sections.overview:
• Normal Sinus Rhythm (NSR) is the physiologic, baseline electrical rhythm of the heart, serving as the benchmark against which all other rhythms are compared.
    ◦ The term "sinus" indicates that the electrical impulse originates in the **sinoatrial (SA) node**, the heart's natural pacemaker.
    ◦ The term "normal" refers to the impulse being generated at a normal rate and conducted properly, resulting in coordinated atrial and ventricular contraction.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ NSR is the result of a healthy, properly functioning cardiac conduction system in the absence of pathologic influences.
• **Pathophysiology (The Normal Conduction Pathway)**
    ◦ **SA Node Firing:** The SA node, located in the upper posterior wall of the right atrium, spontaneously depolarizes at an intrinsic rate of 60-100 times per minute, initiating the cardiac cycle.
    ◦ **Atrial Depolarization:** The impulse spreads through the atria via internodal pathways, causing atrial contraction.
        ▪ Represented by the **P wave** on an EKG.
    ◦ **AV Node Delay:** The impulse reaches the atrioventricular (AV) node and is briefly delayed, allowing time for the ventricles to fill.
        ▪ Represented by the **PR interval**.
    ◦ **Ventricular Depolarization:** The impulse travels down the Bundle of His, through the bundle branches, and into the Purkinje fibers, causing ventricular contraction (systole).
        ▪ Represented by the **QRS complex**.
    ◦ **Ventricular Repolarization:** The ventricles electrically reset and relax (diastole).
        ▪ Represented by the **T wave**.
    ◦ The rate and force are modulated by the **autonomic nervous system**:
        ▪ **Sympathetic stimulation** (e.g., exercise, stress) increases the SA node firing rate.
        ▪ **Parasympathetic (vagal) stimulation** (e.g., rest, sleep) decreases the SA node firing rate.
sections.epidemiology:
• NSR is not a disease and therefore does not have an epidemiology in the traditional sense.
• It is the **most common rhythm** observed in healthy individuals at rest and is considered the physiologic standard across all age groups.
• Its presence is expected in any healthy, stable patient.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• By definition, a patient in NSR is hemodynamically stable and asymptomatic *from their cardiac rhythm*.
• The clinical presentation is that of a healthy individual or a patient whose signs and symptoms are due to an underlying, non-arrhythmic condition (e.g., a patient with pneumonia may have a fever and cough while being in NSR).
sections.diagnostics: • The definitive diagnosis of NSR is made via an **Electrocardiogram (EKG/ECG)**.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent.**
    ◦ The presence of NSR is a sign of a healthy and stable cardiac conduction system.

sections.overview:
• Sinus rhythm with a heart rate less than 60 beats per minute (bpm)
	◦ Originates from the sinoatrial (SA) node, the heart's natural pacemaker
	◦ The electrical impulse is generated correctly and travels through the normal conduction pathway, but at a slower rate
	◦ Defined by a regular rhythm with an upright P wave preceding every QRS complex on an electrocardiogram (EKG)
• Can be a normal physiologic finding (e.g., in athletes, during sleep) or a sign of underlying pathology
	◦ Clinical significance is determined by whether the slow heart rate causes symptoms and hemodynamic instability
sections.etiology: • The pathophysiology centers on **decreased automaticity of the SA node** or blocked conduction near the node.
sections.epidemiology:
• Sinus bradycardia is a very common arrhythmia
• Prevalence increases with age
	◦ Primarily due to the increased incidence of cardiac disease and degenerative changes in the conduction system
• Extremely common in young, healthy, athletic individuals, where it is a benign finding
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation is highly variable and depends on whether the patient is symptomatic
• **Asymptomatic**
	◦ Often an incidental finding on a routine EKG or during vital sign monitoring
	◦ The patient feels well and is hemodynamically stable
• **Symptomatic**
	◦ The patient presents with signs and symptoms of end-organ hypoperfusion due to the low heart rate and resultant decreased cardiac output
	◦ This constitutes an **unstable** patient
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for asymptomatic, physiologic bradycardia (e.g., athletes)
• For pathologic bradycardia, the prognosis is highly dependent on the underlying etiology
• Prognosis is generally **very good** for patients with symptomatic bradycardia due to SSS or AV block who are treated with a permanent pacemaker
• Prognosis is poorer if bradycardia is a manifestation of severe, irreversible heart disease (e.g., large MI)

sections.overview:
• A cardiac rhythm with a **heart rate > 100 bpm** originating from the **sinoatrial (SA) node**.
• Considered a physiologic response to an underlying condition, not a primary arrhythmia.
• **EKG** shows a normal **P wave** preceding every **QRS complex** in a regular, rapid rhythm.
• Management focuses on identifying and treating the **underlying cause**.
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ Results from an increased rate of spontaneous depolarization of the **SA node** mediated by the autonomic nervous system.
        ▪ **Increased Sympathetic Tone:** Release of catecholamines (**epinephrine**, **norepinephrine**) acts on **beta-1 adrenergic receptors** in the SA node, increasing the firing rate.
        ▪ **Decreased Parasympathetic (Vagal) Tone:** Reduced acetylcholine influence on the SA node removes the "braking" effect, allowing the heart rate to rise.
• **Etiologies (Classified by Mechanism)**
    ◦ **Physiologic Stressors**
        ▪ **Exercise**
        ▪ **Pain**
        ▪ Anxiety, fear, emotional distress
    ◦ **Pathologic / Medical Conditions**
        ▪ **Hypovolemia:** Dehydration, hemorrhage, burns
        ▪ **Fever/Infection/Sepsis:** Increased metabolic demand
        ▪ **Hypoxia** (e.g., COPD, pneumonia, high altitude)
        ▪ **Anemia:** Decreased oxygen-carrying capacity requires increased cardiac output
        ▪ **Hypotension/Shock:** Compensatory mechanism to maintain cardiac output
        ▪ **Pulmonary Embolism (PE):** Classic sign due to hypoxia and right heart strain
        ▪ **Hyperthyroidism (Thyrotoxicosis):** Thyroid hormone sensitizes the heart to catecholamines
        ▪ **Myocardial Ischemia/Infarction:** Response to pain and cardiac dysfunction
        ▪ **Heart Failure:** Compensatory mechanism for decreased stroke volume
        ▪ **Myocarditis/Pericarditis**
    ◦ **Pharmacologic / Toxicologic**
        ▪ **Stimulants:** Caffeine, nicotine, cocaine, amphetamines, methamphetamines
        ▪ **Medications:** **Beta-agonists** (albuterol), **anticholinergics** (atropine), dopamine, epinephrine
        ▪ **Withdrawal States:** Alcohol, benzodiazepines, beta-blockers, opioids
sections.epidemiology:
• Extremely common finding in both inpatient and outpatient settings.
• It is a sign, not a disease; its prevalence mirrors the prevalence of its underlying causes.
• Affects all age groups, from infants to the elderly.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The clinical presentation is entirely dependent on the **underlying etiology**.
• The patient may be:
    ◦ **Asymptomatic:** Found incidentally on routine vitals or EKG.
    ◦ **Stable but Symptomatic:** A patient with a fever and URI who feels palpitations.
    ◦ **Unstable:** A hypotensive trauma patient with **hemorrhage**, or a **septic** patient.
• The history is crucial. Inquire about:
    ◦ Recent illness, trauma, medication changes, substance use
    ◦ **Chest pain**, **shortness of breath**
    ◦ Personal or family history of thyroid or heart disease
sections.diagnostics:
• **EKG (First-line and Confirmatory)**
    ◦ **Rate:** **> 100 bpm** (usually 100-160 bpm)
    ◦ **Rhythm:** **Regular**
    ◦ **P waves:** Present and normal morphology. One P wave precedes every QRS complex.
    ◦ **PR Interval:** Normal and constant (0.12-0.20 seconds)
    ◦ **QRS Complex:** Normal duration (< 0.12 seconds) and morphology
• **Laboratory Studies (Guided by clinical suspicion)**
    ◦ **CBC:** To evaluate for **anemia** (low Hgb/Hct) or **infection** (leukocytosis).
    ◦ **BMP/CMP:** To assess for electrolyte abnormalities and **dehydration** (elevated BUN/Cr ratio).
    ◦ **TSH:** To screen for **hyperthyroidism**.
    ◦ **Troponin:** If **myocardial ischemia** is suspected.
    ◦ **D-dimer:** To help rule out **PE** in low-risk patients.
    ◦ **Blood Cultures:** If **sepsis** is suspected.
    ◦ **Urine Toxicology Screen:** If substance use is suspected.
    ◦ **BNP:** If **heart failure** is suspected.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Chest X-Ray (CXR):** To evaluate for **pneumonia**, **pulmonary edema** (heart failure), or other pulmonary pathology.
    ◦ **CT Angiography of the Chest:** Gold standard for diagnosing **pulmonary embolism**.
    ◦ **Venous Doppler of Lower Extremities:** To evaluate for **DVT**.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is entirely dependent on the **underlying cause**.
    ◦ **Excellent:** For physiologic causes or easily reversible conditions (e.g., anxiety, dehydration, fever).
    ◦ **Guarded to Poor:** When it is a sign of a life-threatening condition like **septic shock**, massive **PE**, or acute **MI**.

sections.overview:
• **Premature Atrial Complex (PAC)**, also known as an atrial premature beat (APB) or atrial extrasystole, is a common cardiac arrhythmia characterized by a premature heartbeat originating from an ectopic focus within the atria, outside of the sinoatrial (SA) node.
    ◦ This ectopic impulse fires before the normal SA node impulse, leading to a premature depolarization of the atria and subsequently the ventricles.
    ◦ On an EKG, this manifests as a premature, abnormally shaped P wave followed by a QRS complex and a subsequent pause.
    ◦ PACs are frequently **benign** and **asymptomatic** but can cause **palpitations** and may be a precursor to more significant arrhythmias like **atrial fibrillation**.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• Extremely common, found in >60% of healthy adults on 24-hour **Holter monitoring**.
• Prevalence increases significantly with **age**.
• The frequency and complexity of PACs also increase with **age** and the presence of underlying **heart disease**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The majority of patients are **asymptomatic**, and PACs are found incidentally on an EKG or ambulatory monitor.
• When symptomatic, the presentation is driven by the sensation of an **irregular heartbeat**.
• Symptoms are often intermittent and may be precipitated by known triggers.
sections.diagnostics:
• **12-Lead EKG**
    ◦ The primary tool for diagnosis.
    ◦ Key features:
        ▪ **Premature P wave**: A P wave that occurs earlier than the next expected sinus P wave.
        ▪ **Abnormal P wave morphology**: The P wave is shaped differently from the sinus P waves (it may be inverted, peaked, notched, or biphasic).
        ▪ **Narrow QRS complex**: The QRS is typically <0.12 seconds, identical in morphology to the sinus beats.
        ▪ **Non-compensatory pause**: The R-R interval spanning the PAC is less than two times the preceding R-R interval.
• **Ambulatory Cardiac Monitoring (Holter or Event Monitor)**
    ◦ Indicated for **symptomatic** patients when a standard EKG is non-diagnostic.
    ◦ Quantifies the **"burden"** (frequency) of PACs over 24-48 hours or longer.
    ◦ Correlates symptoms with the arrhythmia.
• **Echocardiogram**
    ◦ Not needed for diagnosis of PACs.
    ◦ Indicated if PACs are very frequent, sustained, or if there is clinical suspicion of underlying **structural heart disease**.
• **Laboratory Tests**
    ◦ **BMP**: To assess electrolytes (potassium, magnesium).
    ◦ **TSH**: To rule out **hyperthyroidism**.
    ◦ **CBC**: To rule out **anemia**.
sections.prognosis:
• In individuals with a **structurally normal heart**, the prognosis is **excellent**.
    ◦ PACs are considered a **benign** finding.
• In older patients and those with **underlying cardiovascular disease**, a high frequency of PACs is associated with an increased risk of:
    ◦ Developing **atrial fibrillation**
    ◦ **Ischemic stroke**
    ◦ **All-cause mortality**

sections.overview:
• A **Premature Ventricular Complex (PVC)** is a common arrhythmia characterized by a premature, ectopic heartbeat originating from an irritable focus within the **ventricles**.
• On an EKG, it appears as an early, **wide**, and bizarrely-shaped **QRS complex** that is **not preceded by a P wave** and is typically followed by a **full compensatory pause**.
• While often benign in individuals with structurally normal hearts, PVCs can be a marker of underlying cardiac pathology and, if frequent, may lead to cardiomyopathy.
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ PVCs arise from an ectopic focus in the ventricular myocardium that depolarizes prematurely, before the normal sinus impulse arrives.
    ◦ The impulse spreads slowly and abnormally through the ventricular muscle rather than the rapid His-Purkinje system.
        ▪ This slow, cell-to-cell conduction is responsible for the characteristic **wide QRS complex (>0.12 seconds)**.
    ◦ The bizarre morphology reflects the abnormal depolarization pathway.
    ◦ The subsequent **compensatory pause** occurs because the sinus node fires on schedule, but the impulse finds the ventricles refractory (unresponsive) after the PVC.
        ▪ The sinus rhythm then resumes, with the next sinus beat occurring at its expected interval from the previous sinus beat.
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Idiopathic (most common)**: No identifiable cause, common in healthy hearts.
    ◦ **Structural Heart Disease**
        ▪ Coronary Artery Disease (CAD), especially post-Myocardial Infarction (MI)
        ▪ Heart Failure (HF) with reduced ejection fraction
        ▪ Cardiomyopathy (dilated, hypertrophic)
        ▪ Valvular heart disease (e.g., mitral valve prolapse)
        ▪ Congenital heart disease
    ◦ **Electrolyte Disturbances**
        ▪ **Hypokalemia**
        ▪ **Hypomagnesemia**
    ◦ **Systemic Conditions**
        ▪ Hypoxia
        ▪ Hyperthyroidism
        ▪ Acidosis
        ▪ Anemia
    ◦ **Pharmacologic / Substance-Induced**
        ▪ **Stimulants**: Caffeine, nicotine, cocaine, amphetamines
        ▪ **Alcohol**
        ▪ **Medications**: Digoxin toxicity, sympathomimetics, antiarrhythmics, tricyclic antidepressants
sections.epidemiology:
• Extremely common in the general population.
• Prevalence increases with age.
• Can be detected in >60% of healthy adults on a 24-hour Holter monitor.
• More prevalent and frequent in patients with underlying structural heart disease.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation ranges from completely asymptomatic (often an incidental finding on EKG or telemetry) to severely symptomatic.
• The clinical significance is largely determined by the presence or absence of underlying heart disease and the frequency of the PVCs.
sections.diagnostics:
• **12-Lead EKG**
    ◦ **Timing**: Premature beat.
    ◦ **QRS**: **Wide (>0.12s)** and bizarre morphology.
    ◦ **P-wave**: No preceding P-wave.
    ◦ **T-wave**: Discordant T-wave (directed opposite to the main QRS vector).
    ◦ **Rhythm**: A **full compensatory pause** is characteristic (the R-R interval spanning the PVC is equal to two normal R-R intervals).
• **Ambulatory EKG Monitoring (Holter Monitor)**
    ◦ **Purpose**: To quantify the PVC "burden" (% of total beats that are PVCs) over 24-48 hours and correlate symptoms with arrhythmias.
        ▪ Crucial for management decisions.
    ◦ Also used to assess for more complex ventricular arrhythmias like non-sustained ventricular tachycardia (NSVT).
• **Echocardiogram**
    ◦ **ESSENTIAL** in the initial workup of frequent PVCs.
    ◦ **Purpose**: To evaluate for underlying **structural heart disease**, particularly left ventricular (LV) size and function (ejection fraction).
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP) or Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP) to assess **potassium**, **magnesium**, **calcium**, and renal function.
    ◦ Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH) to rule out hyperthyroidism.
• **Exercise Stress Test**
    ◦ **Purpose**: To evaluate for ischemic heart disease and to see the effect of exercise on PVCs.
        ▪ PVCs that suppress or disappear with exercise are typically benign.
        ▪ PVCs that increase in frequency or complexity with exercise are more concerning for underlying ischemia.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** in patients with a structurally normal heart.
    ◦ There is no increased risk of mortality.
• **Guarded** in patients with significant underlying **structural heart disease** (e.g., post-MI, LVEF <40%).
    ◦ In this population, frequent PVCs are an independent marker of increased risk for **sudden cardiac death** and all-cause mortality.

sections.overview:
• **Atrial Fibrillation (AFib)** is a **supraventricular tachyarrhythmia** characterized by **chaotic, uncoordinated atrial activation**, resulting in an ineffective atrial contraction and an **irregularly irregular ventricular response**.
    ◦ It is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia encountered in clinical practice.
• Primary concerns with AFib are hemodynamic instability, tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy, and the risk of **thromboembolism**, particularly ischemic stroke.
• **Types of Atrial Fibrillation**
    ◦ **Paroxysmal**: AFib that terminates spontaneously or with intervention within 7 days of onset.
    ◦ **Persistent**: Continuous AFib that is sustained for > 7 days.
    ◦ **Long-standing Persistent**: Continuous AFib for > 12 months.
    ◦ **Permanent**: A joint decision by the patient and clinician has been made to cease further attempts to restore or maintain normal sinus rhythm.
• **Valvular vs. Non-valvular**
    ◦ **Valvular AFib**: AFib in the presence of moderate-to-severe **mitral stenosis** or a **mechanical heart valve**.
    ◦ **Non-valvular AFib (NVAF)**: AFib without the above conditions. This distinction is critical for choosing anticoagulation therapy.
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**: AFib is initiated by a trigger and sustained by a substrate.
    ◦ **Trigger**: Rapidly firing ectopic foci, most commonly originating from the sleeves of myocardial tissue extending into the **pulmonary veins**, initiate the arrhythmia.
    ◦ **Substrate**: Underlying atrial disease (e.g., fibrosis, inflammation, dilation) promotes the propagation of multiple, chaotic, re-entrant wavelets. This disorganized activity prevents coordinated atrial depolarization.
    ◦ This chaotic atrial activity (300-600 bpm) overwhelms the AV node, which acts as a filter. The AV node conducts impulses intermittently and variably, leading to an **irregularly irregular ventricular response**.
    ◦ The loss of coordinated atrial contraction ("atrial kick") can reduce cardiac output by up to 25-30%, which is particularly significant in patients with pre-existing diastolic dysfunction or heart failure.
• **Etiology**: Causes can be cardiac or non-cardiac.
    ◦ **Cardiac**: **Hypertension** (most common), Coronary Artery Disease (CAD), Valvular Heart Disease (especially **mitral stenosis** and regurgitation), Heart Failure (HF), Cardiomyopathy, post-cardiac surgery.
    ◦ **Non-Cardiac/Systemic**: Pulmonary Disease (PE, COPD, OSA), **Hyperthyroidism**, Diabetes Mellitus, Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD), Obesity, excessive alcohol intake (**"Holiday Heart Syndrome"**), electrolyte abnormalities.
sections.epidemiology:
• Most common sustained arrhythmia worldwide.
• Prevalence increases dramatically with age:
    ◦ <0.5% in those <50 years old.
    ◦ ~10% in those >80 years old.
• Slightly more common in men than women.
• More prevalent in individuals of European descent.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation is highly variable, ranging from asymptomatic to severe hemodynamic collapse.
    ◦ **Asymptomatic**: Often an incidental finding on a routine EKG or physical exam.
    ◦ **Symptomatic**: Patients may present with a chief complaint of palpitations, fatigue, or dyspnea.
    ◦ **Complication-related**: The first sign may be a TIA/stroke, a systemic embolic event, or an exacerbation of heart failure.
    ◦ **Hemodynamic Instability**: Hypotension, altered mental status, signs of shock, severe chest pain, or acute pulmonary edema. This constitutes a medical emergency.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Electrocardiogram (ECG)**
    ◦ **Hallmark Findings**
        ▪ **Irregularly irregular R-R intervals**.
        ▪ **No discernible P waves**.
        ▪ Presence of fine, chaotic fibrillatory waves ('f' waves), especially visible in lead V1.
    ◦ QRS is typically narrow (<120 ms) unless there is a pre-existing bundle branch block or rate-related aberrant conduction (**Ashman phenomenon**).
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **TSH**: To rule out hyperthyroidism.
    ◦ **CBC**: To assess for anemia which can exacerbate symptoms.
    ◦ **BMP/CMP**: To check electrolytes (K+, Mg++) and renal/hepatic function (important for medication dosing).
    ◦ **Cardiac Enzymes (Troponin)**: If myocardial ischemia is suspected.
• **Imaging & Monitoring**
    ◦ **Transthoracic Echocardiogram (TTE)**: Essential in all new-onset AFib patients to assess for structural heart disease, valvular pathology, left atrial size, and left ventricular function (LVEF).
    ◦ **Transesophageal Echocardiogram (TEE)**: Gold standard for detecting a left atrial appendage (LAA) thrombus prior to cardioversion.
    ◦ **Ambulatory Monitoring (Holter, Event Monitor)**: Useful for diagnosing paroxysmal AFib if it is not captured on a standard 12-lead ECG.
sections.prognosis:
• AFib is associated with a 1.5 to 2-fold increase in mortality.
• The prognosis is largely dependent on the patient's underlying comorbidities (e.g., age, HF, CAD).
• With appropriate rate/rhythm control and, most importantly, anticoagulation, the risk of major adverse events can be significantly reduced.

sections.overview:
• Atrial Flutter is a **supraventricular tachyarrhythmia** characterized by a rapid, organized, **macro-reentrant circuit** within the atria.
    ◦ This leads to an atrial rate of approximately **250-350 beats per minute (bpm)**.
    ◦ The **AV node acts as a filter**, resulting in a slower, and often regular, ventricular response.
• The two main clinical concerns are **hemodynamic instability** due to rapid ventricular rates and the risk of **thromboembolism**, which is similar to that of atrial fibrillation.
sections.etiology:
• **Core Mechanism:** A large (**macro**) **re-entrant electrical circuit** that continuously circulates within one of the atria.
• **Typical Atrial Flutter** (Most Common, ~90%):
    ◦ The re-entrant circuit is confined to the **right atrium** and travels around the tricuspid annulus.
    ◦ The critical part of this circuit is the **cavotricuspid isthmus (CTI)**, a region of tissue between the inferior vena cava and the tricuspid annulus.
    ◦ **Counter-clockwise (CCW) flutter** is the most common form, producing the classic **"sawtooth" pattern** with negative flutter waves in the **inferior leads (II, III, aVF)**.
• **Atypical Atrial Flutter:**
    ◦ Involves re-entrant circuits that do not use the CTI.
    ◦ Often occurs in the **left atrium** or around areas of **scar tissue** from prior cardiac surgery (e.g., valve repair) or catheter ablation procedures for atrial fibrillation.
• **AV Conduction:**
    ◦ The AV node cannot conduct at the atrial rate of ~300 bpm. It blocks some impulses, leading to a slower ventricular rate.
    ◦ **Fixed AV Block:** Most commonly a **2:1 block**, resulting in a ventricular rate of ~150 bpm. Can also be 3:1 (~100 bpm) or 4:1 (~75 bpm). The ventricular rhythm is **regular**.
    ◦ **Variable AV Block:** The conduction ratio changes, resulting in an **irregularly irregular** ventricular rhythm that can mimic atrial fibrillation.
sections.epidemiology:
• Less common than atrial fibrillation, but they frequently **co-exist**.
• Incidence increases significantly with **age**, particularly after age 60.
• More common in **men** than in women.
• Strongly associated with underlying **structural heart disease**.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Structural Heart Disease:**
    ◦ Ischemic Heart Disease / prior Myocardial Infarction
    ◦ Hypertensive Heart Disease
    ◦ Valvular Heart Disease (especially mitral and tricuspid)
    ◦ Cardiomyopathy (dilated or hypertrophic)
    ◦ Congenital Heart Disease
• **Post-Cardiac Surgery:**
    ◦ Especially after procedures involving atriotomy (e.g., mitral valve surgery, atrial septal defect repair).
• **Pulmonary Disease:**
    ◦ COPD
    ◦ Pulmonary Embolism (acute right heart strain)
    ◦ Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA)
• **Systemic Conditions:**
    ◦ Advanced Age
    ◦ Hyperthyroidism
    ◦ Electrolyte abnormalities (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia)
    ◦ Acute alcohol intoxication (**"Holiday Heart Syndrome"**)
    ◦ Obesity
    ◦ Diabetes Mellitus
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation depends on the ventricular rate, duration of the arrhythmia, and the patient's underlying cardiac function.
• **Hemodynamically Stable:**
    ◦ Patient is alert, normotensive, with no signs of shock or acute heart failure.
• **Hemodynamically Unstable:**
    ◦ Presence of **hypotension, altered mental status, signs of shock, ischemic chest pain, or acute pulmonary edema**.
    ◦ **This is a medical emergency.**
• Can be asymptomatic and found incidentally on EKG.
• **Symptoms:**
    ◦ **Palpitations:** Sensation of a rapid or fluttering heartbeat.
    ◦ **Fatigue / Decreased Exercise Tolerance:** Often the most prominent symptom.
    ◦ **Dyspnea:** Shortness of breath, especially with exertion.
    ◦ **Lightheadedness / Dizziness / Presyncope:** Due to reduced cardiac output from very rapid rates.
    ◦ **Angina:** Chest pain or pressure, especially in patients with underlying coronary artery disease.
    ◦ **Symptoms of Heart Failure:** Worsening edema, orthopnea.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Vitals:**
    ◦ **Tachycardia** (ventricular rate often near **150 bpm**). Blood pressure may be normal or low. Tachypnea may be present.
• **Pulse:**
    ◦ Can be **regular** (with fixed block) or **irregularly irregular** (with variable block).
• **Cardiovascular Exam:**
    ◦ Rapid heart rate.
    ◦ May hear murmurs associated with underlying valvular disease.
    ◦ Signs of heart failure: **Jugular Venous Distention (JVD)**, **S3 gallop**, pulmonary **rales**, peripheral **edema**.
• **Neck Veins:**
    ◦ May see rapid, **"fluttering" jugular venous pulsations**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Electrocardiogram (ECG / EKG): The primary diagnostic tool.**
    ◦ **Atrial Rate:** **250-350 bpm** (typically ~300 bpm).
    ◦ **Ventricular Rate:** A fraction of the atrial rate (e.g., ~150 bpm with **2:1 block**).
    ◦ **Flutter (F) Waves:** The hallmark finding. A continuous, undulating atrial activation pattern.
    ◦ **"Sawtooth" Pattern:** Best visualized in the **inferior leads (II, III, aVF)** and sometimes V1. P waves are absent.
    ◦ **QRS Complex:** Usually narrow (<0.12s) unless a pre-existing bundle branch block or rate-related aberrancy is present.
    ◦ **Rhythm:** Regular if block is fixed; irregular if block is variable.
• **Laboratory Studies:**
    ◦ **TSH:** To rule out hyperthyroidism.
    ◦ **CMP:** To assess electrolytes (K+, Mg++, Ca++) and renal function (important for medication choice).
    ◦ **CBC:** To assess for anemia which could be contributing to tachycardia.
    ◦ **Cardiac Enzymes (Troponin):** If there is concern for ischemia.
• **Echocardiogram (TTE or TEE):**
    ◦ Assesses for structural heart disease, valvular abnormalities, and left ventricular function.
    ◦ **Crucial for identifying left atrial appendage (LAA) thrombus** prior to any attempt at cardioversion if the flutter has been present for >48 hours or duration is unknown.
sections.treatment:
• **Unstable Patient** (Hypotension, AMS, Shock, Ischemic Pain, Acute HF):
    ◦ **Immediate Synchronized Cardioversion:**
        ▪ Initial energy: **50-100 Joules** (biphasic). Atrial flutter is very sensitive to electricity and often converts with low energy.
• **Stable Patient:**
    ◦ **Goal 1: Rate Control** (to improve symptoms and prevent tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy)
        ▪ **1st Line:** **Beta-blockers** (e.g., Metoprolol) OR **Non-dihydropyridine Calcium Channel Blockers** (e.g., Diltiazem).
        ▪ **2nd Line / HF Patients:** Digoxin, Amiodarone.
    ◦ **Goal 2: Rhythm Control** (conversion to normal sinus rhythm)
        ▪ **Electrical Cardioversion:** Preferred method for converting to sinus rhythm. Must ensure proper anticoagulation first.
        ▪ **Pharmacological Cardioversion:** Less effective than for A-fib. **IV Ibutilide** can be used in a monitored setting.
sections.management:
• **Risk Stratification:**
    ◦ Use the **CHA2DS2-VASc** score to assess stroke risk. Atrial flutter carries a similar stroke risk to atrial fibrillation and is managed the same way.
    ◦ **Recommendations:**
        ▪ **Score ≥ 2 (men) or ≥ 3 (women):** Long-term anticoagulation is recommended.
        ▪ **Options:** **Direct Oral Anticoagulants (DOACs)** like Apixaban, Rivaroxaban, Dabigatran are preferred over Warfarin.
• **Anticoagulation around Cardioversion:**
    ◦ If flutter duration is **>48 hours or unknown**, the patient needs **at least 3 weeks** of therapeutic anticoagulation before cardioversion OR a **TEE to rule out thrombus**, followed by **at least 4 weeks** of anticoagulation after successful cardioversion.
• **Rate Control (Long-term):**
    ◦ Long-term oral beta-blockers or non-dihydropyridine CCBs to maintain a ventricular rate typically <110 bpm at rest.
• **Catheter Ablation:**
    ◦ **Highly effective and considered first-line definitive therapy for typical CTI-dependent atrial flutter.**
    ◦ An ablation catheter is used to create a line of scar tissue across the **cavotricuspid isthmus**, which permanently interrupts the re-entrant circuit.
    ◦ Success rates are **>95%**.
sections.complications:
• **Thromboembolic Event:** **Ischemic stroke** is the most feared complication. Systemic embolism can also occur.
• **Tachycardia-Induced Cardiomyopathy:** Persistent, poorly controlled rapid ventricular rates can lead to left ventricular dysfunction and heart failure.
• **Hemodynamic Collapse:** Can occur with very rapid rates, especially in patients with poor baseline cardiac function.
• **Degeneration into Atrial Fibrillation:** Many patients with atrial flutter also have or will develop atrial fibrillation.
sections.prognosis:
• With appropriate anticoagulation, the risk of stroke is significantly reduced.
• **Catheter ablation is curative for typical atrial flutter,** greatly improving quality of life and eliminating the arrhythmia itself.
• Overall prognosis is largely determined by the patient's underlying cardiac and comorbid conditions.

sections.overview:
• **Atrioventricular Nodal Re-entrant Tachycardia (AVNRT)** is the most common type of **paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT)**.
    ◦ A regular, **narrow-complex tachycardia** caused by a **re-entry circuit** located entirely within the **AV node** and the surrounding perinodal atrial tissue.
    ◦ The arrhythmia is characterized by its **abrupt onset and termination**, often described by patients as a "switch being flipped."
    ◦ Typically occurs in individuals without structural heart disease.
sections.etiology:
• The underlying substrate for AVNRT is the presence of **dual AV nodal pathways** with different electrophysiological properties:
    ◦ **Slow Pathway (Alpha Pathway):** Conducts impulses slowly but has a short refractory period (recovers quickly).
    ◦ **Fast Pathway (Beta Pathway):** Conducts impulses rapidly but has a long refractory period (recovers slowly).
• **Mechanism of "Typical" (Slow-Fast) AVNRT** (90% of cases):
    ◦ **Initiation:** A **premature atrial contraction (PAC)** arrives at the AV node.
    ◦ **Anterograde Block:** The Fast Pathway is still in its refractory period from the previous beat and cannot conduct the impulse.
    ◦ **Anterograde Conduction:** The Slow Pathway has a shorter refractory period, so it is "ready" to conduct. The impulse travels slowly down the Slow Pathway to the ventricles, causing the QRS complex.
    ◦ **Retrograde Conduction:** By the time the impulse reaches the bottom of the Slow Pathway, the Fast Pathway has recovered. The impulse can now travel backwards (retrograde) up the now-excitable Fast Pathway to the atria.
    ◦ **Re-entry Circuit:** The impulse re-enters the top of the Slow Pathway, which has also recovered, creating a sustained, circular electrical loop. This loop results in near-simultaneous activation of the atria (retrograde) and ventricles (anterograde), leading to a rapid, regular tachycardia.
• "Atypical" (fast-slow) and "slow-slow" variants are much less common.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Most common form of PSVT**, accounting for ~60% of cases.
• Prevalence is approximately 2.25 per 1,000 persons.
• Can occur at any age but most commonly presents in young adulthood (20s-40s).
• **More common in women** (2:1 to 3:1 female-to-male ratio).
sections.riskFactors:
• **Female gender**
• Middle age
• While often idiopathic in structurally normal hearts, triggers can include:
    ◦ Caffeine
    ◦ Alcohol
    ◦ Stimulant drugs (e.g., sympathomimetics, illicit drugs)
    ◦ Psychological stress or anxiety
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients typically present with an **abrupt onset** of rapid, regular **palpitations**.
• The episodes are paroxysmal, meaning they start and stop suddenly.
• Patients are often anxious and can describe the exact moment the arrhythmia started and stopped.
• The patient may be hemodynamically stable or unstable, depending on the heart rate, duration of the episode, and underlying cardiac function.
• Associated Symptoms:
    ◦ **Palpitations:** Sensation of a rapid, regular, and sometimes forceful heartbeat.
    ◦ **Dizziness or lightheadedness**
    ◦ **Presyncope or syncope** (if the rate is very fast or in patients with underlying heart disease)
    ◦ **Dyspnea** (shortness of breath)
    ◦ **Chest discomfort or tightness** (due to rapid rate, not typically ischemic)
    ◦ **Neck pounding** or fullness (from **cannon A waves**)
    ◦ Anxiety
sections.physicalExam:
• **Vitals:**
    ◦ **Tachycardia** (HR typically 150-250 bpm), regular rhythm.
    ◦ Blood pressure may be low, normal, or high.
• **Cardiovascular:**
    ◦ Tachycardic, regular rhythm.
• **Neck Veins:**
    ◦ **"Frog Sign"**: Visible pulsations in the neck (**cannon A waves**) caused by atrial contraction against a closed tricuspid valve, as the atria and ventricles contract nearly simultaneously.
sections.diagnostics:
• **12-Lead EKG (during tachycardia):** This is the key diagnostic tool.
    ◦ **Rhythm:** Perfectly regular.
    ◦ **Rate:** 150-250 bpm.
    ◦ **QRS:** **Narrow complex (<120 ms)** unless pre-existing bundle branch block or rate-related aberrancy.
    ◦ **P-waves:** Typically not visible as they are buried within the QRS complex due to near-simultaneous atrial and ventricular activation.
    ◦ **High-Yield EKG Findings:**
        ▪ **Pseudo R' wave in lead V1:** A small, terminal positive deflection in V1 that is actually the superimposed retrograde P wave.
        ▪ **Pseudo S' waves in inferior leads (II, III, aVF):** Small, terminal negative deflections in the inferior leads caused by the retrograde P wave.
• **Carotid Sinus Massage or Vagal Maneuvers:** May "break" (terminate) the tachycardia.
• **Adenosine Administration:** Both diagnostic and therapeutic.
    ◦ Transiently blocks the AV node, which interrupts and terminates the re-entry circuit.
    ◦ A normal sinus rhythm is restored after a brief period of asystole.
• **Electrophysiology (EP) Study:** The gold standard for definitive diagnosis.
    ◦ It involves placing catheters in the heart to map the electrical pathways, confirm the presence of dual AV nodal pathways, and induce the arrhythmia.
    ◦ It is typically performed immediately prior to catheter ablation.
sections.treatment:
• **Unstable Patient** (Signs: **hypotension, altered mental status, signs of shock, acute heart failure**)
    ◦ **Immediate synchronized electrical cardioversion.**
• **Stable Patient**
    ◦ **Step 1: Vagal Maneuvers**
        ▪ **Modified Valsalva:** Patient strains against a closed glottis for 15 seconds, followed immediately by being laid supine with a passive leg raise.
        ▪ **Carotid sinus massage** (contraindicated in patients with carotid bruits or history of CVA/TIA).
        ▪ Diving reflex (immersing face in ice water).
    ◦ **Step 2: Pharmacologic Therapy**
        ▪ **Adenosine:** Drug of choice.
            • **Dose:** 6 mg rapid IV push, followed by a 20 mL saline flush.
            • If ineffective, give 12 mg rapid IV push.
            • **MOA:** Blocks AV nodal conduction, terminating the circuit.
            • **Cautions:** Very short half-life (<10 sec). Causes transient flushing, chest pain, dyspnea, and a sense of "impending doom." Use with caution in asthmatics (can cause bronchospasm).
    ◦ **Step 3: Second-Line Agents** (If adenosine is ineffective or contraindicated)
        ▪ **IV Calcium Channel Blockers (non-dihydropyridine):** Verapamil, Diltiazem.
        ▪ **IV Beta-Blockers:** Metoprolol, Esmolol.
sections.management:
• **Catheter Ablation:**
    ◦ **Treatment of choice** for recurrent or symptomatic AVNRT.
    ◦ A catheter is used to deliver radiofrequency energy to selectively **ablate (destroy) the slow pathway**.
    ◦ Highly effective (>95% success rate) and curative.
    ◦ Low complication rate, but a small risk (<1%) of causing **complete heart block** requiring a permanent pacemaker.
• **Chronic Medical Therapy:**
    ◦ For patients who are poor candidates for or decline ablation.
    ◦ Daily oral medications to prevent recurrence.
    ◦ **Beta-blockers** (e.g., metoprolol) or **non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers** (e.g., verapamil, diltiazem).
sections.complications:
• In a structurally normal heart, AVNRT is rarely life-threatening.
• **Syncope** from rapid rates causing decreased cardiac output.
• **Tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy:** A rare complication from very frequent or incessant episodes leading to LV dysfunction.
• Complications of therapy:
    ◦ Adenosine: **Bronchospasm**.
    ◦ Catheter Ablation: **AV block**, vascular access site complications.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent.**
• The condition itself is benign in patients without other heart disease.
• **Catheter ablation is curative** in the vast majority of cases, eliminating the need for long-term medication and significantly improving quality of life.

sections.overview:
• **Ventricular Tachycardia (VT)** is a life-threatening cardiac arrhythmia defined as **three or more consecutive ventricular beats** at a rate of **>100 beats per minute**.
    ◦ The rhythm originates from an ectopic focus within the ventricles.
• VT is classified based on its morphology (monomorphic vs. polymorphic), duration (sustained vs. non-sustained), and the patient's hemodynamic status (stable vs. unstable).
• VT is a major cause of **sudden cardiac death (SCD)**.
• Classifications:
    ◦ **Sustained VT:** Lasts >30 seconds or causes hemodynamic collapse.
    ◦ **Non-sustained VT (NSVT):** Three or more consecutive ventricular beats lasting <30 seconds and terminating spontaneously.
    ◦ **Monomorphic VT:** All QRS complexes have the same morphology, suggesting a single ectopic focus.
    ◦ **Polymorphic VT:** QRS complexes vary in morphology, suggesting multiple ventricular foci.
        ▪ *Torsades de Pointes* is a specific type of polymorphic VT.
sections.etiology:
• The underlying mechanism is typically one of three processes: re-entry, enhanced automaticity, or triggered activity.
    ◦ **Re-entry (Most Common, ~95%):**
        ▪ Requires two distinct electrical pathways with different conduction properties.
        ▪ A common substrate is a myocardial scar (e.g., from a prior MI) which creates an area of slow conduction, allowing a re-entrant circuit to form and perpetuate the tachycardia.
    ◦ **Enhanced Automaticity:**
        ▪ An ectopic focus in the ventricular myocardium depolarizes at a rate faster than the SA node.
        ▪ Often seen in the setting of acute ischemia, electrolyte disturbances, or excessive catecholamines.
    ◦ **Triggered Activity:**
        ▪ Occurs when afterdepolarizations (early or delayed) reach threshold potential and trigger a new action potential.
        ▪ This is the classic mechanism for **Torsades de Pointes**, which is associated with QT prolongation.
• **Common Causes:**
    ◦ **Structural Heart Disease (Most Common Cause):**
        ▪ **Ischemic Heart Disease:** Coronary artery disease, especially a history of **prior myocardial infarction** (most common overall cause).
        ▪ **Non-ischemic Cardiomyopathy:** Dilated cardiomyopathy, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC).
        ▪ **Valvular Disease:** Severe aortic stenosis, mitral valve prolapse.
        ▪ **Infiltrative Disease:** Sarcoidosis, amyloidosis.
    ◦ **No Structural Heart Disease ("Idiopathic VT"):**
        ▪ **Channelopathies:** Long QT syndrome, Brugada syndrome, catecholaminergic polymorphic VT (CPVT).
    ◦ **Other/Reversible Causes:**
        ▪ **Electrolyte Disturbances:** **Hypokalemia**, **hypomagnesemia**, hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia.
        ▪ **Drug Toxicity:** Antiarrhythmics (proarrhythmic effect), tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs), digoxin, stimulants (cocaine, methamphetamine).
        ▪ **Myocarditis.**
        ▪ **Acute MI/Ischemia.**
sections.epidemiology:
• Incidence increases significantly with age and the prevalence of underlying structural heart disease.
• More common in men than women, reflecting the higher prevalence of coronary artery disease.
• Responsible for a significant portion of the ~350,000 annual cases of **sudden cardiac death** in the United States.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation depends on the rate of the VT, its duration, and the patient's underlying cardiac function, ranging from asymptomatic to cardiac arrest.
• **Asymptomatic:**
    ◦ Often seen in brief, self-terminating episodes of non-sustained VT.
• **Hemodynamically Stable:**
    ◦ Patient is conscious with adequate blood pressure.
    ◦ May complain of symptoms but is not in immediate shock.
• **Hemodynamically Unstable:**
    ◦ Patient has a pulse but shows signs of end-organ hypoperfusion: **hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg), altered mental status, signs of shock (cool, clammy skin), ischemic chest pain, or acute heart failure.**
• **Pulseless / Cardiac Arrest:**
    ◦ The patient is unresponsive, apneic, and has no palpable pulse.
    ◦ This is a medical emergency managed with the ACLS algorithm.
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly dependent on the **presence and severity of underlying structural heart disease**.
• In patients with a prior MI and low EF, the prognosis is poor without an ICD.
• In patients with a structurally normal heart ("idiopathic VT"), the prognosis is generally excellent.
• The presence of sustained VT is a powerful independent predictor of mortality.
• ICDs have been shown to significantly improve survival in high-risk populations.

sections.overview:
• **Ventricular Fibrillation (V-Fib or VF)** is a life-threatening cardiac arrhythmia characterized by rapid, disorganized, and ineffective ventricular electrical activity.
• This chaotic state results in the ventricles quivering (fibrillating) rather than contracting coherently.
• Consequently, there is **no effective cardiac output**, leading to systemic circulatory collapse and **sudden cardiac death (SCD)** if not treated immediately with defibrillation.
• It is a **pulseless, shockable rhythm**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology (Causes)**
    ◦ The most common cause is **acute myocardial ischemia or infarction**.
    ◦ Other significant causes include:
        ▪ **Structural Heart Disease**
            • Cardiomyopathy (dilated, hypertrophic)
            • Severe heart failure (especially with EF <35%)
            • Myocarditis
            • Valvular heart disease
        ▪ **Electrolyte Abnormalities**
            • **Hypokalemia / Hyperkalemia**
            • **Hypomagnesemia**
        ▪ **Inherited Arrhythmia Syndromes (Channelopathies)**
            • Long QT Syndrome
            • Brugada Syndrome
            • Catecholaminergic Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia (CPVT)
        ▪ **Drug Toxicity**
            • Antiarrhythmics (proarrhythmic effect)
            • Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs)
            • Cocaine, Methamphetamine
        ▪ **Other**
            • Severe hypoxia or acidosis
            • Hypothermia
            • Blunt chest trauma (Commotio cordis)
            • Electrocution
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ V-Fib is a disorder of disorganized electrical impulse formation and propagation.
    ◦ The underlying mechanism involves multiple, **chaotic, re-entrant electrical circuits** within the ventricular myocardium.
    ◦ Instead of a single, coordinated wave of depolarization, countless micro-reentrant wavelets propagate randomly.
    ◦ This prevents any organized ventricular depolarization and contraction, causing the ventricles to cease functioning as a pump.
    ◦ Stroke volume drops to zero, and profound global ischemia of all vital organs occurs within seconds.
sections.epidemiology:
• V-Fib is the most frequently identified arrhythmia in adult **out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA)**, responsible for a majority of **sudden cardiac deaths**.
• The annual incidence of SCD in the U.S. is estimated to be over 350,000 cases, with V-Fib being the terminal event in most.
• Incidence increases significantly with age, peaking in individuals aged 45-75.
• More common in men than women, reflecting the higher prevalence of **coronary artery disease (CAD)**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is abrupt and catastrophic:
    ◦ **Sudden**, witnessed or unwitnessed **collapse**.
    ◦ Immediate **loss of consciousness**.
    ◦ **Unresponsiveness** to all stimuli.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Diagnosis is made by ECG / Rhythm Monitor.**
    ◦ **ECG Findings:**
        ▪ Chaotic, irregular, disorganized electrical activity.
        ▪ **No identifiable P waves, QRS complexes, or T waves**.
        ▪ The baseline is wavy and erratic.
        ▪ Can be classified as **"coarse V-Fib"** (higher amplitude, more recent onset, better prognosis for defibrillation) or **"fine V-Fib"** (lower amplitude, may be deteriorating towards asystole).
• **Ancillary testing** is performed *after* **Return of Spontaneous Circulation (ROSC)** to identify the underlying cause:
    ◦ **Labs:**
        ▪ **CMP:** Check electrolytes (K+, Mg++, Ca++), renal function.
        ▪ **Cardiac Enzymes:** Troponin to rule out MI.
        ▪ **ABG:** Assess for acidosis and hypoxia.
        ▪ **Toxicology Screen:** If overdose is suspected.
    ◦ **Imaging:**
        ▪ **Post-ROSC 12-Lead ECG:** Look for STEMI, long QT, Brugada pattern.
        ▪ **Echocardiogram:** Assess LV function (EF), wall motion abnormalities, structural disease.
        ▪ **Coronary Angiography:** To identify and treat coronary artery occlusion in cases of MI-induced V-Fib.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is extremely poor without immediate intervention.
• Survival decreases by **7-10% for every minute** that defibrillation is delayed.
• Overall survival to hospital discharge for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest is approximately 10%.
• Prognosis is significantly improved if:
    ◦ The arrest is witnessed.
    ◦ Bystander CPR is initiated.
    ◦ Defibrillation occurs within the first few minutes (e.g., via a public AED).
    ◦ The initial rhythm is **V-Fib/pVT** (shockable rhythms have better outcomes than asystole/PEA).

sections.overview:
• **Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS)** is a spectrum of clinical conditions characterized by acute **myocardial ischemia** or infarction, resulting from a sudden imbalance between myocardial oxygen supply and demand.
    ◦ **Unstable Angina (UA):** Ischemic symptoms suggestive of ACS with **no elevation in cardiac biomarkers**.
        ▪ ECG may show **ST depression**, **T-wave inversion**, or be normal.
    ◦ **Non-ST-Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction (NSTEMI):** Ischemic symptoms with **elevated cardiac biomarkers** (e.g., troponin), but without **ST-segment elevation** on ECG.
        ▪ ECG may show **ST depression**, **T-wave inversion**, or be normal.
    ◦ **ST-Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI):** Ischemic symptoms with **elevated cardiac biomarkers** AND characteristic **ST-segment elevation** on ECG, or new **Left Bundle Branch Block (LBBB)**.
        ▪ Represents a **complete thrombotic occlusion** of a coronary artery.
sections.etiology:
• The overwhelming cause of ACS is the rupture or erosion of an **atherosclerotic plaque** within a coronary artery.
    ◦ **Plaque Rupture:** A vulnerable, lipid-rich plaque with a thin fibrous cap ruptures, exposing its thrombogenic core to the bloodstream.
    ◦ **Thrombus Formation:** This exposure triggers the coagulation cascade and platelet aggregation, leading to the formation of an intracoronary **thrombus**.
    ◦ **Coronary Occlusion:**
        ▪ A **partially occlusive** thrombus or distal embolization causes downstream ischemia, resulting in **UA or NSTEMI**.
        ▪ A **completely occlusive** thrombus blocks all blood flow, causing transmural myocardial infarction, resulting in **STEMI**.
    ◦ Less common causes include **coronary artery vasospasm** (Prinzmetal angina), **coronary artery embolism**, and **spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD)**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Coronary artery disease (CAD)** is the leading cause of death in the United States and worldwide.
• Over 1 million people in the US experience an **ACS** event annually.
• Incidence increases significantly with age.
• Men tend to present at a younger age than women; post-menopause, the incidence in women approaches that of men.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Classic Presentation:** A middle-aged or older patient presenting with acute-onset, retrosternal **chest pain**, often with radiation and associated symptoms.
• **Atypical Presentations:** Common in **women, the elderly, and patients with diabetes**. These patients may present without chest pain, instead reporting:
    ◦ **Dyspnea** (most common anginal equivalent)
    ◦ Epigastric pain or indigestion
    ◦ Nausea/vomiting
    ◦ Diaphoresis
    ◦ Syncope or profound weakness
sections.diagnostics:
• **ECG (EKG):**
    ◦ **Single most important initial test**; must be obtained within 10 minutes of arrival.
    ◦ **STEMI:**
        ▪ New **ST-segment elevation ≥1 mm in 2 contiguous leads**.
        ▪ A new **LBBB** is considered a **STEMI equivalent**.
        ▪ Reciprocal **ST-depressions** are often seen in opposite leads.
    ◦ **NSTEMI / UA:**
        ▪ **ST-segment depression ≥0.5 mm**, dynamic **T-wave inversions**, or a normal ECG.
• **Cardiac Biomarkers:**
    ◦ **Troponin I and T:**
        ▪ **Gold standard**; most sensitive and specific marker for myocardial necrosis.
        ▪ Rises within 2-4 hours, peaks at 12-24 hours, and remains elevated for 7-10 days.
        ▪ **Diagnosis of NSTEMI requires a rise and/or fall of troponin**; serial measurements are crucial.
        ▪ A single negative troponin on presentation does not rule out MI.
    ◦ **CK-MB:**
        ▪ Rises in 4-6 hours, peaks at 12-24 hours, returns to baseline in 48-72 hours.
        ▪ Less specific than troponin but can be useful for detecting **re-infarction**.
• **Chest X-Ray (CXR):**
    ◦ Usually normal.
    ◦ Performed to rule out other causes of chest pain (e.g., aortic dissection, pneumothorax) and assess for complications (e.g., pulmonary edema).
• **Coronary Angiography (Cardiac Catheterization):**
    ◦ **Definitive diagnostic tool ("gold standard")**.
    ◦ Visualizes coronary anatomy, identifies the culprit lesion, and allows for therapeutic intervention (**PCI**).
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly dependent on the extent of myocardial damage (**LVEF is a key predictor**), the presence of complications, and the timeliness of reperfusion therapy.
• Risk stratification tools like the **TIMI score** (for UA/NSTEMI) and **GRACE score** are used to predict mortality and ischemic events.
• **STEMI** has a higher short-term mortality than **NSTEMI**, but long-term mortality can be similar due to underlying disease burden in **NSTEMI** patients.

sections.overview:
• **Stable Angina**, also known as Angina Pectoris, is a clinical syndrome characterized by transient, predictable chest pain or discomfort resulting from **myocardial ischemia**.
    ◦ It occurs when myocardial oxygen demand exceeds supply, most commonly due to a **fixed atherosclerotic obstruction** in one or more coronary arteries.
    ◦ The key features are its **predictable onset** with exertion or emotional stress and its **relief with rest or nitroglycerin**.
    ◦ It is a manifestation of chronic **coronary artery disease (CAD)** and does not involve myocyte necrosis (unlike myocardial infarction).
sections.etiology:
• **Primary Cause**: **Atherosclerotic coronary artery disease (CAD)** is responsible for >90% of cases.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Fixed Stenosis**: A stable atherosclerotic plaque narrows the lumen of a coronary artery. A stenosis of **>70%** is typically required to produce symptoms on exertion.
    ◦ **Supply-Demand Mismatch**:
        ▪ At rest, blood flow is sufficient to meet the myocardium's oxygen needs.
        ▪ During periods of increased demand (e.g., physical exertion, emotional stress), the stenotic artery cannot adequately increase blood flow (dilate) to match the demand.
    ◦ **Myocardial Ischemia**: The resulting imbalance leads to transient, reversible ischemia of the subendocardium.
    ◦ **Symptom Onset**: Ischemia triggers anaerobic metabolism, leading to the accumulation of metabolites like adenosine and lactate, which stimulate local nerve endings, causing the sensation of chest pain.
    ◦ **Symptom Resolution**: When the demand decreases (i.e., with rest), blood flow again becomes adequate, ischemia resolves, and the pain subsides. This entire process is reversible and does not cause permanent myocyte damage (necrosis).
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: A common manifestation of CAD, affecting approximately 10 million people in the United States.
• **Age**: Prevalence increases significantly with age.
• **Sex**: Men are affected at a younger age than women. The incidence in women increases sharply after menopause, eventually approaching that of men.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Non-Modifiable**:
    ◦ **Age**: >45 for men, >55 for women.
    ◦ **Sex**: Male.
    ◦ **Family History**: First-degree relative with premature CAD (male <55 y/o, female <65 y/o).
• **Modifiable**:
    ◦ **Diabetes Mellitus (DM)**: Considered a **CAD risk equivalent**.
    ◦ **Hypertension (HTN)**.
    ◦ **Dyslipidemia**: High LDL, Low HDL.
    ◦ **Cigarette Smoking**.
    ◦ **Obesity**: (BMI > 30 kg/m2).
    ◦ **Sedentary Lifestyle** / Physical Inactivity.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a middle-aged or older adult who complains of intermittent, predictable episodes of chest discomfort. The history is the most critical tool for diagnosis.
• **Character of Pain**:
    ◦ **Quality**: Described as **pressure, heaviness, tightness, squeezing**, or a burning sensation. It is typically not sharp, stabbing, or pleuritic.
    ◦ **Location**: **Substernal**, can radiate to the jaw, neck, shoulders, or left arm.
    ◦ **"Levine's Sign"**: A classic finding where the patient clenches their fist over their sternum to describe the pain.
• **Provoking Factors**:
    ◦ Physical exertion (e.g., walking up a flight of stairs, walking uphill).
    ◦ Emotional stress.
    ◦ Cold weather.
    ◦ Large meals.
• **Palliating Factors**:
    ◦ **Rest**: Symptoms typically resolve within **1-5 minutes** of ceasing the activity.
    ◦ **Nitroglycerin (NTG)**: Sublingual NTG provides rapid relief, usually within 30 seconds to 3 minutes.
• **Duration**: Episodes are brief, typically lasting **2-5 minutes**. Pain lasting >20-30 minutes suggests an **acute coronary syndrome (ACS)**.
• **Associated Symptoms**: Dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea, lightheadedness.
sections.physicalExam:
• The physical exam is often **completely normal** between anginal episodes.
• **Findings may reflect underlying risk factors**:
    ◦ **Hypertension**: Elevated blood pressure reading.
    ◦ **Dyslipidemia**: Xanthelasmas (eyelids), xanthomas (tendons).
    ◦ **Peripheral Artery Disease**: Diminished peripheral pulses, bruits.
• **During an anginal episode (less common to observe)**:
    ◦ Diaphoresis, tachycardia.
    ◦ **S4 gallop**: Due to ischemia-induced ventricular stiffness and decreased compliance.
    ◦ A new, transient mitral regurgitation murmur (due to papillary muscle ischemia).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Initial Workup**:
    ◦ **Electrocardiogram (EKG)**:
        ▪ At rest: Usually **normal** in >50% of patients. May show evidence of a prior MI (Q waves) or non-specific ST-T wave changes.
        ▪ During an anginal episode: May show **transient ST-segment depression** (subendocardial ischemia).
    ◦ **Laboratory Tests**:
        ▪ **Cardiac Enzymes (Troponin I or T)**: **NEGATIVE / NORMAL**. This is a key finding that distinguishes stable angina from ACS.
        ▪ Lipid panel, HbA1c, fasting glucose, CBC, CMP to assess risk factors.
• **Confirmatory & Risk Stratification**:
    ◦ **Stress Testing**: The most important non-invasive test for diagnosis.
        ▪ **Exercise Stress EKG (Treadmill Test)**: Preferred initial test for patients who can exercise and have a normal baseline EKG. Positive test = **ST-segment depression ≥1 mm**, hypotension, or symptoms.
        ▪ **Stress Echocardiogram**: Combines exercise or pharmacologic stress (dobutamine) with ultrasound. Looks for ischemia-induced **regional wall motion abnormalities**.
        ▪ **Myocardial Perfusion Imaging (Nuclear Stress Test)**: Combines exercise or pharmacologic stress (adenosine, regadenoson) with a radiotracer. Looks for **reversible perfusion defects**.
• **Gold Standard (Anatomic Definition)**:
    ◦ **Coronary Angiography (Cardiac Catheterization)**: The definitive diagnostic procedure; it is invasive.
        ▪ Visualizes the coronary anatomy, determines the location and severity of stenosis, and allows for simultaneous intervention (PCI/stent).
        ▪ **Indications**: High-risk stress test results, persistent symptoms despite optimal medical therapy, or inconclusive non-invasive testing.
sections.treatment:
• **Immediate Symptom Relief (Acute Episode)**:
    ◦ **Sublingual Nitroglycerin (SL NTG)**:
        ▪ **Mechanism**: Venodilator decreases preload, which reduces myocardial oxygen demand.
        ▪ **Dosing**: 0.4 mg SL every 5 minutes for up to 3 doses. **Instruct patient to call 911 if pain persists after the first dose.**
• **Long-Term Medical Therapy (Chronic Management)**:
    ◦ **Antiplatelet Therapy (Mortality Benefit)**:
        ▪ **Aspirin**: 81 mg daily (first-line).
        ▪ **Clopidogrel**: If true aspirin allergy.
    ◦ **Beta-Blockers (Mortality Benefit, esp. post-MI)**:
        ▪ **First-line for symptom control** (e.g., Metoprolol, Atenolol).
        ▪ **Mechanism**: Decrease heart rate, contractility, and blood pressure, reducing myocardial oxygen demand.
    ◦ **Statins (Mortality Benefit)**:
        ▪ **High-intensity statin** (e.g., Atorvastatin 40-80 mg, Rosuvastatin 20-40 mg) for all patients with known CAD, regardless of baseline LDL.
    ◦ **Symptom Control (Add-on or Alternative to Beta-Blockers)**:
        ▪ **Calcium Channel Blockers**: (e.g., Amlodipine, Diltiazem). Good for patients who cannot tolerate beta-blockers or need additional symptom control.
        ▪ **Long-Acting Nitrates**: (e.g., Isosorbide mononitrate). Requires a "nitrate-free" interval of 8-12 hours per day to prevent tachyphylaxis.
        ▪ **Ranolazine**: Can be added for refractory symptoms. Does not affect HR or BP.
sections.management:
• **Risk Factor Modification (The ABCDEs)**:
    ◦ **A**: **A**spirin and **A**nti-anginal therapy.
    ◦ **B**: **B**eta-blocker and **B**lood pressure control (<130/80 mmHg).
    ◦ **C**: **C**holesterol management (statins) and **C**igarette cessation.
    ◦ **D**: **D**iet and **D**iabetes management (A1c <7%).
    ◦ **E**: **E**xercise and **E**ducation.
• **Revascularization**:
    ◦ Used for patients with symptoms refractory to optimal medical therapy or for high-risk anatomy.
    ◦ **Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (PCI)**: Angioplasty with stent placement. Best for 1 or 2-vessel disease not involving the left main coronary artery.
    ◦ **Coronary Artery Bypass Graft (CABG) Surgery**: Surgical revascularization. Preferred for **left main coronary artery disease, 3-vessel disease**, or 2-vessel disease in a patient with diabetes.
sections.complications:
• Progression to **Acute Coronary Syndrome** (Unstable Angina, MI).
• **Heart Failure** (secondary to ischemic cardiomyopathy).
• **Arrhythmias** (e.g., ventricular tachycardia).
• **Sudden Cardiac Death**.
sections.prognosis:
• The annual mortality rate for patients with stable angina and normal LV function is approximately 1-2%.
• Prognosis is worse with:
    ◦ Poor left ventricular function (**EF < 50%**).
    ◦ Greater number of diseased coronary vessels (e.g., **left main or 3-vessel disease**).
    ◦ Poorly controlled risk factors.
    ◦ More severe symptoms or ischemia at a low workload on stress testing.

sections.overview:
• Prinzmetal angina, also known as variant angina or vasospastic angina, is a transient and focal **spasm of a coronary artery** that causes a high-grade obstruction, leading to myocardial ischemia.
• Unlike classic stable angina, it occurs **at rest** and is not related to increased myocardial oxygen demand.
• The hallmark is **transient ST-segment elevation** on an ECG during an episode of chest pain, which resolves when the spasm subsides.
sections.etiology:
• **Core Mechanism**: Focal spasm of the smooth muscle layer of a major coronary artery, leading to severe, transient luminal narrowing or complete occlusion.
• **Underlying Abnormality**: The primary cause is believed to be **coronary endothelial dysfunction**.
    ◦ This leads to an imbalance between vasodilating substances (e.g., nitric oxide) and vasoconstricting substances (e.g., endothelin, thromboxane A2).
• **Result**: This dysfunction causes hyperreactivity of the coronary artery smooth muscle to various vasoconstrictive stimuli.
• **Artery State**: The spasm can occur in coronary arteries that are angiographically normal or in those with coexisting, often non-obstructive, atherosclerotic disease. The spasm is the primary ischemic event, not the underlying plaque.
sections.epidemiology:
• Accounts for approximately 2% of hospitalizations for unstable angina.
• More prevalent in **Japanese** populations compared to Western populations.
• Typically affects a **younger patient demographic** (age 40s-50s) than classic atherosclerotic coronary artery disease (CAD).
• Some studies suggest a slight female predominance.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Cigarette Smoking**: The single most important modifiable risk factor.
• **Illicit Drug Use**:
    ◦ **Cocaine** (potent vasoconstrictor)
    ◦ Amphetamines
    ◦ Marijuana
• **Medications**:
    ◦ Triptans (e.g., sumatriptan)
    ◦ Ergot alkaloids (e.g., ergotamine)
• **Other Triggers**:
    ◦ Emotional stress
    ◦ Cold exposure
    ◦ Hyperventilation
    ◦ Magnesium deficiency
    ◦ Alcohol consumption
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a patient experiencing **recurrent episodes of anginal chest pain that occur at rest**.
• Episodes often have a **circadian pattern**, most commonly occurring from **late night to early morning** (midnight to 8 AM).
• Pain is **not precipitated by physical exertion** or emotional stress, although stress can be a trigger.
• Episodes may occur in clusters, with multiple attacks over a period of days to weeks, followed by long periods of remission.
• **Chest Pain**:
    ◦ **Quality**: Substernal, crushing, pressure-like, or squeezing (indistinguishable from typical ACS pain).
    ◦ **Radiation**: May radiate to the neck, jaw, shoulders, or arms.
    ◦ **Duration**: Typically lasts 5 to 15 minutes.
    ◦ **Relief**: Responds promptly to **sublingual nitroglycerin**.
• **Associated Symptoms**:
    ◦ Dyspnea
    ◦ Diaphoresis
    ◦ Nausea / Vomiting
    ◦ Palpitations (due to arrhythmias)
    ◦ Dizziness or syncope (if severe ischemia or arrhythmia occurs)
sections.physicalExam:
• The physical exam is often **completely normal** between episodes.
• **During an episode**:
    ◦ The patient may appear anxious and in distress.
    ◦ Tachycardia and hypertension may be present due to pain-induced sympathetic activation.
    ◦ A transient **S4 gallop** or a new murmur of **mitral regurgitation** may be auscultated due to ischemia-induced left ventricular dysfunction.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Electrocardiogram (ECG)**:
    ◦ **Hallmark Finding** (during an episode): **Transient ST-segment elevation** in the leads corresponding to the affected coronary artery territory.
    ◦ The ECG **returns to baseline** after the chest pain and vasospasm resolve.
    ◦ ST depression or T-wave abnormalities can also occur.
    ◦ The ECG is typically normal between episodes.
• **Ambulatory ECG (Holter Monitoring)**: Useful for capturing spontaneous episodes of ST elevation in patients with frequent symptoms.
• **Cardiac Enzymes (Troponin I/T)**:
    ◦ **Typically normal**.
    ◦ May be slightly elevated if the vasospasm is severe and prolonged enough to cause myocardial necrosis (MI).
• **Coronary Angiography**:
    ◦ **Gold Standard** for definitive diagnosis.
    ◦ Often shows non-obstructive coronary arteries (<50% stenosis).
    ◦ **Provocative Testing**: During angiography, spasm can be induced with intracoronary administration of **acetylcholine** or **ergonovine**.
        ▪ This is diagnostic but carries a risk of inducing prolonged spasm or arrhythmia and is performed only in experienced centers.
• **Exercise Stress Testing**: Usually negative, as symptoms are not exertional.
sections.treatment:
• **Acute Episodes**:
    ◦ **Sublingual Nitroglycerin (NTG)**: First-line therapy for rapid relief of symptoms.
• **Long-Term Prophylaxis (Prevention)**:
    ◦ **First-Line**: **Calcium Channel Blockers (CCBs)** are the cornerstone of therapy.
        ▪ Non-dihydropyridines: **Diltiazem** or **Verapamil**.
        ▪ Dihydropyridines: **Nifedipine** or **Amlodipine**.
    ◦ **Second-Line / Adjunctive**: **Long-acting Nitrates** (e.g., isosorbide mononitrate).
• **Medications to AVOID**:
    ◦ **Non-selective Beta-Blockers** (e.g., propranolol): Can cause unopposed alpha-adrenergic stimulation, potentially worsening vasospasm. **This is a classic contraindication.**
    ◦ Cardioselective beta-blockers should also be used with extreme caution.
    ◦ **Aspirin**: Low-dose (81 mg) is reasonable if co-existing atherosclerosis is present. High doses should be avoided as they can inhibit prostacyclin production and worsen spasm.
sections.management:
• **Risk Factor Modification**:
    ◦ **SMOKING CESSATION** is the most critical intervention.
    ◦ Avoidance of all triggers, especially **cocaine** and other vasoconstrictive substances.
• **Pharmacotherapy**: Titrate CCBs and nitrates to the maximum tolerated dose to prevent symptoms.
• **Patient Education**: Instruct on the proper use of sublingual NTG, recognition of symptoms, and trigger avoidance.
• **Follow-up**: Regular follow-up with cardiology to monitor symptom control and medication side effects.
sections.complications:
• **Acute Myocardial Infarction (MI)**: Can occur if the spasm is severe and prolonged.
• **Life-Threatening Arrhythmias**:
    ◦ Ventricular Tachycardia / Ventricular Fibrillation
    ◦ High-grade Atrioventricular (AV) Block
• **Syncope**
• **Sudden Cardiac Death**
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is generally **excellent** with appropriate medical therapy and risk factor modification (especially smoking cessation).
• The 5-year survival rate is >90%.
• Prognosis is worse for patients with:
    ◦ Coexisting severe, obstructive CAD.
    ◦ Multi-vessel spasm.
    ◦ Development of life-threatening arrhythmias during an ischemic episode.

sections.overview:
• **Silent ischemia** is the presence of objective evidence of myocardial ischemia (e.g., EKG changes, perfusion defects) in the absence of chest pain or other anginal equivalents.
• It is a manifestation of coronary artery disease (CAD) where myocardial oxygen demand exceeds supply, but the patient does not perceive the typical warning sign of **angina**.
• Despite the lack of symptoms, silent ischemia carries the same risk for adverse cardiovascular events (**myocardial infarction**, **sudden cardiac death**) as symptomatic ischemia.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ The underlying cause is identical to symptomatic ischemia: **atherosclerotic coronary artery disease (CAD)**.
    ◦ Fixed coronary artery stenosis or dynamic obstruction (e.g., vasospasm) leads to an imbalance between myocardial oxygen supply and demand, typically triggered by physical exertion or emotional stress.
• **Pathophysiology of "Silence"**
    ◦ The mechanism for the absence of pain is not fully understood but is believed to be due to a "defective anginal warning system." Key theories include:
        ▪ **Cardiac Autonomic Neuropathy**: This is the most widely accepted theory, especially in diabetic patients. Damage to afferent (sensory) cardiac nerves impairs the transmission of pain signals from the myocardium to the central nervous system.
        ▪ **Higher Pain Threshold**: Some individuals may have a naturally higher threshold for pain perception. Elevated levels of endogenous opioids (endorphins) may blunt the perception of ischemic pain.
        ▪ **Altered Cortical Perception**: The brain may process the incoming nociceptive signals differently, failing to recognize them as pain.
        ▪ **Severity/Duration of Ischemia**: Ischemic episodes may be too brief or not severe enough to reach the individual's "anginal threshold," the point at which pain is perceived.
sections.epidemiology:
• Common in patients with known CAD.
• Extremely prevalent in patients with **Diabetes Mellitus**; up to 50% of MIs in diabetics may be silent.
• More common in the **elderly**.
• Also seen in patients after **cardiac transplantation** due to the denervated status of the donor heart.
• Can be the first and only manifestation of CAD in a subset of asymptomatic individuals.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• By definition, patients are **asymptomatic**.
• Silent ischemia is an **incidental finding** discovered during diagnostic testing performed for other reasons (e.g., screening, pre-operative evaluation, follow-up for known CAD).
• It may be discovered after a patient presents with a *complication* of ischemia, such as:
    ◦ New-onset congestive heart failure (CHF)
    ◦ Syncope
    ◦ Ventricular arrhythmia
sections.diagnostics:
• The goal is to find objective evidence of ischemia.
• **Ambulatory EKG (Holter Monitor)**
    ◦ **Best initial test for detecting transient ischemia** during a patient's normal daily routine.
    ◦ Looks for transient **ST-segment depressions (>1 mm)** that are not associated with symptoms noted in the patient's diary.
• **Stress Testing**
    ◦ **Exercise Stress EKG**: The most common provocative test. Positive if it induces 1 mm of horizontal or downsloping ST-segment depression without accompanying chest pain.
    ◦ **Stress Echocardiography**: Assesses for ischemia-induced **regional wall motion abnormalities**. Offers higher sensitivity and specificity than EKG alone.
    ◦ **Myocardial Perfusion Imaging (Nuclear Stress Test - SPECT/PET)**: Detects **reversible perfusion defects** (areas of the heart that receive less blood flow during stress compared to rest). Highly sensitive for identifying the location and extent of ischemia.
• **12-Lead EKG (Resting)**
    ◦ Often normal.
    ◦ May show evidence of a prior silent MI (e.g., pathological Q waves) or non-specific ST-T wave abnormalities.
• **Coronary Angiography (Cardiac Catheterization)**
    ◦ **Gold standard** for defining the anatomy of the coronary arteries.
    ◦ It does not diagnose silent ischemia but confirms the underlying CAD and determines if revascularization is indicated.
sections.prognosis:
• **Poor**. The prognosis of patients with documented silent ischemia is **comparable to that of patients with symptomatic angina**.
• The presence of silent ischemia is a strong independent predictor of future MI and cardiac death.
• The lack of a symptomatic warning sign may prevent the patient from seeking timely medical attention or limiting their activity during an ischemic event, potentially worsening outcomes.

sections.overview:
• **Essential (Primary) Hypertension** is a chronic medical condition characterized by a persistent elevation of systemic arterial blood pressure without an identifiable secondary cause.
• It accounts for approximately 95% of all cases of hypertension.
• It is a major modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, and renal disease.
• Diagnosis is based on multiple blood pressure readings over time, and management involves a combination of lifestyle modifications and pharmacotherapy to reduce the risk of **end-organ damage**.
sections.etiology:
• The term "essential" implies an **idiopathic** etiology.
• The pathophysiology is **multifactorial** and complex, involving an interplay of genetic and environmental factors.
• Key mechanisms include:
    ◦ **Sympathetic Nervous System (SNS) Overactivity:** Increased SNS tone leads to increased heart rate, cardiac output, and peripheral vascular resistance through alpha and beta-adrenergic stimulation.
    ◦ **Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS) Activation:** Inappropriate RAAS activation leads to **vasoconstriction** (via Angiotensin II) and **sodium/water retention** (via Aldosterone), increasing blood volume and pressure.
    ◦ **Renal Sodium and Water Retention:** A primary defect in the kidneys' ability to excrete sodium (**pressure natriuresis**) can lead to volume expansion and increased blood pressure.
    ◦ **Endothelial Dysfunction:** Impaired production of vasodilators (like nitric oxide) and overproduction of vasoconstrictors (like endothelin) contribute to increased peripheral resistance.
    ◦ **Vascular Remodeling:** Chronic high pressure causes structural changes in arteries, including smooth muscle hypertrophy and fibrosis, leading to narrowed lumens and increased stiffness, which further perpetuates hypertension.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** Affects approximately one-third of adults in the United States.
• **Age:** Prevalence increases significantly with age; >60% of individuals over age 60 have hypertension.
• **Race/Ethnicity:** Higher prevalence, earlier onset, and greater severity in **African American** individuals. They also experience a higher rate of complications like **stroke** and **end-stage renal disease (ESRD)**.
• **Gender:** More common in men before age 55; more common in women after age 55 (post-menopause).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The vast majority of patients are **asymptomatic**.
• Hypertension is typically discovered incidentally during a routine physical exam or screening.
• When symptoms do occur, they are often nonspecific or indicative of hypertensive urgency/emergency or **end-organ damage**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Establishing the Diagnosis:**
    ◦ **Office BP Measurement:** Average of 2 readings on 2 separate visits.
    ◦ **Ambulatory BP Monitoring (ABPM):** Gold standard for diagnosis. Useful to rule out **"white coat" hypertension** and identify **"masked" hypertension**. A 24-hour average BP >130/80 mmHg is diagnostic.
    ◦ **Home BP Monitoring (HBPM):** An alternative to ABPM.
• **Initial Workup (To assess for end-organ damage & screen for secondary causes):**
    ◦ **Electrocardiogram (EKG):** To screen for **LVH** (e.g., **Sokolow-Lyon criteria**: S in V1 + R in V5/V6 > 35 mm), ischemia, or prior MI.
    ◦ **Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP/CMP):** Assess electrolytes (Na+, K+), renal function (BUN, Creatinine), and glucose.
    ◦ **Urinalysis (UA):** Screen for **proteinuria** or **hematuria**, suggesting kidney damage.
    ◦ **Urine Albumin-to-Creatinine Ratio (UACR):** More sensitive test for early kidney disease.
    ◦ **Lipid Panel:** Assess for dyslipidemia, a common comorbidity.
    ◦ **Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH):** Rule out thyroid disease as a secondary cause.
    ◦ **Complete Blood Count (CBC):** Baseline assessment.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** with good blood pressure control through lifestyle and medication adherence.
• **Poor** if left untreated, with a significantly increased risk of premature morbidity and mortality from cardiovascular events, stroke, and renal failure.
• The degree of BP elevation and the presence of **end-organ damage** are the primary determinants of prognosis.

sections.overview:
• **Secondary hypertension** is elevated blood pressure due to an identifiable underlying cause.
    ◦ Accounts for 5-10% of cases, unlike primary (essential) hypertension which is idiopathic and accounts for ~95%.
    ◦ Clinical significance lies in its potential for cure or specific treatment by addressing the root cause.
    ◦ Should be suspected in patients with:
        ▪ New-onset hypertension at age <30 or >55.
        ▪ **Resistant hypertension** (uncontrolled on 3 medications including a diuretic).
        ▪ An acute rise in BP over a previously stable baseline.
        ▪ Clinical clues suggestive of a specific etiology.
sections.etiology:
• The underlying causes can be categorized by system (mnemonic **CHAPS**).
• **Renal (Most Common Cause)**
    ◦ **Renal Parenchymal Disease** (e.g., CKD, Glomerulonephritis, Polycystic Kidney Disease)
        ▪ The most common cause of secondary HTN.
        ▪ Pathophysiology involves impaired sodium and water excretion, increased activity of the **Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS)**, and heightened sympathetic nervous system activity.
    ◦ **Renovascular Hypertension**
        ▪ Due to **renal artery stenosis (RAS)**.
        ▪ **Atherosclerosis** (~90% of RAS): Typically affects older men, often with other signs of atherosclerotic disease (CAD, PVD). Usually involves the ostium or proximal third of the renal artery.
        ▪ **Fibromuscular Dysplasia (FMD)** (~10% of RAS): Typically affects younger women (<40). Non-inflammatory, non-atherosclerotic disorder causing stenosis in the mid-to-distal renal artery.
        ▪ Pathophysiology of RAS: Decreased renal perfusion is sensed by the juxtaglomerular apparatus, leading to massive activation of the **RAAS**, resulting in potent vasoconstriction (Angiotensin II) and sodium/water retention (Aldosterone).
• **Endocrine**
