    ◦ **Primary Aldosteronism (Conn's Syndrome)**
        ▪ Caused by an adrenal adenoma or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia.
        ▪ Pathophysiology: Autonomous, excessive aldosterone secretion leads to increased sodium and water reabsorption, causing volume expansion and HTN. It also promotes potassium excretion, leading to **hypokalemia** and metabolic alkalosis. **Renin levels are suppressed**.
    ◦ **Pheochromocytoma**
        ▪ Catecholamine-secreting tumor of the adrenal medulla.
        ▪ Pathophysiology: Tumors secrete excess epinephrine and norepinephrine, leading to potent alpha- and beta-adrenergic stimulation, causing intense vasoconstriction, increased heart rate, and contractility, resulting in sustained or **paroxysmal (episodic) severe hypertension**.
    ◦ **Cushing's Syndrome**
        ▪ Excess cortisol from an adrenal tumor, pituitary tumor (Cushing's disease), or exogenous steroid use.
        ▪ Pathophysiology: Cortisol enhances vascular sensitivity to catecholamines and can have mineralocorticoid effects, leading to fluid retention and HTN.
    ◦ **Thyroid Disease**
        ▪ **Hyperthyroidism**: Causes increased cardiac output and heart rate, leading primarily to **systolic hypertension** with a wide pulse pressure.
        ▪ **Hypothyroidism**: Causes increased systemic vascular resistance, leading primarily to **diastolic hypertension** with a narrow pulse pressure.
    ◦ **Hyperparathyroidism**
        ▪ Elevated PTH and hypercalcemia are associated with HTN, likely through effects on vascular smooth muscle tone.
• **Other Major Causes**
    ◦ **Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA)**
        ▪ A very common and underdiagnosed cause.
        ▪ Pathophysiology: Recurrent nocturnal hypoxia and arousals lead to chronic sympathetic nervous system activation, which persists during waking hours.
    ◦ **Coarctation of the Aorta**
        ▪ Congenital narrowing of the aorta, typically just distal to the left subclavian artery.
        ▪ Pathophysiology: Mechanical obstruction increases pressure proximal to the coarctation (arms, head). Decreased renal blood flow also activates the RAAS.
    ◦ **Drug-Induced / Substance-Induced**
        ▪ Common culprits: **NSAIDs**, oral contraceptives (especially high-estrogen), corticosteroids, decongestants (pseudoephedrine), stimulants (cocaine, amphetamines), certain antidepressants (SNRIs, MAOIs), excessive alcohol.
sections.epidemiology:
• Accounts for **5-10%** of all hypertension cases.
• Prevalence is higher in specific populations:
    ◦ Up to **20-30%** in patients with **resistant hypertension**.
    ◦ More common in children and young adults with HTN.
• **Most common causes overall**: **Renal parenchymal disease** and **Obstructive Sleep Apnea**.
• **Most common curable cause**: **Renovascular hypertension (RAS)**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The "classic" patient presents with one of the following red flags:
    ◦ **Resistant Hypertension**: BP remains >140/90 mmHg despite treatment with at least three antihypertensive agents of different classes, one of which is a diuretic.
    ◦ **Age of Onset**: New HTN in a patient <30 years old (especially without obesity/family history) or >55 years old.
    ◦ **Severity**: Abrupt onset of severe HTN (e.g., stage 2 or hypertensive emergency).
    ◦ **Specific Clues**: Presence of symptoms or lab abnormalities pointing to a specific cause (e.g., unexplained **hypokalemia**).
    ◦ **End-Organ Damage**: Significant target organ damage (e.g., **LVH**, retinopathy, renal insufficiency) that is disproportionate to the duration or level of hypertension.
sections.diagnostics:
• The workup is guided by clinical suspicion.
• **1. Initial Screening Tests (for most suspected cases):**
    ◦ **Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP)**: Look for **hypokalemia** (Primary Aldosteronism) or elevated creatinine/low GFR (Renal Parenchymal Disease).
    ◦ **Urinalysis (UA)**: Proteinuria or hematuria suggests renal parenchymal disease.
    ◦ **TSH**: To screen for thyroid disease.
    ◦ **ECG**: To assess for **LVH** or arrhythmias.
• **2. Confirmatory / Targeted Tests:**
    ◦ Suspected **Primary Aldosteronism**:
        ▪ Test: Plasma Aldosterone Concentration (PAC) and Plasma Renin Activity (PRA) to calculate the **Aldosterone-to-Renin Ratio (ARR)**.
        ▪ Positive Finding: **ARR >20-30** with a PAC >15 ng/dL. Renin will be suppressed.
        ▪ Note: Patient must be off spironolactone, eplerenone, ACEi/ARBs for several weeks before testing.
    ◦ Suspected **Pheochromocytoma**:
        ▪ Test: **Plasma free metanephrines** (high sensitivity) or **24-hour urine for fractionated metanephrines and catecholamines** (high specificity).
        ▪ Follow-up: CT or MRI of the abdomen/pelvis to locate the tumor after biochemical confirmation.
    ◦ Suspected **Cushing's Syndrome**:
        ▪ Test (choose one): 24-hour urinary free cortisol, overnight low-dose dexamethasone suppression test, or late-night salivary cortisol.
    ◦ Suspected **Renovascular HTN (RAS)**:
        ▪ Initial Imaging: Renal duplex ultrasonography (Doppler).
        ▪ Confirmatory Imaging: **CT Angiography (CTA)** or **MR Angiography (MRA)**.
        ▪ Gold Standard: **Renal Arteriography** (invasive, usually reserved for when intervention is planned).
    ◦ Suspected **Coarctation of the Aorta**:
        ▪ Initial Test: **Echocardiogram**.
        ▪ Confirmatory: CT or MR angiography of the chest.
    ◦ Suspected **OSA**:
        ▪ Test: Overnight **polysomnography** (sleep study).
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is generally excellent if the underlying cause is identified and corrected early, before significant end-organ damage occurs.
• In many cases (e.g., adrenalectomy for adenoma, stenting for unilateral FMD), the hypertension can be completely cured.
• If the cause is irreversible (e.g., advanced CKD) or diagnosis is delayed, the prognosis is related to the degree of blood pressure control and existing end-organ damage.

sections.overview:
• **Malignant Hypertension** is a **hypertensive emergency** characterized by severely elevated blood pressure (typically diastolic >120-130 mmHg) accompanied by evidence of **acute, ongoing end-organ damage**
	◦ The hallmark, though not universally present, is **papilledema** on funduscopic exam
	◦ It is a life-threatening condition requiring immediate medical intervention to prevent irreversible organ failure
	◦ It is distinct from hypertensive urgency, where BP is severely elevated but there is no evidence of acute end-organ damage
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
	◦ **Most Common:** Poorly controlled or untreated essential hypertension, especially following abrupt cessation of antihypertensive medications (e.g., clonidine, beta-blockers)
	◦ **Secondary Causes**
		▪ **Renal:** Renal artery stenosis (renovascular hypertension), acute glomerulonephritis, polycystic kidney disease
		▪ **Endocrine:** Pheochromocytoma, Cushing's syndrome, primary aldosteronism
		▪ **Vascular:** Scleroderma renal crisis, vasculitis
		▪ **Drug-Induced:** Cocaine, amphetamines, MAOIs, sympathomimetics
		▪ **Pregnancy-Related:** Eclampsia / pre-eclampsia
• **Pathophysiology**
	◦ **Failure of Autoregulation:** A sudden, severe rise in systemic vascular resistance overwhelms the body's normal blood pressure autoregulatory mechanisms
	◦ **Endothelial Injury:** The intense pressure and mechanical stress damage the endothelial lining of small arteries and arterioles
	◦ **Increased Permeability & Fibrinoid Necrosis:** Damage leads to increased vascular permeability, allowing plasma proteins (like fibrin) to leak into the vessel walls, leading to the characteristic pathologic finding of **fibrinoid necrosis** of the arterioles
	◦ **Vicious Cycle**
		▪ Vessel damage and luminal narrowing cause tissue ischemia, particularly in the kidneys
		▪ Renal ischemia potently activates the **Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS)**
		▪ This leads to profound vasoconstriction (Angiotensin II) and volume expansion (Aldosterone), which further elevates BP, causing more endothelial damage and perpetuating the cycle
	◦ **Microangiopathic Hemolytic Anemia (MAHA):** Red blood cells are sheared and fragmented as they pass through damaged arterioles narrowed by fibrin strands, leading to the formation of **schistocytes**
sections.epidemiology:
• Relatively rare, occurring in <1% of patients with chronic essential hypertension
• Incidence has decreased with effective antihypertensive therapy
• More common in **African American males**
• Typical age of onset is 40-50 years old
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The patient is typically acutely ill and presents with symptoms related to the specific organs being damaged
• The presentation is dramatic and requires immediate assessment in an emergency setting
sections.diagnostics:
• **Labs**
	◦ **CBC with Peripheral Smear:** To look for anemia, thrombocytopenia, and **schistocytes** (hallmark of MAHA)
	◦ **CMP**
		▪ **Elevated BUN/Creatinine:** Indicates acute kidney injury (AKI)
		▪ **Hypokalemia:** May suggest hyperaldosteronism
		▪ Check electrolytes, glucose
	◦ **Urinalysis:** Will show **proteinuria, hematuria**, and often **red blood cell casts**, indicating glomerular damage
	◦ **Cardiac Enzymes (Troponin):** To rule out acute myocardial infarction
	◦ **BNP:** To assess for acute heart failure
	◦ **Urine Toxicology Screen:** If substance use is suspected
• **Imaging & Other Studies**
	◦ **ECG:** May show signs of left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH), strain pattern, or acute ischemia (ST changes)
	◦ **Chest X-ray:** May show cardiomegaly, pulmonary edema ("bat-wing" appearance), or a widened mediastinum (aortic dissection)
	◦ **Non-contrast Head CT:** **Essential for any patient with neurologic symptoms** to rule out intracranial hemorrhage or ischemic stroke
	◦ **Renal Ultrasound:** To evaluate kidney size and rule out obstruction
sections.prognosis:
• **Untreated:** Historically, the 1-year mortality rate was >90%
• **Treated:** With modern therapy, the 5-year survival rate is now >75%
• The most significant predictor of long-term prognosis is the **degree of renal function impairment** at the time of presentation

sections.overview:
• **Orthostatic Hypotension (OH)**, also known as **postural hypotension**, is defined as a **sustained reduction in blood pressure** within 3 minutes of standing or being tilted upright.
• It is a common clinical problem, particularly in the elderly, and represents a failure of the autonomic nervous system to adequately compensate for the gravitational stress of an upright posture.
• The hallmark is symptoms of **cerebral hypoperfusion** (e.g., **dizziness**, **syncope**) that are induced by standing and relieved by sitting or lying down.
    ◦ **Diagnostic Criteria**: A drop in **systolic blood pressure (SBP)** of **≥20 mmHg** OR a drop in **diastolic blood pressure (DBP)** of **≥10 mmHg** within 3 minutes of standing.
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ Normally, standing pulls ~500-1000 mL of blood into the lower extremities and splanchnic circulation, causing a transient drop in cardiac output and blood pressure.
    ◦ **Baroreceptor Reflex (Normal Response)**:
        ▪ Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch detect the pressure drop.
        ▪ They signal the brainstem, which initiates a compensatory sympathetic response (increased heart rate, contractility, and vasoconstriction).
        ▪ This reflex rapidly restores blood pressure and maintains cerebral perfusion.
    ◦ In **Orthostatic Hypotension**, this reflex is impaired.
• **Etiologic Categories**:
    ◦ **Non-Neurogenic OH (Most Common)**:
        ▪ **Volume Depletion**: **Dehydration**, hemorrhage, vomiting/diarrhea, aggressive diuresis.
        ▪ **Medication-Induced**: A very frequent cause.
            • **Antihypertensives**: Diuretics, Alpha-blockers (tamsulosin, prazosin), Beta-blockers, CCBs, ACEi/ARBs.
            • **Vasodilators**: Nitrates, hydralazine, PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil).
            • **Psychotropics**: Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs), MAOIs, phenothiazines.
            • **Dopaminergic agents**: Levodopa.
        ▪ **Cardiogenic**: Conditions that impair cardiac output, such as severe **aortic stenosis**, **heart failure**, constrictive pericarditis, or significant arrhythmias.
        ▪ **Systemic Conditions**: **Adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease)**, severe anemia, prolonged bed rest/deconditioning.
    ◦ **Neurogenic OH**:
        ▪ Caused by failure of the autonomic nervous system itself.
        ▪ **Hallmark**: Orthostatic drop in BP **without** an adequate compensatory increase in heart rate (typically <15 bpm increase).
        ▪ **Primary Autonomic Disorders (Synucleinopathies)**:
            • **Parkinson's Disease**
            • **Multiple System Atrophy (MSA)**
            • **Dementia with Lewy Bodies (DLB)**
            • **Pure Autonomic Failure (PAF)**
        ▪ **Secondary Autonomic Neuropathies**:
            • **Diabetes Mellitus** (long-standing)
            • **Amyloidosis**
            • **Spinal cord injuries**
            • **Paraneoplastic syndromes**
sections.epidemiology:
• Prevalence increases sharply with **age**.
• Affects ~5-10% of community-dwelling adults **>65 years old**.
• Prevalence can be as high as **30-50% in institutionalized elderly patients** (e.g., nursing homes).
• Common in patients with neurodegenerative diseases like **Parkinson's** (~50% prevalence).
sections.riskFactors:
• **Advanced Age (>65)**
• **Polypharmacy**, especially with causative medications
• Neurodegenerative diseases (**Parkinson's**, **MSA**, **DLB**)
• **Diabetes Mellitus** (especially with neuropathy)
• Cardiovascular disease (**CHF**, **aortic stenosis**)
• **Dehydration** / Volume depletion
• Prolonged immobility or bed rest
• Alcohol use
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is an elderly patient on multiple medications (e.g., an alpha-blocker for BPH, a diuretic for HTN) who reports recurrent episodes of **lightheadedness**, **dizziness**, or "nearly blacking out" immediately after getting out of bed or standing up from a chair.
• Symptoms resolve quickly upon sitting or lying down. A history of **falls** is common.
• **Symptoms**:
    ◦ **Most Common**: **Dizziness**, **lightheadedness**, **pre-syncope** (feeling of fainting).
    ◦ **Visual**: **Blurred** or **tunnel vision**.
    ◦ **General**: Generalized **weakness**, fatigue, cognitive slowing ("brain fog").
    ◦ **Less Common but Specific**:
        ▪ Symptoms are consistently triggered by **postural changes** (lying to sitting, sitting to standing).
        ▪ Symptoms worsen in the **morning** (due to nocturnal diuresis), after **large meals** (postprandial hypotension), with **exertion**, in **hot environments**, or after **straining (Valsalva)**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Orthostatic Vitals**: The primary diagnostic tool.
• **Labs**:
    ◦ **CBC**: To rule out anemia.
    ◦ **BMP/CMP**: To assess for electrolyte abnormalities, dehydration (**BUN/Cr ratio >20:1**), and renal function.
    ◦ Consider morning **cortisol** level if adrenal insufficiency is suspected.
• **ECG**: To screen for arrhythmias, evidence of ischemia, or structural abnormalities.
• **Advanced Testing** (if etiology is unclear):
    ◦ **Tilt-Table Test**: A more controlled way to induce orthostatic stress when office vitals are equivocal.
    ◦ **24-hour Ambulatory BP Monitoring**: Can detect **nocturnal hypertension** (common in neurogenic OH) and morning hypotension.
    ◦ **Autonomic Function Testing**: Confirms and characterizes autonomic failure (e.g., Valsalva maneuver, **QSART**).
sections.treatment:
• **Non-Pharmacologic (First-Line)**:
    ◦ **Medication Review**: **Crucial first step.** Discontinue or reduce doses of offending agents whenever possible.
    ◦ **Volume Expansion**: Increase fluid intake (2-3 L/day) and salt intake (6-10 g/day), unless contraindicated (e.g., CHF, renal failure).
    ◦ **Physical Counter-Maneuvers**: Teach patients to perform these at the first sign of symptoms.
    ◦ **Lifestyle/Behavioral Modifications**: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
• **Pharmacologic Therapy**:
    ◦ **Fludrocortisone**: A mineralocorticoid that increases renal sodium and water retention, expanding plasma volume.
    ◦ **Midodrine**: An alpha-1 adrenergic agonist that causes peripheral vasoconstriction.
    ◦ **Droxidopa**: A norepinephrine prodrug. Approved for **neurogenic OH**.
    ◦ **Pyridostigmine**: An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that can be used as an adjunct, especially in **neurogenic OH**.
sections.management:
• **Follow-up**: Regularly assess symptom burden, check for side effects of therapy (especially **supine hypertension**), and monitor electrolytes if on fludrocortisone.
• **Treat the Underlying Cause**: Manage diabetes, optimize heart failure therapy, adjust Parkinson's medications, etc.
sections.complications:
• **Falls and related injuries**: **Fractures** (hip, wrist), **traumatic brain injury** (subdural hematoma).
• **Syncope**.
• Reduced quality of life and functional decline due to fear of falling and activity restriction.
• Increased risk of **cardiovascular events** and **all-cause mortality**.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is highly dependent on the underlying etiology.
    ◦ **Good**: If due to a reversible cause (e.g., medication, dehydration).
    ◦ **Guarded/Poor**: If associated with a progressive neurodegenerative disorder like **Multiple System Atrophy (MSA)**, where OH is a major source of disability and morbidity.
sections.preventionEducation:
• **Patient Education**: Critical for success. Focus on hydration, slow position changes, counter-maneuvers, and fall prevention.
• **Fall Prevention**: Home safety evaluation, appropriate footwear, use of assistive devices (cane, walker).

sections.overview:
• **Left-Sided Heart Failure (L-Sided HF)** is a clinical syndrome where the left ventricle (LV) cannot pump blood effectively to the systemic circulation, or can only do so with abnormally high filling pressures.
    ◦ This leads to a backup of blood into the pulmonary circulation, causing **pulmonary congestion** and respiratory symptoms.
• It is the most common form of heart failure.
• L-Sided HF is broadly categorized into two types based on **Ejection Fraction (EF)**:
    ◦ **Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF)**: Also known as **systolic heart failure**.
        ▪ The LV is weakened and cannot contract forcefully.
        ▪ Defined by an **EF ≤ 40%**.
    ◦ **Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction (HFpEF)**: Also known as **diastolic heart failure**.
        ▪ The LV is stiff and cannot relax or fill properly, despite adequate contractility.
        ▪ Defined by an **EF ≥ 50%**.
sections.etiology:
• The core problem is decreased **cardiac output (CO)** and/or increased pulmonary venous pressure.
• The body's compensatory mechanisms (**RAAS activation**, **sympathetic nervous system activation**) become maladaptive over time, leading to a vicious cycle of:
    ◦ Fluid retention
    ◦ Vasoconstriction
    ◦ Cardiac remodeling
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects over 6 million adults in the United States.
• Incidence increases sharply with age.
• The most common cause of hospitalization for patients over 65.
• HFrEF and HFpEF each account for about 50% of HF cases, with HFpEF becoming more prevalent.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The "classic" patient is an older individual with known cardiac risk factors presenting with a gradual or acute onset of **shortness of breath**.
• The presentation can range from:
    ◦ Chronic, stable **exertional dyspnea**.
    ◦ Acute, life-threatening **pulmonary edema** ("**flash pulmonary edema**").
sections.diagnostics:
• **Labs**
    ◦ **B-type Natriuretic Peptide (BNP)** or **NT-proBNP**
        ▪ **Key diagnostic marker**.
        ▪ Released by ventricles in response to stretch.
        ▪ High levels are very sensitive for HF.
        ▪ A normal level has a high **negative predictive value** (helps rule out HF).
        ▪ **BNP > 100 pg/mL** or **NT-proBNP > 300 pg/mL** is suggestive.
    ◦ **Troponins**: To rule out **acute coronary syndrome (ACS)** as the cause.
    ◦ **CMP**: To assess **renal function (BUN/Cr)** and **electrolytes (Na+, K+)**, which is critical for guiding diuretic therapy.
    ◦ **CBC**: To rule out **anemia** as a contributing cause of dyspnea.
• **Electrocardiogram (ECG)**
    ◦ Often abnormal but non-specific. Can show evidence of underlying cause:
        ▪ **LV hypertrophy (LVH)**
        ▪ Prior **MI (Q waves)**
        ▪ Active **ischemia (ST changes)**
        ▪ Arrhythmias like **atrial fibrillation** (common in HF).
• **Chest X-Ray (CXR)**
    ◦ **A**lveolar edema ("**batwing**" or butterfly pattern)
    ◦ **B** - **Kerley B lines** (short, horizontal lines in the periphery indicating interstitial edema)
    ◦ **C**ardiomegaly (**cardiothoracic ratio > 0.5**)
    ◦ **D**ilated prominent upper lobe vessels (**Cephalization**)
    ◦ **E**ffusion (**pleural effusions**, often bilateral)
• **Echocardiogram (Transthoracic - TTE)**
    ◦ **The single most useful test and gold standard for diagnosis.**
    ◦ Measures the **ejection fraction (EF)**, differentiating HFrEF from HFpEF.
    ◦ Assesses ventricular size, wall thickness, wall motion abnormalities, and valvular function.
    ◦ Provides an estimate of diastolic function.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is generally poor and depends on the underlying etiology, **NYHA functional class**, and adherence to therapy.
• Despite modern therapy, the 5-year mortality rate is approximately 50%.
• Recurrent hospitalizations are common and associated with a worse prognosis.

sections.overview:
• **Right-Sided Heart Failure (RSHF)**, also known as **right ventricular (RV) failure**, is a clinical syndrome characterized by the inability of the right ventricle to pump deoxygenated blood effectively into the pulmonary circulation.
    ◦ This leads to a "backup" of blood in the systemic venous system.
• The hallmark of RSHF is **systemic venous congestion**.
• While it can occur in isolation, it is most commonly a consequence of **left-sided heart failure (LSHF)**.
• When RSHF occurs due to primary pulmonary pathology, it is termed **cor pulmonale**.
sections.etiology:
• The pathophysiology centers on **RV dysfunction** leading to increased right-sided filling pressures (central venous pressure) and subsequent **systemic venous congestion**.
• **Left-Sided Heart Failure (Most Common Cause)**
    ◦ LSHF leads to increased pressure in the pulmonary vasculature (**pulmonary venous hypertension**).
    ◦ This chronic elevation in pressure increases the afterload against which the right ventricle must pump.
    ◦ Over time, the RV hypertrophies and then dilates, eventually failing under the sustained pressure load.
• **Primary Pulmonary Disease (Cor Pulmonale)**
    ◦ **COPD**: Chronic hypoxia causes pulmonary vasoconstriction, leading to pulmonary hypertension and increased RV afterload.
    ◦ **Interstitial Lung Disease (ILD)**: Fibrosis and destruction of the pulmonary capillary bed increases pulmonary vascular resistance.
    ◦ **Pulmonary Embolism (PE)**: A large PE can acutely obstruct the pulmonary artery, causing a sudden, massive increase in RV afterload and acute RSHF. Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) is a chronic cause.
    ◦ **Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA)**: Recurrent nocturnal hypoxia leads to pulmonary hypertension.
• **Primary Pulmonary Hypertension (PAH)**
    ◦ Idiopathic or heritable conditions causing remodeling of the pulmonary arterioles, leading to severely elevated pulmonary artery pressures.
• **Intrinsic RV Myocardial Disease**
    ◦ **Right Ventricular Infarction**: Usually occurs in the setting of an inferior wall MI affecting the right coronary artery.
    ◦ **Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy (ARVC)**: A genetic disorder where RV myocardium is replaced by fibrofatty tissue.
• **Valvular Heart Disease**
    ◦ **Pulmonic Stenosis**: Obstructs RV outflow.
    ◦ **Tricuspid Regurgitation**: Causes RV volume overload.
    ◦ **Tricuspid Stenosis**: Obstructs RV filling (less common).
• **Congenital Heart Disease**
    ◦ **Atrial Septal Defect (ASD)**, **Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD)** can lead to volume/pressure overload on the right side of the heart over time.
sections.epidemiology:
• Heart failure affects over 6 million adults in the United States.
• The epidemiology of RSHF is closely tied to its causes.
    ◦ As **LSHF** is the most common cause, the prevalence of RSHF increases with age and with risk factors for LSHF.
• **Cor pulmonale** accounts for 5-10% of all heart disease cases, with **COPD** being the predominant cause in this subset.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The typical patient presents with symptoms of **fluid overload**.
• The presentation can be gradual (**chronic RSHF** due to LSHF or COPD) or acute (due to a **massive PE** or **RV infarction**).
• The chief complaint is often **bilateral leg swelling**, **increased abdominal girth**, or significant **weight gain** over a short period.
• Dyspnea may be present but is often due to the underlying LSHF or lung disease rather than pulmonary congestion itself.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Echocardiogram (Transthoracic - TTE)**: **The key diagnostic test.**
    ◦ Assesses **RV size**, thickness, and systolic function (e.g., TAPSE).
    ◦ Estimates **pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PASP)**.
    ◦ Identifies valvular pathology (tricuspid/pulmonic).
    ◦ Evaluates left ventricular function to determine if LSHF is the cause.
• **Labs**
    ◦ **BNP / NT-proBNP**: Elevated in heart failure, indicates ventricular stretch. Not specific for RSHF vs. LSHF but useful for confirming a cardiac etiology of symptoms.
    ◦ **Liver Function Tests (LFTs)**: May show elevated bilirubin, AST, ALT, and Alk Phos due to hepatic congestion.
    ◦ **Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP)**: Assess renal function (creatinine, BUN) for **cardiorenal syndrome** and electrolytes (**hyponatremia** is a poor prognostic sign).
• **ECG**
    ◦ May show signs of **RV hypertrophy (RVH)**:
        ▪ Right axis deviation
        ▪ R wave > S wave in V1
        ▪ S wave > R wave in V6 ("S-dominant pattern")
    ◦ May show right atrial enlargement ("**P pulmonale**" - peaked P waves in leads II, III, aVF).
    ◦ In acute cor pulmonale (PE): **S1Q3T3 pattern** (deep S in lead I, Q wave in lead III, inverted T in lead III).
• **Chest X-Ray (CXR)**
    ◦ May show **cardiomegaly** (especially enlargement of the right heart border).
    ◦ **Pleural effusions** (often right-sided or bilateral).
    ◦ May reveal underlying pulmonary cause (e.g., hyperinflation in COPD, interstitial changes in ILD).
• **Right Heart Catheterization**
    ◦ **Gold standard** for definitively measuring right-sided pressures (CVP, RV pressure, pulmonary artery pressure) and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP).
    ◦ Confirms pulmonary hypertension and helps differentiate pre-capillary (pulmonary vascular disease) vs. post-capillary (LSHF) causes.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis for RSHF is generally **poor**, as it often represents an advanced stage of underlying cardiac or pulmonary disease.
• Prognosis is highly dependent on the etiology, the severity of RV dysfunction, and the response to therapy.
• Markers of **poor prognosis** include:
    ◦ Persistent **hyponatremia**
    ◦ Worsening renal function
    ◦ High **BNP** levels
    ◦ The need for inotropic support

sections.overview:
• **Biventricular heart failure** is an advanced stage of heart failure where both the left and right ventricles have failed, leading to inadequate pumping of blood to both the systemic and pulmonary circulations.
• It represents a state of global cardiac dysfunction, manifesting with a combination of symptoms and signs from both left-sided and right-sided heart failure.
• Most commonly, it begins with **left ventricular failure**, which then leads to secondary **right ventricular failure** over time.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Most Common Cause**: **Left-sided heart failure** (of any cause) leading to pulmonary hypertension and subsequent right-sided heart failure.
    ◦ Causes of Left-Sided HF:
        ▪ **Ischemic Heart Disease / Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)**: Most common underlying cause in the US.
        ▪ **Long-standing Hypertension (HTN)**: Leads to left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) and diastolic dysfunction, eventually progressing to systolic failure.
        ▪ **Valvular Disease**: Aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral regurgitation.
    ◦ Causes Affecting Both Ventricles Simultaneously:
        ▪ **Dilated Cardiomyopathy**: Idiopathic, viral (e.g., Coxsackie B), alcoholic, postpartum, toxic (e.g., doxorubicin, cocaine).
        ▪ **High-Output Failure States**: Severe anemia, thyrotoxicosis, beriberi, AV fistulas.
        ▪ **Infiltrative Diseases**: Amyloidosis, sarcoidosis (often presenting as restrictive cardiomyopathy).
• **Pathophysiology**: The process is a cascade of failure:
    ◦ 1. **Initial Left Ventricular (LV) Failure**: The LV weakens and cannot effectively pump oxygenated blood into the systemic circulation.
        ▪ **Decreased Cardiac Output**: Leads to systemic hypoperfusion, causing fatigue, weakness, and activation of neurohormonal systems (RAAS, SNS).
        ▪ **Blood Backup**: Blood backs up from the LV into the left atrium and subsequently into the pulmonary vasculature.
        ▪ **Pulmonary Congestion**: This increased pressure in the pulmonary veins and capillaries (**pulmonary edema**) causes the classic "left-sided" symptoms of dyspnea, orthopnea, and PND.
    ◦ 2. **Progression to Right Ventricular (RV) Failure**:
        ▪ The chronic elevation of pressure in the pulmonary circulation is called **pulmonary hypertension**.
        ▪ The RV, which is a low-pressure chamber designed to pump against the low-resistance pulmonary vasculature, must now pump against this high pressure.
        ▪ This chronic pressure overload causes the RV to hypertrophy, dilate, and eventually fail.
    ◦ 3. **Resulting Biventricular Failure**:
        ▪ The failed RV can no longer effectively pump deoxygenated blood into the lungs.
        ▪ Blood backs up from the RV into the right atrium and then into the systemic venous circulation.
        ▪ This **systemic venous congestion** causes the classic "right-sided" signs: JVD, peripheral edema, ascites, and hepatosplenomegaly.
        ▪ The patient now exhibits a mixed clinical picture of both pulmonary and systemic congestion.
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects over 6 million adults in the United States.
• Leading cause of hospitalization for adults over age 65.
• Incidence and prevalence increase sharply with age.
• **5-year mortality rate** after diagnosis is approximately 50%, highlighting its severity.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A typical patient is an older adult (e.g., a 72-year-old male) with a known history of hypertension and a prior MI who presents to the emergency department with a one-week history of progressive shortness of breath, a 10-pound weight gain, and new swelling in both legs.
• The patient reports needing to sleep upright in a recliner for the past three nights because he can't breathe when lying down.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Labs**
    ◦ **BNP (B-type Natriuretic Peptide) or NT-proBNP**: **Key lab test.**
        ▪ Released from stretched ventricles.
        ▪ A normal level has a high negative predictive value for HF.
        ▪ **BNP >100 pg/mL** is highly suggestive of acute decompensated heart failure.
    ◦ **CMP**: Assess electrolytes (Na+, K+), renal function (**BUN**, **Cr**), and liver enzymes (AST/ALT/Alk Phos may be elevated from congestion).
    ◦ **CBC**: Rule out **anemia** as a contributing cause.
    ◦ **Cardiac Troponins**: Rule out an **acute MI** as the precipitant.
    ◦ **TSH**: Rule out **thyroid dysfunction**.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Echocardiogram (TTE)**: **The single most useful diagnostic tool.**
        ▪ Determines **Ejection Fraction (EF)** to classify as **HFrEF** (Heart Failure with reduced EF, ≤40%) or **HFpEF** (Heart Failure with preserved EF, ≥50%).
        ▪ Assesses ventricular size, wall thickness, wall motion abnormalities, and valvular function.
    ◦ **Chest X-Ray (CXR)**:
        ▪ **Cardiomegaly**: Cardiothoracic ratio > 0.5.
        ▪ **Cephalization**: Prominence of upper lobe pulmonary vessels.
        ▪ **Kerley B lines**: Short, horizontal lines in the periphery, indicating interstitial edema.
        ▪ **Pleural Effusions**: Blunting of costophrenic angles.
        ▪ **Alveolar ("Batwing") Edema**: Hazy opacities in a central distribution.
• **Other Tests**
    ◦ **Electrocardiogram (ECG)**: Not diagnostic for HF itself, but essential for identifying underlying causes like prior **MI** (Q waves), **LVH**, arrhythmias (**atrial fibrillation** is common), or conduction delays (**LBBB**).
sections.prognosis:
• **Biventricular heart failure** is a progressive disease with a poor prognosis.
• Mortality remains high, with an approximate **50% 5-year survival rate** after diagnosis.
• Prognosis is often categorized by:
    ◦ **ACC/AHA Stages**:
        ▪ **Stage A**: At high risk, no structural disease or symptoms.
        ▪ **Stage B**: Structural disease, no symptoms.
        ▪ **Stage C**: Structural disease with prior or current symptoms.
        ▪ **Stage D**: Refractory HF requiring specialized interventions.
    ◦ **NYHA Functional Class**:
        ▪ **Class I**: No limitation of physical activity.
        ▪ **Class II**: Slight limitation. Comfortable at rest.
        ▪ **Class III**: Marked limitation. Comfortable only at rest.
        ▪ **Class IV**: Unable to carry on any physical activity without symptoms; symptoms at rest.

sections.overview:
• **High-Output Heart Failure (HOHF)** is a rare form of heart failure where the cardiac output (CO) is normal or elevated but is insufficient to meet the body's heightened metabolic demands.
    ◦ Unlike typical low-output heart failure (systolic or diastolic), the primary problem is not intrinsic cardiac pump failure.
    ◦ Instead, an underlying condition creates a **hyperdynamic, hypermetabolic state** or a **low-resistance circulatory path (shunting)** that overwhelms a healthy heart.
    ◦ Over time, the chronic volume and pressure overload leads to **cardiac remodeling**, dilation, and eventual pump failure, transitioning to a classic low-output state if left untreated.
sections.etiology:
• The central mechanism of HOHF involves a profound and persistent **decrease in systemic vascular resistance (SVR)** or a significant **arteriovenous (AV) shunt**.
    ◦ This leads to increased venous return (preload) and a compensatory, sustained increase in heart rate and stroke volume, resulting in a high cardiac output.
• **Major Causes and Mechanisms**:
    ◦ **High Metabolic Demand**
        ▪ **Severe Anemia**: Decreased oxygen-carrying capacity leads to tissue hypoxia, triggering profound peripheral **vasodilation** to increase O2 delivery.
        ▪ **Thyrotoxicosis**: Excess thyroid hormone increases basal metabolic rate, has direct positive inotropic/chronotropic effects, and decreases SVR.
        ▪ **Sepsis**: Systemic inflammatory response releases vasodilatory mediators (e.g., nitric oxide), causing a dramatic drop in SVR.
    ◦ **Systemic AV Shunting**
        ▪ **AV Fistulas (AVF)**: Acquired (e.g., for hemodialysis, trauma) or congenital. Blood bypasses high-resistance arterioles/capillaries, shunting directly into the venous system, drastically lowering SVR and increasing venous return.
        ▪ **Paget's Disease of Bone**: Extensive, highly vascular bone lesions create numerous micro-AV shunts.
        ▪ **Cirrhosis / Liver Disease**: Splanchnic vasodilation and formation of portosystemic shunts reduce effective SVR.
    ◦ **Nutritional**
        ▪ **Thiamine (B1) Deficiency (Wet Beriberi)**: Thiamine is a cofactor in aerobic metabolism. Its deficiency impairs cellular energy production, leading to metabolic acidosis and compensatory peripheral vasodilation to improve substrate delivery.
    ◦ **Physiologic**
        ▪ **Pregnancy**: A normal physiologic state of increased blood volume, increased CO, and decreased SVR to support uteroplacental circulation. Can precipitate HOHF in susceptible individuals.
sections.epidemiology:
• HOHF is uncommon, representing a small fraction **(<5%)** of all heart failure cases.
• Its incidence is directly related to the prevalence of the underlying etiologies in a given population (e.g., higher rates of beriberi in areas with malnutrition, or HOHF in patients with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis).
sections.riskFactors:
• **End-stage renal disease (ESRD)** requiring hemodialysis via an **AV fistula**
• Chronic **severe anemia** (e.g., thalassemia, chronic GI bleed)
• Untreated **hyperthyroidism** (Grave's disease, toxic multinodular goiter)
• Chronic alcoholism or malnutrition (risk for **beriberi**)
• Advanced **Paget's disease of bone**
• Chronic liver disease / **cirrhosis**
• History of major trauma leading to an iatrogenic AV fistula
• Myeloproliferative disorders
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The patient presents with classic symptoms of heart failure (e.g., dyspnea, edema) but appears paradoxically **well-perfused and hyperdynamic**.
    ◦ This contrasts sharply with the cool, pale, and vasoconstricted presentation of classic low-output heart failure.
• **Symptoms**:
    ◦ **Dyspnea on exertion (DOE)**
    ◦ **Orthopnea & Paroxysmal Nocturnal Dyspnea (PND)**
    ◦ Bilateral lower extremity **pitting edema**
    ◦ **Ascites**, abdominal fullness
    ◦ Fatigue and weakness (despite high CO, the metabolic demands are even greater)
    ◦ Palpitations or a "pounding" heartbeat
sections.physicalExam:
• **Warm extremities** and flushed skin
• **Bounding, "water-hammer" peripheral pulses**
• **Wide pulse pressure** (e.g., 160/60 mmHg)
sections.diagnostics:
• The goal is to confirm heart failure and, most importantly, identify the high-output state and its underlying cause.
• **Labs**:
    ◦ **BNP or NT-proBNP**: **Elevated**, confirming cardiac wall stress.
    ◦ **CBC**: To identify **severe anemia** (low Hgb/Hct).
    ◦ **TSH, free T4**: To screen for **thyrotoxicosis**.
    ◦ **LFTs**: To evaluate for liver disease.
    ◦ **Thiamine (Vitamin B1) Level**: If **beriberi** is suspected.
    ◦ **Alkaline Phosphatase**: Markedly elevated in **Paget's disease**.
• **Echocardiogram (TTE)**:
    ◦ **Key Finding**: **Normal or supranormal Ejection Fraction (EF > 50-60%)** with left ventricular dilation.
    ◦ Demonstrates a **hyperdynamic left ventricle**.
    ◦ Doppler can be used to estimate a high cardiac output.
    ◦ Rules out primary systolic/diastolic dysfunction or valvular disease.
• **Chest X-ray (CXR)**:
    ◦ Shows signs of **congestive heart failure**: cardiomegaly, pulmonary vascular congestion, Kerley B lines, pleural effusions.
• **Invasive Hemodynamics (Right Heart Catheterization)**:
    ◦ **Gold Standard** for definitive diagnosis, used in unclear cases.
    ◦ **Hallmark Findings**:
        ▪ **High Cardiac Output (CO > 8 L/min) / Cardiac Index (CI > 4.0 L/min/m2)**
        ▪ **Low Systemic Vascular Resistance (SVR < 800 dynes·sec/cm5)**
        ▪ Elevated filling pressures (RAP, PCWP)
        ▪ Low arteriovenous oxygen difference (AVO2 diff)
sections.treatment:
• **Anemia**: Transfuse packed red blood cells (PRBCs); provide iron, B12, or folate as indicated.
• **Thyrotoxicosis**: Anti-thyroid medications (methimazole, PTU), beta-blockers for rate control, radioiodine ablation.
• **AV Fistula**: Surgical ligation or endovascular closure. For dialysis fistulas, surgical banding can reduce flow without sacrificing access.
• **Wet Beriberi**: High-dose parenteral thiamine supplementation. Dramatic improvement is often seen within 24 hours.
• **Paget's Disease**: Bisphosphonates (e.g., zoledronic acid) to decrease bone turnover.
• **Sepsis**: Source control, antibiotics, and hemodynamic support per guidelines.
sections.management:
• **Sodium and Fluid Restriction**: Essential first step to reduce volume overload.
• **Diuretics**: **Loop diuretics (e.g., Furosemide)** are first-line to relieve pulmonary and peripheral congestion.
• **Vasodilators (ACEi/ARBs)**: **Use with extreme caution.** The SVR is already low, and these agents can cause profound hypotension. They are generally not a primary therapy.
• **Beta-Blockers**: Useful in thyrotoxicosis to control heart rate. In other causes, use cautiously as they can blunt the necessary compensatory tachycardia.
sections.complications:
• Irreversible cardiac remodeling leading to chronic systolic or diastolic (low-output) heart failure.
• Development of pulmonary hypertension.
• Atrial and ventricular arrhythmias due to chamber stretch.
• Thromboembolism.
• End-organ damage from chronic congestion (e.g., cardio-renal syndrome, congestive hepatopathy).
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is **excellent** if the underlying cause is identified and corrected early, before significant cardiac remodeling occurs.
• The prognosis is **poor** if the underlying condition is irreversible or if the diagnosis is delayed until the heart has transitioned to a low-output state.

sections.overview:
• **Aortic Stenosis (AS)** is the obstruction of blood flow across the aortic valve, leading to increased resistance to left ventricular (LV) outflow.
	◦ This results in a pressure gradient between the LV and the aorta during systole.
	◦ The LV must generate higher pressures to overcome this obstruction, leading to a cascade of compensatory and eventually maladaptive changes, most notably concentric **left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH)**.
• It is the most common valvular heart disease in developed countries.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• The most common primary valve disease requiring surgery or intervention in Europe and North America.
• Prevalence is strongly age-dependent.
	◦ Affects ~0.4% of the population at age 65, increasing to >10% in those >80 years old.
• Congenital **bicuspid aortic valve** is present in 1-2% of the general population.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Age:** The single greatest risk factor.
• **Congenital Bicuspid Aortic Valve**
• **Male Gender**
• **Hypertension**
• **Hyperlipidemia**
• **Smoking**
• **History of Rheumatic Fever**
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients are typically **asymptomatic for many years**, even with severe AS.
• The onset of symptoms marks a critical turning point and indicates a poor prognosis without intervention.
• The presentation is classically described by a triad of symptoms.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Auscultation**
	◦ **Murmur:** Harsh, **crescendo-decrescendo (diamond-shaped) systolic ejection murmur**, best heard at the **right upper sternal border (RUSB)**.
	◦ **Radiation:** Classically **radiates to the carotid arteries**.
	◦ **Gallavardin Phenomenon:** The murmur may also radiate to the apex, where it sounds more high-pitched or "musical."
	◦ **Maneuvers:** Murmur intensity **increases** with maneuvers that increase preload (squatting, leg raise) and **decreases** with maneuvers that decrease preload (Valsalva, standing).
• **Heart Sounds**
	◦ **Soft or single S2:** The A2 component (aortic valve closure) is delayed and softer due to leaflet immobility, eventually merging with P2.
	◦ **S4 gallop:** Often present due to atrial "kick" against a stiff, non-compliant hypertrophied LV.
• **Palpation**
	◦ **Thrill:** A palpable vibration may be felt at the RUSB or suprasternal notch.
	◦ **Apical Impulse:** Sustained, forceful apical impulse due to LVH.
• **Arterial Pulse**
	◦ **Pulsus Parvus et Tardus:** A weak/diminished (parvus) and delayed (tardus) carotid pulse upstroke. A pathognomonic finding for severe AS.
• **Blood Pressure**
	◦ **Narrowed pulse pressure** (systolic - diastolic) may be seen in severe AS.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Echocardiogram (Transthoracic - TTE):** **GOLD STANDARD** for diagnosis, quantification, and monitoring.
	◦ **Assesses:** Valve morphology (bicuspid, calcification), LV wall thickness (for LVH), LV systolic function (ejection fraction), and quantifies stenosis severity via:
		▪ **Peak Aortic Jet Velocity (Vmax)**
		▪ **Mean Transvalvular Pressure Gradient**
		▪ **Aortic Valve Area (AVA)**
• **Electrocardiogram (ECG/EKG):**
	◦ May be normal.
	◦ Classic finding: **LVH with strain pattern** (deep S waves in V1/V2, tall R waves in V5/V6; ST depressions and T-wave inversions in lateral leads).
	◦ Left atrial enlargement may also be present.
• **Chest X-Ray (CXR):**
	◦ Often normal.
	◦ May show **calcification of the aortic valve**, **post-stenotic dilation of the ascending aorta**, or signs of heart failure (cardiomegaly, pulmonary edema).
• **Cardiac Catheterization:**
	◦ Invasive gold standard but rarely used for diagnosis alone.
	◦ Primarily used pre-operatively to rule out coexisting coronary artery disease (CAD) or if echocardiogram findings are inconclusive.
sections.management:
• **Asymptomatic Patients (Watchful Waiting):**
	◦ **Patient Education:** Instruct patients to immediately report any new symptoms (angina, syncope, dyspnea).
	◦ **Activity:** Advise against strenuous competitive sports if stenosis is severe.
	◦ **Serial Echocardiography:**
		▪ Mild AS: Echo every 3-5 years.
		▪ Moderate AS: Echo every 1-2 years.
		▪ Severe AS: Echo every 6-12 months.
sections.complications:
• **Congestive Heart Failure (CHF)**
• **Sudden Cardiac Death**
• **Arrhythmias** (Atrial Fibrillation is common)
• **Infective Endocarditis**
• **Bleeding:** Heyde's Syndrome (angiodysplasia of the GI tract associated with AS).
sections.prognosis:
• **Asymptomatic Patients:** Prognosis is excellent, with survival rates similar to the age-matched general population.
• **Symptomatic Patients:** Prognosis is **EXTREMELY POOR** without valve replacement. The average survival after symptom onset is:
	◦ **Angina:** 5 years
	◦ **Syncope:** 3 years
	◦ **Heart Failure:** 2 years

sections.overview:
• Aortic Regurgitation (AR), also known as Aortic Insufficiency (AI), is a valvular heart disease characterized by the **retrograde (backward) flow** of blood from the **aorta** into the **left ventricle (LV)** during **diastole**.
    ◦ This occurs due to incomplete closure of the aortic valve leaflets.
    ◦ The resulting **LV volume overload** leads to a series of hemodynamic changes and, if left untreated, eventual heart failure.
    ◦ AR can be **acute or chronic**, with vastly different clinical presentations and management strategies.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• Prevalence increases with age, affecting up to 10% of individuals over 65.
• More common in men.
• In developing nations, **rheumatic heart disease** remains a primary cause.
• In developed nations, **bicuspid aortic valve** and **degenerative disease** are more common.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Chronic AR**
    ◦ Patients often remain **asymptomatic for decades** even with severe AR, due to LV compensation.
    ◦ When symptoms develop, it signifies **LV dysfunction**.
• **Acute AR**
    ◦ Presents as a **cardiovascular collapse**.
    ◦ Patients are critically ill with sudden onset of **severe dyspnea**, **hypotension**, and signs of **cardiogenic shock**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Echocardiogram (TTE/TEE)**
    ◦ **Gold standard** for diagnosis.
    ◦ Confirms the diagnosis and visualizes the regurgitant jet via color Doppler.
    ◦ Assesses severity (e.g., regurgitant fraction, vena contracta width).
    ◦ Evaluates LV size (LVESD, LVEDD) and function (LVEF).
    ◦ Identifies etiology (bicuspid valve, root dilation, vegetations).
• **ECG**
    ◦ May be normal.
    ◦ Classic findings are signs of **LVH** (high voltage in precordial leads, S in V1 + R in V5/V6 > 35mm), left axis deviation, and left atrial enlargement ("P mitrale").
• **Chest X-Ray**
    ◦ **Cardiomegaly** (enlarged, "**boot-shaped**" cardiac silhouette).
    ◦ Dilated ascending aorta.
    ◦ In acute AR or decompensated chronic AR, shows signs of pulmonary edema.
• **Cardiac Catheterization**
    ◦ No longer primary for diagnosis, but can quantify severity via aortography.
    ◦ Primarily used pre-operatively to rule out significant coronary artery disease (CAD).
• **Cardiac MRI (CMR)**
    ◦ Excellent for quantifying regurgitant volume/fraction and assessing LV volumes and function, especially when echo is suboptimal.
sections.prognosis:
• **Asymptomatic with normal LV function:** Excellent prognosis for many years.
• **Onset of symptoms:** Marks a turning point. Without surgery, mortality is high (~10-20% per year).
• **LV dysfunction (LVEF < 50%):** Poor prognosis without surgery.
• **Acute AR:** Extremely high mortality rate (>75%) without emergent surgical intervention.
• With timely AVR, prognosis is excellent, and LV function often improves or normalizes.

sections.overview:
• **Mitral Stenosis (MS)** is a valvular heart disease characterized by the **narrowing of the mitral valve orifice**.
    ◦ This obstruction impedes blood flow from the **left atrium (LA)** to the **left ventricle (LV)** during diastole.
    ◦ The resulting pressure gradient across the valve leads to a cascade of hemodynamic changes, including left atrial enlargement, **pulmonary hypertension**, and eventually **right-sided heart failure**.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• More prevalent in **developing countries** where **rheumatic fever** is endemic.
• In developed countries, it is most often seen in the **elderly (degenerative)** or in immigrants from endemic regions.
• **Sex:** Strong **female predominance** (2:1 to 3:1 ratio).
• **Age of Onset:** Symptoms typically manifest in the 3rd to 4th decade of life.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The clinical course is characterized by a **long latent period** (decades) followed by a gradual progression of symptoms.
• The initial presentation is often precipitated by a physiologic stress that demands increased cardiac output or heart rate, such as:
    ◦ **Pregnancy**
    ◦ **Infection/Fever**
    ◦ Anemia
    ◦ Onset of **atrial fibrillation** with a rapid ventricular response
sections.diagnostics:
• **Echocardiography (TTE/TEE):** **GOLD STANDARD** for diagnosis and assessment of severity.
    ◦ **Visualizes:** Thickened, calcified, and restricted mitral leaflets with diastolic "doming" or a **"hockey-stick" appearance** of the anterior leaflet.
    ◦ **Quantifies Severity:**
        ▪ **Mitral Valve Area (MVA):** Normal is 4-6 cm². Severe MS is **MVA < 1.5 cm²** (very severe < 1.0 cm²).
        ▪ **Mean Pressure Gradient:** Measures the pressure difference across the valve.
    ◦ **Assesses:** LA size, pulmonary artery pressure, RV size and function, and presence of thrombus (TEE is superior for this).
• **Electrocardiogram (ECG):**
    ◦ **P mitrale:** Broad, notched P-wave in lead II (>0.12s) indicating LA enlargement.
    ◦ Biphasic P-wave in V1 with a large negative component.
    ◦ **Atrial fibrillation** is very common.
    ◦ Right axis deviation and RV hypertrophy (tall R wave in V1) suggest significant pulmonary hypertension.
• **Chest X-ray (CXR):**
    ◦ **Left atrial enlargement:** Straightening of the left heart border, a "double density" sign, and splaying of the carina (>90 degrees).
    ◦ **Pulmonary venous congestion:** Cephalization of flow, Kerley B lines (short horizontal lines in the periphery).
    ◦ Pulmonary artery enlargement and RV enlargement in advanced disease.
• **Cardiac Catheterization:**
    ◦ Used when non-invasive tests are inconclusive or to assess for concomitant coronary artery disease before surgery.
    ◦ Directly measures the pressure gradient between the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (LA pressure) and the LV end-diastolic pressure.
sections.prognosis:
• The natural history is a **long, stable asymptomatic period**.
• Once symptoms develop, the prognosis declines rapidly without intervention.
• The 10-year survival rate for untreated symptomatic patients is <15%.
• Successful PMBC or surgery significantly improves symptoms and long-term survival.

sections.overview:
• Mitral Regurgitation (MR) is a valvular heart disorder where the mitral valve fails to close completely during systole, allowing blood to leak backward (regurgitate) from the left ventricle (LV) into the left atrium (LA)
    ◦ This backflow results in a **volume overload** on both the LA and LV, which can be acute or chronic
    ◦ **Chronic MR** leads to compensatory changes like LA and LV dilation and eccentric hypertrophy
    ◦ **Acute MR** is a medical emergency causing a sudden rise in LA pressure and **pulmonary edema**
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• The most common form of significant valvular heart disease in developed nations
• Prevalence increases significantly with age
• **Degenerative MR** (due to MVP) is the most common etiology in the US and Europe
• **Ischemic MR** is also very common
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Chronic MR**:
    ◦ Patients can be asymptomatic for decades
    ◦ Presentation is often insidious with a gradual decline in exercise tolerance
• **Acute MR**:
    ◦ Sudden, severe presentation
    ◦ The patient is critically ill with **cardiogenic shock** and/or **acute pulmonary edema**
sections.diagnostics:
• **Echocardiography (TTE/TEE)**:
    ◦ **Test of choice** for diagnosis, quantification of severity, and determining etiology
    ◦ **Transthoracic Echo (TTE)**: Initial diagnostic test
    ◦ **Transesophageal Echo (TEE)**: Provides superior images of the valve apparatus; often used for pre-operative planning
    ◦ **Key Findings**:
        ▪ Visualizes the **regurgitant jet** with color Doppler
        ▪ Assesses LA and LV size
        ▪ Calculates LVEF and LV end-systolic dimension (LVESD)
• **Electrocardiogram (ECG)**:
    ◦ Can be normal
    ◦ May show **LA enlargement** (**P mitrale**: broad, notched P wave in lead II)
    ◦ May show **LV hypertrophy (LVH)** (voltage criteria)
    ◦ **Atrial fibrillation** is common in chronic MR
• **Chest X-Ray (CXR)**:
    ◦ **Cardiomegaly** due to LA and LV enlargement
    ◦ Signs of pulmonary congestion/edema (**cephalization** of pulmonary vessels, **Kerley B lines**, pleural effusions)
• **Cardiac Catheterization**:
    ◦ Not typically for diagnosis of MR itself
    ◦ Used to assess for concomitant **coronary artery disease (CAD)** prior to surgery, or if non-invasive tests are inconclusive
• **BNP (B-type Natriuretic Peptide)**:
    ◦ Elevated due to ventricular stretch and volume overload
    ◦ Useful for assessing and monitoring associated heart failure
sections.prognosis:
• Dependent on severity, symptoms, and LV function at the time of intervention
• Asymptomatic patients with preserved LV function have a good prognosis
• The development of symptoms or LV dysfunction significantly worsens the prognosis if left untreated
• Surgical repair carries a better long-term prognosis than replacement
• **Acute severe MR** has a very poor prognosis without emergent surgery

sections.overview:
• **Tricuspid Regurgitation (TR)** is the backflow of blood from the right ventricle (RV) into the right atrium (RA) during systole.
	◦ This occurs due to incomplete coaptation (closure) of the tricuspid valve leaflets.
	◦ While mild, physiologic TR is common and benign, **moderate-to-severe TR** is a marker of significant underlying pathology and is associated with increased morbidity and mortality.
	◦ It is often called the "**forgotten valve**," as its clinical significance was historically underappreciated compared to left-sided valve disease.
sections.etiology:
• **Functional (Secondary) TR (>90% of cases)**
	◦ **Pathophysiology:** The valve leaflets and chordae are structurally normal. Regurgitation occurs due to **tricuspid annular dilation** and **RV enlargement/dysfunction**, which prevents the leaflets from coapting properly.
	◦ **Common Causes:**
		▪ **Left-sided heart disease:** This is the most common cause. Mitral stenosis/regurgitation or aortic valve disease leading to pulmonary hypertension and subsequent RV failure.
		▪ **Pulmonary Hypertension (any cause):** Idiopathic PAH, COPD, interstitial lung disease, obstructive sleep apnea, chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH).
		▪ **Right Ventricular Dysfunction:** RV infarction, cardiomyopathy, cor pulmonale.
		▪ **Atrial Fibrillation:** Chronic A-fib can lead to RA and tricuspid annular dilation.
• **Primary (Organic) TR (<10% of cases)**
	◦ **Pathophysiology:** The regurgitation is caused by intrinsic damage to the tricuspid valve apparatus itself (leaflets, chordae tendineae, papillary muscles, or annulus).
	◦ **Common Causes:**
		▪ **Infective Endocarditis:** A classic cause, especially in **IV drug users (IVDU)**.
		▪ **Rheumatic Heart Disease:** Almost always occurs in conjunction with mitral and/or aortic valve disease.
		▪ **Carcinoid Syndrome:** Pathognomonic plaque-like deposits cause the valve leaflets to become fixed and thickened in a semi-open position.
		▪ **Congenital Defects:** **Ebstein's anomaly** (apical displacement of the septal and posterior leaflets into the RV).
		▪ **Iatrogenic:** Damage from pacemaker or ICD leads, or during right heart biopsy.
		▪ **Trauma:** Chest trauma leading to chordal rupture.
		▪ **Myxomatous Degeneration:** Similar to mitral valve prolapse, but affecting the tricuspid valve.
• **Core Pathophysiologic Consequence:**
	◦ Systolic backflow causes RA volume and pressure overload.
	◦ This leads to RA dilation and increased central venous pressure.
	◦ This results in systemic venous congestion and signs/symptoms of **right-sided heart failure**.
sections.epidemiology:
• Mild (physiologic) TR is detectable by echocardiography in up to 70% of healthy adults.
• The prevalence of **moderate-to-severe TR** increases significantly with age.
• It is more common in women and in patients with underlying cardiovascular disease, particularly heart failure and atrial fibrillation.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Most patients with mild-to-moderate TR are asymptomatic.
• Symptoms typically develop gradually as TR becomes severe and right-sided heart failure progresses.
	◦ The presentation is dominated by signs of **systemic fluid overload**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Echocardiography (Transthoracic - TTE):**
	◦ **The diagnostic test of choice.**
	◦ Confirms the diagnosis and grades severity (color Doppler shows regurgitant jet).
	◦ Assesses the cause (functional vs. primary).
	◦ Evaluates RA and RV size and function.
	◦ **Estimates RV systolic pressure (RVSP)**, which is used to estimate pulmonary artery pressure.
• **Electrocardiogram (EKG):**
	◦ Not diagnostic of TR itself, but can show underlying pathology.
	◦ **Right atrial enlargement (RAE):** Tall, peaked P waves (>2.5 mm) in lead II (**P pulmonale**).
	◦ **Right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH):** Right axis deviation, dominant R wave in V1.
	◦ **Atrial fibrillation** is commonly seen.
• **Chest X-Ray (CXR):**
	◦ May show **cardiomegaly** with enlargement of the right atrial and right ventricular silhouettes.
	◦ Pleural effusions may be present due to right-sided heart failure.
• **Cardiac Catheterization:**
	◦ Not typically needed for diagnosis.
	◦ Considered the "gold standard" for measuring intracardiac pressures (RA, RV, PA pressures).
	◦ Primarily used for pre-operative assessment or when non-invasive tests are inconclusive.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis of TR is directly linked to the severity of the regurgitation, the degree of RV dysfunction, and the nature of the underlying etiology.
• **Moderate-to-severe TR** is independently associated with increased mortality, even if asymptomatic.
• Prognosis is generally poor once signs of severe right heart failure (ascites, cachexia) develop.

sections.overview:
• **Pulmonic Stenosis (PS)** is a valvular heart disease characterized by the **obstruction of blood flow** from the **right ventricle (RV)** to the **pulmonary artery (PA)**.
    ◦ This obstruction occurs at the level of the pulmonic valve, leading to an increased pressure load on the right ventricle.
    ◦ While most commonly a **congenital defect**, it can occasionally be acquired.
    ◦ The clinical significance ranges from an incidental, asymptomatic murmur to severe, life-threatening **cyanosis** and **right heart failure**, depending on the degree of stenosis.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• Represents **8-10% of all congenital heart disease (CHD)**.
• One of the most common forms of CHD diagnosed in adults.
• Slight female predominance.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation depends entirely on the severity of the stenosis.
    ◦ **Mild PS**: Often **asymptomatic** and discovered incidentally on physical exam due to a murmur.
    ◦ **Moderate PS**: May be asymptomatic at rest but develop symptoms with exertion.
        ▪ **Dyspnea on exertion (DOE)**
        ▪ **Fatigue**
    ◦ **Severe PS**: Symptoms present at rest or with minimal exertion.
        ▪ **Angina-like chest pain** (due to RV ischemia from high oxygen demand)
        ▪ Exertional **syncope** or presyncope
        ▪ Signs and symptoms of **right-sided heart failure** (edema, ascites, JVD).
    ◦ **Critical PS (Neonates)**: Presents within hours to days of birth with profound **cyanosis** as the ductus arteriosus closes.
        ▪ This is a **medical emergency**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Echocardiogram (TTE)**:
    ◦ **Best initial and primary diagnostic test**.
    ◦ Visualizes valve anatomy (thickened, "doming" leaflets).
    ◦ Doppler measures the peak pressure gradient across the valve to quantify severity:
        ▪ **Mild**: < 30 mmHg
        ▪ **Moderate**: 30-50 mmHg
        ▪ **Severe**: > 50 mmHg
    ◦ Assesses RV size, thickness (**RVH**), and function.
    ◦ Identifies **post-stenotic dilation of the main pulmonary artery**.
• **Electrocardiogram (ECG)**:
    ◦ Normal in mild PS.
    ◦ **Right Axis Deviation (RAD)**.
    ◦ **Right Ventricular Hypertrophy (RVH)**:
        ▪ Tall R wave in V1 (R > S), deep S wave in V6, strain pattern (T-wave inversions in right precordial leads V1-V3).
    ◦ **Right Atrial Enlargement ("P pulmonale")**:
        ▪ Peaked P waves (>2.5 mm) in lead II.
• **Chest X-ray (CXR)**:
    ◦ Often normal.
    ◦ **Post-stenotic dilation of the main pulmonary artery** is a classic finding.
    ◦ **Cardiomegaly** due to RV enlargement may be seen in severe cases ("boot-shaped heart," though more classic for TOF).
    ◦ Pulmonary vascular markings are usually normal or decreased.
• **Cardiac Catheterization**:
    ◦ **Gold standard** for diagnosis, but primarily used when echocardiogram results are unclear or when intervention is planned.
    ◦ Directly measures the pressure gradient between the RV and PA.
    ◦ Allows for concurrent therapeutic intervention (balloon valvuloplasty).
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for individuals with mild stenosis, who typically have a normal life expectancy.
• **Very good** for those who undergo successful balloon valvuloplasty or surgery, with significant improvement in symptoms and hemodynamics.
• Long-term outcomes depend on the degree of residual stenosis, the development of pulmonic regurgitation, and the status of RV function.

sections.overview:
• Dilated Cardiomyopathy (DCM) is the most common type of cardiomyopathy, a disease of the heart muscle characterized by **dilation and impaired contraction (systolic dysfunction) of one or both ventricles**.
    ◦ The hallmark is a dilated, weakened left ventricle, leading to a **reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF)** and signs and symptoms of congestive heart failure.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• Most common cardiomyopathy.
• Prevalence: ~1 in 2,500 individuals.
• Peak incidence is between ages 20 and 50.
• More common in men than women (approx. 3:1).
• More common in African Americans.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is typically one of **insidious, progressive heart failure**.
    ◦ Patients often present with symptoms that have been worsening over weeks to months.
    ◦ They may present with an acute decompensation triggered by an infection, arrhythmia, or medication non-adherence.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Labs**
    ◦ **BNP or NT-proBNP**: **Elevated**.
        ▪ Levels correlate with the severity of heart failure.
        ▪ A normal level has a high negative predictive value for HF.
    ◦ **CMP**: To assess renal function (BUN/Cr), electrolytes (K+, Na+), and liver function (LFTs may be elevated from congestion).
    ◦ **CBC**: To rule out anemia as a contributing cause.
    ◦ **TSH**: To rule out thyroid dysfunction.
    ◦ **Troponins**: May be mildly elevated due to chronic wall stress.
• **ECG**: Often abnormal but non-specific.
    ◦ **Sinus tachycardia** is common.
    ◦ May show **Left Ventricular Hypertrophy (LVH)**, **Left Bundle Branch Block (LBBB)**, poor R-wave progression.
    ◦ Arrhythmias such as **atrial fibrillation** or **ventricular tachycardia** may be present.
• **Chest X-Ray (CXR)**
    ◦ **Cardiomegaly**: Enlarged, "globular" or "balloon-like" cardiac silhouette.
    ◦ Signs of **pulmonary venous congestion**: cephalization of pulmonary vessels, **Kerley B lines**, pleural effusions.
• **Echocardiogram (TTE)**: **Diagnostic test of choice.**
    ◦ **Confirms the diagnosis** by showing:
        ▪ **Left ventricular dilation** (increased LV end-diastolic diameter).
        ▪ **Reduced global systolic function (EF < 40-45%)**.
        ▪ Thin ventricular walls.
    ◦ Can also assess for valvular regurgitation, diastolic function, and mural thrombi.
• **Cardiac MRI with Gadolinium**: The **gold standard** for assessing ventricular volumes and function.
    ◦ Useful to identify specific etiologies like myocarditis, sarcoidosis, or arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (look for late gadolinium enhancement patterns).
• **Cardiac Catheterization**
    ◦ Primarily used to rule out significant **coronary artery disease** as the cause of LV dysfunction (i.e., ischemic cardiomyopathy).
    ◦ Can directly measure cardiac output and filling pressures.
    ◦ **Endomyocardial biopsy** is rarely performed but may be considered if an inflammatory cause (giant cell myocarditis, sarcoidosis) is strongly suspected.
sections.prognosis:
• Variable and depends on the underlying etiology, patient age, comorbidities, and response to GDMT.
• Reversible causes (e.g., alcohol-induced, peripartum) can have an excellent prognosis if the insult is removed.
• Overall 5-year survival is approximately 50%, though this has improved significantly with modern therapies.
• Negative prognostic indicators include **LVEF < 25%**, **NYHA Class IV symptoms**, high **BNP** levels, renal failure, and hyponatremia.

sections.overview:
• **Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM)** is a **genetic** cardiovascular disease characterized by inappropriate and often asymmetric **left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH)** in the absence of another condition that could cause it (e.g., hypertension, aortic stenosis).
• It is a primary cause of **diastolic dysfunction** and can lead to dynamic **left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction**.
• HCM is the most common genetic heart disease and the most frequent cause of **sudden cardiac death (SCD)** in **young athletes**.
sections.etiology:
• Primarily a **genetic** disorder with **autosomal dominant** inheritance.
• Caused by mutations in genes encoding for **sarcomeric proteins** (contractile units of heart muscle).
    ◦ Most common mutations are in the **β-myosin heavy chain (MYH7)** and **myosin-binding protein C (MYBPC3)** genes.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Left Ventricular Hypertrophy (LVH)**
        ▪ Myocyte hypertrophy and disarray, along with interstitial fibrosis, leads to a thickened, stiff, and non-compliant left ventricle.
        ▪ The hypertrophy is typically asymmetric, most commonly affecting the interventricular septum (**Asymmetric Septal Hypertrophy - ASH**).
    ◦ **Diastolic Dysfunction**
        ▪ The stiff, non-compliant ventricle has impaired relaxation and filling.
        ▪ This leads to elevated left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP), which gets transmitted to the left atrium and pulmonary circulation, causing dyspnea.
        ▪ This is the primary cause of symptoms in most patients.
    ◦ **LVOT Obstruction**
        ▪ Occurs in about 70% of symptomatic patients.
        ▪ Caused by:
            ▪ The hypertrophied septum bulging into the outflow tract.
            ▪ **Systolic Anterior Motion (SAM) of the mitral valve**: During systole, the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve is pulled towards the hypertrophied septum, further narrowing the outflow tract.
            ▪ This often causes secondary mitral regurgitation.
    ◦ **Myocardial Ischemia**
        ▪ Can occur even with normal coronary arteries due to increased oxygen demand from the hypertrophied muscle, decreased capillary density, and compression of small intramural coronary arteries.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects approximately 1 in 500 people in the general population.
• **Demographics**: Affects males and females equally and occurs across all races.
• **Presentation**: Can be diagnosed at any age, but often presents in adolescence or young adulthood.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Many patients are **asymptomatic** and are diagnosed during family screening or incidental finding on ECG/echocardiogram.
• The classic presentation is a **young athlete who experiences syncope or sudden cardiac death** during or after exertion.
• Symptoms are often **exertional** due to increased LVOT obstruction and diastolic dysfunction with tachycardia.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Echocardiogram**: **Gold standard for diagnosis**.
    ◦ Shows unexplained LVH, typically asymmetric, with a septal wall thickness **≥15 mm**.
    ◦ Demonstrates **Systolic Anterior Motion (SAM)** of the mitral valve.
    ◦ Doppler shows turbulent flow and an elevated pressure gradient across the LVOT.
    ◦ Assesses diastolic function.
• **Electrocardiogram (ECG)**:
    ◦ Almost always abnormal, but findings are non-specific.
    ◦ **LVH** criteria are often met.
    ◦ Left atrial enlargement.
    ◦ Prominent, deep, narrow **"dagger-like" Q waves** in the inferolateral leads (II, III, aVF, V5, V6) are characteristic.
• **Cardiac MRI (CMR)**:
    ◦ Excellent for confirming the diagnosis if echo is suboptimal.
    ◦ Can quantify the extent and location of hypertrophy.
    ◦ **Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE)** indicates myocardial fibrosis, which is a risk factor for SCD.
• **Genetic Testing**:
    ◦ Can confirm a pathogenic mutation.
    ◦ Crucial for cascade screening of first-degree family members.
• **Ambulatory ECG Monitoring (Holter)**:
    ◦ Used to screen for arrhythmias like NSVT, which is a risk factor for SCD.
sections.prognosis:
• Highly variable; many individuals remain asymptomatic with a normal lifespan.
• For symptomatic patients or those with risk factors, the annual mortality rate is ~1% without an ICD.
• ICDs have significantly improved the prognosis for high-risk individuals.

sections.overview:
• Restrictive Cardiomyopathy (RCM) is the least common of the major cardiomyopathies.
    ◦ Characterized by **non-dilated, stiff ventricles** with impaired ventricular filling (diastolic dysfunction) and relaxation.
    ◦ Systolic function (ejection fraction) is typically preserved until the late stages of the disease.
    ◦ The hallmark is abnormal diastolic function leading to elevated filling pressures and signs of both right- and left-sided heart failure, with **right-sided heart failure often predominating**.
sections.etiology:
• The core pathophysiologic problem is **decreased ventricular compliance** (i.e., stiff ventricles).
    ◦ This stiffness prevents the ventricles from adequately relaxing and filling during diastole, which leads to:
        ▪ A rapid, early rise in diastolic pressure with only a small increase in ventricular volume.
        ▪ High diastolic pressures are transmitted backward to the atria, causing **marked biatrial enlargement**.
        ▪ Elevated atrial pressures are then transmitted to the pulmonary and systemic venous circulations, leading to pulmonary congestion and systemic venous congestion (e.g., peripheral edema, ascites, hepatomegaly).
• **Major Causes:**
    ◦ **Infiltrative Diseases (Most Common)**
        ▪ **Amyloidosis:** The most common cause of RCM in the U.S. Deposition of abnormal protein fibrils (amyloid) in the myocardium. Can be primary (AL amyloidosis from plasma cell dyscrasia) or hereditary/senile (transthyretin-related, ATTR).
        ▪ **Sarcoidosis:** Formation of non-caseating granulomas within the myocardium.
    ◦ **Storage Diseases**
        ▪ **Hemochromatosis:** Iron deposition in the myocardium.
        ▪ **Fabry Disease:** A lysosomal storage disease causing glycosphingolipid accumulation.
        ▪ **Glycogen Storage Diseases**
    ◦ **Fibrosis**
        ▪ **Idiopathic Myocardial Fibrosis:** No identifiable cause.
        ▪ **Radiation-Induced:** Fibrosis secondary to chest radiation therapy.
        ▪ **Scleroderma:** Systemic sclerosis causing myocardial fibrosis.
    ◦ **Endomyocardial Diseases**
        ▪ **Endomyocardial Fibrosis:** Common in tropical regions; fibrosis of the apical endocardium.
        ▪ **Hypereosinophilic Syndrome (Loeffler's endocarditis):** Endocardial fibrosis and thrombus formation due to eosinophilic infiltration.
sections.epidemiology:
• RCM is the least prevalent cardiomyopathy, accounting for ~5% of all cases.
• The incidence and prevalence vary significantly depending on the underlying etiology.
• Amyloidosis is the most common cause in non-tropical, developed countries, typically affecting older adults (>60 years).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients typically present with symptoms of progressive heart failure.
• The classic presentation is **signs and symptoms of right-sided heart failure that are more prominent than left-sided heart failure**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **ECG:**
    ◦ Non-specific ST and T wave changes.
    ◦ Atrial fibrillation is very common.
    ◦ **Classic for Amyloidosis:** **Low-voltage QRS complexes** in the limb leads, which is discordant with the increased ventricular wall thickness seen on echocardiogram (a classic "mismatch").
    ◦ A pseudo-infarct pattern may also be seen.
• **Labs:**
    ◦ **BNP / NT-proBNP:** Markedly elevated, often disproportionately high for the clinical picture.
    ◦ Labs to investigate etiology: Serum and urine protein electrophoresis (SPEP/UPEP) with immunofixation and serum free light chain assay (for amyloidosis), iron studies/ferritin (for hemochromatosis), ACE level (for sarcoidosis).
• **Chest X-ray (CXR):**
    ◦ Mild to moderate cardiomegaly (due to biatrial enlargement, not ventricular dilation).
    ◦ Signs of pulmonary venous congestion (e.g., pleural effusions, Kerley B lines).
• **Echocardiogram (Initial diagnostic test of choice):**
    ◦ **Key Finding:** **Marked biatrial enlargement** with non-dilated, normal-sized ventricles.
    ◦ Thickened ventricular walls may be present.
    ◦ **Preserved LVEF** (systolic function) until late-stage disease.
    ◦ Evidence of severe **diastolic dysfunction** on Doppler imaging.
    ◦ **Amyloidosis-specific:** "Speckled" or granular appearance of the myocardium.
• **Cardiac MRI (CMR) with Gadolinium:**
    ◦ Excellent for tissue characterization and identifying the etiology.
    ◦ Can detect inflammation, fibrosis, and infiltration.
    ◦ **Late Gadolinium Enhancement (LGE):** The pattern can be diagnostic.
        ▪ Diffuse subendocardial LGE is classic for amyloidosis.
        ▪ Patchy, mid-myocardial LGE suggests sarcoidosis.
• **Endomyocardial Biopsy (Gold Standard):**
    ◦ Provides a definitive histologic diagnosis.
    ◦ **Amyloidosis:** Congo red staining shows classic **apple-green birefringence** under polarized light.
    ◦ **Sarcoidosis:** Non-caseating granulomas.
    ◦ **Hemochromatosis:** Iron deposition confirmed with Prussian blue stain.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is generally poor and is highly dependent on the underlying etiology.
• Untreated **AL amyloidosis** has the worst prognosis, with a median survival of less than one year from diagnosis.
• Prognosis is better for etiologies that can be effectively treated, such as hemochromatosis.

sections.overview:
• Infective Endocarditis (IE) is an infection of the endocardial surface of the heart, most commonly affecting the heart valves.
    ◦ It can also involve the mural endocardium or septal defects.
    ◦ The hallmark lesion is a **vegetation**, a mass of platelets, fibrin, microorganisms, and inflammatory cells.
    ◦ IE is classified based on acuity (acute vs. subacute), valve type (native vs. prosthetic), and risk factors (e.g., IV drug use).
    ◦ It is a life-threatening condition requiring prolonged antimicrobial therapy and, frequently, surgical intervention.
sections.etiology:
• The pathogenesis typically involves a sequence of events:
    ◦ **Endothelial Injury**: Turbulent blood flow from pre-existing valvular disease (e.g., mitral valve prolapse, bicuspid aortic valve, rheumatic heart disease) or direct trauma (e.g., catheters, IV drug use) damages the valve endothelium.
    ◦ **Thrombus Formation**: The injury site becomes a nidus for platelet and fibrin deposition, forming a sterile, non-infected thrombus known as **nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis (NBTE)**.
    ◦ **Bacteremia & Colonization**: During transient bacteremia (e.g., from dental work, IV lines, skin infection), circulating microorganisms adhere to the sterile thrombus.
    ◦ **Vegetation Growth**: Bacteria proliferate within the protected platelet-fibrin mesh, forming a mature septic vegetation. This biofilm protects the organisms from host immune defenses and antibiotics.
sections.epidemiology:
• Incidence is increasing, particularly in older adults.
• Male-to-female ratio is approximately 2:1.
• The primary risk has shifted from rheumatic heart disease to degenerative valve disease, prosthetic valves, indwelling medical devices, and IV drug use in developed nations.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation varies widely based on the causative organism and host factors.
    ◦ **Acute IE**: Presents as a rapidly progressive, toxic illness with high fever, chills, and sepsis. Often caused by _S. aureus_.
    ◦ **Subacute IE**: Presents with an indolent course over weeks to months. Symptoms are often nonspecific: low-grade fever, night sweats, fatigue, weight loss. Often caused by _Viridans strep_.
sections.diagnostics: • The diagnosis is made using the **Modified Duke Criteria**.
sections.prognosis:
• Despite advances, in-hospital mortality remains high (15-25%).
• Prognosis is worse for:
    ◦ **_S. aureus_ IE**
    ◦ **Prosthetic valve IE**
    ◦ Elderly patients
    ◦ Those who develop complications like **heart failure**, **stroke**, or **perivalvular abscess**.
• **Right-sided IE** (IVDU) generally has a better prognosis than left-sided IE.

sections.overview:
• **Myocarditis** is an inflammatory disease of the **myocardium** (heart muscle).
    ◦ The inflammation leads to **myocyte injury** and **necrosis**, which can result in a wide spectrum of clinical presentations, from **subclinical disease** to **chest pain**, **arrhythmias**, **heart failure**, **cardiogenic shock**, and **sudden cardiac death**.
