• It is a crucial diagnosis to consider, especially in younger patients presenting with cardiac symptoms, as it can mimic **acute coronary syndrome (ACS)** but has a completely different etiology and management path.
sections.etiology: • The underlying cause is an inflammatory process that damages the heart muscle.
sections.epidemiology:
• More common in **young adults**, with a peak incidence between 20-40 years old.
• Slight **male predominance**.
• Accounts for a significant percentage of **sudden cardiac deaths** in individuals <40 years old, including young athletes.
• True incidence is likely underestimated as many cases are **mild** or **subclinical**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is highly variable and can be categorized into three main syndromes:
    ◦ **"ACS-like" Presentation**:
        ▪ Patient presents with **chest pain**, **elevated troponins**, and **ECG changes (ST elevation)**, prompting a workup for myocardial infarction.
        ▪ This is a very common presentation.
    ◦ **"New-Onset Heart Failure" Presentation**:
        ▪ Patient presents with symptoms of **heart failure** (**dyspnea**, **edema**, **orthopnea**) over days to weeks without a clear prior cause.
    ◦ **"Fulminant" Presentation**:
        ▪ Severe, abrupt onset of **cardiogenic shock**, often requiring intensive care and mechanical circulatory support.
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• Highly variable.
• Approximately **50%** of patients recover fully.
• **25%** develop persistent **left ventricular dysfunction**.
• **12-25%** progress to **end-stage heart failure** requiring transplant or die.
• **Fulminant myocarditis** has a high acute mortality rate, but paradoxically, patients who survive the initial phase have a higher rate of complete recovery compared to those with a more subacute onset.
• **Giant cell myocarditis** has a very poor prognosis with rapid progression.

sections.overview:
• **Pericarditis** is the inflammation of the pericardium, the double-layered fibroelastic sac that encloses the heart.
    ◦ The pericardium consists of a visceral layer (epicardium) and a parietal layer, with the space between them normally containing 15-50 mL of serous fluid.
    ◦ Inflammation can lead to chest pain and an accumulation of fluid (**pericardial effusion**), potentially causing complications like **cardiac tamponade**.
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ Inflammation of the pericardial layers causes vasodilation, increased capillary permeability, and leukocyte infiltration.
    ◦ This can lead to fibrin deposition and fluid exudation into the pericardial space.
    ◦ Pain is thought to arise from the inflamed parietal pericardium, which is innervated by the phrenic nerve.
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Idiopathic**: Most common cause in developed countries; presumed to be viral.
    ◦ **Infectious**
        ▪ **Viral** (most common infectious cause): Often preceded by a URI.
            ▪ **Coxsackievirus A and B**, **Echovirus**, Adenovirus, Influenza, HIV.
        ▪ **Bacterial** (Purulent): Less common, but high mortality.
            ▪ **Staphylococcus aureus**, **Streptococcus pneumoniae**, often from direct extension (pneumonia, empyema) or hematogenous spread.
        ▪ **Tuberculous**: Common in developing countries; insidious onset.
        ▪ **Fungal**: Rare, typically in immunocompromised patients (*Histoplasma, Coccidioides*).
    ◦ **Non-Infectious / Systemic Inflammatory**
        ▪ **Post-Myocardial Infarction**
            ▪ **Early (Peri-infarction pericarditis)**: Occurs within 1-3 days post-MI due to inflammation extending from necrotic myocardium.
            ▪ **Late (Dressler's Syndrome)**: Occurs weeks to months post-MI; an autoimmune/inflammatory response.
        ▪ **Autoimmune / Connective Tissue Disease**: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA), Scleroderma.
        ▪ **Metabolic**: **Uremia** (most common metabolic cause), myxedema.
    ◦ **Iatrogenic / Traumatic**
        ▪ **Post-cardiac surgery (Postpericardiotomy Syndrome)**: Similar mechanism to Dressler's.
        ▪ **Trauma**: Blunt or penetrating chest trauma.
        ▪ **Radiation therapy** to the chest.
        ▪ **Drug-induced**: Procainamide, hydralazine, isoniazid.
    ◦ **Neoplastic**
        ▪ Metastases from lung cancer, breast cancer, lymphoma, or melanoma.
        ▪ Primary tumors (mesothelioma) are rare.
sections.epidemiology:
• Incidence: ~28 cases per 100,000 people per year.
• Accounts for ~5% of ED visits for non-ischemic chest pain.
• More common in men than women.
• Most common in adults aged 20-50 years.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a young, otherwise healthy individual with a sudden onset of severe chest pain, often following a recent viral syndrome.
    ◦ The patient typically appears uncomfortable and may be leaning forward to relieve the pain.
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis requires at least 2 of the following 4 criteria:
    ◦ 1. Typical **pericarditic chest pain**.
    ◦ 2. **Pericardial friction rub**.
    ◦ 3. Widespread **ST-segment elevation** or **PR depression** on ECG.
    ◦ 4. New or worsening **pericardial effusion**.
• **ECG**
    ◦ The most important initial diagnostic tool.
    ◦ **Classic finding**: **Diffuse, concave ST-segment elevation** ("saddle-shaped") and **PR-segment depression** in nearly all leads except aVR and V1 (which show reciprocal ST depression and PR elevation).
    ◦ **Evolution in 4 Stages**:
        ▪ **Stage 1 (Hours to Days)**: Diffuse ST elevation and PR depression.
        ▪ **Stage 2**: Normalization of ST and PR segments; T-wave flattening.
        ▪ **Stage 3**: Widespread, deep, symmetric T-wave inversions.
        ▪ **Stage 4 (Weeks to Months)**: Normalization of ECG.
• **Labs**
    ◦ **Inflammatory Markers**: **Elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) and Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR)** are common and useful for monitoring disease activity and treatment response.
    ◦ **Cardiac Enzymes (Troponin)**: May be mildly elevated due to concurrent inflammation of the epicardium (myopericarditis), but the elevation is not proportional to the degree of ST elevation as seen in an MI.
    ◦ **CBC** (may show leukocytosis), **BUN/Creatinine** (to assess for uremia).
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Chest X-Ray (CXR)**
        ▪ Often normal.
        ▪ If a large chronic effusion (>250 mL) is present, the cardiac silhouette may be enlarged and flask-shaped (**"water bottle heart"**).
    ◦ **Echocardiogram (TTE)**
        ▪ Essential to evaluate for complications.
        ▪ May be normal in uncomplicated pericarditis.
        ▪ **Primary role is to detect pericardial effusion** and assess for signs of **cardiac tamponade** (e.g., diastolic right atrial or ventricular collapse).
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent for acute idiopathic or viral pericarditis, with most recovering completely within weeks.
• Recurrence is the most common long-term problem.
• Prognosis is dependent on the underlying cause; it is worse for malignant, purulent, or tuberculous pericarditis.

sections.overview:
• **Sick Sinus Syndrome (SSS)** is a generalized abnormality of the **sinoatrial (SA) node**, the heart's natural pacemaker.
    ◦ It is not a single disease but a constellation of signs and symptoms caused by **SA node dysfunction**.
    ◦ This dysfunction leads to a variety of arrhythmias, characterized by an inability to generate or transmit an appropriate cardiac impulse.
    ◦ The hallmark of SSS is an **inappropriate heart rate** for the physiologic demand, which can manifest as both slow and fast rhythms.
sections.etiology:
• The underlying pathophysiology is a malfunction of the SA node's **automaticity** (impulse generation) or **conduction** (impulse transmission).
• **Intrinsic Causes (Most Common):**
    ◦ **Idiopathic Degenerative Fibrosis:** The most frequent cause. Age-related, progressive replacement of SA nodal tissue and surrounding atrial myocardium with fibrous, non-conductive tissue.
    ◦ **Ischemia/Infarction:** Especially involving the **Right Coronary Artery (RCA)**, which supplies the SA node in ~60% of individuals.
    ◦ **Infiltrative Diseases:** Amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis.
    ◦ **Inflammatory Conditions:** Myocarditis, pericarditis, rheumatic fever.
    ◦ **Collagen Vascular Disease:** Systemic lupus erythematosus, scleroderma.
    ◦ **Trauma:** Post-cardiac surgery (e.g., atrial septal defect repair).
• **Extrinsic Causes (Often Reversible):**
    ◦ **Pharmacologic:**
        ▪ **Beta-blockers**
        ▪ Non-dihydropyridine Calcium Channel Blockers (**Verapamil**, **Diltiazem**)
        ▪ **Digoxin**
        ▪ **Antiarrhythmics** (e.g., Amiodarone, Sotalol)
        ▪ Certain psychotropic medications
    ◦ **Metabolic/Endocrine:**
        ▪ **Hypothyroidism**
        ▪ Hypothermia
        ▪ Electrolyte abnormalities (especially **hyperkalemia**)
    ◦ **Autonomic Nervous System Imbalance:**
        ▪ Excessive **vagal tone** (e.g., highly trained athletes, carotid sinus hypersensitivity).
sections.epidemiology:
• Primarily a disease of the **elderly**.
    ◦ The mean age of diagnosis is **~68 years**.
• Prevalence increases significantly with age.
• SSS is the most common indication for **permanent pacemaker implantation** in the United States.
• No significant gender or racial predilection.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• SSS manifests as a spectrum of ECG abnormalities, which may be persistent or intermittent.
    ◦ **Persistent Sinus Bradycardia:** Heart rate **<60 bpm** that is not explained by physiologic demands (e.g., sleep, athletic conditioning).
    ◦ **Sinus Pause / Sinus Arrest:** Failure of the SA node to generate an impulse, leading to a pause on ECG.
        ▪ A pause **>3 seconds** is generally considered clinically significant.
    ◦ **Sinoatrial (SA) Exit Block:** The SA node fires, but the impulse is blocked from exciting the atria.
    ◦ **Chronotropic Incompetence:** The inability of the heart rate to increase appropriately in response to exercise or metabolic demand.
    ◦ **Bradycardia-Tachycardia Syndrome (Brady-Tachy Syndrome):** The most specific manifestation.
        ▪ Alternating periods of bradycardia with paroxysmal tachyarrhythmias, most commonly **Atrial Fibrillation (AFib)**, but also atrial flutter or supraventricular tachycardia (SVT).
sections.diagnostics:
• The key to diagnosis is correlating the patient's symptoms with a documented arrhythmia.
• **12-Lead ECG:**
    ◦ **Initial test of choice.**
    ◦ May show **sinus bradycardia**, **sinus pauses**, or **SA exit block**.
    ◦ Crucially, the ECG is often **normal** if the patient is asymptomatic at the time of the test.
• **Ambulatory ECG Monitoring (Holter or Event Monitor):**
    ◦ **The most important diagnostic tool.**
    ◦ **Holter Monitor:** Continuous recording for 24-48 hours. Best for patients with daily or frequent symptoms.
    ◦ **Event Monitor / Mobile Cardiac Telemetry:** Worn for weeks to months. Patient activates recording during symptoms, or it auto-triggers on arrhythmia detection. Best for less frequent symptoms.
    ◦ **Implantable Loop Recorder (ILR):** A small device implanted subcutaneously for long-term monitoring (up to 3 years). Used for very infrequent but severe symptoms like unexplained syncope.
• **Exercise Stress Test:**
    ◦ Primarily used to evaluate for **chronotropic incompetence**.
    ◦ A positive test shows failure to achieve **>80% of the age-predicted maximal heart rate** (220 - age).
• **Labs:**
    ◦ To rule out extrinsic/reversible causes.
    ◦ **TSH** (thyroid function), **BMP** (electrolytes, especially potassium), **Cardiac Enzymes** (if ischemia is suspected).
• **Echocardiogram:**
    ◦ To assess for underlying structural heart disease, which can influence management.
sections.prognosis:
• With a **permanent pacemaker**, the prognosis regarding symptoms and survival is **excellent**.
• Long-term mortality is typically determined by the patient's underlying cardiac disease and other comorbidities, not the SSS itself.

sections.overview:
• First-Degree Atrioventricular (AV) Block is not a true "block" but rather a **delay in conduction** through the AV node or His-Purkinje system.
• On an electrocardiogram (EKG), this manifests as a **prolonged PR interval**.
• Every atrial impulse (P wave) is eventually conducted to the ventricles (QRS complex), resulting in a **1:1 P:QRS ratio**.
• It is the mildest form of AV block and is typically benign and asymptomatic.
sections.etiology:
• The pathophysiology involves a slowing of the electrical impulse as it travels from the atria to the ventricles, with the delay most commonly occurring within the **AV node**.
• **Physiologic (Increased Vagal Tone)**
    ◦ Well-conditioned athletes
    ◦ During sleep
    ◦ Enhanced vagal stimulation
• **Pharmacologic**
    ◦ **Beta-blockers** (e.g., metoprolol, carvedilol)
    ◦ **Non-dihydropyridine Calcium Channel Blockers** (e.g., verapamil, diltiazem)
    ◦ **Digoxin**
    ◦ Antiarrhythmics (e.g., amiodarone, procainamide)
• **Pathologic / Structural**
    ◦ **Ischemic Heart Disease**: Particularly an **inferior wall myocardial infarction** (MI) which can affect the AV nodal artery (a branch of the RCA).
    ◦ **Degenerative/Fibrotic Disease**: Age-related sclerosis of the cardiac conduction system (e.g., Lev's or Lengre's disease).
    ◦ **Infiltrative Diseases**: Sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, hemochromatosis.
    ◦ **Inflammatory/Infectious**: Myocarditis, **Lyme disease**, rheumatic fever, endocarditis.
    ◦ **Electrolyte Abnormalities**: Hyperkalemia.
    ◦ **Congenital** heart defects.
sections.epidemiology:
• Prevalence is approximately 0.5-2% in the healthy, young adult population.
• Incidence increases significantly with age, affecting up to 5-10% of individuals over 60.
• Commonly seen in endurance athletes due to high resting vagal tone.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Almost always an **incidental finding** on a routine EKG, pre-operative screening, or workup for an unrelated condition.
• The patient is typically unaware of the arrhythmia.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Electrocardiogram (EKG)**: The definitive diagnostic tool.
    ◦ Rhythm: Regular
    ◦ PR Interval: **Prolonged (>0.20 seconds or >5 small boxes) and constant.**
    ◦ P:QRS Ratio: **1:1** (every P wave is followed by a QRS complex).
    ◦ QRS Duration: Typically narrow (<0.12 seconds) unless a concomitant bundle branch block is present.
• **Laboratory Studies**: To investigate for reversible causes.
    ◦ Serum electrolytes (especially potassium).
    ◦ Thyroid function tests (TSH).
    ◦ Cardiac enzymes (troponin) if ischemia is suspected.
    ◦ Lyme serology if clinically indicated (e.g., endemic area, rash, arthralgias).
• **Further Evaluation (if indicated)**
    ◦ **Holter or Event Monitor**: If there is suspicion of intermittent, higher-grade AV block (e.g., in a patient with syncope or presyncope).
    ◦ **Echocardiogram**: To assess for underlying structural heart disease.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** in the absence of underlying structural heart disease.
• The prognosis is primarily dictated by the severity of any underlying cardiac condition, not by the first-degree AV block itself.

sections.overview:
• Second-Degree Atrioventricular (AV) Block, Mobitz Type I, also known as the **Wenckebach phenomenon**, is an intermittent block in AV conduction.
• It is characterized by a progressive, beat-to-beat lengthening of the PR interval until an atrial impulse (P wave) is completely blocked and fails to conduct to the ventricles, resulting in a "dropped" QRS complex.
• The cycle then resets with a shorter PR interval, and the pattern repeats.
• This block typically occurs at the level of the **AV node** and is generally considered a benign condition with a low risk of progressing to complete heart block.
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The block is due to a functional, decremental conduction property of the AV nodal tissue.
    ◦ With each successive atrial impulse, the AV node tissue becomes more fatigued, requiring a longer time to repolarize and conduct the next impulse (manifesting as a lengthening PR interval).
    ◦ Eventually, an impulse arrives during the node's refractory period and is not conducted at all.
    ◦ This "dropped beat" provides a pause, allowing the AV node to recover, and the cycle repeats.
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Physiologic (most common)**: Increased vagal tone, which slows AV nodal conduction. Frequently seen in young, healthy athletes and during sleep.
    ◦ **Pharmacologic**: Medications that slow AV nodal conduction.
        ▪ Beta-blockers (e.g., metoprolol, carvedilol)
        ▪ Non-dihydropyridine Calcium Channel Blockers (e.g., verapamil, diltiazem)
        ▪ Digoxin
        ▪ Amiodarone
    ◦ **Ischemic**: Myocardial ischemia or infarction, particularly an **inferior wall MI**, as the right coronary artery (RCA) supplies the AV node in most individuals.
    ◦ **Other Pathologic Causes**: Myocarditis, Lyme disease, post-cardiac surgery (especially valve repair/replacement), infiltrative diseases (amyloidosis, sarcoidosis), electrolyte abnormalities (hyperkalemia).
sections.epidemiology:
• More common than Mobitz Type II.
• Can be a normal variant in up to 10% of the healthy population, especially during sleep.
• Prevalence increases with age and in the presence of underlying structural heart disease.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The vast majority of patients are **asymptomatic**.
• The finding is most often incidental on an EKG, telemetry, or Holter monitor performed for other reasons.
• If symptomatic, the presentation is usually mild and related to the pauses from dropped beats.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Electrocardiogram (EKG) is the primary diagnostic tool.**
    ◦ **Hallmark Finding**: Progressive prolongation of the PR interval over consecutive beats.
    ◦ **Key Feature**: A P wave is eventually not followed by a QRS complex (a "non-conducted" or "dropped" beat).
    ◦ **Rhythm Pattern**: The P-P interval remains regular (atrial rate is constant). The R-R interval progressively shortens prior to the dropped beat.
    ◦ **QRS Complex**: Usually **narrow (<0.12s)** because the level of the block is at or above the AV node (supra-Hisian).
        ▪ A wide QRS may be present if there is a pre-existing bundle branch block.
• **Ambulatory Cardiac Monitoring (Holter or Event Monitor)**: Useful for quantifying the burden of the block, identifying triggers (e.g., only at night), and correlating symptoms with the arrhythmia.
• **Labs**
    ◦ Electrolytes (especially K+)
    ◦ Troponins if ischemia is suspected.
    ◦ Digoxin level if the patient is on the medication.
    ◦ Lyme titers if clinically suspected.
• **Exercise Stress Test**: Can help differentiate the level of the block.
    ◦ In Mobitz I (AV nodal block), conduction often *improves* with exercise due to increased sympathetic tone, and the block may resolve.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** in the absence of underlying structural heart disease.
• Considered a benign rhythm disturbance.
• The prognosis is largely determined by the associated underlying cardiac condition (e.g., post-MI) rather than the AV block itself.

sections.overview:
• **Second-Degree Atrioventricular (AV) Block, Mobitz Type II**, is a serious cardiac conduction abnormality characterized by **intermittent failure** of the atrial impulse to conduct to the ventricles.
    ◦ Unlike Mobitz Type I, this failure occurs **without any preceding, progressive delay** in AV conduction.
    ◦ It represents an **"all-or-none" phenomenon** of the His-Purkinje system.
• Mobitz II is considered an **unstable rhythm** with a high risk of progressing to **complete (third-degree) heart block** and **asystole**.
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The block is located **distal to the AV node (infranodal)**, typically within the Bundle of His or the bundle branches (His-Purkinje system).
    ◦ Because the pathology is below the AV node, the conduction that does occur happens with a normal, constant delay.
    ◦ The issue is a **sudden, unpredictable failure** of the impulse to pass through the diseased infranodal tissue, resulting in **"all-or-none" conduction** and a **constant PR interval** for all conducted beats.
• **Etiology**
    ◦ Mobitz II is almost always a result of underlying structural heart disease.
    ◦ **Ischemic Heart Disease**: Most common cause, especially an **anterior wall myocardial infarction (MI)**, which can damage the bundle branches supplied by the left anterior descending (LAD) artery.
    ◦ **Idiopathic Fibrosis**: Degenerative scarring of the conduction system (e.g., Lengre's or Lev's disease).
    ◦ **Structural Heart Disease**: Cardiomyopathy, valvular disease (especially aortic), congenital heart disease.
    ◦ **Infiltrative Diseases**: Sarcoidosis, amyloidosis.
    ◦ **Iatrogenic**: Following cardiac surgery (e.g., valve replacement) or catheter ablation near the conduction system.
    ◦ **Inflammatory**: Myocarditis, endocarditis.
sections.epidemiology:
• Less common than Mobitz I.
• Prevalence increases with age due to the association with degenerative and ischemic heart diseases.
• Rarely seen in young, healthy individuals or athletes, in contrast to Mobitz I.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation varies from an incidental EKG finding in an asymptomatic patient to a medical emergency.
    ◦ **Asymptomatic**: If dropped beats are infrequent and the underlying heart rate is adequate.
    ◦ **Symptomatic**: Due to transient or sustained **bradycardia** leading to cerebral hypoperfusion.
    ◦ **Hemodynamically Unstable**: Severe bradycardia, hypotension, altered mental status, signs of shock.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Electrocardiogram (EKG)**: The primary diagnostic tool.
    ◦ **Rhythm**: Atrial rate is regular (P waves march out); ventricular rhythm is irregular.
    ◦ **P waves**: Normal morphology and are consistently related to conducted QRS complexes.
    ◦ **PR Interval**: **Constant and unchanging** for all conducted beats before the dropped beat.
    ◦ **QRS Complex**: Often **wide (>0.12s)** because the pathology is in the bundle branches.
    ◦ **Dropped Beats**: A P wave will periodically appear without a subsequent QRS complex. The P-P interval remains constant across the dropped beat.
    ◦ **Conduction Ratio**: May be fixed (e.g., 3:2, 4:3 block) or variable. A 2:1 block can be difficult to distinguish from Mobitz I without a longer rhythm strip showing other patterns.
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **Cardiac Enzymes (Troponin)**: To rule out acute MI.
    ◦ **Electrolytes**: Rule out imbalances (K+, Mg++, Ca++).
    ◦ **TSH**: To rule out thyroid dysfunction.
• **Further Studies**
    ◦ **Ambulatory EKG (Holter Monitor)**: To diagnose intermittent Mobitz II in patients with unexplained syncope or dizziness.
    ◦ **Echocardiogram**: To assess for underlying structural heart disease.
    ◦ **Electrophysiology (EP) Study**: Can be used to confirm the location of the block (infranodal) if the diagnosis is uncertain.
sections.prognosis:
• **Without treatment**: The prognosis is **poor** due to the high likelihood of progression to **complete heart block** and **sudden cardiac death**.
• **With a permanent pacemaker**: The prognosis is **excellent**, and life expectancy is typically similar to that of the general population, dependent on any underlying cardiac comorbidities.

sections.overview:
• **Third-Degree Atrioventricular (AV) Block**, also known as **complete heart block**, is the most severe form of AV block.
    ◦ It is characterized by a **complete failure of electrical impulse conduction** from the atria to the ventricles.
    ◦ There is a **complete dissociation between atrial and ventricular activity**.
    ◦ The atria are typically paced by the sinoatrial (SA) node, while the ventricles are driven by an independent, subsidiary **escape pacemaker** located in the AV junction or the ventricles themselves.
    ◦ This results in a slow, unreliable ventricular rate, often leading to significant **hemodynamic compromise**.
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ In third-degree AV block, there is a complete anatomical or functional block within the heart's conduction system, and no supraventricular impulses are transmitted to the ventricles.
    ◦ **Atrial Depolarization**: The **SA node** functions normally, generating **P waves** at a regular intrinsic rate (e.g., 60-100 bpm).
    ◦ **Ventricular Depolarization**: Since atrial impulses are blocked, a subsidiary pacemaker below the level of the block must take over to pace the ventricles. This is called an "**escape rhythm**."
        ▪ **Junctional Escape**: If the block is at the level of the **AV node**, the pacemaker is in the AV junction. This produces a **narrow QRS complex** at a rate of 40-60 bpm and is generally more stable.
        ▪ **Ventricular Escape**: If the block is infranodal (below the AV node, e.g., Bundle of His or bundle branches), the pacemaker is in the ventricles. This produces a **wide QRS complex** at a slower, less reliable rate of 20-40 bpm. This is highly unstable and carries a poor prognosis without intervention.
• **Etiology**
    ◦ Causes can be categorized as congenital or acquired.
    ◦ **Ischemic/Infarction (Most common cause in adults)**
        ▪ **Inferior Wall MI**: Often causes a block at the **AV node** (supranodal), which is typically transient and resolves with reperfusion. The AV node is supplied by the right coronary artery (**RCA**) in most individuals.
        ▪ **Anterior Wall MI**: Causes an infranodal block due to extensive septal necrosis. This is often permanent and requires a **pacemaker**.
    ◦ **Degenerative/Fibrotic Disease**
        ▪ **Lengre-Lev disease**: Idiopathic progressive fibrosis and calcification of the cardiac conduction system, common in the elderly.
    ◦ **Infectious**
        ▪ **Lyme disease**: A classic cause of reversible heart block.
        ▪ Endocarditis (especially with aortic valve abscess), Chagas disease, rheumatic fever.
    ◦ **Iatrogenic**
        ▪ **Medications**: Beta-blockers, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem), digoxin, amiodarone, adenosine.
        ▪ **Procedures**: Post-cardiac surgery (especially valve replacement), catheter ablation, transcatheter aortic valve replacement (**TAVR**).
    ◦ **Infiltrative/Inflammatory Diseases**
        ▪ Sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, hemochromatosis.
    ◦ **Congenital**
        ▪ Most commonly associated with maternal systemic lupus erythematosus (**SLE**) due to placental transfer of **anti-Ro/SSA antibodies**.
    ◦ **Other**
        ▪ Severe **hyperkalemia**, hypothyroidism, trauma.
sections.epidemiology:
• Incidence increases significantly with age, primarily due to the rise in degenerative fibrotic disease and coronary artery disease.
• The prevalence is estimated at 0.02% to 0.04% in the general population.
• More common in patients with pre-existing structural heart disease.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The clinical presentation depends entirely on the ventricular escape rate and the patient's underlying cardiac function.
• Presentation can range from an incidental finding in an asymptomatic patient to **cardiogenic shock** or **sudden cardiac death**.
• **Hemodynamically Stable**: May be asymptomatic or have mild symptoms like fatigue if the junctional escape rhythm is adequate (e.g., 50 bpm).
• **Hemodynamically Unstable**: Presents with severe symptoms due to low cardiac output from profound **bradycardia** (e.g., ventricular escape rate of 30 bpm). This is a medical emergency.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Electrocardiogram (ECG)**: The primary diagnostic tool.
    ◦ **Hallmark Finding**: **Complete AV dissociation**. **P waves** and **QRS complexes** have no relationship with each other.
    ◦ **Rates**: Atrial rate (**P-P interval**) is faster than the ventricular rate (**R-R interval**).
    ◦ **Rhythm**: Both P waves and QRS complexes are regular ("march out") but independent of one another.
    ◦ **PR Interval**: Completely variable.
    ◦ **QRS Morphology**:
        ▪ **Narrow QRS (<120 ms)**: Indicates a **junctional escape rhythm** (block is at the AV node). Rate: 40-60 bpm.
        ▪ **Wide QRS (≥120 ms)**: Indicates a **ventricular escape rhythm** (block is infranodal). Rate: 20-40 bpm.
• **Laboratory Studies**:
    ◦ **Cardiac Enzymes (Troponin)**: To rule out acute **MI**.
    ◦ **Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP)**: To assess for electrolyte abnormalities (especially **hyperkalemia**) and renal function.
    ◦ **Drug Levels**: Digoxin level, if applicable.
    ◦ **Lyme Titer**: If clinical suspicion is high (e.g., patient from an endemic area).
    ◦ **TSH**: To rule out severe hypothyroidism.
• **Imaging**:
    ◦ **Echocardiogram**: To evaluate for underlying structural heart disease, assess left ventricular function, and identify potential causes like valvular abscess.
sections.prognosis:
• **Untreated**: The prognosis is poor, with a high risk of **syncope**, **asystole**, and **sudden death**, especially with an infranodal (**wide QRS**) escape rhythm.
• **Treated**: With the implantation of a **permanent pacemaker**, the prognosis is generally excellent. The patient's long-term survival is then determined by their underlying comorbidities (e.g., severity of CAD, LV dysfunction).

sections.overview:
• Peripheral Arterial Disease (PAD) is a chronic occlusive disease of the arteries in the extremities (most commonly the lower extremities), caused by **atherosclerosis**.
    ◦ This stenosis or occlusion leads to a reduction in blood flow (**ischemia**), causing symptoms primarily during exertion when oxygen demand exceeds supply.
    ◦ PAD is a significant marker for systemic **atherosclerosis** and is associated with a high risk of **myocardial infarction (MI)**, **stroke**, and **cardiovascular death**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ Over 95% of cases are due to **atherosclerosis**.
    ◦ Less common causes include vasculitis, thrombosis/embolism, fibromuscular dysplasia, and radiation-induced arterial damage.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ Endothelial injury occurs in an artery (e.g., from smoking, HTN).
    ◦ Lipoproteins (LDL) accumulate in the vessel wall (tunica intima).
    ◦ Monocytes are recruited, differentiate into macrophages, and engulf the lipids, forming **foam cells**.
    ◦ These cells, along with smooth muscle cell proliferation, create a fibro-fatty plaque called an **atheroma**.
    ◦ The plaque grows, progressively narrowing the arterial lumen (**stenosis**).
    ◦ When stenosis becomes significant (>50-70%), blood flow is insufficient to meet the metabolic demands of muscles during exercise, causing ischemic pain (**claudication**).
    ◦ Severe stenosis or acute plaque rupture with thrombosis can lead to inadequate blood flow even at rest, causing **critical limb ischemia (CLI)**.
• **Most Common Location**
    ◦ The **superficial femoral artery (SFA)** within the adductor canal (Hunter's canal) is the most common site of stenosis in the lower extremities.
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects approximately 8-12 million people in the U.S.
• Prevalence increases sharply with age:
    ◦ <5% in individuals <50 years, but up to 20% in those >75 years.
• Slightly higher prevalence in men.
• Higher prevalence and worse outcomes in African American populations.
• Crucially, up to 50% of patients with PAD are **asymptomatic**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation exists on a spectrum from asymptomatic to limb-threatening ischemia.
    ◦ **Asymptomatic**: Discovered incidentally on physical exam (e.g., absent pulses) or via screening with an Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI).
    ◦ **Intermittent Claudication**: The classic presentation.
    ◦ **Atypical Leg Pain**: Exertional leg pain that is not typical cramping (e.g., weakness, tiredness). More common than classic claudication.
    ◦ **Critical Limb Ischemia (CLI)**: A chronic state of severe ischemia characterized by ischemic rest pain, non-healing ulcers, or gangrene.
    ◦ **Acute Limb Ischemia (ALI)**: A vascular emergency due to a sudden decrease in limb perfusion, often from an embolus or in-situ thrombosis.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI)**
    ◦ **Best initial test for diagnosis**.
    ◦ Calculation: Ratio of the highest systolic blood pressure at the ankle (dorsalis pedis or posterior tibial) to the highest systolic blood pressure in the arm (brachial).
    ◦ **Interpretation**:
        ▪ > 1.4: Non-compressible, calcified vessels (common in severe DM, CKD). Inconclusive.
        ▪ 0.91 - 1.30: **Normal**.
        ▪ ≤ 0.90: **Diagnostic of PAD**.
        ▪ 0.70 - 0.90: Mild PAD.
        ▪ 0.41 - 0.69: Moderate PAD.
        ▪ ≤ 0.40: **Severe PAD / Critical Limb Ischemia**.
• **Arterial Duplex Ultrasound**
    ◦ First-line imaging modality to localize the lesion and assess stenosis severity.
    ◦ Non-invasive.
• **CT Angiography (CTA) / MR Angiography (MRA)**
    ◦ Provide detailed anatomical mapping of the arterial system.
    ◦ Excellent for pre-operative planning for revascularization.
• **Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA)**
    ◦ **Gold Standard** for vessel imaging.
    ◦ Invasive (catheter-based) procedure that provides the most detailed images.
    ◦ Typically reserved for when an intervention (angioplasty, stenting) is planned.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is dictated more by the patient's overall cardiovascular health than by the limb itself.
• The 5-year mortality rate for patients with PAD is approximately 25-30%.
• For patients with CLI, the 1-year prognosis is poor:
    ◦ ~25% mortality and ~30% major amputation.
• Continued smoking dramatically worsens both limb and life expectancy.

sections.overview:
• **Peripheral Venous Disease (PVD)**, more accurately termed **Chronic Venous Insufficiency (CVI)**, is a spectrum of conditions caused by impaired venous return from the lower extremities.
    ◦ This leads to **venous hypertension**, most commonly in the legs.
    ◦ It ranges in severity from asymptomatic telangiectasias and varicose veins to debilitating edema, skin changes, and venous stasis ulcers.
• It is a chronic, progressive condition distinct from Peripheral Arterial Disease (PAD).
• The **CEAP classification** system (Clinical, Etiologic, Anatomic, Pathophysiologic) is used to standardize its description and severity.
sections.etiology:
• The core pathophysiologic mechanism is **sustained venous hypertension**.
    ◦ This is caused by one or both of the following:
        ▪ **Valvular Incompetence**: Venous valves fail to coapt, allowing for retrograde blood flow (**reflux**).
            ◦ **Primary**: Due to inherent weakness in the vein wall, leading to dilation and valve dysfunction.
            ◦ **Secondary**: Damage to valves from a prior **Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT)**, a condition known as **post-thrombotic syndrome**.
        ▪ **Venous Outflow Obstruction**: Blockage of venous flow, often from a DVT, tumor, or extrinsic compression, which increases distal venous pressure.
• **Pathophysiologic Cascade**: **Venous Hypertension** → Capillary pressure increases → Fluid, proteins (fibrinogen), and RBCs leak into the interstitial space
    ◦ **Edema**: From fluid leakage.
    ◦ **Hyperpigmentation**: Extravasated RBCs break down, and the iron pigment (**hemosiderin**) is deposited in the dermis, causing a brawny, reddish-brown discoloration.
    ◦ **Inflammation & Fibrosis**: Trapped proteins and inflammatory cells lead to chronic inflammation, stasis dermatitis, and eventually **lipodermatosclerosis** (subcutaneous fat is replaced by fibrous tissue).
    ◦ **Ulceration**: Poor tissue oxygenation, impaired healing, and minor trauma lead to the formation of **venous stasis ulcers**.
sections.epidemiology:
• Extremely common, affecting up to 40% of the US population.
• **Varicose veins** are present in 15-25% of adults.
• **Venous ulcers** affect approximately 1% of the adult population.
• Prevalence increases with age.
• More common in women (likely due to hormonal effects and pregnancy).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A typical patient is a middle-aged or older adult, often female, who presents with a chief complaint of **'heavy,' aching, or swollen legs**.
    ◦ The symptoms are characteristically **worse at the end of the day** or after prolonged periods of standing and are **relieved by leg elevation**.
    ◦ They may notice cosmetic changes like spider veins or bulging **varicose veins**, or more advanced signs like skin discoloration and non-healing wounds around the ankle.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Venous Duplex Ultrasound**: **Test of choice**.
    ◦ Non-invasive and highly effective.
    ◦ Identifies the location and severity of **venous reflux** (defined as retrograde flow >0.5 seconds).
    ◦ Can also rule out venous obstruction (e.g., DVT).
• **Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI)**:
    ◦ Essential to perform in any patient with a lower extremity ulcer or signs of advanced PVD.
    ◦ **Purpose**: To rule out coexisting **Peripheral Arterial Disease (PAD)**.
    ◦ **Critical Safety Step**: Compression therapy is the cornerstone of CVI treatment but is **contraindicated in patients with severe PAD (ABI < 0.5)** and used with caution in those with moderate PAD (ABI 0.5-0.9).
• **Trendelenburg Test**: A historical physical exam maneuver to assess for valvular incompetence, largely replaced by duplex ultrasound.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis for life is excellent.
• The condition is chronic and progressive.
• Quality of life can be significantly impacted by pain, edema, and ulceration.
• With consistent management (especially compression), symptoms can be well-controlled and ulcer recurrence can be minimized.
    ◦ Ulcer recurrence rates are >50% without proper compression therapy.

sections.overview:
• **Superficial Venous Thrombosis (SVT)**, also known as **superficial thrombophlebitis**, is a common inflammatory-thrombotic disorder characterized by thrombus formation in a superficial vein, most often in the lower extremities.
• It is distinct from **Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT)**, but they can coexist, and SVT can propagate into the deep venous system.
• The **great saphenous vein** is the most commonly affected vessel.
• While often considered a benign, self-limiting condition, it can cause significant discomfort and has the potential for serious complications, including **DVT** and **Pulmonary Embolism (PE)**.
sections.etiology:
• The pathophysiology of SVT is explained by **Virchow's Triad**:
    ◦ **Venous Stasis**
        ▪ Immobility or prolonged sitting/standing.
        ▪ Venous insufficiency and **varicose veins** (most common predisposing factor).
        ▪ Obesity.
        ▪ Pregnancy.
    ◦ **Endothelial Injury**
        ▪ **Direct trauma** to a vein.
        ▪ **Iatrogenic causes**, such as intravenous (IV) catheters, PICC lines, or infusions of irritating substances (e.g., chemotherapy, potassium chloride).
            ▪ This is the leading cause of upper extremity SVT.
        ▪ Infection (**septic phlebitis**).
    ◦ **Hypercoagulable State**
        ▪ **Malignancy**: Especially pancreatic, lung, and gastrointestinal cancers.
            ▪ Migratory thrombophlebitis is known as **Trousseau's Syndrome**.
        ▪ **Inherited thrombophilias**: Factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation, Protein C/S deficiency.
        ▪ **Acquired states**: Oral contraceptive use (OCPs), hormone replacement therapy (HRT), pregnancy/postpartum period, autoimmune diseases (e.g., Behet's disease, Buerger's disease).
sections.epidemiology:
• More common than **DVT**.
• Incidence is estimated at 3-11% of the general population.
• Slightly more common in women than men.
• Incidence increases with age, particularly after age 60.
• Approximately 5-25% of patients with SVT have a concurrent **DVT**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with a focal area of **pain**, **redness**, and **tenderness** along the course of a superficial vein, often in the leg.
• The onset is usually acute.
• The patient may report a "**lump**" or "**knot**" under the skin.
• Systemic symptoms like high fever or chills are uncommon unless it has progressed to **septic phlebitis**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primarily a clinical diagnosis**; history and physical exam are often sufficient.
• **Venous Duplex Ultrasound**
    ◦ **Test of choice** and gold standard.
    ◦ **Primary Purpose**: To rule out concurrent **DVT**, which is the most critical step in management.
    ◦ **Indications for Ultrasound**:
        ▪ Lower extremity SVT >5 cm in length.
        ▪ Involvement of the **great saphenous vein (GSV)** or **small saphenous vein (SSV)**.
        ▪ Proximity to the **saphenofemoral junction (SFJ)** or **saphenopopliteal junction (SPJ)**.
        ▪ Significant limb swelling or pain suggesting **DVT**.
        ▪ Recurrent SVT.
    ◦ **Ultrasound Findings**: A non-compressible superficial vein containing echogenic material (thrombus).
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **D-Dimer**: Has low specificity and limited utility.
        ▪ A negative result can help rule out **DVT** in low-risk patients, but it is often elevated in isolated SVT, making it unhelpful.
    ◦ **Hypercoagulability Workup**: Not routinely performed.
        ▪ Consider in patients with unprovoked, extensive, or recurrent SVT, or those with a strong personal or family history of VTE.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis for isolated, low-risk SVT is excellent with symptomatic treatment.
• The prognosis is dependent on the presence of underlying risk factors (e.g., **malignancy**) and complications (e.g., development of **DVT**/**PE**).
• High-risk SVT treated appropriately with anticoagulation also has a good prognosis with a significantly reduced risk of **VTE**.

sections.overview: • Deep Venous Thrombosis (DVT) is the formation of a blood clot (thrombus) within a deep vein, most commonly in the lower extremities (e.g., femoral, popliteal, iliac veins). • It is a major component of venous thromboembolism (VTE). • The primary danger of DVT is that the clot can dislodge, travel to the lungs, and cause a life-threatening pulmonary embolism (PE).
sections.etiology: • The formation of a DVT is classically explained by Virchow's Triad, which describes the three broad categories of factors that contribute to thrombosis: ◦ Venous Stasis: Slowing or stagnation of blood flow in the veins. ▪ Causes: Immobilization (post-surgery, long-distance travel, paralysis), obesity, congestive heart failure (CHF), venous insufficiency. ◦ Hypercoagulability (Thrombophilia): An imbalance in clotting factors that favors thrombus formation. ▪ Acquired Causes: Malignancy (most common acquired), pregnancy, estrogen therapy (oral contraceptives, HRT), smoking, nephrotic syndrome, antiphospholipid syndrome. ▪ Inherited Causes: Factor V Leiden (most common inherited), Prothrombin gene mutation, Protein C & S deficiency, Antithrombin deficiency. ◦ Endothelial Injury: Damage to the inner lining (endothelium) of the blood vessel. ▪ Causes: Trauma, surgery (especially orthopedic), indwelling venous catheters (PICC lines), chemotherapy, superficial vein thrombosis. • Pathophysiology: The interplay of these factors leads to platelet aggregation and activation of the coagulation cascade, resulting in the formation of a fibrin-rich thrombus that can obstruct venous outflow.
sections.epidemiology: • Incidence: Affects approximately 1-2 per 1,000 individuals annually. • Age: Incidence increases sharply with age. • Location: Lower extremity DVTs are most common. ◦ Proximal DVT: (Popliteal, femoral, or iliac veins) - Higher risk of embolization to PE. ◦ Distal DVT: (Calf veins) - Lower risk of PE, but can propagate proximally.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • The "classic" presentation is a patient with risk factors who develops unilateral extremity signs and symptoms over a period of hours to days. • However, up to 50% of patients with DVT can be asymptomatic. The clot is discovered incidentally or after a PE has already occurred.
sections.diagnostics: • The diagnostic approach is guided by clinical pre-test probability. ◦ Most often determined by the Wells' Score.
sections.prognosis:
• With timely and appropriate treatment, the prognosis for an isolated DVT is generally good.
• Mortality is primarily associated with the development of a PE or the patient's underlying condition (e.g., malignancy).
• Recurrence risk is significant, especially for unprovoked DVT (~30% at 5 years).

sections.overview:
• Chronic Arterial Occlusive Disease, most commonly referred to as **Peripheral Artery Disease (PAD)**, is a progressive circulatory condition characterized by the **stenosis** or **occlusion** of arteries, leading to reduced blood flow (**ischemia**) to the limbs
• It is primarily caused by **atherosclerosis** and is a manifestation of systemic atherosclerotic disease
• While it can affect the upper extremities, renal, or mesenteric arteries, it most frequently involves the lower extremities
• The clinical spectrum ranges from asymptomatic disease to **intermittent claudication**, and finally to **critical limb ischemia (CLI)**, which is a limb-threatening condition
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Atherosclerosis (>95% of cases)**: The primary cause. It is the same disease process that leads to coronary artery disease (CAD) and cerebrovascular disease (CVD)
    ◦ **Less Common Causes**
        ▪ **Thromboangiitis Obliterans (Buerger's Disease)**
        ▪ **Vasculitis** (e.g., Takayasu arteritis, Giant Cell Arteritis)
        ▪ **Fibromuscular Dysplasia**
        ▪ Trauma
        ▪ Radiation-induced arteritis
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Endothelial Injury**: Chronic injury from risk factors (smoking, HTN, DM) damages the arterial intima
    ◦ **Plaque Formation**: Low-density lipoproteins (LDLs) accumulate in the damaged intima and become oxidized. Macrophages engulf these lipids, forming "foam cells." This initiates an inflammatory cascade, leading to the formation of a fibrous plaque (**atheroma**)
    ◦ **Stenosis**: The **atheroma** grows, progressively narrowing the arterial lumen. This increases resistance and reduces downstream blood flow
    ◦ **Supply-Demand Mismatch**: During exertion (e.g., walking), metabolic demand of the muscles increases. The stenosed artery cannot deliver adequate oxygenated blood, resulting in anaerobic metabolism, lactic acid buildup, and the characteristic pain of **claudication**
    ◦ **Critical Ischemia**: As the **stenosis** worsens, blood flow becomes insufficient even at rest, leading to **rest pain**, tissue **ulceration**, and **gangrene**
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects approximately 8-12 million people in the United States
• Prevalence increases significantly with age: affects ~20% of individuals >65 years old
• Slight male predominance
• Higher prevalence in African American populations
• **Crucially, PAD is a strong marker for systemic atherosclerosis**
    ◦ Patients with PAD have a 3-4 fold increased risk of **myocardial infarction (MI)** and **stroke**
    ◦ The leading cause of death in patients with PAD is cardiovascular disease, not limb-related complications
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation depends on the severity of the disease
    ◦ **Asymptomatic (~20-50%)**: Discovered incidentally on physical exam (e.g., absent pulses) or via screening with an Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI)
    ◦ **Atypical Leg Pain (~40-50%)**: Leg discomfort with exertion that does not consistently resolve with rest or is not classically crampy. The most common presentation
    ◦ **Intermittent Claudication (~10-35%)**: The "classic" presentation
    ◦ **Critical Limb Ischemia (CLI) (~1-2%)**: The most severe form, defined by **rest pain**, **non-healing ulcers**, or **gangrene**
    ◦ **Acute Limb Ischemia (ALI)**: A sudden, severe decrease in limb perfusion, often from thrombosis of a pre-existing plaque or an embolus. Presents with the **"6 P's"**
sections.diagnostics:
• **Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI)**
    ◦ **Best initial test** for diagnosis and screening
    ◦ **Procedure**: Ratio of the highest systolic blood pressure at the ankle (dorsalis pedis or posterior tibial) to the highest systolic blood pressure in the arm (brachial)
    ◦ **Interpretation**
        ▪ **> 1.3**: Non-compressible/calcified vessels (common in DM, CKD). Inaccurate reading; requires further testing
        ▪ **0.91 - 1.30**: Normal
        ▪ **0.70 - 0.90**: Mild PAD
        ▪ **0.41 - 0.69**: Moderate PAD
        ▪ **≤ 0.40**: Severe PAD (correlates with **CLI**)
• **Imaging (used for localization and pre-procedural planning)**
    ◦ **Arterial Duplex Ultrasound**: First-line imaging modality. Non-invasive, visualizes the vessel, and measures flow velocity to identify **stenosis**
    ◦ **CT Angiography (CTA) / MR Angiography (MRA)**: Provide detailed anatomical mapping of the arterial tree. Excellent for planning **revascularization**
    ◦ **Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA)**
        ▪ **Gold Standard**
        ▪ Invasive catheter-based procedure that provides the most detailed images
        ▪ Typically reserved for when an intervention (angioplasty/stenting) is planned simultaneously
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is more related to cardiovascular health than to limb health
• **With claudication**: 5-year mortality rate is 15-30%. The risk of progressing to **CLI** is ~5-10%
• **With CLI**: Prognosis is poor
    ◦ 1-year mortality is ~25%
    ◦ >25% will require major **amputation** within 1 year
• An ABI <0.9 is associated with a two-fold increase in 10-year total mortality

sections.overview:
• **Acute Arterial Occlusive Disease**, also known as **Acute Limb Ischemia (ALI)**, is a vascular emergency characterized by the sudden decrease in arterial blood flow to a limb.
• This abrupt cessation of perfusion threatens limb viability and requires immediate diagnosis and intervention.
• The classic presentation is described by the **"6 P's"**.
• The guiding principle of management is "time is tissue," as irreversible nerve and muscle damage can occur within 4-6 hours of ischemia.
sections.etiology:
• The underlying cause is a sudden blockage of an artery, primarily through two main mechanisms:
    ◦ **Arterial Embolism** (~80% of cases)
        ▪ A thrombus or other material travels from a proximal source and lodges in a more distal, smaller-caliber artery.
        ▪ **Pathophysiology**: The embolus typically lodges at an arterial bifurcation where the vessel narrows (e.g., common femoral bifurcation, popliteal trifurcation). The limb is often otherwise healthy with no pre-existing collateral circulation, leading to a very abrupt and severe presentation.
        ▪ **Common Sources**:
            • **Cardiac (Most Common)**: **Atrial fibrillation** (stasis in the left atrial appendage), recent **myocardial infarction** (left ventricular mural thrombus), ventricular aneurysm, infective endocarditis, or prosthetic heart valves.
            • **Aortic**: Atheroemboli from aortic plaques or thrombus from an aortic aneurysm.
    ◦ **In Situ Thrombosis** (~20% of cases)
        ▪ A blood clot forms directly within an artery at a site of pre-existing pathology.
        ▪ **Pathophysiology**: This is an "acute-on-chronic" event. A pre-existing atherosclerotic plaque in a patient with **Peripheral Artery Disease (PAD)** ruptures or becomes stenotic enough to cause thrombosis. Because of the chronic underlying disease, some collateral circulation may have developed, sometimes making the initial symptoms less severe than an embolic event.
        ▪ **Common Locations**: Superficial femoral artery (SFA), popliteal artery.
    ◦ **Other Less Common Causes**:
        ▪ **Trauma**: Direct arterial injury or dissection.
        ▪ **Aortic Dissection**: The dissection flap can occlude a branch vessel (e.g., iliac or femoral artery).
        ▪ **Iatrogenic**: Complication of arterial catheterization (e.g., cardiac cath).
        ▪ **Hypercoagulable States**.
sections.epidemiology:
• Incidence: Approximately 1.5 cases per 10,000 person-years.
• Strongly associated with increasing age, with the mean age of presentation being 65-75 years.
• Associated with high morbidity and mortality due to the severity of the underlying systemic cardiovascular disease.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is typically dramatic. A patient, often with known cardiovascular risk factors, presents with the sudden onset of a severely **painful, cold, and numb limb**.
• The distinction between an embolic and thrombotic cause is crucial:
    ◦ **Embolic**:
        ▪ Sudden, severe symptoms in a limb with no prior history of claudication.
        ▪ Pulses in the contralateral limb are often normal.
        ▪ A known embolic source (like **A-fib**) is common.
    ◦ **Thrombotic**:
        ▪ May have a more stuttering onset.
        ▪ The patient often has a known history of **PAD** with **claudication**.
        ▪ Physical exam may show signs of chronic ischemia (hair loss, shiny skin, thickened nails) and diminished pulses in the contralateral limb.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Bedside Tests**
    ◦ **Handheld Arterial Doppler**: The essential first step to confirm the absence of blood flow when pulses are not palpable.
    ◦ **Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI)**: Often severely reduced (<0.40) or unobtainable if no Doppler signal is present.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **CT Angiography (CTA)**: **GOLD STANDARD**. It is fast, widely available, and accurately localizes the occlusion, defines the anatomy, and helps plan the intervention (endovascular vs. surgical).
    ◦ **Arterial Duplex Ultrasound**: Non-invasive and useful for identifying the occlusion, but it is operator-dependent and can be time-consuming. A good alternative if CTA is contraindicated (e.g., severe renal failure, contrast allergy).
    ◦ **Conventional Arteriography**: Previously the gold standard, now primarily used during endovascular intervention.
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **CBC, BMP/Chem-7**: Assess renal function (for contrast) and electrolytes (risk of hyperkalemia on reperfusion).
    ◦ **Coagulation Panel (PT/INR, aPTT)**: Baseline before starting heparin.
    ◦ **Creatine Kinase (CK) & Myoglobin**: To assess for **rhabdomyolysis** from muscle ischemia.
    ◦ **Lactate**: A marker of severe tissue ischemia.
    ◦ **Type and Screen**: In case surgery is required.
• **Other**
    ◦ **ECG**: Look for **atrial fibrillation** or evidence of acute **MI**.
    ◦ **Echocardiogram**: Can be done later to identify a cardiac source of emboli.
sections.prognosis:
• Highly time-dependent. Muscle and nerve are very sensitive to ischemia.
• **Viability is threatened at 4-6 hours.**
• **Irreversible damage is likely after 6 hours.**
• **Limb Salvage Rate**: ~85-95% with timely and successful revascularization.
• **Mortality**: Remains high (15-25% at 30 days) primarily due to the patient's underlying cardiac comorbidities.

sections.overview:
• **Raynaud's Disease** is an idiopathic, primary **vasospastic** disorder characterized by an exaggerated vascular response to cold temperature or emotional stress.
• It is distinct from **Raynaud's Phenomenon**, which is a secondary condition caused by an underlying disease or external factor.
• Both conditions manifest as sharply demarcated, episodic color changes of the digits (fingers and toes), and less commonly the nose, ears, or nipples.
• The classic presentation is a **triphasic color change**:
    ◦ **Pallor** (white), followed by
    ◦ **Cyanosis** (blue), and finally
    ◦ **Rubor** (red) upon rewarming.
sections.etiology:
• **Primary Raynaud's (Disease)**
    ◦ **Etiology**: **Idiopathic**. Considered a functional disorder without an underlying pathological cause. It is an exaggeration of normal vasospastic response.
    ◦ **Pathophysiology**
        ▪ **Hyperactivity of Sympathetic Nerves**: Exaggerated **alpha-2 adrenergic receptor** response in digital cutaneous blood vessels leads to profound vasoconstriction.
        ▪ **Endothelial Dysfunction**: A potential imbalance between vasodilators (e.g., nitric oxide) and vasoconstrictors (e.g., endothelin-1) may contribute.
        ▪ There is **no structural abnormality** of the blood vessels themselves.
• **Secondary Raynaud's (Phenomenon)**
    ◦ **Etiology**: Associated with an underlying condition.
        ▪ **Connective Tissue Diseases**: The most common cause. **Scleroderma (Systemic Sclerosis)** is the strongest association (>90% of patients with scleroderma have Raynaud's). Others include Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (**SLE**), **Sjögren's syndrome**, **Dermatomyositis/Polymyositis**, and **Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)**.
        ▪ **Occupational**: Vibration-induced (**vibration white finger**) from using tools like jackhammers or chainsaws.
        ▪ **Drugs**: **Beta-blockers**, amphetamines, sympathomimetics (decongestants), ergotamines, certain chemotherapy agents (**bleomycin**, **cisplatin**).
        ▪ **Arterial Occlusive Disease**: Atherosclerosis, **Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger's disease)**.
        ▪ **Other**: Hypothyroidism, cryoglobulinemia, thoracic outlet syndrome.
    ◦ **Pathophysiology**: Vasospasm is superimposed on a **structural vessel abnormality**, leading to a more severe and often irreversible reduction in blood flow.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects approximately 3-5% of the general population.
• **Primary Raynaud's Disease**
    ◦ Much more common than secondary.
    ◦ **Female-to-Male Ratio**: 5:1.
    ◦ **Typical Onset**: Age 15-30.
• **Secondary Raynaud's Phenomenon**
    ◦ Less common.
    ◦ **Typical Onset**: Age > 40.
    ◦ Onset at an older age is a **red flag** for an underlying disorder.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with a history of their fingers or toes changing color when exposed to cold or during periods of high stress.
• The attacks are **episodic** and resolve with rewarming.
• Patients with **primary disease** often have a long history of mild, symmetric symptoms.
• A new onset of **severe, asymmetric, or progressive symptoms**, especially in a patient over 40, should raise suspicion for a **secondary cause**.
sections.diagnostics:
• The primary goal is to distinguish between **primary** and **secondary** Raynaud's.
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Diagnosis is largely based on a characteristic history and triggered episodes.
• **Nailfold Capillaroscopy**
    ◦ **Purpose**: The single most valuable test to differentiate primary from secondary Raynaud's.
    ◦ **Procedure**: A drop of oil is placed on the nailfold and examined under magnification (dermatoscope or microscope).
    ◦ **Normal (Primary)**: Uniform, hairpin-shaped capillary loops arranged in parallel rows.
    ◦ **Abnormal (Secondary)**: Suggests underlying connective tissue disease. Findings include **giant (dilated) capillary loops**, **capillary hemorrhage**, **avascular areas**, and **architectural disorganization**.
• **Laboratory Studies** (to rule out secondary causes)
    ◦ **Antinuclear Antibody (ANA)**
        ▪ Best initial screening test for autoimmune disease.
        ▪ High sensitivity but low specificity.
        ▪ A negative ANA makes an underlying connective tissue disease highly unlikely.
    ◦ **Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) / C-Reactive Protein (CRP)**
        ▪ Non-specific markers of inflammation.
    ◦ **Specific Autoantibodies** (if ANA is positive)
        ▪ **Anti-Scl-70** (topoisomerase I): Diffuse **Scleroderma**
        ▪ **Anti-centromere**: Limited **Scleroderma (CREST syndrome)**
        ▪ **Anti-dsDNA**, **Anti-Smith**: **SLE**
sections.prognosis:
• **Primary Raynaud's Disease**: **Excellent**. It is a benign condition that does not progress to tissue damage and does not affect life expectancy.
• **Secondary Raynaud's Phenomenon**: **Variable**. The prognosis is determined entirely by the underlying disease. It can be associated with significant morbidity due to **tissue ischemia** and complications.

sections.overview:
• Progressive medical condition characterized by impaired venous return from the lower extremities, leading to **venous hypertension**.
• Results from **venous valvular incompetence**, **venous obstruction**, or a combination of both.
• Sustained increase in venous pressure causes a cascade of pathologic changes, including **edema**, skin changes, and eventual **ulceration**.
sections.etiology:
• The core pathophysiologic mechanism is **ambulatory venous hypertension**.
• **Valvular Incompetence**:
    ◦ **Primary**: Idiopathic weakness of the vein walls and valve leaflets, leading to dilation and failure of the valves to coapt (close properly).
    ◦ **Secondary**: Damage to valves from a prior **deep vein thrombosis (DVT)**, a condition known as **post-thrombotic syndrome**.
• **Venous Obstruction**:
    ◦ Less common, but can result from scarring after a **DVT**, or extrinsic compression from a tumor or other mass.
• **Calf Muscle Pump Failure**:
    ◦ Immobility or paralysis prevents the calf muscles from effectively squeezing deep veins and pumping blood towards the heart.
• **Pathophysiologic Cascade**:
    ◦ Valvular Incompetence → Retrograde blood flow (**reflux**) → Increased venous pressure (**Venous Hypertension**) → Transmission of high pressure to capillaries → Capillary leakage of fluid, proteins, and RBCs into the interstitium.
        ▪ **Fluid Leakage** → **Edema**
        ▪ **RBC Leakage** → **Hemosiderin deposition** → **Hyperpigmentation** (brawny discoloration)
        ▪ **Protein & Fibrinogen Leakage** → Fibrin cuff formation → Impaired O2/nutrient delivery → **Lipodermatosclerosis** & **Ulceration**
        ▪ **Chronic Inflammation** → **Stasis Dermatitis**
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Very common, affecting up to 40% of the U.S. population.
• **Age**: Prevalence increases significantly with age.
• **Sex**: More common in females (likely due to hormonal effects and pregnancy).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Classic patient presentation is an individual with a history of prolonged standing.
• Complains of a progressive, dull, aching, or "heavy" sensation in the legs.
• Symptoms are typically worse at the end of the day or after periods of standing.
• Symptoms are **relieved by leg elevation**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Venous Duplex Ultrasound**:
    ◦ **Test of choice**.
    ◦ Non-invasive, combines imaging of the veins with Doppler flow measurement.
    ◦ **Identifies reflux**: Diagnostic criteria is retrograde flow lasting >0.5 seconds in superficial veins or >1.0 second in deep veins (e.g., femoral, popliteal).
    ◦ Can also rule out obstruction (e.g., **DVT**).
• **Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI)**:
    ◦ Recommended before initiating compression therapy to rule out significant coexisting **Peripheral Artery Disease (PAD)**.
    ◦ High-compression therapy (30-40 mmHg) is contraindicated with an **ABI < 0.5** and should be used with caution for **ABI 0.5-0.8**.
sections.prognosis:
• The condition is chronic and progressive.
• Prognosis for life is excellent, but morbidity and impact on quality of life can be substantial.
• Venous ulcers have a high recurrence rate (>50%) if underlying venous hypertension is not managed with consistent compression therapy.

sections.overview:
• **Varicose veins** are **dilated**, **tortuous**, **elongated superficial veins**, most commonly found in the lower extremities.
• They result from **venous hypertension** caused by **valvular incompetence** and **venous reflux**.
• While often a cosmetic concern, they can cause significant symptoms and lead to complications like **chronic venous insufficiency (CVI)**.
• The **great saphenous vein (GSV)** and its tributaries are most commonly affected.
sections.etiology:
• The core pathophysiologic mechanism is **venous valvular incompetence**.
    ◦ **Valve Failure**: Bicuspid valves within the veins normally prevent the retrograde flow of blood. When these valves fail or become incompetent, blood flows backward (**reflux**), particularly when the patient is standing.
    ◦ **Venous Hypertension**: This reflux leads to pooling of blood in the distal veins, increasing the hydrostatic pressure within the superficial venous system.
    ◦ **Vein Dilation**: Sustained venous hypertension causes the vein walls to stretch, lose elasticity, and become progressively dilated, elongated, and tortuous.
    ◦ **Inflammation & Leakage**: Increased pressure forces fluid, red blood cells, and proteins into the surrounding tissue, leading to edema, inflammation, and skin changes (**stasis dermatitis**, **hyperpigmentation**).
• **Primary Varicose Veins**: Caused by an intrinsic weakness in the vein wall or valves. This is the most common form.
• **Secondary Varicose Veins**: Result from an acquired condition that damages valves or obstructs flow, such as a prior **deep vein thrombosis (DVT)** (i.e., **post-thrombotic syndrome**), arteriovenous (AV) fistula, or extrinsic compression.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Extremely common, affecting up to 25-30% of adult women and 15-20% of adult men.
• **Age**: Prevalence increases significantly with age due to cumulative wear and tear on venous valves.
• **Sex**: More common in women (F > M), likely due to hormonal effects (progesterone) and pregnancy.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patient typically presents with complaints of cosmetically unappealing "**rope-like**" veins on their legs.
• Classic history involves symptoms that worsen throughout the day:
    ◦ Aching
    ◦ Heaviness
    ◦ Swelling
• Symptoms are exacerbated by prolonged standing or sitting and are **relieved by leg elevation** and rest.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primarily a clinical diagnosis.**
• **Venous Duplex Ultrasound**:
    ◦ **Test of choice** to confirm the diagnosis and plan treatment.
    ◦ Non-invasive and highly accurate.
    ◦ **Identifies the source and extent of venous reflux.**
        ▪ Reflux is defined as retrograde flow lasting >0.5 seconds.
    ◦ Maps the anatomy of the incompetent veins (e.g., saphenofemoral junction, great saphenous vein).
    ◦ Rules out obstruction or DVT as a cause of symptoms.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is generally good; varicose veins are a chronic, progressive condition but are not life-threatening.
• Treatment significantly improves quality of life and reduces symptoms.
• **Recurrence** is common, even after successful treatment, as the underlying venous disease process continues.

sections.overview:
• A venous ulcer, also known as a **stasis ulcer**, is a chronic, non-healing wound on the lower leg, typically in the **gaiter area** (**medial malleolus**)
• It is the most common type of lower extremity ulcer, resulting from **chronic venous insufficiency (CVI)** and the subsequent **venous hypertension**
• These ulcers are characterized by their **shallow depth**, **irregular borders**, and association with surrounding skin changes of **stasis dermatitis**
sections.etiology:
• The underlying cause is **Chronic Venous Insufficiency (CVI)** leading to sustained **venous hypertension**
    ◦ **Valvular Incompetence**: Valves within the deep, superficial, or perforating veins of the legs fail
        ▪ Can be due to primary valve failure or secondary to damage from a **deep vein thrombosis (DVT)** (i.e., post-thrombotic syndrome)
    ◦ **Venous Reflux & Stasis**: Failed valves allow for retrograde blood flow (**reflux**), particularly when upright, leading to pooling of blood (**stasis**) in the lower extremities
    ◦ **Venous Hypertension**: Constant stasis and reflux cause pathologically high pressure within the veins of the lower leg
    ◦ **Microcirculatory Damage**: This pressure is transmitted to the capillaries, increasing their permeability
        ▪ Allows macromolecules (like fibrinogen) and red blood cells to leak into the surrounding interstitial tissue
    ◦ **Inflammation & Tissue Injury**
        ▪ **Fibrin Cuffs**: Leaked fibrinogen polymerizes around capillaries, forming "fibrin cuffs" that impair the diffusion of oxygen and nutrients to the skin
        ▪ **Hemosiderin Staining**: Extravasated red blood cells break down, releasing iron pigment (**hemosiderin**) that stains the skin a characteristic brown color
        ▪ **White Cell Trapping**: Leukocytes become activated and trapped in the microcirculation, releasing inflammatory mediators and proteolytic enzymes that contribute to tissue damage
    ◦ **Ulceration**: The resulting skin is ischemic, inflamed, fibrotic, and fragile; minor trauma can lead to a breakdown of this compromised tissue, forming an ulcer that fails to heal due to the poor underlying circulation and chronic inflammation
sections.epidemiology:
• Most common type of leg ulcer, accounting for ~70-80% of all cases
• Prevalence is approximately 1% in the adult population
• Incidence increases significantly with age, most common in patients > 65 years old
• Slightly more common in females than males (F > M), likely due to hormonal influences and pregnancy
• High rate of recurrence, approaching 70% if underlying CVI is not managed
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with a non-healing wound on the lower leg that has been present for weeks to months
    ◦ The ulcer itself is usually located over or superior to the **medial malleolus (gaiter area)**
    ◦ The surrounding skin exhibits classic signs of chronic venous insufficiency
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Diagnosis is primarily based on history and characteristic physical exam findings
• **Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI)**: **Essential first step**
    ◦ Used to rule out significant co-existing **peripheral arterial disease (PAD)**
        ▪ Compression therapy is contraindicated with severe PAD
    ◦ Interpretation:
        ▪ ABI > 0.9: Normal. Safe for full compression
        ▪ ABI 0.5 - 0.9: Mixed arterial/venous disease. Modified/reduced compression may be used with caution
        ▪ ABI < 0.5: Severe PAD. Compression is contraindicated. Refer to vascular surgery
• **Venous Duplex Ultrasound**: **Gold standard** to confirm CVI
    ◦ Identifies the location and severity of venous reflux and/or obstruction in the deep and superficial systems
    ◦ Used to guide further treatment (e.g., vein ablation)
• **Biopsy**: Consider if the ulcer is atypical in appearance, fails to heal despite adequate therapy, or is suspicious for malignancy (e.g., **Marjolin's ulcer** - squamous cell carcinoma)
• **Wound Culture**: Only if clinical signs of infection are present (increased pain, erythema, purulence, odor)
    ◦ Routine cultures are not recommended as all chronic wounds are colonized
sections.prognosis:
• Healing is often slow, taking weeks to months
• With appropriate compression therapy and wound care, healing rates are ~70-85% at 6 months
• The prognosis is dominated by the **high rate of recurrence** (up to 70%) if compression and lifestyle modifications are not maintained

sections.overview:
• Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA), also known as Temporal Arteritis, is a systemic, **granulomatous vasculitis** affecting large and medium-sized arteries, particularly the cranial branches of the aortic arch.
• It is the most common primary vasculitis in adults.
• The condition is considered a **medical emergency** due to the high risk of **irreversible vision loss** if treatment is delayed.
• It has a strong association with **Polymyalgia Rheumatica (PMR)**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**:
    ◦ The exact cause is unknown but is believed to be an immune-mediated process, possibly triggered by an environmental or infectious agent in a genetically susceptible individual.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Immune Activation**: An unknown antigen triggers activation of **CD4+ T-cells** in the adventitia of the arterial wall.
    ◦ **Inflammatory Cascade**: Activated T-cells produce pro-inflammatory cytokines, most notably **Interleukin-6 (IL-6)** and **Interferon-gamma (IFN-γ)**.
    ◦ **Cellular Infiltration**: This cascade recruits macrophages and other inflammatory cells into the vessel wall.
    ◦ **Granuloma Formation**: Macrophages differentiate into epithelioid cells and **multinucleated giant cells**, forming classic **granulomas** within the vessel media and intima.
    ◦ **Vascular Damage**: The intense inflammation leads to fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina, **intimal hyperplasia**, and **luminal occlusion**, resulting in downstream ischemia and end-organ damage (e.g., blindness, stroke, claudication).
sections.epidemiology:
• **Age**: Almost exclusively occurs in individuals **> 50 years old**; the mean age of onset is ~75.
• **Gender**: **Females > Males** (2-3:1 ratio).
• **Geography/Ethnicity**: Most common in individuals of **Northern European / Scandinavian descent**.
    ◦ It is rare in Asian and African populations.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Age > 50** (the single greatest risk factor)
• **Female gender**
• **Northern European ancestry**
• **Genetic predisposition** (associations with certain HLA-DR4 alleles)
• Personal history of **Polymyalgia Rheumatica (PMR)**
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic patient is an elderly female (> 50 years) of Northern European descent who presents with a **new-onset headache**, jaw pain with chewing, scalp tenderness, and constitutional symptoms like fever and fatigue.
• A key presentation feature is transient monocular vision loss (**amaurosis fugax**), which is a harbinger of impending permanent blindness.
• **Constitutional Symptoms**:
    ◦ Low-grade fever, malaise, fatigue
    ◦ Anorexia, weight loss
• **Cranial Ischemia Symptoms**:
    ◦ **Headache (70-90%)**: Usually **new-onset** or a new type of headache. Typically located in the temporal or occipital region, can be unilateral or bilateral, described as dull, boring, or lancinating.
    ◦ **Jaw Claudication (~50%)**: Pain, aching, or fatigue in the masseter muscles with chewing. **Highly specific for GCA.**
    ◦ **Scalp Tenderness (~50%)**: Pain when combing hair, wearing glasses, or resting the head on a pillow.
• **Visual Symptoms (~30%)**: **MEDICAL EMERGENCY.**
    ◦ **Amaurosis Fugax**: Transient, painless, monocular vision loss often described as a "curtain falling over the eye." This is a critical warning sign.
    ◦ **Permanent Vision Loss**: The most feared complication, caused by **Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy (AION)** due to occlusion of the posterior ciliary artery.
    ◦ **Diplopia**: Double vision from ischemia of extraocular muscles.
• **Polymyalgia Rheumatica (PMR) Symptoms (~50%)**:
    ◦ Symmetrical aching and morning stiffness in the proximal joints and muscles (shoulders, neck, hip girdle).
sections.physicalExam:
• **General**:
    ◦ May have a low-grade fever.
• **Head & Neck**:
    ◦ **Temporal Artery**: May be **thickened, nodular, tender** to palpation, with a **reduced or absent pulse**.
    ◦ **Scalp**: Tenderness to palpation.
• **Ophthalmologic Exam**:
    ◦ **Fundoscopy**: May reveal a **pale, edematous (swollen) optic disc**, consistent with **AION**.
    ◦ **Visual Acuity**: May be decreased.
    ◦ **Pupils**: An **afferent pupillary defect (APD)** may be present in the affected eye.
• **Vascular Exam**:
    ◦ Asymmetric blood pressures in the arms or arterial bruits (subclavian, axillary) may suggest large-vessel involvement.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Laboratory Studies**:
    ◦ **Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR)**: Markedly elevated, classically **> 100 mm/hr**. A normal ESR (<30) makes GCA unlikely but does not rule it out.
    ◦ **C-Reactive Protein (CRP)**: Markedly elevated; often more sensitive than ESR.
    ◦ **Complete Blood Count (CBC)**: May show a **normocytic, normochromic anemia** (anemia of chronic disease) and **thrombocytosis** (reactive).
• **Definitive Diagnosis**:
    ◦ **Temporal Artery Biopsy**: The **gold standard**.
        ▪ **Procedure**: A 1-2 cm segment of the artery is surgically excised. Treatment should **NOT** be delayed while awaiting biopsy; steroids do not alter histologic findings for up to 2 weeks.
        ▪ **Histology**: Shows panarteritis with a **mononuclear cell infiltrate**, **granulomatous inflammation**, and characteristic **multinucleated giant cells**.
        ▪ **Caveat**: A negative biopsy does not rule out GCA due to **"skip lesions"** (segmental inflammation). If clinical suspicion remains high, the contralateral side may be biopsied.
• **Imaging**:
    ◦ **Color Doppler Ultrasound**: A non-invasive option that can show a **"halo sign"**—a hypoechoic circumferential thickening of the vessel wall due to edema. It is highly operator-dependent.
    ◦ **MRA / CTA / PET Scan**: Useful for detecting inflammation in the aorta and its major branches (large-vessel GCA).
sections.treatment:
• **GCA without Visual Loss**:
    ◦ **High-Dose Oral Prednisone**: 40-60 mg per day.
• **GCA with Visual Loss (Amaurosis Fugax, Diplopia, or Permanent Loss)**:
    ◦ **IV Pulse Methylprednisolone**: 500 mg - 1 gram IV daily for 3-5 days to rapidly reduce inflammation.
    ◦ Followed by a transition to high-dose oral prednisone (60 mg/day).
• **Adjunctive/Steroid-Sparing Therapy**:
    ◦ **Tocilizumab (Actemra)**: An **IL-6 receptor antagonist**. It is approved for GCA and is often used in conjunction with steroids to allow for a more rapid taper and to maintain remission.
    ◦ **Low-Dose Aspirin (81 mg daily)**: Recommended to reduce the risk of ischemic events like stroke and vision loss.
sections.management:
• **Steroid Taper**: After symptoms and inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP) have normalized (usually 2-4 weeks), a very slow prednisone taper is initiated over **1-2 years**. Relapses are common if tapered too quickly.
• **Monitoring**: Regular clinical follow-up and monitoring of **ESR/CRP** are essential to guide the steroid taper and detect relapses.
• **Prophylaxis for Steroid Toxicity**:
    ◦ **Osteoporosis Prevention**: All patients should receive Calcium, Vitamin D, and a **bisphosphonate** (e.g., alendronate).
    ◦ **Gastrointestinal Protection**: Consider a **proton pump inhibitor (PPI)** for patients at high risk of GI bleeding.
• **Aneurysm Surveillance**: Patients with GCA are at increased long-term risk for **thoracic aortic aneurysms** and dissection. Periodic screening with chest imaging (CT or MRA) is recommended.
sections.complications:
• **Permanent, irreversible monocular or bilateral blindness (most feared)**
• **Cerebrovascular accident (CVA) / Stroke**
• **Thoracic aortic aneurysm and/or dissection** (a major cause of late mortality)
• **Complications of long-term glucocorticoid therapy**:
    ◦ Osteoporosis and fractures
    ◦ Diabetes mellitus
    ◦ Cataracts/glaucoma
    ◦ Cushingoid features
    ◦ Avascular necrosis
    ◦ Increased risk of infection
sections.prognosis:
• With prompt diagnosis and treatment, the prognosis is generally good, and life expectancy is near normal.
• Morbidity is primarily related to **permanent vision loss** if treatment is delayed, and the side effects of long-term steroid use.
• Relapses occur in about 50% of patients, typically during the steroid taper.

sections.overview:
• An aortic aneurysm is a localized or diffuse dilation of the aorta to a diameter of at least 1.5 times its normal size.
    ◦ The normal aortic diameter is ~2 cm, with an aneurysm generally defined as **> 3.0 cm**.
    ◦ Aneurysms are classified by location (abdominal vs. thoracic) and morphology (fusiform vs. saccular).
