    ◦ The primary clinical concern is the risk of rupture, a catastrophic event with extremely high mortality.
• **Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA):** Most common type (~75%). Typically located **infrarenally** (below the renal arteries).
• **Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm (TAA):** Less common. Can involve the aortic root, ascending aorta, aortic arch, or descending aorta.
• **True Aneurysm:** Involves all three layers of the vessel wall (intima, media, adventitia).
• **Pseudoaneurysm (False Aneurysm):** A contained rupture; the vessel wall is breached, and blood is contained by the adventitia or surrounding tissues.
sections.etiology:
• The fundamental pathology is a **degeneration of the aortic wall's structural integrity**, primarily through the degradation of elastin and collagen in the tunica media.
• **Atherosclerosis:** The single most common cause, especially for AAA. Atherosclerotic plaques disrupt the media, leading to weakening.
• **Proteolytic Degradation:** Increased activity of enzymes like **matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)** breaks down elastin and collagen.
• **Inflammation:** Chronic transmural inflammation with an influx of lymphocytes and macrophages is a key feature.
• **Genetic/Hereditary Factors:**
    ◦ **Marfan Syndrome:** Defect in fibrillin-1 gene; strongly associated with ascending TAA and aortic root dilation.
    ◦ **Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (Vascular Type):** Defect in type III collagen; leads to fragile vessels and aneurysms.
    ◦ **Bicuspid Aortic Valve:** A major risk factor for ascending TAA due to altered hemodynamics and intrinsic aortic wall abnormalities.
    ◦ **Loeys-Dietz Syndrome:** Aggressive aneurysm formation.
• **Infection ("Mycotic" Aneurysm):** Bacterial infection (e.g., *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Salmonella*) seeding the aortic wall, leading to rapid expansion and rupture.
• **Vasculitis:** Giant Cell Arteritis, Takayasu Arteritis.
• **Law of Laplace (T = P x r):** Wall tension (T) is proportional to pressure (P) and radius (r). As the aneurysm radius increases, wall tension increases, further promoting expansion and raising the risk of rupture.
sections.epidemiology:
• **AAA:**
    ◦ Prevalence: ~5% in men over 65.
    ◦ Strong male predominance (M:F ratio 4:1).
    ◦ Incidence increases significantly with age.
• **TAA:**
    ◦ Less common than AAA but incidence is rising due to increased imaging.
    ◦ Affects men and women more equally than AAA.
    ◦ Often diagnosed at a slightly younger age, especially when associated with genetic syndromes.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **The vast majority of aortic aneurysms are asymptomatic** and are discovered incidentally on imaging performed for other reasons.
• **Asymptomatic:** Most common presentation.
• **Symptomatic (unruptured):**
    ◦ **AAA:** Vague, deep, gnawing pain in the abdomen, flank, or back. A new-onset of pain in a patient with a known aneurysm is a sign of impending rupture.
    ◦ **TAA:** Chest, back (interscapular), or shoulder pain. Symptoms can arise from compression of adjacent structures:
        ▪ **Hoarseness:** Compression of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve (Ortner's syndrome).
        ▪ **Dysphagia:** Compression of the esophagus.
        ▪ **Dyspnea, cough, stridor:** Compression of the trachea or bronchi.
• **Rupture / Acute Dissection:** A surgical emergency.
    ◦ **AAA Rupture:** Sudden onset of severe, tearing abdominal or back pain, **hypotension**, and a **pulsatile abdominal mass**.
    ◦ **TAA Rupture/Dissection:** Sudden onset of severe, **tearing/ripping chest or interscapular back pain**, syncope, shock, unequal BPs in arms.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Abdominal Ultrasound**
    ◦ **Best initial test** for screening, diagnosis, and surveillance of AAA.
    ◦ Non-invasive, no radiation, cost-effective. Limited by bowel gas and obesity.
• **CT Angiography (CTA)**
    ◦ **Gold standard** for definitive diagnosis and pre-operative planning.
    ◦ Provides precise size, location, extent, and involvement of branch vessels (renal, mesenteric). Requires IV contrast.
• **MRA**
    ◦ Alternative to CTA for pre-operative planning.
    ◦ Used in patients with contrast allergy or renal insufficiency.
• **Chest X-ray**
    ◦ May show a **widened mediastinum** or enlarged aortic knob (TAA). Often an incidental finding.
    ◦ Not sensitive or specific.
• **Bedside US (FAST)**
    ◦ **Used in hemodynamically unstable patients** with suspected AAA rupture to rapidly confirm diagnosis before going to the OR.
    ◦ The goal is rapid confirmation, not detailed measurement. If positive, patient goes directly to surgery.
sections.prognosis:
• **Elective Repair:** Low mortality rate (~2-5%).
• **Ruptured AAA:** Extremely high mortality. **>50% die before reaching the hospital**. Of those who undergo surgery, perioperative mortality is still 30-50%. Overall mortality approaches 80-90%.
• **Aneurysm Growth:** The annual risk of rupture increases exponentially with diameter.
    ◦ < 4.0 cm: < 0.5% / year
    ◦ 5.0 - 5.9 cm: 3-15% / year
    ◦ > 7.0 cm: > 20% / year

sections.overview:
• An **Atrial Septal Defect (ASD)** is a congenital heart defect characterized by a persistent opening in the interatrial septum, allowing blood to flow between the left and right atria.
    ◦ This communication results in a **left-to-right shunt**, as pressure in the left atrium is typically higher than in the right atrium.
    ◦ ASD is one of the most common congenital heart defects diagnosed in adulthood and is classified as an **acyanotic ("pink") heart lesion**.
• There are four main types:
    ◦ **Ostium Secundum (75%)**: Most common type, located in the central portion of the atrial septum (region of the fossa ovalis).
    ◦ **Ostium Primum (15-20%)**: Located in the lower portion of the septum. Often associated with atrioventricular (AV) valve abnormalities (e.g., **cleft mitral valve**) and is considered a form of AV septal defect.
    ◦ **Sinus Venosus (5-10%)**: Located in the superior or inferior aspect of the septum, near the entry of the superior vena cava (SVC) or inferior vena cava (IVC). Often associated with **partial anomalous pulmonary venous return (PAPVR)**.
    ◦ **Coronary Sinus Defect (<1%)**: Rarest type, located at the site where the coronary sinus enters the right atrium.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ Primarily a congenital malformation resulting from improper development of the atrial septum during fetal life.
    ◦ Most cases are sporadic, but some are associated with genetic syndromes (e.g., **Holt-Oram syndrome, Down syndrome**).
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Left-to-Right Shunt**: Postnatally, left atrial (LA) pressure exceeds right atrial (RA) pressure. This pressure gradient drives oxygenated blood from the LA across the defect into the RA.
    ◦ **Right Heart Volume Overload**: The shunted blood mixes with deoxygenated systemic venous return in the RA. This combined volume overloads the right atrium and right ventricle (RV).
    ◦ **Increased Pulmonary Blood Flow**: The volume-overloaded RV pumps excess blood into the pulmonary circulation, leading to increased pulmonary blood flow (PBF). The pulmonary vasculature is normally low-resistance and can accommodate this extra flow for years without a significant rise in pressure.
    ◦ **Chronic Changes**: Over decades, the chronic volume overload causes:
        ▪ Dilation and hypertrophy of the RA and RV.
        ▪ Dilation of the main pulmonary artery.
        ▪ Pulmonary vascular remodeling, leading to **pulmonary hypertension (PHTN)**.
    ◦ **Eisenmenger Syndrome (Late Complication)**: If PHTN becomes severe and irreversible, pulmonary vascular resistance exceeds systemic vascular resistance. This causes the shunt to reverse direction (right-to-left), leading to **cyanosis**, dyspnea, and poor prognosis.
sections.epidemiology:
• Accounts for ~10% of all congenital heart defects.
• One of the most common congenital heart defects to present in adulthood, as many cases are asymptomatic during childhood.
• Prevalence is higher in females than males (F:M ratio 2:1).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Infants/Children**: Usually asymptomatic.
    ◦ Large defects may cause **failure to thrive**, fatigue, or recurrent respiratory infections.
• **Adults (typically 3rd-4th decade)**: Presentation is often insidious.
    ◦ Gradual onset of **exertional dyspnea**, fatigue, and decreased exercise tolerance.
    ◦ **Palpitations**, often due to supraventricular arrhythmias like **atrial fibrillation** or **atrial flutter**.
• **Paradoxical Embolism**
    ◦ A venous thrombus (e.g., **DVT**) can cross the ASD into the systemic circulation, causing a **stroke** or **TIA**.
    ◦ This can be the presenting event in a previously undiagnosed ASD.
• Symptoms of **right-sided heart failure** (e.g., peripheral edema, ascites, JVD) in advanced disease.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Echocardiogram (Transthoracic - TTE)**
    ◦ **Test of choice for diagnosis.**
    ◦ Directly visualizes the defect and determines its size, location, and type.
    ◦ Color Doppler demonstrates the **left-to-right shunt**.
    ◦ Shows evidence of **right heart volume overload** (RA and RV dilation).
    ◦ Can estimate pulmonary artery pressures.
• **Transesophageal Echocardiogram (TEE)**
    ◦ May be needed for better visualization of **sinus venosus defects** or for guiding percutaneous closure.
• **Electrocardiogram (ECG)**
    ◦ **Incomplete Right Bundle Branch Block (rSR' pattern in lead V1)**: Common finding due to RV volume overload and delayed depolarization.
    ◦ **Right Axis Deviation**: Due to RV enlargement.
    ◦ **P-pulmonale (peaked P waves)**: Suggests RA enlargement.
    ◦ **First-degree AV block**: Common with **ostium primum defects**.
    ◦ **Crochetage sign**: A small notch in the peak of the R wave in inferior leads (II, III, aVF); specific but not sensitive.
• **Chest X-Ray (CXR)**
    ◦ **Cardiomegaly**: Specifically RA and RV enlargement.
    ◦ **Prominent/dilated main pulmonary artery**.
    ◦ **Increased pulmonary vascular markings ("shunt vascularity")**: Due to increased blood flow to the lungs.
• **Cardiac Catheterization**
    ◦ Not typically needed for diagnosis.
    ◦ Reserved for cases where echo is inconclusive, to measure pulmonary artery pressures precisely, or to quantify the shunt size (Qp:Qs ratio).
    ◦ Also used for therapeutic percutaneous device closure.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for patients who undergo closure before age 25 and prior to the development of significant **pulmonary hypertension**. Life expectancy is near normal.
• **Good** for patients with closure in adulthood, although the lifetime risk for atrial arrhythmias remains higher than the general population.
• **Poor** once severe, irreversible **pulmonary hypertension (Eisenmenger syndrome)** has developed. Management becomes palliative, and median survival is significantly reduced.

sections.overview:
• A Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD) is a congenital heart defect characterized by an abnormal opening in the interventricular septum, the wall that separates the left and right ventricles.
• This opening allows blood to shunt between the ventricles.
• VSD is the most common congenital heart anomaly.
• The clinical significance depends on the size of the defect and the degree of shunting.
• As it typically involves a left-to-right shunt, it is classified as an **acyanotic** congenital heart disease.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ VSDs are most often sporadic and result from incomplete development of the interventricular septum during embryogenesis (weeks 4-8).
    ◦ They can also be associated with chromosomal abnormalities or teratogenic exposure.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Pressure Gradient**: Post-birth, systemic vascular resistance is high and pulmonary vascular resistance is low. This creates a significant pressure gradient where Left Ventricular (LV) pressure is much higher than Right Ventricular (RV) pressure.
    ◦ **Left-to-Right Shunt**: Blood flows from the high-pressure LV, across the VSD, into the low-pressure RV.
    ◦ **Pulmonary Overcirculation**: The shunted blood, along with the normal venous return to the RV, is ejected into the pulmonary artery, resulting in increased pulmonary blood flow (pulmonary plethora).
    ◦ **LV Volume Overload**: The increased blood flow returns from the lungs to the left atrium (LA) and then to the LV, causing volume overload of the LA and LV, leading to dilation and eccentric hypertrophy.
    ◦ **Clinical Effects**
        ▪ **Small VSD (Restrictive)**: The small opening creates high resistance to flow, limiting the shunt volume. This causes a loud, high-velocity jet murmur but often minimal hemodynamic consequences.
        ▪ **Large VSD (Non-restrictive)**: The large opening allows pressures between the LV and RV to equalize. The shunt volume is large, determined by the ratio of pulmonary to systemic vascular resistance (PVR:SVR). This leads to significant pulmonary overcirculation, LV volume overload, and development of congestive heart failure (CHF).
    ◦ **Long-Term Changes**: Chronic, severe pulmonary overcirculation leads to remodeling of the pulmonary arterioles, causing irreversible **pulmonary hypertension**. If RV pressure eventually exceeds LV pressure, the shunt reverses (**Eisenmenger Syndrome**), becoming a right-to-left shunt, which results in cyanosis.
sections.epidemiology:
• The most common congenital heart defect, accounting for ~30% of all cases.
• Incidence is approximately 2-6 per 1,000 live births.
• **Classification by Location**
    ◦ **Perimembranous (80%)**: Most common type. Located in the upper septum, near the tricuspid and aortic valves.
    ◦ **Muscular (15%)**: Located in the muscular portion of the septum. Often multiple ("Swiss cheese" septum). High rate of spontaneous closure.
    ◦ **Supracristal / Outlet (5%)**: Located in the RV outflow tract, just below the pulmonary valve. High association with aortic valve prolapse and aortic regurgitation. More common in Asian populations.
    ◦ **Inlet (5%)**: Located posterior and inferior, near the tricuspid and mitral valves. Often associated with atrioventricular canal defects (common in Trisomy 21).
sections.riskFactors:
• **Genetic Syndromes**
    ◦ Trisomy 21 (Down Syndrome)
    ◦ Trisomy 18 (Edwards Syndrome)
    ◦ Trisomy 13 (Patau Syndrome)
    ◦ DiGeorge Syndrome (22q11.2 deletion)
• **Maternal Factors**
    ◦ Diabetes mellitus
    ◦ Phenylketonuria (PKU)
    ◦ Alcohol use (Fetal Alcohol Syndrome)
    ◦ Exposure to teratogens (e.g., phenytoin, valproic acid)
    ◦ Infections during pregnancy (e.g., Rubella)
• **Family History**: Increased risk if a first-degree relative has a congenital heart defect.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Small VSD**: Often discovered incidentally due to a loud murmur on routine examination in an otherwise asymptomatic, thriving infant.
• **Moderate to Large VSD**: Symptoms of CHF typically appear at **4-6 weeks of age** as the pulmonary vascular resistance naturally falls, increasing the left-to-right shunt. The presentation includes failure to thrive, feeding difficulties, and respiratory distress.
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ **Small VSD**: Asymptomatic.
    ◦ **Moderate to Large VSD**
        ▪ **Failure to Thrive (FTT)** / Poor weight gain
        ▪ **Diaphoresis (sweating) with feeding**: A classic sign of increased work of breathing and sympathetic overdrive.
        ▪ **Tachypnea**, dyspnea, labored breathing
        ▪ **Fatigue**, especially during feeding (infant may take a long time to feed or fall asleep mid-feed).
        ▪ Recurrent respiratory infections.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Auscultation**
    ◦ **Murmur**: **Loud, harsh, holosystolic (pansystolic) murmur** best heard at the **left lower sternal border (LLSB)**.
    ◦ **Inverse Relationship**: The smaller the VSD, the more turbulent the flow, and the **louder the murmur**.
    ◦ **Thrill**: A palpable thrill is common at the LLSB.
    ◦ **S2**: May be narrowly split with an accentuated P2 if pulmonary hypertension is present.
    ◦ **Diastolic Rumble**: A mid-diastolic rumble may be heard at the apex due to increased blood flow across the mitral valve (relative mitral stenosis).
• **Inspection/Palpation**
    ◦ **Hyperdynamic Precordium**: Visible or palpable hyperactivity of the heart.
    ◦ **PMI**: Apical impulse may be displaced inferiorly and laterally due to LV enlargement.
    ◦ **Signs of CHF**: Tachypnea, hepatomegaly, rales/crackles (less common in infants).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Echocardiogram (with Doppler)**: **Gold standard.**
    ◦ Confirms the diagnosis.
    ◦ Identifies the location, size, and number of defects.
    ◦ Quantifies the shunt magnitude (Qp:Qs ratio).
    ◦ Estimates RV and pulmonary artery pressures.
    ◦ Assesses for chamber enlargement and associated anomalies.
• **Chest X-ray (CXR)**
    ◦ **Small VSD**: Normal.
    ◦ **Large VSD**: **Cardiomegaly** (due to LA and LV enlargement), **increased pulmonary vascular markings** (pulmonary plethora).
• **Electrocardiogram (ECG)**
    ◦ **Small VSD**: Normal.
    ◦ **Large VSD**: **Left Ventricular Hypertrophy (LVH)** is classic due to volume overload. May show **Biventricular Hypertrophy (BVH)** if RV pressures are elevated. Left Atrial Enlargement (LAE) may also be present.
• **Cardiac Catheterization**: Rarely needed for diagnosis. Used to precisely measure pulmonary vascular resistance in older patients before surgical consideration or for transcatheter device closure.
sections.treatment:
• **Small, Asymptomatic VSDs**
    ◦ **Observation**: Many (especially muscular VSDs) close spontaneously, typically within the first 2 years of life.
    ◦ Regular follow-up with cardiology.
    ◦ Endocarditis prophylaxis is generally **not** recommended unless there is a prior history of endocarditis.
• **Moderate to Large, Symptomatic VSDs**
    ◦ Goal: Control CHF symptoms and promote growth.
    ◦ **Medical Management**
        ▪ **Diuretics**: Furosemide (to reduce preload/pulmonary congestion).
        ▪ **Afterload Reduction**: ACE inhibitors (e.g., Captopril, Enalapril) to decrease SVR and promote forward flow, thereby reducing the L->R shunt.
        ▪ **Inotropic Support**: Digoxin (improves contractility, less commonly used now).
        ▪ **Nutritional Support**: High-calorie formula/fortified breast milk to combat FTT. Nasogastric (NG) tube feeding may be necessary.
    ◦ **Surgical Repair**
        ▪ **Indications**: Medically refractory CHF or failure to thrive; Large VSD with evidence of developing pulmonary hypertension (Qp:Qs > 2:1); VSD with associated aortic regurgitation.
        ▪ **Timing**: Typically performed at **3-6 months of age**.
        ▪ **Procedure**: Open-heart surgery with a patch closure (Dacron or pericardium).
sections.management:
• **Follow-up**: Lifelong cardiology follow-up is recommended, even after repair, to monitor for residual shunts, arrhythmias, or valve issues.
• **Endocarditis Prophylaxis**: Recommended for the first **6 months after surgical/device repair** with prosthetic material. Also recommended for life if there is a residual defect near the prosthetic patch.
• **Activity**: No restrictions for small VSDs or after successful repair. Restrictions may apply if significant pulmonary hypertension persists.
sections.complications:
• **Congestive Heart Failure (CHF)**: Most common complication in infancy with large defects.
• **Eisenmenger Syndrome**: Irreversible pulmonary hypertension leading to shunt reversal (R->L), cyanosis, and severe exercise intolerance. This is a late and devastating complication.
• **Infective Endocarditis**: Increased risk due to turbulent blood flow across the defect.
• **Aortic Regurgitation**: Prolapse of an aortic valve cusp into the defect, most common with supracristal VSDs.
• **Arrhythmias**: Can occur pre- or post-operatively (e.g., right bundle branch block is common after surgical repair).
• **Failure to Thrive (FTT)**: Due to increased caloric expenditure from the work of breathing.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for small VSDs, with most closing spontaneously.
• **Excellent** for hemodynamically significant VSDs that are surgically repaired in infancy before the onset of irreversible pulmonary hypertension. Post-repair, patients typically have a normal life expectancy.
• **Poor** for patients who develop Eisenmenger syndrome. Life expectancy is significantly reduced, and management is palliative (heart-lung transplant may be an option).

sections.overview:
• A **Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA)** is a persistent connection between the descending thoracic aorta and the pulmonary artery that results from the failure of the fetal ductus arteriosus to close after birth
    ◦ In fetal circulation, the ductus is a normal and essential structure that shunts blood away from the non-functional lungs
    ◦ After birth, this connection's failure to close leads to a **left-to-right shunt**, causing abnormal blood flow between the two major vessels
sections.etiology:
• **Fetal Circulation**
    ◦ In utero, the **ductus arteriosus** allows oxygenated blood from the placenta (via the right ventricle) to bypass the high-resistance fetal lungs and enter the systemic circulation via the descending aorta
    ◦ The patency of the ductus is maintained by high levels of circulating **prostaglandins (PGE2)** produced by the placenta and **low arterial oxygen tension**
• **Postnatal Closure**
    ◦ At birth, two key events trigger ductal closure:
        ▪ **Increased Oxygen Tension**: The first breaths dramatically increase blood oxygen levels, which inhibits prostaglandin-sensitive channels in the ductal wall, leading to smooth muscle contraction
        ▪ **Decreased Prostaglandins**: The separation of the placenta causes a rapid drop in circulating PGE2 levels, removing the primary stimulus keeping the ductus open
    ◦ Functional closure typically occurs within 12-24 hours, with permanent anatomic closure (fibrosis) by 2-3 weeks
• **Pathophysiology of PDA**
    ◦ Failure of closure results in a persistent connection
    ◦ After birth, systemic vascular resistance becomes higher than pulmonary vascular resistance
    ◦ This pressure gradient creates a **left-to-right shunt**, where oxygenated blood from the aorta flows into the pulmonary artery
    ◦ **Hemodynamic Consequences**
        ▪ **Pulmonary Overcirculation**: Increased blood flow to the lungs
        ▪ **Left Heart Volume Overload**: The increased pulmonary venous return leads to dilation and hypertrophy of the left atrium (**LAE**) and left ventricle (**LVH**)
        ▪ **Wide Pulse Pressure**: During diastole, blood "runs off" from the aorta into the lower-pressure pulmonary artery, causing a lower diastolic blood pressure and thus a wider pulse pressure
        ▪ **Pulmonary Hypertension**: Chronic, high-volume shunting can lead to remodeling of the pulmonary vasculature, increased pulmonary artery pressure, and eventually, irreversible pulmonary hypertension (**Eisenmenger syndrome**)
sections.epidemiology:
• Occurs in approximately 1 in 2,000 live term births
• Significantly more common in **premature infants**, affecting up to 60% of infants born before 28 weeks gestation
• More common in females (2:1 ratio)
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation depends entirely on the size of the PDA and the degree of left-to-right shunting
    ◦ **Small PDA**: Often asymptomatic and discovered incidentally due to a characteristic murmur on routine examination
    ◦ **Moderate to Large PDA**: Presents in infancy with signs of heart failure and poor growth as pulmonary vascular resistance falls in the first few weeks of life
sections.diagnostics:
• **Echocardiogram (with Doppler)**
    ◦ **Gold standard / test of choice**
    ◦ Directly visualizes the patent ductus
    ◦ Doppler flow shows the direction and velocity of the shunt
    ◦ Assesses secondary effects: LA and LV size, pulmonary artery pressure
• **Chest X-Ray (CXR)**
    ◦ **Normal** in a small PDA
    ◦ **Large PDA**: Shows cardiomegaly (specifically LA and LV enlargement) and increased pulmonary vascular markings (**pulmonary plethora**)
• **Electrocardiogram (ECG)**
    ◦ **Normal** in a small PDA
    ◦ **Large PDA**: May show **Left Ventricular Hypertrophy (LVH)** and **Left Atrial Enlargement (LAE)**. Biventricular hypertrophy can be seen if pulmonary hypertension develops
• **Cardiac Catheterization**
    ◦ Primarily used for **therapeutic intervention** (device closure), not for diagnosis
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** with timely diagnosis and closure. Patients live a normal life with no restrictions post-closure
• If a large PDA is left untreated, mortality from heart failure or pulmonary hypertension is high in infancy or early adulthood

sections.overview:
• Most common **cyanotic congenital heart defect**.
• Defined by a constellation of four specific anatomical abnormalities that result from a single embryologic defect: the **anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular (conal) septum**.
• This displacement leads to a **right-to-left shunting** of deoxygenated blood into the systemic circulation, causing central **cyanosis**.
• The severity of the clinical presentation is primarily determined by the degree of **right ventricular outflow tract obstruction (RVOTO)**.
sections.etiology:
• Underlying embryologic cause is the **anterocephalad deviation of the infundibular septum**.
• This single event creates the four cardinal features (mnemonic **PROVe**):
    ◦ **P**ulmonary Stenosis (**Right Ventricular Outflow Tract Obstruction** - **RVOTO**)
        ▪ The displaced septum narrows the pulmonary valve and/or the infundibulum just below the valve.
        ▪ **This is the most critical determinant of clinical severity.**
        ▪ Severe stenosis causes significant obstruction, forcing deoxygenated blood across the VSD.
    ◦ **R**ight **Ventricular Hypertrophy (RVH)**
        ▪ A secondary finding, not a primary defect.
        ▪ The right ventricle hypertrophies as it pumps against both the high pressure of the **RVOTO** and the systemic pressure of the left ventricle (via the VSD).
    ◦ **O**verriding Aorta
        ▪ The displaced septum causes the aorta to sit astride both the left and right ventricles, directly over the VSD.
        ▪ This allows deoxygenated blood from the RV to enter the aorta directly.
    ◦ **V**entricular **Septal Defect (VSD)**
        ▪ The defect is typically large and non-restrictive, located just below the aortic valve.
        ▪ It allows for the equalization of pressures between the right and left ventricles.
• Pathophysiologic Mechanism:
    ◦ The VSD and overriding aorta allow blood to flow from the RV to the aorta.
    ◦ The **RVOTO** makes it difficult for blood to flow from the RV to the pulmonary artery.
    ◦ When pulmonary vascular resistance is high or systemic vascular resistance (**SVR**) is low, the path of least resistance for RV blood is through the VSD into the aorta.
        ▪ This is a **right-to-left shunt**.
    ◦ The shunting of deoxygenated blood into the systemic circulation results in **cyanosis**.
sections.epidemiology:
• Most common **cyanotic** congenital heart disease, accounting for ~10% of all congenital heart defects.
• Incidence is approximately 1 in 2,500 live births.
• Occurs equally in males and females.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation depends entirely on the degree of **RVOTO**.
• **"Pink Tet"**:
    ◦ Infants with mild **RVOTO** may have minimal shunting and be acyanotic or have only intermittent **cyanosis**.
    ◦ They may present later in infancy with a heart murmur and signs of heart failure (due to a left-to-right shunt through the VSD).
• **"Blue Tet"**:
    ◦ Infants with severe **RVOTO** are **cyanotic** at birth or within the first few months of life.
• **"Tet Spells" (Hypercyanotic Spells)**:
    ◦ Paroxysmal episodes of profound **cyanosis** and **hypoxia**.
    ◦ Often precipitated by events that decrease **SVR** (crying, feeding, defecation, waking up) or increase **RVOTO** (infundibular spasm).
    ◦ Pathophysiology:
        ▪ Decreased **SVR** or increased **RVOTO** worsens the **right-to-left shunt**, leading to a sudden drop in arterial oxygen saturation.
        ▪ This creates a vicious cycle of **hypoxia**, acidosis, and further infundibular spasm.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Echocardiogram**:
    ◦ **Diagnostic test of choice**.
    ◦ Directly visualizes all four anatomic abnormalities, assesses the severity of **RVOTO**, and shows the direction of the shunt with color Doppler.
• **Chest X-ray (CXR)**:
    ◦ **"Boot-shaped heart" (Coeur en sabot)**:
        ▪ Caused by **RVH** (which uplifts the cardiac apex) and a concave main pulmonary artery segment.
    ◦ Decreased pulmonary vascular markings (**oligemia**) if **RVOTO** is severe.
• **Electrocardiogram (EKG)**:
    ◦ **Right Ventricular Hypertrophy (RVH)**: Tall R waves in V1, deep S waves in V6.
    ◦ **Right Axis Deviation (RAD)**.
• **Pulse Oximetry**:
    ◦ Shows low oxygen saturation (<95%) that does not improve significantly with supplemental oxygen.
• **Complete Blood Count (CBC)**:
    ◦ **Polycythemia** (elevated hemoglobin/hematocrit) due to chronic **hypoxia**.
sections.prognosis:
• **Untreated**:
    ◦ Poor prognosis.
    ◦ 25% mortality by age 1, 50% by age 5, and rare survival past age 40.
• **Treated**:
    ◦ Excellent prognosis.
    ◦ With timely surgical repair, the 30-year survival rate is >90%.
    ◦ Most patients have a good quality of life, though they require lifelong monitoring and may require further intervention (e.g., pulmonary valve replacement).

sections.overview: • Coarctation of the Aorta (CoA) is a congenital narrowing of the aortic lumen. ◦ Most commonly located just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery at the site of the ductus arteriosus insertion (juxtaductal). • This stenosis creates an obstruction to blood flow, leading to hypertension in the upper extremities and relative hypotension in the lower extremities. • Clinical presentation varies significantly with severity, from cardiogenic shock in newborns to asymptomatic hypertension discovered in adulthood.
sections.etiology: • Etiology ◦ Primarily a congenital defect. ◦ The leading theory is the "ductal tissue theory," where ectopic ductal tissue extends into the aortic wall and constricts when the ductus arteriosus closes after birth. ◦ Strongly associated with certain genetic syndromes. • Pathophysiology ◦ Obstruction & Pressure Gradient: The narrowing creates a significant afterload on the left ventricle (LV) and a pressure gradient across the coarctation. ◦ Proximal Effects (Pre-Coarctation): ▪ Hypertension: Increased blood pressure in the aorta, head, neck, and upper extremities. ▪ Left Ventricular Hypertrophy (LVH): The LV hypertrophies to overcome the high afterload, which can lead to diastolic and eventually systolic heart failure. ◦ Distal Effects (Post-Coarctation): ▪ Hypotension: Decreased blood pressure and blood flow to the abdominal organs and lower extremities. ▪ Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS) Activation: Renal hypoperfusion activates the RAAS, further exacerbating systemic hypertension. ◦ Collateral Circulation: ▪ The body develops an extensive network of collateral vessels to bypass the obstruction. ▪ Key pathways include: • Internal mammary (thoracic) arteries → Anterior intercostal arteries • Subclavian artery branches → Scapular arteries → Posterior intercostal arteries → Descending aorta ▪ These enlarged, pulsatile intercostal arteries can erode the inferior aspect of the ribs, causing "rib notching" on chest X-ray.
sections.epidemiology: • Accounts for 5-8% of all congenital heart defects (CHD). • Male-to-female predominance of approximately 2:1. • Strong association with Turner Syndrome (XO); CoA is found in ~15-20% of patients with Turner Syndrome.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • Presentation is highly dependent on the severity of the coarctation and the patient's age. • Neonates (Severe Coarctation) ◦ Present within the first few days to weeks of life as the ductus arteriosus closes. ◦ Develop sudden signs of cardiogenic shock and severe heart failure: poor feeding, lethargy, tachypnea, respiratory distress, and acidosis. ◦ This is a life-threatening emergency. • Infants & Children (Moderate Coarctation) ◦ May present with failure to thrive, respiratory distress with feeding, or a heart murmur detected on routine exam. • Older Children & Adults (Milder Coarctation) ◦ Often asymptomatic and diagnosed incidentally due to hypertension or a murmur. ◦ May present with symptoms related to hypertension (headaches, epistaxis) or lower extremity hypoperfusion (claudication, cold feet).
sections.diagnostics: • Initial Evaluation ◦ Four-Limb Blood Pressure Measurement: Essential for diagnosis. Confirms the upper-to-lower extremity systolic gradient. ◦ ECG: ▪ May be normal. ▪ In significant cases, shows Left Ventricular Hypertrophy (LVH) (high voltage in precordial leads, left axis deviation). ◦ Chest X-ray (CXR): ▪ "Figure 3" Sign: The indentation of the aorta at the coarctation site with pre- and post-stenotic dilation gives the aortic knob a "3" shape. ▪ Rib Notching: Pathognomonic finding in older children/adults. Bilateral erosion of the inferior surfaces of the 3rd to 8th ribs by enlarged, pulsatile intercostal arteries. • Confirmatory & Definitive Diagnosis ◦ Echocardiogram (Transthoracic): Primary diagnostic tool. ▪ Directly visualizes the coarctation site. ▪ Assesses severity with Doppler (measures pressure gradient). ▪ Evaluates LV function and hypertrophy. ▪ Identifies associated anomalies like a bicuspid aortic valve. • Advanced Imaging (for surgical/interventional planning) ◦ CT Angiography (CTA) or MR Angiography (MRA): ▪ Provide excellent, detailed 3D anatomical images of the entire aorta, the coarctation segment, and the collateral circulation.
sections.prognosis: • With timely repair: Excellent. Most individuals can expect a normal life expectancy and quality of life. • Without repair: Poor. The mean age of death is around 35 years due to complications like heart failure, aortic rupture, or intracranial hemorrhage. • The most common long-term morbidity is systemic hypertension.

sections.overview:
• Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA) is a cyanotic congenital heart defect characterized by **ventriculoarterial discordance**.
	◦ The **aorta arises from the right ventricle (RV)** and the **pulmonary artery arises from the left ventricle (LV)**.
	◦ This creates two separate, parallel circulatory systems instead of a single series circuit.
		▪ Deoxygenated systemic venous blood is pumped back to the body by the RV via the aorta.
		▪ Oxygenated pulmonary venous blood is pumped back to the lungs by the LV via the pulmonary artery.
• This arrangement is incompatible with life unless there is mixing of blood between the two circuits through an associated defect such as an Atrial Septal Defect (ASD), Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD), or Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA).
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
	◦ The defect occurs during embryogenesis (weeks 3-8) due to the failure of the **aorticopulmonary (conotruncal) septum** to spiral correctly as it divides the truncus arteriosus into the aorta and pulmonary artery.
		▪ Instead of spiraling, it divides the vessels in a straight plane.
	◦ The exact cause is typically unknown and multifactorial.
• **Pathophysiology**
	◦ **Parallel Circulation**: Two independent circuits are formed.
		▪ **Systemic Circuit (Deoxygenated)**: Superior/Inferior Vena Cava → Right Atrium → Right Ventricle → Aorta → Systemic Circulation.
		▪ **Pulmonary Circuit (Oxygenated)**: Pulmonary Veins → Left Atrium → Left Ventricle → Pulmonary Artery → Lungs.
	◦ **Requirement for Mixing**: For survival, oxygenated blood must reach the systemic circulation and deoxygenated blood must reach the pulmonary circulation. This "mixing" occurs via shunts:
		▪ **Patent Foramen Ovale (PFO) / Atrial Septal Defect (ASD)**: Allows mixing at the atrial level.
		▪ **Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA)**: Allows mixing between the aorta and pulmonary artery.
		▪ **Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD)**: Allows mixing at the ventricular level.
	◦ The degree of cyanosis is inversely proportional to the amount of mixing. Poor mixing leads to profound hypoxemia and rapid clinical deterioration.
sections.epidemiology:
• Accounts for 5-7% of all congenital heart defects.
• It is the **most common cyanotic heart lesion presenting in the neonatal period** (first 30 days of life).
• Incidence is approximately 20-30 per 100,000 live births.
• There is a **male predominance** (approx. 3:1).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a **full-term male infant** who develops profound central **cyanosis** within the **first few hours of life**.
• The cyanosis is notable for being **unresponsive to supplemental oxygen**.
• The infant often appears otherwise well-developed and comfortable at rest ("**happy blue baby**") initially, but respiratory distress (tachypnea) develops as metabolic acidosis worsens.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Pulse Oximetry**: Low oxygen saturation, typically in the 70s-80s.
• **Hyperoxia Test**
	◦ The infant is placed on 100% inspired oxygen for 10 minutes.
	◦ A post-ductal (e.g., foot) PaO2 is measured.
	◦ In TGA, the PaO2 will show **minimal or no improvement** (typically remains <100 mmHg), distinguishing it from pulmonary causes of cyanosis.
• **Chest X-ray (CXR)**
	◦ Classic finding is the "**egg on a string**" appearance.
		▪ The "egg" is the cardiomegaly from RV enlargement.
		▪ The "string" is the narrow superior mediastinum due to the abnormal anteroposterior alignment of the great vessels and involution of the thymus.
	◦ Pulmonary vascular markings are often increased.
• **Electrocardiogram (ECG)**
	◦ Often normal in the newborn period.
	◦ May show **right axis deviation** and **right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH)** as the RV is the systemic ventricle.
• **Echocardiogram**
	◦ **Gold standard** for diagnosis.
	◦ Directly visualizes the aorta arising from the RV and the pulmonary artery from the LV.
	◦ Identifies the presence and size of associated defects (ASD, VSD, PDA) and assesses coronary artery anatomy, which is crucial for surgical planning.
• **Cardiac Catheterization**
	◦ Primarily therapeutic (**Balloon Atrial Septostomy**) rather than diagnostic.
sections.prognosis:
• **Untreated**: Uniformly fatal.
	◦ 90% mortality by 1 year of age.
• **Treated**: With successful arterial switch surgery, the long-term prognosis is excellent.
	◦ Survival rates are >95% at 20 years.
	◦ Most individuals lead normal, active lives but require lifelong surveillance.

sections.overview:
• Asthma is a chronic, heterogeneous inflammatory disorder of the airways characterized by **airway hyperresponsiveness** and **reversible airflow obstruction**
    ◦ The underlying inflammation leads to recurrent, episodic symptoms such as wheezing, dyspnea, chest tightness, and cough, particularly at night or in the early morning
    ◦ It is a common condition managed with a stepwise approach involving rescue and controller medications
sections.etiology:
• The pathophysiology is a complex interplay of genetic predisposition and environmental triggers, leading to three core features:
    ◦ **Airway Inflammation**
        ▪ The central feature of asthma
        ▪ Primarily driven by **T-helper 2 (Th2) lymphocytes**, which orchestrate an inflammatory cascade involving **eosinophils**, **mast cells**, and **IgE**
        ▪ Mast cell degranulation releases inflammatory mediators like histamine, leukotrienes, and prostaglandins, causing acute bronchoconstriction, mucus production, and vasodilation
        ▪ Eosinophils release proteins that damage airway epithelium
    ◦ **Airway Hyperresponsiveness (AHR)**
        ▪ An exaggerated bronchoconstrictor response to various stimuli (allergens, cold air, exercise, irritants)
        ▪ The inflamed airways are "twitchy" and constrict easily, leading to acute symptoms
    ◦ **Airway Obstruction**
        ▪ Caused by a combination of:
            ▪ **Bronchoconstriction**: Smooth muscle tightening around the airways
            ▪ **Airway Edema**: Swelling of the bronchial wall
            ▪ **Mucus Plugging**: Increased production of thick mucus
        ▪ This obstruction is characteristically **reversible**, either spontaneously or with treatment (e.g., a beta-2 agonist)
    ◦ **Airway Remodeling**
        ▪ In chronic, poorly controlled asthma, structural changes can occur (subepithelial fibrosis, smooth muscle hypertrophy), leading to a fixed, less reversible component of airway obstruction
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects ~8-10% of the U.S. population
• One of the most common chronic diseases of childhood
• **Childhood**: More common in boys
• **Adulthood**: More common in women
• Prevalence, morbidity, and mortality are higher in urban, low-income, and minority populations (particularly African American and Puerto Rican)
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients typically present with a history of episodic respiratory symptoms, ranging from mild, intermittent complaints to a life-threatening acute exacerbation (status asthmaticus)
    ◦ **Triggers**: Symptoms are often precipitated by specific triggers such as exercise, upper respiratory infections, cold air, allergens, or smoke
    ◦ **Diurnal Variation**: Symptoms are classically worse **at night** or in the **early morning hours**
    ◦ **Cough-Variant Asthma**: Some patients may present with a chronic, non-productive cough as their sole symptom
sections.diagnostics:
• **Spirometry (Pulmonary Function Tests - PFTs)**
    ◦ **Gold standard** for diagnosis
    ◦ Shows an **obstructive pattern**:
        ▪ Decreased Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 second (**FEV1**)
        ▪ Decreased **FEV1/FVC ratio** (typically < 0.70 or below the lower limit of normal)
    ◦ **Demonstration of Reversibility**
        ▪ A significant increase in FEV1 (**>12% AND >200 mL**) after administration of a short-acting bronchodilator (SABA) confirms the diagnosis
• **Bronchial Provocation Test**
    ◦ Used when spirometry is non-diagnostic but clinical suspicion remains high
    ◦ Patient inhales a bronchoconstricting agent (e.g., **methacholine** or histamine)
    ◦ A positive test is a **20% fall in FEV1** at a low concentration
    ◦ High negative predictive value
• **Peak Expiratory Flow (PEF) Meter**
    ◦ Excellent for **home monitoring** and assessing response to treatment, not for initial diagnosis
    ◦ A >20% diurnal variation is suggestive of asthma
• **Chest X-ray (CXR)**
    ◦ Often normal
    ◦ Primarily used to rule out other conditions (e.g., pneumonia, pneumothorax, foreign body)
    ◦ During a severe exacerbation, may show signs of **hyperinflation** (flattened diaphragms)
• **Arterial Blood Gas (ABG)**
    ◦ Reserved for severe exacerbations
    ◦ **Initially**: Hypoxemia (low PaO2) with respiratory alkalosis (low PaCO2) due to hyperventilation
    ◦ **Impending Respiratory Failure**: A **"normalizing" or elevated PaCO2** is an ominous sign indicating patient fatigue and imminent failure
• **Other**
    ◦ CBC may show eosinophilia; allergy testing can identify specific triggers
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent with proper diagnosis, education, and adherence to a management plan
• Mortality is rare but often preventable
• Many children experience remission during adolescence, although symptoms may return in adulthood
• Poorly controlled asthma can lead to a progressive decline in lung function

sections.overview: • Clinical diagnosis defined by a chronic productive cough for at least 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years, in a patient in whom other causes of chronic cough have been excluded. • A subtype of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) characterized by inflammation and mucus hypersecretion in the bronchial airways. • The classic phenotype is the "Blue Bloater," referring to: ◦ Cyanosis from hypoxemia. ◦ Peripheral edema from right heart failure.
sections.etiology: Etiology • The overwhelming cause is cigarette smoking (>90% of cases). • Other inhaled irritants: occupational dusts (coal, grain), chemical fumes, and significant indoor/outdoor air pollution. • Recurrent airway infections can contribute. • Rarely, genetic factors like alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (more commonly associated with emphysema but a risk for all COPD). Pathophysiology • Inhalation of Irritants: Chronic exposure to substances like tobacco smoke triggers a persistent inflammatory response in the large and small airways. • Airway Inflammation & Structural Changes: ◦ Goblet Cell Hyperplasia: The number of mucus-secreting goblet cells in the airway epithelium increases dramatically. ◦ Submucosal Gland Hypertrophy: The mucus-secreting glands in the submucosa enlarge. ◦ The Reid Index (ratio of the thickness of the submucosal gland layer to the bronchial wall thickness) is increased to >0.5 (normal is <0.4). • Mucus Hypersecretion & Impaired Clearance: ◦ Excessive, thick mucus is produced, which cannot be effectively cleared by damaged cilia (ciliary dysfunction). ◦ This leads to mucus plugging, narrowing the airway lumen. • Airflow Obstruction: ◦ The combination of inflammation, mucosal edema, and mucus plugging results in progressive, fixed (irreversible) airflow obstruction. • Gas Exchange Abnormalities: ◦ Obstruction leads to severe ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch. ◦ This results in chronic hypoxemia (low PaO2) and hypercapnia (high PaCO2), leading to respiratory acidosis. ◦ Chronic hypoxemia causes reflex pulmonary vasoconstriction, leading to pulmonary hypertension.
sections.epidemiology: • Prevalence: Affects millions of Americans; a major component of COPD, which is the 4th leading cause of death in the US. • Age: Onset typically after age 40. • Gender: Historically more common in men, but the incidence in women is rising and now nearly equal due to changes in smoking patterns.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • The classic patient is an overweight, cyanotic smoker in their 50s or 60s. • Presents with a chief complaint of a chronic, daily "smoker's cough" that produces phlegm, especially in the mornings. • Often reports frequent "chest colds" (acute exacerbations) each winter. • Dyspnea on exertion is common, but they may be comfortable at rest.
sections.diagnostics: • Pulmonary Function Tests (PFTs) / Spirometry: ◦ Gold standard for diagnosis of COPD. ◦ Required finding: Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio < 0.70. ▪ This confirms persistent airflow obstruction. ◦ FEV1 is decreased, and the degree of reduction is used for staging severity (GOLD Criteria). ◦ Increased Residual Volume (RV) and Total Lung Capacity (TLC) due to air trapping. • Chest X-Ray (CXR): ◦ Often nonspecific. May show increased bronchovascular markings ("dirty lungs") and bronchial wall thickening. ◦ Primarily used to rule out other conditions like pneumonia, lung cancer, or heart failure. ◦ Diaphragms are typically normal or rounded (not flattened like in emphysema). • Arterial Blood Gas (ABG): ◦ Reveals chronic respiratory acidosis: low PaO2 (hypoxemia), high PaCO2 (hypercapnia), and compensatory high HCO3-. • Complete Blood Count (CBC): ◦ May show polycythemia (elevated hemoglobin and hematocrit) as a result of chronic hypoxemia stimulating erythropoietin production. • Sputum Culture: ◦ Useful during acute exacerbations to identify bacterial pathogens if there is a poor response to initial therapy.
sections.prognosis: • Chronic bronchitis is a progressive, irreversible disease. • Prognosis is poor without smoking cessation. • The BODE Index (Body mass index, Obstruction [FEV1], Dyspnea [mMRC scale], Exercise capacity [6-minute walk test]) is a validated tool for predicting mortality. • FEV1 is a strong predictor of survival.

sections.overview:
• Emphysema is a major pathologic type of **Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)**
    ◦ Anatomically defined by the **permanent, abnormal enlargement of airspaces** distal to the terminal bronchioles, accompanied by the **destruction of their walls** and without obvious fibrosis
    ◦ This destruction leads to a loss of alveolar surface area for gas exchange and a **loss of elastic recoil**, resulting in expiratory airflow limitation and **air trapping**
    ◦ Clinically, it is characterized by progressive dyspnea
    ◦ The classic patient phenotype is the "**pink puffer**"
sections.etiology:
• The core pathophysiology is an imbalance between **proteases** (e.g., elastase) and **anti-proteases** (e.g., alpha-1 antitrypsin) in the lung
• **Cigarette Smoking (Most Common)**
    ◦ Inhaled irritants incite a chronic inflammatory response in the airways and parenchyma
    ◦ Inflammatory cells (neutrophils, macrophages) are recruited and release proteases, particularly **neutrophil elastase**, which break down elastin and other structural components of the alveolar walls
    ◦ **Oxidative stress** from smoke also inactivates native anti-proteases, tipping the balance toward destruction
    ◦ This process leads to **centriacinar (or centrilobular) emphysema**, which primarily affects the respiratory bronchioles and is most prominent in the **upper lobes**
• **Alpha-1 Antitrypsin (AAT) Deficiency (Genetic)**
    ◦ AAT is a protein produced in the liver that acts as a major inhibitor of neutrophil elastase in the lungs
    ◦ In AAT deficiency, there is an uninhibited breakdown of elastin by elastase, leading to early-onset, severe emphysema
    ◦ This process causes **panacinar (or panlobular) emphysema**, which involves the uniform destruction of the entire acinus and is most prominent in the **lower lobes**
    ◦ Suspect in non-smokers or patients presenting with emphysema at a **young age (<45 years)**. It can also be associated with **liver disease (cirrhosis)**
• **Key Pathophysiologic Consequences**
    ◦ **Loss of Elastic Recoil**: Leads to airway collapse during exhalation, causing airflow obstruction and air trapping
    ◦ **Destruction of Alveolar-Capillary Bed**: Reduces the surface area available for gas exchange, causing a **decreased DLCO** (Diffusing capacity for Carbon Monoxide)
    ◦ **Air Trapping**: Leads to chronic hyperinflation, manifesting as an increased **Total Lung Capacity (TLC)** and **Residual Volume (RV)**
sections.epidemiology:
• Emphysema is a component of COPD, which is the **4th leading cause of death** in the United States
• Prevalence increases with age, most commonly diagnosed in individuals **> 40 years old**
• Strongly associated with a cumulative history of **cigarette smoking** (measured in pack-years)
• AAT deficiency affects approximately 1 in 2,500-5,000 individuals and accounts for 1-2% of all COPD cases
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The "**Pink Puffer**" is the classic archetype for a patient with predominant emphysema
• **History**
    ◦ Long history of slowly progressive **dyspnea on exertion**, often present for years before seeking care
    ◦ May have a minimal, non-productive cough
• **General Appearance**
    ◦ Often thin with evidence of **weight loss (cachexia)** due to the high work of breathing
    ◦ Appears uncomfortable, often sitting in a **tripod position** (leaning forward, hands on knees) to maximize use of accessory respiratory muscles
• **Breathing Pattern**
    ◦ Uses **pursed-lip breathing** to increase intra-airway pressure and prevent premature airway collapse during expiration
    ◦ There is a **prolonged expiratory phase**
sections.diagnostics:
• **Pulmonary Function Tests (PFTs) / Spirometry**: **Gold standard for diagnosis**
    ◦ **Obstructive Pattern**: Decreased **FEV1/FVC ratio < 0.70** (post-bronchodilator) is required for diagnosis
    ◦ **Decreased FEV1**: Correlates with disease severity (GOLD staging)
    ◦ **Increased Lung Volumes**: Increased **Total Lung Capacity (TLC)**, **Functional Residual Capacity (FRC)**, and **Residual Volume (RV)** due to air trapping
    ◦ **Decreased Diffusing Capacity (DLCO)**: A key finding that distinguishes emphysema from pure chronic bronchitis or asthma, caused by the destruction of the alveolar-capillary membrane
• **Chest X-Ray (CXR)**
    ◦ **Hyperinflation**: Over-aeration of the lungs
    ◦ **Flattened Diaphragms**
    ◦ Increased AP diameter (seen on lateral view)
    ◦ **Bullae** (lucent, air-filled spaces >1 cm)
    ◦ Small, vertical-appearing heart ("hanging heart")
• **High-Resolution CT (HRCT) Chest**
    ◦ Most sensitive and specific imaging modality
    ◦ Directly visualizes parenchymal destruction and bullae
    ◦ Can differentiate between centriacinar and panacinar patterns
• **Arterial Blood Gas (ABG)**
    ◦ Early/Mild: May be normal or show mild hypoxemia
    ◦ Advanced: **Chronic respiratory acidosis** with metabolic compensation (↑ PaCO2, ↑ HCO3-, near-normal pH)
• **Alpha-1 Antitrypsin (AAT) Level**
    ◦ Screen all patients diagnosed with COPD, especially those **< 45 years old**, non-smokers, or with a basilar-predominant pattern of emphysema
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is generally poor and the disease is progressive
• **FEV1** is a strong predictor of mortality
• **BODE Index** is a multidimensional scoring system that is a better predictor of mortality than FEV1 alone:
    ◦ **B**ody Mass Index (BMI)
    ◦ **O**bstruction (FEV1)
    ◦ **D**yspnea (mMRC scale)
    ◦ **E**xercise capacity (6-minute walk test)

sections.overview:
• Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is a common, preventable, and treatable disease characterized by **persistent respiratory symptoms** and **airflow limitation** due to airway and/or alveolar abnormalities, usually caused by significant exposure to noxious particles or gases.
    ◦ The airflow limitation is **not fully reversible**.
    ◦ COPD includes two primary phenotypes that often coexist:
        ▪ **Emphysema:** Pathologic diagnosis defined by the permanent enlargement of airspaces distal to the terminal bronchioles, accompanied by the destruction of their walls and without obvious fibrosis.
        ▪ **Chronic Bronchitis:** Clinical diagnosis defined by a chronic productive cough for **three months in each of two successive years** in a patient in whom other causes of chronic cough have been excluded.
sections.etiology:
• The underlying mechanism is a chronic, abnormal inflammatory response of the lungs to noxious stimuli.
• **Emphysema ("Pink Puffer")**
    ◦ **Pathophysiology:**
        ▪ Noxious particles (e.g., cigarette smoke) incite an inflammatory response, leading to an increase in proteases (e.g., elastase) and a decrease in anti-proteases (e.g., alpha-1 antitrypsin).
        ▪ This imbalance leads to the **destruction of alveolar walls and capillary beds**.
        ▪ The loss of alveolar walls results in decreased surface area for gas exchange and, critically, a **loss of elastic recoil**.
        ▪ Loss of elastic recoil causes **airway collapse during exhalation**, leading to air trapping and hyperinflation.
    ◦ **Etiology:**
        ▪ **Cigarette smoking** is the overwhelming cause.
        ▪ **Alpha-1 Antitrypsin (AAT) Deficiency:** A genetic disorder that leads to a lack of protective anti-protease, causing premature, panacinar emphysema, often in younger patients (<45) and non-smokers.
• **Chronic Bronchitis ("Blue Bloater")**
    ◦ **Pathophysiology:**
        ▪ Chronic inflammation of the airways leads to **mucous gland hypertrophy and goblet cell hyperplasia**.
        ▪ This results in excessive mucus production and secretion.
        ▪ Ciliary function is impaired, preventing effective mucus clearance.
        ▪ The combination of mucus plugging and inflammation narrows the airways, leading to obstruction.
    ◦ **Etiology:**
        ▪ **Cigarette smoking** is the most common cause.
        ▪ Occupational dusts, chemicals, and environmental pollution are also contributors.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** 3rd leading cause of death worldwide.
• **Age:** Disease prevalence increases with age; rarely diagnosed in patients <40 years old.
• **Gender:** Historically more common in men, but rates are now nearly equal due to changes in smoking patterns.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation is typically insidious, with a gradual progression of symptoms over years.
• Patients are often former or current smokers over the age of 40.
• The classic phenotypes are useful for understanding pathophysiology but patients often present with a mix of features.
• **Emphysema-Dominant ("Pink Puffer")**:
    ◦ **Primary Symptom:** Severe dyspnea, often with minimal cough.
    ◦ **Appearance:** Thin, cachectic, barrel-chested.
    ◦ **Breathing:** Uses accessory muscles, breathes through pursed lips to maintain airway pressure ("auto-PEEP").
    ◦ **ABG:** Often maintain normal oxygenation (PaO2) and CO2 levels (PaCO2) until late-stage disease by increasing minute ventilation (hence "puffer").
• **Chronic Bronchitis-Dominant ("Blue Bloater")**:
    ◦ **Primary Symptom:** Chronic, productive cough.
    ◦ **Appearance:** Often overweight and cyanotic.
    ◦ **Signs:** Peripheral edema (due to cor pulmonale), noisy lungs with rhonchi and wheezes.
    ◦ **ABG:** Chronic hypoxemia and hypercapnia are common due to severe V/Q mismatch. This drives pulmonary vasoconstriction and polycythemia (hence "blue").
sections.diagnostics:
• **Pulmonary Function Tests (PFTs) / Spirometry:**
    ◦ **THE GOLD STANDARD for diagnosis**.
    ◦ A post-bronchodilator **FEV1/FVC ratio < 0.70** confirms the presence of persistent airflow limitation and thus COPD.
    ◦ **FEV1 (Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 second):** Decreased. The severity of obstruction is classified based on the post-bronchodilator FEV1 % predicted (GOLD stages 1-4).
    ◦ **Lung Volumes:**
        ▪ Increased Total Lung Capacity (TLC) and Residual Volume (RV) indicate air trapping/hyperinflation.
        ▪ Decreased Diffusing Capacity for Carbon Monoxide (DLCO) is characteristic of emphysema due to alveolar destruction.
• **Chest X-Ray (CXR):**
    ◦ Not diagnostic but used to rule out other pathology.
    ◦ **Classic Findings:**
        ▪ **Flattened diaphragms**
        ▪ Increased AP diameter on lateral view
        ▪ Hyperlucency of lung fields
        ▪ Bullae (lucent, air-filled spaces)
• **Arterial Blood Gas (ABG):**
    ◦ Not routine for stable patients.
    ◦ Assesses for hypoxemia and hypercapnia in severe disease or acute exacerbations.
    ◦ **Findings:** Chronic respiratory acidosis (elevated PaCO2) with metabolic compensation (elevated HCO3-).
• **CBC:**
    ◦ May show **polycythemia** (increased hematocrit/hemoglobin) as a response to chronic hypoxemia.
• **Alpha-1 Antitrypsin (AAT) Level:**
    ◦ Screen in patients diagnosed at a young age (<45), non-smokers, or with a strong family history.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is generally poor and the disease is progressive.
• The **BODE Index** is a validated tool for predicting mortality:
    ◦ **B**MI (lower is worse)
    ◦ **O**bstruction (FEV1)
    ◦ **D**yspnea (mMRC scale)
    ◦ **E**xercise capacity (6-minute walk test)
• Frequent exacerbations are associated with a faster decline in lung function and higher mortality.

sections.overview:
• A chronic pulmonary disease characterized by **permanent, irreversible dilation and destruction of the bronchial airways**.
	◦ This structural damage impairs mucociliary clearance, leading to a "vicious cycle" of chronic bacterial infection, airway inflammation, and further structural damage.
	◦ It is classified as an **obstructive lung disease**.
sections.etiology:
• **"Vicious Cycle" Hypothesis** is the underlying mechanism:
	◦ **Initial Insult**: An event (e.g., severe infection, obstruction) damages the airway walls and cilia.
	◦ **Impaired Mucociliary Clearance**: Damaged cilia cannot effectively clear mucus, which then pools in the dilated airways.
	◦ **Chronic Bacterial Colonization/Infection**: Stagnant mucus provides a rich environment for bacterial growth (e.g., *H. influenzae*, *P. aeruginosa*).
	◦ **Neutrophilic Inflammation**: The host immune response releases proteases and inflammatory mediators.
	◦ **Further Airway Damage**: Inflammatory products cause further destruction of cilia, cartilage, and smooth muscle, worsening the condition.
	◦ The cycle repeats, leading to progressive disease.
• **Common Etiologies**:
	◦ **Cystic Fibrosis (CF)**: The single most common cause of severe bronchiectasis in the United States; always consider in young patients.
	◦ **Post-Infectious**: The most common cause of non-CF bronchiectasis.
		▪ Severe childhood pneumonia (e.g., Measles, Pertussis, Adenovirus)
		▪ Tuberculosis (TB)
		▪ Nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM), especially *Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC)*
	◦ **Immunodeficiency**:
		▪ Common Variable Immunodeficiency (CVID)
		▪ Hypogammaglobulinemia
	◦ **Congenital / Genetic (Non-CF)**:
		▪ **Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia (PCD)**: Includes Kartagener's syndrome (situs inversus, chronic sinusitis, bronchiectasis).
		▪ **Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency**
	◦ **Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis (ABPA)**: A hypersensitivity reaction to *Aspergillus fumigatus*, typically in patients with asthma or CF, causing central bronchiectasis.
	◦ **Autoimmune Diseases**:
		▪ Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
		▪ Sjögren's Syndrome
	◦ **Focal Airway Obstruction**:
		▪ Tumor
		▪ Aspirated foreign body
		▪ Bronchial stenosis
	◦ **Idiopathic**: No identifiable cause is found in ~25-50% of cases.
sections.epidemiology:
• Prevalence is increasing, particularly in older adults.
• More common in women than men.
• Non-CF bronchiectasis is more common than CF-related bronchiectasis overall.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Typically presents with a long history of:
	◦ **Persistent productive cough**
	◦ Recurrent respiratory infections ("chest colds") that are slow to resolve, often requiring multiple or prolonged courses of antibiotics.
	◦ Daily sputum production, which may sometimes be tinged with blood.
sections.diagnostics:
• **High-Resolution Computed Tomography (HRCT) of the chest**:
	◦ This is the **diagnostic test of choice**.
	◦ **Key Findings**:
		▪ **Bronchial wall thickening and dilation**: Airways appear larger than the adjacent pulmonary artery (**"signet ring" sign**).
		▪ **Lack of airway tapering**: Bronchi remain wide in the lung periphery.
		▪ Parallel bronchial walls that look like linear opacities (**"tram tracks"**).
		▪ Visible cysts or saccules, sometimes with air-fluid levels.
• **Chest X-ray (CXR)**:
	◦ Often the first imaging test performed but is insensitive and non-specific.
	◦ May show "tram tracks," cystic changes, or increased interstitial markings, but a normal CXR does not rule out bronchiectasis.
• **Pulmonary Function Tests (PFTs)**:
	◦ Show an **obstructive pattern**: decreased FEV1, decreased FEV1/FVC ratio (<0.70).
	◦ Unlike asthma, there is often little to no reversibility with bronchodilators.
• **Sputum Analysis**:
	◦ **Crucial for management**, especially during exacerbations.
	◦ Gram stain and culture to identify bacterial pathogens (e.g., *H. influenzae*, *P. aeruginosa*, *S. aureus*, *M. catarrhalis*).
	◦ AFB smear and culture to test for TB and NTM (especially MAC).
• **Etiology Workup (once diagnosed)**:
	◦ **Sweat chloride test / CFTR genetic testing** (to rule out CF).
	◦ Quantitative immunoglobulin levels (to rule out CVID).
	◦ *Aspergillus* skin testing, precipitins, and total IgE (for ABPA).
	◦ Alpha-1 antitrypsin level.
sections.prognosis:
• A chronic, progressive disease with no cure.
• Prognosis is highly variable and depends on the underlying etiology, severity of lung damage, and frequency of exacerbations.
• Negative prognostic factors include:
	◦ Older age
	◦ Low FEV1
	◦ Chronic colonization with ***Pseudomonas aeruginosa***

sections.overview:
• **Cystic Fibrosis (CF)** is an **autosomal recessive** genetic disorder caused by mutations in the Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator (*CFTR*) gene
• The defect leads to impaired transport of chloride, bicarbonate, and water across epithelial surfaces, resulting in **thick, viscous secretions** in multiple organ systems
• It is a progressive, multi-system disease primarily affecting the respiratory, gastrointestinal (pancreas, liver, intestines), and reproductive tracts
sections.etiology:
• **Genetics**: Mutation in the *CFTR* gene on the long arm of **chromosome 7**
• **Inheritance**: **Autosomal recessive**; an individual must inherit two mutated copies (one from each carrier parent)
• **Most Common Mutation**: **F508del** (a deletion of phenylalanine at position 508) accounts for ~70% of mutations worldwide
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The CFTR protein is an ATP-gated anion channel responsible for transporting chloride and bicarbonate ions out of epithelial cells
    ◦ A defective CFTR protein results in decreased chloride secretion and increased sodium and water reabsorption
    ◦ This dehydrates the mucus layer lining epithelial surfaces, making secretions abnormally thick and sticky
    ◦ **Lungs**: Thick mucus obstructs airways, impairs mucociliary clearance, and creates a favorable environment for chronic bacterial infection and inflammation. This cycle of obstruction -> infection -> inflammation leads to irreversible lung damage (**bronchiectasis**) and eventual respiratory failure
    ◦ **Pancreas**: Thick secretions block pancreatic ducts, preventing digestive enzymes from reaching the small intestine
        ▪ Causes **exocrine pancreatic insufficiency**, leading to maldigestion and malabsorption of fats and proteins
        ▪ Over time, fibrosis can also damage endocrine islets, leading to **CF-related diabetes (CFRD)**
    ◦ **Intestines**
        ▪ Newborns: Abnormally thick intestinal contents can cause **meconium ileus**
        ▪ Older individuals: Can cause **distal intestinal obstruction syndrome (DIOS)**
    ◦ **Hepatobiliary System**: Blockage of bile ducts can lead to focal biliary cirrhosis and portal hypertension
    ◦ **Reproductive Tract**
        ▪ In >95% of males, thick secretions during development lead to **congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens (CBAVD)**, causing obstructive azoospermia and infertility
        ▪ Females may have reduced fertility due to thickened cervical mucus
    ◦ **Sweat Glands**: Defective CFTR channel leads to failure of chloride reabsorption, resulting in excessively high salt content in sweat, which is the basis for the diagnostic sweat test
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: The **most common life-shortening inherited disease among Caucasians** of Northern European descent
• **Incidence**: Approximately 1 in 3,000 live births in the Caucasian population
• **Carrier Frequency**: ~1 in 25 Caucasians
• **Screening**: Included in standard newborn screening panels in all 50 U.S. states
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation varies significantly with age and genotype
• **Newborns/Infants**
    ◦ **Meconium ileus**: Bowel obstruction in a newborn who fails to pass stool
    ◦ **Failure to thrive**: Poor weight gain despite adequate appetite
    ◦ **Steatorrhea**: Frequent, greasy, foul-smelling stools
    ◦ Recurrent respiratory infections, persistent cough
    ◦ Salty-tasting skin
• **Children/Adolescents**
    ◦ Chronic sinopulmonary disease: persistent productive cough, recurrent pneumonia, chronic sinusitis, **nasal polyps**
    ◦ GI symptoms: Poor growth, constipation, **rectal prolapse** (from straining and malnutrition), DIOS
    ◦ Physical signs: **Digital clubbing**
• **Adults**
    ◦ Often present with milder or "atypical" CF
    ◦ May be diagnosed due to chronic pancreatitis, bronchiectasis of unknown cause, or infertility (especially males with CBAVD)
sections.diagnostics:
• **Newborn Screen (NBS)**
    ◦ **Purpose**: Initial screening
    ◦ **Findings**: Elevated **Immunoreactive Trypsinogen (IRT)**
• **Sweat Chloride Test**
    ◦ **Purpose**: **Gold standard** for diagnosis
    ◦ **Findings**: **>60 mmol/L** on two separate occasions is diagnostic; 30-59 mmol/L is intermediate
• **CFTR Genetic Analysis**
    ◦ **Purpose**: Confirmatory testing, identifies mutations
    ◦ **Findings**: Identifies two disease-causing *CFTR* mutations; essential for guiding CFTR modulator therapy
• **Pulmonary Function Tests (PFTs)**
    ◦ **Purpose**: Assess lung function & disease progression
    ◦ **Findings**: **Obstructive pattern** (↓ FEV1, ↓ FEV1/FVC ratio); Air trapping (↑ RV/TLC ratio)
• **Chest Imaging (CXR/CT)**
    ◦ **Purpose**: Assess structural lung damage
    ◦ **Findings**: Hyperinflation, mucus plugging, bronchial wall thickening (**bronchial cuffing**), **bronchiectasis** ("tram tracks")
• **Sputum Culture**
    ◦ **Purpose**: Identify pathogens for targeted therapy
    ◦ **Findings**: Common pathogens include ***S. aureus*** and ***H. influenzae*** (early); ***P. aeruginosa*** (later); ***B. cepacia*** (ominous)
• **Fecal Elastase-1**
    ◦ **Purpose**: Screen for exocrine pancreatic insufficiency
    ◦ **Findings**: **Low** (<200 mcg/g) indicates insufficiency
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis has improved dramatically; the median predicted survival age in the U.S. is now in the **early 50s** and continues to increase, especially with the widespread use of CFTR modulators
• The primary cause of mortality remains progressive respiratory failure

sections.overview:
• A **Pulmonary Embolism (PE)** is an obstruction of the pulmonary artery or one of its branches by a substance (**thrombus**, air, fat, amniotic fluid, or septic embolus) that has traveled from elsewhere in the body through the bloodstream.
    ◦ The vast majority of PEs are caused by a thrombus that originates in the deep venous system of the lower extremities (**Deep Vein Thrombosis - DVT**).
    ◦ PE is a common, life-threatening condition and is considered a part of the spectrum of **Venous Thromboembolism (VTE)**.
sections.etiology:
• **Source:**
    ◦ Over 90% of PEs arise from **DVTs** in the iliac, femoral, or popliteal veins.
    ◦ Upper extremity DVTs (often associated with central lines) are a less common source.
• **Pathophysiology:**
    ◦ Governed by **Virchow's Triad**:
        ▪ **Venous Stasis:** Slowing of blood flow (e.g., prolonged immobilization, surgery, long-haul travel).
        ▪ **Hypercoagulability:** An imbalance in clotting factors favoring thrombosis (e.g., malignancy, oral contraceptives, inherited thrombophilias).
        ▪ **Endothelial Injury:** Damage to the blood vessel wall (e.g., surgery, trauma, catheter placement).
• **Physiologic Consequences:**
    ◦ **Ventilation/Perfusion (V/Q) Mismatch:** The embolus blocks perfusion to a lung region that is still being ventilated, creating "**dead space**." This is the primary cause of **hypoxemia**.
    ◦ **Pulmonary Vascular Resistance (PVR) Increase:** The physical obstruction and release of vasoconstrictive mediators (serotonin, thromboxane) increase **PVR**.
    ◦ **Right Ventricular (RV) Strain:** The increased PVR leads to increased RV afterload. Severe strain can cause **RV dilation and dysfunction**, leading to decreased cardiac output and **obstructive shock**.
sections.epidemiology:
• Third most common cause of cardiovascular death after **myocardial infarction** and **stroke**.
• Incidence is approximately 1 per 1,000 persons per year.
• Mortality is high (~30%) if untreated but drops to <8% with prompt and appropriate treatment.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Strong Risk Factors:**
    ◦ Fracture (hip or leg)
    ◦ Hip or knee replacement surgery
    ◦ Major general surgery
    ◦ Major trauma
    ◦ Spinal cord injury
• **Moderate Risk Factors:**
    ◦ Previous VTE
    ◦ Malignancy (especially active cancer)
    ◦ Immobilization (e.g., bed rest, long-distance travel >4 hours)
    ◦ Central venous catheters
    ◦ Inherited thrombophilias (Factor V Leiden, Prothrombin gene mutation, Protein C/S deficiency)
    ◦ Pregnancy and the postpartum period
    ◦ Estrogen-containing medications (OCPs, HRT)
• **Weak Risk Factors:**
    ◦ Obesity
    ◦ Age > 50
    ◦ Varicose veins
    ◦ Smoking
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation of PE is notoriously variable, ranging from asymptomatic to sudden death.
• It is a great "mimicker" of other cardiopulmonary diseases.
• The hallmark is the **acute/sudden onset** of symptoms in a patient with risk factors.
• **Dyspnea:** Most common symptom (~75-85%). Often sudden in onset.
• **Pleuritic Chest Pain:** Common (~50-65%). Sharp, stabbing pain worse with inspiration.
• **Cough:** (~40-50%)
• **Hemoptysis:** Less common (~10-15%), but a classic finding. Suggests **pulmonary infarction**.
• **Symptoms of DVT:** Unilateral leg pain, swelling, erythema (~30-40%).
• **Syncope/Presyncope:** A sign of a massive PE causing hemodynamic instability.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Tachypnea (RR > 20):** Most common physical exam finding.
• **Tachycardia (HR > 100):** Very common.
• **Hypoxemia (SpO2 < 95%):** Common but not universal.
• **Findings of DVT:** Unilateral lower extremity edema, tenderness, palpable cord, positive Homan's sign (unreliable).
• **Lungs:** Often clear to auscultation. Can have crackles or a pleural friction rub.
• **Cardiovascular:** An accentuated **P2 component** of the second heart sound (S2) may indicate pulmonary hypertension/RV strain.
• **Signs of Massive PE:** **Hypotension** (SBP < 90 mmHg), **jugular venous distention (JVD)**, **cyanosis**.
sections.diagnostics: • The diagnostic approach is guided by **pre-test probability** (clinical suspicion).
sections.management:
• **Disposition:** Use a risk stratification score like the **Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index (PESI)** or simplified PESI (sPESI) to determine if a patient can be managed as an outpatient (low-risk) or requires admission.
• **Duration of Anticoagulation:**
    ◦ **Provoked PE** (transient risk factor like surgery, travel): **3 months**.
    ◦ **Unprovoked PE** (no identifiable risk factor): At least 3 months, often followed by consideration for **extended/indefinite** therapy.
    ◦ **PE in a patient with active cancer:** **Extended/indefinite** therapy (**LMWH** is historically preferred, but **DOACs** are now also used).
sections.complications:
• **Acute:**
    ◦ **Right ventricular failure (Acute Cor Pulmonale)**
    ◦ **Obstructive Shock**
    ◦ **Cardiopulmonary arrest** and **sudden death**
• **Chronic:**
    ◦ **Chronic Thromboembolic Pulmonary Hypertension (CTEPH):** Persistent PVR elevation due to unresolved clot, leading to progressive right heart failure.
    ◦ **Post-PE Syndrome:** Persistent dyspnea and functional limitation despite adequate anticoagulation.
sections.prognosis:
• Highly dependent on the size of the embolus and the patient's underlying cardiopulmonary status.
• Mortality for **massive PE** can be >50%.
• Mortality for hemodynamically stable PE treated appropriately is low (<5%).
• Evidence of **RV dysfunction** on echo or elevated **cardiac biomarkers** worsens the prognosis even in normotensive patients.

sections.overview:
• Pulmonary Hypertension (PH) is a pathophysiological state defined by an elevated mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mPAP) of **> 20 mmHg at rest**, determined by right heart catheterization.
    ◦ It is a hemodynamic condition, not a single disease, resulting from numerous underlying causes.
    ◦ Leads to increased pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR), progressive right ventricular (RV) overload, and eventual right heart failure (**cor pulmonale**), which is the primary cause of death.
    ◦ The World Health Organization (WHO) classifies PH into 5 distinct groups based on etiology, which is critical for guiding diagnosis and treatment.
sections.etiology:
• The central pathophysiologic mechanism involves **vasoconstriction, vascular remodeling** (smooth muscle and endothelial cell proliferation), and **in-situ thrombosis** of the small pulmonary arteries and arterioles, leading to a progressive increase in PVR and mPAP.
    ◦ A key feature is endothelial dysfunction, resulting in an imbalance between vasodilators (e.g., nitric oxide, prostacyclin) and vasoconstrictors (e.g., endothelin-1, thromboxane A2).
• **WHO Classification System (Crucial for Boards):**
    ◦ **Group 1: Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (PAH)**
        ▪ Pathology is confined to the pulmonary arterioles ("**pre-capillary**").
        ▪ **Subtypes:**
            • **Idiopathic (IPAH):** No identifiable cause.
            • **Heritable (HPAH):** Often due to mutations in the *BMPR2* gene.
            • **Drug-and-Toxin-Induced:** Methamphetamines, "fen-phen," Dasatinib.
            • **Associated with (APAH):**
                ◦ **Connective Tissue Disease (CTD):** Most commonly **scleroderma (systemic sclerosis)**.
                ◦ **HIV infection**
                ◦ **Portal hypertension**
                ◦ **Congenital heart disease** (with shunts)
                ◦ **Schistosomiasis**
    ◦ **Group 2: PH due to Left Heart Disease**
        ▪ **The most common cause of PH overall.**
        ▪ Pathophysiology is "**post-capillary**," resulting from passive back-pressure from the failing left heart.
        ▪ **Causes:** Left ventricular systolic or diastolic dysfunction (HFrEF, HFpEF), valvular disease (e.g., mitral stenosis/regurgitation).
    ◦ **Group 3: PH due to Chronic Lung Disease and/or Hypoxia**
        ▪ Pathophysiology is driven by hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction.
        ▪ **Causes:** COPD, Interstitial Lung Disease (ILD), Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA), living at high altitude.
    ◦ **Group 4: Chronic Thromboembolic Pulmonary Hypertension (CTEPH)**
        ▪ Caused by unresolved or recurrent pulmonary emboli that organize into fibrous obstructions in the pulmonary arteries.
        ▪ **This is the only potentially curable form of PH** (via surgery).
    ◦ **Group 5: PH with Unclear or Multifactorial Mechanisms**
        ▪ A miscellaneous group.
        ▪ **Causes:** Hematologic disorders (e.g., sickle cell disease), systemic disorders (e.g., sarcoidosis), metabolic disorders.
sections.epidemiology:
• Overall prevalence is significant, but Group 1 PAH is rare (approx. 15-50 cases per million).
• Group 2 PH (due to LHD) is the most prevalent form.
• Group 1 PAH shows a female predominance (~2:1) and typically presents in young to middle-aged adults (30-60 years).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation is often insidious, with non-specific symptoms leading to a significant delay in diagnosis (average >2 years).
    ◦ The classic patient is a young-to-middle-aged female presenting with progressive, unexplained **dyspnea on exertion**.
    ◦ As the disease progresses, signs of **right heart failure** become more prominent.
sections.diagnostics:
• The diagnostic workup is aimed at confirming the presence of PH, identifying the WHO group, and assessing severity.
• **Best Initial Test (Screening): Transthoracic Echocardiogram (TTE)**
    ◦ Estimates the right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) and pulmonary artery pressure.
    ◦ Assesses RV size, thickness, and function.
    ◦ Evaluates for left heart disease (Group 2) or congenital defects.
• **Gold Standard (Confirmatory): Right Heart Catheterization (RHC)**
    ◦ **Required for definitive diagnosis** and to guide therapy.
    ◦ Directly measures:
        ▪ Mean Pulmonary Arterial Pressure (mPAP)
        ▪ Pulmonary Capillary Wedge Pressure (PCWP) - an estimate of left atrial pressure.
        ▪ Pulmonary Vascular Resistance (PVR)
        ▪ Cardiac Output (CO)
    ◦ **Hemodynamic Definitions:**
        ▪ **PH:** mPAP > 20 mmHg
        ▪ **Pre-capillary PH (Groups 1, 3, 4, 5):** mPAP > 20, **PCWP ≤ 15 mmHg**, PVR ≥ 3 Wood units.
