        ▪ **Post-capillary PH (Group 2):** mPAP > 20, **PCWP > 15 mmHg**.
• **Tests to Determine Etiology (WHO Group):**
    ◦ **Chest X-Ray (CXR):** May show enlarged central pulmonary arteries ("pruning" of peripheral vessels) and RV enlargement (cardiomegaly).
    ◦ **ECG:** May be normal or show signs of RV hypertrophy (right axis deviation, R wave in V1 > S wave) and RV strain (T wave inversions in V1-V3, inferior leads).
    ◦ **V/Q Scan:** **Screening test of choice for CTEPH (Group 4).** Preferred over CTPA for chronic clots.
    ◦ **Pulmonary Function Tests (PFTs):** To diagnose underlying lung disease (Group 3). Often shows a reduced DLCO.
    ◦ **Labs:** CBC, CMP, LFTs, HIV test, ANA panel (for CTD), BNP/NT-proBNP (prognostic marker).
sections.prognosis:
• Without treatment, idiopathic PAH has a very poor prognosis with a median survival of <3 years.
• With modern therapies, the prognosis has significantly improved, but it remains a life-limiting chronic illness.
• Prognosis for other groups is largely determined by the severity and management of the underlying condition.

sections.overview:
• Cor pulmonale is defined as **right ventricular (RV) hypertrophy and/or dilation and dysfunction** caused by **pulmonary hypertension (PH)**
    ◦ PH results from a primary disease of the **lung parenchyma, vasculature, or chest wall**
    ◦ Crucially, it is **NOT** caused by left-sided heart failure or congenital heart disease
    ◦ It represents right-sided heart failure secondary purely to a pulmonary process
• **Acute Cor Pulmonale**
    ◦ RV dilation and failure following a sudden increase in pulmonary artery pressure (e.g., massive **pulmonary embolism**)
• **Chronic Cor Pulmonale**
    ◦ Gradual RV hypertrophy and subsequent dilation due to a slowly progressing underlying lung condition (e.g., **COPD**)
sections.etiology:
• The core pathophysiologic mechanism is **pulmonary hypertension (PH)**, which increases the afterload against which the right ventricle must pump
• **Pathophysiologic Cascade**
    ◦ **Underlying Lung Disease**: A disorder of the lungs, chest wall, or pulmonary vasculature is the starting point
    ◦ **Increased Pulmonary Vascular Resistance (PVR)**: Occurs via two main mechanisms
        ▪ **Hypoxic Pulmonary Vasoconstriction**: Alveolar hypoxia (common in COPD, ILD) causes constriction of small pulmonary arteries to shunt blood away from poorly ventilated areas. Chronic hypoxia leads to sustained, widespread vasoconstriction.
        ▪ **Parenchymal Destruction**: Diseases like emphysema or fibrosis destroy the alveolar septa and associated capillary beds, reducing the total cross-sectional area of the pulmonary vasculature.
    ◦ **Pulmonary Hypertension**: The sustained increase in PVR leads to elevated pressures within the pulmonary arteries (defined as mean PAP ≥ 25 mmHg at rest)
    ◦ **Right Ventricular Strain**: The RV, a thin-walled chamber designed for a low-pressure system, must now pump against high resistance
    ◦ **RV Compensation (Hypertrophy)**: To overcome the increased afterload, the RV myocardium thickens (concentric hypertrophy)
    ◦ **RV Decompensation (Dilation & Failure)**: Over time, the sustained pressure overload overwhelms the RV's compensatory ability, leading to dilation, impaired contractility, and overt right-sided heart failure
• **Most Common Causes**
    ◦ **Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)**: The single most common cause of cor pulmonale
    ◦ **Interstitial Lung Disease (ILD)** (e.g., idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis)
    ◦ **Chronic Thromboembolic Pulmonary Hypertension (CTEPH)**: Recurrent or unresolved pulmonary emboli
    ◦ **Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) / Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome (Pickwickian Syndrome)**: Causes chronic intermittent hypoxia
    ◦ **Cystic Fibrosis**
    ◦ **Chest Wall Deformities**: Severe kyphoscoliosis
    ◦ **Primary Pulmonary Hypertension / Idiopathic Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (IPAH)**
sections.epidemiology:
• Difficult to determine precise incidence as it is a complication of other diseases
• The prevalence directly mirrors that of its underlying causes, especially **COPD**
• Estimated to account for 5-10% of all hospital admissions for heart failure
• Predominantly affects older adults, consistent with the demographics of chronic lung disease
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is often insidious, with symptoms of right heart failure superimposed on the symptoms of the underlying chronic lung disease
• Patients typically present with a gradual worsening of their baseline respiratory status, now with new or worsening signs of fluid overload
sections.diagnostics:
• **ECG**
    ◦ **P pulmonale**: Peaked P waves (>2.5 mm) in inferior leads (II, III, aVF) indicating right atrial enlargement
    ◦ **Right Axis Deviation**
    ◦ **RV Hypertrophy**: R wave > S wave in lead V1; deep S wave in V6
    ◦ **S1Q3T3 pattern** (seen in acute cor pulmonale/PE)
• **Chest X-ray (CXR)**
    ◦ Enlargement of the right atrium, right ventricle, and central pulmonary arteries
    ◦ "**Pruning**" of the peripheral pulmonary vessels
    ◦ Evidence of the underlying lung disease (e.g., hyperinflation, flattened diaphragms in COPD)
• **Echocardiogram (Transthoracic)**
    ◦ **Best initial imaging test** to assess cardiac structure
    ◦ Shows **RV hypertrophy, RV dilation**, and paradoxical septal motion
    ◦ Allows for estimation of the **pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PASP)**
    ◦ Crucially helps **rule out left-sided heart disease** as the cause of the RHF
• **BNP / NT-proBNP**
    ◦ Elevated due to ventricular stretch but is **not specific** for cor pulmonale; can be elevated in any cause of heart failure
• **Right Heart Catheterization**
    ◦ **Gold standard** for diagnosing pulmonary hypertension and confirming cor pulmonale
    ◦ Directly measures pulmonary artery pressure (mean PAP ≥ 25 mmHg at rest)
    ◦ Measures pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP)
        ▪ A **normal PCWP (≤ 15 mmHg)** confirms the PH is **pre-capillary** (i.e., from the lungs) and rules out left heart failure as the cause
• **Other**
    ◦ **PFTs**: To diagnose and quantify the severity of the underlying lung disease
    ◦ **CT Angiography / V/Q Scan**: To evaluate for chronic thromboembolic disease (**CTEPH**)
    ◦ **Sleep Study (Polysomnography)**: If OSA is suspected
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is generally **poor** as cor pulmonale represents an advanced stage of chronic pulmonary disease
• The prognosis is tied directly to the severity and progression of the underlying lung condition
• The presence of cor pulmonale is a significant negative prognostic indicator in patients with COPD
• Median survival after diagnosis can be as low as 2-5 years, but this is highly variable

sections.overview:
• **Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP)** is an acute infection of the pulmonary parenchyma in a patient who has acquired the infection in the community, as distinguished from hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP).
    ◦ Diagnosis is established by the presence of a **new pulmonary infiltrate** on chest imaging combined with clinical signs and symptoms of a lower respiratory tract infection.
    ◦ The decision to treat as an outpatient or inpatient is a critical management step, often guided by clinical scoring systems like **CURB-65**.
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ CAP develops when a pathogen overwhelms the host's lower respiratory tract defenses (e.g., mucociliary clearance, cough reflex, alveolar macrophages).
    ◦ Pathogens are typically introduced via microaspiration from the oropharynx.
    ◦ This leads to an inflammatory response in the alveoli, causing them to fill with exudate (fluid, pus, and cellular debris), a process known as **consolidation**.
    ◦ This alveolar filling impairs gas exchange, leading to **hypoxemia**.
• **Common Pathogens**
    ◦ **Typical Bacteria** (Most Common Overall)
        ▪ ***Streptococcus pneumoniae***: The #1 cause of CAP in all age groups. Gram-positive diplococci.
        ▪ ***Haemophilus influenzae***: Common in patients with underlying lung disease (COPD, bronchiectasis). Gram-negative coccobacilli.
        ▪ ***Moraxella catarrhalis***: Common in elderly patients and those with COPD. Gram-negative diplococci.
        ▪ ***Staphylococcus aureus***: Often occurs post-influenza infection or in IV drug users. Can cause severe, **necrotizing pneumonia**. Gram-positive cocci in clusters.
    ◦ **Atypical Bacteria**
        ▪ ***Mycoplasma pneumoniae***: Common in young adults, college students, military recruits ("**walking pneumonia**"). Lacks a cell wall.
        ▪ ***Chlamydophila pneumoniae***: Similar presentation to *Mycoplasma*.
        ▪ ***Legionella pneumophila***: Associated with contaminated water sources (air conditioners, cooling towers, whirlpools). Causes more severe illness.
    ◦ **Viruses**
        ▪ Influenza A & B
        ▪ Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV)
        ▪ Parainfluenza Virus
        ▪ Adenovirus
        ▪ SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19)
sections.epidemiology:
• One of the most common infectious diseases.
• A leading cause of hospitalization and death, especially in the elderly.
• Incidence is highest during winter months, correlating with viral respiratory season.
• Mortality rate is <1-5% for outpatients but can be as high as 25% for patients requiring ICU admission.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation can be divided into "typical" and "atypical" syndromes, although significant overlap exists.
• **Typical Pneumonia**
    ◦ Characterized by the sudden onset of:
        ▪ High fever, shaking chills (**rigors**)
        ▪ Productive cough with purulent or **rust-colored sputum**
        ▪ **Pleuritic chest pain**
        ▪ Significant dyspnea
        ▪ Patient appears acutely ill.
• **Atypical Pneumonia ("Walking Pneumonia")**
    ◦ Characterized by a more indolent, subacute course:
        ▪ Low-grade fever
        ▪ Dry, **non-productive cough**
        ▪ Prominent constitutional and **extrapulmonary symptoms**: headache, malaise, myalgias, sore throat, GI symptoms.
        ▪ Patient often appears less ill than CXR findings might suggest.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Chest X-Ray (CXR)**
    ◦ The cornerstone of diagnosis. A **new infiltrate** is required.
    ◦ **Findings**
        ▪ **Lobar consolidation**: Classic for *S. pneumoniae*.
        ▪ **Patchy/Interstitial infiltrates**: Often seen in atypical or viral pneumonia.
        ▪ **Cavitary lesions**: Suggestive of *S. aureus*, *Klebsiella*, or anaerobes (abscess).
        ▪ **Pleural effusion**: Fluid in the pleural space.
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **CBC with differential**: **Leukocytosis** (>12,000) with a **left shift** (increased neutrophils/bands) is common in bacterial pneumonia.
    ◦ **CMP**: To assess for dehydration, electrolyte abnormalities (e.g., **hyponatremia with *Legionella***), and renal/hepatic function (important for CURB-65 and antibiotic choice).
    ◦ **Procalcitonin (PCT)**: Can help differentiate bacterial vs. viral etiologies. High levels (>0.5 ng/mL) suggest bacterial infection.
    ◦ **C-Reactive Protein (CRP)**: Non-specific inflammatory marker, usually elevated.
• **Microbiologic Testing (Mainly for Hospitalized Patients)**
    ◦ **Sputum Gram Stain and Culture**: Obtain before antibiotics if possible. A good quality sample has >25 PMNs and <10 squamous epithelial cells per low-power field.
    ◦ **Blood Cultures x2**: Indicated for all severe CAP patients (ICU) and recommended for most hospitalized patients prior to antibiotic administration.
    ◦ **Urinary Antigen Tests**: Rapid tests for *S. pneumoniae* and *Legionella pneumophila* serogroup 1. High specificity.
    ◦ **Nasopharyngeal Swab (PCR)**: For influenza, SARS-CoV-2, and other respiratory viruses.
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent for young, healthy outpatients.
• Mortality increases significantly with age, comorbidities, and severity of illness.
• **CURB-65 score** correlates with mortality:
    ◦ Score 0-1: ~1.5% mortality
    ◦ Score 2: ~9% mortality
    ◦ Score 3-5: ~15-40% mortality

sections.overview:
• **Hospital-Acquired Pneumonia (HAP)** is a pneumonia that is not incubating at the time of hospital admission and occurs **48 hours after admission**; it is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in hospitalized patients.
    ◦ **Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP)**: A subtype of HAP that develops **> 48 hours after endotracheal intubation** and is associated with the highest mortality rates among nosocomial infections.
• **Key Distinction from CAP**: Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP) develops outside of the hospital setting. HAP is distinguished by a different, more resistant spectrum of causative pathogens, most notably *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* and MRSA.
• **Deprecated Term**: **Healthcare-Associated Pneumonia (HCAP)** is an outdated term. Current guidelines focus on assessing individual patient risk factors for **multidrug-resistant (MDR) organisms** rather than the site of care.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• HAP is the second most common nosocomial infection (after UTI).
• It is the **leading cause of death** among all hospital-acquired infections.
• VAP occurs in 9-27% of all mechanically ventilated patients.
• The risk of developing VAP increases by approximately 1-3% for each day of mechanical ventilation.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The diagnosis requires a **new or progressive pulmonary infiltrate on imaging** plus at least two of the following clinical criteria in a patient hospitalized for 48 hours:
    ◦ **Fever** (>38.0C / 100.4F)
    ◦ **Leukocytosis** (>12,000/L) or **Leukopenia** (<4,000/L)
    ◦ **Purulent sputum** (new onset or change in character)
    ◦ Worsening gas exchange (hypoxia, increased O2 requirement)
sections.diagnostics:
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Chest X-Ray (CXR)**: **Essential for diagnosis.** Will show a new or progressive opacity, consolidation, cavitation, or pleural effusion. Can be difficult to interpret in patients with pre-existing ARDS or CHF.
    ◦ **Chest CT**: More sensitive than CXR for identifying infiltrates, abscesses, and empyema.
• **Laboratory**
    ◦ **CBC with differential**: Leukocytosis with a left shift or leukopenia.
    ◦ **Arterial Blood Gas (ABG)**: To quantify hypoxemia and assess acid-base status.
    ◦ **Inflammatory Markers**: Elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) and procalcitonin. **Procalcitonin** is more specific for bacterial infections and can be trended to guide de-escalation of antibiotics.
• **Microbiology (Crucial for targeted therapy)**
    ◦ **Blood Cultures (x2)**: Obtain prior to starting antibiotics.
    ◦ **Lower Respiratory Tract Sampling**
        ▪ **Non-invasive**: Spontaneous or induced sputum sample for Gram stain and culture. Often contaminated by upper airway flora. A good quality sample has >25 neutrophils and <10 squamous epithelial cells per low-power field.
        ▪ **Invasive (for intubated patients)**: **Endotracheal aspirate** is easily obtained. **Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL)** or a **protected specimen brush (PSB)** via bronchoscopy provides a higher-quality sample with less contamination and allows for quantitative cultures.
sections.prognosis:
• Mortality is high, ranging from **20-50%**.
• Prognosis is worse for VAP compared to HAP.
• Negative prognostic factors include infection with MDR organisms (*Pseudomonas*, MRSA, *Acinetobacter*), bacteremia, delayed or inappropriate empiric antibiotics, and severe underlying comorbidities.

sections.overview:
• Atypical pneumonia is a type of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) caused by organisms that are not detectable on a standard Gram stain and are not susceptible to beta-lactam antibiotics
• The term "atypical" originally referred to the **insidious onset** and **extrapulmonary manifestations** that differ from the "typical" abrupt presentation of *Streptococcus pneumoniae*
• It is often referred to as "**walking pneumonia**" because the symptoms are frequently mild enough that patients do not require bed rest or hospitalization
sections.etiology:
• The primary causative organisms lack a cell wall or are obligate intracellular bacteria, which explains their resistance to penicillins and cephalosporins
    ◦ ***Mycoplasma pneumoniae***
        ▪ The **most common cause** of atypical pneumonia, especially in children and young adults
        ▪ It is a small bacterium that **lacks a cell wall**
        ▪ Pathogenesis involves direct attachment to the respiratory epithelial cells, leading to ciliostasis and cell destruction
    ◦ ***Chlamydophila pneumoniae*** (formerly *Chlamydia pneumoniae*)
        ▪ An **obligate intracellular** bacterium
        ▪ It causes a similar, often milder, clinical picture to *Mycoplasma*
        ▪ Commonly associated with **sinusitis** and **hoarseness**
    ◦ ***Legionella pneumophila***
        ▪ An **intracellular gram-negative rod**
        ▪ It is transmitted via inhalation of **contaminated aerosolized water** (e.g., from air conditioning units, cooling towers, humidifiers, whirlpool spas)
        ▪ It infects and multiplies within alveolar macrophages
        ▪ Can cause a more severe illness (**Legionnaires' disease**)
    ◦ **Viruses**
        ▪ Influenza virus, Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), Adenovirus, and SARS-CoV-2 are also common causes of atypical pneumonitis
sections.epidemiology:
• ***Mycoplasma pneumoniae***
    ◦ Peak incidence in school-aged children, military recruits, and college students
    ◦ Epidemics occur in 3-7 year cycles, often in late summer and fall
    ◦ Accounts for up to 20% of all CAP
• ***Chlamydophila pneumoniae***
    ◦ Common worldwide, responsible for 5-15% of CAP cases
    ◦ Outbreaks can occur in closed populations
• ***Legionella pneumophila***
    ◦ Sporadic outbreaks are common
    ◦ More prevalent in the summer and fall
    ◦ Tends to affect **older adults**, **smokers**, and **immunocompromised individuals**
    ◦ Not transmitted person-to-person
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is typically **subacute** and **insidious** over several days to weeks
• Patients often appear non-toxic and are able to continue daily activities, hence the term "**walking pneumonia**"
sections.diagnostics:
• **Chest X-ray (CXR)**
    ◦ The classic finding is **diffuse, patchy, reticulonodular or interstitial infiltrates**, most commonly in the lower lobes
    ◦ Pleural effusions can be seen but are uncommon
    ◦ **Lobar consolidation is rare**, in contrast to typical pneumonia
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **CBC**: WBC count is often normal or only mildly elevated
    ◦ **Sputum Gram Stain**: Reveals few or no bacteria and few neutrophils
• **Pathogen-Specific Testing**
    ◦ ***Mycoplasma pneumoniae***
        ▪ **PCR** of throat swab or sputum is the **test of choice** (sensitive and specific)
        ▪ **Serology** (IgM, IgG): A four-fold rise in IgG titers between acute and convalescent samples is diagnostic
        ▪ **Cold agglutinins**: A bedside test showing clumping of RBCs when cooled. It is classic for board exams but has low sensitivity and specificity
    ◦ ***Legionella pneumophila***
        ▪ **Urine antigen test**: Rapid and highly specific for serogroup 1 (the most common cause of disease), but less sensitive. The **test of choice** for rapid diagnosis
        ▪ **Sputum culture on buffered charcoal yeast extract (BCYE) agar**: The **gold standard**, but slow
        ▪ **Labs**: May show **hyponatremia**, elevated liver function tests (LFTs), and elevated creatine kinase (CK)
    ◦ ***Chlamydophila pneumoniae***
        ▪ **PCR** is the preferred method
        ▪ **Serology**: Difficult to interpret due to high baseline seroprevalence
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis for *Mycoplasma* and *Chlamydophila* pneumonia in healthy individuals is excellent with appropriate treatment
    ◦ The cough may linger for several weeks
• The prognosis for *Legionella* is more guarded, with **mortality rates of 10-15%** in hospitalized patients, and higher in those who are immunocompromised or have delayed treatment

sections.overview:
• Viral pneumonia is an infection of the lung parenchyma caused by a viral pathogen.
• It is a common cause of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), particularly in children and older adults.
• The clinical presentation is often characterized as an "**atypical pneumonia**," with a more gradual onset and prominent constitutional symptoms compared to classic bacterial pneumonia.
• The inflammatory response primarily affects the **interstitial space** rather than causing **lobar consolidation**.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• Accounts for approximately 15-30% of all CAP cases.
• **Seasonality**: Follows predictable patterns.
    ◦ **Influenza**: Peaks in fall and winter.
    ◦ **RSV** & hMPV: Peak in winter and early spring.
• **Outbreaks**: Often occur in closed communities like nursing homes, military barracks, and schools.
• **Pandemics**: Viruses like Influenza and Coronaviruses have pandemic potential.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is often **insidious**, beginning with a **prodrome** of upper respiratory infection (URI) symptoms that progresses over several days.
• **Constitutional symptoms** are typically more prominent than in bacterial pneumonia.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Chest X-Ray (CXR)**
        ▪ **Classic Finding**: **Bilateral, diffuse interstitial infiltrates**.
        ▪ Other patterns: Patchy infiltrates, peribronchial cuffing.
        ▪ Lobar consolidation is uncommon.
    ◦ **Chest CT (High Resolution)**
        ▪ More sensitive than CXR.
        ▪ **Hallmark Finding**: **Ground-glass opacities (GGOs)**, often bilateral and peripheral.
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **CBC with Differential**
        ▪ WBC count can be normal, low, or mildly elevated.
        ▪ Often shows a **lymphocytic predominance** rather than the neutrophilia seen in bacterial infections.
    ◦ **Inflammatory Markers**
        ▪ C-reactive protein (CRP) and Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) are elevated but non-specific.
    ◦ **Procalcitonin (PCT)**
        ▪ **High-yield**: Typically **normal or only minimally elevated (<0.25 ng/mL)**.
        ▪ A high PCT (>0.5 ng/mL) should raise suspicion for a secondary bacterial infection.
• **Pathogen Identification (Gold Standard)**
    ◦ **PCR (NAAT - Nucleic Acid Amplification Test)**: Test of choice for identifying specific viral pathogens.
        ▪ **Sample Source**: Nasopharyngeal swab, sputum, or bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid.
    ◦ **Rapid Antigen Tests**
        ▪ Available for Influenza, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2.
        ▪ They are faster but less sensitive than PCR.
sections.prognosis:
• **Good** in most young, healthy individuals who often recover fully.
• **Guarded to Poor** in elderly patients, those with significant comorbidities, or the immunocompromised.
• Mortality is significantly increased in patients who develop **ARDS** or **secondary bacterial infections**.

sections.overview:
• **Tuberculosis (TB)** is a chronic, granulomatous infectious disease caused by the bacterium ***Mycobacterium tuberculosis***.
    ◦ It primarily affects the lungs (**pulmonary TB**) but can also affect other parts of the body (**extrapulmonary TB**).
    ◦ The clinical spectrum ranges from a dormant, asymptomatic state known as **Latent TB Infection (LTBI)** to a symptomatic, contagious state known as **Active TB Disease**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiologic Agent**: ***Mycobacterium tuberculosis***
    ◦ An **acid-fast bacillus (AFB)**.
    ◦ It is an **obligate aerobe**, which explains its predilection for the highly oxygenated apices of the lungs.
• **Transmission**: Inhalation of **aerosolized droplets** from an individual with active pulmonary TB (e.g., coughing, sneezing, speaking).
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Primary Infection**: Inhaled bacilli reach the alveoli and are phagocytized by alveolar macrophages where they replicate.
    ◦ **Immune Response**: After 2-8 weeks, a **cell-mediated (T-cell) immune response** is mounted, containing the infection by forming **granulomas**.
    ◦ **Granuloma Formation**:
        ▪ The characteristic lesion is a **caseating (cheese-like necrosis) granuloma**.
        ▪ The initial site of infection in the lung is called a **Ghon focus**.
        ▪ The combination of a **Ghon focus** and an associated draining hilar lymph node is called a **Ghon complex**.
    ◦ **Latent TB Infection (LTBI)**:
        ▪ In >90% of immunocompetent individuals, the immune system contains the infection.
        ▪ The bacilli remain **dormant** but viable within the granulomas.
        ▪ The individual is **asymptomatic** and **not infectious**.
    ◦ **Active TB Disease**:
        ▪ Occurs from either failure of initial containment (**primary progressive TB**) or, more commonly, **reactivation of latent infection** years later (**reactivation TB**).
        ▪ Typically due to **waning immunity**.
        ▪ The granuloma breaks down, bacilli multiply, and cause tissue destruction, symptoms, and infectiousness.
sections.epidemiology:
• Globally, approximately one-quarter of the world's population is estimated to have **LTBI**.
• In the United States, TB is less common but disproportionately affects:
    ◦ **Foreign-born individuals** from high-prevalence countries.
    ◦ Residents of **congregate settings** (prisons, homeless shelters).
    ◦ **Immunocompromised** populations.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Latent TB (LTBI)**:
    ◦ **Asymptomatic** by definition.
    ◦ The only positive finding is a TST or IGRA test.
• **Active Pulmonary TB (most common)**:
    ◦ **Insidious onset** over weeks to months with both **constitutional** and **pulmonary symptoms**.
• **Extrapulmonary TB**:
    ◦ Can affect any organ system.
    ◦ **Lymph nodes (Scrofula)**: Most common site.
        ▪ **Painless, matted cervical lymphadenopathy**.
    ◦ **Pleura**:
        ▪ **Pleural effusion**, **pleuritic chest pain**.
    ◦ **Vertebral spine (Pott's Disease)**:
        ▪ **Back pain**, **gibbus deformity**.
    ◦ **Miliary TB**:
        ▪ **Disseminated, hematogenous spread** of bacilli.
        ▪ Presents with a **sepsis-like picture** and organ failure.
        ▪ **"Millet-seed" pattern** on chest x-ray.
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent (>95% cure rate)** for drug-susceptible TB that is diagnosed and treated appropriately.
• Prognosis is significantly worse for patients with:
    ◦ **MDR/XDR-TB**
    ◦ Advanced **immunosuppression** (e.g., low CD4 count in HIV)
    ◦ **Non-adherence** to therapy

sections.overview:
• A pleural effusion is an abnormal accumulation of fluid in the pleural space, the potential space between the visceral pleura (lining the lung) and the parietal pleura (lining the chest wall).
    ◦ Normally, this space contains a small amount (~5-15 mL) of serous fluid that acts as a lubricant.
    ◦ Pathologic accumulation occurs when the rate of fluid formation exceeds the rate of fluid removal by the pleural lymphatics.
sections.etiology:
• The fundamental pathophysiology involves a disruption of the Starling forces that govern fluid movement across capillaries or impaired lymphatic drainage.
• Pleural effusions are broadly classified into **transudates** and **exudates**, a critical distinction for determining the etiology.
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects approximately 1.5 million people in the United States annually.
• The most common causes are CHF, pneumonia, and malignancy.
• Malignant pleural effusions are a common complication of metastatic cancer and carry a poor prognosis.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Congestive heart failure**
• **Malignancy** (especially lung and breast)
• **Bacterial pneumonia**
• **Liver cirrhosis**
• **End-stage renal disease** / Nephrotic syndrome
• **Pulmonary embolism**
• Recent thoracic surgery or trauma
• Autoimmune conditions (e.g., RA, lupus)
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation depends on the size of the effusion, the rate of fluid accumulation, and the underlying disease process. A patient may be asymptomatic with a small effusion discovered incidentally, or present in severe respiratory distress with a large, rapidly accumulating effusion.
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ **Dyspnea**: Most common symptom. Often exertional, but can be present at rest.
    ◦ **Pleuritic Chest Pain**: Sharp, stabbing pain that worsens with deep inspiration or coughing. Suggests pleural inflammation (exudate).
    ◦ **Dry, Non-productive Cough**: Due to irritation or lung compression.
    ◦ **Symptoms of Underlying Disease**:
        ▪ **Fever, chills, productive cough**: Pneumonia
        ▪ **Weight loss, night sweats, hemoptysis**: Malignancy or TB
        ▪ **Orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND), lower extremity edema**: CHF
        ▪ **Jaundice, ascites**: Cirrhosis
sections.physicalExam:
• **Inspection**: May see decreased chest expansion on the affected side.
• **Palpation**: **Decreased tactile fremitus** (fluid insulates and blocks vibration transmission).
• **Percussion**: **Dullness to percussion** over the area of fluid.
• **Auscultation**: **Decreased or absent breath sounds** over the effusion.
• **Auscultation (at superior border)**: May hear egophony ("E" to "A" sound change) and bronchial breath sounds due to compressed lung tissue above the effusion.
• A massive effusion can cause a contralateral **mediastinal shift** (trachea shifts *away* from the effusion).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Initial test of choice.**
• **Chest X-ray (CXR)**
    ◦ **PA/AP View**: **Blunting of the costophrenic angle** is the earliest sign (requires ~250 mL of fluid). A "meniscus sign" may be visible as fluid tracks up the chest wall.
    ◦ **Lateral Decubitus View**: Most sensitive CXR view. Can detect as little as 50 mL of fluid. Fluid layers out on the dependent side.
• **Ultrasound**
    ◦ Highly sensitive for detecting small effusions.
    ◦ Excellent for identifying loculations (septations) and guiding thoracentesis.
• **CT Scan**
    ◦ Not required for simple effusions but is the best test for evaluating underlying lung parenchyma, pleural thickening, loculations, and identifying potential causes like malignancy or empyema ("split pleura sign").
sections.treatment:
• **Transudate**: Focus on systemic disease management (diuresis, etc.).
• **Exudate**: Further investigation to find the local cause (CT chest, cytology, etc.) and treat specifically. For complicated infections, ensure prompt and complete drainage. For recurrent malignant effusions, plan for definitive management with an IPC or pleurodesis.
sections.complications:
• **Empyema**: Infection of the pleural space.
• **Trapped Lung (or Encased Lung)**: A fibrous peel forms on the visceral pleura, preventing the lung from re-expanding after fluid removal.
• **Respiratory Failure**: Large effusions can compromise lung function.
• **Iatrogenic Complications from Thoracentesis**:
    ◦ **Pneumothorax**
    ◦ **Hemothorax**
    ◦ **Re-expansion pulmonary edema** (if >1.5 L is removed too quickly)
    ◦ Infection
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is entirely dependent on the underlying etiology.
• Effusions related to benign, treatable conditions (e.g., uncomplicated pneumonia) have an excellent prognosis.
• Effusions from CHF are associated with advanced heart disease.
• **A malignant pleural effusion is a sign of advanced cancer and has a poor prognosis, with a median survival of 4-12 months.**

sections.overview:
• A **pneumothorax** is the presence of air or gas in the **pleural space** (the potential space between the visceral and parietal pleura), which causes the **lung to collapse** due to a loss of **negative intrapleural pressure**
    ◦ This condition can range from a small, asymptomatic finding to a life-threatening medical emergency
    ◦ It is broadly classified into **spontaneous** (primary or secondary), **traumatic**, and **tension pneumothorax**
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• **PSP (Primary Spontaneous Pneumothorax):**
    ◦ Incidence is highest in **tall, thin males** aged 20-40
    ◦ Male-to-female ratio is ~6:1
• **SSP (Secondary Spontaneous Pneumothorax):**
    ◦ Incidence increases with age, typically occurring in patients >55 years old with underlying lung pathology
• A **bimodal age distribution** is often seen:
    ◦ A peak in the early 20s (**PSP**)
    ◦ Another peak after age 60 (**SSP**)
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is the **sudden onset** of **unilateral, pleuritic chest pain** and **dyspnea** in a patient with known risk factors (e.g., a young male smoker or an elderly patient with COPD)
• The severity of symptoms depends on the size of the pneumothorax and the patient's underlying pulmonary reserve
sections.diagnostics:
• **Chest X-ray (CXR):**
    ◦ **Initial test of choice**
    ◦ An upright expiratory film may accentuate the finding, but an inspiratory film is usually sufficient
    ◦ **Key Finding: Visceral pleural line**
        ▪ A thin white line that defines the edge of the collapsed lung, separated from the parietal pleura by a lucent, air-filled space with no lung markings
    ◦ **Supine CXR** (common in trauma):
        ▪ Look for the **"deep sulcus sign,"** where the costophrenic angle appears abnormally deep and lucent
    ◦ **Mediastinal shift** toward the contralateral side suggests a **tension pneumothorax**
• **Chest CT:**
    ◦ **Most sensitive and specific** imaging modality
    ◦ Used when CXR is equivocal, to differentiate a large bulla from a pneumothorax, or to better quantify the size
• **Ultrasound (POCUS - Point-of-Care Ultrasound):**
    ◦ Highly sensitive and rapid, especially in the ED or trauma setting
    ◦ **Key Findings:**
        ▪ **Absence of lung sliding** ("ants marching" sign is absent)
        ▪ **"Barcode" or "Stratosphere" sign** on M-mode (normal is **"seashore" sign**)
        ▪ **Lung point:** The specific point on the chest wall where the collapsed lung intermittently touches the chest wall; its presence is **pathognomonic** for pneumothorax
• **Arterial Blood Gas (ABG):**
    ◦ Not diagnostic but assesses physiological status
    ◦ Typically shows **hypoxemia** with **respiratory alkalosis** (due to hyperventilation)
sections.prognosis:
• **PSP (Primary Spontaneous Pneumothorax):**
    ◦ Excellent prognosis with treatment, but **recurrence** is common
    ◦ **Smoking cessation** significantly reduces recurrence risk
• **SSP (Secondary Spontaneous Pneumothorax):**
    ◦ Prognosis is more guarded and depends heavily on the severity of the underlying lung disease
    ◦ Mortality is significantly higher than in PSP

sections.overview:
• A **hemothorax** is the accumulation of blood within the **pleural space**, the potential space between the visceral and parietal pleura.
	◦ This condition is a medical emergency that can lead to both **respiratory** and **hemodynamic collapse**.
	◦ The accumulation of blood compresses the ipsilateral lung, causing **atelectasis** and **ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch**, leading to **hypoxia**.
	◦ Significant blood loss into the thorax can result in **hypovolemic shock**.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• **Hemothorax** is primarily associated with **trauma**.
• It occurs in approximately 25% of patients with major **chest trauma**.
• **Penetrating trauma** is more likely to cause significant hemothorax than **blunt trauma**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is highly dependent on the volume and rate of bleeding.
	◦ Often occurs in the setting of **multi-system trauma**.
	◦ Patient may be **anxious**, **pale**, and **diaphoretic**.
	◦ Signs of **respiratory distress** (e.g., **tachypnea**, use of **accessory muscles**).
	◦ Signs of **hypovolemic shock** (e.g., **tachycardia**, **hypotension**, **altered mental status**).
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly dependent on the underlying cause, the rate of blood loss, and the presence of associated injuries.
• Small, isolated hemothoraces have an excellent prognosis.
• **Massive hemothorax** associated with major trauma (e.g., **great vessel injury**) carries a high mortality rate.
	◦ Prompt diagnosis and surgical intervention are key to survival.

sections.overview:
• An empyema (or pyothorax) is a collection of **purulent fluid (pus)** within the **pleural space**, the potential space between the visceral and parietal pleura.
    ◦ Most commonly a complication of **pneumonia** but can also arise from other sources of infection.
    ◦ Represents the final, organized stage of a **parapneumonic effusion**.
    ◦ Management is distinct from simple effusions as it requires both systemic **antibiotics** and **drainage** of the infected pleural fluid.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• Most commonly develops as a complication of **bacterial pneumonia**.
• Occurs in approximately 2-5% of patients hospitalized with pneumonia.
• Incidence is higher in **older adults**, **children**, and **immunocompromised individuals**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Classic presentation: a patient with **pneumonia who fails to improve** despite 48-72 hours of appropriate antibiotic therapy.
    ◦ **Persistent** or **recurrent fever**
    ◦ Worsening **dyspnea**
    ◦ **Pleuritic chest pain**
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• **Mortality rate** is approximately 10-20%.
• Prognosis is worse in **elderly patients**, those with significant **comorbidities**, and when diagnosis or drainage is **delayed**.
• Full recovery of pulmonary function can take several months.

sections.overview:
• Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) is a chronic, progressive, and ultimately fatal fibrosing interstitial lung disease (ILD) of unknown cause.
• It is characterized by the progressive scarring of lung tissue, leading to irreversible loss of lung function.
• The diagnosis of IPF requires the exclusion of other known causes of ILD and is associated with the histopathologic and/or radiologic pattern of **Usual Interstitial Pneumonia (UIP)**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**: 'Idiopathic' by definition, the exact cause is unknown.
• **Pathophysiology**: The current leading hypothesis is a model of **aberrant wound healing**.
	◦ **Repetitive Micro-injury**: Recurrent, unrecognized injury to the alveolar epithelial cells (e.g., from smoking, GERD, environmental toxins).
	◦ **Dysregulated Repair**: An abnormal healing response follows, characterized by epithelial cell dysfunction and apoptosis.
	◦ **Fibroblast Proliferation**: Aberrant signaling pathways (involving growth factors like **TGF-β**) lead to the migration, proliferation, and activation of fibroblasts into myofibroblasts.
	◦ **Excessive Matrix Deposition**: Myofibroblasts excessively deposit extracellular matrix components (e.g., collagen), leading to progressive, irreversible scarring and architectural distortion of the lung parenchyma.
	◦ **Result**: Destruction of normal lung architecture, formation of cystic airspaces (**honeycombing**), and impaired gas exchange.
		▪ This is *not* considered a primarily inflammatory process.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: ~15 per 100,000 persons per year.
• **Prevalence**: Increases significantly with age.
• **Age of Onset**: Typically affects individuals **> 60 years old**.
	◦ Rare before age 50.
• **Sex**: More common in **males** than females (~2:1 ratio).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is typically **insidious and gradually progressive** over months to years.
• A classic vignette is an older male smoker presenting with shortness of breath that he initially attributed to aging or being out of shape.
sections.diagnostics:
• The diagnostic process is aimed at confirming the UIP pattern and excluding all other potential causes of interstitial lung disease.
• **Pulmonary Function Tests (PFTs)**
	◦ **Pattern**: Classic **restrictive** pattern.
	◦ **Spirometry**
		▪ Decreased Forced Vital Capacity (FVC)
		▪ Decreased Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 second (FEV1)
		▪ **Normal or increased FEV1/FVC ratio (> 0.7)**
	◦ **Lung Volumes**: Decreased Total Lung Capacity (TLC).
	◦ **Diffusing Capacity (DLCO)**: **Markedly reduced**, often disproportionately to the reduction in lung volumes.
		▪ Reflects impaired gas exchange across the thickened interstitium.
• **Imaging**
	◦ **Chest X-Ray (CXR)**: Often the initial test.
		▪ Findings: Increased reticular markings (net-like lines), particularly at the **lung bases and periphery**.
		▪ Late findings include low lung volumes and visible honeycombing.
	◦ **High-Resolution Computed Tomography (HRCT) of the Chest**: **The key imaging modality for diagnosis.**
		▪ **Classic UIP Pattern Findings**: **Basilar and subpleural (peripheral) predominance**, **Reticular abnormalities**, **Honeycombing** (clustered cystic air spaces, often in multiple layers), and Traction bronchiectasis and bronchiolectasis.
		▪ **Crucially, there is an *absence* of features suggestive of other diagnoses** (e.g., extensive ground-glass opacities, micronodules, consolidation, pleural plaques).
• **Labs**: Primarily used to rule out other causes.
	◦ ANA, RF, anti-CCP, anti-Scl-70, anti-Jo-1 to screen for connective tissue disease-associated ILD.
• **Surgical Lung Biopsy**
	◦ **When**: Performed when HRCT findings are not classic for a UIP pattern, but clinical suspicion remains high.
	◦ **Method**: Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) is preferred.
	◦ **Histology**: Considered the **gold standard**. Reveals the **histopathologic UIP pattern**: patchy fibrosis, architectural distortion with honeycombing, and scattered collections of myofibroblasts known as **fibroblastic foci**.
sections.prognosis:
• Poor. The disease is universally progressive.
• Median survival from the time of diagnosis is approximately **3-5 years** without treatment.
• Antifibrotic therapy can slow the rate of functional decline but does not halt progression or reverse fibrosis.

sections.overview:
• Sarcoidosis is a multisystem inflammatory disease of unknown etiology, characterized by the hallmark finding of **non-caseating granulomas** in affected organs.
    ◦ While it can affect any organ, the **lungs and intrathoracic lymph nodes** are involved in over 90% of cases.
    ◦ The clinical course is highly variable, ranging from asymptomatic incidental findings to chronic, debilitating disease.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**: Unknown.
    ◦ The leading hypothesis is that it results from an exaggerated cell-mediated immune response to an unidentified antigen (e.g., infectious, environmental) in a genetically susceptible host.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Antigen Exposure**: An unknown antigen is presented to T-helper lymphocytes.
    ◦ **Immune Activation**: This triggers a cascade of **CD4+ T-cell activation** and proliferation.
    ◦ **Granuloma Formation**: Activated CD4+ T-cells release cytokines (e.g., IFN-γ, TNF-α), which recruit and activate macrophages.
        ▪ These macrophages aggregate, differentiate into epithelioid cells, and fuse to form multinucleated giant cells.
        ▪ This collection of immune cells forms a tight, organized structure called a **granuloma**.
    ◦ **Non-Caseating Nature**: Unlike the granulomas in tuberculosis, sarcoid granulomas are typically **non-caseating**, meaning they lack central necrosis.
    ◦ **Organ Dysfunction**: The accumulation of these granulomas in tissues can disrupt normal organ architecture and function, leading to clinical manifestations.
        ▪ Granulomas can also produce active Vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D), leading to **hypercalcemia**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Varies by geography and race.
• **Race**: Highest incidence in **African Americans** (3-4 times higher than Caucasians) and **Northern Europeans** (e.g., Scandinavians).
    ◦ African Americans tend to have more severe and chronic disease.
• **Age**: Bimodal age distribution.
    ◦ The major peak is in young adults aged **20-40 years**.
    ◦ A smaller, second peak occurs in women over 50.
• **Sex**: Slightly higher incidence in females.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Genetic predisposition**: Family history of sarcoidosis, specific HLA alleles.
• **Race/Ethnicity**: African American, Scandinavian descent.
• **Environmental Exposures (Postulated)**:
    ◦ Infectious agents (e.g., *Propionibacterium acnes*, mycobacteria).
    ◦ Inorganic dusts/particles (e.g., occupational exposure for firefighters).
    ◦ Mold and mildew.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation is highly variable.
• **Asymptomatic (~50%)**: Discovered incidentally on a routine chest X-ray showing **bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy**.
• **Systemic/Insidious Onset**: Gradual onset of constitutional symptoms (**fatigue**, **fever**, **night sweats**, **weight loss**) and pulmonary symptoms (**dry cough**, **dyspnea**).
• **Acute Onset (Löfgren's Syndrome)**: A specific, acute presentation with a good prognosis.
    ◦ Classic triad:
        ▪ **Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL)**
        ▪ **Erythema nodosum**
        ▪ **Polyarthralgias** (often ankles) +/- fever.
sections.physicalExam:
• **General**: May have fever, signs of weight loss.
• **Pulmonary**: Often a **normal lung exam**.
    ◦ Fine bibasilar crackles (rales) may be heard in advanced fibrotic disease.
• **Skin**:
    ◦ **Erythema Nodosum**: Tender, warm, red/purple nodules on bilateral shins.
    ◦ **Lupus Pernio**: Violaceous, hardened plaques on the face.
• **Lymphatics**: Palpable, firm, non-tender lymphadenopathy.
• **Ophthalmologic**: Slit-lamp exam may reveal signs of **uveitis** (cells and flare in the anterior chamber).
• **HEENT**: Parotid gland enlargement.
• **Neurologic**: Facial droop (unilateral or bilateral) if **CN VII is involved**.
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis requires three elements:
    ◦ A compatible clinical/radiologic presentation
    ◦ Pathologic evidence of **non-caseating granulomas**
    ◦ Exclusion of other diseases with similar findings.
• **Initial Labs**:
    ◦ **CBC**: May show mild leukopenia.
    ◦ **CMP**: Check for **hypercalcemia** and elevated liver enzymes (LFTs).
    ◦ **ESR/CRP**: Elevated but non-specific.
• **Key Labs**:
    ◦ **Serum ACE (Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme) Level**: Elevated in 40-80% of patients with active disease.
        ▪ Produced by epithelioid cells in granulomas.
        ▪ **Not diagnostic** (low specificity) but can be useful for monitoring disease activity.
• **Imaging**:
    ◦ **Chest X-ray (CXR)**: **Best initial imaging test**.
        ▪ Findings are staged (Scadding Stages):
            ▪ **Stage I**: **Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL)** only.
            ▪ **Stage II**: BHL + parenchymal infiltrates (reticular opacities).
            ▪ **Stage III**: Parenchymal infiltrates only (hilar nodes have resolved).
            ▪ **Stage IV**: Pulmonary fibrosis (volume loss, honeycombing).
    ◦ **High-Resolution CT (HRCT)**: More sensitive than CXR for parenchymal abnormalities.
        ▪ Classic findings include micronodules in a **perilymphatic distribution**.
• **Pulmonary Function Tests (PFTs)**:
    ◦ Typically show a **restrictive pattern**: decreased FVC and FEV1, with a normal or increased FEV1/FVC ratio.
    ◦ **Decreased DLCO** (diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide) is a common and early finding.
• **Tissue Biopsy (Confirmatory)**:
    ◦ **Definitive diagnosis requires biopsy showing non-caseating granulomas.**
    ◦ Site should be the most accessible and least invasive (e.g., skin lesion, palpable lymph node).
    ◦ **Bronchoscopy with endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS)-guided transbronchial needle aspiration (TBNA)** is the procedure of choice for intrathoracic disease.
    ◦ Stains and cultures (for fungi and acid-fast bacilli) must be performed on the biopsy to rule out infection.
• **Other Tests**:
    ◦ **ECG**: Screen for conduction abnormalities (heart block).
    ◦ **Ophthalmologic Exam**: All patients should have a baseline slit-lamp exam to rule out uveitis.
sections.treatment:
• **Asymptomatic patients with Stage I CXR**: **Observation**.
    ◦ High rate of spontaneous remission.
• **Symptomatic or progressive disease**:
    ◦ **First-line**: **Oral Corticosteroids** (e.g., Prednisone 20-40 mg/day with a slow taper over 6-12 months).
    ◦ **Indications for treatment**: Worsening pulmonary symptoms, deteriorating PFTs, or significant extrapulmonary disease (cardiac, neuro, ocular, **hypercalcemia**).
• **Steroid-Sparing Agents**: Used for patients who cannot tolerate steroids or require long-term therapy.
    ◦ **Methotrexate** is the most common second-line agent.
    ◦ Others include Azathioprine, Mycophenolate Mofetil.
• **Refractory Disease**:
    ◦ **TNF-alpha inhibitors** (e.g., Infliximab).
• **Topical Therapy**:
    ◦ **Inhaled corticosteroids** for mild cough.
    ◦ **Topical corticosteroids** for uveitis or skin lesions.
sections.management:
• **Multidisciplinary approach**: Pulmonology, Ophthalmology, Cardiology, etc.
• **Monitoring**: Regular follow-up with serial PFTs, CXR, ECG, and labs (Calcium, ACE).
• **Annual ophthalmologic exam** is recommended for all patients, even if asymptomatic.
• Patient education on disease course and treatment side effects (especially of long-term steroid use).
sections.complications:
• **Pulmonary**: Pulmonary fibrosis, pulmonary hypertension, bronchiectasis.
• **Cardiac**: Complete heart block, ventricular arrhythmias, sudden cardiac death, cardiomyopathy.
• **Ocular**: Glaucoma, cataracts, permanent vision loss.
• **Renal**: Nephrocalcinosis and renal failure due to **hypercalcemia**.
• **Neurologic**: Permanent cranial nerve deficits.
sections.prognosis:
• **Overall prognosis is good.**
• >50% experience spontaneous remission within 2-5 years.
• ~20-30% develop chronic disease.
• <5% mortality, usually due to pulmonary fibrosis or cardiac involvement.
• **Favorable Prognostic Factors**: Stage I CXR, acute onset, **Löfgren's syndrome**, **Erythema nodosum**.
• **Poor Prognostic Factors**: Stage III/IV CXR, insidious onset, **Lupus pernio**, cardiac or neurosarcoidosis, **hypercalcemia**.

sections.overview:
• Small Cell Lung Cancer (SCLC) is a high-grade, aggressive neuroendocrine carcinoma of the lung.
• It is characterized by rapid tumor growth, a high propensity for early metastasis, and a strong association with **cigarette smoking**.
• SCLC accounts for approximately 15% of all lung cancers.
• Unlike Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC), SCLC is typically widespread at diagnosis and is considered a systemic disease, making chemotherapy the cornerstone of treatment rather than surgery.
• It is notorious for its association with various paraneoplastic syndromes.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ Overwhelmingly caused by **cigarette smoking** (>95% of cases).
    ◦ Carcinogens in tobacco smoke lead to a multitude of genetic and molecular aberrations.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Cell of Origin**: Arises from primitive neuroendocrine precursor cells (Kulchitsky cells) in the bronchial epithelium.
    ◦ **Histology**: Characterized by "**small blue round cells**" which are small, poorly differentiated cells with scant cytoplasm, ill-defined borders, finely granular nuclear chromatin (**salt-and-pepper pattern**), and a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio.
        ▪ Nuclear molding and high mitotic activity are classic features.
        ▪ Often referred to as **"oat cell carcinoma"**.
    ◦ **Molecular Genetics**: Involves near-universal inactivation of tumor suppressor genes, most commonly **TP53** and **RB1**.
    ◦ **Neuroendocrine Function**: The tumor cells retain neuroendocrine properties, allowing them to synthesize and secrete various peptide hormones and antibodies, leading to a wide range of paraneoplastic syndromes.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Represents ~15% of all lung cancers.
    ◦ Incidence is decreasing in the U.S. due to lower smoking rates.
• **Demographics**: Typically a disease of older adults, with a peak incidence between ages 60 and 80.
• **Gender**: Historically more common in men, but the gender gap has narrowed significantly with changing smoking patterns.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Cigarette Smoking**: The single most important risk factor. Risk is proportional to the number of pack-years smoked.
• **Secondhand Smoke**: Increased risk.
• **Occupational Exposures**: **Radon gas** (especially in uranium miners), asbestos, and other carcinogens.
• **Genetics**: A family history of lung cancer may slightly increase risk.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• SCLC presents aggressively and rapidly. Patients often have a short duration of symptoms (weeks to months) before seeking medical attention.
• The presentation is dictated by the location of the primary tumor (typically central), the extent of regional spread, the sites of distant metastases, and the presence of paraneoplastic syndromes.
• Most patients (~70%) present with metastatic (**Extensive-Stage**) disease.
• **Constitutional Symptoms**
    ◦ **Weight loss**, anorexia, fatigue, weakness (very common).
• **Symptoms from Primary Tumor (Central Location)**
    ◦ **Cough** (most common symptom)
    ◦ **Dyspnea**
    ◦ **Hemoptysis**
    ◦ Post-obstructive pneumonia
• **Symptoms from Local Invasion / Regional Spread**
    ◦ **Chest pain**
    ◦ **Hoarseness**: Due to recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy.
    ◦ **Dysphagia**: Due to esophageal compression.
    ◦ **Superior Vena Cava (SVC) Syndrome**: Facial plethora, arm/neck swelling, jugular venous distention. A classic SCLC-associated emergency.
• **Symptoms from Metastatic Disease**
    ◦ **Bone pain** (**bone mets**)
    ◦ **Neurologic symptoms**: Headaches, seizures, focal deficits (**brain mets** are very common).
    ◦ Jaundice, abdominal pain (**liver mets**).
• **Symptoms from Paraneoplastic Syndromes**
    ◦ **SIADH**: Euvolemic hyponatremia (lethargy, confusion, seizures).
    ◦ **Cushing's Syndrome**: Ectopic **ACTH** production (hypertension, hyperglycemia, hypokalemia, central obesity).
    ◦ **Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome (LEMS)**: Proximal muscle weakness that **improves with repeated muscle use**, dry mouth, impotence. Caused by antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels.
sections.physicalExam:
• **General**: Cachexia, nicotine-stained fingers.
• **Pulmonary**: May be normal. Can have wheezing, crackles, or signs of consolidation/pleural effusion (dullness to percussion, decreased breath sounds).
• **Signs of Local Spread**
    ◦ Supraclavicular or cervical lymphadenopathy.
    ◦ **SVC Syndrome**: Facial and upper extremity edema, prominent chest wall veins.
    ◦ **Horner's Syndrome**: Ptosis, miosis, anhydrosis (less common than in Pancoast tumors but possible).
• **Signs of Metastases**
    ◦ Hepatomegaly.
    ◦ Focal neurologic deficits.
    ◦ Point tenderness over bones.
• **Signs of Paraneoplastic Syndromes**
    ◦ Confusion, altered mental status (**SIADH**).
    ◦ Proximal muscle weakness, diminished deep tendon reflexes (**LEMS**).
    ◦ Moon facies, purple striae, buffalo hump (**Cushing's**).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Chest X-ray**: Often the first test. Typically shows a **large hilar or perihilar mass** with bulky mediastinal lymphadenopathy.
    ◦ **CT Chest/Abdomen/Pelvis with IV Contrast**: Essential for evaluating the primary tumor, lymph nodes, and common metastatic sites (liver, adrenals).
• **Biopsy (Definitive Diagnosis)**
    ◦ **Bronchoscopy with biopsy** and/or endobronchial ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (EBUS-FNA) is the preferred method for central lesions.
    ◦ CT-guided biopsy for peripheral lesions or metastatic sites.
• **Pathology & Immunohistochemistry (IHC)**
    ◦ Histology shows small, blue, round cells.
    ◦ IHC stains will be positive for neuroendocrine markers: **Chromogranin A**, **Synaptophysin**, and **CD56**.
• **Staging**
    ◦ SCLC is staged differently from NSCLC.
    ◦ **Goal**: To determine if the disease is "**Limited**" or "**Extensive**."
    ◦ **Staging Workup**: **PET/CT** (to identify distant mets) and **MRI of the brain** (high incidence of brain mets at diagnosis) are mandatory.
    ◦ **Limited-Stage Disease (LD-SCLC)**: Tumor is confined to one hemithorax and can be encompassed within a single, tolerable radiation field. Includes ipsilateral mediastinal and supraclavicular nodes. (~30% of patients).
    ◦ **Extensive-Stage Disease (ED-SCLC)**: Tumor has spread beyond one hemithorax, including distant metastases or malignant pleural/pericardial effusion. (~70% of patients).
sections.treatment:
• **Limited-Stage SCLC (LD-SCLC)**
    ◦ **Goal**: Curative intent.
    ◦ **Standard of Care**: **Concurrent Chemoradiation**.
    ◦ **Chemotherapy**: 4-6 cycles of **Cisplatin + Etoposide**.
    ◦ **Radiation**: Concurrent thoracic radiation therapy, typically started with the 1st or 2nd cycle of chemo.
    ◦ **Prophylactic Cranial Irradiation (PCI)**: Offered to patients who achieve a complete or very good partial response after chemoradiation. Significantly reduces the incidence of brain metastases and improves overall survival.
• **Extensive-Stage SCLC (ED-SCLC)**
    ◦ **Goal**: Palliative; to improve survival and quality of life.
    ◦ **Standard of Care**: **Combination Chemotherapy + Immunotherapy**.
    ◦ **Chemo**: 4 cycles of **Carboplatin + Etoposide**.
    ◦ **Immunotherapy**: Concurrent and maintenance **Atezolizumab** or **Durvalumab** (PD-L1 inhibitors).
    ◦ **Radiation**: Used for palliation of symptoms (e.g., painful bone mets, brain mets, bronchial obstruction, SVC compression). PCI is more controversial in ED-SCLC but may be considered in select patients with good response.
sections.management:
• **Symptom Control**: Aggressive management of pain, dyspnea, nausea, and fatigue. Early involvement of palliative care is crucial.
• **Oncologic Emergencies**: Be prepared to manage **SVC syndrome** (radiation, steroids, stenting), **spinal cord compression** (steroids, radiation), and **brain metastases** (steroids, radiation).
• **Paraneoplastic Syndromes**: Treat the underlying malignancy. For **SIADH**, this includes fluid restriction and potentially demeclocycline or vaptans.
• **Surveillance**: After initial treatment, patients are monitored closely with physical exams and serial imaging (CT scans) every 3-6 months to detect recurrence.
sections.complications:
• **Superior Vena Cava (SVC) Syndrome**
• **Brain Metastases**
• **Spinal Cord Compression**
• **Paraneoplastic Syndromes** (**SIADH**, **LEMS**, **Cushing's**)
• **Treatment-related Toxicity**: Myelosuppression, neuropathy (cisplatin), radiation pneumonitis, radiation esophagitis.
sections.prognosis:
• Overall **poor**, though treatment can significantly extend survival.
• **Limited-Stage**: Median survival is approximately 20-25 months with treatment. 5-year survival is ~25%.
• **Extensive-Stage**: Median survival is approximately 12 months with modern chemo-immunotherapy. 5-year survival is <5%.
• **Negative Prognostic Factors**: Extensive-stage disease, poor performance status (ECOG >2), significant weight loss, elevated LDH.

sections.overview:
• **Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC)** is a group of lung malignancies histologically distinct from Small Cell Lung Cancer (SCLC).
• Accounts for approximately **85%** of all lung cancers.
• Generally less aggressive and grows more slowly than SCLC.
• Treatment and prognosis are highly dependent on the specific subtype, stage at diagnosis, and the presence of specific molecular markers.
• Main subtypes include:
    ◦ **Adenocarcinoma**
    ◦ **Squamous Cell Carcinoma**
    ◦ **Large Cell Carcinoma**
sections.etiology:
• **NSCLC** arises from the epithelial cells of the respiratory tract.
• Chronic exposure to carcinogens, primarily from **tobacco smoke**, leads to a cumulative series of genetic and epigenetic mutations.
    ◦ These mutations disrupt normal cell cycle regulation, promoting uncontrolled proliferation and inhibiting apoptosis.
• Specific **driver mutations** can be targeted with specific therapies.
    ◦ Examples: **EGFR, ALK, ROS1, KRAS**
sections.epidemiology:
• Leading cause of **cancer-related death** in both men and women worldwide.
• Accounts for **~85%** of all lung cancers.
• Peak incidence occurs between ages 55 and 85.
• Incidence in men is decreasing, while it is stabilizing in women, reflecting historical smoking patterns.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation varies widely based on tumor location, size, and presence of metastases.
• Many patients are **asymptomatic** at diagnosis, with the lesion found incidentally on imaging.
• **Central Tumors** (often Squamous Cell):
    ◦ **Cough**
    ◦ **Hemoptysis**
    ◦ **Wheezing**
    ◦ **Dyspnea**
    ◦ Post-obstructive pneumonia
• **Peripheral Tumors** (often Adenocarcinoma):
    ◦ Often asymptomatic until late-stage.
    ◦ May present with **pleuritic chest pain** or symptoms of **pleural effusion**.
• **Metastatic Disease**:
    ◦ **Bone pain** (bone)
    ◦ **Headaches**, **seizures**, **focal neurologic deficits** (brain)
    ◦ **Weight loss**, **fatigue** (constitutional)
• **Paraneoplastic Syndromes**: See Complications section.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Chest X-Ray (CXR)**
        ▪ Often the first test.
        ▪ May show a **nodule**, **mass**, **infiltrate**, **atelectasis**, **hilar adenopathy**, or **pleural effusion**.
    ◦ **CT Chest with IV Contrast**
        ▪ **Essential** for characterizing the primary lesion, evaluating for lymph node involvement (**mediastinal staging**), and detecting chest wall/pleural invasion.
    ◦ **PET-CT Scan**
        ▪ Used for **staging** by identifying metabolically active areas of disease (**distant metastases**).
        ▪ Highly sensitive for nodal and distant mets.
    ◦ **MRI Brain**
        ▪ Performed to rule out **brain metastases**, especially in patients with **adenocarcinoma** or any neurologic symptoms.
• **Tissue Biopsy (Required for Diagnosis)**
    ◦ The method depends on tumor location.
    ◦ **Bronchoscopy**: For **central lesions**; allows for direct visualization, biopsy, and brushing.
    ◦ **CT-guided Transthoracic Needle Aspiration (TTNA)**: For **peripheral lesions**.
    ◦ **Thoracentesis**: For patients with **pleural effusion**; cytologic analysis of fluid can be diagnostic.
    ◦ **Endobronchial Ultrasound (EBUS)**: To biopsy **mediastinal lymph nodes** for staging.
• **Molecular Testing**
    ◦ **Crucial** for all diagnosed **non-squamous NSCLC** to guide therapy.
    ◦ Test for driver mutations: **EGFR, ALK, ROS1, BRAF, MET, RET, KRAS**.
    ◦ Test for protein expression: **PD-L1** (to predict response to immunotherapy).
• **Staging**
    ◦ Based on the **TNM** (Tumor, Node, Metastasis) system.
    ◦ The single most important prognostic factor and dictates treatment.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is heavily dependent on the **stage at diagnosis**.
• **Overall 5-year survival rate**: ~25%.
• **Localized disease (Stage I)**: 5-year survival can be as high as 70-90%.
• **Metastatic disease (Stage IV)**: 5-year survival is <10%, though this is improving with targeted and immunotherapies.

sections.overview:
• A carcinoid tumor is a type of slow-growing **neuroendocrine tumor (NET)** that originates from **enterochromaffin cells** (also known as Kulchitsky cells).
    ◦ These cells are found throughout the body, but carcinoid tumors most commonly arise in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract and bronchopulmonary system.
    ◦ They are known for their ability to secrete vasoactive substances, most notably **serotonin**, which can lead to a distinct clinical picture known as **Carcinoid Syndrome**.
sections.etiology:
• **Origin:** Arise from neuroendocrine cells of the APUD system (Amine Precursor Uptake and Decarboxylation).
• **Secretion:** Tumors can be functional (hormone-secreting) or non-functional.
    ◦ Functional tumors produce and secrete various bioactive substances, including:
        ▪ **Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine, 5-HT):** The primary mediator of carcinoid syndrome.
        ▪ Bradykinin & Tachykinins: Potent vasodilators responsible for flushing.
        ▪ Histamine: Primarily secreted by gastric carcinoids, causes atypical flushing.
        ▪ Prostaglandins
• **Carcinoid Syndrome Pathophysiology:**
    ◦ For GI tract tumors (e.g., small bowel), the secreted hormones (like serotonin) enter the portal circulation and are metabolized and inactivated by monoamine oxidase (MAO) in the liver.
    ◦ Therefore, **carcinoid syndrome typically does not occur until the tumor has metastasized to the liver**, allowing the vasoactive substances to bypass hepatic metabolism and enter systemic circulation.
    ◦ Exceptions: Primary tumors outside the portal drainage system (e.g., bronchial, ovarian carcinoids) can cause the syndrome without liver metastasis.
• **Tryptophan Shunting:**
    ◦ Tumor cells use large amounts of dietary tryptophan to synthesize serotonin.
    ◦ This shunts tryptophan away from the production of **niacin (Vitamin B3)**, leading to potential niacin deficiency and **pellagra**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Most Common Sites:**
    ◦ **Gastrointestinal Tract (~65%):** Small intestine (ileum is most common), rectum, appendix, stomach, colon.
    ◦ **Bronchopulmonary System (~25%):** Typically central bronchi.
• **Incidence:** Relatively rare, but incidence is increasing, likely due to improved diagnostic imaging and endoscopy.
• **Age:** Typically diagnosed in the 5th to 6th decade of life.
• **Appendiceal Carcinoids:** Often found incidentally during appendectomy and are the most common appendiceal tumor.
sections.riskFactors:
• Mostly sporadic with no clear cause.
• **Genetic Syndromes:**
    ◦ **Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1 (MEN1):** Strongest known risk factor. Characterized by tumors of the Pituitary, Parathyroid, and Pancreas ("3 P's"). Associated with gastric, thymic, and bronchial carcinoids.
• **Family History:** A positive family history of carcinoid tumor increases risk.
• **Conditions causing hypergastrinemia:** Atrophic gastritis and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome are risk factors for gastric carcinoids.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation depends on the tumor's location, size, and hormonal activity.
    ◦ **Asymptomatic:** Many tumors, especially small ones in the appendix or rectum, are found incidentally.
    ◦ **Local Mass Effect:** Tumor growth can cause obstruction (bowel obstruction), pain, or bleeding (melena/hematochezia).
    ◦ **Carcinoid Syndrome:** Occurs in <10% of patients, almost exclusively in the setting of liver metastases (from GI primary) or a non-portal primary (e.g., bronchial).
• **Symptoms of Carcinoid Syndrome (Classic Triad):**
    ◦ **F**lushing: Episodic, pink-to-violaceous erythema of the face, neck, and upper chest. Lasts minutes to hours. Can be triggered by alcohol, stress, or certain foods (cheese, chocolate).
    ◦ **D**iarrhea: Secretory, watery, explosive, and often accompanied by cramping. Due to serotonin increasing GI motility and secretion.
    ◦ **B**ronchospasm: Wheezing and dyspnea. Less common than flushing or diarrhea.
• **Other Systemic Symptoms:**
    ◦ **Carcinoid Heart Disease:** Fibrotic plaque deposition on the **right-sided heart valves** (tricuspid and pulmonic), leading to tricuspid regurgitation and pulmonic stenosis.
        ▪ Manifests as signs of right-sided heart failure (dyspnea, JVD, edema, ascites).
        ▪ The left side is spared because the lungs metabolize serotonin.
    ◦ **Pellagra:** Niacin deficiency. Classic triad of **D**ermatitis, **D**iarrhea, and **D**ementia.
    ◦ Hypotension (due to vasodilation during flushing episodes).
    ◦ Telangiectasias (chronic facial skin changes).
sections.physicalExam:
• **During a flushing episode:** Obvious cutaneous erythema of the face and upper torso.
• **Skin:**
    ◦ Facial telangiectasias
    ◦ Violaceous skin hue (cyanosis)
• **Cardiovascular:**
    ◦ Murmur of **tricuspid regurgitation** (holosystolic, louder with inspiration).
    ◦ Murmur of **pulmonic stenosis** (systolic ejection murmur).
    ◦ Signs of right heart failure: Jugular venous distension (JVD), peripheral edema, ascites, hepatomegaly.
• **Pulmonary:** Wheezing on auscultation.
• **Abdomen:** Hepatomegaly may be palpable due to liver metastases.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Biochemical Markers (Initial Tests):**
    ◦ **24-hour Urinary 5-HIAA (5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid):** **Best initial test** for diagnosing carcinoid syndrome.
        ▪ 5-HIAA is the main metabolite of serotonin.
        ▪ Patient must avoid serotonin-rich foods (bananas, walnuts, avocados) and certain medications before the test.
    ◦ **Serum Chromogranin A (CgA):** A sensitive but non-specific marker for neuroendocrine tumors.
        ▪ Useful for monitoring disease progression and treatment response.
        ▪ Can be elevated by PPI use.
• **Tumor Localization (Imaging):**
    ◦ **Somatostatin Receptor Scintigraphy (SRS) / Octreoscan:** Functional imaging using radiolabeled octreotide, which binds to somatostatin receptors highly expressed on carcinoid cells. Excellent for identifying primary tumor and metastatic sites.
    ◦ **Gallium-68 DOTATATE PET/CT:** Newer and more sensitive than Octreoscan. Becoming the gold standard for functional imaging.
    ◦ **CT or MRI (Abdomen/Pelvis/Chest):** Provides anatomic detail of the tumor and evaluates for liver, lymph node, and distant metastases.
• **Definitive Diagnosis:**
    ◦ **Biopsy and Histology:** Shows nests of uniform, round cells with "salt-and-pepper" chromatin.
    ◦ **Immunohistochemistry:** Stains positive for neuroendocrine markers like **Synaptophysin** and **Chromogranin A**.
sections.treatment:
• **Localized Disease:**
    ◦ **Surgical resection is the only curative option.**
        ▪ Appendiceal carcinoid <2 cm: Simple appendectomy.
        ▪ Small bowel carcinoid: Wide segmental resection with removal of associated lymph nodes.
• **Metastatic/Unresectable Disease / Symptomatic Control:**
    ◦ **Somatostatin Analogs (e.g., Octreotide, Lanreotide):** **First-line therapy for symptomatic carcinoid syndrome.**
        ▪ They inhibit hormone release from the tumor, controlling flushing and diarrhea.
        ▪ May also have some anti-proliferative effect.
    ◦ **Telotristat:** A tryptophan hydroxylase inhibitor that reduces serotonin production. Used for diarrhea refractory to somatostatin analogs.
    ◦ **Hepatic-directed therapy:** For liver metastases; includes surgical debulking, embolization, or radiofrequency ablation.
    ◦ **Peptide Receptor Radionuclide Therapy (PRRT):** Lutetium-177 (Lutathera). A radiolabeled somatostatin analog delivers targeted radiation to tumor cells.
    ◦ **Targeted Molecular Therapy:** Everolimus (mTOR inhibitor), Sunitinib (tyrosine kinase inhibitor).
    ◦ **Chemotherapy:** Generally reserved for poorly differentiated, high-grade, or rapidly progressive tumors.
sections.management:
• **Pre-operative Management:** Patients undergoing surgery or biopsy must receive **prophylactic IV octreotide** to prevent a **Carcinoid Crisis** (severe, life-threatening episode of flushing, bronchospasm, and hemodynamic instability).
• **Diet:** Avoid triggers like alcohol and large, heavy meals.
• **Symptom Support:** Loperamide for diarrhea, bronchodilators for wheezing.
• **Nutritional Support:** **Niacin supplementation** to prevent or treat pellagra.
• **Cardiac Surveillance:** Regular echocardiograms to monitor for carcinoid heart disease. Valve replacement surgery may be required for severe disease.
• **Long-term Surveillance:** Periodic imaging and biochemical markers (CgA, 5-HIAA) to monitor for recurrence or progression.
sections.complications:
• **Carcinoid Crisis:** Life-threatening hemodynamic instability triggered by anesthesia, surgery, or tumor manipulation.
• **Carcinoid Heart Disease:** Right-sided valvular fibrosis leading to right heart failure.
• **Bowel Obstruction or Ischemia:** From primary tumor growth or mesenteric fibrosis.
• **Liver Metastasis:** Most common site of distant spread.
• **Pellagra:** Niacin (B3) deficiency.
sections.prognosis:
• Highly dependent on the **tumor grade (differentiation), stage (presence of metastases), and primary site.**
• **Localized Disease:** Excellent prognosis; 5-year survival >90%.
• **Distant Metastases:** Prognosis is worse, but the course is often indolent and prolonged. 5-year survival for metastatic disease is ~60-70%.
• **Appendiceal carcinoids** have the best prognosis.
• **Small bowel and lung carcinoids** have an intermediate prognosis.
• Pancreatic and colonic NETs have a poorer prognosis.

sections.overview:
• Smoke inhalation injury is damage to the respiratory tract caused by the inspiration of hot air, particulates, and chemical products of combustion.
    ◦ It is the leading cause of mortality in fire victims, often surpassing thermal burns.
    ◦ The injury is a composite of three distinct mechanisms:
        ▪ **(1) Thermal Injury** to the upper airway
        ▪ **(2) Chemical Irritant Injury** to the lower airways and lung parenchyma
        ▪ **(3) Systemic Chemical Toxicity** from absorbed asphyxiants like carbon monoxide (CO) and cyanide (CN)
    ◦ Clinical presentation can be delayed, and a high index of suspicion is critical for any patient with fire exposure.
sections.etiology:
• **Thermal Injury (Upper Airway)**
    ◦ **Mechanism**: Inhalation of superheated dry air (>150°C).
    ◦ **Location**: Primarily affects the supraglottic structures (oropharynx, larynx). The upper airway is highly efficient at cooling inspired air, protecting the lower tracts.
    ◦ **Pathology**: Causes immediate mucosal edema, erythema, and ulceration, which leads to massive fluid shifts and swelling that can rapidly progress to life-threatening upper airway obstruction.
    ◦ **Exception**: Steam inhalation can carry more thermal energy and cause direct burns to the lower airways.
• **Chemical Irritant Injury (Lower Airway & Parenchyma)**
    ◦ **Mechanism**: Inhalation of toxic chemical products from incomplete combustion of materials (e.g., plastics, wood, upholstery). Common irritants include aldehydes, sulfur oxides, nitrogen oxides, and phosgene.
    ◦ **Pathology**:
        ▪ **Immediate**: These chemicals react with water in the respiratory mucosa to form corrosive substances, causing bronchospasm and ulceration of the bronchial epithelium.
        ▪ **Delayed (24-48 hours)**: A severe inflammatory cascade is initiated, leading to:
            – Increased capillary permeability -> Non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema.
            – Impaired ciliary function and sloughing of bronchial lining -> Mucus plugging, atelectasis.
            – Loss of surfactant -> Alveolar collapse.
        ▪ This entire process can culminate in **Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)**.
• **Systemic Chemical Asphyxiation**
    ◦ **Carbon Monoxide (CO)**:
        ▪ **Mechanism**: Colorless, odorless gas produced by incomplete combustion. Binds to hemoglobin with an affinity ~240x greater than oxygen, forming **carboxyhemoglobin (COHb)**.
        ▪ **Pathology**:
            – Reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood.
            – Causes a **left-shift** in the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve, impairing the release of oxygen to tissues.
            – Directly inhibits cytochrome c oxidase, disrupting cellular respiration.
        ▪ **Result**: Profound systemic and cellular hypoxia.
        ▪ **Note**: **Pulse oximetry (SpO2) is unreliable**, as it cannot distinguish COHb from oxyhemoglobin.
    ◦ **Cyanide (CN)**:
        ▪ **Mechanism**: Released from the combustion of nitrogen-containing polymers (e.g., wool, silk, plastics, foam).
        ▪ **Pathology**: Binds to cytochrome c oxidase in the mitochondria, **blocking the electron transport chain**. This halts aerobic metabolism, forcing cells into anaerobic metabolism.
        ▪ **Result**: Severe **lactic acidosis** and cellular asphyxia, despite adequate oxygen delivery.
sections.epidemiology:
• Present in up to 33% of patients admitted to burn centers.
• Accounts for 60-80% of fire-related deaths.
• The combination of cutaneous burns and inhalation injury drastically increases mortality risk compared to either injury alone.
• Most common in victims of residential fires, particularly those occurring in enclosed spaces.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The clinical course is often biphasic; an initial period of minimal symptoms can be followed by rapid clinical deterioration 24-48 hours later.
• A high index of suspicion is paramount.
• Patients may present with a wide spectrum of signs, from asymptomatic to comatose and in respiratory failure.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Labs**
    ◦ **ABG with Co-oximetry**: **Essential**. Standard ABG (PaO2) and pulse oximetry (SpO2) are unreliable. Co-oximetry directly measures COHb and methemoglobin levels.
        ▪ **Finding**: Elevated COHb level. A "normal" level (<3% for non-smokers, <10% for smokers) does not rule out significant exposure.
    ◦ **Serum Lactate**: An elevated lactate level, especially with a normal COHb, should raise suspicion for **cyanide poisoning**.
    ◦ **Serum CK & Troponin**: To evaluate for rhabdomyolysis and myocardial injury.
    ◦ **CBC, BMP**
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Chest X-Ray**: **Often normal on initial presentation**. 
        ▪ Its primary initial utility is to rule out other pathology (e.g., trauma, aspiration).
        ▪ May later show patchy infiltrates, peribronchial cuffing, atelectasis, or diffuse bilateral opacities consistent with ARDS.
• **Procedures**
    ◦ **Fiberoptic Bronchoscopy**: **The gold standard** for diagnosing the presence and severity of airway injury.
        ▪ Allows for direct visualization of mucosal erythema, edema, ulcerations, necrosis, and soot deposits in the airway.
• **ECG**
    ◦ To screen for ischemia, dysrhythmias, and conduction abnormalities secondary to CO toxicity and hypoxia.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly variable and depends on the severity of inhalation injury, presence of concomitant cutaneous burns, age, and comorbidities.
• The combination of severe burns and inhalation injury carries a mortality rate exceeding 50%.
• Hypoxic brain injury is a major determinant of long-term outcome.

sections.overview:
• **Occupational Lung Disease (OLD)** is a broad category of pulmonary disorders caused by the inhalation of dusts, chemicals, fibers, fumes, or organic antigens in the workplace.
• These diseases range from obstructive conditions like asthma to restrictive, fibrotic diseases known as **pneumoconioses**, and even malignancies.
• A thorough **occupational and environmental history** is the single most critical element in diagnosis.
• The latency period between exposure and symptom onset can be years to decades.
sections.etiology:
• The general mechanism involves inhaled particles overwhelming the lung's mucociliary clearance mechanisms, depositing in the terminal bronchioles and alveoli, which triggers a chronic inflammatory response mediated by alveolar macrophages.
• **Pneumoconioses (Inorganic Dusts)**
    ◦ **Asbestosis**: Inhalation of asbestos fibers, which are ingested by macrophages, leading to chronic inflammation and progressive interstitial fibrosis, characteristically beginning in the **lower lobes** and subpleural regions.
