    ◦ **Silicosis**: Inhalation of crystalline silica particles, which are cytotoxic to alveolar macrophages, perpetuating a fibrotic cycle. Leads to the formation of silicotic nodules, primarily in the **upper lobes**. Impairs macrophage function, increasing susceptibility to **Mycobacterium tuberculosis**.
    ◦ **Coal Worker's Pneumoconiosis (CWP)**: Inhalation of coal dust. Macrophages engulf dust, forming coal macules. In simple CWP, this causes minimal fibrosis. In complicated CWP (**Progressive Massive Fibrosis**), macules coalesce into large fibrotic masses (>1 cm), predominantly in the **upper lobes**.
• **Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis (HP) (Organic Dusts)**
    ◦ Also known as extrinsic allergic alveolitis; an immunologic reaction to inhaled organic antigens (e.g., molds, animal proteins).
        ▪ **Acute**: **Type III hypersensitivity** (immune-complex mediated).
        ▪ **Chronic**: **Type IV hypersensitivity** (cell-mediated) with **non-caseating granuloma** formation.
• **Berylliosis**
    ◦ Inhalation of beryllium dust or fumes triggers a **Type IV (cell-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction** in susceptible individuals, leading to the formation of **non-caseating granulomas**, histologically indistinguishable from sarcoidosis.
• **Occupational Asthma**
    ◦ Airway hyperresponsiveness and inflammation triggered by workplace allergens or irritants. Can be immunologic (IgE-mediated) or non-immunologic (irritant-induced).
sections.epidemiology:
• **Asbestosis**: Shipyard workers, pipefitters, insulation installers, brake mechanics, construction, and demolition workers.
• **Silicosis**: Miners, sandblasters, quarry workers, stone cutters, glass manufacturing, and foundry workers. It is the most common chronic occupational disease worldwide.
• **CWP**: Coal miners.
• **Berylliosis**: Aerospace, nuclear, and electronics industries.
• **Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis**
    ◦ **Farmer's Lung**: Moldy hay (*Saccharopolyspora rectivirgula*).
    ◦ **Bird Fancier's Lung**: Avian proteins in bird droppings/feathers.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation is often insidious, with a long latency period (10-30 years) between first exposure and symptom onset.
• **The occupational history is paramount.**
    ◦ Key questions include:
        ▪ Current and all prior jobs, including job tasks.
        ▪ Known exposures at each job.
        ▪ Use of PPE.
        ▪ Symptoms in relation to work (e.g., better on weekends/vacations suggests occupational asthma or acute HP).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Pulmonary Function Tests (PFTs)**
    ◦ **Pneumoconioses, Chronic HP, Berylliosis**: Show a **restrictive pattern.**
        ▪ Decreased Total Lung Capacity (TLC) and Forced Vital Capacity (FVC).
        ▪ Normal or increased FEV1/FVC ratio (>0.7).
        ▪ **Diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO)** is often the earliest abnormality.
    ◦ **Occupational Asthma**: Shows an **obstructive pattern.**
        ▪ FEV1/FVC ratio (<0.7).
        ▪ Bronchodilator challenge shows reversibility.
        ▪ Workplace-specific peak flow monitoring can confirm.
• **Imaging (Chest X-ray and High-Resolution CT - HRCT)**
    ◦ **Asbestosis**
        ▪ Interstitial fibrosis (reticular or linear opacities), primarily in the **lung bases (lower lobes)**.
        ▪ **Pleural plaques** (calcified or non-calcified thickening of the parietal pleura) are pathognomonic for asbestos exposure.
        ▪ **"Shaggy heart border,"** honeycombing in advanced cases.
    ◦ **Silicosis & CWP**
        ▪ Multiple small, rounded opacities (<1 cm), predominantly in the **upper lobes**.
        ▪ **Eggshell calcification** of hilar lymph nodes is highly specific for silicosis.
        ▪ **Progressive Massive Fibrosis (PMF)**: Opacities coalesce into large masses >1 cm.
    ◦ **Berylliosis**
        ▪ Often mimics sarcoidosis with **bilateral hilar adenopathy** and diffuse interstitial infiltrates.
    ◦ **Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis**
        ▪ **Acute**: Diffuse ground-glass opacities.
        ▪ **Chronic**: Fibrosis, often with mid-to-upper lung predominance.
• **Other Tests**
    ◦ **Bronchoalveolar Lavage (BAL)**: Can be used to rule out other conditions. Asbestos bodies ("ferruginous bodies") may be seen in asbestosis.
    ◦ **Beryllium Lymphocyte Proliferation Test (BeLPT)**: Blood test to confirm beryllium sensitization.
    ◦ **Lung Biopsy**: Rarely needed but provides a definitive diagnosis. Shows specific histology (e.g., non-caseating granulomas in berylliosis/HP, silicotic nodules, asbestos bodies with interstitial fibrosis).
sections.prognosis:
• Generally poor for the fibrotic pneumoconioses, as the damage is irreversible and can progress even after exposure ceases.
• Prognosis depends on the cumulative exposure dose and disease severity at diagnosis.
• Occupational asthma and HP have a good prognosis if diagnosed early and exposure is completely eliminated.
• Development of **PMF**, **cor pulmonale**, or malignancy signifies a very poor prognosis.

sections.overview:
• **Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)** is a chronic condition characterized by symptoms or complications resulting from the reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus or beyond, into the oral cavity, larynx, or lung.
• It is distinguished from simple, occasional heartburn by the **frequency and severity of symptoms** and the presence of mucosal injury.
sections.etiology:
• Primarily a motility disorder caused by **incompetence of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES)**, which allows gastric acid and other contents (pepsin, bile) to reflux back into the esophagus.
    ◦ **Key Pathophysiologic Mechanisms:**
        ▪ **Transient LES Relaxations (TLESRs):** The most common mechanism; the LES relaxes inappropriately, unrelated to swallowing, allowing reflux.
        ▪ **Hypotensive or Weak LES:** A chronically low resting pressure of the LES (<10 mmHg) fails to create an adequate barrier.
        ▪ **Anatomic Disruption:** A **hiatal hernia** can displace the LES into the chest, disrupting the diaphragmatic crura's supportive effect and impairing acid clearance.
        ▪ **Impaired Esophageal Acid Clearance:** Inefficient esophageal peristalsis or reduced saliva production fails to clear refluxed material quickly.
        ▪ **Delayed Gastric Emptying:** Increases gastric volume and pressure, promoting reflux.
• The esophageal mucosa (squamous epithelium) is not equipped to handle corrosive gastric acid (pH 1.5-3.5), leading to inflammation (**esophagitis**), erosions, and potentially long-term cellular changes.
sections.epidemiology:
• Extremely common in Western countries, affecting an estimated **15-20% of the adult population**.
• Prevalence increases with age, peaking between 55-65 years.
• No significant gender predilection, though men are more likely to develop complications like **Barrett's esophagus** and **adenocarcinoma**.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Obesity:** Increased intra-abdominal pressure.
• **Hiatal Hernia**
• **Pregnancy:** Hormonal effects (progesterone relaxes the LES) and increased intra-abdominal pressure.
• **Dietary Triggers:** Fatty or spicy foods, chocolate, caffeine, peppermint, alcohol, acidic foods (citrus, tomatoes).
• **Lifestyle:** Smoking (lowers LES pressure), large meals, lying down soon after eating.
• **Medications that lower LES pressure:**
    ◦ Anticholinergics
    ◦ Calcium Channel Blockers
    ◦ Nitrates
    ◦ Benzodiazepines
    ◦ Progesterone/Estrogen
    ◦ Tricyclic Antidepressants
• **Connective Tissue Disorders:** e.g., Scleroderma (causes esophageal dysmotility).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The "classic" patient presents with postprandial **heartburn** and **regurgitation**, often worse when supine or bending over.
• Symptoms may be intermittent or daily.
• A significant portion of patients may present with atypical or extraesophageal symptoms without classic heartburn.
sections.physicalExam:
• The physical exam is **often unremarkable and normal**.
• May have mild epigastric tenderness on palpation.
• In patients with extraesophageal symptoms, findings may include:
    ◦ Pharyngeal erythema
    ◦ Dental erosions (posterior teeth)
    ◦ Wheezing on lung auscultation
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis (Presumptive Diagnosis):**
    ◦ In patients with classic, uncomplicated symptoms, a diagnosis can be made clinically.
    ◦ The standard approach is an **8-week empiric trial of a Proton Pump Inhibitor (PPI)**.
    ◦ Symptom resolution confirms the diagnosis.
• **Upper Endoscopy (EGD):**
    ◦ **Indications:** **Alarm symptoms**, failure to respond to PPI therapy, or screening for **Barrett's esophagus** in high-risk patients.
    ◦ **Purpose:** Directly visualizes the esophageal mucosa to identify esophagitis, erosions, strictures, hiatal hernia, Barrett's esophagus, and malignancy. Allows for biopsy.
    ◦ *Note: A normal EGD does not rule out GERD (up to 50% of GERD patients have non-erosive reflux disease or NERD).*
• **24-hour Ambulatory pH Monitoring:**
    ◦ **The Gold Standard for diagnosis.**
    ◦ **Indications:** Diagnosis is uncertain, symptoms persist despite PPI therapy, or before anti-reflux surgery.
    ◦ A catheter is placed through the nose into the distal esophagus to measure pH levels over 24 hours, correlating reflux events with patient-reported symptoms.
• **Esophageal Manometry:**
    ◦ Measures the function and pressure of the LES and esophageal body (peristalsis).
    ◦ **Not used to diagnose GERD.**
    ◦ **Main indication:** Pre-operative evaluation before anti-reflux surgery (e.g., Nissen fundoplication) to rule out motility disorders like achalasia or scleroderma.
• **Barium Esophagram (Barium Swallow):**
    ◦ Less sensitive than EGD for diagnosing esophagitis.
    ◦ Useful for evaluating anatomy and identifying hiatal hernias, rings, webs, and strictures.
    ◦ Often the initial test for dysphagia.
sections.treatment:
• **Initial Approach:** For classic symptoms without alarm features, start with lifestyle modifications and an **8-week trial of a standard-dose PPI**.
• **Re-evaluation:** If symptoms resolve, attempt to step down therapy to the lowest effective dose (e.g., low-dose PPI, H2RA, or stopping medication).
• **Failure to Respond:** If symptoms persist after 8 weeks of optimal PPI therapy (e.g., twice-daily dosing), refer to GI for EGD and further workup (e.g., 24-hr pH monitoring).
• **Barrett's Esophagus Management:** Requires long-term PPI therapy and regular EGD surveillance with biopsies to monitor for dysplasia (e.g., every 3-5 years if no dysplasia).
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent for most patients, as symptoms are well-controlled with lifestyle changes and medication.
• The primary concern for long-term morbidity/mortality is the small but significant risk of progression from **Barrett's esophagus to esophageal adenocarcinoma**.

sections.overview:
• Esophagitis is the inflammation of the mucosal lining of the esophagus, which can be acute or chronic and is classified based on its underlying cause
    ◦ Primary symptoms include **odynophagia** (painful swallowing), **dysphagia** (difficulty swallowing), and **retrosternal chest pain**
    ◦ Diagnosis is definitively made via **upper endoscopy (EGD) with biopsy**
    ◦ Treatment is directed at the specific etiology
sections.etiology:
• Esophagitis is a condition resulting from various insults to the esophageal mucosa
    ◦ **Reflux Esophagitis**
        ▪ Most common cause, resulting from the reflux of gastric acid and pepsin into the lower esophagus due to an incompetent lower esophageal sphincter (LES), leading to chemical injury and inflammation
    ◦ **Infectious Esophagitis**
        ▪ Occurs almost exclusively in **immunocompromised** individuals (e.g., HIV/AIDS, transplant recipients, chemotherapy patients, long-term steroid use)
        ▪ ***Candida albicans*:** Fungal overgrowth on the mucosal surface
        ▪ **Cytomegalovirus (CMV):** Viral infection leading to endothelial cell damage, vasculitis, and mucosal ulceration
        ▪ **Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV):** Viral infection causing direct cytopathic effect on squamous epithelial cells
    ◦ **Eosinophilic Esophagitis (EoE)**
        ▪ An immune-mediated, allergic inflammatory condition triggered by food antigens, leading to a Th2-cell-mediated response that recruits a large number of eosinophils to the esophageal epithelium
    ◦ **Pill-Induced Esophagitis**
        ▪ Caused by direct mucosal injury from a medication that remains in contact with the esophageal lining, through a combination of direct caustic effect and local hyperosmolarity
    ◦ **Radiation Esophagitis**
        ▪ Occurs as a side effect of radiation therapy for thoracic malignancies, damaging rapidly dividing epithelial cells
    ◦ **Caustic Esophagitis**
        ▪ Results from the ingestion of corrosive substances (e.g., strong acids or alkalis)
sections.epidemiology:
• **Reflux Esophagitis:** Extremely common, parallels the prevalence of GERD (10-20% of the Western population)
• **Infectious Esophagitis**
    ◦ **Candida:** Most common infectious cause, with highest incidence in HIV patients with **CD4 count <200** cells/L
    ◦ **CMV/HSV:** Occurs in severely immunocompromised patients, typically with **CD4 count <100** cells/L
• **Eosinophilic Esophagitis (EoE):** Prevalence is increasing, typically affecting children and young adults (peak age 20-30s) with a male predominance (3:1) and a strong association with atopic conditions
• **Pill-Induced Esophagitis:** More common in the elderly due to polypharmacy and altered esophageal motility
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic triad of symptoms is **odynophagia, dysphagia, and retrosternal chest pain**
    ◦ The specific history often points to the etiology
        ▪ **Reflux:** Patient complains of chronic **heartburn (pyrosis)** and regurgitation that is worse after meals and when lying down
        ▪ **Infectious:** Patient is known to be **immunocompromised** and presents with severe **odynophagia** that may limit oral intake
        ▪ **EoE:** A **young male with a history of asthma/allergies** presents with dysphagia, particularly to solids; a common presentation is a **food impaction** ("Steakhouse Syndrome")
        ▪ **Pill-Induced:** Patient reports **sudden onset of severe retrosternal pain and odynophagia**, often hours after taking a medication before bed
sections.diagnostics:
• **Upper Endoscopy (EGD) with biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis**
    ◦ **Reflux**
        ▪ Classic Endoscopic Findings: Erythema, friability, linear erosions/ulcers in the distal esophagus. Strictures may be present. (LA Classification used for grading)
        ▪ Biopsy Findings: Non-specific inflammation; may show neutrophils, eosinophils, and basal cell hyperplasia
    ◦ **Candida**
        ▪ Classic Endoscopic Findings: Diffuse, linear, yellow-white plaques or **"cottage cheese" appearance** adherent to the mucosa
        ▪ Biopsy Findings: Yeast and pseudohyphae invading mucosal cells
    ◦ **CMV**
        ▪ Classic Endoscopic Findings: **Large, solitary, shallow, linear ulcers**, typically in the mid-to-distal esophagus
        ▪ Biopsy Findings: Large epithelial cells with intranuclear inclusions (**"Owl's eye" appearance**)
    ◦ **HSV**
        ▪ Classic Endoscopic Findings: Multiple, small, well-demarcated, **"volcano-like" or "punched-out" ulcers**
        ▪ Biopsy Findings: Multinucleated giant cells with nuclear molding and chromatin margination (**Tzanck smear**)
    ◦ **Eosinophilic (EoE)**
        ▪ Classic Endoscopic Findings: **Stacked circular rings ("trachealization" or "felinization")**, linear furrows, white exudates/papules (eosinophilic microabscesses), strictures
        ▪ Biopsy Findings: **≥15 eosinophils per high-power field (eos/hpf)**, which is pathognomonic
    ◦ **Pill-Induced**
        ▪ Classic Endoscopic Findings: One or more discrete ulcers, often with surrounding normal mucosa. May see **"kissing ulcers"** on opposite walls. Typically occurs at sites of narrowing (e.g., aortic arch)
        ▪ Biopsy Findings: Non-specific inflammation and ulceration. May see pill fragments
• **Barium Esophagram**
    ◦ Can be useful as an initial test if a complex stricture is suspected
    ◦ May show ulcers, plaques, or strictures but is less sensitive and specific than EGD and does not allow for biopsy
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is generally **excellent** for most forms of esophagitis (reflux, infectious, pill-induced) if the underlying cause is identified and treated appropriately
• **EoE** is a chronic, relapsing condition that requires long-term management, but the prognosis is good with therapy, and the risk of malignancy is not significantly increased
• The prognosis for chronic reflux esophagitis depends on the development of complications like **Barrett's esophagus**, which requires endoscopic surveillance

sections.overview:
• Achalasia is the most common primary esophageal motility disorder characterized by two key features:
    ◦ **Aperistalsis:** Loss of normal peristaltic contractions in the distal two-thirds of the esophagus.
    ◦ **Impaired Lower Esophageal Sphincter (LES) Relaxation:** The LES fails to relax appropriately in response to swallowing.
• This dysfunction leads to obstruction at the gastroesophageal (GE) junction, causing food and liquid to be retained in the esophagus.
sections.etiology:
• **Primary (Idiopathic) Achalasia:**
    ◦ The most common form (~95% of cases).
    ◦ It is thought to be an autoimmune or post-viral inflammatory process that leads to the destruction of ganglion cells in the **myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus** of the esophageal wall.
    ◦ Specifically, there is a loss of **inhibitory neurons** that release nitric oxide (NO) and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP).
    ◦ This loss of inhibition leads to an imbalance, with unopposed excitatory (cholinergic) stimulation.
    ◦ The end result is a hypertensive, non-relaxing LES and an aperistaltic esophageal body.
• **Secondary Achalasia (Pseudoachalasia):**
    ◦ Occurs when another disease process mimics the symptoms and manometric findings of achalasia.
    ◦ **Malignancy:** Most common cause is adenocarcinoma of the gastric cardia or GE junction directly invading the myenteric plexus.
    ◦ **Chagas Disease:** Caused by the parasite *Trypanosoma cruzi*, which destroys ganglion cells in the GI tract, leading to megaesophagus and megacolon. Endemic to Central and South America.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence:** Approximately 1-2 cases per 100,000 people per year.
• **Prevalence:** Approximately 10 cases per 100,000 people.
• **Age of Onset:** Can occur at any age, but typically diagnosed between ages 25 and 60. A bimodal distribution is sometimes described.
• **Gender:** Affects males and females equally.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Primary Achalasia:**
    ◦ No definitive, modifiable risk factors are known.
    ◦ Potential association with certain autoimmune conditions and viral infections (e.g., Herpes Simplex Virus-1) has been proposed but not proven.
• **Secondary Achalasia:**
    ◦ History of malignancy (gastric, lung, lymphoma).
    ◦ Travel to or residence in endemic areas for Chagas disease.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is typically insidious, with symptoms gradually worsening over months to years.
• The classic triad of symptoms is:
    ◦ **Dysphagia**
    ◦ **Regurgitation**
    ◦ **Weight Loss**
• Patients often learn maneuvers to help esophageal emptying, such as eating slowly, drinking large volumes of water, or arching their back and neck while swallowing.
• **Dysphagia (most common symptom):**
    ◦ Occurs with **both solids and liquids** from the onset. This is a key feature distinguishing it from mechanical obstruction (which typically starts with solids only).
    ◦ Described as a sensation of food "sticking" in the chest.
• **Regurgitation:**
    ◦ Effortless return of undigested food or saliva, especially when lying supine.
    ◦ Can lead to nocturnal coughing, choking, and aspiration.
• **Chest Pain:**
    ◦ Retrosternal, squeezing pain that can occur during or after meals.
    ◦ May mimic angina pectoris.
• **Weight Loss:**
    ◦ Present in the majority of patients due to decreased oral intake.
• **Heartburn (Pyrosis):**
    ◦ Common but is not due to acid reflux. It's caused by the fermentation of retained food in the esophagus, producing lactic acid. It does not respond to proton pump inhibitors (PPIs).
• **Halitosis:**
    ◦ Caused by the decomposition of retained food.
sections.physicalExam:
• The physical exam is often **unremarkable**.
• Findings are typically related to the consequences of the disease:
    ◦ **Cachexia / signs of weight loss:** Decreased muscle mass, temporal wasting.
    ◦ **Halitosis**.
    ◦ **Pulmonary findings (e.g., rales, rhonchi):** If aspiration pneumonia has occurred.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Barium Esophagram (Barium Swallow)**
    ◦ **Role:** Excellent initial imaging test.
    ◦ **Classic Findings:**
        ▪ **"Bird's beak" appearance:** Tapering of the distal esophagus at the non-relaxing LES.
        ▪ **Dilated, sigmoid-shaped esophagus** (megaesophagus) in late-stage disease.
        ▪ **Aperistalsis** (lack of coordinated muscle contractions).
        ▪ Delayed emptying of barium from the esophagus.
• **Esophageal Manometry**
    ◦ **Role:** **Gold standard** for diagnosis. Confirms the diagnosis and classifies the type of achalasia (Chicago Classification).
    ◦ **Key Findings:**
        ▪ **Incomplete LES relaxation** with swallowing (elevated Integrated Relaxation Pressure, or IRP).
        ▪ **Aperistalsis** of the esophageal body.
        ▪ **High resting LES pressure** (often >45 mmHg).
• **Upper Endoscopy (EGD)**
    ◦ **Role:** Essential in all patients to **rule out mechanical obstruction or malignancy (pseudoachalasia)**.
    ◦ **Findings:**
        ▪ Often normal in early disease.
        ▪ May show a dilated esophagus with retained food and saliva.
        ▪ The LES feels tight, but the endoscope can typically be passed into the stomach with gentle pressure ("rosette" appearance).
        ▪ Biopsies are taken to rule out eosinophilic esophagitis or malignancy.
sections.treatment:
• **Pharmacologic Therapy (least effective; for non-surgical candidates):**
    ◦ **Nitrates** (e.g., isosorbide dinitrate)
    ◦ **Calcium Channel Blockers** (e.g., nifedipine)
    ◦ Provide temporary, modest relief. Given before meals.
• **Endoscopic Therapy:**
    ◦ **Pneumatic Dilation (PD):**
        ▪ A balloon is inflated at the GE junction to forcefully stretch and tear the muscle fibers of the LES.
        ▪ Success rate is good (~75-85%) but may require repeat sessions.
        ▪ Main risk: **Esophageal perforation** (~2-4%).
    ◦ **Botulinum Toxin Injection:**
        ▪ Injected directly into the LES via endoscope. It inhibits acetylcholine release, causing muscle paralysis and relaxation.
        ▪ Safe but **temporary** (~6-12 month effect). Best for elderly or frail patients unfit for more invasive procedures.
• **Surgical Therapy:**
    ◦ **Laparoscopic Heller Myotomy (LHM):**
        ▪ **Standard of care.** A surgical incision is made through the muscle layers of the LES, relieving the obstruction.
        ▪ Usually performed with a **partial fundoplication** (e.g., Dor or Toupet) to prevent post-operative GERD.
        ▪ Highest success rate (>90%).
• **Advanced Endoscopic Therapy:**
    ◦ **Per-oral Endoscopic Myotomy (POEM):**
        ▪ A newer, minimally invasive technique where a myotomy is created from within the esophagus using an endoscope.
        ▪ Efficacy is similar to LHM, but may have a higher rate of post-procedure GERD.
sections.management:
• **Young, healthy patients:** Laparoscopic Heller myotomy or pneumatic dilation are first-line options.
• **Elderly/Frail patients:** Botulinum toxin injection or pharmacotherapy.
• Monitor for symptom recurrence.
• Screen for GERD, a common complication of treatment.
• Long-term surveillance for esophageal cancer may be considered, though guidelines are not standardized.
sections.complications:
• **Aspiration Pneumonia:** Due to regurgitation of retained esophageal contents.
• **Megaesophagus:** Progressive, massive dilation of the esophagus over time.
• **Malnutrition and Weight Loss.**
• **Iatrogenic Perforation:** A risk of pneumatic dilation and myotomy.
• **Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma:** Chronic stasis and inflammation increase the risk by approximately 15-50 times over the general population. The risk develops over 15-25 years.
sections.prognosis:
• Achalasia is a chronic, incurable disease, but the prognosis for symptom control is excellent with treatment.
• Over 90% of patients achieve significant long-term symptom relief with myotomy or pneumatic dilation.
• Life expectancy is generally normal, but long-term surveillance for esophageal cancer is a consideration.

sections.overview:
• An **esophageal stricture** is an abnormal narrowing of the esophageal lumen.
	◦ This narrowing is most often caused by **fibrosis** (scar tissue) resulting from chronic inflammation or injury.
	◦ It can be **benign** or **malignant**.
	◦ The primary clinical consequence is **dysphagia** (difficulty swallowing), which typically begins with solids and can progress to liquids.
sections.etiology:
• The underlying pathophysiology involves injury to the esophageal mucosa and submucosa, triggering an inflammatory response.
	◦ Chronic inflammation leads to fibroblast activation, collagen deposition, and ultimately, scar tissue formation (**fibrosis**), which contracts and narrows the lumen.
• **Benign Causes (Most Common)**
	◦ **Peptic Stricture (GERD-related)**: The **most common cause**.
		▪ Chronic exposure of the distal esophagus to gastric acid leads to **reflux esophagitis**.
		▪ The subsequent healing process results in fibrosis and stricture formation, typically in the distal esophagus.
	◦ **Eosinophilic Esophagitis (EoE)**: An immune/antigen-mediated disease characterized by dense eosinophilic infiltration of the esophageal epithelium.
		▪ Chronic inflammation leads to remodeling, fibrosis, and the formation of rings or long, narrow-caliber strictures.
	◦ **Caustic Ingestion**: Ingestion of strong acids or (more commonly) alkali agents causes severe, deep, circumferential burns, leading to extensive fibrosis and severe stricture formation during healing.
	◦ **Iatrogenic**:
		▪ **Radiation-induced**: External beam radiation for thoracic or head/neck cancers can cause esophagitis and subsequent stricture.
		▪ **Post-surgical**: Anastomotic strictures can form at the site of a surgical connection after an esophagectomy.
		▪ **Post-endoscopic procedure**: After procedures like endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) or radiofrequency ablation for Barrett's esophagus.
	◦ **Pill-Induced Esophagitis**: Certain medications can get lodged in the esophagus, causing a localized chemical burn, ulceration, and subsequent stricture.
		▪ Common culprits include **NSAIDs**, **bisphosphonates**, **tetracyclines**, and **potassium chloride**.
	◦ **Infectious Esophagitis**: Rare cause, primarily in immunocompromised patients (e.g., from HSV, CMV, or Candida).
• **Malignant Causes**
	◦ **Primary Esophageal Carcinoma**: **Adenocarcinoma** (often arising from Barrett's esophagus in the distal esophagus) or **Squamous Cell Carcinoma** (associated with smoking/alcohol in the mid-to-upper esophagus).
		▪ The tumor itself narrows the lumen.
	◦ **Extrinsic Compression**: A tumor from an adjacent structure (e.g., lung cancer, mediastinal lymphoma) compresses the esophagus from the outside.
sections.epidemiology:
• Peptic strictures account for ~70-80% of all benign strictures, though their incidence is decreasing due to the widespread use of **Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs)**.
• The incidence of strictures related to **Eosinophilic Esophagitis** is increasing, especially in younger males with a history of **atopy** (asthma, eczema, allergies).
• Malignant strictures are more common in older adults (>50 years).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a patient, often with a long history of **heartburn**, who develops insidious and slowly progressive **dysphagia**.
	◦ They may initially compensate by chewing food more thoroughly, eating slowly, or avoiding certain foods (like steak or bread).
• An acute presentation can be a **food bolus impaction**, which is a medical emergency.
• If malignancy is the cause, the **dysphagia** may progress more rapidly and be associated with **"alarm" symptoms**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Barium Esophagram (Barium Swallow)**: Often the **initial diagnostic test**.
	◦ A radiologic study where the patient swallows a barium contrast agent.
	◦ **Findings**: Can identify the location, length, and diameter of the stricture.
		▪ Smooth, tapered narrowing suggests a benign peptic stricture.
		▪ An irregular, asymmetric, or **"shouldered" appearance** is suspicious for malignancy.
• **Upper Endoscopy (EGD - Esophagogastroduodenoscopy)**: The **gold standard** for diagnosis.
	◦ Allows for direct visualization of the stricture.
	◦ **Crucially, allows for biopsy** to rule out malignancy and diagnose underlying causes like **Eosinophilic Esophagitis** (requires multiple biopsies).
	◦ Can also be therapeutic, as dilation can be performed during the same procedure.
• **Esophageal Manometry**: Not used to diagnose a stricture itself.
	◦ May be used to evaluate for underlying **motility disorders** (e.g., achalasia, scleroderma) if the diagnosis is unclear.
sections.prognosis:
• **Benign Strictures**
	◦ The prognosis for life is excellent.
	◦ Symptomatic recurrence is common, with up to 30-40% of patients requiring repeat dilation within the first year.
	◦ Quality of life can be significantly improved with treatment.
• **Malignant Strictures**
	◦ Prognosis is poor and depends entirely on the stage of the cancer at diagnosis.
	◦ Palliative stenting can improve dysphagia and quality of life in advanced disease.

sections.overview:
• **Esophageal varices** are dilated, tortuous submucosal veins in the distal esophagus
    ◦ A direct consequence of **portal hypertension**, most commonly caused by **cirrhosis**
• Vessels have thin walls and are prone to rupture, leading to life-threatening **upper gastrointestinal (GI) hemorrhage**
• Management focuses on controlling acute bleeding and preventing subsequent episodes
sections.etiology:
• **Core Pathophysiology: Portal Hypertension**
    ◦ **Normal Portal Flow:** The portal vein carries blood from the GI tract, spleen, and pancreas to the liver (normal portal pressure is 5-10 mmHg)
    ◦ **Obstruction:** Resistance to blood flow in the liver (e.g., **cirrhosis**) increases pressure in the portal venous system
        ▪ **Portal hypertension** is defined as a portal venous pressure gradient >10 mmHg
    ◦ **Collateral Circulation:** Increased pressure forces blood into alternative, low-pressure pathways (portosystemic anastomoses)
    ◦ **Variceal Formation:** An anastomosis between the left gastric vein (portal system) and the azygos vein (systemic system) in the esophageal submucosa dilates, forming **varices**
    ◦ **Rupture:** Occurs when vessel wall tension exceeds the elastic limit
        ▪ According to **LaPlace's law**, wall tension increases with both rising portal pressure and increasing variceal radius (size)
        ▪ A portal pressure gradient >12 mmHg is associated with a high risk of bleeding
• **Causes of Portal Hypertension**
    ◦ **Intra-hepatic (Most Common)**
        ▪ **Cirrhosis** (~90% of cases in the US): Scarring and fibrosis of the liver obstruct blood flow. Common causes include alcoholic liver disease, chronic viral hepatitis (B and C), and non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH).
    ◦ **Pre-hepatic**
        ▪ **Portal Vein Thrombosis:** Clot in the portal vein
        ▪ **Splenic Vein Thrombosis:** Often due to pancreatitis
    ◦ **Post-hepatic**
        ▪ **Budd-Chiari Syndrome:** Thrombosis of the hepatic veins
        ▪ **Severe Right-Sided Heart Failure:** Causes hepatic congestion
sections.epidemiology:
• Found in approximately 50% of patients with **cirrhosis**
• Incidence increases with the severity of liver disease (from ~40% in **Child-Pugh Class A** to ~60% in **Class C**)
• The risk of a first variceal hemorrhage is 5-15% per year
• Variceal hemorrhage is the most lethal complication of **cirrhosis**, with a 6-week mortality rate of 15-20% per episode
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Asymptomatic:** Most commonly, varices are asymptomatic and are discovered during screening endoscopy in a patient with known **cirrhosis**
• **Acute Variceal Hemorrhage (Medical Emergency)**
    ◦ Painless, massive **upper GI bleeding**
    ◦ **Hematemesis:** Vomiting of bright red blood or "coffee grounds"
    ◦ **Melena:** Black, tarry stools (digested blood)
    ◦ **Hematochezia:** Bright red blood per rectum (less common, indicates very rapid transit)
    ◦ Symptoms of **hypovolemia**: Dizziness, syncope, weakness
    ◦ Signs of **shock**: **Tachycardia**, **hypotension**, pallor, cool extremities
sections.diagnostics:
• **Initial Lab Work (for acute bleed)**
    ◦ **CBC:** Low hemoglobin/hematocrit, **thrombocytopenia** (due to hypersplenism)
    ◦ **Coagulation Panel (PT/INR, PTT):** Prolonged PT/INR due to decreased synthesis of clotting factors by the liver
    ◦ **Liver Function Tests (LFTs):** Elevated AST/ALT, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase. Low albumin.
    ◦ **Type and Crossmatch:** Essential for blood transfusion
    ◦ **Ammonia:** May be elevated, contributing to **hepatic encephalopathy**
    ◦ **BMP/CMP:** To assess electrolytes and renal function (risk of **hepatorenal syndrome**)
• **Definitive Diagnosis & Screening**
    ◦ **Upper Endoscopy (EGD):** The **gold standard** for diagnosis
        ▪ **Diagnostic:** Directly visualizes **varices**, confirms them as the source of bleeding (e.g., active spurting, overlying clot)
        ▪ **Therapeutic:** Allows for immediate intervention (e.g., **band ligation**)
        ▪ **Screening:** Recommended for all patients at the time of **cirrhosis** diagnosis
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is poor and is dictated by the severity of the underlying liver disease and the presence of bleeding
• **Child-Pugh** and **MELD** scores are used to predict mortality in patients with **cirrhosis**
• Mortality from a single variceal bleed is approximately 15-20%
• The one-year re-bleeding rate without secondary prophylaxis is over 60%

sections.overview: • A Mallory-Weiss tear (MWT) is a non-transmural, longitudinal mucosal laceration of the distal esophagus and/or proximal stomach, most classically occurring at the gastroesophageal (GE) junction. • It is a common cause of acute upper gastrointestinal (UGI) bleeding, typically precipitated by a sudden increase in intra-abdominal pressure.
sections.etiology: • Etiology ◦ The tear is caused by any event that abruptly raises intra-abdominal pressure against a closed glottis, leading to forceful distention and tearing of the gastric cardia or distal esophagus. • Pathophysiology ◦ A sudden, massive increase in pressure occurs within the abdomen and stomach (e.g., during forceful vomiting, retching, coughing). ◦ This pressure is transmitted to the esophagus. ◦ The forceful distention creates a high-pressure gradient across the esophageal wall. ◦ This leads to a shearing force that causes a linear, longitudinal tear in the mucosa and submucosa. ▪ The muscularis propria layer remains intact (distinguishing it from Boerhaave syndrome). ◦ Bleeding occurs from the underlying submucosal arteries and venules exposed by the tear.
sections.epidemiology: • Accounts for approximately 5-10% of all cases of acute UGI bleeding. • More common in males than females (ratio ~3:1). • Can occur at any age but has a peak incidence in individuals aged 40-60. • Strong association with alcohol abuse.
sections.riskFactors: • Alcohol Abuse: The most common risk factor, leading to episodes of forceful vomiting or retching. • Hiatal Hernia: Present in a significant number of patients; weakens the integrity of the GE junction, predisposing it to tearing. • Bulimia Nervosa: Recurrent self-induced vomiting. • Hyperemesis Gravidarum: Severe nausea and vomiting during pregnancy. • Gastroenteritis: Any condition causing severe vomiting. • Iatrogenic: Can be caused during upper endoscopy (rare). • Other: Forceful coughing, straining during bowel movements, seizures, blunt abdominal trauma, CPR.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • The classic presentation involves a patient, often with a history of alcohol use, who presents with acute hematemesis after an episode of forceful, non-bloody vomiting or retching. • Symptoms ◦ Hematemesis: The hallmark symptom. Can be bright red blood or "coffee-ground" emesis. ◦ Melena: Black, tarry stools may develop hours to days later as blood is digested. ◦ Epigastric or Substernal Chest Pain: Often described as a tearing or sharp pain. ◦ Syncope or Presyncope: Symptoms of lightheadedness or fainting if blood loss is hemodynamically significant. ◦ History: Patients will typically report a preceding event of forceful vomiting, retching, or coughing.
sections.physicalExam: • Vital Signs ◦ May be normal. Tachycardia is often the earliest sign of significant blood loss. Hypotension indicates severe volume depletion. • General ◦ Patient may appear pale or diaphoretic if bleeding is severe. • Abdominal Exam ◦ Often benign. May have mild epigastric tenderness. • Rectal Exam ◦ May reveal melena or hematochezia (if bleeding is brisk). • Stigmata of Chronic Disease ◦ Assess for signs of chronic liver disease (jaundice, ascites, caput medusae) to help differentiate from variceal bleeding.
sections.diagnostics: • Initial Labs ◦ CBC: To assess hemoglobin and hematocrit for baseline and to trend blood loss. ◦ Type and Screen/Crossmatch: In anticipation of potential blood transfusion. ◦ Coagulation Panel (PT/INR, PTT): To assess for coagulopathy. ◦ Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP): To evaluate electrolytes, renal function (BUN/Cr ratio is often elevated in UGI bleed), and liver function. • Definitive Diagnosis ◦ Upper Endoscopy (EGD - Esophagogastroduodenoscopy): This is the gold standard diagnostic test. ▪ Diagnostic: Directly visualizes the tear, typically seen as a single, linear, longitudinal mucosal laceration at or near the GE junction, often with an adherent clot or active bleeding. ▪ Therapeutic: Allows for immediate intervention if active bleeding is identified.
sections.treatment: • Place two large-bore (16-18 gauge) IV catheters. • Administer IV crystalloids (Normal Saline or Lactated Ringer's) for volume resuscitation. • Transfuse packed red blood cells (PRBCs) for hemodynamically unstable patients or if hemoglobin drops below 7 g/dL. • Administer an IV Proton Pump Inhibitor (PPI) (e.g., pantoprazole, esomeprazole), often as a continuous infusion. While the tear is not acid-related, reducing gastric acid promotes clot stability and reduces re-bleeding risk. • Administer Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP) or Vitamin K if INR is elevated.
sections.management: • Supportive Care (Majority of Cases) ◦ Over 90% of Mallory-Weiss tears stop bleeding spontaneously. ◦ These patients can be managed with observation, IV fluids, and PPI therapy. • Endoscopic Hemostatic Therapy ◦ Indicated for patients with active bleeding, a visible vessel, or an adherent clot at the time of EGD. ◦ Options include: ▪ Epinephrine Injection: Injected into the submucosa around the tear to cause vasoconstriction and tamponade. ▪ Thermal Coagulation: Using electrocautery to seal the bleeding vessel. ▪ Endoscopic Clipping (Hemoclips): Mechanical closure of the tear and underlying vessel. ◦ *Combination therapy (e.g., epinephrine + clipping) is often most effective.* • Angiographic Embolization ◦ Reserved for patients whose bleeding cannot be controlled with endoscopy. An interventional radiologist selectively embolizes the feeding artery (usually a branch of the left gastric artery). • Surgery ◦ Rarely needed. Reserved as a last resort for refractory, life-threatening hemorrhage. Involves oversewing the tear via gastrotomy.
sections.complications: • Hemorrhagic Shock: Due to massive or uncontrolled blood loss. • Re-bleeding: Can occur in a small percentage of patients, especially those with coagulopathy or portal hypertension. • Death: Rare, with mortality rates <5%, usually related to severe hemorrhage or underlying comorbidities.
sections.prognosis: • Excellent. The vast majority of tears heal spontaneously within 48-72 hours with supportive care. • Re-bleeding is uncommon after initial hemostasis is achieved. • Long-term sequelae are rare.

sections.overview:
• **Boerhaave Syndrome** is a **spontaneous, full-thickness (transmural) perforation** of the esophagus
    ◦ It is a rare but life-threatening surgical emergency resulting from a sudden increase in intra-esophageal pressure, classically associated with **forceful vomiting** or retching
    ◦ The rupture allows gastric contents, air, and oral flora to leak into the mediastinum, leading to **chemical mediastinitis**, rapid bacterial infection, **sepsis**, and **shock**
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ Caused by a sudden, massive increase in intra-esophageal pressure against a closed glottis (**barogenic trauma**), which overcomes the structural integrity of the esophageal wall
    ◦ **Classic Cause**: **Forceful vomiting** or retching (emesis)
    ◦ **Other Causes**: Straining during childbirth, severe coughing or sneezing, heavy lifting, seizures, blunt trauma
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Pressure Spike**: A rapid rise in intraluminal esophageal pressure occurs
    ◦ **Rupture**: The esophagus tears at its weakest point
        ▪ **Location**: Most commonly occurs at the **left posterolateral wall** of the **distal third** of the esophagus, just above the gastroesophageal junction
        ▪ This area is anatomically weaker as it has less muscular support and lacks a serosal layer
    ◦ **Contamination**: Gastric acid, food, bile, and oral bacteria spill into the mediastinum
    ◦ **Inflammatory Cascade**: Leads to chemical mediastinitis, followed by bacterial infection, necrosis, pleural effusion (often left-sided), pneumomediastinum, sepsis, and ultimately multi-organ failure if not treated
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Rare, but has the **highest mortality rate** of any gastrointestinal perforation
• **Demographics**: Typically affects **middle-aged men** (40-60 years old)
• **Sex Predilection**: Male > Female (approx. 5:1)
sections.riskFactors:
• **Alcohol Abuse**: The most common associated risk factor, often leading to binge eating and subsequent forceful vomiting
• **Binge Eating / Large Meals**: Increases gastric volume and the likelihood of emesis
• **Bulimia Nervosa**: Repeated, self-induced vomiting
• **Pre-existing Esophageal Disease**: Conditions like eosinophilic esophagitis, GERD, or Barrett's esophagus may weaken the esophageal wall, though the primary mechanism remains barogenic trauma
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a middle-aged male with a history of alcohol or dietary overindulgence who develops **sudden, excruciating retrosternal chest pain** following an episode of **forceful vomiting**
• Patients often appear acutely ill, toxic, and in significant distress
• The presentation can mimic other life-threatening conditions like MI, aortic dissection, or PE
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ **Severe, acute chest pain**: Cardinal symptom. Described as retrosternal, epigastric, or radiating to the back (interscapular) or left shoulder. Often pleuritic in nature (worse with inspiration)
    ◦ **Vomiting/Retching**: Precedes the onset of pain
    ◦ **Odynophagia**: Painful swallowing
    ◦ **Dysphagia**: Difficulty swallowing
    ◦ **Dyspnea**: Shortness of breath, often from pleural effusion or pneumothorax
    ◦ **Hematemesis**: Can occur but is less common than in a Mallory-Weiss tear
sections.physicalExam:
• **Mackler's Triad**: The classic, pathognomonic triad (present in <50% of cases)
• **Hamman's Sign (Mediastinal Crunch)**: A crunching or crackling sound heard over the precordium with each heartbeat
    ◦ It is pathognomonic but rare
    ◦ Caused by air in the mediastinum being displaced by the heart
• **Systemic Signs**
    ◦ **Tachycardia**
    ◦ **Tachypnea**
    ◦ **Fever**
    ◦ **Diaphoresis**
    ◦ **Hypotension / Shock** (late finding, indicating sepsis)
• **Pulmonary Findings**
    ◦ Decreased breath sounds, dullness to percussion (**pleural effusion**), or hyperresonance (**pneumothorax**), most commonly on the left side
sections.diagnostics:
• **Initial Imaging (CXR)**
    ◦ Often the first test performed in the ED
    ◦ Findings may include:
        ▪ **Pneumomediastinum**: Air in the mediastinum (streaky lucencies)
        ▪ **Left-sided pleural effusion**: Most common finding
        ▪ **Widened mediastinum**
        ▪ **Pneumothorax**
    ◦ **Note**: A normal chest x-ray does not rule out Boerhaave syndrome, especially early in the course
• **Confirmatory Imaging (Contrast Esophagram)**
    ◦ **Test of choice** to confirm the diagnosis and locate the perforation
    ◦ **Procedure**: Start with **water-soluble contrast (Gastrografin)**. It is less inflammatory to the mediastinum if it extravasates
    ◦ If the water-soluble study is negative but clinical suspicion remains high, a **thin barium study** may follow, as barium is more sensitive for detecting small leaks. Barium is contraindicated if aspiration is suspected
• **Chest CT with Oral Contrast**
    ◦ Often used as the initial diagnostic test in many centers due to its speed and availability
    ◦ Highly sensitive for detecting mediastinal air, fluid collections, esophageal wall thickening, and extravasation of contrast
    ◦ Also helps to rule out other differential diagnoses like aortic dissection
• **Labs**
    ◦ Non-specific but helpful for management
    ◦ **CBC**: Leukocytosis with a left shift
    ◦ **CMP**: Metabolic acidosis may be present
    ◦ **Lactate**: Elevated in sepsis
• **Thoracentesis**
    ◦ If a pleural effusion is present, analysis of the fluid can be diagnostic
    ◦ Findings:
        ▪ **High amylase level** (from saliva)
        ▪ **Low pH** (<6.0, from gastric acid)
        ▪ Presence of food particles
sections.management:
• **Surgical Management (Gold Standard)**
    ◦ **Primary surgical repair** of the perforation is the definitive treatment, especially if diagnosed within 24 hours
    ◦ This is typically performed via a **thoracotomy** (left-sided approach is most common)
    ◦ Includes debridement of necrotic tissue and wide drainage of the mediastinum and pleural space
• **Non-Operative Management**
    ◦ Reserved for a highly select group of stable patients with a contained perforation and minimal contamination
    ◦ Includes NPO, IV antibiotics, nutritional support (TPN or feeding jejunostomy), and percutaneous drainage of any fluid collections
• **Endoscopic Management**
    ◦ Newer, less invasive options for select cases
    ◦ Includes **esophageal stenting (SEMS)** to cover the defect or **endoscopic vacuum-assisted closure (endo-VAC)** therapy
sections.complications:
• **Mediastinitis**
• **Sepsis and Septic Shock**
• **Empyema** (pus in the pleural space)
• **Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)**
• **Fistula formation** (esophagopleural, esophagobronchial)
• **Multi-organ failure**
• **Death**
sections.prognosis:
• **Time-dependent**: The single most important prognostic factor is the time from perforation to surgical intervention
    ◦ **Early Diagnosis (<24 hours)**: Mortality rate is approximately 10-25%
    ◦ **Delayed Diagnosis (>24 hours)**: Mortality rate increases dramatically to >50%

sections.overview:
• Gastritis is the inflammation of the gastric mucosa, which is a histological diagnosis confirmed by biopsy showing inflammatory cells.
    ◦ It is distinct from **gastropathy**, which involves epithelial cell damage and regeneration with minimal to no inflammation (e.g., from NSAIDs, alcohol, bile reflux).
    ◦ Gastritis can be classified as acute or chronic, and erosive or non-erosive.
• **Acute Gastritis**: Rapid onset of inflammation, often with neutrophils.
    ◦ Commonly associated with NSAIDs, alcohol, or stress.
• **Chronic Gastritis**: Slower onset with persistent inflammation, featuring lymphocytes and plasma cells.
    ◦ Most commonly caused by *H. pylori* or autoimmune processes.
sections.etiology:
• Gastritis results from an imbalance between mucosal protective factors (mucus, bicarbonate, prostaglandins, blood flow) and mucosal damaging factors (acid, pepsin, exogenous agents).
• **Common Causes:**
    ◦ ***Helicobacter pylori* Infection (Most Common Cause Overall)**
        ▪ **Pathophysiology**: Gram-negative, spiral-shaped bacterium that survives in the acidic stomach by producing **urease**, which converts urea to ammonia, creating a neutral pH microenvironment. It disrupts the mucosal barrier via cytotoxins (e.g., CagA, VacA) and inflammatory mediators, leading to chronic inflammation.
        ▪ **Location**: Typically begins in the **antrum** (Type B Gastritis) and can spread to the body.
    ◦ **NSAIDs and Aspirin**
        ▪ **Pathophysiology**: Systemic inhibition of **cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1)**, which decreases the production of protective **prostaglandins**. This leads to reduced mucus and bicarbonate secretion, decreased mucosal blood flow, and impaired epithelial healing. This is technically a **gastropathy**.
    ◦ **Autoimmune Gastritis (Type A Gastritis)**
        ▪ **Pathophysiology**: Autoantibodies attack gastric parietal cells (leading to decreased acid production - **achlorhydria**) and **intrinsic factor (IF)**. The loss of IF prevents Vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum, leading to **pernicious anemia**.
        ▪ **Location**: Affects the **body and fundus** of the stomach. Achlorhydria leads to a compensatory G-cell hyperplasia and **hypergastrinemia**.
    ◦ **Acute Stress Gastritis**
        ▪ **Pathophysiology**: Splanchnic hypoperfusion in critically ill patients (e.g., sepsis, shock, severe burns, head trauma) leads to mucosal ischemia and breakdown.
        ▪ **Specific types**: **Curling's ulcer** (severe burns), **Cushing's ulcer** (intracranial injury/pressure).
    ◦ **Other Causes**
        ▪ **Alcohol**: Direct toxic effect on the gastric mucosa.
        ▪ **Bile Reflux**: Common after gastric surgery (e.g., gastrectomy).
        ▪ **Radiation / Chemotherapy**: Direct mucosal damage.
        ▪ **Infections (other than *H. pylori*)**: CMV, Herpes simplex, Fungi (in immunocompromised patients).
sections.epidemiology:
• ***H. pylori*-associated gastritis**: Extremely common worldwide, with prevalence exceeding 50% in developing nations. Prevalence increases with age and lower socioeconomic status.
• **NSAID-induced gastropathy**: Very common, especially in the elderly population and those with chronic inflammatory conditions requiring long-term NSAID use.
• **Autoimmune gastritis**: Less common (~5% of chronic gastritis), more prevalent in individuals of Northern European descent and associated with other autoimmune conditions (e.g., Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Type 1 Diabetes).
sections.riskFactors:
• ***H. pylori* infection**
• **Chronic NSAID/aspirin use**
• **Heavy alcohol consumption**
• **Smoking**
• Advanced age
• Critical illness (mechanical ventilation, coagulopathy, shock, sepsis)
• Autoimmune disorders
• Previous gastric surgery
• Chemotherapy or radiation therapy
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The clinical presentation is highly variable; many patients, especially with chronic gastritis, are **asymptomatic**.
• When symptoms are present, they are often nonspecific.
• **Most common presentation**: Dyspepsia (epigastric discomfort/pain).
• **Acute presentation**: May present with sudden onset epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and/or upper GI bleed.
• **Chronic presentation**: Often insidious onset of vague epigastric pain, or presentation with a complication like anemia.
• **Symptoms may include:**
    ◦ **Epigastric pain/burning**: The most common symptom. Often described as a gnawing or burning sensation.
    ◦ Nausea and/or vomiting
    ◦ Anorexia (loss of appetite)
    ◦ Bloating, belching
    ◦ Early satiety
    ◦ **Symptoms of GI Bleeding**: Hematemesis ("coffee-ground" emesis), melena (black, tarry stools).
    ◦ **Symptoms of Anemia**: Fatigue, pallor, weakness, dyspnea on exertion (from chronic blood loss or pernicious anemia).
    ◦ **Neurologic Symptoms (Pernicious Anemia)**: Paresthesias, gait abnormalities, memory changes.
sections.physicalExam:
• Often **unremarkable/normal**.
• **Epigastric tenderness** to palpation may be present.
• **Signs of bleeding**:
    ◦ Pallor (conjunctival) due to anemia.
    ◦ Tachycardia, hypotension (in acute, severe hemorrhage).
    ◦ Positive fecal occult blood test (FOBT) or rectal exam showing melena.
• **Signs of pernicious anemia**:
    ◦ Atrophic glossitis (smooth, beefy red tongue).
    ◦ Neurologic deficits (e.g., decreased vibratory and position sense).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Gold Standard: Upper Endoscopy (EGD) with Biopsy**
    ◦ **Visualization**: Allows direct inspection of the gastric mucosa for erythema, erosions, ulcers, mucosal atrophy (thinning, visible submucosal vessels), or polyps.
    ◦ **Biopsy**: Confirms the diagnosis of gastritis histologically (shows inflammatory infiltrates) and can identify the etiology (e.g., presence of *H. pylori*, metaplasia, atrophy).
• ***H. pylori* Testing**
    ◦ **Invasive (via EGD)**:
        ▪ **Rapid Urease Test**: Biopsy sample is placed in a medium with urea; a color change indicates ammonia production by urease. High sensitivity and specificity.
        ▪ **Histology**: Direct visualization of the organism on the biopsy specimen.
    ◦ **Non-invasive**:
        ▪ **Urea Breath Test**: Patient ingests urea labeled with a carbon isotope. *H. pylori* urease liberates the labeled CO2, which is detected in expired breath. **Test of choice to confirm eradication.**
        ▪ **Stool Antigen Test**: Detects *H. pylori* antigens in the stool. Excellent for initial diagnosis and confirming eradication.
        ▪ **Serology (IgG antibodies)**: Indicates exposure but cannot distinguish between active and past infection. **Not useful for confirming eradication.**
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **CBC**: To detect anemia.
        ▪ Microcytic anemia (low MCV) suggests iron deficiency from chronic blood loss.
        ▪ Macrocytic anemia (high MCV) suggests pernicious anemia (Vitamin B12 deficiency).
    ◦ **Serum Vitamin B12, Iron studies.**
    ◦ **Autoimmune markers (if suspected)**: Anti-parietal cell and anti-intrinsic factor antibodies.
    ◦ **Serum Gastrin**: Markedly elevated in autoimmune gastritis due to achlorhydria.
sections.treatment:
• **General & Supportive Measures**
    ◦ Discontinue offending agents (NSAIDs, alcohol).
    ◦ Symptomatic relief with antacids or acid-suppressive therapy.
• **Acid-Suppressive Therapy**
    ◦ **Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs)**: *Omeprazole, pantoprazole, lansoprazole*. Most effective agents for healing gastric inflammation. Typically given for 4-8 weeks.
    ◦ **H2 Receptor Antagonists (H2RAs)**: *Famotidine, cimetidine*. Less potent than PPIs.
• ***H. pylori* Eradication**
    ◦ **Bismuth Quadruple Therapy (First-line in many regions)**: PPI + Bismuth subsalicylate + Metronidazole + Tetracycline for 10-14 days.
    ◦ **Clarithromycin-based Triple Therapy**: PPI + Clarithromycin + Amoxicillin (or Metronidazole for PCN allergy) for 14 days. Use is limited by high rates of clarithromycin resistance.
• **Autoimmune Gastritis**
    ◦ No treatment to stop the autoimmune process.
    ◦ **Lifelong parenteral Vitamin B12 supplementation** is required to treat/prevent pernicious anemia.
• **Stress Ulcer Prophylaxis**
    ◦ For high-risk, critically ill patients (e.g., on mechanical ventilation >48h, coagulopathy).
    ◦ Prophylaxis with a PPI or H2RA.
sections.management:
• **Follow-up for *H. pylori***: Confirm eradication with a urea breath test or stool antigen test at least 4 weeks after completion of antibiotic therapy and 1-2 weeks after stopping PPIs.
• **Surveillance for Autoimmune Gastritis**: Due to increased risk of gastric adenocarcinoma and carcinoid tumors, periodic endoscopic surveillance (e.g., every 3-5 years) is often recommended.
sections.complications:
• **Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD)**
• **Upper GI Bleeding**
• **Chronic Atrophic Gastritis**
• **Intestinal Metaplasia** (pre-cancerous lesion)
• **Gastric Adenocarcinoma** (risk increased with both chronic *H. pylori* and autoimmune gastritis)
• **MALT Lymphoma** (Mucosa-Associated Lymphoid Tissue lymphoma, strongly associated with *H. pylori*)
• **Pernicious Anemia** (specific to autoimmune gastritis)
• **Gastric Outlet Obstruction** (from chronic inflammation and scarring, rare)
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for acute gastritis or *H. pylori*-associated gastritis if the cause is removed or treated effectively. MALT lymphoma often regresses with *H. pylori* eradication alone.
• **Guarded** for chronic atrophic gastritis and autoimmune gastritis due to the lifelong risk of malignancy, which necessitates surveillance.
sections.preventionEducation: • **Patient Education**: Advise patients to avoid NSAIDs, limit alcohol, and cease smoking.

sections.overview:
• **Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD)** refers to defects in the **gastric** or **duodenal mucosa** that extend through the **muscularis mucosa**.
• It results from an imbalance between **aggressive factors** (gastric acid, pepsin) and **protective mechanisms** (mucus layer, bicarbonate, prostaglandins).
• The two most common forms are **duodenal ulcers (DU)** and **gastric ulcers (GU)**.
sections.etiology:
• PUD develops when the mucosal lining of the stomach or duodenum is damaged, allowing acid and pepsin to cause an ulcer.
• **Core Pathophysiology**: Imbalance between mucosal **protective factors** and **aggressive factors**.
    ◦ **Protective Factors**:
        ▪ Mucus-bicarbonate barrier
        ▪ **Prostaglandins** (stimulate mucus/bicarb secretion, increase mucosal blood flow)
        ▪ Cellular regeneration
        ▪ Adequate mucosal blood flow
    ◦ **Aggressive Factors**:
        ▪ Gastric acid (HCl)
        ▪ Pepsin
        ▪ ***Helicobacter pylori*** infection
        ▪ **NSAIDs**
• **Two Major Causes**:
    ◦ **1. *Helicobacter pylori* Infection**:
        ▪ Gram-negative, spiral-shaped bacterium that colonizes the gastric mucosa.
        ▪ **Mechanism**:
            ▪ Produces **urease**, which converts urea to ammonia (NH3), neutralizing local gastric acid to create a protective cloud for the bacteria.
            ▪ Produces toxins (e.g., CagA, VacA) that directly damage mucosal cells.
            ▪ Induces a chronic inflammatory response (gastritis), which increases acid production and reduces mucosal defenses.
        ▪ Associated with >90% of duodenal ulcers and ~80% of gastric ulcers.
    ◦ **2. Nonsteroidal Anti-inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs)**:
        ▪ Second most common cause.
        ▪ **Mechanism**:
            ▪ **Systemic effect**: Inhibit cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2) enzymes, leading to decreased production of protective **prostaglandins**.
            ▪ **Topical effect**: NSAIDs are weak acids that can directly irritate the gastric mucosa.
• **Other/Rarer Causes**:
    ◦ **Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome (ZES)**: Gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumor (**gastrinoma**) leading to massive gastric acid hypersecretion. Suspect in patients with multiple, severe, or refractory ulcers.
    ◦ **Physiologic Stress ("Stress Ulcers")**: Seen in critically ill patients (e.g., severe burns - ***Curling's ulcer***; head trauma - ***Cushing's ulcer***). Due to systemic hypoperfusion of the GI tract.
    ◦ Viral infections (CMV), Crohn's disease, idiopathic.
sections.epidemiology:
• Lifetime prevalence of ~5-10% in the general population.
• Incidence has decreased due to widespread ***H. pylori*** eradication.
• **Duodenal Ulcers (DU)**: More common than gastric ulcers. Typically affects a younger population (30-55 years).
• **Gastric Ulcers (GU)**: Typically affects an older population (55-70 years).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is **dyspepsia**, which is characterized by **epigastric pain**.
• The nature of the pain can help differentiate between duodenal and gastric ulcers.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Gold Standard**: **Upper Endoscopy (EGD)** with biopsy.
• **Upper Endoscopy (EGD)**:
    ◦ **Diagnostic test of choice**.
    ◦ Allows for direct visualization, biopsy to rule out malignancy (especially for GUs), and testing for ***H. pylori*** (rapid urease test).
    ◦ Can also be used for therapeutic intervention (e.g., stopping a bleed).
• **Barium Upper GI Series**:
    ◦ Used if endoscopy is contraindicated.
    ◦ Less sensitive.
    ◦ Ulcer appears as a well-demarcated crater.
    ◦ Not a first-line test.
• ***H. pylori* Testing**:
    ◦ **Non-Invasive Tests**:
        ▪ **Urea Breath Test (UBT)**:
            ▪ **Test of choice** for initial diagnosis and to **confirm eradication** post-treatment.
            ▪ High sensitivity and specificity.
            ▪ Patient must be off PPIs for 1-2 weeks and antibiotics/bismuth for 4 weeks.
        ▪ **Stool Antigen Assay**:
            ▪ Also excellent for initial diagnosis and confirming eradication.
            ▪ Similar accuracy to UBT and subject to the same medication restrictions.
        ▪ **Serology (IgG antibodies)**:
            ▪ Only indicates **exposure**, not active infection.
            ▪ Cannot be used to confirm eradication as antibodies persist after treatment.
            ▪ Limited clinical utility.
    ◦ **Invasive Tests (via Endoscopy)**:
        ▪ **Rapid Urease Test (CLO test)**: Biopsy sample is placed in a medium with urea; a color change indicates the presence of urease (and thus *H. pylori*).
        ▪ **Histology**: **Gold standard** for detecting *H. pylori*. Stains of the biopsy sample reveal the organism.
• **Laboratory Studies**:
    ◦ **CBC**: Check for **anemia** (normocytic or microcytic if chronic blood loss).
    ◦ **Fasting Serum Gastrin**: Order if suspecting **ZES** (refractory/multiple ulcers, diarrhea). Markedly elevated (>1000 pg/mL) is diagnostic.
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent with eradication of ***H. pylori*** or cessation of **NSAIDs**.
• Recurrence rate is low (<10%) after successful *H. pylori* eradication.
• Recurrence is high if the underlying cause is not addressed.
• Complications (especially **perforation**) carry significant morbidity and mortality.

sections.overview:
• Gastric cancer is a malignancy arising from the lining of the stomach.
• Over 90% of gastric cancers are **adenocarcinomas**.
• It is often diagnosed at an advanced stage due to the nonspecific nature of early symptoms, leading to a generally poor prognosis.
• There are two main histologic subtypes:
    ◦ **Intestinal-type**: more common, resembles intestinal glands, associated with environmental factors.
    ◦ **Diffuse-type**: less common, poorly differentiated, infiltrative, associated with younger age and worse prognosis.
sections.etiology:
• The development of gastric cancer is a multi-step process, often initiated by chronic inflammation.
• **Correa Cascade (Intestinal-Type)**: This is the classic pathway.
    ◦ **Normal Mucosa**
    ◦ **Chronic Gastritis**: Primarily caused by ***Helicobacter pylori* infection**.
    ◦ **Atrophic Gastritis**: Loss of normal gastric glands.
    ◦ **Intestinal Metaplasia**: Gastric epithelium is replaced by intestinal-type epithelium.
    ◦ **Dysplasia**: Pre-cancerous cellular changes.
    ◦ **Adenocarcinoma**.
• ***Helicobacter pylori* Infection**: The single most important etiological agent.
    ◦ It induces chronic inflammation, leading to the cascade described above.
    ◦ The **CagA** (cytotoxin-associated gene A) protein is a key virulence factor that promotes oncogenesis.
• **Diffuse-Type (Signet Ring Cell Carcinoma)**:
    ◦ This type is less associated with *H. pylori*.
    ◦ It is characterized by poorly cohesive, individually infiltrating malignant cells that contain intracellular mucin, pushing the nucleus to the periphery (a **"signet ring" appearance**).
    ◦ This leads to a thickened, rigid stomach wall, a condition known as **linitis plastica** or "leather bottle stomach."
    ◦ It is often associated with **E-cadherin (CDH1) gene mutations**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Global Incidence**: Fifth most common cancer worldwide but a leading cause of cancer-related death.
• **Geographic Variation**: High incidence in **East Asia (Japan, Korea, China)**, Eastern Europe, and South America. Lower incidence in North America and Western Europe.
• **Age**: Incidence increases sharply after age 50; peak incidence in the 7th decade.
• **Sex**: Affects males approximately twice as often as females (2:1 ratio).
sections.riskFactors:
• **Infection**: Chronic ***H. pylori* infection** (strongest risk factor). Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) is also implicated in a small subset.
• **Dietary**:
    ◦ High intake of **salt-preserved, smoked, or pickled foods** (contain high levels of nitrates, which are converted to carcinogenic N-nitroso compounds).
    ◦ Low intake of fruits and vegetables.
• **Lifestyle**: **Smoking** (doubles the risk), heavy alcohol use.
• **Host Factors/Genetics**:
    ◦ Family history of gastric cancer.
    ◦ **Blood Type A**.
    ◦ Hereditary syndromes: **Hereditary Diffuse Gastric Cancer (CDH1 mutation)**, **Lynch syndrome**, **Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP)**.
• **Pre-malignant Conditions**:
    ◦ **Atrophic gastritis** and **intestinal metaplasia**.
    ◦ **Pernicious anemia**.
    ◦ **Menetrier disease** (giant hypertrophic gastropathy).
    ◦ Previous partial gastrectomy (esp. Billroth II anastomosis) >15 years prior.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a patient over 55 with **new-onset, persistent dyspepsia**, often accompanied by "**alarm" features**.
• Unfortunately, early-stage gastric cancer is often **asymptomatic** or causes only vague, nonspecific symptoms, leading to delayed diagnosis.
sections.physicalExam:
• Often unremarkable in early disease.
• **Cachexia and temporal wasting**: Signs of advanced malignancy and malnutrition.
• **Pallor**: Due to chronic **iron-deficiency anemia** from occult bleeding.
• **Palpable epigastric mass**: Indicates a large, locally advanced tumor.
• **Hepatomegaly**: Suggests liver metastasis.
• **Ascites**: Suggests peritoneal carcinomatosis.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Initial Lab Work**:
    ◦ **CBC**: May show **microcytic, hypochromic anemia** (iron deficiency) from chronic GI blood loss.
    ◦ **CMP**: May show elevated LFTs (alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin) with liver metastasis.
• **Definitive Diagnosis**:
    ◦ **Upper Endoscopy (EGD) with Biopsy**: This is the **gold standard**. 
        ▪ Malignant ulcers are typically large with heaped-up, irregular margins.
        ▪ Multiple biopsies (at least 7-8) should be taken from the ulcer edge and base.
• **Staging Workup (Crucial for Treatment Planning)**:
    ◦ **CT scan of Chest/Abdomen/Pelvis with IV contrast**: The primary tool to assess for local tumor extent, lymph node involvement, and distant metastases (liver, lungs).
    ◦ **Endoscopic Ultrasound (EUS)**: Most accurate test for determining the **depth of tumor invasion (T stage)** and assessing **regional lymph nodes (N stage)**.
    ◦ **PET-CT**: Used to detect occult metastatic disease.
    ◦ **Staging Laparoscopy**: Often performed before curative-intent surgery to rule out small peritoneal metastases that may not be visible on CT imaging.
• **Tumor Markers**:
    ◦ CEA, CA 19-9, CA 72-4 may be elevated but are **not sensitive or specific for diagnosis**.
    ◦ They are primarily used to monitor treatment response or detect recurrence in patients with initially elevated levels.
sections.treatment:
• **Early Stage (Localized, Stage 0-I)**:
    ◦ **Endoscopic Resection (EMR/ESD)**: For very early, superficial tumors confined to the mucosa.
    ◦ **Surgical Resection**: The mainstay for curative intent.
        ▪ **Gastrectomy** (subtotal for distal tumors, total for proximal/large tumors) with **lymphadenectomy** (D2 dissection is standard).
• **Locally Advanced (Stage II-III)**:
    ◦ **Perioperative Chemotherapy + Surgery**: This is the standard of care. 
        ▪ Chemotherapy (e.g., **FLOT regimen**) is given before (neoadjuvant) and after (adjuvant) surgery to shrink the tumor and treat micrometastases.
    ◦ Adjuvant chemoradiation may be considered post-operatively.
• **Metastatic (Stage IV) or Unresectable**:
    ◦ **Palliative Chemotherapy**: The goal is to prolong survival and improve quality of life. Combination chemotherapy is standard.
    ◦ **Targeted Therapy**: For tumors that are **HER2-positive** (~20%), adding **Trastuzumab** to chemotherapy improves survival.
    ◦ **Immunotherapy**: **PD-1 inhibitors** (e.g., Pembrolizumab, Nivolumab) are options in select patients.
    ◦ **Palliative Interventions**: Radiation for bleeding/pain, stenting for obstruction, nutritional support.
sections.management:
• **Nutritional Support**: Essential both before and after surgery. Patients may require feeding tubes (jejunostomy tube) post-gastrectomy.
• **Post-Gastrectomy Complications**:
    ◦ **Dumping Syndrome**: Rapid passage of hyperosmolar chyme into the small intestine. Managed with dietary modification (small, frequent, low-carbohydrate meals).
    ◦ **Nutrient Deficiencies**: Lifelong monitoring and supplementation of **Vitamin B12**, iron, calcium, and Vitamin D is required.
• **Surveillance**: Regular follow-up with clinical exams, lab work, and imaging (CT scans) to monitor for recurrence. Endoscopy may also be performed.
sections.complications:
• **GI Bleeding**: From ulceration of the primary tumor.
• **Gastric Outlet Obstruction**: From tumors in the antrum or pylorus.
• **Perforation**: Can lead to peritonitis.
• **Malnutrition and Cachexia**: Due to anorexia, early satiety, and malabsorption.
• **Metastatic Disease**: Liver failure (from mets), malignant ascites, bowel obstruction.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is **highly dependent on the stage at diagnosis**.
• **5-Year Overall Survival**:
    ◦ **Stage I** (localized to mucosa/submucosa): > 70-90%
    ◦ **Stage II**: ~50%
    ◦ **Stage III**: ~20-30%
    ◦ **Stage IV** (metastatic): < 5-10%
• **Diffuse-type** and **signet ring cell** histology have a worse prognosis than intestinal-type.

sections.overview:
• **Celiac disease** is a chronic, immune-mediated enteropathy of the small intestine caused by an inflammatory response to **gluten** and related proteins in genetically susceptible individuals.
◦ This reaction leads to small intestinal mucosal injury, characterized by **villous atrophy**, which results in malabsorption of macro- and micronutrients.
• It is not a food allergy but an **autoimmune disorder**.
sections.etiology:
• The pathophysiology involves an interplay of genetic, environmental, and immunologic factors.
◦ **Environmental Trigger**
▪ Ingestion of **gluten**, a protein found in **wheat, barley, and rye**.
▪ The primary toxic component is a peptide called **gliadin**.
◦ **Genetic Susceptibility**
▪ Strong association with specific Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) class II genes: **HLA-DQ2** (present in ~95% of patients) and **HLA-DQ8** (present in most of the remaining ~5%).
▪ These genes are necessary but not sufficient for disease development.
◦ **Immune Response**
▪ **Gliadin** peptides cross the intestinal epithelial barrier.
▪ In the lamina propria, the enzyme **tissue transglutaminase (tTG)** deamidates the gliadin peptides.
▪ Deamidated gliadin is presented by antigen-presenting cells (APCs) via **HLA-DQ2/DQ8** molecules to CD4+ T-helper cells.
▪ This activates a T-cell-mediated inflammatory cascade, leading to the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IFN-γ).
▪ B-cells are also activated, producing autoantibodies: **anti-tTG**, **anti-endomysial (EMA)**, and **anti-deamidated gliadin peptide (DGP)** antibodies.
◦ **Resulting Histopathologic Damage**
▪ **Villous atrophy**: Blunting or complete loss of the small intestinal villi, reducing the surface area for absorption.
▪ **Crypt hyperplasia**: Elongation of the crypts of Lieberkühn.
▪ **Increased intraepithelial lymphocytes (IELs)**: Infiltration of T-cells into the intestinal lining.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects approximately 1% of the population in Western countries.
• **Demographics**: Can be diagnosed at any age.
◦ Bimodal distribution of presentation: early childhood (6-24 months) and adulthood (3rd-4th decades).
• **Sex**: More common in females (2:1 ratio).
• **Ethnicity**: More prevalent in Caucasians of Northern European descent.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation is highly variable, ranging from classic malabsorptive symptoms to completely asymptomatic.
• Adults are more likely to present with atypical or extra-intestinal manifestations.
• **Classic Presentation** (more common in children)
◦ Chronic diarrhea, **steatorrhea** (pale, foul-smelling, fatty stools), abdominal distention, weight loss, and failure to thrive.
• **Atypical/Extra-intestinal Presentation** (more common in adults)
◦ Symptoms related to nutrient malabsorption or systemic inflammation without prominent GI symptoms.
• **Silent/Asymptomatic**
◦ Positive serology and **villous atrophy** on biopsy but no discernible symptoms.
◦ Often discovered during screening of high-risk individuals.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Important Note**: All testing must be done while the patient is on a **gluten-containing diet**.
• **Serologic Testing (Initial Screening)**
◦ **Best initial test**: **IgA tissue transglutaminase (tTG-IgA) antibody**.
▪ Highly sensitive (>95%) and specific.
◦ **Simultaneously check total serum IgA level** to rule out selective IgA deficiency.
▪ If total IgA is low, the tTG-IgA test will be falsely negative.
◦ **If IgA deficient**: Use IgG-based tests, such as **DGP-IgG** or **tTG-IgG**.
◦ **Other antibodies (less common first-line)**:
▪ **Endomysial IgA (EMA-IgA)**: Highly specific (>99%) but less sensitive and more expensive than tTG-IgA.
▪ **Deamidated Gliadin Peptide (DGP-IgA/IgG)**: Useful in young children (<2 years) and IgA deficient patients.
• **Endoscopy with Biopsy (Confirmatory Gold Standard)**
◦ An esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) with **multiple small bowel biopsies** (at least 4-6) from the second/third portion of the duodenum is required to confirm the diagnosis.
◦ **Characteristic Histologic Findings**:
▪ **Villous atrophy** (blunting or flattening of villi)
▪ **Crypt hyperplasia**
▪ **Increased intraepithelial lymphocytes (IELs)**
◦ Endoscopic findings may include scalloping of duodenal folds, mucosal fissures, or a mosaic pattern, but the mucosa can also appear normal.
• **Other Laboratory Studies**
◦ **CBC**: Microcytic anemia (iron deficiency), macrocytic anemia (folate/B12 deficiency).
◦ **Iron Studies**: Low ferritin, low serum iron, high TIBC.
◦ **CMP**: Hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, hypoalbuminemia, elevated transaminases (AST/ALT).
◦ **Vitamin levels**: Low Vitamin D, B12, folate.
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent with strict adherence to a lifelong **gluten-free diet**.
• Symptoms typically improve within weeks, and histologic changes resolve over months to years.
• Adherence to a GFD reduces the risk of long-term complications, including malignancy, to nearly that of the general population.

sections.overview:
• A **Small Bowel Obstruction (SBO)** is a **mechanical blockage** of the lumen of the small intestine, which prevents the normal transit of intestinal contents (chyme, fluid, and gas).
    ◦ This leads to **proximal accumulation** of these contents, **bowel distention**, and a cascade of physiological disturbances.
    ◦ SBO is a common surgical emergency that can be classified as:
        ▪ **Partial** or **complete**.
        ▪ **Simple** (blood supply intact).
        ▪ **Strangulated** (blood supply compromised), the latter being a life-threatening surgical emergency.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• SBO accounts for **~15% of hospital admissions** for acute abdominal pain in the U.S.
• It is the most common disorder of the small intestine requiring surgery.
• The incidence increases with age, largely due to the increased prevalence of prior abdominal surgeries and malignancy.
• **Adhesions** are the cause in >60% of cases, followed by **hernias** and **neoplasms**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The patient often appears **acutely ill**, in distress from pain, and may be restless.
• Signs of **dehydration** are common, including:
    ◦ **Tachycardia**
    ◦ **Dry mucous membranes**
    ◦ **Poor skin turgor**
• **Fever**, **severe tachycardia**, and **hypotension** are ominous signs suggesting **strangulation**, **sepsis**, or **perforation**.
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• **Simple (non-strangulated) SBO**: **Mortality rate is <5%** with prompt treatment.
• **Strangulated SBO**: **Mortality rate rises significantly to 20-30%**, especially if diagnosis or surgery is delayed.
• **Recurrence**: High.
    ◦ Up to 20% of patients managed non-operatively for adhesive SBO will be readmitted within one year.

sections.overview: • Ileus is a temporary and functional (non-mechanical) inhibition of intestinal motility. ◦ Characterized by the cessation of peristalsis, leading to a backup of gas and fluid within the bowel lumen in the absence of a physical blockage. • Most commonly seen in hospitalized patients, especially after abdominal surgery. • It is critical to differentiate ileus from a mechanical small bowel obstruction (SBO), as their management strategies differ significantly.
sections.etiology: • The pathophysiology involves a complex interplay of neurogenic, hormonal, and inflammatory factors that disrupt normal coordinated bowel motility. • Etiologies: ◦ Post-operative (Most Common): Abdominal or pelvic surgery leads to sympathetic nervous system stimulation and the release of local inflammatory mediators (e.g., cytokines, nitric oxide), which paralyze the gut. This is often called "postoperative ileus." ◦ Medications: ▪ Opioids: Directly bind to mu-receptors in the enteric nervous system, inhibiting peristalsis. ▪ Anticholinergics: Block parasympathetic stimulation, which is crucial for gut motility. ▪ Anesthetics. ◦ Metabolic/Electrolyte Disturbances: ▪ Hypokalemia (classic cause) ▪ Hypomagnesemia ▪ Hyponatremia ▪ Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) ◦ Intra-abdominal Inflammation/Infection: ▪ Pancreatitis ▪ Appendicitis ▪ Diverticulitis ▪ Peritonitis / Sepsis ◦ Retroperitoneal Processes: ▪ Retroperitoneal hemorrhage (e.g., from trauma, leaking AAA) ▪ Renal colic / Pyelonephritis ◦ Systemic Illness: Sepsis, pneumonia (especially lower lobe), myocardial infarction. ◦ Trauma: Spinal cord injury, vertebral fractures. • The final common pathway is the disruption of the neuromuscular apparatus of the intestinal wall. ◦ Increased sympathetic tone (inhibitory) and decreased parasympathetic tone (stimulatory) are key drivers. ◦ Inflammatory cells release substances that are directly toxic to smooth muscle, further inhibiting coordinated contractions.
