sections.epidemiology: • Extremely common in hospitalized patients. • Postoperative ileus occurs in approximately 15-30% of patients undergoing major abdominal surgery. • The incidence is higher after open procedures compared to laparoscopic procedures and after lower GI surgery (e.g., colectomy) compared to upper GI surgery.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • The typical presentation is a hospitalized or post-operative patient who develops progressive abdominal bloating, nausea, and an inability to tolerate an oral diet, usually 24-72 hours after the inciting event (e.g., surgery). • The patient complains of diffuse, constant discomfort rather than the sharp, colicky pain seen in mechanical obstruction.
sections.diagnostics: • The primary goal of the diagnostic workup is to confirm the diagnosis of ileus and, most importantly, to rule out a mechanical obstruction. • Laboratory Studies: ◦ Complete Blood Count (CBC): To evaluate for leukocytosis suggesting an infectious or inflammatory process. ◦ Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP): Crucial for identifying and monitoring electrolyte abnormalities (K+, Mg++, Na+) and assessing renal function/hydration status. ◦ Amylase/Lipase: To rule out pancreatitis as the underlying cause. ◦ Lactate: To assess for bowel ischemia (would be more concerning for obstruction, but can be elevated in severe ileus with hypoperfusion). • Imaging: ◦ Abdominal X-ray Series (KUB Supine & Upright): ▪ Classic Finding: Uniformly dilated loops of both the small and large bowel. ▪ Air is seen throughout the entire GI tract, including the colon and rectum. ▪ May show diffuse air-fluid levels. ▪ This contrasts with SBO, which typically shows dilated small bowel loops with a decompressed (gasless) colon distally. ◦ CT Scan of Abdomen and Pelvis with IV and/or Oral Contrast: ▪ Gold Standard to definitively differentiate ileus from mechanical obstruction. ▪ Ileus Finding: Continuously air- and fluid-filled bowel without a discrete transition point. Contrast material will pass slowly but completely through the bowel. ▪ SBO Finding: Shows a clear transition point with dilated bowel proximally and collapsed bowel distally. ▪ A CT scan can also help identify the underlying cause (e.g., pancreatitis, abscess, retroperitoneal hematoma).
sections.prognosis: • The prognosis is generally excellent. • Ileus is typically a self-limiting condition that resolves within 2-4 days once the underlying cause is managed effectively. • A "prolonged postoperative ileus" is defined as lasting more than 3-5 days after surgery.

sections.overview: • Short Bowel Syndrome (SBS) is a malabsorptive state that occurs as a result of a significant reduction in the length and/or functional capacity of the small intestine, often clinically defined as a remaining small bowel length of less than 200 cm. ◦ This anatomical or functional loss leads to an inability to absorb sufficient water, electrolytes, and nutrients to sustain life without specialized nutritional support, typically parenteral nutrition (PN). ◦ The severity depends on the length of the resected bowel, the specific segments removed (jejunum vs. ileum), and the presence or absence of the colon and ileocecal valve.
sections.etiology: • Etiology: SBS is the direct result of massive surgical resection of the small intestine. ◦ Adults: ▪ Crohn's disease: Multiple resections due to strictures, fistulas, or inflammation. ▪ Mesenteric vascular events: Acute mesenteric ischemia (arterial embolism/thrombosis, venous thrombosis). ▪ Volvulus: Twisting of the intestine leading to ischemia and necrosis. ▪ Trauma: Severe abdominal injury requiring bowel resection. ▪ Radiation enteritis: Chronic damage from radiation therapy. ◦ Pediatrics: ▪ Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC): Most common cause in premature infants. ▪ Intestinal atresia: Congenital absence or closure of a portion of the intestine. ▪ Midgut volvulus: Congenital malrotation leads to twisting. ▪ Gastroschisis: Congenital abdominal wall defect. • Pathophysiology: The core pathology is a drastic reduction in the mucosal surface area available for nutrient and fluid absorption. Specific deficits are determined by the resected segment: ◦ Jejunal Resection: The ileum can adapt and gradually assume the absorptive functions of the jejunum. Patients may tolerate jejunectomy reasonably well if the ileum is intact. ◦ Ileal Resection: More severe consequences, as the ileum is the exclusive site for: ▪ Vitamin B12 absorption. ▪ Bile salt reabsorption (enterohepatic circulation). ▪ Loss of bile salt reabsorption leads to fat malabsorption (steatorrhea), deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), and secretory diarrhea (choleretic diarrhea) from unabsorbed bile salts in the colon. ◦ Ileocecal Valve Resection: Loss of this barrier: ▪ Accelerates intestinal transit time, reducing contact time for absorption. ▪ Allows for reflux of colonic bacteria into the small intestine, leading to Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth (SIBO), which further worsens malabsorption. ◦ Post-Resection Adaptation: The remaining intestine undergoes structural and functional changes over 1-2 years, including villous hypertrophy and increased absorptive capacity per unit length. ◦ Gastric Hypersecretion: Occurs in the early post-operative period due to loss of inhibitory hormones (like peptide YY) from the resected bowel, leading to high-volume fluid losses and potential peptic ulcer disease.
sections.epidemiology: • Relatively rare condition. • Prevalence is estimated at 2-5 cases per million people. • Most common causes in adults are Crohn's disease and mesenteric ischemia. • Most common cause in neonates is necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC).
sections.clinicalPresentation: • The classic presentation is a patient with a known history of extensive small bowel resection who presents with severe, chronic diarrhea, unintentional weight loss, and signs of dehydration and malnutrition. • The presentation depends on the phase after surgery: ◦ Acute Phase (first few weeks): Characterized by massive fluid and electrolyte losses from diarrhea. Patients are entirely dependent on parenteral nutrition (PN). ◦ Adaptation Phase (up to 2 years): The bowel begins to adapt. Diarrhea may lessen, and some nutrients begin to be absorbed. PN dependence may decrease. ◦ Maintenance Phase: Maximum adaptation has occurred. The patient's nutritional needs are stable, though they may still require long-term PN, specialized diets, and/or medications.
sections.diagnostics: • Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on a history of resection and presenting symptoms. • Investigations focus on quantifying malabsorption and identifying specific deficiencies. ◦ Laboratory Studies: ▪ CBC: Anemia (microcytic from iron deficiency; macrocytic from B12/folate deficiency). ▪ CMP: ▪ Electrolytes (hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia). ▪ Bicarbonate (metabolic acidosis). ▪ BUN/Creatinine (pre-renal azotemia from dehydration). ▪ Albumin/Prealbumin (markers of nutritional status). ▪ Vitamin Levels: B12, Folate, Vitamins A, D, E, K. ▪ Mineral Levels: Iron studies (ferritin, TIBC), Zinc, Selenium, Magnesium. ▪ Coagulation Studies: Prothrombin Time (PT) / INR (elevated with Vit K deficiency). ◦ Stool Studies: ▪ 24- to 72-hour fecal fat collection: Gold standard to quantify steatorrhea. ◦ Imaging: ▪ CT or MR Enterography: To evaluate the anatomy of the remaining bowel, identify strictures, or signs of obstruction. ▪ Small Bowel Follow-Through: Can also assess length and transit time.
sections.prognosis: • Prognosis is highly variable and depends on: ◦ Length and location of remaining bowel. ◦ Presence of the ileum and especially the ileocecal valve. ◦ Degree of intestinal adaptation. ◦ Patient age and comorbidities. • Survival has dramatically improved with advances in parenteral nutrition (PN) and therapies like Teduglutide. • 5-year survival for adults dependent on PN is approximately 70-80%. • Mortality is often due to complications of PN (e.g., liver failure, sepsis) rather than SBS itself.

sections.overview:
• Inflammation or infection of one or more diverticula, which are small, bulging pouches that can form in the lining of the digestive system
    ◦ A common complication of **diverticulosis**, the underlying condition of having these pouches
    ◦ While diverticula can occur anywhere in the colon, they are most common in the **sigmoid colon**
    ◦ **Uncomplicated diverticulitis** is managed medically, while **complicated** cases may require intervention or surgery
sections.etiology:
• The pathophysiology begins with the formation of a diverticulum (**diverticulosis**)
    ◦ **Diverticulum Formation**
        ▪ These are "false" diverticula (**pseudodiverticula**) as they only involve the mucosa and submucosa herniating through the muscularis layer of the colon
        ▪ They typically occur at points of weakness where the **vasa recta** (blood vessels) penetrate the colonic wall
    ◦ **Increased Intraluminal Pressure**
        ▪ **Chronic constipation** and a **low-fiber diet** are thought to increase intraluminal pressure, forcing the mucosa to herniate
    ◦ **Obstruction & Perforation**
        ▪ The inflammatory process is initiated when the neck of a diverticulum becomes obstructed, most commonly by a **fecalith** (a hard piece of stool)
        ▪ This obstruction leads to bacterial overgrowth, distension, and ischemia of the pouch
    ◦ **Inflammation & Infection**
        ▪ The compromised blood flow and bacterial proliferation result in **micro- or macro-perforation** of the diverticulum
        ▪ This leak of colonic contents into the pericolic fat triggers an inflammatory response, which can range from:
            ▪ Localized inflammation (**phlegmon**)
            ▪ A contained **abscess**
            ▪ In severe cases, free perforation and **peritonitis**
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence of Diverticulosis**
    ◦ Extremely common and increases with age
    ◦ <10% in individuals under 40 years old
    ◦ ~50% in individuals by age 60
    ◦ ~65-70% in individuals by age 80
• **Incidence of Diverticulitis**
    ◦ Only 10-25% of individuals with diverticulosis will develop diverticulitis in their lifetime
• **Location**
    ◦ **>95%** of cases occur in the **sigmoid colon** in Western populations
    ◦ Right-sided (cecal) diverticulitis is more common in Asian populations
• **Gender**
    ◦ No significant gender predilection
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The "classic" presentation is a patient over 50 years old with a new onset of steady, deep, aching pain in the **left lower quadrant (LLQ)**, which has been present for a few days
• The patient often reports associated:
    ◦ **Fever**
    ◦ **Nausea**
    ◦ A change in bowel habits, most commonly **constipation**
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• **Uncomplicated**
    ◦ Excellent prognosis
    ◦ About 70-80% of patients respond to medical management
• **Recurrence**
    ◦ Approximately 1/3 of patients will have a second episode
• **Complicated**
    ◦ Morbidity and mortality increase significantly with complications, especially **free perforation**

sections.overview:
• **Diverticulosis** is the presence of diverticula, which are sac-like outpouchings of the colonic mucosa and submucosa through the muscularis propria.
    ◦ It is an anatomical finding, not a disease itself.
    ◦ Most individuals with diverticulosis are asymptomatic.
• When complications arise, it is referred to as diverticular disease.
    ◦ **Diverticulosis**: Presence of diverticula (asymptomatic).
    ◦ **Diverticulitis**: Inflammation and/or infection of one or more diverticula.
    ◦ **Diverticular Bleeding**: Hemorrhage from a diverticulum.
sections.etiology:
• Diverticula are **"false" diverticula** (pseudodiverticula) as they only involve the mucosa and submucosa, not all layers of the bowel wall.
    ◦ **Focal Points of Weakness**:
        ▪ Diverticula form at points where the **vasa recta** (nutrient arteries) penetrate the circular muscle layer of the colon.
        ▪ These points create a structural weakness in the colonic wall.
    ◦ **Increased Intraluminal Pressure**:
        ▪ A **low-fiber diet** leads to smaller, harder stools that require higher colonic pressures for propulsion (segmental contraction).
        ▪ This increased pressure, consistent with **Laplace's law** (Pressure = Tension/Radius), pushes the mucosa and submucosa through the weak points where the vasa recta enter.
    ◦ **Location**:
        ▪ The **sigmoid colon** is the most commonly affected segment (~95% of cases) due to its smaller diameter, which generates the highest intraluminal pressure according to Laplace's law.
        ▪ **Right-sided diverticula** are more common in Asian populations.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Age-dependent**:
    ◦ Prevalence increases significantly with age.
        ▪ <10% in individuals under **40 years old**.
        ▪ ~50-70% in individuals over **60 years old**.
• **Geography**:
    ◦ Highly prevalent in **Western, industrialized nations** (USA, Europe, Australia), correlating with a **low-fiber, highly processed diet**.
    ◦ Much less common in Africa and Asia.
• No significant gender predilection.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The vast majority (~80%) of patients with diverticulosis are **asymptomatic**.
• The condition is most often discovered incidentally during a colonoscopy or on imaging performed for other reasons.
• When symptoms are present in the absence of inflammation, it may be termed **Symptomatic Uncomplicated Diverticular Disease (SUDD)**, which can be difficult to distinguish from **Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS)**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Colonoscopy**:
    ◦ **Gold standard** for diagnosis.
    ◦ Directly visualizes the diverticular orifices in the colonic wall.
    ◦ It is the procedure of choice for screening and diagnosis in a **non-acute setting**.
• **CT Abdomen/Pelvis**:
    ◦ Can identify diverticula and colonic wall thickening.
    ◦ It is the **test of choice for suspected acute diverticulitis**, but not typically used to screen for or diagnose uncomplicated diverticulosis.
• **Barium Enema (Contrast Enema)**:
    ◦ Historically used; shows characteristic **saw-tooth appearance** of the colon.
    ◦ Largely replaced by colonoscopy.
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent for asymptomatic diverticulosis.
• The majority of individuals remain asymptomatic for life.
• Lifetime risk of developing **diverticulitis** is approximately 5-15%.
• Lifetime risk of a significant **diverticular hemorrhage** is approximately 5-15%.

sections.overview:
• **Ulcerative Colitis (UC)** is an idiopathic **inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)** characterized by diffuse, continuous inflammation limited to the **mucosal and submucosal layers** of the colon
    ◦ It **invariably involves the rectum** and extends proximally in a contiguous fashion
    ◦ The hallmark clinical feature is **bloody diarrhea**
    ◦ Unlike Crohn's disease, UC:
        ▪ Does not involve the small intestine (except for **"backwash ileitis"** in rare, severe cases)
        ▪ Is **not transmural**
        ▪ Does not form **fistulas** or **strictures**
sections.etiology:
• The exact etiology is unknown, but it is believed to result from a **dysregulated immune response** to intestinal gut flora in a genetically susceptible individual
    ◦ **Immune Dysregulation**
        ▪ An inappropriate and sustained **T-cell-mediated immune response** (predominantly a **Th2 response**) is directed against commensal gut bacteria
        ▪ This leads to the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., **TNF-alpha**, interleukins) that damage the colonic mucosa
    ◦ **Genetic Predisposition**
        ▪ A **positive family history** is a significant risk factor
        ▪ Numerous susceptibility genes have been identified (e.g., `NOD2` is more associated with Crohn's, but other loci are shared)
    ◦ **Environmental Factors**
        ▪ Alterations in the gut microbiome are thought to play a key role
        ▪ The **"hygiene hypothesis"** suggests that reduced exposure to microbes in early life may predispose individuals to autoimmune diseases
    ◦ **Pathology**
        ▪ **Location:** Inflammation begins in the rectum and spreads proximally in a **continuous, uninterrupted pattern**. The extent is variable (proctitis, left-sided colitis, pancolitis)
        ▪ **Depth:** Inflammation is limited to the **mucosa and submucosa**
        ▪ **Histology:** Key findings include **crypt abscesses** (neutrophils accumulating in the crypts of Lieberkühn), distortion of crypt architecture, and depletion of goblet cells. Chronic inflammation leads to mucosal atrophy
        ▪ **Gross Appearance:** The mucosa appears erythematous, friable (bleeds easily on contact), and granular. Loss of haustral folds and the presence of **pseudopolyps** (islands of regenerating mucosa surrounded by ulceration) are common
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence:** ~10-20 per 100,000 persons per year in North America and Europe
• **Prevalence:** ~200 per 100,000 persons
• **Age of Onset:** **Bimodal distribution**, with a primary peak at age 15-30 and a smaller secondary peak at age 50-70
• **Geography:** More common in developed, industrialized nations and urban areas
• **Ethnicity:** Higher incidence in individuals of **Ashkenazi Jewish descent**
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation depends on the extent and severity of the disease. Most patients present with a gradual onset of symptoms over weeks to months
    ◦ **Mild Disease**
        ▪ <4 stools/day (with or without blood)
        ▪ No systemic toxicity
        ▪ Normal inflammatory markers
    ◦ **Moderate Disease**
        ▪ >4 bloody stools/day
        ▪ Mild anemia
        ▪ Minimal signs of systemic toxicity
    ◦ **Severe Disease (Fulminant Colitis)**
        ▪ >6 bloody stools/day
        ▪ Fever (>37.5°C)
        ▪ Tachycardia (>90 bpm)
        ▪ Severe anemia (Hgb <10.5 g/dL)
        ▪ Elevated **ESR/CRP**
sections.diagnostics:
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **CBC:** Anemia (iron deficiency from blood loss), leukocytosis, thrombocytosis (acute phase reactants)
    ◦ **CMP:** Electrolyte abnormalities (diarrhea), hypoalbuminemia (malnutrition, protein-losing enteropathy)
    ◦ **Inflammatory Markers:** Elevated **ESR** and **CRP**
    ◦ **Stool Studies:** Essential to rule out infectious causes (culture, ova & parasites, C. difficile toxin assay)
    ◦ **Fecal Calprotectin/Lactoferrin:** Highly sensitive and specific markers for intestinal inflammation; useful for differentiating IBD from IBS and for monitoring disease activity
    ◦ **Serology:** **Perinuclear Anti-Neutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibody (p-ANCA)** is positive in ~60-70% of UC patients (Contrast with ASCA, more common in Crohn's)
• **Endoscopy**
    ◦ **Colonoscopy with biopsy is the GOLD STANDARD for diagnosis**
    ◦ **Findings:** Continuous, circumferential inflammation starting in the rectum
        ▪ Mucosa is erythematous, edematous, friable, with a granular appearance and loss of normal vascular markings
        ▪ **Pseudopolyps** may be present
    ◦ **NOTE:** In cases of suspected fulminant colitis, a full colonoscopy is contraindicated due to perforation risk. A flexible sigmoidoscopy without air insufflation is preferred
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Abdominal X-ray (KUB):** Used to evaluate for complications like **toxic megacolon** (colonic diameter >6 cm) or perforation (free air under the diaphragm)
    ◦ **Barium Enema (less common now):** Classic finding is a **"lead pipe" or "stovepipe"** appearance, representing the loss of haustral markings due to chronic inflammation
sections.prognosis:
• UC is a **chronic, relapsing-remitting disease**
• With medical management, most patients can achieve long-term remission
• The overall mortality rate is similar to that of the general population, though it is increased in patients with severe disease or complications like CRC
• **Colectomy is curative** for the intestinal disease

sections.overview:
• Crohn Disease (CD) is a type of Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) characterized by chronic, **transmural**, and granulomatous inflammation that can affect **any part of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract**, from "mouth to anus"
    ◦ It most commonly affects the terminal ileum and proximal colon (ileocolitis)
    ◦ The inflammation is typically discontinuous, with affected segments of bowel separated by normal tissue, known as **skip lesions**
    ◦ Unlike Ulcerative Colitis, surgery is not curative
sections.etiology:
• Believed to result from an inappropriate and exaggerated immune response to normal gut flora in a genetically susceptible individual
• **Immune Dysregulation**
    ◦ An overactive T-helper cell (Th1 and Th17) response leads to the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., TNF-alpha, IL-12, IL-23), causing chronic inflammation
• **Genetic Predisposition**
    ◦ Strong association with mutations in the **`NOD2/CARD15` gene**, which is involved in recognizing bacterial components and regulating the innate immune response
• **Environmental Factors**
    ◦ Smoking is a major trigger
    ◦ Other factors include diet, infections, and changes in the gut microbiome
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Transmural Inflammation**
        ▪ Inflammation extends through all layers of the bowel wall (mucosa, submucosa, muscularis, serosa), leading to complications like strictures, fistulas, and abscesses
    ◦ **Gross Appearance**
        ▪ **Skip Lesions:** Discontinuous areas of inflammation
        ▪ **Cobblestoning:** Longitudinal and transverse linear ulcers interspersed with areas of edematous mucosa
        ▪ **Creeping Fat:** Mesenteric fat wraps around the serosal surface of the bowel
        ▪ **Strictures:** Narrowing of the bowel lumen due to fibrosis and scarring
    ◦ **Microscopic Appearance**
        ▪ **Non-caseating granulomas:** A pathognomonic finding, though only present in ~30% of biopsies
        ▪ Lymphoid aggregates and submucosal inflammation are common
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence:** More common in developed, industrialized nations (North America, Northern Europe)
• **Age of Onset:** Bimodal distribution with a primary peak between ages 15-30 and a smaller secondary peak between 60-80
• **Genetics:** Higher incidence in individuals of Ashkenazi Jewish descent
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is highly variable, ranging from insidious onset of chronic symptoms to an acute presentation mimicking appendicitis
• The classic triad is **abdominal pain, non-bloody diarrhea, and weight loss**
sections.diagnostics:
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **CBC:** Anemia (of chronic disease, iron deficiency, or B12 deficiency), thrombocytosis, leukocytosis
    ◦ **CMP:** Hypoalbuminemia (malnutrition, protein-losing enteropathy), electrolyte abnormalities
    ◦ **Inflammatory Markers:** **Elevated ESR and C-Reactive Protein (CRP)**
    ◦ **Fecal Calprotectin:** Highly sensitive marker for intestinal inflammation, useful for differentiating IBD from IBS and monitoring disease activity
    ◦ **Stool Studies:** To rule out infectious causes (e.g., C. diff, ova & parasites)
    ◦ **Serology**
        ▪ **ASCA (Anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies):** Positive in ~60% of CD patients (more specific for CD than UC)
        ▪ **p-ANCA (perinuclear anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies):** Usually negative (more associated with UC)
• **Endoscopy**
    ◦ **Colonoscopy with terminal ileum intubation is the initial test of choice**
    ◦ **Findings:**
        ▪ Skip lesions, cobblestoning, linear/aphthous ulcers
        ▪ Biopsies are taken to confirm diagnosis (look for non-caseating granulomas)
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **CT Enterography (CTE) or MR Enterography (MRE):** Best modalities to evaluate the small bowel, visualize bowel wall thickening, and identify complications like strictures, fistulas, and abscesses
    ◦ **Small Bowel Follow-Through (Barium Study):** Classic finding is the **"string sign"** representing severe narrowing of the terminal ileum. Largely replaced by CTE/MRE
    ◦ **Capsule Endoscopy:** Can visualize the small bowel mucosa but is **contraindicated if a stricture is suspected** due to risk of retention
sections.prognosis:
• Chronic, lifelong relapsing and remitting disease
• Life expectancy is near normal with modern medical management
• Quality of life can be significantly impaired
• Approximately 50% of patients will require surgery within 10 years of diagnosis

sections.overview:
• **Colorectal cancer (CRC)** is a malignancy arising from the epithelial cells lining the colon or rectum.
• The vast majority (>95%) are **adenocarcinomas**.
• Most cases develop from pre-existing adenomatous polyps through a multi-step process known as the **adenoma-carcinoma sequence**.
• CRC is a common and lethal cancer, but it is also highly preventable and curable when detected early through effective screening programs.
sections.etiology:
• CRC develops through two main genetic pathways:
    ◦ **Chromosomal Instability (CIN) Pathway** (~85% of cases):
        ▪ This is the classic "**adenoma-carcinoma sequence**."
        ▪ Characterized by a stepwise accumulation of mutations in tumor suppressor genes and oncogenes.
        ▪ **Step 1: APC gene mutation** (tumor suppressor gene) leads to epithelial hyperproliferation.
        ▪ **Step 2: KRAS gene mutation** (oncogene) allows for the formation of a small adenoma.
        ▪ **Step 3: p53 gene mutation** (tumor suppressor gene) & other mutations lead to malignant transformation into invasive carcinoma.
        ▪ This pathway is associated with most sporadic CRC and **Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP)**.
    ◦ **Microsatellite Instability (MSI) Pathway** (~15% of cases):
        ▪ Characterized by defects in **DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes** (e.g., *MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2*).
        ▪ Defective MMR leads to the accumulation of mutations in short, repetitive DNA sequences called microsatellites.
        ▪ Associated with **Lynch Syndrome** (Hereditary Non-Polyposis Colorectal Cancer or HNPCC) and a subset of sporadic right-sided tumors.
        ▪ Tumors are often poorly differentiated, mucinous, and have a better prognosis stage-for-stage compared to CIN pathway tumors.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence:** **3rd most common cancer** diagnosed in both men and women in the United States.
• **Mortality:** **2nd leading cause of cancer-related death** in the U.S. when men and women are combined.
• **Age:** Incidence increases significantly after age 45-50. The median age at diagnosis is ~66 years.
• **Gender:** Slightly more common in men than women.
• **Race:** **African Americans** have the highest incidence and mortality rates.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Often **asymptomatic** in early stages, highlighting the critical importance of screening.
• Symptoms typically develop with advanced disease and vary by tumor location.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Screening** (for average-risk individuals, starting at age 45):
    ◦ **Tier 1 (Preferred):**
        ▪ **Colonoscopy every 10 years:** The gold standard. Both diagnostic and therapeutic (can remove polyps).
    ◦ **Tier 2 (Acceptable):**
        ▪ **Fecal Immunochemical Test (FIT) annually:** Detects human globin in stool. More specific than gFOBT.
        ▪ **Stool DNA Test (e.g., Cologuard) every 3 years:** Combines FIT with detection of abnormal DNA biomarkers.
        ▪ **CT Colography ("Virtual Colonoscopy") every 5 years.**
    ◦ Any positive non-colonoscopy screening test **must be followed up with a diagnostic colonoscopy**.
• **Diagnosis and Staging:**
    ◦ **Definitive Diagnosis:** **Colonoscopy with biopsy.** Required to confirm the diagnosis of adenocarcinoma.
    ◦ **Laboratory Studies:**
        ▪ **CBC:** To evaluate for anemia (microcytic, hypochromic suggests iron deficiency).
        ▪ **LFTs:** Elevated alkaline phosphatase can suggest liver or bone metastasis.
        ▪ **CEA (Carcinoembryonic Antigen):** **NOT a screening test.** Used as a baseline marker before treatment and for monitoring for recurrence after treatment.
    ◦ **Staging Workup (TNM Staging):**
        ▪ **CT Scan of the Chest, Abdomen, and Pelvis with contrast:** The standard imaging modality to assess for nodal involvement and distant metastatic disease (liver, lungs, peritoneum).
        ▪ **Pelvic MRI:** Standard for staging rectal cancer to assess the depth of tumor invasion (T stage) and lymph node involvement, which guides neoadjuvant therapy decisions.
        ▪ **PET Scan:** May be used in select cases to clarify ambiguous findings on CT or to assess for recurrence.
sections.prognosis:
• The **stage at diagnosis** is the most important prognostic factor.
• **5-Year Survival Rates (Approximate):**
    ◦ **Stage I:** >90%
    ◦ **Stage II:** 65-85%
    ◦ **Stage III:** 40-70% (wide range based on nodal burden)
    ◦ **Stage IV:** <15%

sections.overview: • Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) is a chronic, functional gastrointestinal (GI) disorder characterized by recurrent abdominal pain associated with altered bowel habits (diarrhea, constipation, or both). • It is a diagnosis of exclusion, meaning organic pathology must be ruled out. • IBS does not cause inflammation, permanent intestinal damage, or increase the risk of colorectal cancer. • Sub-classified based on the predominant stool pattern: ◦ IBS with constipation (IBS-C) ◦ IBS with diarrhea (IBS-D) ◦ Mixed IBS (IBS-M) ◦ Unclassified IBS (IBS-U)
sections.etiology: • The pathophysiology of IBS is multifactorial and best conceptualized as a disorder of the brain-gut axis. • Key mechanisms include: ◦ Visceral Hypersensitivity ▪ Increased sensation and pain perception in response to normal stimuli within the gut (e.g., gas, peristalsis). ◦ Altered GI Motility ▪ Abnormal gut motor function leading to either rapid transit (diarrhea) or slow transit (constipation). ◦ Brain-Gut Dysregulation ▪ Altered communication between the central nervous system (CNS) and the enteric nervous system (ENS). ▪ Psychological stress can directly influence gut sensation, motility, and secretion. ◦ Post-Infectious ▪ A subset of patients develops IBS following an episode of acute infectious gastroenteritis. ◦ Gut Microbiome Alterations ▪ Dysbiosis, or an imbalance in the gut flora, may contribute to symptoms like bloating and gas. ▪ Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth (SIBO) has a high degree of overlap with IBS. ◦ Low-Grade Inflammation ▪ Microscopic inflammation and an increased number of mast cells have been observed in the intestinal mucosa of some IBS patients. ◦ Serotonin (5-HT) Pathway Dysregulation ▪ Abnormal serotonin signaling is implicated in IBS, as it is a key neurotransmitter in the ENS regulating motility and sensation.
sections.epidemiology: • Prevalence: Affects approximately 10-15% of the population in Western countries. • Gender: More common in females than males (approx. 2:1 ratio). • Age of Onset: ◦ Typically presents in late adolescence and early adulthood. ◦ New onset after age 50 is less common and warrants a more thorough workup for organic disease.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • The classic presentation is a young female with a long history of chronic, intermittent, cramping abdominal pain, often in the lower abdomen. • The pain is characteristically related to bowel movements (either improved or worsened by defecation) and is associated with a change in the frequency or form of the stool. • Patients often report significant bloating, distention, and a feeling of incomplete evacuation. • Symptoms are often exacerbated by stress or ingestion of certain foods. • Importantly, the patient should have no alarm features.
sections.diagnostics: • IBS is a clinical diagnosis based on symptom criteria after ruling out organic disease.
sections.prognosis: • IBS is a chronic, relapsing-remitting condition. • Prognosis regarding mortality is excellent; life expectancy is normal. • Symptom severity and impact on quality of life are highly variable. • Many patients learn to manage their symptoms effectively with lifestyle modifications and medication.

sections.overview:
• **Pseudomembranous colitis** is an inflammation of the colon caused by the overgrowth of a spore-forming, toxin-producing bacterium, **_Clostridioides difficile_** (formerly _Clostridium difficile_).
• The condition is characterized by severe, watery diarrhea and the formation of **"pseudomembranes"** (yellow-white plaques of inflammatory debris) on the colonic mucosa.
• It is most commonly a complication of **antibiotic therapy**, which disrupts the normal, protective gut flora.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiologic Agent**: **_Clostridioides difficile_**, a Gram-positive, obligate anaerobic, spore-forming bacillus.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Disruption of Normal Colonic Flora**: Broad-spectrum antibiotics eradicate protective commensal bacteria in the gut, creating an environment for **_C. difficile_** to proliferate.
    ◦ **Ingestion and Germination**: Hardy **_C. diff_ spores** are ingested (fecal-oral route) and survive gastric acid. In the colon, they germinate into vegetative, toxin-producing bacteria.
    ◦ **Toxin Production**: The vegetative bacteria produce two key exotoxins:
        ▪ **Toxin A (an enterotoxin)**: Causes intestinal fluid secretion, inflammation, and mucosal injury by disrupting tight junctions between enterocytes.
        ▪ **Toxin B (a cytotoxin)**: More potent than Toxin A, it causes cytoskeletal disruption leading to cell necrosis and apoptosis.
    ◦ **Inflammatory Cascade**: The toxins trigger a profound inflammatory response, attracting neutrophils and leading to epithelial cell death, increased vascular permeability, and fluid secretion.
    ◦ **Pseudomembrane Formation**: The characteristic **pseudomembranes** are formed from an adherent layer of inflammatory cells (neutrophils), fibrin, mucus, and necrotic epithelial cells.
sections.epidemiology:
• The most common cause of infectious, **healthcare-associated diarrhea** in the developed world.
• Primarily affects patients in hospitals and long-term care facilities.
• Incidence is highest in the **elderly population** (>65 years).
• **Hypervirulent strains** (e.g., NAP1/BI/027) are associated with more severe disease and higher mortality.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • A typical presentation involves a hospitalized patient (often elderly) who was recently treated with antibiotics for another infection (e.g., pneumonia, UTI) and now develops acute, profuse, watery diarrhea several days to weeks after starting the antibiotic course.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Stool Studies**:
    ◦ **Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT/PCR)**:
        ▪ **Preferred initial test**.
        ▪ Highly sensitive and specific for **_C. diff_ toxin genes** (*tcdA* and *tcdB*).
        ▪ Can detect asymptomatic carriers, so clinical correlation is essential.
    ◦ **Glutamate Dehydrogenase (GDH) Antigen Assay**:
        ▪ A highly sensitive screening test for the presence of the **_C. diff_** organism.
        ▪ It does not confirm toxin production.
    ◦ **Toxin EIA (Enzyme Immunoassay)**:
        ▪ Detects the actual **Toxin A/B**.
        ▪ Highly specific but has lower sensitivity than NAAT.
    ◦ **Multi-Step Algorithm**:
        ▪ Many labs use a two- or three-step process (e.g., GDH + Toxin EIA, with NAAT as a tie-breaker) to balance sensitivity and specificity.
• **Laboratory Findings**:
    ◦ **CBC**:
        ▪ **Marked leukocytosis** (WBC >15,000/L) is common and can be a marker of severity.
        ▪ A **leukemoid reaction** (WBC >50,000) can occur.
    ◦ **BMP**:
        ▪ Elevated creatinine (**AKI** from dehydration), electrolyte abnormalities.
    ◦ **Albumin**:
        ▪ **Hypoalbuminemia** (<3 g/dL) is a marker of severe disease.
• **Imaging (for Complications)**:
    ◦ **Abdominal X-Ray (KUB)**:
        ▪ Used to look for colonic dilation (**toxic megacolon** >6cm), **ileus**, or free air (**perforation**).
    ◦ **CT Abdomen/Pelvis**:
        ▪ More sensitive for detecting colonic wall thickening (**"accordion sign"**), **pericolonic stranding**, **ascites**, or **perforation**.
• **Endoscopy (Sigmoidoscopy/Colonoscopy)**:
    ◦ Generally **contraindicated** due to risk of **perforation**.
    ◦ Performed only if the diagnosis is in doubt.
    ◦ **Finding**: Characteristic scattered, yellow-white plaques or **"pseudomembranes"** overlying an erythematous and friable mucosa.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is generally good for mild-to-moderate disease if diagnosed and treated promptly.
• Mortality is significantly higher in elderly, immunocompromised patients, and those who develop **fulminant colitis** or **toxic megacolon** (mortality >30-50%).
• **Recurrence** is a major challenge, significantly impacting quality of life.

sections.overview:
• **Hepatitis A** is an acute, self-limiting inflammatory liver disease caused by the Hepatitis A virus (HAV).
• Transmission is primarily through the **fecal-oral route**.
• The illness is typically characterized by an abrupt onset of constitutional and gastrointestinal symptoms followed by **jaundice**.
• It **does not cause chronic liver disease**, and infection confers lifelong immunity.
• The incidence has dramatically decreased in developed nations due to effective vaccination.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**: Hepatitis A Virus (HAV).
• **Virus Type**: A non-enveloped, single-stranded RNA virus from the *Picornaviridae* family.
• **Transmission**: **Fecal-oral route**.
    ◦ Ingestion of food or water contaminated with fecal matter.
    ◦ Person-to-person contact (e.g., household contacts, sexual contact, daycare settings).
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ After ingestion, the virus replicates in the oropharynx and gastrointestinal tract.
    ◦ A transient viremia occurs, seeding the liver.
    ◦ The virus replicates within hepatocytes and is released into the biliary system, then shed in the feces. Fecal shedding begins **before** symptoms appear.
    ◦ Liver injury is not caused directly by the virus (it is non-cytopathic). Instead, damage is **immune-mediated**, resulting from the host's cytotoxic T-cell response to infected hepatocytes.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Has declined by over 95% in the U.S. since the vaccine became available in 1995. 
    ◦ However, outbreaks still occur, often among people experiencing homelessness or persons who use drugs.
• **Global Distribution**: Endemic in regions with poor sanitation and hygiene (parts of Africa, Asia, Central/South America).
• **Incubation Period**: Average **28 days** (range: 15-50 days).
• **Infectivity**: Patients are most contagious during the 1-2 weeks **before** the onset of jaundice/symptoms and for about one week after symptoms begin.
    ◦ Children are often asymptomatic carriers and can be a major source of transmission.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is highly age-dependent.
    ◦ Children <6 years old are often **asymptomatic** or have a mild, anicteric illness.
    ◦ Adults and older children are more likely to be symptomatic.
• The illness typically has two phases:
    ◦ **Prodromal (Pre-icteric) Phase**: Abrupt onset of non-specific viral symptoms lasting several days to a week.
    ◦ **Icteric Phase**: Following the prodrome, patients develop **jaundice**, **dark urine**, and other signs of hepatic dysfunction.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Serology (The Gold Standard)**
    ◦ **Anti-HAV IgM**
        ▪ **Diagnostic of acute Hepatitis A infection**.
        ▪ Appears early in the illness and disappears within 3-6 months.
    ◦ **Anti-HAV IgG (or Total Anti-HAV)**
        ▪ Indicates **past infection or immunity from vaccination**.
        ▪ Appears as IgM declines and persists for life, conferring immunity.
• **Liver Function Tests (LFTs)**
    ◦ **ALT (Alanine Aminotransferase) & AST (Aspartate Aminotransferase)**
        ▪ Markedly **elevated**, often **>1,000 U/L**.
        ▪ Typically, **ALT > AST**.
        ▪ This dramatic rise is a hallmark of acute viral hepatitis.
    ◦ **Total & Direct Bilirubin**
        ▪ **Elevated**, correlating with the degree of jaundice.
    ◦ **Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP)**
        ▪ May be normal or mildly elevated.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** in the vast majority of cases.
• Complete clinical and biochemical recovery is expected within 2-3 months.
• **Hepatitis A does not cause chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, or hepatocellular carcinoma**.
• Infection provides **lifelong immunity** against HAV.

sections.overview:
• **Hepatitis B** is a liver infection caused by the **Hepatitis B virus (HBV)**, a **DNA virus**.
    ◦ It can range from an acute, self-limiting illness to a chronic infection.
    ◦ Chronic infection poses a high risk for death from **cirrhosis** and **hepatocellular carcinoma**.
    ◦ Transmission occurs through **parenteral**, **sexual**, and **perinatal** routes.
    ◦ The risk of developing chronic infection is inversely related to the age at which infection occurs.
• Vaccination is highly effective for prevention.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiologic Agent**: **Hepatitis B Virus (HBV)**, a member of the *Hepadnaviridae* family.
• **Virus Structure**: Partially double-stranded circular DNA virus.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ HBV is **not directly cytopathic**; liver damage is caused by the host's **cytotoxic T-lymphocyte (CD8+)** immune response against infected hepatocytes.
    ◦ The virus replicates in hepatocytes and can integrate its DNA into the host's genome, which is a key mechanism for its **oncogenic potential** (**hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)**), even without cirrhosis.
    ◦ **Acute infection**: A vigorous immune response leads to clearance of the virus and subsequent immunity.
    ◦ **Chronic infection**: An inadequate immune response fails to clear the virus, leading to persistent viral replication, chronic inflammation, and potential progression to **fibrosis**, **cirrhosis**, and **HCC**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Global Prevalence**: Over 290 million people live with chronic hepatitis B, with the highest prevalence in the Western Pacific and African Regions.
• **United States**: Prevalence has significantly decreased due to universal childhood vaccination.
• **Transmission Modes**:
    ◦ **Perinatal (Vertical)**: Mother to child during birth. This is the most common mode worldwide and carries the highest risk (~90%) of leading to chronic infection.
    ◦ **Parenteral (Percutaneous)**: Contaminated needles (**IV drug use**, tattoos, acupuncture), blood transfusions, and occupational exposure.
    ◦ **Sexual**: Transmitted via semen and vaginal fluids.
sections.riskFactors:
• Birth in a region with high **HBV** endemicity (e.g., Asia, sub-Saharan Africa)
• Persons who inject drugs (**PWID**)
• Men who have sex with men (**MSM**)
• Individuals with multiple sexual partners
• Household contacts or sexual partners of **HBV**-infected persons
• Patients on **hemodialysis**
• Healthcare and public safety workers with potential occupational exposure
• Residents and staff of facilities for developmentally disabled persons
• Incarcerated individuals
• Infants born to **HBsAg-positive** mothers
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Incubation Period**: Average 90 days (range 45-160 days).
• **Acute Hepatitis B**:
    ◦ Often **asymptomatic** or subclinical, especially in children.
    ◦ Can present with a "**serum sickness-like**" prodrome: **fever**, **rash**, and **arthralgias**.
    ◦ **Symptoms**:
        ▪ **Prodrome**: **Malaise**, **fever**, **anorexia**, **nausea**, **vomiting**, **abdominal pain (RUQ)**.
        ▪ **Icteric Phase**: **Jaundice**, **dark-colored urine** (bilirubinuria), **pale or clay-colored stools** (acholic stools), **pruritus**.
• **Chronic Hepatitis B**:
    ◦ Most patients are **asymptomatic** for decades.
    ◦ May present with nonspecific symptoms like **fatigue**.
    ◦ Often diagnosed incidentally on routine screening.
    ◦ **Symptoms of decompensated cirrhosis**:
        ▪ **Ascites**, **lower extremity edema**, **jaundice**, **hepatic encephalopathy** (**confusion**, **asterixis**), **gastrointestinal bleeding from varices**.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Acute Findings**:
    ◦ **Scleral icterus**, **jaundiced skin**.
    ◦ **Tender hepatomegaly**.
    ◦ **Splenomegaly** (less common).
• **Chronic Findings**:
    ◦ Exam is often normal.
    ◦ **Stigmata of Chronic Liver Disease** (if cirrhosis is present):
        ▪ **Spider angiomata**, **palmar erythema**, **gynecomastia**, **testicular atrophy**.
        ▪ **Caput medusae** (dilated periumbilical veins).
        ▪ **Ascites** (fluid wave, shifting dullness).
        ▪ **Peripheral edema**.
        ▪ **Asterixis** ("liver flap") in **hepatic encephalopathy**.
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.treatment:
• **Acute Hepatitis B**:
    ◦ **Supportive care** is the mainstay: rest, hydration, nutrition.
    ◦ Avoid **hepatotoxic agents** (e.g., alcohol, acetaminophen).
    ◦ Antiviral therapy is not typically indicated unless the course is severe or **fulminant** (acute liver failure).
• **Chronic Hepatitis B**:
    ◦ **Goal**: Suppress **HBV DNA** replication, normalize **ALT**, and prevent progression to **cirrhosis** and **HCC**. Treatment is suppressive, not curative.
    ◦ **Indications for Treatment**: Patients with high **HBV DNA** levels, elevated **ALT**, and/or significant fibrosis/cirrhosis.
    ◦ **First-Line Pharmacotherapy**: Oral nucleos(t)ide analogues (NAs).
        ▪ **Tenofovir** (TDF or TAF)
        ▪ **Entecavir**
        ▪ These are preferred for high potency and low resistance; treatment is often lifelong.
    ◦ **Second-Line/Alternative**:
        ▪ **Pegylated Interferon alfa-2a (PEG-IFN)**: Given as a finite course (48 weeks). Offers a higher chance of HBsAg clearance but has significant side effects (flu-like symptoms, depression, cytopenias).
sections.management:
• **Monitoring**:
    ◦ Patients on treatment: Monitor **LFTs** and **HBV DNA** every 3-6 months.
    ◦ Inactive carriers (not on treatment): Monitor **LFTs** every 6 months.
• **HCC Screening**:
    ◦ Crucial for all patients with **cirrhosis** and for specific high-risk non-cirrhotic patients (e.g., Asian men >40, family history of HCC).
    ◦ **Abdominal Ultrasound +/- AFP every 6 months**.
sections.complications:
• **Fulminant Hepatic Failure**: Rare (<1%) but life-threatening complication of acute **HBV**.
• **Cirrhosis**: Progressive liver scarring leading to **portal hypertension** (esophageal varices, ascites) and synthetic dysfunction (coagulopathy, hypoalbuminemia).
• **Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC)**: **HBV** is a major cause. **HCC can develop in the absence of cirrhosis** in **HBV**-infected patients.
• **Hepatitis D (Delta Virus) Superinfection**: HDV requires **HBsAg** to replicate; superinfection in a chronic **HBV** carrier can cause rapid progression to cirrhosis.
• **Extrahepatic Manifestations**:
    ◦ **Glomerulonephritis** (membranous or membranoproliferative)
    ◦ **Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN)**
sections.prognosis:
• **Acute Infection**: >95% of immunocompetent adults will clear the virus and develop lifelong immunity.
• **Chronic Infection**: The risk is highly dependent on age at exposure:
    ◦ **Neonates**: ~90%
    ◦ **Children (1-5 years)**: ~30%
    ◦ **Adults**: <5%
• **Untreated Chronic HBV**: Carries a 15-40% lifetime risk of developing **cirrhosis**, **liver failure**, or **HCC**. Effective antiviral therapy significantly reduces these risks.
sections.preventionEducation:
• **Vaccination**:
    ◦ **Highly effective** for prevention.
    ◦ Universal childhood vaccination programs are critical for reducing prevalence.
    ◦ Vaccinate all household and sexual contacts of infected individuals.
• **Patient Education**:
    ◦ Counsel on preventing transmission (**safe sex**, avoid sharing razors/toothbrushes).
    ◦ **Avoid alcohol** completely.
    ◦ Screen for coinfections such as **HCV**, **HDV**, and **HIV**.

sections.overview:
• Hepatitis C is a viral infection of the liver caused by the **Hepatitis C virus (HCV)**, a single-stranded RNA virus.
• It is primarily a **bloodborne pathogen**.
• While the acute infection is often asymptomatic, the majority of cases (~80%) progress to **chronic infection**.
• Chronic HCV is a leading cause of **liver cirrhosis**, **hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)**, and the need for liver transplantation in the United States.
• Treatment has been revolutionized by **Direct-Acting Antivirals (DAAs)**, which offer a cure in over 95% of cases.
sections.etiology:
• **Virus**: **Hepatitis C virus (HCV)**, a single-stranded, enveloped RNA virus of the *Flaviviridae* family.
• **Transmission**: Primarily **parenteral** (blood-to-blood contact).
• **Pathogenesis**:
    ◦ **Infection**: HCV enters the bloodstream and infects **hepatocytes**.
    ◦ **Replication**: The virus replicates within the hepatocytes. Unlike Hepatitis B, HCV is **not directly cytopathic** (it doesn't kill the liver cells itself).
    ◦ **Immune Response**: The host's **T-cell mediated immune response** recognizes and attacks the infected hepatocytes, causing inflammation and liver cell necrosis.
    ◦ **Chronic Inflammation**: The virus has a high mutation rate, creating "quasispecies" that evade the immune system, leading to persistent infection and chronic inflammation.
    ◦ **Fibrosis**: Chronic inflammation triggers hepatic stellate cells to produce collagen, leading to progressive **liver fibrosis**.
    ◦ **Cirrhosis**: Over decades, the extensive fibrosis disrupts liver architecture, leading to **cirrhosis** and its associated complications.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: An estimated 2.4 million people in the U.S. have chronic Hepatitis C.
• **Incidence**: New infections are rising, primarily due to the opioid crisis and increased **injection drug use**.
• **Key Cohorts**:
    ◦ **"Baby Boomers" (born 1945-1965)**: Highest prevalence. Many were infected decades ago via contaminated blood products before routine screening began in 1992.
    ◦ **Persons Who Inject Drugs (PWID)**: Currently the group with the highest incidence of new infections.
• **Genotypes**: There are at least 6 major HCV genotypes. Genotype 1 is the most common in the United States. Modern treatments are often **pan-genotypic**.
sections.riskFactors:
• **High-Risk**:
    ◦ **Current or past injection drug use (most common mode of transmission)**
    ◦ Blood transfusion or organ transplant before July 1992
    ◦ Receipt of clotting factor concentrates before 1987
• **Moderate-Risk**:
    ◦ Chronic hemodialysis
    ◦ Intranasal drug use (sharing straws)
    ◦ Unregulated tattoos or piercings
    ◦ Occupational needlestick injury
    ◦ Children born to HCV-positive mothers (**vertical transmission**, ~5% risk)
• **Lower-Risk**:
    ◦ Sexual contact with an HCV-positive person (more efficient with **HIV co-infection** or high-risk sexual behaviors)
    ◦ Sharing personal items like razors or toothbrushes
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Hepatitis C is often called a "silent epidemic" because it is frequently **asymptomatic for decades**.
• **Acute HCV Infection**:
    ◦ Occurs 2-12 weeks after exposure.
    ◦ **Largely asymptomatic (>80% of cases)**.
    ◦ If symptomatic, presentation is mild and non-specific:
        ▪ Fatigue, malaise
        ▪ Nausea, anorexia
        ▪ **RUQ pain**
        ▪ Low-grade fever
        ▪ **Jaundice** (uncommon)
        ▪ Dark urine, pale stools
• **Chronic HCV Infection**:
    ◦ The insidious, long-term phase.
    ◦ Most patients are **asymptomatic** until they develop advanced liver disease.
    ◦ May have non-specific symptoms like chronic **fatigue**, which is the most common complaint.
• **Decompensated Cirrhosis**:
    ◦ Presentation of end-stage liver disease.
    ◦ This is often the first time a patient becomes symptomatic.
• **Extrahepatic Manifestations**:
    ◦ **Mixed Cryoglobulinemia**: Vasculitis causing a classic triad of **palpable purpura**, **arthralgias**, and **glomerulonephritis**.
    ◦ **Glomerulonephritis**: Especially **Membranoproliferative Glomerulonephritis (MPGN)**.
    ◦ **Porphyria Cutanea Tarda**: Fragile skin, photosensitivity, vesicles/bullae on sun-exposed areas.
    ◦ Lichen planus, sicca syndrome.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Early/Chronic Disease**: Often a completely **normal physical exam**.
• **Advanced Liver Disease (Cirrhosis)**:
    ◦ **General**: **Jaundice**, **scleral icterus**, muscle wasting.
    ◦ **Skin**: **Spider angiomata**, **palmar erythema**, **caput medusae**, ecchymosis.
    ◦ **Abdomen**: **Hepatomegaly** (early cirrhosis) or a shrunken, nodular liver (late cirrhosis), **splenomegaly**, **ascites** (fluid wave, shifting dullness).
    ◦ **Neuro**: **Asterixis** ("liver flap"), confusion, lethargy (signs of **hepatic encephalopathy**).
    ◦ **Endocrine**: **Gynecomastia**, testicular atrophy.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Step 1: Screening (Antibody Test)**
    ◦ **HCV Antibody (Anti-HCV) / (HCV Ab)**: Detects exposure to the virus.
        ▪ If negative, no infection (unless very recent exposure).
        ▪ If positive, it means the person has been infected at some point. **It does not distinguish between active and cleared infection**.
• **Step 2: Confirmation (Viral Load)**
    ◦ **HCV RNA (Quantitative PCR)**: Confirms **active, current infection**.
        ▪ If HCV RNA is detected, the patient has chronic Hepatitis C.
• **Step 3: Pre-Treatment Workup**
    ◦ **HCV Genotype**: Was critical for older therapies; less so for modern pan-genotypic DAAs but still often obtained.
    ◦ **Liver Function Tests (LFTs)**: AST and ALT may be normal or mildly elevated (**ALT > AST** typically, until cirrhosis develops then **AST > ALT**).
    ◦ **Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP)**: Assess bilirubin, albumin, creatinine.
    ◦ **Complete Blood Count (CBC)**: Look for **thrombocytopenia** (suggests portal hypertension/splenomegaly).
    ◦ **Coagulation Panel**: **INR/PT** (prolonged INR indicates synthetic liver dysfunction).
    ◦ **Staging Fibrosis (Assess liver damage)**:
        ▪ **Non-invasive markers**: FIB-4 or APRI score (calculated from CBC/LFTs).
        ▪ **Imaging**: Transient elastography (**FibroScan**) is preferred to measure liver stiffness.
        ▪ **Liver Biopsy**: Gold standard but rarely needed now; reserved for diagnostic uncertainty.
    ◦ **Co-infection screening**: HIV, Hepatitis B (HBV surface antigen, surface antibody, core antibody). **Reactivation of HBV** is a risk during HCV treatment.
sections.treatment:
• **Current Standard: Direct-Acting Antivirals (DAAs)**
    ◦ **Mechanism**: Target specific viral proteins essential for HCV replication.
    ◦ **Advantages**: All-oral, short duration (8-12 weeks), >95% cure rate, minimal side effects.
    ◦ **Common Regimens (Pan-Genotypic)**:
        ▪ *Glecaprevir/Pibrentasvir (Mavyret)*
        ▪ *Sofosbuvir/Velpatasvir (Epclusa)*
• **Old Regimens (Historical)**:
    ◦ **Pegylated Interferon and Ribavirin**: **No longer first-line** due to long treatment course, numerous severe side effects (flu-like symptoms, depression, cytopenias), and lower cure rates.
sections.management:
• **AVOID ALCOHOL**.
• Caution with hepatotoxic drugs (e.g., limit Acetaminophen to <2g/day).
• Counsel on preventing transmission (do not share needles, razors, etc.).
• Patients who had **cirrhosis before** being cured of HCV remain at risk for **HCC**.
    ◦ They require lifelong **HCC surveillance with liver ultrasound +/- AFP every 6 months**.
sections.complications:
• **Hepatic**:
    ◦ **Cirrhosis**: The most common serious complication.
    ◦ **Decompensated Cirrhosis**: **Ascites**, **variceal hemorrhage**, **hepatic encephalopathy**, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
    ◦ **Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC)**: HCV is a major risk factor.
• **Extrahepatic**:
    ◦ **Mixed Cryoglobulinemia**
    ◦ **Membranoproliferative Glomerulonephritis (MPGN)**
    ◦ **Porphyria Cutanea Tarda**
    ◦ Increased risk of **B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma**
sections.prognosis:
• **Without treatment**: ~20-30% of chronically infected individuals will develop **cirrhosis** over 20-30 years.
• **With DAA treatment**: Excellent.
    ◦ Achieving **SVR12 (cure)** halts liver inflammation, can lead to regression of fibrosis, and dramatically reduces the risk of **cirrhosis**, **HCC**, and liver-related death.
• **Prognosis with cirrhosis**: Depends on the severity (Child-Pugh score, MELD score).
    ◦ Even after HCV cure, the risk of **HCC persists**, though it is reduced.

sections.overview:
• Cirrhosis is the final common pathway of chronic liver injury, characterized by irreversible hepatic fibrosis, scarring, and the formation of regenerative nodules.
    ◦ This process disrupts the normal liver architecture and microcirculation, leading to a progressive decline in liver function and the development of **portal hypertension**.
    ◦ Clinically, cirrhosis is classified as **compensated** (asymptomatic or non-specific symptoms) or **decompensated** (presence of complications like ascites, variceal hemorrhage, or encephalopathy).
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology (Most Common in US)**
    ◦ **Alcoholic Liver Disease**: Most common cause in Western countries.
    ◦ **Chronic Viral Hepatitis**: Hepatitis C (historically) and Hepatitis B.
    ◦ **Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD) / Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH)**: Rapidly becoming the leading cause, associated with metabolic syndrome.
• **Other Important Causes**
    ◦ **Autoimmune**: Autoimmune hepatitis, Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC), Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC).
    ◦ **Genetic/Metabolic**: Hemochromatosis (iron overload), Wilson's disease (copper overload), Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.
    ◦ **Vascular**: Budd-Chiari syndrome, veno-occlusive disease, chronic right-sided heart failure (congestive hepatopathy).
    ◦ **Drug-induced**: Methotrexate, amiodarone, isoniazid.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The core mechanism is a cycle of chronic hepatocyte injury, inflammation, and fibrogenesis.
        ▪ **Hepatocyte Injury**: The underlying etiology (e.g., alcohol, virus, fat) causes chronic damage to liver cells.
        ▪ **Inflammation & Cytokine Release**: Damaged hepatocytes release inflammatory signals.
        ▪ **Hepatic Stellate Cell Activation**: This is the key step. Normally quiescent, stellate cells (Ito cells) in the Space of Disse are activated by inflammatory cytokines (like TGF-β).
        ▪ **Fibrogenesis**: Activated stellate cells transform into myofibroblast-like cells that produce and deposit excessive amounts of collagen and extracellular matrix in the liver parenchyma.
        ▪ **Nodule Formation**: Fibrous septa connect portal tracts, encircling and isolating nodules of regenerating hepatocytes.
        ▪ **Architectural Distortion**: This process destroys the normal lobular architecture, leading to two major consequences:
            ▪ **Synthetic Dysfunction**: Loss of functional hepatocyte mass impairs the liver's ability to produce albumin, clotting factors, and metabolize substances like bilirubin and ammonia.
            ▪ **Portal Hypertension**: Fibrosis and nodules increase resistance to portal blood flow, raising pressure within the portal venous system (>5 mmHg gradient).
sections.epidemiology:
• Leading causes in the U.S. are alcohol, NAFLD, and chronic Hepatitis C.
• Prevalence is estimated at 0.15% - 0.27% of the US population.
• Typically diagnosed in individuals aged 45-65.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation depends on whether the disease is **compensated** or **decompensated**.
• **Compensated**: Often asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on routine labs (**thrombocytopenia**, elevated LFTs) or imaging. May present with non-specific symptoms.
• **Decompensated**: Patient presents with one or more of the major complications:
    ◦ **Ascites**: Abdominal distention, weight gain.
    ◦ **Variceal Hemorrhage**: **Hematemesis**, **melena**, hemodynamic instability.
    ◦ **Hepatic Encephalopathy**: Confusion, lethargy, personality changes, **asterixis**.
    ◦ **Jaundice**: Yellowing of the skin and eyes.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Laboratory Findings**
    ◦ **Synthetic Function** (Reflects severity)
        ▪ **Albumin**: Decreased protein synthesis.
        ▪ **PT/INR**: Decreased synthesis of coagulation factors II, VII, IX, X.
        ▪ **Total Bilirubin**: Impaired conjugation and excretion.
    ◦ **CBC**
        ▪ **Thrombocytopenia**: Often the earliest and most reliable sign. Due to splenic sequestration (**hypersplenism**) and decreased thrombopoietin production.
        ▪ **Anemia**, **leukopenia**.
    ◦ **Liver Enzymes** (Reflects ongoing injury, may be normal in end-stage)
        ▪ **AST & ALT**: **AST > ALT** (ratio > 2:1) is highly suggestive of **alcoholic liver disease**.
        ▪ **Alkaline Phosphatase (Alk Phos) & GGT**: Suggests cholestasis.
    ◦ **Electrolytes**
        ▪ **Hyponatremia**: Dilutional, due to inability to excrete free water. A marker of severe disease.
        ▪ **Serum Creatinine**: Assess for **hepatorenal syndrome**.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Ultrasound with Doppler**: First-line imaging. Can show liver nodularity (coarse echotexture), **ascites**, **splenomegaly**, and assess portal vein size and flow direction (**hepatofugal** = reversed flow). Used for **HCC screening**.
    ◦ **Transient Elastography (FibroScan)**: Non-invasive method to measure liver stiffness (fibrosis).
    ◦ **CT/MRI**: Better characterizes liver morphology, nodules, and portal hypertension. Essential for evaluating for **hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)**.
• **Procedures**
    ◦ **Upper Endoscopy (EGD)**: To screen for and treat esophageal **varices**. Recommended in all newly diagnosed cirrhosis patients.
    ◦ **Paracentesis** (if ascites is present)
        ▪ **Diagnostic**: Cell count with differential (PMNs >250/mm³ = **SBP**), albumin, protein, culture.
        ▪ **SAAG (Serum-Ascites Albumin Gradient)**: `SAAG = (Serum Albumin) - (Ascites Albumin)`. A **SAAG ≥ 1.1 g/dL** is highly specific for **portal hypertension**.
    ◦ **Liver Biopsy**: **Gold Standard** for diagnosis. Confirms cirrhosis, can help determine etiology, but is invasive and often not needed if clinical picture is clear.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is assessed using scoring systems:
    ◦ **Child-Pugh Score**: Classifies severity into A, B, and C based on Bilirubin, Albumin, INR, Ascites, and Encephalopathy (Mnemonic: **BAILE**). Used for general prognosis and surgical risk assessment.
        ▪ Class A: Well-compensated (1-year survival ~100%)
        ▪ Class C: Decompensated (1-year survival ~45%)
    ◦ **MELD (Model for End-Stage Liver Disease) Score**:
        ▪ Uses Bilirubin, INR, and Creatinine (**BIC**) to predict 3-month mortality.
        ▪ Primary tool used to prioritize patients on the liver transplant list. Higher score = higher priority.

sections.overview:
• Hepatic Encephalopathy (HE) is a spectrum of potentially reversible neuropsychiatric abnormalities seen in patients with liver dysfunction.
• It is a syndrome of impaired brain function resulting from the liver's inability to detoxify noxious substances absorbed from the gut.
• HE can manifest in patients with acute liver failure or, more commonly, chronic liver disease (cirrhosis) with portal hypertension and portosystemic shunting.
• The clinical presentation ranges from subclinical changes to profound coma.
sections.etiology:
• The pathophysiology of HE is multifactorial, but the central theory involves the accumulation of gut-derived neurotoxins in the systemic circulation that cross the blood-brain barrier.
    ◦ **Ammonia (NH3) Hypothesis**: This is the most widely accepted theory.
        ▪ **Production**: Ammonia is primarily produced in the GI tract by enterocytes from glutamine and by colonic bacteria catabolizing nitrogenous sources (e.g., dietary protein, shed mucosal cells).
        ▪ **Failed Clearance**: Normally, ammonia is absorbed into the portal circulation and efficiently converted to urea in the liver via the urea cycle for excretion by the kidneys.
        ▪ **Pathology**: In liver failure or with portosystemic shunting (e.g., cirrhosis, TIPS), this detoxification process is impaired. Ammonia bypasses the liver and enters the systemic circulation.
        ▪ **Neurotoxicity**: Ammonia readily crosses the blood-brain barrier. In the brain, astrocytes metabolize it to **glutamine**. The accumulation of glutamine within astrocytes creates an osmotic gradient, leading to **astrocyte swelling** and **cerebral edema**. This process also depletes other key molecules, alters neurotransmitter systems (notably increasing inhibitory GABAergic tone and disrupting excitatory glutamate pathways), and ultimately impairs neuronal function.
    ◦ **Other Contributing Factors**:
        ▪ **Systemic Inflammation**: Pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1) from infections can increase blood-brain barrier permeability, synergizing with ammonia to worsen neurotoxicity.
        ▪ **Manganese**: Impaired biliary excretion leads to manganese deposition in the basal ganglia, which can contribute to extrapyramidal symptoms.
        ▪ **Altered Neurotransmission**: Increased activity of the inhibitory GABA system contributes to the CNS depression seen in HE.
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects up to 45% of patients with cirrhosis at some point during their disease.
• The development of overt HE is a sign of decompensated cirrhosis and a poor prognostic indicator.
• Commonly seen as a primary reason for hospitalization in patients with cirrhosis.
• Affects up to 80% of patients with a Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt (TIPS).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is a spectrum of altered mental status and neuromuscular dysfunction.
• Family members often report that the patient is "not acting right," confused, or excessively sleepy.
• Onset can be acute or insidious.
sections.diagnostics:
• HE is a **clinical diagnosis of exclusion**.
• The goal of the workup is to confirm the presence of liver disease, rule out other causes of altered mental status, and identify a precipitating factor.
    ◦ **Laboratory Studies**:
        ▪ **Serum Ammonia**: **Often elevated, but it is NOT a diagnostic test and does NOT correlate with the severity of HE.** Venous ammonia levels are notoriously unreliable due to processing issues (must be placed on ice immediately and run quickly). Use is controversial; primarily helpful if the diagnosis is uncertain. A normal level makes HE less likely but does not rule it out.
        ▪ **Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP)**: Check for hypoglycemia, electrolyte abnormalities (Na+, K+), and renal function (BUN/Cr).
        ▪ **Liver Function Tests (LFTs) & Coags (PT/INR)**: To assess the degree of underlying liver dysfunction.
        ▪ **CBC**: To look for anemia (suggesting GI bleed) or leukocytosis (suggesting infection).
        ▪ **Infectious Workup**: Blood cultures, urinalysis, chest X-ray. If ascites is present, perform a diagnostic **paracentesis** to rule out SBP (cell count with differential, culture).
    ◦ **Imaging**:
        ▪ **Head CT (non-contrast) or MRI**: Primarily to **rule out intracranial pathology** (e.g., subdural hematoma, stroke, mass) as the cause of altered mental status. Imaging is typically normal in HE but may show cerebral edema in severe cases.
sections.prognosis:
• The development of overt HE is a sentinel event in cirrhosis, marking the transition to decompensated disease.
• It is associated with a poor prognosis and high mortality.
• One-year survival after a first episode of overt HE is approximately 40%.
• Three-year survival is approximately 20%.

sections.overview:
• **Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC)** is the most common primary malignancy of the liver, an epithelial tumor arising from hepatocytes
    ◦ Most commonly develops in the setting of chronic liver disease and **cirrhosis**, making the underlying liver function a critical factor in both presentation and management
sections.etiology:
• The primary mechanism is chronic liver injury and inflammation leading to a continuous cycle of hepatocyte death and regeneration, which increases the rate of spontaneous mutations that can lead to malignant transformation
• **Common Pathway:** Chronic inflammation → **Fibrosis** → **Cirrhosis** → **Dysplastic nodules** → **HCC**
• **Viral Oncogenesis**
    ◦ **Hepatitis B Virus (HBV)**
        ▪ A DNA virus that can integrate its own DNA into the host hepatocyte genome
        ▪ Can directly activate host proto-oncogenes or inactivate tumor suppressor genes (e.g., **p53**), allowing for **HCC** development **even in the absence of cirrhosis**
    ◦ **Hepatitis C Virus (HCV)**
        ▪ An RNA virus that does not integrate into the host genome
        ▪ Its oncogenic potential is primarily driven by causing chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and ultimately, **cirrhosis**
• **Chemical Carcinogenesis**
    ◦ **Aflatoxin B1**
        ▪ A mycotoxin produced by *Aspergillus* species found on improperly stored grains (corn, peanuts)
        ▪ Induces a specific mutation in the ***TP53*** **tumor suppressor gene**
    ◦ **Alcohol**
        ▪ Leads to **alcoholic steatohepatitis**, inflammation, and **cirrhosis**
        ▪ Ethanol and its metabolite, acetaldehyde, are directly toxic and carcinogenic
• **Metabolic-Driven Pathway**
    ◦ **Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD/NASH)**
        ▪ Chronic inflammation from **steatohepatitis (NASH)** is a rapidly growing cause of **HCC**, driven by obesity, diabetes, and metabolic syndrome
sections.epidemiology:
• Fifth most common cancer worldwide and the second leading cause of cancer-related death globally
• **Geographic Variation:** High incidence in East Asia and sub-Saharan Africa (endemic **HBV**). Incidence is rising in Western countries due to **HCV** and the **NAFLD** epidemic
• **Age:** Peak incidence is typically > 50 years of age
• **Sex:** Strong male predominance (3:1 to 5:1 male-to-female ratio)
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Asymptomatic:** Often detected during routine surveillance in a patient with known **cirrhosis**
• **Decompensated Liver Disease**
    ◦ A patient with previously stable **cirrhosis** may present with a sudden clinical deterioration, such as new-onset **ascites**, **jaundice**, **variceal hemorrhage**, or **hepatic encephalopathy**
    ◦ This should always raise suspicion for **HCC**
• **Symptomatic Tumor**
    ◦ Less commonly, patients present with symptoms directly related to the tumor, such as **abdominal pain** or a **palpable mass**
sections.diagnostics:
• **Surveillance (Screening)**
    ◦ **Indication:** All patients with **cirrhosis** and select high-risk patients with chronic **HBV** without **cirrhosis**
    ◦ **Method:** **Abdominal Ultrasound** +/- **Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)** every 6 months
• **Tumor Marker**
    ◦ **Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)**
        ▪ An elevated **AFP** (>20 ng/mL) in a high-risk patient is suspicious
        ▪ A very high **AFP** (>400-500 ng/mL) in the presence of a characteristic liver mass is virtually diagnostic of **HCC**
    ◦ **Limitation:** Not sensitive enough for screening alone (can be normal in up to 40% of early **HCC** cases) and can be elevated in other conditions (e.g., active hepatitis flare, other tumors). Primarily used for monitoring treatment response and detecting recurrence
• **Imaging (Definitive Diagnosis)**
    ◦ **Gold Standard:** **Multiphasic CT or MRI with contrast**. In a patient with **cirrhosis**, a biopsy is often NOT needed if characteristic imaging features are present
    ◦ **Hallmark Finding (LI-RADS 5 Criteria):** **Arterial Phase Hyperenhancement (APHE)** followed by **Portal Venous or Delayed Phase "Washout"**
        ▪ **Arterial Phase:** The tumor appears bright because it is fed by the hepatic artery
        ▪ **Venous/Delayed Phase:** The tumor appears dark (hypodense) compared to the surrounding liver parenchyma as the contrast "washes out" of the tumor quickly while remaining in the normal liver tissue
• **Biopsy**
    ◦ **Indications:** Atypical imaging findings or when the diagnosis is uncertain (e.g., a liver mass in a non-cirrhotic patient)
    ◦ **Risks:** Bleeding, infection, and a small risk of **tumor seeding** along the needle tract
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly dependent on the stage at diagnosis and the underlying liver function
• **Early Stage (curative treatment):** 5-year survival rates can exceed 70%
• **Intermediate Stage (TACE):** Median survival is approximately 2-3 years
• **Advanced Stage (systemic therapy):** Median survival is approximately 12-18 months
• **Untreated symptomatic HCC:** Median survival is often less than 6 months

sections.overview: • Cholelithiasis refers to the presence of gallstones within the gallbladder, representing the most common gallbladder pathology. • The condition can be asymptomatic (most common) or symptomatic. ◦ Symptomatic cholelithiasis, also known as biliary colic, occurs when a stone transiently obstructs the cystic duct, causing episodic pain. • It serves as the precursor to most other gallbladder complications, including acute cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis, and gallstone pancreatitis.
sections.etiology: • Gallstones are crystalline structures formed from components of bile. • There are two main types: ◦ Cholesterol Stones (~80-90% in the West) ▪ Result from bile that is supersaturated with cholesterol. ▪ Pathophysiology Triangle: ▪ Cholesterol Supersaturation: The liver secretes bile with an excessive amount of cholesterol relative to bile salts and lecithin. ▪ Gallbladder Hypomotility (Stasis): Incomplete or infrequent emptying of the gallbladder allows time for cholesterol to nucleate and form crystals. ▪ Accelerated Crystal Nucleation: Factors within the bile (e.g., mucin glycoproteins) promote the aggregation of cholesterol microcrystals into macroscopic stones. ◦ Pigment Stones (~10-20%) ▪ Black Stones: ▪ Composed primarily of calcium bilirubinate. ▪ Formed in sterile bile due to supersaturation of unconjugated bilirubin. ▪ Associated with conditions of chronic hemolysis (e.g., sickle cell disease, hereditary spherocytosis) and cirrhosis. ▪ Brown Stones: ▪ Composed of calcium salts of unconjugated bilirubin, cholesterol, and fatty acids. ▪ Form in the setting of biliary tract infection (e.g., E. coli, Klebsiella, Ascaris lumbricoides, Clonorchis sinensis). ▪ Bacteria produce β-glucuronidase, which deconjugates bilirubin, leading to precipitation. ▪ More common in the bile ducts than the gallbladder itself.
sections.epidemiology:
• Extremely common, affecting 10-20% of the adult population in Western countries.
• Prevalence increases with age.
• Higher prevalence in women compared to men (approx. 2-3:1).
• Highest prevalence in Native American and Hispanic populations.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • The majority of individuals with cholelithiasis are asymptomatic and stones are found incidentally on imaging. • When symptomatic, the presentation is biliary colic. ◦ This is a distinct clinical syndrome caused by transient cystic duct obstruction.
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis: • Asymptomatic: Excellent. Most patients remain asymptomatic for life. • Symptomatic: Excellent with elective cholecystectomy, which is curative with low morbidity. • The prognosis worsens significantly if complications develop, particularly acute cholangitis or severe gallstone pancreatitis.

sections.overview:
• Cholecystitis is the inflammation of the gallbladder, most commonly caused by a gallstone obstructing the cystic duct, leading to bile stasis, inflammation, and potential infection.
• It is a primary complication of cholelithiasis (gallstones) and a common cause of acute abdominal pain.
• **Acute Cholecystitis**: Sudden onset of gallbladder inflammation.
    ◦ **Calculous (90-95%)**: Caused by cystic duct obstruction from a gallstone.
    ◦ **Acalculous (5-10%)**: Inflammation without stones, typically seen in critically ill patients.
• **Chronic Cholecystitis**: Long-standing gallbladder inflammation from repeated episodes of obstruction or irritation, leading to fibrosis and thickening of the gallbladder wall.
sections.etiology:
• **Acute Calculous Cholecystitis (Most Common)**
    ◦ **Initial Event**: A gallstone becomes impacted in the cystic duct, causing **persistent obstruction**. This is the key difference from biliary colic, where the obstruction is transient.
    ◦ **Bile Stasis**: Obstructed outflow leads to the accumulation of bile, increasing intraluminal pressure and causing gallbladder distention.
    ◦ **Inflammatory Cascade**: The concentrated bile acts as a chemical irritant. Distention compromises blood flow and lymphatic drainage, leading to mucosal ischemia. This triggers the release of inflammatory mediators (e.g., prostaglandins, lysolecithin).
    ◦ **Bacterial Superinfection**: The inflamed, static environment is prone to secondary bacterial infection in 50-85% of cases. Common organisms include **E. coli** (most common), **Klebsiella**, **Enterococcus**, and **Enterobacter**.
• **Acute Acalculous Cholecystitis**
    ◦ Occurs in the absence of gallstones.
    ◦ **Pathophysiology**: Thought to be caused by gallbladder stasis and ischemia. Bile stasis leads to the formation of biliary sludge, which obstructs the cystic duct. Ischemia results from compromised blood flow in states of systemic hypoperfusion.
    ◦ **Associated Conditions**: Critically ill patients, severe trauma, major surgery, burns, sepsis, prolonged TPN (Total Parenteral Nutrition), and immunosuppression.
• **Chronic Cholecystitis**
    ◦ Results from recurrent bouts of acute or subacute cholecystitis or persistent mechanical irritation from gallstones.
    ◦ Leads to mucosal atrophy, fibrosis, and thickening of the gallbladder wall. The gallbladder becomes stiff and its function is impaired.
    ◦ May progress to a **Porcelain Gallbladder**, a premalignant condition characterized by intramural calcification.
sections.epidemiology:
• One of the most common indications for abdominal surgery in Western countries.
• Acute cholecystitis develops in 10-20% of patients with symptomatic cholelithiasis.
• Incidence increases with age.
• More common in women than men.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a patient with a history of biliary colic who now develops persistent, severe pain.
• The onset often follows a **fatty meal**, which stimulates gallbladder contraction against an obstructed cystic duct.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **CBC**: **Leukocytosis** (12,000-15,000/L) with a **left shift** is characteristic.
    ◦ **LFTs (Liver Function Tests)**
        ▪ May be normal or show mild elevations in ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase (Alk Phos), and total bilirubin.
        ▪ **Marked elevation** of Alk Phos and bilirubin should raise suspicion for **choledocholithiasis** or **cholangitis**.
    ◦ **Amylase/Lipase**: Usually normal or slightly elevated. Significant elevation suggests **gallstone pancreatitis**.
    ◦ **CRP**: Elevated.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Abdominal Ultrasound (RUQ)**: **Initial imaging test of choice**.
        ▪ **Key Findings**:
            ▪ Gallbladder wall thickening (>3 mm)
            ▪ Pericholecystic fluid
            ▪ **Sonographic Murphy's sign** (focal tenderness over the gallbladder when compressed by the transducer probe)
            ▪ Presence of gallstones or sludge
