    ◦ **HIDA Scan (Hepatobiliary Iminodiacetic Acid Scan / Cholescintigraphy)**: **Most specific/accurate test**.
        ▪ **Indication**: Used when ultrasound is equivocal.
        ▪ **Procedure**: A radioactive tracer is injected IV, taken up by hepatocytes, and excreted into the bile.
        ▪ **Positive Finding**: The tracer fills the liver and common bile duct, but the **gallbladder does not visualize**. This indicates cystic duct obstruction.
    ◦ **CT Scan**: Not the primary modality but useful for evaluating complications (e.g., perforation, abscess, emphysematous cholecystitis).
    ◦ **MRI/MRCP**: Excellent for visualizing the biliary tree and detecting choledocholithiasis but not typically needed for an initial cholecystitis diagnosis.
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent with early diagnosis and cholecystectomy. Mortality is <1% for uncomplicated cases.
• Prognosis is worse for elderly patients, those with comorbidities, and in the presence of complications like perforation or gangrene.
• Acute acalculous cholecystitis has a significantly higher mortality rate (up to 50%) due to the underlying critical illness of the patient population.

sections.overview:
• **Choledocholithiasis** is the presence of one or more gallstones in the **common bile duct (CBD)**.
◦ Stones can form *de novo* within the duct (**primary**) or, more commonly, migrate from the gallbladder (**secondary**).
◦ The presence of a stone in the CBD can lead to **biliary obstruction**, which can cause jaundice, pain, and potentially life-threatening complications like **acute cholangitis** or **pancreatitis**.
sections.etiology:
• **Secondary Choledocholithiasis (Most Common, ~95%)**
	◦ Gallstones (**choleliths**), typically cholesterol stones, form in the gallbladder.
	◦ A stone passes from the gallbladder, through the cystic duct, and becomes lodged in the **common bile duct**.
	◦ Obstruction of the CBD prevents bile from flowing from the liver to the duodenum.
	◦ This leads to increased pressure within the biliary tree proximal to the obstruction, causing **ductal dilation**.
	◦ The backup of bile components (**conjugated bilirubin**, bile salts) into the bloodstream leads to **cholestasis** and clinical **jaundice**.
• **Primary Choledocholithiasis (Less Common)**
	◦ Stones form *de novo* within the bile ducts.
	◦ These are typically **brown pigment stones**, composed of **calcium bilirubinate**.
	◦ Associated with conditions that cause **biliary stasis and infection**, such as:
		▪ **Biliary strictures**
		▪ **Sclerosing cholangitis**
		▪ Congenital abnormalities (e.g., **Caroli's disease**)
		▪ Chronic infection with bacteria or parasites (e.g., ***Ascaris lumbricoides***, ***Clonorchis sinensis***).
sections.epidemiology:
• Occurs in **10-20%** of patients with symptomatic **cholelithiasis** (gallstones).
• Incidence increases significantly with **age**.
• More common in **females** than males, reflecting the epidemiology of cholelithiasis.
sections.riskFactors:
• **The "4 Fs":**
	◦ **F**at (obesity)
	◦ **F**emale
	◦ **F**ertile (multiparity, pregnancy due to estrogen effects)
	◦ **F**orty (age > 40)
• **Family history** / genetics
• **Ethnicity** (e.g., Native American, Hispanic)
• **Rapid weight loss** (e.g., post-bariatric surgery)
• **Hemolytic anemias** (e.g., sickle cell disease) - associated with black pigment stones.
• **Biliary stasis** (e.g., TPN, prolonged fasting)
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation can range from **asymptomatic** (found incidentally on imaging) to severe.
• It often presents with **biliary colic** that is more prolonged than typical uncomplicated cholelithiasis, accompanied by signs of obstruction.
• **Symptoms:**
	◦ **Pain:** Severe, constant, or colicky pain in the **Right Upper Quadrant (RUQ)** or **epigastrium**. May radiate to the right shoulder or scapula.
	◦ **Jaundice:** Yellowing of the skin and sclera (**scleral icterus**).
	◦ **Nausea and Vomiting:** Common during episodes of pain.
	◦ **Dark Urine:** Tea-colored or cola-colored urine due to excess conjugated bilirubin being excreted by the kidneys (**bilirubinuria**).
	◦ **Pale Stools:** **Acholic** or clay-colored stools due to the lack of bile pigment (stercobilin) reaching the intestine.
	◦ **Pruritus:** Itching due to the deposition of bile salts in the skin.
	◦ **Fever / Chills:** Suggests a developing complication, specifically **acute cholangitis**.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Vitals:** May be normal. **Tachycardia** or **fever** suggests a complication.
• **General:** **Scleral icterus** and **jaundice** are key findings.
• **Abdomen:**
	◦ **RUQ** or **epigastric tenderness** to palpation.
	◦ **Murphy's Sign:** Typically **NEGATIVE**. The primary issue is in the CBD, not an inflamed gallbladder (as in acute cholecystitis).
	◦ **Courvoisier's Sign:** A palpable, non-tender gallbladder in the presence of jaundice. This is more commonly associated with malignant obstruction (e.g., pancreatic cancer) but can occasionally be seen.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Transabdominal Ultrasound (US):**
	◦ **Best initial imaging test.**
	◦ Key finding: **Dilated common bile duct (> 6 mm)**.
		▪ The CBD may dilate 1 mm per decade of life after age 60.
		▪ A post-cholecystectomy CBD can be normal up to 10 mm.
	◦ Ultrasound is often poor at directly visualizing the stone in the distal CBD due to overlying bowel gas.
• **Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography (MRCP):**
	◦ **Best non-invasive confirmatory test.**
	◦ An MRI that provides detailed, non-invasive images of the biliary and pancreatic ducts.
	◦ Highly sensitive and specific for detecting stones in the CBD.
	◦ Used when LFTs and US are suggestive but the diagnosis is uncertain, or to map anatomy before intervention.
• **Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP):**
	◦ **Gold Standard (Diagnostic and Therapeutic).**
	◦ An endoscopic procedure where a catheter is passed into the biliary ducts and contrast dye is injected to visualize stones via fluoroscopy.
	◦ Allows for immediate therapeutic intervention:
		▪ **Sphincterotomy:** An incision is made in the sphincter of Oddi.
		▪ **Stone extraction:** Stones are removed with a balloon or basket.
		▪ **Stent placement:** If necessary to ensure biliary drainage.
	◦ Reserved for patients with high suspicion and need for intervention due to its risks (**pancreatitis**, bleeding, perforation).
sections.treatment:
• **Definitive Treatment:** **ERCP with biliary sphincterotomy and stone extraction** is the procedure of choice.
• **Subsequent Management:** **Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy** should be performed after the CBD is cleared, ideally during the same hospital admission, to prevent recurrence by removing the source of the stones.
sections.management:
• **Initial Stabilization:**
	◦ **NPO** (Nil per os)
	◦ **IV fluids** for hydration.
	◦ **Analgesia** for pain control (e.g., NSAIDs, opioids).
	◦ **IV antibiotics are indicated ONLY if cholangitis is suspected or confirmed** (e.g., Piperacillin-tazobactam or Ceftriaxone + Metronidazole).
• **Consultation:**
	◦ **Gastroenterology** for ERCP.
	◦ **General Surgery** for cholecystectomy.
sections.complications:
• **Acute Cholangitis:** Biliary obstruction plus bacterial infection. A medical emergency.
	◦ **Charcot's Triad:** **Fever, RUQ Pain, Jaundice**.
	◦ **Reynolds' Pentad:** **Charcot's Triad + Hypotension (shock) and Altered Mental Status**. Indicates severe, suppurative cholangitis with sepsis.
• **Acute Gallstone Pancreatitis:** Obstruction at the **ampulla of Vater** blocks both the CBD and the pancreatic duct, causing pancreatic inflammation.
• **Secondary Biliary Cirrhosis:** Caused by chronic, unresolved biliary obstruction.
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent if diagnosed and treated promptly.
• Morbidity and mortality increase significantly with the development of complications like **acute cholangitis** (mortality ~5-10%) or **pancreatitis**.
• **Reynolds' pentad** carries a very high mortality rate if not treated with emergent biliary decompression (ERCP or percutaneous drainage).

sections.overview:
• **Ascending cholangitis** is an **infection of the biliary tree**, most commonly occurring secondary to **obstruction of the common bile duct (CBD)**
    ◦ **Stasis of bile** from the obstruction allows for **bacterial proliferation** and ascension from the duodenum
    ◦ It is a **medical emergency** requiring prompt antibiotic therapy and biliary decompression
sections.etiology:
• **Core Pathophysiology**: Biliary obstruction leads to biliary stasis, which increases intraductal pressure. This allows for bacterial translocation from the portal circulation or ascension from the duodenum into the sterile biliary tree, leading to infection and inflammation
• **Primary Cause of Obstruction** (85% of cases):
    ◦ **Choledocholithiasis**: A gallstone lodged in the common bile duct
• **Other Causes of Obstruction**:
    ◦ **Malignancy**: Pancreatic cancer, cholangiocarcinoma, ampullary cancer
    ◦ **Benign Strictures**: Post-operative (e.g., after cholecystectomy), primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC)
    ◦ **Iatrogenic**: Post-ERCP, stent occlusion
    ◦ **Parasitic Infections**: *Ascaris lumbricoides*, *Clonorchis sinensis*
    ◦ **Extrinsic Compression**: Pancreatic pseudocyst, duodenal diverticulum
• **Most Common Causative Organisms** (Enteric Flora):
    ◦ **Gram-Negative** (most common):
        ▪ *Escherichia coli* (~25-50%)
        ▪ *Klebsiella* species (~15-20%)
        ▪ *Enterobacter* species (~5-10%)
    ◦ **Gram-Positive**:
        ▪ *Enterococcus* species (~10-20%)
    ◦ **Anaerobes** (less common, seen in severe/recurrent cases):
        ▪ *Bacteroides fragilis*
sections.epidemiology:
• Incidence increases with age, typically affecting patients >50 years old
• The incidence follows the prevalence of its underlying causes, primarily **cholelithiasis**
• No significant gender predilection, though gallstone-related causes are more common in women
sections.riskFactors:
• **Cholelithiasis / Choledocholithiasis** (most significant risk factor)
• History of biliary tract surgery or procedures (e.g., **ERCP**)
• Biliary stents
• Malignancy of the pancreas or biliary tree
• **Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC)**
• Congenital biliary abnormalities (e.g., choledochal cysts)
• Immunosuppression
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a triad of symptoms, which can progress to a pentad in severe cases
• **Charcot's Triad** (present in 50-70% of patients):
    ◦ **Fever / Chills** (often high-spiking)
    ◦ **Right Upper Quadrant (RUQ) Pain**
    ◦ **Jaundice**
• **Reynold's Pentad** (indicates **suppurative cholangitis** with **sepsis/shock**, a **surgical emergency**):
    ◦ **Fever / Chills**
    ◦ **RUQ Pain**
    ◦ **Jaundice**
    ◦ **Hypotension / Shock**
    ◦ **Altered Mental Status / Confusion**
• **Fever and chills**: Often the first and most prominent symptom
• **RUQ abdominal pain**: Can be colicky or constant
• **Jaundice**: Yellowing of the skin and eyes
• **Pruritus**: Itching due to bile salt deposition in the skin
• **Dark urine (biliuria)**: Due to conjugated hyperbilirubinemia
• **Pale stools (acholic stools)**: Due to lack of bilirubin reaching the gut
• Nausea and vomiting
• Malaise and anorexia
sections.physicalExam:
• **General**: Ill-appearing, febrile
• **Vitals**: Tachycardia, fever, **hypotension** (if septic)
• **Skin**: **Jaundice**, **scleral icterus**
• **Abdomen**:
    ◦ **RUQ tenderness** to palpation
    ◦ +/- Hepatomegaly
    ◦ **Murphy's sign is typically absent** (helps distinguish from acute cholecystitis)
• **Neurologic**: Confusion, lethargy (concerning for sepsis/**Reynold's pentad**)
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is based on a combination of clinical, laboratory, and imaging findings (**Tokyo Guidelines**)
• **Initial Imaging Study**:
    ◦ **Abdominal Ultrasound (RUQ)**:
        ▪ **Findings**: **Biliary duct dilation** (CBD >6 mm is suggestive), **pericholecystic fluid**, +/- visible **choledocholithiasis** (low sensitivity for CBD stones)
        ▪ **Primary Role**: Rule out other causes like acute cholecystitis and identify biliary dilation
• **Confirmatory & Therapeutic Gold Standard**:
    ◦ **Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)**:
        ▪ **Diagnostic**: Directly visualizes the biliary tree and can identify stones, strictures, or masses
        ▪ **Therapeutic**: Allows for **sphincterotomy**, **stone extraction**, and **stent placement** for biliary drainage
• **Other Imaging Modalities**:
    ◦ **Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography (MRCP)**:
        ▪ Excellent, non-invasive study to visualize the biliary and pancreatic ducts
        ▪ Often used as a diagnostic step before a therapeutic ERCP
    ◦ **CT Scan with IV Contrast**:
        ▪ Useful for detecting biliary dilation and complications like **liver abscesses**
        ▪ Good for evaluating for malignancy as the cause of obstruction
sections.treatment: • Cholangitis is a **medical emergency** requiring hospitalization and prompt intervention
sections.management:
• The definitive management is **biliary decompression** to relieve the obstruction. The timing depends on the severity
• **Emergent Decompression** (within 24 hours): For patients with severe cholangitis (**Reynold's pentad**, shock, organ dysfunction)
• **Urgent Decompression** (within 24-48 hours): For stable patients who respond to initial antibiotics and fluid resuscitation
sections.complications:
• **Sepsis** and **Septic Shock**
• **Liver abscess**
• Acute Pancreatitis
• Acute Kidney Injury (AKI)
• Multi-organ Dysfunction Syndrome (MODS)
• Biliary cirrhosis (with chronic or recurrent obstruction)
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly dependent on the speed of diagnosis and intervention
• With prompt treatment (antibiotics + decompression): **Mortality rate is <10%**
• With delayed treatment or presence of **Reynold's pentad** (septic shock): **Mortality rate can exceed 50%**
• Advanced age and underlying comorbidities (malignancy, liver disease) worsen the prognosis

sections.overview:
• Acute pancreatitis is an inflammatory condition of the pancreas characterized by **acute onset of abdominal pain** and **elevated pancreatic enzymes** in the blood.
    ◦ The core process involves premature activation of pancreatic digestive enzymes within the pancreas itself, leading to **autodigestion**, inflammation, and potential systemic complications.
    ◦ It ranges in severity from mild, self-limiting disease to severe, **necrotizing pancreatitis** with a high mortality rate.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Approximately 13-45 cases per 100,000 people per year in the U.S.
• **Hospitalizations**: One of the most common gastrointestinal reasons for hospital admission.
• **Demographics**:
    ◦ **Gallstone Pancreatitis**: More common in women and older adults.
    ◦ **Alcoholic Pancreatitis**: More common in men, typically presents earlier in life (30s-40s).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The "classic" presentation is a patient who appears acutely ill with the **sudden onset of severe, constant, and debilitating abdominal pain**.
    ◦ Patients are often restless, trying to find a position of comfort, frequently **leaning forward** or in a **fetal position**, which may offer slight relief.
• **Nausea and vomiting** are almost always present.
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis requires **at least 2 of the following 3 criteria**:
    ◦ 1. Characteristic **acute epigastric abdominal pain radiating to the back**.
    ◦ 2. Serum **lipase** (or amylase) elevation **3 times the upper limit of normal**.
    ◦ 3. Characteristic findings on **cross-sectional imaging** (CT, MRI, or US).
sections.prognosis:
• Prognostic scores help predict severity and mortality.
    ◦ **Ranson's Criteria**: Classic but cumbersome score calculated on admission and at 48 hours. A score of 3 or more indicates severe pancreatitis.
        ▪ **On Admission ("GA LAW")**: **G**lucose >200, **A**ge >55, **L**DH >350, **A**ST >250, **W**BC >16,000
        ▪ **At 48 Hours ("C HOBBS")**: **C**alcium <8, **H**ct fall >10%, **O**xygen (PaO2) <60 mmHg, **B**UN increase >5, **B**ase deficit >4, **S**equestration of fluid >6 L
    ◦ **BISAP Score (Bedside Index of Severity in Acute Pancreatitis)**: Simpler score, calculated within the first 24 hours. One point for each criterion. A score of 3 or more is associated with increased mortality.
        ▪ **B**UN >25 mg/dL
        ▪ **I**mpaired mental status (GCS <15)
        ▪ **S**IRS present (2 criteria)
        ▪ **A**ge >60 years
        ▪ **P**leural Effusion on imaging

sections.overview:
• Progressive and irreversible inflammatory disease of the pancreas characterized by **parenchymal fibrosis**, **calcification**, and destruction.
• Leads to the permanent loss of both **exocrine** (digestive enzyme production) and **endocrine** (insulin/glucagon production) function.
• Unlike acute pancreatitis, the damage in chronic pancreatitis is **not reversible**.
• The clinical course is typically dominated by **chronic pain** and the consequences of pancreatic insufficiency.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology** is commonly classified by the **TIGAR-O** system:
    ◦ **T**oxic-Metabolic: **Alcohol abuse (most common)**, smoking, hypercalcemia, hypertriglyceridemia, chronic kidney disease.
    ◦ **I**diopathic: Second most common cause; no identifiable factor.
    ◦ **G**enetic: Mutations in genes such as *PRSS1* (hereditary pancreatitis), *SPINK1*, and *CFTR* (cystic fibrosis).
    ◦ **A**utoimmune: IgG4-related systemic disease (Type 1) or pancreas-specific (Type 2).
    ◦ **R**ecurrent and severe acute pancreatitis: Post-necrotic changes leading to chronic fibrosis.
    ◦ **O**bstructive: Pancreas divisum (controversial), ductal strictures, tumors (e.g., IPMN, adenocarcinoma), trauma.
• **Pathophysiology**: The core mechanism is a recurrent cycle of inflammation and fibrogenesis, leading to irreversible structural damage.
    ◦ **Initial Injury**: An inciting event (e.g., alcohol toxicity, duct obstruction) causes acinar cell injury and inflammation.
    ◦ **Stellate Cell Activation**: Pancreatic stellate cells, normally quiescent, are activated by inflammatory cytokines (e.g., TGF-β, PDGF).
    ◦ **Fibrosis**: Activated stellate cells transform into myofibroblasts, which deposit large amounts of extracellular matrix proteins (collagen), leading to fibrosis and scarring of the parenchyma.
    ◦ **Ductal Changes**: Intraductal protein plugs calcify, forming stones that obstruct the pancreatic ducts. This increases intraductal pressure, causing further acinar cell atrophy, inflammation, and pain.
    ◦ **Functional Loss**:
        ▪ **Exocrine Insufficiency**: Progressive loss of acinar cells (>90% destruction) leads to a deficiency of digestive enzymes (lipase, amylase, protease), resulting in malabsorption.
        ▪ **Endocrine Insufficiency**: Fibrosis eventually destroys the Islets of Langerhans, leading to impaired glucose regulation and **"pancreatic diabetes"** or Type 3c diabetes mellitus.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Approximately 5-12 cases per 100,000 persons per year in Western countries.
• **Prevalence**: Approximately 50 cases per 100,000 persons.
• **Peak Age of Onset**: 30-40 years for alcohol-related; later for idiopathic.
• **Sex**: More common in males (M:F ratio ~3:1), largely due to the association with alcohol consumption.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation varies based on disease stage.
    ◦ Early disease is characterized by recurrent episodes of acute-on-chronic pancreatitis pain.
    ◦ Late disease is characterized by the classic triad of **pancreatic calcifications**, **steatorrhea**, and **diabetes mellitus**, although this triad is present in less than one-third of patients.
• Patients often present with a long history of recurrent abdominal pain, weight loss, and changes in bowel habits.
sections.diagnostics:
• The diagnosis is often made with a combination of clinical suspicion and characteristic imaging findings.
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **Amylase and Lipase**: **Often normal or only mildly elevated**. They are not reliable for diagnosing chronic pancreatitis as acinar cell mass is depleted.
    ◦ **Fecal Elastase-1**: **Best non-invasive test for pancreatic exocrine insufficiency**. Low levels (<200 mcg/g) are highly specific.
    ◦ **72-hour Fecal Fat Stain (Sudan Stain)**: Gold standard for steatorrhea but cumbersome and rarely performed.
    ◦ **Hemoglobin A1c / Fasting Glucose**: To screen for and monitor endocrine insufficiency (diabetes).
    ◦ **IgG4 levels**: To screen for autoimmune pancreatitis.
    ◦ **Vitamin levels**: Check levels of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) and B12.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Abdominal X-ray (KUB)**: Low sensitivity, but may reveal **pancreatic calcifications** which are highly specific.
    ◦ **Abdominal CT Scan (with contrast)**: **Best initial imaging test**. Can show key findings:
        ▪ **Pancreatic calcifications**
        ▪ **Pancreatic ductal dilation ("chain of lakes" appearance)**
        ▪ **Parenchymal atrophy**
        ▪ Pseudocysts
    ◦ **Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography (MRCP)**: **Best non-invasive test for visualizing the pancreatic duct**. Excellent for detecting strictures, stones, and ductal anatomy without radiation or contrast risk.
    ◦ **Endoscopic Ultrasound (EUS)**: **Most sensitive imaging modality for early or subtle changes** of chronic pancreatitis (e.g., parenchymal lobularity, strands, hyperechoic foci). Allows for fine-needle aspiration (FNA) to rule out malignancy.
    ◦ **Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)**: **Gold standard for visualizing the pancreatic duct** but is invasive and carries a risk of post-ERCP pancreatitis. Now used primarily for therapeutic interventions (e.g., stenting, stone removal) rather than diagnosis.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is generally poor and the disease is progressive.
• Life expectancy is reduced. 10-year mortality is ~30-50%.
• Continued alcohol use and smoking are associated with worse outcomes and faster disease progression.
• Leading causes of death are malignancy, complications of surgery, and consequences of alcohol/tobacco use.

sections.overview:
• Pancreatic cancer is an aggressive malignancy with a very poor prognosis, primarily due to late-stage diagnosis.
• The vast majority (>90%) of cases are **pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC)**, arising from the exocrine ductal epithelium.
• The most common location for tumors is the **head of the pancreas** (~75%), which often presents with biliary obstruction.
• Tumors in the body or tail are typically asymptomatic until they are very large or have metastasized.
sections.etiology:
• **Origin:** Arises from the uncontrolled proliferation of ductal epithelial cells in the pancreas.
• **Genetic Mutations:** A multi-step process involving the accumulation of specific genetic mutations.
    ◦ **KRAS oncogene:** Activating mutation present in >90% of cases (early event).
    ◦ **CDKN2A (p16):** Inactivation.
    ◦ **TP53:** Inactivation.
    ◦ **SMAD4:** Inactivation.
• **Mechanism of Symptoms:**
    ◦ **Tumor in the Head:** Compresses the common bile duct, leading to obstruction of bile flow.
        ▪ This causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, resulting in **jaundice**, **pruritus**, **dark urine**, and **pale (acholic) stools**.
    ◦ **Tumor in the Body/Tail:** Remains "silent" for longer.
        ▪ Symptoms arise from local invasion of nerves (causing severe **back pain**), invasion of surrounding organs, or from metastatic disease.
    ◦ **Exocrine Insufficiency:** Obstruction of the pancreatic duct prevents digestive enzymes from reaching the duodenum, leading to malabsorption, **steatorrhea**, and **weight loss**.
    ◦ **Endocrine Insufficiency:** Destruction of islet cells can lead to new-onset diabetes mellitus.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Mortality:** 4th leading cause of cancer-related death in the United States.
• **Incidence vs. Mortality:** The annual incidence is nearly identical to the annual mortality rate, highlighting its lethality.
• **Peak Incidence:** Age 65-75 years; uncommon before age 45.
• **Sex:** Slightly more common in men.
• **Race:** Higher incidence in **African Americans** compared to other racial groups.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Smoking:** Strongest reversible risk factor; doubles the risk.
• **Age:** Risk increases significantly after age 50.
• **Chronic Pancreatitis:** Major risk factor, increases risk ~10-20 fold.
• **Family History:** A first-degree relative with pancreatic cancer increases risk.
• **Genetic Syndromes:**
    ◦ **BRCA1 and BRCA2** mutations
    ◦ Peutz-Jeghers syndrome
    ◦ Lynch syndrome (HNPCC)
    ◦ Familial atypical multiple mole melanoma (FAMMM) syndrome
• **Diabetes Mellitus:** Long-standing DM is a risk factor.
    ◦ New-onset DM in a patient >50 years old should raise suspicion for pancreatic cancer.
• **Obesity:** Increased BMI is a significant risk factor.
• **Diet:** High intake of red and processed meats; low intake of fruits and vegetables.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The "classic" presentation depends on tumor location:
    ◦ **Pancreatic Head:** A patient presenting with **painless jaundice**. This is the hallmark presentation.
    ◦ **Pancreatic Body/Tail:** A patient presenting with insidious, vague, gnawing epigastric pain that **radiates to the mid-back**.
        ▪ The pain is often worse when supine and relieved by leaning forward.
• **General Presentation:**
    ◦ Significant, unintentional **weight loss**, anorexia, and early satiety are extremely common.
    ◦ A new diagnosis of **diabetes mellitus** in an elderly, non-obese patient is a major red flag.
• **Common Symptoms:**
    ◦ **Constitutional:** Anorexia, cachexia, profound **weight loss**, fatigue.
    ◦ **Abdominal Pain:** Epigastric, vague, gnawing, often radiates to the back.
    ◦ **Jaundice:** Yellowing of the skin and sclerae.
    ◦ **Pruritus:** Severe itching due to bile salt deposition in the skin.
    ◦ **Dark Urine (cola-colored):** Due to excretion of conjugated bilirubin.
    ◦ **Acholic Stools (pale, clay-colored):** Due to lack of bilirubin reaching the gut.
    ◦ **Steatorrhea:** Greasy, foul-smelling stools due to fat malabsorption.
    ◦ **Nausea and Vomiting:** Can be due to duodenal obstruction or biliary obstruction.
    ◦ **Migratory Thrombophlebitis (Trousseau's sign):** Superficial venous thrombosis that appears in different locations over time.
sections.physicalExam:
• **General:** Cachexia, temporal muscle wasting.
• **Skin:** Scleral icterus, jaundice, excoriations from scratching.
• **Abdomen:**
    ◦ **Courvoisier's Sign:** A **palpable, NON-TENDER gallbladder** in the presence of jaundice. This is highly suggestive of malignant obstruction rather than obstruction by a gallstone.
    ◦ Palpable abdominal mass (late finding).
    ◦ Hepatomegaly (from metastases or biliary congestion).
    ◦ Ascites (sign of peritoneal carcinomatosis).
• **Lymph Nodes:**
    ◦ **Virchow's Node:** Palpable left supraclavicular lymph node.
    ◦ **Sister Mary Joseph Nodule:** Palpable periumbilical nodule.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Laboratory Studies:**
    ◦ **LFTs:** Show a **cholestatic pattern**: markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase (Alk Phos) and GGT, with elevated direct (conjugated) bilirubin. AST/ALT may be mildly elevated.
    ◦ **CA 19-9:** The most common tumor marker.
        ▪ **USE:** Primarily for monitoring treatment response and detecting recurrence.
        ▪ **LIMITATIONS:** **NOT for screening or diagnosis.** Can be falsely negative (Lewis antigen negative patients) or falsely elevated in other conditions (e.g., cholangitis, pancreatitis).
• **Initial Imaging:**
    ◦ **Abdominal Ultrasound:** Best initial test for a jaundiced patient. Can show biliary ductal dilation and may identify a mass in the head of the pancreas.
• **Definitive Imaging / Staging:**
    ◦ **Multiphase, contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen (Pancreas Protocol):** The **single best test** for diagnosis, staging (assessing vascular involvement, mets), and determining resectability.
• **Biopsy / Tissue Diagnosis:**
    ◦ **Endoscopic Ultrasound (EUS) with Fine-Needle Aspiration (FNA):** The most sensitive method for detecting small tumors and obtaining a tissue diagnosis.
    ◦ **ERCP (Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography):** Can visualize the biliary and pancreatic ducts, obtain brushings for cytology, and be used **therapeutically to place a stent** to relieve biliary obstruction.
• **"Double Duct" Sign:** Dilation of both the common bile duct and the pancreatic duct seen on ERCP or CT/MRI is highly suggestive of a pancreatic head mass.
sections.treatment:
• **Surgical Resection (Potentially Curative):**
    ◦ Only an option for the ~20% of patients with localized disease without metastasis or major vascular involvement.
    ◦ **Pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple Procedure):** Standard procedure for tumors in the **pancreatic head**. Involves removal of the pancreatic head, duodenum, gallbladder, common bile duct, and distal stomach (antrum).
    ◦ **Distal Pancreatectomy with Splenectomy:** For tumors in the **body or tail**.
• **Chemotherapy:**
    ◦ **Adjuvant:** Given *after* curative surgery to reduce recurrence risk (e.g., FOLFIRINOX).
    ◦ **Neoadjuvant:** Given *before* surgery for borderline-resectable tumors to downstage them.
    ◦ **Palliative:** For unresectable or metastatic disease to improve survival and quality of life (e.g., FOLFIRINOX or Gemcitabine + nab-paclitaxel).
sections.management:
• **Palliative Care:** Should be involved early for all patients to manage symptoms and goals of care.
• **Biliary Obstruction:** Endoscopic stenting via ERCP to relieve jaundice and pruritus.
• **Pain Control:** Aggressive management, often requiring long-acting opioids. Celiac plexus neurolysis can provide significant relief.
• **Exocrine Insufficiency:** **Pancreatic Enzyme Replacement Therapy (PERT)**, such as Creon or Zenpep, taken with all meals and snacks.
• **Malnutrition:** Nutritional counseling, dietary supplements.
• **Gastric Outlet Obstruction:** Surgical bypass (gastrojejunostomy) or endoscopic stenting.
• **VTE Prophylaxis:** Pancreatic cancer is highly thrombogenic.
sections.complications:
• Biliary obstruction and cholangitis
• Cachexia and malnutrition
• Venous thromboembolism (VTE), including DVT and PE
• Severe, intractable pain
• Gastric outlet or duodenal obstruction
• **Post-Surgical (Whipple):** Pancreatic fistula, delayed gastric emptying, hemorrhage, infection.
sections.prognosis:
• **Extremely poor.** It is one of the most lethal malignancies.
• **Overall 5-year survival rate:** < 10%.
• **For patients undergoing complete resection (R0):** 5-year survival improves to ~20-25%.
• Most patients (~80%) present with unresectable or metastatic disease, where median survival is 6-12 months with palliative chemotherapy.

sections.overview:
• Obesity is a chronic, complex, multifactorial disease characterized by excessive adipose tissue accumulation that poses a risk to health.
    ◦ It is not a character flaw or a simple matter of willpower, but rather a medical condition with significant hormonal, genetic, environmental, and behavioral contributors.
    ◦ Diagnosis is primarily based on the **Body Mass Index (BMI)**.
• It is a major driver of morbidity and mortality worldwide, contributing to **cardiovascular disease**, **type 2 diabetes**, certain **cancers**, and other chronic conditions.
• **BMI Classification (Adults):**
    ◦ **< 18.5:** Underweight
    ◦ **18.5 - 24.9:** Normal Weight
    ◦ **25.0 - 29.9:** Overweight
    ◦ **30.0 - 34.9:** Obesity Class I
    ◦ **35.0 - 39.9:** Obesity Class II
    ◦ **≥ 40.0:** Obesity Class III (formerly "morbid obesity")
sections.etiology:
• Obesity results from a long-term positive energy balance (calories consumed > calories expended).
• The underlying pathophysiology is complex and involves an interplay of genetics, neurohormonal regulation, and environmental factors.
• **Neurohormonal Dysregulation:**
    ◦ **Leptin Resistance:** Leptin, a hormone from adipocytes, signals satiety. In obesity, plasma leptin is high but the brain's response is blunted, creating a perceived state of starvation despite ample energy stores, promoting increased food intake and decreased energy expenditure.
    ◦ **Ghrelin:** A hormone from the stomach that stimulates appetite ("hunger hormone"); its regulation can be altered.
    ◦ **Gut Peptides:** Satiety hormones like **GLP-1** and **PYY** may have impaired signaling.
• **Adipose Tissue as an Endocrine Organ:**
    ◦ Visceral adipose tissue secretes pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., **TNF-α, IL-6**) and adipokines.
    ◦ This creates a state of **chronic, low-grade inflammation**, a key driver of insulin resistance and endothelial dysfunction.
• **Insulin Resistance:**
    ◦ Excess free fatty acids (FFAs) from hypertrophied adipocytes interfere with insulin signaling.
    ◦ The pancreas compensates with **hyperinsulinemia**, but beta-cell dysfunction can lead to **type 2 diabetes**.
• **Set-Point Theory:**
    ◦ The body defends a theoretical weight "set point" through metabolic adaptation.
    ◦ During weight loss, Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) decreases more than predicted, making sustained weight loss difficult.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** A global pandemic. In the United States, the prevalence of obesity in adults is **>42%**. The prevalence of severe obesity (BMI ≥ 40) is nearly 10%.
• **Trends:** Prevalence has steadily increased over the past several decades in all age groups.
• **Disparities:** Higher rates are seen in non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic adults compared to non-Hispanic White and Asian adults. Prevalence is also inversely correlated with socioeconomic status and education level.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Genetics:** Strong heritable component (40-70%) influencing appetite, metabolism, and fat distribution.
• **Behavioral:**
    ◦ **Diet:** High intake of energy-dense, processed foods, sugary beverages.
    ◦ **Physical Inactivity:** Sedentary lifestyle.
    ◦ **Sleep:** Insufficient or poor-quality sleep alters appetite-regulating hormones.
• **Environmental & Socioeconomic:**
    ◦ Food environment ("food deserts," high availability of fast food).
    ◦ Lower socioeconomic status and education level.
• **Medications (Iatrogenic Weight Gain):**
    ◦ **Antipsychotics** (especially atypical, e.g., olanzapine, clozapine)
    ◦ **Antidepressants** (e.g., TCAs, mirtazapine, paroxetine)
    ◦ **Anticonvulsants** (e.g., valproic acid, gabapentin)
    ◦ **Glucocorticoids**
    ◦ **Insulin & Sulfonylureas**
• **Secondary Medical Conditions:**
    ◦ **Hypothyroidism**
    ◦ **Cushing's Syndrome**
    ◦ **Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)**
    ◦ **Hypothalamic injury/tumor**
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **History:**
    ◦ Most patients present for a routine visit or for evaluation of a complication (e.g., hypertension, knee pain, sleep apnea symptoms).
    ◦ Weight gain is typically gradual over many years.
    ◦ Patients may report failed attempts at weight loss.
    ◦ A thorough history should assess diet, physical activity, sleep, psychosocial factors, and medication history.
• **Symptoms:**
    ◦ **General:** Fatigue, feeling of poor health.
    ◦ **Pulmonary:** **Dyspnea on exertion**, daytime somnolence, loud snoring (suggestive of **Obstructive Sleep Apnea - OSA**).
    ◦ **Musculoskeletal:** Joint pain (especially knees and back), reduced mobility.
    ◦ **Dermatologic:** Sweating, skin fold rashes (**intertrigo**).
    ◦ **Psychological:** Depression, anxiety, low self-esteem, social stigmatization.
    ◦ **GI:** Symptoms of **GERD**.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Vitals:**
    ◦ Calculate **BMI**.
    ◦ Measure **blood pressure** (may be elevated; use appropriate cuff size).
• **Waist Circumference:**
    ◦ A key indicator of central adiposity and metabolic risk.
    ◦ High Risk: **>40 inches (102 cm) in men, >35 inches (88 cm) in women**.
• **General:** Obese appearance.
• **Head/Neck:** May have a large neck circumference, crowded oropharynx (risk for **OSA**).
• **Skin:**
    ◦ **Acanthosis Nigricans:** Hyperpigmented, velvety plaques in intertriginous areas (axilla, neck); a sign of **insulin resistance**.
    ◦ **Striae:** Stretch marks.
    ◦ **Intertrigo:** Inflammation/fungal infection in skin folds.
• **Cardiovascular:** May have signs of heart failure (JVD, peripheral edema, S3 gallop).
• **Musculoskeletal:** Decreased range of motion, joint tenderness, antalgic gait.
sections.diagnostics:
• The diagnosis of obesity is clinical; lab and diagnostic workup is aimed at screening for comorbidities and ruling out secondary causes.
• **Initial Lab Workup:**
    ◦ **Fasting Lipid Panel:** To screen for dyslipidemia.
    ◦ **Hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c)** or **Fasting Plasma Glucose:** To screen for prediabetes and Type 2 Diabetes.
    ◦ **Liver Function Tests (LFTs):** To screen for **Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD)**.
    ◦ **TSH:** To screen for hypothyroidism.
    ◦ **Fasting Insulin:** Can be a more sensitive marker for insulin resistance.
• **Further Diagnostics (if indicated by H&P):**
    ◦ **ECG:** If signs/symptoms of cardiac disease.
    ◦ **Polysomnography (Sleep Study):** If high suspicion for **OSA** (e.g., STOP-BANG score).
    ◦ **24-hour urine free cortisol** or **Dexamethasone Suppression Test:** If Cushingoid features are present.
sections.treatment:
• **Lifestyle Modifications:**
    ◦ **Diet:** Caloric deficit is key (typically 500-750 kcal/day deficit). No single diet is superior; focus on sustainability (e.g., Mediterranean, DASH).
    ◦ **Physical Activity:** **≥150 minutes/week of moderate-intensity aerobic activity** plus ≥2 days/week of strength training.
    ◦ **Behavioral Therapy:** Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), motivational interviewing, goal setting, self-monitoring.
• **Pharmacotherapy:**
    ◦ **Indications:** BMI **≥ 30**, OR BMI **≥ 27** with at least one weight-related comorbidity (e.g., HTN, T2DM, HLD, OSA).
    ◦ **Mechanisms/Agents:**
        ▪ **GLP-1 Receptor Agonists:** (Most effective class) Semaglutide (Wegovy), Liraglutide (Saxenda), Tirzepatide (Zepbound - GIP/GLP-1 agonist). Promote satiety, slow gastric emptying.
        ▪ **Sympathomimetic/Anticonvulsant:** Phentermine/Topiramate. Appetite suppressant.
        ▪ **Lipase Inhibitor:** Orlistat. Blocks fat absorption (significant GI side effects).
• **Bariatric Surgery:**
    ◦ **Indications:** BMI **≥ 40**, OR BMI **≥ 35** with at least one significant obesity-related comorbidity.
    ◦ **Procedures:**
        ▪ **Sleeve Gastrectomy (most common):** ~80% of the stomach is resected, creating a small "sleeve." Primarily a restrictive procedure.
        ▪ **Roux-en-Y Gastric Bypass (RYGB):** Creates a small gastric pouch and bypasses a portion of the small intestine. Both restrictive and malabsorptive. More effective for T2DM resolution but has higher complication risk.
sections.management:
• **Set Realistic Goals:** An initial goal of **5-10% total body weight loss** within 6 months is achievable and clinically significant for improving health outcomes.
• **Multidisciplinary Team:** Involve dietitians, behavioral therapists, and exercise physiologists.
• **Regular Follow-Up:** Monitor weight, blood pressure, and adherence to therapy. Repeat labs (A1c, lipids) periodically to assess improvement in comorbidities.
• **Address Comorbidities:** Aggressively manage hypertension, dyslipidemia, and diabetes according to standard guidelines.
• **Patient Education:** Educate on the chronic nature of obesity and the need for lifelong management.
sections.complications:
• **Cardiovascular:** Hypertension, Dyslipidemia, Coronary Artery Disease, Heart Failure, Atrial Fibrillation, Stroke.
• **Endocrine/Metabolic:** **Type 2 Diabetes**, **Metabolic Syndrome**, Dyslipidemia, PCOS, Gout.
• **Gastrointestinal:** **Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD/NASH)**, GERD, Cholelithiasis (gallstones).
• **Pulmonary:** **Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA)**, Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome (OHS), Asthma.
• **Musculoskeletal:** **Osteoarthritis** (especially knee & hip), Chronic Low Back Pain.
• **Cancer:** Increased risk of numerous cancers (e.g., Endometrial, Esophageal adenocarcinoma, Colorectal, postmenopausal Breast, Kidney).
• **Reproductive/GU:** Infertility, erectile dysfunction, stress incontinence.
• **Psychosocial:** Depression, anxiety, social stigmatization, decreased quality of life.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is directly related to the degree of obesity and the severity of its complications.
• Morbidity and mortality increase with increasing BMI.
• A modest, sustained weight loss of **5-10%** can significantly improve glycemic control, blood pressure, and lipid levels, thereby improving long-term prognosis.
• Bariatric surgery is associated with significant and durable weight loss and a marked reduction in overall mortality.

sections.overview:
• Malnutrition is a state of nutritional imbalance resulting from a deficiency or excess of energy, protein, and other nutrients, or from impaired nutrient utilization.
    ◦ It encompasses both undernutrition and overnutrition, but in the clinical context, it most often refers to **undernutrition**.
    ◦ Undernutrition leads to measurable adverse effects on tissue/body form and function, and is associated with increased morbidity and mortality.
• Two classic forms of severe protein-energy malnutrition (PEM) are **Marasmus** and **Kwashiorkor**.
    ◦ **Marasmus**: Inadequate intake of all macronutrients (protein, carbohydrates, fats).
        ▪ Characterized by severe wasting of muscle and subcutaneous fat.
    ◦ **Kwashiorkor**: Inadequate protein intake with sufficient (or near-sufficient) caloric intake.
        ▪ Characterized by peripheral edema, ascites, and dermatoses.
    ◦ **Marasmic-Kwashiorkor**: A mixed form with features of both, often seen in chronically ill or hospitalized patients.
sections.etiology:
• Malnutrition develops from one or more of three primary mechanisms:
    ◦ **Inadequate Nutrient Intake**
        ▪ **Causes**: Poverty, food insecurity, anorexia (disease-related or psychiatric), dysphagia, poor dentition, social isolation, substance abuse, restrictive diets.
    ◦ **Impaired Nutrient Absorption or Digestion (Malabsorption)**
        ▪ **Causes**: Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's, ulcerative colitis), celiac disease, short bowel syndrome, chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, post-surgical changes (e.g., gastrectomy).
    ◦ **Increased Metabolic Demand / Nutrient Losses**
        ▪ **Causes**: Hypermetabolic states such as severe trauma, burns, sepsis, major surgery, chronic inflammatory diseases (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis), and malignancy (cancer cachexia). Chronic kidney disease on dialysis, enterocutaneous fistulas.
sections.epidemiology:
• Globally, a major health problem, especially in developing nations and among children.
• In developed countries, it is a "disease of the sick and elderly."
• Prevalence in U.S. hospitalized patients is estimated to be **30-50%**.
• Highly prevalent in long-term care facilities and among individuals with chronic diseases like cancer, COPD, and heart failure.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is often insidious; the chief complaint may be related to the underlying disease, with malnutrition identified on examination or screening.
• A key feature is **unintentional weight loss**.
• Patients may present with generalized weakness, fatigue, apathy, and an increased frequency of infections.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Screening Tools**
    ◦ **MUST** (Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool)
    ◦ **MNA** (Mini Nutritional Assessment) - commonly used in the elderly.
• **Assessment of Weight Loss**
    ◦ **Significant**: >5% in 1 month, >7.5% in 3 months, or >10% in 6 months.
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **Visceral Proteins (Negative Acute Phase Reactants)**
        ▪ **Albumin**:
            ◦ Half-life ~20 days.
            ◦ Low levels (<3.5 g/dL) reflect **chronic malnutrition**.
            ◦ *Caution: Also decreased in inflammation, liver disease, and nephrotic syndrome.*
        ▪ **Prealbumin (Transthyretin)**:
            ◦ Half-life ~2-3 days.
            ◦ More sensitive indicator of **acute nutritional changes** and response to therapy.
    ◦ **CBC**
        ▪ Anemia is common.
            ◦ Microcytic (iron deficiency).
            ◦ Macrocytic (folate or B12 deficiency).
            ◦ Normocytic (anemia of chronic disease).
        ▪ Lymphopenia is a sign of severe malnutrition.
    ◦ **CMP**
        ▪ Electrolyte abnormalities (**K+, Mg2+, PO43** are critical to assess before refeeding).
        ▪ Check renal and liver function.
    ◦ **Specific Nutrient Levels**
        ▪ Iron studies (ferritin, TIBC), Vitamin B12, Folate.
        ▪ Vitamin D (25-hydroxyvitamin D).
        ▪ Thiamine (Vitamin B1), especially in alcoholics.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly variable and depends on the severity of malnutrition, the underlying etiology, and the ability to provide effective nutritional support.
• In hospitalized patients, malnutrition is an independent predictor of increased mortality, morbidity, length of stay, and readmission rates.
• With aggressive and appropriate treatment, nutritional status can be significantly improved.

sections.overview:
• **Osteoarthritis (OA)** is the most common form of arthritis, characterized as a **degenerative joint disease** involving the progressive **loss of articular cartilage**, **subchondral bone remodeling**, **osteophyte formation**, and synovial inflammation.
• It is a disease of the entire joint organ, not merely "wear and tear."
• OA is a leading cause of chronic pain and disability worldwide, primarily affecting **weight-bearing joints** and the **hands**.
sections.etiology:
• OA is a mechanically driven but biologically mediated disease, involving a complex interplay of mechanical stress and an active, cell-mediated process of joint degradation.
• **Primary (Idiopathic) OA**: The most common form, with no identifiable cause, typically associated with aging.
• **Secondary OA**: Occurs due to a known cause, such as trauma, congenital joint abnormalities, metabolic defects (e.g., hemochromatosis), or other inflammatory arthritis (e.g., Rheumatoid Arthritis).
• **Pathophysiologic Cascade**:
    ◦ **Initial Insult**: Excessive mechanical stress or injury damages chondrocytes (cartilage cells).
    ◦ **Chondrocyte Response**: Damaged chondrocytes release pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-1, TNF-α) and matrix-degrading enzymes (matrix metalloproteinases - MMPs, aggrecanases).
    ◦ **Cartilage Degradation**: These enzymes break down the cartilage matrix (proteoglycans and type II collagen), leading to cartilage softening, fibrillation (fissuring), and eventual erosion down to the subchondral bone.
    ◦ **Subchondral Bone Changes**: The underlying bone responds to increased stress by becoming denser (**subchondral sclerosis**). Microfractures can lead to fluid-filled sacs (**subchondral cysts**).
    ◦ **Osteophyte Formation**: The body attempts to stabilize the joint by forming bony outgrowths at the joint margins (**osteophytes** or "bone spurs").
    ◦ **Synovial Inflammation**: Cartilage breakdown products irritate the synovial membrane, causing a mild, secondary synovitis, which further contributes to the inflammatory cycle.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Most common joint disorder in the United States.
• **Age**: Prevalence increases dramatically with age. Rare before 40; highly common in individuals >65.
• **Gender**:
    ◦ Before age 50: More common in men (often due to trauma/occupation).
    ◦ After age 50: Significantly more common in women, particularly affecting the hands and knees.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The typical patient is over 50 years old and presents with an insidious onset of deep, aching joint pain that has progressed over months to years.
• The presentation is typically monoarticular or oligoarticular and **asymmetric**.
• There are **NO systemic symptoms** (e.g., fever, malaise, unintentional weight loss).
• **Commonly Affected Joints**:
    ◦ **Weight-Bearing**: Knees, Hips, Cervical & Lumbar Spine.
    ◦ **Hands**: Distal Interphalangeal (DIP), Proximal Interphalangeal (PIP), and First Carpometacarpal (CMC) joints.
• OA classically **spares** the wrists, Metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints, and ankles.
sections.diagnostics:
• OA is primarily a **clinical diagnosis**. Diagnostics are used to confirm findings and rule out other etiologies.
• **Laboratory Studies**:
    ◦ **Typically all normal**. Labs are ordered to exclude inflammatory conditions.
    ◦ **ESR and CRP**: Normal or minimally elevated.
    ◦ **Rheumatoid Factor (RF) and Anti-CCP**: Negative.
    ◦ **CBC**: Normal.
• **Synovial Fluid Analysis (Arthrocentesis)**:
    ◦ Indicated to rule out septic arthritis or crystal-induced arthropathy (gout/pseudogout).
    ◦ **Appearance**: Clear or straw-colored, viscous.
    ◦ **WBC Count**: **< 2,000 cells/mm³** (non-inflammatory).
    ◦ **Crystals**: Absent.
    ◦ **Culture**: Negative.
• **Imaging**:
    ◦ **X-Ray (Plain Radiograph)**: The primary imaging modality. Findings often correlate poorly with patient symptoms.
        ▪ **Four Cardinal Features of OA on X-Ray**:
            • **J**oint Space Narrowing (asymmetric)
            • **O**steophyte formation (bone spurs)
            • **S**ubchondral **S**clerosis (increased bone density)
            • **S**ubchondral cysts
    ◦ **MRI**: Not needed for routine diagnosis. Useful for evaluating soft tissue structures like menisci, ligaments, or in cases of diagnostic uncertainty.
sections.prognosis:
• OA is a slowly progressive condition with no cure.
• The rate of progression is highly variable.
• Prognosis for life is excellent, but prognosis for joint function and quality of life is variable.
• Joint replacement surgery offers excellent outcomes for pain and function in patients with end-stage disease.

sections.overview:
• Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) is a chronic, systemic, autoimmune inflammatory disease characterized primarily by inflammation of the synovial joints.
• It typically leads to a symmetric, erosive polyarthritis, resulting in progressive joint destruction, deformity, and disability.
• The disease can also have numerous extra-articular manifestations, affecting organs such as the skin, heart, lungs, and eyes.
sections.etiology:
• **Autoimmune Etiology**: The exact trigger is unknown, but it involves a combination of genetic predisposition and environmental factors (e.g., smoking, infections).
• **Genetic Susceptibility**: Strongly associated with the **HLA-DR4** and **HLA-DR1** genes (part of the major histocompatibility complex class II).
• **Pathophysiology Cascade**:
    ◦ An unknown antigen triggers an immune response in a genetically susceptible host.
    ◦ CD4+ T-helper cells are activated, leading to the stimulation of B-cells and macrophages within the synovial tissue.
    ◦ B-cells differentiate into plasma cells and produce autoantibodies:
        ▪ **Rheumatoid Factor (RF)**: An IgM antibody that targets the Fc portion of the patient's own IgG.
        ▪ **Anti-citrullinated peptide antibodies (ACPA / anti-CCP)**: Highly specific for RA. Citrullination is the post-translational modification of arginine to citrulline, which may create neoantigens.
    ◦ Activated macrophages, fibroblasts, and T-cells release pro-inflammatory cytokines, most notably **Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha (TNF-α)**, **Interleukin-1 (IL-1)**, and **Interleukin-6 (IL-6)**.
    ◦ These cytokines promote synovial cell proliferation, leading to the formation of a **pannus**—an aggressive, hyperplastic synovial tissue rich in inflammatory cells.
    ◦ The pannus invades and erodes adjacent articular cartilage and bone, causing the characteristic marginal erosions and joint destruction seen in RA.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects approximately 0.5-1.0% of the adult population worldwide.
• **Gender**: **Female-to-male ratio is 3:1.**
• **Age of Onset**: Can occur at any age, but the peak onset is between **40 and 60 years old.**
sections.riskFactors:
• **Genetic**: Positive family history, presence of **HLA-DRB1** alleles.
• **Environmental**: **Smoking** is the most well-established environmental risk factor.
• **Hormonal**: Female sex. Nulliparity may be a risk factor, while pregnancy and oral contraceptive use may be protective.
• **Infectious Agents (Theorized)**: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), *Porphyromonas gingivalis* (periodontal disease).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is the **insidious onset** of a **symmetric, inflammatory polyarthritis** affecting the small joints of the hands and feet.
• Patients typically report significant morning stiffness and constitutional symptoms.
• **Articular (Joints)**:
    ◦ **Morning Stiffness**: Hallmark symptom. Lasts **> 60 minutes** and **improves with activity/throughout the day.**
    ◦ **Pain & Swelling**: Symmetrical joint involvement.
    ◦ **Joints Most Commonly Affected**:
        ▪ **Hands**: Metacarpophalangeal (MCP), Proximal Interphalangeal (PIP), and wrist joints. **Characteristically spares the Distal Interphalangeal (DIP) joints.**
        ▪ **Feet**: Metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joints.
        ▪ Other: Knees, elbows, shoulders, ankles, cervical spine.
• **Constitutional (Systemic)**:
    ◦ Fatigue, malaise, anorexia, low-grade fever, weight loss.
sections.physicalExam:
• **General**: May appear chronically ill.
• **Joints**:
    ◦ **Synovitis**: Tender, warm, erythematous, swollen joints with a "boggy" or "spongy" feel on palpation.
    ◦ Decreased range of motion.
    ◦ **Grip strength is often reduced.**
• **Hands & Wrists (Late Findings/Chronic Disease)**:
    ◦ **Ulnar Deviation**: At the MCP joints.
    ◦ **Boutonnière Deformity**: Flexion at the PIP joint and hyperextension at the DIP joint.
    ◦ **Swan-Neck Deformity**: Hyperextension at the PIP joint and flexion at the DIP joint.
    ◦ **"Z-Thumb" Deformity**: Flexion of MCP, hyperextension of IP joint.
• **Extra-articular Manifestations**:
    ◦ **Rheumatoid Nodules**: Firm, non-tender, subcutaneous nodules typically found over extensor surfaces (e.g., olecranon, fingers).
    ◦ **Ocular**: Keratoconjunctivitis sicca (secondary Sjögren syndrome), scleritis, episcleritis.
    ◦ **Pulmonary**: Interstitial lung disease (ILD), pleural effusions, pulmonary nodules.
    ◦ **Hematologic**: Anemia of chronic disease, Felty Syndrome (RA + splenomegaly + neutropenia).
    ◦ **Neurologic**: Carpal tunnel syndrome, cervical myelopathy from C1-C2 (atlantoaxial) subluxation.
    ◦ **Vasculitis**: Cutaneous vasculitis (e.g., nail fold infarcts), systemic vasculitis.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Laboratory Studies**:
    ◦ **Autoantibodies**:
        ▪ **Anti-CCP (ACPA)**: **Most specific test for RA (>95%).**
        ▪ **Rheumatoid Factor (RF)**: Sensitive (~80%) but not specific (can be positive in SLE, Sjögren's, hepatitis C, endocarditis, and healthy elderly individuals).
    ◦ **Inflammatory Markers**:
        ▪ **Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) and C-Reactive Protein (CRP)**: Elevated and useful for monitoring disease activity.
    ◦ **CBC**: May show normocytic, normochromic **anemia of chronic disease** and thrombocytosis (reactive).
• **Synovial Fluid Analysis (Arthrocentesis)**:
    ◦ Performed to rule out septic or crystal-induced arthritis.
    ◦ **Appearance**: Turbid, yellow fluid.
    ◦ **WBC Count**: Inflammatory range (**2,000 - 75,000 cells/L**) with a predominance of neutrophils.
    ◦ **Culture**: Negative.
    ◦ **Crystals**: Absent.
• **Imaging**:
    ◦ **X-rays (Hands & Feet)**:
        ▪ **Early Findings**: Soft tissue swelling and periarticular osteopenia.
        ▪ **Late Findings**: **Symmetric joint space narrowing** and **marginal erosions ("rat bite" erosions).**
• **ACR/EULAR 2010 Classification Criteria**:
    ◦ A score-based system (>6/10 = definite RA) based on:
        ▪ **Joint Involvement**: Number and size of joints affected.
        ▪ **Serology**: RF and anti-CCP status.
        ▪ **Acute-Phase Reactants**: ESR and CRP levels.
        ▪ **Duration of Symptoms**: <6 weeks vs. 6 weeks.
sections.treatment:
• **Goals**: Control synovitis, prevent joint erosion, preserve joint function, and manage pain.
• **Referral to a rheumatologist is mandatory.**
• **Symptomatic Management**:
    ◦ **NSAIDs**: For pain and inflammation control. Do not alter disease course.
    ◦ **Glucocorticoids (e.g., Prednisone)**: Used for acute flares and as a "bridge" therapy while waiting for DMARDs to take effect. Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible duration.
• **Disease-Modifying Antirheumatic Drugs (DMARDs)**:
    ◦ **Cornerstone of RA treatment.** Start as soon as diagnosis is confirmed.
    ◦ **Conventional Synthetic DMARDs (csDMARDs)**:
        ▪ **Methotrexate (MTX)**: **First-line agent.** Folate antagonist. **Must supplement with folic acid.**
        ▪ **Major Side Effects**: Hepatotoxicity, myelosuppression, stomatitis, interstitial pneumonitis.
        ▪ **Contraindications**: Pregnancy (teratogenic), severe renal/liver disease.
        ▪ **Leflunomide**: Alternative to MTX.
        ▪ **Sulfasalazine (SSZ)**: Often used in combination therapy.
        ▪ **Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ)**: For mild disease or in combination. **Requires baseline and annual eye exams for retinal toxicity.**
    ◦ **Biologic DMARDs (bDMARDs)**: Used for moderate-to-severe disease, often after MTX failure.
        ▪ **TNF-α Inhibitors**: *Etanercept, Infliximab, Adalimumab, Golimumab, Certolizumab.* **Must screen for latent TB (PPD or IGRA) before initiating.**
        ▪ **Other Biologics**: Abatacept (T-cell modulator), Rituximab (B-cell depleter), Tocilizumab (IL-6 inhibitor).
    ◦ **Targeted Synthetic DMARDs (tsDMARDs)**:
        ▪ **JAK Inhibitors**: *Tofacitinib, Baricitinib, Upadacitinib.* Oral medications for MTX failure.
sections.management:
• **Multidisciplinary Approach**: Rheumatology, physical therapy (PT), occupational therapy (OT).
• **Patient Education**: Disease process, medication adherence, joint protection techniques.
• **Monitoring**: Regular follow-up to assess disease activity (e.g., DAS28 score), monitor for drug toxicity (CBC, LFTs, creatinine for MTX), and adjust treatment.
• **Vaccinations**: Ensure patient is up-to-date, especially pneumococcal, influenza, and herpes zoster vaccines, *before* starting biologic DMARDs. Live vaccines are contraindicated in patients on biologics.
• **Surgical Intervention**: Synovectomy, joint reconstruction, or arthroplasty for severe, end-stage joint destruction.
sections.complications:
• **Musculoskeletal**: Joint destruction and deformity, tendon rupture, osteoporosis.
• **Cervical Spine**: **Atlantoaxial (C1-C2) subluxation**, which can lead to spinal cord compression. Requires pre-operative screening (flexion/extension neck films) before any surgery requiring intubation.
• **Cardiovascular**: **Accelerated atherosclerosis leading to increased risk of MI and stroke (leading cause of mortality).**
• **Pulmonary**: Interstitial lung disease, pleuritis.
• **Hematologic**: Anemia of chronic disease, **Felty's Syndrome (triad of RA, splenomegaly, and neutropenia).**
• **Infection**: Increased risk due to both the disease and immunosuppressive therapies.
sections.prognosis:
• A chronic disease with no cure, but modern treatments have significantly improved outcomes, allowing many patients to achieve remission or low disease activity.
• **Poor Prognostic Factors**: High titers of RF/anti-CCP, early erosions on X-ray, extra-articular manifestations, functional limitation at diagnosis, involvement of many joints.

sections.overview:
• Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA) is the most common chronic rheumatic disease of childhood.
• It is a group of disorders characterized by **arthritis of unknown etiology** that begins **before the age of 16** and persists for **at least 6 weeks**.
• JIA is a diagnosis of exclusion, requiring other causes of childhood arthritis (e.g., infection, malignancy) to be ruled out.
sections.etiology:
• JIA is an **autoimmune disease** resulting from a complex interplay of genetic predisposition and environmental triggers.
    ◦ **Pathophysiology**
        ▪ The immune system mistakenly attacks the body's own tissues, primarily the synovium (the lining of the joints).
        ▪ T-cell activation leads to the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., **TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6**).
        ▪ This cytokine cascade recruits other immune cells to the joint, causing synovial inflammation (synovitis), hypertrophy (pannus formation), and effusion.
        ▪ Chronic inflammation leads to the destruction of cartilage and bone, resulting in joint damage, pain, and loss of function.
    ◦ **Genetics**
        ▪ Strong association with certain human leukocyte antigen (HLA) types (e.g., **HLA-B27** in Enthesitis-related JIA, **HLA-DR4**).
    ◦ **Environmental Triggers**
        ▪ Suspected triggers include viral or bacterial infections that may initiate the autoimmune response in a genetically susceptible individual.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** Affects approximately 1 in 1,000 children.
• **Peak Onset:** Bimodal peaks at **1-3 years** and **8-12 years**.
• **Gender:** Varies by subtype.
    ◦ Oligoarticular JIA: More common in females.
    ◦ Enthesitis-related JIA: More common in males.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation of JIA is heterogeneous and is classified into several subtypes based on the clinical features within the first 6 months of disease.
    ◦ **Oligoarticular** (Most Common: ~50%)
        ▪ Arthritis in **≤ 4 joints**.
        ▪ Typically affects large joints (e.g., **knees**, ankles, elbows).
        ▪ Often **asymmetric**.
        ▪ High risk for **asymptomatic chronic anterior uveitis**, especially if **ANA-positive**.
    ◦ **Polyarticular** (~25%)
        ▪ Arthritis in **≥ 5 joints**.
        ▪ Can be **RF-positive** or **RF-negative**.
        ▪ Often **symmetric**, affecting both large and small joints (hands, feet, wrists).
        ▪ **RF-positive** disease closely resembles adult rheumatoid arthritis and carries a worse prognosis for joint damage.
    ◦ **Systemic (sJIA) / Still's Disease** (~10%)
        ▪ Prominent systemic features with arthritis.
        ▪ Hallmark: **Quotidian fever** (daily high-spiking fevers, often to 39°C), typically in the late afternoon/evening, returning to normal once daily.
        ▪ Classic **evanescent, salmon-colored macular rash** that appears with fever.
        ▪ Other systemic signs: Hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, serositis (pericarditis, pleuritis).
    ◦ **Enthesitis-Related**
        ▪ Arthritis **AND** **enthesitis** (inflammation where tendons/ligaments attach to bone).
        ▪ Common sites of enthesitis: Achilles tendon insertion, plantar fascia.
        ▪ Predominantly affects lower extremity large joints and the axial skeleton (sacroiliac joints, spine).
        ▪ Strong association with **HLA-B27**.
        ▪ More common in males > 6 years old.
    ◦ **Psoriatic**
        ▪ Arthritis **AND** psoriasis.
        ▪ OR Arthritis and at least two of the following: dactylitis, nail pitting/onycholysis, or a first-degree relative with psoriasis.
        ▪ **Dactylitis** ("sausage digit") is characteristic.
sections.diagnostics:
• JIA is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion.
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **Inflammatory Markers:** ESR and CRP (non-specific but correlate with disease activity, especially high in sJIA).
    ◦ **CBC:** Anemia of chronic disease, leukocytosis, and thrombocytosis are common.
    ◦ **Serology**
        ▪ **ANA:** Often positive in Oligoarticular JIA; a key risk factor for developing uveitis.
        ▪ **Rheumatoid Factor (RF) & Anti-CCP:** Used to classify Polyarticular JIA. Presence indicates a more aggressive disease course.
        ▪ **HLA-B27:** Positive in a majority of patients with Enthesitis-related JIA.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **X-rays:** Often normal early in the disease. Later findings include soft tissue swelling, periarticular osteopenia, joint space narrowing, and bony erosions.
    ◦ **Ultrasound:** Useful for detecting synovitis and guiding intra-articular injections.
    ◦ **MRI:** Most sensitive imaging for detecting early synovitis, bone marrow edema, and cartilage damage.
• **Procedures**
    ◦ **Arthrocentesis:** Essential if septic arthritis is suspected. Synovial fluid in JIA is inflammatory (WBC 5,000-60,000/mm3) with a predominance of neutrophils, but culture is negative.
• **Ophthalmologic Exam**
    ◦ **Regular slit-lamp examinations** are mandatory for all JIA patients to screen for uveitis, particularly in high-risk groups (Oligoarticular, ANA-positive).
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly variable and subtype-dependent.
• **Good:** Oligoarticular JIA has the highest rate of remission.
• **Guarded/Poor:** RF-positive polyarticular JIA and Systemic JIA are more likely to persist into adulthood and cause significant joint damage.
• Early diagnosis and aggressive treatment with modern therapies (DMARDs, biologics) have dramatically improved outcomes.

sections.overview:
• Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA) is a chronic, inflammatory, **seronegative spondyloarthropathy** that affects the joints, entheses (sites where tendons and ligaments attach to bone), and skin in individuals with psoriasis.
• It is characterized by stiffness, pain, swelling, and potential for progressive joint destruction.
• The clinical presentation is highly variable, ranging from mild oligoarthritis to severe, deforming polyarthritis and spondylitis.
sections.etiology:
• **Multifactorial:** A combination of genetic predisposition, environmental triggers, and immune dysregulation.
• **Genetic:**
    ◦ Strong association with **HLA-B27** (especially in axial disease) and **HLA-Cw6** (associated with psoriasis).
• **Environmental Triggers:**
    ◦ Physical trauma (**Koebner phenomenon**), infections (e.g., Streptococcal pharyngitis), and certain medications can trigger or exacerbate the disease in genetically susceptible individuals.
• **Pathophysiology:**
    ◦ Primarily an **immune-mediated** process driven by T-cells (Th1 and Th17).
    ◦ Aberrant immune response leads to overproduction of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including **Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha (TNF-α)**, **Interleukin-17 (IL-17)**, and **Interleukin-23 (IL-23)**.
    ◦ This cytokine cascade drives inflammation in the synovium (synovitis), entheses (enthesitis), and bone, leading to synovial hyperplasia, cartilage degradation, bone erosions, and pathologic new bone formation.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** Affects up to **30% of patients with psoriasis**.
• **Age of Onset:** Typically between **30-55 years old**.
• **Sex:** Affects males and females equally (1:1 ratio).
• **Psoriasis Onset:**
    ◦ In ~85% of cases, skin manifestations precede joint disease, often by several years.
    ◦ In ~15%, arthritis can precede or occur concurrently with the skin rash.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Primary Risk Factor:** Existing psoriasis, particularly severe skin or nail disease.
• **Family History:** Positive family history of psoriasis or psoriatic arthritis.
• **Genetic Markers:** Presence of **HLA-B27**.
• **Environmental:** Obesity, smoking, physical trauma, and certain infections.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• PsA is notoriously heterogeneous, with five classic patterns of joint involvement:
    ◦ **Asymmetric Oligoarthritis (Most Common Pattern, ~70%):** Involves ≤4 joints in an asymmetric pattern, often affecting the large joints of the lower extremities like the knees and ankles.
    ◦ **Symmetric Polyarthritis:** Involves ≥5 joints, often in a symmetric pattern mimicking **Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)**.
    ◦ **Distal Interphalangeal (DIP) Predominant:** Classic but less common; affects the DIP joints of the fingers and toes, often associated with nail changes.
    ◦ **Spondylitis:** Inflammation of the axial skeleton, including the sacroiliac joints (sacroiliitis) and spine, presenting as inflammatory back pain.
    ◦ **Arthritis Mutilans (Most Severe, Rare):** Severe, deforming, and destructive arthritis leading to dissolution of bone (osteolysis), resulting in **"telescoping digits."**
• **Joints:** Pain, swelling, and morning stiffness that lasts >30 minutes and improves with activity.
• **Skin:** Pruritic, erythematous plaques with silvery scales, typically on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees), scalp, and gluteal cleft.
• **Nails:** Pitting, onycholysis (separation of nail from nail bed), subungual hyperkeratosis, and **"oil spot" lesions**.
• **Enthesitis:** Pain and tenderness at tendon/ligament insertion sites, commonly the Achilles tendon and plantar fascia.
• **Dactylitis:** Diffuse, painful swelling of an entire finger or toe, giving a **"sausage digit"** appearance.
• **Axial:** Inflammatory back pain, neck pain, or buttock pain that is worse with rest and improves with activity.
• **Systemic:** Fatigue, low-grade fever, malaise.
• **Ocular:** Eye pain, redness, photophobia due to **uveitis**.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Musculoskeletal:**
    ◦ Swollen, tender, and erythematous joints.
    ◦ **Dactylitis:** Uniform swelling of a digit.
    ◦ **Enthesitis:** Point tenderness over affected entheses (e.g., posterior heel, tibial tuberosity).
    ◦ Decreased range of motion of affected joints.
    ◦ Limited spinal flexion (**positive Schober test**) if axial involvement is present.
• **Dermatologic:**
    ◦ Well-demarcated, erythematous plaques with adherent silvery scale.
    ◦ **Nail Pitting:** Small, punctate depressions in the nail plate.
    ◦ **Onycholysis:** Lifting of the nail plate from the nail bed.
• **Ophthalmologic:**
    ◦ Conjunctival injection, ciliary flush (signs of **uveitis**).
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on history, physical exam, and exclusion of other arthritides.
• **CASPAR criteria** are used for classification (requires inflammatory articular disease + ≥3 points):
    ◦ Evidence of current, past, or family history of psoriasis (2 points if current, 1 otherwise).
    ◦ Psoriatic nail dystrophy (1 point).
    ◦ Negative test for **Rheumatoid Factor (RF)** (1 point).
    ◦ **Dactylitis** (current or past) (1 point).
    ◦ Radiographic evidence of juxta-articular new bone formation (1 point).
• **Imaging:**
    ◦ **X-rays (Plain Radiographs):**
        ▪ **Hallmark Finding:** Coexistence of bone erosion and new bone formation.
        ▪ **"Pencil-in-cup" deformity:** Classic, pathognomonic but late finding.
        ▪ **Asymmetric sacroiliitis** and bulky, non-marginal syndesmophytes in the spine.
        ▪ Acro-osteolysis (resorption of terminal phalanges).
        ▪ Juxta-articular "whiskering" (periostitis).
    ◦ **MRI / Musculoskeletal Ultrasound:** More sensitive than X-ray for detecting early inflammation, including synovitis, tenosynovitis, and enthesitis.
sections.treatment:
• **Mild Disease (≤4 joints):**
    ◦ **NSAIDs** (e.g., naproxen, ibuprofen) for symptom control.
    ◦ **Intra-articular glucocorticoid injections** for isolated inflamed joints.
• **Moderate to Severe Disease:**
    ◦ **Conventional Synthetic DMARDs (csDMARDs):**
        ▪ **Methotrexate (MTX)** is the first-line agent, effective for both skin and peripheral arthritis.
        ▪ Leflunomide, Sulfasalazine.
        ▪ *Note:* Hydroxychloroquine is used with caution as it can exacerbate psoriasis.
• **Refractory or Severe Disease / Axial Disease:**
    ◦ **Biologic DMARDs (bDMARDs):**
        ▪ **TNF-α inhibitors:** (First-line biologic) Etanercept, Adalimumab, Infliximab, Golimumab, Certolizumab.
        ▪ **IL-17 inhibitors:** Secukinumab, Ixekizumab.
        ▪ **IL-12/23 inhibitor:** Ustekinumab.
    ◦ **Targeted Synthetic DMARDs (tsDMARDs):**
        ▪ **PDE4 inhibitor:** Apremilast (oral option for mild-moderate disease).
        ▪ **JAK inhibitors:** Tofacitinib, Upadacitinib (oral options for moderate-severe disease).
• **AVOID:** Long-term systemic corticosteroids due to risk of pustular psoriasis flare upon withdrawal.
sections.management:
• **Multidisciplinary Approach:** Collaboration between **Rheumatology** and **Dermatology** is essential.
• **Non-pharmacologic:**
    ◦ **Physical and Occupational Therapy:** To maintain joint function, strength, and range of motion.
    ◦ **Lifestyle Modification:** Smoking cessation, weight management, regular low-impact exercise (swimming, walking).
• **Co-morbidity Screening:** PsA is associated with an increased risk of:
    ◦ **Cardiovascular Disease**
    ◦ **Metabolic Syndrome** (obesity, HTN, dyslipidemia, insulin resistance)
    ◦ Depression & Anxiety
    ◦ Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD)
    ◦ **Uveitis**
    ◦ **Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD)**
sections.complications:
• **Progressive, erosive joint damage** leading to permanent disability.
• **Arthritis Mutilans:** Severe joint destruction.
• **Ankylosis:** Fusion of joints, especially in the spine and SI joints.
• **Extra-articular:** **Uveitis** (can lead to vision loss if untreated), **IBD**.
• **Increased cardiovascular morbidity and mortality** due to chronic systemic inflammation.
sections.prognosis:
• The course of PsA is variable and chronic, often characterized by relapses and remissions.
• Without treatment, the disease is progressive and can lead to significant functional impairment.
• **Poor prognostic factors include:** high number of inflamed joints, **dactylitis**, elevated ESR/CRP, early erosive damage on X-ray, and severe psoriasis.
• Early diagnosis and treatment with DMARDs, especially biologics, have dramatically improved long-term outcomes and can prevent irreversible joint damage.

sections.overview:
• Reactive Arthritis is an acute, non-purulent, inflammatory arthritis that arises as a reaction to a recent infection elsewhere in the body, typically in the gastrointestinal (GI) or genitourinary (GU) tract
	◦ It is a member of the **seronegative spondyloarthropathies**, a group of inflammatory diseases that also includes ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, and enteropathic arthritis
• The classic, though now less commonly seen, triad of symptoms is **arthritis, urethritis, and conjunctivitis**
	◦ The eponymous name "Reiter Syndrome" is now less favored due to the physician's Nazi party affiliation
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
	◦ The condition is triggered by a preceding infection, usually 1-4 weeks prior to the onset of symptoms
	◦ **Genitourinary (GU) Pathogens**
		▪ ***Chlamydia trachomatis*** (most common overall trigger)
	◦ **Gastrointestinal (GI) Pathogens**
		▪ ***Salmonella*** species
		▪ ***Shigella*** species (especially *S. flexneri*)
		▪ ***Yersinia enterocolitica***
		▪ ***Campylobacter jejuni***
		▪ *Clostridioides difficile*
• **Pathophysiology**
	◦ The exact mechanism is believed to be an aberrant autoimmune response to bacterial antigens
	◦ **Molecular Mimicry**: The host immune system, particularly T-cells, mistakenly attacks self-tissues (e.g., synovium) because of a structural similarity between bacterial antigens and host antigens
	◦ **HLA-B27 Association**: There is a very strong genetic predisposition. The presence of the **HLA-B27** antigen is a major risk factor
		▪ It is thought that the HLA-B27 molecule may present arthritogenic bacterial peptides to CD8+ T-cells, initiating the inflammatory cascade
	◦ **Sterile Arthritis**: Viable organisms are **not** present in the affected joint; the synovial fluid is sterile
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Approximately 30-40 cases per 100,000 adults
• **Age of Onset**: Typically affects young adults between the ages of **20 and 40**
• **Sex**
	◦ Post-venereal (Chlamydia-induced) form is more common in **males** (~9:1 ratio)
	◦ Post-enteric (GI-induced) form has an **equal** male-to-female ratio
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a young adult who develops acute onset of joint pain and swelling, typically in a lower extremity, 1-4 weeks after an episode of diarrhea or urethritis
• The presentation is often abrupt and associated with constitutional symptoms
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on a characteristic pattern of symptoms following a known infection
	◦ There is no single pathognomonic test
• **Laboratory Studies**
	◦ **Inflammatory Markers**: **Elevated ESR and CRP** (non-specific)
	◦ **CBC**: May show mild normocytic anemia (anemia of chronic disease) and leukocytosis
	◦ **Serologies**: **Rheumatoid Factor (RF) and Anti-nuclear Antibody (ANA) are negative**
	◦ **Genetic Testing**: **HLA-B27** can support the diagnosis but is not required
• **Infectious Workup**
	◦ **GU**: Urine or urethral/cervical swab for **Chlamydia trachomatis via Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT)**
	◦ **GI**: **Stool culture** if there is a history of recent diarrhea
• **Arthrocentesis (Synovial Fluid Analysis)**
	◦ **ESSENTIAL** to rule out septic arthritis and crystal-induced arthropathy
	◦ **Appearance**: Yellow, cloudy
	◦ **WBC Count**: **Inflammatory** range (typically 2,000-50,000 cells/mm3), with a predominance of neutrophils
	◦ **Culture & Gram Stain**: **NEGATIVE** (sterile fluid)
	◦ **Crystals**: Absent
• **Imaging**
	◦ **X-rays**: Often normal in the early stages. In chronic disease, may show:
		▪ Juxta-articular osteoporosis, joint space narrowing, bony erosions
		▪ Periostitis ("fluffy" new bone formation), especially at sites of enthesitis (e.g., calcaneal spurs)
		▪ Sacroiliitis may be seen on pelvic X-ray
sections.prognosis:
• Most cases are self-limited, with symptoms resolving within **3 to 12 months**
• Up to 50% of patients may experience recurrent episodes of arthritis
• Approximately 15-30% develop chronic arthritis or sacroiliitis
• Patients who are **HLA-B27 positive** tend to have a more severe and prolonged course

sections.overview:
• Gout is a crystal-induced arthropathy characterized by the deposition of **monosodium urate (MSU) crystals** in and around the joints.
• Crystal deposition triggers an intense, episodic inflammatory response, leading to acute arthritis attacks.
• The underlying metabolic cause is **hyperuricemia**, defined as a serum urate level >6.8 mg/dL.
• The classic presentation is a severely painful, red, swollen joint, most famously affecting the first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint, a condition known as **podagra**.
sections.etiology:
• The fundamental cause of gout is **hyperuricemia**, which leads to the supersaturation of uric acid in the blood and other body fluids.
    ◦ Uric acid is the end product of purine metabolism.
    ◦ Hyperuricemia develops via two primary mechanisms:
        ▪ **Underexcretion of Uric Acid (90% of cases)**:
            • This is the most common cause.
            • The kidneys are unable to efficiently excrete uric acid.
            • Can be idiopathic or secondary to conditions like chronic kidney disease (CKD), acidosis, or medications (e.g., diuretics).
        ▪ **Overproduction of Uric Acid (10% of cases)**:
            • Caused by increased purine metabolism.
            • Can result from high dietary purine intake, high cell turnover states (e.g., myeloproliferative disorders, psoriasis, chemotherapy), or rare genetic enzyme defects (e.g., Lesch-Nyhan syndrome).
• **Pathophysiological Cascade**:
