    ◦ Hyperuricemia leads to supersaturation of blood/synovial fluid with uric acid.
    ◦ Precipitation of MSU crystals occurs in cooler, peripheral joints and avascular tissues (e.g., cartilage).
    ◦ Crystals are phagocytosed by synovial macrophages.
    ◦ Activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome.
    ◦ Release of potent pro-inflammatory cytokines, especially **Interleukin-1 (IL-1)**.
    ◦ Massive neutrophil influx into the joint.
    ◦ Intense inflammation, pain, and tissue damage.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects ~4% of adults in the United States.
• **Sex**: Significantly more common in men than women (ratio ~3:1).
    ◦ In women, onset is typically post-menopausal, as estrogen has a mild uricosuric effect.
• **Age**: Incidence increases with age, peaking in the 40s-50s for men.
• **Genetics**: Strong familial component. Higher prevalence in certain ethnic groups (e.g., Pacific Islanders, Māori).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is an **acute, monoarticular, inflammatory arthritis** that develops rapidly over several hours, often waking the patient from sleep.
• The pain is typically excruciating.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Arthrocentesis (Synovial Fluid Analysis) - GOLD STANDARD**
    ◦ **Appearance**: Turbid, yellow, inflammatory fluid.
    ◦ **WBC Count**: Elevated, typically 2,000-50,000/mm³, with a neutrophil predominance.
    ◦ **Microscopy**: 
        ▪ **Pathognomonic finding** under polarized light microscopy: **Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals**.
        ▪ Mnemonic: Crystals are **Y**ellow when para**ll**el to the axis of the compensator and Blue when perpendicular.
    ◦ **Gram Stain & Culture**: Essential to **rule out septic arthritis**, the main differential.
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **Serum Uric Acid**: 
        ▪ Can be misleading; may be **normal or even low** during an acute flare due to inflammatory uricosuria.
        ▪ More useful for long-term management, checked 2 weeks after a flare has resolved.
    ◦ **Inflammatory Markers (ESR, CRP)**: Non-specific but will be elevated during a flare.
    ◦ **BUN/Creatinine**: To assess for underlying CKD.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **X-Ray**: 
        ▪ Often normal in an initial attack.
        ▪ In chronic, advanced gout, shows characteristic **"rat-bite" erosions**: well-defined, "punched-out" erosions with sclerotic margins and overhanging edges.
    ◦ **Ultrasound**: 
        ▪ Highly sensitive for crystal deposition.
        ▪ May show the **"double contour sign"** - a hyperechoic line of MSU crystals overlying the hypoechoic articular cartilage.
sections.prognosis:
• With appropriate treatment and management, the prognosis is excellent.
• Patients can live a normal life with controlled uric acid levels and prevention of flares.
• Untreated or poorly managed gout can lead to chronic pain, joint destruction, and significant disability.

sections.overview:
• Acute inflammatory monoarthritis or oligoarthritis caused by the deposition of **calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD)** crystals in and around joints
    ◦ A form of crystal-induced arthropathy that clinically mimics gout
    ◦ **Calcium Pyrophosphate Deposition (CPPD) disease** is a broader term encompassing a spectrum of clinical presentations, from asymptomatic radiographic findings to acute attacks and chronic degenerative arthritis
sections.etiology:
• Underlying cause is the precipitation of CPPD crystals in articular cartilage, fibrocartilage (e.g., menisci), and synovium
    ◦ **Crystal Formation**: Pathologic formation is driven by elevated extracellular levels of **inorganic pyrophosphate (PPi)** and calcium within the joint cartilage
    ◦ **Genetic/Metabolic Factors**: Mutations in the **ANKH gene** can increase extracellular PPi transport; deficiencies in enzymes that break down PPi (like tissue non-specific alkaline phosphatase - TNAP) can also lead to its accumulation
    ◦ **Crystal Shedding**: Microtrauma or changes in calcium/PPi concentration can cause crystals to shed from the cartilage into the synovial fluid
    ◦ **Inflammatory Cascade**
        ▪ Once in the synovial fluid, CPPD crystals are phagocytosed by neutrophils, monocytes, and synoviocytes
        ▪ This triggers the activation of the **NLRP3 inflammasome** within these cells
        ▪ Inflammasome activation leads to the cleavage and release of potent pro-inflammatory cytokines, primarily **Interleukin-1 (IL-1)**
        ▪ IL-1 orchestrates a robust inflammatory response, recruiting more neutrophils and causing intense pain, swelling, erythema, and warmth
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Strongly associated with aging
    ◦ Radiographic evidence of chondrocalcinosis is seen in ~15% of individuals aged 65-75 and up to 50% of those over 85
• **Symptomatic Disease**: A smaller percentage of those with radiographic findings develop symptomatic disease
• **Gender**: Affects men and women roughly equally
• **Age of Onset**: Typically occurs in individuals > 60 years old
    ◦ Onset before age 50 should prompt a workup for secondary causes
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• CPPD disease has several distinct clinical phenotypes
    ◦ **Acute CPPD Arthritis (Pseudogout)** (~25% of cases)
        ▪ Abrupt, self-limiting attack of severe joint inflammation
        ▪ **Monoarticular** (most common) or oligoarticular
        ▪ **Knee** is the most frequently affected joint (~50% of cases), followed by the **wrist**, shoulder, ankle, and elbow
        ▪ Attacks can be triggered by trauma, surgery, or acute medical illness
    ◦ **Chronic CPPD Inflammatory Arthritis (Pseudo-Rheumatoid Arthritis)** (~5% of cases)
        ▪ Symmetrical, polyarticular inflammatory arthritis
        ▪ Presents with morning stiffness, fatigue, synovitis, and elevated inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP)
        ▪ Can be difficult to distinguish from Rheumatoid Arthritis
    ◦ **Osteoarthritis with CPPD (Pseudo-Osteoarthritis)** (~50% of cases, most common symptomatic form)
        ▪ Chronic, progressive, degenerative arthritis
        ▪ Often affects joints not typical for primary OA, such as the **wrists (radiocarpal joint)**, **metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints**, shoulders, and ankles
        ▪ May present with superimposed acute flares
    ◦ **Asymptomatic CPPD**
        ▪ Incidental radiographic finding of **chondrocalcinosis** without any clinical symptoms
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• Acute attacks are self-limited, usually resolving in days to weeks
• Recurrences are common
• The long-term prognosis is variable
    ◦ Many patients have only intermittent, mild attacks
    ◦ A subset will develop a chronic, progressive arthritis leading to significant disability
• There is no cure

sections.overview:
• Septic arthritis, also known as infectious or bacterial arthritis, is an infection within a synovial joint.
• It is an **orthopedic emergency** due to its potential for rapid cartilage destruction, irreversible joint damage, and systemic sepsis.
• The condition is characterized by an acute onset of a single, swollen, erythematous, and exquisitely painful joint, often accompanied by systemic signs of infection like fever.
• Prompt diagnosis via arthrocentesis and immediate initiation of treatment with antibiotics and joint drainage are critical to preserve joint function and prevent life-threatening complications.
sections.etiology:
• The infection of the synovial space occurs through three main routes:
    ◦ **Hematogenous Seeding (Most Common)**: Bacteria from a distant site of infection (e.g., skin, respiratory tract, urinary tract) travel through the bloodstream and seed the highly vascular synovial membrane.
    ◦ **Direct Inoculation**: Bacteria are introduced directly into the joint from penetrating trauma, intra-articular injections, or arthroscopic/open joint surgery.
    ◦ **Contiguous Spread**: Infection spreads from an adjacent focus, such as osteomyelitis or a soft tissue abscess.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ Once bacteria enter the joint, they proliferate in the synovial fluid, triggering an intense inflammatory response.
    ◦ Neutrophils are recruited, releasing proteolytic enzymes (proteases, collagenases) and cytokines (IL-1, TNF-alpha) that rapidly degrade articular cartilage and subchondral bone.
    ◦ The resulting purulent effusion increases intra-articular pressure, further compromising blood flow and leading to ischemic necrosis of the cartilage.
    ◦ This entire process can cause irreversible joint destruction within 48 hours.
• **Common Causative Organisms**:
    ◦ ***Staphylococcus aureus***: **Most common cause overall (~50%)** in all age groups, including Methicillin-resistant *S. aureus* (**MRSA**).
    ◦ ***Neisseria gonorrhoeae***: A common cause in **young, sexually active adults**.
        ▪ Often presents as part of **Disseminated Gonococcal Infection (DGI)** with a triad of tenosynovitis, dermatitis, and migratory polyarthralgias.
    ◦ **Streptococci** (Group A, B, *S. pneumoniae*): Second most common cause after *S. aureus*.
    ◦ **Gram-negative bacilli** (*E. coli*, *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*): More common in the elderly, immunocompromised patients, and intravenous drug users (**IVDU**).
        ▪ ***Pseudomonas*** is classically associated with **IVDU**.
    ◦ ***Pasteurella multocida***: Associated with **animal bites** (especially cats).
    ◦ ***Borrelia burgdorferi***: **Lyme disease** can present as an oligoarticular inflammatory arthritis, most commonly affecting the knee.
sections.epidemiology:
• Incidence: Approximately 2-10 cases per 100,000 people in the general population.
• Incidence rises to 30-70 cases per 100,000 in patients with risk factors like rheumatoid arthritis or a prosthetic joint.
• **Monoarticular** involvement occurs in 80-90% of cases.
• The **knee** is the most commonly affected joint (~50%), followed by the hip, shoulder, ankle, and wrist.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a patient with an **acute onset** of a single painful, swollen, and warm joint.
• The patient will often present with systemic symptoms and will be reluctant to move the affected joint.
• This is a "can't miss" diagnosis; a high index of suspicion is required.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Synovial Fluid Analysis (Arthrocentesis)**
    ◦ **This is the GOLD STANDARD for diagnosis.**
    ◦ The procedure should be performed immediately if septic arthritis is suspected.
    ◦ **Key Findings**:
        ▪ **Appearance**: Opaque to purulent, yellow/green color.
        ▪ **WBC Count**: **>50,000 cells/mm³** is highly suggestive (often >100,000).
        ▪ **Neutrophil Percentage**: **>75%** (often >90%).
        ▪ **Gram Stain**: Positive in 50-75% of non-gonococcal cases. Guides initial antibiotic choice.
        ▪ **Culture and Sensitivity**: Definitive diagnosis. Essential for tailoring antibiotic therapy.
        ▪ **Glucose**: Low (compared to serum glucose, as bacteria consume it).
        ▪ **Crystals**: Should be performed to rule out co-existing gout or pseudogout.
    ◦ **Synovial Fluid Comparison**:
        ▪ **Normal**: WBCs <200/mm³, PMNs <25%, Clear appearance.
        ▪ **Inflammatory**: WBCs 2,000-50,000/mm³, PMNs >50%, Translucent/Opaque appearance.
        ▪ **Septic**: **WBCs >50,000/mm³**, **PMNs >75%**, **Opaque/Purulent** appearance.
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **CBC with differential**: Leukocytosis with a left shift.
    ◦ **Inflammatory Markers**: **Elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) and Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR).**
        ▪ CRP is more sensitive for acute infection and useful for monitoring treatment response.
    ◦ **Blood Cultures**: Should be drawn before starting antibiotics; positive in ~50% of cases.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Plain Radiographs (X-ray)**:
        ▪ First-line imaging.
        ▪ Often normal in early disease but useful to rule out fracture, osteomyelitis, or other pathology.
        ▪ May show soft tissue swelling and a widened joint space due to effusion.
        ▪ Late findings include joint space narrowing and bony erosions.
    ◦ **Ultrasound**:
        ▪ Excellent for detecting joint effusion and guiding arthrocentesis, especially in deep joints like the hip.
    ◦ **MRI**:
        ▪ Most sensitive for detecting early joint inflammation, associated osteomyelitis, and soft tissue abscesses.
        ▪ Not required for initial diagnosis if arthrocentesis is feasible.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly dependent on the time to diagnosis and treatment.
• Good functional outcomes are possible if treatment is initiated within **24-48 hours** of symptom onset.
• **Poor prognostic factors include**:
    ◦ Delayed treatment
    ◦ Infection of the hip joint
    ◦ Age >60
    ◦ Underlying rheumatoid arthritis
    ◦ Infection with resistant organisms like **MRSA**.

sections.overview:
• Lyme arthritis is a late-stage manifestation of Lyme disease, an infection caused by the spirochete **Borrelia burgdorferi**
• Characterized by intermittent, migratory, and often monoarticular or oligoarticular arthritis
    ◦ Most commonly affects large joints, especially the **knee**
• The arthritis results from an inflammatory response to spirochetes within the joint space
• Diagnosis relies on clinical presentation in an endemic area, supported by **two-tiered serologic testing**
• Treatment with a 28-day course of oral antibiotics is curative for most patients
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**
    ◦ **Borrelia burgdorferi** (in North America)
    ◦ *B. afzelii* and *B. garinii* (in Europe and Asia)
    ◦ It is a gram-negative spirochete
• **Vector**
    ◦ Transmitted via the bite of an infected **Ixodes** species tick (e.g., **Ixodes scapularis** or **deer tick** in the Eastern/Midwestern US)
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Dissemination**: Following initial inoculation, the spirochetes disseminate from the skin via the bloodstream or lymphatics to various tissues, including synovial tissue in the joints
    ◦ **Direct Invasion & Inflammation**: The spirochetes invade the synovium, triggering a robust host inflammatory response, leading to **synovitis**, **effusion**, and cartilage damage
    ◦ **Immune Evasion**: *Borrelia* has mechanisms to evade the immune system, allowing it to persist in tissues
    ◦ **Autoimmunity (in refractory cases)**: In some genetically predisposed individuals (associated with certain HLA-DR alleles), persistent arthritis may occur after bacterial eradication due to molecular mimicry
sections.epidemiology:
• **Geography**
    ◦ Most common tick-borne illness in the United States
    ◦ Highly **endemic** in the **Northeast**, **Mid-Atlantic**, and **Upper Midwest** states (e.g., Connecticut, Massachusetts, New York, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Minnesota)
• **Seasonality**
    ◦ Tick bites and early Lyme disease peak in late spring and summer (May-July)
    ◦ Lyme arthritis typically presents weeks to months later, with cases appearing in the fall and winter
• **Demographics**
    ◦ Bimodal age distribution, with peaks in children (5-14 years) and adults (45-65 years)
    ◦ Slightly more common in males
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A manifestation of **late disseminated Lyme disease**, typically occurring weeks to months (average ~6 months) after the initial tick bite
    ◦ Patients often do not recall the bite or the classic **erythema migrans (EM) rash**
• Classic presentation is the **sudden onset of a markedly swollen, painful joint**
    ◦ The **knee** is the most commonly affected site (>90% of cases)
• Arthritis typically follows an **intermittent course**
    ◦ Attacks last for weeks to months, separated by periods of complete remission
    ◦ Over time, attacks may become less frequent, but in some cases, the arthritis becomes chronic and persistent
• Systemic symptoms like fever and malaise are usually mild or absent at this stage
sections.diagnostics:
• The first step is often to rule out **septic arthritis**, a medical emergency
• **Synovial Fluid Analysis (Arthrocentesis): ESSENTIAL**
    ◦ **Appearance**: Cloudy, yellow
    ◦ **WBC Count**: Inflammatory; typically **20,000 - 60,000 cells/mm3** (can range from 500 to >100,000)
    ◦ **Differential**: **Neutrophil-predominant** (>75% PMNs)
    ◦ **Gram Stain & Culture**: **NEGATIVE**
        ▪ A key finding that helps differentiate it from bacterial septic arthritis
    ◦ **Crystals**: Absent (rules out gout/pseudogout)
• **PCR for *B. burgdorferi* DNA**
    ◦ High specificity but variable sensitivity (~85%)
    ◦ Can be a useful confirmatory test but is not required if serology is positive
• **Serology (Blood Test): Mainstay of diagnosis**
    ◦ The CDC recommends a **two-tiered approach**:
        ▪ **First Tier (Screening)**: Enzyme immunoassay (EIA) or Immunofluorescence Assay (IFA). High sensitivity.
        ▪ **Second Tier (Confirmatory)**: If the first tier is positive or equivocal, a **Western blot** is performed
            ▪ For late disease (>30 days), a positive test requires **5 of 10 IgG bands**
            ▪ The IgM Western blot is often negative or not relevant at this late stage and can be falsely positive
• **Inflammatory Markers**
    ◦ ESR and CRP are non-specifically elevated
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **X-rays**: Usually normal or show only a joint effusion and soft-tissue swelling. Primarily used to rule out other causes (e.g., fracture, advanced osteoarthritis).
    ◦ **MRI/Ultrasound**: Not routinely needed for diagnosis but can confirm effusion and synovitis.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**
    ◦ With timely diagnosis and appropriate antibiotic therapy, >90% of patients achieve complete resolution of their arthritis
• For the ~10% who develop **antibiotic-refractory arthritis**, the prognosis is still very good
    ◦ The inflammation usually resolves over months to years with anti-inflammatory therapy and does not typically cause long-term disability

sections.overview:
• **Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS)** is a chronic, systemic inflammatory disease primarily affecting the **axial skeleton**, especially the **sacroiliac (SI) joints** and spine.
• It is the prototypical **seronegative spondyloarthropathy**.
• The hallmark of AS is **inflammatory back pain** leading to structural damage, new bone formation (**syndesmophytes**), and progressive spinal fusion (**ankylosis**), resulting in significant stiffness and loss of mobility.
• It is also associated with characteristic extra-articular manifestations.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ The exact cause is unknown but involves a strong genetic predisposition, particularly the **HLA-B27 gene**, combined with environmental triggers (e.g., infectious agents, gut microbiome dysbiosis).
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Immune-Mediated Inflammation**: The disease process begins with an immune response at sites of mechanical stress, primarily the **entheses** (sites where tendons and ligaments attach to bone).
    ◦ **Cytokine Cascade**: Infiltration of immune cells (T-cells, macrophages) releases pro-inflammatory cytokines, most notably **Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha (TNF-α)** and **Interleukin-17 (IL-17)**.
    ◦ **Enthesitis & Bone Erosion**: This chronic inflammation leads to enthesitis and subchondral bone marrow edema and erosion. This is the primary lesion in AS.
    ◦ **Reactive Bone Formation**: Following the inflammatory and erosive phase, a reparative process leads to pathologic new bone formation.
    ◦ **Syndesmophytes & Ankylosis**: Fibroblasts differentiate into osteoblasts, forming **syndesmophytes**—thin, vertical bone growths that bridge vertebral bodies. Over time, these syndesmophytes fuse, leading to complete spinal rigidity, or **ankylosis** (the classic **"bamboo spine"**).
sections.epidemiology:
• **Age of Onset**: Typically late adolescence or early adulthood; onset is rare after age 45.
• **Sex**: Strong male predominance (**M:F ratio ~2-3:1**). Females may present with a milder or different disease pattern.
• **Prevalence**: Affects approximately 0.1-0.5% of the U.S. population, with higher prevalence in populations with a higher frequency of the **HLA-B27** allele (e.g., northern Europeans).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a **young male (<40 years)** with an insidious onset of chronic low back pain and stiffness lasting **>3 months**.
• The pain is characterized by inflammatory features:
    ◦ Worse with rest, especially in the **morning** (**morning stiffness >30 minutes**).
    ◦ **Improves with activity and exercise**.
    ◦ Often causes nocturnal awakening (pain in the second half of the night).
    ◦ Pain is typically dull, located in the deep gluteal region, and may alternate sides.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **HLA-B27**: Positive in >90% of Caucasian patients. It is a susceptibility gene, not a diagnostic test. High negative predictive value.
    ◦ **Inflammatory Markers**: **Elevated ESR and CRP** are seen in ~50-70% of patients with active disease but can be normal.
    ◦ **CBC**: May show a normocytic anemia of chronic disease.
    ◦ **Serology**: **Seronegative** by definition; Rheumatoid Factor (RF) and anti-CCP antibodies are absent.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **X-Ray (AP Pelvis)**: The initial imaging of choice.
        ▪ **Sacroiliitis** is the radiographic hallmark.
        ▪ Findings progress from blurring of the joint margins to sclerosis, erosions, and finally complete fusion (ankylosis).
        ▪ Sacroiliitis is typically **bilateral and symmetric**.
    ◦ **X-Ray (Spine)**
        ▪ **Squaring** of vertebral bodies (loss of anterior concavity).
        ▪ **Syndesmophytes**: Thin, vertical ossifications that bridge vertebral bodies.
        ▪ **"Bamboo Spine"**: A late-stage finding where the entire spine is fused by syndesmophytes and ligamentous calcification, appearing as a single, rigid column.
        ▪ **"Dagger sign"**: Calcification of the supraspinous/interspinous ligaments on AP view.
    ◦ **MRI of the Sacroiliac Joints**
        ▪ **The most sensitive imaging modality for early diagnosis**.
        ▪ Can detect active inflammation (**bone marrow edema** on STIR sequences) and sacroiliitis long before changes are visible on plain radiographs.
sections.prognosis:
• The disease course is highly variable.
• With modern therapies (especially biologics), most patients can maintain good function and quality of life.
• Poor prognostic indicators include early hip involvement, high disease activity (**elevated CRP**), poor response to NSAIDs, and smoking.

sections.overview:
• **Enteropathic Arthritis (EnA)** is a form of chronic, inflammatory arthritis associated with **Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD)**, primarily Crohn's Disease and Ulcerative Colitis.
• Classified as one of the **seronegative spondyloarthropathies**, a group of inflammatory joint diseases that are negative for **rheumatoid factor (RF)** and **anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP)** antibodies.
• EnA typically presents in two distinct patterns:
    ◦ A **peripheral arthritis** that often mirrors the activity of the underlying bowel disease.
    ◦ An **axial arthritis** (affecting the spine and sacroiliac joints) that runs an independent course.
sections.etiology:
• The **"Gut-Joint Axis"** is the central concept in the pathophysiology of EnA.
• The proposed mechanism involves:
    ◦ **Increased Intestinal Permeability**: Chronic inflammation in IBD compromises the integrity of the intestinal mucosal barrier ("leaky gut").
    ◦ **Antigenic Translocation**: This allows gut bacteria, microbial products (e.g., lipopolysaccharides), and dietary antigens to cross the barrier and enter the systemic circulation.
    ◦ **Immune System Activation**: These translocated antigens trigger an aberrant systemic immune response.
        ▪ Due to **molecular mimicry**, T-cells activated against these gut antigens may cross-react with similar-appearing antigens in synovial tissue and entheses (sites where tendons and ligaments attach to bone).
    ◦ **Genetic Predisposition**: A strong genetic link exists, particularly with the **HLA-B27** gene, which is present in over 50% of patients with axial involvement.
    ◦ **Cytokine Dysregulation**: Pro-inflammatory cytokines, especially **TNF-alpha**, IL-23, and IL-17, are key mediators driving inflammation in both the gut and the joints.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects approximately 15-20% of patients with IBD.
• **IBD Association**: More common in **Crohn's Disease** than Ulcerative Colitis.
• **Age of Onset**: Typically presents in young adulthood (ages 25-45), mirroring the peak onset of IBD.
• **Gender Distribution**:
    ◦ **Peripheral Arthritis**: Affects males and females equally.
    ◦ **Axial Arthritis**: Shows a male predominance (~3:1), similar to ankylosing spondylitis.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The clinical picture is that of a patient with known or occult IBD who develops musculoskeletal symptoms.
• The arthritis may precede, coincide with, or follow the diagnosis of IBD.
• **Peripheral Arthritis Pattern (More common)**:
    ◦ Typically an **asymmetric, non-erosive oligoarthritis** (affecting < 5 joints).
    ◦ Predominantly affects large joints of the **lower extremities** (knees, ankles).
    ◦ **Activity often parallels IBD flares**.
        ▪ A flare-up of diarrhea and abdominal pain is often accompanied by joint swelling and pain.
• **Axial Arthritis Pattern**:
    ◦ Clinically indistinguishable from **Ankylosing Spondylitis**.
    ◦ Presents with **inflammatory back pain**:
        ▪ Insidious onset, worse with rest/in the morning, improves with activity, nocturnal pain.
    ◦ Can also involve the thoracic spine and cervical spine.
    ◦ **Activity is typically independent of IBD flares**.
        ▪ The back pain and stiffness can persist even when the gut is in remission.
sections.diagnostics:
• This is largely a **clinical diagnosis** made in a patient with IBD and characteristic arthritic symptoms after ruling out other causes.
• **Laboratory Studies**:
    ◦ **Inflammatory Markers**: 
        ▪ **ESR and CRP** (correlate with disease activity but are non-specific).
    ◦ **Serology**:
        ▪ **RF Negative, Anti-CCP Negative** (key for "seronegative" classification).
    ◦ **CBC**:
        ▪ May show **normocytic anemia** of chronic disease or iron deficiency anemia from GI blood loss.
        ▪ **Thrombocytosis** is common during flares.
    ◦ **Genetic Testing**:
        ▪ **HLA-B27** (supportive of axial disease, but not required for diagnosis).
• **Imaging**:
    ◦ **X-rays (Sacroiliac Joints & Spine)**:
        ▪ May be normal early.
        ▪ Later findings include **sacroiliitis** (sclerosis, joint space narrowing, erosions, and eventual fusion/ankylosis).
        ▪ In the spine, look for vertebral body squaring and **syndesmophytes** (bony growths), which can lead to a "**bamboo spine**" appearance in advanced disease.
    ◦ **MRI (Sacroiliac Joints & Spine)**:
        ▪ The most sensitive imaging for detecting *early* inflammation.
        ▪ Will show **bone marrow edema** (active sacroiliitis) on T2/STIR sequences long before X-ray changes are visible.
• **Procedures**:
    ◦ **Arthrocentesis**:
        ▪ Done to rule out **septic** or **crystal-induced arthritis** if a single joint is very inflamed.
        ▪ Synovial fluid will be **inflammatory** (WBC 2,000-50,000/mm3), but with a negative gram stain and culture.
    ◦ **Colonoscopy with Biopsy**:
        ▪ Confirms the diagnosis and activity of underlying IBD.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is highly variable.
• **Peripheral arthritis** tends to have a better prognosis, often remitting with control of the underlying IBD.
• **Axial disease** can be progressive and lead to significant long-term disability if not treated aggressively.
• The advent of biologic therapies (especially **TNF-alpha inhibitors**) has dramatically improved the prognosis and quality of life for patients with moderate-to-severe disease.

sections.overview:
• **Rotator Cuff Tendinopathy** is a spectrum of pathologies affecting the tendons of the rotator cuff muscles, ranging from inflammation and tendinosis (degeneration) to partial- or full-thickness tears.
• It is the most common cause of shoulder pain in adults.
• The condition is often associated with **subacromial impingement**, where the rotator cuff tendons are compressed in the space between the humeral head and the acromion.
• The term "tendinitis" is often a misnomer, as the underlying pathology is typically degenerative (**tendinosis**) rather than purely inflammatory.
• The rotator cuff consists of four muscles and their tendons (**SITS**):
    ◦ **S**upraspinatus (**most commonly affected**)
    ◦ **I**nfraspinatus
    ◦ **T**eres Minor
    ◦ **S**ubscapularis
sections.etiology:
• The pathophysiology is multifactorial, involving both intrinsic and extrinsic factors leading to tendon degeneration and failure.
• **Intrinsic Factors** (Related to the tendon itself):
    ◦ **Degenerative Changes:** Age-related changes lead to disorganized collagen fibers, decreased cellularity, and micro-tears.
    ◦ **Poor Vascularity:** The distal portion of the supraspinatus tendon has a **"critical zone"** of relative hypovascularity, predisposing it to injury and impaired healing.
• **Extrinsic Factors** (External compression/loading):
    ◦ **Subacromial Impingement:** Compression of the rotator cuff tendons, long head of the biceps, and subacromial bursa against the undersurface of the acromion.
        ▪ **Primary Impingement:** Caused by anatomical narrowing of the subacromial space (e.g., bone spurs, Type II or III acromion).
        ▪ **Secondary Impingement:** Caused by functional narrowing due to glenohumeral instability, scapular dyskinesis, or muscular imbalance, leading to abnormal humeral head positioning.
    ◦ **Repetitive Microtrauma:** Overhead activities (e.g., throwing, swimming, painting) cause repeated stress on the tendons, exceeding their capacity to repair.
• The process typically involves a cycle of injury, inflammation, and failed healing, leading to chronic tendinosis, fiber tearing, and potential progression to a full-thickness tear.
sections.epidemiology:
• Most common cause of shoulder pain, accounting for >50% of cases.
• Prevalence increases significantly with age, most common in individuals >40 years old.
• Affects up to 25% of the general population over 60.
• Common in athletes and laborers who perform repetitive overhead motions.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient, typically middle-aged or older, presents with an **insidious onset** of shoulder pain that has progressively worsened over weeks to months.
• The pain is exacerbated by **reaching overhead or behind the back**.
• Patients often report difficulty with activities of daily living such as combing their hair, putting on a coat, or reaching for an item on a high shelf.
• A key feature is **nocturnal pain**, especially when lying on the affected shoulder.
• There may be a history of a minor precipitating injury or no specific event at all.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primarily a clinical diagnosis** based on history and physical exam.
• **X-ray (AP, Scapular-Y, Axillary views):**
    ◦ **First-line imaging.**
    ◦ Mainly used to rule out other pathologies (e.g., glenohumeral arthritis, fracture, calcific tendinitis).
    ◦ May show findings suggestive of chronic impingement: **acromial spurring**, cystic changes in the greater tuberosity, or a **high-riding humeral head** (indicates a large, chronic tear).
• **Musculoskeletal Ultrasound (MSK US):**
    ◦ Excellent for visualizing soft tissues in real-time.
    ◦ Can identify tendinosis, bursitis, and partial- or full-thickness tears.
    ◦ Highly operator-dependent but cost-effective and non-invasive.
• **MRI:**
    ◦ **Gold standard for soft tissue evaluation.**
    ◦ Provides detailed images of tendons, muscles, and ligaments.
    ◦ Used to confirm the diagnosis, determine the size and characteristics of a tear, and assess for muscle atrophy/fatty infiltration prior to surgical planning.
    ◦ Typically reserved for cases that fail conservative management or when a full-thickness tear is suspected in an active individual.
sections.prognosis:
• Generally good.
• Over 75% of patients with impingement syndrome/tendinopathy respond well to conservative management, primarily physical therapy.
• Recovery can be slow, often taking several months.
• Prognosis is worse for patients with large tears, significant muscle atrophy, older age, and poor compliance with rehabilitation.

sections.overview:
• The rotator cuff is a group of four muscles and their associated tendons (the SITS muscles) that stabilize the glenohumeral (shoulder) joint.
• A rotator cuff tear is a common injury involving the rupture of one or more of these tendons.
    ◦ Tears can be **acute** (traumatic) or **chronic** (degenerative) and are classified as **partial-thickness** or **full-thickness**.
    ◦ The **supraspinatus** tendon is the most frequently torn due to its location and function.
• **SITS Muscles & Primary Functions**:
    ◦ **S**upraspinatus: Abduction (initiates first 15 degrees)
    ◦ **I**nfraspinatus: External Rotation
    ◦ **T**eres Minor: External Rotation
    ◦ **S**ubscapularis: Internal Rotation
sections.etiology:
• The pathophysiology depends on the type of tear:
    ◦ **Chronic Degenerative Tears (Most Common)**:
        ▪ **Mechanism**: Repetitive microtrauma, overuse, and age-related tendon degeneration.
        ▪ **Subacromial Impingement**: The supraspinatus tendon passes through the subacromial space. Repetitive overhead motion can cause the tendon to be "pinched" between the acromion and the humeral head, leading to inflammation (tendinitis) and eventual tearing.
        ▪ **Hypovascularity**: The distal portion of the supraspinatus tendon (the "critical zone") has a relatively poor blood supply, impairing its ability to heal from minor injuries and leading to progressive degeneration.
        ▪ **Extrinsic Factors**: **Bone spurs** on the undersurface of the acromion can abrade the tendon.
    ◦ **Acute Traumatic Tears**:
        ▪ **Mechanism**: Occurs from a specific injury.
        ▪ Common causes include a **fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH)**, a sudden pulling motion (e.g., lifting a heavy object), or a **shoulder dislocation**.
        ▪ More common in younger, active individuals.
sections.epidemiology:
• Highly prevalent, with frequency increasing significantly with age.
• Present in ~20% of the general population, rising to >50% in individuals over age 80.
• Many tears, especially in the elderly, can be asymptomatic.
• Most common cause of shoulder pain and disability in adults.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with shoulder pain and weakness. The history is key to differentiating an acute vs. chronic etiology.
• **Chronic Tear**:
    ◦ An older patient (>50) with an insidious onset of anterolateral shoulder pain, worse with overhead activities and at night.
    ◦ They may not recall a specific injury.
• **Acute Tear**:
    ◦ A younger patient who experienced a specific traumatic event, followed immediately by severe pain, a **"popping" sensation**, and significant weakness.
sections.diagnostics:
• **X-rays (AP, Scapular "Y", Axillary views)**:
    ◦ **Purpose**: Initial imaging to rule out other pathology (fractures, arthritis, calcific tendinitis).
    ◦ **Findings in RC Tear**: Often normal. In large, chronic tears, may show a **high-riding humeral head** (superior migration of the humerus due to loss of the cuff's depressor effect) or **bone spurs**.
• **MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging)**:
    ◦ **Gold Standard** for diagnosis.
    ◦ Provides detailed visualization of soft tissues: confirms the presence of a tear, defines its size (partial vs. full), location, degree of tendon retraction, and assesses muscle quality (**fatty atrophy**).
• **Musculoskeletal Ultrasound (MSK US)**:
    ◦ Excellent alternative to MRI; less expensive and allows for dynamic assessment.
    ◦ Highly operator-dependent. Can accurately identify full-thickness tears.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is generally good with appropriate treatment.
• Many patients with chronic tears respond well to conservative management.
• Surgical repair has high success rates for pain relief and functional improvement.
• **Negative prognostic factors**:
    ◦ Large/massive tear size, advanced age, poor tissue quality (**fatty infiltration** of muscle seen on MRI), smoking, and poor compliance with post-operative rehabilitation.

sections.overview:
• **Adhesive Capsulitis** ("**frozen shoulder**") is a clinical syndrome characterized by painful, gradual loss of both **active and passive glenohumeral joint range of motion**.
    ◦ Results from inflammation, fibrosis, and contracture of the joint capsule.
    ◦ Typically follows a predictable course of three overlapping stages:
        ▪ **Painful "freezing" stage**
        ▪ **Stiff "frozen" stage**
        ▪ **"Thawing" resolution stage**
sections.etiology:
• The exact pathophysiology is not fully understood but involves an initial inflammatory synovitis followed by a fibrotic response.
    ◦ **Etiology**
        ▪ **Primary (Idiopathic)**: Occurs without any known cause or preceding trauma; this is the most common form.
        ▪ **Secondary**: Develops as a result of a known cause.
            ▪ **Intrinsic**: Related to the shoulder itself (e.g., **rotator cuff tendinopathy**, biceps tendonitis, fracture).
            ▪ **Extrinsic**: Unrelated to the shoulder structure (e.g., CVA, MI, cervical radiculopathy, breast surgery).
            ▪ **Systemic**: Associated with systemic diseases (e.g., **Diabetes Mellitus**, thyroid disorders, autoimmune disease).
    ◦ **Pathophysiology**
        ▪ **Inflammatory Phase**: An initial hypervascular synovitis develops, with proliferation of fibroblasts and myofibroblasts promoted by pro-inflammatory cytokines.
        ▪ **Fibrotic Phase**: Cells deposit excessive type I and type III collagen, leading to a thickened, fibrotic, and contracted joint capsule.
        ▪ **Key Structures Involved**: Contracture is most prominent in the **rotator interval**, **coracohumeral ligament**, and the **axillary recess** of the inferior glenohumeral ligament, physically restricting joint volume and movement.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects 2-5% of the general population.
• **Age**: Most common between the ages of 40 and 65.
• **Gender**: **Females > Males**.
• **Bilateral Involvement**: Occurs in up to 20-30% of patients, though rarely simultaneously.
• **Recurrence**: Recurrence in the same shoulder is rare.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient, typically a female between 40-65 years old, presents with an **insidious onset** of unilateral shoulder pain that has progressed to significant stiffness.
    ◦ No specific traumatic event is reported.
    ◦ Primary complaint is a **functional deficit**:
        ▪ Difficulty with overhead activities.
        ▪ Difficulty reaching behind their back (e.g., fastening a bra).
        ▪ Difficulty reaching out to the side.
    ◦ **Night pain** is a prominent feature, often disrupting sleep.
sections.diagnostics:
• Adhesive capsulitis is primarily a **clinical diagnosis** based on history and physical exam.
    ◦ **Imaging**
        ▪ **X-rays** (AP, Scapular Y, Axillary views)
            ▪ Usually normal.
            ▪ Main utility is to **rule out other pathologies** such as glenohumeral arthritis, calcific tendonitis, avascular necrosis, or fracture.
            ▪ **Osteopenia** may be seen due to disuse.
        ▪ **MRI / MR Arthrography**
            ▪ Not required for diagnosis but can be used in equivocal cases.
            ▪ **MRI findings**: Thickening of the joint capsule (>4mm) and coracohumeral ligament, with enhancement in the axillary pouch and rotator interval.
            ▪ **MR Arthrography (most specific test)**: Demonstrates a **reduced joint volume** and loss of the axillary recess. The joint will accept less than 10-12 mL of contrast.
        ▪ **Musculoskeletal Ultrasound (MSK US)**
            ▪ Can show thickening of the coracohumeral ligament and hypoechoic tissue in the rotator interval, suggestive of synovitis.
    ◦ **Labs**
        ▪ Not indicated unless ruling out a systemic cause (e.g., TSH for thyroid disease, HbA1c for diabetes).
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is generally good, as the condition is **self-limiting** in most individuals.
    ◦ Over 90% of patients experience significant improvement with conservative management alone.
    ◦ Full recovery can take **1 to 3 years**.
    ◦ Some patients may have a mild but permanent loss of end-range motion that is not functionally limiting.
    ◦ Patients with **diabetes** often have a more severe presentation and a longer, less complete recovery.

sections.overview:
• Inflammation of the subacromial bursa, a fluid-filled sac located between the acromion of the scapula and the rotator cuff tendons.
• Primary function is to reduce friction and allow smooth gliding of the rotator cuff tendons under the acromion during arm elevation.
• A leading cause of shoulder pain and a key component of the broader clinical entity known as **Subacromial Impingement Syndrome**.
• Often coexists with rotator cuff tendinopathy.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Repetitive Microtrauma (Most Common)**: Overuse from repetitive overhead activities (e.g., swimming, throwing, painting, carpentry) leads to chronic irritation and inflammation.
    ◦ **Acute Trauma**: A direct blow to the shoulder or a fall onto an outstretched hand (**FOOSH**) can cause acute bursal inflammation.
    ◦ **Anatomic Factors**: A narrowed subacromial space due to acromial morphology (e.g., a "hooked" **Type III acromion**) or bone spurs can mechanically irritate the bursa.
    ◦ **Associated Conditions**: Often occurs secondary to rotator cuff tendinopathy, scapular dyskinesis, or glenohumeral instability.
    ◦ **Systemic Inflammatory Disease**: Less common causes include rheumatoid arthritis, gout, and pseudogout.
    ◦ **Septic Bursitis**: Rare, but can occur from direct inoculation (e.g., injection) or hematogenous spread.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The core mechanism is **impingement**.
    ◦ The subacromial bursa becomes inflamed, edematous, and thickened, increasing its volume within the fixed subacromial space.
    ◦ During arm abduction or forward flexion, the inflamed bursa and adjacent rotator cuff tendons are compressed between the humeral head and the overlying coracoacromial arch.
    ◦ This compression further exacerbates the inflammation and causes pain, creating a vicious cycle.
sections.epidemiology:
• One of the most common causes of shoulder pain presenting to primary care and orthopedic clinics.
• Peak incidence occurs in individuals aged **40-60**.
• No significant gender predilection, but incidence is higher in populations engaged in **overhead sports or occupations**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The typical patient is a middle-aged individual (e.g., a 45-year-old contractor) who presents with an insidious onset of **anterolateral shoulder pain**.
• The pain is described as a dull ache that is worse with specific movements, particularly **reaching overhead** or behind the back.
• The patient often reports **difficulty sleeping** on the affected side due to pain.
• There is usually no history of acute, specific trauma.
sections.diagnostics:
• Subacromial bursitis is primarily a **clinical diagnosis**; imaging is used to rule out other pathology or in cases refractory to conservative care.
• **X-rays (AP, Scapular-Y, Axillary views)**
    ◦ **Purpose**: To evaluate for fractures, **calcific tendinitis**, glenohumeral arthritis, or bony abnormalities.
    ◦ **Potential Findings**: May reveal a **Type III (hooked) acromion**, subacromial spurring, or a **high-riding humeral head** (suggestive of a chronic, massive rotator cuff tear). Often normal.
• **Musculoskeletal Ultrasound (MSK US)**
    ◦ **Value**: Excellent, cost-effective, dynamic imaging modality for soft tissues.
    ◦ **Findings**: Can show a distended, fluid-filled **subacromial bursa**, bursal thickening, and can assess the integrity of the rotator cuff tendons.
• **MRI**
    ◦ **Value**: **Gold standard** for detailed evaluation of soft tissues.
    ◦ **Indications**: Reserved for cases that fail conservative treatment, or when a high suspicion for a **full-thickness rotator cuff tear** exists.
    ◦ **Findings**: High **T2 signal** (fluid) within the subacromial-subdeltoid bursa, bursal thickening, and definitive assessment of rotator cuff tendons and muscles.
• **Diagnostic Injection**
    ◦ Subacromial injection of a local anesthetic (e.g., lidocaine).
    ◦ Significant pain relief and improved active elevation after the injection strongly supports the diagnosis of subacromial impingement/bursitis.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**.
• The vast majority (>80%) of patients experience significant improvement or complete resolution of symptoms with dedicated conservative management, particularly physical therapy.
• For those who fail conservative care, surgical outcomes are generally good to excellent.

sections.overview:
• Lateral epicondylitis, commonly known as "Tennis Elbow," is an overuse tendinopathy of the common extensor tendon at its origin on the lateral epicondyle of the humerus.
• Despite the "-itis" suffix, the underlying pathology is primarily degenerative (tendinosis) rather than inflammatory, involving angiofibroblastic hyperplasia.
• The **Extensor Carpi Radialis Brevis (ECRB)** tendon is the most commonly affected structure.
• It is the most common cause of elbow pain in adults.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology:**
    ◦ Caused by repetitive microtrauma from overuse of the wrist extensor and forearm supinator muscles.
    ◦ This leads to micro-tears in the common extensor tendon, most notably the ECRB.
    ◦ Activities involving repetitive wrist extension against resistance are the primary cause (e.g., tennis backhand, using a screwdriver, manual labor).
• **Pathophysiology:**
    ◦ The condition is a form of **tendinosis**, a degenerative process, not a true inflammatory tendinitis.
    ◦ Repetitive stress leads to micro-tears and a failed healing response.
    ◦ Histologically, this is characterized by **angiofibroblastic hyperplasia**: a disorganized mix of immature collagen, vascular elements (neovascularization), and fibroblasts.
    ◦ There is a notable absence of acute inflammatory cells (neutrophils, macrophages).
    ◦ The ECRB tendon is particularly vulnerable due to its position and the high tensile forces it endures during wrist extension.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** Affects 1-3% of the general population annually.
• **Age:** Most common between ages 35 and 50.
• **Gender:** Affects males and females equally.
• **Limb:** Occurs most often in the dominant arm.
• **Association:** Despite the name "Tennis Elbow," fewer than 5% of cases are related to tennis. Most are occupational.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Occupational:** Manual labor involving repetitive forearm pronation/supination and wrist extension (e.g., carpenters, plumbers, painters, chefs).
• **Recreational:** Racquet sports (tennis, squash, badminton), especially with poor technique (e.g., leading with the wrist on a backhand shot), improper equipment, or sudden increase in activity.
• **Biomechanical:** Poor technique, weak forearm/shoulder muscles.
• **Other:** Smoking, obesity.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with an **insidious onset** of aching pain over the lateral aspect of the elbow.
• The pain is localized initially but may radiate down the extensor surface of the forearm.
• Patients complain of weakness, particularly in grip strength, often described as "dropping things" (e.g., a coffee cup or milk jug).
• Symptoms are exacerbated by activities that involve wrist extension or gripping.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ **Primary Symptom:** Pain localized to the lateral epicondyle.
    ◦ Pain worsens with activity (gripping, lifting, shaking hands, turning a doorknob).
    ◦ Pain radiation down the posterior forearm.
    ◦ Decreased grip strength, often limited by pain.
    ◦ Morning stiffness around the elbow.
    ◦ No systemic symptoms (fever, chills, malaise).
• **Inspection:** Usually normal; may have mild, localized swelling.
• **Palpation:**
    ◦ **Hallmark sign:** Point tenderness just distal and anterior to the lateral epicondyle (over the ECRB origin).
• **Range of Motion (ROM):**
    ◦ Active and passive ROM of the elbow are typically full and painless.
    ◦ Pain may be reproduced at the end-range of wrist flexion with the elbow in full extension (stretches the extensors).
• **Strength:**
    ◦ Decreased grip strength on the affected side.
    ◦ Pain with **resisted wrist extension**, especially with the elbow extended and forearm pronated.
• **Special Tests (Provocative Maneuvers):**
    ◦ **Cozen's Test:** The examiner stabilizes the patient's elbow while the patient makes a fist, pronates the forearm, and radially deviates and extends the wrist against the examiner's resistance. A positive test is pain at the lateral epicondyle.
    ◦ **Mill's Test:** The examiner passively pronates the patient's forearm, flexes the wrist, and extends the elbow. A positive test is pain at the lateral epicondyle.
    ◦ **"Chair Lift" Test:** The patient is asked to lift a chair with the forearm pronated and elbow extended. A positive test is pain at the lateral epicondyle.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primarily a clinical diagnosis.** History and physical exam are usually sufficient.
• **Imaging is not routinely required** but may be used to rule out other pathology in atypical or refractory cases.
• **X-rays:** Usually normal. May show calcification in the common extensor tendon in chronic cases (>25%) or rule out intra-articular pathology (e.g., arthritis, loose bodies).
• **Musculoskeletal Ultrasound (MSK US):** Can show tendon thickening, hypoechoic areas (degeneration), fibrillar disruption (tears), and neovascularization on Doppler imaging. Highly operator-dependent.
• **MRI:** Most sensitive and specific imaging modality. Can show increased signal intensity and thickening of the ECRB tendon. Reserved for cases where the diagnosis is unclear or for pre-operative planning.
sections.treatment:
• **Conservative management is the mainstay and is successful in >90% of cases.**
• **Phase 1: Pain/Inflammation Control**
    ◦ **Activity Modification:** Relative rest from aggravating activities.
    ◦ **NSAIDs:** Oral or topical for short-term pain relief.
    ◦ **Ice:** Apply for 15 minutes after activity.
    ◦ **Counterforce Brace ("Tennis Elbow Strap"):** Worn just distal to the elbow to dissipate forces on the tendon origin.
• **Phase 2: Rehabilitation**
    ◦ **Physical/Occupational Therapy:** The cornerstone of treatment.
    ◦ **Stretching:** Wrist extensor and flexor stretches.
    ◦ **Strengthening:** **Eccentric strengthening** of the wrist extensors is the most evidence-based exercise.
• **Phase 3: Interventional (for refractory cases)**
    ◦ **Corticosteroid Injection:** Provides good short-term (<6 weeks) pain relief but is associated with poorer long-term outcomes and a higher recurrence rate. Risk of tendon rupture and skin atrophy.
    ◦ **Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) Injection:** Autologous blood product injected to stimulate healing. Evidence is emerging but still mixed.
• **Surgical Management**
    ◦ Reserved for patients who have failed at least 6-12 months of comprehensive conservative treatment.
    ◦ Involves debridement of the pathologic angiofibroblastic tissue from the ECRB tendon origin, followed by tendon repair. Can be performed as an open, percutaneous, or arthroscopic procedure.
sections.management:
• **Patient Education:** Crucial for success. Explain that it is an overuse injury and recovery is often slow (6-12 months). Emphasize the importance of activity modification and adherence to the physical therapy regimen.
• **Ergonomics:** Advise on proper technique for sports and modifications for occupational tasks to reduce strain on the extensors.
• **Follow-up:** Monitor progress every 4-6 weeks. If no improvement after 3 months of conservative therapy, consider imaging or referral.
sections.complications:
• Chronic pain and functional limitation.
• Recurrence of symptoms if underlying risk factors are not addressed.
• **Iatrogenic:**
    ◦ Tendon rupture or skin depigmentation/atrophy following corticosteroid injections.
    ◦ Post-surgical complications (infection, nerve injury, stiffness).
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent.
• 80-95% of patients recover with conservative, non-operative management.
• Full recovery can be slow and may take up to 12-18 months.
• Surgical intervention has a success rate of approximately 85-90% for well-selected patients.

sections.overview: • Medial epicondylitis, commonly known as **"Golfer's Elbow,"** is an overuse tendinopathy affecting the common flexor tendon at its origin on the medial epicondyle of the humerus, characterized by pain and tenderness exacerbated by **resisted wrist flexion** and **forearm pronation**; it is a condition of **tendinosis** (degenerative changes) rather than acute inflammation (tendinitis).
sections.etiology:
• **Mechanism**: Overuse and repetitive microtrauma to the common flexor tendon origin, leading to a failed healing response.
• **Pathology**: Characterized by **angiofibroblastic hyperplasia**, a degenerative process involving disorganized collagen, fibroblast proliferation, and vascular hyperplasia; it is a **tendinosis**, not a true inflammatory tendinitis, as inflammatory cells are typically absent.
• **Affected Muscles (Common Flexor Tendon)**: The primary muscles involved, in order of frequency, are:
    ◦ **Pronator Teres**
    ◦ **Flexor Carpi Radialis (FCR)**
    ◦ Palmaris Longus
    ◦ Flexor Digitorum Superficialis
    ◦ Flexor Carpi Ulnaris (FCU)
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Less common than lateral epicondylitis (Tennis Elbow), with a prevalence of <1% in the general population.
• **Age**: Most common in individuals between **40 and 60 years old**.
• **Sex**: Affects males and females equally.
• **Limb Dominance**: Typically affects the **dominant arm**.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Occupational**: Carpenters, plumbers, construction workers, butchers, chefs (any job requiring forceful, repetitive wrist/finger flexion and pronation).
• **Sports**: Golf, baseball (pitching), tennis (forehand strokes), bowling, weightlifting, javelin throwing.
• **Other**: **Obesity**, **smoking**, and **diabetes** are associated with an increased risk of tendinopathies.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • A typical patient is a 45-year-old who presents with a gradual onset of aching pain on the inner side of their dominant elbow over several weeks. The pain is worse after activities like yard work (e.g., using a screwdriver, hammering) or playing a round of golf. They may report a **weak grip** and difficulty with tasks like turning a doorknob, shaking hands, or picking up a gallon of milk. The pain is localized and does not typically radiate significantly or cause paresthesias.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ **Pain**: Aching pain, localized to the medial epicondyle and proximal forearm.
    ◦ **Onset**: Insidious and gradual.
    ◦ **Aggravating Factors**: Activities requiring **wrist flexion** and **pronation** (e.g., gripping, lifting with palm up, throwing a ball, shaking hands).
    ◦ **Weakness**: Subjective weakness in grip strength.
    ◦ **Stiffness**: Mild elbow stiffness, especially in the morning.
    ◦ **Radiation**: Pain may radiate distally into the forearm but typically does not follow a specific nerve dermatome.
    ◦ **Note**: The **absence of numbness or tingling** is crucial for differentiating from nerve entrapment syndromes.
• **Physical Exam Findings**
    ◦ **Inspection**: Usually normal; no visible erythema, swelling, or deformity.
    ◦ **Palpation**: **Point tenderness** directly over the medial epicondyle, slightly distal and anterior to its most prominent point.
    ◦ **Range of Motion (ROM)**: Typically full and painless active and passive ROM of the elbow. Pain may be elicited at the end-range of wrist extension with the elbow extended.
    ◦ **Strength Testing**: Pain reproduced with **resisted wrist flexion** and **resisted forearm pronation**.
    ◦ **Special Tests**
        ▪ **Golfer's Elbow Test (Provocative Maneuver)**: The examiner palpates the medial epicondyle while passively supinating the forearm and extending the elbow and wrist. A positive test is the reproduction of sharp pain at the medial epicondyle.
        ▪ **Alternate Method**: The patient is asked to make a fist and flex their wrist against resistance with the elbow in extension. Pain over the medial epicondyle indicates a positive test.
sections.diagnostics:
• Medial epicondylitis is primarily a **clinical diagnosis**; imaging is not required for initial diagnosis but may be used to rule out other pathology or in cases refractory to conservative treatment.
• **X-rays (AP/Lateral of Elbow)**
    ◦ **Purpose**: To rule out fracture, osteoarthritis, loose bodies, or osteochondritis dissecans.
    ◦ **Findings**: Usually normal. May occasionally show calcification within the common flexor tendon (**calcific tendinopathy**).
• **Musculoskeletal Ultrasound (MSK US)**
    ◦ **Purpose**: To visualize tendon pathology directly and can be used for dynamic assessment.
    ◦ **Findings**: Tendon thickening, hypoechoic changes, intratendinous calcifications, cortical irregularities at the epicondyle, and **neovascularity** on color Doppler.
• **MRI**
    ◦ **Purpose**: Reserved for confirming the diagnosis in atypical cases, evaluating for concomitant ligamentous injury (e.g., UCL tear), or for pre-operative planning.
    ◦ **Findings**: Increased signal intensity and tendon thickening on T1 and T2-weighted images at the common flexor tendon origin.
sections.treatment:
• **Phase 1: Conservative / First-Line**
    ◦ **Activity Modification**: Relative rest from inciting activities.
    ◦ **Pain/Inflammation Control**
        ▪ **Ice**: Apply for 15-20 minutes after activity.
        ▪ **NSAIDs**: Oral (e.g., ibuprofen, naproxen) or topical (e.g., diclofenac gel) for short-term pain relief.
    ◦ **Counterforce Bracing**: A strap worn just distal to the elbow may dissipate forces at the tendon origin.
• **Phase 2: Rehabilitation**
    ◦ **Physical/Occupational Therapy**: The cornerstone of treatment.
        ▪ **Stretching**: Gentle wrist flexor stretching.
        ▪ **Strengthening**: **Eccentric strengthening exercises** are most effective (e.g., controlled lowering of a weight with the wrist). Progress to concentric exercises.
• **Phase 3: Interventions**
    ◦ **Corticosteroid Injection**: Can provide significant short-term (4-6 weeks) pain relief but evidence shows potential for worse long-term outcomes and a higher recurrence rate. Risk of tendon rupture and skin atrophy.
    ◦ **Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) Injection**: An emerging option; evidence is still evolving but shows some promise for refractory cases.
• **Phase 4: Surgical Intervention**
    ◦ **Indication**: Reserved for severe, debilitating symptoms that have failed at least **6-12 months** of comprehensive conservative management.
    ◦ **Procedure**: Open or percutaneous debridement of the angiofibroblastic tissue (**medial epicondylar release**).
sections.management:
• **Patient Education**: Crucial for success. Explain the nature of the overuse injury, the importance of activity modification, and the rationale for eccentric exercises.
• **Ergonomics**: Advise on proper technique for sports and occupational tasks to prevent recurrence.
• **Timeline**: Counsel patients that recovery is often slow, taking several months.
• **Follow-up**: Re-evaluate in 4-6 weeks after initiating conservative therapy to assess progress and adjust the treatment plan.
sections.complications:
• **Chronic Pain and Functional Limitation**: Most common complication if not managed properly.
• **Tendon Rupture**: Rare, but can be a risk with repeated corticosteroid injections.
• **Iatrogenic Ulnar Nerve Injury**: A significant risk during corticosteroid injection or surgery due to the nerve's proximity to the medial epicondyle.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**: Over **90% of cases resolve** with conservative, non-operative treatment.
• **Recovery Time**: Symptoms typically improve over 6-12 months.
• **Recurrence**: Can recur if the patient returns to the inciting activity without proper conditioning and technique modification.

sections.overview:
• De Quervain Tenosynovitis is a stenosing (narrowing) tenosynovitis of the **first dorsal compartment** of the wrist
    ◦ Involves inflammation and thickening of the tendon sheath (extensor retinaculum) that surrounds the **Abductor Pollicis Longus (APL)** and **Extensor Pollicis Brevis (EPB)** tendons
    ◦ This entrapment causes pain and restricted, non-gliding movement of the tendons at the radial styloid
sections.etiology:
• Primarily caused by **repetitive use** and **overuse** of the thumb and wrist, particularly motions involving forceful gripping combined with ulnar deviation
    ◦ **Pathophysiology**:
        ▪ **Microtrauma**: Repetitive gliding of the APL and EPB tendons within the fibro-osseous tunnel of the first dorsal compartment leads to microtrauma
        ▪ **Inflammation & Thickening**: This trauma incites an inflammatory response, causing the synovial sheath and the overlying extensor retinaculum to thicken and become fibrotic
        ▪ **Stenosis**: The thickening narrows the tunnel (stenosis), increasing friction on the tendons
        ▪ **Impaired Gliding**: The tendons can no longer glide smoothly, leading to pain, catching, and further inflammation, creating a vicious cycle
sections.epidemiology:
• Common cause of wrist pain
• Peak Age: Most common in individuals aged **30-50 years**
• Sex: Significantly more common in **females** (4:1 to 6:1 ratio)
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with an **insidious onset** of aching pain on the **radial side of the wrist**, localized near the base of the thumb
    ◦ The pain is often described as constant, dull, and burning
    ◦ Pain is exacerbated by activity and relieved with rest
    ◦ Patients may report difficulty with simple tasks like opening jars, turning a key, or lifting a child
sections.diagnostics:
• De Quervain Tenosynovitis is a **clinical diagnosis**
    ◦ Imaging is typically not required but can be used to rule out other pathology
    ◦ **X-rays**:
        ▪ **Indication**: To rule out bony pathology such as a scaphoid fracture, radial styloid fracture, or carpometacarpal (CMC) joint arthritis
        ▪ **Findings**: Usually normal in De Quervain's
    ◦ **Ultrasound (Musculoskeletal)**:
        ▪ **Indication**: If the diagnosis is uncertain
        ▪ **Findings**: Can confirm the diagnosis by showing thickening of the extensor retinaculum, increased fluid in the tendon sheath, and thickening/edema of the APL and EPB tendons
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is **excellent**
    ◦ The vast majority of patients achieve complete resolution of symptoms with conservative treatment, particularly corticosteroid injections
    ◦ For the small percentage of patients who require surgery, the success rate is very high (>90%)

sections.overview:
• **Plantar fasciitis** is the most common cause of **heel pain** in adults.
    ◦ It is an overuse injury characterized by inflammation and, more chronically, degenerative changes of the **plantar fascia** at its origin on the **medial calcaneal tuberosity**.
    ◦ It is primarily a **clinical diagnosis** based on a classic history and specific physical exam findings.
sections.etiology:
• **Mechanism**: Repetitive microtrauma and tensile overload at the origin of the **plantar fascia** on the calcaneus.
• **Pathology**: Historically termed "fasciitis," it is now understood to be more of a **degenerative fasciosis** or tendinosis, especially in chronic cases. This involves:
    ◦ Collagen fiber disarray and microtears.
    ◦ Thickening of the fascia.
    ◦ **Angiofibroblastic hyperplasia** (abnormal vascular and fibroblast proliferation).
    ◦ A lack of classic inflammatory cells in chronic specimens.
• The plantar fascia is a thick, fibrous aponeurosis that supports the longitudinal arch of the foot. Stress on this structure, particularly during the **"toe-off" phase of gait**, leads to injury at its weakest point: the calcaneal insertion.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects approximately 10% of the US population over their lifetime.
• **Peak Incidence**: Ages 40-60.
• **Populations**: Very common in **runners** and individuals in occupations requiring **prolonged standing** (e.g., teachers, factory workers, healthcare professionals).
sections.riskFactors:
• **Biomechanical/Anatomic**:
    ◦ **Pes Planus (flat feet)**: Causes increased tensile stress on the fascia.
    ◦ **Pes Cavus (high arches)**: A rigid foot that is a poor shock absorber.
    ◦ **Limited Ankle Dorsiflexion**: Often due to a tight **Achilles tendon** or gastrocnemius/soleus complex. This is a very strong and common association.
    ◦ Leg length discrepancy.
    ◦ Overpronation.
• **Lifestyle/Acquired**:
    ◦ **Obesity / High BMI**: Increased axial load on the foot.
    ◦ **Occupational**: Prolonged standing or walking on hard surfaces.
    ◦ **Training Errors**: Sudden increase in running mileage, intensity, or change in running surface.
    ◦ **Inappropriate Footwear**: Worn-out shoes, poor arch support, minimal cushioning.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a patient complaining of **insidious onset of heel pain**.
• The pain is typically localized to the **plantar medial aspect of the heel**.
• A hallmark feature is **post-static dyskinesia**: severe pain with the **first few steps in the morning** or after a period of inactivity.
    ◦ The pain often improves slightly with initial activity as the fascia "warms up" but then worsens with prolonged weight-bearing or at the end of the day.
• **Location**: Inferior heel, typically at the **medial calcaneal tuberosity**.
• **Character**: Sharp, stabbing, "like stepping on a stone or a nail." Can become a dull ache with chronicity.
• **Onset**: Usually gradual/insidious.
• **Timing**:
    ◦ **Worse**: With first steps in the morning ("**first-step pain**"), after periods of rest, walking barefoot, or climbing stairs.
    ◦ **Better**: After a brief period of walking/activity, but then worsens again with prolonged activity.
• **Bilateral vs. Unilateral**: Most commonly unilateral, but can be bilateral in ~30% of cases.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Inspection**: Generally normal. May see subtle swelling, **pes planus**, or **pes cavus**.
• **Palpation**:
    ◦ **Focal point tenderness** at the plantar fascia's insertion on the **medial calcaneal tuberosity**. This is the most consistent and diagnostic finding.
    ◦ Palpation along the entire fascial band may also elicit tenderness.
• **Special Tests**:
    ◦ **Windlass Test**: Passive dorsiflexion of the great toe tenses the plantar fascia. A positive test elicits pain at the fascial insertion.
    ◦ Assess for **limited ankle dorsiflexion** with the knee both extended (gastrocnemius) and flexed (soleus).
• **Neurologic Exam**: Should be normal. Assess for **Tinel's sign** over the tarsal tunnel to rule out nerve entrapment.
• **Gait**: May observe an **antalgic gait** (limping) to offload the affected heel.
sections.diagnostics:
• Primarily a **clinical diagnosis**. Imaging is not typically required for initial diagnosis.
• **Imaging is indicated if**:
    ◦ Diagnosis is uncertain.
    ◦ Symptoms are atypical (e.g., **night pain, neurologic symptoms**).
    ◦ Conservative treatment fails after several months.
• **Radiographs (X-ray)**:
    ◦ **Purpose**: To rule out other pathology (e.g., **calcaneal stress fracture**, bone cyst, arthritis).
    ◦ **Finding**: May show a **calcaneal spur (heel spur)**.
        ▪ **Clinical Pearl**: A heel spur is an **incidental finding** and is **NOT the cause of the pain**. It is a traction spur that forms in response to stress, and many asymptomatic individuals have them.
• **Musculoskeletal Ultrasound (MSK US)**:
    ◦ Can demonstrate **fascial thickening (>4 mm)**, hypoechogenicity, and perifascial fluid.
    ◦ Useful for guiding injections.
• **MRI**:
    ◦ Rarely needed.
    ◦ Used for refractory cases to evaluate for fascial tears, stress fractures, tumors, or nerve entrapment.
sections.treatment:
• Treatment is overwhelmingly conservative and stepwise. Patient education on the prolonged recovery course (6-12 months) is crucial.
• **Phase 1: First-Line / Conservative (Mainstay of Treatment)**
    ◦ **Stretching**:
        ▪ **Plantar fascia-specific stretching**: Towel stretches, rolling the foot over a frozen water bottle or ball.
        ▪ **Achilles tendon/Calf stretching**: Gastroc and soleus stretches. This is critical.
    ◦ **Activity Modification**: Relative rest; decrease running mileage, avoid high-impact activities.
    ◦ **Supportive Measures**:
        ▪ **Footwear**: Well-cushioned shoes with good arch support. Avoid walking barefoot.
        ▪ **Orthotics**: Over-the-counter or custom heel cups and arch supports.
    ◦ **Pain/Inflammation Control**:
        ▪ **Ice**: Apply to the heel for 15-20 minutes after activity.
        ▪ **NSAIDs**: Oral or topical (e.g., ibuprofen, naproxen) for short-term pain relief.
• **Phase 2: If First-Line Fails (after 6-8 weeks)**
    ◦ **Night Splints**: Worn during sleep to maintain the foot in a dorsiflexed position, preventing nocturnal fascial contracture.
    ◦ **Formal Physical Therapy**: Supervised stretching, strengthening, and manual therapy.
    ◦ **Corticosteroid Injections**: Can provide significant but often temporary pain relief.
        ▪ **WARNING**: Carries a risk of **plantar fascia rupture** and **fat pad atrophy**. Use judiciously, often with ultrasound guidance.
• **Phase 3: Refractory Cases (after 6-12 months of failed conservative therapy)**
    ◦ **Extracorporeal Shockwave Therapy (ESWT)**.
    ◦ **Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) Injections**.
    ◦ **Surgery (Last Resort)**: Partial **plantar fasciotomy** (release of the fascia).
sections.management:
• **Patient Education**: Explain that this is a self-limiting condition, but recovery is slow. Compliance with the daily stretching regimen is the most important factor for success.
• **Address Risk Factors**: Counsel on weight loss, appropriate footwear choices, and proper training techniques for athletes.
• **Follow-up**: Re-evaluate in 4-6 weeks to assess response to initial therapy and advance treatment as needed.
sections.complications:
• **Chronic Heel Pain**: Can lead to significant disability and limitation of daily and recreational activities.
• **Altered Gait Mechanics**: Limping can lead to secondary pain in the knee, hip, or back.
• **Plantar Fascia Rupture**:
    ◦ Can occur spontaneously in chronic cases or iatrogenically after a corticosteroid injection.
    ◦ Presents with an acute **"pop" or tearing sensation**, followed by ecchymosis and pain.
• **Fat Pad Atrophy**: A known complication of repeated corticosteroid injections, leading to permanent loss of natural heel cushioning.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**.
• Over 90% of patients experience resolution of symptoms within 12 months with diligent conservative, non-operative management.
• Recurrence is possible if underlying risk factors are not addressed.

sections.overview:
• Trochanteric bursitis is an inflammation of the bursa overlying the greater trochanter of the femur and is a common cause of lateral hip pain.
• The term is often used interchangeably with **Greater Trochanteric Pain Syndrome (GTPS)**, which is a more accurate and inclusive term describing pain on the lateral aspect of the hip, encompassing not just bursitis but also pathology of the gluteus medius and minimus tendons (tendinopathy or tears).
• For clinical purposes, the initial evaluation and management are similar.
sections.etiology:
• **Mechanism**: The condition arises from repetitive friction and compression of the structures overlying the greater trochanter, where the iliotibial (IT) band repeatedly rubs over the trochanteric bursa and gluteal tendons during hip flexion and extension.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Repetitive Microtrauma**: Overuse or altered biomechanics leads to irritation and inflammation of the bursa.
    ◦ **Gluteal Tendinopathy**: More recent evidence suggests that the primary pathology in most GTPS cases is degenerative tendinopathy or tears of the **gluteus medius** and/or **minimus tendons**, with bursitis being a secondary inflammatory response.
    ◦ **Acute Trauma**: A direct fall or blow to the lateral hip can cause acute hemorrhagic bursitis.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects approximately 1.8 per 1000 patients annually and is one of the most common causes of hip pain in the primary care setting.
• **Age**: Most common in middle-aged to elderly individuals (**40-60 years old**).
• **Sex**: Significantly more common in **females** (Female:Male ratio of **4:1**), likely due to a wider pelvis, which increases the Q-angle and tension on the IT band over the greater trochanter.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Anatomical/Biomechanical**:
    ◦ Female sex
    ◦ Leg-length discrepancy
    ◦ Weakness of hip abductors (**gluteus medius**)
    ◦ Iliotibial (**IT**) **band tightness**
    ◦ Scoliosis
    ◦ Gait abnormalities
• **Comorbidities**:
    ◦ Osteoarthritis (hip or knee)
    ◦ Lumbar spine disease (e.g., degenerative disc disease, radiculopathy)
    ◦ Rheumatoid arthritis
• **Activity-Related**:
    ◦ Repetitive activities like running, stair climbing, or cycling
    ◦ Prolonged standing
    ◦ Previous hip surgery
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Chief Complaint**: Insidious onset of chronic, intermittent, aching **pain over the lateral aspect of the hip**.
• **History**:
    ◦ The patient will often point directly to the bony prominence on the side of their hip (the **greater trochanter**).
    ◦ The pain is exacerbated by activities such as walking, running, climbing stairs, or transitioning from a sitting to a standing position.
    ◦ A classic complaint is the **inability to sleep on the affected side** due to direct pressure.
• **Symptoms**:
    ◦ **Pain**:
        ▪ **Location**: Lateral hip, centered over the greater trochanter. May radiate down the lateral thigh towards the knee but typically **does not go past the knee**.
        ▪ **Character**: Aching, burning, or soreness.
        ▪ **Exacerbating Factors**: Direct pressure (lying on side), prolonged sitting, stair climbing, rising from a chair, walking/running.
        ▪ **Relieving Factors**: Rest.
    ◦ **Night Pain**: Very common and a hallmark symptom, especially when lying on the affected side.
    ◦ **Stiffness**: May report some morning stiffness, but less prominent than in true intra-articular hip pathology.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Inspection**: Generally unremarkable. No visible swelling, erythema, or deformity in chronic cases.
• **Palpation**: **Focal point tenderness** directly over the posterior-lateral aspect of the **greater trochanter**. This is the **most specific physical exam finding**.
• **Range of Motion (ROM)**:
    ◦ **Passive ROM**: Usually normal and painless, which helps differentiate it from intra-articular hip pathology (e.g., osteoarthritis).
    ◦ **Active ROM**: Pain may be elicited at the extremes of abduction, adduction, and external/internal rotation due to stretching or contraction of the affected tissues.
• **Strength Testing**:
    ◦ Pain with **resisted hip abduction**.
    ◦ Pain with resisted external rotation.
• **Special Tests**:
    ◦ **Trendelenburg Test**: A positive test (pelvis drops on the unsupported side when standing on the affected leg) suggests weakness of the **gluteus medius** muscle, a key component of GTPS.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primarily a clinical diagnosis** based on history and physical exam findings.
• **Imaging is not routinely required** but may be ordered to rule out other pathology or if the diagnosis is uncertain.
• **X-rays (AP Pelvis, Lateral Hip)**:
    ◦ **Purpose**: To rule out bony abnormalities, fractures, or significant hip/sacroiliac osteoarthritis.
    ◦ **Findings**: Usually normal. May show calcific tendinitis of the gluteal tendons.
• **Ultrasound**:
    ◦ **Purpose**: Can visualize the bursa (thickening, fluid collection) and assess the integrity of the gluteus medius/minimus tendons for tendinopathy or tears. Useful for guiding injections.
• **MRI**:
    ◦ **Purpose**: The most sensitive test for soft tissue pathology. Reserved for cases refractory to conservative treatment or when a significant gluteal tendon tear is suspected.
    ◦ **Findings**: Will show **high signal intensity (edema)** in the bursa on **T2-weighted images**, as well as any associated tendinopathy or tears.
sections.treatment:
• **Conservative management is the mainstay** and is successful in **>90%** of cases.
• **Tier 1: First-Line Conservative Therapy**
    ◦ **Activity Modification**: Avoid aggravating activities (e.g., reduce running, avoid sleeping on the affected side).
    ◦ **Physical Therapy**: Cornerstone of treatment. Focus on:
        ▪ Stretching the **IT band**, tensor fasciae latae (TFL), and hip flexors.
        ▪ Strengthening the **hip abductors (gluteus medius)** and core stabilizers.
    ◦ **NSAIDs**: Oral (e.g., ibuprofen, naproxen) or topical (e.g., diclofenac gel) for pain and inflammation control.
    ◦ **Ice**: Apply for 15-20 minutes after activity.
• **Tier 2: Injections**
    ◦ **Corticosteroid Injection**: Injection into the trochanteric bursa (often under ultrasound guidance for accuracy) can provide significant pain relief. It can be both diagnostic and therapeutic. Relief may be temporary.
• **Tier 3: Surgical Intervention**
    ◦ **Indication**: Reserved for rare, recalcitrant cases that have failed at least **6-12 months** of comprehensive conservative management.
    ◦ **Procedures**: Arthroscopic or open bursectomy, IT band release, and/or repair of gluteal tendon tears if present.
sections.complications:
• **Of the Condition**:
    ◦ Chronic pain
    ◦ Impaired mobility
    ◦ Gait disturbances
    ◦ Sleep disruption
    ◦ Muscle atrophy from disuse
• **Of Treatment**:
    ◦ **NSAIDs**: GI bleeding, renal dysfunction.
    ◦ **Corticosteroid Injections**: Subcutaneous fat atrophy, skin depigmentation, infection (rare), and potential for tendon rupture if injected directly into a tendon.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**. The vast majority of patients experience complete resolution of symptoms with conservative treatment.
• Recurrence is possible, especially if the underlying biomechanical issues (e.g., abductor weakness, poor flexibility) are not adequately addressed through physical therapy.

sections.overview:
• Patellar tendinopathy, commonly known as **"Jumper's Knee,"** is a chronic overuse injury of the patellar tendon
    ◦ It is primarily a condition of **tendinosis** (degenerative changes) rather than tendinitis (acute inflammation)
    ◦ The pathology involves microtears, collagen disorganization, and a failed healing response from repetitive mechanical loading of the knee extensor mechanism
