    ◦ The most common site of involvement is the tendon's insertion at the **inferior pole of the patella**
sections.etiology:
• **Mechanism:** Caused by repetitive, high-load stress on the patellar tendon, particularly during activities that involve jumping, landing, and rapid deceleration (eccentric loading)
• **Pathophysiology:**
    ◦ **Repetitive Microtrauma:** The extensor mechanism (quadriceps muscle and patellar tendon) is repeatedly overloaded, leading to microscopic tears within the tendon fibers
    ◦ **Failed Healing Response:** The rate of injury exceeds the rate of repair, leading to a degenerative state (**tendinosis**) characterized by:
        ▪ **Collagen Disorganization:** Normal, organized Type I collagen is replaced by weaker, disorganized Type III collagen
        ▪ **Angiofibroblastic Hyperplasia:** A pathological increase in tenocytes, vascular tissue (neovascularization), and nerve endings
        ▪ **Mucoid Degeneration:** Accumulation of ground substance
    ◦ **Lack of Inflammation:** Histological studies show a notable absence of inflammatory cells (e.g., neutrophils, macrophages), which is why the term "tendinopathy" is preferred over "tendinitis"
        ▪ The pain is thought to be mediated by the ingrowth of new nerve endings associated with neovascularization
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** Common in athletes, particularly those participating in sports requiring frequent jumping and explosive movements
• **Affected Sports:** High prevalence in volleyball (up to 45% of elite players) and basketball. Also seen in soccer, track and field (high jump, long jump), and weightlifting
• **Demographics:** Most often affects young male athletes between the ages of 15 and 30
sections.riskFactors:
• **Extrinsic (Modifiable):**
    ◦ **Training Volume/Intensity:** High frequency, duration, or intensity of training; sudden increases in training load
    ◦ **Playing Surface:** Training on hard, unforgiving surfaces
    ◦ **Inadequate Footwear**
• **Intrinsic (Non-modifiable or Less Modifiable):**
    ◦ **Decreased Flexibility:** Tightness in quadriceps, hamstrings, and iliotibial (IT) band
    ◦ **Muscle Imbalance/Weakness:** Weakness in the quadriceps, gluteal muscles, or core stabilizers
    ◦ **Anatomic Variants:** Patella alta (high-riding patella), genu varum/valgum, increased Q-angle, leg length discrepancy
    ◦ **Body Weight:** Higher BMI is a contributing factor
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The typical patient is an athlete who presents with a gradual onset of **activity-related anterior knee pain**
    ◦ The pain is well-localized to the inferior pole of the patella
    ◦ The history does not usually involve a specific traumatic event
    ◦ Pain initially occurred only after activity but has progressed to occurring during activity, potentially interfering with performance or activities of daily living (ADLs)
sections.physicalExam:
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ **Pain:**
        ▪ **Location:** Precisely at the **inferior pole of the patella**
        ▪ **Character:** Sharp or burning pain during activity; a dull ache after activity or at rest
        ▪ **Triggers:** Pain is exacerbated by jumping, running, squatting, and climbing/descending stairs
        ▪ **"Warm-up Phenomenon":** Pain may initially decrease during warm-up but returns as activity continues or after cooling down
    ◦ **Stiffness:** Morning stiffness or stiffness after prolonged sitting ("theater sign," though less specific than for PFPS)
    ◦ **Functional Limitation:** Decreased jumping height, inability to train at full intensity
• **Exam Findings**
    ◦ **Inspection:** Often normal. Mild, localized swelling over the inferior patellar pole or thickening of the proximal tendon may be present in chronic cases. Assess for quadriceps atrophy
    ◦ **Palpation:**
        ▪ **Hallmark Sign: Focal point tenderness to deep palpation at the inferior pole of the patella.** The tendon itself may feel thickened compared to the contralateral side
    ◦ **Range of Motion (ROM):**
        ▪ Active and passive ROM are typically full and painless
        ▪ Pain may be elicited with terminal knee flexion (stretching the tendon) or with resisted knee extension
    ◦ **Strength Testing:** Pain and/or weakness with resisted knee extension, especially when the knee is near full extension
    ◦ **Special Tests:**
        ▪ **Decline Squat:** Performing a single-leg squat on a 25-degree decline board is highly provocative and sensitive for patellar tendinopathy. This test increases the load specifically on the patellar tendon
        ▪ **Basset's Sign:** Tenderness is elicited with palpation of the inferior pole of the patella while the knee is in full extension. The tenderness decreases or disappears when the knee is flexed to 90 degrees (as the tendon is no longer under tension)
sections.diagnostics:
• Patellar tendinopathy is primarily a **clinical diagnosis**
    ◦ Imaging is not typically required unless the diagnosis is uncertain, the condition is refractory to conservative treatment, or to rule out other pathology
• **Musculoskeletal Ultrasound (MSK US):**
    ◦ **Imaging modality of choice**
    ◦ Findings include:
        ▪ **Tendon thickening** (proximal patellar tendon >4-6 mm)
        ▪ **Hypoechoic regions** representing disorganized collagen
        ▪ **Neovascularity** seen on color Doppler, which correlates with pain
• **MRI:**
    ◦ More expensive and less specific than US but excellent for evaluating intra-articular structures and ruling out other diagnoses
    ◦ Findings include:
        ▪ **Thickening of the proximal patellar tendon**
        ▪ **Increased signal intensity** on T2-weighted images
• **X-ray (AP, Lateral, Sunrise views):**
    ◦ Usually normal
    ◦ Primarily used to rule out bony pathology such as:
        ▪ **Sinding-Larsen-Johansson Syndrome** (apophysitis of inferior patellar pole in adolescents)
        ▪ **Osgood-Schlatter Disease** (apophysitis of the tibial tubercle in adolescents)
        ▪ Patellar fracture or bony avulsion
    ◦ May show calcification within the tendon in very chronic cases
sections.treatment:
• **Phase 1: Pain and Load Management**
    ◦ **Relative Rest / Activity Modification:** Avoid provocative activities (e.g., jumping, deep squats). Substitute with low-impact cross-training (swimming, cycling with high seat)
    ◦ **Isometric Exercises:** Sustained quadriceps contractions (e.g., wall sits, seated knee extension holds) have been shown to provide significant analgesia
• **Phase 2: Progressive Strengthening**
    ◦ **Eccentric Exercises (Cornerstone):** Focus on the lengthening phase of muscle contraction. **Decline squats** (single-leg or double-leg) are the classic exercise
    ◦ **Heavy Slow Resistance (HSR) Training:** Involves exercises like leg press and squats performed slowly with heavy weight (e.g., 3 seconds concentric, 3 seconds eccentric). Has shown outcomes equal or superior to eccentrics
    ◦ **Kinetic Chain Strengthening:** Address weakness in glutes, hamstrings, and core muscles
• **Phase 3: Return to Sport**
    ◦ **Plyometrics:** Gradual re-introduction of jumping, landing, and cutting maneuvers
    ◦ **Sport-Specific Drills:** Progressively increase intensity and volume to mimic game demands
sections.management:
• **Physical Therapy:** Formal PT is essential to guide the rehabilitation program, ensure proper form, and manage progression
• **Adjunctive Therapies:**
    ◦ **Patellar Tendon Strap (Cho-Pat Strap) or Taping:** Can provide symptomatic relief for some individuals during activity by altering forces on the tendon
    ◦ **Ice/Cryotherapy:** Useful for pain control after exercise
    ◦ **NSAIDs:** Limited utility as this is not an inflammatory process. Can be used for short-term analgesia but should not be the primary treatment
• **Interventional Options (for refractory cases > 6 months):**
    ◦ **Ultrasound-guided Injections:**
        ▪ **Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP):** Some evidence to support use in chronic cases
        ▪ **Sclerosing Agents (Polidocanol):** Aims to obliterate neovessels and associated nerves
    ◦ **Extracorporeal Shockwave Therapy (ESWT):** Can stimulate healing in chronic tendinopathies
• **Surgery:** Last resort for failed conservative management. Involves debridement of the degenerated tendon tissue
• **AVOID:**
    ◦ **Corticosteroid Injections:** **Generally contraindicated.** Associated with a significant risk of collagen necrosis and subsequent **patellar tendon rupture**
sections.complications:
• **Chronic Pain & Functional Disability:** Inability to participate in sports or desired activities
• **Patellar Tendon Rupture:** A rare but devastating complication, often associated with systemic disease or prior corticosteroid injection. Presents with acute pain, inability to extend the knee, and a palpable defect in the tendon
• **Quadriceps Atrophy:** From disuse due to chronic pain
sections.prognosis:
• **Good** with a structured and consistent conservative management program
• Recovery can be prolonged, often taking **3 to 12 months**
• High rate of recurrence if underlying risk factors (e.g., training errors, biomechanical deficits) are not adequately addressed
• Patient education and adherence are critical

sections.overview: • Iliotibial (IT) Band Syndrome is a common overuse injury and a leading cause of lateral knee pain, particularly in runners and cyclists. ◦ It is characterized by inflammation and irritation of the distal portion of the iliotibial band where it crosses the lateral femoral epicondyle. ◦ It is primarily considered an overuse, non-traumatic inflammatory condition.
sections.etiology: • The IT band is a thick band of fascia that runs along the lateral aspect of the thigh, from the iliac crest to Gerdy's tubercle on the proximal anterolateral tibia. ◦ It is formed by the fascia of the tensor fasciae latae (TFL) and gluteus maximus muscles. • Classic Theory (Friction): Historically, ITBS was thought to be caused by repetitive friction of the posterior edge of the IT band sliding over the lateral femoral epicondyle during knee flexion and extension. • Current Theory (Compression): More recent evidence suggests the primary pathology is the compression of a highly innervated layer of fat and loose connective tissue that lies between the IT band and the lateral femoral epicondyle. ◦ This compression is maximal at approximately 30 degrees of knee flexion, which corresponds to the foot-strike phase of running. ◦ Repetitive compression leads to irritation, inflammation, and pain.
sections.epidemiology: • Most common cause of lateral knee pain in runners. • Accounts for up to 12% of all running-related overuse injuries. • Also prevalent in cyclists, hikers, and military personnel. • Incidence is highest in individuals aged 15-50 who participate in repetitive flexion/extension activities of the knee.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • A patient, typically a runner or cyclist, presents with an insidious onset of lateral knee pain. • The history is crucial and often follows a classic pattern: ◦ Pain develops at a predictable and consistent time/distance during an activity (e.g., "always starts at mile 2 of my run"). ◦ Pain is absent at the beginning of the activity but progressively worsens. ◦ Pain resolves shortly after cessation of the activity. ◦ The patient can often point with one finger to the exact location of the pain.
sections.diagnostics: • ITBS is a clinical diagnosis based on history and physical exam. ◦ Imaging is generally not required unless the diagnosis is uncertain or the patient fails to improve with conservative therapy. • X-rays: ◦ Typically normal. ◦ Useful to rule out bony pathology such as stress fracture or lateral compartment osteoarthritis. • MRI: ◦ The modality of choice if imaging is needed. ◦ Findings: May show thickening of the distal IT band, T2 signal hyperintensity (edema) in the space between the IT band and lateral femoral epicondyle, or a fluid collection (bursitis). ◦ Useful for ruling out intra-articular pathology like a lateral meniscal tear. • Ultrasound: ◦ Can also be used to visualize IT band thickening and inflammation/fluid in the underlying bursa.
sections.prognosis: • Excellent with a dedicated conservative treatment plan. • The vast majority (>90%) of patients recover fully with non-operative management. • Recovery typically takes 4-8 weeks. • Recurrence is common if the underlying biomechanical deficits and training errors are not fully addressed.

sections.overview:
• **Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (CTS)** is the most common entrapment neuropathy, resulting from the compression of the **median nerve** as it passes through the carpal tunnel at the wrist.
    ◦ This compression leads to ischemia and demyelination of the nerve, causing a characteristic pattern of pain, numbness, and paresthesias in the median nerve distribution, and can progress to **motor weakness** and **muscle atrophy** if left untreated.
sections.etiology:
• The carpal tunnel is an inelastic anatomical space.
    ◦ The floor and walls are formed by the carpal bones, and the roof is the **transverse carpal ligament (TCL)**.
    ◦ The tunnel contains nine flexor tendons (4 FDS, 4 FDP, 1 FPL) and the median nerve.
• The pathophysiology is based on **increased pressure within the carpal tunnel**, leading to compression of the median nerve.
    ◦ **Increased Pressure**: Caused by any condition that either decreases the size of the tunnel or increases the volume of its contents.
    ◦ **Nerve Ischemia**: Elevated pressure impairs venous outflow, leading to edema and compromised microcirculation of the nerve (vasa nervorum).
    ◦ **Nerve Damage**:
        ▪ **Early**: Ischemia leads to **segmental demyelination**, slowing nerve conduction. This is often reversible.
        ▪ **Late/Chronic**: Persistent compression leads to **Wallerian degeneration (axonal damage)**, resulting in permanent nerve injury, sensory loss, and muscle atrophy.
• **Key Anatomical Point**: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises *proximal* to the carpal tunnel.
    ◦ Therefore, sensation over the central palm is typically **spared** in CTS.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects 3-6% of the general adult population.
• **Gender**: **Women > Men** (approx. 3:1 ratio).
• **Age**: Peak incidence between **40-60 years of age**.
• **Bilateral Involvement**: Common (~60% of cases), though the dominant hand is usually affected first and more severely.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is typically one of **insidious onset** of sensory symptoms in the median nerve distribution, often **worse at night**.
    ◦ Patients frequently report waking from sleep with numbness and pain, which is relieved by shaking their hand (the **"Flick Sign"**).
    ◦ Symptoms are often exacerbated by activities that involve sustained wrist flexion or extension, such as driving, talking on the phone, or typing.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: CTS is primarily a clinical diagnosis based on a characteristic history and physical exam findings.
• **Confirmatory Testing (Gold Standard)**:
    ◦ **Nerve Conduction Studies (NCS)** and **Electromyography (EMG)**:
        ▪ **Purpose**: To confirm the diagnosis, localize the compression to the wrist, assess severity (demyelinating vs. axonal damage), and rule out other neuropathies.
        ▪ **Findings**: NCS will show **slowed sensory and motor conduction velocity** across the carpal tunnel. EMG can show signs of **denervation** in thenar muscles in severe cases.
        ▪ **Indication**: Often required before surgical intervention or when the diagnosis is uncertain.
• **Imaging**:
    ◦ **Ultrasound**: Can be used to visualize the median nerve, showing swelling proximal to the tunnel and flattening within the tunnel. Can also identify structural causes like cysts. It is becoming a first-line imaging modality.
    ◦ **X-ray**: Not useful for diagnosing CTS itself, but can identify underlying bony abnormalities like fractures or severe arthritis.
    ◦ **MRI**: Rarely indicated. Reserved for cases where a tumor or mass is suspected.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is generally **excellent** with timely diagnosis and appropriate treatment.
• Mild cases often respond well to conservative therapy, especially splinting.
• Surgical release has a **high success rate (>90%)** for relieving pain and paresthesias.
• Recovery of motor function and sensation is less predictable if significant atrophy or axonal damage was present pre-operatively.

sections.overview:
• Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow, commonly known as **Cubital Tunnel Syndrome**, is the second most common compressive neuropathy of the upper extremity after carpal tunnel syndrome.
• It involves the compression or irritation of the ulnar nerve as it passes through the cubital tunnel, a narrow passageway on the medial side of the elbow.
    ◦ This compression leads to **sensory and motor deficits** in the ulnar nerve distribution of the forearm and hand.
sections.etiology:
• The ulnar nerve is vulnerable to compression at the elbow as it passes posterior to the medial epicondyle through the cubital tunnel.
    ◦ The "roof" of this tunnel is formed by the arcuate ligament of Osborne (also called the cubital tunnel retinaculum), which connects the two heads of the flexor carpi ulnaris (FCU) muscle.
• **Mechanisms of Injury:**
    ◦ **Direct Compression:** Prolonged or repetitive direct pressure on the nerve (e.g., resting elbows on a hard surface, "office chair neuropathy").
    ◦ **Traction/Stretching:** Repetitive or sustained elbow flexion (e.g., talking on the phone, sleeping with arms bent) increases tension on the nerve and decreases the volume of the tunnel.
    ◦ **Anatomic Variations:**
        ▪ **Subluxation/Dislocation** of the ulnar nerve over the medial epicondyle during flexion.
        ▪ Presence of an **anconeus epitrochlearis** muscle (an anomalous muscle).
        ▪ Bony abnormalities (osteophytes, **cubitus valgus deformity** from an old fracture).
    ◦ **Systemic Factors:** Conditions like diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, and hypothyroidism can make the nerve more susceptible to compression.
    ◦ **Trauma:** Direct blow, fracture of the medial epicondyle or distal humerus.
    ◦ **Mass Lesions:** Ganglion cysts, tumors, or synovitis compressing the nerve.
• **Pathophysiology:**
    ◦ Chronic compression leads to localized ischemia, inflammation, **demyelination**, and if severe/prolonged, can progress to **axonal loss** and irreversible muscle atrophy.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence:** Approximately 25 per 100,000 person-years.
• **Demographics:** More common in males than females.
    ◦ Can occur at any age but peaks in middle age.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with a **gradual onset** of neurologic symptoms in the ulnar nerve distribution.
• They may complain of "falling asleep" of the **4th and 5th fingers**, particularly at night or when holding the elbow in a flexed position for a prolonged period.
• As the condition progresses, they may report hand weakness, clumsiness, and difficulty with fine motor tasks like buttoning a shirt or opening a jar.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis:** Diagnosis is primarily based on history and physical exam findings.
• **Electromyography (EMG) and Nerve Conduction Studies (NCS):**
    ◦ **Gold standard** for confirming the diagnosis, localizing the site of compression, and determining severity (demyelination vs. axonal loss).
    ◦ NCS will show **slowing of motor conduction velocity** across the elbow segment (>10 m/s decrease compared to the forearm segment is significant).
    ◦ EMG can show signs of **denervation** (e.g., fibrillations, positive sharp waves) in ulnar-innervated muscles.
• **Imaging:**
    ◦ **X-rays:** Useful to rule out bony pathology such as osteophytes, arthritis, or old fractures.
    ◦ **Ultrasound:** Can visualize the nerve directly to assess for swelling, compression, or subluxation. Can also identify space-occupying lesions like a ganglion cyst.
    ◦ **MRI:** Rarely needed but can be useful for evaluating soft tissue masses or complex anatomy.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for mild cases that respond well to conservative treatment.
• **Good** for patients who undergo surgery before the onset of significant muscle atrophy.
    ◦ Most patients experience relief of sensory symptoms.
• **Fair to Poor** if there is long-standing compression with severe muscle wasting and axonal loss on EMG.
    ◦ Motor recovery is often incomplete in these cases.

sections.overview:
• **Trigger finger**, medically known as stenosing tenosynovitis, is a common hand condition.
    ◦ Characterized by inflammation and thickening of the flexor tendon sheath, most notably at the **A1 pulley**.
    ◦ This thickening creates a size mismatch between the flexor tendon and its sheath, causing the tendon to catch or "trigger" as it attempts to glide through the narrowed pulley during finger flexion and extension.
    ◦ The affected finger may become painfully **locked** in a flexed position.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ The condition is most often **idiopathic**.
    ◦ It can be associated with **repetitive or forceful gripping activities** that cause microtrauma to the tendon and pulley system.
    ◦ Strongly associated with underlying systemic diseases, particularly **Diabetes Mellitus**.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Anatomy**
        ▪ The flexor tendons of the fingers pass through a series of fibrous tunnels, or pulleys, that hold them close to the bone.
        ▪ The **A1 pulley**, located at the level of the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint on the volar (palm) side, is the most commonly affected structure.
    ◦ **Inflammation**
        ▪ Inflammation and subsequent thickening (fibrocartilaginous metaplasia) occur in the **A1 pulley** and/or the flexor tendon itself.
    ◦ **Nodule Formation**
        ▪ The constant friction can lead to the formation of a fusiform nodule on the tendon (**Notta's nodule**).
    ◦ **Mechanical Impingement**
        ▪ The thickened tendon or nodule is too large to pass smoothly through the constricted **A1 pulley**.
    ◦ **Triggering**
        ▪ As the finger is flexed, the nodule passes through the pulley.
        ▪ Upon extension, the nodule gets stuck proximal to the pulley, causing a catching sensation.
        ▪ Forceful extension causes the nodule to "pop" back through the pulley, resulting in the characteristic triggering or locking phenomenon.
        ▪ This creates a vicious cycle of friction, inflammation, and further thickening.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**
    ◦ Lifetime risk is approximately 2-3%, but increases to 10% in individuals with **diabetes**.
• **Age**
    ◦ Most common in the 5th and 6th decades of life (age 40-60).
• **Gender**
    ◦ More common in females (Female:Male ratio of 2:1 to 6:1).
• **Affected Digits**
    ◦ Most commonly affects the **ring finger** and **thumb**, followed by the middle, index, and small fingers.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient, typically a middle-aged female, presents with a gradual onset of pain at the base of a finger on the palmar side.
• They report a sensation of **catching** or **locking**, which is often more pronounced in the **morning**.
• They may need to use their other hand to passively extend the affected digit.
• The history may or may not include a preceding history of overuse or repetitive hand activities.
sections.diagnostics:
• Trigger finger is a **clinical diagnosis**; history and physical exam are sufficient.
• **Imaging is not routinely necessary**.
• **X-rays**
    ◦ May be ordered to rule out bony pathology like fracture or severe arthritis.
    ◦ Will be **normal** in trigger finger.
• **Ultrasound**
    ◦ Can be used to visualize thickening of the **A1 pulley** and inflammation of the flexor tendon (tenosynovitis).
    ◦ Typically reserved for atypical cases.
• **Labs**
    ◦ Not indicated unless there is suspicion of an underlying systemic inflammatory condition (e.g., RA factor, uric acid).
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is **excellent**.
• The vast majority of patients achieve complete resolution of symptoms with treatment, whether through corticosteroid injection or surgical release.
• Recurrence is uncommon after surgical release but can occur after injections, particularly in patients with underlying risk factors like **diabetes**.

sections.overview:
• A **ganglion cyst** is a **benign**, non-cancerous, fluid-filled sac (**pseudocyst**) that arises from a joint capsule or tendon sheath, representing the **most common soft-tissue mass** of the hand and wrist.
    ◦ These cysts are filled with a thick, clear, mucinous (**gelatinous**) fluid.
    ◦ They **lack a true epithelial lining**, which differentiates them from true cysts.
sections.etiology:
• The exact etiology is not fully understood, but the leading theory is **mucoid degeneration** of connective tissue.
    ◦ **Mechanism**: **Repetitive microtrauma** or chronic irritation leads to the degeneration of collagen and connective tissue in the joint capsule, ligaments, or tendon sheath.
    ◦ **One-Way Valve**: This process is thought to create a small tear or defect that acts as a **one-way valve**, allowing synovial fluid to be forced out of the joint or sheath into the surrounding soft tissue.
    ◦ **Fluid Concentration**: The extravasated fluid becomes concentrated, viscous, and gelatinous over time, forming the palpable cyst.
    ◦ **Connection**: The cyst typically remains connected to the underlying joint or tendon sheath via a **"stalk"** or "pedicle."
sections.epidemiology:
• **Most Common**: The most common soft-tissue tumor of the hand.
• **Age**: Peak incidence is between **20-40 years old**.
• **Gender**: More common in **women** (Female:Male ratio 3:1).
sections.riskFactors:
• **Repetitive Use**: Activities involving repetitive wrist/hand motion (e.g., gymnastics, typing, musicians).
• **Prior Trauma**: History of joint injury or sprain.
• **Underlying Joint Disease**: **Osteoarthritis**, ligamentous laxity.
• **Gender**: Female.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient, typically a young adult female, presents with a chief complaint of a **"lump"** on their hand or wrist that has appeared gradually over weeks or months.
    ◦ The lump may **fluctuate in size** and is often asymptomatic, but the patient may have mild associated aching.
• **Common Locations**:
    ◦ **Dorsal Wrist (60-70%)**: Most common site, typically arising from the **scapholunate (SL) ligament**.
    ◦ **Volar Wrist (15-20%)**: Second most common, often near the **radial artery** and arising from the radioscaphoid or scaphotrapezial joint.
    ◦ **Dorsal Foot/Ankle**: Can arise from extensor tendons or joints.
    ◦ **Digital Flexor Tendon Sheath**: Presents as a small, firm, pea-sized nodule at the base of a finger (volar aspect), often near the **A1 pulley**.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Inspection**
    ◦ A smooth, well-demarcated, round or oval mass. Overlying skin is typically normal.
• **Palpation**
    ◦ Firm, rubbery, and tense.
    ◦ Typically non-tender to mildly tender.
    ◦ May be mobile or feel fixed to deeper structures, but is not attached to the overlying skin.
• **Special Test - Transillumination**
    ◦ **Hallmark finding**.
    ◦ The cyst will **glow or "transilluminate"** when a penlight is held against it in a darkened room.
        ▪ This confirms its cystic, fluid-filled nature. A solid mass (e.g., giant cell tumor) will not transilluminate.
• **Neurological Exam**
    ◦ Assess sensation and motor function in the distribution of nearby nerves (e.g., median, ulnar).
    ◦ Check for a **Tinel's sign** over the cyst if nerve compression is suspected.
• **Vascular Exam**
    ◦ For volar wrist ganglia, palpate the radial pulse to assess the cyst's proximity to the **radial artery**.
    ◦ An **Allen test** may be performed.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Diagnosis is usually made based on history and physical exam findings, especially **positive transillumination**.
• **Ultrasound (US)**
    ◦ **First-line imaging** if the diagnosis is uncertain.
    ◦ Confirms the **anechoic (cystic)** nature of the mass.
    ◦ Can differentiate from a solid mass and identify the stalk's origin.
    ◦ Useful for guiding aspiration, especially for volar wrist ganglia near the **radial artery**.
• **MRI**
    ◦ Rarely needed.
    ◦ Used for atypical presentations, suspected intra-articular pathology, or for pre-operative planning to define the cyst's anatomy and its relationship to surrounding neurovascular structures.
• **X-ray**
    ◦ Not useful for visualizing the cyst itself.
    ◦ May be ordered to rule out underlying bony pathology, arthritis, or fractures.
sections.treatment:
• **Observation**
    ◦ Indicated for **asymptomatic** cysts.
    ◦ Inform the patient of the benign nature; up to **50% may resolve spontaneously** over time.
    ◦ Avoid "Bible therapy" (smashing with a heavy object) due to risk of injury.
• **Aspiration**
    ◦ A large-bore needle (e.g., 18-gauge) is used to drain the thick, gelatinous fluid.
    ◦ Often combined with a corticosteroid injection (though evidence for its added benefit is mixed).
    ◦ **High recurrence rate (~50%)**.
    ◦ Aspiration of volar wrist ganglia should be done with extreme caution (or under US guidance) due to proximity to the **radial artery**.
• **Surgical Excision**
    ◦ **Most effective treatment** with the lowest recurrence rate (~5-10%).
    ◦ Indicated for symptomatic cysts that fail conservative management or for cysts causing neurovascular compromise.
    ◦ **Key to success**: Complete excision of the cyst, its stalk, and a small portion of the underlying joint capsule or tendon sheath.
sections.management:
• **Asymptomatic cysts**: Reassure and **observe**. Follow up as needed if symptoms develop.
• **Mildly symptomatic cysts**: Consider temporary wrist **splinting** and activity modification. If persistent, offer **aspiration** as the next step, ensuring the patient understands the high recurrence rate.
• **Symptomatic cysts failing conservative care**: Refer to Hand Surgery or Orthopedics for consideration of **surgical excision**.
sections.complications:
• **From the Cyst**
    ◦ **Nerve compression** (e.g., carpal or Guyon's canal syndrome), vascular compression, pain, weakness, cosmetic deformity.
• **From Aspiration**
    ◦ Infection, bleeding, injury to nerves, tendons, or arteries (especially the **radial artery**).
    ◦ **High rate of recurrence**.
• **From Surgery**
    ◦ Standard surgical risks (infection, scar formation, bleeding), **nerve injury** (especially the sensory branch of the radial nerve), joint stiffness, ligamentous instability, recurrence.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**. Ganglion cysts are **benign** and do not undergo malignant transformation.
    ◦ The primary morbidity is related to local symptoms (pain, nerve compression) and the high rate of recurrence with non-surgical treatment.

sections.overview:
• **Mechanical Low Back Pain (LBP)**, also known as lumbosacral strain or sprain, is pain originating from spinal structures including vertebrae, intervertebral discs, facet joints, ligaments, or muscles of the lumbar spine.
    ◦ It is the **most common cause** of low back pain, accounting for over 90% of cases.
    ◦ Characterized by the **absence of specific underlying pathology** (e.g., infection, fracture, malignancy, or nerve root compression).
    ◦ It is a **diagnosis of exclusion** after **"red flag"** conditions have been ruled out.
sections.etiology:
• Mechanical LBP arises from injury or stress to the musculoskeletal structures of the lumbar spine.
    ◦ **Lumbar Strain/Sprain**: Acute injury to the paraspinal muscles (**strain**) or ligaments (**sprain**).
        ▪ Caused by overuse, improper lifting, or sudden twisting movements.
        ▪ Leads to micro-tears, inflammation, and protective muscle spasms.
    ◦ **Degenerative Disc Disease (DDD)**: An age-related process where intervertebral discs lose hydration and height.
        ▪ Can lead to stress on the facet joints and annular tears in the disc, causing localized pain.
    ◦ **Facet Joint Arthropathy (Spondylosis)**: Degenerative osteoarthritis of the zygapophyseal (**facet**) joints.
        ▪ Often occurs secondary to DDD.
    ◦ **Spondylolisthesis (Degenerative)**: Anterior slippage of one vertebra over another due to facet joint degeneration, **without a fracture of the pars interarticularis**.
• The common pathway involves **inflammation**, **muscle spasm**, and **nociceptive pain signaling** from the affected structures.
    ◦ Pain is typically **"mechanical"** in nature, meaning it is influenced by posture and physical activity.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Extremely common, with a lifetime prevalence of up to 85%.
• **Incidence**: Peak incidence occurs between ages 30-50.
• **Disability**: The **leading cause of activity limitation and work absence** worldwide.
    ◦ It is the most common cause of disability in patients under 45 years of age.
• **Course**: Most episodes (approx. 90%) are **acute and self-limiting**, resolving within 4-6 weeks regardless of treatment.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A typical patient presents with an **acute onset** of low back pain, often following a specific precipitating event like lifting a heavy object.
• The pain is localized to the lumbosacral region.
    ◦ It may radiate to the buttocks or posterior thighs but **not** in a dermatomal pattern below the knee.
• The patient's general health is otherwise good, with **no systemic symptoms**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Imaging**
    ◦ For acute (<4-6 weeks) mechanical LBP **without red flags**, imaging is **NOT indicated**.
        ▪ It does not improve outcomes and can lead to unnecessary procedures.
    ◦ **Indications for Imaging**
        ▪ **Presence of Red Flags**
            ▪ Major trauma -> **X-ray** first.
            ▪ Suspected cancer, infection, or epidural abscess -> **MRI with and without contrast** is the study of choice.
            ▪ **Cauda Equina Syndrome** -> **Emergent MRI**.
        ▪ **Failure of Conservative Therapy**
            ▪ No improvement after 4-6 weeks of treatment.
        ▪ **New or Progressive Neurologic Deficit**
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ Not indicated unless red flags for infection (CBC, ESR, CRP) or malignancy are present.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for acute episodes.
    ◦ Over 90% of patients experience significant improvement or complete resolution within 4-6 weeks.
• **Recurrence is common**, with up to 50% of patients having another episode within one year.
• A small percentage (~5-10%) will develop **chronic low back pain**.
    ◦ The presence of **"yellow flags"** is the strongest predictor of chronicity.

sections.overview:
• **Lumbar radiculopathy** is a neurological condition characterized by pain, sensory changes, or weakness in a lower extremity, caused by the compression or irritation of a lumbar spinal nerve root.
    ◦ The most common cause is a **herniated intervertebral disc**, also known as a **herniated nucleus pulposus (HNP)**.
    ◦ The term **"sciatica"** is often used to describe the radiating leg pain associated with this condition, typically affecting the **L4, L5, or S1** nerve roots.
sections.etiology:
• **Anatomy:**
    ◦ The intervertebral disc consists of a gelatinous inner core (**nucleus pulposus**) surrounded by a tough, fibrous outer ring (**annulus fibrosus**).
• **Mechanism:**
    ◦ Degenerative changes or trauma can cause tears in the **annulus fibrosus**, allowing the **nucleus pulposus** to bulge or extrude posteriorly into the spinal canal or intervertebral foramen.
• **Nerve Root Compression:**
    ◦ The herniated disc material can cause:
        ▪ **Mechanical Compression:** Direct pressure on the spinal nerve root.
        ▪ **Chemical Irritation:** The **nucleus pulposus** contains inflammatory mediators (e.g., TNF-alpha) that cause a local inflammatory reaction and chemical irritation of the nerve root.
• **Location of Herniation & Nerve Root Affected (HIGH YIELD):**
    ◦ The most common locations are **L4-L5** and **L5-S1**, as these segments bear the most biomechanical stress.
    ◦ A **posterolateral herniation** (most common type) compresses the *traversing* (lower) nerve root.
        ▪ **L4-L5 disc herniation affects the L5 nerve root.**
        ▪ **L5-S1 disc herniation affects the S1 nerve root.**
    ◦ A **far lateral herniation** (less common) compresses the *exiting* (upper) nerve root at the same level.
        ▪ **Far lateral L4-L5 disc herniation affects the L4 nerve root.**
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** Very common; lifetime prevalence of low back pain is ~80%, with radiculopathy occurring in a significant subset.
• **Peak Incidence:** 30 to 50 years of age.
• **Gender:** Slightly more common in males.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Occupational:** Repetitive lifting, twisting, operating vibrating machinery, prolonged sitting (e.g., truck drivers).
• **Lifestyle:** Sedentary lifestyle, obesity, smoking (impairs disc nutrition).
• **Genetic:** Family history of disc disease.
• **Anatomic:** Tall stature.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Classic Presentation:**
    ◦ A patient (often 30-50 years old) with an acute onset of severe, radiating leg pain, often following a specific event like lifting or twisting.
    ◦ The pain typically overshadows any accompanying low back pain.
• **Symptoms:**
    ◦ **Pain:** Sharp, lancinating, burning, or **"electric shock-like"** pain.
    ◦ **Location:** Begins in the low back or buttock and radiates down the posterior or lateral leg into the foot/toes, following a specific **dermatomal pattern**.
    ◦ **Unilateral:** Symptoms are almost always unilateral.
    ◦ **Aggravating Factors:** Pain is typically worse with activities that increase intrathecal pressure (**Valsalva maneuver**):
        ▪ Coughing, sneezing, straining
        ▪ Lumbar flexion (sitting, bending forward)
    ◦ **Alleviating Factors:** Pain may improve with lying down (supine with knees bent) or standing/walking.
    ◦ **Sensory Symptoms:** **Paresthesias** (numbness, tingling, "pins and needles") in the affected dermatome.
    ◦ **Motor Symptoms:** Subjective **weakness** in the affected myotome (e.g., **"foot drop,"** difficulty with push-off).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primarily a clinical diagnosis.**
    ◦ Imaging is not indicated in the first 4-6 weeks for patients with typical radicular symptoms and no **"red flag" signs**.
• **MRI (Lumbar Spine, without contrast):**
    ◦ **Test of Choice** for visualizing the disc, nerve roots, and soft tissues.
    ◦ **Indications:**
        ▪ **Red Flag Symptoms**
        ▪ Progressive or severe neurologic deficit (e.g., significant **foot drop**)
        ▪ Symptoms persisting >6 weeks despite conservative management
        ▪ Pre-operative planning
• **X-Ray (AP/Lateral):**
    ◦ Limited utility for HNP itself.
    ◦ Useful to rule out other pathologies like fracture, spondylolisthesis, or severe degenerative changes.
• **CT Myelogram:**
    ◦ Alternative to MRI if contraindicated (e.g., pacemaker, certain implants).
• **EMG/NCS:**
    ◦ Can confirm the presence and chronicity of radiculopathy and distinguish it from peripheral neuropathy.
    ◦ Not a first-line test.
sections.management:
• **Acute Phase (0-6 weeks):**
    ◦ Rule out **red flags**.
    ◦ Initiate conservative care: Patient education, NSAIDs, referral to physical therapy.
    ◦ Reassure the patient of the excellent natural history.
• **Subacute Phase (>6 weeks):**
    ◦ If symptoms are unimproved or worsening, obtain an **MRI**.
    ◦ Consider referral to Pain Management (for Epidural Steroid Injection) or Spine Surgery.
sections.complications:
• **Cauda Equina Syndrome:** Compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots. Symptoms include **saddle anesthesia**, bilateral leg weakness/sciatica, and **bowel/bladder dysfunction (urinary retention is most common)**. **This is a neurosurgical emergency.**
• **Permanent Neurologic Deficit:** Persistent weakness (e.g., **foot drop**) or sensory loss.
• **Chronic Pain Syndrome.**
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent.** Over 90% of patients improve significantly with conservative treatment within 3 months.
• The size of the disc herniation on MRI does not always correlate with the severity of symptoms.
    ◦ Large extrusions may be more likely to be resorbed by the body's inflammatory response.
• Recurrence rates are approximately 5-15%.

sections.overview:
• Spinal stenosis is the narrowing of the spinal canal, lateral recess, or neural foramen, leading to compression of the spinal cord, **cauda equina**, and/or nerve roots.
    ◦ This compression results in a clinical syndrome of pain, sensory loss, and weakness.
    ◦ It most commonly affects the lumbar and cervical spine.
• **Central Stenosis**: Narrowing of the central spinal canal, potentially compressing the spinal cord (cervical/thoracic) or the **cauda equina** (lumbar).
• **Foraminal (Lateral) Stenosis**: Narrowing of the **intervertebral foramen** where the nerve root exits, leading to **radiculopathy**.
• **Lateral Recess Stenosis**: Narrowing of the area between the central canal and the foramen, compressing the traversing nerve root.
sections.etiology:
• Spinal stenosis is primarily a **degenerative** condition, though it can be congenital.
    ◦ **Acquired (Most Common, >95%)**: The result of age-related "wear and tear."
        ▪ **Degenerative Spondylosis**: The primary driver. Includes a combination of:
            ▪ **Ligamentum Flavum Hypertrophy**: Thickening of the ligament that connects the laminae of adjacent vertebrae. A major contributor to central canal narrowing.
            ▪ **Facet Joint Arthropathy/Hypertrophy**: **Osteophyte** (bone spur) formation from the facet joints encroaches on the canal and foramen.
            ▪ **Intervertebral Disc Bulging/Herniation**: Loss of disc height and bulging of the annulus fibrosus narrows the canal.
            ▪ **Spondylolisthesis**: Anterior slippage of one vertebra over another, which can kinch the spinal canal.
    ◦ **Congenital**: Less common. Patients are born with a congenitally narrow spinal canal (e.g., in **achondroplasia**). Symptoms present at a much younger age.
• **Pathophysiology**: The narrowing leads to both mechanical compression and vascular ischemia of the neural elements.
    ◦ Standing or walking (**extension**) extends the lumbar spine, which further decreases the canal diameter and exacerbates symptoms (**neurogenic claudication**).
    ◦ **Flexion** (sitting, leaning forward) increases the canal diameter, providing relief.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Very common, increases significantly with age.
• **Age**: Primarily affects individuals **>60 years old**.
• **Location**: **Lumbar spine** is the most common site, followed by the cervical spine. Thoracic stenosis is rare.
• **Significance**: Most common reason for spine surgery in individuals over 65.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is an older adult with an insidious onset and slowly progressive course of back and leg pain.
    ◦ The patient's **history** is the most critical component for diagnosis.
• **Lumbar Stenosis**:
    ◦ Patient complains of **"neurogenic claudication."**
    ◦ They report pain, numbness, or weakness in the legs that is worse with walking or prolonged standing.
    ◦ They often find relief by sitting or leaning forward, such as on a shopping cart (the **"Shopping Cart Sign"**).
• **Cervical Stenosis**:
    ◦ Can present with neck pain, radicular arm symptoms (numbness/weakness in a dermatomal pattern), and/or **myelopathy** (spinal cord compression).
    ◦ **Myelopathy** symptoms include gait instability, loss of fine motor skills (e.g., buttoning a shirt, poor handwriting), and potential bowel/bladder changes.
sections.diagnostics:
• **MRI**: **Gold standard / test of choice.**
    ◦ Directly visualizes neural element compression by soft tissues (disc, **ligamentum flavum**) and bone.
• **X-Ray (AP/Lateral, Flexion/Extension)**: Initial imaging.
    ◦ Can show degenerative changes like decreased disc height, **osteophytes**, and **spondylolisthesis**.
    ◦ Cannot visualize soft tissues or confirm stenosis.
• **CT Myelogram**:
    ◦ Excellent for visualizing bony anatomy and canal dimensions.
    ◦ Used when MRI is contraindicated (e.g., incompatible pacemaker) or inconclusive.
    ◦ Involves injecting contrast into the thecal sac.
• **Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI)**:
    ◦ Can be used to rule out **vascular claudication** if the diagnosis is uncertain.
sections.prognosis:
• Spinal stenosis is a **chronic, progressive** condition.
• Many patients can be managed effectively with **conservative treatment** for years.
• Surgical outcomes are generally favorable for relieving leg pain (**neurogenic claudication**) but are less predictable for relieving low back pain.
• Symptoms can recur over time due to the ongoing degenerative nature of the disease.

sections.overview:
• **Cauda Equina Syndrome (CES)** is a rare but severe **neurosurgical emergency** resulting from the **compression of the cauda equina**—the bundle of lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal nerve roots that descend from the **conus medullaris** (the terminal end of the spinal cord, typically at L1-L2)
    ◦ Acute compression leads to ischemia and neuronal damage, causing a constellation of debilitating symptoms
    ◦ Prompt diagnosis and emergent surgical intervention are critical to prevent **permanent paralysis, incontinence, and sensory loss**
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The core mechanism is **mechanical compression** of the nerve roots of the cauda equina within the lumbar spinal canal. This compression leads to:
        ▪ **Venous Congestion:** Impeded venous outflow causes edema and increased intrathecal pressure
        ▪ **Arterial Ischemia:** Sustained pressure compromises arterial blood supply to the nerve roots
        ▪ **Neuronal Injury:** Ischemia and direct mechanical pressure lead to demyelination, axonal damage, and ultimately, irreversible nerve cell death
• **Etiology (Causes of Compression)**
    ◦ **Most Common (>50%): Massive Lumbar Disc Herniation**
        ▪ Typically a large, central herniation at the L4-L5 or L5-S1 levels
    ◦ **Trauma**
        ▪ Lumbar spine burst fractures, vertebral dislocation, penetrating injuries
    ◦ **Tumors**
        ▪ **Metastatic Disease:** Lung, breast, prostate, renal cell carcinoma
        ▪ **Primary CNS Tumors:** Ependymoma, schwannoma, meningioma
    ◦ **Infection / Inflammation**
        ▪ **Spinal Epidural Abscess:** Often from hematogenous spread (e.g., IV drug use, skin infection) or direct extension
        ▪ **Discitis or Vertebral Osteomyelitis**
    ◦ **Spinal Stenosis**
        ▪ Severe degenerative narrowing of the spinal canal
    ◦ **Iatrogenic**
        ▪ Post-operative hematoma following lumbar surgery
        ▪ Complications from spinal anesthesia/epidural injections (hematoma, abscess)
        ▪ Misplaced surgical hardware
    ◦ **Vascular**
        ▪ Spinal epidural hematoma (spontaneous, often in patients on anticoagulants)
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence:** Rare, estimated at 1 in 33,000 to 1 in 100,000 people
    ◦ Accounts for approximately 1-2% of all lumbar disc herniation surgeries
• **Peak Age:** 30s-50s, aligning with the peak incidence of lumbar disc herniation
• **Sex:** No significant sex predilection
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation can be acute or insidious, but it is always considered an **emergency**
    ◦ The patient typically presents with a combination of **severe low back pain** and neurological deficits
    ◦ The classic presentation involves a **"constellation of red flag symptoms"**
• There are two main patterns:
    ◦ **Acute Onset:** Rapid development of symptoms over hours with no prior history of sciatica
    ◦ **Chronic-to-Acute:** A patient with a history of chronic low back pain and sciatica who experiences a sudden, severe worsening of symptoms, including the onset of bladder/bowel dysfunction and saddle anesthesia
sections.diagnostics:
• **Imaging of Choice: STAT MRI of the Lumbar Spine**
    ◦ This is the gold standard and must be performed emergently
    ◦ It directly visualizes the cauda equina, thecal sac, and the source of compression (e.g., disc herniation, tumor, hematoma)
    ◦ Order **with and without contrast** if tumor, abscess, or inflammatory cause is suspected
• **CT Myelogram**
    ◦ Alternative if MRI is contraindicated (e.g., pacemaker, metallic implants) or unavailable
    ◦ Involves injecting contrast into the thecal sac followed by a CT scan. It is invasive but provides excellent visualization of the spinal canal and nerve roots
• **Labs**
    ◦ Generally not diagnostic for CES itself but crucial for pre-operative workup
    ◦ CBC, CMP, PT/INR, PTT
    ◦ If infection is suspected: ESR, CRP, Blood Cultures
sections.prognosis:
• The single most important prognostic factor is the **duration and severity of symptoms before surgical decompression**
• **Timing:** Surgery within **24-48 hours** offers the best prognosis for recovery of motor, sensory, and visceral function
• **Pre-operative Deficits:** Patients with complete saddle anesthesia and established urinary retention at the time of surgery have a poorer prognosis for functional recovery compared to those with incomplete deficits
• Motor function recovery tends to be better and faster than the recovery of bladder and bowel function

sections.overview:
• A **vertebral compression fracture (VCF)** is a pathologic fracture of a vertebral body, resulting in its collapse.
    ◦ This typically occurs in the anterior portion of the vertebra, leading to a **"wedge-shaped" deformity** on imaging.
    ◦ While they can occur from **high-energy trauma** in healthy individuals, they most commonly represent **fragility fractures** secondary to weakened bone, typically from **osteoporosis**.
        ▪ They are the most common type of fracture associated with osteoporosis.
• The **thoracolumbar junction (T12-L1)** is the most frequently affected region.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Osteoporosis (Most Common)**
        ▪ Decreased **bone mineral density (BMD)** makes vertebrae susceptible to fracture under normal axial loading or from minimal trauma (e.g., coughing, sneezing, bending, lifting a light object).
        ▪ This is the leading cause in patients >50 years old.
    ◦ **Trauma**
        ▪ **High-energy axial load** or **hyperflexion injury** in individuals with normal bone density (e.g., motor vehicle accident, fall from height).
    ◦ **Pathologic Fractures (Non-osteoporotic)**
        ▪ **Malignancy:** **Metastatic disease** (from breast, lung, prostate, kidney cancer) or primary bone tumors (e.g., **Multiple Myeloma**) can weaken the vertebral body.
        ▪ **Infection:** **Osteomyelitis** or **Pott's disease** (tuberculosis of the spine) can destroy vertebral bone.
        ▪ **Metabolic:** Long-term **corticosteroid use**, hyperparathyroidism, osteomalacia.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The vertebral column is divided into three functional columns (**Denis Three-Column Model**).
        ▪ **Anterior Column:** Anterior longitudinal ligament, anterior half of the vertebral body and annulus fibrosus.
        ▪ **Middle Column:** Posterior longitudinal ligament, posterior half of the vertebral body and annulus fibrosus.
        ▪ **Posterior Column:** Pedicles, facets, lamina, spinous processes, and posterior ligaments.
    ◦ A simple compression fracture involves failure of the **anterior column** under compression, while the middle and posterior columns remain intact.
        ▪ This makes most VCFs mechanically **stable** injuries.
    ◦ If the fracture extends into the middle column (a **"burst fracture"**), it is considered **unstable** and carries a high risk of **neurologic injury** from retropulsion of bone fragments into the spinal canal.
sections.epidemiology:
• Extremely common, with an estimated 1.5 million occurring annually in the U.S.
• Prevalence increases dramatically with age.
• Affects ~25% of **postmenopausal women** in the U.S.
    ◦ By age 80, approximately 40% of women will have sustained at least one VCF.
• **Most Common Locations:**
    ◦ **Thoracolumbar Junction (T12-L1):** Highest stress region where the rigid thoracic spine meets the more mobile lumbar spine.
    ◦ Mid-thoracic spine (T7-T8).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is an **elderly patient** (often a postmenopausal female) with a history of **osteoporosis**.
    ◦ Presents with **sudden, acute onset of severe, localized, midline back pain**.
    ◦ The pain often follows an inciting event of **minimal trauma** (e.g., lifting, bending, coughing).
• Up to two-thirds of VCFs may be **asymptomatic** or present with gradual, chronic pain and are discovered incidentally on imaging.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Initial Imaging: Plain Radiographs (AP and Lateral)**
    ◦ **Findings:**
        ▪ **Anterior wedging:** The anterior height of the vertebral body is less than the posterior height.
        ▪ Loss of overall vertebral body height (>20% is significant).
        ▪ Cortical disruption or endplate fracture.
• **Advanced Imaging**
    ◦ **CT Scan**
        ▪ **Indication:** When X-ray is inconclusive, for better visualization of fracture detail, or to assess for suspected **posterior wall involvement (retropulsion)** and **canal compromise**.
        ▪ Essential for surgical planning.
    ◦ **MRI**
        ▪ **Indication:**
            ▪ To determine **acuity:** **Bone marrow edema** on a STIR sequence indicates an **acute or subacute fracture**. This is crucial when deciding on interventions like kyphoplasty.
            ▪ If **neurologic deficits** are present: Best modality to visualize the **spinal cord, nerve roots, and ligaments**.
            ▪ To differentiate **osteoporotic vs. malignant fracture:** Malignant fractures often involve the **pedicles**, have a **convex posterior border**, and may be associated with a **soft tissue mass**.
• **Bone Density Scan (DEXA Scan)**
    ◦ Essential for any patient with a suspected fragility VCF to diagnose and quantify the severity of **osteoporosis**.
    ◦ A **T-score of ≤ -2.5** is diagnostic for **osteoporosis**.
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ Not required for a simple osteoporotic VCF.
    ◦ Consider if **malignancy** or **infection** is suspected: CBC with diff, CMP (check calcium, alkaline phosphatase), ESR, CRP, SPEP/UPEP (for **Multiple Myeloma**).
sections.prognosis:
• Pain from an acute VCF typically improves significantly within 4-6 weeks, although some residual pain may become chronic.
• The presence of one VCF is a very strong predictor of future fractures.
    ◦ A patient with one VCF has a **5-fold increased risk** of a subsequent vertebral fracture.
    ◦ A patient with one VCF has a **2-fold increased risk** of a hip fracture.
• Overall prognosis is tied to the management of the underlying **osteoporosis** and prevention of future falls and fractures.

sections.overview:
• **Spondylolysis** is a unilateral or bilateral defect, most commonly a **stress fracture**, in the **pars interarticularis** of the vertebral arch.
    ◦ It is a common cause of activity-related **low back pain** in adolescents and young athletes.
    ◦ The **pars interarticularis** is the segment of bone connecting the superior and inferior articular processes.
    ◦ This condition can lead to **spondylolisthesis** if bilateral defects allow for anterior slippage of the vertebra.
sections.etiology:
• **Spondylolysis** is considered an **overuse or fatigue fracture** rather than a congenital defect or acute traumatic fracture.
    ◦ **Mechanism**: Repetitive microtrauma from lumbar **hyperextension and rotation** places significant shear stress on the **pars interarticularis**, the weakest point of the neural arch.
    ◦ **Location**: The vast majority of cases (**>90%**) occur at the **L5 vertebra**, followed by L4.
    ◦ **Pathology**: The repetitive stress leads to a stress reaction (**bone marrow edema**), which can progress to a nondisplaced fracture (**spondylolysis**).
        ▪ If bilateral fractures occur, the posterior elements of the vertebra become disconnected from the anterior elements, creating instability that can lead to anterior slippage (**spondylolisthesis**).
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects approximately 6% of the general population.
• **Peak Incidence**: Adolescence (ages 10-15), coinciding with periods of rapid growth and high athletic participation.
• **Sex**: More common in males than females (2:1 to 3:1 ratio).
• **Athletic Population**: Significantly higher prevalence (up to 47%) in athletes participating in sports involving repetitive **hyperextension**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is an adolescent athlete with an insidious onset of **low back pain** that is exacerbated by specific athletic activities and relieved by rest.
    ◦ There is typically no history of a single traumatic event.
sections.diagnostics:
• **X-rays (First-Line Imaging)**
    ◦ **Views**: Anteroposterior (AP), lateral, and bilateral obliques.
    ◦ **Lateral View**: Best for assessing for associated **spondylolisthesis**.
    ◦ **Oblique View**: The classic view for identifying the pars defect, which appears as a radiolucent line or "collar" on the **"Scotty dog."**
        ▪ **Scotty Dog Anatomy**: Ear = Superior articular process; Eye = Pedicle; Nose = Transverse process; Neck = **Pars interarticularis**; Body = Lamina; Front Leg = Inferior articular process.
    ◦ *Note: X-rays can be negative in early stress reactions.*
• **MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging)**
    ◦ **Indication**: High clinical suspicion with negative X-rays.
    ◦ **Findings**: The most sensitive test for detecting early-stage "active" pars lesions (stress reactions), which appear as **bone marrow edema** (high signal on T2/STIR sequences). Also excellent for evaluating soft tissues, intervertebral discs, and nerve roots.
• **CT (Computed Tomography)**
    ◦ **Indication**: Gold standard for defining the bony anatomy of the pars defect.
    ◦ **Findings**: Clearly demonstrates the fracture line and can differentiate between an acute fracture and chronic non-union (pseudoarthrosis). Involves higher radiation exposure.
• **SPECT (Single-Photon Emission Computed Tomography) / Bone Scan**
    ◦ **Indication**: To determine if the pars defect is metabolically **"active"** (acute/subacute) versus **"chronic"** (cold).
    ◦ **Findings**: Increased radiotracer uptake (**"hot spot"**) indicates an active lesion with healing potential. A **"cold"** scan suggests a chronic, stable non-union.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for most patients treated conservatively.
• The majority (>80%) of athletes can return to their previous level of sport after successful conservative management.
• Prognosis for healing is better for acute, unilateral defects identified early.
    ◦ Chronic, bilateral defects are less likely to achieve bony union.

sections.overview: • Scoliosis is a three-dimensional deformity of the spine characterized by a lateral curvature of >10 degrees combined with vertebral rotation. • The curvature is defined by the Cobb angle measured on radiographs. • While often associated with adolescence, it can occur at any age. • The most common form is Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis (AIS).
sections.etiology: • Scoliosis is classified by its cause. ◦ Idiopathic (80% of cases): The cause is unknown. This is the most common type. Sub-classified by age of onset: ▪ Infantile: 0-3 years ▪ Juvenile: 4-9 years ▪ Adolescent (AIS): 10 years to skeletal maturity. Most common type of scoliosis. ◦ Congenital: Caused by vertebral anomalies present at birth. ▪ Failure of formation: Hemivertebrae, wedge vertebrae. ▪ Failure of segmentation: Unilateral bar, block vertebrae. ▪ Often associated with other congenital anomalies (cardiac, renal). ◦ Neuromuscular: Due to muscular imbalance and weakness from an underlying neurologic or muscular disease. ▪ Examples: Cerebral palsy, muscular dystrophy, spinal muscular atrophy, spina bifida, Friedreich's ataxia. ▪ These curves are often severe, progressive ("C-shaped"), and may require earlier surgical intervention. ◦ Syndromic: Associated with a known syndrome. ▪ Examples: Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Neurofibromatosis Type 1, Prader-Willi. ◦ Degenerative (De Novo): Occurs in adults due to asymmetric degeneration of the intervertebral discs and facet joints. • Pathophysiology: The exact mechanism for idiopathic scoliosis is unknown but is thought to be multifactorial (genetic predisposition, hormonal factors, abnormal bone/muscle growth). ◦ The Hueter-Volkmann principle suggests that compressive forces on the concave side of the curve inhibit bone growth, while tensile forces on the convex side stimulate it, leading to a vicious cycle of progressive deformity.
sections.epidemiology: • Prevalence: Affects 2-3% of the adolescent population. • Gender: ◦ Small curves (<10): Equal prevalence in males and females. ◦ Clinically significant curves (>30): Females are 10x more likely to have curve progression requiring treatment. • Age of Onset: Most commonly diagnosed during the pre-pubertal growth spurt (ages 10-15).
sections.clinicalPresentation: • Most commonly discovered during a routine school screening, sports physical, or by a parent. • The patient is usually asymptomatic. • Chief complaint is often cosmetic (e.g., "my clothes don't fit right," "one shoulder is higher," "one hip sticks out"). • Significant back pain is a red flag in AIS and warrants investigation for other causes (e.g., tumor, infection, spondylolysis).
sections.diagnostics: • Imaging: ◦ Initial & Gold Standard: Standing posteroanterior (PA) and lateral full-length spine radiographs (scoliosis series). ▪ "Standing" is critical to assess the curve under gravitational load. ◦ Cobb Angle Measurement: ▪ Used to quantify the magnitude of the curve. ▪ Scoliosis is defined as a Cobb angle > 10 degrees. ▪ Measured by drawing lines along the superior endplate of the most tilted upper vertebra and the inferior endplate of the most tilted lower vertebra. The angle between perpendicular lines drawn from these is the Cobb angle. ◦ Risser Sign: Assesses skeletal maturity by evaluating the ossification of the iliac apophysis (graded 0-5). ▪ Risser 0-2 indicates significant growth remaining; Risser 4-5 indicates skeletal maturity. ◦ MRI of the Spine: ▪ Not routinely indicated for AIS. ▪ Indications (Red Flags): ▪ Atypical curve patterns (e.g., left-sided thoracic curve). ▪ Significant pain. ▪ Abnormal neurologic findings. ▪ Rapid progression. ▪ To rule out intraspinal pathology like a syrinx, tethered cord, or tumor.
sections.prognosis: • Excellent with early diagnosis and appropriate management. • The primary determinant of long-term outcome is the magnitude of the curve at skeletal maturity. • Curves < 30 at maturity are unlikely to progress significantly in adulthood. • Thoracic curves > 50 at maturity tend to progress at a rate of approximately 1 per year throughout life.

sections.overview:
• A **clavicle fracture** is a break in the **collarbone**, one of the most common fractures in the body.
	◦ The clavicle is an S-shaped bone that acts as a strut connecting the sternum to the scapula, providing the only true bony articulation between the upper extremity and the axial skeleton.
	◦ The vast majority of these fractures occur in the **middle third** of the bone and can be managed **non-operatively** with a high rate of union.
sections.etiology:
• **Mechanism of Injury**
	◦ **Most Common:** A fall directly onto the lateral aspect of the shoulder.
	◦ **Second Most Common:** A fall onto an outstretched hand (**FOOSH**).
	◦ **Less Common:** A direct blow to the clavicle itself.
	◦ **Neonates:** Can occur during birth, especially in cases of **shoulder dystocia** or high birth weight.
• **Pathophysiology of Displacement**
	◦ The fracture pattern is dictated by the pull of surrounding muscles on the bone fragments.
	◦ **Medial Fragment:** Pulled **superiorly** and posteriorly by the strong **sternocleidomastoid (SCM) muscle**.
	◦ **Lateral Fragment:** Pulled **inferiorly** and medially by the weight of the arm and the pull of the **pectoralis major** and **latissimus dorsi**.
	◦ This classic displacement pattern creates the characteristic **"step-off" deformity**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence:** Accounts for 2-5% of all fractures in adults and ~35% of all shoulder girdle injuries.
• **Distribution:** Bimodal age distribution.
	◦ **First Peak:** Young, active males (< 30 years old) due to high-energy trauma (e.g., sports, motor vehicle collisions).
	◦ **Second Peak:** Elderly patients (> 70 years old), often women, due to low-energy falls associated with **osteoporosis**.
• **Location of Fracture (Allman Classification)**
	◦ **Group I (Middle Third):** Most common (~80%). The bone is thinnest and has less muscular support here.
	◦ **Group II (Lateral/Distal Third):** Second most common (~15%). These are more unstable due to involvement of the **coracoclavicular (CC) ligaments**.
	◦ **Group III (Medial/Proximal Third):** Least common (~5%). Often requires a **CT scan** to fully evaluate due to overlying structures.
sections.riskFactors:
• Participation in contact sports (football, hockey, rugby).
• Activities with a high risk of falls (cycling, skiing, skateboarding, gymnastics).
• **Osteoporosis**.
• Male gender in the younger population.
• Difficult childbirth / high birth weight (neonates).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The patient typically presents immediately following a traumatic event.
• They will be guarding the injured arm, holding it adducted and close to the body to prevent painful motion.
• The head is often tilted **toward** the affected side and the chin rotated **away** to relax the SCM muscle, reducing tension on the fracture site.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Symptoms**
	◦ Acute, sharp **pain** localized over the clavicle.
	◦ Inability to lift the arm due to pain.
	◦ A **"popping," "cracking," or "snapping"** sound or sensation at the time of injury.
	◦ Sensation of grinding (**crepitus**) with any attempted shoulder movement.
• **Signs (Physical Exam Findings)**
	◦ **Inspection:**
		▪ Visible **deformity, bump, or "step-off"** at the fracture site.
		▪ Swelling, **ecchymosis**, and erythema over the clavicle.
		▪ **Skin tenting:** A critical finding where a sharp bone fragment pushes against the skin, threatening to create an **open fracture**. **This is an indication for urgent surgical consultation.**
		▪ Check for any open wounds, abrasions, or penetrating trauma.
	◦ **Palpation:**
		▪ **Point tenderness** directly over the fracture.
		▪ Palpable **crepitus** with gentle manipulation.
	◦ **Range of Motion:**
		▪ Severely limited and painful active and passive range of motion of the shoulder, especially with abduction and forward flexion.
	◦ **Neurovascular Exam:**
		▪ **Crucial and must be documented.**
		▪ **Neurological:** Assess sensation over the deltoid (**axillary nerve**) and in the **median, ulnar, and radial nerve** distributions. Assess motor strength if pain allows. **Brachial plexus injuries** are a rare but serious association.
		▪ **Vascular:** Palpate distal pulses (radial, ulnar). Check capillary refill. Auscultate the subclavian area for a bruit if a vascular injury is suspected.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Imaging**
	◦ **X-rays:** The primary diagnostic modality.
		▪ **Standard Views:** Anteroposterior (AP) view of the clavicle.
		▪ **Zanca View (10-15° Cephalic Tilt):** Often ordered to better visualize the fracture pattern and degree of superior/inferior displacement without overlap from the ribs and thoracic cage.
	◦ **CT Scan:** Not routinely required.
		▪ **Indications:** Suspected intra-articular extension into the sternoclavicular (SC) or acromioclavicular (AC) joints, severe comminution, preoperative planning, or suspicion of associated injuries (e.g., scapular fracture).
sections.treatment:
• **Non-Operative (Majority of Cases)**
	◦ **Indications:** Minimally displaced or non-displaced middle third fractures. Specifically, fractures with **< 100% displacement** and **< 2 cm of shortening**.
• **Operative (Surgical Fixation - ORIF)**
	◦ **Absolute Indications:**
		▪ **Open fracture**
		▪ Associated **neurovascular injury** requiring repair
		▪ Severe **skin tenting** with impending skin perforation
	◦ **Relative Indications:**
		▪ **> 100% displacement** (fragments are not touching)
		▪ **> 2 cm of shortening**
		▪ Displaced **distal third (Group II) fractures** (high risk of nonunion)
		▪ **"Floating shoulder"** (ipsilateral fractures of the clavicle and scapular neck)
		▪ Polytrauma patient
		▪ Patient preference in active individuals desiring a faster return to function.
sections.management:
• Most patients with isolated, closed fractures are discharged home from the ED with orthopedic follow-up within 1 week.
• Patients with absolute indications for surgery require admission and orthopedic consultation.
• Serial X-rays (e.g., at 1-2 weeks and 6 weeks) to monitor healing and ensure no significant displacement has occurred.
• **Clinical union** (fracture site is non-tender) typically precedes **radiographic union** (callus visible on X-ray).
• **Phase 1 (0-4 weeks):** Sling use, pendulum exercises.
• **Phase 2 (4-8 weeks):** Discontinue sling, begin active-assisted and active ROM exercises as healing progresses.
• **Phase 3 (8-12+ weeks):** Begin strengthening exercises. Return to contact sports is typically not allowed until radiographic evidence of complete union, usually around 3-4 months.
sections.complications:
• **Acute:**
	◦ **Pneumothorax/Hemothorax:** Rare, but can occur with a sharp medial fragment piercing the pleura.
	◦ **Brachial Plexus Injury:** Can occur from the initial trauma or fracture fragments.
	◦ **Subclavian Artery/Vein Injury:** A vascular emergency.
• **Delayed:**
	◦ **Nonunion:** Failure of the fracture to heal. Highest risk is in displaced distal third fractures and significantly displaced mid-shaft fractures, especially in smokers.
	◦ **Malunion:** Healing in a shortened or angulated position. Can lead to cosmetic deformity, pain, and shoulder dysfunction.
	◦ **Post-traumatic Arthritis:** If the fracture extends into the AC or SC joint.
	◦ **Hardware Irritation:** The plate and screws used in ORIF can be prominent under the skin and may require a second surgery for removal after healing.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent.** Most mid-shaft clavicle fractures treated non-operatively heal without significant long-term issues (>95% union rate).
• Operative fixation also has a very high union rate but carries the inherent risks of surgery (infection, nerve damage, anesthesia risk, hardware problems).
• Functional outcomes are generally very good, with most patients returning to their previous level of activity.

sections.overview:
• A **proximal humerus fracture** is a break in the upper part of the humerus bone, which forms the "ball" of the shoulder's ball-and-socket joint (**glenohumeral joint**).
• These fractures involve one or more of four key segments:
    ◦ The **articular surface (humeral head)**
    ◦ The **greater tuberosity**
    ◦ The **lesser tuberosity**
    ◦ The **humeral shaft** (at the level of the surgical neck)
• It is one of the most common fractures in the **elderly** population.
• The majority (~85%) are **minimally displaced** and can be managed non-operatively.
sections.etiology:
• **Mechanism of Injury (MOI):**
    ◦ **Low-Energy (most common):** Fall on an outstretched hand (**FOOSH**) from a standing height, typically in elderly, **osteoporotic** patients.
    ◦ **High-Energy:** Motor vehicle accidents (MVAs), falls from a significant height, or direct, forceful blows to the shoulder. More common in younger patients.
    ◦ **Pathologic:** Fracture through a bone weakened by a tumor (e.g., metastatic disease) or metabolic bone disease.
    ◦ **Seizure/Electric Shock:** May cause a **fracture-dislocation** due to violent, uncontrolled muscle contractions.
• **Pathophysiology:**
    ◦ Fracture patterns are determined by the deforming forces of the muscles that attach to the proximal humerus:
        ▪ **Pectoralis Major:** Pulls the humeral shaft medially and anteriorly.
        ▪ **Supraspinatus:** Pulls the **greater tuberosity** superiorly and posteriorly.
        ▪ **Subscapularis:** Pulls the **lesser tuberosity** medially.
        ▪ **Infraspinatus & Teres Minor:** Pull the **greater tuberosity** posteriorly.
    ◦ These competing forces cause the characteristic displacement of fracture fragments seen on imaging.
sections.epidemiology:
• Third most common fracture type in the **elderly** (>65 years), after **hip fractures** and **distal radius fractures**.
• **Bimodal age distribution:**
    ◦ Young patients with high-energy trauma.
    ◦ Elderly patients with low-energy falls (most common).
• Strong female-to-male predominance (~3:1), especially in the elderly, correlating with the prevalence of **osteoporosis**.
• Incidence increases significantly with age.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient, typically an elderly female, presents after a fall with acute, **severe shoulder pain**.
• They are often supporting the injured arm with their contralateral hand, holding it in an adducted and internally rotated position.
• There is a marked unwillingness to move the affected shoulder due to pain.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Imaging of Choice:** **Radiographs** (X-rays).
• **Standard Views (Trauma Series):**
    ◦ **True AP (Grashey view):** Shows the **glenohumeral joint** in a true anteroposterior plane.
    ◦ **Scapular "Y" View:** Assesses for displacement of the humeral head relative to the glenoid.
    ◦ **Axillary View:** Crucial for identifying **glenohumeral dislocations** and displacement of the tuberosities.
        ▪ If the patient cannot abduct for a standard axillary view, a **Velpeau axillary view** can be obtained.
• **CT Scan:**
    ◦ **Indications:**
        ▪ Evaluation of complex, **comminuted**, or **intra-articular fractures**.
        ▪ Assessment of **fracture-dislocations**.
        ▪ Preoperative planning for surgical fixation.
• **MRI:**
    ◦ Rarely used in the acute setting for the fracture itself.
    ◦ May be used later to evaluate for associated soft tissue injuries, such as a **rotator cuff tear**.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is generally good for **minimally displaced fractures** treated non-operatively.
• For complex, surgically treated fractures, outcomes are more variable.
• Some degree of **residual stiffness and weakness** is common, particularly in the elderly.
• The primary goal of treatment is often a **painless, functional shoulder**, not necessarily a return to pre-injury level of performance.

sections.overview:
• Most common type of shoulder dislocation, accounting for over **95%** of all glenohumeral dislocations.
• Occurs when the humeral head is forcibly displaced from the glenoid fossa to an **anterior** and typically **inferior** position.
• A common, painful orthopedic emergency requiring **prompt reduction**.
• The glenohumeral joint's high degree of mobility makes it inherently less stable and thus susceptible to dislocation.
sections.etiology:
• **Mechanism of Injury**:
    ◦ The classic mechanism is a force applied to the arm while it is in a position of **abduction, external rotation, and extension**.
• **Common Scenarios**:
    ◦ **Falling on an outstretched hand (FOOSH)**.
    ◦ A football quarterback during a throwing motion when tackled.
    ◦ Blocking a shot in basketball or volleyball.
    ◦ Direct posterior blow to the shoulder.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ The force levers the humeral head out of the glenoid fossa, tearing the anterior-inferior joint capsule, ligaments, and glenoid labrum.
    ◦ **Bankart Lesion**: A detachment of the **anterior-inferior glenoid labrum** from the glenoid rim. This is the essential lesion that leads to recurrent anterior instability.
    ◦ **Hill-Sachs Lesion**: A compression fracture or "divot" on the **posterolateral aspect of the humeral head**. It occurs as the humeral head impacts against the anterior glenoid rim during dislocation.
sections.epidemiology:
• The most commonly dislocated major joint in the body.
• Incidence is approximately 24 per 100,000 person-years.
• **Bimodal Distribution**:
    ◦ **Primary Peak**: Young, athletic males (ages 15-29) due to high-energy trauma in sports.
    ◦ **Secondary Peak**: Elderly females (ages 60-80) due to low-energy falls.
• Recurrence is extremely common, especially in younger patients; the rate can be >**90%** in patients under 20 years old.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Age**: Patients < 20 years old have the highest risk of recurrence.
• **Sports Participation**: Contact and collision sports (e.g., football, hockey, rugby, lacrosse).
• **Previous Dislocation**: The single greatest risk factor for a subsequent dislocation.
• **Ligamentous Laxity**: Congenital conditions like Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
• **Glenoid or Humeral Bony Defects**: Glenoid dysplasia or a large Hill-Sachs lesion.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients typically present after an acute traumatic event in significant distress.
• The arm is held in a characteristic position of slight **abduction and external rotation**.
    ◦ The patient holds the affected arm close to their body, supporting it with the contralateral hand.
    ◦ The patient will resist any attempt to **adduct or internally rotate** the arm.
• **Symptoms**:
    ◦ Sudden onset of **severe shoulder pain**.
    ◦ A sensation of the shoulder **"popping out"** or shifting.
    ◦ Inability to move the arm.
    ◦ Visible deformity of the shoulder.
    ◦ Numbness or paresthesias down the arm or in the hand, suggesting nerve involvement.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Inspection**:
    ◦ **"Squared-off" Shoulder**: Loss of the normal rounded contour of the deltoid muscle.
    ◦ The acromion process becomes prominent and palpable superiorly.
    ◦ The humeral head may be palpable anteriorly, just below the coracoid process.
• **Palpation**:
    ◦ Tenderness over the anterior shoulder.
    ◦ A void or "hollowness" may be felt laterally where the humeral head should be.
• **Range of Motion**:
    ◦ Severely limited and guarded due to pain and mechanical block.
• **Neurovascular Exam (CRITICAL - perform before and after reduction)**:
    ◦ **Neurologic**:
        ▪ **Axillary Nerve (C5, C6)**: Most commonly injured nerve.
        ▪ **Motor**: Test deltoid function (abduction). Often difficult due to pain, but ask the patient to "fire" the muscle.
        ▪ **Sensory**: Test sensation over the lateral deltoid (the **"regimental badge" area**).
    ◦ **Vascular**:
        ▪ Palpate the radial pulse and assess capillary refill to rule out injury to the **axillary artery** (rare but limb-threatening).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Imaging of Choice**: Plain Radiographs (X-rays).
• **Standard Views**:
    ◦ **Anteroposterior (AP)**: Shows the humeral head displaced **inferiorly and medially** relative to the glenoid.
    ◦ **Scapular "Y" View**: Crucial for determining the direction of dislocation. The humeral head appears **anterior** to the "Y".
