    ◦ **Axillary View**: The most reliable view to assess the glenohumeral relationship and diagnose subtle subluxations. It clearly shows the anterior displacement but can be difficult to obtain due to patient pain.
• **MRI / MR Arthrogram**:
    ◦ Not indicated for acute diagnosis.
    ◦ Used in the outpatient setting to evaluate for soft-tissue injuries (**Bankart lesions, rotator cuff tears**) and plan for potential surgery.
sections.treatment:
• **Immediate goal is closed reduction**.
• **Analgesia/Sedation**: Procedural sedation (e.g., ketamine, propofol) or intra-articular lidocaine injection is usually required to overcome pain and muscle spasm.
• **Reduction Techniques**:
    ◦ **Stimson Technique**: Patient is prone with the affected arm hanging off the table with weights attached to the wrist.
    ◦ **Traction-Countertraction**: Longitudinal traction is applied to the arm while an assistant provides counter-traction with a sheet across the patient's chest.
    ◦ **Scapular Manipulation**: With the patient prone, the provider rotates the inferior tip of the scapula medially.
    ◦ **Milch Technique**: The arm is gently abducted and externally rotated, followed by direct pressure on the humeral head.
• **Post-Reduction Protocol**
sections.management:
• **Immobilization**: A sling is used for comfort and to protect the joint, typically for 1-3 weeks.
    ◦ Shorter duration is favored in older patients to prevent **adhesive capsulitis**.
• **Physical Therapy**: Essential for recovery. Begins with passive range of motion, progressing to active ROM and finally strengthening exercises focusing on the rotator cuff and scapular stabilizers.
• **Orthopedic Follow-up**: All patients should follow up with an orthopedic specialist.
• **Surgical Intervention (Arthroscopic Bankart Repair)**:
    ◦ **Indications**: Young, high-demand athletes after a first-time traumatic dislocation; recurrent instability; irreducible dislocation; significant associated fractures.
sections.complications:
• **Recurrent Instability**: Most common complication, especially in patients < 20.
• **Neurologic Injury**: **Axillary nerve neuropraxia** is the most common (5-10% of cases). Usually transient and resolves within 3-6 months.
• **Bony Injury**:
    ◦ **Hill-Sachs Lesion** (up to 80% of cases).
    ◦ **Bony Bankart Lesion** (fracture of the anterior glenoid rim).
    ◦ **Associated Fractures**: **Greater tuberosity** of the humerus is most common.
• **Rotator Cuff Tears**: Increasingly common in patients > 40 years old.
• **Vascular Injury**: Axillary artery or vein injury (rare, <1%).
• **Adhesive Capsulitis ("Frozen Shoulder")**: Increased risk with prolonged immobilization.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is generally good for returning to normal function.
• The primary factor influencing long-term outcome is the **risk of recurrence**, which is inversely proportional to the patient's age at the time of the first dislocation.
• Surgical stabilization can significantly reduce the rate of recurrence in high-risk populations.

sections.overview:
• Orthopedic injury where the humeral head displaces posteriorly relative to the glenoid fossa of the scapula
◦ Significantly less common than anterior shoulder dislocation, accounting for only 2-5% of all shoulder dislocations
◦ Frequently missed on initial presentation (up to 50-80% of cases) due to subtle clinical and radiographic findings
◦ Prompt and accurate diagnosis is crucial to prevent long-term complications like chronic instability, pain, and **avascular necrosis**
sections.etiology:
• Mechanism of injury typically involves forceful **internal rotation, adduction, and flexion** of the shoulder
◦ Common causes are remembered by the **"3 E's"**:
▪ **Epilepsy**: Violent, tonic-clonic muscle contractions during a seizure can overpower stabilizing structures
    ◦ The stronger internal rotators (subscapularis, pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi) overpower the external rotators
▪ **Electricity**: Electrocution or high-voltage shock causes severe, involuntary muscle contractions similar to a seizure
▪ **Ethanol / Trauma**: A direct blow to the anterior shoulder or a fall onto an outstretched hand (FOOSH) with the arm in an adducted and internally rotated position
• Pathoanatomically, the injury often involves:
◦ Tearing of the posterior capsule, posterior labrum, and the subscapularis tendon
◦ An impaction fracture on the anteromedial aspect of the humeral head, known as a **reverse Hill-Sachs lesion**, can occur as it impacts the posterior glenoid rim
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Accounts for 2-5% of all glenohumeral dislocations
• **Demographics**: Most commonly affects young, active males (20-40 years old) due to trauma
◦ A second peak is seen in patients with seizure disorders
• **Bilateral dislocations**: While rare, they are almost pathognomonic for a seizure or electrical shock event
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation is often much more subtle than an anterior dislocation
• Patients typically present holding the affected arm in a characteristic position: **adducted and internally rotated**
• Patients will be in significant pain and unwilling to move the arm, particularly into **external rotation**
• Physical appearance:
◦ Anterior shoulder may appear **flattened** with a **prominent coracoid process**
◦ This contrasts with an anterior dislocation where a prominent humeral head creates an anterior bulge (**"squared-off shoulder"**)
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is generally good if the dislocation is diagnosed and reduced acutely
◦ Outcomes are significantly worse for missed or chronic dislocations, often requiring complex open surgery and resulting in some degree of permanent stiffness and pain
• The size of the **reverse Hill-Sachs lesion** is a major prognostic factor for future instability

sections.overview:
• An **Acromioclavicular (AC) joint separation**, commonly known as a "shoulder separation," is an injury to the ligaments that stabilize the AC joint.
    ◦ It is distinct from a glenohumeral (shoulder) dislocation.
    ◦ The injury involves damage to the **acromioclavicular (AC)** and/or **coracoclavicular (CC) ligaments**, leading to a loss of congruity between the distal clavicle and the acromion.
    ◦ Severity is graded using the **Rockwood classification system**, which is based on the direction and degree of clavicular displacement.
sections.etiology:
• **Mechanism of Injury**
    ◦ Typically caused by a **direct blow** to the superolateral aspect of the shoulder (the acromion) with the arm adducted.
        ▪ This force drives the acromion inferiorly and medially relative to the clavicle.
    ◦ Less commonly, it can result from a **fall onto an outstretched hand (FOOSH)**.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The injury represents a sequential failure of the key stabilizing ligaments:
        ▪ **Acromioclavicular (AC) Ligaments:** A relatively weak complex that provides **horizontal (anterior-posterior) stability** to the joint.
        ▪ **Coracoclavicular (CC) Ligaments:** The **primary stabilizers**. This is a very strong complex consisting of two distinct ligaments:
            • **Trapezoid Ligament:** Anterolateral band.
            • **Conoid Ligament:** Posteromedial band.
            • Together, they provide robust **vertical stability**, preventing superior displacement of the distal clavicle.
        ▪ **Deltoid and Trapezius Fascia:** A dynamic muscular envelope that provides secondary stability. Disruption of this fascia occurs in high-grade injuries.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** Accounts for approximately **10%** of all acute shoulder girdle injuries.
• **Demographics:** Most common in **young, physically active individuals**, particularly in the second and third decades of life.
• **Sex:** There is a significant **male predominance** (5:1 to 10:1), largely due to higher participation rates in contact sports.
sections.riskFactors:
• Participation in **contact sports** (e.g., football, hockey, rugby, lacrosse).
• **High-impact activities** (e.g., cycling, skiing, snowboarding, martial arts).
• Occupations involving risk of falls or direct shoulder trauma.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with a history of **acute trauma** (fall, direct blow) to the shoulder.
• They will often be **guarding the injured arm**, holding it in an adducted position and supported by the contralateral hand to relieve pressure on the AC joint.
• They can pinpoint the pain directly to the top of the shoulder.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ **Acute pain** localized to the superior aspect of the shoulder, directly over the AC joint.
    ◦ Pain that is exacerbated by **overhead movements**, lifting, or sleeping on the affected side.
    ◦ Pain with **cross-body adduction** of the arm.
    ◦ A sensation of instability or a visible/palpable **"bump"** or deformity on the superior shoulder.
• **Physical Exam Findings**
    ◦ **Inspection:** Look for swelling, ecchymosis, and a potential **"step-off" deformity** where the distal clavicle is visibly elevated superior to the acromion.
    ◦ **Palpation:** Exquisite **point tenderness** directly over the AC joint. Palpate the entire clavicle and glenohumeral joint to rule out concomitant fractures or dislocation.
    ◦ **Range of Motion:** Active and passive ROM are often limited by pain, especially with abduction >90 degrees and forward flexion.
    ◦ **Provocative Tests:**
        ▪ **Cross-Body Adduction Test (Scarf Test):** Passive adduction of the arm across the patient's chest compresses the AC joint, eliciting sharp pain. This is a **highly sensitive** test for AC joint pathology.
        ▪ **Piano Key Sign:** In higher-grade injuries (Type III+), direct downward pressure on the elevated distal clavicle will reduce it, but it will spring back up upon release, similar to a piano key. This indicates complete **CC ligament rupture**.
    ◦ **Neurovascular Exam:** A thorough distal neurovascular exam is essential but is typically normal.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **X-Rays:** The **primary diagnostic modality**.
        ▪ **AP View:** Standard shoulder view.
        ▪ **Zanca View:** An AP view with a 10-15° cephalic tilt. This is the **best view** to visualize the AC joint in isolation by removing overlapping bony structures (e.g., scapular spine).
        ▪ **Axillary Lateral View:** Essential for evaluating horizontal (anterior-posterior) displacement and diagnosing a **Type IV injury** (posterior displacement).
        ▪ **Stress Views (Weighted Views):** Historically used to differentiate between Type II and III injuries by having the patient hold a 10-15 lb weight. They have largely fallen out of favor due to patient discomfort and limited impact on management.
        ▪ **Bilateral views** can be used to compare the CC interspace of the injured vs. uninjured side.
• **Rockwood Classification (High-Yield)**
    ◦ **Type I:** **Sprain of AC ligament**. CC ligaments are intact. No deformity. Normal X-ray.
    ◦ **Type II:** **Tear of AC ligament**, sprain of CC ligaments. Slight elevation of clavicle (<25% of clavicle height). CC distance is normal or minimally increased.
    ◦ **Type III:** **Complete tear of both AC and CC ligaments**. Obvious superior displacement of the clavicle (25-100% increase in CC distance compared to contralateral side). The clavicle is elevated but remains below the superior border of the acromion on some views.
    ◦ **Type IV:** AC and CC ligaments torn, with **posterior displacement** of the distal clavicle into the trapezius muscle. Best seen on axillary view.
    ◦ **Type V:** **Severe Type III**. Complete tear of AC and CC ligaments plus disruption of the **deltotrapezial fascia**. Gross superior displacement of the clavicle (>100% increase in CC distance).
    ◦ **Type VI:** Very rare. **Inferior displacement** of the distal clavicle below the coracoid or acromion.
sections.treatment:
• **Type I & II:** Almost exclusively **non-operative**.
    ◦ Sling for comfort (1-3 weeks).
    ◦ Ice and NSAIDs for pain and inflammation.
    ◦ Early, gentle range of motion exercises followed by physical therapy for strengthening.
• **Type III:** **Controversial**.
    ◦ **Non-operative:** Often the initial treatment of choice, especially for sedentary individuals. Outcomes are generally good.
    ◦ **Operative:** Considered for high-demand overhead athletes, heavy laborers, or those who fail conservative management. Involves anatomic **CC ligament reconstruction**.
• **Type IV, V, & VI:** Almost always require **operative** management to reduce and stabilize the clavicle.
sections.management:
• **Non-Operative Protocol (Type I, II, most III)**
• **Operative Protocol (Type IV, V, VI, selected III)**
    ◦ Surgical fixation (e.g., **CC ligament reconstruction** with graft, suture button devices).
    ◦ Post-operative immobilization in a sling for 4-6 weeks, followed by a structured physical therapy protocol similar to the non-operative plan but with a more delayed timeline.
sections.complications:
• **Chronic Pain/Instability:** Most common complication, especially with under-rehabilitated or higher-grade injuries.
• **Post-traumatic Osteoarthritis:** Degenerative changes in the AC joint can develop over time.
• **Decreased Range of Motion:** Can result from prolonged immobilization (**adhesive capsulitis**) or residual deformity.
• **Cosmetic Deformity:** A persistent **"bump"** is common in Type III+ injuries, even with good functional outcomes.
• **Surgical Complications:** Hardware failure, infection, fracture, loss of reduction.
sections.prognosis:
• **Type I & II:** **Excellent**. The vast majority of patients return to their pre-injury level of function with non-operative care.
• **Type III:** **Good to excellent**, whether treated operatively or non-operatively. The decision is patient-specific.
• **Type IV, V, VI:** **Good** with appropriate surgical intervention, but recovery is longer and more complex. Some residual deficits may persist.

sections.overview:
• A **supracondylar humerus fracture** is a complete or incomplete fracture of the distal humerus, located in the metaphyseal bone just proximal to the elbow joint's condyles and physis (growth plate)
• It is the **most common elbow fracture in children** and is considered a true **orthopedic emergency** due to the high risk of associated **neurovascular injury**
• The vast majority are **extension-type injuries** resulting from a fall onto an outstretched hand (**FOOSH**)
sections.etiology:
• **Mechanism of Injury**
    ◦ **Extension-Type (>95% of cases)**: Caused by a **Fall On an Outstretched Hand (FOOSH)** with the elbow in hyperextension
        ▪ The olecranon process of the ulna acts as a fulcrum, impacting the weak supracondylar area of the humerus and causing it to fracture
        ▪ The distal fragment is typically displaced **posteriorly** and **medially**
    ◦ **Flexion-Type (<5% of cases)**: Caused by a direct blow to the posterior aspect of a flexed elbow
        ▪ The distal fragment is displaced **anteriorly**
• **Pathophysiology of Injury**
    ◦ The supracondylar region of the humerus in children is a weak point due to its thin cortex and ongoing bone remodeling
    ◦ When the fracture occurs, the sharp proximal fragment can be driven anteriorly, placing the **brachial artery** and **median nerve** at high risk for tethering, contusion, or transection
    ◦ Significant swelling in the antecubital fossa can lead to **compartment syndrome**
sections.epidemiology:
• **Age**: Most common in children aged **5-7 years**
• **Prevalence**: Accounts for approximately 60% of all pediatric elbow fractures and 3% of all pediatric fractures
• **Sex**: Slight male predominance
• **Limb**: More common in the non-dominant arm
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A child typically presents to the emergency department with a history of a fall, usually from a height (e.g., bed, playground equipment), followed by immediate and **severe elbow pain**
• The child will be **guarding the injured limb**, holding it in a flexed position against their body and refusing to move it
sections.diagnostics:
• **Imaging**: X-ray is the primary diagnostic tool
• **Views**: AP and a true Lateral of the elbow are essential
• **Key Radiographic Lines/Signs**
    ◦ **Anterior Humeral Line**: On a true lateral view, a line drawn along the anterior cortex of the humerus should pass through the **middle third of the capitellum**
        ▪ In an extension-type fracture, the capitellum is displaced posteriorly, and this line passes through the anterior third or completely misses it
    ◦ **Fat Pad Sign**: The presence of a **posterior fat pad** is *always abnormal* and indicates an intra-articular effusion (hemarthrosis), suggesting an occult fracture even if no fracture line is visible
        ▪ An elevated anterior fat pad (**"sail sign"**) is also abnormal
    ◦ **Gartland Classification (for Extension-Type Fractures)**: Used to guide treatment
        ▪ **Type I**: **Non-displaced** or minimally displaced (<2 mm)
        ▪ **Type II**: Displaced with the **posterior cortex still intact** (hinged)
        ▪ **Type III**: **Completely displaced** with no cortical contact; high risk of neurovascular injury
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is **excellent** for appropriately and promptly treated fractures
• Most children regain near-full to full range of motion and function
• The prognosis worsens with delayed treatment, severe initial displacement, or the development of complications like **compartment syndrome**

sections.overview:
• Break in the proximal part of the **radius**, one of the two forearm bones forming the elbow joint.
• One of the most common **elbow fractures** in adults.
• Typically results from a **fall onto an outstretched hand (FOOSH)**.
• Injury spectrum ranges from a simple, non-displaced crack to a severely **comminuted fracture** with associated **elbow dislocation** and **ligamentous injury**.
• Diagnosis is confirmed with **radiography**.
• Treatment is guided by fracture pattern and displacement, most commonly using the **Mason Classification**.
sections.etiology:
• **Mechanism of Injury (MOI)**
    ◦ The most common mechanism is a **Fall On an Outstretched Hand (FOOSH)** with the forearm pronated and the elbow in slight flexion.
    ◦ Direct trauma to the elbow is a less common cause.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ An **axial load** is transmitted up the forearm, driving the **radial head** into the **capitellum** of the humerus.
    ◦ A concurrent **valgus force** applied to the elbow can contribute, potentially injuring the **medial collateral ligament (MCL)**.
sections.epidemiology:
• Accounts for approximately **33% of all elbow fractures** and about 2-5% of all fractures in adults.
• Most common in adults between **30-60 years of age**.
• More common in **females** than males (ratio of approx. 2:1).
• Frequently associated with other injuries:
    ◦ **Elbow dislocation**
    ◦ **Coronoid process fractures**
    ◦ Ligamentous tears (e.g., **lateral collateral ligament complex**)
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patient typically presents after a fall, **cradling the injured arm** close to their body.
• Reports an acute onset of **severe elbow pain**.
• **Hesitant to move the arm**, particularly in rotation.
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for **Mason Type I** fractures, with most patients returning to full function.
• **Good to fair** for operatively treated **Mason Type II and III** fractures.
    ◦ Some residual **stiffness** is common, but functional outcomes are generally positive.
• **Guarded** for complex injuries like the **"Terrible Triad"** (**elbow dislocation**, **radial head fracture**, and **coronoid fracture**).
    ◦ These have a high rate of **stiffness** and **instability**.

sections.overview:
• A **Monteggia fracture** is a specific injury pattern defined by a **fracture of the proximal third of the ulna** combined with a **dislocation of the radial head**.
	◦ The ulnar fracture is typically obvious on imaging, but the radial head dislocation can be subtle and is a commonly missed diagnosis.
	◦ Proper identification is critical, as mismanagement leads to significant long-term disability.
	◦ The injury is classified using the **Bado classification system**, which is based on the direction of the radial head dislocation.
sections.etiology:
• The mechanism of injury dictates the fracture pattern and direction of dislocation.
	◦ **Primary Mechanism:** Fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH) with the forearm in forced **hyperpronation** or **hyperextension**.
		▪ The force is transmitted up the forearm. The ulna, being the more rigid bone, fractures first.
		▪ The continued force then travels through the interosseous membrane to the radius, causing the weaker radiocapitellar joint to dislocate.
	◦ **Secondary Mechanism:** A direct blow to the posterior aspect of the forearm.
		▪ This force directly fractures the ulna and pushes the radius out of its articulation with the capitellum.
• The integrity of the "one-bone" forearm ring (composed of the radius, ulna, and their proximal/distal articulations) is disrupted.
	◦ A significant fracture with displacement in one bone almost always results in an injury to the joint at the other end.
sections.epidemiology:
• Relatively uncommon, accounting for <5% of all forearm fractures.
• **Bimodal age distribution:**
	◦ **Peak 1:** Children aged 4-10 years.
	◦ **Peak 2:** Young adults.
• **Bado Type I** is the most common type in both children (>75%) and adults (>60%).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents to the emergency department after a fall or direct blow to the arm, complaining of severe pain and inability to move the elbow or forearm.
• The ulnar fracture deformity may be apparent, but the elbow dislocation can be masked by swelling.
• **Crucial Clinical Point:** Always maintain a high index of suspicion for a radial head dislocation in any patient with a proximal ulna fracture.
	◦ The mantra is to **image the joint above and below** any long bone fracture.
sections.diagnostics:
• **X-rays:**
	◦ **Required Views:**
		▪ AP and lateral views of the **entire forearm**, ensuring both the elbow and wrist joints are included.
	◦ **Key Finding (The Diagnostic Line):** The **Radiocapitellar Line**.
		▪ A line drawn through the center of the radial shaft and neck should **always intersect the capitellum** on *every* radiographic view.
		▪ If this line does not point to the capitellum, the radial head is dislocated, and a Monteggia fracture is diagnosed.
	◦ The ulnar fracture is usually easily visualized on the proximal third of the bone.
	◦ **Bado Classification (based on direction of radial head dislocation):**
		▪ **Type I (60-75%):** **Anterior** dislocation of the radial head. Associated with an anteriorly-angulated (apex posterior) ulnar fracture.
		▪ **Type II (15%):** **Posterior** dislocation of the radial head. Associated with a posteriorly-angulated (apex anterior) ulnar fracture.
		▪ **Type III (5-20%):** **Lateral** or anterolateral dislocation of the radial head. Associated with a fracture of the ulnar metaphysis.
		▪ **Type IV (<5%):** **Anterior** dislocation of the radial head with an associated fracture of **both the radius and ulna**.
sections.prognosis:
• **Children:** Excellent prognosis with prompt diagnosis and treatment.
	◦ Most regain full function with minimal complications.
• **Adults:** Good prognosis, but the risk of complications is higher.
	◦ **Stiffness** (loss of motion) is the most frequent long-term issue.
	◦ Outcomes are directly related to the quality of the ulnar reduction and the stability of the radiocapitellar joint.

sections.overview:
• A **Galeazzi fracture** is an unstable fracture of the **distal third of the radial shaft** with an associated **dislocation or instability of the distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ)**.
    ◦ It is considered a fracture-dislocation of the forearm.
    ◦ Due to its inherent instability, it is often called a **"fracture of necessity,"** as it almost always requires surgical intervention in adults for a good functional outcome.
sections.etiology:
• The primary mechanism of injury is a **fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH)** with the forearm in a **hyperpronated** position, combined with an axial load.
    ◦ **Fracture Mechanism:** The axial load and rotational force cause the radius to fracture at its weakest point, typically the junction of the middle and distal thirds.
    ◦ **DRUJ Dislocation:** The force of the injury is transmitted through the interosseous membrane to the ulna.
        ▪ This disrupts the **Triangular Fibrocartilage Complex (TFCC)** and the radioulnar ligaments, which are the primary stabilizers of the DRUJ, leading to its dislocation.
        ▪ The radius shortens due to the fracture, further exacerbating the DRUJ displacement.
sections.epidemiology:
• Relatively uncommon, accounting for 3-7% of all forearm fractures.
• Most frequently occurs in young to middle-aged adults, with a male predominance.
• Bimodal age distribution:
    ◦ Younger patients: High-energy trauma (e.g., motor vehicle accidents, contact sports).
    ◦ Older patients: Low-energy falls (less common).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with a history of acute trauma to the forearm or wrist, holding the injured arm protectively against their body.
• There is often an obvious deformity of the forearm and wrist.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **X-rays:** The primary diagnostic tool.
        ▪ **Required Views:** AP and Lateral views of the **entire forearm**, including dedicated views of the **wrist and elbow joints.**
        ▪ Failure to include the entire forearm can lead to a missed DRUJ dislocation.
    ◦ **Radiographic Findings:**
        ▪ **Radial Fracture:** Transverse or oblique fracture at the junction of the middle and distal thirds of the radius.
        ▪ **DRUJ Dislocation:**
            ◦ **Widening of the DRUJ space** on the AP view.
            ◦ **Dorsal or volar displacement of the ulna** relative to the radius on the lateral view.
            ◦ **Radial shortening** of >5mm relative to the ulna.
            ◦ Associated **ulnar styloid fracture** (present in ~60% of cases, highly suggestive of TFCC injury and DRUJ instability).
• **CT Scan:** Rarely needed but can be useful for surgical planning in complex fracture patterns or to better evaluate the DRUJ.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** with prompt and accurate diagnosis followed by anatomic ORIF of the radius and stabilization of the DRUJ.
• **Poor outcomes** are strongly associated with a missed DRUJ injury, inadequate radial reduction, or persistent DRUJ instability.
    ◦ The status of the DRUJ is the primary determinant of long-term function.

sections.overview:
• A **Colles fracture** is an extra-articular fracture of the distal radius with **dorsal displacement** and **dorsal angulation** of the distal fragment.
• It is one of the most common fractures of the upper extremity.
• The fracture line is typically located within 2-3 cm of the articular surface of the radius.
• It is often associated with a fracture of the ulnar styloid process.
sections.etiology:
• **Mechanism of Injury (MOI)**
    ◦ The classic mechanism is a **Fall On an Outstretched Hand (FOOSH)** with the wrist in **extension** and the forearm in pronation.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ A compressive force is transmitted from the carpal bones (specifically the scaphoid and lunate) to the distal radius.
    ◦ The force, combined with the extended position of the wrist, causes the distal radial metaphysis (an area of weaker trabecular bone) to fail.
    ◦ The distal fragment is displaced and angulated in a dorsal direction, while the proximal fragment is displaced volarly.
    ◦ Avulsion of the ulnar styloid process occurs in ~60% of cases due to tension on the ulnar collateral ligament.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Bimodal Age Distribution**
    ◦ **Young Adults:** Typically due to high-energy trauma (e.g., motor vehicle accidents, falls from height, contact sports).
    ◦ **Elderly (especially postmenopausal women):** Most common demographic. Typically due to low-energy trauma (e.g., a simple fall from standing height) secondary to **osteoporosis**.
• It is the most common fracture of the distal radius.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Osteoporosis:** The single most significant risk factor. Decreased bone mineral density makes the distal radius highly susceptible to fracture from low-energy falls.
• **Advanced Age:** Associated with decreased bone density, impaired balance, and increased fall risk.
• **Female Gender:** Higher prevalence of **osteoporosis**.
• **Participation in high-risk sports/activities:** Snowboarding, skiing, contact sports.
• **Poor nutrition / Vitamin D deficiency.**
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient, often elderly, presents to the emergency department or urgent care clinic immediately following a fall, cradling their injured wrist.
• They report immediate, severe pain and are unable to use the affected hand.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ Acute, severe pain at the wrist.
    ◦ Rapid onset of swelling and ecchymosis.
    ◦ Obvious deformity of the wrist.
    ◦ Inability to bear weight or move the wrist/hand.
    ◦ Numbness or tingling in the fingers, especially the thumb, index, and middle fingers (suggesting **median nerve** involvement).
• **Exam Findings**
    ◦ **Inspection**
        ▪ **"Dinner Fork" Deformity:** The classic finding. A dorsal displacement of the distal fragment creates a shape resembling a dinner fork when viewed from the side (lateral view).
        ▪ Gross edema and ecchymosis around the wrist.
    ◦ **Palpation**
        ▪ Marked point tenderness over the distal radius.
        ▪ Crepitus may be felt with gentle palpation or movement.
    ◦ **Range of Motion (ROM)**
        ▪ Severely limited and painful active and passive ROM of the wrist (flexion, extension, supination, pronation).
    ◦ **Neurovascular Assessment (CRITICAL)**
        ▪ **Neurologic:**
            ◦ **Median Nerve:** Most commonly injured. Assess sensation over the palmar aspect of the thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the ring finger. Test motor function by having the patient make an "OK" sign (abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis). Paresthesias may indicate **acute carpal tunnel syndrome**.
            ◦ **Ulnar & Radial Nerves:** Assess sensation and motor function in their respective distributions.
        ▪ **Vascular:**
            ◦ Assess radial pulse.
            ◦ Check capillary refill in the nail beds (<2-3 seconds).
            ◦ Note skin color and temperature.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **X-ray:** The primary diagnostic modality.
        ▪ **Views:** Anteroposterior (AP), Lateral, and often Oblique views are required.
        ▪ **Lateral View Findings:**
            ◦ **Dorsal displacement** of the distal radial fragment.
            ◦ **Dorsal angulation** of the distal articular surface.
        ▪ **AP View Findings:**
            ◦ **Radial shortening:** The distal radius appears shorter relative to the ulna (loss of radial height).
            ◦ **Loss of radial inclination:** The normal tilt of the articular surface is reduced or reversed.
            ◦ Assess for an associated ulnar styloid fracture.
    ◦ **CT Scan:**
        ▪ Not routinely ordered.
        ▪ Reserved for complex, severely comminuted, or intra-articular fractures to aid in pre-operative planning.
sections.treatment:
• **Non-Operative (Closed Reduction and Casting/Splinting)**
    ◦ **Indications:** For stable, extra-articular, non-displaced or minimally displaced fractures that are reducible.
    ◦ **Acceptable alignment post-reduction:** <5° dorsal angulation, <2-3 mm radial shortening.
• **Operative (Surgical Fixation)**
    ◦ **Indications:**
        ▪ Unstable fractures.
        ▪ Significant **dorsal angulation (>20°)**
        ▪ Severe comminution
        ▪ Significant **radial shortening (>5mm)**
        ▪ **Intra-articular displacement (>2mm)**
        ▪ **Open fractures**
        ▪ Failure to maintain reduction with closed methods.
    ◦ **Procedures:**
        ▪ **Open Reduction Internal Fixation (ORIF) with a volar plate:** The most common surgical approach. Provides stable fixation, allowing for early ROM.
        ▪ **External Fixation:** Used for severely comminuted or open fractures.
        ▪ **Percutaneous Pinning:** A less invasive option for certain fracture patterns.
sections.management:
• **Initial**
    ◦ Assess and document a thorough neurovascular exam before and after any intervention.
    ◦ Provide adequate analgesia (e.g., NSAIDs, opioids).
    ◦ Reduce and immobilize the fracture.
    ◦ Obtain post-reduction x-rays to confirm acceptable alignment.
• **Follow-Up**
    ◦ Patient should be instructed on RICE (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation).
    ◦ Weekly follow-up with repeat x-rays for the first 2-3 weeks to monitor for loss of reduction.
    ◦ After cast removal, initiate physical or occupational therapy to restore strength and range of motion.
• **Orthopedic Referral**
    ◦ All but the most simple, non-displaced fractures should be referred to orthopedics for management or consultation.
    ◦ Unstable fractures or those with neurovascular compromise require emergent orthopedic consultation.
sections.complications:
• **Acute**
    ◦ **Median Nerve Neuropraxia / Acute Carpal Tunnel Syndrome:** **Most common nerve complication.** Characterized by paresthesias in the median nerve distribution. May require urgent carpal tunnel release if symptoms are severe or do not improve after reduction.
    ◦ **Compartment Syndrome:** A rare but limb-threatening emergency. Suspect with **pain out of proportion** to injury, tense swelling, and pain with passive finger extension. Requires emergent fasciotomy.
    ◦ **Extensor Pollicis Longus (EPL) Tendon Rupture:** Can occur weeks to months post-injury due to ischemia or mechanical irritation from the fracture callus. Patient presents with inability to extend the thumb at the IP joint.
• **Chronic / Late**
    ◦ **Malunion:** **Most common overall complication.** The fracture heals in a non-anatomic position, which can lead to the classic "dinner fork" deformity, decreased ROM (especially supination), wrist pain, and reduced grip strength.
    ◦ **Post-Traumatic Osteoarthritis:** Particularly common with intra-articular fractures.
    ◦ **Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS):** A debilitating condition characterized by severe pain, swelling, stiffness, and autonomic dysfunction (changes in skin color and temperature).
    ◦ **Stiffness (Contracture):** Loss of wrist, finger, or shoulder motion due to prolonged immobilization.
sections.prognosis:
• Generally good, especially in younger patients with non-comminuted, extra-articular fractures.
• Outcomes are dependent on the severity of the initial injury, the quality of the reduction, bone quality, and patient adherence to rehabilitation.
• Elderly patients with **osteoporosis** have a higher risk of complications like **malunion** and chronic stiffness.

sections.overview:
• A **Smith fracture** is a fracture of the distal radius characterized by **volar (palmar) angulation or displacement** of the distal fracture fragment.
    ◦ It is often referred to as a **"reverse Colles' fracture"** because the mechanism of injury and resulting deformity are the opposite of the more common Colles' fracture.
sections.etiology:
• The fracture is typically caused by one of two mechanisms:
    ◦ **Fall Onto a Flexed Wrist (FOFW):** A fall onto the back of the hand, forcing the wrist into hyperflexion. The ground pushes the distal radius fragment in a volar direction.
    ◦ **Direct Blow:** A direct, forceful blow to the dorsal aspect of the wrist.
• The deforming force causes the distal radial fragment to displace and angulate towards the palmar surface of the wrist.
• This fracture is typically extra-articular but can have intra-articular extension.
sections.epidemiology:
• Less common than Colles' fractures.
• Exhibits a bimodal age distribution:
    ◦ **Younger patients (primarily males):** Resulting from high-energy trauma (e.g., motor vehicle accidents, falls from height, contact sports).
    ◦ **Older patients (primarily females):** Resulting from low-energy trauma (e.g., a simple ground-level fall), often secondary to osteoporosis.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Osteoporosis:** The most significant risk factor in the elderly population, leading to fractures from low-energy mechanisms.
• **Advanced age:** Associated with decreased bone mineral density and increased risk of falls.
• **High-impact activities/sports:** Increases risk in younger individuals (e.g., snowboarding, football).
• **Poor balance or neuromuscular disorders:** Increases the risk of falling.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients typically present with a history of a recent fall onto a flexed wrist or a direct blow to the back of the wrist, complaining of immediate, severe pain, swelling, and an obvious deformity.
    ◦ The patient will often be cradling the injured arm with their other hand.
• Key Symptoms:
    ◦ Acute, severe wrist pain.
    ◦ Rapid onset of swelling (edema) and bruising (ecchymosis).
    ◦ Inability to move or bear weight on the wrist.
    ◦ Visible deformity of the wrist.
    ◦ Numbness or tingling in the fingers (paresthesias), particularly in the thumb, index, and middle finger, suggesting **median nerve compression**.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Inspection:**
    ◦ **"Garden spade deformity":** A characteristic visual finding where the wrist profile resembles the curve of a shovel or spade, with the hand appearing volarly displaced relative to the forearm.
    ◦ Significant edema and ecchymosis over the distal forearm and wrist.
• **Palpation:**
    ◦ Point tenderness over the distal radius.
    ◦ Assess for tenderness in the anatomic snuffbox to rule out a concomitant scaphoid fracture.
• **Range of Motion:**
    ◦ Markedly limited and painful. Active and passive ROM testing is often deferred until after imaging to avoid further displacement and pain.
• **Neurovascular Assessment (CRITICAL):**
    ◦ **Neurological:**
        ▪ **Median Nerve:** Most commonly affected nerve due to volar displacement. Assess for sensation over the palmar aspect of the thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the ring finger. Test motor function with thumb opposition ("OK" sign). Suspect **acute carpal tunnel syndrome** if symptoms are present.
        ▪ **Ulnar & Radial Nerves:** Assess sensation and motor function in their respective distributions.
    ◦ **Vascular:**
        ▪ Check the radial and ulnar pulses.
        ▪ Assess capillary refill in the nail beds (<2-3 seconds).
        ▪ Note skin color and temperature.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primary Modality: X-ray**
    ◦ **Required Views:** Anteroposterior (AP) and **Lateral**.
    ◦ **Key Finding:** The **lateral view is essential** for diagnosis. It will clearly demonstrate the characteristic **volar angulation and displacement** of the distal radial fragment.
    ◦ **Other Findings:** The AP view helps assess for intra-articular extension, fracture comminution, radial shortening, and associated **ulnar styloid fracture** (present in ~50% of cases).
• **Secondary Modality: CT Scan**
    ◦ **Indications:** Not routinely needed. Indicated for complex, comminuted, or intra-articular fractures to better define the fracture pattern and assist with pre-operative planning.
sections.treatment:
• **Non-Operative:**
    ◦ **Indications:** Stable, extra-articular, and minimally displaced/angulated fractures that are amenable to closed reduction.
    ◦ **Procedure:**
        ▪ **Initial:** **Sugar tong splint** is applied to allow for swelling while immobilizing the wrist and preventing pronation/supination.
        ▪ **Definitive:** Converted to a **short arm cast** after 7-10 days once initial swelling has subsided. Total immobilization is typically for 4-6 weeks.
• **Operative:**
    ◦ **Indications:** Unstable fractures, significant displacement (>20° angulation, >2mm articular step-off), comminution, intra-articular involvement, open fractures, or failed closed reduction.
    ◦ **Procedure:** **Open Reduction and Internal Fixation (ORIF)** is the most common approach, typically using a **volar locking plate and screws**. This provides stable fixation, allowing for early range of motion.
sections.management:
• **Emergency Department:**
    ◦ Perform a thorough neurovascular exam before and after any intervention.
    ◦ Provide adequate analgesia.
    ◦ Perform closed reduction and apply a **sugar tong splint**.
    ◦ Obtain post-reduction films to confirm acceptable alignment.
    ◦ Discharge with strict instructions for elevation, ice, and pain control.
• **Outpatient Follow-up:**
    ◦ Mandatory orthopedic follow-up within one week.
    ◦ Serial x-rays are obtained to ensure the reduction is maintained.
    ◦ After cast removal, initiate **Physical/Occupational Therapy** to regain strength, flexibility, and function.
sections.complications:
• **Acute:**
    ◦ **Median Nerve Injury / Acute Carpal Tunnel Syndrome:** The most common neurological complication due to direct compression or swelling within the carpal tunnel. May require urgent carpal tunnel release if neurovascularly compromised.
    ◦ **Compartment Syndrome:** A surgical emergency characterized by pain out of proportion, pallor, paresthesias, pulselessness, and paralysis.
    ◦ **Associated Injuries:** Ulnar styloid fracture, Triangular Fibrocartilage Complex (TFCC) tear, scapholunate ligament injury.
• **Delayed/Chronic:**
    ◦ **Malunion:** The most common overall complication. The fracture heals in an unacceptable (volarly angulated) position, leading to the **"garden spade deformity,"** pain, and limited supination.
    ◦ **Post-traumatic Osteoarthritis:** High risk with intra-articular fractures.
    ◦ **Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS):** A chronic pain condition characterized by severe pain, swelling, and autonomic dysfunction.
    ◦ **Tendon Rupture:** Delayed rupture of the **Extensor Pollicis Longus (EPL)** tendon can occur due to irritation over the fracture site.
    ◦ **Nonunion:** Rare.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is generally good for fractures that are anatomically reduced and properly managed.
• Outcomes are worse for patients with significant intra-articular displacement, severe comminution, advanced age, or associated nerve injury.
• Early mobilization after stable fixation (ORIF) can lead to excellent functional recovery.

sections.overview:
• A **scaphoid fracture** is a break in the scaphoid bone, one of the eight small carpal bones in the wrist.
	◦ It is the most commonly fractured carpal bone.
• These fractures are clinically significant and notoriously problematic due to the scaphoid's tenuous, retrograde blood supply.
	◦ This puts it at high risk for complications such as **avascular necrosis (AVN)** and **nonunion**.
• A high index of suspicion is required, as initial radiographs are often negative.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• **Most common carpal fracture** (accounts for ~70% of all carpal fractures).
• **Population**: Most common in young, active males between 15-30 years of age.
• Less common in children and the elderly due to the relative weakness of the distal radius physis (in children) or osteoporotic bone (in the elderly), which tend to fracture first.
sections.riskFactors:
• Participation in high-impact sports (e.g., football, snowboarding, skateboarding, basketball).
• Male gender.
• Young age (15-30).
• Activities with a high risk of falling.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A young patient typically presents to the ED or clinic after a fall, complaining of wrist pain.
• The patient often dismisses the injury as a "**sprain**" because the initial swelling and pain may be subtle and not as dramatic as a distal radius fracture.
	◦ This can lead to a dangerous delay in diagnosis.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Symptoms**
	◦ Pain on the **radial side of the wrist** (thumb side).
	◦ Pain is often dull, deep, and achy.
	◦ Pain worsens with gripping, pinching, or pushing off the wrist.
	◦ Limited range of motion of the wrist, especially with extension and radial deviation.
	◦ Mild swelling and/or bruising on the dorsoradial aspect of the wrist.
• **Exam Findings**
	◦ **Anatomic Snuffbox Tenderness**
		▪ **This is the most sensitive physical exam finding.**
		▪ The **anatomic snuffbox** is a triangular depression on the radial, dorsal aspect of the hand.
		▪ **Borders**: Ulnar border is the tendon of the **extensor pollicis longus (EPL)**. Radial border is the combined tendons of the **abductor pollicis longus (APL)** and **extensor pollicis brevis (EPB)**.
		▪ Tenderness to palpation in this region is highly suspicious for a scaphoid fracture.
	◦ **Scaphoid Tubercle Tenderness**
		▪ Palpation of the scaphoid tubercle on the volar (palmar) aspect of the wrist at the base of the thenar eminence.
	◦ **Pain with Axial Loading of the Thumb**
		▪ Applying longitudinal pressure along the axis of the thumb metacarpal elicits pain at the scaphoid.
	◦ Pain with resisted supination.
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.management:
• **Non-displaced**: Place in a **thumb spica cast/splint** and arrange for orthopedic follow-up.
• **Displaced**: Place in a **thumb spica splint** and obtain an **urgent orthopedic consult** for probable surgical management.
• **Crucial step**: Do NOT discharge as a simple "**sprain**."
• **Option A (Conservative)**: Place the patient in a **thumb spica splint** and have them follow up in 10-14 days for repeat radiographs.
	◦ Advise them to treat it as a fracture.
• **Option B (Definitive)**: Obtain an **MRI** (or CT) to definitively rule in or rule out an occult fracture.
	◦ This is often the preferred approach for athletes or when a definitive diagnosis is needed promptly.
sections.complications:
• **Avascular Necrosis (AVN)**
	◦ Most common and feared complication, especially with **proximal pole fractures**.
	◦ Radiographically seen as increased sclerosis (whiteness) of the proximal fragment.
• **Nonunion or Delayed Union**
	◦ Failure of the fracture to heal, often requiring surgery with bone grafting.
	◦ Risk increases with displacement, proximal location, and delayed diagnosis.
• **Scaphoid Nonunion Advanced Collapse (SNAC Wrist)**
	◦ The long-term consequence of an untreated nonunion.
	◦ This leads to altered wrist kinematics, progressive cartilage wear, and debilitating degenerative arthritis.
• **Malunion**: Healing in an improper position, which can cause pain and limited motion.
• **Osteoarthritis** of the radiocarpal joint.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**: For non-displaced distal pole fractures treated appropriately.
• **Good**: For non-displaced waist fractures diagnosed and immobilized early.
• **Guarded/Poor**: For displaced fractures and proximal pole fractures, which have a high rate of nonunion and **AVN** even with optimal treatment.
• **Key Factor**: Early diagnosis and appropriate immobilization are critical for a good outcome.

sections.overview:
• A **Boxer Fracture** is a common extra-articular fracture of the neck of the **fifth metacarpal bone**
    ◦ Named for the typical mechanism of injury: striking a hard object with a closed fist
    ◦ The fracture typically exhibits **volar (palmar) angulation** of the distal fragment (the metacarpal head) due to the pull of the interosseous muscles
sections.etiology:
• **Mechanism**: **Direct axial load** applied to the metacarpal head with a clenched fist
    ◦ Most commonly occurs when punching a hard, immovable object (e.g., a wall, a door) or during a physical altercation
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ Force is transmitted down the shaft of the 5th metacarpal
    ◦ The **metacarpal neck** is the weakest point and fails under the compressive load, resulting in a **transverse fracture**
    ◦ The flexed position of the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint during impact, combined with the pull of the intrinsic hand muscles (interossei), causes the characteristic **volar displacement/angulation** of the metacarpal head
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Accounts for approximately **10% of all hand fractures** and is the **most common metacarpal fracture**
• **Demographics**: Predominantly affects **young males**, typically between the ages of 15 and 35
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patient typically presents with an acute history of **punching an object**, followed by immediate **pain, swelling, and deformity** over the **ulnar aspect of the hand**
    ◦ Patient will often be guarding the injured hand
sections.diagnostics:
• **Plain Radiographs (X-ray)**
    ◦ **Views**: Anteroposterior (AP), lateral, and oblique views of the hand
        ▪ The **lateral view is the most important** for diagnosis and management, as it allows for accurate measurement of the degree of **volar angulation** of the metacarpal head
    ◦ **Findings**: A **transverse fracture** through the neck of the 5th metacarpal with **volar angulation** of the distal fracture fragment
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is generally **excellent** with appropriate treatment
• Most patients return to their previous level of function
• A cosmetic deformity (**depressed knuckle**) may persist even with acceptable angulation but is rarely functionally significant
• Outcomes are poorer if a **rotational deformity** is missed or if a "**fight bite**" becomes infected

sections.overview:
• An injury to the **ulnar collateral ligament (UCL)** of the thumb's **metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint**.
	◦ The UCL is a critical stabilizer that prevents excessive valgus stress (abduction) of the thumb.
	◦ This injury leads to instability, pain, and weakness, particularly with pincer grasp.
• **Skier's Thumb**: Refers to an **acute** traumatic rupture of the UCL.
• **Gamekeeper's Thumb**: Refers to a **chronic** injury resulting from repetitive stress, leading to ligamentous laxity and instability over time.
sections.etiology:
• The injury is caused by **forced abduction and/or hyperextension** of the thumb at the MCP joint.
	◦ This valgus force stresses the UCL beyond its tensile strength, causing it to sprain (partial tear) or rupture (complete tear).
• **Mechanism**
	◦ A common example is a skier falling while holding a ski pole, which forces the thumb into abduction.
	◦ Other mechanisms include a fall onto an outstretched hand (FOOSH) or having the thumb forcefully bent backward during sports.
• **Pathophysiology**
	◦ **Grade I**: Ligament sprain (stretched fibers), no instability.
	◦ **Grade II**: Partial tear of the ligament, some laxity but a firm endpoint on valgus stress testing.
	◦ **Grade III**: Complete rupture of the ligament, significant instability and no firm endpoint.
	◦ **Stener Lesion**: A critical variant of a complete UCL rupture where the proximal end of the torn ligament is displaced superficially and proximally to the **adductor pollicis aponeurosis**.
		▪ This displaced ligament becomes trapped, preventing it from healing back to its insertion site.
		▪ **A Stener lesion requires surgical intervention.**
sections.epidemiology:
• The most common ligamentous injury of the thumb.
• Most frequently seen in athletes, particularly skiers, accounting for a significant portion of all skiing injuries.
• Also common in football, basketball, rugby, and hockey players.
• Affects males more often than females, consistent with participation in high-risk sports.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with a history of a specific traumatic event involving the thumb.
• They will complain of pain, swelling, and difficulty using the affected hand for gripping or pinching activities.
sections.diagnostics:
• **X-rays (AP, lateral, oblique views of the thumb)**
	◦ **First-line imaging.**
	◦ Primarily used to rule out an associated **avulsion fracture** from the base of the proximal phalanx where the UCL inserts.
		▪ This is known as a "bony Gamekeeper's thumb."
	◦ May be normal in a purely ligamentous injury.
• **Stress Radiography**
	◦ X-rays taken while applying valgus stress.
	◦ Can be used to objectively demonstrate joint space widening and instability.
	◦ Often painful for the patient.
• **MRI**
	◦ **Gold standard for soft tissue evaluation.**
	◦ Highly sensitive and specific for diagnosing UCL tears.
	◦ Crucially, it can identify the presence and location of a **Stener lesion**.
• **Ultrasound**
	◦ Can be used to visualize the UCL and identify tears.
	◦ It is operator-dependent but allows for dynamic testing.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for partial tears treated with immobilization.
• **Good to Excellent** for complete tears treated with timely surgical repair.
• **Poor** for untreated complete tears (especially with a Stener lesion), which almost always leads to chronic instability, weakness, and eventual arthritis.

sections.overview:
• **Nursemaid Elbow**, also known as radial head subluxation or "pulled elbow," is a common and benign musculoskeletal injury in young children.
    ◦ It is a **subluxation**, not a true dislocation, where the head of the radius slips out from under the **annular ligament**.
    ◦ The diagnosis is primarily **clinical**, and treatment involves a simple closed reduction maneuver that provides immediate relief.
sections.etiology:
• **Mechanism of Injury**: Occurs from a sudden longitudinal (axial) traction on a **pronated forearm** with the elbow in **extension**.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ The axial pull on the hand/wrist causes the radial head to be pulled distally through the annular ligament.
    ◦ The annular ligament, which normally encircles the radial neck, slips over the head of the radius.
    ◦ When traction is released, the ligament becomes **entrapped in the radiohumeral joint**.
• **Anatomic Predisposition**:
    ◦ In young children (<5 years), the annular ligament is relatively thin and lax.
    ◦ The radial head is not as developed (more spherical), making it easier for subluxation to occur.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Peak Age**: 1 to 4 years old.
• **Incidence**: Most common upper extremity injury in children under 6 years.
• **Rare after age 5**: The annular ligament becomes thicker and stronger, and the radial head develops a more prominent shape.
• **Sex**: Slightly more common in females.
• **Affected Side**: More common in the **left arm**, possibly because most caregivers are right-handed.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Age**: 1-4 years.
• **Mechanism-related activities**:
    ◦ Lifting or swinging a child by their hands or forearms.
    ◦ Pulling a child's arm to hurry them along or prevent a fall.
    ◦ A fall onto an outstretched hand (less common mechanism).
    ◦ Rolling over in a crib and trapping the arm.
• **History**: Previous history of nursemaid elbow increases the risk of recurrence.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **History**: A classic history of sudden **axial traction** is often reported, with the child crying out in pain immediately after the event.
• **Behavior**: Following the initial pain, the child will pointedly **refuse to use the affected arm**.
• **Position of Arm**: The child holds the arm in a characteristic protective posture:
    ◦ Slightly **flexed** at the elbow.
    ◦ Held close to the body (**adducted**).
    ◦ Forearm is fully **pronated**.
• **Symptoms**:
    ◦ **Acute Pain**: Sudden onset of pain at the time of injury.
    ◦ **Functional Deficit**: The hallmark symptom is the **refusal to use the arm**; the child will not reach for toys or bear weight with that arm.
    ◦ **Minimal Ongoing Pain**: After the initial injury, the child is often not in distress unless the arm is moved, particularly into supination.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Observation**: Note the classic **pronated, slightly flexed posture**; the arm will appear grossly normal.
• **Key Negative Findings**: **Absence** of significant swelling, ecchymosis, erythema, or obvious deformity. These signs would suggest a more serious injury like a fracture.
• **Palpation**: Mild point tenderness may be elicited over the anterolateral aspect of the elbow (over the **radial head**).
• **Range of Motion**:
    ◦ The child will actively **resist any passive attempt at supination** of the forearm.
    ◦ Elbow flexion and extension are often preserved but may be guarded.
• **Neurovascular Exam**: Distal pulses, sensation, and motor function in the hand and fingers should be intact and documented.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primarily a Clinical Diagnosis**: Made based on the characteristic history and physical exam findings.
• **Radiographs (X-rays)**:
    ◦ **Not routinely indicated** if the presentation is classic.
    ◦ **Consider X-rays if**:
        ▪ The mechanism of injury is unclear or involves significant trauma (e.g., high-energy fall).
        ▪ There is focal bony tenderness, significant swelling, or deformity concerning for a **fracture** (especially a **supracondylar fracture**).
        ▪ Reduction attempts are unsuccessful.
    ◦ **Findings**: If obtained, X-rays in an uncomplicated nursemaid elbow are **typically normal**; their main utility is to rule out fracture or dislocation.
sections.treatment:
• **Closed Reduction**: This is the definitive treatment and can be performed without sedation.
• **Reduction Techniques**:
    ◦ **Supination/Flexion Technique**:
        ▪ Place a thumb over the child's radial head.
        ▪ With the other hand, hold the child's wrist.
        ▪ Firmly and quickly **supinate** the child's forearm and then fully **flex** the elbow.
        ▪ A palpable or audible **"click"** or **"pop"** is often felt upon reduction.
    ◦ **Hyperpronation Technique**:
        ▪ Place a thumb over the child's radial head.
        ▪ With the other hand, hold the child's wrist.
        ▪ Firmly **hyperpronate** the forearm.
        ▪ This method is considered by some studies to be more successful and less painful.
• **Confirmation of Successful Reduction**: The most reliable sign is the child **spontaneously beginning to use the arm normally within 5-15 minutes**.
sections.management:
• **Post-Reduction Care**:
    ◦ **Observation**: Observe the child in the clinic for 15-30 minutes post-reduction. Offer them a toy or sticker to encourage them to use the arm.
    ◦ **Immobilization**: Not necessary.
    ◦ **Analgesia**: Typically not needed, but acetaminophen or ibuprofen can be used for residual soreness.
• **Parental Education**:
    ◦ Reassure parents that this is a common, benign injury and not a result of abuse.
    ◦ Educate on prevention: Advise against lifting or swinging the child by the hands or forearms. Instruct them to lift the child from under the axillae.
• **Follow-up**: Not required if reduction is successful and the child returns to normal function.
sections.complications:
• **Recurrence**: The most common complication, occurring in 20-40% of cases. The risk decreases as the child gets older.
• **Failed Reduction**: If 2-3 attempts are unsuccessful, reconsider the diagnosis, obtain radiographs to rule out fracture, and consider orthopedic consultation.
• **Iatrogenic Fracture**: Extremely rare complication from a forceful reduction maneuver.
• **Chronic/Irreducible Subluxation**: Very rare; may occur if the diagnosis is delayed for several days.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**: After successful reduction, there is an immediate and complete return to normal function with no long-term sequelae.
    ◦ The predisposition to subluxation resolves spontaneously around age 5.
sections.preventionEducation:
• **Reassurance**: Reassure parents that this is a common, benign injury and not a result of abuse.
• **Prevention Education**: 
    ◦ Advise against lifting or swinging the child by the hands, wrists, or forearms.
    ◦ Instruct caregivers to lift the child from under the axillae (armpits).

sections.overview:
• A hip fracture is a break in the proximal third of the femur, a common and serious injury primarily affecting the elderly population that is almost always treated surgically
    ◦ These fractures are classified based on their anatomical location, which dictates the treatment approach and potential complications
    ◦ The primary goal of management is to restore function and mobility as quickly as possible to minimize the high rates of morbidity and mortality associated with this injury
sections.etiology:
• **Mechanism of Injury**
    ◦ **Low-Energy (Most Common):** A fall from standing height in an elderly individual with osteoporotic bone. The force is typically applied directly to the greater trochanter
    ◦ **High-Energy:** Motor vehicle accidents, falls from a significant height. This is the more common mechanism in younger patients with healthy bone
    ◦ **Stress Fracture:** Occurs in athletes (e.g., long-distance runners) or military recruits due to repetitive microtrauma
    ◦ **Pathologic Fracture:** Fracture through a bone weakened by a tumor (metastatic or primary), infection, or other metabolic bone disease
• **Anatomic Classification & Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Intracapsular Fractures (Femoral Neck / Subcapital):**
        ▪ Occur within the hip joint capsule
        ▪ The blood supply to the femoral head is tenuous, arising primarily from the **medial femoral circumflex artery** via retinacular vessels
        ▪ Displaced femoral neck fractures can disrupt this blood supply, leading to a high risk of **Avascular Necrosis (AVN)** and **nonunion**
        ▪ **Garden Classification** is used for femoral neck fractures:
            • **Garden I:** Incomplete, valgus impacted
            • **Garden II:** Complete, non-displaced
            • **Garden III:** Complete, partially displaced
            • **Garden IV:** Complete, fully displaced
    ◦ **Extracapsular Fractures (Intertrochanteric / Subtrochanteric):**
        ▪ Occur outside the joint capsule in an area of rich, cancellous bone with an excellent blood supply
        ▪ **AVN is rare**
        ▪ These fractures are associated with more significant **blood loss** and soft tissue injury
        ▪ **Intertrochanteric:** Fracture line runs between the greater and lesser trochanters
        ▪ **Subtrochanteric:** Fracture occurs in the region from the lesser trochanter down to 5 cm distal
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence:** Over 300,000 cases annually in the United States
• **Age:** Vast majority occur in patients >65 years old; average age is ~80
• **Sex:** Females > Males (approx. 3:1 ratio), strongly correlated with the higher prevalence of postmenopausal osteoporosis
sections.riskFactors:
• **Major:**
    ◦ **Advanced Age**
    ◦ **Osteoporosis**
    ◦ **Female Sex**
    ◦ **History of a prior fragility fracture**
• **Other Significant Factors:**
    ◦ Frequent falls / gait instability
    ◦ Dementia or cognitive impairment
    ◦ Low body weight / Frailty
    ◦ Vitamin D deficiency
    ◦ Polypharmacy (especially sedatives, hypnotics, antipsychotics)
    ◦ Corticosteroid use
    ◦ Smoking and excessive alcohol consumption
    ◦ Environmental hazards (e.g., loose rugs)
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is an elderly patient who sustained a low-energy fall and now presents with an inability to ambulate, often found on the floor after a "slip and fall" at home
    ◦ Severe, acute pain in the hip, groin, or thigh
    ◦ Inability to bear weight on the affected leg
    ◦ Pain is exacerbated by any attempted movement of the hip
    ◦ Some patients with impacted or non-displaced fractures may present with less severe pain and may even be able to bear some weight
sections.physicalExam:
• **Classic Deformity (Displaced Fracture):** The affected leg appears **shortened, abducted, and externally rotated**
• Tenderness to palpation over the inguinal region or greater trochanter
• Severe pain with any passive range of motion of the hip (especially internal/external rotation)
• Ecchymosis or swelling may be present around the hip
• Always perform a full neurovascular exam of the lower extremity (pulses, sensation, motor function)
sections.diagnostics:
• **Imaging:**
    ◦ **Initial:**
        ▪ **AP Pelvis X-ray:** Essential for comparison with the contralateral hip and to rule out pelvic fractures
        ▪ **Cross-table (or Axiolateral) Lateral Hip X-ray:** Provides the orthogonal view needed to assess displacement
    ◦ **Occult Fracture:**
        ▪ If clinical suspicion is high but initial X-rays are negative, the patient should be treated as if they have a fracture until proven otherwise
        ▪ **MRI is the gold standard** for diagnosing an occult hip fracture. It is highly sensitive and specific
        ▪ CT scan can be used as an alternative if MRI is unavailable or contraindicated
• **Labs / Pre-operative Evaluation:**
    ◦ CBC (check for anemia from blood loss, especially in extracapsular fractures)
    ◦ BMP/CMP (assess renal function and electrolytes)
    ◦ PT/INR, PTT (coagulation status)
    ◦ Type and Screen
    ◦ ECG and Chest X-ray (standard for pre-operative clearance in the elderly)
sections.treatment:
• **Femoral Neck (Intracapsular):**
    ◦ **Non-displaced/Impacted (Garden I-II):**
        ▪ **Open Reduction and Internal Fixation (ORIF)** with cannulated screws or a sliding hip screw (SHS). Goal is to preserve the native femoral head
    ◦ **Displaced (Garden III-IV):**
        ▪ **Young, active patients:** Urgent ORIF to attempt to salvage the femoral head
        ▪ **Elderly patients:** **Arthroplasty (Hip Replacement)** is preferred due to the high risk of AVN and fixation failure
            • **Hemiarthroplasty:** Replaces only the femoral head. Done for lower-demand patients with no pre-existing hip arthritis
            • **Total Hip Arthroplasty (THA):** Replaces both the femoral head and the acetabulum. Better for active, independent elderly patients or those with pre-existing osteoarthritis
• **Intertrochanteric (Extracapsular):**
    ◦ Goal is stable internal fixation. AVN is not a primary concern
    ◦ **Sliding Hip Screw (SHS):** A large screw into the femoral head fixed to a side plate on the femoral shaft. Best for stable fracture patterns
    ◦ **Cephalomedullary Nail:** An intramedullary rod inserted down the femur with a screw going into the femoral head. Preferred for unstable or reverse obliquity fracture patterns
• **Non-operative Management:** Reserved for the rare cases of non-ambulatory patients with minimal pain or those who are medically unstable for surgery and have a terminal prognosis
sections.management:
• **Pain Control:** Multimodal approach including scheduled opioids, acetaminophen, and regional nerve blocks (fascia iliaca or femoral nerve block) to reduce opioid consumption
• **DVT Prophylaxis:** **CRITICAL.** Begin pharmacologic prophylaxis (e.g., Lovenox, Eliquis) as soon as possible, pre- or post-operatively, unless contraindicated
• **Medical Optimization:** Address and manage comorbidities (CHF, CKD, anemia) prior to surgery
• **Post-operative Care:**
    ◦ **Early Mobilization:** Physical and Occupational Therapy should begin on post-op day 1
    ◦ **Weight-Bearing Status:** Varies by fracture type and fixation (e.g., often weight-bearing as tolerated after arthroplasty)
    ◦ **Osteoporosis Management:** Initiate Vitamin D and calcium supplementation. Consider bisphosphonate therapy
    ◦ **Delirium Prevention:** Avoid anticholinergics and benzodiazepines, maintain sleep-wake cycles, ensure hydration
sections.complications:
• **Immobility-Related:**
    ◦ **DVT / Pulmonary Embolism (PE):** The most dangerous early complication
    ◦ Pneumonia (atelectasis)
    ◦ Decubitus ulcers (pressure sores)
    ◦ Urinary Tract Infections (UTI)
    ◦ Delirium
    ◦ Muscle atrophy
• **Surgical/Fracture-Related:**
    ◦ **Avascular Necrosis (AVN):** High risk with displaced femoral neck fractures
    ◦ **Nonunion:** Failure of the fracture to heal
    ◦ Malunion
    ◦ Infection
    ◦ Implant failure
sections.prognosis:
• **Mortality:** Hip fracture is associated with a significant increase in mortality
    ◦ **1-year mortality rate is as high as 20-30%**
• **Functional Decline:**
    ◦ Less than 50% of patients return to their pre-fracture level of independence
    ◦ A large percentage require assistive devices (walker, cane) or transfer to a long-term care facility

sections.overview:
• A hip dislocation is a traumatic displacement of the femoral head from the acetabulum of the pelvis.
• It is an **orthopedic emergency** requiring prompt reduction to minimize the risk of long-term complications.
• Dislocations are classified by the direction of the femoral head's displacement relative to the acetabulum: **posterior**, **anterior**, or **central**.
sections.etiology:
• Hip dislocations are almost always the result of **high-energy trauma** that overwhelms the stability of the joint, tearing the joint capsule and supporting ligaments.
    ◦ **Posterior Dislocation (~90% of cases)**:
        ▪ **Mechanism**: Caused by an axial load applied to a **flexed, adducted, and internally rotated hip**.
        ▪ **Classic Scenario**: A **"dashboard injury"** in a motor vehicle accident (MVA), where the knee strikes the dashboard, forcing the femoral head posteriorly out of the acetabulum. Also seen in falls from height or contact sports.
        ▪ **Associated Injuries**: Acetabular posterior wall fractures, femoral head fractures (**Pipkin fractures**), and **sciatic nerve injury**.
    ◦ **Anterior Dislocation (~10% of cases)**:
        ▪ **Mechanism**: Caused by forced **abduction, external rotation, and extension** of the hip.
        ▪ **Classic Scenario**: MVA or athletic injury where the hip is forcefully externally rotated and abducted.
        ▪ **Associated Injuries**: Femoral head impaction fractures, femoral nerve injury.
    ◦ **Central Dislocation (Fracture-Dislocation)**:
        ▪ **Mechanism**: A direct, high-energy impact to the lateral aspect of the hip (greater trochanter), driving the femoral head medially through a fractured acetabular floor.
        ▪ This is by definition associated with an **acetabular fracture**.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ The primary concern is the disruption of blood supply to the femoral head.
    ◦ The **medial circumflex femoral artery** provides the majority of the blood supply via the retinacular vessels.
    ◦ Dislocation can stretch, tear, or tamponade these vessels, leading to ischemia and potentially **avascular necrosis (AVN)** of the femoral head.
    ◦ The risk of AVN increases significantly if the hip is not reduced within **6 hours**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Primary demographic**: Young adults (16-40 years) involved in **high-energy trauma**.
• **Bimodal distribution**: A second peak occurs in the elderly population, often from lower-energy mechanisms like falls, especially in patients with a total hip arthroplasty (prosthetic dislocation).
• **Posterior dislocations** are the most common type, accounting for **85-90%** of all traumatic hip dislocations.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The patient typically presents to the emergency department immediately following a significant traumatic event.
• The presentation is dramatic, with the patient in obvious **severe pain** and unable to move the affected limb.
• A detailed history of the mechanism of injury is crucial.
sections.diagnostics:
• **X-ray**:
    ◦ **AP Pelvis and cross-table lateral views** are the initial studies of choice.
    ◦ **Findings**:
        ▪ The femoral head will be visibly displaced from the acetabulum.
        ▪ In **posterior dislocation**, the femoral head appears **smaller** than the contralateral side.
        ▪ In **anterior dislocation**, the femoral head appears **larger**.
    ◦ **Shenton's line** (a smooth arc along the inferior border of the femoral neck and the superior pubic ramus) will be **disrupted**.
    ◦ Carefully inspect for associated fractures of the femoral head/neck or acetabulum.
• **CT Scan**:
    ◦ **A post-reduction CT scan is the standard of care**.
    ◦ **Purpose**:
        ▪ Evaluate for **intra-articular loose bodies** (bone or cartilage fragments).
        ▪ Identify associated, occult fractures not visible on plain films (e.g., femoral head impaction, acetabular rim fracture).
        ▪ Assess the congruity of the joint after reduction.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is good if prompt reduction (**<6 hours**) is achieved with no associated fractures or complications.
• The development of **AVN** or severe **post-traumatic arthritis** significantly worsens the prognosis and often necessitates a total hip arthroplasty in the future.
• Nerve injury recovery is variable.

sections.overview:
• A femoral shaft fracture is a break in the **diaphysis of the femur**, occurring between the lesser trochanter and the supracondylar flare.
• It is a major orthopedic injury typically resulting from **high-energy trauma**.
• These fractures are associated with significant pain, deformity, and **blood loss**, often occurring in the context of **polytrauma**.
• The standard of care is early surgical stabilization, most commonly with an **intramedullary nail**, to restore alignment, facilitate mobilization, and reduce complications.
sections.etiology:
• **Mechanism of Injury**
    ◦ **High-Energy Trauma**: The most common cause in younger individuals.
        ▪ Examples include **motor vehicle accidents (MVAs)**, motorcycle crashes, pedestrian vs. vehicle collisions, **falls from height**, and **gunshot wounds**.
    ◦ **Low-Energy Trauma**: Common in the elderly population due to falls from a standing height, often secondary to underlying **osteoporosis**.
    ◦ **Pathologic Fractures**: The fracture occurs through bone weakened by a pre-existing condition.
        ▪ Examples include **metastatic carcinoma** (breast, lung, prostate, kidney, thyroid), primary bone tumors (e.g., osteosarcoma), or metabolic bone disease.
    ◦ **Atypical Femur Fractures (AFF)**: Transverse or short oblique fractures in the subtrochanteric or diaphyseal region with minimal or no trauma, classically associated with long-term **bisphosphonate use**.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The femur is the largest and strongest bone in the body; therefore, a significant force is required to fracture it.
    ◦ The fracture disrupts the femoral artery's nutrient vessels and surrounding muscle, leading to substantial hemorrhage (1,000-1,500 mL) into the thigh, which can cause **hypovolemic shock**.
    ◦ Powerful surrounding muscles (**quadriceps**, **hamstrings**, **adductors**) exert deforming forces on the fracture fragments, leading to characteristic displacement:
        ▪ **Proximal fragment**: **Flexed** (by **iliopsoas**), **abducted** (by **gluteus medius/minimus**), and **externally rotated**.
        ▪ **Distal fragment**: Pulled **superiorly** (by **hamstrings/quadriceps**) and **posteriorly** (by **gastrocnemius**), causing shortening and angulation.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Bimodal distribution**
    ◦ First peak: Young men aged 15-24 due to **high-energy trauma**.
    ◦ Second peak: Elderly women aged >65 due to low-energy falls complicated by **osteoporosis**.
• Incidence is approximately 10-20 per 100,000 person-years.
• About 5-10% of patients with femoral shaft fractures are **polytrauma victims**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The patient is often a **polytrauma victim** brought in by emergency medical services following a high-energy event.
• The primary survey (**ABCDEs**) per **Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS)** protocol is paramount.
• The femur fracture is a severe and **distracting injury**, but life-threatening injuries to the head, chest, and abdomen must be identified and managed first.
• The patient will be in **severe distress**, unable to move the affected leg.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **X-ray**
        ▪ **AP and Lateral views of the entire femur.** Must include the hip joint proximally and the knee joint distally to rule out associated fractures or dislocations.
        ▪ **AP Pelvis X-ray**: Standard in trauma to rule out associated pelvic ring, acetabular, or **femoral neck fractures**.
        ▪ **AP and Lateral views of the knee, tibia/fibula, and ankle** if there is clinical suspicion of injury.
    ◦ **CT Scan**
        ▪ Not required for routine diagnosis of a diaphyseal fracture.
        ▪ Indicated to further evaluate complex (e.g., **comminuted**, **segmental**) fracture patterns or to rule out a non-displaced **femoral neck fracture** if suspected.
    ◦ **CT Angiography (CTA)**
        ▪ Indicated for **"hard signs" of vascular injury** (e.g., absent pulses, expanding hematoma, pulsatile bleeding) or an **ABI < 0.9**.
• **Labs**
    ◦ **CBC**: To assess for acute blood loss (Hgb/Hct).
    ◦ **Type and Screen/Crossmatch**: In anticipation of significant blood loss and surgery.
    ◦ **Coagulation Panel (PT/INR, PTT)**: Pre-operative assessment.
    ◦ **Lactate / ABG**: To assess for **systemic shock**.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for isolated, closed fractures treated with **IM nailing**. Most patients return to pre-injury function within 6-12 months.
• Prognosis is **guarded** in cases of **open fractures**, severe comminution, associated **vascular injury**, or in the context of **polytrauma**.
• **Elderly patients** face higher rates of mortality (up to 20-30% at one year) and morbidity due to medical comorbidities.

sections.overview:
• A patellar fracture is a break in the **patella (kneecap)**, the large **sesamoid bone** on the anterior aspect of the knee.
• The patella is a critical component of the knee's **extensor mechanism**, including the **quadriceps tendon** and the **patellar tendon**.
    ◦ It acts as a fulcrum, increasing the mechanical advantage of the quadriceps muscle for **knee extension**.
• Fracture can significantly impair this function, leading to an inability to actively extend the knee.
• Treatment decisions are based on **fracture displacement** and the **integrity of the extensor mechanism**.
sections.etiology:
• Patellar fractures occur via two primary mechanisms:
    ◦ **Direct Trauma**
        ▪ **Mechanism**: A direct blow to the anterior knee, such as a fall or a **dashboard injury** in a motor vehicle accident (MVA).
        ▪ **Resulting Fracture Pattern**: Typically results in a **comminuted** (multiple fragments) or **stellate** (star-shaped) fracture. Displacement may be minimal if the surrounding retinaculum remains intact.
    ◦ **Indirect Trauma**
        ▪ **Mechanism**: Sudden, forceful, eccentric contraction of the quadriceps muscle against a flexed knee.
        ▪ **Resulting Fracture Pattern**: Classically results in a **transverse fracture**. These are often **displaced** due to the unopposed pull of the quadriceps and patellar tendons.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The fracture disrupts the continuity of the **extensor mechanism**.
        ▪ If the fracture is **displaced**, the force from the quadriceps can no longer be transmitted to the tibial tubercle, resulting in a loss of active knee extension.
    ◦ The posterior surface of the patella is covered by thick articular cartilage; disruption of this surface significantly increases the risk of **post-traumatic patellofemoral arthritis**.
sections.epidemiology:
• Account for approximately **1% of all skeletal fractures**.
• **Bimodal age distribution**:
