    ◦ **Younger patients (20-50 years)**: More common in males, typically due to high-energy trauma (sports, MVAs).
    ◦ **Older patients (>60 years)**: More common in females, typically due to low-energy falls on osteoporotic bone.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with a history of **acute trauma** to the knee followed by:
    ◦ **Immediate pain**
    ◦ **Swelling**
    ◦ **Inability to ambulate**
• They will often hold the knee in a slightly flexed position to relieve tension.
sections.diagnostics:
• **X-rays**
    ◦ **Standard Views**: Anteroposterior (AP) and **Lateral**.
    ◦ **Lateral View**: The most critical view.
        ▪ It best demonstrates the fracture pattern (e.g., transverse), displacement, and articular surface congruity (**step-off**).
    ◦ **Sunrise View** (also **Merchant** or **Skyline**)
        ▪ Useful for identifying vertical fractures and assessing the patellofemoral joint.
    ◦ Note on **Bipartite Patella**
        ▪ A common normal variant that can be mistaken for a fracture.
        ▪ A bipartite patella is usually superolateral, bilateral, and has smooth, well-corticated edges, unlike the sharp, irregular edges of an acute fracture.
• **CT Scan**
    ◦ Not routinely required.
    ◦ Indicated for complex, **comminuted fractures** to better delineate the fracture pattern for pre-operative planning.
• **Arthrocentesis**
    ◦ Aspiration of the knee joint can be both diagnostic and therapeutic.
    ◦ **Findings**: **Hemarthrosis** is expected.
        ▪ The presence of **fat globules** within the aspirate confirms an **intra-articular fracture**.
    ◦ **Therapeutic**: Draining the tense **hemarthrosis** can provide significant pain relief.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is generally good for **non-displaced fractures** with an **intact extensor mechanism**.
• For operatively treated fractures, outcomes are variable.
    ◦ Most patients regain good function, but many experience residual symptoms like anterior knee pain, stiffness, or weakness.
• The quality of the **articular reduction** is the most important predictor of long-term outcome and the development of arthritis.

sections.overview:
• A **tibial plateau fracture** is an **intra-articular fracture** of the **proximal tibia** involving the articular surface of the knee joint.
    ◦ These fractures result from **high-energy trauma** in younger patients or **low-energy falls** in older, osteoporotic patients.
    ◦ Because they disrupt the knee joint's articular cartilage, they carry a significant risk of long-term complications, most notably **post-traumatic osteoarthritis**.
    ◦ Management is dictated by the fracture pattern, degree of displacement and depression, and patient factors, with the primary goal being the restoration of a stable, congruent, and mobile joint.
sections.etiology:
• The mechanism of injury typically involves a combination of **axial loading with a varus or valgus force**.
    ◦ The femoral condyles are driven into the articular surface of the tibial plateau, causing it to fracture.
• **Valgus Force + Axial Load**:
    ◦ The most common mechanism.
    ◦ The lateral femoral condyle impacts the **lateral tibial plateau**.
    ◦ This often results in a **lateral tibial plateau fracture** (e.g., "**bumper fracture**" or "**fender fracture**" from a car striking the side of a pedestrian's knee).
• **Varus Force + Axial Load**:
    ◦ Less common.
    ◦ The medial femoral condyle impacts the **medial tibial plateau**.
    ◦ These fractures often require more force, as the medial plateau is stronger, and may be associated with more significant soft tissue injury.
• **High-Energy Axial Load**:
    ◦ (e.g., fall from height) Can result in **bicondylar** (both medial and lateral) fractures with significant comminution and depression.
• The **Schatzker Classification** is the most commonly used system to categorize these fractures, guiding treatment and prognosis.
    ◦ **Schatzker I**: Split fracture of the lateral plateau.
    ◦ **Schatzker II**: Split-depression fracture of the lateral plateau (**most common type**).
    ◦ **Schatzker III**: Pure depression of the lateral plateau.
    ◦ **Schatzker IV**: Medial plateau fracture; high-energy, associated with soft tissue injury.
    ◦ **Schatzker V**: Bicondylar (both plateaus) fracture.
    ◦ **Schatzker VI**: Tibial plateau fracture with **diaphyseal dissociation** (separation from the tibial shaft); highest energy injury.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Bimodal distribution**:
    ◦ **Young patients (males > females)**: Result of **high-energy trauma** (motor vehicle accidents, falls from height, high-impact sports).
    ◦ **Elderly patients (females > males)**: Result of **low-energy falls**, often secondary to osteoporosis.
• **Lateral plateau fractures** are more common than medial plateau fractures.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents to the emergency department following an acute traumatic event.
• The presentation is characterized by the acute onset of **severe knee pain**, **swelling**, and an **inability to bear weight** on the affected limb.
• The history should focus on the mechanism of injury (e.g., direction of force, height of fall).
sections.diagnostics:
• **X-rays**:
    ◦ **Required Views**: AP, lateral, and tibial plateau views (AP with 10-15 caudal tilt) or oblique views.
    ◦ **Findings**: Fracture lines, **articular depression (step-off)**, and **condylar widening**.
    ◦ **Lipohemarthrosis**:
        ▪ On a cross-table lateral view, a **fat-fluid level** is visible.
        ▪ This is **pathognomonic for an intra-articular fracture**, as it represents fat from the bone marrow mixing with blood in the joint.
• **CT Scan (Computed Tomography)**:
    ◦ **The gold standard for defining fracture anatomy**.
    ◦ Essential for **pre-operative planning** to visualize the degree of articular depression, comminution, and fracture pattern. It delineates the size and location of key fracture fragments.
• **MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging)**:
    ◦ Not typically used for initial fracture diagnosis.
    ◦ Excellent for evaluating associated **soft-tissue injuries**, such as **meniscal tears** and **ligamentous ruptures** (ACL, MCL, etc.), which occur in up to 50% of cases.
• **CT Angiography (CTA)**:
    ◦ Indicated if there is clinical suspicion of a **vascular injury** (diminished pulses, abnormal ABI, signs of ischemia).
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly dependent on the severity of the initial injury (**Schatzker type**), the quality of the articular reduction, and the presence of associated soft tissue injuries.
• Even with excellent surgical treatment, the risk of developing **post-traumatic osteoarthritis** is high for displaced, intra-articular fractures.
• Many patients do not return to their pre-injury level of high-impact sporting activity.

sections.overview:
• A **tibial shaft fracture** is a break in the diaphysis (shaft) of the **tibia**, the larger of the two bones in the lower leg.
• It is the **most common long bone fracture**.
• Due to the tibia's subcutaneous location along its anteromedial border, these fractures have a high incidence of being **open fractures**.
• The **fibula** is also fractured in over 80% of cases.
• Management depends on the fracture pattern, displacement, degree of soft tissue injury, and patient factors.
sections.etiology:
• Tibial shaft fractures result from the application of force that exceeds the bone's structural capacity.
• The mechanism of injury dictates the fracture pattern.
• **High-Energy Trauma**
    ◦ **Mechanism**: **Motor vehicle accidents (MVA)**, pedestrian vs. auto, **falls from a significant height**, **gunshot wounds (GSW)**.
    ◦ **Pathophysiology**: Involves direct, high-impact forces leading to significant **comminution** (multiple bone fragments), extensive **soft tissue damage**, and a higher likelihood of **open fractures**. This disrupts the periosteal blood supply, complicating healing.
• **Low-Energy Trauma**
    ◦ **Mechanism**: Twisting or rotational forces, such as in skiing or soccer, or a simple fall.
    ◦ **Pathophysiology**: Typically results in simpler fracture patterns like **spiral** or **oblique fractures**. Soft tissue injury is less severe.
• **Pathologic Fractures**
    ◦ **Mechanism**: Fracture through a bone weakened by a pre-existing condition (e.g., **tumor**, **osteoporosis**, **Paget's disease**) with minimal or no trauma.
• **Stress Fractures**
    ◦ **Mechanism**: Repetitive, sub-maximal loading, common in athletes and military recruits.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Most common long bone fracture**.
• **Bimodal age distribution**:
    ◦ **Young males (15-25 years)**: Primarily due to **high-energy trauma** (sports, MVA).
    ◦ **Older females (>65 years)**: Primarily due to **low-energy falls** secondary to **osteoporosis**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents to the emergency department following a traumatic event with acute, severe pain in the lower leg.
• The patient will be **unable to bear weight** on the affected limb.
• There may be an obvious, gross **deformity** of the leg.
• In cases of **high-energy trauma**, the patient may have other life-threatening injuries (**polytrauma**) that require simultaneous evaluation (**ATLS protocol**).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Radiographs (X-rays)**
    ◦ **Standard Views**: Anteroposterior (AP) and Lateral views of the entire tibia and fibula.
    ◦ **Required Inclusions**: Must include the **knee and ankle joints** to rule out associated injuries (e.g., tibial plateau, pilon, or ankle fractures).
    ◦ **What to look for**:
        ▪ Fracture location (proximal/middle/distal third)
        ▪ Pattern (**transverse**, **oblique**, **spiral**, **comminuted**)
        ▪ Displacement
        ▪ Angulation
        ▪ Fibular integrity
• **CT Scan**
    ◦ Not routinely needed for diaphyseal fractures.
    ◦ Indicated for complex fractures, especially those with **intra-articular extension** into the knee (**tibial plateau**) or ankle (**pilon**).
• **Labs**
    ◦ Typically not required for isolated, closed fractures.
    ◦ In **polytrauma** or pre-operative settings: **CBC**, **BMP**, **Type & Screen**, **Coagulation studies**.
• **Classification Systems**
    ◦ **Gustilo-Anderson Classification (for Open Fractures)**: Crucial for guiding treatment (antibiotics, debridement) and predicting infection risk.
    ◦ **Tscherne Classification (for Closed Fractures)**: Grades the severity of the associated soft-tissue injury.
    ◦ **AO/OTA Classification**: A complex alpha-numeric system used by orthopedic surgeons to precisely describe the fracture's location and morphology.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is generally good for **closed fractures** treated appropriately, with union rates >95% for **IM nailing**.
• Healing typically takes **3-6 months**.
• **Open fractures**, severe **soft tissue injury**, and patient comorbidities (**smoking**, **diabetes**) are associated with higher rates of **infection**, **nonunion**, and a more guarded prognosis.

sections.overview:
• A **bimalleolar** or **trimalleolar ankle fracture** is a severe, **unstable** injury involving fractures of two or three malleoli of the ankle joint, respectively.
    ◦ These fractures disrupt the structural integrity of the "**ankle mortise**," the bony arch formed by the tibial plafond and the malleoli that articulates with the talus.
    ◦ Due to their inherent instability, these fractures almost always require **surgical intervention** to restore anatomical alignment and joint congruity.
• Malleoli involved:
    ◦ **Lateral Malleolus**: Distal end of the fibula.
    ◦ **Medial Malleolus**: Distal end of the tibia.
    ◦ **Posterior Malleolus**: Posterior aspect of the distal tibia (tibial plafond).
• Fracture Types:
    ◦ **Bimalleolar Fracture**: Involves both the medial and lateral malleoli.
    ◦ **Trimalleolar Fracture**: Involves the medial, lateral, and posterior malleoli. This is a more severe injury pattern.
sections.etiology:
• These fractures result from significant **rotational forces** applied to the ankle joint, often combined with an axial load.
    ◦ The specific fracture pattern is dictated by the position of the foot and the direction of the force at the time of injury.
• **Mechanism of Injury (MOI)**:
    ◦ Twisting, rotational movements (e.g., foot planted while the body rotates).
    ◦ High-energy trauma: Motor vehicle collisions, falls from height.
    ◦ Low-energy trauma: Simple falls or slips, especially in osteoporotic bone.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ The ankle joint is a "ring" structure composed of the tibia, fibula, talus, and their connecting ligaments (deltoid, syndesmosis).
    ◦ A break in two or more locations within this ring (e.g., medial and lateral malleoli) creates an **unstable joint**.
    ◦ This instability allows the **talus to shift** or subluxate out of its normal position within the mortise, leading to joint incongruity, abnormal joint loading, and rapid development of **post-traumatic arthritis** if not corrected.
    ◦ The most common injury pattern is **supination-external rotation (SER)** according to the Lauge-Hansen classification.
sections.epidemiology:
• Ankle fractures are one of the most common lower extremity fractures treated by orthopedic surgeons.
• There is a **bimodal distribution**:
    ◦ **Young, active males**: High-energy injuries from sports or trauma.
    ◦ **Older females (>60 years)**: Low-energy falls, often complicated by osteoporosis.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The patient typically presents to an emergency department or urgent care center immediately following an acute injury.
• **History**: The patient will report a specific traumatic event, often a "twist" or fall, followed by immediate and severe ankle pain. They may report hearing or feeling a "pop" or "crack."
• **Chief Complaint**: **Severe pain**, swelling, and **inability to bear weight** on the affected leg.
sections.diagnostics:
• **X-ray**:
    ◦ **Standard Views**: Anteroposterior (AP), Lateral, and **Mortise**.
    ◦ **Mortise View**: An AP view with the leg internally rotated 15-20 degrees. This view is essential for assessing the clarity and symmetry of the ankle mortise joint space.
    ◦ **Findings to look for**:
        ▪ Fracture lines in the medial, lateral, and posterior malleoli.
        ▪ **Talar shift**: Widening of the medial clear space (>4-5 mm) on the mortise view indicates deltoid ligament rupture or medial malleolus fracture and is a sign of instability.
        ▪ Disruption of the **syndesmosis** (widened tibiofibular clear space).
• **CT Scan**:
    ◦ Often obtained for **pre-operative planning**, especially for:
        ▪ **Trimalleolar fractures** to assess the size and displacement of the posterior malleolus fragment.
        ▪ **Comminuted** (multi-fragmented) fractures.
        ▪ Suspected articular impaction.
• **MRI**:
    ◦ Rarely used for acute fracture diagnosis. More useful for evaluating purely ligamentous injuries or chronic pain.
sections.prognosis:
• With successful ORIF and diligent rehabilitation, the prognosis is generally good for a return to most activities.
    ◦ Full recovery can take 6-12 months.
• The development of **post-traumatic arthritis** is a significant risk and may lead to chronic pain and functional limitation years after the injury.
• **Trimalleolar fractures** carry a worse prognosis than **bimalleolar fractures** due to the greater initial instability and articular surface involvement.

sections.overview:
• A Maisonneuve fracture is a specific type of unstable ankle injury complex.
    ◦ Defined by a **spiral fracture of the proximal third of the fibula** combined with a disruption of the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis and an injury to the medial ankle structures.
    ◦ The medial injury can be either a fracture of the medial malleolus or a rupture of the deep deltoid ligament.
    ◦ Considered a **spiral fracture equivalent of a high ankle sprain** because the force travels up the interosseous membrane.
    ◦ The key to diagnosis is maintaining a high index of suspicion and examining the entire fibula in any patient with an ankle injury.
sections.etiology:
• The mechanism of injury is a forceful **pronation-external rotation** of the ankle.
• The sequence of injury follows a predictable pattern as the force travels through the ankle and up the leg:
    ◦ **Medial Injury:** Strong external rotation force puts tension on the medial side of the ankle, causing either a rupture of the deltoid ligament or an avulsion fracture of the medial malleolus.
    ◦ **Syndesmotic Injury:** The talus continues to rotate externally within the mortise, tearing the anterior-inferior tibiofibular ligament (AITFL) and the strong interosseous membrane that connects the tibia and fibula.
    ◦ **Proximal Fibula Fracture:** The rotational force is transmitted superiorly along the interosseous membrane until it exits through the proximal fibula, causing a characteristic oblique or spiral fracture.
• This cascade of events results in a highly unstable ankle mortise, as the fibula is no longer tethered to the tibia distally.
sections.epidemiology:
• Accounts for 5-10% of all ankle fractures that require surgical intervention.
• Most commonly seen in young, active individuals.
• Frequently associated with sports injuries involving twisting or pivoting, such as skiing, soccer, and football.
sections.riskFactors:
• Participation in high-impact or pivoting sports.
• Activities with a risk of falls where the foot is planted and the body rotates.
• Any trauma that can produce a strong external rotation force on a pronated or neutral foot.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients typically present with a chief complaint of severe **ankle pain** following a twisting injury.
• They are often unable to bear weight on the affected leg.
• Crucially, the patient may have minimal or no pain at the actual proximal fibula fracture site, focusing all their attention on the more painful ankle.
    ◦ This is the classic pitfall that leads to a missed diagnosis.
• Symptoms include:
    ◦ Severe pain localized to the medial and anterior aspects of the ankle.
    ◦ Sensation of instability or "giving way" at the ankle.
    ◦ Swelling and ecchymosis, primarily around the ankle joint.
    ◦ Pain near the knee or upper leg may be present but is often less pronounced than the ankle pain.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Ankle Inspection:** Significant swelling and ecchymosis, especially medially.
• **Ankle Palpation:** Point tenderness over the deltoid ligament (inferior to the medial malleolus) or over a fractured medial malleolus. Tenderness over the anterior syndesmosis.
• **KEY FINDING: Proximal Fibula Palpation:** Tenderness to palpation over the proximal fibula is the hallmark of this injury. **Always palpate the entire length of the fibula in any ankle injury.**
• **Special Tests for Syndesmotic Instability:**
    ◦ **Squeeze Test (Hopkins' Test):** Compression of the tibia and fibula at mid-calf elicits pain distally at the ankle syndesmosis.
    ◦ **External Rotation Stress Test:** With the knee flexed and the leg stabilized, passive external rotation of the foot elicits pain over the syndesmosis.
• **Neurovascular Exam:** Assess the function of the **common peroneal nerve**, which courses around the fibular neck. Check for foot drop (impaired dorsiflexion) and sensation in the first dorsal webspace.
sections.diagnostics:
• **X-Rays:**
    ◦ **Ankle Series (AP, Lateral, and Mortise views):** Initial imaging study.
        ▪ **Key Finding on Mortise View:** Widening of the **medial clear space** (>5 mm) is a highly sensitive sign of deltoid ligament rupture and an unstable ankle.
        ▪ May also show a widened **tibiofibular clear space** (>6 mm), indicating syndesmotic disruption.
        ▪ A medial malleolus fracture may be visible.
    ◦ **Full-Length Tibia-Fibula Films (AP and Lateral):** **Mandatory** if there is any suspicion of syndesmotic injury on ankle films (e.g., widened medial clear space) or tenderness over the proximal fibula on exam.
        ▪ This view will reveal the proximal fibular fracture and confirm the diagnosis.
    ◦ **Stress Radiographs:** Gravity stress or manual external rotation stress views can be used to unmask ankle mortise instability if initial films are inconclusive.
• **CT/MRI:** Rarely needed for diagnosis but can be useful to evaluate for associated injuries (e.g., posterior malleolus fracture) or in cases of diagnostic uncertainty.
sections.treatment:
• **Non-operative:** Reserved only for extremely poor surgical candidates or non-ambulatory patients with a stable, undisplaced mortise (very rare).
• **Operative (Standard of Care):** **Open Reduction and Internal Fixation (ORIF)**
    ◦ The primary goal is to **anatomically reduce and stabilize the ankle mortise**.
    ◦ The proximal fibular fracture itself is typically **not fixed**; it heals well once the ankle is stabilized.
    ◦ **Syndesmotic Fixation:** The syndesmosis is reduced and stabilized using one or two cortical screws (syndesmotic screws) or a suture-button device (e.g., "TightRope").
    ◦ **Medial Malleolus Fixation:** If the medial malleolus is fractured, it is reduced and fixed with screws. If only the deltoid ligament is torn, it is typically not repaired surgically and will heal once stability is restored.
sections.management:
• **Pre-operative:**
    ◦ Immobilization in a posterior splint.
    ◦ Strict non-weight bearing (NWB).
    ◦ RICE protocol (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation).
    ◦ Analgesia.
    ◦ Urgent orthopedic consultation.
• **Post-operative:**
    ◦ Immobilization in a cast or boot.
    ◦ Strict NWB for 6-8 weeks to allow for ligamentous healing.
    ◦ Transition to progressive weight-bearing in a boot.
    ◦ Physical therapy is critical for regaining range of motion, strength, and proprioception.
    ◦ Hardware (syndesmotic screws) may be removed at 3-6 months, especially in high-demand athletes, to restore normal tibiofibular motion, though this remains controversial.
sections.complications:
• **Missed Diagnosis:** The most significant complication. Failure to diagnose leads to chronic ankle instability, pain, and accelerated post-traumatic osteoarthritis.
• **Common Peroneal Nerve Injury:** Can occur from the initial trauma or iatrogenically during surgery. Results in foot drop.
• **Malunion:** Incorrect reduction of the syndesmosis leads to persistent instability and poor outcomes.
• **Post-traumatic Arthritis:** High risk if the diagnosis is missed or the reduction is not anatomic.
• **Hardware Complications:** Screw breakage, loosening, or pain requiring removal.
• **Stiffness (Arthrofibrosis):** Reduced ankle range of motion.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is **good to excellent** with prompt diagnosis and accurate surgical stabilization of the ankle mortise.
• The quality of the syndesmotic reduction is the most important factor determining long-term outcome.
• Delayed diagnosis or inadequate treatment leads to a poor prognosis with chronic pain and disability.

sections.overview:
• A Jones fracture is a transverse fracture of the proximal fifth metatarsal at the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction.
	◦ It is located in a vascular "watershed" area, which contributes to its notoriously high rate of delayed union and nonunion.
	◦ This specific location and poor healing potential distinguish it from more common and less problematic fractures of the fifth metatarsal, such as an avulsion fracture (Pseudo-Jones).
sections.etiology:
• Mechanism
	◦ The fracture typically occurs from a significant adduction force applied to the forefoot with the ankle in plantar flexion.
	◦ It can also result from repetitive microtrauma or stress loading, common in athletes.
• Pathophysiology
	◦ The fracture site is at the junction of two blood supplies: the nutrient artery supplying the diaphysis and the metaphyseal arteries supplying the base.
		▪ This "watershed" zone has a tenuous blood supply, which impairs the delivery of oxygen and nutrients necessary for bone healing.
	◦ Additionally, the pull from the peroneus brevis and peroneus tertius tendons can distract the fracture fragments, further hindering union.
sections.epidemiology:
• Population
	◦ Most common in young, athletic individuals.
• Incidence
	◦ Accounts for approximately 1.5% of all foot fractures.
	◦ It is less common than the more proximal avulsion fractures of the 5th metatarsal styloid.
• Associated Sports
	◦ Frequently seen in sports involving cutting, pivoting, and running, such as basketball, football, soccer, and dance.
sections.riskFactors:
• High-impact athletic activities
• Sudden increase in training intensity or duration
• Inadequate footwear
• High-arched (cavovarus) foot structure
	◦ This foot type increases pressure and stress on the lateral aspect of the foot.
• Repetitive stress on the lateral foot
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient, typically an athlete, presents with acute lateral foot pain after a twisting injury or with a history of insidious, progressively worsening pain on the outside of the foot.
• They often report hearing or feeling a "pop" at the time of an acute injury and have significant difficulty with weight-bearing.
• Symptoms
	◦ Acute, sharp pain on the lateral border of the midfoot.
	◦ Sensation of a "pop" or "snap" at the time of injury.
	◦ Inability to bear weight or significant pain with ambulation.
	◦ Swelling and ecchymosis (bruising) localized to the lateral foot.
	◦ Aching or pain that worsens with activity and improves with rest (if due to stress mechanism).
sections.physicalExam:
• Inspection
	◦ Visible edema and ecchymosis over the proximal fifth metatarsal.
• Palpation
	◦ Focal point tenderness directly over the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction of the fifth metatarsal.
		▪ This is the key diagnostic finding.
• Range of Motion
	◦ Pain with passive inversion of the foot or active eversion against resistance (due to pull of peroneal tendons).
• Gait
	◦ Antalgic gait or refusal to bear weight on the affected foot.
sections.diagnostics:
• Primary Imaging: Radiographs (X-rays)
	◦ Views: Anteroposterior (AP), lateral, and oblique views of the foot.
		▪ The oblique view is often the most useful for visualizing the fracture line.
	◦ Findings: A sharp, transverse fracture line at the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction (Torg Zone 2), distal to the tuberosity.
	◦ Chronic/Stress Fracture Signs: May show cortical thickening, periosteal reaction, or a widened, sclerotic fracture line, indicating a pre-existing stress injury.
• Advanced Imaging (if needed)
	◦ CT Scan: Useful for pre-operative planning, assessing for nonunion, or when radiographs are equivocal.
	◦ MRI: Can detect early-stage stress reactions or bone marrow edema before a fracture is visible on plain films.
sections.treatment:
• Non-Operative
	◦ Indications: Sedentary individuals, non-displaced fractures, patients who are poor surgical candidates.
	◦ Method: Strict non-weight bearing (NWB) in a short leg cast or boot for 6-8 weeks.
	◦ Outcome: High rate of nonunion (15-30%) and delayed union, often with a prolonged time to recovery.
• Operative
	◦ Indications: Standard of care for athletes and active individuals. Also for displaced fractures (>2 mm) or failure of conservative management.
	◦ Method: Surgical fixation with an intramedullary screw.
		▪ This provides compression across the fracture site, enhances stability, and improves the biological environment for healing.
	◦ Adjuncts: Bone grafting may be used in cases of revision surgery or established nonunion.
sections.management:
• Conservative Management Follow-Up
	◦ Serial radiographs are obtained every 2-4 weeks to monitor for signs of healing.
	◦ Transition to a walking boot and partial weight-bearing only after radiographic evidence of union.
	◦ Physical therapy is initiated to restore range of motion, strength, and proprioception. Full return to activity may take 3-5 months.
• Surgical Management Follow-Up
	◦ Post-operative period of protected weight-bearing (often 2 weeks NWB, then progressive weight-bearing in a boot).
	◦ Allows for a much faster return to sport, typically within 8-12 weeks.
	◦ Radiographs are used to confirm healing before clearance for full activity.
sections.complications:
• Nonunion
	◦ The most significant and common complication.
	◦ Defined as the absence of healing by 3-6 months.
	◦ Often requires surgical intervention with bone grafting.
• Delayed Union
	◦ Fracture heals, but takes longer than the typical 6-8 weeks.
• Refracture
	◦ Occurs after healing, often due to premature return to sport or inadequate initial fixation.
• Sural Nerve Injury
	◦ A risk during the surgical approach, which can cause numbness on the lateral aspect of the foot.
• Hardware Failure/Irritation
	◦ The screw may break or cause irritation, sometimes requiring a second surgery for removal.
sections.prognosis:
• With surgical fixation: Excellent.
	◦ Union rates are >90%, with a reliable and faster return to pre-injury activity levels.
• With non-operative management: Guarded, especially in athletes.
	◦ The high risk of nonunion can lead to prolonged disability and the eventual need for surgery.

sections.overview:
• A stress fracture is a fatigue-induced fracture of the bone caused by repetitive, submaximal stress.
    ◦ Unlike a traumatic fracture from a single, high-force event, a stress fracture develops over time when the rate of bone microdamage exceeds the rate of bone remodeling.
• They are common overuse injuries, particularly in athletes and military recruits.
    ◦ The tibia and metatarsals are among the most frequently affected sites.
sections.etiology:
• The underlying mechanism is an imbalance between bone resorption (**osteoclastic activity**) and bone formation (**osteoblastic activity**).
• **Wolff's Law**: Bone adapts to the loads under which it is placed.
    ◦ Repetitive loading stimulates remodeling.
• **Pathophysiology**: When the frequency and intensity of mechanical stress are too high, osteoclastic activity outpaces osteoblastic repair.
    ◦ This leads to an accumulation of microfractures, which can coalesce into a true fracture line.
• Two primary types:
    ◦ **Fatigue Fracture**: Abnormal stress on a **normal** bone.
        ▪ This is the classic type seen in athletes who suddenly increase the intensity, duration, or frequency of their training ("too much, too soon").
    ◦ **Insufficiency Fracture**: Normal stress on an **abnormal** bone with compromised elastic resistance (e.g., **osteoporosis**, **osteomalacia**, Paget's disease).
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Accounts for up to 20% of all injuries seen in sports medicine clinics.
• **Most Common Locations**:
    ◦ **Tibia**: The single most common location for stress fractures in athletes, particularly runners.
        ▪ The posteromedial cortex is most frequently affected.
    ◦ **Metatarsals**: The **2nd metatarsal** is the most common site in the foot ("**march fracture**"), followed by the 3rd.
        ▪ The 5th metatarsal is also a common, but higher-risk, location.
• **Demographics**:
    ◦ Most common in athletes (running, jumping sports) and military personnel.
    ◦ Higher incidence in females, often associated with the "**Female Athlete Triad**."
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is an athlete or recruit who presents with an **insidious onset** of localized pain.
• The pain is initially mild and occurs only during activity, but it progresses in severity and duration.
• The patient will often be able to pinpoint the exact location of the pain on the bone.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Plain Radiographs (X-rays)**:
    ◦ **First-line imaging test**.
    ◦ Often **negative** for the first 2-4 weeks. Sensitivity is low initially (~15-35%).
    ◦ Late findings (after several weeks) may include:
        ▪ Periosteal reaction or thickening.
        ▪ Cortical thickening (sclerosis).
        ▪ A faint, visible fracture line.
    ◦ **"Dreaded Black Line"**: A transverse fracture line on the anterior cortex of the tibia, indicating high risk for non-union.
• **MRI**:
    ◦ **Gold standard and most sensitive imaging modality**.
    ◦ Can detect stress injuries much earlier than X-rays.
    ◦ Findings include **bone marrow edema** (earliest sign), periosteal reaction, and a visible fracture line.
• **Bone Scintigraphy (Technetium-99m Bone Scan)**:
    ◦ Highly sensitive (detects injury within 2-3 days) but lacks specificity.
    ◦ Shows focal areas of increased radiotracer uptake.
    ◦ Largely replaced by MRI due to better anatomical detail and lack of radiation.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for most low-risk stress fractures when diagnosed early and managed appropriately.
• Healing typically takes **6-8 weeks**, but a full return to sport may take longer.
• Prognosis is more guarded for high-risk fractures, with higher rates of non-union and need for surgery.

sections.overview:
• The **Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL)** is one of the four major ligaments of the knee, connecting the femur to the tibia.
• It is a key stabilizer, primarily preventing anterior translation of the tibia relative to the femur and providing rotational stability.
• An **ACL tear** is a common and significant knee injury, most often occurring in young, athletic populations.
• Can lead to instability and an increased long-term risk of post-traumatic osteoarthritis.
sections.etiology:
• The ACL is an intracapsular but extrasynovial ligament, meaning it has a limited blood supply and poor intrinsic healing potential.
• Tears occur when forces applied to the knee exceed the ligament's tensile strength.
• **Mechanism of Injury**
    ◦ **Non-contact** (70-80% of cases): The most common mechanism involving a combination of deceleration, valgus stress, and external tibial rotation, or forceful hyperextension.
        ▪ Classic for sports involving pivoting, cutting, and jumping (e.g., soccer, basketball, football, skiing).
    ◦ **Contact** (20-30% of cases): A direct blow to the knee, typically to the lateral aspect, creating a valgus force and external rotation.
        ▪ Often injures other structures simultaneously (e.g., MCL, meniscus).
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The injury typically occurs in the mid-substance of the ligament.
    ◦ The tear disrupts mechanoreceptors within the ligament, impairing proprioception.
    ◦ Disruption leads to anterolateral rotational instability of the knee.
    ◦ The immediate, large effusion is a **hemarthrosis** due to the rupture of the middle geniculate artery, which runs with the ligament.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: ~200,000 ACL reconstructions are performed annually in the United States.
• **Age**: Bimodal distribution, with a primary peak in physically active individuals aged 15-25 and a smaller peak in the 30-40 age group.
• **Sex**: Females have a 4-6x higher incidence rate than males participating in the same sports.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Classic history involves an athlete who was planting their foot to cut or pivot, or who landed awkwardly from a jump, reporting an acute event with a distinct onset.
• **History of Present Illness (HPI)**
    ◦ Reports hearing or feeling a **"pop"** at the time of injury.
    ◦ Immediate onset of severe pain.
    ◦ Rapid development of a large knee **effusion** (swelling) within hours.
    ◦ Sensation of the knee **"giving way"** or buckling (instability).
    ◦ Inability to continue playing or bear weight immediately after the injury.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Radiographs (X-ray)**
    ◦ **Views**: AP, lateral, and sunrise views of the knee.
    ◦ **Purpose**: Primarily to rule out associated fractures. Usually normal in an isolated ACL tear.
    ◦ **Key Finding**: **Segond fracture** - an avulsion fracture of the lateral tibial plateau.
        ▪ This finding is **pathognomonic** for an ACL tear.
• **Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)**
    ◦ **Gold standard** for confirming the diagnosis.
    ◦ **Purpose**:
        ▪ Visualizes the ligament tear (full vs. partial thickness).
        ▪ Identifies associated injuries, which are very common:
            • Meniscal tears (especially lateral meniscus in acute tears).
            • Collateral ligament sprains (MCL).
            • Bone bruises (contusions), typically on the lateral femoral condyle and posterolateral tibial plateau from the pivot-shift mechanism.
• **Arthrocentesis**
    ◦ Can be performed for therapeutic relief of a large, painful **hemarthrosis**.
    ◦ Aspiration of blood is indicative of intra-articular injury.
    ◦ The presence of fat globules within the blood suggests an associated intra-articular fracture.
sections.prognosis:
• With successful ACL reconstruction and rehabilitation, ~80-90% of athletes return to some level of sport, with a slightly lower percentage returning to their pre-injury level of competition.
• There is a significant risk of re-injury, with rates of up to 20-25% for a second ACL tear (either ipsilateral or contralateral) in young athletes returning to high-risk sports.

sections.overview:
• The Posterior Cruciate Ligament (PCL) is the **strongest ligament** in the knee, located within the knee joint capsule.
• **Originates** from the anterolateral aspect of the medial femoral condyle and **inserts** onto the posterior tibial fossa.
• Its primary function is to act as the **primary restraint to posterior tibial translation** relative to the femur.
• It also provides secondary restraint to varus, valgus, and external rotation forces.
• PCL injuries are **less common than ACL injuries** and often present with more subtle symptoms, leading to potential delays in diagnosis.
sections.etiology:
• The PCL is injured by significant traumatic force. The mechanism of injury (MOI) dictates the pathophysiology.
• **Mechanism of Injury:**
    ◦ **Direct Blow to Anterior Tibia:** The classic **"dashboard injury"** in a motor vehicle accident (MVA) where the flexed knee strikes the dashboard, forcing the tibia posteriorly.
    ◦ **Fall onto a Flexed Knee:** A fall directly onto the knee with the foot in plantarflexion, driving the tibia backward. Common in sports like football or rugby.
    ◦ **Hyperflexion:** A non-contact injury where the knee is forcefully hyperflexed, crushing the PCL between the posterior tibia and the femur.
    ◦ **Hyperextension:** A severe hyperextension force can injure both the ACL and the PCL.
• **Pathophysiology:**
    ◦ Injury involves stretching or tearing of the ligament fibers.
    ◦ **Grading of Sprains:**
        ▪ **Grade I:** Ligament is stretched, but not torn (microscopic tears). Posterior translation of 1-5 mm.
        ▪ **Grade II:** Partial tear of the ligament. Posterior translation of 6-10 mm, but with a firm endpoint.
        ▪ **Grade III:** Complete rupture of the ligament. Posterior translation >10 mm with a soft or absent endpoint. Often associated with other ligamentous injuries (e.g., PLC).
sections.epidemiology:
• Less common than ACL injuries, accounting for approximately **3-20% of all knee ligament injuries**.
• Incidence is likely under-reported due to subtle presentation and frequent misdiagnosis.
• **Bimodal age distribution:**
    ◦ Young athletes involved in high-impact sports.
    ◦ Individuals involved in high-energy trauma like MVAs.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation of an acute PCL tear can be **subtle** and is often overshadowed by other more apparent injuries.
• Patients may not recall a specific traumatic event or a distinct **"pop"** as is common with ACL tears.
• They often present with **vague posterior knee pain** and a sense of instability, particularly when decelerating or walking down an incline.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Radiographs (X-rays):**
    ◦ **Views:** AP, lateral, and sunrise/merchant views are standard first-line imaging.
    ◦ **Purpose:** To rule out associated fractures (e.g., tibial plateau fracture) or a **PCL avulsion fracture** from its tibial insertion.
    ◦ **Stress Views:** Posterior stress radiographs can be used to objectively quantify posterior tibial translation.
• **Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI):**
    ◦ **Gold Standard** for diagnosis.
    ◦ **Findings:** Directly visualizes the PCL tear (discontinuity, increased signal), identifies the location and grade of the tear, and assesses for associated injuries such as **bone bruises** (classic finding is a **"kissing contusion"** on the anterior tibia and femoral condyle), meniscal tears, chondral damage, and other ligamentous injuries.
sections.prognosis:
• **Isolated Grade I/II:**
    ◦ **Excellent prognosis** with non-operative management.
    ◦ Most patients return to their previous level of function.
• **Isolated Grade III:**
    ◦ **Good prognosis**, but outcomes are more variable.
    ◦ Non-operative treatment may suffice for sedentary individuals, but athletes often require surgery to regain stability.
• **Combined Injuries:**
    ◦ Prognosis is worse and directly related to the severity of the associated injuries.
    ◦ Return to high-level sport is less predictable.

sections.overview:
• The **Medial Collateral Ligament (MCL)**, or tibial collateral ligament, is a broad, flat ligament on the medial aspect of the knee, providing stability.
    ◦ Its primary function is to resist **valgus forces** (forces pushing the knee inward) and provide rotational stability.
• Injury to the MCL is one of the most common knee ligament injuries, typically a sprain or tear from excessive **valgus stress**.
    ◦ Injuries are graded by severity, and most are managed **non-operatively** with excellent outcomes.
sections.etiology:
• **Mechanism of Injury**
    ◦ Most common: A direct blow to the lateral aspect of the knee with the foot planted, forcing the knee into a **valgus position**.
    ◦ Can also occur from non-contact valgus or rotational stress (e.g., planting and cutting in sports, skiing falls).
• **Anatomy**
    ◦ The MCL has two main parts:
        ▪ **Superficial MCL**: The primary stabilizer against valgus stress. It originates from the medial femoral epicondyle and inserts on the medial aspect of the proximal tibia.
        ▪ **Deep MCL**: A thickening of the joint capsule attached to the medial meniscus.
• **Injury Grading**
    ◦ **Grade I (Mild)**: Stretching of the ligament with microscopic tears. The ligament is tender but not lax.
    ◦ **Grade II (Moderate)**: Partial tear of the ligament, causing increased laxity on valgus stress testing but with a **firm endpoint**.
    ◦ **Grade III (Severe)**: Complete rupture of the ligament. The knee is significantly unstable with **no firm endpoint** on valgus stress testing.
sections.epidemiology:
• The **most common ligamentous injury of the knee**.
• High incidence in athletes, particularly in contact sports.
• Sports with the highest incidence include **football, soccer, hockey, and skiing**.
• Affects all ages but is most prevalent in young, active populations.
sections.riskFactors:
• Participation in contact sports (e.g., football, rugby, hockey).
• Sports involving pivoting, cutting, and rapid changes in direction (e.g., soccer, basketball).
• Skiing (valgus-external rotation injuries).
• Poor neuromuscular control or conditioning.
• Previous knee injury or ligamentous laxity.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients typically report an acute traumatic event involving a **valgus force** to the knee.
• May report hearing or feeling a **"pop"** or tearing sensation at the time of injury.
• Presentation includes immediate **medial knee pain** and variable swelling.
• Patients often experience difficulty ambulating or a feeling of **instability**, especially with side-to-side movements.
• **Key Symptoms**
    ◦ **Pain**: Localized over the medial aspect of the knee; can be sharp and intense initially.
    ◦ **Swelling**: Mild to moderate soft tissue swelling over the medial knee. Significant intra-articular effusion is less common unless an associated injury is present (e.g., ACL or meniscal tear).
    ◦ **Instability**: A feeling that the knee is "giving way" or "opening up" on the inner side.
    ◦ **Stiffness**: Difficulty with knee flexion and extension due to pain and swelling.
    ◦ **Ecchymosis**: May develop over the medial knee after 24-48 hours.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Inspection**
    ◦ Visible swelling and ecchymosis over the medial knee.
• **Palpation**
    ◦ **Point tenderness** along the course of the MCL, most often at the proximal insertion on the **medial femoral epicondyle** or the distal insertion on the tibia.
• **Range of Motion**
    ◦ Often limited by pain, especially in full extension.
• **Special Tests**
    ◦ **Valgus Stress Test**: The cornerstone of diagnosis.
        ▪ **Performed at 30° of knee flexion**: This isolates the MCL. Pain or laxity (gapping) compared to the contralateral side indicates an MCL sprain.
            ◦ **Grade I**: Pain with stress, no laxity.
            ◦ **Grade II**: Some laxity is present, but a **firm endpoint** is felt.
            ◦ **Grade III**: Significant laxity with a **soft or no endpoint**.
        ▪ **Performed at 0° of knee flexion (full extension)**: Laxity in full extension suggests a severe injury involving the MCL plus the posterior capsule and possibly a cruciate ligament (ACL/PCL), indicating a **multi-ligamentous injury**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Diagnosis is primarily clinical**, based on history and physical exam findings.
• **X-rays (AP, Lateral)**
    ◦ Recommended to rule out associated fractures, like a tibial plateau fracture in adults or a physeal fracture in children.
    ◦ A **Pellegrini-Stieda lesion** (calcification of the proximal MCL insertion) may be seen in chronic cases.
• **MRI**
    ◦ The **gold standard** for confirming the diagnosis, grading the tear, and evaluating for associated injuries.
    ◦ Not necessary for all suspected MCL injuries but is indicated for:
        ▪ Suspected Grade III tears.
        ▪ Concern for concomitant **ACL, PCL, or meniscal tears**.
        ▪ When valgus laxity is present in full extension.
• **Ultrasound**
    ◦ Can be used to visualize the superficial MCL but is operator-dependent and less effective for deep structures or associated injuries.
sections.treatment:
• The vast majority of isolated MCL injuries (including Grade III) are treated **non-operatively**.
• **Grade I**
    ◦ Conservative management: **RICE** (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation), NSAIDs.
    ◦ Early weight-bearing as tolerated.
    ◦ Physical therapy for ROM and quadriceps strengthening.
    ◦ Return to sport in 1-3 weeks.
• **Grade II**
    ◦ RICE, NSAIDs.
    ◦ **Hinged knee brace** to protect against valgus stress while allowing motion.
    ◦ Weight-bearing as tolerated, may require crutches initially.
    ◦ Physical therapy is crucial.
    ◦ Return to sport in 3-6 weeks.
• **Grade III (Isolated)**
    ◦ Often still managed non-operatively.
    ◦ Longer period of immobilization in a hinged brace, with progressive increases in ROM.
    ◦ Gradual progression of weight-bearing.
    ◦ Extensive rehabilitation is required.
    ◦ Return to sport may take 8-12 weeks or longer.
• **Surgical Intervention**
    ◦ Reserved for rare cases of isolated Grade III tears with persistent valgus instability after conservative management.
    ◦ Indicated primarily for **combined ligamentous injuries** (e.g., MCL + ACL tear).
sections.management:
• **Acute Phase (Week 1)**
    ◦ Focus on controlling pain and inflammation (RICE, NSAIDs) and protecting the ligament (bracing, crutches).
    ◦ Gentle ROM exercises are initiated.
• **Subacute Phase (Weeks 2-6)**
    ◦ Wean off crutches and progress to full weight-bearing.
    ◦ Focus on restoring full ROM and initiating strengthening exercises (quadriceps, hamstrings, hip abductors).
• **Strengthening & Proprioception Phase**
    ◦ Advanced strengthening, balance, and neuromuscular control exercises.
• **Return to Sport Phase**
    ◦ Begin sport-specific drills, agility training, and functional testing.
    ◦ A functional sports brace may be used upon return to play.
    ◦ Clearance requires full ROM, strength nearly equal to the contralateral side, and no instability.
sections.complications:
• **Chronic Valgus Instability**: Most common in improperly rehabilitated or severe injuries.
• **Arthrofibrosis**: Knee stiffness and loss of motion, prevented by early mobilization.
• **Pellegrini-Stieda Syndrome**: Painful calcification of the proximal MCL.
• **Post-traumatic Osteoarthritis**: Increased risk, especially with concomitant injuries.
• **Missed Associated Injuries**: Failure to diagnose concurrent ACL or meniscal tears can lead to poor outcomes.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for isolated Grade I and II injuries treated non-operatively, with >90% returning to pre-injury activity levels.
• **Good to Excellent** for isolated Grade III injuries managed conservatively, though recovery is longer.
• Prognosis for multi-ligamentous injuries is more variable and depends on the specific injuries and success of surgical intervention.

sections.overview:
• The Lateral Collateral Ligament (LCL), also known as the fibular collateral ligament (FCL), is the primary static stabilizer of the lateral aspect of the knee.
    ◦ It is a cord-like extracapsular ligament that runs from the lateral femoral epicondyle to the head of the fibula.
    ◦ Its main function is to resist **varus stress** and, to a lesser extent, external rotation of the tibia.
• LCL injuries are graded on a scale from I to III based on severity.
    ◦ Unlike Medial Collateral Ligament (MCL) injuries, isolated LCL tears are relatively uncommon and are frequently associated with more complex injuries to other knee structures, particularly the **Posterolateral Corner (PLC)**.
    ◦ **Grade I:** Sprain. Ligament fibers are stretched but intact. No significant instability.
    ◦ **Grade II:** Partial tear. Increased laxity with a firm endpoint on varus stress testing.
    ◦ **Grade III:** Complete tear. Significant laxity with no discernible endpoint. Often associated with PLC and/or cruciate ligament injury.
sections.etiology:
• The primary mechanism of injury is excessive **varus force** across the knee, which "gaps" the lateral joint line and stresses the LCL beyond its tensile strength.
    ◦ **Contact Injury:** A direct blow to the anteromedial aspect of the knee, forcing it into varus alignment. This is common in sports like football (tackling) or hockey (a check against the boards).
    ◦ **Non-contact Injury:** A varus force combined with hyperextension or external tibial rotation. This can occur during sudden changes in direction (cutting maneuvers) or awkward landings.
• The LCL is a key component of the Posterolateral Corner (PLC), which also includes the popliteus tendon and the popliteofibular ligament.
    ◦ Forces sufficient to tear the LCL often damage these other structures, leading to significant rotatory and varus instability.
sections.epidemiology:
• LCL injuries are significantly less common than MCL injuries.
• Highest incidence is in young, active individuals, particularly athletes participating in contact sports (e.g., football, soccer, wrestling, hockey).
• Isolated LCL injuries are rare; up to 80% of Grade III LCL tears occur in combination with other ligamentous injuries (e.g., ACL, PCL, PLC).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with a history of a specific traumatic event.
    ◦ They will report a direct blow to the inside of the knee or a non-contact hyperextension/twisting injury.
• The chief complaint is pain localized to the outer aspect of the knee and a possible sensation of instability.
sections.diagnostics:
• **X-rays**
    ◦ Standard AP, lateral, and sunrise views are obtained to rule out fractures.
    ◦ Look for an **avulsion fracture of the fibular head** (arcuate sign), which is pathognomonic for a severe PLC injury.
    ◦ **Bilateral varus stress radiographs** can be used to objectively quantify the degree of lateral compartment gapping.
• **MRI**
    ◦ **Gold standard** for diagnosis.
    ◦ Directly visualizes the LCL to confirm and grade the tear.
    ◦ Essential for identifying associated injuries: PLC structures, ACL/PCL tears, meniscal tears, bone bruises (often seen on the medial femoral condyle and medial tibial plateau from the "kissing" contusion of the varus injury).
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for isolated Grade I and II injuries treated conservatively, with most athletes returning to their prior level of function.
• **Good** for surgically treated isolated Grade III injuries.
• **Fair to Guarded** for combined injuries, especially LCL/PLC/PCL tears.
    ◦ These are complex injuries with a higher risk of residual instability and long-term degenerative changes.

sections.overview:
• The medial meniscus is a C-shaped fibrocartilaginous structure located on the medial aspect of the tibiofemoral joint.
• It acts as a crucial **shock absorber**, distributes load, aids in joint lubrication, and provides secondary stabilization to the knee.
• A medial meniscus tear is one of the most common knee injuries, involving damage to this structure, leading to **pain**, **swelling**, and **mechanical symptoms**.
• Tears are classified by their morphology (e.g., longitudinal, radial, **bucket-handle**) and can be either **acute/traumatic** or **chronic/degenerative**.
sections.etiology:
• **Mechanism of Injury**:
    ◦ **Acute/Traumatic**:
        ▪ Typically occurs in younger, athletic individuals.
        ▪ The classic mechanism is a **non-contact, twisting injury** with the foot planted and the knee in flexion.
        ▪ An axial load combined with femoral internal rotation on a fixed tibia places significant shear stress on the medial meniscus.
    ◦ **Degenerative**:
        ▪ More common in individuals **over 40**.
        ▪ The meniscal tissue weakens and loses elasticity with age.
        ▪ Tears can occur with minimal trauma, such as rising from a squat or a simple twist.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ The meniscus distributes axial loads across the knee. A tear disrupts this function, leading to a concentration of force on the **articular cartilage**.
    ◦ This focal load-bearing can accelerate chondral wear and is a significant risk factor for the development of knee **osteoarthritis**.
    ◦ The inner two-thirds of the meniscus is avascular (the **"white zone"**), having a poor intrinsic healing capacity. The outer one-third is vascular (the **"red zone"**) and has a better potential for healing, especially with surgical repair.
    ◦ **Bucket-handle tear**: A large, displaced longitudinal tear where the inner fragment flips into the intercondylar notch, often causing the knee to **lock**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Extremely common, with an estimated incidence of **60-70 per 100,000** persons per year.
• **Demographics**: Exhibits a **bimodal age distribution**.
    ◦ **Younger patients (<30 years)**: Higher incidence of acute, traumatic tears, often associated with sports.
    ◦ **Older patients (>40 years)**: Higher incidence of degenerative tears.
• **Sex**: **Males** are more commonly affected than females (approx. 2.5:1 ratio), likely due to higher participation in high-risk sports and occupations.
sections.riskFactors:
• **High-impact sports**: Football, soccer, basketball, skiing.
• **Occupations**: Jobs requiring frequent squatting or kneeling (e.g., plumbers, carpenters, coal miners).
• **Age**: Increased risk of degenerative tears with advancing age.
• **Obesity**: Increased load on the knee joint.
• Pre-existing knee instability: Particularly **ACL deficiency**, as the menisci act as secondary stabilizers.
• **Varus or valgus** knee alignment.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Acute Tear**:
    ◦ Patient reports a specific traumatic event, often a twisting motion during sports.
    ◦ They may describe an audible **"pop"** or tearing sensation at the time of injury.
    ◦ Pain is immediate, and a joint **effusion** (swelling) typically develops over the next 12-24 hours.
• **Degenerative Tear**:
    ◦ Patient presents with an **insidious onset** of medial knee pain.
    ◦ They often cannot recall a specific injury.
    ◦ Symptoms are chronic, exacerbated by activities like squatting or pivoting, and may be associated with stiffness and intermittent swelling.
• **Symptoms**:
    ◦ **Pain**: Localized to the medial aspect of the knee, often described as sharp or aching. Worse with twisting, squatting, or pivoting motions.
    ◦ **Mechanical Symptoms**:
        ▪ **Locking**: Inability to fully extend the knee (classic for a displaced **bucket-handle tear**).
        ▪ **Catching or clicking**: Sensation of something moving or getting caught inside the joint.
    ◦ **Swelling (Effusion)**: Typically mild to moderate and may be delayed.
    ◦ **Giving Way**: Sensation of knee instability or buckling.
    ◦ **Limited Range of Motion**: Especially loss of full flexion or extension due to pain or mechanical block.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Inspection**: Mild to moderate joint effusion may be visible. **Quadriceps atrophy** can be present in chronic cases.
• **Palpation**: **Medial joint line tenderness** is the most sensitive and important physical exam finding.
• **Range of Motion**: May be decreased, especially terminal extension if the knee is **locked**.
• **Special Provocative Tests**:
    ◦ **McMurray Test**:
        ▪ With the patient supine, the examiner maximally flexes the knee. The tibia is externally rotated while applying a valgus force. The knee is then slowly extended.
        ▪ **Positive Test**: A palpable or audible **"click"** or "thud" along the medial joint line.
    ◦ **Apley Grind (Compression) Test**:
        ▪ Patient is prone with the knee flexed to 90°. The examiner applies an axial compressive force to the heel while internally and externally rotating the tibia.
        ▪ **Positive Test**: Pain with compression and rotation.
    ◦ **Thessaly Test**:
        ▪ The patient stands on the affected leg with the knee flexed to 20°. The patient then rotates (twists) their body internally and externally.
        ▪ **Positive Test**: Medial joint line pain or a sense of locking/catching. This test is highly sensitive and specific when performed correctly.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Plain Radiographs (X-rays)**:
    ◦ **Views**: AP, lateral, and sunrise (patellofemoral). **Weight-bearing views** are preferred.
    ◦ **Findings**: Usually normal in acute tears. Primary role is to **rule out other pathology** such as fractures, loose bodies, or significant osteoarthritis (joint space narrowing, osteophytes), which would suggest a degenerative tear.
• **Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)**:
    ◦ **Gold standard** for diagnosis.
    ◦ **High sensitivity (>90%) and specificity (>90%)** for detecting meniscal tears.
    ◦ Accurately defines the tear's location, size, and pattern (e.g., bucket-handle, radial) and can identify associated injuries (ACL tear, chondral damage, bone bruising).
• **Diagnostic Arthroscopy**:
    ◦ Historically the gold standard, but now largely replaced by MRI for diagnosis.
    ◦ It is invasive but allows for direct visualization and concurrent treatment.
sections.treatment:
• **Non-operative / Conservative**:
    ◦ **Indications**: Small, stable tears in the periphery; degenerative tears without mechanical symptoms; patients who are poor surgical candidates.
    ◦ **Regimen**:
        ▪ **RICE**: Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation.
        ▪ **NSAIDs**: For pain and inflammation control.
        ▪ **Physical Therapy**: Focus on strengthening the quadriceps and hamstrings, improving range of motion, and neuromuscular control.
        ▪ **Activity Modification**: Avoid aggravating activities like deep squatting and pivoting.
        ▪ **Corticosteroid Injection**: Can provide short-term pain relief, particularly in the setting of co-existing osteoarthritis.
• **Surgical (Knee Arthroscopy)**:
    ◦ **Indications**: Young, active patients; large, complex tears; tears causing mechanical symptoms (**locking**); failure of conservative management.
    ◦ **Procedures**:
        ▪ **Partial Meniscectomy**: Debridement and removal of the torn, unstable portion of the meniscus. This is the most common procedure.
        ▪ **Meniscal Repair**: Suturing the torn edges of the meniscus together. This is preferred for younger patients (<40) with longitudinal tears in the vascular **"red zone"** as it preserves the meniscus and may reduce the long-term risk of osteoarthritis.
sections.management:
• **Initial Management**: For all suspected tears, begin with **RICE and NSAIDs**. Crutches may be used for a short period to assist with ambulation.
• **Diagnostic Pathway**: Obtain **plain radiographs** to rule out bony pathology. If symptoms persist or there is high suspicion for a significant tear (e.g., **locking**), proceed with an **MRI**.
• **Referral**: Refer to an **orthopedic surgeon** for patients with mechanical symptoms, young athletes with significant tears, or those who fail 4-6 weeks of conservative therapy.
• **Post-operative Rehabilitation**:
    ◦ **Partial Meniscectomy**: Rapid rehab protocol. Weight-bearing as tolerated immediately. Return to sport/activity typically within **4-6 weeks**.
    ◦ **Meniscal Repair**: More protected protocol. Often involves a period of non-weight-bearing or limited weight-bearing for **4-6 weeks** and a hinged knee brace to restrict flexion. Return to sport is much slower, often **4-6 months**.
sections.complications:
• **Untreated Tear**: Persistent pain, recurrent effusions, **locking**, and accelerated development of medial compartment **osteoarthritis**.
• **Post-Meniscectomy**: The most significant long-term complication is the **increased risk of developing premature osteoarthritis** due to the loss of the meniscus's shock-absorbing function.
• **Surgical Complications**: Infection, DVT, nerve injury (**saphenous nerve**), stiffness (**arthrofibrosis**), and failure of meniscal repair requiring re-operation.
sections.prognosis:
• **Overall**: Generally good for symptomatic relief.
• **Partial Meniscectomy**: Excellent short-term outcomes with high rates of return to previous activity levels. However, the long-term risk of **osteoarthritis** is increased.
• **Meniscal Repair**: If successful, it offers the best long-term prognosis for preserving joint health. However, it has a higher failure and re-operation rate compared to meniscectomy.
• **Degenerative Tears**: Prognosis is often dictated by the degree of underlying osteoarthritis.

sections.overview:
• C-shaped fibrocartilaginous structure located on the **lateral aspect** of the tibiofemoral joint.
• Primary functions:
    ◦ Act as a **shock absorber**
    ◦ Increase joint congruity and stability
    ◦ Distribute load
    ◦ Aid in lubrication
• More mobile than the medial meniscus due to fewer capsular attachments, making it less prone to injury overall but susceptible to specific injury patterns.
sections.etiology:
• Tears occur through two primary mechanisms:
    ◦ **Acute / Traumatic**
        ▪ Most common in younger, active individuals (< 40 years old).
        ▪ Mechanism: Typically involves a **twisting or rotational force on a flexed, weight-bearing knee**.
            • Examples include sudden pivoting, cutting, or deceleration common in sports.
        ▪ The force compresses and shears the meniscus between the femoral condyle and the tibial plateau, causing it to tear.
    ◦ **Degenerative**
        ▪ More common in older individuals (> 40 years old).
        ▪ Mechanism: Occurs from cumulative microtrauma and age-related changes (dehydration, decreased elasticity) with minimal or no inciting trauma.
            • A simple motion like squatting can cause a tear.
        ▪ Tears are often complex or horizontal in nature.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ A torn meniscus disrupts the normal biomechanics of the knee.
    ◦ It can no longer effectively distribute **"hoop stresses,"** leading to a significant increase in contact pressure on the articular cartilage of the lateral femoral condyle and tibial plateau.
    ◦ This focal pressure accelerates cartilage wear and is a primary driver of **early-onset osteoarthritis**.
sections.epidemiology:
• Less common than medial meniscus tears (Medial:Lateral tear ratio is approximately 2:1 to 3:1).
• **Bimodal distribution**:
    ◦ Peak incidence in active males aged 21-30 years (traumatic).
    ◦ Second peak in individuals aged >50 years (degenerative).
• Often occurs in conjunction with other ligamentous injuries, especially **Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) tears**.
    ◦ An acute ACL tear is frequently associated with a lateral meniscus tear.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The patient's history is crucial for diagnosis.
• **Acute Tear**
    ◦ A young athlete will often report a specific inciting event.
    ◦ They may describe planting their foot, twisting the knee, and feeling or hearing a **"pop"** at the time of injury.
    ◦ This is followed by pain and the gradual onset of a knee effusion over the next **12-24 hours**.
    ◦ They may have been able to continue playing initially but the knee became stiff and swollen later.
• **Degenerative Tear**
    ◦ An older patient may not recall a specific injury.
    ◦ They will describe an insidious onset of lateral-sided knee pain, stiffness, and intermittent swelling, often worse with activities like squatting or twisting.
sections.diagnostics:
• **X-rays (Weight-bearing AP, lateral, and sunrise views)**
    ◦ **First-line imaging** to rule out other pathology.
    ◦ Typically normal in an acute tear.
    ◦ Important for evaluating for fractures, loose bodies, and assessing for degenerative changes like **joint space narrowing**, which may indicate osteoarthritis.
• **MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging)**
    ◦ **Gold standard / Confirmatory test**.
    ◦ Highly sensitive (>90%) and specific for diagnosing meniscal tears.
    ◦ Visualizes the tear itself (location, type, size) and assesses for associated injuries to ligaments, cartilage, and bone (e.g., bone marrow edema).
    ◦ A **Grade 3 signal** (high-intensity signal that extends to an articular surface) on MRI is diagnostic of a tear.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis for symptomatic relief is generally good with both conservative and surgical management.
• Outcomes for meniscal repair are best in young patients with acute, peripheral (**"red zone"**) tears, often done in conjunction with an ACL reconstruction.
• While partial meniscectomy provides excellent short-term relief, it is a known risk factor for the development of osteoarthritis in the long term (10-20 years post-op).

sections.overview: • A lateral ankle sprain is an acute ligamentous injury on the lateral side of the ankle joint, most commonly involving the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL). • It is one of the most common musculoskeletal injuries, resulting from excessive inversion and plantarflexion of the foot. • The injury is graded based on severity, which dictates treatment and prognosis.
sections.etiology: • Mechanism of Injury: The classic mechanism is inversion of a plantarflexed foot. ◦ The ankle is most unstable in plantarflexion, making the lateral ligaments vulnerable. ◦ This commonly occurs when landing from a jump, running on an uneven surface, or stepping into a hole. • Anatomy of the Lateral Ligament Complex: ◦ Anterior Talofibular Ligament (ATFL): The weakest of the three and most commonly injured (>70% of cases). It resists anterior translation of the talus and internal rotation. ◦ Calcaneofibular Ligament (CFL): The second most commonly injured. It is stronger than the ATFL and is typically injured with more significant inversion force, often in a neutral or dorsiflexed position. ◦ Posterior Talofibular Ligament (PTFL): The strongest and least commonly injured. Injury requires a severe force, often associated with ankle dislocation. • Grading of Sprains: ◦ Grade I: ▪ Ligament stretching with microscopic tearing. Mild pain and swelling, minimal loss of function, no mechanical instability. Able to bear weight. ◦ Grade II: ▪ Partial ligament tear. Moderate pain, swelling, and ecchymosis. Mild to moderate instability, pain with weight-bearing, limited range of motion. ◦ Grade III: ▪ Complete ligament rupture. Severe pain, swelling, and ecchymosis. Significant mechanical instability and loss of function. Unable to bear weight.
sections.epidemiology: • Incidence: Extremely common, accounting for up to 25% of all sports-related injuries. • Peak Age: 15-24 years. • Population: High incidence in athletes, particularly in sports requiring jumping and cutting, such as basketball, soccer, and volleyball. • Recurrence: High rate of recurrence (up to 40%), often leading to chronic ankle instability.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • Patient reports an acute event of "twisting" or "rolling" the ankle, often accompanied by an audible "pop" or "snap." • Immediate onset of pain on the lateral aspect of the ankle. • Rapid development of localized swelling and, later, ecchymosis. • Varying degrees of difficulty with weight-bearing, from a slight limp to a complete inability to stand on the affected leg.
sections.diagnostics: • Primarily a clinical diagnosis. • Radiographs (X-rays): ◦ Indicated only if fracture is suspected based on the Ottawa Ankle Rules. ◦ Purpose: To rule out malleolar, talar, or associated foot fractures. ◦ Ottawa Ankle Rules (obtain ankle X-ray series if): ▪ There is bony tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of the lateral malleolus (distal 6 cm). ▪ There is bony tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of the medial malleolus (distal 6 cm). ▪ The patient is unable to bear weight for 4 steps both immediately after the injury and in the emergency department/clinic. ◦ Ottawa Foot Rules (obtain foot X-ray series if): ▪ There is bony tenderness at the base of the 5th metatarsal. ▪ There is bony tenderness at the navicular bone. ▪ The patient is unable to bear weight (as above). • MRI: ◦ Not indicated for acute, uncomplicated sprains. ◦ Reserved for: ▪ Suspected syndesmotic (high ankle) sprain. ▪ Suspected osteochondral lesion of the talus. ▪ Chronic ankle instability despite conservative management. ▪ Diagnostic uncertainty or failure to improve after 4-6 weeks. • Musculoskeletal Ultrasound (MSK US): ◦ Can be used to visualize ligament tears dynamically; highly operator-dependent.
sections.prognosis: • Excellent for most patients who adhere to a structured rehabilitation program. • Return to activity timeline: ◦ Grade I: 1-3 weeks ◦ Grade II: 3-6 weeks ◦ Grade III: 6-12+ weeks • The primary negative prognostic factor is inadequate rehabilitation, which leads to a high rate of recurrence and the development of chronic ankle instability.

sections.overview:
• A high ankle sprain is an injury to the **distal tibiofibular syndesmosis**, the complex of ligaments that connect the distal tibia and fibula, stabilizing the **ankle mortise**.
• It is less common than a traditional lateral ankle sprain but is associated with significantly longer recovery times and greater potential for **chronic instability** if not properly managed.
• The primary ligaments involved are the **anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament (AITFL)**, the **posterior inferior tibiofibular ligament (PITFL)**, and the **interosseous membrane/ligament**.
sections.etiology:
• **Mechanism**
    ◦ The classic mechanism of injury is a forceful **external rotation of the talus/foot** relative to a fixed tibia.
    ◦ This is often combined with excessive **dorsiflexion**.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The external rotation force causes the talus to widen the ankle mortise, placing extreme stress on the syndesmotic ligaments.
    ◦ The **AITFL is the first and most commonly injured** ligament.
    ◦ With increasing force, the injury can progress to involve the interosseous ligament and membrane, and finally the **PITFL**.
    ◦ Severe injuries can lead to a complete rupture of the syndesmosis (**diastasis**), causing gross instability of the ankle joint, often associated with fractures.
sections.epidemiology:
• Accounts for approximately 1-18% of all ankle sprains.
• Incidence is much higher in athletic populations, particularly in high-impact or collision sports.
• **Common sports**
    ◦ American football (especially linemen), soccer, ice hockey, and skiing (due to rigid boots).
sections.riskFactors:
• Participation in contact sports (football, rugby, hockey).
• Sports that involve rigid footwear that fixes the ankle (ski boots, hockey skates).
• Poor neuromuscular control or conditioning.
• Previous ankle injury.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents after an acute traumatic event involving a twisting motion to the ankle, often describing a different mechanism and location of pain than a typical "rolled ankle."
• **History**
    ◦ Forceful twisting of a planted foot, such as being tackled from the outside.
• **Pain Location**
    ◦ The patient will localize pain **anterolaterally and proximal to the ankle joint**, over the area of the syndesmosis.
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ Anterolateral ankle pain located "high" (above the ankle joint).
    ◦ Pain that is worsened by walking, running, or cutting maneuvers.
    ◦ A feeling of instability or "giving way," especially with rotational movements.
    ◦ Swelling may be present but is often less pronounced than in a severe lateral ankle sprain.
• **Functional Status**
    ◦ Significant difficulty or inability to bear weight, especially during the "push-off" phase of gait.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Inspection**
    ◦ Minimal to moderate swelling, often less dramatic than a Grade III lateral ankle sprain.
    ◦ Ecchymosis may be present.
• **Palpation**
    ◦ Point tenderness over the **AITFL** (located between the tibia and fibula, just proximal to the joint line).
    ◦ Tenderness along the interosseous membrane when palpating proximally.
    ◦ **Crucial:** Always palpate the **entire length of the fibula** up to the knee to rule out a **Maisonneuve fracture**.
• **Special Tests (High-Yield)**
    ◦ **Squeeze Test (Hopkins Test)**
        ▪ The examiner compresses the tibia and fibula together at mid-calf.
        ▪ A positive test is pain reproduced distally at the syndesmosis.
    ◦ **External Rotation Stress Test (Kleiger Test)**
        ▪ The examiner stabilizes the leg, holds the foot in a neutral or slightly dorsiflexed position, and applies an external rotation force.
        ▪ A positive test is pain reproduced over the syndesmosis.
    ◦ **Fibular Translation Test**
        ▪ The examiner attempts to translate the fibula anteriorly and posteriorly relative to the tibia.
        ▪ Increased laxity or pain suggests syndesmotic instability.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Radiographs (X-rays)**
    ◦ **Standard Views**: AP, lateral, and **mortise** views of the ankle are essential.
    ◦ **Weight-bearing views are critical** to assess for subtle instability if the patient can tolerate them.
    ◦ **Key Measurements on Mortise/AP Views**
        ▪ **Tibiofibular Clear Space**: >6 mm is abnormal.
        ▪ **Tibiofibular Overlap**: <6 mm on AP or <1 mm on mortise view is abnormal.
        ▪ **Medial Clear Space**: >4-5 mm suggests **deltoid ligament injury** and mortise instability.
    ◦ **Stress Radiographs**: May be used to unmask instability if non-weight-bearing films are normal but clinical suspicion is high.
• **MRI**
    ◦ **Gold standard** for visualizing ligamentous injury.
    ◦ Confirms tears of the **AITFL**, **PITFL**, and interosseous ligament.
    ◦ Can identify associated bone bruises, osteochondral lesions, or other soft tissue injuries.
• **CT Scan**
    ◦ Useful for identifying occult or complex fractures associated with the syndesmotic injury.
sections.treatment:
• **Stable Injuries (no diastasis on weight-bearing or stress imaging)**
    ◦ **Conservative Management**
        ▪ **Phase 1 (Protection):** Strict immobilization in a CAM boot or cast, **non-weight-bearing (NWB)** or protected weight-bearing for 2-4 weeks.
        ▪ **Phase 2 (Rehabilitation):** Gradual progression to full weight-bearing. Physical therapy focused on restoring range of motion, strength, and proprioception.
        ▪ **Phase 3 (Return to Sport):** Sport-specific training. Return criteria include full, pain-free ROM, strength >90% of the contralateral side, and completion of functional tests.
• **Unstable Injuries (diastasis present)**
    ◦ **Surgical Intervention is required.**
    ◦ **Goal:** Anatomically reduce the syndesmosis and provide stable fixation to allow for healing.
    ◦ **Surgical Options**
        ▪ **Syndesmotic Screw Fixation:** One or two screws are placed across the syndesmosis from the fibula into the tibia. May be removed later.
        ▪ **Suture-Button Fixation (e.g., "TightRope"):** A flexible suture construct used instead of rigid screws, allowing for physiologic micro-motion and typically does not require removal.
sections.management:
• The key principle is a prolonged period of protected or **non-weight-bearing** compared to a lateral ankle sprain.
• **Conservative**
    ◦ Follow-up is crucial to ensure stability is maintained. If symptoms persist, repeat imaging or a switch to surgical management may be necessary.
• **Surgical**
    ◦ Post-operative protocol involves a period of NWB in a cast/boot (typically ~6 weeks), followed by progressive weight-bearing and intensive physical therapy.
• **Return to Play**
    ◦ Significantly delayed compared to lateral ankle sprains, often taking **6-12 weeks for conservative care** and **3-6 months for surgical cases.**
sections.complications:
• **Chronic Instability:** Persistent widening of the mortise leading to pain, dysfunction, and early arthritis.
• **Post-Traumatic Arthritis:** Result of altered joint mechanics from chronic instability.
• **Heterotopic Ossification:** Abnormal bone formation within the interosseous membrane, leading to stiffness.
• **Hardware Complications:** Screw breakage, loosening, or pain requiring removal.
• **Arthrofibrosis:** Ankle stiffness and loss of motion.
• **Missed Diagnosis:** The most significant issue, as treating a high ankle sprain like a lateral sprain leads to poor outcomes.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is generally good with accurate diagnosis and appropriate management.
• Unstable injuries treated surgically have good outcomes, though the recovery is lengthy.
• Patients should be counseled that recovery will take **2-3 times longer** than a typical lateral ankle sprain.
• There is a higher risk of persistent symptoms (stiffness, pain with cutting) compared to other sprains.

sections.overview:
• Systemic skeletal disease characterized by **low bone mass** and **microarchitectural deterioration** of bone tissue, leading to enhanced bone fragility and a consequent increase in fracture risk.
    ◦ It is the most common metabolic bone disease.
    ◦ The clinical significance lies in the fractures that result, often from minimal or no trauma (**fragility fractures**).
    ◦ Considered a "**silent disease**" as it is often asymptomatic until a fracture occurs.
sections.etiology:
• The core pathophysiologic mechanism is an **imbalance between bone resorption and bone formation**, where osteoclastic activity (bone breakdown) outpaces osteoblastic activity (bone formation).
• **Primary Osteoporosis**: Most common form.
    ◦ **Type 1 (Postmenopausal)**: Occurs in women after menopause due to **estrogen deficiency**.
