        ▪ ***Cutibacterium acnes*** (formerly *Propionibacterium acnes*): Notably associated with **shoulder** arthroplasty infections.
    ◦ **Polymicrobial Infections (~15%)**
    ◦ **Fungi (*Candida* spp.)**: Rare, usually in severely immunocompromised patients.
sections.epidemiology:
• PJI occurs in **1-2%** of all primary total hip and knee arthroplasties.
• The risk is significantly higher for revision surgeries (**3-5%** or more).
• PJI is the **#1 reason for failure of total knee arthroplasty (TKA)** and a leading cause for failure of total hip arthroplasty (THA).
sections.riskFactors:
• **Diabetes Mellitus** (especially with poor glycemic control, HbA1c > 7)
• **Obesity** (BMI > 40)
• **Immunosuppression** (e.g., corticosteroids, TNF-alpha inhibitors, HIV)
• Inflammatory arthropathies (e.g., **Rheumatoid Arthritis**)
• Malnutrition (low albumin)
• Smoking
• Peripheral vascular disease
• Prior surgery or infection in the same joint
• Nasal colonization with ***S. aureus***
• Revision arthroplasty
• Prolonged operative time (>90-120 minutes)
• Complexity of the surgical procedure
• Post-operative wound complications (e.g., hematoma, delayed healing, dehiscence)
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation is classified by timing, which strongly suggests the etiology and dictates management.
• **Early Onset (<3 Months Post-op)**
    ◦ Presents as an acute post-surgical infection.
    ◦ **Acute onset** of fever, chills, significant joint pain, erythema, swelling, and warmth.
    ◦ Often involves **purulent wound drainage**.
    ◦ Typically caused by virulent organisms like ***S. aureus***.
• **Delayed Onset (3-12 Months Post-op)**
    ◦ Insidious onset with more subtle signs.
    ◦ **Chronic, persistent joint pain** is the primary symptom.
    ◦ May present with implant loosening or a **draining sinus tract**.
    ◦ Systemic symptoms (fever) are often absent.
    ◦ Typically caused by less virulent organisms like ***S. epidermidis*** or ***C. acnes***.
• **Late Onset (>12 Months Post-op)**
    ◦ Usually from **hematogenous seeding**.
    ◦ Presents as an **acute onset of pain and fever in a previously well-functioning joint**.
    ◦ Often preceded by a recent infection (e.g., dental work, UTI, pneumonia).
sections.physicalExam:
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ **Persistent joint pain**, especially **pain at rest** or "start-up pain," distinguishing it from mechanical loosening where pain is activity-related.
    ◦ Localized swelling and warmth.
    ◦ Fever, chills, malaise (more common in acute presentations).
    ◦ Persistent drainage from the surgical wound.
    ◦ Reduced range of motion and inability to bear weight.
• **Exam Findings**
    ◦ Erythema, warmth, and edema over the involved joint.
    ◦ Joint effusion.
    ◦ **A draining sinus tract communicating with the joint is pathognomonic for PJI.**
    ◦ Tenderness to palpation over the joint line or prosthesis.
    ◦ Pain with passive and active range of motion.
    ◦ Evidence of wound dehiscence or poor healing.
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosing PJI requires a combination of clinical, laboratory, and microbiological data.
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) & C-Reactive Protein (CRP)**
        ▪ **Key screening tests** with high sensitivity but low specificity.
        ▪ If both ESR and CRP are normal, PJI is highly unlikely (<1% probability).
        ▪ They are normally elevated in the immediate post-operative period (CRP peaks at day 2-3, ESR peaks at day 5-7). Persistently elevated levels beyond 3-6 months are suspicious.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Plain Radiographs (X-ray)**
        ▪ Initial imaging study.
        ▪ Findings suggesting PJI: **periosteal reaction**, progressive **radiolucent lines** at the bone-cement interface, osteolysis, or implant migration/subsidence.
        ▪ May be completely normal in early PJI.
• **Arthrocentesis (Joint Aspiration)**
    ◦ **The most important diagnostic step**; should be performed before starting antibiotics.
    ◦ Synovial fluid is sent for:
        ▪ **Cell Count & Differential**: Critical for diagnosis.
            • **Knee PJI**: WBC count **> 1,700 cells/L** and/or **> 65%** Polymorphonuclear cells (PMNs).
            • **Hip PJI**: WBC count **> 3,000 cells/L** and/or **> 80%** PMNs.
        ▪ **Aerobic & Anaerobic Cultures**: Essential for identifying the pathogen and sensitivities.
        ▪ **Gram Stain**: Low sensitivity (~20%) but highly specific if positive.
        ▪ **Newer Biomarkers**: Synovial fluid alpha-defensin and leukocyte esterase tests have high accuracy.
• **Intraoperative Findings (Gold Standard)**
    ◦ **Multiple (3-5) tissue samples** are taken from different areas for microbiology and histopathology. Two or more positive cultures with the same organism are highly diagnostic.
    ◦ **Histopathology**: Presence of >5 PMNs per high-power field in tissue surrounding the prosthesis confirms infection.
    ◦ Purulence surrounding the prosthesis is visually diagnostic.
• **Musculoskeletal Infection Society (MSIS) Criteria**
    ◦ A diagnosis of PJI is confirmed if one **Major Criterion** is met, or four of six **Minor Criteria** are met.
    ◦ **Major Criteria**
        ▪ A **sinus tract** communicating with the prosthesis.
        ▪ Two or more positive cultures of the same organism from joint aspirate or intraoperative tissue.
    ◦ **Minor Criteria**
        ▪ Elevated ESR/CRP.
        ▪ Elevated synovial fluid WBC/PMN%.
        ▪ Positive synovial fluid biomarker.
        ▪ Positive single culture.
        ▪ Positive histology.
sections.treatment:
• **Debridement, Antibiotics, and Implant Retention (DAIR)**
    ◦ Also known as "washout," this involves open debridement of all infected tissue and exchange of modular components (e.g., polyethylene liner). The main metal implants are left in place.
    ◦ **Indicated only for**: Acute, early post-op PJI (<3-4 weeks from surgery) OR acute hematogenous PJI with symptoms <3 weeks, in a patient with a stable, well-fixed implant and a known organism sensitive to oral antibiotics.
• **Two-Stage Exchange Arthroplasty**
    ◦ **The gold standard** and most common treatment for chronic PJI in the United States.
    ◦ **Stage 1**: Removal of all prosthetic components, radical debridement of all infected bone and soft tissue, and placement of an **antibiotic-impregnated cement spacer**. This is followed by ~6 weeks of IV antibiotics.
    ◦ **Stage 2**: After a period of being antibiotic-free to ensure the infection is cleared (confirmed by normalized ESR/CRP), the spacer is removed and a new definitive prosthesis is implanted.
• **Single-Stage Exchange (One-Stage)**
    ◦ Removal of components, debridement, and reimplantation of a new prosthesis all in a single operation.
    ◦ Requires a healthy patient with good soft tissues and a known, highly susceptible organism. Higher risk of failure than two-stage.
• **Resection Arthroplasty**
    ◦ Removal of the prosthesis without reimplantation. Results in a shortened, less stable limb but can be a pain-free solution for patients who are too ill to tolerate further complex surgeries.
• **Amputation**
    ◦ A last resort for life-threatening, uncontrollable infection with extensive bone and soft tissue loss.
• **Antibiotic Therapy**
    ◦ Should be guided by culture results.
    ◦ Typically involves **4-6 weeks of pathogen-directed IV antibiotics** after surgery.
    ◦ For Staphylococcal infections on retained hardware (DAIR), **Rifampin is crucial** as it penetrates the biofilm. It should always be used in combination with another agent (e.g., Vancomycin, Cefazolin) to prevent resistance.
    ◦ May be followed by long-term oral suppressive antibiotics in select cases.
sections.management:
• A **multidisciplinary approach** involving Orthopedic Surgery and Infectious Disease is critical for success.
• Infection clearance is monitored by serial **ESR and CRP** levels. Before proceeding to Stage 2 of a two-stage exchange, these markers should normalize or be trending down significantly.
• Patient optimization is key: manage diabetes, encourage smoking cessation, improve nutritional status.
sections.complications:
• Recurrence of infection (failure of treatment)
• Need for multiple additional surgeries
• Persistent pain and functional disability
• Arthrodesis (surgical fusion of the joint)
• **Amputation**
• **Sepsis** and mortality
• Complications from long-term antibiotic therapy (e.g., renal toxicity, C. difficile colitis)
sections.prognosis:
• Eradication of infection is successful in **85-95%** of cases treated with a **two-stage exchange**.
• **DAIR** has a lower success rate, ranging from 60-80%.
• Even with successful eradication, patients often have worse functional outcomes compared to those with an uncomplicated primary arthroplasty.

sections.overview:
• Clinical state resulting from **insufficient production and secretion of thyroid hormones** (thyroxine/T4 and triiodothyronine/T3) by the thyroid gland itself.
• This failure of the gland leads to a characteristic rise in **Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH)** from the anterior pituitary due to a loss of negative feedback.
• It is the **most common cause of hypothyroidism**, accounting for >95% of cases.
• The condition is characterized by a generalized **slowing of metabolic processes**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology (Causes)**
    ◦ **Autoimmune** (most common in iodine-sufficient regions)
        ▪ **Hashimoto's Thyroiditis** (Chronic Lymphocytic Thyroiditis): The number one cause in the United States. Autoantibodies (**Anti-TPO, Anti-Tg**) lead to lymphocyte infiltration and progressive destruction of thyroid follicles.
    ◦ **Iatrogenic**
        ▪ **Post-Thyroidectomy**: Surgical removal of the thyroid gland.
        ▪ **Radioactive Iodine (I-131) Therapy**: Ablation of the thyroid gland, often used to treat hyperthyroidism (e.g., Graves' disease).
        ▪ **External Beam Radiation**: Radiation to the head/neck for malignancies (e.g., lymphoma).
    ◦ **Medications**
        ▪ **Amiodarone**: High iodine content can inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis (**Wolff-Chaikoff effect**). Can also cause a destructive thyroiditis.
        ▪ **Lithium**: Inhibits thyroid hormone release.
        ▪ **Interferon-alpha, Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors** (e.g., Sunitinib).
    ◦ **Iodine Deficiency** (most common cause worldwide).
    ◦ **Congenital Hypothyroidism (Cretinism)**: Thyroid dysgenesis or agenesis.
    ◦ **Infiltrative Diseases** (rare): Amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Gland Failure**: The thyroid gland is damaged or dysfunctional and cannot produce adequate T4 and T3.
    ◦ **Loss of Negative Feedback**: Low circulating levels of T4/T3 are detected by the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary.
    ◦ **Pituitary Response**: The pituitary is not inhibited, so it increases its production and secretion of TSH in an attempt to stimulate the failing thyroid gland.
    ◦ **Clinical Result**: The body's metabolic rate decreases due to the lack of thyroid hormone, leading to systemic signs and symptoms. The hallmark lab finding is an **elevated TSH** with a **low free T4**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects approximately 4-5% of the U.S. population.
• **Sex**: Much more common in **women** than men (ratio approx. 8:1).
• **Age**: Prevalence **increases significantly with age**, particularly after age 60.
• **Subclinical Hypothyroidism**: (Elevated TSH, normal free T4) is even more common, affecting up to 10% of older adults.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is often **insidious**, with a **gradual onset** of non-specific symptoms over months to years.
• Patients present with complaints related to a generalized "**slowing down**" of the body.
• Severity ranges from asymptomatic (subclinical) to life-threatening (**myxedema coma**).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Best Initial Test**: **TSH level**.
    ◦ If TSH is elevated, follow up with a **free T4 (FT4)**.
• **Laboratory Pattern for Primary Hypothyroidism**
    ◦ **High TSH** (>4.5-5.0 mIU/L, varies by lab)
    ◦ **Low Free T4** (<0.8 ng/dL)
• **Laboratory Pattern for Subclinical Hypothyroidism**
    ◦ **High TSH**
    ◦ **Normal Free T4**
• **Autoantibodies** (to determine etiology)
    ◦ **Anti-thyroid peroxidase (Anti-TPO) antibodies**: Highly sensitive and specific for **Hashimoto's thyroiditis**. Present in >90% of cases.
    ◦ **Anti-thyroglobulin (Anti-Tg) antibodies**: Also seen in Hashimoto's but less sensitive.
• **Associated Lab Abnormalities**
    ◦ **Lipids**: Elevated total cholesterol, LDL, and triglycerides.
    ◦ **CBC**: Normocytic, normochromic anemia.
    ◦ **CMP**: Hyponatremia (due to increased ADH).
    ◦ **Enzymes**: Elevated **Creatine Kinase (CK)** from myopathy.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** with adequate and consistent **levothyroxine** replacement therapy.
• Symptoms are reversible, and patients can lead a normal life with normal life expectancy.
• Untreated, it can progress to **myxedema coma**, which carries a high mortality rate.

sections.overview:
• **Graves' Disease** is an autoimmune disorder that is the most common cause of **hyperthyroidism** in iodine-sufficient regions.
	◦ It is characterized by the production of autoantibodies that stimulate the **thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) receptor**, leading to excessive thyroid hormone synthesis and secretion.
	◦ The classic clinical triad, though not always present, consists of **thyrotoxicosis**, **ophthalmopathy (exophthalmos)**, and **dermopathy (pretibial myxedema)**.
sections.etiology:
• **Autoimmune Mechanism**
	◦ The core pathology involves the production of **TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb)**, specifically a type called **Thyroid-Stimulating Immunoglobulin (TSI)**.
• **TSH Receptor Activation**
	◦ TSI binds to and activates the TSH receptor on thyroid follicular cells, mimicking the action of TSH.
• **Unregulated Hormone Production**
	◦ This constant stimulation leads to unregulated, excessive production and release of triiodothyronine (T3) and thyroxine (T4), independent of the normal pituitary feedback loop.
	◦ This results in a **suppressed TSH** level from the pituitary.
• **Extrathyroidal Manifestations**
	◦ The same autoimmune process targets tissues in the orbit and skin.
	◦ T-cell activation and cytokine release cause fibroblasts to produce excess glycosaminoglycans (e.g., hyaluronic acid), leading to inflammation, edema, and tissue remodeling seen in **ophthalmopathy** and **pretibial myxedema**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Most common cause of **hyperthyroidism**, accounting for 60-80% of cases.
• **Sex**: Significantly more common in women (Female:Male ratio **5-10:1**).
• **Age of Onset**: Typically presents between the ages of **20 and 50**.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Genetics**: Strong familial predisposition; associated with **HLA-DR3** and **HLA-B8**.
• **Female Sex**
• **Personal or family history of other autoimmune diseases** (e.g., Type 1 Diabetes, Rheumatoid Arthritis, Pernicious Anemia).
• **Stress**: Major emotional or physical stress can trigger onset.
• **Infection**: Can be a precipitating factor.
• **Postpartum Period**: Increased risk in the year following childbirth.
• **Smoking**: Strongest modifiable risk factor, particularly for the development and severity of **Graves' ophthalmopathy**.
• **High Iodine Intake**: Can precipitate the disease in susceptible individuals.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Classic Vignette**
	◦ A patient, typically a female in her 30s or 40s, presents with a several-week to several-month history of **anxiety**, irritability, **palpitations**, **unintentional weight loss** despite an **increased appetite**, **heat intolerance**, and fatigue.
	◦ They may also complain of changes in their eyes or a visible swelling in their neck.
• **Symptoms by System**
	◦ **Constitutional**: **Weight loss** (despite increased appetite/polyphagia), **heat intolerance**, fatigue, **diaphoresis**.
	◦ **Neuropsychiatric**: **Anxiety**, nervousness, irritability, emotional lability, insomnia, **fine tremor**.
	◦ **Cardiovascular**: **Palpitations**, **tachycardia**, dyspnea on exertion, **atrial fibrillation** (especially in older patients).
	◦ **Gastrointestinal**: **Hyperdefecation** (increased frequency of soft, well-formed stools, not true diarrhea), increased appetite.
	◦ **Musculoskeletal**: Proximal muscle weakness, myopathy.
	◦ **Dermatologic**: Warm, moist, smooth skin; fine, brittle hair; **onycholysis** (Plummer's nails - separation of nail from nail bed).
	◦ **Reproductive**: Oligomenorrhea, amenorrhea, decreased libido.
	◦ **Ocular (Non-infiltrative)**: Stare, **lid lag** (von Graefe's sign).
sections.physicalExam:
• **Vitals**: **Tachycardia** (often >100 bpm), hypertension with a **wide pulse pressure**, possible fever.
• **General**: Anxious, hyperkinetic appearance.
• **Neck**
	◦ **Goiter**: Symmetrically enlarged, non-tender, firm thyroid gland.
	◦ **Thyroid Bruit**: Auscultation over the goiter may reveal a bruit or thrill due to increased vascularity (highly specific for Graves').
• **Eyes (Infiltrative Ophthalmopathy)**
	◦ **Exophthalmos/Proptosis**: Forward protrusion of the eyeballs.
	◦ **Periorbital Edema**: Swelling around the eyes.
	◦ **Lid Retraction**: Gives a characteristic "staring" appearance.
	◦ **Lid Lag**: Upper eyelid lags behind the globe on downward gaze.
	◦ **Conjunctival Injection/Chemosis**: Redness and swelling of the conjunctiva.
	◦ **Extraocular Muscle Dysfunction**: Diplopia, pain with eye movements.
• **Neurologic**
	◦ **Fine Tremor**: Best seen with hands outstretched and a piece of paper on top.
	◦ **Hyperreflexia**: Brisk deep tendon reflexes (DTRs).
• **Cardiovascular**: **Sinus tachycardia**, **atrial fibrillation**, loud S1, systolic flow murmur.
• **Dermatologic**
	◦ **Pretibial Myxedema (Dermopathy)**: Rare (<5% of patients). Waxy, discolored, non-pitting induration of the skin, typically over the shins ("peau d'orange" appearance).
	◦ **Thyroid Acropachy**: Very rare finding; clubbing of the fingers and toes with soft tissue swelling.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Initial Thyroid Function Tests (TFTs)**
	◦ **TSH**: **Low / Suppressed** (<0.01 mIU/L). This is the single best initial screening test.
	◦ **Free T4 and/or Total T3**: **Elevated**. (T3 may be disproportionately higher than T4).
• **Confirmatory Etiologic Tests**
	◦ **TSH Receptor Antibody (TRAb / TSI)**: **Positive**. This is the most specific test for Graves' disease and confirms the autoimmune etiology.
	◦ **Radioactive Iodine Uptake (RAIU) Scan**
		▪ **Finding**: **Diffusely increased iodine uptake** across the entire gland.
		▪ **Purpose**: Differentiates Graves' from other causes of hyperthyroidism (e.g., toxic nodule shows a single "hot" spot; thyroiditis shows very low uptake).
• **Supportive Labs / Imaging**
	◦ **Anti-TPO / Anti-Tg Antibodies**: Often positive but are not specific to Graves'.
	◦ **ECG**: To evaluate for sinus tachycardia or atrial fibrillation.
	◦ **CBC**: May show normocytic anemia.
	◦ **CMP**: May show mild hypercalcemia or elevated alkaline phosphatase.
sections.treatment:
• **Beta-Blockers**
	◦ **Propranolol** is often preferred as it is non-selective and also weakly inhibits the peripheral conversion of T4 to the more active T3.
	◦ Atenolol or Metoprolol can also be used.
	◦ **Purpose**: Controls adrenergic symptoms like **tachycardia**, **palpitations**, **tremor**, and **anxiety**. Does not treat the underlying hyperthyroidism.
• **Antithyroid Drugs (ATDs)**
	◦ **Methimazole (MMI)**: **First-line agent**. Longer half-life (once-daily dosing).
	◦ **Propylthiouracil (PTU)**: **Second-line agent** due to higher risk of severe hepatotoxicity.
		▪ **Preferred in**: **First trimester of pregnancy** (MMI is associated with teratogenicity) and **Thyroid Storm** (also blocks peripheral T4 to T3 conversion).
	◦ **Mechanism**: Inhibit thyroid peroxidase (TPO), thus blocking the synthesis of thyroid hormones.
	◦ **Major Side Effects**:
		▪ **Agranulocytosis**: (**EMERGENCY**) Patient must be counseled to stop the drug and seek immediate medical attention (for a CBC) if they develop **fever and/or sore throat**.
		▪ Hepatotoxicity, vasculitis, rash.
• **Radioactive Iodine (131I) Therapy**
	◦ **Mechanism**: Oral dose of 131I is absorbed by the thyroid and destroys follicular cells over 6-18 weeks.
	◦ **Outcome**: Leads to permanent **hypothyroidism** in >80% of patients, requiring lifelong levothyroxine.
	◦ **Contraindications**: **Pregnancy, breastfeeding, severe ophthalmopathy** (can worsen eye disease).
• **Thyroidectomy**
	◦ **Indications**: Very large goiter with compressive symptoms, suspected malignancy, severe ophthalmopathy, or patient preference/contraindication to RAI.
	◦ **Outcome**: Rapidly effective. Results in permanent **hypothyroidism** requiring lifelong levothyroxine.
	◦ **Risks**: **Hypoparathyroidism** (damage to parathyroid glands -> **hypocalcemia**), **recurrent laryngeal nerve damage** (hoarseness).
sections.management:
• **Initial Phase**: Start beta-blocker for symptoms and an ATD (typically Methimazole). Monitor TFTs every 4-6 weeks until euthyroid.
• **Maintenance**: Once euthyroid, continue ATDs for 12-18 months, then consider a trial of tapering off to see if remission has occurred. Relapse is common.
• **Ophthalmopathy**
	◦ Refer to Ophthalmology.
	◦ Advise strict **smoking cessation**.
	◦ Mild cases: Artificial tears, selenium supplements.
	◦ Moderate-Severe: Glucocorticoids, teprotumumab (Tepezza), or surgical decompression.
• **Thyroid Storm (Thyrotoxic Crisis)**: A life-threatening medical emergency managed in the ICU.
	◦ **Treatment**: Supportive care (IVF, cooling blankets) +
		▪ **Propranolol** (Beta-blockade)
		▪ **PTU** (high dose)
		▪ **Iodine solution** (SSKI or Lugol's) - given *at least 1 hour after* PTU to block hormone release.
		▪ **Glucocorticoids** (e.g., Hydrocortisone) - reduces T4-to-T3 conversion and provides adrenal support.
sections.complications:
• **Thyroid Storm**: Severe, life-threatening thyrotoxicosis.
• **Cardiac**: **Atrial fibrillation** (with risk of thromboembolism), high-output heart failure, cardiomyopathy.
• **Graves' Ophthalmopathy**: Can lead to corneal ulceration, optic neuropathy, and vision loss.
• **Osteoporosis**: Increased bone turnover leads to decreased bone mineral density.
• **Psychosis**
• **Complications of Treatment**: Iatrogenic hypothyroidism, surgical complications, ATD side effects.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is generally **excellent** with treatment.
• Morbidity is related to the complications of thyrotoxicosis (especially cardiac) and extrathyroidal manifestations.
• Mortality is very low but is significant if **thyroid storm** develops or the disease goes untreated.
• Remission can be achieved with ATDs in ~50% of patients, but relapse is common after discontinuing medication.
• Definitive therapies are curative but result in lifelong hypothyroidism.

sections.overview:
• Self-limiting, transient inflammatory condition of the thyroid gland, also known as **De Quervain Thyroiditis** or **Granulomatous Thyroiditis**
• Characterized by **anterior neck pain** and a classic **triphasic clinical course**
    ◦ Initial **hyperthyroid** phase
    ◦ Followed by a **hypothyroid** phase
    ◦ Ultimately a return to a **euthyroid** state
• Believed to be triggered by a **viral infection**
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ Believed to be a **post-viral** inflammatory process
    ◦ Often follows an **upper respiratory infection (URI)** by several weeks
    ◦ **Associated Viruses**: Coxsackievirus, Mumps, Measles, Adenovirus, Influenza, Echovirus, and SARS-CoV-2
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Viral Trigger & Inflammation**: A viral infection or a post-viral immune response triggers an intense inflammatory reaction within the thyroid gland
    ◦ **Follicular Cell Destruction**: Infiltration of lymphocytes, histiocytes, and characteristically, **multinucleated giant cells** (granulomatous inflammation) leads to the destruction of thyroid follicles
    ◦ **Hormone Release (Hyperthyroid Phase)**: The destruction of follicles causes an uncontrolled release of large quantities of pre-formed thyroid hormone (T4 and T3) into the circulation, leading to **thyrotoxicosis**
    ◦ **Depletion (Hypothyroid Phase)**: As the stores of pre-formed hormone are depleted and the inflamed gland is unable to synthesize new hormone, the patient enters a transient **hypothyroid phase**
    ◦ **Recovery (Euthyroid Phase)**: Over weeks to months, the inflammation resolves, the follicular cells regenerate, and the gland resumes normal hormone production, leading to a **euthyroid state**
sections.epidemiology:
• **Age**: Primarily affects adults aged 30-50
• **Sex**: Significantly more common in **females** (Female:Male ratio of 3-5:1)
• **Seasonality**: Incidence is higher in the summer and fall, correlating with enteroviral seasons
sections.clinicalPresentation: • The classic presentation is a middle-aged female with the **acute onset of severe anterior neck pain**, often accompanied by **fever**, **malaise**, and symptoms of **thyrotoxicosis**, typically occurring several weeks after a viral URI.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Laboratory Findings**
    ◦ **Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR)**: **Markedly elevated, often >100 mm/hr**; a classic finding
    ◦ **C-Reactive Protein (CRP)**: Also significantly elevated
    ◦ **Thyroid Function Tests (TFTs)**
        ▪ **Hyperthyroid Phase**: **Low TSH**, High Free T4 and/or T3
        ▪ **Hypothyroid Phase**: **High TSH**, Low Free T4
        ▪ **Recovery Phase**: TSH and Free T4 return to normal
    ◦ **Thyroid Antibodies**: Thyroperoxidase (TPO) and Thyroglobulin (Tg) antibodies are usually negative or present at low titers; TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb) are absent
    ◦ **Thyroglobulin**: Elevated due to release from the damaged gland
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Radioactive Iodine Uptake (RAIU) Scan**
        ▪ **Very low or absent iodine uptake (<5%)** during the thyrotoxic phase
        ▪ This is a critical diagnostic finding that differentiates it from Graves' disease (which has high uptake)
        ▪ The damaged follicular cells are unable to trap iodine
    ◦ **Thyroid Ultrasound**
        ▪ Typically shows a diffusely enlarged gland with ill-defined, **hypoechoic regions** and **decreased vascularity** on color Doppler
        ▪ Useful to rule out suppurative thyroiditis (abscess) or a nodule
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**
• The vast majority of patients experience a **complete and spontaneous recovery** of thyroid function within 12-18 months

sections.overview:
• Postpartum Thyroiditis (PPT) is a transient or permanent autoimmune thyroid dysfunction occurring within the first year after childbirth, miscarriage, or induced abortion.
    ◦ It is characterized by a destructive lymphocytic infiltration of the thyroid gland.
    ◦ The classic presentation is **triphasic**: an initial, often overlooked, thyrotoxic phase, followed by a hypothyroid phase, and finally, a return to a euthyroid state.
    ◦ However, many women present with only one phase.
sections.etiology:
• **Autoimmune**: PPT is considered a variant of **Hashimoto's thyroiditis**, triggered by the postpartum immune rebound.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Pregnancy-induced Immune Suppression**: During pregnancy, the maternal immune system is suppressed to tolerate the semi-allogeneic fetus.
    ◦ **Postpartum Immune Rebound**: After delivery, this suppression wanes, leading to a rebound of the immune system. In genetically susceptible women (often with pre-existing, subclinical thyroid autoimmunity), this rebound triggers an aggressive autoimmune attack on the thyroid gland.
    ◦ **Destructive Process**: The inflammation (lymphocytic infiltration) damages thyroid follicles, causing the unregulated release of pre-formed thyroid hormone (T4 and T3) into the circulation. This causes the initial **thyrotoxic phase**. This is a **destructive process**, not a hyper-productive one like in Graves' disease.
    ◦ **Hormone Depletion**: As the pre-formed hormone stores are depleted and the gland is too damaged to produce new hormone effectively, the patient enters the **hypothyroid phase**.
    ◦ **Recovery**: In most cases, the inflammation subsides, and the thyroid gland gradually recovers its function, leading to a **euthyroid state**.
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects approximately **5-10%** of postpartum women.
• Incidence is much higher (**up to 25%**) in women with other autoimmune conditions, particularly **Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus**.
• More common in women who are positive for **anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies**.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Presence of Anti-TPO antibodies** (strongest predictor)
• History of previous postpartum thyroiditis (**70% recurrence risk**)
• Personal or family history of autoimmune disorders (e.g., Type 1 DM, vitiligo, pernicious anemia)
• History of Hashimoto's or Graves' disease
• Previous miscarriage
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic course is **triphasic**, occurring within 12 months of delivery.
• **Phase 1: Thyrotoxic Phase (1-6 months postpartum)**
    ◦ Often brief (1-2 months) and mild, frequently missed or attributed to the stress of new motherhood.
    ◦ **Symptoms**:
        ▪ Anxiety, irritability, emotional lability
        ▪ Palpitations, tachycardia
        ▪ Heat intolerance, increased sweating
        ▪ Unintentional weight loss (or failure to gain back postpartum weight)
        ▪ Fatigue, insomnia
        ▪ Fine tremor
• **Phase 2: Hypothyroid Phase (3-9 months postpartum)**
    ◦ This is the most common phase at diagnosis, as symptoms are more pronounced and can be confused with postpartum depression.
    ◦ **Symptoms**:
        ▪ **Fatigue, lethargy** (most common symptom)
        ▪ **Depression**, poor concentration ("brain fog")
        ▪ Weight gain, difficulty losing "baby weight"
        ▪ Dry skin, hair loss
        ▪ Constipation
        ▪ Cold intolerance
        ▪ Muscle cramps, weakness
• **Phase 3: Euthyroid Recovery (within 12-18 months postpartum)**
• **Variations**: About one-third of patients present with isolated thyrotoxicosis, one-third with isolated hypothyroidism, and one-third with the classic triphasic pattern.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Thyroid Gland**
    ◦ **Small-to-moderate, diffuse, firm, NON-TENDER goiter** is the hallmark finding.
    ◦ Absence of pain/tenderness helps distinguish it from subacute (de Quervain's) thyroiditis.
• **Thyrotoxic Phase Findings**
    ◦ Tachycardia
    ◦ Fine tremor of outstretched hands
    ◦ Hyperreflexia
    ◦ Warm, moist skin
• **Hypothyroid Phase Findings**
    ◦ Bradycardia
    ◦ Coarse, dry skin
    ◦ Puffy facies, periorbital edema
    ◦ **Delayed relaxation phase of deep tendon reflexes**
    ◦ Hoarseness
sections.diagnostics:
• **Thyroid Function Tests (TFTs)**
    ◦ **TSH**: Best initial test.
        ▪ Thyrotoxic phase: **Low/suppressed TSH**
        ▪ Hypothyroid phase: **Elevated TSH**
    ◦ **Free T4 (FT4)**
        ▪ Thyrotoxic phase: **Elevated FT4**
        ▪ Hypothyroid phase: **Low FT4**
• **Thyroid Autoantibodies**
    ◦ **Anti-TPO antibodies**: Positive in >85% of cases. High levels are strongly suggestive of the diagnosis.
    ◦ **Anti-thyroglobulin (Anti-Tg) antibodies**: May also be positive.
    ◦ **TSH Receptor Antibodies (TRAb)**: **Negative**. A positive result would suggest Graves' disease.
• **Radioactive Iodine Uptake (RAIU) Scan**
    ◦ **Crucial for differentiating the thyrotoxic phase of PPT from Graves' disease.**
    ◦ In PPT, the gland is inflamed and damaged, not overactive, so it does not take up iodine.
    ◦ **RAIU result in PPT**: **LOW or near-absent uptake (<5%)**.
    ◦ RAIU result in Graves' disease: HIGH or diffuse uptake.
sections.treatment:
• Treatment is directed at the symptomatic phase.
• **Thyrotoxic Phase**
    ◦ **Symptomatic control only.** The condition is transient and due to hormone release, not overproduction.
    ◦ **Beta-Blockers**: Propranolol or atenolol for palpitations, tremor, and anxiety.
    ◦ **Antithyroid drugs (e.g., Methimazole, PTU) are NOT indicated and are ineffective.**
• **Hypothyroid Phase**
    ◦ **Levothyroxine (T4 replacement).**
    ◦ **Indications for treatment**:
        ▪ Symptomatic patients
        ▪ **TSH > 10 mIU/L**
        ▪ Patient is planning a subsequent pregnancy
    ◦ Start with a low dose (e.g., 25-50 mcg/day) and titrate based on TSH levels every 4-6 weeks.
• **Asymptomatic/Subclinical**
    ◦ Patients with mild, asymptomatic abnormalities in TFTs can be monitored without treatment.
sections.management:
• **Monitoring**: Regular monitoring of TSH is essential. Check every 4-8 weeks until the patient is stable and euthyroid.
• **Weaning Levothyroxine**: For women started on levothyroxine, a trial of withdrawal should be attempted **6-12 months** after initiation to determine if thyroid function has recovered.
    ◦ If TSH remains normal off medication, they have recovered.
    ◦ If TSH rises, permanent hypothyroidism is likely, and lifelong therapy is needed.
• **Future Pregnancies**: Women with a history of PPT should have TSH checked early in any subsequent pregnancy and again in the postpartum period.
sections.complications:
• **Permanent Hypothyroidism**: Occurs in approximately 20-30% of women.
• **Misdiagnosis**: Symptoms can be mistaken for primary psychiatric conditions like anxiety disorders or postpartum depression, leading to delayed or inappropriate treatment.
• **Cardiovascular strain** during the thyrotoxic phase (rarely significant).
sections.prognosis:
• **Good.**
• Approximately **80%** of women will recover to a euthyroid state within 12-18 months.
• About **20-30%** will develop permanent, overt hypothyroidism requiring lifelong levothyroxine therapy.
• All women with a history of PPT have a significantly increased risk (~50% over 10 years) of developing permanent hypothyroidism later in life.
sections.preventionEducation:
• Counsel on the natural history of the disease.
• Explain the high risk of recurrence (~70%) with future pregnancies.
• Inform them of the increased lifetime risk of developing permanent hypothyroidism.

sections.overview:
• **Hashimoto thyroiditis**, also known as chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis, is an **autoimmune disorder** characterized by gradual destruction of the thyroid gland, leading to **hypothyroidism**.
    ◦ It is the **most common cause of hypothyroidism** in iodine-sufficient regions of the world.
    ◦ Pathophysiology involves T-cell mediated destruction of thyroid follicular cells and the production of autoantibodies against thyroid-specific antigens.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**: **Autoimmune disease** resulting from a combination of genetic susceptibility and environmental triggers.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Genetic Predisposition**: Strong association with specific HLA haplotypes, particularly **HLA-DR3, HLA-DR4, and HLA-DR5**.
    ◦ **Immune-Mediated Destruction**: A breakdown in self-tolerance leads to an autoimmune attack on the thyroid gland.
        ▪ **Cell-mediated immunity**: **CD8+ cytotoxic T-lymphocytes** infiltrate the thyroid and induce apoptosis of thyroid follicular cells (thyrocytes).
        ▪ **Humoral immunity**: B-lymphocytes produce autoantibodies against key thyroid proteins:
            • **Anti-thyroid peroxidase (Anti-TPO) antibodies**: The hallmark of the disease (>90% of patients); they target the enzyme responsible for hormone synthesis.
            • **Anti-thyroglobulin (Anti-Tg) antibodies**: Present in 60-80% of patients; they target the precursor protein for thyroid hormone production.
    ◦ **Glandular Changes**: Chronic inflammation leads to lymphocytic infiltration, fibrosis, and follicular cell destruction.
        ▪ Histology classically shows **lymphocytic infiltrate with germinal centers** and **Hurthle cells** (enlarged eosinophilic follicular cells).
    ◦ **Hormonal Progression**:
        ▪ Initially, the patient may remain euthyroid.
        ▪ A transient hyperthyroid phase, known as **"Hashitoxicosis,"** can occur due to the release of pre-formed hormone from damaged follicles.
        ▪ Over time, progressive destruction leads to decreased T4/T3 production.
        ▪ The pituitary responds by increasing TSH secretion, resulting in the classic lab profile of primary hypothyroidism: **↑ TSH, ↓ Free T4**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: The **most common cause of hypothyroidism** in the United States and other areas with adequate iodine intake.
• **Gender**: Significantly more common in females, with a **female-to-male ratio of approximately 10:1 to 20:1**.
• **Age**: Peak incidence occurs between **30 and 50 years of age**.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Genetics**: Positive family history of thyroid or other autoimmune diseases.
• **Associated Autoimmune Conditions**: High co-occurrence with other autoimmune disorders, such as:
    ◦ Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus
    ◦ Addison's disease
    ◦ Celiac disease
    ◦ Pernicious anemia
    ◦ Rheumatoid arthritis (RA)
    ◦ Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)
    ◦ Sjögren's syndrome
• **Environmental Triggers**:
    ◦ High iodine intake
    ◦ Infections (e.g., Hepatitis C)
    ◦ Certain medications (e.g., amiodarone, lithium, interferon-alpha)
    ◦ Postpartum period
    ◦ Radiation exposure
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The onset is typically **insidious**. Patients often present with **non-specific symptoms** of hypothyroidism or may be diagnosed after an enlarged thyroid (**goiter**) is found on routine examination.
• The presentation can range from asymptomatic with only lab abnormalities to severe **myxedema**.
• **Symptoms by System**:
    ◦ **Constitutional**: **Fatigue**, lethargy, **weight gain** (modest, 5-10 lbs), **cold intolerance**.
    ◦ **Dermatologic**: **Dry, coarse skin**; brittle hair and nails; diffuse, non-scarring hair loss; loss of the outer third of the eyebrows (**Madarosis**).
    ◦ **Neurologic**: Impaired memory and concentration ("brain fog"), depression, paresthesias.
    ◦ **Musculoskeletal**: Myalgias, arthralgias, proximal muscle weakness, cramps.
    ◦ **Cardiovascular**: Bradycardia, dyspnea on exertion, diastolic hypertension.
    ◦ **Gastrointestinal**: **Constipation**, decreased appetite.
    ◦ **Reproductive**: **Menstrual irregularities** (classically **menorrhagia**), infertility, decreased libido.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Thyroid Gland**:
    ◦ Classically a **symmetrically enlarged, firm, non-tender goiter**.
    ◦ Texture is often described as **"rubbery"**.
    ◦ In late stages, the gland may become atrophic and non-palpable.
• **Skin**: 
    ◦ Cool, pale, dry skin.
    ◦ Non-pitting edema (**myxedema**), especially periorbital and peripheral.
• **Cardiovascular**:
    ◦ Bradycardia.
• **Neurologic**:
    ◦ **Delayed relaxation phase of deep tendon reflexes** (Woltman's sign) is a classic finding.
• **General Appearance**:
    ◦ Puffy face (puffy eyes), hoarseness of voice.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Initial Test**: **TSH** is the most sensitive screening test for primary hypothyroidism.
• **Confirmatory Lab Panel**:
    ◦ **TSH**: **Elevated** (typically > 4.5 mIU/L).
    ◦ **Free T4**: **Low** or low-normal.
• **Antibody Testing (to confirm autoimmune etiology)**:
    ◦ **Anti-TPO antibody**: Positive in >90% of cases. **The most specific test for Hashimoto thyroiditis.**
    ◦ **Anti-Tg antibody**: Often positive but less sensitive and specific than Anti-TPO.
• **Other Potential Lab Findings**:
    ◦ **Lipid Panel**: Hyperlipidemia (elevated total cholesterol and LDL).
    ◦ **CBC**: Normocytic, normochromic anemia.
    ◦ **CMP**: Hyponatremia (due to impaired free water excretion).
• **Imaging**:
    ◦ **Ultrasound**: Not routinely required for diagnosis. Performed if a nodule is palpated.
        ▪ Findings suggestive of Hashimoto's include a diffusely **hypoechoic and heterogeneous gland**.
• **Fine-Needle Aspiration (FNA)**:
    ◦ Indicated only for a suspicious or dominant thyroid nodule to rule out malignancy (e.g., lymphoma).
    ◦ Histology shows **lymphocytic infiltrate, germinal centers, and Hurthle cells**.
sections.treatment:
• **Medication**: **Levothyroxine (synthetic T4)** is the mainstay of treatment.
    ◦ **Dosing**:
        ▪ **Healthy, young adults**: Start at a weight-based dose, typically **1.6 mcg/kg/day**.
        ▪ **Elderly (>60) or patients with CAD**: **"Start low and go slow."** Initiate at 12.5-25 mcg/day and titrate up gradually every 4-6 weeks to avoid precipitating cardiac ischemia.
    ◦ **Administration**:
        ▪ Take with water on an empty stomach, **30-60 minutes before the first meal of the day**.
        ▪ Separate from supplements like calcium, iron, and antacids by at least 4 hours, as they impair absorption.
• **Treatment of Subclinical Hypothyroidism** (Elevated TSH, Normal Free T4):
    ◦ **Treat if**:
        ▪ TSH > 10 mIU/L.
        ▪ Patient is symptomatic.
        ▪ Patient is pregnant or planning pregnancy.
        ▪ Presence of a goiter or positive Anti-TPO antibodies.
sections.management:
• **Monitoring**:
    ◦ Check **TSH** levels **6-8 weeks** after initiating or changing the dose.
    ◦ Titrate levothyroxine to achieve a TSH goal within the normal reference range (typically 0.5 - 2.5 mIU/L).
    ◦ Once the dose is stable, monitor **TSH annually**.
• **Special Considerations**:
    ◦ **Pregnancy**: Levothyroxine needs are **increased by 30-50%**. Monitor TSH each trimester and adjust dose accordingly to maintain a trimester-specific TSH goal.
sections.complications:
• **Myxedema Coma**:
    ◦ A rare, life-threatening state of severe, decompensated hypothyroidism.
    ◦ Characterized by **altered mental status (coma), hypothermia, hypotension, bradycardia, and hypoventilation**.
    ◦ This is a medical emergency requiring IV levothyroxine and aggressive supportive care in an ICU setting.
• **Increased risk of other autoimmune disorders**.
• **Increased cardiovascular risk** due to hyperlipidemia and hypertension if left untreated.
• **Infertility and Adverse Pregnancy Outcomes**: Increased risk of miscarriage, pre-eclampsia, and preterm delivery in untreated mothers.
• **Thyroid Lymphoma**: Rare but increased risk of primary B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma of the thyroid gland.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is **excellent** with lifelong, consistent levothyroxine replacement therapy.
• Patients can expect a normal quality of life and life expectancy.
• The condition is permanent and requires lifelong management.

sections.overview:
• A thyroid nodule is a discrete lesion within the thyroid gland that is radiologically distinct from the surrounding thyroid parenchyma.
• They are extremely common, with prevalence increasing with age.
• The primary clinical challenge is to exclude the ~5-15% of nodules that are **malignant**.
• Most nodules are asymptomatic and benign, often discovered incidentally on imaging performed for other reasons (**thyroid incidentaloma**).
• The diagnostic workup is systematic, starting with **TSH** and followed by **thyroid ultrasound** and, if indicated, **Fine-Needle Aspiration (FNA)**.
sections.etiology:
• **Benign Nodules (>90%)**
    ◦ **Colloid Nodules/Adenomatoid Nodules**: Most common type. Focal areas of hyperplastic follicles filled with colloid. Result from cycles of hyperplasia and involution.
    ◦ **Follicular Adenomas**: Benign encapsulated tumors composed of follicular cells. Cannot be distinguished from follicular carcinoma by FNA alone, as diagnosis requires evidence of capsular or vascular invasion on histology.
    ◦ **Thyroid Cysts**: Fluid-filled sacs. Can be simple (purely cystic) or complex (cystic and solid components). Often arise from degeneration of adenomas.
    ◦ **Inflammatory Nodules**: Focal inflammation, most commonly seen in **Hashimoto's thyroiditis**.
• **Malignant Nodules (5-15%)**
    ◦ **Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma (PTC)**: Most common type (~80-85%). Arises from follicular cells. Spreads via **lymphatics**. Least aggressive, excellent prognosis.
    ◦ **Follicular Thyroid Carcinoma (FTC)**: Second most common (~10-15%). Arises from follicular cells. Spreads **hematogenously** (to bone, lung, brain). Prognosis is very good but slightly worse than PTC.
    ◦ **Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma (MTC)**: ~3% of cases. Arises from parafollicular **C-cells** which produce **calcitonin**. Can be sporadic or part of **Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia (MEN) syndromes 2A and 2B**.
    ◦ **Anaplastic Thyroid Carcinoma**: <2% of cases. Highly aggressive and undifferentiated tumor, typically affecting the elderly. Very poor prognosis.
    ◦ **Thyroid Lymphoma**: Rare, usually arises in the setting of pre-existing **Hashimoto's thyroiditis**.
sections.epidemiology:
• Palpable nodules are present in ~5% of women and 1% of men.
• Ultrasound detects nodules in 19-68% of the population, with higher rates in women and the elderly.
• The vast majority are benign.
• **Malignancy** is found in 5-15% of nodules, regardless of whether they are palpable or incidentally discovered.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Patient History**
    ◦ **History of head and neck radiation exposure**, especially in childhood.
    ◦ **Family history of thyroid cancer** (e.g., Medullary thyroid cancer in **MEN2**, papillary cancer in family members).
    ◦ **Extremes of age** (<20 or >60 years).
    ◦ **Male sex**.
    ◦ **Rapid nodule growth**.
    ◦ **Symptoms of compression** (hoarseness, dysphagia).
• **Physical Exam Findings**
    ◦ **Firm or hard consistency**.
    ◦ **Fixation** to adjacent structures.
    ◦ **Vocal cord paralysis** (hoarseness).
    ◦ **Cervical lymphadenopathy**.
• **Ultrasound Findings (High-Risk Features)**
    ◦ **Microcalcifications**.
    ◦ **Irregular margins**.
    ◦ **Hypoechogenicity** (darker than surrounding thyroid tissue).
    ◦ **Taller-than-wide shape**.
    ◦ **Central vascularity**.
    ◦ **Extrathyroidal extension**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The majority of patients are **asymptomatic**, with the nodule found incidentally.
• **Palpable neck mass**: Patient may notice a lump or fullness in their neck.
• **Compressive symptoms**
    ◦ **Dysphagia** (difficulty swallowing).
    ◦ Sensation of a "tickle" in the throat or need to clear throat.
    ◦ **Dyspnea** (shortness of breath), especially when lying down.
    ◦ **Hoarseness** or voice changes (compression of the **recurrent laryngeal nerve**).
    ◦ Neck pain or pressure (rare).
• **Symptoms of Hyperthyroidism** (if nodule is a toxic adenoma)
    ◦ Palpitations, heat intolerance, weight loss, anxiety, tremor.
• **Symptoms of Hypothyroidism** (if nodule is in the setting of **Hashimoto's**)
    ◦ Fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Inspection**: Look for a visible mass, especially with swallowing.
• **Palpation (Thyroid Gland)**
    ◦ Stand behind the seated patient to palpate the thyroid.
    ◦ Have the patient swallow; the thyroid and nodule will move superiorly.
    ◦ **Assess the nodule for**:
        ▪ **Size**: Estimate in centimeters.
        ▪ **Consistency**: Soft, firm, or **hard/rock-like** (suspicious).
        ▪ **Mobility**: Mobile (good) vs. **fixed** to surrounding tissues (suspicious).
        ▪ **Tenderness**: Suggests inflammation (thyroiditis) or hemorrhage into a cyst.
• **Palpation (Neck)**
    ◦ Systematically palpate for **cervical lymphadenopathy** (supraclavicular, deep cervical chains).
• **Other**
    ◦ Check for **tracheal deviation** (seen with very large goiters/nodules).
    ◦ Assess for signs of hyperthyroidism (**tachycardia**, tremor, lid lag) or hypothyroidism (**bradycardia**, delayed reflexes).
sections.diagnostics:
• The workup is systematic and stepwise.
• **History and Physical Exam**: Assess for risk factors listed above.
• **TSH (Thyroid Stimulating Hormone)**: **FIRST and BEST initial test.** This triages the entire workup.
    ◦ **Low TSH (Suppressed)**: Suggests a hyperfunctioning (**"hot"**) nodule.
        ▪ **Next Step**: **Radionuclide Thyroid Scan (I-123)**.
        ▪ **Scan Results**:
            • **"Hot" Nodule** (hyperfunctioning): Takes up the isotope. Very low risk of malignancy (<1%). FNA is generally not needed. Treat the hyperthyroidism.
            • **"Cold" or "Warm" Nodule** (hypofunctioning): Does not take up the isotope. Carries a 5-15% risk of malignancy. Proceed to Ultrasound/FNA.
    ◦ **Normal or High TSH**: Suggests a non-functioning (**"cold"** or indeterminate) nodule.
        ▪ **Next Step**: **Thyroid Ultrasound**. Do NOT order a radionuclide scan.
• **Thyroid Ultrasound**: **BEST imaging modality to characterize the nodule.**
    ◦ Determines size, composition (solid, cystic, mixed), and presence of suspicious features (see risk factors).
    ◦ Guides the decision for FNA.
• **Fine-Needle Aspiration (FNA) Biopsy**: **GOLD STANDARD** for determining if a nodule is benign or malignant.
    ◦ **Indications for FNA are based on nodule size and suspicious ultrasound features**:
        ▪ **High-suspicion features**: FNA if ≥ 1 cm.
        ▪ **Intermediate-suspicion features**: FNA if ≥ 1.5 cm.
        ▪ **Low-suspicion features**: FNA if ≥ 2.0 cm.
        ▪ **Very-low suspicion** (e.g., spongiform, pure cyst): FNA not routinely recommended unless very large or symptomatic.
• **FNA Cytology Results (Bethesda System)**
    ◦ **I. Non-diagnostic**: Insufficient cells. Repeat FNA with ultrasound guidance.
    ◦ **II. Benign**: ~95-99% confidence. Follow with serial ultrasounds.
    ◦ **III. Atypia of Undetermined Significance (AUS/FLUS)**: 5-15% risk of malignancy. Options: Repeat FNA, molecular testing, or diagnostic surgical lobectomy.
    ◦ **IV. Follicular Neoplasm (or Suspicious for Follicular Neoplasm)**: 15-30% risk of malignancy. FNA cannot distinguish between benign follicular adenoma and follicular carcinoma. **Diagnostic surgical lobectomy is usually recommended.**
    ◦ **V. Suspicious for Malignancy**: 60-75% risk of malignancy. **(Total) Thyroidectomy** is recommended.
    ◦ **VI. Malignant**: >97% risk of malignancy. **(Total) Thyroidectomy** is recommended.
• **Other Tests (used in specific situations)**
    ◦ **Serum Calcitonin**: Measure if there is a family history of **MTC** or **MEN2**, or if FNA suggests **MTC**.
    ◦ **Serum Thyroglobulin (Tg)**: Not useful for initial diagnosis. Primarily used as a tumor marker for surveillance **after** total thyroidectomy for differentiated thyroid cancer.
sections.treatment:
• **Benign Nodule (Bethesda II)**
    ◦ **Management**: Conservative management with serial monitoring.
    ◦ **Follow-up**: Repeat ultrasound in 12-24 months. If stable, intervals can be lengthened.
• **Malignant Nodule (Bethesda V/VI)**
    ◦ **Management**: Surgical excision.
    ◦ **Surgery**: **Total or near-total thyroidectomy** is standard. A **lobectomy** may be considered for small (<1 cm), low-risk, unifocal, intrathyroidal papillary carcinomas.
    ◦ **Adjunctive Therapy**: Postoperative **Radioactive Iodine (RAI) ablation** to destroy residual thyroid tissue and micrometastases. **TSH suppression therapy** (with levothyroxine) to prevent cancer recurrence.
• **Indeterminate Nodule (Bethesda III/IV)**
    ◦ **AUS/FLUS (III)**: Repeat FNA, consider molecular testing on the FNA sample to stratify risk, or proceed to **diagnostic lobectomy**.
    ◦ **Follicular Neoplasm (IV)**: **Diagnostic lobectomy** is the standard recommendation. If final pathology shows cancer, a **completion thyroidectomy** may be needed.
• **Toxic Adenoma ("Hot Nodule")**
    ◦ **Radioactive Iodine (I-131) Ablation**: Most common treatment in the US.
    ◦ **Surgery (Thyroid Lobectomy)**: Definitive treatment, preferred for large nodules or compressive symptoms.
    ◦ **Anti-thyroid drugs (Methimazole)**: Can control hyperthyroidism but is not a definitive treatment.
sections.management:
• **Benign Nodules**: Serial ultrasound surveillance. Repeat FNA only if there is significant growth or development of new suspicious features.
• **Malignant Nodules (Post-Thyroidectomy)**
    ◦ Lifelong surveillance for recurrence.
    ◦ Monitor with serial **serum thyroglobulin (Tg)** levels and neck ultrasound.
    ◦ Maintain **TSH suppression** with levothyroxine therapy to a goal level determined by recurrence risk.
sections.complications:
• **Of the Nodule**
    ◦ **Malignant transformation**.
    ◦ **Compressive symptoms**: Airway compromise (rare but serious), dysphagia.
    ◦ **Thyrotoxicosis** from an autonomous ("hot") nodule.
    ◦ **Hemorrhage** into a cyst, causing acute pain and swelling.
• **Of Treatment (Surgery)**
    ◦ **Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve Injury**: Can cause temporary or permanent **hoarseness** (unilateral) or airway obstruction (bilateral).
    ◦ **Hypoparathyroidism**: Due to removal or devascularization of parathyroid glands, leading to **hypocalcemia** (perioral numbness, tingling, **Chvostek/Trousseau signs**).
    ◦ **Hypothyroidism**: Inevitable after total thyroidectomy, requiring lifelong levothyroxine replacement.
    ◦ Bleeding, infection.
sections.prognosis:
• **Benign Nodules**: Excellent prognosis. Do not affect lifespan.
• **Malignant Nodules**
    ◦ **Papillary & Follicular (Differentiated)**: Excellent prognosis, especially in patients <55 years old with small, localized tumors. >98% 20-year survival.
    ◦ **Medullary**: Good prognosis if confined to the thyroid; worsens with lymph node involvement or distant metastases.
    ◦ **Anaplastic**: Dismal prognosis. Median survival is typically 3-6 months.

sections.overview:
• Thyroid cancer is the **most common endocrine malignancy**, originating from the cells of the thyroid gland.
• It typically presents as a **painless, palpable nodule** in the neck.
• There are four main histological types, each with distinct characteristics, treatment approaches, and prognoses.
• The vast majority of thyroid cancers are well-differentiated (**Papillary and Follicular**) and have an **excellent prognosis** with appropriate treatment.
sections.etiology:
• **Papillary (PTC):**
    ◦ Arises from follicular epithelial cells.
    ◦ Characterized by slow growth and a tendency to spread via the **lymphatic system** to cervical lymph nodes.
    ◦ Associated with **BRAF** and **RET/PTC** gene mutations.
    ◦ Histology shows characteristic "**Orphan Annie eye**" nuclei and **psammoma bodies**.
• **Follicular (FTC):**
    ◦ Also arises from follicular epithelial cells.
    ◦ Tends to spread via **hematogenous routes** (bloodstream) to distant sites like bone, lungs, and the CNS.
    ◦ Diagnosis requires histologic evidence of **capsular or vascular invasion**, which cannot be determined by FNA alone.
    ◦ Associated with **RAS** mutations.
• **Medullary (MTC):**
    ◦ Arises from the neuroendocrine **parafollicular C-cells**, which produce calcitonin.
    ◦ **Calcitonin** serves as a crucial tumor marker.
    ◦ About 25% of cases are familial, associated with **Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia (MEN) type 2A and 2B** syndromes, linked to the **RET proto-oncogene** mutation.
• **Anaplastic (ATC):**
    ◦ A highly undifferentiated and aggressive tumor.
    ◦ It is thought to arise from a pre-existing well-differentiated carcinoma (PTC or FTC).
    ◦ It is characterized by rapid, invasive local growth.
    ◦ Associated with **TP53** mutations.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Most common endocrine cancer.**
• Incidence has tripled in the last three decades, largely due to increased detection via imaging.
• **Women are affected 3 times more often than men.**
• Can occur at any age, but peak incidence is between 30-50 years old.
• Anaplastic cancer typically affects individuals >60 years old.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Radiation Exposure:** The single greatest risk factor, especially during childhood (e.g., treatment for lymphoma, Chernobyl disaster).
• **Family History:** MTC (MEN 2 syndromes), Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP), Cowden syndrome.
• **Iodine Deficiency:** A risk factor for **Follicular** cancer.
• **Iodine Excess:** A potential risk factor for **Papillary** cancer.
• **Personal History:** Pre-existing thyroid conditions like goiter or Hashimoto's thyroiditis (though the link is debated for carcinoma, it is a risk factor for primary thyroid lymphoma).
• **Age:** Extremes of age (<20 or >60) are associated with a higher risk of malignancy in a thyroid nodule.
• **Gender:** Male gender is associated with a higher likelihood that a nodule is malignant.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The most common presentation is a **painless, palpable, solitary thyroid nodule.**
• Often discovered incidentally on physical exam or imaging studies (e.g., carotid ultrasound, CT/MRI of the neck).
• A minority of patients present with symptoms related to local invasion or metastasis.
• **Symptoms:**
    ◦ **Usually Asymptomatic.**
    ◦ If symptomatic, may include:
        ▪ **Hoarseness or voice changes:** Suggests involvement of the **recurrent laryngeal nerve**.
        ▪ **Dysphagia:** Difficulty swallowing due to esophageal compression.
        ▪ **Dyspnea/Stridor:** Difficulty breathing due to tracheal compression.
        ▪ **Cough.**
        ▪ Rapid growth of a neck mass.
        ▪ Pain in the neck, jaw, or ear.
        ▪ **MTC Specific:** Diarrhea and flushing (from calcitonin or other secreted peptides).
sections.physicalExam:
• **Palpation of Thyroid:** A **firm, fixed, non-tender nodule** is suspicious for malignancy. Nodules >1 cm are more concerning.
• **Cervical Lymphadenopathy:** Palpable lymph nodes in the anterior or lateral neck suggest regional metastasis.
• **Vocal Cord Paralysis:** Can be assessed via laryngoscopy if hoarseness is present.
sections.diagnostics:
• The workup of a thyroid nodule follows a specific algorithm:
    ◦ **Initial Lab Test: TSH (Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone)**
        ▪ **Low TSH (hyperthyroid):** Suggests a hyperfunctioning ("hot") nodule, which has a very low risk of malignancy.
            ◦ **Next Step:** **Radioiodine Scintigraphy Scan (I-123)**.
            ◦ **"Hot" nodule:** Confirms hyperfunctioning adenoma. Treat the hyperthyroidism.
            ◦ **"Cold" nodule:** Hypofunctioning; carries a 5-10% risk of malignancy. Proceed to Ultrasound and FNA.
        ▪ **Normal or High TSH (euthyroid/hypothyroid):**
            ◦ **Next Step:** **Thyroid Ultrasound.**
    ◦ **Thyroid Ultrasound**
        ▪ The **best initial imaging test** to characterize the nodule.
        ▪ **High-risk features for malignancy:**
            ◦ Hypoechogenicity (appears darker than surrounding tissue).
            ◦ **Microcalcifications.**
            ◦ Irregular margins.
            ◦ **Taller-than-wide shape.**
            ◦ Central vascularity.
        ▪ Ultrasound guides the decision for biopsy.
    ◦ **Fine-Needle Aspiration (FNA) Biopsy**
        ▪ The **gold standard and most accurate diagnostic test** for thyroid nodules.
        ▪ Indicated for nodules >1 cm with suspicious ultrasound features.
        ▪ Cytology is reported using the **Bethesda System**, which stratifies the risk of malignancy.
        ▪ **Limitation:** Cannot distinguish between a benign **follicular adenoma** and a malignant **follicular carcinoma**. Diagnosis of follicular carcinoma requires surgical excision to demonstrate capsular or vascular invasion.
    ◦ **Additional Labs**
        ▪ **Serum Calcitonin:** Measure if MTC is suspected based on family history (MEN 2) or FNA results.
        ▪ **Serum Thyroglobulin (Tg):** **NOT** for initial diagnosis. It is an essential **tumor marker for post-treatment surveillance** of Papillary and Follicular cancers.
sections.management:
• **Post-operative Surveillance is critical.**
• **Papillary & Follicular:**
    ◦ Lifelong **levothyroxine** for TSH suppression.
    ◦ Regular monitoring of **serum Thyroglobulin (Tg)** and anti-Tg antibodies. An undetectable Tg is the goal.
    ◦ Periodic **neck ultrasound** to screen for local recurrence.
• **Medullary:**
    ◦ Monitor **serum Calcitonin** and **Carcinoembryonic Antigen (CEA)** levels.
    ◦ Genetic screening for **RET proto-oncogene** mutation in the patient and family members.
sections.complications:
• **Complications from Surgery:**
    ◦ **Hypoparathyroidism -> Hypocalcemia:** Due to inadvertent removal or devascularization of the parathyroid glands.
        ▪ *Symptoms:* Perioral tingling, paresthesias of fingers/toes, muscle cramps (tetany).
        ▪ *Signs:* **Chvostek's sign** (facial muscle twitch with tapping of facial nerve), **Trousseau's sign** (carpal spasm with BP cuff inflation).
    ◦ **Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve Injury:**
        ▪ *Unilateral:* Hoarseness.
        ▪ *Bilateral:* Airway obstruction and aphonia (medical emergency).
    ◦ **Superior Laryngeal Nerve Injury:** Loss of ability to produce high-pitched sounds.
• **Distant Metastasis:** Lungs and bone are the most common sites.
• **Recurrence:** Local or distant return of the cancer.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for well-differentiated cancers (Papillary and Follicular), especially in patients <55 years. 10-year survival is >95%.
• **Good** for Medullary if confined to the thyroid gland. Prognosis worsens significantly with nodal or distant metastasis.
• **Dismal** for Anaplastic cancer. It is one of the most aggressive human cancers, with a median survival of only 3-6 months.

sections.overview:
• Myxedema coma is a rare, life-threatening endocrine emergency representing the most severe form of hypothyroidism.
• It is a state of decompensated hypothyroidism characterized by a triad of **altered mental status**, **hypothermia**, and a **precipitating event**.
• Despite the name, patients are not always comatose; the condition represents a spectrum of altered consciousness from lethargy to unresponsiveness.
• It is a medical emergency with a high mortality rate requiring immediate recognition and treatment in an ICU setting.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Underlying Cause**: Chronic, severe, and untreated or undertreated hypothyroidism.
        ▪ The most common cause in developed nations is Hashimoto's thyroiditis.
        ▪ Other causes include post-surgical (thyroidectomy) or post-ablative (radioactive iodine) hypothyroidism.
    ◦ **Precipitating Event**: A physiologic stressor overwhelms the body's already compromised homeostatic mechanisms.
        ▪ **Infection (most common)**: Pneumonia, UTI, sepsis.
        ▪ **Drugs**: Sedatives, opioids, anesthetics, lithium, amiodarone.
        ▪ **Exposure**: Prolonged exposure to cold.
        ▪ **Metabolic**: Hypoglycemia, hyponatremia.
        ▪ **Trauma/Surgery**.
        ▪ **Acute Illness**: Myocardial infarction, CVA, GI bleed, heart failure.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Decreased Metabolic Rate**: Profound deficiency of thyroid hormones (T3 and T4) leads to a global decrease in cellular metabolism.
    ◦ **Thermoregulation Failure**: Decreased metabolism leads to reduced thermogenesis, resulting in profound **hypothermia**.
    ◦ **Cardiovascular Collapse**: Decreased T3 reduces cardiac chronotropy (heart rate) and inotropy (contractility), leading to **bradycardia**, decreased cardiac output, and **hypotension**.
        ▪ This can be exacerbated by pericardial effusion.
    ◦ **Respiratory Failure**: The central respiratory drive is blunted, and respiratory muscles weaken.
        ▪ This leads to **hypoventilation**, resulting in **hypercapnia** and **hypoxia**.
    ◦ **Neurologic Dysfunction**: Reduced cerebral blood flow, hypoxia, hypercapnia, hypoglycemia, and hyponatremia all contribute to progressive **altered mental status**, lethargy, and coma.
    ◦ **Myxedema**: Deposition of glycosaminoglycans (hyaluronic acid and chondroitin sulfate) in the interstitial space of various tissues.
        ▪ This causes an osmotic shift of fluid into the interstitium, leading to characteristic **non-pitting edema**, macroglossia, and vocal cord thickening (hoarseness).
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Rare, estimated at 0.22 cases per million per year.
• **Demographics**: Predominantly affects **elderly women** (>60 years old).
• **Seasonality**: More common during the **winter months** due to cold exposure acting as a precipitating factor.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is an **elderly female with a known history of hypothyroidism** who is found unresponsive or severely lethargic at home during the winter.
    ◦ She may have stopped taking her levothyroxine.
    ◦ Family may report a gradual decline in function, increasing lethargy, and confusion preceding the acute decompensation.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Thyroid Function Tests (STAT)**
    ◦ **TSH**: Markedly elevated (often >100 mIU/L) in primary hypothyroidism.
    ◦ **Free T4**: Markedly low.
    ◦ **Free T3**: Markedly low.
• **Metabolic Panel (CMP)**
    ◦ **Hyponatremia**: Common due to an SIADH-like picture (impaired free water excretion).
    ◦ **Hypoglycemia**: Due to impaired gluconeogenesis.
• **Cortisol**
    ◦ **Random or AM Cortisol Level**: **CRITICAL**. Must be drawn before administering steroids.
        ▪ Co-existing adrenal insufficiency (Schmidt syndrome) is possible, and giving thyroid hormone alone can precipitate a fatal adrenal crisis.
• **Arterial Blood Gas (ABG)**
    ◦ **Respiratory acidosis** (elevated pCO2) from hypoventilation.
    ◦ Hypoxemia.
• **Complete Blood Count (CBC)**
    ◦ Anemia (often normocytic, normochromic).
• **Cardiac Markers & Muscle Enzymes**
    ◦ **CK (Creatine Kinase)**: Often elevated due to rhabdomyolysis or myopathy.
    ◦ **Troponin**: To rule out MI as a precipitating cause.
• **Infectious Workup**
    ◦ Blood cultures, urinalysis, chest X-ray to identify a precipitating infection.
• **Electrocardiogram (EKG)**
    ◦ Sinus bradycardia, low voltage QRS complexes, prolonged QT interval, T-wave inversions.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Chest X-ray**: May show cardiomegaly, pericardial or pleural effusions, or pneumonia.
    ◦ **Head CT**: To rule out intracranial pathology as the cause of altered mental status.
sections.prognosis:
• **High mortality rate**: Ranges from 25-60%, even with treatment in an ICU.
• **Negative prognostic factors**: Advanced age, persistent hypothermia, bradycardia, severe hypotension, and delayed diagnosis/treatment.

sections.overview: • A rare, life-threatening exacerbation of thyrotoxicosis characterized by severe, acute multi-organ dysfunction. ◦ Represents the extreme end of the hyperthyroid spectrum. • A clinical diagnosis based on the presence of severe thyrotoxic signs and symptoms, most notably: ◦ High fever ◦ Tachycardia disproportionate to the fever ◦ Central nervous system (CNS) dysfunction ◦ Gastrointestinal (GI) disturbances • A medical emergency requiring immediate admission to an intensive care unit (ICU) and aggressive, multi-faceted treatment.
sections.etiology: • Etiology ◦ Triggered by a precipitating event in a patient with underlying, often undiagnosed or undertreated, thyrotoxicosis. ◦ Most Common Underlying Cause: Graves' disease (~85-90% of cases). ◦ Other Underlying Causes: Toxic multinodular goiter, toxic adenoma, thyroiditis. • Pathophysiology ◦ The exact mechanism is not fully understood, but it is believed to involve a combination of factors: ▪ Rapid Increase in Hormone Levels: A sudden release of stored T4 and T3 into circulation. ▪ Increased Catecholamine Sensitivity: A dramatic upregulation of adrenergic receptors, leading to an exaggerated response to circulating catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine). ▪ Decreased Protein Binding: A decrease in the binding of thyroid hormones to transport proteins, leading to a rapid rise in the biologically active free T4 and T3. ◦ The combination of these factors, triggered by a physiological stressor, overwhelms the body's compensatory mechanisms, leading to a state of decompensated thyrotoxicosis and multi-organ failure.
sections.epidemiology: • Incidence: Rare. Occurs in 1-2% of patients admitted for thyrotoxicosis. • Demographics: More common in women than men (consistent with the prevalence of Graves' disease). • Mortality: ◦ Historically high (up to 100%). ◦ With modern ICU care and prompt treatment, mortality has decreased to 10-20%.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a critically ill patient with a known or unknown history of hyperthyroidism who recently experienced a precipitating event.
• The patient will appear toxic, agitated, and febrile.
• The key features involve dysfunction of four major systems:
    ◦ Thermoregulatory
    ◦ Cardiovascular
    ◦ CNS
    ◦ GI/hepatic
sections.diagnostics: • Thyroid storm is a clinical diagnosis. Do not delay treatment waiting for lab confirmation. • The Burch-Wartofsky Point Scale can be used to estimate the likelihood. ◦ A score >45 is highly suggestive of thyroid storm. • Laboratory Studies ◦ TFTs ▪ TSH: Suppressed to undetectable levels (<0.01 mIU/L). ▪ Free T4 & T3: Markedly elevated. (Note: The absolute hormone levels may not be higher than in uncomplicated thyrotoxicosis). ◦ CBC: Leukocytosis with a left shift (due to stress response and/or underlying infection). ◦ CMP ▪ Hyperglycemia (from catecholamine excess). ▪ Elevated LFTs (especially bilirubin) due to hepatic congestion or direct hepatocellular injury. ▪ Hypercalcemia (from increased bone turnover). ▪ Electrolyte disturbances from GI losses. ◦ Workup for Precipitant: Blood cultures, urinalysis, lactate, troponin, BNP, D-dimer as indicated. • Imaging ◦ ECG: Sinus tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, other supraventricular tachycardias, signs of ischemia. ◦ Chest X-ray: Look for cardiomegaly, pulmonary edema (heart failure), or pneumonia (precipitating cause).
sections.prognosis: • With prompt recognition and aggressive ICU-level treatment, the mortality rate is 10-20%. • Delayed diagnosis or treatment is associated with a much poorer prognosis. • Recovery can be complete if the patient survives the acute event.

sections.overview:
• Autoimmune disorder characterized by **T-cell mediated destruction** of the insulin-producing **beta cells** in the pancreatic islets of Langerhans
• Leads to **absolute insulin deficiency**, resulting in hyperglycemia and a lifelong dependence on exogenous insulin for survival
• Most commonly presents in childhood or adolescence but can occur at any age
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ Combination of **genetic susceptibility** and an **environmental trigger**
    ◦ **Genetic Predisposition**
        ▪ Strongly associated with specific Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) genes on chromosome 6, particularly **HLA-DR3** and **HLA-DR4**
        ▪ A first-degree relative with T1DM increases risk significantly
    ◦ **Environmental Triggers (Proposed)**
        ▪ **Viral infections** (e.g., Coxsackievirus, enteroviruses, mumps, rubella), dietary factors, or other environmental insults are thought to trigger the autoimmune process
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ An environmental trigger initiates an autoimmune response in a genetically susceptible host
    ◦ Autoreactive T-lymphocytes infiltrate the pancreatic islets (**"insulitis"**) and selectively destroy beta cells
    ◦ Autoantibodies are produced and serve as markers of the autoimmune process (e.g., GAD-65, ICA)
    ◦ Symptoms of hyperglycemia do not appear until **80-90% of beta cells have been destroyed**
    ◦ The resulting **absolute insulin deficiency** leads to:
        ▪ **Hyperglycemia**: Glucose cannot enter insulin-dependent tissues (muscle, adipose); unopposed glucagon action promotes hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis
        ▪ **Ketosis**: In the absence of insulin, unrestrained lipolysis occurs, breaking down triglycerides into free fatty acids (FFAs). The liver metabolizes these FFAs into ketone bodies, leading to **diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)**
        ▪ **Catabolism**: Protein and fat stores are broken down, leading to weight loss and muscle wasting
sections.epidemiology:
• Accounts for **5-10%** of all diabetes cases
• **Bimodal age of onset**: Peaks at ages 4-6 years and again in early puberty (10-14 years)
• Affects males and females relatively equally
• Higher prevalence in populations of Northern European descent (e.g., Scandinavia)
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Classic New Onset**
    ◦ Presents over days to weeks with the **"3 Polys"**:
        ▪ **Polyuria**: Osmotic diuresis from hyperglycemia (renal glucose threshold exceeded at ~180 mg/dL)
        ▪ **Polydipsia**: Intense thirst due to dehydration from polyuria
        ▪ **Polyphagia**: Increased hunger due to cellular starvation, despite high blood glucose
    ◦ Accompanied by profound, unintentional **weight loss** and fatigue
• **Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)**
    ◦ About 25-30% of new-onset cases present in DKA, a medical emergency
    ◦ Symptoms include **nausea, vomiting, diffuse abdominal pain, altered mental status**, and dehydration
• **Honeymoon Period**
    ◦ A temporary remission phase that can occur weeks to months after diagnosis and initiation of insulin therapy
    ◦ Residual beta cells function briefly, leading to decreased insulin requirements
    ◦ This period is transient
sections.diagnostics:
• **Diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus** (need 1 of 4):
    ◦ **Fasting Plasma Glucose**: **≥126 mg/dL** on at least two separate occasions
    ◦ **Random Plasma Glucose**: **≥200 mg/dL** in a patient with classic symptoms of hyperglycemia
    ◦ **2-hour Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT)**: Plasma glucose **≥200 mg/dL**
    ◦ **Hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c)**: **≥6.5%** on at least two separate occasions
• **Differentiating T1DM from T2DM**
    ◦ **Autoantibodies**: The key diagnostic differentiator
        ▪ **Anti-Glutamic Acid Decarboxylase (GAD-65)**: Most common
        ▪ **Islet Cell Autoantibodies (ICA)**
        ▪ **Insulin Autoantibodies (IAA)**
        ▪ **Zinc Transporter 8 (ZnT8) Autoantibodies**
    ◦ **C-Peptide Level**: A marker of endogenous insulin production
        ▪ **Low or undetectable C-peptide** confirms little to no insulin production, consistent with **T1DM**
        ▪ Normal or high C-peptide suggests T2DM (insulin resistance)
• **Workup for DKA**
    ◦ **CMP**: **Hyperglycemia, high anion gap metabolic acidosis** (Gap = Na - [Cl + HCO3]), low bicarbonate (<18), **hyperkalemia** (initial) despite total body K+ depletion
    ◦ **Serum Ketones**: Elevated (**beta-hydroxybutyrate** is preferred over urine ketones)
    ◦ **Arterial or Venous Blood Gas (ABG/VBG)**: **pH < 7.30**
    ◦ **Urinalysis**: Glucosuria and ketonuria
sections.prognosis:
• With modern insulin therapy and diligent management, prognosis is good, but life expectancy is still reduced by ~10-13 years compared to the general population
• Tight glycemic control (as shown in the **DCCT trial**) dramatically reduces the risk of **microvascular complications**
• **Cardiovascular disease** remains the leading cause of mortality

sections.overview:
• Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) is a chronic, progressive metabolic disorder characterized by **hyperglycemia** resulting from a combination of **insulin resistance** and a **relative insulin deficiency**.
• Unlike Type 1 DM, which is primarily an autoimmune-mediated absolute destruction of pancreatic beta cells, T2DM involves target organs (liver, muscle, adipose tissue) failing to respond appropriately to insulin, coupled with the pancreas's eventual inability to produce enough insulin to overcome this resistance.
• It is the most common form of diabetes mellitus, accounting for approximately 90-95% of all diagnosed cases.
sections.etiology:
• T2DM is a multifactorial disease with strong genetic and environmental influences.
• The core pathophysiology revolves around two primary defects:
    ◦ **Insulin Resistance**
        ▪ Target cells (skeletal muscle, adipose tissue, liver) show a decreased response to normal circulating levels of insulin.
        ▪ **Muscle**: Decreased glucose uptake after meals.
        ▪ **Adipose Tissue**: Unrestrained lipolysis, leading to increased circulating free fatty acids (FFAs), which worsens **insulin resistance** and contributes to hepatic steatosis.
        ▪ **Liver**: Fails to suppress hepatic glucose production (**gluconeogenesis**), leading to elevated fasting blood glucose.
        ▪ Initially, the pancreatic β-cells compensate by producing more insulin, leading to a state of **hyperinsulinemia**.
    ◦ **Pancreatic β-Cell Dysfunction**
        ▪ Over time, the β-cells become "exhausted" from the constant demand for hypersecretion.
        ▪ There is a progressive decline in insulin secretion in response to glucose.
        ▪ This leads to a **relative insulin deficiency**, where the pancreas can no longer produce enough insulin to overcome the peripheral resistance.
        ▪ Eventually, β-cell mass decreases due to apoptosis.
• Other contributing factors (The "**Ominous Octet**"):
    ◦ **Alpha-cell dysfunction**: Excess glucagon secretion.
    ◦ **Decreased Incretin Effect**: Reduced secretion of GLP-1 and GIP from the gut, which normally stimulate insulin secretion and suppress glucagon.
    ◦ **Increased Renal Glucose Reabsorption**: The kidneys reabsorb more glucose via SGLT2 transporters, contributing to **hyperglycemia**.
    ◦ **Neurotransmitter dysfunction**: Central **insulin resistance** in the brain.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects over 37 million people in the US (~11% of the population). A major global health issue, with prevalence rising worldwide.
• **Age of Onset**: Traditionally diagnosed in adults over 45, but is now increasingly diagnosed in adolescents and young adults due to rising rates of obesity.
• **Demographics**: Higher prevalence in African American, Hispanic/Latino, American Indian, Asian American, and Pacific Islander populations.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Often **asymptomatic** and discovered incidentally on routine laboratory screening.
• Onset is insidious and may be present for years before diagnosis.
• Patients may present with a complication of diabetes (e.g., **neuropathy**, **retinopathy**, non-healing ulcer) or with classic hyperglycemic symptoms.
sections.diagnostics:
• **American Diabetes Association (ADA) Diagnostic Criteria** (any one of the following, confirmed on a subsequent day):
    ◦ **Hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c)**: ≥ 6.5%
    ◦ **Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG)**: ≥ 126 mg/dL (fasting is no caloric intake for at least 8 hours).
    ◦ **2-Hour Plasma Glucose**: ≥ 200 mg/dL during a 75-gram **Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT)**.
    ◦ **Random Plasma Glucose**: ≥ 200 mg/dL in a patient with classic symptoms of **hyperglycemia** or **hyperglycemic crisis**.
• Note: In the absence of unequivocal **hyperglycemia**, the diagnosis requires two abnormal test results from the same sample or in two separate test samples.
• **Categories of Pre-diabetes**:
    ◦ **FPG**: 100-125 mg/dL (**Impaired Fasting Glucose**)
    ◦ **2-Hour OGTT**: 140-199 mg/dL (**Impaired Glucose Tolerance**)
    ◦ **HbA1c**: 5.7% - 6.4%
sections.prognosis:
• T2DM is a lifelong condition that typically progresses over time.
• Life expectancy is reduced by up to 10 years, primarily due to **macrovascular complications** (CAD, stroke).
• Tight glycemic, blood pressure, and lipid control significantly reduces the risk and slows the progression of both **microvascular** and **macrovascular complications**.

sections.overview:
• **Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM)** is defined as carbohydrate intolerance of variable severity with onset or first recognition during pregnancy.
