• It is a state of **hyperglycemia** that develops due to pregnancy-related hormonal changes causing **insulin resistance**.
• GDM typically resolves after delivery but significantly increases the mother's risk of developing **Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM)** later in life and poses risks to the fetus.
sections.etiology:
• **Insulin Resistance**
	◦ During a normal pregnancy, the placenta produces hormones such as **human placental lactogen (hPL)**, progesterone, cortisol, and prolactin.
	◦ These hormones are crucial for fetal growth but also have an **anti-insulin effect**, leading to a state of progressive insulin resistance, particularly in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters.
• **Pancreatic Compensation**
	◦ In most pregnant individuals, the pancreas compensates by increasing insulin production (**beta-cell hyperplasia**) to maintain euglycemia.
• **GDM Development**
	◦ GDM occurs when the maternal pancreatic beta-cells are unable to produce sufficient insulin to overcome the pregnancy-induced insulin resistance.
	◦ This results in relative insulin deficiency and subsequent maternal hyperglycemia.
	◦ The underlying mechanism often involves a pre-existing, subclinical degree of beta-cell dysfunction.
• **Fetal Effects**
	◦ Maternal glucose freely crosses the placenta.
	◦ Maternal hyperglycemia leads to fetal hyperglycemia, stimulating the fetal pancreas to produce excess insulin (**fetal hyperinsulinemia**).
	◦ Insulin acts as a growth hormone in the fetus, leading to excessive growth (**macrosomia**).
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects approximately **6-9%** of pregnancies in the United States.
• Incidence is rising in parallel with the obesity epidemic.
• Prevalence varies by ethnicity, with higher rates in Hispanic, African American, Native American, and Asian populations.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Maternal Age > 35 years**
• **Obesity** (pre-pregnancy BMI > 30 kg/m2)
• **Personal history of GDM** in a prior pregnancy
• **Family history** of diabetes (first-degree relative)
• **Previous delivery of a macrosomic infant** (>4 kg or ~9 lbs)
• Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome (PCOS)
• History of unexplained stillbirth
• Member of a high-risk ethnic group
• Glycosuria on a prior visit
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• GDM is **largely asymptomatic**.
• Diagnosis is almost always made through routine screening, not based on symptoms.
• When symptoms occur, they can include:
	◦ Polyuria (increased urination)
	◦ Polydipsia (increased thirst)
	◦ Polyphagia (increased hunger)
	◦ Blurred vision
	◦ Fatigue
sections.physicalExam:
• The physical exam is **often unremarkable** and not diagnostic for GDM itself.
• Findings may be related to underlying risk factors or complications:
	◦ **High BMI / Obesity**
	◦ **Acanthosis nigricans:** indicates underlying insulin resistance.
	◦ **Fundal height greater than gestational age:** may suggest a **macrosomic fetus** or **polyhydramnios**.
sections.diagnostics: • Screening for GDM is recommended for all pregnant individuals at **24-28 weeks gestation**.
sections.treatment:
• **Diet:** Consultation with a registered dietitian. Focus on a balanced diet with carbohydrate control, distributed across 3 meals and 2-3 snacks to maintain stable glucose levels.
• **Exercise:** At least 30 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise 5 days a week (e.g., walking, swimming) as tolerated.
• **Glucose Monitoring:** Self-monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG) at home, typically **4 times daily** (fasting and 1 or 2 hours after each meal).
• **Insulin:** **First-line and preferred agent.**
	◦ It does not cross the placenta.
	◦ A combination of long-acting (NPH, detemir) and short-acting (aspart, lispro) insulin is often used.
• **Oral Agents:**
	◦ **Metformin:**
		▪ Crosses the placenta; often used as an alternative to insulin due to ease of use.
		▪ Lacks long-term safety data in offspring.
	◦ **Glyburide:** A sulfonylurea.
		▪ **Largely fallen out of favor** as it crosses the placenta and is associated with a higher risk of neonatal hypoglycemia and macrosomia compared to insulin or metformin.
sections.management:
• **Glycemic Goals:**
	◦ Fasting: < 95 mg/dL
	◦ 1-hour postprandial: < 140 mg/dL
	◦ 2-hour postprandial: < 120 mg/dL
• **Fetal Surveillance:** For patients requiring medication or with poor glycemic control.
	◦ **Non-stress tests (NSTs)** and/or **Biophysical Profiles (BPPs)** typically initiated at **32 weeks gestation**, performed once or twice weekly.
	◦ Serial ultrasounds to monitor fetal growth and screen for macrosomia.
• **Delivery Timing:**
	◦ **Well-controlled on diet alone:** Expectant management up to 40w6d.
	◦ **Well-controlled on medication:** Induction of labor recommended between **39w0d and 39w6d**.
	◦ **Poorly controlled:** Earlier delivery may be considered.
• **Intrapartum Management:**
	◦ Monitor glucose levels during labor to prevent neonatal hypoglycemia.
	◦ An insulin drip may be required.
• **Postpartum Follow-up:**
	◦ GDM typically resolves after delivery of the placenta.
	◦ Patients should be screened for overt diabetes at **6-12 weeks postpartum** with a **75-gram, 2-hour OGTT**.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for the pregnancy with good glycemic control.
• **Long-term for Mother:**
	◦ Significant (~50%) lifetime risk of developing **T2DM**.
	◦ This risk can be mitigated by weight loss, diet, and exercise.
• **Long-term for Child:**
	◦ Increased risk for obesity, impaired glucose tolerance, and T2DM later in life.

sections.overview:
• Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) is a life-threatening endocrine emergency characterized by the triad of **hyperglycemia**, **ketosis**, and **anion gap metabolic acidosis**
    ◦ Results from a state of absolute or relative insulin deficiency, leading to severe metabolic derangements
    ◦ Most commonly seen in patients with Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM) but can also occur in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) under conditions of extreme physiologic stress
sections.etiology:
• DKA is triggered by a profound insulin deficiency coupled with an excess of counter-regulatory hormones (glucagon, catecholamines, cortisol, growth hormone)
    ◦ **Etiology (Precipitating Factors - "The 5 I's")**
        ▪ **Infection**: Most common cause (e.g., pneumonia, UTI)
        ▪ **Infarction**: MI, CVA, bowel ischemia
        ▪ **Infraction (Non-compliance)**: Missed or inadequate insulin doses
        ▪ **Infant**: Pregnancy (due to hormonal changes and increased insulin resistance)
        ▪ **Initial** presentation of T1DM
        ▪ Other: Drugs (steroids, SGLT2 inhibitors), trauma, surgery, pancreatitis
    ◦ **Pathophysiology**
        ▪ **Insulin Deficiency & Glucagon Excess → Hyperglycemia**
            ◦ Decreased glucose uptake by peripheral tissues (muscle, fat)
            ◦ Increased hepatic glucose production via unopposed **gluconeogenesis** and **glycogenolysis**
            ◦ Result: Severe hyperglycemia (typically >250 mg/dL)
            ◦ This leads to **osmotic diuresis**, causing profound dehydration, electrolyte loss (Na+, K+, PO4-), and hyperosmolality
        ▪ **Insulin Deficiency & Glucagon Excess → Ketogenesis**
            ◦ Unopposed **lipolysis** in adipose tissue releases free fatty acids (FFAs) into circulation
            ◦ FFAs are transported to the liver and undergo beta-oxidation to Acetyl-CoA
            ◦ Excess Acetyl-CoA is shunted into the **ketogenesis** pathway, producing ketone bodies:
                ▪ **Beta-hydroxybutyrate** (predominant)
                ▪ **Acetoacetate**
                ▪ Acetoacetate can be spontaneously decarboxylated to **acetone**
        ▪ **Ketone Accumulation → Metabolic Acidosis**
            ◦ Beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate are organic acids; their accumulation overwhelms the body's bicarbonate buffering capacity
            ◦ Result: A primary **anion gap metabolic acidosis**
            ◦ The body attempts to compensate via the respiratory system, leading to **Kussmaul respirations** (deep, rapid breathing) to blow off CO2
sections.epidemiology:
• Primarily affects patients with T1DM
• Accounts for ~25% of initial presentations of T1DM
• Can occur in T2DM, particularly in "ketosis-prone" individuals or during severe illness
• A leading cause of hospitalization and mortality in children and young adults with T1DM
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients typically present as acutely ill and may have a rapid onset of symptoms over <24 hours
    ◦ The presentation is a direct consequence of dehydration, hyperglycemia, and acidosis
sections.diagnostics:
• **Diagnostic Criteria (The Triad)**
    ◦ **Hyperglycemia**: Plasma glucose > 250 mg/dL
    ◦ **Metabolic Acidosis**: Arterial pH < 7.30 **AND/OR** Serum Bicarbonate (HCO3) < 18 mEq/L
    ◦ **Ketosis**: Positive serum ketones or moderate/large urine ketones
• **Key Laboratory Findings**
    ◦ **Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP)**
        ▪ **Glucose**: > 250 mg/dL
        ▪ **Bicarbonate (HCO3)**: < 18 mEq/L
        ▪ **Anion Gap**: > 12 [AG = Na - (Cl + HCO3)]; **The anion gap is a critical value to monitor**
        ▪ **Potassium (K+)**: Serum K+ may be normal or elevated on presentation due to extracellular shifts from acidosis, but **total body potassium is always depleted**
        ▪ **Sodium (Na+)**: Often factitiously low (**pseudohyponatremia**) due to the osmotic effect of hyperglycemia
            ▪ Corrected Na = Measured Na + [1.6 * ((Glucose - 100)/100)]
        ▪ **BUN/Creatinine**: Elevated, indicating pre-renal azotemia from dehydration
    ◦ **Serum Ketones**
        ▪ **Beta-hydroxybutyrate is the gold standard** and preferred test
        ▪ More accurate than urine ketones (which primarily measure acetoacetate)
    ◦ **Arterial or Venous Blood Gas (ABG/VBG)**
        ▪ Confirms acidosis (pH < 7.3), low HCO3, and shows compensatory respiratory alkalosis (low pCO2)
    ◦ **Complete Blood Count (CBC)**
        ▪ Leukocytosis is common due to stress, but a significant left shift may indicate an underlying infection
    ◦ **Urinalysis**
        ▪ Strong glucosuria and ketonuria
• **Additional Workup (to find the precipitating cause)**
    ◦ **ECG**: Check for signs of MI or hyper/hypokalemia (peaked T waves vs. U waves)
    ◦ **Chest X-ray**: Rule out pneumonia
    ◦ **Blood and Urine Cultures**: If infection is suspected
    ◦ **Lipase/Amylase**: If pancreatitis is suspected
sections.prognosis:
• Mortality rate is low (<1%) with appropriate and timely treatment in adults
• Prognosis is worse in the elderly and those with severe comorbidities (e.g., MI, sepsis)
• In children, cerebral edema is the leading cause of mortality

sections.overview:
• **Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS)** is a life-threatening endocrine emergency characterized by the triad of:
    ◦ **Severe hyperglycemia**
    ◦ **Hyperosmolality**
    ◦ **Profound dehydration**
• It occurs **without significant ketoacidosis**.
• HHS typically develops in patients with **Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM)**, often in the elderly, and is usually precipitated by an underlying illness or stressor.
• It has a more **insidious onset** (days to weeks) and a **higher mortality rate** compared to Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA).
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology (Precipitating Factors)**: HHS is almost always triggered by a concurrent medical event in a patient with T2DM.
    ◦ **Infections (most common trigger, 50-60%)**: Pneumonia, Urinary Tract Infection (UTI), sepsis.
    ◦ **Acute Illness**: Myocardial infarction, stroke, pancreatitis, pulmonary embolism.
    ◦ **Medication Non-adherence**: Stopping insulin or oral hypoglycemic agents.
    ◦ **New-onset T2DM**: Can be the initial presentation.
    ◦ **Drugs**: Glucocorticoids, thiazide diuretics, sympathomimetics, atypical antipsychotics.
    ◦ **Substance Abuse**: Cocaine, alcohol.
    ◦ **Inadequate fluid intake**: Especially in elderly or debilitated patients who cannot access water freely.
• **Pathophysiology**: The core defect is a **relative insulin deficiency**.
    ◦ There is enough circulating insulin to prevent significant lipolysis and ketogenesis, but not enough to facilitate glucose uptake by peripheral tissues or suppress hepatic gluconeogenesis.
    ◦ **Relative Insulin Deficiency & Glucagon Excess → Severe Hyperglycemia**:
        ▪ Decreased glucose utilization by muscle, fat, and liver.
        ▪ Increased hepatic glucose production (gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis).
        ▪ Blood glucose levels rise to extreme levels (often >1000 mg/dL).
    ◦ **Hyperglycemia → Osmotic Diuresis**:
        ▪ When blood glucose exceeds the renal threshold for reabsorption (~180-200 mg/dL), glucose spills into the urine (**glycosuria**).
        ▪ Glucose acts as an osmotic agent, pulling large volumes of water and electrolytes into the renal tubules.
        ▪ This leads to polyuria and massive fluid loss.
    ◦ **Osmotic Diuresis & Inadequate Fluid Intake → Profound Dehydration & Hyperosmolality**:
        ▪ Patients are often elderly or ill and cannot compensate for fluid losses by drinking enough water (impaired thirst mechanism or physical inability).
        ▪ Severe dehydration develops, with typical water deficits of **8-12 liters**.
        ▪ The loss of free water in excess of solutes leads to a state of extreme **hyperosmolality**, which is the primary driver of the neurological symptoms.
    ◦ **Absence of Significant Ketosis**:
        ▪ The small amount of residual insulin is sufficient to suppress lipolysis (the breakdown of fat into free fatty acids) and subsequent ketogenesis in the liver. This is the key physiological difference from DKA.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Population**: Primarily affects patients with **Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus**.
• **Age**: More common in older adults (mean age 60-70 years).
• **Mortality**: High mortality rate of **5-20%**, significantly higher than that of DKA, largely due to the patient's advanced age, underlying comorbidities, and severity of the precipitating illness.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The onset of HHS is **insidious**, typically developing over several days to weeks, in contrast to the more acute presentation of DKA.
• The clinical picture is dominated by signs of profound **dehydration** and **altered mental status**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Plasma Glucose**: **> 600 mg/dL** (often >1000)
    ◦ Hallmark value. Extremely high.
• **Serum Osmolality**: **> 320 mOsm/kg**
    ◦ Key diagnostic criterion. Drives the neuro symptoms.
• **Arterial/Venous pH**: **> 7.30**
    ◦ Differentiates from DKA. No significant acidosis.
• **Serum Bicarbonate**: **> 18 mEq/L**
    ◦ Differentiates from DKA. Usually normal or slightly low.
• **Anion Gap**: **Normal** or slightly elevated
    ◦ `Na - (Cl + HCO3)`. No significant gap acidosis.
• **Serum/Urine Ketones**: **Negative or small**
    ◦ The defining feature distinguishing HHS from DKA.
• **BUN/Creatinine**: **Markedly elevated** (**prerenal azotemia**)
    ◦ BUN:Cr ratio often > 20:1 due to severe dehydration.
• **Serum Sodium**: Variable (low, normal, or high)
    ◦ **Must calculate corrected sodium!**
• **High-Yield Calculations**:
    ◦ **Effective Serum Osmolality**: `2 * Na + (Glucose / 18)`
    ◦ **Corrected Sodium**: For every 100 mg/dL increase in glucose above 100, sodium is diluted by ~2.4 mEq/L.
        ▪ Formula: `Corrected Na = Measured Na + [2.4 * ((Glucose - 100) / 100)]`
• **Additional Workup (to find the trigger)**:
    ◦ **CBC with differential**: Look for leukocytosis (infection).
    ◦ **Urinalysis & Urine Culture**: Evidence of UTI.
    ◦ **Chest X-Ray**: Evidence of pneumonia.
    ◦ **EKG & Troponins**: To rule out MI.
    ◦ **Blood Cultures**: If sepsis is suspected.
sections.prognosis:
• Mortality rate is high (**5-20%**).
• Prognosis is largely dependent on the patient's age, the severity of the precipitating illness, and the degree of dehydration and hyperosmolality at presentation.

sections.overview:
• A diabetic foot infection (DFI) is any infection below the malleoli in a person with diabetes mellitus.
• Represents a complex clinical problem arising from the interplay of **neuropathy**, **peripheral artery disease (PAD)**, and **immunocompromise**.
• DFIs are a leading cause of non-traumatic **lower extremity amputations** and a major source of morbidity and mortality in diabetic patients.
• They range in severity from superficial cellulitis to deep abscesses, osteomyelitis, and life-threatening necrotizing fasciitis.
sections.etiology:
• The development of DFI is a multi-step process driven by the "pathophysiologic triad" of diabetes:
    ◦ **Peripheral Neuropathy**:
        ▪ **Sensory**: Loss of protective sensation (pain, pressure, temperature) leads to unrecognized trauma (e.g., from ill-fitting shoes, foreign objects).
        ▪ **Motor**: Atrophy of intrinsic foot muscles leads to structural deformities (e.g., **claw toes**, **hammer toes**, prominent metatarsal heads, **Charcot neuroarthropathy**), creating abnormal pressure points and callus formation.
        ▪ **Autonomic**: Decreased sweating (anhidrosis) causes dry, cracked skin, which serves as a portal of entry for bacteria.
    ◦ **Peripheral Artery Disease (PAD)**:
        ▪ Diabetes accelerates atherosclerosis, leading to impaired blood flow to the lower extremities.
        ▪ Reduced perfusion impairs all phases of wound healing, decreases the delivery of antibiotics to the site of infection, and lowers the oxygen tension needed for leukocyte function.
    ◦ **Immunocompromise**:
        ▪ **Hyperglycemia** directly impairs neutrophil function (**chemotaxis**, **opsonization**, and **phagocytosis**).
        ▪ The overall inflammatory response is blunted, which can mask early signs of infection.
• **Microbiology**:
    ◦ **Mild/Acute Infections**: Often **monomicrobial**, typically Gram-positive cocci (e.g., ***Staphylococcus aureus***, Coagulase-negative staphylococci, ***Streptococcus*** species).
    ◦ **Chronic/Severe/Previously Treated Infections**: Almost always **polymicrobial**.
        ▪ Includes Gram-positives, Gram-negatives (e.g., ***Pseudomonas aeruginosa***, ***E. coli***, ***Klebsiella***), and **anaerobes** (e.g., ***Bacteroides***, ***Peptostreptococcus***).
sections.epidemiology:
• Approximately **15-25%** of patients with diabetes will develop a foot ulcer in their lifetime.
• Over **50%** of these ulcers will become infected.
• DFIs are the most common reason for diabetes-related hospitalizations.
• DFIs precede **>80%** of non-traumatic lower extremity amputations in the United States.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The "classic" signs of infection (severe pain, high fever, rigors) may be **absent or blunted** due to neuropathy and immunosuppression.
• Patients often present due to a **non-healing ulcer** with new or worsening local signs.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Laboratory Studies**:
    ◦ **CBC with differential**: Leukocytosis may be present but can be absent in severe cases.
    ◦ **Inflammatory Markers**: **ESR and CRP** are often elevated and are useful for monitoring treatment response.
    ◦ **HbA1c**: To assess long-term glycemic control.
    ◦ **BMP/CMP**: To assess renal function (important for antibiotic dosing) and electrolytes.
    ◦ **Blood Cultures**: Obtain if systemic signs of infection (fever, hypotension) are present.
• **Microbiology**:
    ◦ **Gold Standard**: Deep **tissue culture/biopsy** from the debrided ulcer base or **bone biopsy**.
    ◦ **AVOID**: Superficial wound swabs, as they are contaminated with colonizing flora and do not reflect the true pathogen(s).
• **Imaging**:
    ◦ **Plain Radiographs (X-ray)**:
        ▪ **Initial imaging test of choice**.
        ▪ Can reveal soft tissue gas, foreign bodies, fractures, or Charcot deformities.
        ▪ Findings of **osteomyelitis** (cortical erosion, periosteal reaction, demineralization) may lag behind clinical infection by 2-3 weeks.
    ◦ **Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)**:
        ▪ **Most sensitive and specific** imaging modality for **osteomyelitis** and for detecting deep soft-tissue abscesses.
        ▪ T1-weighted images show decreased signal in infected marrow; T2/STIR images show increased signal (edema).
    ◦ **Nuclear Medicine Scans (Technetium-99m bone scan, Indium-111 labeled WBC scan)**: Used if MRI is contraindicated. Sensitive but not as specific.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is variable and depends on infection severity, presence of PAD, glycemic control, and patient adherence.
• Ulcer recurrence rates are high (**>50% within 3 years**).
• A major lower extremity amputation is associated with a 5-year mortality rate of **50-70%**, which is worse than many cancers.

sections.overview:
• Diabetic neuropathy is nerve damage caused by chronically high blood sugar levels (hyperglycemia) and is one of the most common long-term complications of diabetes mellitus.
• It encompasses a heterogeneous group of syndromes with diverse clinical manifestations.
• The most common form is **Distal Symmetric Polyneuropathy (DSPN)**, which primarily affects sensory and motor nerves in a "stocking-glove" distribution.
• Other forms include autonomic, focal (mononeuropathy), and proximal (radiculoplexus) neuropathies.
• It is a major cause of morbidity, leading to foot ulcers, amputations, and debilitating pain.
sections.etiology:
• The pathophysiology is complex and multifactorial, stemming from chronic hyperglycemia. Key mechanisms include:
	◦ **Metabolic Factors:**
		▪ **Advanced Glycation End-products (AGEs):** Excess glucose binds to proteins and lipids, forming AGEs. These AGEs damage nerve cells and microvasculature by inducing oxidative stress and inflammation.
		▪ **Polyol (Sorbitol) Pathway:** Hyperglycemia shunts excess glucose into the polyol pathway, where aldose reductase converts it to sorbitol. Sorbitol accumulates intracellularly, creating osmotic stress and depleting essential cofactors, leading to nerve cell injury.
		▪ **Protein Kinase C (PKC) Activation:** Hyperglycemia activates PKC, which alters gene expression and leads to vascular dysfunction, including reduced nerve blood flow.
	◦ **Vascular/Ischemic Factors:**
		▪ Diabetes causes microvascular damage to the **vasa nervorum** (the blood vessels supplying the nerves).
		▪ This leads to endothelial dysfunction, impaired vasodilation (due to decreased nitric oxide), and basement membrane thickening, resulting in nerve ischemia and hypoxia.
	◦ **Inflammatory & Immune Mechanisms:**
		▪ Chronic low-grade inflammation and altered immune responses contribute to nerve damage and demyelination.
• The cumulative effect of these pathways is **axonal degeneration** and **segmental demyelination** of peripheral nerves.
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects up to **50%** of all patients with diabetes mellitus over their lifetime.
• Prevalence increases with the **duration of diabetes** and the degree of **hyperglycemia**.
• **Distal Symmetric Polyneuropathy (DSPN)** is the most common form, accounting for ~75% of cases.
• Present in ~8% of newly diagnosed T2DM patients.
• Autonomic neuropathy is also common, with manifestations present in over 20% of patients.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation varies widely depending on the type of neuropathy.
• **Distal Symmetric Polyneuropathy (DSPN):**
	◦ Insidious onset, slowly progressive.
	◦ Symmetric, bilateral symptoms starting in the toes and feet ("stocking" distribution) and progressing proximally. Hands ("glove" distribution) are affected later.
	◦ Sensory symptoms typically precede motor symptoms.
• **Autonomic Neuropathy:**
	◦ Presents with dysfunction of one or more organ systems (cardiovascular, GI, genitourinary).
• **Focal/Multifocal Neuropathy (Mononeuropathy):**
	◦ Sudden onset of deficits in a single nerve distribution.
	◦ Commonly affects cranial nerves (**CN III, IV, VI**) or peripheral nerves (median, ulnar, peroneal).
• **Radiculoplexus Neuropathy (Diabetic Amyotrophy):**
	◦ Acute, asymmetric, severe pain and weakness in the proximal lower extremity (thighs, hips, buttocks).
	◦ Often associated with significant weight loss.
sections.diagnostics:
• Primarily a **clinical diagnosis** in a patient with established diabetes after ruling out other causes.
• **Screening:**
	◦ The American Diabetes Association (ADA) recommends annual screening for DSPN starting at diagnosis for T2DM and 5 years after diagnosis for T1DM.
	◦ Screening includes a careful history and a foot exam including the **10-g monofilament test** AND at least one other test (vibration, pinprick, or ankle reflexes).
• **Laboratory Studies:**
	◦ **HbA1c:** To assess degree of glycemic control.
	◦ Rule out other causes of neuropathy: **Vitamin B12 level**, TSH (thyroid), RPR (syphilis), CMP (renal function).
• **Nerve Conduction Studies (NCS) and Electromyography (EMG):**
	◦ Not routinely required for typical DSPN.
	◦ Indicated for atypical presentations (e.g., asymmetric, rapidly progressive, predominantly motor) to confirm neuropathy and rule out other etiologies.
	◦ Shows evidence of axonal loss and/or demyelination.
sections.prognosis:
• Diabetic neuropathy is a progressive condition.
• Nerve damage is generally **irreversible**.
• The primary goals are to slow progression, manage symptoms, and prevent complications like ulcers and amputations.
• Prognosis is directly related to the quality of glycemic control and management of other risk factors.
• The presence of neuropathy is a strong predictor of increased mortality.

sections.overview:
• **Diabetic Nephropathy (DN)**, also known as **Diabetic Kidney Disease (DKD)**, is a progressive kidney disease caused by damage to the capillaries in the glomeruli
	◦ It is a major **microvascular complication** of both Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes mellitus
• Characterized by a clinical syndrome of persistent **albuminuria** (>300 mg/day), a progressive decline in the **Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)**, and elevated arterial blood pressure
• DN is the leading cause of **chronic kidney disease (CKD)** and **end-stage renal disease (ESRD)** in the United States and other developed nations
sections.etiology:
• The pathophysiology is multifactorial, driven primarily by chronic **hyperglycemia**
• **Hemodynamic Alterations**
	◦ **Glomerular Hyperfiltration**: Chronic **hyperglycemia** leads to afferent (incoming) arteriolar vasodilation and efferent (outgoing) arteriolar vasoconstriction
	◦ **Intraglomerular Hypertension**: This pressure mismatch dramatically increases hydrostatic pressure within the glomerulus, leading to hyperfiltration
	◦ **RAAS Activation**: **Hyperglycemia** activates the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS), leading to increased Angiotensin II, which preferentially constricts the efferent arteriole, further worsening intraglomerular hypertension
• **Metabolic Alterations & Structural Changes**
	◦ **Advanced Glycation End Products (AGEs)**: Non-enzymatic glycation of proteins in the glomerulus leads to the formation of AGEs
		▪ These cross-link proteins (like collagen), causing thickening and reduced elasticity of the **glomerular basement membrane (GBM)** and promoting inflammation and fibrosis
	◦ **Protein Kinase C (PKC) Activation**: **Hyperglycemia** activates PKC, which increases vascular permeability, promotes extracellular matrix deposition, and contributes to fibrosis
	◦ **Polyol Pathway Activation**: Excess glucose is shunted into the polyol pathway, consuming NADPH and leading to **oxidative stress**, which damages podocytes and endothelial cells
• **Histopathological Progression**
	◦ **GBM Thickening**: The earliest structural change
	◦ **Mesangial Expansion**: Proliferation of mesangial cells and deposition of mesangial matrix
	◦ **Nodular Sclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson Lesions)**: Pathognomonic for diabetic nephropathy; these are nodular, eosinophilic accumulations of mesangial matrix
	◦ **Glomerulosclerosis**: Global scarring of the glomerulus, leading to loss of function
sections.epidemiology:
• **Leading cause of ESRD** in the United States
• Develops in approximately **30-40%** of patients with **Type 1 Diabetes (T1DM)**
• Develops in approximately **20-40%** of patients with **Type 2 Diabetes (T2DM)**
• Higher incidence and prevalence in African American, Native American, and Hispanic populations
• Peak incidence
	◦ **T1DM**: 10-20 years after diagnosis
	◦ **T2DM**: Nephropathy may be present at the time of diagnosis due to a long preceding period of undiagnosed **hyperglycemia**
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Asymptomatic in early stages**; the disease is typically detected during routine annual screening
• The first sign is usually **moderately increased albuminuria** (formerly microalbuminuria)
• As the disease progresses, patients may develop symptoms of **nephrotic syndrome** or general **CKD**
• Strongly associated with other microvascular complications, especially **diabetic retinopathy**
	◦ The presence of retinopathy increases the likelihood that proteinuria is due to diabetic nephropathy
sections.diagnostics:
• **Screening (Essential)**
	◦ **Test**: **Spot Urine Albumin-to-Creatinine Ratio (UACR)** on a random urine sample is the preferred screening test
	◦ **Frequency**: Annually
		▪ **T1DM**: Begin 5 years after diagnosis
		▪ **T2DM**: Begin at the time of diagnosis
	◦ **Interpretation of UACR (mg/g)**
		▪ **A1 (Normal to mildly increased)**: < 30 mg/g
		▪ **A2 (Moderately increased / Microalbuminuria)**: 30-300 mg/g
		▪ **A3 (Severely increased / Macroalbuminuria)**: > 300 mg/g
	◦ **Note**: Diagnosis requires **2 of 3 positive tests** within a 3-6 month period to rule out transient causes
• **Monitoring and Staging**
	◦ **Serum Creatinine and eGFR**: Measured at least annually to estimate GFR and stage CKD (G1-G5)
	◦ **BMP**: To monitor for **hyperkalemia** (especially with ACEi/ARB use) and **metabolic acidosis**
• **Renal Biopsy (Gold Standard)**
	◦ **Rarely performed** if the clinical picture is classic (long-standing DM, retinopathy, progressive albuminuria)
	◦ **Indications for Biopsy (atypical features)**
		▪ Absence of **diabetic retinopathy**
		▪ Rapid decline in **GFR**
		▪ Active urinary sediment (**RBC casts**, **hematuria**)
		▪ Sudden onset of **nephrotic syndrome**
		▪ Systemic symptoms (fever, rash, arthralgias)
	◦ **Histology Finding**: **Kimmelstiel-Wilson (KW) lesions** (nodular glomerulosclerosis) are pathognomonic
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is directly related to the degree of **albuminuria** and the rate of **GFR decline**
• **Moderately increased albuminuria** (microalbuminuria) can be slowed or even reversed with intensive glycemic and blood pressure control
• Once **severely increased albuminuria** (macroalbuminuria) and a declining GFR are established, progression to **ESRD** is common, though the rate can be significantly slowed with optimal management
• Patients with DKD have a markedly increased risk of death, primarily from **cardiovascular events**

sections.overview:
• **Diabetic Retinopathy (DR)** is a chronic, progressive microvascular complication of **diabetes mellitus** and is the **leading cause of new-onset blindness** in working-age adults (20-74 years) in developed countries.
• It is characterized by damage to the small blood vessels of the retina, leading to fluid leakage, ischemia, and, in advanced stages, abnormal blood vessel growth.
• The disease is broadly classified into two main stages:
    ◦ **Non-proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (NPDR)**
    ◦ The more severe **Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR)**
sections.etiology:
• The underlying cause is **chronic hyperglycemia**, which initiates a cascade of metabolic and vascular changes in the retina.
• **Hyperglycemia-Induced Damage**
    ◦ **Pericyte Loss**
        ▪ Pericytes are cells that wrap around retinal capillaries, providing structural support.
        ▪ Hyperglycemia leads to their apoptosis (programmed cell death).
        ▪ Loss of pericytes weakens the capillary walls, leading to the formation of **microaneurysms** (the earliest clinical sign).
    ◦ **Basement Membrane Thickening**
        ▪ The membrane surrounding the capillaries becomes abnormally thick, further impairing function and contributing to vessel occlusion.
• **Increased Vascular Permeability**
    ◦ Damaged vessels become "leaky," causing breakdown of the **blood-retina barrier**.
    ◦ This allows plasma fluid, lipids, and proteins to leak into the retinal tissue.
    ◦ **Leakage of fluid** leads to **retinal edema**, particularly **macular edema** if it occurs in the central retina.
    ◦ **Leakage of lipids** leads to the formation of **hard exudates**.
• **Vascular Occlusion & Ischemia**
    ◦ Damaged endothelial cells, thickened basement membranes, and altered blood components lead to capillary occlusion.
    ◦ This results in retinal **ischemia** (lack of oxygen).
    ◦ Ischemic areas appear as **cotton-wool spots** on fundoscopy, which are infarcts of the retinal nerve fiber layer.
• **Proliferative Stage (Response to Ischemia)**
    ◦ Widespread retinal ischemia triggers the upregulation of angiogenic factors, most importantly **Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF)**.
    ◦ VEGF stimulates **neovascularization**: the growth of new, fragile, and abnormal blood vessels on the surface of the retina or optic disc.
    ◦ These new vessels are prone to bleeding (**vitreous hemorrhage**) and can form fibrous scar tissue that contracts, leading to **tractional retinal detachment**.
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects approximately 1 in 3 people with diabetes.
• The prevalence is strongly correlated with the duration of diabetes.
    ◦ **Type 1 DM**: After 20 years, >99% of patients have some degree of DR.
    ◦ **Type 2 DM**: After 20 years, ~60% of patients have some degree of DR.
• **Diabetic Macular Edema (DME)** is the most common cause of vision loss in patients with DR.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients are often **asymptomatic** in the early stages of the disease.
• The diagnosis is frequently made during a routine screening **dilated funduscopic exam**.
• When symptoms develop, it often signifies advanced disease.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Dilated Funduscopic Exam (DFE)**: The cornerstone of screening and diagnosis. Performed by an ophthalmologist or optometrist.
• **Fundus Photography**: Used for documentation, monitoring progression, and telemedicine screening.
• **Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT)**: **Gold standard for diagnosing and quantifying diabetic macular edema**.
    ◦ Provides high-resolution, cross-sectional images of the retina, allowing for precise measurement of retinal thickness.
• **Fluorescein Angiography (FA)**: Involves IV injection of fluorescein dye followed by fundus photography. It is used to:
    ◦ Identify leaking **microaneurysms** and areas of capillary non-perfusion (ischemia).
    ◦ Confirm and locate **neovascularization**.
    ◦ Guide laser treatment.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is good for preserving vision if DR is detected early and treated appropriately.
• Strict control of **glucose, blood pressure, and lipids** can significantly slow progression.
• Once PDR or DME with vision loss develops, the prognosis is more guarded, but modern treatments (**anti-VEGF**, PRP) have drastically improved outcomes and reduced the risk of blindness.

sections.overview:
• **Cushing Syndrome** is a clinical condition resulting from chronic exposure to excess glucocorticoids (cortisol), regardless of the cause
• It is distinct from **Cushing's Disease**, which specifically refers to Cushing Syndrome caused by a pituitary adenoma secreting excess adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)
sections.etiology:
• The etiology is broadly divided into exogenous (iatrogenic) and endogenous causes
• **Exogenous (Iatrogenic) - Most common cause overall**
    ◦ Prolonged administration of high-dose glucocorticoids (e.g., prednisone, dexamethasone) for inflammatory, autoimmune, or post-transplant conditions
• **Endogenous - Rare**
    ◦ Endogenous causes are further classified by their dependence on ACTH
    ◦ **ACTH-Dependent (80% of endogenous cases)**
        ▪ **Cushing's Disease (70%):** A benign pituitary adenoma secretes excessive ACTH, leading to bilateral adrenal hyperplasia and hypercortisolism
        ▪ **Ectopic ACTH Syndrome (10%):** A non-pituitary tumor (paraneoplastic) secretes ACTH
            • Most commonly **Small Cell Lung Cancer (SCLC)**
            • Other causes: Carcinoid tumors (bronchial, pancreatic), medullary thyroid cancer, pheochromocytoma
    ◦ **ACTH-Independent (20% of endogenous cases)**
        ▪ **Adrenal Adenoma (10%):** A benign cortisol-producing tumor on one adrenal gland
        ▪ **Adrenal Carcinoma (5%):** A malignant cortisol-producing tumor. Often produces very high cortisol levels
        ▪ **Micronodular or Macronodular Adrenal Hyperplasia (rare):** Both adrenal glands are enlarged and overproduce cortisol independent of ACTH
• **Pathophysiology:** Excess cortisol exerts exaggerated effects on multiple organ systems
    ◦ **Metabolic:** Increases **gluconeogenesis**, **lipolysis**, and **proteolysis**, leading to **hyperglycemia**, central fat redistribution, and muscle wasting
    ◦ **Catabolic:** Breaks down collagen in skin (thinning, **striae**) and bone (**osteoporosis**)
    ◦ **Immunosuppressive:** Inhibits immune function, increasing risk of infection
    ◦ **Cardiovascular:** Increases vascular sensitivity to catecholamines and can have mineralocorticoid effects, leading to **hypertension** and **hypokalemia**
    ◦ **CNS:** Affects mood, sleep, and cognition
sections.epidemiology:
• **Overall:** The most common cause is iatrogenic steroid use
• **Endogenous:** Rare, with an incidence of 2-5 cases per million people per year
• **Cushing's Disease:** More common in women (3:1 ratio), typically diagnosed between ages 20-50
• **Ectopic ACTH Syndrome:** More common in men, reflecting the epidemiology of **SCLC**
• **Adrenal Tumors:** More common in women
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is often insidious, developing over months to years
• Patients typically present with a combination of progressive central weight gain, skin changes, and new-onset or worsening **hypertension** and **diabetes**
sections.diagnostics:
• A stepwise approach is essential
• **Step 1: Confirm Hypercortisolism (Screening)**
    ◦ Requires at least **two** positive screening tests to confirm
    ◦ **24-Hour Urinary Free Cortisol (UFC):** Measures cortisol excretion over a full day. High sensitivity and specificity
    ◦ **Late-Night Salivary Cortisol:** Cortisol levels are normally at their nadir around midnight. Elevated levels are pathological
    ◦ **Low-Dose (1 mg) Dexamethasone Suppression Test:** Patient takes 1 mg of dexamethasone at 11 PM. A normal response is suppression of morning serum cortisol (<1.8 mcg/dL). Failure to suppress indicates **Cushing Syndrome**
• **Step 2: Determine the Etiology (ACTH Level)**
    ◦ Once hypercortisolism is confirmed, check a plasma **ACTH** level
    ◦ **Low/Suppressed ACTH (<5 pg/mL):** Suggests an **ACTH-independent** cause (adrenal tumor)
        ▪ **Next Step:** Adrenal CT scan to identify adrenal adenoma or carcinoma
    ◦ **Normal to High ACTH (>20 pg/mL):** Suggests an **ACTH-dependent** cause (pituitary vs. ectopic)
• **Step 3: Differentiate Pituitary vs. Ectopic ACTH Source**
    ◦ **High-Dose (8 mg) Dexamethasone Suppression Test:**
        ▪ **Suppression** of cortisol (>50% reduction) points to a **pituitary source (Cushing's Disease)**, as pituitary adenomas retain some sensitivity to negative feedback
        ▪ **No suppression** points to an **ectopic source**, as these tumors do not respond to feedback
    ◦ **Imaging:**
        ▪ **Pituitary MRI with contrast:** Best initial imaging for suspected **Cushing's Disease**
        ▪ **CT of Chest/Abdomen/Pelvis:** Used to search for an ectopic tumor (e.g., SCLC, carcinoid)
    ◦ **Inferior Petrosal Sinus Sampling (IPSS):**
        ▪ **Gold standard** for differentiating pituitary vs. ectopic if imaging is inconclusive
        ▪ Compares ACTH levels from veins draining the pituitary with peripheral levels. A high central-to-peripheral ratio confirms a pituitary source
sections.prognosis:
• **Benign Causes (Adenomas):** Generally good with successful surgical cure, although recovery can take a year or more
• **Malignant Causes (Adrenal Carcinoma, Ectopic SCLC):** Prognosis is poor and depends on the underlying malignancy
• Even after cure, patients have an increased risk of long-term cardiovascular disease and reduced quality of life

sections.overview:
• Addison Disease is **primary adrenal insufficiency**, characterized by the destruction or dysfunction of the entire adrenal cortex.
    ◦ This results in a combined deficiency of **glucocorticoids (cortisol)**, **mineralocorticoids (aldosterone)**, and **adrenal androgens**.
    ◦ The lack of these critical hormones leads to a chronic, progressive, and potentially life-threatening condition marked by an inability to maintain blood pressure, blood glucose, and fluid/electrolyte balance, especially during periods of physiologic stress.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** ~100-140 per million in Western countries.
• **Peak Incidence:** 30-50 years of age.
• **Sex:** Autoimmune Addison's is more common in women (2-3:1).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The onset is typically insidious and non-specific, often delaying diagnosis.
    ◦ Symptoms worsen during periods of stress (infection, surgery, trauma).
• The classic presentation is a patient with chronic fatigue, weakness, and weight loss who develops hypotension and shock during an acute illness (**Adrenal Crisis**).
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• With proper diagnosis, hormone replacement, and patient education on sick day management, the prognosis is excellent, and life expectancy is near-normal.
• Mortality is primarily associated with delayed diagnosis or mismanagement of an **adrenal crisis**.

sections.overview:
• Adrenal crisis (addisonian crisis, acute adrenal insufficiency) is a life-threatening endocrine emergency characterized by the body's inability to produce adequate **cortisol** in response to a physiological stressor.
	◦ This leads to a state of profound **circulatory collapse (shock)**, severe **hypotension**, and metabolic derangements.
• It represents the acute, severe manifestation of adrenal insufficiency, which can be pre-existing or occur acutely due to adrenal gland destruction.
• Immediate recognition and treatment are critical to prevent mortality.
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**: The crisis is driven by a profound deficiency of two key adrenal hormones:
	◦ **Glucocorticoids (Cortisol)**: Deficiency leads to:
		▪ **Cardiovascular Collapse**: Decreased vascular tone and reduced sensitivity of blood vessels to catecholamines, leading to profound vasodilation and **hypotension**.
		▪ **Hypoglycemia**: Impaired gluconeogenesis and increased peripheral glucose utilization.
		▪ **Exaggerated Inflammatory Response**: Uncontrolled release of inflammatory cytokines, contributing to fever and shock.
	◦ **Mineralocorticoids (Aldosterone)**: Deficiency is prominent in primary adrenal insufficiency and leads to:
		▪ **Hypovolemia**: Renal salt wasting (**hyponatremia**) and subsequent water loss.
		▪ **Hyperkalemia** & **Metabolic Acidosis**: Impaired renal excretion of potassium (K+) and hydrogen (H+) ions.
• **Etiology (Causes)**: Typically precipitated by a stressor in a patient with underlying adrenal insufficiency.
	◦ **Stress in a Patient with Chronic Adrenal Insufficiency** (most common cause):
		▪ **Primary Adrenal Insufficiency (Addison's Disease)**: Autoimmune adrenalitis, TB, metastatic cancer, adrenal hemorrhage.
		▪ **Secondary/Tertiary Adrenal Insufficiency**: Pituitary or hypothalamic disease.
		▪ **Precipitating Stressors**: **Infection** (most common), trauma, surgery, dehydration, myocardial infarction, emotional stress.
	◦ **Sudden Withdrawal of Long-Term Glucocorticoid Therapy**: Chronic steroid use suppresses the HPA axis, causing adrenal atrophy; abrupt cessation leaves the patient unable to produce endogenous **cortisol**.
	◦ **Acute Adrenal Hemorrhage or Infarction**:
		▪ **Waterhouse-Friderichsen Syndrome**: Bilateral adrenal hemorrhage classically associated with severe sepsis, especially ***Neisseria meningitidis*** infection.
		▪ Other causes: Anticoagulant therapy, trauma, coagulopathy.
	◦ **Pituitary Apoplexy**: Sudden hemorrhage or infarction of a pituitary adenoma, leading to acute secondary adrenal insufficiency.
sections.epidemiology:
• Relatively rare but carries significant mortality if not treated promptly.
• Incidence in patients with known **primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease)** is approximately 6-8 episodes per 100 patient-years.
• Mortality rate for an adrenal crisis episode is approximately 5-10%, even with modern treatment.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a patient with known (or undiagnosed) adrenal insufficiency who develops an acute illness (e.g., gastroenteritis, pneumonia) and presents with **shock that is refractory to IV fluids and vasopressors**.
• The patient appears critically ill, often with **altered mental status**.
• The presentation can be nonspecific and mimic other severe conditions like **septic shock** or an acute abdomen.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Guiding Principle: DO NOT DELAY TREATMENT** to await diagnostic confirmation. If adrenal crisis is suspected, draw blood for labs and immediately administer treatment.
• **Laboratory Studies (Initial, Emergent)**:
	◦ **Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP)**:
		▪ **Hyponatremia** (universal)
		▪ **Hyperkalemia** (classic for primary AI)
		▪ **Hypoglycemia**
		▪ Non-anion gap metabolic acidosis
		▪ Hypercalcemia (mild)
		▪ Elevated BUN/Creatinine (pre-renal azotemia from hypovolemia)
	◦ **Complete Blood Count (CBC)**: May show eosinophilia, relative lymphocytosis, and neutropenia.
	◦ **Hormone Levels (Draw before giving steroids)**:
		▪ **Random Serum Cortisol**: A level < 5 mcg/dL is highly suggestive. A level > 20 mcg/dL makes the diagnosis unlikely.
		▪ **Plasma ACTH**: Helps differentiate primary vs. secondary AI.
			▪ **High ACTH**: Primary adrenal insufficiency (adrenal gland failure).
			▪ **Low or Inappropriately Normal ACTH**: Secondary/tertiary insufficiency (pituitary/hypothalamic failure).
• **Confirmatory Testing (Done after patient is stabilized)**:
	◦ **ACTH Stimulation Test (Cosyntropin Test)**: The definitive diagnostic test for adrenal insufficiency. An inadequate cortisol response (<18-20 mcg/dL) after administration of synthetic ACTH confirms the diagnosis.
• **Other Studies (to find the precipitant)**:
	◦ Blood cultures, urinalysis, chest x-ray to look for infection.
	◦ CT abdomen if adrenal hemorrhage is suspected.
sections.prognosis:
• With prompt recognition and aggressive treatment, the prognosis is excellent, and patients can recover fully from the acute crisis.
• Delayed diagnosis or treatment is associated with high mortality.

sections.overview:
• Hyperaldosteronism is a condition characterized by the excessive production of aldosterone by the adrenal cortex.
• It is a leading cause of **secondary hypertension**.
• It is broadly divided into two categories:
    ◦ **Primary Hyperaldosteronism (Conn Syndrome):**
        ▪ Aldosterone release is independent of the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS).
        ▪ This results in a **suppressed renin** level.
    ◦ **Secondary Hyperaldosteronism:**
        ▪ Aldosterone release is a result of appropriate RAAS activation due to decreased renal perfusion or other stimuli.
        ▪ This results in an **elevated renin** level.
• The classic triad of findings is **hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis**.
    ◦ However, many patients present with normal potassium levels.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• The most common cause of **secondary hypertension**.
• Affects 5-10% of all patients with hypertension and up to 20% of patients with **resistant hypertension**.
• Peak incidence is between 30-60 years of age.
• **Aldosterone-producing adenomas** are slightly more common in women.
• **Bilateral hyperplasia** has an equal sex distribution.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A typical patient is a 30- to 60-year-old with **difficult-to-control hypertension**.
    ◦ They may have been on multiple antihypertensive medications for years with poor response.
• They may present with symptoms related to **hypokalemia**, such as **muscle weakness** or **cramping**, or be entirely asymptomatic aside from the elevated blood pressure found on routine examination.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Step 1: Screening**
    ◦ **Test:** **Plasma Aldosterone Concentration (PAC) to Plasma Renin Activity (PRA) Ratio**, also called the **Aldosterone-to-Renin Ratio (ARR)**.
    ◦ **Preparation:**
        ▪ Correct **hypokalemia**.
        ▪ If clinically safe, hold interfering medications for 2-4 weeks (especially **MRAs, ACE-I/ARBs, beta-blockers, diuretics**).
    ◦ **Positive Screen:**
        ▪ **ARR > 20-30** ng/dL per ng/mL/hr
        ▪ **AND** Plasma Aldosterone Concentration **(PAC) > 15** ng/dL
• **Step 2: Confirmation**
    ◦ A confirmatory test is performed to verify autonomous aldosterone secretion (i.e., failure to suppress aldosterone with salt loading).
    ◦ **Oral Sodium Loading Test:**
        ▪ Patient consumes a high-sodium diet for 3 days.
        ▪ A 24-hour urine collection on day 3 showing aldosterone excretion **>12 mcg/24h** is positive.
    ◦ **Saline Infusion Test** (more common):
        ▪ Infuse 2 liters of 0.9% normal saline over 4 hours.
        ▪ A post-infusion PAC that fails to suppress to **<5-10 ng/dL** is positive.
• **Step 3: Subtype Classification (Localization)**
    ◦ Differentiates unilateral disease (adenoma) from bilateral disease (hyperplasia) to guide treatment (surgery vs. medical).
    ◦ **Adrenal CT Scan:**
        ▪ A high-resolution CT of the adrenals is the initial imaging test.
        ▪ It can identify a unilateral **adenoma** (typically >1 cm) or signs of **bilateral hyperplasia**.
    ◦ **Adrenal Vein Sampling (AVS):**
        ▪ **The gold standard test for subtype classification**.
        ▪ An interventional radiologist samples blood directly from both adrenal veins and a peripheral vein to measure aldosterone and cortisol.
        ▪ A significant lateralization of aldosterone secretion to one side confirms a unilateral source, making the patient a candidate for **adrenalectomy**.
        ▪ If there is no lateralization, **bilateral adrenal hyperplasia** is the cause.
• **Associated Lab & EKG Findings:**
    ◦ **CMP:** **Hypokalemia** (in ~30-50% of cases), mild **hypernatremia**, elevated serum bicarbonate (**metabolic alkalosis**).
    ◦ **EKG:** May show findings of **hypokalemia**:
        ▪ **U waves**, flattened T waves, ST-segment depression, premature ventricular contractions (PVCs).
sections.prognosis:
• **Unilateral Disease (Post-Adrenalectomy):** Excellent.
    ◦ **Hypokalemia** is cured in >99% of cases.
    ◦ **Hypertension** is cured or significantly improved.
    ◦ The risk of end-organ damage is reduced.
• **Bilateral Disease (Medical Management):** Good with medication adherence.
    ◦ BP can be well-controlled and **hypokalemia** corrected, reducing long-term cardiovascular risk.
    ◦ Requires lifelong therapy and monitoring.

sections.overview:
• A pheochromocytoma is a rare neuroendocrine tumor arising from **chromaffin cells** of the **adrenal medulla**.
	◦ It is characterized by the excessive, uncontrolled secretion of catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine, and to a lesser extent, dopamine).
	◦ This leads to a classic clinical picture of paroxysmal or sustained hypertension and a triad of symptoms: palpitations, headache, and diaphoresis.
• Tumors arising from extra-adrenal chromaffin cells are called **paragangliomas**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
	◦ The tumor originates from **chromaffin cells**, which are neuroendocrine cells responsible for synthesizing, storing, and secreting catecholamines in response to sympathetic nervous system stimulation.
• **Pathophysiology**
	◦ **Tumor Autonomy**: The tumor cells produce and secrete catecholamines independent of normal physiological regulation.
	◦ **Catecholamine Excess**: The tumor releases massive amounts of norepinephrine and epinephrine into circulation.
		▪ **Norepinephrine**: Primarily acts on **alpha-adrenergic receptors**, causing potent vasoconstriction, which leads to severe hypertension.
		▪ **Epinephrine**: Primarily acts on **beta-adrenergic receptors**, leading to increased heart rate (**tachycardia**), increased cardiac contractility, and metabolic effects like **hyperglycemia** (via glycogenolysis/gluconeogenesis) and lipolysis.
	◦ **Paroxysmal Release**: The secretion is often episodic ("paroxysmal"), triggered by factors like stress, surgery, certain medications, or physical pressure on the tumor, leading to characteristic "spells" or "attacks." Some tumors secrete continuously, causing sustained hypertension.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Rare, with an estimated 2-8 cases per 1 million people per year.
• **Prevalence**: Found in ~0.1-0.6% of patients with hypertension.
• **Age of Onset**: Typically diagnosed between the ages of 30 and 50.
• **Gender**: Affects males and females equally.
• **Genetics**: Approximately 40% of cases are associated with a familial genetic mutation.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 2 (MEN 2A & 2B)**
	◦ **MEN 2A**: Pheochromocytoma, Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma, Primary Hyperparathyroidism.
	◦ **MEN 2B**: Pheochromocytoma, Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma, Mucosal Neuromas, Marfanoid habitus.
• **Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) Disease**: Characterized by hemangioblastomas (CNS, retina), clear cell renal cell carcinoma, and pheochromocytomas.
• **Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1)**: Characterized by café-au-lait spots, neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, and optic gliomas.
• **Hereditary Paraganglioma Syndromes**: Caused by mutations in succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) genes (e.g., *SDHB, SDHC, SDHD*).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is highly variable, classically a patient with **paroxysmal, severe hypertension** who experiences episodic "spells."
	◦ These spells can last from minutes to hours and occur with variable frequency.
	◦ Triggers can include surgery, anesthesia, exercise, certain foods (tyramine-rich), or medications (e.g., beta-blockers, TCAs, stimulants).
• **Classic Triad & Symptoms (The "5 P's")**
	◦ **P**ressure (**Hypertension**)
	◦ **P**ain (**Headache**)
	◦ **P**erspiration (**Diaphoresis**)
	◦ **P**alpitations
	◦ **P**allor
	◦ Anxiety, sense of impending doom, panic attacks
	◦ Tremor
	◦ Nausea and vomiting
	◦ Chest or abdominal pain
	◦ Pallor (due to alpha-mediated vasoconstriction)
	◦ **Orthostatic hypotension** (due to intravascular volume depletion)
	◦ **Hyperglycemia** and weight loss
sections.physicalExam:
• **During a Paroxysm**
	◦ **Hypertension**: Can be extreme (e.g., >220/120 mmHg).
	◦ **Tachycardia**: Sinus tachycardia or other tachyarrhythmias.
	◦ **Diaphoresis**: Patient may be visibly sweating.
	◦ **Pallor**: Pale skin.
	◦ **Tremor**.
• **Between Paroxysms**
	◦ The physical exam may be entirely normal.
	◦ Sustained hypertension may be present.
	◦ **Orthostatic hypotension** is a key clue due to chronic volume contraction from persistent alpha-adrenergic stimulation.
• **Signs of Genetic Syndromes**
	◦ **NF1**: **Café-au-lait macules**, neurofibromas.
	◦ **MEN 2B**: **Mucosal neuromas** (lips, tongue), marfanoid habitus.
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is a two-step process: **1. Biochemical confirmation**, followed by **2. Tumor localization**.
• **Step 1: Biochemical Confirmation**
	◦ **Best Initial Tests (Highest Sensitivity)**
		▪ **Plasma free metanephrines**: Measures metabolites of epinephrine and norepinephrine; less affected by short-term stress than catecholamines.
		▪ **24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines and catecholamines**: Measures the total amount secreted over a full day, capturing episodic secretion.
	◦ **Other Tests (Less Sensitive/Specific)**
		▪ Urinary vanillylmandelic acid (VMA).
		▪ Plasma catecholamines (can be falsely elevated by stress of venipuncture).
• **Step 2: Tumor Localization (Imaging)**
	◦ *Perform imaging ONLY after biochemical evidence is confirmed.*
	◦ **First-Line Anatomic Imaging**
		▪ **CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast**: High sensitivity for detecting adrenal tumors (>1 cm).
		▪ **MRI of the abdomen and pelvis**: Preferred for children, pregnant women, and patients with contrast allergy. Pheochromocytomas often appear "lightbulb bright" on T2-weighted images.
	◦ **Functional Imaging (if CT/MRI is negative or to detect metastasis/paragangliomas)**
		▪ **123I-metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) Scintigraphy**: MIBG is a norepinephrine analog taken up by adrenergic tissue.
		▪ **Positron Emission Tomography (PET) Scan**: E.g., Gallium-68 DOTATATE PET/CT is highly sensitive, especially for paragangliomas.
sections.treatment:
• **Preoperative Medical Management**
	◦ **Goal**: Control blood pressure and allow for re-expansion of contracted blood volume.
	◦ **Step A: Alpha-Adrenergic Blockade (ALWAYS START FIRST)**
		▪ **Drug of Choice**: **Phenoxybenzamine** (irreversible, non-selective alpha-blocker).
		▪ **Alternative**: Selective alpha-1 blockers (Doxazosin, Prazosin).
		▪ Titrate dose until blood pressure is controlled and orthostasis is achieved.
	◦ **Step B: Beta-Adrenergic Blockade**
		▪ **Initiate ONLY AFTER 2-3 days of effective alpha-blockade.**
		▪ **Reason**: To avoid "**unopposed alpha-stimulation**." Giving a beta-blocker first will block beta-2 mediated vasodilation, leading to an unopposed alpha-1 vasoconstriction and a paradoxical, severe hypertensive crisis.
		▪ **Drugs**: Propranolol or Metoprolol. Used to control reflex tachycardia caused by alpha-blockade.
	◦ **Volume Expansion**: Encourage a high-sodium diet and fluid intake to reverse catecholamine-induced volume contraction.
• **Definitive Treatment**
	◦ **Surgical Resection**: Complete adrenalectomy, typically performed laparoscopically.
• **Management of Hypertensive Crisis**
	◦ **IV Phentolamine** (short-acting alpha-blocker).
	◦ **IV Sodium Nitroprusside**.
	◦ **IV Nicardipine**.
sections.management:
• **Intraoperative**
	◦ Close monitoring by anesthesia is critical. Expect wide swings in blood pressure, especially during tumor manipulation.
• **Postoperative**
	◦ **Hypotension**: Common after tumor removal due to the abrupt cessation of catecholamine secretion and the lingering effects of alpha-blockade. May require IV fluids and vasopressors.
	◦ **Hypoglycemia**: Can occur due to rebound hyperinsulinemia after the inhibitory effect of catecholamines on insulin secretion is removed.
	◦ If bilateral adrenalectomy is performed, the patient will require lifelong glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement for iatrogenic **Addison's disease**.
• **Long-Term Follow-up**
	◦ Lifelong annual biochemical screening (plasma or urine metanephrines) is recommended to monitor for recurrence or metastasis.
sections.complications:
• **Cardiovascular**: **Hypertensive crisis**, stroke (hemorrhagic or ischemic), myocardial infarction, aortic dissection, **catecholamine-induced cardiomyopathy**, arrhythmias (e.g., ventricular tachycardia).
• **Metastatic Disease**: About 10% of pheochromocytomas are malignant. Common sites of metastasis are bone, liver, and lung.
• **Perioperative**: Extreme hypertension, arrhythmias, hypotension post-resection.
sections.prognosis:
• **Benign, Resected Tumors**: Excellent prognosis with a >95% 5-year survival rate.
• **Malignant (Metastatic) Tumors**: Prognosis is significantly worse and highly variable. The 5-year survival rate is approximately 50-60%.

sections.overview:
• Acromegaly is a rare, chronic endocrine disorder characterized by excessive secretion of **Growth Hormone (GH)** in adults.
• This leads to the insidious and progressive overgrowth of bone, soft tissues, and organs.
• The term "acromegaly" comes from the Greek words for "extremities" (acro) and "great" (megaly), referring to the characteristic enlargement of the hands and feet.
• If excess GH secretion occurs before the closure of the epiphyseal growth plates in childhood, the condition is known as **Gigantism**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Pituitary Adenoma (>95% of cases)**: A benign tumor of the somatotroph cells in the anterior pituitary gland that autonomously secretes excess GH.
        ▪ **Macroadenoma (>1 cm)**: Most common type at diagnosis.
        ▪ **Microadenoma (<1 cm)**: Less common.
        ▪ Some adenomas may co-secrete other hormones, most commonly **Prolactin (PRL)**.
    ◦ **Extra-pituitary Tumors (<5%)**:
        ▪ **Ectopic GHRH secretion**: Neuroendocrine tumors (e.g., carcinoid tumors of the lung, pancreatic islet cell tumors) produce excess **Growth Hormone-Releasing Hormone (GHRH)**, which overstimulates the pituitary to produce GH.
        ▪ **Ectopic GH secretion**: Very rare, from tumors like pancreatic or lung cancers.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **GH Overproduction**: A pituitary adenoma secretes excessive amounts of GH, disrupting the normal negative feedback loop.
    ◦ **IGF-1 Production**: Excess GH stimulates the liver to produce high levels of **Insulin-like Growth Factor 1 (IGF-1)**.
        ▪ IGF-1 is the primary mediator of GH's growth-promoting effects.
    ◦ **Systemic Effects of Excess IGF-1 & GH**:
        ▪ **Somatic Growth**: IGF-1 causes proliferation of bone, cartilage, and soft tissues. In adults, this results in appositional (widening) bone growth, as linear growth is no longer possible.
        ▪ **Metabolic Effects**: GH is a counter-regulatory hormone. Excess GH leads to **insulin resistance**, **hyperglycemia** (can lead to Type 2 DM), and **lipolysis**.
    ◦ **Mass Effect of Tumor**: As the pituitary adenoma grows, it can compress surrounding structures.
        ▪ **Optic Chiasm**: Compression leads to visual field defects, classically **bitemporal hemianopsia**.
        ▪ **Normal Pituitary Tissue**: Compression can cause **hypopituitarism** (deficiencies in TSH, ACTH, LH/FSH).
        ▪ **Cavernous Sinus**: Invasion can cause **cranial nerve palsies** (III, IV, V, VI).
        ▪ **Suprasellar Extension**: Can cause **headaches** and **hydrocephalus**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: 3-4 new cases per million people per year.
• **Prevalence**: Approximately 60 cases per million people.
• **Age of Onset**: Typically diagnosed in middle age (average 40-45 years).
• **Sex**: Affects males and females equally.
• **Diagnostic Delay**: Often a 5-10 year delay from symptom onset to diagnosis due to the insidious nature of the disease.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is often insidious, with patients or family members noticing a gradual change in appearance over many years.
• Patients may present due to a specific comorbidity (e.g., carpal tunnel syndrome, new-onset diabetes) or due to symptoms of the tumor's mass effect (headaches, vision changes).
• A classic patient complaint is an **increasing shoe, glove, or ring size**.
sections.diagnostics:
• The diagnostic approach is a two-step process: 1) Biochemical confirmation of GH excess, 2) Imaging to locate the source.
• **Initial Biochemical Test (Screening)**:
    ◦ **Serum IGF-1**: **Best initial test**.
        ▪ GH secretion is pulsatile, making random GH levels unreliable.
        ▪ IGF-1 levels are stable throughout the day and reflect the 24-hour integrated GH secretion.
        ▪ An elevated level, adjusted for age and sex, is highly suggestive of acromegaly.
• **Confirmatory Biochemical Test**:
    ◦ **Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT) with GH Measurement**: **Gold standard for confirmation**.
        ▪ **Procedure**: Patient ingests a 75g glucose load. GH levels are measured at baseline and at 30, 60, 90, and 120 minutes.
        ▪ **Normal Physiology**: Hyperglycemia (the glucose load) should suppress GH secretion to <1 ng/mL.
        ▪ **Acromegaly Result**: **Failure of GH to suppress** (<1 ng/mL) after a glucose load is diagnostic. GH levels paradoxically remain elevated or may even rise.
• **Other Laboratory Tests**:
    ◦ **Prolactin**: To check for co-secretion by the adenoma.
    ◦ **Fasting glucose, HbA1c**: To screen for diabetes.
    ◦ **Lipid panel**: To screen for dyslipidemia.
    ◦ **TSH, free T4, ACTH, cortisol, LH, FSH, testosterone/estradiol**: To assess for hypopituitarism due to tumor compression.
• **Imaging**:
    ◦ **MRI of the pituitary with gadolinium contrast**: **Imaging modality of choice** to visualize and characterize the pituitary adenoma once the biochemical diagnosis is made.
sections.prognosis:
• **Untreated**: Mortality is 2-3 times higher than the general population, primarily due to cardiovascular, respiratory, and neoplastic complications.
• **Treated**: With successful normalization of GH and IGF-1 levels, life expectancy can return to that of the general population.

sections.overview:
• A rare endocrine disorder characterized by abnormally high linear growth in children and adolescents
• Caused by excessive secretion of **Growth Hormone (GH)** *before* the fusion of the epiphyseal growth plates
    ◦ Results in proportional, accelerated growth, leading to exceptional height
    ◦ It is the childhood counterpart to **acromegaly**, which occurs after epiphyseal plate closure and results in enlargement of acral parts (hands, feet, jaw) without an increase in height
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Pituitary Adenoma (>95% of cases)**
        ▪ The most common cause is a benign, GH-secreting tumor of the anterior pituitary gland (**somatotroph adenoma**)
    ◦ **Genetic Syndromes (Rare)**
        ▪ **McCune-Albright Syndrome**: Characterized by café-au-lait spots, fibrous dysplasia of bone, and endocrine hyperfunction (including excess GH)
        ▪ **Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1 (MEN1)**: Tumors of the pituitary, parathyroid, and pancreas
        ▪ **Carney Complex**: A syndrome of pigmented skin lesions, myxomas, and endocrine tumors
        ▪ **Familial Isolated Pituitary Adenomas (FIPA)**: Genetic predisposition to pituitary adenomas without other features of MEN1 or Carney complex
    ◦ **Ectopic GHRH Production (Very Rare)**
        ▪ Tumors (e.g., pancreatic, lung) can produce Growth Hormone-Releasing Hormone (GHRH), which overstimulates the pituitary to produce GH
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **GH Overproduction**: A pituitary adenoma autonomously secretes excessive amounts of GH, bypassing the normal negative feedback regulation by somatostatin and IGF-1
    ◦ **IGF-1 Stimulation**: High levels of GH stimulate the liver to produce excessive amounts of Insulin-like Growth Factor 1 (IGF-1)
    ◦ **Growth Promotion**: Both GH and IGF-1 act on target tissues
        ▪ In a child with open epiphyseal plates, IGF-1 stimulates chondrocytes in the growth plates, leading to exaggerated longitudinal bone growth (linear growth)
    ◦ **Metabolic Effects**: Excess GH also has direct metabolic effects, including insulin antagonism (leading to **hyperglycemia**), lipolysis, and protein synthesis
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Extremely rare, estimated at 3-4 cases per million per year
• **Age of Onset**: By definition, occurs during childhood or adolescence
• **Sex/Race**: No significant predilection
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Classic presentation is a child or adolescent with **accelerated growth**, often crossing multiple height percentiles on growth charts
    ◦ Onset is insidious and may be mistaken for a simple "growth spurt"
• Patients may also present with symptoms related to the pituitary mass itself
    ◦ **Headaches**
    ◦ **Visual disturbances**
sections.diagnostics:
• A stepwise approach is crucial for diagnosis
• **Biochemical Screening (Initial Test)**
    ◦ **Serum Insulin-like Growth Factor 1 (IGF-1)**
        ▪ The single best screening test
        ▪ GH is secreted in a pulsatile fashion, making a single GH level unreliable
        ▪ IGF-1 levels are stable throughout the day and reflect 24-hour GH secretion
        ▪ An **elevated, age-adjusted IGF-1 level** is highly suggestive
    ◦ **Prolactin**
        ▪ Often co-secreted by pituitary adenomas
• **Biochemical Confirmation (Confirmatory Test)**
    ◦ **Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT) with GH measurement**
        ▪ This is the **gold standard** confirmatory test
        ▪ **Procedure**: Patient ingests a 75g glucose load. GH levels are measured at baseline and serially for 2 hours
        ▪ **Normal Physiology**: Glucose load *suppresses* GH secretion (<1 ng/mL)
        ▪ **Gigantism/Acromegaly**: GH levels **fail to suppress** and may paradoxically rise
• **Tumor Localization (Imaging)**
    ◦ **MRI of the pituitary with gadolinium contrast**
        ▪ The imaging modality of choice to identify and delineate the pituitary adenoma
• **Additional Labs**
    ◦ Assess for other pituitary hormone deficiencies or excesses (**hypopituitarism**) due to tumor compression: TSH, free T4, ACTH, cortisol, LH, FSH, testosterone/estradiol
    ◦ Fasting glucose, HbA1c (to screen for diabetes mellitus)
sections.prognosis:
• With early diagnosis and successful treatment to **normalize GH and IGF-1 levels**, life expectancy can approach that of the general population
• Persistent elevation of GH/IGF-1 levels is associated with a **2-3 fold increase in mortality**, primarily from cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease

sections.overview:
• A **prolactinoma** is a **benign tumor (adenoma)** of the lactotroph cells in the **anterior pituitary gland**.
• It is the most common type of hormone-secreting pituitary tumor.
• The primary pathophysiology involves the autonomous and excessive secretion of **prolactin (PRL)**, leading to a clinical syndrome of **hyperprolactinemia**, which manifests as **hypogonadism, galactorrhea**, and potential **mass effect symptoms**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Sporadic**: The vast majority of cases arise spontaneously with no known cause.
    ◦ **Genetic**: A small percentage are associated with **Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1 (MEN1)**, an autosomal dominant syndrome characterized by tumors of the pituitary, parathyroid, and pancreas (the "3 P's").
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Normal Regulation**: Prolactin secretion from the anterior pituitary is tonically **inhibited** by **dopamine** released from the hypothalamus into the hypophyseal portal system. Thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) can stimulate prolactin release.
    ◦ **Tumor Formation**: A clonal population of lactotroph cells forms an adenoma that secretes prolactin independent of normal hypothalamic control.
    ◦ **Effects of Hyperprolactinemia**
        ▪ **Suppression of GnRH**: High levels of prolactin suppress the pulsatile release of **Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH)** from the hypothalamus.
        ▪ **Hypogonadism**
            ◦ Decreased GnRH leads to decreased secretion of Luteinizing Hormone (LH) and Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH) from the pituitary.
            ◦ **In Females**: Leads to anovulation and decreased estrogen production, causing **amenorrhea or oligomenorrhea, infertility**, and vaginal dryness.
            ◦ **In Males**: Leads to decreased testosterone production, causing **decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, infertility**, and reduced muscle mass.
        ▪ **Galactorrhea**: Prolactin directly stimulates epithelial cells of the breast to produce milk.
    ◦ **Mass Effect**
        ▪ As the adenoma grows (especially **macroadenomas**, >1 cm), it can compress surrounding structures within the sella turcica.
        ▪ **Optic Chiasm Compression**: Classic cause of **bitemporal hemianopsia** (loss of peripheral vision in both visual fields).
        ▪ **Cavernous Sinus Invasion**: Can lead to cranial nerve palsies (CN III, IV, V1, V2, VI).
        ▪ **Headaches**: From stretching of the dura mater.
        ▪ **Hypopituitarism**: Compression of other hormone-producing pituitary cells.
sections.epidemiology:
• Most common type of **functioning pituitary adenoma**, accounting for ~40% of all cases.
• Prevalence is higher in women than in men (~10:1 ratio).
• Peak incidence occurs in women aged 20-50.
• **Presentation Difference**
    ◦ **Women** often present earlier with **microadenomas** (<1 cm) due to the noticeable symptoms of menstrual dysfunction.
    ◦ **Men** often present later with **macroadenomas** (>1 cm) as their symptoms (e.g., decreased libido) are more subtle and may be overlooked.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation depends on the patient's sex, age, and tumor size.
• **Premenopausal Females**: Typically present with the classic triad of **amenorrhea/oligomenorrhea, galactorrhea, and infertility**.
• **Males & Postmenopausal Females**: Presentation is often delayed and more subtle. They are more likely to present with symptoms of a **macroadenoma**.
    ◦ **Males**: **Decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, infertility**.
    ◦ **Mass Effect**: **Headaches, visual field defects**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **Serum Prolactin (PRL) Level**: The cornerstone of diagnosis.
        ▪ **Normal**: < 25 ng/mL
        ▪ **Mild Elevation (25-100 ng/mL)**: Can be caused by many factors (see differentials).
        ▪ **Moderate Elevation (100-200 ng/mL)**: Highly suspicious for prolactinoma.
        ▪ **Marked Elevation (>200 ng/mL)**: **Virtually diagnostic** of a prolactinoma. The level often correlates with tumor size.
    ◦ **Labs to Rule Out Other Causes**
        ▪ **Beta-hCG**: To rule out pregnancy.
        ▪ **TSH and Free T4**: To rule out primary hypothyroidism (high TRH can stimulate PRL).
        ▪ **BUN, Creatinine**: To rule out chronic kidney disease.
    ◦ **Hormonal Evaluation (especially for macroadenomas)**
        ▪ LH, FSH, Testosterone (males), Estradiol (females) to confirm hypogonadism.
        ▪ IGF-1, ACTH, morning cortisol to assess for other pituitary hormone deficiencies.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **MRI of the pituitary with and without gadolinium contrast**: The imaging modality of choice.
    ◦ Confirms the presence of an adenoma.
    ◦ Determines size (**micro-** vs. **macroadenoma**).
    ◦ Assesses for compression of the **optic chiasm** or invasion of the **cavernous sinus**.
• **Ophthalmic Evaluation**
    ◦ **Formal visual field testing (perimetry)**: Required for all patients with macroadenomas or any reported visual symptoms.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is generally **excellent**.
• Dopamine agonists are highly effective, normalizing PRL and shrinking the tumor in over 80-90% of patients.
• Surgical cure rates are high for microadenomas but lower for invasive macroadenomas.
• Recurrence is possible after stopping medical therapy or following surgery.

sections.overview:
• **Central Diabetes Insipidus (CDI)** is a condition characterized by the passage of large volumes of dilute urine (**polyuria**) and compensatory intense thirst (**polydipsia**).
• Caused by a deficiency in the synthesis or secretion of **Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH)** (arginine vasopressin/AVP) from the posterior pituitary gland.
• It is a disorder of **water balance**, not glucose metabolism, distinguishing it from Diabetes Mellitus.
• Without ADH, the collecting ducts of the kidneys are unable to reabsorb water, leading to massive free water loss.
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **ADH Deficiency**: The hypothalamus fails to produce ADH, or the posterior pituitary fails to store and release it.
    ◦ **Impaired Renal Water Reabsorption**: ADH normally acts on V2 receptors in the renal collecting ducts, promoting the insertion of aquaporin-2 water channels.
    ◦ **No ADH Signal**: Without ADH, aquaporin channels are not inserted, and the collecting ducts become impermeable to water.
    ◦ **Massive Water Loss**: Large volumes of dilute, hypotonic urine are excreted.
    ◦ **Compensatory Thirst**: Resulting hyperosmolality and hypernatremia stimulate the thirst center, causing intense **polydipsia**.
• **Etiologies**
    ◦ **Idiopathic/Autoimmune (~30-50%)**: Most common cause, often due to autoimmune destruction of ADH-producing cells.
    ◦ **Trauma**: Accidental head trauma or iatrogenic injury during neurosurgery (especially transsphenoidal pituitary surgery).
    ◦ **Tumors**
        ▪ **Primary**: **Craniopharyngioma** (common in children), pituitary adenoma, germinoma.
        ▪ **Metastatic**: Lung, breast, and leukemia/lymphoma are most common.
    ◦ **Infiltrative/Granulomatous Diseases**: **Sarcoidosis**, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, tuberculosis.
    ◦ **Vascular**: **Sheehan's syndrome** (postpartum pituitary necrosis), pituitary apoplexy, cerebral aneurysm, CVA.
    ◦ **Genetic/Familial**: Rare, typically autosomal dominant inheritance with mutations in the AVP gene.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Rare, affecting approximately 3 in 100,000 individuals.
• **Age**: Can occur at any age; etiology often varies by age group (e.g., craniopharyngioma in children, idiopathic/post-surgical in adults).
• **Sex**: No significant sex predilection.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is the abrupt onset of intense **polyuria** and **polydipsia**.
• The patient reports constant thirst and frequent urination day and night (**nocturia**).
• A key feature is a craving for **ice-cold water**.
• If the thirst mechanism is impaired or the patient lacks access to water, they can rapidly develop signs of severe **dehydration** and **hypernatremia** (e.g., altered mental status, lethargy, seizures).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Initial Lab Workup**
    ◦ **Serum Sodium**: High-normal to high (**Hypernatremia**, >145 mEq/L).
    ◦ **Serum Osmolality**: High (**>295 mOsm/kg**).
    ◦ **Urine Osmolality**: Inappropriately low (**<300 mOsm/kg**, often <100 mOsm/kg).
        ▪ The key finding is **low urine osmolality in the setting of high serum osmolality**.
    ◦ **Urine Specific Gravity**: Low (**<1.005**).
    ◦ **24-hour urine collection**: To quantify volume (>3L/day).
• **Water Deprivation Test (Confirms Diabetes Insipidus)**
    ◦ **Procedure**: Patient is deprived of all fluids; body weight, urine output, urine osmolality, and serum osmolality are measured serially. Test is stopped if patient loses >5% body weight, becomes hypotensive, or serum Na+ >145.
    ◦ **Normal Response**: ADH is released, urine becomes concentrated (Urine Osm >600 mOsm/kg).
    ◦ **DI Response (Central or Nephrogenic)**: Patient continues to produce large volumes of dilute urine despite rising serum osmolality; urine osmolality remains low (<300 mOsm/kg).
• **Desmopressin (DDAVP) Challenge Test (Differentiates Central vs. Nephrogenic DI)**
    ◦ **Procedure**: Performed after the water deprivation test confirms DI. Desmopressin (a synthetic ADH analog) is administered.
    ◦ **Central DI**
        ▪ The kidneys are responsive to ADH but are not receiving it; DDAVP provides the missing signal.
        ▪ **Result**: **Significant increase in urine osmolality (>50% increase)** and decrease in urine volume, confirming the diagnosis of CDI.
    ◦ **Nephrogenic DI**
        ▪ The kidneys are resistant to ADH.
        ▪ **Result**: No significant change in urine osmolality or urine volume.
• **Imaging**
