    ◦ **Brain MRI with contrast**: Indicated in all patients with a new diagnosis of CDI to evaluate the hypothalamus and pituitary for tumors, inflammation, or structural defects.
    ◦ A classic finding is the **absence of the posterior pituitary "bright spot"** on a T1-weighted image, which represents stored ADH.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is generally excellent with lifelong hormone replacement therapy.
• Patients can lead a normal life with normal life expectancy.
• The overall prognosis is often determined by the underlying cause of the CDI (e.g., prognosis is worse if caused by metastatic cancer).

sections.overview:
• **Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone (SIADH)** is a disorder of impaired water excretion caused by the inability to suppress the secretion of antidiuretic hormone (ADH), also known as arginine vasopressin (AVP).
    ◦ Excess ADH leads to increased **free water reabsorption** by the renal collecting ducts.
    ◦ This results in **dilutional hyponatremia**, decreased **serum osmolality**, and **inappropriately concentrated urine**, all in the setting of clinical **euvolemia**.
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Excess ADH Release**: ADH is either produced ectopically (e.g., by a tumor) or released excessively from the posterior pituitary.
    ◦ **Increased Water Reabsorption**: ADH acts on V2 receptors in the renal collecting ducts, increasing the insertion of aquaporin-2 water channels. This leads to a marked increase in free water reabsorption.
    ◦ **Volume Expansion & Natriuresis**: The initial water retention causes a transient, subclinical hypervolemia. This modest volume expansion triggers natriuretic peptides (ANP, BNP), which leads to increased urinary sodium excretion (**natriuresis**).
    ◦ **Euvolemic Hyponatremia**: The combination of water retention (dilution) and urinary sodium loss results in the hallmark state of **euvolemic hypotonic hyponatremia**.
• **Etiologies (Categorized)**
    ◦ **CNS Disorders**: Stroke, subarachnoid hemorrhage, trauma, infection (meningitis, encephalitis), hydrocephalus.
    ◦ **Pulmonary Disorders**
        ▪ **Cancers**: **Small Cell Lung Cancer (SCLC)** is the classic cause (ectopic ADH production).
        ▪ **Infections**: Pneumonia (especially Legionella), tuberculosis, lung abscesses.
    ◦ **Other Malignancies**: Pancreatic, prostate, bladder cancer; lymphomas, sarcomas.
    ◦ **Drugs**
        ▪ **SSRIs** (e.g., fluoxetine, sertraline)
        ▪ **Carbamazepine**, Oxcarbazepine
        ▪ **TCAs** (e.g., amitriptyline)
        ▪ **NSAIDs**
        ▪ Cyclophosphamide, Vincristine
        ▪ MDMA (Ecstasy)
    ◦ **Other Causes**: Post-operative state (pain/nausea are potent ADH stimuli), HIV infection, idiopathic.
sections.epidemiology:
• SIADH is the most common cause of **euvolemic hyponatremia** in hospitalized patients.
• Incidence increases with age, particularly in the elderly population due to polypharmacy and increased prevalence of underlying causes.
• Commonly seen in patients with underlying malignancy or CNS/pulmonary disease.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The clinical presentation is dictated by the **severity** and **acuity** (rate of decline) of the hyponatremia.
    ◦ Patients with chronic, mild hyponatremia may be **asymptomatic**.
    ◦ Patients with an acute, severe drop in sodium can present with life-threatening **neurologic symptoms**.
sections.diagnostics:
• The diagnosis of SIADH is based on meeting specific laboratory criteria after excluding other causes.
• **Essential Diagnostic Criteria**
    ◦ **Hypotonic Hyponatremia**
        ▪ **Serum Na+ < 135 mEq/L**
        ▪ **Serum Osmolality < 275 mOsm/kg**
    ◦ **Inappropriately Concentrated Urine**
        ▪ **Urine Osmolality > 100 mOsm/kg** (usually much higher, often > serum osmolality)
    ◦ **Elevated Urine Sodium**
        ▪ **Urine Na+ > 40 mEq/L** (with normal dietary salt intake)
    ◦ **Clinical Euvolemia**
        ▪ Assessed by physical exam.
    ◦ **Exclusion of Other Causes**
        ▪ Normal renal function (no CKD)
        ▪ Normal adrenal function (rule out adrenal insufficiency with cortisol level)
        ▪ Normal thyroid function (rule out hypothyroidism with TSH)
• **Additional Supportive Labs**
    ◦ **BUN**: Often low (<10 mg/dL) due to dilution.
    ◦ **Serum Uric Acid**: Often low (<4 mg/dL) due to increased urinary clearance.
    ◦ **Chest X-Ray**: To evaluate for pulmonary pathology (e.g., SCLC, pneumonia).
    ◦ **CT/MRI Head**: If a CNS cause is suspected.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is highly dependent on the underlying etiology.
• If SIADH is caused by a reversible factor (e.g., medication, resolving pneumonia), the prognosis is excellent with appropriate management.
• If caused by an underlying malignancy like **SCLC**, the prognosis is poor and dictated by the cancer itself.

sections.overview:
• **Hypopituitarism** is the partial or complete deficiency of one or more hormones secreted by the pituitary gland.
    ◦ It can involve hormones from the anterior pituitary (more common) or the posterior pituitary.
    ◦ Deficiency can be isolated to one hormone or involve multiple hormones.
    ◦ **Panhypopituitarism** refers to the deficiency of all anterior pituitary hormones.
    ◦ The clinical presentation is often insidious and varies widely depending on the specific hormones that are deficient and the acuity of onset.
sections.etiology:
• The underlying pathophysiology involves the destruction, compression, or functional impairment of pituitary tissue or the hypothalamus.
• **Etiologies (Categorized):**
    ◦ **Tumors (Most Common Cause):**
        ▪ **Pituitary Adenomas:** Both secretory and non-secretory adenomas can cause hypopituitarism through mass effect, compressing and destroying normal pituitary tissue.
        ▪ **Craniopharyngioma:** Suprasellar tumor, common in children.
        ▪ **Meningioma, Metastatic Tumors** (e.g., from breast, lung).
    ◦ **Vascular Events:**
        ▪ **Sheehan's Syndrome:** Postpartum pituitary necrosis caused by severe hypotension or shock during childbirth. The pituitary gland enlarges during pregnancy, making it vulnerable to ischemia.
        ▪ **Pituitary Apoplexy:** Acute hemorrhage or infarction into a pre-existing pituitary adenoma. Presents as a **"thunderclap headache,"** visual changes, and acute hypopituitarism. This is a medical emergency.
    ◦ **Iatrogenic:**
        ▪ **Pituitary Surgery:** Transsphenoidal surgery to remove an adenoma is a common cause.
        ▪ **Cranial Radiation:** Radiation therapy for pituitary, nasopharyngeal, or brain tumors can cause a delayed-onset hypopituitarism (months to years later).
    ◦ **Infiltrative / Inflammatory:**
        ▪ **Autoimmune (Lymphocytic) Hypophysitis:** Often occurs in late pregnancy or the postpartum period.
        ▪ **Sarcoidosis:** Granulomatous inflammation.
        ▪ **Hemochromatosis:** Iron deposition.
    ◦ **Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI):** Can cause damage to the pituitary stalk or gland.
    ◦ **Infections:** Tuberculosis, fungal infections, syphilis.
    ◦ **Congenital:** Rare genetic causes leading to pituitary hypoplasia.
• **Pathophysiologic Sequence of Hormone Loss:**
    ◦ There is a typical sequence in which pituitary hormones are lost due to mass effect: **GH → LH/FSH → TSH → ACTH → Prolactin**
    ◦ Mnemonic: **G**o **L**ook **F**or **T**he **A**denoma **P**lease
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** Approximately 45 cases per 100,000 people.
• **Incidence:** Approximately 4 new cases per 100,000 people per year.
• The condition is likely underdiagnosed due to its non-specific and gradual onset.
• The most common cause in adults is a pituitary adenoma or the treatment thereof (surgery/radiation).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is highly variable and depends on the specific hormone deficiencies, the patient's age and sex, and the acuity of onset.
• It is often a slow, insidious process.
• An acute presentation may occur with **pituitary apoplexy**.
sections.diagnostics:
• The workup involves a combination of basal hormone level testing, dynamic stimulation tests, and imaging.
• **Initial Lab Panel (Basal Levels):**
    ◦ **Cortisol Axis:** 8 AM serum cortisol and plasma ACTH. (Low cortisol with a low or inappropriately normal ACTH).
    ◦ **Thyroid Axis:** TSH and Free T4. (Low Free T4 with a low or inappropriately normal TSH).
    ◦ **Gonadal Axis:**
        ▪ Men: Total Testosterone, LH, FSH. (Low testosterone with low/normal LH/FSH).
        ▪ Premenopausal Women: Estradiol, LH, FSH (measured in early follicular phase). (Low estradiol with low/normal LH/FSH).
    ◦ **GH Axis:** Serum IGF-1 (Insulin-like Growth Factor-1). A low IGF-1 suggests GH deficiency.
    ◦ **Prolactin:** Can be low, normal, or even slightly elevated (if a stalk-compressing mass is present, which inhibits dopamine's suppression of prolactin).
• **Confirmatory Dynamic/Stimulation Testing (Gold Standard):**
    ◦ **ACTH Axis:**
        ▪ **Cosyntropin (ACTH) Stimulation Test:** A subnormal cortisol response confirms adrenal insufficiency.
        ▪ The **Insulin Tolerance Test (ITT)** is the gold standard for testing the entire HPA axis but is contraindicated in patients with seizure disorders or coronary artery disease.
    ◦ **GH Axis:**
        ▪ **Insulin Tolerance Test (ITT)** is the gold standard.
        ▪ A GHRH-arginine stimulation test is a safer alternative.
• **Imaging:**
    ◦ **MRI of the pituitary with and without contrast** is the imaging modality of choice to identify structural causes like adenomas, empty sella, or signs of apoplexy.
sections.prognosis:
• With appropriate diagnosis and lifelong hormone replacement therapy, the prognosis is generally excellent, and patients can have a normal life expectancy.
• Morbidity and mortality are increased if the condition is untreated or poorly managed, especially regarding adrenal insufficiency.
• Prognosis can also be influenced by the underlying cause (e.g., a malignant tumor).

sections.overview:
• Endocrine disorder characterized by the excessive and inappropriate secretion of **parathyroid hormone (PTH)** from one or more parathyroid glands
    ◦ Leads to dysregulation of calcium and phosphate metabolism, resulting in **hypercalcemia** and **hypophosphatemia**
• Most common cause of **hypercalcemia** in the outpatient setting
• While many patients are asymptomatic, classic presentations can involve renal, skeletal, gastrointestinal, and neuropsychiatric manifestations
• The definitive treatment is surgical removal of the affected gland(s)
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects approximately 1 in 800 people
• Most common cause of **hypercalcemia** in the **outpatient/ambulatory setting**
    ◦ **Malignancy** is the most common cause in the **inpatient setting**
• **Peak Incidence**: 50-60 years of age
• **Gender**: Affects women 2-3 times more often than men, particularly postmenopausal women
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The majority of patients (~80%) in developed countries are **asymptomatic**
    ◦ Often diagnosed incidentally after a high calcium level is found on routine laboratory testing
• Symptomatic presentation is related to the effects of chronic **hypercalcemia**
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** prognosis following successful **parathyroidectomy**
    ◦ Bone mineral density often improves significantly post-surgery
    ◦ Risk of fractures and kidney stones is reduced
    ◦ Neuropsychiatric symptoms may improve
• For patients managed medically, the prognosis is generally good but requires lifelong monitoring for the development of complications

sections.overview:
• **Secondary hyperparathyroidism (sHPT)** is a condition characterized by the excessive secretion of **parathyroid hormone (PTH)** by the parathyroid glands in response to an underlying disease process, most commonly **hypocalcemia** or **hyperphosphatemia**.
    ◦ Unlike primary hyperparathyroidism where the gland itself is autonomous, in sHPT the glands are functioning correctly but are being **overstimulated**.
• The most common cause is **Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)**, leading to a constellation of findings known as **CKD-Mineral and Bone Disorder (CKD-MBD)**.
sections.etiology:
• The pathophysiology is a compensatory mechanism that becomes maladaptive over time.
• **Chronic Kidney Disease (Most Common Cause)**
    ◦ **Phosphate Retention**: As **Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)** falls, the kidneys are unable to excrete phosphate effectively, leading to **hyperphosphatemia**.
        ▪ High phosphate levels directly stimulate the parathyroid glands to secrete **PTH**.
        ▪ **Hyperphosphatemia** also complexes with calcium in the serum, effectively lowering ionized calcium levels.
    ◦ **Impaired Vitamin D Activation**: The kidneys are responsible for converting 25-hydroxyvitamin D into its active form, **1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol)**, via the enzyme 1-alpha-hydroxylase. In CKD, this enzyme's activity is reduced.
    ◦ **Resulting Hypocalcemia**
        ▪ Decreased calcitriol leads to decreased intestinal absorption of calcium.
        ▪ The combination of these factors results in **hypocalcemia**.
    ◦ **Parathyroid Gland Response**
        ▪ **Hypocalcemia** is the most potent stimulus for **PTH** secretion.
        ▪ **Hyperphosphatemia** directly stimulates **PTH** secretion.
        ▪ Low calcitriol levels reduce the normal negative feedback on the parathyroid glands.
    ◦ **Net Effect**: The parathyroid glands undergo hyperplasia and continuously secrete high levels of **PTH** in an attempt to normalize calcium and phosphate by increasing bone resorption and trying to stimulate the kidneys.
• **Other Causes (Non-Renal)**
    ◦ **Severe Vitamin D Deficiency**: Inadequate sunlight exposure, poor dietary intake, or fat malabsorption (e.g., celiac disease, Crohn's disease, bariatric surgery) leads to decreased intestinal calcium absorption, causing **hypocalcemia** and a subsequent rise in **PTH**.
    ◦ **Malabsorption Syndromes**: Any condition that impairs calcium absorption can lead to chronic **hypocalcemia** and sHPT.
sections.epidemiology:
• Highly prevalent in patients with **Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)**.
• The prevalence increases as **GFR** declines.
• Affects ~30-50% of patients with moderate CKD (Stage 3/4).
• Affects >90% of patients with **End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD)** on dialysis.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Often **asymptomatic** in early stages, with diagnosis made on routine laboratory screening in CKD patients.
• Symptoms, when present, are often related to the underlying CKD (fatigue, edema) or the long-term effects of high **PTH** on the skeletal and vascular systems.
• The clinical picture is dominated by **renal osteodystrophy**, the term for bone disease associated with CKD.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Laboratory Findings are KEY for diagnosis.**
    ◦ **Classic Lab Profile**
        ▪ **PTH** (Parathyroid Hormone): Markedly elevated.
        ▪ **Low or Normal Serum Calcium**: The body's compensatory PTH response may keep calcium in the low-normal range, but the initial driver is **hypocalcemia**.
        ▪ **High Serum Phosphate**: A hallmark finding in CKD-related sHPT.
    ◦ **Other Important Labs**
        ▪ **Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP)**: Elevated due to high bone turnover.
        ▪ **Low 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (Calcitriol)**: Due to impaired renal activation.
        ▪ Low or normal 25-hydroxyvitamin D (storage form).
        ▪ **Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP)** to assess renal function (**BUN**, **Creatinine**, **GFR**).
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **X-rays**: Essential for evaluating **renal osteodystrophy**.
        ▪ **Subperiosteal bone resorption**: **Pathognomonic finding**. Best seen on the radial aspect of the middle phalanges of the 2nd and 3rd fingers. Also seen in the distal clavicles and medial tibia.
        ▪ **"Salt-and-pepper" skull**: Granular, demineralized appearance of the calvarium.
        ▪ **Osteitis fibrosa cystica**: Severe form with **"brown tumors"** (lytic bone lesions filled with fibrous tissue and osteoclasts) and bone cysts.
        ▪ **Rugger-jersey spine**: Sclerotic bands at the vertebral endplates.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is directly tied to the management of the underlying **CKD** and the control of mineral metabolism.
• Poorly controlled sHPT is associated with a significantly increased risk of **fractures**, **cardiovascular events**, and **mortality**.
• Effective management can improve bone health and reduce cardiovascular risk, but morbidity remains high in the **ESRD** population.

sections.overview:
• Hypoparathyroidism is an endocrine disorder characterized by deficient secretion or action of Parathyroid Hormone (PTH)
    ◦ The lack of PTH leads to the hallmark biochemical abnormalities of **hypocalcemia** and **hyperphosphatemia**
    ◦ The clinical manifestations are primarily due to the neuromuscular and cardiac effects of low serum calcium
    ◦ The most common cause is iatrogenic, resulting from damage to or removal of the parathyroid glands during neck surgery
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ PTH is the primary regulator of calcium and phosphate homeostasis. Its main actions are:
        ▪ **Bone:** Stimulates osteoclast activity, leading to bone resorption and release of calcium and phosphate into the circulation
        ▪ **Kidney:**
            ◦ Increases reabsorption of calcium in the distal convoluted tubule
            ◦ Decreases reabsorption of phosphate in the proximal tubule, promoting its excretion
            ◦ Stimulates the enzyme 1-alpha-hydroxylase, which converts inactive 25-hydroxyvitamin D to its active form, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol)
        ▪ **Intestine (Indirectly):** Active Vitamin D (calcitriol) increases the absorption of dietary calcium and phosphate from the gut
    ◦ In hypoparathyroidism, the absence or deficiency of PTH leads to:
        ▪ **Bone Resorption:** Decreased release of calcium from bones
        ▪ **Renal Calcium Reabsorption:** Increased urinary calcium loss
        ▪ **Vitamin D Activation:** Inability to convert 25-hydroxyvitamin D to active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D
        ▪ **Renal Phosphate Reabsorption:** Decreased urinary phosphate excretion
    ◦ The net result is **hypocalcemia** and **hyperphosphatemia**
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Acquired (Most Common):**
        ▪ **Post-Surgical:** Iatrogenic damage or inadvertent removal of parathyroid glands during thyroidectomy, parathyroidectomy, or radical neck dissection. This accounts for ~75% of cases.
        ▪ **Autoimmune:** Isolated or as part of Autoimmune Polyglandular Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1), which also includes adrenal insufficiency and mucocutaneous candidiasis
        ▪ **Radiation-Induced:** Damage from external beam radiation to the neck for malignancies
        ▪ **Infiltrative Diseases:** Hemochromatosis (iron), Wilson's disease (copper), granulomatous disease, or metastatic cancer
        ▪ **Functional Hypoparathyroidism:** Severe **hypomagnesemia** (<1.0 mg/dL) impairs PTH secretion and causes end-organ resistance to PTH
    ◦ **Congenital / Genetic:**
        ▪ **DiGeorge Syndrome (22q11.2 deletion syndrome):** Agenesis or dysgenesis of the parathyroid glands. Associated with classic **CATCH-22** findings:
            ◦ **C**ardiac defects
            ◦ **A**bnormal facies
            ◦ **T**hymic aplasia
            ◦ **C**left palate
            ◦ **H**ypocalcemia/Hypoparathyroidism
sections.epidemiology:
• The most common cause is post-surgical, occurring in up to 30% of patients transiently after total thyroidectomy and 1-3% permanently
• Prevalence of non-surgical hypoparathyroidism is rare
• Autoimmune causes are more common in children and young adults
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation depends on the severity and acuity of the hypocalcemia
    ◦ A patient may present acutely, often days after neck surgery, with classic signs of neuromuscular excitability
    ◦ Chronic cases may be more subtle, with psychiatric, dermatologic, or neurologic complaints
• **Typical Vignette:**
    ◦ A 45-year-old female presents to the ED 3 days after a total thyroidectomy complaining of tingling around her mouth and in her fingertips. She also reports muscle cramps in her hands and feet.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Laboratory Trio (Hallmark Findings):**
    ◦ **Serum Calcium:** Both total and ionized calcium are low
    ◦ **Serum Phosphate:** Increased due to decreased renal excretion
    ◦ **Intact PTH:** Level is low or inappropriately normal in the setting of hypocalcemia
• **Other Essential Labs:**
    ◦ **Serum Magnesium:** **MUST** be checked to rule out hypomagnesemia as the cause
    ◦ **BUN and Creatinine:** To assess renal function and rule out CKD
    ◦ **Vitamin D levels (25-hydroxyvitamin D):** To assess for concurrent deficiency
• **Electrocardiogram (EKG):**
    ◦ **Prolonged QT interval** is the classic finding, which predisposes to ventricular arrhythmias like **Torsades de Pointes**
• **Urinalysis:**
    ◦ **Low 24-hour urinary calcium excretion** is expected due to the lack of PTH-driven calcium reabsorption and overall low serum calcium
sections.prognosis:
• With appropriate treatment and lifelong monitoring, the prognosis is generally good
• Patients may experience a reduced quality of life compared to the general population
• Morbidity and mortality are related to acute complications (arrhythmias, seizures) or long-term complications of therapy (renal failure)

sections.overview:
• Hypercalcemia is an electrolyte abnormality defined as an elevated calcium level in the blood. 
    ◦ Total serum calcium is typically >10.5 mg/dL, or ionized calcium is >5.25 mg/dL.
• It is a relatively common clinical finding.
• Because a significant portion of calcium is bound to albumin, the total calcium level must be corrected for albumin concentration, especially in hypoalbuminemic patients.
    ◦ **Corrected Calcium Formula:** `Corrected Calcium (mg/dL) = Measured Total Ca (mg/dL) + 0.8 * (4.0 - Serum Albumin [g/dL])`
• Mild hypercalcemia is often asymptomatic and discovered incidentally, while severe elevations can be life-threatening.
• The clinical approach is centered on confirming the diagnosis, determining the underlying etiology, and treating based on the severity and symptoms.
sections.etiology:
• The causes of hypercalcemia are broadly divided into two categories: **PTH-mediated** and **non-PTH-mediated**.
    ◦ This distinction is the most critical step in the diagnostic workup.
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects approximately 1-4% of the general population.
• **Primary hyperparathyroidism** is the most frequent cause in ambulatory patients, with a peak incidence in postmenopausal women (women > men, age > 50).
• **Malignancy** is the most common cause in hospitalized patients.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation ranges from asymptomatic (found on routine labs) to a life-threatening medical emergency (hypercalcemic crisis).
• The severity of symptoms depends on both the absolute calcium level and the rate of its rise. 
    ◦ A rapid rise causes more severe symptoms.
• The classic mnemonic for symptoms is: **"Stones, Bones, Groans, Thrones, and Psychiatric Overtones."**
sections.diagnostics:
• The workup is a stepwise process to confirm hypercalcemia and then identify the underlying cause.
• **1. Confirm Hypercalcemia**
    ◦ Repeat serum total calcium.
    ◦ Check serum albumin and calculate **corrected calcium**.
    ◦ If albumin is abnormal or diagnosis is unclear, check **ionized calcium** (the gold standard).
• **2. Determine the Etiology (The Key Step)**
    ◦ Measure an **intact PTH level**. 
        ▪ This is the most important test to differentiate between PTH-mediated and non-PTH-mediated causes.
• **3. Interpret PTH and Subsequent Tests**
    ◦ **If PTH is High or Inappropriately Normal:**
        ▪ **Diagnosis is likely Primary Hyperparathyroidism or FHH.**
        ▪ **Next Step:** Check **24-hour urine calcium**.
            • **High or Normal (>200 mg/24h):** Consistent with **Primary Hyperparathyroidism**.
            • **Low (<100 mg/24h):** Suggests **FHH**. Calculate calcium/creatinine clearance ratio (CCCR). A CCCR <0.01 is highly suggestive of FHH.
    ◦ **If PTH is Low (<20 pg/mL):**
        ▪ **Diagnosis is Non-PTH-Mediated.** The parathyroid glands are appropriately suppressed.
        ▪ **Next Steps (workup for malignancy/other causes):**
            • **PTH-related peptide (PTHrP):** If elevated, strongly suggests humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy.
            • **Vitamin D levels:** Check 25-hydroxyvitamin D (for intoxication) and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (elevated in granulomatous disease/lymphoma).
            • **Serum and Urine Protein Electrophoresis (SPEP/UPEP):** To screen for multiple myeloma.
            • **Imaging:** Chest X-ray or CT to look for malignancy or sarcoidosis.
            • **TSH:** To rule out thyrotoxicosis.
sections.prognosis:
• **Primary Hyperparathyroidism:** Prognosis is excellent following successful parathyroidectomy.
• **Hypercalcemia of Malignancy:** Prognosis is generally poor, as it often signifies advanced-stage cancer.
    ◦ Median survival is often measured in months.
• **Other causes:** Prognosis depends on the successful treatment of the underlying condition.

sections.overview:
• Hypocalcemia is a low level of calcium in the blood.
    ◦ Defined as a total serum calcium level of **<8.5 mg/dL** or an ionized calcium level of **<4.65 mg/dL**.
    ◦ Total calcium must be corrected for low albumin states as a significant portion is albumin-bound.
        ▪ **Corrected Calcium Formula:** `Corrected Ca = Measured Ca + 0.8 * (4.0 - measured albumin)`
    ◦ Ionized calcium is the physiologically active form and the most accurate measure of calcium status.
    ◦ Pathophysiology is based on increased neuromuscular excitability.
sections.etiology:
• Causes are categorized by Parathyroid Hormone (PTH) and Vitamin D regulation.
• **Hypoparathyroidism (Low PTH)**
    ◦ **Post-Surgical**: **Most common cause**, due to accidental removal or damage to parathyroid glands during neck surgery (e.g., thyroidectomy).
    ◦ **Autoimmune**: Autoimmune destruction of the parathyroid glands.
    ◦ **Congenital**: E.g., DiGeorge Syndrome (22q11.2 deletion) with parathyroid hypoplasia.
    ◦ **Hypomagnesemia**: **Crucial** cause; low magnesium impairs PTH secretion and induces end-organ resistance to PTH. Hypocalcemia is refractory to treatment until magnesium is corrected.
• **High PTH (Secondary Hyperparathyroidism)**
    ◦ **Vitamin D Deficiency**: Inadequate intake, malabsorption, or lack of sun exposure leads to decreased intestinal calcium absorption, with a compensatory increase in PTH.
    ◦ **Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)**: **Second most common cause**. Kidneys fail to convert vitamin D to its active form (calcitriol), and hyperphosphatemia binds serum calcium.
    ◦ **Pseudohypoparathyroidism**: End-organ resistance to PTH due to a genetic defect. Labs show high PTH but hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia.
• **Other Causes**
    ◦ **Calcium Chelation/Deposition**
        ▪ **Hyperphosphatemia**: Phosphate binds calcium (e.g., tumor lysis syndrome, rhabdomyolysis).
        ▪ **Acute Pancreatitis**: Free fatty acids chelate calcium (saponification).
        ▪ **Massive Blood Transfusion**: Citrate anticoagulant chelates calcium.
        ▪ **Hungry Bone Syndrome**: After parathyroidectomy, bones rapidly take up calcium and phosphate.
    ◦ **Medications**
        ▪ **Loop Diuretics** (e.g., Furosemide): Increase urinary calcium excretion.
        ▪ **Bisphosphonates, Denosumab**: Inhibit osteoclast activity.
        ▪ **Phenytoin, Phenobarbital**: Accelerate Vitamin D metabolism.
    ◦ **Critical Illness/Sepsis**: Multifactorial etiology.
sections.epidemiology:
• Common in hospitalized patients, affecting up to 70-80% of those in the ICU.
• The **most common outpatient cause** is **post-surgical hypoparathyroidism**.
• High prevalence in patients with **Chronic Kidney Disease** and **Vitamin D deficiency**.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Recent thyroid, parathyroid, or radical neck surgery**
• **Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)**
• **Vitamin D deficiency** (malnutrition, malabsorption, low sun exposure)
• **Alcoholism** (associated with hypomagnesemia)
• **Malabsorption syndromes** (Crohn's disease, celiac disease, short bowel syndrome)
• History of **pancreatitis**
• **Sepsis** or critical illness
• Recipient of **multiple blood transfusions**
• Use of **loop diuretics, bisphosphonates**, or certain anticonvulsants
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation depends on the severity and acuity of the calcium drop.
    ◦ Chronic, mild hypocalcemia may be asymptomatic.
    ◦ A rapid decrease causes dramatic neuromuscular symptoms.
• **Classic Presentation**
    ◦ **Perioral numbness**, **paresthesias** of the hands and feet, and **muscle cramps**.
• **Severe Presentation**
    ◦ **Tetany**, **seizures**, or **laryngospasm**.
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ **Neuromuscular (Most Common)**
        ▪ **Paresthesias**, especially **perioral** and in fingertips/toes.
        ▪ **Muscle cramps** and spasms, especially in the back and lower extremities.
        ▪ **Tetany**: Severe, painful carpopedal spasms (flexion of wrist and MCP joints, extension of IP joints, adduction of thumb).
        ▪ **Laryngospasm**: Can cause stridor and airway obstruction.
    ◦ **Central Nervous System**
        ▪ **Seizures** (focal or generalized).
        ▪ Confusion, irritability, depression.
        ▪ Fatigue.
    ◦ **Cardiovascular**
        ▪ Palpitations, arrhythmias.
        ▪ Hypotension.
        ▪ Signs of congestive heart failure (decreased contractility).
    ◦ **Dermatologic (Chronic)**
        ▪ Dry, coarse skin.
        ▪ Brittle nails.
        ▪ Eczema, psoriasis.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Chvostek's Sign**: Tapping on the facial nerve causes ipsilateral facial muscle contraction (twitching of nose or lip). Less specific.
• **Trousseau's Sign**: Inflating a blood pressure cuff above systolic pressure for 3 minutes induces a **carpal spasm** ("main d'accoucheur"). **More specific** than Chvostek's sign.
• Hyperreflexia / brisk Deep Tendon Reflexes (DTRs).
• **Tetany** (spontaneous carpopedal spasms).
• Possible papilledema (in severe, chronic cases).
• Auscultation may reveal gallops or signs of heart failure.
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.management:
• **Monitoring**: Regularly monitor serum calcium, albumin, magnesium, and phosphate levels during treatment.
• **Address the Underlying Cause**: Definitive management is to treat the root cause (e.g., Vitamin D repletion, managing CKD).
• **Patient Education**: Counsel on the importance of adherence to supplements. For post-surgical patients, educate on the signs/symptoms of hypocalcemia.
• **Dietary**: Encourage intake of calcium-rich foods (dairy, fortified foods, leafy greens).
sections.complications:
• **Laryngospasm**: Can lead to acute airway obstruction and respiratory arrest.
• **Seizures**: Can lead to injury or status epilepticus.
• **Cardiac Arrhythmias**: Prolonged QT can lead to **Torsades de pointes** and sudden cardiac death.
• **Congestive Heart Failure**: Due to negative inotropic effects.
• **Cataracts**: Associated with chronic hypocalcemia.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is generally excellent if the condition is identified and treated promptly.
• Long-term prognosis depends on the reversibility and management of the underlying etiology.
• Chronic hypoparathyroidism requires lifelong supplementation and monitoring.

sections.overview:
• Systemic skeletal disease characterized by **low bone mass** and **microarchitectural deterioration** of bone tissue, leading to enhanced bone fragility and a consequent increase in fracture risk.
    ◦ It is the most common metabolic bone disease.
    ◦ The primary defect is an imbalance between bone resorption (by **osteoclasts**) and bone formation (by **osteoblasts**), resulting in a net loss of bone.
    ◦ A diagnosis is made based on:
        ▪ **Bone mineral density (BMD)** measurements.
        ▪ The presence of a **fragility fracture**.
sections.etiology:
• Bone remodeling is a continuous process involving **osteoclasts** (resorption) and **osteoblasts** (formation).
• Osteoporosis results when resorption outpaces formation.
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects over 10 million Americans, with another 44 million having low bone density (osteopenia).
• **1 in 2 women** and **1 in 4 men** over age 50 will sustain an osteoporosis-related fracture.
• **Postmenopausal Caucasian and Asian women** are at the highest risk.
• **Hip fractures** are a major cause of morbidity and mortality in the elderly.
    ◦ The 1-year mortality rate is as high as 20-30%.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Osteoporosis is a **"silent disease."**
• It is typically asymptomatic until a **fragility fracture** occurs.
    ◦ A **fragility fracture** is one that occurs from a fall from standing height or less, or with minimal to no trauma.
• Common fracture sites:
    ◦ **Vertebral bodies**
    ◦ **Femoral neck (hip)**
    ◦ **Distal radius (Colles' fracture)**
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• With early diagnosis and treatment, bone loss can be slowed or stabilized, significantly reducing fracture risk.
• The prognosis worsens dramatically after a major **fragility fracture**.
• Approximately 20-30% of patients who suffer a **hip fracture** die within one year.
    ◦ Less than half regain their previous level of function.

sections.overview:
• **Osteomalacia** is a metabolic bone disease characterized by the **inadequate or delayed mineralization of osteoid** in mature cortical and cancellous bone.
• It is the adult equivalent of **Rickets**.
• The core defect is a softening of the bones, leading to bone pain, muscle weakness, and an increased risk of fractures.
• This is distinct from **Osteoporosis**, where bone matrix and mineral are lost proportionally, resulting in decreased bone mass but normal mineralization.
• Comparison with Osteoporosis:
    ◦ **Osteomalacia**
        ▪ **Primary Defect**: **Impaired Mineralization** of osteoid
        ▪ **Bone Quality**: Soft, flexible bones
        ▪ **Key Labs**: ↓ Ca, ↓ PO4, ↑ ALP, ↑ PTH
    ◦ **Osteoporosis**
        ▪ **Primary Defect**: **Decreased Bone Mass**
        ▪ **Bone Quality**: Brittle, porous bones
        ▪ **Key Labs**: Labs typically normal
sections.etiology:
• The fundamental cause of osteomalacia is a deficiency in the building blocks required for bone mineralization, primarily **calcium** and **phosphate**.
• The most common cause is **severe Vitamin D deficiency**.
• **Pathophysiology Cascade**:
    ◦ **Vitamin D Deficiency**: Caused by inadequate sun exposure, insufficient dietary intake, or malabsorption.
    ◦ **Decreased Calcium & Phosphate Absorption**: Vitamin D is essential for the intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate. Its absence leads to hypocalcemia and hypophosphatemia.
    ◦ **Hypocalcemia Stimulates PTH**: The parathyroid glands respond to low serum calcium by increasing the secretion of **Parathyroid Hormone (PTH)**, leading to **secondary hyperparathyroidism**.
    ◦ **PTH Effects**:
        ▪ **Bones**: Increases bone resorption (osteoclast activity) to release calcium and phosphate into the blood.
        ▪ **Kidneys**:
            • Increases calcium reabsorption.
            • **Increases phosphate excretion (worsens hypophosphatemia)**. This is a key step.
            • Stimulates the conversion of 25-hydroxyvitamin D to its active form, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol), in an attempt to increase intestinal Ca absorption.
    ◦ **Defective Mineralization**: Despite the body's compensatory efforts, the persistent low serum phosphate and inadequate calcium levels prevent the proper mineralization of newly laid down bone matrix (osteoid). Osteoblasts continue to produce osteoid, but it remains unmineralized, resulting in "soft bones."
• **Major Causes**:
    ◦ **Vitamin D Deficiency**:
        ▪ **Inadequate Sunlight**: Elderly, institutionalized, homebound individuals; northern latitudes.
        ▪ **Dietary Insufficiency**: Lack of fortified foods, strict veganism.
        ▪ **Malabsorption**: Celiac disease, Crohn's disease, gastric bypass, pancreatitis.
        ▪ **Dark Skin Pigmentation**: Melanin acts as a natural sunblock, reducing cutaneous vitamin D synthesis.
    ◦ **Impaired Vitamin D Metabolism**:
        ▪ **Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)**: Kidneys cannot convert 25(OH)D to the active 1,25(OH)2D (calcitriol).
        ▪ **Liver Disease**: Impaired initial hydroxylation to 25(OH)D.
        ▪ **Medications**: Anticonvulsants (e.g., **phenytoin, phenobarbital, carbamazepine**) accelerate the breakdown of vitamin D.
    ◦ **Renal Phosphate Wasting**:
        ▪ Fanconi syndrome, inherited hypophosphatemic rickets.
sections.epidemiology:
• Prevalence is highest in regions with limited sun exposure and among specific populations.
• Commonly affects the **elderly**, particularly those who are **institutionalized or homebound**.
• Higher prevalence in individuals from the Middle East, Northern China, and India due to skin pigmentation and clothing that limits sun exposure.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • A typical patient is an older, homebound adult who presents with a gradual onset of **diffuse bone pain**, **proximal muscle weakness**, and a **waddling gait**. They may have a history of recent falls or a low-trauma fracture. The pain is often described as a dull ache, worse with activity and pressure.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Laboratory Findings (Hallmark Pattern)**:
    ◦ **Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D]**: **Best initial test** to confirm deficiency.
        ▪ Deficiency: <20 ng/mL
        ▪ Insufficiency: 20-29 ng/mL
    ◦ **Serum Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP)**: A very sensitive and common finding, reflecting increased osteoblastic activity.
    ◦ **Serum Parathyroid Hormone (PTH)**: Reflects **secondary hyperparathyroidism**.
    ◦ **Serum Calcium (Hypocalcemia)**: May be normal in early stages due to PTH compensation.
    ◦ **Serum Phosphate (Hypophosphatemia)**: A key finding, driven by PTH-induced renal excretion.
    ◦ **Urine Calcium**: Decreased excretion as the body attempts to conserve calcium.
• **Imaging (X-ray)**:
    ◦ **Pseudofractures (Looser Zones)**:
        ▪ **Pathognomonic finding**.
        ▪ Thin, transverse lucencies running perpendicular to the cortex, often bilateral and symmetric.
        ▪ **Common locations**: Femoral neck, pubic rami, ribs, scapula.
    ◦ Generalized bone demineralization (osteopenia), making it difficult to distinguish from osteoporosis on X-ray alone.
    ◦ **"Codfish vertebrae"**: Biconcave appearance of vertebral bodies due to softening.
• **Bone Biopsy**:
    ◦ **Gold Standard** but rarely performed due to its invasive nature.
    ◦ Shows a widened, unmineralized osteoid seam and increased osteoid volume.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** with appropriate and timely treatment.
• Muscle strength and bone pain typically begin to improve within a few weeks to months.
• Radiologic evidence of healing of pseudofractures can be seen within 2-3 months.
• Skeletal deformities may be permanent in long-standing, severe cases.

sections.overview:
• **Paget disease of bone (osteitis deformans)** is a chronic, focal disorder of bone remodeling that affects older adults.
    ◦ Characterized by an initial phase of excessive bone resorption by hyperactive **osteoclasts**, followed by a compensatory but disorganized and excessive phase of new bone formation by **osteoblasts**.
    ◦ This process results in bone that is **enlarged, structurally weak, highly vascular**, and prone to deformity, pain, fractures, and other complications.
    ◦ While classified under endocrine topics due to its effects on bone metabolism, it is not a primary disorder of calcium, phosphate, or parathyroid hormone regulation.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• **Age**: Primarily affects adults > **55 years old**; rare before age 40.
• **Gender**: Slightly more common in men (**Male:Female ratio 3:2**).
• **Geography**: High prevalence in populations of **Anglo-Saxon descent** (UK, Australia, New Zealand, USA).
    ◦ It is rare in individuals from Asia and Africa.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Largely Asymptomatic**: Over 70% of patients are asymptomatic.
• The disease is often discovered as an **incidental finding** due to:
    ◦ Markedly elevated serum **alkaline phosphatase** on routine blood work.
    ◦ Characteristic findings on an X-ray performed for another reason.
• Symptomatic presentation depends on the location and extent of skeletal involvement.
    ◦ The **pelvis, femur, lumbar spine, skull, and tibia** are most commonly affected.
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• The overall prognosis is **good**, and most individuals have a normal life expectancy.
• Morbidity is primarily related to the development of complications like fractures, deformity, and neurologic impairment.
• The prognosis is extremely poor if **osteosarcoma** develops.

sections.overview:
• A group of metabolic disorders characterized by abnormally elevated levels of lipids (e.g., cholesterol, triglycerides) in the blood
• A major modifiable risk factor for the development of **atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD)**
• Typically **asymptomatic** and identified through routine blood screening
• Management focuses on lifestyle modifications and pharmacotherapy (primarily **statins**) to reduce cardiovascular event risk
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Primary (Familial) Hyperlipidemia**
        ▪ Caused by genetic mutations affecting lipoprotein metabolism
        ▪ **Familial Hypercholesterolemia (FH)**: Most common; autosomal dominant mutation in the **LDL receptor gene**, leading to decreased LDL clearance and extremely high **LDL-C** levels from birth
        ▪ **Familial Combined Hyperlipidemia (FCHL)**: Autosomal dominant; characterized by elevated **LDL-C**, **triglycerides (TGs)**, or both due to hepatic overproduction of VLDL
        ▪ **Dysbetalipoproteinemia (Familial Type III)**: Autosomal recessive; defect in Apolipoprotein E (ApoE) causing accumulation of cholesterol-rich VLDL and chylomicron remnants, presenting with elevated TC and TGs
    ◦ **Secondary (Acquired) Hyperlipidemia**
        ▪ The most common cause in adults, resulting from underlying conditions, medications, or lifestyle
        ▪ **Lifestyle**: High saturated/trans fat diet, obesity, sedentary lifestyle, excessive alcohol
        ▪ **Medical Conditions**
            • **Hypothyroidism**: Decreased LDL receptor activity leads to elevated **LDL-C**
            • **Diabetes Mellitus (Type 2)**: Insulin resistance causes increased VLDL production and decreased clearance, leading to high **TGs** and low HDL
            • **Nephrotic Syndrome**: Increased hepatic lipoprotein synthesis and decreased catabolism lead to high TC and LDL
            • **Cholestatic Liver Disease**: Impaired bile excretion elevates cholesterol
        ▪ **Medications**: Thiazide diuretics, beta-blockers, glucocorticoids, protease inhibitors, atypical antipsychotics
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ Imbalance in the production, processing, and clearance of lipoproteins (VLDL, LDL, HDL)
    ◦ Elevated **atherogenic lipoproteins (primarily LDL)** deposit in the arterial intima, initiating an inflammatory cascade
    ◦ This leads to foam cells, fatty streaks, and eventually complex **atherosclerotic plaques**
    ◦ Plaque rupture can cause thrombosis, leading to **MI** or **stroke**
    ◦ Severe hypertriglyceridemia can cause **acute pancreatitis** through the production of toxic free fatty acids
sections.epidemiology:
• Extremely common in the United States and developed countries
• Approximately 50% of US adults have elevated **LDL-C**
• Prevalence increases with age
• **Familial Hypercholesterolemia** affects approximately 1 in 250 individuals
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Overwhelmingly asymptomatic**
• Most often detected on routine screening via a lipid panel
• Symptoms, when present, are typically due to complications (e.g., angina from CAD) or extremely high lipid levels
sections.diagnostics:
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **Fasting Lipid Panel (9-12 hours)**: The primary diagnostic tool
        ▪ **Total Cholesterol (TC)**: Desirable <200 mg/dL
        ▪ **Low-Density Lipoprotein (LDL-C)**: "Bad cholesterol"; main target of therapy; optimal <100 mg/dL
        ▪ **High-Density Lipoprotein (HDL-C)**: "Good cholesterol"; low is <40 mg/dL (men) or <50 mg/dL (women)
        ▪ **Triglycerides (TGs)**: Normal <150 mg/dL
    ◦ **LDL Calculation (Friedewald Equation)**
        ▪ `LDL = TC - HDL - (TGs / 5)`
        ▪ **Important**: Formula is **invalid if TGs > 400 mg/dL**; a direct LDL measurement is needed in such cases
• **Screening**
    ◦ **USPSTF**: Recommends screening for adults aged 40 to 75 years
    ◦ Consider earlier screening for those with significant risk factors (e.g., strong family history, obesity, diabetes)
• **Secondary Cause Workup**
    ◦ **TSH**: To rule out hypothyroidism
    ◦ **A1c/Fasting Glucose**: To screen for diabetes mellitus
    ◦ **LFTs (AST/ALT)**: To assess for liver disease and establish a baseline before starting statin therapy
    ◦ **Urinalysis/BUN/Cr**: To assess for nephrotic syndrome
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent with effective treatment and adherence to lifestyle modifications
• Primarily dependent on the extent of underlying **ASCVD** at diagnosis and the ability to achieve lipid goals
• Untreated prognosis is poor, especially in familial forms, due to premature **ASCVD** and death

sections.overview:
• Not a single disease, but a **constellation of interconnected metabolic abnormalities**
    ◦ Collectively increases the risk of **atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD)** and **type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM)**
• Considered a **pro-inflammatory** and **pro-thrombotic** state
• Core pathological driver is **insulin resistance**, typically associated with **central (visceral) obesity**
• Diagnosis requires the presence of at least **3 of 5** specific clinical criteria
sections.etiology:
• **Insulin resistance** is the central unifying mechanism
• **Insulin Resistance & Central Obesity**
    ◦ **Visceral Adipose Tissue**
        ▪ Unlike subcutaneous fat, visceral (intra-abdominal) fat is highly metabolically active
        ▪ Releases inflammatory cytokines (e.g., TNF-α, IL-6) and excess free fatty acids (FFAs) directly into the portal circulation
    ◦ **Lipotoxicity**
        ▪ FFAs travel to the liver, pancreas, and muscle, interfering with insulin signaling pathways
        ▪ This causes peripheral tissues (especially muscle and liver) to become less responsive to insulin
    ◦ **Pancreatic Compensation**
        ▪ The pancreatic beta-cells initially compensate by producing more insulin, leading to **hyperinsulinemia**
• **Pathophysiologic Consequences**
    ◦ **Hyperglycemia**
        ▪ Over time, pancreatic beta-cell function declines, and the body can no longer overcome insulin resistance, leading to impaired glucose tolerance and eventually **T2DM**
    ◦ **Atherogenic Dyslipidemia**
        ▪ Insulin resistance in the liver leads to overproduction of VLDL (Very-Low-Density Lipoprotein)
        ▪ This results in the characteristic lipid profile: **high triglycerides (TGs)** and **low HDL cholesterol**
        ▪ It also promotes the formation of small, dense LDL particles, which are highly atherogenic
    ◦ **Hypertension**
        ▪ **Hyperinsulinemia** promotes renal sodium retention and increases sympathetic nervous system activity
        ▪ Endothelial dysfunction, driven by inflammation and oxidative stress, impairs vasodilation
    ◦ **Pro-inflammatory State**
        ▪ Adipose-derived cytokines (adipokines) like TNF-α and IL-6 create a state of chronic, low-grade inflammation, which contributes to endothelial dysfunction and atherosclerosis
    ◦ **Pro-thrombotic State**
        ▪ Increased levels of **plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1)** and **fibrinogen** are often present, impairing fibrinolysis and increasing the risk of thrombosis
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Extremely common, affecting approximately **one-third of adults** in the United States
• **Trends**: The prevalence is increasing worldwide, paralleling the epidemics of obesity and T2DM
• **Demographics**
    ◦ Prevalence increases significantly with **age**
    ◦ It is higher in Hispanic and Native American populations compared to Caucasians and African Americans
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Typically asymptomatic** in its early stages
• Most often identified during routine screening or when a patient presents with one of its individual components (e.g., new-onset hypertension or hyperglycemia)
• The classic patient is overweight or obese, with an **"apple-shaped" body habitus (central obesity)**
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is made based on the **NCEP ATP III (National Cholesterol Education Program Adult Treatment Panel III) criteria**
    ◦ The presence of **≥3 of the following 5 criteria** is diagnostic:
        ▪ **1. Abdominal Obesity** (Waist Circumference)
            ◦ **>102 cm (>40 in)** in men
            ◦ **>88 cm (>35 in)** in women
        ▪ **2. Triglycerides**: **≥150 mg/dL** (or on drug therapy for high TGs)
        ▪ **3. HDL Cholesterol**
            ◦ **<40 mg/dL** in men
            ◦ **<50 mg/dL** in women
            ◦ (Or on drug therapy for low HDL)
        ▪ **4. Blood Pressure**: **≥130/85 mmHg** (or on antihypertensive drug therapy)
        ▪ **5. Fasting Plasma Glucose**: **≥100 mg/dL** (or on drug therapy for hyperglycemia)
• **Other useful lab tests**
    ◦ **HbA1c**: To assess for prediabetes or T2DM
    ◦ **Complete Lipid Panel**: To assess LDL cholesterol
    ◦ **Uric Acid**: Often elevated (hyperuricemia)
    ◦ **Liver Function Tests (LFTs)**: To screen for NAFLD (elevated ALT/AST)
    ◦ **Urine microalbumin-to-creatinine ratio**: To screen for early kidney damage
    ◦ **hs-CRP**: A marker of inflammation, often elevated
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is directly related to the number of MetS components present and the degree to which they are controlled
• Without intervention, the prognosis is poor due to the high likelihood of developing **T2DM** and/or experiencing a major **cardiovascular event**
• With aggressive lifestyle modification and medical management, the prognosis can be significantly improved, and the risk of complications can be substantially reduced

sections.overview:
• Obesity is a complex, chronic, and relapsing multifactorial disease characterized by excessive adiposity, formally defined by the Body Mass Index (BMI)
• It increases the risk for numerous other comorbidities, including cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and certain cancers, leading to increased morbidity and mortality
• Management requires a long-term, comprehensive approach involving lifestyle modification, pharmacotherapy, and potentially surgical intervention
• **BMI (kg/m2)**
    ◦ Underweight: < 18.5
    ◦ Normal weight: 18.5-24.9
    ◦ Overweight: 25.0-29.9
    ◦ **Obesity Class I:** 30.0-34.9
    ◦ **Obesity Class II:** 35.0-39.9
    ◦ **Obesity Class III (Severe Obesity):** ≥ 40.0
sections.etiology:
• Obesity results from a long-term positive energy balance where energy intake exceeds energy expenditure. The pathophysiology is complex and involves a web of genetic, environmental, and neurohormonal factors.
• **Neurohormonal Regulation:** The hypothalamus is the central regulator of appetite and energy expenditure
    ◦ **Leptin:** A hormone produced by adipocytes that signals satiety to the hypothalamus. In most cases of obesity, individuals develop **leptin resistance**, meaning high levels of leptin are present but the brain does not respond appropriately, leading to a failure to suppress appetite
    ◦ **Ghrelin:** A hormone produced primarily by the stomach ("hunger hormone") that stimulates appetite. Levels rise before meals and fall after
    ◦ **Gut Hormones:** Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) and Peptide YY (PYY) are released from the GI tract after a meal and signal satiety
• **Genetic Predisposition:** Polygenic inheritance plays a significant role in susceptibility to weight gain. Rare monogenic causes exist (e.g., MC4R mutation, Prader-Willi syndrome)
• **Environmental Factors:** The "obesogenic environment" includes easy access to high-calorie, palatable foods and a sedentary lifestyle
• **Secondary Causes:**
    ◦ **Endocrine Disorders:** Hypothyroidism, Cushing's syndrome, Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)
    ◦ **Medication-Induced:** Atypical antipsychotics (olanzapine, clozapine), corticosteroids, some antidepressants (TCAs, mirtazapine), insulin, sulfonylureas
• **Adipose Tissue Dysfunction:** Adipose tissue is an active endocrine organ. In obesity, adipocytes become hypertrophic and dysfunctional, leading to a chronic, low-grade inflammatory state and altered secretion of adipokines (e.g., decreased adiponectin, increased inflammatory cytokines like TNF-α and IL-6), which contributes to insulin resistance and other metabolic complications
sections.epidemiology:
• Global pandemic; prevalence has nearly tripled since 1975
• In the United States, the prevalence of obesity was **41.9%** among adults in 2017-2020
• The prevalence of severe obesity (BMI ≥ 40) was **9.2%**
• Significant disparities exist based on race, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status
sections.riskFactors:
• Family history and genetics
• Unhealthy diet (high in processed foods, sugar, and fat)
• Sedentary lifestyle / physical inactivity
• Lower socioeconomic status
• Certain medications (see above)
• Underlying medical conditions (PCOS, hypothyroidism)
• Psychological factors (stress, depression, binge eating disorder)
• Insufficient sleep
• Age (risk increases with age)
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients often present for management of a comorbidity (e.g., HTN, knee pain, T2DM) rather than for obesity itself. It may also be identified incidentally during a routine physical exam
• A thorough history should be taken, including weight history, dietary patterns, physical activity, previous weight loss attempts, and review of systems for obesity-related symptoms
• **Symptoms:**
    ◦ Often asymptomatic
    ◦ When present, symptoms are typically due to comorbidities:
        ▪ **Dyspnea on exertion** (due to deconditioning or underlying cardiopulmonary disease)
        ▪ **Daytime somnolence/Fatigue** (suggestive of Obstructive Sleep Apnea)
        ▪ **Joint pain**, especially in weight-bearing joints (osteoarthritis)
        ▪ Symptoms of **GERD** (heartburn, regurgitation)
        ▪ Low back pain
        ▪ Symptoms of depression or anxiety
sections.physicalExam:
• **Vitals:** **Hypertension** is common
• **Anthropometrics:** BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2. Increased waist circumference (**≥ 40 inches / 102 cm in men; ≥ 35 inches / 88 cm in women**) indicates central adiposity and increased cardiometabolic risk
• **Skin:**
    ◦ **Acanthosis nigricans:** Hyperpigmented, velvety plaques in intertriginous areas (axilla, neck); a sign of insulin resistance
    ◦ **Striae distensae:** Stretch marks
    ◦ **Intertrigo:** Inflammation/rash in skin folds due to moisture and friction
• **Cardiovascular:** Displaced PMI, S3/S4 gallop (if heart failure present), lower extremity edema
• **Pulmonary:** May have decreased breath sounds at the bases
• **Musculoskeletal:** Decreased range of motion, crepitus, or joint-line tenderness in knees/hips. Antalgic gait
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primary Diagnosis:**
    ◦ Calculation of BMI from height and weight
    ◦ Measurement of waist circumference
• **Screening for Comorbidities & Secondary Causes (Initial Lab Workup):**
    ◦ **Fasting Lipid Panel:** To assess for dyslipidemia
    ◦ **Fasting Glucose and/or Hemoglobin A1c:** To screen for prediabetes and type 2 diabetes
    ◦ **Liver Function Tests (ALT, AST):** To screen for Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD)
    ◦ **TSH:** To screen for hypothyroidism
• **Consider in specific cases:**
    ◦ **24-hour urine free cortisol or low-dose dexamethasone suppression test:** If Cushingoid features are present
    ◦ **Sleep study (polysomnography):** If symptoms of OSA are present (snoring, witnessed apneas, daytime sleepiness)
    ◦ **ECG:** To assess for LVH, arrhythmias
sections.treatment:
• **Dietary Therapy:** Caloric reduction (typically by 500-750 kcal/day) to achieve a negative energy balance. Emphasize whole foods (fruits, vegetables, lean proteins). Various diets (e.g., Mediterranean, low-carb) can be effective
• **Physical Activity:** **≥ 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity per week**, spread over several days, plus strength training 2x/week
• **Behavioral Therapy:** Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), motivational interviewing, stimulus control, and self-monitoring to address maladaptive eating behaviors
• **Pharmacotherapy:**
    ◦ **Indications:** BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2 **OR** BMI ≥ 27 kg/m2 with at least one weight-related comorbidity
    ◦ **Key Agents:**
        ▪ **GLP-1 Receptor Agonists:** Semaglutide (Wegovy), Liraglutide (Saxenda), Tirzepatide (Zepbound, also a GIP agonist). Highly effective. MOA: Increases satiety, delays gastric emptying
        ▪ **Phentermine/Topiramate (Qsymia):** Sympathomimetic (suppresses appetite) and antiepileptic (mechanism for weight loss unclear, likely appetite suppression)
        ▪ **Orlistat (Xenical, Alli):** Pancreatic and gastric lipase inhibitor. MOA: Decreases fat absorption. Side effects: Steatorrhea, flatulence
        ▪ **Naltrexone/Bupropion (Contrave):** Opioid antagonist and antidepressant. MOA: Works on hypothalamic appetite centers and dopamine reward pathways
• **Bariatric Surgery:**
    ◦ **Indications:** BMI ≥ 40 kg/m2 **OR** BMI ≥ 35 kg/m2 with at least one severe obesity-related comorbidity
    ◦ **Most Common Procedures:**
        ▪ **Sleeve Gastrectomy (Restrictive):** ~80% of the stomach is removed, creating a small "sleeve." Most common procedure in the US
        ▪ **Roux-en-Y Gastric Bypass (RYGB) (Restrictive + Malabsorptive):** Creates a small gastric pouch that is connected directly to the jejunum, bypassing the rest of the stomach and duodenum
    ◦ Most effective long-term treatment for severe obesity and remission of comorbidities (especially T2DM)
sections.management:
• **Set realistic goals:** Initial goal is **5-10% loss of total body weight** over 6 months. This modest amount provides significant health benefits
• **Multidisciplinary approach:** Involve primary care, registered dietitians, behavioral therapists, and potentially specialists (endocrinology, bariatrics)
• **Regular follow-up:** Monitor weight, blood pressure, and adherence. Repeat labs periodically to monitor comorbidities
• **Address as a chronic disease:** Emphasize that obesity is not a failure of willpower. Long-term, sustained effort is required, and weight regain is common without continued management
sections.complications:
• **Cardiovascular:** Hypertension, Dyslipidemia, Coronary Artery Disease, Congestive Heart Failure, Atrial Fibrillation, Stroke
• **Endocrine/Metabolic:** **Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus**, **Metabolic Syndrome**, PCOS, Gout
• **Pulmonary:** **Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA)**, Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome (Pickwickian syndrome), Asthma
• **GI/Hepatobiliary:** **Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD/NASH)**, GERD, Cholelithiasis (gallstones)
• **Musculoskeletal:** **Osteoarthritis** (especially knee and hip), Chronic Low Back Pain
• **Oncologic:** Increased risk of multiple cancers (e.g., endometrial, breast [postmenopausal], colorectal, esophageal, renal, pancreatic)
• **Psychosocial:** Depression, anxiety, social stigmatization, decreased quality of life
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is directly related to the degree of weight loss and improvement in comorbidities
• A sustained weight loss of **5-10%** can significantly reduce the risk of T2DM and cardiovascular disease and improve blood pressure, lipids, and glycemic control
• Without intervention, obesity is a progressive disease with increasing morbidity and a reduction in life expectancy
• Bariatric surgery offers the best prognosis for significant and sustained weight loss and comorbidity remission in eligible patients

sections.overview:
• Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) is the most common endocrine disorder in women of reproductive age.
• It is a heterogeneous syndrome characterized by a combination of **hyperandrogenism**, **ovulatory dysfunction**, and **polycystic ovarian morphology**.
• It is primarily a clinical diagnosis of exclusion, requiring the ruling out of other conditions that can cause similar signs and symptoms.
• PCOS has significant metabolic, reproductive, and psychological implications.
sections.etiology:
• The exact etiology is unknown but involves a complex interplay of genetic and environmental factors.
• The core pathophysiologic feature is **insulin resistance** and the resultant **compensatory hyperinsulinemia**.
    ◦ **Insulin Resistance & Hyperinsulinemia**
        ▪ Insulin acts on ovarian theca cells, stimulating androgen (testosterone, androstenedione) production.
        ▪ Hyperinsulinemia also suppresses hepatic production of **Sex Hormone-Binding Globulin (SHBG)**.
        ▪ Low SHBG leads to an increase in free, biologically active testosterone, exacerbating hyperandrogenism.
    ◦ **Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Ovarian (HPO) Axis Dysfunction**
        ▪ Altered GnRH pulsatility leads to a preferential secretion of **Luteinizing Hormone (LH)** over Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH).
        ▪ This results in a classic (but not diagnostic) **elevated LH:FSH ratio (>2:1 or 3:1)**.
        ▪ High LH further stimulates ovarian theca cells to produce androgens.
        ▪ Relatively low FSH levels lead to impaired follicular development. Follicles are recruited but fail to mature and ovulate, resulting in multiple small, arrested follicles (cysts).
    ◦ **Chronic Anovulation & Estrogen Imbalance**
        ▪ Anovulation leads to a deficiency of progesterone.
        ▪ Androgens are converted to **estrone** (a type of estrogen) in peripheral adipose tissue.
        ▪ This creates a state of **chronic unopposed estrogen**, which puts the endometrium at risk for hyperplasia and carcinoma.
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects **6-12%** of women of reproductive age.
• The **most common cause of anovulatory infertility**.
• Prevalence of metabolic syndrome in women with PCOS is approximately 30-40%.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Family History:** Strong genetic predisposition.
• **Obesity:** Worsens insulin resistance and hyperandrogenism.
• **Insulin Resistance / Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.**
• **Premature Adrenarche** (early development of pubic hair).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A typical patient is an adolescent or young woman presenting with a chief complaint of **irregular menstrual cycles**, **hirsutism**, persistent **acne**, and often **difficulty losing weight**.
• Key symptoms include:
    ◦ **Menstrual Dysfunction:**
        ▪ **Oligomenorrhea:** <9 menstrual cycles per year or cycles >35 days apart.
        ▪ **Amenorrhea:** Absence of menses for 3 consecutive months.
    ◦ **Hyperandrogenism (Clinical Signs):**
        ▪ **Hirsutism:** Coarse, dark, male-pattern hair growth on the face, chest, back, and abdomen.
        ▪ **Acne:** Typically cystic, persistent beyond adolescence, and resistant to standard treatments.
        ▪ **Androgenic Alopecia:** Male-pattern hair loss (thinning at the crown, frontal scalp).
    ◦ **Infertility:**
        ▪ Difficulty conceiving due to chronic anovulation.
    ◦ **Metabolic Symptoms:**
        ▪ Weight gain or obesity (especially central/abdominal).
        ▪ Difficulty losing weight.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Vitals:**
    ◦ Elevated BMI (>25 kg/m2), may have hypertension.
• **Skin:**
    ◦ **Hirsutism:** Evaluate using the Ferriman-Gallwey scoring system.
    ◦ **Acne Vulgaris:** Face, chest, and back.
    ◦ **Acanthosis Nigricans:** Velvety, hyperpigmented plaques in intertriginous areas (neck, axillae, groin). A cutaneous marker of insulin resistance.
• **General:**
    ◦ Central obesity.
• **Pelvic Exam:**
    ◦ Often normal. May reveal bilateral ovarian enlargement or clitoromegaly (rare, suggests severe hyperandrogenism and warrants workup for a tumor).
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is based on the **Rotterdam Criteria**, requiring **2 out of the following 3 criteria**, after the exclusion of other etiologies:
    ◦ **Oligo- or Anovulation** (evidenced by menstrual history).
    ◦ **Clinical or Biochemical Hyperandrogenism**.
        ▪ **Clinical:** Hirsutism, acne, or androgenic alopecia.
        ▪ **Biochemical:** Elevated total or free testosterone.
    ◦ **Polycystic Ovarian Morphology on Ultrasound**.
        ▪ **Transvaginal Ultrasound:** 12 follicles (2-9 mm) in each ovary OR ovarian volume >10 mL.
        ▪ Classic "string of pearls" appearance.
sections.management:
• **Lifestyle:**
    ◦ Emphasize diet (low-glycemic index) and regular physical activity as the foundation of care.
• **Endometrial Protection:**
    ◦ Ensure regular withdrawal bleeding (via OCPs or cyclic progestins) to prevent endometrial hyperplasia.
    ◦ Investigate any abnormal uterine bleeding with ultrasound and/or endometrial biopsy.
• **Metabolic Screening:**
    ◦ Screen for Type 2 DM with an OGTT at baseline and every 1-3 years.
    ◦ Screen for dyslipidemia with a fasting lipid panel every 2-3 years.
    ◦ Monitor blood pressure at every visit.
• **Mental Health:**
    ◦ Screen for depression, anxiety, and eating disorders.
• **Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA):**
    ◦ High index of suspicion; screen with questionnaires (e.g., STOP-BANG) and refer for a sleep study if indicated.
sections.complications:
• **Metabolic:**
    ◦ Metabolic Syndrome
    ◦ Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
    ◦ Dyslipidemia
    ◦ Hypertension
    ◦ Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD)
• **Reproductive:**
    ◦ Infertility
    ◦ Pregnancy Complications (Gestational Diabetes, Preeclampsia, Preterm Birth)
• **Oncologic:**
    ◦ **Endometrial Cancer** (3x increased risk due to chronic unopposed estrogen)
• **Cardiovascular:**
    ◦ Increased long-term risk of cardiovascular disease
• **Psychological:**
    ◦ Depression, Anxiety, Poor Body Image, Eating Disorders
• **Other:**
    ◦ Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA)
sections.prognosis:
• PCOS is a chronic condition requiring lifelong management.
• With proactive management of metabolic risks and appropriate endometrial surveillance, the long-term prognosis is good.
• Failure to address comorbidities leads to significantly increased morbidity from diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer.

sections.overview:
• Amenorrhea is the absence of menstruation, which is a symptom, not a diagnosis.
• Classification:
    ◦ **Primary amenorrhea**: Absence of menarche by age 15 with normal secondary sexual characteristics, or by age 13 without them.
    ◦ **Secondary amenorrhea**: Absence of menses for >3 months in a woman with previously regular cycles, or >6 months in a woman with previously irregular cycles.
• Endocrine causes disrupt the hormonal signaling of the **Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Ovarian (HPO) axis**, leading to anovulation and cessation of menses.
• The workup involves a systematic evaluation of this axis.
sections.etiology:
• Endocrine amenorrhea results from dysfunction at one or more levels of the HPO axis or from other endocrine glands influencing the axis.
• **Hypothalamic Dysfunction**
    ◦ **Functional Hypothalamic Amenorrhea (FHA)**: The most common cause of secondary amenorrhea.
        ▪ **Pathophysiology**: Decreased pulsatile secretion of **Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH)** from the hypothalamus, leading to decreased FSH and LH from the pituitary, resulting in low estrogen levels and anovulation.
        ▪ **Triggers**:
            ◦ **Excessive Exercise**: High energy expenditure without adequate caloric intake.
            ◦ **Nutritional Deficiency / Low Body Weight**: Anorexia, bulimia, malnutrition (**BMI < 18.5**).
            ◦ **Extreme Psychological Stress**: High cortisol levels can suppress **GnRH**.
        ▪ Often called the **"Female Athlete Triad"**: amenorrhea, disordered eating, and low bone density.
• **Pituitary Dysfunction**
    ◦ **Hyperprolactinemia**
        ▪ **Pathophysiology**: Excess prolactin directly inhibits the pulsatile secretion of **GnRH** from the hypothalamus.
        ▪ **Causes**:
            ◦ **Prolactinoma**: Most common pituitary adenoma.
            ◦ **Medications**: Dopamine antagonists (e.g., antipsychotics like risperidone, haloperidol; antiemetics like metoclopramide).
            ◦ **Primary Hypothyroidism**: Elevated TRH can stimulate prolactin release.
    ◦ **Other Pituitary Causes**
        ▪ **Sheehan's Syndrome**: Postpartum pituitary necrosis due to severe hemorrhage and hypotension during childbirth, leading to panhypopituitarism.
        ▪ **Empty Sella Syndrome**: The sella turcica is not filled with pituitary tissue, leading to hypopituitarism.
        ▪ **Pituitary Tumors (non-prolactinoma)**: Craniopharyngioma or other adenomas can compress the pituitary stalk or gland, disrupting hormone production.
• **Ovarian Dysfunction**
    ◦ **Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)**: The most common endocrine disorder in women of reproductive age.
        ▪ **Pathophysiology**: Complex and multifactorial. Key features include insulin resistance leading to hyperinsulinemia, which stimulates excess ovarian androgen production. This disrupts follicular development and leads to chronic anovulation. Characterized by an elevated **LH:FSH ratio** (>2:1 or 3:1).
    ◦ **Primary Ovarian Insufficiency (POI)**: Also known as premature ovarian failure.
        ▪ **Pathophysiology**: Depletion or dysfunction of ovarian follicles before age 40. The ovaries fail to produce estrogen despite adequate stimulation from the pituitary, resulting in a **hypergonadotropic hypogonadic** state (high **FSH**, high **LH**, low Estrogen).
• **Other Endocrine Disorders**
    ◦ **Thyroid Disease**: Both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism can disrupt the HPO axis.
        ▪ **Hypothyroidism**: Increased TRH can stimulate prolactin. Also, changes in Sex Hormone-Binding Globulin (SHBG) alter hormone balance.
    ◦ **Adrenal Disorders**
        ▪ **Cushing's Syndrome**: Excess cortisol suppresses **GnRH** secretion.
        ▪ **Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH)**: Most commonly due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency. Non-classic (late-onset) forms present with hyperandrogenism and oligo/amenorrhea.
sections.epidemiology:
• **FHA**: Accounts for ~30% of secondary amenorrhea cases. Prevalent in athletes, dancers, and individuals with eating disorders.
• **PCOS**: Affects 5-15% of reproductive-age women. Most common cause of anovulatory infertility.
• **Hyperprolactinemia**: Found in ~10-20% of women with secondary amenorrhea. Prolactinomas are the most common cause.
• **POI**: Affects ~1% of women under 40.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The initial presentation is the absence of menses. The history is critical for narrowing the differential.
• **History**
    ◦ Age of menarche
    ◦ Cycle regularity
    ◦ Stress levels
    ◦ Diet/exercise patterns
    ◦ Weight changes
    ◦ Medication history
    ◦ Signs of hyperandrogenism (**hirsutism**, **acne**)
    ◦ **Galactorrhea**
    ◦ Headaches/visual changes
    ◦ Menopausal symptoms (**hot flashes**, **vaginal dryness**)
sections.diagnostics:
• The workup is a stepwise process.
• **Step 1: First-line Tests**
    ◦ Rule out pregnancy: Urine or serum **hCG** is **ALWAYS** the first step.
    ◦ Initial Hormonal Panel:
        ▪ **TSH**: To screen for thyroid disease.
        ▪ **Prolactin**: To screen for hyperprolactinemia.
        ▪ **FSH**: To assess ovarian function.
• **Step 2: Interpretation and Further Testing**
    ◦ If **TSH is abnormal**: Workup for hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism.
    ◦ If **Prolactin is elevated**: Repeat level. If still high, consider medication causes. Order a **pituitary MRI** to evaluate for a **prolactinoma**.
    ◦ If **FSH is elevated** (>30-40 mIU/mL on two occasions): Suggests **Primary Ovarian Insufficiency (POI)**. Confirms a hypergonadotropic hypogonadic state.
    ◦ If **FSH is low or normal** (and hCG, TSH, Prolactin are normal): Suggests a hypothalamic or pituitary cause (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism) OR anovulation with normal estrogen (like PCOS).
        ▪ **Progestin Challenge Test**: Give medroxyprogesterone acetate for 5-10 days.
            ◦ **Withdrawal bleed occurs (+ test)**: Indicates adequate estrogen and a patent outflow tract. The cause is anovulation (e.g., **PCOS**).
            ◦ **No withdrawal bleed (- test)**: Indicates low estrogen (hypoestrogenic state, e.g., **FHA**) or an outflow tract obstruction (e.g., Asherman's syndrome).
    ◦ If signs of **hyperandrogenism** (suspect PCOS):
        ▪ **Total and Free Testosterone**: Elevated in PCOS.
        ▪ **DHEAS**: Adrenal androgen, to rule out an adrenal tumor.
        ▪ **17-hydroxyprogesterone**: To screen for non-classic **CAH**.
        ▪ **Pelvic Ultrasound**: To look for polycystic morphology of the ovaries ("**string of pearls**").
        ▪ **Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT)** & **Lipid Panel**: To screen for metabolic comorbidities.
sections.prognosis:
• Generally good if the underlying cause is identified and managed appropriately.
• Fertility can often be restored in **FHA**, **PCOS**, and **hyperprolactinemia**.
• Prognosis for natural conception is very poor in **POI**; oocyte donation is the primary option for pregnancy.

sections.overview:
• Male hypogonadism is a clinical syndrome from the failure of the **testes** to produce physiological levels of **testosterone** and/or a normal number of **spermatozoa**.
    ◦ Characterized by low serum **testosterone** levels and associated signs and symptoms.
    ◦ Classified based on the defective level of the **hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis**.
        ▪ **Primary (Hypergonadotropic) Hypogonadism**:
            ◦ Pathophysiology originates in the **testes** (**gonadal failure**).
            ◦ The pituitary gland compensates by producing high levels of **gonadotropins (LH and FSH)**, but the **testes** cannot respond.
        ▪ **Secondary (Hypogonadotropic) Hypogonadism**:
            ◦ Pathophysiology originates in the **hypothalamus** or **pituitary gland**.
            ◦ There is insufficient **gonadotropin (LH, FSH)** secretion, leading to inadequate stimulation of otherwise normal **testes**.
sections.etiology:
• The **HPG axis** is a tightly regulated feedback loop.
    ◦ **Hypothalamus** releases **GnRH** → **Pituitary** releases **LH & FSH** → **Testes** (Leydig cells) produce **testosterone**.
    ◦ **Testosterone** provides negative feedback to the **hypothalamus** and **pituitary**.
    ◦ Disruption at any point causes **hypogonadism**.
sections.epidemiology:
• Prevalence increases significantly with **age**, affecting up to 30-40% of men over 70.
• Highly prevalent in men with comorbidities:
    ◦ **Obesity**: ~40%
    ◦ **Type 2 Diabetes**: ~30-50%
    ◦ **HIV infection**: ~30%
    ◦ **End-stage renal disease**: >50%
• **Klinefelter syndrome** occurs in approximately 1 in 660 live male births.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation varies dramatically depending on the age of onset.
    ◦ **Pre-Pubertal Onset**:
        ▪ Presents as **delayed puberty**.
        ▪ Lack of secondary sexual characteristics (no voice deepening, minimal body/facial hair).
        ▪ **Small testes** and phallus.
        ▪ **Eunuchoid proportions**: arm span > height by >5 cm, long legs relative to trunk.
        ▪ Poor muscle development.
    ◦ **Post-Pubertal (Adult) Onset**:
        ▪ Onset is often insidious with non-specific symptoms; this is the most common clinical scenario.
        ▪ Patients present with complaints of **low energy**, **low libido**, or **erectile dysfunction**.
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• With appropriate diagnosis and treatment, the prognosis is excellent for symptom relief and improvement in quality of life.
• **Bone density**, **muscle mass**, and **anemia** typically improve or resolve with **Testosterone Replacement Therapy (TRT)**.
• Fertility can often be restored in **secondary hypogonadism** but is generally permanent in **primary hypogonadism** (e.g., **Klinefelter syndrome**).
• The prognosis of the underlying cause (e.g., **pituitary adenoma**) dictates the overall long-term outlook.

sections.overview:
• Female hypogonadism is a clinical syndrome resulting from the failure of the ovaries to produce adequate levels of sex steroids (primarily estrogen) and/or to produce oocytes.
    ◦ This failure can originate from a problem within the ovaries themselves (**primary hypogonadism**) or from dysfunction of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis that controls the ovaries (**secondary/tertiary or central hypogonadism**).
    ◦ The clinical presentation depends on the age of onset but universally involves estrogen deficiency and impaired fertility.
    ◦ **Primary Hypogonadism (Hypergonadotropic Hypogonadism)**
        ▪ The defect is at the level of the ovary. The pituitary attempts to compensate by releasing high levels of gonadotropins (FSH, LH), but the ovary cannot respond.
        ▪ **Hallmark Labs**: **High FSH/LH**, **Low Estradiol**
    ◦ **Central Hypogonadism (Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism)**
        ▪ The defect is at the level of the hypothalamus (GnRH release) or pituitary (FSH/LH release). The ovaries are healthy but are not receiving the signal to function.
        ▪ **Hallmark Labs**: **Low or inappropriately normal FSH/LH**, **Low Estradiol**
sections.etiology: • The hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis regulates the female reproductive cycle. Disruption at any level can cause hypogonadism.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Premature Ovarian Insufficiency (POI)**: Affects ~1% of women before age 40 and 0.1% before age 30.
• **Functional Hypothalamic Amenorrhea (FHA)**: Accounts for up to 30% of cases of secondary amenorrhea. Prevalence is significantly higher in competitive athletes and women with eating disorders.
• **Turner Syndrome**: Occurs in approximately 1 in 2,500 live female births.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation varies based on the age of onset.
    ◦ **Pre-pubertal onset**: Presents as **primary amenorrhea** (absence of menarche by age 15) and failure to develop secondary sexual characteristics (e.g., breast development).
    ◦ **Post-pubertal onset**: Presents as **secondary amenorrhea** (cessation of menses for >3 months in a woman with previously regular cycles or >6 months with irregular cycles), oligomenorrhea, or infertility.
    ◦ Patients may also present with symptoms of estrogen deficiency regardless of menstrual status.
sections.diagnostics:
• The diagnostic approach aims to confirm hypogonadism, differentiate between primary and central causes, and identify the underlying etiology.
    ◦ **Initial Workup**
        ▪ **β-hCG**: **ALWAYS** the first step to rule out pregnancy.
        ▪ **Initial Hormonal Panel**
