            • **FSH, LH, Estradiol (E2)**: This is the key differentiating test.
            • **TSH**: To rule out thyroid dysfunction.
            • **Prolactin**: To rule out hyperprolactinemia.
    ◦ **Interpreting Initial Labs**
        ▪ **High FSH (>25 IU/L, repeated on 2 occasions >1 month apart) + Low Estradiol**: Confirms **Primary Hypogonadism (Hypergonadotropic)**.
        ▪ **Low or Inappropriately Normal FSH/LH + Low Estradiol**: Confirms **Central Hypogonadism (Hypogonadotropic)**.
    ◦ **Subsequent Workup Based on Type**
        ▪ **If Primary Hypogonadism (POI) is diagnosed**:
            • **Karyotype**: Essential in women <30 years old to rule out Turner Syndrome (mosaic forms can present later).
            • **FMR1 gene testing**: For Fragile X premutation.
            • **Autoimmune screening**: Anti-adrenal (21-hydroxylase) antibodies, thyroid peroxidase antibodies.
            • **Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH)**: Will be very low; a marker of ovarian reserve.
        ▪ **If Central Hypogonadism is diagnosed**:
            • **MRI of the brain/pituitary**: To evaluate for tumors, infiltrative disease, or congenital abnormalities.
            • **Assess other pituitary hormones**: Cortisol (AM), ACTH, IGF-1 to check for panhypopituitarism.
            • If no structural cause is found and history is suggestive, a diagnosis of FHA is likely.
    ◦ **Ancillary Testing**
        ▪ **Pelvic Ultrasound**: Can reveal a thin endometrial stripe, small uterus, and small ovaries with few antral follicles.
        ▪ **DEXA Scan**: Essential for all women with prolonged hypoestrogenism to assess for osteopenia/osteoporosis.
sections.prognosis:
• With appropriate HRT, the prognosis for managing symptoms and preventing long-term complications (osteoporosis, CVD) is excellent.
• The prognosis for fertility is highly dependent on the etiology.
    ◦ **Excellent** for FHA with appropriate intervention.
    ◦ **Very poor** for POI, with most women requiring oocyte donation to conceive.

sections.overview:
• Hirsutism is the excessive growth of dark, coarse, terminal hair in an androgen-dependent (male-pattern) distribution in females
    ◦ It is a clinical sign of hyperandrogenism, not a disease itself
    ◦ Key locations include the upper lip, chin, chest, upper back, lower back, abdomen, and inner thighs
    ◦ Must be differentiated from **hypertrichosis**, which is generalized, non-sexual hair growth that is not androgen-dependent
sections.etiology:
• Hirsutism results from either:
    ◦ **Increased androgen production** from the ovaries or adrenal glands
    ◦ **Increased end-organ sensitivity** of the hair follicle to normal levels of androgens
• The primary mechanism involves the conversion of testosterone to the more potent **dihydrotestosterone (DHT)** within the hair follicle by the enzyme **5-alpha-reductase**
    ◦ DHT promotes the transformation of vellus hair (fine, soft) into terminal hair (coarse, dark)
• **Common Causes**:
    ◦ **Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)**: **Most common cause (>80%)**. Characterized by ovarian androgen overproduction, often associated with insulin resistance and anovulation
    ◦ **Idiopathic Hirsutism (approx. 10%)**: Hirsutism with regular menses and normal serum androgen levels. Thought to be due to increased 5-alpha-reductase activity in the skin
    ◦ **Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH)**: Most commonly late-onset (non-classic) **21-hydroxylase deficiency**. An autosomal recessive disorder leading to excess adrenal androgen production
    ◦ **Androgen-Secreting Tumors (Ovarian or Adrenal)**: Rare (<0.2%) but critical to identify. Cause rapid onset of severe hirsutism and virilization
        ▪ **Ovarian**: Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors, granulosa-theca cell tumors
        ▪ **Adrenal**: Adrenal adenomas or carcinomas
    ◦ **Cushing's Syndrome**: Excess cortisol from adrenal, pituitary, or ectopic sources. ACTH can stimulate adrenal androgen production
    ◦ **Medications**:
        ▪ Anabolic steroids (e.g., Danazol)
        ▪ Certain progestins in older contraceptives
        ▪ Testosterone
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects approximately 5-10% of reproductive-age women
• Prevalence varies by ethnicity: more common in women of Mediterranean, South Asian, and Middle Eastern descent; less common in women of East Asian and Native American descent
• PCOS is the underlying etiology in the vast majority of cases
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A female patient presents with the chief complaint of "unwanted" or "excessive hair" growth on her face, chest, or abdomen
• The history is critical for determining the underlying cause
• **Key History Questions**:
    ◦ **Onset and Progression**:
        ▪ **Gradual onset** around puberty: Suggests PCOS, CAH, or idiopathic
        ▪ **Rapid onset** and progression: **Red flag for an androgen-secreting tumor**
    ◦ **Menstrual History**: Irregular cycles (oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea) are a hallmark of PCOS
    ◦ **Symptoms of Virilization**: Deepening voice, increased muscle mass, clitoromegaly, temporal balding. **Red flag for a tumor**
    ◦ **Associated Symptoms**: Acne, weight gain, infertility (suggests PCOS). Symptoms of Cushing's (weight gain, easy bruising, striae)
    ◦ **Medication History**: Review for offending agents
    ◦ **Family History**: Inquire about hirsutism, infertility, or diabetes in relatives
sections.diagnostics:
• The goal is to identify the source of androgen excess
• **Initial Laboratory Workup**:
    ◦ **Total Testosterone**: The best initial test
        ▪ Mildly elevated: Suggests PCOS or idiopathic hirsutism
        ▪ **Markedly elevated (>150-200 ng/dL)**: Raises suspicion for an **ovarian tumor**
    ◦ **DHEA-S (Dehydroepiandrosterone Sulfate)**: A specific marker for **adrenal** androgen production
        ▪ Mildly elevated: Can be seen in PCOS or CAH
        ▪ **Markedly elevated (>700 mcg/dL)**: Raises suspicion for an **adrenal tumor**
• **Further Workup Based on Clinical Suspicion**:
    ◦ **If menstrual dysfunction**:
        ▪ LH, FSH (ratio >3:1 suggests PCOS)
        ▪ Prolactin (to rule out hyperprolactinemia)
        ▪ TSH (to rule out thyroid disease)
    ◦ **If suspicion for CAH** (e.g., family history, early onset):
        ▪ **17-Hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP)**: Order an early morning, follicular phase level. Elevated level is diagnostic
    ◦ **If suspicion for Cushing's Syndrome**:
        ▪ 24-hour urinary free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol, or a low-dose dexamethasone suppression test
    ◦ **If screening for metabolic syndrome (in PCOS)**:
        ▪ Fasting glucose and Hemoglobin A1c
        ▪ Fasting lipid panel
• **Imaging**:
    ◦ **Pelvic Ultrasound**: To evaluate for polycystic ovaries or an ovarian tumor
    ◦ **CT or MRI of the Adrenal Glands**: To evaluate for an adrenal tumor if DHEA-S is markedly elevated
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis for managing the symptoms of hirsutism is generally good with consistent treatment
• The overall prognosis depends entirely on the underlying etiology
• For common causes like PCOS and idiopathic hirsutism, the condition is chronic but manageable
• For rare causes like malignancy, the prognosis is guarded and depends on the stage at diagnosis

sections.overview:
• **Congenital Hypothyroidism (CH)** is a condition of **thyroid hormone deficiency present at birth**.
• It is one of the most common, yet treatable, causes of **preventable intellectual disability**.
• Thyroid hormone is essential for normal **brain development, myelination, and physical growth** in the first few years of life.
• The vast majority of infants with CH **appear normal at birth**, making **newborn screening programs crucial** for early detection and intervention.
• Prompt initiation of thyroid hormone replacement therapy leads to **excellent neurodevelopmental outcomes**.
sections.etiology:
• The underlying cause of CH is classified into **primary, central, or transient** forms.
• **Primary Hypothyroidism (95% of cases)** - Defect at the level of the thyroid gland.
    ◦ **Thyroid Dysgenesis (85% of cases)**: An abnormality in the anatomical development of the thyroid gland. This is the **most common cause of CH**.
        ▪ **Ectopic Thyroid**: Most common form of dysgenesis; the gland is located in an abnormal position, most often at the base of the tongue (**lingual thyroid**). It is typically small and produces insufficient hormone.
        ▪ **Thyroid Aplasia**: **Complete absence** of the thyroid gland.
        ▪ **Thyroid Hypoplasia**: The gland is in the correct location but is **underdeveloped and small**.
    ◦ **Dyshormonogenesis (10-15% of cases)**: The thyroid gland is present (and often enlarged, forming a **goiter**) but there is an **inborn error** in one of the steps of thyroid hormone synthesis or secretion (e.g., defects in iodide trapping, organification, or coupling). These are typically **autosomal recessive** disorders.
• **Central (Secondary/Tertiary) Hypothyroidism (5% of cases)**
    ◦ **Secondary**: **Pituitary gland failure** to secrete Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (**TSH**).
    ◦ **Tertiary**: **Hypothalamic failure** to secrete Thyrotropin-Releasing Hormone (**TRH**).
    ◦ Often associated with other **pituitary hormone deficiencies**.
    ◦ **TSH level is inappropriately low or normal** in the setting of a **low T4**.
• **Transient Hypothyroidism**
    ◦ Temporary hypothyroidism that resolves within the first few months or years.
    ◦ Causes include **maternal iodine deficiency**, maternal use of **antithyroid medications** (Methimazole, PTU), or transplacental passage of maternal **TSH-receptor blocking antibodies**.
• **Pathophysiology of Damage**: Lack of **thyroxine (T4)** and **triiodothyronine (T3)** impairs **CNS development**, specifically neuronal differentiation, migration, myelination, and synaptogenesis.
    ◦ This damage is most severe and irreversible during the **first few months of life** when the brain is growing rapidly.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Occurs in approximately **1 in 2,000 to 1 in 4,000** live births.
• **Sex**: More common in **females** (2:1 ratio).
• **Ethnicity**: **Higher incidence** in Hispanic and Asian populations; **lower** in African American populations.
• Thyroid dysgenesis is typically **sporadic**, while dyshormonogenesis is **inherited**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Most infants are asymptomatic** or have very subtle, nonspecific findings at birth.
    ◦ This is due to the partial protective effect of **maternal T4** that crossed the placenta.
• The classic signs and symptoms develop gradually over the first several weeks to months if the condition is not detected and treated.
• The most common presentation today is an **abnormal newborn screening test**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Newborn Screening (NBS)**
    ◦ The **cornerstone of diagnosis**. A blood spot is collected from a heel prick, typically 24-48 hours after birth.
    ◦ Programs either measure **TSH first** or **T4 first** with reflex TSH if T4 is low.
    ◦ An **elevated TSH** and/or **low T4** on the screen is considered a positive result.
• **Confirmatory Serum Testing**
    ◦ An abnormal NBS requires **immediate** confirmatory venous blood draw.
    ◦ **Primary CH (hallmark)**: **High TSH** and **Low Free T4 (FT4)**.
    ◦ **Central CH**: **Low or inappropriately normal TSH** and **Low FT4**.
• **Etiology Determination** (performed after treatment is initiated to avoid delay)
    ◦ **Thyroid Ultrasound**: First-line imaging to assess for the presence, size, and location of the thyroid gland. Non-invasive and readily available.
    ◦ **Radionuclide Scintigraphy Scan** (Technetium-99m or Iodine-123): **Gold standard** for determining etiology.
        ▪ Differentiates between **aplasia** (no uptake), **hypoplasia** (minimal uptake), and an **ectopic gland** (uptake in an abnormal location, e.g., sublingual).
        ▪ Low uptake with a present gland suggests **dyshormonogenesis**.
    ◦ **Bone Age X-ray (knee)**: May show **delayed bone maturation** (absence of distal femoral epiphysis), indicating prenatal onset of hypothyroidism.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** if detected by newborn screening and treated appropriately within the **first 2 weeks of life**.
• Children can achieve **normal intelligence, growth, and development**.
• Prognosis is **poorer** if treatment is **delayed past 4-6 weeks of life** or if management is inconsistent.

sections.overview:
• **Delayed puberty** is defined as the absence of the initial signs of sexual maturation at an age that is more than 2 to 2.5 standard deviations above the population mean.
• It is a common reason for referral to pediatric endocrinology, with the evaluation aiming to differentiate the most common cause, **Constitutional Delay of Growth and Puberty (CDGP)**, from more serious permanent causes.
    ◦ **In Girls:** Absence of breast development (**thelarche**) by age 13 OR absence of menstruation (**menarche**) by age 15.
    ◦ **In Boys:** Absence of testicular enlargement (4 mL volume or 2.5 cm length) by age 14.
• The underlying pathophysiology is categorized into two main groups based on gonadotropin (**LH/FSH**) levels:
    ◦ **Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism (Central):**
        ▪ **Low/normal LH & FSH**.
        ▪ The problem is in the hypothalamus or pituitary. The "signal" to start puberty is absent or insufficient.
    ◦ **Hypergonadotropic Hypogonadism (Primary):**
        ▪ **High LH & FSH**.
        ▪ The problem is in the gonads (testes/ovaries). The pituitary is sending the signal, but the gonads are unable to respond.
sections.etiology:
• The timing of puberty is controlled by the pulsatile release of **Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH)** from the hypothalamus, which stimulates the pituitary to release **Luteinizing Hormone (LH)** and **Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH)**. These gonadotropins act on the gonads to produce sex steroids (testosterone and estrogen).
• **1. Functional Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism (Central & Reversible)**
    ◦ This is a temporary suppression of the Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal (HPG) axis.
    ◦ **Constitutional Delay of Growth and Puberty (CDGP):**
        ▪ The most common cause of delayed puberty overall, especially in boys.
        ▪ It is a benign, often familial, variation of normal development where the HPG axis matures late.
        ▪ Growth velocity slows in the years leading up to puberty, but eventual adult height and sexual development are normal.
    ◦ **Systemic Chronic Illness:**
        ▪ Conditions like inflammatory bowel disease (**Crohn's**), **cystic fibrosis**, **celiac disease**, or chronic kidney disease can suppress the HPG axis due to inflammation and poor nutrition.
    ◦ **Malnutrition / Eating Disorders:**
        ▪ **Anorexia nervosa** or extreme dieting leads to energy deficits that suppress GnRH release.
    ◦ **Excessive Physical Exercise:**
        ▪ Common in elite athletes; high energy expenditure and low body fat suppress the HPG axis.
• **2. Permanent Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism (Central & Permanent)**
    ◦ The HPG axis is permanently impaired.
    ◦ **Congenital:**
        ▪ **Kallmann Syndrome:** Defective migration of GnRH neurons, classically associated with **anosmia** (inability to smell).
        ▪ **Idiopathic Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism (IHH):** GnRH deficiency without anosmia.
        ▪ **Prader-Willi Syndrome, Laurence-Moon Syndrome.**
    ◦ **Acquired:**
        ▪ **CNS Tumors:** **Craniopharyngioma** is the most common tumor causing delayed puberty. Pituitary adenomas (e.g., **prolactinoma**) can also be a cause.
        ▪ **CNS Damage:** Brain radiation, trauma, or severe infection.
• **3. Hypergonadotropic Hypogonadism (Primary Gonadal Failure)**
    ◦ The gonads fail to produce sex steroids despite adequate stimulation from the pituitary (**high FSH/LH**).
    ◦ **Congenital:**
        ▪ **Turner Syndrome (45,XO):** Most common cause of primary ovarian failure in girls.
        ▪ **Klinefelter Syndrome (47,XXY):** Most common congenital cause of primary testicular failure in boys.
        ▪ **Other:** Testicular/ovarian dysgenesis, androgen insensitivity syndrome.
    ◦ **Acquired:**
        ▪ **Chemotherapy/Radiation:** Gonadotoxic treatments for cancer.
        ▪ **Autoimmune Damage:** Autoimmune oophoritis or orchitis.
        ▪ **Trauma/Surgery:** Testicular torsion, orchiectomy.
        ▪ **Infection:** Mumps orchitis.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Delayed puberty** affects approximately 2% of adolescents.
• **CDGP** is the most common cause in boys (~65%) and a significant cause in girls (~30%).
• In girls, **Turner Syndrome** is a primary cause to consider.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents due to concerns from parents or the patient about **short stature** compared to peers and a lack of **secondary sexual characteristics**.
• **Psychosocial distress**, including **anxiety**, **poor body image**, and **bullying**, is a common co-presentation.
sections.diagnostics:
• The diagnostic approach is stepwise, designed to first confirm the delay and then differentiate between the major etiological categories.
• **Step 1: Initial Evaluation**
    ◦ **Bone Age X-ray (Left hand and wrist):**
        ▪ **Delayed Bone Age:** The skeletal age is younger than the chronological age. Highly characteristic of **CDGP** and other functional central causes.
        ▪ **Normal Bone Age:** The skeletal age matches the chronological age. More concerning for **primary gonadal failure** or a permanent central cause.
    ◦ **Initial Laboratory Panel:**
        ▪ **LH, FSH:** The most crucial test to differentiate central vs. primary causes.
        ▪ **Testosterone (boys) / Estradiol (girls):** Will be low in all cases; confirms hypogonadism.
        ▪ **Screening labs for systemic disease:** CBC, CMP, ESR/CRP, TSH, Free T4, Prolactin, IGF-1 (for growth hormone deficiency).
• **Step 2: Interpreting Initial Hormones**
    ◦ **Low/Normal FSH & LH + Low Sex Steroids (Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism - Central Cause)**
        ▪ If bone age is delayed and H&P is suggestive, **CDGP** is likely. Observation may be sufficient.
        ▪ If bone age is normal or neurologic symptoms are present, proceed to brain imaging.
    ◦ **High FSH & LH + Low Sex Steroids (Hypergonadotropic Hypogonadism - Primary Gonadal Failure)**
        ▪ This indicates the problem is with the ovaries or testes. Proceed to karyotyping.
• **Step 3: Confirmatory & Second-Line Testing**
    ◦ **Karyotype Analysis:**
        ▪ Ordered if primary gonadal failure is suspected (**high FSH/LH**).
        ▪ Confirms **Turner Syndrome (45,XO)** or **Klinefelter Syndrome (47,XXY)**.
    ◦ **Brain/Pituitary MRI:**
        ▪ Ordered if a permanent central cause is suspected (e.g., neurologic symptoms, very low/absent gonadotropins, other pituitary hormone deficiencies).
        ▪ Rules out tumors like **craniopharyngioma** or structural defects.
    ◦ **GnRH Stimulation Test:**
        ▪ Can help differentiate **CDGP** from permanent central causes.
        ▪ In **CDGP**, there is typically a pubertal (though blunted) LH response, whereas in permanent IHH, the response is minimal or absent.
sections.prognosis:
• **CDGP:** Excellent. Patients will progress through puberty spontaneously and achieve a normal adult height and full fertility, although they may be slightly shorter on average than their genetic potential.
• **Permanent Causes:** Prognosis depends on the underlying etiology. With appropriate hormone replacement, patients can develop normal secondary sexual characteristics and lead healthy lives. However, **infertility** often remains a major issue.

sections.overview:
• **Precocious Puberty (PP)** is the onset of secondary sexual characteristics before the age of **8 in girls** and **9 in boys**.
    ◦ Represents a premature activation of the reproductive endocrine system.
• Categorized into two main types:
    ◦ **Central Precocious Puberty (CPP)**: **GnRH-dependent**
    ◦ **Peripheral Precocious Puberty (PPP)**: **GnRH-independent**
• Primary goals of evaluation:
    ◦ Identify the underlying cause.
    ◦ Determine the need for treatment to preserve **adult height** and mitigate **psychosocial distress**.
sections.etiology: • Classification is based on the point of activation in the **hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Affects approximately 1 in 5,000 to 1 in 10,000 children.
• **Sex**: Much more common in **girls** than boys (ratio ~10:1).
• **Etiology by Sex**:
    ◦ **Girls**: Over 90% of CPP cases are **idiopathic**.
    ◦ **Boys**: CPP is more likely to be caused by an underlying **CNS pathology** (~50% of cases).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A parent or guardian typically brings the child in for evaluation due to the early appearance of **secondary sexual characteristics**.
• History should focus on:
    ◦ Timing and sequence of pubertal development
    ◦ **Growth velocity**
    ◦ Potential exposures to **exogenous hormones**
• A key part of the history is differentiating **true puberty** (e.g., breast development and pubic hair) from **isolated variants** (e.g., only breast development).
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• **Idiopathic CPP**:
    ◦ **Excellent prognosis** with treatment.
    ◦ Most children achieve a **normal final adult height** and have **normal reproductive function** later in life.
• **PPP or secondary CPP**:
    ◦ Prognosis depends entirely on the **underlying etiology**.

sections.overview:
• Growth Hormone Deficiency (GHD) is a clinical syndrome caused by insufficient secretion of growth hormone (GH) from the anterior pituitary gland.
• It can be congenital or acquired and can manifest in childhood or adulthood.
• In children, it is characterized by **growth failure** and **short stature**.
• In adults, it presents with more subtle findings, including changes in body composition, reduced bone density, and impaired quality of life.
• Diagnosis requires provocative hormonal testing, and treatment involves replacement with recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH).
sections.etiology:
• GH is secreted in a pulsatile fashion by somatotroph cells in the anterior pituitary, primarily under the control of Growth Hormone-Releasing Hormone (GHRH) (stimulatory) and Somatostatin (inhibitory).
• GH acts on the liver and other tissues to produce Insulin-like Growth Factor 1 (IGF-1), which mediates most of the growth-promoting effects of GH.
• **Pathophysiology**: A disruption at any point in the hypothalamic-pituitary-somatotropic axis can cause GHD.
• **Etiologies**:
    ◦ **Congenital (Childhood-Onset)**:
        ▪ **Idiopathic**: Most common cause; no identifiable lesion.
        ▪ **Genetic**: Mutations in genes controlling pituitary development (e.g., *PROP1*, *POU1F1*) or the GH/GHRH pathway.
        ▪ **Structural CNS Defects**:
            • Septo-optic dysplasia
            • Holoprosencephaly
            • Empty sella syndrome
            • Pituitary hypoplasia or aplasia
    ◦ **Acquired (Childhood or Adult-Onset)**:
        ▪ **Pituitary/Hypothalamic Tumors**:
            • **Craniopharyngioma** (most common cause in children)
            • **Pituitary adenoma** (most common cause in adults)
            • Meningioma, glioma, germinoma
        ▪ **Cranial Irradiation**: Treatment for brain tumors or leukemia; causes delayed pituitary dysfunction.
        ▪ **Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI) / Subarachnoid Hemorrhage**: Can damage the pituitary stalk or gland.
        ▪ **Infiltrative/Inflammatory Diseases**:
            • Sarcoidosis
            • Langerhans cell histiocytosis
            • Autoimmune hypophysitis
        ▪ **Infections**: Tuberculosis, meningitis.
        ▪ **Infarction/Hemorrhage**: Sheehan's syndrome (postpartum pituitary necrosis), pituitary apoplexy.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Childhood-Onset GHD (CO-GHD)**: Affects approximately 1 in 4,000 to 1 in 10,000 children.
• **Adult-Onset GHD (AO-GHD)**: Prevalence is estimated at 10-30 cases per million per year, often secondary to pituitary adenomas or their treatment.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation varies significantly based on the age of onset.
    ◦ **Childhood-Onset**:
        ▪ A child presents with concerns of **growth failure**.
        ▪ Parents often notice their child is significantly shorter than peers or not outgrowing clothes.
        ▪ The key feature is a **decreased growth velocity** (crossing percentile lines downward on the growth chart).
    ◦ **Adult-Onset**:
        ▪ An adult presents with **vague, non-specific symptoms**.
        ▪ They may complain of persistent fatigue, low energy, poor mood, and notice changes such as increased abdominal fat.
        ▪ The presentation is often insidious and may be identified during workup for a known pituitary lesion.
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis involves a multi-step process; a single random GH level is useless due to its pulsatile secretion.
• **Initial Screening/Workup (Children)**:
    ◦ **Growth Chart Analysis**: Document **decreased growth velocity** (<5 cm/year in pre-pubertal children).
    ◦ **Bone Age X-ray**: Left hand and wrist X-ray.
        ▪ In GHD, **bone age is delayed** compared to chronological age.
    ◦ **Screening Labs** to rule out other causes of short stature:
        ▪ CBC, CMP, ESR/CRP
        ▪ TSH, Free T4 (hypothyroidism)
        ▪ Karyotype (in girls to rule out Turner Syndrome)
        ▪ Celiac panel (tTG-IgA)
    ◦ **IGF-1 and IGFBP-3 Levels**:
        ▪ These are GH-dependent proteins with longer half-lives than GH, providing an integrated measure of GH secretion.
        ▪ **Low levels** are suggestive of GHD but are not diagnostic on their own (low sensitivity/specificity).
• **Confirmatory Testing: GH Stimulation (Provocative) Tests**:
    ◦ **Indication**: Required to confirm the diagnosis by stimulating the pituitary to release GH and measuring the peak response.
    ◦ **Procedure**: A pharmacologic agent is administered, and blood is drawn at set intervals (e.g., 0, 30, 60, 90, 120 min) to measure GH levels.
    ◦ **Common Agents**:
        ▪ **Insulin Tolerance Test (ITT)**: **Gold standard**. Insulin is given to induce hypoglycemia (glucose <40 mg/dL), a potent stimulus for GH release.
            • *Contraindicated in patients with seizure disorders or coronary artery disease.*
        ▪ **Arginine and/or GHRH Test**: Safer alternatives to ITT.
        ▪ Glucagon, Clonidine, L-DOPA.
    ◦ **Diagnostic Criteria**: Failure of GH to rise above a certain threshold (e.g., <5-10 ng/mL, depending on the assay and protocol) confirms the diagnosis.
        ▪ Most pediatric endocrinologists require **two failed stimulation tests**.
• **Imaging**:
    ◦ **Brain/Pituitary MRI with contrast**: Performed **after** biochemical confirmation of GHD to look for an underlying structural cause (e.g., tumor, empty sella, pituitary hypoplasia).
sections.prognosis:
• **Childhood-Onset**: With early diagnosis and consistent treatment, most children can achieve a final adult height within the normal range, often close to their genetic potential (mid-parental height).
• **Adult-Onset**: Treatment with rhGH can improve body composition, bone density, exercise capacity, and overall quality of life. Effects on mortality are still being studied, but treating associated metabolic disturbances is beneficial.

sections.overview:
• Turner Syndrome (TS) is a genetic disorder affecting individuals with a female phenotype, caused by the complete or partial absence of one X chromosome.
• The core endocrine features are **primary ovarian insufficiency** leading to **hypergonadotropic hypogonadism**, and **short stature**.
• Patients have an increased prevalence of other endocrinopathies, most notably autoimmune hypothyroidism and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Classic Monosomy X (45,X)**: Accounts for approximately 50% of cases, caused by meiotic nondisjunction, typically during paternal gametogenesis, and is not associated with advanced parental age.
    ◦ **Mosaicism (e.g., 45,X / 46,XX)**: Represents approximately 30-40% of cases, involving two or more cell lines, and often results in a milder phenotype.
    ◦ **Structural Abnormalities of the X Chromosome**: Examples include isochromosome Xq (two long arms) or ring chromosome X.
• **Pathophysiology of Endocrine Manifestations**
    ◦ **Gonadal Dysgenesis (Primary Ovarian Insufficiency)**
        ▪ The absence of the second X chromosome leads to accelerated oocyte atresia (apoptosis) during fetal development.
        ▪ Normal ovaries are replaced by bilateral streaks of fibrous tissue ("**streak ovaries**") with few to no remaining follicles.
        ▪ This results in a failure to produce ovarian hormones (estrogen, progesterone) and inhibin B.
        ▪ The lack of negative feedback on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis leads to chronically elevated **FSH and LH** levels (**Hypergonadotropic Hypogonadism**).
    ◦ **Short Stature**
        ▪ Primarily caused by haploinsufficiency of the **SHOX (Short stature HomeobOX) gene**, located on the distal tip of the short arm of the X chromosome.
        ▪ The SHOX gene is crucial for normal long bone growth; having only one copy impairs chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation at the growth plates.
        ▪ This is not a primary growth hormone (GH) deficiency, although GH is the cornerstone of treatment.
    ◦ **Autoimmune Disease**
        ▪ Patients with TS have a higher incidence of autoimmune disorders, particularly **Hashimoto's thyroiditis**.
        ▪ The mechanism is thought to be related to X-linked genes involved in immune tolerance and regulation.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Affects approximately 1 in 2,000 to 1 in 2,500 live female births.
• It is one of the most common sex chromosome abnormalities.
• TS is a very common cause of first-trimester spontaneous abortion, accounting for ~10% of all miscarriages.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation varies by age:
    ◦ **Prenatal**: Abnormal ultrasound findings like **cystic hygroma**, nuchal edema, or hydrops fetalis.
    ◦ **Neonate**: Lymphedema of the hands and feet (puffy appearance), webbed neck (pterygium colli).
    ◦ **Childhood**: **Short stature** is the most common and often the only presenting sign; recurrent otitis media, hearing loss.
    ◦ **Adolescence / Adulthood**: The classic endocrine presentation includes **primary amenorrhea** (failure to menstruate by age 15) and **lack of secondary sexual development** (e.g., failure of breast development).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Definitive Diagnosis**
    ◦ **Karyotype Analysis**: Peripheral blood lymphocyte karyotype is the **gold standard** to confirm 45,X, mosaicism, or structural variants.
• **Endocrine Workup**
    ◦ **Gonadotropins**: **Elevated serum FSH and LH** confirms a hypergonadotropic state, often dramatically high.
    ◦ **Ovarian Hormones**: **Low serum estradiol**.
    ◦ **Ovarian Reserve Markers**: Undetectable or very low **Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH)** and **Inhibin B**.
    ◦ **Thyroid Function**: **TSH and free T4** to screen for autoimmune hypothyroidism (annually).
    ◦ **Metabolic Screen**: **HbA1c** and/or fasting glucose to screen for diabetes (annually after age 10); fasting lipid panel.
• **Associated Anomaly Screening**
    ◦ **Cardiac**: **Echocardiogram** and **cardiac MRI** at diagnosis for all patients to screen for bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation, and aortic root dilation.
    ◦ **Renal**: **Renal ultrasound** at diagnosis to screen for **horseshoe kidney** and other urinary tract anomalies.
    ◦ **Skeletal**: **Bone age X-ray** (left wrist/hand) to assess skeletal maturity. **DEXA scan** in adulthood to monitor for osteoporosis.
sections.prognosis:
• With modern, comprehensive care (GH, HRT, and cardiovascular surveillance), the prognosis is generally good.
• Life expectancy may be slightly reduced, primarily due to the risk of aortic dissection.
• Most individuals can lead healthy, productive lives. Infertility is a major psychosocial issue but does not preclude parenthood through adoption or oocyte donation.

sections.overview:
• Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1 (MEN1), also known as **Wermer's Syndrome**, is a rare, **autosomal dominant** inherited disorder characterized by the development of tumors in multiple endocrine glands.
• The classic triad of affected glands is known as the **"3 Ps"**:
    ◦ **P**arathyroid
    ◦ Anterior **P**ituitary
    ◦ **P**ancreatic neuroendocrine tumors
• Patients may also develop other tumors, including:
    ◦ **Carcinoid tumors**
    ◦ **Adrenal cortical tumors**
    ◦ Skin lesions like **angiofibromas**
sections.etiology:
• **Genetic Mutation**: Caused by a germline mutation in the ***MEN1*** **gene**, located on chromosome **11q13**.
• **Gene Product**: The *MEN1* gene codes for the protein **menin**, which acts as a **tumor suppressor**.
• **Mechanism**: The disease follows **Knudson's "two-hit" hypothesis**:
    ◦ **First Hit**: An individual inherits one mutated (non-functional) copy of the *MEN1* gene in every cell (germline mutation).
    ◦ **Second Hit**: A second, spontaneous (somatic) mutation occurs in the remaining normal copy of the *MEN1* gene within a specific endocrine cell.
    ◦ This loss of both functional copies of the tumor suppressor gene leads to uncontrolled cell proliferation and tumor formation.
• **Inheritance Pattern**: **Autosomal dominant** with high penetrance (>95% by age 50).
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Rare, affecting approximately 1 in 30,000 individuals.
• **Demographics**: Affects males and females equally, with no racial or ethnic predilection.
• **Age of Onset**:
    ◦ Clinical manifestations typically begin in early adulthood (20s-40s), although tumors can develop at any age.
    ◦ **Hyperparathyroidism** is often the first biochemical sign, appearing as early as the teenage years.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The clinical presentation is highly variable and depends on which tumors are present and hormonally active.
• A classic vignette might describe a young adult with **recurrent nephrolithiasis** (from hypercalcemia) and **refractory peptic ulcer disease** (from a gastrinoma).
• The sequence of tumor development varies, but **hyperparathyroidism** is the most common and usually the first manifestation.
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is made based on clinical, biochemical, and genetic criteria.
• **Clinical Criteria**: Presence of 2 of the 3 main MEN1-associated tumors:
    ◦ Parathyroid
    ◦ Pancreatic
    ◦ Pituitary
• **Familial Criteria**: Presence of 1 MEN1-associated tumor in a patient who is a first-degree relative of a known MEN1 patient.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is generally good, but life expectancy is reduced compared to the general population.
• Mortality is primarily driven by **malignant neuroendocrine tumors**, which have metastatic potential, especially:
    ◦ **Duodenopancreatic tumors**
    ◦ **Thymic carcinoid tumors**
• **Hyperparathyroidism** is the most common feature but is rarely a cause of death.

sections.overview:
• Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia (MEN) syndromes are a group of autosomal dominant disorders characterized by the development of tumors in multiple endocrine glands.
• MEN Type 2 is subdivided into MEN 2A and MEN 2B, both caused by mutations in the *RET* proto-oncogene.
    ◦ The key distinction lies in the specific constellation of tumors and clinical features.
• **MEN Type 2A (Sipple Syndrome)**
    ◦ The most common form (~95% of MEN 2 cases).
    ◦ Characterized by the triad of:
        ▪ **M**edullary **T**hyroid **C**arcinoma (MTC) - Occurs in >95% of patients.
        ▪ **P**heochromocytoma - Occurs in ~50% of patients.
        ▪ **P**rimary **H**yperparathyroidism (PHP) - Occurs in ~20-30% of patients.
• **MEN Type 2B**
    ◦ A rarer, more aggressive variant (~5% of MEN 2 cases).
    ◦ Characterized by:
        ▪ **M**edullary **T**hyroid **C**arcinoma (MTC) - Aggressive, early onset. Occurs in 100% of untreated patients.
        ▪ **P**heochromocytoma - Occurs in ~50% of patients.
        ▪ **Mucocutaneous Manifestations**: Mucosal neuromas (lips, tongue, eyelids), intestinal ganglioneuromatosis, and a characteristic **Marfanoid habitus**.
    ◦ Note: Primary hyperparathyroidism is notably **absent** in MEN 2B.
sections.etiology:
• **Genetic Cause**: Caused by a **gain-of-function mutation** in the ***RET*** **proto-oncogene** located on chromosome 10.
• **Inheritance**: Autosomal Dominant with high penetrance.
    ◦ Approximately 50% of cases are familial, and 50% arise from a *de novo* mutation (especially common in MEN 2B).
• **Mechanism**
    ◦ The *RET* gene codes for a receptor tyrosine kinase.
    ◦ The mutation causes constitutive (constant) activation of this receptor, leading to uncontrolled cell growth and tumor formation in specific neuroendocrine cell lines (thyroid C-cells, adrenal medullary cells, parathyroid cells).
• **Genotype-Phenotype Correlation**
    ◦ **MEN 2A**: Most commonly associated with a mutation in **codon 634**.
    ◦ **MEN 2B**: >95% of cases are caused by a specific mutation, **M918T**, in **codon 918**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Rare, affecting approximately 1 in 35,000 individuals.
• **Distribution**
    ◦ MEN 2A accounts for ~95% of all MEN 2 cases.
    ◦ MEN 2B accounts for ~5%.
• **Presentation**
    ◦ MTC is the first and most common manifestation in both subtypes.
    ◦ In MEN 2A, MTC typically presents in early adulthood.
    ◦ In MEN 2B, MTC presents much earlier, often in early childhood, and is more aggressive.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation depends on which tumors are hormonally active. Patients may present due to symptoms of one tumor, a palpable neck mass, findings on family screening, or from the characteristic physical features of MEN 2B.
• **MEN 2A**
    ◦ A patient in their 20s or 30s presents with a firm thyroid nodule. Workup reveals MTC. Further screening uncovers bilateral pheochromocytomas and hypercalcemia due to hyperparathyroidism.
• **MEN 2B**
    ◦ A child or adolescent is evaluated for developmental concerns or GI issues (constipation/diarrhea). The clinician notes thick, bumpy lips, a tall, slender build, and a palpable thyroid nodule. This prompts genetic testing and confirms the diagnosis.
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis relies on a combination of biochemical testing, imaging, and definitive genetic testing.
• **Genetic Testing**
    ◦ **Gold Standard**: ***RET*** **proto-oncogene analysis** confirms the diagnosis and is used to screen at-risk family members.
• **Biochemical Screening** (Annual screening for known carriers)
    ◦ **For MTC**:
        ▪ Serum **calcitonin**. A high basal level is highly suggestive.
        ▪ A pentagastrin or calcium stimulation test can be used if basal levels are equivocal.
        ▪ Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is also a useful tumor marker.
    ◦ **For Pheochromocytoma**:
        ▪ Plasma **free metanephrines** or 24-hour urine fractionated metanephrines and catecholamines.
    ◦ **For Primary Hyperparathyroidism (MEN 2A)**:
        ▪ Serum **calcium** and intact **parathyroid hormone (PTH)**.
        ▪ Expect high or inappropriately normal PTH in the setting of hypercalcemia.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Neck Ultrasound**: To evaluate the thyroid and cervical lymph nodes for MTC.
    ◦ **CT or MRI of the Abdomen/Pelvis**: To locate pheochromocytomas (often bilateral in MEN 2).
    ◦ **Parathyroid Imaging**: Sestamibi scan or neck ultrasound may be used pre-operatively but often not necessary as the surgeon will typically explore all four glands.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is almost entirely dependent on the stage of MTC at the time of diagnosis.
• With early detection through genetic screening and **prophylactic thyroidectomy**, the prognosis is excellent.
• MEN 2B has a worse prognosis than MEN 2A due to the earlier onset and more aggressive nature of MTC.

sections.overview:
• **Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma (MTC)** is a neuroendocrine tumor arising from the **parafollicular C-cells** of the thyroid gland.
    ◦ These cells are responsible for producing **calcitonin**.
    ◦ Unlike papillary and follicular thyroid cancers which arise from follicular cells, MTC does not concentrate iodine.
• Approximately 25% of MTC cases are hereditary, occurring as a component of **Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia (MEN) type 2A** or **2B**, or as **Familial Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma (FMTC)**.
    ◦ The hereditary forms are caused by a germline mutation in the ***RET* proto-oncogene**.
sections.etiology:
• **Cell of Origin:** **Parafollicular cells (C-cells)** of the thyroid, which are derived from the neural crest.
• **Genetic Basis:** All hereditary MTC is caused by an autosomal dominant, gain-of-function mutation in the **`RET` proto-oncogene** on chromosome 10.
• **Pathogenesis:** The `RET` mutation leads to constitutive activation of the RET tyrosine kinase receptor, promoting uncontrolled cell growth and proliferation.
• **Precursor Lesion:** In hereditary MTC, the carcinoma is preceded by a premalignant phase of **C-cell hyperplasia**. This is a key histological distinction from sporadic MTC, which arises de novo.
• **MEN Syndromes:**
    ◦ **MEN 2A:** The most common hereditary form (~90%). Characterized by MTC, **pheochromocytoma** (~50%), and primary **hyperparathyroidism** (~20-30%). MTC is typically the first manifestation.
    ◦ **MEN 2B:** More aggressive variant. Characterized by MTC (100%), **pheochromocytoma** (~50%), **mucosal neuromas**, and a **marfanoid habitus**. MTC in MEN2B presents earlier and is more aggressive than in MEN2A.
    ◦ **Familial Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma (FMTC):** A variant of MEN2A where MTC is the only clinical feature.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** Accounts for 3-5% of all thyroid malignancies.
• **Hereditary vs. Sporadic:**
    ◦ ~75% are **sporadic** (occur in individuals without a predisposing mutation).
    ◦ ~25% are **hereditary** (*RET* mutation-related).
• **Age of Onset:**
    ◦ **Sporadic:** Typically presents in the 5th or 6th decade.
    ◦ **MEN 2A:** Presents in young adulthood (20s-30s).
    ◦ **MEN 2B:** Presents in early childhood, often in the first few years of life.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Primary Risk Factor:** A germline mutation in the **`RET` proto-oncogene**.
• **Family History:** A first-degree relative with MTC, **MEN 2A**, or **MEN 2B**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation varies based on whether it is sporadic or part of a MEN syndrome.
• **Thyroid-related:**
    ◦ Most commonly presents as a solitary, painless, firm **thyroid nodule** or mass in the neck.
    ◦ **Hoarseness**, **dysphagia**, or **dyspnea** due to compression or invasion of local structures.
• **Metastatic Symptoms:**
    ◦ **Cervical lymphadenopathy** is common at presentation (up to 75%).
    ◦ Can also present with symptoms of distant metastases (bone, lung, liver).
• **Hormonal Excess:**
    ◦ High **calcitonin** levels can cause secretory **watery diarrhea** and flushing.
    ◦ MTC can ectopically produce other hormones like ACTH (**Cushing's syndrome**) or vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP).
• **Associated MEN Syndrome Features:**
    ◦ **MEN 2A:** Symptoms of **hyperparathyroidism** ("stones, bones, abdominal groans, and psychiatric overtones") or **pheochromocytoma** (paroxysmal hypertension, palpitations, headache, diaphoresis).
    ◦ **MEN 2B:** Classic physical stigmata are often present from birth or early childhood.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Neck:**
    ◦ A firm, fixed, non-tender **nodule** in the thyroid gland.
    ◦ Palpable **cervical lymphadenopathy**.
• **MEN 2B Specific Findings:**
    ◦ **Mucosal Neuromas:** Bumpy, fleshy nodules on the lips, tongue, and buccal mucosa.
    ◦ **Marfanoid Habitus:** Tall, slender body type with long limbs (high arm-span-to-height ratio).
    ◦ **Ocular:** Thickened corneal nerves (visible on slit-lamp exam).
    ◦ **Skeletal:** High-arched palate, pectus excavatum, scoliosis.
• **Associated Findings:**
    ◦ Check blood pressure and heart rate for evidence of **pheochromocytoma**.
sections.diagnostics:
• A diagnosis of MTC necessitates a full workup for a MEN syndrome.
• **Initial Nodule Evaluation:**
    ◦ **Thyroid Ultrasound:** To characterize the nodule(s) and assess for suspicious lymph nodes.
    ◦ **Fine-Needle Aspiration (FNA):** The primary diagnostic tool.
        ▪ **Cytology:** Spindle-shaped or polygonal cells with "salt and pepper" chromatin.
        ▪ **Amyloid:** Pathognomonic finding of **amyloid deposits** in the stroma (Congo red stain shows apple-green birefringence under polarized light).
• **Biochemical Markers:**
    ◦ **Serum Calcitonin:** **The most important tumor marker.** Levels >100 pg/mL are highly suggestive of MTC. Used for diagnosis, staging, and post-operative surveillance.
    ◦ **Carcinoembryonic Antigen (CEA):** Also elevated and used for surveillance. A rapidly rising CEA indicates a poor prognosis.
• **MEN Syndrome Workup (MANDATORY before surgery):**
    ◦ **Pheochromocytoma Screening:** Plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines.
        ▪ **A pheochromocytoma MUST be ruled out or treated before any surgery to prevent intraoperative hypertensive crisis.**
    ◦ **Hyperparathyroidism Screening:** Serum calcium and parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels.
• **Genetic Testing:**
    ◦ **`RET` Proto-oncogene Analysis:** Should be performed on all patients diagnosed with MTC to identify a germline mutation. If positive, genetic counseling and screening of first-degree relatives is indicated.
• **Staging:**
    ◦ **Neck Ultrasound:** To map cervical lymph nodes.
    ◦ **CT Scan (Neck/Chest/Abdomen) / MRI:** For advanced local disease or suspected distant metastases.
sections.treatment:
• If a **pheochromocytoma** is present, it **MUST be resected first**.
    ◦ Requires pre-operative alpha-adrenergic blockade (e.g., phenoxybenzamine) followed by beta-blockade to control blood pressure and prevent catastrophic hypertensive crisis during thyroid surgery.
• If **hyperparathyroidism** is present, abnormal parathyroid glands are typically removed during the thyroidectomy.
• **Total Thyroidectomy:** Is always the procedure of choice.
• **Central Compartment Neck Dissection:** Prophylactic bilateral central node dissection is standard due to the high rate of early nodal metastasis.
• **Lateral Neck Dissection:** Performed if there is evidence of metastasis to the lateral lymph nodes.
• **Radioactive Iodine (RAI):** **NOT effective.** C-cells do not take up iodine.
• **External Beam Radiation Therapy (EBRT):** May be used for unresectable, recurrent, or residual disease.
• **Systemic Therapy:** Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors (TKIs) that target `RET`, such as **Vandetanib** and **Cabozantinib**, are used for progressive, metastatic disease.
sections.management:
• **Lifelong Surveillance:**
    ◦ Regular monitoring of serum **calcitonin and CEA** levels (e.g., every 6 months). The doubling time of these markers is a strong prognostic indicator.
    ◦ Neck ultrasound to monitor for recurrence.
• **Hormone Replacement:** Lifelong levothyroxine replacement after total thyroidectomy.
• **Genetic Counseling & Family Screening:**
    ◦ All first-degree relatives of a patient with a proven `RET` mutation should undergo genetic testing.
    ◦ **Prophylactic Thyroidectomy:** For family members who test positive for the `RET` mutation. The age for surgery depends on the specific mutation and associated risk (e.g., MEN2B carriers may undergo surgery in the first year of life; MEN2A carriers by age 5-6).
• **Ongoing MEN Surveillance:** Patients require lifelong screening for **pheochromocytoma** and **hyperparathyroidism**.
sections.complications:
• **Surgical Complications:** **Hypoparathyroidism** (transient or permanent), **recurrent laryngeal nerve injury** (hoarseness), bleeding.
• **Tumor-Related:** **Metastatic disease** (to lymph nodes, lung, liver, bone), spinal cord compression, uncontrolled diarrhea.
• **Syndrome-Related:** **Hypertensive crisis** from an undiagnosed **pheochromocytoma**, complications of **hypercalcemia**.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly dependent on the stage at diagnosis and the specific `RET` mutation.
• **MEN 2A:** Generally has a more favorable prognosis than MEN 2B or sporadic MTC due to screening and early intervention.
• **MEN 2B:** Has the most aggressive course and poorest prognosis.
• **Key Prognostic Factors:**
    ◦ Stage at diagnosis (presence of nodal or distant metastases).
    ◦ Post-operative calcitonin levels (undetectable is best).
    ◦ Calcitonin and CEA doubling times.

sections.overview:
• Cellulitis is an acute bacterial infection of the skin, specifically involving the **deeper dermis** and **subcutaneous tissue**
	◦ Characterized by spreading **erythema**, **edema**, **warmth**, and **tenderness**
	◦ Unlike erysipelas, cellulitis has **poorly defined borders**
	◦ A common reason for emergency department visits and hospital admissions
	◦ Typically results from a breach in the skin barrier, allowing pathogenic bacteria to invade
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**
	◦ **Breach in Skin Barrier**: The process begins with a disruption of the epidermis, such as a cut, abrasion, ulcer, insect bite, injection site, or underlying skin condition (e.g., tinea pedis, eczema)
	◦ **Bacterial Inoculation**: Pathogenic bacteria gain entry into the dermis and subcutaneous tissues
	◦ **Infection & Inflammation**: Bacteria multiply and spread along fascial planes, triggering a robust inflammatory response which manifests as the classic signs of erythema, edema, and warmth
• **Common Pathogens**
	◦ **Most Common Overall**
		▪ ***Streptococcus pyogenes*** (Group A Strep): The classic cause of rapidly spreading, **non-purulent cellulitis**
		▪ ***Staphylococcus aureus*** (including **MRSA**): More commonly associated with **purulent cellulitis** (abscess, furuncle) but can also cause non-purulent cellulitis
	◦ **Less Common but High-Yield Pathogens**
		▪ ***Pasteurella multocida***: Associated with **dog** or (especially) **cat bites**
		▪ ***Vibrio vulnificus***: Exposure to **saltwater** or handling raw seafood; can cause severe, **necrotizing cellulitis** with **hemorrhagic bullae**, particularly in patients with liver disease
		▪ ***Pseudomonas aeruginosa***: **Puncture wounds** through footwear ("sneaker puncture"), hot tub folliculitis, or in immunocompromised patients
		▪ ***Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae***: Handling **raw fish or meat** (common in fishermen, butchers)
		▪ ***Capnocytophaga canimorsus***: **Dog bites**, particularly in asplenic or alcoholic patients
sections.epidemiology:
• One of the **most common infectious diseases** seen in clinical practice
• Accounts for millions of ED visits and hundreds of thousands of hospitalizations annually in the U.S.
• Incidence **increases with age**, most commonly affecting middle-aged and older adults
• No significant predilection for sex or race, but risk factors heavily influence prevalence
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patient typically presents with the **acute onset** of a **red**, **swollen**, **warm**, and **painful** area of skin, most commonly on a **lower extremity**
	◦ The onset may have been preceded by a minor injury to the area
	◦ The erythema can spread rapidly over hours to days
• Systemic symptoms like **fever**, **chills**, and **malaise** may be present, suggesting a more severe infection
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primarily a clinical diagnosis**; laboratory and imaging studies are not required for typical, uncomplicated cases
• **Laboratory Studies** (Indicated for systemic toxicity, comorbidities, or failure to respond)
	◦ **CBC with differential**: May show **leukocytosis** with a **left shift**
	◦ **Inflammatory Markers (ESR, CRP)**: Will be elevated but are non-specific; can be used to track response to therapy
	◦ **Blood Cultures**: Low yield (<5%) but should be obtained in patients with signs of sepsis, extensive involvement, or severe immunocompromise
	◦ **Creatine Kinase (CK)**: Order if concerned for myositis or **necrotizing fasciitis** (will be markedly elevated)
• **Imaging** (Not routine; used to rule out other diagnoses)
	◦ **Ultrasound**: Excellent for differentiating simple cellulitis from an underlying **abscess** (will show a hypoechoic or complex fluid collection) or DVT
	◦ **X-ray**: Can identify **soft tissue gas** (suggesting **necrotizing fasciitis**) or underlying osteomyelitis
	◦ **CT/MRI**: More sensitive for deep space infections, abscesses, and **necrotizing fasciitis**; MRI is the most sensitive imaging modality for these complications
• **Microbiology**
	◦ **Wound Culture**: Only useful if there is an open wound, ulcer, or purulent drainage; cultures of intact skin are not recommended
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is **excellent** for uncomplicated cellulitis treated promptly and appropriately
• Most patients respond to antibiotics within **48-72 hours**
• Mortality is low but increases significantly if complications like **sepsis** or **necrotizing fasciitis** develop
• **Recurrence is common (~30%)**, especially in patients with persistent risk factors like lymphedema or venous insufficiency

sections.overview:
• Erysipelas is an acute, superficial bacterial skin infection involving the upper dermis and superficial cutaneous lymphatics.
    ◦ It is a distinct form of cellulitis characterized by a well-demarcated, raised, erythematous plaque with a "**cliff-drop**" border.
    ◦ It is most commonly caused by ***Streptococcus pyogenes*** and often associated with preceding systemic symptoms like fever and chills.
sections.etiology:
• **Primary Pathogen**
    ◦ **Group A β-hemolytic Streptococcus (*Streptococcus pyogenes*)** is responsible for the vast majority of cases.
    ◦ Less common: Group C or G Streptococcus.
    ◦ ***Staphylococcus aureus*** **is NOT a typical cause** of erysipelas, which helps differentiate it from non-purulent cellulitis and purulent skin infections like abscesses.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Portal of Entry**: Bacteria gain entry through a breach in the skin barrier (e.g., fissure from tinea pedis, insect bite, surgical incision, trauma, venous ulcer).
    ◦ **Infection & Spread**: The bacteria invade the upper dermis and rapidly spread through the superficial lymphatic vessels.
    ◦ **Inflammatory Response**: This lymphatic involvement leads to intense, localized erythema, edema, and warmth. The superficial nature of the infection creates the characteristic sharply defined, raised border.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Age**: Bimodal distribution, affecting primarily **infants, young children, and older adults (>60 years)**.
• **Location**
    ◦ **Lower extremities** are the most common site in adults (~80% of cases).
    ◦ **Face** is a classic location, especially in children, often presenting in a "malar" or "butterfly" distribution across the cheeks and nose.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Onset**: Acute and abrupt.
• **Prodrome**: Systemic symptoms such as **fever, chills, malaise, and headache** often precede the skin manifestations by 4-48 hours.
• **Skin Lesion**: A fiery-red, indurated, tender, and edematous plaque develops rapidly.
    ◦ The hallmark feature is a **sharply demarcated, raised, advancing border**.
    ◦ The skin is often described as having a "**peau d'orange**" (orange peel) texture due to lymphatic edema.
    ◦ Vesicles or bullae may form on the surface (bullous erysipelas).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primarily a clinical diagnosis.** History and physical exam are usually sufficient.
• **Laboratory Studies (not routinely needed for uncomplicated cases)**
    ◦ Indicated for systemically ill patients or to rule out sepsis.
        ▪ **CBC**: Leukocytosis with a left shift (neutrophilia).
        ▪ **ESR/CRP**: Markedly elevated, but non-specific.
        ▪ **Blood Cultures**: Low yield (<5%) but should be drawn in febrile, toxic-appearing, or immunocompromised patients.
• **Imaging (not routine)**
    ◦ Used to rule out deeper infections (e.g., abscess, necrotizing fasciitis).
        ▪ **Ultrasound**: Can show dermal thickening and cobblestoning but is often non-specific. Useful for identifying an underlying abscess.
        ▪ **MRI**: Best modality to evaluate for deep tissue involvement if necrotizing fasciitis is suspected.
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent with prompt and appropriate antibiotic therapy.
    ◦ Fever and systemic symptoms typically resolve within 24-48 hours of starting antibiotics.
    ◦ Skin findings improve more slowly over several days to weeks.
• Recurrence is the most common long-term issue, especially if underlying risk factors are not addressed.

sections.overview:
• Common, **highly contagious**, superficial bacterial infection of the **epidermis**
• One of the most frequent skin infections in **children**
• Classically presents in two main forms:
    ◦ **Non-bullous** (**crusted**)
    ◦ **Bullous** (**blistering**)
• A deeper, ulcerative form known as **ecthyma** also exists.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• **Age**: Most common in **children aged 2-5 years**
• **Geography**: More prevalent in **warm, humid climates** and during summer months
• **Setting**: Associated with **poverty**, **crowding**, and **poor personal hygiene**
• **Transmission**: Highly contagious via **direct person-to-person contact** or through **fomites** (e.g., towels, toys, clothing)
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Classic presentation involves a child with **erythematous papules** that evolve into **pustules** or **vesicles**
• These lesions rupture and form a **thick, adherent crust**
• Commonly affects the **face** (especially **perioral** and **perinasal** regions) or **extremities**
sections.diagnostics:
• Primarily a **clinical diagnosis** based on the characteristic appearance of the lesions
• **Gram stain and bacterial culture** are not routinely performed for uncomplicated cases
    ◦ **Indications**:
        ▪ Failure to respond to empiric antibiotic therapy
        ▪ Suspicion of **MRSA**
        ▪ Uncertain diagnosis
        ▪ Public health outbreaks
    ◦ **Procedure**:
        ▪ A swab is taken from the moist base of a **de-crusted lesion** or from the fluid within an intact **bulla**.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** prognosis; with appropriate treatment, most cases resolve within **7-10 days**
• **Non-bullous** and **bullous** forms typically heal **without scarring**
• **Ecthyma** often heals with **scarring**
• **Post-inflammatory pigmentary changes** may occur but usually resolve over time

sections.overview:
• Folliculitis is the inflammation of one or more hair follicles, which can occur anywhere on skin-bearing hair.
• The condition is typically characterized by small, erythematous, often pruritic or tender papules and pustules centered around a hair follicle.
• It can be superficial, involving only the upper part of the follicle, or deep, involving the entire follicle and surrounding dermis.
• While most cases are infectious, non-infectious causes also exist.
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**: The process begins with damage, occlusion, or irritation of the hair follicle, which disrupts the follicular epithelium, allowing microorganisms to invade and lead to an inflammatory response.
• **Etiology (by cause)**:
    ◦ **Bacterial**:
        ▪ **_Staphylococcus aureus_**: The most common infectious cause of folliculitis. Can be Methicillin-sensitive (MSSA) or Methicillin-resistant (MRSA).
        ▪ **_Pseudomonas aeruginosa_**: Classically associated with **"hot tub folliculitis,"** occurring 1-4 days after exposure to contaminated water in hot tubs, whirlpools, or swimming pools.
        ▪ **Gram-negative folliculitis**: Often seen in patients on long-term oral antibiotic therapy for acne vulgaris (e.g., tetracyclines), leading to an overgrowth of organisms like _Klebsiella_, _Enterobacter_, and _Proteus_.
    ◦ **Fungal**:
        ▪ **_Malassezia_ spp.** (formerly _Pityrosporum_): Causes **_Malassezia_ folliculitis**. A common cause of pruritic, monomorphic, acne-like papulopustules on the upper trunk and shoulders. It is technically a yeast.
        ▪ **Dermatophytes** (_Trichophyton_, _Microsporum_): Cause tinea infections that can involve the hair follicle, such as tinea barbae (beard) or tinea capitis (scalp). A deep, inflammatory dermatophyte infection is termed **Majocchi's granuloma**.
    ◦ **Viral**:
        ▪ **Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV)**: **Herpetic folliculitis** can occur, often after shaving, presenting as grouped vesicles or pustules on an erythematous base.
        ▪ **Molluscum contagiosum**: Can incite a follicular reaction.
    ◦ **Parasitic**:
        ▪ **_Demodex folliculorum_**: Mites that can cause a rosacea-like folliculitis.
    ◦ **Non-Infectious / Other**:
        ▪ **Mechanical folliculitis**: Due to friction from tight clothing or shaving (**"razor burn"**).
        ▪ **Occlusion folliculitis**: From topical products like greasy ointments, moisturizers, or industrial oils.
        ▪ **Drug-induced**: Most notably from systemic corticosteroids (**"steroid acne"**), but also lithium, phenytoin, and EGFR inhibitors.
        ▪ **Eosinophilic folliculitis**: An intensely pruritic eruption seen primarily in individuals with advanced **HIV infection** or other forms of immunosuppression.
sections.epidemiology:
• Folliculitis is extremely common and affects individuals of all ages, sexes, and races.
• **_S. aureus_** is the most frequent pathogen worldwide.
• **_Malassezia_ folliculitis** is more common in hot, humid climates and in young to middle-aged adults.
• **"Hot tub" folliculitis** occurs in outbreaks related to contaminated water sources.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation depends on the depth and etiology.
• A patient typically presents with a sudden eruption of **"pimples"** or **"red bumps"** in a hair-bearing area.
• The history should focus on:
    ◦ Recent activities (hot tub use)
    ◦ Shaving habits
    ◦ Current medications (especially antibiotics, steroids)
    ◦ Associated symptoms like itching or pain.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Usually a clinical diagnosis** based on history and physical exam.
• **Gram Stain and Bacterial Culture**:
    ◦ Recommended for recurrent, treatment-refractory, or severe cases.
    ◦ A sample is obtained by unroofing a pustule with a sterile needle or blade and swabbing the purulent material.
    ◦ Helps identify the pathogen and determine antibiotic sensitivities (especially for **MRSA**).
• **KOH Preparation**:
    ◦ Essential if fungal folliculitis is suspected.
    ◦ Lesion scrapings are examined under a microscope.
    ◦ **_Malassezia_**: Shows characteristic budding yeasts and short hyphae (**"spaghetti and meatballs"** appearance).
    ◦ **Dermatophytes**: Shows true, septate hyphae.
• **Viral Culture or PCR**: For suspected herpetic folliculitis.
• **Skin Biopsy**: Rarely necessary. Performed for persistent, atypical cases or to confirm eosinophilic folliculitis. Histology shows a perifollicular inflammatory infiltrate.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis for most cases of superficial folliculitis is excellent, with resolution within 1-2 weeks with proper treatment.
• Recurrence is common if underlying risk factors are not addressed.
• Deep folliculitis (**furuncles/carbuncles**) has a good prognosis with I&D and appropriate antibiotics but carries a higher risk of scarring and complications.

sections.overview:
• A **skin and soft tissue abscess** is a **localized collection of pus** within the **dermis** or **subcutaneous space**.
	◦ It is an **encapsulated infection** that is typically **tender**, **erythematous**, and **fluctuant**.
	◦ The definitive treatment is **incision and drainage (I&D)**.
sections.etiology:
• **Breach in Skin Barrier**
	◦ The process begins with the introduction of bacteria into the subcutaneous tissues via a **hair follicle**, **minor trauma** (e.g., abrasion, puncture wound), or obstruction of a **sebaceous** or **apocrine gland**.
• **Inflammatory Response**
	◦ The host's immune system responds by sending **neutrophils** to the site to combat the invading pathogens.
• **Liquefactive Necrosis**
	◦ Cytokines and bacterial toxins cause **liquefactive necrosis** of surrounding tissue, leading to the formation of **pus** (a collection of dead neutrophils, bacteria, and cellular debris).
• **Encapsulation**
	◦ The body forms a **fibrous capsule** around the purulent material to wall off the infection and prevent its spread.
	◦ This capsule **limits antibiotic penetration**, making **source control (drainage) essential**.
• **Common Pathogens**
	◦ **_Staphylococcus aureus_**: The most common causative organism.
		▪ **Methicillin-Resistant _Staphylococcus aureus_ (MRSA)**, particularly **Community-Associated MRSA (CA-MRSA)**, is now the predominant pathogen in many regions.
	◦ **_Streptococcus pyogenes_ (Group A Strep)**: Often associated with a more significant surrounding **cellulitis**.
	◦ **Polymicrobial/Anaerobes** (e.g., _Bacteroides_, _Peptostreptococcus_)
		▪ Common in abscesses related to the oral cavity, **perineal**, or **perirectal** areas.
sections.epidemiology:
• Skin and soft tissue infections are a leading cause for emergency department visits in the United States.
• The incidence has significantly increased with the emergence of **CA-MRSA** over the past two decades.
• Affects individuals of all ages.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with a **"painful, red bump"** or **"boil"** that has progressively worsened over several days.
	◦ The lesion is often described as **exquisitely tender**.
	◦ Patients may report a "pimple-like" head or **spontaneous drainage** of purulent material.
• **Systemic symptoms** like **fever** and **chills** suggest a more severe or spreading infection.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**
	◦ The diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on history and physical exam findings.
• **Bedside Ultrasound (POCUS)**
	◦ **Best initial imaging modality** to differentiate **cellulitis** from a drainable **abscess**, especially when **fluctuance** is unclear.
	◦ **Findings**
		▪ An abscess appears as a **hypoechoic** or **anechoic** (dark) **fluid collection**, often with a debris-filled, heterogeneous appearance.
		▪ Surrounding tissue may show **"cobblestoning"** (subcutaneous edema).
		▪ Useful for identifying the optimal location for incision and determining the depth of the collection.
• **Wound Culture and Sensitivity**
	◦ **Indications**: **Severe local infection**, **systemic signs of illness**, **recurrent or multiple abscesses**, **failure of initial antibiotic therapy**, or in **immunocompromised patients**.
	◦ **Purpose**: To identify the causative organism and guide targeted antibiotic therapy.
• **Labs (CBC, CRP, Blood Cultures)**
	◦ Indicated only if the patient has **systemic signs of illness** (e.g., **fever**, **tachycardia**, **hypotension**) to evaluate for **sepsis** or **bacteremia**.
• **CT / MRI**
	◦ Rarely needed for uncomplicated cutaneous abscesses.
	◦ Reserved for suspicion of deeper, more extensive infections such as **necrotizing fasciitis**, **pyomyositis**, or **perirectal abscesses** with deep extension.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for simple cutaneous abscesses treated with timely **I&D**.
• The prognosis is more **guarded** in patients with significant **comorbidities**, **delayed treatment**, or the development of severe complications like **sepsis**.

sections.overview:
• **Necrotizing Fasciitis (NF)** is a rare but life-threatening, rapidly progressive soft tissue infection characterized by widespread necrosis of the subcutaneous tissue, fascia, and sometimes muscle
• It is a true **surgical emergency** requiring immediate and aggressive **debridement** and **broad-spectrum antibiotics** to prevent limb loss and mortality
• The infection spreads along fascial planes, leading to thrombosis of microvasculature and subsequent tissue ischemia and necrosis
sections.etiology:
• Classification by microbiology:
	◦ **Type I (Most Common, ~80%): Polymicrobial**
		▪ Caused by a mix of aerobic and anaerobic bacteria (e.g., *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Streptococcus spp.*, Enterobacteriaceae, *Bacteroides*, *Clostridium*)
		▪ Typically occurs in older patients with significant comorbidities (e.g., diabetes, PVD)
		▪ Commonly affects the trunk, perineum (**Fournier's Gangrene**), or post-operative sites
	◦ **Type II: Monomicrobial**
		▪ Most classically caused by **Group A Streptococcus (*Streptococcus pyogenes*)**, the "flesh-eating bacteria"
		▪ May also be caused by community-acquired MRSA (*Staphylococcus aureus*)
		▪ Often affects younger, healthier individuals after minor trauma, and is associated with a high incidence of **Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS)**
	◦ **Type III: Marine Organisms**
		▪ Caused by Gram-negative rods, primarily ***Vibrio vulnificus*** (saltwater exposure, raw oyster ingestion) or ***Aeromonas hydrophila*** (freshwater exposure)
		▪ Rapidly progressive with hemorrhagic bullae
		▪ Strongly associated with patients who have chronic liver disease or are immunocompromised
	◦ **Type IV: Fungal**
		▪ Rare, typically seen in severely immunocompromised patients (e.g., post-transplant)
		▪ Caused by organisms like *Candida* or Zygomycetes
• **Pathophysiology:**
	◦ **Inoculation:** Bacteria enter through a breach in the skin (trauma, surgery, insect bite)
	◦ **Spread:** Infection spreads rapidly along the poorly vascularized deep fascial planes
	◦ **Toxin Production:** Bacteria release enzymes (collagenase, hyaluronidase) and toxins that destroy tissue
	◦ **Vascular Occlusion:** An inflammatory cascade causes thrombosis of the small perforating vessels that supply the overlying skin and subcutaneous tissue
	◦ **Ischemia & Necrosis:** Lack of blood supply leads to liquefactive necrosis of fat and fascia, followed by necrosis of the overlying skin (a late finding). This process also destroys superficial nerves, leading to anesthesia of the skin
	◦ **Systemic Effects:** Massive cytokine release leads to systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), septic shock, and multi-organ failure
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence:** Rare, estimated at 0.4-1.0 cases per 100,000 persons per year
• **Mortality:** High, ranging from 20-40% even with optimal treatment. Mortality approaches 70-80% if septic shock is present
• **Demographics:** Affects all ages, but Type I is more common in older adults with comorbidities
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The hallmark is a **clinical picture that evolves rapidly and is far more severe than the superficial skin findings suggest**
• The patient appears systemically ill and toxic
• **Classic Triad:**
	◦ Tenderness that extends beyond the visible erythema
	◦ Signs of systemic toxicity (fever, tachycardia, hypotension)
	◦ Edema or induration of the soft tissue
sections.diagnostics:
• **Surgical exploration is the definitive gold standard for diagnosis**
	◦ Imaging and labs support clinical suspicion but should **NEVER delay surgical consultation**
• **Surgical Diagnosis:**
	◦ Intraoperatively, a "finger test" may be performed: a blunt instrument or finger passes with little resistance through the normally adherent subcutaneous tissue and fascia ("loss of tissue integrity")
	◦ Findings:
		▪ Gray, necrotic fascia
		▪ Thin, non-purulent "dishwater" fluid
		▪ Lack of bleeding from fascial planes
	◦ Tissue biopsy for Gram stain, culture, and pathology confirms the diagnosis
• **Laboratory Studies:**
	◦ CBC: Marked leukocytosis (>15,000) with a left shift
	◦ CMP: **Hyponatremia** (highly suggestive), elevated BUN/Cr (AKI), acidosis (elevated lactate)
	◦ Inflammatory markers: Markedly elevated CRP (>150 mg/L) and ESR
	◦ CK: Elevated if there is associated myositis or myonecrosis
	◦ Coags: May show signs of DIC
• **LRINEC Score (Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis):**
	◦ A scoring tool to stratify risk. A score ≥ 6 is highly suspicious
	◦ It includes CRP, WBC, Hgb, Na, Creatinine, and Glucose
	◦ *This tool aids suspicion but does not rule out the diagnosis*
• **Imaging:**
	◦ **Plain Radiograph (X-ray):** Can reveal **subcutaneous gas**, which is highly specific but has low sensitivity
	◦ **CT Scan with IV Contrast:** The imaging modality of choice if performed
		▪ Findings include **fascial thickening, fluid collections along fascial planes, inflammatory fat stranding, and subcutaneous gas**
	◦ **Ultrasound/MRI:** Can also show fascial thickening and fluid but are less practical in an emergency
sections.prognosis:
• **Mortality** remains high (20-40%)
• The single most important prognostic factor is the **time from symptom onset to the first surgical debridement**
• Prognosis is worse in patients with delayed diagnosis, inadequate debridement, multiple comorbidities, or truncal/perineal involvement

sections.overview:
• **Sepsis** is a life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection.
• **Septic shock** is a subset of sepsis in which underlying circulatory and cellular/metabolic abnormalities are profound enough to substantially increase mortality.
• It is a medical emergency requiring rapid diagnosis and immediate intervention.
• **Sepsis (Sepsis-3 Definition)**:
    ◦ Suspected or documented infection **plus** an acute increase in the **Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA)** score of ≥2 points.
• **Septic Shock (Sepsis-3 Definition)**:
    ◦ **Sepsis** with persistent **hypotension** requiring **vasopressors** to maintain a **Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP)** of ≥65 mmHg **and** a serum **lactate** level >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation.
• **qSOFA (Quick SOFA)**:
    ◦ A bedside tool to identify patients outside the ICU with suspected infection who are at greater risk for poor outcomes.
    ◦ It is **not** a diagnostic criterion for sepsis.
    ◦ A score of ≥2 suggests a higher risk and prompts further investigation.
        ▪ Respiratory Rate (RR) ≥22/min
        ▪ Altered Mental Status (GCS < 15)
        ▪ Systolic Blood Pressure (SBP) ≤100 mmHg
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**: **Sepsis** is triggered by an infection. Common sources and pathogens include:
    ◦ **Most Common Sources**:
        ▪ **Pneumonia** (most common overall)
        ▪ Intra-abdominal infections (peritonitis, abscess, cholangitis)
        ▪ Urinary Tract Infections (urosepsis, pyelonephritis)
        ▪ Skin and soft tissue infections (cellulitis, necrotizing fasciitis)
        ▪ Bloodstream infections (bacteremia, catheter-related)
    ◦ **Common Pathogens**:
        ▪ **Gram-Positive Bacteria**: *Staphylococcus aureus* (including **MRSA**), *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Enterococcus spp.*
        ▪ **Gram-Negative Bacteria**: *Escherichia coli*, *Klebsiella pneumoniae*, *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, *Enterobacter spp.*
        ▪ **Fungi**: *Candida spp.* (especially in immunocompromised patients)
        ▪ **Viruses**: Influenza, SARS-CoV-2
• **Pathophysiology**: Sepsis is not just an infection, but an overwhelming and injurious host response.
    ◦ **Pathogen Recognition**: Pathogen-associated molecular patterns (**PAMPs**) on microbes are recognized by host immune cells.
    ◦ **Inflammatory Cascade**: This triggers a massive release of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6), leading to a systemic inflammatory response.
    ◦ **Endothelial Dysfunction & Vasodilation**: Cytokines cause widespread endothelial cell damage and induce nitric oxide production, leading to systemic **vasodilation** and a drop in systemic vascular resistance (**SVR**).
    ◦ **Increased Capillary Permeability**: Endothelial damage makes capillaries "leaky," causing fluid to shift from the intravascular space into the interstitium. This leads to profound relative **hypovolemia** and tissue edema.
    ◦ **Coagulopathy**: The inflammatory state activates the coagulation cascade while impairing fibrinolysis, creating a prothrombotic state. This can lead to microthrombi formation in small vessels, further impairing organ perfusion and potentially progressing to **Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC)**.
    ◦ **Myocardial Depression**: Sepsis can cause a reversible **septic cardiomyopathy**, reducing cardiac contractility and cardiac output.
    ◦ **Cellular & Metabolic Dysfunction**: Impaired tissue perfusion (hypoxia) forces cells into anaerobic metabolism, producing **lactate**. Mitochondrial dysfunction further impairs cellular energy production, leading to cell death and organ failure.
sections.epidemiology:
• A leading cause of death in critically ill patients worldwide.
• Incidence is rising due to an aging population, increased use of immunosuppressive drugs, and invasive procedures.
• Mortality rate for **sepsis** is approximately 10-20%.
• Mortality rate for **septic shock** is significantly higher, often exceeding 40%.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The patient typically appears acutely and severely ill.
• The presentation can be highly variable and may be subtle, especially in the elderly.
• Key features are signs of systemic inflammation and organ dysfunction in the setting of a suspected infection.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Labs**
    ◦ **Blood Cultures**: **TWO sets** from different sites, ideally before antibiotic administration.
    ◦ **Lactate**: Key marker of tissue hypoperfusion. Serial measurements are used to guide resuscitation.
    ◦ **CBC with Differential**: **Leukocytosis** (>12,000) or **leukopenia** (<4,000), neutrophilia, "**left shift**" (**bandemia**). **Thrombocytopenia** may be present.
    ◦ **Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP)**:
        ▪ **AKI**: Elevated **BUN** and **Creatinine**.
        ▪ **Liver Dysfunction**: Elevated **LFTs** (AST/ALT), bilirubin.
        ▪ **Electrolytes**: Hyper/hypoglycemia, electrolyte imbalances.
    ◦ **Inflammatory Markers**: C-reactive protein (**CRP**) and **Procalcitonin** (more specific for bacterial infection; can help guide antibiotic therapy).
    ◦ **Coagulation Studies**: PT/INR, PTT, Fibrinogen, D-dimer. Look for evidence of **DIC**.
    ◦ **Arterial Blood Gas (ABG)**: **Metabolic acidosis** (high anion gap due to lactate), potential respiratory compensation or primary respiratory failure.
    ◦ **Source-Specific Labs**: Urinalysis and urine culture, sputum Gram stain and culture, wound cultures, CSF analysis (if indicated).
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Chest X-ray**: To evaluate for **pneumonia** or **ARDS**.
    ◦ **CT/Ultrasound**: To identify intra-abdominal, pelvic, or soft-tissue sources (e.g., abscess, cholecystitis, pyelonephritis).
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is directly related to the severity of illness, underlying comorbidities, and the timeliness of intervention.
• Each hour of delay in administering appropriate antibiotics after the onset of hypotension increases mortality significantly.
• Mortality for **septic shock** remains high (40-50%).
• Survivors often face long-term physical, cognitive, and emotional challenges.

sections.overview:
• **Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS)** is a rare but **life-threatening**, **multi-system inflammatory illness** caused by **exotoxins** produced by specific bacteria, most notably ***Staphylococcus aureus*** and ***Streptococcus pyogenes*** (Group A Strep)
• Characterized by the **acute onset** of **high fever**, **rash**, **hypotension**, and signs of **multi-organ failure**
