• TSS is a **medical emergency** requiring immediate recognition and aggressive treatment
sections.etiology:
• TSS is caused by the systemic effects of potent **toxins**, not by the bacteria invading the bloodstream (bacteremia)
• **Etiologic Agents & Toxins**
    ◦ **Staphylococcal TSS**
        ▪ Caused by toxin-producing strains of ***Staphylococcus aureus***
        ▪ Primary toxin: **Toxic Shock Syndrome Toxin-1 (TSST-1)**
        ▪ Other toxins include staphylococcal enterotoxins B and C
    ◦ **Streptococcal TSS (STSS)**
        ▪ Caused by toxin-producing strains of ***Streptococcus pyogenes*** (Group A Streptococcus, GAS)
        ▪ Primary toxins: **Streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins (Spe)**, primarily SpeA and SpeC
• **Pathophysiology (The "Cytokine Storm")**
    ◦ **Superantigen Activity**: The toxins (TSST-1, SpeA) act as **superantigens**
    ◦ **Bypassing Normal Immunity**: Superantigens bypass the normal antigen-presenting process by directly cross-linking the **Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) class II** on antigen-presenting cells with the **T-cell receptor** on T-lymphocytes
    ◦ **Massive T-Cell Activation**: Leads to the polyclonal activation of a massive number of T-cells (up to 20% of the body's total)
    ◦ **Cytokine Release**: This triggers a "**cytokine storm**"—a catastrophic, systemic release of inflammatory cytokines, including **Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha (TNF-α)**, **Interleukin-1 (IL-1)**, IL-2, and **Interferon-gamma (IFN-γ)**
    ◦ **Systemic Effects**: The cytokine storm causes widespread endothelial damage, leading to:
        ▪ **Capillary Leakage**: Fluid shifts from the intravascular to the extravascular space, causing profound **hypotension**, **shock**, and non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema (**ARDS**)
        ▪ **Vasodilation**: Contributes to hypotension
        ▪ **Fever**: Direct pyrogenic effects
        ▪ **Tissue Damage**: Leads to **multi-organ failure** (renal, hepatic, CNS, etc.)
sections.epidemiology:
• **Staphylococcal TSS**
    ◦ Historically linked to young, menstruating women using high-absorbency tampons
    ◦ Currently, approximately 50% of cases are **non-menstrual**, associated with surgical wounds, nasal packing, burns, or cutaneous lesions
    ◦ **Bacteremia** is uncommon (<5% of cases)
• **Streptococcal TSS (STSS)**
    ◦ Often arises from a deep-seated soft tissue infection (e.g., **necrotizing fasciitis**, myositis, cellulitis)
    ◦ A portal of entry may not be obvious
    ◦ **Bacteremia** is extremely common (>60% of cases)
    ◦ Carries a significantly higher mortality rate than Staphylococcal TSS
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The hallmark of TSS is the **acute onset of illness in a previously healthy individual** that rapidly progresses to shock and **multi-organ failure**
• **Classic Triad**:
    ◦ **High Fever**: Typically >38.9°C (102°F)
    ◦ **Diffuse Erythematous Rash**
    ◦ **Hypotension**: SBP <90 mmHg in adults or orthostatic syncope
sections.diagnostics:
• TSS is primarily a **clinical diagnosis** based on CDC criteria
• Labs support the diagnosis and assess the degree of organ failure
• **CDC Case Definition Highlights**
    ◦ **Fever** >38.9°C
    ◦ **Hypotension** (SBP <90 mmHg)
    ◦ Diffuse erythematous **rash**
    ◦ **Desquamation** (1-2 weeks later)
    ◦ Involvement of **three or more** organ systems:
        ▪ **GI**: Vomiting or diarrhea
        ▪ **Muscular**: Severe myalgia or **CK** >2x normal
        ▪ **Renal**: **BUN/Creatinine** >2x normal or pyuria
        ▪ **Hepatic**: **LFTs** >2x normal
        ▪ **Hematologic**: **Platelets** <100,000/L
        ▪ **CNS**: Disorientation without focal signs
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **CBC**: **Leukocytosis** with a profound **left shift** (immature neutrophils); **thrombocytopenia** is common and a poor prognostic indicator
    ◦ **CMP**: Elevated **BUN/Cr** (AKI), elevated **LFTs** (AST/ALT), hypoalbuminemia, hypocalcemia
    ◦ **CK**: Elevated (rhabdomyolysis/myositis)
    ◦ **Coagulation Studies**: Prolonged PT/PTT, low fibrinogen (suggests DIC)
    ◦ **Blood Cultures**: Crucial differentiator
        ▪ Often **negative** in Staph TSS
        ▪ Often **positive** in Strep TSS
    ◦ **Source Cultures**: Obtain cultures from any suspected source (vagina, wound, nasal packing, throat)
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Chest X-ray**: May show non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema (**ARDS**)
    ◦ **CT/MRI**: If **necrotizing fasciitis** is suspected
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis depends on the causative organism and speed of treatment
• **Staphylococcal TSS**: Mortality is now <5% with prompt treatment
• **Streptococcal TSS (STSS)**: Mortality remains very high, ranging from **30% to 70%**
• Survivors may experience long-term sequelae such as renal impairment, hair and nail loss, and neuropsychological deficits
• **Recurrence** of Staphylococcal TSS can occur (5-30%) in patients who do not develop sufficient antibodies
    ◦ Patients should be counseled to avoid tampons
sections.preventionEducation: • Patients who have had Staphylococcal TSS should be counseled to avoid future tampon use to prevent recurrence.

sections.overview:
• Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP) is an acute infection of the **pulmonary parenchyma** acquired in the community (i.e., outside of a hospital or long-term care facility)
• It is a leading cause of morbidity, mortality, and hospitalization worldwide
• The diagnosis is established by the presence of a **new infiltrate on chest imaging** combined with **clinical signs and symptoms** of a lower respiratory tract infection
• Treatment decisions, including location of care (outpatient vs. inpatient) and antibiotic selection, are guided by risk stratification scores and local pathogen resistance patterns
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Affects millions of adults in the U.S. annually
• **Hospitalization**: A **leading cause of hospitalization** in adults
• **Mortality**: The **most common infectious cause of death**, with mortality highest in elderly patients and those with significant comorbidities
• **Seasonality**: Incidence peaks in the winter months, often following seasonal viral upper respiratory infections
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation can range from a subacute, indolent course (**"walking pneumonia"**) to an acute, fulminant illness
    ◦ **Classic "Typical" Presentation**: **Acute onset** of **high fever**, **productive cough** with **purulent sputum**, **pleuritic chest pain**, and a single, shaking chill (**rigor**)
    ◦ **Classic "Atypical" Presentation**: **Gradual onset** of **low-grade fever**, **dry cough**, and prominent constitutional symptoms like **headache**, **myalgias**, and **malaise**
    ◦ **Elderly Presentation**: Often atypical and subtle
        ▪ May present with **confusion**, **falls**, **weakness**, **lethargy**, or **loss of appetite**, often without fever or significant cough
sections.diagnostics:
• **Chest X-Ray (PA and Lateral)**: The **gold standard for diagnosis**
    ◦ **Findings**: **New infiltrate**, which can be **lobar consolidation**, **interstitial opacities**, or **patchy/diffuse opacities**. **Pleural effusion** may also be present
• **Pulse Oximetry**: To assess for **hypoxemia**
• **Laboratory Studies** (typically for hospitalized patients)
    ◦ **CBC with differential**: **Leukocytosis** with a **left shift** (**neutrophil predominance**) is common in bacterial pneumonia
    ◦ **CMP**: To assess renal function, electrolytes (**hyponatremia** seen with *Legionella*), and liver function
    ◦ **Inflammatory Markers**: C-reactive protein (CRP) and Procalcitonin
        ▪ **Procalcitonin** >0.25 ng/mL suggests a bacterial etiology and can help guide antibiotic therapy
• **Blood Cultures**: Obtain two sets from different sites before starting antibiotics in severe CAP or hospitalized patients
• **Sputum Gram Stain and Culture**: Low sensitivity and specificity but can be helpful if a high-quality sample is obtained before antibiotics
• **Specialized Tests**
    ◦ **Urinary Antigen Tests**: For *S. pneumoniae* and *Legionella pneumophila*. Rapid and useful for guiding therapy
    ◦ **Nasopharyngeal Swab**: For viral pathogens (Influenza, RSV, SARS-CoV-2)
sections.prognosis:
• **Outpatient**: Excellent prognosis, with **mortality <1%**
• **Inpatient (Non-ICU)**: Mortality is approximately **5-10%**
• **Inpatient (ICU)**: Mortality can be **>30%**
• Prognosis is worse in patients with **advanced age**, **multiple comorbidities**, **multilobar involvement**, and **bacteremia**
• Full resolution of symptoms can take several weeks

sections.overview:
• **Hospital-Acquired Pneumonia (HAP)** is a lower respiratory tract infection that was not present or incubating at the time of hospital admission and develops **48 hours after admission**.
    ◦ It is the second most common nosocomial infection and the **leading cause of death** among hospital-acquired infections.
• A significant subtype is **Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP)**, which is a type of HAP that develops **48 hours after endotracheal intubation** and initiation of mechanical ventilation.
• **Note:** The term Healthcare-Associated Pneumonia (HCAP) has been largely abandoned in recent guidelines, as it was found to be overly broad and led to excessive use of broad-spectrum antibiotics.
    ◦ Current guidelines focus on assessing individual patient risk factors for **multidrug-resistant (MDR) organisms**.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• Occurs in **5-15 per 1,000** hospital admissions.
• The **second most common nosocomial infection** after UTIs.
• The **leading cause of mortality** from nosocomial infections.
• **VAP** develops in 10-20% of patients mechanically ventilated for >48 hours.
• Mortality for HAP is estimated at **20-30%**, and for VAP, it can be as high as **50%**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• HAP/VAP should be suspected in any hospitalized or ventilated patient for >48 hours who develops new signs of respiratory compromise.
• The presentation can be subtle, especially in sedated or critically ill patients.
sections.diagnostics:
• A definitive diagnosis requires a new or progressive **radiographic infiltrate** plus **clinical evidence of infection**.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Chest X-Ray (CXR):** **Required for diagnosis**.
        ▪ Look for a **new or progressive infiltrate, consolidation, cavitation, or pleural effusion**.
    ◦ **Chest CT:** Not routinely required but can be useful for complex cases, detecting abscesses, or evaluating for empyema.
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **CBC with differential:** **Leukocytosis** (>12,000/L) with a left shift or **leukopenia** (<4,000/L).
    ◦ **Arterial Blood Gas (ABG):** To assess for **hypoxemia** and **respiratory acidosis**.
    ◦ **Procalcitonin (PCT):** Can be a useful adjunct.
        ▪ An elevated PCT supports a **bacterial etiology**.
        ▪ Serial measurements can help guide antibiotic de-escalation.
    ◦ **Blood Cultures:** Obtain two sets from different sites **before starting antibiotics** to rule out **bacteremia**.
• **Microbiology (Crucial for Targeted Therapy)**
    ◦ **Non-invasive:** **Sputum Gram stain and culture** (low specificity and sensitivity due to contamination with upper airway flora).
    ◦ **Invasive (for VAP):** Lower respiratory tract sampling is preferred for higher diagnostic yield.
        ▪ **Endotracheal aspirate:** Easiest to obtain in a ventilated patient.
        ▪ **Bronchoalveolar Lavage (BAL)** or **Protected Specimen Brush (PSB):** More invasive (requires bronchoscopy) but provides a more accurate sample from the site of infection.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is generally poor due to the severity of underlying illness in affected patients.
• Crude mortality rates for HAP are **20-30%**.
• VAP mortality can reach **50%**.
• Factors associated with poor prognosis include:
    ◦ Infection with **MDR pathogens** (*Pseudomonas*, MRSA, *Acinetobacter*)
    ◦ **Bacteremia**
    ◦ Inappropriate or delayed initial antibiotic therapy
    ◦ Severe underlying comorbidities
    ◦ Development of **ARDS** or **septic shock**

sections.overview:
• Active Tuberculosis (TB) is a contagious, multisystemic infectious disease caused by the bacterium *_Mycobacterium tuberculosis_*.
• It most commonly affects the lungs (pulmonary TB) but can disseminate to involve any organ system (extrapulmonary TB).
• Active disease occurs when the host's immune system fails to contain the initial primary infection or when a latent infection reactivates, leading to clinical signs and symptoms.
• It is characterized by the formation of caseating (necrotizing) granulomas.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**: *_Mycobacterium tuberculosis_*, an obligate aerobic, non-motile, slow-growing bacillus with a unique waxy cell wall rich in mycolic acid. This cell wall makes it resistant to drying, disinfectants, and standard Gram staining; it requires an acid-fast stain (e.g., Ziehl-Neelsen).
• **Transmission**: Inhalation of aerosolized droplets produced by an individual with active pulmonary or laryngeal TB during coughing, sneezing, or speaking.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ 1. **Inhalation & Implantation**: Bacilli are inhaled and reach the alveoli, typically in the mid or lower lung zones.
    ◦ 2. **Macrophage Ingestion**: Alveolar macrophages phagocytose the bacilli but are unable to kill them due to the waxy cell wall. The bacilli replicate inside the macrophages.
    ◦ 3. **Immune Response**: After 2-8 weeks, a cell-mediated (Type IV hypersensitivity) immune response is mounted. T-lymphocytes activate macrophages, enabling them to kill the bacteria. This response walls off the infection, forming a granuloma.
    ◦ 4. **Granuloma Formation (Tubercle)**: The core of the granuloma contains infected macrophages, which may fuse to form multinucleated giant cells (Langhans cells), surrounded by a collar of lymphocytes. This leads to central caseating necrosis (a "cheesy" appearance).
    ◦ 5. **Primary Disease vs. Latent Infection**:
        ▪ **Latent TB Infection (LTBI)**: In >90% of immunocompetent individuals, the granulomas contain the infection, and the individual becomes asymptomatic (PPD/IGRA positive, but not infectious). The primary lung lesion (Ghon focus) and involved lymph node (Ghon complex) may calcify.
        ▪ **Primary Progressive TB**: In ~5% of cases (especially in children or immunocompromised), the immune system fails to contain the initial infection, leading directly to active disease.
    ◦ 6. **Reactivation (Secondary) TB**: The most common form of active TB in adults. The latent infection reactivates months to years later, typically during a period of weakened immunity. Reactivation characteristically occurs in the **apices of the lungs** due to higher oxygen tension, which is favorable for the obligate aerobe *_M. tuberculosis_*. This leads to cavitation, tissue destruction, and potential spread.
sections.epidemiology:
• Globally, TB is one of the leading infectious causes of death.
• Highest prevalence in developing countries, particularly in Southeast Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa, and Eastern Europe.
• In the United States, cases are concentrated among foreign-born individuals from endemic areas, minority populations, and high-risk congregate settings (e.g., correctional facilities, homeless shelters).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is often insidious, developing over weeks to months.
• Patients typically present with a combination of constitutional and pulmonary symptoms.
• A high index of suspicion is required, especially in patients with relevant risk factors.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Chest X-Ray (CXR)**:
    ◦ **Reactivation TB (Classic)**: Infiltrates and **cavitary lesions** in the **apical or posterior segments of the upper lobes**.
    ◦ **Primary TB**: Middle or lower lobe consolidation, **hilar adenopathy**, and pleural effusions are more common. A calcified primary focus + hilar node is a **Ghon complex**.
    ◦ **Miliary TB**: Diffuse, small (1-2mm) nodular opacities throughout both lungs ("millet seed" pattern), indicating hematogenous dissemination.
• **Sputum Microbiology (Definitive Diagnosis)**:
    ◦ **Collection**: Obtain 3 consecutive morning sputum samples (8-24 hours apart). Induction with hypertonic saline may be necessary.
    ◦ **1. AFB Smear Microscopy**: A rapid, presumptive test using Ziehl-Neelsen or Kinyoun stain to visualize acid-fast bacilli. Sensitivity is variable.
    ◦ **2. Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT)**: e.g., Xpert MTB/RIF. **Highly recommended first-line test.** Rapid (results in hours), highly sensitive and specific. Simultaneously detects *_M. tuberculosis_* and resistance to Rifampin.
    ◦ **3. Mycobacterial Culture**: **The gold standard for confirmation.** Requires specialized media (e.g., Löwenstein-Jensen). Very sensitive but slow (can take 2-6 weeks for growth). Essential for definitive species identification and full drug susceptibility testing (DST).
• **Screening Tests (for Latent TB, not for diagnosing Active TB)**:
    ◦ **Tuberculin Skin Test (TST) / PPD**: Measures delayed-type hypersensitivity. Positive result indicates exposure and immune response, not necessarily active disease.
    ◦ **Interferon-Gamma Release Assay (IGRA)**: Blood test (e.g., QuantiFERON-Gold). More specific than TST, not confounded by prior BCG vaccination.
• **Other Labs**: All patients with active TB should be tested for **HIV**. CBC may show normocytic anemia; WBC can be normal or slightly elevated.
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent for drug-susceptible TB if the full course of therapy is completed (>95% cure rate).
• Poor prognosis is associated with drug resistance, HIV co-infection (especially with low CD4 count), malnutrition, advanced age, and non-adherence to treatment.

sections.overview:
• Latent Tuberculosis Infection (LTBI) is a clinical state where an individual is infected with *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* but does not have active, symptomatic TB disease.
• The host's immune system contains the bacteria within granulomas, preventing replication and transmission.
• The individual is **asymptomatic**, has a **normal physical exam**, and is **not infectious**.
• Individuals with LTBI are at risk for future reactivation, leading to active TB disease.
• Diagnosis is made by demonstrating an immune response to TB antigens (via TST or IGRA) in the absence of clinical and radiographic evidence of active disease.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**: Caused by the bacterium ***Mycobacterium tuberculosis***, a slow-growing, aerobic, acid-fast bacillus.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Inhalation**: Infection begins with the inhalation of aerosolized droplets containing *M. tuberculosis* from an individual with active pulmonary TB.
    ◦ **Phagocytosis**: Bacilli reach the alveoli and are phagocytosed by alveolar macrophages, where they can survive and replicate.
    ◦ **Immune Response**: Within 2-8 weeks, a **cell-mediated immune (CMI) response** is mounted. Macrophages present TB antigens to T-lymphocytes (specifically CD4+ T-helper cells).
    ◦ **Granuloma Formation**: Activated T-cells release cytokines, most importantly **Interferon-gamma (IFN-γ)** and **Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha (TNF-α)**.
        ▪ **IFN-γ**: Activates macrophages, enhancing their ability to kill bacilli.
        ▪ **TNF-α**: Crucial for the formation and maintenance of granulomas.
    ◦ **Containment**: A **granuloma** (a collection of immune cells) forms around the bacilli, "walling them off," often with central **caseous necrosis**.
        ▪ The structure in the lung periphery with associated hilar lymph node involvement is called a **Ghon complex**.
        ▪ If calcified, it is a **Ranke complex**.
    ◦ **Latency**: The bacilli remain viable but dormant within the granuloma. Reactivation occurs if the host's CMI wanes.
sections.epidemiology:
• Approximately **one-quarter of the world's population** is estimated to have LTBI.
• In the U.S., LTBI is more prevalent among:
    ◦ Foreign-born individuals from high-burden countries (Asia, Africa, Latin America).
    ◦ Residents and employees of congregate settings (e.g., correctional facilities, homeless shelters, nursing homes).
    ◦ Healthcare workers.
    ◦ Immunocompromised populations.
• The lifetime risk of reactivation for an immunocompetent person with LTBI is **5-10%**, with the highest risk being in the first **2 years** after initial infection.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The defining feature of LTBI is the **complete absence of signs and symptoms**.
• The individual feels entirely well.
• The patient is **asymptomatic**.
• The classic "B symptoms" of active TB (fever, night sweats, weight loss) are absent.
• No cough, hemoptysis, or chest pain.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Normal**.
• There are no abnormal findings on physical examination attributable to LTBI.
• Lungs are clear to auscultation, no lymphadenopathy, no other systemic signs.
sections.diagnostics:
• The goal is to identify an immune response to TB antigens, then rule out active disease.
• **Screening Tests (To detect immune sensitization)**:
    ◦ **Tuberculin Skin Test (TST) / Mantoux Test / PPD**:
        ▪ **Mechanism**: Intradermal injection of purified protein derivative (PPD) antigen. Measures a delayed-type (Type IV) hypersensitivity reaction.
        ▪ **Reading**: Read at 48-72 hours. Measure the diameter of **induration** (palpable hardening), not erythema.
        ▪ **Positive Cutoffs**:
            ▪ **≥5 mm**: HIV-positive, recent contacts of active TB cases, CXR with fibrotic changes suggesting old TB, organ transplant recipients, immunosuppressed (e.g., on TNF-α inhibitors or chronic steroids >15 mg/day prednisone).
            ▪ **≥10 mm**: Recent immigrants (<5 yrs) from high-prevalence areas, IV drug users, residents/employees of high-risk settings (prisons, hospitals, shelters), children <4 years, individuals with high-risk medical conditions (e.g., DM, CKD).
            ▪ **≥15 mm**: Persons with no known risk factors.
        ▪ **Limitations**: False positives from BCG vaccine or non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) infection. False negatives in anergy, recent infection, or overwhelming active disease.
    ◦ **Interferon-Gamma Release Assays (IGRAs)**:
        ▪ **Mechanism**: Blood test (e.g., QuantiFERON-TB Gold, T-SPOT.TB) that measures T-cell release of IFN-γ in response to *M. tb*-specific antigens.
        ▪ **Advantages**: Single visit, **not affected by prior BCG vaccination**, objective lab result. Often preferred for screening individuals with a history of BCG vaccination.
• **Confirmation and Exclusion of Active Disease (Required after positive TST/IGRA)**:
    ◦ **Thorough Symptom Review**: Screen for cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss.
    ◦ **Chest X-ray (CXR)**:
        ▪ **Typical LTBI Finding**: **Normal CXR**.
        ▪ **Possible LTBI Findings**: May show old, healed lesions like a calcified granuloma (**Ghon focus**), calcified hilar nodes, or apical scarring.
        ▪ **Findings Suggesting *Active* TB**: Apical infiltrates, cavitations, hilar/mediastinal adenopathy, pleural effusion, or miliary pattern. If present, further workup (sputum for AFB smear/culture) is required.
sections.treatment:
• **Preferred Regimens**:
    ◦ **Isoniazid (INH) + Rifapentine (RPT)** once weekly for 3 months (3HP). High efficacy and adherence.
    ◦ **Rifampin (RIF)** daily for 4 months (4R). Often used if INH is contraindicated or not tolerated.
    ◦ **Isoniazid (INH) + Rifampin (RIF)** daily for 3 months (3HR).
• **Alternative Regimen**:
    ◦ **Isoniazid (INH)** daily for 9 months (9H). The historical standard, still effective but has lower completion rates.
• **Key Adjunct**:
    ◦ **Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)** must be co-administered with **Isoniazid** to prevent peripheral neuropathy.
sections.management:
• **Baseline Evaluation**:
    ◦ Exclude active TB.
    ◦ Assess for risk factors for hepatotoxicity (liver disease, regular alcohol use, pregnancy/postpartum).
    ◦ Obtain baseline **Liver Function Tests (LFTs)** for patients with risk factors.
    ◦ Review medication list for potential drug-drug interactions (especially with rifampin/rifapentine, which are potent CYP450 inducers).
• **Monitoring**:
    ◦ Monthly clinical evaluation for adherence, signs of active TB, and adverse drug effects.
    ◦ Educate patient on symptoms of **hepatotoxicity**: nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fatigue, dark urine, jaundice. Instruct them to stop medication and call immediately if these occur.
    ◦ Routine LFT monitoring is not required for all, but should be performed for those with baseline abnormalities, liver disease, HIV, pregnancy, or regular alcohol use.
sections.complications:
• **Primary Complication**: **Reactivation into active TB disease**. This can be pulmonary or extrapulmonary (e.g., TB meningitis, Pott's disease of the spine, renal TB).
• **Complications of Treatment**:
    ◦ **Hepatotoxicity** (most common serious side effect, associated with INH and rifamycins).
    ◦ **Peripheral Neuropathy** (INH-induced, preventable with Vitamin B6).
    ◦ **Rifampin/Rifapentine side effects**: Orange discoloration of body fluids, drug-drug interactions, flu-like symptoms, rash.
sections.prognosis:
• **With treatment**: Excellent. A full course of therapy for LTBI reduces the risk of reactivation by approximately **90%**.
• **Without treatment**: The lifetime risk of reactivation is 5-10% for an immunocompetent host. The risk is substantially higher and the prognosis is worse for immunocompromised individuals, especially those with uncontrolled HIV.

sections.overview:
• Pertussis, also known as "**whooping cough**," is a highly contagious, acute respiratory infection caused by the bacterium *Bordetella pertussis*.
    ◦ Characterized by a severe, **paroxysmal cough**.
    ◦ Despite widespread vaccination, it remains a significant cause of morbidity and mortality, especially in **infants**.
    ◦ The clinical course is classically divided into three stages: **catarrhal**, **paroxysmal**, and **convalescent**.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**: *Bordetella pertussis*, a fastidious, gram-negative, aerobic coccobacillus.
• **Transmission**: Spreads via inhalation of aerosolized respiratory droplets from an infected individual.
• **Pathogenesis**:
    ◦ **Attachment**: The bacteria attach to the ciliated respiratory epithelium of the nasopharynx and trachea using virulence factors like filamentous hemagglutinin (FHA) and pertactin.
    ◦ **Toxin Production**: *B. pertussis* does not invade the bloodstream but produces potent exotoxins that cause local and systemic effects.
        ▪ **Pertussis Toxin (PT)**: The major virulence factor. It ADP-ribosylates and inactivates the inhibitory G-protein (Gi), leading to a massive increase in intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP). This impairs immune cell function and causes the characteristic **marked lymphocytosis**.
        ▪ **Tracheal Cytotoxin**: Directly damages and destroys ciliated epithelial cells, leading to impaired mucus clearance (ciliary stasis) and triggering the severe cough.
        ▪ **Adenylate Cyclase Toxin**: Impairs leukocyte chemotaxis and phagocytosis, helping the bacterium evade the host immune response.
    ◦ **Result**: The combination of epithelial damage, ciliary paralysis, and inflammation leads to mucus hypersecretion and the uncontrollable, spasmodic coughing fits characteristic of the disease.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Worldwide distribution. There has been a resurgence in developed countries, including the U.S., due to a combination of waning immunity, improved diagnostics, and a switch to acellular vaccines.
• **High-Risk Populations**:
    ◦ **Infants < 6 months**: Highest risk for severe disease, hospitalization, and death, as they are too young to have completed the primary vaccination series.
    ◦ **Adolescents and Adults**: Often act as reservoirs for transmission to infants due to waning immunity. Their presentation is frequently atypical (persistent cough without a "whoop").
• **Seasonality**: No distinct seasonal pattern, but peaks can occur in summer and fall.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Incomplete or no vaccination**: The single most important risk factor.
• **Waning immunity**: Protection from childhood DTaP vaccine wanes after 5-10 years.
• **Infancy**: Especially neonates and infants < 6 months old.
• **Pregnancy**: Risk to the newborn if the mother is not vaccinated during the third trimester.
• **Close contact** with an infected individual (e.g., household, daycare).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The disease classically progresses through three distinct stages after a 7-10 day incubation period.
• **1. Catarrhal Stage (1-2 weeks)**:
    ◦ Insidious onset, resembles a common cold (URI).
    ◦ Symptoms: Coryza, lacrimation, mild conjunctivitis, low-grade fever, malaise, and a mild, hacking cough that gradually worsens.
    ◦ **Key Point**: The patient is **most contagious** during this stage.
• **2. Paroxysmal Stage (2-8 weeks)**:
    ◦ The hallmark stage of the disease.
    ◦ **Paroxysmal Cough**: Spasms of rapid, consecutive, forceful coughs, often occurring in clusters, especially at night.
    ◦ **Inspiratory "Whoop"**: A high-pitched, forceful inhalation against a narrowed glottis that follows a coughing fit. It may be absent in infants and adults.
    ◦ **Post-tussive Emesis**: Vomiting that occurs immediately after a coughing paroxysm. Highly characteristic.
    ◦ **Apnea**: Common and life-threatening presentation in infants, may occur with or without the cough.
    ◦ Patients appear exhausted and may become cyanotic during coughing spells but are often well-appearing between episodes.
• **3. Convalescent Stage (Weeks to Months)**:
    ◦ Gradual resolution of symptoms.
    ◦ The chronic cough slowly decreases in frequency and severity.
    ◦ Cough may persist for up to 3 months, giving it the name **"100-day cough."**
    ◦ Paroxysms may recur with subsequent upper respiratory infections.
sections.physicalExam:
• **General**: Often unremarkable between coughing paroxysms.
• **During a Paroxysm**:
    ◦ Apparent distress, facial flushing turning to **cyanosis**.
    ◦ Protruding tongue, drooling.
    ◦ Forceful coughing followed by the characteristic **"whoop."**
• **Other findings (due to pressure from coughing)**:
    ◦ **Subconjunctival hemorrhages**
    ◦ **Facial and truncal petechiae**
• **Auscultation**: Lungs are typically clear. The pathology is primarily in the large airways, so rhonchi or crackles are usually absent unless a secondary pneumonia has developed.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Culture**:
    ◦ Nasopharyngeal (NP) swab or aspirate plated on special media (Regan-Lowe or Bordet-Gengou agar).
    ◦ **Gold standard for specificity**, but sensitivity is low and decreases significantly after the first 2 weeks of illness or with prior antibiotic use.
• **Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR)**:
    ◦ **Test of choice.**
    ◦ NP swab or aspirate.
    ◦ Highly sensitive and specific. Best within the first 3-4 weeks of cough onset.
• **Serology (IgG to pertussis toxin)**:
    ◦ Useful later in the disease course (>4 weeks after cough onset) when PCR and culture are likely negative.
    ◦ Requires a single high-titer result or a four-fold rise in paired acute and convalescent samples.
• **Complete Blood Count (CBC)**:
    ◦ Characteristic finding is a marked **leukocytosis (WBC 15,000-100,000)** with a profound **absolute lymphocytosis**.
    ◦ This is caused by PT preventing lymphocytes from entering lymphoid tissue.
• **Chest X-ray**:
    ◦ Usually normal or may show nonspecific perihilar infiltrates or atelectasis.
    ◦ Primarily used to rule out secondary bacterial pneumonia.
sections.treatment:
• **Goal**: Eradicate the bacteria to reduce transmission. Antibiotics have little effect on the clinical course unless started early in the catarrhal stage.
• **First-Line Antibiotics**: Macrolides
    ◦ **Azithromycin**: Preferred agent, especially in infants <1 month.
    ◦ **Clarithromycin**
    ◦ Erythromycin (less favored due to GI side effects and association with infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis if used in neonates).
• **Alternative**:
    ◦ **Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX)**: For patients with macrolide allergy or intolerance. Contraindicated in infants <2 months.
• **Supportive Care**: Crucial, especially for infants. Includes hydration, nutrition, and supplemental oxygen as needed. Avoid cough suppressants.
sections.management:
• **Hospitalization**: Indicated for infants <3-6 months, or any patient with severe paroxysms, apnea, cyanosis, feeding difficulties, or complications like pneumonia.
• **Infection Control**:
    ◦ Place patient on **droplet precautions**.
    ◦ Isolation should continue for 5 days after the initiation of appropriate antibiotic therapy.
    ◦ Pertussis is a **nationally reportable disease**.
• **Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP)**:
    ◦ A full course of a macrolide antibiotic (e.g., Azithromycin) should be given to all **close contacts**, regardless of age or vaccination status.
• **Prevention (Vaccination)**:
    ◦ **DTaP (children)**: Given at 2, 4, 6, 15-18 months, and 4-6 years.
    ◦ **Tdap (adolescents/adults)**: A single booster dose is recommended for adolescents (age 11-12) and for all adults who have not previously received it.
    ◦ **Pregnancy**: A Tdap booster is recommended **during EACH pregnancy**, ideally between 27-36 weeks gestation, to provide passive immunity to the newborn.
sections.complications:
• **Infants & Young Children**:
    ◦ **Apnea** (most common serious complication in infants)
    ◦ **Pneumonia** (secondary bacterial infection is a common cause of death)
    ◦ Seizures
    ◦ Hypoxic encephalopathy
    ◦ Death
• **Adolescents & Adults**:
    ◦ Weight loss
    ◦ Urinary incontinence
    ◦ Syncope
    ◦ Rib fractures from severe coughing
    ◦ Hernias (inguinal, umbilical)
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent in older children and adults. The cough can be prolonged and debilitating but is rarely fatal.
• Guarded in infants <6 months, who account for nearly all pertussis-related deaths. Prognosis depends on the severity of apnea, hypoxia, and secondary complications.

sections.overview:
• Diphtheria is an acute, toxin-mediated infectious disease caused by the bacterium **Corynebacterium diphtheriae**, primarily affecting the mucous membranes of the respiratory tract and the skin.
    ◦ The hallmark of respiratory diphtheria is the formation of a dense, gray, adherent **pseudomembrane** over the pharynx and tonsils.
    ◦ The release of a potent exotoxin can lead to systemic complications, most notably **myocarditis** and **neuropathy**.
    ◦ The disease is rare in developed nations due to widespread vaccination with the DTaP/Tdap vaccine.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**: **Corynebacterium diphtheriae**
    ◦ Gram-positive, non-spore-forming, non-motile, club-shaped (pleomorphic) bacillus.
    ◦ Often appears in "V" or "Y" shapes or clumps resembling **"Chinese letters"** or palisades on microscopy.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ Disease is caused by strains that produce **diphtheria exotoxin**.
        ▪ The gene for the toxin (*tox*) is introduced into the bacteria by a lysogenic bacteriophage (a virus).
    ◦ **Mechanism of Toxin**: The exotoxin inhibits host cell protein synthesis by inactivating **elongation factor-2 (EF-2)** via ADP-ribosylation, leading to cell death and necrosis.
    ◦ **Local Effects**: The toxin causes localized tissue necrosis and a fibrinosuppurative inflammatory response, resulting in the formation of the characteristic **pseudomembrane** (composed of fibrin, dead cells, leukocytes, and bacteria).
    ◦ **Systemic Effects**: The toxin is absorbed into the bloodstream and can damage distant organs, primarily the **heart**, **nervous system**, and **kidneys**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Transmission**: Person-to-person via respiratory droplets or direct contact with cutaneous lesions or contaminated fomites.
• **Reservoir**: Humans are the only known natural reservoir.
• **Incidence**: Extremely rare in the US and other developed countries due to routine childhood vaccination.
    ◦ It remains endemic in regions with low vaccine coverage (e.g., parts of Africa, South America, Asia, Eastern Europe).
    ◦ Outbreaks are typically associated with gaps in immunization.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Unvaccinated or inadequately vaccinated status** (most important risk factor).
• Travel to an endemic area.
• Immunocompromised status.
• Living in crowded or unsanitary conditions.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Incubation Period**: 2 to 5 days.
• Onset is typically gradual.
• Two primary forms:
    ◦ **Respiratory Diphtheria**: The classic and most severe form.
    ◦ **Cutaneous Diphtheria**: Milder, characterized by non-healing skin ulcers.
• **Symptoms**:
    ◦ **General**: Low-grade fever, malaise, chills, fatigue.
    ◦ **Respiratory Diphtheria**:
        ▪ **Severe sore throat** (pharyngitis/tonsillitis).
        ▪ Hoarseness or muffled voice (if larynx is involved).
        ▪ Dysphagia (difficulty swallowing).
        ▪ Bloody or serosanguinous nasal discharge (if nasal passages are involved).
    ◦ **Cutaneous Diphtheria**:
        ▪ A chronic, non-healing ulcer or sore.
        ▪ The lesion is often covered by a gray-brown membrane.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Hallmark Finding**: A thick, gray, leathery, and densely adherent **pseudomembrane** located on the tonsils, pharynx, soft palate, uvula, or larynx.
• **Key Differentiator**: The membrane **bleeds profusely if scraped** or dislodged.
• **Cervical Lymphadenopathy**: Significant anterior cervical adenopathy and surrounding edema can lead to a **"bull neck"** appearance (severe cases).
• **Fetor oris**: Foul-smelling breath.
• **Respiratory**: Stridor, dyspnea, and signs of airway compromise if laryngeal or tracheal involvement occurs.
• **Neurologic**: Cranial nerve palsies (e.g., palatal paralysis leading to a nasal voice), blurred vision (ciliary muscle paralysis).
• **Cutaneous**: "Punched-out" ulcer with a necrotic base and gray membrane.
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is **primarily clinical**; treatment should be initiated immediately based on suspicion and should **NOT** be delayed for laboratory confirmation.
• **Culture**:
    ◦ **Gold Standard** for confirmation.
    ◦ Obtain a sample by swabbing from underneath the edge of the pseudomembrane.
    ◦ Must be plated on special selective media:
        ▪ **Tinsdale agar**: Produces black colonies with brown halos.
        ▪ **Loeffler's medium**: Enhances the growth of *C. diphtheriae*.
• **Toxin Assay**:
    ◦ An isolate must be tested for toxin production to confirm toxigenic diphtheria (e.g., Elek test or PCR for the *tox* gene).
• **Other Labs**:
    ◦ **CBC**: May show leukocytosis.
    ◦ **ECG/EKG**: Essential to monitor for cardiac involvement (arrhythmias, heart block, ST-T wave changes).
sections.treatment:
• **Immediate Hospitalization and Isolation** (respiratory droplet precautions).
• Treatment is URGENT and has two main components:
    ◦ **1. Diphtheria Antitoxin**:
        ▪ **Most critical step**.
        ▪ Neutralizes **unbound circulating toxin** only; does not affect toxin already bound to cells.
        ▪ Obtained from the CDC.
        ▪ It is an equine (horse) serum product, so test for hypersensitivity before administering.
    ◦ **2. Antibiotics**:
        ▪ Purpose: Eradicate the bacteria to halt toxin production and prevent transmission.
        ▪ **First-line**: **Erythromycin** (PO or IV for 14 days) OR **Penicillin G** (IV for 14 days).
        ▪ Clindamycin is an alternative.
• **Supportive Care**:
    ◦ **Airway Management**: Secure the airway via intubation or tracheostomy if there are signs of obstruction from the pseudomembrane.
sections.management:
• **Isolation**: Maintain droplet precautions until two consecutive cultures (taken at least 24 hours apart after antibiotic completion) are negative.
• **Public Health**: Report all suspected cases to local and state health departments immediately.
• **Close Contact Management**:
    ◦ Identify and screen all close contacts for symptoms.
    ◦ Obtain cultures from nose and throat.
    ◦ Administer a diphtheria booster vaccine if not up-to-date.
    ◦ Provide prophylactic antibiotics: a 7-10 day course of oral **Erythromycin** or a single IM dose of **Penicillin G benzathine**.
• **Patient Follow-up**:
    ◦ Monitor with serial ECGs and neurologic exams for complications.
    ◦ Confirm bacteriologic cure with follow-up cultures.
    ◦ Ensure patient completes their primary vaccination series or receives a booster, as natural infection does not guarantee lifelong immunity.
sections.complications:
• **Myocarditis**:
    ◦ **Most common cause of death**.
    ◦ Typically occurs 1-2 weeks after onset of illness.
    ◦ Can manifest as arrhythmias, heart block, or fulminant heart failure.
• **Neuropathy**:
    ◦ Occurs in ~75% of severe cases, usually weeks to months after illness onset.
    ◦ Starts with local paralysis (paralysis of the soft palate) and can progress to cranial neuropathies (diplopia, blurred vision) and a symmetrical, ascending peripheral polyneuropathy similar to Guillain-Barré syndrome.
• **Airway Obstruction**: A medical emergency caused by the pseudomembrane dislodging or extending into the larynx/trachea.
• **Renal**: Acute tubular necrosis from toxemia.
sections.prognosis:
• The case-fatality rate is 5-10% even with treatment.
• Prognosis is worse in the very young (<5 years) and old (>40 years).
• Death is most often due to **airway obstruction** or **myocarditis**.
• Neurologic complications are often reversible but recovery can be slow.

sections.overview:
• **Epiglottitis** is an acute, life-threatening inflammatory condition of the epiglottis and adjacent supraglottic structures (aryepiglottic folds, arytenoids)
    ◦ It is a true medical emergency due to its potential for rapid progression to complete **upper airway obstruction**
• Historically a pediatric disease caused by ***Haemophilus influenzae* type b (Hib)**, the incidence in children has plummeted due to widespread **Hib vaccination**
    ◦ It is now more common in adults, though it can still occur in un/under-immunized children
• Immediate recognition and **airway management** are paramount
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Classic Cause**: ***Haemophilus influenzae* type b (Hib)**
        ▪ Still the primary cause in unvaccinated individuals
    ◦ **Post-Vaccine Era Causes**
        ▪ **Bacterial (most common)**
            - *Streptococcus pneumoniae*
            - *Staphylococcus aureus* (including **MRSA**)
            - Group A *Streptococcus* (GAS)
            - *Haemophilus influenzae* (non-typeable strains)
        ▪ **Viral**: Less common, includes Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), Parainfluenza virus
        ▪ **Fungal**: Rare, primarily in immunocompromised hosts (*Candida*)
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Inoculation**: Pathogens colonize or invade the posterior nasopharynx and travel to the epiglottis
    ◦ **Infection & Inflammation**: Direct bacterial invasion of the epithelial layer of the epiglottis leads to cellulitis
    ◦ **Rapid Edema**: The rich vascular and lymphatic supply of the supraglottic tissues facilitates rapid and massive inflammation and edema
    ◦ **Airway Obstruction**: The swollen, **"cherry-red" epiglottis** and surrounding structures protrude posteriorly, obstructing the airway at the laryngeal inlet
        ▪ This can lead to laryngospasm and complete, abrupt airway occlusion
sections.epidemiology:
• **Pre-Hib Vaccine Era**: Primarily a disease of children aged 2-7 years
• **Post-Hib Vaccine Era**
    ◦ Dramatic (>90%) decrease in pediatric incidence
    ◦ Now more common in adults, with a median age of 45-50 years
    ◦ Pediatric cases are now more often seen in unimmunized or under-immunized children
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is classically described by the **"3 D's"** (Dysphagia, Drooling, Distress) in children, but the overall picture is one of a rapidly deteriorating, **toxic-appearing patient**
    ◦ **Abrupt Onset**: Symptoms develop over hours, not days
    ◦ **High Fever**: Temperature often >39°C (102.2°F)
    ◦ **Toxic Appearance**: Patient appears ill, anxious, and irritable
    ◦ **Tripod Position**: Patient sits leaning forward on their hands, with neck hyperextended and chin thrust forward
        ▪ This is a conscious effort to maximize airway diameter
    ◦ **Sniffing Position**: Similar to the tripod position, the head and neck are extended as if sniffing the air
    ◦ Muffled **"Hot Potato" Voice**: Caused by pharyngeal edema
        ▪ The patient sounds as if they are trying to speak with a mouthful of hot food
    ◦ **Stridor**: A high-pitched inspiratory sound that is a late and ominous sign of severe airway narrowing
        ▪ It may be absent early on
sections.diagnostics:
• **Airway management supersedes all diagnostic procedures.**
• **Clinical Diagnosis**
    ◦ Diagnosis is primarily clinical. A high index of suspicion in a patient with the classic presentation is sufficient to initiate emergency management
• **Direct Laryngoscopy**
    ◦ **Gold Standard** for diagnosis
    ◦ Performed in a controlled setting (Operating Room) by an experienced provider (Anesthesiology or ENT) with full airway equipment, including tracheostomy supplies, immediately available
• **Lateral Neck X-ray**
    ◦ **Only for stable patients** where the diagnosis is uncertain. Moving an unstable patient to radiology is dangerous
    ◦ **Classic Finding: "Thumbprint Sign"**
        ▪ The swollen epiglottis appears as a large, rounded soft tissue shadow resembling the distal phalanx of a thumb
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ Useful but secondary to securing the airway
    ◦ CBC may show leukocytosis with a left shift
    ◦ Blood cultures can identify the causative organism
sections.prognosis:
• With prompt diagnosis, airway management, and antibiotic therapy, the prognosis is excellent
• Mortality rate in hospitalized patients is <1%
• Delayed diagnosis and failure to secure the airway can be fatal

sections.overview:
• Bacterial meningitis is an acute purulent infection and inflammation of the meninges (pia mater, arachnoid mater) and the subarachnoid space.
    ◦ It is a **neurologic emergency** characterized by high morbidity and mortality, requiring immediate diagnosis and empirical antimicrobial therapy.
    ◦ The classic presentation involves fever, nuchal rigidity, and altered mental status.
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Colonization:** Pathogenic bacteria colonize the nasopharynx or another site (e.g., skin, GI tract).
    ◦ **Invasion:** Bacteria invade the bloodstream (bacteremia) through mucosal epithelium.
    ◦ **Meningeal Seeding:** Bacteria cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and enter the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
    ◦ **Inflammatory Cascade:** Bacterial replication in the subarachnoid space triggers a massive inflammatory response. Release of cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1) leads to:
        ▪ Increased BBB permeability -> Vasogenic edema.
        ▪ Leukocyte recruitment (neutrophils) into CSF -> Purulence.
        ▪ Cerebral vasculitis -> Cytotoxic edema and potential for ischemic stroke.
    ◦ **Consequences:** The inflammatory cascade results in **increased intracranial pressure (ICP)**, cerebral edema, and decreased cerebral blood flow, leading to neuronal injury.
• **Common Pathogens by Age Group**
    ◦ **Neonates (<1 month):**
        ▪ **Group B Streptococcus (GBS, *S. agalactiae*)** - Most common
        ▪ *Escherichia coli* (and other gram-negative bacilli)
        ▪ *Listeria monocytogenes*
    ◦ **Infants/Children (1 month - 18 years):**
        ▪ ***Streptococcus pneumoniae***
        ▪ ***Neisseria meningitidis***
        ▪ *Haemophilus influenzae* type b (Hib) - Now rare due to vaccination.
    ◦ **Adults (18 - 50 years):**
        ▪ ***Streptococcus pneumoniae*** - Most common
        ▪ ***Neisseria meningitidis***
    ◦ **Older Adults (>50 years), Alcoholics, Immunocompromised:**
        ▪ ***Streptococcus pneumoniae***
        ▪ *Neisseria meningitidis*
        ▪ ***Listeria monocytogenes***
        ▪ Gram-negative bacilli (e.g., *Klebsiella*, *Pseudomonas*)
    ◦ **Post-neurosurgery or Head Trauma:**
        ▪ *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Staphylococcus epidermidis*, Gram-negative bacilli (*Pseudomonas*)
sections.epidemiology:
• Incidence has dramatically decreased in the U.S. and developed countries due to widespread vaccination against *H. influenzae* type b (Hib), *S. pneumoniae* (PCV13, PPSV23), and *N. meningitidis* (MenACWY, MenB).
• *S. pneumoniae* is now the most common cause of bacterial meningitis in adults in the U.S.
• *N. meningitidis* is known for causing outbreaks in settings of close contact (college dormitories, military barracks).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is often acute, developing over hours to 1-2 days.
• The **classic triad** of **fever, nuchal rigidity, and altered mental status** is present in only ~40-50% of adult patients, but >95% will have at least two of the following four: fever, headache, nuchal rigidity, or altered mental status.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Immediate Steps**
    ◦ Draw **blood cultures** (x2).
    ◦ Administer empiric **antibiotics** and **dexamethasone**.
    ◦ **DO NOT DELAY ANTIBIOTICS FOR LP OR IMAGING.**
    ◦ Assess for contraindications to Lumbar Puncture (LP).
• **Lumbar Puncture (LP) with CSF Analysis**
    ◦ This is the **GOLD STANDARD** for diagnosis.
    ◦ **CT scan of the head should be performed *before* LP** if there is concern for increased ICP that could cause herniation.
        ▪ Indications for pre-LP CT scan:
            ▪ New-onset **s**eizure
            ▪ **I**mmunocompromised state
            ▪ **N**eurologic deficit (focal)
            ▪ **P**apilledema
            ▪ **A**ltered consciousness (significantly depressed)
    ◦ **CSF Analysis - Typical Bacterial Profile:**
        ▪ **Opening Pressure:** **Markedly elevated** (>200-300 mmH2O).
        ▪ **Appearance:** Turbid or purulent.
        ▪ **WBC Count:** **Markedly elevated** (typically >1,000 cells/L, often >5,000).
        ▪ **WBC Differential:** **Neutrophil predominance** (>80%).
        ▪ **Glucose:** **Low** (<40 mg/dL or CSF:serum glucose ratio <0.4).
        ▪ **Protein:** **Elevated** (>100 mg/dL, often >200).
        ▪ **Gram Stain & Culture:** **Definitive diagnosis.** Gram stain is positive in 60-90% of cases. Culture is essential for sensitivities.
        ▪ **PCR:** Can be used for rapid detection of *S. pneumo*, *N. meningitidis*, etc.
• **Other Labs**
    ◦ CBC with differential (leukocytosis with left shift).
    ◦ CMP (check for renal function, electrolytes for SIADH).
    ◦ Coagulation studies (PT/INR, PTT) if petechiae/purpura present (concern for DIC).
    ◦ Inflammatory markers: CRP and Procalcitonin are usually markedly elevated.
sections.prognosis:
• Mortality remains high despite modern therapy (~10-20%).
• Prognosis is worse for pneumococcal meningitis, older age, delayed treatment, and severity of illness on presentation (e.g., coma, seizures).
• Up to 50% of survivors may have long-term neurologic deficits.

sections.overview:
• Viral meningitis, also known as **aseptic meningitis**, is an inflammation of the **meninges** caused by a viral infection.
    ◦ It is the most common type of meningitis and is generally less severe than bacterial meningitis.
    ◦ The clinical course is typically **self-limiting** in immunocompetent individuals, with most patients making a full recovery with supportive care.
    ◦ The key feature distinguishing it from encephalitis is the **absence of significant cerebral parenchymal dysfunction** (i.e., normal mental status, no focal neurologic deficits).
sections.etiology:
• **Most Common Causes**
    ◦ **Enteroviruses** (most common cause, >85% of cases)
        ▪ Coxsackievirus A and B, Echovirus
        ▪ **Transmission**: Fecal-oral, respiratory droplets
        ▪ **Seasonality**: Late summer and early fall
    ◦ **Herpesviruses**
        ▪ **Herpes Simplex Virus 2 (HSV-2)**: Common cause of viral meningitis in adults. Associated with primary genital infection. Can cause recurrent benign lymphocytic meningitis (**Mollaret's meningitis**).
        ▪ **Herpes Simplex Virus 1 (HSV-1)**: More commonly associated with encephalitis, but can cause meningitis.
        ▪ **Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV)**: Can occur with primary infection (chickenpox) or reactivation (shingles).
        ▪ **Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV)**, **Cytomegalovirus (CMV)**: More common in immunocompromised patients.
    ◦ **Arboviruses**
        ▪ West Nile Virus, St. Louis Encephalitis Virus
        ▪ **Transmission**: Mosquito bite
        ▪ **Seasonality**: Summer and fall
    ◦ **Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV)**
        ▪ Can cause aseptic meningitis during the acute seroconversion phase.
    ◦ **Mumps Virus**
        ▪ Once a common cause, now rare due to MMR vaccination.
    ◦ **Lymphocytic Choriomeningitis Virus (LCMV)**
        ▪ Transmitted by exposure to infected rodents (mice, hamsters).
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **1. Entry & Viremia**: The virus enters the host (e.g., GI tract for enterovirus, respiratory tract) and replicates, leading to **viremia** (virus in the bloodstream).
    ◦ **2. CNS Invasion**: The virus crosses the blood-brain barrier or blood-CSF barrier to enter the central nervous system.
    ◦ **3. Meningeal Inflammation**: The virus replicates within the meninges, triggering an inflammatory cascade.
    ◦ **4. Immune Response**: This results in a predominantly **lymphocytic infiltration** into the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), leading to meningeal irritation and the characteristic signs and symptoms.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Viral meningitis is significantly more common than bacterial meningitis.
• **Age**: Bimodal distribution. It is most common in infants and young children (<5 years), with a second, smaller peak in adolescents and young adults.
• **Seasonality**: A distinct peak in incidence occurs in the late summer and early fall, corresponding to the circulation of enteroviruses and arboviruses.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is an acute onset of illness but is typically less severe and fulminant than bacterial meningitis. Patients appear ill but are generally not toxic or moribund.
    ◦ The hallmark is the presence of **meningeal irritation** without signs of cerebral dysfunction.
• **The classic triad** (less common than in bacterial meningitis):
    ◦ **Fever**
    ◦ **Headache**
    ◦ **Nuchal Rigidity** (stiff neck)
sections.diagnostics:
• **Lumbar Puncture (LP) and CSF Analysis is the definitive diagnostic test.**
• **Head CT Scan (prior to LP)**
    ◦ Indicated only if there are signs of **increased intracranial pressure (ICP)** to rule out a mass lesion that could cause herniation.
    ◦ Order a CT first if the patient has:
        ▪ **Papilledema**
        ▪ New-onset **seizure**
        ▪ **Altered mental status**
        ▪ **Focal neurologic deficit**
        ▪ **Immunocompromised** state
• **Typical CSF Findings in Viral Meningitis**
    ◦ **Opening Pressure**: Normal or slightly elevated (<25 cm H2O)
    ◦ **Appearance**: **Clear**
    ◦ **WBC Count**: **Elevated (10-500 cells/L)**
        ▪ A **lymphocytic pleocytosis**
    ◦ **WBC Differential**: **Lymphocytic predominance**
        ▪ *Early on (<48h), may show neutrophils*
    ◦ **Protein**: Normal or mildly elevated (<150 mg/dL)
    ◦ **Glucose**: **Normal** (>40 mg/dL or >60% of serum glucose)
        ▪ **KEY DIFFERENTIATOR from bacterial**
• **Confirmatory Testing**
    ◦ **CSF Viral PCR**: The gold standard for identifying the specific viral pathogen (e.g., Enterovirus, HSV, VZV). High sensitivity and specificity.
    ◦ **Other Labs**: CBC, CMP, blood cultures (to rule out sepsis/bacteremia).
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** in most immunocompetent patients.
    ◦ Viral meningitis is typically a **self-limiting disease** with full recovery expected within 7 to 10 days.
• The prognosis is more guarded for meningitis caused by HSV, VZV, West Nile Virus, and in neonates or immunocompromised individuals, especially if **meningoencephalitis** develops.

sections.overview:
• **Encephalitis** is an acute inflammation of the **brain parenchyma** (the functional tissue of the brain)
    ◦ It is a neurologic emergency
    ◦ It is distinct from meningitis (inflammation of the meninges), although the two can coexist (**meningoencephalitis**)
    ◦ The hallmark of encephalitis that distinguishes it from uncomplicated meningitis is the presence of **altered brain function** (e.g., altered mental status, motor/sensory deficits, personality changes, seizures)
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: ~7 cases per 100,000 annually
• **Distribution**: Occurs worldwide. Specific etiologies have geographic and seasonal patterns
    ◦ **Arboviruses**: More common in summer and early fall when mosquitoes are active. West Nile Virus is endemic throughout North America
    ◦ **HSV**: No seasonal or geographic preference; occurs year-round
• **Age**: Affects all ages, but the very young and the elderly are at highest risk for severe disease
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a rapid onset of the "encephalitis triad":
    ◦ **Fever**
    ◦ **Headache**
    ◦ **Altered Mental Status (AMS)**
• The presence of **AMS and/or focal neurologic deficits** is the key feature that distinguishes encephalitis from simple viral meningitis
• The onset can be over hours to days, often preceded by a non-specific viral prodrome (fever, myalgias, fatigue)
sections.diagnostics:
• **Time is critical**. Begin empiric treatment immediately after lumbar puncture, without waiting for results
• **Lumbar Puncture (LP) & CSF Analysis (THE KEY DIAGNOSTIC TEST)**
    ◦ **Opening Pressure**: Typically elevated
    ◦ **Cell Count**: **Lymphocytic pleocytosis** (elevated WBCs with a predominance of lymphocytes). Neutrophils may dominate in the very early stages
    ◦ **Protein**: Mild to moderately **elevated**
    ◦ **Glucose**: **Normal**. (This helps differentiate from bacterial meningitis, where glucose is low)
    ◦ **CSF PCR**: **The single most important test for etiology**
        ▪ **HSV-1/2 PCR is mandatory in all suspected cases**. High sensitivity and specificity
        ▪ Also order VZV, Enterovirus PCR panels
    ◦ **CSF IgM**: For arboviruses like West Nile Virus
• **Neuroimaging**
    ◦ **MRI of the Brain (with and without contrast)**: **Modality of choice**. More sensitive than CT for showing parenchymal inflammation, edema, and necrosis
        ▪ **HSV Encephalitis classically shows T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in the medial temporal lobes and insular cortex**
    ◦ **CT of the Head (non-contrast)**: Often the first test performed in the ER to rule out other causes of AMS like hemorrhage, tumor, or abscess before performing an LP. It is often normal in early encephalitis
• **Electroencephalogram (EEG)**
    ◦ Shows diffuse, non-specific slowing consistent with encephalopathy
    ◦ Can reveal seizure activity
    ◦ **Periodic Lateralizing Epileptiform Discharges (PLEDs)**, especially over the temporal lobes, are highly suggestive of **HSV encephalitis**
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly dependent on the causative agent, the patient's age and immune status, and the time to initiation of treatment
• **Untreated HSV encephalitis has a mortality rate >70%**
• With prompt acyclovir treatment, mortality for HSV drops to ~20-30%, but a high percentage of survivors have significant long-term neurologic deficits
• Prognosis for arboviral encephalitis varies widely; EEE has a very high mortality rate (~30-70%)

sections.overview:
• A **brain abscess** is a **focal, encapsulated collection of pus** within the brain parenchyma.
    ◦ It begins as a localized area of **cerebritis** (inflammation of brain tissue) and develops into a **necrotic, pus-filled cavity** surrounded by a **vascularized capsule**.
    ◦ It is a **life-threatening neurosurgical emergency** that presents as a **space-occupying lesion** and requires prompt diagnosis and treatment with both antimicrobial therapy and often surgical drainage.
sections.etiology:
• A brain abscess develops through a predictable four-stage process:
    ◦ **Early Cerebritis (Days 1-3):** Localized inflammatory response with perivascular infiltration of inflammatory cells. Poorly demarcated.
    ◦ **Late Cerebritis (Days 4-9):** A necrotic center develops, surrounded by inflammatory cells and marked vasogenic edema.
    ◦ **Early Capsule Formation (Days 10-13):** A thin capsule of fibroblasts and collagen forms around the necrotic center.
    ◦ **Late Capsule Formation (Day 14+):** A well-defined, thick collagenous capsule fully encloses the liquefied necrotic contents.
• **Routes of Infection:**
    ◦ **Contiguous Spread (Most Common, ~50%):** Direct extension from an adjacent infection.
        ▪ **Source -> Abscess Location:**
            • **Otitis Media / Mastoiditis** -> Temporal lobe, Cerebellum
            • **Frontal or Ethmoid Sinusitis** -> Frontal lobe
            • **Dental Infections** -> Frontal lobe
            • **Sphenoid Sinusitis** -> Frontal or Temporal lobe
    ◦ **Hematogenous Spread (~25%):** Seeding from a distant primary infection, often resulting in multiple abscesses, typically at the gray-white matter junction.
        ▪ **Sources:** Chronic pulmonary infections (bronchiectasis, empyema), bacterial endocarditis, skin infections, osteomyelitis, intra-abdominal infections.
        ▪ Associated with **right-to-left cardiac shunts** (e.g., Tetralogy of Fallot) which allow bacteria to bypass pulmonary filtration.
    ◦ **Direct Inoculation (~20%):**
        ▪ Penetrating head trauma
        ▪ Neurosurgical procedures
• **Common Pathogens:**
    ◦ **Polymicrobial** infections are very common.
    ◦ **Most Frequent:**
        ▪ *Streptococcus* species (especially *S. anginosus* group - *S. intermedius*, *S. constellatus*)
        ▪ Anaerobes (*Bacteroides*, *Prevotella*, *Peptostreptococcus*)
    ◦ **Source-Specific Pathogens:**
        ▪ **Trauma/Neurosurgery:** *Staphylococcus aureus*, Gram-negative bacilli (*Pseudomonas*, Enterobacteriaceae)
        ▪ **Otitis/Sinusitis:** *Streptococcus*, *Bacteroides*, *Haemophilus* spp.
        ▪ **Dental source:** *Fusobacterium*, *Prevotella*, *Streptococcus*
        ▪ **Immunocompromised:** *Toxoplasma gondii*, *Nocardia*, Fungi (*Aspergillus*, *Candida*), *Listeria*
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence:** Relatively rare, approximately 0.3-1.3 cases per 100,000 people per year in developed countries.
• **Age:** **Bimodal distribution**, with peaks in childhood (<10 years) and middle age (30-50 years).
• **Sex:** Male-to-female ratio is approximately 2-3:1.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation is typically **subacute**, evolving over days to weeks.
• The classic triad of **headache, fever, and focal neurologic deficit** is present in **less than 50%** of patients.
• The most common presenting symptom is **headache**.
• Symptoms are due to a combination of infection and the mass effect of the lesion.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Imaging (Definitive Diagnostic Modality):**
    ◦ **MRI with gadolinium contrast is the gold standard.**
        ▪ **Classic finding:** A **ring-enhancing lesion** on T1-weighted post-contrast images.
        ▪ The lesion has a hypointense (dark) center representing pus, a smooth, thin, enhancing rim (capsule), and surrounding hyperintensity (bright) on T2/FLAIR images representing vasogenic edema.
    ◦ Diffusion-Weighted Imaging (DWI) is highly characteristic, showing **restricted diffusion** (bright signal) in the abscess cavity, helping differentiate it from necrotic tumors.
    ◦ **CT with contrast:**
        ▪ Alternative if MRI is contraindicated or unavailable.
        ▪ Also shows a ring-enhancing lesion with surrounding edema but is less sensitive, especially for early cerebritis.
• **Laboratory Studies:**
    ◦ **CBC:** Leukocytosis may be present but is non-specific.
    ◦ **Inflammatory markers:** ESR and C-reactive protein (CRP) are usually elevated but non-specific.
    ◦ **Blood cultures:** Obtain before starting antibiotics. Positive in only ~10-35% of cases but can guide therapy if positive.
• **Biopsy / Aspiration:**
    ◦ **Stereotactic-guided needle aspiration** is the procedure of choice for both diagnosis and therapy.
    ◦ Pus should be sent for Gram stain, aerobic/anaerobic/fungal/mycobacterial cultures, and pathology.
• **Lumbar Puncture (LP):**
    ◦ **STRONGLY CONTRAINDICATED** in patients with a suspected brain abscess due to the risk of **uncal or tonsillar herniation** from the mass effect.
    ◦ If performed, CSF findings are non-specific (pleocytosis, elevated protein, normal/low glucose).
sections.prognosis:
• With modern neuro-imaging, surgical techniques, and antibiotics, the mortality rate has dropped significantly from >40% to **5-15%**.
• **Poor Prognostic Factors:**
    ◦ Delayed diagnosis and treatment
    ◦ Low GCS / Coma at presentation
    ◦ Ventricular rupture
    ◦ Multiple or deep-seated abscesses
    ◦ Immunocompromised state
• Significant neurologic morbidity occurs in 30-50% of survivors.

sections.overview:
• Lyme disease is the most common vector-borne illness in the United States and Europe, caused by the spirochete bacterium **_Borrelia burgdorferi_** and transmitted to humans through the bite of infected **_Ixodes_** species ticks (deer ticks).
• It is a multisystem inflammatory disease with a clinical course typically divided into three stages: early localized, early disseminated, and late disseminated disease.
• Early recognition and treatment are crucial to prevent progression to later, more severe stages.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Organism**: Caused by gram-negative spirochetes of the **_Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato_** complex.
    ◦ **USA**: Primarily **_Borrelia burgdorferi_**. *B. mayonii* is a less common cause in the upper Midwest.
    ◦ **Europe/Asia**: **_B. afzelii_** (associated with skin manifestations) and **_B. garinii_** (associated with neurologic manifestations).
• **Vector**: Transmitted by the bite of an infected **_Ixodes_** tick.
    ◦ **Eastern/Midwestern US**: **_Ixodes scapularis_** (deer tick).
    ◦ **Western US**: **_Ixodes pacificus_** (western black-legged tick).
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Transmission**: An infected tick attaches and feeds; spirochetes migrate from the tick's midgut to salivary glands. Transmission typically requires the tick to be attached for **36-48 hours**.
    ◦ **Inoculation**: Spirochetes are injected into the skin, where they multiply and migrate outward, causing the characteristic **erythema migrans (EM)** rash.
    ◦ **Dissemination**: The bacteria spread from the skin via lymphatic vessels and the bloodstream to other tissues, particularly the **joints**, **nervous system**, and **heart**.
    ◦ **Inflammatory Response**: The clinical manifestations are primarily due to the host's inflammatory and immune response to the spirochetes, rather than direct tissue damage from a bacterial toxin.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Geography**: Highest incidence in the **Northeast**, **Mid-Atlantic**, and **Upper Midwest** regions of the United States. Also prevalent in forested areas of Europe and Asia.
• **Incidence**: The CDC estimates ~476,000 cases per year in the US, making it the most common vector-borne disease.
• **Seasonality**: Most cases occur in late spring and summer (**May-August**), coinciding with the peak activity of nymphal-stage **_Ixodes_** ticks, which are small and often go unnoticed.
sections.riskFactors:
• Living in or traveling to an endemic, wooded, or grassy area.
• Outdoor occupations (e.g., landscaping, forestry).
• Recreational activities like hiking, camping, and gardening.
• Having pets that can carry ticks into the home.
• Failure to use tick repellents (e.g., **DEET**, **Picaridin**) or perform tick checks.
• Improper tick removal.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Lyme disease presentation is classically divided into three stages, which may overlap.
• **Stage 1: Early Localized Disease (3-30 days post-bite)**
    ◦ Characterized by the hallmark skin lesion, **Erythema Migrans (EM)**.
    ◦ Accompanied by non-specific, flu-like symptoms:
        ▪ Fatigue, malaise, lethargy
        ▪ Fever and chills
        ▪ Myalgias and arthralgias
        ▪ Headache
        ▪ The EM rash is often asymptomatic (not painful or pruritic).
• **Stage 2: Early Disseminated Disease (Weeks to months post-bite)**
    ◦ Occurs as the spirochete spreads throughout the body, involving the skin, nervous system, and heart.
    ◦ **Key Manifestations**:
        ▪ Multiple EM lesions
        ▪ **Neurologic**: Headache, stiff neck, unilateral or **bilateral facial nerve (CN VII) palsy**, meningitis, radiculoneuropathy (sharp, shooting nerve pain).
        ▪ **Cardiac**: Palpitations, dizziness, lightheadedness, syncope, chest pain, or dyspnea due to **AV block**.
        ▪ **General**: Worsening fatigue and malaise.
• **Stage 3: Late Disseminated Disease (Months to years post-bite)**
    ◦ Occurs in untreated or inadequately treated patients.
    ◦ **Key Manifestations**:
        ▪ **Musculoskeletal**: Intermittent or persistent swelling and pain in one or a few large joints (especially the **knee**).
        ▪ **Neurologic**: Subtle cognitive difficulties ("**brain fog**"), memory impairment, peripheral neuropathy (distal paresthesias).
sections.physicalExam:
• **Skin**:
    ◦ **Erythema Migrans (EM)**: An expanding erythematous macule or papule, typically >5 cm in diameter. The classic **"bull's-eye"** or targetoid appearance (central clearing) is seen in <20% of cases; more commonly, it is a uniformly erythematous, expanding patch.
    ◦ **Multiple EM lesions**: A sign of disseminated disease.
• **Neurologic**:
    ◦ **Cranial Neuropathy**: **Facial nerve (CN VII) palsy** is the most common finding. Assess for facial asymmetry, inability to wrinkle forehead, close eye tightly, or smile symmetrically.
    ◦ **Meningeal Signs**: Nuchal rigidity, Kernig's sign, or Brudzinski's sign may be present with meningitis.
    ◦ **Radiculopathy/Peripheral Neuropathy**: Assessed with sensory and motor testing.
• **Cardiovascular**:
    ◦ Bradycardia or an irregular rhythm on auscultation, suggesting **AV heart block**.
• **Musculoskeletal**:
    ◦ Signs of arthritis in a large joint (most often the **knee**): Effusion (swelling), warmth, tenderness to palpation, and decreased range of motion. Typically monoarticular or oligoarticular.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Early Localized Disease (Typical EM Rash)**:
    ◦ Diagnosis is **clinical**.
    ◦ If a patient has a characteristic EM rash and a history of possible tick exposure in an endemic area, **serologic testing is not recommended** as it is often negative in this early stage.
    ◦ Treatment should be initiated immediately based on clinical findings.
• **Disseminated or Late Disease**:
    ◦ **Two-Tiered Serologic Testing (CDC Recommended)**:
        ▪ **First Tier**: Enzyme Immunoassay (EIA) or Immunofluorescence Assay (IFA).
            ◦ This test is sensitive but not highly specific.
            ◦ If negative, no further testing is needed.
            ◦ If positive or equivocal, proceed to the second tier.
        ▪ **Second Tier**: **Western Blot**.
            ◦ This test is more specific and confirms the diagnosis by detecting antibodies to specific *_B. burgdorferi_* proteins.
            ◦ IgM is useful within the first month of infection; IgG becomes positive later and can persist for years.
    ◦ **Ancillary Testing**:
        ▪ **ECG**: For any patient with cardiac symptoms (e.g., palpitations, syncope) to evaluate for **AV block**.
        ▪ **Lumbar Puncture**: For patients with signs of meningitis or CNS involvement. CSF analysis shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, and normal glucose. CSF PCR has low sensitivity but is highly specific.
        ▪ **Arthrocentesis**: For patients with joint effusion. Synovial fluid shows an inflammatory picture (WBC 25,000-100,000/L, predominantly neutrophils), with negative gram stain and culture. PCR of synovial fluid is highly sensitive for Lyme arthritis.
sections.treatment:
• **Prophylaxis (Post-Exposure)**:
    ◦ A single dose of **Doxycycline 200 mg** can be given if ALL of the following criteria are met:
        ▪ Attached tick identified as an adult or nymphal *_I. scapularis_* tick.
        ▪ Tick attached for ≥36 hours.
        ▪ Prophylaxis started within 72 hours of tick removal.
        ▪ Local rate of tick infection with *_B. burgdorferi_* is ≥20%.
        ▪ Doxycycline is not contraindicated.
• **Early Localized Disease (EM rash)**:
    ◦ **First Line**: **Doxycycline** 100 mg PO BID for 10-14 days.
    ◦ **Alternatives** (for children <8, pregnant/lactating women): **Amoxicillin** 500 mg PO TID or **Cefuroxime** 500 mg PO BID for 14 days.
• **Early Disseminated Disease**:
    ◦ **Uncomplicated** (e.g., facial palsy, mild carditis/1st degree AV block): **Doxycycline** 100 mg PO BID for 14-21 days.
    ◦ **Severe** (e.g., meningitis, 2nd/3rd degree AV block): **Ceftriaxone** 2 g IV daily for 14-28 days. Hospitalization and cardiac monitoring required for high-degree AV block.
• **Late Disease (Lyme Arthritis)**:
    ◦ **First Line**: **Doxycycline** 100 mg PO BID for 28 days.
    ◦ **Refractory Arthritis** (persistent synovitis after oral course): A second course of oral antibiotics or a 2-4 week course of IV **Ceftriaxone**.
sections.management:
• **Follow-up**: Patients should be monitored for resolution of symptoms. Most symptoms resolve within weeks of treatment, though fatigue and myalgias may linger.
• **Jarisch-Herxheimer Reaction**: A transient worsening of symptoms (fever, chills, myalgias) within 24 hours of starting antibiotic therapy, due to a massive release of spirochete antigens. It is self-limiting and managed with supportive care (e.g., antipyretics). Patients should be warned of this possibility.
• **Post-Treatment Lyme Disease Syndrome (PTLDS)**:
    ◦ A subset of patients report persistent symptoms (fatigue, pain, "**brain fog**") for >6 months after appropriate treatment.
    ◦ The etiology is unclear, but **additional long-term antibiotic therapy has not been shown to be effective and is not recommended**.
    ◦ Management is supportive and symptomatic.
sections.complications:
• **Cardiac**: Complete (**third-degree**) **heart block**, myopericarditis, cardiomegaly.
• **Neurologic**: Post-Lyme encephalopathy (memory loss, cognitive slowing), chronic axonal polyneuropathy, meningoencephalitis.
• **Musculoskeletal**: Chronic, erosive arthritis (rare).
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**: The vast majority of patients who are diagnosed and treated early make a full and rapid recovery.
• **Good to Fair**: Patients with later-stage disease usually respond well to treatment, but recovery may be slower, and some symptoms (e.g., arthralgias, fatigue) may persist for months.
• **PTLDS**: Affects a minority (~10%) of patients and can cause significant long-term morbidity, though it typically improves slowly over time.
sections.preventionEducation:
• Education on tick avoidance is key:
    ◦ Use insect repellent containing **DEET** or **Picaridin** on exposed skin and clothing.
    ◦ Wear light-colored, long-sleeved clothing to easily spot ticks.
    ◦ Perform daily, full-body tick checks after being in endemic, wooded, or grassy areas.
    ◦ Promptly and properly remove attached ticks with fine-tipped tweezers, pulling upward with steady, even pressure.

sections.overview:
• Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever (RMSF) is the most severe and most frequently reported rickettsial illness in the United States.
    ◦ It is a tick-borne disease caused by the bacterium *Rickettsia rickettsii*.
• Despite its name, it is most prevalent in the southeastern and south-central US.
• The classic presentation involves a triad of **fever**, **headache**, and a characteristic **rash**, though not all patients will present with all three.
• RMSF is a medical emergency; delayed diagnosis and treatment can lead to severe multi-organ dysfunction and death.
• Empirical treatment should be initiated based on clinical suspicion alone, without waiting for confirmatory lab results.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiologic Agent**: *Rickettsia rickettsii*, an obligate intracellular, gram-negative coccobacillus.
• **Vector**: Hard-shelled ticks.
    ◦ **American Dog Tick** (*Dermacentor variabilis*): Primary vector in the Eastern & Central US.
    ◦ **Rocky Mountain Wood Tick** (*Dermacentor andersoni*): Primary vector in the Western US.
    ◦ **Brown Dog Tick** (*Rhipicephalus sanguineus*): Vector in parts of the Southwest (e.g., Arizona).
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Inoculation**: Bacteria are transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected tick after several hours of attachment (typically 6-10 hours).
    ◦ **Dissemination**: *R. rickettsii* spreads via the lymphatic system and bloodstream.
    ◦ **Endothelial Invasion**: The primary target is the vascular endothelial cell lining of small and medium-sized blood vessels throughout the body.
    ◦ **Vasculitis**: The bacteria replicate within the endothelial cells, causing direct cellular injury, which triggers a host inflammatory response. This leads to a systemic vasculitis.
    ◦ **Vascular Permeability**: The widespread vasculitis increases vascular permeability, leading to:
        ▪ Leakage of plasma into the interstitial space.
        ▪ Resulting edema (peripheral, pulmonary, cerebral), hypovolemia, and hypotension.
        ▪ Loss of electrolytes, causing **hyponatremia**.
    ◦ **Microthrombi & Hemorrhage**: Damage to the endothelium also activates platelets and the coagulation cascade, leading to microthrombi formation, which can cause ischemia and organ damage. Damage and vessel leakage result in petechial and purpuric lesions.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Geography**:
    ◦ The name is a misnomer. The highest incidence is *not* in the Rocky Mountains.
    ◦ Most common in the "Tick Belt" of the south-central and southeastern US.
    ◦ Over 60% of cases occur in 5 states: **North Carolina**, **Oklahoma**, **Arkansas**, **Tennessee**, and **Missouri**.
• **Seasonality**: Peak incidence occurs during spring and summer months (**April - September**), consistent with peak tick activity.
• **Incidence**: The most common fatal tick-borne disease in the US.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The early presentation of RMSF is notoriously non-specific, often mimicking a common viral illness.
• **Incubation Period**: 2-14 days after tick bite (average 7 days).
• **History of Tick Bite**:
    ◦ Importantly, a known tick bite is only reported in ~50-60% of cases.
    ◦ Its absence does not rule out the diagnosis.
• **Classic Triad**: **Fever**, **severe headache**, and **rash**.
    ◦ This triad is only present in a small minority of patients during the first 3 days of illness.
    ◦ Its development later in the course should strongly suggest the diagnosis.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Diagnosis is primarily clinical**.
    ◦ Treatment should be initiated empirically based on suspicion and should **NEVER** be delayed while awaiting confirmatory tests.
