• **Supportive Lab Findings (Non-specific)**:
    ◦ **CBC**:
        ▪ **Thrombocytopenia** (very common).
        ▪ Normal WBC early on (may become leukopenic or leukocytic later).
        ▪ Mild anemia.
    ◦ **CMP**:
        ▪ **Hyponatremia** (very common, due to SIADH-like effect or fluid shifts).
        ▪ Elevated hepatic transaminases (ALT/AST).
        ▪ Elevated bilirubin.
        ▪ Elevated BUN/Creatinine (AKI).
• **Confirmatory Serologic Testing (Retrospective)**:
    ◦ **Gold Standard**: Indirect Immunofluorescence Assay (IFA) for IgM and IgG antibodies to *R. rickettsii*.
        ▪ A single acute-phase titer is not sufficient.
        ▪ A **four-fold or greater rise** in antibody titers between an acute specimen (first week of illness) and a convalescent specimen (2-4 weeks later) is required for confirmation.
• **Other Tests**:
    ◦ **PCR**: Can detect rickettsial DNA in blood or tissue.
        ▪ Best performed on a skin biopsy of a rash lesion (eschar if present).
        ▪ Blood PCR has low sensitivity early in the course.
    ◦ **Immunohistochemistry (IHC)**: Staining of a skin biopsy can detect the organism in endothelial cells and is highly specific.
sections.prognosis:
• With prompt treatment (within the first 5 days), the mortality rate is < 5%.
• Without treatment or with delayed treatment, the mortality rate can be as high as 20-30%.
• Poor prognostic factors include advanced age, male sex, delayed treatment, and absence of a rash ("**spotless fever**").

sections.overview:
• Ehrlichiosis is a tick-borne infectious disease caused by obligate intracellular bacteria of the genus **_Ehrlichia_**.
	◦ The primary pathogen in the United States is **_Ehrlichia chaffeensis_**, which causes **Human Monocytic Ehrlichiosis (HME)**.
	◦ It typically presents as an acute, non-specific febrile illness characterized by fever, headache, and myalgias.
	◦ Key laboratory findings include **leukopenia**, **thrombocytopenia**, and **elevated liver transaminases**.
	◦ Prompt diagnosis and treatment with **doxycycline** are crucial to prevent severe complications.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agents**
	◦ **_Ehrlichia chaffeensis_**: Most common cause, leading to **Human Monocytic Ehrlichiosis (HME)**.
	◦ **_Ehrlichia ewingii_**: Less common, primarily affects immunocompromised patients.
	◦ **_Ehrlichia muris eauclairensis_**: Newly identified species in the upper Midwest.
• **Microbiology**
	◦ Gram-negative, obligate intracellular coccobacilli.
• **Vector**
	◦ **Lone Star Tick** (_Amblyomma americanum_).
• **Reservoir**
	◦ White-tailed deer are the primary animal reservoir.
• **Pathophysiology**
	◦ **Transmission**: The tick injects the bacteria into the bloodstream during a blood meal.
	◦ **Cellular Invasion**: _E. chaffeensis_ primarily infects and replicates within **monocytes and macrophages**. _E. ewingii_ infects granulocytes.
	◦ **Replication**: Inside the host cell's phagosome, the bacteria multiply, forming characteristic intracellular microcolonies called **morulae** (Latin for "mulberry").
	◦ **Systemic Effects**: The infection triggers a systemic inflammatory response. The release of cytokines leads to fever, myalgias, and headache. The infection and subsequent destruction of host cells lead to leukopenia and thrombocytopenia. Liver involvement causes elevated transaminases. Vascular endothelial injury can occur in severe cases, leading to increased permeability and organ damage.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Geography**: Most prevalent in the **southeastern, south-central, and mid-Atlantic United States**.
	◦ High-incidence states include Missouri, Arkansas, Oklahoma, Tennessee, and Virginia.
• **Seasonality**: Peak incidence occurs from **April to September**, coinciding with the activity of adult and nymphal Lone Star ticks.
• **Demographics**: Incidence is highest in males and individuals over 50 years of age.
sections.riskFactors:
• Residence in or travel to an endemic area.
• Outdoor occupations (e.g., forestry, landscaping).
• Outdoor recreational activities (e.g., hiking, camping, hunting).
• Exposure to tick-infested areas (wooded, grassy areas).
• **Immunocompromised state** (e.g., HIV, organ transplant, malignancy) increases the risk for severe disease.
• Failure to use tick repellents or perform tick checks.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Incubation Period**: 1-2 weeks after tick bite. Many patients (~50%) do not recall a specific bite.
• **Onset**: Typically **abrupt**.
• **General Appearance**: Patients often present with a **non-specific, flu-like illness**. The clinical presentation is frequently indistinguishable from anaplasmosis.
• **Symptoms**
	◦ **Constitutional (most common)**
		▪ **Fever (>90%)**: Often high-grade (>39C / 102F).
		▪ **Headache (70-90%)**: Can be severe and retro-orbital.
		▪ **Malaise & Myalgias (60-80%)**: Diffuse muscle aches and fatigue are very common.
	◦ **Gastrointestinal (20-70%)**
		▪ Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, anorexia, abdominal pain.
	◦ **Neurologic (20%)**
		▪ Confusion, altered mental status, photophobia, stiff neck (meningismus). More common in severe disease.
	◦ **Dermatologic (~30% of adults, ~60% of children)**
		▪ Non-pruritic, maculopapular or petechial rash.
		▪ Typically appears late in the first week of illness.
		▪ **Usually spares the palms and soles** (a key feature distinguishing it from Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever).
sections.physicalExam:
• **Vitals**: **Fever** is the most common finding. Tachycardia and hypotension may be present in severe cases.
• **General**: Patient may appear **ill or "toxic."**
• **Skin**: **Rash** may be present, typically on the trunk and extremities.
• **Abdomen**: **Hepatosplenomegaly** may be palpable in a minority of cases.
• **Neurologic**: **Altered mental status**, confusion, or signs of meningeal irritation.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Initial Labs (Highly Suggestive Findings)**
	◦ **CBC**
		▪ **Thrombocytopenia** (low platelets) - present in >80% of cases.
		▪ **Leukopenia** (low WBC count) - especially lymphopenia early on.
		▪ Mild normocytic, normochromic anemia.
	◦ **CMP**
		▪ **Elevated liver transaminases (AST/ALT)** - often 2-3x the upper limit of normal.
		▪ Hyponatremia.
• **Confirmatory Tests**
	◦ **PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction)**
		▪ **Test of choice** during the acute illness (first week).
		▪ Detects _Ehrlichia_ DNA in whole blood. High specificity but sensitivity decreases after doxycycline is started.
	◦ **Serology (Indirect Immunofluorescence Assay - IFA)**
		▪ Detects IgM and IgG antibodies.
		▪ Not useful for acute diagnosis, as antibodies take 1-2 weeks to develop.
		▪ A **four-fold rise in IgG titer** between acute and convalescent samples (2-4 weeks apart) is the gold standard for confirmation.
	◦ **Peripheral Blood Smear**
		▪ May reveal **intracytoplasmic morulae** in monocytes.
		▪ This finding is **pathognomonic** but has very low sensitivity (<10%) and should not be relied upon for diagnosis.
sections.treatment:
• **Key Principle**: Treatment should be started **empirically** based on clinical and epidemiological suspicion. **Do NOT wait for confirmatory testing.**
• **First-Line (Adults and Children of all ages)**
	◦ **Doxycycline** 100 mg PO BID.
	◦ **Duration**: Continue for at least 3 days after the fever subsides, typically for a total of 10-14 days.
• **Alternative**
	◦ **Rifampin** may be considered in pregnant patients, although recent CDC guidance supports using doxycycline as benefits outweigh risks.
• **Note**: Chloramphenicol and sulfonamides are not effective and may worsen the disease.
sections.management:
• **Supportive Care**: IV fluids for dehydration, antipyretics for fever control.
• **Hospitalization**: Indicated for patients with severe symptoms (e.g., altered mental status, significant cytopenias, respiratory distress) or those unable to tolerate oral medication.
• **Monitoring**: Clinical improvement (fever reduction) is typically seen within 24-48 hours of starting doxycycline. Monitor CBC and LFTs, which should begin to normalize.
sections.complications:
• Delayed diagnosis and treatment increase the risk of severe complications, which can include:
	◦ **Neurologic**: **Meningoencephalitis**, seizures, coma.
	◦ **Respiratory**: **Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)**.
	◦ **Hematologic**: **Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC)**, severe hemorrhage.
	◦ **Systemic**: **Septic shock-like syndrome**, **multi-organ failure** (renal, hepatic).
	◦ **Opportunistic infections** in immunocompromised patients.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** if treated early with **doxycycline**. Most patients recover fully.
• Fever typically resolves within 24-48 hours of appropriate therapy.
• The case-fatality rate is approximately **1-3%** but is significantly higher in those with delayed treatment or who are immunocompromised.
sections.preventionEducation:
• Counsel patients on tick bite prevention:
	◦ Use DEET-containing insect repellent.
	◦ Treat clothing and gear with permethrin.
	◦ Perform thorough tick checks after being outdoors.
	◦ Remove attached ticks promptly and correctly with fine-tipped tweezers.

sections.overview:
• An acute, tick-borne febrile illness caused by the obligate intracellular bacterium *Anaplasma phagocytophilum*.
• Transmitted by the **Ixodes scapularis** (deer tick), the same vector responsible for **Lyme disease** and **Babesiosis**.
• The disease is characterized by a non-specific, flu-like presentation with hallmark laboratory findings of **leukopenia**, **thrombocytopenia**, and **elevated liver transaminases**.
• Prompt diagnosis and treatment with **doxycycline** are crucial for a favorable outcome.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**: *Anaplasma phagocytophilum*, a small, gram-negative, obligate intracellular bacterium.
• **Vector**:
    ◦ **Primary Vector (Eastern/Midwestern US)**: *Ixodes scapularis* (black-legged or deer tick).
    ◦ **Primary Vector (Western US)**: *Ixodes pacificus* (western black-legged tick).
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Transmission**: The bacterium is transmitted through the saliva of an infected tick during a blood meal, typically requiring 24-48 hours of attachment.
    ◦ **Target Cell**: *A. phagocytophilum* has a specific tropism for **granulocytes**, primarily **neutrophils**.
    ◦ **Replication**: Once inside the neutrophil, the bacteria replicate within vacuoles, forming characteristic microcolonies called **morulae** (Latin for "mulberry," due to their clustered appearance).
    ◦ **Systemic Effects**:
        ▪ Infection of hematopoietic cells and subsequent cytokine dysregulation (e.g., TNF-alpha, IFN-gamma) leads to bone marrow suppression and peripheral destruction of blood cells.
        ▪ This process results in the classic lab findings:
            • **Leukopenia**: Primarily neutropenia from infection and destruction of neutrophils.
            • **Thrombocytopenia**: From decreased production and increased peripheral consumption/sequestration.
            • **Elevated transaminases**: Mild inflammatory infiltrates in the liver lead to hepatocellular injury.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Geography**: Most common in the Northeast and Upper Midwest of the United States. The geographic distribution mirrors that of Lyme disease.
    ◦ Key states include Minnesota, Wisconsin, New York, and the New England states.
    ◦ Also present on the West Coast.
• **Seasonality**: Peak incidence occurs during late spring and early summer (May-July), with a smaller peak in the fall (October-November), corresponding with the activity of nymphal and adult *Ixodes* ticks.
• **Demographics**: Affects all ages, but severity and incidence of hospitalization are higher in individuals >50 years old and those who are immunocompromised.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presents as an acute, undifferentiated febrile illness, typically 1-2 weeks after a tick bite.
• Many patients (~75%) do not recall the tick bite.
• The onset of symptoms is usually abrupt.
• **Key Feature**: Unlike Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever (RMSF), a **rash is very rare** (<10%) in Anaplasmosis.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Do not delay treatment pending confirmatory test results.**
• **Initial Laboratory Studies (Key Findings)**:
    ◦ **CBC**:
        ▪ **Thrombocytopenia**: Often the first and most consistent abnormality.
        ▪ **Leukopenia**: Due to neutropenia.
    ◦ **CMP**:
        ▪ **Elevated Liver Transaminases (ALT/AST)**: Typically mild-to-moderate elevation (2-4x upper limit of normal).
• **Confirmatory Tests**:
    ◦ **PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction)**:
        ▪ **Test of choice** during the acute illness (first week).
        ▪ Detects *Anaplasma* DNA in whole blood. High sensitivity and specificity.
    ◦ **Peripheral Blood Smear**:
        ▪ May reveal **intracytoplasmic morulae** within neutrophils.
        ▪ **Pathognomonic but insensitive** (<20% sensitivity). A negative smear does not rule out the diagnosis.
    ◦ **Serology (Indirect Immunofluorescence Assay - IFA)**:
        ▪ Detects IgG antibodies. Not useful for acute diagnosis as antibodies take 1-2 weeks to develop.
        ▪ Primarily used for retrospective confirmation. A four-fold increase in titer between acute and convalescent samples (2-4 weeks apart) is diagnostic.
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent with prompt diagnosis and treatment with **doxycycline**.
• The fatality rate is low (<1%) but can be up to 5% in hospitalized patients.
• Most patients recover fully without long-term sequelae.

sections.overview:
• Babesiosis is a **tick-borne parasitic disease** caused by protozoa of the genus *Babesia*.
    ◦ The parasite **infects and lyses red blood cells (RBCs)**, leading to a **malaria-like syndrome** characterized by **fever**, **chills**, and **hemolytic anemia**.
    ◦ It is transmitted primarily by the ***Ixodes scapularis*** **tick**, the same vector responsible for **Lyme disease** and **anaplasmosis**.
    ◦ While many infections are asymptomatic, it can cause severe, life-threatening illness, particularly in **asplenic**, **elderly**, or **immunocompromised** individuals.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Organism**: Intraerythrocytic protozoan parasite of the genus *Babesia*.
    ◦ **Primary US Species**: ***Babesia microti***
    ◦ **European Species**: *Babesia divergens* (typically more severe)
• **Vector**: ***Ixodes scapularis*** (deer tick or blacklegged tick).
• **Reservoir**: The primary reservoir is the white-footed mouse (*Peromyscus leucopus*). Deer are important for the tick life cycle but are not competent reservoirs for *Babesia*.
• **Transmission**:
    ◦ **Tick Bite**: Most common route. The tick must be attached for approximately 36-48 hours.
    ◦ **Blood Transfusion**: A significant non-vector route, as donated blood is not routinely screened.
    ◦ **Congenital**: Rare transplacental transmission.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ An infected tick injects sporozoites into the human host during a blood meal.
    ◦ Sporozoites invade erythrocytes (RBCs).
    ◦ Inside the RBC, they undergo asexual reproduction (binary fission), forming merozoites. This can create characteristic "tetrads."
    ◦ The replication process leads to RBC lysis, releasing more merozoites to infect other RBCs.
    ◦ The resulting **hemolysis** and host inflammatory response (cytokine release) cause the clinical signs and symptoms:
        ▪ **Anemia**: From RBC destruction.
        ▪ **Fever, Chills, Sweats**: From inflammatory cytokine release (e.g., TNF-alpha).
        ▪ **Jaundice & Dark Urine**: From elevated bilirubin and hemoglobinuria due to hemolysis.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Geography**: Primarily found in specific endemic regions:
    ◦ **Northeast US**: New England (especially coastal islands like Nantucket, Martha's Vineyard, Block Island), New York (Long Island, Hudson Valley).
    ◦ **Upper Midwest US**: Wisconsin, Minnesota.
• **Seasonality**: Peak incidence during late spring and summer (May through October), coinciding with peak activity of nymphal-stage *Ixodes* ticks.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Incubation Period**: 1-4 weeks after tick bite.
• **Spectrum of Illness**:
    ◦ **Asymptomatic**: Common in young, healthy individuals.
    ◦ **Mild-to-Moderate**: Gradual onset of a flu-like or malaria-like illness.
    ◦ **Severe**: Rapidly progressive, life-threatening disease, almost exclusively in high-risk individuals.
• **Typical Presentation**: A patient from an endemic area presents in the summer with a gradual onset of **fever**, **drenching sweats**, and **profound fatigue** that is out of proportion to the fever.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Initial Laboratory Studies**:
    ◦ **CBC**:
        ▪ **Hemolytic Anemia**: Normocytic, normochromic anemia (↓ Hgb/Hct).
        ▪ **Thrombocytopenia**: Very common.
        ▪ WBC: Can be normal, decreased, or elevated.
    ◦ **Hemolysis Labs**:
        ▪ **Elevated LDH**
        ▪ **Elevated indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin**
        ▪ **Decreased haptoglobin**
        ▪ Reticulocytosis
    ◦ **CMP**: Mildly elevated LFTs (AST/ALT), elevated BUN/Creatinine (in severe cases indicating AKI).
    ◦ **Urinalysis**: May show hemoglobinuria and proteinuria.
• **Definitive Diagnosis**:
    ◦ **Peripheral Blood Smear (Giemsa or Wright stain)**:
        ▪ **Intraerythrocytic ring forms** (may resemble *Plasmodium falciparum*, but *Babesia* rings can be pleomorphic, multiple per cell, and lack pigment).
        ▪ **"Maltese Cross" formation**: A tetrad of merozoites. **Pathognomonic but rarely seen**.
    ◦ **PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction)**:
        ▪ **Most sensitive and specific test for acute infection**.
        ▪ Test of choice for confirming diagnosis, especially with low parasitemia.
    ◦ **Serology (Indirect Immunofluorescent Assay - IFA)**:
        ▪ Detects IgG and IgM antibodies.
        ▪ Not useful for acute diagnosis as antibodies take weeks to develop. Best for confirming a recent or past infection.
sections.prognosis:
• **Immunocompetent/Young Patients**: Excellent. Most recover fully, many are asymptomatic.
• **High-Risk Patients (Asplenic, Elderly, Immunocompromised)**: Guarded. **Mortality can reach up to 20%** even with treatment. Relapses are possible, especially in the immunocompromised.

sections.overview:
• ***Chlamydia trachomatis*** infection is the most common reportable bacterial **sexually transmitted infection (STI)** in the United States.
• It is caused by an obligate intracellular, gram-negative bacterium.
• The infection is frequently **asymptomatic**, which contributes to its high prevalence and facilitates transmission.
• If left untreated, it can lead to serious reproductive and other health complications, particularly in women.
sections.etiology:
• **Organism**: *Chlamydia trachomatis*, an obligate intracellular gram-negative bacterium that lacks a traditional peptidoglycan cell wall.
• **Serovars & Associated Diseases**:
    ◦ **Serovars D-K**: Cause urogenital infections (**cervicitis**, **urethritis**, **PID**), **proctitis**, adult **inclusion conjunctivitis**, and neonatal infections. This is the most common group.
    ◦ **Serovars L1, L2, L3**: Cause **Lymphogranuloma Venereum (LGV)**, an invasive infection of lymphatics and lymph nodes.
    ◦ **Serovars A, B, C**: Cause **Trachoma**, a chronic eye infection that is a leading cause of preventable blindness worldwide (rare in the US).
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ *C. trachomatis* has a unique biphasic life cycle.
        ▪ **Elementary Body (EB)**: The small, dense, metabolically inactive **infectious** form. It is extracellular and binds to columnar or transitional epithelial cells (e.g., cervix, urethra, rectum, conjunctiva).
        ▪ **Reticulate Body (RB)**: Once inside the host cell, the EB reorganizes into the larger, metabolically active **replicative** form. It replicates via binary fission within a membrane-bound vacuole called an inclusion body.
        ▪ **Release**: After 48-72 hours, RBs condense back into EBs. The host cell ruptures (lysis), releasing new EBs to infect adjacent cells.
    ◦ **Mechanism of Injury**: Most tissue damage (e.g., **tubal scarring**, **infertility**) is not caused directly by the bacterium but by the host's own **prolonged inflammatory immune response** to the infection.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Most frequently reported bacterial infectious disease in the U.S.
• **Incidence**: Highest rates are among adolescents and young adults aged 15-24.
• **Gender**: Rates are significantly higher in women, likely reflecting increased screening practices in this population.
• **Transmission**:
    ◦ Sexual contact (vaginal, anal, or oral).
    ◦ **Vertical transmission** from an infected mother to her infant during vaginal delivery.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The hallmark of chlamydia is that it is frequently **asymptomatic** (>70% of women and >50% of men have no symptoms).
• When symptoms do occur, the incubation period is typically 7-21 days after exposure.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Gold Standard**: **Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT)** is the preferred method due to its high sensitivity and specificity.
• **Specimen Collection**:
    ◦ **Women**: **Vaginal swab** (self or clinician-collected) is the preferred specimen. Endocervical swabs or first-catch urine are also acceptable.
    ◦ **Men**: **First-catch urine** is the preferred specimen. Urethral swabs are an alternative.
    ◦ **Extragenital Sites**: Pharyngeal and rectal swabs should be collected based on sexual history (e.g., for all **MSM**).
• **Screening Recommendations (CDC)**:
    ◦ Annual screening of all sexually active women aged <25 years.
    ◦ Annual screening of women ≥25 years with risk factors.
    ◦ Screen all pregnant women at their first prenatal visit and again in the third trimester if at continued risk.
    ◦ Annual screening for all sexually active **MSM** at sites of contact (urethra, rectum, pharynx).
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is excellent if diagnosed and treated early. The infection is easily cured with antibiotics.
• However, **reinfection** is common.
• The long-term prognosis is worse if complications such as **PID** have already occurred, as **tubal scarring** and subsequent **infertility** can be permanent.

sections.overview:
• Gonorrhea is a common **sexually transmitted infection (STI)** caused by the bacterium ***Neisseria gonorrhoeae***.
	◦ It primarily infects the **mucous membranes** of the **urogenital tract**, **rectum**, **pharynx**, and **conjunctiva**.
	◦ Often **asymptomatic**, especially in women, it can lead to significant complications if left untreated, including **pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)**, **infertility**, and **disseminated infection**.
	◦ Due to rising **antibiotic resistance**, adherence to current treatment guidelines is critical.
	◦ It is a **nationally notifiable disease**.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent:** ***Neisseria gonorrhoeae***, a **gram-negative intracellular diplococcus**.
• **Pathophysiology:**
	◦ **Attachment:** The bacterium uses **pili (fimbriae)** and **Opa proteins** to attach to **columnar epithelial cells** of mucosal surfaces (e.g., cervix, urethra, pharynx).
	◦ **Invasion:** It invades the host cells and multiplies, triggering a robust **inflammatory response** characterized by a **neutrophilic influx**.
	◦ **Evasion of Host Defense:** *N. gonorrhoeae* has mechanisms to evade the host immune system, including **antigenic variation** of its surface proteins, which prevents the development of long-term protective immunity.
	◦ **Tissue Damage:** The **inflammatory response** leads to the characteristic **purulent discharge** (pus), which is composed of live and dead bacteria, neutrophils, and epithelial cells. This local inflammation can lead to fibrosis and scarring (e.g., **urethral strictures**, **fallopian tube damage**).
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence:** **Second most commonly reported bacterial infectious disease** in the United States, after **Chlamydia**.
• **Prevalence:** Highest rates are seen in **adolescents and young adults (ages 15-24)**.
• **Trends:** Rates have been increasing, and there is a significant public health concern regarding the emergence of **antibiotic-resistant strains** (e.g., cephalosporin-resistant).
• **Transmission:** Transmitted through **sexual contact** (vaginal, anal, or oral) involving the penis, vagina, mouth, or anus. **Perinatal transmission** from mother to newborn can occur during childbirth.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation varies significantly based on the site of infection and the patient's sex. Many infections are **asymptomatic**.
• **Incubation Period:** Typically 2-7 days.
• **Uncomplicated Urogenital Infection (Men):**
	◦ **Urethritis:** The most common presentation. Characterized by sudden onset of **dysuria** and a copious, **purulent, yellow-green urethral discharge**.
• **Uncomplicated Urogenital Infection (Women):**
	◦ **Cervicitis:** Often **asymptomatic** (~50% of cases). When symptomatic, presents with **vaginal pruritus**, increased **vaginal discharge (mucopurulent)**, **intermenstrual bleeding**, and **dysuria**.
• **Anorectal Gonorrhea:**
	◦ Often **asymptomatic**. May present with **anal discharge**, pruritus, tenesmus, or rectal bleeding/pain. Common in MSM and women who engage in anal intercourse.
• **Pharyngeal Gonorrhea:**
	◦ Usually **asymptomatic**. Can present as a **sore throat** or **pharyngitis** with **cervical lymphadenopathy**. Acquired through oral sex.
• **Conjunctivitis:**
	◦ **Adults:** Rare, usually from **autoinoculation**. Presents with marked **purulent discharge**, chemosis, and eyelid swelling.
	◦ **Neonates (Ophthalmia Neonatorum):** Acquired during vaginal delivery. Presents 2-5 days after birth with bilateral copious **purulent discharge** and eyelid edema. Can lead to **corneal ulceration** and **blindness** if not treated promptly.
• **Disseminated Gonococcal Infection (DGI):**
	◦ Occurs when the organism invades the bloodstream. More common in women.
	◦ **Classic Triad:**
		▪ 1. **Tenosynovitis:** Inflammation of tendon sheaths, most often in the hands/wrists or feet/ankles.
		▪ 2. **Dermatitis:** **Papular, pustular, or hemorrhagic skin lesions**, often on the distal extremities.
		▪ 3. **Polyarthralgias:** **Asymmetric migratory joint pain**.
	◦ **Purulent Arthritis:** Can also present as a frank **septic monoarthritis**, most commonly affecting the **knee**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT):**
	◦ **Gold standard** for diagnosis. Highly sensitive and specific.
	◦ **Acceptable Specimens:**
		▪ **Urine (first-catch)**
		▪ **Endocervical or vaginal swabs** (women)
		▪ **Urethral swab** (men)
		▪ **Pharyngeal and rectal swabs** (based on sexual history)
• **Gram Stain:**
	◦ Shows **gram-negative intracellular diplococci** within **neutrophils**.
	◦ Highly specific (>99%) and sensitive (>95%) for symptomatic urethritis in men.
	◦ Low sensitivity (~50%) for endocervical, pharyngeal, or rectal infections, so not recommended for these sites.
• **Culture:**
	◦ Requires specific media (**Thayer-Martin agar**).
	◦ Less sensitive than NAAT but is essential for **antimicrobial susceptibility testing**, which is crucial for monitoring resistance patterns and managing treatment failures.
• **Co-infection Testing:** All patients diagnosed with gonorrhea should also be tested for other STIs, including **Chlamydia, HIV, and syphilis**.
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent for **uncomplicated gonorrhea** when treated early and appropriately.
• The prognosis becomes more guarded if complications like **PID** or **DGI** develop.
• Long-term sequelae of PID (**infertility**, **ectopic pregnancy**) can be permanent.
• **Reinfection** is common.

sections.overview:
• Trichomoniasis is a highly prevalent, curable **sexually transmitted infection (STI)** caused by a protozoan parasite.
    ◦ It is one of the most common causes of **vaginitis** in women.
    ◦ In men, the infection is frequently **asymptomatic**, making them important reservoirs for transmission.
    ◦ The infection is associated with significant complications, including adverse pregnancy outcomes and an increased risk of HIV acquisition and transmission.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**: ***Trichomonas vaginalis***, a single-celled, anaerobic, flagellated protozoan parasite.
• **Transmission**: Primarily through sexual contact (penile-vaginal, vulva-vulva).
    ◦ Fomite transmission is rare.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ ***T. vaginalis*** adheres to the squamous epithelial cells of the genitourinary tract.
    ◦ The organism causes direct cell damage and cytotoxicity, leading to microulcerations in the epithelium.
    ◦ This triggers a robust local inflammatory response, with an influx of neutrophils, lymphocytes, and other immune cells, resulting in the characteristic purulent discharge and erythema.
    ◦ The parasite also increases the local pH of the vagina (typically >4.5), which disrupts the normal lactobacilli-dominant flora and can contribute to the malodorous discharge.
sections.epidemiology:
• One of the most common non-viral STIs worldwide.
• The CDC estimates over 2 million infections in the U.S. annually.
• Prevalence is higher in women than in men.
• Disproportionately affects Black women and individuals in resource-limited settings.
• A significant number of infections (~70-85%) are **asymptomatic** or minimally symptomatic, especially in men, facilitating ongoing transmission.
sections.riskFactors:
• Multiple sexual partners
• New sexual partner
• History of prior STIs
• Lack of condom use
• Douching (disrupts normal vaginal flora)
• Lower socioeconomic status
• Incarceration
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The clinical presentation is highly variable, ranging from completely **asymptomatic** to severe, acute inflammation.
    ◦ **Incubation Period**: 4 to 28 days.
• **Female Presentation**:
    ◦ Typically presents as **vaginitis**.
    ◦ Symptoms can be acute or chronic and may be exacerbated during or after menses.
• **Male Presentation**:
    ◦ Most commonly **asymptomatic**.
    ◦ If symptoms are present, they manifest as **non-gonococcal urethritis (NGU)**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **NAAT (Nucleic Acid Amplification Test)**
    ◦ **GOLD STANDARD**.
    ◦ Can be performed on vaginal/cervical swabs, urine (both male & female).
    ◦ Detects *T. vaginalis* RNA or DNA.
    ◦ Sensitivity/Specificity: Highest Sensitivity (>95%) & Specificity.
• **Wet Mount (Saline Microscopy)**
    ◦ **Classic finding: Pear-shaped, flagellated, motile trophozoites**.
    ◦ Also shows increased polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMNs).
    ◦ Requires a fresh sample and immediate evaluation, as motility is lost as the sample cools.
    ◦ Sensitivity/Specificity: Low Sensitivity (~50-70%), High Specificity.
• **Vaginal pH**
    ◦ **Elevated pH > 4.5** (normal is 3.8-4.5).
    ◦ Helps differentiate from candidiasis (normal pH) but overlaps with BV.
    ◦ Sensitivity/Specificity: Non-specific.
• **Whiff Test**
    ◦ Addition of 10% KOH may release an amine ("fishy") odor.
    ◦ Less common than with BV but can be positive.
    ◦ Sensitivity/Specificity: Non-specific.
• **Rapid Antigen/DNA Probe Tests**
    ◦ Point-of-care tests with better sensitivity than wet mount but less than NAAT.
    ◦ Sensitivity/Specificity: Moderate-High Sensitivity.
• **Culture**
    ◦ Was previously the gold standard before NAAT.
    ◦ High specificity but takes 3-7 days for results.
    ◦ Sensitivity/Specificity: High Sensitivity (75-95%).
sections.treatment:
• **First-Line Recommended Regimen**:
    ◦ **Metronidazole 500 mg PO BID for 7 days**
        ▪ *Slightly higher cure rates than single-dose therapy.*
• **Alternative Regimen**:
    ◦ **Metronidazole 2 grams PO as a single dose**
        ▪ *Useful for improving adherence.*
    ◦ **Tinidazole 2 grams PO as a single dose**
        ▪ *Often better tolerated with fewer GI side effects, but more expensive.*
sections.management:
• **Partner Therapy**: Prescribe treatment for all sexual partners from the preceding 60 days.
    ◦ **Expedited Partner Therapy (EPT)** is recommended where legal.
• **Follow-up**:
    ◦ Test-of-cure is not routinely needed.
    ◦ **Retesting is recommended for all sexually active women ~3 months after treatment** due to high rates of reinfection.
• **Screening**: Screen for other common STIs, including HIV, syphilis, gonorrhea, and chlamydia.
sections.complications:
• **Increased risk of HIV acquisition and transmission** (2-3 fold increase).
• **Females**:
    ◦ Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID)
    ◦ Infertility
    ◦ Cervical neoplasia
• **Pregnancy**:
    ◦ Preterm delivery
    ◦ Premature rupture of membranes (PROM)
    ◦ Low birth weight infant
• **Males**:
    ◦ Epididymitis
    ◦ Prostatitis
    ◦ Infertility (rare)
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** with appropriate antimicrobial therapy and treatment of partners.
• Cure rates are >90% with recommended regimens.
• Reinfection is common if partners are not treated concurrently.
sections.preventionEducation:
• **Abstinence**: Counsel patients to abstain from sexual intercourse until they and their partner(s) have completed the full course of therapy and are asymptomatic (approx. 7 days after last dose).
• **Alcohol Avoidance**: Crucial counseling point. Instruct patients to **avoid all alcohol consumption** during treatment and for 24 hours after completing Metronidazole (or 72 hours for Tinidazole) due to the risk of a **disulfiram-like reaction** (flushing, tachycardia, nausea/vomiting, headache).
• **Medication Side Effects**: Common side effects of metronidazole include metallic taste, nausea, and headache.

sections.overview:
• Syphilis is a complex, multi-stage **sexually transmitted infection (STI)** caused by the spirochete bacterium ***Treponema pallidum***.
• Known as "**The Great Imitator**," its clinical manifestations can mimic many other diseases.
• It progresses through distinct stages (**primary**, **secondary**, **latent**, and **tertiary**) if left untreated.
• **Diagnosis** is primarily based on **serologic testing**, and the treatment of choice for all stages is **Penicillin G**.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**
    ◦ ***Treponema pallidum*** subspecies *pallidum*, a motile, corkscrew-shaped **spirochete** bacterium.
• **Transmission**
    ◦ Primarily through direct contact with an infectious lesion (**chancre**) during sexual activity (vaginal, anal, or oral).
    ◦ Can also be transmitted vertically from mother to fetus (**congenital syphilis**) or, rarely, via blood transfusion.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Inoculation**: The spirochete enters the body through microscopic abrasions in the skin or mucous membranes.
        ▪ The **incubation period** averages 3 weeks (range 10-90 days).
    ◦ **Local Proliferation**: Organisms multiply at the site of entry, forming the primary **chancre**.
    ◦ **Dissemination**: Even before the **chancre** appears, spirochetes disseminate via the lymphatic system and bloodstream to distant sites.
    ◦ **Immune Response**: The host immune response is responsible for both clearing spirochetes and causing tissue damage.
        ▪ The characteristic lesion of syphilis is an **obliterative endarteritis** (inflammation of the inner lining of small arteries), resulting in **ischemia** and **necrosis**.
        ▪ This vasculitis is present in all stages.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**
    ◦ Rates of **primary** and **secondary syphilis** have been increasing in the United States, particularly since the early 2000s.
• **High-Risk Populations**
    ◦ **Men who have sex with men (MSM)** account for the majority of new cases.
    ◦ Individuals with **HIV co-infection**.
    ◦ Populations with limited access to healthcare.
    ◦ Illicit drug use (especially methamphetamine).
• **Congenital Syphilis**
    ◦ Rates are also rising, mirroring the increase in **primary** and **secondary syphilis** among women of childbearing age.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • Syphilis presentation is divided into stages, each with a distinct clinical picture.
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent for **primary** and **secondary syphilis** when treated appropriately.
• **Latent syphilis** treated with penicillin has a very good prognosis for preventing late-stage complications.
• In **tertiary syphilis**, treatment can halt disease progression, but **neurologic** and **cardiovascular damage** is often irreversible.

sections.overview:
• **Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV)** is a **retrovirus** that targets and destroys **CD4+ T-helper lymphocytes**, leading to progressive immunodeficiency.
• **Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS)** is the most advanced stage of HIV infection, characterized by:
    ◦ A severely compromised immune system (**CD4 count <200 cells/mm3**).
    ◦ The presence of specific **opportunistic infections** or malignancies (**AIDS-defining illnesses**).
• Without treatment, HIV infection progresses to AIDS in an average of 8-10 years.
• Modern **antiretroviral therapy (ART)** can suppress viral replication, preserve immune function, and allow individuals with HIV to live a near-normal lifespan.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**: Caused by the **Human Immunodeficiency Virus**, a lentivirus (a type of retrovirus).
    ◦ **HIV-1**: The most common and pathogenic type worldwide.
    ◦ **HIV-2**: Less common, less easily transmitted, and typically causes a slower progression to AIDS. Primarily found in West Africa.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Viral Entry**: The virus's outer envelope protein, **gp120**, binds to the **CD4 receptor** on T-helper cells. This allows binding to a coreceptor, either **CCR5** or **CXCR4**. The viral protein **gp41** then facilitates membrane fusion.
    ◦ **Reverse Transcription**: The viral enzyme **reverse transcriptase** converts single-stranded viral RNA into double-stranded proviral DNA.
    ◦ **Integration**: The viral enzyme **integrase** inserts the proviral DNA into the host cell's genome, making the infection permanent.
    ◦ **Replication**: The host cell's machinery is hijacked to transcribe and translate viral DNA into new viral components.
    ◦ **Assembly & Budding**: New viral components are assembled and bud off from the cell membrane.
    ◦ **Maturation**: The viral enzyme **protease** cleaves long protein chains into functional proteins, creating a mature, infectious virion.
    ◦ This cycle leads to a progressive decline in **CD4+ T-cells**, crippling cell-mediated immunity.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Worldwide**: >38 million people are living with HIV. Sub-Saharan Africa is the most affected region.
• **United States**: ~1.2 million people are living with HIV.
• **Populations at highest risk in the U.S.**:
    ◦ **Men who have sex with men (MSM)** account for the majority of new diagnoses.
    ◦ Disproportionate impact on Black/African American and Hispanic/Latino populations.
    ◦ Persons who inject drugs (PWID).
• **Transmission**: Occurs via blood, semen, pre-seminal fluid, rectal fluids, vaginal fluids, and breast milk.
    ◦ **Sexual Contact**: Unprotected anal intercourse carries the highest risk.
    ◦ **Parenteral**: Sharing contaminated needles.
    ◦ **Perinatal (Vertical)**: Mother-to-child transmission during pregnancy, childbirth, or breastfeeding. ART dramatically reduces this risk to <1%.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Acute Retroviral Syndrome (ARS)**:
    ◦ Occurs 2-4 weeks after initial infection.
    ◦ Presents as a nonspecific, **mononucleosis-like illness**.
    ◦ Characterized by a high viral load and high infectivity.
    ◦ Symptoms resolve spontaneously in 1-2 weeks.
• **Clinical Latency (Asymptomatic HIV Infection)**:
    ◦ Follows the acute phase and can last for many years (average 8-10 years without treatment).
    ◦ Patients are typically asymptomatic or may have persistent generalized lymphadenopathy.
    ◦ The virus actively replicates at a low level, and the CD4 count gradually declines.
• **Symptomatic HIV Infection / AIDS**:
    ◦ As the CD4 count falls below 500 cells/mm3, patients become susceptible to infections.
    ◦ A diagnosis of **AIDS** is made when the **CD4 count drops <200 cells/mm3** or an **AIDS-defining illness** develops.
    ◦ Patients present with constitutional symptoms and/or opportunistic infections and malignancies.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Screening & Diagnosis Algorithm**:
    ◦ **Initial Test**: **4th Generation HIV-1/2 Immunoassay**.
        ▪ This combination test detects both **HIV p24 antigen** and **HIV-1/2 antibodies**.
        ▪ p24 antigen appears earlier than antibodies, shortening the "window period."
    ◦ **Confirmatory Test**: If the initial test is positive, an **HIV-1/HIV-2 Antibody Differentiation Immunoassay** is performed to confirm the diagnosis and distinguish between HIV-1 and HIV-2.
• **Monitoring Disease Progression & Treatment Efficacy**:
    ◦ **CD4+ T-cell Count**:
        ▪ Measures immune status (Normal is 500-1500 cells/mm3).
        ▪ Key thresholds determine the need for opportunistic infection (OI) prophylaxis.
        ▪ Checked at baseline and every 3-6 months.
    ◦ **HIV Viral Load (Quantitative RNA PCR)**:
        ▪ Measures the amount of virus in the blood.
        ▪ The goal of ART is an **"undetectable"** viral load (<20-50 copies/mL).
        ▪ Checked at baseline, before starting ART, and regularly to monitor treatment response.
• **Baseline & Other Important Labs**:
    ◦ Genotypic resistance testing (to guide ART selection).
    ◦ CBC, CMP, lipid panel, urinalysis.
    ◦ Screening for Hepatitis A, B, and C.
    ◦ Screening for STIs (syphilis, gonorrhea, chlamydia).
    ◦ **HLA-B*5701 screening**: Required before starting **Abacavir** due to risk of fatal hypersensitivity reaction.
    ◦ Tuberculosis screening (PPD or IGRA).
sections.prognosis:
• **Untreated**: Progression to AIDS in ~10 years, with death typically occurring 1-2 years after an AIDS diagnosis.
• **Treated**: With early diagnosis and consistent adherence to ART, life expectancy for people with HIV approaches that of the general population. Prognosis is excellent.

sections.overview:
• **Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID)** is an infectious and inflammatory disorder of the upper female genital tract.
    ◦ It is not a single diagnosis but a spectrum of disease that can include any combination of **endometritis**, **salpingitis**, **oophoritis**, and **tubo-ovarian abscess (TOA)**.
    ◦ It is most often the result of a sexually transmitted infection ascending from the cervix and vagina.
    ◦ Prompt diagnosis and treatment are critical to prevent long-term complications, most notably **infertility**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ Most commonly caused by **_Neisseria gonorrhoeae_** and **_Chlamydia trachomatis_**, which are responsible for ~50% of cases.
    ◦ Often **polymicrobial**, with other pathogens including anaerobes (_Peptostreptococcus_, _Bacteroides_), **_Gardnerella vaginalis_**, **_Haemophilus influenzae_**, enteric Gram-negative rods (_E. coli_), and **_Streptococcus agalactiae_**.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Ascending Infection**: Microorganisms from the cervix or vagina ascend into the upper genital tract.
    ◦ **Breach of Endocervical Barrier**: Factors like menstruation (loss of mucus plug, retrograde flow), sexual intercourse, or instrumentation (e.g., IUD insertion) can facilitate this ascent.
    ◦ **Inflammation and Damage**: The infection spreads along the endometrial surface to the fallopian tubes (**salpingitis**) and potentially to the ovaries and surrounding peritoneum.
    ◦ **Tubal Damage**: Inflammation leads to damage of the ciliated epithelial cells of the fallopian tubes, causing scarring, adhesions, and potential occlusion, which is the basis for sequelae like **infertility** and **ectopic pregnancy**.
sections.epidemiology:
• Most common in sexually active women, particularly adolescents and young adults aged **15-25**.
• A leading cause of preventable **infertility** in the United States.
• Incidence has been declining due to better screening and treatment for chlamydia and gonorrhea.
sections.riskFactors:
• Multiple sexual partners
• Unprotected intercourse
• Age **< 25 years**
• Prior history of **PID** or other **STIs**
• Instrumentation of the uterus (e.g., IUD insertion, termination of pregnancy, endometrial biopsy)
    ◦ Note: Risk with IUDs is highest in the first **3 weeks post-insertion**.
• Vaginal douching (alters normal flora and may propel bacteria upward)
• **Bacterial Vaginosis (BV)**
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation can range from asymptomatic or subclinical to severe, acute illness; a high index of suspicion is required.
• The classic patient is a young, sexually active female with recent onset of **bilateral lower abdominal pain**, often during or shortly after menses.
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ **Bilateral lower abdominal or pelvic pain** (most common symptom)
    ◦ **Abnormal vaginal discharge** (often purulent, yellow/green)
    ◦ **Abnormal uterine bleeding** (intermenstrual or post-coital)
    ◦ **Dyspareunia** (painful intercourse)
    ◦ **Fever and chills**
    ◦ Nausea and/or vomiting
    ◦ Dysuria or urinary frequency
sections.physicalExam:
• **Abdominal Exam**
    ◦ Suprapubic tenderness, which may be bilateral.
    ◦ Rebound tenderness or guarding suggests peritoneal involvement.
• **Pelvic Exam (Key to Diagnosis)**
    ◦ **Cervical Motion Tenderness (CMT)**: Also known as the **"Chandelier Sign."** This is a hallmark finding.
    ◦ **Uterine tenderness** on bimanual exam.
    ◦ **Adnexal tenderness** on bimanual exam (can be unilateral or bilateral).
    ◦ **Purulent or mucopurulent discharge** from the cervical os.
• **Systemic Signs**
    ◦ **Fever** (>38.3°C / 101°F)
sections.diagnostics:
• PID is primarily a **clinical diagnosis**; a low threshold for empiric treatment is recommended due to severe complications of delayed therapy.
• **Minimum Diagnostic Criteria (CDC Guidelines)**
    ◦ Lower abdominal/pelvic pain in a sexually active young woman at risk for STIs.
    ◦ **PLUS** one or more of the following on pelvic exam:
        ▪ **Cervical motion tenderness**
        ▪ **Uterine tenderness**
        ▪ **Adnexal tenderness**
• **Supportive Criteria (Increase specificity)**
    ◦ Oral temperature **> 101°F (38.3°C)**
    ◦ Abnormal cervical or vaginal mucopurulent discharge
    ◦ Abundant **WBCs** on saline microscopy of vaginal secretions ("wet prep")
    ◦ Elevated **ESR** or **C-reactive protein (CRP)**
    ◦ Positive nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) for **_N. gonorrhoeae_** or **_C. trachomatis_**.
• **Lab Studies**
    ◦ **Pregnancy Test (Beta-hCG)**: **MANDATORY** to rule out ectopic pregnancy.
    ◦ **NAAT for Gonorrhea & Chlamydia**: Cervical swab is preferred.
    ◦ **CBC with differential**: May show leukocytosis with a left shift.
    ◦ **Wet Prep / Microscopy**: To check for WBCs and rule out trichomoniasis and BV.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Transvaginal Ultrasound**: Not required for diagnosis but helpful to rule out other pathology or identify complications. Findings may include:
        ▪ Thickened, fluid-filled fallopian tubes (**hydrosalpinx**)
        ▪ Free pelvic fluid
        ▪ **Tubo-ovarian abscess (TOA)**: Complex, multiloculated adnexal mass.
• **Definitive Diagnosis (Rarely used)**
    ◦ **Laparoscopy**: Considered the **"gold standard"** but is invasive and reserved for uncertain diagnoses or surgical emergencies. It visualizes purulent drainage from fimbriae and inflamed tubes.
sections.treatment:
• **Outpatient Regimen (for mild-to-moderate PID)**
    ◦ **Ceftriaxone** 500 mg IM x 1 dose
    ◦ **PLUS Doxycycline** 100 mg PO BID x 14 days
    ◦ **PLUS Metronidazole** 500 mg PO BID x 14 days
• **Inpatient Regimen (see Management for admission criteria)**
    ◦ **Option 1**
        ▪ **Cefotetan** 2g IV q12h **OR** **Cefoxitin** 2g IV q6h
        ▪ **PLUS Doxycycline** 100 mg PO or IV q12h
    ◦ **Option 2 (Penicillin allergy)**
        ▪ **Clindamycin** 900 mg IV q8h
        ▪ **PLUS** **Gentamicin** loading dose IV/IM followed by maintenance dose
    ◦ Transition to oral therapy (e.g., Doxycycline +/- Metronidazole) after 24-48 hours of clinical improvement to complete a **14-day total course**.
sections.management:
• **Criteria for Hospitalization**
    ◦ Inability to exclude a surgical emergency (e.g., appendicitis)
    ◦ Suspected or confirmed **Tubo-ovarian Abscess (TOA)**
    ◦ **Pregnancy**
    ◦ Severe illness (high fever, nausea/vomiting, severe pain)
    ◦ Inability to tolerate or follow an oral regimen
    ◦ Failure of outpatient therapy within 72 hours
• **Intrauterine Device (IUD)**
    ◦ The IUD does **NOT** need to be removed if the patient is responding well to antibiotic therapy.
    ◦ Consider removal if there is no clinical improvement after 48-72 hours.
sections.complications:
• **Tubo-ovarian Abscess (TOA)**: An inflammatory mass involving the fallopian tube, ovary, and adjacent pelvic organs. May require drainage or surgery if it does not respond to IV antibiotics or if rupture is suspected.
• **Infertility**: The most common serious complication. Risk increases with each episode of PID (1 episode ≈ 10% risk; 3 episodes ≈ 50% risk).
• **Ectopic Pregnancy**: Damaged fallopian tubes increase the risk **7 to 10-fold**.
• **Chronic Pelvic Pain**: Caused by pelvic adhesions and chronic inflammation.
• **Fitz-Hugh-Curtis Syndrome (Perihepatitis)**
    ◦ Inflammation of the liver capsule and adjacent peritoneum, leading to adhesions that look like **"violin strings."**
    ◦ Presents with pleuritic **right upper quadrant (RUQ) pain** that may be referred to the right shoulder.
sections.prognosis:
• With early and appropriate treatment, the prognosis for resolving the acute infection is excellent.
• The long-term prognosis regarding fertility and chronic pain depends on the severity of the initial infection and the number of recurrent episodes. Each subsequent infection dramatically increases the risk of permanent tubal damage.
sections.preventionEducation:
• **Partner Management**
    ◦ All sexual partners within the preceding **60 days** must be evaluated and treated empirically for gonorrhea and chlamydia to prevent reinfection.
    ◦ **Expedited Partner Therapy (EPT)** may be an option.
• **Patient Education & Follow-Up**
    ◦ Patients should be re-evaluated in **48-72 hours** to assess for clinical improvement.
    ◦ Advise **abstinence** from sexual intercourse until treatment is complete and symptoms have resolved.
    ◦ Discuss safe sex practices and risk reduction.

sections.overview:
• **Chancroid** is a sexually transmitted infection (STI) caused by the bacterium ***Haemophilus ducreyi***.
• Characterized by **painful genital ulcers** and **suppurative inguinal lymphadenopathy (buboes)**.
• While rare in developed nations, it is a significant cause of genital ulcer disease (GUD) in parts of Africa, Asia, and the Caribbean.
• The presence of an open sore significantly increases the risk of **HIV transmission**.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Organism**: ***Haemophilus ducreyi***, a fastidious, gram-negative coccobacillus.
• **Transmission**: Primarily through sexual contact via **microabrasions** in the skin or mucous membranes.
• **Pathogenesis**:
    ◦ **Inoculation**: Bacteria enter through a break in the epithelium.
    ◦ **Incubation Period**: Typically **3-10 days**.
    ◦ **Lesion Formation**: A tender papule evolves into a pustule, which then erodes to form the characteristic ulcer.
        ▪ The organism produces a **cytolethal distending toxin (CDT)**, which contributes to ulcer formation by inducing host cell apoptosis.
    ◦ **Lymphatic Spread**: The organism spreads to regional lymph nodes, causing an intense inflammatory response that leads to **lymphadenitis (bubo formation)**.
        ▪ Buboes can become **fluctuant**, suppurate, and spontaneously rupture if untreated.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Rare in the U.S. and Europe, but endemic in many resource-limited areas, particularly parts of Africa, Asia, and the Latin America/Caribbean region.
• **Outbreaks**: In developed countries, outbreaks are often associated with **commercial sex work** and **illicit drug use**.
• **Gender**: More commonly diagnosed in **men**; women may be **asymptomatic carriers**.
• **Coinfection**: High rates of coinfection with **HIV**, **HSV**, and **syphilis**.
    ◦ The presence of a chancroid ulcer increases **HIV acquisition and transmission risk by 10- to 50-fold**.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Unprotected sexual intercourse**
• **Multiple sexual partners**
• **Commercial sex work** (client or provider)
• Travel to **endemic areas**
• Low socioeconomic status
• **Illicit drug use**
• Being **uncircumcised**
• Pre-existing **HIV infection**
sections.clinicalPresentation: • A patient, typically male, presents with the **acute onset** of one or more **painful genital sores** **3-10 days** after a sexual encounter, often with a partner from an endemic region. This may be accompanied by a **painful, swollen lump in the groin area**.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Symptoms**:
    ◦ **Primary Lesion**: **Extremely painful genital ulcer(s)**.
    ◦ **Lymphadenopathy**: **Painful, tender swelling** in the inguinal region (groin).
    ◦ **Systemic Symptoms**: Fever, chills, and malaise are uncommon.
    ◦ **Female-Specific**: May experience dysuria, dyspareunia, or vaginal discharge. Ulcers on the cervix or vaginal walls may be less painful and go unnoticed.
• **Physical Exam Findings**:
    ◦ **Ulcer(s)**:
        ▪ **Appearance**: A deep, well-demarcated ulcer with **ragged, undermined edges**.
        ▪ **Base**: **Friable** (bleeds easily) and covered with a malodorous, purulent gray or yellow exudate.
        ▪ **Consistency**: The ulcer base is typically **soft** (a "**soft chancre**"), in contrast to the hard chancre of syphilis.
        ▪ **Pain**: **Exquisitely tender** to palpation.
        ▪ **Number**: Often presents as multiple ulcers due to **auto-inoculation ("kissing lesions")**.
        ▪ **Location (Male)**: Prepuce, coronal sulcus, glans, frenulum, shaft.
        ▪ **Location (Female)**: Labia, fourchette, vestibule, clitoris, perianal, cervix, vagina.
    ◦ **Inguinal Lymphadenopathy (Bubo)**:
        ▪ Occurs in ~50% of patients, typically 1-2 weeks after the ulcer appears.
        ▪ Usually **unilateral**, tender, and erythematous.
        ▪ Can become **fluctuant** (filled with pus).
        ▪ May **spontaneously rupture**, forming a draining sinus tract.
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is often **clinical** due to the difficulty of definitive testing for the fastidious organism *H. ducreyi*.
• **Probable Clinical Diagnosis (CDC Criteria)**: All four criteria must be met:
    ◦ One or more **painful genital ulcers** are present.
    ◦ The clinical presentation is typical for chancroid.
    ◦ **No evidence of *Treponema pallidum* (syphilis)** by darkfield microscopy or negative serology (RPR/VDRL) at least 7 days after ulcer onset.
    ◦ A test for **Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV)** from the ulcer exudate is negative.
• **Definitive Diagnosis**:
    ◦ **Culture**: Requires special, enriched media. Sensitivity is <80% and not widely available.
    ◦ **Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT/PCR)**: The **preferred method**. Highly sensitive and specific, but not widely available.
    ◦ **Gram Stain**: Smear from the ulcer base may show gram-negative coccobacilli in a "**school of fish**" or "**railroad track**" arrangement. Low sensitivity and specificity.
sections.treatment:
• **Goal**: Cure the infection, resolve symptoms, prevent transmission, and re-test for other STIs.
• **CDC Recommended Regimens**:
    ◦ **Azithromycin** 1 g PO in a single dose
    ◦ **Ceftriaxone** 250 mg IM in a single dose
• **Alternative Regimens**:
    ◦ **Ciprofloxacin** 500 mg PO BID for 3 days (*Contraindicated in pregnancy/lactation*)
    ◦ **Erythromycin** base 500 mg PO QID for 7 days
sections.management:
• **Follow-Up**: Patients should be re-examined **3-7 days** after starting therapy.
    ◦ Symptomatic improvement should occur within 3 days.
    ◦ Objective ulcer healing should be evident within 7 days.
• **Bubo Management**: Fluctuant lymph nodes should be drained via **needle aspiration** or incision and drainage to provide relief and prevent rupture.
• **Partner Management**: All sexual partners within the 10 days preceding symptom onset should be examined and treated, regardless of symptoms.
• **Counseling**:
    ◦ Abstain from sexual contact until ulcers have completely healed.
    ◦ Counsel on safe sex practices and risk reduction.
• **STI Screening**: All patients should be tested for **HIV** and **syphilis** at diagnosis and again in 3 months if initial tests are negative.
sections.complications:
• **Ruptured bubo** with fistula formation
• Extensive **scarring** of genital tissue
• **Phimosis** or **paraphimosis** in uncircumcised men
• Balanoposthitis
• Significantly increased risk of **HIV acquisition and transmission**
sections.prognosis:
• With appropriate antibiotic therapy, the prognosis is **excellent** and a full cure is expected.
• Healing may be slower in **HIV-positive** individuals and **uncircumcised men**.
• **Scarring** may be a permanent sequela.
• **Reinfection** is possible as no long-term immunity develops.

sections.overview:
• A chronic, lifelong **sexually transmitted infection (STI)** caused by the **Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV)**.
• Most commonly caused by **HSV-2**, though **HSV-1** is an increasing cause of first-episode genital infections.
• Characterized by recurrent, painful **vesicular** or **ulcerative lesions** on the genitals, perineum, or anorectal area.
• After primary infection, the virus establishes **latency** in the **sacral dorsal root ganglia** and can reactivate periodically.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**: **Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV)**, an enveloped, double-stranded DNA virus.
    ◦ **HSV-2**: Primary cause of **recurrent** genital herpes (~85-90% of cases).
    ◦ **HSV-1**: Traditionally associated with orolabial herpes ("cold sores"), but an increasingly common cause of **primary** genital herpes, often due to oral-genital contact.
        ▪ Recurrences are **less frequent** with genital HSV-1 than with genital HSV-2.
• **Transmission**:
    ◦ Direct contact with infectious lesions (vesicular fluid, ulcers).
    ◦ Contact with mucosal surfaces or genital/oral secretions from an infected person.
    ◦ **Asymptomatic viral shedding**: Transmission can occur even in the absence of visible lesions. This is a major driver of the epidemic.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Primary Infection**: The virus enters through breaks in the skin or mucous membranes, undergoes local replication at the inoculation site, causing characteristic lesions.
    ◦ **Latency**: The virus travels via retrograde axonal transport to the sensory dorsal root ganglia (typically the **sacral ganglia** for genital herpes) where it establishes lifelong latency.
    ◦ **Reactivation**: Various triggers (e.g., stress, illness, immunosuppression, menses, trauma) cause the virus to reactivate and travel via anterograde axonal transport back to the initial site of infection, causing recurrent lesions.
sections.epidemiology:
• One of the most common **STIs** worldwide.
• In the United States, the seroprevalence of **HSV-2** in persons aged 14-49 is approximately 12%.
• Seroprevalence is higher in women than men.
• A significant majority (>80%) of individuals with HSV-2 infection are unaware of their status because their symptoms are mild, atypical, or unrecognized.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The clinical course is highly variable, ranging from asymptomatic to severe.
• **Primary (First-Episode) Infection**:
    ◦ **Incubation Period**: 2-12 days (average 4 days).
    ◦ Often the most severe episode.
    ◦ **Prodrome**: May begin with tingling, burning, itching, or pain at the inoculation site.
    ◦ **Systemic Symptoms**: Common; includes **fever**, **headache**, **malaise**, and **myalgias**.
    ◦ **Local Symptoms**: **Painful genital lesions**, **dysuria** (especially in women), tender **inguinal lymphadenopathy**, and vaginal/urethral discharge.
    ◦ Lesions can last 2-4 weeks if untreated.
• **Recurrent Infection**:
    ◦ Typically less severe and shorter in duration than the primary infection.
    ◦ **Prodrome**: Common (tingling, itching, burning) and often precedes lesions by hours to days.
    ◦ **Systemic Symptoms**: Rare.
    ◦ Lesions are usually fewer in number, more localized, and heal more quickly (within 5-10 days).
• **Asymptomatic Infection**:
    ◦ Many individuals are seropositive but report no history of genital lesions.
    ◦ They can still experience **asymptomatic viral shedding**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Preferred Method (Gold Standard): Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR)**
    ◦ Highest sensitivity and specificity.
    ◦ Can differentiate between **HSV-1** and **HSV-2**.
    ◦ Test of choice for **active lesions** (swab the base of an unroofed vesicle) and for diagnosing **HSV meningitis** from CSF.
• **Viral Culture**:
    ◦ Once the standard, now largely replaced by PCR.
    ◦ Requires live virus; sensitivity decreases rapidly as lesions begin to heal.
    ◦ Specificity is high, but sensitivity is low (~50%).
• **Tzanck Smear**:
    ◦ Scraping from the base of a vesicle is stained (Wright-Giemsa or Papanicolaou).
    ◦ **Finding**: **Multinucleated giant cells** and eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions (Cowdry A bodies).
    ◦ **Limitation**: Low sensitivity and specificity. Cannot differentiate between HSV-1, HSV-2, and Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV). Primarily of historical significance or a classic "buzzword" finding.
• **Serology (Blood Test)**:
    ◦ Detects type-specific **IgG antibodies** (glycoprotein G).
    ◦ **Use**: Useful for confirming diagnosis in patients with a history of recurrent lesions but negative PCR/culture, or for screening asymptomatic partners.
    ◦ **Limitation**: Takes 3-6 weeks (up to 12 weeks) to become positive after primary infection (**seroconversion**). Not useful for diagnosing an acute outbreak.
    ◦ IgM testing is **not recommended** due to poor performance.
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent for immunocompetent individuals; it is a chronic condition but not life-threatening.
• Recurrences tend to become **less frequent and less severe** over time.
• Genital **HSV-2** recurs more frequently than genital **HSV-1**.

sections.overview:
• **Human Papillomavirus (HPV)** is the most common **sexually transmitted infection (STI)** worldwide.
• It is a DNA virus with over 150 identified genotypes.
• Infections are often **asymptomatic** and transient, cleared by the immune system within 1-2 years.
• Persistent infection with specific HPV types can lead to clinical disease, ranging from benign anogenital warts (**condyloma acuminata**) to various anogenital and oropharyngeal cancers.
• The primary distinction is between **low-risk HPV types**, which cause warts, and **high-risk (oncogenic) HPV types**, which can lead to malignancy.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**: Human Papillomavirus, a non-enveloped, double-stranded DNA virus of the Papillomaviridae family.
• **Transmission**: Primarily through direct skin-to-skin or mucosal contact, most commonly via sexual activity (vaginal, anal, oral).
    ◦ Vertical transmission from mother to infant during childbirth is possible but rare.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ HPV gains access to the basal layer of the stratified squamous epithelium through micro-abrasions.
    ◦ The virus infects basal keratinocytes and integrates its DNA, utilizing the host cell's machinery for replication.
    ◦ As keratinocytes differentiate and migrate to the surface, the virus expresses its proteins, assembles new virions, and is shed.
• **Key Genotypes**:
    ◦ **Low-Risk (Non-oncogenic)**: **HPV 6 and 11** are responsible for >90% of cases of **condyloma acuminata** (genital warts) and recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP).
    ◦ **High-Risk (Oncogenic)**: **HPV 16 and 18** cause ~70% of cervical cancers and a significant proportion of anal, vulvar, vaginal, penile, and oropharyngeal cancers. Other high-risk types include 31, 33, 45, 52, 58.
• **Mechanism of Oncogenesis (High-Risk HPV)**:
    ◦ The viral oncoproteins **E6** and **E7** are central to malignant transformation.
    ◦ **E6 Protein**: Binds to and promotes the degradation of the **p53 tumor suppressor gene product**.
    ◦ **E7 Protein**: Binds to and inactivates the **retinoblastoma (pRb) tumor suppressor protein**, leading to uncontrolled cell cycle progression.
    ◦ This combination results in genomic instability and accumulation of mutations, leading to dysplasia (e.g., CIN) and eventual carcinoma.
sections.epidemiology:
• Most sexually active individuals will acquire an HPV infection at some point in their lives.
• Peak incidence occurs in the late teens and early 20s.
• The majority (~90%) of new HPV infections are cleared by the immune system within 2 years and are clinically insignificant.
• Prevalence of **high-risk HPV** is a key factor in the incidence of **cervical cancer** worldwide.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation depends on the HPV type and the host immune response.
• **Asymptomatic**: The most common presentation. Patients are unaware they are infected.
• **Condyloma Acuminata (Genital Warts)**: Patient presents with single or multiple "bumps" or "growths" in the anogenital area.
• **Abnormal Pap Smear**: Patient is asymptomatic but screening cytology reveals abnormalities (e.g., **ASC-US, LSIL, HSIL**) leading to further investigation.
• **Symptoms of HPV-Related Cancer**:
    ◦ **Cervical**: **Post-coital bleeding**, intermenstrual bleeding, or abnormal vaginal discharge.
    ◦ **Anal**: Rectal bleeding, pain, or a palpable mass.
    ◦ **Oropharyngeal**: Persistent sore throat, dysphagia, odynophagia, neck mass.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Genital Warts**: Primarily a **clinical diagnosis** based on visual inspection.
    ◦ **Biopsy (shave or punch)**: Recommended if the diagnosis is uncertain, lesions are atypical (pigmented, ulcerated, indurated), do not respond to standard therapy, or if the patient is immunocompromised.
    ◦ **Acetowhitening**: Application of 3-5% acetic acid turns lesions white. **No longer recommended for routine screening** due to low specificity (can be positive with inflammation, trauma, or other conditions).
• **Cervical Cancer Screening (Asymptomatic Females)**:
    ◦ **Papanicolaou (Pap) Test**: Cytology to detect cellular abnormalities (dysplasia).
    ◦ **HPV DNA Testing**: Detects the presence of high-risk HPV DNA. Can be used for primary screening, co-testing with cytology, or as a reflex test for abnormal Pap results.
• **Anal Cancer Screening (High-Risk Populations e.g., MSM, HIV+)**:
    ◦ **Anal Pap smear** followed by **high-resolution anoscopy (HRA)** if abnormal.
sections.prognosis:
• **Genital Warts**: The prognosis is good. Warts can resolve spontaneously (in months to years), remain unchanged, or increase in size/number. **Recurrence** after treatment is common (~30%).
• **HPV Infection**: Most infections (~90%) **clear spontaneously** within 2 years. Persistent infection with high-risk types carries a risk of progression to cancer over decades.
• **HPV-related Cancers**: Prognosis is dependent on the type, location, and stage at diagnosis.

sections.overview:
• Influenza ("the flu") is an **acute, febrile respiratory illness** caused by the **influenza virus**
    ◦ Typically occurs in seasonal epidemics, primarily during the fall and winter months
    ◦ The hallmark is the **abrupt onset** of systemic symptoms (fever, myalgia, headache) and respiratory symptoms (cough, sore throat)
    ◦ Usually self-limiting but can cause severe complications, hospitalization, and death, especially in **high-risk populations**
sections.etiology:
• **Virus**: Caused by the **Influenza virus**, a member of the **Orthomyxoviridae** family (single-stranded RNA virus)
• **Types**
    ◦ **Influenza A**: Most common and virulent type
        ▪ Subtyped based on two surface glycoproteins: **Hemagglutinin (HA)** and **Neuraminidase (NA)**
        ▪ Responsible for most seasonal epidemics and all pandemics
    ◦ **Influenza B**: Causes seasonal epidemics but is generally less severe than Influenza A
        ▪ Does not cause pandemics
    ◦ **Influenza C**: Causes mild, sporadic respiratory illness; not a significant cause of epidemics
• **Key Concepts**
    ◦ **Antigenic Drift**: Minor point mutations in the HA and NA genes
        ▪ Leads to slightly different viral strains each year
        ▪ Reason for annual epidemics and the need for a new vaccine each season
        ▪ **(Drift = Epidemics)**
    ◦ **Antigenic Shift**: A major, abrupt genetic reassortment of the viral genome
        ▪ Typically occurs when animal and human influenza viruses co-infect an intermediate host (e.g., a pig)
        ▪ Creates a novel virus to which humans have little or no immunity
        ▪ **(Shift = Pandemics)**
        ▪ This phenomenon is exclusive to **Influenza A**
• **Pathogenesis**
    ◦ **Transmission**: Inhaled via respiratory droplets
    ◦ **Entry**: Virus uses **hemagglutinin (HA)** to bind to sialic acid receptors on respiratory epithelial cells
    ◦ **Replication**: Virus enters the host cell, replicates, and new virions are assembled
    ◦ **Release**: New virions are released from the cell via budding, a process facilitated by **neuraminidase (NA)**, which cleaves the virus from the host cell receptor, destroying the cell
    ◦ **Host Response**: Cell damage and the host's inflammatory response (cytokine release) are responsible for systemic and respiratory symptoms
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Affects 5-20% of the population annually in the U.S.
• **Seasonality**: Typically October to May in the Northern Hemisphere (peaks in December-February)
• **Transmission**: Primarily through **respiratory droplets** from coughing and sneezing; also by contact with fomites
• **Incubation Period**: Short, typically **1-4 days** (average 2 days)
• **Infectious Period**: Adults are typically infectious from 1 day before symptom onset to 5-7 days after; children can be infectious for >10 days
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is an **abrupt onset** of illness
    ◦ Patients can often pinpoint the exact time they began to feel sick
    ◦ This is a key feature that distinguishes influenza from the more gradual onset of the common cold
sections.diagnostics:
• Clinical diagnosis is often sufficient in healthy outpatients during peak influenza season
• Testing is recommended for:
    ◦ Hospitalized patients with suspected influenza
    ◦ Outpatients at high risk for complications
    ◦ Patients for whom a diagnosis will change clinical management
• **RT-PCR**
    ◦ **Description**: **Gold Standard.** Detects viral RNA. Nasopharyngeal swab is preferred specimen.
    ◦ **Sensitivity**: **High (>95%)**
    ◦ **Specificity**: **High (>99%)**
    ◦ **Notes**: Can differentiate between A/B and subtypes. Most accurate test.
• **Rapid Influenza Diagnostic Test (RIDT)**
    ◦ **Description**: Detects viral antigens. Nasal or throat swab.
    ◦ **Sensitivity**: Low to Moderate (50-70%)
    ◦ **Specificity**: High (>95%)
    ◦ **Notes**: Fast results (<15 min). **A negative RIDT does not rule out influenza**, especially during high prevalence.
• **Viral Culture**
    ◦ **Description**: Cell culture to grow the virus.
    ◦ **Sensitivity**: High
    ◦ **Specificity**: High
    ◦ **Notes**: Slow (3-10 days). Used primarily for public health surveillance and research.
• **Chest X-Ray (CXR)**
    ◦ Indicated if pneumonia is suspected (e.g., dyspnea, hypoxia, abnormal lung exam)
    ◦ **Primary viral pneumonia**: Often shows **bilateral interstitial infiltrates**
    ◦ **Secondary bacterial pneumonia**: May show **focal lobar consolidation**
sections.prognosis:
• **Uncomplicated Influenza**: Excellent. Self-limiting illness that typically resolves within 3-7 days, though cough and malaise may persist for >2 weeks
• **Complicated Influenza**: Morbidity and mortality are significantly higher in high-risk groups, primarily due to pneumonia and exacerbations of underlying chronic conditions

sections.overview:
• Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) is an infectious disease caused by the novel **severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2)**.
	◦ It primarily manifests as a respiratory illness, with a clinical spectrum ranging from asymptomatic infection to critical illness, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and death.
	◦ The disease was declared a global pandemic by the World Health Organization (WHO) in March 2020.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**: SARS-CoV-2, an enveloped, single-stranded RNA beta-coronavirus.
• **Transmission**: Primarily through inhalation of respiratory droplets and aerosols generated when an infected person coughs, sneezes, speaks, or breathes.
	◦ Fomite transmission is less common.
• **Viral Entry**: The virus's **Spike (S) protein** binds with high affinity to the **Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptor** on host cells.
	◦ ACE2 receptors are highly expressed on alveolar epithelial cells of the lungs, as well as in the heart, kidneys, and gastrointestinal tract, explaining the multi-organ involvement.
• **Pathophysiology**:
	◦ **Viral Replication**: After cell entry, the virus replicates, leading to cell lysis and propagation.
	◦ **Inflammatory Response**: The initial infection triggers a robust innate and adaptive immune response.
	◦ **Cytokine Storm**: In severe cases, a dysregulated, hyperinflammatory response occurs, characterized by a massive release of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-6, TNF-α). This "**cytokine storm**" is a key driver of lung injury and multi-organ damage.
	◦ **Lung Injury**: Direct viral damage and inflammation lead to diffuse alveolar damage, pulmonary edema, and impaired gas exchange, potentially culminating in **Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)**.
	◦ **Endothelial Dysfunction & Thrombosis**: SARS-CoV-2 can infect endothelial cells, leading to widespread endothelialitis, a prothrombotic state, and micro- and macro-thromboses (e.g., pulmonary embolism, DVT, stroke).
sections.epidemiology:
• **First Identified**: Wuhan, China, in December 2019.
• **Incubation Period**: Typically 4-5 days, with a range of 2-14 days.
• **Infectious Period**: Individuals are most infectious from ~2 days before symptom onset to ~5-7 days after.
	◦ Asymptomatic and presymptomatic transmission is a major driver of spread.
• **Variants**: Multiple variants of concern have emerged (e.g., Alpha, Delta, Omicron), characterized by changes in transmissibility, virulence, and immune evasion.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is highly variable.
• **Asymptomatic**: No symptoms.
• **Mild**: Symptoms of an upper respiratory infection (URI) without shortness of breath or abnormal chest imaging.
• **Moderate**: Evidence of lower respiratory disease by clinical assessment or imaging, with SpO2 ≥ 94% on room air.
• **Severe**: SpO2 < 94% on room air, PaO2/FiO2 ratio <300 mmHg, respiratory rate > 30 breaths/min, or lung infiltrates > 50%.
• **Critical**: Respiratory failure, septic shock, and/or multiple organ dysfunction.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Viral Testing (Confirmatory)**
	◦ **NAAT (Nucleic Acid Amplification Test) / RT-PCR**: Gold standard.
		▪ Highly sensitive and specific.
		▪ Typically uses a nasopharyngeal, oropharyngeal, or nasal swab.
	◦ **Rapid Antigen Test**: Detects viral proteins.
		▪ Less sensitive than PCR but provides rapid results (15-30 min).
		▪ Useful for screening and in symptomatic individuals.
• **Laboratory Findings** (Associated with Severity/Prognosis, not for diagnosis)
	◦ **CBC**: **Lymphopenia** is a classic finding.
	◦ **Inflammatory Markers**: **Elevated C-reactive protein (CRP), ferritin, D-dimer, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), procalcitonin**.
	◦ **Coagulation**: **Elevated D-dimer** is strongly associated with severe disease and thromboembolic risk.
• **Imaging**
	◦ **Chest X-Ray (CXR)**: Classic findings are **bilateral, peripheral ground-glass opacities (GGOs)** and/or consolidations, often in the lower lobes.
		▪ May be normal in early or mild disease.
	◦ **Chest CT**: More sensitive than CXR.
		▪ Shows widespread, peripheral, bilateral GGOs with or without consolidation.
		▪ A "crazy-paving" pattern can be seen.
sections.prognosis:
• Highly variable; >80% of infections are mild-to-moderate.
• **Mortality** is significantly higher in the elderly, unvaccinated, and those with multiple comorbidities.
• The requirement for mechanical ventilation is associated with high mortality (~30-50%).
• **Vaccination** dramatically reduces the risk of severe disease and death.

sections.overview:
• Measles, also known as **Rubeola**, is a highly contagious, acute viral illness caused by the measles virus.
    ◦ Characterized by a classic prodrome of fever and the **"3 C's" (Cough, Coryza, Conjunctivitis)**, followed by a pathognomonic enanthem (**Koplik spots**) and a maculopapular exanthem (rash) that spreads in a **cephalocaudal pattern**.
    ◦ While typically self-limiting, it can cause severe complications, particularly in young children and adults.
    ◦ It is a vaccine-preventable disease via the MMR (Measles, Mumps, Rubella) vaccine.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**:
    ◦ **Causative Agent**: Measles morbillivirus.
    ◦ **Virus Family**: *Paramyxoviridae*.
    ◦ **Virus Type**: Single-stranded, negative-sense RNA virus.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Transmission**: Primarily via **respiratory droplets** (airborne).
        ▪ The virus can remain infectious in the air for up to 2 hours.
    ◦ **Incubation Period**: 10-14 days.
    ◦ **Viral Lifecycle**:
        ▪ 1. **Inoculation**: Virus enters the respiratory tract and infects alveolar macrophages and dendritic cells.
        ▪ 2. **Local Replication**: Spreads to local lymphoid tissue (tracheobronchial lymph nodes).
        ▪ 3. **Primary Viremia**: Virus enters the bloodstream, spreading to the reticuloendothelial system (spleen, lymph nodes, thymus).
        ▪ 4. **Secondary Viremia**: Occurs 5-7 days after initial infection, leading to widespread dissemination to skin, conjunctiva, respiratory tract, and other organs.
    ◦ **Immune Response & Rash**: The characteristic morbilliform rash is a T-cell mediated immune response targeting infected endothelial cells in dermal capillaries.
        ▪ It is NOT a direct result of viral replication in the skin.
    ◦ **Immunosuppression**: The virus infects lymphocytes (CD4+ T-cells, B-cells) and antigen-presenting cells, leading to a transient but profound immunosuppression that can last for weeks to months.
        ▪ This state, sometimes called **"immune amnesia,"** increases susceptibility to secondary bacterial infections.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Dramatically reduced in countries with high MMR vaccination rates.
    ◦ Outbreaks still occur in pockets of unvaccinated individuals.
    ◦ It remains a major cause of childhood mortality worldwide.
• **Population**: Primarily affects unvaccinated children.
    ◦ Infants too young for vaccination and immunocompromised individuals are also at high risk.
• **Contagiousness**: Extremely high.
    ◦ R-naught (R0) is estimated at **12-18**.
    ◦ One infected individual can infect 90% of their susceptible close contacts.
