• **Infectious Period**: From **4 days before** the onset of the rash to **4 days after**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The clinical course unfolds in distinct stages over approximately 1-2 weeks.
• A typical case involves an unvaccinated child presenting with a high fever for several days, followed by the development of a rash that starts on the head and spreads downwards.
• The child appears quite ill during the febrile and eruptive phases.
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is often made clinically, but laboratory confirmation is crucial for public health surveillance and outbreak control.
• **Serology (Best Initial Test)**:
    ◦ **Measles-specific IgM antibody** in serum.
        ▪ Becomes positive ~3 days after rash onset and is diagnostic of acute infection.
    ◦ **Measles-specific IgG antibody**:
        ▪ A four-fold or greater rise in titer between acute and convalescent samples confirms diagnosis.
• **RT-PCR (Reverse Transcriptase PCR)**:
    ◦ Highly sensitive and specific for detecting measles virus RNA.
    ◦ Preferred specimens: **Throat swab**, nasopharyngeal swab, or urine.
    ◦ Most effective when collected within the first few days of the rash.
• **Supportive Labs**:
    ◦ CBC may show leukopenia and lymphopenia.
sections.prognosis:
• In healthy, well-nourished individuals in developed nations, the prognosis is generally excellent.
• Case-fatality rates are significantly higher (up to 25%) in developing countries, largely due to malnutrition (especially Vitamin A deficiency) and lack of access to care.
• Poor prognostic factors include young age (<5 years), malnutrition, and immunodeficiency.

sections.overview:
• Acute, systemic viral illness caused by the mumps virus, a member of the *Paramyxoviridae* family
    ◦ Characterized by the classic presentation of **parotitis** (painful swelling of the parotid salivary glands)
    ◦ While typically a self-limited childhood disease, it can cause significant complications, especially in post-pubertal individuals
    ◦ Incidence has been dramatically reduced by the widespread use of the Measles, Mumps, and Rubella (MMR) vaccine
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**: **Mumps virus**, a single-stranded RNA virus from the genus *Rubulavirus* in the *Paramyxoviridae* family
• **Transmission**: Primarily through **respiratory droplets**, direct contact with saliva, or fomites
    ◦ Humans are the only natural host
• **Pathogenesis**:
    ◦ The virus enters the respiratory tract and replicates in the nasopharynx and regional lymph nodes
    ◦ A primary viremia occurs, disseminating the virus to target tissues
        ▪ Target tissues include salivary glands (especially the **parotid glands**), testes, ovaries, pancreas, and the central nervous system (CNS)
    ◦ The incubation period is typically **16-18 days** (range 12-25 days)
    ◦ The characteristic parotid swelling is due to inflammation and edema within the gland
sections.epidemiology:
• **Pre-vaccine Era**: Mumps was a ubiquitous childhood illness
• **Post-vaccine Era**: Incidence has decreased by >99% in countries with routine vaccination programs
• **Current Trends**: Outbreaks still occur, primarily in **congregate settings** such as college campuses, military barracks, and close-knit communities
    ◦ These outbreaks often affect vaccinated individuals due to **waning immunity**
• **Peak Incidence**: Late winter and spring
• **Communicability**: Patients are most infectious from 2 days before to 5 days after the onset of parotitis
sections.clinicalPresentation: • A typical presentation is an unvaccinated or under-vaccinated adolescent or young adult from a college campus who presents with a prodrome of fever and malaise, followed by the development of unilateral or bilateral painful swelling of the cheek and jaw area.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Often made clinically based on parotitis in the setting of an outbreak
• **Laboratory Confirmation** (required for sporadic cases)
    ◦ **Best Initial Test**: **Serum mumps-specific IgM antibody**
        ▪ Positive IgM indicates acute infection
    ◦ **Most Specific Test / Gold Standard**: **RT-PCR** of a buccal swab, saliva, urine, or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)
        ▪ This is most sensitive within the first few days of symptom onset
• **Supportive Lab Findings**
    ◦ **Leukopenia** with a relative lymphocytosis is common
    ◦ **Serum amylase** is typically elevated due to parotitis (salivary amylase) and/or pancreatitis (pancreatic amylase)
        ▪ Serum lipase is more specific for pancreatitis
• **Lumbar Puncture** (if CNS symptoms are present)
    ◦ CSF analysis will show classic findings of **aseptic (viral) meningitis**:
        ▪ Pleocytosis with a **lymphocytic predominance**
        ▪ Mildly elevated protein
        ▪ **Normal glucose**
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for uncomplicated cases; the illness is typically self-limited and resolves within 2 weeks
• Life-long immunity generally follows natural infection
• Prognosis is worse if rare complications like encephalitis occur
• Sterility is a feared but very rare consequence, even with bilateral orchitis

sections.overview:
• Rubella, also known as **German Measles** or **"3-day measles,"** is a mild, self-limiting viral illness in children and adults.
• Primary clinical significance lies in its devastating teratogenic effects when infection occurs during early pregnancy, leading to **Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS)**.
• Widespread use of the **MMR (Measles, Mumps, Rubella) vaccine** has made postnatal infection rare in developed countries, shifting the focus to prevention and recognition of CRS.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent:** Rubella virus, an enveloped, single-stranded RNA virus from the **Togaviridae** family (genus *Rubivirus*).
• **Transmission:** Primarily through inhalation of infectious respiratory droplets. It can also be transmitted transplacentally from mother to fetus.
• **Pathophysiology (Postnatal):**
    ◦ Virus enters the respiratory tract and replicates in the nasopharynx and regional lymph nodes.
    ◦ A primary viremia occurs, spreading the virus throughout the body.
    ◦ A secondary viremia follows, leading to the characteristic rash and other systemic symptoms.
    ◦ The patient is contagious from approximately 7 days before to 7 days after the onset of the rash.
• **Pathophysiology (Congenital):**
    ◦ During maternal viremia, the virus crosses the placenta and infects the fetus.
    ◦ The risk and severity of fetal damage are highest during the **first trimester** (up to 85% risk of defects if infected in the first 8-10 weeks).
    ◦ The virus causes fetal cell necrosis, apoptosis, and chromosomal abnormalities, leading to vasculopathy and widespread organ damage.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence:** Dramatically reduced worldwide due to vaccination. In the U.S., rubella is considered eliminated, but imported cases still occur.
• **Outbreaks:** Typically occur in unvaccinated or under-vaccinated populations.
• **Reservoir:** Humans are the only known reservoir.
• **Seasonality:** Historically, peaks occurred in late winter and early spring.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Postnatal (Acquired) Rubella:**
    ◦ Often a mild, subclinical infection.
    ◦ When symptomatic, it presents as a classic viral exanthem with a prodrome of low-grade fever, malaise, and prominent lymphadenopathy, followed by a maculopapular rash.
• **Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS):**
    ◦ A neonate born to a mother infected during early pregnancy presents with a constellation of birth defects, classically involving the eyes, ears, and heart.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Serology is the mainstay of diagnosis.**
    ◦ **Rubella-specific IgM:**
        ▪ Presence indicates a **recent primary infection**.
        ▪ Typically detectable shortly after rash onset and persists for several weeks.
    ◦ **Rubella-specific IgG:**
        ▪ Indicates **past infection or immunity** from vaccination.
        ▪ A **four-fold rise** in IgG titers between acute and convalescent sera (collected 2-4 weeks apart) confirms recent infection.
• **Viral Detection (RT-PCR or Culture):**
    ◦ Can be performed on nasopharyngeal swabs, throat swabs, or urine.
    ◦ More commonly used to confirm CRS in infants, who may shed the virus for up to a year.
• **Prenatal Screening:**
    ◦ All pregnant women should be screened for rubella immunity (IgG status) at their first prenatal visit.
sections.prognosis:
• **Postnatal Rubella:** Excellent. It is a self-limiting illness with complete recovery.
• **Congenital Rubella Syndrome:** Highly variable and depends on the extent and severity of the defects. Can lead to lifelong disability and a shortened lifespan.

sections.overview:
• Roseola infantum, also known as **exanthem subitum** or **sixth disease**, is a common, self-limiting viral illness of early childhood.
    ◦ Classically characterized by a distinct clinical sequence: **3 to 5 days of high fever** that resolves abruptly, followed immediately by the appearance of a maculopapular rash.
• It is a benign condition, but the high fever can be alarming to parents and is a common cause of **febrile seizures**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiologic Agent**
    ◦ Primarily caused by **Human Herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6)**, specifically HHV-6B.
    ◦ A smaller percentage of cases are caused by **Human Herpesvirus 7 (HHV-7)**.
• **Virus Family**
    ◦ Member of the Herpesviridae family.
    ◦ Like other herpesviruses, it can establish lifelong latency in the host after the primary infection.
• **Transmission**
    ◦ Spread primarily through **respiratory droplets** (saliva) from asymptomatic contacts.
    ◦ The virus replicates in leukocytes and salivary glands.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Incubation Period**: Approximately 5-15 days after exposure.
    ◦ **Viremia**: The virus enters the bloodstream, leading to a viremic phase responsible for the abrupt onset of **high fever** (the prodromal phase).
    ◦ **Immune Response & Rash**: The rash (exanthem) is believed to be an **immune-mediated response** (antigen-antibody complex formation) that occurs as the child's immune system clears the viremia.
        ▪ This explains the classic timing: the rash appears only *after* the fever has resolved.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Age**: Predominantly affects infants and toddlers.
    ◦ Peak incidence is between **6 and 15 months of age**.
• **Prevalence**: It is a ubiquitous virus.
    ◦ Over 90% of children have been infected and are seropositive for HHV-6 by age 2.
• **Seasonality**: Occurs year-round with a slight peak in the spring and fall.
• **Transmission**: Humans are the only known reservoir.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a **biphasic illness** in a typically well-appearing, alert infant or toddler.
    ◦ A sudden **high fever** for several days, followed by the development of a rash once the fever subsides.
• **Classic Vignette**
    ◦ A 10-month-old infant is brought to the clinic with a rash. The parents report the child had a **high fever (up to 40°C / 104°F)** for the past 4 days, during which they were fussy but still relatively active. This morning, the fever completely disappeared, and a pink, spotty rash appeared on the child's chest and back.
sections.diagnostics:
• Primarily a **clinical diagnosis**; laboratory testing is rarely necessary in an immunocompetent child with a classic presentation.
• **Laboratory Findings** (if performed)
    ◦ **CBC**: May show **leukopenia** and **lymphocytopenia** initially, followed by relative lymphocytosis.
    ◦ **Serology**: IgG and IgM antibody tests for HHV-6 can confirm diagnosis but are not used for routine clinical management.
• **Workup**
    ◦ Further investigation (e.g., blood cultures, urinalysis) should be considered in infants with fever to rule out more serious bacterial infections, especially if the presentation is atypical or the child appears ill.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**; in healthy children, roseola is a benign illness with complete recovery expected.
• Infection confers lifelong immunity to the specific virus type (HHV-6 or HHV-7).

sections.overview:
• Varicella, commonly known as chickenpox, is a highly contagious acute infectious disease caused by the **Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV)**.
• Characterized by a **pruritic, vesicular rash** that appears in **successive crops**.
• While typically a benign, self-limiting illness in healthy children, it can cause significant morbidity and mortality in adults, neonates, and immunocompromised individuals.
• Primary infection confers lifelong immunity, but the virus establishes latency in the **dorsal root ganglia** and can reactivate later in life as **Herpes Zoster (shingles)**.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**: **Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV)**, a member of the Human Herpesvirus family (HHV-3) and a double-stranded DNA virus.
• **Transmission**:
    ◦ Primarily via inhalation of **respiratory droplets** from an infected person.
    ◦ Also via direct contact with fluid from **vesicular lesions**.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Inoculation**: Virus enters the mucosa of the upper respiratory tract or conjunctiva.
    ◦ **Replication**: VZV replicates in regional lymph nodes (e.g., tonsils).
    ◦ **Primary Viremia**: Occurs 4-6 days post-infection, disseminating the virus to organs like the liver and spleen.
    ◦ **Secondary Viremia**: Occurs ~14 days post-infection, leading to widespread dissemination to the skin and mucous membranes, resulting in the characteristic **vesicular rash**.
    ◦ **Latency**: After the primary infection resolves, VZV becomes latent in the sensory **dorsal root ganglia** and reactivation later in life causes **Herpes Zoster (Shingles)**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Dramatically decreased (>90%) in the U.S. since the introduction of the **varicella vaccine** in 1995.
    ◦ **"Breakthrough" infections** in vaccinated individuals are possible but are typically much milder.
• **Peak Incidence**: Historically, in children <10 years old.
• **Seasonality**: More common in late winter and early spring in temperate climates.
• **Contagiousness**: Extremely high, with a secondary attack rate among susceptible household contacts of ~90%.
• **Period of Infectivity**: From 1-2 days *before* the rash appears until all lesions have fully **crusted over** (typically 5-7 days after rash onset).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The clinical course begins with a **prodrome** followed by the classic **exanthem**.
• **Prodrome**:
    ◦ Occurs 1-2 days before the rash; more common and pronounced in adults.
    ◦ Symptoms include low-grade fever, malaise, anorexia, headache, and myalgias.
• **Exanthem (Rash)**: The hallmark of the disease.
    ◦ **Distribution**: Begins on the face and trunk (**"centripetal distribution"**) and spreads to the extremities.
        ▪ Lesions can occur on **mucous membranes** (mouth, conjunctiva, vagina).
    ◦ **Appearance**: Intensely **pruritic** lesions that progress through stages:
        ▪ **Macule** (red spot)
        ▪ **Papule** (raised bump)
        ▪ **Vesicle** (clear, fluid-filled blister on an erythematous base - **"dewdrop on a rose petal"**)
        ▪ **Pustule** (cloudy fluid)
        ▪ **Crusting/Scabbing**
    ◦ **Key Feature**: The presence of lesions in **all stages of development simultaneously** on any one part of the body.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primarily a clinical diagnosis** based on the characteristic polymorphic rash.
• Lab confirmation is reserved for atypical cases, severe disease, or immunocompromised hosts.
• **PCR of vesicular fluid or scabs**: The test of choice, highly sensitive and specific for VZV DNA.
• **Tzanck Smear**: A rapid test showing **multinucleated giant cells**.
    ◦ A classic finding for herpesvirus infections (VZV, HSV) but is not specific for VZV and has low sensitivity compared to PCR.
• **Serology (IgG, IgM)**: Can confirm immunity (**VZV IgG**) or recent primary infection (**VZV IgM**), but less useful for acute diagnosis.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** in healthy children; typically a self-limiting illness with complete recovery.
• **Guarded** in adults and the immunocompromised due to a higher risk of severe complications.
• Primary infection provides **lifelong immunity** to varicella, but VZV remains latent with the potential for reactivation as **herpes zoster**.

sections.overview:
• **Herpes Zoster**, commonly known as **shingles**, is an acute, painful, **unilateral vesicular eruption** that occurs in a restricted **dermatomal distribution**
◦ Caused by the **reactivation** of the latent **Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV)** from the dorsal root or cranial nerve ganglia
◦ The primary infection with VZV causes **varicella (chickenpox)**
sections.etiology:
• **Etiologic Agent**: **Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV)**, also known as **Human Herpesvirus 3 (HHV-3)**
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Primary Infection (Varicella/Chickenpox)**: The individual is first infected with VZV, typically in childhood, leading to a diffuse vesicular rash
    ◦ **Latency**: After the primary infection resolves, the virus is not cleared from the body. It becomes latent, establishing a lifelong dormant infection within the sensory neurons of the dorsal root ganglia and cranial nerve ganglia
    ◦ **Reactivation**: Due to a decline in VZV-specific cell-mediated immunity (often associated with aging or immunosuppression), the virus reactivates. It then travels down the sensory nerve axon to the skin surface of the corresponding dermatome
    ◦ **Eruption**: Viral replication in the epidermis causes localized inflammation, neuronal damage, and the characteristic vesicular rash and neuralgia
sections.epidemiology:
• **Lifetime Risk**: Approximately **1 in 3 people** in the United States will develop shingles in their lifetime
• **Incidence**: Over 1 million cases occur annually in the US
• **Age**: The incidence and severity of shingles increase sharply with age, particularly after age 50, due to **immunosenescence** (age-related decline in immune function)
• **Vaccination**: The widespread use of the **varicella vaccine** in children has decreased the incidence of chickenpox. The use of the **zoster vaccine (Shingrix)** is decreasing the incidence of shingles in vaccinated adults
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The clinical course typically progresses through three phases
    ◦ **Prodromal Phase (Pre-eruptive)**
        ▪ Lasts 1-5 days before the rash appears
        ▪ Patients experience sensory symptoms in the affected dermatome
    ◦ **Acute Eruptive Phase**
        ▪ The characteristic rash appears and evolves over 7-10 days
        ▪ Pain is often most severe during this phase
    ◦ **Chronic Phase**
        ▪ For some patients, this phase is characterized by **Postherpetic Neuralgia (PHN)**, where pain persists for months or years after the rash has healed
sections.diagnostics:
• Primarily a **clinical diagnosis**; the history and pathognomonic rash are usually sufficient
• Laboratory testing is reserved for atypical cases (e.g., absence of rash, immunocompromised patient with disseminated disease)
• **Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR)**
    ◦ **Test of choice**
    ◦ Highly sensitive and specific
    ◦ Performed on unroofed vesicular fluid, a crust, or CSF
    ◦ Can differentiate VZV from HSV
• **Direct Fluorescent Antibody (DFA) Staining**
    ◦ Rapid and sensitive
    ◦ Differentiates VZV from HSV
• **Tzanck Smear**
    ◦ A historical test involving scraping the base of a vesicle
    ◦ Shows **multinucleated giant cells**
    ◦ It is sensitive but not specific for VZV (also positive for HSV)
sections.prognosis:
• **Immunocompetent**: The rash typically resolves within 2-4 weeks. Prognosis is excellent
• **PHN**: Develops in 10-15% of all patients, but the risk rises to >30% in patients over 60. Pain can persist for months to years, significantly impacting quality of life
• **Immunocompromised**: Higher risk for complications, dissemination, and prolonged course

sections.overview:
• **Rabies** is a viral zoonotic neuroinvasive disease that causes progressive and fatal **encephalitis**.
• It is caused by lyssaviruses, primarily the **Rabies lyssavirus**.
• The virus is transmitted from the saliva of an infected animal to a human, typically through a bite.
• It travels via peripheral nerves to the central nervous system (CNS).
• Once clinical symptoms appear, the disease is nearly **100% fatal**.
• It is almost **100% preventable** with prompt and appropriate **post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP)**.
    ◦ **PEP** includes wound care, administration of **human rabies immune globulin (HRIG)**, and a series of rabies vaccine injections.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**: **Rabies lyssavirus**, a single-stranded, negative-sense, enveloped RNA virus of the *Rhabdoviridae* family.
    ◦ It has a characteristic **bullet shape**.
• **Transmission**: Primarily through the saliva of an infected animal via a bite.
    ◦ Scratches contaminated with saliva or direct saliva contact with mucous membranes or broken skin can also transmit the virus.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Inoculation & Local Replication**: The virus enters the host through a bite and replicates slowly within myocytes (muscle cells) at the inoculation site.
    ◦ **Neuroinvasion**: The virus binds to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction to enter the peripheral nervous system.
    ◦ **Retrograde Axonal Transport**: The virus travels up the peripheral nerves towards the CNS at a rate of approximately 1-2 cm per day.
        ▪ The incubation period is directly related to the distance of the bite from the CNS (e.g., a bite on the face has a shorter incubation period than a bite on the foot).
    ◦ **CNS Infection**: The virus replicates rapidly within the brain, causing severe **encephalitis**.
        ▪ It has a predilection for the hippocampus, brainstem, and cerebellum, leading to the characteristic behavioral and autonomic symptoms.
    ◦ **Centrifugal Spread**: From the CNS, the virus spreads centrifugally via anterograde axonal transport to highly innervated sites.
        ▪ Includes the **salivary glands** (enabling further transmission), skin (especially hair follicles at the nape of the neck), cornea, and other organs.
• **Pathognomonic Finding (Histology)**: **Negri bodies**.
    ◦ Eosinophilic, sharply demarcated, intracytoplasmic inclusions found in infected neurons (especially hippocampal pyramidal cells and cerebellar Purkinje cells).
sections.epidemiology:
• **Worldwide**: Over 59,000 deaths annually, mostly in Asia and Africa.
    ◦ >95% of human cases are transmitted by **dogs**.
• **United States**: Human rabies is rare (~1-3 cases per year).
    ◦ **Primary Vector**: **Bats** are the most common source of human rabies infection in the U.S.
        ▪ Bat bites may be small, difficult to see, and go unnoticed.
    ◦ **Other Terrestrial Vectors**: **Raccoons** (most common rabid animal on the East Coast), **skunks**, and **foxes** are major reservoirs.
• Rodents (squirrels, chipmunks, mice, rats) and lagomorphs (rabbits) are rarely found to be infected with rabies and have not been known to transmit it to humans.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Incubation Period**: Highly variable, typically **3 weeks to 3 months**, but can range from days to years.
    ◦ Dependent on the location and severity of the bite, and the viral load.
• **Prodromal Phase (2-10 days)**:
    ◦ Nonspecific flu-like symptoms: fever, malaise, headache, anorexia, nausea, vomiting.
    ◦ **Pathognomonic Clue**: Paresthesias, pain, or intense pruritus **at the site of the bite/inoculation** is present in 50-80% of cases and is a major red flag.
• **Acute Neurologic Phase (2-7 days)**: The disease manifests in one of two forms.
    ◦ **Furious (Encephalitic) Rabies (~80% of cases)**:
        ▪ Characterized by hyperactivity, agitation, confusion, and fluctuating consciousness.
        ▪ **Hydrophobia**: Painful, violent, involuntary pharyngeal and laryngeal spasms when attempting to drink water or even at the sight/sound of water.
        ▪ **Aerophobia**: Spasms triggered by a draft of air on the face.
        ▪ Other findings: **Hypersalivation** ("foaming at the mouth"), autonomic dysfunction (hyperpyrexia, tachycardia), seizures.
    ◦ **Paralytic (Dumb) Rabies (~20% of cases)**:
        ▪ Characterized by an **ascending, flaccid paralysis** beginning in the bitten limb and spreading symmetrically or asymmetrically.
        ▪ Often misdiagnosed as **Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS)**.
        ▪ Fever and headache are common, but signs of cerebral irritation (**hydrophobia, aerophobia**) are minimal or absent.
• **Coma and Death**: Both forms progress to coma, autonomic collapse, and death, typically within 2 weeks of symptom onset.
sections.diagnostics:
• Antemortem diagnosis is difficult and often clinical; no single test is sufficient and multiple samples should be collected.
• **Saliva**: **RT-PCR** for rabies virus RNA.
    ◦ Multiple samples should be taken.
• **Nuchal (nape of the neck) Skin Biopsy**: This is a very high-yield test.
    ◦ **RT-PCR** and **direct fluorescent antibody (DFA)** staining for viral antigen in cutaneous nerves at the base of hair follicles.
• **Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF)**:
    ◦ CSF analysis shows mild pleocytosis and elevated protein.
    ◦ Test for **anti-rabies antibodies** (in unvaccinated patients) and viral RNA by **RT-PCR**.
• **Serum**: Test for **anti-rabies antibodies**.
    ◦ Only useful in an unvaccinated individual, as antibodies do not appear until late in the disease.
• **Postmortem Diagnosis (Gold Standard)**: **DFA test on brain tissue** (brainstem, cerebellum) to detect viral antigens.
    ◦ Histology can reveal **Negri bodies**.
sections.prognosis:
• Once clinical symptoms appear, rabies is nearly **100% fatal**.
    ◦ Death usually occurs within 2 weeks.
• With timely and appropriate **PEP**, rabies is nearly **100% preventable**.

sections.overview:
• Infectious Mononucleosis (IM) is a clinical syndrome most commonly caused by the **Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV)**.
• Characterized by the classic triad of:
    ◦ **Fever**
    ◦ **Pharyngitis**
    ◦ **Posterior cervical lymphadenopathy**
• The illness is typically self-limited but notable for profound fatigue that can persist and the risk of significant complications, most notably **splenic rupture**.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**: **Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV)**, a member of the Human Herpesvirus family (HHV-4).
• **Transmission**: Primarily through saliva ("the kissing disease"), but can also be transmitted via blood transfusion or organ transplant.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ EBV initially infects the oropharyngeal epithelial cells.
    ◦ The virus then spreads to underlying lymphoid tissue, specifically targeting **B-lymphocytes** by binding to the CD21 receptor.
    ◦ This leads to a massive B-cell proliferation and the production of heterophile antibodies (the basis for the Monospot test).
    ◦ The host's immune system mounts a vigorous response with **CD8+ cytotoxic T-lymphocytes** which target the infected B-cells.
    ◦ These activated, large T-cells are the characteristic **"atypical lymphocytes"** seen on a peripheral blood smear.
    ◦ The clinical signs and symptoms of mono (fever, lymphadenopathy, pharyngitis) are largely due to this intense T-cell immune response.
    ◦ Like all herpesviruses, EBV establishes lifelong latency within B-lymphocytes.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Over 90% of adults worldwide are seropositive for EBV.
• **Age**: Symptomatic infectious mononucleosis has a peak incidence in adolescents and young adults aged **15-24 years**.
• **Socioeconomics**:
    ◦ In developing countries, infection often occurs in early childhood and is typically asymptomatic or presents as a mild illness.
    ◦ In developed countries, primary infection is often delayed until adolescence, leading to the classic symptomatic presentation.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The typical presentation is an adolescent or young adult with an insidious onset of a prodrome (malaise, headache, and low-grade fever).
• This progresses over 1-2 weeks to the classic triad of symptoms.
• The illness generally lasts 2-4 weeks, but fatigue and malaise can linger for months.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Screening Test: Heterophile Antibody Test (Monospot)**
    ◦ Detects IgM antibodies that agglutinate horse or sheep red blood cells.
    ◦ Quick and inexpensive.
    ◦ Sensitivity is ~75% in the first week, increasing to >90% by the third week.
    ◦ A negative test early in the illness does not rule out mono.
• **Complete Blood Count (CBC) with Differential**
    ◦ **Lymphocytosis**: Absolute lymphocyte count >4,500/mcL or >50% of total WBCs.
    ◦ **Atypical Lymphocytes**: **>10%** atypical lymphocytes on peripheral smear is a hallmark finding.
        ▪ These are large, reactive CD8+ T-cells, also known as **Downey cells**.
• **EBV-Specific Serology**
    ◦ Used when the Monospot is negative but clinical suspicion remains high.
    ◦ **Viral Capsid Antigen (VCA) IgM**: Indicates **acute/current infection**. Appears early and disappears after 3-6 months.
    ◦ **VCA IgG**: Indicates **current or past infection**. Appears after IgM and persists for life.
    ◦ **Epstein-Barr Nuclear Antigen (EBNA) IgG**: Marker of **past infection**. Appears late (6-12 weeks after symptom onset) and persists for life. Its presence rules out acute mononucleosis.
• **EBV Serology Interpretation Summary**
    ◦ **Acute Infection**:
        ▪ **VCA-IgM**: Positive
        ▪ **VCA-IgG**: Positive
        ▪ **EBNA-IgG**: Negative
    ◦ **Past Infection**:
        ▪ **VCA-IgM**: Negative
        ▪ **VCA-IgG**: Positive
        ▪ **EBNA-IgG**: Positive
• **Liver Function Tests (LFTs)**: Mildly elevated AST and ALT are seen in >80% of patients.
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent for most immunocompetent individuals.
• The acute illness is self-limited and typically resolves within 2-4 weeks.
• Fatigue is the most persistent symptom and can last for several months in some individuals.
• Death is very rare and is usually due to **splenic rupture**, **airway obstruction**, or neurologic complications.

sections.overview:
• Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a ubiquitous, double-stranded DNA virus belonging to the Herpesviridae family, specifically Human Herpesvirus 5 (HHV-5).
• Like other herpesviruses, it establishes lifelong latency after primary infection with the potential for reactivation.
• Clinical disease from CMV is highly dependent on the host's immune status.
    ◦ In **immunocompetent** individuals, it is typically asymptomatic or causes a mild, self-limited **mononucleosis-like illness**.
    ◦ It is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in **immunocompromised** patients (e.g., transplant recipients, HIV/AIDS).
    ◦ It is the most common **congenital viral infection**, leading to significant long-term sequelae like **hearing loss** and **developmental delay**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**: Caused by Cytomegalovirus (CMV), a member of the Betaherpesvirinae subfamily.
• **Transmission**: Occurs via direct contact with infected bodily fluids, including saliva, urine, blood, tears, semen, breast milk, and cervical secretions.
    ◦ It can also be transmitted vertically (in utero, perinatally) or through blood transfusions and organ transplantation.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Primary Infection**: The virus replicates in epithelial cells of the respiratory tract, salivary glands, and kidneys.
    ◦ **Latency**: CMV establishes a latent infection primarily within myeloid progenitor cells in the bone marrow.
    ◦ **Reactivation**: **Immunosuppression** (e.g., due to HIV, chemotherapy, or anti-rejection medications) allows the virus to reactivate, leading to high-level replication and viremia.
    ◦ **Cellular Effects**: CMV infection causes characteristic cellular enlargement (cytomegaly) and the formation of a pathognomonic large, basophilic intranuclear inclusion body surrounded by a clear halo, famously described as an **"owl's eye"** appearance on histology.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Extremely common worldwide, with seroprevalence ranging from 50-100% in the adult population, increasing with age and in lower socioeconomic settings.
• **Congenital Infection**: The most common congenital viral infection in the United States, affecting ~1 in 200 newborns.
• **High-Risk Populations**: Disease is most severe in transplant recipients (especially solid organ and hematopoietic stem cell) and individuals with advanced HIV/AIDS.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The clinical presentation is divided into three major syndromes:
    ◦ **Congenital CMV**:
        ▪ ~90% are asymptomatic at birth.
        ▪ Symptomatic newborns (**"cytomegalic inclusion disease"**) present with:
            • **Intrauterine Growth Restriction (IUGR)** and low birth weight.
            • **Hepatosplenomegaly** and jaundice.
            • **Thrombocytopenia** with petechiae/purpura (**"blueberry muffin" rash**).
            • **Neurologic**: **Microcephaly**, seizures, and characteristic **periventricular calcifications** on head CT/MRI.
            • **Sensorineural Hearing Loss (SNHL)**: The most common sequela, can be present at birth or develop later.
    ◦ **Immunocompetent Host (CMV Mononucleosis)**:
        ▪ Often asymptomatic.
        ▪ When symptomatic, presents as a **mononucleosis-like illness**:
            • Prolonged fever, malaise, myalgias, arthralgias.
            • Mildly tender lymphadenopathy (less prominent than EBV).
            • Mild hepatitis (elevated LFTs).
        ▪ **Key Distinction from EBV**: Severe exudative pharyngitis and marked posterior cervical lymphadenopathy are less common. The **heterophile antibody (Monospot) test is negative**.
    ◦ **Immunocompromised Host**:
        ▪ Represents reactivation or severe primary infection. Disease is often site-specific.
        ▪ **Retinitis**: The most common manifestation in AIDS (**CD4 <50**).
            • Presents with floaters, scotomas, or decreased peripheral vision.
            • Fundoscopy reveals a characteristic **"pizza pie" or "ketchup and cheese"** appearance (hemorrhages and fluffy yellow-white exudates).
            • High risk for **retinal detachment** and blindness.
        ▪ **Gastrointestinal Disease**:
            • **Esophagitis**: Odynophagia. Endoscopy shows **large, linear, deep ulcers**.
            • **Colitis**: Diarrhea (often bloody), abdominal pain, fever. Can lead to perforation.
        ▪ **Pneumonitis**: Common and severe in transplant patients.
            • Presents with dyspnea, nonproductive cough, fever, and interstitial infiltrates on CXR.
        ▪ **Neurologic Disease**: Encephalitis, ventriculitis, or polyradiculopathy.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Immunocompetent (Mononucleosis)**:
    ◦ **CBC**: Lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes.
    ◦ **CMP**: Elevated LFTs (transaminitis).
    ◦ **Heterophile Antibody (Monospot) Test**: **Negative**.
    ◦ **CMV Serology**: Positive CMV IgM antibody confirms acute infection. IgG indicates past exposure.
• **Immunocompromised & Congenital**:
    ◦ **CMV DNA PCR (Quantitative)**: **Test of choice**.
        ▪ Detects and quantifies viral load in blood, CSF, or other fluids.
        ▪ Used for diagnosis and to monitor treatment response.
    ◦ **Histopathology**: Tissue biopsy (e.g., from GI tract) showing large cells with classic **"owl's eye" intranuclear inclusions** is diagnostic for invasive disease.
    ◦ **Congenital Diagnosis**: CMV PCR on newborn urine or saliva within the first 3 weeks of life.
    ◦ **Neuroimaging (Congenital)**: Head CT/MRI showing **periventricular calcifications**.
sections.prognosis:
• **Immunocompetent**: Excellent; full recovery is expected.
• **Congenital**: Highly variable.
    ◦ Asymptomatic neonates have a better prognosis, but 10-15% still develop **SNHL**.
    ◦ Symptomatic infants have a high rate of severe, permanent neurologic deficits.
• **Immunocompromised**: Guarded.
    ◦ Depends on the site of disease, underlying immune status, and response to therapy.
    ◦ CMV **retinitis** is sight-threatening, and **pneumonitis** is life-threatening.

sections.overview:
• Parvovirus B19 is a single-stranded DNA virus causing a spectrum of disease based on patient age and hematologic/immunologic status, including:
    ◦ **Erythema Infectiosum (Fifth Disease)** in children
    ◦ Acute **arthropathy** in adults
    ◦ **Transient aplastic crisis** in patients with hemolytic anemias
    ◦ **Hydrops fetalis** in fetuses
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**: Caused by Parvovirus B19, a small, non-enveloped, single-stranded DNA virus from the *Parvoviridae* family.
• **Transmission**: Primarily through **respiratory droplets**. Can also be transmitted vertically (mother to fetus) and via blood products.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Viral Tropism**: The virus has a specific affinity for **erythroid progenitor cells** in the bone marrow by binding to the **P antigen** (globoside) on the cell surface.
    ◦ **Cell Lysis**: The virus replicates within these cells, leading to their lysis and a temporary **cessation of erythropoiesis** (red blood cell production).
    ◦ **Clinical Manifestations**:
        ▪ **Healthy Individuals**: The temporary halt in RBC production is clinically insignificant. The classic "slapped cheek" rash is an **immune complex-mediated** phenomenon that occurs *after* viremia has resolved.
        ▪ **Patients with Hemolytic Anemia**: (e.g., Sickle Cell Disease, Thalassemia, Hereditary Spherocytosis): These patients rely on rapid RBC production. A sudden halt leads to a severe drop in hemoglobin, causing a **transient aplastic crisis**.
        ▪ **Fetuses**: High rate of RBC production makes them susceptible. Infection can lead to severe fetal anemia, high-output heart failure, and subsequent **hydrops fetalis**.
        ▪ **Adults**: A robust immune response often leads to immune complex deposition in the synovium, causing an acute, symmetric **arthropathy**.
        ▪ **Immunocompromised Patients**: Inability to produce neutralizing antibodies allows for persistent infection, leading to **chronic pure red cell aplasia** and chronic anemia.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Very common worldwide. Seroprevalence increases with age; >50% of adults are IgG positive, indicating past infection and immunity.
• **Peak Incidence**: Most common in children aged 4-10 years.
• **Seasonality**: Outbreaks are common in late winter and spring.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Exposure to Children**: Parents, teachers, daycare workers.
• **Underlying Hemolytic Anemia**: Sickle cell disease, hereditary spherocytosis, thalassemia.
• **Immunocompromised State**: HIV/AIDS, transplant recipients, congenital immunodeficiency.
• **Pregnancy**: Non-immune (IgG negative) pregnant women are at risk for fetal complications.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation depends entirely on the host:
    ◦ **Erythema Infectiosum (Fifth Disease)**: Classic presentation in immunocompetent children.
    ◦ **Acute Arthropathy**: Most common presentation in adults, especially women.
    ◦ **Transient Aplastic Crisis**: Presents in patients with chronic hemolytic anemias.
    ◦ **Hydrops Fetalis**: Fetal complication following maternal infection.
    ◦ **Chronic Anemia**: Seen in immunocompromised patients.
• **Prodrome (common to most forms)**:
    ◦ Low-grade fever, headache, malaise, coryza.
    ◦ This phase corresponds with peak viremia and contagiousness.
• **Erythema Infectiosum**:
    ◦ Initially, fiery red rash on the cheeks ("**slapped cheeks**").
    ◦ 1-4 days later, a **lacy, reticular, maculopapular rash** appears on the trunk and extremities.
    ◦ Rash may wax and wane for weeks, often exacerbated by heat, sun, or stress.
• **Arthropathy**:
    ◦ Acute onset of **symmetric polyarthritis**, primarily affecting small joints (hands, wrists, knees, ankles).
    ◦ Can be associated with morning stiffness, mimicking rheumatoid arthritis.
• **Transient Aplastic Crisis**:
    ◦ Sudden onset of severe weakness, fatigue, pallor, and dyspnea.
    ◦ **No rash or fever** is typically present during the crisis.
• **Maternal Infection**:
    ◦ Often asymptomatic or presents with mild flu-like symptoms and/or arthralgias. The risk is primarily to the fetus.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Erythema Infectiosum**:
    ◦ Bright erythematous, indurated plaques on the cheeks, with **perioral and circumoral sparing**.
    ◦ Reticular (lace-like) erythematous rash on the trunk and extremities.
• **Arthropathy**:
    ◦ Swelling, tenderness, and effusion in affected joints (e.g., MCPs, PIPs, wrists, knees).
• **Transient Aplastic Crisis**:
    ◦ Profound **pallor** of skin and conjunctiva.
    ◦ Tachycardia, systolic flow murmur.
    ◦ **Absence of hepatosplenomegaly**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Often sufficient for classic Fifth Disease in a healthy child.
• **Serology (Test of Choice)**:
    ◦ **Parvovirus B19 IgM**: Indicates an acute or recent infection. Appears ~10 days after exposure and can persist for 3-6 months.
    ◦ **Parvovirus B19 IgG**: Indicates past infection and immunity. Appears ~2 weeks after exposure and persists for life.
• **Complete Blood Count (CBC)**:
    ◦ **Aplastic Crisis**: Severe normocytic anemia, **reticulocytopenia (<0.5%)** is the hallmark finding. Leukocytes and platelets are usually normal.
    ◦ **Fifth Disease/Healthy Adult**: May show mild anemia, lymphopenia, or be entirely normal.
• **PCR for Parvovirus B19 DNA**:
    ◦ Used to diagnose infection in **immunocompromised patients** who may fail to mount an antibody response.
    ◦ Used to confirm fetal infection via amniotic fluid or cordocentesis.
sections.treatment:
• **Erythema Infectiosum / Arthropathy**:
    ◦ **Supportive care**: Treatment is symptomatic.
    ◦ **NSAIDs** for arthralgias and fever.
    ◦ Reassurance; the condition is self-limiting.
• **Transient Aplastic Crisis**:
    ◦ **Admission to hospital**.
    ◦ **Packed Red Blood Cell (PRBC) transfusion** is the mainstay of treatment.
    ◦ Place patient on **droplet precautions** as they are viremic and contagious.
• **Chronic Anemia (Immunocompromised)**:
    ◦ **Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG)**: Provides neutralizing antibodies to clear the persistent infection.
• **Hydrops Fetalis**:
    ◦ Requires management by Maternal-Fetal Medicine (MFM).
    ◦ May require **intrauterine blood transfusion**.
sections.management:
• **Infection Control**:
    ◦ Patients with Fifth Disease are contagious *before* the rash appears. By the time the rash is visible, they are generally no longer infectious.
    ◦ Patients in aplastic crisis *are* contagious and require droplet precautions.
• **Pregnant Women**:
    ◦ If a non-immune pregnant woman is exposed, her serology (IgM and IgG) should be checked.
    ◦ If acute infection is confirmed, she requires **serial fetal ultrasounds** to monitor for signs of anemia and hydrops fetalis.
sections.complications:
• **Hydrops Fetalis**: Severe fetal anemia, heart failure, edema, and potential fetal demise. Risk is highest with infection during the **second trimester**.
• **Transient Aplastic Crisis**: Life-threatening anemia in at-risk individuals.
• **Chronic Red Cell Aplasia**: Persistent anemia in immunocompromised hosts.
• **Rare**: Myocarditis, hepatitis, papular-purpuric "gloves and socks" syndrome.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for immunocompetent children and adults. The rash and arthritis resolve completely without sequelae.
• **Good** for transient aplastic crisis if identified and treated promptly with transfusion.
• **Variable** for fetal infection. The overall risk of fetal loss after maternal infection is ~5-10%, but prognosis improves significantly with early detection and intrauterine transfusion.
sections.preventionEducation:
• Inform parents that Fifth Disease is a mild, self-limited illness.
• Educate patients with hemolytic anemias about the signs of aplastic crisis (sudden pallor, fatigue) and to seek immediate medical attention.

sections.overview:
• Malaria is a life-threatening, mosquito-borne infectious disease caused by protozoan parasites of the genus *Plasmodium*.
• It is characterized by cyclical fevers, chills, sweats, and hemolysis.
• ***Plasmodium falciparum*** is the most virulent species and is responsible for the majority of severe disease and deaths.
• The disease is a major public health problem in tropical and subtropical regions worldwide.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• **Geographic Distribution**: Predominantly in tropical and subtropical regions.
    ◦ The highest burden is in sub-Saharan Africa (>90% of cases), with other significant areas including Southeast Asia, the Eastern Mediterranean, and the Americas.
• **Population**: Young children (<5 years), pregnant women, and non-immune travelers are at the highest risk for severe disease and death.
• **In the US**: Malaria is primarily seen in travelers, immigrants, or military personnel returning from endemic areas.
sections.riskFactors:
• Travel to or residence in a malaria-endemic region.
• Lack of or non-adherence to malaria chemoprophylaxis.
• Nighttime exposure in endemic areas (since *Anopheles* mosquitoes are nocturnal feeders).
• Pregnancy.
• Immunocompromised status (e.g., HIV).
• Asplenia (functional or anatomic).
• Children under 5 years of age in endemic regions.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a **malarial paroxysm**: a cyclical pattern of symptoms lasting 6-10 hours.
    ◦ **Cold Stage**: Intense chills and rigors.
    ◦ **Hot Stage**: High fever (40-41°C / 104-106°F), headache, vomiting.
    ◦ **Sweating Stage**: Profuse diaphoresis, resolution of fever, exhaustion.
• **Fever Patterns** (Classic, but often not seen early in infection):
    ◦ **Tertian Fever** (every 48 hours): *P. vivax, P. ovale, P. falciparum*.
    ◦ **Quartan Fever** (every 72 hours): *P. malariae*.
    ◦ ***P. falciparum*** infection often presents with a less regular, continuous, or daily fever pattern initially.
• Any fever in a returned traveler from an endemic area should be considered malaria until proven otherwise.
• **Associated Symptoms**:
    ◦ **Core Symptoms**: Fever, chills, sweats.
    ◦ **Constitutional**: Headache, profound malaise, fatigue.
    ◦ **Musculoskeletal**: Myalgias, arthralgias.
    ◦ **GI**: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain.
    ◦ **Respiratory**: Cough, chest pain.
sections.physicalExam:
• **General**: Fever, pallor (due to anemia), jaundice (due to hemolysis).
• **Abdomen**: **Splenomegaly** is a common finding. Hepatomegaly may also be present.
• **Signs of Severe Malaria (*P. falciparum*)**:
    ◦ **Neurologic**: Altered mental status, confusion, seizures, coma (**cerebral malaria**).
    ◦ **Respiratory**: Tachypnea, signs of pulmonary edema/ARDS.
    ◦ **Cardiovascular**: Tachycardia, hypotension, signs of shock.
    ◦ **Renal**: Oliguria, dark urine (hemoglobinuria).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Gold Standard: Light Microscopy**
    ◦ **Thick Blood Smear**: More sensitive. Used to detect the *presence* of parasites. A negative thick smear makes malaria unlikely.
    ◦ **Thin Blood Smear**: Less sensitive. Used for *species identification* and to calculate **parasitemia** (% of infected RBCs), which is crucial for prognosis and management decisions.
    ◦ *Specific findings*:
        ▪ *P. falciparum*: Ring forms, appliqué forms (rings at periphery of RBC), multiple rings in one RBC, banana-shaped gametocytes.
• **Rapid Diagnostic Tests (RDTs)**
    ◦ Antigen-detection immunoassays (e.g., BinaxNOWTM).
    ◦ Detect parasite antigens like HRP-2 (*P. falciparum* specific) and pLDH (pan-specific).
    ◦ Useful in settings without microscopy but should be confirmed with a smear. False negatives can occur at very low or very high parasitemia.
• **Supportive Laboratory Findings**:
    ◦ **CBC**: Normocytic, normochromic anemia; **thrombocytopenia** is very common; leukocyte count can be low, normal, or high.
    ◦ **CMP**: Elevated indirect bilirubin, elevated LFTs, elevated creatinine (in AKI).
    ◦ **LDH**: Elevated due to hemolysis.
    ◦ **Glucose**: Hypoglycemia can occur, especially in severe disease.
sections.management:
• **Admission criteria**: All patients with severe malaria, *P. falciparum* infection (especially non-immune travelers), children, pregnant women, or those unable to tolerate oral medication.
• **Monitoring**: Daily blood smears to monitor for decreasing parasitemia, CBC, renal and liver function tests, glucose.
sections.complications:
• **Cerebral Malaria**: Unarousable coma, seizures. Highest mortality rate.
• **Severe Anemia**: From massive RBC destruction and bone marrow suppression.
• **Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)**: Non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema.
• **Acute Kidney Injury (AKI)**: **"Blackwater Fever"** - massive intravascular hemolysis leads to hemoglobinuria, dark urine, and renal failure.
• **Metabolic Acidosis**: Often lactic acidosis from tissue hypoxia.
• **Hypoglycemia**: Increased glucose consumption by parasites and host.
• **Circulatory Collapse / Shock**.
• **Splenic Rupture** (rare).
sections.prognosis:
• **Uncomplicated Malaria**: Excellent if diagnosed and treated promptly and correctly.
• **Severe Malaria**: Mortality remains high (10-20%) even with optimal treatment. Neurologic deficits can persist in survivors of cerebral malaria.
sections.preventionEducation:
• **Prevention (The "ABCDs")**:
    ◦ **A**wareness of risk in travel destination.
    ◦ **B**ite prevention: Insect repellents (DEET), permethrin-treated clothing, insecticide-treated bed nets (ITNs), staying indoors from dusk to dawn.
    ◦ **C**hemoprophylaxis: Based on destination. Common options include Atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone), Doxycycline, and Mefloquine.
    ◦ **D**iagnosis: Seek prompt medical evaluation for any fever post-travel.

sections.overview:
• Toxoplasmosis is a systemic parasitic disease caused by the obligate intracellular protozoan **_Toxoplasma gondii_**.
◦ While infection is often asymptomatic in immunocompetent individuals, it can cause severe and life-threatening disease in **immunocompromised hosts** (especially those with **HIV/AIDS**) and in the developing fetus through **congenital transmission**.
◦ It is a major cause of **focal brain lesions** in AIDS patients and is a component of the **TORCH** congenital infections.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**: **_Toxoplasma gondii_**, a protozoan parasite.
• **Definitive Host**: **Felines** (domestic cats and their relatives) are the only hosts where the parasite can complete its sexual reproductive cycle.
• **Intermediate Hosts**: Humans, birds, and other mammals.
• **Life Cycle & Forms**:
    ◦ **Oocysts**: Shed in cat feces. Become infectious after sporulating in the environment (1-5 days).
    ◦ **Tachyzoites**: The rapidly multiplying form responsible for acute infection and tissue destruction. This form crosses the placenta.
    ◦ **Bradyzoites**: A slow-growing, dormant form that encysts in host tissues (brain, muscle, eye). Responsible for latent infection and reactivation.
• **Pathogenesis**:
    ◦ **Transmission**: Humans are infected primarily via three routes:
        ▪ **Foodborne**: Ingesting tissue cysts (bradyzoites) in undercooked or raw meat (especially pork, lamb, venison).
        ▪ **Zoonotic**: Ingesting oocysts from sources contaminated with cat feces (e.g., unwashed vegetables, contaminated water, cleaning a litter box).
        ▪ **Congenital (Transplacental)**: A pregnant woman with a **primary** infection passes tachyzoites to the fetus.
    ◦ **Infection**: After ingestion, the cysts/oocysts release parasites that transform into tachyzoites. They invade host cells, replicate, and spread hematogenously throughout the body.
    ◦ **Immune Response**: In an immunocompetent host, the immune system controls the tachyzoite proliferation, leading to the formation of dormant tissue cysts (bradyzoites), resulting in a latent, lifelong infection.
    ◦ **Reactivation**: In an **immunocompromised host** (e.g., AIDS, transplant recipient), the dormant bradyzoites can reactivate, transform back into tachyzoites, and cause severe, disseminated disease, most commonly affecting the brain (**toxoplasmic encephalitis**).
sections.epidemiology:
• One of the most common human infections worldwide; approximately one-third of the global population is estimated to be seropositive.
• In the United States, prevalence is ~11%.
• Toxoplasmic encephalitis is a major **AIDS-defining illness**, typically occurring in patients with a **CD4 count < 100 cells/L** who are not on appropriate prophylaxis.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Immunocompromised state**: HIV/AIDS (**CD4 < 100**), organ transplant recipients, patients on chemotherapy or high-dose corticosteroids.
• **Pregnancy**: Primary infection during gestation poses a risk for congenital transmission.
• **Dietary**: Consumption of raw or undercooked meat.
• **Environmental**:
    ◦ Owning a cat (especially one that hunts outdoors).
    ◦ Cleaning cat litter boxes.
    ◦ Gardening or playing in soil/sandboxes contaminated with cat feces.
    ◦ Drinking contaminated, untreated water.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The clinical syndrome depends on the host's immune status.
• **Immunocompetent Host**:
    ◦ >80% are asymptomatic.
    ◦ Symptomatic cases present as a mild, self-limited, **mononucleosis-like illness**.
    ◦ Symptoms: Fever, malaise, headache, sore throat, myalgias, symmetrical non-tender **lymphadenopathy** (especially posterior cervical).
• **Immunocompromised Host (Toxoplasmic Encephalitis)**:
    ◦ Most common presentation is a subacute onset of **focal neurological deficits**.
    ◦ Presents as encephalitis with headache, altered mental status, fever, and seizures.
    ◦ Symptoms: **Headache** (most common), confusion, lethargy, fever, focal weakness/hemiparesis, sensory loss, seizures, cranial nerve palsies, ataxia.
• **Congenital Toxoplasmosis**:
    ◦ Spectrum of disease severity. Many infants are asymptomatic at birth but develop symptoms later.
    ◦ **Classic Triad**:
        ▪ **Chorioretinitis** (most common late finding)
        ▪ **Hydrocephalus**
        ▪ **Intracranial Calcifications** (diffuse)
    ◦ The risk of transmission increases with gestational age, but the severity of fetal disease is greatest with infection in the first trimester.
    ◦ Symptoms at birth: May have jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, rash, microcephaly or macrocephaly (from hydrocephalus). Later in life, may develop vision loss, hearing loss, or developmental delays.
• **Ocular Toxoplasmosis**:
    ◦ Most common cause of infectious **posterior uveitis**.
    ◦ Typically results from reactivation of a congenital infection.
    ◦ Symptoms: Unilateral blurred vision, **floaters**, scotoma, photophobia, and eye pain.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Immunocompetent**:
    ◦ **Lymphadenopathy**: Bilateral, symmetric, non-tender, particularly involving the posterior cervical chain.
• **Cerebral (Immunocompromised)**:
    ◦ **Fever**
    ◦ **Altered Mental Status**: Ranging from lethargy to coma.
    ◦ **Focal Neurologic Deficits**: Hemiparesis, aphasia, ataxia, cranial nerve palsies.
• **Ocular**:
    ◦ **Fundoscopy**: **Necrotizing retinochoroiditis**. Classic finding is a fluffy, yellow-white lesion with indistinct borders (**"headlights in the fog"**) due to overlying vitritis. Healed lesions appear as pigmented scars.
• **Congenital**:
    ◦ Microcephaly or macrocephaly
    ◦ Hepatosplenomegaly
    ◦ Jaundice
    ◦ Petechial or purpuric rash (**"blueberry muffin" rash**)
sections.diagnostics:
• **Serology**:
    ◦ **IgG**: Indicates past or chronic infection. A positive IgG in an immunocompromised patient with consistent symptoms is highly suggestive.
    ◦ **IgM**: Indicates acute or recent infection (within the last year). Essential for diagnosing primary infection in pregnant women.
    ◦ **IgG Avidity Test**: Helps distinguish recent (<4 months) from past infection in pregnant women. High avidity suggests an older infection, making congenital transmission less likely.
• **Imaging (Cerebral Toxoplasmosis)**:
    ◦ **Brain MRI with contrast (preferred)** or CT with contrast:
        ▪ **Characteristic finding**: **Multiple, bilateral, ring-enhancing lesions**, often located in the **basal ganglia** and **corticomedullary junction**.
        ▪ A single lesion is less common and raises suspicion for **CNS Lymphoma**.
• **Lumbar Puncture & CSF Analysis**:
    ◦ Performed if diagnosis is uncertain.
    ◦ CSF may show mild pleocytosis and elevated protein.
    ◦ **CSF PCR for _T. gondii_ DNA**: High specificity but moderate sensitivity. A positive result is diagnostic, but a negative result does not rule out disease.
• **Definitive Diagnosis**:
    ◦ **Brain Biopsy**: Gold standard for cerebral toxoplasmosis but is invasive. Reserved for patients who fail to respond to empiric therapy, to differentiate from **CNS lymphoma**. Histology shows tachyzoites at the periphery of necrotic lesions.
sections.treatment:
• **Immunocompetent (symptomatic)**: Usually self-limiting. If severe/persistent, treat with the regimen below for 2-4 weeks.
• **Cerebral / Disseminated / Ocular Disease**:
    ◦ **First-line Therapy (Acute Phase)**: Combination of **Pyrimethamine + Sulfadiazine + Leucovorin**.
    ◦ **Leucovorin (folinic acid)** is essential to prevent the bone marrow suppression (thrombocytopenia, neutropenia) caused by pyrimethamine, a folate antagonist.
    ◦ **Alternative**: Pyrimethamine + Clindamycin + Leucovorin (for patients with sulfa allergy).
• **Pregnant Women (Primary Infection)**:
    ◦ **<18 weeks gestation**: **Spiramycin** (macrolide antibiotic) to prevent fetal transmission.
    ◦ **≥18 weeks gestation or confirmed fetal infection**: **Pyrimethamine + Sulfadiazine + Leucovorin**. (Pyrimethamine is teratogenic and avoided in the 1st trimester).
• **Congenital Infection (in the newborn)**: Treat infant for 1 year with Pyrimethamine + Sulfadiazine + Leucovorin.
sections.management:
• **Prophylaxis in HIV**:
    ◦ **Indication**: Seropositive (*Toxo* IgG+) patients with **CD4 count < 100 cells/L**.
    ◦ **Primary Prophylaxis Drug**: **Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX, Bactrim)**, one DS tablet daily.
    ◦ **Discontinuation**: May be stopped when CD4 count is >200 cells/L for >3 months on ART.
• **Maintenance Therapy (Secondary Prophylaxis)**:
    ◦ After completing acute treatment for toxoplasmic encephalitis, patients must receive lifelong suppressive therapy (e.g., lower dose Pyrimethamine + Sulfadiazine + Leucovorin) unless immune reconstitution occurs (CD4 > 200 for >6 months).
sections.complications:
• **Neurologic**: Permanent deficits (cognitive impairment, seizures, motor deficits) after toxoplasmic encephalitis.
• **Ocular**: Vision loss, blindness.
• **Congenital**: Intellectual disability, seizures, deafness, blindness, death.
• **Disseminated Disease (rare)**: Pneumonitis, myocarditis, hepatitis.
sections.prognosis:
• **Immunocompetent**: Excellent, typically a full recovery.
• **Toxoplasmic Encephalitis**: With treatment, clinical improvement is seen in >90% of patients within 14 days. However, mortality remains significant, and relapse is common without maintenance therapy.
• **Congenital**: Highly variable. Severe neonatal disease has a poor prognosis. Infants asymptomatic at birth are at risk for long-term sequelae without treatment.
sections.preventionEducation:
• Cook meat to safe temperatures (e.g., 165°F / 74°C).
• Wash hands, cutting boards, and utensils thoroughly after contact with raw meat.
• Pregnant and immunocompromised individuals should **avoid cleaning cat litter boxes**. If unavoidable, wear gloves and a mask, and clean the box daily.
• Wear gloves when gardening.
• Wash all fruits and vegetables.

sections.overview:
• Giardiasis is a common gastrointestinal infection caused by the flagellated protozoan parasite ***Giardia lamblia*** (also known as *G. intestinalis* or *G. duodenalis*).
• It is a leading cause of **waterborne diarrheal disease** worldwide.
• Transmission occurs via the **fecal-oral route**, typically through ingestion of contaminated water or food, or by person-to-person contact.
• The hallmark of the disease is acute or chronic **non-bloody, malabsorptive diarrhea** characterized by **steatorrhea** (fatty, greasy, foul-smelling stools).
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**: ***Giardia lamblia***, a protozoan parasite.
• **Life Cycle**:
    ◦ **Infection**: Ingestion of dormant, environmentally resistant **cysts**.
        ▪ Cysts are the infective stage and are resistant to chlorination.
    ◦ **Excystation**: In the acidic environment of the stomach and duodenum, the cysts transform into motile, flagellated **trophozoites**.
    ◦ **Replication**: Trophozoites are the active, pathogenic stage.
        ▪ They attach to the mucosal surface of the duodenum and jejunum via a ventral sucking disk.
        ▪ They do **not** invade the intestinal wall.
    ◦ **Pathology**: Attachment of trophozoites leads to epithelial damage, **villous atrophy/blunting**, and crypt hyperplasia.
        ▪ This disrupts the absorptive capacity of the small intestine, causing malabsorption of fats and carbohydrates.
    ◦ **Encystation**: As trophozoites pass into the colon, they revert to the cyst form.
    ◦ **Excretion**: Cysts are passed in the feces, completing the cycle.
        ▪ Shedding can be intermittent.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: The **most common intestinal protozoal infection** in the United States and worldwide.
• **Transmission**: **Fecal-oral route**.
    ◦ **Waterborne**: Most common source.
        ▪ Contaminated streams, lakes, wells, and municipal water supplies.
        ▪ Classic scenario involves **hikers/campers** drinking untreated surface water.
    ◦ **Person-to-person**: High-risk in **daycare centers** and institutional settings due to poor hygiene.
    ◦ **Foodborne**: Less common, but occurs when food is contaminated by an infected handler.
sections.riskFactors:
• Drinking untreated water from lakes, streams, or wells (**"beaver fever"**).
• Travel to endemic areas (e.g., developing countries, parts of Russia).
• Children attending **daycare centers** (and their household contacts).
• Immunocompromised states, particularly **IgA deficiency** and hypogammaglobulinemia.
• Oral-anal sexual contact.
• Poor sanitation and hygiene.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Incubation Period**: 1 to 3 weeks (average 7-10 days).
• **Spectrum of Illness**:
    ◦ **Asymptomatic Carrier**: Common (~50% of cases).
    ◦ **Acute Giardiasis**: Sudden onset of symptoms lasting 1-3 weeks.
    ◦ **Chronic Giardiasis**: Symptoms can be continuous or intermittent, lasting for months.
        ▪ This form is more associated with significant **malabsorption** and **weight loss**.
• **Hallmark Symptom**: Diarrhea that is characteristically:
    ◦ Profuse and watery initially.
    ◦ Progresses to **greasy, frothy, foul-smelling stools (steatorrhea)**.
    ◦ **Non-bloody** (as there is no tissue invasion).
• **Other Common Symptoms**:
    ◦ Malaise, fatigue.
    ◦ Abdominal cramps and bloating.
    ◦ **Excessive flatulence** and **sulfurous ("rotten egg") burps/belching**.
    ◦ Nausea (vomiting is less common).
    ◦ Anorexia and significant **weight loss** (especially in chronic cases).
• **Fever**: Is uncommon or low-grade.
sections.physicalExam:
• The physical exam is often unremarkable.
• **Abdomen**: May have mild, diffuse tenderness or distention. Bowel sounds may be hyperactive.
• **General**:
    ◦ Signs of **dehydration** (tachycardia, dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor) in acute, severe cases.
    ◦ Evidence of **weight loss** or malnutrition in chronic infections.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Stool Studies (Primary Method)**:
    ◦ **Stool Antigen Assay (EIA, DFA)**: **Test of choice**.
        ▪ Highly sensitive (>90%) and specific.
        ▪ Rapid results.
    ◦ **Stool Ova & Parasites (O&P) Microscopy**:
        ▪ Classic test but less sensitive than antigen assays.
        ▪ Requires examination of **3 separate stool samples** collected over several days because cyst shedding is intermittent.
        ▪ Can identify both **cysts** and motile **trophozoites** (trophozoites are typically only seen in fresh, liquid stool).
• **Less Common Methods**:
    ◦ **Duodenal Aspiration / Biopsy**: Invasive and rarely needed.
        ▪ Used in difficult cases where stool studies are negative but suspicion is high.
        ▪ Biopsy shows **villous atrophy**.
    ◦ **String Test (Entero-Test)**: Involves swallowing a weighted gelatin capsule attached to a string to sample duodenal contents.
        ▪ Rarely used today.
sections.treatment:
• **First-Line Agents**:
    ◦ **Tinidazole**: 2 g PO single dose. Often preferred due to single-dose regimen and better side effect profile.
    ◦ **Metronidazole**: 250 mg PO TID for 5-7 days. Effective but has more side effects (metallic taste, nausea) and requires multiple doses. **Must advise patient to avoid alcohol due to disulfiram-like reaction**.
    ◦ **Nitazoxanide**: 500 mg PO BID for 3 days. Broad-spectrum anti-parasitic; good option, especially for children (available as a suspension).
• **Special Populations**:
    ◦ **Pregnancy**: Treatment often deferred until after the first trimester. If severe, **Paromomycin** (a non-absorbable aminoglycoside) is the preferred agent.
    ◦ **Asymptomatic Carriers**: Treatment is generally not recommended unless they are in high-risk settings (e.g., food handlers, daycare workers) to prevent spread.
sections.management:
• **Supportive Care**:
    ◦ **Rehydration**: Oral or IV fluids are crucial, especially in acute diarrhea.
    ◦ Dietary management is typically not necessary, but avoiding lactose may help temporarily.
• **Follow-up**: Test-of-cure is not routinely indicated unless symptoms persist or recur.
sections.complications:
• **Dehydration** and electrolyte imbalance.
• **Chronic malabsorption** leading to significant weight loss, vitamin deficiencies (fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, K), and failure to thrive in children.
• **Post-infectious lactose intolerance**: Temporary condition due to damage to the intestinal brush border. Can persist for weeks to months after infection resolves.
• **Post-infectious IBS**: Some patients develop IBS-like symptoms after the infection has cleared.
• **Reactive arthritis** (rare).
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent for most immunocompetent patients who receive treatment.
• Symptoms typically resolve within a few days of starting appropriate therapy.
• Infections can be more severe and difficult to eradicate in individuals with **IgA deficiency** or other immune defects.
sections.preventionEducation:
• Practice good **hand hygiene**, especially after using the toilet and before handling food.
• Avoid drinking untreated water from natural sources.
• When hiking/camping, purify water by **boiling for at least 1 minute** or using a filter with a pore size of **<1 micron**.
    ▪ Chemical disinfection with iodine can be less reliable against *Giardia* cysts.
• Avoid swallowing water while swimming in pools, lakes, or rivers.

sections.overview:
• Infection caused by the protozoan parasite **_Entamoeba histolytica_**.
    ◦ Primarily acquired through the **fecal-oral route** by ingesting cysts from contaminated food or water.
    ◦ The clinical spectrum ranges from **asymptomatic carriage** (most common) to invasive disease.
        ▪ **Intestinal Amebiasis** (amebic colitis/dysentery).
        ▪ **Extraintestinal Amebiasis**, most notably **amebic liver abscess**.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent:** **_Entamoeba histolytica_**, a protozoan parasite.
    ◦ It is important to distinguish it from the morphologically identical but non-pathogenic **_Entamoeba dispar_**.
• **Transmission:** **Fecal-oral route**.
• **Lifecycle & Pathogenesis:**
    ◦ **Ingestion:** Humans ingest the environmentally resistant, quadrinucleate **cysts** (infective stage).
    ◦ **Excystation:** Cysts pass through the stomach and excyst in the small intestine, releasing **trophozoites**.
    ◦ **Colonization:** Trophozoites colonize the large intestine.
        ▪ **Non-invasive:** In most cases (>90%), trophozoites remain in the intestinal lumen, feed on bacteria, and form new cysts. These individuals become asymptomatic carriers who pass infectious cysts in their feces.
        ▪ **Invasive:** In a minority of cases, trophozoites adhere to and invade the colonic epithelium. They release cytotoxic substances (amoebapores, cysteine proteases) that cause cell lysis and tissue necrosis.
    ◦ **Ulceration:** This invasion leads to the formation of classic **"flask-shaped" ulcers** in the colonic mucosa, which are deep with a narrow neck and wide base.
    ◦ **Hematogenous Spread:** Trophozoites can penetrate blood vessels and travel via the portal circulation to the liver, causing an **amebic liver abscess**.
        ▪ Less commonly, they can spread to the lungs, brain, or skin.
    ◦ **Encystation:** In the colon, trophozoites revert to the cyst form, which are then passed in the stool, continuing the cycle.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Global Burden:** A major cause of parasitic morbidity and mortality worldwide, with an estimated 50 million cases of invasive disease and 100,000 deaths annually.
• **Geographic Distribution:** Prevalent in developing countries with poor sanitation, particularly in Mexico, Central and South America, tropical Asia, and Africa.
• **In the US:** Primarily seen in travelers to endemic regions, immigrants, and individuals in institutionalized settings.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation varies based on the site and severity of infection.
• **Asymptomatic Infection (90%):**
    ◦ Patient is a **"cyst passer"** with no symptoms. This is the most common presentation.
• **Intestinal Amebiasis (Amebic Colitis):**
    ◦ Gradual onset (1-3 weeks) of symptoms ranging from mild to severe.
    ◦ **Amebic Dysentery:** A severe form of intestinal amebiasis characterized by **bloody diarrhea**.
• **Extraintestinal Amebiasis:**
    ◦ Occurs when trophozoites spread beyond the colon.
    ◦ **Amebic Liver Abscess:** The most common form of extraintestinal disease.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Intestinal Amebiasis**
    ◦ **Primary Lab Tests**
        ▪ **Stool Antigen Detection (EIA) or PCR:** **Test of choice**. High sensitivity/specificity; distinguishes **_E. histolytica_** from **_E. dispar_**.
    ◦ **Imaging**
        ▪ Not routinely used.
        ▪ Colonoscopy may show **flask-shaped ulcers** but carries a risk of perforation and is generally avoided.
    ◦ **Other Tests**
        ▪ **Stool O&P (Ova & Parasites):** Can identify cysts or trophozoites. **Trophozoites containing ingested RBCs (erythrophagocytosis)** are pathognomonic. Low sensitivity; requires 3+ samples.
    ◦ **Supportive Lab Findings**
        ▪ Leukocytosis may be present.
• **Amebic Liver Abscess**
    ◦ **Primary Lab Tests**
        ▪ **Serology (Antibody Test, e.g., ELISA):** **Test of choice**. Highly sensitive (>95%) for extraintestinal disease. Titers become positive ~7-10 days into illness.
    ◦ **Imaging**
        ▪ **Abdominal Ultrasound:** Best initial imaging test. Shows a single, round, hypoechoic, well-defined lesion, typically in the **posterior-superior aspect of the right lobe**.
        ▪ **CT/MRI:** Provides more detail. Shows a well-demarcated, round lesion with a peripheral enhancing rim (**"rim enhancement"**).
    ◦ **Other Tests**
        ▪ **Abscess Aspiration:** NOT for routine diagnosis. Done if diagnosis is uncertain, no response to therapy, or high risk of rupture.
        ▪ Fluid is typically thick, reddish-brown, and odorless (**"anchovy paste"**). Microscopy of fluid is often negative.
    ◦ **Supportive Lab Findings**
        ▪ **Leukocytosis (without eosinophilia)**, elevated Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP), elevated ESR/CRP, mild anemia.
sections.prognosis:
• **Uncomplicated Amebiasis:** Excellent with appropriate treatment.
• **Amebic Liver Abscess:** Mortality is very low (<1%) with timely medical therapy.
• **Complicated Disease:** Prognosis worsens significantly with complications like perforation, toxic megacolon, or abscess rupture (especially into the pericardium, which carries high mortality).

sections.overview:
• Intestinal infection caused by parasitic nematodes (roundworms), a major type of **soil-transmitted helminth (STH)** infection.
• The primary pathology is caused by chronic intestinal blood loss, leading to **iron deficiency anemia**.
• The two main species infecting humans are:
    ◦ *Necator americanus*
    ◦ *Ancylostoma duodenale*
• Infection occurs when **filariform larvae** from contaminated soil penetrate intact skin.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• Primarily found in **tropical and subtropical regions** with poor sanitation.
• Highest prevalence in Sub-Saharan Africa, Southeast Asia, China, and Latin America.
• Transmitted via contact with soil contaminated with human feces containing hookworm larvae.
    ◦ It is **not** spread directly from person to person.
• **Children** and **pregnant women** are most vulnerable to the consequences of anemia.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Clinical presentation depends on the **worm burden** and the host's nutritional status; light infections are often asymptomatic.
• **Acute Phase (Larval Migration):**
    ◦ **Dermal:** Localized, pruritic, papulovesicular rash at the site of skin penetration (**"ground itch"**), usually on the feet. Lasts a few days.
    ◦ **Pulmonary:** Transient, dry cough, wheezing, and low-grade fever as larvae migrate through the lungs (**Loeffler-like syndrome**). Often mild and unrecognized.
• **Chronic Phase (Intestinal Infection):**
    ◦ This is the most common presentation, dominated by symptoms of **iron deficiency anemia** and malnutrition.
    ◦ The onset is insidious, developing over months to years.
    ◦ Patients present with **fatigue**, **weakness**, and **decreased exercise tolerance**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Stool Examination (Ova & Parasites):**
    ◦ **Definitive diagnosis** through microscopic identification of hookworm eggs in a stool sample.
    ◦ Quantitative methods (e.g., Kato-Katz) can estimate worm burden based on eggs per gram of feces.
    ◦ Note: The eggs of *N. americanus* and *A. duodenale* are morphologically indistinguishable.
• **Complete Blood Count (CBC):**
    ◦ **Microcytic, hypochromic anemia:**
        ▪ Low Hemoglobin/Hematocrit
        ▪ Low **MCV (<80 fL)**
        ▪ Low MCHC
    ◦ **Eosinophilia:**
        ▪ A key clue, especially in early or acute infection.
        ▪ May be less prominent in chronic infection.
• **Iron Studies:**
    ◦ Shows classic iron deficiency picture:
        ▪ **Low serum ferritin**
        ▪ Low serum iron
        ▪ **High TIBC** (Total Iron Binding Capacity)
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** with appropriate anthelmintic and iron therapy.
• Anemia and other nutritional deficiencies are fully reversible.
• The main challenge is the high rate of **re-infection** in endemic areas if sanitation and hygiene are not improved.

sections.overview:
• Enterobiasis, commonly known as **pinworm infection**, is the **most common helminthic infection** in the United States and Western Europe.
    ◦ Caused by the nematode *Enterobius vermicularis*.
    ◦ Characterized by **intense perianal pruritus**, especially at night.
    ◦ Primarily affects **school-aged children**.
    ◦ Spread via **fecal-oral transmission** and is common within households and institutions.
    ◦ Diagnosis is typically made with the **"tape test."**
    ◦ Treatment with antihelminthic medication is highly effective, though **reinfection is common**.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Organism:** *Enterobius vermicularis*, a human-specific intestinal nematode (roundworm).
• **Life Cycle & Pathophysiology:**
    ◦ **Ingestion:** Humans ingest infective pinworm eggs via contaminated hands, food, water, or fomites (e.g., bedding, clothing, toys).
    ◦ **Hatching:** Eggs hatch in the small intestine (duodenum), releasing larvae.
    ◦ **Maturation:** Larvae migrate to the cecum, appendix, and ascending colon, where they mature into adult worms over 2-6 weeks.
    ◦ **Migration:** After mating, the gravid female migrates to the perianal region, **typically at night**.
    ◦ **Oviposition (Egg Laying):** The female worm emerges from the anus and deposits thousands of microscopic, sticky eggs on the perianal skin, causing **intense pruritus**.
    ◦ **Autoinfection & Transmission:**
        ▪ The eggs become infective within 4-6 hours.
        ▪ **Autoinfection:** Scratching the perianal area contaminates the fingers and fingernails with eggs, which are then transferred back to the mouth.
        ▪ **Transmission:** Eggs are shed onto surfaces where they can survive for 2-3 weeks and be ingested by others.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** Most common helminthic infection in the United States.
• **Most Affected Population:** **School-aged children (5-10 years old)**.
• **Settings:** Prevalent in crowded environments such as daycare centers, schools, and institutional facilities.
• **Geography:** Worldwide distribution, more common in temperate climates.
• **Transmission:** Humans are the only natural host; transmission is strictly **person-to-person** via the **fecal-oral route**.
sections.riskFactors:
• Age 5-10 years
• Overcrowded living conditions (e.g., institutionalization, large families)
• Poor personal hygiene (especially inadequate handwashing)
• Nail-biting (**onychophagia**)
• Having an infected family member or classmate
• Not changing underwear daily
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Hallmark Symptom:** **Nocturnal perianal pruritus** (intense anal itching that is worse at night).
    ◦ Leads to restlessness, irritability, and **insomnia**.
    ◦ Parent may report seeing **"small white worms"** in the perianal region at night or on the surface of the stool.
• **Associated Symptoms:**
    ◦ **Enuresis** (bedwetting) may be associated with the infection.
    ◦ In females, worms can migrate to the genital area, causing **vulvovaginitis** with pruritus and vaginal discharge.
    ◦ Nonspecific, mild abdominal pain or nausea (uncommon).
• **Many individuals are asymptomatic carriers.**
sections.physicalExam:
• The physical exam is often unremarkable.
• **Perianal region:** May show erythema, inflammation, and **linear excoriations** from intense scratching.
• **Visualization of worms:** Occasionally, adult female worms (small, white, thread-like, ~1 cm long) may be seen in the perianal folds.
• **Females:** Possible signs of **vulvovaginitis**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primary Diagnostic Test: "Scotch Tape Test" / Cellophane Tape Test**
    ◦ **Procedure:** A piece of clear adhesive tape is pressed firmly against the perianal skin, then placed adhesive-side down onto a glass microscope slide.
    ◦ **Timing:** The test should be performed **first thing in the morning**, before bathing or a bowel movement.
        ▪ Sensitivity is increased by performing the test on **3 consecutive mornings** (>90% sensitivity vs. ~50% for a single test).
    ◦ **Microscopy:** Microscopic examination of the tape reveals characteristic pinworm eggs.
