        ▪ **Egg Morphology:** **Plano-convex (oval with one flattened side), described as "D-shaped."**
• **Other Tests (Low Yield):**
    ◦ **Stool for Ova & Parasites (O&P):** **Not recommended** as eggs are deposited on the perianal skin, not passed in the feces.
    ◦ **CBC:** Eosinophilia is typically **absent or mild**.
    ◦ **"Flashlight Test":** Visual inspection of the perianal area 2-3 hours after the child has fallen asleep may reveal motile adult female worms.
sections.treatment:
• **Pharmacologic Therapy:**
    ◦ **Albendazole:** 400 mg PO single dose.
    ◦ **Mebendazole:** 100 mg PO single dose.
    ◦ **Pyrantel Pamoate:** 11 mg/kg (max 1 g) PO single dose. Available over-the-counter.
• **Crucial Dosing Schedule:**
    ◦ The single dose should be **repeated in 2 weeks**.
    ◦ **Rationale:** The first dose kills adult worms, but not eggs. The second dose kills newly hatched worms.
• **Who to Treat:**
    ◦ **Treat the patient and ALL household members/close contacts simultaneously**, regardless of symptoms, to prevent reinfection.
sections.management:
• **Patient Education is Key to Preventing Reinfection:**
    ◦ **Hygiene Measures:**
        ▪ **Strict handwashing:** Emphasize washing with soap and water after using the toilet, before meals, and upon waking.
        ▪ **Fingernails:** Keep fingernails trimmed short and clean. Discourage nail-biting.
        ▪ **Bathing:** Encourage daily morning showers or baths to wash away eggs deposited overnight.
    ◦ **Clothing/Bedding:**
        ▪ On the morning after the first dose of medication, **wash all bedding, towels, and pajamas in hot water** and dry on a hot setting.
    ◦ **Environmental Cleaning:**
        ▪ Regular cleaning and vacuuming of the house, especially the bedroom, can help remove environmental eggs.
sections.complications:
• Complications are **rare** and the infection is generally benign.
• **Secondary bacterial skin infection** (e.g., cellulitis, pyoderma) from excoriations due to intense scratching.
• **Female Genitourinary Tract:** Aberrant migration of worms can lead to **vulvovaginitis**, endometritis, salpingitis, and pelvic inflammatory disease.
• **Appendicitis:** Rarely, a bolus of pinworms can obstruct the appendiceal lumen.
• **Urinary Tract Infection:** Can occur, though uncommon.
• Sleep deprivation and emotional distress from chronic pruritus.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is **excellent** with proper treatment.
• Morbidity and mortality are extremely low.
• **Reinfection is very common** if hygiene measures are not strictly followed and if household contacts are not treated concurrently.

sections.overview:
• Scabies is a highly contagious parasitic skin infestation caused by the mite ***Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis***
• Characterized by an **intensely pruritic, papular rash** caused by a **delayed-type (Type IV) hypersensitivity reaction** to the mite, its eggs, and its feces (scybala)
• The pathognomonic lesion is the **burrow**, a thin, serpiginous track created by the female mite in the epidermis
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**: ***Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis***, an obligate human parasite
• **Transmission**: Primarily through prolonged, direct **skin-to-skin contact**
    ◦ Fomite transmission (bedding, clothing) is less common but possible, especially in cases of **crusted scabies**
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ The fertilized female mite burrows into the **stratum corneum** of the epidermis
    ◦ She lays 2-3 eggs per day and deposits feces (scybala) within the burrow
    ◦ The eggs hatch into larvae in 3-4 days, which then mature into adult mites on the skin surface
    ◦ The intense pruritus and inflammatory rash are caused by a **Type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction** to the mite, eggs, and scybala
    ◦ **Initial Infestation**: Symptoms appear **3-6 weeks** after exposure, the time it takes for sensitization to occur
    ◦ **Re-infestation**: Symptoms appear much faster, within **1-3 days**, due to pre-existing immunity
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects millions of people worldwide annually
• Occurs across all ages, races, and socioeconomic groups
• Prevalence is highest in resource-poor, tropical regions
• Outbreaks are common in settings with **crowded conditions** such as nursing homes, long-term care facilities, prisons, and daycare centers
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is the insidious onset of a **severely pruritic rash**
• The patient's chief complaint is an **unrelenting itch** that dramatically **worsens at night**, often disrupting sleep
• A key historical clue is the presence of similar symptoms in **household members or close contacts**
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primarily a clinical diagnosis** based on characteristic history (**nocturnal pruritus**, itchy contacts) and physical exam findings (**burrows** in classic locations)
• **Skin Scraping (Mineral Oil Prep)**: Confirmatory test
    ◦ **Procedure**: A drop of mineral oil is placed over a burrow. The burrow is then scraped with a #15 scalpel blade. The scrapings are placed on a glass slide and examined under low power microscopy
    ◦ **Positive Finding**: Visualization of **mites, eggs, or scybala** (fecal pellets)
    ◦ **Note**: A **negative scrape does not rule out scabies**, as the mite burden can be low (10-15 mites in classic scabies)
• **Dermoscopy**: Can be used to visualize the "**delta-wing jet**" sign (the mite's head and forelegs)
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** with prompt and proper treatment of the patient and **all close contacts**
• **Re-infestation** is common if contacts are not treated **simultaneously** or if environmental decontamination is inadequate
• **Crusted scabies** carries a **higher morbidity and mortality**, often related to the patient's underlying immunosuppression and risk of secondary sepsis

sections.overview:
• Pediculosis is an **infestation of the skin by lice** (obligate, blood-sucking ectoparasites).
    ◦ Three distinct species infest humans:
        ▪ **Pediculosis Capitis**: **Head lice** (*Pediculus humanus capitis*)
        ▪ **Pediculosis Corporis**: **Body lice** (*Pediculus humanus corporis*)
        ▪ **Pediculosis Pubis (Pthiriasis)**: **Pubic** or "**crab**" **lice** (*Pthirus pubis*)
sections.etiology:
• **Organisms**: Wingless insects of the order Anoplura.
    ◦ Host-specific and cannot survive off a human host for more than 1-2 days.
• **Life Cycle**:
    ◦ **Nit (Egg)**
        ▪ Female louse lays eggs and cements them to the base of a hair shaft (capitis, pubis) or clothing fibers (corporis).
        ▪ Nits are oval, typically 0.8 mm long, and hatch in 7-10 days.
    ◦ **Nymph**
        ▪ An immature louse that hatches from the nit.
        ▪ Undergoes three molts over 7-10 days to become an adult.
    ◦ **Adult Louse**
        ▪ Lives for approximately 30 days.
        ▪ Feeds on host blood several times daily.
        ▪ An adult female can lay several nits per day.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Pruritus** is caused by a **delayed-type (Type IV) hypersensitivity reaction** to proteins in louse saliva injected during blood feeding.
    ◦ Initial infestation may be **asymptomatic for 4-6 weeks** until sensitization occurs.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Pediculosis Capitis**
    ◦ Most common in **children aged 3-11 years**.
    ◦ Prevalence is higher in females and Caucasians.
    ◦ Transmission is primarily via **direct head-to-head contact**.
        ▪ Fomite transmission (e.g., hats, combs, bedding) is less common but possible.
• **Pediculosis Corporis**
    ◦ Associated with populations in **crowded conditions with poor hygiene** (e.g., homeless individuals, refugees).
    ◦ Transmitted through **infested clothing, bedding, and towels**.
    ◦ **Unique role as a disease vector**.
• **Pediculosis Pubis**
    ◦ Considered a **Sexually Transmitted Infection (STI)**.
    ◦ Most common in young, sexually active adults.
    ◦ Transmission is primarily through **sexual contact**.
        ▪ Fomite transmission is possible but less frequent.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Pediculosis Capitis**
    ◦ Classic patient: A 6-year-old female with persistent **scalp itching** and irritability for two weeks.
    ◦ Itching is often **worse behind the ears and at the back of the neck**.
    ◦ Parent may report seeing "**little white dots**" (nits) in the hair that cannot be brushed out.
• **Pediculosis Corporis**
    ◦ Classic patient: A 55-year-old man experiencing **homelessness** presents with severe, **generalized pruritus**, especially around the waist and in the axillae.
    ◦ Skin may appear **thickened and hyperpigmented** with multiple **linear excoriations**.
• **Pediculosis Pubis**
    ◦ Classic patient: A 22-year-old male with **intense itching in the genital region**.
    ◦ Often reports a **new sexual partner** within the last month.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Based on **visualization of live lice or nits** on the hair/clothing.
• **Wet Combing**: The **most sensitive method** for detecting *P. capitis*.
    ◦ A **fine-toothed nit comb** is passed through wet, conditioned hair from scalp to end.
    ◦ Lice are trapped on the comb and can be visualized against a white background.
• **Wood's Lamp**: Nits may fluoresce a pale blue, but this is not a highly sensitive or specific test.
• **STI Screening**: Patients diagnosed with **pediculosis pubis** should be **screened for other STIs**.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** with appropriate pharmacologic treatment and environmental control.
• **Treatment failure** is most often due to:
    ◦ Non-adherence
    ◦ Improper application
    ◦ Resistance to therapy
    ◦ **Re-infestation** from an untreated contact or fomite.

sections.overview:
• Candidiasis is an opportunistic fungal infection caused by yeast from the genus *Candida*.
    ◦ ***Candida albicans*** is the most common species.
    ◦ It is a normal commensal organism of the skin, gastrointestinal tract, and female genital tract.
• Infection (candidiasis) occurs due to overgrowth, typically following a disruption of the normal flora, a breach in mucosal/cutaneous barriers, or in the setting of **immunosuppression**.
• Presentations range from benign superficial mucocutaneous infections (e.g., thrush, vaginitis) to life-threatening invasive, disseminated disease (**candidemia**).
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ ***Candida albicans***: Most common cause (>80% of cases).
    ◦ **Non-albicans species**: Increasingly common, especially in nosocomial settings. Important examples include *_C. glabrata_*, *_C. parapsilosis_*, and *_C. krusei_* (notably resistant to **fluconazole**).
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ *Candida* exists as a commensal yeast. Pathogenesis begins with a disruption of the host's defenses or local environment.
    ◦ **Adherence**: The organism adheres to host epithelial or endothelial cells.
    ◦ **Transformation**: It converts from its unicellular yeast form to an invasive, filamentous form with **pseudohyphae** and hyphae. This morphologic shift is critical for tissue invasion.
    ◦ **Invasion**: The hyphae penetrate host tissues, causing local inflammation and damage.
    ◦ **Dissemination**: In immunocompromised hosts, the organism can enter the bloodstream (**candidemia**) and seed distant organs.
sections.epidemiology:
• *Candida* is a ubiquitous organism found worldwide.
• **Oropharyngeal Candidiasis (Thrush)**: Common in infants, elderly denture wearers, and immunocompromised individuals (especially **HIV/AIDS**).
• **Vulvovaginal Candidiasis (VVC)**: Extremely common; affects up to 75% of women at least once in their lifetime.
• **Invasive Candidiasis**: A leading cause of **nosocomial bloodstream infections**, particularly in intensive care unit (ICU) patients.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Immunosuppression**
    ◦ **HIV/AIDS** (**CD4 count <200** cells/L is a major risk for esophageal candidiasis)
    ◦ Chemotherapy-induced **neutropenia**
    ◦ Chronic **corticosteroid use** (inhaled or systemic)
    ◦ Solid organ or hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients
• **Disruption of Normal Flora**
    ◦ **Broad-spectrum antibiotic** use
• **Metabolic/Endocrine**
    ◦ Uncontrolled **Diabetes Mellitus** (hyperglycemia promotes yeast growth)
• **Breach of Cutaneous/Mucosal Barriers**
    ◦ Indwelling catheters (central venous, urinary)
    ◦ Dentures
    ◦ Macerated skin (obesity, moist environments)
    ◦ Burns or recent major surgery (especially abdominal)
• **Other**
    ◦ Pregnancy
    ◦ High-estrogen oral contraceptives
    ◦ Newborns (immature immune system)
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Oropharyngeal (Thrush)**: Painless, **white plaques** on buccal mucosa, tongue, or palate.
• **Esophageal**: Substernal **dysphagia**, **odynophagia** (painful swallowing), retrosternal chest pain.
• **Vulvovaginal (VVC)**: Intense vulvar **pruritus**, burning, and **thick, white vaginal discharge**.
• **Cutaneous (Intertrigo)**: **Erythematous rash** in skin folds (axilla, groin, inframammary) with **satellite lesions**.
• **Diaper Dermatitis**: **Beefy-red rash** involving skin folds in the diaper area with **satellite pustules**.
• **Invasive (Candidemia)**: Presents as **sepsis**: fever, chills, hypotension, tachycardia. May have non-specific symptoms or signs of end-organ seeding.
• **Endocarditis**: New or changing heart murmur, fever, **large vegetations** on valves.
• **Endophthalmitis**: Eye pain, vision changes, **"cotton ball" lesions** seen on fundoscopic exam.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ **Oropharyngeal**: Mouth soreness, cottony feeling, loss of taste, pain with eating.
    ◦ **Esophageal**: **Odynophagia**, **dysphagia**, retrosternal chest pain.
    ◦ **Vulvovaginal**: Intense vulvar **itching (pruritus)**, burning, soreness, **dyspareunia** (painful intercourse).
    ◦ **Cutaneous**: Itching, burning, stinging in affected skin folds.
    ◦ **Systemic**: **Fever, chills, myalgias, altered mental status** (non-specific signs of sepsis).
• **Physical Exam Findings**
    ◦ **Oropharyngeal**
        ▪ **Creamy white plaques** on oral mucosa or tongue that are **easily scrapeable**, revealing an underlying erythematous base.
        ▪ **Angular Cheilitis**: Fissures and erythema at the corners of the mouth.
    ◦ **Vulvovaginal**
        ▪ Vulvar and vaginal erythema and swelling.
        ▪ Thick, white, adherent, **"cottage cheese-like" discharge**.
        ▪ Vaginal pH is typically normal (<4.5).
    ◦ **Cutaneous**
        ▪ **"Beefy-red" erythema** in skin folds (intertriginous areas).
        ▪ Distinct **satellite macules, papules, or pustules** at the periphery of the main rash are characteristic.
    ◦ **Invasive/Disseminated**
        ▪ Signs of **sepsis** (fever, hypotension, tachycardia).
        ▪ Fundoscopic exam may reveal chorioretinal lesions or Roth spots (**endophthalmitis**).
        ▪ Skin exam may show diffuse erythematous maculopapular lesions.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Often sufficient for uncomplicated thrush, VVC, or intertrigo in a patient with classic findings and risk factors.
• **KOH Prep (Microscopy)**
    ◦ **Test of choice** for mucocutaneous infections.
    ◦ Skin scraping, oral swab, or vaginal discharge is placed on a slide with 10% Potassium Hydroxide (KOH).
    ◦ **Finding**: **Budding yeast and pseudohyphae**.
• **Fungal Culture**
    ◦ Used for speciation and antifungal susceptibility testing, especially in recurrent or refractory cases.
    ◦ Essential for blood, sterile fluids, or tissue samples.
• **Endoscopy with Biopsy and Brushing**
    ◦ **Gold standard** for diagnosing **esophageal candidiasis**.
    ◦ Endoscopy shows characteristic linear, **white-yellow plaques**.
• **Blood Cultures**
    ◦ The standard for diagnosing **candidemia**. Can have low sensitivity.
• **(1,3)-Beta-D-Glucan Assay**
    ◦ A serum marker for invasive fungal infections. Sensitive but not specific to *Candida*.
    ◦ Can be useful in high-risk, neutropenic patients.
sections.treatment:
• **Oropharyngeal**
    ◦ **Topical (mild)**: Nystatin "swish and swallow" or clotrimazole troches (lozenges).
    ◦ **Systemic (moderate-severe or refractory)**: Oral **fluconazole**.
• **Esophageal**
    ◦ **Requires systemic therapy**.
    ◦ **First-line**: Oral or IV **fluconazole**.
    ◦ **Refractory/Severe**: Voriconazole or an **echinocandin** (e.g., caspofungin).
• **Vulvovaginal (Uncomplicated)**
    ◦ **Topical**: OTC azoles (e.g., clotrimazole, miconazole) for 1-7 days.
    ◦ **Oral**: **Fluconazole 150 mg PO x 1 dose**.
• **Cutaneous (Intertrigo)**
    ◦ **Topical**: Nystatin, clotrimazole, or miconazole cream. Keep area clean and dry.
• **Candidemia (Invasive)**
    ◦ **First-line (critically ill/neutropenic)**: **Echinocandin** (e.g., caspofungin, micafungin).
    ◦ **Alternative (stable, non-neutropenic)**: Fluconazole (if susceptible).
    ◦ **Severe/Resistant**: Amphotericin B.
    ◦ **Crucial step**: **Remove central venous catheter** if it is the suspected source.
sections.management:
• **Primary Goal**: Eradicate the infection and prevent recurrence.
• **Address Underlying Risk Factors**
    ◦ Optimize glycemic control in diabetic patients.
    ◦ Re-evaluate the need for broad-spectrum antibiotics or corticosteroids.
    ◦ Ensure proper denture hygiene.
• **Follow-up**
    ◦ **For candidemia, an ophthalmology consult is mandatory** to rule out endophthalmitis.
    ◦ Re-evaluate patients with mucocutaneous infections if symptoms do not resolve with initial therapy.
sections.complications:
• **Mucocutaneous**: Can become chronic and recurrent, significantly impacting quality of life.
• **Esophageal**: Stricture formation, perforation (rare).
• **Invasive/Candidemia**
    ◦ **Septic shock** and multi-organ failure.
    ◦ **End-organ seeding**:
        ▪ **Endophthalmitis** (can lead to blindness)
        ▪ **Endocarditis**
        ▪ **Osteomyelitis** / Septic Arthritis
        ▪ CNS infection (meningitis, brain abscesses)
        ▪ Liver and spleen abscesses
sections.prognosis:
• **Mucocutaneous**: Excellent with appropriate treatment. Recurrence is common if underlying risk factors persist.
• **Invasive/Candidemia**: Guarded. **Mortality remains high (30-50%)** despite antifungal therapy, largely due to the severity of the patient's underlying conditions.
sections.preventionEducation:
• For intertrigo, advise keeping skin folds clean and dry. Use of barrier powders can be helpful.
• For recurrent VVC, advise wearing cotton underwear and avoiding douching.

sections.overview:
• Cryptococcosis is an invasive, systemic fungal infection caused by the encapsulated yeast *Cryptococcus*.
• The primary route of infection is inhalation of spores, leading to an initial pulmonary infection that is often asymptomatic.
• In immunocompromised individuals, the organism can disseminate, with a strong predilection for the central nervous system (CNS), causing the most common and feared manifestation: **cryptococcal meningoencephalitis**.
• It is a major opportunistic infection and a leading cause of meningitis in patients with advanced HIV/AIDS.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiologic Agents**
    ◦ ***Cryptococcus neoformans***: Most common species worldwide. Found in soil contaminated with bird (especially pigeon) droppings. Primarily affects immunocompromised hosts.
    ◦ ***Cryptococcus gattii***: Found in association with certain trees (e.g., eucalyptus). Can cause disease in both immunocompromised and immunocompetent hosts. Geographically more restricted (e.g., Pacific Northwest, Australia).
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Inhalation**: Desiccated yeast cells or spores are inhaled into the alveoli.
    ◦ **Primary Pulmonary Infection**: In the lungs, the organism rehydrates and develops its characteristic thick **polysaccharide capsule**. This capsule is a key virulence factor, as it is antiphagocytic and protects the yeast from the host immune response.
    ◦ **Containment or Dissemination**
        ▪ **Immunocompetent Host**: Cell-mediated immunity (T-cells, macrophages) typically contains the infection, often forming a granuloma. The infection may remain latent or be cleared.
        ▪ **Immunocompromised Host**: Defective T-cell immunity allows the yeast to replicate unchecked.
    ◦ **Hematogenous Spread**: The organism disseminates from the lungs via the bloodstream.
    ◦ **CNS Invasion**: *Cryptococcus* has a strong neurotropism. It crosses the blood-brain barrier and proliferates in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), leading to meningoencephalitis. The proliferation in the subarachnoid space obstructs CSF outflow, leading to a dangerous **increase in intracranial pressure (ICP)**.
sections.epidemiology:
• Worldwide distribution.
• *C. neoformans* is the most common cause of fungal meningitis globally.
• Incidence is highest in regions with a high prevalence of HIV/AIDS, particularly sub-Saharan Africa.
• In developed countries, it is most often seen in patients with other forms of immunosuppression (transplant, malignancy, corticosteroid use).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation varies by site of infection and host immune status.
• **Pulmonary Cryptococcosis**
    ◦ Often asymptomatic and incidentally found on imaging.
    ◦ Symptomatic disease can present as a subacute pneumonia with cough (productive or non-productive), dyspnea, low-grade fever, and pleuritic chest pain.
• **CNS Cryptococcosis (Meningoencephalitis)**
    ◦ **This is the most common and severe presentation.**
    ◦ **Subacute onset** over days to weeks (distinguishes from acute bacterial meningitis).
    ◦ **Headache**: Most common symptom (>80%), often severe, persistent, and progressively worsening.
    ◦ **Fever** and **malaise**.
    ◦ **Altered Mental Status**: Lethargy, confusion, personality changes, coma.
    ◦ **Nuchal Rigidity**: Present in <50% of cases, especially in severely immunocompromised patients who cannot mount a strong inflammatory response.
    ◦ **Focal Neurologic Deficits**: Cranial nerve palsies (esp. CN VI - abducens nerve palsy causing diplopia), vision/hearing loss, seizures.
• **Disseminated Cryptococcosis**
    ◦ **Cutaneous Lesions**: Papules, nodules, or ulcers, often with **central umbilication**, mimicking molluscum contagiosum. Can be the first sign of disseminated disease.
    ◦ Can also involve bone, prostate, and other organs.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Lumbar Puncture (LP) is the essential diagnostic procedure for suspected CNS disease.**
• **Opening Pressure (OP)**
    ◦ **CRITICAL to measure.** Frequently **elevated (>20 cm H2O)**.
    ◦ An OP >25 cm H2O requires aggressive management.
• **CSF Analysis**
    ◦ WBC: Mildly elevated (<50 cells/L) with a **lymphocytic predominance**.
    ◦ Glucose: **Low**.
    ◦ Protein: **High**.
• **India Ink Stain**
    ◦ Microscopic visualization of encapsulated, budding yeast.
    ◦ Rapid but has low sensitivity (~50-80%).
    ◦ Classic "halo" appearance.
• **Cryptococcal Antigen (CrAg) Test**
    ◦ **TEST OF CHOICE.**
    ◦ Can be performed on CSF and serum.
    ◦ Latex agglutination or enzyme immunoassay.
    ◦ Highly sensitive (>95%) and specific.
    ◦ High titers correlate with fungal burden.
• **Fungal Culture**
    ◦ **Gold standard** for diagnosis.
    ◦ Confirms species and allows for antifungal susceptibility testing.
    ◦ Can take several days to grow.
• **Serum CrAg**
    ◦ Useful for screening high-risk (CD4 <100) patients and diagnosing disseminated disease.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Brain MRI with contrast**: More sensitive than CT. May be normal or show meningeal enhancement, hydrocephalus, or characteristic **"soap bubble lesions"** (gelatinous pseudocysts) in the basal ganglia.
    ◦ **Chest X-ray / CT**: For pulmonary disease. Findings are non-specific and can include nodules, consolidation, infiltrates, or hilar adenopathy.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis depends heavily on baseline immune status, mental status at presentation, management of ICP, and access to care.
• In high-resource settings, mortality for cryptococcal meningitis is 10-20%.
• In low-resource settings, mortality can exceed 70%.
• Significant neurologic sequelae are common among survivors.

sections.overview:
• Histoplasmosis is a systemic fungal infection caused by the dimorphic fungus *Histoplasma capsulatum*.
• It is the most common endemic mycosis in the United States.
• Infection occurs via inhalation of fungal spores (microconidia) from soil contaminated with bird or bat droppings.
• The clinical spectrum ranges from asymptomatic infection to life-threatening progressive disseminated disease, largely dependent on the host's immune status and the size of the inoculum.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent:** *Histoplasma capsulatum*, a thermally dimorphic fungus.
    ◦ **Environment (<37°C):** Exists as a **mold** (mycelial form) in soil.
    ◦ **Host Body (37°C):** Converts to a **yeast** form within tissues.
• **Transmission:** Inhalation of airborne microconidia from disturbed soil.
• **Pathogenesis:**
    ◦ **Inhalation:** Spores are inhaled and deposited into the alveoli.
    ◦ **Phagocytosis:** Alveolar macrophages phagocytose the spores.
    ◦ **Conversion:** Inside the warm environment of the macrophage, the mold converts into its pathogenic yeast form.
    ◦ **Replication & Spread:** The yeast replicates within the macrophages, surviving the host's initial phagocytic defense. Infected macrophages travel via lymphatics to regional (hilar, mediastinal) lymph nodes and can then disseminate hematogenously.
    ◦ **Immune Response:** A competent T-cell mediated (cellular) immune response is critical for control. T-cells activate macrophages, leading to the formation of granulomas to contain the yeast. In most immunocompetent hosts, this contains the infection, often resulting in calcified granulomas visible on later imaging.
    ◦ **Dissemination:** In individuals with impaired cellular immunity (e.g., AIDS, transplant recipients), the yeast cannot be contained and disseminates throughout the reticuloendothelial system (liver, spleen, bone marrow, lymph nodes) and other organs.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Geography:** Endemic to specific regions, most notably the **Ohio and Mississippi River Valleys** in the United States. Also found in parts of Central and South America, Africa, and Asia.
• **Reservoir:** Soil enriched with nitrogen from **bird or bat droppings (guano)**.
• **Common Exposures:** Caving (**spelunking**), cleaning chicken coops, excavation, demolition of old buildings, and disturbing soil under bird roosts.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Exposure-Related:**
    ◦ Living in an endemic area.
    ◦ Occupations/hobbies: Farming, construction, landscaping, spelunking.
• **Host-Related (for severe or disseminated disease):**
    ◦ **Immunocompromised States:**
        ▪ HIV/AIDS, especially with **CD4 count < 150 cells/L**.
        ▪ Solid organ or hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients.
        ▪ Patients on immunosuppressive therapies (e.g., **TNF-alpha inhibitors**, high-dose corticosteroids, chemotherapy).
        ▪ Hematologic malignancies (lymphoma, leukemia).
    ◦ **Extremes of age:** Infants and elderly.
    ◦ **Pre-existing Lung Disease:** Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a risk factor for developing chronic cavitary histoplasmosis.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Clinical Syndromes:** The presentation depends on the inoculum size and host immunity.
    ◦ **Asymptomatic (~90%):** Most immunocompetent individuals have no symptoms. Infection is only identified by later findings (e.g., calcified granulomas on CXR) or positive serology.
    ◦ **Acute Pulmonary Histoplasmosis:** Occurs in immunocompetent hosts after a moderate-to-large exposure. Typically a self-limited, flu-like illness.
    ◦ **Chronic Cavitary Histoplasmosis:** Occurs almost exclusively in patients with pre-existing structural lung disease (e.g., COPD). It is a progressive and destructive pulmonary disease that mimics reactivation tuberculosis.
    ◦ **Progressive Disseminated Histoplasmosis (PDH):** A severe, systemic, and potentially fatal illness that occurs in immunocompromised individuals. Characterized by hematogenous spread to multiple organs.
• **Symptoms:**
    ◦ **Acute Pulmonary:**
        ▪ Fever, chills
        ▪ Non-productive cough
        ▪ Myalgias, arthralgias
        ▪ Headache
        ▪ Substernal chest pain
        ▪ Fatigue
    ◦ **Chronic Cavitary:**
        ▪ Productive cough
        ▪ Dyspnea
        ▪ Low-grade fever, night sweats
        ▪ Significant **weight loss**, malaise (constitutional **"B" symptoms**)
    ◦ **Progressive Disseminated:**
        ▪ Persistent fever, profound fatigue, weight loss
        ▪ **Hepatosplenomegaly**-related symptoms (abdominal fullness, pain)
        ▪ **Mucocutaneous lesions:** Painful **oral or nasopharyngeal ulcers** are classic.
        ▪ **Pancytopenia**-related symptoms: Pallor (anemia), easy bruising/petechiae (thrombocytopenia), recurrent infections (leukopenia).
        ▪ Adrenal insufficiency (less common): Nausea, vomiting, hypotension.
        ▪ CNS involvement (less common): Headache, altered mental status, seizures.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Acute Pulmonary:**
    ◦ Often unremarkable. May have fever. Auscultation can be normal or reveal rales/crackles.
• **Chronic Cavitary:**
    ◦ Rales, rhonchi, or signs of consolidation, particularly in the upper lobes. Cachexia may be present.
• **Progressive Disseminated:**
    ◦ **Hepatosplenomegaly**
    ◦ **Lymphadenopathy** (generalized)
    ◦ **Oral/Pharyngeal Ulcers**
    ◦ **Skin lesions:** Papules, pustules, nodules, or ulcerative lesions.
    ◦ Pallor, petechiae, ecchymoses (signs of **pancytopenia**).
    ◦ Hypotension (if adrenal involvement).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Labs:**
    ◦ **CBC:** May show **pancytopenia** in disseminated disease.
    ◦ **LFTs:** Elevated **Alkaline Phosphatase** and **LDH** are characteristic of disseminated disease.
    ◦ **Ferritin:** Can be markedly elevated.
• **Imaging:**
    ◦ **Chest X-ray / CT Chest:**
        ▪ *Acute:* Focal infiltrates, **hilar or mediastinal lymphadenopathy**.
        ▪ *Chronic:* **Apical infiltrates and cavitations**, mimicking TB.
        ▪ *Healed/Past Infection:* **Calcified granulomas** (histoplasmoma) or calcified hilar lymph nodes. **"Buckshot" calcifications** (multiple small calcified nodules) can be seen after heavy exposure.
• **Specific Tests:**
    ◦ **Antigen Detection:**
        ▪ **BEST INITIAL TEST** for acute pulmonary or disseminated disease.
        ▪ Detects *H. capsulatum* polysaccharide antigen in **urine** and/or serum.
        ▪ High sensitivity (>90%) in PDH.
        ▪ Also used to monitor treatment response.
    ◦ **Culture:**
        ▪ **GOLD STANDARD**.
        ▪ Can be cultured from sputum, blood, bone marrow, or tissue biopsy.
        ▪ *Limitation:* Very slow growth (can take 2-4 weeks).
    ◦ **Histopathology (Biopsy):**
        ▪ Visualization of small, oval, budding yeasts **within macrophages** on tissue stain (GMS or PAS).
        ▪ Provides a rapid diagnosis.
    ◦ **Serology (Antibody testing):**
        ▪ Detects IgM and IgG antibodies.
        ▪ Useful for subacute or chronic pulmonary disease.
        ▪ *Limitations:* Takes weeks to become positive; may be negative in immunocompromised patients.
sections.treatment:
• **Asymptomatic/Mild Acute:**
    ◦ No treatment needed for immunocompetent individuals.
• **Moderate-to-Severe Acute Pulmonary:**
    ◦ **Itraconazole** for 6-12 weeks.
• **Chronic Cavitary:**
    ◦ **Itraconazole** for at least 12 months.
• **Progressive Disseminated (PDH) or Severe Acute:**
    ◦ **Induction (for sick patients):** **Liposomal Amphotericin B** IV for 1-2 weeks.
    ◦ **Step-down/Consolidation:** **Itraconazole** PO for a total of at least 12 months.
• **CNS Histoplasmosis:**
    ◦ Requires a longer course, starting with high-dose Liposomal Amphotericin B followed by Itraconazole.
• **Note:** Therapeutic drug monitoring of itraconazole levels is recommended.
sections.management:
• **Follow-up:**
    ◦ Clinical improvement is key.
    ◦ In disseminated disease, urine/serum antigen levels should be monitored; a decline indicates effective treatment.
• **Prophylaxis:**
    ◦ **Primary Prophylaxis:** Itraconazole may be considered for patients with AIDS (**CD4 < 150**) in highly endemic areas.
    ◦ **Secondary Prophylaxis (Suppression):** Patients with treated PDH who remain significantly immunocompromised (e.g., AIDS, transplant) require long-term (often lifelong) suppressive therapy with itraconazole to prevent relapse.
sections.complications:
• **Mediastinal Granuloma:** Enlarged lymph nodes that can compress adjacent structures.
• **Fibrosing Mediastinitis:** A rare but severe complication from an exaggerated immune response, leading to excessive fibrosis that encases and obstructs great vessels (e.g., SVC syndrome), airways, or the esophagus.
• **Adrenal Insufficiency:** Due to granulomatous destruction of the adrenal glands in PDH.
• **CNS Involvement:** Meningitis or focal brain lesions (histoplasmomas).
• **ARDS:** Can occur in severe acute pulmonary histoplasmosis.
sections.prognosis:
• **Immunocompetent (Acute):** Excellent; most cases are self-limited.
• **Chronic Cavitary:** Good with treatment, but pulmonary damage can be progressive if untreated.
• **Progressive Disseminated:** **High mortality (>80%) if untreated**. With prompt and appropriate therapy, mortality is reduced to ~25%, but relapse is possible if immunosuppression persists.

sections.overview:
• Blastomycosis is a systemic **pyogranulomatous** infection caused by the dimorphic fungus **_Blastomyces dermatitidis_**.
• Infection is acquired via **inhalation of fungal spores (conidia)** from the environment.
• The primary site of infection is the **lungs**, but it can disseminate hematogenously to other sites:
    ◦ Most commonly: **skin**, **bones**, and **genitourinary system**.
• Clinical presentation ranges from **asymptomatic infection** to **acute or chronic pneumonia**, and can progress to a widely disseminated, life-threatening disease, particularly in **immunocompromised individuals**.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Organism:** **_Blastomyces dermatitidis_** (and the less common _B. gilchristii_).
• **Dimorphic Fungus:** This is a key characteristic.
    ◦ In the environment (soil, <37°C): Exists as a **mold** (mycelial form) that produces infectious spores (**conidia**).
    ◦ In the body (host tissue, 37°C): Converts to its pathogenic **yeast** form.
• **Pathogenesis:**
    ◦ **Inhalation:** Microconidia are inhaled from disturbed soil or decaying organic matter.
    ◦ **Deposition:** Spores deposit in the alveoli.
    ◦ **Conversion:** At body temperature (37°C), the conidia transform into the larger, pathogenic yeast form.
    ◦ **Yeast Characteristics:** The yeast is large, spherical, and thick-walled, classically described as having a **single, broad-based bud**. This thick wall helps it evade phagocytosis by alveolar macrophages.
    ◦ **Inflammatory Response:** The host mounts a mixed inflammatory response, characterized by both neutrophils (pyo-) and macrophages/granulomas (-granulomatous), hence "**pyogranulomatous**."
    ◦ **Dissemination:** The yeast can spread from the lungs via the bloodstream (hematogenously) to distant organs.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Geographic Distribution:** Endemic to specific regions of North America.
    ◦ **Mississippi and Ohio River Valleys**
    ◦ **Great Lakes region** (including Canadian provinces)
    ◦ **Southeastern United States**
• **Environment:** Found in moist, acidic soil rich in organic material, such as decaying wood and leaves. Outbreaks are often associated with soil disruption.
• **Demographics:** Affects both **immunocompetent** and **immunocompromised** individuals. Higher incidence in men, possibly due to increased occupational or recreational exposure (e.g., farming, forestry, construction, hunting).
sections.riskFactors:
• **Geographic Exposure:** Living in or traveling to an **endemic area** is the primary risk factor.
• **Occupational/Recreational Exposure:** Activities that disturb soil:
    ◦ Farming, excavation, construction
    ◦ Forestry, landscaping
    ◦ Hunting, camping, hiking
• **Host Factors (for severe/disseminated disease):**
    ◦ **Immunosuppression:**
        ▪ **HIV/AIDS** (especially CD4 count < 200 cells/L)
        ▪ Solid organ or hematopoietic stem cell transplant
        ▪ Chronic use of corticosteroids or other immunosuppressants (e.g., **TNF-alpha inhibitors**)
        ▪ Malignancy
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is highly variable, ranging from asymptomatic to fulminant. The incubation period is typically 3-6 weeks but can be longer.
• **Pulmonary Disease (Most Common, ~50% of symptomatic cases):**
    ◦ **Acute Pneumonia:** Mimics community-acquired bacterial pneumonia. Presents with abrupt onset of fever, chills, productive cough, myalgias, and pleuritic chest pain.
    ◦ **Chronic Pneumonia:** More insidious onset, mimics tuberculosis or lung cancer. Presents with low-grade fever, night sweats, weight loss, and chronic productive cough.
    ◦ **Severe Disease:** Can progress to **Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)** with diffuse, bilateral infiltrates.
• **Extrapulmonary Disseminated Disease:** Occurs in 25-40% of symptomatic patients.
    ◦ **Cutaneous (2nd most common):** Lesions are often the presenting sign. Classically **verrucous (wart-like)** or **ulcerative**. They are typically well-demarcated with irregular, violaceous borders and may have central clearing or crusted microabscesses at the periphery. Usually painless.
    ◦ **Osseous:** **Lytic bone lesions** can occur in long bones, vertebrae, and ribs. Presents as localized bone pain, swelling, or a draining sinus tract.
    ◦ **Genitourinary (GU):** Common in males, involving the prostate and epididymis. Presents with **prostatitis** (dysuria, perineal pain) or **epididymo-orchitis**.
    ◦ **Central Nervous System (CNS):** Rare but life-threatening. Can cause **meningitis** or intracranial/epidural **abscesses**. Presents with headache, focal neurologic deficits, confusion, or seizures.
• **Associated Symptoms:**
    ◦ **Constitutional:** Fever, chills, malaise, night sweats, weight loss.
    ◦ **Pulmonary:** Cough (productive or non-productive), dyspnea, chest pain.
    ◦ **Cutaneous:** A non-healing, painless skin lesion that may be described as a "wart" or "ulcer."
    ◦ **Osseous:** Deep, aching bone pain.
    ◦ **GU:** Dysuria, pelvic/perineal pain, scrotal swelling.
    ◦ **CNS:** Headache, altered mental status, seizures.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Vitals:** Fever may be present. Tachypnea and hypoxia in severe pulmonary disease.
• **Lungs:** Can be normal or may have rales, rhonchi, or signs of consolidation.
• **Skin:** Carefully inspect for the characteristic **verrucous plaques** or **ulcerated nodules** with heaped-up, violaceous borders.
• **Musculoskeletal:** Point tenderness over affected bones, erythema, swelling.
• **Genitourinary:** Prostatic tenderness on DRE; scrotal/epididymal tenderness and swelling.
• **Neurologic:** Nuchal rigidity, cranial nerve palsies, focal deficits.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Microscopy:**
    ◦ **Method:** Direct visualization of specimens (sputum, bronchoalveolar lavage [BAL] fluid, pus, tissue biopsy) using KOH prep, wet mount, or specific fungal stains (GMS, PAS).
    ◦ **Finding:** **Large, thick-walled, spherical yeast with a single, broad-based bud.** This finding is **diagnostic**.
• **Fungal Culture:**
    ◦ **Method:** Culture of sputum, BAL fluid, tissue, pus, blood, or urine.
    ◦ **Finding:** **Gold standard** for diagnosis. Growth may be slow (2-4 weeks). Lab must be notified of suspicion for a dimorphic fungus due to biohazard risk of mold form.
• **Antigen Detection:**
    ◦ **Method:** Enzyme immunoassay (EIA) detects _Blastomyces_ galactomannan antigen in urine or serum.
    ◦ **Finding:** High sensitivity, especially in disseminated or severe pulmonary disease. Useful for rapid diagnosis and for monitoring treatment response. Can **cross-react with _Histoplasma_**.
• **Imaging:**
    ◦ **Chest X-ray / CT:** Findings are **non-specific**. Can show focal consolidation, nodules, masses (mimicking malignancy), miliary pattern, or diffuse interstitial infiltrates. Cavitation can occur but is less common than in TB. Hilar adenopathy is uncommon.
• **Histopathology (Biopsy):**
    ◦ **Method:** Skin, lung, or bone biopsy.
    ◦ **Finding:** Shows **pyogranulomatous inflammation** and the characteristic yeast forms. Skin biopsy often shows **pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia**, which can be mistaken for squamous cell carcinoma.
sections.management:
• **Monitoring:** Follow patients for clinical improvement (resolution of symptoms, weight gain) and radiographic clearing.
• **Drug Levels:** For patients on long-term **itraconazole**, checking serum drug levels is recommended to ensure adequate absorption and therapeutic concentration.
• **LFTs:** Monitor liver function tests for patients on **azole therapy**.
• **Antigen Levels:** Serial urine/serum antigen testing can be used to monitor response to therapy; levels should decline with effective treatment.
• **CNS Disease:** Requires follow-up imaging and may require repeat lumbar punctures.
sections.complications:
• **ARDS** (from severe pulmonary infection)
• **CNS infection:** Brain abscess, meningitis
• **Spinal cord compression** from vertebral osteomyelitis
• **Massive hemoptysis**
• **Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC)** and multi-organ failure in severe disease
sections.prognosis:
• **Immunocompetent patients** with mild-to-moderate disease treated appropriately have an **excellent prognosis** (>90% cure rate).
• **Prognosis is worse** for patients with:
    ◦ Severe disease requiring hospitalization (especially **ARDS**)
    ◦ **CNS involvement**
    ◦ Significant underlying **immunosuppression**
• Mortality for ARDS or CNS blastomycosis can be **>40%** even with treatment.

sections.overview: • Coccidioidomycosis, commonly known as "Valley Fever" or "San Joaquin Valley Fever," is a systemic mycosis caused by the dimorphic fungus Coccidioides. • Acquired via inhalation of airborne arthroconidia. • The clinical spectrum is broad, ranging from an asymptomatic infection (~60% of cases) to a self-limited acute pulmonary illness, to severe, progressive, and potentially fatal disseminated disease. • It is endemic to the arid regions of the southwestern United States, Mexico, and parts of Central and South America.
sections.etiology: • Causative Agents: Coccidioides immitis (primarily in California) and Coccidioides posadasii (in Arizona, Texas, Mexico, and South America). ◦ Both are clinically indistinguishable. • Dimorphic Fungus: It exists in two distinct forms: ◦ Mold (in soil): At ambient temperature in the soil, it grows as a mold with hyphae that segment into infectious, barrel-shaped arthroconidia. ◦ Yeast (in host): At body temperature (37°C) within the lungs, the inhaled arthroconidia transform into large, thick-walled spherules. • Pathogenesis: ◦ Inhalation: Arthroconidia are aerosolized from disturbed soil (e.g., by wind, construction, farming) and inhaled into the lungs. ◦ Transformation: Inside the lungs, arthroconidia convert to spherules. ◦ Replication: The spherule enlarges and develops internal septations, forming hundreds of endospores. ◦ Rupture: The spherule ruptures, releasing the endospores into surrounding tissue. Each endospore can then develop into a new spherule, propagating the infection. ◦ Immune Response: Cell-mediated immunity (T-lymphocytes) is critical for containing the infection. A deficient cell-mediated immune response allows for dissemination.
sections.epidemiology: • Geography: Endemic to arid, alkaline soils in the Lower Sonoran Life Zone. ◦ United States: Southwestern US, particularly Arizona (Maricopa, Pima, Pinal counties) and California's San Joaquin Valley. Also found in New Mexico, west Texas, Nevada, and Utah. • Transmission: Inhalation of airborne arthroconidia. ◦ NOT transmitted from person to person. ◦ Outbreaks are often associated with dust-generating events like dust storms, earthquakes, and construction. • Incidence: An estimated 60% of primary infections are asymptomatic or subclinical.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • The presentation can be divided into three main categories: ◦ Asymptomatic Infection: (~60%) Identified only by a positive serologic test or skin test conversion. ◦ Acute Primary Pulmonary Coccidioidomycosis ("Valley Fever"): (~40%) Occurs 1-3 weeks after exposure. Typically a self-limited, flu-like illness. ◦ Disseminated Coccidioidomycosis: (<1%) Infection spreads hematogenously from the lungs to other parts of the body. Can be devastating.
sections.diagnostics: • Laboratory Studies ◦ CBC: Peripheral eosinophilia is a classic and highly suggestive finding. Leukocytosis may be present. ◦ ESR/CRP: Markedly elevated, but non-specific. • Serology (Primary method for diagnosis) ◦ IgM Antibodies: Detected by enzyme immunoassay (EIA) or immunodiffusion. ▪ Appear 1-3 weeks after symptom onset, indicating acute/recent infection. ▪ Often fade by 3-6 months. ◦ IgG Antibodies: Detected by complement fixation (CF) or immunodiffusion. ▪ Appear 2-8 weeks after onset. ▪ Titers correlate with disease severity. ▪ High or rising IgG CF titers (e.g., >1:32) are concerning for dissemination. • Imaging ◦ Chest X-Ray / CT Chest: Findings are highly variable. ▪ Hilar or mediastinal lymphadenopathy ▪ Focal or diffuse infiltrates ▪ Nodules or thin-walled cavities ("cavitary lesions") ▪ Pleural effusion • Microscopy and Histopathology ◦ Sputum, bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid, or tissue biopsy (e.g., skin, bone). ◦ Staining with KOH prep, GMS, or PAS reveals characteristic large spherules (20-60 µm) containing endospores. This is diagnostic. • Culture ◦ Gold Standard for diagnosis. ◦ EXTREME BIOHAZARD: The mold form grown in culture produces highly infectious arthroconidia. The laboratory MUST be notified of suspected Coccidioides to ensure proper biosafety precautions.
sections.prognosis: • Primary Pulmonary Infection: Excellent in immunocompetent hosts; most cases resolve spontaneously. The presence of erythema nodosum is a good prognostic sign. • Disseminated Disease: Guarded. Morbidity is high, and prolonged therapy is required. • Meningitis: Without treatment, it is uniformly fatal. With lifelong suppressive therapy, the prognosis has improved but significant neurologic morbidity can remain.

sections.overview:
• Refers to a spectrum of diseases caused by the fungus *Aspergillus*, a ubiquitous mold found in soil, water, and decaying vegetation.
• The clinical presentation is highly dependent on the host's immune status and underlying lung pathology, ranging from a benign allergic reaction to a rapidly fatal invasive infection.
• The four main clinical syndromes are:
    ◦ **Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis (ABPA)**: A hypersensitivity reaction to *Aspergillus* antigens in patients with asthma or cystic fibrosis.
    ◦ **Aspergilloma**: A "fungus ball" (mycetoma) that colonizes a pre-existing lung cavity.
    ◦ **Chronic Pulmonary Aspergillosis (CPA)**: A long-term, destructive but non-invasive or semi-invasive infection in patients with underlying lung disease.
    ◦ **Invasive Aspergillosis (IA)**: A life-threatening, rapidly progressive infection characterized by angioinvasion, occurring almost exclusively in severely immunocompromised individuals.
sections.etiology:
• Etiologic Agent
    ◦ Primarily **Aspergillus fumigatus**.
    ◦ Other species include *A. flavus*, *A. niger*, and *A. terreus*.
• Transmission: Inhalation of airborne conidia (spores), which are ubiquitous in the environment.
• Pathophysiology by Syndrome:
    ◦ **ABPA**
        ▪ An immune-mediated inflammatory response, not a true infection.
        ▪ Inhaled spores trigger **Type I (IgE-mediated)** and **Type III (immune complex)** hypersensitivity reactions in the airways.
        ▪ This leads to excessive mucus production, eosinophilic inflammation, and airway damage, resulting in bronchiectasis.
    ◦ **Aspergilloma**
        ▪ Spores are inhaled and settle in a pre-existing pulmonary cavity (e.g., from prior TB, sarcoidosis, or bullous emphysema).
        ▪ The fungus germinates and grows into a tangled mass of hyphae, forming a ball.
        ▪ It does **not** invade surrounding lung tissue but can cause local inflammation and erode nearby blood vessels, leading to hemoptysis.
    ◦ **CPA**
        ▪ Occurs in patients with structural lung disease but who are not severely immunocompromised.
        ▪ It is a chronic, indolent process of local fungal invasion and inflammation, leading to cavity formation, fibrosis, and progressive destruction of lung parenchyma.
    ◦ **Invasive Aspergillosis (IA)**
        ▪ In severely immunocompromised hosts (especially neutropenic patients), inhaled spores are not cleared by macrophages and neutrophils.
        ▪ They germinate into hyphae, which have a propensity for **angioinvasion** (invading blood vessels).
        ▪ This leads to thrombosis, tissue infarction, necrosis, and hematogenous dissemination to other organs (brain, skin, liver, kidney).
sections.epidemiology:
• *Aspergillus* is ubiquitous worldwide.
• The incidence of invasive disease is directly related to the size of the at-risk immunocompromised population (e.g., transplant recipients, patients on chemotherapy).
• ABPA is seen in 1-2% of patients with asthma and 7-10% of patients with cystic fibrosis.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • The presentation varies dramatically depending on the specific syndrome.
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• **ABPA**: Good with treatment, but is a chronic condition with relapses.
• **Aspergilloma**: Depends on the severity of hemoptysis and underlying lung function. Excellent if successfully resected.
• **CPA**: Variable. Can be stable for years or progress to respiratory failure.
• **IA**: **Very poor**. Mortality remains high (50-80%) even with appropriate therapy, especially in allogeneic HSCT recipients.

sections.overview:
• Tinea, also known as dermatophytosis or "**ringworm**," is a superficial fungal infection of keratinized tissues, including the skin (epidermis), hair, and nails.
    ◦ It is caused by a group of fungi called dermatophytes.
    ◦ The clinical name is typically based on the anatomical location of the infection (e.g., Tinea pedis for the foot).
    ◦ These infections are extremely common and are generally not life-threatening but can cause significant discomfort and cosmetic concern.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**: Caused by dermatophyte fungi from three main genera:
    ◦ ***Trichophyton*** (most common, affects skin, hair, and nails)
        ▪ *T. rubrum* is the most common cause worldwide.
    ◦ ***Microsporum*** (affects skin and hair)
        ▪ *M. canis* is often acquired from cats or dogs.
    ◦ ***Epidermophyton*** (affects skin and nails)
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ Dermatophytes are keratinophilic, meaning they feed on keratin.
    ◦ They produce enzymes called **keratinases** that digest the keratin in the stratum corneum, hair shafts, and nail plates.
    ◦ The infection remains superficial, rarely invading deeper tissues in immunocompetent hosts.
    ◦ The host's cell-mediated immune response to the fungal antigens and metabolic byproducts causes the inflammation, erythema, scaling, and pruritus seen clinically.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: One of the most common infectious diseases worldwide.
• **Transmission**:
    ◦ **Direct contact**: Human-to-human (anthropophilic), animal-to-human (zoophilic), or soil-to-human (geophilic).
    ◦ **Indirect contact**: Via fomites such as contaminated towels, clothing, bedding, and floors (e.g., locker rooms, public showers).
• **Environment**: More common in warm, humid climates.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Tinea is classified by the affected body part ("Tinea" + Latin location).
• **Tinea Corporis (Body)**: The classic "**ringworm**."
    ◦ Presents as a solitary or multiple, pruritic, erythematous, annular (ring-shaped) plaque.
    ◦ Features a raised, advancing scaly border and **central clearing**.
• **Tinea Pedis (Foot - "Athlete's Foot")**: Most common dermatophytosis.
    ◦ **Interdigital type**: Most common pattern. Presents with scaling, erythema, and maceration in the web spaces, especially between the 3rd and 4th toes.
    ◦ **Moccasin type (Hyperkeratotic)**: Diffuse, fine scaling covering the soles and sides of the feet, resembling a moccasin. Often associated with tinea manuum on one hand (**"two feet, one hand" syndrome**).
    ◦ **Vesiculobullous type**: Inflammatory variant with vesicles or bullae, typically on the medial foot.
• **Tinea Cruris (Groin - "Jock Itch")**:
    ◦ Pruritic, erythematous patches with a sharp, demarcated border that spreads from the groin folds onto the upper inner thighs.
    ◦ The central portion of the patch is often reddish-brown with some scaling.
    ◦ **Key Differentiator**: The **scrotum is typically spared**, unlike in Candidal intertrigo.
• **Tinea Capitis (Scalp)**: Primarily affects children.
    ◦ **Ectothrix**: Infection on the outside of the hair shaft. Presents as scaly patches with alopecia. "Gray patch" tinea capitis is a classic example.
    ◦ **Endothrix**: Infection within the hair shaft. Presents with hair shafts breaking off at the scalp level, creating a "**black dot**" appearance.
    ◦ **Kerion**: A severe, inflammatory, boggy, purulent mass with significant hair loss. Caused by an intense immune reaction to the fungus. Can lead to scarring alopecia. Often associated with posterior cervical lymphadenopathy.
• **Tinea Manuum (Hand)**:
    ◦ Often presents as unilateral, diffuse dry scaling on the palm and fingers. Often seen with tinea pedis ("two feet, one hand" syndrome).
• **Tinea Barbae (Beard Area)**:
    ◦ Inflammatory follicular papules and pustules in the beard and mustache area of adult men.
• **Tinea Unguium (Nails - Onychomycosis)**:
    ◦ Nails become thickened, brittle, and discolored (yellow-brown).
    ◦ Presents with subungual hyperkeratosis (debris under the nail), and onycholysis (separation of the nail plate from the bed).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Best Initial Test: KOH Preparation**
    ◦ **Procedure**: Scrape scales from the active border of the lesion onto a glass slide, add a drop of 10-20% potassium hydroxide (KOH), gently heat, and examine under a microscope.
    ◦ **Finding**: The KOH dissolves the keratinocytes, making the fungal elements visible. The classic finding is **septate hyphae** ("spaghetti") and sometimes spores ("meatballs").
• **Gold Standard: Fungal Culture**
    ◦ Uses Sabouraud agar.
    ◦ Takes 2-4 weeks for results but can identify the specific species.
    ◦ Indicated for failed treatment, atypical presentations, or required for initiating systemic therapy for tinea capitis/unguium.
• **Wood's Lamp (UV-A light)**
    ◦ Limited utility as the most common species (*Trichophyton*) do not fluoresce.
    ◦ *Microsporum* species (*M. canis*, *M. audouinii*) will show a characteristic **blue-green fluorescence**.
    ◦ Useful for differentiating from Erythrasma (caused by *Corynebacterium minutissimum*), which fluoresces a **coral-red** color.
• **Biopsy with PAS stain**
    ◦ Rarely necessary, reserved for cases where diagnosis is unclear.
    ◦ The Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain highlights fungal elements in tissue.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**: Most superficial tinea infections respond well to appropriate therapy.
• **Recurrence**: Common if underlying risk factors (e.g., moisture, exposure) are not addressed.
• **Onychomycosis**: Has a lower cure rate (~50-75%) and higher relapse rate compared to skin infections.
• **Tinea Capitis**: Prognosis is good, but a kerion can result in permanent hair loss.

sections.overview:
• Fifth Disease, also known as **Erythema Infectiosum**, is a common, mild viral exanthem in children caused by **Parvovirus B19**
• Classically characterized by a **"slapped cheek"** facial rash, followed by a **lacy, reticular rash** on the trunk and extremities
• While benign in healthy children, it can cause significant complications in those with hemolytic anemias, immunocompromised individuals, and pregnant women
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**: **Parvovirus B19**, a non-enveloped, single-stranded DNA virus; the only human pathogen in the *Erythroparvovirus* genus
• **Transmission**: Primarily through **respiratory droplets**
    ◦ Can also be transmitted via vertical transmission (mother to fetus) and blood products
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Viral Tropism**: Parvovirus B19 has a unique affinity for **erythroid progenitor cells** in the bone marrow by binding to the P antigen (globoside) on the cell surface
    ◦ **Viremic Phase (First Week)**: The virus replicates in the bone marrow, causing lysis of red blood cell precursors, leading to a temporary halt in erythropoiesis
        ▪ This results in a transient drop in reticulocytes and hemoglobin
        ▪ During this phase, the patient experiences non-specific flu-like symptoms (fever, malaise) and is **highly contagious**
    ◦ **Immune-Complex Phase (Second/Third Week)**: The characteristic rash and arthralgias appear after viremia resolves
        ▪ Symptoms are caused by the deposition of **IgM and IgG immune complexes** in the capillaries of the skin and synovial tissues
        ▪ The patient is **no longer contagious** once the rash appears
sections.epidemiology:
• **Peak Incidence**: School-aged children (4-10 years old)
• **Seasonality**: Outbreaks are common in late winter and spring
• **Seroprevalence**: Very common; up to 60% of adults are seropositive for **Parvovirus B19 IgG**, indicating past infection and immunity
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The illness typically follows a biphasic course
    ◦ **Prodromal Phase**: Mild, non-specific viral symptoms that precede the rash by 2-5 days
    ◦ **Exanthem Phase**: The characteristic rash appears as the initial symptoms subside
• Adult presentation may be different, often with minimal or absent rash but prominent arthralgias
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is typically **clinical** in healthy children with the characteristic rash and does not require laboratory testing
• **When to Test**:
    ◦ Atypical presentation
    ◦ Suspected complications (aplastic crisis, hydrops fetalis)
    ◦ Confirming infection in a pregnant or immunocompromised patient
• **Laboratory Tests**:
    ◦ **Serology (Most Common)**:
        ▪ **Parvovirus B19 IgM**: Indicates acute or recent infection; appears within 10 days of exposure and can persist for several months
        ▪ **Parvovirus B19 IgG**: Indicates past infection and immunity; appears within 2 weeks and persists for life
    ◦ **Complete Blood Count (CBC)**:
        ▪ In healthy individuals: Often normal or may show mild lymphopenia or neutropenia
        ▪ In **aplastic crisis**: Severe anemia (drop in Hgb >2 g/dL), **marked reticulocytopenia (<0.1%)**, and decreased WBC/platelet counts
    ◦ **PCR**: Detects Parvovirus B19 DNA
        ▪ Highly sensitive and specific
        ▪ The test of choice for immunocompromised patients who may not mount a reliable antibody response
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for healthy children and adults, with complete recovery expected
• The transient aplastic crisis is serious but typically resolves within 1-2 weeks with supportive care
• Fetal loss rate is approximately 5-10% if maternal infection occurs before 20 weeks gestation; risk is much lower in the third trimester

sections.overview:
• Scarlet fever, also known as scarlatina, is a systemic illness resulting from an infection with a specific strain of **_Streptococcus pyogenes_** (Group A Streptococcus, GABHS).
    ◦ It is classically characterized by the triad of **fever**, **pharyngitis**, and a characteristic **exanthem (rash)**.
• The rash and systemic symptoms are not caused by the bacteria itself, but by an **erythrogenic toxin** produced by the organism.
• It is primarily a disease of childhood.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiologic Agent**: Infection with an exotoxin-producing strain of **_Streptococcus pyogenes_** (Group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus).
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ GABHS colonizes the pharynx (most common) or, less commonly, a skin wound ("surgical scarlet fever").
    ◦ The specific bacterial strain produces one of three **streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins (SpeA, SpeB, or SpeC)**.
    ◦ These toxins act as **superantigens**, leading to a massive, nonspecific activation of T-cells and the release of inflammatory cytokines.
    ◦ This results in a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction, causing diffuse vasodilation and inflammation, which manifests as the characteristic erythematous rash and systemic symptoms.
    ◦ Prior exposure to the toxin confers lifelong type-specific immunity to the rash, but not to future GABHS infections, which is why scarlet fever is rare in adults.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Age**: Most common in children aged **5-15 years**.
    ◦ Rare in children <3 years due to circulating maternal anti-exotoxin antibodies and in adults due to acquired immunity.
• **Transmission**: Respiratory droplets from coughing or sneezing, or direct contact with an infected individual or carrier.
• **Seasonality**: Predominantly occurs in the late fall, winter, and early spring, mirroring the seasonality of streptococcal pharyngitis.
• **Setting**: Outbreaks are common in settings of close contact, such as schools and daycare centers.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The illness typically begins with a prodrome of **fever** and **sore throat**.
• The characteristic rash appears **12-48 hours** after the onset of fever.
• The patient is often irritable, febrile, and complains of significant throat pain (**odynophagia**), headache, and malaise.
• Abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting are also common, particularly in younger children.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Best Initial Test**: **Rapid Antigen Detection Test (RADT)** for GABHS from a throat swab.
    ◦ High specificity but variable sensitivity.
• **Gold Standard**: **Throat Culture**.
    ◦ Perform if **RADT is negative** in a child or adolescent with high clinical suspicion for GABHS.
    ◦ In adults, a negative RADT does not typically require culture confirmation due to the low risk of **acute rheumatic fever**.
• **Supportive Labs** (not required for diagnosis):
    ◦ **CBC**: Leukocytosis with neutrophilia ("left shift") and possible eosinophilia.
    ◦ **Inflammatory markers**: Elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR).
    ◦ **Antistreptolysin O (ASO) Titer**: Retrospective evidence of recent strep infection.
        ▪ Not useful for diagnosing acute disease but helpful in diagnosing post-streptococcal sequelae (**ARF**, **PSGN**).
sections.prognosis:
• With timely and appropriate antibiotic therapy, the prognosis is **excellent**.
• Fever typically resolves within 24-48 hours of starting antibiotics.
• The rash fades within a week, often followed by **desquamation**.
• The risk of complications, especially **acute rheumatic fever (ARF)**, is dramatically reduced with treatment.

sections.overview:
• **Hand-Foot-Mouth Disease (HFMD)** is a common, highly contagious, and typically self-limiting viral illness most frequently affecting infants and young children.
• It is characterized by a classic triad of clinical findings:
    ◦ A painful **oral enanthem** (sores in the mouth)
    ◦ A **maculopapular or vesicular rash** on the hands and feet
    ◦ Often a low-grade fever
• While usually a mild disease, certain causative agents can lead to severe **neurologic complications**.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agents**
    ◦ Caused by viruses from the **Picornaviridae** family, genus *Enterovirus*.
    ◦ **Coxsackievirus A16** is the most common cause in the United States, typically resulting in mild, uncomplicated illness.
    ◦ **Enterovirus 71 (EV-A71)** is notorious for causing more severe disease, including significant neurologic complications (e.g., **encephalitis**, **aseptic meningitis**, **acute flaccid paralysis**) and is associated with large outbreaks, particularly in Asia.
    ◦ Other serotypes like **Coxsackievirus A6** can cause a more widespread and atypical rash.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Transmission**: Primarily via **fecal-oral route**. Also spread through respiratory droplets (saliva, sputum, nasal mucus) and direct contact with vesicle fluid or fomites.
    ◦ **Incubation Period**: 3 to 6 days.
    ◦ **Mechanism**: The virus initially replicates in the lymphoid tissues of the lower intestine (Peyer's patches) and the pharynx, leading to a viremia which allows the virus to seed target organs like the oral mucosa and skin.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Peak Incidence**: Infants and children under 5 years of age.
• **Seasonality**: Predominantly occurs in the **summer and early fall** in temperate climates.
• **Setting**: Outbreaks are common in group settings like **daycare centers, preschools, and summer camps** due to close contact and suboptimal hygiene among children.
• **Geography**: Worldwide distribution.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Age**: < 5 years old.
• **Environment**: Attending daycare or school.
• **Hygiene**: Poor handwashing practices.
• **Immune Status**: Immunocompromised individuals may experience more severe or prolonged illness.
• **Close Contact**: Living in crowded conditions or having a sibling with the infection.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient, typically a young child, presents after a 1-2 day **prodrome** of low-grade fever, malaise, and anorexia.
• The parent reports the child is irritable and refusing to eat or drink due to **mouth pain**.
• Shortly after the prodrome, a characteristic rash appears in the mouth and on the hands and feet.
• **Prodromal Symptoms**
    ◦ Low-grade fever (100-102°F / 38-39°C)
    ◦ Malaise, fussiness, irritability
    ◦ Anorexia (poor appetite)
    ◦ Sore throat / Mouth pain (**odynophagia**)
    ◦ Abdominal pain, occasionally diarrhea
• **Ensuing Symptoms**
    ◦ Painful oral lesions
    ◦ Non-pruritic (but sometimes tender) skin rash on hands and feet
sections.physicalExam:
• **Oral Enanthem (Mouth Lesions)**
    ◦ Erythematous macules that progress to vesicles on an erythematous base.
    ◦ Vesicles rapidly rupture, forming **shallow, painful, yellowish-gray ulcers surrounded by an erythematous halo**.
    ◦ **Location**: Primarily **anterior oral cavity**—buccal mucosa, tongue, and hard palate. Spares the posterior pharynx.
• **Exanthem (Skin Rash)**
    ◦ **Distribution**: Classic locations are the **palms and soles**. Also common on the dorsal surfaces of hands/feet, buttocks, and occasionally knees/elbows.
    ◦ **Appearance**:
        ▪ Maculopapular lesions that can progress to **vesicles**.
        ▪ Vesicles are often oval or elliptical, 2-10 mm in size, with a "grayish" appearance.
        ▪ They are non-pruritic and non-tender to palpation.
        ▪ The rash typically resolves without crusting or scarring.
sections.diagnostics:
• Primarily a **clinical diagnosis** based on characteristic history and physical exam findings (age, season, oral enanthem + exanthem on hands/feet).
• **Laboratory testing is rarely indicated** in uncomplicated cases.
• **Indications for Testing**: Severe or atypical disease, public health outbreak investigations.
• **Viral Culture or RT-PCR**: Can be performed on samples from stool, throat swabs, or vesicular fluid to identify the specific enterovirus serotype.
    ◦ Stool samples have the highest yield.
• **Serology**: Not useful for acute diagnosis.
• **CSF Analysis**: If meningitis is suspected, will show a **lymphocytic pleocytosis** with normal glucose and normal or slightly elevated protein (typical for aseptic/viral meningitis).
sections.treatment:
• **Supportive care is the mainstay of therapy.** There is no specific antiviral agent available.
• **Analgesia and Antipyretics**
    ◦ **Acetaminophen or Ibuprofen** for fever and pain management.
    ◦ *Avoid Aspirin* in children due to the risk of Reye's syndrome.
• **Hydration**
    ◦ Encourage oral fluids (water, milk, electrolyte solutions). Cold liquids and popsicles can be soothing.
    ◦ Avoid acidic or spicy foods/beverages that can irritate oral ulcers.
    ◦ **IV fluids** may be necessary for patients with significant dehydration due to odynophagia.
• **Topical Oral Anesthetics**
    ◦ Mixtures like **"Magic Mouthwash"** (e.g., liquid diphenhydramine and Maalox) can provide temporary relief.
    ◦ Use viscous lidocaine with extreme caution in young children due to risk of toxicity, seizures, and suppression of the gag reflex.
sections.management: • Advise parents on the signs of dehydration (decreased urine output, dry mucous membranes, no tears, lethargy) and the rare but serious signs of neurologic complications (severe headache, stiff neck, confusion, seizures).
sections.complications:
• **Dehydration**: The most common complication, resulting from refusal to drink due to painful oral lesions.
• **Aseptic (Viral) Meningitis**: Headache, nuchal rigidity, photophobia. More common with **EV-A71**.
• **Encephalitis / Acute Flaccid Myelitis**: Rare but severe neurologic complications, strongly associated with **EV-A71**.
• **Myocarditis / Pericarditis**: Very rare.
• **Onychomadesis**: Painless shedding of the nails, typically occurring 1-2 months after the acute illness. The nails regrow normally.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**. The vast majority of children recover completely within 7 to 10 days without any long-term sequelae.
• Prognosis is more guarded for infants and those who develop severe neurologic or cardiopulmonary complications from **EV-A71**.
sections.preventionEducation:
• **Patient Education**: Reassure parents about the benign, self-limiting nature of the illness (usually resolves in 7-10 days).
• **Hygiene and Prevention**
    ◦ Stress the importance of **frequent and thorough handwashing**, especially after diaper changes or using the toilet.
    ◦ Disinfect contaminated surfaces and fomites.
• **Isolation**: Children should be kept out of daycare or school while they have a fever or weeping blisters. Viral shedding in stool can persist for weeks, making complete containment difficult.

sections.overview:
• *Clostridioides difficile* infection (CDI) is a gastrointestinal illness caused by the gram-positive, spore-forming, anaerobic bacillus, ***C. difficile***.
• It is the most common cause of **healthcare-associated infectious diarrhea**.
• The clinical spectrum ranges from mild, self-limiting diarrhea to severe, life-threatening conditions such as **pseudomembranous colitis** and **toxic megacolon**.
• Pathogenesis is driven by the production of toxins (**Toxin A** and **Toxin B**) that cause colonic inflammation and mucosal damage, typically following the disruption of normal gut flora by **antibiotic therapy**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ Causative agent: ***Clostridioides difficile*** (formerly *Clostridium difficile*).
    ◦ **Gram-positive**, **spore-forming**, **obligate anaerobic bacillus**.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Disruption of Normal Colonic Microbiota**: Typically caused by antibiotic use, which allows *C. difficile* to proliferate.
    ◦ **Fecal-Oral Transmission**: Ingestion of hardy, acid-resistant *C. difficile* spores from contaminated surfaces or hands.
    ◦ **Germination & Colonization**: Spores survive gastric acid, germinate into vegetative bacteria in the colon, and multiply.
    ◦ **Toxin Production**: The vegetative bacteria produce two primary exotoxins:
        ▪ **Toxin A (an enterotoxin)**: Binds to the brush border of the gut, causing inflammation, increased fluid secretion, and watery diarrhea.
        ▪ **Toxin B (a cytotoxin)**: More potent than Toxin A. Causes actin depolymerization, leading to destruction of the cellular cytoskeleton, cell death (apoptosis), and the formation of characteristic **pseudomembranes** (yellow-white plaques of inflammatory cells, fibrin, and necrotic debris).
    ◦ **Hypervirulent Strain (BI/NAP1/027)**: Produces significantly more Toxin A and B, and a third binary toxin, leading to more severe disease.
sections.epidemiology:
• Most common cause of **nosocomial (hospital-acquired) infectious diarrhea** in the United States and Europe.
• **Transmission**: **Fecal-oral route**.
    ◦ Spores are highly resilient and can persist on environmental surfaces (bedrails, toilets, medical equipment) for months.
    ◦ They are frequently transmitted via the hands of healthcare workers.
• **Highest incidence**: Hospitalized or institutionalized elderly patients.
• **Community-acquired CDI (CA-CDI)**: Increasing in incidence, often affecting younger individuals without traditional risk factors.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a patient who develops new-onset, profuse **watery diarrhea** during or shortly after a course of antibiotics.
• The onset of symptoms is typically **5-10 days** after starting antibiotics but can be delayed for up to 10 weeks after cessation.
• The disease exists on a spectrum from mild diarrhea to fulminant, life-threatening colitis.
sections.diagnostics:
• **When to Test**
    ◦ Only test stool from **symptomatic patients** (i.e., new-onset, unexplained diarrhea).
    ◦ Do not test asymptomatic patients or test for "proof of cure," as patients can remain colonized.
    ◦ Stool sample must be **loose/unformed**.
• **Stool Testing**
    ◦ **Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT/PCR)**: **Best initial test**.
        ▪ Highly sensitive for *C. diff* toxin genes.
        ▪ A negative result effectively **rules out CDI**.
        ▪ A positive result confirms the presence of a toxigenic strain but does not distinguish active infection from asymptomatic carriage.
    ◦ **Multi-step Algorithm (recommended)**: Combines a sensitive test with a specific one.
        ▪ Start with **GDH antigen test + Toxin EIA** OR **NAAT + Toxin EIA**.
        ▪ If both are positive, the result is positive for CDI.
        ▪ If tests are discordant (e.g., NAAT positive, Toxin EIA negative), the result is indeterminate and may reflect colonization. Clinical correlation is key.
• **Lab Findings (Blood)**
    ◦ **Leukocytosis**: WBC > 15,000 cells/L is a criterion for **severe disease**.
    ◦ **Acute Kidney Injury**: Serum creatinine ≥1.5 times baseline is a criterion for **severe disease**.
    ◦ **Hypoalbuminemia**: < 3.0 g/dL is a marker of **severe disease** and poor prognosis.
• **Imaging (reserved for severe/complicated cases)**
    ◦ **Abdominal X-ray (KUB)**: To evaluate for colonic dilation (**toxic megacolon** is defined as >6 cm dilation) or free air (perforation).
    ◦ **CT Abdomen/Pelvis**: More sensitive for showing marked colonic wall thickening (**accordion sign**), pericolic stranding, and ascites.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is generally good for mild-to-moderate disease treated appropriately.
• Mortality is significantly increased in elderly patients, those with multiple comorbidities, and those who develop severe or fulminant disease.
• **Fulminant colitis** carries a mortality rate of **30-50%**.
• The risk of recurrence is:
    ◦ **~25%** after a first episode
    ◦ **~45%** after a second
    ◦ **>60%** after three or more episodes.

sections.overview:
• *Salmonella* is a genus of **motile**, **gram-negative**, **facultative anaerobic rods** belonging to the Enterobacteriaceae family, representing a major cause of foodborne illness.
• The clinical spectrum ranges from self-limited gastroenteritis to life-threatening systemic illness known as **enteric (typhoid) fever**.
• Two main clinical entities are caused by different serotypes:
    ◦ **Non-typhoidal Salmonella (NTS):** Causes acute **gastroenteritis** (e.g., *S. Typhimurium*, *S. Enteritidis*).
    ◦ **Typhoidal Salmonella:** Causes **enteric fever** (e.g., *S. Typhi*, *S. Paratyphi*).
sections.etiology:
• **Organism**
    ◦ **Gram-negative**, flagellated (**motile**) rod.
    ◦ **Non-lactose fermenter**.
    ◦ Produces **hydrogen sulfide (H2S)**, which appears as **black colonies on Hektoen agar**.
• **Transmission**
    ◦ **Fecal-oral route**.
    ◦ Ingestion of contaminated food (poultry, eggs, dairy products, produce) or water.
    ◦ Direct contact with infected animals (especially **reptiles** like turtles, snakes, lizards) or their environment.
• **Pathogenesis**
    ◦ **Gastroenteritis (Non-typhoidal)**
        ▪ After ingestion, *Salmonella* survives gastric acid and invades epithelial cells of the small and large intestines, particularly the **M cells of Peyer's patches**.
        ▪ Triggers a massive acute inflammatory response, recruiting neutrophils into the intestinal lumen.
        ▪ This inflammation damages the mucosa, leading to increased fluid secretion and an **"inflammatory diarrhea."**
        ▪ The infection typically remains localized to the intestine in immunocompetent hosts.
    ◦ **Enteric (Typhoid) Fever (Typhoidal)**
        ▪ *S. Typhi* and *S. Paratyphi* are more invasive; after penetrating the intestinal epithelium, they are engulfed by macrophages.
        ▪ Possess a **Vi (virulence) capsule** that allows them to survive and replicate *within* macrophages.
        ▪ Infected macrophages transport the bacteria via the lymphatic system to the **reticuloendothelial system** (liver, spleen, bone marrow, lymph nodes).
        ▪ Leads to a sustained **bacteremia** and the systemic symptoms of enteric fever.
        ▪ A **chronic carrier state** can be established, with bacteria colonizing the **gallbladder**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Non-typhoidal**
    ◦ A leading cause of bacterial foodborne illness in the U.S. and worldwide.
    ◦ Incidence is highest in summer and fall.
    ◦ Outbreaks are often linked to contaminated poultry, eggs, and produce.
• **Typhoidal**
    ◦ Rare in developed countries; primarily seen in **travelers** returning from endemic regions (South Asia, Southeast Asia, Africa, Latin America).
    ◦ Endemic in areas with poor sanitation and unsafe drinking water.
    ◦ **Humans are the only reservoir**.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Host Factors**
    ◦ **Immunocompromised**: HIV/AIDS, malignancy, transplant recipients, corticosteroid use.
    ◦ **Extremes of age**: Infants (<1 year) and elderly (>65 years).
    ◦ **Reduced Gastric Acidity**: Achlorhydria, PPIs, H2-blockers, gastrectomy.
    ◦ **Sickle Cell Disease**: Markedly increased risk for *Salmonella* **bacteremia** and **osteomyelitis**.
    ◦ **Asplenia**: Increased risk for invasive disease.
    ◦ **Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD)**: Disrupted gut mucosa facilitates invasion.
• **Exposure Factors**
    ◦ Consumption of raw or undercooked eggs, poultry, meat, or unpasteurized dairy.
    ◦ Contact with **reptiles** (turtles, lizards, snakes) or amphibians.
    ◦ Travel to developing countries.
    ◦ Occupational exposure (veterinarians, poultry workers).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Non-typhoidal Gastroenteritis**
    ◦ **Incubation period**: 6-72 hours.
    ◦ **Abrupt onset** of nausea, vomiting, and crampy abdominal pain.
    ◦ Followed by **fever** (38-39°C) and diarrhea.
    ◦ Diarrhea is typically watery and large-volume but can be mucoid or grossly bloody (**inflammatory diarrhea**).
    ◦ Symptoms are usually **self-limited**, lasting 3-7 days.
