• **Enteric (Typhoid) Fever**
    ◦ **Incubation period**: 7-14 days.
    ◦ Insidious onset with a characteristic stepwise progression of fever over the first week.
    ◦ **Week 1**: Rising **"stepwise" fever**, malaise, headache, chills, and constipation or **"pea soup" diarrhea**.
    ◦ **Week 2**: **Sustained high fever**. Patient appears toxic. Classic findings include:
        ▪ **Relative bradycardia** (pulse-temperature dissociation or **Faget sign**).
        ▪ Faint, salmon-colored maculopapular rash known as **"rose spots"** on the trunk and abdomen.
        ▪ Abdominal distension/pain.
        ▪ **Hepatosplenomegaly** may develop.
    ◦ **Week 3**: Continued high fevers with potential for severe complications like **intestinal perforation** and **hemorrhage** if untreated.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Gastroenteritis**
    ◦ Fever.
    ◦ **Signs of dehydration**: tachycardia, hypotension, dry mucous membranes, decreased skin turgor.
    ◦ Diffuse abdominal tenderness on palpation.
    ◦ Hyperactive bowel sounds.
• **Enteric Fever**
    ◦ Ill-appearing, toxic patient with **sustained high fever**.
    ◦ **Relative Bradycardia (Faget Sign)**: Heart rate is lower than expected for the degree of fever.
    ◦ **Rose Spots**: Faint, blanching, salmon-colored macules, 2-4 mm in diameter, primarily on the chest and abdomen. Appear in week 2 and are often transient.
    ◦ **Hepatosplenomegaly**.
    ◦ Abdominal tenderness and distension.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Stool Culture**: **Gold standard** for diagnosing *Salmonella* gastroenteritis.
• **Blood Culture**: **Essential for diagnosing enteric fever**, with the highest yield during the first week of illness. Also indicated for suspected bacteremia in NTS.
• **Bone Marrow Culture**: The **most sensitive** diagnostic test for enteric fever (>90%), but invasive. Useful if blood cultures are negative after antibiotic administration.
• **Complete Blood Count (CBC)**: Often shows **leukopenia** and **neutropenia** in enteric fever. May be normal or show mild leukocytosis in gastroenteritis.
• **Liver Function Tests (LFTs)**: Often mildly elevated in enteric fever.
• **Serology (Widal Test)**: **Not recommended** for acute diagnosis due to poor sensitivity and specificity.
sections.treatment:
• **Non-typhoidal Gastroenteritis**
    ◦ **Supportive Care**: Mainstay of treatment for uncomplicated cases; focus on oral or IV **rehydration**.
    ◦ **Antibiotics**: **Not routinely recommended** as they do not shorten illness and may prolong the fecal carrier state.
        ▪ **Indications for Antibiotics**:
            ◦ Severe illness (high fever, severe diarrhea, hospitalization).
            ◦ High-risk patients: Infants <3 months, adults >50 with atherosclerosis, **immunocompromised**, **sickle cell disease**, patients with prosthetic joints or heart valves.
        ▪ **Antibiotic Choice (if indicated)**:
            ◦ Adults: **Ciprofloxacin** or **Levofloxacin**.
            ◦ Children/Pregnancy: **Ceftriaxone** or **Azithromycin**.
• **Enteric (Typhoid) Fever**
    ◦ **Antibiotics are always required**.
    ◦ **First-line**: **Fluoroquinolones** (e.g., **Ciprofloxacin**), but resistance is widespread. Susceptibility testing is crucial.
    ◦ **Alternative/Resistant Strains**: **Ceftriaxone (IV)** or **Azithromycin (oral)** are now often preferred.
• **Chronic Carrier State (*S. Typhi* in Gallbladder)**
    ◦ Prolonged course of a fluoroquinolone (e.g., **Ciprofloxacin for 4-6 weeks**).
    ◦ **Cholecystectomy** may be required for eradication, especially if gallstones are present.
sections.management:
• **Infection Control**: Standard contact precautions and emphasis on hand hygiene.
• **Public Health**: Salmonellosis is a **reportable disease**; notify public health departments to investigate outbreaks.
• **Symptom Management**: Antipyretics for fever.
    ◦ **Antidiarrheal agents (loperamide) are generally contraindicated** in inflammatory diarrhea, as they may increase the risk of toxic megacolon.
sections.complications:
• **Gastroenteritis**
    ◦ Severe dehydration, electrolyte abnormalities, bacteremia.
    ◦ **Reactive arthritis (Reiter's syndrome)**.
• **Enteric Fever**
    ◦ **Gastrointestinal hemorrhage and perforation** (most serious, typically in the 3rd week).
    ◦ Toxic megacolon, cholecystitis, pancreatitis.
    ◦ Neurologic: Encephalopathy, meningitis.
    ◦ Cardiovascular: Myocarditis, pericarditis.
    ◦ Relapse.
• **Bacteremia / Focal Infections** (more common with NTS in high-risk groups)
    ◦ **Osteomyelitis** (especially in **Sickle Cell Disease**).
    ◦ Endocarditis, **mycotic aneurysm** (especially in elderly with atherosclerosis).
    ◦ Meningitis (infants).
sections.prognosis:
• **Non-typhoidal Gastroenteritis**: **Excellent**. Typically self-limited in healthy individuals. Mortality is very low (<1%) but higher in the elderly and immunocompromised.
• **Enteric Fever**: **Good with prompt antibiotic therapy** (mortality rate <1%). If left untreated, the mortality rate can be as high as 10-30%.
sections.preventionEducation:
• Counsel on proper food handling (cook poultry thoroughly), avoiding cross-contamination, and hand washing, especially after handling raw meat or reptiles.
• Travelers to endemic areas should be advised on food and water precautions ("boil it, cook it, peel it, or forget it") and typhoid vaccination.

sections.overview:
• Shigellosis is an acute bacterial infectious gastroenteritis caused by species of the genus *Shigella*
    ◦ It is a major cause of **bacillary dysentery**, characterized by frequent, small-volume, **bloody, and mucoid stools**
    ◦ The illness is typically marked by an abrupt onset of **high fever**, **abdominal cramps**, and **tenesmus**
    ◦ It is highly contagious due to a very low infectious dose and is primarily transmitted via the **fecal-oral route**
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**: *Shigella* species, which are **Gram-negative**, non-motile, non-spore-forming, facultative anaerobic rods belonging to the Enterobacteriaceae family
    ◦ ***S. sonnei***: Most common species in the developed world (e.g., United States). Usually causes a milder, watery diarrhea
    ◦ ***S. flexneri***: Most common species in developing countries
    ◦ ***S. dysenteriae***: Most severe form. Produces **Shiga toxin**, which can lead to severe complications like **Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS)**
    ◦ ***S. boydii***: Less common
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Transmission**: **Fecal-oral route**. Ingestion of contaminated food, water, or direct person-to-person contact
    ◦ **Low Infectious Dose**: Highly virulent; as few as **10-100 organisms** can cause infection
    ◦ **Invasion**: *Shigella* is acid-resistant and survives transit through the stomach. It primarily invades the **terminal ileum and colon**
    ◦ **Mechanism**: It invades M cells in Peyer's patches and subsequently spreads laterally to adjacent colonic epithelial cells using the host cell's actin polymerization ("**actin rockets**"). This cell-to-cell spread allows it to evade host immune defenses in the lumen
    ◦ **Inflammation**: The invasion triggers a massive inflammatory response, leading to mucosal ulceration, abscess formation, and necrosis. This results in the characteristic stool containing blood, mucus, and pus (leukocytes)
    ◦ **Toxin Production**: *S. dysenteriae* produces **Shiga toxin**, an exotoxin that inhibits protein synthesis by cleaving the 60S ribosomal subunit, leading to endothelial damage, cell death, and contributing to the severity of dysentery and risk of HUS
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Global disease, with highest burden in developing nations with poor sanitation
• **Primary Population**: Predominantly affects **children under 5 years of age**
• **Common Settings**: Outbreaks are common in crowded settings with suboptimal hygiene, such as **daycare centers**, nursing homes, prisons, and residential institutions
• **Transmission**: The "**Four Fs**": **F**ingers, **F**lies, **F**ood, and **F**eces
• **Seasonality**: In temperate climates, incidence peaks in the summer and early fall
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is biphasic:
    ◦ **Early Phase (Prodrome)**: Begins 1-4 days after exposure. Characterized by watery, non-bloody diarrhea, crampy abdominal pain, and high fever. This is due to enterotoxin activity in the small intestine
    ◦ **Later Phase (Invasive/Colonic)**: Follows 1-2 days later. The infection localizes to the colon, leading to the classic dysentery syndrome
sections.diagnostics:
• **Stool Studies**
    ◦ **Stool Culture**: **Definitive diagnosis**. Isolates the organism and allows for antimicrobial susceptibility testing
        ▪ **Media**: **MacConkey agar** (non-lactose fermenting colonies), **Hektoen (HE) agar** (green colonies, no black H2S production like *Salmonella*)
    ◦ **Stool Microscopy**: Presence of numerous **fecal leukocytes (WBCs)** and red blood cells (RBCs) is highly suggestive of an invasive bacterial process like Shigellosis
    ◦ **Stool PCR Panels**: Rapid molecular tests (e.g., GI pathogen panels) are increasingly used for faster diagnosis but may not provide susceptibility data
• **Blood Work**
    ◦ **CBC**: May show **leukocytosis** with a prominent **left shift (bandemia)**. Hemoconcentration if dehydrated. If HUS is suspected, look for **anemia** and **thrombocytopenia**
    ◦ **BMP**: To assess for **electrolyte disturbances** and **acute kidney injury** (elevated BUN/Creatinine)
sections.prognosis:
• In healthy individuals with access to care, shigellosis is typically **self-limiting** and resolves within 5-7 days
• Prognosis is excellent for infections caused by ***S. sonnei***
• Morbidity and mortality are significantly higher with ***S. dysenteriae*** infections, in malnourished children, infants, the elderly, and in cases complicated by **HUS** or **toxic megacolon**

sections.overview:
• *Campylobacter* is a genus of Gram-negative bacteria and a leading cause of bacterial gastroenteritis worldwide, with ***Campylobacter jejuni*** being the most common species causing human disease
    ◦ Infection, known as campylobacteriosis, typically presents as an acute, self-limiting diarrheal illness
    ◦ Classically associated with the consumption of **undercooked poultry**
    ◦ Infamous for its potential post-infectious complication, **Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS)**
sections.etiology:
• **Organism**
    ◦ Gram-negative, motile, curved or **"S-shaped" / "seagull-wing"** rods
    ◦ Microaerophilic (requires low oxygen) and thermophilic (grows best at elevated temperatures, **42°C**, which is the internal body temperature of birds)
• **Species**
    ◦ ***C. jejuni***: Accounts for >90% of human infections
    ◦ ***C. coli***: Less common, often associated with pigs
    ◦ ***C. fetus***: Rare cause of gastroenteritis; more likely to cause systemic infections (bacteremia, septic thrombophlebitis) in immunocompromised individuals and neonates
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Ingestion:** A low infectious dose (as few as 500 organisms) is required. Sources are typically contaminated food (poultry), unpasteurized milk, or contaminated water
    ◦ **Colonization:** The organism's motility allows it to penetrate the viscous mucous layer of the small and large intestines
    ◦ **Invasion & Inflammation:** *Campylobacter* adheres to and invades intestinal epithelial cells, triggering a significant local inflammatory response that causes cell damage, leading to exudate, fluid loss, and bleeding into the lumen
    ◦ **Toxin Production:** Produces **cytolethal distending toxin (CDT)**, which arrests the host cell cycle and leads to cell death, contributing to mucosal damage
    ◦ **Molecular Mimicry (GBS):** The lipooligosaccharide (LOS) on the surface of some *C. jejuni* strains resembles human gangliosides found on nerve cell axons
        ▪ The host's immune response (antibodies) against the bacterial LOS can cross-react with these neural gangliosides, leading to acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy, i.e., Guillain-Barré Syndrome
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence:** One of the most common causes of bacterial diarrhea in the United States and worldwide
• **Transmission:** Fecal-oral route. Primarily a foodborne zoonosis
• **Reservoir:** Gastrointestinal tracts of various animals, especially **chickens** and cattle
• **Seasonal Peak:** Occurs more frequently in the summer and early fall
• **Demographics:** Bimodal age distribution, with peaks in children <5 years old and young adults (15-29 years old)
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Incubation Period:** Typically 2-5 days (range 1-10 days)
• **Prodrome:** A 12-24 hour prodrome of fever, headache, myalgia, and malaise is common before the onset of GI symptoms
• **Gastrointestinal Phase**
    ◦ Characterized by the abrupt onset of severe abdominal cramping followed by diarrhea
    ◦ Diarrhea is initially watery and voluminous, but within 1-2 days frequently becomes bloody and mucoid
    ◦ The illness is typically self-limited, lasting about one week
sections.diagnostics:
• **Stool Studies (Definitive Diagnosis)**
    ◦ **Stool Culture:** The gold standard
        ▪ Requires special laboratory conditions: a selective medium (e.g., Skirrow or Campy BAP) and incubation in a microaerophilic (5% O2, 10% CO2) environment at **42°C**
    ◦ **Stool PCR:** Many hospitals now use multiplex GI PCR panels which are rapid and sensitive for detecting *Campylobacter* DNA along with other pathogens
    ◦ **Stool Microscopy**
        ▪ **Fecal Leukocytes & Erythrocytes:** Usually present, indicating an inflammatory process
        ▪ **Gram Stain:** May reveal characteristic **"S-shaped" or "gull-wing" rods**, but sensitivity is low
• **Blood Work**
    ◦ **CBC:** May show leukocytosis with a left shift
    ◦ **CMP:** To assess for electrolyte abnormalities and dehydration (e.g., hypokalemia, metabolic acidosis)
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis for uncomplicated gastroenteritis is **excellent**
• The illness is typically self-limiting and resolves within 5-7 days without specific therapy
• Prognosis is more guarded for patients who develop GBS, although most make a significant recovery with supportive care (e.g., IVIG, plasmapheresis)
    ◦ Some may have permanent neurological deficits

sections.overview:
• Vibrio species are motile, curved (comma-shaped), **gram-negative rods** found in aquatic environments, particularly brackish or saltwater.
• The two most clinically significant species are:
    ◦ ***Vibrio cholerae***: The causative agent of **cholera**, a toxigenic disease characterized by severe, life-threatening secretory diarrhea.
    ◦ ***Vibrio parahaemolyticus***: A common cause of **seafood-associated gastroenteritis** and wound infections.
• **Cholera** is characterized by severe diarrhea, while **V. parahaemolyticus** causes a milder, often self-limited gastroenteritis or potentially severe wound infections.
sections.etiology:
• **Microbiology**: **Gram-negative**, facultative anaerobic, **motile** (single polar flagellum), **comma-shaped** rods.
• **Oxidase-positive**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **V. cholerae**:
    ◦ Primarily found in developing countries with inadequate water purification and sanitation.
    ◦ Endemic in parts of Africa, Southeast Asia, and Latin America.
    ◦ Outbreaks are common after natural disasters (e.g., hurricanes, earthquakes) that disrupt water supplies.
• **V. parahaemolyticus**:
    ◦ The leading cause of **seafood-associated gastroenteritis** in the United States and worldwide.
    ◦ Found naturally in coastal marine environments.
    ◦ Infections are more common in warmer months (**"summer diarrhea"**).
sections.riskFactors:
• **V. cholerae**:
    ◦ Travel to an endemic region.
    ◦ Consumption of contaminated water or food.
    ◦ **Achlorhydria** or **hypochlorhydria** (e.g., chronic PPI use, gastrectomy).
    ◦ **Blood type O** (associated with more severe disease).
• **V. parahaemolyticus**:
    ◦ Consumption of raw or undercooked shellfish, especially **oysters**.
    ◦ Exposure of open wounds to seawater or brackish water.
    ◦ Pre-existing liver disease (**cirrhosis**), **hemochromatosis**, or immunocompromised states (increased risk for severe disease and sepsis).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **V. cholerae**:
    ◦ Presents with the abrupt onset of severe, voluminous, watery diarrhea.
    ◦ The patient appears acutely ill, lethargic, and rapidly becomes dehydrated.
    ◦ The key feature is the sheer volume of fluid loss, which can exceed 1 liter per hour.
    ◦ Vomiting may also be present.
    ◦ **Fever is notably absent**.
• **V. parahaemolyticus**:
    ◦ **Gastroenteritis**:
        ▪ Presents as an acute, self-limited illness with watery diarrhea, abdominal cramping, nausea, and vomiting.
        ▪ Symptoms begin within 24 hours of exposure.
    ◦ **Wound Infection**:
        ▪ Presents as cellulitis with erythema, edema, and pain at the site of a wound exposed to seawater.
        ▪ Can rapidly progress to **hemorrhagic bullae** and **necrotizing fasciitis**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Stool Studies**:
    ◦ **Gross Inspection**:
        ▪ **"Rice-water" appearance** is classic for cholera.
    ◦ **Microscopy**:
        ▪ **Cholera**: No fecal leukocytes or erythrocytes. Dark-field microscopy may show motile, **comma-shaped bacilli**.
        ▪ **V. parahaemolyticus**: Fecal leukocytes and erythrocytes may be present.
    ◦ **Stool Culture**:
        ▪ **Definitive test**.
        ▪ Requires a special selective medium: **Thiosulfate-Citrate-Bile salts-Sucrose (TCBS) agar**.
            ▪ ***V. cholerae*** ferments sucrose and produces **yellow colonies**.
            ▪ ***V. parahaemolyticus*** does not ferment sucrose and produces **green colonies**.
• **Laboratory Studies**:
    ◦ **CBC**: **Elevated hematocrit** and hemoglobin (hemoconcentration) from dehydration.
    ◦ **BMP/CMP**:
        ▪ **Hyponatremia**, **Hypokalemia**.
        ▪ **Elevated BUN and Creatinine** (pre-renal azotemia from dehydration).
        ▪ **Metabolic Acidosis** (non-anion gap) due to bicarbonate loss in stool.
        ▪ **Hypoglycemia** (especially in children).
sections.management:
• **Fluid Status**: Closely monitor vital signs, urine output, and mental status.
    ◦ **"Cholera cots"** (cots with a hole to collect and measure stool output) are used in epidemic settings.
• **Electrolytes**: Monitor and replete potassium as needed.
• **Nutrition**: Resume feeding as soon as vomiting subsides and the patient is rehydrated.
• **Public Health**: Cholera is a **reportable disease**. Public health efforts focus on ensuring access to safe drinking water and proper sanitation.
• **Contraindications**: **Anti-motility agents** (e.g., loperamide) are contraindicated in severe disease as they can increase toxin-related complications.
sections.complications:
• **Severe Dehydration**, **Hypovolemic Shock**, **Multi-organ failure**
• **Acute Kidney Injury** (pre-renal)
• **Severe Electrolyte Disturbances**:
    ◦ **Hypokalemia** can lead to cardiac arrhythmias, paralytic ileus.
• **Metabolic Acidosis**
• **Hypoglycemia**
• For *V. parahaemolyticus* wound infections: **Necrotizing Fasciitis**, **Sepsis**, and **Limb Loss**.
sections.prognosis:
• **V. cholerae**:
    ◦ With prompt and adequate rehydration, the mortality rate is **<1%**.
    ◦ Without treatment, mortality can be as high as **50-60%**.
• **V. parahaemolyticus**:
    ◦ Gastroenteritis has an excellent prognosis.
    ◦ The prognosis for severe wound infections or sepsis depends on the speed of diagnosis and intervention, with mortality rates being significantly higher.

sections.overview:
• **Norovirus** is a highly contagious single-stranded RNA virus belonging to the *Caliciviridae* family.
	◦ It is the leading cause of **acute gastroenteritis (AGE)** outbreaks worldwide, affecting all age groups.
	◦ Often referred to as the "**stomach flu**," it is not related to influenza.
• The illness is characterized by the **acute onset** of **nausea**, **projectile vomiting**, **watery non-bloody diarrhea**, and **abdominal cramps**.
• It is typically **self-limiting** in healthy individuals but can cause **severe dehydration** and complications in vulnerable populations.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
	◦ **Non-enveloped, single-stranded RNA virus** from the *Caliciviridae* family.
		▪ Multiple genogroups exist, with **GII.4** being responsible for the majority of human outbreaks.
• **Transmission**
	◦ **Fecal-oral route (primary)**: Direct contact with an infected person.
	◦ **Fomites**: Consuming food or water contaminated with the virus. Touching contaminated surfaces and then the mouth.
	◦ **Aerosolization**: Inhalation of aerosolized viral particles from vomitus.
• **Pathophysiology**
	◦ **Ingestion**: Ingestion of a very low infectious dose (as few as 10-100 viral particles).
	◦ **Infection**: The virus targets and infects **enterocytes** of the small intestine, primarily the jejunum.
	◦ **Intestinal Damage**: Leads to **blunting of the intestinal villi**, causing malabsorption of fats and carbohydrates.
		▪ This results in a **malabsorptive, osmotic diarrhea**.
		▪ It does not cause significant mucosal invasion or inflammation.
	◦ **Symptom Onset**: The rapid onset of symptoms is due to **delayed gastric emptying** (causing nausea and vomiting) and the malabsorptive diarrhea.
		▪ The diarrhea is non-inflammatory and therefore **non-bloody**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: **Most common cause of epidemic gastroenteritis** globally.
	◦ Accounts for ~20% of all AGE cases.
• **Setting**: Outbreaks are common in **crowded, semi-closed environments**.
	◦ **Classic Settings**: Cruise ships, nursing homes, hospitals, schools, daycares, military barracks, restaurants.
• **Seasonality**: Predominantly occurs in the **winter months**, leading to the nickname "**winter vomiting disease**."
• **Incubation Period**: Very short, typically **12 to 48 hours**.
• **Duration of Illness**: Brief, lasting **24 to 72 hours**.
• **Viral Shedding**: Can occur for up to **2 weeks** (or longer in immunocompromised hosts) after symptom resolution, contributing to its high transmissibility.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is marked by an **abrupt onset** of severe gastrointestinal distress in a person who was previously well.
• The patient will typically report being around others with similar symptoms.
• The illness is **intense but brief**.
sections.diagnostics:
• Primarily a **clinical diagnosis**.
	◦ Laboratory confirmation is not necessary for most sporadic cases in healthy individuals.
• **When to Test**: Testing is reserved for outbreak investigations (public health), immunocompromised patients, or when the diagnosis is uncertain in a severely ill patient.
• **Gold Standard Test**: Stool testing with **Real-time Reverse Transcriptase-Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR)**.
• **Laboratory Studies** (if concerned for dehydration/complications):
	◦ **Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP)**: To assess for electrolyte abnormalities (**hyponatremia, hypokalemia**) and **acute kidney injury** (elevated BUN/Creatinine).
	◦ **Stool Studies**: **Fecal leukocytes** and **occult blood** will be **negative**, consistent with a non-inflammatory diarrheal process.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** in immunocompetent individuals.
• The illness is **self-limiting**, with full recovery typically within 1-3 days.
• Morbidity and mortality are significantly higher in the very young, the elderly, and the immunocompromised, primarily due to complications from **severe dehydration**.

sections.overview:
• **Rotavirus** is a highly contagious virus that is the leading cause of severe, **dehydrating gastroenteritis** in infants and young children worldwide.
• It is characterized by an **abrupt onset of vomiting** followed by profuse, **watery diarrhea**.
• While the illness is typically self-limited, the resulting **dehydration** is the primary cause of morbidity and mortality.
• The introduction of routine **rotavirus vaccination** has dramatically reduced the incidence and severity of the disease in many countries.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Virus:** Member of the *Reoviridae* family.
    ◦ **Structure:** Non-enveloped, double-stranded RNA virus. Its name derives from its characteristic "wheel-like" (Latin: *rota*) appearance on electron microscopy.
    ◦ **Serogroups:** Group A is responsible for >90% of human infections.
• **Transmission**
    ◦ Primarily **fecal-oral route**.
    ◦ The virus is extremely stable and can survive on fomites for extended periods. It is highly infectious, with a very small inoculum required for infection.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Infection:** The virus infects and destroys mature enterocytes at the tips of the villi in the small intestine, primarily the duodenum and jejunum.
    ◦ **Villus Blunting:** Destruction of enterocytes leads to villous atrophy and blunting. This impairs the intestine's absorptive capacity.
    ◦ **Malabsorption (Osmotic Diarrhea):**
        ▪ The damaged villi result in decreased production of brush-border enzymes, particularly **lactase**.
        ▪ The inability to break down complex carbohydrates (like lactose) creates a high osmotic load in the intestinal lumen, drawing water in and causing **osmotic diarrhea**.
    ◦ **Secretion (Secretory Diarrhea):**
        ▪ Rotavirus produces a viral enterotoxin, **NSP4**, which increases intracellular calcium concentration in enterocytes.
        ▪ This disrupts cellular transport processes, leading to chloride secretion into the lumen and causing a **secretory diarrhea**.
    ◦ **Result:** The combination of osmotic and secretory mechanisms produces the characteristic large-volume, **watery diarrhea** that can rapidly lead to severe **dehydration** and electrolyte imbalances.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Global:** The most common cause of severe diarrhea in children under 5 years old worldwide. A major cause of infant mortality in developing nations.
• **Pre-Vaccine Era:**
    ◦ Nearly every child was infected by age 5.
    ◦ Disease peaked in the winter months in temperate climates, earning it the nickname "winter vomiting disease."
• **Post-Vaccine Era:**
    ◦ In countries with routine vaccination, there has been a >80% reduction in rotavirus-related hospitalizations and emergency department visits.
    ◦ The distinct seasonality has also become less pronounced.
• **Peak Incidence:** Most severe disease occurs in children **6 months to 2 years of age**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A classic clinical vignette describes an **unvaccinated infant or toddler**, typically in the winter, who develops an **abrupt onset of vomiting** and **low-grade fever**.
    ◦ Within 24-48 hours, the child develops **frequent, large-volume, non-bloody, watery diarrhea**.
    ◦ The patient often appears irritable or lethargic due to **dehydration**.
• **Incubation Period:** ~48 hours.
• **Course of Illness:**
    ◦ Vomiting and fever usually resolve within 2-3 days.
    ◦ The diarrhea is the most prominent and persistent symptom, lasting 5-8 days.
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is typically made clinically based on the classic history and presentation.
• Laboratory confirmation is usually reserved for atypical cases, public health surveillance, or severely ill patients.
• **Stool Studies:**
    ◦ **Stool Antigen Test (Enzyme Immunoassay - EIA):**
        ▪ The most common, rapid, and cost-effective diagnostic test.
        ▪ High sensitivity and specificity.
    ◦ **Stool PCR:**
        ▪ More sensitive; often used in outbreak investigations.
    ◦ **Stool analysis:**
        ▪ Fecal leukocytes are typically absent.
        ▪ Stool is negative for occult blood.
• **Serum Labs (indicated for moderate-to-severe dehydration):**
    ◦ **Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP):** To assess for electrolyte abnormalities (**hyponatremia**, **hypernatremia**, **hypokalemia**) and evidence of pre-renal azotemia (**elevated BUN/Creatinine**).
    ◦ **Serum Bicarbonate:** May be low, indicating a **non-anion gap metabolic acidosis** from bicarbonate loss in stool.
sections.prognosis:
• In developed countries with access to rehydration therapy, the prognosis is excellent, and mortality is rare.
• The illness is self-limited and typically resolves completely within 5-8 days without long-term sequelae.
• In resource-limited settings, it remains a leading cause of childhood mortality due to untreated severe **dehydration**.

sections.overview:
• Tetanus is a severe, often fatal neurologic disease caused by the neurotoxin **tetanospasmin**, produced by the bacterium *Clostridium tetani*.
    ◦ Characterized by progressive, painful muscle rigidity and spasms.
    ◦ Not contagious from person to person and is an entirely vaccine-preventable disease.
• The classic presentation involves **trismus** ("lockjaw"), followed by a **descending pattern** of muscle spasms.
• Diagnosis is **clinical**, and treatment is focused on supportive care, neutralization of unbound toxin, and eradication of the bacteria.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**: *Clostridium tetani*
    ◦ Gram-positive, obligate anaerobic, spore-forming bacillus (rod).
    ◦ Spores are highly resilient and found ubiquitously in soil, dust, and animal (especially horse) feces.
    ◦ Spores can appear as a "tennis racket" or "drumstick" on microscopy.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Entry**: Spores are introduced into the body, typically through a puncture wound, laceration, crush injury, burn, or injection site. The wound provides the necessary anaerobic environment for germination.
    ◦ **Germination**: In the anaerobic wound environment, spores germinate into vegetative, toxin-producing bacteria.
    ◦ **Toxin Production**: The bacteria produce **tetanospasmin**, a potent neurotoxin.
    ◦ **Toxin Transport**: Tetanospasmin travels via retrograde axonal transport from the peripheral nerves to the central nervous system (spinal cord and brainstem).
    ◦ **Mechanism of Action**: The toxin binds irreversibly to presynaptic nerve terminals of inhibitory interneurons.
        ▪ It acts as a protease, cleaving synaptobrevin (a SNARE protein), which blocks the release of inhibitory neurotransmitters **GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid)** and **glycine**.
    ◦ **Result**: Loss of central inhibition leads to unopposed alpha motor neuron firing, resulting in sustained, tonic muscle contraction (**spastic paralysis**) and painful spasms.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Global**: More common in low-income countries with low vaccination rates and poor obstetric care (leading to neonatal tetanus from umbilical stump contamination).
• **United States**: Rare due to high vaccination rates, with approximately 30 cases reported annually.
• **Demographics in US**: Primarily affects individuals who are unvaccinated or inadequately vaccinated, particularly:
    ◦ Adults >60 years old with waning immunity.
    ◦ Individuals with diabetes (e.g., foot ulcers).
    ◦ Intravenous drug users.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Inadequate Immunization**: The single most important risk factor.
• **Tetanus-prone wounds**:
    ◦ Puncture wounds (e.g., nails, splinters).
    ◦ Wounds contaminated with soil, dust, or feces.
    ◦ Crush injuries.
    ◦ Burns or frostbite.
    ◦ Avulsions and major lacerations.
    ◦ Intravenous drug use (skin popping).
    ◦ Non-sterile procedures (e.g., piercings, tattoos, childbirth, abortion).
    ◦ Chronic wounds (e.g., diabetic foot ulcers).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Incubation Period**: Typically 3 to 21 days (average 8-10 days).
    ◦ A shorter incubation period correlates with more severe disease and a worse prognosis.
• **Pattern**: Classically presents with a **descending pattern** of muscle rigidity.
• **Sensorium**: The patient remains **fully conscious and alert** with a clear sensorium, which can make the experience particularly terrifying.
• **Fever**: Usually absent or low-grade unless a secondary infection is present.
• **Symptoms**:
    ◦ **Presenting Symptom**: **Trismus ("Lockjaw")** is the most common and earliest sign; patients complain of jaw pain or stiffness.
    ◦ Neck stiffness and pain.
    ◦ **Dysphagia** (difficulty swallowing).
    ◦ Painful, involuntary muscle spasms, often triggered by minor stimuli (noise, light, touch).
    ◦ Abdominal rigidity.
    ◦ Back pain and stiffness.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Trismus**: Inability to open the mouth fully due to masseter muscle spasm.
• **Risus Sardonicus**: A characteristic facial expression combining a sardonic "grin" with elevated eyebrows, caused by facial muscle spasms.
• **Opisthotonos**: Severe, sustained spasm of the paraspinal muscles causing hyperextension and arching of the back.
• **Board-like abdominal rigidity**.
• **Generalized Spasms**: Intense, painful, whole-body spasms that can be strong enough to cause fractures.
• **Autonomic Instability** (in severe cases):
    ◦ Tachycardia, labile hypertension, profuse sweating (**diaphoresis**), arrhythmias. This is a late and ominous sign.
• **Spatula Test**: Touching the posterior pharynx with a spatula elicits a reflex masseter spasm (biting down) instead of the normal gag reflex. High specificity.
sections.diagnostics:
• Tetanus is a **clinical diagnosis** based on history and physical exam findings.
    ◦ There are no specific laboratory tests to confirm it.
• **Wound Cultures**: Often negative for *C. tetani* and are not reliable for diagnosis.
• **Labs**: Generally non-specific.
    ◦ **CBC** may be normal.
    ◦ **CK** can be elevated due to **rhabdomyolysis** from severe muscle contractions.
• **CSF**: Normal.
• **EMG**: May show continuous motor unit activity but is not required for diagnosis.
sections.treatment:
• **Human Tetanus Immune Globulin (TIG)**: Administer a single IM dose of 3000-5000 units. TIG can only neutralize circulating toxin that has not yet bound to nerve terminals.
• **Wound Debridement**: Thoroughly clean and debride the wound to remove spores and necrotic tissue.
• **Antibiotics**: **Metronidazole** (500 mg IV q6-8h) is the drug of choice.
    ◦ **Penicillin G** is an alternative but is a GABA antagonist and may theoretically worsen spasms.
• **Benzodiazepines**: Mainstay of therapy. **Diazepam** or **Lorazepam** IV are used to enhance GABA-mediated inhibition. Often requires very high, continuous doses.
• If spasms are uncontrolled with benzodiazepines, use neuromuscular blocking agents (e.g., vecuronium) with mechanical ventilation.
• **Magnesium Sulfate**: Can help stabilize blood pressure and control spasms.
• **Labetalol** or other short-acting agents for hypertension and tachycardia.
sections.management:
• **Supportive Care**: Place the patient in a **dark, quiet room** to minimize external stimuli (noise, light, touch) that can trigger spasms.
• **Immunization**: **Tetanus infection does not confer immunity**.
    ◦ All patients with tetanus should receive a full course of active immunization with the tetanus toxoid vaccine (e.g., Tdap or Td) once they have recovered.
    ◦ The first dose should be given during hospitalization, at a separate site from the TIG injection.
• **Nutrition and Hydration**: Often requires enteral or parenteral nutrition due to dysphagia and prolonged ICU stay.
sections.complications:
• **Respiratory**:
    ◦ Laryngospasm
    ◦ Aspiration pneumonia
    ◦ Respiratory failure/arrest
• **Musculoskeletal**:
    ◦ Vertebral compression fractures
    ◦ Long bone fractures
    ◦ **Rhabdomyolysis** leading to acute kidney injury
• **Autonomic**:
    ◦ Labile hypertension/hypotension
    ◦ Arrhythmias
    ◦ Sudden cardiac arrest
• **Other**:
    ◦ DVT/PE due to immobility
    ◦ Nosocomial infections
sections.prognosis:
• With modern ICU care, mortality in the US is approximately 10-20%.
• Mortality is much higher in developing countries and in neonates or the elderly.
• Recovery is slow, taking weeks to months, as it requires the sprouting of new nerve terminals.
    ◦ Full recovery is possible.
• Predictors of poor prognosis include:
    ◦ Short incubation period (<7 days)
    ◦ Rapid progression of symptoms
    ◦ Development of autonomic dysfunction

sections.overview:
• **Botulism** is a rare but life-threatening **neuroparalytic illness** caused by **botulinum neurotoxin (BoNT)** produced by the bacterium ***Clostridium botulinum***
	◦ The toxin acts at the neuromuscular junction to cause a **symmetric, descending flaccid paralysis**
	◦ It is considered a **medical and public health emergency**
	◦ The classic clinical presentation is an **afebrile** patient with a **normal sensorium** who develops **acute, bilateral cranial neuropathies** followed by **symmetric descending weakness**
sections.etiology:
• **Etiologic Agent**: ***Clostridium botulinum***
	◦ Gram-positive, obligate anaerobic, spore-forming rod
	◦ Spores are heat-resistant and ubiquitous in soil
• **Toxin**: **Botulinum neurotoxin (BoNT)**
	◦ One of the most potent lethal substances known
	◦ Eight serotypes exist (A-H); types A, B, E, and F cause most human disease
• **Pathophysiology**
	◦ The toxin is absorbed into the bloodstream and travels to peripheral cholinergic nerve terminals (neuromuscular junction, autonomic ganglia)
	◦ It binds **irreversibly** to the presynaptic membrane and is internalized
	◦ Inside the nerve terminal, the toxin's light chain (a zinc-endopeptidase) cleaves **SNARE proteins** (e.g., SNAP-25, synaptobrevin)
	◦ Cleavage of SNARE proteins prevents the fusion of acetylcholine (ACh)-containing vesicles with the cell membrane
	◦ This **blocks the presynaptic release of acetylcholine**
	◦ The result is a failure of neurotransmission, leading to muscle weakness and **flaccid paralysis**
	◦ Recovery requires the sprouting of new nerve terminals and the formation of new synapses, which is a slow process (weeks to months)
sections.epidemiology:
• **Infant Botulism**: Most common form in the U.S.
	◦ Occurs in infants <12 months old who ingest ***C. botulinum* spores** (e.g., from **honey** or contaminated soil/dust), which then germinate and produce toxin in the gut
• **Foodborne Botulism**
	◦ Caused by **ingestion of pre-formed toxin** in contaminated food, typically from improperly preserved or **home-canned**, low-acid foods (e.g., green beans, corn, beets)
• **Wound Botulism**
	◦ Occurs when ***C. botulinum* spores contaminate a wound**, germinate in the anaerobic environment, and produce toxin
	◦ Increasingly associated with subcutaneous or intramuscular injection of **"black tar" heroin**
• **Iatrogenic Botulism**
	◦ Results from an overdose of botulinum toxin used for cosmetic (e.g., Botox) or therapeutic purposes
• **Inhalation Botulism**
	◦ Does not occur naturally but is a significant **bioterrorism concern**
sections.riskFactors:
• **Infant Botulism**: Age < 1 year, consumption of **honey**, exposure to soil/dust (e.g., from construction sites).
• **Foodborne Botulism**: Consumption of **home-canned foods**, preserved fish, fermented foods, or other improperly stored food items.
• **Wound Botulism**: Traumatic wounds contaminated with soil, **injection drug use** ("skin popping").
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The hallmark of botulism is an **acute onset of symmetric, descending flaccid paralysis in an afebrile patient with a clear sensorium**
	◦ **Incubation Period**
		▪ Foodborne: 12-36 hours (range: 6 hours to 10 days)
		▪ Wound: ~7 days
	◦ Progression is typically from cranial nerves to the upper extremities, trunk, and then lower extremities
• **Symptoms**
	◦ **Cranial Nerve Palsies (The "4 D's")**
		▪ **Diplopia**: Blurry or double vision (often the first symptom)
		▪ **Dysphagia**: Difficulty swallowing
		▪ **Dysarthria**: Slurred speech
		▪ **Dysphonia**: Hoarse or weak voice
	◦ **Autonomic Dysfunction**
		▪ Dry mouth (xerostomia)
		▪ Fixed, dilated pupils (mydriasis)
		▪ Urinary retention
		▪ Constipation / ileus
		▪ Orthostatic hypotension
	◦ **Descending Muscle Weakness**
		▪ Weakness of neck muscles ("floppy head")
		▪ Symmetric weakness in shoulders and arms, progressing to lower limbs
		▪ Shortness of breath, progressing to respiratory failure
	◦ **Infant-Specific Symptoms**
		▪ Constipation (often the earliest sign)
		▪ Poor feeding, weak suck
		▪ Lethargy, diminished facial expression
		▪ Weak, altered cry
		▪ Loss of head control ("floppy baby")
sections.physicalExam:
• **General**: Alert and oriented patient, often anxious. **Afebrile**.
• **HEENT/Neuro**
	◦ Bilateral ptosis
	◦ **Pupils**: **Dilated and poorly reactive or non-reactive to light (mydriasis)**
	◦ Extraocular muscle palsies (e.g., CN VI palsy causing disconjugate gaze)
	◦ Bilateral facial weakness
	◦ Diminished or absent gag reflex
• **Motor Exam**
	◦ Symmetric, descending weakness
	◦ Hypotonia
• **Deep Tendon Reflexes (DTRs)**: Diminished or absent
• **Sensory Exam**: **SENSATION IS INTACT**. This is a critical finding.
• **Respiratory**: Use of accessory muscles, paradoxical breathing pattern, leading to respiratory arrest
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is primarily **clinical**. Do not delay treatment while awaiting test results.
• **Confirmatory Tests**
	◦ **Toxin Assay (Mouse Bioassay)**: Gold standard. Detects BoNT in patient's serum, stool, gastric aspirate, or a food sample.
		▪ Results take several days.
	◦ **Culture**: Anaerobic culture of stool (infant) or wound tissue for ***C. botulinum***
• **Electromyography (EMG) / Repetitive Nerve Stimulation (RNS)**
	◦ Highly suggestive finding: **Brief, low-amplitude motor unit potentials** on EMG
	◦ **Incremental response (facilitation) to high-frequency (20-50 Hz) repetitive nerve stimulation**. This post-activation facilitation is characteristic.
• **Ancillary Tests (to rule out other diagnoses)**
	◦ **CSF Analysis**: Typically normal (acellular with normal protein), helping to differentiate from Guillain-Barr Syndrome
	◦ **Brain Imaging (CT/MRI)**: Normal
sections.treatment:
• **Adults/Children (>1 year)**: **Heptavalent Botulism Antitoxin (BAT)**, derived from equine sources
• **Infants (<1 year)**: **Botulism Immune Globulin Intravenous (BIG-IV, BabyBIG)**, derived from human sources
• **Wound Botulism**: Penicillin G or metronidazole is indicated to eradicate the organism, but only **AFTER** antitoxin has been administered
• **Foodborne/Infant Botulism**: Antibiotics are **NOT** recommended, as bacterial lysis may increase toxin release in the gut
• **AVOID AMINOGLYCOSIDES**, as they can potentiate neuromuscular blockade
sections.management:
• **Supportive Care is Paramount**
	◦ **Respiratory Monitoring**: Meticulous monitoring of respiratory status with serial measurements of vital capacity and negative inspiratory force (NIF). Elective intubation and **mechanical ventilation** are often required for impending respiratory failure.
	◦ **Nutritional Support**: Dysphagia necessitates enteral feeding (e.g., nasogastric tube).
	◦ **Autonomic Care**: Management of urinary retention (catheterization), constipation, and orthostatic hypotension.
	◦ **General ICU Care**: DVT prophylaxis, pressure ulcer prevention, physical therapy.
• **Public Health**: Botulism is a **reportable disease**. Immediately notify local and state health departments and the CDC to investigate the source and prevent further cases.
sections.complications:
• Acute respiratory failure (most common cause of death)
• Prolonged mechanical ventilation
• Nosocomial infections (ventilator-associated pneumonia, catheter-associated UTI)
• Aspiration pneumonia
• Complications of immobility (DVT, PE, contractures, pressure ulcers)
sections.prognosis:
• With timely diagnosis, antitoxin administration, and modern intensive care (especially mechanical ventilation), the mortality rate has decreased from >50% to **<5%**
• Recovery is **very slow (weeks to months)** as it requires the regeneration of presynaptic nerve terminals
• Most patients eventually make a full or near-full recovery, but fatigue and shortness of breath can persist for years

sections.overview:
• Anthrax is an acute infectious disease caused by the spore-forming, gram-positive bacterium ***Bacillus anthracis***.
    ◦ It is primarily a zoonosis, affecting herbivores, but can be transmitted to humans through contact with infected animals or their products.
    ◦ It is not typically transmitted person-to-person.
    ◦ It is a significant public health concern due to its potential use as a bioterrorism agent.
    ◦ Clinical presentation depends on the route of exposure, leading to four main forms: **cutaneous**, **inhalational**, **gastrointestinal**, and **injectional**.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent:** ***Bacillus anthracis***, a large, aerobic, gram-positive, encapsulated, spore-forming rod.
• **Transmission:** Occurs via inoculation of spores through broken skin, inhalation, ingestion, or injection.
• **Pathogenesis:**
    ◦ **Spores:** Highly resilient and can remain dormant in soil for decades. Once inside a host, they are phagocytosed by macrophages.
    ◦ **Germination:** Spores germinate into vegetative bacteria within macrophages and travel to regional lymph nodes.
    ◦ **Toxin Production:** Vegetative bacteria multiply and release a tripartite exotoxin, the primary virulence factor.
• **Virulence Factors:**
    ◦ **Poly-D-glutamic Acid Capsule:** Antiphagocytic, protecting the bacteria from the host's immune system.
    ◦ **Anthrax Toxin (Tripartite):**
        ▪ **Protective Antigen (PA):** Binds to host cell receptors and facilitates the entry of EF and LF into the cell.
        ▪ **Edema Factor (EF):** An adenylate cyclase that increases intracellular cAMP levels, leading to massive edema and disruption of cell function.
        ▪ **Lethal Factor (LF):** A zinc metalloprotease that cleaves MAP kinases (MAPK), leading to apoptosis, cytokine dysregulation, septic shock, and death.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Reservoir:** Primarily soil and infected herbivorous animals (cattle, sheep, goats, horses).
• **Human Infection:** Occurs through occupational or environmental exposure.
• **Cutaneous:** Most common form worldwide (>95%). Acquired via handling infected animal products (hides, wool, meat). Known as **"woolsorter's disease"** or **"hide-porter's disease."**
• **Inhalational:** Associated with processing contaminated animal fibers or with bioterrorism.
• **Gastrointestinal:** Rare; from ingesting undercooked meat from infected animals.
• **Injectional:** Seen in heroin users in Europe, from injecting drugs contaminated with anthrax spores.
• **Bioterrorism:** Spores can be aerosolized for mass exposure, primarily causing inhalational anthrax.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Occupational:** Veterinarians, farmers, livestock producers, tannery workers, woolsorters.
• **Environmental:** Living in endemic agricultural areas.
• **Laboratory personnel** working with *B. anthracis*.
• **Injection drug use** (in certain regions).
• **Bioterrorism event exposure.**
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation varies significantly based on the route of exposure.
• **Cutaneous Anthrax:**
    ◦ Incubation period: 1-12 days.
    ◦ Begins as a small, pruritic, painless papule resembling an insect bite.
    ◦ Evolves over 2-6 days into a vesicle or bulla, which then erodes to form a necrotic ulcer.
    ◦ Classic finding is a **painless black eschar** surrounded by significant non-pitting edema.
    ◦ Regional lymphadenopathy and systemic symptoms (fever, malaise) may be present.
• **Inhalational Anthrax:**
    ◦ Incubation period: 1-7 days (can be up to 60 days).
    ◦ **Biphasic Illness:**
        ▪ **Phase 1 (Prodromal):** Nonspecific flu-like symptoms: fever, malaise, myalgia, nonproductive cough, mild chest discomfort. Lasts 2-4 days. Patients may show transient improvement.
        ▪ **Phase 2 (Fulminant):** Abrupt onset of high fever, severe dyspnea, diaphoresis, cyanosis, and shock. Stridor may occur due to airway compression from massive lymphadenopathy. Patients rapidly deteriorate. **Hemorrhagic mediastinitis** is a hallmark.
• **Gastrointestinal Anthrax:**
    ◦ Incubation period: 1-7 days.
    ◦ **Oropharyngeal form:** Oral/esophageal ulcers, sore throat, dysphagia, cervical lymphadenopathy, and edema.
    ◦ **Intestinal form:** Nausea, vomiting (**hematemesis**), bloody diarrhea, severe abdominal pain, and ascites. Can mimic an acute abdomen. High risk of bowel perforation and sepsis.
• **Injectional Anthrax:**
    ◦ Presents similarly to cutaneous anthrax but at the site of injection.
    ◦ Characterized by severe soft tissue infection, often with massive edema and lack of a well-defined eschar.
    ◦ Can progress to **necrotizing fasciitis**, **compartment syndrome**, and systemic disease more rapidly than cutaneous anthrax.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Cutaneous:**
    ◦ **Painless black, depressed eschar** with a surrounding vesicular border.
    ◦ Starts as a pruritic papule, evolves to a vesicle, then a painless ulcer with the central eschar.
    ◦ Extensive, non-pitting, **"malignant" edema** surrounding the lesion.
    ◦ Regional lymphadenopathy.
• **Inhalational:**
    ◦ **Early:** Fever, fatigue, myalgia, nonproductive cough, chest pressure.
    ◦ **Late/Fulminant:**
        ▪ Sudden severe respiratory distress, **stridor**, use of accessory muscles, cyanosis, diaphoresis, chest pain, confusion.
        ▪ Fever, tachycardia, tachypnea.
        ▪ Signs of shock: **hypotension**, altered mental status.
        ▪ Lung auscultation may be unremarkable initially.
• **Gastrointestinal:**
    ◦ Severe abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting of blood (**hematemesis**), **bloody diarrhea**, fever, ascites.
    ◦ Diffuse abdominal tenderness, guarding, rebound tenderness.
    ◦ Cervical edema and lymphadenopathy (oropharyngeal form).
• **Injectional:**
    ◦ Marked soft tissue edema disproportionate to the skin lesion.
    ◦ Erythema, vesicle/ulcer formation (eschar may be absent).
    ◦ **"Skin popping"** track marks.
    ◦ Signs of **necrotizing fasciitis** or **compartment syndrome**.
    ◦ Signs of systemic toxicity.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Gram Stain & Culture:** **Gold Standard.**
    ◦ Gram stain of vesicle fluid, eschar edge, blood, pleural fluid, or CSF shows large, gram-positive rods, often in **"boxcar" chains**.
    ◦ Culture on blood agar shows non-hemolytic, tenacious colonies.
• **Blood Cultures:** Should be drawn in all suspected cases of systemic anthrax (inhalational, GI, severe cutaneous).
• **Chest X-Ray / CT Scan (for suspected inhalational anthrax):**
    ◦ **Classic finding: Widened mediastinum** due to hemorrhagic mediastinitis and lymphadenitis.
    ◦ Pleural effusions are common (often hemorrhagic).
    ◦ Infiltrates or consolidation are less common early on.
• **PCR:** Rapid identification of *B. anthracis* DNA from clinical samples (blood, lesion swab, pleural fluid).
• **Lumbar Puncture:**
    ◦ Perform if meningeal signs are present.
    ◦ CSF is often hemorrhagic with a high protein count, low glucose, and gram-positive rods.
sections.treatment:
• **Contact CDC and public health authorities immediately.**
• **Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) for Bioterrorism Event:**
    ◦ **Ciprofloxacin** OR **Doxycycline** for 60 days.
    ◦ A 3-dose series of anthrax vaccine is also recommended if available.
• **Cutaneous Anthrax (uncomplicated, no systemic signs):**
    ◦ **Oral Ciprofloxacin** or **Doxycycline** for 7-10 days.
• **Inhalational / Systemic / Cutaneous with Systemic Signs (e.g., head/neck involvement, extensive edema):**
    ◦ **Requires multi-drug IV therapy and hospitalization.**
    ◦ **Primary Regimen:** IV **Ciprofloxacin** OR IV **Doxycycline** PLUS a second bactericidal agent (e.g., Clindamycin, Rifampin, Meropenem, Linezolid).
    ◦ **Antitoxin Therapy:** A monoclonal antibody (e.g., **raxibacumab**, obiltoxaximab) or anthrax immune globulin (AIG) should be added to neutralize circulating toxins.
    ◦ Treat for at least 14 days or until clinically stable, then complete a 60-day total course with oral antibiotics.
sections.management:
• **Supportive Care:** Crucial for systemic anthrax.
    ◦ ICU admission for aggressive hemodynamic support (fluids, vasopressors).
    ◦ Mechanical ventilation for respiratory failure.
    ◦ Thoracentesis for large pleural effusions causing respiratory compromise.
• **Infection Control:**
    ◦ Standard precautions are sufficient for patient care. Person-to-person transmission is not documented.
    ◦ Laboratory specimens should be handled with appropriate biosafety precautions.
• **Public Health:** Anthrax is a nationally notifiable disease. All suspected cases must be reported to local and state health departments.
sections.complications:
• Sepsis and septic shock
• **Hemorrhagic meningitis** (a common complication of systemic anthrax)
• Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC)
• Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)
• Bowel perforation (GI anthrax)
• Death
sections.prognosis:
• **Cutaneous (treated):** Mortality < 1%.
• **Cutaneous (untreated):** Mortality up to 20%.
• **Gastrointestinal:** Mortality 25-60%.
• **Inhalational (even with treatment):** High mortality, estimated at 45-80%. Early diagnosis and aggressive treatment are critical to survival.

sections.overview:
• Leptospirosis is a worldwide **zoonotic disease** caused by spirochetes of the genus ***Leptospira***.
    ◦ It is transmitted to humans through direct or indirect contact with the urine of infected animals, typically via contaminated water or soil.
    ◦ The clinical presentation is broad, ranging from a mild, self-limiting febrile illness to a severe, life-threatening condition known as **Weil's disease**, characterized by **jaundice**, **renal failure**, and **hemorrhage**.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**: Pathogenic spirochetes from the genus ***Leptospira***, most notably ***Leptospira interrogans***.
    ◦ These are thin, coiled, gram-negative bacteria with hooked ends.
• **Transmission**:
    ◦ Primary reservoirs are **rodents** (especially rats), but also dogs, cattle, pigs, and wild animals.
    ◦ Animals shed leptospires in their **urine**, contaminating soil and water.
    ◦ Human infection occurs when the spirochetes enter the body through cuts or abrasions in the skin, or via mucous membranes (eyes, nose, mouth).
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Entry & Bacteremia (Leptospiremic Phase)**: After entry, the organism disseminates hematogenously throughout the body. This is the first phase, characterized by flu-like symptoms.
    ◦ **Endothelial Damage**: Leptospires damage the endothelial lining of small blood vessels, leading to **vasculitis**, increased capillary permeability, and hemorrhage.
    ◦ **Organ Invasion**: Organisms invade and cause damage to various organs, particularly the liver (hepatocellular necrosis), kidneys (tubulointerstitial nephritis), and lungs (capillary injury leading to hemorrhage).
    ◦ **Immune Phase**: The second phase of illness is mediated by the host's immune response. The clearance of organisms can lead to an inflammatory cascade, causing **aseptic meningitis**, uveitis, and worsening organ dysfunction (e.g., **Weil's disease**).
sections.epidemiology:
• **Distribution**: Worldwide, but has the highest incidence in **tropical and subtropical regions** (e.g., Southeast Asia, the Caribbean, South America).
• **Incidence**: Often underdiagnosed. Outbreaks are commonly associated with **heavy rainfall or flooding**.
• **Seasonality**: Peaks during summer and fall in temperate climates and during rainy seasons in the tropics.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is classically **biphasic**, though many patients may not exhibit two distinct phases.
• **Incubation Period**: Typically 5-14 days (range 2-30 days).
• **Anicteric Leptospirosis** (90% of cases):
    ◦ **Phase 1 (Leptospiremic/Septicemic Phase)**: Lasts 3-7 days.
        ▪ Abrupt onset of high fever, chills, rigors, headache (often retro-orbital), and severe myalgias.
    ◦ **Phase 2 (Immune Phase)**: After a brief period of improvement (1-3 days), fever and other symptoms may recur.
        ▪ This phase is associated with the appearance of IgM antibodies.
        ▪ **Aseptic meningitis** is a common manifestation.
• **Icteric Leptospirosis / Weil's Disease** (5-10% of cases):
    ◦ Severe, life-threatening form.
    ◦ Characterized by the triad of **jaundice**, **acute kidney injury (AKI)**, and **hemorrhagic diathesis**.
    ◦ Often presents as a single, progressive illness without a clear biphasic course.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Laboratory Findings (Nonspecific but suggestive)**:
    ◦ **CBC**: **Leukocytosis with left shift**, **thrombocytopenia**. Anemia may be present due to hemorrhage.
    ◦ **CMP**:
        ▪ **AKI**: **Elevated BUN and Creatinine**.
        ▪ **Hepatic**: Elevated bilirubin (predominantly direct/conjugated), elevated alkaline phosphatase, mildly elevated AST/ALT (typically <5x ULN).
    ◦ **CK**: Often elevated due to myositis/rhabdomyolysis.
    ◦ **Urinalysis**: Proteinuria, pyuria, hematuria.
• **Specific Diagnostic Tests**:
    ◦ **Serology**:
        ▪ **Gold standard is the Microscopic Agglutination Test (MAT)**. Requires acute and convalescent sera to demonstrate a four-fold rise in titer. It is complex and not widely available.
    ◦ **ELISA**: Detects IgM antibodies; more widely available for initial diagnosis but less specific than MAT.
    ◦ **PCR**: Highly sensitive and specific for detecting *Leptospira* DNA.
        ▪ **Test of choice in the first week of illness** (leptospiremic phase) on blood or CSF.
        ▪ Can be used on urine after the first week.
    ◦ **Culture**: Definitive but difficult and slow (takes weeks). Requires special media. Blood/CSF cultures are positive in the first week; urine cultures are positive after the first week.
sections.prognosis:
• **Anicteric form**: Excellent prognosis, with mortality near 0%. Full recovery is expected.
• **Icteric form (Weil's Disease)**: Mortality rate is 5-15%, and can be >50% if SPHS develops.
• Early diagnosis and initiation of antibiotics and supportive care significantly improve outcomes.

sections.overview:
• *Pneumocystis jirovecii* Pneumonia (PCP), formerly known as *Pneumocystis carinii* pneumonia, is a life-threatening opportunistic fungal infection of the lungs.
• It is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in immunocompromised individuals, most classically recognized as an **AIDS-defining illness**.
• The clinical presentation is typically a subacute onset of progressive **dyspnea on exertion**, **non-productive cough**, and **fever**.
• Diagnosis relies on identifying the organism in respiratory samples, supported by characteristic imaging and laboratory findings.
• Treatment is primarily with high-dose **Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX)**, and adjunctive corticosteroids are crucial in cases of significant **hypoxemia**.
sections.etiology:
• **Organism**
    ◦ *Pneumocystis jirovecii* is a ubiquitous, unicellular, yeast-like fungus.
    ◦ It was previously misclassified as a protozoan.
• **Transmission**
    ◦ Airborne.
    ◦ Most individuals are exposed during early childhood and remain asymptomatic carriers.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Reactivation**: In an immunocompromised host (especially with defective cell-mediated immunity), latent organisms reactivate and proliferate within the alveoli.
    ◦ **Alveolar Attachment**: The trophic forms of the fungus attach to Type I pneumocytes.
    ◦ **Inflammation & Damage**: This attachment and proliferation provoke an intense inflammatory response, leading to damage of the alveolar-capillary membrane.
    ◦ **Exudate Formation**: The alveoli fill with a characteristic proteinaceous, foamy, eosinophilic exudate composed of organisms, host cells, and cellular debris.
        ▪ This exudate is sometimes described as having a **"honeycomb" appearance** on pathology.
    ◦ **Impaired Gas Exchange**: The alveolar filling and inflammation lead to a severe ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) mismatch and a diffusion impairment.
        ▪ This results in the hallmark finding of **profound hypoxemia**, often disproportionate to clinical or radiographic findings.
        ▪ This is quantified by an **increased A-a gradient**.
sections.epidemiology:
• Ubiquitous in the environment worldwide.
• The most common opportunistic infection in patients with HIV/AIDS.
• The incidence has dramatically decreased in developed countries due to the widespread use of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART/ART) and routine PCP prophylaxis.
• Still a significant threat in undiagnosed or non-adherent HIV patients and a growing concern in non-HIV immunocompromised populations (e.g., transplant recipients, patients on chronic steroids or chemotherapy).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Classic Triad**
    ◦ **Progressive Dyspnea on Exertion (DOE)**: The most common symptom, often insidious over days to weeks.
    ◦ **Fever**
    ◦ **Non-productive, dry cough**
• **Onset**
    ◦ **In HIV patients**: Subacute, indolent onset over several weeks.
    ◦ **In non-HIV immunocompromised patients**: Often a more acute, fulminant presentation.
• Constitutional symptoms like fatigue, night sweats, and weight loss are common.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **Arterial Blood Gas (ABG)**
        ▪ Shows **hypoxemia (low PaO2) and respiratory alkalosis** (low PaCO2 from tachypnea).
        ▪ A key finding is an **elevated Alveolar-arterial (A-a) oxygen gradient** (>35 mmHg is indicative of severe disease).
    ◦ **Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH)**
        ▪ Markedly elevated (>220 U/L, often >500) in >90% of cases.
        ▪ It is non-specific but has a high negative predictive value (a normal LDH makes PCP unlikely).
    ◦ **(1,3)-Beta-D-Glucan**
        ▪ An assay for a component of fungal cell walls.
        ▪ It is sensitive but not specific for PCP.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Chest X-ray (CXR)**
        ▪ Classic finding is **bilateral, diffuse, interstitial "ground-glass" infiltrates**, often in a perihilar or **"bat-wing" distribution**.
        ▪ The CXR can be normal in 10-20% of early cases.
        ▪ Atypical findings include nodules, pneumatoceles, cysts (especially in upper lobes), and pneumothorax.
    ◦ **High-Resolution Chest CT (HRCT)**
        ▪ More sensitive than CXR.
        ▪ Shows extensive patchy or diffuse **"ground-glass" opacities**.
• **Definitive Diagnosis (Microorganism Identification)**
    ◦ **Specimen Collection**
        ▪ **Induced Sputum**: First-line, non-invasive method. Sensitivity is variable (50-90%).
        ▪ **Bronchoalveolar Lavage (BAL)**: **Procedure of choice** when induced sputum is negative or cannot be obtained. Sensitivity is >95%.
    ◦ **Staining**
        ▪ **Methenamine Silver** or **Toluidine Blue O**: Stains the cyst walls, which may appear as **"crushed ping-pong balls"** or cup-shaped structures.
        ▪ **Giemsa** or **Wright-Giemsa**: Stains the intracystic sporozoites and trophic forms.
        ▪ **Direct Fluorescent Antibody (DFA)**: A monoclonal antibody stain that is highly sensitive and specific.
sections.prognosis:
• Mortality rate with treatment is approximately **10-20%** in HIV-infected patients.
• Prognosis is significantly worse in non-HIV immunocompromised patients, with mortality rates of **30-60%**.
• The need for mechanical ventilation is a poor prognostic indicator.

sections.overview:
• **Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC)** is an infection caused by a group of nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM), primarily *Mycobacterium avium* and *Mycobacterium intracellulare*.
• MAC causes two main clinical syndromes:
    ◦ **Disseminated MAC Disease**: An opportunistic infection occurring almost exclusively in severely immunocompromised individuals, classically in HIV/AIDS patients with **CD4 counts < 50 cells/L**.
    ◦ **Pulmonary MAC Disease**: A chronic, progressive lung infection typically seen in patients with underlying structural lung disease or in a specific patient phenotype (thin, elderly women).
• It is an environmental organism and is not transmitted from person to person.
sections.etiology:
• **Organisms**: MAC is composed of two main slow-growing, acid-fast bacilli:
    ◦ *Mycobacterium avium*
    ◦ *Mycobacterium intracellulare*
• **Source**: Ubiquitous in the environment, found in soil, dust, and natural water sources (including treated municipal water systems and biofilms in pipes).
• **Transmission**: Inhalation or ingestion of the organisms from the environment. There is **no person-to-person transmission**.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Host Defense**: A healthy immune system, particularly robust cell-mediated immunity (macrophages, CD4+ T-helper cells), effectively contains the organism.
    ◦ **Disseminated Disease**: In a severely immunocompromised host (e.g., **CD4 < 50**), the host cannot form effective granulomas to contain the bacteria. After initial entry via the lungs or GI tract, the organisms replicate within macrophages and disseminate via the bloodstream and lymphatics to multiple organs, especially the reticuloendothelial system (liver, spleen, bone marrow, lymph nodes).
    ◦ **Pulmonary Disease**: In immunocompetent individuals with structural lung defects (e.g., COPD, bronchiectasis), inhaled organisms colonize damaged airways. A chronic, slow inflammatory response leads to further bronchiectasis, scarring, and nodule formation.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Disseminated MAC**: Incidence has dramatically decreased in high-income countries due to the widespread use of effective **antiretroviral therapy (ART)** for HIV. It remains a significant AIDS-defining illness in untreated or non-adherent patients.
• **Pulmonary MAC**: The most common form of NTM lung disease in the United States. Incidence is increasing, particularly among older adults. Two classic patient profiles exist:
    ◦ Older men with a history of smoking and underlying COPD.
    ◦ Post-menopausal, thin, non-smoking women, often with scoliosis or pectus excavatum ("**Lady Windermere Syndrome**").
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation varies significantly based on the syndrome.
• **Disseminated MAC Disease (in AIDS)**:
    ◦ Insidious onset of non-specific, systemic symptoms.
    ◦ **Constitutional "B-symptoms"** are classic: persistent **fever**, drenching **night sweats**, progressive **weight loss/wasting**.
    ◦ **Gastrointestinal**: Chronic watery **diarrhea**, malabsorption, abdominal pain.
    ◦ **Hematologic**: **Anemia**, **pancytopenia** from bone marrow infiltration.
    ◦ **Hepatosplenomegaly**, generalized **lymphadenopathy**.
• **Pulmonary MAC Disease**:
    ◦ Indolent course over months to years.
    ◦ Chronic, persistent **cough**, often productive of purulent sputum.
    ◦ **Fatigue**, **malaise**, and low-grade fevers.
    ◦ **Dyspnea** on exertion.
    ◦ **Hemoptysis** (can be recurrent).
    ◦ Unintentional **weight loss**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Initial Laboratory Studies (Suggestive)**:
    ◦ **CBC**: **Anemia of chronic disease** (normocytic, normochromic) is very common in disseminated disease. **Pancytopenia** may be present.
    ◦ **CMP**: **Markedly elevated Alkaline Phosphatase (Alk Phos)** is a classic finding in disseminated disease due to hepatic and bone marrow infiltration. LDH may also be elevated.
• **Definitive Diagnosis (Isolation of MAC)**:
    ◦ **Acid-Fast Bacilli (AFB) Smear & Culture**: This is the **gold standard**.
    ◦ **Specimen Source**:
        ▪ **Disseminated Disease**: **Blood cultures** for mycobacteria (using specific BACTEC or Isolator systems). **Bone marrow aspirate/biopsy** has a very high yield.
        ▪ **Pulmonary Disease**: Requires specific criteria to differentiate colonization from true infection:
            • **Clinical**: Compatible symptoms.
            • **Radiographic**: Nodules, cavities, or bronchiectasis on CXR/CT.
            • **Microbiologic**: Positive culture from **2 separate sputum samples** OR positive culture from **1 bronchial wash/lavage** OR biopsy showing granulomatous inflammation with a positive culture.
• **Imaging**:
    ◦ **Chest X-ray / High-Resolution CT (HRCT) for Pulmonary Disease**:
        ▪ Classic "**Nodular Bronchiectatic**" form: **Bronchiectasis** (tram tracks, signet ring sign) and multiple small (<1 cm) centrilobular nodules ("**tree-in-bud**" opacities). Most commonly affects the **right middle lobe and lingula**.
        ▪ "**Upper Lobe Cavitary**" form: **Fibrocavitary disease** in the upper lobes, resembling reactivation TB, typically seen in male smokers with COPD.
    ◦ **Abdominal CT for Disseminated Disease**: May show **hepatosplenomegaly** and diffuse intra-abdominal **lymphadenopathy**.
sections.prognosis:
• **Disseminated Disease**: Without treatment in the pre-ART era, median survival was 4-6 months. With effective anti-MAC therapy and ART, the prognosis is dramatically improved and is primarily determined by the recovery of the immune system.
• **Pulmonary Disease**: Treatment is long and arduous with cure rates of ~60-80%. It is not typically a rapidly fatal disease but causes significant morbidity and a progressive decline in lung function and quality of life. Relapse can occur after treatment completion.

sections.overview:
• **CMV Retinitis** is a severe, **sight-threatening opportunistic infection** of the retina caused by **Cytomegalovirus (CMV)**.
    ◦ It is the most common serious ocular complication of Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (**AIDS**) and a leading cause of **blindness** in this population, particularly when the immune system is severely compromised.
    ◦ Characterized by **full-thickness necrotizing retinitis** that, if left untreated, progresses to irreversible vision loss.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiologic Agent**: **Cytomegalovirus (CMV)**, also known as **Human Herpesvirus 5 (HHV-5)**, a double-stranded DNA virus.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Latency & Reactivation**: Most of the population is seropositive for CMV, which remains latent. In states of **severe cellular immunodeficiency** (primarily failure of T-cell surveillance), the virus **reactivates**.
    ◦ **Hematogenous Spread**: The reactivated virus spreads through the bloodstream to the highly vascular retina.
    ◦ **Retinal Infection**: CMV infects retinal cells, leading to direct cytopathic effects.
    ◦ **Necrosis**: The virus causes **full-thickness retinal necrosis**, resulting in cell death and tissue destruction, accompanied by edema and hemorrhage from damaged retinal blood vessels.
    ◦ **Progression**: Infection typically starts in the periphery and spreads **centripetally** along vascular arcades toward the macula and optic nerve, leading to progressive visual field loss and ultimately blindness.
sections.epidemiology:
• Primarily affects **severely immunocompromised** individuals.
• Historically a major **AIDS-defining illness**.
    ◦ Incidence has dramatically decreased (>80%) since the advent of effective **Antiretroviral Therapy (ART)**.
• Still occurs in patients with undiagnosed HIV, poor adherence to ART, or ART failure.
• Also seen in other immunocompromised states:
    ◦ Solid organ and hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients.
    ◦ Patients on high-dose chemotherapy or chronic immunosuppressive agents (e.g., corticosteroids).
• The key determinant in HIV patients is the **CD4+ T-cell count**.
    ◦ The risk is highest with a **CD4 count < 50 cells/L**.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • A patient with a known history of **advanced AIDS** or another **immunocompromised** state presents with a **gradual onset** of **unilateral** (but can become bilateral) visual disturbances that are typically **painless**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Presumptive Clinical Diagnosis**: Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on characteristic fundoscopic findings in a high-risk, immunocompromised patient.
    ◦ Sufficient to initiate treatment.
    ◦ Example: Patient with a **CD4 < 50**.
• **Ophthalmology Consult**: **Urgent** referral is mandatory for dilated fundoscopic examination by an ophthalmologist.
• **Confirmatory (if needed)**:
    ◦ **PCR of aqueous or vitreous humor**: High sensitivity and specificity for CMV DNA.
        ▪ Reserved for atypical cases or when the diagnosis is uncertain.
• **Supportive Lab Work**:
    ◦ HIV test and **CD4 count**.
    ◦ Quantitative serum CMV PCR (**CMV viral load**) to assess systemic disease burden.
sections.prognosis:
• **Untreated**: Universally poor.
    ◦ Leads to progressive retinal necrosis and **blindness** within 3-6 months.
• **Treated (with modern ART)**: Excellent.
    ◦ With prompt anti-CMV therapy and effective **ART**, vision can be stabilized, and the prognosis for long-term control is very good.
    ◦ The risk of **retinal detachment** remains a lifelong concern for the affected eye.

sections.overview:
• **Meningococcemia** is a life-threatening, invasive bacterial infection caused by ***Neisseria meningitidis***.
    ◦ It is characterized by the presence of meningococci in the bloodstream (**bacteremia**), leading to a systemic inflammatory response.
    ◦ This condition is a true medical emergency, capable of progressing from non-specific symptoms to **septic shock**, **disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)**, **multi-organ failure**, and death within hours.
    ◦ Its hallmark clinical sign is a **non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash**.
    ◦ It can occur with or without concurrent meningitis.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**: ***Neisseria meningitidis***, an encapsulated, aerobic, gram-negative diplococcus.
• **Virulence Factors**:
    ◦ **Polysaccharide Capsule**: Antiphagocytic, allowing the organism to evade the host immune system. Serogroups (A, B, C, Y, W) are defined by their capsular polysaccharides.
    ◦ **Pili**: Mediate attachment to nasopharyngeal epithelial cells.
    ◦ **IgA Protease**: Cleaves host IgA at mucosal surfaces, facilitating colonization.
    ◦ **Lipooligosaccharide (LOS)**: The key endotoxin.
        ▪ When released during bacterial lysis, LOS triggers a massive, uncontrolled inflammatory cascade via activation of Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4).
• **Pathophysiologic Cascade**:
    ◦ **Colonization**: The organism colonizes the human nasopharynx (the only known reservoir).
    ◦ **Invasion**: Bacteria invade the bloodstream, often following a preceding viral upper respiratory infection that damages mucosal integrity.
    ◦ **Endotoxemia**: Rapid bacterial multiplication and lysis releases massive amounts of LOS into the circulation.
    ◦ **Cytokine Storm**: LOS stimulates the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6), leading to systemic inflammation.
    ◦ **Endothelial Damage**: Cytokines and LOS directly damage vascular endothelial cells, causing increased capillary permeability ("leaky vessels") and fluid shifts into the extravascular space, leading to **hypotension** and **shock**.
    ◦ **Coagulopathy (DIC)**: Widespread endothelial damage activates the coagulation cascade, leading to microthrombi formation (consuming platelets and clotting factors) and subsequent hemorrhage. This process manifests as **purpura fulminans**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Reservoir**: Humans are the only natural host. Asymptomatic nasopharyngeal carriage is common (5-10% of the general population).
• **Transmission**: Direct contact with large-droplet respiratory secretions. Requires close contact (e.g., coughing, kissing, sharing utensils).
• **Age Distribution**: Bimodal peaks:
    ◦ Infants < 1 year old.
    ◦ Adolescents and young adults (16-23 years).
• **Setting**: Outbreaks are associated with crowded living conditions, such as college dormitories, military barracks, and prisons.
• **Trends**: Incidence in the United States has dramatically decreased due to routine vaccination (MenACWY and MenB).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is classically abrupt and **fulminant**.
    ◦ A previously healthy individual can become critically ill in under 24 hours.
• **Initial Phase (Non-specific)**: **Fever**, chills, malaise, **myalgias** (often severe and disproportionate), arthralgias.
• **Progressive Phase**: Rapid deterioration with **hypotension**, tachycardia, **altered mental status**, and the development of the characteristic **rash**.
• **Meningitis**: About 50% of patients with meningococcemia also have meningitis, presenting with **headache**, **nuchal rigidity**, and **photophobia**.
• **Septic Shock**: The end result of the inflammatory cascade, characterized by **refractory hypotension** and **end-organ hypoperfusion**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Do not delay empiric antibiotics for diagnostic procedures.**
    ◦ If meningococcemia is suspected, treat immediately after drawing blood cultures.
• **Blood Cultures**: **Gold standard for diagnosis.**
    ◦ Should be drawn prior to antibiotic administration.
• **CBC with Differential**:
    ◦ **Leukocytosis** with a **left shift** is common.
    ◦ **Leukopenia** is a poor prognostic sign.
    ◦ **Thrombocytopenia** is a hallmark of **DIC**.
• **Coagulation Panel (PT, PTT, Fibrinogen, D-dimer)**:
    ◦ **DIC findings**:
        ▪ Prolonged PT/PTT
        ▪ Low fibrinogen
        ▪ Elevated D-dimer
• **Lumbar Puncture (LP)**:
    ◦ Perform if the patient is stable and meningitis is suspected.
    ◦ **Contraindicated** in patients with severe coagulopathy or signs of markedly elevated ICP (**papilledema**, **Cushing's triad**).
• **CSF Analysis**:
    ◦ High opening pressure, high WBC (neutrophil-predominant), high protein, low glucose.
• **CSF Gram Stain**: May reveal gram-negative diplococci.
• **CSF Culture**: Definitive for meningitis.
• **Gram Stain and Culture of Skin Lesions**: Aspiration or punch biopsy of purpuric lesions can yield the organism.
• **PCR**: Highly sensitive and specific for *N. meningitidis* on blood or CSF samples.
sections.prognosis:
• **Mortality**: Remains high at 10-15% even with optimal therapy.
• **Fulminant Meningococcemia**: Mortality approaches 40-50%. Death can occur within 6-12 hours of symptom onset.
• **Poor Prognostic Factors**: **Hypotension** on presentation, rapid development of **purpura fulminans**, absence of meningitis (paradoxically, a purely systemic response is often more severe), **leukopenia**, severe **thrombocytopenia/DIC**.

sections.overview:
• **Epiglottitis** is a **life-threatening medical emergency** characterized by inflammation and swelling of the epiglottis and adjacent supraglottic structures.
    ◦ This swelling can rapidly progress to complete **upper airway obstruction**.
• Historically a pediatric disease caused by *Haemophilus influenzae* type b (Hib), its epidemiology has shifted towards adults due to widespread **Hib vaccination**.
• The cornerstone of management is immediate **airway protection**.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• **Pre-Hib Vaccine Era**:
    ◦ Primarily a disease of children aged 2-6 years.
• **Post-Hib Vaccine Era**:
    ◦ Incidence in children has decreased by >90%.
    ◦ **Epiglottitis is now more common in adults than children**.
    ◦ Adult incidence is approximately 1-4 cases per 100,000 per year.
    ◦ Mean age for adults is ~45 years.
    ◦ Slight male predominance.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is typically **acute** and **fulminant**, with patients progressing from a mild sore throat to **respiratory arrest** within hours.
• Patients appear acutely ill and **toxic**.
• **Classic Pediatric Presentation**:
    ◦ **Rapid onset** of **high fever**, **severe sore throat**, and signs of **respiratory distress** in a previously healthy-appearing child.
