    ◦ The child will often assume a **characteristic posture** to maintain airway patency.
• **Adult Presentation**:
    ◦ May have a more **subacute onset** over 1-2 days.
    ◦ The most common presenting complaint is a **severe sore throat**, often disproportionate to physical exam findings.
    ◦ **Odynophagia** and **voice changes** are also common.
    ◦ **Respiratory distress** may be a later finding.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Airway management supersedes all diagnostic procedures.**
• Diagnosis is primarily **clinical**.
• **Definitive Diagnosis**:
    ◦ **Direct Fiberoptic Laryngoscopy**:
        ▪ Performed in a controlled environment (operating room).
        ▪ **Finding**: A **swollen, edematous, cherry-red epiglottis**.
• **Imaging (ONLY for stable patients where suspicion is lower)**:
    ◦ **Lateral Neck X-ray**:
        ▪ **Classic Finding**: **"Thumbprint sign"** or **"thumb sign"**.
        ▪ The swollen epiglottis appears as a large, rounded soft tissue shadow resembling the distal phalanx of a thumb.
        ▪ Other findings: **Thickened aryepiglottic folds**, loss of the vallecular air space.
• **Labs (obtain after airway is secure)**:
    ◦ CBC: **Leukocytosis** with a **left shift**.
    ◦ Blood Cultures: May identify the causative organism.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** with prompt diagnosis and airway management.
• Mortality rate is **<1%** in hospitalized patients.
• Mortality rises significantly if the airway becomes obstructed prior to intervention.

sections.overview:
• Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS) is an acute, severe, toxin-mediated illness characterized by a classic triad of **high fever**, profound **hypotension**, and a diffuse, erythematous **"sunburn-like" rash**.
    ◦ It rapidly progresses to **multi-organ failure** and constitutes a medical emergency.
    ◦ TSS is caused by exotoxins produced by *Staphylococcus aureus* (Staphylococcal TSS) or *Streptococcus pyogenes* (Streptococcal TSS), which act as **superantigens**, triggering a massive, uncontrolled inflammatory response or **"cytokine storm."**
sections.etiology:
• TSS is not caused by the bacteria invading the bloodstream directly (bacteremia is rare in Staph TSS), but by the systemic effects of potent exotoxins that function as **superantigens**.
• **Staphylococcal TSS**
    ◦ **Organism:** Toxin-producing strains of *Staphylococcus aureus*.
    ◦ **Toxin:** Primarily **Toxic Shock Syndrome Toxin-1 (TSST-1)**. Other staphylococcal enterotoxins (A, B, C) are implicated in non-menstrual cases.
    ◦ **Pathophysiology:**
        ▪ The **superantigen (TSST-1)** bypasses typical antigen processing.
        ▪ It directly cross-links the T-cell receptor (TCR) with the MHC class II complex on antigen-presenting cells.
        ▪ This results in the non-specific activation of a massive number of T-cells (up to 20% of the body's total), leading to a **cytokine storm**.
        ▪ The massive release of IL-1, IL-2, TNF-alpha, and IFN-gamma causes systemic inflammation, widespread capillary leakage, vasodilation, fever, hypotension, rash, and multi-organ dysfunction.
• **Streptococcal TSS (STSS)**
    ◦ **Organism:** Invasive Group A *Streptococcus* (*S. pyogenes*).
    ◦ **Toxin:** **Streptococcal Pyrogenic Exotoxins (SpeA, SpeC)** are the primary superantigens.
    ◦ **Pathophysiology:**
        ▪ The mechanism is similar to Staph TSS (**superantigen-mediated cytokine storm**).
        ▪ However, STSS is almost always associated with an underlying invasive streptococcal infection (e.g., necrotizing fasciitis, myositis, cellulitis).
        ▪ **Bacteremia is common (>60% of cases)**, making it a more invasive and often more fulminant disease.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Staphylococcal TSS**
    ◦ Historically associated with high-absorbency tampon use in the 1980s.
    ◦ Incidence has decreased, but cases still occur.
    ◦ Currently, **>50% of cases are non-menstrual**, affecting all ages and genders.
• **Streptococcal TSS**
    ◦ Occurs as a complication of invasive Group A Strep (GAS) disease.
    ◦ Can affect any age group but is more common in the very young and the elderly.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The patient is acutely ill, often presenting with a rapid onset of symptoms mimicking sepsis.
• The clinical course is one of swift deterioration to shock and multi-organ failure, often within hours.
• In STSS, a key feature can be **severe, localized pain that is out of proportion** to the visible physical findings, heralding an underlying deep tissue infection like necrotizing fasciitis.
sections.diagnostics:
• TSS is a **clinical diagnosis** based on the CDC case criteria.
• Labs are used to confirm multi-organ involvement.
• **CDC Case Criteria for Staphylococcal TSS (Probable Case)**
    ◦ Fever >38.9°C (102°F)
    ◦ **Hypotension** (SBP <90 mmHg)
    ◦ Diffuse erythematous **rash**
    ◦ **Desquamation** (1-2 weeks post-onset)
    ◦ Involvement of **three or more** organ systems:
        ▪ **GI:** Vomiting or diarrhea at onset.
        ▪ **Muscular:** Severe myalgia or CPK >2x ULN.
        ▪ **Mucous Membrane:** Vaginal, oropharyngeal, or conjunctival hyperemia.
        ▪ **Renal:** BUN or Creatinine >2x ULN.
        ▪ **Hepatic:** AST, ALT, or Bilirubin >2x ULN.
        ▪ **Hematologic:** Platelets <100,000/L.
        ▪ **CNS:** Disorientation without focal neurologic signs.
    ◦ Negative serology for RMSF, measles, and leptospirosis.
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **CBC:** Leukocytosis with a marked left shift, **thrombocytopenia**, normocytic anemia.
    ◦ **CMP:**
        ▪ BUN/Creatinine (AKI)
        ▪ AST/ALT, Bilirubin (hepatic injury)
        ▪ Calcium, Albumin
    ◦ **Coags:** PT/PTT, D-dimer (consistent with DIC).
    ◦ **CPK:** Markedly elevated (rhabdomyolysis).
• **Cultures**
    ◦ **Blood Cultures:** Typically **NEGATIVE** in Staph TSS; often **POSITIVE** in STSS.
    ◦ **Site Cultures:** Obtain from any potential source (vagina, wound, nares, throat).
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Chest X-ray:** May show non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema (ARDS).
    ◦ **CT/MRI:** Crucial if suspecting a deep tissue infection (necrotizing fasciitis, myositis, occult abscess).
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly dependent on the speed of diagnosis and initiation of aggressive therapy.
• **Staphylococcal TSS**
    ◦ Mortality rate is low (<3%) with appropriate care.
    ◦ Recurrence can occur if a localized source is not fully eradicated.
• **Streptococcal TSS**
    ◦ Mortality remains very high (**30-70%**), reflecting the severity of the underlying invasive infection.

sections.overview:
• Septic shock is a life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection, leading to profound circulatory, cellular, and metabolic abnormalities.
    ◦ It is a subset of sepsis characterized by persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain a mean arterial pressure (MAP) of ≥ 65 mmHg and a serum lactate level >2 mmol/L, despite adequate fluid resuscitation.
    ◦ It represents a form of **distributive shock**, where widespread vasodilation and increased capillary permeability lead to relative hypovolemia and tissue hypoperfusion.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• Sepsis is a leading cause of mortality and critical illness worldwide.
• Incidence is rising due to an aging population, more invasive procedures, and increased use of immunosuppressive drugs.
• Septic shock has a hospital mortality rate of approximately **20-40%**.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Extremes of age** (infants and elderly >65)
• **Immunosuppression** (chemotherapy, chronic steroid use, HIV/AIDS, organ transplant)
• **Chronic Diseases** (diabetes, cirrhosis, chronic kidney disease, COPD, heart failure)
• **Recent surgery or hospitalization**
• **Indwelling devices** (central venous catheters, urinary catheters, endotracheal tubes)
• **Malignancy**
• **Alcoholism or drug abuse**
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The patient often appears "toxic" or acutely ill; the presentation can be non-specific, especially in the elderly who may present with only altered mental status.
• The clinical picture is one of infection plus signs of systemic hypoperfusion and organ dysfunction.
• **Constitutional Symptoms**
    ◦ Fever, chills, rigors, malaise, weakness.
• **Neurologic Symptoms**
    ◦ Altered mental status, confusion, lethargy, anxiety.
• **Cardiopulmonary Symptoms**
    ◦ Shortness of breath, palpitations, lightheadedness, dizziness.
• **Source-Specific Symptoms**
    ◦ **Pneumonia:** Cough, sputum production, pleuritic chest pain.
    ◦ **UTI:** Dysuria, frequency, urgency, flank pain.
    ◦ **Abdominal:** Abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Vitals (Key to diagnosis)**
    ◦ **Hypotension:** SBP < 90 mmHg or **MAP < 65 mmHg**.
    ◦ **Tachycardia:** Heart rate > 90 bpm.
    ◦ **Tachypnea:** Respiratory rate > 22 breaths/min.
    ◦ **Fever (>38.3°C / 101°F) or Hypothermia (<36°C / 96.8°F)**.
• **General Appearance**
    ◦ Acutely ill, diaphoretic, lethargic or agitated.
• **Skin**
    ◦ **Early ("Warm Shock"):** Warm, flushed, dry skin due to peripheral vasodilation (hyperdynamic state).
    ◦ **Late ("Cold Shock"):** Cool, clammy, cyanotic, or mottled skin (cutis marmorata) due to shunting of blood to vital organs (hypodynamic state).
    ◦ Delayed capillary refill (>2 seconds).
• **HEENT**
    ◦ Dry mucous membranes.
• **Lungs**
    ◦ Rales, crackles, or rhonchi (pneumonia, ARDS).
• **Cardiovascular**
    ◦ Tachycardia, bounding pulses (early) or thready pulses (late).
• **Abdomen**
    ◦ May have tenderness, rigidity, or guarding if an intra-abdominal source.
• **Neurologic**
    ◦ Altered mental status (Glasgow Coma Scale < 15), confusion, obtundation.
• **Extremities**
    ◦ Peripheral edema due to capillary leak.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Chest X-Ray (CXR):** To evaluate for pneumonia or ARDS.
• **CT / Ultrasound:** To identify a potential source (e.g., CT abdomen/pelvis for abscess, renal ultrasound for hydronephrosis/pyelonephritis).
• **Echocardiogram:** To assess cardiac function and rule out cardiogenic shock.
sections.treatment:
• **Airway & Breathing**
    ◦ Ensure patent airway; intubate for mechanical ventilation if respiratory failure or inability to protect airway.
    ◦ Provide supplemental oxygen.
• **Circulation**
    ◦ **Fluid Resuscitation**
        ▪ **Begin immediately** for hypotension or lactate ≥ 4 mmol/L.
        ▪ Administer **30 mL/kg of isotonic crystalloid** (Lactated Ringer's or Normal Saline) within the **first 3 hours**.
        ▪ Monitor for signs of fluid overload (pulmonary edema).
    ◦ **Vasopressors**
        ▪ If hypotension persists despite adequate fluid resuscitation (i.e., MAP remains <65 mmHg), start vasopressors.
        ▪ **Norepinephrine (Levophed) is the first-line agent.**
        ▪ **Vasopressin or Epinephrine** can be added as second-line agents if the MAP goal is not met with norepinephrine alone.
        ▪ An arterial line should be placed for accurate, continuous blood pressure monitoring.
• **Infection Control: Empiric Antibiotics**
    ◦ **Administer broad-spectrum IV antibiotics as soon as possible, ideally within 1 HOUR** of recognition.
    ◦ Choice of agent(s) depends on suspected source, local resistance patterns, and patient risk factors (e.g., healthcare exposure).
    ◦ **Common Empiric Regimen:** Vancomycin (for MRSA) + a broad-spectrum beta-lactam (e.g., Piperacillin-tazobactam [Zosyn] or Cefepime).
    ◦ De-escalate/tailor therapy once culture and sensitivity results are available.
sections.management:
• **Source Control**
    ◦ Identify and treat the underlying source of infection. This may require surgery (e.g., debridement of necrotic tissue, drainage of an abscess) or removal of an infected device (e.g., central line).
• **Corticosteroids**
    ◦ Consider IV hydrocortisone for patients with refractory septic shock (persistent hypotension despite adequate fluids and high-dose vasopressors).
• **Supportive Care**
    ◦ **Glycemic Control:** Maintain blood glucose < 180 mg/dL.
    ◦ **DVT Prophylaxis:** Use pharmacologic (e.g., heparin, enoxaparin) or mechanical prophylaxis.
    ◦ **Stress Ulcer Prophylaxis:** Use PPIs or H2 blockers.
    ◦ **Mechanical Ventilation:** Use low tidal volume ventilation for patients with ARDS.
• **Monitoring**
    ◦ Monitor MAP, heart rate, respiratory rate, temperature, and oxygen saturation continuously.
    ◦ Monitor urine output (goal > 0.5 mL/kg/hr).
    ◦ **Follow serial lactate levels** to assess the adequacy of resuscitation (lactate clearance).
sections.complications:
• **Multi-Organ Dysfunction Syndrome (MODS):** Progressive failure of two or more organ systems.
• **Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)**
• **Acute Kidney Injury (AKI):** May require renal replacement therapy (dialysis).
• **Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC)**
• **Hepatic Failure**
• **Limb ischemia/necrosis** due to high-dose vasopressors or microthrombi.
• **Post-Sepsis Syndrome:** Long-term cognitive, psychological, and physical impairments in survivors.
sections.prognosis:
• Mortality remains high, ranging from 20-40%, and increases with the severity of organ dysfunction and delay in treatment.
• Early recognition and adherence to guideline-based bundles are associated with improved survival.
• Factors associated with poor prognosis include advanced age, comorbidities, persistent high lactate, and failure to achieve hemodynamic stability.

sections.overview:
• **Iron Deficiency Anemia (IDA)** is a **microcytic, hypochromic anemia** resulting from insufficient iron stores in the body.
    ◦ **Iron** is essential for the synthesis of **heme**, a critical component of **hemoglobin**.
    ◦ A lack of iron leads to decreased **hemoglobin production** and the formation of smaller, paler red blood cells.
• It is the most common cause of **anemia** and the most prevalent nutritional deficiency worldwide.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• Most common cause of **anemia** worldwide, affecting over 1.5 billion people.
• Prevalence is highest in developing countries due to **malnutrition** and **parasitic infections**.
• In developed nations, the highest-risk groups are:
    ◦ Toddlers
    ◦ Adolescent girls
    ◦ Women of childbearing age
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is often **insidious**, with symptoms developing slowly as the **anemia** worsens.
• A classic vignette might describe:
    ◦ A young, menstruating female complaining of chronic **fatigue** and **weakness**.
    ◦ An elderly male with new-onset **fatigue** found to have a positive **fecal occult blood test**.
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is generally **excellent** if the underlying cause is identified and corrected.
    ◦ The **anemia** is fully reversible with **iron supplementation**.
• The overall prognosis is determined by the underlying etiology (e.g., the prognosis for IDA due to **menorrhagia** is much better than IDA due to **colon cancer**).

sections.overview: • Anemia of Chronic Disease (ACD), also known as Anemia of Inflammation, is a common type of anemia that occurs in patients with chronic inflammatory conditions, infections, or malignancies. ◦ It is the second most common type of anemia worldwide after iron deficiency anemia (IDA) and the most common cause of anemia in hospitalized patients. ◦ Initially, it presents as a normocytic, normochromic anemia, but it can become microcytic over time. ◦ The underlying mechanism is an inflammatory process that leads to decreased RBC production and survival due to altered iron homeostasis.
sections.etiology: • The pathophysiology of ACD is driven by inflammatory cytokines and the master iron-regulating hormone, hepcidin. ◦ Increased Inflammatory Cytokines ▪ Chronic diseases (autoimmune, infectious, malignant) trigger a sustained inflammatory response, leading to elevated levels of cytokines like Interleukin-6 (IL-6), TNF-alpha, and Interferon-gamma. ◦ Hepcidin Upregulation ▪ IL-6 is the primary stimulus for the liver to increase its production of hepcidin. ▪ Hepcidin is the central molecule in ACD pathophysiology, functioning to decrease the amount of available serum iron. ◦ Hepcidin's Effects on Iron Homeostasis ▪ Hepcidin binds to and degrades ferroportin, the only known cellular iron exporter. ▪ Effect on Macrophages: Ferroportin on macrophages is degraded, trapping recycled iron from old RBCs within the reticuloendothelial system (RES), a process known as iron sequestration. ▪ Effect on Enterocytes: Ferroportin on duodenal enterocytes is degraded, blocking dietary iron absorption. ◦ Other Cytokine-Mediated Effects ▪ Suppressed Erythropoiesis: Inflammatory cytokines directly inhibit the proliferation of erythroid progenitor cells in the bone marrow. ▪ Blunted Erythropoietin (EPO) Response: The kidneys produce less EPO than expected for the degree of anemia, and the bone marrow's response to EPO is impaired. ▪ Reduced RBC Lifespan: There is a modest decrease in the survival of red blood cells. • The net result is a functional iron deficiency: total body iron stores are adequate or high, but the iron is locked away and unavailable for incorporation into hemoglobin.
sections.epidemiology: • The most common cause of anemia in hospitalized or chronically ill patients. • The second most common cause of anemia globally, after iron deficiency anemia. • Prevalence increases with age, corresponding to the increased prevalence of chronic diseases in the elderly.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The clinical presentation is often dominated by the symptoms of the underlying chronic disease.
• The anemia develops gradually, allowing for physiological adaptation, so it may be discovered incidentally on routine lab work.
sections.diagnostics: • Diagnosis is made by identifying a normocytic (or mildly microcytic) anemia in the setting of a chronic inflammatory condition, confirmed with characteristic iron studies that rule out IDA. ◦ Complete Blood Count (CBC) ▪ Hemoglobin/Hematocrit: Mild to moderate reduction (Hgb typically 8-10 g/dL). ▪ MCV (Mean Corpuscular Volume): ▪ Initially Normocytic (MCV 80-100 fL). ▪ Becomes Microcytic (MCV < 80 fL) in ~25-50% of long-standing cases. ▪ Reticulocyte Count: Low or inappropriately normal for the degree of anemia, indicating inadequate bone marrow production. ◦ Iron Studies (The Key to Diagnosis) ▪ Serum Iron: Low (similar to IDA). ▪ TIBC (Total Iron-Binding Capacity): Low or Normal (in contrast to High in IDA). ▪ Transferrin Saturation (%): Normal or Low (in contrast to Very Low in IDA). ▪ Serum Ferritin: High or Normal (in contrast to Very Low in IDA). ▪ Key Differentiator: The combination of low TIBC and high/normal ferritin is pathognomonic for ACD. Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant and is elevated by the underlying inflammation. ◦ Inflammatory Markers ▪ Elevated C-reactive protein (CRP). ▪ Elevated Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR). ◦ Bone Marrow Biopsy (Rarely performed for diagnosis) ▪ Shows abundant iron stores within macrophages (stains positive with Prussian blue). ▪ Shows decreased iron within erythroblasts (sideroblasts).
sections.prognosis: • The prognosis is entirely dependent on the prognosis of the underlying chronic disorder. • Resolution or improvement of the underlying disease typically leads to resolution or improvement of the anemia. • The presence and severity of ACD often correlate with the severity of the underlying inflammatory condition.

sections.overview: • Vitamin B12 (Cobalamin) deficiency anemia is a type of macrocytic, megaloblastic anemia characterized by impaired DNA synthesis, leading to ineffective erythropoiesis. ◦ Distinguished by the presence of both hematologic and neurologic abnormalities. ◦ The deficiency can result from insufficient intake, but more commonly from malabsorption.
sections.etiology: • Etiology (Causes) ◦ Impaired Absorption (Most Common) ▪ Pernicious Anemia: Autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells, leading to a lack of Intrinsic Factor (IF), which is essential for B12 absorption in the terminal ileum. This is the most common cause in Western populations. ▪ Gastric Abnormalities: Atrophic gastritis, gastrectomy, bariatric surgery (e.g., Roux-en-Y). These reduce parietal cells or alter the GI tract. ▪ Intestinal Disorders: Crohn's disease affecting the terminal ileum, ileal resection, celiac disease, bacterial overgrowth, or infection with the fish tapeworm (Diphyllobothrium latum). ▪ Medications: Long-term use of Metformin, Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs), and H2 receptor antagonists. ◦ Decreased Intake ▪ Strict vegans or vegetarians who do not consume animal products or fortified foods. ▪ Elderly individuals with "tea and toast" diets. ▪ Chronic alcoholism. • Pathophysiology ◦ Vitamin B12 is a crucial cofactor for two key enzymes: ▪ Methionine Synthase: Converts homocysteine to methionine. This reaction is also folate-dependent. Deficiency leads to an accumulation of homocysteine and impaired DNA synthesis. ▪ Methylmalonyl-CoA Mutase: Converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA. Deficiency leads to an accumulation of methylmalonic acid (MMA). ◦ Hematologic Effects: Impaired DNA synthesis causes nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony. Red blood cell precursors (megaloblasts) are large with immature nuclei, leading to intramedullary hemolysis and ineffective erythropoiesis. ◦ Neurologic Effects: The accumulation of MMA is believed to be toxic to myelin, leading to demyelination of the dorsal and lateral columns of the spinal cord (subacute combined degeneration).
sections.epidemiology:
• More common in older adults, with prevalence increasing significantly after age 60.
• Pernicious anemia is more common in individuals of Northern European descent.
• Prevalence is increasing due to the rising popularity of vegan diets and widespread use of PPIs and Metformin.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • The onset is typically insidious and slow. Patients often present with vague, non-specific symptoms. • The classic triad is weakness, sore tongue, and paresthesias, but not all are required. • A key feature is the combination of an anemic state with unexplained neurologic symptoms.
sections.diagnostics: • Complete Blood Count (CBC) ◦ Anemia (Low Hgb/Hct) ◦ MCV > 100 fL (Macrocytosis) ◦ MCH is elevated, MCHC is normal ◦ Low reticulocyte count ◦ Can see leukopenia and thrombocytopenia in severe cases (pancytopenia) • Peripheral Blood Smear ◦ Hypersegmented neutrophils (>5 lobes) - PATHOGNOMONIC ◦ Macrocytes and macro-ovalocytes • Confirmatory Serum Tests ◦ Low Serum Vitamin B12 Level (<200 pg/mL). Note: levels can be borderline (200-300). ◦ Elevated Serum Methylmalonic Acid (MMA): Most specific test for B12 deficiency. ◦ Elevated Serum Homocysteine: Also elevated in folate deficiency, renal failure. • Etiology Workup ◦ Anti-Intrinsic Factor Antibodies: High specificity for pernicious anemia. ◦ Anti-parietal cell antibodies: Sensitive but not specific. ◦ Schilling Test: Historical, no longer used clinically. • Key Diagnostic Differentiator ◦ B12 Deficiency ▪ Serum MMA: Elevated ▪ Neurologic Sx: Present ▪ Serum Homocysteine: Elevated ◦ Folate Deficiency ▪ Serum MMA: Normal ▪ Neurologic Sx: Absent ▪ Serum Homocysteine: Elevated
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent with early diagnosis and treatment.
• Hematologic abnormalities are fully reversible.
• Neurologic recovery is variable and depends on the duration and severity of the deficiency prior to treatment.

sections.overview:
• Folate deficiency anemia is a type of **macrocytic, megaloblastic anemia** resulting from insufficient levels of folate (Vitamin B9).
	◦ Folate is a crucial water-soluble vitamin essential for the synthesis of purines and pyrimidines, the building blocks of DNA.
	◦ A deficiency impairs DNA replication and cell division, particularly affecting rapidly dividing cells like hematopoietic precursors in the bone marrow and gastrointestinal epithelial cells.
	◦ The hallmark of this condition is large, immature red blood cells (megaloblasts) in the bone marrow and macrocytes on the peripheral smear.
	◦ It is clinically distinguished from Vitamin B12 deficiency by the **absence of neurological symptoms**.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• More common in populations with poor dietary habits, including individuals with alcohol use disorder, the elderly, and those living in poverty.
• Prevalence has decreased significantly in countries with mandatory folic acid fortification of grains (e.g., United States, Canada).
• Remains a significant issue in pregnant women and individuals with malabsorptive disorders globally.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The onset is typically insidious and gradual.
• Patients present with non-specific symptoms of anemia.
• A thorough history focusing on diet, alcohol use, medications, and underlying medical conditions is crucial.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Complete Blood Count (CBC)**
	◦ **Anemia**: Decreased Hemoglobin (Hgb) and Hematocrit (Hct).
	◦ **Macrocytosis**: **Elevated MCV (> 100 fL)**.
	◦ Elevated MCH (mean corpuscular hemoglobin).
	◦ Normal MCHC (mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration).
	◦ Elevated RDW (red cell distribution width).
	◦ Severe cases may show leukopenia and thrombocytopenia (pancytopenia).
• **Peripheral Blood Smear**
	◦ **Hypersegmented neutrophils**: Pathognomonic finding; defined as >5% of neutrophils with 5 lobes or any neutrophil with 6 lobes.
	◦ **Macrocytes / Macro-ovalocytes**: Large, oval-shaped red blood cells.
	◦ Anisocytosis and Poikilocytosis.
	◦ Basophilic stippling may be seen.
• **Confirmatory Serum Studies**
	◦ **Low Serum Folate**: < 4 ng/mL (diagnostic, but can be falsely normalized by a single folate-rich meal).
	◦ **Normal Serum Vitamin B12**: **Must be checked** to rule out a concurrent deficiency.
	◦ **Elevated Serum Homocysteine**: A sensitive indicator of folate (or B12) deficiency.
	◦ **Normal Serum Methylmalonic Acid (MMA)**: **The key differentiating lab test from B12 deficiency, in which MMA is elevated.**
• **Reticulocyte Count**: Low or inappropriately normal for the degree of anemia, indicating a production problem.
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent with supplementation.
• The hematologic abnormalities are fully reversible with treatment.
• Prognosis depends on the ability to correct the underlying cause.

sections.overview:
• Aplastic Anemia (AA) is a rare, life-threatening bone marrow failure disorder characterized by **pancytopenia** (anemia, neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia) and a corresponding **hypocellular bone marrow**
• It is not a malignancy; rather, it is a failure of the hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) to produce mature blood cells, leading to an "empty" or fatty marrow
sections.etiology:
• The underlying mechanism is the destruction or suppression of pluripotent hematopoietic stem cells. This can be acquired or inherited.
• **Acquired Aplastic Anemia (80-85% of cases)**
    ◦ **Idiopathic (~70%)**
        ▪ The most common form
        ▪ Believed to be an **autoimmune** process where cytotoxic T-lymphocytes (CD8+) attack and destroy hematopoietic stem cells
    ◦ **Drugs**
        ▪ Chloramphenicol (classic association), sulfonamides, carbamazepine, phenytoin, methimazole/propylthiouracil (PTU), gold
    ◦ **Toxins**
        ▪ Benzene, pesticides, toluene
    ◦ **Infections**
        ▪ Viral hepatitis (seronegative hepatitis), Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), HIV, Parvovirus B19 (classically causes transient red cell aplasia, but can trigger AA)
    ◦ **Radiation**
        ▪ High-dose exposure
    ◦ **Pregnancy**
        ▪ Rare, often resolves post-partum
    ◦ **Associated Conditions**
        ▪ Can co-exist with or evolve from Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH)
• **Inherited/Congenital Aplastic Anemia (15-20%)**
    ◦ These are bone marrow failure syndromes that typically present in childhood
    ◦ **Fanconi Anemia**
        ▪ Autosomal recessive
        ▪ The most common inherited form
        ▪ Characterized by progressive pancytopenia *plus* congenital anomalies (short stature, abnormal thumbs/radii, cafe-au-lait spots, renal abnormalities)
    ◦ **Dyskeratosis Congenita**
        ▪ Classic triad of abnormal skin pigmentation, nail dystrophy, and oral leukoplakia
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**
    ◦ Rare, 2-5 cases per million people per year
• **Age Distribution**
    ◦ Exhibits a **bimodal** age distribution with two distinct peaks:
        ▪ Adolescents and young adults (15-25 years)
        ▪ Older adults (>60 years)
• **Gender/Race**
    ◦ No significant gender or racial predilection
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is usually insidious over weeks to months
• Patients present with signs and symptoms directly related to the deficiency of each cell line
• A previously healthy young person presenting with fatigue, bleeding, and infections should raise high suspicion
sections.diagnostics:
• **CBC with Differential**
    ◦ The initial and most important test
    ◦ **Pancytopenia**
        ▪ **Anemia:** Normocytic, normochromic anemia (Hgb <10 g/dL)
        ▪ **Thrombocytopenia:** Platelets often <50,000/L
        ▪ **Neutropenia:** Absolute Neutrophil Count (ANC) <1,500/L
    ◦ **Reticulocyte Count**
        ▪ Markedly **low** (reticulocytopenia), indicating a marrow production failure
• **Peripheral Blood Smear**
    ◦ Shows a paucity of all cell lines
    ◦ RBCs are normocytic and normochromic
    ◦ **No abnormal cells** (e.g., no blasts, no dysplastic cells)
        ▪ This helps differentiate from leukemia and Myelodysplastic Syndrome (MDS)
• **Bone Marrow Aspiration and Biopsy**
    ◦ **THE GOLD STANDARD / DEFINITIVE DIAGNOSTIC TEST**
    ◦ **Hallmark Finding:** **Marked hypocellularity** with extensive replacement by adipocytes (fat cells)
    ◦ Described as a **"hypocellular marrow"** or **"fatty marrow"**
    ◦ Absence of malignant infiltrates or significant fibrosis
• **Additional Workup (to rule out other causes/associations)**
    ◦ **PNH Testing:** Flow cytometry for CD55 and CD59 on RBCs/WBCs
    ◦ **Cytogenetics/Genetic Testing:** To rule out MDS and inherited syndromes like Fanconi Anemia (chromosome breakage analysis)
    ◦ **Vitamin B12 and Folate levels:** To rule out severe megaloblastic anemia
    ◦ **Viral Serologies:** Hepatitis panel, EBV, CMV, HIV
• **Severity Classification (Camitta Criteria for Severe Aplastic Anemia - SAA)**
    ◦ Bone marrow cellularity <25% **PLUS** at least two of the following:
        ▪ ANC < 500/L
        ▪ Platelet count < 20,000/L
        ▪ Absolute reticulocyte count < 20,000/L (or corrected retic < 1%)
sections.prognosis:
• **Untreated SAA**
    ◦ Grave prognosis, with mortality >80% within 1-2 years due to infection or bleeding
• **With Allogeneic HSCT (young patient, matched sibling)**
    ◦ Excellent prognosis, with >80-90% long-term survival
• **With Immunosuppressive Therapy (IST)**
    ◦ Overall response rate is 60-70%
    ◦ The 5-year survival rate is approximately 75%, but relapse and clonal evolution remain risks

sections.overview:
• A rapid reduction in red blood cell (RBC) mass due to hemorrhage
	◦ Primary clinical consequences stem from **intravascular volume depletion (hypovolemia)**, leading to hemodynamic instability and shock, not from the anemia itself
	◦ The drop in hemoglobin (Hgb) and hematocrit (Hct) is often delayed due to the time required for hemodilution (extravascular fluid shifting into the vascular space)
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• Highly prevalent in emergency and critical care settings
• Trauma is a leading cause in younger populations
• GI bleeding is a more common cause in older populations and those with comorbid conditions
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation is dominated by signs and symptoms of hypovolemia and depends on the volume and rate of blood loss, ranging from mild orthostatic dizziness to overt hypovolemic shock
	◦ **Classes of Hemorrhage:**
		▪ **Class I Hemorrhage (<15% blood loss):** Minimal symptoms, near-normal vitals
		▪ **Class II Hemorrhage (15-30% blood loss):** Tachycardia, tachypnea, anxiety, decreased pulse pressure
		▪ **Class III Hemorrhage (30-40% blood loss):** Marked tachycardia, hypotension, confusion, decreased urine output
		▪ **Class IV Hemorrhage (>40% blood loss):** Severe tachycardia and hypotension, lethargy/coma, negligible urine output; immediately life-threatening
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• Highly dependent on the **rate and volume of blood loss**, the patient's underlying comorbidities (especially cardiovascular disease), and the ability to rapidly control the source of bleeding
• Prognosis is excellent if the bleeding is controlled quickly and the patient is otherwise healthy
• Mortality is high in massive hemorrhage, elderly patients, and those with significant comorbidities

sections.overview:
• **Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia (AIHA)** is an acquired, heterogeneous group of disorders characterized by the destruction of **red blood cells (RBCs)** mediated by **autoantibodies** against antigens on the RBC surface.
    ◦ This leads to a shortened RBC lifespan and subsequent **anemia**.
• The hallmark of AIHA is a positive **Direct Antiglobulin Test (DAT)**, also known as the **Direct Coombs test**.
• AIHA is broadly classified based on the thermal characteristics of the autoantibody:
    ◦ **Warm AIHA (WAIHA)**
        ▪ Most common type (~70-80%).
        ▪ Mediated by **IgG antibodies** that react optimally at core body temperature (37°C).
        ▪ Hemolysis is predominantly **extravascular**.
    ◦ **Cold AIHA**
        ▪ Includes **Cold Agglutinin Disease (CAD)** and **Paroxysmal Cold Hemoglobinuria (PCH)**.
        ▪ **Cold Agglutinin Disease (CAD)**: Mediated by **IgM antibodies** that bind RBCs at colder temperatures (<37°C), typically in the peripheral circulation. Hemolysis is predominantly **intravascular** via **complement activation**.
        ▪ **Paroxysmal Cold Hemoglobinuria (PCH)**: Rare type mediated by a biphasic **IgG antibody** (**Donath-Landsteiner antibody**).
    ◦ **Drug-Induced AIHA**
        ▪ Caused by medications that trigger an immune response against RBCs.
sections.etiology: • The core mechanism is a loss of **self-tolerance**, leading to the production of **antibodies** that target one's own RBCs.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: 1-3 cases per 100,000 people per year.
• **Warm AIHA**: Can occur at any age but is more common in middle-aged women. Most common type overall.
• **Cold AIHA**: Primarily affects adults over 50.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • The presentation can range from an insidious onset of **chronic anemia** to a fulminant, life-threatening **hemolytic crisis**.
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• Highly variable and depends on the underlying etiology, severity, and response to therapy.
• **Idiopathic WAIHA** often responds well to first-line therapy, but relapses are common.
• AIHA secondary to **lymphoproliferative disorders** (e.g., **CLL**) has a prognosis tied to the underlying malignancy.
• **Primary CAD** is often a chronic, indolent disease manageable with cold avoidance and intermittent therapy.

sections.overview:
• Hereditary Spherocytosis (HS) is an inherited genetic disorder of the **red blood cell (RBC) membrane**.
• It is characterized by the production of intrinsically defective RBCs that are spherical (**spherocytes**) rather than the normal biconcave disc shape.
• These abnormal cells are less deformable and are prematurely sequestered and destroyed by the **spleen**, leading to a chronic **extravascular hemolytic anemia** of varying severity.
• The clinical presentation is classically defined by the triad of **anemia, splenomegaly, and jaundice**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**:
    ◦ Caused by mutations in genes that code for RBC membrane structural proteins which form the cytoskeleton.
    ◦ **Inheritance**: Primarily **Autosomal Dominant** (~75% of cases). Autosomal recessive and de novo mutations account for the rest.
    ◦ **Most Common Defective Proteins**:
        ▪ **Ankyrin (ANK1 gene)**: Most common defect (~50%)
        ▪ Spectrin (alpha and beta chains)
        ▪ Band 3 protein
        ▪ Protein 4.2
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Membrane Instability**: The genetic defect leads to a deficiency in key structural proteins, weakening the vertical connections between the lipid bilayer and the underlying membrane cytoskeleton.
    ◦ **Loss of Surface Area**: The unstable membrane loses small fragments (microvesicles), decreasing the surface area-to-volume ratio of the cell.
    ◦ **Spherocyte Formation**: To accommodate its volume with a reduced surface area, the RBC assumes a spherical shape.
    ◦ **Splenic Sequestration**: Rigid spherocytes become trapped in the narrow inter-endothelial slits of the spleen (cords of Billroth).
    ◦ **Extravascular Hemolysis**: Trapped spherocytes are phagocytized by splenic macrophages, leading to chronic hemolysis.
sections.epidemiology:
• The most common inherited hemolytic anemia in people of **Northern European descent**.
• Prevalence is approximately 1 in 2,000 to 1 in 5,000 in this population.
• Affects all ethnic groups but is less common in individuals of African or Asian descent.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Family History**: The single greatest risk factor.
    ◦ An affected parent with an autosomal dominant form of HS has a 50% chance of passing the condition to each child.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Severity exists on a spectrum:
    ◦ **Mild HS (~20-30%)**: Patients may be asymptomatic with only mild anemia or compensated hemolysis. Often diagnosed incidentally on lab work.
    ◦ **Moderate HS (~60-70%)**: The "classic" presentation. Patients experience noticeable anemia, intermittent jaundice (often exacerbated by infection or stress), significant splenomegaly, and are at high risk for gallstones.
    ◦ **Severe HS (~5%)**: Presents in infancy or early childhood with severe, transfusion-dependent anemia, marked splenomegaly, and skeletal abnormalities (e.g., **frontal bossing**) from massive bone marrow expansion.
• **Symptoms of Anemia**:
    ◦ Fatigue, pallor, dyspnea on exertion, exercise intolerance.
• **Symptoms of Hemolysis**:
    ◦ **Jaundice**: Yellowing of the skin.
    ◦ **Scleral Icterus**: Yellowing of the whites of the eyes.
    ◦ **Dark Urine**: Due to increased urobilinogen (not hemoglobinuria).
• **Symptoms of Splenomegaly**:
    ◦ Left upper quadrant (LUQ) abdominal fullness, early satiety.
• **Symptoms of Complications**:
    ◦ Biliary colic (RUQ pain) from **pigment gallstones**.
sections.physicalExam:
• **General**: Pallor.
• **HEENT**: **Scleral icterus**.
• **Abdomen**: **Splenomegaly** is a cardinal sign, present in >75% of patients. Palpable spleen tip in the LUQ. Hepatomegaly may also be present.
• **Skin**: **Jaundice**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **CBC with Differential**:
    ◦ **Anemia** (↓ Hgb/Hct): Normocytic or mild microcytic.
    ◦ **↑ MCHC (Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin Concentration) >36 g/dL**: The **hallmark lab finding**, caused by cellular dehydration and loss of membrane surface area.
    ◦ **↑ RDW (Red Cell Distribution Width)**: High degree of variation in RBC size.
• **Peripheral Blood Smear**:
    ◦ **Spherocytes**: Small, dense (hyperchromic) RBCs that **lack central pallor**.
    ◦ **Polychromasia**: Bluish-tinged, larger RBCs (reticulocytes), indicating a robust bone marrow response.
• **Hemolysis Labs**:
    ◦ **↑ Reticulocyte Count**: Bone marrow is compensating for the hemolysis.
    ◦ **↑ Indirect (Unconjugated) Bilirubin**: Product of heme breakdown.
    ◦ **↑ Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH)**: Released from destroyed RBCs.
    ◦ **↓ Haptoglobin**: Binds free hemoglobin; consumed during hemolysis.
• **Confirmatory Tests**:
    ◦ **Osmotic Fragility Test (Classic)**: **Increased osmotic fragility**. Spherocytes lyse more easily in hypotonic salt solutions.
    ◦ **Eosin-5'-maleimide (EMA) Binding Test (Modern)**: Preferred screening test (flow cytometry) with high sensitivity and specificity. **Decreased fluorescence** indicates a deficiency of RBC membrane proteins.
    ◦ **Direct Antiglobulin Test (DAT / Coombs Test)**: **NEGATIVE**. This is crucial for differentiating HS from **autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA)**, which is Coombs positive.
sections.treatment:
• **Supportive Care**:
    ◦ **Folic Acid Supplementation (1 mg daily)**: Essential for all patients. Chronic hemolysis causes rapid RBC turnover, which can deplete folate stores and lead to a megaloblastic crisis.
    ◦ **Blood Transfusions**: Used for severe anemia or during aplastic crises.
• **Definitive Treatment**:
    ◦ **Splenectomy**: The definitive treatment for moderate to severe HS.
        ▪ **Mechanism**: Removes the primary site of RBC destruction. This does not correct the underlying RBC defect but eliminates the hemolysis, thus "curing" the anemia.
        ▪ **Indications**: Severe anemia requiring transfusions, symptomatic splenomegaly, poor growth in children, or severe quality of life impairment.
        ▪ **Timing**: Usually delayed until after age 6 to reduce the risk of **overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI)**.
sections.management:
• **Post-Splenectomy Care**:
    ◦ **Prophylactic Antibiotics**: Daily penicillin is often prescribed, especially for children and for at least the first few years post-op in adults.
• **Monitoring**:
    ◦ Regular CBC to monitor anemia.
    ◦ Abdominal ultrasound periodically to screen for **pigment gallstones**.
sections.complications:
• **Aplastic Crisis**:
    ◦ A sudden, life-threatening drop in hemoglobin due to cessation of erythropoiesis, characterized by a very **low reticulocyte count (<1%)**.
    ◦ Most common trigger: **Parvovirus B19 infection**, which directly infects and destroys RBC precursors.
• **Cholelithiasis (Pigment Gallstones)**:
    ◦ Very common due to chronic hyperbilirubinemia.
    ◦ Can lead to cholecystitis or choledocholithiasis.
    ◦ A cholecystectomy is often performed at the time of splenectomy.
• **Megaloblastic Crisis**:
    ◦ Anemia worsens due to a superimposed **folate deficiency**, impairing RBC production.
• **Overwhelming Post-Splenectomy Infection (OPSI)**:
    ◦ A rare but life-threatening sepsis caused by **encapsulated bacteria**, with a high mortality rate.
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent. With proper management (folic acid, timely splenectomy for severe cases), patients typically have a normal life expectancy and good quality of life.
• Splenectomy is highly effective at controlling the anemia.
sections.preventionEducation:
• **Pre-Splenectomy Vaccinations**:
    ◦ Crucial to administer at least 2 weeks before surgery. Vaccinate against **encapsulated organisms**:
        ▪ *Streptococcus pneumoniae* (Pneumovax 23, Prevnar 13)
        ▪ *Haemophilus influenzae* type B (HiB)
        ▪ *Neisseria meningitidis* (Meningococcal vaccine)
• **Post-Splenectomy Patient Education**:
    ◦ Patients must be aware of their lifelong risk of **OPSI**.
    ◦ Any fever >38°C (100.4°F) is a medical emergency requiring immediate evaluation and empiric antibiotics.

sections.overview:
• **Sickle Cell Disease (SCD)** is a group of inherited, **autosomal recessive** red blood cell disorders.
    ◦ Characterized by the presence of abnormal hemoglobin, called **hemoglobin S (HbS)**.
    ◦ Under conditions of deoxygenation, HbS polymerizes, causing red blood cells (RBCs) to deform into a rigid, crescent or "sickle" shape.
    ◦ These sickled cells lead to two primary pathological processes: **chronic hemolysis** and **vaso-occlusion**, resulting in a wide range of systemic complications.
sections.etiology:
• **Genetic Mutation**: A single point mutation in the beta-globin gene (*HBB*) on chromosome 11.
    ◦ This causes a substitution of valine for glutamic acid at the 6th position of the beta-globin chain.
• **Hemoglobin Types**:
    ◦ **HbSS (Sickle Cell Anemia)**: **Homozygous** form, most common and most severe.
    ◦ **HbSC**: Heterozygous, one sickle gene and one hemoglobin C gene. Generally milder than HbSS.
    ◦ **HbS-beta thalassemia**: One sickle gene and one beta-thalassemia gene. Severity depends on the type of beta-thalassemia mutation.
    ◦ **HbAS (Sickle Cell Trait)**: **Heterozygous carrier state**. One normal hemoglobin A gene and one sickle gene. Generally asymptomatic but can have complications in extreme conditions (e.g., high altitude, extreme exertion). Offers protection against malaria.
• **Pathophysiology Cascade**:
    ◦ **Triggers**: Low oxygen tension (**hypoxia**), **acidosis**, **dehydration**, **infection**, or **cold exposure**.
    ◦ **Polymerization**: Deoxygenated HbS molecules link together, forming long, rigid polymers.
    ◦ **Sickling**: These polymers distort the RBC into the characteristic crescent shape. This process is initially reversible with re-oxygenation.
    ◦ **Vaso-occlusion**: The rigid, sticky sickled cells cannot pass through small capillaries. They clump together, obstructing blood flow and causing downstream tissue ischemia, infarction, and severe pain (**vaso-occlusive crisis**).
    ◦ **Hemolysis**: Sickled RBCs are fragile and have a shortened lifespan (10-20 days vs. 120 days for normal RBCs). They are destroyed by the spleen (**extravascular hemolysis**) and in circulation (**intravascular hemolysis**), leading to chronic anemia.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Most common in individuals of African, Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, and Indian subcontinent descent.
    ◦ The high prevalence in these regions is due to the selective advantage of the **sickle cell trait (HbAS)** against *Plasmodium falciparum* malaria.
• **In the United States**:
    ◦ Affects approximately 100,000 Americans.
    ◦ Occurs in about 1 in every 365 Black or African American births.
    ◦ **Sickle cell trait (HbAS)** is found in about 1 in 13 Black or African American babies.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The clinical presentation is highly variable, ranging from chronic, low-grade symptoms to acute, life-threatening crises.
• **Vaso-Occlusive Crisis (VOC) / Pain Crisis**: The **hallmark of SCD**.
    ◦ Sudden onset of severe pain in bones (femur, humerus, tibia), back, chest, or abdomen due to ischemic tissue injury.
• **Acute Chest Syndrome (ACS)**: A life-threatening emergency.
    ◦ Defined as a **new pulmonary infiltrate** on chest X-ray plus fever, cough, chest pain, dyspnea, or hypoxia.
    ◦ Can be caused by infection, fat embolism from bone marrow infarction, or pulmonary infarction.
• **Splenic Sequestration Crisis**:
    ◦ Most common in young children before the spleen fibroses (**autosplenectomy**).
    ◦ Characterized by a rapid, painful enlargement of the spleen and a sudden **drop in hemoglobin**, leading to **hypovolemic shock**.
• **Aplastic Crisis**:
    ◦ A temporary cessation of RBC production, often triggered by **Parvovirus B19** infection.
    ◦ Presents with a rapid drop in hemoglobin and a profoundly **low reticulocyte count**.
• **Stroke**:
    ◦ Can be ischemic or hemorrhagic.
    ◦ A major cause of morbidity, especially in children.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Newborn Screening**: Standard in all 50 U.S. states.
• **Hemoglobin Electrophoresis**: **Gold standard** for diagnosis.
• **HbSS**: Predominantly HbS, no HbA, small amount of HbF.
• **HbAS (Trait)**: ~60% HbA, ~40% HbS.
• **Complete Blood Count (CBC)**:
    ◦ **Normocytic, normochromic anemia** (baseline Hgb 6-9 g/dL).
    ◦ **Reticulocytosis** (chronically elevated, 10-25%).
    ◦ **Leukocytosis** and **thrombocytosis** are common at baseline.
• **Peripheral Blood Smear**:
    ◦ **Sickled cells (drepanocytes)**.
    ◦ **Howell-Jolly bodies** (nuclear remnants in RBCs, pathognomonic for **functional asplenia**).
    ◦ Target cells.
• **Labs During Crisis**:
    ◦ Hgb may drop significantly (aplastic, sequestration crises).
    ◦ **Reticulocyte count** will be very low (<1%) in an **aplastic crisis**.
    ◦ Markers of hemolysis (elevated indirect bilirubin, LDH; low haptoglobin).
• **Imaging**:
    ◦ **Chest X-ray**: Essential for diagnosing **Acute Chest Syndrome** (new infiltrate).
    ◦ **MRI/CT of Head**: To evaluate for stroke.
    ◦ **MRI of Bones**: To evaluate for avascular necrosis or osteomyelitis.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis has improved dramatically with comprehensive care.
• In high-resource countries, median life expectancy is now into the 40s-60s.
• Morbidity remains high, and quality of life can be significantly impacted by chronic pain and organ damage.
• Leading causes of death are **acute chest syndrome**, infection, and end-organ failure.

sections.overview:
• Sickle Cell Trait (SCT) is a **benign carrier state**, not a disease.
    ◦ Occurs in individuals who have inherited one gene for normal hemoglobin (**HbA**) and one gene for sickle hemoglobin (**HbS**).
    ◦ The genetic makeup is referred to as **HbAS**.
• Unlike Sickle Cell Disease (SCD), individuals with SCT have more **HbA** than **HbS**.
    ◦ This high percentage of normal hemoglobin prevents the chronic, widespread red blood cell (RBC) sickling and clinical manifestations seen in SCD.
• The vast majority of individuals are **asymptomatic** and have a normal life expectancy.
• Clinical issues are rare and typically only arise under conditions of **extreme physiologic stress**.
sections.etiology:
• **Genetics**
    ◦ **Autosomal recessive** inheritance pattern.
    ◦ Individuals are **heterozygous** for the beta-globin gene, possessing one normal allele (A) and one sickle allele (s).
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The presence of the s allele leads to the production of sickle hemoglobin (**HbS**).
    ◦ In individuals with SCT, the total hemoglobin is composed of approximately **50-60% HbA** and **35-45% HbS**.
    ◦ The predominance of normal **HbA** prevents the extensive polymerization of **HbS** that characterizes SCD.
    ◦ RBC sickling is rare but can be provoked by severe, systemic conditions such as:
        ▪ **Profound Hypoxia** (e.g., high altitude, unpressurized aircraft)
        ▪ **Extreme Dehydration**
        ▪ **Severe Acidosis**
        ▪ **Extreme Physical Exertion**
    ◦ When these triggers occur, deoxygenated **HbS** can polymerize, causing RBCs to deform into a rigid, sickle shape, which can lead to **microvascular occlusion** in specific organs (notably the renal medulla and spleen).
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**
    ◦ Most common in populations from sub-Saharan Africa, the Mediterranean, the Middle East, and India.
    ◦ **United States:** Affects approximately 8-10% of African Americans.
        ▪ About **1 in 13 African American** babies is born with SCT.
• **Evolutionary Advantage**
    ◦ The high prevalence is due to the **heterozygote advantage**, where SCT provides significant protection against severe forms of ***Plasmodium falciparum* malaria**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The overwhelming majority of individuals are **completely asymptomatic** and unaware of their status until identified through screening.
• Presentation is most often an incidental finding on a **newborn screening panel** or hemoglobin electrophoresis ordered for other reasons.
• Symptoms, if they occur, are episodic and directly related to a specific **physiological stressor**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Screening**
    ◦ **Newborn Screening:** Standard in all 50 U.S. states.
    ◦ **Hemoglobin Solubility Tests** (e.g., Sickledex)
        ▪ Rapid and inexpensive.
        ▪ Detects the presence of HbS but **cannot differentiate between SCT (HbAS) and SCD (HbSS)**.
        ▪ Not used for definitive diagnosis.
• **Confirmatory Testing (Gold Standard)**
    ◦ **Hemoglobin Electrophoresis** or **High-Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC)**.
    ◦ **Classic Result for SCT:**
        ▪ **HbA: 50-60%**
        ▪ **HbS: 35-45%**
        ▪ HbF and HbA2: Normal levels.
• **Laboratory Findings**
    ◦ **CBC:** **Normal**. No anemia. Normal RBC count, hemoglobin, hematocrit, and RBC indices (MCV, MCH, MCHC).
    ◦ **Peripheral Smear:** **Normal**. Sickled cells are not present.
    ◦ **Urinalysis**
        ▪ May show microscopic or gross **hematuria**.
        ▪ May also show **hyposthenuria** (low urine specific gravity, ~1.010), indicating an impaired ability to concentrate urine.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent.**
• Life expectancy is **normal** and not different from the general population without the trait.
• The vast majority of individuals lead full, healthy lives with no medical issues related to SCT.

sections.overview:
• Alpha thalassemia is a group of inherited **microcytic, hemolytic anemias** characterized by reduced or absent synthesis of the alpha-globin chains of hemoglobin.
• Hemoglobin A (HbA), the primary adult hemoglobin, is a tetramer of two alpha chains and two beta chains (α2β2).
• A deficiency in alpha-globin chains leads to an excess of other chains (beta or gamma), which form unstable tetramers, causing premature red blood cell (RBC) destruction (**hemolysis**) and ineffective erythropoiesis.
• The clinical severity is directly proportional to the number of deleted alpha-globin genes, ranging from an asymptomatic carrier state to a lethal in-utero condition.
sections.etiology:
• **Genetics**: Caused by **gene deletions** on the short arm of **chromosome 16**.
    ◦ There are four alpha-globin genes in a normal individual, two on each chromosome (αα/αα).
• **Pathophysiology**: The core issue is an imbalance between alpha-globin and beta-globin chain production.
    ◦ Decreased alpha-chain synthesis leads to a relative excess of beta-chains (in adults) or gamma-chains (in fetuses/newborns).
    ◦ These excess chains pair up to form unstable tetramers:
        ▪ **Hemoglobin H (HbH)**: Tetramers of four **beta-chains (β4)**. HbH is unstable, prone to oxidation, and precipitates within RBCs to form **Heinz bodies**. These damaged RBCs are cleared by the spleen, leading to chronic extravascular hemolysis.
        ▪ **Hemoglobin Barts (Hb Barts)**: Tetramers of four **gamma-chains (γ4)**. This is seen in fetuses and newborns. Hb Barts has an extremely high affinity for oxygen and does not release it to tissues, leading to severe tissue hypoxia and is incompatible with postnatal life.
• **Clinical Syndromes Based on Number of Gene Deletions**:
    ◦ **One deletion** (-α/αα): **Silent Carrier**
        ▪ Asymptomatic, hematologically normal or borderline low MCV.
    ◦ **Two deletions** (-α/-α or --/αα): **Alpha Thalassemia Trait (Minor)**
        ▪ Mild **microcytic anemia**, usually asymptomatic.
    ◦ **Three deletions** (--/-α): **Hemoglobin H (HbH) Disease**
        ▪ Moderate to severe **microcytic, hemolytic anemia**. Clinically significant.
    ◦ **Four deletions** (--/--): **Hydrops Fetalis / Hb Barts**
        ▪ Lethal in utero or shortly after birth without intervention. Severe anemia.
• **Cis vs. Trans Deletion** (in 2-gene deletion):
    ◦ **Trans (-α/-α)**: One deletion on each chromosome. Common in **African** populations. Offspring can inherit trait but are not at risk for HbH disease.
    ◦ **Cis (--/αα)**: Both deletions on the same chromosome. Common in **Southeast Asian** populations. A couple where both partners have the cis-deletion have a 25% chance of having a child with **Hydrops Fetalis**.
sections.epidemiology:
• Most common in regions where malaria is or was endemic, suggesting a selective advantage.
• High prevalence in:
    ◦ **Southeast Asia** (highest prevalence of severe forms)
    ◦ **Mediterranean** regions
    ◦ **Africa**
    ◦ The Middle East
sections.riskFactors:
• **Family history** of thalassemia.
• **Ethnic background** from endemic regions (**Southeast Asian, African, Mediterranean**).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation depends entirely on the number of gene deletions.
    ◦ **Silent Carrier (1 deletion)**: Asymptomatic. Discovered incidentally or through family screening.
    ◦ **Alpha Thalassemia Trait (2 deletions)**: Typically asymptomatic. May have mild fatigue. Often discovered incidentally on a CBC showing persistent **microcytic anemia** without another cause (e.g., normal iron studies).
    ◦ **HbH Disease (3 deletions)**: Presents with chronic **hemolytic anemia** of variable severity. Symptoms are often exacerbated by oxidative stress (infection, certain drugs).
    ◦ **Hydrops Fetalis (4 deletions)**: Presents in utero with severe anemia, massive fluid accumulation (**ascites, pleural/pericardial effusions**), heart failure, and hepatosplenomegaly. Usually results in stillbirth or neonatal death.
• Symptoms from **Chronic Anemia**:
    ◦ Fatigue, weakness, pallor, exercise intolerance, shortness of breath.
• Symptoms from **Hemolysis**:
    ◦ **Jaundice**, dark urine (urobilinogen), scleral icterus.
• Symptoms from **Ineffective Erythropoiesis** (in severe cases):
    ◦ Bone pain, pathologic fractures due to marrow expansion.
sections.physicalExam:
• **General**: Pallor, **jaundice**.
• **Abdomen**: **Splenomegaly** is common due to sequestration of damaged RBCs and extramedullary hematopoiesis. Hepatomegaly may also be present.
• **HEENT**: **Frontal bossing**, prominent maxilla ("**chipmunk facies**") in severe, transfusion-dependent cases due to bone marrow expansion.
sections.diagnostics:
• **CBC with Differential**:
    ◦ **Microcytic anemia**: Low Hemoglobin/Hematocrit, **very low MCV** (often 60-75 fL).
    ◦ **Low MCH/MCHC** (**hypochromic**).
    ◦ **RBC count**: Often **normal or high** for the degree of anemia (a key differentiator from iron deficiency anemia, where RBC count is typically low).
    ◦ **RDW**: Usually normal in trait and elevated in HbH disease.
• **Peripheral Blood Smear**:
    ◦ **Microcytic, hypochromic** RBCs.
    ◦ **Target cells (codocytes)**.
    ◦ Anisopoikilocytosis (variation in size and shape).
    ◦ **Basophilic stippling**.
    ◦ **Heinz Bodies**: With supravital staining (e.g., crystal violet), precipitated HbH appears as small intracellular inclusions, giving a **"golf ball" appearance** to the RBC.
• **Iron Studies**: **CRITICAL** for differential diagnosis.
    ◦ Serum iron, ferritin, and transferrin saturation are **NORMAL or INCREASED**. This rules out iron deficiency.
• **Hemoglobin Electrophoresis**:
    ◦ **Newborn Screen**: Detects **Hb Barts** (γ4).
    ◦ **Adults with HbH Disease**: Shows a fast-migrating band representing **HbH (β4)**, typically comprising 5-30% of total hemoglobin.
    ◦ **Alpha Thal Trait**: Adult electrophoresis is often **normal**, as the proportions of HbA, HbA2, and HbF are unaffected. This is a key difference from beta-thalassemia trait, which shows an elevated HbA2.
• **Definitive Diagnosis**:
    ◦ **Genetic testing (DNA analysis)** is the gold standard to confirm the diagnosis and identify the specific number and type of gene deletions.
sections.treatment:
• **Silent Carrier / Alpha Thal Trait**:
    ◦ **No treatment required**.
    ◦ Important to **avoid unnecessary iron supplementation**, which can lead to iron overload.
    ◦ The main intervention is **genetic counseling** to assess risk for offspring.
• **HbH Disease**:
    ◦ **Folic acid supplementation** (1 mg/day) to support RBC production.
    ◦ **Avoidance of oxidative stressors**, including sulfa drugs and certain antimalarials.
    ◦ **Episodic blood transfusions** during periods of severe anemia (e.g., aplastic crisis, severe infection).
    ◦ **Splenectomy** may be considered in patients with severe hemolysis, massive splenomegaly, and high transfusion requirements.
• **Hydrops Fetalis**:
    ◦ Historically fatal.
    ◦ Aggressive **intrauterine blood transfusions** may allow for survival to term, but the child will require lifelong chronic transfusion therapy and/or hematopoietic stem cell transplant. Prognosis remains poor.
sections.management:
• **Monitoring (for HbH Disease)**: Regular follow-up with a hematologist, including monitoring CBC, growth, and development.
• **Iron Overload**: For patients receiving chronic transfusions, monitor ferritin levels and manage iron overload with **chelation therapy** (e.g., deferoxamine, deferasirox, deferiprone).
sections.complications:
• **Iron overload (hemosiderosis)**: From chronic transfusions, leading to damage of the heart, liver, and endocrine organs.
• **Cholelithiasis (pigment gallstones)**: Due to chronic hemolysis and increased bilirubin turnover.
• **Splenomegaly**: Can lead to hypersplenism, worsening anemia and causing abdominal discomfort.
• **Aplastic Crisis**: Acute, severe anemia often triggered by **Parvovirus B19** infection, which temporarily shuts down erythropoiesis.
• **Skeletal Deformities**: From massive expansion of the bone marrow.
• **Increased susceptibility to infection**, especially after splenectomy.
sections.prognosis:
• **Silent Carrier & Trait**: Normal life expectancy and quality of life.
• **HbH Disease**: Variable, but with modern management, most patients have a near-normal life expectancy. Morbidity is related to anemia severity and complications of treatment (e.g., iron overload).
• **Hydrops Fetalis**: Almost universally fatal in utero or perinatally unless aggressive and specialized intrauterine transfusions are performed.
sections.preventionEducation:
• **Patient Education**: Counsel on the genetic nature of the disease and avoidance of oxidative drugs/triggers.
• **Genetic Counseling**: Essential for all patients and their families to understand inheritance patterns and risks for future pregnancies.

sections.overview:
• Autosomal recessive inherited hemoglobinopathy characterized by a quantitative defect in hemoglobin synthesis
    ◦ Results from reduced (+) or absent (0) synthesis of the **beta-globin chains** of hemoglobin A (HbA)
    ◦ Imbalance of globin chain production leads to ineffective erythropoiesis, hemolysis, and chronic anemia of varying severity
    ◦ The clinical spectrum ranges from asymptomatic carriers (**thalassemia minor**) to severe, transfusion-dependent anemia (**thalassemia major**)
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ Caused by mutations in the **HBB gene** on chromosome 11, which codes for the beta-globin chain
    ◦ An **autosomal recessive** disorder
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Reduced/Absent Beta-Globin Synthesis**: Leads to a decreased production of Hemoglobin A (α2β2)
    ◦ **Relative Excess of Alpha-Globin Chains**: Unpaired alpha-globin chains are highly unstable and precipitate within red blood cell (RBC) precursors in the bone marrow
    ◦ **Ineffective Erythropoiesis**: The alpha-chain precipitates damage the cell membrane, leading to premature destruction (apoptosis) of RBC precursors within the bone marrow, which is the primary cause of anemia
    ◦ **Hemolysis**: The few RBCs that mature and enter circulation are damaged and have a shortened lifespan, being rapidly cleared by macrophages in the spleen and liver (extravascular hemolysis)
    ◦ **Compensatory Mechanisms**
        ▪ **Massive Erythroid Hyperplasia**: The bone marrow expands dramatically to compensate for the anemia, leading to skeletal deformities
        ▪ **Extramedullary Hematopoiesis**: Hematopoiesis occurs outside the bone marrow, primarily in the liver and spleen, contributing to massive hepatosplenomegaly
        ▪ **Increased HbF Production**: Synthesis of fetal hemoglobin (HbF, α2γ2) persists but is insufficient to fully compensate
    ◦ **Iron Overload (Hemosiderosis)**
        ▪ Occurs via repeated blood transfusions (primary cause) and increased gastrointestinal iron absorption due to suppressed hepcidin
sections.epidemiology:
• Most common in individuals of **Mediterranean** (Greek, Italian), **Middle Eastern**, **North African**, and **Southeast Asian** descent
• The high carrier frequency in these regions is thought to be due to a selective advantage (heterozygote advantage) against severe malaria
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation depends on the number of defective beta-globin alleles (one vs. two) and the specific mutation's severity
• **Beta Thalassemia Major (Cooley's Anemia)**
    ◦ Homozygous (β0/β0 or severe β+/β+)
    ◦ Presents in infancy (**6-24 months of age**) as fetal hemoglobin (HbF) levels decline
    ◦ Infants develop severe, life-threatening anemia, failure to thrive, pallor, and irritability
    ◦ Requires lifelong blood transfusions for survival
• **Beta Thalassemia Intermedia**
    ◦ Milder homozygous or compound heterozygous forms
    ◦ Presents later in childhood or even early adulthood
    ◦ Moderate anemia that is **not transfusion-dependent** at diagnosis, though transfusions may be needed during times of stress (e.g., infection, pregnancy)
• **Beta Thalassemia Minor (Trait)**
    ◦ Heterozygous (one normal, one mutated allele)
    ◦ Usually **asymptomatic**
    ◦ Typically discovered incidentally on a complete blood count (CBC) showing a mild microcytic anemia
sections.diagnostics:
• **CBC with Peripheral Smear**
    ◦ **Microcytic, hypochromic anemia** (Low MCV, low MCH/MCHC)
    ◦ **MCV is disproportionately low** for the degree of anemia (e.g., MCV < 70 fL with Hgb of 10 g/dL)
    ◦ **Normal RDW** (in contrast to iron deficiency anemia, where it is often elevated)
    ◦ **Peripheral Smear**: Poikilocytosis and anisocytosis
        ▪ Key findings include **target cells (codocytes)**, teardrop cells (dacrocytes), and **basophilic stippling**
• **Iron Studies**
    ◦ Essential to differentiate from iron deficiency anemia
    ◦ Serum iron, ferritin, and transferrin saturation are **normal or elevated**
• **Hemoglobin Electrophoresis / HPLC (Confirmatory Test)**
    ◦ **Beta Thalassemia Major**
        ▪ HbA: Markedly decreased or absent
        ▪ **HbF: Markedly elevated** (often >90%)
        ▪ HbA2: Variable
    ◦ **Beta Thalassemia Minor (Trait)**
        ▪ **Pathognomonic finding: Elevated HbA2 (>3.5%)**
        ▪ HbF: Normal or slightly elevated
• **Imaging (in severe disease)**
    ◦ **Skull X-ray**: Classic "**hair-on-end**" or "**crew-cut**" appearance due to diploic space expansion from erythroid hyperplasia
    ◦ **Bone X-rays**: Show cortical thinning and a widened marrow space
sections.prognosis:
• **Thalassemia Major**: Untreated, it is fatal in early childhood. With modern transfusion and chelation therapy, life expectancy is well into mid-adulthood (40-50s+). Cardiac disease remains the leading cause of death.
• **Thalassemia Intermedia**: Variable prognosis but often a near-normal lifespan, albeit with significant morbidity.
• **Thalassemia Minor**: Normal life expectancy and quality of life.

sections.overview:
• **Polycythemia Vera (PV)** is a chronic, clonal **myeloproliferative neoplasm (MPN)** characterized by the overproduction of all three hematopoietic cell lines (erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets), but most prominently red blood cells (**erythrocytosis**).
    ◦ This leads to increased red blood cell mass, blood volume, and blood viscosity, predisposing patients to **thrombotic** and **hemorrhagic** events.
    ◦ It is driven by a somatic mutation, most commonly in the ***JAK2*** gene.
sections.etiology:
• **Core Defect:** An acquired gain-of-function mutation in a hematopoietic stem cell.
• **Genetic Marker:** Over 95% of PV cases are associated with the **JAK2 V617F mutation**.
    ◦ The Janus Kinase 2 (**JAK2**) protein is a tyrosine kinase involved in signal transduction pathways for hematopoietic growth factors, including erythropoietin (EPO).
    ◦ The V617F mutation causes the JAK2 protein to be constitutively active, meaning it is "always on," even in the absence of EPO.
• **Pathophysiologic Cascade:**
    ◦ **Constitutive Activation:** The mutated stem cell proliferates uncontrollably without normal growth factor regulation.
    ◦ **Erythroid Proliferation:** The proliferation is most pronounced in the erythroid (RBC) lineage, leading to an expanded red cell mass independent of EPO levels.
    ◦ **Panmyelosis:** The mutation also drives the proliferation of megakaryocytes (platelets) and granulocytes (WBCs), resulting in thrombocytosis and leukocytosis.
    ◦ **Negative Feedback:** The high red blood cell mass suppresses renal production of EPO. Therefore, a hallmark of PV is an **elevated Hgb/Hct with a low serum EPO level**.
    ◦ **Hyperviscosity:** The increased cellular components, particularly RBCs, thicken the blood, impairing microcirculation.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** Relatively rare, affecting ~2-3 per 100,000 people.
• **Median Age at Diagnosis:** 60 years. It is uncommon in individuals under 40.
• **Gender:** Slight male predominance (1.5:1).
sections.riskFactors:
• **Primary "Risk Factor":** The acquired somatic **JAK2 V617F mutation**. This is not an inherited risk.
• **Age:** Incidence increases significantly with age.
• **Environmental Exposure (weak association):** Long-term exposure to benzene or ionizing radiation may be linked, but the association is not strong.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Many patients are **asymptomatic** at diagnosis, with the condition discovered incidentally on a routine Complete Blood Count (CBC).
• When symptomatic, the presentation is often related to hyperviscosity or complications from thrombosis.
• The classic patient is a middle-aged male complaining of headaches, dizziness, and a strange itching sensation after showering.
• **Hyperviscosity-Related Symptoms:**
    ◦ **Neurologic:** Headache, dizziness, vertigo, tinnitus, visual disturbances (scotomata, blurred vision).
    ◦ **Constitutional:** Generalized fatigue, weakness, dyspnea.
• **Pathognomonic / Classic Symptoms:**
    ◦ **Aquagenic Pruritus:** Intense itching, typically after a hot bath or shower. Caused by mast cell and basophil degranulation.
    ◦ **Erythromelalgia:** Intermittent burning pain, warmth, and redness in the hands and feet. Caused by microvascular thrombi and relieved by aspirin.
• **Complication-Related Symptoms:**
    ◦ **Thrombosis:** Symptoms of DVT, PE, MI, TIA, or CVA. Unexplained thrombosis in unusual sites (e.g., portal vein, splenic vein, or hepatic vein-**Budd-Chiari syndrome**) should raise suspicion for an MPN.
    ◦ **Bleeding:** Epistaxis, gum bleeding, or GI bleeding. This is a paradoxical effect due to dysfunctional platelets (acquired von Willebrand syndrome).
    ◦ **Abdominal Fullness:** Early satiety or LUQ pain due to splenomegaly.
    ◦ **Gout:** Due to high cell turnover leading to hyperuricemia.
sections.physicalExam:
• **General:** **Plethora** (a ruddy, reddish-purple complexion of the face, hands, and feet).
• **HEENT:** **Conjunctival plethora** (engorged, dark red conjunctival vessels).
• **Abdomen:** **Splenomegaly** is present in ~75% of patients. Hepatomegaly is less common.
• **Skin:** Excoriations from scratching, facial flushing.
• **Cardiovascular:** Hypertension is common.
sections.diagnostics:
• The diagnostic approach follows the WHO 2016 criteria, which requires meeting all 3 major criteria or the first 2 major criteria and the minor criterion.
• **Major Criteria:**
    ◦ **Elevated Hemoglobin/Hematocrit:**
        ▪ Hgb > 16.5 g/dL (men) or > 16.0 g/dL (women)
        ▪ Hct > 49% (men) or > 48% (women)
        ▪ OR Elevated red cell mass
    ◦ **Bone Marrow Biopsy:** Hypercellularity for age with **panmyelosis** (proliferation of erythroid, granulocytic, and megakaryocytic lineages).
    ◦ **Presence of JAK2 mutation:** ***JAK2*** **V617F** or ***JAK2*** **exon 12 mutation**.
• **Minor Criterion:**
    ◦ **Subnormal (low) serum erythropoietin (EPO) level.**
• **Typical Diagnostic Workup:**
    ◦ **CBC with Differential:** Initial test. Shows **erythrocytosis**, often with **thrombocytosis** and/or **leukocytosis**. Basophilia and eosinophilia are common.
    ◦ **JAK2 V617F Mutation Analysis:** The most important confirmatory test. Positive in >95% of PV patients.
    ◦ **Serum EPO Level:** If JAK2 is positive, a low EPO level helps confirm the diagnosis and distinguishes it from secondary polycythemia.
    ◦ **Bone Marrow Aspiration & Biopsy:** Not always required for diagnosis if the other criteria are met, but is often performed to confirm panmyelosis, assess for fibrosis, and perform cytogenetics.
sections.treatment:
• **Low-Risk Patients** (Age < 60 and no history of thrombosis):
    ◦ [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
• **High-Risk Patients** (Age ≥ 60 OR a history of thrombosis):
    ◦ **First-Line:** **Hydroxyurea**.
    ◦ **Second-Line:** **Interferon-alfa** (often preferred in younger patients or women desiring pregnancy) or **Ruxolitinib** (a JAK1/2 inhibitor) for patients intolerant or resistant to hydroxyurea.
sections.management:
• **Routine Monitoring:** Regular CBCs to ensure Hct remains < 45%.
• **Symptom Control:**
    ◦ **Pruritus:** Antihistamines, SSRIs (e.g., paroxetine), or ruxolitinib.
    ◦ **Gout/Hyperuricemia:** Allopurinol.
• **Cardiovascular Risk Reduction:** Aggressively manage hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and smoking.
sections.complications:
• **Thrombosis:** **Most common cause of morbidity and mortality**. Includes both arterial (MI, CVA) and venous (DVT, PE, **Budd-Chiari syndrome**) events.
• **Hemorrhage:** Paradoxical bleeding due to platelet dysfunction.
• **Disease Transformation:**
    ◦ **Post-PV Myelofibrosis ("Spent Phase"):** The bone marrow becomes fibrotic, leading to cytopenias (especially anemia), progressive splenomegaly, and severe constitutional symptoms.
    ◦ **Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) or Myelodysplastic Syndrome (MDS):** Occurs in a small percentage of patients, with the risk increased by long-term treatment with cytoreductive agents like hydroxyurea.
sections.prognosis:
• With treatment, the prognosis is generally good, with a median survival of **over 20 years**.
• Without treatment, median survival is less than 2 years due to thrombotic complications.
• The leading causes of death are thrombosis and transformation to AML or myelofibrosis.

sections.overview:
• **Essential Thrombocythemia (ET)** is a chronic **myeloproliferative neoplasm (MPN)** characterized by a sustained, clonal proliferation of megakaryocytes in the bone marrow.
    ◦ This leads to an excessive number of platelets in the peripheral blood (**thrombocytosis**).
• The primary clinical consequences are an increased risk of **thromboembolic events** (blood clots) and, paradoxically, **hemorrhagic events** (bleeding).
• Many patients are **asymptomatic** at diagnosis.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ ET is caused by acquired somatic mutations in a hematopoietic stem cell, leading to uncontrolled growth.
    ◦ The key driver mutations are:
        ▪ **JAK2 (Janus kinase 2) V617F mutation**: Most common, present in **~50-60%** of patients. This is a gain-of-function mutation that causes the cell to proliferate continuously, independent of normal growth factor signaling (e.g., thrombopoietin).
        ▪ **CALR (calreticulin) mutation**: Second most common, found in **~20-30%** of patients. Mutually exclusive with **JAK2** and **MPL** mutations.
        ▪ **MPL (myeloproliferative leukemia virus oncogene) mutation**: The thrombopoietin receptor gene. Less common, seen in **~3-5%** of patients.
        ▪ **Triple-Negative**: ~10-15% of patients lack any of these three driver mutations.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The mutated stem cell gives rise to a clone of megakaryocytes that are hypersensitive to or independent of thrombopoietin.
    ◦ This results in massive, unregulated production and release of platelets into the circulation.
    ◦ These platelets are often functionally abnormal, which contributes to both the thrombotic and hemorrhagic tendencies.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Approximately 1-2.5 cases per 100,000 people per year.
• **Median Age at Diagnosis**: ~60 years old. It can occur at any age but is rare in children.
• **Gender**: Slightly more common in women (female-to-male ratio of ~2:1).
sections.riskFactors:
• **Primary "Risk Factor"**: The presence of an acquired somatic mutation (**JAK2, CALR, MPL**).
• **Risk Factors for Thrombosis** (Crucial for Treatment decisions):
    ◦ **Age > 60 years**
    ◦ **Prior history of thrombosis** (arterial or venous)
    ◦ Presence of **JAK2 V617F mutation**
    ◦ Coexisting cardiovascular risk factors (hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, smoking)
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Over 50% of patients are **asymptomatic** at diagnosis, with thrombocytosis discovered incidentally on a routine **complete blood count (CBC)**.
• When symptomatic, presentation is related to either thrombosis, hemorrhage, or microvascular disturbances.
    ◦ **Thrombotic Events**
        ▪ **Deep vein thrombosis (DVT)**, **pulmonary embolism (PE)**, **myocardial infarction (MI)**, **cerebrovascular accident (CVA/stroke)**, **transient ischemic attack (TIA)**, or thrombosis in unusual sites (e.g., portal, hepatic, mesenteric veins).
    ◦ **Hemorrhagic Events**
        ▪ Less common than thrombosis.
        ▪ Typically occurs with extreme thrombocytosis (**platelets > 1,000,000/L**).
        ▪ Presents as **epistaxis**, gingival bleeding, **easy bruising**, or **GI bleeding**.
    ◦ **Vasomotor/Microvascular Symptoms** (due to platelet aggregation in small vessels)
        ▪ **Erythromelalgia**: Classic finding. Intense, burning pain, redness, and warmth in the hands and feet. **Relieved by aspirin**.
        ▪ **Headaches**, dizziness, visual disturbances (**amaurosis fugax**), or **paresthesias**.
    ◦ **Constitutional Symptoms**
        ▪ Fatigue, low-grade fever, weight loss (less common than in other MPNs like PMF or CML).
sections.physicalExam:
• The physical exam is often **completely normal**.
• **Splenomegaly**: Palpable in ~40-50% of patients. Usually mild and non-tender.
• **Hepatomegaly**: Less common (~20%).
• **Skin Findings**: 
    ◦ Livedo reticularis, signs of digital ischemia, petechiae, or ecchymoses.
    ◦ Erythematous and warm extremities if **erythromelalgia** is present.
sections.diagnostics:
• **CBC with Differential**
    ◦ **Hallmark**: Sustained platelet count **> 450,000/L**. Often >600,000/L.
    ◦ **WBC**: May be normal or mildly elevated (leukocytosis).
    ◦ **Hemoglobin/Hematocrit**: Usually normal (this helps distinguish it from Polycythemia Vera).
• **Peripheral Blood Smear**
    ◦ Marked thrombocytosis with large, giant, or bizarre-shaped platelets.
    ◦ Platelet clumps are common.
• **Bone Marrow Aspiration and Biopsy (Confirmatory)**
    ◦ **Required for diagnosis** to confirm ET and exclude other MPNs.
    ◦ Shows hypercellularity with a marked proliferation of large, mature-appearing megakaryocytes, often in clusters.
    ◦ No significant increase in reticulin fibrosis (to exclude Primary Myelofibrosis).
    ◦ No features of CML, MDS, or PV.
• **Genetic/Molecular Testing**
    ◦ Test for **JAK2 V617F** mutation first.
    ◦ If negative, test for **CALR** and **MPL** mutations.
• **Exclusion of Reactive Thrombocytosis**
    ◦ **Iron Studies**: Rule out iron deficiency anemia (a common cause of reactive thrombocytosis).
    ◦ **Inflammatory Markers (ESR, CRP)**: Elevated in reactive states (inflammation, infection).
    ◦ **BCR-ABL1 Gene**: Test to exclude Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML).
• **WHO 2016 Diagnostic Criteria**: Requires meeting all 4 major criteria OR the first 3 major criteria and the 1 minor criterion.
    ◦ **Major Criteria**:
        ▪ Platelet count ≥ 450 x 10⁹/L.
        ▪ Bone marrow biopsy showing proliferation mainly of the megakaryocytic lineage with increased numbers of large, mature megakaryocytes. No significant increase in granulopoiesis or erythropoiesis.
