        ▪ **Caveat**: Can be falsely positive/negative during acute thrombosis or in patients on anticoagulants (heparin, DOACs)
    ◦ **Confirmatory Test**: **Genetic Testing (PCR)**
        ▪ Directly detects the G1691A mutation in the *F5* gene
        ▪ **Gold standard** for diagnosis
        ▪ Unaffected by anticoagulants or acute thrombosis
sections.treatment:
• **Acute VTE Treatment**
    ◦ **Anticoagulation** is the mainstay
    ◦ **First-line**: Direct Oral Anticoagulants (**DOACs**) like Apixaban or Rivaroxaban
    ◦ **Other options**
        ▪ Low-Molecular-Weight Heparin (LMWH, e.g., Enoxaparin), often used for initial treatment, bridging to warfarin, or monotherapy in cancer/pregnancy
        ▪ Unfractionated Heparin (UFH), used for hemodynamically unstable patients or severe renal failure
        ▪ Warfarin (Vitamin K antagonist), requires bridging and INR monitoring
    ◦ **Thrombolysis or Thrombectomy**: Reserved for massive, life-threatening PE with hemodynamic instability
sections.management:
• **Asymptomatic Carrier (No history of VTE)**
    ◦ **No long-term anticoagulation is needed**
    ◦ **Focus on counseling and risk reduction**
        ▪ Avoid estrogen-containing OCPs (progestin-only methods are safer)
        ▪ Smoking cessation
        ▪ Weight management
    ◦ **Provide VTE prophylaxis** during high-risk periods (e.g., major surgery, prolonged immobilization, pregnancy/postpartum)
• **Patient with a Factor V Leiden-associated VTE**
    ◦ **Duration of anticoagulation** is the key decision
    ◦ **First provoked VTE** (e.g., post-surgery): Standard course of anticoagulation (typically 3 months). The FVL status does not usually extend therapy.
    ◦ **First unprovoked VTE**: **Long-term or indefinite anticoagulation** is generally recommended due to the high risk of recurrence
    ◦ **Recurrent unprovoked VTE**: **Lifelong anticoagulation** is indicated
• **Pregnancy Management**
    ◦ For pregnant carriers with a personal history of VTE or a strong family history, **prophylactic LMWH** is often recommended during pregnancy and the postpartum period
sections.complications:
• **Recurrence of VTE**
• **Post-Thrombotic Syndrome (PTS)**: Chronic venous insufficiency following a DVT, causing chronic leg pain, swelling, and skin changes
• **Chronic Thromboembolic Pulmonary Hypertension (CTEPH)**: A rare but serious long-term consequence of PE leading to right heart failure
• **Complications of Anticoagulation**: **Bleeding** is the primary risk
sections.prognosis:
• For asymptomatic carriers, the prognosis is excellent, and life expectancy is normal. Most will never experience a VTE.
• For individuals who experience a VTE, the prognosis is generally good with appropriate anticoagulation
• Morbidity and mortality are primarily related to the severity of the initial VTE event (especially a massive PE) and its long-term complications

sections.overview:
• Prothrombin Gene Mutation (PGM) is an inherited **thrombophilia** characterized by a specific genetic mutation that leads to **elevated levels of prothrombin (Factor II)**, a key protein in the coagulation cascade
    ◦ This results in a **hypercoagulable state** and an increased lifetime risk for **venous thromboembolism (VTE)**
    ◦ It is the second most common inherited thrombophilia in Caucasian populations, after **Factor V Leiden**
    ◦ Most carriers remain asymptomatic
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ Genetic disorder with an **autosomal dominant** inheritance pattern and incomplete penetrance
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Gene**: A point mutation occurs in the prothrombin gene (F2 gene) on chromosome 11
    ◦ **Mutation**: A single nucleotide substitution of **guanine (G) for adenine (A) at position 20210** in the 3' untranslated region (3'-UTR) of the gene. This is denoted as the **G20210A mutation**
    ◦ **Mechanism**: This mutation does not alter the structure of the prothrombin protein itself. Instead, it increases the stability of prothrombin messenger RNA (mRNA)
    ◦ **Result**: Increased mRNA stability leads to more efficient translation, resulting in **elevated plasma concentrations of prothrombin (Factor II)**, typically 1.5 times the normal level
    ◦ **Consequence**: The higher baseline level of prothrombin creates a prothrombotic state. Upon activation of the coagulation cascade, more thrombin is generated, which in turn converts more fibrinogen to fibrin, promoting excessive clot formation
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: The second most common inherited cause of hypercoagulability
• **Population**: Primarily affects individuals of **European (Caucasian) descent**, with a prevalence of 2-3%
    ◦ It is rare in African, Asian, and Native American populations
• **Genotype**
    ◦ **Heterozygous**: The vast majority of affected individuals are heterozygous (one copy of the mutation). This confers a ~3-5 fold increased relative risk of VTE
    ◦ **Homozygous**: Rare, but carries a significantly higher thrombotic risk
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The majority of individuals with the mutation will **remain asymptomatic** their entire lives
• The classic presentation is a **venous thromboembolic event (VTE)**
    ◦ **Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT)**: Most common presentation, typically in the lower extremities
    ◦ **Pulmonary Embolism (PE)**: Can be the first manifestation, with or without clinical evidence of DVT
• **Typical Scenarios for Presentation**
    ◦ An initial VTE at a younger age (<50 years)
    ◦ An unprovoked or "idiopathic" VTE (no clear inciting factor)
    ◦ Recurrent VTE
    ◦ Thrombosis in an unusual site (e.g., cerebral, portal, or mesenteric veins)
• **Association with arterial thrombosis (MI, stroke) is weak and controversial**
• May be associated with an increased risk of recurrent pregnancy loss, though this link is less established than with other thrombophilias like Antiphospholipid Syndrome
sections.diagnostics:
• **Who to Test**
    ◦ Initial VTE before age 50, especially if unprovoked
    ◦ Recurrent unprovoked VTE
    ◦ VTE in unusual sites (cerebral, mesenteric, portal veins)
    ◦ VTE associated with pregnancy, postpartum, or OCP use
    ◦ Individuals with a first-degree relative with a known high-risk thrombophilia
• **Definitive Diagnosis**
    ◦ **Genetic Testing**: A **PCR-based DNA test** from a blood sample is the gold standard to identify the **G20210A mutation**
        ▪ This test can be performed at any time, as it is not affected by acute thrombosis or anticoagulation therapy
• **Supporting/Other Labs**
    ◦ **Prothrombin (Factor II) level**: May be elevated but is not used for diagnosis due to overlap with normal ranges
• **Diagnosis of Acute VTE**
    ◦ **D-dimer**: A sensitive but non-specific test. High negative predictive value helps rule out VTE in low-risk patients
    ◦ **Venous Doppler Ultrasound**: First-line imaging for suspected DVT
    ◦ **CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA)**: Gold standard for diagnosing PE
    ◦ **V/Q Scan**: Alternative for PE diagnosis in patients with contraindications to CTPA (e.g., severe renal insufficiency, contrast allergy)
sections.prognosis:
• The overall prognosis for asymptomatic carriers is **excellent**
    ◦ Most will never experience a thrombotic event
• The absolute annual risk of a first VTE in a heterozygous carrier is low (<1%)
• Following a VTE, prognosis is generally very good with appropriate anticoagulation
    ◦ Morbidity and mortality are related to the severity of the thrombotic event (e.g., a massive PE) and the development of long-term complications like PTS or CTEPH

sections.overview:
• **Protein C deficiency** is an inherited or acquired **hypercoagulable state** (thrombophilia) characterized by a quantitative or qualitative defect in Protein C.
• Protein C is a vitamin K-dependent zymogen that, when activated, functions as a natural **anticoagulant** by inactivating pro-coagulant **Factors Va** and **VIIIa**.
• Deficiency leads to insufficient downregulation of the coagulation cascade, resulting in an increased lifetime risk for **venous thromboembolism (VTE)**.
• The two hallmark, though rare, clinical presentations are **warfarin-induced skin necrosis** and **neonatal purpura fulminans**.
sections.etiology:
• **Normal Physiology**
    ◦ Protein C is synthesized in the liver and is **vitamin K-dependent**.
    ◦ It is activated by the **thrombin-thrombomodulin complex** on endothelial cell surfaces.
    ◦ **Activated Protein C (APC)**, along with its cofactor **Protein S**, proteolytically cleaves and inactivates **Factors Va** and **VIIIa**.
    ◦ This inactivation slows down thrombin generation, acting as a crucial negative feedback loop in the coagulation cascade.
• **Pathophysiology of Deficiency**
    ◦ **Inherited (Primary)**
        ▪ **Autosomal dominant** mutation in the ***PROC* gene**.
        ▪ **Type I (Quantitative)**: Most common (85-90%). Reduced synthesis of Protein C, leading to **low antigen** and **low functional activity** levels.
        ▪ **Type II (Qualitative)**: Less common. Normal production of a dysfunctional protein, leading to **normal antigen** levels but **low functional activity**.
        ▪ **Heterozygous**: Mild deficiency. Most common inherited form. Patients have ~50% of normal Protein C activity and are at increased risk for **VTE**, typically in adulthood.
        ▪ **Homozygous/Compound Heterozygous**: Severe deficiency. Extremely rare. Leads to **neonatal purpura fulminans**, a life-threatening condition of widespread microvascular thrombosis.
    ◦ **Acquired (Secondary)**
        ▪ More common than inherited deficiency.
        ▪ **Decreased synthesis**: Liver disease, vitamin K deficiency.
        ▪ **Increased consumption**: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (**DIC**), severe infection/sepsis, acute thrombosis.
        ▪ **Drug-induced**: **Warfarin therapy** (Protein C has a short half-life and is depleted faster than pro-coagulant factors II, IX, X), chemotherapy (**L-asparaginase**).
sections.epidemiology:
• **Heterozygous Inherited Deficiency**: Affects approximately **1 in 200 to 1 in 500** individuals in the general population.
• **Clinically Significant VTE**: Only a fraction of those with the genetic trait develop thrombosis. The lifetime risk of VTE in heterozygotes is significantly elevated but not absolute.
• **Homozygous Deficiency**: Extremely rare, estimated at **1 in 4 million** births.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The majority of heterozygous individuals remain **asymptomatic** throughout life.
• **Classic Presentation**: **Venous thromboembolism (VTE)** at a young age (<50 years), often unprovoked or with a minor trigger.
    ◦ **Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT)**: Most common manifestation.
    ◦ **Pulmonary Embolism (PE)**: Can be the initial presentation.
• **Other Presentations**
    ◦ Recurrent VTE.
    ◦ Thrombosis in **unusual sites** (e.g., cerebral, mesenteric, portal veins).
    ◦ Strong family history of thrombosis.
• **Specific, High-Yield Presentations**
    ◦ **Warfarin-induced Skin Necrosis**
        ▪ A rare but classic complication. Occurs 3-10 days after starting warfarin, especially with large loading doses and without heparin bridging.
        ▪ The rapid drop in Protein C (half-life ~6-8 hrs) before the drop in pro-coagulant factors (II, IX, X) creates a transient **hypercoagulable state**, leading to microthrombi in dermal vessels.
    ◦ **Neonatal Purpura Fulminans**
        ▪ Seen in **homozygous** or compound heterozygous infants shortly after birth.
        ▪ Presents as widespread, rapidly progressing **purpuric skin lesions** that become necrotic, indicative of extensive microvascular thrombosis.
        ▪ Often associated with **DIC** and is life-threatening.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Initial VTE Workup**
    ◦ **D-Dimer**: High negative predictive value to rule out VTE in low-risk patients.
    ◦ **Duplex Ultrasound**: Imaging modality of choice to diagnose DVT.
    ◦ **CT Angiography (CTA)**: Gold standard for diagnosing PE.
• **Specific Workup for Protein C Deficiency**
    ◦ **Timing is critical**: Testing should be performed when the patient is stable, not during an acute thrombotic event, and off anticoagulants (warfarin for 2 weeks, DOACs for 48 hours).
        ▪ Acute thrombosis and anticoagulants can **falsely lower** Protein C levels.
    ◦ **Screening/Initial Test**: **Protein C Functional Assay (Activity Level)**.
        ▪ This is the best test as it detects both quantitative (Type I) and qualitative (Type II) defects.
    ◦ **Confirmatory Test**: **Protein C Antigenic Assay (Level)**.
        ▪ Helps differentiate between types:
            ▪ **Type I**: ↓ Activity, ↓ Antigen.
            ▪ **Type II**: ↓ Activity, Normal Antigen.
    ◦ **Genetic Testing**: Analysis of the ***PROC* gene** can confirm an inherited deficiency but is not typically required for clinical management.
sections.prognosis:
• **Heterozygotes**: With appropriate management and awareness, the prognosis is excellent with a normal life expectancy. Morbidity is related to thrombotic events and treatment complications.
• **Homozygotes**: Historically fatal in infancy. With early recognition and aggressive treatment (Protein C concentrate, anticoagulation), survival has significantly improved, but it remains a condition with high morbidity.

sections.overview:
• Inherited or acquired **hypercoagulable disorder** characterized by an increased risk for **venous thromboembolism (VTE)**.
    ◦ **Protein S** is a vitamin K-dependent glycoprotein that functions as a critical cofactor for **Activated Protein C (APC)** in the anticoagulant pathway.
        ▪ A deficiency leads to reduced inactivation of coagulation **factors Va and VIIIa**, tipping the hemostatic balance towards a **prothrombotic state**.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects approximately 0.1-0.2% of the general population.
• **VTE Population**: Found in 2-5% of patients presenting with a first-time **VTE**.
• Most **heterozygous individuals** remain asymptomatic throughout their lives.
    ◦ The risk of thrombosis is significantly increased when other risk factors are present.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The hallmark of Protein S deficiency is **venous thromboembolism (VTE)**.
    ◦ First **VTE** at a young age (<50 years old).
    ◦ **Unprovoked VTE** (i.e., no identifiable provoking risk factor).
    ◦ **Recurrent VTE**.
    ◦ **VTE at unusual sites**: Cerebral, mesenteric, portal, or hepatic veins.
    ◦ Strong **family history** of **VTE**.
• **Warfarin-induced skin necrosis**: A rare but classic complication where warfarin initiation (without heparin bridging) causes a transient **hypercoagulable state**, leading to thrombosis in the dermal microvasculature.
• **Neonatal Purpura Fulminans**: Seen in rare **homozygous infants**; widespread thrombosis and hemorrhagic skin necrosis, often fatal.
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• With appropriate management and anticoagulation, life expectancy is generally normal.
• Morbidity is related to the complications of **VTE** (post-thrombotic syndrome, CTEPH) and the risks of anticoagulation (bleeding).
• The prognosis for **neonatal purpura fulminans** is very poor.

sections.overview: • An inherited or acquired hypercoagulable disorder characterized by a defect in antithrombin, a key endogenous anticoagulant. ◦ Type I: Quantitative defect. ◦ Type II: Qualitative defect. • Impairs the body's ability to inactivate clotting factors, primarily thrombin (Factor IIa) and Factor Xa, leading to a significantly increased risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE). • Classic presentation: A young patient with an unprovoked or recurrent VTE, often with a positive family history. • A key clinical clue is "heparin resistance."
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology: • Inherited: Affects approximately 1 in 2,000 to 1 in 5,000 individuals in the general population. • Found in ~1% of patients with a history of VTE. • Accounts for 2-3% of inherited thrombophilias. • The first thrombotic event typically occurs at a young age, often before age 50.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • The most common presentation is an unprovoked VTE in a patient < 50 years old. • Recurrent VTE is a hallmark feature. • Thrombosis in unusual locations: ◦ Cerebral veins, mesenteric veins, portal vein, hepatic veins (Budd-Chiari syndrome). • Strong family history of VTE. • Warfarin-induced skin necrosis (rare, more classic for Protein C/S deficiency but can occur). • Heparin Resistance: A patient being treated for a VTE requires unexpectedly high doses of unfractionated heparin to achieve a therapeutic aPTT.
sections.diagnostics: • Initial VTE workup ◦ Imaging confirms the clot (e.g., Lower Extremity Compression Ultrasound for DVT, CT Angiography for PE). • Thrombophilia workup (for AT Deficiency) ◦ Timing is critical: Testing should be performed when the patient is stable, NOT during an acute VTE or while on certain anticoagulants (heparin, DOACs), as these can falsely lower AT activity levels. ▪ Wait at least 2-4 weeks after stopping anticoagulation. ◦ Screening Test: Antithrombin Functional Assay (Activity Assay). ▪ This is the best initial test as it detects both quantitative and qualitative defects. ◦ Confirmatory/Typing Test: Antithrombin Antigenic Assay (Immunologic Assay). ▪ Measures the amount of AT protein. ▪ Differentiates between types: • Type I: Low Activity, Low Antigen • Type II: Low Activity, Normal Antigen
sections.prognosis: • With proper diagnosis and management (especially long-term anticoagulation after a VTE), life expectancy is generally normal. • The lifetime risk of VTE in untreated individuals with inherited deficiency is high (up to 50%). • The risk of recurrence after a first event is >50% without continued anticoagulation.

sections.overview:
• **Antiphospholipid Antibody Syndrome (APS)** is a systemic autoimmune disorder characterized by a **hypercoagulable state** leading to recurrent arterial or venous thrombosis and/or pregnancy morbidity.
• The diagnosis is confirmed by the persistent presence of specific autoantibodies known as **antiphospholipid antibodies (aPL)**.
• APS can be **primary** (occurring alone) or **secondary** (associated with another autoimmune disease, most commonly **Systemic Lupus Erythematosus - SLE**).
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Autoimmune**. The exact trigger is often unknown (**idiopathic/primary APS**).
    ◦ It can be **secondary** to other conditions like **SLE**, other autoimmune diseases, malignancies, or certain infections (e.g., syphilis, HIV).
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Autoantibody Production**: The body produces autoantibodies—primarily **Lupus Anticoagulant (LA)**, **Anticardiolipin Antibodies (aCL)**, and **Anti-β2 Glycoprotein I Antibodies (anti-β2GPI)**.
    ◦ **Target Binding**: These antibodies do not directly target phospholipids but rather bind to phospholipid-binding plasma proteins, with **β2-glycoprotein I** being the main target.
    ◦ **Prothrombotic Cascade**: The binding of these autoantibodies to their targets on the surfaces of endothelial cells and platelets initiates a prothrombotic state through multiple mechanisms:
        ▪ **Endothelial cell activation**: Promotes a procoagulant surface.
        ▪ **Platelet activation and aggregation**: Leads to thrombus formation.
        ▪ **Complement activation**: Contributes to inflammation and thrombosis.
        ▪ **Interference with natural anticoagulants**: Impairs the function of proteins like Protein C.
    ◦ **Paradoxical aPTT Prolongation**: In the laboratory (*in vitro*), **Lupus Anticoagulant** antibodies interfere with the phospholipid-dependent reagents used in the aPTT test, causing a falsely elevated result. However, *in vivo*, these same antibodies are **prothrombotic**, creating a hypercoagulable state.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Approximately 40-50 cases per 100,000 people.
• **Incidence**: ~5 new cases per 100,000 people per year.
• **Demographics**
    ◦ **Gender**: Predominantly affects women (F:M ratio ~5:1).
    ◦ **Age of Onset**: Typically diagnosed in young to middle-aged adults (30-40 years old).
• **Association**: Found in 30-40% of patients with **SLE**.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Primary**: Genetic predisposition (e.g., HLA-DR7).
• **Secondary**:
    ◦ **Autoimmune Disease**: **Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)** is the strongest association. Also Sjögren's syndrome, Rheumatoid Arthritis.
    ◦ **Infections**: Syphilis, HIV, Hepatitis C, COVID-19.
    ◦ **Malignancy**: Particularly lymphoproliferative disorders.
    ◦ **Drugs**: Procainamide, hydralazine, phenytoin, chlorpromazine.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation is highly variable but is defined by a thrombotic event or pregnancy morbidity in the presence of aPL.
• **Venous Thrombosis**
    ◦ Most common manifestation (~30% of patients).
    ◦ **Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT)** of the lower extremities is classic.
    ◦ **Pulmonary Embolism (PE)**.
    ◦ Less common sites: renal, hepatic (Budd-Chiari syndrome), or cerebral veins.
• **Arterial Thrombosis**
    ◦ **Stroke** or **Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA)** are the most common arterial events, especially in patients <50 years old.
    ◦ Myocardial Infarction (MI).
    ◦ Peripheral arterial occlusion.
• **Obstetric Complications**
    ◦ Recurrent, unexplained early miscarriages (<10 weeks gestation).
    ◦ One or more unexplained fetal deaths at or beyond 10 weeks gestation.
    ◦ Premature birth (<34 weeks) due to severe **preeclampsia**, **eclampsia**, or **placental insufficiency**.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ **Thrombosis-related**
        ▪ **DVT**: Unilateral leg pain, swelling, erythema, warmth.
        ▪ **PE**: Pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, tachypnea, cough, hemoptysis.
        ▪ **Stroke/TIA**: Acute onset of focal neurologic deficits (e.g., unilateral weakness, aphasia, visual changes).
    ◦ **Obstetric**: History of recurrent pregnancy loss or late-term pregnancy complications.
    ◦ **Other**
        ▪ Headaches (migraine-like).
        ▪ Memory loss or cognitive dysfunction.
        ▪ Arthralgias, myalgias (especially if secondary to SLE).
• **Physical Exam Findings**
    ◦ **Vascular**
        ▪ **Livedo reticularis** or **livedo racemosa**: A purplish, lace-like rash on the skin, especially on extremities, that persists with warming.
        ▪ Evidence of DVT (Homan's sign is unreliable).
        ▪ Skin ulcers or gangrene from arterial occlusion.
    ◦ **Neurologic**: Focal deficits corresponding to a stroke territory.
    ◦ **Cardiac**
        ▪ Heart murmurs, particularly **mitral regurgitation**, may suggest nonbacterial thrombotic vegetations (**Libman-Sacks endocarditis**).
    ◦ **Hematologic**: Petechiae or purpura if significant **thrombocytopenia** is present.
sections.diagnostics: • Diagnosis requires meeting at least **one clinical criterion** AND **one laboratory criterion** (Revised Sapporo/Sydney Criteria).
sections.treatment:
• **Asymptomatic with aPL**: Risk factor modification. Low-dose aspirin (81 mg) may be considered, especially in high-risk profiles (e.g., "triple-positive" serology, SLE).
• **Thrombotic Event**
    ◦ **Long-term anticoagulation**.
    ◦ **Warfarin (Coumadin)** is the treatment of choice. Target INR is typically **2.0-3.0**.
    ◦ A higher INR target (3.0-4.0) or addition of aspirin may be considered for recurrent arterial events.
    ◦ **DOACs (e.g., rivaroxaban, apixaban) are NOT recommended**, especially in high-risk (triple-positive) patients, due to increased risk of arterial thrombosis compared to warfarin.
• **APS in Pregnancy**
    ◦ **Warfarin is teratogenic** and is contraindicated.
    ◦ **Low-Dose Aspirin (LDA) + Prophylactic or Therapeutic LMWH (e.g., enoxaparin)** is the standard of care.
        ▪ **With prior obstetric complications only**: LDA + prophylactic LMWH.
        ▪ **With a prior thrombotic event**: LDA + therapeutic LMWH.
• **Catastrophic APS (CAPS)**: A medical emergency.
    ◦ Requires aggressive, multi-modal therapy.
sections.management:
• **Primary Prevention**: Aggressive management of cardiovascular risk factors (hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, smoking cessation).
• **Contraception**: **Avoid estrogen-containing oral contraceptives** due to increased thrombosis risk. Progestin-only pills or IUDs are safer alternatives.
• **Monitoring**: Regular INR checks for patients on warfarin.
• **Surgery/Immobility**: Requires perioperative bridging with LMWH.
sections.complications:
• **Recurrent Thrombosis**: High risk of recurrence without adequate anticoagulation.
• **Post-thrombotic syndrome**: Chronic leg pain, swelling, and ulcers after DVT.
• **Pulmonary Hypertension**: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH).
• **Catastrophic APS (CAPS)**: Rare but life-threatening. Characterized by widespread small vessel thrombosis leading to multi-organ failure. High mortality (~50%).
• **Valvular Heart Disease**: Thickening and vegetations on heart valves (**Libman-Sacks**).
• **Cognitive Dysfunction**: "Brain fog" or memory issues, potentially from microthrombi.
sections.prognosis:
• With proper anticoagulation, the survival rate is generally good.
• Morbidity remains high due to the risk of recurrent thrombosis, complications of anticoagulation, and pregnancy loss.
• **Worse prognosis** is associated with:
    ◦ **"Triple-positive" serology** (LA + aCL + anti-β2GPI).
    ◦ High titers of antibodies.
    ◦ Recurrent thrombosis, especially arterial events.
    ◦ Concomitant **SLE**.
sections.preventionEducation: • Counsel on signs/symptoms of thrombosis and bleeding, medication adherence, and the need for specialized care during pregnancy.

sections.overview:
• Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) is a malignant hematologic disorder characterized by the clonal proliferation and accumulation of immature lymphoid precursor cells, known as **lymphoblasts**, in the bone marrow, peripheral blood, and other tissues
• This uncontrolled proliferation disrupts normal hematopoiesis, leading to bone marrow failure and its consequent cytopenias (anemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia)
• ALL is the **most common malignancy in children** but can also affect adults, where it carries a poorer prognosis
• It is classified primarily into B-cell ALL and T-cell ALL based on the cell of origin
sections.etiology:
• The core pathophysiology of ALL is a **genetic mutation** in a single lymphoid progenitor cell, which confers a survival and proliferative advantage, leading to clonal expansion
• The development of these cells is arrested at an early, immature stage (lymphoblast)
    ◦ **Clonal Proliferation**: The mutated lymphoblasts proliferate uncontrollably within the bone marrow
    ◦ **Marrow Infiltration & Failure**: These malignant cells "crowd out" and suppress the normal hematopoietic stem cells, leading to a failure to produce mature, functional blood cells
        ▪ **Anemia**: Decreased red blood cell (RBC) production
        ▪ **Thrombocytopenia**: Decreased platelet production
        ▪ **Neutropenia**: Decreased neutrophil production
    ◦ **Extramedullary Spread**: Lymphoblasts can exit the bone marrow and infiltrate other organs, including:
        ▪ Central Nervous System (CNS)
        ▪ Testes
        ▪ Liver, Spleen, and Lymph Nodes
        ▪ Thymus (especially in T-cell ALL)
• The specific genetic abnormalities (e.g., translocations) are critical for prognosis and targeted therapy
    ◦ For example, the **Philadelphia chromosome (t(9;22))** creates the **BCR-ABL1 fusion gene**, a key driver in a subset of ALL
sections.epidemiology:
• **Most common childhood cancer**, accounting for ~25% of all pediatric malignancies and ~75% of all childhood leukemias
• **Peak Incidence**: Ages **2 to 5 years**
• **Bimodal Age Distribution**: A second, smaller peak occurs in adults over the age of 50
• Slightly more common in males than females
• More common in White and Hispanic populations than in Black populations
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The clinical presentation is typically acute, with symptoms developing over days to weeks
• The presentation is a direct result of bone marrow failure and tissue infiltration by lymphoblasts
• Patients, often children, present with non-specific symptoms that can be mistaken for common viral illnesses before the pattern of cytopenias becomes apparent
sections.diagnostics:
• **Initial Lab Work**
    ◦ **CBC with Differential**: The key initial test. Findings may include:
        ▪ **Anemia** (normocytic, normochromic)
        ▪ **Thrombocytopenia**
        ▪ **WBC count**: Can be low, normal, or markedly elevated (>100,000/L)
        ▪ **The hallmark is the presence of circulating lymphoblasts** on the differential
    ◦ **Peripheral Blood Smear**
        ▪ Visual confirmation of **lymphoblasts**: large cells with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic (N:C) ratio, scant agranular cytoplasm, and fine, dispersed chromatin
        ▪ **Auer rods are ABSENT** (Their presence is pathognomonic for AML)
• **Confirmatory Test**
    ◦ **Bone Marrow Aspiration & Biopsy**: **Gold standard for diagnosis**
        ▪ Reveals a **hypercellular marrow** that is replaced by a homogeneous population of **>20% lymphoblasts**
• **Blast Characterization & Risk Stratification**
    ◦ **Flow Cytometry (Immunophenotyping)**: Essential. Differentiates ALL from AML and subtypes ALL into B-cell or T-cell lineage by identifying specific cell surface markers (CD antigens)
        ▪ **ALL marker**: **TdT** (terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase) is positive in >95% of cases
        ▪ **B-cell markers**: CD10, CD19, CD20, CD22
        ▪ **T-cell markers**: CD2, CD3, CD5, CD7, CD8
    ◦ **Cytogenetics (Karyotyping) & Molecular Studies (FISH, PCR)**: Critical for prognosis and treatment
        ▪ Identifies chromosomal abnormalities like the **Philadelphia chromosome (t(9;22), BCR-ABL1 fusion)**, which is a poor prognostic factor but is targetable with tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs)
• **Staging & Other Tests**
    ◦ **Lumbar Puncture (LP)**: **Mandatory in all newly diagnosed patients** to evaluate for CNS involvement. CSF is sent for cell count, chemistry, and cytology
    ◦ **Chemistry Panel (CMP)**: Assess for **Tumor Lysis Syndrome (TLS)**: K+, Phosphate, Uric Acid, Ca2+, LDH, Creatinine
    ◦ **Chest X-ray**: To evaluate for a **mediastinal mass** (suspicious for T-cell ALL)
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly dependent on age and cytogenetic risk factors
    ◦ **Children**: Overall excellent prognosis, with cure rates approaching **90%**
    ◦ **Adults**: Significantly poorer prognosis, with cure rates around **40-50%**
• **Favorable Prognostic Factors**
    ◦ Age **1-10 years** at diagnosis
    ◦ Initial WBC **< 50,000/L**
    ◦ B-cell immunophenotype
    ◦ Hyperdiploidy (>50 chromosomes)
    ◦ Rapid response to induction therapy
    ◦ No CNS involvement at diagnosis
    ◦ Absence of poor-risk cytogenetics
• **Unfavorable Prognostic Factors**
    ◦ Age <1 year or >10 years (especially adults)
    ◦ Initial WBC **> 50,000/L**
    ◦ Mature B-cell or T-cell immunophenotype
    ◦ Hypodiploidy (<44 chromosomes)
    ◦ Slow response / persistent MRD
    ◦ CNS involvement at diagnosis
    ◦ **Philadelphia Chromosome (t(9;22))**

sections.overview:
• **Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML)** is a malignant neoplasm of the hematopoietic system characterized by the rapid proliferation and clonal expansion of immature myeloid progenitor cells (**myeloblasts**) in the bone marrow and blood.
• This uncontrolled proliferation leads to the suppression of normal hematopoiesis, resulting in **bone marrow failure** and its associated complications: **anemia**, **thrombocytopenia**, and **neutropenia**.
• AML is the most common acute leukemia in adults and is considered a **medical emergency** requiring prompt diagnosis and treatment.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ Most cases of AML are ***de novo***, arising without a known precursor.
    ◦ **Secondary AML** can develop from pre-existing hematologic disorders (e.g., **myelodysplastic syndrome [MDS]**) or as a result of prior exposure to chemotherapy or radiation (**therapy-related AML**).
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The core defect is a series of acquired **genetic mutations** in a myeloid progenitor cell that confer a survival and proliferative advantage, leading to clonal expansion.
    ◦ Key pathophysiologic steps include:
        ▪ **Block in Differentiation:** The myeloid blasts fail to mature into functional granulocytes, monocytes, erythrocytes, or platelets.
        ▪ **Uncontrolled Proliferation:** The blasts divide rapidly, accumulating in the bone marrow.
        ▪ **Suppression of Normal Hematopoiesis:** The leukemic blasts "crowd out" and inhibit the growth of normal hematopoietic stem cells, leading to the hallmark clinical findings of **pancytopenia**:
            • **Anemia:** Decreased red blood cell production.
            • **Thrombocytopenia:** Decreased platelet production.
            • **Neutropenia:** Decreased functional neutrophil production.
        ▪ **Infiltration:** Leukemic blasts can infiltrate extramedullary sites, including the spleen, liver, lymph nodes, skin, and central nervous system (CNS).
sections.epidemiology:
• Most common **acute leukemia in adults**.
• Incidence increases significantly with age.
• **Median age at diagnosis is ~68 years**.
• Slightly more common in males than females.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Advanced Age:** The single most important risk factor.
• **Prior Chemotherapy:** Especially with alkylating agents (e.g., cyclophosphamide) or topoisomerase II inhibitors (e.g., etoposide).
• **Prior Radiation Therapy.**
• **Pre-existing Hematologic Disorders:**
    ◦ Myelodysplastic Syndrome (MDS)
    ◦ Myeloproliferative Neoplasms (e.g., CML, polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia)
    ◦ Aplastic Anemia
• **Genetic Syndromes:**
    ◦ **Down Syndrome (Trisomy 21)**
    ◦ Fanconi Anemia
    ◦ Bloom Syndrome
• **Environmental/Chemical Exposure:**
    ◦ **Benzene**
    ◦ Smoking
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation is typically acute, with symptoms developing over days to weeks. The clinical picture is a direct consequence of **bone marrow failure**. Patients often present with non-specific constitutional symptoms and signs related to one or more cytopenias.
• **Symptoms due to Anemia:**
    ◦ Fatigue, weakness, lethargy
    ◦ Dyspnea on exertion
    ◦ Pallor
    ◦ Dizziness, headaches
• **Symptoms due to Thrombocytopenia:**
    ◦ Easy bruising (**ecchymosis**)
    ◦ Pinpoint red/purple spots (**petechiae**)
    ◦ Epistaxis (nosebleeds)
    ◦ Gingival (gum) bleeding
    ◦ Menorrhagia
• **Symptoms due to Neutropenia (Lack of functional WBCs):**
    ◦ **Fever**
    ◦ Recurrent or severe infections (e.g., pneumonia, cellulitis, **sepsis**)
• **Constitutional Symptoms:**
    ◦ Fever, night sweats, unintentional weight loss
• **Infiltrative Symptoms:**
    ◦ Bone pain (due to marrow expansion)
    ◦ Abdominal fullness (if hepatosplenomegaly is present)
    ◦ Swollen, bleeding gums (**gingival hyperplasia**)
• **Leukostasis Symptoms (WBC >100,000/L):**
    ◦ Neurologic: Headache, confusion, vision changes
    ◦ Pulmonary: Dyspnea, hypoxia
sections.physicalExam:
• **General:** Pallor, fever, signs of infection.
• **Skin:** Petechiae, ecchymoses, purpura.
• **Leukemia Cutis:** Violaceous, non-tender skin nodules or plaques from leukemic infiltration.
• **HEENT:**
    ◦ **Gingival hyperplasia** (boggy, swollen gums), particularly common in monocytic subtypes (M4, M5).
    ◦ Mucosal bleeding.
    ◦ Fundoscopic exam may reveal retinal hemorrhages (**Roth spots**).
• **Abdomen:** Hepatosplenomegaly (present in ~50% of cases, but typically mild).
• **Lymphatics:** Lymphadenopathy (less common and less prominent than in ALL).
• **Musculoskeletal:** Sternal tenderness or bone pain.
sections.diagnostics:
• **CBC with Differential:** The initial and most crucial test.
    ◦ **Anemia:** Normocytic, normochromic.
    ◦ **Thrombocytopenia:** Often severe (<50,000/L).
    ◦ **WBC Count:** Can be low, normal, or markedly high.
    ◦ **Circulating myeloblasts** are typically present on the differential.
• **Peripheral Blood Smear:**
    ◦ Confirms the presence of **myeloblasts:** Large cells with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic (N:C) ratio, fine (immature) chromatin, and prominent nucleoli.
    ◦ **Auer Rods:** **Pathognomonic for AML**. These are needle-like, eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions formed by the fusion of azurophilic granules.
• **Bone Marrow Aspiration and Biopsy:** **Gold standard for diagnosis.**
    ◦ **Hypercellular marrow** replaced by leukemic blasts.
    ◦ **Diagnostic Criteria: ≥20% myeloblasts** in the bone marrow or peripheral blood.
    ◦ Samples are sent for flow cytometry, cytogenetics, and molecular testing.
• **Flow Cytometry:** Identifies cell surface markers (CD markers) to confirm myeloid lineage (e.g., **CD13, CD33, CD117, Myeloperoxidase [MPO]**) and rule out ALL.
• **Cytogenetics and Molecular Studies:** Critical for prognosis and treatment decisions.
    ◦ Identifies chromosomal abnormalities (e.g., translocations, deletions).
    ◦ **t(15;17)** is diagnostic for **Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (APL)**.
    ◦ Mutations like ***FLT3***, ***NPM1***, ***CEBPA*** are key prognostic markers.
• **Coagulation Studies (PT, PTT, Fibrinogen):** Essential to screen for **Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC)**, especially in APL.
• **Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP) & Labs for Tumor Lysis Syndrome:** Check electrolytes, uric acid, LDH, creatinine, and phosphorus before starting therapy.
sections.treatment:
• **Induction Chemotherapy:** Goal is to achieve complete remission (<5% blasts in marrow).
    ◦ **Standard Regimen: "7 + 3"**
        ▪ **7** days of continuous infusion **Cytarabine** (Ara-C).
        ▪ **3** days of an anthracycline (e.g., **Daunorubicin** or **Idarubicin**).
• **Consolidation (Post-Remission) Therapy:** Goal is to eradicate residual disease and prevent relapse.
    ◦ Options depend on risk stratification (based on cytogenetics/molecular markers):
        ▪ **Favorable Risk:** Several cycles of high-dose Cytarabine (HiDAC).
        ▪ **Intermediate/Poor Risk:** **Allogeneic Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplant (HSCT)** is often the preferred consolidation if the patient is a suitable candidate.
• **Special Case: Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (APL / M3 Subtype):**
    ◦ **Treatment:** **All-Trans Retinoic Acid (ATRA)** + **Arsenic Trioxide (ATO).**
    ◦ ATRA is a differentiating agent that forces the leukemic promyelocytes to mature, resolving the coagulopathy (DIC). This is a non-chemotherapy approach for low-risk APL.
sections.management:
• **Supportive Care is Critical:**
    ◦ **Infection Management:**
        ▪ **Febrile neutropenia is a medical emergency.** Immediate workup and empiric broad-spectrum IV antibiotics are required.
        ▪ Prophylaxis against bacterial, fungal (e.g., posaconazole), and viral (e.g., acyclovir) infections.
    ◦ **Transfusion Support:**
        ▪ **Packed Red Blood Cells (pRBCs)** for symptomatic anemia or Hgb <7-8 g/dL.
        ▪ **Platelets** for thrombocytopenia (prophylactically for platelets <10,000/L or for active bleeding).
    ◦ **Tumor Lysis Syndrome (TLS) Prophylaxis:**
        ▪ Aggressive IV hydration, allopurinol (to block uric acid production), and rasburicase (for high-risk patients) to prevent renal failure from hyperuricemia.
    ◦ **Leukostasis Management (WBC > 100,000/L):**
        ▪ Medical emergency requiring urgent cytoreduction via induction chemotherapy or **leukapheresis**.
sections.complications:
• **Febrile Neutropenia and Sepsis:** Most common cause of mortality during induction therapy.
• **Tumor Lysis Syndrome (TLS):** Metabolic emergency caused by rapid cell death, leading to **hyperuricemia**, **hyperkalemia**, **hyperphosphatemia**, and secondary **hypocalcemia**, which can cause acute kidney injury and cardiac arrhythmias.
• **Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC):** Widespread activation of clotting leads to a consumptive coagulopathy, resulting in both thrombosis and severe bleeding. **Strongly associated with APL.**
• **Leukostasis:** Hyperviscosity from a very high blast count leads to sludging in the microvasculature, primarily affecting the lungs (hypoxia) and CNS (stroke, confusion).
• **Hemorrhage:** Severe thrombocytopenia and DIC can lead to life-threatening bleeding (e.g., intracranial, GI).
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly variable and depends on several factors, with **cytogenetics and molecular markers being the most important**.
• **Favorable Prognosis:**
    ◦ t(8;21), inv(16), t(15;17) (APL)
    ◦ *NPM1* or *CEBPA* mutations (in the absence of *FLT3-ITD*)
• **Poor Prognosis:**
    ◦ Complex karyotype (>3 abnormalities)
    ◦ Deletions of chromosome 5 or 7
    ◦ *FLT3-ITD* mutation
• **Other negative prognostic factors:**
    ◦ Older age (>60)
    ◦ Poor performance status
    ◦ High initial WBC
    ◦ Therapy-related AML

sections.overview: • Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) is a low-grade (indolent), mature B-cell neoplasm characterized by the progressive accumulation of functionally incompetent monoclonal B-lymphocytes. It is the most common leukemia in adults in Western countries, primarily affecting the elderly and is often discovered incidentally on a routine complete blood count (CBC). ◦ When the disease is primarily located in the lymph nodes with minimal blood involvement (absolute lymphocyte count <5,000/L), it is termed Small Lymphocytic Lymphoma (SLL). CLL and SLL are considered different manifestations of the same underlying disease.
sections.etiology: • Etiology: The exact cause is unknown. Unlike other leukemias, there is no strong association with radiation, chemotherapy, or specific viral infections. A strong genetic predisposition exists. • Pathophysiology: The core defect is the clonal proliferation of mature B-cells that are resistant to apoptosis (programmed cell death). This leads to a gradual accumulation—rather than rapid overproduction—of these cells in the peripheral blood, bone marrow, lymph nodes, and spleen. ◦ Immunophenotype: The neoplastic B-cells express a unique combination of surface markers, crucial for diagnosis: ▪ B-cell markers: CD19, CD20 (characteristically dim), CD23 ▪ T-cell marker: CD5 (The co-expression of CD5 on a B-cell is a key feature of CLL) ◦ Functional Incompetence: Despite their mature appearance, these lymphocytes are immunologically dysfunctional, leading to hypogammaglobulinemia and impaired immune response.
sections.epidemiology: • Incidence: Most common leukemia in the Western world. • Age: Median age at diagnosis is ~70 years. It is rare in individuals under 40. • Sex: Male-to-female ratio is approximately 2:1. • Race: More common in Caucasians; less common in individuals of Asian descent.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • The majority of patients (>70%) are asymptomatic at diagnosis. The disease is typically discovered incidentally on a routine CBC showing a high lymphocyte count.
sections.diagnostics: • CBC with Differential: ◦ Hallmark finding: Sustained absolute lymphocytosis > 5,000/L. ◦ Peripheral smear shows a predominance of small, mature-appearing lymphocytes. ◦ Pathognomonic: Smudge cells (or "basket cells") - fragile leukemic lymphocytes that are crushed during slide preparation. ◦ Normocytic, normochromic anemia and/or thrombocytopenia may be present in later stages. • Flow Cytometry of Peripheral Blood: ◦ The definitive diagnostic test. Confirms the diagnosis by identifying a monoclonal B-cell population with the characteristic immunophenotype: CD19+, CD5+, CD23+, and dim CD20+. • Bone Marrow Aspiration & Biopsy: ◦ Not required for diagnosis but is performed prior to initiating treatment to assess the extent of marrow infiltration and evaluate the cause of cytopenias. ◦ Shows >30% infiltration by lymphocytes. • Prognostic Workup (Essential before treatment): ◦ FISH/Cytogenetics: To detect chromosomal abnormalities. ▪ del(17p) and TP53 mutation are the most important adverse prognostic factors and predict poor response to chemoimmunotherapy. ◦ IgVH (Immunoglobulin Heavy Chain Variable region) Gene Mutation Status: Mutated IgVH confers a better prognosis; unmutated IgVH confers a worse prognosis. ◦ Serum beta-2 microglobulin: High levels correlate with a larger tumor burden and worse prognosis. ◦ Direct Coombs Test: To screen for autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
sections.prognosis: • The clinical course is highly variable, with survival ranging from 2 to >20 years. Prognosis is now best determined by molecular features rather than just clinical stage (Rai/Binet systems). • Favorable Prognostic Factors: ◦ Mutated IgVH status ◦ del(13q) as the sole cytogenetic abnormality ◦ Low beta-2 microglobulin • Unfavorable Prognostic Factors: ◦ del(17p) or TP53 mutation (Worst) ◦ del(11q) ◦ Unmutated IgVH status ◦ High beta-2 microglobulin ◦ Rapid lymphocyte doubling time

sections.overview:
• **Chronic Myelogenous Leukemia (CML)** is a myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by the excessive production of mature and maturing granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils).
    ◦ It is defined by a specific cytogenetic abnormality, the **Philadelphia chromosome**, which results from a translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22.
    ◦ The disease typically progresses through three phases if left untreated: a **chronic phase**, an **accelerated phase**, and a terminal **blast crisis**.
    ◦ The advent of **tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs)** has revolutionized treatment, transforming CML from a fatal leukemia into a manageable chronic condition for most patients.
sections.etiology:
• **Core Genetic Defect:** A reciprocal translocation between the long arms of chromosome 9 and chromosome 22, denoted as **t(9;22)(q34;q11)**.
    ◦ **The Philadelphia Chromosome (Ph):** This translocation results in a shortened chromosome 22, known as the **Philadelphia chromosome**.
    ◦ **The Fusion Gene:** The translocation creates a novel fusion gene called ***BCR-ABL1***. The *ABL1* gene (from chromosome 9) is fused to the *BCR* (breakpoint cluster region) gene (on chromosome 22).
    ◦ **Pathogenic Protein:** The *BCR-ABL1* gene encodes for a constitutively active **BCR-ABL1 tyrosine kinase**. This protein is always "on."
• **Mechanism of Disease:** The unregulated tyrosine kinase activity drives cellular processes that lead to:
    ◦ **Uncontrolled Proliferation:** The kinase activates multiple signaling pathways (e.g., RAS, JAK-STAT) that promote cell division.
    ◦ **Inhibition of Apoptosis:** The malignant cells become resistant to programmed cell death.
    ◦ **Altered Adhesion:** The leukemic cells have reduced adhesion to bone marrow stroma, allowing for their premature release into the peripheral blood.
• **Result:** A massive expansion of the granulocytic cell line in the bone marrow, peripheral blood, and extramedullary sites like the spleen and liver.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence:** Accounts for 15-20% of all adult leukemias.
• **Median Age at Diagnosis:** 60-65 years. Can occur at any age but is rare in children.
• **Sex:** Slight male predominance (1.5:1).
sections.riskFactors:
• The only clearly established risk factor is **high-dose ionizing radiation** exposure (e.g., atomic bomb survivors, radiation therapy for other cancers).
• Most cases are sporadic with no identifiable risk factor.
• Not associated with smoking, chemotherapy, or specific viral infections. No strong hereditary component.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Asymptomatic:** Up to 50% of patients are asymptomatic at diagnosis, discovered incidentally on a routine complete blood count (CBC) showing marked leukocytosis.
• **Symptomatic:** When symptoms occur, they are typically insidious and related to the hypermetabolic state and organ infiltration.
    ◦ **Constitutional "B" Symptoms:** Fatigue, malaise, unintentional weight loss, low-grade fever, night sweats.
    ◦ **Splenomegaly-related:**
        ▪ Left upper quadrant (LUQ) abdominal pain or discomfort.
        ▪ **Early satiety** or feeling of fullness due to the enlarged spleen compressing the stomach.
    ◦ **Anemia-related:** Weakness, dyspnea on exertion, pallor.
    ◦ **Platelet Dysfunction:** Bleeding (epistaxis, bruising) or thrombosis (less common).
    ◦ **Hyperuricemia-related (from high cell turnover):** Gouty arthritis, nephrolithiasis.
    ◦ **Leukostasis (rarely, with extreme WBC >500k):** CNS symptoms (blurry vision, confusion, headache), priapism, respiratory distress.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Splenomegaly:** The most common and prominent physical finding, present in over 50% of patients. It can be massive, extending below the umbilicus.
• **Hepatomegaly:** Less common and less pronounced than splenomegaly.
• **Pallor:** Due to anemia.
• **Ecchymoses or Petechiae:** Evidence of bleeding due to platelet dysfunction.
• **Sternal Tenderness:** Due to bone marrow expansion.
• Lymphadenopathy and skin infiltration are rare in the chronic phase.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Initial Test (Best Initial Test):**
    ◦ **CBC with Differential:**
        ▪ **Marked Leukocytosis:** WBC count is dramatically elevated, typically >100,000/µL.
        ▪ **"Left Shift":** Shows the full spectrum of granulocyte maturation, from myeloblasts to mature neutrophils. **Myelocytes** are characteristically prominent ("myelocyte bulge"). Blasts are typically <5%.
        ▪ **Basophilia and Eosinophilia:** Absolute **basophilia** is a universal finding and a hallmark of CML.
        ▪ **Thrombocytosis:** Platelet count is often elevated.
        ▪ **Anemia:** Usually normocytic, normochromic.
• **Confirmatory Tests (Most Specific / Gold Standard):**
    ◦ **Cytogenetics (Karyotyping) of Bone Marrow:** **Gold standard** for identifying the **Philadelphia chromosome [t(9;22)]**.
    ◦ **Molecular Testing (FISH or RT-PCR):** Detects the ***BCR-ABL1* fusion gene** or its mRNA transcript.
        ▪ **Quantitative PCR (qPCR)** is the most sensitive test, used for both diagnosis and for monitoring treatment response (**Minimal Residual Disease**).
• **Other Important Labs:**
    ◦ **Leukocyte Alkaline Phosphatase (LAP) Score:**
        ▪ The LAP score is **LOW** in CML because the malignant neutrophils are biochemically abnormal.
        ▪ This helps distinguish CML from a ***leukemoid reaction*** (a reactive, non-malignant leukocytosis due to severe infection or inflammation), where the LAP score would be **HIGH**.
    ◦ **Bone Marrow Aspiration & Biopsy:**
        ▪ Shows **hypercellularity** with marked granulocytic hyperplasia.
        ▪ Used to confirm the diagnosis and, crucially, to determine the phase of the disease by quantifying the percentage of blasts.
    ◦ **Serum Uric Acid:** Often elevated due to high cell turnover.
sections.treatment:
• **Cornerstone of Therapy:** **Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors (TKIs)**. These drugs specifically target and inhibit the BCR-ABL1 protein.
• **First-Line TKIs:**
    ◦ **Imatinib (Gleevec)** - The first-generation TKI.
    ◦ **Dasatinib, Nilotinib, Bosutinib** - Second-generation TKIs, often preferred first-line due to faster and deeper responses.
• **Treatment for Resistance/Intolerance:**
    ◦ If a patient is resistant or intolerant to a first-line TKI, switch to another TKI.
    ◦ For patients with the **T315I mutation**, which confers resistance to most TKIs, **Ponatinib** (a third-generation TKI) is effective.
• **Allogeneic Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplant (HSCT):**
    ◦ The only potentially curative therapy.
    ◦ Now reserved for patients who are resistant/intolerant to multiple TKIs or who present in an advanced phase (accelerated or blast crisis).
sections.management:
• **Goal of Therapy:** Achieve and maintain a deep, durable molecular response, preventing progression to advanced phases.
• **Monitoring Response:**
    ◦ **Hematologic Response:** Normalization of CBC and resolution of splenomegaly.
    ◦ **Cytogenetic Response:** Disappearance of the Ph chromosome on karyotyping.
    ◦ **Molecular Response:** Measured by **quantitative PCR (qPCR) for *BCR-ABL1* transcripts**. This is the most sensitive method and the primary tool for long-term monitoring. The goal is to achieve a **Major Molecular Response (MMR)** or deeper.
• **Monitoring Schedule:** qPCR is typically performed every 3 months until a stable MMR is achieved, then can be spaced out to every 6 months.
• **Side Effect Management:** Address TKI-specific adverse effects (e.g., fluid retention/edema with imatinib, pleural effusions with dasatinib, pancreatitis/vascular events with nilotinib).
sections.complications:
• **Progression to Advanced Phases (Natural history without treatment):**
    ◦ **Accelerated Phase:** Defined by ≥15% basophils, persistent thrombocytopenia/thrombocytosis unresponsive to therapy, or 10-19% blasts in blood or marrow.
    ◦ **Blast Crisis:** The terminal phase, defined by **≥20% blasts** in the blood or bone marrow. The disease behaves like an acute leukemia (AML in ~70% of cases, ALL in ~30%). Prognosis is very poor.
• **TKI Resistance:** Development of mutations (like T315I) in the *BCR-ABL1* kinase domain.
• **Thromboembolic or Bleeding Events.**
• **Leukostasis:** Rare complication from hyperviscosity due to extremely high WBC counts.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent in the Chronic Phase:** With TKI therapy, the 10-year survival rate for patients in the chronic phase is >80-90%, approaching that of the general population.
• **Poor in Advanced Phases:** Prognosis is significantly worse once the disease progresses to the accelerated phase or blast crisis. Median survival in blast crisis is measured in months.

sections.overview:
• Myelodysplastic Syndromes (MDS) are a group of clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorders characterized by **ineffective hematopoiesis**.
    ◦ This leads to peripheral blood cytopenias despite a typically **hypercellular** or normocellular bone marrow.
    ◦ The core problem is dysregulated blood cell production and maturation (dysplasia), resulting in poor-quality cells that undergo apoptosis in the marrow before reaching circulation.
    ◦ MDS is considered a pre-leukemic or pre-malignant condition due to its significant risk of transformation into **Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML)**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Primary (de novo) MDS**
        ▪ The majority of cases (~80-90%).
        ▪ The cause is unknown, arising from somatic mutations in a hematopoietic stem cell.
    ◦ **Therapy-related MDS (t-MDS)**
        ▪ Occurs as a late complication of cytotoxic chemotherapy (especially **alkylating agents**, **topoisomerase II inhibitors**) or radiation therapy used to treat prior malignancies.
        ▪ T-MDS often has a worse prognosis.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Clonal Mutation**
        ▪ A single hematopoietic stem cell acquires one or more genetic mutations.
    ◦ **Proliferation**
        ▪ This mutated clone outcompetes normal stem cells, leading to its dominance in the bone marrow.
    ◦ **Dysplasia & Apoptosis**
        ▪ The clonal cells have impaired differentiation and maturation.
        ▪ This "dysplasia" creates morphologically abnormal cells in all three lineages (erythroid, myeloid, megakaryocytic).
        ▪ These defective cells are prone to premature programmed cell death (apoptosis) within the bone marrow.
    ◦ **Ineffective Hematopoiesis**
        ▪ The result is a paradox: a **hypercellular bone marrow** that is busy making cells, but **peripheral blood cytopenias** because the cells are defective and die before being released.
    ◦ **AML Transformation**
        ▪ Accumulation of additional mutations can block cell differentiation entirely, leading to a buildup of immature blast cells.
        ▪ When blasts reach **20%** in the bone marrow, the diagnosis changes from MDS to **AML**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Age**
    ◦ Primarily a disease of the elderly; median age at diagnosis is **~70 years**.
    ◦ It is rare in individuals <50.
• **Sex**
    ◦ Slight male predominance.
• **Incidence**
    ◦ Approximately 4-5 cases per 100,000 people per year, but this rises significantly in those over 60.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Many patients are **asymptomatic** at diagnosis, with MDS found incidentally on a routine complete blood count (CBC).
• Symptomatic presentation is directly related to the specific cytopenia(s) present.
sections.diagnostics:
• The diagnosis requires a combination of peripheral blood and bone marrow analysis.
• **CBC with Differential**
    ◦ The initial clue.
    ◦ May show one or more cytopenias:
        ▪ **Anemia**: Usually **macrocytic (MCV > 100 fL)** but can be normocytic.
        ▪ **Neutropenia**
        ▪ **Thrombocytopenia**
    ◦ Can present as a single cytopenia, bicytopenia, or pancytopenia.
• **Peripheral Blood Smear**
    ◦ Look for dysplastic features:
        ▪ **WBCs**: **Pseudo-Pelger-Hut anomaly** (bilobed, "pince-nez" nuclei in neutrophils), hypogranular or agranular neutrophils.
        ▪ **RBCs**: Macrocytes, ovalomacrocytes, basophilic stippling.
        ▪ **Platelets**: Giant platelets, hypogranular platelets.
• **Bone Marrow Aspiration and Biopsy (Definitive Diagnosis)**
    ◦ **Cellularity**: Typically **hypercellular** for the patient's age.
    ◦ **Dysplasia**: Morphologic evidence of dysplasia in ≥10% of the cells in one or more lineages (dyserythropoiesis, dysgranulopoiesis, dysmegakaryopoiesis).
    ◦ Special stain (Prussian blue) may show **ring sideroblasts**: erythroblasts with iron-laden mitochondria encircling the nucleus.
    ◦ **Blast Percentage**: **Crucial for diagnosis and prognosis.** Blasts are <20% of total nucleated cells. **If blasts are ≥20%, it is classified as AML.**
• **Cytogenetics (Karyotyping) / FISH**
    ◦ Performed on bone marrow aspirate to identify chromosomal abnormalities.
    ◦ Key for prognosis and guiding treatment.
    ◦ Common abnormalities include: **del(5q)**, del(7q), trisomy 8.
• **Other Labs**
    ◦ Rule out other causes of cytopenias: Vitamin B12, folate levels.
    ◦ Serum erythropoietin (EPO) level: helps predict response to treatment.
    ◦ Iron studies.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly variable and is best predicted by the **IPSS-R score**.
• Factors determining prognosis:
    ◦ **Bone marrow blast percentage** (higher is worse).
    ◦ **Karyotype (cytogenetics)** (complex or poor-risk abnormalities are worse).
    ◦ **Severity of cytopenias** (deeper cytopenias are worse).
• Median survival can range from less than a year for very high-risk disease to over 8 years for very low-risk disease.

sections.overview:
• **Hodgkin Lymphoma (HL)** is a malignancy of the lymphatic system characterized by the presence of a specific neoplastic cell, the **Reed-Sternberg cell**, within a reactive inflammatory cell infiltrate.
• It is one of the two major types of lymphoma, the other being Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma (NHL).
• HL is distinguished from NHL by its characteristic histology, a typically orderly and contiguous pattern of spread through lymph node chains, and a generally better prognosis with modern therapy.
• There are two main subtypes:
    ◦ **Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma (cHL):** Accounts for ~95% of cases. Characterized by classic **Reed-Sternberg cells**.
    ◦ **Nodular Lymphocyte-Predominant Hodgkin Lymphoma (NLPHL):** Accounts for ~5% of cases. Characterized by **"popcorn" cells** (lymphocytic and histiocytic cells).
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology:** The exact cause is unknown. There is a strong association with the **Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV)**, which is found in the tumor cells of approximately 40-50% of classical HL cases. Immunosuppression (e.g., HIV) is also a significant risk factor.
• **Pathophysiology:**
    ◦ HL arises from germinal center or post-germinal center B-lymphocytes that have undergone malignant transformation.
    ◦ The hallmark is the **Reed-Sternberg (RS) cell**, a large, multinucleated cell with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli, often described as having an **"owl's eye" appearance**.
    ◦ A key feature of HL is that the malignant RS cells constitute only a small fraction (~1-2%) of the tumor mass. The bulk of the tumor consists of a reactive infiltrate of non-neoplastic cells (lymphocytes, eosinophils, neutrophils, plasma cells).
    ◦ These RS cells secrete various cytokines and chemokines that recruit the surrounding inflammatory cells, which in turn support the survival and proliferation of the RS cells and contribute to the systemic **"B" symptoms**.
    ◦ The disease typically spreads in a **contiguous, predictable pattern** from one lymph node group to adjacent ones.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Bimodal Age Distribution:** There are two distinct peaks of incidence:
    ◦ Young adulthood (ages 15-35)
    ◦ Older adulthood (ages >55)
• **Sex:** More common in males than females (M:F ratio ~1.5:1).
• **Incidence:** Less common than Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma, accounting for approximately 10% of all lymphomas.
sections.riskFactors:
• **EBV Infection:** A history of infectious mononucleosis increases the risk ~3-fold.
• **Immunosuppression:** HIV infection, solid organ transplant recipients, congenital immunodeficiency.
• **Family History:** A first-degree relative with Hodgkin Lymphoma.
• **Autoimmune Diseases:** Rheumatoid arthritis, sarcoidosis.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The "classic" patient is a young adult presenting with a persistent, painless mass in the neck.
• **Painless Lymphadenopathy (most common):** Firm, rubbery, non-tender enlarged lymph nodes.
    ◦ Most common sites: **Cervical**, **supraclavicular**, and **mediastinal**.
• **"B" Symptoms (present in ~40% of patients):** These have prognostic significance.
• **Pruritus:** Generalized itching, can be severe.
• **Fatigue & Malaise:** Common and nonspecific.
• **Chest Symptoms:** Cough, chest pain, or shortness of breath due to a large mediastinal mass.
• **Pel-Ebstein Fever:** A rare finding of cyclical fevers that rise and fall over a period of 1-2 weeks.
• **Alcohol-Induced Lymph Node Pain:** A rare but highly specific symptom where ingestion of alcohol causes pain at the site of nodal disease.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Lymphadenopathy:** Palpable, non-tender, firm, and rubbery lymph nodes. Matted nodes (groups of nodes that feel connected) may be present.
• **Mediastinal Mass:** May lead to signs of **Superior Vena Cava (SVC) syndrome** (facial plethora, JVD, arm swelling) if large enough to cause compression.
• **Hepatosplenomegaly:** Palpable enlargement of the liver and/or spleen, indicating more advanced disease.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Biopsy (Gold Standard):**
    ◦ **Excisional lymph node biopsy** is required for diagnosis. It allows for assessment of the node's architecture.
    ◦ Fine-Needle Aspiration (FNA) is **inadequate** as it does not provide tissue architecture.
    ◦ **Histology:** Identification of **Reed-Sternberg cells** in a reactive cellular background confirms classical HL.
• **Laboratory Studies:**
    ◦ **CBC with differential:** May show normocytic anemia, neutrophilia, eosinophilia, or lymphopenia.
    ◦ **Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) & C-Reactive Protein (CRP):** Often elevated; ESR is an important prognostic factor.
    ◦ **Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH):** May be elevated; also a prognostic factor.
    ◦ **Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP):** To assess renal and hepatic function prior to therapy.
    ◦ HIV and Hepatitis B/C serologies.
• **Staging Imaging:**
    ◦ **PET/CT Scan:** The current standard of care for initial staging, assessing response to therapy, and detecting relapse. It combines anatomical detail (CT) with functional information about metabolic activity (PET).
    ◦ **CT of Neck, Chest, Abdomen, and Pelvis (with contrast):** Was the historical standard and is still used to define the extent of nodal and extranodal disease.
• **Staging System:**
    ◦ **Cotswolds-modified Ann Arbor Staging System:**
        ▪ **Stage I:** Involvement of a single lymph node region.
        ▪ **Stage II:** Involvement of 2 lymph node regions on the same side of the diaphragm.
        ▪ **Stage III:** Involvement of lymph node regions on both sides of the diaphragm.
        ▪ **Stage IV:** Diffuse or disseminated involvement of one or more extralymphatic organs (e.g., bone marrow, liver, lung).
    ◦ **Modifiers:**
        ▪ **A:** Asymptomatic.
        ▪ **B:** Presence of **"B" symptoms**.
        ▪ **X:** Bulky disease (mass >10 cm or >1/3 of transthoracic diameter).
        ▪ **E:** Extranodal extension from an adjacent lymph node site.
sections.treatment:
• **Chemotherapy (Mainstay):**
    ◦ **ABVD Regimen:** The most common frontline regimen for classical HL.
        ▪ **A**driamycin (Doxorubicin)
        ▪ **B**leomycin
        ▪ **V**inblastine
        ▪ **D**acarbazine
• **Radiation Therapy (RT):**
    ◦ Often used in combination with chemotherapy for early-stage (I-II) disease.
    ◦ Modern technique is **Involved-Site Radiation Therapy (ISRT)**, which targets only the originally involved lymph nodes to minimize toxicity.
• **Relapsed/Refractory Disease:**
    ◦ High-dose chemotherapy followed by **autologous stem cell transplant**.
    ◦ Targeted therapies: **Brentuximab Vedotin** (anti-CD30 antibody-drug conjugate).
    ◦ Immunotherapy: **Checkpoint inhibitors** (e.g., Nivolumab, Pembrolizumab).
sections.management:
• **Staging Workup:** Complete history, physical, labs, and PET/CT are essential to determine the stage and guide treatment decisions.
• **Treatment Response Assessment:** Interim and end-of-treatment PET/CT scans are used to evaluate response (Deauville score).
• **Fertility Preservation:** Chemotherapy can cause infertility. Counseling and options like sperm banking or oocyte cryopreservation should be discussed with young patients before starting treatment.
• **Survivorship Care:** Long-term follow-up is critical to monitor for relapse and manage long-term treatment complications.
sections.complications:
• **Secondary Malignancies:**
    ◦ **Solid Tumors:** Increased risk of breast cancer, lung cancer, and GI cancers, particularly in areas that received radiation.
    ◦ **Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) / Myelodysplastic Syndrome (MDS):** A risk from chemotherapy.
• **Cardiovascular Disease:**
    ◦ **Coronary Artery Disease:** Risk increased by mediastinal radiation.
    ◦ **Cardiomyopathy:** A known side effect of Doxorubicin (Adriamycin).
• **Pulmonary Toxicity:**
    ◦ **Pulmonary Fibrosis:** A risk from Bleomycin and chest radiation.
• **Endocrinopathy:**
    ◦ **Hypothyroidism:** Common after neck radiation.
    ◦ **Infertility:** Risk from several chemotherapy agents.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent:** Hodgkin Lymphoma is one of the most curable cancers.
• The overall 5-year survival rate is **>85%**.
• **Prognosis depends on stage and risk factors:**
    ◦ Early-stage (I-IIA) disease has a cure rate of >90%.
    ◦ Advanced-stage (III-IV) disease has a cure rate of 75-80%.
• **Poor prognostic factors include:** Advanced age, male sex, **"B" symptoms**, high ESR, bulky disease, and advanced stage.

sections.overview:
• Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma (NHL) is a heterogeneous group of malignancies arising from lymphocytes (B-cells, T-cells, or NK-cells).
    ◦ Characterized by the clonal proliferation of lymphoid cells in lymphoid tissues, such as lymph nodes, spleen, bone marrow, and extranodal sites.
    ◦ Unlike Hodgkin Lymphoma, NHL is defined by the **absence of Reed-Sternberg cells**.
    ◦ Encompasses a wide spectrum of diseases, ranging from slow-growing (indolent) to very aggressive.
    ◦ B-cell lymphomas account for the vast majority (~85-90%) of cases in the United States.
sections.etiology:
• NHL results from malignant transformation of a lymphocyte at a specific stage of its differentiation.
    ◦ This is driven by genetic mutations, such as chromosomal translocations, that lead to the overexpression of oncogenes or the inhibition of tumor suppressor genes.
    ◦ This dysregulation causes uncontrolled cell proliferation and evasion of apoptosis.
    ◦ **Clonal Proliferation**: A single mutated lymphoid cell proliferates, creating a clone of malignant cells.
    ◦ **Cell of Origin**:
        ▪ Can be B-lymphocytes (~85%), T-lymphocytes (~15%), or rarely NK-cells.
        ▪ The specific subtype of NHL depends on the cell of origin and its developmental stage.
    ◦ **Key Genetic Events**:
        ▪ **Follicular Lymphoma**: t(14;18) translocation → overexpression of the anti-apoptotic gene **BCL-2**.
        ▪ **Burkitt Lymphoma**: t(8;14) translocation → overexpression of the **c-myc** proto-oncogene, a potent driver of cell proliferation.
        ▪ **Mantle Cell Lymphoma**: t(11;14) translocation → overexpression of **Cyclin D1**, promoting cell cycle progression.
sections.epidemiology:
• More common than Hodgkin Lymphoma.
• The 7th most common cancer in the U.S.
• Incidence increases significantly with age; the median age at diagnosis is **~67 years**.
• Slightly more common in males and Caucasians.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is highly variable depending on the subtype and sites of involvement.
• Most patients present with **painless, persistent lymphadenopathy**.
• Unlike Hodgkin Lymphoma, which often presents with contiguous, localized nodal spread, NHL frequently presents with disseminated, non-contiguous disease at diagnosis.
• Extranodal involvement is common.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Biopsy (Gold Standard)**:
    ◦ **Excisional lymph node biopsy** is required for diagnosis and subtyping.
        ▪ It provides crucial information on cell morphology and tissue architecture.
    ◦ *Fine Needle Aspiration (FNA) is inadequate as it does not preserve architecture.*
• **Laboratory Studies**:
    ◦ **CBC with differential**: To assess for anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, or circulating lymphoma cells.
    ◦ **Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP)**: Evaluate renal and hepatic function.
    ◦ **LDH (Lactate Dehydrogenase)**: Important prognostic marker; elevated levels correlate with tumor burden and cell turnover.
    ◦ **Uric Acid**: Marker of high cell turnover; elevated levels increase the risk of Tumor Lysis Syndrome.
    ◦ **Viral Serologies**: HIV, HBV, HCV, EBV.
• **Immunohistochemistry & Flow Cytometry**:
    ◦ Performed on the biopsy sample to determine the cell lineage (B-cell vs. T-cell) and specific protein markers (e.g., **CD20** on B-cells).
• **Staging Workup (Ann Arbor Staging)**:
    ◦ **Imaging**:
        ▪ **CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis with contrast** is standard.
        ▪ **PET/CT scan** is now the preferred modality for initial staging and assessing treatment response, as it identifies metabolically active tumor sites.
    ◦ **Bone Marrow Biopsy and Aspirate**:
        ▪ To determine if the marrow is involved (Stage IV disease).
    ◦ **Lumbar Puncture with CSF analysis**:
        ▪ For patients with high-risk subtypes (e.g., Burkitt, DLBCL) or neurologic symptoms to rule out CNS involvement.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly variable and depends on the subtype, stage, and patient-specific factors.
• **Indolent lymphomas**: Long median survival (many years), but relapses are common and they are generally not curable.
• **Aggressive lymphomas**: Can be cured in a significant proportion of patients (~60-70% for DLBCL) with intensive therapy, but are rapidly fatal if left untreated.
• **International Prognostic Index (IPI)**:
    ◦ Used for aggressive lymphomas to stratify risk.
    ◦ Based on 5 factors ("APLES"):
        ▪ **A**ge > 60
        ▪ **P**erformance Status (ECOG ≥ 2)
        ▪ **L**DH elevated
        ▪ **E**xtranodal sites > 1
        ▪ **S**tage III or IV
    ◦ *The more risk factors present, the worse the prognosis.*

sections.overview:
• Burkitt Lymphoma (BL) is a **highly aggressive**, mature B-cell Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma (NHL).
• It is one of the **fastest-growing human tumors**, with a doubling time of approximately 24 hours.
• The disease is characterized by a specific chromosomal translocation involving the **c-MYC oncogene**, leading to uncontrolled cellular proliferation.
• Despite its aggressive nature, it is often curable with intensive, short-course chemotherapy.
sections.etiology:
• **Cell of Origin**: Mature B-lymphocyte (germinal center B-cell).
• **Pathognomonic Genetic Defect**: Translocation of the **c-MYC oncogene** on chromosome 8.
    ◦ **t(8;14)**: Most common (~85%); the c-MYC gene is moved next to the immunoglobulin heavy chain (IgH) gene locus on chromosome 14, leading to its overexpression.
    ◦ **t(2;8)** and **t(8;22)**: Less common variants; move c-MYC next to the immunoglobulin kappa or lambda light chain loci, respectively.
• **Mechanism**: Overexpression of the c-MYC protein, a transcription factor, drives cells into continuous proliferation and blocks differentiation, resulting in rapid tumor growth.
• **Viral Association**: **Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV)** is strongly associated, particularly with the endemic variant.
    ◦ EBV is thought to be a "first hit" that immortalizes B-cells, with the c-MYC translocation being the "second hit" that drives malignant transformation.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Endemic (African) Burkitt Lymphoma**:
    ◦ **Geography**: Primarily in equatorial Africa ("lymphoma belt").
    ◦ **Demographics**: Mainly affects children (peak age 4-7 years).
    ◦ **Association**: Strong association with **EBV (>95%)** and co-infection with chronic malaria.
• **Sporadic (Non-endemic) Burkitt Lymphoma**:
    ◦ **Geography**: Worldwide, including North America and Europe.
    ◦ **Demographics**: Primarily affects children and young adults but can occur at any age.
    ◦ **Association**: Weaker association with **EBV (~20-30%)**.
• **Immunodeficiency-Associated Burkitt Lymphoma**:
    ◦ **Population**: Occurs in patients with significant immunosuppression, most commonly **HIV/AIDS**; also seen in post-transplant patients.
    ◦ **CD4 Count**: Typically occurs when CD4 count is >200 cells/L, unlike other AIDS-defining lymphomas.
sections.riskFactors:
• **EBV infection** (especially for endemic and immunodeficiency-associated types)
• **Chronic malaria** (cofactor in endemic regions, thought to reduce immune surveillance of EBV)
• **Immunodeficiency** (HIV/AIDS, post-transplant immunosuppression)
• **Age**: Primarily a disease of children and young adults.
• **Geography**: Living in equatorial Africa (for endemic type).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation is marked by a **rapidly enlarging tumor mass**; symptoms develop over days to weeks.
• The site of primary involvement differs by variant:
    ◦ **Endemic**: Most commonly presents as a large mass of the **jaw or facial bones**. Can also involve kidneys, ovaries, or meninges.
    ◦ **Sporadic**: Most commonly presents as an **abdominal mass**, typically in the **ileocecal region**. Patients may present with abdominal pain, distention, or signs of bowel obstruction/intussusception.
    ◦ **Immunodeficiency-Associated**: Often presents with widespread disease, including lymph node involvement, bone marrow, and CNS.
• **Constitutional "B" symptoms**: Fever, drenching night sweats, and unintentional weight loss (>10% of body weight in 6 months).
• Symptoms related to mass location:
    ◦ **Jaw/Face**: Facial swelling, jaw pain, proptosis, tooth loosening.
    ◦ **Abdomen**: Abdominal pain, bloating, nausea, vomiting, change in bowel habits, GI bleeding.
    ◦ **CNS**: Headache, cranial nerve palsies, seizures, altered mental status.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Palpable Mass**: A firm, non-tender, rapidly growing mass in the jaw, orbit, or abdomen.
• **Abdomen**: Abdominal distention, tenderness, ascites, hepatosplenomegaly. Bowel sounds may be high-pitched (obstruction) or absent (ileus).
• **Head/Neck**: Facial asymmetry, proptosis, cervical lymphadenopathy.
• **Neurologic**: Cranial nerve deficits (e.g., CN VII palsy), signs of meningeal irritation.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Biopsy**: **Excisional biopsy** of an involved lymph node or tumor mass is the gold standard for diagnosis.
• **Histopathology**:
    ◦ **"Starry sky" appearance**: A classic but not pathognomonic finding.
        ▪ **"Sky"**: Diffuse sheet of medium-sized, monotonous lymphoid cells with basophilic cytoplasm and round nuclei.
        ▪ **"Stars"**: Benign tangible-body macrophages that have phagocytosed apoptotic tumor cells.
    ◦ **High mitotic rate** and numerous apoptotic bodies.
• **Immunohistochemistry / Flow Cytometry**:
    ◦ **Positive for**: CD19, **CD20**, CD10, BCL6, surface IgM.
    ◦ **High proliferation index**: **Ki-67 is nearly 100%**.
    ◦ **Negative for**: TdT, BCL2.
• **Cytogenetics**: Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) or karyotyping to confirm **t(8;14)** or its variants.
• **Laboratory Studies**:
    ◦ **LDH**: Markedly elevated (reflects high tumor burden and rapid cell turnover).
    ◦ **Uric Acid**: Elevated (risk for tumor lysis syndrome).
    ◦ **CBC**: May show anemia, thrombocytopenia, or leukocytosis if bone marrow is involved.
    ◦ **CMP**: Assess renal function (BUN, creatinine) and electrolytes prior to therapy.
• **Staging Workup**:
    ◦ **Imaging**: CT of chest/abdomen/pelvis and/or PET/CT scan to determine the extent of disease.
    ◦ **Bone Marrow Biopsy**: To assess for marrow involvement.
    ◦ **Lumbar Puncture (LP)**: CSF analysis (cytology, flow cytometry) is **mandatory** for all patients to rule out CNS involvement.
sections.treatment:
• **Chemotherapy Regimens**: Often include high doses of cyclophosphamide, methotrexate, cytarabine, and vincristine.
    ◦ Examples: **CODOX-M/IVAC**, **R-hyper-CVAD**, **CALGB 10002**.
• **Rituximab (R)**: An anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody, is now standardly added to most chemotherapy regimens.
• **CNS Prophylaxis**: **Mandatory for ALL patients** due to high risk of CNS relapse. Typically consists of intrathecal (IT) methotrexate and/or cytarabine.
• **Role of Surgery/Radiation**:
    ◦ **Surgery**: Limited to initial diagnostic biopsy. Debulking is not recommended.
    ◦ **Radiation**: Limited role; may be considered for CNS disease or palliation.
sections.management:
• **Tumor Lysis Syndrome (TLS)**: This is a medical emergency and a major concern due to the high proliferation rate and exquisite chemosensitivity of the tumor.
    ◦ **Prophylaxis is CRITICAL**:
        ▪ **Aggressive IV hydration**: To maintain high urine output.
        ▪ **Allopurinol** (blocks uric acid production) or **Rasburicase** (breaks down existing uric acid) for high-risk patients.
        ▪ **Monitoring**: Frequent monitoring of electrolytes (K+, PO4, Ca2+), uric acid, and renal function, especially during the first few days of chemotherapy.
• **Supportive Care**: Management of chemotherapy side effects, including myelosuppression (neutropenic fever protocols), mucositis, and nausea/vomiting.
sections.complications:
• **Tumor Lysis Syndrome (TLS)**: Hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, hyperuricemia, acute kidney injury, arrhythmias, seizures.
• **Bowel Obstruction / Perforation**: From large abdominal masses.
• **CNS Involvement**: Can lead to permanent neurologic deficits.
• **Chemotherapy Toxicity**: Profound myelosuppression leading to infection/sepsis, mucositis, infertility.
• **Secondary Malignancies**: Long-term risk from chemotherapy.
sections.prognosis:
• **Highly curable**: Despite its aggressiveness, Burkitt Lymphoma is very sensitive to chemotherapy.
