        ▪ Symptoms: Yawning, euphoria, depression, irritability, food cravings, neck stiffness, constipation.
    ◦ **Aura:**
        ▪ Occurs in ~25% of patients.
        ▪ Focal, reversible neurological symptoms that usually last **5-60 minutes** and precede or accompany the headache.
        ▪ **Visual (most common):**
            ▪ **Scintillating Scotoma:** Classic aura; an arc or band of absent vision with a shimmering or flickering border.
            ▪ **Fortification Spectra:** Zig-zag lines resembling a fortress wall.
            ▪ **Photopsia** (flashes of light).
        ▪ **Sensory:** Paresthesias (tingling) or numbness, typically affecting one side of the face or an extremity.
        ▪ **Language:** Aphasia or word-finding difficulty.
        ▪ **Motor (rare):** Hemiplegic migraine with unilateral weakness.
    ◦ **Headache Phase:**
        ▪ Lasts **4 to 72 hours** (untreated or unsuccessfully treated).
        ▪ **POUND** mnemonic:
            ▪ **P**ulsating or throbbing quality
            ▪ **O**ne-day duration (4-72 hrs)
            ▪ **U**nilateral location (can be bilateral in ~40%)
            ▪ **N**ausea and/or vomiting
            ▪ **D**isabling intensity (moderate to severe)
        ▪ **Associated Symptoms:**
            ▪ **Photophobia:** Sensitivity to light.
            ▪ **Phonophobia:** Sensitivity to sound.
            ▪ Osmophobia: Sensitivity to smells.
            ▪ **Cutaneous Allodynia:** Pain from a stimulus that does not normally provoke pain (e.g., brushing hair, wearing glasses).
    ◦ **Postdrome:**
        ▪ Occurs after the headache resolves, lasting up to 24-48 hours.
        ▪ "Migraine hangover" feeling.
        ▪ Symptoms: Fatigue, difficulty concentrating, mood changes, residual head soreness.
sections.physicalExam:
• The physical and neurological exam is typically **normal** between migraine attacks.
• **During an acute attack:**
    ◦ Patient may appear ill and prefer to be in a dark, quiet room.
    ◦ **Photophobia**, **phonophobia**.
    ◦ Scalp tenderness or **allodynia** may be present.
    ◦ Transient focal neurologic deficits corresponding to the aura may be observed but should resolve.
• **Crucial Purpose of Exam:** Rule out secondary causes of headache (i.e., "red flags").
    ◦ Check for **papilledema**, **nuchal rigidity**, focal neurological deficits (that don't fit a typical aura), and altered mental status.
sections.diagnostics:
• Migraine is primarily a **clinical diagnosis** based on patient history and a normal physical exam.
• **Diagnostic Criteria (ICHD-3 beta):**
    ◦ **Migraine without Aura:** At least 5 attacks fulfilling criteria:
        ▪ Headache lasts 4-72 hours.
        ▪ Has 2 of the following: **unilateral**, **pulsating**, moderate-to-severe pain, aggravation by routine physical activity.
        ▪ During headache, has 1 of the following: **nausea/vomiting**, **photophobia** AND **phonophobia**.
• **Neuroimaging (CT or MRI):**
    ◦ Not routinely indicated.
    ◦ Indicated if "red flags" are present to rule out secondary causes.
    ◦ Use the **SNOOPP** mnemonic:
        ▪ **S**ystemic symptoms (**fever**, weight loss, cancer, HIV)
        ▪ **N**eurologic symptoms or signs (confusion, **seizure**, focal deficit)
        ▪ **O**nset is new (especially if >50 years old) or sudden ("**thunderclap**" headache)
        ▪ **O**ther associated conditions (head trauma, pregnancy)
        ▪ **P**revious headache history is different (change in frequency, severity, or clinical features)
        ▪ **P**apilledema
sections.management:
• **Patient Education:** Critical for success. Explain the nature of migraine, treatment goals, and realistic expectations.
• **Headache Diary:** Helps identify triggers and track headache frequency and response to treatment.
• **Lifestyle Modifications:**
    ◦ **Trigger Avoidance:** Identify and avoid personal triggers.
    ◦ **Sleep Hygiene:** Maintain a regular sleep schedule.
    ◦ **Stress Management:** Biofeedback, cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), relaxation techniques.
    ◦ **Regular Exercise:** Can reduce migraine frequency.
• **Limit Abortive Medications:** To prevent **Medication Overuse Headache (MOH)**.
    ◦ Limit use of triptans/combination analgesics to <10 days/month.
    ◦ Limit simple analgesics to <15 days/month.
sections.complications:
• **Chronic Migraine:** Headache occurring on ≥15 days per month for >3 months, which has the features of migraine headache on at least 8 days per month.
• **Medication Overuse Headache (MOH):** "Rebound headache" caused by the frequent use of acute medications. A very common reason for migraine treatment failure.
• **Status Migrainosus:** A debilitating migraine attack lasting for more than 72 hours.
• **Migrainous Infarction:** A rare complication where a stroke occurs during a typical migraine with aura attack, and neuroimaging confirms an infarct.
• **Persistent Aura without Infarction:** Aura symptoms that persist for >1 week without evidence of infarction on imaging.
sections.prognosis:
• Migraine is a chronic condition, but the prognosis for managing symptoms is generally good with appropriate treatment and lifestyle modifications.
• It is not life-threatening but can severely impact daily functioning and quality of life.
• Headache frequency often decreases with age, particularly in women after menopause.

sections.overview:
• A primary headache disorder and the most common of the **trigeminal autonomic cephalgias** (TACs).
    ◦ Characterized by recurrent, excruciatingly **severe, strictly unilateral attacks** of orbital, supraorbital, or temporal pain.
    ◦ Attacks are associated with **ipsilateral cranial autonomic symptoms**.
• The name "cluster" refers to the tendency for attacks to occur in cyclical periods (**cluster periods**) followed by periods of remission.
• Often described as one of the most painful conditions known to medicine.
sections.etiology:
• The exact pathophysiology is not fully understood but is thought to involve two key mechanisms:
    ◦ **Hypothalamic Activation**
        ▪ The posterior hypothalamus is considered the central generator for cluster attacks.
        ▪ Functional imaging shows activation of the ipsilateral posterior hypothalamus during an attack.
        ▪ Explains the striking **circadian rhythmicity** of attacks (e.g., occurring at the same time each day, frequently at night, and during specific seasons).
    ◦ **Trigeminovascular System and Parasympathetic Activation**
        ▪ Activation of the **trigeminal-autonomic reflex** is central to the symptoms.
        ▪ Pain is mediated by the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve.
        ▪ Activation leads to the release of vasoactive neuropeptides like **Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide (CGRP)**, causing painful neurogenic inflammation and vasodilation.
        ▪ This reflex also activates cranial **parasympathetic pathways**, resulting in the characteristic **ipsilateral autonomic symptoms** (lacrimation, rhinorrhea, conjunctival injection).
        ▪ **Sympathetic pathway impairment** can cause ipsilateral ptosis and miosis (a partial **Horner's syndrome**).
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Relatively rare, affecting ~0.1% of the population.
• **Sex**: Strong male predominance (**M:F ratio ~3:1** to 4:1).
• **Age of Onset**: Typically between **20 and 40 years old**.
• **Episodic vs. Chronic**:
    ◦ **Episodic (80-90%)**: Patients experience cluster periods lasting weeks to months, followed by remission periods lasting months to years.
    ◦ **Chronic (10-20%)**: Attacks occur without significant remission periods (remission < 3 months per year).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Classic patient: A middle-aged male, often a smoker, who is awakened 1-2 hours after falling asleep by a **sudden, severe, unilateral headache**.
• The pain is so intense that the patient is **agitated, unable to sit still**, and may be seen **pacing, rocking**, or even banging their head against a wall.
• Attack characteristics:
    ◦ Builds to a peak rapidly.
    ◦ Lasts less than 3 hours before abruptly resolving.
• Attacks may occur multiple times a day for several weeks before disappearing completely for a long period.
sections.diagnostics:
• Cluster headache is a **clinical diagnosis** based on a characteristic history fulfilling the ICHD-3 criteria.
• **Imaging**:
    ◦ **Brain MRI with and without contrast** is recommended for all patients with a new diagnosis of cluster headache.
    ◦ **Purpose**: To rule out secondary causes and structural lesions that can mimic cluster headache (e.g., pituitary adenoma, carotid artery dissection, cavernous sinus pathology, aneurysm).
        ▪ The MRI is almost always normal in primary cluster headache.
• **Labs**: No specific laboratory tests are indicated.
sections.prognosis:
• Cluster headache is not a life-threatening condition, but it causes **severe disability** and a profound reduction in quality of life.
• It is a **lifelong condition** for most, with cluster periods recurring throughout life.
• The frequency and duration of cluster periods may decrease with age in some individuals.

sections.overview:
• Medication Overuse Headache (MOH), also known as **rebound headache**, is a chronic secondary headache disorder caused by the regular, long-term use of medications to treat acute headaches.
    ◦ Characterized by a paradoxical **increase in headache frequency** and a decrease in the effectiveness of acute medications.
    ◦ The headache typically resolves or reverts to its previous episodic pattern after the overused medication is discontinued.
sections.etiology:
• The exact pathophysiology is not fully understood but is thought to be multifactorial, involving central nervous system changes.
    ◦ **Central Sensitization**: Chronic exposure to acute headache medication is believed to lower the pain perception threshold in the brainstem (trigeminal nucleus caudalis) and higher cortical areas, making the brain more susceptible to generating pain signals.
    ◦ **Receptor Dysregulation**:
        ▪ **Serotonin (5-HT) System**: Chronic use of triptans and other analgesics can lead to downregulation of 5-HT receptors, altering natural pain modulation.
        ▪ **Opioid System**: Overuse of opioids leads to changes in endogenous opioid receptors, contributing to a pro-nociceptive (pain-promoting) state.
    ◦ **Genetic Predisposition**: A potential genetic susceptibility may make certain individuals more prone to developing MOH.
    ◦ **Behavioral Factors**: Operant conditioning, where temporary relief reinforces repeated medication use, can contribute to the cycle of overuse.
• **Commonly Implicated Medications** (in order of risk):
    ◦ **Highest Risk**: Opioids (oxycodone, hydrocodone), Butalbital-containing compounds (Fioricet, Fiorinal).
    ◦ **High Risk**: Triptans, Combination analgesics containing caffeine (Excedrin).
    ◦ **Moderate Risk**: Ergots (dihydroergotamine).
    ◦ **Lower Risk**: Simple analgesics - NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen), Acetaminophen.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects approximately 1-2% of the general population.
• **Demographics**: More common in **women** than men (ratio of 3-4:1), reflecting the higher prevalence of primary headache disorders like migraine in women.
• **Age**: Peak incidence is between 40-50 years old.
• **Clinical Setting**: MOH is one of the most common diagnoses in specialized headache clinics.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The typical patient presents with a history of an episodic headache disorder (e.g., migraine) that has transformed over months to years into a **chronic, near-daily headache**.
    ◦ Patients report their headaches are becoming more frequent and their acute "rescue" medications are no longer working as well.
    ◦ They often take medication preemptively out of fear of a developing headache.
    ◦ The headache pattern is often a constant, low-grade background pain, punctuated by more severe attacks.
sections.diagnostics:
• MOH is a **clinical diagnosis** based on the International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition (ICHD-3) criteria.
    ◦ **Key ICHD-3 Criteria**:
        ▪ Headache present on **≥15 days/month** in a patient with a pre-existing headache disorder.
        ▪ Regular overuse for **>3 months** of one or more acute headache medications.
            ◦ **≥10 days/month**: Triptans, opioids, ergots, combination analgesics.
            ◦ **≥15 days/month**: Simple analgesics (NSAIDs, acetaminophen).
        ▪ The headache pattern cannot be better explained by another diagnosis.
    ◦ **Diagnostic Tools**:
        ▪ **Detailed History**: The most important tool. Focus on headache frequency, evolution over time, and a meticulous medication history (type, dose, frequency).
        ▪ **Headache Diary**: Essential for diagnosis and management. It provides objective data on headache days and medication intake, confirming the pattern of overuse.
        ▪ **Neuroimaging (CT/MRI)**: Not indicated for MOH diagnosis. It should only be performed if there are **red flag** findings (e.g., thunderclap onset, new neurological deficit, new onset after age 50, significant change in headache pattern) to exclude other secondary causes.
sections.prognosis:
• With comprehensive treatment (withdrawal + prevention), the prognosis is generally good.
    ◦ Approximately **50-70%** of patients successfully revert to their prior episodic headache pattern.
    ◦ **Relapse is common**, occurring in up to 40% of patients within 5 years, highlighting the importance of ongoing management.
    ◦ Negative prognostic factors include overuse of **opioids or butalbital**, long duration of overuse, and coexisting psychiatric disorders.

sections.overview:
• Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH), formerly known as Pseudotumor Cerebri, is a clinical syndrome characterized by **elevated intracranial pressure (ICP)** in the absence of a mass lesion, hydrocephalus, or other identifiable cause.
• Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) composition is normal.
• The primary morbidity associated with IIH is **permanent vision loss** due to chronic papilledema.
sections.etiology:
• The term "idiopathic" signifies that the exact cause is unknown.
• The leading theories suggest a disturbance in CSF dynamics, likely due to:
    ◦ **Impaired CSF Absorption**: Reduced outflow of CSF through the arachnoid granulations into the dural venous sinuses.
    ◦ **Venous Outflow Obstruction**: Stenosis of the transverse venous sinuses is found in a majority of patients, leading to increased venous pressure that impedes CSF absorption.
        ▪ It is unclear if the stenosis is a cause or a result of the elevated ICP.
    ◦ **Increased CSF Production**: This is a less favored theory.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Classic Patient Profile**: **Obese woman of childbearing age**.
• **Incidence**:
    ◦ General population: ~1-2 per 100,000.
    ◦ Obese women (age 20-44): Rises to ~20 per 100,000.
• **Female-to-Male Ratio**: Approximately 9:1.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The typical patient is an obese young woman who presents with a persistent, daily **headache** and **visual disturbances**.
• The onset of symptoms is usually gradual.
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is based on the **Modified Dandy Criteria**, which requires:
    ◦ Symptoms and signs of increased ICP.
    ◦ No localizing neurological findings (except for **CN VI palsy**).
    ◦ **Normal CSF composition**.
    ◦ **Elevated opening pressure** on lumbar puncture.
    ◦ Neuroimaging that rules out another etiology.
• **Diagnostic Workup**:
    ◦ **Neuroimaging (MUST be done before LP)**:
        ▪ **MRI of the brain with MR Venography (MRV)** is the preferred study.
        ▪ **Purpose**: To rule out an intracranial mass, hydrocephalus, and cerebral venous sinus thrombosis.
        ▪ **Supportive Findings for IIH**: Empty sella turcica, flattening of the posterior sclera, distention of the optic nerve sheath, and transverse venous sinus stenosis.
    ◦ **Lumbar Puncture (LP)**:
        ▪ Performed **AFTER imaging** has ruled out a mass lesion to prevent cerebral herniation.
        ▪ **Key Diagnostic Finding**: **Elevated opening pressure >25 cmH2O** (in the lateral decubitus position).
        ▪ **CSF Analysis**: Must be **normal** (cell count, protein, glucose).
    ◦ **Ophthalmologic Evaluation**:
        ▪ Formal visual field testing and optical coherence tomography (OCT) to quantify papilledema and monitor for optic nerve damage.
sections.prognosis:
• With timely diagnosis and treatment, the prognosis for vision is generally good.
• The degree of **permanent vision loss** is directly related to the severity and duration of **papilledema** at presentation.
• Symptoms can recur, particularly with weight regain. IIH is often a chronic condition requiring long-term management.

sections.overview:
• **Temporal (Giant Cell) Arteritis (GCA)** is a systemic, granulomatous **large-vessel vasculitis** affecting extracranial branches of the carotid artery, especially the **temporal artery**.
    ◦ It is a neurologic **medical emergency** due to its potential to cause irreversible ischemic damage to the optic nerve, brain, and other structures.
    ◦ The underlying pathology is luminal occlusion from vessel wall inflammation, leading to end-organ ischemia.
    ◦ The most feared neurologic complication is **permanent vision loss**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ The exact cause is unknown.
    ◦ Believed to be a **T-cell-mediated autoimmune process** triggered by an unknown antigen in a genetically susceptible individual (associated with **HLA-DR4**).
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Immune Activation**: An unknown antigen presented by dendritic cells in the vessel adventitia activates CD4+ T-cells.
    ◦ **Inflammatory Cascade**: Activated T-cells differentiate (Th1, Th17), releasing pro-inflammatory cytokines like **interferon-gamma (IFN-γ)** and **Interleukin-6 (IL-6)**.
    ◦ **Vessel Wall Damage**
        ▪ Macrophages are recruited and form **multinucleated giant cells**.
        ▪ Granulomatous inflammation disrupts the internal elastic lamina.
        ▪ Vascular smooth muscle cells proliferate, leading to intimal hyperplasia and severe **luminal narrowing or occlusion**.
    ◦ **Ischemia**: The stenotic or occluded vessel results in downstream tissue ischemia, causing neurologic signs and symptoms (e.g., **optic nerve ischemia causing blindness**, vertebrobasilar ischemia causing **stroke**).
sections.epidemiology:
• **Age**: Almost exclusively affects individuals **> 50 years old**; median age of onset is 75.
• **Gender**: Female-to-male ratio is approximately 2-3:1.
• **Geography/Ethnicity**: Most common in individuals of **Northern European** or Scandinavian descent.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Age > 50** (strongest risk factor)
• **Female gender**
• **Northern European ancestry**
• Personal or family history of **Polymyalgia Rheumatica (PMR)**
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient, typically an elderly female, presents with a **new-onset, unilateral headache** and constitutional symptoms.
    ◦ May report **transient visual disturbances** (a critical warning sign) or **jaw pain with chewing** (jaw claudication).
• The presentation of neurologic manifestations can be abrupt and severe.
• Approximately 50% of patients with GCA also have concurrent **Polymyalgia Rheumatica (PMR)**, characterized by proximal muscle stiffness and aching in the shoulder and pelvic girdles.
sections.physicalExam:
• **General**
    ◦ May have a low-grade fever.
• **Head & Neck**
    ◦ **Temporal Artery**: May be **thickened**, **tender to palpation**, nodular, or have a **reduced/absent pulse**.
    ◦ **Scalp**: Tenderness to light touch over the temporal or occipital regions.
• **Neurologic Exam**
    ◦ **Visual Acuity**: Decreased in the affected eye.
    ◦ **Visual Fields**: Assess for field cuts.
    ◦ **Pupils**: **Afferent Pupillary Defect (APD)** or "Marcus Gunn pupil" may be present in the affected eye with optic neuropathy.
    ◦ **Fundoscopy**: A **pale, edematous (swollen) optic disc** is the classic finding of **Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy (AION)**.
    ◦ **Extraocular Movements**: Assess for palsies causing diplopia.
• **Vascular Exam**
    ◦ **Asymmetric blood pressures** between arms (>15 mmHg difference suggests subclavian artery involvement).
    ◦ Auscultation for bruits over the carotid, subclavian, or axillary arteries.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Labs**
    ◦ **Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR)**: Markedly elevated, typically **>50 mm/hr**, often >100 mm/hr. Highly sensitive.
    ◦ **C-Reactive Protein (CRP)**: Markedly elevated. Often more sensitive than ESR and normalizes faster with treatment.
    ◦ **CBC**: May show a **normocytic anemia** (anemia of chronic disease) and **thrombocytosis** (reactive).
• **Biopsy**
    ◦ **Temporal Artery Biopsy**: **Gold standard** for diagnosis.
        ▪ A 1-2 cm segment is excised.
        ▪ Histology shows panarteritis with infiltration of lymphocytes, macrophages, and characteristic **multinucleated giant cells**.
    ◦ **Important**: A negative biopsy does not rule out GCA due to **"skip lesions"**. Treatment should **NOT** be delayed while awaiting the biopsy. Biopsy can remain positive for up to 2 weeks after starting steroids.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Color Doppler Ultrasound**: Can be used for rapid, non-invasive diagnosis. The **"halo sign"** (a hypoechoic ring around the vessel lumen) is highly specific for vessel wall edema/inflammation.
    ◦ **MRA/CTA/PET Scan**: Useful for evaluating for large-vessel involvement beyond the temporal artery (e.g., aorta, subclavian).
sections.treatment:
• **With Vision Loss or Neurologic Symptoms**: **IV Methylprednisolone** 1000 mg daily for 3 days.
• **Without Vision Loss**: **Oral Prednisone** 40-60 mg daily (or 1 mg/kg/day).
• **Tocilizumab (Actemra)**: An **IL-6 receptor antagonist**. Now often used first-line in combination with steroids to allow for a more rapid steroid taper and reduce long-term steroid toxicity.
• **Low-Dose Aspirin (81 mg daily)**: Recommended to reduce the risk of ischemic events (vision loss, stroke).
sections.management:
• **Steroid Taper**: After the initial high dose, prednisone is tapered very slowly over **1-2 years**, guided by the patient's symptoms and normalization of inflammatory markers (**ESR/CRP**).
• **Relapse Monitoring**: Patients must be monitored for relapse of symptoms, which often occurs during the steroid taper.
• **Prophylaxis for Steroid Complications**
    ◦ **Osteoporosis**: Calcium and Vitamin D supplementation. Consider bisphosphonates.
    ◦ **Gastric Protection**: Proton Pump Inhibitor (PPI) or H2 blocker.
    ◦ **Pneumocystis Pneumonia (PJP)**: Prophylaxis (e.g., Bactrim) should be considered for patients on high-dose, long-term steroids.
• **Aortopathy Surveillance**: Patients with GCA are at increased risk for late-onset **aortic aneurysm and dissection**. Regular imaging (e.g., CTA) may be warranted.
sections.complications:
• **Neurologic**
    ◦ **Permanent, irreversible blindness** (unilateral or bilateral)
    ◦ **Ischemic stroke** (especially vertebrobasilar)
    ◦ Cranial and peripheral neuropathies
• **Vascular**
    ◦ **Aortic aneurysm** (thoracic is most common)
    ◦ **Aortic dissection**
• **Iatrogenic (from treatment)**
    ◦ Complications of long-term glucocorticoid use: **osteoporosis**, vertebral compression fractures, **cataracts**, **glaucoma**, diabetes, Cushingoid features, weight gain, immunosuppression.
sections.prognosis:
• With prompt treatment, the prognosis for survival is excellent.
• The primary source of morbidity is **permanent vision loss** and **side effects from long-term steroid therapy**.
• If vision loss has already occurred, it is almost always **irreversible**.
• **Relapses are common**, affecting up to 50% of patients.

sections.overview:
• A **Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA)** is a transient episode of neurological dysfunction caused by focal brain, spinal cord, or retinal ischemia, **without** acute infarction.
    ◦ Often referred to as a "**warning stroke**."
    ◦ The modern definition is tissue-based: a transient ischemic event where symptoms resolve and imaging (specifically **Diffusion-Weighted MRI**) shows no evidence of a new, permanent infarct.
        ▪ This contrasts with the traditional definition which was based on symptom duration (<24 hours).
• A TIA is a **neurologic emergency**, as it signals a very high short-term risk of a completed ischemic stroke.
sections.etiology:
• The underlying mechanism is a temporary disruption of blood flow to a specific area of the brain, leading to a focal oxygen deficit (ischemia) that is not severe or prolonged enough to cause permanent tissue death (infarction).
• The causes are identical to those of ischemic stroke:
    ◦ **Embolic (Most Common)**: A clot or debris travels from a proximal source and lodges in a smaller cerebral artery.
        ▪ **Cardioembolic (~20%)**: Clot formation in the heart, most commonly due to **Atrial Fibrillation**. Other sources include valvular disease, ventricular aneurysm post-MI, or endocarditis.
        ▪ **Artery-to-Artery**: An embolus breaks off from an atherosclerotic plaque in a large artery (e.g., carotid bifurcation, aortic arch) and travels distally.
    ◦ **Thrombotic (Large Artery)**: In-situ thrombus formation on top of an atherosclerotic plaque within a large intracranial or extracranial artery (e.g., internal carotid, middle cerebral, vertebral).
    ◦ **Lacunar (Small Vessel)**: Occlusion of small, penetrating arteries deep within the brain (e.g., basal ganglia, pons, thalamus).
        ▪ Typically due to lipohyalinosis or microatheroma, strongly associated with chronic **hypertension** and **diabetes**.
    ◦ **Cryptogenic**: No identifiable cause after a thorough workup.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Approximately 200,000 to 500,000 cases annually in the United States.
• **Prevalence**: True prevalence is likely underestimated as many patients do not seek medical care.
• **Age**: Incidence increases significantly with age, doubling each decade after age 55.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is characterized by the **sudden, abrupt onset** of a **focal neurologic deficit**.
• The key feature is the **transient nature** of the symptoms, which typically resolve within minutes to an hour.
• Patients often present to the emergency department *after* their symptoms have completely resolved, making a detailed history the most critical part of the evaluation.
sections.diagnostics:
• A TIA workup is a stroke workup, done urgently to identify the cause and stratify the risk of future stroke.
• **IMMEDIATE Imaging**:
    ◦ **Non-contrast CT Head**:
        ▪ **First-line test** to rapidly rule out intracranial hemorrhage or other mimics (e.g., tumor).
        ▪ It is usually normal in a TIA.
• **Definitive Brain Imaging**:
    ◦ **MRI Brain with Diffusion-Weighted Imaging (DWI)**:
        ▪ **Gold standard**.
        ▪ A TIA is confirmed when there are no new signs of acute infarction on DWI.
        ▪ If DWI is positive, the diagnosis is changed to an acute ischemic stroke, regardless of symptom duration.
• **Vascular Imaging (To find the source)**:
    ◦ **Carotid Ultrasound (Doppler)**: Initial non-invasive test to assess for carotid artery stenosis.
    ◦ **CT Angiography (CTA)** or **MR Angiography (MRA)** of the head and neck: Provides more detailed imaging of intracranial and extracranial vessels.
• **Cardiac Evaluation (To find the source)**:
    ◦ **Electrocardiogram (EKG)**: To screen for **atrial fibrillation** or evidence of recent MI.
    ◦ **Echocardiogram (TTE or TEE)**: To evaluate for cardioembolic sources (e.g., LV thrombus, valvular vegetations, patent foramen ovale).
    ◦ **Continuous Cardiac Monitoring (Telemetry/Holter)**: To detect paroxysmal A-fib.
• **Laboratory Studies**:
    ◦ Fingerstick glucose (to rule out hypoglycemia)
    ◦ CBC, CMP
    ◦ PT/INR, PTT
    ◦ Lipid Panel
    ◦ HbA1c
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly dependent on the underlying etiology and control of risk factors.
• The **ABCD2 score** is a clinical tool used to stratify the short-term (2-day) risk of stroke after a TIA.
    ◦ **A**ge: ≥ 60 years (+1 point)
    ◦ **B**lood Pressure: SBP ≥ 140 or DBP ≥ 90 mmHg at presentation (+1 point)
    ◦ **C**linical Features:
        ▪ **Unilateral weakness** (+2 points)
        ▪ **Speech disturbance** without weakness (+1 point)
    ◦ **D**uration of Symptoms:
        ▪ ≥ 60 minutes (+2 points)
        ▪ 10-59 minutes (+1 point)
    ◦ **D**iabetes: History of DM (+1 point)
• **Interpretation (2-Day Stroke Risk)**:
    ◦ **0-3 points**: Low risk (~1%)
    ◦ **4-5 points**: Moderate risk (~4%)
    ◦ **6-7 points**: High risk (~8%)
• Patients with a score ≥ 3 are typically recommended for hospital admission.

sections.overview:
• An ischemic stroke, or "**brain attack**," is a sudden loss of brain function due to a disruption of the blood supply to a part of the brain.
• It is a **neurological emergency** resulting from focal cerebral, spinal, or retinal infarction.
• Ischemic strokes account for approximately 87% of all strokes and are caused by the occlusion of a cerebral artery, most commonly by a thrombus or an embolus.
• The core principle of management is "**Time is Brain**," as rapid diagnosis and intervention are critical to salvaging brain tissue (the **ischemic penumbra**) and improving patient outcomes.
sections.etiology:
• The underlying pathophysiology is the cessation of blood flow, leading to a cascade of cellular events.
    ◦ **Ischemic Cascade**:
        ▪ **Energy Failure**: Lack of oxygen and glucose delivery halts aerobic metabolism, leading to a rapid depletion of ATP.
        ▪ **Ion Pump Failure**: Na+/K+ pumps fail, causing an influx of Na+, Cl-, and Ca2+, and an efflux of K+.
        ▪ **Cytotoxic Edema**: The ionic shift draws water into the cell, causing cellular swelling and lysis.
        ▪ **Excitotoxicity**: Depolarization triggers the release of excitatory neurotransmitters (e.g., glutamate), which overstimulate neighboring neurons, leading to further calcium influx and cell death.
        ▪ **Inflammation & Apoptosis**: An inflammatory response and programmed cell death pathways are activated, extending the area of injury.
    ◦ **Major Subtypes/Causes**:
        ▪ **Thrombotic Stroke (Large Artery Atherosclerosis)**: A blood clot (thrombus) forms locally on an atherosclerotic plaque within a large cerebral artery (e.g., carotid artery, MCA, vertebral artery), leading to occlusion.
        ▪ **Embolic Stroke**: A clot or debris forms elsewhere in the body and travels to the brain to occlude a vessel.
            • **Cardioembolic (20% of cases)**: Most commonly from **atrial fibrillation**, where stasis of blood in the left atrial appendage allows clot formation. Other sources include valvular disease, ventricular thrombi post-MI, and endocarditis.
            • **Artery-to-Artery Embolism**: A piece of a thrombus from a large proximal artery (e.g., carotid plaque) breaks off and lodges in a smaller distal artery.
        ▪ **Lacunar Stroke (Small Vessel Disease)**: Occlusion of small, penetrating arteries deep within the brain (e.g., basal ganglia, thalamus, pons).
            • Strongly associated with chronic **hypertension** and diabetes mellitus.
            • Results in small (<15 mm) infarcts.
        ▪ **Cryptogenic Stroke**: Stroke of undetermined cause after a thorough workup.
        ▪ **Other Causes**: Hypercoagulable states, arterial dissection, vasculitis, sickle cell disease.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Approximately 800,000 strokes per year in the United States.
• **Prevalence**: Ischemic stroke is the 5th leading cause of death and the leading cause of serious, long-term disability in the U.S.
• **Demographics**: Risk increases significantly with age, doubling each decade after age 55. Higher incidence and mortality in men (at younger ages) and in African American and Hispanic populations.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is characterized by the **sudden, abrupt onset of focal neurological deficits**.
• The specific signs and symptoms depend on the vascular territory affected.
• Patients are often brought in by family who witness the event.
• The most important historical point is the **"last known well" time**, which dictates eligibility for acute treatments.
sections.diagnostics:
• **IMMEDIATE (STAT) Orders**:
    ◦ **Non-Contrast Head CT**: **The single most important initial test.**
        ▪ Its primary purpose is to **rule out hemorrhagic stroke**, which is a contraindication to thrombolytic therapy.
        ▪ Ischemic changes may not be visible for several hours ("normal" CT is common in early ischemic stroke).
    ◦ **Fingerstick Blood Glucose**: To rule out hypoglycemia, a common stroke mimic.
• **Further Workup**:
    ◦ **Neuroimaging**:
        ▪ **CT Angiography (CTA) of Head and Neck**: Identifies large vessel occlusion (LVO) to determine candidacy for mechanical thrombectomy.
        ▪ **CT Perfusion**: Can identify the ischemic penumbra (tissue at risk but still salvageable).
        ▪ **MRI Brain**: **Gold standard for diagnosing ischemic stroke.** The **Diffusion-Weighted Imaging (DWI)** sequence is highly sensitive and can detect ischemia within minutes of onset.
    ◦ **Labs**: CBC, CMP, PT/INR, PTT, Troponin, Lipid Panel.
    ◦ **Cardiac Evaluation**:
        ▪ **ECG**: Essential to screen for atrial fibrillation.
        ▪ **Echocardiogram (TTE/TEE)**: To look for cardiac sources of emboli (e.g., LV thrombus, patent foramen ovale).
        ▪ **Telemetry/Holter Monitor**: For prolonged monitoring for paroxysmal A-fib.
    ◦ **Vascular Studies**:
        ▪ **Carotid Doppler Ultrasound**: To assess for carotid artery stenosis.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly variable and depends on the initial severity of the stroke, patient's age, comorbidities, and timeliness of treatment.
• The **NIHSS score** on admission is a strong predictor of outcome.
• Roughly 1/3 of patients have a good functional recovery, 1/3 are left with a significant disability, and 1/3 die.
• Mortality at 1 year is approximately 25%.

sections.overview:
• **Intracerebral Hemorrhage (ICH)** is a subtype of hemorrhagic stroke characterized by bleeding directly into the **brain parenchyma**.
    ◦ This leads to the formation of a **hematoma**, which causes direct neuronal damage, increases **intracranial pressure (ICP)**, and can lead to **brain herniation**.
• It is a **neurological emergency** with high rates of morbidity and mortality.
• Differentiating it from **ischemic stroke** is a critical first step, as treatments are diametrically opposed.
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Vessel Rupture**: A weakened blood vessel ruptures, leaking blood into the brain tissue.
    ◦ **Hematoma Formation**: The extravasated blood forms a space-occupying lesion (hematoma).
    ◦ **Primary Injury**: The hematoma exerts mechanical pressure (**mass effect**) on surrounding brain tissue, destroying it and causing immediate neurologic deficits.
    ◦ **Secondary Injury**: Over the next hours to days, secondary injury occurs via:
        ▪ **Increased Intracranial Pressure (ICP)**: The fixed volume of the skull cannot accommodate the extra blood, leading to increased ICP, decreased **cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP)**, and ischemia.
        ▪ **Cytotoxic Edema**: Blood breakdown products (e.g., thrombin, iron) trigger inflammatory cascades, leading to vasogenic and cytotoxic edema around the hematoma.
        ▪ **Neurotoxicity**: Blood components are directly toxic to neurons.
• **Etiology (Causes)**
    ◦ **Hypertensive Vasculopathy (Most Common)**: Chronic hypertension leads to **lipohyalinosis** and **fibrinoid necrosis** of small penetrating arteries (e.g., lenticulostriate arteries), making them prone to rupture.
        ▪ **Typical Locations**: **Basal ganglia (putamen)**, **thalamus**, **pons**, **cerebellum**.
    ◦ **Cerebral Amyloid Angiopathy (CAA)**: Deposition of beta-amyloid in the walls of small- to medium-sized cortical arteries weakens them.
        ▪ **Typical Locations**: **Lobar (cortical or subcortical)**, often in older, non-hypertensive patients.
        ▪ Prone to recurrence.
    ◦ **Anticoagulation/Thrombolytic Therapy**: Iatrogenic cause from medications like warfarin, DOACs, heparin, or tPA.
    ◦ **Vascular Malformations**:
        ▪ **Arteriovenous Malformation (AVM)**: Tangle of abnormal vessels; common cause in younger patients.
        ▪ **Cavernous Malformation (Cavernoma)**: Clusters of thin-walled vessels; often present with seizures or recurrent small bleeds.
    ◦ **Brain Tumors**: Highly vascular primary (e.g., **glioblastoma**) or metastatic tumors (e.g., **melanoma**, **renal cell carcinoma**, **choriocarcinoma**) can bleed.
    ◦ **Sympathomimetic Drug Use**: **Cocaine** and **amphetamines** cause a rapid, severe rise in blood pressure, leading to vessel rupture.
    ◦ **Trauma**: Often classified separately but is a common cause of parenchymal bleeding.
sections.epidemiology:
• Accounts for **10-15% of all strokes** but is responsible for a disproportionately high percentage of stroke-related mortality.
• Incidence increases significantly with age.
• Higher incidence in men and in certain ethnic populations (e.g., East Asian, African American).
• 30-day mortality rate is approximately **40-50%**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is the **sudden onset of a focal neurologic deficit** that **progressively worsens over minutes to hours**.
    ◦ This is in contrast to an **ischemic stroke** (often maximal at onset) or a **subarachnoid hemorrhage** (often an instantaneous **"thunderclap" headache**).
• Patients often present with signs of **elevated ICP**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Initial Imaging (STAT)**
    ◦ **Non-contrast Head CT**: The **best initial test**.
        ▪ It is fast, widely available, and highly sensitive for acute hemorrhage, which appears **hyperdense (bright white)**.
        ▪ It is essential to rule out hemorrhage before considering any treatment for ischemic stroke.
• **Further Imaging (to determine etiology)**
    ◦ **CT Angiography (CTA)**: Can identify underlying vascular lesions (aneurysm, AVM) and the **"spot sign"**-foci of active contrast extravasation within the hematoma, which predicts hematoma expansion and poor outcome.
    ◦ **MRI/MRA**: More sensitive for underlying causes like cavernous malformations, tumors, or evidence of prior microbleeds (suggesting CAA or hypertensive vasculopathy). Usually performed after the patient is stabilized.
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **CBC**: Check for thrombocytopenia.
    ◦ **Coagulation Studies (PT/INR, PTT)**: Essential to identify coagulopathy.
    ◦ **Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP)**: Assess electrolytes and renal function.
    ◦ **Toxicology Screen**: For cocaine, amphetamines.
    ◦ **Type and Screen**: In case surgical intervention is needed.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is generally poor and depends on several factors.
• The **ICH Score** is a widely used tool to predict 30-day mortality:
    ◦ **GCS Score** (lower is worse)
    ◦ **ICH Volume** (>30 mL is worse)
    ◦ **Intraventricular Hemorrhage** (presence is worse)
    ◦ **Infratentorial Location** (pons/cerebellum is worse)
    ◦ **Age** (≥80 is worse)
    ▪ A higher score correlates with higher mortality.
• Only about 20% of survivors regain full functional independence.

sections.overview:
• A **subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH)** is bleeding into the **subarachnoid space**, the area between the arachnoid mater and the pia mater that contains cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)
• It is a type of **hemorrhagic stroke** and a true neurologic emergency with high morbidity and mortality
• The most common cause of spontaneous (non-traumatic) SAH is a **ruptured saccular ("berry") aneurysm**
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Spontaneous (85% of cases):**
        ▪ **Ruptured Saccular (Berry) Aneurysm:** The most common cause (~85%). These are thin-walled outpouchings of arteries, typically at bifurcations in the **Circle of Willis**. Most common locations are the **anterior communicating artery (ACOM)**, **posterior communicating artery (PCOM)**, and **middle cerebral artery (MCA)**.
        ▪ **Arteriovenous Malformation (AVM):** Tangle of abnormal blood vessels.
        ▪ **Vasculitis**
        ▪ **Cerebral Amyloid Angiopathy**
        ▪ **Cocaine/Amphetamine use**
    ◦ **Traumatic:** Head trauma is the most common overall cause of SAH, but clinical management and workup differ from spontaneous SAH.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ A vessel (usually an aneurysm) ruptures, releasing arterial blood under high pressure directly into the subarachnoid space
    ◦ This causes a sudden, dramatic increase in **intracranial pressure (ICP)**
    ◦ The blood irritates the meninges and cerebral blood vessels
    ◦ Increased ICP can lead to decreased **cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP)**, causing global cerebral ischemia and loss of consciousness
    ◦ Blood products can obstruct the flow of CSF through arachnoid granulations, leading to acute or delayed **hydrocephalus**
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence:** Approximately 10 per 100,000 person-years.
• **Peak Age:** 50-60 years.
• **Sex:** Slightly more common in females (~1.5:1).
• Responsible for ~5% of all strokes.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a patient who develops a **sudden, intensely severe headache**, often during a period of physical exertion or stress (e.g., Valsalva, sexual activity, defecation)
• Many patients will have a transient **loss of consciousness**
• A significant minority (~20%) experience a **"sentinel headache"** days to weeks prior, caused by a small, self-limited leak from the aneurysm
sections.diagnostics:
• **Non-Contrast CT Head:**
    ◦ **Best initial test.**
    ◦ Highly sensitive (>95%) within the first 6-12 hours of symptom onset.
    ◦ Blood appears hyperdense (white) in the sulci, fissures, and basal cisterns.
    ◦ The **Fisher Grade** is a CT-based scale used to predict the risk of vasospasm.
• **Lumbar Puncture (LP):**
    ◦ **Indicated if CT is negative but clinical suspicion remains high.**
    ◦ Must be performed only after a negative CT scan to rule out a mass lesion that could cause herniation.
    ◦ Wait at least 6-12 hours from symptom onset for RBCs to lyse.
    ◦ **Key Findings:**
        ▪ **Xanthochromia:** Yellow/pink discoloration of the CSF supernatant after centrifugation. This is pathognomonic for SAH and is caused by the breakdown of hemoglobin to bilirubin.
        ▪ **Elevated Opening Pressure.**
        ▪ **Persistently elevated RBC count** in all four collection tubes (distinguishes from a traumatic tap).
• **Cerebral Angiography:**
    ◦ **Performed after SAH is confirmed** to identify the source of bleeding (e.g., aneurysm, AVM).
    ◦ **CT Angiography (CTA)** is the most common initial modality.
    ◦ **Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA)** is the **gold standard** for detecting aneurysms and is often used for treatment planning or if CTA is negative.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly variable and depends on the patient's initial clinical condition.
• Overall mortality is high (~25-50%), with many deaths occurring before reaching the hospital.
• Of the survivors, about 50% have significant, permanent neurologic disability.
• **Clinical Grading Scales:**
    ◦ **Hunt and Hess Scale:** Grades severity based on clinical presentation (e.g., headache, nuchal rigidity, focal deficit, coma). Higher grade correlates with poorer prognosis.
    ◦ **World Federation of Neurological Surgeons (WFNS) Scale:** Uses GCS and motor deficit.

sections.overview:
• **Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis (CVST)** is the formation of a blood clot (thrombus) within the dural venous sinuses, cerebral veins, or both.
• This obstruction impedes venous drainage from the brain, leading to venous congestion and increased **intracranial pressure (ICP)**.
• This can result in a wide spectrum of clinical presentations, ranging from isolated headache to focal neurological deficits, seizures, and coma.
• Unlike arterial strokes, CVST often affects younger individuals, particularly women, and has a more variable and subacute onset.
• Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial for a favorable outcome.
sections.etiology:
• The pathophysiology of CVST is rooted in **Virchow's triad**:
    ◦ **Hypercoagulable State:** Conditions that increase the propensity for blood to clot. This is the most common underlying cause.
    ◦ **Venous Stasis:** Slowing of blood flow, often due to local compression or systemic conditions.
    ◦ **Endothelial Injury:** Damage to the vessel lining, which can be caused by infection, inflammation, or trauma.
• **Pathophysiological Cascade:**
    ◦ **Thrombus Formation:** A thrombus forms in a dural sinus (e.g., superior sagittal, transverse) or a cortical vein.
    ◦ **Venous Outflow Obstruction:** The clot blocks normal venous drainage.
    ◦ **Increased Venous & Capillary Pressure:** Blood backs up, leading to venous congestion.
    ◦ **Cerebral Edema:** Increased pressure forces fluid out of the vasculature into the brain parenchyma, causing vasogenic edema. This is a primary cause of increased ICP and headache.
    ◦ **Cerebral Infarction/Hemorrhage:** Severe congestion can lead to ischemia and venous infarction. These infarcts are often hemorrhagic because the high venous pressure causes fragile capillaries to rupture.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence:** Relatively rare, estimated at 5-15 cases per million people per year.
• **Age:** Primarily affects younger adults, with a mean age of 30-40 years.
• **Sex:** Strong female predominance (~3:1 ratio), largely due to gender-specific risk factors like oral contraceptive use, pregnancy, and the puerperium.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is notoriously variable, making it a diagnostic challenge. It can be acute, subacute, or chronic.
• **Most Common Presentation:** Subacute onset of a progressive, persistent headache over days to weeks.
• **Key Syndromes:**
    ◦ **Isolated Intracranial Hypertension:** Presents with headache, papilledema, and visual disturbances, mimicking idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri).
    ◦ **Focal Neurological Deficits:** Presents with signs of venous infarction or hemorrhage, mimicking an arterial stroke (e.g., hemiparesis, aphasia, hemianopia). Seizures are common.
    ◦ **Encephalopathy:** Presents with altered mental status, confusion, delirium, or coma, often associated with bilateral thalamic involvement or widespread edema.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Initial Lab Work:**
    ◦ **D-dimer:**
        ▪ High sensitivity but low specificity.
        ▪ A negative D-dimer in a low-risk patient can help rule out CVST.
        ▪ A positive result is non-specific and requires imaging.
    ◦ **CBC, CMP, Coagulation studies (PT/INR, PTT).**
    ◦ **Hypercoagulable workup:** Order after the acute phase, as acute thrombosis can transiently lower levels of proteins C, S, and antithrombin.
• **Neuroimaging (Essential for Diagnosis):**
    ◦ **Non-contrast Head CT:** Often the first test performed.
        ▪ May be normal in ~30% of cases.
        ▪ **"Dense Delta Sign" / "Dense Triangle Sign":** Hyperdensity (clot) within the superior sagittal sinus.
        ▪ **"Cord Sign":** Hyperdense thrombosed cortical vein.
        ▪ May show signs of venous infarction (edema, hemorrhage) that do not conform to an arterial territory.
    ◦ **CT Venography (CTV):** Excellent for diagnosis. A contrast-enhanced CT focused on the venous system.
        ▪ Shows a **"filling defect"** in the affected sinus.
        ▪ **"Empty Delta Sign":** On contrast-enhanced images, contrast enhances the walls of the sinus, surrounding the non-enhancing central thrombus.
    ◦ **MRI with MR Venography (MRV):** **Gold standard** / test of choice due to high sensitivity and specificity without radiation.
        ▪ **MRI:** Shows the consequences of the thrombus (edema, infarction, hemorrhage). The clot itself can be visualized.
        ▪ **MRV:** Directly visualizes the venous sinuses and demonstrates an absence of flow (**"flow void"**) or a filling defect in the affected sinus.
• **Lumbar Puncture (LP):**
    ◦ Not for diagnosis, but may be performed to rule out meningitis if suspected.
    ◦ **Typical Findings:** Elevated opening pressure. CSF is often normal but can show elevated protein or red blood cells.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is generally better than for arterial stroke.
• **Mortality:** Acute mortality is relatively low (~5-10%).
• **Recovery:** >80% of survivors have a good functional outcome with partial or complete recovery.
• **Poor Prognostic Factors:**
    ◦ Presentation with coma or altered mental status
    ◦ Presence of hemorrhage or venous infarction on imaging
    ◦ Underlying malignancy or CNS infection
    ◦ Involvement of deep cerebral veins

sections.overview:
• A focal (or partial) seizure originates within a localized network of neurons in one cerebral hemisphere, with clinical manifestations depending on the specific area of the brain affected
• Focal seizures are classified based on the level of consciousness during the event
    ◦ **Focal Aware Seizure** (formerly Simple Partial Seizure)
        ▪ Consciousness and awareness are fully maintained
        ▪ The patient can recall the event
        ▪ Symptoms can be motor, sensory, autonomic, or psychic
    ◦ **Focal Impaired Awareness Seizure** (formerly Complex Partial Seizure)
        ▪ Consciousness and/or awareness are altered or lost
        ▪ The patient may appear awake but is unresponsive or confused and has no memory (or a vague memory) of the event
        ▪ Often associated with **automatisms**
    ◦ **Focal to Bilateral Tonic-Clonic Seizure** (formerly Secondarily Generalized Seizure)
        ▪ The seizure begins focally (with or without a preceding **aura**) and then spreads to involve both cerebral hemispheres, resulting in a generalized tonic-clonic convulsion
sections.etiology:
• Focal seizures result from a localized, abnormal, hypersynchronous electrical discharge of a group of neurons (the "**epileptogenic focus**")
    ◦ This can be caused by any process that disrupts normal cortical structure or function
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ An imbalance between excitatory (e.g., **glutamate**) and inhibitory (e.g., **GABA**) neurotransmission within a specific cortical region
• **Common Etiologies (Structural)**
    ◦ **Cerebrovascular Disease**: Most common cause in adults >60 years (e.g., post-stroke scar tissue)
    ◦ **Brain Tumors**: Primary or metastatic
    ◦ **Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI)**: Cortical scarring is highly epileptogenic
    ◦ **Hippocampal Sclerosis**: Atrophy and scarring of the hippocampus; the most common cause of focal epilepsy, particularly in the temporal lobe
    ◦ **Cortical Dysplasia/Malformations**: Developmental abnormalities of the cortex
    ◦ **Infections**: CNS infections like meningitis, encephalitis (especially HSV), neurocysticercosis, brain abscess
• **Other Etiologies**
    ◦ **Genetic**: Certain channelopathies or genetic syndromes
    ◦ **Autoimmune**: Autoimmune encephalitis (e.g., anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis)
    ◦ **Metabolic**: While often causing generalized seizures, focal seizures can occur
    ◦ **Idiopathic/Cryptogenic**: No identifiable cause is found
sections.epidemiology:
• Focal seizures are the most common type of seizure in adults with epilepsy, accounting for ~60% of cases
• Incidence shows a **bimodal distribution**: highest in young children and in the elderly (>65 years)
    ◦ The rise in the elderly population is primarily due to the increased prevalence of stroke, neurodegenerative disease, and brain tumors
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation is highly variable and directly correlates with the location of the **epileptogenic focus**
    ◦ The patient may present after a first-time seizure or with a history of recurrent events
    ◦ The history from the patient (if awareness was preserved) or a witness is the most crucial part of the evaluation
• **Aura**
    ◦ A focal aware seizure that precedes a focal impaired awareness or bilateral tonic-clonic seizure
    ◦ The symptoms of the **aura** (e.g., rising epigastric sensation, déjà vu, specific smell) can help localize the seizure onset zone
• **Postictal State**
    ◦ A period of confusion, lethargy, or focal neurological deficits (e.g., **Todd's paralysis**) following the seizure
    ◦ The duration is variable
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• Variable and depends heavily on the underlying etiology
• Approximately two-thirds of patients will achieve seizure freedom with the first or second ASD tried
• The remaining one-third have **drug-resistant epilepsy**, which carries a higher morbidity
• Prognosis is generally worse if there is an underlying progressive structural lesion (e.g., high-grade tumor)

sections.overview:
• A Generalized Tonic-Clonic (GTC) seizure, formerly known as **"grand mal,"** is a type of generalized seizure that affects the entire brain from onset.
• Characterized by an abrupt loss of consciousness followed by two distinct phases:
    ◦ A **tonic** (stiffening) phase
    ◦ A **clonic** (rhythmic jerking) phase
• The event is typically followed by a **postictal state** of confusion, lethargy, and amnesia for the event.
• GTC seizures are the most dramatic and widely recognized form of epileptic seizure.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Genetic / Idiopathic**
        ▪ Primary generalized epilepsy syndromes (e.g., Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy).
        ▪ No identifiable structural or metabolic cause.
    ◦ **Structural**
        ▪ **Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI)**
        ▪ **Stroke** (especially hemorrhagic)
        ▪ **Brain tumors** (primary or metastatic)
        ▪ **CNS Infections** (meningitis, encephalitis, brain abscess)
        ▪ Congenital malformations (e.g., cortical dysplasia)
        ▪ Neurodegenerative disorders (e.g., Alzheimer's disease)
    ◦ **Metabolic**
        ▪ **Hypoglycemia**
        ▪ **Electrolyte disturbances**: Hyponatremia, hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia
        ▪ **Uremia** (renal failure)
        ▪ Hepatic encephalopathy
        ▪ Hypoxia / Anoxia
    ◦ **Toxic / Substance-Related**
        ▪ **Alcohol withdrawal**
        ▪ Drug intoxication/overdose (e.g., cocaine, amphetamines, TCAs, isoniazid)
        ▪ Medication side effects or withdrawal (e.g., benzodiazepine withdrawal)
    ◦ **Other**
        ▪ High fever (**febrile seizures** in young children)
        ▪ **Eclampsia** (in pregnancy)
        ▪ Autoimmune encephalitis
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The fundamental mechanism is a sudden, abnormal, synchronous, and excessive electrical discharge of a large network of cortical neurons across both **cerebral hemispheres**.
    ◦ This results from an imbalance between excitatory (**glutamate**-mediated) and inhibitory (**GABA**-mediated) neurotransmission, leading to a state of neuronal **hyperexcitability** that spreads rapidly throughout the brain.
    ◦ This widespread cortical involvement causes the immediate loss of consciousness and symmetric motor manifestations characteristic of a GTC seizure.
sections.epidemiology:
• Lifetime prevalence of a single seizure is ~10%.
• **Epilepsy** (recurrent unprovoked seizures) affects about 1-2% of the population.
• Incidence shows a **bimodal distribution**: highest in early childhood and in adults over 60 years of age.
• GTC seizures are one of the most common seizure types encountered in clinical practice.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The seizure follows a classic, stereotyped sequence of events.
• **Prodrome**
    ◦ Some patients experience nonspecific symptoms (e.g., mood changes, headache) hours to days before a seizure.
• **Aura**
    ◦ A true aura is a focal seizure with preserved awareness. If an aura precedes a GTC, it is classified as a **focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure**, not a primary GTC.
• **Ictal Phase (The Seizure Itself)**
    ◦ **Sudden Loss of Consciousness**
        ▪ Patient abruptly becomes unresponsive and falls, often without warning.
    ◦ **Tonic Phase (10-20 seconds)**
        ▪ Generalized, sustained contraction of all muscles; body becomes **rigid** and stiff.
        ▪ Opisthotonic posturing (arching of the back) may occur.
        ▪ **Ictal cry**: A loud moan or cry as air is forcefully expelled through a contracted larynx.
        ▪ **Apnea** and **cyanosis** due to contraction of respiratory muscles.
        ▪ Eyes are open with upward deviation of the eyeballs; pupils are dilated.
    ◦ **Clonic Phase (30-90 seconds)**
        ▪ Symmetric, rhythmic, violent **jerking** of the extremities.
        ▪ Frothing at the mouth (salivation mixed with air).
        ▪ Possible **tongue biting** (classically the lateral aspect).
        ▪ Autonomic signs: **Tachycardia**, **hypertension**, diaphoresis.
        ▪ **Urinary and/or fecal incontinence** are common.
• **Postictal Phase (Minutes to Hours)**
    ◦ Initially, the patient is unresponsive with flaccid muscles and deep, labored breathing.
    ◦ Gradual return of consciousness, but patient is typically in a state of marked **confusion**, disorientation, and lethargy.
    ◦ Common complaints include severe **headache**, **myalgias**, and exhaustion.
    ◦ The patient has complete **amnesia** for the ictal event.
sections.diagnostics:
• The workup for a first-time GTC seizure aims to identify the underlying cause.
• **Initial Bedside/Stat Labs**
    ◦ **Fingerstick Glucose**: Immediately rule out **hypoglycemia**.
    ◦ **Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP)**: Check for Na+, Ca++, Mg++, glucose, BUN/Cr (uremia), and liver function.
    ◦ **CBC**: Evaluate for signs of infection.
    ◦ **Pregnancy Test (hCG)**: In all women of childbearing age to rule out **eclampsia**.
    ◦ **Toxicology Screen & Blood Alcohol Level**: If substance use is suspected.
• **Further Labs**
    ◦ **Creatine Kinase (CK)**: Will be elevated due to **rhabdomyolysis** from intense muscle contraction.
    ◦ **Prolactin**: Often elevated for 15-60 minutes after a GTC seizure (helps differentiate from psychogenic non-epileptic seizures).
• **Neuroimaging**
    ◦ **Non-contrast Head CT**: **Initial imaging of choice in the emergency department** to rule out acute intracranial hemorrhage, mass effect, or large structural lesions.
    ◦ **Brain MRI**: **Most sensitive imaging modality** to evaluate for subtle structural causes (e.g., tumor, stroke, cortical dysplasia, mesial temporal sclerosis). The gold standard for epilepsy workup, usually performed outpatient.
• **Electroencephalogram (EEG)**
    ◦ **The key test** to confirm an epileptic tendency and classify seizure type.
    ◦ **Interictal EEG**: May show generalized spike-wave or polyspike-and-wave discharges.
    ◦ A normal EEG does not rule out epilepsy.
• **Lumbar Puncture (LP)**
    ◦ Indicated if **meningitis** or **encephalitis** is suspected (e.g., patient has fever, nuchal rigidity, or persistent altered mental status).
sections.prognosis:
• Variable and highly dependent on the underlying etiology.
• With appropriate AED therapy, approximately **60-70%** of patients can achieve seizure freedom.
• Prognosis is generally better for **idiopathic generalized epilepsy** than for epilepsy secondary to a major structural brain lesion.
• Poorly controlled seizures, especially frequent GTCs, are associated with a higher risk of complications and mortality.

sections.overview:
• An absence seizure is a type of **generalized, non-convulsive (non-motor) seizure** characterized by a brief, sudden lapse of consciousness.
    ◦ The hallmark is a **"staring spell"** where the individual abruptly stops all activity and appears to be daydreaming.
    ◦ Consciousness returns as suddenly as it was lost, with **no postictal confusion** or memory of the event.
    ◦ These seizures typically last for a few seconds and can occur dozens to hundreds of times per day, often leading to misdiagnosis as inattentiveness or **ADHD**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ Primarily **genetic**.
    ◦ Multiple genes are implicated, many of which code for **ion channels**, particularly **T-type calcium channels** and **GABA receptors**.
    ◦ A strong family history of epilepsy is common.
    ◦ It is not caused by brain injury or structural abnormalities.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ Involves abnormal, synchronous electrical activity within the **thalamocortical circuits**.
    ◦ **Thalamic Relay Neurons**: These neurons normally operate in a tonic firing mode during wakefulness and an oscillatory/burst-firing mode during sleep. In absence seizures, there is a pathological shift to the oscillatory mode during wakefulness.
    ◦ **T-type Calcium Channels**: The low-threshold **T-type calcium channels** in the thalamus are crucial for initiating these burst-firing patterns.
    ◦ **GABAergic Inhibition**: This burst firing activates GABAergic neurons in the reticular nucleus of the thalamus, which in turn hyperpolarizes the thalamic relay neurons, creating a feedback loop.
    ◦ **EEG Correlation**: This rhythmic, oscillating circuit activity between the thalamus and the cerebral cortex generates the characteristic **3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges** seen on EEG.
        ▪ **Ethosuximide's** mechanism of action is the specific blockade of these **T-type calcium channels**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Peak Incidence**: Primarily a disorder of childhood, with peak onset between **4 and 10 years of age**.
• **Prevalence**: Accounts for 10-17% of all pediatric epilepsies.
• **Gender**: Slight female predominance (approximately 2:1).
sections.riskFactors:
• **Family History**: The single most significant risk factor is a positive family history of absence seizures or other generalized epilepsies.
• **Age**: The 4-10 year old age group is the highest risk window for developing **Childhood Absence Epilepsy (CAE)**.
• **Specific Epilepsy Syndromes**: Associated with syndromes like **Childhood Absence Epilepsy (CAE)** and **Juvenile Absence Epilepsy (JAE)**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a school-age child whose teacher reports episodes of **"daydreaming," "zoning out,"** or **"not paying attention"** in class.
    ◦ The parent may report that the child has brief periods of unresponsiveness during conversation or meals.
• **Onset/Offset**: Abrupt, without warning or aura.
• **Recovery**: Immediate, with a full return to baseline. The child is typically unaware that a seizure has occurred.
• **Frequency**: Can be very frequent, often occurring multiple times per hour.
• **Triggers**: Seizures can often be provoked by **hyperventilation**, and sometimes by photic stimulation or drowsiness.
• **Hallmark Symptom**: **Behavioral arrest** with a blank, staring expression.
    ◦ The patient is unresponsive to verbal or tactile stimuli.
• **Duration**: Brief, typically lasting **5-15 seconds** (rarely > 20 seconds).
• **Automatisms**: Subtle motor signs may be present, especially in longer seizures.
    ◦ **Eyelid myoclonia / fluttering** (~3 per second)
    ◦ **Lip smacking** or chewing movements
    ◦ Subtle fumbling of the hands or picking at clothes
• **Postictal State**: **ABSENT**. This is a key differentiating feature.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Interictal Exam**
    ◦ The neurological examination between seizures is **completely normal**. There are no focal deficits.
• **Ictal Exam**
    ◦ If a seizure is witnessed or provoked in the clinic (e.g., with 3 minutes of **hyperventilation**), the examiner will observe:
        ▪ Cessation of all activity (e.g., stops counting or talking mid-sentence).
        ▪ Unresponsive staring.
        ▪ Possible subtle automatisms.
        ▪ Immediate resumption of activity after the event.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Electroencephalogram (EEG)**: **Gold standard** for diagnosis.
    ◦ **Classic Finding**: **Generalized, symmetric 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges**.
    ◦ The background EEG is otherwise normal.
    ◦ **Provocation Maneuver**: **Hyperventilation** for 3-5 minutes during the EEG is a highly effective method for inducing a clinical seizure and its corresponding EEG pattern, confirming the diagnosis.
• **Neuroimaging (MRI/CT)**
    ◦ **Generally not indicated** for typical absence seizures with a normal neurological exam.
    ◦ It may be considered if there are atypical features, a focal neurological deficit, or if the seizures are refractory to treatment, to rule out a structural lesion.
• **Labs**
    ◦ Basic labs (CBC, CMP) are usually normal but may be done as part of a standard new-onset seizure workup.
sections.treatment:
• **First-Line Therapy (for pure absence seizures)**
    ◦ **Ethosuximide**: **Drug of choice**. It is highly effective and specific for absence seizures with the most favorable side effect profile. It works by blocking **T-type calcium channels**.
• **Alternative First-Line / Broad-Spectrum**
    ◦ **Valproic Acid (Valproate)**: Equally effective and is the preferred agent if the patient has **co-existing generalized tonic-clonic (GTC) seizures**. It has a higher risk of side effects (hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, weight gain, teratogenicity).
• **Second-Line / Adjunctive Therapy**
    ◦ **Lamotrigine**: Less effective than ethosuximide or valproic acid but is a reasonable alternative, especially if others are not tolerated. Requires slow titration due to risk of **Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS)**.
• **!! DRUGS TO AVOID !!** Certain anti-seizure medications can **exacerbate** absence seizures:
    ◦ Carbamazepine
    ◦ Oxcarbazepine
    ◦ Phenytoin
    ◦ Gabapentin
    ◦ Tiagabine
sections.management:
• **Driving Restrictions**: For adolescents with absence epilepsy (e.g., **JAE**), counseling on state-specific driving laws (requiring a specified seizure-free period) is mandatory.
• **Monitoring**: Regular follow-up to assess seizure control, monitor for medication side effects (e.g., LFTs with valproate), and determine when/if to wean medication after a prolonged seizure-free period (typically 2 years).
sections.complications:
• **Academic Difficulties**: Frequent, unrecognized seizures lead to significant gaps in learning and poor school performance.
• **Social Stigma**: Can be misinterpreted as rudeness, lack of interest, or intellectual disability.
• **Progression to Other Seizure Types**: A subset of patients, particularly those with **JAE**, will develop **generalized tonic-clonic seizures**.
• **Medication Side Effects**: 
    ◦ GI upset, fatigue (**ethosuximide**)
    ◦ Hepatotoxicity, weight gain (**valproic acid**)
    ◦ Rash/SJS (**lamotrigine**)
• **Accidental Injury**: Rare due to the brief, non-convulsive nature, but possible if a seizure occurs during activities like swimming or crossing a street.
sections.prognosis:
• **Generally excellent**, especially for **Childhood Absence Epilepsy (CAE)**.
• **Remission**: Approximately **70-80%** of children with CAE will become seizure-free and successfully discontinue medication in their teenage years.
• **Factors for Poorer Prognosis**: 
    ◦ Onset after age 10
    ◦ Presence of **GTC seizures**
    ◦ Resistance to initial medication therapy.
sections.preventionEducation:
• **Patient/Family Education**: Crucial for explaining the nature of the seizures, distinguishing them from behavioral issues, and stressing the importance of medication adherence.
• **School Communication**: A letter or communication with the child's school/teacher is vital to explain the condition, manage academic expectations, and ensure the child is not penalized for seizure-related inattention.

sections.overview:
• **Status Epilepticus (SE)** is a life-threatening neurological emergency characterized by a prolonged seizure or a series of seizures without a return to baseline consciousness between them.
• The modern definition from the International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE) defines two critical time points:
    ◦ **Time Point 1 (T1):** The point at which a seizure is considered abnormally prolonged and treatment should be initiated. For generalized **tonic-clonic** SE, this is **5 minutes**.
    ◦ **Time Point 2 (T2):** The point at which there is a risk of long-term consequences (e.g., neuronal death, injury). For generalized **tonic-clonic** SE, this is **30 minutes**.
• Two main types:
    ◦ **Convulsive Status Epilepticus (CSE):** Characterized by repetitive, overt **tonic-clonic movements**. This is the most common and dangerous form.
    ◦ **Non-Convulsive Status Epilepticus (NCSE):** Characterized by seizure activity on **EEG** without the overt convulsions. Patients present with **altered mental status**, confusion, or coma. It is often underdiagnosed.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence:** 10-40 per 100,000 people annually.
• **Distribution:** Bimodal age distribution, with peaks in children <1 year and adults >60 years.
• **Mortality:** In-hospital mortality is high, ranging from 15-25%, largely dependent on the underlying etiology.
    ◦ Mortality is highest in the elderly and in cases caused by **anoxia** or acute brain injury.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The patient presents in one of two ways:
    ◦ **Overtly seizing:** Continuous, generalized **tonic-clonic movements**, often with impaired consciousness, **cyanosis**, and autonomic instability (tachycardia, hypertension).
    ◦ **Post-ictal or confused:** The patient may have stopped convulsing by the time of arrival but has not returned to their neurologic baseline.
        ▪ This is a critical point to consider **NCSE**.
• **Non-Convulsive SE (NCSE) Presentation:**
    ◦ Profound, unexplained **altered mental status**.
    ◦ **"Subtle SE"**: May see minor motor signs like facial twitching, **nystagmus**, or eye deviation.
    ◦ Presents as confusion, stupor, or coma.
    ◦ High index of suspicion is required.
sections.diagnostics:
• The workup is performed concurrently with stabilization and treatment.
• **Immediate Bedside Tests:**
    ◦ **Fingerstick Glucose:** **THE FIRST STEP**. **Hypoglycemia** is a common, reversible cause.
    ◦ **ABCs:** **Airway**, **Breathing**, **Circulation**. Place on cardiac monitor, pulse oximetry.
• **Laboratory Studies:**
    ◦ **CMP:** Check for electrolytes (Na+, Ca2+, Mg2+), glucose, renal function (BUN/Cr), liver function.
    ◦ **CBC:** Look for signs of infection (**leukocytosis**).
    ◦ **Troponin & CK:** To assess for cardiac strain and **rhabdomyolysis**.
    ◦ **Toxicology Screen (Urine & Serum):** To rule out overdose or intoxication.
    ◦ **Serum AED Levels:** For patients on anti-epileptic medications.
    ◦ **Blood Gas (ABG/VBG):** To assess for **acidosis**, **hypoxia**, **hypercarbia**.
• **Imaging:**
    ◦ **Non-contrast Head CT:** **Essential initial imaging** to rule out acute **intracranial hemorrhage**, large tumor, or stroke.
    ◦ **Head MRI:** More sensitive for subtle structural lesions, but typically performed after the patient is stabilized.
• **Specialized Tests:**
    ◦ **Lumbar Puncture (LP):** Indicated if there is suspicion of **meningitis** or **encephalitis** (fever, **nuchal rigidity**).
        ▪ Perform *after* the **CT scan** to rule out a mass lesion that could cause herniation.
    ◦ **EEG (Electroencephalogram):** **The gold standard for diagnosis**, especially for **NCSE**.
        ▪ It confirms ongoing seizure activity and helps guide therapy.
        ▪ Continuous **EEG** (cEEG) is essential for managing refractory SE.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is primarily determined by the **underlying etiology** and the **duration of the seizure**.
• SE caused by **anoxia/hypoxia** has a very poor prognosis.
• SE due to **AED non-adherence** has a relatively good prognosis if treated promptly.
• Longer duration of SE is associated with higher mortality and greater neurologic morbidity.
• The elderly have a significantly higher mortality rate.

sections.overview:
• A febrile seizure is a convulsion in a child caused by a spike in body temperature, often from an infection, occurring in otherwise neurologically healthy children between the ages of **6 months and 5 years**
    ◦ The diagnosis requires a fever (**>38C / 100.4F**) and the exclusion of any intracranial infection (meningitis, encephalitis), metabolic disturbance, or history of afebrile seizures
• Febrile seizures are categorized as either **simple** or **complex**, a distinction critical for management and prognosis
    ◦ **Simple Febrile Seizure (SFS):** Most common type (~80-85%)
        ▪ **Duration:** < 15 minutes
        ▪ **Type:** Generalized (typically tonic-clonic)
        ▪ **Frequency:** Occurs only once in a 24-hour period
        ▪ **Post-ictal:** Brief period of drowsiness, returns to baseline quickly
    ◦ **Complex Febrile Seizure (CFS):** Less common, but carries slightly higher risk
        ▪ **Duration:** ≥ 15 minutes (prolonged)
        ▪ **Type:** Focal features (e.g., shaking of only one limb or side of the body)
        ▪ **Frequency:** More than one seizure in a 24-hour period
sections.etiology:
• The exact mechanism is not fully understood but is believed to be multifactorial
    ◦ **Pathophysiology:** A developing nervous system has a lower seizure threshold. Fever, particularly a **rapid rise in temperature**, is thought to act as a catalyst by increasing neuronal excitability. Pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-1) released during an infection can also cross the blood-brain barrier and have a direct pro-convulsant effect
    ◦ **Etiology (Fever Source):** The fever is almost always caused by a benign infection, most commonly viral
        ▪ **Most Common Viral Causes:** Human Herpesvirus 6 (**HHV-6**, associated with Roseola Infantum), Influenza virus, Adenovirus, Parainfluenza virus
        ▪ **Bacterial Causes:** Less common but can include Otitis Media, Pharyngitis, and UTI
        ▪ **Post-vaccination:** A low risk of febrile seizure exists 1-2 weeks after certain live-virus vaccines (e.g., **MMR**) and within 24-48 hours of inactivated vaccines (e.g., DTaP)
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** Occurs in **2-5%** of all children in the U.S. and Europe
• **Peak Incidence:** **12-18 months** of age
• **Age Range:** By definition, occurs between 6 months and 5 years
• **Gender:** Slight male predominance
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a previously well child who develops a fever from a common illness (e.g., URI), followed by a sudden-onset convulsion
• **History:** Caregivers report a sudden loss of consciousness and rhythmic shaking of the extremities
• **Seizure Type:** Most often a **generalized tonic-clonic seizure**
    ◦ **Tonic Phase:** Body becomes stiff, arms and legs extend
    ◦ **Clonic Phase:** Rhythmic jerking of extremities
    ◦ May also be associated with upward eye deviation, transient apnea, or cyanosis
• **Post-ictal State:** Following the seizure, the child is typically drowsy, confused, and lethargic for a short period before returning to their neurologic baseline
sections.diagnostics:
• For a first-time **simple** febrile seizure in a well-appearing, fully immunized child, **no routine diagnostic workup is necessary** beyond identifying the fever source
• **Lumbar Puncture (LP):** This is the most critical diagnostic consideration to rule out meningitis/encephalitis
    ◦ **Strongly Consider/Recommended In:**
        ▪ Any child with **meningeal signs** (nuchal rigidity, positive Kernig/Brudzinski)
        ▪ Infants **< 6 months** of age
        ▪ A child whose immunizations are deficient or unknown (especially for *H. influenzae* type B and *S. pneumoniae*)
        ▪ A child who has received antibiotics prior to the seizure, as this can mask signs of meningitis
        ▪ Persistent lethargy or altered mental status
• **Laboratory Studies (CBC, BMP, glucose):** Not routinely indicated
    ◦ Consider if there are signs of dehydration, a complex seizure, or if the history suggests an underlying metabolic disorder
• **Electroencephalogram (EEG):** Not recommended for a first-time simple febrile seizure
    ◦ Consider for complex febrile seizures or if there is concern for an underlying epilepsy syndrome
• **Neuroimaging (CT/MRI):** Not indicated for simple febrile seizures
    ◦ Consider in cases of focal seizures, trauma, persistently abnormal neurologic exam, or macrocephaly
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**
• The overwhelming majority of children who experience febrile seizures have no long-term neurologic sequelae
• Intelligence, school performance, and behavior are unaffected

sections.overview:
• Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is a chronic, immune-mediated, inflammatory, and neurodegenerative disease of the central nervous system (CNS) characterized by **demyelination**, **axonal damage**, and the formation of sclerotic **plaques** in the brain and spinal cord
    ◦ The clinical hallmark is the presentation of neurologic symptoms that are **"disseminated in time and space,"** meaning different symptoms occur at different times and affect different parts of the CNS
sections.etiology:
• The exact etiology is unknown but is believed to be a multifactorial process involving genetic susceptibility and environmental triggers
• **Immune-Mediated Process**
    ◦ MS is considered an autoimmune disease where the body's immune system, specifically **T-cells**, mistakenly attacks the CNS
• **Pathophysiology Cascade**
    ◦ **T-cell Activation**: Autoreactive T-cells become activated in the periphery, likely triggered by an environmental factor (e.g., a virus) in a genetically susceptible individual
    ◦ **Blood-Brain Barrier (BBB) Disruption**: These activated T-cells cross the BBB and enter the CNS
    ◦ **Inflammatory Attack**: Once in the CNS, T-cells release inflammatory cytokines, which recruit other immune cells (B-cells, macrophages)
    ◦ **Demyelination**: The inflammatory cascade targets and destroys **myelin**, the protective sheath around nerve axons, and the **oligodendrocytes** that produce it
    ◦ **Axonal Damage**: Underlying axons are damaged and can be transected, leading to irreversible neurologic disability
    ◦ **Plaque Formation**: Areas of demyelination and inflammation eventually heal with glial scarring (gliosis), forming the characteristic sclerotic plaques
sections.epidemiology:
• **Age of Onset**: Typically between **20 and 40 years old**
• **Gender**: Affects **women 2-3 times more** often than men
• **Geography**: More common in regions **farther from the equator** (e.g., North America, Europe, Australia), suggesting a role for environmental factors like Vitamin D levels
• **Prevalence**: Most common non-traumatic cause of neurologic disability in young adults
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Clinically Isolated Syndrome (CIS)**
    ◦ The first clinical episode of neurologic symptoms lasting at least 24 hours, suggestive of MS
    ◦ Not all patients with CIS will develop MS
• **Relapsing-Remitting MS (RRMS)**
    ◦ Most common form (~85% of initial diagnoses)
    ◦ Characterized by clearly defined attacks (relapses) of new or worsening neurologic symptoms
    ◦ Relapses are followed by periods of partial or complete recovery (remissions)
    ◦ There is no apparent progression of disability between relapses
• **Secondary Progressive MS (SPMS)**
    ◦ Follows an initial relapsing-remitting course
