    ◦ The disease begins to progress more steadily, with or without occasional relapses
    ◦ Disability gradually worsens over time
• **Primary Progressive MS (PPMS)**
    ◦ ~15% of cases
    ◦ Characterized by worsening neurologic function from the onset of symptoms, without early relapses or remissions
    ◦ Typically presents with a progressive myelopathy (spinal cord disease)
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is clinical, supported by MRI, CSF analysis, and evoked potentials, based on the **McDonald Criteria**
    ◦ The goal is to demonstrate **Dissemination in Space (DIS)** and **Dissemination in Time (DIT)**
• **MRI (Brain and Spinal Cord with and without Gadolinium)**
    ◦ **Test of choice** for confirming MS
    ◦ **T2-weighted images** are best for visualizing demyelinating plaques
    ◦ **Characteristic Lesion Locations (for DIS)**
        ▪ **Periventricular**: Ovoid lesions perpendicular to the lateral ventricles (**Dawson's Fingers**)
        ▪ **Juxtacortical**: Lesions touching the cerebral cortex
        ▪ **Infratentorial**: Lesions in the cerebellum, brainstem, or pons
        ▪ **Spinal Cord**: Lesions in the spinal cord
    ◦ **Gadolinium-enhancing lesions**: Indicate active inflammation and breakdown of the BBB (used to establish DIT)
    ◦ **T1-weighted images**: May show **"black holes,"** representing areas of permanent axonal damage and brain atrophy
• **Lumbar Puncture (CSF Analysis)**
    ◦ Performed if MRI is inconclusive or presentation is atypical
    ◦ **Key Finding**: **Oligoclonal Bands (OCBs)** of IgG found in the CSF but **not** in the serum
        ▪ Present in >95% of MS patients
    ◦ **Other Findings**: Mild lymphocytic pleocytosis (<50 cells/L), elevated IgG index
• **Evoked Potentials (EPs)**
    ◦ Measure the speed of nerve conduction along sensory pathways
    ◦ **Visual Evoked Potentials (VEPs)** are the most useful, showing slowed conduction in the optic nerve, often even in patients without a history of optic neuritis
sections.prognosis:
• Highly variable; MS is not typically considered a fatal disease, but it does reduce life expectancy by an average of 5-10 years
• **Favorable Prognostic Factors**
    ◦ Female sex
    ◦ Onset before age 40
    ◦ Relapsing-remitting course
    ◦ Initial symptoms are sensory or optic neuritis
    ◦ Low relapse rate in the first few years
• **Unfavorable Prognostic Factors**
    ◦ Male sex
    ◦ Onset after age 40
    ◦ Primary progressive course
    ◦ Initial symptoms are motor or cerebellar
    ◦ High early relapse rate or poor recovery from first attack

sections.overview:
• Acute Disseminated Encephalomyelitis (ADEM) is an immune-mediated inflammatory disorder of the central nervous system (CNS) characterized by widespread demyelination.
• It is typically a **monophasic** illness that occurs following a recent viral or bacterial infection, or less commonly, a vaccination.
• The hallmark of ADEM is a rapid onset of **multifocal neurological deficits** accompanied by **encephalopathy** (altered mental status).
sections.etiology:
• ADEM is considered a post-infectious autoimmune process, with the primary proposed mechanism being **molecular mimicry**.
    ◦ **Antecedent Trigger**: The patient is exposed to a viral or bacterial antigen (from an infection) or a foreign protein (from a vaccine).
    ◦ **Immune Activation**: The immune system mounts a response, creating T-cells and antibodies against the foreign antigen.
    ◦ **Cross-Reactivity**: Due to structural similarities between the foreign antigens and CNS myelin proteins (e.g., myelin basic protein [MBP], myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein [MOG]), activated T-cells and antibodies cross the blood-brain barrier.
    ◦ **CNS Attack**: These immune components mistakenly attack the host's own myelin sheath, leading to perivascular inflammation, edema, and multifocal demyelination, resulting in the abrupt onset of widespread neurological dysfunction.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Rare, estimated at 0.4-0.8 per 100,000 people per year.
• **Age**: Primarily a disease of **children and young adults**, with a median age of onset between 5 and 8 years; it can occur in adults but is less common.
• **Sex**: Slight male predominance.
• **Seasonality**: More common in winter and spring, which corresponds to the peak season for many viral infections.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a child or young adult who had a mild febrile illness (e.g., upper respiratory infection) 1-4 weeks prior.
• Patients present with a **rapidly progressive onset** of both focal/multifocal neurological deficits and encephalopathy.
• Symptoms typically evolve over hours to days.
sections.diagnostics:
• ADEM is a clinical diagnosis supported by imaging and CSF analysis, after ruling out direct CNS infection.
• **Brain & Spine MRI with and without contrast**
    ◦ **The single most important diagnostic test.**
    ◦ **Classic Findings**: Multiple, bilateral, but **asymmetric** lesions.
    ◦ **Lesion Characteristics**: Large (>1-2 cm), poorly demarcated ("fluffy" or "cloud-like") T2/FLAIR hyperintensities.
    ◦ **Location**:
        ▪ Primarily involve cerebral **white matter**.
        ▪ **Deep gray matter involvement** (thalami, basal ganglia) is common and highly characteristic of ADEM.
        ▪ Brainstem, cerebellum, and spinal cord are also frequently affected.
    ◦ **Enhancement**: Variable; may show diffuse, nodular, or ring enhancement.
    ◦ **Key Feature**: All lesions typically appear to be of the **same age**, consistent with a monophasic event.
• **Lumbar Puncture & CSF Analysis**
    ◦ **Opening Pressure**: Can be normal or elevated.
    ◦ **WBC**: Mild lymphocytic pleocytosis (typically 50-200 cells/L).
    ◦ **Protein**: Mildly elevated (typically <100 mg/dL).
    ◦ **Glucose**: Normal.
    ◦ **Oligoclonal Bands**: **Usually absent.** Their presence suggests a diagnosis of Multiple Sclerosis (MS), though they can be transiently positive in a minority of ADEM cases.
• **Lab Studies**
    ◦ CBC may show leukocytosis.
    ◦ ESR/CRP may be elevated (non-specific).
    ◦ Serologies for suspected infectious triggers (e.g., *Mycoplasma*, EBV) can be helpful.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is generally **favorable**, with most patients (especially children) making a full or near-full recovery.
• Recovery may take weeks to months.
• Mortality rate is low (~1-3%).
• Poor prognostic indicators include:
    ◦ Very young age.
    ◦ Fulminant onset with severe deficits.
    ◦ Poor response to initial steroid therapy.

sections.overview:
• **Myasthenia Gravis (MG)** is a chronic autoimmune, neuromuscular disorder characterized by fluctuating, fatigable weakness of skeletal muscles.
• Caused by autoantibodies directed against components of the postsynaptic membrane at the **neuromuscular junction (NMJ)**, most commonly the **acetylcholine receptor (AChR)**.
• The hallmark of MG is muscle weakness that **worsens with repetitive use** and **improves with rest**.
sections.etiology:
• **Autoimmune Pathogenesis**: A Type II hypersensitivity reaction where the body produces IgG autoantibodies targeting proteins in the postsynaptic membrane of the neuromuscular junction.
    ◦ **Primary Target (85% of cases)**: **Acetylcholine Receptors (AChR)**.
        ▪ Antibodies bind to AChRs, leading to:
            • **Blockade** of acetylcholine binding sites.
            • **Complement-mediated destruction** of the postsynaptic membrane, flattening the junctional folds.
            • **Increased internalization and degradation** of AChRs.
    ◦ The net result is a reduced number of functional AChRs, leading to a decreased end-plate potential. With repetitive nerve stimulation, acetylcholine release diminishes naturally, and in MG patients, the reduced number of receptors cannot generate a sufficient end-plate potential to trigger muscle contraction, resulting in **fatigable weakness**.
    ◦ **Other Targets**:
        ▪ **Anti-MuSK (Muscle-Specific Kinase) Antibodies**: Found in ~40% of AChR-seronegative patients. MuSK is crucial for clustering AChRs at the NMJ. **Anti-MuSK MG** often presents with more prominent bulbar and respiratory weakness.
        ▪ **Anti-LRP4 (Lipoprotein-related protein 4) Antibodies**: A less common target in "double seronegative" (AChR- and MuSK-negative) patients.
• **Role of the Thymus**: The thymus gland is implicated in the pathogenesis.
    ◦ **Thymic Hyperplasia**: Found in ~65% of patients.
    ◦ **Thymoma (Thymic tumor)**: Found in ~10-15% of patients.
    ◦ The thymus is believed to be a site of initial T-cell and B-cell sensitization against AChR proteins.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Approximately 14-20 cases per 100,000 population.
• **Incidence**: Bimodal age distribution.
    ◦ **Early Peak**: Women in their 20s-30s.
    ◦ **Late Peak**: Men in their 60s-80s.
• **Gender**: Overall, women are affected more frequently than men (approx. 3:2 ratio), especially in the early-onset group.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Thymic abnormalities**: **Thymoma** or thymic hyperplasia.
• **Female gender** (for early-onset).
• **Genetic predisposition**: Associated with certain HLA types (e.g., HLA-B8, HLA-DR3).
• **Personal or family history of other autoimmune diseases** (e.g., Lupus, Rheumatoid Arthritis, Autoimmune Thyroiditis).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a patient with specific, **fatigable muscle weakness** that is **worse at the end of the day** or after exertion. Symptoms fluctuate in intensity.
    ◦ **Ocular MG**: Weakness is confined to the eyelids and extraocular muscles. This is the initial presentation in >50% of patients.
    ◦ **Generalized MG**: Weakness affects ocular, bulbar, limb, and/or respiratory muscles. Approximately 85% of patients with ocular onset will progress to generalized MG within 2 years.
• **Ocular Symptoms**:
    ◦ **Ptosis**: Asymmetrical, drooping of one or both eyelids.
    ◦ **Diplopia**: Double vision, often horizontal or vertical.
• **Bulbar (Cranial Nerves) Symptoms**:
    ◦ **Dysarthria**: Slurred, "nasal" speech that worsens during conversation.
    ◦ **Dysphagia**: Difficulty swallowing liquids and solids, risk of aspiration.
    ◦ **Fatigable Chewing**: Weakness of jaw muscles during a meal.
    ◦ **Facial Weakness**: "**Myasthenic snarl**" on smiling; difficulty puffing cheeks.
• **Limb/Axial Symptoms**:
    ◦ **Proximal > Distal Weakness**: Difficulty climbing stairs, rising from a chair, combing hair, or lifting objects.
    ◦ **Neck Weakness**: "**Dropped head syndrome**" due to weak neck extensors.
• **Respiratory Symptoms**:
    ◦ **Shortness of breath**, especially with exertion or when supine (orthopnea).
    ◦ Can progress to respiratory failure (**Myasthenic Crisis**).
• **Key Negative Findings**: Sensation, cognition, and deep tendon reflexes (DTRs) are typically **normal**. Pupillary responses are spared.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Inspection**: Observe for **ptosis**, facial asymmetry, or a "**snarling**" expression.
• **Ocular Exam**:
    ◦ **Sustained Upward Gaze (60 seconds)**: Provokes or worsens **ptosis**.
    ◦ **Extraocular Movements (EOMs)**: May reveal dysconjugate gaze that does not conform to a single cranial nerve palsy.
    ◦ **Cogan's Lid Twitch**: Brief upward twitch of the ptotic eyelid when the patient quickly shifts gaze from downward to primary position.
• **Motor Exam**:
    ◦ **Fatigability Testing**: Repetitive abduction of the arms or repeated sit-to-stand maneuvers will demonstrate progressive weakness.
    ◦ **Strength**: Often proximal weakness (deltoids, hip flexors) and prominent neck flexor weakness.
• **Reflexes**: DTRs are **preserved**.
• **Sensation**: **Intact** throughout.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Bedside/Office Tests**:
    ◦ **Ice Pack Test**: Applying an ice pack over a ptotic eyelid for 2-5 minutes.
        ▪ **Improvement in ptosis is a positive test**.
        ▪ Mechanism: Cold inhibits acetylcholinesterase activity, increasing ACh availability.
        ▪ High specificity.
• **Serology (Antibody Testing) - First Line**:
    ◦ **AChR-binding antibodies**: Positive in ~85% of generalized MG and ~50% of pure ocular MG. **Highly specific**.
    ◦ **Anti-MuSK antibodies**: Order if AChR-Ab is negative. Positive in ~40% of seronegative generalized MG.
• **Electrophysiology**:
    ◦ **Repetitive Nerve Stimulation (RNS)**: Low-frequency (2-3 Hz) stimulation of a motor nerve shows a **decremental response** (>10% decrease in the compound muscle action potential amplitude).
    ◦ **Single-Fiber Electromyography (SFEMG)**: **Most sensitive diagnostic test**. Detects increased "**jitter**" (variability in timing between two muscle fiber action potentials from the same motor unit) and "**blocking**".
• **Imaging**:
    ◦ **Chest CT or MRI**: **Mandatory** in all newly diagnosed MG patients to rule out **thymoma** or thymic hyperplasia.
• **Pulmonary Function Tests (PFTs)**:
    ◦ **Forced Vital Capacity (FVC)** and **Negative Inspiratory Force (NIF)** are used to monitor respiratory status, especially in patients at risk for myasthenic crisis.
sections.treatment:
• **1. Symptomatic Therapy**:
    ◦ **Acetylcholinesterase Inhibitors**: **Pyridostigmine (Mestinon)**.
        ▪ MOA: Increases the amount of acetylcholine available at the NMJ.
        ▪ Use: First-line symptomatic treatment.
        ▪ Side Effects: Cholinergic (diarrhea, abdominal cramps, salivation, bradycardia).
• **2. Chronic Immunomodulating Therapies**:
    ◦ **Corticosteroids (e.g., Prednisone)**: Mainstay of immunosuppressive therapy.
    ◦ **Steroid-Sparing Agents**: Azathioprine, Mycophenolate Mofetil, Tacrolimus. Used for long-term management to reduce steroid dose and side effects.
• **3. Rapid, Short-Term Immunomodulating Therapies (for crisis or exacerbations)**:
    ◦ **Plasmapheresis (PLEX)**: Directly removes autoantibodies from the blood.
    ◦ **Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG)**: Modulates the immune system and neutralizes autoantibodies.
• **4. Surgical**:
    ◦ **Thymectomy**:
        ▪ **Mandatory** for all patients with a **thymoma**.
        ▪ Recommended for most AChR-Ab positive patients with generalized MG, typically under age 60, to increase the probability of remission or clinical improvement.
sections.management:
• **Avoidance of Triggering Medications**:
    ◦ **Antibiotics**: Aminoglycosides, Fluoroquinolones, Macrolides.
    ◦ **Cardiovascular**: Beta-blockers, Procainamide, Quinidine.
    ◦ **Other**: Magnesium (high IV doses), certain muscle relaxants, botulinum toxin.
• **Myasthenic Crisis Management**: This is a neurologic emergency.
    ◦ **Definition**: Life-threatening weakness of respiratory muscles leading to respiratory failure.
    ◦ **Management**: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.complications:
• **Myasthenic Crisis**: Acute respiratory failure requiring ventilation. The most life-threatening complication.
• **Aspiration Pneumonia**: Secondary to bulbar muscle weakness and dysphagia.
• **Thymoma**: Can be locally invasive, though metastasis is rare.
• **Complications from Treatment**:
    ◦ Long-term steroid use (osteoporosis, hyperglycemia, Cushing's syndrome).
    ◦ Immunosuppressant side effects (bone marrow suppression, opportunistic infections).
sections.prognosis:
• With modern treatment, the prognosis is generally very good.
• Most patients can achieve significant improvement in symptoms and lead relatively normal lives.
• Mortality rate is low (<5%) and is usually related to **myasthenic crisis**.
• **Thymectomy** can induce remission in a subset of patients.

sections.overview:
• **Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome (LEMS)** is a rare autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction
• Characterized by a triad of **proximal muscle weakness**, **autonomic dysfunction**, and **areflexia**
• It is a **presynaptic disorder** caused by antibodies directed against **voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs)** on the motor nerve terminal, which impairs the release of acetylcholine (ACh)
• Approximately 50-60% of cases are associated with an underlying malignancy, most commonly **Small Cell Lung Cancer (SCLC)**, making it a significant paraneoplastic syndrome
• Unlike Myasthenia Gravis, muscle weakness in LEMS characteristically improves with brief, repeated muscle exertion, a phenomenon known as **post-exercise facilitation**
sections.etiology:
• LEMS is an antibody-mediated autoimmune disease
    ◦ **Target**: The primary target is the **P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channel (VGCC)** located on the presynaptic motor nerve terminal
    ◦ **Mechanism**:
        ▪ Autoantibodies bind to VGCCs
        ▪ This binding leads to cross-linking and internalization of the channels, reducing the number of functional VGCCs
        ▪ When an action potential reaches the nerve terminal, the reduced number of VGCCs results in decreased calcium influx
        ▪ Calcium influx is the critical trigger for the release of acetylcholine (ACh) vesicles into the synaptic cleft
        ▪ The reduced calcium influx leads to a **significant decrease in the quantity of ACh released** per nerve impulse
        ▪ The amount of ACh released is insufficient to generate a normal end-plate potential and trigger a muscle fiber contraction, resulting in weakness
    ◦ **Facilitation Phenomenon**: With rapid, repetitive nerve stimulation (i.e., exercise), calcium can accumulate within the presynaptic terminal faster than it is removed
        ▪ This buildup of intracellular calcium eventually reaches a threshold sufficient to trigger more ACh vesicle release, leading to a temporary improvement in muscle strength
    ◦ **Two Main Forms**:
        ▪ **Paraneoplastic LEMS (~50-60%)**: Strongly associated with **Small Cell Lung Cancer (SCLC)**
            ▪ The SCLC tumor cells express VGCCs on their surface
            ▪ The immune system creates antibodies against these tumor channels, which then cross-react with the VGCCs at the neuromuscular junction
        ▪ **Non-paraneoplastic (Idiopathic) LEMS (~40-50%)**: Occurs in the absence of cancer and is considered a primary autoimmune disorder
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: **Rare**, affecting approximately 3-4 per million people worldwide
• **Paraneoplastic LEMS**:
    ◦ Median age of onset: ~60 years
    ◦ More common in males, reflecting the demographics of smoking-related SCLC
• **Non-paraneoplastic LEMS**:
    ◦ Bimodal age distribution, with peaks around age 35 and 60
    ◦ No significant gender predominance
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The onset is typically insidious and slowly progressive over months to years
• Patients often present with complaints related to proximal leg weakness
• **Classic Triad**:
    ◦ **Symmetric Proximal Muscle Weakness**:
        ▪ Primarily affecting the legs
        ▪ Patients report difficulty rising from a chair, climbing stairs, or walking
        ▪ Arm weakness (difficulty combing hair, lifting objects) can also occur but is usually less severe
    ◦ **Hyporeflexia or Areflexia**: Deep tendon reflexes (DTRs) are diminished or absent
    ◦ **Autonomic Dysfunction**: Often an early and prominent feature
sections.diagnostics:
• **Electrophysiology (NCS/EMG)**: **Gold standard** for diagnosis
    ◦ **Repetitive Nerve Stimulation (RNS)**:
        ▪ At **low frequency (2-3 Hz)**, a **decremental response** (a progressive decrease in the compound muscle action potential, or CMAP, amplitude) is seen, similar to MG
        ▪ After a brief period of maximal exercise (10 seconds), a **dramatic incremental response (>100% increase in CMAP amplitude)** is observed
            ▪ This post-exercise facilitation is **pathognomonic for LEMS**
        ▪ At **high frequency (20-50 Hz)**, a similar incremental response is seen
• **Serology**:
    ◦ **Anti-VGCC antibody test**: Positive in 85-95% of patients. Confirms the diagnosis and the autoimmune etiology
• **Malignancy Workup**: **Mandatory for all newly diagnosed LEMS patients**
    ◦ **Chest CT with and without contrast** is the initial imaging test of choice to screen for SCLC
    ◦ If the initial CT is negative, consider a PET scan
    ◦ If all imaging is negative, surveillance with repeat chest CTs should be performed every 6 months for at least 2 years
sections.prognosis:
• **Paraneoplastic LEMS**: The prognosis is directly tied to the stage and response of the underlying **SCLC**, which is generally poor
• **Non-paraneoplastic LEMS**: The condition is chronic but does not typically affect life expectancy. Symptoms can be well-managed with treatment, though complete remission is uncommon

sections.overview:
• Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), commonly known as Lou Gehrig's disease, is a progressive, fatal, neurodegenerative disease characterized by the destruction of both **upper motor neurons (UMN)** and **lower motor neurons (LMN)**.
    ◦ This leads to progressive muscle weakness, atrophy, and eventual paralysis.
• Crucially, the following are typically spared until very late stages:
    ◦ Sensory function
    ◦ Cognition (in most cases)
    ◦ Extraocular movements
    ◦ Bowel/bladder control
• It is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**:
    ◦ The exact cause is unknown in most cases.
    ◦ **Sporadic ALS (SALS)**: Accounts for ~90-95% of all cases with no clear identifiable cause.
    ◦ **Familial ALS (FALS)**: Accounts for ~5-10% of cases and is caused by genetic mutations.
        ▪ Most common gene mutations: **C9orf72** and **SOD1** (superoxide dismutase 1).
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ Involves the degeneration and death of motor neurons.
    ◦ **Upper Motor Neurons (UMNs)**: Located in the precentral gyrus (motor cortex); their degeneration leads to loss of inhibitory control.
    ◦ **Lower Motor Neurons (LMNs)**: Located in the anterior horn of the spinal cord and brainstem motor nuclei; their degeneration leads to muscle denervation.
• **Proposed Mechanisms**:
    ◦ **Glutamate Excitotoxicity**: Excessive glutamate levels cause neuronal damage and death. This is the target of Riluzole.
    ◦ **Oxidative Stress**: Damage from free radicals, particularly relevant in SOD1 mutations.
    ◦ **Protein Aggregation**: Abnormal protein clumps (e.g., TDP-43) accumulate within neurons, disrupting cellular function.
    ◦ **Neurofilament Dysfunction**: Disruption of the neuronal cytoskeleton.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: ~2 per 100,000 people annually.
• **Prevalence**: ~5 per 100,000 people.
• **Age of Onset**: Typically between 55-75 years.
• **Sex**: Slightly more common in men (M:F ratio 1.5:1).
sections.riskFactors:
• **Definitive**:
    ◦ **Age**: The single greatest risk factor.
    ◦ **Family History**: Positive genetic mutation (FALS).
• **Probable/Possible**:
    ◦ **Male Sex**
    ◦ **Cigarette Smoking**
    ◦ **Military Service**: Veterans have a higher risk, though the reason is unclear.
    ◦ **Environmental Exposures** (e.g., lead, pesticides - evidence is debated).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is insidious and progressive.
• **Classic Onset**: **Asymmetric limb weakness**.
    ◦ A patient may notice difficulty with fine motor tasks (buttoning a shirt, turning a key), tripping over their feet (**foot drop**), or weakness in a hand or shoulder.
• **Two main patterns of onset**:
    ◦ **Limb-Onset (~75%)**: Symptoms begin in the arms or legs. This is the most common presentation.
    ◦ **Bulbar-Onset (~25%)**: Symptoms begin with muscles of speech, swallowing, and chewing (**dysarthria**, **dysphagia**). This form often has a more rapid progression and poorer prognosis.
• **Hallmark Feature**: The **combination of UMN and LMN signs** in the same region, or UMN signs in some regions and LMN signs in others.
• **LMN Symptoms (Loss of direct innervation)**:
    ◦ Painless, progressive muscle weakness
    ◦ Muscle atrophy (wasting)
    ◦ **Fasciculations** (visible muscle twitching)
    ◦ Muscle cramps
• **UMN Symptoms (Loss of inhibition)**:
    ◦ Muscle **spasticity** (stiffness, velocity-dependent increased tone)
    ◦ Slowness of movement
    ◦ Poorly coordinated movements
• **Bulbar Symptoms**:
    ◦ **Dysarthria**: Slurred, nasal, or quiet speech.
    ◦ **Dysphagia**: Difficulty swallowing solids and/or liquids.
    ◦ **Sialorrhea**: Drooling due to impaired swallowing of saliva.
    ◦ **Pseudobulbar Affect**: Pathological, uncontrollable episodes of laughing or crying that are incongruent with mood.
• **Respiratory Symptoms (Late-stage)**:
    ◦ Dyspnea on exertion, progressing to dyspnea at rest
    ◦ Orthopnea (difficulty breathing while lying flat)
    ◦ Morning headaches (due to nocturnal hypercapnia)
• **What is SPARED**:
    ◦ Sensation (pain, temperature, vibration, proprioception)
    ◦ Bowel and bladder function
    ◦ Extraocular movements
    ◦ Cognition (though an overlap with **frontotemporal dementia [FTD]** exists in ~15% of cases).
sections.diagnostics:
• ALS is a clinical diagnosis supported by electrodiagnostic studies and exclusion of other conditions.
• **Electromyography (EMG) & Nerve Conduction Studies (NCS)**:
    ◦ The single most important diagnostic test.
    ◦ **EMG**: Shows evidence of **widespread, active and chronic denervation** (fibrillation potentials, positive sharp waves) and reinnervation (large motor unit potentials) in at least 3 limbs or 2 limbs + bulbar muscles.
    ◦ **NCS**: **Motor and sensory nerve conduction studies are typically normal**. This is critical to rule out peripheral neuropathies.
• **MRI of Brain and Cervical Spine**:
    ◦ Essential to **rule out structural mimics** like cervical spondylotic myelopathy, spinal cord tumors, syringomyelia, or brain lesions (e.g., MS plaques, stroke).
    ◦ MRI is **normal** in ALS, though subtle hyperintensity along corticospinal tracts (T2/FLAIR) may be seen.
• **Laboratory Studies**:
    ◦ Used to rule out other causes.
    ◦ Includes CBC, CMP, TSH, Vitamin B12, CK (often mildly elevated), Lyme serology, heavy metal screen.
• **Pulmonary Function Tests (PFTs)**:
    ◦ Establish a baseline and monitor disease progression.
    ◦ **Forced Vital Capacity (FVC)** is the key measurement.
        ▪ A drop to <50% predicted often necessitates discussion of ventilatory support.
sections.management:
• **Respiratory**:
    ◦ Regular PFT monitoring (**FVC**).
    ◦ **Non-invasive ventilation (NIV)**, such as BiPAP, is the cornerstone for managing respiratory insufficiency. It improves survival and quality of life.
    ◦ Discussion of mechanical ventilation via tracheostomy as an end-of-life choice.
• **Nutrition**:
    ◦ Early placement of a **percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tube** when dysphagia becomes significant or weight loss occurs.
        ▪ This prevents aspiration and malnutrition.
• **Symptom Control**:
    ◦ **Spasticity**: Baclofen, tizanidine, physical therapy.
    ◦ **Sialorrhea (drooling)**: Anticholinergics (glycopyrrolate, amitriptyline), botulinum toxin injections to salivary glands.
    ◦ **Pseudobulbar Affect**: Dextromethorphan/quinidine (Nuedexta).
    ◦ **Cramps**: Stretching, quinine (use with caution), mexiletine.
• **Rehabilitation**:
    ◦ **Physical & Occupational Therapy**: Maintain mobility, prevent contractures, provide assistive devices (braces, walkers, wheelchairs).
    ◦ **Speech-Language Pathology**: Swallowing strategies, communication aids (voice banking, eye-gaze communication devices).
• **Palliative Care & Advanced Directives**: Introduce early to address symptom burden and end-of-life goals.
sections.complications:
• **Respiratory Failure**: Most common cause of death.
• **Aspiration Pneumonia**: Due to dysphagia.
• **Malnutrition & Dehydration**: Due to dysphagia.
• **Thromboembolism (DVT/PE)**: Due to immobility.
• **Pressure Ulcers**
• **Joint Contractures**
sections.prognosis:
• **Invariably fatal**.
• **Median survival is 3-5 years** from symptom onset.
    ◦ ~20% of patients live >5 years, and ~10% live >10 years.
• **Negative Prognostic Factors**:
    ◦ Bulbar onset
    ◦ Older age at onset
    ◦ Rapid progression of symptoms
    ◦ Early respiratory involvement (low initial FVC)

sections.overview:
• Condition characterized by diffuse, symmetric damage to peripheral nerves, resulting in a combination of sensory, motor, and/or autonomic deficits.
    ◦ Dysfunction typically begins in the longest nerves first and progresses proximally, leading to a classic **"stocking-glove" distribution** of symptoms.
    ◦ It is a syndrome resulting from a wide array of underlying systemic diseases, toxic exposures, or hereditary conditions.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects an estimated 2-7% of the general population.
• Prevalence increases significantly with age.
• **Diabetic polyneuropathy** is the most common form, affecting up to 50% of patients with long-standing diabetes.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The onset is typically **insidious and slowly progressive**.
• Patients usually present with sensory complaints in the feet that gradually ascend up the legs.
    ◦ Hand involvement occurs later, once symptoms have reached the knees, creating the characteristic **"stocking-glove" pattern**.
• The presentation is almost always **symmetric**.
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• Highly dependent on the underlying etiology.
• **Reversible/Treatable causes** (e.g., B12 deficiency, medication-induced) carry a good prognosis if identified and treated early.
• For **progressive conditions** like diabetic neuropathy, the prognosis is fair to poor in terms of symptom reversal.
    ◦ The goal is to slow progression and manage symptoms.
• Hereditary neuropathies are typically slowly progressive with no cure.

sections.overview:
• **Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathy (DPN)** is the most common chronic complication of diabetes mellitus.
• Refers to nerve damage caused by **chronic hyperglycemia** and associated metabolic derangements.
• Classic presentation is a **distal symmetric sensorimotor polyneuropathy**.
    ◦ Typically affects the longest nerves first (feet and hands) in a symmetric pattern.
    ◦ Involves both sensory and motor fibers.
• Sensory symptoms usually precede motor deficits.
• It is a **diagnosis of exclusion** after other potential causes of peripheral neuropathy have been ruled out.
sections.etiology:
• The pathophysiology is multifactorial with **chronic hyperglycemia** as the central pathogenic factor. Key proposed mechanisms include:
    ◦ **Polyol Pathway (Sorbitol-Aldose Reductase Pathway)**
        ▪ In hyperglycemic states, excess glucose is shunted into this pathway.
        ▪ Glucose is converted to sorbitol by aldose reductase, which is then converted to fructose.
        ▪ **Sorbitol accumulation** within nerve cells creates osmotic stress, leading to cellular injury and reduced nerve conduction velocity.
    ◦ **Advanced Glycation End Products (AGEs)**
        ▪ Non-enzymatic binding of glucose to proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids forms AGEs.
        ▪ AGEs accumulate in the endoneurial microvasculature and nerve fibers, leading to structural damage, inflammation, and increased oxidative stress.
    ◦ **Oxidative Stress**
        ▪ Hyperglycemia increases the production of **reactive oxygen species (ROS)**, overwhelming the body's antioxidant defenses.
        ▪ ROS directly damage neurons, Schwann cells, and microvascular endothelial cells, leading to axonal degeneration and demyelination.
    ◦ **Microvascular Insufficiency**
        ▪ Diabetes-induced damage to the **vasa nervorum** (the small blood vessels supplying the nerves) leads to endothelial dysfunction, vasoconstriction, and reduced nerve blood flow.
        ▪ This results in nerve ischemia and hypoxia, contributing to nerve fiber loss.
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects up to **50%** of patients with long-standing diabetes.
• Prevalence increases with the duration of diabetes and the severity of hyperglycemia.
• In **Type 1 DM (T1DM)**, DPN is rare in the first 5 years but prevalence rises significantly thereafter.
• In **Type 2 DM (T2DM)**, up to 10-20% of patients have evidence of DPN at the time of diagnosis, as hyperglycemia may have been present for years.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The hallmark of DPN is a **distal, symmetric, "stocking-glove" distribution**.
    ◦ Symptoms typically begin in the toes and ascend up the legs before appearing in the fingers and hands.
• **Pattern:** Distal to proximal.
• **Fiber Involvement:**
    ◦ **Small fibers** (pain, temperature) are often affected first.
    ◦ Followed by **large fibers** (vibration, proprioception).
• **Progression:** Insidious onset and slow progression.
• **Timing:** Symptoms are often worse at night.
sections.diagnostics:
• DPN is primarily a **clinical diagnosis** based on a thorough history and physical exam in a patient with diabetes.
• **Screening**
    ◦ Annual screening for all patients with T2DM starting at diagnosis.
    ◦ Annual screening for T1DM patients 5 years after diagnosis.
    ◦ Screening includes:
        ▪ History of symptoms
        ▪ Visual foot inspection
        ▪ Testing with **10-g monofilament** AND one other modality (vibration, pinprick, or reflexes).
• **Laboratory Tests** (to rule out other causes)
    ◦ **HbA1c:** To assess glycemic control.
    ◦ Vitamin B12 level and/or methylmalonic acid.
    ◦ Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH).
    ◦ Complete Blood Count (CBC).
    ◦ Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP) to assess for renal failure (uremic neuropathy).
• **Nerve Conduction Studies (NCS) & Electromyography (EMG)**
    ◦ Not routinely required for diagnosis of typical DPN.
    ◦ **Indications:** Atypical presentation (e.g., asymmetric, motor-predominant, rapid progression), or if the diagnosis is uncertain.
    ◦ **Expected Findings:** Show evidence of a distal, axonal, sensorimotor polyneuropathy (decreased nerve conduction velocities and amplitudes).
sections.prognosis:
• DPN is a progressive and generally irreversible condition.
• The primary goal is to **slow progression** and **prevent complications**.
• **Strict glycemic control** from the time of diabetes diagnosis is the most effective way to improve the long-term prognosis.
• The presence of DPN is a strong independent predictor of increased morbidity and all-cause mortality in patients with diabetes.

sections.overview:
• Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (CTS) is the most common compressive mononeuropathy, resulting from the entrapment and compression of the **median nerve** as it passes through the carpal tunnel at the wrist.
    ◦ This compression leads to ischemia and demyelination of the nerve, causing a constellation of sensory and motor symptoms in the median nerve distribution of the hand.
sections.etiology:
• The underlying pathophysiology is **increased pressure within the carpal tunnel**, a rigid fibro-osseous canal. This pressure compromises the microcirculation of the median nerve, leading to nerve ischemia, impaired axoplasmic flow, and eventual demyelination and axonal damage.
• **Etiologies are broadly categorized as:**
    ◦ **Decreasing the size of the tunnel:**
        ▪ Trauma: Distal radius fractures, carpal bone dislocation/fracture.
        ▪ Anatomic variants: Bony abnormalities, space-occupying lesions (ganglion cysts, lipomas).
    ◦ **Increasing the volume of the contents:**
        ▪ **Inflammatory:** Tenosynovitis of the flexor tendons (e.g., in Rheumatoid Arthritis).
        ▪ **Fluid shifts:** Pregnancy, hypothyroidism (myxedema), renal failure.
        ▪ **Metabolic:** Gout, amyloidosis.
    ◦ **Dynamic/Repetitive Stress:**
        ▪ Repetitive wrist flexion/extension or use of vibrating tools leads to inflammation and thickening of the transverse carpal ligament and flexor tenosynovium.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Most common entrapment neuropathy.**
• Prevalence: 3-6% of the general population.
• **Gender:** Women > Men (approx. 3:1 ratio).
• **Peak Age:** 40-60 years.
• Bilateral involvement is common (>50% of cases), though the dominant hand is usually affected first and more severely.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic patient is a middle-aged woman with an insidious onset of numbness and tingling in her hand.
    ◦ Symptoms are **worse at night** and often **awaken her from sleep**.
    ◦ The patient may report needing to "shake her hand out" to get relief (this is known as the **Flick Sign**).
• Symptoms are often exacerbated by activities like driving, holding a phone, or typing.
• As the condition progresses, patients may report dropping objects, clumsiness with fine motor tasks (e.g., buttoning a shirt), and weakness in the thumb.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis:** CTS is primarily a clinical diagnosis based on a characteristic history and physical exam.
• **Electromyography (EMG) and Nerve Conduction Studies (NCS):**
    ◦ **Gold standard** for confirming the diagnosis, assessing severity, and ruling out other neuropathies.
    ◦ **NCS:** Will show **slowed sensory and motor nerve conduction velocity** across the carpal tunnel.
    ◦ **EMG:** Can show signs of denervation (e.g., fibrillation potentials) in the thenar muscles in severe, chronic cases.
• **Ultrasound:**
    ◦ Increasingly used as a first-line imaging modality.
    ◦ Can show flattening or swelling (increased cross-sectional area) of the median nerve at the carpal tunnel.
    ◦ Useful for identifying structural causes like a ganglion cyst.
• **X-ray:**
    ◦ Not routine, but useful to evaluate for bony abnormalities or arthritis if there is a history of trauma.
• **MRI:**
    ◦ Rarely needed; reserved for cases where a tumor or mass is suspected.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** with timely diagnosis and treatment.
• Conservative measures are effective for many mild cases.
• Surgical carpal tunnel release has a **>90% success rate** for relieving symptoms, especially pain and paresthesias.
• Motor recovery (strength) and recovery from severe sensory loss may be slow and incomplete if the nerve damage was severe or long-standing prior to surgery.

sections.overview: • Ulnar neuropathy is the second most common compressive mononeuropathy of the upper extremity, after Carpal Tunnel Syndrome. • It results from the compression, traction, or irritation of the ulnar nerve at any point along its course. • The two most common sites of entrapment are: ◦ The cubital tunnel at the elbow (most common) ◦ Guyon's canal at the wrist • The condition presents with sensory and/or motor deficits in the ulnar nerve distribution, affecting the little finger, the medial half of the ring finger, and the intrinsic hand muscles.
sections.etiology: • The underlying mechanism is mechanical compression or traction of the ulnar nerve, leading to ischemia, demyelination, and if chronic, axonal loss.
sections.epidemiology:
• Second most common upper extremity compressive neuropathy.
• Incidence is higher in men than women.
• Peak incidence occurs in middle age.
• Common in occupations or activities requiring repetitive or sustained elbow flexion.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients typically present with an insidious onset of sensory symptoms in the ulnar nerve distribution.
• They may complain of numbness or tingling when talking on the phone, driving, or sleeping with their elbows bent.
• As the condition progresses, they may report:
    ◦ Hand weakness
    ◦ Clumsiness
    ◦ Dropping objects
    ◦ Difficulty with fine motor tasks like buttoning a shirt
• Pain is often described as an ache at the medial elbow that can radiate up the arm or down into the hand.
sections.diagnostics: • Clinical Diagnosis: The diagnosis is primarily based on history and physical exam findings. • Electrodiagnostic Studies (EMG/NCS): ◦ Gold Standard to confirm the diagnosis, localize the site of compression (elbow vs. wrist), and determine the severity (demyelination vs. axonal loss). ◦ NCS: Will show focal slowing of motor conduction velocity across the elbow (>10 m/s decrease compared to other segments). ◦ EMG: Can detect fibrillations or positive sharp waves in ulnar-innervated muscles, indicating denervation (axonal loss). • Imaging: ◦ Ultrasound: Can directly visualize the nerve to identify swelling, compression, or instability (subluxation). It is often the initial imaging modality of choice. ◦ X-ray: Useful to rule out bony pathology such as osteophytes, arthritis, or old fractures contributing to compression. ◦ MRI: Provides excellent detail of the nerve and surrounding soft tissues; used for surgical planning or if the diagnosis is unclear.
sections.prognosis: • Excellent for mild cases treated early with conservative measures. • Good for surgical decompression performed before the onset of significant muscle atrophy. ◦ Sensory symptoms often improve more readily than motor deficits. • Poor for chronic cases with severe, long-standing compression and marked axonal loss on EMG. ◦ Motor recovery, in particular, is unpredictable and often incomplete in these cases.

sections.overview:
• Meralgia Paresthetica (MP) is a sensory mononeuropathy caused by the entrapment or compression of the **Lateral Femoral Cutaneous Nerve (LFCN)**.
    ◦ This results in pain, paresthesias (tingling), and sensory loss in the anterolateral aspect of the thigh.
    ◦ It is a **purely sensory** condition with **no motor weakness** or reflex changes, which is a key distinguishing feature.
sections.etiology:
• **Core Mechanism**: Compression of the **Lateral Femoral Cutaneous Nerve (LFCN)**.
• **Anatomical Course**: The LFCN is a pure sensory nerve originating from the L2 and L3 spinal nerve roots of the lumbar plexus.
    ◦ It travels from the pelvis and exits inferior to the inguinal ligament, just medial to the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS).
• **Site of Compression**: The most common site of entrapment is where the nerve passes under or through the inguinal ligament.
• **Causes of Compression**:
    ◦ **External Pressure**:
        ▪ Tight clothing, belts (e.g., "tight pants syndrome")
        ▪ Tool belts (common in construction workers)
        ▪ Seatbelts in motor vehicle accidents
        ▪ Body armor or duty belts in law enforcement/military
    ◦ **Increased Intra-abdominal Pressure**:
        ▪ **Obesity** (most common cause)
        ▪ **Pregnancy**
        ▪ Ascites
        ▪ Large abdominal tumors
    ◦ **Iatrogenic (Post-Surgical)**:
        ▪ Anterior approach hip replacement surgery
        ▪ Iliac crest bone graft harvesting
        ▪ Pelvic osteotomy
        ▪ Appendectomy or other pelvic/abdominal surgeries
    ◦ **Trauma**:
        ▪ Direct blow to the hip or pelvis
        ▪ Pelvic fractures
    ◦ **Metabolic**:
        ▪ **Diabetes mellitus** (nerves are more susceptible to compression)
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Approximately 4 per 10,000 person-years.
• **Age**: Most common in middle-aged individuals (30-60 years).
• **Sex**: Slightly more common in males, but occurs frequently in both sexes.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Obesity** (strongest risk factor)
• **Pregnancy**
• **Diabetes Mellitus**
• Age 40-60
• Wearing tight clothing, especially around the waist and hips
• Occupations requiring heavy tool belts (e.g., carpenters, police officers)
• Recent hip or pelvic surgery
• Scar tissue near the inguinal ligament
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A middle-aged patient, often with a history of **obesity**, **diabetes**, or an occupation involving a heavy belt, presents with a complaint of numbness, tingling, or burning pain isolated to a "patch" on the outer or front part of one thigh.
    ◦ The onset is typically gradual.
    ◦ Symptoms are often aggravated by prolonged standing or walking and are relieved by sitting.
    ◦ The patient will explicitly deny any leg weakness, difficulty walking (other than due to pain), or changes in bowel/bladder function.
• **Sensory Disturbances (Primary Symptoms)**:
    ◦ **Paresthesias**: Tingling, "pins and needles" sensation.
    ◦ **Hypoesthesia**: Numbness or reduced sensation to light touch.
    ◦ **Dysesthesia**: An unpleasant, abnormal sensation (often described as burning or "skin crawling") that can be provoked by light touch (**allodynia**).
• **Pain**:
    ◦ **Character**: Burning, stinging, aching, or sharp.
    ◦ **Location**: Well-demarcated area on the **anterolateral thigh**.
• **Key Negative**: **NO motor weakness**. The patient will not complain of the leg "giving way."
sections.physicalExam:
• **Inspection**: Usually normal.
    ◦ May see hair loss or shiny skin in the affected area due to chronic rubbing by the patient.
• **Palpation**: Possible point tenderness just medial (~1-2 cm) to the **anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS)**.
• **Neurological Exam**:
    ◦ **Sensation**: Altered sensation (to pinprick or light touch) in the distribution of the **LFCN** (anterolateral thigh).
        ▪ The area of sensory change is often well-defined by the patient.
    ◦ **Motor Strength**: **Completely normal (5/5)**.
        ▪ Test hip flexors (iliopsoas), knee extensors (quadriceps), ankle dorsiflexors, and plantar flexors.
    ◦ **Reflexes**: Patellar and Achilles reflexes are **normal and symmetric (2+)**.
• **Special Tests**:
    ◦ **Pelvic Compression Test**: Patient lies on their side (unaffected side down). The examiner applies firm, downward pressure on the iliac crest for 45-60 seconds.
        ▪ **Relief of symptoms is a positive test**, as this maneuver slackens the inguinal ligament and reduces compression on the nerve. (High specificity).
    ◦ **Tinel's Sign**: Tapping over the inguinal ligament medial to the **ASIS** may reproduce the symptoms.
    ◦ **Negative Straight Leg Raise (SLR)**: Rules out nerve root impingement/**radiculopathy**.
sections.diagnostics:
• Meralgia Paresthetica is primarily a **clinical diagnosis**; diagnostic studies are typically reserved for atypical cases or to rule out other pathology.
• **Imaging**:
    ◦ **Lumbar Spine X-ray or MRI**: Not required for typical MP.
        ▪ Ordered to rule out **lumbar radiculopathy** (e.g., herniated disc, spinal stenosis) if there is any back pain, weakness, or reflex change.
    ◦ **Pelvic CT or MRI**: To rule out a retroperitoneal or pelvic mass compressing the nerve.
• **Electrophysiologic Studies**:
    ◦ **Nerve Conduction Studies (NCS)**: Can be used to confirm the diagnosis by demonstrating abnormal sensory nerve conduction of the **LFCN**.
        ▪ Often compared to the contralateral, asymptomatic side.
    ◦ **Electromyography (EMG)**: Will be **normal** in the leg muscles.
        ▪ Its primary role is to rule out radiculopathy or plexopathy, which would show abnormal findings (e.g., fibrillations, positive sharp waves).
• **Diagnostic Nerve Block**:
    ◦ An injection of local anesthetic (e.g., lidocaine) around the **LFCN** near the **ASIS**.
    ◦ **Complete but temporary relief of symptoms is both diagnostic and therapeutic.**
    ◦ Ultrasound guidance is often used for accuracy.
sections.treatment:
• **Tier 1: Conservative / Lifestyle Modification**
    ◦ **Patient Education**: Reassure the patient about the benign nature of the condition.
    ◦ **Activity Modification**: Avoid activities that precipitate symptoms (e.g., prolonged standing).
    ◦ **Remove Compression**: Wear loose-fitting pants and underwear; avoid heavy belts.
    ◦ **Weight Loss**: Crucial for overweight and obese patients.
• **Tier 2: Pharmacotherapy**
    ◦ **Simple Analgesics**: NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) for pain.
    ◦ **Neuropathic Pain Agents**: For persistent or severe burning pain.
        ▪ Anticonvulsants: **Gabapentin**, Pregabalin
        ▪ TCAs: **Amitriptyline**, Nortriptyline
    ◦ **Topical Agents**: Lidocaine patch, capsaicin cream applied over the affected area.
• **Tier 3: Interventional**
    ◦ **Local Corticosteroid Injection**: Anesthetic + steroid injection around the **LFCN** near the **ASIS**, often under ultrasound guidance.
        ▪ Can provide relief for weeks to months.
• **Tier 4: Refractory Cases**
    ◦ **Pulsed Radiofrequency Ablation** of the **LFCN**.
    ◦ **Surgical Decompression (Neurolysis)** or **Neurectomy** (transection of the nerve).
        ▪ Reserved for severe, intractable cases that have failed all other treatments.
        ▪ Neurectomy results in permanent numbness.
sections.management:
• The initial approach is always conservative; advise **weight loss** and **loose clothing** for 4-8 weeks.
• If symptoms persist, initiate neuropathic pain medication (e.g., **gabapentin**).
• For patients with significant pain impacting quality of life, an ultrasound-guided **corticosteroid injection** is an excellent next step.
• Referral to pain management or surgery is appropriate only after failure of conservative and medical therapies.
• In pregnant patients, symptoms typically resolve spontaneously after delivery.
sections.complications:
• Complications from the condition itself are related to quality of life:
    ◦ Chronic pain and dysesthesia
    ◦ Sleep disturbance
    ◦ Difficulty with activities of daily living
• Complications from treatment can include:
    ◦ Skin atrophy or infection from injections
    ◦ Post-neurectomy **neuroma formation** (painful nerve stump)
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is **generally excellent**.
• The majority of cases resolve with conservative measures, especially if the underlying cause (e.g., tight clothing, pregnancy) is removed.
• Symptoms can be recurrent if risk factors like **obesity** are not addressed.
• Surgical intervention has variable success rates.

sections.overview:
• Acute, idiopathic, **unilateral peripheral facial nerve (Cranial Nerve VII) palsy**
    ◦ Results in paralysis or significant weakness of the muscles of facial expression on one side of the face
    ◦ It is a **diagnosis of exclusion**
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ The cause is idiopathic by definition, but there is a strong association with the reactivation of **Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV-1)**
    ◦ Other potential viral triggers include Herpes Zoster Virus (VZV), Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), and Cytomegalovirus (CMV)
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The proposed mechanism is inflammation and edema of the facial nerve
    ◦ This swelling causes compression of the nerve within its narrow course through the **facial canal** of the temporal bone (specifically the labyrinthine segment)
    ◦ The compression leads to ischemia, demyelination, and subsequent nerve dysfunction (neuropraxia)
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Approximately 20-30 cases per 100,000 people annually
• **Age**: Can occur at any age, but peaks are seen in young to middle-aged adults (15-45 years)
• **Sex**: Affects males and females equally
• **Laterality**: Left and right sides are affected with equal frequency; recurrence occurs in ~7% of patients
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with a **rapid and progressive onset** (over hours to a maximum of 72 hours) of unilateral facial weakness
    ◦ May report waking up in the morning and noticing facial drooping in the mirror
    ◦ Often a preceding viral prodrome or postauricular pain
    ◦ The patient is alert and oriented, with no other neurological deficits
sections.diagnostics:
• Bell Palsy is a **clinical diagnosis of exclusion**
• **Laboratory Tests**
    ◦ Not routinely indicated
    ◦ Consider Lyme serology (ELISA) in endemic areas or with a history of tick exposure
• **Imaging (CT/MRI)**
    ◦ Not required for typical presentations meeting all criteria for Bell Palsy
    ◦ **Indications for imaging (MRI with gadolinium preferred)**:
        ▪ Atypical presentation (e.g., slow onset > 3 weeks, involvement of other cranial nerves)
        ▪ No improvement after 4 months
        ▪ Presence of other neurological signs suggesting a central cause
        ▪ Recurrent ipsilateral palsy
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for most patients
• Some improvement is typically seen within **3 weeks**
• ~85% of patients achieve near-normal to normal facial function within 3-6 months, especially if treated early
• **Poor Prognostic Indicators**:
    ◦ Advanced age (>60)
    ◦ **Complete paralysis** at presentation (House-Brackmann grade VI)
    ◦ Severe pain at onset
    ◦ Associated comorbidities like diabetes mellitus

sections.overview:
• **Trigeminal Neuralgia (TN)**, also known as *tic douloureux*, is a chronic neuropathic pain disorder characterized by severe, **paroxysmal**, **unilateral facial pain**.
	◦ The pain follows the distribution of one or more branches of the **Trigeminal Nerve (Cranial Nerve V)**.
	◦ It is often described as one of the most painful conditions known.
	◦ The diagnosis is primarily **clinical**, based on the characteristic history of the pain.
sections.etiology:
• The pathophysiology is centered on irritation or damage to the trigeminal nerve, leading to **focal demyelination** and subsequent aberrant nerve signaling (**ephaptic transmission**), where non-painful stimuli are interpreted as painful.
• **Classical Trigeminal Neuralgia** (~80-90% of cases)
	◦ Caused by **neurovascular compression** at the trigeminal root entry zone (REZ) in the posterior fossa.
		▪ The **Superior Cerebellar Artery (SCA)** is the most common offending vessel.
	◦ Chronic pulsatile compression from the artery leads to demyelination of the nerve, causing hyperexcitability and abnormal signal transmission.
• **Secondary (Symptomatic) Trigeminal Neuralgia** (~10-20%)
	◦ Caused by an identifiable underlying structural lesion or disease.
		▪ **Multiple Sclerosis (MS):** A demyelinating plaque at the trigeminal nerve root entry zone is a classic cause, especially in younger patients (<40) or those with bilateral symptoms.
		▪ **Tumors:** Cerebellopontine angle tumors (e.g., **acoustic neuroma**, **meningioma**), cysts, or schwannomas compressing the nerve.
		▪ **Arteriovenous Malformation (AVM)** or other vascular anomalies.
		▪ Post-herpetic neuralgia or post-traumatic injury.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence:** Approximately 4-13 per 100,000 people per year.
• **Age of Onset:** Typically occurs after age 50.
	◦ Onset before age 40 should raise suspicion for a secondary cause, particularly **Multiple Sclerosis**.
• **Gender:** More common in females than males (approx. 2:1 ratio).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient, typically a female over 50, presents with a chief complaint of **sudden, severe, recurrent episodes of facial pain** on one side of the face.
• The patient often winces or grimaces during an attack (the **"tic"**).
• They may hold their face to protect it from any stimuli and may have developed **avoidance behaviors** (e.g., not brushing teeth, avoiding talking, eating soft foods).
• Between attacks, the patient is typically **asymptomatic**.
sections.diagnostics:
• Trigeminal neuralgia is primarily a **clinical diagnosis** based on the pathognomonic history.
• **Imaging**
	◦ **Brain MRI with and without contrast** is the imaging modality of choice.
		▪ **Purpose:** To rule out secondary causes like **MS plaques**, **tumors**, or **AVMs**.
	◦ **High-Resolution Sequences** (e.g., FIESTA, CISS): Specialized thin-slice MRI sequences are used to visualize the trigeminal nerve and identify any **neurovascular compression**.
• **Labs**
	◦ Not indicated unless another condition (e.g., Giant Cell Arteritis) is suspected in the differential.
sections.prognosis:
• **Trigeminal Neuralgia** is a chronic condition, often characterized by periods of **remission and exacerbation**.
• Medical therapy often loses efficacy over time (**tachyphylaxis**).
• **Microvascular Decompression (MVD)** offers the best chance for long-term, medication-free pain relief.
	◦ Initial success rates of ~80-90%.
	◦ However, pain can recur in 10-20% of patients within 10 years.

sections.overview:
• **Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS)** is an **acute, immune-mediated, inflammatory polyradiculoneuropathy** characterized by **rapidly progressive, ascending, and symmetric muscle weakness or paralysis**.
    ◦ It primarily affects the **peripheral nervous system**, leading to **demyelination** and/or **axonal damage**.
    ◦ GBS is considered a **medical emergency** due to the potential for rapid **respiratory failure**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ GBS is typically a **post-infectious disorder**; approximately two-thirds of patients report an antecedent respiratory or gastrointestinal infection, usually 1-4 weeks prior to the onset of neurologic symptoms.
        ▪ **Most Common Preceding Pathogen:** ***Campylobacter jejuni*** (associated with more severe, axonal forms of GBS).
        ▪ **Other Associated Pathogens:** Cytomegalovirus (CMV), Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV), *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*, Influenza virus, Zika virus.
        ▪ **Other Triggers (Less Common):** Recent vaccination (e.g., influenza, meningococcal), surgery, trauma, bone marrow transplant.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The core mechanism is **molecular mimicry**.
        ▪ The body produces antibodies against an infectious agent (e.g., lipo-oligosaccharides on the *C. jejuni* cell wall).
        ▪ These antibodies cross-react with structurally similar gangliosides and glycolipids that are components of the peripheral nerve myelin sheath or the axon itself.
        ▪ This triggers an autoimmune attack involving T-cells and macrophages, which strip the myelin from the peripheral nerves (**demyelination**) or, less commonly, damage the axon directly.
        ▪ The resulting demyelination or axonal injury impairs nerve conduction, leading to muscle weakness, sensory changes, and areflexia.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence:** Rare, affecting approximately 1-2 per 100,000 people annually worldwide.
• **Age:** Can occur at any age, but shows a bimodal distribution with peaks in young adulthood and in older adults (ages 50-80).
• **Gender:** Slightly more common in males (Male:Female ratio 1.5:1).
sections.riskFactors:
• **Antecedent Infection:** The single greatest risk factor.
• **Gastroenteritis**, especially from ***C. jejuni***.
• Upper respiratory tract infection (viral).
• Recent surgery or trauma.
• Immunization (very rare association, benefits of vaccination far outweigh the minimal risk).
• Malignancy (e.g., lymphoma).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a patient who reports a recent "stomach flu" or "cold" and now presents with **weakness that started in their feet and is "crawling up" their legs** over a few days.
• The progression is rapid, with symptoms peaking within **2 to 4 weeks**.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ **Motor (Hallmark):**
        ▪ **Progressive, ascending, symmetric muscle weakness**.
        ▪ Often begins in the lower extremities and ascends to the trunk, upper extremities, and cranial nerves.
        ▪ Can progress to **flaccid quadriplegia**.
    ◦ **Sensory:**
        ▪ **Paresthesias** (tingling, "pins and needles") in the hands and feet are common and often precede weakness.
        ▪ Sensory loss is typically mild compared to motor deficits.
        ▪ Neuropathic pain, especially in the lower back, buttocks, and thighs, is reported in over 50% of patients.
    ◦ **Cranial Nerves:**
        ▪ Involvement is common (>50% of cases).
        ▪ **Bilateral facial nerve (CN VII) palsy** is highly characteristic.
        ▪ **Bulbar weakness** (CN IX, X, XII) can cause dysphagia, dysarthria, and difficulty managing secretions.
        ▪ Oculomotor nerve (CN III, IV, VI) involvement can cause ophthalmoplegia.
    ◦ **Autonomic Dysfunction:**
        ▪ Occurs in ~70% of cases and can be life-threatening.
        ▪ Tachycardia (most common), bradycardia, arrhythmias.
        ▪ Labile blood pressure (hypertension or orthostatic hypotension).
        ▪ Urinary retention, ileus, loss of sweating.
• **Physical Exam Findings**
    ◦ **Motor:** Symmetric, flaccid weakness, typically greater distally than proximally in the early stages.
    ◦ **Reflexes:** ***Loss of Deep Tendon Reflexes (DTRs) / areflexia*** is a cardinal sign. May be initially present but diminishes or disappears within days.
    ◦ **Cranial Nerves:** Assess for facial droop (ask patient to smile, close eyes tightly), dysarthria, and gag reflex.
    ◦ **Sensory:** Often minimal to no objective sensory loss despite subjective paresthesias. Vibratory and position sense may be affected.
    ◦ **Gait:** Ataxia or inability to ambulate.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) Analysis via Lumbar Puncture (LP):**
    ◦ **Classic Finding:** ***Albuminocytologic dissociation***.
    ◦ **High Protein:** (>55 mg/dL) due to inflammation and breakdown of nerve roots.
    ◦ **Normal WBC count:** (<10 cells/mm3), indicating a non-infectious process.
    ◦ *Note:* CSF protein may be normal in the first week of symptoms, peaking at 2-4 weeks.
• **Electromyography (EMG) and Nerve Conduction Studies (NCS):**
    ◦ **Most specific test for GBS**, confirms the diagnosis.
    ◦ Findings are consistent with **demyelination**:
        ▪ Slowed nerve conduction velocities.
        ▪ Prolonged distal latencies.
        ▪ Conduction block or temporal dispersion.
    ◦ Usually performed 1-2 weeks after symptom onset when findings are most apparent.
• **Pulmonary Function Tests (PFTs):**
    ◦ **Crucial for monitoring respiratory status**, not for diagnosis.
    ◦ **Forced Vital Capacity (FVC):** Measures the amount of air that can be exhaled. A sharp decline suggests impending respiratory failure.
    ◦ **Negative Inspiratory Force (NIF):** Measures inspiratory muscle strength.
    ◦ **Indications for intubation:**
        ▪ FVC < 20 mL/kg
        ▪ NIF < -30 cm H2O
        ▪ Signs of clinical respiratory distress (hypoxia, accessory muscle use).
• **Imaging:**
    ◦ MRI of the spine may be done to rule out other causes like transverse myelitis or spinal cord compression. It may show enhancement of the cauda equina nerve roots.
sections.treatment:
• **Note:** Treatment is aimed at halting the autoimmune process and does not repair existing damage. Early treatment is crucial.
• **First-Line Therapies (Equally effective):**
• **Therapies to AVOID:**
    ◦ ***Corticosteroids (e.g., Prednisone) are NOT effective in GBS and should NOT be used.***
sections.management:
• **Supportive care is the cornerstone of management.**
• **Hospitalization:** All patients with suspected GBS should be hospitalized for monitoring. Severe cases require ICU admission.
• **Respiratory Monitoring:** Serial PFTs (FVC, NIF) every 4-8 hours. Have a low threshold for elective intubation.
• **Autonomic Monitoring:** Continuous cardiac and blood pressure monitoring. Treat hypotension with IV fluids/pressors and hypertension with short-acting agents (e.g., labetalol).
• **DVT Prophylaxis:** Immobility necessitates prophylaxis with subcutaneous heparin or LMWH, plus compression stockings.
• **Pain Control:** Neuropathic pain is common. Treat with gabapentin, carbamazepine, or TCAs.
• **Nutrition & Hydration:** May require an NG tube if dysphagia is present.
• **Rehabilitation:** Early involvement of physical, occupational, and speech therapy is vital for recovery.
sections.complications:
• **Respiratory Failure:** Most life-threatening complication, occurring in up to 30% of patients.
• **Autonomic Instability:** Cardiac arrhythmias, profound hypotension/hypertension, cardiovascular collapse.
• **Thromboembolism (DVT/PE):** Due to prolonged immobility.
• **Aspiration Pneumonia:** Resulting from bulbar weakness and dysphagia.
• **Nosocomial Infections:** Sepsis, ventilator-associated pneumonia, UTIs.
• **Pressure Ulcers / Contractures:** Complications of immobility.
• **Chronic Neuropathic Pain & Fatigue:** Can persist long after motor recovery.
sections.prognosis:
• **Mortality:** ~3-7%, usually due to respiratory failure, autonomic dysfunction, or sepsis.
• **Recovery:**
    ◦ ~85% of patients achieve a full and functional recovery, although it may take months to years.
    ◦ ~20% are left with significant long-term neurological deficits (e.g., persistent weakness).
    ◦ ~3% may experience a relapse.
• **Poor Prognostic Indicators:**
    ◦ Older age (>60)
    ◦ Rapidly progressive weakness
    ◦ Severe weakness at nadir (quadriplegia)
    ◦ Need for mechanical ventilation
    ◦ Preceding *C. jejuni* infection (associated with axonal variant)

sections.overview:
• Chronic Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy (CIDP) is an acquired, immune-mediated disorder of the peripheral nervous system characterized by progressive or relapsing-remitting, symmetric sensorimotor deficits.
• It is the **chronic counterpart to acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP), the most common form of Guillain-Barr Syndrome (GBS)**.
    ◦ The key differentiating factor is the time course: CIDP symptoms progress for **>8 weeks**, whereas GBS symptoms peak within 4 weeks.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ Primarily **idiopathic and immune-mediated**.
    ◦ It is not typically preceded by a specific infection in the same way GBS is, though some cases may follow an illness or vaccination.
    ◦ It can be associated with other systemic conditions.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Autoimmune Attack**: An autoimmune response, involving both cellular (T-cell mediated) and humoral (antibody-mediated) immunity, targets components of the peripheral nerve myelin sheath and Schwann cells.
    ◦ **Demyelination**: Macrophages strip the myelin from the peripheral nerves, leading to segmental demyelination. This process impairs nerve signal conduction.
    ◦ **Mechanism of Deficit**: The slowed or blocked nerve conduction along multiple motor and sensory nerves results in the clinical manifestations of weakness, sensory loss, and areflexia.
    ◦ **Chronic Nature**: Unlike the self-limited process in GBS, the inflammatory process in CIDP is persistent or recurrent, leading to chronic demyelination and secondary axonal damage over time. Repeated cycles of demyelination and remyelination can lead to "onion bulb" formations on nerve biopsy.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Relatively rare, estimated at 1-9 cases per 100,000 people.
• **Age of Onset**: Can occur at any age, but there is a bimodal distribution with peaks in young adulthood and again in older age (50s-60s).
• **Gender**: Slightly more common in males (M:F ratio 2:1).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is one of **insidious, slowly progressive, symmetric weakness** affecting both proximal and distal muscles, accompanied by sensory loss.
• The course can be:
    ◦ **Slowly progressive**: A steady decline in function over months to years.
    ◦ **Relapsing-remitting**: Episodes of neurological worsening followed by periods of partial or complete recovery.
• Patients typically present with complaints of difficulty walking, climbing stairs, rising from a chair, or using their hands for fine motor tasks.
• The progression over **more than 8 weeks** is the hallmark that distinguishes it from GBS.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Electrophysiologic Studies (EMG/NCS)**
    ◦ **The most important diagnostic test**. Confirms a demyelinating process and is required for diagnosis.
    ◦ Key findings include:
        ▪ **Markedly slowed nerve conduction velocities (NCVs)**.
        ▪ Prolonged distal motor latencies.
        ▪ Evidence of **conduction block** or temporal dispersion.
        ▪ Prolonged or absent F-wave responses.
• **Lumbar Puncture (CSF Analysis)**
    ◦ Classic finding is **albuminocytologic dissociation**:
        ▪ **Elevated CSF protein** (>45 mg/dL).
        ▪ **Normal white blood cell count** (<10 cells/L).
    ◦ This finding is identical to GBS, making the clinical timeline crucial for differentiation.
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ To rule out mimics and associated conditions.
    ◦ CBC, CMP, HbA1c, TSH, Vitamin B12 level.
    ◦ Serum and urine protein electrophoresis (SPEP/UPEP) with immunofixation to screen for monoclonal gammopathy (e.g., MGUS).
    ◦ HIV, Hepatitis B/C serologies.
• **Nerve Biopsy (Rarely needed)**
    ◦ Reserved for atypical cases or when electrodiagnostic studies are inconclusive.
    ◦ Shows evidence of segmental demyelination, inflammatory infiltrates, and classic **"onion bulb"** formations (concentric layers of Schwann cells from cycles of de- and re-myelination).
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is variable but generally favorable with treatment.
• Approximately **two-thirds of patients respond well** to initial immunotherapy.
• A monophasic progressive course has a better prognosis than a relapsing-remitting course.
• Despite treatment, many patients are left with some residual sensory or motor deficits. A minority may become wheelchair-dependent.

sections.overview:
• Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) and Becker Muscular Dystrophy (BMD) are **X-linked recessive**, progressive muscular dystrophies caused by mutations in the *DMD* gene, which codes for the protein **dystrophin**.
    ◦ They are part of a spectrum of diseases called "dystrophinopathies."
• **Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD)**: The more severe form.
    ◦ Caused by a mutation (often frameshift) that leads to a **near-complete absence** of functional dystrophin.
    ◦ Presents in early childhood with rapid progression.
• **Becker Muscular Dystrophy (BMD)**: The milder form.
    ◦ Caused by a mutation (often in-frame) that produces a **partially functional, truncated** dystrophin protein.
    ◦ Presents later in childhood or adolescence with slower progression.
sections.etiology:
• **Gene**: Mutation in the dystrophin (*DMD*) gene located on the **X chromosome (Xp21)**.
    ◦ It is the largest known human gene, making it susceptible to spontaneous mutations.
• **Protein**: Dystrophin is a crucial structural protein in muscle cells (myocytes).
    ◦ It acts as a "shock absorber," anchoring the intracellular actin cytoskeleton to the dystroglycan complex in the cell membrane (sarcolemma), which in turn connects to the extracellular matrix.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Defective Dystrophin**: In DMD, dystrophin is **absent**. In BMD, it is **reduced** in amount or size.
    ◦ **Sarcolemma Instability**: Without functional dystrophin, the sarcolemma becomes fragile and is easily damaged during muscle contraction and relaxation.
    ◦ **Increased Permeability**: Microtears in the sarcolemma lead to an influx of extracellular **calcium (Ca2+)**.
    ◦ **Cell Death Cascade**: Elevated intracellular Ca2+ activates proteases, leading to mitochondrial damage, inflammation, and **myocyte necrosis**.
    ◦ **Fibrofatty Replacement**: Damaged muscle fibers are progressively replaced by adipose and fibrous connective tissue.
        ▪ This leads to the characteristic **pseudohypertrophy** and profound muscle weakness.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Inheritance**: **X-linked recessive**.
    ◦ Primarily affects males.
    ◦ Females are typically carriers but can be mildly symptomatic ("**manifesting carriers**").
• **Incidence**:
    ◦ **DMD**: ~1 in 3,500 to 5,000 live male births.
    ◦ **BMD**: ~1 in 18,000 to 30,000 live male births.
• **Mutations**: Approximately two-thirds of cases are inherited from a carrier mother; one-third are due to new, spontaneous (*de novo*) mutations.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **DMD**: Presents between ages 2-5.
    ◦ Parents report child is a "**late walker**," clumsy, has frequent falls, and struggles to climb stairs or keep up with peers.
    ◦ **Loss of ambulation** typically occurs by age 12.
• **BMD**: Presents later, from age 5 to early adulthood (average age ~12).
    ◦ Patients present with muscle cramping, fatigue, or mild weakness.
    ◦ Ambulation is often preserved into the 30s or beyond.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Initial Lab Test (Screening)**:
    ◦ **Serum Creatine Kinase (CK)**: Markedly elevated.
        ▪ **DMD**: 10-100 times the upper limit of normal (often >10,000-20,000 U/L). Highest in early childhood and declines as muscle mass is lost.
        ▪ **BMD**: Elevated, but typically lower than in DMD (e.g., 5-50x normal).
    ◦ **AST/ALT** may also be elevated (as they are present in muscle), which can be mistaken for liver disease.
• **Confirmatory Test**:
    ◦ **Genetic Testing (DNA analysis)**: **Gold standard**.
        ▪ Identifies deletions, duplications, or point mutations in the *DMD* gene.
        ▪ Confirms the diagnosis and can distinguish between DMD and BMD.
• **Ancillary/Historical Tests**:
    ◦ **Muscle Biopsy**: Performed if genetic testing is inconclusive.
        ▪ **Histology**: Shows variation in muscle fiber size, necrotic/regenerating fibers, and extensive endomysial connective tissue (**fibrofatty replacement**).
        ▪ **Immunostaining for Dystrophin (DMD)**: Shows **absent or severely reduced** (<3%) dystrophin staining.
        ▪ **Immunostaining for Dystrophin (BMD)**: Shows **reduced or abnormally sized** dystrophin staining.
    ◦ **Echocardiogram (Echo) & ECG**: Essential for baseline cardiac evaluation and ongoing monitoring for **cardiomyopathy**.
    ◦ **Pulmonary Function Tests (PFTs)**: To monitor respiratory muscle strength.
sections.prognosis:
• **DMD**: Without intervention, **loss of ambulation** occurs around age 12, with death in the late teens or early 20s.
    ◦ With modern comprehensive care (steroids, ventilation, cardiac management), life expectancy has extended into the 30s and sometimes 40s.
    ◦ Death is typically from **respiratory failure** or **cardiomyopathy**.
• **BMD**: Highly variable.
    ◦ Ambulation may be maintained well into adulthood.
    ◦ Many patients have a near-normal lifespan, though **cardiomyopathy** remains a significant cause of morbidity and mortality.

sections.overview:
• Parkinson Disease (PD) is a chronic, progressive neurodegenerative disorder primarily affecting the motor system.
• It is characterized by the cardinal features of a **resting tremor**, **bradykinesia**, **rigidity**, and **postural instability**.
• The disease also involves significant non-motor symptoms.
• It is the second most common neurodegenerative disease after Alzheimer disease.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ Primarily **idiopathic** (>90% of cases).
    ◦ A smaller percentage is linked to genetic mutations (e.g., *SNCA*, *LRRK2*, *PARK7* genes).
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The core pathology is the progressive **loss of dopaminergic neurons** in the **substantia nigra pars compacta**, which is part of the basal ganglia in the midbrain.
        ▪ These neurons project to the striatum (caudate and putamen), and their loss leads to a significant **deficiency of dopamine**.
    ◦ This dopamine depletion disrupts the balance of the basal ganglia's motor circuits (the direct and indirect pathways), resulting in a net inhibition of the thalamus and reduced excitatory input to the motor cortex.
        ▪ The ultimate effect is a disruption of smooth, controlled movement, leading to the characteristic motor symptoms.
    ◦ The histopathological hallmark is the presence of **Lewy bodies**, which are abnormal intracytoplasmic eosinophilic aggregates of **alpha-synuclein protein** within the remaining neurons.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** Affects approximately 1% of the population over age 60.
• **Incidence:** Increases sharply with age.
    ◦ Mean age of onset is ~60 years.
    ◦ Early-onset PD (<50 years) is less common and more likely to have a genetic link.
• **Sex:** Slightly more common in men than women (M:F ratio ~1.5:1).
sections.riskFactors:
• **Definite:**
    ◦ **Advancing age** (strongest risk factor)
    ◦ Family history / certain genetic mutations
• **Probable:**
    ◦ Male sex
    ◦ Environmental exposures (pesticides, herbicides, heavy metals)
    ◦ History of head trauma
• **Protective Factors (Negative Associations):**
    ◦ Cigarette smoking
    ◦ Caffeine consumption
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Onset:** Insidious and gradual.
• **Laterality:** Symptoms typically begin **asymmetrically**, affecting one side of the body first before progressing to become bilateral over years.
• The classic presentation is a patient (often in their 60s) who notices a slight tremor in one hand at rest, a general slowness in daily activities, softer speech (**hypophonia**), or smaller handwriting (**micrographia**).
    ◦ Family members may notice a lack of facial expression (**masked facies**).
sections.physicalExam:
• **General Observation:** Stooped posture, **masked facies** (**hypomimia**).
• **Gait:**
    ◦ **Shuffling gait** with short steps.
    ◦ **Festinating gait:** Progressive shortening of stride and quickening of pace, often leading to falls.
    ◦ **En bloc turning:** Turning the whole body as a single unit, rather than pivoting.
    ◦ Decreased or absent arm swing.
• **Motor Exam:**
    ◦ **Tremor:** Observe for the classic resting **pill-rolling tremor**.
    ◦ **Tone:** Assess for **cogwheel** or **lead-pipe rigidity** at the wrist, elbow, and neck.
    ◦ **Bradykinesia:** Assessed by rapid alternating movements (e.g., finger tapping, hand opening/closing, foot tapping); look for slowness and reduction in amplitude.
• **Special Tests:**
    ◦ **Pull Test:** Stand behind the patient and pull them backward by the shoulders. A positive test (**retropulsion**) is a fall or taking more than 2 steps backward to regain balance, indicating **postural instability**.
    ◦ **Myerson's Sign (Glabellar Tap Reflex):** Repetitive tapping on the glabella (forehead) produces a sustained blink response. Non-specific but often present.
sections.diagnostics:
• Parkinson Disease is a **clinical diagnosis**.
    ◦ There are no definitive blood tests or standard imaging to diagnose idiopathic PD.
• **Diagnostic Criteria:** Based on the UK Parkinson's Disease Society Brain Bank Clinical Diagnostic Criteria:
    ◦ **Bradykinesia** is required.
    ◦ Plus at least one of the following: **muscular rigidity**, **resting tremor**, or **postural instability**.
• **Supportive Evidence:** A dramatic and sustained response to **levodopa** is highly suggestive of PD.
• **Imaging:**
    ◦ **MRI of the Brain:** Primarily used to **rule out other pathologies** (e.g., stroke, tumor, normal pressure hydrocephalus). Usually normal in idiopathic PD.
    ◦ **Dopamine Transporter Scan (DaTscan):** A nuclear medicine scan that visualizes dopamine transporters in the brain.
        ▪ Can help differentiate PD from conditions like Essential Tremor but cannot distinguish PD from other parkinsonian syndromes (e.g., MSA, PSP).
        ▪ Not routinely used for initial diagnosis.
sections.management:
• **Initial Therapy:** Decision is individualized based on age, symptom severity, and lifestyle.
    ◦ **Younger patients (<65):** Often start with a **Dopamine Agonist** or **MAO-B inhibitor** to delay levodopa use.
    ◦ **Older patients (>65)** or those with significant functional impairment: **Levodopa/Carbidopa** is the preferred initial agent.
• **Management of Motor Complications:**
    ◦ **"Wearing-off":** Increase levodopa dose/frequency, add a **COMT inhibitor** or **MAO-B inhibitor**.
    ◦ **Dyskinesias:** Reduce levodopa dose, add **Amantadine**.
• **Non-pharmacologic Management:** Essential for all stages.
    ◦ **Physical & Occupational Therapy:** To improve gait, balance, strength, and ability to perform activities of daily living (ADLs).
    ◦ **Speech Therapy:** For **hypophonia** and **dysphagia**.
    ◦ **Nutrition:** High-fiber diet for constipation. Protein can interfere with levodopa absorption, so medication should be taken 30-60 min before meals.
    ◦ Patient and family education and support.
sections.complications:
• **Falls** and related fractures due to **postural instability**.
