• **Neuropsychiatric disturbances:** Psychosis, hallucinations (often a side effect of medication), depression, dementia (**Parkinson Disease Dementia**).
• **Aspiration pneumonia** secondary to **dysphagia**.
• Autonomic failure leading to severe **orthostatic hypotension** or constipation.
• Medication-related side effects (**dyskinesias**, impulse control disorders).
sections.prognosis:
• PD is a progressive disorder without a cure.
• The rate of progression is highly variable among individuals.
• Life expectancy is reduced compared to the general population, but many patients live for 15-20 years after diagnosis.
• Mortality is typically due to secondary complications such as pneumonia or falls, not the disease itself.

sections.overview:
• Essential Tremor (ET) is the **most common movement disorder**
• A progressive neurological condition characterized primarily by a **bilateral action tremor** (both postural and kinetic) of the hands and forearms
    ◦ Can also affect the head, voice, and lower limbs
• Distinct from Parkinson's disease as it is **not associated with bradykinesia, rigidity, or a resting tremor**
• While often considered benign, it can cause significant functional disability and social embarrassment
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ The exact cause is unknown, but a strong genetic component is well-established
    ◦ **Genetics**
        ▪ Approximately 50-70% of cases are familial, inherited in an **autosomal dominant** pattern with variable penetrance
        ▪ Several genetic loci have been identified, but no single gene is responsible for all cases
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ Not fully understood, but considered a disorder of the central nervous system, not the peripheral nerves or muscles
    ◦ **Cerebellar Dysfunction**
        ▪ The leading theory involves dysfunction within the **cerebello-thalamo-cortical circuit**, which is responsible for coordinating and timing movements
    ◦ **Pathological Findings**
        ▪ Post-mortem studies show a loss of **Purkinje cells** in the cerebellum
        ▪ There may also be evidence of cerebellar cortical atrophy
    ◦ **Neurotransmitter Imbalance**
        ▪ A primary hypothesis involves dysfunction of **GABAergic** neurons, leading to oscillatory activity in the motor pathways
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Most common movement disorder worldwide, affecting up to 1% of the general population and up to 5% of individuals over age 65
• **Age of Onset**: Can occur at any age but has a **bimodal distribution**, with peaks in the 2nd decade (adolescence/young adulthood) and the 6th decade (older adulthood)
• **Gender**: Affects men and women equally
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Typically presents with a **slowly progressive, symmetric tremor** of the hands that is most noticeable during volitional movement
• Chief complaint is often difficulty with fine motor tasks like writing, using utensils, or drinking from a glass
• Patient may report the tremor is:
    ◦ Exacerbated by **stress, anxiety, or fatigue**
    ◦ Temporarily relieved by a small amount of **alcohol**
• The neurological exam is otherwise normal
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**
    ◦ Diagnosis is made based on history and physical exam findings
    ◦ There are no specific blood tests or imaging studies to confirm ET
• **Diagnosis of Exclusion**
    ◦ Laboratory and imaging tests are used to rule out other causes of tremor
• **Labs**
    ◦ **TSH**: To rule out hyperthyroidism
    ◦ **CMP**: To rule out hepatic or renal dysfunction
    ◦ **Ceruloplasmin**: Consider in patients <40 years old to rule out Wilson's disease
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Brain MRI**
        ▪ Not routinely indicated
        ▪ Consider if there are atypical features (e.g., sudden onset, unilateral tremor, other focal neurological deficits) to rule out a structural lesion (e.g., stroke, tumor)
    ◦ **DaTscan (Dopamine Transporter Scan)**
        ▪ **Normal** in ET
        ▪ Can be used to differentiate from Parkinson's disease, which shows decreased dopamine transporter uptake in the striatum
sections.prognosis:
• The condition is **slowly progressive** over many years
• It **does not affect life expectancy**
• The degree of disability varies widely
    ◦ Some individuals have a very mild tremor that never requires treatment
    ◦ Others develop severe, disabling tremors

sections.overview:
• Huntington Disease (HD) is a progressive, fatal, autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder.
• Clinically characterized by a classic triad of **motor dysfunction (chorea)**, **cognitive decline (dementia)**, and **psychiatric disturbances**.
• Caused by an expansion of a CAG trinucleotide repeat in the huntingtin (*HTT*) gene.
    ◦ This leads to selective neuronal loss, most prominently in the **caudate nucleus and putamen** of the basal ganglia.
• There is no cure, and treatment is focused on managing symptoms.
sections.etiology:
• **Genetic Defect**: Autosomal dominant mutation in the **Huntingtin (*HTT*) gene** located on the short arm of **chromosome 4**.
• **Mutation Type**: **CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion**, which codes for an abnormally long polyglutamine (polyQ) tract in the huntingtin protein.
• **Pathogenesis**:
    ◦ The mutant huntingtin protein (mHTT) misfolds and aggregates, forming toxic intracellular inclusions in neurons.
    ◦ This leads to mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired axonal transport, and ultimately, neuronal cell death.
    ◦ The most severely affected cells are the **GABAergic medium spiny neurons** in the **striatum (caudate and putamen)**.
    ◦ Loss of these inhibitory neurons leads to disinhibition of the thalamus, resulting in hyperkinetic movements like chorea.
• **CAG Repeat Lengths**: The number of repeats correlates with disease onset and severity.
    ◦ **< 26 repeats**: Normal; unaffected.
    ◦ **27-35 repeats**: Intermediate; unaffected but at risk for expansion in offspring (premutation).
    ◦ **36-39 repeats**: Reduced penetrance; may or may not develop symptoms, often with later onset.
    ◦ **≥ 40 repeats**: Full penetrance; individual will develop HD.
• **Anticipation**: A phenomenon where the disease appears at an earlier age and with greater severity in successive generations.
    ◦ This is due to the instability of the CAG repeat, which tends to expand further during meiosis, particularly during **paternal transmission (spermatogenesis)**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Most common in populations of European descent (~5-10 per 100,000).
    ◦ Less common in Asian and African populations.
• **Age of Onset**: Typically between **30 and 50 years old**.
• **Juvenile HD**:
    ◦ Onset before age 20 (<10% of cases).
    ◦ Often associated with very large CAG repeats (>60).
    ◦ More commonly inherited from the father.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The onset is insidious.
• A typical patient is a 35-50 year old who presents with subtle, unintentional jerky movements, clumsiness, or changes in personality like irritability, apathy, or depression.
• There is often a positive family history, although it may be concealed or misdiagnosed in previous generations (e.g., "died of nervous illness," "alcoholism," or "schizophrenia").
sections.diagnostics:
• **Genetic Testing**: **The definitive and confirmatory test.**
    ◦ A blood test analyzes the *HTT* gene for the number of CAG repeats.
    ◦ Performed in symptomatic individuals to confirm the diagnosis.
    ◦ **Predictive testing** is available for asymptomatic at-risk individuals.
        ▪ Requires extensive pre- and post-test genetic counseling.
• **Neuroimaging (CT or MRI)**: Not diagnostic but highly supportive.
    ◦ The classic finding is **atrophy of the caudate nucleus and putamen**.
        ▪ This atrophy leads to the secondary enlargement of the anterior horns of the lateral ventricles, giving them a **"boxcar ventricle"** appearance on coronal views.
    ◦ Generalized cerebral atrophy is seen in later stages.
sections.prognosis:
• **Incurable and universally fatal**.
• The disease progresses relentlessly over **15-20 years** from the time of symptom onset.
• Death is typically due to a complication (e.g., pneumonia, fall) rather than the primary pathology itself.

sections.overview:
• **Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS)**, also known as **Willis-Ekbom disease**, is a common sensorimotor neurological disorder characterized by an irresistible urge to move the legs, typically accompanied by uncomfortable or unpleasant sensations.
• Symptoms are characteristically:
    ◦ Worse during periods of rest or inactivity.
    ◦ Have a circadian pattern with worsening in the evening or at night.
    ◦ Are transiently relieved by movement.
• RLS is a major cause of sleep disturbance and can significantly impair quality of life.
sections.etiology:
• The exact pathophysiology is not fully understood but is thought to involve two primary mechanisms:
    ◦ **Central Nervous System (CNS) Iron Dysregulation**:
        ▪ There is a state of "**brain iron deficiency**" despite normal peripheral iron stores.
        ▪ Iron is a crucial cofactor for tyrosine hydroxylase, the rate-limiting enzyme in the synthesis of **dopamine**.
        ▪ Reduced iron levels in key brain areas (e.g., substantia nigra, putamen) lead to impaired **dopamine** production and receptor function.
    ◦ **Dopaminergic System Dysfunction**:
        ▪ The dopaminergic pathways, particularly the A11 pathway that projects to the spinal cord, are implicated in modulating sensory input.
        ▪ Dysfunction in this system leads to a state of spinal cord hyperexcitability, resulting in the characteristic sensory symptoms and motor restlessness.
        ▪ The circadian nature of symptoms may be linked to the natural diurnal fluctuation of **dopamine** levels, which are lowest at night.
• RLS can be classified as:
    ◦ **Primary (Idiopathic)**: Most common form, often has a strong genetic component with an early age of onset (<45 years).
    ◦ **Secondary**: Caused by or strongly associated with an underlying medical condition or medication.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects 5-15% of the general adult population in Western countries.
• **Gender**: More common in women than men (approx. 2:1 ratio).
• **Age**: Prevalence and severity increase with age. Onset can occur at any age, but clinically significant symptoms are most common in middle-aged and older adults.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a patient complaining of difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep.
• They describe an "**uncontrollable**" or "**overwhelming**" need to move their legs when trying to relax in the evening, such as when watching TV or lying in bed.
• They may report that their sleep partner complains of them kicking or thrashing at night.
• The patient often experiences significant **daytime sleepiness** and fatigue due to poor sleep quality.
sections.diagnostics:
• RLS is a **clinical diagnosis** based on the 4 essential criteria (URGE).
• **Laboratory Studies (to rule out secondary causes)**:
    ◦ **Serum Ferritin and Iron Panel (TIBC, serum iron)**:
        ▪ **Essential for all patients.**
        ▪ A ferritin level **< 75 ng/mL** warrants iron supplementation.
    ◦ **Complete Blood Count (CBC)**: To assess for anemia.
    ◦ **Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP) / Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP)**: To assess renal function (BUN, Creatinine) and electrolytes.
• **Other Studies**:
    ◦ **Polysomnography (Sleep Study)**:
        ▪ Not required for the diagnosis of RLS.
        ▪ Its primary role is to evaluate for **Periodic Limb Movements of Sleep (PLMS)**, which are rhythmic extensions and flexions of the limbs during sleep.
        ▪ **PLMS** are present in >80% of patients with RLS.
        ▪ A sleep study can also help rule out other sleep disorders like obstructive sleep apnea that may be contributing to symptoms.
sections.prognosis:
• RLS is a chronic condition with no cure.
• Prognosis for symptom control is generally good with appropriate management.
• Symptoms can fluctuate, with periods of remission and exacerbation.
• In **secondary RLS** (e.g., pregnancy-induced), symptoms often resolve once the underlying cause is treated.

sections.overview:
• Tourette Syndrome (TS) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by the presence of multiple motor tics and at least one vocal (phonic) tic.
    ◦ Tics are typically repetitive, stereotyped, and involuntary, though they can be **temporarily suppressed**.
• The onset is in childhood, and the severity follows a characteristic **waxing and waning course**.
    ◦ Often peaks in early adolescence and improves in adulthood.
• TS is frequently associated with **comorbid psychiatric conditions**, most notably **ADHD** and **OCD**.
    ◦ These comorbidities often cause more functional impairment than the tics themselves.
sections.etiology:
• The exact etiology is unknown but is understood to be a combination of genetic and environmental factors.
• **Genetics**
    ◦ Strong genetic component; it is one of the most heritable neuropsychiatric disorders of childhood.
    ◦ Multiple susceptibility genes are likely involved.
• **Neurobiology**
    ◦ The leading theory involves dysfunction in the **cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical (CSTC) circuits**.
• **Dopamine Dysregulation**
    ◦ This is the primary hypothesis.
    ◦ It suggests hyperactivity or hypersensitivity of postsynaptic **dopamine D2 receptors** in the striatum (part of the basal ganglia).
    ◦ This leads to a "failure of inhibition" in the motor and limbic pathways, resulting in unwanted movements and sounds (tics).
    ◦ This is supported by the efficacy of dopamine-blocking agents in treating tics.
• **Other Neurotransmitters**
    ◦ Serotonin and norepinephrine systems may also be involved, which could explain the high comorbidity with OCD and ADHD.
• **PANDAS/PANS**
    ◦ Pediatric Autoimmune Neuropsychiatric Disorders Associated with Streptococcal Infections (PANDAS) is a hypothesis suggesting that a post-streptococcal autoimmune process can trigger an abrupt onset or exacerbation of tics and OCD.
    ◦ This remains a controversial but recognized clinical entity.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects up to 1% of school-aged children.
• **Gender**: **Males are affected 3-4 times more often** than females.
• **Age of Onset**: Typically between **4 and 6 years old**.
    ◦ Tics almost always appear before age 18.
• **Peak Severity**: Tics usually worsen and peak in severity around ages **10-12 years**.
• **Course**: Tics often improve significantly during late adolescence and early adulthood.
    ◦ A majority of patients experience a marked reduction in tic severity by adulthood.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient, typically a 7-year-old boy, is brought to the clinic by his parents due to "strange habits."
• Parents report tics for the past year:
    ◦ **Motor tics**: Persistent **eye blinking** and **facial grimacing**.
    ◦ **Vocal tics**: Recently started making a **throat-clearing sound**.
• Tic Characteristics:
    ◦ Worse when stressed or excited.
    ◦ Decrease when focused on an enjoyable activity.
    ◦ Can be suppressed for a short time, but then seem to burst out even worse.
• Associated Comorbid Features:
    ◦ Significant trouble paying attention in school (suggestive of **ADHD**).
    ◦ Very particular about how things are arranged on his desk (suggestive of **OCD**).
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is **purely clinical** based on history and observation, using the DSM-5 criteria.
    ◦ No lab tests or imaging can confirm TS.
• **DSM-5 Diagnostic Criteria**
    ◦ **Both multiple motor tics and one or more vocal tics** have been present at some time during the illness, though not necessarily concurrently.
    ◦ The tics may wax and wane in frequency but have persisted for **more than 1 year** since the first tic onset.
    ◦ Onset is **before age 18 years**.
    ◦ The disturbance is not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance or another medical condition.
• **Labs/Imaging**
    ◦ Not routinely indicated.
    ◦ May be considered if the presentation is atypical (e.g., sudden onset in adolescence, other neurological signs).
        ▪ An MRI of the brain.
        ▪ Labs (e.g., serum ceruloplasmin to rule out Wilson's disease, ASO titer for PANDAS).
sections.prognosis:
• The long-term prognosis is generally **favorable**.
• Tics typically **peak in severity around ages 10-12** and then decline through adolescence.
• By early adulthood:
    ◦ About **one-third of individuals become tic-free**.
    ◦ Another third have mild tics that are not impairing.
    ◦ The final third have persistent tics that may require ongoing management.
• Comorbid conditions like **OCD and anxiety** may persist into adulthood and often cause more long-term morbidity than the tics themselves.

sections.overview:
• Neurological condition characterized by the **compression** or **irritation** of a **cervical nerve root** as it exits the spinal column.
	◦ This compression leads to a constellation of symptoms, including **pain**, **sensory deficits** (paresthesias), and/or **motor weakness** that radiates from the neck into the distribution of the affected nerve root (**dermatome** and **myotome**).
	◦ It is colloquially known as a "**pinched nerve**" in the neck.
sections.etiology:
• The underlying cause is **nerve root compression**, which can be due to mechanical compression, inflammation, or both.
	◦ The specific etiology often correlates with patient age.
• **Degenerative Changes (Spondylosis)** - Most common cause overall, especially in **older adults (>50 years)**:
	◦ **Foraminal Stenosis**: Narrowing of the **intervertebral foramen** (the opening where the nerve root exits) due to:
		▪ **Osteophyte formation**: Bony spurs from the uncovertebral joints (Luschka) or facet joints.
		▪ **Degenerative Disc Disease (DDD)**: Loss of disc height reduces foraminal space.
		▪ **Ligamentum Flavum Hypertrophy**: Thickening of the ligament further narrows the space.
• **Herniated Nucleus Pulposus (HNP)** - Most common cause in **younger patients (<50 years)**:
	◦ The soft, gel-like center of an intervertebral disc protrudes through a tear in the outer **annulus fibrosus**, directly impinging on the nerve root.
		▪ This is often posterolateral.
• **Less Common Causes**:
	◦ Trauma (e.g., fracture leading to foraminal narrowing)
	◦ Spinal tumors (e.g., schwannoma, neurofibroma)
	◦ Spinal infection (e.g., epidural abscess, discitis)
	◦ Synovial cysts
• **Note**: The **C7 nerve root** is the most commonly affected, followed by **C6**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects approximately 85 per 100,000 people.
• **Peak Incidence**: Bimodal distribution.
	◦ **4th decade (30-40s)**: Primarily due to acute **disc herniation**.
	◦ **6th-7th decades (50-60s)**: Primarily due to degenerative **foraminal stenosis**.
• **Most Common Levels**:
	◦ **C7**: ~45-60% of cases
	◦ **C6**: ~20-25% of cases
	◦ **C5 & C8**: Less common
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with an insidious or acute onset of **neck pain** that **radiates** into the shoulder, arm, or hand.
	◦ The pain is often described as **sharp**, **shooting**, or "**electric**."
• Patients may hold their head tilted **away** from the affected side to relieve tension on the nerve root.
• Symptoms are often exacerbated by neck movements, particularly **extension** and **rotation/lateral bending toward** the symptomatic side.
• A key historical feature is the relief of symptoms when the patient places their hand on top of their head (**Shoulder Abduction Relief Sign**).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Plain Radiographs (X-rays)**
	◦ **Views**: AP, lateral, oblique.
	◦ **Findings**: Can show chronic **degenerative changes** like decreased disc height, **osteophytes**, and **foraminal narrowing** (best seen on oblique views). Useful to rule out fracture or instability. Often the first imaging test.
• **Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)**
	◦ **Gold standard / test of choice**.
	◦ Provides excellent visualization of soft tissues, including the **spinal cord**, **nerve roots**, and **intervertebral discs**.
	◦ Directly shows **nerve root compression** from a **herniated disc** or **stenosis**.
	◦ Usually performed without contrast.
• **Computed Tomography (CT) Myelogram**
	◦ Alternative to MRI when contraindicated (e.g., pacemaker).
	◦ Involves injecting contrast into the **thecal sac** to visualize the spinal cord and nerve roots with CT imaging.
	◦ Excellent bony detail.
• **Electromyography (EMG) / Nerve Conduction Studies (NCS)**
	◦ Not for initial diagnosis but useful to:
		▪ Confirm the diagnosis if imaging is equivocal.
		▪ Assess the severity and chronicity of nerve damage.
		▪ Differentiate **radiculopathy** from **peripheral neuropathies** (e.g., carpal tunnel syndrome, ulnar neuropathy).
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**. The natural history is generally favorable.
• **75-90%** of patients improve with **conservative management** alone.
• Symptoms often resolve spontaneously over weeks to several months.
• Recurrence is possible.

sections.overview:
• **Lumbar radiculopathy** is a condition characterized by pain, sensory changes, and/or motor weakness resulting from the compression or irritation of a nerve root in the lumbar spine.
	◦ **"Sciatica"** is a common term used to describe radiculopathy involving the sciatic nerve, which originates from the **L4-S3 nerve roots** and is the most frequent presentation.
	◦ The hallmark is **neuropathic pain** radiating from the low back or buttock down the leg in a specific nerve root distribution (dermatome).
sections.etiology:
• The underlying cause is nerve root impingement, which leads to both mechanical compression and chemical irritation.
• **Most Common Cause (>90%): Herniated Nucleus Pulposus (HNP)**
	◦ The soft, gel-like nucleus pulposus extrudes through a tear in the annulus fibrosus of the intervertebral disc.
	◦ **Posterolateral herniation** is the most common type, as the posterior longitudinal ligament is weakest laterally.
		▪ It typically compresses the nerve root **exiting one level below** (e.g., an L4-L5 disc herniation compresses the L5 nerve root).
• **Other Causes:**
	◦ **Lumbar Spinal Stenosis:** Narrowing of the spinal canal, often from degenerative changes like ligamentum flavum hypertrophy or facet joint osteoarthritis.
	◦ **Spondylolisthesis:** Anterior slippage of one vertebra over another.
	◦ **Degenerative Disc Disease (DDD):** Leads to bone spur (osteophyte) formation that can encroach on the neural foramen.
	◦ **Less Common:** Tumors, epidural abscess, epidural hematoma, synovial cysts, trauma.
• **Pathophysiology:**
	◦ **Mechanical Compression:** Direct pressure on the nerve root and its blood supply (vasa nervorum) leads to ischemia and impaired nerve conduction.
	◦ **Chemical Irritation:** The nucleus pulposus releases inflammatory mediators (e.g., phospholipase A2, TNF-alpha) that cause a robust inflammatory response and chemical irritation of the nerve root, contributing significantly to the pain.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Peak Incidence:** Age 30-50 years for HNP-related radiculopathy.
• **Lifetime Prevalence:** Estimated between 10% to 40%.
• **Most Commonly Affected Nerve Roots:**
	◦ **L5:** Most common (~45-50% of cases)
	◦ **S1:** Second most common (~40-45% of cases)
	◦ L4: Less common
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a patient complaining of **unilateral low back pain** that **radiates down the leg past the knee**, typically in a well-defined **dermatomal pattern**.
	◦ The onset can be acute (often after a specific event like lifting) or insidious.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis:** Lumbar radiculopathy is primarily a clinical diagnosis.
	◦ Imaging is **not** indicated in the first 4-6 weeks for typical cases without **red flags**.
• **Imaging:**
	◦ **MRI (Non-contrast): Imaging modality of choice.**
		▪ Indicated for:
			▪ Presence of **red flag** symptoms.
			▪ Failure of 4-6 weeks of conservative management.
			▪ Pre-operative planning.
		▪ Excellent visualization of soft tissues, including discs, nerve roots, and ligaments.
	◦ **X-Rays (AP/Lateral):**
		▪ Limited utility for radiculopathy itself but can identify bony abnormalities like fractures, spondylolisthesis, or severe degenerative changes.
		▪ Often a first step if there is a concern for bony pathology.
	◦ **CT Myelogram:**
		▪ Used when MRI is contraindicated (e.g., incompatible hardware).
		▪ Involves injecting contrast into the thecal sac.
• **Electromyography (EMG) / Nerve Conduction Studies (NCS):**
	◦ Useful to confirm the diagnosis, determine acuity/severity, and differentiate from other conditions like peripheral neuropathy or plexopathy.
	◦ Not typically used for initial diagnosis.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent.** The vast majority of patients (>80-90%) improve significantly with conservative treatment within 3 months.
• Spontaneous regression of the herniated disc material is common over time.
• Surgery is effective for faster pain relief in appropriately selected candidates, but long-term outcomes at 1-2 years are often similar to non-operative care.

sections.overview:
• **Cauda Equina Syndrome (CES)** is a rare but severe neurological condition and a **true neurosurgical emergency**.
• Caused by the compression of the nerve roots of the cauda equina, the bundle of nerves located at the distal end of the spinal cord (typically below the L1-L2 vertebrae).
• Compression leads to a constellation of symptoms including **severe low back pain**, **radiculopathy**, **lower extremity weakness**, **saddle anesthesia**, and **bowel/bladder dysfunction**.
• **Prompt diagnosis** and **surgical intervention** are critical to prevent permanent neurological deficits.
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The underlying mechanism is mechanical compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots (L2-S5) that constitute the cauda equina.
    ◦ This compression leads to venous congestion, intraneural edema, and ultimately, ischemic damage to the nerve roots, resulting in axonal injury and neurological dysfunction.
• **Etiology (Causes of Compression)**
    ◦ **Most Common (~45%): Massive Lumbar Disc Herniation**
        ▪ A large, often central, disc herniation at the L4-L5 or L5-S1 level is the leading cause.
    ◦ **Spinal Stenosis**
        ▪ Severe narrowing of the spinal canal from degenerative changes (e.g., facet hypertrophy, ligamentum flavum thickening).
    ◦ **Trauma**
        ▪ Lumbar spine fractures (e.g., burst fractures) that displace bone fragments into the canal.
    ◦ **Tumors**
        ▪ Primary spinal tumors (e.g., ependymoma, schwannoma) or metastatic disease (e.g., from lung, breast, prostate cancer).
    ◦ **Infection/Inflammation**
        ▪ Spinal epidural abscess, discitis, or arachnoiditis.
    ◦ **Iatrogenic**
        ▪ Post-operative hematoma, misplaced surgical hardware, complications from spinal anesthesia.
    ◦ **Vascular**
        ▪ Spinal epidural hematoma (can be spontaneous in patients on anticoagulants), spinal AVM.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence:** Rare, estimated at 1-3 per 100,000 people.
• **Prevalence:** Accounts for 2-6% of all lumbar disc surgeries.
• **Peak Age:** 30s-40s, consistent with the peak incidence of lumbar disc herniation.
• **Gender:** No significant gender predilection.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation can be acute or insidious.
• **Acute Presentation**
    ◦ Rapid onset of severe symptoms over hours.
    ◦ Often associated with a specific event like lifting a heavy object.
• **Gradual Presentation**
    ◦ Slower progression of symptoms over weeks or months, often seen in cases of spinal stenosis or tumor growth.
• **Incomplete vs. Complete CES**
    ◦ **Incomplete (CES-I):** Patient has subjective signs of sphincter dysfunction (e.g., altered urinary sensation, difficulty voiding) but no objective urinary retention or overflow incontinence.
        ▪ This stage has a better prognosis with surgery.
    ◦ **Complete (CES-R):** Characterized by painless urinary retention and overflow incontinence.
        ▪ The bladder is no longer under executive control.
        ▪ Prognosis is significantly worse.
• The classic presentation is a patient with a history of back pain who develops **new-onset, bilateral leg pain/weakness**, **saddle anesthesia**, and **urinary retention**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Emergent MRI of the Lumbar Spine (without and with contrast)**
        ▪ This is the **gold standard** and study of choice.
        ▪ Directly visualizes the cauda equina, thecal sac, and the source of compression.
        ▪ Contrast is useful to identify tumors, abscesses, or inflammation.
    ◦ **CT Myelogram**
        ▪ The best alternative if MRI is contraindicated (e.g., incompatible pacemaker, metallic foreign body) or unavailable.
        ▪ Involves injecting contrast into the thecal sac followed by a CT scan.
• **Labs**
    ◦ Generally not diagnostic for CES itself but can help identify underlying causes.
    ◦ **CBC with differential, ESR, CRP:** To evaluate for infection (epidural abscess).
    ◦ **Coagulation studies (PT/INR, PTT):** If epidural hematoma is suspected.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly dependent on the **severity and duration of symptoms before decompression**.
• Patients with **incomplete CES (CES-I)** who undergo surgery have a much better chance of neurological recovery than those with **complete CES (CES-R)**.
• **Urinary retention** at presentation is a poor prognostic indicator.
• Motor deficits tend to recover better than sphincter and sexual function.
• Even with timely surgery, a full recovery is not guaranteed.

sections.overview:
• **Neurologic emergency** resulting from extrinsic pressure on the spinal cord or its vascular supply.
• This compression leads to a cascade of events including edema, ischemia, and direct neuronal injury, culminating in progressive and potentially irreversible neurologic deficits.
• The clinical presentation often follows a predictable pattern: **pain**, followed by **motor weakness**, **sensory deficits**, and finally, **autonomic dysfunction** (bowel/bladder/sexual).
• Prompt diagnosis and treatment are critical to preserve neurologic function.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology (Causes)**
    ◦ **Malignancy (Most Common Cause of non-traumatic compression)**
        ▪ **Metastatic Disease (~85%)**: Primary tumors that commonly metastasize to the spine include **Breast**, **Lung**, **Prostate**, **Kidney**, and **Multiple Myeloma**.
        ▪ **Primary CNS Tumors**: Ependymoma, astrocytoma, meningioma.
    ◦ **Infection**
        ▪ **Spinal Epidural Abscess (SEA)**: Often from hematogenous spread (e.g., *Staphylococcus aureus*) or direct extension.
        ▪ **Tuberculosis (Pott's Disease)**: Tuberculous spondylitis leading to vertebral collapse.
    ◦ **Trauma**
        ▪ **Vertebral Fracture/Dislocation**: Bone fragments impinge on the cord.
        ▪ **Spinal Epidural Hematoma (SEH)**: Can be traumatic or spontaneous (especially with anticoagulation).
    ◦ **Degenerative Disease**
        ▪ **Herniated Intervertebral Disc**: Most common in cervical and lumbar regions.
        ▪ **Spinal Stenosis**: Narrowing of the spinal canal.
        ▪ **Spondylolisthesis**: Anterior slippage of one vertebra over another.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Direct Compression**: The mass or structure physically impinges on the spinal cord.
    ◦ **Venous Congestion**: Compression of the epidural venous plexus obstructs venous outflow, leading to **vasogenic edema** of the spinal cord white matter.
        ▪ This edema further increases pressure and worsens the compression.
    ◦ **Arterial Ischemia**: As pressure rises, arterial blood flow to the cord is compromised, leading to infarction and irreversible neuronal death.
        ▪ This is a late and catastrophic event.
sections.epidemiology:
• Occurs in 5-10% of all cancer patients.
• Metastatic disease is the cause in ~70% of cases.
• **Location**: The **thoracic spine** is the most common site (~60-70%) due to its long length and relatively narrow canal diameter.
    ◦ The lumbar spine is second (~20%), and the cervical spine is third (~10%).
• Spinal epidural abscess has an incidence of ~2-8 cases per 10,000 hospital admissions.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is a classic progression of symptoms.
• A high index of suspicion is required, especially in patients with known risk factors.
• The "textbook" case is a patient with a known history of cancer who develops new, progressive, localized back pain.
• **Clinical Progression**: **Pain** → **Weakness** → **Sensory Loss** → **Autonomic Dysfunction**
sections.diagnostics:
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **MRI with and without contrast of the ENTIRE SPINE**: This is the **gold standard and imaging test of choice**.
        ▪ "Entire spine" is crucial as multiple metastatic lesions ("**skip mets**") are common.
        ▪ MRI clearly visualizes the cord, nerve roots, and surrounding soft tissues.
    ◦ **CT Myelogram**: Used when MRI is contraindicated (e.g., pacemaker, certain metallic implants).
        ▪ Involves a lumbar puncture to inject contrast into the thecal sac.
    ◦ **Plain X-Rays**: Limited utility.
        ▪ May show lytic/blastic lesions or vertebral body collapse but can be normal in up to 33% of cases.
        ▪ **A normal x-ray does NOT rule out spinal cord compression.**
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ Not diagnostic for compression but helpful for etiology.
    ◦ **CBC, ESR, CRP, Blood Cultures**: If suspecting epidural abscess.
    ◦ **Tumor markers** (e.g., PSA) if malignancy is suspected.
sections.prognosis:
• The **single most important prognostic factor is the patient's neurologic status at the time of treatment**.
• Patients who are **ambulatory** before treatment have a >80% chance of remaining ambulatory.
• Patients who are **non-ambulatory** have a <10% chance of regaining the ability to walk.
• The underlying etiology also heavily influences prognosis (e.g., prognosis is poor with widely metastatic lung cancer).
• Rapidly progressing symptoms carry a worse prognosis than slowly developing ones.

sections.overview:
• **Cervical Spondylotic Myelopathy (CSM)** is a condition characterized by dysfunction and **compression of the spinal cord** in the cervical spine due to age-related, degenerative changes (**spondylosis**).
• It is the **most common cause of spinal cord dysfunction** in adults over the age of 55.
• CSM is a progressive condition where chronic compression leads to spinal cord ischemia, inflammation, and neuronal damage, resulting in a constellation of neurologic signs and symptoms.
• The clinical picture is defined by **upper motor neuron (UMN) signs** below the level of compression and potentially **lower motor neuron (LMN) signs** at the level of compression.
sections.etiology:
• CSM is caused by the narrowing of the sagittal diameter of the cervical spinal canal, leading to **chronic spinal cord compression**, involving both static and dynamic factors.
    ◦ **Etiology**: Chronic, degenerative "wear and tear" of the cervical spine (**spondylosis**).
    ◦ **Pathophysiologic Mechanisms**:
        ▪ **Static Factors (Chronic Compression)**:
            • **Osteophytes**: Bony spurs form on vertebral bodies, compressing the ventral aspect of the cord.
            • **Disc Herniation/Bulging**: Degenerated discs lose height and bulge posteriorly.
            • **Ligamentum Flavum Hypertrophy**: The ligament along the posterior aspect of the spinal canal thickens and buckles inward.
            • **Ossification of the Posterior Longitudinal Ligament (OPLL)**: The PLL becomes calcified, severely narrowing the canal.
        ▪ **Dynamic Factors (Repetitive Injury)**:
            • Normal neck movements (**flexion/extension**) cause repetitive microtrauma to a spinal cord that has no room to move within the narrowed canal.
            • **Flexion** stretches the cord over anterior osteophytes, while **extension** causes the ligamentum flavum to buckle into the cord posteriorly.
        ▪ **Cellular Result**: Chronic compression leads to ischemia, demyelination, gray matter neuronal loss, and reactive gliosis within the spinal cord.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Most common cause of spinal cord dysfunction in adults > 55 years old**.
• Prevalence increases directly with age.
• Radiographic evidence of cervical spondylosis is present in >90% of individuals by age 60, but only a fraction develop symptomatic myelopathy.
• Slight male predominance.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is typically **insidious** and **slowly progressive**, often over months to years.
• Patients are often misdiagnosed initially with "old age" or other neurologic conditions.
• The course is often **stepwise**, with periods of stability followed by neurologic decline.
• **Hallmark Presentation**: An older adult presenting with a progressive, **clumsy and spastic gait**, often accompanied by **loss of fine motor skills** in the hands and neck stiffness.
sections.diagnostics:
• **MRI of the Cervical Spine**: **The gold standard** and investigation of choice.
    ◦ Directly visualizes **spinal cord compression**.
    ◦ Shows the cause of stenosis (disc herniation, osteophytes, ligamentum flavum hypertrophy).
    ◦ **T2-weighted images** may show **signal hyperintensity** within the cord, indicating edema, inflammation, or myelomalacia (permanent damage).
        ▪ This is a **poor prognostic indicator**.
• **Cervical X-rays (AP/Lateral, Flexion/Extension)**:
    ◦ Can reveal degenerative changes: osteophytes, disc space narrowing, loss of lordosis.
    ◦ Flexion/extension views can assess for instability (**spondylolisthesis**).
    ◦ Cannot visualize the spinal cord.
• **CT Scan**:
    ◦ Superior for evaluating bony anatomy (e.g., **OPLL**, osteophytes).
    ◦ Often used for pre-operative planning.
• **CT Myelogram**:
    ◦ Used when MRI is contraindicated (e.g., pacemaker, certain implants).
    ◦ Involves injecting contrast into the thecal sac to outline the spinal cord and nerve roots.
sections.prognosis:
• The natural history is **stepwise neurologic deterioration**.
• Surgery successfully halts progression in the majority of patients.
• The degree of neurologic recovery is variable.
• **Negative Prognostic Indicators**:
    ◦ Symptoms present for > 1 year before surgery.
    ◦ Advanced age.
    ◦ Severe myelopathy at time of diagnosis (e.g., gait assistance needed, bowel/bladder symptoms).
    ◦ **T2 signal hyperintensity on MRI**.

sections.overview:
• Spinal stenosis is the narrowing of the spinal canal, lateral recesses, or neural foramina, leading to compression of the spinal cord, cauda equina, and/or nerve roots
    ◦ This compression results in a constellation of neurologic signs and symptoms
    ◦ The condition most commonly affects the lumbar and cervical spine due to their greater mobility and susceptibility to degenerative changes
• **Central Stenosis**: Narrowing of the central spinal canal, potentially compressing the spinal cord (cervical/thoracic) or the cauda equina (lumbar)
• **Foraminal/Lateral Recess Stenosis**: Narrowing of the openings where nerve roots exit the spinal canal, leading to radiculopathy
sections.etiology: • Spinal stenosis is broadly classified into congenital and acquired causes, with acquired being far more common
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: A very common condition, with prevalence increasing significantly with age
• **Age**: Most symptomatic patients are **>60 years old**
• **Location**: The **lumbar spine** is the most frequently affected region, followed by the cervical spine. Thoracic stenosis is rare
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is typically one of **insidious onset and slow progression**
    ◦ Symptoms are often posture-dependent and exacerbated by specific activities
• **Lumbar Stenosis**: Patient is often an older adult complaining of buttock and bilateral leg pain, numbness, or weakness that is worse with walking and standing, and relieved by sitting or leaning forward
• **Cervical Stenosis**: Patient may present with neck pain, radicular arm symptoms, or signs of myelopathy such as gait imbalance, loss of fine motor skills in the hands, and widespread weakness or spasticity
sections.diagnostics:
• **X-Rays (AP/Lateral, Flexion/Extension)**
    ◦ Initial imaging
    ◦ Can show spondylosis, spondylolisthesis, loss of disc height
    ◦ Cannot visualize soft tissues or neural compression
• **MRI**
    ◦ **Diagnostic test of choice**
    ◦ Directly visualizes the spinal canal, cord, cauda equina, nerve roots, discs, and ligaments, confirming the location and severity of stenosis
• **CT Myelogram**
    ◦ Used when MRI is contraindicated (e.g., incompatible pacemaker)
    ◦ Involves a CT scan after injection of intrathecal contrast, providing excellent bony detail and outlining neural compression
• **EMG/NCS**
    ◦ Not for primary diagnosis
    ◦ Can help differentiate from peripheral neuropathy or confirm a specific radiculopathy
sections.prognosis:
• **Lumbar Stenosis**
    ◦ The natural history is variable
    ◦ Many patients remain stable or improve with conservative care
    ◦ Surgery is highly effective for relieving leg symptoms (claudication) but less reliable for back pain
• **Cervical Myelopathy**
    ◦ More guarded prognosis
    ◦ The natural history is one of stepwise neurologic deterioration
    ◦ Surgery is effective at **halting progression**, but neurologic recovery is often incomplete
    ◦ Earlier diagnosis and treatment lead to better outcomes

sections.overview:
• Bacterial meningitis is a pyogenic infection of the leptomeninges (arachnoid and pia mater) and the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) within the subarachnoid space.
• It is characterized by an acute onset of fever, headache, and signs of meningeal inflammation.
• Bacterial meningitis is a **medical emergency** requiring immediate diagnostic evaluation and empiric antimicrobial therapy to prevent high rates of morbidity and mortality.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• Incidence has dramatically decreased in developed countries due to routine vaccination against ***H. influenzae* type b (Hib)**, ***S. pneumoniae* (PCV13, PPSV23)**, and ***N. meningitidis* (MenACWY, MenB)**.
• ***S. pneumoniae*** is the most common cause in adults.
• ***N. meningitidis*** is known for causing epidemics, particularly in college dormitories and military barracks (the "meningitis belt" of sub-Saharan Africa has the highest global incidence).
sections.riskFactors:
• **Extremes of age:** Neonates and the elderly.
• **Immunocompromised state:** Asplenia (anatomic or functional), complement deficiency, HIV, alcoholism, diabetes mellitus.
• **Lack of vaccination.**
• **Crowded living conditions:** College dorms, military barracks, prisons.
• **Contiguous infection:** Otitis media, sinusitis, mastoiditis.
• **Direct inoculation:** Recent neurosurgery, head trauma with basilar skull fracture causing a CSF leak.
• **Cochlear implants.**
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is typically acute, evolving over several hours to 2 days.
• The **classic triad** is **fever, nuchal rigidity, and altered mental status (AMS)**.
    ◦ However, less than 50% of patients present with all three.
    ◦ The absence of all three findings virtually rules out bacterial meningitis.
• **Headache:** Severe, generalized, and often the most prominent symptom.
• **Fever & Chills**
• **Nuchal Rigidity:** Stiff neck, pain with neck movement.
• **Altered Mental Status:** Confusion, lethargy, delirium, stupor, or coma.
• **Photophobia & Phonophobia**
• **Nausea & Vomiting:** Often due to increased ICP.
• **Seizures** (focal or generalized)
• **Myalgias**
• **Petechial/Purpuric Rash:** Classic for meningococcemia (*N. meningitidis*), non-blanching.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Vitals:** Fever, tachycardia, hypotension (if septic shock).
• **General:** Toxic or ill-appearing.
• **HEENT/Neck:**
    ◦ **Nuchal Rigidity:** Resistance to passive neck flexion.
• **Neurologic:**
    ◦ **Meningeal Signs:**
        ▪ **Brudzinski's Sign:** Passive neck flexion causes involuntary flexion of the hips and knees.
        ▪ **Kernig's Sign:** With the patient supine and hip flexed to 90°, resistance to passive knee extension is a positive sign.
        ▪ *Note: These signs have low sensitivity but higher specificity.*
    ◦ **Altered Mental Status:** Assess using the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS).
    ◦ **Focal Neurologic Deficits:** Cranial nerve palsies (esp. CN III, IV, VI, VIII), hemiparesis, aphasia.
    ◦ **Papilledema:** Sign of elevated ICP (a late and ominous finding).
• **Dermatologic:**
    ◦ **Petechiae/Purpura:** Non-blanching rash, may progress to purpura fulminans in severe meningococcemia.
sections.diagnostics:
• **TIME IS BRAIN. Do not delay empiric antibiotics for diagnostic procedures.**
    ◦ If LP is delayed for a CT scan, administer antibiotics *after* drawing blood cultures but *before* the patient leaves for CT.
• **Blood Cultures:** Obtain 2 sets immediately.
• **Lumbar Puncture (LP) with CSF Analysis:**
    ◦ **The definitive diagnostic test.**
    ◦ **Perform LP immediately UNLESS contraindications exist.**
    ◦ **Indications for CT Head prior to LP:**
        ▪ Immunocompromised state
        ▪ History of CNS disease (e.g., mass, stroke)
        ▪ New-onset seizure (<1 week)
        ▪ Papilledema
        ▪ Altered consciousness (significantly depressed)
        ▪ Focal neurologic deficit
• **CSF Analysis Findings in Bacterial Meningitis:**
    ◦ **Opening Pressure:** **Markedly Elevated (>200)**
    ◦ **Appearance:** **Turbid / Purulent**
    ◦ **WBC Count:** **Elevated (>1000)**
    ◦ **WBC Differential:** **Neutrophil (>80%)**
    ◦ **Glucose:** **Markedly Decreased (<40)**
    ◦ **Protein:** **Markedly Elevated (>200)**
    ◦ **Gram Stain:** **Often positive (60-90%)**
• **Other Labs:** CBC, CMP, coagulation studies (PT/INR, PTT), blood glucose (to calculate CSF/serum ratio), lactate.
sections.management:
• **Admission:** Admit to ICU for close monitoring.
• **Isolation:** **Droplet precautions** for suspected *N. meningitidis* or *H. influenzae* meningitis for at least 24 hours after initiating effective antibiotic therapy.
• **Supportive Care:**
    ◦ IV fluids for hydration and blood pressure support.
    ◦ Control of seizures (e.g., lorazepam).
    ◦ Management of increased ICP (elevate head of bed, mannitol, hyperventilation as a temporizing measure).
• **Chemoprophylaxis for Contacts (*N. meningitidis*):**
    ◦ **Indicated for:** Close contacts (household members, intimate kissing, sharing utensils, unprotected exposure to respiratory secretions like during intubation).
    ◦ **Regimens:**
        ▪ **Rifampin** (600 mg PO BID x 2 days)
        ▪ **Ciprofloxacin** (500 mg PO x 1 dose)
        ▪ **Ceftriaxone** (250 mg IM x 1 dose)
sections.complications:
• **Neurologic:** Sensorineural hearing loss (most common sequela), cognitive impairment, seizures, hydrocephalus, cranial nerve palsies, ischemic stroke.
• **Systemic:** Sepsis/septic shock, Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC), Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS).
• **Waterhouse-Friderichsen Syndrome:** Adrenal gland hemorrhage and failure, classically associated with severe meningococcemia, leading to shock and death.
sections.prognosis:
• Mortality remains high: ~20% for pneumococcal and 5-15% for meningococcal meningitis.
• Up to 50% of survivors experience long-term neurologic sequelae.
• Poor prognostic factors include advanced age, low GCS at presentation, signs of high ICP, seizures, and delay in treatment.

sections.overview:
• Viral meningitis, also known as **aseptic meningitis**, is an inflammation of the meninges caused by a viral infection.
• It is the most common type of meningitis and is generally less severe than bacterial meningitis.
• The clinical course is typically self-limited with an **excellent** prognosis in immunocompetent individuals.
• The primary challenge in management is distinguishing it from the more life-threatening **bacterial meningitis**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Enteroviruses (most common cause, >85%)**
        ▪ Coxsackievirus (A and B)
        ▪ Echovirus
    ◦ **Herpesviruses**
        ▪ **Herpes Simplex Virus Type 2 (HSV-2)** - a common cause of recurrent meningitis.
        ▪ **Herpes Simplex Virus Type 1 (HSV-1)** - more commonly associated with encephalitis.
        ▪ **Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV)**
        ▪ **Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV)**
    ◦ **Arboviruses**
        ▪ **West Nile Virus**
        ▪ St. Louis Encephalitis Virus
    ◦ **Others**
        ▪ **Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV)** - can present as acute meningitis during seroconversion.
        ▪ **Mumps virus** (less common due to MMR vaccine).
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Entry & Replication:** The virus enters the host (typically respiratory or GI tract) and undergoes primary replication at the site of entry and in regional lymph nodes.
    ◦ **Viremia:** The virus spreads into the bloodstream, allowing it to disseminate.
    ◦ **CNS Invasion:** The virus crosses the blood-brain barrier (BBB) or the blood-CSF barrier to enter the central nervous system.
    ◦ **Inflammation:** Viral replication within the meninges triggers an inflammatory response characterized by a **lymphocytic infiltration** into the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), leading to meningeal irritation.
sections.epidemiology:
• More common than bacterial meningitis.
• Incidence peaks in the **late summer and early fall**, corresponding to the peak season for enteroviruses.
• Affects all age groups but is most common in infants and children.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presents as an acute illness that develops over hours to a few days.
• Patients generally appear less toxic and acutely ill than those with bacterial meningitis.
• The classic triad of **fever, headache, and nuchal rigidity** is common but may not always be present.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Lumbar Puncture (LP) with CSF Analysis is the definitive test.**
    ◦ A head CT should be performed **before LP** if there are signs of significantly increased intracranial pressure (**papilledema, focal neurologic deficits, new-onset seizures, severely altered mental status**) to rule out a mass lesion.
• **Typical CSF Findings in Viral Meningitis**
    ◦ **Opening Pressure:** Normal or slightly elevated (<25 cm H2O)
        ▪ Differentiating Feature (vs. Bacterial): Markedly elevated in bacterial meningitis
    ◦ **Appearance:** Clear
        ▪ Differentiating Feature (vs. Bacterial): Turbid or purulent in bacterial meningitis
    ◦ **WBC Count:** Elevated (10 - 1,000 cells/L)
        ▪ Differentiating Feature (vs. Bacterial): Markedly elevated (>1,000) in bacterial
    ◦ **WBC Differential:** **Lymphocytic predominance**
        ▪ Differentiating Feature (vs. Bacterial): **Neutrophilic predominance** in bacterial
    ◦ **Protein:** Normal or mildly elevated (<150 mg/dL)
        ▪ Differentiating Feature (vs. Bacterial): Markedly elevated (>200) in bacterial
    ◦ **Glucose:** **Normal** (>40 mg/dL or > 2/3 serum glucose)
        ▪ Differentiating Feature (vs. Bacterial): **Low** (<40 mg/dL) in bacterial
    ◦ **Gram Stain:** Negative
        ▪ Differentiating Feature (vs. Bacterial): Positive in ~60-80% of bacterial cases
    ◦ **Bacterial Culture:** Negative
        ▪ Differentiating Feature (vs. Bacterial): Positive in bacterial cases
• **Confirmatory Tests**
    ◦ **CSF PCR:** Gold standard for identifying the specific causative virus (e.g., Enterovirus, HSV, VZV). High sensitivity and specificity.
    ◦ **Serology/Viral Cultures:** Less commonly used for diagnosis in the acute setting.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for most immunocompetent patients.
• Viral meningitis is typically a self-limited disease.
• Full recovery is expected within **7 to 10 days**, although post-viral fatigue and headaches can persist for weeks.

sections.overview:
• Encephalitis is an acute inflammation of the brain parenchyma, the functional tissue of the brain.
• It is a neurological emergency characterized by the classic triad of **fever, headache, and altered mental status (AMS)**.
• The clinical presentation can range from mild to life-threatening.
• The key feature distinguishing encephalitis from meningitis is the presence of significant cerebral dysfunction (e.g., AMS, seizures, focal neurological deficits).
• When inflammation involves both the brain and the meninges, it is termed **meningoencephalitis**.
• Prompt diagnosis and treatment are critical to reduce morbidity and mortality.
sections.etiology: • The etiology can be broadly divided into infectious and autoimmune causes.
sections.epidemiology:
• Incidence is approximately 5-10 cases per 100,000 people per year.
• **HSV encephalitis** is sporadic and occurs year-round.
• **Arboviral encephalitis** is seasonal, peaking in late summer and early fall, corresponding with mosquito and tick seasons.
• Certain causes have geographic predilections (e.g., EEE in the eastern U.S.).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is typically an **acute onset** of symptoms over hours to days.
• The hallmark is **altered brain function**.
• **Classic Triad:**
    ◦ **Fever**
    ◦ **Headache** (often severe)
    ◦ **Altered Mental Status (AMS):** Can range from mild confusion and lethargy to profound coma. Personality and behavioral changes are common.
• **Associated Findings:**
    ◦ **Focal Neurologic Deficits:** Hemiparesis, aphasia, cranial nerve palsies.
    ◦ **Seizures:** Focal or generalized seizures are very common.
    ◦ Movement disorders (tremors, parkinsonism), ataxia.
sections.diagnostics:
• A multi-modal approach is required for diagnosis.
• **Brain Imaging (MRI)**
    ◦ **Modality of choice.**
    ◦ Identifies parenchymal inflammation, edema, necrosis, or hemorrhage. Rules out other pathologies.
    ◦ **Key Findings:**
        ▪ **HSV:** Asymmetric hypersignal/edema in the **inferomedial temporal lobes** and orbitofrontal region.
        ▪ **ADEM:** Multifocal, bilateral white matter lesions.
• **Brain Imaging (CT)**
    ◦ **Initial test in the ED.**
    ◦ Primarily used to rule out contraindications to LP (mass lesion, midline shift, hemorrhage).
    ◦ Often normal in early encephalitis. May show low-density areas in the temporal lobes in later HSV.
• **Lumbar Puncture (LP)**
    ◦ **Essential for diagnosis.**
    ◦ Must be performed unless contraindicated. Provides CSF for analysis.
• **CSF Analysis**
    ◦ Differentiates etiology and confirms CNS inflammation.
    ◦ **Viral (Typical):**
        ▪ **WBC:** (10-500 cells/L), **lymphocytic predominance**
        ▪ **Protein:** Mildly elevated
        ▪ **Glucose:** **Normal**
        ▪ **Opening Pressure:** Normal to mildly elevated
• **CSF PCR**
    ◦ **Definitive test for specific viral etiology.**
    ◦ **HSV PCR is CRITICAL and should be sent on all suspected cases.** Also send for VZV, enterovirus, CMV based on clinical suspicion.
• **Electroencephalogram (EEG)**
    ◦ Assesses for seizure activity (including non-convulsive status epilepticus) and can show characteristic patterns.
    ◦ Diffuse slowing is common. **PLEDs (Periodic Lateralizing Epileptiform Discharges)** over the temporal lobes are highly suggestive of HSV encephalitis.
• **Lab Studies (Blood)**
    ◦ Includes CBC, CMP, blood cultures, HIV test, serologies (for arboviruses, etc.).
    ◦ Leukocytosis may be present. Serologies can help but PCR is more rapid for diagnosis.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly variable and depends on the specific etiology, patient's age and immune status, and the time to treatment.
• **HSV Encephalitis:**
    ◦ Mortality is **>70% if untreated**.
    ◦ With prompt acyclovir, mortality drops to **~20%**, but a large proportion of survivors have significant long-term neurological deficits.
• **Eastern Equine Encephalitis (EEE):**
    ◦ Mortality rate of 30-70% with severe and permanent sequelae in most survivors.
• **West Nile Virus:**
    ◦ Mortality is lower (~10%), but a "polio-like" flaccid paralysis can be a permanent complication.
• **Anti-NMDA Receptor Encephalitis:**
    ◦ Generally has a better prognosis with immunotherapy, though recovery can be slow and relapses can occur.

sections.overview:
• A **brain abscess** is a focal, encapsulated collection of pus within the brain parenchyma.
    ◦ It is a **life-threatening neurological emergency**.
    ◦ Begins as a localized area of inflammation (**cerebritis**) and evolves into a collection of necrotic, purulent material surrounded by a vascularized capsule.
    ◦ Acts as an expanding intracranial mass, leading to **increased intracranial pressure (ICP)** and **focal neurological deficits**.
sections.etiology:
• A brain abscess develops via one of three main mechanisms:
    ◦ **Contiguous (Direct) Spread (45-50%)**: Infection spreads from an adjacent structure.
        ▪ **Otitis Media / Mastoiditis**: Spreads to the temporal lobe or cerebellum.
        ▪ **Paranasal Sinusitis (Frontal, Ethmoid)**: Spreads to the frontal lobe.
        ▪ **Dental Infections** (e.g., periapical abscess): Spreads to the frontal lobe.
        ▪ **Orbital Cellulitis**: Spreads to the frontal lobe.
    ◦ **Hematogenous (Bloodborne) Spread (25%)**: Bacteria from a distant site travel through the bloodstream and seed the brain, typically at the grey-white matter junction.
        ▪ These abscesses are often **multiple**.
        ▪ **Pulmonary Sources**: Lung abscess, empyema, bronchiectasis, AV malformations.
        ▪ **Cardiac Sources**: Infective endocarditis, **cyanotic congenital heart disease** (e.g., Tetralogy of Fallot) which creates a **right-to-left shunt**.
        ▪ **Other Sources**: Pelvic infections, abdominal infections (e.g., diverticulitis), IV drug use.
    ◦ **Direct Inoculation (10%)**:
        ▪ Penetrating head trauma.
        ▪ Post-neurosurgical procedures (craniotomy, shunt placement).
• **Pathophysiology Stages**:
    ◦ **Stage 1: Early Cerebritis (Days 1-3)**: Localized inflammation and perivascular inflammatory infiltrate without necrosis.
    ◦ **Stage 2: Late Cerebritis (Days 4-9)**: A central necrotic core develops, surrounded by a larger area of inflammation and cerebral edema.
    ◦ **Stage 3: Early Capsule Formation (Days 10-13)**: A thin collagenous capsule begins to form around the necrotic core.
    ◦ **Stage 4: Late Capsule Formation (Day 14+)**: A thick, well-defined capsule fully encloses the abscess.
• **Common Pathogens**:
    ◦ **Immunocompetent Host**: Often polymicrobial.
        ▪ *Streptococcus* species (*S. anginosus, S. intermedius*).
        ▪ Anaerobes (*Bacteroides*, *Prevotella*).
        ▪ *Staphylococcus aureus* (especially post-trauma/neurosurgery).
    ◦ **Immunocompromised Host**:
        ▪ *Toxoplasma gondii* (most common in HIV/AIDS).
        ▪ *Nocardia*.
        ▪ Fungi (*Aspergillus*, *Candida*, *Cryptococcus*).
        ▪ *Listeria monocytogenes*.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Relatively rare, approx. 0.3-1.3 cases per 100,000 people per year in developed countries.
• **Age**: Bimodal distribution, with peaks in childhood and in the 4th-5th decades of life.
• **Sex**: Male-to-female ratio is approximately 2-3:1.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation is often subacute, evolving over days to weeks, mimicking any space-occupying lesion.
• The **classic triad of fever, headache, and focal neurologic deficit** is present in **less than 50%** of patients.
• **Headache**: Most common symptom (~70%).
    ◦ Typically dull, constant, and poorly localized.
    ◦ Worsens with valsalva (coughing, sneezing).
• **Fever**: Present in only about 50% of cases at presentation.
• **Altered Mental Status**: Can range from mild drowsiness to coma, depending on the degree of increased ICP.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Lumbar Puncture (LP) is CONTRAINDICATED** as the first step due to the risk of uncal or tonsillar herniation from the mass effect.
    ◦ If performed, CSF may show elevated protein, pleocytosis, and normal glucose, but it is non-specific and risky.
• **Laboratory Studies**:
    ◦ **CBC with differential**: Leukocytosis is common but not universal.
    ◦ **ESR and CRP**: Elevated, but non-specific markers of inflammation.
    ◦ **Blood Cultures**: Obtain prior to antibiotic administration. Positive in only ~10-35% of cases but can guide therapy if positive.
• **Imaging (Essential for Diagnosis)**:
    ◦ **CT Head with IV Contrast**:
        ▪ **Best initial test** in an emergency setting.
        ▪ Classic finding is a **ring-enhancing lesion** with a hypodense center (pus/necrosis) and surrounding vasogenic edema (hypodensity).
        ▪ The ring represents the inflamed, vascularized capsule.
    ◦ **MRI Brain with Gadolinium**:
        ▪ **Gold standard / Most sensitive test**.
        ▪ **T1 with contrast**: Shows a smooth, thin-walled **ring-enhancing lesion**.
        ▪ **T2**: Shows a hyperintense (bright) area of surrounding edema.
        ▪ **Diffusion-Weighted Imaging (DWI)**: This is a key sequence.
            ▪ The central core of the abscess shows **restricted diffusion** (appears bright on DWI, dark on ADC map), which helps differentiate it from a necrotic tumor.
• **Definitive Diagnosis**:
    ◦ **Stereotactic brain biopsy or aspiration**: Allows for drainage and collection of pus for Gram stain, culture (aerobic, anaerobic, fungal, AFB), and sensitivity testing.
sections.prognosis:
• With modern diagnosis and treatment, the mortality rate is now **<10-15%**.
• Prognosis depends heavily on the patient's neurologic status at presentation (**GCS score** is a strong predictor).
• Poor prognostic factors include delayed diagnosis, **rupture into ventricles**, multiple abscesses, and severe immunocompromise.
• Up to 50% of survivors may have long-term neurological sequelae.

sections.overview:
• A concussion is a **mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI)** caused by biomechanical forces to the head, resulting in a **functional disturbance** of the brain rather than a structural one
• Characterized by a complex pathophysiological process that affects neurons and leads to a temporary and transient alteration in brain function
• Diagnosis is clinical, as standard neuroimaging (CT/MRI) is typically normal
• Loss of consciousness is **not** required for a diagnosis
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Direct Impact**: A blow to the head (e.g., helmet-to-helmet collision, hitting head on the ground)
    ◦ **Acceleration-Deceleration Injury**: Rapid change in head velocity without direct impact (e.g., whiplash in a motor vehicle accident) causing coup-contrecoup injury
    ◦ **Common Causes**: Sports-related injuries, motor vehicle accidents (MVAs), falls, assaults, blast injuries (military)
• **Pathophysiology (The Neurometabolic Cascade)**
    ◦ **Initial Injury**: Biomechanical forces cause stretching and shearing of neuronal axons
    ◦ **Ion Channel Disruption**: An abrupt, indiscriminate efflux of **potassium (K+)** out of neurons and influx of **calcium (Ca2+)** and sodium (Na+) into neurons
    ◦ **Excitatory Neurotransmitter Release**: Massive release of excitatory neurotransmitters (primarily **glutamate**), which binds to NMDA receptors, further exacerbating the Ca2+ influx and neuronal dysfunction
    ◦ **Energy Crisis**: The Na+/K+ pump works overtime to restore ionic balance, consuming large amounts of ATP, leading to a state of **hyperglycolysis**
    ◦ **Metabolic Mismatch**: This period of high energy demand occurs simultaneously with a period of **reduced cerebral blood flow**, creating a critical "energy crisis" or "metabolic mismatch"
    ◦ **Mitochondrial Dysfunction**: The intracellular Ca2+ overload impairs mitochondrial function, reducing ATP production and leading to lactate accumulation
    ◦ **Axonal Injury & Inflammation**: The cascade can lead to cytoskeletal damage, impaired axonal transport, and a local inflammatory response, contributing to prolonged symptoms
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: An estimated 1.6 to 3.8 million sports-related concussions occur in the U.S. annually; many go unreported
• **Age Distribution**: Bimodal peak
    ◦ **Adolescents/Young Adults (15-24 years)**: Primarily due to sports and risk-taking behaviors
    ◦ **Older Adults (>65 years)**: Primarily due to falls
• **High-Risk Sports**: American football, ice hockey, lacrosse, wrestling, soccer, and basketball
• **Sex**: Females report a higher incidence of concussion in comparable sports, potentially due to weaker neck musculature, hormonal differences, or higher reporting rates
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents after a known or suspected head injury
• The **Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is 13-15**
• The patient may or may not have experienced a loss of consciousness (LOC) or amnesia (anterograde or retrograde)
• Symptoms often evolve over minutes to hours following the injury
• The key is the presence of neurological symptoms in the setting of a recent head trauma with a non-focal neurological exam
sections.diagnostics:
• **Diagnosis is CLINICAL** based on history and physical exam
• **Neuroimaging (Non-contrast Head CT)**
    ◦ **Purpose**: To **rule out structural intracranial injury** (e.g., hemorrhage, fracture), NOT to diagnose the concussion itself
    ◦ **Indications (e.g., Canadian CT Head Rule, PECARN for pediatrics)**
        ▪ GCS < 15 two hours after injury
        ▪ Suspected open or depressed skull fracture
        ▪ Signs of basilar skull fracture (Battle's sign, raccoon eyes, hemotympanum)
        ▪ Vomiting ≥ 2 episodes
        ▪ Age ≥ 65 years
        ▪ Amnesia before impact > 30 minutes
        ▪ Focal neurologic deficit
        ▪ Dangerous mechanism of injury (e.g., ejected from vehicle, fall from >3 feet)
• **MRI**
    ◦ More sensitive for subtle axonal injury but not typically used in the acute setting unless there is persistent focal neurologic deficit with a negative CT
• **Neuropsychological Testing (e.g., ImPACT)**
    ◦ Not for acute diagnosis
    ◦ Used to obtain objective cognitive data to help guide return-to-play/learn decisions, especially in cases of prolonged recovery
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for the majority of patients
• **80-90%** of concussions resolve spontaneously within **7-14 days** in adults (can be up to 4 weeks in adolescents)
• **10-20%** of individuals will go on to develop Post-Concussion Syndrome
• **Prognostic Factors for Prolonged Recovery**: History of prior concussion, female sex, younger age (adolescents), history of migraines, mood disorders, and a high initial symptom burden

sections.overview:
• **Diffuse Axonal Injury (DAI)** is a severe form of **traumatic brain injury (TBI)** characterized by **widespread, microscopic shearing of long connecting axons** in the white matter of the brain.
	◦ Caused by traumatic **acceleration-deceleration** or **rotational forces**, typically from high-impact events.
	◦ The clinical hallmark is a **profound neurological deficit**, most commonly immediate and prolonged coma, that is disproportionately severe compared to the initial findings on **non-contrast head CT**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
	◦ **Mechanism**: Caused by high-velocity **acceleration-deceleration** and **rotational (shearing)** forces. The brain, having a different density and consistency than the skull, moves at a different rate, causing axons to stretch, twist, and tear.
	◦ **Common Causes**:
		▪ High-speed motor vehicle accidents (most common).
		▪ Falls from a significant height.
		▪ Assaults / violent shaking.
		▪ **Abusive Head Trauma** (formerly Shaken Baby Syndrome) in infants.
• **Pathophysiology**: A process involving primary and secondary injury cascades.
	◦ **Primary Injury** (at moment of impact):
		▪ Mechanical stretching and shearing of axons, primarily at junctions of tissues with different densities (e.g., **grey-white matter junction**).
		▪ Immediate tearing (axotomy) can occur but is less common than the secondary process.
	◦ **Secondary Injury** (hours to days post-injury):
		▪ The initial stretching disrupts the axonal cytoskeleton, halting normal **axoplasmic transport**.
		▪ Proteins and organelles accumulate proximal to the injury site, causing focal axonal swelling, forming **axonal retraction bulbs** (a key histopathological finding).
		▪ This swelling triggers an influx of calcium and initiates degenerative cascades.
		▪ Ultimately, the axon disconnects from its distal segment (secondary axotomy), leading to Wallerian degeneration.
sections.epidemiology:
• One of the most common and devastating types of **TBI**.
• Accounts for a significant portion of mortality and long-term disability in TBI patients.
• Highest incidence in **young adult males**, consistent with the demographics of major trauma.
• Present in approximately **50% of patients with severe TBI** who require hospitalization.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Hallmark**: **Immediate loss of consciousness** at the time of injury. **No lucid interval.**
• The patient typically presents in a **coma** (Glasgow Coma Scale [GCS] ≤ 8).
• The severity of the coma and its duration are key features.
• Patients may exhibit signs of autonomic dysfunction (**sympathetic storming**), such as hypertension, hyperthermia, and diaphoresis.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Non-Contrast Head CT**:
	◦ **Role**: The **initial imaging modality of choice** in all head trauma to rapidly rule out life-threatening, surgically correctable lesions (e.g., epidural/subdural hematoma, large contusion).
	◦ **Findings in DAI**: Often appears **normal or near-normal**, creating the classic "**clinical-radiological dissociation**" (patient is comatose but CT is unimpressive).
	◦ **Subtle Signs**:
		▪ May show small, punctate hemorrhages (<1 cm) at the **grey-white matter junction**, in the **corpus callosum**, or in the **dorsolateral brainstem**.
		▪ May also see diffuse cerebral edema.
• **MRI of the Brain**:
	◦ **Role**: The **gold standard** and most sensitive imaging modality for diagnosing and grading DAI. It is typically performed after the patient is stabilized.
	◦ **Key Sequences**:
		▪ **Gradient Echo (GRE) or Susceptibility-Weighted Imaging (SWI)**: Extremely sensitive for detecting microhemorrhages, which appear as "blooming" hypointense (black) foci.
		▪ **T2-FLAIR**: Shows non-hemorrhagic lesions as hyperintense (bright) areas of edema.
		▪ **Diffusion-Weighted Imaging (DWI)**: Can detect cytotoxic edema in injured axons within hours of injury, appearing as areas of restricted diffusion (bright spots).
	◦ **Adams-Gennarelli Grading System** (based on MRI findings):
		▪ **Grade I**: Axonal injury confined to the lobar white matter (**grey-white junction**).
		▪ **Grade II**: Lesions in the **corpus callosum** (in addition to Grade I findings).
		▪ **Grade III**: Lesions in the **brainstem**, typically the dorsolateral quadrant (in addition to Grade I & II findings). **Worst prognosis.**
sections.prognosis:
• Generally **poor**, with high rates of mortality and severe long-term disability.
• Prognosis is strongly correlated with:
	◦ Initial GCS score.
	◦ Duration of coma.
	◦ Pupillary response on admission.
	◦ Patient age.
	◦ **Grade of DAI on MRI** (Grade III carries a dismal prognosis).
• Recovery is often prolonged and incomplete.

sections.overview:
• An **epidural hematoma (EDH)** is a collection of blood in the potential space between the inner surface of the skull and the **dura mater**.
• It is a **neurosurgical emergency**, typically caused by **trauma**, that can lead to a rapid increase in **intracranial pressure (ICP)**, brain herniation, and death if not treated promptly.
• The classic presentation involves a **"lucid interval"** between the initial injury and subsequent neurological decline, although this is not always present.
sections.etiology:
• **Mechanism**
    ◦ Typically results from a direct, **blunt force trauma** to the head, often over the **temporal** or **temporoparietal region**.
• **Source of Bleeding**
    ◦ **Arterial (90% of cases)**
        ▪ The most common source is a tear of the **Middle Meningeal Artery (MMA)**, which is vulnerable as it runs in a groove on the inner surface of the temporal bone.
    ◦ **Venous (10%)**
        ▪ Can result from a tear of a **dural venous sinus** or diploic veins.
        ▪ Venous EDHs tend to expand more slowly.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ A **skull fracture** (present in ~85-95% of adult cases) lacerates the underlying vessel.
    ◦ High-pressure arterial blood dissects the dura mater away from the inner table of the skull, creating a hematoma.
    ◦ Because the dura is tightly adherent to the skull at the **suture lines**, the hematoma is confined and expands inward, compressing the underlying brain tissue.
        ▪ This confinement creates its characteristic **biconvex shape**.
    ◦ The rapidly expanding mass increases ICP, leading to decreased cerebral perfusion and risk of **brain herniation** (most commonly **uncal herniation**).
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**
    ◦ Accounts for 1-4% of all **traumatic brain injuries (TBIs)**.
• **Age**
    ◦ Primarily affects **adolescents and young adults** (peak incidence 10-30 years).
    ◦ It is less common in the elderly and very young (<2 years) because the dura is more adherent to the skull, making it harder to dissect.
• **Sex**
    ◦ More common in males (M:F ratio 4:1), reflecting higher rates of trauma in this population.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The **"classic" presentation** occurs in only a minority of patients (~20-30%) but is high-yield for exams.
• **Classic Triad**
    ◦ **Initial Loss of Consciousness (LOC)**
        ▪ A brief concussion at the moment of impact.
    ◦ **Lucid Interval**
        ▪ The patient regains consciousness and appears neurologically intact for a period of minutes to several hours.
    ◦ **Rapid Neurological Decline**
        ▪ As the hematoma expands and ICP rises, the patient experiences a rapid deterioration in mental status (drowsiness, confusion, coma), severe headache, vomiting, and focal neurological deficits.
• **Common Presentation**
    ◦ Many patients do not have a **lucid interval**.
    ◦ They may present with confusion, persistent headache, or may have been unconscious since the time of injury.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Imaging (Gold Standard)**
    ◦ **Non-contrast Head CT**
        ▪ **Classic Finding**: A **lens-shaped (lenticular), biconvex** hyperdense (bright white) collection of blood.
        ▪ **Location**: Confined by suture lines; **does not cross suture lines**. It may, however, cross the midline (e.g., cross the falx cerebri or tentorium cerebelli).
        ▪ **Associated Findings**: May show significant **mass effect**, including **midline shift**, compression of the lateral ventricles, and effacement of sulci. A **"swirl sign"** (mixed density within the hematoma) suggests active, ongoing bleeding. **Skull fractures** are often visible.
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **CBC**: To establish baseline hemoglobin/hematocrit and platelet count.
    ◦ **Coagulation studies (PT/INR, PTT)**: To assess for underlying coagulopathy.
    ◦ **Type and Screen/Crossmatch**: In anticipation of surgery.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is generally **excellent** if the hematoma is evacuated promptly before significant neurological decline.
• Mortality rate is low (<10%) with rapid surgical intervention.
• **Key prognostic factors** are the patient's pre-operative **GCS score**, pupillary exam findings, and the time from injury to surgery.
• **Poor prognostic indicators**
    ◦ Low **GCS** on presentation
    ◦ Bilateral **fixed and dilated pupils**
    ◦ Large hematoma volume
    ◦ Significant delay in treatment

sections.overview:
• A subdural hematoma (SDH) is a collection of blood in the potential space between the dura mater and the arachnoid mater
• It is one of the most common types of traumatic intracranial mass lesions
• Unlike epidural hematomas, which are typically arterial, subdural hematomas result from the tearing of low-pressure **bridging veins**
• This leads to a slower accumulation of blood that spreads out over the surface of the brain, creating a characteristic **crescent shape** on imaging
• SDH can be classified as acute, subacute, or chronic based on the timing of onset
sections.etiology:
• **Mechanism:** The primary mechanism is the tearing of cortical **bridging veins** as they cross the subdural space to drain into the dural venous sinuses
• **Pathophysiology:**
    ◦ **Trauma (Acceleration-Deceleration Injury):** Sudden head movement (e.g., fall, motor vehicle accident, assault) causes the brain to move within the cranium
    ◦ **Shear Force:** The brain's momentum creates a shearing force on the bridging veins, which are relatively fixed at their point of entry into the dural sinuses
    ◦ **Venous Tearing & Bleeding:** The veins tear, leading to low-pressure venous bleeding into the subdural space
    ◦ **Mass Effect:** As blood accumulates, it exerts pressure on the underlying cerebral cortex, leading to increased intracranial pressure (ICP), midline shift, and potentially cerebral herniation
• **Cerebral Atrophy:** In elderly patients and those with chronic alcoholism, brain atrophy increases the distance the bridging veins must travel, stretching them and making them more susceptible to tearing from even minor trauma
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence:** Occurs in approximately 1-5 per 100,000 people per year
• **Bimodal Distribution:**
    ◦ **Young Patients:** Typically associated with severe, high-energy trauma (e.g., MVA)
    ◦ **Elderly Patients (>60 years):** Most common group, often resulting from a simple ground-level fall. The incidence increases significantly with age
sections.riskFactors:
• **Advanced Age:** Due to cerebral atrophy and increased fall risk
• **Chronic Alcoholism:** Contributes to cerebral atrophy, coagulopathy, and falls
• **Anticoagulant / Antiplatelet Therapy:** (e.g., Warfarin, DOACs, Aspirin, Clopidogrel)
• **Coagulopathy:** Liver disease, hemophilia
• **Arachnoid Cysts**
• **History of Recurrent Falls**
• **Shaken Baby Syndrome:** Classic cause in infants
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation varies dramatically based on acuity
• **Acute SDH:**
    ◦ Occurs within **72 hours** of injury
    ◦ Often presents with a significantly decreased level of consciousness (coma, stupor) immediately following a high-impact trauma
    ◦ A "lucid interval" can occur but is much less common than with epidural hematomas
    ◦ Rapid neurological deterioration is common
• **Subacute SDH:**
    ◦ Presents **3 to 21 days** after injury
    ◦ Gradual onset of neurological symptoms
    ◦ Headache, drowsiness, confusion, or mild focal deficits
• **Chronic SDH:**
    ◦ Presents **>21 days** after injury
    ◦ Extremely common in the elderly
    ◦ The initial trauma may be minor and often forgotten by the patient
    ◦ Insidious onset and may mimic other conditions like dementia, stroke, or a brain tumor
    ◦ Classic presentation: An elderly patient on anticoagulation with a remote history of a fall now presenting with weeks of progressive confusion, gait disturbance, and headache
sections.physicalExam:
• **Symptoms:**
    ◦ **Headache:** Most common symptom, often described as constant and worsening
    ◦ **Altered Mental Status:** Confusion, drowsiness, lethargy, coma
    ◦ **Nausea and Vomiting:** Signs of increased ICP
