    ◦ **Gait Disturbance / Ataxia**
    ◦ **Focal Neurological Deficits:**
        ▪ Contralateral weakness (hemiparesis)
        ▪ Aphasia (if dominant hemisphere is affected)
        ▪ Sensory deficits
    ◦ **Seizures**
• **Exam Findings:**
    ◦ **Vitals:** Watch for **Cushing's Triad** (a late and ominous sign of brainstem compression/herniation)
    ◦ **Neurological Exam:**
        ▪ **Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS):** Essential for initial assessment and monitoring
        ▪ **Pupils:** Anisocoria (unequal pupils), with an **ipsilateral fixed and dilated pupil** (\"blown pupil\") is a classic sign of uncal herniation compressing the oculomotor nerve (CN III). This is a neurosurgical emergency.
        ▪ **Motor:** Contralateral hemiparesis or posturing (decorticate, decerebrate)
        ▪ **Reflexes:** Hyperreflexia, positive Babinski sign (upgoing toe)
sections.diagnostics:
• **Initial Imaging of Choice:** **Non-contrast Head CT**
    ◦ **Appearance:** **Crescent-shaped (crescentic)** collection of blood overlying the cerebral hemisphere
    ◦ **Key Feature:** It **crosses suture lines** but does not cross dural reflections (e.g., falx cerebri, tentorium cerebelli)
    ◦ **Density by Age of Hematoma:**
        ▪ **Acute (<3 days):** **Hyperdense** (bright white) compared to brain parenchyma
        ▪ **Subacute (3-21 days):** **Isodense** (same density as brain parenchyma). Can be subtle and easily missed; look for sulcal effacement or midline shift as indirect signs
        ▪ **Chronic (>21 days):** **Hypodense** (dark grey/black) compared to brain parenchyma
• **MRI Brain:**
    ◦ More sensitive than CT, especially for identifying **isodense subacute SDH**, membranes within a chronic SDH, or acute-on-chronic hemorrhage (re-bleeding)
    ◦ Not typically the first-line test in an acute setting due to time and availability
• **Labs:**
    ◦ **CBC:** Check for anemia or thrombocytopenia
    ◦ **Coagulation Studies (PT/INR, PTT):** Crucial for all patients, especially those on anticoagulants, to guide reversal
sections.treatment:
• **Conservative/Non-Surgical Management:**
    ◦ **Indications:** Small SDH (<10 mm thick), no significant midline shift (<5 mm), and a GCS > 8 with no major focal deficits
    ◦ **Treatment:** Hospital admission for close observation, serial neurological exams, and repeat head CTs
• **Surgical Management:**
    ◦ **Indications:** Symptomatic patients, hematoma thickness >10 mm, or midline shift >5 mm
    ◦ **Procedures:**
        ▪ **Craniotomy:** For **acute SDH**. A large bone flap is temporarily removed to allow for direct visualization and evacuation of the solid clot and control of bleeding
        ▪ **Burr Hole Trephination:** For **chronic SDH**, where the hematoma is liquefied. One or two small holes are drilled in the skull to drain the fluid, often with a temporary drain left in place
        ▪ **Craniectomy:** A portion of the skull is removed and not immediately replaced to allow a swollen brain to expand (decompressive craniectomy)
sections.management:
• **Initial Stabilization (ABCs):** Intubate for airway protection if **GCS ≤ 8**
• **Management of Increased ICP:**
    ◦ **Elevate head of bed** to 30 degrees
    ◦ **Hyperosmolar therapy:** **Mannitol** or **hypertonic saline (3% NaCl)** to draw fluid out of the brain parenchyma
• **Seizure Prophylaxis:** Levetiracetam (Keppra) is often used in the setting of severe traumatic brain injury
• **Reversal of Anticoagulation:**
    ◦ **Warfarin:** Vitamin K and Prothrombin Complex Concentrate (PCC)
    ◦ **DOACs:** Specific reversal agents (e.g., Andexanet Alfa, Idarucizumab) or PCC
• **Blood Pressure Control:** Maintain adequate cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP = MAP - ICP) while avoiding hypertension that could worsen bleeding
sections.complications:
• Increased ICP
• Cerebral Herniation (Uncal, Subfalcine)
• Seizures
• Re-accumulation of the hematoma
• Permanent neurological deficits (e.g., weakness, cognitive impairment)
• Hydrocephalus
• Infection (post-surgical)
sections.prognosis:
• Highly dependent on the patient's initial GCS, age, pupillary findings, and time to surgical intervention
• **Acute SDH:** Carries a very high mortality rate (50-90%), as it is often associated with severe underlying primary brain injury
• **Chronic SDH:** Prognosis is generally good with surgical evacuation, although cognitive and functional recovery can be incomplete in elderly patients

sections.overview:
• **Increased Intracranial Pressure (ICP)** is a life-threatening neurologic emergency defined as a sustained elevation of pressure within the cranial vault
    ◦ Normal ICP in a supine adult is **5-15 mmHg**
    ◦ Sustained ICP > **20-22 mmHg** requires intervention
• The condition arises when compensatory mechanisms for managing volume within the fixed space of the skull are overwhelmed, leading to reduced cerebral perfusion, ischemia, and potential for brain herniation
sections.etiology:
• The pathophysiology is governed by the **Monro-Kellie Doctrine**, which states that the skull is a rigid, non-expansible container with a fixed volume
    ◦ This volume is composed of three components:
        ▪ **Brain Parenchyma** (~80%)
        ▪ **Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF)** (~10%)
        ▪ **Blood** (arterial and venous) (~10%)
    ◦ An increase in the volume of any one component must be compensated by a decrease in the volume of another
    ◦ When this compensation fails, ICP rises
• The rise in ICP reduces **Cerebral Perfusion Pressure (CPP)**, which is the pressure gradient driving blood flow to the brain
    ◦ **CPP = Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) - Intracranial Pressure (ICP)**
    ◦ Decreased CPP leads to cerebral ischemia and cytotoxic edema, which further increases brain volume and exacerbates the ICP rise, creating a vicious cycle
• Etiologies are categorized by the component causing the volume increase:
    ◦ **Increased Brain Parenchyma Volume**:
        ▪ **Mass Lesions**: Brain tumors, hematomas (epidural, subdural, intraparenchymal), abscesses
        ▪ **Cerebral Edema**:
            ◦ **Cytotoxic**: Cellular swelling from ischemia (e.g., large ischemic stroke, anoxic brain injury)
            ◦ **Vasogenic**: Breakdown of the blood-brain barrier (e.g., tumors, abscesses, inflammation)
    ◦ **Increased CSF Volume**:
        ▪ **Hydrocephalus**: Impaired absorption (communicating) or obstruction of flow (non-communicating)
        ▪ **Increased Production**: Choroid plexus papilloma (rare)
        ▪ **Infection**: Meningitis can impair CSF absorption at the arachnoid granulations
    ◦ **Increased Blood Volume**:
        ▪ **Hemorrhage**: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH)
        ▪ **Venous Outflow Obstruction**: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, jugular vein compression
        ▪ **Hypercapnia**: CO2 is a potent vasodilator, increasing cerebral blood flow
    ◦ **Idiopathic**:
        ▪ **Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH)** (formerly Pseudotumor Cerebri)
sections.epidemiology:
• Incidence is highly dependent on the underlying cause
• **Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI)** is a leading cause in young adults
• Stroke and CNS tumors are more common causes in older adults
• **Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH)** classically affects young, obese females of childbearing age
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation ranges from subtle and insidious to acute and catastrophic
• Patients may present with nonspecific complaints that progress rapidly to neurologic devastation
• A high index of suspicion is critical
• The constellation of **headache**, **vomiting**, and **altered mental status** should always raise concern for increased ICP
sections.diagnostics:
• **Initial Test of Choice: CT Head without Contrast**
    ◦ **Purpose**: Rapidly identify hemorrhage, mass effect, midline shift, effacement of sulci/cisterns, or hydrocephalus
    ◦ **Findings**: Loss of grey-white differentiation, compressed ventricles, herniation
• **MRI Brain with and without Contrast**
    ◦ **Purpose**: More sensitive than CT for detecting tumors, abscesses, ischemia, and venous sinus thrombosis. Usually obtained after initial stabilization
• **Lumbar Puncture (LP)**
    ◦ **CRITICAL**: LP is **CONTRAINDICATED** in patients with suspected increased ICP due to a mass lesion or obstructive hydrocephalus
        ▪ Removing CSF from the lumbar space can create a pressure gradient, precipitating fatal **cerebral herniation**
    ◦ **Indications**: Permissible *after* imaging has ruled out a mass lesion. Used to measure opening pressure and analyze CSF in suspected meningitis or IIH
• **ICP Monitoring**
    ◦ **Gold Standard**: Direct measurement of intracranial pressure
    ◦ **Method**: An intraventricular catheter, most commonly an **External Ventricular Drain (EVD)**, is placed
        ▪ An EVD is both diagnostic (measures ICP) and therapeutic (can drain CSF)
    ◦ **Indications**: Typically for severe TBI (**GCS ≤ 8**) with abnormal CT findings, or in patients with clinical signs of increased ICP
sections.prognosis:
• Highly variable and dependent on the etiology, severity, duration of elevated ICP, and timeliness of intervention
• The initial GCS score is a strong prognostic indicator
• Poor prognostic factors include prolonged ICP elevation, presence of **Cushing's triad**, and fixed, dilated pupils

sections.overview: • Alzheimer Disease (AD) is a progressive, irreversible neurodegenerative disorder characterized by cognitive decline and memory impairment. ◦ It is the most common cause of dementia worldwide, accounting for 60-80% of all cases. ◦ The pathology involves the extracellular deposition of beta-amyloid plaques and the intracellular accumulation of neurofibrillary tangles, leading to synaptic dysfunction, neuronal loss, and macroscopic brain atrophy.
sections.etiology: • The exact etiology is multifactorial, involving genetic and environmental factors. • The two core pathological hallmarks are: ◦ Amyloid-Beta (Aβ) Plaques (Extracellular) ▪ Result from the abnormal cleavage of the Amyloid Precursor Protein (APP) by β-secretase and γ-secretase. ▪ This produces insoluble Aβ42 monomers, which aggregate into oligomers and eventually form dense, extracellular plaques. ▪ These plaques disrupt synaptic function, trigger neuroinflammation, and are considered neurotoxic. This is the basis of the "amyloid cascade hypothesis." ◦ Neurofibrillary Tangles (NFTs) (Intracellular) ▪ Composed of hyperphosphorylated tau protein. ▪ Normally, tau protein stabilizes microtubules, which are essential for intracellular transport within the neuron. ▪ In AD, tau becomes hyperphosphorylated, causing it to detach from microtubules and aggregate into insoluble paired helical filaments, forming NFTs. ▪ This leads to microtubule collapse, impaired axonal transport, and eventual neuronal cell death. • Other Key Pathophysiologic Features: ◦ Cholinergic Deficit: Significant loss of cholinergic neurons, particularly in the nucleus basalis of Meynert, leading to a deficiency in the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. This is the target of cholinesterase inhibitors. ◦ Synaptic Dysfunction: Synapse loss is an early feature and correlates strongly with the severity of cognitive impairment. ◦ Neuroinflammation: Chronic activation of microglia and astrocytes surrounding plaques contributes to neuronal damage.
sections.epidemiology: • Most common cause of dementia. • Prevalence doubles approximately every 5 years after age 65. • Affects ~10% of individuals over 65. • Affects ~30-40% of individuals over 85. • Slightly more common in women, partly due to longer life expectancy. • Higher incidence in African American and Hispanic populations compared to Caucasians.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • The presentation is typically one of an insidious onset and gradual progression of cognitive decline. • The patient is often brought in by a family member who has noticed changes. • The patient themselves may lack insight into their deficits (anosognosia). • The classic initial presentation is impairment in short-term memory.
sections.diagnostics: • AD is a clinical diagnosis, supported by testing that helps confirm the pattern of decline and rule out other causes. • Lab Studies (Dementia Workup): To rule out reversible causes. ◦ CBC, CMP (electrolytes, glucose, renal/hepatic function). ◦ TSH (to rule out hypothyroidism). ◦ Vitamin B12 and Folate. ◦ Consider RPR/VDRL for syphilis and HIV testing if risk factors are present. • Neuroimaging: ◦ MRI (preferred) or Non-contrast CT: Primarily used to exclude other pathologies (e.g., stroke, tumor, subdural hematoma, normal pressure hydrocephalus). ◦ Characteristic Finding in AD: Cortical atrophy, especially pronounced medial temporal lobe (hippocampal) atrophy. ◦ Advanced Imaging (Specialized Centers): ▪ FDG-PET Scan: Shows a characteristic pattern of bilateral temporoparietal hypometabolism. ▪ Amyloid PET Scan: Can directly visualize Aβ plaques in the brain. • CSF Analysis (for atypical cases): ◦ Low levels of CSF Amyloid-Beta 42 (Aβ42 is deposited in brain plaques, so less is in the CSF). ◦ High levels of CSF total-Tau and phospho-Tau (released from damaged neurons). • Neuropsychological Testing: Formal, detailed assessment by a neuropsychologist to characterize and quantify deficits across multiple cognitive domains.
sections.prognosis: • Incurable and progressive. • The average survival time from diagnosis is 8-10 years, but the range is wide (3-20 years). • Death is typically due to a complication (e.g., pneumonia) rather than AD itself.

sections.overview:
• Vascular Dementia (VaD) is the **second most common type of dementia** after Alzheimer's Disease (AD).
• It is a heterogeneous group of cognitive disorders caused by cerebrovascular disease and brain injury from ischemic or hemorrhagic events.
• Unlike the slow, progressive memory loss typical of AD, VaD often presents with a **stepwise decline** in cognitive function, where abilities deteriorate suddenly after a vascular event (e.g., a stroke), followed by periods of stability.
• The hallmark is prominent impairment in **executive function** rather than memory loss in the early stages.
sections.etiology:
• The underlying mechanism is neuronal death due to cerebral ischemia or hemorrhage, leading to disruption of neural circuits necessary for cognition.
• **Large Vessel Disease (Multi-infarct Dementia)**
    ◦ Caused by multiple cortical strokes, typically from thrombosis or embolism (e.g., from atrial fibrillation, carotid artery stenosis).
    ◦ The cognitive deficits depend on the cumulative volume and location of the infarcts.
• **Small Vessel Disease (Subcortical Ischemic Dementia)**
    ◦ This is the most common cause.
    ◦ Chronic ischemia from disease of small, penetrating arteries and arterioles (lipohyalinosis, microatheroma) leads to:
        ▪ **Lacunar Infarcts:** Small infarcts in deep brain structures (basal ganglia, thalamus, internal capsule, brainstem).
        ▪ **White Matter Lesions (Leukoaraiosis):** Diffuse demyelination and axonal loss in the periventricular and deep white matter. This disrupts the frontal-subcortical circuits critical for executive function. Binswanger's disease is a severe form of this.
• **Strategic Infarct Dementia**
    ◦ A single, well-placed infarct in a critical brain region (e.g., thalamus, hippocampus, angular gyrus) can cause significant cognitive impairment.
• **Hemorrhagic Events**
    ◦ Intracerebral hemorrhage, microbleeds, or subarachnoid hemorrhage can destroy brain tissue and lead to dementia.
• **Hypoperfusion**
    ◦ Global cerebral hypoperfusion (e.g., from cardiac arrest, severe hypotension) can cause watershed infarcts and diffuse brain injury.
• **Mixed Dementia**
    ◦ Very common in the elderly.
    ◦ Co-existence of both VaD and Alzheimer's Disease pathology.
sections.epidemiology:
• Accounts for ~15-20% of all dementia cases.
• Prevalence doubles every 5.3 years and strongly increases with age.
• Slightly more common in men than women.
• Higher incidence in populations with high rates of stroke and cardiovascular disease.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is highly variable and depends on the location and severity of the underlying cerebrovascular disease.
• **Classic Presentation:** **Stepwise deterioration** in cognitive function.
    ◦ A patient's baseline function abruptly declines after a clinical or subclinical stroke, followed by a plateau, until the next event causes another decline.
• **Subcortical Ischemic VaD**
    ◦ More gradual, insidious onset that can mimic AD.
    ◦ However, **executive dysfunction** (problems with planning, organizing, problem-solving, multitasking) and **slowed processing speed (bradyphrenia)** are typically the earliest and most prominent features, often preceding significant memory loss.
• Cognitive deficits are often accompanied by focal neurological signs.
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is clinical, supported by neuroimaging and neuropsychological testing.
• **Labs**
    ◦ Rule out reversible causes of cognitive decline.
    ◦ CBC, CMP, **TSH**, **Vitamin B12**, Folate.
    ◦ RPR or VDRL to screen for neurosyphilis.
• **Neuroimaging (Essential)**
    ◦ Establishes the presence of cerebrovascular disease.
    ◦ **MRI of the Brain (preferred modality)**
        ▪ More sensitive than CT.
        ▪ **Findings:** Cortical or subcortical infarcts, extensive **white matter hyperintensities (leukoaraiosis)**, multiple **lacunar infarcts**, cerebral microbleeds.
    ◦ **CT of the Head**
        ▪ Can identify larger, older strokes but is less sensitive for small vessel ischemic changes.
        ▪ Useful to rule out acute hemorrhage or mass lesions.
• **Neuropsychological Testing**
    ◦ Characterizes the pattern and severity of cognitive impairment.
    ◦ Typically reveals prominent deficits in **executive function** and processing speed, with relative sparing of episodic memory in the early stages.
    ◦ Helps differentiate from other dementias like AD.
• **Diagnostic Criteria (e.g., NINDS-AIREN)**
    ◦ Require evidence of cognitive decline, cerebrovascular disease on imaging, and a temporal relationship between the two.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is generally **poorer than for Alzheimer's Disease**.
• The course is variable and depends on the control of vascular risk factors and the occurrence of new strokes.
• Mortality is higher due to the comorbid cardiovascular disease.
• Median survival from diagnosis is approximately **3-5 years**.

sections.overview:
• **Lewy Body Dementia (LBD)** is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder and the second most common cause of degenerative dementia after Alzheimer's disease.
• Characterized by a "triad" of symptoms:
    ◦ Progressive cognitive decline (especially in **executive** and **visuospatial function**)
    ◦ **Parkinsonism**
    ◦ Recurrent, well-formed **visual hallucinations**
• Core pathology involves abnormal deposits of a protein called **alpha-synuclein** in the brain, forming structures known as **Lewy bodies**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ The exact cause is unknown; most cases are sporadic.
    ◦ A small percentage are linked to genetic mutations (e.g., ***SNCA***, ***SNBC***, ***GBA*** genes).
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Alpha-Synucleinopathy**: Characterized by the misfolding and aggregation of the **alpha-synuclein** protein.
    ◦ **Lewy Bodies & Lewy Neurites**: These aggregates form abnormal intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions called **Lewy bodies** and abnormal neurites called **Lewy neurites**.
    ◦ **Location of Deposits**:
        ▪ **Cortex**: Widespread cortical **Lewy bodies** lead to cognitive impairment, dementia, and psychiatric symptoms (hallucinations).
        ▪ **Brainstem (Substantia Nigra)**: Deposits here disrupt the dopaminergic pathways, leading to parkinsonian motor symptoms.
    ◦ **Neurotransmitter Deficits**: Involves significant deficits in two key neurotransmitters:
        ▪ **Dopamine**: Loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra causes **parkinsonism**.
        ▪ **Acetylcholine**: Profound cholinergic deficits (often more severe than in Alzheimer's) contribute to cognitive fluctuations, hallucinations, and gait instability.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Accounts for approximately 10-25% of all dementia cases.
• **Age of Onset**: Typically occurs after age 50, with the average age of onset between 60-75.
• **Sex**: Slightly more common in men than women.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Age**: The single greatest risk factor.
• **Genetics**:
    ◦ Family history of LBD or Parkinson's disease.
    ◦ Certain gene variants, including ***APOE e4*** (also a risk for Alzheimer's), ***GBA***, and ***SNCA***.
• **Comorbidities**: A history of **REM Sleep Behavior Disorder** is a very strong predictor.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation is often insidious, with a combination of cognitive, motor, and psychiatric symptoms appearing early in the disease course.
• A key feature is the day-to-day or even hour-to-hour **fluctuation** in attention and alertness, which can be mistaken for delirium.
    ◦ Patients may have "good days" where they are relatively lucid and "bad days" where they are confused, drowsy, and have disorganized speech.
• **Severe Neuroleptic Sensitivity**: Profound worsening of **parkinsonism**, confusion, or development of autonomic instability in response to antipsychotic medications (especially typical agents like **haloperidol**).
• **Autonomic Dysfunction**: **Orthostatic hypotension**, syncope, constipation, urinary incontinence.
• **Cognitive Profile**: Early and prominent deficits in **executive function** (planning, problem-solving) and **visuospatial skills** (getting lost, difficulty judging distances), with relative preservation of memory in the early stages compared to Alzheimer's.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Cognitive Assessment**
    ◦ **MoCA (Montreal Cognitive Assessment)** is often more sensitive than the MMSE for detecting the executive and visuospatial deficits common in LBD.
    ◦ Observe for **fluctuating attention** and alertness during the interview.
• **Neurological Exam**
    ◦ **Motor**: Symmetric **bradykinesia**, **cogwheel rigidity**, **shuffling gait**, **postural instability** (positive pull test). **Resting tremor** is often absent or mild.
    ◦ **Autonomic**: Check for **orthostatic hypotension** (a drop in SBP ≥ 20 mmHg or DBP ≥ 10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing).
sections.diagnostics:
• LBD is primarily a **clinical diagnosis** based on the presence of core clinical features.
• **"The 1-Year Rule"**: A key diagnostic concept.
    ◦ **LBD**: Dementia develops *before*, *concurrently with*, or *within one year* of the onset of parkinsonian motor symptoms.
    ◦ **Parkinson's Disease Dementia (PDD)**: A patient has a well-established diagnosis of Parkinson's disease for more than one year *before* developing dementia.
• **Supportive Diagnostic Imaging**
    ◦ **DaTscan (Ioflupane I-123 SPECT Scan)**: High-yield test that measures the density of dopamine transporters in the brain.
        ▪ **Positive/Abnormal**: Shows reduced dopamine transporter uptake in the basal ganglia. Supports a diagnosis of LBD (or other synucleinopathies like Parkinson's).
        ▪ **Normal**: Makes LBD less likely; suggests Alzheimer's, vascular dementia, or another etiology.
    ◦ **Brain MRI/CT**: Primarily used to rule out other causes (e.g., stroke, tumors, normal pressure hydrocephalus).
        ▪ May show generalized cortical atrophy but classically shows less severe medial temporal lobe/hippocampal atrophy than seen in Alzheimer's disease.
• **Other Supportive Tests**
    ◦ **Polysomnography (Sleep Study)**: Can confirm the diagnosis of RBD by demonstrating **REM sleep without atonia**.
sections.treatment:
• **Cognitive Symptoms**
    ◦ **First-line**: Cholinesterase inhibitors (**Rivastigmine**, Donepezil). Rivastigmine is FDA-approved and can improve cognition, apathy, and hallucinations.
    ◦ **Second-line/Adjunct**: Memantine (NMDA receptor antagonist).
• **Motor (Parkinsonian) Symptoms**
    ◦ **Carbidopa/Levodopa**: Can be used cautiously at the lowest effective dose.
        ▪ **Warning**: May worsen psychosis and hallucinations in many patients.
    ◦ Avoid dopamine agonists.
• **Psychosis / Hallucinations**
    ◦ **EXTREME CAUTION**: Patients have **severe neuroleptic sensitivity**.
    ◦ Typical antipsychotics (e.g., **Haloperidol**) and many atypical agents (e.g., **Risperidone**, **Olanzapine**) are **contraindicated** as they can cause irreversible parkinsonism, sedation, and a NMS-like state.
    ◦ **Safest Options (if necessary)**: Low-dose **Quetiapine** or **Pimavanserin**. Clozapine is effective but requires frequent blood monitoring.
• **REM Sleep Behavior Disorder**
    ◦ **First-line**: **Melatonin** (high dose).
    ◦ **Second-line**: **Clonazepam** (use with caution in the elderly due to risk of falls and confusion).
sections.management:
• **Multidisciplinary Team**: Involve physical therapy (gait/balance), occupational therapy (ADLs), speech therapy (swallowing), social work, and palliative care.
• **Safety First**
    ◦ Implement fall precautions.
    ◦ Address driving safety early.
    ◦ Evaluate home environment for safety modifications.
• **Medication Review**: Regularly review all medications and discontinue any with strong anticholinergic or sedative properties.
• **Caregiver Education & Support**: Educate caregivers about the fluctuating nature of the illness, medication side effects, and prognosis. Connect them with support groups.
sections.complications:
• Frequent falls and associated injuries (e.g., hip fractures).
• Severe adverse reactions to antipsychotic medications.
• Aspiration pneumonia due to dysphagia.
• Urinary tract infections.
• Significant caregiver burnout.
sections.prognosis:
• LBD is a progressive, incurable disease.
• The rate of decline is typically faster than in Alzheimer's disease.
• Average survival after diagnosis is approximately **5-8 years**.
• Death is often due to complications such as pneumonia or falls.

sections.overview:
• **Frontotemporal Dementia (FTD)** is a clinical syndrome caused by a group of progressive neurodegenerative disorders characterized by the selective **atrophy of the frontal and anterior temporal lobes**.
• Unlike Alzheimer's disease, FTD typically presents with profound changes in **personality, social behavior, and/or language**, while memory and visuospatial skills are relatively preserved in the early stages.
• It is a leading cause of **early-onset dementia**, with a typical age of onset between 45 and 65.
• There are two main clinical phenotypes:
    ◦ **Behavioral Variant FTD (bvFTD)**: The most common form (~60%), characterized by changes in personality, behavior, and executive function.
    ◦ **Primary Progressive Aphasia (PPA)**: Characterized by a progressive loss of language function. It has two main subtypes relevant to FTD:
        ▪ **Nonfluent/Agrammatic Variant (nfvPPA)**
        ▪ **Semantic Variant (svPPA)**
sections.etiology:
• FTD is pathologically defined as a type of **Frontotemporal Lobar Degeneration (FTLD)**.
• The underlying pathology is heterogeneous and is classified by the type of abnormal protein aggregates found in neurons and glial cells.
    ◦ **FTLD-Tau (Tauopathy)**:
        ▪ Caused by abnormal aggregation of hyperphosphorylated tau protein.
        ▪ Associated with mutations in the microtubule-associated protein tau (`MAPT`) gene.
        ▪ The classic histological finding is the **Pick body**, a spherical, silver-staining intraneuronal inclusion.
    ◦ **FTLD-TDP (TDP-43 Proteinopathy)**:
        ▪ **Most common underlying pathology (~50% of cases)**.
        ▪ Caused by aggregation of TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43).
        ▪ Strongly associated with mutations in the `C9orf72` gene (most common genetic cause of both FTD and ALS) and the `GRN` (progranulin) gene.
    ◦ **FTLD-FUS**:
        ▪ Least common type, caused by aggregation of Fused in Sarcoma (FUS) protein.
• The specific proteinopathy and the location of the brain atrophy determine the clinical phenotype.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Second most common cause of dementia in individuals under 65 (after Alzheimer's disease).
• **Age of Onset**: Typically between **45 and 65 years old**; much earlier than typical Alzheimer's.
• **Genetics**: A strong genetic component is present in up to 40% of cases, with about 10-15% having a clear autosomal dominant inheritance pattern.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation depends on the variant.
• A classic vignette describes a patient in their 50s brought in by family due to insidious and progressive changes in personality.
• The patient often lacks insight into their changes (**anosognosia**) and may appear unconcerned.
    ◦ **bvFTD Presentation**: Family reports the patient has become apathetic, socially inappropriate (e.g., making offensive comments), impulsive (e.g., reckless spending), or developed strange eating habits. They may neglect personal hygiene.
    ◦ **PPA Presentation**: Family reports the patient has increasing difficulty speaking or understanding words. They may struggle to find the right word or produce grammatically correct sentences.
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is clinical, supported by neuropsychological testing and imaging. There is no single diagnostic biomarker.
    ◦ **Neuropsychological Testing**:
        ▪ Essential to objectively document the pattern of cognitive deficits.
        ▪ In bvFTD, tests will reveal severe impairment in **executive functions** with relatively preserved memory.
        ▪ In PPA, **language domains** will be predominantly affected.
    ◦ **Structural Imaging (MRI or CT)**:
        ▪ **Key Finding**: Focal, often asymmetric, **atrophy of the frontal and/or anterior temporal lobes**.
        ▪ MRI is preferred for its superior resolution.
    ◦ **Functional Imaging (FDG-PET or SPECT)**:
        ▪ Shows **hypometabolism** or hypoperfusion in the frontal and/or temporal lobes, corresponding to the areas of atrophy.
    ◦ **Laboratory Tests**:
        ▪ Used to rule out other causes of dementia (e.g., CBC, CMP, TSH, Vitamin B12, RPR, HIV).
    ◦ **Lumbar Puncture (CSF)**:
        ▪ Not diagnostic for FTD but can help rule out Alzheimer's.
        ▪ In FTD, CSF levels of Aβ-42 and p-tau are typically normal, whereas in AD, Aβ-42 is low and p-tau is high.
    ◦ **Genetic Counseling & Testing**:
        ▪ Considered for patients with a strong family history.
sections.prognosis:
• FTD is an incurable, progressive, and fatal neurodegenerative disease.
• The average survival is approximately **7 to 13 years** from symptom onset.
• Prognosis is worse if associated with motor neuron disease (FTD-ALS).

sections.overview:
• Cerebral Palsy (CP) is a group of permanent, **non-progressive motor disorders** that affect the development of movement and posture.
• It is caused by a disturbance or lesion in the developing fetal or infant brain.
• The motor disorder is often accompanied by disturbances of sensation, perception, cognition, communication, and behavior, as well as by epilepsy and secondary musculoskeletal problems.
• The motor impairment is the central feature, but the associated conditions often cause more disability than the motor disorder itself.
sections.etiology:
• CP is caused by an injury to the brain that occurs before, during, or within the first few years after birth.
    ◦ The injury is static (non-progressive), but the clinical manifestations may change over time as the child's nervous system matures.
• **Timing of Brain Insult**:
    ◦ **Prenatal (~75-80%)**: Majority of cases.
        ▪ Intrauterine infections (TORCH: Toxoplasmosis, Other [Syphilis, Varicella, Zika], Rubella, Cytomegalovirus, Herpes)
        ▪ Congenital brain malformations (e.g., schizencephaly)
        ▪ Maternal health issues (e.g., preeclampsia, thyroid disorders, diabetes)
        ▪ Placental insufficiency, intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR)
    ◦ **Perinatal (~10-15%)**:
        ▪ **Hypoxic-Ischemic Encephalopathy (HIE)**: Perinatal asphyxia.
        ▪ **Prematurity Complications**: The single greatest risk factor. Includes:
            ▪ **Periventricular Leukomalacia (PVL)**: Ischemic injury to the white matter adjacent to the lateral ventricles. Hallmark lesion in premature infants.
            ▪ **Intraventricular Hemorrhage (IVH)**: Bleeding into the brain's ventricular system.
        ▪ **Kernicterus**: Brain damage from severe neonatal hyperbilirubinemia.
    ◦ **Postnatal (~10%)**:
        ▪ CNS Infections (e.g., bacterial meningitis, viral encephalitis)
        ▪ Traumatic Brain Injury (accidental or non-accidental)
        ▪ Neonatal or infantile stroke
        ▪ Anoxia (e.g., near-drowning)
• **Pathophysiology by CP Type**:
    ◦ **Spastic CP**: Damage to the motor cortex or corticospinal tracts (pyramidal system). Results in Upper Motor Neuron (UMN) signs.
    ◦ **Dyskinetic CP**: Damage to the basal ganglia. Results in inability to control muscle tone and movement.
    ◦ **Ataxic CP**: Damage to the cerebellum. Results in impaired coordination and balance.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: ~2-3 per 1,000 live births. It is the most common motor disability of childhood.
• **Most Common Type**: **Spastic CP** accounts for ~80% of all cases.
    ◦ Spastic diplegia is strongly associated with prematurity.
• The prevalence of CP increases dramatically with decreasing gestational age and birth weight.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The hallmark of CP is a **delay in achieving motor milestones**.
    ◦ Diagnosis is rarely made at birth and is typically suspected within the first 1-2 years of life.
• The chief complaint from parents is often "my baby isn't rolling over/sitting up/crawling" or "he seems very stiff/floppy."
• **Classification by Motor Abnormality**:
    ◦ **Spastic (Most Common)**: Characterized by increased muscle tone (**hypertonia**) and velocity-dependent resistance to passive stretch (**spasticity**).
        ▪ **Spastic Diplegia**: Affects both legs > arms. Strongly associated with prematurity. Classic **"scissoring" gait**.
        ▪ **Spastic Hemiplegia**: Affects one side of the body (arm > leg). Often presents with early hand preference (<1 year).
        ▪ **Spastic Quadriplegia**: Affects all four limbs, trunk, and often bulbar muscles. Most severe form, high association with intellectual disability and seizures.
    ◦ **Dyskinetic (Extrapyramidal)**: Characterized by involuntary, uncontrolled, recurring movements.
        ▪ **Athetoid**: Slow, writhing, involuntary movements, especially in distal extremities.
        ▪ **Dystonic**: Sustained or intermittent muscle contractions causing twisting and repetitive movements or abnormal postures.
    ◦ **Ataxic (Rare)**: Characterized by problems with balance, coordination, and depth perception. Patients often have a wide-based, unsteady gait and intention tremor.
    ◦ **Mixed**: Combination of motor types (e.g., spasticity with dyskinetic movements).
sections.diagnostics:
• CP is a **clinical diagnosis** based on a detailed history and neurologic exam over time. There is no single diagnostic test for CP.
• **Neuroimaging**:
    ◦ **MRI of the Brain**: **Imaging modality of choice**. Can identify underlying structural abnormalities, such as:
        ▪ **Periventricular leukomalacia (PVL)**
        ▪ **Focal arterial infarct (stroke)**
        ▪ Brain malformations
        ▪ Signs of **HIE**
    ◦ Cranial ultrasound may be used in neonates to screen for **IVH** or **PVL**.
• **EEG**: To evaluate for seizures if suspected.
• **Screening**:
    ◦ Hearing and vision screening is essential due to high rates of deficits.
• **Genetic/Metabolic Testing**: To rule out progressive neurodegenerative or metabolic disorders if the clinical picture is atypical or there is regression of skills.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly variable and depends on the severity of motor impairment and the presence of comorbidities.
• The **Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS)** is a 5-level scale used to classify a child's motor function and predict ambulatory potential.
    ◦ **Level I**: Walks without limitations.
    ◦ **Level V**: Transported in a manual wheelchair; severe limitations in head and trunk control.
• Most children with CP (>90%) survive into adulthood.
• The best predictors of inability to ambulate are the failure to sit independently by age 2 and the persistence of primitive reflexes.
• Severe intellectual disability and uncontrolled epilepsy are poor prognostic factors.

sections.overview:
• Group of major congenital malformations caused by the incomplete closure of the embryonic neural tube during the 3rd to 4th week of gestation.
	◦ The neural tube is the precursor to the central nervous system (CNS), which includes the brain and spinal cord.
	◦ Failure of closure can occur anywhere along the neuraxis, leading to a spectrum of anomalies.
• The two most common NTDs are **Anencephaly** (anterior/cranial neuropore fails to close) and **Spina Bifida** (posterior/caudal neuropore fails to close).
	◦ **Anencephaly**
		▪ Absence of the forebrain, cerebrum, and cranial vault.
		▪ Incompatible with life.
	◦ **Spina Bifida**
		▪ Incomplete closure of the vertebral column.
		▪ **Spina Bifida Occulta**: Mildest form. Defect in the vertebral arch without protrusion of meninges or spinal cord. Often asymptomatic.
		▪ **Spina Bifida Cystica**: A visible cystic mass protrudes through the bony defect.
			▪ **Meningocele**: Protrusion of the meninges and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) into the sac. The spinal cord remains in its normal position.
			▪ **Myelomeningocele**: Most common and severe form. Protrusion of meninges, CSF, *and* elements of the spinal cord/nerves into the sac. Results in neurologic deficits.
sections.etiology:
• The primary cause is the failure of **neurulation**, the process where the neural plate folds to form the neural tube.
	◦ This process should be complete by day 28 of gestation.
• **Pathophysiology**: The etiology is multifactorial, involving a complex interplay of genetic predisposition and environmental factors.
	◦ **Folate Metabolism**: The most critical factor is a deficiency in **folic acid (Vitamin B9)**.
		▪ Folate is essential for nucleotide synthesis, DNA repair, and methylation.
		▪ Inadequate folate levels during the periconceptional period disrupt the rapid cell proliferation required for neural tube closure.
	◦ **Genetic Factors**: Polymorphisms in genes involved in folate metabolism, such as the **MTHFR (methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase)** gene, increase susceptibility.
	◦ **Mechanism of Damage**: In open defects (e.g., myelomeningocele), the exposed neural tissue is damaged by direct chemical trauma from amniotic fluid and mechanical trauma, leading to progressive neurologic injury in utero.
sections.epidemiology:
• Incidence has decreased by >50% in the United States since the mandatory fortification of cereal grains with folic acid in 1998.
• Current U.S. incidence is approximately 0.3 per 1,000 live births.
• Higher prevalence in certain ethnic groups (e.g., Hispanic, Celtic) and lower in others (e.g., African American, Ashkenazi Jewish).
• **Myelomeningocele** is the most common form of spina bifida.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation depends on the type and location of the defect.
• **Prenatal**
	◦ Often detected during routine prenatal screening via maternal serum labs or fetal ultrasound.
• **Postnatal**
	◦ **Anencephaly**
		▪ Obvious at birth.
		▪ Absence of the cranial vault with exposed, disorganized brain tissue ("**frog-like**" appearance).
	◦ **Spina Bifida Occulta**
		▪ Often an incidental finding.
		▪ May present with a cutaneous sign over the lumbosacral area:
			▪ **Sacral hair tuft**
			▪ **Sacral dimple** (especially if deep or >5mm from anus)
			▪ Hemangioma or nevus
			▪ Subcutaneous lipoma
	◦ **Meningocele / Myelomeningocele**
		▪ Visible, **sac-like protrusion** on the back, most commonly in the lumbosacral region.
		▪ The sac may be thin and translucent or covered by skin.
		▪ If ruptured, CSF will be leaking.
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• **Anencephaly**: Uniformly fatal.
• **Spina Bifida Occulta/Meningocele**: Generally excellent prognosis with normal lifespan and function.
• **Myelomeningocele**
	◦ With modern surgical and medical management, >90% of individuals survive into adulthood.
	◦ Face significant lifelong disabilities.
	◦ The **level of the spinal lesion** is the primary determinant of motor function.
	◦ Intelligence is often in the normal range, but learning disabilities are common.

sections.overview:
• **Hydrocephalus** is an excessive accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid (**CSF**) within the brain's ventricular system, leading to **ventricular dilation** and **increased intracranial pressure (ICP)**.
    ◦ Results from an imbalance between CSF production and absorption.
    ◦ In pediatrics, it can be congenital or acquired, presenting differently based on age and cranial suture fusion.
• **Two Primary Types:**
    ◦ **Non-communicating (Obstructive) Hydrocephalus**: CSF flow is blocked *within* the ventricular system, preventing it from reaching the subarachnoid space for absorption.
        ▪ This is the most common type in pediatrics.
    ◦ **Communicating (Non-obstructive) Hydrocephalus**: CSF flows freely through the ventricular system, but its absorption is impaired at the level of the arachnoid granulations.
sections.etiology:
• The underlying pathophysiology is an imbalance in CSF dynamics.
    ◦ **CSF Production**: Primarily produced by the **choroid plexus** within the ventricles.
    ◦ **CSF Circulation**: Flows from lateral ventricles → foramen of Monro → third ventricle → cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius) → fourth ventricle → foramina of Luschka and Magendie → subarachnoid space.
    ◦ **CSF Absorption**: Reabsorbed into the venous system via the **arachnoid granulations**.
• **Mechanisms of Hydrocephalus:**
    ◦ **Obstruction of CSF Flow (Non-communicating)**:
        ▪ **Aqueductal Stenosis**: Narrowing of the cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius. *Most common cause of congenital hydrocephalus.*
        ▪ **Tumors**: **Posterior fossa tumors** (e.g., medulloblastoma, ependymoma, astrocytoma) can compress the 4th ventricle or cerebral aqueduct.
        ▪ **Congenital Malformations**:
            ◦ **Arnold-Chiari II Malformation**: Herniation of the cerebellar tonsils and brainstem through the foramen magnum, often associated with **myelomeningocele**.
            ◦ **Dandy-Walker Malformation**: Agenesis/hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis and cystic dilation of the 4th ventricle.
        ▪ **Intraventricular Hemorrhage (IVH)**: Blood clots can obstruct CSF pathways, common in premature infants.
    ◦ **Impaired CSF Absorption (Communicating)**:
        ▪ **Post-hemorrhagic**: Subarachnoid hemorrhage or IVH can cause inflammation and scarring of the arachnoid granulations.
        ▪ **Post-infectious**: Bacterial or viral **meningitis** can lead to fibrosis and blockage of the arachnoid granulations.
    ◦ **Excessive CSF Production (Rare)**:
        ▪ **Choroid Plexus Papilloma/Carcinoma**: A rare tumor that overproduces CSF.
sections.epidemiology:
• Occurs in approximately 1-2 per 1,000 live births.
• Incidence is significantly higher in **premature infants**, primarily due to the risk of **intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH)**.
• Often associated with other congenital anomalies, particularly **neural tube defects** (e.g., **myelomeningocele**).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation varies significantly with age due to the state of the cranial sutures.
• **Infants (Open Sutures/Fontanelles)**:
    ◦ The skull can expand to accommodate rising **ICP**, so classic signs of increased ICP may be absent initially.
    ◦ The presentation is dominated by signs of an **enlarging head**.
    ◦ **Hallmark**: Abnormally rapid increase in **head circumference**.
• **Toddlers/Older Children (Fused Sutures)**:
    ◦ The skull is a rigid box.
    ◦ Presentation is dominated by signs and symptoms of **increased intracranial pressure (ICP)**.
    ◦ Often present with **headache**, **vomiting**, and **vision changes**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Cranial Ultrasound**:
    ◦ The initial imaging modality of choice in infants with an **open anterior fontanelle**.
    ◦ It is non-invasive, portable, and avoids radiation.
    ◦ Shows ventricular size effectively.
• **CT Scan (Non-contrast)**:
    ◦ The preferred test for acute settings or when ultrasound is inadequate.
    ◦ Quickly identifies **ventricular enlargement (ventriculomegaly)**.
    ◦ Can detect acute **hemorrhage** or **mass effect**.
• **MRI of the Brain**:
    ◦ The **gold standard** for diagnosis.
    ◦ Provides superior anatomical detail to identify the underlying etiology (e.g., **tumor**, **aqueductal stenosis**, **Chiari malformation**).
    ◦ Often performed once the patient is stable.
• **Lumbar Puncture (LP)**:
    ◦ **GENERALLY CONTRAINDICATED** in suspected **non-communicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus** due to the high risk of **tonsillar herniation**.
    ◦ May be performed in **communicating hydrocephalus** to measure opening pressure or analyze CSF (e.g., post-meningitis).
sections.prognosis:
• Highly dependent on the underlying etiology.
• Prognosis is worse with severe underlying conditions like major **IVH**, **CNS tumors**, or significant **congenital malformations**.
• With timely treatment for conditions like isolated **aqueductal stenosis**, many children can have normal or near-normal cognitive development.
• Most children will require at least one **shunt revision** in their lifetime.

sections.overview:
• **Syncope** is a **transient loss of consciousness (TLoC)** characterized by **rapid onset**, **short duration**, and **spontaneous, complete recovery**.
    ◦ Caused by transient global **cerebral hypoperfusion**.
• While most syncope is due to **cardiovascular** or **reflex-mediated (vasovagal)** causes, a thorough neurologic evaluation is critical to identify high-risk conditions that mimic syncope, such as **seizures** or **stroke**.
• True "**neurologic syncope**" is rare; the goal is typically to differentiate true syncope from a primary neurologic event causing TLoC.
sections.etiology:
• Neurologic causes of TLoC are not typically true syncope (i.e., not from global hypoperfusion) but rather mimics that must be ruled out.
    ◦ **Seizure**: The most common neurologic mimic.
        ▪ Caused by **abnormal, excessive, or synchronous neuronal activity** in the brain.
        ▪ TLoC occurs due to disruption of consciousness-maintaining networks (e.g., **reticular activating system**), not from hypoperfusion.
    ◦ **Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency (VBI)**: **Transient ischemic attack (TIA)** or **stroke** in the **posterior circulation** (vertebral and basilar arteries).
        ▪ This is a rare cause of TLoC and is almost always accompanied by other **brainstem symptoms** (e.g., **vertigo**, **diplopia**, **ataxia**).
        ▪ Hypoperfusion is localized to the brainstem, not global.
    ◦ **Subclavian Steal Syndrome**: **Stenosis** of the **subclavian artery** proximal to the origin of the **vertebral artery**.
        ▪ **Arm exertion** on the affected side shunts blood flow from the contralateral vertebral artery down the ipsilateral vertebral artery (**retrograde flow**) to supply the arm, "stealing" it from the brainstem and causing posterior circulation symptoms, including TLoC.
    ◦ **Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH)**: A sudden, massive increase in **intracranial pressure (ICP)** can lead to a compensatory rise in systemic blood pressure (**Cushing's reflex**), followed by a precipitous drop in **cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP = MAP - ICP)**, causing TLoC.
    ◦ **Basilar Artery Migraine**: A rare cause of TLoC, typically in younger patients, associated with other **brainstem aura symptoms**.
        ▪ The mechanism is thought to be related to **vasospasm** and **cortical spreading depression**.
sections.epidemiology:
• Neurologic causes account for a small fraction (<5%) of all TLoC presentations in the emergency department.
• **Generalized seizures** are the most common neurologic cause of TLoC.
• **VBI** is an uncommon cause of **isolated syncope**; TLoC occurs in only about 10% of cases and is almost always associated with other **focal neurologic signs**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The **history** is the most critical tool; a **witness account** is invaluable as the patient often presents after a TLoC event.
• The key is to elicit features that are atypical for simple syncope and suggestive of a neurologic cause.
• **Red flags** include:
    ◦ TLoC during a **supine state**
    ◦ Lack of a typical **vasovagal prodrome**
    ◦ **Prolonged confusion** after the event
    ◦ Associated **focal neurologic symptoms**
sections.diagnostics:
• **Initial Tests (for all syncope patients)**:
    ◦ **ECG**: Essential to rule out **arrhythmia** or **structural heart disease**.
    ◦ **Fingerstick Glucose**: Rule out **hypoglycemia**.
    ◦ **Orthostatic Vitals**: Rule out **orthostatic hypotension**.
• **Neurologic-Specific Workup (indicated by red flag symptoms or exam findings)**:
    ◦ **Non-contrast Head CT**: **First-line imaging** for TLoC associated with new **headache ("thunderclap")**, **head trauma**, or **focal neurologic deficit**.
        ▪ Rules out hemorrhage (**SAH**, **ICH**).
    ◦ **Brain MRI/MRA**: More sensitive than CT for detecting **acute ischemia** (especially posterior circulation), **tumor**, or structural abnormalities.
        ▪ MRA visualizes cerebral vasculature.
    ◦ **Electroencephalogram (EEG)**: The **gold standard** for diagnosing a **seizure disorder**.
        ▪ Indicated if there is high clinical suspicion for seizure (e.g., **aura**, **tonic-clonic activity**, **post-ictal state**).
    ◦ **Carotid & Vertebral Artery Duplex Ultrasound**: Non-invasive test to assess for **stenosis** or abnormal flow patterns, particularly for suspected **VBI** or **subclavian steal syndrome**.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is entirely dependent on the underlying etiology.
    ◦ **Vasovagal Syncope**: **Excellent prognosis**, benign condition.
    ◦ **Seizure**: Generally good with effective antiepileptic therapy, but depends on underlying cause.
    ◦ **TIA/Stroke**: Higher risk of subsequent **stroke** and **cardiovascular events**.
    ◦ **SAH**: **High morbidity and mortality** (~40-50% mortality at 30 days).

sections.overview:
• **Vertigo** is the false sensation of motion (spinning, tilting, or rocking) of the self or the environment.
• It is a subtype of **dizziness** and must be differentiated from **pre-syncope**, **disequilibrium**, or non-specific lightheadedness.
• The most critical clinical task is to distinguish between benign **peripheral causes** (involving the **vestibular labyrinth** or **vestibulocochlear nerve**) and potentially life-threatening **central causes** (involving the **brainstem** or **cerebellum**).
    ◦ **Peripheral vertigo** is far more common, but **central vertigo** is a **can't-miss diagnosis**.
• Comparison:
    ◦ **PERIPHERAL VERTIGO**
        ▪ **Location:** **Labyrinth**, **Vestibulocochlear Nerve (CN VIII)**
        ▪ **Prevalence:** ~80-90% of cases
        ▪ **Severity:** Often **severe**, intense, "the worst room spin"
        ▪ **Urgency:** Generally benign, manageable outpatient
    ◦ **CENTRAL VERTIGO**
        ▪ **Location:** **Brainstem**, **Cerebellum**
        ▪ **Prevalence:** ~10-20% of cases
        ▪ **Severity:** Often less intense, more of a vague imbalance
        ▪ **Urgency:** Potential emergency, often requires admission
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• **Overall:** Vertigo affects approximately 20-30% of the population at some point.
• **BPPV**:
    ◦ Most common cause of recurrent vertigo.
    ◦ Prevalence increases with age, peaking between 50-70 years.
• **Vestibular Neuritis/Labyrinthitis**:
    ◦ Often occurs in young to middle-aged adults, frequently following a viral URI.
• **Meniere's Disease**:
    ◦ Typically presents between ages 40-60.
• **Central Causes**:
    ◦ Incidence mirrors that of their underlying conditions (e.g., stroke risk factors increase with age; MS is more common in young women).
sections.clinicalPresentation: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**:
    ◦ For classic peripheral syndromes (like **BPPV**), the diagnosis is often made by **history and physical exam alone**.
• **Imaging**:
    ◦ **MRI Brain with DWI** (Diffusion-Weighted Imaging):
        ▪ **Test of choice** for suspected **central vertigo**.
        ▪ Essential for detecting **acute posterior circulation stroke**, **MS plaques**, or tumors.
        ▪ An MRI is indicated for any patient with vertigo plus any **neurological sign/symptom**, new **severe headache**, or **risk factors for stroke**.
    ◦ **CT Head**:
        ▪ Often the first test in the ED.
        ▪ Good for ruling out **hemorrhage** but has **poor sensitivity for acute posterior circulation infarcts**.
        ▪ A **negative CT does not rule out a central cause**.
    ◦ **MRA/CTA**:
        ▪ Can evaluate the **vertebrobasilar arteries** for stenosis or dissection.
• **Audiometry**:
    ◦ Formal hearing test used to confirm and quantify **hearing loss** in suspected **Meniere's disease** or **Labyrinthitis**.
sections.prognosis:
• **Peripheral:** Generally excellent.
    ◦ **BPPV** is highly treatable.
    ◦ **Vestibular neuritis** typically resolves over weeks to months, though some residual imbalance can persist.
    ◦ **Meniere's disease** is chronic but can be managed.
• **Central:** Highly variable and dependent on the etiology, location, and extent of the CNS lesion.
    ◦ Prognosis can range from complete recovery (**TIA**) to severe disability or death (large **brainstem stroke**).

sections.overview:
• Acne vulgaris is a chronic inflammatory disease of the **pilosebaceous unit**
    ◦ Characterized by the formation of **comedones**, **papules**, **pustules**, **nodules**, and **cysts**
    ◦ Primarily affects areas with a high density of sebaceous follicles, such as the face, neck, chest, upper back, and shoulders
sections.etiology:
• Multifactorial process involving four key pathogenic factors:
    ◦ **Follicular Hyperkeratinization**
        ▪ Abnormal proliferation and differentiation of keratinocytes in the follicular infundibulum leads to plugging of the follicle, forming a **microcomedone**
        ▪ This is the initial step
    ◦ **Increased Sebum Production**
        ▪ **Androgens** (especially during puberty) stimulate sebaceous glands to produce excess sebum
        ▪ This oily substance mixes with the excess keratinocytes, further plugging the follicle
    ◦ **Proliferation of *Cutibacterium acnes***
        ▪ This anaerobic bacterium (formerly *Propionibacterium acnes*) is a normal resident of the skin flora but proliferates in the anaerobic, lipid-rich environment of the plugged follicle
    ◦ **Inflammation**
        ▪ *C. acnes* produces enzymes and chemotactic factors that attract neutrophils and trigger a host inflammatory response, leading to the development of **papules**, **pustules**, **nodules**, and **cysts**
• **Lesion Progression**:
    ◦ **Microcomedone** (Subclinical)
    ◦ **Closed Comedone** (Whitehead)
    ◦ **Open Comedone** (Blackhead)
    ◦ **Inflammatory Papule/Pustule**
    ◦ **Nodule/Cyst**
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Extremely common, affecting **80-85%** of individuals between ages 12 and 24
• **Age of Onset**: Typically begins in **puberty**. Can persist into adulthood, especially in women ("**adult female acne**")
• **Gender**: Affects males and females equally in adolescence, though males often have more severe disease. Adult acne is more common in females
• **Race**: No racial predilection, but **post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH)** is more common and pronounced in patients with skin of color
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients typically present with a complaint of "**pimples**," "**blackheads**," or "**zits**" on the face, neck, chest, or back
• The onset is usually gradual during adolescence
• The history should include:
    ◦ Age of onset
    ◦ Previous treatments and their efficacy
    ◦ Hormonal history in females (**menstrual regularity**)
    ◦ Medication history
    ◦ The psychological impact of the disease
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**
    ◦ Diagnosis is made based on history and the characteristic physical exam findings (presence of **comedones** is **pathognomonic**)
• **Laboratory Studies** (rarely needed)
    ◦ Consider hormonal workup (**total testosterone**, **DHEA-S**, **LH/FSH ratio**) in female patients who present with adult-onset acne accompanied by signs of **hyperandrogenism**
        ▪ Signs include **hirsutism**, **irregular menses**, or **virilization**
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is generally **good**
• Acne is typically a **self-limited** disease that resolves by the late teens or early 20s
    ◦ However, it can persist into adulthood
• With appropriate and consistent treatment, most cases can be well-controlled, and the risk of long-term complications like **scarring** can be significantly reduced

sections.overview:
• Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory skin condition characterized by a **relapsing-remitting course** of central facial **erythema**, **flushing**, **telangiectasias**, **papules**, and **pustules**.
• It typically affects adults and is distinguished from acne vulgaris by the **absence of comedones**.
• The condition can significantly impact a patient's quality of life and may involve **ocular** and **phymatous changes**.
sections.etiology:
• The exact etiology is unknown, but it is considered a multifactorial inflammatory disorder involving:
    ◦ **Neurovascular Dysregulation**:
        ▪ Exaggerated response to triggers (heat, stress, etc.) leads to **flushing** and **persistent erythema** due to vasodilation and increased blood flow.
        ▪ Dysfunctional transient receptor potential (TRP) ion channels on sensory nerves are implicated.
    ◦ **Innate Immune System Dysfunction**:
        ▪ An abnormal immune response leads to elevated levels of antimicrobial peptides like **cathelicidin LL-37**.
        ▪ In rosacea patients, these peptides are processed into pro-inflammatory fragments that promote inflammation, erythema, and telangiectasia formation.
    ◦ **Microorganisms**:
        ▪ An increased density of ***Demodex folliculorum*** mites within pilosebaceous units is strongly associated with rosacea.
        ▪ It is believed that the mites or the bacteria they carry (*Bacillus oleronius*) trigger an inflammatory immune response.
        ▪ The role of ***H. pylori*** is controversial and less established.
    ◦ **Genetic Predisposition**:
        ▪ A positive family history is common, suggesting a genetic component.
    ◦ **UV Radiation**:
        ▪ Chronic sun exposure is a well-established trigger and exacerbating factor, leading to dermal matrix degradation and vascular damage.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Age of Onset**: Typically between **30 and 50 years**.
• **Sex**: More commonly diagnosed in females, but males tend to have more severe disease, particularly **rhinophyma**.
• **Prevalence**: Affects approximately 1-10% of the population.
• **Ethnicity**: Most common in fair-skinned individuals of Northern European or Celtic descent (Fitzpatrick skin types I-II).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Rosacea is classified into four major subtypes, and patients can present with features of more than one subtype.
    ◦ **Erythematotelangiectatic Rosacea (ETR)**:
        ▪ **Persistent central facial erythema** ("red face").
        ▪ Recurrent, prolonged **flushing** in response to triggers.
        ▪ Visible **telangiectasias** (fine, dilated blood vessels).
        ▪ Skin may be sensitive, stinging, or burning.
    ◦ **Papulopustular Rosacea (PPR)**:
        ▪ Persistent central facial erythema with transient **papules** and/or **pustules**.
        ▪ Often mistaken for acne, but **comedones (blackheads/whiteheads) are absent**.
        ▪ Inflammatory lesions tend to be symmetric on the cheeks, chin, and forehead.
    ◦ **Phymatous Rosacea**:
        ▪ Characterized by **skin thickening** and irregular surface nodularities.
        ▪ Most commonly affects the nose (**rhinophyma**), but can also involve the chin (gnathophyma), forehead (metophyma), or ears (otophyma).
        ▪ Associated with prominent pores and sebaceous hyperplasia.
        ▪ Predominantly affects men.
    ◦ **Ocular Rosacea**:
        ▪ Can precede, coincide with, or occur without skin manifestations (in up to 20% of cases).
        ▪ **Symptoms** include foreign body sensation, dryness, burning, stinging, itching, photosensitivity, and blurred vision.
        ▪ **Signs** include blepharitis, conjunctivitis, lid margin telangiectasias, styes (hordeola), and chalazia.
        ▪ Can lead to serious complications like **keratitis** if untreated.
sections.diagnostics:
• Rosacea is a **clinical diagnosis** based on a thorough history and physical exam.
• **Diagnostic Criteria (at least one primary feature)**:
    ◦ **Persistent Erythema**: Characteristic centrofacial distribution.
    ◦ **Phymatous Changes**.
• **Major Features (two or more support diagnosis)**:
    ◦ **Flushing**
    ◦ **Papules and pustules**
    ◦ **Telangiectasias**
    ◦ **Ocular manifestations**
• **Skin Biopsy**:
    ◦ Rarely necessary. Performed only in atypical cases to rule out other conditions (e.g., lupus, sarcoidosis).
    ◦ Histology would show a perivascular and perifollicular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate with dermal edema and telangiectasias.
sections.prognosis:
• Rosacea is a chronic condition with **no cure**.
• The prognosis for controlling symptoms and preventing progression is generally good with consistent treatment and management.
• The course is characterized by periods of **exacerbation and remission**.
• Without treatment, the condition tends to worsen over time.

sections.overview:
• **Bullous Pemphigoid (BP)** is the most common autoimmune subepidermal blistering disease.
	◦ Characterized by large, **tense, fluid-filled bullae** on erythematous or urticarial-like skin, accompanied by **intense pruritus**.
	◦ Primarily affects the **elderly**.
	◦ Core pathology involves autoantibodies targeting components of the **hemidesmosome**, leading to a separation of the epidermis from the underlying dermis.
sections.etiology:
• **Autoimmune Process**
	◦ Caused by the production of **IgG autoantibodies** (primarily IgG1 and IgG4) directed against two key protein components of **hemidesmosomes**.
	◦ Hemidesmosomes are structures that anchor basal keratinocytes of the epidermis to the underlying basement membrane.
	◦ **Target Antigens**
		▪ **BPAG1 (BP230):** An intracellular protein that helps connect keratin intermediate filaments to the hemidesmosome.
		▪ **BPAG2 (BP180):** A transmembrane collagen protein (collagen XVII) that spans the basement membrane. Antibodies against BP180 are considered more pathogenic.
	◦ **Pathologic Cascade**
		▪ IgG autoantibodies bind to BPAG1 and BPAG2 at the basement membrane zone (BMZ).
		▪ This binding activates the **complement cascade**, leading to the accumulation of C3.
		▪ Inflammatory cells, particularly **eosinophils** and neutrophils, are recruited to the site.
		▪ These cells release proteases that degrade the hemidesmosomal proteins and the BMZ.
		▪ The epidermis separates from the dermis, creating a **subepidermal cleft**.
		▪ Fluid fills this space, forming a tense bulla.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Most common** autoimmune blistering disease in Western countries.
• Primarily a disease of the **elderly**.
	◦ **Age of Onset:** Typically >60 years, with a mean age of ~80 years.
	◦ **Incidence:** Increases significantly with age.
• **Sex:** No significant predilection; affects males and females equally.
• **Race:** No major racial predilection.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Advanced Age:** The single most significant risk factor.
• **Neurologic Diseases:** Strong association with conditions like:
	◦ Dementia (especially Alzheimer's)
	◦ Parkinson's disease
	◦ Cerebrovascular accident (stroke)
	◦ Multiple sclerosis
• **Medications (Drug-Induced BP):**
	◦ Diuretics (especially **Furosemide**)
	◦ NSAIDs
	◦ ACE inhibitors (Captopril)
	◦ Penicillamine
	◦ Biologics (e.g., **PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint inhibitors** for cancer)
• **Physical Triggers:** Trauma, burns, radiation therapy, UV light (less common).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Prodromal Phase**
	◦ Can precede blisters by weeks to months.
	◦ **Intense, generalized pruritus** is the hallmark symptom.
	◦ Non-specific skin lesions may appear, such as eczematous patches, papules, or **urticarial plaques** (resembling hives).
• **Bullous Phase**
	◦ Eruption of large (>1 cm), **tense bullae** filled with clear or serosanguinous fluid.
	◦ Bullae arise on normal-appearing skin, erythematous patches, or urticarial plaques.
	◦ **Location:** Most commonly on the trunk, abdomen, and flexural areas (axillae, groin, inner thighs).
	◦ Ruptured bullae leave behind raw, painful erosions that subsequently crust over.
• **Key Symptoms**
	◦ **Pruritus (Itching):** The most prominent and debilitating symptom. Often severe and may disrupt sleep.
	◦ **Pain/Soreness:** Primarily from ruptured bullae (erosions).
	◦ **Stinging/Burning:** Sensation from active lesions.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Skin Lesions**
	◦ **Bullae:** **Tense, dome-shaped blisters** that are difficult to rupture with pressure.
	◦ **Urticarial Plaques:** Edematous, erythematous plaques, often annular or serpiginous.
	◦ **Erosions and Crusts:** Seen where bullae have ruptured.
• **Nikolsky Sign: NEGATIVE**
	◦ Firm lateral pressure on perilesional skin does not induce epidermal separation or blister formation.
	◦ This is because the blister is deep (subepidermal), and the epidermal cell-to-cell junctions are intact.
• **Mucous Membrane Involvement**
	◦ **Uncommon** (occurs in ~10-20% of patients).
	◦ When present, it is typically mild and involves oral erosions. Significantly less common and severe than in Pemphigus Vulgaris.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Skin Biopsy (Gold Standard)**
	◦ Two biopsies are required:
		▪ **1. Punch Biopsy for Histology (H&E Stain):**
			◦ **Site:** Edge of an intact, fresh blister.
			◦ **Findings:** A **subepidermal split** (separation between the epidermis and dermis) with a prominent inflammatory infiltrate rich in **eosinophils**.
		▪ **2. Punch Biopsy for Direct Immunofluorescence (DIF):**
			◦ **Site:** *Perilesional* (normal-appearing) skin, typically within 1-2 cm of an active lesion.
			◦ **Findings:** This is the most specific test. It reveals a **linear deposition of IgG and/or C3** along the basement membrane zone (BMZ).
• **Serology (Blood Tests)**
	◦ **Indirect Immunofluorescence (IIF):** Detects circulating anti-BMZ IgG antibodies in the patient's serum.
	◦ **Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA):** Highly specific and quantitative test that detects circulating antibodies to **BPAG1 (BP230)** and **BPAG2 (BP180)**. Useful for confirming diagnosis and monitoring disease activity.
sections.treatment:
• **Goal:** Suppress inflammation and autoantibody production, reduce pruritus, and promote healing of lesions.
• **First-Line**
	◦ **Mild/Localized Disease:** **High-potency topical corticosteroids** (e.g., Clobetasol propionate 0.05% cream/ointment).
	◦ **Moderate-to-Severe/Widespread Disease:** **Systemic corticosteroids** (e.g., Prednisone 0.5-1.0 mg/kg/day), followed by a slow taper.
• **Steroid-Sparing Adjuvants** (Used to reduce long-term steroid toxicity)
	◦ **Doxycycline:** Often combined with nicotinamide for its anti-inflammatory effects. A good option for elderly patients who cannot tolerate high-dose steroids.
	◦ **Immunosuppressants:** Azathioprine, Mycophenolate Mofetil, Methotrexate.
• **Refractory Disease**
	◦ **Rituximab** (anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody): Depletes B-cells.
	◦ **IVIG, Dupilumab, Omalizumab** have also been used.
sections.management:
• **Dermatology Consultation:** Essential for diagnosis and management.
• **Wound Care:** Gentle skin cleansing, use of non-adherent dressings on erosions. Sterile rupture of large, tense bullae can relieve pain.
• **Pruritus Control:** Oral antihistamines (e.g., hydroxyzine, diphenhydramine).
• **Patient Education:** Discuss the chronic nature of the disease, treatment side effects, and the importance of adherence.
• **Monitoring for Complications of Therapy**
	◦ With systemic steroids, monitor blood pressure, blood glucose, and bone density (DEXA scan).
	◦ Consider prophylaxis for **Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP)** in patients on high-dose immunosuppression.
sections.complications:
• **Secondary Bacterial Infection:** Cellulitis or sepsis from open erosions (most common cause of death).
• **Fluid & Electrolyte Imbalance:** If large areas of skin are denuded.
• **Scarring and Dyspigmentation:** Post-inflammatory hyper- or hypopigmentation.
• **Iatrogenic Complications (from treatment)**
	◦ **Systemic Steroids:** Osteoporosis, hyperglycemia/diabetes, hypertension, cataracts, weight gain, adrenal suppression, immunosuppression.
	◦ **Immunosuppressants:** Bone marrow suppression, hepatotoxicity, increased risk of infection and malignancy.
sections.prognosis:
• The disease often follows a chronic, relapsing-remitting course that can last for years.
• Remission can be achieved with treatment, but relapse is common, especially during steroid tapering.
• There is an **increased mortality rate** compared to the age-matched general population, primarily from complications like sepsis and adverse effects of long-term immunosuppressive therapy in a frail, elderly population.

sections.overview:
• Pemphigus Vulgaris (PV) is a rare, life-threatening, chronic autoimmune blistering (bullous) disease that causes flaccid, easily ruptured blisters and painful erosions on the skin and mucous membranes.
    ◦ It is the most common form of pemphigus.
• The hallmark of the disease is **acantholysis**, which is the loss of adhesion between keratinocytes in the epidermis, leading to intraepidermal blister formation.
sections.etiology:
• **Autoimmune Mechanism**: PV is a **Type II Hypersensitivity Reaction**.
• **Autoantibodies**: Pathogenic **IgG** autoantibodies are produced against specific cell-to-cell adhesion proteins (cadherins) in the desmosomes of keratinocytes.
• **Target Antigens**:
    ◦ **Desmoglein 3 (Dsg3)**: Predominantly expressed in the deep layers of the epidermis and on mucosal surfaces.
        ▪ Antibodies against Dsg3 are primarily responsible for the **mucosal lesions**.
    ◦ **Desmoglein 1 (Dsg1)**: Predominantly expressed in the superficial layers of the epidermis.
        ▪ Antibodies against Dsg1 are primarily responsible for **cutaneous (skin) lesions**.
• **Pathologic Process**:
    ◦ IgG antibodies bind to Dsg1 and/or Dsg3 on keratinocytes.
    ◦ This binding disrupts desmosomal adhesion, leading to a loss of cohesion between epidermal cells (**acantholysis**).
    ◦ The separation occurs within the epidermis (**intraepidermal split**), typically just above the basal cell layer.
    ◦ This separation results in the formation of a fragile, **flaccid bulla** that ruptures easily, leaving a painful erosion.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Rare, approximately 0.1-0.5 cases per 100,000 people per year.
• **Age of Onset**: Typically affects middle-aged and older adults (40-60 years).
• **Sex**: Affects males and females equally.
• **Ethnicity**: Higher incidence in individuals of Ashkenazi Jewish and Mediterranean descent.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Genetic Predisposition**: Strong association with certain HLA class II alleles, particularly **HLA-DRB1*0402**.
• **Drug-Induced**: Certain medications can trigger PV, most notably:
    ◦ **Penicillamine**
    ◦ **Captopril** (and other ACE inhibitors)
    ◦ Piroxicam (NSAID)
    ◦ Phenobarbital
• **Other**: Association with other autoimmune diseases (e.g., myasthenia gravis, thymoma) has been reported.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The disease typically begins insidiously with mucosal involvement, which can precede skin lesions by weeks to months.
• **Mucosal Lesions**:
    ◦ The vast majority of patients (>80%) present with **painful oral erosions** first.
    ◦ These appear as ill-defined, irregular, and often persistent ulcers.
    ◦ Any mucosal surface can be affected, including oropharynx, nasopharynx, larynx, esophagus, conjunctiva, and anogenital region.
• **Cutaneous Lesions**:
    ◦ Develop after mucosal onset.
    ◦ Appear as **flaccid, fragile bullae** on normal-appearing or erythematous skin.
    ◦ The bullae rupture very easily, leaving behind large, painful, denuded erosions that bleed and are slow to heal.
    ◦ Lesions often appear on the scalp, face, chest, axillae, and groin.
    ◦ Healing typically occurs without scarring but with post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.
• **Associated Symptoms**:
    ◦ **Severe oral pain**: Can lead to dysphagia, odynophagia, and subsequent weight loss and malnutrition.
    ◦ **Skin pain/burning**: The erosions are extremely painful.
    ◦ **Pruritus**: Usually absent or mild (a key feature distinguishing it from Bullous Pemphigoid).
    ◦ **Hoarseness**: If laryngeal mucosa is involved.
    ◦ **Epistaxis**: If nasal mucosa is involved.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Oral Cavity**: Multiple, irregular, friable erosions on the buccal mucosa, palate, gingiva, and tongue. Intact bullae are rarely seen in the mouth due to trauma.
• **Skin**: Flaccid bullae of varying sizes. Widespread, weeping or crusted erosions.
• **Nikolsky Sign: POSITIVE**
    ◦ The application of gentle, lateral pressure on perilesional (normal-appearing) skin results in the separation of the epidermis and blister formation. This indicates acantholysis.
• **Asboe-Hansen Sign (Bulla Spread Sign): POSITIVE**
    ◦ Gentle pressure on the top of an intact bulla forces the fluid to spread under the skin away from the point of pressure, causing the bulla to enlarge.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Biopsy (Gold Standard)**: Two punch biopsies are required.
    ◦ 1. **For Histopathology (H&E stain)**: Taken from the **edge of an active blister**.
        ▪ Shows an **intraepidermal split** just above the basal layer.
        ▪ **Acantholysis** (loss of cell-to-cell adhesion) is visible.
        ▪ The basal keratinocytes remain attached to the basement membrane, resembling a **"row of tombstones"**.
    ◦ 2. **For Direct Immunofluorescence (DIF)**: Taken from **perilesional** (normal-appearing) skin.
        ▪ Shows **net-like or "chicken wire" pattern** of intercellular IgG and C3 deposits throughout the epidermis. This is pathognomonic.
• **Serology**:
    ◦ **Indirect Immunofluorescence (IIF)**: Detects circulating anti-desmoglein IgG antibodies in the patient's serum.
    ◦ **Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA)**: Detects and quantifies circulating **anti-Dsg1 and anti-Dsg3 antibodies**.
        ▪ This is useful for confirming the diagnosis and monitoring disease activity and response to treatment.
sections.treatment:
• **Goal**: To stop blister formation, promote healing of erosions, and achieve long-term remission while minimizing side effects.
• **First-Line Therapy**:
    ◦ **Systemic Corticosteroids**: High-dose **prednisone** (1-2 mg/kg/day) is the mainstay to gain initial control.
    ◦ **Rituximab (Anti-CD20 Monoclonal Antibody)**: Increasingly used as a first-line agent along with corticosteroids due to its high efficacy and steroid-sparing effects.
• **Steroid-Sparing Adjuvants**: Added to reduce the cumulative dose and side effects of long-term steroid use.
    ◦ **Mycophenolate Mofetil (MMF)**
    ◦ **Azathioprine**
• **Refractory Disease**:
    ◦ Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG)
    ◦ Cyclophosphamide
    ◦ Plasmapheresis
• **Local Care**:
    ◦ Meticulous wound care for erosions (treat like burns).
    ◦ Topical corticosteroids and/or antibiotics.
    ◦ Antiseptic mouthwashes.
sections.management:
• **Multidisciplinary Approach**: Requires collaboration between Dermatology, Internal Medicine, Dentistry, and Nutrition.
• **Wound Care**: Non-adherent dressings to protect erosions and prevent secondary infection.
• **Pain Management**: Crucial for comfort and to ensure adequate oral intake.
• **Nutritional Support**: A soft or liquid diet may be necessary. Enteral feeding may be required in severe cases.
• **Monitoring**:
    ◦ Clinical monitoring of lesion counts.
    ◦ Serological monitoring of anti-Dsg1 and anti-Dsg3 antibody titers via ELISA to guide therapy tapering.
• **Prophylaxis**: Patients on long-term immunosuppression require prophylaxis for osteoporosis (calcium/vitamin D, bisphosphonates) and opportunistic infections (e.g., TMP-SMX for PJP).
sections.complications:
• **Secondary Infection**: Bacterial or fungal infection of skin erosions is common and can lead to **sepsis**, which is the leading cause of death.
• **Fluid and Electrolyte Imbalance**: Due to extensive loss of epidermal barrier function.
• **Malnutrition and Dehydration**: From severe, painful oral lesions.
• **Iatrogenic Complications**: Side effects from long-term systemic corticosteroids and immunosuppressants are significant (e.g., Cushing's syndrome, diabetes, osteoporosis, cataracts, opportunistic infections, adrenal suppression).
sections.prognosis:
• **Without treatment**: The disease is often fatal, with mortality rates exceeding 75% primarily due to sepsis and electrolyte imbalance.
• **With treatment**: Mortality has been reduced to <10%. The course is chronic and characterized by relapses and remissions.
    ◦ Death is now more commonly due to complications of therapy rather than the disease itself.

sections.overview:
• A **lipoma** is the most common **benign soft tissue tumor**, composed of mature adipose cells (adipocytes).
    ◦ It presents as a **slow-growing**, **soft**, **mobile**, and typically **painless** subcutaneous mass.
    ◦ While they can occur anywhere on the body, they are most frequently found on the trunk, neck, shoulders, and upper extremities.
    ◦ Diagnosis is primarily clinical, and treatment is usually observation or simple surgical excision for cosmetic reasons or symptomatic lesions.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ The exact cause is unknown.
    ◦ There is a genetic component, with some cases showing **chromosomal translocations**, particularly involving region 12q13-15.
    ◦ Trauma has been suggested as a potential trigger ("**post-traumatic lipoma**"), though this link is not definitively established.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ A lipoma is a **benign neoplastic proliferation** of mature, univacuolated adipocytes.
    ◦ These fat cells are histologically identical to normal fat cells but are contained within a thin, **fibrous capsule** that separates them from the surrounding tissue.
    ◦ They do not undergo malignant transformation, though a deep, atypical lipoma (well-differentiated liposarcoma) can be difficult to distinguish clinically.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Most common **benign soft tissue tumor**, affecting approximately 1 in 100 people.
• **Age of Onset**: Most commonly appear between the ages of **40 and 60**. They are uncommon in children.
