• **Gender**: Some sources cite a slight male predominance, while others report equal distribution. **Multiple lipomas** are more common in men.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Genetics**: **Familial multiple lipomatosis** (autosomal dominant condition).
• **Associated Syndromes**
    ◦ **Gardner Syndrome**: An autosomal dominant condition characterized by intestinal polyps, osteomas, and soft tissue tumors, including lipomas.
    ◦ **Madelung's Disease (Benign Symmetric Lipomatosis)**: Characterized by large, non-encapsulated lipomas around the neck and shoulders, creating a "**horse collar**" or "**Madelung's collar**" appearance. Strongly associated with **alcohol abuse**.
    ◦ **Dercum's Disease (Adiposis Dolorosa)**: Characterized by multiple, **painful lipomas**. More common in obese, postmenopausal women.
• **Obesity**: While lipomas are composed of fat, their development is not directly proportional to a patient's weight. They can occur in individuals of any body habitus.
• **Minor Trauma**: A debated risk factor.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with the incidental finding of a **slow-growing**, **non-tender lump** under the skin that has been present for months to years.
    ◦ The primary complaint is often cosmetic, or concern about the nature of the growth.
    ◦ They rarely cause symptoms unless they are large or in a location that compresses a nerve.
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ **Asymptomatic**: The vast majority of lipomas are painless and cause no symptoms.
    ◦ **Pain/Tenderness**: Can occur if the lipoma compresses a peripheral nerve or if it is an **angiolipoma** (a subtype containing blood vessels).
    ◦ **Cosmetic Concern**: A common reason for seeking medical evaluation and treatment.
    ◦ **Restricted Movement**: Very large lipomas located near a joint can mechanically interfere with the range of motion.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Palpation**: Feels **soft**, **"doughy"**, or **rubbery** in consistency.
• **Mobility**: **Freely mobile** and not attached to the overlying skin or underlying fascia.
• **"Slip Sign"**: The edges of the tumor are easily palpable and feel as though they slip out from under the examining fingers.
• **Borders**: **Well-circumscribed** and encapsulated.
• **Location**: Most commonly located in the **subcutaneous tissue** of the trunk, neck, posterior shoulders, and proximal extremities.
• **Size**: Typically 1-3 cm in diameter, but can grow much larger (**giant lipoma >5 cm**).
• **Overlying Skin**: Normal in appearance, without discoloration, inflammation, or ulceration. A central punctum is absent (helping to distinguish it from an epidermoid cyst).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: The diagnosis is almost always made based on the characteristic findings on history and physical exam.
• **Imaging (not routinely necessary for small, classic lesions)**
    ◦ **Ultrasound**: The **initial imaging modality** of choice if there is diagnostic uncertainty. A lipoma appears as a **well-defined**, **encapsulated**, **compressible**, **hyperechoic mass** parallel to the skin, with no significant internal blood flow on Doppler.
    ◦ **MRI**: The **gold standard** for differentiating a lipoma from a malignant **liposarcoma**, especially for **large (>5 cm)**, **deep (subfascial)**, or **rapidly growing lesions**. A lipoma will have signal intensity identical to that of subcutaneous fat on all pulse sequences and will "disappear" (show **signal suppression**) on fat-suppression sequences.
• **Biopsy/Histology**
    ◦ **Excisional biopsy** is the definitive diagnostic procedure and is also therapeutic.
    ◦ **Histology**: Confirms the diagnosis by showing a thin, fibrous capsule surrounding a lobulated collection of **mature, univacuolated adipocytes** with **no cellular atypia**, pleomorphism, or mitotic figures.
sections.treatment:
• **Conservative Management / Observation**
    ◦ The standard approach for asymptomatic lipomas with a clear clinical diagnosis.
    ◦ Provide patient reassurance regarding the benign nature of the lesion.
• **Surgical Excision**
    ◦ **Standard of care** for symptomatic or cosmetically bothersome lipomas.
    ◦ **Indications**: Pain, nerve compression, restricted movement, cosmetic concern, diagnostic uncertainty.
    ◦ **Procedure**: Performed under local anesthesia via a simple elliptical incision. The **entire lipoma, including its capsule**, is dissected and removed to prevent recurrence.
• **Steroid Injections**: Intralesional injections of triamcinolone can cause localized fat atrophy, shrinking the lipoma. May not result in complete resolution and is less common.
• **Liposuction**: An alternative for removing large lipomas in cosmetically sensitive areas to minimize scarring. Has a **higher rate of recurrence** than complete excision.
sections.management:
• **If Asymptomatic**: Explain that no treatment is necessary. Instruct the patient on **"red flag" signs** that warrant re-evaluation (**rapid growth**, **new pain**, **skin changes**).
• **If Symptomatic/Cosmetic Concern**: Discuss the risks and benefits of surgical excision, including **scarring**, **bleeding**, **infection**, and **recurrence** (<5% with complete excision).
sections.complications:
• **Complications of the Lipoma (Rare)**
    ◦ Compression of adjacent nerves, causing pain or neuropathy.
    ◦ Cosmetic disfigurement.
    ◦ Interference with joint movement (if very large and near a joint).
• **Complications of Excision**
    ◦ **Scarring**
    ◦ **Hematoma or Seroma**
    ◦ **Wound Infection**
    ◦ **Nerve Damage** (to nearby cutaneous nerves)
    ◦ **Recurrence** (if the capsule is not completely removed)
sections.prognosis: • The prognosis is **excellent**. Lipomas are **benign** lesions with **no malignant potential**. **Recurrence** after complete surgical excision is **uncommon (<5%)**.

sections.overview:
• An **Epidermal Inclusion Cyst (EIC)**, also commonly but incorrectly called a "**sebaceous cyst**," is a **benign**, **keratin-filled** subcutaneous nodule
    ◦ It is the most common type of cutaneous cyst
    ◦ Formed by the proliferation of epidermal cells within a circumscribed space in the dermis
    ◦ The cyst wall is composed of stratified squamous epithelium, identical to the epidermis, which produces and sheds keratin into the enclosed cyst cavity
sections.etiology:
• The core pathophysiology is the sequestration of epidermal cells within the dermis, which can occur via two primary mechanisms:
    ◦ **Occlusion of a Pilosebaceous Follicle**
        ▪ The most common cause
        ▪ The opening of a hair follicle becomes blocked, leading to the accumulation of keratinaceous debris within the follicular canal
        ▪ The follicle expands, forming a cyst
    ◦ **Traumatic Implantation**
        ▪ Epidermal cells are driven deep into the dermis as a result of trauma, a surgical procedure, or even a minor wound (e.g., a needle stick)
        ▪ These displaced cells continue to proliferate and produce keratin, forming a cyst
• The result in both cases is a dermal cyst lined by true epidermis (including a granular layer) that is filled with laminated, soft, yellow keratin
• If the cyst wall **ruptures**, the keratinous contents are released into the surrounding dermis, inciting a robust **foreign-body inflammatory reaction**, leading to pain, erythema, and swelling
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: The most common cutaneous cyst
• **Age**: Can occur at any age but is most common in young and middle-aged adults (3rd and 4th decades)
• **Sex**: More common in men (M:F ratio 2:1)
• **Location**: Can appear anywhere on the body but has a predilection for hair-bearing areas, particularly the face, scalp, neck, back, chest, and scrotum
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with a complaint of a "**lump**" or "**bump**" under the skin that has been present for months to years and has grown slowly
• Often, the presentation is for cosmetic reasons or because the lesion has become acutely **inflamed**, **painful**, and **enlarged**
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is almost always made clinically based on history and physical exam findings
    ◦ **Clinical Diagnosis**: Based on the characteristic **mobile, subcutaneous nodule** with a **central punctum**
    ◦ **Ultrasound**: Rarely necessary
        ▪ Can be used to differentiate from other soft tissue masses if the diagnosis is uncertain
        ▪ It will show a **well-circumscribed, hypoechoic dermal mass**
    ◦ **Biopsy / Histopathology**: Performed if there is clinical suspicion for **malignancy** (e.g., rapid growth, ulceration, fixation to underlying structures, location in an unusual area) or if the diagnosis is unclear
    ◦ **Histology**: Shows a cyst located in the dermis lined by **stratified squamous epithelium** with an intact **granular layer** (distinguishing it from a pilar cyst), filled with **laminated keratin**
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is **excellent** as Epidermal inclusion cysts are **benign** lesions
• With **complete surgical excision** of the cyst capsule, the cure rate is high and **recurrence is rare**

sections.overview:
• A **Seborrheic Keratosis (SK)** is the most common **benign epithelial tumor** of the skin.
    ◦ Characterized by a benign proliferation of immature **keratinocytes**.
    ◦ Often described as having a waxy, **"stuck-on" appearance**.
    ◦ Extremely common in middle-aged and older adults.
    ◦ They have **no malignant potential** and are not contagious.
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**: A **benign, localized proliferation of epidermal keratinocytes**.
    ◦ The exact cause is unknown, but it is considered part of the natural **aging process** of the skin.
• **Genetic Factors**:
    ◦ Somatic mutations in the ***FGFR3*** (Fibroblast Growth Factor Receptor 3) and ***PIK3CA*** genes are frequently found, suggesting a genetic component to their development.
• **Not Viral**:
    ◦ Unlike warts (verrucae), SKs are not caused by the **Human Papillomavirus (HPV)** and are not transmissible.
• **Sun Exposure**:
    ◦ While they can appear on sun-exposed skin, they also commonly occur in sun-protected areas, suggesting sun exposure is a contributing factor but not the sole cause.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Extremely common. The prevalence increases significantly with age.
• **Age**: Rare in individuals under 30; most common in those **over 50**.
    ◦ Nearly **90%** of individuals over age 60 have at least one SK.
• **Sex**: Affects males and females equally.
• **Race/Ethnicity**: More common in individuals with lighter skin types (Caucasians and Asians).
    ◦ A specific variant, ***dermatosis papulosa nigra***, consists of multiple small, dark papules on the face and neck and is very common in individuals of African or Asian descent.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Advanced Age**: The single greatest risk factor.
• **Genetics**: A familial predisposition is often noted.
• **Sun Exposure**: May play a role in the development on sun-exposed sites.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients typically present due to **cosmetic concerns** or fear of malignancy.
• They may report a new "mole" or "growth" that has appeared and **slowly enlarged** over months to years.
• The number of lesions can range from a single growth to hundreds.
• **Symptoms**:
    ◦ **Asymptomatic**: The vast majority of SKs cause no symptoms.
    ◦ **Pruritus**: Can occasionally be itchy.
    ◦ **Irritation**: May become inflamed, red, or crusted if traumatized or rubbed by clothing, which can cause bleeding.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Appearance**: Classically described as a well-demarcated, **"stuck-on"** or "pasted-on" papule or plaque.
• **Color**: Highly variable; can be skin-colored, tan, brown, or black.
• **Texture**: Surface can be waxy, greasy, velvety, or **verrucous** (wart-like) and may feel crumbly.
• **Shape**: Usually round or oval.
• **Size**: Varies from a few millimeters to several centimeters.
• **Key Features**:
    ◦ **Horn Cysts**: Small, whitish or yellowish keratin-filled cysts embedded in the surface. Best seen with a dermatoscope.
    ◦ **Comedo-like Openings**: Keratin-filled invaginations of the epidermis that appear as small dark plugs on the surface.
• **Location**: Most common on the trunk, face, scalp, and upper extremities.
    ◦ They **spare** the palms, soles, and mucous membranes.
• **Special Sign**:
    ◦ **Sign of Leser-Trélat**: The **sudden, explosive onset** of multiple, often pruritic, seborrheic keratoses.
        ▪ This is a rare **paraneoplastic sign** associated with an underlying internal malignancy, most commonly a **gastrointestinal adenocarcinoma** (e.g., stomach, colon).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: The diagnosis is almost always made based on the classic clinical appearance.
• **Dermoscopy**: A handheld dermatoscope is the key diagnostic tool.
    ◦ It enhances visualization of the surface and helps differentiate SKs from other lesions, especially **melanoma**.
    ◦ **Dermoscopic Findings**:
        ▪ **Comedo-like openings** (dark plugs)
        ▪ **Milia-like cysts** (horn cysts)
        ▪ **Cerebriform pattern** (brain-like appearance with fissures and ridges)
        ▪ **Sharp demarcation**
• **Biopsy (Shave or Punch)**: Indicated only if the diagnosis is uncertain or if there is concern for malignancy.
    ◦ **Indications for Biopsy**:
        ▪ Atypical features (e.g., lack of characteristic findings on dermoscopy)
        ▪ **Rapid growth**
        ▪ Persistent **bleeding** or **ulceration**
        ▪ Intense inflammation
        ▪ Failure to respond to treatment like cryotherapy
sections.treatment:
• **Reassurance**: As SKs are **benign**, no treatment is medically necessary. This is the primary management for asymptomatic, clinically obvious lesions.
• **Treatment Modalities for symptomatic lesions or cosmetic concerns**:
    ◦ **Cryotherapy**: Liquid nitrogen is applied to the lesion. This is the most common, quickest, and most cost-effective treatment.
        ▪ **Side effect**: Can cause **hypopigmentation**, which is more noticeable in darker skin types.
    ◦ **Curettage**: The lesion is scraped off with a curette, often after light anesthesia.
        ▪ May be combined with electrodessication to control bleeding. Provides an excellent cosmetic result.
    ◦ **Shave Excision/Biopsy**: The lesion is shaved off with a scalpel.
        ▪ This is the preferred method if there is any **diagnostic uncertainty**, as it provides a tissue specimen for pathology.
    ◦ **Electrodessication**: Use of an electric current to destroy the tissue.
    ◦ **Laser Ablation**: CO2 or Er:YAG lasers can be used to vaporize the lesion.
sections.management:
• **Patient Education**: Reassure the patient of the **benign nature** of the growth.
    ◦ Explain that it is not cancerous, not contagious, and that new lesions may appear over time as part of the aging process.
• **Cosmetic Considerations**: Inform patients that removal for purely cosmetic reasons is generally **not covered by insurance**.
• **Follow-up**: No routine follow-up is required for lesions diagnosed with high confidence.
    ◦ Advise patients to seek re-evaluation for any skin lesion that **grows rapidly, changes color, bleeds, or ulcerates**.
• **Suspicious Lesions**: If the **Sign of Leser-Trélat** is suspected, an urgent workup for an underlying malignancy (especially GI) is warranted, including age-appropriate cancer screening (e.g., colonoscopy, endoscopy) and imaging.
sections.complications:
• **Irritation/Inflammation**: The most common issue, usually from friction.
• **Bleeding**: Can occur with minor trauma.
• **Misdiagnosis**: The most significant potential complication is misdiagnosing a **nodular melanoma** as a benign SK, leading to a delay in treatment.
    ◦ **When in doubt, biopsy.**
• **Treatment Complications**:
    ◦ Scarring
    ◦ Hypo- or hyperpigmentation (especially post-cryotherapy)
    ◦ Incomplete removal or recurrence
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**. Seborrheic keratosis is a completely **benign condition** with no potential for malignant transformation.
• New lesions are likely to develop throughout the patient's life.

sections.overview:
• A **Cherry Angioma**, also known as a **Campbell de Morgan spot** or **senile angioma**, is a common, **benign** cutaneous **vascular proliferation**.
    ◦ Composed of clusters of **dilated capillaries** and post-capillary venules.
• Lesions are typically small, bright **cherry-red** to violaceous **papules**.
    ◦ Appear most frequently on the **trunk** and proximal extremities.
• Most common type of **angioma**.
• Prevalence increases significantly with **age**.
sections.etiology:
• Exact etiology is **unknown**.
• Pathophysiology involves a **benign proliferation** of **endothelial cells** lining capillaries.
    ◦ **Vascular Proliferation**: True **capillary malformations**, not malignant tumors.
        ▪ Represent a localized proliferation of dilated capillaries and venules in the **papillary dermis**.
    ◦ **Genetic Factors**: A genetic component is suspected as they can run in families; specific gene mutations have not been consistently identified.
    ◦ **Hormonal Influence**: Hormonal changes, such as those in **pregnancy**, may be associated with an increase in their number and size.
    ◦ **Chemical Exposure**: Some studies suggest a link between **eruptive cherry angiomas** and exposure to certain chemicals like **bromides** or **mustard gas**, but this is not a common cause.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Extremely **common** in the general population.
• **Age of Onset**:
    ◦ Typically begin to appear in the 3rd or 4th decade of life (after age 30).
    ◦ Their number and size increase progressively with advancing age.
        ▪ By age 75, over 75% of individuals have multiple cherry angiomas.
• **Sex**: Affects males and females equally.
• **Race**: Occur in all races, but may be less readily visible on darker skin types.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients usually present for one of two reasons:
    ◦ **Cosmetic Concern**: Unhappy with the appearance of the red spots.
    ◦ **Concern for Malignancy**: Worry that a new or changing spot could be skin cancer.
• The presentation is almost always a small, **asymptomatic red papule** that has been present for years and has grown slowly, or the patient has noticed an increasing number of similar lesions over time.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Diagnosis is made clinically based on the characteristic appearance on physical exam.
• **Dermoscopy**:
    ◦ The primary diagnostic tool used to confirm the **vascular nature** of the lesion and confidently rule out mimics.
• **Biopsy (Shave or Punch)**:
    ◦ Rarely necessary.
    ◦ Indicated only if the diagnosis is uncertain, particularly if **melanoma** is suspected.
    ◦ **Indications for Biopsy**:
        ▪ **Atypical features** (irregular border, multiple colors other than red/purple).
        ▪ **Rapid growth** or change.
        ▪ Spontaneous **bleeding** or **ulceration** without trauma.
        ▪ Uncertainty on dermoscopy.
• **Histology**:
    ◦ Shows a proliferation of dilated, congested capillaries and venules lined by **benign endothelial cells** in the **papillary dermis**.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** prognosis.
• Cherry angiomas are entirely **benign** with no potential for **malignant transformation**.
• They are **persistent** lesions; they do not resolve spontaneously.
• The number of lesions tends to **increase** throughout a person's life.

sections.overview:
• An Infantile Hemangioma (IH), commonly known as a "strawberry hemangioma," is a **benign vascular tumor** of infancy.
• It is the most common tumor in this age group.
• Characterized by a unique life cycle:
    ◦ **Rapid proliferation** in the first few months of life.
    ◦ Followed by a **plateau phase**.
    ◦ Then slow, **spontaneous involution** over several years.
• While most are self-resolving and require no treatment, some can cause significant complications depending on their size, location, and morphology.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ The exact cause is unknown.
    ◦ Leading hypothesis suggests an origin from placental tissue (chorionic villous mesenchyme) or endothelial progenitor cells.
    ◦ Localized tissue **hypoxia** during early development is also thought to play a role, stimulating angiogenesis via pathways like **Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF)**.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ IHs are true tumors resulting from the rapid proliferation of endothelial cells that form aberrant blood vessels.
    ◦ They are distinct from vascular malformations, which are structural anomalies present at birth that grow proportionally with the child.
• **Histologic Marker**
    ◦ IHs are uniquely positive for **Glucose Transporter 1 (GLUT-1)**, a pathognomonic marker that distinguishes them from nearly all other vascular anomalies.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Occurs in 4-5% of infants, making it the most common tumor of infancy.
• **Sex**: More common in females (3:1 to 5:1 ratio).
• **Race**: Significantly more common in Caucasian infants.
• **Birth Weight**: Higher incidence in premature and low birth weight infants.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Prematurity / Low Birth Weight (<1500g)** (Strongest risk factor)
• Female sex
• Caucasian race
• Multiple gestations (e.g., twins)
• Advanced maternal age
• History of placental abnormalities (placenta previa, preeclampsia)
• Chorionic villus sampling
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Appearance at Birth**
    ◦ Often absent at birth or may present as a subtle precursor lesion, such as a pale patch (anemic nevus), a small area of telangiectasias, or a red macule ("herald patch").
• **Clinical Course (Phases)**
    ◦ **Proliferative Phase (Rapid Growth)**: Begins in the first few weeks of life and continues for the first 5-9 months. This is when the lesion becomes most prominent.
    ◦ **Plateau Phase**: Growth stabilizes, typically around 9-12 months of age.
    ◦ **Involution Phase (Regression)**: Begins around 1 year of age and continues for several years (can last until age 5-10). The lesion gradually softens, flattens, and the color fades from bright red to a dull purple or gray.
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ Most are **asymptomatic**.
    ◦ Symptoms are location-dependent and arise from complications:
        ▪ **Pain**: Significant if **ulceration** occurs.
        ▪ **Bleeding**: Usually minor oozing from trauma or ulceration.
        ▪ **Functional Impairment**:
            • **Vision changes**: If located on the eyelid (**periorbital**).
            • **Stridor / Difficulty Breathing**: If located in the airway (**subglottic**).
            • **Difficulty Feeding**: If located on the lip or in the oral cavity.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Classification by Depth**
    ◦ **Superficial (most common, "strawberry")**: Bright red, lobulated, non-blanching papule, nodule, or plaque with a firm, rubbery texture.
    ◦ **Deep**: Bluish or skin-colored subcutaneous mass. Softer and more compressible.
    ◦ **Mixed (Compound)**: Features both superficial and deep components.
• **Classification by Distribution**
    ◦ **Localized (Focal)**: Most common; a single discrete lesion.
    ◦ **Segmental**: Large, plaque-like hemangioma that follows a neuroectodermal distribution (e.g., covering a large area of the face or a limb). These have a higher risk of complications and underlying syndromes.
• **Involution Findings**
    ◦ During regression, the color fades, and the lesion softens.
    ◦ After involution, the skin may be normal or may show residual changes like atrophy, wrinkling, telangiectasias, or a fibrofatty residuum.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primarily a clinical diagnosis** based on the characteristic history (appearance after birth, rapid growth) and physical exam findings.
• **Imaging (indicated for specific cases)**
    ◦ **Ultrasound with Doppler**: First-line imaging modality.
        ▪ Confirms the diagnosis by showing a **high-flow vascular mass**.
        ▪ Useful for differentiating from other lesions (e.g., venous malformations, cysts) and assessing the depth of deep hemangiomas.
    ◦ **MRI**: Indicated for large, deep, or segmental hemangiomas.
        ▪ Evaluates the extent of tissue involvement, especially in the orbit, airway, or liver.
        ▪ Essential for evaluating suspected **PHACES syndrome**.
• **Biopsy**: Rarely necessary.
    ◦ Performed only if the diagnosis is uncertain.
    ◦ The key finding is **GLUT-1 positivity**.
sections.treatment:
• **Active Non-intervention ("Watchful Waiting")**: The standard of care for most small, uncomplicated IHs that do not pose a functional or cosmetic risk.
• **Indications for Treatment**
    ◦ **Life-threatening location**: Airway (**subglottic**), liver (**high-output heart failure**).
    ◦ **Functional Impairment**: Vision (**periorbital**), hearing, feeding.
    ◦ **Ulceration**: Especially if painful, bleeding, or recurrent.
    ◦ **Significant Disfigurement**: Large facial lesions or those in cosmetically sensitive areas.
    ◦ Associated with underlying syndromes (e.g., **PHACES**).
• **First-Line Therapy**
    ◦ **Oral Propranolol**: A non-selective beta-blocker.
        ▪ Mechanism includes vasoconstriction, inhibition of VEGF, and induction of apoptosis in endothelial cells.
        ▪ Requires careful initiation with monitoring of heart rate, blood pressure, and glucose.
• **Other Therapies**
    ◦ **Topical Timolol (gel)**: A beta-blocker used for small, thin, superficial lesions.
    ◦ **Systemic Corticosteroids (e.g., Prednisolone)**: Historically first-line, now second-line due to side effect profile (growth retardation, immunosuppression, cushingoid features).
    ◦ **Pulsed Dye Laser (PDL)**: Effective for treating **ulceration** and residual telangiectasias after involution.
    ◦ **Surgical Excision**: Considered for pedunculated lesions, lesions that fail medical therapy, or for correction of residual fibrofatty tissue after involution.
sections.management:
• **Education & Reassurance**: Crucial for parents. Explain the natural history of proliferation and involution. Use serial photographs to track progress and demonstrate regression.
• **Monitoring**: Schedule regular follow-up visits (e.g., every 1-3 months during the proliferative phase) to monitor for growth and complications.
• **Wound Care**: For ulcerated lesions, use gentle cleansing, barrier ointments, and non-adherent dressings.
• **Referral**: Prompt referral to a specialist (Pediatric Dermatology, Vascular Anomalies Clinic) is indicated for any high-risk hemangioma (e.g., large, segmental, periorbital, "beard" distribution, lumbosacral).
sections.complications:
• **Ulceration**: Most common complication (~15%). Leads to pain, bleeding, infection, and scarring. Highest risk in areas of friction (lips, neck, anogenital).
• **Amblyopia ("Lazy Eye")**: A major risk with **periorbital hemangiomas** due to direct visual axis obstruction or induced astigmatism. **This is an ophthalmologic emergency.**
• **Airway Obstruction**: Hemangiomas in the **"beard" distribution** (chin, neck, mandible) have a high association with **subglottic hemangiomas**, which can cause **biphasic stridor** and life-threatening respiratory distress.
• **Permanent Disfigurement**: Scarring, atrophy, or fibrofatty residual tissue after involution.
• **High-Output Cardiac Failure**: A rare complication seen with very large or multiple hepatic hemangiomas.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for the vast majority of cases.
• Most lesions involute spontaneously with good to excellent cosmetic outcomes.
• **Rule of Involution**: Approximately 50% resolution by age 5, 70% by age 7, and >90% by age 9.
• Residual skin changes occur in ~50% of cases, but are often minor.

sections.overview:
• A **benign**, soft, flesh-colored or hyperpigmented **pedunculated (stalk-like) papule**
	◦ Commonly known as a **skin tag**
	◦ A very common **fibroepithelial polyp** that typically occurs in areas of **skin friction**
	◦ Medically **harmless** but can be a cosmetic concern or become irritated
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
	◦ The exact cause is unknown but is thought to be **multifactorial**
	◦ Contributing Factors:
		▪ **Friction** from skin rubbing against skin or clothing is a major factor
		▪ **Hormonal influences** (e.g., during pregnancy)
		▪ Growth factors associated with **insulin resistance**
		▪ **Genetic predisposition** has been observed
• **Pathophysiology**
	◦ Histologically, consists of a central **fibrovascular core** containing loose collagen fibers and small capillaries
	◦ Covered by a normal or slightly thinned (acanthotic) epidermis
	◦ It is a **benign outgrowth** of normal skin components
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Extremely common, affecting up to **50-60%** of the adult population
• **Age of Onset**: Prevalence increases significantly with age, most commonly developing after the age of **40**
• **Sex**: Affects males and females equally
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients typically present requesting removal for **cosmetic reasons** or because the lesions have become **irritated** by clothing or jewelry
• Patients may describe them as "**hanging pieces of skin**" that have been present for years and may have slowly increased in number or size
sections.diagnostics:
• The diagnosis is **purely clinical**, based on the characteristic appearance and location
• A **dermatoscope** can be used to visualize the structure, which typically shows a papillomatous surface with a central vessel
• **Biopsy is not necessary** unless the diagnosis is uncertain or there are atypical features to rule out other lesions like neurofibromas, nevi, or malignancy
	◦ **Atypical features** include: rapid growth, ulceration, bleeding without trauma, firmness
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** prognosis
	◦ Acrochordons are entirely **benign** and do not undergo malignant transformation
	◦ They persist unless removed and new lesions are common to develop over a person's lifetime

sections.overview:
• A **dermatofibroma** (also known as a **benign fibrous histiocytoma**) is a very common, **benign** cutaneous nodule composed of a proliferation of fibroblasts and histiocytes in the dermis
    ◦ Typically a firm, small papule or nodule, most frequently found on the lower extremities
    ◦ While it is a **benign** tumor with no **malignant potential**, it is clinically significant because it can mimic other lesions, most notably **nodular melanoma**
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ The exact cause is unknown; it is widely considered a reactive fibroblastic/histiocytic proliferation that occurs in response to minor, often unnoticed, trauma
    ◦ Common triggers include:
        ▪ Insect bites (e.g., mosquito, tick)
        ▪ **Folliculitis**
        ▪ Shaving injuries
        ▪ Minor puncture wounds
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ A localized, non-neoplastic proliferation of dermal spindle cells (fibroblasts) and histiocytes
    ◦ These cells produce excess collagen, which becomes entrapped within the lesion, contributing to its firmness
• **Histology**
    ◦ A well-demarcated but unencapsulated proliferation of spindle-shaped cells arranged in short bundles, often in a **"storiform"** (cartwheel) pattern in the dermis
    ◦ A key feature is **"collagen trapping"**, where the proliferating cells surround and entrap existing dermal collagen bundles, especially at the periphery of the lesion
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Extremely common
• **Age**: Most common in adults, typically appearing between ages 20-50; rare in children
• **Sex**: More common in females than males (approx. 2:1 ratio)
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients typically present with a single, slow-growing or stable "spot" on an extremity that has been present for months to years
• It is often found incidentally during a skin exam
• The patient may report that the lesion appeared after an insect bite or minor injury in the area
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**
    ◦ Diagnosis is most often made clinically based on the characteristic history and physical exam findings, especially a positive **Fitzpatrick sign**
• **Dermoscopy**
    ◦ Can increase diagnostic certainty and help differentiate from **melanoma**
• **Biopsy**
    ◦ Performed if the diagnosis is uncertain, the lesion is atypical (e.g., rapidly growing, ulcerated, >1.5 cm), or to rule out **malignancy**
    ◦ **Excisional biopsy** is both diagnostic and curative
    ◦ **Shave biopsy** is generally inadequate as it does not sample the deep dermal component, leading to incomplete removal and likely recurrence
    ◦ **Punch biopsy** can be used for definitive histologic diagnosis if excision is not immediately planned
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**
• Dermatofibromas are entirely **benign** and have **no potential for malignant transformation**
• Once formed, they are typically stable and persist for life, although rare cases of spontaneous regression have been reported

sections.overview:
• **Solar Purpura** (also known as **Actinic Purpura**, **Senile Purpura**, or **Bateman's Purpura**) is a common, benign dermatologic condition characterized by recurrent, non-inflammatory **ecchymoses** (bruises) on sun-exposed skin, particularly the dorsal forearms and hands of elderly individuals.
    ◦ Results from the extravasation of blood into the dermis following minor, often unnoticed, trauma.
    ◦ It is a manifestation of severe, long-term **photodamage** and is **not** associated with any underlying hematologic abnormality or coagulopathy.
sections.etiology:
• The underlying cause is chronic, cumulative **ultraviolet (UV) radiation exposure**, which leads to significant damage to the dermal connective tissue.
    ◦ **Pathophysiology**:
        ▪ **Dermal Atrophy**: Years of UV exposure degrade collagen and elastin fibers in the dermis, a process known as **solar elastosis**.
        ▪ **Vascular Fragility**: The supporting dermal connective tissue that surrounds and cushions the superficial dermal blood vessels becomes weak and atrophic.
        ▪ **Vessel Rupture**: The fragile, poorly supported capillaries and venules are highly susceptible to rupture from minor shearing forces or trauma.
        ▪ **Blood Extravasation**: Blood leaks from the ruptured vessels into the surrounding atrophic dermis.
        ▪ **Lesion Formation**: Because the dermis is atrophic, the extravasated blood spreads easily, forming large, well-demarcated, dark purple macules.
        ▪ **Slow Resolution**: Clearance of the extravasated red blood cells by macrophages is slow in aged skin, leading to prolonged lesion duration and residual hemosiderin staining (brown pigmentation).
sections.epidemiology:
• **Age**: Primarily affects older adults, typically **> 65 years**. Prevalence increases significantly with age.
• **Prevalence**: Extremely common, affecting up to **12% of individuals over 50** and a much higher percentage of those in their 80s and 90s.
• **Sex**: Affects men and women equally.
• **Skin Type**: More common and appears earlier in **fair-skinned individuals** (Fitzpatrick types I-III) with a history of significant sun exposure.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The typical patient is an elderly individual who presents with a complaint of **"easy bruising"** on their arms or hands.
    ◦ They often **cannot recall a specific traumatic event** that caused the lesions.
    ◦ The patient will deny symptoms of a systemic bleeding disorder, such as epistaxis, gingival bleeding, or melena.
    ◦ The history should focus on sun exposure, medication use (especially steroids and blood thinners), and a lack of systemic bleeding symptoms.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Diagnosis is made clinically based on the characteristic history and physical exam findings in an appropriate patient population.
• **Laboratory Studies**:
    ◦ **Not indicated** for a classic presentation.
    ◦ A workup is only necessary if the diagnosis is uncertain or if there are signs of a systemic bleeding disorder (e.g., purpura in non-sun-exposed areas, petechiae, mucosal bleeding, **palpable purpura**).
    ◦ If performed, labs will be **normal**:
        ▪ **CBC with platelets**: Normal platelet count.
        ▪ **PT/INR and PTT**: Normal coagulation times.
• **Skin Biopsy**:
    ◦ Rarely necessary.
    ◦ Performed only to rule out other conditions, such as vasculitis.
    ◦ Histology shows extravasated erythrocytes in an atrophic dermis with marked **solar elastosis**. There is **no evidence of perivascular inflammation**.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**.
    ◦ The condition is chronic and lesions will likely recur throughout the patient's life.
    ◦ However, it is a benign process with no associated mortality or systemic morbidity.
    ◦ Individual lesions fade over 1-3 weeks.

sections.overview:
• A common melanocytic nevus (plural: nevi), also known as a "common mole," is a **benign**, localized **proliferation of melanocytes** (nevus cells)
• These are extremely common skin lesions found on almost all individuals
• Their clinical significance lies primarily in their differentiation from **malignant melanoma**
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**: A combination of genetic predisposition and ultraviolet (UV) radiation exposure
    ◦ **Genetics**: Activating mutations in genes like **BRAF** or, less commonly, **NRAS** are found in the vast majority of **benign** nevi
        ▪ These mutations trigger a limited, controlled proliferation of melanocytes
    ◦ **UV Exposure**: Sun exposure, particularly during childhood and adolescence, is a major factor in determining the total number of nevi an individual develops
• **Pathophysiology**: Nevi are formed by clusters of melanocytes, called **nevus cells**, which group together in "nests"
    ◦ The location of these nests within the skin layers determines the type of nevus
        ▪ **Junctional Nevus**: Nests are located at the dermo-epidermal junction (DEJ)
        ▪ **Compound Nevus**: Nests are located at the DEJ **and** within the dermis
        ▪ **Intradermal Nevus**: Nests are located exclusively within the dermis
• **Maturation Sequence**: Nevi typically evolve over a person's lifetime in a predictable pattern
    ◦ Starts as a flat **junctional** nevus in childhood
    ◦ Grows and becomes a slightly raised **compound** nevus in adolescence/early adulthood
    ◦ Matures into a flesh-colored, dome-shaped **intradermal** nevus in later adulthood
    ◦ May eventually involute and disappear in old age
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Extremely common; most adults have 10-40 nevi
• **Incidence**: Typically appear during childhood and early adulthood
    ◦ The development of new nevi is uncommon after age 40 and should be viewed with higher suspicion
• **Demographics**: More common in individuals with fair skin (**Fitzpatrick skin types I-II**)
    ◦ The number of nevi peaks in the third or fourth decade of life and then gradually decreases
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presents as a small, **well-circumscribed** skin lesion
• Can be a **macule** (flat) or a **papule** (raised)
• Color is typically **uniform**, ranging from tan and brown to skin-colored or black
• Lesions are generally stable, changing very slowly and predictably over years
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: The diagnosis is most often made based on history and physical examination alone
• **Dermoscopy**
    ◦ A handheld dermatoscope is a crucial tool
    ◦ It uses magnification and polarized light to visualize subsurface skin structures
    ◦ **Benign** nevi show specific, organized patterns (e.g., **reticular/network**, **globular**, **cobblestone**)
• **Biopsy**
    ◦ Indicated if there is suspicion for **melanoma** (lesion meets **ABCDE criteria**, is an "**ugly duckling**," or is persistently symptomatic)
• **Gold Standard**: **Excisional biopsy**
    ◦ This is the preferred method for any suspicious pigmented lesion, performed with 1-3 mm margins
    ◦ It allows the pathologist to evaluate the entire lesion architecture and depth (**Breslow depth**), which is critical for staging if it is **melanoma**
• **Shave or Punch Biopsy**
    ◦ May be performed, but are less ideal as they may not provide an adequate sample for depth assessment, potentially leading to mis-staging of an early **melanoma**
    ◦ Never use shave biopsy if **melanoma** is highly suspected
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**
    ◦ By definition, a common melanocytic nevus is a **benign** lesion with no potential for metastasis and does not affect life expectancy
    ◦ The prognosis is only altered if **melanoma** develops

sections.overview:
• An atypical (dysplastic) nevus is a **benign melanocytic nevus** that shares clinical and/or histologic features with malignant melanoma.
• These lesions are considered potential **precursors to melanoma** and are significant markers for an **increased risk** of developing melanoma elsewhere on the body.
• They are not cancerous but represent a step along the continuum of melanocyte proliferation that can, in some cases, lead to malignancy.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ The development of atypical nevi is multifactorial, involving a combination of **genetic predisposition** and environmental factors, primarily **ultraviolet (UV) radiation exposure**.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Genetic Mutations**
        ▪ Germline mutations, particularly in the **CDKN2A** tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 9p21, are strongly associated with **Familial Atypical Multiple Mole Melanoma (FAMMM) syndrome**.
        ▪ Somatic mutations in genes like **BRAF** and **NRAS** are also found.
    ◦ **Melanocyte Proliferation**
        ▪ Atypical nevi are characterized by a disordered proliferation of melanocytes with both architectural and cytologic atypia.
    ◦ **UV Radiation**
        ▪ UV exposure induces DNA damage in melanocytes, promoting mutations and the development of both atypical nevi and melanoma.
        ▪ **Intermittent, high-intensity sun exposure** (e.g., blistering sunburns) is particularly damaging.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Common, affecting an estimated 2-8% of the Caucasian population.
• **Age of Onset**: Typically begin to appear around puberty and continue to develop into the 4th or 5th decade of life. Common nevi usually stop appearing after age 30.
• **Demographics**: More common in fair-skinned individuals (**Fitzpatrick skin types I and II**) with a history of significant sun exposure.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Personal or family history of melanoma**
• **Personal history of multiple atypical nevi**
• **High total body nevus count** (>50-100 moles)
• **Fair skin phenotype**: Light skin, hair, and eye color; tendency to burn rather than tan.
• History of **excessive sun exposure**, especially **blistering sunburns** in childhood/adolescence.
• **Genetic syndromes**: e.g., **FAMMM syndrome**.
• **Immunosuppression** (e.g., organ transplant recipients, chronic lymphocytic leukemia).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients typically present for evaluation of a "**new mole**," a "**changing mole**," or an "**unusual-looking mole**."
• Often discovered incidentally during a routine **full-body skin examination (FBSE)**.
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ **Usually asymptomatic**.
    ◦ The presence of symptoms is a **red flag** for potential malignant transformation.
    ◦ **Concerning symptoms include**:
        ▪ **Pruritus** (itching)
        ▪ **Bleeding** (especially without trauma)
        ▪ **Tenderness** or pain
        ▪ **Ulceration**
sections.physicalExam:
• **ABCDE Criteria**: Atypical nevi often fulfill some, but not all, of the criteria used to screen for melanoma.
    ◦ **A - Asymmetry**: One half of the mole does not match the other.
    ◦ **B - Border**: Irregular, scalloped, notched, or poorly defined borders.
    ◦ **C - Color**: Variegation; multiple shades of tan, brown, black, and sometimes pink or red within a single lesion.
    ◦ **D - Diameter**: Often ≥6 mm, but can be smaller.
    ◦ **E - Evolving**: Any change in size, shape, color, elevation, or symptoms over time.
• **Morphology**: Can be macular (flat), papular (raised), or a combination.
• **Classic Appearance ("Fried Egg" or "Targetoid")**: Characterized by a central, darker, raised papule surrounded by a flatter, lighter brown macular ring.
• **Location**: Most common on the **trunk** (especially the back) and sun-exposed areas, but can occur anywhere, including sun-protected areas like the scalp, breasts, and buttocks.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Dermoscopy**
    ◦ A handheld skin surface microscope used to visualize subsurface structures and patterns.
    ◦ Findings suggesting atypia include an **atypical pigment network**, **irregular dots/globules**, and **asymmetry** of pattern/color.
• **Biopsy (Gold Standard)**
    ◦ Histopathologic examination is required for definitive diagnosis.
    ◦ **Method of Choice**: **Deep shave biopsy or a narrow excisional biopsy** that includes the full thickness of the lesion.
    ◦ **AVOID superficial shave biopsies** if melanoma is suspected:
        ▪ This can transect the base of the lesion, making it impossible for the pathologist to accurately measure the **Breslow depth**, the single most important prognostic factor for melanoma.
• **Histopathology**
    ◦ Findings include:
        ▪ **Architectural Disorder**: Asymmetry, **nests of melanocytes bridging adjacent rete ridges**, and extension beyond the dermal-epidermal junction (lentiginous proliferation).
        ▪ **Cytologic Atypia**: Melanocytes are enlarged with **irregular nuclear contours**, **hyperchromasia**, and prominent nucleoli.
        ▪ **Grading**: Pathologists often grade atypia as **mild, moderate, or severe**. Severe atypia can be difficult to distinguish from melanoma in situ.
sections.treatment:
• **Biopsy-Proven Mild or Moderate Atypia with Clear Margins**: No further treatment is typically required. The patient is managed with routine surveillance.
• **Biopsy-Proven Severe Atypia**: Often treated as **melanoma in situ**.
    ◦ **Re-excision with 5 mm margins** is standard practice to ensure complete removal and rule out an associated melanoma.
• **Positive Margins on Initial Biopsy**: **Re-excision** is generally recommended for nevi with moderate-to-severe atypia to ensure complete removal. The decision for mild atypia is provider-dependent.
sections.management:
• **Professional Surveillance**:
    ◦ **Low-Risk Patients** (few atypical nevi, no personal/family hx of melanoma): Annual **full-body skin exams (FBSE)**.
    ◦ **High-Risk Patients** (many atypical nevi, personal/family hx of melanoma): More frequent FBSE (e.g., every 3-12 months).
    ◦ **Total Body Photography / Sequential Digital Dermoscopy**: Useful tools for monitoring high-risk patients to objectively track changes in nevi over time.
sections.complications:
• **Transformation to Melanoma**: The risk of any single atypical nevus transforming into melanoma is **low**.
• **Increased Lifetime Risk of Melanoma**: The primary significance of having atypical nevi is their role as a powerful marker for an increased risk of developing melanoma **de novo** (from normal-appearing skin) elsewhere on the body.
    ◦ Risk increases with the number of atypical nevi.
    ◦ Patients with **>5 atypical nevi** have a **~6-fold increased risk of melanoma**.
• **Psychosocial**: Anxiety and "mole-phobia" due to the association with melanoma risk.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis for an individual atypical nevus is **excellent**, as it is a benign lesion.
• The patient's overall prognosis is determined by their lifetime risk of developing melanoma and the stage at which any future melanoma is detected.
• **Early detection through regular surveillance** dramatically improves melanoma prognosis.
sections.preventionEducation:
• **Patient Education is Key**:
    ◦ **Sun Protection**: Emphasize **broad-spectrum sunscreen (SPF 30+)**, sun-protective clothing, hats, and avoiding peak sun hours (10 am - 4 pm).
    ◦ **Self-Skin Exams (SSE)**: Teach patients how to perform monthly SSEs to identify new or changing lesions.

sections.overview:
• A Congenital Nevus (plural: nevi), also known as a Congenital Melanocytic Nevus (CMN), is a benign proliferation of melanocytes that is present at birth or develops within the first few months of life
    ◦ These "birthmarks" range widely in size, from a few millimeters to covering vast areas of the body
• The primary clinical significance is their potential for malignant transformation into **melanoma**, a risk that correlates directly with the size of the nevus
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ Caused by a somatic mosaic mutation in melanocyte precursor cells during embryogenesis
        ▪ The most commonly identified mutations are in the **NRAS** and, less frequently, **BRAF** genes
        ▪ These are sporadic mutations and are not typically inherited
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The mutation occurs in a neural crest-derived cell (melanoblast), leading to a localized, benign proliferation of these cells
    ◦ The depth of the nevus cells can extend from the epidermis down through the dermis and even into subcutaneous fat, which is a key differentiator from acquired nevi
    ◦ The timing of the mutation during fetal development determines the ultimate size of the nevus; earlier mutations result in larger nevi
sections.epidemiology:
• **Small CMN (<1.5 cm):** Very common, occurring in approximately **1 in 100** live births
• **Medium CMN (1.5-19.9 cm):** Occur in approximately **1 in 1,000** live births
• **Large/Giant CMN (≥20 cm):** Rare, occurring in approximately **1 in 20,000** live births
sections.riskFactors:
• As this is a congenital condition resulting from a sporadic somatic mutation, there are no established maternal or environmental risk factors
    ◦ The "risk" is a random event during fetal development
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A pigmented lesion is noted at birth or within the first few months
    ◦ It is typically **asymptomatic**
    ◦ The nevus grows in proportion to the child's growth
    ◦ Over time, the lesion may become darker, thicker, more elevated, and often develops coarse terminal hairs (**hypertrichosis**)
• Parents often present with concerns about the appearance of the "birthmark" or its potential for cancer
• **Red flag symptoms** suggesting malignant change include:
    ◦ Pruritus (itching)
    ◦ Pain or tenderness
    ◦ Bleeding
    ◦ Ulceration
    ◦ Rapid growth of a new nodule within the nevus
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis:** Diagnosis is primarily made based on history (present at birth) and physical examination findings
• **Dermoscopy:** Can be used to evaluate pigment patterns but is often non-specific in congenital nevi
• **Biopsy**
    ◦ **Indication:** Performed for any part of the nevus showing suspicious changes (e.g., ABCDE criteria, new persistent nodule, ulceration)
    ◦ **Method:** An excisional or deep shave/punch biopsy of the suspicious area is preferred
    ◦ **Pathology:** Shows melanocytes in the epidermis and extending into the reticular dermis, often surrounding adnexal structures (hair follicles, glands) and blood vessels. Differentiating from melanoma can be challenging for pathologists
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **MRI of Brain and Spine:** Indicated for infants with **large/giant posterior axial CMN** or **multiple satellite nevi (>20)** to screen for **neurocutaneous melanosis (NCM)**
        ▪ Should be performed within the first 6 months of life before myelination is complete
sections.treatment:
• **Small & Medium CMN**
    ◦ **Conservative Management:** The standard of care. Involves regular clinical follow-up and patient/parent education on monthly self-skin exams
    ◦ **Surgical Excision:** Can be considered for cosmetic reasons or if a lesion is in a location prone to trauma/irritation. Excision is mandatory if there is a clinical or histologic suspicion of melanoma
• **Large & Giant CMN**
    ◦ **Multidisciplinary Approach:** Requires management by a dermatologist and a plastic surgeon
    ◦ **Prophylactic Surgical Excision:** Often recommended to reduce the lifetime risk of melanoma and for cosmetic/functional improvement. This is complex and may involve:
        ▪ **Serial (staged) excision:** The nevus is removed in sections over time
        ▪ **Tissue expansion:** A balloon expander is placed under adjacent normal skin to stretch it, creating excess skin to use for closure after nevus removal
        ▪ **Skin grafting:** The nevus is excised and replaced with a skin graft
    ◦ **Non-excisional therapies (Dermabrasion, Curettage, Laser):** Controversial. May improve cosmetic appearance but do not remove deep dermal nevus cells, carrying a risk of leaving residual cells that could become malignant and obscuring future clinical detection
sections.management:
• **Patient Education**
    ◦ Teach ABCDE criteria for melanoma detection (Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation, Diameter >6mm, Evolving)
    ◦ Emphasize the importance of **strict sun protection** (sunscreen, protective clothing) as UV exposure is a risk factor for melanoma development in any pigmented lesion
    ◦ Instruct on regular self/parental skin checks
• **Follow-up Schedule**
    ◦ **Small/Medium:** Annual skin exams with a primary care provider or dermatologist
    ◦ **Large/Giant:** More frequent follow-up with a dermatologist, typically every 6-12 months. Baseline clinical photography is highly recommended to monitor for changes
• **NCM Screening**
    ◦ For at-risk infants (large/giant posterior axial nevi, multiple satellites), perform a baseline neurologic exam and schedule an MRI of the brain/spine
sections.complications:
• **Malignant Transformation (Melanoma)**
    ◦ The most significant complication
    ◦ Lifetime risk is directly proportional to the size of the nevus
        ▪ **Small/Medium CMN:** Risk is very low (<1%)
        ▪ **Large/Giant CMN:** Risk is significantly higher, estimated at **5-10% over a lifetime**. Importantly, about half of these melanomas develop before age 10
• **Neurocutaneous Melanosis (NCM)**
    ◦ A rare, non-cancerous proliferation of melanocytes in the leptomeninges of the central nervous system
    ◦ **Association:** Occurs almost exclusively in patients with large/giant posterior axial CMN or numerous satellite nevi
    ◦ **Clinical Manifestations:** Can be asymptomatic or present with hydrocephalus, seizures, cranial nerve palsies, and developmental delay
    ◦ **Prognosis:** Poor, especially for symptomatic patients
• **Psychosocial Impact**
    ◦ Large or cosmetically sensitive lesions can cause significant psychological distress, bullying, and body image issues
sections.prognosis:
• **Small/Medium CMN:** Excellent prognosis. The risk of melanoma is extremely low
• **Large/Giant CMN:** Guarded prognosis. Depends on the development of melanoma or NCM. With regular surveillance and prophylactic excision where appropriate, the outcome can be improved
• **NCM:** Prognosis is poor, with high morbidity and mortality, particularly if symptoms develop in the first two years of life

sections.overview:
• A Port-Wine Stain (PWS), also known as **nevus flammeus**, is a congenital, low-flow **capillary malformation** of the dermal blood vessels.
• Presents **at birth** as a flat, pink-to-reddish-purple patch on the skin.
• Grows proportionally with the child and **persists throughout life**, often darkening and thickening over time.
    ◦ Unlike other common infantile birthmarks (e.g., nevus simplex, infantile hemangioma).
• Most commonly an isolated cosmetic finding but can be associated with underlying syndromes.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ Caused by a somatic, mosaic, gain-of-function mutation in the **GNAQ gene**.
        ▪ This is a postzygotic mutation, occurring after fertilization in a single cell during embryonic development and is therefore **not inherited**.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The **GNAQ mutation** leads to constitutive activation of the MAPK signaling pathway, resulting in the progressive dilation (**ectasia**) of post-capillary venules within the dermis.
    ◦ This is a **malformation** (abnormal vessel structure) and not a hemangioma (a benign tumor characterized by endothelial proliferation).
        ▪ The vessels are simply enlarged and engorged with blood.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Occurs in approximately **0.3%** of newborns.
• **Gender**: Affects males and females equally.
• **Race**: Occurs in all races and ethnicities.
• **Location**: Can occur anywhere on the body, but >80% are found on the head and neck.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **History**
    ◦ Parents report a "birthmark" that was **present at birth**.
    ◦ It has grown proportionally with the child and has **not faded or involuted**.
    ◦ The lesion is typically asymptomatic.
    ◦ The primary concern is often cosmetic.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**
    ◦ The diagnosis is almost always made clinically based on the characteristic history and physical exam findings.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ Not required for isolated PWS.
    ◦ Indicated only when suspecting an associated syndrome.
        ▪ **MRI of the Brain with Contrast**: Indicated for facial PWS involving the ophthalmic (**V1**) distribution of the trigeminal nerve to screen for ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomatosis seen in **Sturge-Weber Syndrome**.
        ▪ **Doppler Ultrasound / MRI of Limb**: Indicated for a large PWS on an extremity to evaluate for underlying venous malformations and limb overgrowth seen in **Klippel-Trenaunay Syndrome**.
• **Ophthalmology Consultation**
    ◦ **Mandatory** for any PWS involving the eyelids or periorbital region (V1/V2 distribution) to screen for **glaucoma**.
    ◦ Annual eye exams are required.
• **Skin Biopsy**
    ◦ Rarely necessary.
    ◦ Histology shows dilated, thin-walled capillaries and post-capillary venules in the superficial dermis.
sections.prognosis:
• **Isolated PWS**: Excellent prognosis.
    ◦ The lesion is benign and management is focused on cosmetic improvement and monitoring.
• **Syndromic PWS**: Prognosis is dependent on the severity of the associated systemic manifestations (e.g., severity of glaucoma, seizure control in SWS, or degree of limb-length discrepancy in KTS).

sections.overview:
• Telangiectasias are small, permanently dilated blood vessels (capillaries, venules, arterioles) located in the superficial dermis.
• They present as visible, fine, red-to-purple lines, webs, or net-like patterns on the skin or mucous membranes.
• While often a benign cosmetic concern, they can be a key cutaneous marker for significant underlying systemic diseases.
• They are characteristically **blanchable** with pressure (diascopy).
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology:** The core mechanism is the dilation of pre-existing superficial dermal blood vessels. This can result from:
    ◦ **Vessel Wall Weakness:** Loss of perivascular connective tissue (collagen and elastin) support, leading to vessel dilation under normal intravascular pressure.
    ◦ **Vasodilation:** Chronic vasodilation due to inflammatory mediators, hormonal influences, or neurovascular dysregulation.
    ◦ **Neovascularization:** Formation of new blood vessels, often in response to tissue injury or malignancy.
• **Etiology:** Telangiectasias are broadly classified as primary (congenital/hereditary) or secondary (acquired).
    ◦ **Acquired (More Common):**
        ▪ **Actinic Damage:** Chronic sun exposure (photoaging) is the most common cause, leading to dermal atrophy and loss of vessel support.
        ▪ **Rosacea:** Chronic inflammatory condition of the face characterized by erythema, papules/pustules, and prominent facial telangiectasias.
        ▪ **Hormonal Influence:** Elevated estrogen levels (e.g., pregnancy, oral contraceptives, chronic liver disease) can lead to **spider angiomas** (spider nevi).
        ▪ **Chronic Liver Disease/Cirrhosis:** Impaired estrogen metabolism leads to spider angiomas, typically on the upper trunk, face, and arms.
        ▪ **Connective Tissue Disease:**
            • **Systemic Sclerosis (Scleroderma):** Especially in **CREST syndrome**, presenting as mat-like telangiectasias on the face, hands, and mucous membranes. Also seen as nailfold capillary changes.
            • **Dermatomyositis:** Periungual (nailfold) telangiectasias are common.
        ▪ **Corticosteroid Use:** Prolonged use of potent topical or systemic steroids causes skin atrophy, making vessels more visible and fragile.
        ▪ **Radiation Therapy:** Radiation dermatitis leads to chronic skin changes, including permanent telangiectasias in the treatment field.
        ▪ **Venous Hypertension:** Increased pressure in lower extremity veins leads to telangiectasias ("spider veins") on the ankles and legs.
        ▪ **Malignancy:** **Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC)** classically presents as a pearly papule with fine, arborizing telangiectasias on its surface.
        ▪ **Carcinoid Syndrome:** Associated with episodic flushing which can lead to fixed facial telangiectasias over time.
    ◦ **Congenital / Genetic:**
        ▪ **Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia (HHT / Osler-Weber-Rendu Syndrome):** Autosomal dominant disorder characterized by telangiectasias on skin and mucosa (lips, tongue, nose, GI tract) and visceral arteriovenous malformations (AVMs).
        ▪ **Ataxia-Telangiectasia:** Autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder. Presents with the classic triad of cerebellar **ataxia**, oculocutaneous **telangiectasias** (especially conjunctiva), and **immunodeficiency**.
        ▪ **Sturge-Weber Syndrome:** Neurocutaneous disorder featuring a facial port-wine stain (capillary malformation) and associated leptomeningeal angiomas.
sections.epidemiology:
• Extremely common in the general population, with prevalence increasing with age.
• Actinically induced telangiectasias are most common in fair-skinned individuals (Fitzpatrick types I-II) with a history of significant sun exposure.
• Rosacea affects an estimated 16 million people in the US, primarily adults aged 30-60.
• HHT has a prevalence of approximately 1 in 5,000-10,000.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with a complaint of "broken capillaries," "spider veins," or persistent red marks on the skin, often for cosmetic reasons.
• A thorough history is crucial to screen for symptoms of underlying disease:
    ◦ Recurrent nosebleeds (epistaxis) or GI bleeding (melena) -> **HHT**
    ◦ Heartburn, dysphagia, or cold, painful fingers (Raynaud's) -> **Scleroderma/CREST**
    ◦ Easy flushing, facial papules -> **Rosacea**
    ◦ Jaundice, ascites, or history of hepatitis/alcoholism -> **Liver Disease**
    ◦ A non-healing "pimple" that sometimes bleeds -> **BCC**
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primarily a clinical diagnosis** based on history and physical exam.
• **Dermoscopy:** Handheld magnification helps visualize vessel morphology (e.g., arborizing vessels in BCC).
• **Workup for Suspected Underlying Disease:**
    ◦ **Liver Disease:** LFTs, albumin, coagulation panel (PT/INR), hepatitis panel.
    ◦ **Connective Tissue Disease:** ANA, anti-centromere antibody (highly specific for CREST), anti-Scl-70 (diffuse scleroderma).
    ◦ **HHT:**
        ▪ CBC to check for anemia.
        ▪ Screening for AVMs is critical:
            • Contrast echocardiogram ("bubble study") for pulmonary AVMs.
            • Brain MRI/MRA for cerebral AVMs.
            • Endoscopy for GI lesions.
• **Skin Biopsy:** Indicated only if there is a suspicion of malignancy (e.g., rule out BCC).
sections.prognosis:
• For isolated, benign telangiectasias (e.g., from sun damage), the prognosis is excellent. It is purely a cosmetic issue.
• The overall prognosis is **entirely dependent on the underlying etiology**. It can range from excellent to poor based on the severity and management of the associated systemic condition.

sections.overview:
• **Plaque psoriasis (psoriasis vulgaris)** is the most common form of psoriasis, accounting for approximately 80-90% of cases.
• It is a chronic, immune-mediated, inflammatory skin disorder characterized by the **hyperproliferation of keratinocytes**.
• The classic presentation involves **well-demarcated, erythematous plaques** with an overlying, **silvery-white scale**.
    ◦ These lesions are typically found on **extensor surfaces**, the **scalp**, and the **lumbosacral region**.
• It is a systemic disease with significant associated comorbidities, most notably **psoriatic arthritis**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**: Multifactorial, involving a combination of **genetic predisposition** and **environmental triggers**.
• **Pathophysiology**: A **T-cell-mediated autoimmune process**.
    ◦ **Trigger**: An environmental factor (e.g., infection, trauma) activates antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells) in the skin.
    ◦ **Activation**: Dendritic cells present an antigen to naive T-cells, causing them to differentiate into inflammatory helper T-cells (Th1, Th17, Th22).
    ◦ **Inflammatory Cascade**: These activated T-cells migrate into the dermis and epidermis and release pro-inflammatory cytokines, most importantly:
        ▪ **Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha (TNF-α)**
        ▪ **Interleukin-17 (IL-17)**
        ▪ **Interleukin-23 (IL-23)**
    ◦ **Hyperproliferation**: These cytokines stimulate keratinocytes to proliferate at an accelerated rate (cell turnover in **3-5 days** vs. the normal 28-30 days), leading to epidermal thickening (**acanthosis**) and the characteristic plaque formation.
        ▪ Incomplete keratinocyte maturation leads to the retention of nuclei in the stratum corneum (**parakeratosis**), which contributes to the silvery scale.
• **Histology**:
    ◦ **Acanthosis**: Epidermal hyperplasia (thickening).
    ◦ **Parakeratosis**: Retention of nuclei in the stratum corneum.
    ◦ **Munro's microabscesses**: Collections of neutrophils in the stratum corneum.
    ◦ Dilated, tortuous capillaries in the papillary dermis.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects 2-3% of the world's population.
• **Age of Onset**: Bimodal distribution:
    ◦ **Early onset**: 20-30 years of age (often associated with **HLA-Cw6** and a stronger family history).
    ◦ **Late onset**: 50-60 years of age.
• **Gender**: Affects males and females equally.
• **Ethnicity**: More common in Caucasians; less common in African and Asian populations.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Genetic**: **Family history is the strongest risk factor.**
    ◦ Specific genetic locus: **HLA-Cw6** is strongly associated with early-onset psoriasis.
• **Environmental Triggers**:
    ◦ **Infection**: **Streptococcal pharyngitis** (classic trigger for guttate psoriasis, which can precede plaque psoriasis). **HIV** infection can cause severe flares.
    ◦ **Trauma**: Physical trauma to the skin (cuts, burns, surgery) can induce lesions in susceptible individuals (**Koebner phenomenon**).
    ◦ **Medications**:
        ▪ **B**eta-blockers
        ▪ **L**ithium
        ▪ **A**ntimalarials (e.g., Hydroxychloroquine)
        ▪ **N**SAIDs
        ▪ **S**teroid withdrawal (rapid, systemic withdrawal)
    ◦ **Lifestyle**: Smoking, excessive alcohol consumption, obesity.
    ◦ **Stress**: Psychological or emotional stress.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The hallmark lesion is a **well-demarcated, erythematous plaque** with a thick, **silvery-white, lamellar scale**.
    ◦ Plaques can be of varying sizes, may coalesce, and are typically symmetrical.
• **Common Locations**:
    ◦ **Extensor surfaces**: Elbows, knees.
    ◦ **Scalp**: Often presents as severe "dandruff" with well-defined plaques.
    ◦ **Lumbosacral region / Gluteal cleft**.
    ◦ Can also involve nails, ears, and intertriginous areas (inverse psoriasis).
• **Symptoms**:
    ◦ **Pruritus**: The most common symptom, ranging from mild to severe.
    ◦ **Pain, burning, or stinging** of the lesions.
    ◦ **Joint Pain/Stiffness**: Suggests concomitant **Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA)**. Morning stiffness lasting >30 minutes is a red flag.
    ◦ **Psychosocial Impact**: Significant impact on quality of life, leading to anxiety, depression, and social stigmatization.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Skin**:
    ◦ **Plaques**: As described above (well-demarcated, erythematous, silvery scale).
    ◦ **Auspitz Sign**: Pinpoint bleeding observed after the removal of a psoriatic scale. Caused by the exposure of underlying, dilated dermal capillaries.
    ◦ **Koebner Phenomenon (Isomorphic Response)**: Development of new psoriatic lesions at sites of skin trauma.
• **Nails**: Nail involvement occurs in ~50% of patients.
    ◦ **Nail Pitting**: Small, punctate depressions on the nail plate.
    ◦ **Onycholysis**: Separation of the nail plate from the nail bed.
    ◦ **"Oil Drop" or "Salmon Patch" Sign**: Translucent, yellow-red discoloration of the nail bed.
    ◦ **Subungual Hyperkeratosis**: Thickening and scaling under the nail.
• **Joints**: Examine for signs of **Psoriatic Arthritis**.
    ◦ **Dactylitis ("Sausage Digit")**: Diffuse swelling of an entire finger or toe.
    ◦ **Enthesitis**: Inflammation at sites of tendon/ligament insertion (e.g., Achilles tendonitis, plantar fasciitis).
    ◦ Swelling, tenderness, and decreased range of motion in affected joints (can be asymmetric oligoarthritis, symmetric polyarthritis, or involve DIP joints).
sections.diagnostics:
• Primarily a **clinical diagnosis** based on characteristic history and physical exam findings.
• **Biopsy**: A punch biopsy can be performed for confirmation in atypical cases or to rule out other conditions (e.g., cutaneous T-cell lymphoma).
    ◦ Histopathology will show the classic findings of **acanthosis, parakeratosis, and Munro's microabscesses**.
• **Labs**: Not required for diagnosis of cutaneous disease.
    ◦ May be used to screen for comorbidities (lipids, glucose) or to monitor systemic therapies (CBC, CMP for methotrexate).
    ◦ Inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) may be elevated, especially with active **Psoriatic Arthritis**.
sections.treatment:
• **Severity Classification (Body Surface Area - BSA)**:
    ◦ **Mild**: <3% BSA
    ◦ **Moderate**: 3-10% BSA
    ◦ **Severe**: >10% BSA or involvement of hands, feet, face, or genitals.
sections.management:
• **Emollients**: Use liberally to hydrate skin, reduce scaling, and alleviate pruritus.
• **Comorbidity Screening**: Regularly screen for and manage associated conditions:
    ◦ **Psoriatic Arthritis**: Use screening tools (e.g., PEST questionnaire) and ask about joint pain/stiffness at every visit.
    ◦ **Cardiovascular Disease**: Monitor blood pressure, lipids.
    ◦ **Metabolic Syndrome**: Monitor weight, glucose, waist circumference.
    ◦ **Depression/Anxiety**: Screen for mental health issues.
sections.complications:
• **Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA)**: Develops in up to 30% of patients. Can lead to irreversible joint damage if untreated.
• **Metabolic Syndrome & Cardiovascular Disease**: Increased risk of hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes mellitus, MI, and stroke.
• **Psychosocial Morbidity**: High rates of depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation.
• **Erythrodermic Psoriasis**: A severe, unstable form where >90% of the BSA is involved. 
    ◦ Can be life-threatening due to risk of infection, electrolyte imbalance, and high-output cardiac failure. **Medical emergency.**
• **Pustular Psoriasis**: Another severe form characterized by widespread sterile pustules and systemic symptoms (fever, malaise).
sections.prognosis:
• Psoriasis is a **chronic, lifelong condition** with a relapsing-remitting course.
• There is **no cure**, but modern treatments can achieve significant clearing and dramatically improve quality of life.
• Life expectancy may be slightly reduced in patients with severe disease, primarily due to the increased risk of cardiovascular events.
sections.preventionEducation:
• **Patient Education**: Crucial for managing a chronic disease. Discuss the nature of the disease, trigger avoidance, and the importance of treatment adherence.
• **Lifestyle Modification**: Counsel on weight loss, smoking cessation, and reducing alcohol intake.

sections.overview:
• **Guttate psoriasis** is an acute, eruptive, inflammatory dermatosis characterized by the sudden onset of small (1-10 mm), discrete, **"drop-like"** erythematous papules and plaques with a fine, silvery scale.
    ◦ It is a distinct clinical variant of psoriasis, most commonly seen in children and young adults.
    ◦ The eruption is strongly associated with a preceding **Group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal (GABHS) infection**, typically pharyngitis.
    ◦ While often self-limiting, it can be the initial presentation of what later becomes chronic plaque psoriasis.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ The primary trigger is an infection, most classically **Group A Beta-Hemolytic Streptococcal (GABHS) pharyngitis** (*Streptococcus pyogenes*).
        ▪ The psoriasis eruption typically occurs 1-3 weeks after the infection.
    ◦ Other less common triggers include viral infections (URI, Varicella), stress, and certain medications (e.g., beta-blockers, lithium, abrupt withdrawal of systemic corticosteroids).
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The mechanism is thought to be an immune-mediated reaction involving **molecular mimicry**.
        ▪ A patient with a genetic predisposition to psoriasis is infected with GABHS.
        ▪ T-cells are activated to target specific streptococcal antigens (e.g., M protein).
        ▪ These activated T-cells mistakenly cross-react with similar-looking self-antigens (e.g., keratin) found in the skin.
        ▪ This triggers a T-helper cell (Th1 and Th17) inflammatory cascade in the dermis and epidermis.
        ▪ The inflammation leads to keratinocyte hyperproliferation, resulting in the characteristic erythematous papules and silvery scale.
sections.epidemiology:
• Accounts for approximately 2% of all psoriasis cases.
• Predominantly affects children, adolescents, and adults under 30 years of age.
• It is often the first manifestation of psoriasis in a patient.
• No significant sex predilection.
• Associated with specific HLA alleles, particularly **HLA-Cw6**, which confers susceptibility.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Recent GABHS infection**: Pharyngitis, tonsillitis, or perianal streptococcal dermatitis. This is the single most important risk factor.
• **Genetic predisposition**: Personal or family history of psoriasis.
• **Age**: Children and young adults (<30).
• Other infections: Viral upper respiratory infections.
• Psychological stress.
• **Koebner phenomenon**: Trauma to the skin can induce lesions.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient, typically a child or young adult, presents with the **abrupt onset of a widespread rash**.
• The history often includes a **sore throat, fever, or malaise 1-3 weeks prior** to the rash's appearance.
• The eruption is often mildly pruritic but can be asymptomatic.
• The rash appears suddenly over a period of days to weeks.
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ **Pruritus**: Mild to moderate itching is common.
    ◦ **Cosmetic concern**: The sudden, widespread nature of the rash is often distressing to patients.
    ◦ **Symptoms of preceding infection**: Residual sore throat, tonsillar swelling, or fever may be present.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Lesion Morphology**
    ◦ **"Guttate"** (Latin *gutta*, meaning "drop") **papules**: Multiple, small (1-10 mm), discrete, round-to-oval papules and thin plaques.
    ◦ **Color**: Salmon-pink to erythematous.
    ◦ **Scale**: Fine, silvery-white, superficial scale that may be less prominent than in plaque psoriasis.
• **Distribution**
    ◦ Widespread and symmetric.
    ◦ Primarily involves the **trunk and proximal extremities**.
    ◦ The face, scalp, palms, and soles are often spared.
• **Associated Signs**
    ◦ **Auspitz Sign**: Pinpoint bleeding upon gentle scraping or removal of the scale (may be present).
    ◦ **Koebner Phenomenon**: Development of new lesions at sites of skin trauma (e.g., scratches).
    ◦ **Pharyngeal exam**: May reveal erythema, tonsillar exudates, or petechiae suggestive of recent streptococcal pharyngitis.
sections.diagnostics:
• Primarily a **clinical diagnosis** based on the characteristic history and physical exam findings.
• **Supportive Laboratory Tests**
    ◦ **Throat Culture or Rapid Strep Test**: To detect active GABHS infection. May be negative if the infection has resolved.
    ◦ **Antistreptolysin O (ASO) Titer**: **Crucial test.** An elevated or rising titer confirms a recent streptococcal infection, even if the throat culture is negative.
    ◦ **Skin Biopsy**
        ▪ Rarely necessary but can be performed if the diagnosis is uncertain.
        ▪ Histopathology shows classic psoriatic features: **acanthosis** (epidermal hyperplasia), **parakeratosis** (retained nuclei in the stratum corneum), **Munro's microabscesses** (neutrophil collections in the stratum corneum), and a perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate.
sections.treatment:
• **Treat Underlying Infection**
    ◦ If GABHS infection is confirmed or strongly suspected, a course of antibiotics is recommended to eradicate the organism and prevent complications like rheumatic fever.
    ◦ **First-line**: Penicillin VK or Amoxicillin.
    ◦ **PCN Allergy**: Azithromycin or Clindamycin.
• **Topical Therapy**
    ◦ **Medium-potency topical corticosteroids** (e.g., triamcinolone 0.1%).
    ◦ **Vitamin D analogs** (e.g., calcipotriene, calcitriol).
    ◦ **Emollients**: To reduce scaling and pruritus.
• **Phototherapy**
    ◦ **Narrowband UVB (NB-UVB) is the treatment of choice** for extensive guttate psoriasis. It is highly effective and often leads to rapid clearance.
    ◦ Sunlight exposure (heliotherapy) can also be beneficial.
• **Systemic Therapy**
    ◦ Generally reserved for cases that fail to respond to topicals and phototherapy.
    ◦ Options include methotrexate, cyclosporine, acitretin, or biologics (e.g., TNF-alpha inhibitors, IL-17/23 inhibitors).
sections.management:
• **Symptom Control**: Advise gentle skin care, use of moisturizers, and lukewarm baths to manage pruritus.
• **Follow-up**: Schedule follow-up appointments to monitor for resolution, recurrence, or progression to plaque psoriasis.
sections.complications:
• **Progression to Chronic Plaque Psoriasis**: This is the most significant complication, occurring in approximately one-third of patients.
• **Post-inflammatory Pigmentary Changes**: Hyperpigmentation or hypopigmentation after lesions resolve.
• **Psychosocial Distress**: The sudden, visible nature of the rash can cause significant anxiety and self-consciousness.
• **Erythrodermic Psoriasis**: A rare but severe complication where the rash becomes confluent and involves >90% of the body surface area.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is generally good.
• **Spontaneous resolution** occurs in many patients within weeks to months, even without treatment.
• The clinical course can be divided into thirds:
    ◦ ~1/3 of patients experience complete, long-term remission.
    ◦ ~1/3 have recurrent episodes of guttate psoriasis, often triggered by new infections.
    ◦ ~1/3 progress to develop chronic plaque psoriasis.
sections.preventionEducation:
• **Patient Education**: Explain the link between strep infection and the rash. Reassure them that the condition is often self-limiting but carries a risk of evolving into chronic psoriasis.
