• **Prevention**: Prompt diagnosis and treatment of future streptococcal infections may help prevent flares.

sections.overview:
• Pustular psoriasis is a rare and severe variant of psoriasis characterized by the eruption of widespread, **sterile pustules** on an erythematous base.
    ◦ It is not an infection; the pustules contain non-infectious, **neutrophilic exudate**.
• It can be classified into generalized and localized forms.
    ◦ **Generalized pustular psoriasis (GPP)** is a potentially **life-threatening** medical emergency.
sections.etiology:
• Pustular psoriasis is an autoinflammatory skin disorder driven by dysregulation of the innate and adaptive immune systems.
• **Etiology (Triggers)**:
    ◦ **Medication Withdrawal**: **Abrupt withdrawal of systemic corticosteroids** is a classic trigger.
    ◦ **Medications (Initiation)**: Lithium, beta-blockers, NSAIDs, antimalarials, terbinafine.
    ◦ **Infections**: Especially upper respiratory infections (e.g., streptococcal pharyngitis).
    ◦ **Metabolic/Electrolyte Imbalance**: **Hypocalcemia**.
    ◦ **Pregnancy**: Hormonal changes can trigger "**impetigo herpetiformis**."
    ◦ **Stress**: Physical or emotional stress.
    ◦ **Local Irritants**: Strong topical agents, excessive UV light (sunburn).
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Genetic Predisposition**: Strong association with mutations in the **IL36RN gene**, which encodes the IL-36 receptor antagonist, leading to unopposed pro-inflammatory signaling.
    ◦ **Immune Cascade**: Triggering factors activate dendritic cells and T-cells (Th1/Th17 pathways).
    ◦ **Cytokine Release**: Massive release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including **TNF-α, IL-17, IL-23**, and especially **IL-36**.
    ◦ **Neutrophil Chemotaxis**: These cytokines cause a massive influx of neutrophils into the epidermis.
    ◦ **Pustule Formation**: Neutrophils accumulate in the superficial epidermis, forming characteristic **sterile pustules** known as **spongiform pustules of Kogoj**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Rare, affecting <1% of all psoriasis patients.
• **Age of Onset**: Can occur at any age; GPP has a bimodal distribution (early adulthood and >50 years).
• **Gender**: Affects males and females equally.
• **Association**: Approximately 30% of patients with GPP have a prior history of **psoriasis vulgaris** (plaque psoriasis).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation varies significantly by subtype.
• **Generalized (von Zumbusch)**:
    ◦ **Abrupt onset** of fiery red, painful erythema that spreads over large areas of the body within hours.
    ◦ Followed by the eruption of numerous, pinpoint (2-3 mm), sterile, monomorphic pustules.
    ◦ Pustules coalesce into large purulent collections, often described as "**lakes of pus**."
    ◦ The patient is **acutely ill**, appears **toxic**, and has significant **systemic symptoms**.
• **Localized (Palmoplantar Pustulosis - PPP)**:
    ◦ Chronic, relapsing eruption of yellow-brown pustules on the **palms and soles**.
    ◦ Pustules are set in an erythematous, scaly base.
    ◦ Often functionally disabling due to pain and fissuring.
• **Localized (Acrodermatitis Continua of Hallopeau - ACH)**:
    ◦ Rare, chronic, and persistent pustular eruption of the **fingertips, toes, and nail beds**.
    ◦ Can lead to severe nail dystrophy (onychodystrophy), nail loss (anonychia), and resorption of the distal phalanx (osteolysis).
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is primarily clinical, with laboratory and histologic findings for confirmation and management.
• **Laboratory Studies**:
    ◦ **CBC**: **Leukocytosis** (often >20,000/L) with a marked **neutrophilia** and **left shift**.
    ◦ **CMP**: **Hypocalcemia**, hypoalbuminemia, electrolyte abnormalities (due to fluid loss).
    ◦ **Inflammatory Markers**: Markedly elevated **CRP** and **ESR**.
    ◦ **Blood Cultures**: Performed to rule out sepsis; should be negative.
    ◦ **Bacterial Culture of Pustule**: Gram stain and culture will be **negative (sterile)**, helping to differentiate from bacterial infection.
• **Histopathology (Skin Biopsy)**:
    ◦ **Confirmatory finding**: **Kogoj's spongiform pustules** - collections of neutrophils in the superficial epidermis.
    ◦ Other findings: Acanthosis (epidermal thickening), parakeratosis, and a perivascular inflammatory infiltrate.
sections.prognosis:
• **GPP**: With modern treatment, the acute flare can be controlled, but the disease follows a **chronic, relapsing course**.
    ◦ Prognosis depends on the severity of the flare and the presence of comorbidities.
    ◦ Mortality is now low with aggressive management but remains a risk.
• **Localized**: Not life-threatening but can be chronic, refractory to treatment, and cause significant morbidity and impact on quality of life.

sections.overview:
• Erythrodermic psoriasis (EP), or psoriatic erythroderma, is a severe, unstable, and rare variant of psoriasis.
    ◦ Characterized by widespread, fiery **erythema** and **exfoliation** (scaling) affecting at least **90% of the body surface area (BSA)**.
    ◦ Considered a **medical emergency** due to its potential for life-threatening systemic complications, including:
        ▪ **High-output cardiac failure**
        ▪ **Sepsis**
        ▪ Severe metabolic derangements
    ◦ Requires prompt hospitalization and aggressive systemic treatment.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology (Triggers)**
    ◦ Can develop gradually from chronic plaque psoriasis or arise acutely from a specific trigger.
    ◦ **Most common trigger**: **Abrupt withdrawal of potent topical or systemic corticosteroids**.
    ◦ **Medications**: Lithium, antimalarials, beta-blockers, NSAIDs.
    ◦ **Infections**: Systemic infections (e.g., streptococcal pharyngitis, HIV).
    ◦ **Systemic illness**: Electrolyte imbalance (especially **hypocalcemia**).
    ◦ **Other**: Excessive alcohol consumption, severe emotional stress, phototherapy burns.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ An extreme and dysregulated T-cell-mediated inflammatory response (**Th1, Th17 pathways**) involving cytokines like **TNF-alpha, IL-17, and IL-23**.
    ◦ This leads to massive cutaneous vasodilation and a dramatically increased rate of epidermal cell turnover.
    ◦ The consequences are:
        ▪ **Impaired Barrier Function**: Leads to massive transepidermal water loss (TEWL), protein loss, and electrolyte loss.
        ▪ **Thermodysregulation**: Profound heat loss from vasodilation causes **hypothermia** and compensatory shivering.
        ▪ **Hemodynamic Changes**: Increased cutaneous blood flow shunts a large volume of blood to the skin, potentially leading to **high-output cardiac failure**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Rare, affecting approximately 1-2% of all patients with psoriasis.
• **Demographics**: More common in adult males (Male:Female ratio 3:1).
• **Onset**: Can occur at any age but is most common in middle-aged adults, often in patients with a long-standing history of unstable plaque psoriasis.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Pre-existing, unstable plaque psoriasis**.
• Poor adherence to psoriasis treatment.
• **Recent withdrawal from systemic or high-potency topical steroids**.
• Systemic infection.
• Comorbidities such as HIV or alcoholism.
• Use of provoking medications (lithium, antimalarials).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients typically present as acutely ill, distressed, and uncomfortable.
• Presentation is characterized by a rapid, generalized "explosion" of pre-existing psoriasis or the de novo appearance of diffuse erythema.
• Patients often report feeling intensely cold and may be shivering uncontrollably, despite having warm, erythematous skin.
• **Cutaneous Symptoms**
    ◦ Intense, widespread **pruritus** (itching) and skin pain or a burning sensation.
• **Systemic Symptoms**
    ◦ **Chills**, shivering
    ◦ **Malaise**, profound fatigue
    ◦ **Arthralgias** (joint pain)
    ◦ Lower extremity **edema** (due to **hypoalbuminemia** and capillary leak)
sections.physicalExam:
• **Skin**
    ◦ **Fiery, bright-red erythema** involving **≥90% of the BSA**.
    ◦ Skin is warm and edematous to the touch.
    ◦ Fine, branny scales that often desquamate (peel) in large sheets (**exfoliative dermatitis**).
    ◦ Pre-existing psoriatic plaques may be obscured by the generalized erythema.
    ◦ "**Islands of sparing**" (patches of uninvolved skin) are characteristically absent, distinguishing it from other erythrodermas like Pityriasis Rubra Pilaris (PRP).
• **Nails**
    ◦ Severe nail changes are common, including pitting, onycholysis, subungual hyperkeratosis, and "oil drop" spots.
• **Hair**
    ◦ **Telogen effluvium** (diffuse hair shedding) may occur weeks to months after the acute episode.
• **Systemic Findings**
    ◦ **Tachycardia** (due to dehydration and increased cardiac output).
    ◦ Peripheral **edema**.
    ◦ Generalized **lymphadenopathy** (dermatopathic).
    ◦ **Fever** or **hypothermia**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Diagnosis is primarily clinical**, based on history and the characteristic physical exam finding of erythroderma (≥90% BSA involvement).
• **Skin Biopsy**
    ◦ A punch biopsy can confirm the diagnosis of psoriasis and help rule out other causes of erythroderma (e.g., CTCL, drug reaction).
    ◦ Histology shows characteristic psoriatic features: acanthosis, parakeratosis with neutrophils (**Munro's microabscesses**), and a perivascular inflammatory infiltrate.
• **Laboratory Studies (Essential for Management)**
    ◦ **CBC**: May show leukocytosis and normocytic anemia (anemia of chronic disease).
    ◦ **CMP**: Crucial to monitor for:
        ▪ **Electrolyte abnormalities** (**hypocalcemia**, **hypomagnesemia**).
        ▪ **Hypoalbuminemia** (due to protein loss through skin).
        ▪ **Renal dysfunction** (↑ BUN/Cr from dehydration).
    ◦ **Inflammatory Markers**: Elevated ESR and CRP.
    ◦ **Blood Cultures**: To rule out sepsis if the patient is febrile.
sections.treatment:
• **Supportive Care (Paramount)**
    ◦ **Fluid & Electrolyte Management**: Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation.
    ◦ **Thermoregulation**: Maintain a warm environment; use warming blankets to prevent **hypothermia**.
    ◦ **Wound & Skin Care**: Gentle skin handling, bland emollients (e.g., petrolatum), cool compresses, and oatmeal baths.
        ▪ **AVOID** extensive use of topical steroids due to systemic absorption.
    ◦ **Nutritional Support**: High-protein, high-calorie diet.
• **Systemic Therapy (First-Line)**
    ◦ **Cyclosporine**: Rapid onset of action, highly effective for acute control.
    ◦ **Infliximab** (TNF-α inhibitor): Rapid onset, very effective in inducing remission.
    ◦ **IL-17 inhibitors** (Secukinumab, Ixekizumab): Rapid and potent action.
• **Systemic Therapy (Second-Line / Slower Onset)**
    ◦ **Methotrexate**: Slower onset, but effective for long-term control.
    ◦ **Acitretin** (retinoid): Useful, especially in combination therapy, but slow onset and teratogenic.
• **AVOID**: **Systemic corticosteroids should be avoided** as they can provide temporary relief but are associated with severe, life-threatening rebound flares upon tapering or withdrawal.
sections.management:
• **Inpatient**
    ◦ Meticulous monitoring of vital signs, fluid intake/output, temperature, electrolytes, and signs of secondary infection.
• **Outpatient**
    ◦ Once stabilized, patients require long-term management with a systemic agent (biologics are often preferred) to prevent relapse.
• **Multidisciplinary Care**
    ◦ Involve dermatology, internal medicine, and potentially nutrition and social work.
sections.complications:
• **Hemodynamic**: **High-output cardiac failure** from persistent cutaneous vasodilation.
• **Metabolic**: Dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, **hypoalbuminemia**.
• **Infectious**: Secondary bacterial skin infection (**cellulitis, sepsis**) from a compromised skin barrier.
• **Thermoregulatory**: **Hypothermia** due to excessive heat loss.
• **Renal**: **Acute kidney injury** (prerenal azotemia) from dehydration.
sections.prognosis:
• Erythrodermic psoriasis is a **life-threatening condition**.
    ◦ Mortality rates have decreased with modern biologic therapies but remain significant if treatment is delayed.
• The primary causes of death are **sepsis** and **cardiovascular collapse**.
• With appropriate and timely management, the acute episode can be controlled, but patients require lifelong monitoring and treatment as it follows a relapsing course.
sections.preventionEducation:
• **Patient Education**
    ◦ Crucial counseling on avoiding known triggers (e.g., abrupt medication changes, excessive alcohol).

sections.overview: • Benign, acute, self-limiting papulosquamous exanthem.
sections.etiology:
• Exact etiology is unknown
• Leading hypothesis: Reactivation of **Human Herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6)** and/or **Human Herpesvirus 7 (HHV-7)**
• The condition is not considered contagious
• Pathophysiology:
    ◦ An immune-mediated response to viral reactivation
    ◦ Involves a T-cell mediated inflammatory response
sections.epidemiology:
• **Peak Incidence**: Adolescents and young adults, typically between ages **10 and 35**
• **Sex**: Slightly more common in females
• **Seasonality**: Slight increase in cases noted in the **spring and autumn**
• Seen worldwide and in all races
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Typical Patient: A healthy adolescent or young adult presenting with a new-onset rash
• Prodrome (may precede the eruption):
    ◦ Malaise
    ◦ Headache
    ◦ Pharyngitis
    ◦ Low-grade fever
• History of Eruption:
    ◦ Begins with the appearance of a single, larger lesion 1-2 weeks before the generalized rash develops
sections.physicalExam:
• **Herald Patch**:
    ◦ A single, initial lesion that precedes the generalized eruption
• Generalized Rash:
    ◦ Smaller, similar-appearing lesions develop after the herald patch
    ◦ Classic distribution on the trunk follows skin cleavage lines, creating a "**Christmas tree**" pattern
sections.diagnostics:
• Pityriasis rosea is a **clinical diagnosis** based on characteristic history and physical exam findings
• Lab tests are **not routinely necessary**
• **KOH Preparation**:
    ◦ Performed on scale from a lesion to rule out tinea corporis
    ◦ Result in pityriasis rosea: **Negative**
• **Serologic Test for Syphilis (RPR or VDRL)**:
    ◦ **Crucial to consider** in any sexually active patient with a papulosquamous eruption, as secondary syphilis is a great mimicker
    ◦ Differentiating feature: Syphilis rash often involves the **palms and soles**
• **Skin Biopsy**:
    ◦ Rarely needed
    ◦ Shows nonspecific findings if performed (e.g., superficial perivascular dermatitis)
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**
• Spontaneous resolution usually occurs within **6-8 weeks** (range 2 weeks to 3 months)
• Recurrence is rare (~2-3%)

sections.overview:
• Lichen Planus (LP) is a chronic, immune-mediated, inflammatory mucocutaneous disorder that affects the skin, hair, nails, and mucous membranes.
    ◦ Characterized by the **"6 P's"**: **Pruritic**, **Planar** (flat-topped), **Polygonal**, **Purple Papules** and **Plaques**.
    ◦ A key diagnostic feature is the presence of **Wickham's striae**, which are fine, lace-like white lines on the surface of the lesions.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ The exact cause is unknown (idiopathic).
    ◦ It is considered a T-cell-mediated autoimmune or inflammatory condition.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ A cell-mediated cytotoxic immune response, primarily involving **CD8+ T-lymphocytes**, is directed against basal keratinocytes.
    ◦ These T-cells recognize a modified self-antigen on the surface of keratinocytes, leading to apoptosis (programmed cell death) of these cells.
    ◦ This inflammatory process at the dermoepidermal junction results in the characteristic clinical and histological findings.
• **Histology (Key Findings)**
    ◦ **Hyperkeratosis**: Thickening of the stratum corneum.
    ◦ **Hypergranulosis**: Thickening of the granular layer.
    ◦ **"Saw-tooth" pattern** of rete ridges.
    ◦ Dense, **band-like (lichenoid) lymphocytic infiltrate** at the dermoepidermal junction.
    ◦ **Civatte bodies**: Apoptotic keratinocytes in the lower epidermis/upper dermis.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects approximately 0.5-2% of the general population.
• **Age of Onset**: Most common in middle-aged adults, typically between 30 and 60 years old. It is rare in children.
• **Gender**: Slight female predominance (approximately 3:2 female-to-male ratio).
• **Race**: No significant racial predilection.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• LP can manifest in several distinct forms and locations; a thorough exam of skin, mouth, genitals, scalp, and nails is essential.
• **Cutaneous LP (Classic)**
    ◦ Lesions typically appear on the flexor surfaces of the wrists, forearms, ankles, and presacral area.
    ◦ Characterized by the **"6 P's"**: **Pruritic**, **Planar**, **Polygonal**, **Purple Papules** and **Plaques**.
    ◦ **Wickham's striae** may be visible on the surface, especially with magnification or application of mineral oil.
    ◦ **Koebner phenomenon** is often present (new lesions developing at sites of trauma or scratching).
• **Oral LP (OLP)**
    ◦ Occurs in ~50% of patients with cutaneous LP; can also occur in isolation.
    ◦ **Reticular OLP (most common)**: Asymptomatic, lace-like white plaques (**Wickham's striae**) on the buccal mucosa.
    ◦ **Erosive/Ulcerative OLP**: Painful, erythematous, raw areas with ulceration. Higher risk of malignant transformation.
    ◦ **Plaque-like OLP**: Resembles leukoplakia, more common in smokers.
• **Nail LP**
    ◦ Occurs in ~10% of cases.
    ◦ Findings include thinning of the nail plate, longitudinal ridging and fissuring, and **dorsal pterygium** (scarring from the nail fold onto the nail bed, a pathognomonic finding).
• **Lichen Planopilaris (LPP)**
    ◦ LP of the scalp, leading to **scarring alopecia**.
    ◦ Characterized by perifollicular erythema and scale.
• **Hypertrophic LP**
    ◦ Thick, verrucous (wart-like), extremely pruritic plaques, most often on the shins.
• **Genital LP**
    ◦ Can present as papules, plaques, or painful erosions on the glans penis, vulva, or in the vagina.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Often made based on the characteristic history and physical exam findings (the **"6 P's"** and **Wickham's striae**).
• **Punch Biopsy**: The **gold standard** for diagnosis, especially in atypical cases or to rule out malignancy (e.g., a non-healing oral erosion).
    ◦ Histopathology will show the classic findings (saw-tooth rete ridges, band-like infiltrate).
• **Hepatitis C Serology**: Recommended for all patients diagnosed with lichen planus due to the strong association.
• **Direct Immunofluorescence (DIF)**: Can be performed on a biopsy specimen to help differentiate from other autoimmune blistering diseases.
    ◦ Shows shaggy, linear deposits of fibrinogen at the dermoepidermal junction.
sections.prognosis:
• **Cutaneous LP**: Generally a good prognosis. It is often self-limiting, with about two-thirds of cases resolving within 1-2 years, although recurrences are common.
• **Oral, Nail, Scalp, and Hypertrophic LP**: Tend to follow a more chronic, relapsing-remitting course that can persist for many years and be more resistant to treatment.

sections.overview:
• Lichen Simplex Chronicus (LSC), also known as **Neurodermatitis**, is a secondary skin disorder resulting from chronic, habitual scratching or rubbing of a primary pruritic lesion or even normal skin.
• It is not a primary disease but rather the skin's reaction to repetitive physical trauma.
• The hallmark of LSC is the development of a well-demarcated, thickened, lichenified plaque with exaggerated skin markings.
• The condition is driven by a self-perpetuating **itch-scratch cycle**.
sections.etiology:
• The pathophysiology of LSC is centered on the **itch-scratch cycle**:
    ◦ **Initial Trigger**: A stimulus causes an initial sensation of pruritus, which can be an underlying dermatosis (e.g., atopic dermatitis, insect bite), a sensory neuropathy, or a psychological stressor.
    ◦ **Scratching/Rubbing**: The individual responds to the itch with vigorous, repetitive scratching or rubbing of the affected area.
    ◦ **Inflammatory Response & Epidermal Changes**: The mechanical trauma induces an inflammatory response and stimulates keratinocyte proliferation, leading to:
        ▪ **Acanthosis**: Thickening of the epidermis (stratum spinosum).
        ▪ **Hyperkeratosis**: Thickening of the stratum corneum.
        ▪ **Nerve Fiber Proliferation**: Dermal nerve fibers become hypertrophied and sensitized, lowering the threshold for pruritus.
    ◦ **Perpetuation of the Cycle**: The thickened, inflamed skin with sensitized nerves becomes even itchier, leading to more scratching, which further thickens the skin, locking the patient in a vicious cycle.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Peak Incidence**: Adults aged 30-50 years.
• **Sex**: More common in females than males (~2:1).
• **Associated Conditions**: Frequently seen in patients with a history of atopic dermatitis, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), or depression.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Underlying Pruritic Dermatoses**: Atopic dermatitis, contact dermatitis, psoriasis, xerosis (dry skin), insect bites, fungal infections.
• **Psychological Conditions**: Anxiety, depression, stress, OCD.
• **History of Atopy**: Personal or family history of asthma, allergic rhinitis, or eczema.
• **Female Gender**.
• **Venous Insufficiency**: Can lead to stasis dermatitis, a common trigger on the lower legs.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with a chief complaint of a single, chronically itchy patch of skin that has been present for months to years.
• The pruritus is often described as paroxysmal and overwhelming, leading to an uncontrollable urge to scratch.
• The itch is characteristically worse during periods of inactivity, stress, or at night, often leading to sleep disturbances.
• Patients may admit to scratching the area unconsciously or during sleep.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ **Pruritus**: The hallmark symptom. It is intense, localized, and often described as burning or stinging.
        ▪ Scratching provides temporary relief, often followed by more intense itching.
    ◦ **Pain/Soreness**: May be present from deep excoriations.
    ◦ **Sleep Disturbance**: Due to nocturnal pruritus.
• **Exam Findings**
    ◦ **Primary Lesion**: A solid, well-demarcated, firm, rough **plaque** with minimal to no scaling.
    ◦ **Lichenification**: The pathognomonic finding where the epidermis is thickened and normal skin lines are exaggerated, creating a **"washboard"** or "tree bark" appearance.
    ◦ **Color**: Can be erythematous, violaceous, or most commonly, hyperpigmented (especially in chronic lesions and skin of color).
        ▪ The center of the plaque may be more thickened and hyperpigmented, with a less-affected, erythematous border.
    ◦ **Secondary Lesions**: Excoriations, erosions, and crusting from scratching are common. Fissures may be present.
    ◦ **Distribution**: Typically occurs in areas accessible to scratching.
        ▪ **Common sites**: Nape of the neck (**lichen nuchae**), scrotum/vulva, upper thighs, ankles (especially lateral malleoli), shins, wrists, and extensor forearms.
    ◦ Usually **unilateral** and solitary, though multiple plaques can occur.
sections.diagnostics:
• LSC is almost always a **clinical diagnosis** based on the characteristic history and physical exam findings.
• **KOH Prep**:
    ◦ Can be performed if tinea corporis is on the differential to rule out a fungal infection.
    ◦ It will be negative in LSC.
• **Skin Biopsy (Punch Biopsy)**:
    ◦ Rarely necessary.
    ◦ Indicated if the diagnosis is uncertain, the lesion is atypical, or there is a concern for malignancy (e.g., Squamous Cell Carcinoma).
    ◦ **Histology Findings**:
        ▪ Irregular acanthosis
        ▪ Hyperkeratosis
        ▪ Hypergranulosis
        ▪ A chronic perivascular inflammatory infiltrate in the dermis.
sections.treatment:
• **First-Line Therapy**:
    ◦ **High-Potency Topical Corticosteroids**: The mainstay of treatment.
        ▪ Examples: Clobetasol propionate 0.05%, Betamethasone dipropionate 0.05%.
        ▪ Applied once or twice daily for 2-4 weeks.
    ◦ **Occlusion**: Applying the steroid under an occlusive dressing (e.g., plastic wrap, hydrocolloid dressing) overnight dramatically increases potency and penetration, and provides a physical barrier to scratching.
    ◦ **Intralesional Corticosteroids**: For very thick, refractory plaques.
        ▪ Example: Triamcinolone acetonide (Kenalog) injected directly into the plaque.
• **Second-Line / Adjunctive Therapy**:
    ◦ **Antihistamines**: Sedating antihistamines (e.g., **Hydroxyzine**, Diphenhydramine) are useful at night to reduce nocturnal scratching and aid sleep.
        ▪ Non-sedating antihistamines are generally not effective for the pruritus of LSC.
    ◦ **Topical Calcineurin Inhibitors**: (Tacrolimus, Pimecrolimus). Good for facial or genital areas where long-term steroid use is undesirable.
    ◦ **Doxepin Cream 5%**: Has potent topical H1 and H2 receptor antagonist properties.
    ◦ **Keratolytics**: Preparations containing salicylic acid or urea can help reduce scale and hyperkeratosis, improving steroid penetration.
sections.management:
• **Patient Education**: Crucial for success. Explain the itch-scratch cycle and emphasize that scratching is the cause of the lesion, not just a symptom.
• **Behavioral Modification**:
    ◦ Instruct the patient to consciously avoid scratching or rubbing.
    ◦ Keep fingernails trimmed short.
    ◦ Consider wearing gloves or socks over the hands at night.
    ◦ Covering the plaque with a dressing (e.g., Unna boot for lower leg lesions, simple bandage) can be very effective.
• **Stress Management**: Address and manage underlying anxiety or stress, as these are common triggers.
• **Emollients**: Frequent use of bland emollients can help hydrate the skin and reduce dryness-related itching.
sections.complications:
• **Secondary Bacterial Infection (Impetiginization)**: Most commonly with *Staphylococcus aureus* or *Streptococcus pyogenes*.
    ◦ Presents with honey-colored crusting, weeping, or purulence.
• **Pigmentary Changes**: Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (common) or hypopigmentation can be permanent.
• **Scarring**: Can occur from deep excoriations.
• **Psychosocial Impact**: Decreased quality of life, sleep disturbance, and emotional distress.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is good if the itch-scratch cycle can be successfully interrupted.
• However, LSC is a chronic condition with a high rate of recurrence, especially if the underlying trigger is not addressed or if scratching behavior resumes.
• Long-term management and behavioral changes are key to preventing relapse.

sections.overview:
• Dermatitis Herpetiformis (DH) is a chronic, intensely pruritic, autoimmune blistering skin disease.
• It is considered the specific cutaneous (skin) manifestation of **celiac disease**.
• The rash is characterized by symmetrically distributed, grouped (**herpetiform**) papules and vesicles, predominantly on the extensor surfaces of the body.
• While it is a skin disease, its origin lies in the gastrointestinal immune response to **gluten**.
sections.etiology:
• The pathophysiology is directly linked to **gluten sensitivity**.
    ◦ **Gluten Ingestion**: In genetically predisposed individuals, ingestion of gluten (specifically its gliadin component) triggers an immune response in the small intestine.
    ◦ **tTG and Immune Response**: The intestinal enzyme **tissue transglutaminase (tTG)** deamidates gliadin, creating a more immunogenic compound. This leads to the production of **IgA antibodies** against both gliadin and tTG (IgA anti-tTG).
    ◦ **Molecular Mimicry**: **Epidermal transglutaminase (eTG or TG3)**, an enzyme found in the skin, is structurally similar to tTG. The IgA antibodies produced in the gut cross-react with eTG in the skin.
    ◦ **Immune Complex Deposition**: IgA-eTG **immune complexes** deposit at the dermal-epidermal junction, specifically at the tips of the dermal papillae.
    ◦ **Inflammation and Blistering**: This deposition activates the complement cascade and recruits neutrophils. The neutrophils release proteases and other inflammatory mediators, causing separation of the epidermis from the dermis and forming **subepidermal blisters** (microabscesses).
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Approximately 10-40 per 100,000 people.
• **Association with Celiac Disease**: Nearly 100% of patients with DH have celiac disease, although up to 75% may have no overt gastrointestinal symptoms.
• **Age of Onset**: Most commonly presents in young adults (15-40 years), but can occur at any age.
• **Sex**: Slight male predominance (M:F ratio ~1.5:1).
• **Race/Ethnicity**: Predominantly affects Caucasians of Northern European descent. It is rare in individuals of African or Asian descent.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic patient is a young to middle-aged adult of Northern European descent presenting with a chronic, intensely itchy rash that comes and goes.
• The primary complaint is **severe pruritus**, often described as a burning or stinging sensation that precedes the eruption of visible skin lesions.
• Many patients are unaware of any underlying gastrointestinal issues.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Skin Biopsy (Gold Standard)**: Two separate biopsies are required from different sites.
    ◦ **Biopsy #1: Lesional Skin (for H&E Staining)**
        ▪ **Site**: Taken from the edge of a fresh, intact papule or vesicle.
        ▪ **Findings**: A **subepidermal blister** containing a dense infiltrate of neutrophils. **Neutrophilic microabscesses** are seen at the tips of the dermal papillae.
    ◦ **Biopsy #2: Perilesional Skin (for Direct Immunofluorescence - DIF)**
        ▪ **Site**: Taken from normal-appearing skin adjacent (within 1 cm) to an active lesion.
        ▪ **Findings (Pathognomonic)**: **Granular IgA deposits** in the dermal papillae.
• **Serology (To confirm underlying Celiac Disease)**
    ◦ **IgA tissue transglutaminase antibody (IgA tTG)**: The single best serologic test for diagnosis and monitoring. Highly sensitive and specific.
    ◦ **IgA endomysial antibody (IgA EMA)**: Highly specific but less sensitive and more operator-dependent than IgA tTG.
    ◦ **Total Serum IgA**: Should be checked concurrently. A selective IgA deficiency can cause a false-negative result on IgA-based tests. If deficient, use IgG-based tests (e.g., IgG-tTG, IgG-DGP).
• **Small Bowel Biopsy**
    ◦ Historically required but may be deferred if skin biopsy and serology are definitively positive for DH.
    ◦ Confirms the diagnosis of celiac disease by showing characteristic **villous atrophy**.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is **excellent** with adherence to a strict gluten-free diet.
• The skin disease can be fully controlled, and the risk of long-term complications like **lymphoma** is significantly reduced.
• DH is a lifelong condition that requires permanent dietary modification.
• Relapses of the rash are common with intentional or unintentional gluten exposure.

sections.overview:
• Acute Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus (ACLE) is the most common subtype of cutaneous lupus.
    ◦ Typically manifests as a **photosensitive rash** that arises in conjunction with a flare of **Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)**.
    ◦ The classic presentation is the **"malar"** or **"butterfly" rash**.
    ◦ The presence of ACLE is a strong indicator of **active systemic disease** and is included in the diagnostic criteria for SLE.
    ◦ Lesions are transient and heal **without scarring**, though post-inflammatory pigment changes can occur.
sections.etiology:
• ACLE is an autoimmune-mediated inflammatory condition driven by a **Type III hypersensitivity reaction**.
    ◦ The pathophysiology involves a complex interplay of genetic predisposition, environmental triggers, and immune dysregulation.
• **Genetic Susceptibility**
    ◦ Associated with specific HLA alleles, particularly **HLA-DR2** and **HLA-DR3**.
• **Environmental Triggers**
    ◦ **UV radiation** is the most significant trigger.
        ▪ It induces apoptosis in keratinocytes, leading to the exposure of nuclear autoantigens (e.g., DNA, histones).
• **Immune Dysregulation**
    ◦ Loss of self-tolerance leads to the production of autoantibodies, primarily **antinuclear antibodies (ANA)**, **anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA)**, and **anti-Smith (anti-Sm)**.
    ◦ These autoantibodies form immune complexes with the exposed nuclear antigens.
    ◦ Immune complexes deposit at the **dermoepidermal junction (DEJ)** and in small blood vessels.
    ◦ This deposition activates the complement cascade and recruits inflammatory cells (lymphocytes, neutrophils), resulting in an **interface dermatitis** and subsequent tissue damage.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Peak Incidence**: Age 20-40 (women of childbearing age).
• **Sex**: Strong female predominance (**9:1** female-to-male ratio).
• **Race/Ethnicity**: More common and often more severe in African American, Hispanic, and Asian populations compared to Caucasians.
• **Association**: Occurs in 30-60% of patients with SLE.
    ◦ Its presence strongly correlates with **active systemic disease**, particularly **lupus nephritis** and **arthritis**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• ACLE typically presents abruptly, often following sun exposure.
• Patients usually appear systemically unwell, with constitutional symptoms coinciding with the rash.
• **Localized ACLE**
    ◦ The most common form.
    ◦ Presents as the classic **malar rash ("butterfly rash")**: a well-demarcated, confluent, erythematous, edematous maculopapular rash on the cheeks and nasal bridge.
    ◦ Crucially, it **spares the nasolabial folds**.
• **Generalized ACLE**
    ◦ A more widespread, photosensitive, **morbilliform (measles-like)** or exanthematous eruption.
    ◦ Occurs on sun-exposed areas such as the "V" of the neck, upper back, shoulders, and extensor surfaces of the arms and hands.
    ◦ Often **spares the knuckles** (differentiates from Dermatomyositis).
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is often made clinically but should be confirmed with serology and/or biopsy.
• **Serology (Essential for SLE workup)**
    ◦ **ANA (Antinuclear Antibody)**: Highly **sensitive** (>95%) for SLE but not specific. The first test to order if lupus is suspected.
    ◦ **Anti-dsDNA** and **Anti-Sm**: Highly **specific** for SLE. Anti-dsDNA levels often correlate with disease activity, especially nephritis.
    ◦ **Anti-Ro (SSA) / Anti-La (SSB)**: May also be positive. Anti-Ro is associated with photosensitivity and Subacute Cutaneous Lupus.
    ◦ **Complement levels (C3, C4)**: Often **decreased** during active disease flares due to consumption by immune complexes.
    ◦ **Inflammatory Markers**: Elevated ESR and CRP.
    ◦ **CBC**: May show cytopenias (**anemia**, **leukopenia**, **thrombocytopenia**).
    ◦ **Urinalysis with microscopy**: Screen for proteinuria and cellular casts to evaluate for **lupus nephritis**.
• **Skin Biopsy**
    ◦ **Punch biopsy** from an active lesion for **histopathology (H&E stain)** shows:
        ▪ **Vacuolar interface dermatitis**: Vacuolization of the basal keratinocyte layer.
        ▪ Perivascular and periadnexal lymphocytic infiltrate.
        ▪ Increased dermal mucin.
    ◦ Biopsy from perilesional skin for **Direct Immunofluorescence (DIF)** shows:
        ▪ **Lupus Band Test**: A granular band of **IgG, IgM, and/or C3** deposited along the dermoepidermal junction.
        ▪ A positive lupus band in sun-protected, non-lesional skin is highly specific for SLE.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis of the skin lesions is excellent; they resolve **without scarring**.
• The overall patient prognosis is entirely dependent on the severity and management of the underlying **systemic lupus erythematosus**, particularly the extent of major organ involvement (e.g., kidneys, CNS).

sections.overview:
• **Subacute Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus (SCLE)** is a distinct, **photosensitive**, **non-scarring**, **non-atrophic** subtype of cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CLE).
    ◦ It presents with characteristic **annular** or **papulosquamous** plaques primarily on **sun-exposed areas**.
    ◦ SCLE is strongly associated with **anti-Ro/SSA antibodies** and occupies an intermediate position in the lupus spectrum, with more systemic involvement than **Discoid Lupus (DLE)** but less than **Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)**.
    ◦ Approximately 50% of patients with SCLE also meet the criteria for SLE, although they typically have a milder systemic course.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology (Multifactorial)**
    ◦ **Genetic Predisposition:** Strong association with **HLA-DR3**.
    ◦ **Environmental Triggers:**
        ▪ **UV Radiation:** The most significant trigger. UV light induces apoptosis of keratinocytes, leading to the externalization of nuclear autoantigens (like **Ro/SSA**), which are then targeted by the immune system.
        ▪ **Drugs:** A significant portion of cases are drug-induced. The rash appears months to years after starting the medication and resolves upon discontinuation.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ An autoimmune response driven by autoreactive T-cells and autoantibodies.
    ◦ **Type III & IV Hypersensitivity:** The process involves both antibody-mediated and cell-mediated immunity.
    ◦ **Key Steps:**
        ▪ A trigger (e.g., UV light, drug) causes keratinocyte damage.
        ▪ Nuclear antigens, particularly **Ro/SSA** and **La/SSB**, are exposed on the cell surface.
        ▪ Autoreactive T-cells recognize these antigens and initiate an inflammatory cascade.
        ▪ B-cells produce autoantibodies (**Anti-Ro/SSA**) which form immune complexes.
        ▪ This leads to a lymphocytic attack on the basal layer of the epidermis, resulting in the characteristic **interface dermatitis** seen on histology.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** Second most common form of cutaneous lupus after **DLE**.
• **Age:** Typically affects young to middle-aged adults.
• **Sex:** Strong **female predominance** (~4:1).
• **Race:** More common in Caucasians compared to other forms of lupus.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Female sex**
• **Caucasian race**
• **Age 20-50**
• **Genetic predisposition (HLA-DR3)**
• **Significant UV light exposure** (occupational or recreational)
• **Smoking**
• **Medications (Drug-Induced SCLE):**
    ◦ **Hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ)**
    ◦ **Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs)**
    ◦ **Terbinafine**
    ◦ **Calcium Channel Blockers**
    ◦ **TNF-alpha inhibitors**
    ◦ **Griseofulvin**
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient, often a middle-aged Caucasian female, presents with a **non-itchy**, **non-painful** rash that appeared on her upper chest, back, and arms after **sun exposure**.
    ◦ She may also complain of mild, intermittent **joint pain** and **fatigue**.
    ◦ The rash has been present for several weeks to months and may have a circular or scaly appearance.
• **Cutaneous Symptoms:**
    ◦ The rash is the primary symptom.
    ◦ Usually asymptomatic but can be mildly pruritic or have a burning sensation.
• **Systemic Symptoms (present in ~50% of cases, usually mild):**
    ◦ **Most Common:** **Arthralgias/arthritis** (**non-erosive**).
    ◦ **Fatigue**, **myalgias**, **low-grade fever**.
    ◦ Severe systemic involvement (significant renal or CNS disease) is uncommon.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Morphology:** Two primary patterns (**annular** or **papulosquamous**) can coexist.
• **Key Characteristics:**
    ◦ **Non-scarring & Non-atrophic:** Lesions heal without scarring, though **post-inflammatory hypopigmentation** or **telangiectasias** are common. This is a key feature distinguishing it from **DLE**.
• **Distribution:**
    ◦ **Photosensitive Pattern:** Strongly favors **sun-exposed areas**.
    ◦ **Common Sites:** "V" of the neck, upper chest, upper back, shoulders, extensor surfaces of the arms, dorsal hands.
    ◦ **Sparing:** Typically **spares the central face** (malar area is more typical of Acute Cutaneous Lupus), and often **spares the knuckles** (unlike the **Gottron's papules** of **dermatomyositis**).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Biopsy (Gold Standard for skin lesion):**
    ◦ **Punch Biopsy:** Taken from the active border of a lesion.
    ◦ **Histology (H&E stain):** Shows **interface dermatitis** with a lymphocytic infiltrate along the dermoepidermal junction and vacuolar degeneration of basal keratinocytes.
        ▪ Apoptotic keratinocytes (**civatte bodies**) may be present.
• **Direct Immunofluorescence (DIF):**
    ◦ Shows granular deposits of IgG and/or C3 along the dermoepidermal junction ("**Lupus Band Test**").
• **Serology:**
    ◦ **ANA (Antinuclear Antibody):** Positive in ~80% of patients. A good screening test.
    ◦ **Anti-Ro/SSA antibodies:** **KEY DIAGNOSTIC MARKER.** Positive in >70% of patients.
    ◦ **Anti-La/SSB antibodies:** Can also be positive, often along with Anti-Ro/SSA.
    ◦ **Anti-dsDNA & Anti-Sm:** Usually negative. Their presence suggests a higher risk for severe **SLE**.
• **Baseline Labs (to screen for systemic involvement):**
    ◦ **CBC with differential:** To check for **cytopenias** (leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia).
    ◦ **CMP:** To assess renal and hepatic function.
    ◦ **Urinalysis with urine protein/creatinine ratio:** To screen for **lupus nephritis**.
sections.treatment:
• **Topical Therapy (for limited disease):**
    ◦ **Topical Corticosteroids:** High-potency (e.g., clobetasol) for body, mid-potency for sensitive areas.
    ◦ **Topical Calcineurin Inhibitors:** Tacrolimus or pimecrolimus. Good steroid-sparing agents, especially for intertriginous areas.
• **Systemic Therapy (for widespread or refractory disease):**
    ◦ **First-Line Systemic:** **Antimalarials** (**Hydroxychloroquine** or Chloroquine).
        ▪ Takes 2-3 months to see effect.
    ◦ **Second-Line Systemic:**
        ▪ **Methotrexate**
        ▪ **Mycophenolate Mofetil**
        ▪ **Dapsone**
    ◦ **Systemic Corticosteroids (e.g., Prednisone):** Used for short-term control of severe flares but avoided for long-term management due to side effects.
sections.management:
• **Monitoring:**
    ◦ Regular follow-up with dermatology and/or rheumatology.
    ◦ **Baseline and annual ophthalmology exams** for patients on antimalarials to screen for **retinal toxicity**.
    ◦ Periodic lab monitoring (CBC, CMP, UA) to screen for development or progression of systemic disease.
• **Drug-Induced SCLE:**
    ◦ The primary management is **discontinuation of the offending drug**.
    ◦ Lesions typically resolve over 2-6 months.
sections.complications:
• **Post-inflammatory pigmentary changes:** Hypo- or hyperpigmentation at the site of healed lesions.
• **Development of SLE:** About 50% of patients with SCLE meet criteria for **SLE**, although it is typically mild (musculoskeletal and mucocutaneous involvement).
• **Neonatal Lupus Erythematosus (NLE):**
    ◦ Maternal **Anti-Ro/SSA antibodies** can cross the placenta and affect the fetus.
    ◦ This can cause a transient rash and cytopenias in the newborn.
    ◦ The most feared complication is **irreversible congenital heart block**.
    ◦ Any woman with SCLE of childbearing age should be counseled on this risk.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis for the skin disease is generally good with treatment, although the course is chronic with relapses and remissions.
• The overall prognosis depends on the extent of systemic involvement. As severe organ damage is rare, the long-term prognosis is very good for most patients.
• **Drug-induced SCLE** has an excellent prognosis with complete resolution after drug withdrawal.
sections.preventionEducation:
• **Patient Education:** Counsel extensively on sun protection and adherence to medication.
• **Strict Sun Protection:** This is the most critical element of management.
    ◦ Broad-spectrum (UVA/UVB) sunscreen with SPF 30+.
    ◦ Sun-protective clothing (UPF fabrics), wide-brimmed hats.
    ◦ Avoidance of peak sun hours (10 am - 4 pm).
• **Smoking Cessation:** Smoking can decrease the efficacy of antimalarials.

sections.overview:
• **Discoid Lupus Erythematosus (DLE)** is the most common form of **Chronic Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus (CCLE)**.
• It is a chronic, scarring, photosensitive autoimmune skin disorder.
• Characterized by well-demarcated, **erythematous plaques** with **adherent scale** and **follicular plugging**.
• Lesions typically heal with **atrophy**, **scarring**, and **dyspigmentation**.
• While DLE can be an isolated skin condition, approximately 5-10% of patients may develop **Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ The exact cause is unknown, but it involves a combination of genetic susceptibility, environmental triggers, and an autoimmune response.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Autoimmune Reaction**: It is a **T-cell mediated** autoimmune process directed against **basal keratinocytes** in the skin.
    ◦ **UV Radiation Trigger**: **UV light** is a major trigger. It induces apoptosis in keratinocytes, exposing nuclear and cytoplasmic antigens. In genetically predisposed individuals, this leads to an inflammatory cascade.
    ◦ **Interface Dermatitis**: The hallmark histologic finding is a dense lymphocytic infiltrate at the **dermal-epidermal junction (DEJ)**, which attacks and damages the basal cell layer.
    ◦ **Immune Complex Deposition**: Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) reveals granular deposition of immunoglobulins (IgG, IgM) and complement (C3) along the DEJ, known as a positive **"Lupus Band Test."**
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Most common form of **cutaneous lupus**.
• **Age of Onset**: Peak incidence is between ages 20 and 40.
• **Sex**: Affects females more than males (approx. 2-3:1 ratio).
• **Race/Ethnicity**: More common and often more severe in individuals with darker skin tones, especially those of African descent.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The typical patient is a young to middle-aged adult who presents with one or more chronic, persistent, **scaly red plaques** in **sun-exposed areas**, particularly the face, scalp, or ears.
• The lesions are often **asymptomatic** but may be mildly **pruritic** or **tender**.
• They develop slowly and persist for months to years, worsening with sun exposure.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Skin Biopsy**: The gold standard for diagnosis.
    ◦ A punch biopsy should be taken from the active edge of a lesion.
• **Histopathology (H&E stain)**
    ◦ Shows **interface dermatitis** (vacuolar degeneration of the basal layer), a **perivascular** and **periadnexal lymphocytic infiltrate**, **follicular plugging**, and increased **dermal mucin**.
• **Direct Immunofluorescence (DIF)**
    ◦ Reveals a granular band of IgG, IgM, and/or C3 deposition along the dermal-epidermal junction (positive **Lupus Band Test**).
• **Laboratory Workup (to screen for systemic involvement)**
    ◦ **Antinuclear Antibody (ANA)**: Positive in only ~20% of patients with isolated DLE. A high titer may indicate a higher risk for developing SLE.
    ◦ **CBC with differential**: To screen for anemia, leukopenia, or thrombocytopenia.
    ◦ **CMP**: To assess renal and hepatic function.
    ◦ **Urinalysis with microscopy**: To screen for proteinuria or cellular casts (**lupus nephritis**).
    ◦ **Anti-dsDNA** and **Anti-Sm antibodies**: Highly specific for SLE; usually negative in isolated DLE.
sections.prognosis:
• The skin disease itself is a **chronic, relapsing condition**.
• With treatment, lesions can be controlled, but **scarring is permanent**.
• For patients with isolated DLE (not progressing to SLE), the overall prognosis is excellent, and life expectancy is normal.
• If **SLE** develops, the prognosis is determined by the extent and severity of systemic organ involvement.

sections.overview:
• **Granuloma Annulare (GA)** is a **benign**, **self-limiting** inflammatory dermatosis of unknown etiology.
    ◦ Characterized by dermal papules and **annular (ring-shaped) plaques**.
    ◦ The underlying pathology involves a focal degeneration of collagen (**necrobiosis**) surrounded by a wall of histiocytes, forming a **"palisading granuloma"**.
    ◦ While most commonly localized and asymptomatic, it can present in generalized, subcutaneous, or perforating forms.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Idiopathic** in most cases.
    ◦ Considered a **Type IV delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction** to an unknown antigen.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ An unknown trigger (e.g., insect bite, trauma, infection) initiates an inflammatory cascade.
    ◦ **Cell-mediated immunity** is the primary driver, involving activated **T-helper 1 (Th1) lymphocytes**.
    ◦ Th1 cells release cytokines, particularly **interferon-gamma (IFN-γ)**.
    ◦ IFN-γ activates macrophages (histiocytes).
    ◦ These activated histiocytes aggregate in the dermis, surrounding a central zone of degenerated collagen and mucin deposits, forming a classic **necrobiotic "palisading" granuloma**.
    ◦ The process leads to the formation of clinically visible papules that often coalesce into annular plaques.
• **Potential Triggers**
    ◦ Minor trauma (**Koebner phenomenon**)
    ◦ Insect bites
    ◦ Infections (e.g., EBV, HIV, Hepatitis C, TB)
    ◦ Sun exposure
    ◦ Medications (e.g., allopurinol, TNF-alpha inhibitors)
    ◦ Tuberculin skin tests
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Relatively common dermatosis.
• **Gender**: Affects **females** more than males (approx. 2:1 ratio).
• **Age**: Bimodal age distribution.
    ◦ **Localized GA**: Most common in children and adults under 30.
    ◦ **Generalized GA**: More common in older adults (40-60 years).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **1. Localized GA (Most Common, ~75% of cases)**
    ◦ Presents as one or several **annular** or arcuate plaques.
    ◦ Size ranges from 1-5 cm.
    ◦ **Classic Location**: **Dorsum of hands and feet**, ankles, elbows, and knees. Typically spares palms and soles.
• **2. Generalized GA (~15% of cases)**
    ◦ Widespread eruption of numerous papules or small annular plaques.
    ◦ Often **symmetrical**, involving the trunk, neck, and extremities.
    ◦ More likely to be **pruritic** and associated with systemic disease (DM, lipids).
• **3. Subcutaneous GA ("Pseudo-rheumatoid nodules")**
    ◦ Presents as firm, deep dermal or **subcutaneous nodules**.
    ◦ Typically found in children on the **anterior shins**, hands, scalp, and buttocks.
    ◦ Can be mistaken for rheumatoid nodules.
• **4. Perforating GA (Rare)**
    ◦ Papules with **central umbilication** or crusting.
    ◦ Represents transepidermal elimination of the necrobiotic collagen.
    ◦ Often occurs on the hands and fingers and may be **pruritic**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**
    ◦ Diagnosis is most often made based on the characteristic clinical appearance (**annular, non-scaly plaques** in a typical location).
• **KOH Preparation**
    ◦ Should be performed if tinea corporis is on the differential.
    ◦ A KOH prep will be **negative** in GA.
• **Skin Biopsy (Punch or Excisional)**
    ◦ **Indication**: Atypical presentation, diagnostic uncertainty, or failure to respond to therapy.
    ◦ **Histopathology (Gold Standard)**: The findings are pathognomonic.
        ▪ **"Palisading granuloma"**: A collection of histiocytes (macrophages) and lymphocytes arranged in a fence-like ("palisading") pattern in the upper and mid-dermis.
        ▪ **Necrobiosis**: The histiocytes surround a central zone of degenerated collagen fibers.
        ▪ **Mucin Deposition**: Increased mucin is found within the central necrobiotic zone (best visualized with an Alcian blue or colloidal iron stain).
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ Consider screening for associated conditions, especially in generalized GA:
        ▪ **HbA1c or Fasting Glucose**: To rule out diabetes mellitus.
        ▪ **Lipid Panel**: To assess for dyslipidemia.
        ▪ **TSH**: To screen for thyroid dysfunction.
sections.prognosis:
• **Localized GA**: Excellent prognosis.
    ◦ Approximately 50-75% of cases **resolve spontaneously**, typically within 2 years.
    ◦ Recurrences are common.
• **Generalized GA**: More chronic and persistent course.
    ◦ Spontaneous resolution is less likely.
    ◦ Lesions may persist for a decade or longer.

sections.overview:
• Common, acquired disorder of **hyperpigmentation**
• Characterized by **symmetric**, irregularly shaped, brown to grayish-brown **macules and patches**
• Occurs on **sun-exposed areas** of the skin, most commonly the face
• Particularly prevalent in women of reproductive age with darker skin phototypes
• While benign, it can cause significant cosmetic concern and psychological distress
sections.etiology:
• Primarily a disorder of **melanocyte hyperfunction**, not an increase in the number of melanocytes
• **Key Pathogenic Factors**:
    ◦ **UV Radiation**: The single most important exacerbating factor
        ▪ UV light stimulates melanocytes to produce more melanin
        ▪ It also increases levels of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (α-MSH) and Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF) in the skin
    ◦ **Hormonal Influence**: Estrogen and progesterone are potent stimulators of melanogenesis
        ▪ Explains the strong association with **pregnancy**, **oral contraceptive pills (OCPs)**, and **hormone replacement therapy (HRT)**
    ◦ **Genetic Predisposition**: A positive family history is reported in over 50% of patients
    ◦ **Vascular Component**: Lesional skin shows increased vascularity
        ▪ VEGF, produced by keratinocytes after UV exposure, stimulates both angiogenesis and melanogenesis
• **Cellular Mechanism**:
    ◦ Hyperfunctional melanocytes produce an excessive amount of melanin
    ◦ This melanin is transferred to surrounding keratinocytes in the epidermis (**epidermal melasma**)
    ◦ In some cases, disruption of the basement membrane allows melanin to fall into the papillary dermis, where it is engulfed by macrophages (melanophages), leading to **dermal melasma**
    ◦ **Mixed melasma** involves both epidermal and dermal pigment deposition
sections.epidemiology:
• **Gender**: Affects **females** much more commonly than males (approx. 9:1 ratio)
• **Age**: Typically develops in women of **reproductive age (20-40 years)**
• **Skin Type**: More common and clinically more apparent in individuals with **darker skin tones** (Fitzpatrick skin types III-VI)
• **Prevalence**: Affects millions of people worldwide, with higher rates in areas with intense sun exposure
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **History**:
    ◦ Typically a woman of childbearing age
    ◦ Reports the **gradual onset** of **asymptomatic dark patches** on her face
    ◦ Common history of **pregnancy**, **OCP use**, and significant **sun exposure**
• **Classic Patterns of Facial Involvement**:
    ◦ **Centrofacial (Most Common)**: Forehead, cheeks, upper lip, nose, and chin
    ◦ **Malar**: Predominantly on the cheeks and nose
    ◦ **Mandibular**: Along the jawline
• Extra-facial involvement (e.g., forearms, neck) is rare but possible
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primarily a clinical diagnosis** based on characteristic history and physical exam findings
• **Wood's Lamp** is the most useful in-office tool to help classify the type and predict treatment response
• **Dermoscopy** can also help visualize pigment patterns
• **Skin Biopsy**:
    ◦ Rarely necessary
    ◦ Performed only if the diagnosis is uncertain or to rule out other conditions (e.g., malignancy)
    ◦ Histology would show increased melanin in the epidermis and/or dermis, without an increase in the number of melanocytes
sections.prognosis:
• **Benign** condition with no associated mortality or systemic effects
• Clinical course is **chronic** with frequent **relapses**, especially after sun exposure
• Prognosis for improvement is better for **epidermal melasma** than for **dermal melasma**
• Spontaneous resolution can occur after pregnancy or discontinuation of hormonal triggers, but it is not guaranteed

sections.overview:
• Vitiligo is an acquired, chronic **autoimmune disorder** characterized by the progressive destruction of melanocytes, resulting in **well-demarcated, depigmented (milk-white) macules and patches** on the skin
	◦ Can also affect hair (**leukotrichia**) and mucous membranes
	◦ The condition is not contagious or life-threatening but can cause significant psychosocial distress
sections.etiology:
• The exact etiology is multifactorial, involving a combination of genetic susceptibility and environmental triggers
• The predominant theory is **autoimmune-mediated destruction of melanocytes**
• **Pathophysiology**
	◦ **Autoimmune Theory (Primary)**: An autoimmune response, primarily mediated by **cytotoxic CD8+ T lymphocytes**, targets and destroys melanocytes
		▪ These T-cells recognize melanocyte-specific antigens (e.g., MART-1, tyrosinase) and induce apoptosis
	◦ **Genetic Susceptibility**: A positive family history is present in ~20-30% of cases. Genes associated with immune regulation (e.g., *NLRP1*, *PTPN22*) are implicated
	◦ **Oxidative Stress**: An imbalance in the redox state within melanocytes leads to an accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which can be toxic to the cells and trigger an autoimmune response
	◦ **Environmental Triggers**: Physical trauma (**Koebner phenomenon**), severe sunburn, emotional stress, or illness can precipitate or exacerbate vitiligo in genetically susceptible individuals
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects 0.5-2% of the global population
• **Age of Onset**: Can occur at any age, but ~50% of cases begin before age 20, with a peak incidence between 10 and 30 years old
• **Demographics**: Affects all races and sexes equally
	◦ It is cosmetically more apparent and can be more socially stigmatizing in individuals with darker skin tones
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Vitiligo is classified based on the distribution of lesions:
	◦ **Non-segmental Vitiligo (NSV)**
		▪ **Most common form (~90%)**
		▪ Characterized by **bilateral, often symmetrical** distribution
		▪ Commonly affects periorificial areas (mouth, eyes), extensor surfaces (hands, elbows, knees), and areas of friction
		▪ Tends to be progressive and unpredictable
		▪ Subtypes include generalized, acrofacial, universalis, and mucosal
	◦ **Segmental Vitiligo (SV)**
		▪ Less common (~5-10%)
		▪ **Unilateral, dermatomal, or quasi-dermatomal** distribution
		▪ Typically has an earlier age of onset, spreads rapidly within its segment, and then **stabilizes**
		▪ Less frequently associated with autoimmune diseases compared to NSV
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: The diagnosis is typically made based on the characteristic clinical findings
• **Wood's Lamp**: Essential to confirm depigmentation and delineate the extent of the disease
• **Skin Biopsy**: Rarely necessary but can confirm the diagnosis in atypical cases
	◦ Histology reveals a **complete absence of melanocytes** and melanin pigment in the epidermis
	◦ An inflammatory lymphocytic infiltrate may be seen at the margins of active lesions
• **Screening Labs**: Recommended to assess for associated autoimmune conditions, particularly thyroid disease
	◦ **TSH** (with reflex T4) - to screen for thyroid disorders
	◦ **CBC with differential** - to screen for pernicious anemia (macrocytosis)
	◦ **Fasting glucose or HbA1c** - to screen for diabetes mellitus
	◦ **ANA** - if other signs/symptoms of rheumatologic disease are present
sections.prognosis:
• The course is highly variable and unpredictable
• **Non-segmental vitiligo** is typically chronic and progressive
• **Segmental vitiligo** often stabilizes after a period of rapid spread
• **Favorable Prognostic Factors for Repigmentation**
	◦ Lesions on the face/neck
	◦ Recent onset of disease
	◦ Younger age
• **Poor Prognostic Factors for Repigmentation**
	◦ Lesions on acral sites (hands, feet) and lips
	◦ Presence of **leukotrichia** (white hair)
	◦ Longer disease duration

sections.overview:
• Post-inflammatory pigmentary alteration (PIPA) is an acquired disorder of pigmentation that occurs following an inflammatory or traumatic insult to the skin.
• It can manifest as either:
    ◦ **Post-Inflammatory Hyperpigmentation (PIH)**, which is an excess of melanin deposition.
    ◦ **Post-Inflammatory Hypopigmentation**, which is a loss of melanin.
• It is not a primary disease but a sequela of a separate underlying condition.
• PIH is significantly more common, especially in individuals with darker skin tones.
sections.etiology: • The underlying cause is cutaneous inflammation or injury.
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects individuals of all ages and sexes.
• **PIH** is significantly more common and more severe in individuals with **darker skin phototypes (Fitzpatrick III-VI)**.
    ◦ It is one of the most frequent reasons for dermatologic consultation in this population.
• Post-inflammatory hypopigmentation is less common and can occur in any skin type.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Asymptomatic macules or patches** that are located at the site of previous inflammation.
• The shape and distribution of the pigmentary change often **mirror the original inflammatory lesion** (e.g., linear marks from a scratch, follicular papules from acne).
• The onset is after the primary inflammatory process has subsided.
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is almost always **clinical**, based on history and physical exam.
• **History**: Elicit a clear history of a preceding rash, lesion, or injury in the affected area.
• **Wood's Lamp Exam**:
    ◦ **PIH**:
        ▪ **Epidermal PIH** appears more conspicuous (accentuated).
        ▪ **Dermal PIH** shows no enhancement.
    ◦ **Hypopigmentation**:
        ▪ Useful to differentiate from vitiligo.
        ▪ Post-inflammatory hypopigmentation is **off-white** and margins are **indistinct**; it may not enhance significantly.
        ▪ Vitiligo shows complete depigmentation and appears as a bright, **"chalk-white" or "ivory-white"** area with **sharp borders**.
• **Biopsy**:
    ◦ Rarely necessary; performed only if the diagnosis is uncertain.
    ◦ **PIH**: Shows increased melanin in the epidermis and/or melanophages in the dermis.
    ◦ **Hypopigmentation**: Shows reduced or absent melanin in the epidermis.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is generally good but highly variable.
• **Epidermal PIH**: Usually resolves completely within 6-12 months with appropriate treatment and sun protection.
• **Dermal PIH**: Much more difficult to treat and can take years to resolve or may be permanent.
• **Post-inflammatory Hypopigmentation**: Excellent prognosis. Typically resolves completely over several months to a year once the underlying inflammation is controlled.

sections.overview:
• Acanthosis Nigricans (AN) is a common, benign skin disorder characterized by symmetric, velvety, hyperpigmented, and sometimes papillomatous (wart-like) plaques.
	◦ It primarily affects intertriginous areas (skin folds) such as the axillae, posterior neck, and groin.
• AN is not a disease itself but rather a **cutaneous marker of an underlying systemic condition**.
	◦ The most common association is with insulin resistance, but it can also be a paraneoplastic sign of an internal malignancy.
sections.etiology:
• The pathophysiology of AN involves the **proliferation of keratinocytes and dermal fibroblasts**.
	◦ This proliferation is stimulated by various growth factors.
• **Insulin Resistance-Associated AN (Most Common):**
	◦ **Mechanism:** In states of insulin resistance (e.g., obesity, Type 2 DM, PCOS), the pancreas produces excess insulin (hyperinsulinemia) to overcome peripheral resistance.
	◦ At these high concentrations, **insulin binds to and activates Insulin-like Growth Factor-1 (IGF-1) receptors** on keratinocytes and dermal fibroblasts.
		▪ This activation stimulates cellular proliferation, leading to the characteristic epidermal thickening (acanthosis) and hyperpigmentation.
• **Malignancy-Associated AN (Paraneoplastic):**
	◦ **Mechanism:** Malignant cells secrete growth factors that stimulate epidermal proliferation.
	◦ The most commonly implicated factor is **Transforming Growth Factor-alpha (TGF-α)**, which binds to the Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR) on keratinocytes.
	◦ This form of AN is often more abrupt in onset, severe, and extensive.
• **Other Causes:**
	◦ **Drug-Induced:** Medications like nicotinic acid (niacin), systemic corticosteroids, and oral contraceptives can induce AN, often through mechanisms involving insulin resistance.
	◦ **Genetic/Familial:** Rare syndromes can cause AN without overt insulin resistance or malignancy.
sections.epidemiology:
• Prevalence is directly related to the prevalence of obesity and type 2 diabetes.
• Affects all ages and genders but is more common in adults.
• Higher prevalence in populations with a higher risk of insulin resistance, including **Native Americans, Hispanics, and African Americans**.
• Malignancy-associated AN is rare, typically affecting middle-aged or older adults (>40 years).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The onset is typically **insidious and asymptomatic**.
• Patients usually seek medical attention due to the cosmetic appearance of the skin, often described as looking "dirty" and being unable to be washed off.
• **Red Flag Presentation (suggests malignancy):**
	◦ Sudden, explosive onset
	◦ Rapid progression and widespread distribution
	◦ Associated pruritus (itching)
	◦ Involvement of mucous membranes, palms, or soles
	◦ Patient is non-obese, older, and has constitutional symptoms (e.g., weight loss).
sections.diagnostics:
• The diagnosis of AN is clinical, but a workup is **mandatory** to identify the underlying cause.
• **Skin Biopsy:** Rarely necessary. Performed only if the diagnosis is uncertain.
	◦ Histology shows hyperkeratosis and papillomatosis with minimal acanthosis.
• **Laboratory Workup (for benign AN):**
	◦ **First-line:** Fasting blood glucose and **Hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c)** to screen for diabetes/prediabetes.
	◦ Fasting lipid panel.
	◦ Fasting insulin level (to directly assess for hyperinsulinemia).
• **Malignancy Workup (if suspected based on red flags):**
	◦ Age-appropriate cancer screening.
	◦ **Upper endoscopy (EGD)** and/or colonoscopy to evaluate for GI malignancy, especially gastric adenocarcinoma.
	◦ CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis.
sections.prognosis:
• **Benign AN:** Prognosis is excellent.
	◦ The skin lesions may improve or resolve completely with successful treatment of the underlying cause (e.g., weight loss, glycemic control).
• **Malignant AN:** Prognosis is **poor**, as it usually signifies an aggressive and often advanced-stage internal malignancy.
	◦ The prognosis is that of the underlying cancer.

sections.overview:
• Atopic Dermatitis (AD), commonly known as eczema, is a chronic, relapsing, inflammatory, and intensely pruritic skin disease
    ◦ It is the most common form of eczema and is often associated with a personal or family history of other atopic diseases (allergic rhinitis, asthma)
    ◦ The defining feature is a defective skin barrier, leading to **xerosis** (dry skin) and increased susceptibility to environmental irritants and allergens
        ▪ This drives a cycle of inflammation and pruritus
    ◦ The distribution of lesions characteristically changes with age
sections.etiology:
• The pathophysiology of AD is multifactorial, involving a complex interplay of genetic predisposition, skin barrier dysfunction, immune dysregulation, and environmental factors
    ◦ **Genetic Predisposition**
        ▪ Strong familial link
        ▪ Key mutations in the **filaggrin gene (`FLG`)** are a major risk factor
            ▪ Filaggrin is a crucial protein for epidermal barrier function; its deficiency leads to increased transepidermal water loss (TEWL) and easier penetration of allergens and microbes
    ◦ **Immune Dysregulation**
        ▪ Characterized by a **T-helper 2 (Th2) cell-dominant inflammatory response**
        ▪ Th2 cells release key cytokines like **Interleukin-4 (IL-4)**, **Interleukin-5 (IL-5)**, and **Interleukin-13 (IL-13)**
            ▪ These cytokines promote IgE production, eosinophilia, and further impair skin barrier function, perpetuating the inflammatory cycle
    ◦ **Skin Barrier Dysfunction**
        ▪ Primary defect, even in unaffected skin
        ▪ Caused by genetic factors (`FLG` mutations) and inflammation
        ▪ Results in **xerosis** and a lower threshold for irritation
    ◦ **The "Itch-Scratch Cycle"**
        ▪ Pruritus is a primary symptom, not just a consequence of the rash ("the itch that rashes")
        ▪ Scratching further damages the already compromised skin barrier, causing more inflammation, histamine release, and subsequently, more itching
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects 15-20% of children and 1-3% of adults worldwide
• **Age of Onset**: Typically begins in early childhood
    ◦ ~60% of cases develop by age 1
    ◦ ~85% of develop by age 5
• **Course**: Often improves with age; many children "outgrow" it, but it can persist into or develop in adulthood
• **Demographics**: Occurs in all races and ethnicities
    ◦ Higher prevalence in developed countries, supporting the "hygiene hypothesis"
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The location and morphology of AD lesions characteristically vary by age
    ◦ **Infants (birth to 2 years)**
        ▪ **Distribution**: Typically affects the face (especially cheeks), scalp, and **extensor surfaces** of the limbs (knees, elbows)
        ▪ **Morphology**: Presents as erythematous, weeping, crusting papules and plaques
        ▪ **Classic Pearl**: The **diaper area is almost always spared** due to moisture occlusion
    ◦ **Children (2 years to puberty)**
        ▪ **Distribution**: Shifts to the **flexural surfaces**, especially the **antecubital and popliteal fossae**. Also common on the wrists, ankles, and neck
        ▪ **Morphology**: Lesions are less exudative. Characterized by scaly, erythematous papules and plaques. **Lichenification** (thickening of the skin with accentuated skin lines from chronic scratching) becomes prominent
    ◦ **Adults**
        ▪ **Distribution**: Predominantly flexural, but also frequently involves the hands, neck, face (especially eyelids), and upper chest. Can be more localized or generalized
        ▪ **Morphology**: Chronic AD predominates with significant **lichenification** and **xerosis**. Fissuring of the hands and feet can be disabling
sections.diagnostics:
• AD is a **clinical diagnosis** based on history and characteristic physical exam findings (morphology, age-specific distribution, chronicity, pruritus, and personal/family atopic history)
• **Laboratory Tests (not for routine diagnosis)**
    ◦ **Serum IgE**: Often elevated but is non-specific and not diagnostic
    ◦ **Bacterial/Viral Culture**: Indicated if a secondary infection is suspected (e.g., honey-colored crusting suggesting impetigo, or monomorphic vesicles suggesting eczema herpeticum)
    ◦ **Skin Biopsy**: Rarely needed. Performed only in atypical or treatment-refractory cases to rule out other conditions (e.g., cutaneous T-cell lymphoma)
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is generally good. Up to 60-70% of children experience significant improvement or complete resolution by adolescence
• Factors associated with persistent disease include severe early-onset AD, a strong family history of AD, and coexisting allergic rhinitis or asthma

sections.overview:
• Contact dermatitis is an inflammatory **eczematous skin reaction** resulting from direct contact with an external substance. It is broadly divided into two main categories:
    ◦ **Irritant Contact Dermatitis (ICD)**: The more common type (~80%). A **non-immunologic inflammatory reaction** caused by direct cytotoxic damage to the skin barrier from an offending chemical or physical agent.
    ◦ **Allergic Contact Dermatitis (ACD)**: A less common type (~20%). A delayed, **Type IV hypersensitivity reaction** (T-cell mediated) that occurs after sensitization to a specific allergen.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• One of the most common **occupational skin diseases**.
• **ICD** accounts for approximately 80% of all contact dermatitis cases.
• **ACD** accounts for the remaining 20%.
• Affects all ages and ethnicities.
• High prevalence in certain occupations: **healthcare workers**, **food handlers**, **hairdressers**, **mechanics**, **cleaners**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A thorough **history** is critical to identify the causative agent. Key questions should focus on occupation, hobbies, new products, topical medications, and potential plant exposures.
• **Onset**
    ◦ **Irritant Contact Dermatitis (ICD)**: Hours after exposure (strong irritant) or gradual (weak irritant).
    ◦ **Allergic Contact Dermatitis (ACD)**: Delayed: **12-72 hours** after re-exposure.
• **Prior Exposure**
    ◦ **Irritant Contact Dermatitis (ICD)**: Not required.
    ◦ **Allergic Contact Dermatitis (ACD)**: **Sensitization** (prior exposure) is required.
• **Distribution**
    ◦ **Irritant Contact Dermatitis (ICD)**: **Sharply demarcated**, confined strictly to site of contact.
    ◦ **Allergic Contact Dermatitis (ACD)**: May **spread beyond the site of contact**; borders can be less distinct.
• **Classic Example**
    ◦ **Irritant Contact Dermatitis (ICD)**: "**Dishpan hands**" from detergents; **diaper dermatitis**.
    ◦ **Allergic Contact Dermatitis (ACD)**: **Linear vesicles** from **poison ivy**; rash under a watch buckle (**nickel**).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Diagnosis is primarily based on a detailed **history** and a **physical exam** that reveals a characteristic morphology and distribution.
• **Patch Testing**
    ◦ **Gold standard** for identifying the causative allergen in **ACD**.
    ◦ Standardized allergens are applied to the patient's back on adhesive patches.
    ◦ Patches are removed at **48 hours**, and the skin is evaluated for reactions at **48 and 72-96 hours**.
    ◦ A **positive test** shows **erythema**, **papules**, or **vesicles** at the allergen site.
    ◦ **Not used for ICD**.
• **KOH Preparation**: Can be performed on skin scrapings to **rule out tinea** (fungal infection), which can mimic chronic contact dermatitis of the hands or feet.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** if the causative agent is identified and strictly avoided.
• May become **chronic**, **relapsing**, and difficult to control if the agent cannot be identified or if exposure is unavoidable (e.g., in an occupational setting).

sections.overview:
• **Nummular Dermatitis**, also known as discoid eczema, is a chronic, inflammatory skin condition
    ◦ Characterized by well-demarcated, **coin-shaped (nummular)** or oval plaques of eczematous skin
    ◦ It is **intensely pruritic** and follows a **relapsing-remitting course**
• The etiology is not fully understood, but **skin barrier dysfunction (xerosis)** is a key contributing factor
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ The exact cause is **unknown** but is considered multifactorial
    ◦ It is **not contagious**
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Skin Barrier Disruption**: The primary defect is thought to be a compromised epidermal barrier
        ▪ Leads to increased **transepidermal water loss (TEWL)** and **xerosis** (dry skin)
    ◦ **Inflammatory Cascade**: This barrier dysfunction allows environmental irritants and allergens to penetrate the epidermis
        ▪ Triggers a **T-cell-mediated inflammatory response**
    ◦ **Bacterial Colonization**: Lesions are frequently colonized with ***Staphylococcus aureus***
        ▪ The bacteria can act as **superantigens**, exacerbating the inflammation and causing weeping and crusting
    ◦ **Histology**: Shows a non-specific finding common to all forms of eczema
        ▪ **Spongiotic dermatitis** (intercellular edema in the epidermis)
        ▪ **Acanthosis** (epidermal thickening)
        ▪ A perivascular infiltrate of lymphocytes, eosinophils, and mast cells
sections.epidemiology:
• **Bimodal Age Distribution**
    ◦ First peak: Young adult **women** (ages 15-25)
    ◦ Second peak: Older **men** (ages 50-65)
• **Prevalence**: More common in **winter months** due to lower humidity and increased **xerosis**
• **Association**: Can occur in patients with or without a history of **atopic dermatitis**
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **History**
    ◦ Patients typically report the sudden onset of **intensely itchy, round spots**, often on the **arms or legs**
    ◦ The spots may have started as small bumps or blisters that merged together
    ◦ The **pruritus** is often **severe** and may interfere with sleep
    ◦ There is often a personal or family history of **atopic conditions**, though not always
    ◦ Patients frequently report **dry skin**, especially during the winter
sections.diagnostics:
• Nummular dermatitis is primarily a **clinical diagnosis** based on history and the characteristic appearance of **pruritic, coin-shaped eczematous plaques** on a background of **xerotic skin**
• **Potassium Hydroxide (KOH) Prep**
    ◦ **Essential to perform** to rule out **tinea corporis** (ringworm), the main differential diagnosis
    ◦ A **negative KOH prep** (no hyphae or spores) supports the diagnosis of nummular dermatitis
• **Bacterial Culture & Sensitivity**
    ◦ Indicated if **secondary bacterial infection** is suspected (e.g., significant crusting, pustules, purulence, or failure to respond to initial therapy)
    ◦ ***S. aureus*** is the most common pathogen
• **Patch Testing**
    ◦ Consider in persistent or recalcitrant cases to rule out an underlying **allergic contact dermatitis**
• **Skin Biopsy**
    ◦ **Rarely necessary**
    ◦ Performed only if the diagnosis is uncertain or if there is suspicion for another condition like **cutaneous T-cell lymphoma**
sections.prognosis:
• Nummular dermatitis is a **chronic condition** with a **high rate of recurrence**
    ◦ Lesions often **recur in the same locations**
• While complete cure is uncommon, the condition can be **well-managed and controlled** with consistent skin care and appropriate treatment during flares

sections.overview:
• Seborrheic dermatitis is a common, chronic, or relapsing inflammatory skin condition that primarily affects seborrhea-prone (oily) regions of the body.
    ◦ It is not contagious.
    ◦ In its mildest form, it is known as **dandruff** (pityriasis capitis).
    ◦ In infants, it is commonly called **"cradle cap."**
sections.etiology:
• The exact cause is multifactorial and not fully understood, but it involves an inflammatory reaction to a common skin commensal, the yeast ***Malassezia*** (specifically *M. globosa* and *M. furfur*).
    ◦ ***Malassezia* Yeast:** This lipophilic yeast is a normal part of the skin flora. In susceptible individuals, the yeast metabolizes triglycerides in sebum, releasing pro-inflammatory free fatty acids (e.g., oleic acid).
    ◦ **Host Immune Response:** An abnormal or exaggerated immune response to *Malassezia* and its metabolites is the key driver of inflammation. This leads to increased skin cell turnover.
    ◦ **Sebum Production:** The condition thrives in areas with high sebaceous gland activity. Hormonal changes, particularly androgens, can influence sebum production.
