    ◦ **Epidermal Barrier Dysfunction:** The inflammation disrupts the stratum corneum, leading to the characteristic scaling and flaking.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** Affects approximately 3-10% of the general population. Dandruff, the mildest form, affects up to 50%.
• **Age:** Bimodal age distribution:
    ◦ **Infancy:** First 3 months of life (**"cradle cap"**).
    ◦ **Adulthood:** Post-puberty, with a peak incidence between 30-60 years.
• **Sex:** Slightly more common in males.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Immunosuppression**
    ◦ **HIV/AIDS:** Very common and often severe. Severity can correlate with CD4 count decline.
    ◦ Organ transplant recipients.
• **Neurologic and Psychiatric Conditions**
    ◦ **Parkinson's disease (highly associated)**
    ◦ Stroke (CVA)
    ◦ Epilepsy
    ◦ Spinal cord injury
    ◦ Depression
• **Genetic predisposition**
• **Physical or emotional stress**
• **Cold, dry weather**
• **Certain medications:** Lithium, haloperidol, psoralen.
• **Obesity and alcohol use**
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Infants:** Presents as **"cradle cap"** - thick, yellow, greasy, adherent plaques on the scalp vertex.
    ◦ It is typically non-pruritic and self-limited.
    ◦ Can also affect the face and diaper area.
• **Adults:** Presents with a chronic, relapsing course of **"dandruff"** or erythematous patches with greasy scales in characteristic locations.
    ◦ Flares are common, often triggered by stress or seasonal changes.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ **Pruritus:** Varies from absent/mild to moderate. It is often the primary complaint.
    ◦ **Flaking/Scaling:** Visible flakes on skin, hair, and clothing.
    ◦ **Burning sensation:** Can occur, especially on the face.
    ◦ **Cosmetic concerns:** Erythema and scaling can cause significant psychosocial distress.
• **Exam Findings**
    ◦ **Morphology:** Ill-defined erythematous patches or thin plaques with overlying scale.
    ◦ **Scale:** Can be fine and white (pityriasiform) or greasy and yellow/orange.
    ◦ **Distribution (Key to Diagnosis):**
        ▪ **Scalp:** Diffuse erythema and scaling. May have a distinct border along the hairline (**"seborrheic crown"**).
        ▪ **Face:** Most common sites are the **nasolabial folds**, glabella, eyebrows, and eyelids (seborrheic blepharitis).
        ▪ **Ears:** Postauricular, conchal bowl, and external auditory canal.
        ▪ **Chest:** Presternal area, often in a "petaloid" (flower-like) or annular pattern.
        ▪ **Intertriginous Areas:** Axillae, inframammary folds, groin, and anogenital cleft. Presents as moist, erythematous, macerated patches.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primarily a clinical diagnosis** based on the characteristic morphology and distribution of the rash.
• **KOH Preparation**
    ◦ Can be performed to rule out tinea (dermatophytosis), especially on the scalp (tinea capitis) or body (tinea corporis).
    ◦ KOH prep will be **negative for hyphae** in seborrheic dermatitis.
• **Skin Biopsy**
    ◦ Rarely necessary.
    ◦ Performed only if the diagnosis is uncertain or there's a poor response to treatment.
    ◦ Histology shows parakeratosis, acanthosis, spongiosis, and a superficial perivascular inflammatory infiltrate.
sections.treatment:
• **Scalp (Dandruff/Adult Seborrheic Dermatitis):**
    ◦ **First-line:** Medicated shampoos used 2-3 times weekly. Rotate agents to prevent tachyphylaxis.
        ▪ **Antifungals:** **Ketoconazole 2%** (Rx) or 1% (OTC), **selenium sulfide**, ciclopirox.
        ▪ **Keratolytics:** Salicylic acid, coal tar.
        ▪ **Anti-inflammatory:** Zinc pyrithione.
    ◦ **Second-line:** Topical corticosteroids (e.g., fluocinolone solution, clobetasol foam) for short-term use during flares to control inflammation and pruritus.
• **Face and Body:**
    ◦ **First-line:**
        ▪ Topical antifungals: **Ketoconazole 2% cream**.
        ▪ Low-potency topical corticosteroids: **Hydrocortisone 1%** or **desonide 0.05% cream** for flares (use for <2 weeks to avoid side effects).
    ◦ **Second-line (Steroid-sparing):**
        ▪ Topical calcineurin inhibitors: **Pimecrolimus cream** or **tacrolimus ointment**. Excellent for facial use to avoid steroid-induced atrophy.
• **Infants (Cradle Cap):**
    ◦ **Conservative:** Reassurance. Apply emollients (baby oil, petroleum jelly) to soften crusts, followed by gentle removal with a soft brush and washing with a mild baby shampoo.
    ◦ **Medical:** If persistent, can use low-potency hydrocortisone cream or ketoconazole 2% shampoo/cream sparingly.
• **Severe or Refractory Disease:**
    ◦ Consider oral antifungals (itraconazole or fluconazole).
    ◦ Oral isotretinoin may be used in rare, severe cases.
sections.management:
• **Patient Education:** Emphasize the chronic, relapsing nature of the condition. Explain that the goal is control, not cure.
• **Maintenance Therapy:** Once a flare is controlled, regular use of medicated shampoos (1-2 times/week) or creams can help prevent recurrence.
• **Trigger Avoidance:** Counsel patients on managing stress and avoiding harsh soaps or known irritants.
sections.complications:
• **Secondary bacterial infection (impetiginization):** Due to scratching and skin barrier breakdown.
• **Side effects of treatment:** Skin atrophy, telangiectasias, and hypopigmentation from long-term, potent topical steroid use, especially on the face or in skin folds.
• **Psychosocial impact:** Can affect self-esteem due to the visible nature of the condition.
• **Erythroderma:** Rare complication where the rash becomes generalized, affecting >90% of body surface area.
sections.prognosis:
• **Infantile form:** Excellent. Usually self-resolves by 6-12 months of age.
• **Adult form:** Considered a chronic condition. While symptoms can be effectively controlled with treatment, it tends to follow a relapsing and remitting course throughout life.

sections.overview:
• Dyshidrotic eczema, also known as pompholyx, is a type of endogenous eczema characterized by a pruritic vesicular eruption on the palms, soles, and lateral aspects of the digits.
• It follows a chronic, relapsing-remitting course.
• The name "dyshidrotic" is a misnomer, as the condition is not caused by abnormal sweating, although it is often associated with hyperhidrosis.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ The exact cause is often **idiopathic**.
    ◦ It is considered a reaction pattern triggered by various endogenous and exogenous factors.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The underlying mechanism is not fully understood.
    ◦ It involves an inflammatory reaction leading to **spongiosis**, which is intraepidermal edema.
    ◦ This edema accumulates and forms vesicles.
    ◦ The thick stratum corneum of the acral skin (palms and soles) prevents the small vesicles from rupturing easily, causing them to appear deep-seated.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** Accounts for 5-20% of cases of hand eczema.
• **Age of Onset:** Most common in young adults, typically between **20 and 40 years of age**.
• **Sex:** May have a slight female predominance (2:1 ratio).
• **Seasonality:** Flares are more common in warmer weather (spring and summer months).
sections.riskFactors:
• **Atopic Diathesis:** Strong personal or family history of atopic dermatitis, allergic rhinitis, or asthma.
• **Hyperhidrosis:** Excessive sweating of the hands and feet is a common association.
• **Contact Allergens:** Sensitivity to metals, particularly **nickel**, cobalt, and chromate.
• **Environmental Factors:** Frequent water exposure, occlusive gloves, and irritating detergents ("wet work").
• **Systemic Factors:** Emotional stress, smoking.
• **Id Reaction:** A dermatophytid reaction to a distant fungal infection, most commonly **tinea pedis**.
• **Medications:** Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) has been reported as a trigger.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with a sudden onset of an intensely itchy rash on their hands and/or feet.
• The pruritus often precedes the appearance of visible lesions.
• The eruption is most often bilateral and symmetric.
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ **Intense Pruritus:** This is the hallmark and most debilitating symptom.
    ◦ **Burning Sensation or Pain:** Especially as vesicles enlarge or when fissures develop.
    ◦ **Sensation of Tightness** in the affected skin.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Deep-seated, tense vesicles** with clear fluid, classically described as resembling **"tapioca pudding"**.
• Location: Primarily on the **lateral and palmar aspects of the fingers**, palms, and soles.
• Vesicles are typically small (1-2 mm) but may coalesce to form larger **bullae**.
• The surrounding skin may be non-erythematous initially, but can become red and edematous.
• After 1-3 weeks, the vesicles resolve, either by rupturing or reabsorption.
• This leads to a phase of **scaling, desquamation, erythema, and lichenification** (skin thickening from chronic scratching).
• **Painful fissures** and cracks can develop, particularly over joints.
• Pitting, transverse ridging (Beau's lines), and dystrophy of the nail plate can occur if the nail matrix is affected.
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is primarily **clinical**, based on the characteristic history and physical exam findings.
• **KOH Preparation:** Essential if scaling is present, especially on the feet, to rule out tinea pedis (dermatophytosis) which could be the source of an id reaction.
• **Bacterial Culture & Sensitivity:** Perform if signs of secondary infection are present (e.g., pustules, purulent drainage, honey-colored crusting) to rule out impetiginization, commonly by *S. aureus*.
• **Patch Testing:** Consider in chronic or refractory cases to identify a potential allergic contact dermatitis (e.g., nickel allergy).
• **Biopsy:** Rarely necessary. Histology would show characteristic **spongiosis** (intraepidermal edema), intraepidermal vesicles, and a superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate.
sections.treatment:
• **First-Line (Mild-to-Moderate):**
    ◦ **High-potency topical corticosteroids** (e.g., Clobetasol, Fluocinonide) in an ointment base. Apply for a limited course (2-4 weeks).
• **Second-Line (Severe or Refractory):**
    ◦ **Systemic Corticosteroids:** A short course of oral prednisone (e.g., 0.5-1 mg/kg/day) with a taper over 2-4 weeks for severe, acute flares.
    ◦ **Topical Calcineurin Inhibitors:** Tacrolimus or Pimecrolimus can be used for maintenance to reduce steroid reliance.
    ◦ **Phototherapy:** PUVA (psoralen + UVA) or narrowband UVB.
• **Third-Line (Severe, Chronic, Recalcitrant):**
    ◦ Systemic immunosuppressants such as methotrexate, cyclosporine, or mycophenolate mofetil.
    ◦ Biologics (e.g., Dupilumab).
• **Adjunctive Therapies:**
    ◦ **Cool compresses** (e.g., Burow's solution) to soothe acute inflammation and weeping.
    ◦ **Drainage of large bullae:** Can be performed with a sterile needle to relieve pain, leaving the vesicle roof intact as a biological dressing.
    ◦ **Oral antihistamines:** For symptomatic relief of pruritus (e.g., Hydroxyzine, Diphenhydramine), especially at night.
    ◦ **Antibiotics:** For secondary bacterial infections (e.g., Dicloxacillin, Cephalexin).
sections.management:
• **Skin Care:**
    ◦ Use lukewarm water and gentle, soap-free cleansers.
    ◦ Pat skin dry gently.
    ◦ Apply **thick emollients or barrier creams** (e.g., petroleum jelly) multiple times daily, especially after hand washing.
• **Trigger Avoidance:**
    ◦ Avoid known contact allergens (e.g., nickel).
    ◦ Wear protective gloves for wet work (vinyl gloves with cotton liners underneath are ideal).
    ◦ Manage stress.
• **Treat Associated Conditions:**
    ◦ Aggressively treat hyperhidrosis (e.g., topical aluminum chloride).
    ◦ Promptly treat tinea pedis with topical or oral antifungals.
sections.complications:
• **Secondary Bacterial Infection (Impetiginization):** Most common complication, usually with *Staphylococcus aureus*. Presents as pustules, erosions, and honey-colored crusts.
• **Lichenification:** Skin thickening from chronic rubbing and scratching.
• **Painful Fissures:** Can limit function of the hands and feet.
• **Nail Dystrophy:** Pitting and ridging from chronic inflammation near the nail matrix.
• **Psychosocial Impact:** Significant effect on quality of life due to severe itching, pain, and cosmetic appearance.
sections.prognosis:
• The condition follows a **chronic, relapsing-remitting course**.
• Individual flares typically resolve within 3-4 weeks, but recurrence is the rule.
• Many patients experience spontaneous improvement with age.
• The prognosis is significantly better if an avoidable trigger (like a contact allergen) can be identified.

sections.overview: • Perioral dermatitis is a common inflammatory facial skin eruption characterized by clusters of erythematous papules, papulopustules, and sometimes vesicles. ◦ Despite its name, it is considered a variant of rosacea rather than a true eczematous dermatitis. ◦ The eruption classically occurs around the mouth, nose, and eyes. ◦ A key diagnostic feature is the sparing of the skin directly adjacent to the vermilion border of the lips.
sections.etiology: • The exact etiology is unknown, but it is considered an inflammatory process, not an infection. • The pathophysiology is thought to be related to a disruption of the epidermal barrier and an altered cutaneous microflora. ◦ Primary Trigger: The most significant contributing factor is the use of topical corticosteroids. ▪ Prolonged use leads to skin barrier dysfunction, follicular inflammation, and a rebound flare upon cessation. ◦ Other Triggers: Inhaled and nasal corticosteroids can also trigger the condition. ◦ Epidermal Barrier Dysfunction: Heavy, occlusive moisturizers, thick cosmetics, and certain sunscreens can block pilosebaceous units and disrupt skin barrier function. ◦ Microorganisms: An overgrowth of follicular microorganisms like Demodex mites or Fusobacterium species may play a role in the inflammatory response. ◦ Other Factors: Fluoridated toothpaste and hormonal fluctuations have also been implicated as potential triggers.
sections.epidemiology: • Primary Demographic: Most commonly affects young women, typically between the ages of 16 and 45. • Prevalence: Accounts for approximately 90% of cases in women. • Other Populations: Can occur in men and children, but it is far less common.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • A patient, typically a young woman, presents with a persistent rash around her mouth that has been present for weeks to months. ◦ May report a history of using over-the-counter or prescribed hydrocortisone cream on the area, which initially helped but now seems to make the rash worse or cause a significant flare when she stops using it. ◦ The main complaint is often cosmetic.
sections.diagnostics: • Clinical Diagnosis: Diagnosis is almost always made based on the characteristic history and classic physical exam findings (papules/pustules with vermilion border sparing). • Biopsy: Rarely necessary. If performed, histopathology shows a perifollicular and perivascular lymphohistiocytic inflammatory infiltrate. • Culture: A bacterial culture of a pustule can be performed to rule out staphylococcal folliculitis if the diagnosis is uncertain, but it is not routinely required.
sections.prognosis: • Excellent: With proper treatment and trigger avoidance, the prognosis is excellent and most cases resolve completely. • Recurrence: Recurrence is common if triggers, particularly topical corticosteroids, are reintroduced.

sections.overview:
• Diaper dermatitis, commonly known as diaper rash, is a general term for an acute **inflammatory skin reaction** in the region covered by a diaper.
    ◦ It is most commonly a form of **irritant contact dermatitis**.
    ◦ While typically benign, it causes significant discomfort for the infant and concern for caregivers.
sections.etiology:
• The pathophysiology is multifactorial, primarily driven by a **compromised skin barrier**.
• **Irritant Contact Dermatitis (Most Common Type)**:
    ◦ **Moisture**: Prolonged exposure to moisture (urine, feces) leads to **skin maceration**, softening the stratum corneum and increasing its permeability.
    ◦ **Friction**: The diaper and its contents physically rub against the skin, disrupting the epidermal barrier.
    ◦ **pH Change**: Fecal bacteria (e.g., *Proteus*, *Providencia*) produce urease, which converts urea from urine into ammonia. This **raises the skin's pH** (normal is ~5.5).
    ◦ **Enzyme Activity**: Elevated pH activates fecal **proteases and lipases** (trypsin, chymotrypsin), which further damage the skin barrier and cause inflammation.
    ◦ **Conclusion**: A synergistic effect of moisture, friction, increased pH, and enzymatic activity leads to irritant dermatitis.
• **Candidal Dermatitis (Common Superinfection)**:
    ◦ Caused by ***Candida albicans***, a yeast that thrives in the warm, moist, and macerated environment created by irritant dermatitis.
    ◦ Often occurs after a primary irritant rash has been present for **>72 hours** or following a course of oral **antibiotics** which disrupts the infant's normal gut and skin flora.
sections.epidemiology:
• One of the most frequent dermatologic conditions in infancy.
• Peak incidence occurs between **9 and 12 months** of age.
• Affects approximately 25-35% of diaper-wearing infants at any given time.
• Slightly higher incidence in formula-fed infants compared to breastfed infants (due to higher stool pH).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Parents typically report a new-onset rash in the diaper area, often associated with infant fussiness or crying, especially during diaper changes.
    ◦ The history should focus on:
        ▪ Diapering habits
        ▪ Diet
        ▪ Recent illnesses (especially **diarrhea**)
        ▪ Medication use
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is almost always **clinical**, based on history and physical exam findings.
• **KOH Preparation**:
    ◦ Can be performed on scrapings from a **satellite lesion** to confirm *Candida*.
    ◦ Will reveal **budding yeast and pseudohyphae**.
    ◦ This is rarely necessary in practice due to the classic clinical appearance.
• **Culture**:
    ◦ A bacterial culture can be done if a **secondary bacterial infection** (impetigo) is suspected (e.g., **honey-colored crusting**).
• **Skin Biopsy**:
    ◦ Reserved for severe, atypical, or treatment-refractory cases to rule out less common diagnoses (e.g., **Langerhans cell histiocytosis**).
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is **excellent**.
• Most cases of uncomplicated diaper dermatitis resolve within **3-7 days** with appropriate management.
• Recurrence is common if preventive measures are not consistently followed.

sections.overview:
• Prurigo Nodularis (PN) is a chronic inflammatory skin disease characterized by intensely pruritic, firm, hyperkeratotic, and often excoriated nodules.
• The condition is driven by a self-perpetuating **itch-scratch cycle**.
    ◦ Intense pruritus leads to chronic scratching, which causes the development of characteristic skin lesions.
    ◦ These lesions are themselves pruritic, thus continuing the cycle.
• PN significantly impacts quality of life due to severe itch and the disfiguring nature of the lesions.
sections.etiology:
• The exact etiology is not fully understood; it is a complex disease state involving the skin, immune system, and nervous system.
• **Core Mechanism**: The **itch-scratch cycle** is central to its pathophysiology.
    ◦ **Initial Trigger**: An underlying dermatologic, systemic, neurologic, or psychiatric condition causes initial, severe pruritus.
    ◦ **Repetitive Trauma**: The patient scratches, rubs, or picks at the skin in response to the itch.
    ◦ **Pathologic Changes**: Chronic mechanical trauma leads to:
        ▪ **Epidermal Hyperplasia (Acanthosis)**: Thickening of the epidermis.
        ▪ **Dermal Fibrosis**: Thickening of the dermis with dense collagen.
        ▪ **Neural Hypertrophy/Hyperplasia**: An increase in the number and size of cutaneous nerve fibers, making skin more sensitive to itch.
        ▪ **Inflammatory Infiltrate**: Presence of eosinophils, mast cells, neutrophils, and lymphocytes.
• **Immunology**: PN is considered a **Type 2 inflammatory disease**.
    ◦ **Key Cytokines**: Interleukin-4 (IL-4), Interleukin-13 (IL-13), and Interleukin-31 (IL-31) are significantly upregulated.
        ▪ **IL-31**: Known as a key "itch cytokine," it directly stimulates sensory nerves to cause pruritus.
        ▪ **IL-4 & IL-13**: Drive chronic inflammation, disrupt skin barrier function, and contribute to fibrotic changes in nodules.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Uncommon, but likely underdiagnosed.
• **Age of Onset**: Typically affects middle-aged to older adults (50-65 years).
• **Race/Ethnicity**: Higher prevalence and disease severity are noted in **African Americans**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The hallmark is a patient history of an **intense, debilitating, and chronic itch** for months to years, often preceding visible lesions.
• Patients report a deep, unrelenting itch leading to uncontrollable scratching.
• There is a profound negative impact on sleep, work, and social functioning.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Primarily made based on characteristic history of severe chronic pruritus and the presence of typical nodules on physical exam.
• **Skin Biopsy (Punch or Excisional)**:
    ◦ **Indication**: Performed to confirm the diagnosis, especially in atypical cases, or to rule out malignancy (e.g., **Squamous Cell Carcinoma**, **Keratoacanthoma**, **Cutaneous Lymphoma**).
    ◦ **Histopathology Findings (High-Yield)**:
        ▪ Massive epidermal thickening (**acanthosis**) and hyperkeratosis.
        ▪ Thickened papillary dermis with vertically oriented collagen bundles.
        ▪ **Thickened and increased number of nerve fibers (neural hypertrophy)** - a **pathognomonic feature**.
        ▪ Mixed inflammatory infiltrate, often with prominent eosinophils.
• **Laboratory Workup**: Ordered to investigate for underlying systemic causes.
    ◦ CBC with differential (to check for anemia, eosinophilia, polycythemia)
    ◦ Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP) (to assess renal and hepatic function)
    ◦ TSH (thyroid function)
    ◦ HIV and Hepatitis C serologies
    ◦ Fasting glucose/HbA1c
sections.prognosis:
• PN is a chronic disease with a relapsing-remitting course.
• It is often difficult to achieve complete, long-term remission.
• Prognosis is significantly improved when an underlying cause is identified and treated.
• The advent of highly effective targeted biologics like dupilumab has dramatically improved the outlook for patients with moderate-to-severe, refractory disease.

sections.overview:
• **Hidradenitis Suppurativa (HS)**, also known as acne inversa, is a chronic, recurrent, inflammatory skin disease of the **hair follicle**.
    ◦ It is not a primary infection nor a disease of the sweat glands.
    ◦ HS characteristically affects **intertriginous skin areas** (areas where skin rubs together) and is defined by painful, deep-seated inflammatory **nodules**, **abscesses**, **sinus tracts**, and progressive **scarring**.
sections.etiology:
• The pathophysiology is not fully elucidated but is understood as a multi-step process initiated by **follicular occlusion**.
    ◦ **Follicular Occlusion**: The primary event is **hyperkeratosis of the follicular epithelium**, leading to a blockage of the pilosebaceous unit.
        ▪ This creates a keratin-plugged, dilated follicle (comedone).
    ◦ **Follicular Rupture**: The blocked follicle distends and eventually ruptures, releasing its contents (keratin, sebum, bacteria) into the surrounding dermis.
    ◦ **Inflammatory Response**: This dermal spillage triggers a massive, foreign-body-type inflammatory cascade.
        ▪ Neutrophils, lymphocytes, and macrophages are recruited, leading to the formation of painful nodules and abscesses.
        ▪ This is a key point: HS is an **auto-inflammatory** disease, not a primary infection.
    ◦ **Chronic Inflammation & Tissue Destruction**: The persistent inflammatory state leads to the formation of **sinus tracts** (subcutaneous tunnels lined by epithelium), fibrosis, and hypertrophic "rope-like" scars.
    ◦ **Genetic & Immune Factors**: There is a strong genetic predisposition.
        ▪ A dysregulated immune response, particularly involving **TNF-alpha**, **IL-17**, and **IL-23**, perpetuates the inflammation.
    ◦ Note: The involvement of apocrine glands is considered secondary, resulting from the extension of inflammation from the nearby hair follicle.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects approximately **1%** of the population.
• **Gender**: More common in **females** (Female:Male ratio **3:1**).
• **Age of Onset**: Typically occurs after puberty, most commonly in the **2nd and 3rd decades** of life (ages 20-29).
    ◦ Disease activity often decreases after menopause.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient, typically a **young adult female who smokes**, presents with a history of recurrent, painful **"boils"** in the **armpits** or **groin**.
    ◦ The lesions are chronic, lasting for weeks, and often drain **purulent, foul-smelling fluid** before healing with significant **scarring**.
    ◦ The patient reports a significant negative impact on quality of life due to pain and embarrassment.
sections.diagnostics:
• HS is a **clinical diagnosis** based on three key criteria:
    ◦ **Typical Lesions**: Nodules, abscesses, sinus tracts.
    ◦ **Typical Location**: Axillae, groin, anogenital, inframammary regions.
    ◦ **Chronicity & Recurrence**: The lesions are long-lasting and recurrent.
• **Lab Studies**: Generally not required for diagnosis.
    ◦ May show non-specific signs of inflammation (elevated CRP, ESR, leukocytosis).
• **Bacteriology**: Swabs of draining lesions are often polymicrobial and reflect colonization, not causation.
    ◦ Swabs are primarily useful to rule out a primary staphylococcal abscess or identify secondary infection (e.g., **MRSA**) guiding acute antibiotic choice.
• **Biopsy**: Rarely needed.
    ◦ May be performed in atypical cases or to rule out **Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)** in a chronic, non-healing lesion.
sections.prognosis:
• HS is a **chronic, lifelong disease** with a relapsing and remitting course.
• There is **no cure**, but treatment can manage symptoms, reduce flare frequency, and prevent progression.
• **Early and aggressive management** is key to preventing the development of irreversible tissue damage (Stage III disease).
• The disease has a profound negative impact on quality of life, comparable to conditions like psoriasis, heart failure, or COPD.

sections.overview:
• Urticaria (hives) is a common skin condition characterized by the development of **wheals** (transient, circumscribed, edematous, and erythematous plaques), **angioedema** (swelling of the deeper dermis and subcutaneous tissues), or both.
◦ Classified based on duration:
    ▪ **Acute Urticaria**: Lasts **< 6 weeks**; often due to an identifiable trigger like an infection, food, or medication.
    ▪ **Chronic Urticaria**: Lasts **> 6 weeks**; the cause is often idiopathic or autoimmune and is subdivided into Chronic Spontaneous Urticaria (CSU) and Chronic Inducible Urticaria (CIndU).
sections.etiology:
• The central pathogenic event is the **degranulation of cutaneous mast cells and basophils**, leading to the release of inflammatory mediators.
    ◦ **Primary Mediator**: **Histamine**.
    ◦ **Other Mediators**: Prostaglandins, leukotrienes, cytokines, bradykinin.
    ◦ These mediators cause:
        ▪ **Vasodilation**: Leads to erythema (redness).
        ▪ **Increased Vascular Permeability**: Leads to fluid extravasation and the formation of edematous wheals.
        ▪ **Sensory Nerve Stimulation**: Leads to intense **pruritus** (itching).
• **Mechanisms of Mast Cell Degranulation**:
    ◦ **IgE-Mediated (Type I Hypersensitivity)**: Classic allergic pathway where an allergen cross-links IgE antibodies on the mast cell surface, triggering degranulation.
        ▪ Examples: Foods (peanuts, shellfish), drugs (penicillin), insect venom.
    ◦ **Non-IgE-Mediated (Direct Mast Cell Degranulation)**: Certain substances can directly cause mast cell degranulation without IgE involvement.
        ▪ Examples: Opiates, vancomycin, radiocontrast media.
    ◦ **Autoimmune**: In many cases of Chronic Spontaneous Urticaria (CSU), autoantibodies (IgG) target either the IgE molecule itself or its high-affinity receptor (FcεRI) on mast cells, causing chronic activation.
    ◦ **Physical Stimuli (CIndU)**: Triggers like pressure, cold, heat, or vibration directly activate mast cells through various, often poorly understood, mechanisms.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Lifetime Prevalence**: Approximately 20% of the population will experience urticaria at some point.
• **Acute Urticaria**: Very common, especially in children, often associated with viral infections.
• **Chronic Urticaria**: Affects about 0.5-1% of the population.
• **Peak Incidence**: 20-40 years of age.
• **Sex Predilection**: More common in females (2:1 ratio).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with a sudden onset of skin lesions accompanied by intense itching.
• History should focus on identifying a potential trigger (new food, medication, recent illness, physical exposure).
• It is crucial to inquire about symptoms of **anaphylaxis** (shortness of breath, wheezing, throat tightness, dizziness, hypotension).
• The hallmark of urticaria is the **transient nature of individual lesions**.
    ◦ Each wheal appears and resolves completely **within 24 hours** without leaving any residual marking (e.g., bruising, scaling).
    ◦ New lesions may appear as old ones fade, giving the impression of a continuous rash.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Acute Urticaria**: Usually a **clinical diagnosis**; no laboratory workup is necessary if the cause is clear and it is not associated with anaphylaxis.
• **Chronic Urticaria (>6 weeks)**: Workup aims to rule out underlying conditions and identify triggers.
    ◦ **First-Line Labs**:
        ▪ **CBC with differential** (to screen for eosinophilia or systemic inflammation).
        ▪ **ESR and/or CRP** (inflammatory markers).
    ◦ **Second-Line Labs** (based on H&P):
        ▪ **TSH and anti-TPO antibodies**: To screen for autoimmune thyroid disease, a common comorbidity.
        ▪ Hepatitis panel, stool O&P if infectious etiology is suspected.
• **Provocation Testing (for CIndU)**:
    ◦ **Ice Cube Test**: Place an ice cube on the forearm for 5-10 minutes; wheal formation upon rewarming is diagnostic for **cold urticaria**.
    ◦ Stroking the skin with a tongue depressor to elicit **dermatographism**.
• **Skin Biopsy**: Indicated if lesions are atypical:
    ◦ Last > 24-48 hours.
    ◦ Are painful rather than pruritic.
    ◦ Leave behind purpura or bruising (petechiae/ecchymosis).
    ◦ **Findings**: A biopsy can differentiate simple urticaria (perivascular infiltrate without vessel wall destruction) from **urticarial vasculitis** (leukocytoclasis, fibrinoid necrosis of vessel walls).
sections.prognosis:
• **Acute Urticaria**: Excellent; the vast majority of cases resolve spontaneously within days to a few weeks.
• **Chronic Urticaria**: Variable and unpredictable.
    ◦ Approximately 50% of patients with CSU experience remission within 1 year.
    ◦ However, symptoms can persist for 5-10 years or longer in a significant minority.
    ◦ Chronic inducible urticarias often have a longer course than CSU.

sections.overview:
• Localized, well-demarcated, **non-pitting edema** affecting the deep dermal, subcutaneous, or submucosal tissues.
• Most commonly involves the face, lips, tongue, larynx, extremities, and gastrointestinal tract.
• The primary danger is **laryngeal edema**, which can lead to rapid **airway compromise** and asphyxiation.
• Pathophysiology is broadly divided into two main categories, which dictates clinical presentation and treatment:
    ◦ **Mast Cell (Histaminergic) Mediated**:
        ▪ The most common type.
        ▪ Associated with **urticaria** and **pruritus**.
        ▪ Responds to standard allergy treatments.
    ◦ **Bradykinin-Mediated**:
        ▪ Less common but critical to identify.
        ▪ **Not** associated with **urticaria** or **pruritus**.
        ▪ Does **not** respond to **epinephrine**, **antihistamines**, or **steroids**.
sections.etiology: • The core mechanism is transient, localized **vasodilation** and increased **vascular permeability**, leading to plasma extravasation into the deep tissues.
sections.epidemiology:
• **General**: Affects up to 25% of the population at some point.
• **Mast Cell-Mediated**: The most common form overall.
• **ACE Inhibitor-Induced**:
    ◦ Occurs in 0.1-0.7% of patients on **ACE inhibitors**.
    ◦ More common in **African Americans**, women, and smokers.
• **Hereditary Angioedema (HAE)**: Rare, with a prevalence of approximately 1 in 50,000.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient presents with acute onset of **asymmetric, non-pitting swelling**.
• The history is critical for determining the underlying cause.
    ◦ Key questions revolve around new medications (especially **ACE inhibitors**), allergic triggers, personal or family history of similar episodes, and associated symptoms (**itching**, **hives**, **abdominal pain**).
• The most urgent consideration is **airway involvement**.
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is primarily clinical.
• Labs are used to confirm suspected **bradykinin-mediated angioedema**, not for acute management.
• **Initial Assessment**:
    ◦ **ABCs** take priority.
    ◦ **Laryngoscopy** (flexible fiberoptic) is the gold standard to directly visualize **laryngeal edema** if **airway compromise** is suspected.
• **Laboratory Studies (for suspected HAE/AAE)**:
    ◦ **Screening Test**: **C4 complement level**.
        ▪ C4 is consumed in the pathway leading to bradykinin production.
        ▪ A **low C4 level** during or between attacks is highly suggestive of **HAE** or **AAE**.
        ▪ A normal C4 makes **HAE Type I/II** very unlikely.
    ◦ **Confirmatory Tests**:
        ▪ **C1-INH quantitative (antigenic) level**: Low in **HAE Type I**.
        ▪ **C1-INH functional assay**: Low in both **HAE Type I and II**.
        ▪ **C1q level**: Used to differentiate HAE from AAE.
            ▪ C1q is **normal in HAE** but **low in AAE**.
• **Allergy Testing**: May be useful later to identify triggers for IgE-mediated angioedema.
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent if the airway is managed appropriately and the correct diagnosis is made.
• Mortality is almost exclusively due to **airway obstruction**.
• For **HAE**, prognosis has dramatically improved with the availability of specific on-demand and prophylactic therapies.

sections.overview:
• **Erythema Multiforme (EM)** is an acute, self-limiting, immune-mediated **hypersensitivity reaction**.
    ◦ Characterized by distinctive **target-like lesions** on the skin.
    ◦ May also involve one or more **mucous membranes**.
• The condition exists on a spectrum, classically divided into **EM minor** and **EM major**.
• It is crucial to distinguish EM from **Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS)** and **Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN)**, which are now considered separate, more severe entities.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Infections (>90% of cases)**
        ▪ **Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV-1 and HSV-2)**: The **most common precipitant**, especially for **recurrent EM**. The rash typically appears 1-3 weeks after a herpetic outbreak.
        ▪ ***Mycoplasma pneumoniae***: The **second most common cause**, particularly in children and adolescents.
        ▪ Other viruses (Adenovirus, EBV, CMV, VZV) and bacteria (Group A Strep) are less common triggers.
    ◦ **Drugs (<10% of cases)**
        ▪ **Sulfa drugs**
        ▪ **Anticonvulsants** (Phenytoin, Carbamazepine, Barbiturates)
        ▪ **NSAIDs**
        ▪ **Allopurinol**
        ▪ Antibiotics (e.g., penicillins)
    ◦ **Idiopathic**: No clear cause identified in some cases.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ EM is a **Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity reaction**.
    ◦ It is mediated by cytotoxic **T-lymphocytes (CD8+)** that target keratinocytes.
    ◦ In **HSV-associated EM**, viral DNA fragments are transported to keratinocytes by immune cells. These fragments are expressed on the cell surface, leading T-cells to recognize them as foreign and initiate **apoptosis** (cell death).
    ◦ This inflammatory cascade results in **epidermal necrosis** and **dermal edema**, creating the characteristic **"target" morphology**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Age**: Most common in young adults, typically between **20-40 years old**. Can occur at any age.
• **Sex**: Slight **male predominance**.
• **Incidence**: Relatively common, though exact figures are difficult to obtain due to its self-limiting nature.
• **Seasonality**: May show a slight peak in **spring and autumn**, possibly mirroring the incidence of HSV outbreaks.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Onset**: **Acute**, developing over several days.
• **Prodrome**: May be preceded by 1-7 days of low-grade **fever**, **malaise**, **myalgias**, **headache**, or **sore throat**.
• **Course**: The condition is **self-limiting**, typically resolving within **2-4 weeks without scarring**, although **post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation** may occur.
sections.physicalExam:
• Lesions appear **abruptly** and **symmetrically**.
• They often begin on the **extensor surfaces** of the extremities (dorsal hands, feet, elbows, knees) and spread **centripetally** (towards the trunk).
• **Palms and soles** are commonly involved.
sections.diagnostics:
• Primarily a **clinical diagnosis** based on history and the presence of **typical target lesions**.
• **Skin Biopsy**
    ◦ Not always necessary but performed in **atypical cases** to rule out other conditions (e.g., SJS, bullous pemphigoid).
    ◦ **Findings**: **Perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate**, **dermal edema**, and focal **keratinocyte necrosis**.
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ Generally not required for diagnosis but useful for identifying the **underlying trigger**.
    ◦ **HSV PCR or culture** from a preceding herpetic lesion.
    ◦ ***Mycoplasma* serology (IgM)** or PCR from a throat swab.
    ◦ CBC, CMP, ESR/CRP are non-specific but may show inflammation.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**.
• **EM Minor**: Resolves completely in **2-4 weeks without scarring**.
• **EM Major**: Takes longer to resolve (**3-6 weeks**) and has a higher risk of complications (especially ocular), but **mortality is very rare**.
• **Recurrence** is common, particularly in **HSV-triggered cases**, if prophylactic antivirals are not used.

sections.overview:
• Erythema Nodosum (EN) is an acute, nodular, erythematous inflammatory condition of the subcutaneous fat.
    ◦ It is a form of **panniculitis**—specifically, a **septal panniculitis without vasculitis**.
    ◦ EN is considered a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction to a variety of underlying stimuli.
    ◦ It is often a cutaneous marker for an underlying systemic disease, infection, or drug reaction.
    ◦ The lesions are self-limited and resolve without scarring.
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ EN is a Type IV delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction.
    ◦ The mechanism involves the formation of immune complexes that deposit in and around the venules of the subcutaneous fat septa, triggering an inflammatory cascade.
    ◦ The key histologic feature is **septal panniculitis** (inflammation of the fibrous septa between fat lobules) **without primary vasculitis**.
• **Etiology**
    ◦ EN is a reactive process; the underlying trigger can be identified in about 50% of cases.
    ◦ **Idiopathic (Most Common)**: Up to 50% of cases have no identifiable cause.
    ◦ **Infections (Common)**
        ▪ **Streptococcal Infection**: Most common identifiable cause, especially in children (following streptococcal pharyngitis).
        ▪ **Tuberculosis (TB)**: A classic and important association.
        ▪ **Endemic Fungi**: *Coccidioidomycosis* ("Valley Fever"), *Histoplasmosis*, *Blastomycosis*.
        ▪ **Other Bacteria**: *Yersinia*, *Salmonella*, *Shigella*, *Campylobacter*, *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*.
    ◦ **Systemic Inflammatory Diseases**
        ▪ **Sarcoidosis**: A very strong association. The triad of EN, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, and polyarthralgias is known as **Löfgren's Syndrome**.
        ▪ **Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD)**: Crohn's Disease > Ulcerative Colitis.
        ▪ **Behçet's Disease**.
    ◦ **Medications**
        ▪ **Oral Contraceptives (OCPs)**.
        ▪ **Sulfonamides** (e.g., sulfasalazine, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole).
        ▪ **Penicillins**.
    ◦ **Pregnancy**: Can be a trigger, especially in the second trimester.
    ◦ **Malignancy**: Less common, but associated with lymphoma, leukemia.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Age**: Most common in young adults, typically 20-40 years old.
• **Sex**: Strong female predilection (Female:Male ratio of 3-6:1).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A typical patient is a young woman who presents with the acute onset of tender, red nodules on the shins.
• This is often accompanied by systemic symptoms like fever, malaise, and joint pain.
• She may report a recent sore throat, diarrheal illness, or starting a new medication (like OCPs).
sections.diagnostics:
• The diagnosis is often clinical; the workup is aimed at identifying the underlying cause.
• **Initial Workup (Essential)**
    ◦ **Chest X-ray (CXR)**: Crucial to evaluate for **bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy** (suggesting sarcoidosis/Löfgren's Syndrome) or evidence of TB or fungal infection.
    ◦ **CBC with differential**: May show leukocytosis.
    ◦ **Inflammatory Markers**: ESR and CRP are almost always elevated.
• **Workup Based on Suspicion**
    ◦ **ASO Titer or Throat Culture**: To rule out recent streptococcal infection.
    ◦ **PPD Skin Test or IGRA**: To screen for Tuberculosis.
    ◦ **Stool Cultures**: If GI symptoms are present (for *Yersinia*, *Salmonella*, etc.).
    ◦ **Pregnancy Test (hCG)**.
• **Biopsy**
    ◦ **Indication**: Rarely needed; reserved for atypical cases where the diagnosis is uncertain.
    ◦ **Procedure**: A deep incisional biopsy is required to obtain an adequate sample of subcutaneous fat. A punch biopsy is often insufficient.
    ◦ **Histology**: Confirms **septal panniculitis without vasculitis**.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis for the skin lesions is **excellent**, with spontaneous resolution within weeks to months.
• The overall prognosis is entirely dependent on the successful identification and management of the underlying etiology.

sections.overview:
• **Acute Generalized Exanthematous Pustulosis (AGEP)** is a rare, **severe cutaneous adverse reaction (SCAR)** characterized by the acute onset of **numerous, small, sterile, non-follicular pustules** on a background of widespread **edematous erythema**.
	◦ It is most commonly triggered by **medications** and is typically accompanied by **high fever** and **neutrophilia**.
	◦ Despite its dramatic presentation, AGEP is usually self-limiting with an excellent prognosis upon withdrawal of the offending agent.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Rare, estimated at 1-5 cases per million people per year.
• **Age**: Can occur at any age, but most common in adults.
• **Sex**: Slight female predominance.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Latency Period**: **Rapid onset**, usually within **48 hours** of drug exposure, but can be up to 2 weeks.
• **Prodrome**: Often begins with a **high fever (>38C)** and malaise.
• **Eruption**:
	◦ Starts as a burning or pruritic, edematous erythema, often beginning on the **face or in intertriginous areas** (axillae, groin).
	◦ The rash rapidly generalizes within hours to a few days.
	◦ **Hundreds to thousands of small (<5 mm), non-follicular, pinhead-sized pustules** erupt on the erythematous base.
• **Resolution**: After drug cessation, pustules resolve spontaneously over 1-2 weeks, followed by a characteristic superficial, "**collarette-like" desquamation**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Diagnosis is primarily clinical**, based on history (drug timeline) and physical exam.
• **Laboratory Studies**:
	◦ **CBC**:
		▪ **Marked neutrophilic leukocytosis** is characteristic.
		▪ Eosinophilia may be present in about 30% of cases but is less pronounced than in DRESS.
	◦ **CMP**:
		▪ May show transient, mild elevation of liver transaminases (AST/ALT) or mild renal insufficiency (elevated BUN/Cr).
	◦ **Inflammatory Markers**:
		▪ Elevated CRP and ESR.
• **Skin Biopsy (Confirmatory)**:
	◦ **Classic finding**: **Spongiform subcorneal and/or intraepidermal pustules**.
	◦ Prominent edema of the papillary dermis.
	◦ Perivascular inflammatory infiltrate with abundant neutrophils and some eosinophils.
• **Patch Testing**:
	◦ Can be performed 4-6 weeks after resolution to help identify the causative drug.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**.
• Most cases are self-limiting, with resolution of fever and pustules within 1-2 weeks of drug withdrawal.
• Mortality rate is low (<5%), typically occurring in elderly patients with significant comorbidities.

sections.overview:
• Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (HSP), now preferentially called **IgA Vasculitis (IgAV)**, is the most common systemic small-vessel vasculitis in children.
• It is characterized by the deposition of IgA-containing immune complexes in the walls of small blood vessels, primarily affecting the skin, joints, gastrointestinal (GI) tract, and kidneys.
• The hallmark of the disease is its cutaneous manifestation: **palpable purpura**, typically distributed on the lower extremities and buttocks.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ The exact cause is unknown, but it is widely considered an immune-mediated process, often triggered by an antecedent infection.
    ◦ **Most Common Trigger**: Group A β-hemolytic Streptococcus (GABHS) upper respiratory infection (URI), occurring 1-3 weeks prior to symptom onset.
    ◦ **Other Triggers**: Other bacteria (Mycoplasma), viruses (EBV, Varicella), certain medications (e.g., antibiotics, NSAIDs), and insect bites.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ An antigenic trigger (e.g., a pathogen) elicits an abnormal immune response.
    ◦ This leads to the production of aberrantly glycosylated IgA1 antibodies.
    ◦ The body forms IgG autoantibodies against these abnormal IgA1 molecules, creating large IgA-IgG immune complexes.
    ◦ These complexes deposit in the walls of small vessels (capillaries, arterioles, venules) in target organs.
    ◦ Deposition activates the complement system (alternative pathway), leading to neutrophil recruitment and inflammation.
    ◦ The resulting inflammation damages vessel walls, causing extravasation of red blood cells into the surrounding tissue.
        ▪ This process is termed **leukocytoclastic vasculitis**.
        ▪ The inflammation and hemorrhage are what make the purpura "palpable."
sections.epidemiology:
• **Age**: Primarily a disease of childhood, with 90% of cases occurring in patients <10 years old.
    ◦ The peak incidence is between ages 4 and 6.
• **Sex**: Slight male predominance (Male:Female ratio 1.5:1).
• **Seasonality**: Higher incidence in the fall, winter, and spring, correlating with the prevalence of URIs.
• **Prevalence**: Most common systemic vasculitis in the pediatric population.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a child who recently recovered from a sore throat or cold and now develops a characteristic rash on their legs, along with potential joint pain, abdominal cramping, and/or blood in the urine.
• The full **classic tetrad** includes:
    ◦ **Palpable Purpura** (present in 95-100% of cases)
    ◦ **Arthritis/Arthralgia** (~75%)
    ◦ **Abdominal Pain** (~50%)
    ◦ **Renal Disease** (~20-50%)
• The cutaneous findings are almost always the presenting feature.
sections.diagnostics:
• IgAV is a **clinical diagnosis** based on the EULAR/PRINTO/PRES criteria:
    ◦ **Palpable purpura** (mandatory criterion) plus at least one of the following:
        ▪ Diffuse abdominal pain
        ▪ Arthritis or arthralgia
        ▪ Renal involvement (hematuria and/or proteinuria)
        ▪ Biopsy showing predominant IgA deposition
• **Laboratory Studies (to support diagnosis and rule out differentials)**
    ◦ **CBC**: Platelet count is **normal or elevated (thrombocytosis)**.
        ▪ This is essential to differentiate from thrombocytopenic purpuras (e.g., ITP, TTP, leukemia).
    ◦ **Coagulation Studies (PT, PTT, INR)**: **Normal**.
    ◦ **Urinalysis (UA) with Microscopy**: **CRITICAL** for assessing renal involvement.
        ▪ Look for hematuria and/or proteinuria.
    ◦ **Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP)**: Assess BUN and creatinine for renal function.
    ◦ **ASO Titer / Throat Culture**: May be positive for recent GABHS infection.
    ◦ **Serum IgA**: Elevated in ~50% of patients, but has low sensitivity and specificity.
        ▪ Not required for diagnosis.
• **Biopsy**
    ◦ **Skin Biopsy**: The **gold standard** for confirming vasculitis if the diagnosis is uncertain.
        ▪ **Light Microscopy (H&E stain)**: Shows **leukocytoclastic vasculitis** in post-capillary venules (neutrophilic infiltrate, nuclear debris, fibrinoid necrosis).
        ▪ **Direct Immunofluorescence (DIF)**: **Pathognomonic finding** is granular **IgA deposition** in the vessel walls.
    ◦ **Renal Biopsy**: Indicated for severe or progressive nephritis.
        ▪ Shows **mesangial IgA deposition**, identical to IgA nephropathy (Berger disease).
sections.prognosis:
• **Generally excellent**: IgAV is typically a self-limiting disease, with most cases resolving completely within 4-6 weeks.
• **Recurrence**: Occurs in up to one-third of patients, usually within the first year.
    ◦ Recurrent episodes are typically milder.
• **Long-term prognosis is determined entirely by the degree of renal involvement.**

sections.overview:
• A simple exanthematous drug eruption, also known as a morbilliform or maculopapular drug eruption, is the most common type of cutaneous adverse drug reaction.
    ◦ It is a T-cell mediated (**Type IV**) hypersensitivity reaction characterized by a widespread, symmetric, erythematous maculopapular rash that appears **7-14 days** after starting a new medication.
    ◦ It is considered "simple" due to the absence of systemic symptoms, mucosal involvement, or organ damage, distinguishing it from **severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCARs)**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ Caused by a hypersensitivity reaction to a medication.
    ◦ **Most Common Culprits**
        ▪ **Antibiotics:** Penicillins (especially **ampicillin/amoxicillin**), Sulfonamides (e.g., Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole), Cephalosporins.
        ▪ **Anticonvulsants:** Carbamazepine, Phenytoin, Lamotrigine.
        ▪ **Allopurinol**
        ▪ **NSAIDs**
        ▪ **Thiazide diuretics**
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Type IV (Delayed-Type) Hypersensitivity Reaction:** This is a cell-mediated immune response, not an IgE-mediated (Type I) reaction like urticaria or anaphylaxis.
    ◦ **Mechanism**
        ▪ The drug or its metabolites act as a hapten, binding to carrier proteins in the skin.
        ▪ These new antigens are processed by antigen-presenting cells (Langerhans cells) and presented to drug-specific T-lymphocytes.
        ▪ Upon activation, these T-cells proliferate and release cytokines (like IFN-gamma and TNF-alpha), leading to inflammation and the characteristic skin rash.
    ◦ The **7-14 day delay** on first exposure represents the time needed for this primary T-cell sensitization and expansion.
        ▪ On re-exposure, the reaction can occur much faster (**1-3 days**).
sections.epidemiology:
• Accounts for ~90% of all cutaneous drug eruptions.
• Incidence is approximately 1-5% for users of high-risk medications.
• Can occur at any age, in any race, and affects both sexes, with a slight predilection for females.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Specific Medications:** Certain drugs (see Etiology) have a higher incidence.
• **Viral Infections:** Concurrent viral infections can increase risk.
    ◦ The classic example is the high incidence (~90%) of a morbilliform rash when **amoxicillin is given to a patient with Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) mononucleosis**.
• **Immunocompromised States:** Patients with **HIV** have a significantly higher risk (up to 50-60%) of drug eruptions, especially to sulfonamides.
• **Genetic Predisposition:** Certain HLA alleles are associated with increased risk for specific drugs (though this is more strongly linked to SCARs).
• **History of Prior Drug Eruption:** A previous reaction increases the likelihood of future reactions.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **History is key:** The patient will report starting a new medication **7-14 days prior** to rash onset.
    ◦ If it's a re-exposure, the onset may be within **24-72 hours**.
• The rash typically begins on the **trunk and upper extremities** and then becomes more widespread and confluent over several days, spreading centrifugally (outward) to the distal extremities.
• Patients may report mild malaise or a low-grade fever, but are otherwise systemically well.
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ **Pruritus:** This is the **hallmark symptom** and can range from mild to intense. It is almost always present.
    ◦ **Low-grade fever:** Temperature typically < 38.5C (101.3F).
    ◦ Mild malaise.
    ◦ **Crucially, there is an ABSENCE of:**
        ▪ high fever, severe pain, mucosal pain/erosions, dyspnea, hypotension, or signs of organ injury.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Morphology**
    ◦ **Maculopapular ("Morbilliform")**: Composed of erythematous macules (flat spots <1 cm) and papules (raised bumps <1 cm).
    ◦ Lesions may start as small, discrete spots and then become **confluent** (merge together) to form larger patches and plaques.
• **Distribution**
    ◦ **Symmetrical and widespread.**
    ◦ Typically starts on the **trunk** and spreads to the extremities.
    ◦ Facial involvement can occur, but significant facial edema is a red flag for **DRESS**.
    ◦ Palm and sole involvement is possible but less common.
• **Key Negative Findings on Exam**
    ◦ **No mucosal involvement:** Oral, ocular, and genital mucosa are clear.
    ◦ **No blisters, bullae, or pustules.**
    ◦ **No purpura.**
    ◦ **Negative Nikolsky sign** (top layer of skin does not slough off with gentle pressure).
    ◦ **No significant lymphadenopathy.**
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primarily a clinical diagnosis** based on morphology of the rash and a thorough medication history (including OTCs and supplements).
• **Labs (generally not necessary for simple cases)**
    ◦ If the diagnosis is uncertain or there is concern for a severe reaction, labs may be ordered.
    ◦ **CBC with differential:**
        ▪ Typically normal. Mild eosinophilia may be present but significant eosinophilia (>1500/L) is a red flag for **DRESS**.
    ◦ **CMP:**
        ▪ Liver function tests (AST/ALT) and creatinine are normal. Abnormalities suggest organ involvement (**DRESS**).
• **Skin Biopsy**
    ◦ Rarely needed. If performed, shows a nonspecific perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate, sometimes with eosinophils. It is primarily used to rule out other conditions.
sections.treatment:
• **Topical Corticosteroids:** Medium-to-high potency (e.g., triamcinolone 0.1% cream) applied BID to affected areas can reduce inflammation and pruritus.
• **Oral Antihistamines:** Second-generation (cetirizine, loratadine) for daytime use and first-generation (diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine) for nighttime use due to sedative effects.
• **Systemic Corticosteroids**
    ◦ Generally **not required or recommended** for simple eruptions.
    ◦ May be considered for very severe or persistent cases after SCARs have been definitively ruled out.
sections.management:
• **Patient Education**
    ◦ Inform the patient of the offending drug. The drug should be listed as an allergy in their medical record.
    ◦ Educate them to avoid the specific drug and structurally related medications in the future.
    ◦ Provide strict "return to clinic" or "go to ED" instructions if they develop any signs of a severe reaction (high fever, blisters, mouth sores, facial swelling, difficulty breathing, severe skin pain).
• **Follow-Up**
    ◦ The rash should begin to improve within a few days of stopping the drug and typically resolves over **1-2 weeks**.
    ◦ The rash may temporarily worsen for 24-48 hours after drug cessation, which is normal.
    ◦ Resolution is often followed by a fine **desquamation** (peeling) and possible post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.
sections.complications:
• Complications are rare in a truly simple exanthematous eruption.
• **Misdiagnosis:** The most significant risk is failing to recognize a developing **severe cutaneous adverse reaction (SCAR)**.
• **Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation:** Can occur after the rash resolves, especially in individuals with darker skin tones.
• **Excoriations and secondary bacterial infection:** From intense scratching.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent.**
• The condition is self-limiting upon withdrawal of the offending agent.
• Full recovery without long-term sequelae is the expected outcome.

sections.overview:
• An urticarial drug eruption is a common, acute cutaneous adverse drug reaction characterized by the development of **wheals (hives)**, **angioedema**, or both.
• It is typically a **Type I (IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction** to a medication.
• The eruption is defined by **intensely pruritic**, **transient**, **erythematous**, and **edematous plaques**.
• The cornerstone of management is the identification and **discontinuation of the offending drug**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**: Caused by a systemic medication. Common culprits include:
    ◦ **Antibiotics**: **Penicillins** and related beta-lactams (e.g., cephalosporins) are the most frequent cause. Sulfonamides are also common.
    ◦ **Aspirin and NSAIDs**: Can induce both IgE-mediated and non-allergic (pseudoallergic) urticaria.
    ◦ **Opiates**: Cause direct mast cell degranulation (non-IgE mediated).
    ◦ **Radiocontrast media**: Can cause both IgE-mediated and direct mast cell degranulation.
    ◦ **ACE Inhibitors**: Primarily cause **angioedema** (without urticaria) via bradykinin accumulation, but are an important consideration.
    ◦ **Monoclonal antibodies** and other biologics.
• **Pathophysiology**: Two primary mechanisms:
    ◦ **Immunologic (Type I Hypersensitivity)**:
        ▪ **Sensitization**: On first exposure, the drug (or its metabolite) acts as a hapten, binding to a carrier protein to form an antigen. This is presented to B-lymphocytes, which differentiate into plasma cells and produce drug-specific IgE antibodies.
        ▪ **Elicitation**: Upon re-exposure, the drug cross-links the IgE antibodies bound to the surface of mast cells and basophils.
        ▪ **Degranulation**: This cross-linking triggers the release of pre-formed inflammatory mediators, primarily **histamine**, as well as leukotrienes and prostaglandins.
        ▪ **Clinical Effect**: These mediators cause vasodilation (erythema) and increased vascular permeability, leading to fluid extravasation into the dermis (**wheal**).
    ◦ **Non-Immunologic (Pseudoallergic)**:
        ▪ Certain drugs can directly stimulate mast cell degranulation without involving IgE antibodies.
        ▪ Examples: Opiates, vancomycin (**"Red Man Syndrome"**), and some radiocontrast agents.
        ▪ NSAIDs can also induce urticaria by shunting arachidonic acid metabolism towards the production of pro-inflammatory leukotrienes.
sections.epidemiology:
• Urticarial drug eruptions are one of the most common types of cutaneous adverse drug reactions.
• They account for a significant portion of all drug-induced skin reactions.
• Can occur at any age, in any race, and affects both sexes, though some studies suggest a slight female predominance.
• Occurs in ~2-5% of hospitalized patients receiving medications.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The **clinical history** is paramount. A thorough medication history, including timing of administration, is critical.
• **Timing**:
    ◦ The reaction typically occurs within **minutes to hours** after drug administration in a previously sensitized individual.
    ◦ In a first-time exposure, it may take **7-14 days** for sensitization to occur, with the rash appearing late in the treatment course or even after it has finished.
• The patient presents with an acute onset of an **intensely itchy rash**.
    ◦ They may report associated swelling of the lips, tongue, or around the eyes (**angioedema**).
• In severe cases, the patient may report symptoms of **anaphylaxis**: difficulty breathing, wheezing, throat tightness, dizziness, or syncope.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primarily a clinical diagnosis** based on a characteristic history and physical exam.
• **Laboratory studies are not routinely necessary** for uncomplicated urticaria.
• **CBC with differential**:
    ◦ May show eosinophilia, but this is non-specific.
• **ESR/CRP**:
    ◦ May be elevated but are also non-specific.
• **Skin Biopsy**:
    ◦ Rarely performed.
    ◦ If done (e.g., to rule out urticarial vasculitis), it shows dermal edema with a sparse perivascular inflammatory infiltrate, often containing eosinophils.
• **Allergy Testing (Skin Prick, Intradermal)**:
    ◦ Can be performed by an allergist to confirm the causative agent *after* the acute reaction has completely resolved.
    ◦ It carries a risk of inducing another reaction.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for most cases once the offending drug is identified and withdrawn.
• Symptoms typically begin to improve within **24-48 hours** of drug cessation and fully resolve within days to a week.
• The prognosis depends on the severity of the reaction; **anaphylaxis** can be fatal if not treated promptly.

sections.overview: • A Lichenoid Drug Eruption is a cell-mediated (Type IV) hypersensitivity reaction to a systemic medication that clinically and/or histologically mimics idiopathic Lichen Planus (LP). • It is characterized by the appearance of pruritic, violaceous, flat-topped papules and plaques. • The key to diagnosis and management is identifying and discontinuing the causative drug. • The latency period between starting a drug and the rash appearing can be highly variable, ranging from weeks to over a year.
sections.etiology: • Etiology ◦ Caused by a systemic medication. The list of offending drugs is extensive, but high-yield culprits include: ▪ Antihypertensives: • Thiazide diuretics (especially Hydrochlorothiazide - HCTZ) • ACE Inhibitors (-prils, e.g., lisinopril, captopril) • Beta-blockers (-olols, e.g., propranolol, metoprolol) ▪ Antimalarials: Hydroxychloroquine, chloroquine ▪ NSAIDs: Ibuprofen, naproxen ▪ Metals: Gold salts (classic but less common now), mercury ▪ Anticonvulsants: Carbamazepine, phenytoin ▪ Others: Allopurinol, Penicillamine, TNF-alpha inhibitors (e.g., infliximab, adalimumab) • Pathophysiology ◦ Type IV (Delayed) Hypersensitivity Reaction: It is a T-cell mediated inflammatory response. ◦ Mechanism: ▪ The drug or its metabolite acts as a hapten, binding to a self-protein (carrier) within the skin. This new complex is recognized as foreign. ▪ Antigen-presenting cells (APCs), such as Langerhans cells, process this antigen and present it to T-helper cells. ▪ This activates cytotoxic CD8+ T-cells, which migrate to the skin and attack basal keratinocytes that express the drug-antigen complex on their surface. ▪ This targeted attack on the basal layer of the epidermis leads to apoptosis of keratinocytes and the characteristic "interface dermatitis" seen on histology.
sections.epidemiology: • Incidence: Less common than other drug eruptions like morbilliform exanthems. • Age: More common in middle-aged and older adults, likely due to increased medication use (polypharmacy). • Sex/Race: No significant predilection, but incidence is tied to the prescription patterns of causative drugs. • Latency Period: Highly variable and a key clinical feature. Can develop from 2-3 weeks to over a year after drug initiation, making the historical connection challenging.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • Onset: Typically subacute to chronic. • Distribution: ◦ Often begins on the trunk and extremities. Can be more widespread and symmetric compared to idiopathic LP. ◦ A photodistribution (sun-exposed areas like face, neck, dorsal hands/arms) is a strong clue for a drug-induced cause. • Morphology: ◦ Lesions are papules and plaques. ◦ Color: Violaceous (purple-hued), erythematous, or dusky-brown. ◦ Shape: Polygonal or irregularly shaped; can be less well-defined than classic LP. ◦ Surface: Flat-topped ("lichenoid") with a fine scale. May appear more eczematous or psoriasiform than classic LP.
sections.diagnostics: • Thorough Medication History: This is the most crucial diagnostic step. ◦ Obtain a detailed list of all current and recently started medications, including prescription, over-the-counter (OTC), and herbal supplements. ◦ Note the start date for each. • Skin Biopsy (Punch Biopsy): ◦ Confirms the "lichenoid" pattern of inflammation. ◦ Histology Findings: ▪ Lichenoid Interface Dermatitis: A dense, band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermal-epidermal (D-E) junction that obscures the border. ▪ Vacuolar degeneration of the basal keratinocyte layer. ▪ Apoptotic keratinocytes (Civatte or colloid bodies) in the lower epidermis or upper dermis. ▪ Key Histologic Clue: The presence of eosinophils in the infiltrate is more suggestive of a drug-induced etiology than idiopathic LP. Parakeratosis may also be present. • Labs: ◦ Generally not required for diagnosis but may be used to rule out other conditions (e.g., ANA for lupus, LFTs for hepatitis). ◦ A CBC may show peripheral eosinophilia.
sections.prognosis: • Excellent once the causative drug is identified and discontinued. • Resolution is slow but steady over a period of weeks to months (sometimes up to a year). • Relapse will occur if the patient is re-challenged with the same medication.

sections.overview:
• Erythroderma, also known as exfoliative dermatitis, is a severe, generalized inflammation of the skin characterized by **diffuse erythema and scaling involving greater than 90% of the body surface area (BSA)**.
    ◦ It is not a specific disease but rather a cutaneous reaction pattern to a variety of underlying conditions.
    ◦ Erythroderma is considered a **dermatologic emergency** due to its potential for profound metabolic and systemic decompensation.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** A rare condition.
• **Age:** Predominantly affects adults, with a mean age of onset > 50 years.
• **Sex:** More common in males (**M:F ratio of 2:1 to 4:1**).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with a rapidly progressing, generalized, **fiery-red rash** associated with systemic illness.
• The history is critical and should focus on:
    ◦ Timeline of rash onset and progression.
    ◦ Personal or family history of skin disease (e.g., **psoriasis**, **eczema**).
    ◦ Recent medication changes (new prescriptions, dose changes).
    ◦ Constitutional **"B" symptoms** (e.g., **fever**, **night sweats**, **weight loss**) to screen for malignancy.
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly dependent on the underlying etiology.
    ◦ **Good:** **Drug-induced erythroderma** typically resolves with withdrawal of the offending agent.
    ◦ **Variable/Chronic:** Caused by **psoriasis** or **atopic dermatitis**, often follows a relapsing-remitting course.
    ◦ **Poor:** Associated with malignancy (e.g., **CTCL**) or in elderly, debilitated patients where complications are more likely.

sections.overview:
• **Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS)** is a severe, life-threatening, **immune-mediated mucocutaneous reaction** characterized by extensive **necrosis and detachment of the epidermis**
    ◦ It is considered a **dermatologic emergency**
    ◦ SJS is part of a spectrum of disease with **Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN)**, differentiated by the percentage of **body surface area (BSA)** with skin detachment
        ▪ **SJS:** <10% BSA detachment
        ▪ **SJS/TEN Overlap:** 10-30% BSA detachment
        ▪ **TEN:** >30% BSA detachment
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Drugs (>80% of cases):** The most common cause. Onset is typically 1-3 weeks after drug initiation.
        ▪ **"S-A-T-A-N" mnemonic:**
            ◦ **S**ulfa drugs (e.g., Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole)
            ◦ **A**llopurinol
            ◦ **T**etracyclines (less common)
            ◦ **A**nticonvulsants (Lamotrigine, Carbamazepine, Phenytoin, Phenobarbital)
            ◦ **N**SAIDs (oxicam type, e.g., piroxicam)
    ◦ **Infections:** The most common non-drug cause, especially in children.
        ▪ ***Mycoplasma pneumoniae*** (most common infectious cause)
        ▪ Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV)
        ▪ **HIV** (patients with HIV have a significantly higher risk)
    ◦ **Idiopathic:** No clear cause identified in a subset of cases.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ Considered a **Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity reaction**.
    ◦ The offending drug or metabolite acts as a hapten, binding to host cells and triggering a cytotoxic T-cell (CD8+) response.
    ◦ Activated T-cells release **granulysin**, a cytolytic protein that induces widespread **keratinocyte apoptosis** (programmed cell death).
    ◦ This massive apoptosis leads to the separation of the epidermis from the dermis.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence:** Rare, affecting approximately 1-2 people per million per year.
• **Mortality:**
    ◦ **SJS** has a mortality rate of ~10%.
    ◦ The rate increases significantly with progression to **TEN** (>30%).
• **Demographics:**
    ◦ Can occur at any age, in any race, and in both sexes.
    ◦ Incidence is higher in patients with **HIV** and **active cancer**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Prodrome:** Begins 1-3 days before the rash with non-specific, flu-like symptoms:
    ◦ Fever (>39C / 102.2F)
    ◦ Malaise, myalgias, arthralgias
    ◦ Headache
    ◦ Pharyngitis
• **Cutaneous Eruption:**
    ◦ Starts with ill-defined, erythematous macules, often with purpuric centers.
    ◦ Lesions typically begin on the face and trunk and spread symmetrically.
    ◦ Progresses to **atypical target lesions** (2 zones of color, dusky center, indistinct border).
    ◦ Lesions coalesce, forming **flaccid bullae** that slough off with minimal pressure, leaving behind raw, denuded dermis.
• **Mucosal Involvement:** A hallmark of SJS.
    ◦ Occurs in >90% of cases and **at least two mucosal surfaces** are typically involved.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primarily a clinical diagnosis** based on history (drug exposure) and physical exam findings (**characteristic rash**, **positive Nikolsky sign**, **mucosal involvement**).
• **Skin Biopsy (Gold Standard for confirmation):**
    ◦ Shows **full-thickness epidermal necrosis** and a subepidermal split.
    ◦ Dermal inflammatory infiltrate is characteristically sparse.
    ◦ Immunofluorescence is negative, helping to rule out autoimmune blistering diseases.
• **Laboratory Studies (for management and prognosis, not diagnosis):**
    ◦ **CBC:** Anemia, lymphopenia. **Neutropenia** is a poor prognostic sign.
    ◦ **CMP:** Assess for electrolyte abnormalities, renal dysfunction (prerenal azotemia), and low albumin.
    ◦ **Blood cultures:** To rule out sepsis.
    ◦ **CRP/ESR:** Markedly elevated.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is determined using the **SCORTEN** scale on day 1 and 3 of admission. It predicts mortality based on 7 independent risk factors.
• **SCORTEN Variables (1 point each):**
    ◦ **A**ge > 40 years
    ◦ **M**alignancy present
    ◦ **H**eart rate > 120 bpm
    ◦ **I**nitial **BSA** detachment > 10%
    ◦ **B**UN > 28 mg/dL
    ◦ **B**icarbonate < 20 mEq/L
    ◦ **G**lucose > 252 mg/dL
• Mortality increases exponentially with a higher **SCORTEN** score.

sections.overview:
• **Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN)** is a rare, life-threatening, and severe mucocutaneous adverse drug reaction characterized by extensive necrosis and detachment of the epidermis.
• It represents the most severe end of a spectrum of diseases that includes **Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS)**.
    ◦ The distinction is based on the percentage of **Body Surface Area (BSA)** with epidermal detachment:
        ▪ **Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS)**: <10% BSA detachment
        ▪ **SJS/TEN Overlap**: 10-30% BSA detachment
        ▪ **Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN)**: >30% BSA detachment
• TEN is considered a **medical emergency** requiring immediate hospitalization, typically in a burn unit or intensive care unit (ICU).
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Drugs (>80% of cases)**: The most common cause. Onset is typically 1-3 weeks after starting a new medication.
        ▪ **High-Risk Medications (S.A.T.A.N.)**:
            ▪ **S**ulfa antibiotics (e.g., Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole)
            ▪ **A**llopurinol
            ▪ **T**etracyclines (e.g., Minocycline)
            ▪ **A**nticonvulsants (e.g., Lamotrigine, Carbamazepine, Phenytoin, Phenobarbital)
            ▪ **N**SAIDs (oxicam type, e.g., Piroxicam)
            ▪ Nevirapine (NNRTI)
    ◦ **Infections (less common)**:
        ▪ *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*
        ▪ Cytomegalovirus (CMV)
        ▪ HIV
    ◦ **Malignancy**:
        ▪ Lymphoma, leukemia
    ◦ **Idiopathic**: No clear cause identified in a minority of cases.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ Considered a **Type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity reaction**.
    ◦ The offending drug acts as a hapten, which is processed and presented by antigen-presenting cells via the Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC).
    ◦ This triggers a massive, cell-mediated cytotoxic reaction against keratinocytes.
    ◦ **Key Mediator: Granulysin**. This cytotoxic protein is secreted by **Cytotoxic T-Lymphocytes (CTLs)** and **Natural Killer (NK) cells**, inducing widespread **keratinocyte apoptosis** (programmed cell death).
    ◦ This apoptosis leads to separation of the epidermis from the dermis at the dermo-epidermal junction, resulting in bullae formation and full-thickness epidermal sloughing.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Rare, affecting approximately 1-2 persons per million per year.
• **Mortality**: High, ranging from 25-35%.
• **Demographics**: Can affect any age but is more common in adults. Slightly higher incidence in females.
• **Increased Risk**: Patients with **HIV** have a ~1000-fold increased risk, particularly with sulfa drugs.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Prodrome (1-3 days prior to rash)**
    ◦ Flu-like symptoms: **fever (>39C or 102.2F)**, malaise, myalgias, arthralgias.
    ◦ Sore throat, cough, headache.
    ◦ Ocular symptoms: burning, itching, photophobia.
• **Cutaneous Eruption**
    ◦ Initial rash is often ill-defined, erythematous macules with purpuric centers (**"atypical targets"**).
    ◦ Begins on the face and trunk, spreading symmetrically and rapidly.
    ◦ Lesions are associated with significant pain and a burning sensation.
    ◦ Over 1-4 days, the macules coalesce, and the epidermis begins to wrinkle and detach, forming large, flaccid bullae that slough off in sheets.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primarily a clinical diagnosis** based on history (new medication), characteristic rash progression, **positive Nikolsky sign**, and extensive mucosal involvement.
• **Skin Biopsy (Gold Standard for Confirmation)**
    ◦ A frozen section can provide rapid results.
    ◦ **Histopathology**: Shows **full-thickness epidermal necrosis** with subepidermal cleavage (separation at the dermo-epidermal junction). The dermal infiltrate is characteristically sparse (**"pauci-inflammatory"**).
• **Laboratory Studies (for management and prognosis, not diagnosis)**
    ◦ **CBC**: Anemia, **lymphopenia** (poor prognostic sign).
    ◦ **CMP**: Electrolyte abnormalities (from fluid loss), hypoalbuminemia, elevated LFTs.
    ◦ **BUN/Creatinine**: To assess for acute kidney injury.
    ◦ **Blood cultures**: To rule out sepsis.
    ◦ **Serum Bicarbonate & Glucose**: Part of the **SCORTEN score**.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is poor, with mortality rates of 25-35%.
• The **SCORTEN score** is a validated tool used on day 1 and day 3 to predict mortality. One point is given for each of the 7 criteria:
    ◦ **A**ge > 40 years
    ◦ **M**alignancy (presence of)
    ◦ **H**eart Rate > 120 bpm
    ◦ **E**pidermal detachment on admission > 10% BSA
    ◦ **R**enal: BUN > 28 mg/dL (or Urea > 10 mmol/L)
    ◦ **S**erum Glucose > 252 mg/dL (> 14 mmol/L)
    ◦ **B**icarbonate < 20 mEq/L
• **SCORTEN Score & Mortality**: 0-1 (~3%), 2 (~12%), 3 (~35%), 4 (~58%), 5 (>90%).

sections.overview:
• Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms (DRESS), also known as Drug-Induced Hypersensitivity Syndrome (DIHS), is a severe, idiosyncratic, delayed-type (Type IVb) hypersensitivity reaction.
• It is characterized by a classic triad of **widespread rash**, **eosinophilia** (or atypical lymphocytosis), and **internal organ involvement**.
• The defining feature is a long latency period of **2-8 weeks** between drug initiation and symptom onset.
• It carries a significant mortality rate (~10%), primarily due to fulminant hepatitis.
sections.etiology:
• **Cause**: An adverse reaction to a specific medication.
• **Pathophysiology**: A complex, T-cell mediated **Type IVb delayed hypersensitivity reaction**.
    ◦ **Drug-Specific T-Cell Activation**: The offending drug or its metabolite binds to HLA molecules on antigen-presenting cells, leading to the activation and clonal expansion of drug-specific CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells.
    ◦ **Cytokine Storm**: These activated T-cells release a flood of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IL-5 (which is critical for eosinophil proliferation and activation), IFN-γ, and TNF-α.
    ◦ **Viral Reactivation**: A key feature distinguishing DRESS from other drug reactions is the reactivation of latent human herpesviruses, most notably **Human Herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6)**, but also EBV, CMV, and HHV-7. Viral reactivation is thought to amplify the immune response and contribute to the severity and duration of the syndrome.
• **Common Offending Drugs**:
    ◦ **Aromatic Anticonvulsants**: **Carbamazepine**, **Phenytoin**, Phenobarbital, Lamotrigine.
    ◦ **Allopurinol**: A very common cause, especially in the elderly.
    ◦ **Sulfonamides**: Sulfasalazine, **Dapsone**, Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
    ◦ **Antibiotics**: Minocycline, Vancomycin.
    ◦ **Antiretrovirals**: Abacavir, Nevirapine.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Rare, estimated at 1 in 1,000 to 1 in 10,000 drug exposures.
• **Demographics**: Affects all ages, races, and sexes, but certain genetic predispositions increase risk in specific populations.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Genetic Predisposition (High-Yield)**: Strong associations exist between specific HLA alleles and drug-induced DRESS.
• **HLA-B*5801**: Increased risk with **Allopurinol**, particularly in Han Chinese and Thai populations.
• **HLA-A*3101**: Increased risk with **Carbamazepine** in Northern European populations.
• **HLA-B*1502**: Strongly associated with Carbamazepine-induced SJS/TEN, but also a risk factor for DRESS in some Asian populations.
