• **Viral Co-infection**: Latent or active HHV-6, EBV, or CMV.
• **Drug-Related**: Rapid dose escalation (e.g., lamotrigine), high daily dosage.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is marked by a **long latency period of 2-8 weeks** following the initiation of the culprit drug.
• The illness typically begins with a non-specific prodrome before the characteristic rash appears.
• **Symptoms**:
    ◦ **Constitutional**: **High fever (>38.5C)**, malaise, fatigue, pharyngitis.
    ◦ **Dermatologic**: An intensely **pruritic (itchy) rash**.
    ◦ **Lymphatics**: Tender, swollen lymph nodes (lymphadenopathy).
    ◦ **Systemic**: Symptoms depend on the organ involved:
        ▪ **Hepatic**: Right upper quadrant pain, jaundice.
        ▪ **Pulmonary**: Cough, dyspnea.
        ▪ **Renal**: Decreased urine output, edema.
        ▪ **Cardiac**: Chest pain, shortness of breath.
sections.physicalExam:
• **General**: Febrile, ill-appearing patient.
• **Skin**:
    ◦ **Morbilliform (measles-like) eruption** is the most common initial presentation, often starting on the face/upper trunk and spreading to the extremities.
    ◦ **Prominent facial edema**, especially periorbital, is a characteristic and early sign.
    ◦ The rash progresses to become **confluent, infiltrated, and edematous**, potentially evolving into **exfoliative dermatitis** or **erythroderma** (>90% body surface area involvement).
    ◦ Pustules, vesicles, or targetoid lesions can be present.
    ◦ **Mucous membrane involvement** (e.g., cheilitis, conjunctivitis) is seen in ~50% of cases but is typically **mild** compared to Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS)/Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN).
• **Lymph**: Generalized, tender lymphadenopathy.
• **Systemic**:
    ◦ **Hepatomegaly** and/or splenomegaly.
    ◦ Rales or crackles on lung auscultation (pneumonitis).
    ◦ Tachycardia, muffled heart sounds (myocarditis).
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is clinical, supported by lab findings and ruling out other causes.
• The **RegiSCAR criteria** are often used for definitive diagnosis.
• **Laboratory Studies**:
    ◦ **CBC with Differential**:
        ▪ **Eosinophilia**: Hallmark finding. Count often **>1,500 cells/L**. May be delayed.
        ▪ **Atypical Lymphocytosis**: Also a very common and characteristic finding.
        ▪ Anemia, thrombocytopenia may also be present.
    ◦ **Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP)**:
        ▪ **Elevated Liver Transaminases (ALT/AST)**: The most common sign of organ involvement. Can range from mild elevation to fulminant hepatic necrosis.
        ▪ **Elevated BUN and Creatinine**: Indicates acute interstitial nephritis (AIN).
    ◦ **Inflammatory Markers**: Elevated CRP and ESR.
    ◦ **Viral Serology/PCR**: Can test for **HHV-6 reactivation** to support the diagnosis.
• **Skin Biopsy**: Not always necessary but can be useful to exclude other conditions. Findings include a dense, perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate, often with eosinophils.
• **Imaging**:
    ◦ **Chest X-ray or CT**: To evaluate for interstitial pneumonitis.
sections.treatment:
• **First-Line**: **Systemic Corticosteroids**.
    ◦ Dose: **Prednisone 1 mg/kg/day** (or equivalent).
    ◦ **Crucial Point**: Requires a **very slow taper over 8-12 weeks** or longer. Rapid tapering can cause a severe relapse of the disease.
• **Topical Therapy**: High-potency topical corticosteroids for skin symptoms.
• **Second-Line (for severe/steroid-refractory cases)**:
    ◦ Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG)
    ◦ Cyclosporine
    ◦ Mycophenolate Mofetil
sections.management:
• **Inpatient Monitoring**: Daily monitoring of CBC (for eosinophils), CMP (for liver/renal function), and clinical status is essential.
• **Outpatient Follow-up**: Continue to monitor labs weekly to monthly during the steroid taper.
sections.complications:
• **Acute**:
    ◦ **Fulminant Hepatic Failure** (most common cause of death).
    ◦ Acute Interstitial Nephritis leading to renal failure.
    ◦ Myocarditis, pericarditis.
    ◦ Pneumonitis, ARDS.
    ◦ Encephalitis, thyroiditis, colitis.
• **Long-Term**:
    ◦ Increased risk of developing **autoimmune diseases**, such as Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), Type 1 Diabetes, and Autoimmune Thyroiditis (Grave's or Hashimoto's).
sections.prognosis:
• **Mortality**: Approximately **10%**.
• **Cause of Death**: Most commonly due to **fulminant hepatitis**, followed by myocarditis.
• **Recovery**: The course is often prolonged, lasting weeks to months. Relapses are common if steroids are tapered too quickly.
sections.preventionEducation:
• Counsel the patient to **strictly avoid the culprit drug for life**.
• Inform them of potential cross-reactivity with structurally similar medications (e.g., other aromatic anticonvulsants).
• Provide a medical alert bracelet or wallet card.

sections.overview:
• **Impetigo** is a highly contagious, superficial bacterial skin infection affecting the epidermis.
	◦ It is one of the most common skin infections in children.
• It primarily manifests in two forms: **non-bullous** (crusted) and **bullous** (blistering).
	◦ A deeper, ulcerative form is known as **ecthyma**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
	◦ **_Staphylococcus aureus_**
		▪ The most common cause of both **non-bullous** and **bullous** impetigo.
		▪ Methicillin-resistant _S. aureus_ (**MRSA**) can also be a cause.
	◦ **_Streptococcus pyogenes_** (Group A β-hemolytic Strep, GABHS)
		▪ A common cause of **non-bullous** impetigo, often co-infecting with _S. aureus_.
• **Pathophysiology**
	◦ The infection begins with a break in the skin barrier (e.g., insect bite, cut, eczema), allowing bacteria to colonize the superficial epidermis.
	◦ **Non-Bullous Impetigo**
		▪ Bacteria produce proteases that break down host tissue.
		▪ The host immune response leads to the formation of vesicles or pustules.
		▪ These rupture, and the serous fluid dries, mixing with bacterial debris to form the characteristic crust.
	◦ **Bullous Impetigo**
		▪ Caused exclusively by strains of _S. aureus_ that produce exfoliative toxins (ETA, ETB).
		▪ These toxins target and cleave **desmoglein-1**, a protein that holds epidermal cells together in the stratum granulosum.
		▪ This targeted cleavage (**acantholysis**) causes intraepidermal separation, leading to the formation of flaccid bullae filled with clear or yellow fluid.
		▪ This is a localized form of **Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS)**.
sections.epidemiology:
• Most common bacterial skin infection in children, with a peak incidence in ages 2-5.
• More prevalent in warm, humid climates and during summer months.
• Spreads easily in crowded environments like daycares and schools through direct contact.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Patient Profile**
	◦ Typically occurs in young children.
• **History of Lesions**
	◦ Initial lesions are small red spots (macules/papules), often around the nose or mouth.
	◦ These quickly evolve into small blisters (vesicles/pustules) that rupture.
	◦ The exudate dries to form a distinctive **yellowish-brown, 'honey-colored' crust**.
• **Associated Symptoms**
	◦ Lesions are typically **non-painful**.
	◦ **Pruritus (itching)** is common.
	◦ Scratching can spread the infection to other areas (autoinoculation), causing new spots to appear nearby.
• **Systemic Symptoms**
	◦ Systemic symptoms like **fever** are generally absent.
sections.diagnostics:
• Primarily a **clinical diagnosis** based on the characteristic appearance of the lesions.
• **Gram Stain and Bacterial Culture**
	◦ Recommended in cases of treatment failure, atypical presentation, or suspicion of **MRSA**.
	◦ Sample is obtained from the moisture beneath a crust or fluid from an intact pustule/bulla.
	◦ Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in **clusters** (_S. aureus_) or **chains** (_S. pyogenes_).
	◦ Culture confirms the organism and provides antibiotic sensitivities.
• **Biopsy**
	◦ Rarely necessary.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** prognosis.
	◦ With appropriate treatment, lesions typically resolve within 7-10 days.
• Post-inflammatory pigmentary changes may occur but usually fade over time.
• Recurrence is possible, especially if underlying risk factors (e.g., nasal carriage of _S. aureus_, atopic dermatitis) are not addressed.

sections.overview:
• Erysipelas is a specific type of **superficial cellulitis**, an acute infection of the upper dermis and superficial lymphatics
• It is clinically characterized by a **raised, intensely erythematous plaque** with a **sharply demarcated border** that distinguishes it from surrounding normal skin
sections.etiology:
• **Primary Pathogen**
	◦ **_Streptococcus pyogenes_ (Group A β-hemolytic Streptococcus)** is the causative agent in the vast majority of cases
	◦ Less commonly, Groups C or G streptococci
	◦ **_Staphylococcus aureus_ is RARELY** a cause of classic erysipelas
• **Pathophysiology**
	◦ **Portal of Entry**: Bacteria enter the skin through a breach in the epidermal barrier
		▪ Common entry points include minor trauma, insect bites, surgical incisions, **tinea pedis** (especially interdigital maceration), or chronic skin conditions like stasis ulcers or eczema
	◦ **Invasion & Spread**: The bacteria invade the upper dermis and proliferate
	◦ **Inflammatory Response**: The infection spreads rapidly through the superficial lymphatic vessels
		▪ This lymphatic involvement is responsible for the classic **raised, well-demarcated appearance** and intense inflammation (erythema, edema, warmth)
sections.epidemiology:
• **Age**: Primarily affects young children and older adults (>60 years)
• **Location**
	◦ **Adults**: Most commonly affects the **lower extremities** (~85% of cases)
	◦ **Children**: The **face** (**malar or "butterfly" distribution**) is a more common location
• No significant gender or racial predilection
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Onset**: Typically abrupt and acute
• **Prodrome**: Often preceded by systemic symptoms for 4-48 hours before the rash appears
	◦ **Fever, chills, malaise, headache**
• **Skin Lesion**: A small erythematous patch rapidly progresses to a **fiery-red, indurated, tense, and shiny plaque**
	◦ The area is **exquisitely tender** and warm to the touch
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primarily a clinical diagnosis** based on the characteristic physical exam findings
• **Laboratory Studies** (often not required for mild cases)
	◦ **CBC**: **Leukocytosis** with a neutrophilic predominance ("**left shift**") is common
	◦ **Inflammatory Markers**: Elevated **C-reactive protein (CRP)** and **Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR)**
	◦ **Blood Cultures**: Low yield (<5% positive) but should be obtained in systemically ill or immunocompromised patients to rule out bacteremia
• **Imaging**
	◦ Generally not indicated
	◦ **Ultrasound or MRI** may be used if there is suspicion of a deeper infection, such as an abscess or necrotizing fasciitis
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent with prompt and appropriate antibiotic therapy
• Fever typically resolves within 24-72 hours of starting antibiotics; skin changes resolve more slowly over 1-2 weeks
• **Recurrence is common** (~30% of patients), especially if underlying risk factors are not managed

sections.overview:
• Acute bacterial infection of the skin involving the **deeper dermis** and **subcutaneous tissue**.
• Manifests as a spreading area of **erythema**, **warmth**, **swelling**, and **tenderness**.
• Characterized by **ill-defined, non-palpable borders**, distinguishing it from **erysipelas** (superficial, sharply demarcated).
• Typically occurs after a breach in the **skin barrier**, allowing bacteria to invade.
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Breach in Skin Barrier**: The process begins with a break in the skin (e.g., trauma, fissure, ulcer, insect bite, **tinea pedis**).
    ◦ **Bacterial Inoculation**: Pathogenic bacteria gain entry into the dermis and subcutaneous tissues.
    ◦ **Inflammatory Response**: Bacteria proliferate and release toxins, triggering an acute inflammatory response.
        ▪ This leads to the classic signs: **vasodilation** (**erythema**, **warmth**), increased **vascular permeability** (**edema**), and cytokine/bradykinin release (**pain**).
    ◦ **Spread**: The infection spreads laterally through the subcutaneous planes and can involve lymphatic channels, causing **lymphangitis**.
• **Common Pathogens**
    ◦ **Most Common Overall**
        ▪ ***Streptococcus pyogenes*** (**Group A Strep**): Classically causes diffuse, rapidly spreading cellulitis without a focal point of purulence.
        ▪ ***Staphylococcus aureus*** (including **MRSA**): Often associated with a **purulent focus**, such as a furuncle, carbuncle, or abscess.
    ◦ **Specific Clinical Scenarios**
        ▪ **Animal Bites** (Cat/Dog): ***Pasteurella multocida***, *Capnocytophaga canimorsus*.
        ▪ **Human Bites**: ***Eikenella corrodens***, anaerobes.
        ▪ **Saltwater Exposure**: ***Vibrio vulnificus*** (high mortality, especially in patients with liver disease).
        ▪ **Freshwater Exposure**: ***Aeromonas hydrophila***.
        ▪ **Puncture Wound** (through shoe): ***Pseudomonas aeruginosa***.
        ▪ **Immunocompromised Host**: Broader spectrum including Gram-negative rods, fungi.
sections.epidemiology:
• One of the most common infectious disease-related reasons for **hospitalization** in the U.S.
• Incidence **increases with age**, most common in middle-aged and older adults.
• The **lower extremities** are the most frequently affected site (>80% of cases).
• No significant difference in incidence between sexes.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patient typically presents with the acute onset of a localized area of skin that is **red**, **swollen**, **warm**, and **painful**.
• Symptoms often develop over 1-2 days and progressively worsen.
• The patient may also experience systemic symptoms such as **fever**, **chills**, and **malaise**, especially with rapidly spreading or severe infection.
• A history of a preceding minor skin injury may or may not be present.
sections.diagnostics:
• Cellulitis is **primarily a clinical diagnosis**.
• Ancillary testing is reserved for patients with **systemic toxicity**, **extensive disease**, underlying comorbidities, or **failure of initial therapy**.
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **CBC with differential**: May show **leukocytosis** with a neutrophilic predominance ("**left shift**").
    ◦ **Inflammatory Markers**: Elevated **C-reactive protein (CRP)** and **Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR)** are common but non-specific.
        ▪ Can be useful to track response to therapy.
    ◦ **Blood Cultures**: Low yield (~5%) in uncomplicated cellulitis.
        ▪ Indicated for patients with **SIRS/sepsis criteria**, extensive disease, or severe immunosuppression.
    ◦ **Creatine Kinase (CK)**: Order if concern for **necrotizing fasciitis** (will be markedly elevated).
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Ultrasound**: Highly useful at the bedside to differentiate uncomplicated cellulitis from a **drainable abscess** (appears as a hypoechoic or anechoic fluid collection) or to rule out DVT.
    ◦ **X-ray**: Can show soft tissue swelling.
        ▪ Primarily used to rule out osteomyelitis or **subcutaneous gas** (a sign of **necrotizing fasciitis**).
    ◦ **CT / MRI**: Not routinely needed.
        ▪ Reserved for cases where **necrotizing fasciitis** or **deep space infection** is suspected and clinical diagnosis is uncertain.
        ▪ **MRI** is the most sensitive imaging modality for these conditions.
• **Microbiology**
    ◦ **Wound/Pus Culture**: Indicated for **purulent cellulitis** (after I&D), open wounds, or animal bites.
    ◦ **Needle Aspiration/Biopsy**: Low yield in non-purulent cellulitis.
        ▪ Considered for immunocompromised patients or in cases of treatment failure.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is **excellent** for uncomplicated cellulitis treated promptly with appropriate antibiotics.
• **Recurrence is common** (~30%), especially if underlying risk factors (lymphedema, venous insufficiency) are not managed.
• Mortality is low but increases significantly with complications like **sepsis** or **necrotizing fasciitis**, or in patients with severe comorbidities.

sections.overview:
• Folliculitis is the **inflammation** of one or more hair follicles, which can be superficial or deep and occur anywhere with hair
	◦ Characterized by **erythematous papules or pustules** centered around a hair follicle
	◦ Can be **infectious** (bacterial, fungal, viral) or **non-infectious** (mechanical, inflammatory)
sections.etiology:
• Pathophysiology involves **follicular damage or occlusion**, allowing microorganisms to invade the follicular unit and cause inflammation
• **Infectious Causes**
	◦ **Bacterial (Most Common)**
		▪ ***Staphylococcus aureus***: Most frequent cause; common skin flora that becomes pathogenic when follicular epithelium is compromised (includes **MSSA** and **MRSA**)
		▪ ***Pseudomonas aeruginosa***: Associated with **"Hot Tub Folliculitis"** from contaminated water in hot tubs, pools, or spas
		▪ **Gram-negative folliculitis**: Can occur in patients on long-term antibiotics for acne (e.g., *Klebsiella*, *Enterobacter*, *Proteus*)
	◦ **Fungal**
		▪ ***Malassezia spp.*** (formerly *Pityrosporum*): Causes **Pityrosporum folliculitis**, presenting as monomorphic, pruritic papules and pustules on the upper trunk and shoulders
		▪ **Dermatophytes** (*Trichophyton spp.*): Causes **Tinea barbae** (beard) or tinea capitis
		▪ ***Candida albicans***: Occurs in occluded, moist areas, especially in immunocompromised or diabetic patients
	◦ **Viral**
		▪ **Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV)**: Causes **herpetic folliculitis**, presenting as grouped vesicles or pustules
		▪ **Molluscum contagiosum**: Can induce a perifollicular inflammatory reaction
• **Non-Infectious/Inflammatory Causes**
	◦ **Mechanical Folliculitis**: Due to friction from tight clothing or trauma from shaving (**Pseudofolliculitis barbae** - ingrown hairs)
	◦ **Eosinophilic Folliculitis**: Intensely pruritic papules and pustules, strongly associated with advanced **HIV/AIDS** (CD4 <250-300 cells/L)
	◦ **Drug-induced Folliculitis**: Caused by medications like corticosteroids, lithium, phenytoin, and EGFR inhibitors
sections.epidemiology:
• Very common condition affecting all ages, sexes, and races
• ***P. aeruginosa*** folliculitis often occurs in outbreaks related to contaminated recreational water
• ***Malassezia*** folliculitis is more common in young adults in warm, humid climates
• **Pseudofolliculitis barbae** is most prevalent in individuals with tightly curled hair who shave closely
sections.clinicalPresentation: • Patients present with an acute eruption of small, **tender, or pruritic papules and/or pustules** in hair-bearing areas
sections.diagnostics:
• Primarily a **clinical diagnosis** based on history and physical exam
• **Gram Stain and Bacterial Culture**
	◦ Indicated for recurrent, treatment-refractory, or severe cases
	◦ Sample obtained by unroofing a pustule and swabbing purulent material
	◦ Identifies the organism (e.g., ***S. aureus***) and determines antibiotic sensitivities (crucial for **MRSA**)
• **KOH Preparation**
	◦ Used if a fungal etiology is suspected
	◦ Examines skin scrapings or pustule contents under a microscope
		▪ ***Malassezia***: Shows **"spaghetti and meatballs"** pattern (budding yeasts and hyphae)
		▪ **Dermatophyte**: Shows **septate hyphae**
• **Skin Biopsy**
	◦ Rarely necessary; performed for persistent, atypical, or suspected non-infectious cases (e.g., **eosinophilic folliculitis**)
	◦ Histology shows a **perifollicular inflammatory infiltrate**
• **Viral Culture or Tzanck Smear**
	◦ Performed if **herpetic folliculitis** is suspected
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for most cases of superficial folliculitis, often resolving with conservative care
• Deep folliculitis (**furuncles/carbuncles**) has a good prognosis with appropriate therapy but may lead to **scarring**
• **Recurrence is common** if underlying risk factors are not addressed

sections.overview:
• A **furuncle** (or "boil") is a deep, painful infection of a single hair follicle and the surrounding tissue, which forms an abscess.
• A **carbuncle** is a more severe and extensive infection that involves a cluster of interconnected furuncles.
    ◦ Carbuncles are larger, deeper, and form a suppurative lesion that drains through multiple openings in the skin.
• **Furuncle**: Infection of **one** hair follicle and surrounding dermis.
• **Carbuncle**: Aggregate of **multiple** interconnected furuncles.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• Furuncles and carbuncles are extremely common skin and soft tissue infections (SSTIs).
• Occur more frequently in areas with hair follicles subjected to friction and perspiration, such as the neck, face, axillae, buttocks, and thighs.
• Increased incidence in settings of close personal contact (e.g., athletic teams, military barracks, prisons, households).
• The prevalence of CA-MRSA as a cause has significantly increased over the past two decades.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Colonization with *S. aureus*** (especially nasal carriage)
• Immunocompromised states (Diabetes Mellitus, HIV, malignancy, chemotherapy)
• Poor hygiene
• Obesity
• Living in crowded conditions or close contact with an infected individual
• Skin trauma (e.g., abrasions, shaving nicks)
• Occlusive clothing
• Hyperhidrosis (excessive sweating)
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with a "painful boil" or "spider bite" that started as a small red bump and has rapidly enlarged over several days.
    ◦ The lesion is extremely tender to palpation.
    ◦ For carbuncles or severe furuncles, the patient may also present with systemic symptoms like fever and malaise.
• **Localized**:
    ◦ Intense, localized pain and tenderness
    ◦ Erythema (redness) and swelling
    ◦ Sensation of pressure or fullness
    ◦ Spontaneous purulent drainage may occur
• **Systemic (more common with carbuncles)**:
    ◦ Fever
    ◦ Chills
    ◦ Malaise
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is primarily **clinical**, based on history and physical exam findings.
• **Wound Culture (Gram Stain and Sensitivity)**:
    ◦ **Indication**: Essential for guiding antibiotic therapy. Should be obtained from purulent drainage whenever incision and drainage is performed.
    ◦ **Purpose**: Identifies the causative organism and determines antibiotic susceptibility (e.g., distinguishes MRSA from MSSA).
• **Ultrasound**:
    ◦ Useful to confirm the presence and extent of a drainable fluid collection (abscess) when fluctuance is unclear on physical exam. It helps differentiate an abscess from simple cellulitis.
• **Blood Work (CBC, Blood Cultures)**:
    ◦ **Indication**: Reserved for patients with signs of systemic illness (fever, hypotension, tachycardia) to assess for leukocytosis and bacteremia.
sections.management:
• **Wound Care**: Instruct the patient on how to care for the wound post-I&D, including dressing changes and keeping the area clean and dry.
• **Follow-up**: Schedule a follow-up appointment in 24-48 hours for packing removal and wound check.
• **Patient Education**:
    ◦ Emphasize hand hygiene.
    ◦ Advise against sharing personal items (towels, razors).
    ◦ Counsel on signs of worsening infection (spreading redness, increased pain, fever).
• **Recurrent Furunculosis**:
    ◦ Screen for and manage underlying risk factors (e.g., check HbA1c for diabetes).
    ◦ Consider decolonization protocol for *S. aureus*:
        ▪ **Intranasal Mupirocin (Bactroban) ointment** twice daily for 5-7 days.
        ▪ Use of antiseptic cleansers like **chlorhexidine** wash.
sections.complications:
• Cellulitis or erysipelas (spreading infection)
• Bacteremia and sepsis
• Metastatic infection (e.g., endocarditis, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis)
• **Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis**: A life-threatening complication of furuncles located in the **"danger triangle" of the face** (from the corners of the mouth to the bridge of the nose). Venous drainage from this area leads directly to the cavernous sinus.
• Scarring
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for uncomplicated furuncles treated with timely I&D.
• Recurrence is common, especially in individuals with persistent risk factors or nasal colonization with *S. aureus*.
• Carbuncles and infections in immunocompromised hosts have a higher risk of complications but generally have a good prognosis with appropriate, aggressive treatment.

sections.overview:
• A **localized collection of pus** (purulent material) that accumulates in a tissue, organ, or confined space
	◦ Result of the body's **inflammatory response** to an infection, typically bacterial
	◦ The defining feature is a central core of **necrotic leukocytes** (neutrophils) and tissue debris, often encapsulated by a **fibrous wall (pyogenic membrane)** that isolates the infection from surrounding tissue
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• Abscesses are extremely common and occur in all age groups
• **Cutaneous abscesses** are one of the most frequent **skin and soft tissue infections (SSTIs)** seen in emergency departments
• The incidence of **CA-MRSA** as the primary cause of cutaneous abscesses has significantly increased over the past two decades
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation varies based on location (cutaneous vs. deep/internal)
	◦ **Cutaneous Abscess**
		▪ Patients typically present with a new or enlarging **painful, localized mass** on the skin
		▪ The area is **red, swollen, and warm**
		▪ May or may not be **spontaneously draining pus**
	◦ **Deep Abscess** (e.g., intra-abdominal, psoas, hepatic)
		▪ Presentation can be insidious
		▪ Patients often present with non-specific systemic symptoms like **fever, chills, malaise, and anorexia**, along with **localized pain** (e.g., abdominal pain, flank pain)
		▪ A palpable mass is rare
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for simple cutaneous abscesses treated promptly with I&D
• **Guarded** for deep, large, or multi-loculated abscesses, especially in immunocompromised or critically ill patients
	◦ Mortality is associated with the development of **sepsis**

sections.overview:
• Necrotizing fasciitis (NF) is a rare, life-threatening, and rapidly progressive infection of the deep soft tissues.
    ◦ Spreads quickly along the fascial planes, causing widespread necrosis of the subcutaneous tissue and fascia.
    ◦ The overlying skin may initially appear unaffected, masking the severity of the underlying destruction.
    ◦ NF is a **true surgical emergency** requiring immediate diagnosis and aggressive intervention to prevent limb loss, systemic toxicity, and death.
    ◦ Often referred to by the layman's term "flesh-eating bacteria."
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Rare, estimated at 0.4 to 1.0 cases per 100,000 people per year in the US.
• **Mortality**: High, ranging from 20% to 30% even with aggressive treatment.
• **Location**: Can occur anywhere on the body, but most common on the extremities, perineum (**Fournier's gangrene**), and trunk.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a patient with a rapidly progressing soft tissue infection whose systemic signs of toxicity and severe pain are **wildly out of proportion** to the initial cutaneous findings.
    ◦ What may look like simple cellulitis can be a devastating underlying infection.
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is primarily clinical, but labs and imaging can support suspicion.
    ◦ **Definitive diagnosis is made in the operating room.**
• **Surgical Exploration (Gold Standard)**
    ◦ Direct visualization of necrotic fascia.
    ◦ Fascia appears gray and dull, does not bleed when cut, and separates easily from underlying tissue ("**finger test**" - blunt dissection with a finger meets no resistance).
    ◦ Tissue is sent for Gram stain and culture.
• **Laboratory Findings**
    ◦ **LRINEC Score (Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis)**: A scoring system to stratify risk.
        ▪ A score of **6 is suspicious**, and **8 is highly predictive**.
        ▪ *This tool should never delay surgical consultation.*
        ▪ Components: CRP (>150), WBC (>15), Hemoglobin (<13.5), Sodium (<135), Creatinine (>1.6), Glucose (>180).
    ◦ **Leukocytosis** with a profound left shift.
    ◦ **Hyponatremia** (common and significant).
    ◦ Elevated **Creatine Kinase (CK)** indicating muscle involvement.
    ◦ Elevated **Lactate**, indicating tissue hypoperfusion.
    ◦ Signs of AKI (elevated BUN/Cr) and DIC (thrombocytopenia, elevated INR).
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Should NOT delay surgery.** Used for equivocal cases or to assess the extent of disease.
    ◦ **CT Scan**: Best initial imaging test.
        ▪ Findings include **subcutaneous gas**, fascial thickening (>3 mm), fluid collections, and fat stranding.
    ◦ **Plain X-ray**: May show subcutaneous gas but is very insensitive.
sections.prognosis:
• Mortality remains high (20-30%).
• Poor prognostic factors include:
    ◦ Delay in diagnosis and surgical debridement (>24 hours)
    ◦ Age > 60
    ◦ Presence of comorbidities (especially Diabetes and PVD)
    ◦ Truncal or perineal involvement
    ◦ Development of septic shock

sections.overview:
• **Tinea corporis**, commonly known as "**ringworm**," is a superficial **dermatophyte** infection of the glabrous skin (skin of the trunk, extremities, and face)
    ◦ Characterized by the classic presentation of an **annular** (ring-shaped), **erythematous**, **scaling plaque** with **central clearing**
    ◦ It is one of the most common fungal infections worldwide
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ Caused by dermatophytic fungi that metabolize keratin in the skin, hair, and nails
    ◦ **Most Common Organism**: **Trichophyton rubrum**
    ◦ Other common species include *Trichophyton mentagrophytes* and *Microsporum canis*
    ◦ **Transmission**
        ▪ **Anthropophilic**: Human-to-human (direct contact, fomites)
        ▪ **Zoophilic**: Animal-to-human (e.g., ***M. canis*** from cats/dogs)
        ▪ **Geophilic**: Soil-to-human (rare)
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The **dermatophyte** invades the stratum corneum of the epidermis
    ◦ Fungal enzymes (keratinases) digest keratin, allowing the organism to proliferate
    ◦ The host's cell-mediated immune response causes inflammation, leading to erythema and pruritus
    ◦ The infection spreads centrifugally (outward) from the point of inoculation, creating an **annular** lesion
    ◦ As the immune system clears the fungus from the center of the lesion, **central clearing** develops, while the advancing, inflamed border remains active
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Worldwide distribution. More common in warm, humid climates
• **Age**: Affects all ages, but is particularly common in children and young adults
• **Setting**: Outbreaks can occur in settings with close physical contact, such as schools, daycare centers, and among athletes (especially wrestlers, known as **tinea gladiatorum**)
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with a complaint of an "itchy, **ring-shaped rash**" that has been slowly enlarging over several days to weeks
• The history may include exposure to an infected person or animal, or participation in high-risk activities
• Lesions can be single or multiple and may appear on any part of the body, most commonly the trunk and limbs
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Often made based on the classic history and physical exam findings
• **KOH Preparation (Potassium Hydroxide Microscopy)**
    ◦ **Procedure**: Vigorously scrape scales from the active, advancing border of the lesion onto a glass slide. Add a drop of 10-20% KOH solution and a coverslip. Gently heat the slide to dissolve keratinocytes.
    ◦ **Finding**: Visualization of **segmented (septate) hyphae** confirms the diagnosis of a **dermatophyte** infection
    ◦ This is the most cost-effective and rapid confirmatory test
• **Fungal Culture (Sabouraud's Agar)**
    ◦ **Gold standard** for identifying the specific species
    ◦ Indicated for atypical presentations, treatment failure, or when KOH is negative but suspicion remains high
    ◦ Results take 2-4 weeks
• **Wood's Lamp Examination**
    ◦ Most **tinea corporis** caused by ***T. rubrum*** does **not** fluoresce
    ◦ Some ***Microsporum*** species (*M. canis*, *M. audouinii*) may show a blue-green fluorescence
    ◦ Primarily useful for tinea capitis
• **Skin Biopsy with PAS Stain**
    ◦ Rarely needed
    ◦ Reserved for cases where the diagnosis is uncertain and other diagnoses (e.g., granuloma annulare, psoriasis) are being considered
    ◦ Histology shows hyphae in the stratum corneum
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** with appropriate treatment
• Lesions typically resolve completely, although post-inflammatory pigment changes may take months to fade
• **Recurrence** is common if underlying risk factors are not addressed or if treatment is not completed

sections.overview:
• Tinea capitis is a dermatophyte fungal infection of the hair follicles and scalp skin.
• It is the most common dermatophytosis of childhood.
• The infection invades the hair shaft and follicle, leading to **scaling**, inflammation, and **alopecia** (hair loss).
• Prompt diagnosis and treatment with **systemic antifungals** are crucial to prevent permanent hair loss and transmission.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ Caused by dermatophyte fungi, primarily from the genera *Trichophyton* and *Microsporum*.
    ◦ **Most common cause in the U.S.**: ***Trichophyton tonsurans***.
    ◦ **Common cause from pets** (cats/dogs): ***Microsporum canis***.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Inoculation**: Fungal arthrospores from an infected person, animal, or fomite (e.g., comb, hat) contact the scalp.
    ◦ **Invasion**: Spores germinate and invade the stratum corneum and then penetrate the hair follicle.
    ◦ **Hair Shaft Invasion Patterns**:
        ▪ **Endothrix**: Fungal spores are found *inside* the hair shaft.
            ◦ Hairs become brittle and break at the scalp surface, creating a **"black dot" appearance**.
            ◦ Classic Organism: ***T. tonsurans***.
        ▪ **Ectothrix**: Fungal spores are found *outside* the hair shaft, forming a sheath.
            ◦ Hairs break a few millimeters above the scalp, leaving stubs.
            ◦ Classic Organism: ***M. canis***.
    ◦ **Host Response**: The host's immune system mounts a response to the fungus, leading to inflammation, scaling, and pruritus.
        ▪ An exaggerated T-cell mediated response can result in a **kerion**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Primary Population**: Prepubertal children, typically ages 3-7.
• **Gender**: Slightly more common in males.
• **Geography**: More prevalent in urban, overcrowded environments.
• **Race**: Higher incidence in African American children, potentially due to hair care practices and hair structure.
sections.riskFactors:
• Age (prepubertal)
• Crowded living conditions (daycare, schools)
• Lower socioeconomic status
• Contact with infected individuals or asymptomatic carriers
• Sharing fomites (combs, brushes, hats, pillows)
• Contact with infected pets (kittens and puppies are common vectors for *M. canis*)
• Participation in contact sports (e.g., wrestling)
• Immunocompromised state
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A parent typically brings in a child due to one or more patches of hair loss on the scalp that may be scaly or itchy.
• The presentation is highly variable and can be inflammatory or non-inflammatory.
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ **Pruritus**: Can range from absent to severe.
    ◦ **Scalp pain or tenderness**: Especially with inflammatory types like a kerion.
    ◦ **Hair loss**: The primary complaint.
    ◦ Visible scaling or flaking ("dandruff").
sections.physicalExam:
• **Lymphadenopathy**: **Posterior cervical, postauricular, or occipital lymphadenopathy is a very common and key finding.**
• **Alopecia**: One or more patches of hair loss with broken hairs.
• **Morphologic Patterns**:
    ◦ **"Black Dot" Tinea Capitis**:
        ▪ Most common pattern, caused by ***T. tonsurans*** (**endothrix**).
        ▪ Broken hair shafts at the level of the scalp create a "dotted" appearance.
        ▪ May have mild to moderate scaling and inflammation.
    ◦ **"Gray Patch" Tinea Capitis**:
        ▪ Well-demarcated, circular patch of alopecia with fine, gray-white scales.
        ▪ Hairs are broken 1-3 mm above the scalp.
        ▪ Often caused by ***Microsporum spp.*** (**ectothrix**).
    ◦ **Kerion**:
        ▪ **A severe, inflammatory reaction** to the fungus.
        ▪ Presents as a **boggy, indurated, purulent, and friable mass** with significant alopecia.
        ▪ This is a hypersensitivity reaction, NOT a bacterial abscess (though secondary infection can occur).
        ▪ High risk for permanent **scarring alopecia**.
    ◦ **Favus**:
        ▪ Chronic infection, rare in the U.S.
        ▪ Caused by *T. schoenleinii*.
        ▪ Characterized by **scutula**: yellow, cup-shaped crusts composed of hyphae and skin debris, often with a "mousy" odor.
        ▪ Leads to significant **scarring alopecia**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Often made based on classic presentation (**scaling alopecia** + **occipital lymphadenopathy** in a child). Confirmation is recommended.
• **Wood's Lamp Examination**:
    ◦ Shining a black light on the scalp.
    ◦ **Positive (bright blue-green fluorescence)**: Suggests *Microsporum* species (*M. canis*, *M. audouinii*).
    ◦ **Negative (no fluorescence)**: Characteristic of ***T. tonsurans***, the most common cause.
        ▪ **A negative exam does not rule out tinea capitis.**
• **KOH Prep (Potassium Hydroxide)**:
    ◦ **Best initial test.**
    ◦ Scalp scrapings and plucked hairs are placed on a slide with KOH.
    ◦ Microscopy reveals hyphae and spores.
    ◦ Can differentiate endothrix vs. ectothrix patterns.
• **Fungal Culture**:
    ◦ **Gold standard for diagnosis.**
    ◦ Identifies the exact species, which can be useful for epidemiology and treatment failures.
    ◦ Takes 2-4 weeks for results.
sections.treatment:
• **First-Line Agents**:
    ◦ **Griseofulvin**:
        ▪ Classic treatment of choice, especially for *Microsporum*.
        ▪ Dose: 20-25 mg/kg/day of microsize formulation for 6-8 weeks.
        ▪ **Administration**: Must be taken with a **fatty meal** (e.g., milk, ice cream) to enhance absorption.
        ▪ Monitoring: LFTs at baseline and periodically for long courses.
    ◦ **Terbinafine**:
        ▪ Highly effective for ***T. tonsurans*** and often preferred due to shorter course (4-6 weeks).
        ▪ Less effective for *Microsporum*.
        ▪ Dosing is weight-based.
• **Adjunctive Therapy**:
    ◦ **Antifungal Shampoo** (Ketoconazole 2% or Selenium Sulfide 2.5%):
        ▪ Use 2-3 times per week.
        ▪ **Does not cure the infection** but decreases spore shedding and reduces transmissibility.
        ▪ Should be used by the patient and household contacts.
• **Treatment of Kerion**:
    ◦ In addition to systemic antifungals, a short course of **oral corticosteroids** (e.g., Prednisone 1-2 mg/kg/day for 1-2 weeks) is recommended to reduce inflammation and decrease the risk of permanent **scarring alopecia**.
sections.management:
• **Patient Education**: Emphasize the importance of medication adherence for the full course and taking griseofulvin with a fatty meal.
• **Fomite Control**: Wash all combs, brushes, hats, pillowcases, and bedding in hot water to prevent reinfection and spread.
• **Screen Household Contacts**: Examine close family members for signs of infection or asymptomatic carriage. Treat carriers with antifungal shampoo.
• **Return to School**: Children may return to school once systemic therapy has been initiated.
• **Follow-up**: Re-evaluate in 4-8 weeks to assess for clinical improvement. Treatment should continue until clinical and mycological cure is achieved.
sections.complications:
• **Cicatricial (Scarring) Alopecia**: Permanent hair loss, the most significant complication. Highest risk with **kerion** and **favus**.
• **Id (Dermatophytid) Reaction**: An allergic, sterile vesicular rash that can appear on the face, trunk, or hands in response to the fungal antigens.
• **Secondary Bacterial Infection (Impetiginization)**: Superimposed bacterial infection, especially with kerion.
• **Psychosocial Distress**: Significant impact on self-esteem due to hair loss.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** with early diagnosis and appropriate, full-course systemic therapy.
• Hair regrowth typically begins within 4-6 weeks of starting treatment and can take 6-12 months to be complete.
• Prognosis is guarded if significant scarring has already occurred.

sections.overview:
• **Tinea cruris** (jock itch) is a superficial **dermatophyte** (fungal) infection of the inguinal folds, proximal inner thighs, and buttocks.
    ◦ A form of dermatophytosis that specifically affects the groin region.
    ◦ Characterized by a **pruritic**, **erythematous**, and **scaling rash**, typically with a **raised, advancing border** and **central clearing**.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Organisms**
    ◦ Primarily caused by **dermatophytes**, which are fungi that metabolize keratin in the skin, hair, and nails.
        ▪ ***Trichophyton rubrum***: Most common cause worldwide.
        ▪ ***Epidermophyton floccosum***: Second most common cause.
        ▪ *Trichophyton mentagrophytes*.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Inoculation**: Fungal spores (arthroconidia) from an external source (fomites, **autoinoculation from tinea pedis**) or endogenous flora adhere to the stratum corneum in the groin.
    ◦ **Germination & Growth**: In the presence of **warmth, moisture, and maceration**, the spores germinate into hyphae.
    ◦ **Invasion**: The dermatophytes are keratinophilic and invade the superficial, keratinized layers of the epidermis, producing enzymes called **keratinases** to digest keratin.
    ◦ **Inflammatory Response**: The host's cell-mediated immune system recognizes fungal antigens, leading to an inflammatory response that manifests as **erythema, scaling, and pruritus**.
        ▪ The most intense inflammation is seen at the **advancing edge** of the infection where the fungus is most active.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: A very common dermatologic condition.
• **Demographics**
    ◦ Significantly more common in **males** (male-to-female ratio ~3:1).
    ◦ Most frequently affects adolescents and young adult men.
• **Geography**
    ◦ More common in **hot, humid climates** and during summer months.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with a complaint of a persistent, **intensely itchy rash** in the groin that has been **slowly expanding** over several weeks.
    ◦ They may report that it worsens with sweating or physical activity.
    ◦ They often have a history of recent athletic activity or live in a warm environment.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**
    ◦ Diagnosis is most often made based on the characteristic history and physical exam findings.
• **KOH Preparation (Potassium Hydroxide)**
    ◦ **Indication**: To confirm the diagnosis, especially in atypical cases or if unresponsive to initial therapy.
    ◦ **Procedure**: Scrape scales from the most active area (the **advancing border**) onto a glass slide. Add a drop of 10-20% KOH solution, cover with a coverslip, and gently heat.
    ◦ **Positive Finding**: Visualization of **segmented, septate hyphae**.
• **Fungal Culture (Sabouraud's agar)**
    ◦ **Indication**: The gold standard, but not routinely performed due to the time required (2-4 weeks for results). Reserved for cases refractory to treatment or if the KOH prep is negative despite high clinical suspicion.
    ◦ **Benefit**: Identifies the specific causative species.
• **Wood's Lamp Examination**
    ◦ **Finding**: Tinea cruris-causing dermatophytes **do not fluoresce**.
    ◦ **Utility**: Useful for ruling out **Erythrasma**, which is caused by *Corynebacterium minutissimum* and fluoresces a characteristic **coral-red**.
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent with appropriate treatment and adherence to preventative management strategies.
• **Recurrence** is common if underlying risk factors (e.g., hyperhidrosis, obesity, untreated tinea pedis) are not addressed.

sections.overview:
• Tinea pedis, commonly known as "**athlete's foot**," is a superficial fungal infection of the skin on the feet, primarily affecting the soles, interdigital spaces, and sides of the feet.
• It is the **most common dermatophyte infection** worldwide.
• Caused by dermatophytic fungi that thrive in warm, moist environments and colonize the keratinized tissue of the stratum corneum.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology (Causative Organisms):**
    ◦ **_Trichophyton rubrum_**: The most common cause worldwide. Often leads to chronic, moccasin-type infections.
    ◦ **_Trichophyton interdigitale_** (formerly _T. mentagrophytes_): Often associated with inflammatory or vesiculobullous presentations.
    ◦ **_Epidermophyton floccosum_**: A less common cause.
• **Pathophysiology:**
    ◦ **Inoculation:** Dermatophytes from a contaminated surface (e.g., shower floor, shared towels) come into contact with the host's skin.
    ◦ **Adherence & Germination:** The fungi adhere to corneocytes in the stratum corneum. A warm, moist environment (from sweat and occlusive footwear) promotes germination.
    ◦ **Invasion:** The dermatophytes produce enzymes called **keratinases**, which digest keratin, allowing the fungi to invade and proliferate within the non-living, keratinized stratum corneum.
    ◦ **Host Response:** The host's cell-mediated immune system responds to the fungal antigens, leading to inflammation, erythema, pruritus, and scaling. The infection rarely invades deeper tissues in immunocompetent individuals.
sections.epidemiology:
• The most prevalent dermatophytosis globally.
• **Prevalence:** Affects up to 15% of the general population.
• **Sex:** More common in males than females.
• **Age:** More common in adolescents and young adults, with prevalence increasing with age.
• **Environment:** More common in warm, humid climates and among individuals who frequent communal facilities (gyms, pools, military barracks).
sections.riskFactors:
• Use of **occlusive footwear** (e.g., boots, athletic shoes).
• **Hyperhidrosis** (excessive sweating).
• Use of communal showers, locker rooms, or swimming pools.
• **Immunocompromised states** (e.g., diabetes mellitus, HIV, immunosuppressive therapy).
• Peripheral vascular disease (PVD).
• Pre-existing **onychomycosis** (serves as a fungal reservoir).
• Participation in sports.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Symptoms:**
    ◦ **Pruritus (itching):** The most common and hallmark symptom.
    ◦ Burning or stinging sensation.
    ◦ Malodor.
    ◦ Pain, especially if fissures are present or with the vesiculobullous type.
    ◦ Patients with the moccasin type may be relatively asymptomatic, complaining only of "dryness" or "scaling."
• **Clinical Patterns:**
    ◦ **Interdigital Type:**
        ▪ The **most common** presentation.
        ▪ Primarily affects the webspace between the **4th and 5th toes**.
        ▪ Presents as scaling, erythema, **maceration** (soggy, white skin), and fissures.
    ◦ **Moccasin Type (Chronic Hyperkeratotic):**
        ▪ Characterized by fine, silvery-white scale with underlying pink, tender skin.
        ▪ Affects the soles, heels, and lateral borders of the feet in a **"moccasin" distribution**.
        ▪ Often bilateral and may be asymptomatic or mistaken for dry skin.
        ▪ Strongly associated with **_T. rubrum_**.
    ◦ **Vesiculobullous Type (Inflammatory):**
        ▪ Presents as pruritic, sometimes painful, **vesicles or bullae** on an erythematous base.
        ▪ Typically located on the medial foot, especially the instep and sole.
        ▪ Represents an acute inflammatory response to the fungus.
    ◦ **Ulcerative Type:**
        ▪ A severe variant, often seen in **immunocompromised or diabetic patients**.
        ▪ Characterized by rapidly spreading vesiculopustules and ulcers, often with secondary bacterial infection.
        ▪ Associated with significant pain, purulence, and cellulitis risk.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Interdigital:** **Maceration**, scaling, and erythema in the toe webspaces. Fissures may be present at the base of the toes.
• **Moccasin:** Diffuse **hyperkeratosis** and fine, white scaling covering the plantar surface and sides of the feet. Often bilateral. Look for associated onychomycosis.
• **Vesiculobullous:** Clustered **vesicles or bullae**, typically on the sole or instep.
• **Associated Findings:**
    ◦ **"Two feet, one hand" syndrome:** A classic pattern of moccasin-type tinea pedis on both feet and tinea manuum (fungal infection of the hand) on one hand, typically the dominant hand used for scratching the feet.
    ◦ **Onychomycosis:** Thickened, yellowed, and brittle toenails may be present, acting as a reservoir for infection.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis:** Often made based on a classic history and physical exam findings.
• **KOH Preparation (Potassium Hydroxide Prep):**
    ◦ **Procedure:** Scrape scales from the active border of a lesion onto a microscope slide. Add a drop of 10-20% KOH, gently heat, and examine under a microscope.
    ◦ **Findings:** Confirmatory test that reveals **segmented (septate) hyphae**. This is the most rapid and cost-effective diagnostic test.
• **Fungal Culture (e.g., Sabouraud agar):**
    ◦ **Gold Standard** for speciation but takes several weeks for results.
    ◦ Indicated for atypical presentations, failed treatment, or when KOH is negative but clinical suspicion remains high.
• **Wood's Lamp:**
    ◦ **Not useful.** The dermatophytes that cause tinea pedis do not fluoresce.
sections.treatment:
• **Topical Therapy (First-line for uncomplicated interdigital, mild moccasin, and vesiculobullous disease):**
    ◦ **Allylamines:** **Terbinafine 1% cream** (highly effective). Apply BID for 1-4 weeks.
    ◦ **Azoles:** Clotrimazole, miconazole (OTC), ketoconazole, econazole. Apply BID for 4 weeks.
    ◦ **Other:** Ciclopirox, butenafine.
    ◦ Treatment should continue for at least 1 week after clinical resolution.
• **Oral (Systemic) Therapy (Indicated for severe, extensive, or refractory cases, especially moccasin-type, and for patients with onychomycosis or immunosuppression):**
    ◦ **Terbinafine:** 250 mg PO daily for 2-6 weeks. **Drug of choice.** Requires baseline and periodic LFT monitoring.
    ◦ **Itraconazole:** 200 mg PO daily for 2-4 weeks. Potent CYP3A4 inhibitor with many drug interactions. Requires LFT monitoring.
    ◦ **Fluconazole:** 150 mg PO once weekly for 2-6 weeks. Less effective than terbinafine or itraconazole for dermatophytes.
sections.complications:
• **Secondary Bacterial Infection:** Fissures and erosions provide a portal of entry for bacteria (_Staphylococcus aureus_, _Streptococcus pyogenes_), leading to **cellulitis** or lymphangitis. This is the most common serious complication.
• **Onychomycosis (Tinea Unguium):** The infection can spread from the skin to the toenails.
• **Id (Dermatophytid) Reaction:** An autoimmune/allergic eczematous reaction at a distant site (commonly the hands) in response to fungal antigens. The vesicles of an Id reaction are sterile (KOH negative).
• **Tinea Corporis/Cruris:** Autoinoculation can spread the infection to the body or groin.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is generally excellent with appropriate treatment.
• However, **recurrence is very common**, especially if risk factors and preventative measures are not addressed.
• Chronic moccasin-type tinea pedis is more difficult to eradicate and has a higher rate of recurrence.
sections.preventionEducation:
• **Patient Education is CRITICAL for preventing recurrence:**
    ◦ **Foot Hygiene:** Wash feet daily and dry thoroughly, especially between the toes.
    ◦ **Footwear:** Wear breathable shoes (leather, mesh). Avoid occlusive, synthetic materials. Alternate shoes daily to allow them to dry completely.
    ◦ **Socks:** Wear moisture-wicking socks (cotton, wool) and change them daily or more often if feet are sweaty.
    ◦ **Antifungal Powders/Sprays:** Use antifungal powders (e.g., miconazole powder) in shoes and on feet to keep them dry.
    ◦ **Public Areas:** Wear sandals or water shoes in communal showers, locker rooms, and pool areas.
    ◦ **Treat reservoirs:** Concurrently treat onychomycosis if present to prevent reinfection of the skin.

sections.overview:
• Tinea manuum is a superficial **dermatophyte** infection of the skin on one or both hands, affecting either the palmar or dorsal surfaces.
• Often misdiagnosed as other common hand dermatoses like contact dermatitis or psoriasis.
• The classic presentation is often **unilateral** and is frequently associated with a concurrent **tinea pedis** infection.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ Caused by dermatophytic fungi that metabolize **keratin** in the skin, hair, and nails.
    ◦ **Most Common Organism**: **_Trichophyton rubrum_** (accounts for ~80% of cases).
    ◦ **Other Common Organisms**: _Trichophyton mentagrophytes_, _Epidermophyton floccosum_.
    ◦ **Zoophilic sources**: _Microsporum canis_ (from cats/dogs).
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Inoculation**: The fungus is transmitted to the hand via direct contact with an infected person (anthropophilic), animal (zoophilic), soil (geophilic), or a fomite.
        ▪ Most commonly, it occurs via **autoinoculation** from scratching one's own **tinea pedis** (athlete's foot).
    ◦ **Invasion**: Dermatophytes produce enzymes called **keratinases**, which allow them to invade and colonize the non-living, keratinized **stratum corneum** of the epidermis.
    ◦ **Inflammation**: The clinical signs of erythema, scaling, and pruritus are due to the host's **cell-mediated immune response** to fungal antigens.
sections.epidemiology:
• More common in adults than children.
• Higher prevalence in males.
• Occurs worldwide but is more common in hot, humid climates.
• Less common than tinea pedis, tinea cruris, or tinea corporis.
• Often seen in individuals with manual labor jobs or those who wear occlusive gloves for prolonged periods.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is highly variable but classically falls into two main patterns:
    ◦ **Hyperkeratotic (Dry-Type)**
        ▪ Most common presentation, often affecting the **palm**.
        ▪ Presents as diffuse, fine, white, powdery scaling, particularly within the palmar creases (**accentuated dermatoglyphics**).
        ▪ May be subtle and often mistaken for "dry skin" or chronic irritant contact dermatitis.
        ▪ Usually **unilateral**.
    ◦ **Inflammatory (Annular/Ringworm Type)**
        ▪ More common on the **dorsum** of the hand.
        ▪ Presents as a classic "ringworm" lesion: an **annular** (ring-shaped) or **arcuate** (curved) plaque.
        ▪ Features a raised, erythematous, scaling, and sometimes vesicular border with **central clearing**.
        ▪ Typically more pruritic and acute in onset than the hyperkeratotic type.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Best Initial Test: KOH Preparation**
    ◦ **Procedure**: Scrape scales from the **active border** of a lesion onto a glass slide. Add a drop of 10-20% potassium hydroxide (KOH), apply a coverslip, and gently heat.
    ◦ **Findings**: Visualization of **segmented, branching hyphae** under microscopy confirms the diagnosis.
• **Gold Standard: Fungal Culture**
    ◦ **Procedure**: Use Sabouraud dextrose agar.
    ◦ **Use**: Confirms the diagnosis and identifies the specific species. It is more sensitive than KOH prep but takes several weeks for results. Useful in cases of failed treatment or atypical presentation.
• **Skin Biopsy with PAS stain**
    ◦ Rarely necessary.
    ◦ A **periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain** will highlight fungal elements in the stratum corneum.
    ◦ Reserved for cases where the diagnosis is uncertain despite other tests.
• **Wood's Lamp**
    ◦ Not useful, as _Trichophyton_ species do not fluoresce.
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent with appropriate diagnosis and treatment.
• Recurrence is common if predisposing factors, especially concurrent **tinea pedis**, are not identified and eliminated.

sections.overview:
• **Tinea versicolor** (also known as **pityriasis versicolor**) is a common, benign, superficial fungal infection of the stratum corneum caused by the dimorphic, lipophilic yeast of the *Malassezia* genus, a component of normal skin flora
    ◦ Characterized by the development of multiple, well-demarcated, **hypo- or hyperpigmented macules**, primarily on the trunk and upper extremities
    ◦ It is **not contagious**
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Organism**: Overgrowth of *Malassezia* species, most commonly ***Malassezia globosa*** and ***Malassezia furfur***
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ *Malassezia* is a dimorphic yeast, meaning it can exist in both a yeast (spore) form and a mycelial (hyphal) form
    ◦ In tinea versicolor, the harmless yeast form, which is part of the normal skin flora, transforms into its pathogenic, filamentous (mycelial) form
    ◦ This overgrowth is thought to be triggered by factors like heat, humidity, and oily skin
• **Pigmentary Changes**
    ◦ **Hypopigmentation**
        ▪ The fungus produces **azelaic acid**, a dicarboxylic acid that inhibits the enzyme **tyrosinase** in epidermal melanocytes
        ▪ This blocks the conversion of tyrosine to melanin, leading to lighter-colored macules that fail to tan with sun exposure
    ◦ **Hyperpigmentation**
        ▪ The mechanism is less clear but is thought to be related to an inflammatory response and the presence of larger-than-normal melanosomes, causing a brown or reddish-brown appearance
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Most common in regions with **hot and humid climates** (tropical and subtropical areas)
• **Age**: Primarily affects **adolescents and young adults** due to peak sebaceous gland activity, which produces the lipids the yeast feeds on
• **Sex**: Affects males and females equally
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patient typically presents with a complaint of a **non-pruritic rash** that has been present for weeks to months
• The rash is often first noticed during summer or after sun exposure because the affected skin **does not tan**, making the hypopigmentation more obvious
• The lesions are multiple, small, discrete macules that may coalesce into larger patches over time
sections.diagnostics:
• **Potassium Hydroxide (KOH) Prep**
    ◦ **Test of choice** for confirmation
    ◦ **Procedure**: Skin scrapings from a lesion are placed on a slide with a drop of 10-20% KOH solution
    ◦ **Classic Finding**: A "**spaghetti and meatballs**" pattern, which represents a mixture of short, cigar-butt **hyphae (spaghetti)** and clusters of yeast **spores (meatballs)**
• **Wood's Lamp Examination**
    ◦ **Procedure**: The affected skin is examined under a Wood's lamp (UV-A light) in a dark room
    ◦ **Finding**: Lesions often exhibit a **pale yellow to yellow-green fluorescence**
        ▪ *Note*: This test has low sensitivity, as fluorescence may be absent if the patient has recently showered
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is excellent, as the infection responds well to treatment
• However, the **rate of recurrence is high (>60%)**, especially for individuals living in predisposing climates or with ongoing risk factors

sections.overview:
• Onychomycosis is a fungal infection of the nail apparatus, which includes the nail plate, nail bed, and nail matrix.
    ◦ It is the most common cause of nail dystrophy.
    ◦ While often considered a cosmetic issue, it can cause pain, disability, and serve as a portal of entry for secondary bacterial infections, especially in diabetic or immunocompromised patients.
• The term **tinea unguium** specifically refers to onychomycosis caused by dermatophytes.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Dermatophytes (~90% of cases)**
        ▪ ***Trichophyton rubrum*** is the most common causative organism worldwide.
        ▪ *Trichophyton mentagrophytes* is also common.
    ◦ **Yeasts (~5-10% of cases)**
        ▪ *Candida albicans* is the most frequent yeast isolate, often affecting fingernails and associated with chronic paronychia or mucocutaneous candidiasis.
    ◦ **Non-dermatophyte Molds (<5% of cases)**
        ▪ *Aspergillus spp.*, *Fusarium spp.*, *Scopulariopsis brevicaulis*.
        ▪ Often considered opportunistic pathogens, infecting nails that are already damaged by trauma or other disease.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The infection typically begins with the invasion of the nail bed or nail plate by the fungal organism.
    ◦ Fungi, particularly dermatophytes, produce **keratinases**, enzymes that digest keratin, the primary structural protein of the nail.
    ◦ This enzymatic breakdown leads to the separation of the nail plate from the underlying nail bed (**onycholysis**).
    ◦ The space created becomes filled with keratinaceous debris, resulting in a thickened, crumbly nail (**subungual hyperkeratosis**).
    ◦ The infection spreads proximally towards the nail matrix, the site of nail growth. If the matrix becomes infected, permanent nail dystrophy can occur.
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects approximately 10% of the general population.
• Prevalence increases dramatically with age, affecting up to 50% of individuals over 70.
• **Toenails are affected far more often than fingernails** (ratio of ~10:1).
    ◦ This is attributed to slower nail growth, reduced blood supply, and the dark, moist environment inside shoes.
• More common in males than females.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• There are four main clinical subtypes:
    ◦ **Distal and Lateral Subungual Onychomycosis (DLSO)**
        ▪ **Most common type.**
        ▪ Fungus invades the hyponychium (under the distal nail edge) or lateral nail fold and spreads proximally under the nail plate.
        ▪ Presents as a white, yellow, or brown area at the tip of the nail that slowly enlarges.
    ◦ **Superficial White Onychomycosis (SWO)**
        ▪ Fungus directly invades the dorsal (top) surface of the nail plate.
        ▪ Presents as well-demarcated, opaque, "chalky" white patches on the nail surface.
        ▪ These patches can be scraped off.
        ▪ Commonly caused by *T. mentagrophytes*.
    ◦ **Proximal Subungual Onychomycosis (PSO)**
        ▪ **Least common type in healthy individuals.**
        ▪ Fungus invades via the cuticle and proximal nail fold, infecting the nail plate from its base.
        ▪ Presents as a white or yellowish area near the lunula that moves distally as the nail grows.
        ▪ **Strongly associated with immunosuppression, particularly HIV.** Its presence should prompt an HIV workup in at-risk patients.
    ◦ **Total Dystrophic Onychomycosis**
        ▪ The end-stage result of any of the above types.
        ▪ Characterized by a completely thickened, crumbly, and destroyed nail plate.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical diagnosis alone is unreliable (<50% accuracy).**
• **Mycological confirmation is the standard of care before initiating systemic therapy.**
• **Potassium Hydroxide (KOH) Preparation**
    ◦ **Best initial test.**
    ◦ Subungual debris is scraped from the affected nail, placed on a slide with 10-20% KOH solution, and heated gently.
    ◦ KOH dissolves human keratinocytes, leaving fungal elements visible.
    ◦ Microscopy reveals **septate hyphae**.
    ◦ Quick and inexpensive but operator-dependent.
• **Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) Stain**
    ◦ **Gold standard diagnostic test** with the highest sensitivity (>90%).
    ◦ A clipped portion of the affected nail is sent to pathology.
    ◦ The PAS stain highlights fungal elements in pink/red.
• **Fungal Culture**
    ◦ Identifies the specific causative organism, which can guide therapy (e.g., terbinafine is less effective against *Candida* and molds).
    ◦ Requires several weeks for growth and is prone to false negatives and contamination.
sections.prognosis:
• Cure rates with systemic therapy vary. Mycological cure (negative labs) is achieved in ~75% of patients with terbinafine.
• Clinical cure (normal-appearing nail) is lower due to residual dystrophy.
• **Recurrence is common**, occurring in 20-50% of patients even after successful treatment.
• Prognosis is worse in older patients and those with significant comorbidities (diabetes, PVD).

sections.overview:
• Cutaneous candidiasis is a superficial fungal infection of the skin caused by yeast from the *Candida* genus, an opportunistic infection thriving in warm, moist, and macerated environments
    ◦ The infection typically manifests in **intertriginous areas** (skin folds) and is characterized by **erythematous plaques with satellite lesions**
    ◦ Diagnosis is often clinical but can be confirmed with a **KOH preparation**
sections.etiology:
• **Etiologic Agent**: Primarily **_Candida albicans_** (>90% of cases)
    ◦ Other species like _C. tropicalis_ and _C. glabrata_ can also be causative agents, especially in immunocompromised hosts
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ *Candida* is a normal commensal organism on the skin, GI tract, and GU tract
    ◦ Infection occurs when there is a disruption of the skin barrier or an alteration in the host's local or systemic immunity
    ◦ Key factors for overgrowth include moisture, warmth, occlusion, and maceration of the skin
    ◦ *Candida* transforms from its benign yeast form to its pathogenic **pseudohyphal/hyphal form**, which invades the stratum corneum
    ◦ The organism releases enzymes (proteases, phospholipases) that damage host tissue and elicit an inflammatory response, leading to the characteristic rash
sections.epidemiology:
• *Candida* infections are ubiquitous and occur worldwide
• Affects all ages, but is most common at the extremes of age (**infants, elderly**)
• Higher prevalence in **obese individuals, diabetics, and the immunocompromised**
• **Diaper candidiasis** is one of the most common dermatoses in infancy
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation varies by location but shares common features
    ◦ **Intertrigo**: Infection of the large skin folds (axillae, groin, inframammary, gluteal cleft, pannus)
        ▪ Presents as **"beefy red,"** well-demarcated, erythematous plaques with surrounding **satellite papules and pustules**
        ▪ Often associated with burning and pruritus
    ◦ **Diaper Candidiasis**: A common form of diaper dermatitis
        ▪ Erythematous patches in the perineal region that, unlike irritant dermatitis, **prominently involve the skin folds (creases)**
        ▪ Classic satellite lesions are present
    ◦ **Erosio Interdigitalis Blastomycetica**: Candidal infection of the web spaces between the fingers or toes, most commonly the 3rd and 4th digits
        ▪ Presents with erythema, maceration, and fissuring
        ▪ Common in individuals with frequent water exposure (e.g., dishwashers)
    ◦ **Candidal Paronychia**: Inflammation of the nail fold
        ▪ Presents with painful, erythematous swelling of the proximal or lateral nail folds
        ▪ May have purulent discharge
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Often sufficient based on the characteristic **"beefy red"** plaques with **satellite lesions** in an intertriginous location
• **KOH Preparation (Potassium Hydroxide)**
    ◦ **Procedure**: Skin scrapings from the edge of a lesion are placed on a slide with a drop of 10-20% KOH and gently heated
    ◦ **Finding**: Confirmatory test shows **budding yeast and pseudohyphae** (differentiates from dermatophytes which show true septate hyphae)
• **Fungal Culture**: Not routinely necessary but can be used in cases of treatment failure or atypical presentation to confirm the species and determine antifungal sensitivities
• **Wood's Lamp Examination**
    ◦ *Candida* does **not** fluoresce, which helps differentiate it from erythrasma (fluoresces coral-red)
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** in immunocompetent individuals with appropriate treatment and management of underlying risk factors
• **Recurrence is common** if predisposing factors (moisture, obesity, hyperglycemia) are not controlled
• Prognosis is more guarded in **severely immunocompromised patients** due to the risk of systemic dissemination

sections.overview:
• **Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV)** is a ubiquitous, **double-stranded DNA virus** that causes **lifelong latent infections** characterized by periodic reactivation.
    ◦ Cutaneous HSV infections manifest as localized, **grouped vesicles on an erythematous base**.
    ◦ There are two main types:
        ▪ **HSV-1:** Classically associated with **orofacial lesions ("cold sores")**.
        ▪ **HSV-2:** Classically associated with **anogenital lesions**.
        ▪ Due to changing sexual practices, there is significant crossover in the location of infection for both types.
    ◦ Primary infection can be accompanied by systemic symptoms, while recurrent episodes are typically milder and often preceded by a **prodrome**.
sections.etiology:
• **Virus:**
    ◦ Family **Herpesviridae**.
    ◦ **HSV-1:** Primarily associated with orofacial infections.
    ◦ **HSV-2:** Primarily associated with genital infections.
• **Transmission:**
    ◦ Direct contact with active lesions, saliva, or genital secretions.
    ◦ **Asymptomatic viral shedding** is a common mode of transmission.
• **Pathophysiology:**
    ◦ **Primary Infection:**
        ▪ The virus enters through breaks in the skin or mucous membranes.
        ▪ It then replicates within the epidermis and dermis, causing cell lysis and leading to the characteristic vesicular eruption.
    ◦ **Latency:**
        ▪ The virus travels via **retrograde axonal transport** along sensory nerves to the corresponding dorsal root ganglia, where it establishes a lifelong latent infection.
        ▪ **HSV-1:** Typically resides in the **trigeminal ganglia**.
        ▪ **HSV-2:** Typically resides in the **sacral ganglia**.
    ◦ **Reactivation:**
        ▪ Various triggers (e.g., stress, UV light, illness) cause the virus to reactivate.
        ▪ It then travels via **anterograde axonal transport** down the same sensory nerve to the skin or mucosa, causing a recurrent outbreak, often in the same location as the primary infection.
sections.epidemiology:
• HSV is one of the most common human infections globally.
• **HSV-1:** Seroprevalence is >50% in the U.S. adult population, with most primary infections occurring in childhood.
• **HSV-2:** Seroprevalence is ~12-15% in the U.S. adult population, strongly correlated with sexual activity.
• Genital herpes caused by **HSV-1** is becoming increasingly common, especially in younger populations.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Primary Infection:**
    ◦ Often more severe and prolonged than recurrent episodes.
    ◦ May be associated with systemic symptoms like fever, headache, malaise, and myalgias.
    ◦ Lesions can be widespread and painful.
    ◦ *Example: **Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis*** in children involves extensive vesicular lesions of the oral mucosa, gums, and pharynx.
• **Recurrent Infection:**
    ◦ Typically less severe and of shorter duration.
    ◦ Usually localized to a specific area.
    ◦ Often preceded by a **prodrome**.
• **Specific Clinical Syndromes:**
    ◦ **Herpes Labialis:** "Cold sores" or "fever blisters." The most common presentation of recurrent **HSV-1**. Lesions on the vermilion border of the lips.
    ◦ **Genital Herpes:** Vesicles and erosions on the external genitalia, perineum, buttocks, or cervix. Associated with pain, itching, **dysuria**, and **tender inguinal lymphadenopathy**.
    ◦ **Herpetic Whitlow:** Infection of the finger, typically the distal phalanx. Often seen in healthcare workers or children who suck their thumb. Characterized by an erythematous, swollen, and vesiculopustular lesion.
    ◦ **Herpes Gladiatorum:** Seen in athletes with close skin-to-skin contact (e.g., wrestlers, rugby players). Lesions typically appear on the head, neck, and trunk.
    ◦ **Eczema Herpeticum (Kaposi's Varicelliform Eruption):** A dermatologic emergency. A disseminated HSV infection superimposed on pre-existing atopic dermatitis or other skin diseases. Characterized by widespread, monomorphic, **"punched-out" erosions**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis:** Often sufficient if the presentation is classic.
• **Confirmatory Tests (from an active lesion):**
    ◦ **Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR):** **Test of choice.**
        ▪ Highest sensitivity and specificity.
        ▪ Can differentiate **HSV-1** vs. **HSV-2**.
    ◦ **Viral Culture:** High specificity but lower sensitivity than PCR, especially as lesions begin to heal. Was previously the gold standard.
• **Supportive/Older Tests:**
    ◦ **Tzanck Smear:** Rapid bedside test.
        ▪ Involves scraping the base of a vesicle and staining (Wright-Giemsa).
        ▪ Shows **multinucleated giant cells** and ballooning keratinocytes.
        ▪ Low sensitivity and specificity; does not differentiate HSV from VZV.
    ◦ **Direct Fluorescent Antibody (DFA) Staining:** Rapid results, can differentiate HSV types. Less sensitive than PCR.
    ◦ **Serology (Type-Specific IgG):**
        ▪ Detects IgG antibodies to **HSV-1** and **HSV-2**.
        ▪ **Not useful for diagnosing an acute outbreak.**
        ▪ Useful for: confirming a diagnosis in patients with a history of recurrent but atypical lesions, identifying asymptomatic carriers, and counseling serodiscordant couples.
sections.prognosis:
• In immunocompetent hosts, cutaneous HSV is a benign, self-limiting condition. The virus establishes **lifelong latency**.
• Recurrences generally become less frequent and less severe over time.
• Prognosis is more guarded in immunocompromised patients, neonates, or those with complications like **encephalitis** or **eczema herpeticum**.

sections.overview:
• Varicella, commonly known as chickenpox, is a highly contagious acute infectious disease caused by the **Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV)**.
    ◦ Characterized by a prodrome of fever and malaise followed by the eruption of a **pruritic, vesicular rash** that appears in successive crops.
    ◦ While typically a benign, self-limiting illness in healthy children, it can cause significant morbidity and mortality in adults, newborns, and immunocompromised individuals.
    ◦ The virus establishes lifelong latency in the dorsal root ganglia and can reactivate later in life as **Herpes Zoster (Shingles)**.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**: **Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV)**, a member of the Human Herpesvirus family (HHV-3).
• **Virus Type**: Enveloped, double-stranded DNA virus.
• **Transmission**
    ◦ Inhalation of aerosolized respiratory droplets.
    ◦ Direct contact with vesicular fluid from skin lesions.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Inoculation**: VZV enters the respiratory tract or conjunctiva.
    ◦ **Primary Replication**: The virus replicates in the nasopharynx and regional lymph nodes.
    ◦ **Primary Viremia**: Virus disseminates via the bloodstream to the liver, spleen, and other reticuloendothelial organs.
    ◦ **Secondary Viremia**: After a second phase of replication, a larger secondary viremia occurs approximately 10-21 days post-infection (incubation period).
    ◦ **Cutaneous Manifestation**: The virus spreads to capillary endothelial cells and the epidermis, causing the characteristic vesicular rash.
    ◦ **Latency**: After the primary infection resolves, VZV travels via retrograde axonal transport to the dorsal root ganglia, where it establishes a latent infection.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Has decreased by >90% in the United States since the implementation of the routine two-dose varicella vaccination program.
• **Peak Season**: Late winter and early spring in temperate climates.
• **Age**: Primarily a disease of childhood, with peak incidence historically in children <10 years old.
• **Contagious Period**: Highly contagious.
    ◦ The period of infectivity is from **1-2 days before the onset of the rash until all lesions have fully crusted over** (typically 5-7 days after rash onset).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient, typically an unvaccinated child, presents with a 1-2 day **prodrome**.
    ◦ Low-grade fever
    ◦ Malaise
    ◦ Anorexia
• This is followed by the development of an **intensely pruritic rash**.
    ◦ Begins on the face and trunk (**"centripetal"**) and spreads to the extremities.
    ◦ The rash is notable for the simultaneous presence of lesions in various stages of development.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**
    ◦ Diagnosis is almost always made clinically based on the pathognomonic rash and exposure history.
• **Laboratory Confirmation** (reserved for atypical or severe cases)
    ◦ **PCR of vesicular fluid**
        ▪ The test of choice.
        ▪ Highest sensitivity and specificity for detecting VZV DNA.
    ◦ **Tzanck Smear**
        ▪ A historical test showing **multinucleated giant cells** and eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions (Cowdry A inclusions).
        ▪ It is rapid but has low sensitivity and is not specific (also positive for HSV).
    ◦ **Direct Fluorescent Antibody (DFA) Staining**
        ▪ More sensitive and specific than Tzanck smear.
    ◦ **Serology (IgM/IgG)**
        ▪ Useful for confirming recent infection (IgM) or determining immune status (IgG).
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** in healthy children, with recovery leading to lifelong immunity to chickenpox.
• Morbidity and mortality are significantly higher in adults, newborns, and immunocompromised individuals.
• The virus remains latent in the dorsal root ganglia and can reactivate years later as **Herpes Zoster (Shingles)**.

sections.overview:
• **Herpes Zoster**, commonly known as **shingles**, is an acute, painful, **unilateral vesicular eruption** that occurs in a restricted **dermatomal distribution**
    ◦ Caused by the **reactivation** of the latent **Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV)**, the same virus that causes varicella (**chickenpox**)
    ◦ After the primary chickenpox infection resolves, the virus becomes dormant in the **dorsal root ganglia**, cranial nerve ganglia, or autonomic ganglia, where it can reactivate later in life
sections.etiology:
• **Etiologic Agent**: **Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV)**, also known as **Human Herpesvirus 3 (HHV-3)**
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Primary Infection**: The individual is first infected with VZV, leading to varicella (**chickenpox**). The virus spreads hematogenously and infects skin epithelial cells
    ◦ **Latency**: After the primary infection resolves, the virus travels via **retrograde axonal transport** from skin lesions to sensory nerves and establishes a latent infection within the **dorsal root or cranial nerve ganglia**
    ◦ **Reactivation**: A **decline in VZV-specific cell-mediated immunity** allows the virus to reactivate
    ◦ **Replication & Spread**: The reactivated virus replicates within the ganglion, causing intense inflammation, **neuronal necrosis**, and **neuralgia**. It then travels down the sensory nerve (**anterograde transport**) to the corresponding dermatome of the skin
    ◦ **Clinical Manifestation**: Viral replication in epidermal cells leads to the characteristic **vesicular rash**. The associated **ganglionitis** and **neuritis** cause the prodromal and persistent pain
