sections.epidemiology:
• **Lifetime Risk**: Approximately **1 in 3 people** in the United States will develop shingles in their lifetime
• **Incidence**: Incidence sharply **increases with age**. It is relatively uncommon in individuals <50 years old but rises dramatically thereafter
• **Population**: Affects all races and genders equally. It is most common in **older adults** and **immunocompromised individuals**
• **Vaccination Impact**: The widespread use of the **recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix)** is expected to decrease the incidence and severity of shingles and its complications
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation typically follows a distinct progression:
    ◦ **Prodromal Phase (1-3 days before rash)**:
        ▪ Localized **pain** (burning, throbbing, stabbing), **pruritus**, or **paresthesias** (tingling, numbness) within a single dermatome
        ▪ Systemic symptoms may be present: **fever**, **headache**, **malaise**, fatigue
        ▪ The pain can be mistaken for other conditions like myocardial infarction, pleurisy, or cholecystitis depending on the dermatome
    ◦ **Acute Eruptive Phase (Lasts 2-4 weeks)**:
        ▪ **Erythematous macules and papules** appear in a **unilateral dermatomal distribution**
        ▪ These rapidly progress to form **vesicles**, which may coalesce
        ▪ Vesicles become **pustular** or **hemorrhagic** within 3-4 days
        ▪ **Crusting** occurs over the next 7-10 days
        ▪ **Pain** is a prominent feature throughout this phase
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primarily a clinical diagnosis** based on the characteristic **unilateral, dermatomal vesicular rash**
• **Confirmatory Testing** (if diagnosis is uncertain):
    ◦ **PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction)**:
        ▪ **Test of choice**
        ▪ Highly sensitive and specific
        ▪ A sample is obtained by unroofing a vesicle and swabbing the base
        ▪ Can **differentiate VZV from HSV**
    ◦ **Tzanck Smear**:
        ▪ A classic but less sensitive/specific test
        ▪ A scraping from the vesicle base is stained, revealing **multinucleated giant cells**
        ▪ **Cannot differentiate VZV from HSV**
    ◦ **Direct Fluorescent Antibody (DFA) Staining**:
        ▪ More rapid and sensitive than a Tzanck smear
sections.prognosis:
• **Immunocompetent Host**: The prognosis is generally excellent. The rash typically resolves within 2-4 weeks
• **PHN**: Develops in 10-15% of all patients, but the risk is >50% in patients over 60 who are not treated with antivirals
• **Immunocompromised Host**: Higher risk of complications, including dissemination and death

sections.overview:
• **Molluscum contagiosum (MC)** is a common, benign, self-limiting viral infection of the skin
    ◦ Caused by a **poxvirus** and characterized by the appearance of discrete, small, **dome-shaped papules** with **central umbilication**
    ◦ Primarily affects children, sexually active adults, and immunocompromised individuals
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**: **Molluscum Contagiosum Virus (MCV)**, a large, double-stranded DNA virus belonging to the *Poxviridae* family
    ◦ Four subtypes exist (MCV-1 to MCV-4)
        ▪ **MCV-1** is the most common cause in children
        ▪ **MCV-2** is more frequently seen in sexually transmitted cases and in HIV-positive individuals
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The virus inoculates the epidermis through direct contact, fomites, or autoinoculation
    ◦ It replicates exclusively within the cytoplasm of keratinocytes in the epidermis
    ◦ The virus produces proteins that inhibit the host's innate immune response, allowing the lesions to persist
    ◦ Infected keratinocytes enlarge, forming large, eosinophilic, intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies known as **Henderson-Patterson bodies** or "molluscum bodies"
    ◦ These bodies contain mature virions and are extruded from the central umbilication of the papule, contributing to transmission
• **Transmission**
    ◦ **Direct skin-to-skin contact**: Most common route
    ◦ **Fomites**: Sharing towels, sponges, razors, or sports equipment (e.g., wrestling mats)
    ◦ **Autoinoculation**: Spreading the virus from one part of the body to another by scratching or touching a lesion
    ◦ **Sexual transmission**: Common in adults, resulting in lesions on the genitals, lower abdomen, and inner thighs
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: A common childhood skin infection worldwide
• **Peak Incidence**
    ◦ Bimodal distribution: Children aged 2-5 years and young, sexually active adults
    ◦ A third peak can be seen in immunocompromised patients
• **Environment**: More common in warm, humid climates and in institutional settings (e.g., daycare)
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The appearance of single or, more commonly, multiple cutaneous lesions
• Patients are often brought in by parents due to cosmetic concerns or fear of a more serious condition
• In adults, presentation is often due to concern about a sexually transmitted infection
• Immunocompromised patients may present with hundreds of lesions, including giant or atypical forms
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Diagnosis is almost always made based on the characteristic appearance of the lesions (**dome-shaped papules** with **central umbilication**)
• **Dermoscopy**: May show a central, polylobular, white-to-yellowish amorphous structure with surrounding crown-like vessels
• **Skin Biopsy** (rarely needed)
    ◦ Performed for atypical or uncertain cases, especially in immunocompromised hosts to rule out fungal infections (e.g., cryptococcosis) or malignancy
    ◦ **Histology**: Shows pathognomonic **Henderson-Patterson bodies**
        ▪ Large, eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies within the keratinocytes of the epidermis
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**
• In immunocompetent individuals, MC is **self-limiting**
    ◦ Lesions typically resolve spontaneously without scarring over a period of 6-18 months, although some may persist for up to 4 years
• Once resolved, immunity is conferred, though reinfection with a different viral subtype is possible
    ◦ The virus does not have a latent phase like herpesviruses

sections.overview:
• **Verruca Vulgaris**, or the **common wart**, is a benign, self-limited epidermal proliferation caused by infection with the **Human Papillomavirus (HPV)**.
    ◦ These lesions typically present as **hyperkeratotic**, **flesh-colored papules** with a rough, **verrucous surface**.
    ◦ While they can occur anywhere, they are most frequently found on the hands, fingers, and knees.
    ◦ The diagnosis is primarily clinical, and although many warts resolve spontaneously, treatment is often sought for cosmetic reasons, symptoms, or to prevent spread.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiologic Agent**: **Human Papillomavirus (HPV)**, a non-enveloped, double-stranded DNA virus.
• **Specific Strains**
    ◦ Most commonly caused by **HPV types 2 and 4**.
    ◦ Also associated with types 1, 3, 27, 29, and 57.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Inoculation**: HPV enters the epidermis through microscopic breaks or trauma in the skin barrier.
    ◦ **Infection**: The virus infects the **basal keratinocytes** of the epidermis.
    ◦ **Proliferation**: HPV E6 and E7 oncoproteins interfere with host tumor suppressor genes (**p53** and **pRb**), leading to uncontrolled cellular proliferation (**acanthosis**) and delayed keratinocyte maturation.
    ◦ **Lesion Formation**: This results in the characteristic clinical findings of **hyperkeratosis** (thickened stratum corneum), **papillomatosis** (undulating epidermal surface), and **acanthosis** (thickened epidermis).
    ◦ **Histologic Hallmark**: Presence of **koilocytes** - keratinocytes with a pyknotic (shrunken, irregular) nucleus surrounded by a perinuclear halo. This is pathognomonic for HPV infection.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Extremely common, affecting an estimated 7-12% of the general population.
• **Peak Incidence**: Children and young adults (ages 5-20).
• **Occupational Risk**: Increased incidence in handlers of meat, poultry, and fish ("**butcher's warts**").
• **Transmission**
    ◦ Direct person-to-person contact.
    ◦ Fomites (e.g., towels, razors, surfaces).
    ◦ **Autoinoculation**: Spreading the virus from one part of the body to another (e.g., through scratching or nail-biting).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Classic Lesion**: Firm, well-demarcated, **hyperkeratotic papule** or nodule with a rough, **verrucous** (cauliflower-like) surface.
• **Size**: Varies from 1 mm to >1 cm.
• **Color**: Skin-colored, pink, tan, or grayish-brown.
• **Location**: Most commonly on hands (dorsal surfaces, digits), periungual areas, elbows, and knees. Can occur anywhere on the skin.
• **Number**: May be solitary or multiple.
    ◦ Multiple lesions often appear in a linear configuration due to **autoinoculation** (**Koebner phenomenon**).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: The diagnosis is almost always made based on history and physical exam findings.
• **Paring**: Use of a scalpel to shave down the lesion is both a diagnostic and therapeutic maneuver, revealing **thrombosed capillaries**.
• **Dermoscopy**: Can help visualize the **thrombosed capillaries** (appearing as red or black dots) and **papillomatous surface**.
• **Biopsy**: Rarely necessary.
    ◦ Indicated if the diagnosis is uncertain, the lesion is refractory to standard treatments, or there is suspicion of malignancy (e.g., ulcerated, bleeding, atypical location in an elderly or **immunocompromised** patient).
    ◦ Histology will show **hyperkeratosis**, **papillomatosis**, and **koilocytes**.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**.
• Warts are benign and often self-resolve, particularly in healthy children.
• Recurrence after treatment is common (~30%) because the virus may persist in clinically normal-appearing skin surrounding the treated lesion.
• Warts in **immunocompromised** individuals are often more numerous, larger, and more recalcitrant to therapy.

sections.overview:
• Plantar warts, or **verruca plantaris**, are common, benign epidermal growths caused by the **Human Papillomavirus (HPV)**.
    ◦ They occur on the plantar surfaces (soles) of the feet.
    ◦ Due to the pressure of walking, these warts tend to grow inward (**endophytic**) and are often covered by a thick layer of callus, which can make them painful.
    ◦ Diagnosis is typically clinical, and while many resolve spontaneously, various treatments are available for symptomatic or persistent lesions.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**: **Human Papillomavirus (HPV)**, a non-enveloped, double-stranded DNA virus.
• **Specific Serotypes**: Most commonly caused by **HPV types 1, 2, 4, 27, and 57**.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Inoculation**: The virus enters the epidermis through microscopic breaks or abrasions in the skin, often in a moist environment.
    ◦ **Infection**: HPV infects the **basal keratinocytes** of the epidermis.
    ◦ **Proliferation**: The virus promotes benign proliferation of these infected epithelial cells, leading to **acanthosis** (epidermal thickening), **papillomatosis** (undulation of the epidermis), and **hyperkeratosis** (thickening of the stratum corneum).
    ◦ **Clinical Lesion**: This cellular proliferation results in the characteristic wart.
        ▪ The inward, or **endophytic**, growth pattern is a direct result of pressure from standing and walking.
        ▪ The visible "black dots" are **thrombosed capillaries** that have been pushed to the surface by the proliferating tissue.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Extremely common, affecting 7-10% of the general population.
• **Peak Incidence**: Most prevalent in children and young adults, with a peak between ages 12-16.
• **Transmission**: Spread through direct contact with the virus, either from another person's wart or, more commonly, from contaminated surfaces like locker room floors, public showers, and pool decks.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Location**: Found exclusively on the plantar surface of the foot, most commonly over pressure points such as the heel, metatarsal heads, and toes.
• **Morphology**
    ◦ Can present as a single lesion or as multiple lesions.
    ◦ Multiple, closely grouped warts may coalesce to form a larger, plaque-like lesion known as a **mosaic wart**.
• **Appearance**
    ◦ Typically a well-demarcated, rough, **hyperkeratotic papule or plaque**.
    ◦ The surface may appear **verrucous** (cauliflower-like) or may be covered by a smooth callus.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: The diagnosis is almost always made clinically based on the characteristic history and physical exam findings.
• **Diagnostic Procedure**: **Paring the lesion** with a scalpel is the single most useful maneuver. This confirms the diagnosis by revealing:
    ◦ Disruption of skin lines.
    ◦ Punctate bleeding from **thrombosed capillaries**.
• **Biopsy**: Rarely necessary. Indicated only if the diagnosis is uncertain, the lesion is refractory to standard treatments, or if there is suspicion of malignancy (e.g., **verrucous carcinoma**, **amelanotic melanoma**).
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**. Plantar warts are benign and self-limited.
• **Spontaneous Resolution**: Occurs in approximately 65% of cases within 2 years, especially in immunocompetent children.
• **Recurrence**: Recurrence after treatment is common (up to 30%) because the virus can persist in clinically normal-appearing skin surrounding the treated area.

sections.overview:
• **Condyloma acuminata**, commonly known as **genital warts**, are benign proliferative lesions of the skin and mucous membranes.
    ◦ They are one of the most common sexually transmitted infections (STIs) globally, caused by the **Human Papillomavirus (HPV)**.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**: **Human Papillomavirus (HPV)**, a non-enveloped, double-stranded DNA virus.
• **Key Strains**:
    ◦ **>90% of cases are caused by low-risk, non-oncogenic HPV types 6 and 11.**
    ◦ High-risk, oncogenic types (e.g., HPV 16, 18, 31, 33), which are primarily associated with dysplasia and cancer, can occasionally cause anogenital warts.
    ◦ Co-infection with multiple HPV types is common.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ HPV infects the basal keratinocytes of the epidermis, typically through micro-abrasions in the skin or mucous membranes during sexual contact.
    ◦ The virus integrates its DNA into the host cell genome, expressing viral proteins (E6 and E7) that interfere with tumor suppressor proteins (p53 and pRb), leading to uncontrolled cell proliferation.
    ◦ This results in epidermal hyperplasia (acanthosis) and the formation of a macroscopic wart.
    ◦ Histologic examination reveals **koilocytes**, which are pathognomonic for HPV infection.
        ▪ These are squamous epithelial cells with a perinuclear halo (cytoplasmic vacuolization) and a wrinkled, pyknotic nucleus.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: The **most common viral STI** in the United States.
• **Incidence**: Highest among sexually active individuals aged 15-29.
• **Transmission**:
    ◦ Primarily through direct skin-to-skin contact during vaginal, anal, or oral sex.
    ◦ Vertical transmission from mother to infant during childbirth can occur, potentially causing recurrent respiratory papillomatosis.
    ◦ Fomite transmission is rare but possible.
• Most HPV infections are transient and cleared by the immune system within 1-2 years without causing clinical disease.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a sexually active patient who notes the appearance of new, **painless "bumps"** in the anogenital region.
    ◦ Lesions can be solitary or multiple and may have been present for weeks to months.
    ◦ The primary complaint is often cosmetic.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primarily a clinical diagnosis** based on the characteristic appearance of the lesions on physical exam.
• **Acetic Acid Application ("Acetowhitening")**:
    ◦ Application of 3-5% acetic acid causes HPV-infected tissue to turn white.
    ◦ This test is **not recommended for routine diagnosis** due to low sensitivity and very low specificity (can be positive with inflammation, psoriasis, or normal tissue).
• **Biopsy for Histopathology**:
    ◦ Indicated if:
        ▪ The diagnosis is uncertain.
        ▪ Lesions are atypical (e.g., pigmented, indurated, ulcerated, fixed).
        ▪ Warts are refractory to standard treatment.
        ▪ The patient is immunocompromised (higher risk of malignancy).
    ◦ **Finding**: Will show **koilocytosis**.
• **HPV DNA/RNA testing**: **NOT** used for the diagnosis of genital warts. Its role is in cervical cancer screening.
• **Serology**: Not clinically useful for diagnosis.
sections.prognosis:
• In many immunocompetent individuals, genital warts may resolve spontaneously within months to 2 years.
• Treatment can clear visible warts, but **recurrence is common (~25-65%)** within 3-6 months because of persistent subclinical infection.
• The underlying HPV infection can persist for years, even in the absence of visible warts.

sections.overview:
• Intensely pruritic, highly contagious skin infestation caused by the mite *Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis*
	◦ Characterized by a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction to the mite, its eggs, and its feces (scybala)
		▪ Results in **severe itching (especially at night)** and a papular rash with **pathognomonic burrows**
	◦ Transmitted primarily through direct, prolonged skin-to-skin contact
sections.etiology:
• **Etiologic Agent**: The mite *Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis*, an obligate human ectoparasite
• **Pathophysiology**
	◦ **Infestation**: The impregnated female mite burrows into the stratum corneum of the epidermis
	◦ **Reproduction**: She lays 2-3 eggs per day within the burrow, where they hatch into larvae in 3-4 days
	◦ **Hypersensitivity Reaction**: The hallmark pruritus and inflammatory rash are a **Type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity reaction** to the mite, its eggs, and its feces
	◦ **Timeline**
		▪ **Primary Infestation**: Sensitization takes **3-6 weeks**. The patient is contagious during this asymptomatic period
		▪ **Re-infestation**: Symptoms develop rapidly within **1-3 days** due to pre-existing immunity
	◦ The mite cannot survive off a human host for more than 48-72 hours
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects millions worldwide annually; endemic in many tropical and resource-poor regions
• **Transmission**
	◦ **Primary**: Prolonged, direct skin-to-skin contact (e.g., holding hands, sexual contact)
	◦ **Secondary (Less Common)**: Fomites (infested bedding, clothing, furniture)
		▪ This route is more significant in **Crusted (Norwegian) Scabies** due to the high mite burden
• **Outbreaks**: Common in crowded settings like nursing homes, long-term care facilities, military barracks, prisons, and daycare centers
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a patient complaining of a new-onset, severe, generalized itching that is unrelenting and significantly interferes with sleep
	◦ The itching is often described as being **worst at night** or after a hot shower
	◦ Other household members may have similar symptoms
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Scabies is most often diagnosed based on the classic history (**intense nocturnal pruritus**) and physical exam findings (characteristic rash distribution)
• **Skin Scraping (Scabies Prep)**
	◦ **Indication**: Definitive diagnosis; **gold standard**
	◦ **Procedure**: A drop of mineral oil is placed over a burrow or non-excoriated papule. The lesion is scraped with a #15 scalpel blade. The scrapings are placed on a glass slide and examined under a microscope
	◦ **Positive Finding**: Visualization of **mites, eggs, or scybala (fecal pellets)**
• **Dermoscopy**: Can be used to visualize the mite (**"delta wing"** or **"jetliner"** sign) at the end of a burrow, avoiding the need for a scraping
• **Adhesive Tape Test**: A simpler, less sensitive alternative where clear tape is firmly applied to a lesion, removed, and examined under a microscope
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent with proper and timely treatment of the patient and all contacts
• Re-infestation is common if contacts are not treated simultaneously
• **Crusted scabies** carries higher morbidity if not treated aggressively

sections.overview:
• **Pediculosis capitis** is a common ectoparasitic infestation of the scalp by the head louse, ***Pediculus humanus capitis***.
• The louse is an obligate human parasite that feeds on blood from the scalp.
• The condition is characterized by intense **pruritus**.
• It is most prevalent in school-aged children and is transmitted primarily through direct **head-to-head contact**.
• It is **not associated with poor hygiene**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiologic Agent**: ***Pediculus humanus capitis***.
• **Life Cycle**: The life cycle is approximately 30 days and occurs entirely on the human host.
    ◦ **Nit (Egg)**: The female louse lays eggs (nits) and cements them to the hair shaft, typically within 6 mm of the scalp for warmth and incubation. Nits hatch in 7-10 days.
    ◦ **Nymph**: An immature louse that hatches from the nit. It undergoes three molts over about 7-10 days before becoming an adult.
    ◦ **Louse (Adult)**: A 2-3 mm long, wingless, grayish-white insect. Adult lice feed on host blood several times a day and can survive for up to 30 days on a host but die within 1-2 days if they fall off.
• **Pathophysiology of Symptoms**: The primary symptom, **pruritus**, is caused by a **delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction (Type IV)** to proteins in louse saliva injected during blood meals. It may take 4-6 weeks for sensitization to occur after an initial infestation, which is why early cases can be asymptomatic.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects millions of people worldwide annually, with highest rates in the United States among children aged 3-11.
• **Demographics**:
    ◦ **Age**: Most common in preschool and elementary school-aged children.
    ◦ **Sex**: More common in **females** than males, likely due to longer hair and greater frequency of head-to-head contact.
    ◦ **Race**: More common in Caucasians. Less common in African Americans, possibly due to the oval shape of the hair shaft, which is more difficult for the louse's claws to grasp.
• **Transmission**:
    ◦ **Primary**: Direct **head-to-head contact**.
    ◦ **Secondary (Rare)**: Fomites such as hats, combs, brushes, headphones, bedding, and towels. Lice **cannot jump or fly**.
sections.riskFactors:
• School or daycare attendance
• Overcrowded living conditions
• Close contact with an infested individual (e.g., household members, sleepovers)
• Female gender
• Age 3-11 years
• Sharing of personal items like combs, hats, or headphones
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A parent typically brings in a school-aged child with the chief complaint of an **intensely itchy scalp**, which may be **worse at night**.
• The parent may report seeing "bugs" or **"dandruff that doesn't flake off."**
• The child may be irritable or have difficulty sleeping due to the pruritus.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Symptoms**:
    ◦ **Hallmark Symptom**: **Scalp pruritus**, especially on the **occipital** and **post-auricular scalp**.
    ◦ Tickling sensation or a feeling of movement on the scalp.
    ◦ Irritability and difficulty sleeping (lice are more active in the dark).
    ◦ Can be asymptomatic, particularly in the first few weeks of a primary infestation.
• **Physical Exam Findings**:
    ◦ **Definitive Diagnosis**: Visualization of a **live adult louse or nymph**. This is often difficult as they move quickly and avoid light.
    ◦ **Nits**: Ovoid, 1mm, grayish-white to yellowish-brown specks firmly cemented to one side of the hair shaft.
    ◦ **Viable nits**: Usually found **within 6 mm** (~1/4 inch) of the scalp. They are typically pearly, yellow, or brown.
    ◦ **Non-viable/hatched nits (casings)**: Found **>6 mm from the scalp**, appear white and more translucent. They are not indicative of an active infestation.
    ◦ **Common Locations**: **Retroauricular** (behind the ears) and **posterior occipital scalp** are classic locations to find lice and nits.
    ◦ **Excoriations**: Due to scratching.
    ◦ **Posterior cervical and posterior auricular lymphadenopathy**: Common reactive finding due to scalp inflammation and potential secondary infection.
    ◦ **"Louse dirt" (Frass)**: Reddish-brown or black specks on the scalp, pillow, or clothing, representing louse feces.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primary Method**: Clinical diagnosis via direct visualization on physical exam.
• **Wet-Combing**: **Gold standard** and most sensitive method for detection.
    ◦ **Procedure**: Apply conditioner to wet hair to immobilize lice. Use a fine-toothed louse comb to systematically comb through the hair from the scalp to the ends. Wipe the comb on a white paper towel after each pass to inspect for lice and nits.
• **Wood's Lamp**: Nits and their casings may fluoresce a pale blue, but this is not a standard diagnostic tool.
sections.treatment:
• **Permethrin 1% lotion (Nix)**: A neurotoxin that causes paralysis and death in lice.
    ◦ **Application**: Apply to damp, towel-dried hair, leave on for 10 minutes, then rinse.
    ◦ **Efficacy**: Pediculicidal but has limited ovicidal activity. **Must repeat treatment in 7-10 days** to kill newly hatched nymphs. Widespread resistance is a major issue.
• **Pyrethrins with Piperonyl Butoxide (RID)**: Neurotoxin derived from chrysanthemum flowers.
    ◦ **Application**: Apply to dry hair, leave on for 10 minutes, then rinse.
    ◦ **Efficacy**: Pediculicidal only. **Must repeat treatment in 7-10 days**. Contraindicated in patients with chrysanthemum or ragweed allergy.
• **Ivermectin 0.5% lotion (Sklice)**: Paralyzes and kills lice.
    ◦ **Application**: Apply once to dry hair, leave on for 10 minutes, then rinse.
    ◦ **Efficacy**: Highly effective, pediculicidal, and partially ovicidal. Generally does not require re-treatment.
• **Spinosad 0.9% topical suspension (Natroba)**: Causes neuronal excitation leading to paralysis and death.
    ◦ **Application**: Apply once to dry hair, leave on for 10 minutes, then rinse.
    ◦ **Efficacy**: Highly effective, pediculicidal, and ovicidal. Generally does not require re-treatment.
• **Malathion 0.5% lotion (Ovide)**: An organophosphate cholinesterase inhibitor.
    ◦ **Application**: Apply to dry hair, let air dry, leave on for 8-12 hours, then rinse.
    ◦ **Efficacy**: Highly effective, pediculicidal, and ovicidal.
    ◦ **Caution**: **Flammable**; keep away from heat sources (hair dryers, curling irons).
• **Benzyl Alcohol 5% lotion (Ulesfia)**: Suffocates lice by obstructing their respiratory spiracles.
    ◦ **Application**: Apply to dry hair, leave on for 10 minutes, then rinse.
    ◦ **Efficacy**: Pediculicidal only. **Must repeat treatment in 7 days**. Non-neurotoxic mechanism.
sections.management:
• **Patient Education**:
    ◦ Reassure families that head lice are not a sign of poor hygiene and do not transmit disease.
    ◦ Explain the life cycle and the importance of correct application and timing of re-treatment for pediculicides.
• **Mechanical Removal**: Continue **wet-combing** with a louse comb every 2-3 days for 2 weeks after treatment to remove any remaining nits and lice.
• **Environmental Decontamination**:
    ◦ Wash clothing, bedding, and towels used by the infested person in the 2 days prior to treatment in **hot water (>130F or 54C)** and dry on high heat.
    ◦ Items that cannot be washed can be **sealed in a plastic bag for 2 weeks**.
    ◦ Soak combs and brushes in hot water for 5-10 minutes.
    ◦ Extensive home cleaning is generally unnecessary as fomite transmission is rare.
• **Contact Management**:
    ◦ All household members and close contacts should be examined for head lice.
    ◦ **Treat only those with evidence of active infestation** (live lice or viable nits). Prophylactic treatment is not recommended.
• **Return to School**:
    ◦ The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) and National Association of School Nurses (NASN) recommend that a child should **not be restricted from school attendance** because of head lice.
    ◦ **"No-nit" policies are discouraged**.
    ◦ The child can return to school after the first treatment has been administered.
sections.complications:
• **Secondary Bacterial Infection (Impetigo)**: Most common complication.
    ◦ Excoriations from scratching can become superinfected with ***Staphylococcus aureus*** or ***Streptococcus pyogenes***.
    ◦ Presents with **honey-colored crusting**.
    ◦ Requires treatment with topical or oral antibiotics.
• **Lice-Borne Disease**: ***Pediculus humanus capitis*** is **not** a known vector for other diseases, unlike the body louse (*Pediculus humanus corporis*).
• **Psychosocial**: Anxiety, embarrassment, social stigma, and insomnia.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**. With proper treatment and management, infestation can be fully eradicated.
• Failure is typically due to non-compliance, improper application of pediculicides, or re-infestation from an untreated contact.
• **Drug resistance** is an increasing cause of treatment failure.

sections.overview: • Pediculosis Corporis is an infestation of the body by the louse Pediculus humanus humanus. ◦ Unlike head lice or pubic lice, body lice do not live on the human body itself but rather in the seams of clothing and bedding. ◦ They move onto the skin only to feed, typically at night. • The clinical presentation is primarily driven by a hypersensitivity reaction to louse saliva, resulting in intense pruritus. • Crucially, body lice are known vectors for serious infectious diseases.
sections.etiology: • Causative Organism: Pediculus humanus humanus, a 2-4 mm long, six-legged, wingless insect. This is a subspecies distinct from the head louse (Pediculus humanus capitis). • Lifecycle: The entire lifecycle (egg to adult) takes approximately 3 weeks. ◦ Nit (Egg): Female lice lay eggs (nits) in the seams of clothing or bedding. Nits hatch in about 1 week. ◦ Nymph: Hatched nits become nymphs, which mature into adults over about 9-12 days. ◦ Adult: Adult lice can live for about 30 days and feed on human blood 3-5 times per day. They die within 1-2 days if separated from a human host and its associated clothing. • Pathophysiology: Symptoms are not caused by the bite itself, but by an allergic/hypersensitivity reaction to antigens present in the louse's saliva injected during feeding. This delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction causes intense pruritus.
sections.epidemiology: • Distribution: Worldwide. • Population: Primarily affects individuals in conditions of poverty, crowding, and poor personal hygiene. It is rare in individuals with access to regular bathing and laundering of clothes/bedding. • Setting: Commonly associated with homeless populations, refugees, victims of natural disasters, and soldiers in wartime conditions. • Transmission: ◦ Direct contact with an infested person. ◦ More commonly, via contact with infested clothing, bedding, and other fomites.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • A patient, often from a high-risk group, presents with a chief complaint of severe, generalized itching that is often worse at night. • The patient may report seeing "bugs" on their clothes but rarely on their body. • The history will reveal a lack of access to regular laundry and bathing facilities.
sections.diagnostics: • Clinical Diagnosis: The diagnosis is primarily made based on the characteristic history, symptoms, and physical exam findings in a patient with known risk factors. • Definitive Diagnosis: Identification of live lice or nits in the seams of clothing or on bedding. ◦ A magnifying glass can be helpful. • Skin Biopsy: Rarely indicated. If performed, it shows a non-specific inflammatory infiltrate with eosinophils. • Lab work: Not required for diagnosis, but consider screening for louse-borne diseases in endemic areas or with suggestive symptoms (e.g., fever, rash).
sections.prognosis: • Excellent with effective treatment of the patient and decontamination of their environment. • Recurrence is common if the underlying socioeconomic and hygiene issues are not addressed.

sections.overview:
• **Ectoparasitic infestation** of coarse body hair, primarily in the **pubic region**, caused by the louse **_Phthirus pubis_**
    ◦ Commonly known as "**crabs**" due to the louse's appearance
    ◦ Typically considered a **sexually transmitted infestation (STI)**
• Cardinal symptom is **intense pruritus** in the affected area
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Organism**: **_Phthirus pubis_** (the pubic or crab louse)
• **Morphology**
    ◦ A **1-2 mm**, six-legged insect with a broad, **crab-like body** and large front **claws (pincers)** adapted for grasping coarse hair fibers
    ◦ Visually distinct from head and body lice
• **Life Cycle**
    ◦ **Nits (Eggs)**: Small, oval, yellowish-white eggs firmly cemented to the base of hair shafts
        ▪ Hatch in **6-10 days**
    ◦ **Nymphs**: Immature lice that mature into adults over **2-3 weeks**
    ◦ **Adults**: Live for **3-4 weeks** on a human host, feeding on blood 4-5 times per day
        ▪ Cannot survive more than **24-48 hours** away from a human host
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ Infestation occurs via **direct contact**
    ◦ The **intense pruritus** is a **delayed hypersensitivity reaction** to proteins in the louse's **saliva**, which is injected into the skin during blood feeding
sections.epidemiology:
• **Transmission**
    ◦ Primarily through **sexual contact**
    ◦ Less common routes include close, non-sexual contact or contact with infested **fomites** (bedding, towels, clothing)
• **Prevalence**
    ◦ Occurs worldwide and affects all socioeconomic levels
    ◦ Most common in sexually active individuals, especially **adolescents** and **young adults**
    ◦ It is not a nationally reportable disease, so exact prevalence is unknown
• **Co-infection**
    ◦ A high rate of co-infection with other **STIs** exists
    ◦ A diagnosis of pubic lice should prompt a **full STI workup**
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A **sexually active patient** presents with the chief complaint of persistent and **intense itching (pruritus)** in the genital region
    ◦ May be **worse at night**
• Patient may report seeing small, crawling "**bugs**" or "**dots**" in their pubic hair
• The patient may have a history of a **new sexual partner**
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**
    ◦ Diagnosis is confirmed by visualizing at least one **live louse** or **nit** on the hair shafts in the affected area
    ◦ A **magnifying glass** or **dermatoscope** can be helpful
• **Microscopy**
    ◦ A suspected louse or nit can be removed with forceps, placed on a slide with mineral oil, and examined under a microscope for definitive identification
• **STI Screening**
    ◦ Due to the high correlation, all patients diagnosed with pediculosis pubis should be **screened for other STIs**
        ▪ Including **gonorrhea**, **chlamydia**, **syphilis**, and **HIV**
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is **excellent** with proper treatment and adherence to management guidelines
• **Treatment failure** is most often due to:
    ◦ **Non-compliance**
    ◦ **Improper application** of medication
    ◦ **Re-infestation** from an untreated partner or contaminated fomites

sections.overview:
• Bedbug bites are cutaneous inflammatory reactions to the saliva of the bedbug, **_Cimex lectularius_** or **_Cimex hemipterus_**.
• The clinical presentation is typically **pruritic**, **erythematous macules** or **papules** on exposed skin, often appearing in a characteristic **linear** or **clustered pattern**.
• While the bites cause significant discomfort and psychological distress, bedbugs are **not known to be significant vectors** for infectious diseases.
• Diagnosis is **clinical**, and management focuses on symptomatic relief and, most importantly, **eradication** of the environmental infestation.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ Caused by the nocturnal, hematophagous (blood-feeding) ectoparasite **_Cimex lectularius_** (common bedbug) or **_Cimex hemipterus_** (tropical bedbug).
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The bedbug pierces the skin and injects saliva containing **anesthetic** and **anticoagulant** properties, which allows it to feed undetected for several minutes.
    ◦ The skin reaction is a **delayed-type (Type IV) hypersensitivity response** to foreign proteins in the bedbug's saliva.
        ▪ An immediate (**Type I**) **IgE-mediated reaction** can also occur.
    ◦ Initial exposure may produce no reaction. **Sensitization** occurs with repeated bites, leading to a more rapid and intense inflammatory response.
    ◦ The inflammatory cascade involves lymphocytes, eosinophils, and mast cells, resulting in localized **erythema**, **edema**, and intense **pruritus**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Distribution**: Worldwide, with a significant resurgence in North America, Europe, and Australia.
• **Incidence**: Affects all individuals regardless of age, sex, socioeconomic status, or hygiene.
• **Transmission**: Bedbugs are passively transported via luggage, clothing, furniture, and other personal belongings. They do not fly or jump.
• **Environment**: Infestations are common in areas with high occupant turnover, such as hotels, apartments, dormitories, shelters, and public transportation.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patient typically presents with a complaint of multiple **"bug bites"** that appeared overnight or upon waking.
• The patient reports intensely **itchy red bumps**.
• Lesions are most often located on skin areas that are **exposed during sleep**, such as the face, neck, arms, hands, and trunk.
• A key historical clue is a **linear** or **grouped arrangement** of the bites.
• Inquire about **recent travel**, new furniture, and whether other household members have similar symptoms.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**
    ◦ Diagnosis is primarily based on the characteristic history and physical exam findings.
• **Definitive Diagnosis**
    ◦ Relies on finding evidence of the infestation in the patient's dwelling. This includes:
        ▪ Visual identification of a live or dead bedbug (adults are **reddish-brown**, **oval**, **flat**, ~5 mm long).
        ▪ Finding shed **exoskeletons** (casings).
        ▪ Observing small, dark **fecal spots** (digested blood) on mattresses, sheets, or furniture.
• **Skin Biopsy**
    ◦ Rarely necessary.
    ◦ If performed, it shows a nonspecific superficial and deep **perivascular infiltrate** with lymphocytes, histiocytes, and numerous **eosinophils**.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for individual skin lesions, which typically self-resolve within 1-2 weeks.
• The overall prognosis depends entirely on the successful **eradication** of the environmental infestation.
• **Recurrence** is very common if the source of the bedbugs is not identified and eliminated.

sections.overview:
• **Alopecia Areata (AA)** is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory disorder that targets anagen (growing) hair follicles, resulting in **non-scarring hair loss**.
    ◦ It typically presents as smooth, well-demarcated, circular patches of hair loss on the scalp or other hair-bearing areas.
    ◦ The clinical course is highly unpredictable, characterized by spontaneous remissions and relapses.
sections.etiology:
• **Autoimmune T-Cell Mediated Attack**: The core mechanism is a T-cell (primarily CD8+) mediated autoimmune attack against the hair follicle bulb.
• **Collapse of Immune Privilege**: Hair follicles in the anagen phase normally have "immune privilege," a state that protects them from the immune system.
    ◦ In AA, this privilege is lost, allowing immune cells to recognize hair follicle autoantigens as foreign and attack them.
• **Inflammatory Infiltrate**: Histologically, this is seen as a dense lymphocytic infiltrate around the hair bulb, classically described as a **"swarm of bees."**
• **Genetic Predisposition**: A strong genetic component exists, with associations to specific HLA genes (e.g., HLA-DR, HLA-DQ) that are involved in antigen presentation.
    ◦ This explains the link to other autoimmune diseases.
• **Triggers**: While the underlying cause is autoimmune, environmental triggers (e.g., viral infections, stress, trauma) may precipitate disease onset in genetically susceptible individuals.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects approximately 2% of the population in their lifetime.
• **Age of Onset**: Can occur at any age, but there is a bimodal peak in childhood and young adulthood (most cases present before age 40).
• **Sex**: Affects males and females equally.
• **Ethnicity**: Occurs in all ethnic groups.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Onset**: Typically sudden onset of asymptomatic, well-demarcated, round or oval patches of complete hair loss.
• **Location**: Most common on the scalp, but can affect any hair-bearing skin, including the beard (**alopecia barbae**), eyebrows, and eyelashes.
• **Skin Appearance**: The underlying skin within the patches is smooth, non-inflamed, and non-scarred.
    ◦ There is no scaling, erythema, or atrophy.
    ◦ Follicular openings remain visible.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Diagnosis is usually made based on history and characteristic physical exam findings.
• **Dermoscopy (Trichoscopy)**: A handheld dermatoscope can aid in diagnosis by revealing:
    ◦ **Yellow dots**: Dilated follicular openings filled with sebum/keratin.
    ◦ **Black dots**: "Cadaverized hairs" (remnants of hair broken at the scalp level).
    ◦ **Exclamation point hairs**.
• **Scalp Biopsy**: Rarely necessary.
    ◦ Performed in atypical cases to rule out scarring alopecia.
• **Histology**: Shows a characteristic **peribulbar lymphocytic infiltrate ("swarm of bees")** around anagen hair follicles without evidence of scarring.
• **Laboratory Studies**:
    ◦ Not required for diagnosis of AA.
    ◦ Consider screening for associated conditions, especially **TSH** and free T4 to rule out thyroid disease.
    ◦ KOH prep or fungal culture can be performed if tinea capitis is suspected.
    ◦ RPR/VDRL if "moth-eaten" alopecia of secondary syphilis is on the differential.
sections.prognosis:
• The course is highly variable and difficult to predict.
• **Favorable Prognostic Factors**:
    ◦ Adult onset
    ◦ Limited, patchy involvement
    ◦ First episode
    ◦ Spontaneous regrowth within one year
• **Poor Prognostic Factors**:
    ◦ Prepubertal onset
    ◦ Extensive involvement (AT/AU)
    ◦ **Ophiasis pattern**
    ◦ Associated nail disease (pitting, trachyonychia)
    ◦ Long duration of hair loss
    ◦ Coexisting atopy or other autoimmune diseases

sections.overview:
• **Androgenetic Alopecia (AGA)** is the most common cause of hair loss in both men and women.
• It is a **non-scarring, progressive** condition characterized by the **miniaturization** of hair follicles and the conversion of **terminal hairs to vellus hairs** in a characteristic pattern.
    ◦ Commonly known as **male-pattern baldness** or **female-pattern hair loss**.
• The condition is driven by a combination of **genetic predisposition** and the action of **androgens**.
sections.etiology:
• AGA is a genetically determined condition with an **androgen-dependent mechanism**.
    ◦ **Genetic Susceptibility**
        ▪ Polygenic inheritance pattern.
        ▪ A positive **family history** is a major risk factor.
    ◦ **Androgen-Mediated Mechanism**
        ▪ **Testosterone** is converted to the more potent androgen **dihydrotestosterone (DHT)** by the enzyme **5-alpha-reductase** (primarily Type 2) located in the dermal papilla of hair follicles.
        ▪ **DHT binds to androgen receptors** in susceptible scalp follicles.
        ▪ This binding triggers a process called **follicular miniaturization**.
        ▪ **Miniaturization**: The **anagen (growth) phase** of the hair cycle becomes progressively shorter, while the **telogen (resting) phase** lengthens.
        ▪ Over successive cycles, large, pigmented **terminal hairs** are replaced by short, fine, non-pigmented **vellus hairs**.
        ▪ Eventually, the follicle may cease to produce hair altogether.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Extremely common; the most frequent cause of hair loss worldwide.
• **Men**: Affects up to **50% of Caucasian men by age 50** and **80% by age 70**.
• **Women**: Affects up to **40% of Caucasian women by age 70**.
• **Race**: Most prevalent in Caucasians; less common in individuals of Asian, African American, and Native American descent.
• **Onset**: Can begin any time after puberty, but typically presents in the 20s-40s for men and often post-menopausally for women.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is a **gradual, progressive, and patterned** hair thinning without signs of inflammation or scarring.
    ◦ **Male Pattern**
        ▪ Typically follows the **Hamilton-Norwood classification scale**.
        ▪ Begins with **bitemporal recession** (receding hairline) and subsequent thinning at the **vertex (crown)**.
        ▪ Over time, these areas coalesce, leaving a rim of hair at the occipital and temporal scalp (areas that are not androgen-sensitive).
    ◦ **Female Pattern**
        ▪ Typically follows the **Ludwig classification scale**.
        ▪ Characterized by **diffuse thinning over the central scalp** with a widened midline part.
        ▪ Crucially, there is **preservation of the frontal hairline**.
        ▪ A common description is the **"Christmas tree" pattern**, where the part is widest frontally and tapers posteriorly.
sections.diagnostics:
• The diagnosis is almost always **clinical**, based on history and physical exam.
    ◦ **Clinical Diagnosis**: A classic history of gradual thinning in a characteristic pattern is usually sufficient.
• **Dermoscopy**: Confirms the diagnosis by visualizing **follicular miniaturization**.
• **Laboratory Studies** (Not routine for men)
    ◦ Indicated for women to rule out other causes, especially if presentation is atypical, rapid, or accompanied by signs of **hyperandrogenism** (e.g., hirsutism, severe acne, menstrual irregularity).
    ◦ **TSH**: Rule out thyroid disease.
    ◦ **CBC, Ferritin**: Rule out iron deficiency anemia.
    ◦ **Total & Free Testosterone, DHEA-S**: Assess for hyperandrogenism (e.g., PCOS).
• **Scalp Biopsy**
    ◦ Rarely necessary; performed only if the diagnosis is uncertain or to rule out a scarring alopecia.
    ◦ A 4-mm punch biopsy would show a **decreased terminal-to-vellus hair ratio (< 4:1)**.
sections.prognosis:
• AGA is a **chronic and progressive** condition.
• Without treatment, hair loss will continue at a variable rate.
• With consistent treatment, progression can be significantly **slowed or halted** in the majority of patients.
• The **earlier treatment is initiated**, the better the potential outcome, as it is more effective at preventing further loss than at regrowing lost hair.

sections.overview:
• Telogen Effluvium (TE) is the second most common cause of **alopecia**.
    ◦ It is a **non-scarring, diffuse hair loss** characterized by an abrupt, excessive shedding of resting (**telogen**) hairs.
    ◦ This occurs after a triggering event pushes a large number of growing (**anagen**) follicles into a premature resting state.
    ◦ The condition is typically **self-limiting**, with hair regrowth occurring once the underlying trigger is removed or resolves.
sections.etiology:
• The pathophysiology of TE is rooted in the disruption of the normal hair growth cycle.
    ◦ **Normal Hair Cycle**:
        ▪ **Anagen (Growth Phase):** Lasts 2-6 years. ~85-90% of scalp hairs are in this phase.
        ▪ **Catagen (Transitional Phase):** Lasts 1-2 weeks. Follicle shrinks. ~1% of hairs.
        ▪ **Telogen (Resting Phase):** Lasts 2-4 months. ~10-15% of hairs. The hair shaft is anchored by a "**club hair**" and is eventually shed to make way for a new anagen hair.
    ◦ **Pathophysiology of TE**:
        ▪ A significant physiologic or emotional stressor causes a large number of anagen follicles to prematurely and synchronously enter the telogen phase.
        ▪ These hairs then remain in the telogen phase for their typical duration (about 3 months) before being shed.
        ▪ This synchronous shedding results in a clinically apparent, **diffuse hair loss**.
        ▪ The key is the **premature termination of the anagen phase**.
    ◦ **Common Triggers**:
        ▪ **Physiologic Stress**:
            ▪ Childbirth (**postpartum telogen effluvium**)
            ▪ High fever / severe infection (e.g., COVID-19, influenza)
            ▪ Major surgery
            ▪ Severe trauma
            ▪ **Rapid weight loss** / crash dieting
        ▪ **Emotional Stress**:
            ▪ Death of a loved one, divorce, major life change
        ▪ **Medical Conditions**:
            ▪ **Thyroid disorders** (hypo- and hyperthyroidism)
            ▪ **Nutritional deficiencies** (esp. **iron**, but also zinc, biotin, protein)
        ▪ **Medications**:
            ▪ Beta-blockers, anticoagulants, retinoids (isotretinoin, high-dose vitamin A), ACE inhibitors, lithium.
            ▪ Starting or stopping oral contraceptives can also be a trigger.
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects all ages, sexes, and races.
• More commonly diagnosed and reported in women, likely due to greater concern over hair thinning.
• It is the most common cause of **diffuse hair loss in women**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **History is key.** The patient reports an **abrupt onset of increased hair shedding**, typically **2-4 months after an identifiable trigger**.
• The chief complaint is often finding large amounts of hair in the shower drain, on a pillow, or in a hairbrush.
• Patients describe a **diffuse thinning** of hair over the entire scalp, not concentrated in one area.
    ◦ They may note their ponytail feels thinner or their part line appears wider.
sections.diagnostics:
• TE is primarily a **clinical diagnosis** based on history and physical exam.
• **Laboratory Studies (to identify underlying triggers)**:
    ◦ **CBC:** To rule out anemia.
    ◦ **TSH:** To rule out thyroid dysfunction.
    ◦ **Ferritin:** The most important test to assess for **iron deficiency**, which is a very common and reversible cause. A level <40-70 ng/mL may be implicated even if within the lab's normal range.
    ◦ Consider Vitamin D, zinc levels.
• **Trichoscopy (Dermoscopy)**:
    ◦ Can be used to examine the scalp and hair shafts.
    ◦ In TE, it shows **empty follicular openings** and **normal hair shaft diameters**.
    ◦ It is useful for differentiating TE from androgenetic alopecia (which shows hair shaft diameter variability/miniaturization).
• **Scalp Biopsy**:
    ◦ Rarely necessary. Performed if the diagnosis is uncertain or to rule out scarring alopecia.
    ◦ **Findings:** A horizontal section will show an increased percentage of **telogen follicles** (typically >20%; normal is 10-15%). There is no significant inflammation.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent.** For acute telogen effluvium with an identifiable and removable trigger, the prognosis is **full hair recovery**.
• Regrowth typically begins within **3-6 months** after the trigger is gone.
• If the trigger is ongoing (e.g., chronic illness, persistent nutritional deficiency), the condition can become **Chronic Telogen Effluvium**.

sections.overview:
• **Anagen effluvium** is a rapid, diffuse, non-scarring hair loss caused by an acute insult to the hair follicle during the **anagen (growth) phase**.
    ◦ This insult abruptly arrests the mitotic activity of the hair matrix cells, leading to a weakened, malformed hair shaft that fractures and sheds easily.
    ◦ It is most classically associated with **chemotherapy**.
    ◦ The hair loss is typically extensive and begins within days to weeks of the inciting event.
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The core mechanism is the **sudden cessation of mitosis** in the rapidly dividing cells of the hair bulb matrix.
        ▪ **Anagen Phase**: Approximately 85-90% of scalp hairs are in the **anagen (growth) phase** at any given time. This phase is characterized by high metabolic and mitotic activity.
        ▪ **The Insult**: A cytotoxic, inflammatory, or metabolic insult directly damages these highly active matrix cells.
        ▪ **Arrested Growth**: Mitosis stops, leading to the production of a weakened, narrowed, or incompletely keratinized hair shaft.
        ▪ **Shaft Fracture & Shedding**: The hair shaft becomes constricted and fragile, causing it to break off within the follicle or at the scalp surface. This results in rapid, widespread shedding of anagen hairs.
    ◦ This is distinct from **Telogen Effluvium**, where a stressor causes hairs to prematurely enter the telogen (resting) phase, with shedding occurring 2-4 months later.
• **Etiology (Causes)**
    ◦ **Chemotherapy (Most Common)**
        ▪ Alkylating agents (e.g., **cyclophosphamide**)
        ▪ Antimetabolites (e.g., **methotrexate**, **5-fluorouracil**)
        ▪ Mitotic inhibitors (e.g., taxanes like **paclitaxel**, **docetaxel**; vinca alkaloids)
    ◦ **Radiation Therapy**
        ▪ Affects hair follicles only within the direct radiation field.
    ◦ **Toxins / Poisoning**
        ▪ Heavy metals: **Thallium** (classic board question), **arsenic**, **mercury**, **lead**
        ▪ **Boric acid**, **colchicine**
    ◦ **Severe Malnutrition**
        ▪ Profound protein-energy malnutrition (**Kwashiorkor**)
        ▪ Severe zinc or biotin deficiency
    ◦ **Autoimmune Diseases**
        ▪ **Pemphigus vulgaris** (oral erosions are key)
        ▪ Severe, diffuse **Alopecia Areata** (can present similarly)
sections.epidemiology:
• Incidence is directly related to the prevalence of the underlying causes, particularly cancer treatment.
• Affects up to **65% of patients receiving chemotherapy**.
    ◦ The likelihood and severity depend on the specific drug, dose, duration, and route of administration.
• No specific predilection for age, sex, or ethnicity, other than through exposure to causative agents.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **History is Key**: The diagnosis is often made from the patient's history.
    ◦ **Onset**: Abrupt and dramatic onset of hair shedding, typically **7-14 days** after exposure to the inciting agent (e.g., first cycle of chemotherapy).
    ◦ **Pattern**: Diffuse hair loss affecting the entire scalp, often leading to near-total (**alopecia totalis**) or total body hair loss (**alopecia universalis**).
    ◦ **Associated History**: Patient will report recent initiation of chemotherapy, radiation therapy, or known toxin exposure.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primarily a clinical diagnosis** based on a clear history of a causative exposure followed by rapid, diffuse hair loss.
• **Hair Pull Test & Microscopic Exam**: The most useful and rapid diagnostic step to confirm the type of hair being shed (**dystrophic anagen vs. telogen club hair**).
• **Scalp Biopsy**: Rarely necessary. If performed, it would show:
    ◦ Anagen follicles with marked **follicular necrosis**, **pigment clumping (melanin incontinence)**, and **matrix degeneration**.
    ◦ Absence of significant perifollicular inflammation (helps differentiate from alopecia areata).
• **Lab Tests**: Generally not indicated unless the etiology is unclear, in which case a toxicology screen (e.g., for heavy metals) may be considered.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for hair regrowth.
• Once the insult is removed, hair follicles (which are not permanently destroyed) re-enter a normal anagen phase.
• Visible regrowth typically begins within **1-3 months** and becomes substantial by **3-6 months**.
• Full recovery is expected in most cases.

sections.overview: • Hirsutism is the excess growth of terminal hair (coarse, dark, thick) in females in an androgen-dependent (male-pattern) distribution. ◦ This includes areas like the upper lip, chin, chest, linea alba, lower back, and inner thighs. • It is a clinical sign of hyperandrogenism (excess androgens) or increased hair follicle sensitivity to androgens, not a disease itself. • It is crucial to differentiate hirsutism from hypertrichosis, which is generalized, non-sexual hair growth that is not androgen-dependent.
sections.etiology: • The underlying mechanism is either excessive androgen production from the ovaries or adrenal glands, or increased sensitivity of the hair follicle to normal androgen levels. • The enzyme 5-alpha-reductase in the hair follicle converts testosterone to the more potent dihydrotestosterone (DHT), which stimulates the transformation of vellus hair to terminal hair. • Common Causes (by Source): ◦ Ovarian (Most Common) ▪ Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS): The most common cause (>80%). Characterized by anovulation, hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound. Often associated with insulin resistance. ▪ Androgen-Secreting Ovarian Tumors: Rare but serious. Examples include Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors. Suspect with rapid onset of severe hirsutism and virilization. ◦ Adrenal ▪ Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH): Most commonly due to a 21-hydroxylase deficiency. The "non-classic" or "late-onset" form presents post-puberty with hirsutism and menstrual irregularities. ▪ Cushing's Syndrome: Excess cortisol can be associated with excess adrenal androgen production. ▪ Androgen-Secreting Adrenal Tumors: Rare but must be considered with very high DHEA-S levels. ◦ Idiopathic Hirsutism ▪ Hirsutism with normal ovulatory function and normal serum androgen levels. ▪ Thought to be due to increased peripheral 5-alpha-reductase activity or altered androgen receptor sensitivity. A diagnosis of exclusion. ◦ Iatrogenic / Medications ▪ Anabolic steroids (e.g., testosterone, DHEA supplements) ▪ Danazol ▪ Progestins with high androgenic activity
sections.epidemiology: • Affects approximately 5-10% of reproductive-aged women. • Prevalence varies by ethnicity, with higher rates in women of Mediterranean, South Asian, and Middle Eastern descent. • PCOS is the underlying cause in over 80% of cases. • Idiopathic hirsutism accounts for 5-15% of cases. • Tumors are a rare cause (<0.5%).
sections.clinicalPresentation: • The presentation is guided by the onset, severity, and associated symptoms. A thorough history is critical. • Key History Questions: ◦ Onset and Progression: ▪ Gradual, peripubertal onset: Suggests a benign cause like PCOS or idiopathic hirsutism. ▪ Rapid, severe onset (especially post-menopausal): RED FLAG for an androgen-secreting tumor. ◦ Menstrual History: Irregular menses (oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea) is a hallmark of PCOS. ◦ Signs of Virilization: Voice deepening, clitoromegaly, increased muscle mass, temporal balding. These are RED FLAGS for very high androgen levels, strongly suggesting a tumor. ◦ Medication/Supplement History: Inquire about steroids, DHEA, etc. ◦ Family History.
sections.diagnostics: • The workup is aimed at identifying the source of androgen excess. • Initial Laboratory Workup: ◦ Total Testosterone: The best initial test. ▪ Mildly elevated: Suggests PCOS or idiopathic. ▪ > 200 ng/dL: RED FLAG. Highly suspicious for an androgen-secreting tumor. ◦ DHEA-S (Dehydroepiandrosterone Sulfate): ▪ Marker for adrenal androgen production. ▪ Mildly elevated: Can be seen in PCOS or CAH. ▪ > 700 mcg/dL: RED FLAG. Highly suspicious for an adrenal tumor. • Further Labs (if indicated by history/exam): ◦ 17-Hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP): Order if CAH is suspected. Best drawn in the early morning during the follicular phase of the menstrual cycle. ◦ Prolactin: If menstrual dysfunction or galactorrhea is present. ◦ TSH: To rule out thyroid dysfunction as a cause of menstrual irregularity. ◦ Cortisol: 24-hour urinary free cortisol or overnight dexamethasone suppression test if Cushing's syndrome is suspected. ◦ Fasting Glucose and Lipid Panel: To screen for metabolic syndrome in patients with suspected PCOS. • Imaging: ◦ Transvaginal Pelvic Ultrasound: Indicated if a palpable adnexal mass, very high testosterone, or to confirm polycystic ovarian morphology for PCOS diagnosis. ◦ CT or MRI of Adrenal Glands: Indicated if DHEA-S is markedly elevated.
sections.prognosis:
• For benign causes like PCOS and idiopathic hirsutism, the prognosis is excellent with regard to health, but it is a chronic condition requiring lifelong management.
• The prognosis for hirsutism caused by a tumor depends on whether the tumor is benign or malignant and the stage at diagnosis.
• Hair growth typically resumes if medical therapy is discontinued.

sections.overview:
• Onychomycosis is a fungal infection of the nail apparatus, including the nail plate, nail bed, and nail matrix.
• It is the most common cause of nail dystrophy.
• The term **tinea unguium** specifically refers to onychomycosis caused by dermatophytes.
• This condition is often chronic, difficult to treat, and has a high rate of recurrence.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects approximately 10% of the general population.
• Prevalence increases significantly with age:
    ◦ <1% in children, but up to 50% in individuals over 70.
• More common in toenails than fingernails (ratio of ~10:1).
• Slightly more common in men than women.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Onychomycosis is classified into several clinical subtypes based on the pattern of nail invasion.
• **Distal and Lateral Subungual Onychomycosis (DLSO)**
    ◦ **Most common subtype (~90%)**.
    ◦ Fungus invades the hyponychium and distal nail bed.
    ◦ Starts as a white, yellow, or brown discoloration at the distal or lateral edge of the nail and spreads proximally.
    ◦ Associated with subungual hyperkeratosis and onycholysis.
• **White Superficial Onychomycosis (WSO)**
    ◦ Less common (~10%).
    ◦ Caused by direct fungal invasion of the dorsal (top) surface of the nail plate.
    ◦ Presents as well-demarcated, "chalky" white patches or islands on the nail plate.
    ◦ The affected areas can often be easily scraped off.
    ◦ Most commonly caused by *T. mentagrophytes*.
• **Proximal Subungual Onychomycosis (PSO)**
    ◦ **Rarest subtype in the general population**.
    ◦ Fungus enters via the cuticle (proximal nail fold) and invades the nail plate from underneath.
    ◦ Presents as a white or yellowish area near the lunula that moves distally as the nail grows.
    ◦ **Strongly associated with immunosuppression, particularly HIV/AIDS**. Its presence should prompt an HIV workup in at-risk individuals.
• **Endonyx Onychomycosis (EO)**
    ◦ Fungus invades the interior of the nail plate directly without causing nail bed inflammation.
    ◦ Presents with milky white discoloration but notably **lacks subungual hyperkeratosis or onycholysis**.
• **Total Dystrophic Onychomycosis (TDO)**
    ◦ The end-stage of any of the above subtypes.
    ◦ The entire nail unit is involved, resulting in a thickened, crumbling, and dystrophic nail plate.
sections.diagnostics:
• Confirmation of fungal infection is crucial before initiating long-term systemic therapy.
• **KOH Preparation (Potassium Hydroxide)**
    ◦ **Procedure:** Nail clippings and subungual debris are placed on a slide with 10-20% KOH solution and gently heated.
    ◦ **Findings:** The KOH dissolves keratin, making fungal elements more visible. Look for **septate hyphae**.
    ◦ **Utility:** Rapid, inexpensive, in-office test. Operator-dependent with moderate sensitivity.
• **Fungal Culture**
    ◦ **Procedure:** Sample is plated on media like Sabouraud agar.
    ◦ **Findings:** Identifies the specific species of fungus.
    ◦ **Utility:** High specificity but low sensitivity. Takes 2-4 weeks for results. Useful for guiding therapy if non-dermatophytes are suspected.
• **Nail Clipping with PAS Stain (Periodic Acid-Schiff)**
    ◦ **Procedure:** A clipped portion of the affected nail is sent for histopathology.
    ◦ **Findings:** The PAS stain highlights fungal elements (hyphae, spores) in pink/red against a light background.
    ◦ **Utility:** **The most sensitive and specific test ("Gold Standard")**.
• **PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction)**
    ◦ **Procedure:** Detects fungal DNA from a nail sample.
    ◦ **Utility:** High sensitivity and specificity, rapid results. Becoming more common but is more expensive.
sections.prognosis:
• With appropriate systemic therapy, mycological cure rates (negative culture/KOH) can be 60-80%.
• Clinical cure rates (completely clear nail) are lower, around 40-60%.
• **Recurrence rates are high**, estimated at 15-25% within 2 years, even after successful treatment.
• Prognosis is worse in patients with significant risk factors (e.g., uncontrolled diabetes, PVD).

sections.overview:
• Paronychia is an inflammation or infection of the tissue folds surrounding the nail plate (the perionychium)
    ◦ It is the most common hand infection in the United States
    ◦ Classified based on duration
        ▪ **Acute Paronychia**: Duration of less than 6 weeks. Typically caused by a bacterial pathogen following a break in the skin
        ▪ **Chronic Paronychia**: Duration of 6 weeks or more. Typically a multifactorial inflammatory condition, often with secondary fungal colonization, related to chronic irritant exposure
sections.etiology:
• The protective barrier between the nail plate and the nail fold (the cuticle or eponychium) is compromised, allowing pathogens to enter
    ◦ **Acute Paronychia**
        ▪ **Mechanism**: Direct or indirect trauma to the cuticle or nail fold creates a portal of entry for bacteria
        ▪ **Common Causes of Trauma**: **Nail biting** (onychophagia), aggressive manicuring, hangnails, finger sucking (in children), ingrown nails
        ▪ **Causative Organisms**
            ◦ **Most Common**: ***Staphylococcus aureus*** (including MRSA)
            ◦ Others: ***Streptococcus pyogenes***, ***Pseudomonas***, Proteus species
            ◦ Oral Flora (associated with nail biting/finger sucking): Anaerobes like ***Fusobacterium***, ***Peptostreptococcus***, and ***Eikenella corrodens***
    ◦ **Chronic Paronychia**
        ▪ **Mechanism**: A chronic, irritant-induced dermatitis of the nail fold. Repetitive exposure to moisture, allergens, or irritants (e.g., soaps, detergents, chemicals) damages the cuticle. This leads to chronic inflammation, swelling, and separation of the nail fold from the nail plate, creating a space for opportunistic colonization
        ▪ **Causative Organisms**
            ◦ **Most Common**: ***Candida albicans*** is the primary colonizer, not necessarily the primary cause
            ◦ Bacterial superinfection can also occur
sections.epidemiology:
• The most common infection of the hand
• More common in females than males (ratio approx. 3:1), often linked to manicures and "wet work"
• **Acute paronychia** is common in both children (finger sucking) and adults (trauma)
• **Chronic paronychia** is frequently seen in occupations with prolonged water or chemical exposure
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with pain, swelling, and redness localized to one of the lateral or proximal nail folds
    ◦ The onset of symptoms helps differentiate between acute (rapid, over hours to days) and chronic (insidious, over weeks to months)
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is almost always **clinical** based on history and physical exam
    ◦ **Laboratory Studies**: Typically not required for uncomplicated cases
    ◦ **Gram Stain and Culture**: Indicated for
        ▪ Severe or refractory cases
        ▪ Suspected **MRSA**
        ▪ Immunocompromised patients
        ▪ A sample can be obtained by expressing pus or by lifting the nail fold with a needle
    ◦ **KOH Prep**: Can be performed on nail fold scrapings in chronic cases to look for ***Candida*** pseudohyphae
    ◦ **Imaging (X-ray)**: Rarely needed
        ▪ Consider if there is suspicion for a retained foreign body or **osteomyelitis** of the distal phalanx (e.g., severe pain, elevated inflammatory markers, failure to improve with drainage)
sections.prognosis:
• **Acute**: Excellent with appropriate and timely treatment
• **Chronic**: Generally good, but the condition often follows a relapsing and remitting course
    ◦ Patient adherence to management strategies is the most important factor for long-term success

sections.overview:
• A **felon** is a **closed-space abscess** of the **distal pulp** or pad of a finger or thumb.
• It is a true orthopedic emergency because the unique anatomy of the fingertip, with its multiple vertical fibrous septa, creates a non-compliant space.
• As pus accumulates, pressure builds rapidly, acting as a **compartment syndrome** of the fingertip.
• This can lead to compression of digital arteries, resulting in **tissue necrosis**, **osteomyelitis**, and **septic arthritis** if not treated urgently with **incision and drainage**.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects individuals of all ages.
• More common in adults, particularly those who perform manual labor or are at risk for penetrating fingertip injuries.
• Incidence is increased in patients with **diabetes mellitus** and those who are **immunocompromised**.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Penetrating trauma** to the fingertip.
• Occupations: Manual laborers, carpenters, gardeners, healthcare workers.
• Medical Conditions: **Diabetes mellitus** (especially with home glucose monitoring), **immunosuppression** (HIV, chronic steroid use).
• Behaviors: Nail biting, aggressive manicures, hangnail manipulation.
• Untreated **paronychia**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with a history of a minor penetrating injury to the fingertip 1-5 days prior, complaining of a rapid onset of severe, localized pain that has become progressively worse and is now **throbbing** and unbearable.
    ◦ The pain is often described as disproportionate to the visible signs and is worse when the hand is in a dependent position.
• **Symptoms**:
    ◦ **Severe, throbbing, constant pain** in the **distal pad** of the digit.
    ◦ Swelling and redness of the fingertip.
    ◦ Sensation of pressure or fullness.
    ◦ Pain worsened by dependency (hanging hand down) and relieved by elevation.
    ◦ Possible decreased sensation in the fingertip (a late sign due to nerve compression).
sections.physicalExam:
• **Location**: Swelling, erythema, and induration are **strictly confined to the distal pulp** and do not cross the DIP joint flexion crease.
• **Palpation**:
    ◦ **Exquisite point tenderness** over the volar pulp.
    ◦ The fingertip is tense, firm, and often warm to the touch.
    ◦ **Fluctuance** may be present but is often difficult to appreciate due to the tense, septated nature of the pulp space.
• **Inspection**:
    ◦ The area may appear shiny and taut.
    ◦ A central area of pallor or necrosis may be visible if vascular compromise has occurred.
• **Range of Motion**:
    ◦ Pain with passive motion of the DIP joint is usually minimal unless the infection has spread to cause **septic arthritis**.
• **Systemic Signs**:
    ◦ Check for ascending **lymphangitis** (red streaks up the arm) and tender epitrochlear or axillary lymphadenopathy.
    ◦ **Fever** is uncommon unless the infection is severe or systemic.
sections.diagnostics:
• The diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on history and physical exam findings.
• **X-ray (AP, Lateral, and Oblique views)**:
    ◦ Not for initial diagnosis, but essential to rule out complications.
    ◦ **Findings**:
        ▪ Look for a retained radiopaque **foreign body**.
        ▪ Assess for **osteomyelitis** (bony erosion, periosteal reaction); these changes are typically not visible until 1-2 weeks after symptom onset.
        ▪ Evaluate for **septic arthritis** (joint space narrowing) of the DIP joint.
        ▪ Check for soft tissue gas, suggesting an anaerobic infection.
• **Ultrasound**:
    ◦ Can be a useful adjunct to confirm the presence of a drainable fluid collection (**abscess**).
    ◦ Helps differentiate a felon from cellulitis (which would not have a discrete collection).
    ◦ Can be used to guide the incision for drainage.
• **Labs**:
    ◦ WBC and inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR) may be elevated but are non-specific and often normal in localized infections.
• **Wound Culture**:
    ◦ **Crucial**. Obtain pus during I&D for Gram stain, culture, and sensitivity to guide antibiotic therapy.
sections.treatment:
• **Anesthesia**:
    ◦ **Digital nerve block** is essential for adequate drainage.
    ◦ **NEVER use epinephrine** in the anesthetic solution, as it can cause vasospasm and digital ischemia/necrosis.
• **Incision & Drainage (I&D)**:
    ◦ **Goal**: To decompress the pulp space, drain the pus, and disrupt the fibrous septa to prevent re-accumulation.
    ◦ **Technique**:
        ▪ **Unilateral Longitudinal Incision**: The preferred method. The incision is made on the non-contact (ulnar side of index/middle/ring fingers, radial side of thumb/small finger) aspect of the distal phalanx, just dorsal to the neurovascular bundle.
        ▪ **Midline Longitudinal Volar Incision**: An alternative, made directly over the area of maximal fluctuance. Avoids neurovascular structures but may result in a painful scar on the gripping surface.
        ▪ **AVOID**: "Fish-mouth" or "hockey-stick" incisions are no longer recommended due to high complication rates (unstable finger pad, nerve injury, poor healing).
    ◦ **Procedure**: After incision, a small hemostat is inserted to bluntly dissect and break up all septa, ensuring complete drainage. The wound is then copiously irrigated with sterile saline.
    ◦ **Packing**: The wound is loosely packed with a small strip of iodoform or plain gauze to allow for continued drainage.
• **Antibiotics**:
    ◦ Used as an adjunct to I&D.
    ◦ **Empiric coverage** should target ***S. aureus*** (including **MRSA**) and ***Streptococcus***.
    ◦ **Oral options**: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Bactrim) or Doxycycline (for **MRSA**) **PLUS** Cephalexin (Keflex) or Amoxicillin-Clavulanate (Augmentin) (for Strep). Clindamycin can be used as monotherapy.
    ◦ **IV options (for severe infection)**: Vancomycin or Linezolid.
    ◦ Antibiotic choice should be narrowed based on culture and sensitivity results.
sections.management:
• **Post-I&D Care**:
    ◦ The hand should be **splinted** in a position of function and **strictly elevated** above the heart to minimize edema and pain.
    ◦ **Pain Control**: NSAIDs and/or opioid analgesics.
    ◦ **Tetanus Prophylaxis**: Administer if not up-to-date.
• **Follow-up**:
    ◦ The patient should be re-evaluated in **24-48 hours**.
    ◦ Packing is typically removed at the first follow-up visit.
    ◦ Begin warm soaks or saline irrigations to promote drainage and healing by secondary intention.
sections.complications:
• **Osteomyelitis** of the distal phalanx (most common serious complication).
• **Infectious flexor tenosynovitis**.
• **Septic arthritis** of the DIP joint.
• Pulp necrosis and skin sloughing.
• Chronic pain, fingertip numbness, or neuroma formation.
• Unstable finger pad from improper incision technique.
• Sepsis (rare).
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** with prompt diagnosis and appropriate surgical drainage. Full recovery is expected.
• **Poor** if treatment is delayed. Delayed treatment can lead to the complications listed above, potentially resulting in chronic pain, stiffness, or the need for amputation of the distal phalanx.

sections.overview:
• Psoriatic nail dystrophy, or psoriatic onychodystrophy, refers to the characteristic changes in the fingernails and toenails that occur in patients with psoriasis
    ◦ It is a common manifestation of the disease, affecting up to 50% of patients with psoriasis and over 80% of patients with **psoriatic arthritis (PsA)**
    ◦ Nail involvement can be an isolated finding but often co-exists with skin and joint disease
    ◦ The presence of nail psoriasis is a significant predictor for the development of **PsA**
• The specific nail changes observed depend on whether the psoriatic inflammation affects the nail matrix or the nail bed
sections.etiology:
• Psoriatic nail disease is an immune-mediated inflammatory condition driven by a combination of genetic predisposition and environmental triggers
    ◦ **Genetics**: Strong association with specific HLA alleles, particularly **HLA-Cw6**
    ◦ **Pathophysiology**: The process mirrors cutaneous psoriasis, involving T-cell-mediated inflammation with dysregulation of cytokines, primarily **TNF-alpha, IL-17, and IL-23**
• **Nail Matrix Involvement**: Inflammation of the nail matrix (the tissue from which the nail plate grows) disrupts normal nail formation (onychosynthesis)
    ◦ **Proximal Matrix**: Affects the superficial nail plate, causing **pitting**
    ◦ **Distal Matrix**: Affects the deeper nail plate, causing **leukonychia** or **nail plate crumbling**
• **Nail Bed Involvement**: Inflammation of the nail bed and hyponychium leads to:
    ◦ **Onycholysis**: Separation of the nail plate from the nail bed
    ◦ **"Oil Drop" / "Salmon Patch"**: Localized areas of psoriatic inflammation in the nail bed
    ◦ **Subungual Hyperkeratosis**: Increased proliferation and scaling of the nail bed epidermis
    ◦ **Splinter Hemorrhages**: Rupture of dilated, tortuous capillaries in the nail bed
• **Koebner Phenomenon**: Trauma or injury to the nail or surrounding digit can trigger or exacerbate psoriatic nail changes
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects approximately 10-55% of all patients with psoriasis
• **Association with PsA**: Significantly more common in patients with **psoriatic arthritis**, with a prevalence of **80-90%**
• **Predictive Value**: The presence and severity of nail psoriasis are strong independent risk factors for the development of **PsA**
• **Onset**: Can occur at any age, often developing years after the initial skin diagnosis
    ◦ In ~5-10% of cases, nail changes may precede skin or joint findings
• **Distribution**: Fingernails are more commonly affected than toenails
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is highly variable, ranging from a single pitted nail to severe dystrophy of all twenty nails
• It can cause significant cosmetic disfigurement and functional disability
• Patients may present with complaints about the appearance of their nails or with symptoms of pain and difficulty with manual tasks
• It is crucial to examine the nails in any patient with joint pain or a rash, even if they do not mention nail issues
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is typically **clinical**, based on characteristic nail findings in a patient with a personal or family history of psoriasis or **PsA**
    ◦ **Primary Tool**: Clinical examination of all 20 nails
    ◦ **Dermoscopy**: Can help visualize nail bed capillaries (dilated, tortuous) and differentiate from onychomycosis
• **Rule out Onychomycosis**: Because psoriatic nails can be secondarily infected with fungus and the presentations can mimic each other, it's often necessary to perform:
    ◦ **KOH preparation** of nail clippings/debris
    ◦ **Fungal culture**
    ◦ **Nail clipping with PAS (Periodic acid-Schiff) stain**, which has the highest sensitivity
• **Nail Biopsy**: Rarely performed but is the **gold standard** for a definitive diagnosis if needed
    ◦ Performance is limited due to pain and risk of permanent nail damage
sections.prognosis:
• Psoriatic nail disease is a chronic, relapsing condition
