• It is often refractory to topical treatments alone
• Systemic and biologic therapies offer the best chance for significant improvement or clearance, but relapse can occur upon cessation of treatment
• The presence of nail disease indicates a more severe psoriatic phenotype and warrants closer monitoring for comorbidities, especially **PsA**

sections.overview:
• A **pressure (decubitus) ulcer**, also known as a **pressure injury** or **pressure sore**, is a localized injury to the skin and/or underlying tissue, usually over a **bony prominence**
• The injury results from sustained **pressure**, or pressure in combination with **shear** and/or **friction**, which leads to **tissue ischemia and necrosis**
• These ulcers are staged based on the depth of tissue destruction
sections.etiology:
• The primary mechanism is **sustained external pressure** that exceeds the arteriolar end-capillary pressure (typically >32 mmHg), occluding blood flow and lymphatic drainage, leading to:
    ◦ **Ischemia**: Deprivation of oxygen and nutrients to the tissue
    ◦ **Hypoxia**: Reduced oxygen levels cause a shift to anaerobic metabolism, leading to lactic acid accumulation and a drop in tissue pH
    ◦ **Cell Death**: Prolonged ischemia leads to irreversible cell damage and necrosis
    ◦ **Reperfusion Injury**: When pressure is relieved, the return of blood flow can introduce inflammatory mediators and oxygen-free radicals, causing further tissue damage
• **Key Contributing Forces**:
    ◦ **Pressure**: Perpendicular force compressing tissues between a bony prominence and an external surface
    ◦ **Shear**: Parallel force created when skin stays stationary but underlying tissue and bone shift (e.g., sliding down in a hospital bed), which stretches and distorts blood vessels
    ◦ **Friction**: The force of two surfaces moving across one another (e.g., dragging a patient across bed linens), which can strip the epidermis and increase susceptibility to pressure injury
    ◦ **Moisture**: Macerates the skin, weakening its integrity and making it more vulnerable to pressure, shear, and friction (e.g., from incontinence, sweat, wound drainage)
sections.epidemiology:
• Highly prevalent in healthcare settings, particularly long-term care facilities, hospitals (especially ICUs), and rehabilitation centers
• Highest incidence in elderly patients (>65 years old), individuals with spinal cord injuries, and the critically ill
• Most common locations are over bony prominences:
    ◦ **Sacrum/Coccyx (~40%)**
    ◦ **Greater Trochanter**
    ◦ **Ischial Tuberosity**
    ◦ **Heels**
    ◦ **Lateral Malleolus**
sections.clinicalPresentation: • A patient at risk (e.g., an elderly, **bed-bound** resident of a **nursing home** with multiple comorbidities) is noted to have a new area of skin discoloration, blistering, or an open sore over a **bony prominence** during a routine skin assessment
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primarily a clinical diagnosis** based on history and physical exam
• **Wound Culture**:
    ◦ Indicated for wounds with clinical signs of infection (new/increasing pain, purulent drainage, erythema, warmth, fever)
    ◦ **Needle aspiration or tissue biopsy is the gold standard**, as surface swabs often reflect colonization, not true infection
• **Laboratory Studies**:
    ◦ **CBC**: To assess for leukocytosis (infection)
    ◦ **ESR/CRP**: Non-specific inflammatory markers, useful for tracking response to treatment for osteomyelitis
    ◦ **Serum Albumin/Prealbumin**: To assess nutritional status
    ◦ **Blood Cultures**: If sepsis or bacteremia is suspected
• **Imaging**:
    ◦ **Plain X-ray**: Initial imaging to evaluate for bony abnormalities or gas in soft tissues, but has low sensitivity for early osteomyelitis
    ◦ **MRI**: **Most sensitive and specific imaging modality for diagnosing underlying osteomyelitis**
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly variable and depends on the ulcer stage, patient comorbidities, nutritional status, and the quality of care
• **Stage 1 and 2** ulcers typically heal with appropriate intervention
• **Stage 3 and 4** ulcers are very difficult to heal, have high rates of recurrence, and are associated with increased **morbidity and mortality**, particularly in the elderly

sections.overview:
• A chronic, non-healing wound on the lower extremity, typically the ankle, caused by sustained **venous hypertension** and **chronic venous insufficiency (CVI)**.
• It is the most common type of lower extremity ulceration.
• Represents a final, severe manifestation of CVI.
sections.etiology:
• The underlying cause is **Chronic Venous Insufficiency (CVI)**.
• The pathophysiology follows a sequence known as the **"ambulatory venous hypertension"** cascade:
    ◦ **Valvular Incompetence:** Valves in the deep, superficial, or perforator veins of the legs fail.
        ▪ This is often secondary to prior **deep vein thrombosis (DVT)**, trauma, or congenital weakness.
    ◦ **Venous Reflux:** Blood flows retrograde (backwards) down the leg instead of towards the heart, especially during standing or walking.
    ◦ **Venous Hypertension:** The reflux leads to persistently elevated pressure in the veins of the lower leg.
    ◦ **Microcirculatory Changes:**
        ▪ Capillaries become distended and permeable.
        ▪ **Fluid & Macromolecules Leak:** Plasma, red blood cells (RBCs), and fibrinogen leak into the surrounding interstitial tissue, causing edema.
        ▪ **Fibrin Cuffs:** Fibrinogen polymerizes into fibrin, forming "cuffs" around capillaries that impair the diffusion of oxygen and nutrients to the skin.
        ▪ **Hemosiderin Deposition:** Extravasated RBCs break down, releasing iron which deposits as hemosiderin, causing the characteristic brawny, hyperpigmented skin.
        ▪ **Inflammation:** Trapped leukocytes release inflammatory mediators, leading to chronic inflammation, tissue damage, and fibrosis.
    ◦ **Tissue Breakdown:** The skin becomes hypoxic, malnourished, and fibrotic (**lipodermatosclerosis**), leading to the formation of an ulcer that heals poorly.
sections.epidemiology:
• Accounts for **~80%** of all lower extremity ulcers.
• Prevalence increases significantly with age, affecting 1-3% of the elderly population.
• More common in females than males.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with a chronic, slowly enlarging wound on the lower leg that has been present for weeks to months and has failed to heal with simple dressings.
• The ulcer is often surrounded by signs of CVI.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis:** Diagnosis is often made based on the characteristic history and physical exam findings.
• **Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI):**
    ◦ **ESSENTIAL initial test** to rule out significant coexisting **Peripheral Arterial Disease (PAD)** before initiating compression therapy.
    ◦ **ABI > 0.9:** Normal. Safe for full compression.
    ◦ **ABI 0.5 - 0.9:** Mixed arterial-venous disease. Reduced compression is required.
    ◦ **ABI < 0.5:** Severe PAD. **Compression is contraindicated**. Refer to vascular surgery.
• **Venous Duplex Ultrasound:**
    ◦ **Gold standard** for confirming CVI.
    ◦ Identifies the location and severity of venous reflux and/or obstruction.
    ◦ Helps guide potential surgical or endovenous interventions.
• **Wound Culture:**
    ◦ Only indicated for clinical signs of infection (spreading erythema, purulence, fever, increased pain), not for routine colonization.
• **Biopsy:**
    ◦ Consider if the ulcer is atypical in appearance, recalcitrant to standard therapy, or rapidly enlarging, to rule out malignancy (e.g., **Marjolin's ulcer**).
sections.prognosis:
• Healing is often slow, taking weeks to months.
• **High recurrence rate (up to 70%)** if the underlying venous hypertension is not managed and the patient is non-compliant with compression therapy.
• Prognosis improves significantly with diligent compression, lifestyle changes, and correction of underlying venous reflux.

sections.overview:
• An Arterial Insufficiency Ulcer (also known as an ischemic ulcer) is a **full-thickness wound** that develops due to inadequate arterial blood supply to the lower extremities.
• These ulcers are a direct consequence of advanced **Peripheral Artery Disease (PAD)** and represent a state of **critical limb ischemia (CLI)**.
• They are characterized by **severe pain**, a **"punched-out" appearance**, and are typically located on the **distal aspects** of the limb.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ The underlying cause is advanced **Peripheral Artery Disease (PAD)**.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Atherosclerosis**: This is the primary mechanism. Systemic atherosclerosis leads to the formation of fibrofatty plaques within the arterial lumen, causing progressive stenosis and occlusion.
    ◦ **Reduced Blood Flow (Ischemia)**: Stenosis reduces blood flow (perfusion) to the distal tissues, particularly during increased metabolic demand (exercise) or in the resting state in severe disease.
    ◦ **Tissue Hypoxia & Malnutrition**: The resulting ischemia deprives tissues of essential oxygen and nutrients required for cellular metabolism and viability.
    ◦ **Tissue Breakdown**: Minor trauma, pressure, or even spontaneous breakdown of atrophic, ischemic skin overwhelms the tissue's compromised ability to heal.
    ◦ **Ulceration & Necrosis**: The tissue dies, leading to the formation of a necrotic, poorly healing ulcer. The lack of blood flow prevents the normal inflammatory and proliferative phases of wound healing.
sections.epidemiology:
• Less common than venous ulcers, accounting for approximately 10-25% of all lower extremity ulcers.
• Prevalence is directly correlated with the prevalence of **PAD**.
• Incidence increases significantly with age, most common in patients **> 60 years old**.
• Slightly higher prevalence in males.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The typical patient is an older individual with a history of **smoking** or **diabetes** who presents with a painful, non-healing wound on a toe or foot.
• The patient often reports a history of **intermittent claudication** that has progressed to **rest pain**.
• The onset may be spontaneous or follow minor, often unnoticed, trauma.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI)**
    ◦ **First-line, cornerstone of diagnosis.** Compares systolic blood pressure at the ankle to the arm.
    ◦ **< 0.9**: Diagnostic of **PAD**.
    ◦ **< 0.4**: Suggests severe **PAD** / **Critical Limb Ischemia**.
    ◦ **> 1.4**: Indicates **non-compressible, calcified arteries** (common in diabetics); the result is unreliable.
        ▪ Proceed to a **Toe-Brachial Index (TBI)**.
• **Toe-Brachial Index (TBI)**
    ◦ Used when **ABI is >1.4**.
    ◦ A **TBI < 0.7** is diagnostic of **PAD**.
• **Arterial Duplex Ultrasound**
    ◦ Non-invasive imaging to visualize blood flow and locate specific areas of stenosis or occlusion.
• **Angiography (CTA, MRA, or DSA)**
    ◦ Used for pre-procedural planning before revascularization.
    ◦ **Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA)** is the **gold standard**, allowing for both diagnosis and concurrent endovascular intervention.
• **Labs**
    ◦ HgbA1c, lipid panel, CBC, CMP to assess and manage underlying risk factors.
• **Wound Culture & X-ray**
    ◦ If signs of infection are present (erythema, purulence) or to rule out **osteomyelitis**.
sections.prognosis:
• **Guarded.** The development of an arterial ulcer signifies end-stage **PAD**.
• Without revascularization, the 1-year limb **amputation rate is >50%**.
• Mortality is high due to associated systemic disease.
    ◦ Patients with **CLI** have a 1-year mortality rate of approximately 25%.
    ◦ The 5-year mortality rate is up to 70%, primarily from cardiovascular causes.

sections.overview: • A diabetic foot ulcer (DFU) is a full-thickness wound penetrating the dermis, located below the ankle in a patient with diabetes mellitus. ◦ It is a major complication of diabetes, resulting from the combined effects of peripheral neuropathy and peripheral artery disease (PAD). ◦ DFUs are the most common precursor to non-traumatic lower extremity amputations and are associated with significant morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs. ◦ The pathophysiology is a "perfect storm" of sensory loss, motor dysfunction, autonomic changes, and impaired wound healing.
sections.etiology: • The development of a DFU is multifactorial, primarily driven by three key pathologic processes stemming from chronic hyperglycemia: ◦ 1. Peripheral Neuropathy: The cornerstone of DFU pathogenesis. ▪ Sensory Neuropathy: Leads to Loss of Protective Sensation (LOPS). Patients cannot feel minor trauma (e.g., a pebble in a shoe, pressure from ill-fitting footwear, or thermal injury), allowing unrecognized injuries to progress to ulceration. ▪ Motor Neuropathy: Causes intrinsic muscle atrophy in the foot, leading to structural deformities such as hammer toes, claw toes, and a prominent "rocker-bottom" appearance in severe cases (Charcot foot). These deformities create abnormal pressure points, particularly over the metatarsal heads. ▪ Autonomic Neuropathy: Results in decreased sweating (anhidrosis), leading to dry, cracked, and fissured skin. This compromises the skin's barrier function, creating a portal of entry for bacteria. ◦ 2. Peripheral Artery Disease (PAD): ▪ Diabetes accelerates atherosclerosis, leading to stenosis or occlusion of lower extremity arteries. ▪ This results in ischemia, which impairs the delivery of oxygen, nutrients, and immune cells to the tissue. ▪ Poor perfusion directly inhibits all phases of wound healing and increases the risk of infection and gangrene. ◦ 3. Immunocompromise: ▪ Hyperglycemia impairs leukocyte function (e.g., chemotaxis, phagocytosis). ▪ This leads to a diminished inflammatory response and a decreased ability to fight off infection, allowing minor wounds to become severely infected. • The Typical Sequence: ◦ A patient with sensory neuropathy sustains minor, unfelt trauma over a high-pressure point (e.g., metatarsal head). ◦ The skin breaks down. ◦ Due to PAD, the wound has inadequate blood supply to heal. ◦ Due to immunocompromise, it becomes easily infected.
sections.epidemiology: • Lifetime risk of developing a DFU for a person with diabetes is 15-25%. • DFUs precede over 80% of non-traumatic lower extremity amputations in diabetic patients. • The 5-year mortality rate after a major amputation is alarmingly high, reported to be between 40-70%, which is worse than many common cancers. • Recurrence rate is high: >40% within 1 year and >60% within 3 years.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • A patient typically presents with a non-healing wound on the foot, often discovered incidentally (e.g., noticing drainage on a sock). ◦ The ulcer is characteristically painless due to underlying neuropathy. • Location: Most common over areas of high pressure. ◦ Plantar surface of metatarsal heads (especially 1st MTP joint) ◦ Dorsal aspect of hammer toes ◦ Heel ◦ Tips of the toes
sections.diagnostics: • Labs ◦ HbA1c: To assess long-term glycemic control. ◦ CBC with differential: Leukocytosis may indicate infection. ◦ ESR and CRP: Inflammatory markers; useful for tracking treatment response for deep infections like osteomyelitis. • Imaging ◦ Plain X-ray (Weight-bearing AP, lateral, oblique views): First-line imaging. Can reveal: ▪ Soft tissue gas (gas gangrene - a surgical emergency). ▪ Foreign bodies. ▪ Bone deformities (Charcot foot). ▪ Signs of osteomyelitis (cortical erosion, periosteal reaction, lytic lesions) - Note: findings may lag by 2 weeks. ◦ MRI: Gold standard for diagnosing osteomyelitis and assessing soft tissue abscesses. Highly sensitive and specific. • Microbiology ◦ Wound Culture: Deep tissue or bone biopsy after debridement is required. Superficial swabs are unreliable as they only identify colonizing bacteria. • Vascular Studies ◦ ABI / TBI (Toe-Brachial Index): Non-invasive screening for PAD. ◦ Arterial Duplex Ultrasound: To localize and quantify stenosis. ◦ CT Angiography (CTA) or MR Angiography (MRA): For detailed vascular mapping prior to revascularization.
sections.prognosis:
• Guarded. Even with healing, recurrence rates are extremely high.
• The presence of a DFU is a marker for increased mortality.
• The 5-year mortality rate after a DFU diagnosis is approximately 40%.
• The 5-year mortality after a major amputation is >50%, rivaling that of many advanced cancers.

sections.overview:
• A lower extremity chronic wound resulting from the simultaneous presence of **both Chronic Venous Insufficiency (CVI) and Peripheral Arterial Disease (PAD)**.
    ◦ This combination makes diagnosis and treatment more complex than for ulcers of a single etiology.
    ◦ The presence of arterial disease limits the use of standard compression therapy, the mainstay for venous ulcers, creating a therapeutic challenge.
• Accounts for approximately 15-25% of all lower extremity ulcers.
sections.etiology:
• Pathophysiology is a synergistic combination of venous hypertension and arterial insufficiency.
    ◦ **Venous Component (CVI)**
        ▪ Caused by incompetent valves in deep and/or perforating veins, leading to venous reflux and pooling of blood in the lower extremities.
        ▪ Results in **venous hypertension**, which increases capillary hydrostatic pressure.
        ▪ Fluid, red blood cells, and fibrinogen leak into the interstitial space, causing edema, inflammation, hemosiderin deposition, and lipodermatosclerosis.
        ▪ The compromised tissue becomes fragile and prone to breakdown from minor trauma, leading to ulceration.
    ◦ **Arterial Component (PAD)**
        ▪ Primarily caused by **atherosclerosis**, which narrows or occludes arteries supplying the lower extremities.
        ▪ Leads to **tissue ischemia** due to reduced blood flow, depriving tissues of oxygen and essential nutrients.
        ▪ Ischemia impairs all phases of wound healing (inflammation, proliferation, remodeling) and can lead to tissue necrosis and ulcer formation.
    ◦ **Combined Effect**
        ▪ Venous congestion further compromises the already poor arterial inflow by increasing local tissue pressure.
        ▪ Arterial ischemia prevents the delivery of oxygen and nutrients needed to heal the damage caused by venous hypertension.
        ▪ This vicious cycle results in a persistent, difficult-to-heal ulcer.
sections.epidemiology:
• Prevalence increases with age, most common in patients > 65 years old.
• Accounts for up to 25% of all lower extremity ulcers.
• Often underdiagnosed, as clinicians may focus on the more obvious signs of either venous or arterial disease alone.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The clinical presentation is a hybrid of venous and arterial ulcers, often with overlapping and confusing features.
• The patient is typically elderly with multiple comorbidities (**DM**, **HTN**, **HLD**, **CAD**).
• The ulcer may have been present for months to years, with failed previous treatments.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI)**: **THE key diagnostic test**; mandatory for any lower extremity ulcer.
    ◦ Compares systolic blood pressure at the ankle to the arm.
    ◦ **ABI < 0.9**: Confirms **PAD**.
    ◦ **Mixed-etiology ulcers often have an ABI between 0.5 and 0.8**.
    ◦ **ABI < 0.5**: Severe **PAD**; healing is unlikely without revascularization.
    ◦ **ABI > 1.3**: Suggests calcified, non-compressible arteries (common in diabetics).
        ▪ Perform a **Toe-Brachial Index (TBI)** instead.
        ▪ A **TBI < 0.7** is abnormal.
• **Vascular Studies**
    ◦ **Arterial Duplex Ultrasound**: Non-invasive imaging to identify the location and severity of arterial stenosis or occlusion.
    ◦ **Venous Duplex Ultrasound**: Non-invasive imaging to confirm venous reflux and rule out **DVT**.
• **Labs**
    ◦ **HbA1c** (to assess glycemic control).
    ◦ Lipid panel.
    ◦ **CBC** (to rule out anemia which can worsen ischemia).
    ◦ **CMP** (to assess renal function prior to potential contrast studies).
• **Wound Culture**: Only if clinical signs of infection are present (increased pain, erythema, purulent drainage, odor).
• **Biopsy**: If the ulcer is atypical or fails to heal with appropriate therapy.
    ◦ To rule out malignancy (e.g., **Marjolin's ulcer** - squamous cell carcinoma arising in a chronic wound).
sections.prognosis:
• Guarded; healing is slower and more complicated than for single-etiology ulcers.
• Recurrence rates are high, especially if underlying risk factors are not aggressively managed.
• Prognosis is significantly improved by successful revascularization and consistent adherence to compression and risk factor modification.

sections.overview:
• Stasis dermatitis is a common inflammatory dermatosis of the lower extremities occurring in patients with chronic venous insufficiency (CVI).
    ◦ It is a cutaneous manifestation of underlying venous hypertension, which leads to capillary leakage, inflammation, and subsequent skin changes.
    ◦ It exists on a spectrum of CVI, often preceding more severe complications like lipodermatosclerosis and venous ulceration.
sections.etiology:
• The core pathophysiologic driver is **venous hypertension**, most commonly due to **chronic venous insufficiency (CVI)**.
    ◦ **Valvular Incompetence**: Valves in the deep or perforating veins of the lower extremities fail. This prevents the efficient return of blood to the heart.
    ◦ **Venous Reflux & Hypertension**: Gravity causes blood to pool in the lower leg veins, leading to sustained high pressure (venous hypertension).
    ◦ **Capillary Damage**: Increased hydrostatic pressure is transmitted to the dermal capillaries, causing them to become dilated and permeable.
    ◦ **Fluid & Macromolecule Leakage**: Plasma, fibrinogen, and red blood cells (RBCs) leak into the dermal interstitium.
        ▪ **Edema**: Leakage of fluid causes pitting edema.
        ▪ **Fibrin Cuffs**: Fibrinogen polymerizes into fibrin, forming "fibrin cuffs" around capillaries, which impairs oxygen and nutrient exchange, leading to tissue hypoxia.
        ▪ **Hemosiderin Staining**: RBCs break down, and the iron-containing pigment (hemosiderin) is deposited in the dermis, causing the characteristic reddish-brown discoloration.
    ◦ **Inflammation**: The leaked molecules and tissue hypoxia trigger a chronic inflammatory response, leading to the eczematous changes of dermatitis (erythema, scaling, pruritus).
sections.epidemiology:
• **Age**: Predominantly affects middle-aged and elderly individuals, with prevalence increasing significantly after age 50.
• **Sex**: More common in women, likely due to hormonal influences and pregnancy.
• **Prevalence**: Affects approximately 6-7% of the population over 50. CVI itself is even more common.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Chronic Venous Insufficiency (CVI)** (the underlying cause)
• **History of Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT)** (post-thrombotic syndrome damages valves)
• **Increasing Age**
• **Family History** of venous disease
• **Female Sex**
• **Multiple Pregnancies** (hormonal effects, IVC compression)
• **Obesity** (increases intra-abdominal pressure)
• **Prolonged Standing or Sitting** (occupational risk)
• **Congestive Heart Failure (CHF)**
• **History of leg surgery or trauma**
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is typically chronic and progressive. It almost always affects the lower legs, often bilaterally, though it can be asymmetric.
    ◦ **Location**: Classically begins around the **medial malleolus** (the "gaiter area") and can spread circumferentially up the calf.
    ◦ **Progression**:
        ▪ **Early**: Intermittent pitting edema, mild erythema, pruritus.
        ▪ **Established**: Chronic edema, hyperpigmentation, scaling, and eczematous plaques.
        ▪ **Advanced**: Lipodermatosclerosis, ulceration, atrophie blanche.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ **Pruritus (itching)**: Can be intense and is a hallmark symptom.
    ◦ **Leg Heaviness/Aching**: A dull ache that worsens with dependency (standing/sitting).
    ◦ **Symptom Relief with Elevation**: A key historical feature.
    ◦ **Pain**: Usually associated with ulceration or acute inflammation.
    ◦ **Swelling** in the affected leg(s).
• **Physical Exam Findings**
    ◦ **Edema**: Pitting edema, especially in the pretibial area and around the ankles.
    ◦ **Erythema**: Ill-defined erythema, which may be subtle in darker skin tones.
    ◦ **Scaling and Crusting**: Eczematous changes, sometimes with serous weeping ("wet" dermatitis).
    ◦ **Hemosiderin Deposition**: Reddish-brown, brawny discoloration, often with pinpoint "cayenne pepper" macules.
    ◦ **Varicose Veins**: Often visible.
    ◦ **Lipodermatosclerosis**: A late-stage finding. Subcutaneous fat is replaced by fibrosis, leading to induration, hardening, and tapering of the lower leg. This creates the classic **"inverted champagne bottle"** or **"bowling pin"** appearance.
    ◦ **Atrophie Blanche**: White, scar-like, star-shaped plaques, often with surrounding telangiectasias. Represents areas of healed ulcers and poor microcirculation.
    ◦ **Venous Stasis Ulcers**: Shallow, moist, irregularly bordered ulcers located over bony prominences, most commonly the **medial malleolus**.
    ◦ **Pulses**: Pedal pulses (dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial) are typically **present and normal**, which helps differentiate from arterial disease.
sections.diagnostics:
• Stasis dermatitis is primarily a **clinical diagnosis** based on history and physical exam findings.
• **Venous Duplex Ultrasound**: **Gold standard/confirmatory test.**
    ◦ Identifies venous reflux and valvular incompetence.
    ◦ It is also essential to rule out an underlying DVT as the cause of acute symptoms.
• **Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI)**: Crucial to perform before initiating compression therapy to rule out significant coexisting Peripheral Arterial Disease (PAD).
    ◦ **ABI < 0.9**: Suggests PAD; use caution with compression.
    ◦ **ABI < 0.5**: Severe PAD; compression is **contraindicated**.
• **Skin Biopsy**: Rarely needed. Performed if the diagnosis is uncertain, to rule out malignancy (e.g., squamous cell carcinoma in a chronic ulcer), vasculitis, or other inflammatory dermatoses.
• **Patch Testing**: Useful if a superimposed allergic contact dermatitis is suspected (e.g., allergy to topical antibiotics like neomycin or components of wound dressings).
sections.treatment:
• **Compression Therapy**
    ◦ **Graduated Compression Stockings**: 20-30 mmHg or 30-40 mmHg are standard. Must be worn daily.
    ◦ **Multi-layer Compression Wraps / Unna Boot**: Used for patients with active ulceration or severe edema.
• **Topical Corticosteroids**
    ◦ Used to control inflammation and pruritus during acute flares.
    ◦ Medium-to-high potency (e.g., **triamcinolone 0.1% ointment**) applied for 1-2 weeks.
• **Skin Care and Barrier Repair**
    ◦ Liberal use of bland emollients (e.g., petroleum jelly, Aquaphor, CeraVe) to restore the skin barrier.
    ◦ Use gentle, soap-free cleansers.
sections.management:
• **Patient Education**: Critical for long-term success. Emphasize that this is a chronic condition requiring lifelong management.
• **Lifestyle Modification**:
    ◦ Weight loss in obese patients.
    ◦ Regular exercise, especially ankle flexion activities (e.g., walking), to engage the calf muscle pump.
    ◦ Avoidance of prolonged periods of standing or sitting.
• **Ulcer Management**: Debridement, appropriate wound dressings, and infection control.
• **Referral**: Refer to a Vascular Surgeon for severe, refractory CVI.
    ◦ Procedural options include endovenous thermal ablation or sclerotherapy for incompetent superficial veins.
sections.complications:
• **Venous Stasis Ulceration**: The most common and significant complication.
• **Secondary Bacterial Infection**: Cellulitis or impetigo can develop in eczematous or ulcerated skin.
• **Allergic Contact Dermatitis**: High rate of sensitization to topical agents (antibiotics, preservatives in creams).
• **Lipodermatosclerosis**: Permanent fibrotic changes to the skin and subcutaneous tissue.
• **Atrophie Blanche**: Permanent scarring.
• **Hemorrhage**: Minor trauma to superficial varicosities can cause significant bleeding.
• **Squamous Cell Carcinoma (Marjolin's Ulcer)**: A rare but deadly complication arising in a chronic, non-healing venous ulcer.
sections.prognosis:
• Stasis dermatitis is a chronic, lifelong condition that can be well-managed but not cured.
• With strict adherence to elevation and compression therapy, the prognosis for controlling symptoms and preventing ulcers is good.
• Recurrence is very common with non-adherence.

sections.overview:
• Pyoderma Gangrenosum (PG) is a rare, non-infectious, inflammatory skin disorder characterized by the rapid development of painful, necrotic ulcers.
• Despite its name, it is not caused by an infection ('pyoderma') nor is it a form of gangrene.
• It is classified as a **neutrophilic dermatosis**, meaning the underlying pathology involves an abnormal accumulation of neutrophils in the skin.
• PG is often associated with underlying systemic diseases and is considered a **diagnosis of exclusion**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ The exact cause is unknown (idiopathic), but it is considered an autoinflammatory or immune-mediated disorder.
    ◦ It is not an infection.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Neutrophil Dysfunction**: Characterized by dysregulated neutrophil trafficking and activation.
        ▪ In response to a trigger (often unknown or minor trauma), neutrophils massively infiltrate the dermis, releasing destructive enzymes (e.g., elastase, collagenase) and reactive oxygen species.
    ◦ **Immune Dysregulation**: Involves both innate and adaptive immune systems.
        ▪ Elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-8, and IL-17 are implicated.
    ◦ **Pathergy**: A hallmark feature in ~30% of cases.
        ▪ It is an exaggerated, abnormal response to minor skin trauma (e.g., a needle stick, biopsy, or insect bite) that results in the formation of a new PG lesion or the worsening of an existing one.
        ▪ This has critical implications for management (i.e., avoiding surgical debridement).
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Rare, estimated at 3-10 cases per million people per year.
• **Age of Onset**: Typically occurs in adults between 40-60 years of age. Can occur at any age but is rare in children.
• **Sex**: Slightly more common in females.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Initial Lesion**: Typically begins as a small, tender, inflammatory papule, pustule, or nodule, often mistaken for an insect bite, furuncle, or folliculitis.
• **Progression**: The initial lesion rapidly breaks down over days, evolving into an exquisitely painful ulcer.
• **Classic Ulcer**: The mature ulcer expands quickly and has characteristic features:
    ◦ **Borders**: Irregular, **violaceous** (purplish-red), **undermined**, and **boggy**. The border is often raised and dusky.
    ◦ **Base**: Purulent, necrotic, and hemorrhagic base. Despite the 'purulent' appearance, cultures are typically sterile.
    ◦ **Location**: Most common on the lower extremities (especially the anterior shin/pretibial area), but can occur anywhere, including the trunk, face, and peristomal sites in patients with ostomies.
sections.diagnostics:
• PG is a **diagnosis of exclusion**. There is no specific laboratory test or histopathologic finding that is pathognomonic.
    ◦ The workup is aimed at ruling out other causes of ulcers.
• **Biopsy**
    ◦ **Purpose**: Primarily to **rule out other conditions** like infection, malignancy, or vasculitis.
    ◦ **Procedure**: A deep punch or wedge biopsy from the inflammatory ulcer edge is required.
    ◦ **Histology**: Shows a massive, dense neutrophilic infiltrate in the dermis, often with dermal edema and necrosis. It is a 'neutrophilic dermatosis.'
        ▪ Importantly, true leukocytoclastic vasculitis is typically absent, though secondary vessel inflammation can be seen.
• **Wound Cultures**
    ◦ **Purpose**: To rule out bacterial, fungal, or mycobacterial infection.
    ◦ **Result in PG**: Typically sterile or grow only normal skin flora.
• **Laboratory Workup** (to screen for underlying disease)
    ◦ CBC with differential (leukemia, anemia)
    ◦ Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP)
    ◦ Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) & C-Reactive Protein (CRP) (will be elevated but are non-specific)
    ◦ Serum Protein Electrophoresis (SPEP) and Urine Protein Electrophoresis (UPEP) with immunofixation (for monoclonal gammopathy)
    ◦ Rheumatoid Factor (RF), Anti-CCP antibodies
    ◦ ANCA (to help differentiate from vasculitis)
sections.prognosis:
• The course is often chronic and relapsing.
• Healing is slow, often taking months to years.
• Prognosis is highly variable and often depends on the control of the underlying systemic disease.
• Mortality is generally related to the associated systemic illness rather than PG itself.

sections.overview:
• A superficial burn, also known as a **first-degree burn**, is the least severe type of burn
    ◦ Involves injury confined to the **outermost layer of the skin, the epidermis**
    ◦ Characterized by **erythema** (redness), **pain**, and dryness, but **does not produce blisters**
    ◦ These burns typically heal within 3-7 days **without scarring**
    ◦ The classic example is a mild **sunburn**
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Thermal**
        ▪ Most common cause
        ▪ Brief exposure to hot liquids (**scalds**), hot surfaces, or flash flames
    ◦ **Radiation**
        ▪ Overexposure to ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun (**sunburn**) or tanning beds
        ▪ Also seen with radiation therapy for cancer
    ◦ **Chemical**
        ▪ Brief exposure to mild irritants or acids
    ◦ **Electrical**
        ▪ Rarely causes an isolated superficial burn; usually associated with more significant deeper injury
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ Tissue injury to the **epidermis** triggers an acute inflammatory response
    ◦ Release of inflammatory mediators (e.g., prostaglandins, histamine, kinins) from damaged keratinocytes
    ◦ These mediators cause local **vasodilation** and increased capillary permeability
        ▪ Vasodilation leads to **erythema** (redness) and warmth
        ▪ Mild leakage of plasma into the interstitium causes minor edema, but not enough to separate the epidermis from the dermis to form blisters
    ◦ Prostaglandins and other mediators sensitize local nociceptors (pain receptors), resulting in **pain and tenderness**
    ◦ The damaged epidermis typically desquamates (peels) in several days as new epithelial cells regenerate from the basal layer
sections.epidemiology:
• Extremely common; one of the most frequent types of injuries seen in outpatient and emergency settings
• Occurs in all age groups
• Children and the elderly are particularly susceptible to **scald injuries**
• **Sunburn** is a major cause, especially in individuals with lighter skin phototypes (Fitzpatrick I-II) and during summer months
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient presents with a history of recent exposure to a noxious source (e.g., "I was out in the sun all day," "I spilled hot coffee on my arm")
• The onset of pain and redness is typically within a few hours of the injury
• The primary complaint is **pain**, which can be significant despite the superficial nature of the injury
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**
    ◦ Diagnosis is made based on history and physical exam findings alone
• **No laboratory or imaging studies** are required for an isolated, uncomplicated superficial burn
• Assessment of **Total Body Surface Area (TBSA)**
    ◦ Can be done using the "**Rule of Nines**" (for adults) or the **Lund-Browder chart** (for children)
    ◦ Primarily used for guiding fluid resuscitation in deeper, more extensive burns
    ◦ It is still good practice to document the approximate TBSA involved
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**
• Healing typically occurs within **3 to 7 days**
• There is **no scarring**, although temporary pigment changes may occur

sections.overview:
• A partial-thickness burn, also known as a second-degree burn, is an injury that damages the epidermis and extends into the dermis.
    ◦ This category is further subdivided into **superficial partial-thickness** and **deep partial-thickness** burns, which differ in their depth, clinical appearance, and prognosis.
    ◦ The key feature distinguishing them from first-degree burns is the presence of **blistering** and damage to the dermal layer.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Thermal (most common)**
        ▪ **Scalds:** Hot liquids or steam (common in children).
        ▪ **Flame:** Direct contact with fire.
        ▪ **Contact:** Touching a hot object (e.g., stove, iron).
        ▪ **Flash:** Intense heat from an explosion.
    ◦ **Chemical:** Contact with strong acids or alkalis.
    ◦ **Electrical:** Passage of electrical current through tissue.
    ◦ **Radiation:** Severe sunburn or exposure to radiation sources.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ Tissue damage extends from the epidermis into the dermis, damaging blood vessels, nerve endings, and dermal appendages (hair follicles, sweat glands).
    ◦ An intense inflammatory response is triggered, causing significant vasodilation and a dramatic increase in capillary permeability.
        ▪ This increased permeability allows protein-rich plasma to leak from the intravascular space into the interstitium, leading to edema and the formation of **blisters (bullae)**.
    ◦ **Superficial Partial-Thickness**
        ▪ Damage is limited to the epidermis and the papillary (upper) dermis.
        ▪ Nerve endings are irritated and exposed, causing significant **pain**.
        ▪ The vascular network is largely intact, leading to **brisk blanching**.
    ◦ **Deep Partial-Thickness**
        ▪ Damage extends into the deeper reticular dermis.
        ▪ More nerve endings are destroyed, which can result in **less pain** compared to superficial burns.
        ▪ Blood vessels are more damaged, leading to **sluggish or absent blanching**.
        ▪ Glandular tissue and hair follicles are often damaged.
sections.epidemiology:
• Burns are a major cause of morbidity worldwide.
• In the U.S., approximately 486,000 people receive medical treatment for burns annually.
• **Scald burns** are the most common type in children under 5 years old.
• Flame burns are more common in older children and adults.
• Most burns occur in the home.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The patient's history is critical.
    ◦ A detailed account of the incident helps determine the burn agent, duration of contact, and potential for associated injuries (e.g., **inhalation injury** in a house fire, trauma from an explosion).
• The patient will present with an acutely **painful, blistered, and edematous** area of skin following a known exposure.
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on history and physical exam.
• The main diagnostic tasks are to determine the **depth** of the burn and the **Total Body Surface Area (TBSA)** involved.
    ◦ **TBSA Estimation**
        ▪ **Rule of Nines (Adults):** A rapid estimation method.
            • Head: 9%
            • Each Arm: 9%
            • Anterior Torso: 18%
            • Posterior Torso: 18%
            • Each Leg: 18%
            • Genitalia/Perineum: 1%
        ▪ **Lund-Browder Chart:** More accurate, especially for pediatric patients, as it accounts for changes in body proportions with age.
        ▪ **Palmar Method:** The surface of the patient's palm (including fingers) represents ~1% TBSA. Useful for small or scattered burns.
    ◦ **Laboratory Studies (for major burns >20% TBSA or suspected systemic effects)**
        ▪ **CBC:** To assess for **hemoconcentration** (elevated Hct) from fluid loss.
        ▪ **CMP:** To monitor electrolytes (**hyperkalemia** initially), BUN/Cr (renal function), and albumin (protein loss).
        ▪ **CK-MB / Troponin:** If electrical injury is suspected, to rule out cardiac muscle damage.
        ▪ **Urinalysis:** To check for **myoglobinuria** (**rhabdomyolysis**) in deep or electrical burns.
        ▪ **ABG with Carboxyhemoglobin:** Essential if **inhalation injury** is suspected.
sections.prognosis:
• **Superficial Partial-Thickness**
    ◦ Excellent prognosis.
    ◦ Typically heals within 2-3 weeks via re-epithelialization.
    ◦ Scarring is minimal, though pigment changes are common.
• **Deep Partial-Thickness**
    ◦ Healing takes longer (3-8 weeks) and often occurs by scar formation rather than re-epithelialization.
    ◦ There is a high risk of significant **hypertrophic scarring** and **contractures**.
    ◦ Skin grafting may be required for optimal functional and cosmetic outcomes.

sections.overview:
• A severe injury that destroys all layers of the skin, including the epidermis and the entire dermis, extending into the subcutaneous fat.
    ◦ These are classified as **third-degree** burns.
    ◦ When the injury extends deeper, damaging underlying muscle, tendon, and bone, it is classified as a **fourth-degree** burn.
    ◦ Due to the complete destruction of dermal nerve endings, the central area of the burn is insensate.
    ◦ Full-thickness burns do not heal by re-epithelialization and require surgical intervention (skin grafting) for closure.
    ◦ They are associated with significant systemic complications, including burn shock, and carry a high risk of morbidity and mortality.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• Bimodal age distribution: peaks in children <5 years old (scalds are common) and young adults 18-35 years old (flame burns).
    ◦ A third peak occurs in the elderly.
• **Flame burns** are the most common cause of burn-related deaths.
• Most burns occur in the home.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patient presents following a significant thermal, chemical, or electrical injury.
• The primary focus is the **ABCDEs** (Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure).
• Suspect **inhalation injury** if the burn occurred in an enclosed space, or if there is facial/neck swelling, hoarseness, carbonaceous sputum, or singed nasal hairs.
• The patient may be in **hypovolemic shock** with hypotension and tachycardia.
• The burn wound itself will be the most obvious finding on exposure.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Lab Studies**
    ◦ **CBC**: Initially shows high hematocrit (**hemoconcentration**) from fluid loss.
    ◦ **CMP**: Monitor for electrolyte abnormalities (**hyperkalemia** initially from cell lysis, then **hypokalemia**), renal function (BUN/Cr), and albumin (**hypoalbuminemia**).
    ◦ **CK (Creatine Kinase)**: Markedly elevated in electrical burns or deep burns with muscle damage, indicating **rhabdomyolysis**.
    ◦ **ABG with Carboxyhemoglobin (CO-Hgb)**: Essential if inhalation injury or carbon monoxide poisoning is suspected.
    ◦ **Lactate**: To assess for shock and adequacy of resuscitation.
    ◦ **Urinalysis**: Check for **myoglobinuria** (dark, tea-colored urine) in **rhabdomyolysis**.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Chest X-ray**: To evaluate for inhalation injury (may show **ARDS**, but is often normal initially).
    ◦ **Bronchoscopy**: Gold standard for diagnosing the level and severity of airway injury.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis depends heavily on:
    ◦ **TBSA burned**
    ◦ **Patient age** (very young and very old have worse outcomes)
    ◦ Presence of **inhalation injury** (significantly increases mortality)
• **Baux Score**: A classic predictor of mortality, calculated as **Patient Age + % TBSA**.
    ◦ A score >140 is generally considered non-survivable.

sections.overview:
• Burn shock is a complex, life-threatening condition that occurs after a major burn injury (typically >20% Total Body Surface Area).
    ◦ It is a combination of **distributive shock** (due to systemic inflammation and vasodilation) and **hypovolemic shock** (due to massive fluid loss from the intravascular space).
    ◦ The underlying pathophysiology is a systemic inflammatory response leading to a profound increase in capillary permeability, causing fluid to shift into the interstitial space.
    ◦ Prompt and aggressive fluid resuscitation is the cornerstone of management to prevent end-organ hypoperfusion and failure.
sections.etiology:
• The pathophysiology of burn shock is a two-phase process involving both a local and a systemic response.
• **Local Response (Jackson's Burn Model):**
    ◦ **Zone of Coagulation:** Central area of the burn with the most intense heat. Cells are irreversibly damaged and necrosed.
    ◦ **Zone of Stasis:** Surrounds the central zone. Characterized by decreased tissue perfusion. This tissue is potentially salvageable with adequate resuscitation but can progress to necrosis without it.
    ◦ **Zone of Hyperemia:** Outermost zone. Tissue perfusion is increased due to vasodilation. This tissue will typically recover unless severe sepsis or prolonged hypoperfusion occurs.
• **Systemic Response (The "Leaky Capillaries"):**
    ◦ **Massive Inflammatory Mediator Release:** A major burn triggers a Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS). Damaged tissue releases a "cytokine storm" including histamine, prostaglandins, leukotrienes, TNF-alpha, and interleukins.
    ◦ **Increased Capillary Permeability:** These mediators cause a dramatic increase in microvascular permeability, not just at the burn site but **systemically**.
    ◦ **Intravascular Fluid Loss:** Plasma, electrolytes, and proteins (especially albumin) leak from the intravascular space into the interstitial space. This leads to:
        ▪ **Profound Intravascular Hypovolemia:** Leads to decreased cardiac preload, decreased cardiac output, and systemic hypoperfusion (shock).
        ▪ **Massive Edema:** Both at the burn site and in non-burned tissues.
    ◦ **Cardiovascular Effects:**
        ▪ **Initial Phase (Ebb Phase):** Decreased cardiac output and increased systemic vascular resistance (SVR) due to hypovolemia and catecholamine release. Myocardial depressant factors are also released.
        ▪ **Later Phase (Flow Phase):** After resuscitation, a hypermetabolic state with increased cardiac output and decreased SVR develops.
    ◦ **Hemoconcentration:** Loss of plasma volume from the vascular space leads to an increased hematocrit.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence:** Approximately 486,000 burn injuries receive medical treatment annually in the US.
• **Etiology:**
    ◦ Flame/Fire: ~43%
    ◦ Scalds (hot liquid/steam): ~34%
    ◦ Direct contact with hot object: ~9%
    ◦ Electrical: ~4%
    ◦ Chemical: ~3%
• **Mortality:** The risk of death increases significantly with larger burn size (%TBSA), advanced age, and the presence of inhalation injury.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient with a significant burn presents with evidence of thermal injury and progressive signs of shock.
    ◦ The presentation evolves over the first 24-48 hours.
    ◦ Initially, blood pressure may be normal due to compensatory vasoconstriction, but tachycardia is almost always present.
    ◦ As fluid shifts continue without resuscitation, signs of hypoperfusion become evident.
    ◦ **Massive edema** is a hallmark finding that develops over hours.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Labs:**
    ◦ **CBC:**
        ▪ **Elevated Hct (hemoconcentration)** is a classic initial finding.
    ◦ **CMP:**
        ▪ **Hyperkalemia** (early, from cell lysis).
        ▪ **Hyponatremia** (from fluid shifts).
        ▪ BUN/Creatinine (to assess for AKI).
        ▪ Glucose (hyperglycemia from stress response).
    ◦ **ABG with Carboxyhemoglobin (COHb):**
        ▪ Assess for metabolic acidosis (from hypoperfusion) and carbon monoxide poisoning.
        ▪ Standard pulse oximetry is unreliable in CO poisoning.
    ◦ **CK (Creatine Kinase) & Urine Myoglobin:**
        ▪ Essential for electrical burns or suspected rhabdomyolysis.
    ◦ **Type and Screen:**
        ▪ In case of associated trauma or need for future surgery.
    ◦ **Lactate:**
        ▪ Key marker of systemic hypoperfusion.
• **Imaging:**
    ◦ **Chest X-ray:**
        ▪ May be normal initially.
        ▪ Used to rule out associated trauma and establish a baseline.
        ▪ Later may show infiltrates or ARDS.
    ◦ **EKG:**
        ▪ Mandatory for all electrical burns and patients with cardiac history.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis depends heavily on three key factors:
    ◦ **% TBSA burned**
    ◦ **Patient Age**
    ◦ **Presence of Inhalation Injury**
• **Baux Score:** A simple prognostic indicator = **Patient Age + %TBSA**.
    ◦ A score > 140 is associated with very high mortality.
    ◦ The presence of inhalation injury adds ~20% mortality to any given burn size.

sections.overview:
• **Actinic Keratosis (AK)**, also known as solar keratosis, is a common, pre-malignant lesion of the epidermis caused by chronic, cumulative exposure to ultraviolet (UV) radiation
    ◦ It is considered a precursor lesion to **squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)**, specifically SCC in situ or invasive SCC
• AKs represent atypical keratinocytes confined to the epidermis
• They are a significant marker for chronically sun-damaged skin and an increased risk for all forms of skin cancer
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ The primary cause is long-term exposure to **ultraviolet (UV) radiation**, primarily UVB (290-320 nm) and to a lesser extent UVA (320-400 nm)
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ UV radiation induces DNA damage in epidermal keratinocytes
    ◦ The most common mutation occurs in the **TP53 tumor suppressor gene**, leading to impaired apoptosis (programmed cell death) of damaged cells
    ◦ This allows for the clonal proliferation and survival of atypical keratinocytes
    ◦ These atypical cells are confined to the epidermis and **do not breach the basement membrane**
        ▪ If they do, the lesion has progressed to invasive SCC
    ◦ The concept of **"field cancerization"** describes a large area of sun-damaged skin (e.g., the entire scalp) containing multiple clinical and subclinical AKs, all at risk for malignant transformation
sections.epidemiology:
• One of the most common dermatologic diagnoses, especially in older adults
• Prevalence increases significantly with age and cumulative sun exposure
• More common in individuals living closer to the equator
• **Gender**: More prevalent in males, likely due to higher rates of cumulative occupational and recreational sun exposure
• **Race**: Significantly more common in fair-skinned individuals (Fitzpatrick skin types I and II)
sections.riskFactors:
• **Primary Risk Factor**: Chronic, cumulative sun exposure
• **Host Factors**
    ◦ Fitzpatrick skin types I and II (fair skin, light hair/eyes, easily burns)
    ◦ Increasing age
    ◦ Male gender
    ◦ Personal history of AK or other skin cancers (BCC, SCC, melanoma)
• **Medical Factors**
    ◦ **Immunosuppression**: Organ transplant recipients, patients on chronic immunosuppressive therapy, and those with hematologic malignancies (e.g., CLL) have a drastically increased risk of AK and progression to SCC
    ◦ Genetic syndromes predisposing to UV damage (e.g., xeroderma pigmentosum, albinism)
• **Other Exposures**
    ◦ Ionizing radiation
    ◦ Arsenic exposure
    ◦ Phototherapy (e.g., PUVA)
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients typically present with one or more small, rough spots on chronically sun-exposed areas
    ◦ Common locations: **face, scalp (especially in bald men), ears (helices), neck, dorsal forearms, and hands**
• Lesions are often discovered incidentally during an exam or because the patient notes a persistent rough or scaly area
• Multiple lesions are common
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ Often **asymptomatic**
    ◦ May be pruritic, tender, or have a stinging sensation
    ◦ Patients often describe the lesion as a **"rough patch"** or **"sandpaper spot"** that may intermittently flake off and recur
sections.physicalExam:
• **Palpation**: Often **"better felt than seen"**
    ◦ The key finding is a **rough, sandpaper-like texture** on palpation
• **Inspection**
    ◦ **Morphology**: Solitary or multiple, ill-defined erythematous macules, papules, or plaques
    ◦ **Scale**: Adherent, hyperkeratotic scale that can be yellow, white, or dirty brown
    ◦ **Size**: Typically ranges from 3 to 10 mm
    ◦ **Base**: The base of the lesion is typically erythematous (pink or red)
• **Special Variants**
    ◦ **Cutaneous Horn**: A conical, dense, hyperkeratotic projection
        ▪ The base of a cutaneous horn can harbor an AK or an underlying SCC, warranting biopsy
    ◦ **Actinic Cheilitis**: AK occurring on the vermilion border of the lip, most commonly the **lower lip**
        ▪ Presents as persistent dryness, scaling, and blurring of the lip margin
        ▪ Has a higher rate of progression to SCC than cutaneous AK
    ◦ **Pigmented AK**: Contains melanin, appearing as a brownish papule
        ▪ Must be differentiated from lentigo maligna
sections.diagnostics:
• The diagnosis is **primarily clinical**, based on history and characteristic physical exam findings
• **Dermoscopy** can aid in visualization, showing a **"strawberry pattern"** (erythematous pseudo-network around hair follicles)
• **Skin Biopsy (Shave or Punch)** is indicated if there is suspicion for SCC
    ◦ "Red flags" for progression include:
        ▪ **Induration** (firmness at the base)
        ▪ **Ulceration** or bleeding
        ▪ **Rapid growth**
        ▪ **Tenderness/Pain**
        ▪ Diameter > 1 cm
        ▪ Failure to respond to appropriate therapy
sections.treatment:
• **Lesion-Directed Therapies**
    ◦ **Cryotherapy (Liquid Nitrogen)**: Most common treatment for isolated lesions. Causes localized blistering and crusting, with resolution in 1-2 weeks
    ◦ **Curettage +/- Electrodessication**: Scraping the lesion off with a curette
• **Field-Directed Therapies**
    ◦ **Topical Fluorouracil (5-FU)**: A pyrimidine analog that inhibits DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells. Applied for several weeks, causes marked inflammation, erythema, and erosions before healing. High efficacy
    ◦ **Topical Imiquimod**: An immune response modifier that stimulates a local immune reaction against the atypical cells. Also causes a significant inflammatory response
    ◦ **Photodynamic Therapy (PDT)**: Application of a topical photosensitizer (e.g., aminolevulinic acid) followed by exposure to a specific wavelength of light (blue or red light), which selectively destroys the atypical cells
    ◦ **Topical Diclofenac**: A topical NSAID, less irritating than 5-FU or imiquimod but may be less effective
    ◦ **Chemical Peels / Laser Resurfacing**: Can be effective for widespread facial AKs
sections.management:
• **Follow-up**: Regular full-body skin examinations are crucial
    ◦ **Frequency**: Every 6-12 months, or more frequently for high-risk patients (immunosuppressed, history of multiple skin cancers)
sections.complications:
• The most significant complication is **progression to Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)**
• The risk per lesion per year is low (~0.1-1%), but the cumulative lifetime risk for a patient with multiple AKs is significant (up to 10%)
• SCC arising from AK is typically low-grade, but has the potential for metastasis
• Other complications include pain, bleeding, secondary infection, and cosmetic disfigurement from the lesions or their treatment
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis for individual AKs treated appropriately is excellent
• However, the presence of AKs serves as a powerful marker for significant cumulative sun damage, placing the patient at a **lifelong increased risk for developing SCC, BCC, and melanoma**
• Prognosis is worse in immunosuppressed patients, who have a much higher rate of progression to aggressive SCC
sections.preventionEducation:
• **Patient Education is CRITICAL**
    ◦ **Sun Protection**: Emphasize daily use of broad-spectrum sunscreen (SPF 30+), wearing sun-protective clothing (hats, long sleeves), and avoiding peak sun hours (10 am - 4 pm)
    ◦ **Skin Self-Exams**: Teach patients to monitor their skin for new or changing lesions, focusing on the "red flags" for SCC

sections.overview:
• Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC) is the **most common human malignancy**.
    ◦ A non-melanoma skin cancer arising from the basal cells of the epidermis and its adnexal structures (hair follicles).
    ◦ Characterized by **slow growth**, local invasion, and a **very low rate of metastasis**.
    ◦ Typically appears on **sun-exposed skin**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ Primary cause is DNA damage from **ultraviolet (UV) radiation**, particularly UVB.
    ◦ Other causes include ionizing radiation, arsenic exposure, and genetic predisposition.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ UV radiation induces the formation of pyrimidine dimers in DNA, leading to mutations.
    ◦ The key pathway involved is the **Hedgehog (Hh) signaling pathway**.
    ◦ Mutations, most commonly in the **PTCH1 (Patched-1) tumor suppressor gene**, lead to uncontrolled activation of this pathway.
    ◦ This dysregulation results in the uncontrolled proliferation of basaloid cells, forming the tumor.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Most common cancer worldwide**.
• Incidence: >4 million cases diagnosed annually in the U.S.
• More common in **males** than females.
• Incidence increases sharply with age, typically affecting individuals **> 50 years old**.
• Higher prevalence in fair-skinned individuals (Fitzpatrick skin types I and II) and in geographic locations with high sun exposure (closer to the equator, higher altitudes).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• BCC has several clinical subtypes, each with a distinct appearance:
    ◦ **Nodular BCC (Most Common: ~60%)**
        ▪ Classically a **pink or flesh-colored papule** with a **pearly or translucent** quality.
        ▪ Often has overlying **telangiectasias** (small, dilated blood vessels).
        ▪ May have a **rolled border** and central ulceration (often called a **"rodent ulcer"**).
        ▪ Most common on the head and neck, especially the nose.
    ◦ **Superficial BCC (~30%)**
        ▪ Appears as a pink or red, slightly scaly patch or plaque.
        ▪ May have a fine, thread-like, slightly raised border.
        ▪ Often mistaken for eczema, psoriasis, or actinic keratosis.
        ▪ Most common on the trunk and extremities.
    ◦ **Morpheaform / Sclerosing / Infiltrative BCC (~5-10%)**
        ▪ The most aggressive subtype.
        ▪ Appears as a white, yellow, or flesh-colored, scar-like plaque.
        ▪ Borders are often ill-defined and indistinct.
        ▪ Firm, indurated, and may be depressed below the skin surface.
        ▪ High risk for recurrence due to subclinical extension.
    ◦ **Pigmented BCC**
        ▪ Similar to nodular BCC but contains melanin (brown, blue, or black pigment).
        ▪ Can be mistaken for malignant melanoma.
        ▪ Key differentiating features are the presence of a pearly sheen, rolled border, and telangiectasias.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Definitive Diagnosis**: **Biopsy with histopathology**.
• **Biopsy Technique**
    ◦ **Shave biopsy** is the most common and preferred method for most suspected BCCs.
    ◦ **Punch biopsy** can be used for flat or pigmented lesions.
• **Dermoscopy**: A handheld tool used to magnify and illuminate the skin, revealing specific features not visible to the naked eye (e.g., arborizing vessels, blue-gray ovoid nests, spoke wheel areas).
• **Histopathology Findings**
    ◦ Nests of **basaloid cells** with scant cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nuclei, showing **peripheral palisading** (nuclei at the edge of nests align in a row) and **stromal retraction** (clefts/spaces between the tumor and surrounding stroma).
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for the vast majority of cases.
• The 5-year cure rate with appropriate treatment is **>95%**.
• Mortality is extremely low and is almost always due to uncontrolled local invasion or rare metastasis from a neglected, aggressive tumor.

sections.overview:
• Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC) is the **second most common type of skin cancer** after Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC).
    ◦ It is a malignant proliferation of suprabasal epidermal keratinocytes.
    ◦ While most cases are localized with a high cure rate, a subset can be aggressive, with potential for local recurrence, perineural invasion, and distant metastasis.
    ◦ The most common precursor lesion is **Actinic Keratosis (AK)**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ The primary cause is cumulative exposure to **ultraviolet (UV) radiation**, particularly UVB.
    ◦ UV light induces DNA damage, primarily causing pyrimidine dimers, which leads to mutations in key regulatory genes.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The most commonly mutated gene in SCC is the **TP53 tumor suppressor gene**.
    ◦ This mutation disrupts normal cell cycle control and apoptosis (programmed cell death), allowing for the uncontrolled proliferation of atypical keratinocytes.
• **Other Causes**
    ◦ **Human Papillomavirus (HPV)**: Especially in anogenital and periungual SCC.
    ◦ **Chronic Inflammation/Scarring**: SCC can arise in chronic wounds, burns, or scars (**Marjolin's Ulcer**).
    ◦ **Immunosuppression**: Impaired immune surveillance significantly increases risk.
    ◦ **Carcinogen Exposure**: Arsenic, industrial tars, radiation.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Second most common skin cancer, with over 1 million cases diagnosed annually in the U.S.
• **Affected Population**: Primarily affects older individuals (>50 years).
• **Sex**: More common in males than females (approx. 2:1 ratio), likely due to higher cumulative sun exposure.
• **Risk Groups**: Highest incidence in fair-skinned individuals (Fitzpatrick types I and II) living in areas with high sun exposure.
sections.riskFactors:
• **UV Exposure**: History of extensive sun exposure, sunburns, or tanning bed use.
• **Phenotype**: Fair skin, light hair, blue/green eyes (Fitzpatrick I-II).
• **Immunosuppression**: **Organ transplant recipients** are at a ~65-250 fold increased risk. Patients with HIV or chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) are also at high risk.
• **Precursor Lesions**: **Actinic Keratosis (AK)**, Bowen's disease (SCC in situ).
• **Chronic Wounds**: Non-healing ulcers, burn scars, osteomyelitis sinus tracts.
• **Genetic Syndromes**: Xeroderma pigmentosum, Oculocutaneous Albinism.
• **History**: Personal or family history of skin cancer.
• **Ionizing Radiation**: Prior radiation therapy.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a **non-healing, growing lesion** in a sun-exposed area that may bleed with minimal trauma.
• Lesions are typically found on the head, neck, forearms, and dorsal hands.
• SCC can present in several forms:
    ◦ **Papule or Plaque**: Erythematous, indurated (firm), and scaly.
    ◦ **Nodule**: Firm, hyperkeratotic, may have a central ulceration.
    ◦ **Ulcer**: A persistent, shallow or excavated sore with a red base and firm, raised borders.
    ◦ **Cutaneous Horn**: A conical, dense, hyperkeratotic projection.
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ Often asymptomatic.
    ◦ **Pruritus** (itching).
    ◦ **Tenderness or pain**, especially with perineural invasion.
    ◦ **Bleeding** that is spontaneous or follows minor trauma (friable).
    ◦ A sensation of a "sore that doesn't heal."
sections.physicalExam:
• **Inspection**:
    ◦ **Morphology**: Erythematous, indurated papule, plaque, or nodule.
    ◦ **Surface**: Typically has overlying scale, crust, hyperkeratosis, or ulceration.
    ◦ **Borders**: Often ill-defined.
• **Palpation**:
    ◦ **Induration**: The lesion feels firm, thickened, and deep upon palpation.
    ◦ **Fixation**: Check if the lesion is mobile or fixed to underlying structures.
    ◦ **Regional Lymphadenopathy**: Palpate regional lymph nodes (e.g., cervical, preauricular, axillary, inguinal) to assess for potential metastasis.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Gold Standard**: **Biopsy with histopathology**.
• **Biopsy Technique**:
    ◦ **Shave Biopsy**: Suitable for superficial, papular lesions.
    ◦ **Punch Biopsy**: Preferred for plaques or nodules to assess depth of invasion.
    ◦ **Excisional Biopsy**: Can be diagnostic and therapeutic for smaller, well-defined lesions.
• **Histopathology Findings**:
    ◦ Invasion of atypical, pleomorphic keratinocytes into the dermis or beyond.
    ◦ Cells feature large, hyperchromatic nuclei and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm.
    ◦ **Keratin pearls**: Pathognomonic finding of well-differentiated SCC, appearing as eosinophilic, concentric layers of squamous cells with central keratinization.
sections.treatment:
• **Surgical (First-Line)**
    ◦ **Mohs Micrographic Surgery**: Highest cure rate (~99%) and maximal tissue preservation. **Treatment of choice** for high-risk SCCs (face, ears, hands, feet), large or recurrent tumors, or in immunosuppressed patients.
    ◦ **Standard Surgical Excision**: Used for lower-risk tumors in non-critical areas. Requires 4-6 mm clinical margins.
• **Destructive Methods**
    ◦ **Curettage & Electrodesiccation (C&E)**: For small, low-risk, primary tumors in non-critical sites.
    ◦ **Cryotherapy**: Primarily for precursor lesions (AK) or SCC in situ (Bowen's disease).
• **Non-Surgical**
    ◦ **Radiation Therapy**: For non-surgical candidates or as adjuvant therapy for high-risk tumors (e.g., with perineural invasion).
    ◦ **Topical Therapy (for SCC in situ)**: Topical 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU), Imiquimod.
    ◦ **Systemic Therapy (for metastatic disease)**: Immunotherapy (e.g., PD-1 inhibitors like Cemiplimab, Pembrolizumab) or chemotherapy.
sections.management:
• **Follow-up**: Essential for early detection of recurrence or new primary skin cancers.
    ◦ **High-Risk SCC**: Full body skin exams every 3-6 months for 2 years, then annually.
    ◦ **Low-Risk SCC**: Full body skin exams every 6-12 months for 2 years, then annually.
sections.complications:
• **Local Recurrence**: Higher risk with inadequate excision or high-risk features.
• **Metastasis**: Risk is ~3-5%. Most common site is regional lymph nodes. Distant metastases (lung, liver, brain) are rare but carry a poor prognosis.
• **Perineural Invasion (PNI)**: Tumor cells track along nerves. Associated with pain, numbness, and higher recurrence rates.
• **Cosmetic/Functional Deficit**: Resulting from large tumors or extensive surgical excision, especially on the face or hands.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for most localized cutaneous SCC, with a 5-year cure rate >95% with appropriate treatment.
• **Prognosis worsens** with high-risk features:
    ◦ **Size**: >2 cm in diameter.
    ◦ **Depth**: Invasion beyond the subcutaneous fat.
    ◦ **Location**: Ear, lip, central face.
    ◦ **Histology**: Poorly differentiated.
    ◦ **Etiology**: Arising in a scar or chronic wound (**Marjolin's ulcer**).
    ◦ **Host**: Immunosuppression.
• **Metastatic SCC**: 5-year survival rate drops significantly to <50%.
sections.preventionEducation:
• **Patient Education**:
    ◦ **Sun Protection**: Emphasize broad-spectrum sunscreen (SPF 30+), sun-protective clothing, hats, and avoidance of peak sun hours (10 am - 4 pm).
    ◦ **Self-Skin Exams**: Teach patients to perform monthly self-exams to identify new or changing lesions.

sections.overview:
• **Melanoma** is a malignant neoplasm of **melanocytes**, the pigment-producing cells derived from the neural crest.
• While it accounts for less than 5% of all skin cancers, it is responsible for the vast majority of skin cancer-related deaths due to its high potential for early **metastasis**.
• It can arise from a pre-existing nevus or de novo.
• The most common locations are sun-exposed skin, but it can also occur in non-sun-exposed areas, mucous membranes, the uveal tract of the eye, and the leptomeninges.
sections.etiology:
• **Melanoma** develops from the malignant transformation of melanocytes.
• The primary etiologic agent is **ultraviolet (UV) radiation** exposure, particularly UVA and UVB.
    ◦ **UVB (290-320 nm):** Directly damages melanocyte DNA, causing the formation of cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers (CPDs), leading to signature C>T or CC>TT mutations.
    ◦ **UVA (320-400 nm):** Generates reactive oxygen species, causing oxidative DNA damage.
• **Genetic Mutations:** A stepwise accumulation of genetic mutations leads to malignant transformation and progression.
    ◦ Key pathways involved:
        ▪ **MAP Kinase Pathway:** Activating mutations are common.
            • **BRAF (V600E):** Most common mutation (~50% of cutaneous melanomas). Leads to constitutive activation of the signaling pathway, promoting cell proliferation.
            • **NRAS:** Second most common (~20%).
        ▪ **Tumor Suppressor Genes:** Inactivating mutations.
            • **CDKN2A:** Encodes p16 (cell cycle inhibitor); germline mutations are associated with familial melanoma (**Familial Atypical Multiple Mole Melanoma - FAMMM syndrome**).
            • **PTEN:** Inactivation is also common.
• **Growth Phases:**
    ◦ **Radial (Horizontal) Growth Phase:** Malignant cells proliferate laterally within the epidermis and superficial dermis. Little to no metastatic potential.
    ◦ **Vertical Growth Phase:** Cells invade downwards into the deeper dermis and gain access to blood vessels and lymphatics, conferring metastatic potential. This is the critical step for disease progression.
sections.epidemiology:
• Incidence is rising faster than any other preventable cancer in the United States.
• It is one of the most common cancers in young adults (especially women aged 25-29).
• Overall incidence is higher in men than in women.
• Significantly more common in fair-skinned individuals (**Fitzpatrick skin types I and II**) and those living closer to the equator.
• Less common in individuals with darker skin (**Fitzpatrick V and VI**), but when it occurs, it is often in non-sun-exposed areas (e.g., **acral** or **mucosal**) and is frequently diagnosed at a later, more advanced stage.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation varies based on the melanoma subtype. The most common sign is a new or changing skin lesion.
• **Superficial Spreading Melanoma (SSM):**
    ◦ **Most common type (~70%).**
    ◦ Often arises in a pre-existing nevus.
    ◦ Long radial growth phase before vertical invasion.
    ◦ Typically presents as a flat or slightly elevated macule or plaque with irregular borders and color variegation.
• **Nodular Melanoma:**
    ◦ **Second most common type (~15-20%).**
    ◦ Aggressive, with early vertical growth and poor prognosis.
    ◦ Presents as a rapidly growing, darkly pigmented (blue-black), dome-shaped or pedunculated papule or nodule. Often uniform in color.
    ◦ May ulcerate and bleed easily.
• **Lentigo Maligna Melanoma:**
    ◦ ~5-10% of cases.
    ◦ Occurs in older individuals on chronically sun-damaged skin (face, neck, forearms).
    ◦ Begins as a tan or brown macule (**lentigo maligna** or "**Hutchinson's freckle**") that slowly enlarges over years (long radial growth phase) before developing a nodular component (invasion).
• **Acral Lentiginous Melanoma:**
    ◦ <5% of cases, but the **most common type in darker-skinned individuals** (African Americans, Asians, Hispanics).
    ◦ Arises on palms, soles, and beneath the nail plate (**subungual**).
    ◦ Often presents as a dark brown/black, irregularly shaped macule or patch.
    ◦ Subungual melanoma may present as a longitudinal melanonychia (dark streak in the nail) that widens or involves the nail fold (**Hutchinson's sign**).
• **Amelanotic Melanoma:**
    ◦ ~5% of cases; lacks pigment.
    ◦ Presents as a pink, red, or flesh-colored papule or nodule.
    ◦ Often misdiagnosed as basal cell carcinoma, pyogenic granuloma, or a benign inflammatory lesion, leading to delayed diagnosis and a worse prognosis.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Biopsy is mandatory for any suspicious lesion.**
• **Gold Standard: Full-thickness excisional biopsy** with 1-3 mm clinical margins.
    ◦ This technique allows the pathologist to measure the full tumor depth (**Breslow thickness**) without transecting the base.
• **Alternatives:** A deep shave (saucerization) or a punch biopsy may be used for large lesions or cosmetically sensitive areas, but it must be deep enough to include the reticular dermis.
    ◦ A superficial shave biopsy is inadequate and should be avoided.
• **Histopathology Report:** Key prognostic information includes:
    ◦ **Breslow Thickness (in mm):** The single most important prognostic factor. Measured from the granular layer of the epidermis to the deepest point of tumor invasion.
    ◦ **Ulceration:** Presence or absence is a powerful, independent prognostic factor.
    ◦ **Mitotic Rate:** Number of mitoses per square millimeter (mitoses/mm2).
    ◦ **Clark Level:** Anatomic level of invasion (less commonly used for staging now but may be reported).
    ◦ Presence of lymphovascular invasion, microsatellites, and regression.
• **Staging Workup (for invasive melanoma):**
    ◦ **Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy (SLNB):** Recommended for melanomas with Breslow depth >0.8 mm or those <0.8 mm with adverse features (e.g., ulceration, high mitotic rate).
        ▪ The status of the sentinel node is the most important prognostic factor for patients without clinical metastasis.
    ◦ **Imaging:** For patients with positive nodes or signs of distant disease (Stage III/IV), imaging such as PET/CT, CT of chest/abdomen/pelvis, and/or brain MRI is used.
    ◦ **Labs:** Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is a prognostic marker in metastatic disease.
    ◦ **Molecular Testing:** Tumor tissue is tested for **BRAF V600E** and other mutations (NRAS, c-KIT) to guide systemic therapy in advanced disease.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is excellent for thin, localized melanomas and poor for advanced, metastatic disease.
• **Key Prognostic Factors (in order of importance for localized disease):**
    ◦ 1. **Breslow Thickness:** The single most important factor. Thicker tumors have a worse prognosis.
    ◦ 2. **Tumor Ulceration:** Presence is a poor prognostic sign.
    ◦ 3. **Sentinel Lymph Node Status:** Positive SLN significantly worsens prognosis.
    ◦ 4. **Mitotic Rate:** Higher rate indicates more rapid proliferation and worse prognosis.
• **5-Year Survival Rates (Approximate):**
    ◦ Localized (Stage I/II): >95%
    ◦ Regional (Stage III): ~60-70%
    ◦ Distant (Stage IV): ~25-30%

sections.overview: • Merkel Cell Carcinoma (MCC) is a rare but highly aggressive primary neuroendocrine carcinoma of the skin. ◦ It has a high propensity for local recurrence, regional lymph node metastasis, and distant spread. ◦ Typically presents as a rapidly growing, painless, reddish-purple nodule on sun-exposed skin in elderly, fair-skinned, or immunosuppressed individuals. ◦ Diagnosis is confirmed by biopsy with specific immunohistochemical staining. ◦ Management is multidisciplinary and requires aggressive staging and treatment.
sections.etiology: • There are two primary, distinct etiologic pathways for MCC development: ◦ Viral Pathogenesis (~80% of cases): ▪ Caused by the integration of the Merkel Cell Polyomavirus (MCPyV) into the host cell's DNA. ▪ MCPyV is a common, usually asymptomatic virus in the general population. ▪ In MCC, a clonal integration of the viral genome occurs, leading to the expression of viral oncoproteins (Large T and Small T antigens). ▪ These oncoproteins inactivate host tumor suppressor proteins, primarily the Retinoblastoma protein (pRb), driving uncontrolled cell proliferation. ▪ Virus-positive tumors typically have a low tumor mutational burden. ◦ UV-Induced Pathogenesis (~20% of cases): ▪ Caused by extensive DNA damage from chronic ultraviolet (UV) radiation exposure. ▪ These tumors are MCPyV-negative. ▪ They are characterized by a very high tumor mutational burden with a classic "UV signature" (C>T transitions). ▪ Mutations in key tumor suppressor genes like TP53 and RB1 are common. • The cell of origin is debated but is thought to be a dermal fibroblast or an early B-cell progenitor, not the Merkel cell itself.
sections.epidemiology: • Incidence: Rare, approximately 0.7 cases per 100,000 person-years in the U.S., but the incidence is rapidly increasing. • Age: Primarily a disease of the elderly; median age at diagnosis is ~75 years. • Sex: Slight male predominance (approx. 1.5:1). • Race: Overwhelmingly affects Caucasians and fair-skinned individuals (Fitzpatrick types I-II).
sections.clinicalPresentation: • The classic presentation is a solitary, rapidly growing nodule on sun-exposed skin. ◦ Most common location is the head and neck (~50%), followed by the extremities and trunk. • The lesion often goes unnoticed or is misdiagnosed initially due to its non-specific appearance.
sections.diagnostics: • Biopsy (Definitive Diagnosis): ◦ A full-thickness biopsy (deep punch, incisional, or excisional) is required. ◦ Shave biopsies are inadequate as they do not allow for assessment of tumor depth or lymphovascular invasion. ◦ Histology: Shows sheets of small, round, blue cells with scant cytoplasm, granular chromatin ("salt and pepper"), a high mitotic rate, and frequent necrosis. • Immunohistochemistry (IHC): ◦ Essential to differentiate MCC from other small round blue cell tumors. ◦ Positive (+): ▪ Cytokeratin 20 (CK-20) in a characteristic perinuclear dot-like pattern (highly specific). ▪ Neuroendocrine markers such as Synaptophysin, Chromogranin A, and Neuron-Specific Enolase (NSE). ◦ Negative (-): ▪ Thyroid Transcription Factor-1 (TTF-1) - helps rule out small cell lung cancer metastasis. ▪ S-100 - helps rule out melanoma. ▪ Leukocyte Common Antigen (LCA) - helps rule out lymphoma. • Staging Workup (Essential): ◦ Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy (SLNB): Recommended for ALL patients with clinically negative nodes due to a high rate (~30%) of occult (microscopic) nodal metastasis. ◦ Imaging: Cross-sectional imaging is mandatory to assess for distant disease. ▪ PET/CT scan is the preferred modality. ▪ CT of the chest/abdomen/pelvis with contrast is an alternative. ▪ Brain MRI if neurologic symptoms are present.
sections.prognosis: • Prognosis is heavily dependent on the stage at diagnosis; MCC is more lethal than melanoma at comparable stages. • Overall 5-Year Survival: ~60% ◦ Stage I: ~80% ◦ Stage II: ~60% ◦ Stage III (Nodal Disease): ~40-50% ◦ Stage IV (Distant Metastasis): <20% • Negative prognostic factors include male sex, immunosuppression, large tumor size, and truncal location.

sections.overview:
• **Mycosis Fungoides (MF)** is the most common type of **Cutaneous T-Cell Lymphoma (CTCL)**.
    ◦ A low-grade, non-Hodgkin lymphoma characterized by the clonal proliferation of malignant, skin-homing, mature **CD4+ T-helper lymphocytes**.
• The disease course is typically indolent and chronic, classically progressing through three clinical stages: **patch, plaque, and tumor**.
• The name "Mycosis Fungoides" is a historical misnomer, as it is not a fungal infection; it was named for the mushroom-like appearance of the tumors in advanced disease.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ The exact cause is unknown (**idiopathic**).
    ◦ It is not considered hereditary or contagious.
    ◦ Chronic antigenic stimulation and genetic/environmental factors have been proposed but are not proven.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Malignant Clone**: A clone of mature **CD4+ T-helper cells** undergoes malignant transformation.
