    ◦ **Skin-Homing**: These malignant T-cells express specific cell adhesion molecules (e.g., **Cutaneous Lymphocyte Antigen - CLA**) that cause them to preferentially traffic to and accumulate in the skin.
    ◦ **Epidermotropism**: A key feature where the malignant T-cells infiltrate the epidermis without causing significant spongiosis (edema).
    ◦ **Progression**: Over time, these cells proliferate, leading to visible skin lesions. In advanced stages, the malignant cells can lose their skin-homing properties and spread to lymph nodes, peripheral blood, and visceral organs.
    ◦ **Histologic Hallmark**: Collections of atypical lymphocytes in the epidermis, known as **Pautrier's microabscesses**, are pathognomonic but not always present.
        ▪ The lymphocytes themselves often have convoluted, "**cerebriform**" nuclei.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Most common CTCL, accounting for ~50% of cases.
• **Age of Onset**: Typically affects older adults, with a median age of diagnosis between 55 and 60 years. Rare in children.
• **Sex**: Male-to-female ratio is approximately 2:1.
• **Race**: Higher incidence in Black individuals compared to White individuals.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is highly variable and often mimics benign inflammatory dermatoses for years, leading to a significant delay in diagnosis (average 3-6 years).
• **Classic Triad of Progression**:
    ◦ **Patch Stage**: Flat, erythematous to brownish, possibly scaly lesions with irregular borders. Can be mistaken for eczema, psoriasis, or tinea.
    ◦ **Plaque Stage**: Lesions become raised, indurated, and more infiltrated. Often annular or serpiginous in shape with a violaceous hue.
    ◦ **Tumor Stage**: Nodules or tumors develop, which may arise from pre-existing plaques or de novo. These are prone to ulceration and secondary infection.
• **Location**: Lesions have a predilection for non-sun-exposed areas, classically in the **"bathing trunk" distribution** (buttocks, groin, hips, lower trunk, axillae).
• **Szary Syndrome**: A related but distinct, more aggressive leukemic variant of CTCL characterized by the triad of:
    ◦ **Erythroderma** (>80% body surface area redness)
    ◦ Lymphadenopathy
    ◦ The presence of malignant T-cells (**Szary cells**) in the peripheral blood.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Definitive Diagnosis**: **Skin biopsy** is the gold standard.
    ◦ **Multiple biopsies** from different lesion types are often required, as early stages can be histologically non-specific.
    ◦ A **punch biopsy** of the thickest, most indurated lesion is preferred.
• **Histopathology**:
    ◦ **Epidermotropism**: Atypical lymphocytes with hyperchromatic, convoluted (**cerebriform**) nuclei infiltrating the epidermis.
    ◦ **Pautrier's Microabscesses**: Intraepidermal collections of these atypical lymphocytes. Pathognomonic for MF.
    ◦ Superficial, band-like lymphoid infiltrate in the upper dermis.
• **Immunohistochemistry (IHC)**:
    ◦ Stains confirm the T-cell lineage: **CD3+**, **CD4+**.
    ◦ Malignant cells often show loss of pan-T-cell antigens, most commonly **CD7-**.
    ◦ A high CD4:CD8 ratio (>4:1) within the infiltrate is supportive.
• **Staging Workup** (for plaque, tumor, or extensive disease):
    ◦ **Labs**: CBC with differential, peripheral smear (to look for **Szary cells**), CMP, LDH.
    ◦ **Flow Cytometry**: To quantify circulating malignant T-cells in peripheral blood.
    ◦ **Imaging**: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or PET/CT to evaluate for lymph node and visceral involvement.
    ◦ **Lymph Node Biopsy**: If nodes are suspicious on exam or imaging.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly dependent on the stage at diagnosis.
• **Early Stage (IA)**: Excellent prognosis. The disease is indolent, and life expectancy is typically normal or near-normal.
• **Advanced Stage**: Prognosis worsens significantly with increasing skin burden (tumors, erythroderma), and especially with extracutaneous (nodal, visceral, or blood) involvement.
• The 5-year overall survival for Stage IA is >95%, while for Stage IV disease it can be <25%.

sections.overview:
• **Plaque psoriasis** is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory skin disease characterized by well-demarcated, erythematous plaques with silvery-white scale.
• Biologic therapies are reserved for patients with moderate-to-severe disease who have failed, have contraindications to, or are intolerant of topical therapies, phototherapy, and conventional systemic agents (e.g., methotrexate, cyclosporine).
• Biologics are monoclonal antibodies or fusion proteins engineered to target specific cytokines or cell surface receptors involved in the psoriatic inflammatory cascade.
    ◦ The three main classes used in psoriasis are **TNF-alpha inhibitors**, **IL-17 inhibitors**, and **IL-23 inhibitors**.
sections.etiology:
• Psoriasis results from a combination of genetic predisposition and environmental triggers, leading to aberrant activation of the innate and adaptive immune systems.
• The core pathophysiology involves a self-amplifying inflammatory loop driven by the **IL-23/Th17 axis**.
    ◦ **Initiation**: An environmental trigger (e.g., infection, trauma) causes keratinocytes to release danger signals.
    ◦ **Activation**: Antigen-presenting cells (APCs), particularly dendritic cells, are activated, migrate to lymph nodes, and present an unknown antigen to naive T-cells.
    ◦ **The IL-23/Th17 Axis**:
        ▪ APCs release key cytokines, including **Interleukin-23 (IL-23)** and **Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha (TNF-alpha)**.
        ▪ **IL-23** is critical for the differentiation and maintenance of a specific subset of T-helper cells called **Th17 cells**.
        ▪ Activated Th17 cells produce pro-inflammatory cytokines, most importantly **Interleukin-17 (IL-17)**, as well as IL-22.
    ◦ **Amplification & Plaque Formation**:
        ▪ **IL-17** and **TNF-alpha** act on keratinocytes, causing them to hyperproliferate (leading to acanthosis and thick plaques), produce more inflammatory mediators, and recruit neutrophils into the epidermis (forming **Munro's microabscesses**).
        ▪ This cycle of inflammation becomes self-sustaining, leading to the chronic nature of the disease.
• **Biologic Targets**:
    ◦ **TNF-alpha inhibitors** block the action of TNF-alpha, a pleiotropic cytokine that amplifies the inflammatory response.
    ◦ **IL-17 inhibitors** directly block IL-17 or its receptor, interrupting its direct effects on keratinocytes.
    ◦ **IL-23 inhibitors** block IL-23, preventing the differentiation and activation of the pathogenic Th17 cells, acting "upstream" in the inflammatory cascade.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects 2-3% of the worldwide population.
• **Age of Onset**: Bimodal distribution; peaks at age 20-30 and again at age 50-60.
• **Sex**: Males and females are equally affected.
• **Comorbidities**: Associated with **psoriatic arthritis (PsA)** in up to 30% of patients. Also strongly associated with **metabolic syndrome**, **cardiovascular disease**, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), and **depression**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The typical presentation is a patient with a chronic history of **pruritic, scaling rashes** that wax and wane.
• Lesions are often **symmetrically distributed**.
• The disease significantly impacts quality of life, causing social stigma, anxiety, and depression.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Diagnosis is almost always made based on the characteristic clinical findings.
• **Skin Biopsy**: Performed if the diagnosis is uncertain.
    ◦ Histology reveals:
        ▪ **Acanthosis**: Epidermal hyperplasia.
        ▪ **Parakeratosis**: Retention of nuclei in the stratum corneum.
        ▪ **Munro's Microabscesses**: Collections of neutrophils in the stratum corneum.
        ▪ Dilated, tortuous capillaries in the dermal papillae.
• **Labs (Pre-Biologic Screening)**: These are **essential** before initiating therapy.
    ◦ **Tuberculosis Screening**: Tuberculin Skin Test (PPD) or Interferon-Gamma Release Assay (IGRA, e.g., Quantiferon-TB Gold).
    ◦ **Hepatitis Panel**: HBsAg, anti-HBs, anti-HBc, anti-HCV.
    ◦ **Complete Blood Count (CBC)** with differential.
    ◦ **Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP)** to assess liver and kidney function.
    ◦ Consider **HIV screening**.
sections.prognosis:
• Psoriasis is a **chronic, non-curable disease** characterized by relapses and remissions.
• Biologic therapies have revolutionized management, enabling a majority of patients with moderate-to-severe disease to achieve significant (**PASI 75**) or near-complete (**PASI 90/100**) skin clearance.
• Treatment dramatically improves quality of life but requires lifelong therapy, as discontinuation typically leads to relapse.

sections.overview:
• **Dupilumab** (brand name **Dupixent**) is a human monoclonal antibody and a first-line biologic agent for the treatment of **moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis (AD)**.
    ◦ Indicated for patients whose disease is not adequately controlled with topical therapies or when those therapies are not advisable.
    ◦ By targeting the key drivers of **Type 2 inflammation**, it effectively reduces both the signs (lesions) and symptoms (**pruritus**) of AD, significantly improving quality of life.
sections.etiology:
• **Atopic Dermatitis Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Skin Barrier Dysfunction**
        ▪ Genetic mutations, most notably in the **filaggrin gene (*FLG*)**, lead to a compromised epidermal barrier.
        ▪ This results in increased transepidermal water loss (**TEWL**), leading to **xerosis** (dry skin), and allows for easier entry of allergens and microbes.
    ◦ **Immune Dysregulation**
        ▪ AD is characterized by a dominant **Type 2 inflammatory response**, driven by **T-helper 2 (Th2) cells**.
        ▪ Th2 cells produce key cytokines: **Interleukin-4 (IL-4)** and **Interleukin-13 (IL-13)**.
        ▪ **IL-4 and IL-13 functions**:
            - Promote **IgE** production from B-cells.
            - Recruit **eosinophils** and mast cells.
            - Directly stimulate sensory neurons, causing intense **pruritus**.
            - Further downregulate filaggrin and other structural proteins, worsening the skin barrier defect.
        ▪ This creates a self-perpetuating "**itch-scratch**" cycle.
• **Dupilumab Mechanism of Action (MOA)**
    ◦ **Dupilumab** is a monoclonal antibody that targets the **Interleukin-4 receptor alpha subunit (IL-4Rα)**.
    ◦ The **IL-4Rα** is a shared component of both the **IL-4** and **IL-13** receptor complexes.
    ◦ By binding to **IL-4Rα**, Dupilumab **simultaneously blocks the signaling pathways of both IL-4 and IL-13**.
    ◦ This dual inhibition effectively dampens the **Type 2 inflammatory cascade**, leading to reduced eosinophilia, lower IgE levels, improved skin barrier function, and a significant reduction in **pruritus** and inflammation.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Atopic Dermatitis** is one of the most common chronic inflammatory skin diseases.
• Affects up to **20% of children** and **3-7% of adults** worldwide.
• Typically begins in early childhood, with ~60% of cases developing in the first year of life.
• Often the first manifestation of the "**atopic march**," a progression from AD to allergic rhinitis and asthma.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The typical candidate for **Dupilumab** is a patient with **moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis** who presents with:
    ◦ Widespread, persistent, or frequently recurring eczematous lesions.
    ◦ **Failure of, intolerance to, or contraindication to** maximal topical therapy (e.g., mid-to-high potency topical corticosteroids, topical calcineurin inhibitors).
    ◦ Significant negative impact on quality of life, including severe **pruritus**, sleep disturbance, anxiety, or depression.
sections.diagnostics:
• Atopic Dermatitis is a **clinical diagnosis** based on history and characteristic physical exam findings (**pruritus**, typical morphology/distribution, chronic course, atopic history).
• **Laboratory Tests**
    ◦ Not required for diagnosis.
    ◦ Serum **IgE** is often elevated but is non-specific.
• **Skin Biopsy**
    ◦ Rarely necessary; may be performed to rule out other conditions (e.g., cutaneous T-cell lymphoma).
    ◦ Histology would show **spongiosis** in acute lesions and **acanthosis/hyperkeratosis** in chronic lesions.
sections.prognosis:
• **With Dupilumab**
    ◦ Excellent for most patients, with significant and sustained improvement in signs, symptoms (especially **pruritus**), and quality of life.
    ◦ It is a long-term controller therapy, not a cure; symptoms typically return upon discontinuation.
• **Natural History of AD**
    ◦ Chronic, relapsing-remitting course.
    ◦ Many children experience improvement or resolution by adolescence, but it can persist or develop de novo in adulthood.

sections.overview:
• **Hidradenitis Suppurativa (HS)**, also known as **acne inversa**, is a chronic, recurrent, inflammatory skin disease of the hair follicle
    ◦ Characteristically affects intertriginous skin areas (**axillae**, **groin**, **inframammary**, **perineal regions**)
    ◦ Presents with painful, deep-seated inflammatory **nodules** and **abscesses** that progress to form draining **sinus tracts** and hypertrophic **scarring**
• **Adalimumab (Humira)** is a recombinant human IgG1 monoclonal antibody that specifically binds to and neutralizes **Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha (TNF-α)**
    ◦ It is currently the **only FDA-approved biologic therapy** for the treatment of moderate to severe Hidradenitis Suppurativa
    ◦ Its use is a cornerstone of therapy for patients who have failed conventional treatments
sections.etiology:
• **Core Defect:** The primary event is **follicular occlusion** of the pilosebaceous unit, not an infection of the apocrine (sweat) glands, which is a common misconception
• **Pathologic Cascade:**
    ◦ **Follicular Hyperkeratosis:** The follicle becomes plugged with keratin
    ◦ **Follicular Rupture:** The blocked follicle dilates and eventually ruptures, releasing keratin, sebum, and bacteria into the dermis
    ◦ **Inflammatory Response:** This dermal spillage triggers a massive, foreign-body-type inflammatory reaction. Neutrophils and other immune cells are recruited
    ◦ **Immune Dysregulation:** HS is an immune-mediated inflammatory disease
        ▪ There is an upregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines, particularly **TNF-α**, **IL-1**, **IL-17**, and **IL-23**
• **Role of TNF-α:** TNF-α is a key cytokine that drives the chronic inflammation seen in HS. It promotes the recruitment of inflammatory cells, leading to tissue destruction, abscess formation, and the development of sinus tracts
• **Mechanism of Adalimumab:** Adalimumab binds to soluble and membrane-bound TNF-α, preventing it from interacting with its receptors (TNFR1 and TNFR2). This blockade downregulates the inflammatory cascade, reducing the clinical signs and symptoms of HS
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** Approximately 1-4% of the general population
• **Gender:** Affects females more than males (approx. 3:1 ratio)
• **Age of Onset:** Typically occurs after puberty, with peak incidence between ages 20-30. It is rare before puberty or after menopause, suggesting a hormonal influence
• **Race/Ethnicity:** Higher prevalence and severity reported in African Americans
sections.riskFactors:
• **Genetics:** Positive family history in 30-40% of patients (autosomal dominant inheritance suggested)
• **Smoking:** **Very strong association.** Nicotine may alter follicular keratinization and immune response
• **Obesity / Metabolic Syndrome:** Strong association. Increased skin friction, hormonal alterations from adipose tissue, and a pro-inflammatory state contribute
• **Hormonal Factors:** Flares are often linked to the menstrual cycle
• **Mechanical Stress:** Friction from tight clothing can exacerbate the condition
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Location:** Predilection for intertriginous areas rich in apocrine glands
    ◦ **Axillae** (most common)
    ◦ **Inguinofemoral** (groin) folds
    ◦ **Perineal** and **perianal** regions
    ◦ **Inframammary** folds
    ◦ **Buttocks**
• **Symptoms:**
    ◦ **Pain:** The hallmark symptom; often severe, debilitating, and out of proportion to physical findings
    ◦ **Purulent or Serosanguinous Drainage:** Often malodorous, leading to social embarrassment
    ◦ **Pruritus:** Can be intense in and around lesions
    ◦ **Reduced Mobility:** Scarring and contractures can limit the range of motion, especially in the axillae
    ◦ **Psychosocial Distress:** High rates of depression, anxiety, and social isolation
• **Disease Course:** Characterized by a chronic, relapsing-remitting course. Patients experience recurrent, painful flares that lead to progressive scarring and disability. The disease significantly impacts quality of life due to pain, malodorous drainage, and disfigurement
sections.physicalExam:
• **Primary Lesions:**
    ◦ Deep-seated, tender, erythematous inflammatory **nodules**
    ◦ Painful **abscesses** (can be sterile or secondarily infected)
• **Secondary / Chronic Lesions:**
    ◦ **"Tombstone" Comedones:** Open, double-or-triple-headed comedones are **pathognomonic**
    ◦ **Sinus Tracts:** Dermal or subcutaneous tunnels that connect inflammatory lesions and drain purulent material
    ◦ **Fistulas:** Abnormal connections between tracts and the skin surface
    ◦ **Scarring:** Can be atrophic (thin) or hypertrophic ("rope-like" fibrotic bands)
• **Hurley Staging System (Crucial for determining treatment):**
    ◦ **Stage I:** Abscess formation (single or multiple) without sinus tracts or scarring
    ◦ **Stage II:** Recurrent abscesses with sinus tracts and scarring; lesions are separated by normal-appearing skin
    ◦ **Stage III:** Diffuse or near-diffuse involvement with multiple interconnected sinus tracts and abscesses across an entire area
sections.diagnostics:
• HS is a **clinical diagnosis** based on three key criteria:
    ◦ **Typical Lesions:** Nodules, abscesses, sinus tracts
    ◦ **Typical Location:** Axilla, groin, inframammary, etc.
    ◦ **Chronicity and Recurrence:** History of repeated flares
• **Labs:** Not diagnostic. CBC may show leukocytosis; ESR and CRP may be elevated, reflecting systemic inflammation
• **Bacterial Cultures:** Often reveal polymicrobial growth or normal skin flora. They are useful to rule out primary infection (e.g., MRSA abscess) but do not diagnose HS
• **Biopsy:** Rarely necessary. Performed if there is suspicion of **Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)** in a chronic lesion. Histology shows follicular occlusion and perifollicular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate
sections.treatment:
• **Adjunctive Therapies:**
    ◦ **Pain Control:** NSAIDs, acetaminophen, neuropathic agents (gabapentin)
    ◦ **Acute Flares:** Intralesional corticosteroids, incision and drainage (I&D) of fluctuant abscesses
    ◦ **Topicals:** Topical clindamycin for mild disease or as an adjunct
    ◦ **Systemic Antibiotics:** Often used for their anti-inflammatory effects (e.g., Doxycycline, Clindamycin + Rifampin)
    ◦ **Surgery:** For refractory disease, options include deroofing of sinus tracts or wide local excision
sections.management:
• **Monitoring on Adalimumab:**
    ◦ Assess for signs/symptoms of infection before each dose
    ◦ Monitor for injection site reactions
    ◦ Periodic labs (CBC, LFTs) every 3-6 months
    ◦ Annual TB screening
    ◦ Regular skin exams due to a small increased risk of non-melanoma skin cancer
sections.complications:
• **Of the Disease:**
    ◦ **Scarring and Contractures:** Leading to lymphedema and limited mobility
    ◦ **Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC):** A rare but serious complication (**Marjolin's ulcer**) that can arise in chronic, draining sinus tracts
    ◦ **Anemia of Chronic Disease**
    ◦ **Fistula Formation:** Urethral, bladder, rectal fistulas
    ◦ **Systemic Comorbidities:** Associated with metabolic syndrome, inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's), and spondyloarthropathies
• **Of Adalimumab Therapy:**
    ◦ **Infections:** Increased risk of bacterial, fungal, and opportunistic infections
    ◦ **Injection Site Reactions:** Erythema, pain, swelling
    ◦ **Malignancy:** Small increased risk of lymphoma and non-melanoma skin cancer
    ◦ **Demyelinating Disease:** Rare but can be precipitated or exacerbated
    ◦ **Drug-induced Lupus**
sections.prognosis:
• HS is a chronic disease with no cure. The course is variable but often progressive without effective treatment
• Adalimumab has been shown in landmark clinical trials (**PIONEER I & II**) to significantly reduce the number of inflammatory lesions and improve quality of life
• Early intervention and multimodal therapy (medical, surgical, lifestyle) provide the best chance of controlling the disease and preventing long-term complications
sections.preventionEducation:
• **Patient Education:**
    ◦ Disease is chronic, not curable, but manageable
    ◦ Counsel on **smoking cessation** and **weight management**
    ◦ Proper wound care and use of non-occlusive dressings

sections.overview:
• Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) is a clinical syndrome characterized by a rapid decline in renal function, occurring over hours to days, defined by an increase in serum creatinine (SCr), a decrease in urine output (UOP), or both.
• AKI results in the failure to excrete nitrogenous waste products and maintain fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base homeostasis.
• It is a spectrum of injury, not a single disease, and is broadly categorized based on the location of the primary insult: Prerenal, Intrinsic (Renal), and Postrenal.
    ◦ **KDIGO Definition:** An increase in SCr by 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours, OR an increase in SCr to 1.5 times baseline within the prior 7 days, OR a urine volume <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours.
sections.etiology: • The pathophysiology is best understood by classifying AKI into three main categories.
sections.epidemiology:
• Occurs in 5-7% of all hospitalized patients.
• Incidence is up to 30-50% in ICU patients.
• Most common cause in outpatients: **Prerenal AKI**.
• Most common cause in hospitalized patients: **Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN)**, often from ischemic or nephrotoxic insults.
• Postrenal is the least common cause overall (~5%).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Often asymptomatic and identified incidentally on routine lab work (**rising BUN/SCr**).
• Patients may present with symptoms related to the underlying cause (e.g., sepsis, heart failure) or with symptoms of uremia and volume overload if the AKI is severe.
• **Oliguria** (<400-500 mL/day) or **anuria** (<100 mL/day) may be present but is not required for diagnosis (non-oliguric AKI is common).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Lab Studies:**
    ◦ **BMP/CMP:**
        ▪ **Serum Creatinine (SCr):** Hallmark of AKI.
        ▪ **Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN):** Also rises, but less specific than creatinine.
        ▪ **BUN:SCr Ratio: >20:1** suggests prerenal cause (urea is reabsorbed with water).
        ▪ **Hyperkalemia:** Life-threatening complication.
        ▪ **Metabolic Acidosis:** Anion gap or non-anion gap; look for low serum bicarbonate (HCO3-).
        ▪ **Hyperphosphatemia / Hypocalcemia.**
    ◦ **CBC:**
        ▪ May show anemia (if chronic) or signs of infection/inflammation.
        ▪ **Eosinophilia** may suggest AIN.
    ◦ **Urinalysis (UA) & Urine Studies (CRUCIAL FOR DIAGNOSIS):**
        ▪ **Urine Microscopy (Sediment Exam):**
            • **Prerenal:** Bland sediment, may see hyaline casts.
            • **ATN:** **Muddy brown granular casts** (pathognomonic), renal tubular epithelial cells.
            • **AIN:** **WBC casts**, eosinophiluria.
            • **Glomerulonephritis:** **RBC casts**, dysmorphic RBCs.
        ▪ **Urine Chemistry:**
            • **Fractional Excretion of Sodium (FENa):** (Urine Na x Serum Cr) / (Serum Na x Urine Cr) x 100
                ◦ **FENa <1%:** Suggests prerenal state (tubules are working and avidly reabsorbing Na).
                ◦ **FENa >2%:** Suggests ATN (damaged tubules cannot reabsorb Na).
                ◦ *Note: FENa is unreliable in patients on diuretics.*
            • **Fractional Excretion of Urea (FEUrea):** Used if patient is on diuretics.
                ◦ **FEUrea <35%:** Suggests prerenal state.
• **Imaging:**
    ◦ **Renal Ultrasound:** **First-line imaging test for ALL new AKI cases.**
        ▪ Primarily used to rule out a postrenal (obstructive) cause by looking for **hydronephrosis**.
        ▪ Also assesses kidney size (small kidneys suggest CKD).
    ◦ **Bladder Scan:** Non-invasive bedside tool to assess for post-void residual volume.
• **Renal Biopsy:**
    ◦ **Indication:** Reserved for cases where the diagnosis remains unclear after a non-invasive workup, particularly when suspecting intrinsic causes like glomerulonephritis or AIN that may benefit from specific therapy (e.g., immunosuppression).
sections.prognosis:
• Highly variable and depends on the underlying etiology, severity, baseline health, and presence of comorbidities.
• Mortality for hospitalized AKI is ~20%, and >50% for ICU patients with AKI requiring dialysis.
• Full recovery of renal function is possible, especially in prerenal and postrenal causes.
• ATN can resolve, but patients are at a significantly increased risk for developing **CKD** in the future.

sections.overview:
• **Prerenal Acute Kidney Injury (AKI)** is the **most common form of AKI**, accounting for 60-70% of cases.
    ◦ It is a functional, reversible condition caused by **decreased renal perfusion (hypoperfusion)** in the absence of structural damage to the kidney parenchyma itself.
    ◦ The glomeruli and tubules are initially intact but are not being adequately supplied with blood, leading to a drop in the **Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)**.
    ◦ If the underlying cause of hypoperfusion is not corrected promptly, it can progress to intrinsic renal damage, specifically **Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN)**.
sections.etiology:
• The core pathophysiology is a **decrease in renal blood flow (RBF)**, which leads to a decreased **GFR**.
    ◦ In response to this perceived hypovolemia, the kidneys activate compensatory mechanisms to preserve salt and water, leading to the characteristic laboratory findings.
• **Pathophysiologic Response**
    ◦ **Decreased RBF** leads to **Decreased GFR**.
    ◦ **RAAS Activation**: Renin is released, leading to Angiotensin II and Aldosterone production.
        ▪ **Angiotensin II**: Causes systemic vasoconstriction and preferential constriction of the **efferent arteriole** to maintain GFR.
        ▪ **Aldosterone**: Promotes sodium and water reabsorption in the distal tubule and collecting duct.
    ◦ **ADH (Vasopressin) Release**: Promotes free water reabsorption in the collecting ducts, leading to concentrated urine.
    ◦ **Sympathetic Nervous System Activation**: Causes systemic vasoconstriction and **afferent arteriole** constriction to divert blood to vital organs.
• **Etiologic Categories**
    ◦ **1. True Hypovolemia** (Decreased Intravascular Volume)
        ▪ **Hemorrhage**: Trauma, GI bleed, surgical blood loss.
        ▪ **Renal Losses**: Over-diuresis, adrenal insufficiency.
        ▪ **GI Losses**: Vomiting, diarrhea, NG tube suction.
        ▪ **Cutaneous Losses**: Burns, sweating, fever.
        ▪ **Poor Oral Intake**: Dehydration.
    ◦ **2. Decreased Effective Circulating Volume** (Fluid is present but not in the vasculature)
        ▪ **Congestive Heart Failure (CHF)**: Low cardiac output leads to poor renal perfusion.
        ▪ **Cirrhosis (Hepatorenal Syndrome)**: Systemic vasodilation and splanchnic pooling of blood reduces effective volume.
        ▪ **Nephrotic Syndrome**: Massive protein loss leads to low oncotic pressure and third-spacing of fluid.
        ▪ **Sepsis/Anaphylaxis**: Systemic vasodilation and capillary leak leads to relative hypovolemia.
    ◦ **3. Pharmacologic Causes** (Impaired Renal Autoregulation)
        ▪ **NSAIDs** (e.g., ibuprofen, naproxen): Inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, causing unopposed constriction of the **afferent arteriole**, reducing blood flow into the glomerulus.
        ▪ **ACE Inhibitors / ARBs** (e.g., lisinopril, losartan): Block Angiotensin II, causing dilation of the **efferent arteriole**, reducing glomerular filtration pressure.
        ▪ **Cyclosporine/Tacrolimus**: Cause afferent arteriole vasoconstriction.
    ◦ **4. Renal Artery Occlusion**
        ▪ Bilateral **renal artery stenosis** (or unilateral stenosis in a solitary kidney).
        ▪ Renal artery thrombosis or embolism.
sections.epidemiology:
• The **most common cause of AKI**, representing up to 70% of community-acquired and 40% of hospital-acquired cases.
• Incidence is highest in **critically ill patients**, especially in the ICU setting.
• More common in the **elderly population** due to comorbidities and polypharmacy.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The clinical presentation is typically dominated by the signs and symptoms of the **underlying disorder** causing the renal hypoperfusion.
• The AKI itself is often an **incidental laboratory finding**.
    ◦ The patient does not present *because* of prerenal AKI; they present with heart failure, sepsis, or dehydration, and the AKI is discovered during the workup.
sections.diagnostics:
• The goal of diagnostics is to identify AKI and differentiate prerenal causes from intrinsic or postrenal causes.
• **Serum Labs**
    ◦ **Serum Creatinine (SCr)** and **Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN)**.
    ◦ **BUN:Cr Ratio > 20:1**: This is the hallmark finding.
        ▪ Urea is passively reabsorbed with sodium and water in the proximal tubule. In a hypoperfused state, increased water reabsorption leads to a disproportionate rise in BUN compared to creatinine.
• **Urine Studies** (Crucial for differentiation)
    ◦ **Urine Sodium (UNa): < 20 mEq/L**.
        ▪ The kidney is avidly reabsorbing sodium to restore volume.
    ◦ **Fractional Excretion of Sodium (FENa): < 1%**.
        ▪ The gold standard for prerenal state. Represents the percentage of filtered sodium that is excreted.
        ▪ Note: Can be falsely elevated by recent diuretic use.
        ▪ Formula: `FENa = [(Urine Na x Serum Cr) / (Serum Na x Urine Cr)] x 100`
    ◦ **Urine Osmolality: > 500 mOsm/kg**.
        ▪ The kidneys are maximally concentrating the urine in response to ADH to conserve water.
    ◦ **Urine Specific Gravity: > 1.020**.
        ▪ Reflects concentrated urine.
• **Urine Sediment (Urinalysis with Microscopy)**
    ◦ **Bland/Benign**: Typically shows no cells or casts.
        ▪ **Hyaline casts** (precipitated Tamm-Horsfall protein from low flow/concentrated urine) may be present.
        ▪ This is a key finding that differentiates it from the **muddy brown casts of ATN**.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Renal Ultrasound**: Primarily used to **rule out postrenal AKI** by looking for hydronephrosis (obstruction).
        ▪ In prerenal AKI, the kidneys will appear normal.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** if the underlying cause is identified and corrected promptly.
    ◦ Renal function typically returns to baseline within days.
• The overall prognosis is determined by the severity of the **underlying disease** (e.g., sepsis, cardiogenic shock) rather than the prerenal AKI itself.

sections.overview:
• **Intrinsic Acute Kidney Injury (AKI)**, or intra-renal AKI, is a form of kidney injury from direct damage to the kidney parenchyma itself.
    ◦ Damage can affect the tubules, interstitium, glomeruli, or renal vasculature.
    ◦ Unlike **pre-renal AKI** (perfusion issue) or **post-renal AKI** (obstruction issue), intrinsic AKI involves structural damage within the kidney.
    ◦ It is the most common cause of AKI in hospitalized patients.
    ◦ The most frequent subtype is **Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN)**.
sections.etiology: • Intrinsic AKI is categorized based on the primary site of injury within the kidney parenchyma.
sections.epidemiology:
• Accounts for approximately 50% of all AKI cases in hospitalized patients.
• **ATN** is the cause in ~85% of these intrinsic AKI cases.
• Incidence is highest in critically ill patients, particularly those in the ICU with sepsis or multi-organ failure.
sections.riskFactors:
• Pre-existing **Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)**
• **Diabetes Mellitus**
• Advanced age
• Volume depletion / Dehydration
• **Sepsis**
• Heart failure or liver failure (cirrhosis)
• Exposure to **nephrotoxins** (contrast, aminoglycosides, NSAIDs)
• Major surgery (especially cardiothoracic or vascular)
• **Hypotension**
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is often dominated by the underlying illness (e.g., fever and hypotension in sepsis; signs of heart failure).
• The key finding is a **rise in serum creatinine (Cr)** and **Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN)**, with or without a decrease in urine output (**oliguria** <400-500 mL/day or **anuria** <100 mL/day).
• Patients may be asymptomatic in early stages, with AKI being detected solely on lab work.
• Symptoms are often nonspecific and related to **uremia** or fluid overload.
    ◦ Malaise, fatigue, weakness
    ◦ Nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite
    ◦ Shortness of breath (due to fluid overload/pulmonary edema)
    ◦ Confusion, lethargy, asterixis (signs of **uremia**)
• **Specific Symptom Constellations**:
    ◦ **AIN-specific triad** (classic but only seen in 10-15% of cases): **Fever**, **maculopapular rash**, **arthralgias**.
    ◦ **GN-specific**: **Edema** (periorbital, peripheral), **dark/cola-colored urine** (**hematuria**), **hypertension**.
sections.physicalExam:
• **General**: Assess volume status.
• **Volume Overload**: Pitting edema, pulmonary rales/crackles, elevated JVP, S3 gallop.
• **Volume Depletion**: Tachycardia, hypotension, dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor.
• **Specific Clues to Etiology**:
    ◦ **AIN**: **Maculopapular rash**.
    ◦ **GN/Vasculitis**: **Palpable purpura**, **livedo reticularis**, **malar rash** (lupus).
    ◦ **Atheroemboli**: **Livedo reticularis**, **blue toes**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Renal Ultrasound**: Essential first imaging step.
    ◦ **Primary Role**: Rule out post-renal obstruction (**hydronephrosis**).
    ◦ Findings in intrinsic AKI are often nonspecific but may show enlarged, echogenic kidneys.
sections.treatment:
• **Stop the Offending Agent**: Discontinue any nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, PPIs, etc.).
• **Restore Perfusion**: If ischemic, treat the underlying cause (e.g., antibiotics and vasopressors for septic shock, fluids for hypovolemia).
sections.management:
• Achieve and maintain euvolemia.
    ◦ Carefully monitor daily weights, intake, and output.
    ◦ For oliguric/anuric patients with volume overload, fluid restriction is necessary.
• **Loop Diuretics** (e.g., Furosemide) can be used to manage fluid overload but **DO NOT** treat the underlying AKI or shorten its course. They are contraindicated in volume-depleted patients.
• **Hyperkalemia**: This is a medical emergency.
    ◦ **Stabilize membrane**: Calcium gluconate.
    ◦ **Shift K+ intracellularly**: Insulin with dextrose, albuterol.
    ◦ **Remove K+ from body**: Kayexalate, patiromer, or hemodialysis.
• Monitor and correct phosphate, calcium, and magnesium abnormalities.
• Treat severe **metabolic acidosis** (pH < 7.1-7.2 or bicarb < 15) with IV sodium bicarbonate.
• Adjust doses of all renally excreted medications. Avoid further nephrotoxins.
• **Dialysis**:
    ◦ Indicated for severe, life-threatening complications refractory to medical management.
    ◦ **Indications (Mnemonic: AEIOU)**:
        ▪ **A**: **Acidosis** (severe, refractory)
        ▪ **E**: **Electrolytes** (refractory **hyperkalemia**)
        ▪ **I**: **Intoxications** (salicylates, lithium, ethylene glycol)
        ▪ **O**: **Overload** (refractory fluid overload/pulmonary edema)
        ▪ **U**: **Uremia** (symptomatic: pericarditis, encephalopathy, seizures)
sections.complications:
• **Metabolic**: **Hyperkalemia**, **metabolic acidosis**, **hyperphosphatemia**.
• **Cardiovascular**: **Volume overload**, **pulmonary edema**, hypertension, arrhythmias (from **hyperkalemia**).
• **Uremic**: Encephalopathy, pericarditis, platelet dysfunction (bleeding).
• **Long-term**: Increased risk of developing or progression of **Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)** and **End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD)**.
sections.prognosis:
• Highly variable and depends on the underlying cause, severity, patient age, and comorbidities.
• Mortality is high (>50%) for AKI in the ICU setting, largely due to the severity of the underlying illness (e.g., sepsis).
• Prognosis for drug-induced AIN is generally good if the offending agent is stopped promptly.
• Many survivors of severe AKI do not fully recover baseline renal function and are left with some degree of **CKD**.

sections.overview:
• **Postrenal Acute Kidney Injury (AKI)** is a form of kidney failure caused by the **obstruction of urine flow** from the kidneys.
    ◦ This obstruction leads to a backup of urine and an increase in pressure within the urinary tract (ureters, renal pelvis, and tubules).
    ◦ The elevated pressure opposes glomerular filtration, leading to a rapid decrease in the **Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)** and subsequent **azotemia** (accumulation of BUN and creatinine).
    ◦ Accounts for approximately 5-10% of all AKI cases.
    ◦ It is the most readily **reversible** form of AKI if the obstruction is identified and relieved promptly.
    ◦ For AKI to occur, the obstruction must affect **both kidneys** (bilateral obstruction) or a **single functioning kidney**.
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **1. Obstruction:** A physical blockage occurs anywhere along the urinary tract, from the renal calyces to the urethral meatus.
    ◦ **2. Increased Pressure:** The blockage prevents urine drainage, causing a retrograde increase in hydrostatic pressure within the ureters, renal pelvis, and Bowman's space of the nephrons.
    ◦ **3. Decreased GFR:** The elevated pressure in Bowman's space directly opposes the hydrostatic pressure that drives glomerular filtration, reducing the net filtration pressure and causing a sharp decline in GFR.
    ◦ **4. Renal Effects:** Initially, renal blood flow may increase as a compensatory mechanism, but it soon decreases due to afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction. Prolonged obstruction leads to tubular damage, interstitial inflammation, and eventually fibrosis, which can cause irreversible kidney damage.
• **Etiology (Categorized by Location)**
    ◦ **Urethra / Bladder Outlet Obstruction (BOO) - Most Common**
        ▪ **Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH):** The most common cause in older men.
        ▪ **Prostate Cancer**
        ▪ **Urethral Stricture**
        ▪ **Blocked Foley Catheter**
        ▪ **Neurogenic Bladder:** Due to spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis, or diabetes.
        ▪ **Anticholinergic Medications:** Can cause urinary retention.
    ◦ **Ureteral Obstruction (Must be bilateral or unilateral in a solitary kidney)**
        ▪ **Intrinsic:**
            • **Nephrolithiasis (Kidney Stones):** Especially at the ureterovesical junction (UVJ).
            • **Blood Clots**
            • **Sloughed Papillae** (papillary necrosis)
        ▪ **Extrinsic Compression:**
            • **Malignancy:** Cervical, prostate, bladder, colorectal cancers causing retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy or direct invasion.
            • **Retroperitoneal Fibrosis**
            • **Aortic Aneurysm**
    ◦ **Renal Pelvis / Intrarenal Obstruction**
        ▪ **Nephrolithiasis** (e.g., large staghorn calculi)
        ▪ **Tumors** (e.g., transitional cell carcinoma)
        ▪ **Crystal Deposition:** Uric acid (tumor lysis syndrome), acyclovir, sulfonamides.
sections.epidemiology:
• Accounts for 5-10% of AKI hospital admissions.
• Bimodal age distribution:
    ◦ **Young Children:** Often due to congenital anomalies (e.g., posterior urethral valves).
    ◦ **Older Adults (>60 years):**
        ▪ Predominantly in men due to **BPH** and **prostate cancer**.
        ▪ In women, often related to **pelvic malignancies** (cervical, ovarian) or pelvic organ prolapse.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation can be dramatic (**acute anuria**) or subtle (gradual decline in urine output).
• A classic presentation is an elderly male with a history of **BPH** who presents with **anuria** or **oliguria** and lower abdominal discomfort.
• The patient may have symptoms related to the underlying cause (e.g., **flank pain** from a kidney stone) or symptoms of uremia (**nausea**, **confusion**, malaise) if the condition is advanced.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP)**
        ▪ **Serum Creatinine (Cr) and Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN):** The hallmark of AKI.
        ▪ **BUN:Cr Ratio:** Often >20:1 initially, as increased intratubular pressure enhances urea reabsorption (similar to prerenal state). This is not a reliable differentiator.
        ▪ **Hyperkalemia:** A life-threatening emergency resulting from decreased renal excretion.
        ▪ **Metabolic Acidosis:** (Low bicarbonate) due to impaired acid excretion.
    ◦ **Urinalysis (UA)**
        ▪ Often bland or unremarkable.
        ▪ May show **hematuria** (stones, malignancy, trauma from catheter), **pyuria** (infection), or crystals (e.g., uric acid, calcium oxalate).
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Renal and Bladder Ultrasound (US)**
        ▪ **THE KEY DIAGNOSTIC TEST.**
        ▪ Rapid, non-invasive, and highly sensitive for detecting **hydronephrosis** (dilation of the renal pelvis and calyces) and **hydroureter**.
        ▪ Can also identify a distended bladder, large stones, or masses.
    ◦ **Bedside Bladder Scan**
        ▪ A quick, initial test to measure post-void residual (PVR) volume.
        ▪ A PVR > 200 mL is highly suggestive of bladder outlet obstruction.
    ◦ **Non-contrast CT of Abdomen/Pelvis**
        ▪ The imaging modality of choice for suspected **nephrolithiasis**.
        ▪ Can also demonstrate hydronephrosis and may identify the site and cause of obstruction (e.g., retroperitoneal mass).
    ◦ **CT Urogram (with contrast)**
        ▪ Used to delineate the anatomy of the urinary tract and identify the exact location/cause of obstruction.
        ▪ Often performed after initial kidney function has been stabilized due to the risk of contrast-induced nephropathy.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** if the obstruction is recognized and relieved promptly.
    ◦ Renal function often returns to baseline or near-baseline within 7-14 days.
• The degree of recovery depends on the duration and completeness of the obstruction.
• Prognosis is worse if the obstruction was present for weeks to months, as this can lead to irreversible kidney damage.
• The patient's overall prognosis is also heavily influenced by the underlying etiology (e.g., metastatic cancer vs. a benign kidney stone).

sections.overview:
• Form of **intrinsic acute kidney injury (AKI)** characterized by the injury and necrosis of renal tubular epithelial cells
    ◦ **Most common cause of AKI** in hospitalized patients
• Leads to a rapid decline in renal function, resulting in the retention of waste products (urea, creatinine) and dysregulation of fluid and electrolytes
• The damage is potentially **reversible** if the underlying cause is corrected
sections.etiology: • Broadly classified into two major categories based on the mechanism of injury: **Ischemic** and **Nephrotoxic**
sections.epidemiology:
• Cause of **~50% of all cases of AKI** in hospitalized patients
• Incidence is highest in **critically ill patients**, affecting up to 25% of patients in the ICU
• **Sepsis** and **major surgery** are the leading causes in the inpatient setting
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Clinical presentation is often dominated by the **underlying illness** (e.g., **fever** and **hypotension** in sepsis; **muscle pain** in rhabdomyolysis)
• Diagnosis is frequently made based on routine laboratory monitoring that reveals a **sudden rise in serum creatinine**
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly variable and depends on the underlying cause, severity of illness, and patient comorbidities
• **Mortality rate is high (40-50%)** in critically ill patients, often due to the underlying condition (e.g., sepsis) rather than the ATN itself
• For survivors, renal function typically recovers over several weeks to months
    ◦ A significant portion may not return to their baseline renal function and may develop **CKD**

sections.overview:
• **Acute Interstitial Nephritis (AIN)** is a cause of **Acute Kidney Injury (AKI)** characterized by an **inflammatory infiltrate** in the renal interstitium and tubules.
    ◦ This process spares the glomeruli and renal vasculature initially.
    ◦ It is most often a hypersensitivity reaction to a medication or other exposure, leading to a sudden deterioration in renal function.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology (Causes):**
    ◦ **Drugs (>70% of cases):** The most common cause. The reaction is idiosyncratic and not dose-dependent.
        ▪ **Antibiotics:** Penicillins (especially methicillin, ampicillin), Cephalosporins, Sulfonamides (including TMP-SMX), Rifampin, Ciprofloxacin.
        ▪ **NSAIDs:** Ibuprofen, naproxen, indomethacin, celecoxib. (Often presents with nephrotic-range proteinuria and a less prominent systemic inflammatory response).
        ▪ **Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs):** Omeprazole, pantoprazole. A growing and often-missed cause.
        ▪ **Diuretics:** Thiazides, Furosemide.
        ▪ **Others:** Allopurinol, Cimetidine, Phenytoin.
    ◦ **Infections (~15%):**
        ▪ **Bacterial:** *Streptococcus*, *Legionella*, *Mycoplasma*.
        ▪ **Viral:** Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV), Cytomegalovirus (CMV), HIV.
    ◦ **Systemic / Autoimmune Diseases (~5%):**
        ▪ **Sarcoidosis**
        ▪ **Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)**
        ▪ **Sjögren's syndrome**
        ▪ **TINU syndrome** (Tubulointerstitial Nephritis and Uveitis)
• **Pathophysiology:**
    ◦ AIN is primarily a **cell-mediated (Type IV) hypersensitivity reaction**.
    ◦ The offending agent (e.g., a drug) acts as a **hapten**, binding to a protein within the tubular basement membrane.
    ◦ This complex is processed by antigen-presenting cells and presented to T-cells.
    ◦ Activated T-cells infiltrate the renal interstitium, releasing cytokines that recruit other inflammatory cells (macrophages, eosinophils, plasma cells).
    ◦ This inflammatory response leads to interstitial edema and tubular cell injury, impairing renal function and causing **AKI**.
    ◦ A **Type I (IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity** may also contribute, explaining the presence of eosinophils and rash.
sections.epidemiology:
• Accounts for approximately 15-20% of cases of unexplained **AKI** in hospitalized patients.
• The incidence is likely underestimated as a renal biopsy is often not performed.
• Can occur at any age, but incidence increases with age due to polypharmacy.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The onset of symptoms is variable, typically occurring **5 days to several weeks** after exposure to the offending agent (average 10-14 days).
• The classic presentation is a patient who was recently started on a new medication (e.g., an antibiotic for an infection) and now develops a rising creatinine.
• **Classic Triad (present in only 10-15% of patients):**
    ◦ **Fever**
    ◦ **Rash**
    ◦ **Eosinophilia**
sections.diagnostics:
• **Laboratory Findings (Blood):**
    ◦ **Serum Creatinine and BUN:** The hallmark of **AKI**.
    ◦ **Peripheral Eosinophilia:** Found in up to 80% of drug-induced **AIN** but is non-specific.
    ◦ **Elevated IgE levels:** May be seen.
• **Laboratory Findings (Urine):**
    ◦ **Urinalysis (UA):**
        ▪ **Sterile Pyuria:** Presence of WBCs in the absence of bacteria (negative culture). This is a classic finding.
        ▪ **Hematuria:** Microscopic hematuria is common.
        ▪ **Mild Proteinuria:** Usually non-nephrotic (<3.5 g/day).
            ▪ *Exception: NSAID-induced AIN can cause nephrotic-range proteinuria*.
    ◦ **Urine Microscopy:**
        ▪ **WBC Casts:** **Pathognomonic for interstitial inflammation/pyelonephritis**, but only seen in a minority of cases. Their presence is highly suggestive of **AIN** in the right clinical context.
    ◦ **Urine Eosinophils (Hansel or Wright stain):**
        ▪ Classically associated with **AIN**, but has **poor sensitivity and specificity**.
        ▪ Can be positive in other conditions (UTI, ATN, atheroemboli) and negative in confirmed **AIN**.
        ▪ Not routinely recommended.
    ◦ **Fractional Excretion of Sodium (FENa):**
        ▪ Usually **>1%**, consistent with intra-renal tubular damage.
• **Imaging:**
    ◦ **Renal Ultrasound:** Primarily used to rule out other causes of **AKI**, such as post-renal obstruction. Kidneys may appear normal-sized or enlarged and echogenic due to interstitial edema.
• **Definitive Diagnosis:**
    ◦ **Renal Biopsy (Gold Standard):**
        ▪ Indicated when the diagnosis is uncertain, if there's no improvement after stopping the suspected agent, or if steroid therapy is being considered.
        ▪ **Histology:** Shows diffuse or patchy **interstitial inflammatory infiltrate** (lymphocytes, macrophages, eosinophils, plasma cells) and **tubulitis** (inflammatory cells invading the tubular basement membrane).
sections.prognosis:
• Generally good if the offending agent is identified and removed promptly.
• Over 60-70% of patients recover renal function, though some may be left with residual CKD.
• **Poor prognostic factors:**
    ◦ Delayed diagnosis and treatment (>2 weeks).
    ◦ Prolonged oliguria/anuria.
    ◦ Advanced age.
    ◦ Significant interstitial fibrosis on biopsy.
• NSAID-induced **AIN** has a generally worse prognosis for full recovery.

sections.overview:
• Acute Glomerulonephritis (AGN) is an immunologically mediated inflammation of the glomeruli, the kidney's primary filtering units, leading to damage of the glomerular capillary walls
• Results in the abrupt onset of the characteristic **nephritic syndrome**
    ◦ **Hematuria** (red blood cells in the urine)
    ◦ **Hypertension** (due to sodium and water retention)
    ◦ **Edema** (due to fluid retention)
    ◦ **Azotemia** (elevated BUN and creatinine)
    ◦ **Oliguria** (decreased urine output)
• The hallmark finding is hematuria with **RBC casts** in the urine, which is **pathognomonic** for glomerular bleeding
sections.etiology:
• The underlying mechanism is typically a **Type III Hypersensitivity Reaction**
    ◦ Involves the formation and deposition of antigen-antibody immune complexes within the glomeruli
    ◦ These complexes activate the complement cascade, leading to an inflammatory response, leukocyte infiltration, and damage to the glomerular structure
• **Major Causes**
    ◦ **Post-Infectious Glomerulonephritis (PIGN)**
        ▪ **Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN)**: The classic prototype
            • Occurs after infection with specific nephritogenic strains of **Group A β-hemolytic Streptococcus (GAS)**
            • **Latency Period**: Glomerulonephritis appears **1-3 weeks** after streptococcal pharyngitis or **3-6 weeks** after streptococcal skin infection (impetigo)
            • Antibiotics treat the infection and prevent rheumatic fever but do **not** prevent the development of PSGN
        ▪ **Non-Streptococcal PIGN**
            • Bacterial: Staphylococcal (endocarditis, shunt infections), Pneumococcal
            • Viral: Hepatitis B/C, HIV, CMV, EBV
            • Fungal/Parasitic: Malaria, Toxoplasmosis
    ◦ **Systemic Autoimmune Diseases (Secondary GN)**
        ▪ **IgA Nephropathy (Berger's Disease)**: The most common cause of primary GN worldwide
            • Characterized by IgA deposition in the glomerular mesangium
            • Classic presentation: Gross hematuria that occurs **concurrently (syn-pharyngitic)** with a URI or GI infection
        ▪ **Lupus Nephritis**: A common and serious complication of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)
        ▪ **ANCA-Associated Vasculitis**: (Pauci-immune GN - few immune deposits on biopsy)
            • Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (Wegener's)
            • Microscopic Polyangiitis
        ▪ **Anti-Glomerular Basement Membrane (Anti-GBM) Disease / Goodpasture's Syndrome**
            • Antibodies attack the type IV collagen in the glomerular and alveolar basement membranes, causing both glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage
sections.epidemiology:
• **PSGN**: Primarily a disease of **children (ages 5-15)**, though it can occur in adults
    ◦ More common in males (2:1 ratio)
    ◦ Incidence has decreased in developed countries due to prompt treatment of streptococcal infections
• **IgA Nephropathy**: Most common in young adults, particularly in Asian populations
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic vignette is a child who had a sore throat or skin rash 2 weeks prior and now presents with **puffy eyes, dark urine, and high blood pressure**
• The onset is abrupt
sections.diagnostics:
• **Urinalysis (UA) with Microscopy**: **Most important initial test**
    ◦ **Hematuria**: >3 RBCs per high-power field
    ◦ **RBC Casts**: **Pathognomonic for glomerulonephritis**; indicates bleeding is from the glomerulus
    ◦ **Dysmorphic RBCs (Acanthocytes)**: RBCs with a distorted shape from passing through the damaged glomerulus
    ◦ **Proteinuria**: Usually mild to moderate (sub-nephrotic range, <3.5 g/day)
• **Blood Tests**
    ◦ **Renal Function Panel**
        ▪ **Elevated BUN and Creatinine** (azotemia)
        ▪ BUN:Cr ratio is often >20:1 initially (pre-renal component)
    ◦ **Serologic Studies (to determine etiology)**
        ▪ **Antistreptolysin O (ASO) Titer**: Elevated in 80-90% of cases following GAS pharyngitis
        ▪ **Anti-DNase B Titer**: A more sensitive marker, especially for post-impetigo GN
        ▪ **Complement Levels (C3/C4)**: **Low C3** with normal C4 is characteristic of PSGN. Low C3 and C4 suggest lupus nephritis
        ▪ **ANCA, ANA, Anti-GBM antibodies**: Order if a systemic cause is suspected
• **Renal Biopsy**: **Gold standard for diagnosis** but not routinely performed for typical post-streptococcal cases in children
    ◦ **Indications**: Atypical presentation, rapidly progressive course, suspected non-PSGN cause, significant AKI, or no improvement after 4-6 weeks
    ◦ **PSGN Findings**: Enlarged, hypercellular glomeruli on light microscopy. Granular ("lumpy-bumpy") deposits of IgG and C3 on immunofluorescence
sections.prognosis:
• **Children**: Excellent. >95% achieve complete recovery of renal function. Proteinuria resolves in months, but microscopic hematuria may persist for 1-2 years
• **Adults**: More guarded prognosis. Higher rates of progression to CKD and persistent hypertension

sections.overview:
• **Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)** is defined as the presence of kidney damage or a decreased Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) < 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 for a period of **three months or more**, irrespective of the cause
• It is a progressive loss of renal function, culminating in **End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD)** if untreated
• The diagnosis and staging are crucial for management and slowing progression
sections.etiology:
• **Major Causes**
    ◦ **Diabetes Mellitus (Diabetic Nephropathy)**: The leading cause (~40%). Hyperglycemia leads to glomerulosclerosis, basement membrane thickening, and mesangial expansion
    ◦ **Hypertension (Hypertensive Nephrosclerosis)**: Second leading cause (~25%). Sustained high blood pressure causes arteriosclerosis of renal arterioles, leading to ischemia and glomerulosclerosis
    ◦ **Glomerulonephritis**: Primary or secondary inflammation of the glomeruli (e.g., IgA nephropathy, Lupus nephritis)
    ◦ **Polycystic Kidney Disease (PCKD)**: A genetic disorder causing numerous cysts to grow in the kidneys
    ◦ **Obstructive Uropathy**: Chronic blockage of the urinary tract (e.g., BPH, kidney stones, tumors) leading to hydronephrosis and parenchymal damage
    ◦ **Other**: Tubulointerstitial nephritis (often from drugs like **NSAIDs**), renovascular disease, multiple myeloma
• **Pathophysiology (Final Common Pathway)**
    ◦ **Initial Insult**: The primary disease damages a subset of nephrons
    ◦ **Compensatory Hyperfiltration**: The remaining, healthy nephrons hypertrophy and increase their individual GFR to compensate for the lost function
    ◦ **Intraglomerular Hypertension**: This compensatory mechanism leads to high pressure within the glomeruli
    ◦ **Glomerular Damage**: Over time, this pressure causes glomerular scarring (**glomerulosclerosis**) and proteinuria
    ◦ **Fibrosis**: This process leads to progressive tubulointerstitial fibrosis and further nephron loss, creating a vicious cycle of decline
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects approximately 15% of the US adult population
• Prevalence increases significantly with age
• Higher prevalence in individuals with diabetes, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease
• Disproportionately affects African American, Hispanic, and Native American populations
• A significant portion of individuals with early-stage CKD are undiagnosed
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• CKD is often a **"silent disease"** and is **asymptomatic in its early stages (Stages 1-3)**
    ◦ It is frequently discovered incidentally on routine lab work (e.g., elevated serum creatinine, abnormal urinalysis)
• As the disease progresses to **Stages 4-5**, symptoms of **uremia** (the accumulation of waste products in the blood) begin to manifest
sections.diagnostics:
• **GFR Estimation**
    ◦ **Serum Creatinine (SCr)**: Used to estimate GFR; rises as GFR falls
    ◦ **eGFR (estimated GFR)**: Calculated using formulas like the **CKD-EPI** equation (preferred); essential for staging
    ◦ **BUN**: Also elevates, but is less specific than creatinine
        ▪ A **BUN:Cr ratio > 20:1** suggests pre-renal causes
• **Markers of Kidney Damage**
    ◦ **Urinalysis (UA)**
        ▪ **Proteinuria/Albuminuria**: A key marker that indicates glomerular damage
        ▪ **Casts**: **Broad, waxy casts** are classic for advanced CKD/ESRD
        ▪ Hematuria, pyuria, or other casts (RBC, WBC) may point to the underlying etiology (e.g., glomerulonephritis)
    ◦ **Urine Albumin-to-Creatinine Ratio (UACR)**: The **preferred test** for quantifying albuminuria from a spot urine sample
        ▪ A1 (Normal to mildly increased): < 30 mg/g
        ▪ A2 (Moderately increased): 30-300 mg/g (formerly "microalbuminuria")
        ▪ A3 (Severely increased): > 300 mg/g (formerly "macroalbuminuria")
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Renal Ultrasound**
        ▪ **Key initial imaging study**
        ▪ Assesses kidney size; in most forms of CKD, kidneys are **small, shrunken, and echogenic (bright)**
        ▪ **Exceptions**: Kidneys may be normal/large in diabetic nephropathy (early), PCKD, and HIV-associated nephropathy
        ▪ Rules out obstruction (hydronephrosis)
• **Renal Biopsy**
    ◦ Not routinely performed for CKD
    ◦ Indicated when the cause is unclear, there is rapid GFR decline, or there is suspicion for a specific glomerulonephritis
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is inversely related to GFR stage and albuminuria grade
    ◦ Higher stage and higher albuminuria level confer a worse prognosis for both kidney failure and all-cause mortality
• The disease is progressive and irreversible, but the rate of decline can be slowed significantly with aggressive management of BP, diabetes, and proteinuria
• The leading cause of death is not renal failure itself, but **cardiovascular disease**

sections.overview:
• End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD), also known as Stage 5 Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD), represents the final, permanent stage of kidney failure.
    ◦ Defined by a **glomerular filtration rate (GFR) < 15 mL/min/1.73 m2** or the requirement for **renal replacement therapy (RRT)**, such as dialysis or kidney transplantation.
• At this stage, the kidneys have lost nearly all of their ability to excrete waste products, concentrate urine, and perform their critical endocrine and metabolic functions, leading to the systemic syndrome of **uremia**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology (Most Common Causes in the U.S.)**
    ◦ **Diabetes Mellitus (Diabetic Nephropathy)**: The leading cause (~45-50%).
        ▪ Hyperglycemia leads to glomerulosclerosis and tubulointerstitial fibrosis.
    ◦ **Hypertension (Hypertensive Nephrosclerosis)**: The second leading cause (~25-30%).
        ▪ Chronic high pressure damages the small arteries of the kidneys, leading to ischemia and scarring.
    ◦ **Glomerulonephritis**: Inflammation of the glomeruli (e.g., IgA nephropathy, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis).
    ◦ **Polycystic Kidney Disease (PCKD)**: An inherited disorder causing numerous cysts to grow in the kidneys.
    ◦ **Obstructive Uropathy**: Chronic blockage of the urinary tract (e.g., BPH, nephrolithiasis, tumors).
• **Pathophysiology**: ESRD is the endpoint of a common pathway of progressive nephron loss, regardless of the initial insult.
    ◦ **Nephron Loss**: The primary disease process destroys a critical mass of nephrons.
    ◦ **Compensatory Hyperfiltration**: The remaining viable nephrons undergo hypertrophy and hyperfiltration to maintain GFR.
    ◦ **Glomerular Hypertension & Sclerosis**: This sustained hyperfiltration increases intraglomerular pressure, leading to endothelial injury, proteinuria, and ultimately glomerulosclerosis and interstitial fibrosis.
    ◦ **Vicious Cycle**: As more nephrons are destroyed, the burden on the remaining ones increases, accelerating the process until GFR falls to a critical level (<15 mL/min).
• **Systemic Consequences of Renal Failure**
    ◦ Waste Product Accumulation: Inability to excrete urea, creatinine, and other nitrogenous wastes leads to **uremia**.
    ◦ Fluid & Electrolyte Imbalance
        ▪ **Volume Overload**: Impaired sodium and water excretion leads to edema, hypertension, and heart failure.
        ▪ **Hyperkalemia**: Life-threatening inability to excrete potassium.
        ▪ **Hyperphosphatemia & Hypocalcemia**: Decreased phosphate excretion and impaired activation of Vitamin D.
        ▪ **Metabolic Acidosis**: Impaired excretion of H+ ions and reduced bicarbonate reabsorption.
    ◦ Endocrine Dysfunction
        ▪ **Anemia**: Decreased production of **erythropoietin (EPO)**.
        ▪ **Renal Osteodystrophy**: A complex bone disease resulting from **secondary hyperparathyroidism** (due to hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia) and lack of activated Vitamin D (calcitriol).
sections.epidemiology:
• Prevalence: Over 800,000 people in the U.S. are living with ESRD.
• Incidence: Over 130,000 new cases are diagnosed each year.
• Demographics: Incidence is significantly higher in African American, Hispanic, and Native American populations compared to Caucasians.
• Mortality: The leading cause of death in ESRD patients is **cardiovascular disease**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients often present insidiously after a long period of asymptomatic CKD.
• The presentation is typically dominated by the signs and symptoms of **uremia** or a major complication (e.g., pulmonary edema, hyperkalemic emergency).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ Serum Chemistry
        ▪ **GFR < 15 mL/min/1.73 m2** (calculated via CKD-EPI equation).
        ▪ **BUN and Creatinine** (BUN:Cr ratio often >20:1 but can be variable).
        ▪ **Potassium (Hyperkalemia)**.
        ▪ **Phosphate (Hyperphosphatemia)**.
        ▪ **Calcium (Hypocalcemia)**.
        ▪ **Bicarbonate (Metabolic Acidosis with an Anion Gap)**.
        ▪ **PTH** (secondary hyperparathyroidism).
    ◦ CBC
        ▪ **Normocytic, normochromic anemia** due to EPO deficiency.
        ▪ Platelet dysfunction may be present despite a normal platelet count.
    ◦ Urinalysis
        ▪ Variable proteinuria and hematuria depending on the underlying cause.
        ▪ Urine sediment may show **broad, waxy casts**, which are indicative of advanced renal disease and stasis in dilated tubules.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Renal Ultrasound**: The key imaging modality.
        ▪ Classic finding: **Small, bilateral, echogenic (scarred) kidneys.**
        ▪ Exceptions: Kidneys may be large or normal-sized in diabetic nephropathy, PCKD, HIV-associated nephropathy, and amyloidosis.
        ▪ Also useful to rule out hydronephrosis (obstruction).
• **ECG**
    ◦ May show signs of hyperkalemia (**peaked T waves**, widened QRS, loss of P waves) or left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH).
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is generally poor without transplantation.
• The 5-year survival rate for patients on dialysis is approximately **40%**.
• The 5-year survival rate for patients receiving a deceased donor kidney transplant is >85%, and >95% for a living donor transplant.

sections.overview:
• **Diabetic Nephropathy (DN)** is a progressive kidney disease characterized by **albuminuria**, **hypertension**, and a progressive decline in the **glomerular filtration rate (GFR)**.
    ◦ It is a **microvascular complication** of both Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes mellitus and is the single leading cause of **chronic kidney disease (CKD)** and **end-stage renal disease (ESRD)** in the United States.
• Pathologic hallmarks include **glomerular basement membrane (GBM) thickening**, **mesangial expansion**, and **glomerulosclerosis**.
• Early detection through screening and aggressive management are critical to slowing its progression.
sections.etiology:
• **Chronic hyperglycemia** is the primary driver of DN, initiating a cascade of metabolic and hemodynamic changes within the kidney.
• **Hemodynamic Alterations**
    ◦ Hyperglycemia leads to **afferent** (incoming) **arteriolar vasodilation** and **efferent** (outgoing) **arteriolar vasoconstriction**, primarily mediated by **angiotensin II**.
    ◦ This results in **increased intraglomerular pressure** and **glomerular hyperfiltration**.
    ◦ This sustained pressure causes mechanical stress on the glomeruli, leading to podocyte injury and progressive glomerular damage.
• **Metabolic Pathways**
    ◦ **Advanced Glycation End Products (AGEs)**
        ▪ Non-enzymatic glycation of proteins in the GBM and mesangium leads to the formation of AGEs.
        ▪ These products cause cross-linking of collagen, leading to **GBM thickening**, increased permeability, and promotion of pro-inflammatory and pro-fibrotic cytokines (e.g., TGF-β).
    ◦ **Protein Kinase C (PKC) Activation**
        ▪ Hyperglycemia activates the PKC pathway, which increases vascular permeability, promotes endothelial dysfunction, and stimulates the production of extracellular matrix proteins, contributing to **mesangial expansion** and **fibrosis**.
    ◦ **Polyol Pathway**
        ▪ Excess glucose is shunted into the polyol pathway, where it is converted to **sorbitol**.
        ▪ This process depletes NADPH, reducing the capacity of cells to counter oxidative stress, leading to cellular injury.
• **Overall Result**: These pathways converge to cause progressive structural damage:
    ◦ Glomerular basement membrane thickening.
    ◦ Mesangial cell proliferation and extracellular matrix expansion.
    ◦ Podocyte effacement (damage to the cells that form the filtration barrier).
    ◦ Nodular glomerulosclerosis (**Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions**).
    ◦ Ultimately, global glomerulosclerosis, tubulointerstitial fibrosis, and a decline in GFR.
sections.epidemiology:
• The single most common cause of **ESRD** in the developed world.
• Affects approximately 20-40% of all patients with diabetes.
• While the risk is higher in Type 1 Diabetes (T1DM), the greater prevalence of Type 2 Diabetes (T2DM) means that the majority of patients with DN have T2DM.
• Higher incidence and faster progression in **African Americans, Hispanic Americans, and Native Americans**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Most patients are **asymptomatic** in the early stages.
• The disease is typically identified during routine annual screening (urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio).
• In later stages, patients may present with signs and symptoms of worsening kidney function or nephrotic syndrome.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Screening & Monitoring**
    ◦ **Urine Albumin-to-Creatinine Ratio (UACR)** on a spot urine sample: The preferred screening test.
        ▪ **A1 (Normal/Mild)**: <30 mg/g
        ▪ **A2 (Moderately Increased / "Microalbuminuria")**: 30-300 mg/g. **This is the earliest clinical sign of DN.**
        ▪ **A3 (Severely Increased / "Macroalbuminuria")**: >300 mg/g. Often in the nephrotic range (>3.5 g/day).
    ◦ **Serum Creatinine and eGFR**: To stage CKD and monitor the rate of progression.
    ◦ **Screening Schedule**: Annually, beginning at diagnosis for T2DM and 5 years after diagnosis for T1DM.
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **Urinalysis**: May show proteinuria and glycosuria.
        ▪ **The sediment is typically bland** (no RBCs, WBCs, or cellular casts), which helps distinguish it from glomerulonephritis.
        ▪ Waxy casts may be seen in advanced CKD.
    ◦ **CMP/BMP**
        ▪ Elevated BUN and Creatinine (decreased eGFR).
        ▪ **Hyperkalemia** (impaired excretion).
        ▪ Low serum bicarbonate (**metabolic acidosis**).
    ◦ **CBC**: **Normocytic, normochromic anemia** (due to decreased erythropoietin production by the failing kidneys).
    ◦ **HbA1c**: To assess glycemic control.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Renal Ultrasound**: Typically performed to rule out other causes (e.g., obstruction).
        ▪ Kidneys may be normal-sized or enlarged in the early hyperfiltration stage but become small and echogenic in advanced disease.
• **Kidney Biopsy**
    ◦ **Rarely indicated.** Reserved for atypical presentations:
        ▪ Absence of diabetic retinopathy.
        ▪ Rapid decline in GFR.
        ▪ **Active urine sediment** (RBCs, cellular casts).
        ▪ Acute onset of nephrotic syndrome.
    ◦ Pathognomonic finding: **Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules** (nodular glomerulosclerosis).
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is directly related to the degree of **albuminuria** and the rate of GFR decline.
• Progression is variable but can be significantly slowed with intensive management of blood pressure, blood glucose, and proteinuria.
• Even with optimal treatment, many patients will experience a slow, progressive decline in renal function over decades.
• Mortality is high, predominantly from **cardiovascular events** rather than kidney failure itself.

sections.overview:
• Hypertensive nephrosclerosis, also known as benign nephrosclerosis, is kidney damage caused by chronic, poorly controlled **hypertension**.
• It is a progressive disease characterized by the hardening (**sclerosis**) of the small arteries and arterioles in the kidneys.
• This vascular damage leads to ischemia, **glomerulosclerosis**, interstitial fibrosis, and a gradual decline in renal function.
• It is a leading cause of **Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)** and **End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD)**, particularly in the elderly and African American populations.
• The process is typically slow and insidious, often remaining **asymptomatic** until significant renal function is lost.
sections.etiology:
• The primary etiology is **long-standing systemic hypertension**.
• The pathophysiology is a direct result of hemodynamic stress on the renal vasculature:
    ◦ **Vascular Injury**: Chronic high pressure damages the endothelial lining of the afferent arterioles, leading to increased permeability and leakage of plasma proteins into the arteriolar walls.
    ◦ **Hyaline Arteriolosclerosis**: The deposition of this proteinaceous material thickens the vessel walls and narrows the lumen, a hallmark of benign nephrosclerosis.
    ◦ **Renal Ischemia**: The narrowed arteriolar lumens reduce blood flow to the glomeruli and tubules, causing chronic ischemia.
    ◦ **Glomerular Damage**: Ischemia leads to **glomerulosclerosis** (scarring of the glomeruli) and glomerular collapse. Some glomeruli may experience **hyperfiltration injury** as a compensatory mechanism, which accelerates their own demise.
    ◦ **Tubulointerstitial Fibrosis**: Chronic ischemia causes tubular atrophy and scarring of the surrounding interstitial tissue.
    ◦ **RAAS Activation**: Renal ischemia can activate the **Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS)**, further elevating systemic blood pressure and creating a vicious cycle.
• Note: In cases of **malignant (or accelerated) hypertension**, a more severe form called **hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis** occurs, characterized by "**onion-skinning**" of the arteriolar walls and **fibrinoid necrosis**, leading to a much more rapid decline in renal function.
sections.epidemiology:
• The **second most common cause of ESRD** in the United States, after diabetic nephropathy.
• Prevalence is strongly linked to the prevalence of hypertension.
• Incidence and severity are significantly higher in **individuals of African descent**, who may progress to ESRD at a rate 4-5 times higher than Caucasians.
• The risk increases with age.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Poorly controlled or long-standing hypertension** (most important)
• **African American ancestry**
• Older age
• Male sex
• Genetic predisposition (e.g., **APOL1 gene variants** in African Americans)
• **Diabetes Mellitus** (accelerates vascular damage)
• Obesity
• Smoking
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is typically insidious.
• Patients are often **asymptomatic** in the early to moderate stages of the disease.
• The condition is usually discovered incidentally on routine laboratory work showing an elevated serum creatinine or mild proteinuria.
• The patient will have a **long-standing history of hypertension**, which may be inadequately treated or undiagnosed.
• Evidence of hypertensive **end-organ damage** in other systems is common (e.g., cardiomegaly, retinopathy).
• **Symptoms**:
    ◦ **Early Stages**: None. The patient feels well.
    ◦ **Late Stages (Advanced CKD)**: Symptoms are non-specific and related to uremia.
        ▪ Fatigue, weakness
        ▪ Nausea, loss of appetite
        ▪ Pruritus (itching)
        ▪ Fluid retention (peripheral or pulmonary edema)
        ▪ Nocturia
    ◦ Symptoms of uncontrolled hypertension: headaches, dizziness, blurred vision.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Elevated Blood Pressure**: The hallmark finding.
• **Fundoscopic Exam**: May reveal signs of **hypertensive retinopathy**:
    ◦ Arteriolar narrowing
    ◦ **AV (arteriovenous) nicking**
    ◦ Copper or silver wiring
    ◦ Hemorrhages or exudates
• **Cardiovascular Exam**:
    ◦ Loud S2 heart sound
    ◦ **S4 gallop** (due to a stiff, non-compliant left ventricle)
    ◦ Displaced or sustained apical impulse (PMI) suggestive of **Left Ventricular Hypertrophy (LVH)**.
• **Late CKD findings**:
    ◦ Pallor (due to anemia of CKD)
    ◦ Peripheral edema
    ◦ Uremic frost (rare, in severe uremia)
sections.diagnostics:
• Hypertensive nephrosclerosis is often a **diagnosis of exclusion**, made in a patient with long-standing HTN, slowly progressive CKD, and mild proteinuria.
• **Laboratory Studies**:
    ◦ **Serum Creatinine / BUN**: Gradually and progressively elevated.
    ◦ **Estimated GFR (eGFR)**: Decreased and shows a slow decline over years.
    ◦ **Urinalysis (UA)**:
        ▪ **Proteinuria**: Typically **mild to moderate (<1 g/day)**. This is a key distinguishing feature.
        ▪ **Urinary Sediment**: Generally **bland** (few or no cells or casts). Occasional hyaline casts may be present.
    ◦ **Urine Albumin-to-Creatinine Ratio (UACR)**: A more sensitive measure for detecting early proteinuria.
• **Imaging**:
    ◦ **Renal Ultrasound**: A key diagnostic modality.
        ▪ The classic finding is **bilaterally small (atrophic) and echogenic (hyperechoic) kidneys** with cortical thinning, consistent with chronic scarring.
        ▪ Kidneys are typically symmetric.
• **Other Tests**:
    ◦ **ECG**: May show criteria for **Left Ventricular Hypertrophy (LVH)**.
• **Renal Biopsy**:
    ◦ **Definitive diagnosis**, but **rarely performed** in clinical practice.
    ◦ **Histologic Findings**: **Hyaline arteriolosclerosis**, fibrointimal hyperplasia of larger arteries, **glomerulosclerosis**, and **tubulointerstitial fibrosis**.
sections.treatment:
• **Blood Pressure Goal**: **< 130/80 mmHg** (per ACC/AHA and KDIGO guidelines).
• **Pharmacotherapy**:
    ◦ **First-Line Agents**: **ACE Inhibitors** (e.g., lisinopril, enalapril) or **ARBs** (e.g., losartan, valsartan).
        ▪ These agents are preferred because they reduce both systemic BP and intraglomerular pressure (by dilating the efferent arteriole), providing a specific **renal-protective effect**.
        ▪ They also have anti-proteinuric properties.
    ◦ **Second/Third-Line Agents**:
        ▪ **Thiazide Diuretics** (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone) are excellent for volume and BP control, especially in African American patients. (Use **loop diuretics** like furosemide for **GFR <30 mL/min**).
        ▪ **Calcium Channel Blockers** (long-acting, e.g., amlodipine, nifedipine).
    ◦ Most patients will require **two or more antihypertensive agents** to achieve their goal BP.
sections.management:
• **Lifestyle Modifications**:
    ◦ **Sodium Restriction**: <2 grams/day (**DASH diet** is highly recommended).
    ◦ Weight loss, regular exercise, smoking cessation.
• **Management of CKD**:
    ◦ **Proteinuria monitoring**: Regular UACR checks.
    ◦ **Avoidance of Nephrotoxins**: Especially **NSAIDs**, IV contrast when possible.
    ◦ **Anemia management**: Iron supplementation, erythropoietin-stimulating agents (ESAs).
    ◦ **Mineral & Bone Disease management**: Phosphate binders, vitamin D analogs.
    ◦ **Metabolic Acidosis management**: Sodium bicarbonate.
• **Referral**: Refer to a nephrologist when **eGFR < 30 mL/min** or if the diagnosis is uncertain.
• **Renal Replacement Therapy (RRT)**: Plan for dialysis or transplantation when the patient approaches ESRD (**eGFR < 15 mL/min**).
sections.complications:
• Progression to **End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD)**
• Increased risk of **Cardiovascular Disease** (MI, CVA, CHF, PVD) - this is the leading cause of death in CKD patients.
• Accelerated atherosclerosis
• **Left Ventricular Hypertrophy (LVH)** and diastolic heart failure
• **Malignant hypertension** and hypertensive emergency
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is directly related to the **degree of blood pressure control** and the amount of proteinuria.
• Excellent BP control can significantly slow or even halt the progression of GFR decline.
• Poorly controlled HTN leads to a more rapid progression to ESRD.
• The presence of heavy proteinuria is a poor prognostic sign.
• Prognosis is generally worse for African American patients due to higher rates of HTN and genetic predispositions.

sections.overview:
• Nephritic syndrome is a clinical syndrome characterized by **glomerular inflammation (glomerulonephritis)**, leading to damage of the capillary walls.
• This damage results in a classic clinical presentation involving hematuria, hypertension, and acute kidney injury.
• It is defined by the presence of an "active" urinary sediment containing red blood cells (RBCs) and pathognomonic **RBC casts**.
• This stands in contrast to nephrotic syndrome, which is primarily a disorder of podocyte damage leading to massive proteinuria.
• **The Nephritic Pentad (Classic Presentation):**
    ◦ **Hematuria** (cola or tea-colored urine)
    ◦ **Hypertension** (due to salt and water retention)
