    ◦ **Oliguria** (decreased urine output)
    ◦ **Azotemia** (elevated BUN and Creatinine)
    ◦ **Edema** (often periorbital and peripheral)
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology:** The core mechanism is **immune-mediated inflammation** of the glomeruli.
    ◦ **Immune Complex Deposition:** Antigens (e.g., streptococcal proteins) and antibodies form immune complexes that circulate and deposit within the glomerular capillaries.
    ◦ **Complement Activation:** The deposited immune complexes activate the complement cascade.
    ◦ **Inflammatory Response:** This triggers an influx of inflammatory cells (neutrophils, macrophages).
    ◦ **Glomerular Damage:** Release of cytokines and proteases causes proliferation of glomerular cells and damage to the capillary endothelium and glomerular basement membrane (GBM).
    ◦ **Clinical Manifestations:**
        ▪ **Hematuria/RBC Casts:** Damage to the GBM creates pores large enough for RBCs to leak into Bowman's space.
        ▪ **Hypertension/Edema/Oliguria:** The inflammatory process reduces the glomerular filtration rate (GFR), leading to decreased filtration of sodium and water, causing volume expansion, hypertension, and edema.
• **Common Etiologies:**
    ◦ **Post-Infectious Glomerulonephritis (PIGN):**
        ▪ **Post-Streptococcal GN (PSGN):** Most common cause in children. Occurs **1-3 weeks after** a Group A β-hemolytic streptococcal (GABHS) pharyngitis or **3-6 weeks after** a skin infection (impetigo).
    ◦ **IgA Nephropathy (Berger's Disease):**
        ▪ Most common cause of primary glomerulonephritis worldwide.
        ▪ Characterized by IgA deposition in the glomerular mesangium.
        ▪ Classic presentation is gross hematuria that occurs **concurrently with or 1-2 days after** a URI or GI infection (**synpharyngitic hematuria**).
    ◦ **Rapidly Progressive Glomerulonephritis (RPGN):**
        ▪ A severe syndrome characterized by rapid loss of kidney function and **crescent formation** on kidney biopsy.
        ▪ **Type I (Anti-GBM Disease):**
            • **Goodpasture's Syndrome:** Antibodies against the GBM and alveolar basement membranes. Presents with glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage (hemoptysis).
        ▪ **Type II (Immune-Complex Mediated):**
            • Can be a complication of severe PSGN, Lupus Nephritis, or IgA nephropathy.
        ▪ **Type III (Pauci-Immune):**
            • Associated with ANCA (Antineutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibodies).
            • **Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA, formerly Wegener's):** Affects upper respiratory tract, lungs, and kidneys. **c-ANCA** positive.
            • **Microscopic Polyangiitis (MPA):** Affects kidneys and lungs but not the upper respiratory tract. **p-ANCA** positive.
    ◦ **Lupus Nephritis:**
        ▪ Kidney involvement in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE). Can present as nephritic, nephrotic, or mixed picture.
    ◦ **Membranoproliferative Glomerulonephritis (MPGN):**
        ▪ Can have both nephritic and nephrotic features.
sections.epidemiology:
• **PSGN:** Primarily affects children aged 5-15. More common in developing countries.
• **IgA Nephropathy:** Most common in children and young adults (2nd-3rd decades). Higher prevalence in East Asian and Caucasian populations. More common in males.
• **Lupus Nephritis:** Most common in females of childbearing age, particularly of African American, Hispanic, and Asian descent.
• **Anti-GBM Disease:** Bimodal age distribution, with peaks in young men (20s-30s) and older adults (60s-70s).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation can be acute and dramatic.
• A classic vignette is a child who had a sore throat two weeks ago and is now brought to the clinic with "puffy eyes" (periorbital edema) and dark, "Coca-Cola colored" urine.
• An adult may present with new-onset hypertension, leg swelling, and decreased urine output after a recent upper respiratory infection.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Urinalysis (UA) with Microscopy:** **Single most important initial test.**
    ◦ **Hematuria:** >3 RBCs/high-power field.
    ◦ **RBC Casts:** **Pathognomonic for glomerulonephritis.** Indicates bleeding is from the glomerulus.
    ◦ **Dysmorphic RBCs:** Cells are misshapen from passing through the damaged GBM.
    ◦ **Proteinuria:** Present but usually **sub-nephrotic** (<3.5 g/24 hours).
• **Blood Tests:**
    ◦ **Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP):** Shows **↑ BUN** and **↑ Serum Creatinine** (azotemia). May show hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis.
    ◦ **Complete Blood Count (CBC):** May show normocytic, normochromic anemia due to hemodilution or decreased erythropoietin production.
• **Serologic Workup (tailored to clinical suspicion):**
    ◦ **PSGN:** Anti-streptolysin O (ASO) titers, Anti-DNase B titers.
    ◦ **Complement Levels:** **↓ C3** is characteristic of PSGN and lupus nephritis.
    ◦ **Lupus:** (+) ANA, (+) Anti-dsDNA.
    ◦ **ANCA-associated Vasculitis:** (+) c-ANCA (GPA), (+) p-ANCA (MPA).
    ◦ **Goodpasture's:** (+) Anti-GBM antibodies.
• **Imaging:**
    ◦ **Renal Ultrasound:** Primarily used to rule out other causes of AKI (e.g., hydronephrosis from obstruction). Kidneys may appear normal or slightly enlarged.
• **Renal Biopsy:** **Gold standard for definitive diagnosis.**
    ◦ Indicated when the diagnosis is unclear, presentation is severe (RPGN), or to guide specific immunosuppressive therapy.
    ◦ Findings can include hypercellularity, immune deposits on immunofluorescence (e.g., "lumpy-bumpy" IgG/C3 deposits in PSGN), and crescents in RPGN.
sections.prognosis:
• **PSGN in children:** Excellent. >95% make a full recovery.
• **PSGN in adults:** More guarded; higher rates of progression to chronic kidney disease.
• **IgA Nephropathy:** Variable. About 20-30% of patients progress to ESRD over 20 years.
• **RPGN:** Poor prognosis without rapid diagnosis and aggressive treatment. Often leads to permanent kidney failure.

sections.overview:
• Nephrotic syndrome is a clinical syndrome characterized by a collection of signs and symptoms caused by glomerular damage.
    ◦ It is not a single disease but a manifestation of underlying kidney disease that alters the permeability of the glomerular capillary wall.
    ◦ The hallmark is massive proteinuria, which leads to the other classic findings.
    ◦ **The classic tetrad of Nephrotic Syndrome**:
        ▪ **Heavy Proteinuria**: >3.5 g / 24 hours
        ▪ **Hypoalbuminemia**: Serum albumin <3.5 g/dL
        ▪ **Peripheral Edema**: Due to low plasma oncotic pressure
        ▪ **Hyperlipidemia**: Elevated total cholesterol, LDL, and triglycerides
sections.etiology:
• The underlying pathophysiology involves damage to the **podocytes** (glomerular epithelial cells) of the glomerular filtration barrier.
    ◦ This damage leads to an increase in permeability to large proteins, particularly **albumin**.
    ◦ **Pathophysiologic Cascade**:
        ▪ **Podocyte Damage**: Injury to podocytes disrupts the glomerular filtration barrier's size and charge selectivity.
        ▪ **Massive Proteinuria**: Large amounts of protein, primarily **albumin**, leak from the blood into the urine.
        ▪ **Hypoalbuminemia**: As urinary protein loss exceeds the liver's capacity for **albumin** synthesis, serum **albumin** levels drop.
        ▪ **Edema**: Decreased plasma oncotic pressure (due to low **albumin**) causes fluid to shift from the intravascular space to the interstitial space, resulting in generalized edema (anasarca).
            • The body attempts to compensate by retaining sodium and water via the RAAS system, which worsens the edema.
        ▪ **Hyperlipidemia**: In response to **hypoalbuminemia** and decreased oncotic pressure, the liver increases synthesis of lipoproteins (VLDL, LDL), leading to hypercholesterolemia and hypertriglyceridemia.
            • Lipid clearance is also reduced.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Children**:
    ◦ Incidence is ~2-7 cases per 100,000.
    ◦ **Minimal Change Disease** accounts for >80% of cases.
• **Adults**:
    ◦ Incidence is ~3 cases per 100,000.
    ◦ Causes are more varied:
        ▪ **FSGS** is the most common primary cause in African Americans.
        ▪ **Membranous Nephropathy** is the most common primary cause in Caucasians.
        ▪ **Diabetic Nephropathy** is the most common secondary cause overall.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients typically present with the gradual onset of swelling.
• A child may be brought in by a parent who notices **puffiness around the eyes** (periorbital edema) in the morning.
• An adult may present with new-onset swelling in the feet and ankles that progresses up the legs.
• The patient may also report:
    ◦ Recent weight gain
    ◦ Fatigue
    ◦ **Foamy urine**
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• **Minimal Change Disease**:
    ◦ Excellent prognosis, especially in children.
    ◦ >90% respond to corticosteroids, although relapses are common.
    ◦ Progression to ESRD is rare.
• **FSGS**:
    ◦ Variable prognosis.
    ◦ About 50% progress to ESRD within 10 years.
    ◦ Poorer prognosis in those who do not respond to treatment.
• **Membranous Nephropathy**:
    ◦ Follows the "rule of thirds":
        ▪ One-third spontaneously remit.
        ▪ One-third remain proteinuric but stable.
        ▪ One-third progress to ESRD.
• **Diabetic Nephropathy**:
    ◦ A leading cause of ESRD worldwide.
    ◦ Prognosis is dependent on glycemic and blood pressure control.

sections.overview:
• IgA Nephropathy (IgAN), also known as **Berger's Disease**, is the most common primary glomerulonephritis worldwide.
    ◦ It is an immune-complex-mediated kidney disease characterized by the deposition of immunoglobulin A (IgA) in the glomerular mesangium.
    ◦ The clinical course is highly variable, ranging from asymptomatic microscopic hematuria to rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis leading to end-stage renal disease (ESRD).
sections.etiology:
• The pathogenesis is best explained by a "multi-hit" hypothesis, primarily involving abnormal IgA1 molecules:
    ◦ **Hit 1: Abnormal Glycosylation**
        ▪ Patients produce an abnormal form of IgA1 with deficient O-linked galactose residues in the hinge region. This is known as **galactose-deficient IgA1 (Gd-IgA1)**.
    ◦ **Hit 2: Autoantibody Production**
        ▪ The body recognizes Gd-IgA1 as foreign and produces autoantibodies (typically IgG) against these abnormal sugar residues.
    ◦ **Hit 3: Immune Complex Formation**
        ▪ The Gd-IgA1 and the anti-Gd-IgA1 IgG autoantibodies bind to form large, circulating immune complexes.
    ◦ **Hit 4: Mesangial Deposition & Injury**
        ▪ These immune complexes deposit in the glomerular mesangium, activating the complement system, which leads to glomerular damage manifesting as hematuria and proteinuria.
• **Mucosal Link**
    ◦ Triggers like upper respiratory or GI infections lead to a surge in IgA (including Gd-IgA1) production, which can precipitate an acute flare or macroscopic hematuria.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** Most common primary glomerulonephritis globally.
• **Peak Incidence:** 2nd and 3rd decades of life.
• **Gender:** Male-to-female ratio is approximately 2:1.
• **Geography/Race:** Highest prevalence in East Asians and Caucasians. It is significantly less common in individuals of African descent.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Genetic Predisposition:** Familial clustering and associations with specific HLA alleles.
• **Mucosal Infections:** Frequent URIs, pharyngitis, or gastroenteritis can trigger clinical manifestations.
• **Associated Conditions:**
    ◦ **IgA Vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein Purpura):** Considered a systemic form of IgAN.
    ◦ **Celiac Disease**
    ◦ **Dermatitis Herpetiformis**
    ◦ **Chronic Liver Disease (especially cirrhosis):** Impaired clearance of IgA complexes.
    ◦ **HIV, Ankylosing Spondylitis**
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is highly variable:
    ◦ **Classic Presentation (40-50%):** Recurrent episodes of **macroscopic (gross) hematuria** that occur **synpharyngitically** - meaning within 1-3 days of an upper respiratory or GI infection.
    ◦ **Asymptomatic Microscopic Hematuria (30-40%):** Most common presentation overall, often discovered incidentally on a routine urinalysis. May be accompanied by mild proteinuria.
    ◦ **Nephrotic Syndrome (<10%):** Heavy proteinuria (>3.5 g/day), hypoalbuminemia, edema, and hyperlipidemia.
    ◦ **Rapidly Progressive Glomerulonephritis (RPGN) (<10%):** Rare but severe, characterized by a rapid decline in GFR and often associated with crescents on biopsy.
    ◦ **Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD):** Some patients present with established CKD, hypertension, and proteinuria with no prior history of gross hematuria.
• Associated Symptoms:
    ◦ **"Cola-colored" or "tea-colored" urine:** During episodes of gross hematuria.
    ◦ **Flank Pain:** May occur during acute episodes due to capsular swelling.
    ◦ **Edema:** Peripheral or periorbital edema if proteinuria is significant.
    ◦ **Fatigue / Malaise:** Non-specific symptoms of CKD or active nephritis.
    ◦ **Symptoms of trigger infection:** Sore throat, cough, fever, diarrhea.
sections.physicalExam:
• The physical exam is often **normal**.
• **Hypertension** is the most common and significant clinical sign.
• **Peripheral or periorbital edema** may be present in patients with nephrotic-range proteinuria.
• If associated with **IgA Vasculitis (HSP)**, look for:
    ◦ Palpable purpura (especially on lower extremities and buttocks)
    ◦ Arthralgias/arthritis
    ◦ Abdominal pain
sections.diagnostics:
• **Urinalysis (UA)**
    ◦ **Hallmark:** Persistent microscopic or macroscopic hematuria.
    ◦ **Key Finding:** **Dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts**, indicating a glomerular source of bleeding.
    ◦ Proteinuria: Varies from none to nephrotic range.
• **Urine Protein Quantification**
    ◦ Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) or a 24-hour urine collection is essential to quantify proteinuria, which is a key prognostic marker.
• **Blood Tests**
    ◦ **Serum Creatinine / BUN:** To assess glomerular filtration rate (GFR).
    ◦ **Serum IgA levels:** Elevated in up to 50% of patients, but it is **neither sensitive nor specific** for diagnosis.
    ◦ **Complement Levels (C3, C4):** Typically **normal**. This helps differentiate IgAN from other GNs like post-streptococcal GN or lupus nephritis.
• **Kidney Biopsy**
    ◦ **GOLD STANDARD** for definitive diagnosis.
    ◦ **Light Microscopy (LM):** Mesangial hypercellularity and mesangial matrix expansion.
    ◦ **Immunofluorescence (IF):** **Pathognomonic finding is dominant or co-dominant granular IgA deposits in the mesangium.** C3 and IgG/IgM may also be present.
    ◦ **Electron Microscopy (EM):** Confirms electron-dense immune deposits within the mesangium.
sections.treatment:
• **Supportive Care / Low-Risk Patients:** (Proteinuria <0.5-1 g/day, normal GFR)
    ◦ Monitoring of BP, GFR, and proteinuria.
• **First-Line for Proteinuria (High-Risk):** (Persistent proteinuria >0.5-1 g/day)
    ◦ **ACE Inhibitors or ARBs:** Cornerstone of therapy. Titrate to maximum tolerated dose to achieve BP control (<130/80 mmHg) and reduce proteinuria.
    ◦ **SGLT2 Inhibitors:** Now recommended for CKD patients with proteinuria (e.g., dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) regardless of diabetes status, as an add-on to ACEi/ARB.
• **Immunosuppression:** (For patients with persistent proteinuria >1 g/day despite 3-6 months of optimized supportive care)
    ◦ **Corticosteroids:** A 6-month course of systemic glucocorticoids is the primary recommendation.
    ◦ **Other agents:** Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), cyclophosphamide, or rituximab may be considered in severe or rapidly progressive disease.
sections.management:
• **Routine Monitoring:** Regular checks of blood pressure, serum creatinine (eGFR), and UPCR (e.g., every 3-6 months) to track disease progression and response to therapy.
• **Blood Pressure Control:** Strict target of **<130/80 mmHg**.
• **Lifestyle Modification:** Low sodium diet (<2g/day), smoking cessation, maintaining a healthy weight.
• **Patient Education:** Avoid NSAIDs, which can worsen kidney function.
sections.complications:
• Progressive Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)
• **End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD)** requiring dialysis or transplantation (occurs in 20-30% of patients over 20 years).
• Hypertension and associated cardiovascular disease.
• **Recurrence post-transplantation:** IgA deposits can recur in the allograft in up to 50% of cases, leading to graft loss in a subset.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is highly variable. The "rule of thirds" is a classic but oversimplified model:
    ◦ 1/3 achieve spontaneous remission.
    ◦ 1/3 develop stable, non-progressive CKD.
    ◦ 1/3 progress to ESRD.
• **Major Risk Factors for Poor Prognosis:**
    ◦ **Persistent proteinuria > 1 g/day**
    ◦ **Hypertension**
    ◦ **Reduced GFR** at time of diagnosis
    ◦ **Severe histologic features on biopsy** (e.g., tubular atrophy, interstitial fibrosis, crescents)

sections.overview:
• **Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN)** is an acute nephritic syndrome that develops after an infection with a specific nephritogenic strain of **Group A β-hemolytic Streptococcus** (*S. pyogenes*)
    ◦ It is a classic example of an immune complex-mediated (**Type III hypersensitivity**) renal disease
    ◦ The hallmark clinical presentation is the abrupt onset of **hematuria**, **edema**, and **hypertension** in a child 1-6 weeks after a streptococcal infection (**pharyngitis** or **impetigo**)
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ Caused by infection with **nephritogenic strains** of **Group A β-hemolytic Streptococcus (GAS) / *Streptococcus pyogenes***
    ◦ Follows two primary types of infections:
        ▪ **Pharyngitis (strep throat):** Latent period of **1-3 weeks**
        ▪ **Impetigo (skin infection):** Latent period of **3-6 weeks**
• **Pathophysiology (Type III Hypersensitivity)**
    ◦ **Infection:** A patient is infected with a nephritogenic strain of GAS
    ◦ **Immune Complex Formation:** The body forms antibodies against specific streptococcal antigens (e.g., streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin B [SpeB], nephritis-associated plasmin receptor [NAPlr]), which circulate in the bloodstream
    ◦ **Deposition:** The immune complexes deposit in the glomeruli, primarily in the **subepithelial space**
    ◦ **Complement Activation:** Deposited complexes activate the **alternative complement pathway**, leading to the characteristic **low serum C3 level**
    ◦ **Inflammation & Damage:** Complement activation triggers an inflammatory cascade, attracting neutrophils and macrophages, causing glomerular inflammation and damage
    ◦ **Clinical Effect:** Glomerular damage reduces the Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) and disrupts the filtration barrier
        ▪ **Reduced GFR:** Leads to salt and water retention, causing **Edema**, **Hypertension**, and **Oliguria**
        ▪ **Damaged Barrier:** Leads to leakage of RBCs and protein, causing **Hematuria (cola-colored urine)** and **Proteinuria**
sections.epidemiology:
• **Age:** Primarily a disease of children, with a peak incidence between **5 and 12 years old**
    ◦ Uncommon in children under 3 and in adults over 40
• **Sex:** Slight male predominance (2:1)
• **Geography/Setting:** More common in developing countries and areas with crowded living conditions
    ◦ **Post-pharyngitis PSGN:** More common in colder climates during the winter
    ◦ **Post-impetigo PSGN:** More common in warmer, humid climates during the summer
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a child who develops an acute nephritic syndrome 1-3 weeks after recovering from a sore throat or 3-6 weeks after a skin infection
• The parent typically brings the child in due to **puffy eyes (periorbital edema)** and **dark, "cola-colored" urine**
sections.diagnostics:
• **Urinalysis (UA) with Microscopy: CRITICAL TEST**
    ◦ **Hematuria:** Gross or microscopic
    ◦ **Red Blood Cell (RBC) Casts:** **Pathognomonic for glomerulonephritis**
    ◦ **Dysmorphic RBCs (acanthocytes):** Indicates a glomerular source of bleeding
    ◦ **Proteinuria:** Usually mild to moderate (sub-nephrotic range, <3.5 g/day)
    ◦ **Oliguria:** Urine output <1 mL/kg/hr in children
• **Blood Tests**
    ◦ **Renal Function Panel:**
        ▪ **Elevated BUN and Serum Creatinine** (azotemia)
    ◦ **Serologic Evidence of Strep Infection:**
        ▪ **Antistreptolysin O (ASO) Titer:** Elevated after **pharyngitis**. May be normal in post-impetigo PSGN
        ▪ **Anti-DNase B Titer:** Elevated after **both pharyngitis and impetigo**. More sensitive for post-impetigo cases
    ◦ **Complement Levels:**
        ▪ **Low C3 and/or CH50:** A hallmark finding
        ▪ **Normal C4:** Differentiates it from other conditions like lupus nephritis where both C3 and C4 are low
        ▪ *Note: C3 levels typically normalize within 6-8 weeks of onset*
• **Renal Biopsy**
    ◦ **Rarely indicated in children** with a typical history and lab findings
    ◦ **Indications:** Atypical features (e.g., anuria, rapidly rising creatinine), nephrotic-range proteinuria, normal complement levels, or failure to improve (persistent low C3 >8 weeks, worsening renal function)
    ◦ **Findings:**
        ▪ **Light Microscopy:** Diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis (hypercellular glomeruli)
        ▪ **Immunofluorescence (IF):** Granular ("lumpy-bumpy" or "starry sky") deposits of **IgG and C3** along the glomerular basement membrane (GBM)
        ▪ **Electron Microscopy (EM):** Large, electron-dense **subepithelial "humps"** (Characteristic finding)
sections.prognosis:
• **Children: Excellent**
    ◦ Over 95% have a complete recovery of renal function
• **Adults: Guarded**
    ◦ Only 50-60% achieve full recovery
    ◦ A significant portion may develop chronic kidney disease (CKD), persistent hypertension, or end-stage renal disease (ESRD) years later

sections.overview:
• **Anti-glomerular basement membrane (Anti-GBM) disease** is a rare, small-vessel vasculitis characterized by autoantibodies directed against an antigen in the basement membranes of the kidneys and lungs, leading to a classic clinical dyad of **rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN)** and **diffuse alveolar hemorrhage**.
• **Anti-GBM Disease**: The broad term for the condition, which may be limited to the kidneys (~30-40% of cases) or involve both kidneys and lungs.
• **Goodpasture's Syndrome**: The specific presentation involving both glomerulonephritis AND pulmonary hemorrhage. It is a true medical emergency.
sections.etiology:
• **Autoimmune Etiology**: The disease is caused by the production of **IgG autoantibodies** against a specific target: the **alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen**.
• **Target Location**: Type IV collagen is a crucial structural component of basement membranes, particularly in the **glomeruli (GBM)** and the **pulmonary alveoli (ABM)**.
• **Mechanism of Injury (Type II Hypersensitivity Reaction)**:
    ◦ **Antibody Binding**: Circulating anti-GBM IgG antibodies bind to their target antigens on the GBM and ABM.
    ◦ **Complement Activation**: This binding activates the classical complement pathway.
    ◦ **Inflammatory Cascade**: Complement activation recruits neutrophils and other inflammatory cells.
    ◦ **Tissue Damage**: Recruited cells release proteases and reactive oxygen species, leading to destruction of the basement membranes.
• **Pathologic Result**:
    ◦ **Kidneys**: Damage to the GBM causes breaks, allowing proteins and red blood cells to leak into Bowman's space. This triggers a severe inflammatory response, leading to the formation of **crescents** (cellular proliferation in Bowman's space) and **rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN)**.
    ◦ **Lungs**: Damage to the ABM results in bleeding into the alveolar spaces, causing **diffuse alveolar hemorrhage**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Rare, approximately 1-2 cases per million per year.
• **Age Distribution**: Bimodal peak:
    ◦ **First peak (20s-30s)**: Predominantly males, classic pulmonary-renal syndrome is more common.
    ◦ **Second peak (60s-70s)**: M:F ratio is more equal, kidney-limited disease is more common.
• **Genetics**: Strong association with **HLA-DRB1*1501**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation is typically acute and severe over days to weeks. Pulmonary symptoms may precede renal symptoms.
• A classic vignette is a **young male smoker** who presents with **hemoptysis and hematuria** after a recent upper respiratory infection.
• Patients often present with a prodrome of constitutional symptoms before the onset of organ-specific manifestations.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Serology**:
    ◦ **Anti-GBM Antibodies**: The key diagnostic test. Highly specific (>95%) and sensitive.
    ◦ **ANCA (Anti-Neutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibodies)**: Check in all patients. Up to 30% of anti-GBM patients are "double-positive" for both anti-GBM and ANCA, which can affect treatment and prognosis.
• **Urinalysis (UA) with Microscopy**:
    ◦ **Hematuria** (dysmorphic RBCs)
    ◦ **Red Blood Cell (RBC) Casts**: Pathognomonic for glomerulonephritis.
    ◦ Proteinuria (usually sub-nephrotic, <3.5 g/day).
• **Renal Function Panel**:
    ◦ **Elevated BUN and Creatinine**: Often rising rapidly, indicating RPGN.
• **Complete Blood Count (CBC)**:
    ◦ **Normocytic, normochromic anemia**: Due to a combination of hemorrhage, renal failure (decreased erythropoietin), and inflammation.
• **Imaging**:
    ◦ **Chest X-ray (CXR)**: Bilateral, diffuse alveolar infiltrates, often in a central or "bat-wing" distribution, sparing the costophrenic angles.
• **Biopsy (Gold Standard)**:
    ◦ **Renal Biopsy**: Provides the definitive diagnosis.
        ▪ **Light Microscopy**: Shows diffuse, necrotizing glomerulonephritis with extensive **crescent formation** in most glomeruli.
        ▪ **Immunofluorescence (Pathognomonic)**: Reveals smooth, **linear IgG deposition** along the entire length of the glomerular basement membrane. Described as "ribbon-like."
sections.prognosis:
• **Patient Survival**: With aggressive modern therapy, one-year survival is >80%. Death is usually from massive pulmonary hemorrhage or complications of immunosuppression.
• **Renal Survival**: Highly dependent on renal function at the time of diagnosis.
• **Poor prognostic indicators**:
    ◦ Serum creatinine >5.7 mg/dL at presentation.
    ◦ Requiring dialysis at presentation.
    ◦ >50% crescents on initial kidney biopsy.
    ◦ Patients with these features are unlikely to recover renal function.
• **Relapse**: Is rare (<5%) once antibody production has ceased, unlike in ANCA vasculitis where relapse is common.

sections.overview:
• **Membranous Nephropathy (MN)** is a major cause of **nephrotic syndrome** in non-diabetic adults.
    ◦ It is an immune-mediated glomerular disease characterized by the formation of immune complexes on the outer (**subepithelial**) side of the **glomerular basement membrane (GBM)**.
    ◦ This leads to **GBM thickening** and **podocyte injury**, resulting in significant **proteinuria**.
    ◦ MN can be **primary (idiopathic)** or **secondary** to other conditions.
sections.etiology: • The core pathophysiology involves **immune complex deposition** in the **subepithelial space** of the glomerular capillaries, triggering a cascade that damages the glomerular filtration barrier.
sections.epidemiology:
• The **most common cause of primary nephrotic syndrome** in non-diabetic Caucasian adults.
• Peak incidence between ages **50 and 60**.
• Male-to-female ratio is approximately 2:1.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Insidious onset** of symptoms.
• Patients typically present with the full clinical picture of **nephrotic syndrome**:
    ◦ **Heavy Proteinuria** (>3.5 g/day)
    ◦ **Hypoalbuminemia** (<3.5 g/dL)
    ◦ **Peripheral Edema**
    ◦ **Hyperlipidemia**
sections.diagnostics:
• **Urinalysis (UA)**
    ◦ **Heavy proteinuria** (3+ or 4+ on dipstick)
    ◦ Microscopic hematuria is present in ~50% of cases
    ◦ **Oval fat bodies** are characteristic of nephrotic syndrome
        ▪ "Maltese crosses" under polarized light
• **Urine Protein Quantification**
    ◦ **24-hour urine collection:** Protein >3.5 grams/24 hours
    ◦ **Spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR):** >3.5 mg/mg is indicative of nephrotic-range proteinuria
• **Serum Labs**
    ◦ **Hypoalbuminemia:** Serum albumin <3.5 g/dL (often <2.5 g/dL)
    ◦ **Hyperlipidemia:** Elevated total cholesterol, LDL, and triglycerides
    ◦ **BMP:** May show normal or elevated BUN and creatinine, depending on the severity and chronicity of the disease
• **Serology (Crucial for Diagnosis)**
    ◦ **Anti-PLA2R Antibody:** A highly specific test for primary MN.
        ▪ A positive test in a patient with nephrotic syndrome is virtually diagnostic.
        ▪ Titers can be followed to monitor disease activity.
    ◦ **Workup for Secondary Causes:** ANA (for SLE), Hepatitis B/C serologies, age-appropriate cancer screening (e.g., colonoscopy, mammogram, chest X-ray/CT).
• **Renal Biopsy (Gold Standard):** Confirms the diagnosis and provides prognostic information.
    ◦ **Light Microscopy (LM):** Diffuse thickening of the **glomerular basement membrane (GBM)** with little or no cellular proliferation.
    ◦ **Immunofluorescence (IF):** Shows **diffuse granular deposits** of **IgG** (mainly IgG4) and **C3** along the capillary walls.
    ◦ **Electron Microscopy (EM):** The pathognomonic finding.
        ▪ Shows **subepithelial electron-dense immune deposits**.
        ▪ This creates the classic **"spike and dome"** appearance, where the "domes" are the immune deposits and the "spikes" are new GBM material laid down between them by podocytes.
        ▪ Also shows effacement (flattening) of podocyte foot processes.
sections.prognosis:
• Follows the **"Rule of Thirds"**:
    ◦ **1/3** undergo spontaneous remission.
    ◦ **1/3** have persistent, non-progressing proteinuria.
    ◦ **1/3** progress to **ESRD**.
• **Poor prognostic factors:**
    ◦ Male sex
    ◦ Older age at onset
    ◦ Persistent nephrotic-range proteinuria (>8 g/day)
    ◦ Elevated serum creatinine at presentation
    ◦ Development of tubulointerstitial fibrosis on biopsy.

sections.overview:
• Glomerular disorder characterized by the **abrupt onset of nephrotic syndrome**
    ◦ Most common cause of primary **nephrotic syndrome in children**
    ◦ Named "minimal change" because glomeruli appear **normal under light microscopy**
    ◦ Definitive diagnosis is via **electron microscopy**, which reveals the pathognomonic finding of **diffuse effacement (fusion) of podocyte foot processes**
    ◦ Clinical hallmark is the **nephrotic syndrome tetrad**: massive proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, hyperlipidemia, and generalized edema
    ◦ Highly responsive to **corticosteroid therapy**, especially in children
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• Most common cause of **nephrotic syndrome in children**, accounting for ~90% of cases under age 10
• Peak incidence is between **2 and 6 years of age**
• Slight male predominance in children (approx. 2:1)
• Less common in adults, accounting for 10-25% of primary nephrotic syndrome cases
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Classic presentation is a previously healthy child who develops the **sudden onset of generalized edema**
    ◦ Often occurs following a minor infection, such as an upper respiratory tract infection
• Presentation is dominated by the signs and symptoms of **nephrotic syndrome**
• Unlike nephritic syndromes, **hypertension** and **hematuria** are typically absent
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent in children**: Over 90% achieve complete remission with steroids
• **Relapses are common** (~50-75% experience at least one), especially within the first year after initial treatment
    ◦ **Frequent relapsers**: Defined as 4 relapses in 12 months
    ◦ **Steroid-dependent**: Relapse occurs during the steroid taper or right after stopping
• Progression to end-stage renal disease (ESRD) is **very rare** in classic steroid-responsive MCD
• Prognosis in adults is generally good, but remission rates are lower and the time to response is longer compared to children

sections.overview:
• Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is a clinicopathologic syndrome, not a single disease.
• It is characterized by a pattern of kidney damage featuring scarring (sclerosis) in **some** glomeruli (**focal**) and in specific parts of the affected glomeruli (**segmental**).
• The fundamental pathology is injury to the **podocytes**, the cells that form the final barrier of the glomerular filtration system.
• This damage leads to massive protein leakage into the urine, resulting in **nephrotic syndrome**.
• FSGS is a leading cause of **end-stage renal disease (ESRD)** among glomerular diseases.
sections.etiology:
• The core pathophysiologic event in FSGS is **podocyte injury**.
    ◦ **Podocyte Damage**: Injury to podocytes leads to their detachment from the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) and/or effacement (flattening) of their foot processes.
    ◦ **Proteinuria**: The damaged filtration barrier becomes highly permeable to proteins, particularly albumin, resulting in heavy proteinuria.
    ◦ **Sclerosis**: The denuded areas of the GBM adhere to Bowman's capsule, leading to the formation of scar tissue (sclerosis). This scarring is irreversible and impairs glomerular function.
    ◦ **Progression**: As more glomeruli become sclerotic, the remaining healthy glomeruli undergo hyperfiltration to compensate, which can cause further podocyte stress and injury, creating a vicious cycle that leads to progressive loss of kidney function.
• **Classification of Etiologies**:
    ◦ **Primary (Idiopathic) FSGS**: The most common form (~80% of cases). It is thought to be caused by a circulating permeability factor or an underlying immune dysregulation that directly targets podocytes.
    ◦ **Secondary FSGS**: Occurs as a response to a known insult or underlying condition.
        ▪ **Viral Infections**: **HIV-associated nephropathy (HIVAN)** is a classic example, particularly the "collapsing variant." Also Parvovirus B19, CMV, EBV.
        ▪ **Drug-Induced**: **Heroin**, pamidronate, anabolic steroids, lithium.
        ▪ **Maladaptive Response**: Occurs due to glomerular hyperfiltration in states of reduced nephron mass.
            ▪ Obesity
            ▪ Sickle cell disease
            ▪ Chronic vesicoureteral reflux (reflux nephropathy)
            ▪ Prior kidney injury or congenital solitary kidney.
        ▪ **Genetic FSGS**: Mutations in genes that code for podocyte structural proteins (e.g., NPHS1, NPHS2). Most notably, **APOL1 gene variants** are strongly associated with a higher risk of FSGS, particularly in individuals of African ancestry.
sections.epidemiology:
• The **most common cause of primary nephrotic syndrome in adults** in the United States, especially in African American and Hispanic populations.
• Accounts for approximately 35% of all cases of nephrotic syndrome in adults and 50% of cases in African Americans.
• Incidence is rising, partly due to the obesity epidemic.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is the abrupt or insidious onset of **nephrotic syndrome**.
    ◦ **Heavy Proteinuria**: >3.5 grams / 24 hours.
    ◦ **Hypoalbuminemia**: <3.5 g/dL.
    ◦ **Edema**: Due to low oncotic pressure and sodium retention.
    ◦ **Hyperlipidemia / Lipiduria**: Due to increased hepatic lipoprotein synthesis and loss of lipid-regulating proteins in the urine.
• Some patients may present with sub-nephrotic proteinuria and preserved renal function, while others may present with rapidly progressive renal failure.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Lab Studies**
    ◦ **Urinalysis (UA)**
        ▪ **4+ protein** on dipstick.
        ▪ Microscopic exam may show **oval fat bodies** (renal tubular cells that have absorbed lipids) which have a characteristic **"Maltese cross"** appearance under polarized light.
        ▪ Microscopic hematuria may be present.
    ◦ **Urine Protein Quantification**
        ▪ **24-hour urine collection**: Gold standard for quantifying proteinuria. Nephrotic range is **>3.5 g/day**.
        ▪ **Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR)**: A convenient spot test. A UPCR of **>3.5** correlates with nephrotic-range proteinuria.
    ◦ **Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP)**
        ▪ **Hypoalbuminemia** (<3.5 g/dL).
        ▪ **Elevated BUN and Creatinine** (indicates decreased GFR).
        ▪ Electrolyte abnormalities.
    ◦ **Lipid Panel**
        ▪ **Elevated total cholesterol and triglycerides.**
    ◦ **Serologic Workup** (to rule out secondary causes)
        ▪ HIV test, Hepatitis B & C panel.
        ▪ ANA (for lupus), ANCA (for vasculitis) if clinically suspected.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Renal Ultrasound**: Primarily to assess kidney size, echogenicity, and rule out any structural or obstructive causes. Kidneys may be normal-sized or enlarged.
• **Definitive Diagnosis: Renal Biopsy**
    ◦ A kidney biopsy is **required** for definitive diagnosis. Findings include:
        ▪ **Light Microscopy (LM)**: Shows sclerosis and hyalinosis in **some** (focal) glomeruli, and within those affected glomeruli, only a **portion** (segmental) is scarred.
        ▪ **Immunofluorescence (IF)**: Typically negative or shows non-specific, "trapped" deposits of IgM and C3 in the sclerotic areas. This helps distinguish it from other glomerular diseases like membranous nephropathy or lupus nephritis.
        ▪ **Electron Microscopy (EM)**: Reveals **diffuse effacement (flattening) of the podocyte foot processes**. This is the key ultrastructural finding but is not specific to FSGS (also seen in Minimal Change Disease).
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is variable and significantly worse than Minimal Change Disease.
• Approximately 50% of patients with primary FSGS progress to ESRD within 10 years.
• **Key Prognostic Factors**
    ◦ **Response to Therapy**: Patients who achieve remission have a much better prognosis.
    ◦ **Degree of Proteinuria**: Persistent nephrotic-range proteinuria is a poor sign.
    ◦ **Renal Function at Presentation**: Higher initial creatinine is associated with a worse outcome.
    ◦ **Histologic Variant**: The **"collapsing variant"** has a very poor prognosis with rapid progression to ESRD.

sections.overview: • Acute Interstitial Nephritis (AIN) is a form of acute kidney injury (AKI) characterized by inflammation and edema of the renal interstitium and tubules. ◦ This process typically spares the glomeruli and renal vasculature. ◦ It is most often an immunologically-mediated hypersensitivity reaction to an offending agent, leading to a decline in renal function.
sections.etiology: • Etiology (Causes): AIN is broadly caused by drugs, infections, or systemic autoimmune diseases. ◦ Drugs (>70% of cases): The most common cause. ▪ Antibiotics: Penicillins (especially methicillin, ampicillin), Cephalosporins, Sulfonamides (e.g., Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole), Rifampin, Ciprofloxacin. ▪ NSAIDs: Both non-selective (ibuprofen, naproxen) and COX-2 inhibitors. ▪ Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs): Omeprazole, pantoprazole, etc. (A common and often overlooked cause). ▪ Diuretics: Thiazides, Furosemide. ▪ Anticonvulsants: Phenytoin, Carbamazepine. ▪ Others: Allopurinol, Cimetidine, Checkpoint inhibitors. ◦ Infections (~15% of cases): ▪ Bacterial: Streptococcus, Legionella, Mycoplasma. ▪ Viral: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), Cytomegalovirus (CMV), HIV. ▪ Fungal/Other: Histoplasmosis, Leptospirosis. ◦ Systemic / Autoimmune Diseases (~5% of cases): ▪ Sarcoidosis ▪ Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) ▪ Sjögren's Syndrome ▪ TINU Syndrome: Tubulointerstitial Nephritis and Uveitis syndrome. ◦ Idiopathic: No clear cause is identified. • Pathophysiology: ◦ AIN is primarily a Type IV (T-cell mediated) delayed hypersensitivity reaction. A Type I (IgE-mediated) reaction may also contribute. ◦ Mechanism (Drug-Induced): ▪ The offending drug or its metabolite acts as a hapten. ▪ The hapten binds to a native protein on the tubular basement membrane, forming a complete antigen. ▪ This antigen is processed by antigen-presenting cells. ▪ T-cells are activated and infiltrate the renal interstitium. ▪ These T-cells release cytokines, leading to the recruitment of other inflammatory cells (macrophages, eosinophils, plasma cells). ▪ This inflammatory infiltrate causes direct tubular cell injury (tubulitis) and interstitial edema, leading to impaired tubular function and a decrease in GFR (i.e., AKI). ◦ NSAID-induced AIN has a distinct pathophysiology. It is often associated with minimal change disease or membranous nephropathy, leading to nephrotic-range proteinuria.
sections.epidemiology: • Responsible for approximately 15-20% of cases of unexplained AKI. • The incidence is likely under-reported as definitive diagnosis requires a renal biopsy, which is not always performed. • Drug-induced AIN is the most common form in developed countries. • Incidence is increasing, likely due to the aging population, polypharmacy, and increased use of causative agents like PPIs.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • The presentation is often non-specific, primarily manifesting as an acute rise in serum creatinine. • The "classic triad" is taught but is only present in 10-15% of cases. ◦ Classic Triad: ▪ Fever ▪ Maculopapular Rash ▪ Eosinophilia • Onset is typically 7-10 days after starting a new drug but can range from 1 day to several months. • NSAID-induced AIN often has a much longer latency period (months) and is less likely to present with systemic hypersensitivity features.
sections.diagnostics: • Labs (Serum): ◦ Serum Creatinine (sCr) and BUN: The hallmark finding of AKI. ◦ Peripheral Eosinophilia: Often present, but its absence does not rule out AIN. ◦ Elevated IgE: May be seen, suggesting a Type I hypersensitivity component. • Labs (Urine): ◦ Urinalysis (UA): ▪ Sterile Pyuria: WBCs in urine without bacteria (negative culture). This is a key finding. ▪ WBC Casts: Pathognomonic for interstitial inflammation/pyelonephritis, but only seen in a minority of AIN cases. Highly suggestive if present. ▪ Microscopic Hematuria: Common. ▪ Mild to Moderate Proteinuria: Usually non-nephrotic (<1 g/day). ▪ Exception: NSAID-induced AIN can have nephrotic-range proteinuria >3.5 g/day. ◦ Urine Eosinophils: ▪ Detected with Wright or Hansel stain. ▪ Low sensitivity and specificity. Its presence is suggestive but not diagnostic, and its absence is not exclusionary. No longer widely relied upon. • Imaging: ◦ Renal Ultrasound: Primarily used to rule out other causes of AKI, especially post-renal obstruction. Kidneys may appear normal-sized or enlarged and hyperechoic. • Gold Standard: ◦ Renal Biopsy: Provides the definitive diagnosis. ▪ Histology Findings: Diffuse or patchy interstitial inflammatory infiltrate (lymphocytes, macrophages, eosinophils, plasma cells), interstitial edema, and tubulitis (inflammatory cells invading the tubular epithelium).
sections.prognosis: • The prognosis is generally good if the causative agent is identified and withdrawn promptly. • Most patients experience partial or complete recovery of renal function, though it may take weeks to months. • Negative Prognostic Factors: ◦ Delayed diagnosis and withdrawal of the offending drug (>2 weeks). ◦ Advanced age. ◦ Severe and prolonged AKI (especially if dialysis is required). ◦ Extensive interstitial fibrosis found on biopsy.

sections.overview:
• Chronic Interstitial Nephritis (CIN), also known as Chronic Tubulointerstitial Nephritis (CTIN), is a clinical and pathologic entity characterized by chronic inflammation and fibrosis of the renal interstitium and tubules.
• This process leads to progressive tubular atrophy and dysfunction, which ultimately results in a gradual, irreversible decline in renal function (**Chronic Kidney Disease** - CKD).
• The onset is **insidious**, and patients are often asymptomatic until significant renal impairment has occurred.
• Unlike glomerulonephritis, the glomeruli are typically spared until late in the disease course.
sections.etiology:
• The underlying mechanism involves a persistent insult to the renal tubules and interstitium, triggering a sustained inflammatory response that transitions from cellular infiltration to fibrosis.
• **Etiology (Causes):**
    ◦ **Drugs (Most Common Cause):**
        ▪ **Analgesics:** Long-term, high-dose use of NSAIDs or combination analgesics (e.g., phenacetin, aspirin, acetaminophen). This is often termed **"Analgesic Nephropathy."**
        ▪ **Lithium:** Used for bipolar disorder; causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and CIN.
        ▪ **Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs):** Increasingly recognized cause, can progress from AIN to CIN.
        ▪ **Calcineurin Inhibitors:** Cyclosporine and tacrolimus (used in transplant medicine).
        ▪ Certain Antivirals & Antibiotics: Chronic use.
    ◦ **Toxins / Environmental Exposure:**
        ▪ **Heavy Metals:** Lead (Saturnine nephropathy), Cadmium.
        ▪ **Aristolochic Acid:** Found in some Chinese herbal remedies; causes Balkan endemic nephropathy and aristolochic acid nephropathy.
    ◦ **Systemic / Immunologic Diseases:**
        ▪ **Sjögren's Syndrome**
        ▪ **Sarcoidosis** (can present as granulomatous interstitial nephritis)
        ▪ **IgG4-related disease**
        ▪ **Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)**
    ◦ **Anatomic / Obstructive Uropathy:**
        ▪ **Vesicoureteral Reflux (VUR): "Reflux Nephropathy"** is a classic cause, especially with superimposed infections. Chronic backflow of urine leads to scarring.
        ▪ **Chronic Urinary Tract Obstruction:** BPH, kidney stones, tumors.
    ◦ **Infections:**
        ▪ **Chronic Pyelonephritis:** Recurrent or persistent bacterial infections, often in the setting of VUR or obstruction.
    ◦ **Metabolic Disorders:**
        ▪ **Chronic Hypercalcemia** (e.g., from hyperparathyroidism)
        ▪ **Chronic Hypokalemia**
        ▪ **Hyperuricemia** (Urate nephropathy)
        ▪ **Hyperoxaluria**
    ◦ **Hematologic / Malignant Disorders:**
        ▪ **Multiple Myeloma** (Light chain cast nephropathy)
        ▪ **Sickle Cell Disease**
    ◦ **Idiopathic:** A significant portion of cases have no identifiable cause.
• **Pathophysiology:**
    ◦ **Initial Injury:** A drug, toxin, or disease process directly injures the renal tubular epithelial cells or the interstitial capillaries.
    ◦ **Inflammatory Infiltration:** The injury recruits a persistent, low-grade infiltrate of mononuclear cells (lymphocytes, macrophages, plasma cells) into the interstitium.
    ◦ **Fibrosis Cascade:** These inflammatory cells release pro-fibrotic cytokines (e.g., TGF-β). This activates interstitial fibroblasts, transforming them into myofibroblasts.
    ◦ **Extracellular Matrix Deposition:** Myofibroblasts produce and deposit excessive extracellular matrix components, like collagen, leading to **interstitial fibrosis**.
    ◦ **Tubular Atrophy & Dysfunction:** The fibrosis encases and "strangles" the tubules, disrupting their function and blood supply, leading to **tubular atrophy**. This impairs the kidney's ability to concentrate urine, reabsorb solutes, and secrete acids.
    ◦ **Secondary Glomerulosclerosis:** As interstitial fibrosis worsens, it leads to periglomerular fibrosis and ischemic injury to the glomeruli, causing secondary glomerulosclerosis and a further decline in GFR. This is the final common pathway to **End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD)**.
sections.epidemiology:
• Accounts for approximately 10-15% of cases of **End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD)**.
• The true incidence is likely underestimated because the disease is often clinically silent and a definitive diagnosis requires a kidney biopsy, which is not always performed.
• Drug-induced CIN is a leading and potentially preventable cause.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is typically **insidious and asymptomatic** in the early stages.
    ◦ It is often discovered incidentally on routine laboratory work showing a gradual rise in serum creatinine over months to years.
• There are no classic "triad" symptoms like in Acute Interstitial Nephritis (fever, rash, eosinophilia).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Laboratory Studies:**
    ◦ **BMP/CMP:**
        ▪ **Elevated BUN and Serum Creatinine** with a reduced eGFR.
        ▪ **Hyperkalemia** (due to impaired tubular secretion).
        ▪ **Non-anion gap metabolic acidosis** (hyperchloremic) due to Type 1 (distal) or Type 4 (hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism) Renal Tubular Acidosis (RTA).
    ◦ **CBC:**
        ▪ **Normocytic, normochromic anemia** disproportionate to the degree of renal failure, due to decreased erythropoietin (EPO) production by the damaged interstitium.
    ◦ **Urinalysis (UA):**
        ▪ **Bland urinary sediment** is common.
        ▪ **Sterile Pyuria:** Presence of white blood cells (WBCs) without evidence of bacterial infection.
        ▪ **WBC casts:** A key finding, though not always present.
        ▪ Mild to moderate proteinuria: Typically **non-nephrotic range** (<3.5 g/day, often <1-2 g/day).
        ▪ Heavy proteinuria suggests a primary glomerular disease.
        ▪ Eosinophiluria: Less common than in AIN but can be seen.
• **Imaging:**
    ◦ **Renal Ultrasound:** This is a key imaging modality.
        ▪ Classic finding: **Bilaterally small or shrunken, echogenic (scarred) kidneys.**
        ▪ May show cortical thinning.
        ▪ In Analgesic Nephropathy, may see **papillary calcifications**.
        ▪ Can rule out obstruction (hydronephrosis).
• **Definitive Diagnosis:**
    ◦ **Kidney Biopsy:** Gold standard, but not always necessary if the clinical picture and history are classic.
        ▪ **Histology:** Shows **interstitial fibrosis, tubular atrophy, and a mononuclear inflammatory cell infiltrate** (lymphocytes, macrophages).
        ▪ Glomeruli and blood vessels are typically normal until late stages.
sections.prognosis:
• Highly variable and depends on the underlying cause and the degree of fibrosis at the time of diagnosis.
    ◦ If the offending agent is removed early, renal function may stabilize or even improve slightly.
• Once significant fibrosis is established, the damage is **irreversible**, and the disease typically progresses to **ESRD**, although the rate of decline may be slowed with good management.

sections.overview:
• Renal Papillary Necrosis (RPN) is a form of nephropathy involving coagulative necrosis of the renal medullary pyramids and papillae.
    ◦ The renal papillae have a tenuous blood supply, making them highly susceptible to ischemic injury.
• Damage leads to sloughing of the papilla, which can cause **hematuria** and urinary tract obstruction.
• It is not a primary disease but rather a complication of an underlying condition.
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The final common pathway is **ischemia** of the renal papilla.
        ▪ The blood supply to the renal medulla and papillae is provided by the vasa recta, which is a low-pressure, low-flow vascular system.
        ▪ The hypertonic environment of the medulla also contributes to cellular stress.
        ▪ Any condition that compromises this delicate blood flow can lead to ischemia, coagulative necrosis, and subsequent sloughing of the papillary tip.
    ◦ **NSAIDs**: Inhibit prostaglandins (PGE2), which are crucial for vasodilation of the vasa recta. Loss of this vasodilation leads to vasoconstriction and medullary ischemia.
    ◦ **Diabetes**: Microangiopathy (diabetic nephropathy) damages the vasa recta, impairing blood flow. Increased susceptibility to infection (pyelonephritis) also contributes.
    ◦ **Sickle Cell Disease/Trait**: Sickling of RBCs in the hypoxic, hyperosmolar medullary environment causes microvascular occlusion and ischemia.
    ◦ **Obstruction/Infection**: Increased intraluminal pressure from obstruction or inflammation from pyelonephritis can compress the vasa recta, reducing blood flow.
• **Etiology**
    ◦ The causes can be remembered with the mnemonic **POSTCARDS**:
        ▪ **P** - Pyelonephritis (especially in diabetics or with obstruction)
        ▪ **O** - Obstruction of the urinary tract
        ▪ **S** - **Sickle Cell Disease** (and trait)
        ▪ **T** - Tuberculosis (renal)
        ▪ **C** - Cirrhosis of the liver / Chronic alcoholism
        ▪ **A** - Analgesic abuse (especially **NSAIDs**)
        ▪ **R** - Renal transplant rejection
        ▪ **D** - **Diabetes Mellitus**
        ▪ **S** - Systemic Vasculitis
sections.epidemiology:
• More common in women, largely due to higher rates of analgesic nephropathy and urinary tract infections.
• Prevalence is highest in patients with one or more of the major risk factors, particularly **diabetes**, **sickle cell disease**, and chronic **NSAID** use.
• Typically affects adults over 40.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation can range from asymptomatic to fulminant renal failure and sepsis.
• **Acute Presentation**
    ◦ Abrupt onset of **flank pain** or abdominal pain (**renal colic**), gross **hematuria**, and fever/chills if a secondary infection is present.
        ▪ The pain is often caused by the passage of sloughed papillary tissue down the ureter.
• **Chronic/Insidious Presentation**
    ◦ May be asymptomatic or present with intermittent, microscopic **hematuria**, **sterile pyuria**, mild proteinuria, and a gradual decline in renal function (rising creatinine).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **Urinalysis (UA)**: The most important initial test.
        ▪ **Hematuria** (gross or microscopic).
        ▪ **Pyuria** (WBCs in urine), which may be **sterile** (no growth on culture) if not caused by infection.
        ▪ Mild proteinuria.
        ▪ Necrotic papillary tissue may be seen on microscopy.
    ◦ **Urine Culture**: To rule out or confirm a concomitant urinary tract infection.
    ◦ **Complete Blood Count (CBC)**: May show leukocytosis (infection) or anemia (from chronic disease or blood loss).
    ◦ **Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP)**: To assess renal function (**BUN, Creatinine**), which may be elevated (AKI or CKD).
• **Imaging**
    ◦ Imaging is crucial for diagnosis.
    ◦ **CT Urogram (with and without contrast)**: **Best diagnostic modality**.
        ▪ Findings include medullary cavitation, irregularities of the papillary tips, and hydronephrosis if obstruction is present.
        ▪ The classic finding is the **"ring shadow" sign**, where contrast material surrounds a sloughed, non-opacified papilla within the collecting system.
    ◦ **Intravenous Pyelogram (IVP)**: Historically the gold standard, but now largely replaced by CT. Excellent for board exam questions.
        ▪ Classic findings include the **"egg-in-a-cup"** or **"lobster claw" deformity**, representing contrast filling a cavity in the medulla where a papilla has necrosed.
    ◦ **Renal Ultrasound**: Useful for screening.
        ▪ Can detect hydronephrosis from obstruction and may show echogenic, non-shadowing material (the sloughed papilla) in the collecting system.
        ▪ Less sensitive for direct visualization of necrosis.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is highly variable and depends on the underlying etiology, the extent of renal damage, and whether the causative factor can be removed or controlled.
• Prognosis is generally good if the insult (e.g., **NSAIDs**) is identified and removed early in a patient with otherwise normal renal function.
• Prognosis is poorer in patients with uncontrolled systemic diseases like diabetes or in cases of bilateral, extensive necrosis leading to significant renal failure.

sections.overview:
• **Analgesic Nephropathy** is a form of **chronic kidney disease (CKD)** characterized by **chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis** and **renal papillary necrosis**.
◦ Caused by the long-term, excessive consumption of combination analgesic medications.
◦ While incidence has decreased since the removal of **phenacetin**, it remains an important cause of CKD, particularly from chronic **NSAID** use.
◦ Damage is often insidious and progresses slowly over years.
sections.etiology:
• **Core Mechanism**: **Ischemic injury** to the renal medulla and papillae.
◦ The renal medulla is a relatively low-oxygen environment, making it highly susceptible to further reductions in blood flow.
• **Prostaglandin Inhibition**: Prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2) are crucial for maintaining medullary blood flow via vasodilation of the afferent arteriole and medullary vessels.
◦ **NSAIDs** (e.g., ibuprofen, naproxen) and **Aspirin**: Block COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes, leading to decreased prostaglandin synthesis.
▪ This causes vasoconstriction and reduces medullary blood flow, resulting in ischemia and, eventually, **papillary necrosis**.
• **Oxidative Damage**:
◦ **Acetaminophen**: In high doses, it depletes intracellular glutathione, leaving renal cells vulnerable to oxidative damage from its toxic metabolites (e.g., NAPQI).
◦ **Phenacetin** (historical): Its metabolites (including acetaminophen) caused direct oxidative injury.
• **Pathological Progression**:
◦ **Medullary Ischemia**: Chronic vasoconstriction leads to ischemic damage.
◦ **Papillary Necrosis**: The tips of the renal papillae, being the most distal part of the medullary blood supply, undergo necrosis.
◦ **Sloughing**: Necrotic papillae may slough off, potentially causing ureteric obstruction.
◦ **Chronic Tubulointerstitial Nephritis**: The cortical tubules that drain into the damaged papillae undergo atrophy and fibrosis, surrounded by a chronic inflammatory infiltrate, leading to the characteristic **"bumpy"** or irregular kidney contour.
• **Combination Therapy**: The risk is greatest with combination analgesics (e.g., aspirin + NSAID + acetaminophen/caffeine), as the different agents cause injury through multiple mechanisms.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Has significantly decreased in many countries after the ban of phenacetin-containing analgesics.
• **Demographics**: Classically affects **middle-aged to older women** (Female > Male).
• **Association**: Strongly associated with patients who have chronic pain syndromes, such as **chronic headaches**, back pain, or musculoskeletal disorders, leading to high cumulative analgesic intake over many years.
sections.riskFactors:
• **High Cumulative Dose**: The most significant risk factor. Typically **>1 kg of NSAIDs** or **>3 kg of acetaminophen** over a lifetime.
• **Long-Term Use**: Daily use for **>3 years**.
• **Combination Analgesics**: Use of multiple agents simultaneously (especially historic phenacetin-containing compounds).
• **Female Sex**.
• **Underlying Conditions**: **Dehydration**, pre-existing renal disease, **heart failure**, or **cirrhosis** (states where renal blood flow is highly prostaglandin-dependent).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is often insidious and patients may be asymptomatic for years until significant renal dysfunction develops.
• The classic vignette is a **middle-aged female with a history of chronic headaches or arthritis** who has been taking over-the-counter pain medications for many years and now presents with signs of CKD.
• **Symptoms**:
◦ **Early**:
▪ Often asymptomatic.
▪ **Nocturia** or **polyuria** may be early signs due to impaired urinary concentrating ability from tubular damage.
◦ **Later** (as CKD progresses):
▪ Vague constitutional symptoms: **Fatigue**, weakness, malaise.
▪ Nausea, anorexia, pruritus (**uremic symptoms**).
▪ **Flank pain** (can be acute and colicky if a sloughed papilla causes ureteric obstruction).
▪ Gross or microscopic **hematuria**.
▪ Recurrent **Urinary Tract Infections (UTIs)**.
sections.physicalExam:
• Often unremarkable in the early stages.
• **Hypertension**: Very common, present in >50% of patients.
• **Pallor**: Due to **anemia of chronic disease**.
• **Edema**: Peripheral or periorbital edema with advanced CKD and fluid retention.
• "Prematurely aged" appearance (a classic but non-specific description).
• Costovertebral angle (**CVA**) tenderness may be present during an episode of obstruction.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Non-contrast Helical CT**: **The imaging modality of choice.**
◦ **Findings**:
▪ Small, shrunken, bilaterally affected kidneys.
▪ Irregular, **"bumpy" renal contours** due to cortical scarring over necrotic papillae.
◦ **Papillary Calcifications**: The most specific finding.
◦ **"Ring Shadow" sign**: A calcified, sloughed papilla seen within the collecting system.
• **Renal Ultrasound**:
◦ May show small, echogenic kidneys with irregular outlines.
◦ Can also detect hydronephrosis if a sloughed papilla is causing obstruction.
• **Intravenous Pyelogram (IVP)**:
◦ Historically used but now largely replaced by CT due to the risk of contrast-induced nephropathy.
◦ It was excellent for visualizing the **"ring shadow" sign**.
sections.treatment:
• **CESSATION OF OFFENDING AGENT(S)**: This is the single most important intervention.
◦ All suspected analgesics, particularly **NSAIDs**, must be discontinued immediately and permanently.
sections.management:
• **Blood Pressure Control**: Aggressive BP management is critical.
◦ **ACE inhibitors or ARBs** are first-line agents, though serum creatinine and potassium must be monitored closely upon initiation.
• **Hydration**: Maintain adequate fluid intake to support renal perfusion.
• **Manage CKD Complications**:
◦ **Anemia**: Iron supplementation, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs).
◦ **Metabolic Acidosis**: Oral sodium bicarbonate.
◦ **Mineral and Bone Disorder**: Phosphate binders, vitamin D analogs.
• **Nephrology Referral**: All patients should be managed in consultation with a nephrologist.
• **Urologic Surveillance**: Due to the high risk of **urothelial carcinoma**, patients may require periodic surveillance with urine cytology or cystoscopy.
• **Renal Replacement Therapy**: Dialysis or kidney transplantation for patients who progress to **end-stage renal disease (ESRD)**.
sections.complications:
• **End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD)**: Progressive fibrosis leads to irreversible loss of kidney function.
• **Urothelial Carcinoma (Transitional Cell Carcinoma)**: Significantly increased risk (up to 8-10 times) of cancer involving the renal pelvis, ureter, or bladder.
◦ This risk persists even after stopping analgesics.
• **Acute Ureteric Obstruction**: Caused by a sloughed papilla lodging in the ureter, presenting as acute renal colic or acute kidney injury.
• **Hypertension**.
• **Cardiovascular Disease**: Accelerated atherosclerosis is common in all forms of CKD.
sections.prognosis:
• Highly variable and depends on the degree of renal dysfunction at the time of diagnosis.
• If analgesics are stopped early, renal function may stabilize or even show modest improvement.
• If diagnosed with advanced CKD, progression to **ESRD** is likely, even after discontinuation of the drugs.
• The lifetime risk of **urothelial cancer** remains elevated regardless of renal outcome.
sections.preventionEducation:
• **Patient Education**: Crucial for ensuring compliance and preventing relapse of analgesic use.
◦ Help patient find alternative pain management strategies.

sections.overview:
• **Renal Artery Stenosis (RAS)** is the narrowing or blockage of one or both renal arteries, most commonly due to **atherosclerosis** or **fibromuscular dysplasia**.
• This stenosis leads to decreased renal perfusion, which triggers the **Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS)**, resulting in **renovascular hypertension**.
• If severe and bilateral, it can also lead to **ischemic nephropathy** and chronic kidney disease.
• It is a major cause of **secondary hypertension**.
sections.etiology:
• There are two primary causes of Renal Artery Stenosis:
    ◦ **Atherosclerotic RAS (~90% of cases):**
        ▪ **Etiology:** Caused by the same process as **coronary artery disease (CAD)** and **peripheral vascular disease (PVD)**. Atherosclerotic plaques build up and narrow the artery lumen.
        ▪ **Location:** Typically affects the **ostium and proximal 1/3** of the renal artery.
        ▪ **Population:** Primarily affects older individuals (>50 years) with other evidence of atherosclerosis.
    ◦ **Fibromuscular Dysplasia (FMD) (~10% of cases):**
        ▪ **Etiology:** A non-atherosclerotic, non-inflammatory vascular disease causing abnormal cell growth in the arterial wall, leading to areas of stenosis, aneurysm, or dissection.
        ▪ **Location:** Typically affects the **mid-to-distal** portions of the renal artery and may involve branch vessels.
        ▪ **Population:** Primarily affects younger women (age 15-50).
• **Pathophysiology Cascade:**
    ◦ **Decreased Renal Perfusion:** Stenosis reduces blood flow to the affected kidney.
    ◦ **RAAS Activation:** The juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA) of the affected kidney senses this hypoperfusion and releases **renin**.
    ◦ **Angiotensin II Production:** Renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I. Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme (ACE) then converts angiotensin I to **angiotensin II**.
    ◦ **Systemic Effects of Angiotensin II:**
        ▪ **Potent Vasoconstriction:** Causes a rapid increase in systemic blood pressure.
        ▪ **Aldosterone Release:** Stimulates the adrenal cortex to release aldosterone.
    ◦ **Aldosterone Effects:** Promotes sodium and water retention (and potassium excretion) by the kidneys, increasing blood volume and further elevating blood pressure.
    ◦ **Result:** Severe, difficult-to-control **renovascular hypertension** and potential **hypokalemia**. In bilateral disease, the lack of a "healthy" kidney to excrete sodium leads to volume overload and progressive renal failure (**ischemic nephropathy**).
sections.epidemiology:
• **Atherosclerotic RAS:** Found in 10-40% of patients with **refractory hypertension** and in >40% of patients with hypertensive **end-stage renal disease (ESRD)**. Prevalence increases with age.
• **FMD:** The most common cause of **secondary hypertension** in young and middle-aged women.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The clinical presentation is often that of a patient with severe or difficult-to-control hypertension. Suspect RAS in patients with:
    ◦ **Resistant Hypertension:** Uncontrolled blood pressure despite being on 3 antihypertensive agents of different classes, one of which is a diuretic.
    ◦ **Acute Kidney Injury (AKI):** A significant rise in serum creatinine (>30%) after initiation of an **ACE inhibitor or ARB**. This is a classic board question finding.
    ◦ **New-onset Severe Hypertension:** Especially in patients <30 years old (suspect **FMD**) or >55 years old (suspect **atherosclerosis**).
    ◦ Unexplained **Renal Failure** or asymmetric kidney sizes on imaging.
    ◦ Recurrent **Flash Pulmonary Edema:** Sudden onset, severe pulmonary edema in a patient with severe hypertension, often suggesting severe bilateral RAS.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Laboratory Studies:**
    ◦ **BMP:** Check for elevated creatinine/BUN (renal insufficiency) and **hypokalemia** (from secondary hyperaldosteronism).
    ◦ **Plasma Renin Activity:** May be elevated but is non-specific.
    ◦ **Urinalysis:** Usually benign but may show mild proteinuria.
• **Imaging (Screening & Non-invasive):**
    ◦ **Renal Duplex Ultrasound:** **First-line screening test.**
        ▪ Assesses renal artery blood flow velocities (Peak Systolic Velocity >200 cm/sec is suggestive) and kidney size (atrophy or asymmetry >1.5 cm).
        ▪ It is non-invasive and uses no contrast but is highly operator-dependent and limited by body habitus.
    ◦ **CT Angiography (CTA):**
        ▪ Excellent anatomical detail.
        ▪ Requires IV iodinated contrast, posing a risk of **contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN)**.
    ◦ **MR Angiography (MRA):**
        ▪ Also provides excellent detail.
        ▪ Uses gadolinium contrast, which carries a risk of **nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF)** in patients with GFR < 30 mL/min.
• **Confirmatory / Gold Standard:**
    ◦ **Renal Angiography:** **The definitive gold standard.**
        ▪ An invasive catheter-based procedure that provides the best visualization of the renal arteries.
        ▪ It is both diagnostic and allows for therapeutic intervention (angioplasty/stenting) in the same session.
sections.prognosis:
• **FMD:** Excellent prognosis. Revascularization is often highly effective or curative.
• **Atherosclerotic RAS:** Prognosis is largely determined by the patient's overall cardiovascular disease burden. Medical management is effective for many, but mortality is higher due to associated comorbidities (MI, stroke).

sections.overview:
• **Renal Vein Thrombosis (RVT)** is the formation of a thrombus within the main renal vein or its tributaries.
• This obstruction of venous outflow leads to renal congestion, increased intrarenal pressure, and potential kidney damage.
• RVT can present acutely with dramatic symptoms or chronically with a more insidious course.
• It is often a complication of an underlying systemic condition rather than a primary renal disease.
sections.etiology:
• The pathophysiology of RVT is rooted in **Virchow's Triad**:
    ◦ **Hypercoagulability (Most Common Cause in Adults)**
        ▪ **Nephrotic Syndrome**: This is the single most important association. Massive proteinuria leads to the urinary loss of anticoagulant proteins, primarily **Antithrombin III**. The liver also increases production of procoagulant factors (e.g., fibrinogen).
        ▪ **Membranous Nephropathy** is the glomerulopathy most frequently associated with RVT.
        ▪ **Malignancy**: Especially **Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC)**, which can directly invade the renal vein. Also associated with other abdominal cancers.
        ▪ **Inherited Thrombophilias**: Factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation, Protein C/S deficiency.
        ▪ **Acquired Hypercoagulable States**: Antiphospholipid syndrome, oral contraceptive use, pregnancy.
    ◦ **Endothelial Injury**
        ▪ **Trauma**: Direct injury to the abdomen, flank, or back.
        ▪ **Surgery**: Especially renal transplant, nephrectomy, or other retroperitoneal procedures.
        ▪ **Indwelling Catheters**: Central venous catheters extending near the renal veins.
        ▪ **Inflammation**: Vasculitis or severe pyelonephritis.
    ◦ **Venous Stasis**
        ▪ **Extrinsic Compression**: Retroperitoneal fibrosis, tumors, lymphadenopathy, or an aortic aneurysm compressing the renal vein.
        ▪ **Severe Dehydration**: Especially in neonates and infants, leading to hemoconcentration and sluggish blood flow.
        ▪ **Anatomical**: "**Nutcracker Syndrome**" (compression of the left renal vein between the superior mesenteric artery and the aorta).
• **Pathophysiologic Sequence**:
    ◦ Thrombus formation → Obstruction of venous outflow → Increased renal venous pressure → Renal congestion & interstitial edema → Decreased arterial perfusion and glomerular filtration rate (GFR) → **Acute Kidney Injury (AKI)** or **Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Adults**: Most commonly associated with **nephrotic syndrome**.
    ◦ Incidence is highest in patients with **membranous nephropathy** (up to 50%).
• **Neonates/Infants**: The most common cause is severe **dehydration** or perinatal asphyxia.
    ◦ It is the most common non-catheter-related thrombosis in this age group.
• The **left renal vein** is more commonly affected than the right due to its longer course and its compression between the SMA and aorta.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation varies dramatically based on the acuity and extent of the thrombosis.
• **Acute RVT**:
    ◦ Sudden, severe onset.
    ◦ Often unilateral.
    ◦ **Classic triad**:
        ▪ **Sudden, severe flank/loin pain**
        ▪ **Gross hematuria**
        ▪ **Worsening proteinuria** (or new-onset in a previously unaffected patient)
    ◦ Associated with nausea, vomiting, and fever.
    ◦ Rapid decline in renal function (**oliguria/anuria**, rising creatinine).
• **Chronic RVT**:
    ◦ Insidious, slow onset; may be clinically silent and found incidentally.
    ◦ Nonspecific symptoms like dull flank discomfort.
    ◦ Gradual decline in renal function.
    ◦ **Persistent or worsening proteinuria** is a key sign.
    ◦ Symptoms may be dominated by the underlying cause (e.g., edema from nephrotic syndrome).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **Urinalysis**: **Hematuria** (microscopic or gross), **Proteinuria** (often nephrotic range >3.5 g/day), may see **red blood cell casts**.
    ◦ **Renal Function Panel (BMP/CMP)**: Elevated **BUN** and **Creatinine** (indicates AKI/CKD).
    ◦ **CBC**: May show hemoconcentration in dehydration.
    ◦ **LDH**: Can be elevated due to renal tissue infarction.
    ◦ **Coagulation studies/Hypercoagulability workup**: To identify an underlying thrombophilia if the cause is not apparent.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Renal Ultrasound with Doppler**: **Best initial imaging test**. It is non-invasive and can show an enlarged kidney, lack of venous flow, or a visible thrombus.
    ◦ **CT Angiography (CTA) or MR Angiography (MRA)**: More sensitive and specific. Considered the **diagnostic standard** for confirming RVT. Can clearly visualize the thrombus, its extent (e.g., into the IVC), and potential causes like tumors or compression.
        ▪ *Caution: Contrast may be contraindicated in severe AKI.*
    ◦ **Conventional Venography**: **Gold standard** but invasive and rarely used due to the excellent quality of CTA/MRA. Reserved for cases where other imaging is inconclusive and intervention is planned.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly dependent on the underlying etiology, whether the thrombosis is unilateral or bilateral, and the degree of renal injury.
• With timely anticoagulation, the prognosis for renal recovery in unilateral RVT is generally good.
• Prognosis is poorer in cases associated with **malignancy** or in those who develop severe **AKI** or ESRD.

sections.overview:
• A hypertensive emergency is defined as a severe elevation in blood pressure (typically **Systolic >180 mmHg** or **Diastolic >120 mmHg**) associated with evidence of new or worsening **target-organ damage**.
    ◦ When the kidney is the primary organ affected, it is termed a hypertensive emergency with acute renal injury.
    ◦ This condition, also known as **malignant hypertension** or **accelerated-malignant hypertension**, represents a medical emergency requiring immediate blood pressure reduction with intravenous agents to prevent irreversible organ damage and death.
    ◦ The hallmark is **acute kidney injury (AKI)** superimposed on, or as the initial presentation of, severe hypertension.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ Most Common: Non-adherence to or abrupt discontinuation of antihypertensive medication in a patient with pre-existing essential hypertension.
    ◦ Renal Parenchymal Disease: Acute glomerulonephritis, lupus nephritis.
    ◦ Renovascular Disease: **Renal artery stenosis** (atherosclerotic or fibromuscular dysplasia).
    ◦ Endocrine Causes: Pheochromocytoma, Cushing's syndrome, primary aldosteronism.
    ◦ Drug-Induced: Cocaine, amphetamines, phencyclidine (PCP), MAOIs with tyramine-rich foods, sympathomimetics.
    ◦ Pregnancy-Related: Preeclampsia, eclampsia, HELLP syndrome.
    ◦ Systemic Disorders: Scleroderma (scleroderma renal crisis), thrombotic microangiopathies (TTP/HUS), systemic vasculitis.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ Failure of Autoregulation: The kidneys normally maintain constant blood flow and glomerular filtration rate (GFR) across a wide range of systemic pressures. In a hypertensive emergency, the extreme BP elevation overwhelms this autoregulatory capacity.
    ◦ Endothelial Injury: The intense pressure and shear stress damage the endothelial lining of the small arteries and arterioles in the kidney.
    ◦ Increased Permeability & **Fibrinoid Necrosis**: Endothelial damage leads to increased vascular permeability, allowing plasma proteins and fibrin to leak into the vessel walls. This process results in **fibrinoid necrosis** of the arterioles, a pathognomonic finding.
    ◦ Vicious Cycle of RAAS Activation: The resulting ischemia from vessel narrowing is sensed by the juxtaglomerular apparatus, which triggers a massive release of renin. This activates the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS), leading to profound vasoconstriction (via Angiotensin II) and volume retention (via Aldosterone), which further exacerbates the hypertension.
    ◦ Ischemia & Microangiopathy: The cycle of vasoconstriction and vessel damage leads to downstream ischemia, glomerular damage, and a decline in GFR. Mechanical damage to red blood cells passing through narrowed, fibrin-filled vessels can cause **Microangiopathic Hemolytic Anemia (MAHA)**.
    ◦ Result: The end result is a rapid decline in renal function (**acute kidney injury**), characterized by a rising serum creatinine and oliguria.
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects approximately 1-2% of patients with chronic hypertension.
• More common in males than females.
• Higher incidence and prevalence in African American populations, who often present at a younger age and with more severe organ damage.
• The mean age of presentation is 40-50 years.
• Acute renal injury is one of the most common forms of end-organ damage seen in hypertensive emergencies.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The patient is often in moderate to severe distress and appears acutely ill.
• The presentation is dominated by the severely elevated blood pressure and symptoms related to **end-organ damage**.
    ◦ While the chief complaint may be neurological (headache, confusion) or cardiovascular (chest pain), evidence of renal injury is found on initial workup.
• The history often reveals a known diagnosis of hypertension with poor follow-up or recent cessation of medications.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP/CMP)
        ▪ **Elevated BUN and Creatinine** (defining AKI), hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis (low bicarbonate).
    ◦ Urinalysis with Microscopy (**KEY TEST**)
        ▪ **Proteinuria** (can be in nephrotic range).
        ▪ **Hematuria** (gross or microscopic).
        ▪ Urine Sediment: **Red Blood Cell (RBC) casts** are highly suggestive of glomerular injury (glomerulonephritis or malignant hypertension).
    ◦ Complete Blood Count (CBC) with Peripheral Smear
        ▪ Anemia, thrombocytopenia.
        ▪ **Schistocytes (fragmented RBCs)** on peripheral smear indicate **MAHA**.
    ◦ LDH and Haptoglobin
        ▪ Elevated LDH and low haptoglobin further support the diagnosis of **MAHA**.
    ◦ Cardiac Enzymes (Troponin)
        ▪ To rule out associated myocardial infarction.
    ◦ B-type Natriuretic Peptide (BNP)
        ▪ To assess for acute heart failure.
• **Imaging & Other Tests**
    ◦ Electrocardiogram (EKG)
        ▪ Look for signs of left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH), strain pattern, or acute ischemia/infarction.
    ◦ Chest X-Ray
        ▪ May show cardiomegaly, pulmonary edema ("bat-wing" appearance), or a widened mediastinum (aortic dissection).
    ◦ Renal Ultrasound with Doppler
        ▪ To rule out obstructive uropathy and assess kidney size. Doppler can evaluate for **renal artery stenosis**.
    ◦ Non-contrast Head CT
        ▪ Indicated for any patient with neurologic symptoms to rule out intracranial hemorrhage or ischemic stroke.
sections.prognosis:
• Historically (pre-treatment era): Mortality was >90% within one year.
