• Currently: With prompt and appropriate treatment, the one-year survival rate is >90%.
• However, long-term morbidity remains high. Up to 20-40% of survivors may develop **ESRD** requiring dialysis.
• Prognosis is directly related to the severity of the initial renal injury and the effectiveness of long-term blood pressure control.

sections.overview:
• Thrombotic Microangiopathy (TMA) is a pathologic process, not a single disease, characterized by the formation of microthrombi in arterioles and capillaries, leading to a triad of:
    ◦ **Microangiopathic Hemolytic Anemia (MAHA):** Mechanical shearing of RBCs by fibrin strands in the microvasculature.
    ◦ **Thrombocytopenia:** Platelet consumption in the formation of microthrombi.
    ◦ **End-Organ Ischemia/Damage:** Most notably affecting the kidneys and brain.
• The two primary TMA syndromes are **Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP)** and **Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS)**.
    ◦ While they share the core features of MAHA and thrombocytopenia, their underlying pathophysiology, typical patient population, and primary organ involvement differ.
• **Renal injury is a hallmark feature, particularly in HUS.**
sections.etiology: • The central event in all TMAs is widespread endothelial injury and subsequent microvascular thrombosis.
sections.epidemiology:
• **TTP:** More common in adults (median age 40). Higher incidence in females and individuals of African descent.
• **HUS:**
    ◦ **STEC-HUS:** Primarily a disease of **children < 5 years old**. Often occurs in outbreaks related to contaminated food.
    ◦ **aHUS:** Can occur at any age, including adults.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation can be abrupt. Suspect TMA in any patient with unexplained anemia and thrombocytopenia.
• **Classic TTP Pentad (rarely all present, suspect with just MAHA + Thrombocytopenia):**
    ◦ **F**ever
    ◦ **A**nemia (Microangiopathic Hemolytic)
    ◦ **T**hrombocytopenia
    ◦ **R**enal Dysfunction (often mild)
    ◦ **N**eurologic Symptoms (dominant feature)
• **Classic HUS Triad:**
    ◦ **A**nemia (Microangiopathic Hemolytic)
    ◦ **T**hrombocytopenia
    ◦ **A**cute Kidney Injury (AKI) (dominant feature)
sections.diagnostics:
• **TMA is a medical emergency. Diagnosis is clinical and confirmed by labs.**
• **Key Initial Labs (Essential for Diagnosis):**
    ◦ **CBC:** Normocytic anemia with low hemoglobin/hematocrit; **Thrombocytopenia** (platelets often <30,000/L).
    ◦ **Peripheral Blood Smear:** **PATHOGNOMONIC FINDING:** **Schistocytes** (fragmented RBCs, "helmet cells").
    ◦ **CMP / Renal Panel:** **Elevated BUN and Creatinine** (AKI); electrolyte abnormalities (hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis).
• **Hemolysis Labs:**
    ◦ **High LDH** (Lactate Dehydrogenase) - often markedly elevated.
    ◦ **Low Haptoglobin** - consumed by binding free hemoglobin.
    ◦ **High Indirect (Unconjugated) Bilirubin**.
• **Coagulation Studies (PT, aPTT):** **Typically NORMAL**. This is a key feature distinguishing TMA from Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC).
• **Direct Coombs Test:** **Negative**. Rules out autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
• **Urinalysis:** Hematuria, proteinuria.
• **Confirmatory / Etiology-Specific Labs:**
    ◦ **ADAMTS13 Activity Level:** Order immediately if TTP is suspected. **Activity <10% is diagnostic for TTP.**
    ◦ **Stool Culture & Shiga Toxin Assay:** For patients with diarrhea to confirm STEC-HUS.
    ◦ **Complement Pathway Studies (C3, C4, CH50):** For suspected aHUS.
sections.prognosis:
• **TTP:** Untreated, mortality is >90%. With emergent PEX, survival is >80-90%. Relapse can occur in 30-40% of patients.
• **STEC-HUS:** In children, mortality is <5% with supportive care. However, up to 30% may develop long-term renal complications (CKD, HTN). Prognosis is worse in adults.
• **aHUS:** Historically very poor, with ~50% progressing to ESRD or death within a year. With complement inhibitors, >80% can achieve renal recovery if started early.

sections.overview:
• Acute pyelonephritis is an infection of the upper urinary tract, specifically involving the renal parenchyma and the renal pelvis.
• It is considered a **complicated urinary tract infection (UTI)**.
• The infection leads to an inflammatory response causing tissue damage, which can be acute and, if recurrent, can lead to chronic kidney scarring.
• It is a more serious condition than cystitis (lower UTI) and requires prompt diagnosis and treatment to prevent systemic complications.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Most Common**: **_Escherichia coli_** (accounts for ~80-90% of cases).
    ◦ Other common gram-negative organisms: _Klebsiella pneumoniae_, _Proteus mirabilis_ (associated with stones), _Enterobacter spp._
    ◦ Gram-positive organisms (less common): _Enterococcus faecalis_, _Staphylococcus saprophyticus_.
    ◦ In hospitalized or catheterized patients, consider nosocomial organisms like _Pseudomonas aeruginosa_.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Ascending Infection (Most Common)**: Bacteria from the perineum colonize the urethra, ascend into the bladder (causing cystitis), and then continue up the ureters to the renal pelvis and parenchyma.
        ▪ This is often facilitated by vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) or obstruction.
    ◦ **Hematogenous Spread (Less Common)**: Bacteria from a distant infection site (e.g., endocarditis, IV drug use) seed the kidneys via the bloodstream.
        ▪ This is more common with organisms like _Staphylococcus aureus_.
    ◦ Once in the kidney, bacteria provoke an intense neutrophilic inflammatory response, leading to renal edema, interstitial inflammation, and tubular necrosis.
sections.epidemiology:
• More common in women than men due to anatomical factors (shorter urethra).
• Peak incidence occurs in young, sexually active women (15-29 years).
• A second peak occurs in older adults, often associated with urinary tract obstruction (e.g., BPH in men, prolapse in women) and instrumentation.
• It is the most common serious medical complication of pregnancy.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The patient typically appears systemically ill.
• The presentation is more severe than a simple lower UTI.
• The **classic triad** is **fever, flank pain, and nausea/vomiting**.
• The onset is usually acute over hours to a couple of days.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Lab Studies**
    ◦ **Urinalysis (UA) with microscopy (most important initial test)**
        ▪ **Pyuria**: >10 WBCs/hpf is the key finding.
        ▪ **Bacteriuria**: Presence of bacteria.
        ▪ **Positive Leukocyte Esterase**: Suggests presence of WBCs.
        ▪ **Positive Nitrites**: Specific for gram-negative bacteria (e.g., *E. coli*).
        ▪ **WBC Casts**: **Pathognomonic for pyelonephritis.** These indicate inflammation within the kidney itself.
        ▪ Hematuria (microscopic or gross) may be present.
    ◦ **Urine Culture and Sensitivity**: **Mandatory** for all patients with suspected pyelonephritis to confirm the diagnosis, identify the organism, and guide antibiotic selection.
    ◦ **Complete Blood Count (CBC)**: Shows **leukocytosis with a neutrophilic predominance ("left shift")**.
    ◦ **Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP)**: Assess renal function (BUN, Creatinine) and electrolytes, especially if the patient is vomiting or septic.
    ◦ **Blood Cultures**: Obtain in all hospitalized patients or those who appear septic to rule out bacteremia.
• **Imaging (Not required for uncomplicated cases)**
    ◦ **Indications**: Severe illness, sepsis, failure to improve after 48-72 hours of appropriate antibiotics, recurrent episodes, or suspicion of obstruction or abscess.
    ◦ **Modality of Choice**: **CT scan of abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast**.
        ▪ Can identify hydronephrosis, perinephric stranding, abscess formation, emphysematous changes, or obstructing stones.
    ◦ **Renal Ultrasound**: Useful alternative, especially in pregnant patients or to quickly assess for hydronephrosis (obstruction) or large abscesses.
        ▪ Less sensitive than CT for subtle parenchymal changes.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is excellent for uncomplicated pyelonephritis in healthy individuals who receive prompt and appropriate treatment.
• Mortality is low (<1%) but increases significantly in the elderly, those with multiple comorbidities, or if complicated by sepsis or abscess.

sections.overview:
• Chronic Pyelonephritis (CPN) is a progressive renal disorder characterized by **interstitial inflammation, fibrosis, and scarring of the renal parenchyma, particularly the cortex and calyces**
• It results from recurrent or persistent renal infections, often in the setting of an underlying structural or functional urinary tract abnormality
• Unlike acute pyelonephritis, CPN represents **irreversible histologic damage** and subsequent renal dysfunction
• Can lead to chronic kidney disease (CKD), hypertension, and end-stage renal disease (ESRD)
sections.etiology:
• CPN develops from repeated insults to the renal parenchyma, primarily driven by two major mechanisms:
    ◦ **Reflux Nephropathy**
        ▪ This is the most common cause, especially in children
        ▪ **Vesicoureteral Reflux (VUR):** An incompetent vesicoureteral sphincter allows retrograde flow of urine from the bladder into the ureters and renal pelvis
        ▪ During micturition, infected urine is forced into the kidney under high pressure, leading to "intrarenal reflux"
        ▪ This combination of bacterial infection and inflammation leads to a focal immune response, subsequent scar formation, and eventual destruction of nephrons
    ◦ **Chronic Obstructive Pyelonephritis**
        ▪ More common in adults
        ▪ Long-standing obstruction (e.g., nephrolithiasis, BPH, strictures, tumors) leads to urinary stasis
        ▪ Stasis promotes bacterial growth and persistent or recurrent infections
        ▪ Increased intrapelvic pressure causes parenchymal atrophy, while infection leads to inflammation and fibrosis
• **Histopathology**
    ◦ Grossly, the affected kidney is often small, shrunken, and irregularly scarred, with a thinned cortex
    ◦ Microscopically, key findings include:
        ▪ Interstitial fibrosis and a mononuclear infiltrate (lymphocytes, plasma cells)
        ▪ Tubular atrophy and dilation
        ▪ **"Thyroidization of the kidney":** A classic finding where atrophic tubules fill with eosinophilic, proteinaceous material (colloid casts), resembling thyroid follicles
sections.epidemiology:
• **Bimodal age distribution**
    ◦ **Childhood:** Primarily associated with congenital VUR. More common in females.
    ◦ **Adulthood:** Often related to obstructive causes like kidney stones, BPH, or neurogenic bladder.
• Overall more common in females due to a higher incidence of UTIs
• CPN is a significant cause of ESRD, particularly in the pediatric population
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is often insidious and may be asymptomatic for years, with many patients diagnosed incidentally or when complications arise
• **Insidious onset** of renal insufficiency or hypertension
• History of recurrent UTIs, particularly in childhood
• Presentation during an **acute-on-chronic exacerbation**, with symptoms of acute pyelonephritis (fever, flank pain, dysuria)
sections.diagnostics:
• **Imaging is the cornerstone of diagnosis.**
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **Urinalysis (UA):** Often abnormal but nonspecific. May show pyuria (WBCs), bacteriuria, mild proteinuria.
        ▪ **WBC casts** are highly suggestive of renal parenchymal inflammation and may be seen during an acute exacerbation
    ◦ **Urine Culture:** May be positive during an active infection or negative between episodes
    ◦ **Complete Blood Count (CBC):** Leukocytosis with a left shift during acute exacerbations. Anemia of chronic disease may be present with CKD.
    ◦ **Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP):** Elevated BUN and creatinine (azotemia) with a decreased GFR indicate renal insufficiency
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Renal Ultrasound:** Often the initial study. Findings include:
        ▪ Asymmetric kidney size
        ▪ A small, contracted, scarred kidney
        ▪ **Cortical thinning**
        ▪ Hydronephrosis if obstruction is present
    ◦ **CT Scan (with and without contrast):** More sensitive and specific than ultrasound; the definitive imaging modality for scarring
        ▪ Clearly demonstrates **focal cortical scarring**, overlying **blunted or clubbed calyces**
    ◦ **Voiding Cystourethrogram (VCUG):** The gold standard for diagnosing and grading VUR, primarily used in the pediatric workup
    ◦ **Renal Scintigraphy (DMSA Scan):** A nuclear medicine scan highly sensitive for detecting cortical scarring. Often used to assess functional renal mass and monitor disease progression in children.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis depends on whether the disease is unilateral or bilateral, the degree of renal function at diagnosis, and the ability to control underlying causes and hypertension
    ◦ **Unilateral disease** with a normal contralateral kidney generally has an excellent prognosis for overall renal function
    ◦ **Bilateral disease** carries a significant risk of progression to ESRD

sections.overview:
• A **renal abscess** is a localized collection of purulent material (pus) within the renal parenchyma.
• Considered a severe, life-threatening complication of an upper urinary tract infection, commonly evolving from inadequately treated or complicated **acute pyelonephritis**.
• Forms due to **liquefactive necrosis** of infected renal tissue.
• May be confined to the kidney (**renal abscess**) or extend into the surrounding space (**perinephric abscess**).
sections.etiology:
• **Ascending Infection** (Most common, ~80% of cases)
    ◦ Begins as a lower UTI (cystitis) that ascends to the kidney, causing **acute pyelonephritis**.
    ◦ Infection progresses from focal inflammation (acute focal bacterial nephritis or lobar nephronia) to **tissue necrosis and liquefaction**, forming an abscess, particularly in cases of obstruction (e.g., nephrolithiasis, stricture) or in compromised hosts.
    ◦ **Common Organisms**: Gram-negative enteric bacteria
        ▪ ***Escherichia coli*** (most common)
        ▪ *Klebsiella pneumoniae*
        ▪ *Proteus mirabilis*
        ▪ *Enterococcus spp.*
• **Hematogenous Spread** (Less common)
    ◦ Bacteria from a distant infection site (e.g., **endocarditis**, skin infection, osteomyelitis) seed the highly vascular renal cortex via the bloodstream.
    ◦ More likely to result in multiple, smaller cortical abscesses.
    ◦ **Common Organisms**:
        ▪ ***Staphylococcus aureus*** (classic association, especially in IV drug users)
sections.epidemiology:
• Relatively uncommon but serious sequela of complicated UTIs.
• Occurs in approximately 1-2% of all patients hospitalized for **acute pyelonephritis**.
• No significant gender or age predilection, but incidence is higher in patients with underlying risk factors.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Classic presentation involves a patient being treated for pyelonephritis who **fails to improve clinically after 48-72 hours** of appropriate IV antibiotic therapy.
    ◦ Patient often remains **febrile and symptomatic** despite treatment.
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent with prompt diagnosis, appropriate antibiotic therapy, and effective drainage.
• Mortality is low (<5%) in appropriately treated patients.
• Prognosis worsens significantly with delayed diagnosis, development of **sepsis**, presence of multiple comorbidities, or in immunocompromised individuals.

sections.overview:
• **Xanthogranulomatous Pyelonephritis (XGP)** is a rare, severe, and chronic form of destructive pyelonephritis.
• It is a benign, inflammatory condition characterized by the destruction of the renal parenchyma, which is replaced by granulomatous tissue containing **lipid-laden macrophages (foam cells or xanthoma cells)**.
• Typically results in a **non-functioning kidney** and is almost always **unilateral**.
• Clinically important as it can closely mimic **renal cell carcinoma (RCC)**, earning it the name "**the great mimicker**."
sections.etiology:
• XGP is believed to be an atypical, incomplete immune response to a chronic bacterial infection, almost always in the setting of long-standing urinary tract obstruction.
    ◦ **Primary Cause**: Chronic urinary tract obstruction and superimposed infection.
    ◦ **Obstruction**: Most commonly caused by a large, infected renal calculus, classically a **staghorn calculus** (fills the renal pelvis and calyces).
        ▪ Other causes include ureteropelvic junction (UPJ) obstruction or tumors.
    ◦ **Infection**: The most common pathogens are gram-negative bacteria, particularly:
        ▪ **Proteus mirabilis** (most common)
        ▪ **Escherichia coli**
        ▪ *Pseudomonas*, *Klebsiella*, and *Enterococcus* are less common.
    ◦ **Pathophysiological Cascade**:
        ▪ **Obstruction & Stasis**: Obstruction leads to urinary stasis, providing a nidus for chronic bacterial infection.
        ▪ **Chronic Inflammation**: The persistent infection triggers a chronic inflammatory response.
        ▪ **Macrophage Dysfunction**: The inflammatory process and bacterial endotoxins impair local circulation and lymphatic drainage, leading to hemorrhage and necrosis. Macrophages are recruited to clear cellular debris, but their lipid processing ability is overwhelmed.
        ▪ **Foam Cell Formation**: Macrophages phagocytose large amounts of lipids from necrotic tissue, transforming into characteristic **lipid-laden macrophages (xanthoma cells)**.
        ▪ **Granuloma & Destruction**: These xanthoma cells, along with lymphocytes, plasma cells, and neutrophils, form granulomas that progressively replace and destroy the normal renal parenchyma, leading to a large, non-functioning kidney.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: A rare condition, accounting for <1% of all cases of chronic pyelonephritis.
• **Demographics**:
    ◦ **Age**: Most common in middle-aged adults (45-65 years).
    ◦ **Sex**: Strong female predominance (Female:Male ratio of 2:1 to 4:1), likely due to the higher incidence of UTIs in women.
• **Laterality**: Almost exclusively **unilateral**. Bilateral involvement is exceedingly rare and often fatal.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Nephrolithiasis**: Long-standing kidney stones, especially **staghorn calculi**.
• **Chronic/Recurrent UTIs**.
• **Urinary Tract Obstruction**: Anatomic abnormalities (e.g., UPJ obstruction), tumors, neurogenic bladder.
• **Immunosuppression**: **Diabetes mellitus** is a significant risk factor.
• **History of urologic procedures**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is often insidious and non-specific, leading to delayed diagnosis.
• Patients typically have a long-standing history of vague, constitutional symptoms and recurrent UTIs that respond poorly to standard antibiotic therapy.
• **Classic Vignette**: A middle-aged diabetic woman with a history of kidney stones presenting with months of flank pain, fever, and weight loss.
• **Constitutional Symptoms**:
    ◦ Malaise, fatigue
    ◦ Fever, chills
    ◦ Weight loss, anorexia
• **Localized Symptoms**:
    ◦ **Dull, persistent flank pain** (most common symptom)
    ◦ Gross or microscopic hematuria
    ◦ Symptoms of recurrent or persistent UTI (dysuria, frequency, urgency)
sections.physicalExam:
• **Fever**: Often low-grade but can be high.
• **Costovertebral Angle (CVA) Tenderness**: Present in the majority of patients.
• **Palpable Flank Mass**: A firm, often tender mass may be palpable due to the enlarged, inflamed kidney.
• **Cutaneous Draining Fistula**: A rare but classic finding where a fistula forms between the kidney and the skin (renocutaneous fistula).
• Signs of sepsis (tachycardia, hypotension) in severe cases.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Ultrasound (US)**: Often the initial study.
    ◦ **Findings**: Enlarged kidney, loss of normal corticomedullary differentiation, central echogenic focus with shadowing (calculus), hydronephrosis, and multiple hypoechoic collections representing abscesses or dilated calyces.
• **CT Scan (with and without contrast)**: **Diagnostic modality of choice**.
    ◦ **Classic Finding (Pathognomonic)**: **"Bear Paw Sign"**.
        ▪ This refers to a severely hydronephrotic, non-functioning kidney where the renal parenchyma is replaced by multiple, low-density, fluid-filled calyces surrounding a contracted renal pelvis. The appearance resembles the paw of a bear.
    ◦ **Other Key Findings**:
        ▪ Enlarged, non-functioning kidney.
        ▪ Large central calculus (**staghorn**).
        ▪ Thickened perinephric fascia (Gerota's fascia).
        ▪ Perinephric fat stranding, abscesses, and inflammatory extension into adjacent structures (psoas muscle, colon, spleen).
        ▪ The wall of the dilated calyces often enhances with contrast.
sections.treatment:
• **Pre-operative Stabilization**:
    ◦ **IV Antibiotics**: Broad-spectrum antibiotics are given to control systemic infection and reduce local inflammation, making surgery safer.
    ◦ **Percutaneous Drainage**: If a large abscess is present or to decompress a severely obstructed system, a percutaneous nephrostomy tube may be placed.
• **Surgical Intervention**:
    ◦ **Total Nephrectomy**: **The definitive treatment** for the vast majority of cases where the disease is diffuse and the kidney is non-functional. The surgery can be challenging due to severe perinephric inflammation and adhesions.
    ◦ **Partial Nephrectomy**: May be considered in very rare cases of focal XGP (Stage I) where the disease is confined to one pole of the kidney, especially in a solitary kidney.
sections.complications:
• **Sepsis and Septic Shock**
• **Abscess Formation**: Perinephric, psoas, or hepatic abscesses.
• **Fistula Formation**: Renocutaneous, renocolonic, renoduodenal.
• **Local Invasion**: Extension of inflammation into adjacent structures like the colon, spleen, diaphragm, or psoas muscle.
• **Surgical Complications**: Hemorrhage, injury to the bowel or spleen, wound infection.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is **excellent** following nephrectomy, as XGP is a benign condition.
• The removal of the non-functioning, infected kidney resolves the chronic infection and systemic symptoms.
• Morbidity and mortality are primarily related to surgical complications or untreated sepsis from a delayed diagnosis.

sections.overview:
• Calcium oxalate stones are the **most common type of nephrolithiasis** (kidney stones), accounting for approximately 75-80% of all cases.
	◦ They are hard mineral deposits formed within the kidneys or urinary tract when urine becomes supersaturated with calcium and oxalate.
	◦ These stones are composed primarily of calcium oxalate monohydrate (whewellite) or calcium oxalate dihydrate (weddellite).
	◦ They are characteristically **hard** and **radiopaque**, making them visible on standard X-rays.
sections.etiology:
• The formation of calcium oxalate stones (lithogenesis) is a multifactorial process involving urinary supersaturation, nucleation, crystal growth, and aggregation.
• **Supersaturation**
	◦ The fundamental requirement is urine that is supersaturated with stone-forming constituents, primarily calcium and oxalate.
	◦ Key factors leading to supersaturation:
		▪ **Low Urine Volume (Dehydration)**: The most common and correctable risk factor. Concentrated urine increases the concentration of all solutes, promoting crystallization.
		▪ **Hypercalciuria**: Abnormally high levels of calcium in the urine (>250 mg/day in men, >200 mg/day in women). This is the most common metabolic abnormality found in calcium stone formers.
			◦ **Absorptive**: Increased intestinal absorption of dietary calcium.
			◦ **Resorptive**: Increased mobilization of calcium from bone (e.g., **primary hyperparathyroidism**).
			◦ **Renal Leak**: Impaired renal tubular reabsorption of calcium.
		▪ **Hyperoxaluria**: High levels of oxalate in the urine (>40 mg/day).
			◦ **Dietary**: High intake of oxalate-rich foods (e.g., spinach, rhubarb, nuts, beets).
			◦ **Enteric**: Secondary to fat malabsorption (e.g., **Crohn's disease**, Roux-en-Y gastric bypass). Unabsorbed fatty acids bind to intestinal calcium, leaving oxalate free to be absorbed into the bloodstream and excreted by the kidneys.
			◦ **Primary**: Rare genetic disorders causing overproduction of oxalate.
		▪ **Hypocitraturia**: Low levels of urinary citrate (<320 mg/day).
			◦ Citrate is a key inhibitor of stone formation as it binds with urinary calcium, forming a soluble complex and preventing it from binding with oxalate. It also directly inhibits crystal growth and aggregation.
			◦ Often caused by chronic diarrhea, metabolic acidosis, or high animal protein intake.
• **Nucleation, Growth, and Aggregation**
	◦ Once the urine is supersaturated, a crystal nidus (nucleus) can form. This nucleus then grows and aggregates with other crystals to form a macroscopic stone.
	◦ This process is often initiated on the surface of the renal papilla at sites called **Randall's plaques**, which are collections of calcium phosphate in the basement membrane.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Lifetime prevalence is ~12% in men and ~6% in women.
• **Incidence**: Increasing worldwide, linked to diet and lifestyle.
• **Peak Age**: 30-50 years.
• **Sex**: Men > Women (ratio approx. 2:1).
• **Geography**: Higher prevalence in hot, arid climates (e.g., the "**Stone Belt**" in the Southeastern US) due to increased risk of dehydration.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is an adult patient presenting with the acute onset of **severe, unilateral flank pain**.
• The patient is often diaphoretic, tachycardic, and unable to find a comfortable position ("**writhing in pain**").
• The pain's location may migrate as the stone moves down the ureter.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Urinalysis (UA)**
	◦ **Hematuria**: Microscopic or gross is the hallmark finding.
	◦ **Crystalluria**: May show **envelope-shaped (dihydrate)** or **dumbbell-shaped (monohydrate)** calcium oxalate crystals.
	◦ **Urine pH**: Typically 5.5 - 6.8.
		▪ A very alkaline pH >7.2 would suggest struvite stones.
		▪ A very acidic pH <5.5 would suggest uric acid stones.
	◦ **Leukocyte esterase / Nitrites**: Presence suggests concurrent UTI.
• **Lab Studies**
	◦ **Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP/CMP)**: Assess renal function (BUN, Creatinine) and serum calcium (to screen for hyperparathyroidism).
	◦ **Complete Blood Count (CBC)**: To evaluate for leukocytosis, which may indicate infection.
• **Imaging**
	◦ **Non-contrast Helical CT of Abdomen/Pelvis**: **Gold standard** for diagnosing nephrolithiasis.
		▪ High sensitivity (>95%) and specificity.
		▪ Can detect stone size, location, and density.
		▪ Evaluates for secondary signs like hydronephrosis or perinephric stranding.
		▪ Helps rule out other causes of abdominal pain.
	◦ **Renal Ultrasound**
		▪ **First-line imaging in pregnant patients and children** to avoid radiation.
		▪ Excellent for detecting hydronephrosis (indirect sign of obstruction).
		▪ Less sensitive for small stones (<5mm) or stones in the mid-ureter.
	◦ **Kidneys, Ureters, Bladder (KUB) X-ray**
		▪ Calcium oxalate stones are **radiopaque** and visible on KUB.
		▪ Used primarily to monitor the passage of a known stone, not for initial diagnosis. Less sensitive than CT.
• **Metabolic Workup** (for recurrent stone formers or high-risk patients)
	◦ **Two 24-hour urine collections**: Measures total urine volume, pH, calcium, oxalate, citrate, uric acid, sodium, and creatinine to identify underlying metabolic abnormalities and guide preventative therapy.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis for a single stone event is excellent with appropriate treatment.
• **Recurrence** is common.
	◦ Without preventative measures, the 5-year recurrence rate is approximately 50%.
• With dietary changes and medical therapy, recurrence rates can be significantly reduced.

sections.overview:
• Form of **nephrolithiasis** (kidney stones) composed of crystallized uric acid.
• Accounts for approximately 5-10% of all urinary calculi in the United States.
• The defining characteristic is a persistently **acidic urinary environment**.
• Unlike common calcium oxalate stones, uric acid stones are typically **radiolucent** on plain film radiography (KUB).
• Strongly associated with metabolic conditions such as **gout**, **obesity**, and **diabetes mellitus**.
sections.etiology:
• The formation of uric acid stones (urolithiasis) is governed by the "**uric acid stone triad**":
    ◦ **Low Urine pH (Persistent Acidity):**
        ▪ This is the **most critical factor**.
        ▪ Uric acid is poorly soluble in urine with a pH < 5.5, causing it to precipitate into solid crystals.
        ▪ Patients with metabolic syndrome, insulin resistance, or chronic diarrhea often have impaired renal ammonia excretion, leading to persistently acidic urine.
    ◦ **Hyperuricosuria (High Uric Acid in Urine):**
        ▪ Provides the substrate for stone formation.
        ▪ **Exogenous Overload:** High dietary intake of **purines** (e.g., red meat, organ meats, shellfish).
        ▪ **Endogenous Overproduction:** Conditions like **gout**, myeloproliferative disorders, or **tumor lysis syndrome** where high cell turnover increases uric acid production.
    ◦ **Low Urine Volume (Dehydration):**
        ▪ Concentrates urinary solutes, including uric acid, increasing the likelihood of supersaturation and precipitation.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** Comprise 5-10% of all kidney stones in Western countries.
• **Sex:** More common in men than women (Men:Women ratio ~2:1).
• **Age:** Peak incidence occurs in middle age (40-60 years).
• **Geography:** Higher prevalence in hot, arid climates (due to dehydration) and in areas with diets high in animal protein ("**Gout Belt**" in the southeastern United States).
sections.riskFactors:
• **Metabolic:** **Gout**, Metabolic Syndrome, **Diabetes Mellitus Type 2**, **Obesity**.
• **Urinary:** Persistently **acidic urine pH (<5.5)**.
• **Dietary:** High **purine** diet (red meat, organ meats, certain seafood), high fructose intake.
• **Volume Status:** Chronic **dehydration**, chronic diarrheal states (e.g., inflammatory bowel disease, ileostomy) which lead to bicarbonate loss and volume depletion.
• **Medications:** Thiazide and loop diuretics, uricosuric agents without adequate hydration/alkalinization.
• **Genetic/Malignant:** Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, myeloproliferative disorders, chemotherapy (**tumor lysis syndrome**).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is **acute renal colic**.
    ◦ Patient appears in severe distress, often writhing in pain and unable to find a comfortable position.
    ◦ Onset is typically sudden and severe.
• **Symptoms:**
    ◦ **Pain:** Severe, **colicky** (waxing and waning) **flank pain**.
        ▪ The location of pain depends on the location of the stone:
            - **Upper Ureter/UPJ:** Pain is primarily in the flank/CVA.
            - **Mid-Ureter:** Pain radiates anteriorly and inferiorly toward the lower abdomen.
            - **Distal Ureter/UVJ:** Pain radiates to the groin, testicle (in males), or labia (in females); may be associated with urinary urgency, frequency, and dysuria.
    ◦ **Hematuria:** Gross or microscopic hematuria is common (>90% of cases).
    ◦ **Nausea & Vomiting:** Common due to the severity of pain (stimulation of celiac ganglion).
    ◦ **Fever/Chills:** **Red flag** suggesting an obstructed and infected kidney, a urologic emergency.
sections.physicalExam:
• **General:** Patient appears anxious, diaphoretic, and in obvious pain; often pacing or shifting position.
• **Vitals:** **Tachycardia** and **hypertension** are common due to pain. **Fever** suggests concurrent infection.
• **Abdomen:** May have mild abdominal tenderness. Guarding and rebound tenderness are absent (distinguishes from peritonitis).
• **Back:** **Positive Costovertebral Angle (CVA) Tenderness** on percussion is the hallmark finding.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Laboratory Studies:**
    ◦ **Urinalysis (UA) with Microscopy:** The most important initial lab test.
        ▪ **pH:** Persistently **acidic (<5.5)** is highly suggestive.
        ▪ **Hematuria:** Microscopic or gross.
        ▪ **Crystalluria:** May show characteristic **rhomboid, diamond, or needle-shaped** uric acid crystals.
        ▪ **Leukocyte Esterase/Nitrites/WBCs:** Suggests concurrent infection.
    ◦ **Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP):** To assess renal function (BUN, Creatinine) and electrolytes.
    ◦ **Serum Uric Acid:** May be elevated but can be normal.
    ◦ **CBC:** To evaluate for leukocytosis, which can indicate inflammation or infection.
• **Imaging:**
    ◦ **Non-contrast Helical CT of the Abdomen/Pelvis:** **GOLD STANDARD** for diagnosing nephrolithiasis.
        ▪ Can detect virtually all stone types (including uric acid), sizes, and locations, as well as secondary signs like **hydronephrosis** or perinephric stranding.
    ◦ **Renal Ultrasound:** Best alternative when radiation is a concern (e.g., pregnancy).
        ▪ Excellent for detecting **hydronephrosis** (obstruction) and stones within the kidney, but less sensitive for small or ureteral stones.
    ◦ **KUB (Kidney, Ureter, Bladder) X-ray:** **LOW YIELD**.
        ▪ Uric acid stones are **radiolucent** and therefore typically not visible on a plain X-ray, which is a key distinguishing feature from radiopaque calcium stones.
sections.treatment:
• **Pain Control:**
    ◦ **NSAIDs (e.g., Ketorolac):** First-line treatment; reduces ureteral inflammation and spasm.
    ◦ **Opioids (e.g., Morphine):** For severe pain unresponsive to NSAIDs.
• **Hydration:** IV or oral fluids to promote stone passage.
• **Medical Expulsive Therapy (MET):** For stones <10 mm, especially in the distal ureter.
    ◦ **Alpha-blockers (e.g., Tamsulosin):** Relaxes smooth muscle in the distal ureter to facilitate stone passage.
• **Urological Intervention:** Required for:
    ◦ Stones >10 mm
    ◦ Failed medical therapy / uncontrolled pain
    ◦ Signs of obstruction with infection (fever)
    ◦ **Acute kidney injury**
    ◦ **Procedures:** Ureteroscopy with laser lithotripsy, Extracorporeal Shock Wave Lithotripsy (ESWL), Percutaneous Nephrolithotomy (PCNL).
sections.management:
• **Fluid Intake:**
    ◦ **Goal:** Produce >2.5 liters of urine per day.
    ◦ **Method:** Increase fluid intake (water is best).
• **Urine Alkalinization:**
    ◦ **Goal:** Maintain urine pH between **6.0 and 6.5** (pH > 7.0 increases risk of calcium phosphate stones).
    ◦ **Method:** **Potassium Citrate** is the first-line medication; it is metabolized to bicarbonate, which alkalinizes the urine.
• **Dietary Modification:**
    ◦ **Limit Purine Intake:** Decrease consumption of red meat, organ meats, and shellfish.
    ◦ **Increase Fruits/Vegetables:** Naturally alkalinizing and provide citrate.
    ◦ **Limit High-Fructose Corn Syrup.**
• **Pharmacologic Uric Acid Reduction:**
    ◦ **Indication:** Recurrent stones despite above measures, or co-existing gout/tophaceous disease.
    ◦ **Method:** **Allopurinol** or Febuxostat (xanthine oxidase inhibitors) to decrease systemic uric acid production.
sections.complications:
• **Urinary Tract Obstruction:** Can lead to **hydronephrosis** and **acute kidney injury (AKI)**.
• **Infection:** Obstructed urinary flow increases risk of **pyelonephritis** and **urosepsis** (a life-threatening emergency).
• **Ureteral Stricture or Perforation:** Can occur from stone passage or surgical intervention.
• **Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD):** Recurrent stones and obstructions can lead to permanent kidney damage.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis for an acute stone event is excellent with appropriate management.
• The recurrence rate is high (~50% within 5 years) if underlying risk factors are not addressed.
• Long-term prophylactic management is crucial for preventing recurrence and preserving renal function.

sections.overview:
• Struvite stones, also known as **infection stones** or **triple phosphate stones**, are composed of magnesium ammonium phosphate and sometimes carbonate apatite.
	◦ Almost exclusively associated with urinary tract infections (UTIs) caused by **urease-producing bacteria**.
	◦ Can grow very rapidly, often forming large, branching stones known as **staghorn calculi** that fill the renal pelvis and calyces.
	◦ Account for approximately 10-15% of all urinary calculi.
sections.etiology:
• Formation is driven by a urinary tract infection with specific **urease-producing bacteria**.
	◦ **Infection**:
		▪ The most common organism is ***Proteus mirabilis***.
		▪ Other organisms include *Klebsiella*, *Pseudomonas*, *Providencia*, and *Staphylococcus*.
		▪ ***E. coli***, the most common cause of UTIs, is typically **not** urease-producing.
	◦ **Urease Action**:
		▪ The enzyme urease hydrolyzes urea into ammonia (NH3) and carbon dioxide (CO2).
	◦ **Urine Alkalinization**:
		▪ Ammonia combines with water to form ammonium (NH4+) and hydroxide ions (OH-).
		▪ The increase in hydroxide ions makes the urine highly **alkaline (pH > 7.2)**.
	◦ **Precipitation**:
		▪ The alkaline environment decreases the solubility of phosphate.
		▪ Magnesium, ammonium, and phosphate precipitate to form magnesium ammonium phosphate crystals, which aggregate into a stone.
	◦ **Rapid Growth**:
		▪ The stone acts as a foreign body and a nidus for bacteria, creating a vicious cycle of persistent infection and rapid stone growth.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Constitute 10-15% of all kidney stones.
• **Gender**: More common in **females** (2:1 to 3:1 ratio), consistent with their higher incidence of UTIs.
• **Age**: Can occur at any age but is more common in individuals with recurrent UTIs or underlying urinary tract abnormalities.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The clinical presentation can be insidious and is often dominated by symptoms of the underlying **UTI** rather than classic, acute renal colic.
• Patients may present with a history of **recurrent UTIs** that are difficult to eradicate.
• A large **staghorn calculus** may be asymptomatic for a long time and discovered incidentally on imaging.
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is good if the stone is completely removed and the underlying UTI is successfully treated and controlled.
• The recurrence rate is high (>50%) if stone fragments remain (**residual stone burden**) or if recurrent UTIs are not prevented.
• Large **staghorn calculi** can lead to significant loss of renal function in the affected kidney over time.

sections.overview:
• Cystine stones are a rare type of kidney stone resulting from **cystinuria**, an inherited metabolic disorder.
	◦ Cystinuria is characterized by impaired reabsorption of dibasic amino acids-**C**ystine, **O**rnithine, **L**ysine, and **A**rginine (COLA)-in the proximal convoluted tubules of the kidneys.
		▪ Of these, only cystine is poorly soluble in urine, leading to crystallization and stone formation.
	◦ These stones are often **recurrent**, can grow very large (**staghorn calculi**), and typically present in childhood or early adulthood.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
	◦ An **autosomal recessive** genetic disorder.
	◦ Caused by mutations in one of two genes:
		▪ **`SLC3A1`**: Encodes the rBAT protein, a heavy subunit of the amino acid transporter.
		▪ **`SLC7A9`**: Encodes the b(0,+)AT protein, a light subunit of the amino acid transporter.
• **Pathophysiology**
	◦ The genetic defect causes a faulty amino acid transport system in the apical membrane of the proximal convoluted tubule cells (and the small intestine).
	◦ This transporter is responsible for reabsorbing the dibasic amino acids: **C**ystine, **O**rnithine, **L**ysine, and **A**rginine.
	◦ Failure of reabsorption leads to high concentrations of these amino acids in the urine (**aminoaciduria**).
	◦ Cystine has very **low solubility**, especially in acidic urine (pH < 7.0).
	◦ When the concentration of cystine exceeds its solubility limit, it precipitates out of solution, forming crystals.
	◦ These crystals aggregate to form macroscopic stones (calculi).
		▪ Ornithine, lysine, and arginine are highly soluble and do not form stones.
sections.epidemiology:
• Accounts for only **1-2%** of all adult urinary calculi.
• Significantly more common in the pediatric population, accounting for **6-10%** of kidney stones in children.
• **Age of Onset**: Typically presents in the second or third decade of life, but can occur at any age, including infancy.
• No significant difference in prevalence based on sex.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is identical to other forms of nephrolithiasis.
	◦ The key clinical clue is the **patient's age and history**.
		▪ A young patient with their first stone or any patient with recurrent, frequent stone formation should raise suspicion for a metabolic cause like cystinuria.
• **Acute renal colic**: Severe, paroxysmal, unilateral flank pain.
	◦ Pain often radiates anteroinferiorly to the groin, testicles, or labia as the stone migrates down the ureter.
	◦ Patient is typically writhing in pain, unable to find a comfortable position.
	◦ May be accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and diaphoresis.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Urinalysis (UA)**
	◦ **Microscopy**: The **pathognomonic** finding is **hexagonal crystals**. These are flat, colorless, and six-sided.
	◦ **pH**: Urine is often acidic (pH < 6.0).
	◦ **Hematuria**: Microscopic or gross hematuria is usually present.
	◦ **Pyuria/Bacteriuria**: May be present if there is a concurrent UTI.
• **Confirmatory Urine Testing**
	◦ **24-Hour Urine Collection**: Gold standard for diagnosis and management.
		▪ Measures total cystine excretion. **Excretion > 250 mg/day** is diagnostic of cystinuria.
	◦ **Sodium Cyanide-Nitroprusside Test**: A qualitative screening test.
		▪ A positive result (a magenta or purple color change) indicates high levels of urinary cystine.
• **Imaging**
	◦ **Non-contrast Helical CT (Abdomen/Pelvis)**: The **imaging modality of choice** for acute flank pain to diagnose nephrolithiasis.
		▪ Cystine stones are composed of sulfur and are **faintly radio-opaque** or **radiolucent**. They appear as "ground-glass" on CT and are less dense (400-600 Hounsfield Units) than calcium stones.
	◦ **Kidney-Ureter-Bladder (KUB) X-ray**: Often **negative** because cystine stones are poorly visualized.
		▪ May show smooth, rounded, ground-glass stones, especially if large.
	◦ **Renal Ultrasound**: Useful for identifying hydronephrosis (indicative of obstruction) and stones within the kidney.
		▪ Less sensitive for ureteral stones.
• **Stone Analysis**
	◦ If a stone is passed or surgically removed, **infrared spectroscopy or X-ray diffraction** provides a definitive diagnosis, showing a composition of nearly 100% cystine.
sections.prognosis:
• Cystinuria is a lifelong condition with a **very high recurrence rate** if left untreated.
• With aggressive and consistent management (especially hydration and alkalinization), the prognosis for preserving renal function is **good**.
• **Patient compliance** is the single most important factor determining long-term outcomes.
• A small percentage of patients may develop CKD or ESRD, particularly those with poor adherence to therapy or who require numerous surgical interventions.

sections.overview:
• **Nephrolithiasis**, commonly known as kidney stones or renal calculi, is the formation of solid mineral and salt deposits within the urinary tract.
• These stones can cause severe **pain**, **obstruction**, and **infection**.
• While many stones pass spontaneously, some require medical or surgical intervention.
• Evaluation focuses on diagnosing the acute event, relieving symptoms, and identifying underlying causes to prevent recurrence.
sections.etiology:
• The fundamental process is **urine supersaturation**.
    ◦ The concentration of a solute (e.g., calcium, oxalate, uric acid) exceeds its solubility, leading to crystal formation (nucleation).
    ◦ These crystals can aggregate and grow, forming a macroscopic stone.
• **Key Factors** influencing stone formation:
    ◦ **Low Urine Volume**: The single most important factor; concentrated urine increases supersaturation.
    ◦ **Urinary Chemistry Imbalance**:
        ▪ **Promoters**: High urinary excretion of calcium, oxalate, or uric acid.
        ▪ **Inhibitors**: Low urinary levels of citrate and magnesium, which normally prevent crystal formation.
    ◦ **Abnormal Urine pH**:
        ▪ **Acidic urine (pH < 5.5)**: Promotes uric acid and cystine stone formation.
        ▪ **Alkaline urine (pH > 7.2)**: Promotes struvite (infection) stone formation.
• **Major Stone Types**:
    ◦ **Calcium Oxalate (~80%)**:
        ▪ **Most common type**.
        ▪ **Appearance**: **Radiopaque** on KUB.
        ▪ **Urine**: Typically acidic or neutral pH.
        ▪ **Crystals**: Dihydrate (envelope-shaped), Monohydrate (dumbbell-shaped).
        ▪ **Causes**: Idiopathic hypercalciuria, hyperparathyroidism, high oxalate diet.
    ◦ **Struvite (Magnesium Ammonium Phosphate) (~10-15%)**:
        ▪ Known as **"Infection Stones."**
        ▪ **Appearance**: **Radiopaque**; can form large **staghorn calculi** that fill the renal collecting system.
        ▪ **Pathophysiology**: Associated with recurrent UTIs from **urease-producing organisms** (e.g., *Proteus mirabilis*, *Klebsiella*). Urease splits urea into ammonia, making the urine alkaline.
        ▪ **Crystals**: Coffin-lid shaped.
    ◦ **Uric Acid (~5-10%)**:
        ▪ **Appearance**: **Radiolucent** on KUB, but visible on CT.
        ▪ **Pathophysiology**: Associated with high purine intake (red meat), gout, dehydration, and acidic urine.
        ▪ **Crystals**: Rhomboid or rosette-shaped.
    ◦ **Cystine (~1%)**:
        ▪ **Appearance**: Faintly **radiopaque** (ground-glass appearance).
        ▪ **Pathophysiology**: Rare autosomal recessive genetic disorder (cystinuria) causing impaired renal reabsorption of cystine.
        ▪ **Crystals**: Pathognomonic **hexagonal** crystals.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Lifetime Prevalence**: ~10-12% in men, ~5-7% in women.
• **Peak Onset**: 20-50 years of age.
• **Gender**: Men > Women (ratio 2:1), though the gap is narrowing.
• **Recurrence Rate**: High; ~50% within 5 years without preventative measures.
• **Geography**: More common in hot, arid climates ("Stone Belt" of the southeastern U.S.).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is the abrupt onset of severe, **colicky** (waxing and waning) **unilateral flank pain**.
    ◦ Often accompanied by **nausea and vomiting**.
    ◦ The patient is typically unable to find a comfortable position and is often seen writhing or pacing ("renal colic dance").
• The location of pain often correlates with the stone's position as it migrates down the ureter.
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent for a single episode with proper management.
• Morbidity is related to pain, obstruction, and infection.
• The primary long-term concern is the high rate of recurrence (~50% at 5 years) if preventative measures are not implemented.

sections.overview: • Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD) is the most common inherited kidney disease, characterized by the progressive development and enlargement of numerous bilateral renal cysts. ◦ This leads to massive kidney enlargement, distortion of renal architecture, and ultimately, a decline in renal function, often culminating in End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD). ◦ ADPKD is a systemic disease with significant extra-renal manifestations, most notably liver cysts and intracranial "berry" aneurysms.
sections.etiology: • Etiology (Genetics) ◦ Caused by a mutation in one of two genes: ▪ `PKD1` (Chromosome 16): Accounts for ~85% of cases. Encodes the protein Polycystin-1. Associated with a more severe phenotype and earlier onset of ESRD (median age ~55). ▪ `PKD2` (Chromosome 4): Accounts for ~15% of cases. Encodes the protein Polycystin-2. Associated with a milder phenotype and later onset of ESRD (median age ~75). ◦ Inheritance pattern is autosomal dominant, meaning an affected parent has a 50% chance of passing the gene to each child. • Pathophysiology ◦ Ciliopathy: Polycystin-1 and -2 are located in the primary cilia of renal tubular epithelial cells. These cilia act as mechanosensors. ◦ "Two-Hit" Hypothesis: An individual inherits one mutated allele ("first hit"). A spontaneous somatic mutation in the remaining normal allele ("second hit") in a single tubular cell leads to a complete loss of polycystin function in that cell. ◦ Cyst Formation: The loss of function leads to: ▪ Altered Calcium Signaling: Dysregulation of intracellular calcium. ▪ Increased cAMP: Leads to increased cell proliferation and chloride-driven fluid secretion into the tubule lumen. ▪ Cell Proliferation: Epithelial cells multiply, forming a focal outpouching. ▪ Fluid Secretion: The pouch fills with fluid, detaches from the parent tubule, and becomes an independent cyst. ◦ Disease Progression: Cysts progressively enlarge, compressing adjacent healthy nephrons, causing ischemia, fibrosis, and inflammation. This process activates the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS), leading to early and severe hypertension, which further accelerates kidney damage.
sections.epidemiology: • Prevalence: Affects 1 in 400 to 1 in 1,000 live births. • ESRD Cause: Accounts for 5-10% of all cases of ESRD requiring renal replacement therapy. • Demographics: Occurs worldwide with no racial or ethnic predilection. Affects males and females equally. • Penetrance: Nearly 100% penetrant, meaning almost all individuals with the mutation will develop cysts by late adulthood.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • Patients are often asymptomatic for decades and may be diagnosed incidentally on imaging. • Symptoms typically begin between the ages of 30 and 50. • The most common initial presentations are hypertension, flank pain, or hematuria.
sections.diagnostics: • Imaging (Primary Diagnostic Tool) ◦ Renal Ultrasound: Test of choice for diagnosis in patients with a positive family history. It is non-invasive and cost-effective. ◦ Age-Based Diagnostic Criteria (Ravine Criteria) for patients with positive family history: ▪ Age 15-39: 3 cysts (unilateral or bilateral) ▪ Age 40-59: 2 cysts in each kidney ▪ Age 60: 4 cysts in each kidney ◦ CT or MRI: More sensitive than ultrasound. Used for atypical cases, evaluating complications (hemorrhage, complex cysts), and for precisely measuring Total Kidney Volume (TKV), which is a key marker for disease progression and eligibility for certain treatments. • Laboratory Studies ◦ Urinalysis: May show hematuria, mild proteinuria, and reduced urine specific gravity (isosthenuria) due to impaired concentrating ability. ◦ Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP): BUN and creatinine are often normal early in the disease but rise as GFR declines. ◦ CBC: May show anemia of chronic kidney disease (later stages) or occasionally erythrocytosis (early stages, from erythropoietin production by cysts). • Screening for Intracranial Aneurysms ◦ MRA (Magnetic Resonance Angiography) or CTA (CT Angiography) of the head. ◦ Indications for Screening: ▪ Personal or family history of intracranial aneurysm or subarachnoid hemorrhage. ▪ High-risk occupations (e.g., pilots, surgeons). ▪ Patient anxiety/request. ▪ Prior to major elective surgery. • Genetic Testing ◦ Not routinely used for diagnosis. Reserved for cases with equivocal imaging, young potential kidney donors, or for family planning.
sections.prognosis: • The disease is universally progressive, but the rate of progression varies widely. • With modern management (especially BP control), life expectancy has improved significantly. • Prognosis is worse for patients with the `PKD1` mutation, large kidney volume, and early-onset hypertension. • Survival after kidney transplantation is excellent and comparable to that of transplant recipients without ADPKD.

sections.overview: • Autosomal Recessive Polycystic Kidney Disease (ARPKD) is a rare, inherited ciliopathy characterized by the development of non-obstructive, fusiform cysts in the renal collecting ducts and congenital hepatic fibrosis ◦ Typically presents in the perinatal period or early childhood with significant renal and hepatic morbidity and mortality ◦ Unlike Autosomal Dominant PKD (ADPKD), which presents in adulthood with large macrocysts, ARPKD is defined by microcysts and severe, early-onset disease
sections.etiology: • Genetic Mutation ◦ Caused by mutations in the _PKHD1_ gene (Polycystic Kidney and Hepatic Disease 1) on chromosome 6 ◦ This gene encodes for the protein fibrocystin (also known as polyductin) • Ciliopathy ◦ Fibrocystin is an integral membrane protein located in the primary cilia of renal tubular cells and biliary epithelial cells, which act as cellular sensors • Pathophysiology ◦ Renal ▪ Defective fibrocystin disrupts normal ciliary function and cell signaling pathways ▪ This leads to abnormal tubular cell proliferation, apoptosis, and fluid secretion, resulting in diffuse, fusiform (spindle-shaped) dilation of the renal collecting ducts ▪ This creates numerous microscopic cysts, leading to massively enlarged kidneys, progressive interstitial fibrosis, and ultimately End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD) ◦ Hepatic ▪ The same genetic defect affects the biliary system, causing a "ductal plate malformation" ▪ This leads to abnormal development of the intrahepatic bile ducts, resulting in congenital hepatic fibrosis and biliary dysgenesis ▪ This fibrosis obstructs portal venous flow, leading to portal hypertension ▪ In some cases, saccular dilation of the intrahepatic bile ducts can occur, a condition known as Caroli disease
sections.epidemiology: • Incidence ◦ Relatively rare, occurring in approximately 1 in 20,000 to 1 in 40,000 live births • Demographics ◦ Affects males and females equally, with no specific ethnic predilection • Significance ◦ One of the most common causes of significant genetic renal disease in infancy and childhood
sections.clinicalPresentation: • Presentation varies based on the age of onset and severity of organ involvement • Perinatal/Neonatal (Most Common & Severe) ◦ Oligohydramnios detected on prenatal ultrasound due to poor fetal urine output ◦ This leads to the Potter sequence ▪ Pulmonary hypoplasia ▪ Flattened facies (low-set ears, recessed chin) ▪ Limb deformities (clubfoot) ◦ Severe respiratory distress at birth is the most immediate life-threatening problem ◦ Massively enlarged, palpable kidneys causing abdominal distension ◦ Severe systemic hypertension often present within the first few weeks of life • Infantile/Juvenile ◦ For those who survive the neonatal period, presentation is more variable ◦ Failure to thrive and poor growth ◦ Symptoms of declining renal function (polyuria, polydipsia due to poor concentrating ability) ◦ Recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs) ◦ Hypertension ◦ Signs of portal hypertension become more prominent ▪ Hepatosplenomegaly ▪ Thrombocytopenia (from splenic sequestration) ▪ Esophageal/gastric variceal bleeding (hematemesis, melena)
sections.diagnostics: • Prenatal Diagnosis ◦ Ultrasound ▪ Bilateral, large, hyperechoic kidneys ▪ Oligohydramnios ▪ Empty fetal bladder • Postnatal Diagnosis ◦ Labs ▪ BMP/CMP: Elevated BUN and creatinine, metabolic acidosis, hyponatremia (due to impaired urinary concentration) ▪ Urinalysis: Low specific gravity, proteinuria, hematuria ▪ CBC: May show anemia (due to CKD), thrombocytopenia, and leukopenia (if hypersplenism is present) ▪ LFTs: Usually normal or only mildly elevated, as hepatic fibrosis does not cause primary hepatocellular failure ◦ Imaging (Primary Diagnostic Modality) ▪ Renal Ultrasound: The cornerstone of diagnosis ▪ Bilateral, symmetrically enlarged kidneys ▪ Diffusely hyperechoic/echogenic parenchyma ▪ Loss of corticomedullary differentiation ▪ Microcysts are typically too small to be resolved individually ▪ Abdominal Ultrasound: To evaluate liver. Shows hepatomegaly, increased liver echotexture (fibrosis), splenomegaly, portal vein dilation, and possible biliary cysts (Caroli disease) ◦ Genetic Testing ▪ Molecular genetic testing for _PKHD1_ mutations confirms the diagnosis ◦ Biopsy ▪ Renal or liver biopsy is rarely necessary but can be used for definitive diagnosis if imaging and genetics are inconclusive
sections.prognosis: • Highly variable and dependent on the severity of the phenotype, particularly the degree of pulmonary hypoplasia • Perinatal Presentation ◦ Mortality rate is high (~30-40%) in the neonatal period, primarily due to respiratory failure • Survival ◦ For those who survive infancy, the 10-year survival rate is approximately 80% • Long-Term ◦ Almost all survivors will develop ESRD, with about 50% requiring renal replacement therapy by age 10 ◦ Morbidity from portal hypertension is also a significant long-term concern

sections.overview:
• **Medullary Sponge Kidney (MSK)** is a congenital developmental malformation of the kidney characterized by **cystic dilation** and **ectasia** of the precalyceal collecting ducts (**Ducts of Bellini**) within the medullary pyramids.
• This structural abnormality leads to **urinary stasis**, which predisposes patients to:
    ◦ **Medullary nephrocalcinosis**
    ◦ Recurrent **nephrolithiasis** (kidney stones)
    ◦ **Urinary tract infections (UTIs)**
• Despite these complications, **renal function (GFR) is typically well-preserved** throughout life.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ MSK is a **non-hereditary, developmental anomaly** that occurs during nephrogenesis.
    ◦ The vast majority of cases are **sporadic**.
    ◦ Rare familial cases and associations with congenital hemihypertrophy syndromes (e.g., **Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome**) have been reported.
    ◦ It is not considered a true inherited disease.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Structural Defect**: The core issue is malformation of the terminal collecting ducts, leading to saccular, cystic, or fusiform dilations.
    ◦ **Urinary Stasis**: The ectatic ducts impair the normal flow of urine, causing stasis within the medullary pyramids.
    ◦ **Nephrocalcinosis/Nephrolithiasis**: Urinary stasis promotes the supersaturation and precipitation of calcium salts (primarily calcium phosphate and calcium oxalate), leading to:
        ▪ Formation of microcalculi that aggregate in the dilated ducts (**medullary nephrocalcinosis**).
        ▪ These stones can then detach and pass into the collecting system, causing symptomatic **nephrolithiasis**.
    ◦ **Metabolic Abnormalities**: Many patients with MSK also have underlying metabolic defects, most commonly **hypercalciuria** (high urine calcium) and **hypocitraturia** (low urine citrate), which further increase the risk of stone formation.
    ◦ **Infection**: Stagnant urine provides a nidus for bacterial growth, increasing the risk for recurrent **UTIs** and **pyelonephritis**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Estimated to be between 1 in 5,000 to 1 in 20,000 in the general population. However, it is likely underdiagnosed.
• **Demographics**: Found in approximately 12-20% of patients who are evaluated for recurrent **calcium nephrolithiasis**.
• **Age of Onset**: Typically diagnosed in adolescents and young to middle-aged adults (ages 20-50) when they present with symptoms from stones or UTIs.
• **Sex**: Slight female predominance has been reported.
sections.riskFactors:
• MSK is a congenital condition, so there are no preventable risk factors for developing the anatomic abnormality itself.
• **Associated conditions (rare)**:
    ◦ **Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome**
    ◦ **Ehlers-Danlos syndrome**
    ◦ Congenital hemihypertrophy
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The majority of individuals with MSK are **asymptomatic**, and the condition is often discovered incidentally on imaging performed for other reasons.
• When symptomatic, patients typically present with one of the following:
    ◦ **Recurrent Nephrolithiasis**: Most common presentation. Patients experience episodes of acute, **colicky flank pain**, **hematuria**, and nausea/vomiting associated with stone passage.
    ◦ **Recurrent UTIs**: Symptoms include **dysuria**, **frequency**, **urgency**, and occasionally fever and flank pain if **pyelonephritis** develops.
    ◦ **Hematuria**: Can be gross or microscopic, often related to stone passage.
    ◦ **Chronic Flank Pain**: Some patients report a dull, chronic ache in the flank region, even in the absence of an obstructing stone or infection.
• Key Symptoms:
    ◦ **Colicky flank pain** radiating to the groin (renal colic from stones)
    ◦ **Hematuria** (gross or microscopic)
    ◦ **Dysuria, urinary frequency, urgency** (from UTI)
    ◦ **Fever, chills, nausea, vomiting** (from pyelonephritis or severe renal colic)
    ◦ Dull, chronic flank or abdominal pain
sections.physicalExam:
• The physical exam is **typically unremarkable and non-contributory** in asymptomatic patients or between acute episodes.
• **During an acute event**:
    ◦ **Costovertebral angle (CVA) tenderness** may be present during passage of a kidney stone or with **pyelonephritis**.
    ◦ **Fever** and **tachycardia** may be present with infection.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Computed Tomography (CT)**:
    ◦ **Non-contrast helical CT** is the modality of choice for evaluating acute flank pain and is excellent for identifying stones.
    ◦ **Definitive Diagnosis**: A **CT Urogram** (with contrast) is the **gold standard**. It reveals:
        ▪ **Medullary nephrocalcinosis**: Clusters of calcifications within the renal medullary pyramids.
        ▪ **Papillary blush**: On excretory phase images, contrast material pools in the dilated collecting ducts, creating a striated or "blush" appearance.
• **Intravenous Pyelogram (IVP)**:
    ◦ The historical gold standard, now rarely used but images are classic for board exams.
    ◦ Shows the **"bouquet of flowers"** or **"paint brush" appearance** as contrast fills the ectatic collecting ducts.
• **Kidney, Ureter, Bladder (KUB) X-ray**:
    ◦ Can show clusters of calcifications in the characteristic pyramidal distribution of **medullary nephrocalcinosis**.
• **Renal Ultrasound**:
    ◦ Less sensitive for diagnosis.
    ◦ May show **hyperechoic medullary pyramids** secondary to calcifications, but cannot visualize the ductal ectasia itself.
sections.treatment:
• **Acute Nephrolithiasis**:
    ◦ **Pain control**: NSAIDs (e.g., ketorolac), opioids.
    ◦ **Hydration**: IV or oral fluids.
    ◦ **Medical Expulsive Therapy**: Alpha-blockers (e.g., tamsulosin) for distal ureteral stones.
    ◦ **Urologic Intervention**: Ureteroscopy or shock wave lithotripsy (SWL) for large, obstructing, or intractable stones.
• **Acute UTI/Pyelonephritis**:
    ◦ Appropriate antibiotic therapy based on urine culture and sensitivity.
sections.management:
• **High Fluid Intake**: **Cornerstone of therapy**. Goal is to produce >2.5 L of urine per day to dilute stone-forming solutes.
• **Dietary Modification**:
    ◦ **Low sodium diet** (<2g/day) is crucial, as high sodium intake increases calcium excretion.
    ◦ **Normal dietary calcium intake** (1000-1200 mg/day). Calcium restriction is counterproductive as it increases oxalate absorption.
    ◦ Low animal protein diet may be beneficial.
• **Pharmacologic Therapy (guided by 24-hour urine results)**:
    ◦ **Potassium Citrate**: Treatment of choice for **hypocitraturia**. It alkalinizes the urine and citrate binds to calcium, inhibiting stone formation.
    ◦ **Thiazide Diuretics** (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone): Treatment of choice for **hypercalciuria**. They increase calcium reabsorption in the distal tubule, lowering urine calcium.
• **Surveillance**: Regular follow-up with Nephrology or Urology for monitoring.
sections.complications:
• Recurrent **nephrolithiasis**
• Recurrent **UTIs** and **pyelonephritis**
• **Obstructive uropathy**
• **Chronic kidney disease (CKD)**: **Rare**, but can occur secondary to recurrent obstruction or severe, repeated infections. Progression to end-stage renal disease (ESRD) is very uncommon.
• Chronic pain
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis for renal function is **excellent**. MSK is considered a benign condition that does not typically progress to renal failure.
• The primary morbidity is related to the frequency and severity of kidney stones and UTIs, which can significantly impact quality of life.
• Life expectancy is normal.

sections.overview:
• A **horseshoe kidney** is the most common congenital renal fusion anomaly
	◦ Consists of two distinct, functioning kidneys that are fused at their lower poles by a band of tissue (**isthmus**) composed of either renal parenchyma or fibrous tissue
	◦ This fusion occurs early in embryological development, causing the kidneys to be trapped in the lower abdomen during their normal ascent, typically by the **inferior mesenteric artery (IMA)**
	◦ While many individuals are **asymptomatic**, the abnormal anatomy predisposes them to a variety of urological complications
sections.etiology:
• **Embryology**
	◦ During normal fetal development (weeks 7-9), the kidneys (metanephric blastemas) originate in the pelvis and ascend to their final position in the retroperitoneum
	◦ **Fusion Event**: In a horseshoe kidney, the lower poles of the developing kidneys are positioned abnormally close together in the pelvis and fuse before ascent
	◦ **Arrested Ascent**: As the fused kidney attempts to ascend, the isthmus gets caught on the root of the **Inferior Mesenteric Artery (IMA)**, which arises from the aorta. This prevents the kidney from reaching its normal height
• **Anatomical Consequences**
	◦ **Location**: The kidney lies lower in the abdomen than normal, typically at the level of the L3-L5 vertebrae
	◦ **Malrotation**: The renal pelvis and ureters are often directed anteriorly or anteromedially, rather than medially
	◦ **Ureteral Course**: The ureters must pass over the anterior surface of the isthmus, which can lead to drainage issues
• **Pathophysiology of Complications**
	◦ The altered anatomy (anteriorly-directed renal pelves, high ureteral insertion, ureters draping over the isthmus) leads to impaired urinary drainage and **stasis**, which is the underlying cause for most complications like stones, infection, and obstruction
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Approximately 1 in 400 to 1 in 600 live births
• **Sex Predilection**: Male-to-female ratio is approximately 2:1
• It is the most common of all renal fusion abnormalities
sections.riskFactors:
• **Turner Syndrome (45,X0)**: The most common and strongest syndromic association
• **Trisomy 18 (Edwards Syndrome)**
• **Trisomy 13 (Patau Syndrome)**
• **Trisomy 21 (Down Syndrome)**
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Asymptomatic (Majority)**: Over 60% of individuals are asymptomatic, and the condition is often discovered as an incidental finding on imaging performed for other reasons
• **Symptomatic Presentation**: When symptoms occur, they are typically due to one of the complications. Patients may present with:
	◦ Vague, chronic abdominal or flank pain
	◦ Symptoms of a **urinary tract infection (UTI)**
	◦ Symptoms of **nephrolithiasis** (renal colic, hematuria)
	◦ A palpable, firm, midline abdominal mass (rare)
• **Key Symptoms**
	◦ **Pain**: Dull, aching pain in the flank or lower abdomen that may radiate to the groin. Pain may worsen with hyperextension (**Rovsing's sign** for horseshoe kidney)
	◦ **Hematuria**: Gross or microscopic, often due to stones or infection
	◦ **Recurrent UTIs**: Frequency, urgency, dysuria, fever
	◦ **Nausea & Vomiting**: Can be associated with obstruction (**Dietl's crisis** - intermittent, severe flank pain and N/V from acute UPJ obstruction)
	◦ **Symptoms of Renal Stones**: Severe, colicky flank pain
sections.physicalExam:
• **Often Unremarkable**: The physical exam is usually normal
• **Palpable Mass**: In thin individuals, a firm, non-tender, deep midline abdominal mass may be palpable below the umbilicus
• **Rovsing's Sign (for horseshoe kidney)**: Hyperextension of the spine causes abdominal pain and nausea by compressing the renal isthmus between the aorta and the vertebral column. (Note: this is different from Rovsing's sign for appendicitis)
• **Stigmata of Associated Syndromes**: Look for features of **Turner Syndrome** (e.g., webbed neck, wide-spaced nipples, short stature)
sections.diagnostics:
• **Laboratory Studies**
	◦ **Urinalysis (UA)**: To evaluate for hematuria, pyuria, bacteriuria, or crystalluria
	◦ **Urine Culture**: If infection is suspected
	◦ **Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP)**: To assess renal function (BUN, Creatinine)
• **Imaging**
	◦ **Initial Test**: **Abdominal Ultrasound** is often the first imaging modality used. It can show the low-lying position of the kidneys and the fusion of the lower poles
	◦ **Gold Standard / Confirmatory Test**: **CT Urogram** (CT with and without contrast) is the best imaging modality
		▪ Provides excellent anatomical detail of the fused kidneys, the isthmus, the collecting systems, the ureters, and its relationship to the IMA and other structures
		▪ It is also the best test for identifying complications like stones, hydronephrosis, or masses
	◦ **Voiding Cystourethrogram (VCUG)**: Performed to diagnose **vesicoureteral reflux (VUR)**, especially in children with recurrent UTIs
	◦ **Radionuclide Renal Scan (MAG3 or DTPA)**: A functional study used to quantify differential renal function and assess the severity of a **ureteropelvic junction (UPJ) obstruction**
sections.treatment:
• **Asymptomatic Patients**: No treatment is required. Management focuses on surveillance
• **Symptomatic Patients**: Treatment is directed at the specific complication
	◦ **UPJ Obstruction**: Surgical correction via **pyeloplasty**
	◦ **Nephrolithiasis**
		▪ Standard management: Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL), ureteroscopy, or percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL)
		▪ PCNL can be more challenging due to the abnormal kidney position
	◦ **Vesicoureteral Reflux (VUR)**
		▪ Low-grade: Observation or prophylactic antibiotics
		▪ High-grade/symptomatic: Surgical correction (ureteral reimplantation)
	◦ **Malignancy**: Treatment follows standard oncologic protocols, typically involving partial or radical nephrectomy
sections.management:
• **Routine Follow-Up**: Asymptomatic patients should have annual follow-up including blood pressure measurement, urinalysis, and serum creatinine
• **Surveillance Imaging**: Periodic renal ultrasound (e.g., every 1-2 years) is often recommended to monitor for the development of hydronephrosis or renal masses
sections.complications:
• **Ureteropelvic Junction (UPJ) Obstruction**: The **most common complication** (up to 35% of symptomatic patients), leading to **hydronephrosis**. Caused by a high insertion of the ureter on the renal pelvis
• **Nephrolithiasis**: Increased incidence (20-60%) due to urinary stasis
• **Recurrent UTIs & Pyelonephritis**: Due to urinary stasis and/or VUR
• **Vesicoureteral Reflux (VUR)**: Occurs in up to 50% of children with horseshoe kidney
• Increased Susceptibility to **Trauma**: The isthmus is vulnerable to compression and fracture during blunt abdominal trauma
• Increased Risk of **Malignancy**
	◦ **Wilms Tumor (Nephroblastoma)**: 2-fold increased risk
	◦ **Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC)**: Slightly increased risk
	◦ **Transitional Cell Carcinoma**: Increased risk, often occurring in the isthmus
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is generally **excellent**, and life expectancy is normal for individuals without complications
• Morbidity is directly related to the presence and severity of associated urological complications
sections.preventionEducation:
• **Hydration**: Counsel on maintaining adequate fluid intake to reduce the risk of stone formation
• **Trauma Prevention**: Advise patients to avoid high-impact contact sports. The anterior position of the renal isthmus over the spine makes it highly susceptible to injury from blunt abdominal trauma
• **Symptom Recognition**: Educate patients to seek medical care for symptoms of UTI, stones, or obstruction

sections.overview:
• Primary acid-base disorder characterized by a decrease in serum bicarbonate (HCO3), leading to a decrease in blood pH
• Renal causes stem from the kidney's inability to perform its two primary roles in acid-base homeostasis:
    ◦ Reabsorbing filtered bicarbonate
    ◦ Excreting the daily non-volatile acid load (~1 mEq/kg/day)
• Renal metabolic acidosis is broadly divided into two categories based on the serum anion gap:
    ◦ **High Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis (AGMA)**: Caused by the failure to excrete endogenous acids (e.g., sulfates, phosphates) in advanced kidney disease (**Uremia**)
    ◦ **Normal Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis (NAGMA)** / **Hyperchloremic**: Caused by the failure to reabsorb bicarbonate or secrete H+ ions, as seen in **Renal Tubular Acidosis (RTA)**
sections.etiology: • The kidneys regulate acid-base balance through proximal tubule HCO3 reabsorption and distal tubule H+ secretion (acid excretion), primarily as ammonium (NH4+)
sections.epidemiology:
• **Uremic Acidosis**:
    ◦ Common; prevalence increases with the severity of CKD
    ◦ Affects millions of patients with advanced kidney disease worldwide
• **RTA**:
    ◦ Relatively rare compared to uremic acidosis
    ◦ **Type 1**: Can be hereditary or acquired (e.g., associated with autoimmune diseases)
    ◦ **Type 2**: Rare in adults, most often associated with multiple myeloma
    ◦ **Type 4**: The most common form of RTA, frequently seen in patients with diabetes, mild-to-moderate CKD, or those on medications that block the RAAS system
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation is often dominated by the underlying disease (e.g., CKD, lupus)
• The acidosis itself may be an incidental laboratory finding
• In severe, acute cases, patients may present with respiratory distress as a compensatory mechanism
sections.diagnostics:
• A stepwise approach is crucial
• **Step 1: Confirm Metabolic Acidosis**
    ◦ **Arterial Blood Gas (ABG)**: pH < 7.35, HCO3 < 22 mEq/L, and compensatory respiratory alkalosis (low PaCO2)
    ◦ **Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP)**: Low HCO3 (or CO2 content). Check BUN/Cr for evidence of CKD
• **Step 2: Calculate the Serum Anion Gap (AG)**
    ◦ **Formula**: AG = Na+ - (Cl + HCO3). Normal is 8-12 mEq/L
    ◦ **High AG (>12)**: Suggests **Uremic Acidosis**
        ▪ The diagnosis is confirmed by a low GFR (<25 mL/min)
    ◦ **Normal AG (8-12)**: Suggests **RTA** or a non-renal cause like diarrhea
• **Step 3: If NAGMA, Differentiate Renal vs. GI Cause**
    ◦ **Calculate the Urine Anion Gap (UAG)**
        ▪ **Formula**: UAG = (Urine Na+ + Urine K+) - Urine Cl
    ◦ **Positive UAG (> 0)**: Suggests a **renal cause (RTA)**
        ▪ The kidneys are unable to excrete ammonium (NH4+Cl), the primary form of renal acid excretion. This leads to a relative deficit of urine Cl
    ◦ **Negative UAG (< 0)**: Suggests a **GI cause (e.g., diarrhea)**
        ▪ The kidneys are working properly and are excreting large amounts of NH4+Cl to compensate for bicarbonate loss from the gut. This leads to a high urine Cl and a negative UAG
• **Step 4: Differentiate RTA Types**
    ◦ **Check Serum Potassium (K+)**
        ▪ **Hypokalemia**: Type 1 or Type 2 RTA
        ▪ **Hyperkalemia**: Type 4 RTA
    ◦ **Check Urine pH**
        ▪ If hypokalemic, a **urine pH > 5.5** during systemic acidosis is diagnostic of **Type 1 RTA**
        ▪ If hypokalemic and urine pH is variable (can be < 5.5), suspect **Type 2 RTA**. Look for Fanconi syndrome (glycosuria with normal blood glucose, phosphaturia)
• **RTA Type Summary**
    ◦ **Type 1 (Distal)**
        ▪ Defect: H+ Secretion
        ▪ Serum K+: **↓ K+**
        ▪ Urine pH: **> 5.5**
        ▪ Key Association: Kidney stones, Sjögren's
    ◦ **Type 2 (Proximal)**
        ▪ Defect: HCO3 Reabsorption
        ▪ Serum K+: **↓ K+**
        ▪ Urine pH: **< 5.5 (variable)**
        ▪ Key Association: Fanconi syndrome, Myeloma
    ◦ **Type 4 (Hyperkalemic)**
        ▪ Defect: Aldosterone Effect
        ▪ Serum K+: **↑ K+**
        ▪ Urine pH: **< 5.5**
        ▪ Key Association: Diabetes, ACE-I/ARB use
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is generally tied to the underlying etiology and the stage of kidney disease
• For **RTA**, the prognosis is excellent if acidosis and electrolyte imbalances are corrected, though the underlying disease may carry its own prognosis
• For **uremic acidosis**, prognosis is dictated by the progression of CKD to ESRD. Correcting acidosis may slow CKD progression

sections.overview:
• Metabolic alkalosis is a primary acid-base disorder characterized by an elevated serum bicarbonate (HCO3) concentration and a consequent increase in arterial **pH > 7.45**.
• The respiratory system compensates by hypoventilating to retain CO2, leading to an elevated PaCO2.
• Renal causes of metabolic alkalosis are conditions where the kidneys are the primary driver for either the generation or, more commonly, the *maintenance* of the alkalotic state.
• These causes are typically characterized by being **saline-resistant** (high urine chloride), indicating that the kidneys are unable to excrete bicarbonate effectively despite volume expansion.
sections.etiology:
• The pathophysiology involves two distinct phases:
    ◦ **Generation Phase:** An initial event causes a net gain of HCO3 or a net loss of non-volatile acid (H+) from the body.
    ◦ **Maintenance Phase:** The kidneys fail to excrete the excess HCO3, perpetuating the alkalosis.
        ▪ This is the key step in renal-mediated metabolic alkalosis and is typically driven by **chloride depletion**, **volume contraction (RAAS activation)**, and/or **hypokalemia**.
• **Key Renal Mechanisms:**
    ◦ **Mineralocorticoid Excess:**
        ▪ **Pathophysiology:** Excess aldosterone or other mineralocorticoids act on the principal cells of the distal tubule and collecting duct, leading to increased activity of the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) and the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase. The resulting reabsorption of Na+ creates a negative electrical potential in the lumen, which drives the secretion of K+ (via ROMK channels) and H+ (via H+-ATPase in intercalated cells).
        ▪ **Result:** H+ loss into the urine generates new HCO3, while K+ loss causes **hypokalemia**. The volume expansion from Na+ retention causes **hypertension**.
        ▪ **Examples:**
            • **Primary Hyperaldosteronism (Conn's Syndrome):** Aldosterone-producing adenoma or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia.
            • **Secondary Hyperaldosteronism:** High renin states like **renal artery stenosis**.
            • **Apparent Mineralocorticoid Excess:** Genetic defect in 11-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase 2, which normally inactivates cortisol. Can also be induced by licorice (glycyrrhizic acid).
    ◦ **Diuretic Therapy (Loop and Thiazide):**
        ▪ **Pathophysiology:** This is often called **"contraction alkalosis."**
            • 1. **Chloride and Volume Depletion:** Diuretics block NaCl reabsorption, leading to natriuresis and volume contraction, which activates the RAAS system.
            • 2. **Increased Distal Na+ Delivery:** More Na+ reaches the collecting ducts.
            • 3. **Aldosterone-Mediated H+/K+ Secretion:** The activated RAAS (high aldosterone) promotes Na+ reabsorption in exchange for K+ and H+ secretion in the collecting ducts, causing **hypokalemia** and generating HCO3.
    ◦ **Inherited Renal Tubulopathies:**
