    ◦ **Ultrasound:** Often the initial imaging modality. AMLs typically appear as a well-defined, **hyperechoic (bright)** mass due to high fat content.
    ◦ **CT Scan (Non-Contrast):** **Diagnostic test of choice.** The pathognomonic finding is a renal mass containing macroscopic fat, identified by **negative Hounsfield units (-20 to -80 HU)**.
    ◦ **CT with Contrast / CT Angiography:** Excellent for assessing vascularity, identifying aneurysms (>5 mm is high risk), and detecting active contrast extravasation in an acute bleed.
    ◦ **MRI:** Superior for characterizing **fat-poor AMLs**, which are a diagnostic challenge. Fat appears bright on T1/T2 weighted images and demonstrates signal loss on fat-suppressed sequences.
    ◦ **Biopsy:** **RARELY performed and generally contraindicated** due to a high risk of inducing severe hemorrhage. It is only considered in diagnostically uncertain cases where a fat-poor AML cannot be distinguished from Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC).
sections.treatment:
• **Active Surveillance**
    ◦ For **asymptomatic AMLs < 4 cm**.
    ◦ Involves periodic imaging (e.g., annual ultrasound) to monitor for growth.
• **Selective Arterial Embolization (SAE)**
    ◦ **First-line intervention** for both acute hemorrhage and prophylaxis.
    ◦ **Indications:** Acutely bleeding AML, or prophylactic treatment for asymptomatic tumors **> 4 cm**, tumors with aneurysms > 5 mm, or in women of childbearing age.
    ◦ **Procedure:** Catheter-based occlusion of the feeding arteries to the AML, causing it to shrink and devascularize while preserving healthy kidney tissue.
• **mTOR Inhibitors (Everolimus, Sirolimus)**
    ◦ FDA-approved for TSC-associated AMLs.
    ◦ Works by inhibiting the overactive mTOR pathway, causing significant tumor shrinkage. An excellent option for patients with large or bilateral tumors where preserving renal function is paramount.
• **Surgery**
    ◦ **Partial Nephrectomy (Nephron-sparing):** An option for larger tumors if SAE is unsuccessful or unavailable.
    ◦ **Radical Nephrectomy:** Reserved for massive, uncontrollable hemorrhage or if malignancy cannot be ruled out.
sections.management:
• **Asymptomatic, < 4 cm:** Active surveillance with annual or biennial imaging.
• **Asymptomatic, > 4 cm:** Prophylactic intervention is recommended due to increased risk of rupture. **SAE is the preferred modality.** mTOR inhibitors are a key option for TSC patients.
• **Symptomatic (Pain/Bleeding) or Pregnant Patient with AML > 4 cm:** Treat regardless of size. SAE is first-line.
• **Acute Rupture (Wunderlich Syndrome):**
    ◦ [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.complications:
• **Hemorrhage:** The most significant and feared complication, leading to **Wunderlich Syndrome**.
• **Anemia:** Due to acute or chronic blood loss.
• **Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD):** Can occur in patients with TSC due to a large, bilateral tumor burden or from multiple interventions compromising renal parenchyma.
• **Post-Embolization Syndrome:** A common, self-limited condition after SAE characterized by fever, flank pain, and leukocytosis.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for most patients with sporadic AML.
• The condition is benign, and mortality is almost exclusively related to the complications of hemorrhage.
• With modern management (surveillance and early intervention with SAE), the risk of life-threatening hemorrhage is low.
• Prognosis in TSC is more guarded and depends on the overall disease burden (neurologic, pulmonary, and renal manifestations).

sections.overview:
• Clinical syndrome characterized by the rapid breakdown (lysis) of **striated muscle tissue**.
    ◦ This process releases intracellular muscle constituents into the systemic circulation, including **myoglobin**, **creatine kinase (CK)**, **potassium**, and **phosphate**.
• The primary and most severe renal complication is **Acute Kidney Injury (AKI)**.
    ◦ Specifically a form of pigment-induced nephropathy leading to **Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN)**.
    ◦ The massive release of **myoglobin** overwhelms the renal system's filtering capacity, leading to direct tubular toxicity and obstruction, ultimately causing renal failure.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• Incidence is estimated at 26,000 cases per year in the United States.
• Rhabdomyolysis accounts for approximately 7-10% of all cases of **AKI**.
• More common in males, individuals in the military, and victims of natural disasters or mass casualty events.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is often dominated by the underlying cause (e.g., trauma, sepsis, overdose).
• The classic triad of symptoms is present in less than 10% of patients.
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• Generally good if recognized and treated early with aggressive fluid resuscitation.
• Mortality is low (<10%) in patients who do not develop **AKI**.
• Prognosis is significantly worse if severe **AKI** develops, especially if dialysis is required.
• The underlying cause of the rhabdomyolysis is a major determinant of the overall outcome.

sections.overview:
• **Post-Obstructive Diuresis (POD)** is a **polyuric state** that occurs after the relief of a significant, prolonged, and typically **bilateral urinary tract obstruction**.
	◦ It is characterized by a **massive urine output**, often exceeding **200 mL/hour** for at least two consecutive hours, or **>3 Liters in 24 hours**.
	◦ POD represents the kidney's attempt to excrete excess urea, sodium, and water that accumulated during the obstructive period.
	◦ It can be either **physiologic** (appropriate and self-limiting) or **pathologic** (inappropriate, leading to severe volume depletion and electrolyte disturbances).
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• Occurs in up to 50% of patients following relief of chronic urinary obstruction.
• The incidence of clinically significant (**pathologic**) POD is lower.
• Most commonly seen in elderly males due to the high prevalence of BPH.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a patient with a known or suspected **urinary tract obstruction** (e.g., an elderly male with BPH and **anuria** for 24 hours) who undergoes a bladder catheterization (e.g., Foley catheter placement).
	◦ **Initially:** The patient may present with symptoms of **Acute Kidney Injury (AKI)** and **urinary retention**.
	◦ **Immediately following relief:** A dramatic and sustained increase in urine output begins. The urine is often clear and copious.
sections.diagnostics:
• POD is a **clinical diagnosis** based on high urine output after relieving an obstruction. The diagnostic workup is focused on identifying the cause of obstruction and monitoring for complications.
	◦ **Diagnosis Confirmation**
		▪ Urine output **> 200 mL/hr for 2 consecutive hours**.
		▪ Urine output **> 3 L / 24 hours**.
	◦ **Laboratory Studies**
		▪ **Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP/CMP):** Crucial for monitoring.
		▪ **BUN/Creatinine:** Will be elevated initially and should trend down.
			▪ A **BUN:Cr ratio >20:1** suggests a pre-renal state from the obstruction.
		▪ **Electrolytes:** Monitor for **hyponatremia, hypernatremia, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and hypophosphatemia**.
		▪ **Serial monitoring (q4-6 hours initially) is essential**.
	◦ **Urine Studies**
		▪ **Urine Osmolality & Urine Electrolytes:** Helps differentiate physiologic vs. pathologic POD.
			▪ **Physiologic:** Urine Na+ is high; urine osmolality is near plasma osmolality (~300 mOsm/kg).
			▪ **Pathologic:** Urine Na+ is high; urine osmolality is low/hypotonic (<150-200 mOsm/kg), indicating an inability to concentrate urine.
	◦ **Imaging**
		▪ **Bladder Scan (Bedside Ultrasound):** Confirms **urinary retention** prior to catheterization.
		▪ **Renal Ultrasound:** To evaluate for **hydronephrosis** and assess for upper tract obstruction.
	◦ **EKG:** To evaluate for cardiac manifestations of electrolyte abnormalities (e.g., **peaked T-waves** in hyperkalemia, **U-waves** in hypokalemia).
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is generally **excellent** if POD is recognized early and managed appropriately with careful fluid and electrolyte monitoring.
• The long-term prognosis depends on the degree of recovery from the underlying acute kidney injury and the nature of the primary cause of the obstruction.
• The diuresis phase typically resolves within 24-72 hours as tubular function recovers and solute/volume balance is restored.

sections.overview:
• Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) in shock is a rapid decline in renal function due to systemic circulatory failure and critical end-organ hypoperfusion.
• The injury is primarily perfusion-dependent, beginning as **prerenal azotemia** that can rapidly progress to intrinsic renal damage, most commonly **Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN)**, if the shock state is not reversed promptly.
• AKI is defined by a rise in serum creatinine (SCr), a decrease in urine output, or both.
• The **KDIGO (Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes)** criteria are the standard for diagnosing and staging AKI.
sections.etiology:
• The final common pathway for AKI in all shock states is **renal hypoperfusion** leading to decreased glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and renal ischemia.
• **The Spectrum of Injury**:
    ◦ **Prerenal Azotemia (The Compensatory Phase)**:
        ▪ Systemic hypotension leads to decreased renal blood flow.
        ▪ The kidney activates compensatory mechanisms: **RAAS activation**, sympathetic nervous system stimulation, and ADH release.
        ▪ **Efferent arteriole vasoconstriction** (via Angiotensin II) occurs to a greater degree than afferent constriction, attempting to maintain GFR.
        ▪ The renal tubules are intact and functional, avidly reabsorbing sodium and water to restore systemic volume.
        ▪ This state is **reversible** with restoration of renal perfusion.
    ◦ **Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN) (The Decompensated/Injury Phase)**:
        ▪ Prolonged or severe hypoperfusion overwhelms compensatory mechanisms.
        ▪ Ischemia leads to injury and death of the renal tubular epithelial cells, particularly in the proximal tubule and thick ascending limb.
        ▪ Dead cells slough off into the tubular lumen, forming casts and causing obstruction.
        ▪ The loss of tubular integrity impairs the kidney's ability to reabsorb sodium and concentrate urine.
        ▪ This represents **intrinsic renal damage** and takes longer to resolve.
• **Pathophysiology by Shock Type**:
    ◦ **Hypovolemic Shock** (e.g., hemorrhage, severe dehydration):
        ▪ **Etiology**: Decreased intravascular volume → decreased preload → decreased cardiac output → systemic hypoperfusion.
    ◦ **Cardiogenic Shock** (e.g., acute MI, severe heart failure):
        ▪ **Etiology**: Primary pump failure → decreased cardiac output → systemic hypoperfusion and venous congestion.
    ◦ **Distributive Shock** (e.g., sepsis, anaphylaxis):
        ▪ **Etiology**: Massive vasodilation → decreased systemic vascular resistance (SVR) → relative hypovolemia and maldistribution of blood flow.
        ▪ **Sepsis is unique**: In addition to hypoperfusion, systemic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and microthrombi contribute directly to renal injury.
    ◦ **Obstructive Shock** (e.g., cardiac tamponade, massive pulmonary embolism):
        ▪ **Etiology**: Physical obstruction to blood flow → impaired cardiac filling → decreased cardiac output → systemic hypoperfusion.
sections.epidemiology:
• AKI occurs in over 50% of patients in the Intensive Care Unit (ICU).
• **Sepsis** is the single most common cause of AKI in critically ill patients, accounting for approximately 50% of cases.
• The development of AKI in a patient with shock dramatically increases mortality.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The clinical presentation is dominated by the signs and symptoms of the underlying shock state, with AKI being a secondary finding.
    ◦ **Profound Hypotension**: Systolic BP <90 mmHg or MAP <65 mmHg.
    ◦ **Tachycardia**
    ◦ **Tachypnea**
    ◦ **Altered Mental Status**: Confusion, lethargy, obtundation.
    ◦ **Oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/hr) or Anuria** is the classic renal sign.
sections.diagnostics:
• The goal is to diagnose and stage AKI, differentiate prerenal from intrinsic (ATN), and identify the cause of shock.
• **Laboratory Studies**:
    ◦ **Basic/Complete Metabolic Panel (BMP/CMP)**:
        ▪ **Serum Creatinine (SCr)**: Key diagnostic marker.
        ▪ **Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN)**: Rises disproportionately in prerenal states.
        ▪ **BUN:SCr Ratio**:
            ▪ **>20:1 suggests Prerenal Azotemia**.
            ▪ **<15:1 suggests Intrinsic AKI (ATN)**.
        ▪ **Hyperkalemia, Hyperphosphatemia, Hypocalcemia**
        ▪ **Metabolic Acidosis** (low bicarbonate, anion gap may be elevated).
    ◦ **Urinalysis with Microscopy**:
        ▪ **Prerenal**: High specific gravity (>1.020), bland sediment (hyaline casts).
        ▪ **ATN**: Isosthenuria (specific gravity ~1.010), **muddy brown granular casts (pathognomonic)**, renal tubular epithelial cells.
    ◦ **Urine Chemistry**:
        ▪ **Fractional Excretion of Sodium (FENa)**: (Urine Na / Plasma Na) / (Urine Cr / Plasma Cr) x 100
            ▪ **FENa < 1% suggests Prerenal** (kidney is conserving sodium).
            ▪ **FENa > 2% suggests ATN** (damaged tubules cannot reabsorb sodium).
            ▪ *Note: Less reliable in patients on diuretics. Use FEUrea in these cases.*
    ◦ **Arterial Blood Gas (ABG)**: To assess for metabolic acidosis and oxygenation status.
    ◦ **Serum Lactate**: Key marker of systemic hypoperfusion and tissue hypoxia.
    ◦ **Additional Labs for Shock Workup**: CBC, cardiac enzymes (troponin), BNP, coagulation studies, blood cultures.
• **Imaging**:
    ◦ **Renal Ultrasound with Doppler**: Essential to rule out a postrenal (obstructive) cause. Also assesses kidney size and echogenicity.
    ◦ **Chest X-ray, Echocardiogram, CT Scan**: To identify the underlying cause of shock (e.g., pneumonia, heart failure, PE, hemorrhage).
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is poor and largely dependent on the severity and reversibility of the underlying shock state.
• The development of AKI requiring RRT in the setting of shock is associated with a mortality rate exceeding 50%.
• Survivors of severe AKI are at high risk for developing CKD in the future.

sections.overview:
• Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS) is a clinical syndrome characterized by the classic triad of:
    ◦ **Microangiopathic Hemolytic Anemia (MAHA)**
    ◦ **Thrombocytopenia**
    ◦ **Acute Kidney Injury (AKI)**
• It is the most common cause of **acute kidney injury** in otherwise healthy children, particularly those under 5 years of age.
• The most frequent form is "typical" or "diarrhea-positive" (D+) HUS, which is preceded by a diarrheal illness, most often caused by **Shiga toxin-producing *E. coli* (STEC)**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Primary Cause (>90% of cases):** Infection with **Shiga toxin-producing *E. coli* (STEC)**, with the serotype **O157:H7** being the most notorious.
    ◦ Other pathogens include ***Shigella dysenteriae*** type 1 and, rarely, other non-O157 STEC strains.
    ◦ This is distinct from ***atypical HUS (aHUS)***, which is caused by genetic defects in the alternative complement pathway and is not associated with diarrhea.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Ingestion & Infection:** A child ingests the pathogen (e.g., in contaminated food). The bacteria colonize the large intestine.
    ◦ **Toxin Production & Absorption:** The bacteria produce **Shiga toxin (Stx)**. The toxin damages the intestinal lining, causing **hemorrhagic colitis (bloody diarrhea)**, and then enters the systemic circulation.
    ◦ **Endothelial Damage:** The Shiga toxin has a high affinity for globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) receptors, which are highly expressed on the surface of vascular endothelial cells, particularly within the **renal glomeruli** and cerebral vasculature.
    ◦ **Microthrombi Formation:** Toxin binding leads to endothelial cell activation, inflammation, and apoptosis. This exposes the subendothelial matrix, triggering localized platelet activation and aggregation, forming widespread **platelet-rich microthrombi** in the small vessels of the kidneys and other organs.
    ◦ **Manifestation of the Triad:**
        ▪ **Microangiopathic Hemolytic Anemia:** As red blood cells (RBCs) attempt to pass through the partially occluded microvasculature, they are subjected to high shear stress and are fragmented. This creates **schistocytes** (helmet cells) seen on the peripheral smear. These damaged RBCs are rapidly cleared, leading to intravascular hemolysis.
        ▪ **Thrombocytopenia:** Platelets are consumed in the formation of the widespread microthrombi, leading to a low circulating platelet count.
        ▪ **Acute Kidney Injury:** The microthrombi occlude the glomerular capillaries, leading to glomerular ischemia, decreased glomerular filtration rate (GFR), and subsequent acute tubular necrosis.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Age:** Primarily a disease of young children, with a peak incidence between **6 months and 5 years of age**.
• **Incidence:** The most common cause of pediatric **AKI** in the United States.
• **Seasonality:** More common during the summer and early fall months, corresponding to peak *E. coli* season.
• **Transmission:** Occurs in outbreaks or as sporadic cases.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation follows a distinct two-phase course:
    ◦ **Prodromal Phase (precedes HUS by ~5-10 days):**
        ▪ A gastrointestinal illness characterized by severe abdominal cramps, watery diarrhea that progresses to **bloody diarrhea (hemorrhagic colitis)** within a few days.
        ▪ Vomiting and low-grade fever may also be present.
    ◦ **HUS Phase:**
        ▪ As the diarrhea improves or resolves, the child suddenly becomes acutely ill.
        ▪ Rapid onset of weakness, lethargy, irritability, and pallor.
        ▪ **Decreased urine output (oliguria)** or complete cessation of urine (**anuria**) is a cardinal sign of developing AKI.
sections.diagnostics:
• **CBC with Peripheral Smear:**
    ◦ **Anemia:** **Normocytic, normochromic hemolytic anemia** (Hgb often <8 g/dL).
    ◦ **Thrombocytopenia:** Platelet count typically <150,000/L, often <60,000/L.
    ◦ **Peripheral Smear:** **Schistocytes (fragmented RBCs, helmet cells) are the hallmark finding.**
• **Labs for Hemolysis:**
    ◦ **Elevated LDH** (Lactate Dehydrogenase): A sensitive marker of hemolysis.
    ◦ **Elevated indirect bilirubin.**
    ◦ **Decreased haptoglobin** (binds free hemoglobin).
    ◦ **Negative Coombs test:** Rules out autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
• **Renal Function Panel / BMP:**
    ◦ **Elevated BUN and Creatinine** (azotemia).
    ◦ **Electrolyte abnormalities:** **Hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia.**
    ◦ **Metabolic acidosis** (low bicarbonate).
• **Urinalysis (UA):**
    ◦ **Hematuria** (microscopic or gross).
    ◦ **Proteinuria**.
    ◦ **RBC casts** may be present.
• **Stool Studies:**
    ◦ Stool culture for ***E. coli* O157:H7** (requires special **sorbitol-MacConkey agar**, as O157:H7 does not ferment sorbitol).
    ◦ Stool assay for **Shiga toxin** (PCR or EIA).
• **Key Lab Pattern:** **Anemia with schistocytes + Thrombocytopenia + High BUN/Creatinine = HUS until proven otherwise.**
• Coagulation studies (PT, PTT) are typically **normal**, helping to distinguish it from DIC.
sections.prognosis:
• Overall prognosis in children with typical D+ HUS is good with modern supportive care.
• **>95% survive the acute illness.**
• Most children (~70-85%) recover full renal function.
• Poor prognostic indicators include:
    ◦ Prolonged **anuria** (>1 week)
    ◦ Severe **CNS involvement**
    ◦ Need for extensive dialysis

sections.overview:
• Most common cause of **nephrotic syndrome** in the pediatric population (approx. 80-90% of cases)
    ◦ A glomerular disorder characterized by the abrupt onset of massive **proteinuria**
        ▪ Leads to the full nephrotic syndrome tetrad: **proteinuria**, **hypoalbuminemia**, **edema**, and **hyperlipidemia**
    ◦ The name "minimal change" refers to glomeruli appearing normal under light microscopy
    ◦ Definitive diagnosis is made by electron microscopy, revealing characteristic **effacement (flattening) of podocyte foot processes**
    ◦ The hallmark of pediatric MCD is its excellent response to **corticosteroid therapy**
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• Most common cause of **nephrotic syndrome** in children (~80-90%)
• Peak incidence between **2 and 6 years of age**
• Slight male predominance (~2:1)
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Classic presentation: a **previously healthy toddler or young child** who develops the **sudden onset of generalized edema** over a few days to weeks
    ◦ The child is typically well-appearing despite the dramatic swelling and is often **normotensive**
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent in children**
    ◦ The vast majority (>90%) of children are **steroid-sensitive** and achieve remission
    ◦ While relapses are common, renal function is preserved long-term
    ◦ Most children outgrow the tendency to relapse by late adolescence or early adulthood
• Prognosis is guarded for the small minority with **steroid-resistant disease**
    ◦ This group has a higher risk of progressing to **end-stage renal disease (ESRD)**

sections.overview:
• Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) is a non-malignant, age-related enlargement of the prostate gland.
    ◦ This proliferation of prostatic stromal and epithelial cells primarily occurs in the **periurethral (transitional) zone**, leading to compression of the prostatic urethra.
    ◦ The resulting obstruction causes a constellation of symptoms known as **Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms (LUTS)**, which can be categorized as obstructive (voiding) or irritative (storage) symptoms.
    ◦ BPH is not a precursor to prostate cancer, but the two can coexist.
sections.etiology:
• The pathophysiology of BPH is hormonally dependent and multifactorial, involving both static and dynamic components.
    ◦ **Hormonal Influence**
        ▪ The prostate requires androgens for growth. Testosterone is converted to the more potent androgen, **dihydrotestosterone (DHT)**, by the enzyme **5-alpha reductase (Type 2)** within prostate stromal cells.
        ▪ **DHT** is the primary mediator of prostatic growth, binding to androgen receptors with high affinity and promoting cellular hyperplasia.
        ▪ Aging leads to a relative increase in estrogen compared to testosterone, which may also increase the activity of **DHT** and sensitize the prostate to its effects.
    ◦ **Components of Obstruction**
        ▪ **Static Component:** The physical enlargement of the prostate gland itself, which encroaches on and compresses the prostatic urethra and bladder neck, causing mechanical obstruction. This is the target of 5-alpha reductase inhibitors.
        ▪ **Dynamic Component:** Increased smooth muscle tone within the prostate stroma and bladder neck, mediated by **alpha-1 adrenergic receptors**. Increased sympathetic nervous system activity can worsen this component, causing functional obstruction. This is the target of alpha-blockers.
sections.epidemiology:
• BPH is extremely common and is the most frequent cause of **bladder outlet obstruction** in men.
• The prevalence is strongly correlated with age.
    ◦ Rare in men < 40 years old.
    ◦ ~50% of men have histologic evidence of BPH by age 60.
    ◦ ~90% of men have histologic evidence by age 85.
• Approximately 50% of men with histologic BPH will develop clinically significant symptoms.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The typical patient is a male over the age of 50 presenting with a gradual onset and slow progression of **lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS)**.
• Patients may complain of difficulty initiating urination, a weak stream, and waking up multiple times at night to urinate.
• The severity of symptoms can be quantified using the **American Urological Association (AUA) Symptom Index** or the **International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS)**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **History**
    ◦ Utilize the **AUA Symptom Index (IPSS)** to quantify symptom severity (Mild: 0-7, Moderate: 8-19, Severe: 20-35).
• **Urinalysis (UA) with culture**
    ◦ Essential initial test to rule out **infection (UTI)** and **hematuria** (which may suggest bladder cancer or stones).
• **Basic Labs**
    ◦ **Serum Creatinine / BUN:** To assess for renal impairment and potential post-renal azotemia from obstruction.
    ◦ **Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA):** Optional. Not a diagnostic test for BPH, but used to screen for prostate cancer and can help guide treatment (larger prostates have higher PSAs). A baseline is often obtained.
• **Post-Void Residual (PVR) Volume**
    ◦ Measured via bladder ultrasound or catheterization.
    ◦ **Normal:** < 50 mL
    ◦ **Abnormal/Significant:** > 200 mL suggests inadequate bladder emptying.
• **Uroflowmetry**
    ◦ Measures urine flow rate. A low peak flow rate (<10-15 mL/sec) is indicative of obstruction.
• **Cystoscopy**
    ◦ Not routine. Indicated for **hematuria**, suspicion of **urethral stricture**, or before surgical intervention.
• **Transrectal Ultrasound (TRUS)**
    ◦ Not for routine BPH diagnosis. Used to accurately measure prostate volume (important for choosing 5-alpha reductase inhibitors) and to guide prostate biopsy if cancer is suspected.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is excellent.
• BPH is a benign, manageable condition.
• With appropriate treatment, most men experience significant improvement in quality of life.
• The primary goals are symptom relief and prevention of long-term complications.

sections.overview:
• **Acute Prostatitis** is a serious bacterial infection and inflammation of the prostate gland, categorized as **NIH Category I prostatitis**
• Presents with an abrupt onset of systemic symptoms (**fever**, **chills**) and urogenital symptoms (**dysuria**, **perineal pain**)
• Considered a **complicated urinary tract infection (UTI)** in males
• Requires prompt diagnosis and treatment with antibiotics that have good prostatic tissue penetration
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The primary mechanism is **ascending infection** from the urethra or reflux of infected urine from the bladder into the prostatic ducts
    ◦ Bacteria colonize prostatic tissue, leading to an intense inflammatory response, edema, and potential micro-abscess formation
    ◦ Less common routes include direct extension from adjacent structures or hematogenous seeding
• **Etiologic Agents**
    ◦ Causative organisms vary with age and risk factors
    ◦ **Men > 35 years old** (and men < 35 who do not practice high-risk sexual behavior)
        ▪ **_Escherichia coli_** (most common, ~80%)
        ▪ _Proteus_ spp.
        ▪ _Klebsiella_ spp.
        ▪ _Enterococcus_ spp.
        ▪ _Pseudomonas aeruginosa_
    ◦ **Men < 35 years old** (and men > 35 who practice high-risk sexual behavior)
        ▪ **_Neisseria gonorrhoeae_**
        ▪ **_Chlamydia trachomatis_**
sections.epidemiology:
• Acute bacterial prostatitis is the **most common urologic diagnosis in men under 50** years of age
• Accounts for a significant number of physician visits for genitourinary complaints
• Has a **bimodal distribution**
    ◦ One peak in younger, sexually active men (20-40 years)
    ◦ Another in older men (>60 years), often associated with **benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)** and urologic procedures
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patient is typically a male who appears acutely ill, often with systemic signs of infection and an abrupt presentation
• Classic triad includes **fever**, **irritative voiding symptoms**, and **perineal pain**
• History should focus on urinary symptoms, sexual history, and recent urologic procedures
sections.diagnostics:
• **Urinalysis (UA)**
    ◦ Will show **pyuria** (WBCs), **bacteriuria**, and often hematuria
• **Urine Culture & Sensitivity**
    ◦ **Essential for diagnosis and to guide antibiotic therapy**
    ◦ A midstream urine sample is required
    ◦ Critical if initial treatment fails
• **Complete Blood Count (CBC)**
    ◦ **Leukocytosis** with a left shift (neutrophilia) is expected
• **Blood Cultures**
    ◦ Obtain in patients who are systemically ill, septic, or immunocompromised
• **Inflammatory Markers**
    ◦ C-reactive protein (CRP) and Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) will be elevated
• **Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA)**
    ◦ Will be markedly elevated due to inflammation
    ◦ **PSA should NOT be checked during the acute illness**
        ▪ It is not a reliable marker for cancer in this setting and can cause undue patient anxiety
        ▪ If indicated for cancer screening, it should be rechecked weeks to months after the infection has resolved
• **Imaging (Not routinely indicated)**
    ◦ **Transrectal Ultrasound (TRUS)** or **CT scan with contrast** should be performed if a **prostatic abscess** is suspected
        ▪ i.e., patient fails to improve after 48-72 hours of appropriate antibiotic therapy, or has persistent fever/bacteremia
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is generally **excellent for a full recovery** with prompt and adequate antibiotic therapy
• A small percentage of patients may develop **chronic bacterial prostatitis** or chronic pelvic pain syndrome
• Mortality is low but increases significantly if complicated by **sepsis**

sections.overview:
• **Chronic Prostatitis** is a clinical syndrome characterized by a combination of urologic symptoms and chronic pelvic pain, lasting for **at least 3 months**.
• It is not a single disease but a spectrum of conditions affecting the prostate gland and surrounding tissues.
• The **NIH has established a classification system** to categorize prostatitis syndromes:
    ◦ **Category I: Acute Bacterial Prostatitis**: Acute infection of the prostate, not covered here.
    ◦ **Category II: Chronic Bacterial Prostatitis (CBP)**: Recurrent UTIs and persistent bacterial infection of the prostate.
    ◦ **Category III: Chronic Prostatitis/Chronic Pelvic Pain Syndrome (CP/CPPS)**: The most common type. Pelvic pain for >3 months with no evidence of bacterial infection.
        ▪ **IIIA**: Inflammatory CP/CPPS (WBCs present in semen/prostatic secretions).
        ▪ **IIIB**: Non-inflammatory CP/CPPS (No WBCs present).
    ◦ **Category IV: Asymptomatic Inflammatory Prostatitis**: WBCs found in prostatic secretions/tissue incidentally (e.g., during infertility workup or after prostate biopsy), but the patient has no symptoms.
• This guide focuses on **Category II (CBP)** and **Category III (CP/CPPS)**.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• One of the most common urologic diagnoses in men under 50.
• Prevalence is estimated at 8-16% of the male population.
• **CP/CPPS (Category III) accounts for >90% of all prostatitis cases**.
• **Chronic Bacterial Prostatitis (Category II)** is relatively rare, accounting for only 5-10% of cases.
• Peak incidence occurs in men aged 35-50.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The typical patient is a male between 35 and 50 years old presenting with a long-standing, waxing and waning history of **pelvic pain** and **lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS)**.
• The symptoms have been present for **at least 3 months**.
• Patients often express significant frustration due to the chronic nature of their symptoms and previous unsuccessful treatments.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Urinalysis (UA) and Urine Culture**
    ◦ Essential initial tests.
    ◦ Performed to rule out a simple UTI.
    ◦ May be normal or show **pyuria/bacteriuria**.
• **Pre- and Post-Prostatic Massage Urinalysis and Culture (Simplified Meares-Stamey Test)**
    ◦ **Procedure**
        ▪ Patient provides a mid-stream urine sample (**Pre-massage**).
        ▪ Clinician performs a DRE with vigorous **prostatic massage** for ~1 minute to express prostatic fluid into the urethra.
        ▪ Patient provides a urine sample immediately after the massage (**Post-massage**).
    ◦ **Interpretation**
        ▪ **Category II (CBP)**: A significant increase in bacteria (**10-fold**) in the post-massage sample compared to the pre-massage sample.
        ▪ **Category IIIA (Inflammatory CP/CPPS)**: A significant increase in WBCs (**>10/hpf**) in the post-massage sample, but cultures are negative.
        ▪ **Category IIIB (Non-inflammatory CP/CPPS)**: No significant increase in WBCs or bacteria.
• **Semen Analysis/Culture**
    ◦ Can also be used to look for WBCs and bacteria.
• **Labs**
    ◦ **PSA**: May be mildly elevated due to inflammation but is non-specific. Should normalize after treatment.
• **Imaging (Not routinely indicated)**
    ◦ **Transrectal Ultrasound (TRUS)**: To rule out a **prostatic abscess** or ejaculatory duct obstruction.
    ◦ **CT/MRI of Pelvis**: To rule out other pelvic pathology if the diagnosis is uncertain.
• **Urodynamics/Cystoscopy**
    ◦ Considered for patients with significant **voiding symptoms** or if alternative diagnoses (e.g., bladder neck obstruction, interstitial cystitis) are suspected.
sections.prognosis:
• **Category II (CBP)**
    ◦ Prognosis is fair to good.
    ◦ Bacterial eradication can be achieved in ~60-80% of cases with appropriate antibiotic therapy, but **relapses can occur**.
• **Category III (CP/CPPS)**
    ◦ Prognosis for a complete cure is poor.
    ◦ However, with a multimodal management approach, a majority of patients can achieve significant and sustained symptom improvement.
    ◦ The condition often follows a **relapsing-remitting pattern**.

sections.overview:
• Prostate cancer is a malignant tumor of the prostate gland.
• It is the most common non-skin cancer in men.
• The vast majority (>95%) are **adenocarcinomas** that arise from the glandular tissue of the prostate.
• It is typically a slow-growing cancer, often asymptomatic in its early stages.
• Most frequently discovered through screening with a Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA) blood test and/or a Digital Rectal Exam (DRE).
sections.etiology:
• **Cellular Origin**
    ◦ Arises from the epithelial cells of the prostate gland's acini.
• **Histology**
    ◦ Over 95% are **adenocarcinomas**.
    ◦ Other rare types include small cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and sarcomas.
• **Hormonal Influence**
    ◦ The growth of prostate cancer is heavily dependent on androgens, primarily **testosterone** and its more potent metabolite, **dihydrotestosterone (DHT)**.
    ◦ Androgens bind to androgen receptors in prostate cells, promoting growth and proliferation.
• **Anatomic Location**
    ◦ Approximately 70-80% of prostate cancers originate in the **peripheral zone** of the prostate, which is the area most accessible to a Digital Rectal Exam (DRE).
    ◦ About 10-20% arise in the transitional zone and 5% in the central zone.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Second most common cancer in men worldwide (after skin cancer).
• **Mortality**: Second leading cause of cancer-related death in men (after lung cancer).
• **Age**: Incidence increases significantly after age 50. The median age at diagnosis is ~66 years. It is rare in men under 40.
• **Race/Ethnicity**: **African American** men have the highest incidence and mortality rates (approximately 1.5x higher incidence and 2x higher mortality than Caucasian men). Asian American and Hispanic men have lower rates.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Non-modifiable**
    ◦ **Age**: Strongest risk factor. Risk increases dramatically after age 50.
    ◦ **Race**: **African American** ethnicity.
    ◦ **Family History**: Having a first-degree relative (father, brother, son) with prostate cancer doubles the risk. Risk is higher if the relative was diagnosed at a young age (<65).
    ◦ **Genetic Mutations**: Inherited mutations in genes like **BRCA1** and **BRCA2** (especially BRCA2) and Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) increase risk.
• **Modifiable/Possible**
    ◦ **Diet**: High intake of red meat and high-fat dairy products may increase risk.
    ◦ **Obesity**: Associated with more aggressive disease and higher mortality.
    ◦ **Agent Orange exposure** (for Vietnam veterans).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Early/Localized Disease**
    ◦ Most commonly **asymptomatic** and detected during screening.
• **Locally Advanced Disease**
    ◦ Patients may develop obstructive or irritative urinary symptoms.
• **Advanced/Metastatic Disease**
    ◦ Patients may present with symptoms related to metastases, without having had any prior urinary symptoms.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Digital Rectal Exam (DRE)**
    ◦ Early-stage cancer may not be palpable (normal DRE).
    ◦ Classic findings for suspicious cancer include a hard, indurated, **nodular**, or **asymmetric** prostate gland.
• **Advanced Disease**
    ◦ Palpable supraclavicular or inguinal lymphadenopathy.
    ◦ Lower extremity lymphedema.
    ◦ Focal neurologic deficits if spinal cord compression is present.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Screening**
    ◦ **Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA)**
        ▪ A glycoprotein produced by prostate cells. Normal levels are typically <4 ng/mL, but this is age-dependent.
        ▪ PSA is prostate-specific, not cancer-specific. Can be elevated in BPH, prostatitis, recent ejaculation, or prostate instrumentation.
    ◦ **Digital Rectal Exam (DRE)**
    ◦ Screening decisions (e.g., AUA guidelines) are based on shared decision-making with the patient, typically starting the discussion between ages 50-55 for average-risk men.
• **Definitive Diagnosis**
    ◦ **Transrectal Ultrasound (TRUS)-guided Biopsy**
        ▪ **Gold standard** for diagnosis. Performed if PSA is elevated or DRE is abnormal.
        ▪ Multiple core samples are taken from different regions of the prostate.
• **Staging and Grading**
    ◦ **Gleason Score**
        ▪ Pathological grading system based on tissue architecture from the biopsy.
        ▪ Two most common patterns are graded 1-5 and added together (e.g., 3+4=7).
        ▪ A higher score indicates a more aggressive, poorly differentiated tumor.
            ▪ Gleason 6: Well-differentiated (low-grade)
            ▪ Gleason 7: Moderately-differentiated (intermediate-grade)
            ▪ Gleason 8-10: Poorly-differentiated (high-grade)
    ◦ **TNM Staging System**
        ▪ Describes the extent of the tumor (T), lymph node involvement (N), and distant metastasis (M).
    ◦ **Staging Imaging**
        ▪ Used for intermediate to high-risk disease or suspected metastasis.
        ▪ **Radionuclide Bone Scan**: To detect bone metastases.
        ▪ **CT scan of Abdomen/Pelvis**: To assess pelvic lymph nodes and visceral organs.
        ▪ **MRI of Prostate**: Can help define the extent of the primary tumor.
sections.treatment:
• **Localized Disease (Confined to Prostate)**
    ◦ **Active Surveillance**: For very low-risk or low-risk disease (low Gleason score, low PSA, small tumor volume). Involves regular monitoring with PSA, DRE, and repeat biopsies. Treatment is initiated if the disease shows signs of progression.
    ◦ **Radical Prostatectomy (RP)**: Surgical removal of the entire prostate gland, seminal vesicles, and ampullae of the vas deferens.
    ◦ **Radiation Therapy (RT)**
        ▪ **External Beam Radiation Therapy (EBRT)**: Radiation delivered from an external source.
        ▪ **Brachytherapy**: Implantation of radioactive seeds directly into the prostate gland.
• **Locally Advanced Disease (Extends beyond prostate capsule)**
    ◦ Typically combination therapy: **EBRT + Androgen Deprivation Therapy (ADT)**.
    ◦ Radical prostatectomy may be an option in select patients.
• **Metastatic Disease**
    ◦ **Androgen Deprivation Therapy (ADT)**: The cornerstone of treatment. Aims to lower testosterone to castrate levels.
        ▪ **GnRH Agonists**: **Leuprolide**, Goserelin. Cause an initial testosterone flare before downregulation. Often given with an anti-androgen initially.
        ▪ **GnRH Antagonists**: **Degarelix**. No testosterone flare.
        ▪ **Orchiectomy**: Surgical castration, less commonly used.
    ◦ **Chemotherapy**: **Docetaxel** is often used for hormone-refractory or high-volume metastatic disease.
    ◦ **Novel Anti-androgen Agents**: Abiraterone, Enzalutamide. Used for castrate-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC).
    ◦ **Bone-modifying agents**: Zoledronic acid, Denosumab to reduce skeletal-related events.
sections.management:
• **Post-treatment Surveillance**
    ◦ Monitor serum **PSA** levels regularly. After radical prostatectomy, PSA should be undetectable (<0.2 ng/mL). A rising PSA after treatment is termed "biochemical recurrence" and may require salvage therapy.
• **Managing Treatment Side Effects**
    ◦ **Post-Prostatectomy**: **Erectile dysfunction** and **urinary incontinence** are the most common long-term complications.
    ◦ **Post-Radiation**: Erectile dysfunction, radiation proctitis (bowel irritation/bleeding), cystitis.
    ◦ **ADT Side Effects**: Hot flashes, loss of libido, erectile dysfunction, osteoporosis, gynecomastia, weight gain, fatigue, and increased risk of cardiovascular events and diabetes.
sections.complications:
• **From Disease Progression**
    ◦ **Metastasis**: Most commonly to **bone** (axial skeleton), lymph nodes, lung, and liver.
    ◦ **Spinal Cord Compression**: An oncologic emergency requiring immediate steroids and radiation/surgery.
    ◦ **Pathologic Fractures**: Due to osteoblastic bone metastases weakening the bone.
    ◦ **Bladder Outlet Obstruction / Ureteral Obstruction**: Can lead to acute kidney injury.
• **From Treatment**
    ◦ See Management section above.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly dependent on the stage and grade (**Gleason score**) at the time of diagnosis.
• **Localized Disease**: Excellent prognosis. 5-year relative survival rate is nearly 100%.
• **Distant (Metastatic) Disease**: Poor prognosis. 5-year relative survival rate is approximately 30%.

sections.overview:
• Testicular torsion is a urologic emergency caused by the twisting (torsion) of the spermatic cord, which cuts off the blood supply to the testicle
    ◦ Leads to venous congestion, arterial ischemia, and subsequent infarction of the testis if not treated promptly
    ◦ It is a clinical diagnosis that requires immediate surgical intervention to prevent testicular loss
    ◦ The mantra is **"time is testis"**
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ The underlying cause is most often an anatomical anomaly known as the **"bell clapper" deformity**
        ▪ Normally, the testis is secured to the scrotal wall posteriorly by the tunica vaginalis
        ▪ In the bell clapper deformity, the tunica vaginalis has an abnormally high attachment on the spermatic cord, allowing the testicle to hang freely and rotate within the scrotum, much like a clapper inside a bell
        ▪ This deformity is often bilateral
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The testis and spermatic cord twist, typically in a medial direction
    ◦ Venous outflow is obstructed first due to the lower pressure in the veins, leading to venous congestion, edema, and hemorrhage
    ◦ As intrastesticular pressure increases, arterial inflow is compromised, leading to ischemia
    ◦ Prolonged ischemia (>6 hours) leads to irreversible damage, infarction, and necrosis of the testicular tissue
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**
    ◦ Approximately 1 in 4,000 males under the age of 25 per year
• **Age Distribution**
    ◦ Exhibits a **bimodal distribution**
        ▪ **Perinatal period (neonates):** Often extravaginal torsion (torsion of the entire cord and tunica vaginalis)
        ▪ **Puberty (peak age 12-18 years):** Most common period, typically intravaginal torsion associated with the bell clapper deformity
• Can occur at any age but is rare after 30
• The left testis is slightly more commonly affected
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is an adolescent male who is awakened from sleep with **severe, acute testicular pain**
    ◦ The onset is abrupt and is often associated with systemic symptoms like **nausea and vomiting** due to the severity of the pain
    ◦ There is usually no history of fever or urinary symptoms
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**
    ◦ Testicular torsion is primarily a clinical diagnosis
    ◦ If clinical suspicion is high, proceed directly to surgical exploration without delaying for imaging
• **Testicular Doppler Ultrasound**
    ◦ The diagnostic modality of choice when the diagnosis is uncertain
    ◦ **Findings**
        ▪ Demonstrates **decreased or absent blood flow** to the affected testis
        ▪ The contralateral testis is used as a control
        ▪ May also show a "whirlpool sign," which is the coiled, twisted spermatic cord
• **Urinalysis (UA)**
    ◦ Typically normal
    ◦ A UA with pyuria and bacteriuria would suggest an infectious etiology like epididymitis
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis for testicular salvage is directly dependent on the duration of torsion
    ◦ **< 6 hours:** 90-100% salvage rate
    ◦ **12-24 hours:** 20-50% salvage rate
    ◦ **> 24 hours:** < 10% salvage rate

sections.overview:
• **Epididymitis** is the inflammation or infection of the epididymis, the coiled tube at the posterior aspect of the testicle responsible for sperm transport and maturation.
	◦ It is the most common cause of **scrotal pain** in adult males in the outpatient setting.
	◦ Often accompanied by inflammation of the testis (orchitis), a condition known as **epididymo-orchitis**.
	◦ Categorized as **acute** (<6 weeks) or **chronic** (>3 months of symptoms).
sections.etiology:
• The underlying mechanism is typically a **retrograde infection**, where pathogens ascend from the urethra or bladder to the epididymis.
• Causative organisms are strongly stratified by age and risk factors:
	◦ **Men < 35 years & Sexually Active Men**: Most common pathogens are sexually transmitted infections (STIs).
		▪ ***Chlamydia trachomatis*** (most common overall)
		▪ ***Neisseria gonorrhoeae***
	◦ **Men > 35 years & those practicing insertive anal intercourse**: Most common pathogens are enteric organisms, often associated with bladder outlet obstruction (e.g., BPH) or recent urologic instrumentation.
		▪ ***Escherichia coli*** (most common in this group)
		▪ *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*
		▪ *Klebsiella pneumoniae*
		▪ *Proteus* species
	◦ **Prepubertal Boys**: Less common.
		▪ Often associated with urinary tract anomalies.
		▪ Caused by coliform bacteria (*E. coli*) or can be post-viral (e.g., mumps, coxsackievirus).
• **Non-infectious Causes**:
	◦ **Amiodarone**: Can cause sterile, chemical epididymitis.
	◦ **Trauma**: Direct injury or strain.
	◦ **Vasculitis**: e.g., IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura).
	◦ **Tuberculosis**: A rare cause, usually in endemic areas or immunocompromised patients.
sections.epidemiology:
• Most common in men aged 19-35.
• Annual incidence is approximately 1 in 1,000 men.
• Accounts for over 600,000 medical visits per year in the United States.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A male patient typically presents with a **gradual onset** of unilateral **scrotal pain** and swelling developing over several hours to days.
	◦ Pain may radiate to the groin, flank, or lower abdomen.
	◦ Systemic symptoms like **fever** and **chills** may be present.
	◦ Lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) may be present.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Laboratory Studies**
	◦ **Urinalysis (UA) with culture**: Will often show **pyuria** (10 WBC/hpf) and bacteriuria. A culture is essential to guide therapy in the >35 age group.
	◦ **Urethral Swab / Urine Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT)**: The **gold standard** for detecting *N. gonorrhoeae* and *C. trachomatis* in all sexually active men.
	◦ **Complete Blood Count (CBC)**: May show **leukocytosis** with a left shift.
	◦ **Inflammatory Markers**: C-reactive protein (CRP) and Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) may be elevated but are non-specific.
• **Imaging**
	◦ **Scrotal Doppler Ultrasound**: This is the **imaging test of choice**. Its primary purpose is to **rule out testicular torsion**, a surgical emergency.
		▪ **Findings in Epididymitis**: Increased blood flow (**hyperemia**) to the epididymis and sometimes the testis, an enlarged/thickened epididymis, reactive hydrocele, and scrotal wall thickening.
		▪ **Findings in Torsion**: **Decreased or absent testicular blood flow**.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is **excellent** if treated promptly and appropriately with antibiotics.
	◦ Most patients experience significant improvement within 48-72 hours.
	◦ Delayed treatment increases the risk of complications.

sections.overview: • Orchitis is an inflammation of one or both testicles, most often caused by a bacterial or viral infection. ◦ Isolated orchitis is uncommon; it usually occurs in conjunction with epididymitis, a condition known as epididymo-orchitis. • The primary goals in evaluating a patient with testicular pain are to differentiate orchitis from testicular torsion (a surgical emergency) and to identify the causative pathogen to guide treatment.
sections.etiology: • The pathophysiology depends on the causative agent.
sections.epidemiology: • Isolated orchitis is rare; epididymo-orchitis is the most common cause of scrotal pain in adults. • Bacterial: Bimodal distribution. ◦ Peak incidence in young, sexually active men (19-35 years). ◦ Second peak in older men (>60 years) with BPH or other urologic pathology. • Viral (Mumps): The incidence has dramatically decreased since the widespread use of the MMR vaccine. ◦ Occurs in approximately 20-30% of post-pubertal males who contract mumps.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A male patient presents with acute or subacute onset of testicular pain, tenderness, and swelling.
    ◦ The history is critical to determine the likely etiology (e.g., sexual history, recent urinary procedures, or a viral prodrome with parotid swelling).
• Systemic symptoms like fever and malaise are common.
sections.diagnostics: • The primary goal is to rule out testicular torsion. • Scrotal Ultrasound with Color Doppler: ◦ Test of choice for acute scrotal pain. ◦ Findings: Increased blood flow (hyperemia) to the inflamed testis and/or epididymis. ◦ Reliably distinguishes orchitis from torsion, which shows decreased or absent blood flow. ◦ Can also identify complications like abscess or reactive hydrocele. • Urinalysis (UA) with culture: ◦ Will often show pyuria (WBCs) and/or bacteriuria in bacterial cases. • Urethral Swab or Urine Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT): ◦ Standard test for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis in all sexually active men. • Labs: ◦ CBC may show leukocytosis with a left shift. ◦ Inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR) may be elevated but are nonspecific. • Viral Serology: ◦ Mumps IgM/IgG can be ordered if mumps is suspected and the diagnosis is uncertain.
sections.prognosis: • The prognosis for bacterial orchitis is excellent if treated promptly with appropriate antibiotics. ◦ Pain typically subsides within 3 days, but swelling may persist for weeks. • For mumps orchitis, the prognosis is generally good, but the risk of testicular atrophy and subfertility is significant, particularly with bilateral disease.

sections.overview:
• A hydrocele is a pathological collection of **serous fluid** within the **tunica vaginalis** of the scrotum, the potential space surrounding the testicle.
    ◦ One of the most common causes of **painless scrotal swelling**.
• Hydroceles are broadly classified into two types: communicating and non-communicating.
    ◦ **Communicating Hydrocele**
        ▪ Caused by a patent processus vaginalis (**PPV**), allowing peritoneal fluid to flow into the scrotum.
        ▪ The swelling often **fluctuates in size**.
        ▪ This type is common in infants.
    ◦ **Non-communicating Hydrocele**
        ▪ Occurs when the processus vaginalis is closed, but there is an **imbalance between fluid secretion and absorption** by the tunica vaginalis.
        ▪ This is the most common type in adults.
sections.etiology:
• The underlying pathophysiology differs based on the type of hydrocele.
• **Communicating (Congenital)**
    ◦ **Mechanism**: Failure of the **processus vaginalis to close** after the testicular descent during fetal development.
    ◦ **Process**
        ▪ The patent processus vaginalis (**PPV**) creates a direct channel between the peritoneal cavity and the scrotum.
        ▪ Peritoneal fluid can then freely move into the scrotum, especially with **increased intra-abdominal pressure** (e.g., crying, straining).
        ▪ The size of the hydrocele may therefore **increase during the day and decrease at night** when the patient is supine.
• **Non-communicating (Acquired)**
    ◦ **Mechanism**: An **imbalance of fluid production and reabsorption** by the membranes of the tunica vaginalis.
        ▪ The processus vaginalis is obliterated.
    ◦ **Causes**
        ▪ **Idiopathic**: Most common cause in adults.
        ▪ **Inflammatory**: Secondary to **epididymitis** or **orchitis**.
        ▪ **Trauma**: Scrotal injury leading to inflammation or bleeding.
        ▪ **Tumor**: Underlying **testicular neoplasm** can cause a **reactive hydrocele**.
        ▪ **Infection**: **Filariasis** (in endemic areas), tuberculosis.
        ▪ **Iatrogenic**: Post-surgical (e.g., hernia repair, varicocelectomy).
sections.epidemiology:
• **Infants**
    ◦ Very common. Occurs in approximately **1-5% of newborn males**.
    ◦ More common in **premature infants**.
    ◦ The majority are **communicating** and **resolve spontaneously** within the first year of life.
• **Adults**
    ◦ Most common in men **over 40**.
    ◦ The incidence increases with age.
    ◦ The vast majority are **non-communicating** and **acquired**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A male patient, either an infant or an adult, presents with a complaint of a **swollen scrotum**.
• The onset is typically **gradual and painless**.
• In infants with a **communicating hydrocele**, parents may report that the swelling is **smaller in the morning and larger by the evening** or after periods of crying.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primarily a Clinical Diagnosis**
    ◦ Diagnosis is often made based on history and physical exam findings, especially positive **transillumination**.
• **Scrotal Ultrasound (US)**
    ◦ **Indication**: This is the diagnostic **test of choice**, especially in adults, to confirm the diagnosis and, more importantly, to **rule out underlying testicular pathology** (e.g., **testicular cancer**).
    ◦ **Findings**
        ▪ Ultrasound will show an **anechoic (black) fluid collection** surrounding the testicle, and it allows for clear visualization of the testicular parenchyma to ensure it is normal.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is **excellent**.
• Most congenital hydroceles **resolve without any intervention**.
• Surgical hydrocelectomy has a success rate of **over 95%** with a low risk of recurrence and complications.

sections.overview:
• A **varicocele** is the **dilation** (varicosity) of the **pampiniform plexus veins** within the **spermatic cord**.
    ◦ It is analogous to a varicose vein in the leg but occurs in the scrotum.
    ◦ It is the most common correctable cause of **male infertility**.
sections.etiology:
• The underlying cause is incompetent or congenitally absent valves in the gonadal (testicular) vein, leading to retrograde blood flow, increased hydrostatic pressure, and subsequent venous dilation.
• **Primary (Idiopathic) Varicocele**
    ◦ Most common type.
    ◦ **Left-Sided Predominance (~90%)**: Due to anatomical factors.
        ▪ **Longer Course**: The left gonadal vein is longer than the right.
        ▪ **Angle of Insertion**: The **left gonadal vein** drains into the **left renal vein** at a 90-degree angle, creating higher pressure. The right gonadal vein drains directly into the **inferior vena cava (IVC)** at an oblique angle.
        ▪ **"Nutcracker Effect"**: The **left renal vein** can be compressed between the **superior mesenteric artery (SMA)** and the **aorta**, increasing pressure which is transmitted back down the left gonadal vein.
• **Secondary Varicocele**
    ◦ Caused by extrinsic compression or obstruction of the gonadal vein.
    ◦ Much less common.
    ◦ Can be caused by a retroperitoneal or renal mass (e.g., **Renal Cell Carcinoma** with tumor thrombus), abdominal mass, or retroperitoneal fibrosis.
    ◦ **Clinical Red Flag**: Suspicion for an underlying obstructive cause should be raised for a:
        ▪ Sudden-onset varicocele in an older man
        ▪ Right-sided varicocele
        ▪ Varicocele that does not decompress when the patient is supine
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects ~15-20% of the general male population.
• Found in ~35-40% of men presenting with **primary infertility**.
• Typically develops during puberty and adolescence.
• Vast majority **(~90%) are left-sided**; ~10% are bilateral.
• Isolated right-sided varicoceles are rare (<1%).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Most are **asymptomatic** and discovered incidentally on physical exam or during an infertility workup.
• When symptomatic, patients report a dull, aching, or **"heavy" sensation** in the scrotum.
• Symptoms are classically worse at the end of the day, with prolonged standing, or during strenuous activity.
• Symptoms are typically relieved by lying down (**supine position**).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**
    ◦ The diagnosis is primarily made by physical examination.
• **Scrotal Doppler Ultrasound**
    ◦ **Indication**: Confirms the diagnosis, especially in equivocal exams or obese patients. Also used to accurately measure testicular volumes and rule out other scrotal pathology.
    ◦ **Findings**:
        ▪ Dilation of **pampiniform plexus veins** (typically **>3 mm**)
        ▪ Demonstration of **retrograde venous flow** during **Valsalva maneuver**.
• **Semen Analysis**
    ◦ **Indication**: Essential for all men with a varicocele who are concerned about fertility.
    ◦ **Classic Findings (The "Stress Pattern")**:
        ▪ Decreased sperm motility (**asthenospermia**)
        ▪ Decreased sperm count (**oligospermia**)
        ▪ Poor sperm morphology (**teratospermia**)
        ▪ Often referred to as **OAT syndrome** (Oligoasthenoteratozoospermia).
• **Abdominal Imaging (CT or Renal Ultrasound)**
    ◦ **Indication**: Reserved for suspected **secondary varicocele** (i.e., new onset, purely right-sided, or fails to decompress when supine).
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent for asymptomatic cases requiring no intervention.
• Following successful repair:
    ◦ **Semen Parameters**: Improve in ~60-70% of men.
    ◦ **Pregnancy Rates**: Spontaneous pregnancy is achieved in ~30-40% of couples within a year.
    ◦ **Testicular Growth**: Adolescents with testicular atrophy often demonstrate "catch-up" growth after repair.

sections.overview:
• A **spermatocele**, also known as an **epididymal cyst**, is a **benign**, **painless**, **fluid-filled sac** that develops in the **epididymis**
    ◦ The epididymis is the coiled tube located on the **superior and posterior aspect of the testicle** that helps transport sperm
    ◦ The cyst contains a **milky or cloudy fluid** which may include **non-viable spermatozoa**
    ◦ They are typically found at the **head of the epididymis** (**caput epididymidis**)
    ◦ Spermatoceles are **common** and do **not affect fertility** or increase the risk of **testicular cancer**
sections.etiology:
• The exact etiology is often unknown (**idiopathic**)
• The prevailing theory is that spermatoceles arise from a **blockage or obstruction** in one of the **efferent ductules** within the epididymis
    ◦ **Mechanism**: An obstruction prevents the normal outflow of sperm and seminal fluid from the **rete testis** into the **epididymis**
    ◦ **Result**: This leads to a **cystic dilation** of the ductule, forming a **retention cyst**
        ▪ The cyst wall is composed of **cuboidal epithelium**
    ◦ **Contents**: The fluid within the spermatocele consists of **sperm**, **cellular debris**, **lymphocytes**, and **proteinaceous fluid**, giving it a characteristic **cloudy appearance**
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Very common, found in approximately **30% of men** undergoing scrotal ultrasound for any reason
• **Age**: Most commonly discovered in men aged **40 to 60**, but can occur at any age after puberty
• **Incidence**: True incidence is difficult to determine as most are asymptomatic and go undiagnosed
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is an **asymptomatic** male who incidentally discovers a **small, non-tender lump** in his scrotum during self-examination or a routine physical exam
• It is one of the most common causes of a **scrotal mass**
• The patient is typically unconcerned but seeks evaluation to rule out malignancy
sections.physicalExam:
• **History and Physical Exam** are often sufficient for a presumptive diagnosis
    ◦ The key is palpating a **distinct, cystic mass separate from the testis** that **transilluminates**
sections.diagnostics:
• **Scrotal Ultrasound (Test of Choice)**
    ◦ **Purpose**: Confirms the diagnosis, differentiates it from other scrotal pathologies (especially **testicular tumors**), and assesses the testicle
    ◦ **Findings**: Ultrasound will show a **well-defined, anechoic (black), cystic lesion** in the **head of the epididymis**, with **no internal blood flow** on Doppler imaging
        ▪ The adjacent **testicular parenchyma** will appear **normal**
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is **excellent**
• A spermatocele is a **benign condition** with **no malignant potential** and does not inherently affect **testicular function** or **fertility**
• With observation, most patients remain **asymptomatic**
• For those undergoing surgery for symptoms, relief is common, though surgical risks must be considered

sections.overview:
• Malignancy arising from the germ cells or stromal cells of the testicle.
• Most common solid tumor in men aged **15-35**.
• One of the most **curable solid neoplasms** due to high sensitivity to chemotherapy and accurate staging/surveillance protocols.
• >95% are **Germ Cell Tumors (GCTs)**, broadly divided into:
    ◦ **Seminomas**
    ◦ **Non-Seminomas (NSGCTs)**
• The distinction between seminoma and NSGCT is critical as it dictates treatment and prognosis.
sections.etiology:
• Exact etiology is unknown; believed to originate from a precursor lesion called **intratubular germ cell neoplasia (ITGCN)**.
• **Histological Types:**
    ◦ **Germ Cell Tumors (GCTs) - 95%**
        ▪ **Seminomas (~50% of GCTs):**
            • Arise from spermatogonia.
            • Tend to be slower-growing and remain localized for longer.
            • Highly sensitive to radiation therapy.
            • Tumor markers: May produce **-hCG**; **NEVER produce AFP**.
        ▪ **Non-Seminomatous Germ Cell Tumors (NSGCTs) (~50% of GCTs):**
            • A heterogeneous group, often appearing as mixed tumors.
            • More aggressive, metastasize earlier via hematogenous and lymphatic routes.
            • Subtypes include:
                ▪ **Embryonal Carcinoma:** Highly malignant, early metastasis.
                ▪ **Yolk Sac (Endodermal Sinus) Tumor:** Most common testicular tumor in infants/children <3 years. Produces **AFP**. Histology shows **Schiller-Duval bodies**.
                ▪ **Choriocarcinoma:** Highly aggressive with early hematogenous spread (especially to lungs and brain). Produces high levels of **-hCG**, which can lead to gynecomastia and hyperthyroidism.
                ▪ **Teratoma:** Composed of cells from all three germ layers. Mature teratomas are typically benign in children but are considered malignant in post-pubertal males with potential for metastasis.
    ◦ **Non-Germ Cell Tumors (Sex Cord-Stromal Tumors) - <5%**
        ▪ **Leydig Cell Tumors:** Can secrete androgens, leading to precocious puberty in boys or gynecomastia in men.
        ▪ **Sertoli Cell Tumors:** Often hormonally silent but can produce estrogen.
        ▪ **Gonadoblastoma:** Rare, typically occurs in patients with gonadal dysgenesis.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Peak Incidence:** Age **15-35**.
• Most common solid malignancy in young men.
• More common in **Caucasian men** than in African American or Asian men.
• Incidence is higher in individuals with a personal or family history of the disease.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Classic presentation: a **painless, solid testicular mass or nodule** discovered incidentally or during routine exam.
• Patients may also report a dull ache or a sensation of **"heaviness"** in the scrotum.
• A small percentage (~10%) may present with **acute pain** due to intratesticular hemorrhage or infarction.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Scrotal Ultrasound**
    ◦ **Best initial imaging test**.
    ◦ Confirms the presence of a mass and determines if it is **intratesticular (highly suspicious for cancer)** versus extratesticular (usually benign).
• **Serum Tumor Markers**
    ◦ Essential for diagnosis, staging, and monitoring response to treatment.
    ◦ **Must be drawn BEFORE the orchiectomy**.
    ◦ **Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP):** Elevated in NSGCTs (especially Yolk Sac Tumors). **NEVER elevated in pure seminoma**.
    ◦ **Beta-human Chorionic Gonadotropin (-hCG):** Elevated in many NSGCTs (especially choriocarcinoma) and some seminomas (~15%).
    ◦ **Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH):** A non-specific marker of tumor burden and cell turnover; correlates with prognosis.
• **Radical Inguinal Orchiectomy**
    ◦ The **gold standard for diagnosis and initial treatment**.
    ◦ The entire testicle and spermatic cord are removed through an inguinal incision to prevent tumor seeding.
    ◦ Provides definitive histologic diagnosis.
    ◦ **A trans-scrotal biopsy is absolutely contraindicated** as it disrupts lymphatic drainage pathways and can seed the scrotum, worsening prognosis.
• **Staging Workup (Post-Orchiectomy)**
    ◦ **CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis** with contrast to evaluate for retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy and distant metastases.
    ◦ Brain MRI or PET scan if symptoms of brain metastasis are present or with high-risk disease (e.g., choriocarcinoma).
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent overall prognosis**, especially when diagnosed early.
• Overall **5-year survival rate is >95%**.
• Even with metastatic disease, the 5-year survival rate is >70%, making it a model for curable cancer.
• Seminomas generally have a slightly better prognosis than non-seminomas at similar stages.

sections.overview:
• Phimosis is the inability to retract the prepuce (foreskin) proximally over the glans penis.
• It is categorized into two main types:
    ◦ **Physiologic Phimosis**: This is a normal developmental condition in infants and young children.
        ▪ The foreskin is non-retractile due to congenital adhesions between the prepuce and the glans.
        ▪ It typically resolves spontaneously without intervention.
    ◦ **Pathologic Phimosis (Acquired)**: This is a true, non-retractile foreskin due to distal scarring of the prepuce.
        ▪ It occurs in uncircumcised males at any age and is the result of inflammation, infection, or trauma.
        ▪ It does not resolve spontaneously and often requires treatment.
sections.etiology:
• **Physiologic Phimosis**
    ◦ Results from normal congenital adhesions between the inner preputial epithelium and the glandular epithelium.
    ◦ As the child grows, intermittent erections and accumulation of desquamated epithelial cells (smegma) gradually separate these adhesions.
    ◦ The preputial orifice naturally widens and becomes retractable over time.
    ◦ Forceful retraction can cause micro-tears, bleeding, and subsequent scarring, converting a physiologic condition into a pathologic one.
• **Pathologic Phimosis**
    ◦ The underlying mechanism is inflammation and fibrosis leading to a constricting, inelastic ring at the preputial orifice.
    ◦ **Common Causes**:
        ▪ **Recurrent Balanoposthitis**: Chronic inflammation from bacterial or fungal infections leads to scar tissue formation.
        ▪ **Forcible Retraction**: Trauma from repeated attempts to retract a physiologic phimosis causes micro-fissures that heal with scarring.
        ▪ **Poor Hygiene**: Accumulation of smegma and irritants can lead to chronic inflammation.
        ▪ **Balanitis Xerotica Obliterans (BXO)**: Also known as penile Lichen Sclerosus. This is a chronic, progressive inflammatory dermatosis and is the most common cause of pathologic phimosis in adults and children. It is characterized by whitish, indurated, and atrophic plaques that lead to severe scarring of the prepuce, glans, and sometimes the urethral meatus.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Physiologic**
    ◦ Present in >95% of newborn males.
    ◦ Retractability increases with age:
        ▪ ~50% by age 1
        ▪ ~90% by age 3
        ▪ ~99% by age 16-18
• **Pathologic**
    ◦ Affects approximately 1-2% of uncircumcised adult males.
    ◦ The incidence increases with age, often associated with comorbidities like diabetes.
    ◦ BXO is the underlying cause in a significant portion of cases requiring circumcision for phimosis.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation varies based on the type and severity.
• **Physiologic**
    ◦ Most commonly identified during a routine well-child check.
    ◦ The parent or child is typically asymptomatic.
    ◦ Parents may express concern about the non-retractile foreskin or the presence of "smegma pearls" (trapped desquamated cells), which are benign.
• **Pathologic**
    ◦ Patients present with symptoms.
    ◦ An older child or adult will complain about the inability to retract the foreskin, which may have been previously retractile.
    ◦ The presentation may be acute (due to infection) or chronic.
sections.diagnostics:
• The diagnosis is **clinical**, based on history and physical examination.
• **No imaging is necessary**.
• **Labs are generally not required**, but consider:
    ◦ **Swab for Culture & Sensitivity**: If purulent discharge is present, to guide antibiotic therapy.
    ◦ **KOH Prep**: To check for Candida if fungal balanitis is suspected.
    ◦ **HbA1c / Blood Glucose**: In adults with recurrent balanitis to screen for undiagnosed Diabetes Mellitus.
    ◦ **Biopsy**: Rarely needed but may be performed by a urologist if BXO diagnosis is uncertain or if there is a suspicion of malignancy (e.g., penile squamous cell carcinoma).
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**.
• Physiologic phimosis resolves spontaneously in almost all cases.
• Pathologic phimosis responds very well to treatment, whether with topical steroids or surgery.
    ◦ Circumcision is curative.

sections.overview:
• **Paraphimosis** is a **urologic emergency** that occurs in uncircumcised or partially circumcised males.
    ◦ It is defined by the inability to reduce (pull forward) a retracted foreskin back over the **glans penis**.
    ◦ The retracted foreskin becomes trapped behind the **coronal sulcus**, forming a tight, constricting band.
    ◦ This band impairs venous and lymphatic drainage from the glans, leading to severe **pain**, **edema**, and ultimately, **arterial compromise**, **ischemia**, and **necrosis** if not treated promptly.
• **Paraphimosis vs. Phimosis**:
    ◦ **Paraphimosis**: Retracted foreskin is **trapped** behind the glans (can't be pulled forward). This is an **emergency**.
    ◦ **Phimosis**: Foreskin is too tight and **cannot be retracted** over the glans. This is not typically an emergency unless it causes **urinary obstruction**.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• Relatively uncommon, affecting approximately 1% of **uncircumcised males** over the age of 16.
• Has a **bimodal age distribution**:
    ◦ **Adolescents**: Often due to vigorous sexual activity or forcible retraction.
    ◦ **Elderly men**: Often iatrogenic, related to **catheterization** and care in long-term facilities.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient presents with acute onset of severe **penile pain** and **swelling**.
    ◦ The history often reveals a precipitating event such as recent **catheterization**, sexual activity, or cleaning where the foreskin was not reduced.
• Patients may delay seeking care due to embarrassment.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Paraphimosis is a clinical diagnosis**.
    ◦ It is made based on the characteristic history and physical exam findings.
• **No imaging or laboratory studies are necessary for diagnosis**.
• A **doppler ultrasound** may be used in rare, equivocal cases or to assess arterial flow if **necrosis** is suspected, but this should **never** delay attempts at reduction.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** with prompt diagnosis and treatment.
    ◦ Full recovery is expected.
• **Poor** if treatment is delayed (>24 hours), leading to a high risk of **ischemic tissue damage** and **necrosis**.

sections.overview:
• Priapism is a persistent penile erection lasting more than 4 hours that is not associated with sexual stimulation or desire.
    ◦ It is a **urologic emergency** that requires prompt evaluation and management to prevent permanent erectile dysfunction.
    ◦ There are three main types:
        ▪ **Ischemic (Low-Flow):** The most common type (~95%). A true **urologic emergency** caused by impaired venous outflow from the corpora cavernosa, leading to a compartment syndrome of the penis.
        ▪ **Non-ischemic (High-Flow):** Uncommon. Caused by unregulated, high arterial inflow, typically from a fistula. It is not an emergency.
        ▪ **Stuttering (Recurrent):** Recurrent, self-limiting episodes of **ischemic priapism**.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence:** ~1.5 per 100,000 person-years.
• **Distribution:** Bimodal age distribution:
    ◦ Ages 5-10 (primarily due to **Sickle Cell Disease**).
    ◦ Ages 20-50 (primarily idiopathic or medication-induced).
• **Sickle Cell Disease:** Affects up to 40% of males with SCD at some point in their lifetime.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The patient presents with a persistent erection lasting longer than 4 hours, unrelated to sexual desire.
• The key differentiating feature in the history is the presence or absence of pain.
    ◦ **Ischemic:** Presents with severe, progressive penile pain.
    ◦ **Non-ischemic:** Typically painless or only mildly uncomfortable.
• A thorough history of medications, drug use, trauma, and underlying medical conditions (especially SCD) is crucial.
sections.diagnostics: • The primary goal of diagnostics is to differentiate **ischemic** from **non-ischemic priapism**.
sections.prognosis:
• **Ischemic:** The prognosis for erectile function depends entirely on the **duration of the erection before successful treatment**.
    ◦ **< 12 hours:** Good prognosis.
    ◦ **12-24 hours:** ~50% recover erectile function.
    ◦ **> 24 hours:** Poor prognosis.
• **Non-ischemic:** Excellent prognosis. Erectile function is typically preserved as there is no ischemia.

sections.overview:
• Peyronie Disease (PD) is an acquired, localized fibrotic disorder of the **tunica albuginea** of the penis.
    ◦ Characterized by the formation of fibrous, non-compliant plaques, leading to penile pain, curvature, shortening, and erectile dysfunction (ED).
    ◦ The condition progresses through two distinct phases:
        ▪ An initial **acute inflammatory phase**
        ▪ A subsequent **chronic fibrotic (stable) phase**
sections.etiology:
• The exact etiology is believed to be multifactorial, with the most accepted theory involving repetitive microtrauma to the erect penis (e.g., during intercourse).
    ◦ **Initial Trauma:** Microvascular injury to the tunica albuginea initiates an inflammatory cascade.
    ◦ **Aberrant Wound Healing:** In genetically susceptible individuals, this healing process is dysregulated, leading to fibrin deposition.
    ◦ **Plaque Formation:** Instead of normal fibrinolysis, there is an upregulation of profibrotic cytokines like **TGF-β1**, which stimulates fibroblasts to excessively produce and deposit collagen, elastin, and fibrin, forming a dense, inelastic plaque.
    ◦ **Clinical Manifestations:** The non-compliant plaque restricts the expansion of the tunica albuginea during an erection, causing the penis to bend or deform toward the side of the plaque.
• **Acute Phase:**
    ◦ Lasts 6-18 months.
    ◦ Characterized by active inflammation, plaque evolution, and often **penile pain** with or without erections.
    ◦ Penile deformity may change or worsen during this phase.
• **Chronic (Stable) Phase:**
    ◦ Inflammation subsides, and pain typically resolves.
    ◦ The plaque becomes a dense, often calcified, stable scar.
    ◦ The penile deformity stabilizes and no longer changes.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** Affects an estimated 3-9% of adult men.
    ◦ The true prevalence is likely higher due to patient embarrassment and underreporting.
• **Age of Onset:** Most commonly diagnosed in men aged **40-70 years**, with a peak incidence in the mid-50s.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A middle-aged male typically presents with a complaint of a "new bend" in his penis during erection, which may or may not be painful.
• He may report a palpable lump or hardened area on the shaft of the penis.
• The patient often expresses significant distress regarding sexual function, body image, and the ability to have intercourse.
• He may also report co-existing erectile dysfunction, either as a result of the deformity, vascular compromise, or psychological stress.
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is primarily **clinical**, based on history and physical exam.
    ◦ **Patient Photographs:** Home photos of the erect penis can help document the deformity without requiring an in-office induced erection.
    ◦ **Penile Doppler Ultrasound:**
        ▪ **Primary Role:** To visualize and characterize plaques (size, location, presence of **calcification**).
        ▪ **Secondary Role:** To assess cavernous arterial inflow and rule out vasculogenic erectile dysfunction, especially if surgical intervention is considered.
            ▪ Performed after an intracavernosal injection.
    ◦ **Questionnaires:** Peyronie's Disease Questionnaire (PDQ) is used to assess symptom bother and impact on quality of life.
    ◦ Imaging such as CT or MRI is generally not indicated.
sections.prognosis:
• The natural history is variable:
    ◦ ~10-15% may experience spontaneous improvement.
    ◦ ~40-50% will stabilize.
    ◦ ~40-45% will worsen.
• Pain from the acute phase resolves in >90% of men within 12-18 months.
• Treatment can significantly improve sexual function and quality of life, but a complete return to pre-disease anatomy is rare.
    ◦ The primary goal of intervention is a **functionally straight penis**.

sections.overview:
• Penile cancer is a rare malignancy, primarily affecting older, uncircumcised males.
    ◦ The vast majority of cases are **Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)**, arising from the epithelium of the penis.
    ◦ The most common locations are the glans and the prepuce (foreskin).
    ◦ It typically presents as a non-healing lesion, such as a mass, ulcer, or papule.
    ◦ Early diagnosis is critical, as the prognosis is strongly tied to the presence or absence of lymph node metastasis.
sections.etiology:
• **Primary Driver**: Chronic inflammation and infection with high-risk strains of **Human Papillomavirus (HPV)**, particularly **types 16 and 18**.
