• **Pathogenesis**:
    ◦ **HPV Infection**: HPV E6 and E7 oncoproteins inactivate tumor suppressor genes p53 and pRb, respectively, leading to uncontrolled cell proliferation.
    ◦ **Chronic Inflammation**: Conditions like **phimosis** (inability to retract the foreskin) lead to the accumulation of **smegma**. Smegma is a chronic irritant containing desquamated cells, oils, and bacteria, promoting an inflammatory state that can lead to dysplasia and carcinoma.
• **Progression**:
    ◦ The disease typically progresses from a pre-malignant state, such as **Carcinoma in Situ (CIS)**, to invasive carcinoma.
        ▪ **Erythroplasia of Queyrat**: Velvety red plaque on the glans or prepuce (CIS).
        ▪ **Bowen's Disease**: Scaly, gray-white plaque on the penile shaft (CIS).
• **Histology**: **Squamous Cell Carcinoma accounts for >95% of cases.** Other rare types include melanoma, basal cell carcinoma, and sarcoma.
• **Spread**: The primary route of metastasis is lymphatic. It spreads in a predictable pattern:
    ◦ Superficial inguinal nodes
    ◦ Deep inguinal nodes
    ◦ Pelvic (iliac) nodes.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Rare in developed nations like the United States and Europe (<1 case per 100,000 men).
• **Prevalence**: Significantly higher in developing countries in Africa, Asia, and South America, where circumcision is less common and hygiene standards may be lower.
• **Demographics**: Primarily a disease of older men, with a peak incidence in the **6th to 8th decades of life**. It is exceedingly rare in men who underwent neonatal circumcision.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Phimosis**: The single strongest risk factor.
• **HPV Infection (types 16, 18, 31, 33)**: A major causative agent.
• **Lack of Circumcision**: Particularly neonatal circumcision, which is nearly 100% protective.
• **Poor Personal Hygiene**: Leads to smegma accumulation.
• **Smoking**: Carcinogens are secreted in urine, leading to topical exposure.
• **Age**: Risk increases significantly after age 60.
• **Chronic Inflammatory Conditions**: Balanitis, lichen sclerosus.
• **Immunosuppression**: HIV infection, organ transplant recipients.
• **PUVA (Psoralen + UVA) Therapy**: Used for treating psoriasis.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is an older, uncircumcised male who notices a persistent lesion on his penis.
    ◦ The lesion may have been present for months to years and is often ignored or self-treated initially.
    ◦ Patients may present late due to embarrassment or fear.
• **Symptoms**:
    ◦ **Painless lump, mass, or ulcer** on the penis (most common presenting symptom).
    ◦ Change in skin color or texture of the glans or foreskin.
    ◦ Persistent sore that fails to heal.
    ◦ Bleeding from the lesion.
    ◦ Foul-smelling discharge, especially under a tight foreskin.
    ◦ **New or worsening phimosis** in an adult male (can obscure the primary tumor).
    ◦ **Palpable lump in the groin** (inguinal lymphadenopathy).
    ◦ Late-stage symptoms: dysuria, urinary retention, pain, constitutional symptoms (weight loss, fatigue).
sections.physicalExam:
• **Inspection of the Lesion**:
    ◦ **Location**: Most commonly on the **glans**, followed by the prepuce, then the shaft.
    ◦ **Appearance**: Can be **papillary/exophytic** (cauliflower-like) or **ulcerative/flat**. May appear as a reddish, velvety patch (**Erythroplasia of Queyrat**) or a scaly plaque (**Bowen's disease**).
    ◦ **Foreskin**: Must be retracted fully. If phimosis is present, a dorsal slit may be required to visualize the underlying glans.
• **Palpation**:
    ◦ **Primary Lesion**: Assess for size, induration, and fixation to underlying structures (**corpora cavernosa**).
    ◦ **Inguinal Lymph Nodes**: This is a critical part of the exam. Carefully palpate both inguinal regions for enlarged, firm, fixed, or matted lymph nodes. Up to 50% of palpable nodes are inflammatory, but they must be investigated.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Definitive Diagnosis**:
    ◦ **Punch or Excisional Biopsy**: **Required for diagnosis.** This provides histological confirmation and grading.
• **Staging Workup (to assess extent of disease)**:
    ◦ **Local Staging (T-stage)**: Physical exam is often sufficient. Penile MRI may be used to assess the depth of invasion into the **corpora cavernosa** if unclear.
    ◦ **Nodal Staging (N-stage)**:
        ▪ **Clinically Negative Nodes (no palpable lumps)**: For tumors >T1G2, a **dynamic sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB)** is the standard of care to detect micrometastases.
        ▪ **Clinically Positive Nodes (palpable lumps)**: **Fine-needle aspiration (FNA)** of the suspicious node. If positive, a therapeutic inguinal lymph node dissection is warranted.
    ◦ **Metastatic Workup (M-stage)**:
        ▪ **CT Chest/Abdomen/Pelvis or PET/CT**: Indicated for patients with high-risk tumors (e.g., high grade, large size) or confirmed inguinal node metastasis to look for distant disease.
sections.treatment:
• **Carcinoma in Situ (CIS)**:
    ◦ **Topical therapy**: 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) cream, Imiquimod cream.
    ◦ **Ablative therapy**: Laser ablation (CO2, Nd:YAG).
    ◦ **Surgical**: Circumcision (if lesion is on prepuce), wide local excision.
• **Localized Invasive Cancer (T1-T2): Penis-Sparing Techniques**
    ◦ **Wide Local Excision**: For small lesions.
    ◦ **Glansectomy**: Removal of the glans with skin graft reconstruction.
    ◦ **Mohs Micrographic Surgery**: Provides maximal tissue preservation.
    ◦ **Partial Penectomy**: Removal of the distal part of the penis.
• **Locally Advanced Cancer (T3-T4)**:
    ◦ **Partial or Total Penectomy**: More aggressive surgery is required for tumors invading deep structures. A total penectomy requires creation of a perineal urethrostomy for urination.
• **Nodal Disease (N+)**:
    ◦ **Inguinal Lymph Node Dissection (ILND)**: Therapeutic removal of lymph nodes.
    ◦ **Adjuvant Therapy**: Chemotherapy or radiation may be given after surgery if there is extensive nodal disease.
• **Metastatic Disease (M1)**:
    ◦ **Systemic Chemotherapy**: Palliative intent. Common regimens include TIP (Paclitaxel, Ifosfamide, Cisplatin).
    ◦ **Palliative Radiation**: For symptomatic bone or brain metastases.
sections.management:
• **Multidisciplinary Team**: Requires collaboration between urology, medical oncology, radiation oncology, pathology, and often psychosocial support/psychiatry.
• **Surveillance**: Post-treatment follow-up is crucial for detecting recurrence.
    ◦ **Schedule**: Physical exam (including inguinal palpation) every 3-6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.
    ◦ **Imaging**: CT scans as clinically indicated for high-risk patients.
• **Patient Education**: Counsel on smoking cessation, safe sexual practices, and self-examination. Address the significant psychological, sexual, and body image impacts of treatment.
sections.complications:
• **Disease-Related**: Urethral obstruction, pain, bleeding, fistula formation.
• **Treatment-Related**:
    ◦ **Surgical**:
        ▪ **Penectomy**: Altered urinary stream (may require sitting to urinate), sexual dysfunction, severe body image issues.
        ▪ **Inguinal Lymph Node Dissection**: High risk of **lymphedema** of the legs and scrotum, wound infection, skin flap necrosis, DVT/PE.
    ◦ **Chemotherapy/Radiation**: Standard systemic side effects (myelosuppression, neuropathy, nephrotoxicity) and local skin reactions.
sections.prognosis:
• The **single most important prognostic factor is the presence and extent of lymph node metastasis.**
    ◦ **Node-Negative Disease**: Excellent prognosis; 5-year survival rate is >90%.
    ◦ **Inguinal Node-Positive Disease**: Prognosis drops significantly; 5-year survival is ~50-70%.
    ◦ **Pelvic Node-Positive or Distant Metastatic Disease**: Poor prognosis; 5-year survival is <10%.

sections.overview:
• Acute cystitis is an infection and inflammation of the lower urinary tract, specifically the bladder.
• It is one of the most common bacterial infections encountered in outpatient medicine.
• Classified as either **uncomplicated** or **complicated**.
    ◦ **Uncomplicated**: Occurs in a healthy, non-pregnant, premenopausal female with a structurally and functionally normal urinary tract.
    ◦ **Complicated**: Occurs in patients with factors that increase the risk of treatment failure. This includes males, pregnant patients, diabetics, immunosuppressed individuals, those with indwelling catheters, or underlying urologic abnormalities (e.g., stones, obstruction, VUR).
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology (Causative Organisms)**
    ◦ **_Escherichia coli_ (E. coli)**: The most common pathogen, accounting for **75-95%** of uncomplicated cases.
    ◦ **_Staphylococcus saprophyticus_**: The second most common cause, particularly in young, sexually active women (**"honeymoon cystitis"**).
    ◦ **_Klebsiella pneumoniae_**
    ◦ **_Proteus mirabilis_**: Associated with urease production, leading to alkaline urine and **struvite stone** formation.
    ◦ **_Enterococcus faecalis_**
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The primary mechanism is an **ascending infection**.
        ▪ **Colonization**: Uropathogenic bacteria, typically from the host's own fecal flora, colonize the periurethral area.
        ▪ **Ascension**: Bacteria ascend the urethra into the bladder. This is facilitated by the shorter female urethra and mechanical factors like sexual intercourse.
        ▪ **Adherence & Invasion**: Bacteria with virulence factors (e.g., fimbriae/pili) adhere to the urothelium, resisting the flushing mechanism of urination and triggering an inflammatory response.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Extremely common, especially in females.
• **Gender**: Women > Men (lifetime risk for women is >50%). The short female urethra is a key predisposing factor.
• **Age**: Bimodal peaks in women:
    ◦ Young, sexually active women (18-30 years).
    ◦ Postmenopausal women (due to estrogen deficiency and changes in vaginal flora).
• **Males**: UTIs in men are uncommon and are generally considered **complicated** until proven otherwise, often suggesting an underlying anatomical or functional abnormality (e.g., BPH, prostatitis).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The patient is typically a female presenting with the abrupt onset of **lower urinary tract symptoms**.
• The presentation is classic for localized bladder inflammation **without systemic signs**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Urinalysis (UA)**: The primary diagnostic test. A mid-stream clean-catch sample is preferred.
    ◦ Key findings include:
        ▪ **Pyuria**: Presence of white blood cells (WBCs). Indicated by **+ Leukocyte Esterase** on dipstick or >5-10 WBCs/hpf on microscopy.
        ▪ **Bacteriuria**: Presence of bacteria. Indicated by **+ Nitrites** on dipstick (specific for gram-negative enterobacteriaceae like **_E. coli_** which convert urinary nitrates to nitrites).
        ▪ **Hematuria**: Presence of red blood cells (RBCs) is common.
• **Urine Culture and Sensitivity (C&S)**: The **gold standard**, but not required for all cases.
    ◦ **Indications for Culture**:
        ▪ **Complicated UTI** (males, pregnancy, diabetes, etc.)
        ▪ Symptoms not characteristic of simple cystitis
        ▪ Failure to respond to initial therapy
        ▪ Recurrent symptoms (<1 month after treatment)
    ◦ A positive culture is typically defined as **10^5 CFU/mL**, although lower counts can be significant in symptomatic patients.
• **Imaging (Ultrasound, CT)**: Generally **not indicated** for uncomplicated cystitis. Reserved for patients with suspected complications, anatomical abnormalities, obstruction, or recurrent infections.
sections.prognosis:
• **Uncomplicated Cystitis**: Excellent. With appropriate antibiotic therapy, symptoms typically resolve within 24-48 hours.
• **Complicated Cystitis**: Generally good, but the prognosis is more dependent on the underlying complicating factor and the patient's overall health status.

sections.overview:
• **Hemorrhagic cystitis (HC)** is a diffuse inflammatory condition of the bladder characterized by **bleeding from the bladder mucosa**
    ◦ The clinical spectrum ranges from microscopic hematuria with mild irritative voiding symptoms to **severe, life-threatening gross hematuria** with clot formation, urinary retention, and potential for systemic complications like anemia and renal failure
    ◦ It is not a primary diagnosis but rather a consequence of an underlying infectious, chemical, or radiation-induced insult to the urothelium
sections.etiology:
• The underlying pathophysiology involves damage to the transitional epithelium (**urothelium**) and blood vessels of the bladder wall, leading to mucosal erosion, edema, and hemorrhage
• **Major Causes**
    ◦ **Chemotherapy-Induced**
        ▪ **Pathophysiology:** Caused by alkylating agents like **cyclophosphamide** and **ifosfamide**
        ▪ These drugs are metabolized in the liver to toxic metabolites, primarily **acrolein**, which is excreted in the urine
        ▪ **Acrolein** directly irritates the bladder urothelium, causing inflammation, ulceration, and bleeding
        ▪ This is the most classic and high-yield cause
    ◦ **Radiation-Induced**
        ▪ **Pathophysiology:** Pelvic radiation therapy causes progressive obliterative endarteritis of small blood vessels in the bladder wall
        ▪ This leads to chronic ischemia, tissue hypoxia, mucosal friability, and the development of fragile **telangiectasias** that are prone to bleeding
        ▪ Can present acutely during therapy or, more commonly, have a delayed onset months to years after radiation is complete
    ◦ **Infectious**
        ▪ **Viral**
            ▪ **BK virus (polyomavirus):** A major cause in immunocompromised patients, especially post-hematopoietic stem cell transplant (**HSCT**). The virus remains latent in the renal tubules and reactivates during periods of intense immunosuppression
            ▪ **Adenovirus:** Commonly seen in children and immunocompromised adults
            ▪ Other viruses: Cytomegalovirus (CMV), Influenza A
        ▪ **Bacterial:** While standard bacterial cystitis (*E. coli*, *Klebsiella*, *Proteus*) can cause microscopic hematuria, it is a less common cause of severe HC compared to viral or chemical etiologies
        ▪ **Fungal:** *Candida*, *Aspergillus*
    ◦ **Toxins:** Exposure to certain industrial chemicals (e.g., aniline dyes, toluidine)
sections.epidemiology:
• The incidence is highest in specific at-risk populations
• **Chemotherapy:** Occurs in 10-40% of patients receiving **cyclophosphamide** or **ifosfamide** without prophylaxis
• **Radiation:** Delayed HC affects 5-10% of patients who undergo pelvic radiotherapy
• **HSCT:** **BK virus-associated HC** occurs in 10-25% of allogeneic HSCT recipients
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients present with a classic triad of symptoms, with severity varying dramatically
• The key feature is **visible blood in the urine** in the setting of **irritative voiding symptoms**
• The presentation can be acute and dramatic, especially in cases of chemotherapy-induced or viral HC
sections.diagnostics:
• **Urinalysis (UA)**
    ◦ Will show **large RBCs** (gross or microscopic hematuria)
    ◦ May show pyuria (WBCs), proteinuria
    ◦ Leukocyte esterase and nitrites may be positive if a bacterial co-infection is present
• **Urine Culture and Sensitivity:** Essential to rule out or identify a bacterial cause
• **Urine Viral Studies**
    ◦ **Urine PCR for BK virus and adenovirus** is critical in immunocompromised or post-HSCT patients
• **Labs**
    ◦ **Complete Blood Count (CBC):** To assess hemoglobin and hematocrit for anemia and to check platelet count
    ◦ **Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP):** To evaluate renal function (BUN/Creatinine), especially important if urinary obstruction is suspected
    ◦ **Coagulation studies (PT/INR, PTT):** To rule out an underlying coagulopathy
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Renal and Bladder Ultrasound (US):** Excellent initial test. Can visualize bladder wall thickening, intraluminal clots, and assess for **hydronephrosis**, which would indicate upper tract obstruction
    ◦ **CT Urogram:** Used to evaluate the entire urinary tract (kidneys, ureters, bladder) to rule out other causes of hematuria such as renal cell carcinoma, urothelial carcinoma, or nephrolithiasis
• **Cystoscopy**
    ◦ **Gold standard for diagnosis**
    ◦ Allows direct visualization of the bladder mucosa, which typically appears diffusely erythematous, edematous, and friable
    ◦ Can identify specific bleeding points, **telangiectasias** (common in radiation cystitis), or ulcerations
    ◦ Can be both diagnostic and therapeutic (e.g., clot evacuation, fulguration of bleeders)
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is highly dependent on the etiology, severity, and the patient's underlying condition
• Chemotherapy-induced HC often resolves once the drug is cleared
• Viral HC in transplant patients can be persistent and difficult to manage
• **Radiation-induced HC often has a chronic, relapsing-remitting course and can be challenging to treat, carrying a more guarded prognosis for quality of life.**

sections.overview:
• **Interstitial Cystitis (IC)**, also known as **Bladder Pain Syndrome (BPS)**, is a chronic clinical syndrome characterized by **pelvic pain**, pressure, or discomfort perceived to be related to the urinary bladder, accompanied by at least one other urinary symptom such as persistent **urgency** or **frequency**
• It is a **diagnosis of exclusion**, made only after ruling out other identifiable causes like **urinary tract infection (UTI)**, bladder cancer, or prostatitis
• The condition significantly impacts quality of life
sections.etiology:
• The exact etiology is unknown and likely multifactorial. Leading theories include:
    ◦ **Urothelial/GAG Layer Dysfunction**: A defect in the glycosaminoglycan (GAG) layer lining the bladder may allow toxic substances in urine to penetrate the bladder wall, leading to tissue inflammation, nerve irritation, and pain
    ◦ **Mast Cell Activation**: An increased number of activated mast cells in the bladder submucosa and detrusor muscle release histamine and other inflammatory mediators, contributing to neurogenic inflammation and pain
    ◦ **Neurogenic Inflammation & Central Sensitization**: Chronic bladder inflammation may lead to upregulation of sensory nerve fibers and neuronal hypersensitivity, causing the brain to perceive non-painful stimuli as painful (**allodynia**) and amplify pain signals (**hyperalgesia**)
    ◦ **Autoimmune Component**: Strong association with other autoimmune and systemic inflammatory conditions such as Sjögren's syndrome, lupus, fibromyalgia, and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects an estimated 3-8 million women and 1-4 million men in the United States
• **Gender**: Predominantly affects females (**Female:Male ratio ~9:1**)
• **Age of Onset**: Typically presents in young to middle-aged adults, with a mean age of onset around 40 years
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic patient is a woman in her 30s-40s presenting with a long history of "**recurrent UTIs**" despite persistently **negative** urine cultures
• The primary complaint is chronic **pelvic pain** referred to the bladder that waxes and wanes, often exacerbated by specific triggers
    ◦ Accompanied by debilitating urinary **frequency** and **urgency**
sections.diagnostics:
• A **diagnosis of exclusion** based on clinical symptoms in the absence of other identifiable pathology
• **Urinalysis (UA) with Microscopic Exam & Urine Culture**
    ◦ **Essential first step** to rule out **UTI**
    ◦ In IC/BPS, UA and culture are typically **negative**
    ◦ Microscopic hematuria can be present
• **Urine Cytology**
    ◦ Recommended in patients with risk factors for bladder cancer (e.g., >40 years old, history of smoking, gross hematuria) to rule out carcinoma in situ
• **Urodynamic Studies**
    ◦ Not required for diagnosis but can be useful to rule out detrusor overactivity or bladder outlet obstruction
    ◦ May show low functional bladder capacity and pain with bladder filling
• **Cystoscopy with Hydrodistention**
    ◦ Considered the gold standard for visualizing the bladder wall and supporting the diagnosis
    ◦ **Hunner's Lesions**
        ▪ Distinct, reddish-brown inflammatory lesions with small vessels radiating towards a central scar
        ▪ May bleed or fissure with hydrodistention
        ▪ **Pathognomonic for IC/BPS** but found in only 10-20% of patients
    ◦ **Glomerulations**
        ▪ Diffuse, pinpoint petechial hemorrhages seen on the bladder wall after hydrodistention
        ▪ This finding is non-specific but supportive of the diagnosis
sections.prognosis:
• IC/BPS is a chronic, non-progressive condition
    ◦ It is not life-threatening and does not increase the risk of developing bladder cancer
• The clinical course is typically one of waxing and waning symptoms (flares and remissions)
• While there is no cure, a majority of patients can achieve significant symptom control and improved quality of life with long-term, multimodal management

sections.overview:
• Bladder cancer is a malignancy arising from the epithelial lining of the urinary bladder.
    ◦ It is the most common malignancy of the urinary system.
• The vast majority (>90%) of bladder cancers are **Urothelial Carcinomas** (previously known as Transitional Cell Carcinomas or TCC), reflecting the type of cells that line the bladder.
• The clinical course and treatment are primarily dictated by the depth of tumor invasion, specifically whether the tumor is **non-muscle invasive** (NMIBC) or **muscle-invasive** (MIBC).
    ◦ **NMIBC**: Has a high rate of recurrence but is generally not life-threatening.
    ◦ **MIBC**: Is aggressive and has a high potential for metastasis.
sections.etiology:
• The primary mechanism involves prolonged contact of urinary carcinogens with the urothelium of the bladder wall.
• **Urothelial (Transitional Cell) Carcinoma (>90%)**
    ◦ Arises from the transitional epithelial cells lining the bladder.
    ◦ Carcinogens (e.g., from **tobacco smoke**, industrial chemicals) are filtered by the kidneys, concentrated in the urine, and sit in the bladder, leading to DNA damage and malignant transformation over time.
• **Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC) (~5%)**
    ◦ Associated with chronic inflammation and irritation of the bladder lining, leading to squamous metaplasia and subsequent malignant change.
    ◦ Common causes include chronic indwelling Foley catheters, chronic UTIs, and infection with *Schistosoma haematobium*.
• **Adenocarcinoma (~2%)**
    ◦ A rare type arising from glandular cells.
    ◦ Can be associated with urachal remnants (a remnant of the fetal structure connecting the bladder to the umbilicus) or bladder exstrophy.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: 4th most common cancer in men in the United States.
• **Gender**: Men > Women (approx. 3:1 ratio).
• **Age**: Primarily a disease of older adults, with the median age at diagnosis being ~73 years.
• **Geography**: Higher incidence in industrialized nations (Western Europe, North America) and in regions like Egypt and the Middle East where *Schistosoma haematobium* is endemic (associated with SCC).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is an older male smoker who presents with **painless gross hematuria**.
    ◦ The hematuria is often intermittent.
• Some patients may be asymptomatic and diagnosed based on incidental microscopic hematuria.
• Others may present with irritative voiding symptoms that can mimic a urinary tract infection (UTI) or benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Initial Workup for Hematuria**
    ◦ **Urinalysis (UA) with Microscopy**
        ▪ Confirms hematuria (>3 RBCs/high-power field).
        ▪ May also show pyuria.
    ◦ **Urine Cytology**
        ▪ Microscopic examination of exfoliated cells in the urine.
        ▪ It has high specificity but low sensitivity, especially for low-grade tumors.
        ▪ More useful for detecting high-grade tumors and carcinoma in situ (CIS).
• **Definitive Diagnosis & Staging**
    ◦ **Cystoscopy**
        ▪ **The gold standard for diagnosis**.
        ▪ A flexible or rigid scope is inserted through the urethra to directly visualize the entire bladder mucosa.
        ▪ Any suspicious lesions (papillary tumors, red patches) are noted.
    ◦ **Transurethral Resection of Bladder Tumor (TURBT)**
        ▪ This procedure is both diagnostic and therapeutic.
        ▪ It is performed under anesthesia in the operating room.
        ▪ The urologist uses a resectoscope to excise the tumor.
        ▪ The resected tissue is sent to pathology to determine tumor type, grade, and depth of invasion (i.e., if the **muscularis propria** is involved).
• **Upper Tract Evaluation & Staging Imaging**
    ◦ **CT Urography (CT-IVP)**
        ▪ The imaging modality of choice.
        ▪ A multiphasic CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with and without IV contrast.
        ▪ It evaluates the bladder for tumor extent and assesses the kidneys and ureters for synchronous upper tract urothelial cancers.
        ▪ It also helps detect lymph node involvement and distant metastases.
    ◦ **MRI Urography**
        ▪ An alternative if CT contrast is contraindicated.
    ◦ **Chest CT / Bone Scan**
        ▪ Used to evaluate for distant metastases in patients with confirmed muscle-invasive disease.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly dependent on **tumor grade** and **stage** (depth of invasion).
• **NMIBC**
    ◦ 5-year survival is excellent (>90%).
    ◦ However, the recurrence rate is high (50-70%), and a small percentage (~15%) will progress to muscle-invasive disease.
• **MIBC**
    ◦ More guarded prognosis.
    ◦ 5-year survival with radical cystectomy is approximately 50-70%.
• **Metastatic Disease**
    ◦ Poor prognosis, with a 5-year survival rate of <15%.

sections.overview:
• **Neurogenic bladder** is a broad term for bladder dysfunction (either **flaccid** or **spastic**) caused by damage to the central or peripheral nerves that control urination.
    ◦ The bladder may fail to store urine, fail to empty urine, or both.
• The primary goals of management are to protect the upper urinary tract (kidneys), achieve urinary continence, and improve the patient's quality of life.
• The clinical presentation and treatment are dictated by the location and nature of the neurologic lesion.
sections.etiology:
• The control of micturition is complex, involving the cerebral cortex, **pontine micturition center (PMC)**, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves.
    ◦ Disruption at any level can cause neurogenic bladder.
• The pathophysiology is best understood by classifying the lesion as **Upper Motor Neuron (UMN)** or **Lower Motor Neuron (LMN)**.
sections.epidemiology:
• The prevalence directly correlates with the prevalence of the underlying neurologic disorders.
• ~**80%** of patients with **MS** will develop bladder dysfunction.
• ~**80%** of patients with **spina bifida** have neurogenic bladder.
• Up to **75%** of **spinal cord injury** patients experience neurogenic bladder.
• Long-standing **Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus** are common causes of LMN-type bladder dysfunction.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is highly variable and depends on the underlying neurologic lesion.
• Patients present with **storage symptoms**, **voiding symptoms**, or a combination.
• The history is crucial and should focus on both urinary symptoms and a detailed neurologic review of systems (bowel/sexual function, weakness, numbness, gait changes).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Initial Workup**
    ◦ **Urinalysis & Urine Culture**: Rule out **urinary tract infection (UTI)**, which can mimic or exacerbate symptoms.
    ◦ **Post-Void Residual (PVR) Volume**
        ▪ **Crucial first step**.
        ▪ Measured with a bladder scanner or straight catheterization immediately after voiding.
        ▪ **Normal**: < 50 mL
        ▪ **Abnormal**: > 100-200 mL suggests inadequate emptying (common in LMN/flaccid bladder or **DSD**).
    ◦ **Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP)**: Assess renal function (**BUN**, **Creatinine**).
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Renal and Bladder Ultrasound**: Assesses for **hydronephrosis**, bladder stones, bladder wall thickening, and provides a non-invasive PVR. **Essential for monitoring upper tract health**.
• **Specialized Testing**
    ◦ **Urodynamic Studies**: **The gold standard for diagnosis**.
        ▪ Measures bladder pressures, volume, and flow during filling and voiding.
        ▪ Differentiates detrusor overactivity from underactivity, assesses bladder compliance, and can definitively identify **Detrusor-Sphincter Dyssynergia (DSD)**.
    ◦ **Videourodynamics**: Combines urodynamics with fluoroscopy to visualize bladder neck and sphincter function during voiding.
    ◦ **MRI of Brain and/or Spine**: To identify or characterize the underlying neurologic cause if unknown.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis depends entirely on the underlying neurologic condition and the quality of bladder management.
• With diligent management (especially **CIC** and regular monitoring), renal function can be preserved, and quality of life can be significantly improved.
• Poor compliance or inadequate management can lead to life-threatening complications like **renal failure** and **sepsis**.

sections.overview:
• Urethritis is the inflammation of the urethra, most commonly due to a **sexually transmitted infection (STI)**.
• It is a major cause of **urethral discharge**, **dysuria**, and **pruritus**, primarily in sexually active individuals.
• The condition is broadly classified into two categories based on the causative organism:
    ◦ **Gonococcal Urethritis (GU)**, caused by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*.
    ◦ **Nongonococcal Urethritis (NGU)**, caused by other pathogens, most notably *Chlamydia trachomatis*.
• Prompt diagnosis and treatment are essential to prevent complications and further transmission.
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The pathogen gains entry to the urethra, typically during sexual contact, and adheres to the mucosal epithelial cells.
    ◦ This triggers an inflammatory response characterized by the influx of **polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMNs)**, leading to mucosal swelling, erythema, and the production of urethral discharge (exudate).
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Gonococcal Urethritis (GU)**
        ▪ **_Neisseria gonorrhoeae_**: A **gram-negative intracellular diplococcus**. Accounts for approximately 10-20% of cases.
    ◦ **Nongonococcal Urethritis (NGU)**
        ▪ **_Chlamydia trachomatis_**: The most common cause of NGU (15-40% of cases). An obligate intracellular bacterium.
        ▪ **_Mycoplasma genitalium_**: An increasingly recognized cause (15-25%), particularly implicated in persistent or recurrent NGU.
        ▪ **_Trichomonas vaginalis_**: More common cause of vaginitis in women, but can cause NGU in men (5-15%).
        ▪ **_Ureaplasma urealyticum_**: Role is controversial but considered a potential pathogen.
        ▪ **Viral Causes**: Less common; include Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) and Adenovirus.
        ▪ **Non-infectious Causes**: Rare; can result from trauma (e.g., catheterization), chemical irritation (spermicides, soaps), or reactive arthritis.
sections.epidemiology:
• One of the most common STI syndromes diagnosed in men in the United States.
• Highest incidence is in sexually active individuals aged 15-29.
• NGU is more prevalent than GU in most developed countries.
• A significant proportion of cases, especially those caused by *Chlamydia* and *Mycoplasma*, are **asymptomatic**, contributing to silent transmission.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a male complaining of **urethral discharge** and/or **dysuria**.
• The onset and character of symptoms can provide clues to the etiology.
• **Incubation Period**
    ◦ **GU**: Typically shorter, around 2-7 days.
    ◦ **NGU**: Typically longer, around 7-21 days.
• A significant number of patients, particularly with NGU, may be **asymptomatic**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT)**
    ◦ **Gold Standard** for detecting _N. gonorrhoeae_ and _C. trachomatis_.
    ◦ Highly sensitive and specific.
    ◦ **Specimen**: First-catch urine (preferred in men) or urethral swab.
• **Gram Stain of Urethral Smear**
    ◦ Rapid, point-of-care test.
    ◦ **Presumptive GU**: Presence of **gram-negative intracellular diplococci (GNID)** within PMNs.
    ◦ **Urethritis confirmed**: **≥2 PMNs** per oil immersion field. If PMNs are present but no GNID, it's presumptively NGU.
• **Urine Dipstick**
    ◦ May show positive leukocyte esterase, but lacks specificity.
    ◦ Not used for definitive diagnosis.
• **Culture for Gonorrhea**
    ◦ Less sensitive than NAAT but necessary for antimicrobial susceptibility testing, especially in cases of suspected treatment failure ("test-of-cure").
• **_M. genitalium_ & _T. vaginalis_ Testing**
    ◦ Consider NAAT for these organisms in cases of persistent or recurrent NGU.
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent for uncomplicated urethritis when diagnosed and treated promptly with appropriate antibiotics.
• Recurrence is common but is usually due to reinfection from an untreated partner rather than treatment failure.
• Persistent NGU can be challenging and may require further testing for less common pathogens like *M. genitalium*.

sections.overview:
• Gonococcal Urethritis (GU) is a common sexually transmitted infection (STI) of the urethra caused by the bacterium *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*.
    ◦ Characterized by an **abrupt onset** of symptoms, most notably **purulent urethral discharge** and **dysuria**.
    ◦ It is the second most commonly reported bacterial STI in the United States.
    ◦ Prompt diagnosis and treatment are crucial to prevent complications and further transmission.
    ◦ Co-infection with *Chlamydia trachomatis* is common.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Organism**: ***Neisseria gonorrhoeae***
    ◦ A gram-negative, non-motile, non-spore-forming diplococcus.
    ◦ Classic description: **"Gram-negative intracellular diplococcus"** seen within neutrophils on a Gram stain.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Attachment**: The gonococcus uses surface pili and Opa proteins to attach to the columnar epithelial cells of the anterior urethra.
    ◦ **Invasion**: The bacteria penetrate the host cells and multiply, establishing infection in the subepithelial connective tissue.
    ◦ **Inflammatory Response**: The infection triggers a robust host inflammatory response, characterized by a massive influx of neutrophils.
    ◦ **Clinical Manifestations**: The accumulation of neutrophils, dead epithelial cells, and bacteria results in the characteristic thick, **purulent urethral discharge** (exudate). The inflammation of the urethral mucosa causes **dysuria**.
sections.epidemiology:
• One of the most common reportable infectious diseases in the U.S.
• Incidence is highest in adolescents and young adults (ages **15-24**).
• Higher prevalence in men who have sex with men (MSM).
• Rising rates of **antimicrobial resistance** (especially to fluoroquinolones and macrolides) are a major public health concern.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Typically presents in a sexually active male with an **abrupt onset** of symptoms after a recent sexual encounter.
• **Incubation Period**: Short, typically **2-7 days**.
• The "classic" presentation is a male complaining of "burning on urination" and a "drip from my penis."
• Up to 10% of men may be asymptomatic carriers, acting as a reservoir for transmission.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Preferred Method - NAAT**:
    ◦ **Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT)** is the gold standard for diagnosis due to its high sensitivity and specificity.
    ◦ **Sample**: First-catch urine (patient should not have voided for at least 1 hour) is the preferred sample in men. A urethral swab is an alternative.
    ◦ NAAT panels almost always test for *N. gonorrhoeae* and *C. trachomatis* simultaneously.
• **Gram Stain**:
    ◦ A urethral swab specimen can be examined under a microscope.
    ◦ **Finding**: **Gram-negative intracellular diplococci** within polymorphonuclear leukocytes (neutrophils).
    ◦ Highly specific (>99%) but less sensitive (~95%) than NAAT. It is useful for a rapid, presumptive diagnosis in symptomatic men.
• **Culture**:
    ◦ Requires a urethral swab specimen plated on **Thayer-Martin agar** (or other selective medium).
    ◦ **Primary Utility**: Essential for **antimicrobial susceptibility testing**, which is critical for monitoring and responding to antibiotic resistance.
• **Routine STI Screening**:
    ◦ All patients diagnosed with gonorrhea should also be tested for other STIs, including Chlamydia, HIV, and syphilis.
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent for uncomplicated urethritis when treated promptly and appropriately with effective antibiotics.
• Untreated infections can lead to complications.
• Reinfection is common if risk behaviors continue and partners are not treated.
• The primary long-term concern is the continued emergence of **antimicrobial resistance**.

sections.overview:
• **Nongonococcal Urethritis (NGU)** is inflammation of the urethra not caused by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*.
• The most common identifiable infectious cause is ***Chlamydia trachomatis***.
• It is the most frequently reported bacterial **sexually transmitted infection (STI)** in the United States.
• Chlamydia is often referred to as a **"silent" infection** because the majority of cases, particularly in women, are **asymptomatic**, which facilitates its transmission.
• Untreated, it can lead to serious reproductive health complications.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Most Common Cause:** ***Chlamydia trachomatis*** (serovars D-K) is responsible for approximately 15-55% of NGU cases.
    ◦ **Other Causes:**
        ▪ *Mycoplasma genitalium* (increasingly recognized)
        ▪ *Ureaplasma urealyticum*
        ▪ *Trichomonas vaginalis*
        ▪ Viruses (e.g., Adenovirus, HSV)
• **Pathophysiology of *Chlamydia trachomatis***
    ◦ *C. trachomatis* is an **obligate intracellular gram-negative bacterium** and cannot be visualized on a standard Gram stain.
    ◦ It has a unique **biphasic life cycle**:
        ▪ **Elementary Body (EB):** The infectious, extracellular, metabolically inactive form. It attaches to and enters host columnar epithelial cells (urethra, cervix, conjunctiva, etc.).
        ▪ **Reticulate Body (RB):** The non-infectious, intracellular, metabolically active, replicating form. Inside the host cell, EBs transform into RBs.
    ◦ RBs replicate via binary fission within a cellular inclusion.
    ◦ After ~48-72 hours, RBs reorganize back into EBs.
    ◦ The host cell lyses, releasing the new EBs to infect adjacent cells, perpetuating the infection and causing an inflammatory response.
sections.epidemiology:
• Most common reportable bacterial **STI** in the U.S.
• Highest prevalence is among sexually active individuals **aged 15-24**.
• Higher rates are seen in minority ethnic/racial groups and in **men who have sex with men (MSM)**.
• A significant reservoir of infection exists due to a high rate of **asymptomatic cases** (>70% in females, up to 50% in males).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient often presents due to symptoms of urethral irritation or during routine STI screening.
• The incubation period is typically **7 to 21 days**.
• Many patients, especially females, are entirely **asymptomatic** and are diagnosed via screening.
• The onset of symptoms is often **gradual** and **milder** than in gonococcal urethritis.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Gold Standard: Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT)**
    ◦ Highly sensitive and specific.
    ◦ **Preferred Samples:**
        ▪ **Men:** **First-catch urine**.
        ▪ **Women:** **Vaginal swab** (can be self-collected) is preferred over endocervical swabs or urine due to higher sensitivity.
    ◦ NAAT can also be performed on rectal and pharyngeal swabs in at-risk populations (e.g., MSM).
• **Urethral Smear (Gram Stain)** - in symptomatic males:
    ◦ **Classic NGU Finding:** Presence of **≥2 WBCs per oil immersion field** AND **absence of gram-negative intracellular diplococci (GNID)**.
    ◦ This distinguishes NGU from gonococcal urethritis, which characteristically shows **GNID**.
• **Urinalysis:**
    ◦ May show **pyuria** (WBCs in urine) in the absence of bacteriuria on culture.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is **excellent** with early diagnosis and appropriate antibiotic therapy; the infection resolves without sequelae.
• If left untreated or in cases of repeat infection, the risk of long-term complications, particularly **infertility in women**, increases significantly.

sections.overview:
• **Urethral stricture** is an abnormal narrowing of the urethra caused by **scar tissue (fibrosis)** in the submucosal layer and the surrounding corpus spongiosum (**spongiofibrosis**)
    ◦ This scarring reduces the luminal diameter, leading to obstruction of urine flow from the bladder
    ◦ It is almost exclusively a disease of males due to their longer urethra
    ◦ The clinical presentation is dominated by **obstructive voiding symptoms**
sections.etiology:
• The underlying pathophysiology involves injury to the urethral epithelium or the underlying corpus spongiosum, which incites an inflammatory response, leading to fibroblast proliferation and collagen deposition, resulting in a scar that contracts and narrows the urethral lumen
• **Common Etiologies**:
    ◦ **Iatrogenic (Most Common, ~45%)**
        ▪ Traumatic urethral catheterization (prolonged or difficult placement)
        ▪ Transurethral surgery (e.g., TURP, cystoscopy, resection of bladder tumors)
        ▪ Prior hypospadias repair
    ◦ **Idiopathic (~30%)**
        ▪ No identifiable cause
    ◦ **Traumatic (non-iatrogenic)**
        ▪ **Straddle Injury**: A direct blow to the perineum (e.g., falling on a bicycle frame or fence) crushes the bulbar urethra against the pubic symphysis, representing the classic cause of a **bulbar urethral stricture**
        ▪ **Pelvic Fracture**: Associated with disruption of the **posterior urethra** (membranous or prostatic urethra)
    ◦ **Inflammatory / Infectious**
        ▪ **Gonococcal Urethritis**: Historically a common cause, leading to long, often multifocal strictures
        ▪ **Non-gonococcal urethritis** (e.g., *Chlamydia trachomatis*)
        ▪ **Lichen Sclerosus (LS)**: Also known as **Balanitis Xerotica Obliterans (BXO)**, a chronic inflammatory skin condition that frequently causes **meatal stenosis** and **fossa navicularis strictures**
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects approximately 0.6% of susceptible men
• **Age**: Incidence shows a bimodal distribution
    ◦ Younger men: Often related to trauma
    ◦ Older men: Predominantly iatrogenic causes (catheterization, BPH procedures) and idiopathic
• **Sex**: Almost exclusively occurs in males; female urethral stricture is very rare
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The typical patient is a male presenting with a gradual onset and slow progression of **obstructive voiding symptoms** over months to years
    ◦ They may report a "slowing down" of their stream since a prior procedure or trauma
• **Recurrent UTIs** or **acute urinary retention** can be the initial presentation
sections.diagnostics:
• **Initial Evaluation**
    ◦ **Uroflowmetry**: Objective measure of urine flow rate
        ▪ The classic finding is a **low peak flow rate (Qmax < 10-12 mL/s)** with a prolonged, flattened, **"plateau-shaped"** voiding curve
    ◦ **Post-Void Residual (PVR)**: Measured by bladder ultrasound or catheterization
        ▪ An **elevated PVR** indicates inefficient bladder emptying
    ◦ **Urinalysis and Urine Culture**: To rule out an active UTI, which should be treated before any instrumentation
• **Definitive Imaging**
    ◦ **Retrograde Urethrogram (RUG)**: **GOLD STANDARD** diagnostic test for **anterior urethral strictures** (penile, bulbar)
        ▪ Contrast is injected into the urethral meatus, and an x-ray is taken to outline the entire length of the anterior urethra
        ▪ It defines the **location, length, and severity** of the stricture
    ◦ **Voiding Cystourethrogram (VCUG)**: Often performed concurrently with RUG
        ▪ The bladder is filled with contrast, and images are taken while the patient voids
        ▪ It is the best test for evaluating the **posterior urethra** (bladder neck, prostatic urethra)
• **Direct Visualization**
    ◦ **Cystourethroscopy**: Allows direct visualization of the stricture, assessment of the scar tissue's appearance, and evaluation of the lumen's caliber
        ▪ It is also used to assess the bladder for secondary changes like trabeculation or calculi
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is excellent with **urethroplasty**, which is considered curative with success rates of **85-95%**
• The prognosis is poor with endoscopic management (**dilation** or **DVIU**) as the sole treatment, with recurrence rates exceeding **50%** within the first year
    ◦ Each subsequent endoscopic attempt has an even lower chance of success

sections.overview:
• Epididymo-orchitis is the inflammation of the epididymis (epididymitis) and/or the testicle (orchitis)
    ◦ It most commonly begins as an infection in the epididymis that spreads to the ipsilateral testicle
    ◦ It is the most frequent cause of **scrotal pain** in adults in the outpatient setting
    ◦ The primary clinical challenge is to differentiate it from **testicular torsion**, which is a **urologic emergency**
sections.etiology:
• The condition is typically caused by the **retrograde ascent of pathogens** from the lower urinary tract (urethra, bladder, prostate) into the epididymis via the vas deferens
    ◦ **Men < 35 years (Sexually Transmitted)**: The most common pathogens are sexually transmitted
        ▪ ***Chlamydia trachomatis*** (most common overall in this group)
        ▪ ***Neisseria gonorrhoeae***
    ◦ **Men > 35 years (Urinary Pathogens)**: The most common pathogens are enteric organisms that cause urinary tract infections, often associated with **bladder outlet obstruction** (e.g., BPH) or recent urologic instrumentation
        ▪ ***Escherichia coli*** (most common overall in this group)
        ▪ *Klebsiella pneumoniae*
        ▪ *Proteus mirabilis*
        ▪ *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*
    ◦ **Prepubertal Boys & Geriatric Patients**:
        ▪ Primarily caused by enteric organisms (*E. coli*), often associated with underlying urogenital anomalies
    ◦ **Viral Orchitis**:
        ▪ **Mumps virus** is the classic cause of isolated orchitis, though less common now due to MMR vaccination
        ▪ Other viruses include Coxsackie, EBV, and Varicella
    ◦ **Other Causes**:
        ▪ **Amiodarone**: Can cause a sterile, non-infectious chemical epididymitis
        ▪ Trauma, autoimmune disease (e.g., Beçhet's syndrome, IgA vasculitis/HSP)
sections.epidemiology:
• Most common cause of **scrotal pain** in adults
• **Bimodal age distribution**:
    ◦ Peak 1: Young, sexually active men (18-35 years)
    ◦ Peak 2: Older men (>50 years) with BPH or other urologic issues
• Approximately 600,000 cases per year in the United States
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A male patient presents with a **gradual onset** of **unilateral scrotal pain, swelling, and erythema** that has developed over several days
• The patient may also report associated urinary symptoms or fever
• This contrasts with the **sudden, severe onset** of pain seen in **testicular torsion**
sections.diagnostics:
• **Scrotal Ultrasound with Color Doppler**:
    ◦ **Initial imaging test of choice** to rule out **testicular torsion**
    ◦ **Findings**:
        ▪ Enlarged, hypoechoic epididymis and/or testis
        ▪ **Increased blood flow (hyperemia)** to the affected structures
        ▪ Reactive hydrocele and scrotal wall thickening are common
• **Urinalysis (UA) with Urine Culture**:
    ◦ **UA**: Will often show **pyuria** (10 WBC/hpf) and/or **bacteriuria**
    ◦ **Culture**: Identifies the causative organism and guides antibiotic therapy in non-STI cases
• **STI Testing**:
    ◦ **Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT)** of a first-catch urine or urethral swab is the gold standard for detecting *N. gonorrhoeae* and *C. trachomatis*
• **Laboratory Studies**:
    ◦ **CBC**: May show **leukocytosis** with a left shift
    ◦ **Inflammatory Markers (CRP, ESR)**: May be elevated but are non-specific
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is **excellent** if diagnosed early and treated with appropriate antibiotics
• Delays in treatment increase the risk of complications like **testicular atrophy** and **infertility**
• **Mumps orchitis** carries a higher risk of subsequent **testicular atrophy**

sections.overview:
• Prostatitis is inflammation of the prostate gland and surrounding tissues, classified into four categories by the National Institutes of Health (NIH).
    ◦ **Category I: Acute Bacterial Prostatitis (ABP)**
        ▪ An acute infection of the prostate gland.
        ▪ Presents as a systemic illness (**fever**, **chills**) with severe urogenital symptoms.
    ◦ **Category II: Chronic Bacterial Prostatitis (CBP)**
        ▪ A chronic or recurrent bacterial infection of the prostate.
        ▪ Characterized by relapsing UTIs with the same organism and more subtle, intermittent symptoms.
    ◦ **Category III: Chronic Prostatitis/Chronic Pelvic Pain Syndrome (CP/CPPS)**
        ▪ The most common type (>90% of cases).
        ▪ Chronic genitourinary pain in the absence of a proven bacterial infection.
        ▪ **IIIa:** Inflammatory (leukocytes present in prostatic secretions/urine).
        ▪ **IIIb:** Non-inflammatory (no leukocytes).
    ◦ **Category IV: Asymptomatic Inflammatory Prostatitis**
        ▪ Incidental finding of prostate inflammation (leukocytes) on biopsy or in semen, without symptoms.
        ▪ Usually requires no treatment.
sections.etiology:
• **Acute Bacterial (Category I):** Caused by an ascending infection from the urethra or reflux of infected urine into the prostatic ducts.
    ◦ **Most Common Organisms (>80%):** Gram-negative enterics, primarily ***E. coli***.
    ◦ Other common pathogens:
        ▪ *Proteus*, *Klebsiella*, *Enterococcus*, *Pseudomonas*.
    ◦ In sexually active men <35 years old, consider ***Neisseria gonorrhoeae*** and ***Chlamydia trachomatis***.
• **Chronic Bacterial (Category II):** Results from a persistent bacterial nidus within the prostate, often due to undertreated acute prostatitis.
    ◦ Pathogens are similar to ABP.
    ◦ **Bacterial biofilms** form on prostatic stones (corpora amylacea), making eradication difficult.
• **Chronic Pelvic Pain Syndrome (Category III):** Pathophysiology is poorly understood and likely multifactorial. Proposed mechanisms include:
    ◦ Past, unproven infection leading to a chronic inflammatory or autoimmune state.
    ◦ **Neurogenic inflammation** and central sensitization.
    ◦ **Pelvic floor muscle dysfunction** (hypertonicity).
    ◦ Psychological factors (stress, anxiety, depression).
sections.epidemiology:
• Most common urologic diagnosis in men < 50 years old.
• Third most common in men > 50 years old (after BPH and prostate cancer).
• Lifetime prevalence is estimated to be 10-15%.
• **CP/CPPS (Category III)** accounts for 90-95% of all prostatitis cases.
• **Acute Bacterial Prostatitis (Category I)** is the least common form.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Acute Bacterial Prostatitis:**
    ◦ A male patient presenting with an **abrupt onset of high fever, chills, and malaise**, associated with significant perineal or low back pain and severe lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS).
    ◦ The patient often appears systemically ill.
• **Chronic Bacterial Prostatitis:**
    ◦ A male patient with a history of **recurrent, relapsing UTIs** caused by the same pathogen.
    ◦ Symptoms are intermittent and milder than in acute prostatitis.
    ◦ The patient is typically afebrile and does not appear ill between episodes.
• **Chronic Pelvic Pain Syndrome:**
    ◦ A male patient (often <50) whose primary complaint is **chronic pain (≥3 months)** in the pelvic region (perineum, testicles, suprapubic area).
    ◦ Voiding symptoms and pain with ejaculation are common.
    ◦ Patient appears well, and there is no history of positive urine cultures.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Urinalysis (UA)**
    ◦ **Acute Bacterial (I):** **Pyuria**, bacteriuria, hematuria.
    ◦ **Chronic Bacterial (II) & CPPS (III):** Often normal. May show leukocytes.
• **Urine Culture**
    ◦ **Acute Bacterial (I):** **Positive** for a uropathogen.
    ◦ **Chronic Bacterial (II) & CPPS (III):** Typically negative on standard mid-stream samples.
• **Prostatic Fluid Culture**
    ◦ **Acute Bacterial (I):** **NOT PERFORMED** (massage contraindicated).
    ◦ **Chronic Bacterial (II) & CPPS (III):** **Key diagnostic test (2-glass or 4-glass test)**. Culture of Expressed Prostatic Secretions (EPS) or post-massage urine (VB3) is performed.
        ▪ **2-Glass Test:** Collect mid-stream urine (VB2), then perform DRE with massage, then collect post-massage urine (VB3). **Positive for CBP if VB3 has >10x bacteria count of VB2.**
• **CBC**
    ◦ **Acute Bacterial (I):** **Leukocytosis** with a left shift.
    ◦ **Chronic Bacterial (II) & CPPS (III):** Normal.
• **Inflammatory Markers (CRP/ESR)**
    ◦ **Acute Bacterial (I):** Elevated.
    ◦ **Chronic Bacterial (II) & CPPS (III):** Normal.
• **Blood Cultures**
    ◦ **Acute Bacterial (I):** Obtain if patient is septic or hospitalized.
    ◦ **Chronic Bacterial (II) & CPPS (III):** Not indicated.
• **PSA**
    ◦ **Acute Bacterial (I):** **Markedly elevated**. Do not check acutely for cancer screening. It will return to baseline after treatment.
    ◦ **Chronic Bacterial (II) & CPPS (III):** Can be normal or mildly elevated.
• **Imaging (TRUS or CT)**
    ◦ **Acute Bacterial (I):** Not routine. Indicated if patient fails to improve on antibiotics to **rule out a prostatic abscess**.
    ◦ **Chronic Bacterial (II) & CPPS (III):** Not routine. May be used to rule out other pathology in refractory cases.
sections.prognosis:
• **Acute Bacterial Prostatitis:** Excellent with prompt and adequate antibiotic therapy. Most men recover fully.
• **Chronic Bacterial Prostatitis:** Guarded. Relapse rates are high (~50%) due to poor antibiotic penetration and bacterial biofilm formation.
• **CP/CPPS:** A chronic condition with a waxing and waning course. Complete cure is rare, but a multimodal approach can significantly improve symptoms and quality of life.

sections.overview:
• Urethritis is the inflammation of the urethra, most commonly caused by a **sexually transmitted infection (STI)**.
	◦ It is a major cause of morbidity and a key public health issue due to its potential for serious complications and efficient transmission.
	◦ The primary clinical distinction is between **Gonococcal Urethritis (GU)**, caused by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*, and **Non-Gonococcal Urethritis (NGU)**, most commonly caused by *Chlamydia trachomatis*.
sections.etiology:
• Inflammation is triggered by the direct invasion of the urethral columnar epithelium by a pathogenic microorganism.
• **Gonococcal Urethritis (GU)**
	◦ **Organism:** *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*, a **gram-negative intracellular diplococcus**.
	◦ **Pathophysiology:** The organism attaches to and penetrates columnar epithelial cells of the distal urethra. This elicits a robust neutrophilic inflammatory response, resulting in a copious, purulent exudate (pus).
• **Non-Gonococcal Urethritis (NGU)**
	◦ **Organism(s):**
		▪ ***Chlamydia trachomatis*** **(Most common, ~20-40% of cases):** An obligate intracellular bacterium. It causes inflammation that is typically less intense than gonorrhea, leading to a more mucoid or watery discharge.
		▪ ***Mycoplasma genitalium*** **(~15-30% of cases):** A bacterium lacking a cell wall. It is an increasingly recognized cause, notable for high rates of macrolide resistance.
		▪ ***Trichomonas vaginalis*** **(~5% of cases):** A motile protozoan. More commonly associated with vaginitis in women but is a significant cause of NGU in men.
		▪ **Other causes:** Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), adenovirus, *Ureaplasma urealyticum*.
• **Co-infection:** Co-infection with *N. gonorrhoeae* and *C. trachomatis* is common (up to 40% of patients with gonorrhea also have chlamydia).
	◦ This is the basis for routine dual-pathogen testing and often empiric co-treatment.
sections.epidemiology:
• Gonorrhea and Chlamydia are two of the most commonly reported infectious diseases in the United States.
• Highest incidence is in sexually active adolescents and young adults (**ages 15-24**).
• Higher prevalence in **men who have sex with men (MSM)**.
• Rates of both infections, along with antibiotic resistance (especially in *N. gonorrhoeae* and *M. genitalium*), are rising globally.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a sexually active male complaining of **dysuria** and/or **urethral discharge**.
• A significant percentage of infections, particularly Chlamydia, can be **asymptomatic**.
• **Gonococcal Urethritis (GU)**
	◦ **Onset:** Abrupt, with a short incubation period (typically **2-8 days**).
	◦ **Symptoms:** More severe **dysuria**.
	◦ **Discharge:** Copious, opaque, **purulent (thick, yellow-green) discharge**.
• **Non-Gonococcal Urethritis (NGU)**
	◦ **Onset:** More subacute or insidious, with a longer incubation period (typically **7-21 days for Chlamydia**).
	◦ **Symptoms:** Mild to moderate **dysuria**, often described as itching or burning.
	◦ **Discharge:** Scant to moderate, **mucoid (whitish)** or **serous (clear) discharge**.
		▪ Many patients may only notice crusting at the meatus in the morning.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Gold Standard: Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT)**
	◦ **Sample:** First-catch urine (at least 1 hour after last void) is the preferred sample in men. Urethral swabs are an alternative.
	◦ **Tests for:** *N. gonorrhoeae* and *C. trachomatis*. NAATs are also available for *M. genitalium* and *T. vaginalis*.
	◦ Highly sensitive and specific.
• **Microscopy (Point-of-Care Testing)**
	◦ **Gram Stain of Urethral Smear:**
		▪ **Presumptive GU:** Presence of **gram-negative intracellular diplococci (GNIDs)** within polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMNs). Highly specific (>99%) in symptomatic men.
		▪ **Evidence of Urethritis (for NGU diagnosis):** Presence of **≥2 WBCs (PMNs) per oil immersion field**.
	◦ **Urine Microscopy:**
		▪ Presence of **pyuria (≥10 WBCs/high-power field)** on the sediment of a first-void urine sample suggests urethritis.
• **Culture**
	◦ Gonococcal culture (Thayer-Martin agar) is less sensitive than NAAT but is essential for **antibiotic susceptibility testing**, which is critical due to rising resistance.
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent for **uncomplicated urethritis** when treated promptly and appropriately.
• Full cure is expected.
• **Reinfection is common** due to untreated partners.
• The prognosis is worse if complications like **PID** or **DGI** develop, which can have long-term sequelae.

sections.overview:
• **Stress Urinary Incontinence (SUI)** is the **involuntary leakage of urine** during activities that increase **intra-abdominal pressure** (e.g., coughing, sneezing, laughing, lifting, exercising).
    ◦ It is a problem of **urethral support and closure**, not a bladder muscle (**detrusor**) problem.
    ◦ Leakage occurs when the pressure inside the bladder exceeds the pressure in the urethra in the absence of a **detrusor contraction**.
sections.etiology:
• Continence is maintained when urethral pressure is greater than bladder pressure. SUI results from a failure of this mechanism due to one or both of the following:
    ◦ **Urethral Hypermobility**
        ▪ This is the most common cause.
        ▪ Weakness of the **pelvic floor muscles** (levator ani) and pelvic connective tissue (endopelvic fascia) fails to provide adequate support for the bladder neck and proximal urethra.
        ▪ During increased **intra-abdominal pressure**, the bladder neck and urethra descend ("drop") and rotate away from the anterior vaginal wall.
        ▪ This prevents the urethra from closing effectively against its supportive layer, leading to leakage.
    ◦ **Intrinsic Sphincter Deficiency (ISD)**
        ▪ This refers to a weakness of the **urethral sphincter muscle** itself.
        ▪ The urethral "valve" is unable to generate enough resting resistance to hold back urine, even with minimal or no urethral movement.
        ▪ Often results from previous pelvic surgery (e.g., prior incontinence surgery), pelvic radiation, trauma, or neurologic conditions.
        ▪ Patients with ISD often experience more severe leakage with minimal exertion.
sections.epidemiology:
• The most common type of urinary incontinence in women, especially those under 60.
• Affects an estimated 15-50% of adult women.
• Prevalence increases with age.
• Less common in men, where it is almost always iatrogenic, most commonly after **radical prostatectomy**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a patient (typically a parous, middle-aged woman) who reports episodes of **involuntary urine leakage**.
    ◦ The leakage is **predictable** and occurs immediately following a **physical trigger**.
    ◦ The amount can range from a few drops to a complete soaking.
    ◦ Importantly, the patient **does not feel an urge** to urinate before the leakage event.
    ◦ They may report limiting physical activities or social engagements due to fear of leakage.
sections.diagnostics:
• **History**
    ◦ The most important diagnostic tool.
    ◦ A detailed history can often differentiate SUI from other types of incontinence.
• **Urinalysis (UA) & Urine Culture**
    ◦ **Mandatory** to rule out **urinary tract infection (UTI)**, which can cause transient incontinence.
    ◦ Also checks for hematuria and glucosuria.
• **Post-void Residual (PVR) Volume**
    ◦ Measured via bladder scanner or catheterization immediately after voiding.
    ◦ Rules out **urinary retention** and **overflow incontinence**.
    ◦ **Normal PVR (<50-100 mL)** is expected in pure SUI.
• **Voiding Diary**
    ◦ A 3-day diary helps quantify the problem, identify triggers, and confirm the diagnosis by documenting leakage episodes relative to physical activity.
• **Urodynamic Studies**
    ◦ **Not required** for the initial diagnosis of uncomplicated SUI.
    ◦ **Indications**:
        ▪ Diagnostic uncertainty (e.g., mixed stress/urge symptoms).
        ▪ Planning for surgical intervention.
        ▪ History of prior incontinence or prolapse surgery.
        ▪ Associated neurologic conditions.
    ◦ Confirms SUI by demonstrating urine leakage with increased abdominal pressure in the absence of a detrusor contraction.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is generally **excellent**.
• **Conservative management** can lead to significant symptom improvement or resolution in many motivated patients.
• **Surgical management** with a **mid-urethral sling** offers high long-term cure and satisfaction rates (80-90%).
• Symptoms can recur over time, particularly with significant weight gain or development of new risk factors.

sections.overview:
• **Urge incontinence** is the involuntary leakage of urine immediately preceded by or associated with a sudden, compelling desire to urinate (**urgency**)
    ◦ A key symptom of the **Overactive Bladder (OAB)** syndrome, which is defined by urinary urgency, with or without urge incontinence, and usually accompanied by **frequency** and **nocturia**
• The hallmark is the inability to delay urination once the sensation of bladder fullness is perceived
sections.etiology:
• The underlying pathophysiology is **detrusor overactivity**
    ◦ Refers to involuntary, uninhibited contractions of the bladder's detrusor muscle during the filling phase
    ◦ This occurs when the central nervous system's (specifically the pontine micturition center) inhibitory control is lost
• Etiologies can be classified as:
    ◦ **Idiopathic**: The most common cause, where no specific underlying pathology is identified
    ◦ **Neurogenic**: Disruption of CNS inhibitory pathways
        ▪ **Stroke (CVA)**: Lesions in the frontal lobe or pontine micturition center
        ▪ **Parkinson's Disease**: Loss of dopaminergic inhibition
        ▪ **Multiple Sclerosis (MS)**: Demyelinating plaques in the spinal cord
        ▪ **Spinal Cord Injury**: Disruption of pathways between the brain and the sacral spinal cord
        ▪ **Dementia**: Loss of cortical inhibition
    ◦ **Non-Neurogenic (Bladder Irritation)**:
        ▪ **Urinary Tract Infection (UTI)**: Inflammation irritates the bladder wall
        ▪ **Bladder Stones (Calculi)**: Mechanical irritation
        ▪ **Bladder Cancer / Carcinoma in situ**: Mucosal abnormalities act as an irritant
        ▪ **Interstitial Cystitis / Bladder Pain Syndrome**
        ▪ **Bladder Outlet Obstruction (e.g., BPH)**: Can lead to secondary detrusor instability
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects millions of adults worldwide
• Prevalence increases significantly with age
• More common in women than men
• It is the most common type of incontinence in the elderly population
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Classic presentation is a patient (often an older female) reporting episodes of leaking a **large amount of urine** after experiencing a sudden, intense need to urinate
    ◦ They often **cannot make it to the toilet in time**
• The patient may describe specific **triggers**, such as hearing running water, washing hands, or putting a key in the door upon arriving home
• Patients also typically complain of frequent urination throughout the day (**frequency**) and waking multiple times at night to void (**nocturia**)
sections.diagnostics:
• **History**: The most important diagnostic tool
    ◦ Clarify the nature of leakage, **frequency**, **urgency**, **nocturia**, fluid intake, and potential triggers
• **Bladder Diary**: A 3-day record of fluid intake, voiding times, volume voided, and incontinent episodes
    ◦ Helps quantify the problem and identify patterns
• **Urinalysis (UA) with Culture**: **Essential initial test**
    ◦ Rules out **UTI** and **hematuria**
        ▪ **Hematuria** requires further workup for malignancy
• **Post-Void Residual (PVR) Volume**: Measured via bladder ultrasound scanner or catheterization
    ◦ A **low PVR (<50 mL)** is consistent with urge incontinence
    ◦ A **high PVR (>200 mL)** suggests incomplete emptying and points toward overflow incontinence or a mixed picture
• **Urodynamic Studies**: **Gold standard** for confirming **detrusor overactivity**
    ◦ A cystometrogram measures bladder pressure during filling, demonstrating involuntary detrusor contractions
    ◦ **Indicated for**:
        ▪ Diagnostic uncertainty
        ▪ Failure of initial therapy
        ▪ Prior to surgical intervention
    ◦ Not required for initial, uncomplicated diagnosis
sections.prognosis:
• **Urge incontinence** is a chronic condition, but symptoms can be significantly managed in most patients
• Behavioral therapies alone can produce a significant improvement or cure in a majority of patients
• While not life-threatening, its impact on quality of life can be severe if left untreated

sections.overview:
• **Overflow incontinence** is the involuntary leakage of urine from an **overdistended bladder**
    ◦ Occurs when the bladder is unable to empty properly, causing urinary pressure to exceed the resistance of the urethral sphincter, leading to frequent or constant **dribbling of urine**
    ◦ This condition results from either **bladder outlet obstruction** or **impaired detrusor muscle contractility** (detrusor underactivity)
sections.etiology:
• The underlying mechanism is **urinary retention**, leading to a high **post-void residual (PVR)** volume
• Pathophysiology can be divided into two primary categories:
    ◦ **Bladder Outlet Obstruction (BOO):** An anatomical or functional blockage prevents urine outflow
        ▪ **Mechanical Obstruction**
            - **Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH):** Most common cause in men; enlarged prostate compresses the urethra
            - **Prostate Cancer:** Malignant growth obstructs the urethral outflow tract
            - **Urethral Stricture:** Scarring and narrowing of the urethra from prior infection, instrumentation, or trauma
            - **Pelvic Organ Prolapse (e.g., Cystocele):** In women, the bladder herniates into the vagina, kinking the urethra
        ▪ **Functional Obstruction**
            - **Detrusor-Sphincter Dyssynergia:** Lack of coordination between bladder contraction and external sphincter relaxation, often seen in **spinal cord injury**
    ◦ **Detrusor Underactivity (Acontractile/Hypocontractile Bladder):** The detrusor muscle is too weak to generate a sufficient contraction to fully empty the bladder
        ▪ **Neurologic Causes:** Damage to the nerves controlling the bladder
            - **Diabetes Mellitus (Diabetic Cystopathy):** Peripheral neuropathy affects bladder sensation and motor function
            - **Multiple Sclerosis (MS)**
            - **Spinal Cord Injury or Tumors**
            - **Parkinson's Disease**
            - Damage from **pelvic surgery** (e.g., hysterectomy, radical prostatectomy)
        ▪ **Medication-Induced:** Drugs that decrease bladder contractility or increase sphincter tone
            - **Anticholinergics** (e.g., oxybutynin, diphenhydramine)
            - **Opioids**
            - **Calcium Channel Blockers**
            - **Alpha-adrenergic agonists**
        ▪ **Overdistension Injury:** Chronic overstretching of the bladder leads to muscle damage
sections.epidemiology:
• More common in **older adults**
• Prevalence increases with age
• In men, the most common cause is **BPH**
• In women, it is less common and often related to pelvic organ prolapse or prior pelvic surgery
• Common in individuals with **neurogenic bladder** from conditions like diabetes mellitus or spinal cord injury
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A typical patient is an older male with a history of **BPH** presenting with both **obstructive** and **irritative** voiding symptoms
• Reports constant **"dampness"** or **dribbling of urine** throughout the day and night
• May also complain of:
    ◦ A **weak stream**
    ◦ **Straining to urinate**
    ◦ A sensation that the bladder never fully empties
• In severe cases, the patient may present with **acute urinary retention** and **suprapubic pain**
sections.diagnostics:
• **Post-Void Residual (PVR) Volume**
    ◦ **Key diagnostic test**
    ◦ Measured via bladder ultrasound scanner or straight catheterization immediately after voiding
    ◦ **PVR > 200-300 mL is highly suggestive** of overflow incontinence/urinary retention
• **Urinalysis and Urine Culture**
    ◦ To rule out **urinary tract infection (UTI)**, which can cause or mimic symptoms
• **Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP)**
    ◦ To assess renal function (BUN, Creatinine)
    ◦ Chronic urinary retention can lead to **obstructive uropathy**, **hydronephrosis**, and **post-renal acute kidney injury (AKI)** or **chronic kidney disease (CKD)**
• **Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA)**
    ◦ In men, if DRE is abnormal or prostate cancer is suspected
• **Renal Ultrasound**
    ◦ To evaluate for **hydronephrosis** or **hydroureter**, indicating upper tract damage from chronic obstruction
• **Urodynamic Studies**
    ◦ **Gold standard** for differentiating between **bladder outlet obstruction** and **detrusor underactivity**
    ◦ Measures bladder pressures during filling and voiding (cystometry)
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is generally **good** if the underlying cause is identified and treated promptly
• For reversible causes like medication side effects or **BPH**, treatment can lead to a complete resolution of symptoms
• For irreversible causes like severe diabetic neuropathy or spinal cord injury, management is focused on preventing complications and improving quality of life, often requiring lifelong intermittent catheterization

sections.overview:
• Defined by the International Continence Society (ICS) as the complaint of involuntary leakage of urine associated with both **urgency** (Urgency Urinary Incontinence - UUI) and **effort or physical exertion** such as coughing or sneezing (Stress Urinary Incontinence - SUI)
• Represents a combination of two distinct pathophysiologies occurring in the same patient
• One component often predominates, and identifying the most bothersome symptom is key to management
sections.etiology:
• Pathophysiology is a combination of the mechanisms underlying SUI and UUI
    ◦ **Stress Urinary Incontinence (SUI) Component**
        ▪ Caused by failure of the urethral sphincter mechanism to remain closed during increases in intra-abdominal pressure due to:
            ▪ **Urethral Hypermobility**: Weakness of pelvic floor muscles and connective tissue supports allows the bladder neck and proximal urethra to descend during exertion, preventing efficient pressure transmission and leading to leakage
            ▪ **Intrinsic Sphincter Deficiency (ISD)**: The urethral sphincter is weak and cannot generate enough resistance, which can result from prior pelvic surgery, radiation, or neurologic damage
    ◦ **Urgency Urinary Incontinence (UUI) Component**
        ▪ Caused by **detrusor overactivity**, characterized by involuntary contractions of the detrusor muscle during bladder filling
        ▪ These contractions create a sudden, compelling urge to void that cannot be suppressed
        ▪ Often idiopathic but can be neurogenic (e.g., from stroke, MS, spinal cord injury)
    ◦ In MUI, both urethral incompetence and detrusor overactivity coexist
sections.epidemiology:
• Extremely common, particularly in women
• Prevalence increases significantly with age; it is the most common type of incontinence in older women
• Estimates suggest 30-50% of all women with urinary incontinence have the mixed type
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patient presents with urinary leakage featuring both stress and urge components
• The history is paramount, with patients endorsing scenarios like **"I leak when I cough or laugh, but I also have episodes where I get a sudden, strong urge and can't make it to the bathroom in time."**
• The clinical goal is to determine which component is more bothersome to the patient, as this will guide initial therapy
sections.diagnostics:
• **History**: The single most important diagnostic tool; validated questionnaires can be helpful
• **Bladder Diary**: Patient records fluid intake, voiding times, volume voided, and leakage episodes (with triggers) over 3-7 days. **Essential** for characterizing the type and severity of incontinence
• **Urinalysis (UA) with Culture**: **Mandatory** on initial evaluation to rule out urinary tract infection (UTI), hematuria, or glucosuria
• **Post-Void Residual (PVR) Volume**: Measured via bladder scanner or catheterization; a high PVR (>150-200 mL) suggests urinary retention and possible overflow incontinence
• **Urodynamic Studies**: Not required for initial, uncomplicated diagnosis. Indicated when:
    ◦ The diagnosis is uncertain after initial workup
    ◦ Conservative therapy has failed
    ◦ Surgical intervention for SUI is planned (to assess for occult detrusor overactivity)
    ◦ There is suspicion of a complex voiding dysfunction (e.g., high PVR, neurologic disease)
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis for symptom improvement is generally good with a structured, multi-modal approach
• Complete "cure" can be challenging; management focuses on improving quality of life
• Patient adherence to conservative therapies is a major predictor of success
• Surgical correction of the SUI component is highly effective but may not resolve, and can occasionally worsen, the UUI component

sections.overview:
• **Pelvic Organ Prolapse (POP)** is the herniation or descent of pelvic organs from their normal anatomical position into or through the vaginal canal, resulting from a failure of the pelvic support structures (muscles, ligaments, fascia)
    ◦ **Cystocele (Anterior Prolapse)**: Prolapse of the **anterior vaginal wall**, resulting in the herniation of the **bladder**; often referred to as a "dropped bladder"
    ◦ **Rectocele (Posterior Prolapse)**: Prolapse of the **posterior vaginal wall**, resulting in the herniation of the **rectum**
sections.etiology:
• The pelvic organs are supported by a "hammock" of muscles (the levator ani complex) and connective tissue (endopelvic fascia); POP occurs when this support system is damaged or weakened, leading to organ descent
    ◦ **Direct Muscle Trauma**: **Vaginal childbirth** can cause direct injury, stretching, or tearing of the levator ani muscles and perineal body
    ◦ **Connective Tissue Damage**: Stretching and tearing of the endopelvic fascia (e.g., pubocervical fascia in cystocele, rectovaginal fascia in rectocele) during childbirth or from chronic pressure
    ◦ **Neuropathic Injury**: Stretching of the **pudendal nerve** during delivery can lead to pelvic floor muscle denervation and subsequent atrophy and weakness
    ◦ **Hormonal Effects**: **Post-menopause**, decreased estrogen levels lead to atrophy and weakening of vaginal mucosa and connective tissues, predisposing to prolapse
    ◦ **Chronic Pressure**: Conditions that chronically increase intra-abdominal pressure (e.g., **obesity**, **chronic cough**, **chronic constipation**) put constant strain on the pelvic floor, leading to gradual weakening
sections.epidemiology:
• Extremely common, affecting up to 50% of parous women to some degree, though many are asymptomatic
• The lifetime risk for a woman to undergo surgery for POP or incontinence is approximately 10-20%
• Prevalence increases significantly with **age**, peaking in the 7th and 8th decades of life
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic patient is a **multiparous**, **postmenopausal** woman presenting with a complaint of a "**bulge**" or "**pressure**" in her vagina
    ◦ Symptoms are often described as worse after long periods of standing or at the end of the day and are relieved by lying down
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is primarily **clinical**, based on history and physical exam
    ◦ **Urinalysis & Urine Culture**: To rule out urinary tract infection, especially with urinary symptoms
    ◦ **Post-void Residual (PVR) Volume**: Measured via bladder scanner or catheterization; an elevated PVR can indicate significant **urinary retention** secondary to urethral kinking from a large cystocele
    ◦ **Urodynamic Studies**: Not routine; considered for patients with complex urinary symptoms (e.g., mixed incontinence) or to unmask "**occult**" **stress incontinence** prior to surgical repair
sections.prognosis:
• With conservative management, many patients experience significant improvement in quality of life
• Surgical outcomes are generally good for symptom relief, but anatomical recurrence rates can be as high as 30% or more over time
• Recurrence is more likely in patients with significant underlying risk factors (e.g., obesity, connective tissue disease)
