sections.overview: • Pelvic Floor Dysfunction (PFD) is a broad term for a range of disorders that occur when the pelvic floor muscles and connective tissues are impaired ◦ The pelvic floor is a "hammock" of muscles (primarily the levator ani and coccygeus muscles) that supports the pelvic organs (bladder, uterus/prostate, rectum) ◦ Plays a crucial role in urinary continence, fecal continence, sexual function, and lumbopelvic stability • PFD can manifest as either hypotonicity (weakness) leading to incontinence and prolapse, or hypertonicity (tightness/spasm) leading to pain and obstructive voiding/defecation
sections.etiology: • The underlying cause is a failure of the pelvic floor muscles to contract or relax in a coordinated manner • Hypotonicity (Weakness/Laxity) ◦ Patho: Direct injury, stretching, or denervation of the levator ani muscles and pudendal nerve, leading to inadequate support for pelvic organs and insufficient closure pressure of the urethra and anus ◦ Causes: ▪ Childbirth: Vaginal delivery is the most significant cause, especially with forceps/vacuum assistance, prolonged second stage of labor, or large fetal size ▪ Chronic Increased Intra-abdominal Pressure: Chronic coughing (COPD), chronic constipation/straining, obesity, heavy lifting ▪ Aging/Menopause: Atrophy of tissues due to estrogen loss weakens supportive structures ▪ Connective Tissue Disorders: Ehlers-Danlos, Marfan syndrome • Hypertonicity (Spasm/Overactivity) ◦ Patho: The pelvic floor muscles are in a state of constant or near-constant contraction and fail to relax appropriately, which can be a protective response to pain or trauma. This "non-relaxing" state causes pain and can obstruct the outflow tracts of the bladder and rectum ◦ Causes: ▪ Trauma: Pelvic fractures, falls on the coccyx, sexual assault ▪ Surgery: Hysterectomy, episiotomy, hemorrhoidectomy ▪ Pain Syndromes: Endometriosis, interstitial cystitis, vulvodynia, pudendal neuralgia ▪ Psychological: Stress, anxiety, history of abuse ▪ Postural Dysfunction: Poor posture leading to chronic muscle guarding
sections.epidemiology:
• Extremely common, affecting up to 25% of women in the US
• Prevalence increases with age and parity
• Often underdiagnosed and underreported due to patient embarrassment
• While more common in women, men can also be affected, often presenting with chronic prostatitis-like symptoms, post-prostatectomy incontinence, or constipation
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is highly variable and depends on the specific type of dysfunction (hypo- vs. hypertonic) and the organs affected
• Patients often present with a constellation of seemingly unrelated symptoms involving the urinary, bowel, and sexual systems, often accompanied by pain
• A common presentation is a multiparous, middle-aged woman complaining of urinary leakage when she coughs or laughs, combined with a sensation of pelvic pressure or a "bulge"
• Another common presentation is a young woman with chronic pelvic pain, painful intercourse, and difficulty with bowel movements
sections.diagnostics: • PFD is primarily a clinical diagnosis based on history and physical exam • Urinalysis & Culture: Rule out UTI, which can mimic urgency/frequency symptoms • Post-void Residual (PVR): Bladder scan or catheterization to assess for incomplete emptying • Urodynamic Studies: Indicated for complex incontinence, suspected obstruction, or prior to surgery. Measures bladder pressures during filling and voiding to differentiate stress vs. urge incontinence and identify detrusor overactivity • Anorectal Manometry: Measures pressures of the anal sphincter. Used to evaluate fecal incontinence or chronic constipation/obstructed defecation • Defecography: A video X-ray or MRI that visualizes the rectum and pelvic floor during defecation. Excellent for diagnosing rectoceles and paradoxical contraction • Cystoscopy: To rule out bladder pathology (e.g., interstitial cystitis, masses)
sections.prognosis:
• Generally good, especially for patients who are motivated and adherent to conservative therapies like PFPT
• Many patients experience significant improvement or resolution of symptoms
• Surgical outcomes for stress incontinence and prolapse are also generally favorable but carry risks of recurrence and complications (e.g., mesh erosion)
• The condition can be chronic and may require long-term management strategies

sections.overview:
• A **urethral diverticulum** is a localized, epithelium-lined outpouching or sac that forms along the urethra
	◦ It communicates with the urethral lumen, leading to the collection and stagnation of urine
• This condition is predominantly found in **females** and is often underdiagnosed due to its varied and non-specific symptoms
• The classic presentation involves a triad of symptoms, but patients rarely present with all three
• Diagnosis requires a high index of suspicion, and management is primarily **surgical** for symptomatic individuals
sections.etiology:
• The vast majority of urethral diverticula in adults are **acquired**
• The leading theory involves the obstruction and subsequent infection of the **periurethral glands (Skene's glands)**
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** Estimated to occur in 1-6% of the adult female population
	◦ It is likely underdiagnosed
• **Gender:** Almost exclusively a condition of **females**
	◦ It is extremely rare in males
• **Age of Onset:** Most commonly diagnosed in women between the ages of **30 and 60**
sections.riskFactors:
• **Recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs)**
• **Urethral trauma**
	◦ Vaginal childbirth (instrumented delivery, perineal tears)
	◦ Urethral instrumentation (e.g., catheterization, cystoscopy)
• **Previous urethral or pelvic surgery**
• **Urethral strictures**
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is often vague and mimics other urologic and gynecologic conditions
	◦ A patient may have a long history of lower urinary tract symptoms (**LUTS**) that have been refractory to standard treatments
• The classic triad, often referred to as the **"3 D's,"** includes:
	◦ **D**ysuria (painful urination)
	◦ Post-void **D**ribbling
	◦ **D**yspareunia (painful intercourse)
• **Key Clinical Point:** While classic, the full triad is present in only 5-20% of patients
	◦ **Post-void dribbling** is the most specific symptom
sections.physicalExam:
• **Primary Finding:** A palpable, tender, fluctuant, or firm mass located on the **anterior vaginal wall**, underlying the urethra
• **Pathognomonic Sign:** Expression of **purulent material or urine** from the urethral meatus upon compression or **"milking"** of the suburethral mass
• The mass may vary in size and consistency
• Urethral tenderness may be present without a distinct mass
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.treatment:
• **Asymptomatic Patients:** Observation may be considered, with counseling on the risks of infection, stone formation, and malignancy
• **Symptomatic Patients:** **Surgical excision** is the definitive treatment
	◦ **Procedure:** **Transvaginal diverticulectomy**
		▪ **Technique:** An incision is made in the anterior vaginal wall, the diverticular sac is carefully dissected away from surrounding tissues and the urethra, the sac is completely excised, and the communication to the urethra is closed meticulously in multiple, non-overlapping layers
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis with complete surgical excision by an experienced surgeon is **excellent**
• Cure rates are reported to be over 90%
• Recurrence is more likely with incomplete excision, infection, or large/complex diverticula

sections.overview:
• Urethral prolapse is the complete, circumferential eversion of the distal urethral mucosa through the external urethral meatus.
    ◦ Appears as a round, often **"donut-shaped,"** erythematous, and friable mass at the urethral opening.
    ◦ It is a **benign condition** most commonly seen in a **bimodal distribution**: pre-pubertal girls and post-menopausal women.
sections.etiology:
• The exact pathophysiology is not fully understood but is believed to be multifactorial, stemming from a combination of **poor tissue support** and **increased intra-abdominal pressure**.
    ◦ **Weak Submucosal Attachments**: The primary underlying factor is weakness of the submucosal connective tissues that anchor the distal urethral mucosa to the underlying muscularis layer.
    ◦ **Hypoestrogenism**: Estrogen is crucial for maintaining the tone, vascularity, and integrity of urogenital tissues.
        ▪ **Pre-pubertal girls**: Have a naturally low estrogen state before puberty.
        ▪ **Post-menopausal women**: Experience a significant decline in estrogen, leading to **urogenital atrophy**.
        ▪ Low estrogen leads to atrophic, thin, and friable tissues that are more susceptible to eversion.
    ◦ **Increased Intra-abdominal Pressure**: An acute or chronic increase in pressure acts as a trigger, forcing the poorly supported mucosa outward. Common triggers include:
        ▪ Severe **coughing spells** (e.g., asthma, respiratory infections)
        ▪ **Constipation** and straining during defecation
        ▪ Vomiting
        ▪ Heavy lifting
        ▪ Trauma
    ◦ The combination of weak tissue support (low estrogen) and a triggering event (increased pressure) leads to the mucosal prolapse.
sections.epidemiology:
• Urethral prolapse has a distinct **bimodal age** and demographic distribution.
    ◦ **Peak 1: Pre-pubertal Girls**
        ▪ Typically occurs between ages 4 and 10.
        ▪ **Highest incidence in pre-pubertal African-American girls.** The reason for this racial predilection is unknown.
    ◦ **Peak 2: Post-menopausal Women**
        ▪ Typically Caucasian women.
    ◦ Overall, it is an uncommon condition.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient (or the parent of a child) typically presents with the chief complaint of a **"lump"** or **"mass"** at the vaginal opening and/or **perineal bleeding**.
    ◦ The onset can be sudden after a coughing fit or straining.
sections.diagnostics:
• Urethral prolapse is a **clinical diagnosis** made based on history and characteristic physical exam findings.
    ◦ **No imaging is typically required.**
    ◦ **Urinalysis (UA)**: May be performed to rule out a concurrent urinary tract infection (UTI).
        ▪ **Hematuria** may be present.
    ◦ **Complete Blood Count (CBC)**: Can be considered if there is concern for anemia from chronic or significant bleeding.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is **excellent**.
    ◦ The vast majority of cases resolve completely with either medical or surgical management.
    ◦ The condition is **benign** and does not have malignant potential.
    ◦ Recurrence is possible but is also manageable.

sections.overview:
• **Bladder Pain Syndrome (BPS)**, formerly **Interstitial Cystitis (IC)**, is a chronic clinical syndrome characterized by **pelvic pain, pressure, or discomfort** perceived to be related to the urinary bladder
    ◦ This sensation is typically accompanied by at least one other urinary symptom, such as persistent **urgency** or **frequency**
    ◦ BPS/IC is a **diagnosis of exclusion**, made after ruling out conditions like urinary tract infection, bladder cancer, or endometriosis
    ◦ Broadly categorized into two subtypes:
        ▪ **Ulcerative**: Characterized by the presence of **Hunner's lesions**
        ▪ **Non-ulcerative**: Far more common
sections.etiology:
• The exact etiology is unknown and likely multifactorial
• Several leading theories exist:
    ◦ **Urothelial Dysfunction (GAG Layer Theory)**
        ▪ A defective **glycosaminoglycan (GAG) layer** in the bladder lining may allow irritants (e.g., potassium, urea) to penetrate the bladder wall, triggering an inflammatory response and activating sensory nerves
    ◦ **Mast Cell Activation**
        ▪ Increased numbers of activated **mast cells** in the bladder wall release **histamine**, cytokines, and other inflammatory mediators, contributing to neurogenic inflammation and pain
    ◦ **Neurogenic Inflammation & Central Sensitization**
        ▪ Chronic bladder irritation leads to hypersensitivity of pelvic sensory nerves (C-fibers)
        ▪ This can cause **central sensitization**, where the central nervous system amplifies pain signals, leading to **allodynia** (perceiving non-painful stimuli like bladder filling as painful)
    ◦ **Autoimmune Component**
        ▪ BPS/IC has a strong association with other autoimmune and inflammatory disorders such as **Sjögren's syndrome**, **lupus**, and **IBS**, suggesting a possible autoimmune cause in some patients
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects an estimated 3-8 million women and 1-4 million men in the United States
• **Gender**: Predominantly affects women, with a female-to-male ratio of approximately **9:1**
• **Age of Onset**: The median age of onset is **40 years**, but it can occur at any age
• **Comorbidities**: High rate of co-occurrence with other chronic pain syndromes such as **irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)**, **fibromyalgia**, **endometriosis**, **vulvodynia**, and **chronic fatigue syndrome**
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic patient is a woman in her 40s with a long history of **"recurrent UTIs"** despite persistently **negative urine cultures**
• Reports **chronic suprapubic or pelvic pain**
    ◦ Characteristically **exacerbated as her bladder fills** and is **transiently relieved upon urination**
• Accompanied by significant **urinary frequency**, **urgency**, and **nocturia**
• Symptoms have been present for **>6 weeks** in the absence of any other identifiable cause, severely impacting quality of life
sections.diagnostics:
• BPS/IC is a **diagnosis of exclusion**; the workup aims to rule out other conditions
• **Initial Workup (Essential)**
    ◦ **History & Physical Exam**: A detailed history focusing on the relationship between pain and bladder filling/emptying is paramount
    ◦ **Urinalysis (UA) & Urine Culture**: 
        ▪ **Required first step**
        ▪ UA is typically normal (may show **microhematuria**)
        ▪ Urine culture is **negative**
    ◦ **Symptom Questionnaires**: PUF (Pelvic Pain and Urgency/Frequency) or O'Leary-Sant Symptom Index can be used to quantify symptom severity
• **Secondary Workup (When Indicated)**
    ◦ **Post-void Residual (PVR)**: To rule out incomplete bladder emptying
    ◦ **Urine Cytology**: To rule out bladder cancer, especially in patients **>50**, with a **smoking history**, or with **macroscopic hematuria**
    ◦ **Urodynamics**: Not routine for diagnosis; may show low functional bladder capacity and pain with filling
    ◦ **Cystoscopy with Hydrodistention**: A key procedure performed under anesthesia
        ▪ **Purpose**: Allows direct visualization of the bladder wall and assessment of bladder capacity
        ▪ **Diagnostic Findings**:
            ▪ **Hunner's Lesions**: Focal, friable, erythematous lesions with a central coagulum that bleed easily. **Pathognomonic for Ulcerative IC** (found in 5-10% of cases)
            ▪ **Glomerulations**: Diffuse, pinpoint petechial hemorrhages seen on the bladder wall after hydrodistention. A supportive but **non-specific** finding
        ▪ *Note: A visually normal bladder does not exclude a diagnosis of Non-ulcerative BPS/IC*
sections.prognosis:
• BPS/IC is a **chronic condition** with a **relapsing-remitting course**
• There is **no cure**, but a significant majority of patients can achieve substantial symptom control with a long-term, multimodal management plan
• Prognosis is generally better for patients with **Hunner's lesions** that are appropriately treated

sections.overview: • Malignancy arising from the epithelial lining of the urinary bladder, making it the most common malignancy of the urinary system. ◦ The vast majority of cases are urothelial carcinoma (formerly known as transitional cell carcinoma or TCC). ◦ The clinical course and treatment are primarily dictated by the tumor's grade (low vs. high) and stage, specifically whether it is non-muscle-invasive or muscle-invasive. ◦ The classic presentation is painless hematuria in an older adult, especially a smoker.
sections.etiology: • The pathophysiology involves the malignant transformation of the urothelium, the specialized epithelial layer lining the bladder, due to prolonged contact with carcinogens excreted in the urine, leading to DNA damage and neoplastic growth. ◦ Histological Types: ▪ Urothelial Carcinoma (UC / TCC): ◦ Accounts for >90% of all bladder cancers in the US and Europe. ◦ Arises from the transitional epithelial cells of the urothelium. ◦ Can be papillary (finger-like projections) or sessile (flat). ▪ Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC): ◦ Accounts for ~5% of cases in the US. ◦ Associated with chronic irritation and inflammation of the bladder, leading to squamous metaplasia and subsequent malignant transformation. ◦ Key associations: Chronic indwelling catheters, recurrent UTIs, bladder stones (calculi), and worldwide, infection with _Schistosoma haematobium_ (a parasitic fluke). ▪ Adenocarcinoma: ◦ Rare (~2% of cases). ◦ Arises from glandular elements. ◦ Often associated with a patent urachal remnant at the bladder dome. ◦ Staging Distinction: ▪ Non-Muscle-Invasive Bladder Cancer (NMIBC): Confined to the mucosa (Ta, Tis) or submucosa/lamina propria (T1). Accounts for ~75% of new diagnoses. ▪ Muscle-Invasive Bladder Cancer (MIBC): Invades the muscularis propria (detrusor muscle) (T2) or beyond. This is a critical distinction as it requires much more aggressive treatment.
sections.epidemiology: • Incidence: 4th most common cancer in men in the US. • Age: Primarily a disease of older adults; median age at diagnosis is ~73 years. • Gender: Men > Women (approx. 3:1 to 4:1 ratio). • Race: More common in White individuals compared to African American or Hispanic individuals.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • The classic presentation is an older male smoker who presents with painless gross hematuria. ◦ The patient may report that the hematuria was intermittent, leading to a delay in seeking care. • While hematuria is the hallmark, some patients may present with irritative voiding symptoms that can be mistaken for a UTI or BPH.
sections.diagnostics: • Initial Workup: ◦ Urinalysis (UA) with Microscopy: To confirm hematuria (>3 RBCs/high-power field). May also show pyuria. ◦ Urine Culture: To rule out infectious causes. ◦ Urine Cytology: ▪ Microscopic examination of shed urothelial cells in urine. ▪ High specificity but low sensitivity, especially for low-grade tumors. ▪ More useful for high-grade tumors and CIS. ◦ Imaging: ▪ CT Urogram (or MR Urogram): Best initial imaging test for hematuria evaluation. ◦ A multiphasic CT scan (non-contrast, arterial, venous, and delayed/excretory phases) that visualizes the entire urinary tract (kidneys, ureters, bladder). ◦ It can identify bladder masses/wall thickening and rule out upper tract tumors. • Definitive Diagnosis: ◦ Cystoscopy with Biopsy: THE GOLD STANDARD for diagnosis. ▪ A flexible or rigid scope is inserted through the urethra to directly visualize the bladder lining. ▪ Any suspicious lesions are biopsied. ◦ Transurethral Resection of Bladder Tumor (TURBT): ▪ This procedure is both diagnostic and therapeutic. ▪ It uses a resectoscope to remove the visible tumor(s). ▪ The resected tissue is sent to pathology to determine tumor type, grade, and depth of invasion (i.e., if muscle is present and if it's invaded), which is crucial for staging.
sections.prognosis: • Prognosis is highly dependent on tumor grade and stage (depth of invasion) at diagnosis. • NMIBC: 5-year survival is excellent (>90%), but recurrence rates are high (50-70%). • MIBC: 5-year survival for localized disease treated with cystectomy is ~60-70%. • Metastatic Disease: Prognosis is poor, with a 5-year survival rate of <15%.

sections.overview:
• Prostate cancer is a malignant neoplasm of the prostate gland, overwhelmingly classified as **adenocarcinoma**.
• It is one of the most common cancers in men, with a highly variable clinical course ranging from indolent to aggressive.
• Most tumors arise in the **peripheral zone** of the prostate, making them potentially palpable on a digital rectal exam (DRE).
• The growth of prostate cancer is typically **androgen-dependent**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ The exact cause is unknown; it is a multifactorial process involving genetic predisposition, hormonal influences, and environmental factors.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Cell of Origin**: Originates from glandular epithelial cells, hence **adenocarcinoma** is the predominant histologic type (>95%).
    ◦ **Hormonal Influence**: Prostate cells are stimulated by androgens.
        ▪ Testosterone is converted to the more potent **dihydrotestosterone (DHT)** by the enzyme **5-alpha-reductase**.
        ▪ DHT binds to androgen receptors, promoting growth and proliferation.
    ◦ **Location**: Approximately 70-80% of cancers develop in the **peripheral zone**.
    ◦ **Metastasis**: Spreads via three main routes:
        ▪ **Direct Extension**: Into the seminal vesicles, bladder neck.
        ▪ **Lymphatic Spread**: To pelvic lymph nodes (obturator nodes are typically the first to be involved).
        ▪ **Hematogenous Spread**: Primarily to bone, especially the axial skeleton. Classically causes **osteoblastic** (bone-forming) metastases.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: The most common non-skin cancer in men in the United States.
• **Mortality**: The second leading cause of cancer-related death in men (after lung cancer).
• **Age**: Risk increases significantly after age 50; median age at diagnosis is ~66 years.
• **Race/Ethnicity**
    ◦ **Highest incidence and mortality**: African American men, who also tend to be diagnosed younger with more aggressive disease.
    ◦ **Intermediate incidence**: Caucasian men.
    ◦ **Lowest incidence**: Asian and Hispanic men.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Non-modifiable (Major Factors)**
    ◦ **Advancing Age**: The single strongest risk factor.
    ◦ **Race**: African American ethnicity.
    ◦ **Family History**: Risk doubles with a first-degree relative; higher if multiple relatives are affected or diagnosed at a young age (<55).
    ◦ **Genetic Mutations**: Inherited mutations in genes like **BRCA1/BRCA2** and Lynch syndrome (HNPCC).
• **Potentially Modifiable**
    ◦ **Diet**: High intake of animal fats and red meat.
    ◦ **Obesity**: Associated with more aggressive disease.
    ◦ **Agent Orange Exposure**: Recognized risk factor by the VA.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The majority of men with early-stage prostate cancer are **asymptomatic**.
• The disease is most often detected due to an abnormal screening test, either an elevated **Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA)** level or a suspicious finding on a **Digital Rectal Exam (DRE)**.
• Symptomatic presentation usually signifies locally advanced or metastatic disease.
• **Early/Localized Disease**
    ◦ **Typically asymptomatic**.
• **Locally Advanced Disease** (causing bladder outlet obstruction)
    ◦ Obstructive voiding symptoms: Hesitancy, weak stream, intermittency, incomplete emptying.
    ◦ Irritative voiding symptoms: Frequency, urgency, nocturia.
    ◦ Hematuria or hematospermia (less common).
• **Metastatic Disease**
    ◦ **Bone Pain**: Most common symptom of metastatic disease, especially in the lower back, hips, or pelvis.
    ◦ **Pathologic Fractures**.
    ◦ **Spinal Cord Compression**: A neurologic emergency. Presents with severe back pain, lower extremity weakness, sensory deficits, or bowel/bladder incontinence.
    ◦ **Constitutional Symptoms**: Unexplained weight loss, fatigue (rare until very advanced disease).
sections.physicalExam:
• **Digital Rectal Exam (DRE)**
    ◦ **Normal Prostate**: Smooth, firm (consistency of the tip of the nose), non-tender, and symmetrical with a palpable median sulcus.
    ◦ **Suspicious Findings**
        ▪ **Hard nodule** or area of **induration**.
        ▪ Glandular asymmetry.
        ▪ Obliteration of the median sulcus.
        ▪ A fixed, non-mobile gland suggests extraprostatic extension.
• **General Exam**
    ◦ Assess for lower extremity lymphedema (suggests pelvic nodal disease).
    ◦ Palpate for supraclavicular or inguinal lymphadenopathy.
    ◦ Percuss spine for tenderness (suspicious for bone metastases).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Initial Evaluation**
    ◦ **Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA)**: A glycoprotein produced by prostate epithelial cells.
        ▪ **Not cancer-specific**; can be elevated in BPH, prostatitis, or after urologic procedures.
        ▪ Generally, **PSA > 4.0 ng/mL** is considered abnormal, but risk is a continuum.
        ▪ PSA velocity and free/total PSA ratio can add specificity.
    ◦ **Digital Rectal Exam (DRE)**.
• **Definitive Diagnosis**
    ◦ **Transrectal Ultrasound (TRUS)-guided Biopsy**: The **gold standard** for diagnosis. Multiple core samples are taken.
• **Pathology & Staging**
    ◦ **Gleason Grading System**: Based on histologic architecture; the two most predominant patterns are graded (1-5) and added together.
    ◦ **Gleason Score**: Ranges from 6 to 10.
        ▪ **Score 6**: Well-differentiated (low-grade).
        ▪ **Score 7 (3+4 or 4+3)**: Moderately-differentiated (intermediate-grade).
        ▪ **Scores 8-10**: Poorly-differentiated (high-grade, aggressive).
    ◦ **Staging (TNM System)**: Determines the extent of cancer spread.
    ◦ **Imaging for staging**: Used for intermediate to high-risk disease.
        ▪ **Radionuclide Bone Scan**: To detect **osteoblastic** bone metastases.
        ▪ **CT or MRI of Abdomen/Pelvis**: To assess for lymph node involvement and local extension.
        ▪ **PSMA-PET Scan**: A newer, more sensitive imaging modality for detecting metastatic disease.
sections.treatment:
• **Localized Disease (Confined to the Prostate)**
    ◦ **Active Surveillance**: For low-risk disease (Gleason 6, low PSA, small tumor volume). Involves monitoring to defer treatment.
    ◦ **Radical Prostatectomy (RP)**: Surgical removal of the prostate gland, seminal vesicles, and ampullae of the vas deferens.
    ◦ **Radiation Therapy (RT)**
        ▪ **External Beam Radiation Therapy (EBRT)**: Radiation from an external source.
        ▪ **Brachytherapy**: Implantation of radioactive seeds directly into the prostate.
• **Locally Advanced Disease**
    ◦ Typically a combination of **Radiation Therapy + Androgen Deprivation Therapy (ADT)**.
• **Metastatic Disease**
    ◦ **Androgen Deprivation Therapy (ADT)**: The cornerstone of treatment.
        ▪ **LHRH Agonists** (e.g., Leuprolide): Cause an initial testosterone flare followed by downregulation.
        ▪ **GnRH Antagonists** (e.g., Degarelix): Directly block GnRH receptors without a flare.
        ▪ **Surgical Castration (Orchiectomy)**.
    ◦ **Chemotherapy** (e.g., Docetaxel): For hormone-refractory or high-volume metastatic disease.
    ◦ **Novel Hormonal Agents** (e.g., Abiraterone, Enzalutamide): Used for castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC).
    ◦ **Palliative Radiation**: For symptomatic bone metastases.
sections.management:
• **Screening**
    ◦ Controversial; **shared decision-making** is recommended by the USPSTF for men aged 55-69.
• **Post-Treatment Surveillance**
    ◦ **PSA monitoring**: The primary method for detecting recurrence.
        ▪ After prostatectomy, PSA should become undetectable (<0.2 ng/mL). A rising PSA indicates **biochemical recurrence**.
        ▪ After radiation, PSA will drop to a low point (nadir) but will not be undetectable.
    ◦ Monitoring for and managing treatment-related side effects.
sections.complications:
• **From the Disease**
    ◦ Bladder outlet obstruction leading to urinary retention and hydronephrosis.
    ◦ **Spinal cord compression** from vertebral metastases (EMERGENCY).
    ◦ Pathologic fractures.
    ◦ Pain from bone metastases.
• **From Treatment**
    ◦ **Radical Prostatectomy**: **Erectile dysfunction** and **urinary incontinence** (stress) are the most common long-term side effects.
    ◦ **Radiation Therapy**: Erectile dysfunction, radiation proctitis, radiation cystitis.
    ◦ **Androgen Deprivation Therapy (ADT)**: Hot flashes, decreased libido, osteoporosis, gynecomastia, weight gain, fatigue, increased risk of metabolic syndrome.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly dependent on stage and grade at diagnosis.
• **Localized Disease**: Excellent prognosis, with a 5-year relative survival rate of nearly 100%.
• **Regional Disease**: Excellent prognosis, 5-year survival is also nearly 100%.
• **Distant (Metastatic) Disease**: Poor prognosis, with a 5-year relative survival rate of approximately 30%.
• **Key Prognostic Factors**
    ◦ **Gleason Score** (histologic grade).
    ◦ **TNM Stage** (extent of disease).
    ◦ **PSA level** at the time of diagnosis.

sections.overview:
• Testicular cancer is the most common solid malignancy affecting males between the ages of 15 and 35.
    ◦ It arises from germ cells within the testicles and is one of the most curable solid neoplasms, with an overall 5-year survival rate exceeding 95%.
    ◦ The two main categories are **Germ Cell Tumors (GCTs)** (>95% of cases) and Non-Germ Cell Tumors (sex cord-stromal tumors).
        ▪ GCTs are further divided into **Seminomas** and **Non-seminomas (NSGCTs)**, a distinction critical for prognosis and treatment.
sections.etiology:
• **Origin**: Most testicular cancers arise from a precursor lesion known as **intratubular germ cell neoplasia (ITGCN)**.
• **Germ Cell Tumors (GCTs)**: Derived from primordial germ cells.
    ◦ **Seminomas (~50% of GCTs)**:
        ▪ Composed of uniform cells resembling primitive gonocytes.
        ▪ Tend to be slower-growing and remain localized to the testis for longer.
        ▪ Highly sensitive to radiation therapy.
        ▪ Histology: Large cells with clear cytoplasm and a central nucleus (**"fried egg" appearance**).
    ◦ **Non-seminomatous GCTs (NSGCTs)**:
        ▪ A heterogeneous group that is generally more aggressive than seminomas.
        ▪ Often presents with mixed cell types.
        ▪ Subtypes include:
            • **Embryonal Carcinoma**: Poorly differentiated, aggressive, with early metastatic potential.
            • **Yolk Sac (Endodermal Sinus) Tumor**: Most common testicular tumor in infants and children. Histology shows **Schiller-Duval bodies**. Produces **alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)**.
            • **Choriocarcinoma**: Highly aggressive with rapid hematogenous spread (especially to lungs and brain). Produces high levels of **beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG)**.
            • **Teratoma**: Composed of cells from all three germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm). Mature teratomas are typically benign in children but can be malignant in adults. Often chemoresistant.
• **Non-Germ Cell Tumors (<5%)**:
    ◦ **Leydig Cell Tumors**: Can be hormonally active, producing androgens (causing precocious puberty in boys) or estrogens (causing gynecomastia in men).
    ◦ **Sertoli Cell Tumors**: Typically benign, can also produce hormones.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Peak Incidence**: Ages 15-35.
• **Prevalence**: Relatively rare, accounting for ~1% of all cancers in men.
• **Demographics**: More common in Caucasian men than in African American or Asian men. Incidence is highest in Scandinavia and Western Europe.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Cryptorchidism (undescended testicle)**: The single most significant risk factor. Risk is elevated in both the undescended and contralateral testis. Orchiopexy reduces risk but does not eliminate it; its main benefit is allowing for easier surveillance.
• **Personal history** of testicular cancer in the contralateral testis.
• **Family history** of testicular cancer (especially in a father or brother).
• **Intratubular germ cell neoplasia (ITGCN)**.
• **HIV infection**.
• **Klinefelter syndrome** (47, XXY).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a young man who self-discovers a nodule or **painless swelling** in one testicle, often with a dull ache or sensation of **"heaviness"** in the lower abdomen or scrotum.
• Approximately 10% of patients present with symptoms of metastatic disease.
• **Painless, solid testicular mass or nodule** (most common presenting symptom).
• Sensation of scrotal **heaviness** or fullness.
• Dull ache in the lower abdomen, groin, or scrotum.
• Acute testicular pain (~10%), often due to intratumoral hemorrhage or infarction.
• **Symptoms of Metastasis**:
    ◦ **Back pain**: Retroperitoneal lymph node metastasis.
    ◦ **Cough, dyspnea, or hemoptysis**: Pulmonary metastasis.
    ◦ **Lower extremity edema**: IVC compression from retroperitoneal mass.
    ◦ **Neurologic symptoms**: Brain metastasis.
• **Hormonally-mediated symptoms** (rare, <10%):
    ◦ **Gynecomastia**: Due to **β-hCG** production (seen with choriocarcinoma).
sections.physicalExam:
• **Mass**: Firm, non-tender, fixed (indurated) mass that is part of the testicular parenchyma and cannot be separated from it.
• **Transillumination**: The mass **will not** transilluminate (differentiates from a hydrocele).
• **Testicular Atrophy**: The contralateral testis may show signs of atrophy.
• **Lymphadenopathy**: Palpate for supraclavicular or inguinal lymphadenopathy.
• **Abdominal Exam**: Check for a palpable abdominal mass (suggesting large-volume retroperitoneal disease).
• **Gynecomastia**: Note any breast tissue development.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Scrotal Ultrasound**: **Best initial test**. Confirms the presence of an intratesticular mass (highly suspicious for malignancy) versus an extratesticular mass (usually benign).
• **Tumor Markers (Serum)**: Obtain **before** orchiectomy, as levels guide staging, prognosis, and monitoring.
    ◦ **Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)**: Elevated in many NSGCTs (especially Yolk Sac Tumors). **A pure seminoma will NEVER produce AFP**. If AFP is elevated, the tumor contains a non-seminomatous component.
    ◦ **Beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG)**: Can be elevated in both NSGCTs (especially choriocarcinoma) and some seminomas (~15%).
    ◦ **Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)**: A non-specific marker of cell turnover and tumor burden; correlates with prognosis.
• **Radical Inguinal Orchiectomy**: This is the gold standard for **both diagnosis (histopathology) and initial treatment**. The testicle and spermatic cord are removed through a groin incision.
    ◦ **A trans-scrotal biopsy is CONTRAINDICATED** due to the risk of tumor seeding and disruption of lymphatic drainage pathways, which can upstage the patient and worsen prognosis.
• **Staging**: After orchiectomy, perform imaging to assess for metastasis.
    ◦ **CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis** is standard for detecting nodal (retroperitoneal) and visceral metastases.
sections.treatment:
• **All Stages**: Initial step is **radical inguinal orchiectomy**.
• **Stage I (localized) Seminoma**:
    ◦ **Active surveillance** (preferred for low-risk).
    ◦ Adjuvant therapy: Single-dose **carboplatin** or radiation therapy to para-aortic nodes.
• **Stage I NSGCT**:
    ◦ **Active surveillance** for low-risk patients (no lymphovascular invasion).
    ◦ Adjuvant therapy for high-risk patients: 1-2 cycles of **BEP chemotherapy** or retroperitoneal lymph node dissection (RPLND).
• **Advanced Disease (Metastatic)**:
    ◦ **Seminoma**: Radiation therapy for localized nodal disease or combination chemotherapy (e.g., **EP**: Etoposide, Platinum/Cisplatin) for more advanced disease.
    ◦ **NSGCT**: Primary treatment is chemotherapy with **BEP** (**B**leomycin, **E**toposide, **P**latinum/Cisplatin). Post-chemotherapy **RPLND** is often required to resect any residual masses.
sections.management:
• **Sperm Banking**: Should be offered to all patients **before** initiating any treatment (orchiectomy, chemotherapy, radiation, or RPLND) as all can impair fertility.
• **Surveillance**: Post-treatment follow-up is critical. It involves a strict schedule of:
    ◦ Physical exams
    ◦ Serial serum tumor markers (AFP, β-hCG)
    ◦ Imaging (CT scans, chest x-rays)
• **Long-term monitoring**: Patients are at risk for hypogonadism, cardiovascular disease, and secondary malignancies from chemo/radiation.
sections.complications:
• **Metastasis**: Primarily via lymphatics to the **retroperitoneal lymph nodes**. Hematogenous spread to the lungs, liver, bone, and brain can also occur.
• **Treatment-Related Complications**:
    ◦ **RPLND**: Retrograde ejaculation (leading to infertility).
    ◦ **Chemotherapy (BEP)**:
        ▪ **B**leomycin: Pulmonary fibrosis.
        ▪ **E**toposide: Secondary leukemia.
        ▪ **P**latinum (Cisplatin): Nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, peripheral neuropathy.
    ◦ **Radiation**: Increased risk of secondary malignancies.
    ◦ **Hypogonadism**: Requires testosterone replacement therapy.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**. The overall 5-year survival rate is >95%.
• For disease confined to the testis (Stage I), survival is ~99%.
• Even with distant metastatic disease, the 5-year survival is approximately 75-80% due to the high chemosensitivity of these tumors.
• Seminomas generally have a slightly better prognosis than NSGCTs stage-for-stage.

sections.overview:
• Penile cancer is a rare malignancy of the external male genitalia.
• The vast majority (>95%) of cases are **Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)**.
• It typically arises from the epithelium of the glans penis, the coronal sulcus, or the inner surface of the prepuce (foreskin).
• The disease progresses from precursor lesions known as **Penile Intraepithelial Neoplasia (PeIN)**.
• Early detection and treatment are crucial, as prognosis is heavily dependent on the stage at diagnosis, particularly the status of the inguinal lymph nodes.
sections.etiology:
• Penile cancer development follows two primary pathways:
    ◦ **HPV-Related Pathway** (approx. 30-50% of cases):
        ▪ Associated with high-risk **Human Papillomavirus (HPV) types 16 and 18**.
        ▪ The virus integrates its DNA into host cells, and the expression of viral oncoproteins E6 and E7 leads to the inactivation of tumor suppressor genes p53 and pRb, respectively.
        ▪ This results in uncontrolled cellular proliferation and malignant transformation.
        ▪ Typically leads to basaloid or warty-type SCC.
    ◦ **Non-HPV-Related Pathway**:
        ▪ Associated with **chronic inflammation** and dermatological conditions.
        ▪ Conditions like **phimosis** (inability to retract the foreskin) lead to the accumulation of **smegma** (a mix of desquamated cells and oils), which acts as a chronic irritant and potential carcinogen.
        ▪ Chronic inflammatory skin conditions, most notably **Lichen Sclerosus** (also known as Balanitis Xerotica Obliterans), are strong predisposing factors.
        ▪ This pathway typically leads to the more common, well-differentiated types of SCC.
• In both pathways, the initial step is the development of a pre-malignant lesion, **Penile Intraepithelial Neoplasia (PeIN)**, which can then progress to invasive SCC.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence:** Rare in developed nations like the United States and Europe (<1 per 100,000 men).
• **Prevalence:** Much higher in parts of South America, Africa, and Asia where HPV prevalence is high and neonatal circumcision is not routine.
• **Age:** Primarily a disease of older men, with a peak incidence in the **6th to 8th decade of life**. It is very rare in men under 40.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The typical patient is an elderly, uncircumcised male who presents with a persistent, non-healing lesion on his penis that has been present for several months to years.
• Delays in seeking care are common due to embarrassment or fear.
• The most common location for the primary tumor is the **glans (48%)**, followed by the **prepuce (21%)**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Biopsy of the Primary Lesion:**
    ◦ **Gold Standard:** A definitive diagnosis requires a tissue sample.
    ◦ **Punch or excisional biopsy** is performed on the suspicious lesion. This confirms the diagnosis of SCC and determines its grade and depth of invasion.
• **Staging (TNM System):**
    ◦ **T (Tumor):** Assess local invasion.
        ▪ Physical exam is the primary tool.
        ▪ **Penile MRI with contrast** can be used to evaluate the depth of invasion into underlying structures (e.g., corpus spongiosum or cavernosum), which is critical for planning organ-sparing surgery.
    ◦ **N (Nodes):** Assess inguinal lymph node involvement. This is the **most important prognostic factor**.
        ▪ **Clinically Negative Nodes (cN0):** For tumors T1G2, a **dynamic sentinel lymph node biopsy (DSNB)** is the standard of care to detect micrometastases.
        ▪ **Clinically Positive Nodes (cN1/cN2):** **Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA)** of the suspicious node is performed. If positive, the patient requires an inguinal lymph node dissection.
    ◦ **M (Metastasis):** Assess for distant spread.
        ▪ **CT scan of the chest/abdomen/pelvis** or a **PET/CT scan** is recommended for patients with palpable inguinal nodes or high-risk disease to rule out distant metastases.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is almost entirely dependent on the **presence and extent of lymph node metastasis**.
• **Node-Negative Disease:** 5-year disease-specific survival is excellent (>90%).
• **Node-Positive Disease:** Survival drops significantly.
    ◦ One positive inguinal node: ~70-80% 5-year survival.
    ◦ Multiple or bilateral inguinal nodes: ~20-50% 5-year survival.
    ◦ Pelvic node involvement: <20% 5-year survival.
• **Distant Metastatic Disease:** Prognosis is very poor, with a median survival of <1 year.

sections.overview:
• A tear or rupture of the urethra, the tube that carries urine from the bladder out of the body
    ◦ These injuries are urologic emergencies, most commonly seen in males due to their longer urethra
• Broadly classified based on anatomical location:
    ◦ **Posterior urethral injuries** (prostatic and membranous urethra)
        ▪ Typically severe and associated with major trauma (e.g., pelvic fractures)
    ◦ **Anterior urethral injuries** (bulbar and penile urethra)
        ▪ Often caused by direct perineal trauma (e.g., straddle injuries)
• Prompt diagnosis and management are critical to prevent long-term complications like stricture, incontinence, and erectile dysfunction
sections.etiology:
• Urethral injuries are almost exclusively caused by trauma
    ◦ The mechanism differs by location
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: A relatively uncommon injury but significant in the context of trauma
• **Demographics**: Overwhelmingly occurs in **males**
• **Association with Pelvic Fractures**: Approximately 5-10% of patients with pelvic fractures will have a concomitant posterior urethral injury
• **Location**:
    ◦ Anterior injuries are more common overall
    ◦ Posterior injuries are more severe and more frequently associated with life-threatening polytrauma
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a **trauma patient**, often from an MVC, with evidence of a pelvic fracture who is unable to urinate
• Suspicion for urethral injury should be extremely high in any male patient with a pelvic fracture or significant perineal trauma
sections.diagnostics:
• The most critical step in diagnosis is to **suspect the injury and AVOID blind urethral catheterization**
• **Gold Standard: Retrograde Urethrogram (RUG)**
    ◦ **Indication**: Mandatory in any patient with suspected urethral injury (e.g., blood at meatus, pelvic fracture with inability to void) *before* attempting Foley catheter placement
    ◦ **Procedure**: A small catheter is placed just inside the urethral meatus, and 20-30 mL of water-soluble contrast is gently injected under fluoroscopy or with a plain X-ray
    ◦ **Findings**: **Extravasation of contrast** outside the normal urethral lumen confirms the diagnosis of a urethral tear/rupture
        ▪ The location of the extravasation determines if it's an anterior or posterior injury
• **Other Imaging**
    ◦ **Pelvic X-ray / CT Scan**: Essential to evaluate for associated pelvic fractures
    ◦ **CT Cystogram**: Often performed during trauma evaluation to rule out a concurrent bladder rupture
sections.prognosis:
• Survival is dictated by the severity of associated injuries (e.g., pelvic hemorrhage)
• Prognosis for urethral function depends on the injury type
    ◦ **Anterior injuries** generally have a better prognosis with lower rates of long-term complications
    ◦ **Posterior injuries** have a high rate of morbidity
        ▪ Even with successful surgical repair, a significant percentage of patients will experience some degree of urethral stricture, erectile dysfunction, or incontinence

sections.overview:
• Bladder rupture is a disruption of the bladder wall integrity, leading to urine leakage into surrounding spaces
    ◦ It is a urologic emergency, most commonly associated with significant trauma, particularly pelvic fractures
    ◦ Ruptures are classified based on location relative to the peritoneal reflection: **extraperitoneal** or **intraperitoneal**
    ◦ Prompt diagnosis and management are crucial to prevent complications like peritonitis and sepsis
sections.etiology:
• Bladder ruptures are primarily caused by trauma, with the mechanism of injury dictating the type of rupture
    ◦ **Blunt Trauma (Most Common)**
        ▪ Accounts for >80% of cases, typically from motor vehicle collisions (MVCs), falls, or crush injuries
        ▪ **Extraperitoneal Rupture (~60%)**
            • Strongly associated with **pelvic fractures**
            • Injury occurs from direct perforation by a bony fragment or shearing forces on the anterolateral bladder wall
            • Urine leaks into the perivesical space (Space of Retzius) but remains outside the peritoneal cavity
        ▪ **Intraperitoneal Rupture (~30%)**
            • Results from a sudden, forceful increase in intravesical pressure (e.g., direct blow to a distended bladder)
            • Rupture occurs at the **bladder dome**, the weakest and most mobile part
            • Urine spills directly into the peritoneal cavity
        ▪ **Combined Rupture (~10%)**: Features of both intraperitoneal and extraperitoneal rupture
    ◦ **Penetrating Trauma**
        ▪ Caused by gunshot or stab wounds to the lower abdomen or pelvis
        ▪ Almost always managed surgically due to the high likelihood of associated visceral and vascular injuries
    ◦ **Iatrogenic Injury**
        ▪ Can occur during urologic procedures (e.g., TURBT), gynecologic surgery (hysterectomy), colorectal surgery, or difficult Foley catheter placement
    ◦ **Spontaneous Rupture (Rare)**
        ▪ Occurs without acute trauma
        ▪ Associated with chronic bladder inflammation, bladder cancer, neurogenic bladder, bladder outlet obstruction, or excessive alcohol consumption
sections.epidemiology:
• Occurs in 5-10% of patients with pelvic fractures
• Conversely, ~80% of bladder ruptures from blunt trauma are associated with a pelvic fracture
• Extraperitoneal ruptures are more common than intraperitoneal ruptures (ratio ~2:1)
• Higher incidence in males, reflecting higher rates of high-impact trauma
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a trauma patient with the following triad:
    ◦ **Gross hematuria**
    ◦ **Suprapubic pain or tenderness**
    ◦ **Inability to void** (despite a feeling of bladder fullness)
• Patients may also present with hemodynamic instability due to associated injuries (e.g., pelvic hemorrhage)
sections.diagnostics:
• **Urinalysis**: Will show gross or microscopic hematuria
• **Labs**
    ◦ **CBC**: To assess for hemorrhage (low Hgb/Hct)
    ◦ **CMP**: May show elevated BUN and creatinine (Cr) with a BUN:Cr ratio >20:1, hyperkalemia, and hyponatremia
        ▪ These changes are due to peritoneal reabsorption of urea and electrolytes from extravasated urine in an **intraperitoneal rupture**
• **Imaging (Gold Standard): Retrograde Cystography**
    ◦ **CT Cystogram**: The preferred modality in the trauma setting
        ▪ Highly sensitive and specific and allows for simultaneous evaluation of other abdominopelvic injuries
    ◦ **Procedure**
        ▪ A Foley catheter is inserted, and the bladder is fully drained
        ▪ The bladder is passively filled with 350-400 mL of water-soluble contrast
        ▪ CT images are obtained with the bladder full and again **after the bladder is drained** (post-drainage films)
    ◦ **Findings for Extraperitoneal Rupture**: Contrast extravasation is seen in the perivesical space, often in a **"flame-shaped" or "starburst" pattern**, confined to the pelvis
    ◦ **Findings for Intraperitoneal Rupture**: Contrast material is seen free in the abdomen, **outlining bowel loops**, filling the paracolic gutters, and surrounding the liver and spleen
    ◦ **Conventional (Plain Film) Cystography**: An alternative if CT is unavailable, involving AP, oblique, and post-drainage pelvic X-rays
• **AP Pelvis X-ray**: Crucial in all trauma patients to identify pelvic fractures
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis for bladder healing is **excellent** with timely and appropriate treatment
• Overall morbidity and mortality are primarily determined by the **severity of associated injuries** (e.g., head trauma, major vascular injury, pelvic hemorrhage), not the bladder rupture itself

sections.overview:
• Testicular trauma is a urologic emergency due to potential for **testicular rupture**, hemorrhage, and loss of function (fertility, hormone production).
• Classified into **blunt trauma** (most common) and **penetrating trauma**.
• The primary goal is to distinguish a simple contusion/hematoma from a **testicular rupture**, which requires urgent **surgical intervention** to maximize **testicular salvage**.
sections.etiology:
• **Mechanism**
    ◦ The testes are compressed against the pubic symphysis or pelvic bones by a **direct blow**.
• **Blunt Trauma (90% of cases)**
    ◦ **Source**: Sports injuries (baseball, martial arts), motor vehicle accidents, assault, straddle injuries.
    ◦ **Pathophysiology**:
        ▪ **Contusion**: Bruising of testicular parenchyma without capsule disruption.
        ▪ **Intratesticular Hematoma**: Bleeding within the testicular parenchyma.
        ▪ **Hematocele**: Blood collection within the space of the tunica vaginalis.
        ▪ **Testicular Rupture (Fracture)**: A surgical emergency where a tear in the **tunica albuginea** leads to extrusion of seminiferous tubules.
        ▪ **Testicular Dislocation**: The testis is displaced from the scrotum into the inguinal canal, abdomen, or perineum.
• **Penetrating Trauma (<10% of cases)**
    ◦ **Source**: Gunshot wounds, stab wounds, animal bites.
    ◦ **Pathophysiology**: Direct violation of the scrotum and **tunica albuginea**, almost always requiring surgical exploration.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Primary Population**: Most common in **males aged 15-40**.
• **Incidence**: Accounts for a significant portion of urologic emergencies in young men.
• **Setting**: **Sports-related injuries** are the leading cause in adolescents and young adults.
sections.riskFactors:
• Participation in **high-impact or contact sports** (e.g., martial arts, football, baseball).
• Occupations with risk of physical trauma (e.g., military, law enforcement).
• Motorcycle accidents.
• Pre-existing **undescended testicle (cryptorchidism)** for injuries to the inguinal region.
• Anatomical predisposition to torsion (e.g., **bell clapper deformity**), as trauma can precipitate a torsion event.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **History**
    ◦ Patient typically presents after a known traumatic event (direct blow, kick, straddle injury) followed by immediate and **severe pain**.
    ◦ Pain may be intense enough to cause a **vasovagal response** with nausea, vomiting, and diaphoresis.
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ **Severe, acute scrotal or testicular pain**.
    ◦ **Scrotal swelling** and significant enlargement.
    ◦ **Nausea and vomiting**.
    ◦ **Ecchymosis** (bruising) of the scrotum, which can develop over hours.
    ◦ Lower abdominal pain (referred pain).
    ◦ Difficulty ambulating due to pain.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Inspection**
    ◦ **Scrotal asymmetry**, significant **edema**, and **ecchymosis**.
    ◦ Scrotum may appear tense and much larger than baseline.
• **Palpation**
    ◦ **Extreme tenderness** to palpation over the affected testis.
    ◦ Scrotum is often tense and firm due to a large hematoma or hematocele.
    ◦ **Loss of normal landmarks**: It is often difficult to distinguish the testis from the epididymis due to massive swelling, suggesting significant injury.
    ◦ A palpable defect in the testicle may suggest rupture but is rarely appreciated due to swelling.
    ◦ Assess testicular position: A **high-riding, horizontal testicle** suggests concurrent **testicular torsion**.
• **Cremasteric Reflex**
    ◦ May be present in simple trauma/rupture but is typically **absent** in **testicular torsion**.
• **Empty Hemiscrotum**
    ◦ Suggests **testicular dislocation**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Scrotal Ultrasound with Color Doppler**
    ◦ This is the **imaging modality of choice**; highly sensitive and specific for testicular rupture.
    ◦ **Key Findings on US**:
        ▪ **Testicular Rupture**: Disruption or discontinuity of the echogenic line of the **tunica albuginea**. A heterogeneous testicular parenchyma indicates contusion, hematoma, or ischemia. Extrusion of testicular contents.
        ▪ **Hematocele**: Collection of complex fluid (blood) around the testis.
        ▪ **Parenchymal Integrity**: Can differentiate between intratesticular and extratesticular hematomas.
        ▪ **Vascular Flow**: Doppler is crucial to assess blood flow. **Absent flow is diagnostic for testicular torsion**.
• **Urinalysis**
    ◦ Performed to rule out associated injury to the urethra or bladder (hematuria).
• **Surgical Exploration**
    ◦ This is the **gold standard** for both diagnosis and treatment if ultrasound is equivocal or clinical suspicion remains high.
sections.treatment:
• **Conservative Management (for contusion, small hematoma, intact tunica)**
    ◦ Scrotal support and elevation.
    ◦ Ice packs.
    ◦ Strict rest.
    ◦ Analgesia (NSAIDs, opioids).
    ◦ Close follow-up with urology.
• **Surgical Management (for testicular rupture, penetrating trauma, large hematocele, or uncertain diagnosis)**
    ◦ **Urgent Surgical Exploration** is required.
    ◦ **Orchiectomy (Testicle Removal)**: Performed if the testis is non-salvageable (e.g., massive destruction >50%, irreparable vascular injury).
sections.management:
• **Emergency Department**
    ◦ [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
• **Post-operative / Follow-up**
    ◦ Patients managed non-operatively should be re-evaluated to ensure the hematoma is resolving and pain is improving.
    ◦ Post-operative patients require routine wound care and follow-up.
sections.complications:
• **Testicular Atrophy**: Most common long-term complication.
• **Infertility / Subfertility**: Can result from loss of tissue, epididymal damage, or anti-sperm antibodies.
• **Hypogonadism**: Impaired testosterone production. Usually occurs with bilateral injury or if contralateral testis was compromised.
• **Chronic Scrotal Pain (Orchialgia)**.
• **Abscess formation / Infection**.
• **Testicular Necrosis requiring Orchiectomy**.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly dependent on the type of injury and the **time to intervention**.
• For **testicular rupture**, surgical repair within **72 hours** is associated with a testicular salvage rate of **>80%**.
• Delays beyond 72 hours significantly decrease the salvage rate and increase the likelihood of requiring an **orchiectomy**.
• Prognosis for simple contusions is excellent with conservative management.

sections.overview:
• **Primary amenorrhea** is the failure of menses to occur by a specific age, defined by one of two criteria:
    ◦ **No menarche by age 15** in the presence of normal growth and **secondary sexual characteristics** (e.g., breast development, pubic hair).
    ◦ **No menarche by age 13** in the absence of **secondary sexual characteristics**.
• It is a symptom, not a diagnosis, and always warrants a thorough investigation to identify the underlying cause.
• The workup is systematic and often follows an algorithm based on the presence or absence of a **uterus** and **secondary sexual characteristics**.
sections.etiology: • The causes of **primary amenorrhea** are best categorized by the level of the **hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis** affected, plus **outflow tract abnormalities**.
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects approximately 1-3% of women of reproductive age.
• The most common causes are:
    ◦ **Gonadal dysgenesis** (including **Turner Syndrome**): ~50%
    ◦ **Müllerian agenesis (MRKH)**: ~15%
    ◦ **Constitutional delay of puberty**: ~10%
    ◦ **Transverse vaginal septum**/**imperforate hymen**: ~5%
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The chief complaint is the 'failure to start menstruating.'
• The clinical approach is dichotomized based on the presence or absence of **secondary sexual characteristics** (**breasts**):
    ◦ **Breasts Present, Uterus Present**: Suggests an **outflow obstruction** (e.g., **imperforate hymen**) or HPO axis dysfunction that occurred after puberty began.
    ◦ **Breasts Present, Uterus Absent**: Classic presentation for **Müllerian Agenesis (MRKH)** or **Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (AIS)**.
    ◦ **Breasts Absent, Uterus Present**: Suggests profound **estrogen deficiency**, indicating a problem at the level of the ovary (**hypergonadotropic**) or hypothalamus/pituitary (**hypogonadotropic**).
    ◦ **Breasts Absent, Uterus Absent**: Extremely rare; may be seen in certain forms of **gonadal dysgenesis** or enzymatic defects.
sections.diagnostics:
• A stepwise, algorithmic approach is essential.
• **Step 1: Initial Workup**
    ◦ **Beta-hCG**: ALWAYS the first test to rule out **pregnancy**.
    ◦ **Pelvic Ultrasound**: The most important initial imaging study.
        ▪ Determines the presence or absence of a **uterus**, creating the primary branch point in the diagnostic algorithm.
• **Step 2: Uterus is ABSENT on Ultrasound**
    ◦ Obtain **Karyotype** (46,XX or 46,XY?) and **Serum Testosterone Level**.
        ▪ **Karyotype 46,XX** + Normal Female Testosterone: Diagnosis is **Müllerian Agenesis (MRKH)**.
        ▪ **Karyotype 46,XY** + Normal or High Male Testosterone: Diagnosis is **Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (AIS)**.
• **Step 3: Uterus is PRESENT on Ultrasound**
    ◦ Check **FSH** and **LH** levels.
    ◦ **High FSH** (>20 IU/L): **Hypergonadotropic Hypogonadism** (problem is at the ovary).
        ▪ **Next Step**: **Karyotype**.
        ▪ **45,X**: Confirms **Turner Syndrome**.
        ▪ **46,XX**: Suggests **Premature Ovarian Failure**.
        ▪ **46,XY**: Suggests **Swyer Syndrome**.
    ◦ **Low or Normal FSH** (<5 IU/L): **Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism** (problem is 'central' - pituitary or hypothalamus).
        ▪ **Next Steps**: Check **Prolactin** and **TSH**.
        ▪ If **Prolactin** is high, workup for **prolactinoma**.
        ▪ If **TSH** is abnormal, workup for **thyroid disease**.
        ▪ If Prolactin and TSH are normal, perform a **Brain MRI** to rule out pituitary/hypothalamic tumors or structural anomalies (e.g., **craniopharyngioma**, **empty sella**).
        ▪ If MRI is normal, consider **Functional Hypothalamic Amenorrhea** or **Constitutional Delay**.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis for life is generally excellent for most causes.
• The main impact is on **fertility**; with modern **assisted reproductive technologies**, many patients can have biological children (e.g., a patient with **MRKH** using a **gestational carrier**).
• **Morbidity** is related to the underlying condition (e.g., cardiac issues in **Turner's**, **bone density loss**).

sections.overview:
• Secondary amenorrhea is the cessation of menses for **3 consecutive months** in a woman who previously had regular menstrual cycles, or for **6 consecutive months** in a woman with a history of irregular cycles.
• It is a symptom, not a diagnosis, and prompts a workup to identify the underlying cause.
• The most common cause of secondary amenorrhea is **pregnancy**.
sections.etiology: • The causes are best categorized by the level of the **Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Ovarian (HPO) axis** that is disrupted.
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects approximately 3-5% of adult women.
• Prevalence is much higher in specific populations, such as elite athletes (up to 65%) and women with eating disorders.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The chief complaint is the **absence of menses**.
• A thorough history is critical to guide the workup. Key historical points include:
    ◦ **Menstrual History:** Age of menarche, cycle length and regularity prior to amenorrhea.
    ◦ **Obstetric History:** History of pregnancies, complications during delivery (e.g., postpartum hemorrhage for Sheehan's), history of D&C.
    ◦ **Lifestyle:** Diet, exercise habits, recent stressors, changes in weight.
    ◦ **Symptoms of Hyperandrogenism:** Hirsutism, acne, hair loss.
    ◦ **Symptoms of Estrogen Deficiency:** Hot flashes, vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, mood changes.
    ◦ **Neurologic Symptoms:** Headaches, visual field changes (**bitemporal hemianopsia**) suggest pituitary mass.
    ◦ **Other Endocrine Symptoms:** Galactorrhea, fatigue, cold intolerance, palpitations, changes in skin/hair.
sections.diagnostics:
• A stepwise, algorithmic approach is essential.
• **Step 1: Rule out Pregnancy**
    ◦ **Urine or Serum β-hCG:** ALWAYS the first test.
• **Step 2: Initial Lab Workup**
    ◦ **TSH:** To rule out thyroid dysfunction.
    ◦ **Prolactin:** To rule out hyperprolactinemia.
    ◦ **FSH:** To screen for ovarian insufficiency.
• **Step 3: Progestin Challenge Test**
    ◦ **Purpose:** To assess for a competent endometrium and adequate endogenous estrogen levels.
    ◦ **Method:** Administer oral medroxyprogesterone acetate (Provera) 10 mg daily for 7-10 days.
    ◦ **Interpretation:**
        ▪ **(+) Positive Test (Withdrawal Bleeding Occurs):** Indicates that the outflow tract is patent and there is sufficient estrogen to have proliferated the endometrium. The problem is **anovulation**.
            • Common Causes: PCOS, mild hypothalamic dysfunction.
        ▪ **(-) Negative Test (No Withdrawal Bleeding):** Indicates either:
            • **Hypoestrogenism:** Not enough estrogen to build up the endometrium (problem with hypothalamus, pituitary, or ovary).
            • **Outflow Tract Obstruction:** e.g., Asherman's syndrome.
• **Step 4: Further Evaluation Based on Initial Results & Progestin Challenge**
    ◦ **If Prolactin is High:** Repeat the level. If still high, consider an **MRI of the pituitary** to look for a prolactinoma.
    ◦ **If TSH is Abnormal:** Treat the underlying thyroid disorder.
    ◦ **If Progestin Challenge is Negative (No Bleed):**
        ▪ Check **FSH and LH**.
        ▪ **High FSH (>30-40 mIU/mL):** Indicates **primary ovarian insufficiency (POI)**. The pituitary is trying to stimulate an unresponsive ovary.
        ▪ **Low or Normal FSH/LH:** Indicates a **hypothalamic or pituitary problem**. The command centers are not working. Consider an **MRI of the brain**.
        ▪ To differentiate between hypoestrogenism and an outflow tract obstruction, perform an **Estrogen-Progestin Challenge**: give estrogen for 21 days, add progestin for the last 10 days.
            • If bleeding occurs, the cause is hypoestrogenism.
            • If no bleeding, the cause is an **outflow tract obstruction (Asherman's)**. This is often bypassed in favor of imaging.
• **Step 5: Imaging**
    ◦ **Pelvic Ultrasound:** Essential for evaluating PCOS ("string of pearls" appearance), uterine anatomy, and endometrial stripe thickness.
    ◦ **Brain/Pituitary MRI:** Indicated for high prolactin, low/normal FSH with hypoestrogenism, or neurological symptoms.
    ◦ **Hysterosalpingogram (HSG) or Saline-Infusion Sonohysterography:** To evaluate for Asherman's syndrome.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is generally excellent and highly dependent on the underlying cause.
• Many causes (FHA, PCOS, hyperprolactinemia, thyroid disease) are reversible or highly manageable with return of menses and fertility.
• Prognosis for fertility is poor in **primary ovarian insufficiency (POI)** and may require donor oocytes.

sections.overview:
• A form of abnormal uterine bleeding characterized by infrequent menstrual periods
• Defined as a menstrual cycle length of **more than 35 days but less than 6 months**
◦ A cycle length greater than 6 months (or 3 missed cycles for a previously regular woman) is classified as **secondary amenorrhea**
• Oligomenorrhea is a symptom, not a diagnosis, and it typically reflects an underlying issue with ovulation (oligo-ovulation) or hormonal regulation, most commonly dysfunction of the **hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis**.
sections.etiology:
• The underlying cause is almost always related to disruption of the normal **HPO axis**, leading to infrequent or absent ovulation (anovulation)
• **Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)**
◦ **Pathophysiology**: The most common cause. Characterized by **hyperandrogenism**, ovulatory dysfunction, and polycystic ovaries
▪ **Insulin resistance** is a key factor, leading to increased LH pulse frequency, which in turn stimulates theca cells to produce androgens. This androgen excess disrupts follicular development, causing anovulation
• **Hypothalamic Dysfunction (Functional Hypothalamic Amenorrhea - FHA)**
◦ **Pathophysiology**: Decreased pulsatile secretion of **Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH)** from the hypothalamus. This leads to low levels of LH and FSH, resulting in low estrogen and anovulation
◦ **Causes**: Excessive exercise, significant weight loss (e.g., eating disorders like anorexia nervosa), and high levels of emotional or physical stress
▪ This triad (low energy availability, menstrual dysfunction, low bone density) is known as the **Female Athlete Triad**
• **Hyperprolactinemia**
◦ **Pathophysiology**: Elevated prolactin levels suppress GnRH secretion from the hypothalamus, leading to anovulation
◦ **Causes**: Pituitary adenoma (**prolactinoma**), medications (e.g., antipsychotics, TCAs, metoclopramide), **hypothyroidism** (high TRH stimulates prolactin), or idiopathic
• **Thyroid Disease**
◦ **Pathophysiology**: Both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism can disrupt the HPO axis
▪ **Hypothyroidism**: Increased TRH can stimulate prolactin release. Also alters metabolism of sex hormones
▪ **Hyperthyroidism**: Increases sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), altering free estrogen and androgen levels
• **Perimenopause / Primary Ovarian Insufficiency (POI)**
◦ **Pathophysiology**: Depletion of ovarian follicles leads to decreased estrogen production and loss of negative feedback on the pituitary. This results in an **elevated FSH level** as the pituitary tries to stimulate the failing ovaries
• **Immature HPO Axis**
◦ **Pathophysiology**: Common in the first 1-2 years after menarche. The HPO axis is still maturing, leading to anovulatory cycles
▪ This is generally a diagnosis of exclusion in adolescents
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects approximately 10-15% of women of reproductive age
• **PCOS** is the most common cause, accounting for a significant portion of cases
• More prevalent in athletes, women with eating disorders, and those with high levels of stress
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The patient is a female of reproductive age presenting with a chief complaint of "irregular periods," "skipped periods," or "my cycle is too long"
• The history is the most critical tool for narrowing the differential diagnosis
◦ Key questions should focus on cycle length, associated symptoms (**hair growth**, **acne**, **milk discharge**), lifestyle factors (diet, exercise, stress), and medical history
sections.diagnostics:
• The workup proceeds in a stepwise, logical fashion
• **Rule out Pregnancy**
◦ **Urine hCG** or **serum β-hCG** is the essential first step
• **Initial Hormonal Panel**
◦ **TSH**: To screen for thyroid disease
◦ **Prolactin**: To screen for hyperprolactinemia
• **Further Endocrine Evaluation** (if initial tests are normal and suspicion remains)
◦ **FSH and LH**
▪ **LH:FSH ratio >2:1 or 3:1** is suggestive of **PCOS** (but not diagnostic)
▪ **Elevated FSH** (>25-30 IU/L) suggests ovarian insufficiency/perimenopause
▪ **Low/Normal FSH & LH** suggests a central (hypothalamic or pituitary) cause
◦ **Testosterone (Total and Free)**: Elevated in PCOS
◦ **DHEA-S**: To assess for an adrenal source of androgens. Markedly high levels may suggest an androgen-secreting tumor
◦ **17-hydroxyprogesterone**: Screen for non-classic **congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH)**, a PCOS mimic. Best drawn in the early morning follicular phase
• **Metabolic Workup** (if PCOS is suspected)
◦ **2-hour oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT)**: Gold standard for diagnosing impaired glucose tolerance/diabetes in PCOS
◦ **Fasting lipid panel**
◦ **HbA1c**
• **Imaging**
◦ **Pelvic Ultrasound (Transvaginal)**
▪ To evaluate for polycystic-appearing ovaries (**"string of pearls"** appearance: 12-20 follicles per ovary or increased ovarian volume)
▪ To measure **endometrial stripe thickness**. A thick stripe (>4-5 mm in postmenopausal, variable in premenopausal) in an anovulatory patient raises concern for **endometrial hyperplasia**
◦ **Brain MRI**
▪ Indicated if **prolactin is significantly elevated** (>100 ng/mL) or if there are neurologic symptoms to evaluate for a **pituitary adenoma**
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis for resolving oligomenorrhea is generally excellent if the underlying cause is identified and treated appropriately
• Fertility can often be restored
• The long-term health prognosis depends on managing associated risks, such as metabolic syndrome in **PCOS** or bone loss in **FHA**

sections.overview:
• A form of **Abnormal Uterine Bleeding (AUB)** defined by a menstrual cycle frequency of **less than 21 days**.
• Characterized by regular, but overly frequent, menstruation.
• The underlying physiologic defect is typically a **shortened follicular phase** of the menstrual cycle, leading to early ovulation.
• A common complaint, particularly at the extremes of reproductive age (**adolescence** and **perimenopause**).
sections.etiology:
• The core pathophysiologic mechanism is **dysfunction of the Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Ovarian (HPO) axis**, which disrupts normal hormonal cycling.
    ◦ This leads to a shortened follicular phase, premature follicular development, and an earlier LH surge, resulting in more frequent ovulation and menstruation.
• **Common Causes**:
    ◦ **Endocrine/Hormonal (Most Common)**:
        ▪ **Perimenopause**: As ovarian reserve declines, FSH levels rise, leading to accelerated follicular development and shorter, often irregular, cycles.
        ▪ **Puberty/Menarche**: An immature HPO axis can lead to irregular ovulatory patterns and short cycles.
        ▪ **Anovulatory or Dysovulatory Cycles**: Common in conditions like **Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)**, where hormonal imbalances disrupt normal follicle maturation.
        ▪ **Thyroid Dysfunction**: Both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism can disrupt HPO axis function.
        ▪ **Hyperprolactinemia**: Elevated prolactin suppresses GnRH, leading to ovulatory dysfunction.
    ◦ **Systemic Factors**:
        ▪ **Psychological Stress**: Can alter GnRH pulsatility from the hypothalamus.
        ▪ **Excessive Exercise / Low Body Weight**: Can lead to hypothalamic amenorrhea, but may initially present with shorter cycles.
    ◦ **Infections**:
        ▪ **Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID)**: Can cause endometritis and intermenstrual bleeding that may be perceived by the patient as frequent periods.
    ◦ **Structural Lesions**:
        ▪ While less common as a direct cause of a shortened cycle, conditions like uterine **fibroids** or **polyps** can cause intermenstrual bleeding that mimics polymenorrhea.
sections.epidemiology:
• Most prevalent at the **extremes of reproductive age**:
    ◦ **Adolescents**: Immediately following menarche due to an immature HPO axis.
    ◦ **Perimenopausal women (age >40)**: Due to declining ovarian function.
• Exact prevalence is difficult to determine as it often overlaps with other AUB patterns like **heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia)**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient will typically present with the chief complaint of "getting my period too often" or "my cycle is only 2 or 3 weeks long."
• The key to the diagnosis is a meticulous **menstrual history**, focusing on the frequency, regularity, duration, and volume of bleeding.
• It is critical to differentiate true polymenorrhea from **intermenstrual or breakthrough bleeding**.
sections.diagnostics:
• The workup is aimed at ruling out pregnancy, identifying systemic causes, and evaluating for structural abnormalities.
• **Initial Lab Tests (All Patients)**:
    ◦ **Beta-hCG (Urine or Serum)**: **ALWAYS the first step** to rule out pregnancy-related bleeding.
    ◦ **Complete Blood Count (CBC)**: To assess for **anemia**.
    ◦ **TSH**: To screen for thyroid dysfunction.
• **Second-Line Lab Tests (Based on H&P)**:
    ◦ **Prolactin**: If galactorrhea, pituitary symptoms, or irregular cycles.
    ◦ **FSH, LH, Estradiol**: To evaluate for **perimenopause** (elevated FSH) or **PCOS** (elevated LH:FSH ratio, typically >2:1).
    ◦ **Coagulation Studies (vWF, PT/PTT)**: If heavy bleeding (**menorrhagia**) is also a component, especially in adolescents.
• **Imaging**:
    ◦ **Transvaginal Ultrasound (TVUS)**: **First-line imaging modality**.
        ▪ Used to evaluate for structural abnormalities like **fibroids**, **polyps**, **adenomyosis**, and to measure **endometrial stripe thickness**.
• **Procedures**:
    ◦ **Endometrial Biopsy**: Indicated to rule out **endometrial hyperplasia** or **carcinoma** in patients with risk factors:
        ▪ Age **> 45** with AUB.
        ▪ Age **< 45** with risk factors for endometrial cancer (e.g., **obesity**, **PCOS**, **unopposed estrogen exposure**).
        ▪ Failure of medical management or persistent AUB.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is generally **excellent** once the underlying cause is identified and appropriately treated.
• For functional causes like **perimenopause** or **stress**, management may be required for a longer duration until the underlying physiologic state changes (i.e., menopause occurs).

sections.overview:
• **Dysmenorrhea** is the medical term for painful menstruation and is one of the most common gynecologic complaints.
• It is broadly categorized into two types:
    ◦ **Primary Dysmenorrhea**: Recurrent, crampy, lower abdominal pain that occurs during menstruation **in the absence of any demonstrable pelvic pathology**.
        ▪ Typically begins within 6-12 months of menarche.
    ◦ **Secondary Dysmenorrhea**: Painful menstruation caused by an **underlying organic pelvic pathology**.
        ▪ It can begin at any time after menarche but is more common in women over 25.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Extremely common, affecting 50-90% of reproductive-age women.
    ◦ It is a leading cause of recurrent short-term school and work absenteeism.
• **Primary Dysmenorrhea**: Most common in adolescents and women in their early 20s.
    ◦ Onset is typically within 1-2 years of menarche, once ovulatory cycles are established.
• **Secondary Dysmenorrhea**: Prevalence increases with age, most commonly presenting in women aged 25 and older.
sections.clinicalPresentation: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• **Primary Dysmenorrhea**: Excellent.
    ◦ Symptoms typically lessen with age and often improve significantly after childbirth.
    ◦ Most patients respond well to **NSAIDs** and/or hormonal therapy.
• **Secondary Dysmenorrhea**: Variable.
    ◦ Prognosis depends entirely on the underlying pathology, its severity, and the effectiveness of its specific treatment.

sections.overview:
• Abnormal Uterine Bleeding (AUB) is a broad term for bleeding from the uterine corpus that is abnormal in regularity, volume, frequency, or duration; it is a symptom, not a diagnosis.
	◦ The International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) established the **PALM-COEIN** classification system to standardize etiology.
	◦ The goal of the workup is to identify the underlying cause and rule out **malignancy**, especially in at-risk populations.
	◦ Older terms (menorrhagia, metrorrhagia, menometrorrhagia) are replaced by more descriptive terms like **Heavy Menstrual Bleeding (HMB)** and **Intermenstrual Bleeding (IMB)**.
sections.etiology: • The **PALM-COEIN** system is the standard for classifying the causes of AUB.
sections.epidemiology:
• AUB is one of the most common gynecologic complaints, affecting up to 30% of women of reproductive age.
• It has a bimodal peak incidence:
	◦ **Adolescence**: Due to an immature **hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis** causing ovulatory dysfunction (AUB-O).
	◦ **Perimenopausal period**: Due to waning ovarian function, **anovulatory cycles** (AUB-O), and an increased prevalence of structural lesions like **fibroids** and **malignancy**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation varies by underlying etiology; the key is to characterize the bleeding pattern.
	◦ **Heavy Menstrual Bleeding (HMB)**:
		▪ Defined as excessive menstrual blood loss (>80 mL per cycle) or bleeding that interferes with quality of life.
		▪ Patients may report soaking through pads/tampons every 1-2 hours or passing large clots.
	◦ **Intermenstrual Bleeding (IMB)**:
		▪ Bleeding that occurs between regular menstrual cycles.
	◦ **Postcoital Bleeding**:
		▪ Suggests a cervical lesion (e.g., **polyp**, **cervicitis**, **cancer**) until proven otherwise.
	◦ **Irregular Bleeding**:
		▪ Unpredictable frequency and flow, classic for ovulatory dysfunction (AUB-O).
	◦ **Postmenopausal Bleeding**:
		▪ Any bleeding that occurs >12 months after the final menstrual period.
sections.diagnostics: • The workup is tiered based on age, risk factors, and clinical suspicion.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is excellent for benign causes of AUB with correct diagnosis and treatment.
• For **malignancy**, prognosis depends on the histologic type, grade, and stage at diagnosis.
	◦ **Endometrial cancer** is often diagnosed early due to the symptom of **postmenopausal bleeding**, leading to a generally good prognosis.

sections.overview:
• Premenstrual Syndrome (PMS) is a clinical syndrome characterized by a cluster of recurrent physical, behavioral, and psychological symptoms that occur in a predictable, cyclical pattern during the **luteal phase** of the menstrual cycle.
    ◦ Symptoms must be severe enough to cause significant distress or interfere with daily functioning and must resolve shortly after the onset of menstruation, followed by a symptom-free period in the follicular phase.
• A more severe variant with predominantly psychological symptoms is termed **Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD)**.
sections.etiology:
• The exact etiology is unknown but is strongly linked to the cyclical fluctuations of ovarian steroid hormones, specifically **estrogen and progesterone**, during the luteal phase.
    ◦ **Central Serotonin (5-HT) Dysregulation**: This is the leading theory.
