        ▪ Normal ovarian hormone cycling appears to trigger a central nervous system response in susceptible individuals, leading to a decrease in serotonin levels or altered serotonin receptor sensitivity.
        ▪ Serotonin is crucial for mood, appetite, and sleep regulation, which explains the predominance of affective symptoms.
        ▪ The efficacy of SSRIs in treating PMS strongly supports this hypothesis.
    ◦ **GABA System**:
        ▪ Allopregnanolone, a metabolite of progesterone, is a potent positive modulator of GABA-A receptors (similar to benzodiazepines).
        ▪ In most women, this has a calming effect.
        ▪ In women with PMS, a paradoxical anxiogenic effect may occur due to altered receptor sensitivity or fluctuations in allopregnanolone levels.
    ◦ **Genetic Predisposition**: A familial link suggests a genetic component to susceptibility.
• Importantly, PMS is **not caused by a hormone imbalance**, but rather an abnormal response to normal hormonal changes.
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects up to **75%** of menstruating women to some degree.
• Clinically significant PMS meeting diagnostic criteria occurs in **20-30%** of menstruating women.
• **PMDD**, the severe form, affects **3-8%**.
• Symptoms typically begin in the 20s or 30s and may worsen with age, often peaking in the late 30s to early 40s.
• Symptoms cease after menopause.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The hallmark of PMS is the **timing of symptoms**.
    ◦ The patient is a menstruating female who reports a predictable pattern of symptoms that:
        ▪ Begin during the **luteal phase** (the 1-2 weeks leading up to menses).
        ▪ Peak in the days just before menses begins.
        ▪ **Resolve within 4 days** of the onset of menses.
        ▪ Are absent during the **follicular phase** (the week after her period ends).
• The patient will often complain that these symptoms disrupt her work, school, or personal relationships.
sections.diagnostics:
• The diagnosis of PMS is **clinical**, based entirely on history and confirmed with prospective charting.
    ◦ **Symptom Diary/Calendar**: This is the **gold standard for diagnosis**.
        ▪ The patient must chart her symptoms daily for at least **two consecutive menstrual cycles**.
        ▪ This confirms the link to the luteal phase and the presence of a symptom-free follicular phase, distinguishing PMS from chronic mood disorders.
    ◦ **ACOG Diagnostic Criteria for PMS**:
        ▪ At least **one** affective and **one** somatic symptom from the lists above.
        ▪ Symptoms occur during the **5 days before menses** in each of the 3 prior menstrual cycles.
        ▪ Symptoms are relieved within **4 days of the onset of menses**.
        ▪ Symptoms do not recur until at least **cycle day 13**.
        ▪ Symptoms are present in the absence of any pharmacologic therapy, hormone ingestion, or drug/alcohol use.
        ▪ Symptoms cause identifiable dysfunction in social or economic performance.
    ◦ **Laboratory Studies**:
        ▪ **Not used for diagnosis**, but to rule out differential diagnoses.
            ▪ **TSH**: To rule out hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism.
            ▪ **CBC**: To rule out anemia as a cause of fatigue.
            ▪ **hCG**: To rule out pregnancy.
sections.prognosis:
• With appropriate management, the prognosis is excellent, and most women experience significant symptom relief.
• PMS is a chronic condition that typically recurs cyclically until menopause.
• Symptoms resolve completely after menopause (naturally or surgically induced).

sections.overview:
• Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD) is a severe, disabling form of Premenstrual Syndrome (PMS) classified in the DSM-5 as a Depressive Disorder.
    ◦ The defining characteristic is a cluster of severe mood, behavioral, and physical symptoms that occur cyclically during the **luteal phase** of the menstrual cycle and remit within a few days of the onset of menses.
    ◦ The key distinguishing feature from PMS is the presence of **clinically significant distress or functional impairment** (e.g., in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning).
sections.etiology:
• PMDD is **not caused by a hormonal imbalance**, but rather an abnormal central nervous system (CNS) response to normal cyclical fluctuations in ovarian hormones (estrogen and progesterone).
    ◦ **Serotonin (5-HT) Dysregulation:**
        ▪ The primary hypothesis is that gonadal steroids modulate serotonergic systems.
        ▪ Women with PMDD appear to have altered serotonin receptor sensitivity and decreased serotonin activity during the luteal phase, leading to mood and behavioral symptoms.
        ▪ This explains the rapid efficacy of SSRIs.
    ◦ **GABA System & Allopregnanolone:**
        ▪ Allopregnanolone, a progesterone metabolite, is a positive allosteric modulator of the GABA-A receptor (similar to benzodiazepines).
        ▪ In susceptible individuals, there may be a paradoxical anxiogenic or dysphoric response to the normal luteal phase rise in allopregnanolone levels.
    ◦ **Genetic Predisposition:**
        ▪ A genetic component is likely, involving genes related to hormone signaling and serotonin transport (e.g., ESR1, HTR1A).
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** Affects approximately 3-8% of menstruating women.
• **Age of Onset:** Can occur anytime after menarche, but most commonly presents in the late 20s to early 30s.
• Symptoms cease after menopause.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with a history of recurrent, predictable symptoms that begin 1-2 weeks before her period and severely impact her life.
    ◦ She will report feeling "out of control," "not herself," or experiencing intense interpersonal conflicts specifically during this time.
• A crucial element of the history is the presence of a **symptom-free period** during the **follicular phase** (the week after her period ends).
sections.diagnostics:
• The diagnosis is clinical and based on DSM-5 criteria, confirmed by prospective charting.
    ◦ **Gold Standard:** **Prospective symptom charting** for at least **two consecutive menstrual cycles**.
        ▪ Tools like the Daily Record of Severity of Problems (DRSP) are used.
        ▪ This confirms the cyclical nature of the symptoms, their severity, and their remission after menses, which is essential to distinguish PMDD from an exacerbation of another underlying disorder.
    ◦ **Labs (to rule out other etiologies):**
        ▪ **TSH:** To rule out hypothyroidism.
        ▪ **CBC:** To rule out anemia (fatigue).
        ▪ **hCG:** To rule out pregnancy.
    ◦ Hormone levels (FSH, LH, estrogen, progesterone) are **not indicated** as they are typically normal.
sections.prognosis:
• With treatment, the prognosis is **excellent**.
    ◦ Most women experience significant symptom relief with first or second-line therapies.
• PMDD is a chronic condition that will persist throughout the reproductive years unless treated.
• Symptoms resolve definitively with menopause (natural or induced).

sections.overview:
• Endometriosis is a chronic, inflammatory, **estrogen-dependent** condition characterized by the presence of **endometrial-like tissue** (glands and stroma) outside of the uterine cavity.
    ◦ These ectopic implants respond to hormonal fluctuations of the menstrual cycle, leading to proliferation, bleeding, and local inflammation.
    ◦ This process results in the cardinal symptoms of **chronic pelvic pain**, **dysmenorrhea**, **dyspareunia**, and **infertility**.
    ◦ The severity of symptoms does not necessarily correlate with the extent of the disease.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ The exact etiology is unknown, but several theories exist:
        ▪ **Sampson's Theory (Retrograde Menstruation)**: The most widely accepted theory. Endometrial fragments are transported backward through the fallopian tubes during menstruation and implant onto pelvic structures.
        ▪ **Coelomic Metaplasia Theory**: Peritoneal cells (which share a common embryologic origin with endometrial cells) undergo metaplastic transformation into endometrial tissue. This explains endometriosis in individuals without a uterus or in unusual locations.
        ▪ **Lymphatic/Vascular Spread Theory**: Endometrial tissue is transported via the lymphatic system or blood vessels to distant sites, explaining rare cases of thoracic or central nervous system endometriosis.
        ▪ **Stem Cell Theory**: Progenitor/stem cells from the bone marrow or endometrium travel to the peritoneum and differentiate into endometrial tissue.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Hormonal Response**: Ectopic implants contain estrogen and progesterone receptors. Estrogen stimulates their growth and proliferation.
    ◦ **Inflammation**: Cyclical bleeding from these implants into the surrounding tissue incites a significant inflammatory response.
    ◦ **Pain Generation**: The body releases inflammatory mediators (prostaglandins, cytokines, nerve growth factor), which sensitize nerve fibers and cause pain.
    ◦ **Fibrosis & Adhesions**: Chronic inflammation leads to scarring, fibrosis, and the formation of adhesions, which can distort pelvic anatomy, tether organs, and contribute to chronic pain and infertility.
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects approximately **10% of women** of reproductive age.
• Prevalence is much higher in symptomatic populations:
    ◦ **30-50%** of women with infertility.
    ◦ **Up to 80%** of women with chronic pelvic pain.
• Most commonly diagnosed in women in their 20s and 30s.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a woman of reproductive age with a chief complaint of pelvic pain that has worsened over time.
    ◦ The pain is typically cyclical, beginning 1-2 days before menses and lasting through the cycle.
    ◦ She may also report deep dyspareunia and difficulty conceiving.
    ◦ It's crucial to remember that some patients may be asymptomatic and diagnosed incidentally during surgery for other reasons.
• **Classic Triad**:
    ◦ **Cyclic pelvic pain (Dysmenorrhea)**
    ◦ **Dyspareunia**
    ◦ **Infertility**
sections.diagnostics:
• **Definitive Diagnosis**: **Laparoscopy with biopsy and histologic confirmation.**
    ◦ **Visualization**: Allows direct inspection of the pelvis. Lesions can appear as classic **"powder-burn"** (black/blue), red, white, or clear vesicles. Adhesions and endometriomas may also be seen.
    ◦ **Biopsy**: Histology showing endometrial glands and stroma confirms the diagnosis.
• **Presumptive Diagnosis**: A clinical diagnosis is often made based on a classic history and physical exam, allowing for initiation of empiric medical therapy without immediate surgery.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Transvaginal Ultrasound (TVUS)**: First-line imaging modality.
        ▪ Primary role is to identify **endometriomas ("chocolate cysts")**, which appear as unilocular or multilocular cysts with homogenous, low-level internal echoes (**"ground-glass" appearance**).
        ▪ Can also identify deep infiltrating disease and suggest adhesions (e.g., "kissing ovaries").
        ▪ A normal ultrasound does not rule out endometriosis.
    ◦ **MRI**: Not routine. Reserved for surgical planning in cases of suspected deep infiltrating endometriosis (e.g., bowel or bladder involvement) to map the extent of disease.
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **CA-125**: **Not a diagnostic marker.** It is non-specific and can be elevated in endometriosis, fibroids, PID, and ovarian cancer. May be used to follow disease progression in some established cases, but has a limited role.
sections.prognosis:
• Endometriosis is a chronic and recurrent disease.
• Symptoms typically resolve after menopause (natural or surgical) due to estrogen deprivation.
• Without post-operative medical suppression, the 5-year recurrence rate of pain after conservative surgery is approximately **40-50%**.
• Fertility can often be achieved with appropriate surgical and/or assisted reproductive techniques.

sections.overview:
• Benign gynecologic condition characterized by the presence of **ectopic endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium** (the muscular wall of the uterus)
    ◦ This misplaced tissue leads to diffuse uterine enlargement, hypertrophy, and hyperplasia of the surrounding myometrium
    ◦ Often referred to as "endometriosis interna"
    ◦ A major cause of **heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB)** and **dysmenorrhea** in women, particularly in their late reproductive years
sections.etiology:
• The exact etiology is unknown, but the most widely accepted theory is the **invagination theory**
    ◦ **Pathogenesis**: This theory proposes that a disruption or break in the **endometrial-myometrial junction (EMJ)** allows the basal layer of the endometrium to invade the underlying myometrium
    ◦ **Triggers for Invagination**: This disruption is thought to be caused by "microtrauma" from events like:
        ▪ Childbirth (uterine hyperperistalsis and placental separation)
        ▪ Uterine instrumentation (e.g., D&C, C-section, myomectomy)
• **Hormonal Influence**
    ◦ Adenomyosis is an **estrogen-dependent** condition
    ◦ The ectopic endometrial tissue within the myometrium responds to cyclical hormonal changes, leading to bleeding within the uterine muscle
    ◦ This intramyometrial bleeding causes an inflammatory response, smooth muscle hypertrophy, and hyperplasia, resulting in a diffusely enlarged, tender, and "boggy" uterus
• **Disease Regression**
    ◦ Symptoms and uterine size typically regress after menopause due to the decline in estrogen
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: True prevalence is difficult to determine as definitive diagnosis requires hysterectomy; estimates range from 20% to 65% in hysterectomy specimens
• **Peak Incidence**: Most commonly diagnosed in women in their **40s and 50s**
• **Demographics**: Significantly more common in **multiparous** women compared to nulliparous women
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a **perimenopausal, multiparous woman** (e.g., G4P4, age 45) complaining of:
    ◦ Progressively worsening **heavy menstrual bleeding**
    ◦ Severe **menstrual cramps**
    ◦ Significant impact on her quality of life
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is often presumptive, based on clinical findings and imaging; the definitive diagnosis is histological
• **Transvaginal Ultrasound (TVUS)**: **First-line imaging modality**
    ◦ **Key Findings**:
        ▪ **Globular, symmetrically enlarged uterus**
        ▪ Asymmetric myometrial wall thickening (posterior wall is most common)
        ▪ Poorly defined endometrial-myometrial junction
        ▪ **Myometrial cysts** (anechoic \"lakes\" or swiss-cheese appearance)
        ▪ Linear, hyperechoic striations radiating from the endometrium (\"Venetian blind\" shadowing)
• **MRI**: The **most accurate non-invasive imaging test**, reserved for cases where ultrasound is inconclusive
    ◦ **Key Finding**: **Thickening of the junctional zone (JZ) to >12 mm** (a normal JZ is typically <5 mm)
• **Histopathology**: **Definitive diagnosis (\"gold standard\")**
    ◦ Requires a hysterectomy specimen
    ◦ Microscopic examination reveals endometrial glands and stroma located at least 2.5 mm deep within the myometrium
• **Other Labs**:
    ◦ **Beta-hCG**: To rule out pregnancy
    ◦ **CBC**: To assess for anemia due to heavy menstrual bleeding
    ◦ **Endometrial biopsy**: To rule out endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma in patients >45 years with abnormal uterine bleeding, or younger patients with risk factors
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent prognosis as adenomyosis is a **benign condition**
• Symptoms are completely resolved by **menopause** or with **hysterectomy**
• Medical management is effective in controlling symptoms for many patients until menopause

sections.overview:
• Uterine leiomyomas, commonly known as **fibroids** or myomas, are benign (non-cancerous) monoclonal tumors arising from the smooth muscle cells (myocytes) and fibroblasts of the myometrium.
• They are the most common benign gynecologic tumors in women.
• Their growth is hormonally sensitive, primarily to **estrogen** and **progesterone**.
• They are classified based on their location within the uterus:
    ◦ **Intramural**: Within the uterine wall (most common type).
    ◦ **Submucosal**: Protrude into the uterine cavity.
        ▪ Most likely to cause **heavy bleeding** and **fertility issues**.
    ◦ **Subserosal**: Protrude from the outer surface of the uterus.
        ▪ Can become **pedunculated** (attached by a stalk).
    ◦ **Cervical**: Located in the cervix (rare).
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ The exact cause is unknown, but development is a multifactorial process involving genetic, hormonal, and growth factor influences.
    ◦ They are considered monoclonal, meaning each tumor arises from a single mutated cell.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Hormonal Influence**: Leiomyoma cells have a higher concentration of estrogen and progesterone receptors than normal myometrial cells.
        ▪ **Estrogen**: Promotes proliferation of smooth muscle cells.
        ▪ **Progesterone**: Upregulates growth factors (e.g., TGF-β) and contributes to cell proliferation.
    ◦ **Growth Factors**: Growth factors like insulin-like growth factor (IGF) and transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) also play a significant role in tumor growth.
    ◦ **Growth Pattern**: Fibroids typically grow during the reproductive years when hormone levels are high and regress or shrink after **menopause** due to hormonal deprivation.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Extremely common, affecting up to 70-80% of women by age 50.
• **Peak Incidence**: Age 30s and 40s, leading up to menopause.
• **Race/Ethnicity**: 2-3 times more common in **African American** women compared to Caucasian women.
    ◦ They also tend to present at an earlier age with larger, more numerous, and more symptomatic fibroids.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Majority are **asymptomatic**: Often discovered incidentally during a routine pelvic exam or on imaging.
• **Symptomatic Presentation** (depends on size, number, and location):
    ◦ **Abnormal Uterine Bleeding (AUB)**: Most common presenting symptom.
    ◦ **Bulk-Related Symptoms**: Due to uterine enlargement and pressure on adjacent organs.
    ◦ **Reproductive Dysfunction**: Infertility or obstetric complications.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Initial Test of Choice**: **Pelvic Ultrasound** (**Transvaginal** is superior for detail).
    ◦ Shows well-circumscribed, round, hypoechoic masses with acoustic shadowing.
    ◦ Confirms presence, number, size, and location of fibroids.
• **Lab Tests**
    ◦ **Pregnancy Test (hCG)**: Rule out pregnancy as a cause of uterine enlargement and bleeding.
    ◦ **Complete Blood Count (CBC)**: To assess for **iron deficiency anemia** from heavy bleeding.
• **Other Imaging / Procedures**
    ◦ **Saline Infusion Sonohysterography (SIS)**: Ultrasound with saline infused into the uterine cavity.
        ▪ Excellent for delineating **submucosal fibroids** and differentiating them from endometrial polyps.
    ◦ **MRI**: The most accurate imaging modality for mapping the number, size, and location of all fibroids.
        ▪ Used for complex cases or pre-operative planning, especially for myomectomy.
    ◦ **Hysteroscopy**: Direct visualization of the uterine cavity.
        ▪ Both diagnostic and therapeutic for **submucosal fibroids**.
• **Biopsy**
    ◦ **Endometrial Biopsy**: **Does not diagnose fibroids**.
        ▪ Performed in women >45 years with **AUB** (or younger with risk factors) to rule out concurrent endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is **excellent** as leiomyomas are benign.
• Malignant transformation into a **leiomyosarcoma** is extremely rare (<0.5%) and is not thought to be a direct malignant degeneration of a pre-existing fibroid.
• Symptoms typically resolve completely after **menopause**.
• Fibroids may recur after myomectomy.

sections.overview:
• Chronic Pelvic Pain (CPP) is a common and complex condition defined as non-cyclical or cyclical pain perceived in the pelvis or lower abdomen, lasting for **at least 6 months**
    ◦ It is a symptom, not a single diagnosis, and is often multifactorial, involving gynecologic, urologic, gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal, and neurologic systems
    ◦ The pain frequently leads to significant functional disability and a decreased quality of life
    ◦ The underlying pathophysiology often involves central sensitization, where the central nervous system becomes amplified to pain signals
sections.etiology:
• CPP arises from a complex interplay of visceral and somatic organ systems, neuromuscular dysfunction, and central nervous system modulation
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Visceral Hyperalgesia**: Increased pain perception from pelvic organs due to nerve sensitization
    ◦ **Central Sensitization**: The primary mechanism; prolonged nociceptive input from the pelvis leads to neuroplastic changes in the spinal cord and brain, resulting in an amplified pain response, allodynia (pain from non-painful stimuli), and hyperalgesia (exaggerated pain response)
    ◦ **Pelvic Floor Muscle Dysfunction**: Chronic pain leads to guarding and hypertonicity of the pelvic floor muscles (e.g., levator ani), which becomes a pain generator itself
    ◦ **Nerve Entrapment/Neuropathy**: Injury or irritation to nerves like the pudendal, ilioinguinal, or genitofemoral nerves
• **Etiologies by System**
    ◦ **Gynecologic (Most Common)**
        ▪ **Endometriosis**: Ectopic endometrial tissue that bleeds cyclically, causing inflammation, adhesions, and pain
        ▪ **Adenomyosis**: Endometrial tissue within the myometrium, leading to a diffusely enlarged, "boggy" uterus
        ▪ **Adhesions**: Scar tissue from prior surgery (C-section, hysterectomy), infection (PID), or endometriosis
        ▪ **Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID)**: Chronic infection/inflammation can lead to adhesions and hydrosalpinx
        ▪ **Leiomyomas (Fibroids)**: Can cause pain through mass effect, degeneration, or torsion
        ▪ **Ovarian Remnant Syndrome**: Residual ovarian tissue post-oophorectomy that can become cystic and painful
        ▪ **Pelvic Congestion Syndrome**: Pelvic varicosities leading to a dull, aching pain worse with prolonged standing
    ◦ **Urologic**
        ▪ **Interstitial Cystitis / Bladder Pain Syndrome (IC/BPS)**: Chronic inflammation of the bladder wall. Classic symptom is pain with bladder filling, relieved by urination
        ▪ **Chronic/Recurrent UTIs**
        ▪ **Urethral Syndrome**
    ◦ **Gastrointestinal**
        ▪ **Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS)**: A primary consideration. Pain is often related to defecation and associated with changes in stool frequency/form
        ▪ **Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD)**: Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis
        ▪ **Chronic Constipation**
        ▪ **Diverticulitis**
    ◦ **Musculoskeletal**
        ▪ **Pelvic Floor Muscle Spasm/Hypertonicity**: A very common contributor and consequence of CPP
        ▪ **Myofascial Pain Syndrome**: Trigger points in the abdominal wall, pelvic floor, or back muscles
        ▪ **Piriformis Syndrome**
        ▪ **Coccydynia**
    ◦ **Neurologic**
        ▪ **Pudendal Neuralgia**: Nerve entrapment causing burning pain/numbness in the perineum
        ▪ **Abdominal Wall Nerve Entrapment** (e.g., ilioinguinal, iliohypogastric)
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects approximately **15-25%** of women aged 18-50
• Accounts for 10-20% of all outpatient gynecology visits
• Accounts for up to 40% of diagnostic laparoscopies
• A specific etiology is not found in up to 60% of cases, highlighting the role of central sensitization
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is highly variable, and a thorough history is the most critical diagnostic tool
    ◦ Patients often present with a long history of pelvic pain evaluated by multiple providers without a definitive diagnosis or effective treatment
    ◦ The pain significantly impacts daily activities, work, sleep, and relationships
sections.diagnostics:
• **Initial Lab Workup**
    ◦ **Urine hCG**: Rule out pregnancy
    ◦ **Urinalysis & Culture**: Rule out UTI
    ◦ **CBC with differential**: Look for signs of infection or anemia
    ◦ **STI Screening**: Gonorrhea and chlamydia NAA testing
    ◦ **ESR/CRP**: Non-specific markers of inflammation
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Transvaginal Ultrasound (TVUS)**: First-line imaging
        ▪ Can identify leiomyomas, adenomyosis (heterogeneous myometrium), endometriomas ("chocolate cysts"), and hydrosalpinx
        ▪ Often normal in cases of adhesions or early endometriosis
    ◦ **MRI**: More detailed evaluation for deep infiltrating endometriosis, adenomyosis, or complex masses
• **Procedures (Diagnostic & Therapeutic)**
    ◦ **Diagnostic Laparoscopy**: **Gold standard** for diagnosing endometriosis and adhesions
        ▪ Allows for direct visualization and simultaneous treatment (e.g., ablation of implants, lysis of adhesions)
    ◦ **Cystoscopy**: To diagnose interstitial cystitis (may show Hunner's ulcers or glomerulations after hydrodistention)
    ◦ **Colonoscopy**: If GI symptoms are prominent, to rule out IBD
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is variable and depends on the underlying etiology, duration of symptoms, and patient engagement in a multidisciplinary treatment plan
• CPP is a chronic condition; complete cure is often not possible. The goal is long-term management and functional improvement
• Recurrence is common, especially after surgical interventions for endometriosis or adhesions if the underlying inflammatory process is not addressed

sections.overview:
• **Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID)** is an acute infection and inflammation of the upper female genital tract, including the uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries, and may involve adjacent pelvic structures.
    ◦ It is a spectrum of inflammatory disorders including any combination of endometritis, salpingitis, oophoritis, and **tubo-ovarian abscess (TOA)**.
• PID is a serious complication of **sexually transmitted infections (STIs)** and can lead to significant long-term morbidity.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Most Common:** *Neisseria gonorrhoeae* and *Chlamydia trachomatis* are implicated in ~50% of cases.
    ◦ **Polymicrobial:** PID is most often a polymicrobial infection. Other organisms include:
        ▪ Anaerobes (*Prevotella*, *Peptostreptococcus*)
        ▪ *Mycoplasma genitalium*
        ▪ *Gardnerella vaginalis*
        ▪ *Haemophilus influenzae*
        ▪ Enteric Gram-negative rods (*E. coli*)
        ▪ *Streptococcus agalactiae*
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Ascending Infection:** The primary mechanism is the ascent of microorganisms from the vagina and cervix into the upper genital tract.
    ◦ **Mucosal Barrier Breakdown:** Infection of the cervix (cervicitis) disrupts the endocervical canal's protective mucosal barrier, allowing organisms to ascend.
    ◦ **Progression of Infection:**
        ▪ **Cervicitis:** Infection starts at the cervix.
        ▪ **Endometritis:** Infection ascends to the endometrium.
        ▪ **Salpingitis:** Infection spreads to the fallopian tubes. This is the most critical event, as inflammation damages the ciliated epithelial cells responsible for ovum transport. This damage leads to tubal scarring, adhesions, and potential occlusion.
        ▪ **Oophoritis/Peritonitis:** Infection can extend to the ovaries and the pelvic peritoneum.
    ◦ **Abscess Formation:** A severe, walled-off infection can lead to a **tubo-ovarian abscess (TOA)**.
sections.epidemiology:
• Primarily affects sexually active women, with the highest incidence in those aged 15-25.
• One of the most common serious infections in women of reproductive age.
• The incidence has been decreasing in the US, likely due to increased screening and treatment for chlamydia.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A sexually active young woman presents with a new onset of **lower abdominal or pelvic pain**, often associated with vaginal discharge and fever.
• The presentation can range from asymptomatic or subclinical to severe, acute illness.
• Subclinical PID is common and a major cause of long-term complications.
sections.diagnostics:
• PID is primarily a **clinical diagnosis**.
• Empiric treatment should be initiated in sexually active young women with pelvic/lower abdominal pain if no other cause is identified and if one or more of the following **minimum clinical criteria** are present on pelvic exam:
    ◦ **Cervical motion tenderness** OR
    ◦ **Uterine tenderness** OR
    ◦ **Adnexal tenderness**
• **Supportive Diagnostic Tests:**
    ◦ **Pregnancy Test (Urine or Serum-hCG):** **MANDATORY** to rule out ectopic pregnancy.
    ◦ **Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT):** For *N. gonorrhoeae* and *C. trachomatis* from a vaginal or endocervical swab.
    ◦ **Saline Microscopy (Wet Mount) of Vaginal Fluid:** May show abundant white blood cells (WBCs).
    ◦ **Inflammatory Markers:** Elevated Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) or C-reactive protein (CRP).
    ◦ **CBC:** May show leukocytosis with a left shift.
• **More Specific/Invasive Tests (Not required for diagnosis):**
    ◦ **Transvaginal Ultrasound (TVUS):**
        ▪ Often the first-line imaging.
        ▪ Findings may include: Thickened, fluid-filled fallopian tubes (hydrosalpinx/pyosalpinx), Free pelvic fluid, **Tubo-ovarian complex** or **tubo-ovarian abscess (TOA)**.
        ▪ A normal ultrasound does not rule out PID.
        ▪ Primarily used to exclude other etiologies (e.g., ovarian torsion, ectopic).
    ◦ **Laparoscopy:**
        ▪ The **gold standard** for diagnosis but rarely performed due to its invasive nature.
        ▪ Reserved for cases of diagnostic uncertainty or failure to respond to therapy.
        ▪ Allows direct visualization of tubal inflammation, adhesions, and purulent exudate.
sections.prognosis:
• With early diagnosis and appropriate antibiotic therapy, the short-term prognosis for cure of infection is excellent.
• The long-term prognosis is variable and depends on the severity of the infection, the number of episodes, and the promptness of treatment.
    ◦ The risk of long-term sequelae (infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pain) remains significant.

sections.overview:
• A **Tubo-Ovarian Abscess (TOA)** is an encapsulated, inflammatory mass involving the fallopian tube, ovary, and occasionally adjacent pelvic organs (e.g., bowel, bladder).
• It is a serious, potentially life-threatening complication of **Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID)**.
• A TOA represents the endpoint of an ascending infection from the lower genital tract, resulting in a collection of pus within the adnexa.
• Prompt diagnosis and treatment are crucial to prevent **rupture** and preserve future fertility.
sections.etiology:
• **Mechanism**: TOA is almost always a consequence of an ascending infection. Pathogens travel from the vagina and cervix, through the uterus (**endometritis**), and into the fallopian tubes (**salpingitis**).
• **Progression**:
    ◦ **Salpingitis**: Infection and inflammation of the fallopian tube lead to purulent exudate.
    ◦ **Tissue Damage**: The inflammatory process damages the fimbriae and tubal epithelium.
    ◦ **Ovarian Involvement**: The infection spreads to the adjacent ovary, causing oophoritis. The structures become edematous and adherent.
    ◦ **Abscess Formation**: The body walls off the infection, creating a complex, encapsulated collection of pus that obliterates the normal tubo-ovarian anatomy.
• **Microbiology**:
    ◦ **Polymicrobial**: TOAs are typically polymicrobial, involving a mix of aerobes and anaerobes.
    ◦ **Initial Pathogens**: Often initiated by sexually transmitted organisms like ***Neisseria gonorrhoeae*** and ***Chlamydia trachomatis***.
    ◦ **Secondary Invaders**: The initial infection creates an anaerobic environment, allowing for the overgrowth of other bacteria from the vaginal flora. Common isolates include:
        ▪ **Anaerobes**: *Bacteroides fragilis*, *Peptostreptococcus*, *Prevotella* spp.
        ▪ **Aerobes/Facultative**: *Escherichia coli*, *Gardnerella vaginalis*, *Streptococcus* spp.
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects primarily sexually active, reproductive-aged women.
• Occurs in approximately 15-35% of women hospitalized for PID.
• The incidence has decreased with improved screening and treatment for STIs.
• Can occur, though less commonly, in postmenopausal women, often associated with underlying malignancy or other pelvic pathology.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Prior history of PID** (strongest risk factor)
• Multiple sexual partners
• Age 15-25 years
• History of sexually transmitted infections (STIs)
• Lack of barrier contraception (condoms)
• **Intrauterine device (IUD)**, particularly within the first 3 weeks of insertion
• Recent uterine instrumentation (e.g., D&C, IUD insertion, hysteroscopy)
• Vaginal douching
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation can range from subacute and indolent to an acute surgical emergency.
• Typically, a young woman presents with an acute onset of **severe, constant lower abdominal pain**, **fever**, and signs of systemic illness.
• A patient with a **ruptured TOA** will present with an **acute abdomen**, signs of **peritonitis**, and potential **hemodynamic instability** (tachycardia, hypotension).
• **Symptoms**:
    ◦ **Acute, severe lower abdominal or pelvic pain** (most common symptom, often bilateral but can be unilateral)
    ◦ **Fever and chills**
    ◦ **Purulent vaginal discharge**
    ◦ Nausea and vomiting
    ◦ Abnormal uterine bleeding (intermenstrual or postcoital)
    ◦ Malaise and generalized weakness
sections.physicalExam:
• **General**: Febrile, tachycardic, appears ill/toxic.
• **Abdominal Exam**:
    ◦ Marked tenderness in lower quadrants.
    ◦ **Rebound tenderness** and **guarding** suggest peritoneal irritation or rupture.
• **Pelvic Exam**:
    ◦ **Cervical Motion Tenderness (CMT)**: Exquisite pain on manipulation of the cervix, often called the **"Chandelier Sign."**
    ◦ **Adnexal Tenderness**: Severe, usually unilateral, tenderness on palpation of the adnexa.
    ◦ **Palpable Adnexal Mass**: A tender, complex, fixed, and ill-defined mass is often palpable.
    ◦ **Purulent discharge** from the cervical os.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Laboratory Studies**:
    ◦ **Pregnancy Test (Serum or Urine hCG)**: **ALWAYS the first step** to rule out ectopic pregnancy, a key differential.
    ◦ **CBC with differential**: **Leukocytosis** (>10,000/L) with a neutrophilic predominance ("**left shift**") is common.
    ◦ **Inflammatory Markers**: Elevated Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) and C-Reactive Protein (CRP).
    ◦ **Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT)**: For ***N. gonorrhoeae*** and ***C. trachomatis*** from a cervical or vaginal swab.
    ◦ **Blood Cultures**: Obtain if the patient is septic or severely ill.
• **Imaging**:
    ◦ **Transvaginal Ultrasound (TVUS)**: **Initial imaging modality of choice.**
        ▪ **Classic Finding**: A complex, multiloculated, thick-walled adnexal mass with internal debris or fluid-fluid levels. The borders between the tube and ovary are often indistinct ("**cogwheel sign**" or loss of tissue planes).
    ◦ **CT Scan with IV Contrast**:
        ▪ Useful when the diagnosis is uncertain, to rule out other intra-abdominal pathology (e.g., appendicitis, diverticulitis), or to evaluate for abscess rupture.
        ▪ Findings are similar to ultrasound: thick-walled, rim-enhancing fluid collection in the adnexa.
sections.treatment:
• **Hospitalization is required for all patients with a suspected TOA.**
• **IV Antibiotics (Broad-Spectrum)**: The cornerstone of therapy, providing coverage for GC/Chlamydia, gram-negatives, and anaerobes.
    ◦ **CDC Recommended Parenteral Regimens**:
        ▪ **Regimen 1**: **Ceftriaxone** 1g IV q24h OR **Cefoxitin** 2g IV q6h **PLUS Doxycycline** 100mg IV/PO q12h **PLUS Metronidazole** 500mg IV/PO q12h.
        ▪ **Regimen 2**: **Clindamycin** 900mg IV q8h **PLUS Gentamicin** loading dose then maintenance dose.
• **Transition to Oral Therapy**:
    ◦ Continue IV antibiotics until the patient shows significant clinical improvement (afebrile, decreased pain, resolving leukocytosis) for at least 24-48 hours.
    ◦ Transition to an oral regimen such as **Doxycycline** 100mg BID + **Metronidazole** 500mg BID to complete a **14-day total course**.
sections.management:
• **Medical Management**:
    ◦ IV antibiotics are successful in ~70% of cases for unruptured TOAs.
    ◦ Patients should be monitored closely for response to therapy (improvement in fever, pain, and WBC count) within 48-72 hours.
• **Surgical / Interventional Management**:
    ◦ **Indications**:
        ▪ [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
    ◦ **Procedures**:
        ▪ **Image-Guided Drainage**: CT or ultrasound-guided percutaneous or transvaginal drainage is a less invasive option for stable patients.
        ▪ **Surgical Drainage/Excision**: Laparoscopy or laparotomy for drainage, lysis of adhesions, and often unilateral **salpingo-oophorectomy** (removal of the affected tube and ovary).
sections.complications:
• **Acute**:
    ◦ **Rupture**: Can lead to diffuse **peritonitis**, **sepsis**, **septic shock**, and death. Mortality is significantly higher.
    ◦ **Sepsis**
    ◦ **Fitz-Hugh-Curtis Syndrome** (perihepatitis)
• **Chronic/Long-Term**:
    ◦ **Infertility**: High risk (~50%) due to tubal damage, scarring, and adhesions.
    ◦ **Ectopic Pregnancy**: 5-10 fold increased risk.
    ◦ **Chronic Pelvic Pain**: Due to pelvic adhesions.
    ◦ Hydrosalpinx
    ◦ Recurrent PID/TOA
sections.prognosis:
• **Unruptured TOA**: Good prognosis with prompt and appropriate antibiotic therapy. Mortality is <1%.
• **Ruptured TOA**: Significantly higher mortality rate (5-10%), even with aggressive surgical and medical management.
• Long-term morbidity related to fertility and chronic pain is high, regardless of successful initial treatment.

sections.overview:
• Ovarian torsion is a gynecologic emergency characterized by the partial or complete twisting (rotation) of the ovary on its ligamentous supports (the infundibulopelvic ligament and the utero-ovarian ligament).
• This rotation obstructs the ovarian blood supply, initially impeding venous and lymphatic outflow, followed by cessation of arterial inflow, leading to ovarian edema, ischemia, infarction, and necrosis if not promptly corrected.
• The fallopian tube often twists along with the ovary, making **adnexal torsion** a more accurate term.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ Torsion occurs when an ovary becomes unstable, allowing it to twist around its pedicle, most often caused by an **ovarian mass** acting as a lead point.
    ◦ **Benign Neoplasms**: **Dermoid cysts** (mature cystic teratomas) are classically associated with torsion. Other benign cysts (serous/mucinous cystadenomas, corpus luteum cysts) are also common causes.
    ◦ **Physiologic Cysts**: Large corpus luteum cysts, particularly in the first trimester of pregnancy, are a frequent cause.
    ◦ **Ovarian Hyperstimulation**: Caused by assisted reproductive technology (ART), leading to large, bilateral, heavy ovaries.
    ◦ **Anatomical Factors**: In children and adolescents, excessively long utero-ovarian ligaments can predispose to torsion even without a mass.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Rotation**: The ovary and adnexa twist on the vascular pedicle.
    ◦ **Venous/Lymphatic Occlusion**: Low-pressure veins and lymphatic vessels are compressed first, leading to impaired drainage, vascular congestion, and ovarian edema.
    ◦ **Arterial Occlusion**: As intra-ovarian pressure from edema increases, it eventually exceeds arterial pressure, cutting off arterial blood supply.
    ◦ **Ischemia & Infarction**: Lack of arterial blood flow leads to ischemia and eventual hemorrhagic infarction and necrosis of the ovarian tissue.
sections.epidemiology:
• Occurs most commonly in women of **reproductive age** (15-30 years).
• Has a bimodal distribution, with peaks in adolescence and the 30s.
• Can occur at any age, from pre-puberty to post-menopause.
• Accounts for approximately 3% of all gynecologic emergencies.
• **Right ovary is more commonly affected** than the left (ratio ~3:2).
    ◦ **Reasoning**: The utero-ovarian ligament is longer on the right, and the sigmoid colon on the left side may physically limit the mobility of the left adnexa.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Ovarian mass > 5 cm** (greatest risk factor)
• Benign gynecologic neoplasms (especially **dermoid cysts**)
• **Pregnancy** (especially 8-16 weeks gestation due to corpus luteum cyst and ligamentous laxity)
• Ovulation induction / Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART)
• Prior history of ovarian torsion
• Previous pelvic surgery (adhesions can alter anatomy)
• Pre-pubertal age group (due to elongated ovarian ligaments)
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a patient of reproductive age with the **sudden onset of severe, unilateral pelvic pain**, frequently associated with **nausea and vomiting**.
    ◦ The pain may have been intermittent for hours or days prior to becoming constant, representing episodes of torsion and spontaneous detorsion.
    ◦ The patient often appears distressed and may be writhing in pain.
• **Pain**
    ◦ **Onset**: Acute, sudden.
    ◦ **Character**: Sharp, stabbing, cramping, or colicky.
    ◦ **Location**: Unilateral lower abdomen/pelvic region.
    ◦ **Radiation**: May radiate to the flank, back, or groin.
    ◦ **Severity**: Moderate to severe.
• **Nausea and Vomiting**
    ◦ Present in ~70% of cases. A key associated symptom.
• **Low-grade Fever**
    ◦ May be present.
• **Nonspecific Symptoms**
    ◦ Possible urinary urgency or bowel symptoms due to local irritation.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Vitals**
    ◦ Tachycardia may be present due to pain.
    ◦ A low-grade fever (<101°F / 38.3°C) is possible.
• **Abdominal Exam**
    ◦ Marked unilateral tenderness in the lower quadrant.
    ◦ Guarding and rebound tenderness may be present, suggesting peritoneal irritation.
• **Pelvic Exam (Bimanual)**
    ◦ **Unilateral adnexal tenderness** is the most consistent finding.
    ◦ A **palpable adnexal mass** is often present.
    ◦ Cervical motion tenderness (CMT) may be present but is typically less pronounced than in Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Labs**
    ◦ **Serum β-hCG**: **Crucial** to rule out ectopic pregnancy.
    ◦ **CBC**: May show mild leukocytosis.
    ◦ **Urinalysis**: To rule out UTI or nephrolithiasis.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Pelvic Ultrasound with Doppler** is the **imaging modality of choice**.
    ◦ **Grayscale US Findings**
        ▪ **Unilaterally enlarged ovary** (>4 cm or significantly larger than the contralateral ovary).
        ▪ **Ovarian edema**: Hypoechoic stroma with peripherally displaced follicles ("string of pearls" appearance).
        ▪ Free pelvic fluid (hemorrhage or reactive fluid).
        ▪ Abnormal ovarian location (e.g., midline).
        ▪ An underlying ovarian cyst or mass is often identified.
    ◦ **Doppler Flow Findings**
        ▪ **Decreased or absent blood flow (venous and/or arterial)** within the ovary is a specific sign.
        ▪ **However, presence of normal Doppler flow DOES NOT rule out torsion.** Blood flow may be preserved in early or incomplete torsion.
        ▪ **Whirlpool Sign**: A specific sonographic sign showing the twisted vascular pedicle.
• **Definitive Diagnosis**
    ◦ Made by **direct visualization** during surgery (diagnostic laparoscopy).
sections.treatment:
• **Surgical Intervention**: **Laparoscopy** is the preferred approach.
• **Procedure of Choice**
    ◦ **Salpingo-oophorectomy (Removal of Ovary and Tube)**: Reserved for cases where the ovary is obviously necrotic, an abscess has formed, or there is a high suspicion of malignancy.
sections.complications:
• **Ovarian Necrosis/Infarction**: Loss of the ovary and its endocrine/reproductive function.
• **Infertility**: If the ovary is removed and the contralateral ovary is compromised.
• **Infection/Abscess Formation**
• **Hemorrhage**
• **Peritonitis**
• **Recurrence of Torsion** (risk is 10-20% if oophoropexy is not performed).
• **Thromboembolic event** (rare).
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** with prompt diagnosis and surgical intervention (within 6-8 hours of symptom onset).
• Ovarian salvage rates are >90% with timely treatment.
• Delayed diagnosis leads to a higher rate of oophorectomy due to necrosis.
• Future fertility is generally good, as the contralateral ovary can compensate.

sections.overview:
• Functional ovarian cysts are **benign**, fluid-filled sacs that form on or in the ovary during the normal menstrual cycle.
• Directly related to the process of ovulation and are the most common type of ovarian mass in women of reproductive age.
• Almost always **benign** and typically resolve spontaneously.
• Three main types:
    ◦ **Follicular**
    ◦ **Corpus Luteum**
    ◦ **Theca Lutein**
sections.etiology:
• Arise from the normal physiologic function of the ovaries.
• **Follicular Cyst**
    ◦ The **most common** type of functional cyst.
    ◦ Forms when a mature ovarian follicle **fails to ovulate** or **fails to regress** (involute) after ovulation.
        ▪ The follicle continues to grow, filling with fluid.
    ◦ Typically **unilateral**, thin-walled, and filled with clear fluid.
• **Corpus Luteum Cyst**
    ◦ Forms after ovulation when the corpus luteum **fails to break down** and instead seals off, filling with fluid or blood.
    ◦ May prolong the luteal phase and cause menstrual cycle abnormalities due to progesterone production.
    ◦ If the cyst bleeds into itself, it is termed a **hemorrhagic corpus luteum cyst**.
    ◦ Often larger, thicker-walled, and more prone to **rupture** and **hemorrhage** than follicular cysts.
• **Theca Lutein Cyst**
    ◦ The least common type.
    ◦ Caused by excessive stimulation of theca cells by **high levels of human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)**.
    ◦ Almost always **bilateral**, multiple, and filled with straw-colored fluid.
    ◦ Associated conditions:
        ▪ **Molar pregnancy** (gestational trophoblastic disease)
        ▪ Multiple gestations
        ▪ Ovulation induction therapy (e.g., clomiphene, gonadotropins)
sections.epidemiology:
• Extremely common in **reproductive-aged women**.
• The most frequent cause of ovarian enlargement.
• Incidence peaks during reproductive years (post-menarche, pre-menopause).
• Rare before menarche and significantly less common after menopause.
    ◦ Any **postmenopausal adnexal mass** requires a more thorough workup for malignancy.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The majority are **asymptomatic** and discovered incidentally on pelvic exam or imaging.
• When symptomatic, presentation varies:
    ◦ Mild, dull pelvic ache
    ◦ Severe, **acute pain** due to complications like **rupture** or **torsion**
sections.diagnostics:
• **Pelvic Ultrasound (Transvaginal preferred)**: The primary diagnostic modality.
    ◦ **Simple Cyst (Classic Follicular)**: Smooth, thin-walled, unilocular, **anechoic** (black) appearance.
    ◦ **Corpus Luteum Cyst**: Often appears as a "complex" cyst with thicker walls and peripheral vascularity.
        ▪ Doppler flow shows a characteristic **"ring of fire"** due to high vascularity.
    ◦ **Hemorrhagic Cyst**: Complex appearance with internal echoes in a fine, lacy, or reticular pattern (**"fishnet"** or **"cobweb"** appearance) due to fibrin strands.
    ◦ **Theca Lutein Cyst**: Large, **bilateral**, multiseptated cystic masses.
• **Urine Pregnancy Test (hCG)**
    ◦ **MANDATORY** in all reproductive-age females presenting with pelvic pain or an adnexal mass to rule out **ectopic pregnancy**.
    ◦ An elevated hCG also points towards a corpus luteum of pregnancy or theca lutein cysts.
• **CBC**: To evaluate for **anemia** if significant hemorrhage from rupture is suspected.
• **Tumor Markers (e.g., CA-125)**
    ◦ **NOT** routinely indicated in premenopausal women with a simple cyst on ultrasound.
    ◦ CA-125 lacks specificity in this population (can be elevated in endometriosis, fibroids, PID).
    ◦ More useful in postmenopausal women or if ultrasound findings are suspicious for malignancy.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**.
• The vast majority of functional cysts are **benign** and **self-limiting**.
• Recurrence is common throughout the reproductive years but ceases after menopause.

sections.overview:
• Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) is the most common endocrinopathy in women of reproductive age.
• A heterogeneous disorder characterized by a combination of **hyperandrogenism**, **ovulatory dysfunction**, and **polycystic ovarian morphology**.
• Fundamentally a metabolic disorder with significant reproductive and long-term health implications, including an increased risk for type 2 diabetes mellitus and cardiovascular disease.
sections.etiology:
• The exact etiology is unknown; it is considered a multifactorial disorder with genetic and environmental components.
• The core pathophysiology revolves around **insulin resistance** and **hyperandrogenism**.
• **Insulin Resistance & Hyperinsulinemia**
    ◦ Most patients with PCOS (~70%), particularly those who are obese, have **insulin resistance**.
    ◦ The resulting hyperinsulinemia has two primary effects:
        ▪ **Ovarian Effect:** Directly stimulates theca cells in the ovaries to produce androgens (testosterone, androstenedione).
        ▪ **Hepatic Effect:** Decreases hepatic production of **sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG)**.
            ▪ Low SHBG leads to an increase in the level of *free*, biologically active testosterone, exacerbating the signs of **hyperandrogenism**.
• **Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Ovarian (HPO) Axis Dysfunction**
    ◦ There is an increased frequency of Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) pulses from the hypothalamus.
    ◦ This favors pituitary production of **Luteinizing Hormone (LH)** over Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH).
    ◦ The result is a characteristically **elevated LH:FSH ratio** (often >2:1 or 3:1).
    ◦ **High LH** further stimulates ovarian theca cells to produce androgens.
    ◦ **Relatively low FSH** is insufficient to promote full maturation of ovarian follicles, leading to follicular arrest, anovulation, and the formation of multiple small cysts seen on ultrasound.
• **Summary Vicious Cycle:** **Insulin Resistance** → Hyperinsulinemia → Ovarian Androgen Production & ↓ **SHBG** → **Hyperandrogenism** → Disruption of HPO Axis (↑ LH/FSH ratio) → Anovulation & Polycystic Ovaries
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects **5-15%** of reproductive-age women worldwide.
• The **most common cause of anovulatory infertility**.
• Prevalence of metabolic syndrome in patients with PCOS is approximately 30-40%.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a young woman in her late teens or early 20s who presents with **irregular menstrual cycles**, **hirsutism**, and/or **acne**.
• May also report difficulty losing weight or a history of infertility.
sections.diagnostics:
• PCOS is a **diagnosis of exclusion**.
• The **Rotterdam Criteria** (2003) are most commonly used, requiring **2 of the following 3 criteria** to be met:
    ◦ **Oligo- and/or Anovulation** (e.g., irregular cycles)
    ◦ **Clinical and/or Biochemical Hyperandrogenism**
        ▪ **Clinical:** **Hirsutism**, **acne**, or **androgenic alopecia**.
        ▪ **Biochemical:** Elevated serum total or free **testosterone**.
    ◦ **Polycystic Ovaries on Ultrasound**
        ▪ **"String of pearls" appearance:** ≥12 follicles measuring 2-9 mm in diameter per ovary.
        ▪ Increased ovarian volume (>10 mL).
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is generally good with appropriate management and lifestyle modifications.
• The primary source of morbidity is the long-term metabolic and cardiovascular complications.
• Early diagnosis and intervention are key to mitigating these risks.

sections.overview:
• **Lichen Sclerosus (LS)** is a chronic, inflammatory mucocutaneous disorder characterized by marked inflammation, epithelial thinning, and dermal sclerosis.
    ◦ Primarily affects the **anogenital skin**, leading to significant **pruritus**, pain, and architectural changes.
    ◦ While benign, it carries a small but significant risk of progression to **squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)**.
sections.etiology:
• The exact etiology is unknown but is considered multifactorial, with the leading theory pointing to an **autoimmune process**.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ An inflammatory cascade, likely triggered by an unknown antigen in a genetically susceptible individual, leads to a T-cell-mediated response.
    ◦ This results in damage to the basal keratinocytes.
    ◦ Chronic inflammation leads to **sclerosis** (hyalinization) of the papillary dermis, which appears as the characteristic white color.
    ◦ The epidermis becomes atrophic and fragile, leading to symptoms.
• **Key Histologic Features**
    ◦ **Hyperkeratosis** with follicular plugging.
    ◦ **Atrophic** (thinned) **epidermis**.
    ◦ **Homogenization and sclerosis** of the papillary dermis.
    ◦ A band-like (**lichenoid**) lymphocytic infiltrate just below the sclerotic zone.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects approximately 1 in 300 to 1 in 1000 individuals, but is likely underdiagnosed.
• **Sex**: Strong female predominance (F:M ratio ~6-10:1).
• **Age**: Exhibits a **bimodal age distribution**
    ◦ Prepubertal girls
    ◦ Postmenopausal women (most common)
• **Location**: **Anogenital region** is affected in 85-95% of cases.
    ◦ Extragenital sites (trunk, neck, axillae) are rare.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic patient is a postmenopausal woman presenting with **intractable vulvar itching** that is often worse at night.
    ◦ May report pain, especially with intercourse, and changes in the appearance of her vulva.
• In children, it can present as itching and constipation due to fear of pain from anal fissures.
• In men, it is known as **Balanitis Xerotica Obliterans (BXO)** and typically presents with **phimosis** and **meatal stenosis**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Often made based on characteristic history and classic physical exam findings.
• **Confirmatory Test (Gold Standard)**: **Punch biopsy** of an active lesion.
• **Indications for Biopsy**:
    ◦ Atypical presentation (e.g., pigmented, red, or asymmetric lesions).
    ◦ Diagnostic uncertainty.
    ◦ Failure to respond to high-potency topical steroid therapy.
    ◦ **Suspicion of malignancy**: Any **indurated**, **ulcerated**, or persistently **hyperkeratotic** area must be biopsied to rule out SCC.
• **Labs**: No specific labs for LS, but consider screening for associated autoimmune conditions (e.g., TSH) based on clinical suspicion.
sections.prognosis:
• With consistent treatment, symptoms can be well-controlled for most patients.
• The condition is **chronic** and requires lifelong maintenance therapy and monitoring.
• Architectural changes (scarring) are often permanent.
• The risk of **SCC** remains even with good symptom control, necessitating lifelong surveillance.

sections.overview:
• **Lichen Simplex Chronicus (LSC)** is a **secondary skin disorder** resulting from **chronic, repetitive scratching or rubbing** of the skin.
• It is not a primary disease but rather the skin's reaction to a persistent physical trauma.
• On the vulva, it manifests as localized, thickened, and leathery skin plaques (**lichenification**) driven by an intractable **"itch-scratch-itch cycle."**
• LSC is considered a localized form of **neurodermatitis**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ LSC is initiated by any condition that causes **chronic vulvar pruritus**.
    ◦ The initial trigger leads to a self-perpetuating **cycle of itching and scratching**.
    ◦ **Primary Triggers**
        ▪ **Dermatologic:** Atopic dermatitis, contact dermatitis (allergic or irritant), psoriasis, lichen sclerosus, seborrheic dermatitis.
        ▪ **Infectious:** Recurrent candidiasis, tinea cruris.
        ▪ **Neuropathic:** Pudendal nerve entrapment, radiculopathy.
        ▪ **Psychogenic:** Anxiety, stress, depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Initial Pruritic Stimulus:** A trigger (e.g., contact dermatitis from a scented soap) causes an initial sensation of itch.
    ◦ **Scratching/Rubbing:** The patient scratches the area for relief.
    ◦ **Epidermal Trauma:** Mechanical trauma from scratching damages keratinocytes, causing the release of inflammatory mediators (cytokines, prostaglandins).
    ◦ **Inflammation & Nerve Sensitization:** These mediators cause inflammation and sensitize or stimulate proliferation of local nerve fibers, intensifying the sensation of pruritus.
    ◦ **Itch-Scratch Cycle:** The intensified itch leads to more vigorous and prolonged scratching, which further damages the skin, releases more mediators, and perpetuates the cycle.
    ◦ **Lichenification:** Chronic rubbing and scratching leads to protective epidermal thickening (**acanthosis**) and **hyperkeratosis**, resulting in the characteristic leathery, lichenified plaques.
sections.epidemiology:
• More common in females, with a peak incidence between ages **30-50**.
• Frequently associated with a personal or family history of **atopy** (atopic dermatitis, asthma, allergic rhinitis).
• Often co-exists with **anxiety disorders** or significant psychological stress.
sections.riskFactors:
• History of **atopic dermatitis, eczema, or psoriasis**.
• Underlying vulvar dermatoses (e.g., **lichen sclerosus**).
• **Allergic or irritant contact dermatitis** (e.g., from soaps, detergents, douches, sanitary pads, synthetic fabrics).
• History of **anxiety, depression, or obsessive-compulsive disorder**.
• **Chronic moisture and occlusion** in the vulvar area.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with a chief complaint of **severe, unrelenting vulvar itching** that has been present for months or years.
• The itching is often described as **paroxysmal** (occurring in attacks) and is characteristically worse **at night** or during periods of rest, leading to significant sleep disturbance and distress.
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ **Hallmark Symptom:** Severe, chronic **pruritus**, often with a burning or stinging sensation.
    ◦ Soreness or raw feeling from excoriations.
    ◦ Pain, especially if fissures have developed.
    ◦ **Dyspareunia** (painful intercourse) due to skin irritation and fissuring.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Lesion:** Typically a **well-demarcated** or ill-defined, **thickened plaque**.
• **Lichenification:** The key finding. The skin appears **leathery, firm, and thickened** with markedly **accentuated skin lines**.
• **Color:** May be erythematous, violaceous, or **hyperpigmented** (brown/gray), especially in chronic lesions or skin of color. Hypopigmentation can also occur post-inflammation.
• **Excoriations:** Linear scratch marks are prominent and are evidence of the ongoing cycle.
• **Fissures/Erosions:** May be present within the plaque due to intense scratching.
• **Location:** Most commonly affects areas easily reached for scratching:
    ◦ Labia majora
    ◦ Clitoral hood
    ◦ Perineal body
• Crucially, LSC typically **spares the vestibule and vagina**.
sections.diagnostics:
• Primarily a **clinical diagnosis** based on the characteristic history of chronic itch and the physical finding of lichenification.
• **Punch Biopsy:** Indicated if:
    ◦ The diagnosis is uncertain.
    ◦ The lesion is refractory to standard treatment.
    ◦ There is suspicion of malignancy (e.g., ulceration, persistent erosion, atypical features).
• **Histology Findings:**
    ◦ **Hyperkeratosis:** Thickening of the stratum corneum.
    ◦ **Acanthosis:** Thickening of the stratum spinosum (epidermal hyperplasia).
    ◦ **Papillomatosis:** Irregular undulation of the dermal-epidermal junction.
    ◦ Chronic dermal inflammatory infiltrate (lymphocytes, histiocytes).
• **Ancillary Tests:**
    ◦ **KOH prep / Fungal culture:** To rule out tinea or candidiasis as a primary trigger.
    ◦ **Patch testing:** If allergic contact dermatitis is suspected.
sections.treatment:
• **First-Line Therapy:**
    ◦ **High-potency to super-potent topical corticosteroids:**
        ▪ **Clobetasol propionate 0.05%** ointment or Halobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment.
        ▪ **Dosing:** Apply once daily at bedtime for 2-4 weeks, then taper to 2-3 times per week for maintenance as symptoms improve. Ointments are preferred over creams as they are more lubricating and less irritating.
• **Second-Line / Adjunctive Therapies:**
    ◦ **Antihistamines:** Sedating antihistamines (e.g., **Hydroxyzine**, Diphenhydramine) at bedtime to reduce nighttime scratching and help with sleep.
    ◦ **Topical Calcineurin Inhibitors:** Tacrolimus or Pimecrolimus can be used as steroid-sparing maintenance therapy once inflammation is controlled.
    ◦ **Intralesional Steroids:** Triamcinolone injections may be used for very thick, localized, refractory plaques.
    ◦ **Psychotropic Medications:** SSRIs (e.g., Doxepin) may be helpful, especially if there is a significant anxiety or depressive component.
sections.management:
• **Patient Education is CRITICAL:**
    ◦ **Explanation of the Itch-Scratch Cycle:** Help the patient understand that scratching is the problem, not the solution.
    ◦ **Vulvar Care Measures:**
        ▪ Use lukewarm water and a gentle, soap-free cleanser (e.g., Cetaphil, Dove sensitive) or water alone.
        ▪ Pat the area dry; do not rub.
        ▪ Wear loose-fitting, cotton underwear and avoid tight pants.
        ▪ Avoid all potential irritants: scented soaps, bubble baths, douches, fabric softeners, scented sanitary products.
    ◦ **Behavioral Modification:**
        ▪ Keep fingernails short.
        ▪ Apply cool compresses or emollients for symptomatic relief instead of scratching.
        ▪ Stress reduction techniques (e.g., mindfulness, meditation).
sections.complications:
• Secondary bacterial infection (**impetiginization**) from scratching.
• Fissuring and ulceration.
• Permanent skin changes (dyspigmentation, scarring).
• Significant impact on quality of life, sleep, and sexual function.
• **Low risk of Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC):** While LSC itself is not considered premalignant, the state of chronic inflammation, especially when superimposed on an underlying condition like lichen sclerosus, can slightly increase the risk of SCC. Any non-healing or suspicious area requires biopsy.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is generally good for symptom control with consistent adherence to treatment and behavioral modifications.
• It is a chronic condition characterized by relapses and remissions.
• Recurrence is common if treatment is stopped prematurely or if triggers are not managed.

sections.overview:
• Vulvodynia is a chronic pain syndrome characterized by vulvar pain, burning, or discomfort lasting at least **3 months**, without an identifiable cause such as infection, inflammation, neoplasia, or a specific neurologic disorder.
    ◦ It is a **diagnosis of exclusion**.
    ◦ The pain can be constant or intermittent, localized or generalized, and is often described as burning, stinging, or rawness.
• **Key Subtypes**:
    ◦ **Localized Vulvodynia**: Pain is confined to a specific area of the vulva, most commonly the vestibule.
        ▪ **Provoked Vestibulodynia (PVD)**: The most common subtype. Pain is triggered by touch or pressure, such as during sexual intercourse (**dyspareunia**), tampon insertion, gynecologic exams, or wearing tight clothing.
        ▪ **Unprovoked or Spontaneous**: Pain occurs without a clear trigger.
        ▪ **Mixed**: Both provoked and unprovoked pain are present.
    ◦ **Generalized Vulvodynia**: Pain is diffuse and affects multiple areas of the vulva (e.g., clitoris, labia majora/minora, vestibule).
        ▪ It can be provoked, unprovoked, or mixed.
sections.etiology:
• The etiology is multifactorial and not fully understood; it is considered a neuropathic pain condition.
• Key proposed mechanisms include:
    ◦ **Neuropathic Changes**: Proliferation of nerve endings (**neuroproliferation**) in the vestibular mucosa, leading to peripheral and central nervous system sensitization.
        ▪ This results in **allodynia** (pain from a stimulus that does not normally provoke pain) and **hyperalgesia** (an exaggerated response to a painful stimulus).
    ◦ **Musculoskeletal Dysfunction**: **Hypertonicity**, tenderness, and instability of the pelvic floor muscles are extremely common and can contribute significantly to pain.
    ◦ **Inflammatory Response**: Increased local concentration of inflammatory mediators and mast cell proliferation/activation in the affected tissues.
    ◦ **Hormonal Factors**: A possible link to long-term use of low-dose combined oral contraceptives (OCPs), which may alter vestibular tissue structure and hormone receptor sensitivity.
    ◦ **Genetic Predisposition**: Polymorphisms in genes related to inflammatory responses may increase susceptibility.
    ◦ **Psychosocial Factors**: While not a cause, conditions like anxiety, depression, and pain catastrophizing can modulate the pain experience and are often comorbid.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects up to 16% of women in their lifetime.
• **Age of Onset**: Can occur at any age, but most commonly presents in women of reproductive age (18-40 years).
• **Diagnosis Delay**: There is often a significant delay (average 3-7 years) between symptom onset and diagnosis due to a lack of provider awareness and patient hesitation to report symptoms.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with a chief complaint of chronic "vulvar burning," "vaginal pain," or "pain with intercourse" that has been present for months or years.
• They have often seen multiple providers and tried numerous ineffective treatments (e.g., multiple courses of antifungals/antibiotics).
• The history reveals a significant negative impact on sexual function, quality of life, and psychological well-being.
sections.diagnostics:
• Vulvodynia is a **diagnosis of exclusion**; the diagnostic process is aimed at ruling out other causes of vulvar pain.
• **History**: Detailed history of pain (onset, duration, quality, triggers) and review of systems.
• **Physical Exam**: Includes visual inspection and the **cotton swab test**.
• **Tests to Rule Out Other Conditions**:
    ◦ **Vaginal Wet Mount & KOH Prep**: To exclude Candida and bacterial vaginosis.
    ◦ **Vaginal pH**.
    ◦ **Cultures or NAAT**: To screen for STIs (e.g., Herpes Simplex Virus, Chlamydia, Gonorrhea, Trichomonas) if indicated.
    ◦ **Vulvar Biopsy**: **Only indicated if there is a visible lesion** to rule out dermatoses (e.g., lichen sclerosus, lichen planus) or neoplasia (e.g., VIN).
        ▪ Biopsy in classic vulvodynia is typically non-specific or shows mild chronic inflammation.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is variable; with a dedicated, multidisciplinary treatment plan, most patients can achieve significant symptom reduction and functional improvement.
• It is often a chronic condition that requires long-term management rather than a "cure."
• For carefully selected patients with **provoked vestibulodynia**, **vestibulectomy** offers a high rate of success.

sections.overview:
• Vulvovaginal Candidiasis (VVC), commonly known as a "yeast infection," is an infection of the vulva and/or vagina caused by an overgrowth of *Candida* species.
• It is the second most common cause of vaginitis after bacterial vaginosis.
• VVC is not considered a sexually transmitted infection (STI), as *Candida* is a commensal organism in the vaginal flora of many asymptomatic women.
• The clinical focus is on distinguishing it from other causes of vaginitis and categorizing it as either **uncomplicated** or **complicated** to guide appropriate therapy.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**:
    ◦ **_Candida albicans_**: The causative organism in 80-90% of cases.
    ◦ **Non-albicans species**: Less common, but important as they may be resistant to standard therapies. Includes _C. glabrata_ and _C. tropicalis_. These are more frequently seen in recurrent or complicated cases.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ VVC is not caused by acquiring the organism, but rather by the **overgrowth** of *Candida* that is already part of the normal vaginal flora.
    ◦ This overgrowth occurs when the vaginal ecosystem is disrupted. Key factors include:
        ▪ **Loss of Protective Flora**: A decrease in commensal *Lactobacillus* species, which normally produce lactic acid and hydrogen peroxide to suppress yeast growth.
        ▪ **Favorable Environment**: Increased glycogen/glucose levels (e.g., in diabetes, pregnancy) provide a substrate for yeast proliferation.
        ▪ **Immune Suppression**: A compromised local or systemic immune response allows the yeast to proliferate unchecked.
    ◦ Once overgrowth occurs, *Candida* transitions from its yeast (budding) form to its invasive hyphal form.
    ◦ The hyphae invade the vaginal epithelium, triggering an inflammatory response that causes the classic symptoms of itching, burning, and erythema.
sections.epidemiology:
• VVC is extremely common. It is estimated that ~75% of women will have at least one episode in their lifetime.
• Approximately 40-50% will have a second episode, and 5-8% will develop recurrent VVC (RVVC).
• It is most common during the reproductive years, likely due to hormonal influences (estrogen).
• It is uncommon before menarche and after menopause unless the patient is on hormone replacement therapy.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The typical patient is a female of reproductive age presenting with the acute onset of intense vulvar itching.
• The primary complaint is almost always **pruritus**, which can range from mild to debilitating.
• She may report a change in vaginal discharge and discomfort during urination or intercourse.
• She may also report a recent course of antibiotics or a history of poorly controlled diabetes.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Vaginal pH**:
    ◦ **Normal (3.8 to 4.5)**.
    ◦ This is a key finding that helps differentiate VVC from bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis, both of which cause an elevated pH (>4.5).
• **Saline Wet Mount (Microscopy)**:
    ◦ A sample of vaginal discharge is mixed with 0.9% normal saline.
    ◦ Reveals **budding yeast**, **hyphae**, or **pseudohyphae**.
• **10% KOH Prep**:
    ◦ Adding potassium hydroxide (KOH) to the sample lyses epithelial cells, making the yeast, hyphae, and pseudohyphae **easier to visualize**.
    ◦ This is the most specific office-based test.
• **Whiff-Amine Test**:
    ◦ **Negative**. A drop of KOH is added to the discharge sample; no "fishy" odor is produced.
    ◦ A positive test is characteristic of bacterial vaginosis.
• **Vaginal Culture**:
    ◦ Not routinely performed for initial, uncomplicated cases.
    ◦ **Indicated for**:
        ▪ Recurrent VVC.
        ▪ Persistent symptoms after treatment.
        ▪ Negative microscopy with high clinical suspicion.
    ◦ A culture is essential to identify non-albicans species like _C. glabrata_, which require different treatment.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis for **uncomplicated** VVC is excellent, with high cure rates (>90%) after a standard course of therapy.
• **Recurrent** VVC can be challenging and frustrating for the patient but is often manageable with long-term suppressive therapy.

sections.overview:
• **Bacterial Vaginosis (BV)** is the most common cause of vaginal discharge in women of reproductive age.
• It is not considered a sexually transmitted infection (STI) but is associated with sexual activity.
• BV is a polymicrobial clinical syndrome resulting from a **dysbiosis** of the vaginal microbiome.
    ◦ This involves a decrease in the concentration of the normally protective, hydrogen peroxide and lactic acid-producing **`Lactobacillus`** species.
    ◦ It also involves a significant overgrowth of **anaerobic bacteria**.
sections.etiology:
• **Normal Flora**
    ◦ A healthy vaginal ecosystem is dominated by `Lactobacillus` species (e.g., `L. crispatus`, `L. jensenii`).
    ◦ These bacteria produce **lactic acid**, creating an acidic vaginal environment (**pH 3.8-4.5**).
    ◦ They also produce **hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)**, which is microbicidal to anaerobic bacteria.
• **Pathophysiology (Dysbiosis)**
    ◦ **Disruption**: An inciting event (e.g., douching, new sexual partner) disrupts the `Lactobacillus` population.
    ◦ **pH Increase**: With fewer lactobacilli, lactic acid production decreases, causing the vaginal pH to rise **above 4.5**.
    ◦ **Anaerobic Overgrowth**: The higher pH creates a favorable environment for the proliferation of anaerobes.
        ▪ Key organisms include: `Gardnerella vaginalis`, `Atopobium vaginae`, `Prevotella` species, `Mobiluncus` species.
    ◦ **Biofilm Formation**: These organisms, particularly `Gardnerella`, create a dense, adherent polymicrobial **biofilm** on the vaginal epithelium, which makes eradication difficult and contributes to high recurrence rates.
    ◦ **Symptom Production**: The overgrown anaerobic bacteria produce enzymes that break down vaginal peptides into volatile amines, which are responsible for the characteristic **malodorous "fishy" odor**.
    ◦ **Lack of Inflammation**: BV is a **vaginosis**, not a vaginitis, with a notable lack of a significant inflammatory response (WBCs/leukocytes).
sections.epidemiology:
• Most common cause of vaginitis, accounting for 40-50% of cases.
• Prevalence varies significantly by population, ranging from 10% to 50% in reproductive-aged women.
• Higher prevalence in women who are sexually active.
sections.riskFactors:
• New or multiple sexual partners
• Female sexual partners
• **Douching** (a major, modifiable risk factor)
• Lack of condom use
• Cigarette smoking
• Presence of an IUD
• Recent antibiotic use
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a malodorous, **"fishy" vaginal discharge** that is often worse after unprotected intercourse or during menses.
• Up to 50% of women may be **asymptomatic** and diagnosed incidentally.
• **Vaginal Discharge**
    ◦ **Character**: Thin, homogenous, milky-gray or white.
    ◦ **Amount**: Mild to moderate.
• **Odor**
    ◦ **Character**: Unpleasant, stale, **"fishy" odor**.
    ◦ **Timing**: Often noticed after intercourse (semen is alkaline) or menses (blood is alkaline).
• **Absence of Inflammatory Symptoms**
    ◦ Pruritus (itching), dysuria, and dyspareunia are typically **absent or minimal**; their presence should raise suspicion for a co-infection or alternative diagnosis.
sections.physicalExam:
• **External Genitalia**: Typically normal, without erythema or edema.
• **Speculum Exam**
    ◦ **Discharge**: A thin, homogenous, gray-white discharge is seen coating the vaginal walls; it is not typically adherent or curd-like.
    ◦ **Vaginal Mucosa**: Appears normal, with no signs of inflammation (erythema, petechiae, or edema).
    ◦ **Cervix**: Appears normal.
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is typically made clinically using **Amsel's Criteria**; at least **3 of the 4** criteria must be met.
    ◦ **1. Clinical Finding**: Thin, gray-white, homogenous discharge.
    ◦ **2. Vaginal pH**: **> 4.5** (use pH paper on a sample from the lateral vaginal wall).
    ◦ **3. Whiff Test**: **Positive "whiff-amine" test**: A distinct fishy odor is released upon adding a drop of 10% potassium hydroxide (KOH) to the vaginal discharge sample.
    ◦ **4. Microscopy**: **Clue Cells** on saline wet mount.
        ▪ Squamous epithelial cells with borders obscured by adherent coccobacilli, giving a "stippled" or granular appearance.
        ▪ **Presence of >20% clue cells per high-power field is diagnostic.**
• **Microscopy Findings (Saline Wet Mount)**
    ◦ **Presence**: **Clue cells**.
    ◦ **Absence**: Few to no WBCs, and a marked decrease or absence of large lactobacilli rods.
sections.treatment:
• Treatment is recommended for all symptomatic women.
• Treatment of asymptomatic women is recommended prior to gynecologic surgery or if pregnant to reduce complication risks.
• **Primary Regimens**
    ◦ **Metronidazole** 500 mg PO twice daily for 7 days
    ◦ **Metronidazole gel** 0.75%, one applicator (5g) intravaginally once daily for 5 days
    ◦ **Clindamycin cream** 2%, one applicator (5g) intravaginally at bedtime for 7 days
• **Alternative Regimens**
    ◦ **Clindamycin** 300 mg PO twice daily for 7 days
    ◦ **Tinidazole** 2g PO once daily for 2 days
    ◦ **Secnidazole** 2g PO as a single dose
• **Counseling Points**
    ◦ **Metronidazole/Tinidazole**: Avoid alcohol during and for 24-72 hours after treatment due to risk of **disulfiram-like reaction**. A metallic taste is a common side effect.
    ◦ **Clindamycin Cream**: It is oil-based and may weaken latex condoms and diaphragms.
sections.management:
• **Partner Treatment**: Routine treatment of male sexual partners is **not recommended** as it has not been shown to reduce recurrence.
• **Pregnancy**
    ◦ Treat all symptomatic pregnant women to reduce the risk of preterm birth.
    ◦ **Preferred Regimens**: Oral **Metronidazole** or Oral **Clindamycin** for 7 days.
    ◦ Avoid topical agents as they have not been shown to be as effective in preventing complications.
• **Recurrent BV** (defined as ≥3 documented episodes in 12 months)
    ◦ Consider a longer initial course of therapy (e.g., 10-14 days).
    ◦ Consider suppressive therapy, such as Metronidazole gel 0.75% twice weekly for 4-6 months after the initial treatment course.
    ◦ Address risk factors, especially **douching**.
sections.complications:
• **Obstetric**
    ◦ **Preterm labor** and delivery
    ◦ Premature rupture of membranes (PPROM)
    ◦ Chorioamnionitis
    ◦ Postpartum endometritis
• **Gynecologic / Infectious**
    ◦ Increased risk of **Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID)**
    ◦ Post-operative infections after gynecologic procedures (e.g., hysterectomy, abortion)
    ◦ Increased susceptibility to and transmission of STIs, including **HIV**, HSV-2, gonorrhea, and chlamydia.
sections.prognosis:
• The short-term cure rate with standard therapy is high (>80%).
• However, **recurrence is very common**, with over 50% of women experiencing a recurrence within 12 months.

sections.overview:
• Trichomoniasis is a common, curable sexually transmitted infection (STI) caused by the protozoan parasite ***Trichomonas vaginalis***.
• It is the most prevalent non-viral STI worldwide.
• While it can infect both males and females, clinical disease is far more common in females.
• Infection can range from **asymptomatic carriage** (especially in males) to severe, acute inflammatory disease of the urogenital tract.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent:** ***Trichomonas vaginalis***, a single-celled, anaerobic, flagellated protozoan.
    ◦ It exists only in the **trophozoite stage** (no cyst stage).
• **Transmission:** Primarily through **sexual contact** (penile-vaginal, vulva-vulva).
    ◦ Vertical transmission from mother to infant during childbirth is possible but rare.
• **Pathophysiology:**
    ◦ The organism adheres to the squamous epithelium of the urogenital tract (vagina, urethra, prostate).
    ◦ It causes direct damage to epithelial cells and elicits a significant local host **inflammatory response** (recruitment of neutrophils).
