    ◦ *T. vaginalis* alters the vaginal microenvironment by consuming arginine, leading to increased production of nitric oxide and other cytotoxic substances.
    ◦ It raises the normal vaginal pH (typically **>4.5**), which disrupts the protective lactobacilli-dominant flora and facilitates the growth of other anaerobic bacteria.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** Estimated 2-3 million new cases annually in the United States.
    ◦ It is more common than chlamydia and gonorrhea combined.
• **Demographics:**
    ◦ More common in females than males.
    ◦ Prevalence increases with age.
    ◦ Disproportionately affects African American women.
• **Co-infection:** Frequently co-exists with other STIs, particularly **bacterial vaginosis (BV)**, chlamydia, gonorrhea, and **HIV**.
sections.riskFactors:
• Multiple sexual partners
• New sexual partner
• History of prior STIs
• Lack of condom use
• Lower socioeconomic status
• Incarceration
• Exchanging sex for money or drugs
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The clinical presentation exists on a spectrum; up to **70-85%** of infected individuals are **asymptomatic** or have minimal symptoms.
    ◦ Males are significantly more likely to be asymptomatic carriers than females.
• **Classic Female Presentation:** Acute vaginitis with a characteristic discharge.
    ◦ **Vaginal Discharge:** Often profuse, thin, and frothy. Classically described as **yellow-green to gray** in color.
    ◦ **Odor:** Malodorous, often described as **"fishy"**.
    ◦ **Vulvovaginal Irritation:** Pruritus (itching), soreness, erythema.
    ◦ **Dysuria:** Burning with urination (often due to urine contacting inflamed vulvar tissue).
    ◦ **Dyspareunia:** Pain during sexual intercourse.
    ◦ **Lower Abdominal Pain:** Less common, but may be present.
• **Classic Male Presentation:** Usually asymptomatic. If symptomatic, presents as non-gonococcal urethritis.
    ◦ **Largely Asymptomatic** (up to 75%).
    ◦ **Urethritis:** The most common symptom.
        ▪ Mucoid or purulent urethral discharge (often scant).
        ▪ Dysuria.
        ▪ Urethral pruritus.
    ◦ **Less Common:** Epididymitis, prostatitis.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Female Exam Findings:**
    ◦ **Vulva/Vagina:** Erythema and edema of the vulva and vaginal mucosa.
    ◦ **Discharge:** A pool of **frothy, yellow-green discharge** may be visible in the vaginal vault.
    ◦ **Cervix:** The pathognomonic finding is **colpitis macularis or "strawberry cervix"**, characterized by punctate hemorrhages on the cervix.
        ▪ This finding is highly specific but only seen in **~10% of cases** on direct visualization (more common on colposcopy).
• **Male Exam Findings:**
    ◦ Often unremarkable.
    ◦ May have scant urethral discharge, sometimes only expressed after milking the urethra.
    ◦ No characteristic findings.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Wet Mount (Saline Microscopy)**
    ◦ **Description:** Vaginal fluid mixed with 0.9% saline and viewed under a microscope.
    ◦ **Findings:** **Motile, pear-shaped, flagellated trichomonads.** Also see increased polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMNs).
    ◦ **Notes:** Standard office-based test. **Operator-dependent and low sensitivity (60-70%).** Requires live organisms.
• **NAAT (Nucleic Acid Amplification Test)**
    ◦ **Description:** Amplifies parasite DNA or RNA.
    ◦ **Findings:** Positive or negative result.
    ◦ **Notes:** **GOLD STANDARD.** Highest sensitivity (>95%) and specificity. Can be performed on vaginal, endocervical, or urine samples. Urine is the preferred sample for males.
• **Rapid Antigen Tests**
    ◦ **Description:** Point-of-care immunochromatographic dipstick tests.
    ◦ **Findings:** Positive or negative result.
    ◦ **Notes:** Faster than NAATs, more sensitive than microscopy. Good for office settings without microscopy.
• **Culture**
    ◦ **Description:** InPouch TV system.
    ◦ **Findings:** Organism growth.
    ◦ **Notes:** Previously the gold standard before NAATs. High sensitivity but takes 3-7 days for results. Now used mainly for suspected antimicrobial resistance testing.
• **Ancillary Tests**
    ◦ **Vaginal pH:** Measure with pH paper.
        ▪ **Finding:** **pH > 4.5** (almost always).
    ◦ **Whiff-Amine Test:** Add 10% KOH to vaginal fluid.
        ▪ **Finding:** **Positive whiff test** (amine odor) may be present (~20% of cases).
    ◦ **Notes:** These findings are non-specific and also classic for **bacterial vaginosis (BV)**.
• **Screening**
    ◦ The CDC recommends screening for *T. vaginalis* in all **HIV-positive women annually** and at entry to care.
    ◦ Consider screening in high-prevalence settings (e.g., correctional facilities, STI clinics).
sections.management:
• **Follow-up:** A "test of cure" is not needed for asymptomatic individuals post-treatment.
• **Retesting:** Retesting is recommended for all sexually active females **3 months after treatment** due to the very high rate of reinfection (~17% in 3 months).
• **Persistent Infection:**
    ◦ First, assess for non-adherence or reinfection from an untreated partner.
    ◦ For suspected resistance, consider Tinidazole if Metronidazole was used, or a longer course of Metronidazole (2g PO daily for 7 days).
    ◦ Consult with an ID specialist for refractory cases.
sections.complications:
• **Increased HIV Risk:** Trichomoniasis causes genital inflammation, which **increases the risk of both acquiring and transmitting HIV** by 2-3 fold.
• **Pregnancy:** Associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes including:
    ◦ Premature rupture of membranes (PROM)
    ◦ Preterm delivery
    ◦ Low birth weight
• **Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID):** Can facilitate ascending infection, leading to PID.
• **Infertility:** Can be a consequence of PID (tubal factor infertility).
• **Male Complications (Rare):** Epididymitis, prostatitis, decreased sperm motility.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is **excellent** with appropriate antimicrobial therapy.
• Cure rates are **>95%** when the patient and partners are treated correctly.
• **Reinfection** is the most common cause of treatment failure.
sections.preventionEducation: • Counsel on safe sex practices, condom use, and the importance of partner notification and treatment.

sections.overview:
• Inflammation of the uterine cervix caused by the bacterium *Chlamydia trachomatis*.
• Most commonly reported **bacterial sexually transmitted infection (STI)** in the United States.
• Key feature: Frequently **asymptomatic**, leading to under-diagnosis.
• If untreated, can lead to significant long-term complications, most notably **Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID)**.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**: *Chlamydia trachomatis* (serovars D-K).
• **Microbiology**:
    ◦ An **obligate intracellular bacterium**, meaning it can only replicate inside a host cell.
    ◦ Lacks the ability to produce its own ATP.
• **Pathogenesis**:
    ◦ *C. trachomatis* has a unique biphasic life cycle:
        ▪ **Elementary Body (EB)**: The small, **infectious**, metabolically inactive form that **enters** host columnar epithelial cells of the endocervix. (**E** for **Enters**).
        ▪ **Reticulate Body (RB)**: The larger, non-infectious, metabolically active form that **replicates** within the host cell. (**R** for **Replicates**).
• **Mechanism**:
    ◦ The EB enters the cell via endocytosis and transforms into an RB.
    ◦ The RB undergoes binary fission, creating numerous new RBs.
    ◦ These RBs then reorganize and condense back into EBs.
    ◦ The host cell eventually lyses, releasing the new EBs to infect adjacent cells.
    ◦ This cell destruction and the associated host inflammatory response cause the clinical signs of cervicitis (edema, erythema, discharge, friability).
sections.epidemiology:
• Most common **reportable bacterial** STI in the U.S.
• Highest prevalence in sexually active adolescents and young adults, particularly **women aged 15-24**.
• **Asymptomatic carriage** is common, facilitating transmission.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The **majority of cases (>70%) are asymptomatic**.
• When symptoms do occur, they are often non-specific and may have a gradual onset.
• The infection is often discovered during routine screening.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Gold Standard**: **Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT)**.
    ◦ Highly sensitive and specific.
• **Sample Collection**:
    ◦ **Vaginal Swab**: Preferred method for females (can be self-collected or clinician-collected); highest sensitivity.
    ◦ **Endocervical Swab**: An alternative to vaginal swab.
    ◦ **Urine Sample**: Less sensitive than swabs in females but is a non-invasive option.
• **Other Lab Findings (Non-Specific)**:
    ◦ **Wet Mount**: May show an increased number of polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMNs / WBCs) but cannot diagnose Chlamydia. Useful for ruling out co-infections like BV or Trichomonas.
• **Screening Recommendations (CDC)**:
    ◦ Annual screening for all sexually active women < 25 years old.
    ◦ Annual screening for women ≥ 25 years old with risk factors.
    ◦ Screen all pregnant women at their first prenatal visit.
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent with early diagnosis and appropriate treatment.
• The risk of long-term sequelae like infertility increases significantly with each subsequent infection and with delayed treatment.

sections.overview:
• Gonococcal cervicitis is a sexually transmitted infection (STI) of the endocervix caused by the bacterium **_Neisseria gonorrhoeae_**.
• It is a common cause of cervical inflammation and **mucopurulent discharge**.
• A significant portion of cases are **asymptomatic**, making screening of at-risk populations crucial.
• Untreated, it can ascend the female genital tract, leading to serious complications such as **Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID)**, **infertility**, and **ectopic pregnancy**.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**: **_Neisseria gonorrhoeae_**, a **gram-negative intracellular diplococcus**.
• **Transmission**: Occurs via sexual contact (vaginal, anal, or oral).
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **_N. gonorrhoeae_** has a strong affinity for the **columnar epithelial cells** of the endocervix. It attaches to these mucosal cells via **pili** and **Opa proteins**.
    ◦ The bacterium invades the host cells, multiplies, and eventually causes cell lysis.
    ◦ This process triggers a robust inflammatory response characterized by a **neutrophilic infiltrate**.
    ◦ The resulting inflammation leads to tissue damage, causing the characteristic findings of **mucopurulent discharge**, **cervical edema**, and **friability**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Second most commonly reported bacterial STI** in the United States, after Chlamydia.
• Highest incidence is among sexually active adolescents and young adults, particularly those aged **15-24**.
• Significant geographic, racial, and ethnic disparities exist, with higher rates in certain regions and among minority populations.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Often Asymptomatic**: Up to 70% of females with gonococcal cervicitis may be asymptomatic.
• **Symptomatic Presentation**:
    ◦ When symptoms occur, they typically develop within 10 days of exposure.
    ◦ The most common presenting complaint is a **change in vaginal discharge**.
    ◦ Patients may also present with **postcoital or intermenstrual bleeding**.
    ◦ **Dysuria** may be present due to concurrent urethritis.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Gold Standard**: **Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT)** is the most sensitive and specific test for detecting *_N. gonorrhoeae_*.
• **Specimen Source**:
    ◦ **Endocervical or vaginal swabs** are preferred.
    ◦ Self-collected vaginal swabs are equivalent to clinician-collected swabs.
    ◦ **Urine NAAT** is an option but is less sensitive in females compared to males.
• **Gram Stain**:
    ◦ A sample of the endocervical discharge can be gram-stained.
    ◦ The finding of **gram-negative intracellular diplococci** is highly specific but has low sensitivity (~50%) and is not recommended for routine diagnosis.
• **Culture**:
    ◦ Not routinely used for diagnosis but is essential for **antibiotic susceptibility testing**, especially in cases of suspected treatment failure.
    ◦ Requires collection on **Thayer-Martin** or other selective media.
• **Co-testing**:
    ◦ All patients should be tested for other STIs, particularly **Chlamydia trachomatis** (high rate of co-infection), HIV, and syphilis.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** with prompt and appropriate antibiotic therapy.
• Full recovery is expected for uncomplicated cervicitis.
• Prognosis becomes guarded if complications like **PID** develop, as this can lead to permanent reproductive tract damage.
• **Reinfection** is common.

sections.overview:
• **Condyloma acuminata** (genital warts) are benign epithelial growths occurring in the anogenital region
    ◦ They are one of the most common clinical manifestations of **Human Papillomavirus (HPV)** infection and represent the most common viral **sexually transmitted infection (STI)** in the United States
    ◦ While generally benign, they cause significant patient anxiety and morbidity
• The condition is caused by **low-risk HPV types**, distinct from the high-risk types associated with dysplasia and malignancy.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**: **Human Papillomavirus (HPV)**, a non-enveloped, double-stranded DNA virus
• **Specific Types**:
    ◦ **>90% of cases are caused by low-risk HPV types 6 and 11**
    ◦ Other less common low-risk types include 42, 43, and 44
    ◦ Co-infection with high-risk (oncogenic) types like **HPV 16, 18, 31, and 33** is possible
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Transmission**: The virus is transmitted through direct skin-to-skin contact, typically during sexual activity (vaginal, anal, or oral)
    ◦ **Infection**: HPV infects the basal keratinocytes of the squamous epithelium, usually through micro-abrasions in the skin or mucous membranes
    ◦ **Viral Replication**: The virus utilizes the host cell's machinery to replicate. Viral oncoproteins E6 and E7 interfere with host tumor suppressor proteins (p53 and pRb), leading to unregulated cell proliferation
    ◦ **Lesion Formation**: This uncontrolled proliferation results in the characteristic papillomatous, verrucous growths (warts)
    ◦ **Histology**: The hallmark cellular change is the presence of **koilocytes**—squamous epithelial cells with a perinuclear halo and a wrinkled, enlarged nucleus
sections.epidemiology:
• The most common viral **STI** in the U.S.
• Highest prevalence is in sexually active individuals aged 15-25
• An estimated 80% of sexually active individuals will acquire an HPV infection by age 50, though most are asymptomatic and clear the infection spontaneously within 2 years
• Prevalence has been decreasing in vaccinated populations
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients typically present with a complaint of a new "bump," "growth," or "rash" in the genital or perianal area
• The appearance can be insidious, with lesions growing slowly over weeks to months
• Lesions can be single or multiple, and may coalesce into large plaques
• Often discovered incidentally by the patient or during a routine physical or pelvic exam
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primary method**: **Clinical diagnosis** based on visual inspection of characteristic lesions
• **Acetic Acid Application (Aceto-whitening)**:
    ◦ Application of 3-5% acetic acid causes warts to turn white (**"acetowhite"**)
    ◦ **Not recommended for routine diagnosis** due to low sensitivity and specificity (can be positive with inflammation, psoriasis, or dysplasia)
• **Biopsy**:
    ◦ Not routinely necessary
    ◦ Indicated if:
        ▪ Diagnosis is uncertain
        ▪ Lesions are atypical (e.g., pigmented, indurated, ulcerated, fixed)
        ▪ Lesions are refractory to standard treatment
        ▪ Patient is **immunocompromised** (higher risk of dysplasia/SCC)
    ◦ Histology reveals **koilocytic atypia**, acanthosis, and papillomatosis
• **HPV DNA/RNA testing**:
    ◦ **NOT recommended** for the diagnosis of genital warts
    ◦ These tests are used for cervical cancer screening
sections.prognosis:
• Spontaneous resolution occurs in ~30% of cases within 4 months, especially in immunocompetent individuals
• **Recurrence after treatment is common (~25-30%)** within 3 months, as the virus can remain latent in surrounding, clinically normal-appearing tissue
• The host immune system typically clears or suppresses the virus over 1-2 years in most healthy individuals

sections.overview:
• Cervical dysplasia refers to the presence of precancerous, abnormal cell growth on the surface lining (epithelium) of the cervix
• It is not cancer but can progress to cervical cancer if left untreated and is most often discovered through routine cervical cancer screening (Pap test)
• **Squamous Intraepithelial Lesion (SIL):** The term used in the Bethesda System for reporting Pap test (cytology) results
    ◦ **Low-Grade Squamous Intraepithelial Lesion (LSIL):** Represents early, mild cellular changes
        ▪ Correlates with **Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia grade 1 (CIN 1)** on histology
        ▪ High potential for spontaneous regression
    ◦ **High-Grade Squamous Intraepithelial Lesion (HSIL):** Represents more significant, moderate-to-severe cellular changes
        ▪ Correlates with **CIN 2** and **CIN 3** on histology
        ▪ Has a higher risk of progressing to invasive cervical cancer
• **Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia (CIN):** The term used for histological diagnosis from a biopsy specimen
    ◦ **CIN 1:** Mild dysplasia (affecting the lower 1/3 of the epithelium)
    ◦ **CIN 2:** Moderate dysplasia (affecting up to 2/3 of the epithelium)
    ◦ **CIN 3:** Severe dysplasia / **Carcinoma in situ** (affecting more than 2/3 to the full thickness of the epithelium)
sections.etiology:
• The primary cause is a **persistent infection with high-risk oncogenic strains of Human Papillomavirus (HPV)**
• **Causative Agent:** HPV, a double-stranded DNA virus
• **High-Risk HPV Types:** **HPV 16 and 18** are responsible for ~70% of cervical cancers and a majority of **HSIL** cases
    ◦ Other high-risk types include 31, 33, 45, 52, 58
• **Low-Risk HPV Types:** **HPV 6 and 11** primarily cause anogenital warts (condyloma acuminata) and are rarely associated with cancer
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ HPV infects basal epithelial cells of the cervix, typically at the **squamocolumnar junction (Transformation Zone)**, an area of active metaplasia
    ◦ Most HPV infections are transient and cleared by the immune system within 1-2 years
    ◦ **Persistent infection** with a high-risk HPV type is required for dysplasia to develop
    ◦ The virus integrates its DNA into the host cell's genome
    ◦ Two key viral oncoproteins are expressed:
        ▪ **E6 Oncoprotein:** Binds to and promotes the degradation of the **p53 tumor suppressor protein**
        ▪ **E7 Oncoprotein:** Binds to and inactivates the **retinoblastoma (pRb) tumor suppressor protein**
    ◦ Inactivation of these "gatekeepers" of the cell cycle leads to unregulated cell proliferation, accumulation of genetic mutations, and progression from normal cells to **LSIL**, then to **HSIL**, and potentially to invasive squamous cell carcinoma over several years
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** Most common in women of reproductive age
    ◦ Peak incidence for **LSIL/CIN 1** is in women aged 25-29
• **Incidence:** Peak incidence for **HSIL/CIN 2-3** is in women aged 30-39
• **Progression:** The average time from initial HPV infection to development of invasive cancer is 10-15 years
• **Impact of Vaccination:** Widespread HPV vaccination has significantly reduced the incidence of high-grade dysplasia and cervical cancer in vaccinated populations
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The vast majority of women with cervical dysplasia are **completely asymptomatic**
• The condition is almost always detected during routine cervical cancer screening
sections.diagnostics:
• The diagnosis is a multi-step process involving screening, colposcopy, and histologic confirmation
• **Screening Tests (Cytology and/or HPV Testing)**
    ◦ **Papanicolaou (Pap) Test:** A cytology smear that identifies abnormal cells
        ▪ Results are reported using the Bethesda System (e.g., **LSIL**, **HSIL**, **ASC-US**)
    ◦ **HPV DNA Test:** Detects the presence of **high-risk HPV DNA**
        ▪ Can be done as a primary screen, co-test with cytology, or as a triage test for abnormal Pap results
• **Colposcopy**
    ◦ The standard follow-up for abnormal screening results (e.g., **HSIL**, persistent **LSIL**)
    ◦ A binocular microscope is used to visualize the cervix under magnification
    ◦ **Acetic Acid (3-5%) Application:** Dehydrates cells, causing abnormal cells (with high nuclear density) to turn white, a finding called **acetowhite epithelium**
    ◦ **Lugol's Solution (Iodine)**
        ▪ Normal, mature squamous cells are rich in glycogen and will stain a dark brown ("Lugol's positive")
        ▪ Dysplastic and cancerous cells are glycogen-poor and will **fail to stain** (remain yellow or mustard-colored, "Lugol's negative")
    ◦ Abnormal findings that guide biopsy: **acetowhite changes**, **mosaicism**, **punctation**, **atypical vessels**
• **Biopsy (Histology - The Gold Standard)**
    ◦ **Cervical Punch Biopsy:** Tissue samples are taken from the most abnormal-appearing areas identified during colposcopy
        ▪ This provides the definitive histologic diagnosis (**CIN 1, 2, or 3**)
    ◦ **Endocervical Curettage (ECC):** Sampling of the endocervical canal with a curette
        ▪ Performed when colposcopy is unsatisfactory (entire transformation zone not seen), the lesion extends into the canal, or **HSIL** is suspected
        ▪ **Contraindicated in pregnancy**
sections.prognosis:
• **LSIL (CIN 1):** Excellent prognosis with a high rate of spontaneous regression without treatment
• **HSIL (CIN 2/3):** Excellent prognosis with appropriate treatment
    ◦ Cure rates after an excisional procedure are >90%
• If **HSIL (specifically CIN 3)** is left untreated, the risk of progression to invasive cancer is estimated to be 30-50% over 10-30 years

sections.overview:
• Combined Hormonal Contraception (CHC) refers to birth control methods containing both a synthetic **estrogen** and a **progestin**
• Among the most effective and widely used reversible contraceptive methods
• Available formulations:
    ◦ **Oral contraceptive pills (OCPs)**
    ◦ **Transdermal patch**
    ◦ **Vaginal ring**
• Functions:
    ◦ Primary: **Prevent pregnancy**
    ◦ Secondary (non-contraceptive benefits):
        ▪ Regulation of the menstrual cycle
        ▪ Reduction in risk for certain cancers
sections.etiology:
• Mechanism of Action: Multi-faceted, primarily aimed at preventing **ovulation**
    ◦ **Primary Mechanism: Suppression of Ovulation**
        ▪ Exogenous estrogen and progestin exert **negative feedback on the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis**
        ▪ Suppresses pulsatile release of **Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH)**
        ▪ Leads to decreased secretion of **Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH)** and **Luteinizing Hormone (LH)**
        ▪ **Inhibition of FSH** prevents follicular development
        ▪ **Elimination of the mid-cycle LH surge** is the key step preventing ovulation
    ◦ **Secondary Mechanisms**:
        ▪ **Thickening of Cervical Mucus**: Progestin creates a barrier impeding sperm transport
        ▪ **Endometrial Atrophy/Alteration**: Becomes thin, atrophic, and non-receptive to implantation
        ▪ **Altered Tubal Motility**: May slow ovum transport
• **Component Roles**:
    ◦ **Estrogen (usually Ethinyl Estradiol - EE)**:
        ▪ Primarily stabilizes the endometrium to prevent irregular bleeding (**breakthrough bleeding**)
        ▪ Potentiates the action of the progestin
    ◦ **Progestin**:
        ▪ Provides most of the contraceptive effect via **ovulation suppression** and **cervical mucus thickening**
        ▪ Different generations have varying androgenic and metabolic profiles
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: **OCPs** are the most common form of reversible contraception used by women in the United States
• **User Demographics**: Most prevalent among younger women (ages 15-29)
• **Efficacy**:
    ◦ **Perfect Use**: >99% effective (failure rate <1%)
    ◦ **Typical Use**: ~93% effective (failure rate ~7%)
        ▪ Discrepancy is due to user error (e.g., missed pills, incorrect patch/ring use)
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Healthy patient seeking a reliable, reversible method of contraception
• Patient seeking treatment for non-contraceptive benefits such as:
    ◦ **Dysmenorrhea** (painful periods)
    ◦ **Menorrhagia** (heavy menstrual bleeding)
    ◦ Irregular menstrual cycles
    ◦ **Acne vulgaris** or **hirsutism**
    ◦ Symptom control for **Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)** or **endometriosis**
• Patient may also present with side effects after initiating a CHC
sections.diagnostics:
• For a healthy individual with no contraindications based on a thorough medical history, **no routine laboratory tests are required** before initiating CHCs
• A **urine pregnancy test (UPT)** should be performed if there is any suspicion of pregnancy
• Consider a **lipid panel** in patients with a family history of premature cardiovascular disease or known dyslipidemia
sections.prognosis:
• **Contraceptive Efficacy**: Excellent when used correctly
• **Overall Health**: Excellent for appropriately screened, healthy, non-smoking individuals
• **Long-Term Benefits (Protective Effects)**:
    ◦ **Ovarian Cancer**: ~50% risk reduction with long-term use; protection persists for years after stopping
    ◦ **Endometrial Cancer**: ~50% risk reduction; protection persists for years after stopping
    ◦ **Colorectal Cancer**: Reduced risk
    ◦ **Benign Breast Disease**: Reduced risk of fibrocystic changes and fibroadenomas

sections.overview:
• **Progestin-Only Contraception (POC)** utilizes a synthetic progestin to prevent pregnancy without estrogen, making it a suitable option for individuals with contraindications to estrogen-containing methods.
    ◦ POCs are available in several forms, each with a distinct delivery system, duration of action, and user-dependency profile:
        ▪ **Pill (POP):** A daily oral tablet, often called the "minipill."
        ▪ **Injection (DMPA):** An intramuscular or subcutaneous injection given every 3 months (**Depo-Provera**).
        ▪ **Implant:** A subdermal rod placed in the upper arm that lasts for 3 years (**Nexplanon**).
sections.etiology:
• The mechanism of action (MOA) varies slightly by method but is centered on progestogenic effects.
    ◦ **Primary MOA (All Methods): Thickening of cervical mucus.**
        ▪ This creates a physical barrier that prevents sperm penetration into the upper reproductive tract.
        ▪ This is the most consistent and important mechanism, especially for the **progestin-only pill**.
    ◦ **Secondary MOAs:**
        ▪ **Inhibition of Ovulation:** This is the dominant MOA for the **implant** and **injection**, which consistently suppress the **LH surge**. Ovulation is inhibited in only ~50% of cycles with the **POP**.
        ▪ **Endometrial Thinning/Atrophy:** Progestin creates an unfavorable, atrophic endometrium that is not receptive to the implantation of a fertilized egg.
        ▪ **Slowing of Tubal Motility:** May slow the transport of the ovum through the fallopian tube.
sections.epidemiology:
• POCs are a crucial contraceptive option for specific populations, including:
    ◦ **Postpartum** and **breastfeeding** women: Progestin does not affect milk supply, unlike estrogen.
    ◦ Women with **contraindications to estrogen** (e.g., history of **VTE**, smoker >35 years old, **migraine with aura**).
• The subdermal implant (a **LARC** - Long-Acting Reversible Contraceptive) has one of the highest efficacy rates and continuation rates of all reversible methods.
• **DMPA** is widely used, particularly among younger populations, but has a higher discontinuation rate, often due to side effects.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient will present seeking contraception and may be an ideal candidate for a POC if they have the following characteristics:
    ◦ Desire for contraception and have a **contraindication to estrogen**.
    ◦ Are in the immediate **postpartum** period or are **breastfeeding**.
    ◦ Desire a long-acting method with low user failure (implant, injection).
    ◦ Suffer from **dysmenorrhea** or **heavy menstrual bleeding** (**amenorrhea** induced by the implant or DMPA can be therapeutic).
    ◦ Have difficulty with adherence to a daily pill regimen.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Pregnancy Test:** A urine hCG test is required before initiating any method to rule out existing pregnancy.
• **Routine Labs:** No routine laboratory monitoring (e.g., lipids, LFTs) is required for healthy individuals using POCs.
• **DMPA-Specific:**
    ◦ A **DXA scan** to assess bone mineral density (BMD) is **not routinely recommended**.
    ◦ It may be considered for long-term users (>2 years) who have other significant risk factors for osteoporosis (e.g., chronic steroid use, history of fragility fracture).
• **Workup for Abnormal Bleeding:** If bleeding is persistent or concerning, workup may include:
    ◦ STI screening (chlamydia, gonorrhea).
    ◦ Pap test (if due).
    ◦ TSH.
    ◦ Pelvic ultrasound.
sections.prognosis:
• Refers to contraceptive efficacy (failure rates with 1 year of typical use).
    ◦ **Implant:** <0.1% (The most effective reversible method available).
    ◦ **Injection (DMPA):** ~6% (Failure is almost always due to a late or missed injection).
    ◦ **Pill (POP):** ~9% (Failure is primarily due to incorrect or inconsistent use).

sections.overview:
• Intrauterine Devices (IUDs) are a form of Long-Acting Reversible Contraception (LARC) placed into the uterine cavity.
    ◦ They are T-shaped, highly effective (>99%), and offer long-term contraception without requiring user adherence.
    ◦ Return to fertility is rapid upon removal.
• There are two main categories:
    ◦ **Copper IUD (Cu-IUD):** Non-hormonal (e.g., ParaGard).
        ▪ Approved for up to 10-12 years.
        ▪ Can also be used for emergency contraception.
    ◦ **Hormonal / Levonorgestrel IUD (LNG-IUD):** Releases a progestin, levonorgestrel (e.g., Mirena, Kyleena, Liletta, Skyla).
        ▪ Approved for 3-8 years depending on the device.
        ▪ Has non-contraceptive benefits like treating **heavy menstrual bleeding**.
sections.etiology: • The mechanism of action differs significantly between the two types.
sections.epidemiology:
• IUDs are one of the most effective forms of reversible contraception, with typical-use failure rates of <1% per year (0.8% for Cu-IUD, 0.1-0.4% for LNG-IUDs).
• Use has been steadily increasing in the United States, especially among nulliparous individuals.
• LARCs (IUDs and implants) are recommended as first-line contraceptive options for most women, including adolescents, by ACOG and the AAP.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patient presents requesting a highly effective, long-term, low-maintenance ("get it and forget it") form of contraception.
• Patient may present for non-contraceptive benefits, primarily management of **heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB)**, endometriosis-associated pain, or endometrial hyperplasia (LNG-IUD only).
• Patient presents for scheduled follow-up or with a complication/side effect (see below).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Pre-Insertion:**
    ◦ **Urine pregnancy test (UPT):** Mandatory immediately before insertion.
    ◦ **STI Screening:** Screen for Gonorrhea and Chlamydia based on risk factors (age <25, new/multiple partners) per CDC guidelines.
        ▪ Treatment can occur with the IUD in place.
    ◦ Cervical cytology (Pap test) should be up to date but is not required for insertion.
• **Post-Insertion / Complication Workup:**
    ◦ **Missing Strings:**
        ▪ 1. Rule out pregnancy with UPT.
        ▪ 2. Gently probe the endocervical canal with a cytobrush or cotton swab to locate strings that may have retracted.
        ▪ 3. If strings are not found, order a **pelvic ultrasound** to confirm intrauterine location.
        ▪ 4. If not visualized on ultrasound, an **abdominal X-ray (KUB)** is needed to locate a potential intraperitoneal device from an unrecognized perforation.
    ◦ **Suspected PID:** Cervical cultures, wet prep, CBC.
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent. One of the most effective contraceptive methods available.
• Continuation rates are high due to lack of user-dependence.
• Full and rapid return to fertility upon removal.
• LNG-IUD provides excellent long-term management for **HMB**, often avoiding the need for more invasive procedures like hysterectomy.

sections.overview:
• Emergency Contraception (EC) refers to methods of contraception used to prevent pregnancy after **unprotected sexual intercourse (UPSI)** or **contraceptive failure**.
• EC is a **time-sensitive** intervention and is most effective the sooner it is used.
• The primary mechanisms involve preventing or delaying **ovulation**; EC is **not an abortifacient** and will not terminate an established pregnancy.
• Major options include oral **levonorgestrel (LNG)**, oral **ulipristal acetate (UPA)**, and the **copper intrauterine device (IUD)**.
sections.etiology:
• The mechanism of action varies by the method used. The primary goal is to prevent pregnancy before **implantation** occurs.
• **Copper IUD (Paragard)**
    ◦ **Primary Mechanism:** The copper ions create a sterile intrauterine **inflammatory reaction** that is **spermicidal** and **ovicidal**. This prevents fertilization.
    ◦ **Secondary Mechanism:** If fertilization has occurred, it impairs **implantation** by altering the endometrium. It is effective both pre- and post-fertilization but is used pre-implantation.
• **Ulipristal Acetate (UPA) (ella)**
    ◦ **Mechanism:** A **selective progesterone receptor modulator (SPRM)**. Its primary action is to **delay or inhibit ovulation** by suppressing the **LH surge**. It is effective even when taken close to the time of ovulation.
    ◦ It may also have some effects on the endometrium that could inhibit implantation, but **ovulation inhibition** is the main mechanism.
• **Levonorgestrel (LNG) (Plan B One-Step, and others)**
    ◦ **Mechanism:** A high-dose **progestin**. Its primary action is to **delay or inhibit ovulation**. It is most effective **before the LH surge begins**.
    ◦ It may also thicken **cervical mucus**, which hinders sperm transport.
    ◦ It is ineffective once ovulation has occurred.
• **Combined Oral Contraceptives (Yuzpe Method)**
    ◦ **Mechanism:** High doses of estrogen and progestin **inhibit ovulation**.
    ◦ This method is rarely used today due to lower efficacy and higher rates of side effects (nausea, vomiting) compared to other options.
sections.epidemiology:
• Approximately 1 in 4 sexually active women in the U.S. have used EC.
• Usage is highest among women aged **20-24**.
• Common reasons for use include **contraceptive failure** (e.g., condom breakage) or inconsistent/no use of contraception.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patient presents requesting EC after an episode of **UPSI** or **contraceptive failure**.
• The key historical elements to obtain are:
    ◦ **Time since intercourse:** This is the most critical factor in determining options and efficacy.
    ◦ **Date of Last Menstrual Period (LMP):** To assess the phase of the menstrual cycle and rule out a possible pre-existing pregnancy.
    ◦ Regularity of menstrual cycles.
    ◦ Medical history and current medications: To identify contraindications or drug interactions.
    ◦ History of prior EC use.
    ◦ In cases of **sexual assault**, follow appropriate institutional protocols for care, counseling, and forensic evidence collection.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Urine Pregnancy Test (hCG):** The most important test.
    ◦ Perform prior to providing EC to rule out an **existing pregnancy**.
    ◦ Note: a **negative test** does not rule out a very recent pregnancy from the UPSI in question, only a pre-existing one.
• **STI Screening:** Offer based on patient's risk factors and history (e.g., chlamydia, gonorrhea, HIV, syphilis).
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent for preventing pregnancy when used correctly and within the recommended timeframe.
• **Failure rates** are low but not zero. The risk of pregnancy after a single act of UPSI is reduced by **>95%** with the **copper IUD** and by **50-98%** with **oral methods**.

sections.overview:
• **Female sterilization** is a **permanent method of contraception** that works by blocking or removing the fallopian tubes to prevent fertilization.
• It is one of the most effective and widely used methods of contraception globally.
• The two primary procedures are:
    ◦ **Tubal ligation**: Occluding the tubes.
    ◦ **Bilateral salpingectomy**: Removing the tubes.
        ▪ The standard of care is shifting towards **bilateral salpingectomy** due to its added benefit of significantly reducing the risk of **ovarian cancer**.
• Sterilization can be performed at various times:
    ◦ **Postpartum** (immediately after childbirth).
    ◦ As an **interval procedure** (unrelated to a recent pregnancy).
    ◦ Opportunistically during other abdominal or pelvic surgeries (e.g., cholecystectomy, hysterectomy).
sections.etiology:
• This is a surgical intervention, not a disease process.
• **Mechanism of Action**:
    ◦ Creates a physical barrier in the fallopian tubes, preventing sperm from reaching the oocyte for fertilization.
    ◦ Ovarian function (hormone production and ovulation) remains intact.
• **Methods of Occlusion/Removal**:
    ◦ **Tubal Ligation (Occlusion)**:
        ▪ **Clips** (e.g., Filshie, Hulka): Mechanically clamp the tube shut, leading to necrosis and separation.
        ▪ **Rings** (e.g., Falope, Yoon): A silicone band is placed around a knuckle of the fallopian tube, causing ischemia and scarring.
        ▪ **Electrocautery** (Bipolar/Unipolar): Destroys a segment of the tube using electrical current. Bipolar is more common and safer.
        ▪ **Suture Ligation** (e.g., **Pomeroy**, Parkland): A segment of the tube is tied off with suture and then excised. The **Pomeroy** technique is very common in postpartum procedures.
    ◦ **Salpingectomy (Removal)**:
        ▪ **Partial**: Removal of a portion of the tube.
        ▪ **Total/Complete (Bilateral Salpingectomy)**: Complete removal of both fallopian tubes. This is the **preferred method**.
• **Ovarian Cancer Pathophysiology Link**:
    ◦ A significant proportion of high-grade serous **ovarian cancers** are now believed to originate in the fimbriated end of the fallopian tube (**serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma, or STIC**).
    ◦ Removing the tubes (**salpingectomy**) removes this precursor tissue, drastically reducing the risk.
sections.epidemiology:
• One of the most common contraceptive methods in the United States and worldwide.
• The leading method of contraception for women over 35 in the U.S.
• Prevalence increases with age and parity.
• Approximately 25% of female contraception users in the U.S. rely on sterilization.
• **Postpartum sterilization** accounts for a large number of procedures.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patient is typically a healthy female who has completed childbearing and desires **permanent contraception**.
• The "presentation" is an elective consult for counseling and scheduling.
• The key component is a thorough discussion of:
    ◦ The patient's reproductive goals.
    ◦ Understanding of the procedure's **permanence**.
    ◦ Review of all alternative contraceptive methods.
• Must confirm the decision is voluntary and well-informed.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Pre-operative**:
    ◦ **Urine hCG**: **MANDATORY** to rule out pregnancy on the day of surgery.
    ◦ Up-to-date **Pap smear** (cervical cancer screening).
    ◦ **STI screening** (e.g., for gonorrhea and chlamydia) to prevent post-procedural **PID**.
    ◦ **CBC** may be obtained as a baseline, especially if significant blood loss is a concern.
• **Post-operative (If Complications are Suspected)**:
    ◦ **CBC**: To evaluate for **leukocytosis** (infection) or a drop in hemoglobin/hematocrit (**hemorrhage**).
    ◦ **Pelvic/Abdominal Ultrasound**: Can identify **hematoma** or **abscess** formation.
    ◦ **CT Scan**: More detailed imaging if **bowel injury** or intra-abdominal abscess is suspected.
• **Confirmation of Sterility**:
    ◦ Not routinely performed.
    ◦ **Hysterosalpingogram (HSG)** may be used to evaluate for tubal patency in cases of suspected **method failure** (i.e., subsequent pregnancy).
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent. One of the most effective forms of contraception, with a typical-use **failure rate of <1%**.
• **Salpingectomy** provides a significant, lifelong reduction in the risk of **epithelial ovarian cancer**.
• Surgical **mortality** is extremely low (~1-2 per 100,000 procedures).

sections.overview:
• A vasectomy is a minor surgical procedure for **permanent male contraception**.
• Involves the transection, ligation, or occlusion of the **vas deferens** bilaterally to prevent sperm from entering the ejaculate.
• Considered one of the safest and most effective forms of birth control.
• Does not affect male hormone production (**testosterone**), libido, erectile function, or the sensation of orgasm.
• The volume of ejaculate is only minimally reduced (~5%), as sperm constitutes a very small portion of the total semen volume.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**: Elective surgical intervention.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ The procedure mechanically obstructs the **vas deferens**, a duct that transports sperm from the epididymis to the ejaculatory ducts.
    ◦ Sperm production in the **seminiferous tubules** of the testes continues normally.
    ◦ Sperm mature in the epididymis but are unable to pass the point of occlusion.
    ◦ Trapped sperm are broken down and reabsorbed by the body (**phagocytosis**), a natural process that also occurs with unused sperm in non-vasectomized men.
    ◦ The seminal vesicles and prostate gland continue to produce the fluid components of semen, so ejaculation still occurs, but the ejaculate is **azoospermic** (sperm-free).
    ◦ **Leydig cell** function is unaffected; therefore, testosterone production and secondary sexual characteristics remain unchanged.
sections.epidemiology:
• One of the most common methods of contraception in the United States, with approximately 500,000 procedures performed annually.
• The typical patient is a male over age 30 in a stable, monogamous relationship who has completed his family.
• It is more common, less invasive, less expensive, and has a lower complication rate than female **tubal ligation**.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Indications**:
    ◦ Patient desires **permanent sterilization**.
    ◦ The patient has completed family planning.
    ◦ Medical contraindication for a partner to use other forms of contraception.
• **Relative Contraindications**:
    ◦ Previous scrotal surgery (e.g., hernia repair, hydrocelectomy, orchiopexy) which can cause scarring and make the vas deferens difficult to isolate.
    ◦ **Bleeding diathesis** or current anticoagulant therapy.
    ◦ Active scrotal skin infection or genitourinary infection (e.g., epididymitis, STI).
    ◦ Large **varicocele** or **hydrocele**.
    ◦ **Chronic scrotal pain** or history of testicular cancer.
• **Absolute Contraindications**:
    ◦ Patient uncertainty or decisional conflict.
    ◦ Evidence of patient being coerced by a partner or family.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• An otherwise healthy male presents to an outpatient clinic (primary care or urology) for consultation regarding permanent contraception.
• The patient should be able to articulate a clear and stable decision to forego future fertility.
• The clinical visit focuses on counseling, education, and physical examination to ensure the patient is an appropriate candidate.
• **Symptoms**:
    ◦ **Pre-Procedure**: Asymptomatic.
    ◦ **Immediate Post-Procedure (Expected)**:
        ▪ Mild to moderate **scrotal pain**, aching, or discomfort.
        ▪ **Scrotal bruising** and swelling.
        ▪ A small amount of bleeding or oozing from the incision site.
        ▪ Symptoms typically resolve within 1-2 weeks.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Pre-Operative Exam is Crucial**:
    ◦ **Scrotal Contents**: Normal testes bilaterally in size and consistency. No masses.
    ◦ **Vas Deferens**: The vas should be easily palpable bilaterally within the spermatic cord.
        ▪ It feels firm and cord-like, often described as "al dente spaghetti."
        ▪ Confirming the presence of both vasa is essential.
    ◦ **Assess for Abnormalities**: Screen for inguinal hernia, varicocele, hydrocele, spermatocele, or epididymal cysts that might complicate the procedure.
    ◦ **Skin**: Check for any active lesions, cysts, or infections on the scrotal skin.
sections.diagnostics:
• The primary diagnostic test is performed **after** the procedure to confirm its success.
• **Post-Vasectomy Semen Analysis (PVSA)**:
    ◦ **Gold standard** for confirming sterility.
    ◦ **Timing**: Performed 8-16 weeks post-procedure, and after a minimum of 20 ejaculations, to clear residual sperm from the distal reproductive tract.
    ◦ **Success Criteria (AUA Guidelines)**:
        ▪ **Azoospermia**: No sperm seen on analysis.
        ▪ **Rare Non-Motile Sperm (RNMS)**: A very low number of non-motile sperm (typically defined as <100,000 non-motile sperm/mL) is also considered a successful vasectomy, as these are not clinically significant for pregnancy.
    ◦ **Failure**: The presence of any **motile sperm** on PVSA after the clearing phase indicates procedural failure (**recanalization**) and requires repeat vasectomy or continued use of contraception.
sections.treatment:
• **Anesthesia**: Local anesthetic (e.g., lidocaine) injected into the skin and spermatic cord sheath.
• **Surgical Techniques**:
    ◦ **Occlusion Methods (often used in combination)**:
        ▪ **Ligation**: Sutures are used to tie off the ends of the vas.
        ▪ **Excision**: A small segment of the vas is removed.
        ▪ **Thermal Cautery**: The mucosal lining of the vas is destroyed with heat to promote scarring and closure.
        ▪ **Fascial Interposition**: The testicular end of the vas is covered with the vasal sheath, creating a tissue barrier between the two severed ends to prevent recanalization. This is a critical step for improving success rates.
        ▪ **Clips**: Metal clips may be used to occlude the vas ends.
sections.management:
• **Pre-Operative Care**:
    ◦ **Counseling is paramount**. Must cover:
        ▪ The **permanence** of the procedure.
        ▪ The procedure is not effective immediately; **backup contraception is required** until sterility is confirmed by PVSA.
        ▪ Potential for failure (early and late **recanalization**, ~1 in 2000).
        ▪ Risks and complications (bleeding, infection, **PVPS**).
        ▪ Alternatives (e.g., tubal ligation, IUD, condoms).
    ◦ **Informed consent** must be obtained.
• **Post-Operative Care**:
    ◦ **Rest and Ice**: Rest for 24-48 hours. Apply ice packs to the scrotum for 20-minute intervals.
    ◦ **Scrotal Support**: Wear supportive underwear or an athletic supporter.
    ◦ **Pain Control**: NSAIDs (ibuprofen) or acetaminophen.
    ◦ **Activity**: Avoid strenuous activity, heavy lifting, and sports for about one week.
    ◦ **Sexual Activity**: Can resume in about one week, but **MUST use another form of contraception**.
    ◦ **Follow-up**: PVSA as described in the Diagnostics section.
sections.complications:
• **Early (<2 weeks)**:
    ◦ **Hematoma/Bleeding**: Most common complication (1-5%). Can range from minor bruising to a large, painful **scrotal hematoma** requiring drainage.
    ◦ **Infection**: Cellulitis of the incision site or deeper abscess. Low risk, especially with NSV.
• **Late (>2 weeks)**:
    ◦ **Post-Vasectomy Pain Syndrome (PVPS)**: Chronic, debilitating scrotal pain lasting >3 months. Incidence is 1-2%. Etiology is multifactorial (nerve entrapment, epididymal congestion, granuloma).
    ◦ **Sperm Granuloma**: Painful or painless lump at the vasectomy site due to sperm leakage.
    ◦ **Failure (Recanalization)**: The severed ends of the vas deferens grow back together. Early failure is due to technical error; late failure is spontaneous. Overall failure rate is <1%.
    ◦ **Psychological**: Regret (rare if counseling was adequate).
• **Disproven Associations**: Large-scale studies have shown **NO** increased risk of **prostate cancer**, **testicular cancer**, or **cardiovascular disease**.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**.
• Failure rate is very low, with a pregnancy risk of approximately **1 in 2,000** after sterility is confirmed.
• Vasectomy is safer and more effective than female tubal ligation.
• While vasectomy reversal (**vasovasostomy**) is possible, it is technically demanding, expensive, and not guaranteed to restore fertility. Success rates decrease as more time passes since the vasectomy.

sections.overview:
• **Anovulation** is the failure of the ovary to release an oocyte during the menstrual cycle.
• It is a major cause of female infertility, accounting for approximately **25-30% of cases**.
• Chronic anovulation presents clinically as **amenorrhea** or **oligomenorrhea**.
• The underlying cause is a disruption of the **hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis**, which can occur at any level (hypothalamus, pituitary, or ovary).
• Diagnosis involves a systematic hormonal evaluation, and treatment is aimed at correcting the underlying cause to induce ovulation.
sections.etiology:
• Anovulation is classified by the World Health Organization (**WHO**) based on gonadotropin (FSH/LH) and estrogen levels.
    ◦ This framework is essential for diagnosis and treatment.
sections.epidemiology:
• Anovulation is responsible for infertility in approximately **25-30% of couples** seeking treatment.
• **PCOS is the single most common cause of anovulatory infertility**, affecting 5-10% of reproductive-aged women.
• **Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea** accounts for about 10-15% of anovulation cases.
• **Premature ovarian insufficiency** affects about 1% of women under 40.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The primary presenting complaint is **infertility**, defined as the inability to conceive after 12 months of regular, unprotected intercourse (or 6 months if the female partner is ≥35 years old).
• The hallmark of anovulation is **menstrual dysfunction**.
sections.diagnostics:
• The diagnostic workup is a stepwise process to identify the underlying etiology.
• **Rule out Pregnancy**:
    ◦ Always the first step.
    ◦ **Urine or serum β-hCG**.
• **Initial Hormonal Screening**:
    ◦ **TSH**: To rule out thyroid disease.
    ◦ **Prolactin**: To rule out hyperprolactinemia.
    ◦ **FSH**: To differentiate between ovarian (high FSH), hypothalamic/pituitary (low/normal FSH), and HPO dysfunction (normal FSH).
• **Further Evaluation based on Initial Labs**:
    ◦ **If FSH is HIGH (>20-30 mIU/mL)**:
        ▪ Suspect ovarian insufficiency (**WHO Group III**).
        ▪ Repeat FSH and estradiol level on a separate day to confirm.
        ▪ Consider karyotype (for **Turner syndrome**) and FMR1 premutation testing.
    ◦ **If FSH is LOW or NORMAL**:
        ▪ Suspect hypothalamic/pituitary cause (**WHO I or II**).
        ▪ Proceed with:
            • **LH**: An **LH:FSH ratio >2:1 or 3:1** is suggestive of **PCOS**.
            • **Androgen Panel**: Total and free testosterone, DHEAS. Elevated levels support a diagnosis of **PCOS**.
    ◦ **If Prolactin is HIGH**:
        ▪ Repeat level while fasting.
        ▪ If persistently elevated, especially >100 ng/mL, order a **pituitary MRI** to evaluate for a prolactinoma.
• **Progestin Challenge Test**:
    ◦ **Purpose**: To assess for endogenous estrogen production and a patent outflow tract.
    ◦ **Procedure**: Administer oral medroxyprogesterone acetate (**Provera**) 10 mg daily for 5-10 days.
    ◦ **Results**:
        ▪ **Withdrawal Bleeding Occurs**: Confirms the presence of sufficient estrogen and a normal outflow tract. This indicates anovulation (e.g., **PCOS**).
        ▪ **No Withdrawal Bleeding**: Indicates either low estrogen (hypoestrogenic state like **FHA**) or an outflow tract obstruction (e.g., **Asherman syndrome**).
• **Imaging**:
    ◦ **Transvaginal Pelvic Ultrasound**: Essential for evaluating ovarian morphology.
        ▪ **"String of pearls" appearance** (12-20 small follicles per ovary) is a key criterion for **PCOS**.
        ▪ Also used to assess endometrial stripe thickness.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for **WHO Group II (PCOS)** and **hyperprolactinemia** with appropriate treatment.
    ◦ Live birth rates are high.
• **Good** for **WHO Group I**, but requires more intensive therapy with injectable gonadotropins.
• **Very Poor** for **WHO Group III (ovarian insufficiency)** for achieving pregnancy with autologous oocytes.
    ◦ Success with **donor eggs** is high and dependent on the egg donor's age.

sections.overview:
• Tubal factor infertility refers to the inability to conceive due to structural abnormalities, blockage, or damage to the fallopian tubes.
• The fallopian tubes play a critical role in reproduction by capturing the oocyte after ovulation, serving as the site of fertilization, and transporting the resulting embryo to the uterus for implantation.
• Any process that obstructs this pathway or damages the delicate ciliated epithelium of the tubes can lead to infertility.
• It accounts for approximately **25-35%** of all cases of female infertility.
sections.etiology:
• The underlying pathophysiology involves inflammation, scarring (adhesions), and occlusion of the fallopian tubes, which impairs oocyte capture, sperm-egg interaction, and embryo transport.
• **Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID)**
    ◦ The most common cause.
    ◦ Ascending infection, most notably from ***Chlamydia trachomatis*** and ***Neisseria gonorrhoeae***, leads to salpingitis (inflammation of the tubes).
    ◦ The subsequent healing process creates scar tissue and adhesions, leading to tubal blockage.
    ◦ *Chlamydia* is particularly insidious as it often causes a "silent," subclinical infection that results in significant tubal damage.
• **Pelvic Surgery**
    ◦ Any abdominal or pelvic surgery (e.g., appendectomy, ovarian cystectomy, myomectomy) can lead to the formation of post-operative adhesions that distort or obstruct the tubes.
• **Endometriosis**
    ◦ Endometrial implants in the pelvis can cause a significant inflammatory reaction, leading to adhesions that encase the ovaries and tubes (peritubal adhesions), distorting their anatomy and function.
• **Previous Ectopic Pregnancy**
    ◦ The ectopic pregnancy itself can damage the tube.
    ◦ Furthermore, surgical treatment (salpingostomy or salpingectomy) can result in scarring or removal of the tube.
• **Hydrosalpinx**
    ◦ A specific form of distal tubal blockage where the end of the fallopian tube (fimbriae) is occluded, causing the tube to fill with serous fluid.
    ◦ This fluid is embryotoxic and can leak back into the uterine cavity, decreasing IVF implantation rates.
• **Congenital Tubal Abnormalities**
    ◦ Rare causes include agenesis or malformations of the tubes.
sections.epidemiology:
• Accounts for **25-35%** of female infertility cases.
• Incidence is directly correlated with the prevalence of sexually transmitted infections (STIs), particularly *Chlamydia trachomatis*.
• A single episode of PID increases the risk of tubal infertility by ~10-15%; this risk rises to over 50% after three or more episodes.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The primary presentation is **infertility**, defined as the inability to conceive after 12 months of regular, unprotected intercourse (or 6 months if the female partner is ≥35 years old).
• Patients are often **asymptomatic** apart from the inability to conceive.
• The patient may provide a history consistent with one of the risk factors (e.g., "I was treated for a bad infection years ago," "I had surgery for an ovarian cyst").
sections.diagnostics:
• The goal is to assess the patency (openness) of the fallopian tubes.
• **Hysterosalpingogram (HSG)**
    ◦ **First-line imaging test** for evaluating tubal patency.
    ◦ **Procedure:** Radiopaque contrast dye is injected through the cervix into the uterine cavity and fallopian tubes under fluoroscopy.
    ◦ **Findings:**
        ▪ **Normal (Patent):** Dye fills the uterine cavity, outlines the fallopian tubes, and then freely **spills** into the peritoneal cavity.
        ▪ **Abnormal (Blocked):** Dye stops at a certain point.
            ◦ *Proximal occlusion:* Blockage near the uterus.
            ◦ *Distal occlusion:* Blockage near the fimbrial end, often associated with a **hydrosalpinx** (dilated, club-like appearance of the tube).
    ◦ HSG also evaluates the uterine cavity for abnormalities like fibroids or polyps.
• **Laparoscopy with Chromotubation**
    ◦ **The gold standard** for assessing tubal and pelvic pathology.
    ◦ **Procedure:** A minimally invasive surgery where a camera is inserted into the abdomen. Methylene blue dye is injected through the cervix, and the surgeon directly visualizes whether the dye spills from the fimbriated ends of the tubes.
    ◦ **Advantages:** Allows for direct visualization of adhesions, endometriosis, and other pelvic pathologies. Also allows for simultaneous treatment (e.g., lysis of adhesions).
• **Saline Infusion Sonohysterography (SIS) / HyCoSy**
    ◦ An ultrasound-based alternative. Saline or a contrast agent is infused into the uterus to assess the uterine cavity and tubal patency via transvaginal ultrasound. Less definitive for tubal evaluation than HSG but avoids radiation.
• ***Chlamydia* Antibody Testing**
    ◦ A blood test for IgG antibodies to *C. trachomatis*.
    ◦ A positive result indicates past exposure and significantly increases the likelihood of tubal factor infertility, helping to guide the decision to proceed with HSG or laparoscopy.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis for natural conception is **poor** with significant tubal damage, especially bilateral distal occlusion (hydrosalpinx).
• The success of surgical repair depends heavily on the extent and location of the damage. Prognosis is better for lysis of minimal adhesions than for neosalpingostomy for a large hydrosalpinx.
• The prognosis for achieving pregnancy via **IVF is excellent**, as it bypasses the tubal pathology. Success rates are primarily dictated by the female partner's age and ovarian reserve.

sections.overview:
• **Male factor infertility** refers to any condition in a male partner contributing to a couple's inability to conceive after one year of regular, unprotected intercourse (or 6 months if the female partner is >35 years old)
    ◦ A contributing factor in approximately **50%** of all infertile couples
    ◦ The sole cause in about **20-30%** of cases
    ◦ Evaluation focuses on issues with sperm production (**spermatogenesis**), function, or delivery (**ejaculation**)
sections.etiology:
• Male infertility can be categorized into three main groups:
    ◦ **Pre-testicular** causes
    ◦ **Testicular** causes
    ◦ **Post-testicular** causes
sections.epidemiology:
• Infertility affects ~15% of couples attempting to conceive
• A male factor is identified in ~50% of these cases
• **Varicoceles** are found in ~15% of the general male population but in ~40% of men with primary infertility
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The primary presentation is the **couple's inability to achieve pregnancy**
• The male partner is often entirely asymptomatic
• Workup is typically initiated after 12 months of unsuccessful, regular, unprotected intercourse (or 6 months if female partner >35)
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for correctable causes like endocrine abnormalities or obstruction
• **Good** for men with **varicoceles** who undergo repair, though benefit is debated
• **Variable to Poor** for natural conception in cases of **primary testicular failure**
• **Excellent** for achieving pregnancy via **IVF with ICSI** even with severe male factor, provided sperm can be found/retrieved
    ◦ Prognosis for sperm retrieval is better in **obstructive azoospermia** (>90%) than **non-obstructive azoospermia** (~50%)

sections.overview:
• **Hyperprolactinemia** is an endocrine disorder characterized by pathologically elevated levels of prolactin (PRL) in the blood.
• Prolactin's primary function is to stimulate milk production (**lactation**) after childbirth.
• Sustained high levels of prolactin disrupt the normal pulsatile secretion of **Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH)** from the hypothalamus.
    ◦ This disruption leads to suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (**HPG**) axis, resulting in **hypogonadism** and its associated reproductive consequences, such as infertility, menstrual dysfunction, and sexual dysfunction.
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The central mechanism is the **inhibition of GnRH release** from the hypothalamus by elevated prolactin.
        ▪ ↓ **Pulsatile GnRH Secretion**
        ▪ ↓ **Luteinizing Hormone (LH)** & **Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH)** Secretion from the pituitary.
        ▪ ↓ LH & FSH leads to:
            ▪ **In Females:** Anovulation, impaired follicular development, and decreased estrogen production → **oligomenorrhea/amenorrhea**, infertility, vaginal dryness.
            ▪ **In Males:** Decreased testosterone production from Leydig cells → **decreased libido**, **erectile dysfunction (ED)**, reduced spermatogenesis, infertility.
    ◦ **Dopamine**, secreted by the hypothalamus, is the primary physiologic **inhibitor** of prolactin release.
        ▪ Any process that reduces dopamine's effect on the pituitary can cause hyperprolactinemia.
• **Etiologies**
    ◦ **Physiologic (Non-pathologic)**
        ▪ **Pregnancy & Lactation:** Most common physiologic cause.
        ▪ Nipple stimulation / chest wall stimulation
        ▪ Stress (physical or emotional)
        ▪ Exercise
        ▪ Sleep
    ◦ **Pathologic**
        ▪ **Pituitary Adenomas (Prolactinomas):** **Most common pathologic cause.** These are benign tumors of lactotroph cells in the anterior pituitary.
            ▪ **Microadenoma:** < 10 mm (< 1 cm) in diameter.
            ▪ **Macroadenoma:** ≥ 10 mm (≥ 1 cm) in diameter.
        ▪ **Pharmacologic (Drug-Induced):** Extremely common. Caused by dopamine antagonists or dopamine-depleting agents.
            ▪ **Antipsychotics:** **Risperidone**, haloperidol, phenothiazines (e.g., chlorpromazine). *Second-generation antipsychotics are common culprits.*
            ▪ **Antiemetics:** **Metoclopramide**, prochlorperazine, domperidone.
            ▪ **Antihypertensives:** Verapamil, methyldopa.
            ▪ **Antidepressants:** TCAs, SSRIs (less common, usually mild elevation).
            ▪ **Opioids.**
        ▪ **Systemic Disease**
            ▪ **Primary Hypothyroidism:** A classic association. Decreased T4/T3 → increased **TRH (Thyrotropin-Releasing Hormone)** from the hypothalamus. TRH stimulates not only TSH but also **prolactin secretion**.
            ▪ **Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD):** Decreased clearance of prolactin.
            ▪ **Cirrhosis.**
        ▪ **Other Pituitary/Hypothalamic Causes**
            ▪ **Stalk Compression ("Stalk Effect"):** Any mass (e.g., non-functioning adenoma, craniopharyngioma) that compresses the pituitary stalk can block the flow of inhibitory dopamine to the anterior pituitary, leading to increased prolactin.
            ▪ Empty sella syndrome, radiation, infiltrative diseases (sarcoidosis).
        ▪ **Idiopathic:** No identifiable cause found after a thorough workup.
sections.epidemiology:
• More common in **females**, with a peak incidence between ages 25-34.
• Prevalence is estimated at ~0.4% in the general population.
• **Prolactinomas** are the most common type of hormone-secreting (functional) pituitary tumor.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation depends on gender and tumor size.
• **Premenopausal Female:** Presents with a triad of **amenorrhea (or oligomenorrhea)**, **galactorrhea**, and **infertility**.
• **Male:** Often presents later with less specific symptoms of hypogonadism like **decreased libido**, **erectile dysfunction**, and **infertility**.
    ◦ They are more likely to present with mass effect symptoms from a macroadenoma.
• **Mass Effect Presentation (from Macroadenoma):** Patient presents with **headaches** and **visual field defects**, most classically **bitemporal hemianopsia** due to compression of the optic chiasm.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Step 1: Initial Lab Workup**
    ◦ **Serum Prolactin Level:** The first and most important test.
        ▪ Normal: <20-25 ng/mL (varies by lab).
        ▪ **>200 ng/mL:** Almost always indicative of a **prolactinoma**.
        ▪ **25-150 ng/mL:** Can be caused by medications, hypothyroidism, stalk compression, or a microprolactinoma.
    ◦ **Beta-hCG:** **ALWAYS** rule out pregnancy in a female of reproductive age.
    ◦ **TSH:** To rule out primary hypothyroidism as the cause.
    ◦ **BUN/Creatinine:** To rule out renal failure.
    ◦ **Comprehensive Medication Review:** Critical to identify pharmacologic causes.
• **Step 2: Imaging (if indicated)**
    ◦ **Pituitary MRI with contrast:** The gold standard imaging modality.
    ◦ Indicated if prolactin is significantly elevated and other causes are ruled out, or if mass effect symptoms are present.
    ◦ Distinguishes microadenomas from macroadenomas and identifies other sellar/suprasellar masses.
• **Note on "Hook Effect"**
    ◦ Very large tumors (giant prolactinomas) can oversaturate the assay, leading to a falsely low or moderately elevated prolactin level.
    ◦ If a large mass is seen on MRI with only a moderately high prolactin, the lab should be asked to repeat the test on a diluted sample.
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent for most patients.
• Medical therapy with dopamine agonists is highly effective (>80-90%) in normalizing prolactin and restoring fertility.
• Surgical cure rates are high for microadenomas but lower for macroadenomas.
• Recurrence is common if medical therapy is discontinued.

sections.overview:
• **Premature Ovarian Insufficiency (POI)**, formerly known as premature ovarian failure, is a clinical syndrome defined by the **loss of normal ovarian function before the age of 40**
    ◦ Characterized by **amenorrhea** (or **oligomenorrhea**) and **elevated gonadotropin levels (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism)** due to a depletion or dysfunction of ovarian follicles
    ◦ Represents a spectrum of declining ovarian function and, unlike menopause, can be intermittent
        ▪ 5-10% of women experience spontaneous ovulation and even pregnancy after diagnosis
sections.etiology:
• The underlying cause is often unknown
• Results from either:
    ◦ A **rapid depletion of the primordial follicle pool**
    ◦ A **dysfunction of existing follicles**
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects approximately **1% of women by age 40**
• Affects 1 in 1,000 women by age 30
• Affects 1 in 10,000 women by age 20
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a **woman under the age of 40** who presents with:
    ◦ **Menstrual cycle disturbances**
        ▪ **Oligomenorrhea** (infrequent periods)
        ▪ **Secondary amenorrhea** (cessation of periods for >3 months)
    ◦ **Symptoms of estrogen deficiency**
    ◦ A primary concern of **infertility**
sections.diagnostics: • Diagnosis requires a **high index of suspicion** in any **woman <40 with menstrual irregularities**
sections.prognosis:
• With appropriate **HRT**, the prognosis for managing symptoms and reducing long-term health risks is **excellent**
• Life expectancy can be normalized with treatment
• **Infertility** remains the most significant and often irreversible complication
• Spontaneous remission and pregnancy are rare but possible (5-10%)

sections.overview:
• **Erectile Dysfunction (ED)** is the consistent or recurrent inability to attain and/or maintain a penile erection sufficient for satisfactory sexual performance.
• It is a common medical condition that can significantly impact quality of life.
• Importantly, ED is often a manifestation of underlying systemic disease, particularly **cardiovascular disease (CVD)**, and should be considered a potential early marker for **endothelial dysfunction**.
sections.etiology:
• Penile erection is a complex neurovascular event requiring intact psychological, neurologic, hormonal, and vascular systems.
• The primary mechanism involves parasympathetic stimulation leading to the release of **Nitric Oxide (NO)** from cavernous nerve terminals and endothelial cells.
	◦ **NO** activates guanylate cyclase, which converts GTP to **cyclic GMP (cGMP)**.
	◦ **cGMP** causes relaxation of the cavernous smooth muscle, leading to vasodilation of the helicine arteries.
	◦ This increased arterial inflow engorges the corpora cavernosa with blood.
	◦ The engorgement compresses the subtunical venules against the tunica albuginea, reducing venous outflow and trapping blood, thus producing a rigid erection.
	◦ Erection subsides when **Phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE-5)** breaks down cGMP.
• **Classification of Etiologies:**
	◦ **Vascular (most common organic cause):**
		▪ **Arterial Insufficiency:** **Atherosclerosis**, **hypertension**, **hyperlipidemia**, **diabetes mellitus**. Reduced blood flow into the corpora.
		▪ **Veno-occlusive Dysfunction:** Inability to trap blood within the corpora cavernosa due to **venous leakage**.
	◦ **Neurogenic:**
		▪ **Central:** Spinal cord injury, **Multiple Sclerosis (MS)**, Parkinson's disease, stroke.
		▪ **Peripheral:** Radical prostatectomy or cystectomy (**cavernous nerve damage**), **diabetic neuropathy**, pelvic trauma.
	◦ **Hormonal (Endocrinologic):**
		▪ **Hypogonadism (low testosterone):** Decreases libido and may affect erection quality.
		▪ **Hyperprolactinemia:** Suppresses gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), leading to secondary hypogonadism.
		▪ **Thyroid disorders:** Both hyper- and hypothyroidism can contribute.
	◦ **Psychogenic:**
		▪ Performance anxiety, depression, stress, relationship conflicts, "spectatoring."
		▪ Characterized by a **sudden onset**, situational nature, and **preservation of nocturnal/morning erections**.
	◦ **Iatrogenic / Medication-Induced:**
		▪ **Antihypertensives:** Thiazide diuretics, beta-blockers.
		▪ **Antidepressants:** SSRIs, SNRIs.
		▪ **Antipsychotics.**
		▪ **5-alpha-reductase inhibitors:** Finasteride, dutasteride.
		▪ **H2-receptor antagonists:** Cimetidine.
		▪ **Recreational drugs:** Alcohol, nicotine, opioids.
sections.epidemiology:
• Prevalence increases significantly with age.
• Affects approximately **50% of men aged 40-70 years** to some degree.
• **Severe ED** affects 5% of men at age 40 and increases to 15% at age 70.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A male patient, typically >40 years old, presents with a complaint of difficulty achieving or sustaining an erection.
• The **history** is the most critical diagnostic tool.
• Key aspects of the history include:
	◦ **Onset and Duration:** **Gradual onset** suggests an organic cause (e.g., vascular); **sudden onset** is more typical of **psychogenic ED**.
	◦ **Severity and Rigidity:** Differentiating partial from complete inability.
	◦ **Situational vs. Global:** Erections with masturbation but not with a partner suggest a **psychogenic component**.
	◦ **Presence of Nocturnal/Morning Erections:** Their presence strongly suggests intact vascular and neurologic function, pointing towards a **psychogenic etiology**.
	◦ **Associated Symptoms:** Decreased libido (suggests **hypogonadism**), penile curvature (**Peyronie's disease**), claudication (**vascular disease**).
	◦ Thorough review of medical/surgical history, medications, and social history (smoking, alcohol).
sections.diagnostics:
• **History:**
	◦ The most important initial step.
	◦ Using a validated questionnaire like the **International Index of Erectile Function (IIEF-5)** is recommended.
• **Initial Laboratory Workup:**
	◦ **Fasting glucose or HbA1c:** Screen for diabetes.
	◦ **Lipid panel:** Assess for hyperlipidemia and CVD risk.
	◦ **Morning total testosterone:** Screen for **hypogonadism** (must be drawn between 8-10 AM). If low, repeat with free testosterone, LH, and FSH.
• **Optional Labs (based on H&P):**
	◦ **TSH:** If thyroid disease is suspected.
	◦ **Prolactin:** If low libido and low testosterone are present.
	◦ **PSA:** Age-appropriate screening.
• **Specialized Testing (rarely needed, performed by urology):**
	◦ **Nocturnal Penile Tumescence (NPT) Testing:** Uses a device (e.g., RigiScan) to differentiate psychogenic from organic ED by measuring erections during sleep.
	◦ **Penile Duplex Ultrasound:** In-office injection of a vasodilator (e.g., alprostadil) followed by ultrasound to measure arterial inflow and venous outflow.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis for restoring sexual function is excellent with modern therapies.
• The overall health prognosis depends on the underlying etiology.
• The onset of ED confers an **increased risk for future cardiovascular events** (MI, stroke) and all-cause mortality, independent of other risk factors.

sections.overview:
• Male hypogonadism is a clinical syndrome resulting from the failure of the testes to produce physiological levels of testosterone (androgen deficiency) and/or a normal number of spermatozoa (impaired spermatogenesis).
    ◦ The reproductive impact stems directly from these deficiencies, leading to infertility and related symptoms.
    ◦ It is fundamentally classified into two categories based on the level of the Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal (HPG) axis that is defective.
• **Primary Hypogonadism (Hypergonadotropic Hypogonadism):**
    ◦ Testicular failure.
    ◦ The pituitary gland produces high levels of Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH) and Luteinizing Hormone (LH) in an attempt to stimulate the failing testes, but the testes cannot respond.
    ◦ Characterized by **low testosterone** with **high LH/FSH**.
• **Secondary Hypogonadism (Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism):**
    ◦ Hypothalamic or pituitary failure.
    ◦ The testes are normal but are not stimulated adequately due to insufficient production of GnRH, LH, or FSH.
    ◦ Characterized by **low testosterone** with **low or inappropriately normal LH/FSH**.
sections.etiology:
• The HPG axis is central to male reproduction:
    ◦ **Hypothalamus** secretes Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH).
    ◦ **Anterior Pituitary** is stimulated by GnRH to secrete LH and FSH.
    ◦ **Testes:**
        ▪ **LH** stimulates **Leydig cells** to produce testosterone.
        ▪ **FSH** stimulates **Sertoli cells** to support spermatogenesis.
    ◦ Testosterone provides negative feedback to the hypothalamus and pituitary.
• **Primary Hypogonadism (Testicular Failure)**
    ◦ **Congenital:**
        ▪ **Klinefelter Syndrome (XXY):** Most common congenital cause. Leads to seminiferous tubule dysgenesis.
        ▪ **Cryptorchidism:** Undescended testes.
        ▪ **Anorchia:** Congenital absence of testes.
    ◦ **Acquired:**
        ▪ **Orchitis:** Inflammation of the testes (e.g., mumps).
        ▪ **Trauma or Torsion:** Physical damage or vascular compromise.
        ▪ **Chemotherapy/Radiation:** Gonadotoxic effects.
        ▪ **Varicocele:** Dilation of pampiniform plexus can impair testicular function and spermatogenesis.
        ▪ **Autoimmune damage.**
• **Secondary Hypogonadism (Hypothalamic/Pituitary Failure)**
    ◦ **Congenital:**
        ▪ **Kallmann Syndrome:** GnRH deficiency associated with anosmia (inability to smell).
        ▪ **Prader-Willi Syndrome:** Complex genetic disorder.
        ▪ **Idiopathic hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (IHH).**
    ◦ **Acquired:**
        ▪ **Pituitary Tumors:** Prolactinomas are common; high prolactin inhibits GnRH release.
        ▪ **Infiltrative Diseases:** Hemochromatosis (iron deposition), sarcoidosis.
        ▪ **Head Trauma/Surgery/Radiation.**
        ▪ **Systemic Illness:** Severe chronic illness, malnutrition, or critical illness can suppress the HPG axis.
        ▪ **Medications:** Opioids, glucocorticoids, and **anabolic steroids** (exogenous androgens suppress the HPG axis).
        ▪ **Obesity:** Increased aromatase activity in adipose tissue converts testosterone to estradiol, which suppresses LH.
sections.epidemiology:
• Prevalence increases with age, affecting up to 30-40% of men over 60 ("andropause").
• Commonly associated with chronic conditions like obesity, type 2 diabetes, and HIV.
• **Klinefelter syndrome** occurs in approximately 1 in 600 live male births.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation depends on the age of onset. For reproductive impact, the focus is on post-pubertal onset.
• The chief complaint is often **infertility**, decreased libido, or erectile dysfunction.
• The patient may report they and their partner have been unable to conceive after 12 months of unprotected intercourse.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Initial Lab Work-up:**
    ◦ **Total Testosterone:** The first-line test. Must be drawn in the **early morning (8-10 AM)** due to diurnal variation. Low is generally considered <300 ng/dL.
    ◦ **Confirmation:** If the initial level is low, repeat the test on a separate morning.
    ◦ Consider **Free Testosterone** or **Bioavailable Testosterone** if total testosterone is borderline or if SHBG abnormalities are suspected (e.g., obesity, elderly).
• **Differentiating Primary vs. Secondary:**
    ◦ **LH and FSH:**
        ▪ **High LH/FSH** + **Low Testosterone** Primary Hypogonadism.
        ▪ **Low or Inappropriately Normal LH/FSH** + **Low Testosterone** Secondary Hypogonadism.
• **Infertility-Specific Work-up:**
    ◦ **Semen Analysis:** **The single most important test for male infertility.** Assesses sperm concentration (count), motility (movement), and morphology (shape). This should be obtained after 2-5 days of abstinence.
• **Etiology-Specific Work-up:**
    ◦ If **Primary** is suspected:
        ▪ **Karyotype:** To rule out **Klinefelter syndrome (47, XXY)**.
    ◦ If **Secondary** is suspected:
        ▪ **Prolactin:** To rule out a prolactinoma.
        ▪ **Iron Studies/Ferritin:** To rule out hemochromatosis.
        ▪ **MRI of the Pituitary:** To evaluate for tumors, infiltrative disease, or structural abnormalities.
sections.prognosis:
• **Symptom control:** Prognosis is excellent with TRT for men not seeking fertility.
• **Fertility:**
    ◦ **Secondary Hypogonadism:** Good prognosis. Fertility can often be restored with clomiphene or gonadotropin therapy.
    ◦ **Primary Hypogonadism:** Poor prognosis for natural conception. Depends heavily on the underlying cause and the success of ART.

sections.overview:
• Male infertility is the inability of a male to cause pregnancy in a fertile female.
    ◦ It accounts for approximately 50% of infertility cases, either as a primary cause or a contributing factor.
    ◦ **Sperm abnormalities** are the most common cause of male infertility.
    ◦ The evaluation focuses on identifying and treating reversible causes, while assisted reproductive technologies (ART) offer solutions for irreversible conditions.
• Key terminology based on semen analysis (SA):
