    ◦ **Aspermia:** Complete lack of semen.
    ◦ **Azoospermia:** Absence of sperm in the ejaculate.
    ◦ **Oligospermia:** Low sperm concentration (<15 million/mL).
    ◦ **Asthenospermia:** Reduced sperm motility (<40% total motility or <32% progressive motility).
    ◦ **Teratospermia:** Abnormal sperm morphology (<4% normal forms).
    ◦ **Oligoasthenoteratospermia (OAT):** A combination of low count, low motility, and abnormal morphology.
sections.etiology: • The causes of sperm abnormalities can be systematically categorized into three groups:
sections.epidemiology:
• Infertility affects ~15% of couples attempting to conceive.
• A male factor is identified in ~50% of these cases.
• A specific cause for male infertility is identified in only 30-40% of cases; the remainder are classified as idiopathic.
• **Varicoceles** are present in ~15% of the general male population but in ~40% of men with primary infertility.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The primary presentation is a **couple's inability to conceive after 1 year of regular, unprotected intercourse** (or 6 months if the female partner is >35 years old).
    ◦ The male partner is often asymptomatic.
    ◦ The initial evaluation of the couple should involve both partners concurrently.
sections.diagnostics: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent:** For men with correctable conditions like hypogonadotropic hypogonadism or ductal obstruction.
• **Good:** **Varicocelectomy** improves semen parameters in ~60-70% of men, with pregnancy rates of ~30-40%.
• **Guarded/Poor for natural conception:** For men with primary testicular failure (e.g., **Klinefelter**, **AZFa/b microdeletions**).
    ◦ However, the prognosis for achieving pregnancy via **IVF/ICSI with TESE** is often good.
• The advent of **ICSI** has dramatically improved the prognosis for nearly all forms of severe male factor infertility.

sections.overview:
• The **first trimester** of pregnancy encompasses the period from the first day of the Last Menstrual Period (LMP) to the end of the 13th week (13 weeks and 6 days).
• This period is characterized by **fertilization**, **implantation**, rapid embryonic development (**organogenesis**), and significant maternal hormonal and physiological changes.
• It is a critical window for fetal development and is associated with the highest risk of **spontaneous abortion**.
• Clinical management focuses on confirming pregnancy viability and location, establishing an accurate gestational age, and initiating comprehensive prenatal care.
sections.etiology:
• **Fertilization**
    ◦ Typically occurs in the ampulla of the fallopian tube, where a sperm fuses with an ovum to form a zygote.
• **Implantation**
    ◦ The zygote undergoes cleavage divisions, becoming a morula and then a **blastocyst**.
    ◦ The blastocyst implants into the uterine endometrium (now called the decidua) approximately 6-12 days after fertilization.
• **Hormonal Axis**
    ◦ The **syncytiotrophoblast** (outer layer of the blastocyst) begins to secrete **human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)**.
    ◦ **hCG** "rescues" the **corpus luteum** in the ovary, stimulating it to continue producing progesterone.
    ◦ **Progesterone** maintains the uterine lining, prevents uterine contractions, and supports the early pregnancy.
    ◦ The placenta gradually takes over progesterone production from the corpus luteum around 8-10 weeks gestation.
• **Embryogenesis**
    ◦ The embryonic period (weeks 3-8) is the most critical phase of **organogenesis**.
    ◦ The three primary germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm) differentiate to form all major organ systems.
    ◦ This is the period of greatest susceptibility to **teratogens**.
sections.epidemiology:
• The vast majority of conceptions result in a successful first trimester.
• **Spontaneous Abortion (SAB)** is the most common complication.
    ◦ Approximately 15-20% of clinically recognized pregnancies end in miscarriage, with over 80% of these losses occurring in the first trimester.
• The true rate of pregnancy loss is likely higher, including "chemical pregnancies" where implantation fails before the pregnancy is clinically recognized.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Advanced Maternal Age (AMA)**: Age >35 is associated with an increased risk of chromosomal abnormalities and spontaneous abortion.
• **Teratogen Exposure**: Alcohol, tobacco, certain medications (e.g., ACE inhibitors, isotretinoin, valproic acid), illicit drugs, and radiation.
• **Uncontrolled Chronic Maternal Disease**: Diabetes mellitus (poor glycemic control), hypertension, thyroid disease, autoimmune disorders (e.g., SLE, antiphospholipid syndrome).
• **Infections**: **TORCH infections** (Toxoplasmosis, Other [Syphilis, Varicella, Parvovirus], Rubella, Cytomegalovirus, Herpes).
• **Uterine Abnormalities**: Uterine septum, large fibroids.
• **Nutritional Deficiencies**: Particularly **folic acid deficiency**.
• **Previous History**: Prior SAB, ectopic pregnancy, or preterm birth.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents to the clinic for confirmation of pregnancy after a missed menstrual period and a positive home pregnancy test.
• The visit focuses on confirming the diagnosis, establishing gestational age, and initiating prenatal care.
• **Common Symptoms**
    ◦ **Amenorrhea**: Hallmark symptom; cessation of menses.
    ◦ **Nausea and Vomiting ("Morning Sickness")**: Extremely common, caused by rising hCG and estrogen levels. Can occur at any time of day.
    ◦ **Breast Tenderness and Enlargement**: Due to hormonal stimulation (estrogen and progesterone).
    ◦ **Fatigue**: Profound fatigue is very common.
    ◦ **Urinary Frequency**: Increased uterine size places pressure on the bladder, and hormonal changes increase renal blood flow.
    ◦ **Food Cravings or Aversions**
    ◦ **Mood Swings**
    ◦ **Light Spotting**: Implantation bleeding can occur around the time of the expected period.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Vitals**: Generally stable. Blood pressure may begin to slightly decrease near the end of the first trimester.
• **Uterine Sizing (Bimanual Exam)**
    ◦ **6-8 weeks**: Uterus is enlarged to the size of a small pear/orange.
    ◦ **8-10 weeks**: Uterus is the size of a large orange/grapefruit.
    ◦ **12 weeks**: Uterus is palpable just above the pubic symphysis.
• **Cervical/Vaginal Signs**
    ◦ **Chadwick's Sign**: Bluish/purplish discoloration of the cervix and vagina due to increased vascularity.
    ◦ **Goodell's Sign**: Softening of the cervix.
    ◦ **Hegar's Sign**: Softening of the uterine isthmus (the area between the cervix and uterine body).
• **Breast Exam**: Increased nodularity, enlarged areolae, prominent Montgomery's tubercles.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Transvaginal Ultrasound (TVUS)**
    ◦ The **gold standard** for evaluation in the first trimester.
    ◦ **Visualization Timeline**:
        ▪ **Gestational Sac**: ~5 weeks gestation (or **β-hCG** >1500-2000 mIU/mL).
        ▪ **Yolk Sac**: ~5.5 weeks. The first structure seen within the gestational sac.
        ▪ **Fetal Pole with Cardiac Activity**: ~6 weeks.
sections.treatment:
• **Prenatal Vitamins**: Daily supplementation is essential.
    ◦ **Folic Acid**: Crucial for preventing **neural tube defects**.
        ▪ **Standard Risk**: 0.4 - 0.8 mg (400-800 mcg) daily.
        ▪ **High Risk** (e.g., prior NTD, on anti-epileptic drugs): 4 mg daily.
    ◦ **Iron**: To prevent/treat maternal anemia.
    ◦ **Calcium & Vitamin D**: For fetal skeletal development.
sections.management:
• **Symptom Management**
    ◦ **Nausea/Vomiting**: First-line is **Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine)** alone or in combination with **Doxylamine**. Advise small, frequent meals.
• **Follow-up Schedule**
    ◦ Prenatal visits are typically scheduled **every 4 weeks** during the first trimester.
• **Immunizations**
    ◦ Inactivated **influenza vaccine** is recommended and safe in any trimester.
    ◦ **Live vaccines** (MMR, Varicella) are **contraindicated**.
sections.complications:
• **Spontaneous Abortion (SAB)**: Most common complication.
• **Ectopic Pregnancy**
• **Hyperemesis Gravidarum**: Severe nausea and vomiting causing >5% weight loss, dehydration, and electrolyte abnormalities.
• **Subchorionic Hemorrhage**: Bleeding between the chorion and the uterine wall.
sections.prognosis:
• For a confirmed intrauterine pregnancy with documented fetal cardiac activity, the prognosis is **excellent**.
• The risk of miscarriage drops significantly after fetal heart tones are detected (to <5% after 8 weeks).
• The majority of uncomplicated first-trimester pregnancies will progress to term with a good outcome.
sections.preventionEducation:
• **Patient Counseling and Education**
    ◦ **Diet**: Avoid raw/undercooked meat, unpasteurized dairy (**Listeria** risk), and high-mercury fish (e.g., shark, swordfish).
    ◦ **Substances**: Advise complete cessation of alcohol, tobacco, and illicit drugs.
    ◦ **Medication Review**: Discontinue or switch any known **teratogenic** medications.
    ◦ **Activity**: Encourage regular, moderate exercise. Avoid high-impact sports or activities with a risk of abdominal trauma.
    ◦ **Warning Signs**: Counsel on when to seek care (e.g., heavy vaginal bleeding, severe abdominal pain, fever, loss of fluid from the vagina).

sections.overview:
• An **ectopic pregnancy** is the implantation of a fertilized ovum outside of the uterine endometrial cavity.
• It is a **life-threatening gynecologic emergency** and the **leading cause of maternal mortality** in the first trimester.
• The vast majority (>95%) of ectopic pregnancies occur in the **fallopian tube**.
    ◦ **Most Common Location**: **Ampulla** of the fallopian tube (~70%).
    ◦ **Other Tubal Locations**: **Isthmus** (~12%), **Fimbriae** (~11%), **Interstitial/Cornual** (~2%).
    ◦ **Non-Tubal Locations** (<5%): Ovary, cervix, abdomen, cesarean scar.
sections.etiology:
• The underlying mechanism involves any factor that **impedes or delays the transit** of the fertilized embryo from the fallopian tube to the uterine cavity.
    ◦ **Delayed Transit**: Inflammation, scarring, or adhesions within the fallopian tube (e.g., from prior infections or surgery) slow the embryo's journey.
    ◦ **Implantation**: The embryo reaches the blastocyst stage while still in the tube and hatches from its zona pellucida.
    ◦ **Invasion**: Trophoblastic cells implant into the tubal wall, which lacks the thick, protective decidua of the uterus.
    ◦ **Growth & Sequelae**: The invading trophoblasts erode into the tubal vasculature, establishing a blood supply. As the pregnancy grows, it can lead to:
        ▪ **Tubal Rupture**: The thin tubal wall stretches and eventually ruptures, causing catastrophic **intraperitoneal hemorrhage**.
        ▪ **Tubal Abortion**: The pregnancy detaches from the tubal wall and is expelled through the fimbriated end into the peritoneal cavity.
sections.epidemiology:
• Occurs in approximately **1-2% of all pregnancies** in the United States.
• Accounts for **~6% of all pregnancy-related deaths**.
• The **leading cause of maternal death** in the first trimester.
• Incidence has been increasing, likely due to better diagnostic methods and increased prevalence of risk factors (e.g., STIs, ART).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation is highly variable, ranging from asymptomatic to hemodynamic shock.
• Suspect ectopic pregnancy in any sexually active female of reproductive age with **abdominal pain** or **vaginal bleeding**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **Quantitative serum β-hCG**
        ▪ The single most important lab test.
        ▪ In a normal intrauterine pregnancy (IUP), β-hCG should **double approximately every 48-72 hours** in the first trimester.
        ▪ In an ectopic pregnancy, β-hCG levels **rise inappropriately** (suboptimal rise), plateau, or fall slowly.
        ▪ A single value is not diagnostic; serial measurements are key.
    ◦ **Serum Progesterone**
        ▪ A level **< 5 ng/mL** has a very high specificity for a **non-viable pregnancy** (either ectopic or impending abortion).
        ▪ A level **> 20 ng/mL** is highly suggestive of a **viable IUP**.
        ▪ Values between 5 and 20 are indeterminate.
    ◦ **CBC**: To assess for anemia from acute or chronic blood loss.
    ◦ **Blood Type and Rh Status**: Essential for Rhogam administration in Rh-negative mothers and for potential blood transfusion.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Transvaginal Ultrasound (TVUS)**
        ▪ The **imaging modality of choice**.
        ▪ **Discriminatory Zone**: The β-hCG level at which an IUP should be visible on TVUS (typically **1,500 - 2,000 mIU/mL**).
        ▪ **Key Findings**:
            • **Definitive Diagnosis**: Visualization of a **gestational sac with a yolk sac or fetal pole** in the adnexa.
            • **Presumptive Diagnosis**: An **empty uterus** with a β-hCG level **above the discriminatory zone**.
            • **Other Suggestive Findings**:
                ▪ Complex adnexal mass (separate from the ovary).
                ▪ **"Tubal Ring"** or **"Ring of Fire"** sign on color Doppler (hypervascular ring around the ectopic).
                ▪ **Free fluid (echogenic)** in the posterior cul-de-sac (Morison's pouch), highly suggestive of **hemoperitoneum and rupture**.
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent with early diagnosis and treatment. Maternal mortality is <0.1% when managed appropriately.
• Prognosis for future fertility depends on the condition of the contralateral tube and the type of treatment received.
• Overall, **~65% of women** who have had an ectopic pregnancy will have a successful subsequent IUP.

sections.overview:
• A threatened abortion is defined by uterine bleeding in a pregnant patient before **20 weeks of gestation**.
	◦ There is **no cervical dilation** or expulsion of **products of conception (POC)**.
• It indicates a spontaneous abortion (miscarriage) may occur, but the pregnancy is still **potentially viable**.
• It is a clinical diagnosis requiring evaluation to rule out other causes of first-trimester bleeding and to assess pregnancy viability.
sections.etiology:
• The exact cause is often unknown (idiopathic).
• The pathophysiology involves bleeding from the decidual vessels at the maternal-fetal interface.
• **Most Common Association:**
	◦ Fetal **chromosomal abnormalities** (e.g., trisomies) are the underlying cause of many pregnancies that ultimately miscarry and may present as a threatened abortion.
• **Maternal Factors:**
	◦ **Implantation Bleeding:** Physiologic bleeding as the blastocyst embeds in the endometrium.
	◦ **Subchorionic Hematoma:** A collection of blood between the chorionic membrane and the uterine wall; a common ultrasound finding in threatened abortion.
	◦ **Maternal Infections:** Systemic (e.g., pyelonephritis) or local (e.g., cervicitis).
	◦ **Endocrine Issues:** Luteal phase defect, uncontrolled diabetes, thyroid disease.
	◦ **Uterine Abnormalities:** Fibroids, polyps, uterine septum.
	◦ **Trauma**.
sections.epidemiology:
• Extremely common, occurring in **20-25%** of all clinically recognized pregnancies.
• Approximately **50%** of patients with a threatened abortion will progress to a spontaneous abortion (incomplete, complete, or missed).
• The remaining 50% will have the bleeding resolve and the pregnancy will continue to term.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A pregnant patient, typically in the first trimester (<12 weeks), presents with a chief complaint of **vaginal bleeding**.
	◦ The bleeding may be accompanied by **mild cramping**.
• The patient is often anxious about the viability of her pregnancy.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Transvaginal Ultrasound (TVUS):**
	◦ Primary goal is to confirm an **intrauterine pregnancy (IUP)** to rule out ectopic pregnancy.
	◦ Assess viability by looking for a **fetal heartbeat (FHB)**; its presence significantly improves prognosis.
	◦ Identify other potential causes of bleeding, such as a **subchorionic hematoma**.
	◦ Confirm gestational age via Crown-Rump Length (CRL).
• **Quantitative beta-hCG (-hCG):**
	◦ A single level confirms pregnancy but does not determine viability.
	◦ **Serial -hCG levels** (measured 48-72 hours apart) are essential.
		▪ In a normal IUP, the level should rise appropriately (typically doubling every 48-72 hours).
		▪ A slow-rising or falling level suggests a non-viable pregnancy or ectopic.
• **Lab Work:**
	◦ **CBC:** To assess for anemia if bleeding is significant.
	◦ **Blood Type & Rh Status:** **ESSENTIAL**. If the mother is Rh-negative, she requires Rho(D) immune globulin (RhoGAM).
	◦ **Progesterone Level:**
		▪ A level <5 ng/mL is highly suggestive of a non-viable pregnancy.
		▪ A level >20-25 ng/mL is reassuring for a viable IUP.
sections.prognosis:
• The single most important prognostic factor is the **presence of fetal cardiac activity on ultrasound**.
• If an IUP with a fetal heartbeat is confirmed, **over 90% of these pregnancies will continue successfully to term**.
• Prognosis is poorer with advanced maternal age, heavier bleeding, or a co-existing subchorionic hematoma.

sections.overview:
• **Spontaneous Abortion (SAB)**, or **miscarriage**, is the non-induced loss of a pregnancy before 20 weeks of gestation.
• The key differentiating factors are the state of the **cervical os** and the passage of **products of conception (POC)**.
• **Inevitable Abortion**
    ◦ The process of miscarriage has started and cannot be stopped.
    ◦ The cervical os is **open**.
    ◦ The products of conception have **not yet passed**.
    ◦ The pregnancy is non-viable.
• **Incomplete Abortion**
    ◦ The cervical os is **open**.
    ◦ **Some**, but not all, of the products of conception have been expelled from the uterus.
• **Complete Abortion**
    ◦ The cervical os is **closed**.
    ◦ **All** products of conception have been expelled from the uterus.
sections.etiology:
• The underlying cause is often multifactorial, but the most common etiologies for any first-trimester SAB are:
    ◦ **Chromosomal Abnormalities (Most Common)**
        ▪ Account for >50% of all SABs.
        ▪ **Aneuploidy** (e.g., trisomies, monosomy X) is the most frequent cause.
    ◦ **Maternal Factors**
        ▪ **Systemic Disease**: Uncontrolled diabetes mellitus (especially with high HbA1c), thyroid disease, severe hypertension, SLE, antiphospholipid syndrome.
        ▪ **Uterine Abnormalities**: Uterine septum, bicornuate uterus, large submucosal fibroids, Asherman syndrome (intrauterine adhesions).
        ▪ **Infections**: **TORCH infections** (Listeria, Toxoplasma, Parvovirus B19, Rubella, CMV, Herpes).
        ▪ **Endocrinopathies**: Luteal phase defect, PCOS.
    ◦ **Environmental/Toxic Exposures**
        ▪ Heavy alcohol use, smoking, cocaine, high doses of radiation.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The process begins with hemorrhage into the decidua basalis, leading to necrosis and inflammation.
    ◦ This stimulates uterine contractions and cervical dilation, resulting in the expulsion of the products of conception.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Spontaneous abortion** is the most common complication of early pregnancy.
• Occurs in 15-20% of all clinically recognized pregnancies.
• The actual rate is likely higher, as many occur before a pregnancy is clinically recognized.
• 80% of SABs occur in the first trimester (<13 weeks).
sections.clinicalPresentation: • The typical presentation is a pregnant patient in the first trimester (<20 weeks, but most commonly 6-12 weeks) who presents with **vaginal bleeding** and/or **abdominopelvic pain/cramping**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Lab Studies**
    ◦ **Quantitative β-hCG**
        ▪ Essential for diagnosis and follow-up.
        ▪ In **inevitable/incomplete abortion**, β-hCG levels are inappropriately low or are falling on serial measurements.
        ▪ In **complete abortion**, β-hCG levels will fall rapidly and should eventually return to zero (<5 mIU/mL).
    ◦ **CBC**
        ▪ To assess for anemia due to hemorrhage.
    ◦ **Blood Type and Rh Status**
        ▪ **CRITICAL**: All **Rh-negative** mothers must receive **Rho(D) immune globulin (Rhogam)** to prevent isoimmunization.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Transvaginal Ultrasound (TVUS)**
        ▪ The gold standard diagnostic tool.
        ▪ **Inevitable Abortion**: Intrauterine pregnancy (IUP) is present, often in the lower uterine segment. An open cervical canal may be visible. Fetal cardiac activity may be present or absent.
        ▪ **Incomplete Abortion**: **Thickened, irregular endometrial stripe (>15 mm)**. Heterogeneous material (**retained products of conception - RPOC**) seen within the uterus. No gestational sac or fetus identifiable.
        ▪ **Complete Abortion**: **Empty uterus with a thin, uniform endometrial stripe (<15 mm)**. No evidence of an IUP or RPOC.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis for future fertility is excellent after a single spontaneous abortion.
• The risk of **recurrent miscarriage** increases after 2-3 consecutive losses, warranting a workup.
• Most women go on to have successful subsequent pregnancies.

sections.overview:
• A missed abortion, also known as a silent miscarriage or early fetal demise, is the intrauterine death of an embryo or fetus prior to 20 weeks of gestation, **without** the spontaneous passage of products of conception (POC).
    ◦ The key features are a **closed cervical os** and retained POC.
    ◦ It is often discovered incidentally during a routine prenatal ultrasound when fetal cardiac activity is absent.
sections.etiology:
• **Chromosomal Abnormalities (Most Common Cause):** Accounts for >50% of all first-trimester losses.
    ◦ **Autosomal Trisomies:** Trisomy 16 is the most frequent. Trisomies 13, 18, and 21 are also common.
    ◦ **Monosomy X:** Turner Syndrome (45,X0).
    ◦ **Polyploidy:** Triploidy, tetraploidy.
• **Pathophysiology:**
    ◦ Embryonic or fetal demise occurs.
    ◦ The corpus luteum and developing placenta cease production of hormones (progesterone, hCG).
    ◦ However, the normal physiological process of uterine contractions and cervical dilation fails to initiate.
    ◦ The deceased fetus and other products of conception are retained within the uterus.
• **Other Causes:**
    ◦ **Maternal Systemic Disease:** Uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, chronic hypertension, thyroid disease, SLE.
    ◦ **Uterine Abnormalities:** Septate uterus, uterine fibroids (especially submucosal), intrauterine adhesions (Asherman syndrome).
    ◦ **Thrombophilias:** Antiphospholipid syndrome, Factor V Leiden.
    ◦ **Infections:** Less common, but TORCH infections (Toxoplasmosis, Other, Rubella, Cytomegalovirus, Herpes) can be implicated.
    ◦ **Endocrine Factors:** Luteal phase defect (inadequate progesterone).
sections.epidemiology:
• Spontaneous abortion (miscarriage) occurs in 15-20% of all clinically recognized pregnancies.
• The majority (>80%) of spontaneous abortions occur in the **first trimester** (<13 weeks).
• Missed abortion represents a significant portion of these first-trimester losses.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Advanced Maternal Age (AMA):** >35 years old is the single most significant risk factor, due to the increased rate of fetal aneuploidy.
• **Previous Spontaneous Abortion:** The risk increases with each successive loss.
• **Paternal Age:** Advanced paternal age (>40) is also associated with a slightly increased risk.
• **Maternal Medical Conditions:** See Etiology section.
• **Lifestyle Factors:** Smoking, excessive alcohol or caffeine intake, illicit drug use.
• **Uterine Structural Abnormalities.**
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is an **asymptomatic patient** who presents for a routine prenatal visit.
    ◦ The diagnosis is often an incidental finding on ultrasound.
    ◦ The uterine size on exam may be smaller than expected for the calculated gestational age.
• **Symptoms:**
    ◦ **Often NONE.** This is the hallmark of a missed abortion.
    ◦ **Regression of Pregnancy Symptoms:** The most common reported symptom is the disappearance of nausea, vomiting, and breast tenderness.
    ◦ **Vaginal Spotting:** Mild, dark brown or prune-colored discharge may be present, but significant bleeding is absent.
    ◦ **Abdominal Cramping:** Typically absent or very mild.
    ◦ **Absence of Quickening:** In the second trimester, the patient may note the absence of perceived fetal movement.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Vitals:** Typically stable and unremarkable.
• **Abdominal Exam:** Uterus may be non-tender and feel **smaller than expected for gestational age**.
• **Pelvic Exam:**
    ◦ **Cervical Os:** **CLOSED**. This is a critical and defining finding.
    ◦ **Bleeding:** No active bleeding from the os. Scant, old (brown) blood may be noted in the vaginal vault.
    ◦ **Uterus:** May be slightly enlarged but, again, smaller than expected for dates.
    ◦ **Adnexa:** No adnexal masses or tenderness (helps rule out ectopic).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Transvaginal Ultrasound (TVUS) - Gold Standard:**
    ◦ **Key Finding:** Absence of fetal cardiac activity in an embryo/fetus that is of a size where a heartbeat should be present.
    ◦ **Diagnostic Criteria (one of the following):**
        ▪ **No cardiac activity** in an embryo with a crown-rump length (CRL) **7 mm**.
        ▪ **No embryo** in a gestational sac with a mean sac diameter (MSD) **25 mm** (termed anembryonic gestation or "blighted ovum").
        ▪ Absence of an embryo with a heartbeat 2 weeks after a scan that showed a gestational sac without a yolk sac.
        ▪ Absence of an embryo with a heartbeat 11 days after a scan that showed a gestational sac with a yolk sac.
• **Quantitative Serum -hCG:**
    ◦ Levels will be **inappropriately low for gestational age**.
    ◦ **Serial -hCG levels** (drawn 48-72 hours apart) will show a **plateau or decline**, rather than the expected doubling seen in a viable early pregnancy.
        ▪ This is confirmatory but ultrasound is definitive.
sections.treatment:
• **Expectant Management:**
    ◦ **Method:** Awaiting the spontaneous passage of tissue without intervention.
    ◦ **Pros:** Avoids medication side effects and surgical risks. Most natural option.
    ◦ **Cons:** Can take days to weeks, leading to emotional distress. Unpredictable timing of bleeding/cramping. Higher risk of incomplete abortion requiring eventual surgery. Success rate ~80% but decreases with advancing gestational age.
• **Medical Management:**
    ◦ **Method:** **Misoprostol (Cytotec)**, a prostaglandin E1 analog, administered vaginally, buccally, or orally. Often preceded by Mifepristone for higher efficacy. Causes cervical ripening and uterine contractions.
    ◦ **Pros:** Avoids surgery and anesthesia. Can be done in the privacy of the patient's home.
    ◦ **Cons:** Significant cramping and heavy bleeding. Risk of incomplete abortion (~15-20%) requiring D&C. Nausea/vomiting/diarrhea are common side effects.
• **Surgical Management:**
    ◦ **Method:** **Dilation and Curettage (D&C)** or Manual Vacuum Aspiration (MVA) to physically remove the POC.
    ◦ **Pros:** Most effective and definitive treatment (>95% success). Quickest resolution. Allows for histopathologic or genetic analysis of the tissue.
    ◦ **Cons:** Invasive. Requires anesthesia. Risks include uterine perforation, cervical laceration, hemorrhage, infection, and intrauterine adhesions (**Asherman syndrome**).
• **Essential Ancillary Management:**
    ◦ **Rh(D) Immune Globulin (RhoGAM):** Administer to all **Rh-negative** mothers to prevent isoimmunization.
    ◦ **Emotional Support:** Acknowledge the loss and provide resources for grief counseling.
sections.complications:
• **Hemorrhage:** Can occur with any management option, but risk is higher with expectant and medical management.
• **Infection (Septic Abortion):** Retained POC can become infected. Presents with fever, uterine tenderness, and purulent discharge.
• **Incomplete Abortion:** Failure to pass all POC, requiring subsequent D&C.
• **Asherman Syndrome:** Intrauterine adhesions/scarring as a rare complication of D&C, which can lead to future infertility or recurrent pregnancy loss.
• **Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC):** Rare complication, more associated with second-trimester fetal demise where the POC is retained for many weeks.
sections.prognosis:
• **Maternal physical prognosis is excellent.**
• **Future Fertility:** Generally unaffected. Most women go on to have successful pregnancies.
• **Recurrence Risk:** A single miscarriage does not significantly increase the risk for the next pregnancy. The risk increases after 2-3 consecutive losses, prompting a workup for recurrent pregnancy loss.
• **Psychological:** The emotional impact can be significant. Grief, anxiety, and depression are common and should be addressed.

sections.overview:
• Gestational Trophoblastic Disease (GTD) is a spectrum of rare, pregnancy-related tumors that arise from the abnormal proliferation of trophoblastic tissue of the placenta.
	◦ The spectrum ranges from benign, non-invasive hydatidiform moles to malignant, metastatic neoplasms (Gestational Trophoblastic Neoplasia, or GTN).
• **Two main categories of hydatidiform mole (molar pregnancy):**
	◦ **Complete Hydatidiform Mole:**
		▪ Diploid.
		▪ Characterized by diffuse hydropic swelling of chorionic villi and diffuse trophoblastic proliferation.
		▪ **No fetal tissue is present.**
	◦ **Partial Hydatidiform Mole:**
		▪ Triploid.
		▪ Characterized by focal hydropic swelling of villi, focal trophoblastic proliferation, and the **presence of fetal tissue** (which is always non-viable).
sections.etiology:
• GTD results from aberrant fertilization events.
• **Complete Mole (46,XX or 46,XY):**
	◦ **Pathogenesis:** Fertilization of an anucleated ovum ("empty egg") by a single sperm that then duplicates its chromosomes (resulting in 46,XX, most common) or by two separate sperm (resulting in 46,XY).
	◦ **Key Feature:** All genetic material is of **paternal origin**.
	◦ **Result:** No embryo/fetus develops. The placenta is replaced by a mass of edematous, grape-like chorionic villi. The trophoblastic tissue produces extremely high levels of human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG).
• **Partial Mole (69,XXY, 69,XXX, or 69,XYY):**
	◦ **Pathogenesis:** Fertilization of a normal, haploid ovum by two sperm (dispermy).
	◦ **Key Feature:** Triploid karyotype, containing both maternal and paternal genetic material.
	◦ **Result:** An abnormal, non-viable fetus is often present. The placenta shows a mixture of normal and hydropic villi. hCG levels are elevated, but typically not as dramatically as in a complete mole.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence:** Approximately 1 in 1,000 pregnancies in the United States and Europe.
• **Geographic Variation:** Significantly higher incidence in Southeast Asia and the Philippines (~1 in 100 pregnancies).
• **Relative Frequency:** Complete moles are more common than partial moles.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The "classic" presentation is now less common due to routine first-trimester ultrasound. However, it is critical to recognize for board exams.
• **Classic Triad:**
	◦ Vaginal bleeding
	◦ Uterine size larger than gestational age
	◦ Markedly elevated serum hCG
• Most common presenting symptom is **painless vaginal bleeding in the first trimester**.
• Patients may present with symptoms of severe pregnancy-related conditions occurring unusually early, such as **pre-eclampsia before 20 weeks gestation**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **LABORATORY STUDIES**
	◦ **Quantitative Serum β-hCG:** The hallmark diagnostic test.
		▪ **Extremely elevated for gestational age**, often **>100,000 mIU/mL**.
		▪ A level this high is highly suggestive of a complete mole.
	◦ **Complete Blood Count (CBC):** May show anemia (microcytic or normocytic) due to blood loss.
	◦ **Thyroid Function Tests (TSH, free T4):** To evaluate for hyperthyroidism. TSH will be low, T4 will be high.
	◦ **Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP):** To assess for electrolyte abnormalities from hyperemesis and renal/liver function if pre-eclampsia is suspected.
	◦ **Blood Type and Rh Status:** Crucial for administration of Rho(D) immune globulin if the patient is Rh-negative.
• **IMAGING**
	◦ **Pelvic Ultrasound:** The primary imaging modality.
		▪ **Complete Mole:** Classic finding is a "central heterogeneous mass with numerous anechoic spaces," described as a **"snowstorm"** or **"cluster of grapes"** appearance. No fetus, no amniotic fluid. Bilateral theca lutein cysts are often seen.
		▪ **Partial Mole:** Shows a thickened, cystic placenta along with fetal tissue (which may be growth-restricted or have anomalies).
• **PATHOLOGY**
	◦ **Histopathology:** Provides the definitive diagnosis after uterine evacuation. Tissue analysis confirms the characteristic molar changes and differentiates between complete and partial moles.
sections.prognosis:
• **Benign Molar Pregnancy:** Excellent. With proper uterine evacuation and hCG follow-up, the cure rate is nearly 100%.
• **Future Fertility:** Generally preserved. Subsequent pregnancies are usually normal, though there is a slightly increased risk of a repeat mole.
• **GTN:** Prognosis is also excellent. Even metastatic disease has a high cure rate with appropriate chemotherapy.

sections.overview:
• **Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM)** is defined as glucose intolerance with onset or first recognition during pregnancy.
• Typically arises in the **second or third trimester** when placental hormones create a state of **insulin resistance**.
• It is distinct from pre-existing Type 1 or Type 2 diabetes discovered during pregnancy.
• GDM usually **resolves after delivery** but significantly increases the mother's risk of developing **Type 2 DM** later in life.
sections.etiology:
• **Hormonal Influence:**
    ◦ During a normal pregnancy, the placenta produces hormones like **human placental lactogen (hPL)**, cortisol, and progesterone.
    ◦ These hormones are essential for fetal growth but also have an **anti-insulin effect**, leading to a state of physiologic **insulin resistance**.
• **Beta-Cell Dysfunction:**
    ◦ In most pregnant individuals, the pancreatic beta-cells compensate by increasing insulin production to overcome this resistance and maintain euglycemia.
• **GDM Development:**
    ◦ In women who develop GDM, the pancreatic beta-cell function is **insufficient** to overcome the pregnancy-induced insulin resistance.
    ◦ This results in relative insulin deficiency and subsequent **hyperglycemia**.
    ◦ GDM is essentially a **"stress test"** for the pancreas, unmasking a predisposition to Type 2 diabetes.
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects approximately **2-10%** of pregnancies in the United States.
• Incidence is rising in parallel with the global increase in obesity and **Type 2 DM**.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Maternal Age > 25** (especially >35)
• **Pre-pregnancy BMI > 25 kg/m2** (overweight) or **>30 kg/m2** (obese)
• **Previous history of GDM** in a prior pregnancy
• **History of a macrosomic infant** (>4,000g or 9 lbs)
• **Family history of diabetes** (first-degree relative)
• **Ethnicity:** Hispanic, African American, Native American, South or East Asian, Pacific Islander
• **Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)**
• Previous unexplained stillbirth
• **Glycosuria** at the first prenatal visit
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• GDM is most often **asymptomatic**.
• The "presentation" is typically a **positive screening test** performed at **24-28 weeks gestation**.
• On occasion, a patient may present with symptoms of **hyperglycemia** if blood glucose levels are significantly elevated.
    ◦ **Polyuria** (increased urination)
    ◦ **Polydipsia** (increased thirst)
    ◦ **Polyphagia** (increased hunger) - difficult to distinguish from normal pregnancy symptoms
    ◦ Fatigue
    ◦ Blurred vision
sections.physicalExam:
• Physical exam is typically **unremarkable** and not diagnostic.
• **Fundal height may be large for gestational age (LGA)** secondary to fetal **macrosomia**.
• **Acanthosis nigricans** may be present, indicating underlying **insulin resistance**.
• Maternal **hypertension** may co-exist, particularly in obese patients.
sections.diagnostics:
• Universal screening is recommended for all pregnant women.
• **Timing:**
    ◦ Average-risk women: **24-28 weeks gestation**
    ◦ High-risk patients: Screen earlier (at the first prenatal visit)
• **Screening Strategies:** There are two primary strategies for diagnosis.
sections.treatment:
• **Diet:**
    ◦ Controlled carbohydrate diet, often with consultation from a registered dietitian.
    ◦ Focus on complex carbohydrates distributed throughout the day in 3 meals and 2-3 snacks to maintain stable glucose levels.
• **Exercise:**
    ◦ At least 30 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise 5 days a week (if no obstetric contraindications).
• **Insulin:**
    ◦ **First-line medication and gold standard**.
    ◦ **Does not cross the placenta**.
    ◦ Various regimens (NPH, long-acting, rapid-acting) can be used.
• **Metformin:**
    ◦ Oral agent that **crosses the placenta**.
    ◦ Considered a reasonable alternative to insulin.
    ◦ Lacks long-term safety data for offspring compared to insulin.
• **Glyburide:**
    ◦ Oral sulfonylurea that stimulates insulin secretion.
    ◦ **Crosses the placenta** and is associated with a **higher risk of neonatal hypoglycemia and macrosomia** compared to insulin or metformin.
    ◦ Generally considered **second-line** to insulin and metformin.
sections.management:
• **Self-Monitoring of Blood Glucose (SMBG):**
    ◦ Patients typically check their blood sugar **4 times daily**:
        ▪ Once upon waking (fasting)
        ▪ 1 or 2 hours after breakfast, lunch, and dinner
• **Glycemic Targets (ACOG):**
    ◦ **Fasting:** <95 mg/dL
    ◦ **1-hour postprandial:** <140 mg/dL
    ◦ **2-hour postprandial:** <120 mg/dL
• **Fetal Monitoring:**
    ◦ **Growth Ultrasounds:** Every 4-6 weeks in the third trimester to assess for **macrosomia (LGA)** or growth restriction (SGA).
    ◦ **Antepartum Surveillance:** For patients requiring medication.
        ▪ Typically starts at **32 weeks gestation** with twice-weekly **nonstress tests (NSTs)** and/or **biophysical profiles (BPPs)**.
• **Delivery Timing:**
    ◦ **Well-controlled on diet alone:** Expectant management until 39-40 weeks.
    ◦ **Well-controlled on medication:** Induction of labor recommended at **39 weeks**.
    ◦ **Poorly controlled:** May require earlier delivery (~37-38 weeks).
• **Intrapartum:** Monitor glucose levels and consider an insulin drip if needed.
• **Postpartum:**
    ◦ Discontinue all GDM medications after delivery.
    ◦ Screen for persistent diabetes at **4-12 weeks postpartum** with a **75-g 2-hour OGTT**.
sections.prognosis:
• **Maternal:**
    ◦ Excellent for the pregnancy if well-controlled.
    ◦ Glucose levels typically normalize immediately postpartum.
    ◦ The major long-term risk is the development of **Type 2 DM**.
• **Fetal:**
    ◦ Excellent if GDM is well-controlled.
    ◦ Complications are directly related to the degree of maternal **hyperglycemia**.

sections.overview:
• Chronic Hypertension (CHTN) in pregnancy is defined as hypertension (BP ≥140/90 mmHg) present **before pregnancy**, diagnosed **before 20 weeks of gestation**, or persisting for more than 12 weeks postpartum.
• This condition complicates 1-5% of pregnancies and is a major risk factor for adverse maternal and fetal outcomes, primarily due to the high risk of developing **superimposed preeclampsia** and **placental insufficiency**.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects approximately 1-5% of all pregnancies.
• The prevalence is **increasing** due to rising rates of **obesity** and **delayed childbearing** (advanced maternal age).
• Higher prevalence in **non-Hispanic Black women**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Most commonly, patients are **asymptomatic**.
• The diagnosis is made based on blood pressure measurements taken during routine prenatal care.
    ◦ Key diagnostic feature: Elevated blood pressure (≥140/90 mmHg) on at least two occasions, at least 4 hours apart, **before the 20th week of gestation**.
• May have a documented history of hypertension prior to conception.
sections.diagnostics:
• The goal is to:
    ◦ **Confirm the diagnosis**
    ◦ **Assess for end-organ damage**
    ◦ Establish a baseline to monitor for the development of **superimposed preeclampsia**
sections.prognosis:
• Generally good for both mother and fetus with appropriate prenatal care, BP control, and surveillance.
• The prognosis worsens significantly if **superimposed preeclampsia** develops.
• Women with CHTN in pregnancy have an increased risk of developing **cardiovascular disease** later in life.

sections.overview:
• New-onset hypertension (**systolic blood pressure ≥140 mmHg** or **diastolic blood pressure ≥90 mmHg**) on at least two occasions, at least four hours apart, after **20 weeks of gestation** in a previously normotensive woman.
• Diagnosis requires the **absence of proteinuria** and the absence of signs or symptoms of severe features (end-organ damage) characteristic of preeclampsia.
• It is considered a provisional diagnosis, as up to 25-50% of cases may progress to preeclampsia.
• The condition typically resolves by 12 weeks postpartum.
sections.etiology:
• The exact etiology is not fully understood but is believed to be a milder form of the same pathophysiologic process that causes preeclampsia, with the central theory involving **abnormal placentation**.
    ◦ **Impaired Trophoblastic Invasion**: In a normal pregnancy, cytotrophoblasts invade the maternal uterine spiral arteries, transforming them from narrow, high-resistance vessels into wide, low-resistance vessels, which allows for a massive increase in blood flow to the placenta.
    ◦ **Placental Hypoperfusion**: In GH (and preeclampsia), this remodeling process is incomplete. The spiral arteries remain narrow, leading to placental hypoperfusion, hypoxia, and ischemia.
    ◦ **Release of Anti-Angiogenic Factors**: The ischemic placenta releases anti-angiogenic factors (e.g., soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 [sFlt-1] and soluble endoglin [sEng]) into the maternal circulation.
    ◦ **Systemic Endothelial Dysfunction**: These factors cause widespread maternal endothelial cell dysfunction, leading to:
        ▪ **Vasoconstriction**: Causing hypertension.
        ▪ **Increased Vascular Permeability**: Leads to edema and proteinuria if it progresses to preeclampsia.
        ▪ In GH, this process is limited primarily to vasoconstriction without the significant systemic damage seen in preeclampsia.
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects approximately 6% of all pregnancies.
• More common in nulliparous (first-time pregnant) women.
• One of the four major categories of hypertensive disorders in pregnancy, along with preeclampsia/eclampsia, chronic hypertension, and chronic hypertension with superimposed preeclampsia.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Nulliparity** (first pregnancy) - strongest risk factor
• Previous pregnancy with a hypertensive disorder
• Multiple gestation (twins, triplets)
• Maternal age > 40 years or < 18 years
• Pre-pregnancy BMI ≥30 (obesity)
• Pre-existing medical conditions:
    ◦ Chronic kidney disease
    ◦ Diabetes mellitus (pre-gestational)
    ◦ Chronic hypertension
• Family history of preeclampsia or gestational hypertension (especially in a mother or sister)
• New paternity
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Most commonly detected as an **incidental finding** of elevated blood pressure during a routine prenatal visit in the second half of pregnancy (after 20 weeks).
• The patient is typically asymptomatic and feels well.
• **Usually asymptomatic.**
    ◦ The absence of symptoms is a key feature distinguishing it from preeclampsia with severe features.
    ◦ If the following symptoms develop, it suggests progression to preeclampsia:
        ▪ Persistent, new-onset headache
        ▪ Visual disturbances (scotomata, blurry vision, flashing lights)
        ▪ Right upper quadrant (RUQ) or epigastric pain
        ▪ Sudden, non-dependent edema (face, hands)
sections.physicalExam:
• **Blood Pressure**: SBP ≥**140 mmHg** or DBP ≥**90 mmHg** on two separate readings at least 4 hours apart.
• **Remainder of Exam**: Typically unremarkable.
• **No** hyperreflexia or clonus.
• **No** RUQ or epigastric tenderness.
• Fundoscopic exam is normal (no papilledema).
• Mild peripheral edema may be present but is common in normal pregnancy and is not a diagnostic criterion.
sections.diagnostics:
• The primary goals of the diagnostic workup are to confirm hypertension and, most importantly, to **rule out preeclampsia**.
• **Blood Pressure Monitoring**: Accurate, repeated measurements are foundational.
• **Laboratory Studies** (to assess for end-organ damage):
    ◦ **Urinalysis**: Dipstick for protein. If 1+ or greater, follow up with a quantitative test.
    ◦ **Urine Protein-to-Creatinine Ratio (UPCR)**: A spot urine test. A ratio of ≥**0.3** is diagnostic for proteinuria.
    ◦ **24-Hour Urine Collection**: The gold standard for quantifying proteinuria. ≥**300 mg** of protein in 24 hours is diagnostic.
    ◦ **Complete Blood Count (CBC)**: To assess for thrombocytopenia (platelets < 100,000/microL).
    ◦ **Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP)**:
        ▪ To assess renal function (serum creatinine > 1.1 mg/dL or doubling of baseline).
        ▪ To assess for liver involvement (AST/ALT levels > 2x the upper limit of normal).
• **Fetal Assessment**:
    ◦ **Ultrasound**: To estimate fetal weight and assess for Fetal Growth Restriction (FGR).
    ◦ **Nonstress Test (NST)** or **Biophysical Profile (BPP)**: To assess fetal well-being, especially as the pregnancy nears term.
• In pure Gestational Hypertension, all laboratory results (urine protein, platelets, creatinine, liver enzymes) will be normal.
sections.treatment:
• **Antihypertensive Medications** (indicated for persistent SBP ≥150-160 or DBP ≥100-110):
    ◦ **Labetalol** (Beta-blocker): First-line. Avoid in patients with asthma, COPD, or bradycardia.
    ◦ **Nifedipine** (Calcium Channel Blocker): First-line, particularly extended-release formulations.
    ◦ **Methyldopa** (Alpha-2 Agonist): Long history of safety but less effective and may cause sedation/fatigue.
• **CONTRAINDICATED MEDICATIONS**:
    ◦ **ACE Inhibitors** (e.g., lisinopril)
    ◦ **ARBs** (e.g., losartan)
    ◦ **Direct Renin Inhibitors** (e.g., aliskiren)
sections.management:
• **Expectant Management** (if < 37 weeks gestation):
    ◦ **Maternal Surveillance**:
        ▪ Weekly (or more frequent) office visits for BP checks.
        ▪ Weekly laboratory assessment for preeclampsia (CBC, CMP, urine protein).
        ▪ Patient education on warning signs of preeclampsia.
    ◦ **Fetal Surveillance**:
        ▪ Weekly Nonstress Test (NST) or Biophysical Profile (BPP).
        ▪ Serial ultrasounds (every 3-4 weeks) to monitor for Fetal Growth Restriction (FGR).
• **Delivery (Definitive Treatment)**:
    ◦ **Timing**: Delivery is recommended at **37 0/7 weeks gestation**.
        ▪ Earlier delivery is indicated if the patient develops severe hypertension or progresses to preeclampsia.
• **Intrapartum**:
    ◦ Monitor BP closely.
    ◦ **Magnesium Sulfate** for seizure prophylaxis is NOT indicated for gestational hypertension but should be started if severe features develop or it progresses to preeclampsia.
• **Postpartum**:
    ◦ Continue to monitor BP for at least 72 hours postpartum and again at 7-10 days. BP can often peak in the first few days after delivery.
    ◦ If hypertension persists past 12 weeks postpartum, the diagnosis is changed to Chronic Hypertension.
sections.complications:
• **Maternal**:
    ◦ **Progression to Preeclampsia (~25-50%)**, Eclampsia, or HELLP syndrome.
    ◦ Placental abruption.
    ◦ Increased risk of Cesarean delivery.
    ◦ Future cardiovascular disease: Women with a history of GH have a significantly increased long-term risk of developing chronic hypertension, ischemic heart disease, and stroke.
• **Fetal/Neonatal**:
    ◦ **Fetal Growth Restriction (FGR)** / Intrauterine Growth Restriction (IUGR).
    ◦ Oligohydramnios (low amniotic fluid).
    ◦ Preterm delivery (often iatrogenic, due to worsening maternal condition).
    ◦ Perinatal mortality (increased risk compared to normotensive pregnancies).
sections.prognosis:
• The short-term prognosis for both mother and fetus is generally good with appropriate surveillance and timely delivery.
• BP typically normalizes within 12 weeks postpartum.
• The most significant long-term consequence is the increased lifetime risk of cardiovascular disease for the mother.

sections.overview:
• **Preeclampsia** is a multisystem progressive disorder characterized by the new onset of **hypertension** and either **proteinuria** or **end-organ dysfunction** after 20 weeks of gestation in a previously normotensive individual.
• It is a major cause of maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality.
• The spectrum of the disease ranges from mild features to **preeclampsia with severe features**, **eclampsia** (seizures), and **HELLP syndrome**.
• The definitive cure is the delivery of the fetus and placenta.
sections.etiology:
• The exact etiology is not fully understood, but the central defect is **abnormal placentation**.
    ◦ **Defective Spiral Artery Remodeling**: In a normal pregnancy, cytotrophoblasts invade the maternal spiral arteries, transforming them from narrow, high-resistance vessels into wide, low-resistance vessels to accommodate increased blood flow to the placenta. In preeclampsia, this invasion is incomplete.
    ◦ **Placental Hypoperfusion & Ischemia**: The poorly remodeled spiral arteries lead to decreased placental perfusion and hypoxia.
    ◦ **Endothelial Cell Dysfunction**: The ischemic placenta releases anti-angiogenic factors (e.g., soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 or **sFlt-1**) and pro-inflammatory factors into the maternal circulation.
    ◦ **Systemic Response**: These circulating factors cause widespread maternal endothelial cell dysfunction, leading to:
        ▪ **Vasoconstriction & Increased Vascular Tone**: Causing hypertension.
        ▪ **Increased Vascular Permeability**: Fluid shifts from the intravascular to the interstitial space, causing edema (peripheral, pulmonary) and proteinuria (due to glomerular capillary damage).
        ▪ **Activation of the Coagulation Cascade**: Leading to thrombocytopenia and, in severe cases, Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC).
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects approximately 2-8% of pregnancies worldwide.
• A leading cause of maternal death, preterm birth, and **intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR)**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Often asymptomatic and identified during a routine prenatal visit with elevated blood pressure and proteinuria on urinalysis.
• Typically presents after 20 weeks gestation, most commonly in the third trimester.
• Can also present for the first time in the postpartum period (usually within the first 48 hours, but up to 6 weeks).
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is based on ACOG (American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists) criteria.
    ◦ **Diagnostic Criteria**: Requires both **Blood Pressure** and **Proteinuria/End-Organ Dysfunction** criteria to be met.
        ▪ **1. Blood Pressure**:
            ◦ **Systolic BP 140 mmHg OR Diastolic BP 90 mmHg** on two occasions at least 4 hours apart after 20 weeks gestation.
            ◦ OR **Systolic BP 160 mmHg OR Diastolic BP 110 mmHg** once (severe range).
        ▪ **2. AND EITHER Proteinuria OR End-Organ Dysfunction**:
            ◦ **Proteinuria**:
                ▪ 300 mg per 24-hour urine collection.
                ▪ Urine protein/creatinine ratio 0.3.
                ▪ Dipstick reading of 2+ (use only if other quantitative methods are not available).
            ◦ **End-Organ Dysfunction (in the absence of proteinuria)**:
                ▪ **Thrombocytopenia**: Platelets < 100,000/L.
                ▪ **Renal Insufficiency**: Serum creatinine > 1.1 mg/dL or a doubling of the serum creatinine.
                ▪ **Impaired Liver Function**: Elevated transaminases to twice the normal concentration (AST/ALT > 2x ULN).
                ▪ **Pulmonary Edema**.
                ▪ **New-onset cerebral or visual disturbances**.
• **Preeclampsia with Severe Features** is diagnosed if the patient has new-onset hypertension plus any of the following:
    ◦ Systolic BP 160 or Diastolic BP 110.
    ◦ **Thrombocytopenia** (< 100,000/L).
    ◦ Impaired liver function (elevated LFTs, severe RUQ/epigastric pain).
    ◦ Progressive renal insufficiency (creatinine > 1.1 mg/dL).
    ◦ **Pulmonary edema**.
    ◦ New-onset cerebral or visual disturbances.
• **Lab Workup**:
    ◦ **CBC**: To assess for thrombocytopenia and hemolysis.
    ◦ **Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP)**: To assess renal function (Creatinine, BUN) and liver function (AST, ALT).
    ◦ **Uric Acid**: Often elevated in preeclampsia.
    ◦ **Urinalysis (U/A)** and **Urine Protein/Creatinine Ratio** or **24-hour urine for protein**.
    ◦ **Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH)**: To assess for hemolysis (part of HELLP workup).
• **Fetal Assessment**:
    ◦ **Nonstress Test (NST)** and/or **Biophysical Profile (BPP)**: To assess fetal well-being.
    ◦ **Ultrasound for Fetal Growth**: To assess for IUGR.
    ◦ **Doppler Velocimetry of Umbilical Artery**: To assess placental function.
sections.prognosis:
• BP and proteinuria typically resolve by 12 weeks postpartum.
• If hypertension persists beyond 12 weeks postpartum, the diagnosis is changed to chronic hypertension.
• A history of preeclampsia, especially with severe features or early onset, significantly increases a woman's long-term risk for **cardiovascular disease**, including chronic hypertension, ischemic heart disease, stroke, and venous thromboembolism.

sections.overview:
• **Severe Preeclampsia** is a multisystem disorder of pregnancy characterized by **new-onset hypertension** (≥140/90 mmHg) after 20 weeks of gestation, accompanied by signs of significant **end-organ damage**.
    ◦ It is a more dangerous progression from preeclampsia without severe features and represents a life-threatening condition for both the mother and fetus.
    ◦ The "severe features" are specific clinical and laboratory findings that indicate a high risk for complications such as **eclampsia**, **HELLP syndrome**, **stroke**, and **placental abruption**.
• The definitive cure is delivery of the fetus and placenta.
sections.etiology:
• The exact etiology is unknown, but the core pathophysiologic process is **abnormal placentation**.
    ◦ **Defective Spiral Artery Remodeling**: In a normal pregnancy, cytotrophoblasts invade the maternal spiral arteries, transforming them from narrow, high-resistance vessels into wide, low-resistance vessels to ensure adequate placental blood flow. In preeclampsia, this invasion is incomplete.
    ◦ **Placental Ischemia**: The failure of remodeling leaves the spiral arteries narrow and vasospastic, leading to placental hypoperfusion, hypoxia, and ischemia.
    ◦ **Endothelial Cell Dysfunction**: In response to ischemia, the stressed placenta releases anti-angiogenic factors (e.g., soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 or sFlt-1) and pro-inflammatory mediators into the maternal circulation.
    ◦ **Systemic Effects**: These factors cause widespread maternal **endothelial cell dysfunction**, leading to:
        ▪ **Vasospasm**: Causes hypertension and reduced organ perfusion.
        ▪ **Increased Capillary Permeability**: Leads to proteinuria (glomerular damage) and edema (including pulmonary edema).
        ▪ **Activation of the Coagulation Cascade**: Can lead to thrombocytopenia and, in severe cases, DIC.
• This systemic endothelial damage manifests as the clinical "severe features" affecting the brain, liver, kidneys, and cardiovascular system.
sections.epidemiology:
• Preeclampsia complicates 2-8% of pregnancies worldwide.
• Approximately 25% of preeclampsia cases will present with severe features.
• It is a leading cause of maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality globally.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a pregnant patient beyond 20 weeks gestation who develops **severely elevated blood pressure** and complains of symptoms related to **end-organ damage**.
    ◦ The onset can be abrupt.
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is made based on **ACOG** (American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists) criteria.
• **Preeclampsia with Severe Features** is diagnosed by:
    ◦ **SBP ≥ 160 mmHg** or **DBP ≥ 110 mmHg** on two occasions at least 4 hours apart.
    ◦ OR **BP ≥ 140/90 mmHg** with any of the following new-onset conditions:
        ▪ **Thrombocytopenia**: Platelet count < 100,000/microL.
        ▪ **Renal Insufficiency**: Serum creatinine > 1.1 mg/dL or a doubling of the serum creatinine in the absence of other renal disease.
        ▪ **Impaired Liver Function**: Elevated blood concentrations of liver transaminases (AST or ALT) to twice the upper limit of normal.
        ▪ **Pulmonary Edema**.
        ▪ **New-onset cerebral or visual disturbances**.
• Note: Significant **proteinuria** is no longer required for diagnosis if other severe features are present.
• **Initial Laboratory Workup**:
    ◦ **CBC with platelets**: To assess for thrombocytopenia and hemoconcentration.
    ◦ **Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP)**: To assess liver enzymes (AST, ALT) and renal function (BUN, creatinine).
    ◦ **Urine Protein/Creatinine Ratio** or **24-hour urine collection for protein**: To quantify proteinuria (≥0.3 or ≥300mg/24h respectively is abnormal).
    ◦ **Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH)**: To screen for hemolysis (part of **HELLP syndrome** workup).
• **Fetal Assessment**:
    ◦ **Non-stress Test (NST)**: To assess fetal well-being.
    ◦ **Biophysical Profile (BPP)**: Comprehensive assessment of fetal well-being.
    ◦ **Ultrasound for Fetal Growth**: To evaluate for **intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR)**.
sections.prognosis:
• With prompt diagnosis and management, maternal and fetal prognosis is generally good, though morbidity is significant.
• Symptoms typically resolve within days to weeks after delivery.
• **Long-Term**: A history of severe preeclampsia significantly increases a woman's lifetime risk of developing:
    ◦ **Chronic hypertension**
    ◦ **Cardiovascular disease**

sections.overview:
• Eclampsia is a life-threatening obstetric emergency defined as the new onset of generalized, **tonic-clonic seizures** in a patient with **preeclampsia**.
• It represents one of the most severe manifestations of the hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.
• The diagnosis does not require the presence of **proteinuria** if other signs of **preeclampsia** (e.g., **hypertension**, **thrombocytopenia**, elevated liver enzymes) are present.
• It can occur antepartum, intrapartum, or postpartum.
sections.etiology:
• Eclampsia is the neurological culmination of **preeclampsia**.
• The exact pathophysiology is rooted in the same process as **preeclampsia**:
    ◦ **Abnormal Placentation**: Inadequate trophoblastic invasion of the maternal spiral arteries leads to poor placental perfusion and ischemia.
    ◦ **Endothelial Dysfunction**: The ischemic placenta releases anti-angiogenic factors (e.g., soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 or sFlt-1) into the maternal circulation.
    ◦ **Systemic Vasospasm & Injury**: These factors cause widespread maternal endothelial cell damage, leading to:
        ▪ Intense vasospasm (causing **hypertension**).
        ▪ Increased vascular permeability (causing edema and **proteinuria**).
        ▪ Activation of the coagulation cascade (can lead to **HELLP**/**DIC**).
    ◦ **Cerebral Involvement**: Vasospasm and endothelial injury affect the cerebral vasculature, leading to a breakdown of the blood-brain barrier.
        ▪ This results in cerebral vasogenic edema, hyperperfusion, and ischemia.
        ▪ This neuronal irritation and dysfunction ultimately precipitates a **seizure**.
• This process is often described as a form of **Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome (PRES)**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**:
    ◦ Occurs in approximately 0.5-1% of patients with mild **preeclampsia** and 2-3% of patients with **preeclampsia** with severe features.
• **Timing of Onset**:
    ◦ **Antepartum**: ~50%
    ◦ **Intrapartum**: ~25%
    ◦ **Postpartum**: ~25% (most within the first 48 hours, but can occur up to 6 weeks postpartum).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a pregnant or postpartum patient who develops a generalized **tonic-clonic seizure**.
    ◦ The **seizure** is often self-limited, lasting 60-90 seconds, followed by a postictal phase of confusion or combativeness.
• Many patients will have preceding signs and symptoms of **preeclampsia** with severe features.
sections.diagnostics:
• The diagnosis of eclampsia is **clinical**: a new-onset **seizure** in the setting of **preeclampsia**.
• Workup is focused on assessing maternal and fetal stability and evaluating for complications.
• **Laboratory Studies**:
    ◦ **CBC with peripheral smear**: To assess for **thrombocytopenia** (<100,000/L) and hemolysis (schistocytes), key components of **HELLP syndrome**.
    ◦ **Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP)**:
        ▪ **LFTs (AST/ALT)**: Elevated liver enzymes suggest **HELLP syndrome**.
        ▪ **Creatinine**: To assess for renal insufficiency.
        ▪ **Uric Acid**: Often elevated in **preeclampsia**.
    ◦ **Urinalysis**: To quantify **proteinuria** (≥2+ on dipstick, or protein/creatinine ratio ≥0.3).
    ◦ **LDH**: Elevated level suggests hemolysis.
• **Imaging**:
    ◦ **Maternal**: Head CT or MRI is **not required for diagnosis** but should be performed if the presentation is atypical (e.g., focal deficits, prolonged coma, **seizure** onset >48 hours postpartum) to rule out other CNS pathology.
    ◦ **Fetal**:
        ▪ **Continuous Fetal Monitoring**: To assess for fetal bradycardia (common during maternal **seizure**), late decelerations, or loss of variability.
        ▪ **Ultrasound**: To assess fetal growth, amniotic fluid volume, and perform a biophysical profile (BPP).
sections.prognosis:
• With prompt and appropriate treatment, maternal mortality is low in developed countries.
• Women with a history of eclampsia have an increased risk of **preeclampsia** in future pregnancies.
• There is an increased long-term risk of cardiovascular disease (chronic **hypertension**, ischemic heart disease, stroke) for women who have had **preeclampsia**/eclampsia.
• Fetal prognosis is largely dependent on gestational age at delivery and the severity of complications like placental abruption.

sections.overview:
• **HELLP syndrome** is a life-threatening obstetric complication considered a severe variant or complication of **preeclampsia**.
    ◦ The name is an acronym for its key laboratory findings: **H**emolysis, **E**levated **L**iver enzymes, and **L**ow **P**latelet count.
• It is a form of **microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA)** that occurs during pregnancy and can lead to significant maternal and fetal morbidity and mortality.
• Prompt recognition and **delivery** are crucial.
sections.etiology:
• The exact etiology is unknown, but it is thought to be a severe manifestation of **abnormal placentation**, leading to widespread maternal endothelial and microvascular injury.
    ◦ **Abnormal Placentation**: Inadequate cytotrophoblast invasion of maternal spiral arteries leads to poor placental perfusion, placental ischemia, and release of anti-angiogenic factors (like **sFlt-1**) into the maternal circulation.
    ◦ **Endothelial Dysfunction**: These circulating factors cause systemic endothelial cell dysfunction and damage, leading to widespread **vasospasm**, increased vascular permeability, and activation of the coagulation cascade.
    ◦ **Pathophysiologic Triad**:
        ▪ **Hemolysis (Microangiopathic Hemolytic Anemia)**: Endothelial damage leads to the deposition of fibrin strands in the microvasculature. Red blood cells are sheared as they pass through these narrowed vessels, creating fragmented RBCs (**schistocytes**) and leading to **intravascular hemolysis**. This is evidenced by **elevated LDH** and **bilirubin**.
        ▪ **Elevated Liver Enzymes**: Fibrin deposition in the hepatic sinusoids obstructs blood flow, leading to **periportal necrosis** and hepatocellular injury. This causes liver swelling and distension of the Glisson's capsule, resulting in the characteristic **right upper quadrant (RUQ) pain** or **epigastric pain**. This damage releases **AST** and **ALT** into the bloodstream.
        ▪ **Low Platelets (Thrombocytopenia)**: Endothelial injury exposes subendothelial collagen, which triggers platelet adhesion and aggregation. The activated platelets are consumed at sites of vascular damage, leading to a rapid drop in the circulating platelet count.
sections.epidemiology:
• Occurs in 0.5-0.9% of all pregnancies.
• Develops in 10-20% of women with **severe preeclampsia** or **eclampsia**.
• **Timing**:
    ◦ ~70% of cases develop antepartum, typically between 27 and 37 weeks' gestation (third trimester).
    ◦ ~30% of cases develop postpartum, usually within the first 48 hours but can be up to 7 days.
• More common in Caucasian women and those with multiparity.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is often rapid and can be dramatic.
• Patients may present with non-specific symptoms that can be mistaken for a viral illness; a high index of suspicion is required.
• The classic presentation involves a triad of **RUQ pain**, **nausea/vomiting**, and **malaise** in a late-trimester pregnant patient.
• Notably, **15-20% of patients with HELLP syndrome are normotensive**, and **proteinuria** may be absent or mild, which can delay diagnosis.
sections.diagnostics: • Diagnosis is made based on characteristic laboratory findings in a pregnant or postpartum woman.
sections.prognosis:
• With prompt diagnosis and treatment, maternal prognosis is generally good.
• Maternal mortality is approximately 1-3%.
• Labs (platelets, LFTs) usually nadir around 24-48 hours postpartum and begin to improve, typically normalizing within 3-7 days.
    ◦ Failure to improve postpartum suggests an alternative diagnosis (e.g., **TTP/HUS**).
• High risk of recurrence (~20-25%) in subsequent pregnancies.

sections.overview:
• **Hyperemesis Gravidarum (HG)** is a severe and intractable form of nausea and vomiting of pregnancy (NVP)
	◦ Distinguished from typical "morning sickness" by its severity, leading to significant maternal metabolic derangements
	◦ Classic triad includes:
		▪ **Persistent vomiting**
		▪ **Weight loss of >5%** of pre-pregnancy body weight
		▪ **Ketonuria**
	◦ HG is a **diagnosis of exclusion** that requires hospitalization in severe cases for fluid and electrolyte management
sections.etiology:
• The exact etiology is multifactorial and not fully understood, but it is strongly associated with hormonal changes
	◦ **Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (hCG)**: Leading theory
		▪ hCG levels peak around 9-12 weeks gestation, coinciding with the peak of HG symptoms
		▪ Conditions with higher hCG levels (e.g., **molar pregnancy**, **multiple gestations**) have a significantly higher incidence of HG
		▪ hCG has a similar alpha-subunit to TSH, which can lead to **transient gestational hyperthyroidism** (suppressed TSH, elevated free T4)
	◦ **Estrogen & Progesterone**:
		▪ These hormones slow gastric motility and may lower the esophageal sphincter tone, contributing to nausea and reflux
	◦ **GDF15 (Growth Differentiation Factor 15)**: A newer theory
		▪ The GDF15 protein, produced by the placenta, acts on receptors in the brainstem's vomiting center
		▪ Higher maternal sensitivity to GDF15 is strongly linked to HG
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects 0.3-3% of all pregnancies
• It is the most common reason for hospitalization in the first half of pregnancy
• Timeline:
	◦ **Onset**: Typically begins between 4-6 weeks gestation
	◦ **Peak**: Symptoms peak around 9 weeks gestation
	◦ **Resolution**: Symptoms usually subside by 16-20 weeks, but can persist longer in a minority of patients
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient in the first trimester (typically <16 weeks) presents with relentless nausea and vomiting, unable to tolerate oral liquids or solids
	◦ They often appear ill, fatigued, and dehydrated
• The key is the **inability to maintain hydration and nutrition orally**
sections.diagnostics:
• HG is a **clinical diagnosis of exclusion**
• The goal of the workup is to confirm the metabolic consequences and rule out other causes
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is excellent for both mother and fetus with proper management
• Symptoms typically resolve by 20 weeks gestation
• There is a high recurrence rate in subsequent pregnancies
• The maternal psychological toll can be significant

sections.overview:
• **Intrauterine Growth Restriction (IUGR)**, also known as Fetal Growth Restriction (FGR), is a condition in which a fetus fails to achieve its genetically determined growth potential.
    ◦ Pathologically defined by an **Estimated Fetal Weight (EFW)** or **Abdominal Circumference (AC)** less than the 10th percentile for gestational age on ultrasound, coupled with evidence of fetal compromise (e.g., abnormal Doppler studies).
    ◦ Distinct from **Small for Gestational Age (SGA)**, which describes a fetus with an EFW <10th percentile without evidence of pathology.
        ▪ An SGA fetus may be constitutionally small and healthy.
        ▪ IUGR is always pathological.
• **Two Main Types**:
    ◦ **Symmetric IUGR (~20%)**: 
        ▪ Onset is early in gestation (<20 weeks).
        ▪ Characterized by a global, proportional reduction in the size of all organs, including the head.
    ◦ **Asymmetric IUGR (~80%)**: 
        ▪ Onset is later in gestation (late 2nd or 3rd trimester).
        ▪ Characterized by disproportionate growth, where head growth is relatively preserved at the expense of abdominal/somatic growth. This is known as **"brain-sparing."**
sections.etiology:
• IUGR results from any condition that limits the supply of oxygen and nutrients to the fetus.
• Causes can be categorized as maternal, fetal, or placental.
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects 3-10% of all pregnancies.
• Accounts for a significant proportion of perinatal morbidity and mortality.
• IUGR fetuses have a 6-10 fold increased risk of perinatal death compared to appropriately grown fetuses.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Often an **incidental finding** during routine prenatal care.
• The primary clinical sign is a **fundal height that is smaller than expected** for the gestational age.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Ultrasound Biometry (Diagnostic Standard)**
    ◦ **Estimated Fetal Weight (EFW)**: Calculated using BPD, HC, AC, and FL. **EFW <10th percentile** is the primary diagnostic criterion.
    ◦ **Abdominal Circumference (AC)**: The **single most sensitive parameter** for detecting IUGR, as it reflects liver size and subcutaneous fat, which are diminished early in asymmetric IUGR.
    ◦ **HC/AC Ratio**:
        ▪ Normally, this ratio decreases as gestation advances.
        ▪ In **asymmetric IUGR**, this ratio is **elevated (>1)** due to brain-sparing (preserved HC, small AC).
        ▪ In symmetric IUGR, the ratio is typically normal.
• **Assessment of Fetal Well-being (Critical for Management)**
    ◦ **Umbilical Artery (UA) Doppler Velocimetry**:
        ▪ **The most important surveillance tool for managing IUGR.** It assesses placental resistance to blood flow.
        ▪ **Normal**: Low-resistance waveform with robust forward flow during diastole.
        ▪ **Abnormal**: Increased Systolic/Diastolic (S/D) ratio, indicating increased placental resistance.
        ▪ **Absent End-Diastolic Flow (AEDF)**: Indicates severe placental dysfunction.
        ▪ **Reversed End-Diastolic Flow (REDF)**: A pre-terminal finding indicating extremely high resistance and impending fetal demise.
    ◦ **Biophysical Profile (BPP)**: Score of 0 or 2 for five components (total score /10):
        ▪ **B**reathing movements (1+ episode of 30s)
        ▪ **A**mniotic fluid index (AFI >5cm or single deepest pocket >2cm)
        ▪ **T**one (1+ episode of flexion/extension)
        ▪ **M**ovement (3+ body movements)
        ▪ **N**on-stress test (NST) (Reactive)
        ▪ *Interpretation*: 8-10 is reassuring; 6 is equivocal; 4 is non-reassuring and often prompts delivery.
    ◦ **Amniotic Fluid Index (AFI)**:
        ▪ **Oligohydramnios (AFI <5 cm)** is common with IUGR due to decreased renal perfusion and urine output.
        ▪ It is a sign of chronic uteroplacental insufficiency and a poor prognostic indicator.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly variable and depends on:
    ◦ Underlying etiology (aneuploidy carries a poor prognosis).
    ◦ Gestational age at onset and delivery.
    ◦ Severity of growth restriction.
    ◦ **Umbilical artery Doppler findings** (**REDF** is associated with the highest perinatal mortality).

sections.overview:
• Fetal macrosomia refers to a newborn who is significantly larger than average for their gestational age. It is formally defined by birth weight, not by prenatal estimates.
• While there is some variation, it is most commonly defined as:
    ◦ **Birth weight > 4,000 grams (8 lbs 13 oz)** regardless of gestational age.
    ◦ **Birth weight > 4,500 grams (9 lbs 15 oz)** is a more specific cutoff used by ACOG for recommending cesarean delivery in certain cases.
    ◦ **Large for Gestational Age (LGA):** A fetus or neonate with an estimated fetal weight (EFW) or birth weight **>90th percentile** for a given gestational age.
• Macrosomia is a major risk factor for maternal and neonatal morbidity during labor and delivery, most notably **shoulder dystocia**.
sections.etiology:
• The primary driver of fetal overgrowth is an environment of excess fuel (glucose, amino acids, free fatty acids) provided by the mother.
• **Pedersen Hypothesis (Primary Mechanism):** This is the classic explanation, particularly in diabetic mothers.
    ◦ **Maternal Hyperglycemia:** Poorly controlled maternal diabetes (pre-gestational or gestational) leads to high blood glucose levels.
    ◦ **Glucose Transport:** Glucose freely crosses the placenta into fetal circulation.
    ◦ **Fetal Hyperglycemia:** The fetus develops high blood glucose levels.
    ◦ **Fetal Hyperinsulinemia:** The fetal pancreas responds by producing excess insulin.
    ◦ **Anabolic Growth:** Insulin is a potent fetal growth hormone. High insulin levels promote the uptake of glucose and amino acids, leading to:
        ▪ Increased fat deposition (adiposity), particularly around the trunk and shoulders.
        ▪ Organomegaly (hepatosplenomegaly, cardiomegaly).
        ▪ Accelerated somatic growth.
• **Other Factors:** In non-diabetic mothers, the pathophysiology is less clear but likely involves genetic predisposition, maternal obesity (leading to insulin resistance and increased availability of lipids and amino acids), and excessive caloric intake.
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects approximately **10%** of all live births in the United States.
• The incidence of birth weights >4500g is approximately 1.5%.
• The prevalence is increasing worldwide, paralleling the rising rates of maternal obesity and diabetes.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Fetal macrosomia is typically suspected during routine prenatal care.
• The most common presenting sign is a **uterine size larger than expected for gestational age**.
• The patient may report feeling "very large" or experiencing more discomfort than in previous pregnancies, but these are non-specific.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Prenatal Diagnosis is an *estimation* and is notoriously inaccurate.**
• **Ultrasound (US) Biometry:** This is the primary modality for estimating fetal weight.
    ◦ Measurements include: Biparietal Diameter (BPD), Head Circumference (HC), **Abdominal Circumference (AC)**, and Femur Length (FL).
    ◦ **The AC is the single most important measurement**, as macrosomic infants have disproportionately larger abdomens.
    ◦ These measurements are entered into formulas (e.g., Hadlock) to calculate an **Estimated Fetal Weight (EFW).**
    ◦ **Limitation:** The margin of error for EFW in the third trimester can be 15% or more, and accuracy decreases as weight increases.
• **Laboratory Tests:**
    ◦ **Gestational Diabetes Screening:** All pregnant patients are screened between 24-28 weeks.
        ▪ **1-Hour 50g Glucose Challenge Test (GCT):** Screening test.
        ▪ **3-Hour 100g Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT):** Confirmatory diagnostic test if GCT is abnormal.
sections.prognosis:
• **Maternal:** Prognosis is generally excellent, but morbidity from PPH, severe lacerations, or emergent C-section is increased.
• **Neonatal:** Prognosis is excellent for the majority of infants. However, a small percentage can suffer permanent disability from severe birth trauma (e.g., permanent brachial plexus palsy) or hypoxic brain injury.

sections.overview:
• **Placenta previa** is an obstetric complication in which the placenta abnormally implants in the lower uterine segment, partially or completely covering the internal cervical os.
    ◦ This position can cause **severe bleeding** during pregnancy and delivery.
    ◦ It is a leading cause of **antepartum (third-trimester) hemorrhage**.
• **Types**:
    ◦ **Complete Previa**: The placenta completely covers the internal cervical os.
    ◦ **Partial Previa**: The placenta partially covers the internal os.
    ◦ **Marginal Previa**: The edge of the placenta is within 2 cm of the internal os but does not cover it.
    ◦ **Low-Lying Placenta**: The placenta is implanted in the lower uterine segment, and its edge is >2 cm from the internal os.
        ▪ Many low-lying placentas diagnosed in the second trimester will resolve via "**placental migration**" as the uterus grows.
sections.etiology:
• The exact etiology is unknown, but it is theorized to be related to conditions that damage or scar the endometrium of the upper uterine segment, leading to placental implantation in the less vascular, lower uterine segment.
• As the pregnancy progresses, the lower uterine segment begins to thin, efface, and dilate in preparation for labor.
    ◦ This process disrupts the placental attachment at the cervix, tearing blood vessels and leading to **painless bleeding**.
    ◦ **Bleeding occurs without uterine contractions**.
sections.epidemiology:
• Occurs in approximately **1 in 200 pregnancies** at term (0.5%).
• Incidence is higher on second-trimester ultrasounds, but up to **90% of cases diagnosed before 20 weeks' gestation resolve** due to uterine growth and apparent "**placental migration**" away from the cervix.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a patient in the **late second or third trimester** (typically after 28 weeks) who experiences a sudden onset of **painless, bright red vaginal bleeding**.
• The initial bleeding episode is often **self-limited** but may be **recurrent** and progressively heavier with each subsequent episode.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Initial & Gold Standard Test: Transvaginal Ultrasound (TVUS)**
    ◦ Confirms the diagnosis and precisely localizes the placenta in relation to the internal cervical os.
    ◦ **TVUS is safe and more accurate** than transabdominal ultrasound for this diagnosis.
• **Laboratory Studies**:
    ◦ **CBC**: To assess for anemia and establish a baseline hemoglobin/hematocrit.
