    ◦ **Type & Screen (or Crossmatch)**: Essential for potential blood transfusion.
    ◦ **Coagulation Studies (PT/PTT, Fibrinogen)**: To rule out coagulopathy, especially with heavy bleeding.
• **Fetal Monitoring**:
    ◦ **Cardiotocography (CTG)**: **Non-stress test (NST)** to assess fetal well-being.
sections.prognosis:
• With access to modern obstetric care, including ultrasound for diagnosis and planned **C-section** for delivery, the prognosis for both mother and fetus is generally good.
• The greatest risks are associated with **uncontrolled hemorrhage** and complications from **preterm delivery**.

sections.overview:
• Placental abruption (abruptio placentae) is the premature separation of a normally implanted placenta from the uterine wall, occurring after 20 weeks of gestation and prior to the delivery of the fetus.
    ◦ This separation disrupts fetal oxygen and nutrient supply and can cause significant maternal hemorrhage.
    ◦ It is a serious obstetric emergency.
• The bleeding is typically maternal in origin, but fetal bleeding can occur if villi are disrupted.
sections.etiology: • The primary event is the rupture of maternal spiral arteries within the decidua basalis, leading to bleeding and the formation of a retroplacental hematoma. ◦ As the hematoma expands, it shears the placenta from the uterine wall, causing further separation and bleeding. • Mechanism ◦ Vascular Rupture: Degenerative changes in the small maternal arterioles of the decidua lead to rupture. ◦ Hematoma Formation: A hematoma forms between the placenta and the uterine wall. ◦ Placental Separation: The pressure of the expanding hematoma dissects the placenta away from its attachment site. • Bleeding Types ◦ Revealed (External): Blood tracks down between the membranes and the uterine wall, escaping through the cervix. Vaginal bleeding is visible. ◦ Concealed (Internal): Blood is trapped behind the placenta. This can be more dangerous as the extent of blood loss is not externally visible, potentially delaying diagnosis and leading to a falsely reassuring clinical picture. • Pathophysiologic Consequences ◦ Fetal Compromise: Separation reduces the surface area for gas and nutrient exchange, leading to fetal hypoxia, acidosis, and potential demise. ◦ Myometrial Irritation: Extravasated blood is a potent irritant to the myometrium, causing uterine hypertonicity (tetanic contractions) and tenderness. ◦ DIC: The damaged decidual tissue releases large amounts of thromboplastin into maternal circulation, triggering the coagulation cascade and potentially leading to Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC).
sections.epidemiology: • Incidence: Occurs in approximately 0.5-1% of all pregnancies. • Timing: Most commonly occurs in the third trimester. • Significance: Accounts for ~15% of all perinatal deaths.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • The classic triad includes: ◦ Painful vaginal bleeding ◦ Abdominal or back pain ◦ High-frequency, low-amplitude uterine contractions • Severity is graded: ◦ Grade 1 (Mild): Slight vaginal bleeding, localized uterine tenderness, normal maternal VS, no fetal distress. ◦ Grade 2 (Moderate): Moderate bleeding, significant uterine tenderness/tetany, maternal tachycardia, orthostatic changes, signs of fetal distress. ◦ Grade 3 (Severe): Severe bleeding (may be concealed), uterine tetany (board-like rigidity), maternal shock, fetal demise, and often DIC.
sections.diagnostics: • Abruption is a CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS based on history and physical exam. • Ultrasound ◦ Main purpose is to rule out placenta previa as a cause of bleeding. ◦ Low sensitivity (~50%) for directly visualizing an abruption. A retroplacental hematoma is diagnostic if seen, but its absence does not rule out abruption. • Laboratory Studies ◦ CBC: To assess for anemia and thrombocytopenia. ◦ Type & Crossmatch: Essential for potential transfusion. ◦ Coagulation Profile: PT, PTT, and fibrinogen levels to screen for DIC (fibrinogen < 200 mg/dL is concerning). ◦ Kleihauer-Betke (KB) Test: Detects fetal red blood cells in maternal circulation. Used to quantify fetal-maternal hemorrhage to guide Rho(D) immune globulin dosing in Rh-negative mothers.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly dependent on the severity of the separation, the gestational age at which it occurs, and the time to delivery.
• Maternal mortality is low (<1%) with modern management but morbidity is significant.
• Perinatal mortality rate is approximately 10-20%, primarily due to prematurity and hypoxia.
• High risk of recurrence in subsequent pregnancies (~10-15%).

sections.overview:
• **Placenta Accreta Spectrum (PAS)** is a range of conditions characterized by **abnormal, deep attachment of the placental chorionic villi** into the **myometrium** (uterine muscle wall)
    ◦ It results from a **defect in the decidua basalis layer**, which normally creates a barrier between the placenta and the myometrium
    ◦ The hallmark of this condition is the **inability of the placenta to properly separate** from the uterine wall after delivery, leading to **severe, life-threatening postpartum hemorrhage**
    ◦ The spectrum is classified by the depth of placental invasion:
        ▪ **Placenta Accreta:** Chorionic villi attach directly to the myometrium without invading it. (Most common, ~75% of cases)
        ▪ **Placenta Increta:** Chorionic villi invade *into* the myometrium. (~15% of cases)
        ▪ **Placenta Percreta:** Chorionic villi invade *through* the myometrium and uterine serosa, potentially invading adjacent organs like the bladder or rectum. (Most severe, ~5% of cases)
sections.etiology:
• The core pathophysiologic defect is an absence or deficiency of the **decidua basalis**, specifically the **Nitabuch's layer**
    ◦ This fibrinoid layer normally forms between the placenta and the myometrium, acting as a cleavage plane and preventing excessive placental invasion
    ◦ When this layer is damaged or absent, typically due to prior uterine surgery and scarring, the chorionic villi can directly contact and invade the myometrium
        ▪ This leads to neovascularization and a disorganized, tenacious placental attachment that cannot separate cleanly after childbirth
        ▪ Attempts to manually separate the placenta cause tearing of uterine blood vessels, resulting in **catastrophic hemorrhage**
sections.epidemiology:
• The incidence of PAS has risen dramatically over the past several decades, paralleling the rise in **cesarean delivery rates**
• Current estimated incidence: approximately **1 in 272 to 1 in 533** pregnancies
    ◦ This represents a nearly 10-fold increase since the 1970s
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The "classic" presentation occurs at the time of delivery, though many cases are now diagnosed antenatally
    ◦ **Antenatal:** Most patients are **asymptomatic**
        ▪ If placenta previa is also present, the patient may experience **painless vaginal bleeding** in the second or third trimester
    ◦ **Intrapartum/Postpartum:** The diagnosis is often made when the **placenta fails to deliver** within 30 minutes of the infant
        ▪ Any attempt at manual extraction results in **profuse, torrential, and life-threatening hemorrhage**
sections.diagnostics:
• **Prenatal Diagnosis is Key**
• **Ultrasound (US)**
    ◦ **Gold Standard for Screening & Diagnosis**
    ◦ Findings:
        ▪ **Loss of the retroplacental "clear space":** The normal hypoechoic zone between the placenta and myometrium is obliterated
        ▪ **Placental Lacunae:** Multiple large, irregular vascular spaces within the placenta, giving it a "Swiss cheese" or "moth-eaten" appearance
        ▪ **Myometrial thinning:** Myometrium overlying the placenta is <1 mm thick
        ▪ **Bladder wall irregularity:** Disruption of the line between the uterine serosa and bladder wall
        ▪ **Color Doppler:** Turbulent blood flow crossing from placenta into the myometrium or beyond
    ◦ Notes:
        ▪ Best performed between 18-24 weeks gestation
        ▪ Transvaginal US is often superior for evaluating the lower uterine segment
• **MRI**
    ◦ Used as adjunctive imaging to confirm US findings, especially with:
        ▪ Posterior placenta
        ▪ Suspected **placenta percreta** (to delineate the extent of invasion into adjacent organs like the bladder)
    ◦ Notes:
        ▪ Not used for routine screening due to cost and limited availability
        ▪ Best at confirming the depth of invasion
• **Labs**
    ◦ Not diagnostic prenatally; used for delivery planning and management
    ◦ **Prenatal:** CBC, Type & Screen
    ◦ **Intrapartum:** Type & Crossmatch (for multiple units of PRBCs, FFP, platelets), CBC, Coagulation panel (PT/INR, PTT, fibrinogen)
    ◦ Essential for preparing for **massive transfusion protocol**
• **Definitive Diagnosis**
    ◦ **Histopathology** of the hysterectomy specimen after delivery
    ◦ This is the only way to make a definitive diagnosis and classify the exact depth of invasion
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly dependent on **prenatal diagnosis** and management at an experienced tertiary care center
• With a planned, multidisciplinary approach, maternal mortality is significantly reduced to **<1%**
• In cases of an unanticipated accreta discovered at delivery, maternal morbidity and mortality are **substantially higher**

sections.overview:
• Multiple gestation refers to a pregnancy with more than one fetus, with a twin pregnancy being the most common form.
• Clinical significance lies in the substantially increased risk for both maternal and fetal complications compared to singleton pregnancies.
• The single most important determinant of pregnancy outcome is **chorionicity** (the number of placentas), which dictates the level of surveillance and management.
sections.etiology: • Multiple gestations are classified by **zygosity** (genetic origin) and **chorionicity/amnionicity** (placental and membrane structure).
sections.epidemiology:
• The rate of monozygotic twins is constant worldwide at approximately **1 in 250 births**.
• The rate of dizygotic twins varies significantly by race, geography, and use of assisted reproductive technology (ART).
    ◦ Highest rates in populations of African descent.
    ◦ Lowest rates in populations of Asian descent.
• The overall rate of multiple gestations has increased dramatically in recent decades, primarily due to the increased use of ART and advanced maternal age.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation is often one of "exaggerated" pregnancy signs and symptoms.
• A high index of suspicion is key, especially in patients with known risk factors.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Ultrasound (US)**: The **gold standard** for diagnosis.
    ◦ Confirms the number of fetuses.
    ◦ Crucially determines **chorionicity** and **amnionicity**, ideally in the first trimester (10-14 weeks) when it is most accurate.
        ▪ **Dichorionic:** Thick dividing membrane (>2mm), **"Lambda" or "Twin Peak" sign** (a triangular projection of placental tissue into the inter-twin membrane).
        ▪ **Monochorionic:** Thin dividing membrane (<2mm), **"T" sign** (membrane joins the placenta at a 90-degree angle with no intervening placental tissue).
        ▪ **Monoamniotic:** Absence of a dividing membrane between fetuses.
    ◦ Used for serial growth scans and fetal surveillance throughout pregnancy.
• **Laboratory Findings**
    ◦ **Maternal Serum Alpha-Fetoprotein (msAFP)**: Significantly elevated.
    ◦ **Beta-hCG**: Higher than expected for gestational age.
    ◦ Note: These are non-specific and are not used for diagnosis, but may be an incidental finding prompting an ultrasound.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is generally good with intensive prenatal surveillance and management.
• However, the perinatal mortality rate is 3-6 times higher than for singleton pregnancies.
• The primary determinant of prognosis is the **gestational age at delivery** and the presence or absence of major complications, particularly those related to monochorionicity.

sections.overview:
• **Post-term pregnancy**, also known as **postdates** or **prolonged pregnancy**, is a pregnancy that extends to or beyond **42 weeks and 0 days** of gestation (≥ 294 days) from the first day of the last menstrual period (LMP).
• It is associated with a significant increase in **perinatal morbidity and mortality** due to progressive **placental dysfunction** and **fetal compromise**.
• Management focuses on accurate dating, **antenatal surveillance**, and timely **induction of labor**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Most Common Cause: Inaccurate Dating**: Miscalculation of the estimated due date (EDD) based on an unreliable LMP.
    ◦ **Idiopathic (Majority of true cases)**: The precise mechanism for the initiation of labor is unknown, and its failure to occur is often idiopathic.
    ◦ **Fetal Factors**
        ▪ **Anencephaly**: Lack of a developed fetal hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis fails to produce the cortisol surge needed to initiate labor.
        ▪ Fetal adrenal hypoplasia.
    ◦ **Placental Factors**
        ▪ **Placental sulfatase deficiency**: A rare, X-linked recessive disorder that impairs placental estrogen synthesis, a key component for labor initiation.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The primary pathophysiologic process is **placental senescence (aging)**, which leads to **uteroplacental insufficiency**.
        ▪ Results in **reduced uteroplacental blood flow** and **impaired nutrient/gas exchange**, which can cause chronic **fetal hypoxia** and malnutrition.
    ◦ This placental dysfunction leads to two major fetal consequences:
        ▪ **Oligohydramnios**: Decreased placental perfusion leads to reduced fetal renal blood flow, causing decreased fetal urine output, which increases the risk of **umbilical cord compression**.
        ▪ **Macrosomia vs. Growth Restriction**: Depending on placental function, the fetus may continue to grow, leading to **macrosomia** (>4500g) and increased risks of birth trauma, or experience **intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR)** and develop **postmaturity (dysmaturity) syndrome** if placental function declines.
sections.epidemiology:
• Incidence is approximately 5-10% of all pregnancies.
• The rate has been decreasing due to more accurate gestational age assessment with **first-trimester ultrasound** and more liberal policies for **inducing labor at 41 weeks**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The patient presents for routine prenatal care with a confirmed gestational age of **≥ 42 0/7 weeks**.
• The primary presentation is the date itself; the patient may or may not be symptomatic.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Confirmation of Gestational Age**
    ◦ This is the single most important initial step.
    ◦ **Gold Standard**: **First-trimester ultrasound** measuring **crown-rump length (CRL)** is the most accurate method.
• **Antenatal Fetal Surveillance**
    ◦ Initiated at **41 0/7 weeks** and typically performed twice weekly until delivery.
    ◦ **Nonstress Test (NST)**
        ▪ Monitors fetal heart rate in response to fetal movement; a **"reactive" NST** is reassuring.
    ◦ **Amniotic Fluid Index (AFI)**
        ▪ Ultrasound measurement of the fluid in four quadrants of the uterus.
        ▪ **Oligohydramnios** (AFI **< 5 cm**) is an indication for delivery.
    ◦ **Biophysical Profile (BPP)**
        ▪ Combines an NST with four ultrasound parameters (fetal breathing, gross body movements, fetal tone, amniotic fluid volume).
        ▪ Scored out of 10: a score of **8-10** is reassuring, **6** is equivocal (may require repeat testing or delivery), and **≤ 4** is non-reassuring and indicates delivery.
sections.prognosis:
• With appropriate **antenatal surveillance** and timely **induction of labor** (typically between **41-42 weeks**), the prognosis for both mother and baby is generally excellent.
• The risks increase significantly with **expectant management beyond 42 weeks**.

sections.overview:
• Normal labor (eutocia) is a physiologic process characterized by sequential, progressive effacement and dilation of the cervix, coupled with descent of the fetus through the pelvis, culminating in the expulsion of the fetus and placenta
• It is typically divided into three, sometimes four, stages
• The process relies on the interplay of the **"Three P's"**:
    ◦ **Power:** Uterine contractions and maternal expulsive efforts
    ◦ **Passenger:** The fetus (size, lie, presentation, position)
    ◦ **Passage:** The maternal bony pelvis and soft tissues
sections.etiology:
• The initiation of labor is a complex cascade involving maternal and fetal factors that shift the uterus from a state of quiescence to active contractility
    ◦ **Progesterone Withdrawal:** Functional withdrawal of progesterone's inhibitory effect on myometrial contractility
    ◦ **Increased Estrogen:** Estrogen dominance upregulates myometrial gap junctions, oxytocin receptors, and prostaglandin synthesis, increasing uterine excitability
    ◦ **Oxytocin:** Released from the posterior pituitary, it is a potent uterotonic agent. Its receptor concentration in the myometrium increases dramatically near term
    ◦ **Prostaglandins (PGE2, PGF2):** Produced by the placenta, amnion, and chorion. They are critical for cervical ripening (softening and effacement) and stimulating myometrial contractions
    ◦ **Fetal HPA Axis:** Fetal cortisol release is thought to be a trigger for the hormonal cascade leading to labor
    ◦ **Ferguson Reflex:** A neuroendocrine positive feedback loop
        ▪ Stretch receptors in the lower uterine segment/cervix are stimulated by the fetal presenting part
        ▪ Signals hypothalamus to release oxytocin from the posterior pituitary
        ▪ Oxytocin stimulates uterine contractions
        ▪ Further descent and cervical stretch
sections.epidemiology:
• **Term Pregnancy:** Normal labor typically occurs at term, defined as 37 0/7 weeks to 41 6/7 weeks of gestation
• **Mode of Delivery (US):** Approximately 68% of births are vaginal, while 32% are via Cesarean section
• **Onset of Labor:** Approximately 85% of term pregnancies will begin labor spontaneously. The remainder are induced for maternal or fetal indications
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients presenting in labor typically report a combination of the following:
    ◦ Regular, painful uterine contractions that increase in frequency, duration, and intensity
    ◦ **Rupture of membranes (ROM)**, which may present as a sudden gush or a slow, steady trickle of clear or pale yellow fluid
    ◦ Passage of the mucus plug, often with a small amount of blood (**"bloody show"**)
    ◦ Persistent low back pain that may radiate to the abdomen
    ◦ A sensation of pelvic pressure or a feeling of needing to have a bowel movement as the fetus descends
sections.diagnostics:
• Labor is a **clinical diagnosis** based on regular uterine contractions that cause cervical change
• **Confirmation of Rupture of Membranes (ROM):**
    ◦ **Sterile Speculum Exam:** Look for **pooling** of fluid in the posterior fornix
    ◦ **Nitrazine Test:** Amniotic fluid is alkaline (pH >7.1), turning nitrazine paper blue
        ▪ *False positives: blood, semen, bacterial vaginosis.*
    ◦ **Ferning Test:** Amniotic fluid dried on a microscope slide forms a crystalline "fern" pattern
        ▪ *Most specific test.*
• **Group B Strep (GBS) Status:** Check prenatal record for results of 36-37 week rectovaginal culture. If positive, unknown, or preterm, initiate intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis
• **Ultrasound:** Bedside ultrasound can confirm fetal presentation and assess amniotic fluid volume
• **Labs:** Admission labs typically include CBC and Type & Screen
sections.prognosis:
• For an uncomplicated, normal labor and delivery at term, the prognosis for both the mother and infant is excellent
• Maternal recovery from a vaginal birth is typically faster than from a Cesarean section

sections.overview:
• **Preterm labor (PTL)** is defined as the onset of regular uterine contractions accompanied by cervical change (dilation and/or effacement) occurring before 37 completed weeks of gestation
    ◦ It is distinct from preterm *birth*, which is delivery before 37 weeks
    ◦ PTL is a major cause of perinatal morbidity and mortality, primarily due to the complications of prematurity in the neonate
    ◦ Management focuses on delaying delivery to allow for administration of corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity
sections.etiology:
• The exact mechanism is often unknown, but PTL is considered a pathologic syndrome initiated by multiple factors, with four primary proposed pathways:
    ◦ **Pathologic Uterine Activation / Stretch**
        ▪ **Overdistension** of the uterus from multiple gestation (e.g., twins) or polyhydramnios can trigger myometrial contractility
        ▪ Premature activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis (maternal or fetal stress)
    ◦ **Inflammation / Infection**
        ▪ **Intrauterine infections** (**chorioamnionitis**) are a well-established cause
        ▪ Extra-uterine infections (e.g., pyelonephritis, appendicitis, periodontal disease) can cause systemic inflammation
        ▪ Inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α) and prostaglandins are produced, which stimulate uterine contractions and cervical ripening
    ◦ **Decidual Hemorrhage / Ischemia**
        ▪ Bleeding at the decidual-chorionic interface (e.g., **placental abruption**) releases thrombin
        ▪ Thrombin is a potent uterotonic agent that directly stimulates contractions
        ▪ Uteroplacental ischemia can also lead to decidual necrosis and inflammation
    ◦ **Cervical Factors**
        ▪ **Cervical insufficiency** or a pathologically **short cervix** may be less able to resist the forces of uterine contractions
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects approximately 10-12% of all births in the United States
• The **leading cause of neonatal morbidity and mortality**
• Significant racial and ethnic disparities exist, with non-Hispanic Black women having the highest rates of preterm birth
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A pregnant patient between **20 and 36 6/7 weeks of gestation** presenting with symptoms of labor
    ◦ The key to diagnosis is differentiating true labor from benign uterine activity (**Braxton-Hicks contractions**) by identifying documented **cervical change**
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Based on gestational age (20 0/7 - 36 6/7 weeks) plus one of the following:
    ◦ Regular uterine contractions **AND**
    ◦ **Cervical change** (dilation ≥3 cm or effacement ≥80%) OR cervical change on subsequent exams
• **Fetal Monitoring**
    ◦ **Tocodynamometry**: External monitoring to confirm frequency and duration of contractions
    ◦ **Continuous Fetal Heart Rate Monitoring**: To assess fetal well-being
• **Transvaginal Ultrasound (TVUS)**
    ◦ **Measures cervical length**
    ◦ A **short cervix** (<25 mm before 24 weeks) is a strong predictor of preterm birth risk
• **Fetal Fibronectin (fFN)**
    ◦ A glycoprotein "glue" at the maternal-fetal interface
    ◦ **High Negative Predictive Value**: A negative result means there is a >99% chance of *not* delivering within the next 7-14 days; useful for deciding whom *not* to admit or treat
    ◦ Performed between 24-34 weeks on symptomatic patients with an intact membrane and minimal cervical dilation (<3 cm)
• **Lab Studies**
    ◦ Urinalysis and urine culture to rule out UTI
    ◦ **GBS culture** if status is unknown
    ◦ Wet mount to rule out vaginitis/BV
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is directly related to the gestational age at delivery, with survival and outcomes improving dramatically for each week delivery is delayed
    ◦ **< 23 weeks**: Generally considered pre-viable; survival is rare
    ◦ **24 weeks**: ~50% survival, high rates of severe morbidity
    ◦ **28 weeks**: >90% survival
    ◦ **34 weeks**: Survival rates approach that of term infants, but still at risk for minor morbidities

sections.overview:
• **Premature Rupture of Membranes (PROM)** is the rupture of the chorioamniotic membrane before the onset of regular uterine contractions (i.e., before labor begins)
    ◦ It can occur at any gestational age
    ◦ **Term PROM**: Rupture of membranes at or after **37 0/7 weeks** gestation before the onset of labor
    ◦ **Preterm PROM (PPROM)**: Rupture of membranes at **< 37 0/7 weeks** gestation
        ▪ This is a major cause of preterm birth and associated neonatal morbidity and mortality
    ◦ **Prolonged PROM**: Rupture of membranes lasting for more than **24 hours** before the onset of labor
        ▪ This increases the risk of infection
    ◦ **Latency Period**: The time from membrane rupture to the onset of labor
sections.etiology:
• The exact cause is often multifactorial or unknown, but the final common pathway is a weakening of the chorioamniotic membranes
    ◦ **Pathophysiologic Process**: Involves enzymatic degradation of the collagen in the extracellular matrix of the amnion and chorion
    ◦ **Inflammation/Infection**: Subclinical or overt intra-amniotic infection (e.g., from ascending vaginal flora like **GBS**, **_E. coli_**, or **bacterial vaginosis**) is a primary trigger
        ▪ Bacteria produce proteases (collagenases, elastases) and phospholipases that weaken the membranes and stimulate prostaglandin production, which can lead to contractions
    ◦ **Mechanical Stress**: Overdistension of the uterus can cause physical stretching and weakening of the membranes
        ▪ **Polyhydramnios**
        ▪ **Multiple gestation**
    ◦ **Cellular Changes**: Programmed cell death (apoptosis) in the amniotic membrane
    ◦ **Nutritional Deficiencies**: Deficiencies in copper or ascorbic acid (Vitamin C) can impair collagen synthesis
sections.epidemiology:
• **Term PROM**: Occurs in approximately 8-10% of all term pregnancies
• **PPROM**: Complicates approximately 3% of all pregnancies in the U.S.
    ◦ PPROM is responsible for approximately one-third of all preterm births
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A pregnant patient presents with a complaint of leaking fluid from the vagina
    ◦ The presentation can range from a sudden, large "gush" of clear fluid to a more insidious, intermittent, or slow trickle of fluid
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is primarily clinical, confirmed with bedside and laboratory tests
    ◦ **Nitrazine Test**
        ▪ **Procedure**: A sterile swab is used to collect fluid from the vaginal fornix and is applied to nitrazine paper
        ▪ **Positive Finding**: Paper turns **blue** (**pH > 6.5**)
        ▪ **Notes**: Amniotic fluid is alkaline (pH 7.1-7.3) while normal vaginal secretions are acidic (pH 4.5-6.0). **False Positives**: Blood, semen, **bacterial vaginosis**, alkaline antiseptics
    ◦ **Ferning Test**
        ▪ **Procedure**: Fluid from the posterior fornix is swabbed onto a glass slide and allowed to air dry completely
        ▪ **Positive Finding**: A "fern-like" pattern of crystallization is observed under a microscope
        ▪ **Notes**: Caused by the estrogen and NaCl content of amniotic fluid. More specific than nitrazine. **False Negatives**: Insufficient fluid, contamination with blood or cervical mucus
    ◦ **Ultrasound (U/S)**
        ▪ **Procedure**: Transabdominal ultrasound to assess amniotic fluid index (AFI)
        ▪ **Positive Finding**: **Oligohydramnios** (**AFI < 5 cm**) is supportive of the diagnosis but not diagnostic on its own
        ▪ **Notes**: A normal AFI does not rule out PROM. Useful for assessing fetal presentation and well-being
    ◦ **Commercial Tests** (e.g., AmniSure)
        ▪ **Procedure**: Immunoassay that detects **Placental Alpha Microglobulin-1 (PAMG-1)** in vaginal fluid
        ▪ **Positive Finding**: Positive test result
        ▪ **Notes**: Highly specific and sensitive. Useful when the clinical picture is unclear
sections.prognosis:
• Highly dependent on the **gestational age** at which rupture occurs
• At term, the prognosis for both mother and infant is excellent with appropriate management
• In PPROM, the primary driver of neonatal outcome is the degree of prematurity
• The risk of chorioamnionitis increases with the duration of membrane rupture

sections.overview:
• Preterm Premature Rupture of Membranes (PPROM) is the rupture of the amniotic and chorionic membranes **before 37 0/7 weeks of gestation** and **before the onset of labor**.
	◦ This event leads to the leakage of amniotic fluid.
	◦ PPROM is a leading cause of preterm birth and is responsible for a significant proportion of perinatal morbidity and mortality.
• Definitions:
	◦ **PPROM:** Rupture of membranes < 37 weeks gestation, prior to labor onset.
	◦ **PROM (Premature Rupture of Membranes):** Rupture of membranes ≥ 37 weeks gestation, prior to labor onset.
	◦ **Preterm Labor:** Uterine contractions causing cervical change < 37 weeks gestation, *with intact membranes*.
sections.etiology:
• The integrity of the fetal membranes is compromised through a multifactorial process, not a single cause.
• The final common pathway is the weakening and eventual rupture of the chorion and amnion.
• **Inflammation/Infection:**
	◦ This is the most widely accepted theory.
	◦ Subclinical intra-amniotic infection (e.g., from *Ureaplasma*, *Mycoplasma*, bacterial vaginosis) triggers an inflammatory cascade.
	◦ Maternal or fetal immune cells release pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α).
		▪ Cytokines stimulate the production of proteases, such as **matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)**, which degrade collagen and elastin within the fetal membranes.
	◦ Prostaglandins are also released, which can stimulate uterine contractions and further weaken membranes.
• **Mechanical Stress:**
	◦ Overdistension of the uterus can place excessive physical stress on the membranes.
	◦ Examples: Polyhydramnios, multiple gestations.
• **Decidual Hemorrhage/Abruption:**
	◦ Bleeding at the maternal-fetal interface (e.g., placental abruption) can lead to membrane breakdown.
• **Genetic Predisposition:**
	◦ Some individuals may have underlying connective tissue disorders or genetic variants that predispose them to weaker membranes.
sections.epidemiology:
• Accounts for approximately **3%** of all pregnancies in the United States.
• Responsible for roughly **one-third** of all preterm births.
• A major contributor to neonatal morbidity, mortality, and long-term disability due to the consequences of prematurity.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a patient reporting a sudden **"gush" of clear fluid** from the vagina.
• The presentation can be more subtle, described as a steady, watery leakage or just a feeling of persistent wetness.
• The fluid is typically odorless or may have a slightly sweet smell, in contrast to the ammonia smell of urine.
sections.diagnostics:
• The diagnosis is primarily clinical, confirmed with laboratory tests on the vaginal fluid collected during the SSE.
• **Nitrazine Test:**
	◦ **Principle:** Tests the pH of the fluid. Amniotic fluid is alkaline (pH 7.1-7.3), while the normal vaginal environment is acidic (pH 4.5-6.0).
	◦ **Result:** A swab of the fluid applied to nitrazine paper will turn **dark blue** (pH >6.5), indicating an alkaline pH consistent with amniotic fluid.
	◦ **False Positives:** Blood, semen, bacterial vaginosis, alkaline antiseptics.
• **Ferning Test:**
	◦ **Principle:** The electrolytes (sodium chloride) in amniotic fluid crystallize in a characteristic pattern when dried.
	◦ **Procedure:** A sample of the fluid is placed on a glass slide and allowed to air dry completely.
	◦ **Result:** Microscopic examination reveals a delicate, branching, "fern-like" pattern of crystals (arborization).
	◦ **False Positive:** Cervical mucus can sometimes produce a "pseudo-ferning" pattern, but it is less distinct.
• **Ultrasound:**
	◦ **Finding:** **Oligohydramnios** (low amniotic fluid index [AFI] <5 cm) is supportive of the diagnosis but is not diagnostic on its own (membranes can rupture with a normal AFI).
	◦ **Utility:** Essential for assessing gestational age, fetal presentation, fetal well-being (Biophysical Profile), and placental location.
• **Commercial Immunoassays (e.g., AmniSure):**
	◦ **Principle:** Detects placental alpha microglobulin-1 (PAMG-1), a protein found in high concentrations in amniotic fluid.
	◦ **Utility:** Very high sensitivity and specificity; useful in equivocal cases.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly dependent on the **gestational age at rupture** and the **latency period** achieved.
• Approximately 50% of patients with PPROM deliver within one week of membrane rupture.
• Neonatal survival increases dramatically with each week of advancing gestation.
• The use of corticosteroids, latency antibiotics, and magnesium sulfate has significantly improved neonatal outcomes.

sections.overview:
• Chorioamnionitis, now more commonly termed **Intra-amniotic Infection (IAI)**, is an acute inflammation and infection of the fetal membranes (chorion and amnion), amniotic fluid, placenta, and potentially the fetus.
    ◦ It is a significant cause of maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality, strongly associated with preterm labor and preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM).
    ◦ Diagnosis is primarily clinical, and management involves prompt administration of broad-spectrum antibiotics and delivery of the fetus.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• Occurs in approximately 2-5% of term pregnancies.
• Incidence is significantly higher in preterm births, especially those involving PPROM (up to 40-70%).
• Accounts for a substantial portion of early-onset neonatal sepsis.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Prolonged Rupture of Membranes (ROM):** The single greatest risk factor. Classically defined as >18 hours.
• **Preterm Premature Rupture of Membranes (PPROM)**
• Preterm labor
• Prolonged labor (especially with ruptured membranes)
• **Multiple digital vaginal exams** (introduces bacteria)
• Internal fetal or uterine monitoring (e.g., Fetal Scalp Electrode, Intrauterine Pressure Catheter)
• Nulliparity
• Genital tract infections (e.g., Bacterial Vaginosis, STIs, GBS colonization)
• Previous history of IAI
• Meconium-stained amniotic fluid
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a pregnant patient (often with ruptured membranes) who develops a fever during labor.
    ◦ The constellation of signs and symptoms points toward an intrauterine source of infection.
• Symptoms include:
    ◦ Fever / Chills
    ◦ Malaise
    ◦ Lower abdominal pain or pelvic pain
    ◦ Purulent or foul-smelling vaginal discharge / amniotic fluid
sections.physicalExam:
• **Maternal Fever:** Temperature **39.0C (102.2F)** on one occasion OR **38.0-38.9C (100.4-102.1F)** on two occasions at least 30 minutes apart.
• **Uterine Fundal Tenderness:** Pain upon palpation of the uterus, distinct from contraction pain.
• **Maternal Tachycardia:** Heart rate >120 bpm.
• **Fetal Tachycardia:** Fetal heart rate >160 bpm for 10 minutes.
• **Purulent or Malodorous Amniotic Fluid:** Visible at the cervical os or on a sterile speculum exam.
sections.diagnostics:
• IAI is primarily a **clinical diagnosis**.
    ◦ The gold standard (amniocentesis) is invasive and rarely used for this indication.
sections.management:
• **Intrapartum:**
    ◦ Initiate IV antibiotics immediately upon diagnosis of Suspected IAI.
    ◦ Proceed with delivery via induction or augmentation.
    ◦ Provide continuous maternal and fetal monitoring.
    ◦ Notify the neonatal care team of the IAI diagnosis to prepare for potential neonatal complications.
• **Postpartum:**
    ◦ **Vaginal Delivery:** Antibiotics are typically discontinued after delivery if the patient is afebrile and risk factors for endometritis are low.
        ▪ Some providers give at least one additional postpartum dose.
    ◦ **Cesarean Delivery:** At least one additional dose of antibiotics is recommended.
        ▪ Therapy is continued until the patient is afebrile and asymptomatic for 24-48 hours.
sections.prognosis:
• **Maternal:** Generally good with prompt diagnosis and treatment with antibiotics and delivery.
• **Neonatal:** Varies significantly based on gestational age at delivery and severity of the infection.
    ◦ The primary source of long-term morbidity associated with IAI is in the neonate, particularly the risk of neurodevelopmental delay and cerebral palsy.

sections.overview:
• Labor dystocia, commonly known as **"failure to progress,"** is the abnormal or difficult progression of labor.
• It is the leading indication for **primary cesarean delivery** in the United States.
• Dystocia is broadly characterized by a slower-than-normal rate of cervical dilation in the active phase of labor or a complete cessation of progress (**arrest**), including arrest of dilation or arrest of fetal descent.
• The diagnosis and management are framed around the **"Three P's"**: **Powers**, **Passenger**, and **Passage**.
sections.etiology:
• The underlying cause of labor dystocia can be attributed to one or more abnormalities in the **"Three P's"** of labor.
    ◦ **Powers (Uterine Contractions)**
        ▪ **Hypotonic uterine dysfunction**: The most common cause. Uterine contractions are either too weak, too infrequent, or not synchronized to effectively dilate the cervix.
        ▪ **Hypertonic or incoordinate uterine dysfunction**: Less common. Contractions are frequent and painful but are uncoordinated and ineffective at causing cervical change. Often seen in the latent phase.
    ◦ **Passenger (Fetus)**
        ▪ **Fetal Macrosomia**: Large fetal size (>4000-4500g) can lead to a mismatch with the maternal pelvis.
        ▪ **Fetal Malpresentation**: Any presentation other than occiput anterior (OA).
            - **Occiput Posterior (OP)**: Most common malpresentation, often leads to a longer, more painful labor (**"back labor"**).
            - **Breech, Transverse Lie, Face/Brow Presentation**: These often represent an absolute contraindication to vaginal delivery.
        ▪ **Fetal Anomalies**: Conditions like hydrocephalus can increase the size of the presenting part.
    ◦ **Passage (Pelvis and Soft Tissues)**
        ▪ **Cephalopelvic Disproportion (CPD)**: A true mismatch between the size of the fetal head and the maternal pelvis. The pelvis may be too small or abnormally shaped (e.g., android or platypelloid pelvis).
        ▪ **Soft Tissue Obstruction**: Obstructions in the birth canal, such as a full bladder, uterine fibroids, ovarian tumors, or cervical stenosis.
sections.epidemiology:
• Labor dystocia complicates approximately 8-11% of all labors.
• It is the most common indication for **primary cesarean delivery**, accounting for roughly 60% of cases.
• More common in **nulliparous women** compared to multiparous women.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The patient is a laboring woman whose progress, as monitored by serial cervical examinations, is not meeting expected milestones.
• She may report **exhaustion**, severe pain (especially **back pain** with OP position), and frustration with the lack of progress despite experiencing contractions.
sections.diagnostics:
• Labor dystocia is a **clinical diagnosis** based on established criteria for abnormal labor progression.
    ◦ **Definition of Active Phase Labor Arrest (ACOG Criteria):**
        ▪ Patient must be in the active phase (**6 cm dilated**) with **ruptured membranes**.
        ▪ **AND** one of the following:
            - **No cervical change for 4 hours** despite **adequate** uterine contractions (>200 MVUs).
            - **No cervical change for 6 hours** with **inadequate** uterine contractions.
    ◦ **Diagnostic Tools:**
        ▪ **Partogram**: A graphical representation of labor progress (dilation, station vs. time) used to identify deviations from the normal labor curve.
        ▪ **Intrauterine Pressure Catheter (IUPC)**: The gold standard for objectively diagnosing inadequate uterine "**Powers**."
        ▪ **Bedside Ultrasound**: Can confirm fetal presentation, position, and estimate fetal weight if not already known.
sections.prognosis:
• With appropriate and timely intervention (oxytocin, cesarean section), the prognosis for both mother and infant is generally excellent.
• The primary consequence is the increased rate of **operative delivery** and its associated risks.
• Women who have a C-section for labor dystocia have a higher risk of requiring a **repeat C-section** in subsequent pregnancies.

sections.overview:
• **Shoulder dystocia** is an obstetric emergency occurring during vaginal delivery when the fetal head has been delivered, but the anterior shoulder becomes impacted behind the maternal pubic symphysis.
    ◦ Less commonly, the posterior shoulder can be impacted on the sacral promontory.
• This impaction prevents the delivery of the remainder of the fetal body.
• Requires immediate recognition and a sequence of specific maneuvers to release the shoulder and prevent significant fetal and maternal morbidity and mortality.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ The fundamental cause is a size discrepancy between the fetal bisacromial diameter (the distance between the shoulders) and the maternal pelvic dimensions.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Failure of Rotation**: Normally, after the head delivers, the fetal shoulders rotate into the oblique diameter of the pelvis. In shoulder dystocia, this rotation fails, and the shoulders attempt to enter the pelvis in a direct anterior-posterior diameter.
    ◦ **Impaction**: The anterior fetal shoulder becomes wedged behind the symphysis pubis.
    ◦ **Cord Compression**: The delivered head and neck are outside the vagina, while the chest, containing the umbilical cord, is compressed within the birth canal.
        ▪ This leads to rapidly progressing fetal **hypoxia**, **acidosis**, and potential brain injury or death if not resolved quickly.
    ◦ **Brachial Plexus Stretch**: Excessive lateral traction on the fetal head to dislodge the shoulder stretches the brachial plexus nerves (C5-T1), leading to nerve injury (**palsy**).
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Occurs in approximately 0.2% to 3% of all vertex vaginal deliveries.
• The incidence is rising, likely due to increasing rates of fetal **macrosomia** secondary to maternal obesity and diabetes.
• Over 50% of shoulder dystocia cases occur in infants with normal birth weights and in mothers with no identifiable risk factors, making it an unpredictable event.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The diagnosis is made in real-time during delivery based on a cardinal sign:
    ◦ The fetal head delivers but then retracts against the maternal perineum. This is the pathognomonic **"Turtle Sign."**
• The delivery of the body does not occur with the next contraction and gentle, routine axial traction.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Shoulder dystocia** is a **clinical diagnosis** made intrapartum.
    ◦ There are **no laboratory or imaging studies** to confirm the diagnosis at the moment it occurs.
    ◦ The diagnosis is confirmed when the routine delivery of the shoulders is unsuccessful after the delivery of the head.
• **Antepartum Ultrasound**:
    ◦ Can be used to estimate fetal weight (EFW) and identify **macrosomia** (a risk factor), but it has a high margin of error (+/- 15%) and is a poor predictor of shoulder dystocia.
    ◦ Prophylactic C-section based on EFW is controversial but may be considered for:
        ▪ EFW >5,000 g in a non-diabetic mother.
        ▪ EFW >4,500 g in a diabetic mother.
sections.prognosis:
• **Neonate**:
    ◦ The majority of infants (>95%) delivered after shoulder dystocia have no permanent injuries.
    ◦ Over 80% of brachial plexus palsies resolve spontaneously within 6-12 months.
    ◦ Fractures typically heal well without intervention.
• **Maternal**:
    ◦ Physical prognosis is excellent.
    ◦ The primary long-term concern is the increased risk of shoulder dystocia in future pregnancies and the associated psychological trauma.
    ◦ A discussion about elective C-section for subsequent pregnancies is warranted.

sections.overview:
• An umbilical cord prolapse is an acute obstetric emergency in which the umbilical cord descends into the lower uterine segment, preceding or lying alongside the fetal presenting part, after the rupture of membranes.
    ◦ This can lead to compression of the cord between the fetus and the maternal pelvis or cervix.
    ◦ Cord compression obstructs blood flow through the umbilical vessels, causing rapid fetal hypoxemia, acidosis, and potentially irreversible neurological damage or death if not managed immediately.
• There are three main types:
    ◦ **Overt Prolapse:** The cord is ahead of the presenting part and can be seen or palpated in the vagina or at the introitus. Most common type.
    ◦ **Occult Prolapse:** The cord is alongside the presenting part but has not advanced past it. Cannot be seen or felt on exam. Suspected with FHR changes.
    ◦ **Funic (Cord) Presentation:** The cord is between the presenting part and the cervix, but the membranes are still intact. Not a true prolapse but a major risk factor for one upon ROM.
sections.etiology:
• The underlying cause is any condition that creates a space between the fetal presenting part and the maternal pelvic inlet, allowing the cord to slip through.
• **Pathophysiological Cascade:**
    ◦ **Prolapse:** The umbilical cord descends ahead of the presenting part, typically following rupture of membranes (ROM).
    ◦ **Compression:** The cord becomes trapped and compressed between the descending fetal part (usually the head) and the maternal bony pelvis, cervix, or vagina.
    ◦ **Vascular Occlusion:**
        ▪ **Umbilical Vein:** The thin-walled vein is compressed first, cutting off oxygenated blood flow from the placenta to the fetus.
        ▪ **Umbilical Arteries:** The thicker-walled arteries are compressed next, preventing deoxygenated blood from returning to the placenta.
        ▪ **Vasospasm:** Exposure of the cord to the cooler temperature of the vagina can also induce vasospasm, further restricting blood flow.
    ◦ **Fetal Consequences:** The occlusion leads to rapid-onset fetal hypoxia, hypercarbia, and metabolic/respiratory acidosis. This manifests as severe, prolonged bradycardia on fetal heart rate (FHR) monitoring.
    ◦ **Outcome:** If compression is not relieved promptly, it results in hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE), cerebral palsy, or fetal demise.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence:** Occurs in approximately 0.1% to 0.6% of all deliveries (roughly 1 in 300).
• **Presentation-Specific Incidence:**
    ◦ Cephalic presentation: ~0.5%
    ◦ Frank Breech: ~1%
    ◦ Complete Breech: ~5%
    ◦ Footling Breech: ~15% (highest risk)
    ◦ Transverse Lie: ~20%
sections.clinicalPresentation: • The classic presentation is the **sudden onset of severe, prolonged fetal bradycardia or profound, recurrent variable decelerations on the fetal heart rate monitor**, often occurring immediately after rupture of membranes (spontaneous or artificial).
sections.diagnostics:
• The diagnosis is made **clinically** and does not require imaging or labs.
    ◦ **Definitive Diagnosis:** Direct visualization of the cord at the introitus OR palpation of the cord during a sterile vaginal exam.
    ◦ **High Index of Suspicion:** Any sudden, severe change in FHR tracing, especially after ROM, should prompt an immediate SVE to rule out cord prolapse.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is highly dependent on the **duration and severity of cord compression.**
• With rapid recognition and delivery (typically within 30 minutes), neonatal outcomes are generally excellent.
• Prolonged delays lead to a significant increase in perinatal morbidity and mortality.

sections.overview:
• **Operative Vaginal Delivery (OVD)** refers to a vaginal birth assisted by either **forceps** or a **vacuum extractor**.
    ◦ The device is applied to the fetal head to provide traction and assist the mother's pushing efforts to expedite delivery.
• It is performed during the **second stage of labor** as an alternative to **cesarean delivery** when specific indications are met and strict prerequisites are fulfilled.
• The choice between **forceps** and **vacuum** depends on the clinical scenario, fetal position, and operator experience.
• **Vacuum-assisted delivery** is now more common than **forceps delivery** in the United States.
sections.etiology:
• The need for **OVD** arises when spontaneous vaginal delivery is unlikely or when rapid delivery is required for maternal or fetal benefit.
• **Indications for OVD**:
    ◦ **Prolonged Second Stage of Labor**: The most common indication.
        ▪ **Nulliparous**: >3 hours of pushing with regional anesthesia, or >2 hours without.
        ▪ **Multiparous**: >2 hours of pushing with regional anesthesia, or >1 hour without.
    ◦ **Maternal Exhaustion**: The mother is unable to generate effective pushing efforts.
    ◦ **Non-Reassuring Fetal Status**: A suspicious or abnormal fetal heart rate tracing (e.g., **recurrent late decelerations**, **bradycardia**, minimal variability) in the second stage of labor where delivery is imminent.
    ◦ **Maternal Medical Conditions**: Conditions where prolonged pushing (**Valsalva maneuver**) is contraindicated or should be shortened.
        ▪ **Cardiac**: **Aortic stenosis**, **pulmonary hypertension**, some congenital heart diseases.
        ▪ **Neurologic**: **Intracranial aneurysm**, certain neuromuscular disorders.
        ▪ **Pulmonary**: Severe restrictive lung disease.
sections.epidemiology:
• **OVD** accounts for approximately 3% of all vaginal deliveries in the United States.
• The rate of **OVD** has been declining over the past few decades, while the rate of primary **cesarean delivery** for second-stage arrest has increased.
• **Vacuum extraction** is used in about 80% of OVDs, while **forceps** are used in about 20%.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient in the **second stage of labor** (cervix **fully dilated to 10 cm**) who develops one of the indications for **OVD** (e.g., **fetal bradycardia**, **prolonged pushing** without descent).
• The fetal head is engaged in the pelvis, and the provider determines that a vaginal delivery can be safely accomplished with assistance.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Assessment**: The decision is primarily based on clinical evaluation of labor progress and maternal/fetal status.
• **Continuous Fetal Heart Rate Monitoring**: Essential to assess fetal well-being before and during the procedure.
• **Intrapartum Ultrasound**: Can be used to confirm fetal head position if the digital exam is uncertain.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is generally excellent for both mother and infant when **OVD** is performed for the correct indication by a skilled operator.
• A successful **OVD** avoids the morbidity of a **cesarean delivery** (e.g., longer recovery, infection, VTE, future uterine rupture risk).
• Most neonatal complications (e.g., **cephalohematoma**, **facial nerve palsy**) are transient and resolve completely.
• Maternal risk of long-term **pelvic floor dysfunction** (incontinence, prolapse) is increased compared to spontaneous vaginal delivery.

sections.overview:
• A **Cesarean delivery (C-section)** is a major abdominal surgical procedure used to deliver a fetus through incisions in the abdomen (**laparotomy**) and uterus (**hysterotomy**).
• It is performed when a vaginal delivery is not feasible or poses a greater risk to the mother or fetus.
• While potentially life-saving, it is associated with increased maternal and neonatal morbidity compared to vaginal delivery.
• The rate in the United States is approximately 32%.
sections.etiology:
• A **Cesarean delivery** is not a disease but a treatment for underlying maternal or fetal conditions.
    ◦ The indications (etiologies) are the primary drivers for the procedure.
• **Common Indications for Cesarean Delivery**:
    ◦ **Labor Dystocia / Failure to Progress**: The most common indication.
        ▪ **Arrest of Active Labor**: No cervical change for 4 hours with adequate uterine contractions or 6 hours with inadequate contractions.
        ▪ **Arrest of Descent**: No fetal descent after 1 hour of pushing (2 hours for nulliparous).
    ◦ **Previous Uterine Surgery**:
        ▪ **Prior Classical Cesarean Section**: A vertical incision in the upper, contractile portion of the uterus carries a high risk (4-9%) of **uterine rupture** during a subsequent trial of labor. This is an absolute indication for a repeat C-section.
        ▪ **Prior Myomectomy**: If the surgery entered or significantly disrupted the uterine cavity.
    ◦ **Non-reassuring Fetal Status (Fetal Distress)**:
        ▪ Indicated by a **Category III fetal heart rate tracing** (e.g., recurrent late decelerations, severe variable decelerations, bradycardia, sinusoidal pattern) that is non-responsive to conservative measures (oxygen, position change, IV fluids).
    ◦ **Fetal Malpresentation**:
        ▪ **Breech Presentation**: Buttocks or feet presenting first. **External cephalic version (ECV)** may be attempted, but if unsuccessful or contraindicated, C-section is the standard of care.
        ▪ **Transverse Lie**: Fetus is positioned horizontally across the uterus.
    ◦ **Placental Abnormalities**:
        ▪ **Placenta Previa**: The placenta partially or completely covers the internal cervical os, blocking the exit. Vaginal delivery would cause catastrophic hemorrhage.
        ▪ **Placental Abruption**: Premature separation of the placenta from the uterine wall. An emergent C-section is required if there is significant bleeding or fetal distress.
        ▪ **Vasa Previa**: Fetal blood vessels run over the cervical os, unprotected by the umbilical cord or placenta. Rupture of membranes can tear these vessels, leading to rapid fetal exsanguination.
    ◦ **Maternal Indications**:
        ▪ **Active Genital Herpes Infection**: To prevent neonatal transmission during vaginal passage.
        ▪ **High Viral Load HIV**: To reduce vertical transmission.
        ▪ **Maternal Hemodynamic Instability**: In cases of trauma or severe preeclampsia where prolonged labor is unsafe.
    ◦ **Emergencies**:
        ▪ **Umbilical Cord Prolapse**: The umbilical cord descends ahead of the presenting fetal part, leading to cord compression and fetal hypoxia. This is a true obstetric emergency.
        ▪ **Uterine Rupture**: Tearing of the uterine wall, often at the site of a prior scar.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: ~32% of all births in the U.S. (The WHO suggests an ideal rate of 10-15%).
• **Most Common Indication**: **Labor dystocia**, often followed by repeat C-section, non-reassuring fetal status, and malpresentation.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is that of the underlying indication requiring the C-section.
• **Scheduled/Elective**:
    ◦ Patient presents at a scheduled time, usually asymptomatic.
    ◦ Indication is known (e.g., malpresentation confirmed by ultrasound, **placenta previa**, planned repeat C-section).
• **Urgent/Intrapartum**: Patient is in labor.
    ◦ **Failure to Progress**: Prolonged labor course with lack of cervical dilation or fetal descent noted on serial cervical exams.
    ◦ **Fetal Distress**: An abnormal fetal heart rate pattern is observed on the monitor.
    ◦ **Placental Abruption**: Presents with **painful, dark red vaginal bleeding** and a **rigid, tender uterus**.
    ◦ **Placenta Previa**: Presents with **painless, bright red vaginal bleeding**.
• **Emergent**: A sudden, life-threatening event.
    ◦ **Cord Prolapse**: Sudden, severe fetal **bradycardia** immediately following rupture of membranes. The cord may be palpable on vaginal exam.
    ◦ **Uterine Rupture**: Sudden onset of intense abdominal pain, loss of fetal station, and fetal distress.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Continuous Fetal Heart Rate Monitoring (Cardiotocography)**: Essential for assessing fetal well-being during labor.
• **Ultrasound**:
    ◦ Confirms fetal presentation (**breech**, **transverse**).
    ◦ Confirms placental location (**previa**).
    ◦ Can help diagnose **abruption** (retroplacental hematoma).
    ◦ Estimates fetal weight (**macrosomia**).
• **Sterile Speculum & Digital Cervical Exams**:
    ◦ Used to assess labor progress and diagnose conditions like **cord prolapse**.
    ◦ **Note**: A digital vaginal exam is **contraindicated** in known or suspected **placenta previa**.
• **Laboratory Studies**:
    ◦ **CBC**: To establish baseline hemoglobin/hematocrit.
    ◦ **Type and Screen**: To prepare for potential blood transfusion.
sections.prognosis:
• Overall prognosis is excellent for both mother and infant.
• Maternal mortality is low but significantly higher than with vaginal delivery (approx. 2.2 vs 0.2 per 100,000 births).
• The decision to perform a C-section involves balancing the immediate risks of surgery against the risks of vaginal delivery in a specific clinical scenario.
• Patients with a prior low-transverse C-section can be candidates for a **Trial of Labor After Cesarean (TOLAC)**, with a ~70% success rate of achieving a **Vaginal Birth After Cesarean (VBAC)**.

sections.overview:
• Postpartum Hemorrhage (PPH) is a severe, potentially life-threatening obstetric emergency characterized by excessive bleeding following childbirth. It is a leading cause of maternal morbidity and mortality worldwide.
    ◦ **Classic Definition**: Cumulative blood loss of **>500 mL** following a vaginal delivery or **>1,000 mL** following a cesarean delivery.
    ◦ **ACOG 2017 Updated Definition**: Cumulative blood loss of **1,000 mL** OR bleeding associated with signs/symptoms of hypovolemia within 24 hours of birth, regardless of the route of delivery.
    ◦ **Primary PPH**: Occurs within the first 24 hours postpartum (most common).
    ◦ **Secondary (or Delayed) PPH**: Occurs between 24 hours and 12 weeks postpartum.
sections.etiology:
• The causes of PPH are classically remembered by the mnemonic **"The 4 T's"**.
    ◦ **Tone (Uterine Atony) - ~80% of cases**
        ▪ **Pathophysiology**: The myometrium fails to contract adequately after delivery. Normally, uterine contraction compresses the spiral arteries at the placental implantation site, achieving hemostasis. In atony, these vessels remain open and continue to bleed profusely.
        ▪ This is the **most common cause** of PPH.
    ◦ **Trauma (Lacerations/Rupture) - ~15%**
        ▪ **Pathophysiology**: Bleeding occurs from lacerations of the genital tract or uterine rupture, despite a well-contracted (firm) uterus.
        ▪ **Locations**: Perineum, vagina, cervix, or uterus (uterine rupture is a catastrophic event).
        ▪ **Causes**: Precipitous delivery, operative vaginal delivery (forceps, vacuum), large infant, episiotomy.
    ◦ **Tissue (Retained Products of Conception) - ~5%**
        ▪ **Pathophysiology**: Retained placental fragments or membranes act as a foreign body, preventing the uterus from contracting fully and uniformly.
        ▪ **Causes**: Incomplete placental separation, placenta accreta spectrum, succenturiate placental lobe.
    ◦ **Thrombin (Coagulopathy) - ~<1%**
        ▪ **Pathophysiology**: A pre-existing or acquired clotting disorder prevents normal hemostasis. The patient is unable to form clots to stop the bleeding.
        ▪ **Causes**:
            ▪ **Pre-existing**: Von Willebrand disease, hemophilia.
            ▪ **Acquired**: Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC) from severe preeclampsia, HELLP syndrome, amniotic fluid embolism, sepsis, or massive hemorrhage itself (dilutional coagulopathy).
sections.epidemiology:
• Occurs in 1-5% of all deliveries.
• Accounts for approximately 25% of maternal deaths worldwide.
• Uterine atony is the cause in about 80% of cases.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The patient presents with persistent, heavy vaginal bleeding after delivery.
    ◦ The clinical picture can evolve rapidly from stable to profound shock.
    ◦ Initial vital signs may be normal due to physiologic compensation, with tachycardia being the earliest sign of hypovolemia.
sections.diagnostics:
• PPH is primarily a **clinical diagnosis** based on estimated blood loss and patient stability. Labs and imaging help guide management and determine the underlying cause.
    ◦ **Laboratory Studies**
        ▪ **CBC**: To assess baseline and serial hemoglobin/hematocrit and platelet count.
        ▪ **Type & Crossmatch**: Essential for blood product transfusion.
        ▪ **Coagulation Panel**: PT, PTT, INR, and **fibrinogen**.
            ▪ A low **fibrinogen** level (<200 mg/dL) is an early and strong predictor of severe PPH.
    ◦ **Imaging**
        ▪ **Bedside Ultrasound**: Can be used to quickly identify retained products of conception (RPOC) or hematomas.
sections.prognosis:
• With prompt recognition, a multidisciplinary team approach, and adherence to established protocols, the prognosis is generally good in well-resourced settings.
• Delayed diagnosis or management significantly increases the risk of severe morbidity and mortality.

sections.overview:
• **Postpartum endometritis** is an infection of the **decidua** (the pregnancy endometrium), which may extend into the myometrium (**endomyometritis**) and parametrium (**parametritis**).
• It is the most common cause of **postpartum infection and fever**.
• The diagnosis is primarily **clinical**, based on the presence of **postpartum fever**, **uterine tenderness**, and **tachycardia**.
• Treatment involves prompt initiation of broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics.
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**: An **ascending infection** of the uterine cavity from the normal flora of the vagina and cervix. After delivery, the uterine environment is highly susceptible to infection due to:
	◦ The raw placental implantation site providing a rich culture medium.
	◦ The presence of lochia (blood, tissue, mucus) which also serves as a growth medium.
	◦ Disruption of the endocervical barrier and a dilated cervix.
	◦ Micro-lacerations and trauma to the genital tract.
• **Microbiology**: The infection is almost always **polymicrobial**, involving a mixture of aerobes and anaerobes.
	◦ **Common Aerobes**: **Group B Streptococcus (GBS)**, **Group A Streptococcus (GAS)**, ***Enterococcus***, ***Escherichia coli***, ***Gardnerella vaginalis***.
	◦ **Common Anaerobes**: ***Bacteroides*** spp., ***Peptostreptococcus***, ***Prevotella*** spp.
	◦ **Less Common**: ***Chlamydia trachomatis*** (often associated with late-onset endometritis, >1 week postpartum).
sections.epidemiology:
• Occurs in 1-3% of vaginal deliveries.
• Incidence is significantly higher following **Cesarean delivery**, ranging from 5-15% even with antibiotic prophylaxis.
	◦ Without prophylaxis, the rate can be as high as 30%.
• It is the **leading cause of postpartum fever**.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Single most significant risk factor: Cesarean section**.
• **Prolonged rupture of membranes (PROM)** (>18-24 hours).
• **Prolonged labor** (>12 hours), especially with multiple cervical examinations.
• Internal fetal/uterine monitoring.
• Manual removal of the placenta.
• Pre-existing lower genital tract infection (e.g., bacterial vaginosis, GBS colonization, chlamydia).
• Low socioeconomic status.
• Anemia.
• Operative vaginal delivery (forceps, vacuum).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a postpartum patient (typically **2-3 days** after delivery, but can occur up to 6 weeks) who develops a fever, tachycardia, and abdominal pain.
• Onset is usually within the first 10 days postpartum.
• **Symptoms**
	◦ **Fever** (>38.0C / 100.4F) and chills (hallmark).
	◦ **Lower abdominal or pelvic pain**.
	◦ **Malaise**, fatigue.
	◦ **Foul-smelling lochia** (may be purulent or bloody).
	◦ Headache.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Fever**: Temperature 38.0C (100.4F) on two occasions at least 6 hours apart, after the first 24 hours postpartum.
• **Tachycardia**: Often disproportionate to the degree of fever.
• **Uterine Tenderness**: **Exquisite fundal tenderness** on abdominal palpation and/or bimanual exam is the key finding.
• **Purulent or foul-smelling lochia** may be observed on pelvic exam.
• **Subinvolution**: Uterus may be boggy, soft, and larger than expected for the number of days postpartum.
• **Rule out other sources**: It is critical to perform a full exam to rule out other causes of fever (check breasts for mastitis, C/S incision for wound infection, perineum for laceration infection, and assess for CVA tenderness for pyelonephritis).
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is primarily **clinical**.
	◦ Lab work and imaging are supportive and help rule out other causes or identify complications.
• **Labs**
	◦ **CBC**: **Leukocytosis** (WBC >15,000-20,000) with a left shift is common but non-specific, as leukocytosis is normal in the postpartum period.
	◦ **Blood Cultures**: Recommended for patients with high fever (>39C), signs of sepsis, or who do not respond to initial antibiotic therapy.
	◦ **Urinalysis and Urine Culture**: To rule out UTI/pyelonephritis.
• **Imaging (Not routinely indicated)**
	◦ Performed if the patient fails to respond to 48-72 hours of appropriate IV antibiotics.
	◦ **Pelvic Ultrasound**: To evaluate for **retained products of conception (RPOC)** or uterine abscess.
	◦ **Pelvic CT with contrast**: More sensitive for diagnosing pelvic abscess, **septic pelvic thrombophlebitis**, or ovarian vein thrombosis.
sections.treatment:
• **Inpatient admission and IV antibiotics** are required.
• **First-Line Regimen (Gold Standard):**
	◦ **Clindamycin 900 mg IV q8h + Gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV q24h**
		▪ *Rationale*: Excellent broad-spectrum coverage for polymicrobial infections. Clindamycin covers most anaerobes and gram-positive cocci. Gentamicin covers gram-negative aerobes.
• **Alternative Regimens:**
	◦ Ampicillin-sulbactam
	◦ Piperacillin-tazobactam
	◦ A cephalosporin (e.g., Cefoxitin, Cefotetan)
• **Add Ampicillin** to the Clindamycin/Gentamicin regimen if suspecting ***Enterococcus*** or known **GBS colonization**.
• **Duration**: Continue IV therapy until the patient is clinically improved and has been **afebrile for 24-48 hours**.
• **Oral Antibiotics**: Routine use of oral antibiotics after successful IV therapy is **not generally recommended** for uncomplicated endometritis.
sections.management:
• For patients who fail to improve on first-line therapy, management may include:
	◦ Adding Ampicillin for ***Enterococcus*** coverage.
	◦ Performing imaging (US or CT) to look for complications (abscess, **RPOC**, **septic pelvic thrombophlebitis**).
	◦ Broadening antibiotic coverage.
sections.complications:
• **Sepsis** / Septic Shock
• **Pelvic abscess** / Peritonitis
• Wound infection or dehiscence
• **Septic Pelvic Thrombophlebitis (SPT)**
	◦ A rare but serious complication involving thrombosis of the ovarian or pelvic veins.
	◦ Suspect in a patient with persistent "picket-fence" fevers despite broad-spectrum antibiotics.
	◦ Diagnosis is often clinical or confirmed by CT/MRI.
	◦ Treatment involves adding anticoagulation (e.g., heparin) to the antibiotic regimen.
• Long-term: Infertility, ectopic pregnancy (due to tubal scarring).
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is **excellent** with prompt diagnosis and treatment with appropriate IV antibiotics.
• Most patients show significant clinical improvement within 48-72 hours.
• Mortality is very low in the developed world.

sections.overview:
• **Postpartum (Lactational) Mastitis** is an inflammation of the breast parenchyma, often caused by infection, occurring in women who are breastfeeding.
    ◦ It typically presents with a localized, painful, erythematous area on one breast, accompanied by systemic symptoms like fever and myalgias.
• A **Breast Abscess** is a localized collection of pus within the breast tissue, representing a severe complication of unresolved or inadequately treated mastitis.
sections.etiology:
• **Primary Cause:** Milk stasis leading to ductal obstruction.
    ◦ Incomplete emptying of the breast allows milk to stagnate, providing a rich medium for bacterial growth.
• **Infectious Agent:** The most common pathogen is **_Staphylococcus aureus_**.
    ◦ Methicillin-resistant _S. aureus_ (MRSA) should be considered in cases of treatment failure, hospital-acquired infection, or high community prevalence.
    ◦ Other less common organisms include _Streptococcus pyogenes_, _Escherichia coli_, and _Bacteroides_ species.
• **Mechanism:**
    ◦ **Milk Stasis:** Caused by poor latch, infrequent feedings, or abrupt weaning.
    ◦ **Ductal Obstruction:** Stagnant milk thickens and obstructs a milk duct.
    ◦ **Bacterial Entry:** Bacteria from the infant's nasopharynx or the mother's skin colonize the stagnant milk, typically entering through small cracks or fissures in the nipple.
    ◦ **Infection & Inflammation:** Bacterial proliferation leads to an inflammatory response in the surrounding breast tissue, causing the classic signs of mastitis.
    ◦ **Abscess Formation:** If the infection is not effectively treated, neutrophils and inflammatory debris become walled off by a fibrous capsule, forming a collection of pus (abscess).
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects up to 20% of breastfeeding women.
• Most common in the **first 6 weeks postpartum**, but can occur at any time during lactation.
• **Primiparous** (first-time) mothers are at higher risk.
• Typically a **unilateral** condition.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Milk Stasis:**
    ◦ Ineffective milk removal (poor latch, tongue-tie in infant)
    ◦ Infrequent or missed feedings
    ◦ Abrupt weaning
    ◦ Oversupply of milk
    ◦ Pressure on the breast (e.g., tight-fitting bra, seatbelt)
• **Nipple Trauma:**
    ◦ Cracked, fissured, or damaged nipples provide a portal of entry for bacteria.
• **Maternal Factors:**
    ◦ Previous history of mastitis
    ◦ Maternal stress and fatigue
    ◦ Malnutrition
• **Other:**
    ◦ Use of a manual breast pump with improper flange fit.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The typical patient is a breastfeeding woman, 2-6 weeks postpartum, who presents with an acute onset of a painful, red, swollen area on one breast, accompanied by systemic, flu-like symptoms.
• **Local Symptoms:**
    ◦ Unilateral breast pain (often intense and constant)
    ◦ Breast tenderness, swelling, and warmth
    ◦ Erythema (redness)
    ◦ A palpable lump or hardened area
• **Systemic Symptoms:**
    ◦ Fever (>38.3C or 101F)
    ◦ Chills
    ◦ Myalgias (body aches)
    ◦ Malaise and fatigue
    ◦ Headache
sections.physicalExam:
• **Inspection:**
    ◦ Localized erythema, often in a **wedge-shaped pattern**.
    ◦ Edema and swelling of the affected breast segment.
• **Palpation:**
    ◦ **Mastitis:** A firm, indurated, tender, and warm area.
    ◦ **Abscess:** A distinct, palpable, **fluctuant mass**. Tenderness is often exquisite over the abscess.
• **Regional Nodes:**
    ◦ Tender ipsilateral axillary lymphadenopathy may be present.
• **Vitals:**
    ◦ Fever, tachycardia.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Mastitis:**
    ◦ Primarily a **clinical diagnosis**. Laboratory tests and imaging are not routinely required for uncomplicated cases.
• **Breast Abscess / Complicated Mastitis:**
    ◦ **Ultrasound:** **Diagnostic modality of choice**. Differentiates between simple mastitis (cellulitis/phlegmon) and a drainable abscess.
        ▪ **Abscess appearance on US:** A well-defined, complex, anechoic or hypoechoic fluid collection with a thick, irregular wall and posterior acoustic enhancement. May see swirling debris within.
    ◦ **Milk Culture & Sensitivity:** Recommended for:
        ▪ Severe or recurrent infections
        ▪ Hospital-acquired infections
        ▪ Failure to respond to initial antibiotic therapy within 48-72 hours
    ◦ **Blood Cultures:** If the patient appears septic.
    ◦ **CBC:** May show leukocytosis with a left shift, but is non-specific.
sections.management:
• **Follow-up:** Patients should be re-evaluated in **24-48 hours**.
• **Lack of Improvement:** If symptoms do not improve, reconsider the diagnosis. Perform a breast ultrasound to rule out an abscess and consider the possibility of a resistant organism or inflammatory breast cancer.
sections.complications:
• **Breast Abscess** (most common)
• Recurrent mastitis
• Sepsis (rare)
• Premature cessation of breastfeeding
• Breast fistula formation
• Scarring or breast deformity after I&D
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent with prompt diagnosis and appropriate management.
• Most women recover fully without long-term sequelae.
• Recurrence rate is higher if underlying causes (e.g., poor latch) are not corrected.
sections.preventionEducation:
• **Patient Education:** Reassure the patient that it is safe and highly recommended to continue breastfeeding from both breasts. The infection will not harm the infant. Stopping abruptly will worsen milk stasis and the infection.
• **Lactation Consultant Referral:** Highly recommended to address underlying issues like poor latch to prevent recurrence.

sections.overview:
• Postpartum blues, commonly known as **"baby blues,"** is a transient, mild, and self-limiting mood disturbance that occurs in the first two weeks after childbirth.
    ◦ Characterized by emotional lability, tearfulness, anxiety, and irritability.
• It is considered a normal adjustment reaction to the physiological and psychosocial changes of the postpartum period.
• It is distinct from the more severe postpartum psychiatric disorders like postpartum depression (PPD) and postpartum psychosis.
sections.etiology:
• The exact etiology is not fully understood but is believed to be multifactorial, involving a combination of hormonal, psychological, and social factors.
• **Hormonal Changes:**
    ◦ The primary proposed mechanism is the rapid and profound drop in reproductive hormones, specifically **estrogen and progesterone**, that occurs immediately following delivery of the placenta.
    ◦ The abrupt withdrawal of these neuroactive steroids is thought to destabilize mood-regulating neurotransmitter systems.
• **Neurotransmitter Dysregulation:**
    ◦ Fluctuations in serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine systems may be involved.
    ◦ Elevated levels of monoamine oxidase A (**MAO-A**), an enzyme that breaks down these neurotransmitters, have been observed in the early postpartum period.
• **Psychosocial Stressors:** The transition to motherhood involves significant stressors that contribute to mood changes:
    ◦ **Sleep deprivation**
    ◦ Physical discomfort and recovery from childbirth
    ◦ Emotional stress of new parental responsibilities
    ◦ Feelings of being overwhelmed and loss of personal freedom
sections.epidemiology:
• Extremely common, affecting an estimated **50-85%** of all new mothers.
• Occurs across all cultures, ethnicities, and socioeconomic strata.
• Prevalence does not seem to be significantly affected by parity (first-time vs. subsequent births), although primiparous mothers may report more stress.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a new mother who is **2 to 4 days postpartum** and reports sudden, unprovoked episodes of crying and emotional lability.
• She may feel happy and bonded with her infant one moment and then sad and overwhelmed the next.
• She remains oriented, rational, and her ability to function and care for her infant is **intact**.
• The symptoms are distressing but do not cause significant functional impairment.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Diagnosis is entirely clinical,** based on the characteristic symptoms, timing (onset within days of delivery), and transient nature.
• **No laboratory or imaging studies are indicated** for the diagnosis of postpartum blues.
• **Screening Tools:**
    ◦ The **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)** is a validated 10-item questionnaire used to screen for postpartum depression.
    ◦ While not designed for "blues," it is a valuable tool to use at the first postpartum visit to establish a baseline and screen for PPD.
    ◦ A score >10 suggests possible depression and warrants further evaluation.
• Consider labs to rule out other causes if symptoms are atypical or persistent:
    ◦ **TSH:** To rule out postpartum thyroiditis.
    ◦ **CBC:** To rule out anemia causing fatigue.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent.**
• Symptoms typically peak around the 5th day postpartum and resolve spontaneously without intervention by **day 10-14 postpartum.**

sections.overview:
• **Postpartum Depression (PPD)** is a **major depressive episode** with onset during pregnancy or within the first year following delivery
• It is a DSM-5 specifier ("**with peripartum onset**") for a major depressive disorder (MDD) episode
• PPD is characterized by symptoms of depression, severe anxiety, and exhaustion that significantly impair a woman's ability to care for herself and her infant
• It is more persistent and severe than the "**postpartum blues**" but less severe than **postpartum psychosis**
sections.etiology:
• The etiology of PPD is multifactorial, involving a complex interplay of biological, genetic, and psychosocial factors
    ◦ **Hormonal Fluctuations**: A rapid and dramatic drop in **estrogen** and **progesterone** levels immediately following childbirth is a primary suspected trigger. Fluctuations in thyroid hormones (e.g., **postpartum thyroiditis**) can also mimic or contribute to depressive symptoms.
    ◦ **Neurotransmitter Dysregulation**: Similar to MDD, there is believed to be dysregulation in neurotransmitter systems, particularly **serotonin**, **norepinephrine**, and **dopamine**. The neuroactive steroid **allopregnanolone** (a progesterone metabolite) rapidly declines post-delivery, affecting GABA-A receptor function, which is linked to mood and anxiety.
    ◦ **Psychosocial Stressors**:
        ▪ Sleep deprivation
        ▪ Physical recovery from childbirth
        ▪ The immense responsibility of caring for a newborn
        ▪ Lack of social support
        ▪ Marital or financial stress
    ◦ **Genetic Predisposition**: A personal or family history of mood disorders significantly increases susceptibility.
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects approximately **10-15%** of new mothers
• Can also occur in fathers and adoptive parents
• Onset is most common within the **first 3 months postpartum** but can occur anytime within the first year
• It is one of the most common medical complications of childbirth
• Significantly **underdiagnosed** and undertreated due to stigma and symptom overlap with normal postpartum changes
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient, typically a mother within one year of childbirth, presents with persistent low mood and functional impairment
• She may not volunteer depressive symptoms and instead complain of fatigue, anxiety, or somatic symptoms
• The presentation often centers on her perceived inadequacies as a mother
• A concerned partner or family member may initiate the visit
• Symptoms must be present for **at least 2 weeks**
sections.diagnostics:
• **Screening**
    ◦ Universal screening is recommended at postpartum and well-child visits
• **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)**
    ◦ 10-item questionnaire
    ◦ A score of **10** indicates a high likelihood of depression
    ◦ **Question #10 asks about self-harm and must be reviewed regardless of the total score**
• **Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9)**
    ◦ Also a valid screening tool
• **Diagnosis**
    ◦ Primarily a clinical diagnosis based on **DSM-5 criteria** for MDD with the "**peripartum onset**" specifier
• **Laboratory Tests (to rule out contributing medical conditions)**
