    ◦ **TSH and Free T4**: To screen for **postpartum thyroiditis**
    ◦ **CBC**: To screen for **postpartum anemia**
sections.prognosis:
• With appropriate and timely treatment, the **prognosis is excellent**. Most women experience significant improvement or full remission.
• Without treatment, PPD **can last for months or become chronic**.
• There is a **high risk of recurrence (~50%)** in subsequent pregnancies. Prophylactic treatment should be considered.

sections.overview:
• Postpartum Psychosis (PPP) is the most severe form of postpartum psychiatric illness, considered a **psychiatric emergency**.
• Characterized by a rapid and dramatic onset of psychotic symptoms within the first **2-4 weeks** following childbirth.
    ◦ Symptoms include **delusions**, **hallucinations**, and **disorganized thought/behavior**.
• Distinct from postpartum blues and postpartum depression due to the presence of psychosis and the acuity of onset.
• Poses a significant risk of **suicide** and **infanticide**, necessitating immediate hospitalization and treatment.
sections.etiology:
• The exact etiology is not fully understood but is believed to be multifactorial.
• Key proposed mechanisms include:
    ◦ **Hormonal Shifts**:
        ▪ Abrupt withdrawal of placental steroids, particularly **estrogen** and **progesterone**, after delivery.
        ▪ Dysregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis is also implicated.
    ◦ **Neurotransmitter Dysregulation**:
        ▪ Imbalances in **dopamine**, **serotonin**, and **GABA** systems, similar to those seen in bipolar disorder and schizophrenia.
    ◦ **Genetic Predisposition**:
        ▪ There is a strong genetic component.
        ▪ PPP is often considered a manifestation of an underlying **bipolar disorder**.
    ◦ **Immune System Dysregulation**:
        ▪ Postpartum inflammatory or autoimmune processes may contribute.
        ▪ Some cases may be related to autoimmune encephalitis (e.g., anti-NMDAR encephalitis).
    ◦ **Sleep Deprivation**:
        ▪ Severe sleep disruption in the postpartum period can be a significant physiological stressor and trigger.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Relatively rare, affecting **1-2 per 1,000** live births.
• **Onset**: Typically has a dramatic and rapid onset, usually within the **first 2 weeks postpartum**, with 50% of cases presenting in the first week.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient's concerned family member typically reports a **sudden, dramatic change** in the mother's mental state and behavior days to weeks after delivery.
• The patient may appear **agitated**, **confused**, **paranoid**, or **euphoric**.
• She often **lacks insight** into her illness and may be suspicious of healthcare providers.
• The presentation is marked by **rapidly fluctuating moods** and **bizarre behavior**.
• Family members often describe the patient as "not herself" or "a completely different person."
sections.diagnostics:
• PPP is a clinical diagnosis.
• The workup is aimed at **ruling out organic causes** of psychosis.
    ◦ **Labs**:
        ▪ **CMP**: Rule out electrolyte abnormalities, hypoglycemia, hepatic or renal dysfunction.
        ▪ **CBC with differential**: Rule out infection/sepsis.
        ▪ **TSH with T4/T3**: Rule out postpartum thyroiditis or thyroid storm.
        ▪ **Urine toxicology screen**: Rule out substance-induced psychosis.
        ▪ **Ammonia level**: If concern for hepatic encephalopathy.
    ◦ **Imaging**:
        ▪ **Head CT or MRI**: Indicated for patients with new focal neurological deficits, seizures, or atypical presentation to rule out CNS pathology (e.g., mass, stroke, hemorrhage).
    ◦ **Other**:
        ▪ Consider **EEG** if seizures are suspected.
        ▪ Consider **lumbar puncture** if meningitis/encephalitis is suspected.
        ▪ Consider **autoimmune panel** (e.g., anti-NMDAR antibodies) in atypical cases.
sections.prognosis:
• **With treatment**: The prognosis for the acute episode is **generally good**, with most women returning to their premorbid level of functioning.
• **Without treatment**: The prognosis is poor, with high rates of **suicide** and **infanticide**.
• **Long-term**:
    ◦ There is a high risk (~70%) of developing **Bipolar Disorder**.
    ◦ Recurrence risk in subsequent pregnancies is over 50%.

sections.overview:
• **Fibrocystic breast changes (FBC)** are the most common benign breast condition, characterized by a spectrum of non-cancerous histologic changes in the breast tissue.
	◦ It is not a disease but rather an exaggerated physiological response of breast tissue to cyclical hormonal fluctuations.
	◦ Key features include **fibrosis** (overgrowth of fibrous tissue), **adenosis** (proliferation of glandular tissue), and **cyst formation**.
	◦ It is crucial to differentiate these benign changes from **malignancy**.
sections.etiology:
• The exact etiology is not fully understood, but it is strongly linked to **hormonal imbalance**, particularly an exaggerated response to **estrogen** and **progesterone**.
	◦ **Hormonal Influence:** Repetitive stimulation of breast tissue by ovarian hormones during the menstrual cycle is the primary driver.
		▪ **Estrogen:** Promotes the proliferation of ductal and stromal tissue.
		▪ **Progesterone:** Stimulates the development of lobules and acini.
	◦ **Pathologic Process:** An imbalance, particularly **estrogen dominance** or **progesterone deficiency**, leads to:
		▪ **Stromal Fibrosis:** Proliferation of connective tissue.
		▪ **Cyst Formation:** Ducts become blocked and dilate, filling with fluid to form cysts (microcysts or macrocysts).
		▪ **Adenosis:** Increase in the number and size of glandular lobules.
	◦ **Cyclical Nature:** These changes result in tissue that feels **lumpy, dense, and tender**, with symptoms typically peaking during the late **luteal phase (premenstrual)** and subsiding after menstruation begins.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** Extremely common, affecting an estimated 30-60% of women.
• **Peak Incidence:** Most common in women of reproductive age, typically between **20 and 50 years old**.
• **Post-Menopause:** Symptoms and findings usually diminish or resolve after menopause due to the cessation of ovarian hormone production, unless the patient is on **hormone replacement therapy (HRT)**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A 35-year-old female presents to the clinic with a chief complaint of "**painful, lumpy breasts**" that has been occurring for several months.
	◦ She notes that the pain and lumpiness are worst in the week leading up to her menstrual period and improve significantly once her period starts.
	◦ She denies any **bloody nipple discharge**, skin changes, or a single dominant, **fixed mass**.
sections.diagnostics:
• The primary goal of the diagnostic workup is to exclude **malignancy**.
• **Imaging**
	◦ **Breast Ultrasound:** **Best initial test for a palpable mass in women < 30 years old.**
		▪ It is excellent for differentiating a simple fluid-filled cyst from a solid mass.
		▪ **Simple Cyst:** Appears as a well-circumscribed, anechoic (black) lesion with posterior acoustic enhancement.
	◦ **Mammogram:** Standard imaging for women > 40 years old.
		▪ May be performed in younger women if suspicion is high.
		▪ Findings can include dense, glandular tissue, and round or oval masses (cysts).
		▪ It is less sensitive in young women due to naturally dense breast tissue.
• **Aspiration/Biopsy**
	◦ **Fine-Needle Aspiration (FNA):** Can be both diagnostic and therapeutic.
		▪ **Procedure:** A needle is used to aspirate fluid from a palpable cyst.
		▪ **Diagnostic Findings:** If the fluid is **non-bloody** (straw-colored or green) and the mass **resolves completely** upon aspiration, it is considered a benign simple cyst and no further workup is needed. The fluid is typically discarded.
		▪ **Therapeutic:** Draining a large, tense cyst provides immediate pain relief.
		▪ **Red Flags Requiring Biopsy:** **Bloody aspirate**, palpable mass **persists after aspiration**, or the cyst **recurs rapidly**.
	◦ **Core Needle Biopsy or Excisional Biopsy:** **Definitive diagnosis.**
		▪ Indicated for any **solid mass**, **complex cyst**, or suspicious finding on imaging (e.g., **BI-RADS 4 or 5**).
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is **excellent**.
• Fibrocystic breast changes are **benign**.
• Symptoms are chronic and cyclical but typically **resolve completely with menopause**.
• The main concern is distinguishing these changes from **malignancy** and managing the associated pain and anxiety.

sections.overview:
• Most common **benign tumor** of the female breast
• **Biphasic tumor** composed of two tissue types:
    ◦ Stromal (fibrous)
    ◦ Epithelial (glandular)
• Typically found in **young women** and is hormonally responsive
    ◦ Often grows during **pregnancy** and involutes after **menopause**
sections.etiology:
• Exact etiology is unknown but development is strongly linked to **estrogen sensitivity**
• Considered a hyperplastic or proliferative lesion rather than a true neoplasm
• **Hormonal Influence**
    ◦ Proliferation of stromal and epithelial cells is stimulated by **estrogen**
    ◦ Estrogen receptors are often present in the tissue
• **Growth Pattern**
    ◦ Arises from a breast lobule
    ◦ Grows by expanding and compressing surrounding breast tissue, accounting for its **well-circumscribed** and non-infiltrative nature
• **Types**
    ◦ **Simple Fibroadenoma**: Homogenous tissue composition
    ◦ **Complex Fibroadenoma**: Contains other proliferative changes such as cysts (>3mm), sclerosing adenosis, epithelial calcifications, or papillary apocrine changes
        ▪ This type carries a slightly higher relative risk for future breast cancer
sections.epidemiology:
• Most common **benign breast tumor**
• **Peak Incidence**: Women of reproductive age, typically between **20 and 35 years old**
• Uncommon in postmenopausal women unless they are on hormone replacement therapy (HRT)
• Accounts for up to 50% of all breast biopsies, rising to 75% for biopsies in women under 20
sections.riskFactors:
• **Age**: Young, reproductive age (20s-30s)
• **Hormonal Exposure**
    ◦ **Early menarche**
    ◦ Use of oral contraceptives before age 20
    ◦ **Nulliparity**
• **Genetics**: Increased incidence in patients with Carney complex
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Classic presentation is a young woman discovering a **painless, palpable lump** during self-exam or a routine clinical exam
    ◦ The mass is the primary and often only symptom
• The mass is typically **slow-growing** and may fluctuate slightly in size with the menstrual cycle
• **No Associated Symptoms**: Typically no nipple discharge, skin changes (dimpling, erythema), or systemic symptoms
• Some patients may report mild tenderness, especially pre-menstrually
sections.physicalExam:
• **Palpation**: The mass is classically described as:
    ◦ **Firm and Rubbery**
    ◦ **Smooth**
    ◦ **Well-circumscribed** with distinct borders
    ◦ **Highly Mobile** and easily movable within the breast tissue (a key finding often called a **"breast mouse"**)
• **Shape**: Round or ovoid
• **Size**: Typically 1-3 cm in diameter
    ◦ "**Giant fibroadenomas**" are >5 cm
• **Location**: Most commonly found in the **upper outer quadrant (UOQ)** of the breast
• **Associated Findings**: No axillary lymphadenopathy or overlying skin or nipple changes
sections.diagnostics:
• The workup follows the **"Triple Assessment"** protocol:
    ◦ Clinical breast exam
    ◦ Imaging
    ◦ Biopsy
sections.treatment:
• **Conservative Management / Observation**
    ◦ **Most common approach**
    ◦ Indicated for small (<3 cm), asymptomatic, biopsy-proven benign fibroadenomas
    ◦ Involves serial clinical exams and/or ultrasounds (e.g., every 6-12 months for 1-2 years) to monitor for stability
    ◦ Many will shrink and involute over time
• **Surgical Excision (Lumpectomy)**
    ◦ **Indications**:
        ▪ Rapid growth
        ▪ Large size (>3-5 cm) causing cosmetic deformity or symptoms
        ▪ Patient preference or significant anxiety
        ▪ Atypical features on biopsy or inconclusive results
        ▪ Suspicion for Phyllodes tumor
• **Cryoablation**
    ◦ A minimally invasive alternative to surgery where a probe is used to freeze and destroy the tumor tissue
    ◦ An option for smaller (<4 cm), biopsy-proven fibroadenomas
sections.management:
• **Reassurance**: After a definitive diagnosis, reassure the patient of the benign nature of the lesion and the very low risk of malignant transformation
• **Shared Decision-Making**: Discuss the pros and cons of observation versus removal
• **Follow-up Plan**: If observing, establish a clear follow-up schedule
• **Breast Self-Awareness**: Encourage continued routine self-exams and clinical breast exams
sections.complications:
• **Malignant Transformation**: Extremely rare (<0.1% risk), but carcinoma can arise within a fibroadenoma
• **Growth**: Can enlarge, especially during pregnancy or with HRT, potentially causing discomfort or cosmetic issues
• **Patient Anxiety**: The presence of any breast lump can cause significant psychological distress
• **Surgical Risks**: If excised, risks include scarring, hematoma, infection, and changes in breast contour
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** prognosis
• Fibroadenomas are benign and do not increase the overall risk of breast cancer
    ◦ **Complex fibroadenomas** confer a very slight increase in relative risk
• Recurrence is uncommon after complete excision
• Many spontaneously regress, particularly after menopause

sections.overview:
• **Mastitis** is an inflammation of the breast parenchyma, which may or may not be accompanied by infection.
    ◦ Most commonly associated with lactation (**puerperal** or **lactational mastitis**) but can also occur in non-lactating women (**non-puerperal mastitis**).
    ◦ Typically presents as a painful, erythematous, and warm area on the breast, often with systemic symptoms like fever and myalgias.
    ◦ Prompt diagnosis and treatment are crucial to prevent complications such as abscess formation.
sections.etiology:
• **Lactational (Puerperal) Mastitis**
    ◦ **Primary Cause**: **Milk stasis** from a blocked duct is the initiating event.
    ◦ **Pathophysiology**:
        ▪ **Milk Stasis**: Incomplete emptying of a milk duct due to poor latch, infrequent feeding, or mechanical obstruction (e.g., tight bra).
        ▪ **Increased Intraductal Pressure**: The stagnant milk increases pressure within the lobule, causing leakage of milk components into the surrounding breast tissue.
        ▪ **Inflammatory Response**: This leakage triggers a non-infectious, sterile inflammatory response.
        ▪ **Infectious Mastitis**: Stagnant, nutrient-rich milk provides an ideal culture medium for bacteria from the infant's nasopharynx or the mother's skin, which can enter the ductal system (often through a cracked or traumatized nipple) leading to a secondary infection.
    ◦ **Most Common Organism**: **Staphylococcus aureus**
    ◦ **Other Organisms**: *Streptococcus pyogenes*, *Escherichia coli*, Coagulase-negative staphylococci.
• **Non-Lactational Mastitis (e.g., Periductal Mastitis)**
    ◦ **Pathophysiology**: Often related to duct ectasia and inflammation of the periductal tissue.
        ▪ Strongly associated with **smoking**, which can cause squamous metaplasia of the ductal epithelium, leading to blockage by keratin plugs.
        ▪ This can result in a sterile inflammatory response or become secondarily infected.
    ◦ **Organisms**: Often polymicrobial, including Staph, Strep, and anaerobes.
sections.epidemiology:
• Occurs in up to 33% of lactating women.
• **Peak Incidence**: Most common in the **first 6 weeks postpartum**, but can occur at any time during lactation.
• Unilateral presentation is far more common than bilateral.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • A lactating woman, typically 2-6 weeks postpartum, presents with the acute onset of a focal area of breast tenderness, swelling, and erythema, accompanied by systemic signs of infection.
sections.diagnostics:
• Primarily a **clinical diagnosis**.
    ◦ Laboratory tests and imaging are not routinely required for uncomplicated cases.
• **When to Test**:
    ◦ **Breast Milk Culture & Sensitivity**: Indicated if:
        ▪ Severe or life-threatening infection.
        ▪ No response to initial empiric antibiotics within 48-72 hours.
        ▪ Recurrent mastitis.
        ▪ Hospital-acquired infection.
    ◦ **Imaging (Ultrasound)**: **Test of choice** to differentiate simple mastitis from a **breast abscess**.
        ▪ **Indications**:
            • Palpable mass or suspicion of fluctuance on exam.
            • Failure to improve clinically after 48-72 hours of appropriate antibiotic therapy.
        ▪ **Findings**: An abscess will appear as a complex, walled-off fluid collection.
    ◦ **Mammogram/Biopsy**: Considered in non-lactating women or if symptoms persist after treatment to rule out **Inflammatory Breast Cancer (IBC)**.
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent with prompt and appropriate treatment.
    ◦ Most women recover fully without long-term sequelae and can continue to breastfeed successfully.

sections.overview:
• A **breast abscess** is a localized collection of **pus** within the breast tissue, resulting from an unresolved or severe infection.
• It is most commonly a complication of **mastitis**.
• Abscesses are classified as **lactational (puerperal)** or **non-lactational**.
• They present as a **painful, tender, fluctuant mass** and require **drainage** for resolution.
sections.etiology:
• **Pathogenesis**
    ◦ A breast abscess typically begins as **mastitis** (inflammation of breast parenchyma).
    ◦ Bacteria invade the breast tissue, often through a crack or fissure in the nipple or via the milk ducts.
    ◦ If the infection is not adequately treated or if a duct becomes severely blocked, the inflammatory response leads to **liquefactive necrosis** and the formation of a walled-off collection of **pus**.
• **Lactational (Puerperal) Abscess**
    ◦ The **most common type**.
    ◦ Occurs in **breastfeeding** women.
    ◦ **Patho**: **Milk stasis** provides a culture medium for bacteria, which enter through nipple trauma from infant feeding. Unresolved infectious **mastitis** progresses to abscess formation.
• **Non-Lactational Abscess**
    ◦ Less common.
    ◦ **Central/Subareolar**: Often associated with **squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts (Zuska's disease)**, leading to duct blockage, inflammation, and infection. Strongly associated with **smoking**.
    ◦ **Peripheral**: Unrelated to major ducts. Can be associated with underlying conditions like **diabetes**, **immunosuppression**, or **trauma**.
• **Microbiology**
    ◦ **Most Common Overall**: ***Staphylococcus aureus*** (including Methicillin-resistant *S. aureus* - **MRSA**).
    ◦ **Others**: Streptococcal species.
    ◦ **Non-lactational/Subareolar**: Often **polymicrobial**, including anaerobes (*Bacteroides*, *Peptostreptococcus*).
sections.epidemiology:
• Occurs in approximately 5-10% of women with infectious **mastitis**.
• Primarily affects women of reproductive age, most commonly during the first **6 weeks of lactation**.
• Non-lactational abscesses are less frequent and can occur at any age, with a peak in the 4th decade.
sections.riskFactors:
• Inadequately treated **mastitis**
• First-time mother
• Improper breastfeeding technique / poor infant latch
• Cracked or damaged nipples
• **Milk stasis** / Incomplete breast emptying
• Use of a breast pump
• Tight-fitting bras
• Previous history of mastitis
• **Cigarette smoking** (strongest risk factor for subareolar abscesses)
• **Diabetes mellitus**
• **Obesity**
• **Immunosuppression**
• Nipple piercings
• Duct ectasia or periductal mastitis
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient with a breast abscess typically presents with a history of recent or ongoing **mastitis**.
• The classic scenario is a lactating woman who was started on antibiotics for **mastitis** 7-10 days prior but has **failed to improve** or has worsened, now presenting with a **well-defined, palpable mass** and persistent systemic symptoms.
sections.physicalExam:
**Symptoms**
• Localized, intense **breast pain** and tenderness
• **Fever, chills, and malaise** (systemic signs of infection)
• Palpable, **tender lump** or swelling in the breast
• **Erythema** and **warmth** of the overlying skin
• Spontaneous **purulent drainage** from the nipple (less common)

**Physical Exam Findings**
• **Inspection**: 
    ◦ Overlying **erythema, edema, and warmth** of the skin. Skin may appear shiny or taut.
    ◦ **Peau d'orange** appearance is possible but is a red flag for **inflammatory breast cancer**.
• **Palpation**:
    ◦ **Fluctuance**: A palpable fluid wave is the **classic sign** of a drainable abscess.
    ◦ A distinct, **tender, indurated mass** may be felt if the abscess is deep or not yet fully "mature."
    ◦ Tender **axillary lymphadenopathy** may be present.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Often made based on a history of **mastitis** and the finding of a new, **tender, fluctuant mass**.
• **Imaging**:
    ◦ **Breast Ultrasound**: **Diagnostic modality of choice**.
        ▪ Confirms the presence of a fluid collection.
        ▪ Differentiates abscess from simple **cellulitis/phlegmon**.
        ▪ Determines the size, location, and complexity (unilocular vs. multilocular).
        ▪ Essential for guiding needle aspiration or drainage.
    ◦ **Findings**: A complex, thick-walled, hypoechoic or anechoic fluid collection with irregular borders, posterior acoustic enhancement, and possibly internal debris or septations.
• **Laboratory Studies**:
    ◦ **CBC**: May show **leukocytosis** with a neutrophilic predominance ("**left shift**").
    ◦ **Culture and Sensitivity**: Pus obtained from drainage should always be sent for Gram stain, culture, and sensitivity to guide antibiotic therapy, especially to identify **MRSA**.
• **Biopsy**: Consider if the abscess is non-lactational, recurrent, or fails to resolve with standard treatment to rule out underlying malignancy, particularly **Inflammatory Breast Cancer (IBC)**.
sections.treatment:
• **Needle Aspiration**:
    ◦ **First-line treatment** for most abscesses, especially if <5 cm and unilocular.
    ◦ Performed under **ultrasound guidance**.
    ◦ Less invasive, better cosmetic outcome.
    ◦ May require serial aspirations every 2-3 days until resolved.
• **Incision and Drainage (I&D)**:
    ◦ Indicated for **large (>5 cm)**, complex, **multiloculated** abscesses, or those that fail needle aspiration.
    ◦ An incision is made over the area of maximal fluctuance (often in a circumareolar or curvilinear fashion for cosmesis), the pus is evacuated, loculations are broken up, and the cavity is irrigated. A drain or packing may be placed.
• **Empiric Therapy (target *S. aureus*)**:
    ◦ **Dicloxacillin** 500 mg PO QID
    ◦ **Cephalexin** (Keflex) 500 mg PO QID
    ◦ **If MRSA is suspected or prevalent**:
        ▪ **Clindamycin** 300-450 mg PO TID
        ▪ **Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Bactrim)** 1-2 DS tabs PO BID
        ▪ **Doxycycline** 100 mg PO BID (generally avoided in breastfeeding mothers, but short courses may be considered).
• **IV Antibiotics (for severe infection/sepsis)**: **Vancomycin**, **Clindamycin**.
• Therapy should be tailored to **culture and sensitivity** results once available. Duration is typically 10-14 days.
sections.management:
• **Lactation Support**:
    ◦ **CONTINUE BREASTFEEDING** or pumping from the affected breast. This is critical to promote drainage and prevent milk stasis.
    ◦ The milk is safe for a healthy, full-term infant.
    ◦ If feeding is too painful, pump the affected side and feed from the unaffected breast.
• **Symptomatic Relief**:
    ◦ **Analgesics**: **NSAIDs** (Ibuprofen) and/or Acetaminophen.
    ◦ **Warm compresses** applied to the area before feeding/pumping can aid drainage.
• **Follow-up**:
    ◦ Close clinical follow-up is essential (e.g., in 2-3 days) to assess for resolution.
    ◦ Repeat ultrasound may be necessary if symptoms do not improve.
sections.complications:
• Recurrence of abscess
• **Mammary duct fistula** (a tract from a subareolar duct to the skin)
• Scarring or breast deformity
• **Sepsis** (rare)
• Delayed diagnosis of **breast cancer** (if the abscess is masking a mass or is mistaken for **IBC**)
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is **excellent** with timely diagnosis, complete drainage, and appropriate antibiotic therapy.
• Most women recover fully without long-term sequelae.
• Recurrence rates are higher in non-lactational, **smoking-associated** abscesses.

sections.overview:
• Galactorrhea is the secretion of a milky, nipple discharge from the breast in a person who is not pregnant or breastfeeding.
• It is a clinical sign of an underlying issue, most commonly **hyperprolactinemia**.
• The discharge is typically bilateral and can occur in both females and males.
• The workup focuses on identifying and treating the root cause, which ranges from physiologic changes and medication side effects to systemic disease and pituitary tumors.
sections.etiology:
• The central mechanism is almost always **hyperprolactinemia**.
	◦ Prolactin secretion is tonically inhibited by **dopamine** from the hypothalamus.
	◦ Disruption of this inhibition leads to **hyperprolactinemia**.
• **Key Causes of Hyperprolactinemia**:
	◦ **Pituitary Adenomas (Prolactinomas)**:
		▪ **The most common pathologic cause.**
		▪ Benign tumors of lactotroph cells in the anterior pituitary that autonomously secrete prolactin.
		▪ **Microadenomas** (<10 mm) are more common in women.
		▪ **Macroadenomas** (≥10 mm) are more common in men and can cause mass effect symptoms (**headaches**, **visual changes**).
	◦ **Pharmacologic (Very High-Yield)**:
		▪ **Dopamine Antagonists**: Block dopamine's inhibitory effect on prolactin.
		▪ **Antipsychotics**: Especially first-generation (e.g., haloperidol) and second-generation (e.g., **risperidone**, paliperidone).
		▪ **Antiemetics**: Metoclopramide, prochlorperazine.
		▪ Other Medications:
			• **Antidepressants**: TCAs, SSRIs (less common).
			• **Antihypertensives**: Verapamil, methyldopa.
			• **Opioids**.
			• **H2-receptor antagonists** (e.g., cimetidine).
	◦ **Hypothalamic/Pituitary Stalk Disruption ("Stalk Effect")**:
		▪ Any mass, infiltrative disease, or trauma that compresses the pituitary stalk can block dopamine from reaching the pituitary, leading to disinhibition and mild-moderate **hyperprolactinemia** (typically <150 ng/mL).
		▪ Causes include non-secreting pituitary adenomas, craniopharyngiomas, sarcoidosis, trauma, or radiation.
	◦ **Systemic Disease**:
		▪ **Primary Hypothyroidism**: Increased TRH (Thyrotropin-releasing hormone) not only stimulates TSH but also weakly stimulates prolactin release.
		▪ **Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)**: Decreased clearance of prolactin from the circulation.
		▪ **Cirrhosis**: Impaired hormone metabolism.
	◦ **Physiologic Causes**:
		▪ **Pregnancy & Postpartum**: Normal physiologic state.
		▪ **Chest Wall Stimulation**: Frequent nipple stimulation, suckling, herpes zoster (shingles) of the chest wall, thoracotomy scars, or even tight clothing can cause a neurogenic-mediated increase in prolactin.
		▪ **Stress**: Physical or psychological stress.
	◦ **Idiopathic**:
		▪ No identifiable cause is found after a thorough workup.
sections.epidemiology:
• Most common in women aged **20-35**.
• Prevalence of **hyperprolactinemia** is approximately 1% in the general population.
• **Prolactinomas** account for ~40% of all pituitary adenomas.
• Galactorrhea is uncommon in postmenopausal women and rare in men.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a premenopausal woman complaining of **bilateral milky nipple discharge** and **menstrual irregularities** (oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea).
• A male patient may present with decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, and gynecomastia.
• If a large pituitary **macroadenoma** is present, the patient may complain of **headaches** and **visual field defects**.
sections.diagnostics:
• The diagnostic workup is a stepwise process to rule out common causes and identify the underlying etiology.
• **Initial Laboratory Tests**:
	◦ **hCG**: **ALWAYS THE FIRST STEP** in a premenopausal female to rule out pregnancy.
	◦ **Serum Prolactin Level**:
		▪ Normal: <25 ng/mL.
		▪ Mildly elevated (25-100 ng/mL): Can be due to medications, stress, hypothyroidism, or stalk effect.
		▪ Moderately elevated (100-200 ng/mL): Suggestive of a microprolactinoma but can still be other causes.
		▪ **Markedly elevated (>200 ng/mL): Essentially diagnostic of a prolactinoma.**
		▪ **Hook Effect**: Be aware that giant adenomas can paradoxically show a falsely low or normal prolactin level on immunoassay. If clinical suspicion is high, the lab should be asked to repeat the test with serial dilutions.
	◦ **TSH**: To rule out primary hypothyroidism as the cause. If TSH is high, check a free T4.
	◦ **BUN and Creatinine**: To assess renal function and rule out CKD.
• **Imaging**:
	◦ **Pituitary MRI with contrast**: This is the **gold standard** for visualizing the pituitary gland.
	◦ **Indication**: Indicated if prolactin level is elevated and pregnancy, hypothyroidism, and medication causes have been ruled out.
	◦ It can differentiate between micro- and macroadenomas and assess for optic chiasm compression.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is **excellent**.
• Most patients with **prolactinomas** respond very well to medical therapy with dopamine agonists.
• For other causes, correcting the underlying disorder typically resolves the galactorrhea.

sections.overview:
• Benign proliferation of **glandular breast tissue** in males.
• Results from an imbalance between **estrogen and androgen** action on the breast tissue.
• Must be differentiated from **pseudogynecomastia**, which is the accumulation of adipose (fatty) tissue in the breast area without glandular proliferation.
• Can be **unilateral or bilateral** and may be tender.
sections.etiology:
• The core pathophysiologic mechanism is an **increased estrogen-to-androgen ratio**.
    ◦ This imbalance can arise from:
        ▪ **Increased Estrogen Production**
            • **Testicular tumors** (Leydig or Sertoli cell tumors)
            • **Adrenal tumors**
            • Increased peripheral conversion of androgens to estrogens via **aromatase** (seen in obesity, liver disease, and aging).
        ▪ **Decreased Androgen Production (Hypogonadism)**
            • **Primary:** **Klinefelter syndrome (XXY)**, testicular trauma, orchitis, testicular failure.
            • **Secondary:** Pituitary or hypothalamic tumors/disorders.
        ▪ **Androgen Insensitivity Syndromes**
            • Tissues are unable to respond to androgens.
        ▪ **Increased Binding of Androgens**
            • Increased levels of **sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG)**, seen in hyperthyroidism and liver disease, bind testosterone more avidly than estrogen, leading to a higher ratio of free estrogen.
• **Classification by Cause**
    ◦ **Physiologic:** Occurs at three distinct life stages.
        ▪ **Neonatal:** Due to high levels of maternal estrogen crossing the placenta. Resolves in weeks.
        ▪ **Pubertal:** A transient imbalance during mid-puberty where estrogen levels rise before testosterone levels fully catch up. Typically resolves within 1-2 years.
        ▪ **Senescent (Older Age):** Due to a combination of decreased testicular testosterone production and increased peripheral aromatization of androgens in adipose tissue.
    ◦ **Pathologic**
        ▪ **Systemic Disease:** Chronic liver disease (impaired estrogen metabolism), chronic kidney disease (CKD), **hyperthyroidism**, malnutrition/refeeding syndrome.
        ▪ **Neoplasms:** Testicular, adrenal, or ectopic **hCG-producing tumors** (e.g., lung cancer).
        ▪ **Primary or Secondary Hypogonadism:** Including **Klinefelter syndrome**.
    ◦ **Pharmacologic (Medication-Induced):** A very common cause.
        ▪ Mnemonic: **"Some Drugs Create Awesome Knockers"**
        ▪ **S**pironolactone
        ▪ **D**igoxin
        ▪ **C**imetidine, Ketoconazole
        ▪ **A**nti-androgens (for prostate cancer), Anabolic steroids
        ▪ **K**etoconazole (again)
        ▪ Other notable drugs: Finasteride, metronidazole, methyldopa, some antiretrovirals (Efavirenz), marijuana, heroin, amphetamines.
    ◦ **Idiopathic:** No identifiable cause is found in ~25% of cases.
sections.epidemiology:
• Shows a **tri-modal age distribution**, corresponding to the physiologic causes.
    ◦ **Infancy:** >60% of male newborns.
    ◦ **Puberty:** Affects up to 60-70% of adolescent boys, peaking at age 13-14.
    ◦ **Older Adulthood:** Prevalence increases with age, affecting >50% of men over age 50.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A male patient, often an adolescent or older adult, presents with a chief complaint of **"breast enlargement"** or a **"lump under the nipple."**
• The onset can be gradual.
• It can be **unilateral or bilateral**.
• Patients may also report **tenderness**.
• The **psychological impact** (embarrassment, anxiety) can be a significant part of the presentation.
sections.diagnostics:
• The workup is guided by the history and physical exam.
• For classic **pubertal gynecomastia** with a normal exam, no further workup is needed beyond reassurance.
• **Initial Laboratory Studies** (if pathologic cause is suspected):
    ◦ **hCG:** To rule out **hCG-secreting tumors** (testicular, lung).
    ◦ **LH & Testosterone** (total and free): To evaluate for **hypogonadism**.
    ◦ **Estradiol:** Elevated in certain tumors or liver disease.
    ◦ **TSH & Free T4:** To rule out **hyperthyroidism**.
    ◦ **Prolactin:** **Prolactinomas** can cause hypogonadism.
    ◦ **LFTs** (AST, ALT, Bilirubin): To assess for liver disease.
    ◦ **BUN & Creatinine:** To assess for renal failure.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ Indicated if the mass is suspicious for **malignancy** (hard, fixed, eccentric, associated skin changes) or if lab work is abnormal.
    ◦ **Mammogram:** The primary imaging modality to differentiate gynecomastia from **male breast cancer**.
    ◦ **Breast Ultrasound:** Can help differentiate solid vs. cystic masses and evaluate for abscess.
    ◦ **Testicular Ultrasound:** Indicated if a testicular mass is palpated or if hormone levels (high hCG, high estradiol, low LH) suggest a testicular tumor.
• **Further Studies**
    ◦ **Karyotyping (XXY):** If **Klinefelter syndrome** is suspected (small, firm testes; hypogonadism).
    ◦ **Biopsy:** If imaging and clinical findings cannot rule out malignancy.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is **excellent**.
• **Physiologic gynecomastia** (newborn and pubertal) typically resolves spontaneously.
• Gynecomastia due to a treatable cause (e.g., medication) often regresses once the cause is removed.
• **Long-standing gynecomastia** (>1 year) is more likely to become **fibrotic** and less likely to resolve without surgical intervention.

sections.overview:
• Cervical cancer is a malignancy arising from the cells of the cervix, the lower part of the uterus that connects to the vagina.
• It is most commonly caused by persistent infection with high-risk strains of **Human Papillomavirus (HPV)**.
• The disease progresses slowly from pre-cancerous lesions (**cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, or CIN**) to invasive carcinoma.
• Due to effective screening programs (**Pap test**, **HPV testing**) and **HPV vaccination**, the incidence and mortality have significantly decreased in developed nations.
• The two main histological types are **Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)** and **Adenocarcinoma**.
sections.etiology:
• **Primary Etiology**: Persistent infection with **high-risk (oncogenic) Human Papillomavirus (HPV)**.
    ◦ **High-Risk HPV Types**: **HPV 16 and 18** are responsible for ~70% of all cervical cancers. Other high-risk types include 31, 33, 45, 52, 58.
    ◦ **Low-Risk HPV Types**: **HPV 6 and 11** cause **condyloma acuminata** (genital warts) but have very low malignant potential.
• **Pathogenesis**:
    ◦ **Infection**: HPV infects immature basal cells of the squamous epithelium at the **squamocolumnar junction (SCJ)**, also known as the **transformation zone (T-zone)**.
        ▪ This is the most common site for cervical neoplasia.
    ◦ **Oncogene Integration**: The virus integrates its DNA into the host cell's genome. The key viral oncoproteins are **E6 and E7**.
        ▪ **E6 protein** binds to and promotes the degradation of the **p53 tumor suppressor protein**.
        ▪ **E7 protein** binds to and inactivates the **retinoblastoma (Rb) tumor suppressor protein**.
    ◦ **Uncontrolled Proliferation**: Inactivation of these two critical tumor suppressors allows for uncontrolled cell division, resistance to apoptosis, and accumulation of genetic mutations, leading to malignant transformation.
• **Progression**: The process is typically slow, occurring over 10-15 years.
    ◦ Normal Cervical Epithelium → Low-Grade Squamous Intraepithelial Lesion (**LSIL** / **CIN 1**) → High-Grade Squamous Intraepithelial Lesion (**HSIL** / **CIN 2/3**) → Invasive Carcinoma.
• **Histologic Types**:
    ◦ **Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)**: Accounts for ~80% of cases. Arises from the ectocervix.
    ◦ **Adenocarcinoma**: Accounts for ~15-20% of cases. Arises from the glandular cells of the endocervical canal. Often more difficult to detect via Pap smear.
sections.epidemiology:
• A leading cause of cancer death for women in developing countries lacking screening programs.
• Incidence and mortality in the United States have decreased by over 75% since the introduction of the **Pap test**.
• **Bimodal age distribution** for invasive cancer: peaks at ages **35-44** and again at **60-64**.
    ◦ Precursor lesions (CIN) peak in women aged 20-30.
• Invasive cervical cancer is an **AIDS-defining illness**.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Greatest Risk Factor**: Persistent infection with **high-risk HPV**.
• **Immunosuppression**: **HIV**, organ transplant recipients, chronic corticosteroid use.
• **Sexual History**: Early onset of sexual activity (<18 years), multiple sexual partners, a male partner with multiple previous partners.
• **Cigarette Smoking**: A direct carcinogen and cofactor for HPV persistence.
• **High Parity**: Multiple full-term pregnancies.
• **Long-term Oral Contraceptive Use** (>5 years).
• History of other STIs: **Chlamydia trachomatis**, **Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV)**.
• **Low Socioeconomic Status**: Associated with barriers to screening and follow-up.
• **In-utero Diethylstilbestrol (DES) exposure**: Increased risk for **clear cell adenocarcinoma** of the cervix and vagina.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Early-stage disease is typically **ASYMPTOMATIC** and is most often detected by abnormal cervical cancer screening.
• Symptomatic presentation usually indicates more advanced, invasive disease.
• **Most common symptom**: **Postcoital bleeding** (spotting or bleeding after intercourse).
• Irregular or heavy vaginal bleeding (intermenstrual or postmenopausal).
• Watery, mucoid, or purulent vaginal discharge, which may be malodorous.
• Pelvic pain or low back pain (often a late sign suggesting extension to the pelvic sidewalls or nerve involvement).
• Dyspareunia (painful intercourse).
• **Advanced Disease Symptoms**:
    ◦ Unilateral leg edema, sciatic pain (pelvic wall involvement).
    ◦ Urinary symptoms (**hematuria**, fistula) from bladder invasion.
    ◦ Rectal symptoms (tenesmus, fistula) from bowel invasion.
    ◦ Constitutional symptoms: weight loss, fatigue.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Speculum Exam**:
    ◦ May appear normal in early stages.
    ◦ **Visible lesion**: A friable, bleeding mass; an exophytic (fungating) growth; an ulcerative lesion; or a polypoid mass.
    ◦ **Barrel-shaped cervix**: Suggests a large endocervical tumor expanding the cervical stroma.
• **Bimanual Exam**:
    ◦ Assess for cervical firmness, irregularity, and size.
    ◦ Palpate for **parametrial induration** or nodularity, which indicates local extension of the tumor.
• **Rectovaginal Exam**:
    ◦ Essential for clinical staging.
    ◦ Assesses for involvement of the uterosacral ligaments and parametria.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Screening (Secondary Prevention)**
    ◦ **Cervical Cytology (Pap Test)**: Reports using the Bethesda system (e.g., ASC-US, LSIL, HSIL).
        ▪ May show **koilocytes** (squamous epithelial cells with a perinuclear halo), which are pathognomonic for HPV infection.
    ◦ **High-Risk HPV DNA Testing**: Can be done as a primary screen, co-test with cytology, or as a reflex test for **ASC-US**.
• **Definitive Diagnosis & Staging**
    ◦ **Colposcopy**: A magnified view of the cervix after application of **acetic acid**, which causes dysplastic areas to turn white (**acetowhite changes**).
        ▪ Allows for visually directed biopsies.
    ◦ **Cervical Biopsy**: **The gold standard for diagnosis**. A tissue sample is taken from the most abnormal-appearing area.
    ◦ **Endocervical Curettage (ECC)**: Sampling of the endocervical canal; performed if the transformation zone is not fully visualized or if adenocarcinoma is suspected.
• **Staging Workup**
    ◦ **Cervical cancer is STAGED CLINICALLY** using the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system.
    ◦ Staging is based on physical exam (bimanual, rectovaginal), colposcopy, biopsy, and limited imaging (chest X-ray, IVP) or procedures (cystoscopy, proctoscopy) if bladder/rectal involvement is suspected.
    ◦ **Modern imaging (CT, MRI, PET)** is used extensively for **treatment planning** to assess tumor size, lymph node status, and distant mets, but does not formally change the FIGO clinical stage.
        ▪ **Pelvic MRI**: Best for evaluating local tumor extent.
        ▪ **PET/CT**: Best for detecting nodal and distant metastases.
sections.treatment:
• **Pre-invasive Disease (CIN 2/3)**:
    ◦ **Excisional Procedures**: **LEEP** (Loop Electrosurgical Excision Procedure) or **Cold Knife Conization (CKC)**.
• **Stage IA1 (Microinvasive)**:
    ◦ Cone biopsy or simple hysterectomy.
• **Stage IA2, IB1, IIA1 (Early-stage invasive)**:
    ◦ **Radical Hysterectomy with Pelvic Lymph Node Dissection** OR
    ◦ **Primary External Beam Radiation Therapy (EBRT) + Brachytherapy** (internal radiation).
    ◦ Outcomes for surgery and radiation are equivalent; choice depends on patient age and comorbidities.
• **Stage IB2, IIA2 through IVA (Locally Advanced)**:
    ◦ **STANDARD OF CARE**: **Definitive Chemoradiation**.
    ◦ **EBRT + concurrent weekly Cisplatin-based chemotherapy** (acts as a radiosensitizer), followed by **brachytherapy**.
• **Stage IVB (Metastatic Disease)**:
    ◦ **Systemic Chemotherapy** (e.g., cisplatin, paclitaxel) +/- targeted therapy (**Bevacizumab**, an anti-VEGF monoclonal antibody).
    ◦ Palliative radiation for symptom control (e.g., bleeding, pain).
sections.management:
• **Primary Prevention**: **HPV Vaccination** (**Gardasil 9**). Recommended for all adolescents before sexual debut.
• **Secondary Prevention**: Routine cervical cancer screening with **Pap** and/or **HPV testing** according to national guidelines (e.g., ACOG, USPSTF).
• **Tertiary Prevention (Surveillance after Treatment)**:
    ◦ Follow-up visits every 3-6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.
    ◦ Includes history, physical exam (including pelvic/rectovaginal exam), and Pap smears of the vaginal cuff.
    ◦ Imaging (CT or PET) as indicated for symptoms concerning for recurrence.
sections.complications:
• **From Disease Progression**:
    ◦ **Ureteral obstruction** → **Hydronephrosis** → **Renal Failure** (a common cause of death).
    ◦ Hemorrhage from the tumor.
    ◦ Fistula formation (vesicovaginal or rectovaginal).
    ◦ Pain from nerve or bone involvement.
• **From Treatment**:
    ◦ **Surgical**: Lymphedema, bladder/bowel dysfunction, sexual dysfunction, infertility.
    ◦ **Radiation**: Radiation cystitis/proctitis, vaginal stenosis, ovarian failure/menopause, pelvic fractures.
    ◦ **Chemotherapy**: Nephrotoxicity (cisplatin), neurotoxicity, myelosuppression.
sections.prognosis:
• The most important prognostic factor is the **stage at diagnosis**.
• **5-Year Survival Rates (approximate)**:
    ◦ Stage I: >90%
    ◦ Stage II: 60-80%
    ◦ Stage III: 30-50%
    ◦ Stage IV: <20%

sections.overview:
• **Endometrial cancer** is the most common gynecologic malignancy in the United States.
• Arises from the epithelial cells of the **endometrium**, the inner lining of the uterus.
• Primarily a disease of **postmenopausal women**.
    ◦ Often diagnosed at an early stage due to its hallmark symptom of **postmenopausal bleeding**.
• The vast majority are **estrogen-dependent adenocarcinomas** with a favorable prognosis when confined to the uterus.
sections.etiology:
• The pathophysiology is classically divided into two types:
• **Type I (Estrogen-Dependent)** (~80% of cases)
    ◦ **Mechanism**: Caused by **unopposed estrogen stimulation** of the endometrium. 
        ▪ Excess estrogen, without the counteracting effects of progesterone, leads to continuous proliferation of the endometrial lining.
        ▪ This progresses from simple hyperplasia → complex hyperplasia → **atypical hyperplasia** (endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia, EIN) → invasive adenocarcinoma.
    ◦ **Histology**: Typically low-grade, **endometrioid adenocarcinoma**.
    ◦ **Presentation**: Tends to affect younger, perimenopausal, or early postmenopausal women.
    ◦ **Prognosis**: Generally favorable due to low grade and early detection.
• **Type II (Estrogen-Independent)** (~20% of cases)
    ◦ **Mechanism**: Arises spontaneously in an atrophic endometrium, not driven by estrogen.
        ▪ Associated with mutations in genes like **p53**.
    ◦ **Histology**: More aggressive subtypes, such as **serous, clear cell, or high-grade endometrioid carcinoma**.
    ◦ **Presentation**: Tends to affect older, postmenopausal women.
    ◦ **Prognosis**: Poorer, as these tumors are more aggressive and often diagnosed at a more advanced stage.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Most common gynecologic cancer in developed countries.
    ◦ 4th most common cancer in women in the U.S. (after breast, lung, and colorectal).
• **Peak Age**: Median age at diagnosis is **62 years**.
    ◦ Primarily a postmenopausal disease.
• **Racial Disparities**: Black women have a slightly lower incidence but a significantly higher mortality rate, often due to diagnosis with more aggressive (Type II) subtypes at a later stage.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Classic presentation: a **postmenopausal woman with new-onset vaginal bleeding or spotting**.
    ◦ **Any postmenopausal bleeding** should be investigated to rule out endometrial cancer.
• In premenopausal or perimenopausal women, it may present as a change in menstrual pattern, such as **heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia)** or **intermenstrual bleeding**.
sections.diagnostics:
• The diagnostic workup follows a stepwise approach, particularly for the classic presentation of **postmenopausal bleeding**.
• **Initial Imaging (for PMB): Transvaginal Ultrasound (TVUS)**
    ◦ **Purpose**: To measure the **endometrial stripe thickness**.
    ◦ **Interpretation (Postmenopausal Patient)**:
        ▪ **≤ 4 mm**: Low probability of cancer. Observation is appropriate if bleeding resolves.
        ▪ **> 4 mm**: Suspicious for hyperplasia or malignancy. **Requires tissue sampling.**
    ◦ *Note: TVUS is less useful in premenopausal women due to cyclical changes in endometrial thickness.*
• **Tissue Sampling (Definitive Diagnosis)**
    ◦ **Gold Standard**: **Endometrial Biopsy**.
        ▪ An office-based procedure using a thin catheter (e.g., Pipelle) to suction a sample of the endometrium.
        ▪ High sensitivity (>90%) for detecting endometrial cancer.
    ◦ **Dilation and Curettage (D&C) with Hysteroscopy**:
        ▪ Performed if office biopsy is non-diagnostic, stenosis prevents office biopsy, or if focal pathology is suspected.
        ▪ Hysteroscopy allows direct visualization of the uterine cavity to guide biopsies.
• **Pre-operative Staging Workup (once cancer is confirmed)**
    ◦ **Pelvic MRI**: Best imaging modality to assess the depth of **myometrial invasion** and **cervical stroma involvement**.
    ◦ **CT Chest/Abdomen/Pelvis**: To evaluate for metastatic disease (lymph nodes, lung, liver).
    ◦ **Tumor Markers**: **CA-125** may be elevated in advanced or high-grade disease; it is not a screening tool but can be used to monitor treatment response.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is generally excellent for early-stage disease.
• Key prognostic factors include:
    ◦ **Surgical Stage**: The single most important factor.
    ◦ **Histologic Grade (1-3)**: How differentiated the tumor cells are.
    ◦ **Histologic Subtype**: Endometrioid (favorable) vs. Serous/Clear Cell (unfavorable).
    ◦ **Depth of Myometrial Invasion**: Deeper invasion is associated with higher risk of nodal metastasis.
    ◦ **Lymphovascular Space Invasion (LVSI)**: Presence of tumor cells in blood or lymphatic vessels.
• **5-Year Survival Rates by Stage**:
    ◦ **Stage I**: 85-90%
    ◦ **Stage II**: 70-80%
    ◦ **Stage III**: 50-60%
    ◦ **Stage IV**: <20%

sections.overview:
• Ovarian cancer is a malignancy arising from the ovary, fallopian tube, or peritoneum.
• It is the **leading cause of death from gynecologic cancer** in the United States, primarily because it is often diagnosed at an advanced stage.
• The vast majority (>90%) of ovarian cancers are **epithelial** in origin.
• It typically presents with vague, non-specific symptoms, earning it the nickname "**the silent killer**."
• The cornerstone of diagnosis and treatment is **surgical exploration and staging**, followed by chemotherapy.
sections.etiology:
• The exact etiology is unknown, but the most accepted theory is related to repeated trauma and repair to the ovarian epithelium during **incessant ovulation**, which provides more opportunities for malignant transformation.
• **Histological Types:**
    ◦ **Epithelial Tumors (~90%):** Arise from the surface epithelium of the ovary.
        ▪ **Serous Carcinoma (70-80%):** Most common type. Often bilateral. **Psammoma bodies** are a classic histological finding.
        ▪ **Endometrioid Carcinoma (~10%):** Often associated with **endometriosis** or endometrial cancer.
        ▪ **Mucinous Carcinoma (~10%):** Can become very large. May be associated with **pseudomyxoma peritonei** if it originates from an appendiceal primary.
        ▪ **Clear Cell Carcinoma (~5%):** Associated with **endometriosis** and **hypercalcemia**.
    ◦ **Germ Cell Tumors (~5%):** Arise from oocytes. Typically occur in younger women (<30 years old).
        ▪ **Dysgerminoma:** Malignant, radiosensitive. Associated with elevated **LDH**.
        ▪ **Teratoma:** Can be mature (benign, "**dermoid cyst**"), immature (malignant), or monodermal (e.g., **Struma ovarii**, which produces thyroid hormone).
        ▪ **Yolk Sac Tumor (Endodermal Sinus Tumor):** Aggressive. Produces **alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)**. **Schiller-Duval bodies** are pathognomonic.
    ◦ **Sex Cord-Stromal Tumors (~2%):** Arise from the connective tissue of the ovary. Often hormonally active.
        ▪ **Granulosa Cell Tumor:** Produces **estrogen**. Can cause precocious puberty in children or postmenopausal bleeding in adults. **Call-Exner bodies** on histology.
        ▪ **Sertoli-Leydig Cell Tumor:** Produces **androgens**. Can cause hirsutism and virilization.
sections.epidemiology:
• **5th leading cause of cancer death** in women in the U.S.
• **Most lethal gynecologic malignancy.**
• Peak incidence is in the 6th and 7th decades of life (postmenopausal).
• Germ cell tumors are more common in women under 30.
• ~75% of women are diagnosed with advanced-stage disease (**Stage III or IV**).
sections.riskFactors:
• **Risk Factors:**
    ◦ **Age:** Risk increases with age.
    ◦ **Genetics/Family History:** **Single greatest risk factor.**
        ▪ **BRCA1/BRCA2** gene mutations (associated with breast and ovarian cancer)
        ▪ **Lynch Syndrome (HNPCC)** (associated with colorectal, endometrial, and ovarian cancer)
    ◦ **Nulliparity** (or low parity)
    ◦ **Early Menarche / Late Menopause:** More lifetime ovulatory cycles.
    ◦ **Infertility**
    ◦ **Endometriosis**
• **Protective Factors:**
    ◦ **Oral Contraceptive Pills (OCPs):** 5+ years of use can decrease risk by 50%.
    ◦ **Multiparity / Breastfeeding:** Suppresses ovulation.
    ◦ **Tubal Ligation / Salpingectomy:** Reduces risk, supporting the theory that many high-grade serous cancers originate in the fallopian tube.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a postmenopausal woman with vague, persistent gastrointestinal or pelvic symptoms.
• The insidious onset and non-specific nature of symptoms lead to delayed diagnosis.
• Patients are often treated for IBS, constipation, or gastritis before the true diagnosis is considered.
• **Symptoms:**
    ◦ **Abdominal bloating** or increased abdominal girth
    ◦ **Pelvic or abdominal pain/pressure**
    ◦ **Early satiety** or difficulty eating
    ◦ **Urinary frequency or urgency**
    ◦ Constitutional symptoms in advanced disease: fatigue, weight loss, anorexia.
    ◦ Acute symptoms (less common): Ovarian torsion, rupture of a cystic tumor.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Abdominal Exam:**
    ◦ **Ascites:** Fluid wave, shifting dullness, distension.
    ◦ Palpable abdominal or omental mass.
• **Pelvic Exam:**
    ◦ **Adnexal mass:** Often solid, fixed, irregular, and non-tender.
    ◦ Nodularity in the cul-de-sac (pouch of Douglas).
• **Signs of Metastasis:**
    ◦ **Sister Mary Joseph Nodule:** Palpable nodule in the umbilicus.
    ◦ **Pleural effusion:** Decreased breath sounds, dullness to percussion.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Initial Workup (for a suspected adnexal mass):**
    ◦ **Pelvic Ultrasound:** **Transvaginal Ultrasound (TVUS)** is the initial imaging modality of choice.
        ▪ **Malignant features:** Solid components, thick septations (>2-3 mm), papillary projections, increased vascularity (Doppler flow), ascites.
        ▪ **Benign features:** Simple, thin-walled, anechoic cyst.
    ◦ **Tumor Markers:**
        ▪ **CA-125 (Cancer Antigen 125):**
            ◦ **NOT a screening tool** for the general population due to low specificity.
            ◦ Best used to monitor treatment response or detect recurrence in a known cancer.
            ◦ Can be elevated in many benign conditions (endometriosis, fibroids, PID, cirrhosis, pregnancy).
        ▪ **For young patients (<40) with a complex mass (suspicion for germ cell tumor):**
            ◦ **AFP (Alpha-fetoprotein):** Yolk sac tumors.
            ◦ **hCG (human Chorionic Gonadotropin):** Choriocarcinoma, embryonal carcinoma.
            ◦ **LDH (Lactate Dehydrogenase):** Dysgerminomas.
• **Pre-Operative Staging & Definitive Diagnosis:**
    ◦ **CT Scan of Abdomen/Pelvis with contrast:** Used to assess for metastatic disease (lymphadenopathy, omental caking, carcinomatosis) and for surgical planning.
    ◦ **Definitive Diagnosis:** **Surgical exploration and histological analysis.**
        ▪ Biopsy of an adnexal mass is generally **AVOIDED** due to the risk of rupturing a malignant cyst and seeding the peritoneum (upstaging the cancer).
        ▪ Patients with high suspicion of malignancy should be referred to a **Gynecologic Oncologist** for surgery.
    ◦ **Staging:** **FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) staging is surgical.**
        ▪ **Stage I:** Limited to one or both ovaries.
        ▪ **Stage II:** Pelvic extension (uterus, tubes, other pelvic tissues).
        ▪ **Stage III:** Peritoneal implants outside the pelvis and/or positive retroperitoneal lymph nodes. (Most common stage at diagnosis).
        ▪ **Stage IV:** Distant metastases (e.g., liver parenchyma, lung).
sections.treatment:
• **Surgical Management (Cytoreductive Surgery):**
    ◦ **Goal:** To remove all visible tumor. Optimal debulking (<1 cm of residual disease) is a key prognostic factor.
    ◦ **Procedure includes:**
        ▪ Total abdominal hysterectomy (TAH)
        ▪ Bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (BSO)
        ▪ Omentectomy
        ▪ Pelvic and para-aortic lymph node dissection
        ▪ Peritoneal washings for cytology
        ▪ Biopsies of any suspicious peritoneal surfaces
• **Chemotherapy:**
    ◦ **First-line:** Intravenous (IV) platinum-based agent + a taxane.
        ▪ **Carboplatin + Paclitaxel (Taxol)** is the standard regimen.
    ◦ Usually administered adjuvantly (after surgery) for all but the earliest, low-grade stages.
• **Targeted Therapy:**
    ◦ **PARP Inhibitors** (e.g., Olaparib): Used as maintenance therapy, especially effective in patients with **BRCA mutations**.
    ◦ **Bevacizumab (Avastin):** An anti-VEGF antibody that can be added to chemotherapy.
sections.management:
• **Surveillance:** After primary treatment, patients are monitored for recurrence.
    ◦ Regular physical and pelvic exams.
    ◦ Serial **CA-125 levels** (if initially elevated). A rising CA-125 often precedes clinical or radiographic evidence of recurrence.
    ◦ Imaging (CT/PET) is reserved for when there is clinical or biochemical suspicion of recurrence.
• **Genetic Counseling & Testing:** All patients with epithelial ovarian cancer should be offered genetic counseling and testing for **BRCA1/2** and Lynch syndrome.
    ◦ This has implications for targeted therapy (PARP inhibitors) and for family members.
sections.complications:
• **Malignant Bowel Obstruction:** A common and difficult-to-manage complication in advanced/recurrent disease.
• **Malignant Ascites and Pleural Effusion:** Can cause significant respiratory distress and discomfort. Requires paracentesis/thoracentesis.
• **Venous Thromboembolism (VTE):** High risk due to malignancy and pelvic mass effect.
• **Malnutrition/Cachexia:** Due to early satiety, nausea, and disease burden.
• **Chemotherapy-Induced Side Effects:** Neuropathy, nephrotoxicity, myelosuppression, alopecia.
sections.prognosis:
• The **stage at diagnosis** is the most important prognostic factor.
• **5-Year Overall Survival:**
    ◦ **Stage I:** >90%
    ◦ **Stage II:** ~70%
    ◦ **Stage III:** ~40%
    ◦ **Stage IV:** <20%
• Other factors influencing prognosis include tumor grade, histologic subtype, and the success of primary cytoreductive surgery.

sections.overview:
• Vulvar cancer is a relatively rare gynecologic malignancy arising from the external female genitalia (vulva), which includes the labia majora, labia minora, clitoris, and perineum.
• The vast majority of cases are **Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)**.
• It typically presents in postmenopausal women and is often associated with a long-standing history of vulvar pruritus.
• Diagnosis is confirmed by biopsy, and prognosis is primarily determined by the status of the inguinal lymph nodes.
sections.etiology:
• There are two main distinct etiopathogenic pathways for vulvar SCC:
    ◦ **HPV-Associated Pathway**
        ▪ Accounts for ~30-40% of cases.
        ▪ More common in **younger, premenopausal women**.
        ▪ Caused by persistent infection with **high-risk HPV types (16, 18, 33)**.
        ▪ HPV oncoproteins **E6 and E7** inactivate tumor suppressor genes **p53 and Rb**, respectively, leading to uncontrolled cell proliferation.
        ▪ The precursor lesion is **Vulvar Intraepithelial Neoplasia (VIN)**, now more specifically termed **High-Grade Squamous Intraepithelial Lesion (HSIL)**.
        ▪ Often multifocal and has a "warty" or "basaloid" histology.
    ◦ **HPV-Independent Pathway**
        ▪ Accounts for the majority (~60-70%) of cases.
        ▪ More common in **older, postmenopausal women** (>70 years).
        ▪ Associated with chronic inflammatory dermatoses, most notably **Lichen Sclerosus**.
        ▪ Pathogenesis involves chronic inflammation leading to genetic alterations, often **p53 mutations** independent of HPV.
        ▪ The precursor lesion is **differentiated VIN (dVIN)**.
        ▪ Typically unifocal and has a "keratinizing" histology.
• Other, less common types:
    ◦ **Vulvar Melanoma**: Second most common type (~5%).
    ◦ **Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC)**: Typically indolent course.
    ◦ **Paget's Disease of the Vulva**: Intraepithelial adenocarcinoma; may be associated with an underlying invasive cancer.
    ◦ **Bartholin Gland Carcinoma**: Rare adenocarcinoma.
sections.epidemiology:
• Accounts for ~5% of all gynecologic malignancies.
• Primarily a disease of older women; median age at diagnosis is **~68 years**.
• There is a bimodal age distribution reflecting the two pathways:
    ◦ A smaller peak at age 40-50 (HPV-related)
    ◦ A larger peak at age 70-80 (non-HPV related)
• Incidence is slowly increasing, particularly among younger women.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is an **elderly woman with a long history of vulvar pruritus** who notices a new lump, mass, or non-healing ulcer.
• Presentation is often delayed due to patient embarrassment or misattribution of symptoms to "aging" or a yeast infection.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Definitive Diagnosis**
    ◦ **Punch Biopsy**: The gold standard.
        ▪ A 3-5 mm punch biopsy should be taken from the thickest, most abnormal-appearing area of the lesion.
        ▪ If multiple lesions are present, multiple biopsies may be necessary.
• **Staging Workup** (once cancer is confirmed)
    ◦ **Full Pelvic Exam**: To assess for vaginal, cervical, or rectal involvement.
    ◦ **Cystoscopy/Proctoscopy**: If there is suspicion of bladder or rectal invasion.
    ◦ **Imaging**: For locally advanced or metastatic disease.
        ▪ **CT scan (Chest/Abdomen/Pelvis)** or **PET/CT** to evaluate for distant metastasis and pelvic/inguinal lymph node involvement.
        ▪ **MRI of the pelvis** can be useful to assess the extent of local tumor invasion.
• Staging is done surgically according to the **FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics)** system.
sections.prognosis:
• The **single most important prognostic factor is the status of the inguinal-femoral lymph nodes**.
• **5-Year Survival Rates**:
    ◦ **Stage I (Node-Negative)**: >90%
    ◦ **Stage II (Node-Negative)**: ~80%
    ◦ **Stage III (Node-Positive)**: ~50-60%
    ◦ **Stage IV (Distant Metastasis)**: <15%

sections.overview:
• Vaginal cancer is a rare malignancy arising from the tissues of the vagina, accounting for 1-2% of all gynecologic cancers.
• The most common histological type is **Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)**.
• It is primarily a disease of postmenopausal women.
• Strongly associated with **Human Papillomavirus (HPV)** infection.
• The precursor lesion is known as **Vaginal Intraepithelial Neoplasia (VAIN)**.
• Diagnosis is confirmed by biopsy, and staging is done clinically.
• Treatment is highly dependent on the stage and location of the tumor but most often involves radiation therapy.
sections.etiology:
• Vaginal cancer is classified by its cell of origin, and the pathophysiology is closely linked to the histological subtype.
    ◦ **Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)** (~85-90%)
        ▪ Arises from the squamous epithelium lining the vagina.
        ▪ Pathophysiology is analogous to cervical cancer, most commonly caused by persistent infection with **high-risk HPV types (16, 18)**.
        ▪ Develops from a precancerous lesion, **Vaginal Intraepithelial Neoplasia (VAIN)**.
        ▪ Most commonly found in the **upper one-third of the posterior vaginal wall**.
    ◦ **Adenocarcinoma** (~5-10%)
        ▪ Arises from glandular cells.
        ▪ **Clear Cell Adenocarcinoma** is a specific subtype associated with **in utero exposure to Diethylstilbestrol (DES)**.
        ▪ Non-DES-related adenocarcinomas can also occur, typically in older women.
    ◦ **Melanoma** (~3%)
        ▪ Arises from melanocytes in the vaginal mucosa.
        ▪ Highly aggressive with a poor prognosis.
        ▪ Most commonly found in the **lower one-third of the vagina**.
    ◦ **Sarcoma** (<3%)
        ▪ Arises from mesenchymal tissue (muscle, connective tissue) within the vaginal wall.
        ▪ **Sarcoma botryoides (Embryonal Rhabdomyosarcoma)** is a rare type seen almost exclusively in infants and children < 5 years old, presenting as a **"grape-like" mass** protruding from the vagina.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Rare, constituting 1-2% of GYN malignancies.
• **Age**: Primarily affects postmenopausal women.
    ◦ The median age at diagnosis for **SCC** is **60-70 years**.
    ◦ **Clear Cell Adenocarcinoma** (DES-related) has a peak incidence in younger women (ages 15-25).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The majority of patients are **asymptomatic** in the early stages.
    ◦ The lesion is often found incidentally on a routine pelvic exam or Pap smear.
• When symptomatic, the presentation is often nonspecific.
• The most common presenting symptom is **abnormal vaginal bleeding**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Pap Smear**
    ◦ May show atypical cells (ASC-US, LSIL, HSIL) or malignant cells.
    ◦ It is a screening tool, not a diagnostic one.
    ◦ A normal Pap does not rule out vaginal cancer if a lesion is visible.
• **Colposcopy**
    ◦ Examination of the vagina under magnification after application of acetic acid.
    ◦ Helps to identify abnormal areas and guide biopsy.
• **Biopsy of the visible lesion**
    ◦ **This is the gold standard for diagnosis.**
    ◦ An office-based punch biopsy is typically sufficient.
• **Staging**
    ◦ Vaginal cancer is **CLINICALLY STAGED** according to the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system.
    ◦ This is a critical distinction from surgically staged cancers (e.g., ovarian, endometrial).
• **Staging workup includes**
    ◦ Physical exam (bimanual, rectovaginal).
    ◦ Cystoscopy.
    ◦ Proctoscopy.
    ◦ Chest X-ray.
• **Optional imaging** (for treatment planning, not for staging)
    ◦ CT, MRI, or PET/CT can help assess tumor volume and lymph node involvement.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is highly **stage-dependent**.
• **Overall 5-year survival**: ~45-50%
• **5-year survival by stage** (approximate):
    ◦ **Stage I**: 70-80%
    ◦ **Stage II**: 45-55%
    ◦ **Stage III**: 30-40%
    ◦ **Stage IV**: <20%
• Tumors in the lower vagina tend to have a worse prognosis due to early spread to inguinal lymph nodes.

sections.overview:
• **Gestational Trophoblastic Disease (GTD)** is a spectrum of tumors arising from the trophoblastic cells of the placenta
    ◦ Encompasses premalignant conditions like **hydatidiform moles** and malignant conditions known as **Gestational Trophoblastic Neoplasia (GTN)**
    ◦ GTN includes **invasive mole**, **choriocarcinoma**, **placental site trophoblastic tumor (PSTT)**, and **epithelioid trophoblastic tumor (ETT)**
    ◦ Characterized by abnormal proliferation of placental tissue and markedly high levels of human chorionic gonadotropin (**-hCG**)
    ◦ With appropriate diagnosis and management, even metastatic GTN is highly curable
sections.etiology:
• GTD results from aberrant fertilization events, with pathophysiology differing based on the specific entity
    ◦ **Hydatidiform Mole (Molar Pregnancy)**
        ▪ **Complete Mole**: Characterized by diploid genetics (46,XX or 46,XY) of **paternal origin**, resulting from an anuclear ovum fertilization. Pathology reveals no fetal tissue, diffuse hydropic (grape-like) swelling of chorionic villi, and diffuse trophoblastic proliferation. Carries a higher risk of malignant transformation into GTN (~15-20%).
        ▪ **Partial Mole**: Characterized by triploid genetics (69,XXX or 69,XXY) from a normal ovum fertilized by two sperm or a single diploid sperm. Pathology shows fetal tissue, an amniotic sac, and both normal and hydropic villi with focal trophoblastic proliferation. Carries a lower risk of malignant transformation (~1-5%).
    ◦ **Gestational Trophoblastic Neoplasia (GTN)**: Malignant transformation or persistence of trophoblastic tissue
        ▪ **Invasive Mole**: A complete mole that invades the myometrium or uterine vessels. It is locally invasive but rarely metastasizes.
        ▪ **Choriocarcinoma**: A highly aggressive, malignant tumor of cytotrophoblasts and syncytiotrophoblasts that **lacks chorionic villi**. It spreads hematogenously, most commonly to the **lungs**, followed by the vagina, liver, and brain. Can follow any type of pregnancy (50% after molar pregnancy, 25% after normal term pregnancy, 25% after abortion or ectopic).
        ▪ **Placental Site Trophoblastic Tumor (PSTT)**: A rare, slow-growing tumor arising from intermediate trophoblasts at the placental implantation site. Produces low levels of -hCG but high levels of human placental lactogen (hPL).
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Relatively rare in North America and Europe (~1 in 1,000-1,500 pregnancies)
• **Geographic Variation**: Significantly more common in Southeast Asia and parts of Latin America (~1 in 100-500 pregnancies)
• **Age**: Incidence follows a bimodal distribution, with the highest risk at the extremes of reproductive age (**<20 years and >40 years**)
sections.clinicalPresentation: • The "classic" presentation is a patient in the first or early second trimester with signs and symptoms of a grossly abnormal pregnancy.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Quantitative Serum -hCG**: The single most important laboratory test
    ◦ **Finding**: Markedly elevated, often **>100,000 mIU/mL**. A level this high is highly suggestive of a complete mole.
    ◦ Partial moles may have normal or only slightly elevated levels.
• **Pelvic Ultrasound**: The primary imaging modality
    ◦ **Complete Mole**: Classic finding is a **"snowstorm"** or **"cluster of grapes"** appearance. This represents a heterogeneous mass of anechoic spaces (hydropic villi) filling the uterine cavity, with no fetus or amniotic sac.
    ◦ **Partial Mole**: Shows a coexisting (often nonviable) fetus, amniotic fluid, and a thickened, cystic placenta with a "Swiss cheese" appearance.
• **Chest X-ray (CXR)**: Essential baseline study for all patients to screen for pulmonary metastases, the most common site of spread for choriocarcinoma.
• **Histopathology**: Definitive diagnosis is made by histologic examination of tissue obtained from uterine evacuation.
sections.prognosis:
• **Hydatidiform Mole**: Excellent prognosis; nearly 100% cure rate with evacuation and surveillance
• **Low-Risk GTN**: Excellent prognosis; cure rates approach 100% with single-agent chemotherapy
• **High-Risk GTN**: Very good prognosis; cure rates are 80-90% with multi-agent chemotherapy
• Future fertility is preserved in the vast majority of patients treated with chemotherapy

sections.overview:
• Breast cancer is a malignancy arising from the epithelial cells of the ducts or lobules of the breast.
• It is the most common non-skin cancer in women and the second leading cause of cancer-related death in women.
• The disease spectrum ranges from non-invasive (in situ) carcinoma to invasive and metastatic cancer.
• Diagnosis is confirmed by biopsy, and treatment is multidisciplinary, involving surgery, radiation, and systemic therapies tailored to the tumor's specific biological characteristics.
sections.etiology:
• **Origin**: Arises from the **terminal duct-lobular unit (TDLU)** of the breast.
• **Progression**: The typical progression involves normal epithelium → hyperplasia → atypical hyperplasia → **ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS)** or **lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS)** → invasive carcinoma.
• **Hormonal Influence**: The majority of breast cancers are hormone-sensitive. Estrogen promotes the growth of cancer cells by binding to **estrogen receptors (ER)** on the tumor.
• **Genetic Mutations**: Acquired or inherited mutations in tumor suppressor genes (e.g., ***p53***) or proto-oncogenes (e.g., ***HER2***) drive malignant transformation. Inherited mutations in DNA repair genes (e.g., ***BRCA1***, ***BRCA2***) significantly increase lifetime risk.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Most common cancer diagnosed in women worldwide (excluding non-melanoma skin cancer).
• **Mortality**: Second leading cause of cancer death in women (after lung cancer).
• **Age**: Risk increases with age; median age at diagnosis is ~62 years.
• **Race/Ethnicity**: Higher incidence in non-Hispanic white women, but higher mortality in non-Hispanic Black women (often diagnosed at a later stage with more aggressive subtypes).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The most common presentation is a **painless, hard, fixed (non-mobile), irregular breast mass** discovered by the patient or on a clinical exam.
• **Breast Mass/Lump**: Most common symptom.
• **Nipple Changes**:
    ◦ **Retraction or Inversion**: New-onset pulling in of the nipple.
    ◦ **Discharge**: **Spontaneous, unilateral, bloody, or serosanguinous** discharge is suspicious.
    ◦ **Scaling/Eczematous Rash**: Suggestive of **Paget's disease**.
• **Skin Changes**:
    ◦ **Dimpling or Puckering**: Caused by traction on **Cooper's ligaments**.
    ◦ **Erythema, Edema, Warmth**: Suggests **inflammatory breast cancer**.
    ◦ **Peau d'orange** ("skin of an orange"): Edema caused by lymphatic blockage.
• **Axillary Lump**: Palpable **axillary lymphadenopathy** may be the first sign.
• **Breast Pain (Mastalgia)**: Less common (<10% of cases), but can be a presenting symptom.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Inspection**: (Patient seated, arms at sides, then raised, then on hips)
    ◦ Look for asymmetry, skin dimpling, erythema, nipple retraction, or visible masses.
• **Palpation**: (Patient supine with arm over head)
    ◦ **Mass**: Note location, size, consistency (**hard** vs. soft), mobility (**mobile** vs. **fixed**), and borders (**well-circumscribed** vs. **irregular**).
    ◦ **Lymph Nodes**: Systematically palpate the axillary (central, lateral, pectoral, subscapular) and supraclavicular lymph nodes for any enlargement or fixation.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Mammography**:
    ◦ **Screening**: Standard CC and MLO views.
    ◦ **Diagnostic**: Includes additional spot compression and magnification views.
    ◦ **Suspicious Findings**: **Spiculated mass**, **architectural distortion**, **asymmetric density**, malignant-appearing **microcalcifications** (**pleomorphic**, **linear**, **branching**).
• **Ultrasound**:
    ◦ Excellent for differentiating **cystic vs. solid lesions**.
    ◦ Used to guide **core needle biopsy**.
    ◦ **Suspicious Findings**: **Hypoechoic mass**, **irregular margins**, "**taller-than-wide**" orientation, **posterior acoustic shadowing**.
• **Breast MRI**:
    ◦ Not a screening tool for the general population. Used for:
        ▪ High-risk screening (***BRCA*** carriers, history of chest radiation).
        ▪ Evaluating extent of disease in newly diagnosed cancer.
        ▪ Evaluating for recurrence.
sections.management:
• **Screening**:
    ◦ **USPSTF**: Biennial mammography for women aged 50-74. Recommends shared decision-making for women aged 40-49.
    ◦ **ACS**: Annual mammography for women aged 45-54, then biennial or annual for women 55+. Recommends offering screening starting at age 40.
• **High-Risk Management**: For ***BRCA*** carriers or those with a strong family history.
    ◦ **Increased surveillance**: Annual mammogram + annual breast MRI starting at age 25-30.
    ◦ **Chemoprevention**: **Tamoxifen** or **Raloxifene**.
    ◦ **Prophylactic mastectomy** and/or salpingo-oophorectomy.
• **Post-Treatment Surveillance**:
    ◦ Regular follow-up with history and physical exam.
    ◦ Annual diagnostic mammogram on the remaining breast tissue.
    ◦ No routine role for blood tumor markers (CEA, CA 15-3) or imaging in asymptomatic patients.
sections.complications:
• **Disease-Related**:
    ◦ **Metastasis**: To **bone** (most common), **lung**, **liver**, and **brain**.
    ◦ **Hypercalcemia of Malignancy**: Associated with bone metastases.
• **Treatment-Related**:
    ◦ **Lymphedema**: Chronic swelling of the arm on the side of axillary surgery/radiation.
    ◦ **Surgical Complications**: Seroma, infection, chronic pain.
    ◦ **Radiation Complications**: Dermatitis, fatigue, pneumonitis (rare).
    ◦ **Chemotherapy Side Effects**: Myelosuppression, nausea/vomiting, alopecia, neuropathy.
    ◦ **Endocrine Therapy Side Effects**:
        ▪ **Tamoxifen**: Hot flashes, increased risk of **VTE** and **endometrial cancer**.
        ▪ **Aromatase Inhibitors**: Arthralgias, myalgias, **osteoporosis**.
    ◦ **Targeted Therapy Side Effects**:
        ▪ **Trastuzumab**: **Cardiotoxicity** (reversible decline in LV function); requires regular echocardiograms.
sections.prognosis:
• The **most important prognostic factor is the stage** at diagnosis, specifically the **axillary lymph node status**.
• **Favorable Prognostic Factors**:
    ◦ No lymph node involvement
    ◦ Small tumor size (<2 cm)
    ◦ Well-differentiated (Low grade)
    ◦ **ER/PR-positive** status
• **Unfavorable Prognostic Factors**:
    ◦ **Lymph node positivity** (prognosis worsens with an increasing number of positive nodes)
    ◦ Large tumor size
    ◦ Poorly differentiated (High grade)
    ◦ **HER2-positive** status (though prognosis has improved dramatically with targeted therapy)
    ◦ **Triple-Negative Breast Cancer (TNBC)**: (**ER-negative**, **PR-negative**, **HER2-negative**). Associated with a poor prognosis due to aggressive biology and lack of targeted therapies.

sections.overview:
• **Blepharitis** is a common, chronic, inflammatory condition of the eyelid margins, frequently causing eye discomfort and irritation.
• It can be broadly classified into two main types based on anatomical location:
    ◦ **Anterior Blepharitis**: Inflammation primarily affecting the area around the base of the eyelashes. It is often associated with bacterial overgrowth (**Staphylococcus**) or **seborrheic dermatitis**.
    ◦ **Posterior Blepharitis**: Inflammation affecting the inner eyelid margin, primarily involving dysfunction of the meibomian glands (**Meibomian Gland Dysfunction** or **MGD**).
• Often, patients present with a mixed picture of both anterior and posterior blepharitis.
sections.etiology:
• **Anterior Blepharitis**
    ◦ **Staphylococcal Type**: Caused by an overgrowth of bacteria, most commonly **Staphylococcus aureus**, at the lash base. Bacterial exotoxins trigger an inflammatory response, leading to irritation, erythema, and the formation of hard, fibrinous crusts (**collarettes**).
    ◦ **Seborrheic Type**: Strongly associated with generalized **seborrheic dermatitis** (dandruff of the scalp, eyebrows, etc.). Characterized by greasy, flaky scales on the lid margins. Less inflammation is seen compared to the staphylococcal type.
    ◦ **Demodex Type**: Infestation of the lash follicles by **Demodex** mites can contribute to inflammation.
• **Posterior Blepharitis**
    ◦ The core pathophysiology is **Meibomian Gland Dysfunction (MGD)**.
    ◦ The meibomian glands, which secrete the lipid layer of the tear film, become obstructed and/or produce abnormal secretions (meibum).
    ◦ This leads to:
        ▪ **Tear Film Instability**: The altered lipid layer causes rapid tear evaporation, leading to **evaporative dry eye disease**.
