        ▪ **Inflammation**: Stagnant, altered meibum is irritating and promotes the growth of bacteria (e.g., *Propionibacterium acnes*), whose lipases break down lipids into pro-inflammatory free fatty acids.
    ◦ Strongly associated with skin conditions like **acne rosacea**.
sections.epidemiology:
• Extremely common ophthalmologic condition, accounting for a significant percentage of patient visits.
• Affects all ages, genders, and ethnicities.
• Prevalence increases with age, particularly forms associated with MGD and rosacea.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients typically present with a chronic history of **bilateral eye irritation**.
• The presentation is often characterized by periods of **exacerbation and remission**.
• Symptoms are frequently worse in the **morning upon awakening** due to the accumulation of debris and inflammatory mediators overnight.
sections.diagnostics:
• Primarily a **clinical diagnosis** based on history and physical exam findings with a slit-lamp.
• **Tear Break-Up Time (TBUT)**:
    ◦ A drop of fluorescein is instilled, and the time it takes for dry spots to appear on the cornea is measured.
    ◦ A TBUT **<10 seconds is abnormal** and suggests tear film instability, common in posterior blepharitis.
• **Cultures**:
    ◦ Rarely performed.
    ◦ Indicated for cases that are severe, recalcitrant to therapy, or unilateral, to rule out unusual infection or malignancy.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis for vision is **excellent**.
• Blepharitis is a chronic disease characterized by **exacerbations and remissions**.
• The goal of management is control of symptoms and prevention of complications.
• With consistent adherence to lid hygiene and treatment, most patients can be managed effectively.

sections.overview:
• A hordeolum (stye) is an acute, localized pyogenic (pus-forming) infection or abscess of the eyelid.
    ◦ It typically arises from an obstructed gland at the eyelid margin.
• Hordeola are classified based on the gland involved:
    ◦ **External Hordeolum:** Infection of a gland of Zeis (sebaceous) or a gland of Moll (apocrine sweat gland).
        ▪ Located at the base of the eyelashes.
        ▪ This is the more common type and what is classically referred to as a "stye."
    ◦ **Internal Hordeolum:** Infection of a Meibomian gland within the tarsal plate of the eyelid.
        ▪ Tends to be larger, more painful, and may point toward the conjunctival surface of the eyelid.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Organism:**
    ◦ The most common pathogen is **_Staphylococcus aureus_** (>90% of cases).
    ◦ Less commonly, coagulase-negative staphylococci or other skin flora are involved.
• **Pathophysiology:**
    ◦ **Obstruction:** The duct of an eyelid margin gland (Meibomian, Zeis, or Moll) becomes blocked by inspissated secretions, dead skin cells, or debris.
    ◦ **Stasis & Proliferation:** The blockage creates a static environment, allowing commensal bacteria (primarily _S. aureus_) to proliferate.
    ◦ **Infection & Abscess:** Bacterial multiplication leads to an acute inflammatory response, suppurative infection, and the formation of a small abscess characterized by pus, localized edema, erythema, and pain.
sections.epidemiology:
• Extremely common ophthalmologic condition seen in primary care, urgent care, and ophthalmology settings.
• Affects individuals of all ages, genders, and ethnicities with no significant predilection.
• Incidence is slightly higher in individuals with chronic blepharitis or certain skin conditions.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with the **acute onset** of a painful, red, swollen lump on the eyelid.
• They may describe it as a "pimple" on their eyelid.
• The onset is usually rapid, developing over 1-2 days.
• Vision is typically unaffected.
sections.diagnostics:
• Hordeolum is a **clinical diagnosis**; no laboratory or imaging studies are required for typical presentations.
• **Culture & Sensitivity:**
    ◦ May be considered for recurrent hordeola, cases unresponsive to standard therapy, or if MRSA is suspected.
    ◦ The specimen is obtained by swabbing purulent discharge after drainage.
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent; most hordeola resolve spontaneously or with conservative treatment within 1-2 weeks.
• Recurrence is common, especially in patients with underlying risk factors like blepharitis or rosacea, which should be managed concurrently.

sections.overview:
• A **chalazion** is a common, sterile, chronic, lipogranulomatous inflammatory lesion of the meibomian gland.
    ◦ It results from the obstruction of a gland duct, leading to the retention of sebaceous secretions.
    ◦ This retained material incites a non-infectious, granulomatous inflammatory reaction in the surrounding tarsal plate.
    ◦ It is crucial to differentiate a **chalazion** from a **hordeolum (stye)**, which is an acute, painful, pyogenic infection.
sections.etiology:
• **Obstruction**:
    ◦ The process begins with the blockage of a meibomian gland duct.
    ◦ These are modified sebaceous glands located within the tarsal plates of the eyelids that produce meibum, the lipid layer of the tear film.
• **Secretion Retention**:
    ◦ The obstruction prevents the normal drainage of meibum, causing the lipid secretions to accumulate and distend the gland.
• **Extravasation & Inflammation**:
    ◦ The distended gland may rupture, releasing lipids and keratinous debris into the surrounding tarsal plate tissue.
• **Granulomatous Response**:
    ◦ The body recognizes these lipids as foreign material and mounts a sterile, granulomatous inflammatory response.
    ◦ This involves the recruitment of chronic inflammatory cells, such as lymphocytes, plasma cells, macrophages, and giant cells, which form a "**lipogranuloma**."
    ◦ This is the palpable nodule characteristic of a **chalazion**.
    ◦ It is an inflammatory process, not an infectious one.
sections.epidemiology:
• Extremely common ophthalmologic condition.
• Affects individuals of all ages, but peak incidence is in adults aged 30-50.
• No significant predilection for sex or race.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Meibomian Gland Dysfunction (MGD)**: The most significant risk factor.
    ◦ Characterized by altered meibum quality (thickened, cloudy) and quantity.
• **Blepharitis**: Chronic inflammation of the eyelid margins.
• **Rosacea**: Particularly ocular rosacea, which is strongly associated with MGD and blepharitis.
• **Seborrheic Dermatitis**: Can affect the eyelids and contribute to ductal obstruction.
• **History of previous chalazia**.
• Poor eyelid hygiene.
• Hyperlipidemia (a theoretical, less established association).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with a complaint of a slowly enlarging, **non-painful lump** on their eyelid that has been present for several weeks to months.
    ◦ It can occur on the upper or lower eyelid but is more common on the upper lid due to the higher number of meibomian glands.
• **Symptoms**:
    ◦ **Primary Symptom**: A painless or minimally tender, localized eyelid nodule or swelling.
    ◦ Foreign body sensation or mild irritation.
    ◦ Tearing (epiphora).
    ◦ If the **chalazion** becomes very large, it can press on the cornea, causing **blurred vision** due to induced mechanical astigmatism.
    ◦ Cosmetic concern over the appearance of the "bump."
sections.physicalExam:
• **Inspection**:
    ◦ A visible, discrete, subcutaneous nodule within the eyelid.
    ◦ The overlying skin is typically non-erythematous and mobile.
• **Palpation**:
    ◦ A firm, rubbery, **non-tender nodule** embedded within the tarsal plate.
    ◦ It is typically located away from the eyelid margin.
• **Eyelid Eversion**:
    ◦ A key examination technique.
    ◦ Eversion of the affected lid often reveals a focal, yellowish or erythematous, elevated granulomatous lesion on the palpebral conjunctival surface.
• **Associated Findings**:
    ◦ Look for evidence of underlying risk factors like **MGD** (inspissated glands, capped orifices), **blepharitis** (crusting, telangiectasias of the lid margin), or **rosacea** (facial erythema, telangiectasias, papules/pustules).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: The diagnosis is made based on the characteristic history and physical exam findings.
• **Biopsy**: Rarely needed.
    ◦ Indicated for atypical presentations, particularly a recurrent **chalazion** in the same location in an older adult.
    ◦ This is to rule out malignancy, most notably **Sebaceous Gland Carcinoma**, which can mimic a **chalazion**.
sections.treatment:
• **Warm Compresses**: The cornerstone of treatment.
    ◦ Apply a warm, clean washcloth to the closed eyelid for 10-15 minutes, 2-4 times per day.
    ◦ This helps liquefy the inspissated meibum.
• **Lid Massage**:
    ◦ Gentle massage of the eyelid towards the lid margin immediately after warm compresses can help express the gland's contents.
• **Eyelid Hygiene**:
    ◦ Regular cleaning of the eyelid margins with a commercial lid scrub or diluted baby shampoo, especially if **blepharitis** is present.
• **Intralesional Steroid Injection**:
    ◦ A small amount of triamcinolone is injected directly into the **chalazion**.
    ◦ This reduces the inflammation and often leads to resolution.
    ◦ *Risk*: Skin depigmentation (a hypopigmented spot), which can be more noticeable in darker-skinned individuals.
• **Incision and Curettage (I&C)**: A definitive surgical procedure.
    ◦ Performed under local anesthesia.
    ◦ The eyelid is everted, a vertical incision is made on the conjunctival side (to avoid a cutaneous scar), and the granulomatous contents are curetted (scooped out).
sections.management:
• **Referral**: Refer to an ophthalmologist if:
    ◦ The diagnosis is uncertain.
    ◦ The lesion is very large and affecting vision.
    ◦ For consideration of steroid injection or I&C.
    ◦ If there is any suspicion of malignancy.
sections.complications:
• **Mechanical Astigmatism**: A large **chalazion**, especially on the upper lid, can exert pressure on the cornea, temporarily altering its shape and causing **blurred vision**.
• **Cosmetic Deformity**: A persistent, visible lump on the eyelid.
• **Secondary Infection**: Rarely, a sterile **chalazion** can become secondarily infected, forming an abscess requiring drainage.
• **Complications from Treatment**:
    ◦ Skin depigmentation or atrophy from steroid injection.
    ◦ Scarring, lid notching, or eyelash damage from I&C (rare).
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**. The vast majority of chalazia resolve either spontaneously with conservative treatment or with minor intervention (injection or I&C).
• Recurrence is common, especially if underlying risk factors like **MGD** or **rosacea** are not addressed.
sections.preventionEducation:
• **Patient Education**:
    ◦ Explain the chronic nature of the condition and the importance of consistent adherence to conservative therapy.
    ◦ Manage patient expectations regarding the timeline for resolution.
• **Prevention**: For patients with recurrent chalazia, management should focus on treating underlying conditions.
    ◦ Daily lid hygiene and warm compresses.
    ◦ Management of **MGD** and **blepharitis**.
    ◦ Systemic treatment for **rosacea** (e.g., oral doxycycline) may be necessary.

sections.overview:
• **Entropion** is the inward turning (inversion) of the eyelid margin, causing the eyelashes and skin to rub against the ocular surface (cornea and conjunctiva)
    ◦ This condition most commonly affects the **lower eyelid** and leads to significant irritation, pain, and potential vision-threatening complications if left untreated
    ◦ It is the direct opposite of **Ectropion**, where the eyelid turns outward
sections.etiology:
• Entropion is classified based on its underlying cause
    ◦ **Involutional (Age-Related)**: The most common type. Pathophysiology is multifactorial
        ▪ **Horizontal Lid Laxity**: Attenuation and stretching of the medial and lateral canthal tendons, leading to an unstable eyelid
        ▪ **Disinsertion of Lower Lid Retractors**: The muscles that pull the lower lid down and keep it against the globe weaken and detach from the tarsal plate
        ▪ **Overriding of the Preseptal Orbicularis Oculi**: The preseptal portion of the eyelid-closing muscle (orbicularis oculi) moves superiorly and overrides the pretarsal portion during blinking, forcing the lid margin to roll inward
    ◦ **Cicatricial**: Caused by scarring and contracture of the posterior lamella (conjunctiva and tarsal plate), which pulls the eyelid margin inward
        ▪ **Causes**: **Trachoma** (leading cause worldwide), chemical burns, **ocular cicatricial pemphigoid (OCP)**, **Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS)**, previous eyelid surgery, or trauma
    ◦ **Spastic**: Occurs due to forceful, sustained contraction of the orbicularis oculi muscle
        ▪ Often triggered by ocular irritation, inflammation, or post-operative pain, creating a vicious cycle: irritation → spasm → entropion → more irritation
    ◦ **Congenital**: Rare. Results from improper development of the lower eyelid retractor aponeurosis or other structural abnormalities of the eyelid
sections.epidemiology:
• Primarily a condition of the **elderly**, with prevalence increasing significantly after age 60
• **Involutional entropion** is the most common form in developed countries
• **Cicatricial entropion** is more prevalent in regions where **trachoma** is endemic (e.g., parts of Africa, Asia, and the Middle East)
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient, typically elderly, presents with a chief complaint of **chronic eye irritation**, **foreign body sensation**, and **excessive tearing** in one or both eyes
    ◦ The symptoms may be intermittent initially, often worse with forceful blinking or squeezing the eyes shut
sections.diagnostics:
• Entropion is a **clinical diagnosis** made on physical examination
• **Slit-lamp examination with fluorescein staining** is crucial to assess the degree of corneal damage
• A conjunctival biopsy may be performed by ophthalmology if an autoimmune condition like ocular cicatricial pemphigoid is suspected
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is **excellent** with timely surgical intervention; surgical success rates are very high
• If left untreated, the prognosis is poor due to the high risk of progressive **corneal damage**, which can lead to **blindness**

sections.overview:
• Ectropion is the **eversion**, or outward turning, of the eyelid margin
    ◦ It most commonly affects the **lower eyelid**
    ◦ This condition disrupts the normal anatomical apposition of the lid to the globe, leading to inadequate tear drainage and **corneal exposure**
sections.etiology:
• Ectropion is classified based on its underlying cause:
    ◦ **Involutional (Most Common)**
        ▪ Also known as **senile ectropion**
        ▪ Caused by age-related changes, primarily **horizontal lid laxity** from stretching and dehiscence of the medial and lateral canthal tendons
        ▪ Weakness of the **orbicularis oculi muscle** (the muscle that closes the eye) also contributes
        ▪ The lid essentially sags under its own weight
    ◦ **Cicatricial**
        ▪ Caused by scarring and contracture of the skin and underlying tissues of the eyelid, which pulls the lid margin away from the globe
        ▪ Common causes include **facial burns**, trauma, chronic dermatitis, or previous eyelid surgery (e.g., **blepharoplasty**)
    ◦ **Paralytic**
        ▪ Results from weakness or paralysis of the **orbicularis oculi muscle** due to **facial nerve (CN VII) palsy**
            ▪ **Bell's palsy** is a classic cause
        ▪ The loss of muscle tone allows the eyelid to droop outward
    ◦ **Mechanical**
        ▪ Occurs when a mass or tumor on or near the eyelid margin physically weighs down or pushes the eyelid outward
        ▪ Examples include large **chalazia** or eyelid neoplasms (e.g., **basal cell carcinoma**)
sections.epidemiology:
• Primarily a condition of the **elderly**, with incidence increasing significantly with age
• **Involutional ectropion** is the most prevalent form
• Slightly more common in males
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient, typically elderly, presents with complaints of a "**watery eye**," **irritation**, and **redness**
    ◦ The symptoms are often **chronic** and **progressively worsening**
    ◦ They may report constantly dabbing their eye with a tissue, which can further exacerbate the lid laxity and skin irritation
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**
    ◦ The diagnosis is made primarily through a thorough history and physical examination of the eyelids and ocular surface
• **Slit-Lamp Examination**
    ◦ Essential for assessing the severity of the ectropion, evaluating the health of the conjunctiva, and examining the cornea for signs of **exposure keratopathy**
• **Fluorescein Staining**
    ◦ Used during the slit-lamp exam to highlight any **corneal epithelial defects**, **abrasions**, or **ulcers**
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis with surgical intervention is **excellent**
    ◦ Surgical repair has a high success rate, and symptoms typically resolve completely once the eyelid's anatomical position is restored
• The prognosis for vision depends on the severity of **corneal damage** prior to treatment

sections.overview:
• Dacryocystitis is an infection or inflammation of the **nasolacrimal sac**, located in the medial canthal region of the eye.
• Most commonly caused by an **obstruction** of the **nasolacrimal duct (NLD)**, which leads to stasis of tears and secondary bacterial overgrowth.
• It can present in two forms:
    ◦ **Acute Dacryocystitis**: Characterized by the sudden onset of **pain**, **erythema**, **edema**, and **tenderness** over the lacrimal sac, often with **purulent discharge**.
    ◦ **Chronic Dacryocystitis**: Characterized by persistent **epiphora** (tearing) and a **mucoid** or **mucopurulent discharge**, with minimal inflammatory signs.
sections.etiology:
• The primary mechanism is the **obstruction** of the **nasolacrimal duct (NLD)**, which prevents normal tear drainage from the lacrimal sac into the nasal cavity.
    ◦ **Obstruction**: Can be congenital (e.g., persistent membrane of Hasner in infants) or acquired (e.g., idiopathic stenosis, trauma, tumors, dacryoliths).
    ◦ **Stasis**: Tears become trapped and stagnant within the lacrimal sac.
    ◦ **Infection**: The stagnant tear fluid serves as a rich culture medium for bacteria, leading to infection and inflammation of the sac.
• **Common Pathogens**:
    ◦ **Acute**:
        ▪ *Staphylococcus aureus* (**most common**)
        ▪ *Streptococcus pneumoniae*
        ▪ *Staphylococcus epidermidis*
        ▪ *Haemophilus influenzae* (more common in children)
    ◦ **Chronic**:
        ▪ *Staphylococcus epidermidis*
        ▪ Anaerobic species (e.g., *Propionibacterium acnes*)
        ▪ *Candida* species (less common)
sections.epidemiology:
• **Bimodal age distribution**:
    ◦ **Infants**: Due to congenital NLD obstruction.
    ◦ **Adults**: Primarily affects individuals over 40 years of age.
• **Gender**: More common in females, likely due to a narrower duct diameter.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation depends on whether the condition is acute or chronic.
• **Acute**:
    ◦ Patient presents with a rapid onset of symptoms over hours to days.
    ◦ The chief complaints are severe **pain**, **redness**, and **swelling** on one side of the nose near the eye.
• **Chronic**:
    ◦ Patient presents with a long-standing history of persistent **tearing** and intermittent **discharge**, often without significant pain or inflammation.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primarily a clinical diagnosis** based on history and characteristic physical exam findings.
• **Culture and Sensitivity**: A sample of expressed **purulent discharge** can be sent to guide antibiotic therapy, especially in severe, recurrent, or hospital-acquired cases.
• **Imaging (not routine for uncomplicated cases)**:
    ◦ **CT scan of the orbits and sinuses**: Indicated if there is suspicion of **orbital cellulitis**, **abscess**, **tumor**, or significant trauma, or for pre-operative planning for a DCR.
    ◦ **Dacryocystography (DCG)**: An X-ray with contrast dye to visualize the lacrimal drainage system and identify the site of obstruction. Typically done by ophthalmology in the workup for chronic dacryocystitis.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for acute cases that are treated promptly with antibiotics.
• **Recurrence is common** if the underlying NLD obstruction is not surgically corrected.
• DCR surgery has a very **high success rate (>90%)** in resolving symptoms of chronic dacryocystitis and preventing recurrence.

sections.overview:
• **Dacryoadenitis** is the inflammation of the **lacrimal gland**, the almond-shaped gland responsible for producing the aqueous component of tears
	◦ Located in the **superotemporal** (upper-outer) portion of the orbit
• The condition can be classified as **acute** or **chronic** based on onset and duration
	◦ **Acute dacryoadenitis** is typically infectious and painful
	◦ **Chronic dacryoadenitis** is more often due to non-infectious systemic inflammatory disorders and is less painful
sections.etiology: • The underlying cause determines the classification
sections.epidemiology:
• **Acute**: More common in children and young adults, often associated with viral syndromes like mumps or mononucleosis
• **Chronic**: More common in adults, particularly middle-aged women, due to the higher prevalence of autoimmune conditions like **Sjögren's** and **sarcoidosis**
• **Bilateral involvement** is rare in acute cases but is seen in ~60% of chronic cases, strongly suggesting a systemic etiology
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation varies significantly between acute and chronic forms
• **Acute**:
	◦ Patient presents with **rapid onset** (hours to days) of severe **unilateral pain**, **swelling**, and **redness** over the outer one-third of the upper eyelid
	◦ May be accompanied by systemic symptoms like **fever**, **malaise**, and **preauricular lymphadenopathy**
• **Chronic**:
	◦ Patient presents with a **gradual**, often **painless**, **enlargement of the lacrimal gland** over weeks to months
	◦ It is frequently **bilateral**
	◦ The primary complaint may be a visible lump, eyelid fullness, or symptoms of **dry eye (keratoconjunctivitis sicca)**
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is often clinical, but further workup is guided by suspicion of the underlying cause
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Based on the classic history and physical exam findings
• **Laboratory Studies**:
	◦ **CBC with differential**: **Leukocytosis** with a left shift suggests bacterial infection; **atypical lymphocytes** suggest EBV
	◦ **Inflammatory Markers**: Elevated **ESR** and **CRP** are non-specific but indicate inflammation
	◦ **Serologies** (for chronic/systemic disease):
		▪ **ACE (Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme)**: Elevated in **sarcoidosis**
		▪ **ANA, RF, Anti-SSA (Ro), Anti-SSB (La)**: For **Sjögren's syndrome** and other rheumatologic conditions
		▪ **ANCA**: For **granulomatosis with polyangiitis**
		▪ **TSH, T4, TSI**: For **Graves' disease**
• **Imaging**:
	◦ **CT Scan of the Orbits (with contrast)**: Best initial imaging test
		▪ Shows an enlarged, diffusely enhancing lacrimal gland
		▪ Crucial for differentiating dacryoadenitis from an abscess, orbital cellulitis, or a lacrimal gland tumor
	◦ **MRI of the Orbits**: Provides superior soft tissue detail but is less commonly used for initial diagnosis
• **Biopsy**:
	◦ **Gold standard for chronic dacryoadenitis**
	◦ Indicated if the condition is refractory to treatment or if malignancy is suspected
	◦ Histopathology reveals the underlying cause (e.g., **non-caseating granulomas** for sarcoidosis, **lymphocytic infiltrate** for Sjögren's, lymphoma)
sections.prognosis:
• **Acute**: Excellent. Viral cases are self-resolving, and bacterial cases respond well to antibiotics
• **Chronic**: Guarded to good. The prognosis depends on the nature and control of the underlying systemic disease
	◦ The condition can be recurrent

sections.overview:
• Viral conjunctivitis, commonly known as "**pink eye**," is an inflammation of the **conjunctiva** caused by a viral infection.
• It is the most common cause of infectious conjunctivitis.
• Characterized by its **acute onset**, **watery discharge**, and **highly contagious** nature.
• While typically a benign and **self-limiting** condition, it can cause significant discomfort and, in some cases, lead to complications involving the cornea.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Adenovirus**: The most common cause (~65-90% of cases), highly contagious, and responsible for seasonal epidemics.
        ▪ **Pharyngoconjunctival Fever (PCF)**: Caused by adenovirus serotypes 3, 4, and 7; presents with a classic triad of **fever**, **pharyngitis**, and **follicular conjunctivitis**.
        ▪ **Epidemic Keratoconjunctivitis (EKC)**: Caused by adenovirus serotypes 8, 19, and 37; a more severe form that frequently involves the **cornea**.
    ◦ **Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV)**: Important to identify as it requires specific antiviral treatment; often **unilateral** and may present with **vesicular skin lesions** on the eyelid.
    ◦ **Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV)**: Associated with chickenpox or shingles (**Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus**).
    ◦ **Enterovirus** (e.g., Coxsackievirus): Often causes **acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis**.
    ◦ **Others**: Influenza, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), measles, mumps.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The virus directly infects conjunctival epithelial cells, leading to a host inflammatory response.
    ◦ This results in **vasodilation** (redness), increased vascular permeability (**edema/chemosis**), and stimulation of tear production (**watery discharge**).
    ◦ Lymphoid tissue within the conjunctiva becomes hyperplastic, forming characteristic **follicles**.
sections.epidemiology:
• The most common overall cause of **infectious conjunctivitis**.
• More common in adults than children, although children in daycare/school settings are frequently affected.
• Occurs year-round but with peaks in the summer and fall.
• Spreads easily in crowded environments like schools, military barracks, and healthcare facilities.
• **Transmission**: Highly contagious via **direct contact** with ocular secretions, **respiratory droplets**, and contaminated **fomites** (towels, pillows, doorknobs).
sections.riskFactors:
• Exposure to an infected individual.
• Recent or concurrent **upper respiratory infection (URI)**.
• Crowded living or working conditions (schools, offices, daycare).
• Use of public swimming pools ("**swimming pool conjunctivitis**").
• Poor hand hygiene.
• Contact lens wear.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A typical patient presents with the **acute onset** of a red, irritated, watery eye.
• The infection often begins **unilaterally** but frequently spreads to the contralateral eye within 24-48 hours.
• The patient may report a recent "cold" or sick contacts at home, school, or work.
• The chief complaint is often a **gritty, foreign body sensation** and **watery discharge**, distinguishing it from the thick, purulent discharge of bacterial conjunctivitis or the intense itching of allergic conjunctivitis.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ **Acute onset** of unilateral or bilateral conjunctival redness.
    ◦ **Watery (serous)** or mucoserous discharge.
    ◦ **Gritty, sandy, or foreign body sensation**.
    ◦ Mild itching (less prominent than in allergic conjunctivitis).
    ◦ Mild photophobia.
    ◦ Eyelid edema and crusting, especially upon waking.
    ◦ Associated systemic symptoms: **fever**, malaise, **sore throat**, **URI symptoms**.
• **Physical Exam Findings**
    ◦ **Visual Acuity**: Should be normal. If reduced, suspect corneal involvement (**keratitis**).
    ◦ **Conjunctiva**:
        ▪ **Diffuse conjunctival injection** ("beefy red" appearance).
        ▪ **Chemosis** (conjunctival edema).
        ▪ **Follicular reaction**: **Hallmark finding**. Multiple small, dome-shaped nodules (hyperplastic lymphoid tissue) most prominent on the inferior palpebral conjunctiva.
        ▪ **Subconjunctival hemorrhage**: Petechial or diffuse hemorrhages may be present.
    ◦ **Cornea**:
        ▪ Usually clear.
        ▪ **Punctate Epithelial Keratitis (PEK)**: Fine, scattered corneal lesions visible with fluorescein stain and cobalt blue light.
        ▪ **Subepithelial Infiltrates (SEIs)**: A later finding (7-10 days after onset) in **EKC**. Granular, white deposits in the anterior stroma that can cause glare and decreased vision.
    ◦ **Lymphatics**:
        ▪ **Preauricular lymphadenopathy**: A tender, palpable lymph node in front of the ear on the affected side. **This is a highly specific sign for viral conjunctivitis.**
    ◦ **Eyelids**: Mild edema, possible associated dermatitis (in **HSV/VZV**).
sections.diagnostics:
• Primarily a **clinical diagnosis** based on a thorough history and characteristic physical exam findings (**watery discharge**, **follicular reaction**, **preauricular lymphadenopathy**).
• **Lab tests are rarely indicated** but may be used in atypical cases, outbreaks, or to rule out HSV.
    ◦ **PCR or viral culture** of conjunctival swabs can confirm the specific virus.
    ◦ **Rapid antigen tests** (e.g., AdenoPlus) are available for in-office detection of adenovirus.
• **Fluorescein Staining / Slit Lamp Exam**:
    ◦ Not mandatory in primary care for uncomplicated cases.
    ◦ **Indicated if**: vision loss, severe pain, photophobia, or suspected corneal involvement.
    ◦ Used to identify corneal abrasions, **PEK**, or the pathognomonic **dendritic ulcers** of **HSV keratitis**.
sections.treatment:
• The mainstay of treatment is **supportive care**, as most cases are **self-limiting**.
• **Supportive Measures**:
    ◦ **Cool compresses**: To reduce eyelid edema and provide symptomatic relief.
    ◦ **Artificial tears / Lubricating drops**: (e.g., Refresh, Systane) PRN for irritation and gritty sensation.
• **Pharmacologic (Symptomatic Relief Only)**:
    ◦ **Topical antihistamine/decongestant drops**: (e.g., Naphazoline/Pheniramine) can be used short-term for itching and redness.
• **Key "Don'ts"**:
    ◦ **Antibiotic drops are NOT indicated** and do not treat the virus.
    ◦ **Topical corticosteroids are CONTRAINDICATED** in primary care. They can prolong viral shedding and cause a severe, sight-threatening "geographic ulcer" if the cause is undiagnosed **HSV**. Steroids should only be initiated by an ophthalmologist.
• **Specific Antiviral Therapy**:
    ◦ Reserved for non-adenoviral causes. **Prompt ophthalmology referral is required.**
    ◦ **HSV**: Topical ganciclovir gel or trifluridine drops. Oral acyclovir may be added.
    ◦ **VZV**: High-dose oral antivirals (acyclovir, valacyclovir, famciclovir).
sections.management:
• **Patient Education is CRITICAL** to prevent transmission.
    ◦ **Contagious Period**: Patients are contagious as long as their eyes are red and tearing (typically 7-14 days).
    ◦ **Hand Hygiene**: Emphasize meticulous and frequent hand washing with soap and water or alcohol-based hand sanitizer.
    ◦ **Avoid Touching Eyes**: Instruct patient to avoid rubbing or touching their eyes.
    ◦ **Personal Items**: Do not share towels, pillows, washcloths, makeup, or eye drops.
    ◦ **Contact Lenses**: Discontinue wear until complete resolution of symptoms. Discard the old lenses, case, and solution.
    ◦ **Return to Work/School**: Policies vary, but generally, individuals should stay home until eye discharge has resolved.
sections.complications:
• **Subepithelial Infiltrates (SEIs)**: Can persist for weeks to months and may cause blurred vision, glare, and photophobia.
• **Keratitis** (corneal inflammation).
• **Pseudomembrane/Membrane Formation**: Severe inflammation can lead to fibrinous sheets on the palpebral conjunctiva that can cause scarring if not removed.
• **Corneal scarring** (rare).
• **Secondary bacterial infection** (uncommon).
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**. Most adenoviral cases are **self-limiting** and resolve completely within 1-3 weeks without long-term sequelae.
• Vision-affecting complications like persistent **SEIs** can occur, especially with **EKC**, but are less common.

sections.overview:
• Bacterial conjunctivitis, commonly known as **"pink eye,"** is an inflammation of the conjunctiva caused by a bacterial infection.
    ◦ Characterized by **conjunctival injection** (redness) and a **purulent or mucopurulent discharge**.
    ◦ While often self-limiting, it is **highly contagious** and typically treated with topical antibiotics to shorten the duration of illness, prevent complications, and reduce transmission.
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Direct inoculation** of bacteria onto the conjunctival surface leads to an acute inflammatory response.
        ▪ This involves **vasodilation** of conjunctival vessels (causing erythema) and recruitment of neutrophils, resulting in a characteristic **purulent exudate**.
        ▪ The infection is typically limited to the conjunctiva and does not involve the cornea or deeper ocular structures in uncomplicated cases.
• **Common Pathogens**
    ◦ **Adults**
        ▪ ***Staphylococcus aureus*** (most common)
        ▪ ***Streptococcus pneumoniae***
        ▪ ***Haemophilus influenzae***
    ◦ **Children**
        ▪ ***Haemophilus influenzae*** (especially non-typeable)
        ▪ ***Streptococcus pneumoniae***
        ▪ ***Moraxella catarrhalis***
        ▪ Often associated with concurrent otitis media.
    ◦ **Neonates (Ophthalmia Neonatorum)**
        ▪ ***Neisseria gonorrhoeae***: **Medical Emergency**.
            ▪ Presents at 2-5 days of life with **hyperacute, copious purulent discharge**.
            ▪ Can rapidly lead to **corneal ulceration and perforation**.
        ▪ ***Chlamydia trachomatis***: Most common overall cause in newborns.
            ▪ Presents at 5-14 days of life with mucoid to purulent discharge and conjunctival swelling.
    ◦ **Contact Lens Wearers**
        ▪ ***Pseudomonas aeruginosa***.
        ▪ This is a critical association due to the high risk of sight-threatening **bacterial keratitis**.
sections.epidemiology:
• Extremely common, especially in the pediatric population.
• Accounts for 50-75% of conjunctivitis cases in children.
• **Highly contagious** and spreads easily via **direct contact** with ocular secretions or contaminated fomites (towels, pillows, makeup).
• Outbreaks are common in schools and daycare centers.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with an acute onset of a red, irritated eye.
    ◦ The presentation is often **unilateral initially**, with spread to the contralateral eye within 24-48 hours.
    ◦ The hallmark feature is discharge that causes the eyelids to be **matted or "stuck shut,"** particularly upon awakening.
sections.diagnostics:
• Bacterial conjunctivitis is primarily a **clinical diagnosis** based on history and physical exam findings.
• **Cultures and Gram stain are NOT routinely performed** for mild-to-moderate cases.
• **Indications for culturing**:
    ◦ **Hyperacute**, severe, or **copious purulent discharge** (to rule out ***N. gonorrhoeae***).
    ◦ **Neonatal conjunctivitis**.
    ◦ **Contact lens wearers** (to identify ***Pseudomonas***).
    ◦ Recurrent cases or those unresponsive to initial antibiotic therapy.
    ◦ Immunocompromised patients.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**.
• Most cases are **self-limiting** within 7-10 days without treatment.
• Topical antibiotic therapy shortens the clinical course to 2-3 days, reduces the risk of complications, and decreases transmissibility.

sections.overview: • Allergic conjunctivitis is an inflammatory response of the conjunctiva to an allergen, mediated by a Type I (IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction. • It is the most common cause of eye itching and is not contagious. • Characterized by: ◦ Bilateral ocular pruritus (itching) ◦ Conjunctival injection (redness) ◦ Tearing ◦ Chemosis (conjunctival swelling) • Major subtypes include: ◦ Seasonal Allergic Conjunctivitis (SAC): Acute episodes corresponding to seasonal allergens (e.g., pollen). Most common type. ◦ Perennial Allergic Conjunctivitis (PAC): Chronic, year-round symptoms from non-seasonal allergens (e.g., dust mites, animal dander). ◦ Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis (VKC): Severe, chronic form, typically affecting young males in warm, dry climates. Can involve the cornea. ◦ Atopic Keratoconjunctivitis (AKC): Severe, chronic form associated with atopic dermatitis. Can lead to significant corneal complications and vision loss. ◦ Giant Papillary Conjunctivitis (GPC): Caused by mechanical irritation and an immune response to foreign bodies on the ocular surface, most commonly contact lenses or ocular prostheses.
sections.etiology: • Allergic conjunctivitis is a classic Type I IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction. • Pathophysiology Steps: ◦ Sensitization Phase: ▪ Initial exposure to a specific allergen (e.g., pollen, dander). ▪ Allergen is processed by antigen-presenting cells (APCs) on the conjunctiva. ▪ APCs present the antigen to T-helper 2 (Th2) cells. ▪ Th2 cells release cytokines (IL-4, IL-13) that stimulate B-cells to differentiate into plasma cells. ▪ Plasma cells produce allergen-specific Immunoglobulin E (IgE) antibodies. ▪ IgE antibodies bind to the surface of mast cells and basophils located in the conjunctiva, "sensitizing" them. ◦ Effector (Re-exposure) Phase: ▪ Upon subsequent exposure, the allergen cross-links the IgE antibodies on the surface of sensitized mast cells. ▪ This triggers mast cell degranulation, releasing a cascade of inflammatory mediators. ▪ Early Phase (minutes): Release of pre-formed mediators like histamine. ▪ Histamine binds to H1 receptors on nerve endings, causing intense itching (pruritus). ▪ Histamine binds to H1 and H2 receptors on blood vessels, causing vasodilation (redness/injection) and increased vascular permeability (edema/chemosis). ▪ Late Phase (4-6 hours): Synthesis and release of new mediators (leukotrienes, prostaglandins, cytokines) and recruitment of inflammatory cells like eosinophils, neutrophils, and lymphocytes, which prolongs the inflammatory response.
sections.epidemiology: • Extremely common, affecting 15-40% of the population. • SAC and PAC are the most prevalent forms. • Frequently co-exists with other atopic conditions (the "atopic triad"). ◦ Approximately 70-80% of patients with allergic rhinitis have concurrent allergic conjunctivitis. • VKC is more common in young males (ages 5-20) in warm, dry climates. • AKC typically affects adults (ages 30-50) with a history of atopic dermatitis.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • A patient, often with a known history of seasonal allergies, presents with the acute onset of: ◦ Bilateral, intensely itchy, red, and watery eyes. • Symptoms often begin shortly after a known allergen exposure (e.g., spending time outdoors during high pollen counts, interacting with a pet). • The patient may also complain of concurrent sneezing and nasal congestion.
sections.diagnostics: • Primarily a clinical diagnosis based on characteristic history (acute onset, bilateral itching, known allergies) and physical exam findings. • Fluorescein Stain: ◦ Should be performed to rule out corneal abrasion, ulceration, or herpetic keratitis, especially in patients with pain, photophobia, or suspected VKC/AKC. ◦ The cornea should be clear (no epithelial defects). • Lab Tests (rarely indicated for routine cases): ◦ Conjunctival Scraping: ▪ May reveal eosinophils, supporting an allergic etiology. ▪ Not routinely performed. ◦ Allergy Testing: ▪ Skin prick testing or serum IgE testing can help identify specific offending allergens but is not necessary to diagnose the conjunctivitis itself.
sections.prognosis: • Excellent for SAC and PAC. Symptoms are typically self-limited or well-controlled with treatment. • VKC often resolves after puberty. • AKC is a chronic condition that can lead to significant morbidity and requires long-term management by an ophthalmologist.

sections.overview:
• A pterygium is a **benign**, degenerative condition characterized by a **triangular, fibrovascular growth** of the bulbar conjunctiva that extends onto the **cornea**.
	◦ Commonly referred to as **"surfer's eye."**
• The lesion typically originates in the **interpalpebral fissure**, most often on the **nasal side**, and grows horizontally towards the center of the cornea.
• While benign, it can cause significant symptoms and **visual impairment** if it progresses.
sections.etiology:
• The exact pathophysiology is multifactorial but is strongly linked to chronic exposure to **ultraviolet (UV-B) radiation**.
	◦ **UV Damage**: Chronic UV exposure leads to photodamage of **limbal stem cells** at the junction of the cornea and sclera.
		▪ These stem cells normally act as a barrier, preventing conjunctival epithelial cells from migrating onto the corneal surface.
	◦ **Barrier Breakdown**: Damage to these stem cells compromises the barrier function.
	◦ **Abnormal Proliferation**: This allows conjunctival tissue, including fibroblasts, blood vessels, and inflammatory cells, to proliferate and invade the superficial **corneal stroma**.
	◦ **Tissue Remodeling**: The process involves chronic inflammation, angiogenesis (new blood vessel formation), and elastotic degeneration of collagen fibers, resulting in the characteristic fleshy growth.
		▪ **Mutations in the p53 tumor suppressor gene** (a common result of UV damage) are often found in pterygium tissue.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Varies significantly with geographic location.
	◦ Much higher in regions with high UV exposure, particularly in the **"Pterygium Belt,"** an area 37 degrees north and south of the equator.
• **Age**: More common in adults, with prevalence increasing after age 40.
• **Sex**: Higher incidence in **males**, likely due to higher rates of outdoor occupational exposure.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Primary**: Chronic exposure to **UV-B radiation**.
• **Environmental**: Living in hot, dry, windy, and dusty climates (microtrauma to the ocular surface).
• **Occupational**: Outdoor workers (e.g., farmers, fishermen, construction workers).
• **Geographic**: Living at high altitudes or near the equator.
• **Other**: Genetic predisposition, chronic eye irritation, inflammation.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients typically present with a cosmetic complaint of a visible growth on their eye that has been slowly enlarging over months to years.
• The growth is most commonly located on the **nasal conjunctiva** and extends onto the cornea.
• It is often **bilateral** but can be asymmetrical.
• The lesion may become intermittently inflamed and red.
• **Symptoms** may include:
	◦ **Asymptomatic**: Many small pterygia are asymptomatic.
	◦ **Irritation**: Foreign body sensation, grittiness, itching, burning.
	◦ **Redness**: Due to inflammation and vascularity.
	◦ **Dryness or Tearing**: Disruption of the normal tear film.
	◦ **Blurred Vision**: Occurs as the pterygium grows onto the cornea and induces **astigmatism** by physically altering the corneal curvature.
	◦ **Vision Obstruction**: In advanced cases, the growth may cover the pupil, directly obstructing the **visual axis**.
	◦ **Diplopia (rare)**: Very large lesions can restrict extraocular movements.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Slit-lamp examination** is the key diagnostic tool.
• **Appearance**: A **triangular, wing-shaped, fleshy, fibrovascular mass** extending from the bulbar conjunctiva onto the corneal surface.
	◦ The "apex" or head of the pterygium is on the cornea.
• **Location**: Almost always in the **interpalpebral zone** (exposed area between eyelids), with a strong predilection for the **nasal side**.
• **Vascularity**: Can appear pale and atrophic (inactive) or hyperemic and inflamed (active).
• **Stocker's Line**: A classic associated finding.
	◦ It is a brownish or yellowish line of **iron deposition** in the corneal epithelium located just anterior to the advancing head of the pterygium.
	◦ Indicates chronicity.
sections.diagnostics:
• The diagnosis is **overwhelmingly clinical**, based on the characteristic appearance and location on physical exam (especially **slit-lamp**).
• **Visual Acuity**: To assess for vision changes.
• **Corneal Topography**: May be used to measure the degree of induced **astigmatism**, particularly for surgical planning.
• **Biopsy/Histopathology (Rarely needed)**: Performed if the lesion has an atypical appearance (e.g., rapid growth, unusual pigmentation) to rule out malignancy, such as conjunctival squamous cell carcinoma.
sections.treatment:
• **Conservative / Medical Management (First-line for mild cases)**:
	◦ **Lubrication**: **Artificial tears** to alleviate irritation, dryness, and foreign body sensation.
	◦ **Anti-inflammatories** (for symptomatic inflammation/redness):
		▪ Topical NSAIDs (e.g., ketorolac).
		▪ Short course of topical corticosteroids (e.g., loteprednol, prednisolone).
• **Surgical Excision**:
	◦ **Surgical Technique**:
		▪ Simple excision alone has a very high **recurrence rate** (up to 80%).
		▪ The standard of care is **excision with conjunctival autograft** or **amniotic membrane transplantation**. A piece of the patient's own healthy conjunctiva (autograft) or a piece of amniotic membrane is used to cover the bare sclera where the pterygium was removed.
			• This acts as a new barrier and dramatically **reduces the recurrence rate** to <10%.
		▪ **Adjunctive Therapies**: **Mitomycin C** (an anti-metabolite) may be applied intraoperatively to inhibit fibroblast proliferation and reduce recurrence, especially in high-risk cases.
sections.management:
• For asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic patients, a **"watch and wait"** approach is appropriate.
• **Follow-up**: Monitor annually or semi-annually to document size (serial photography is useful) and assess for progression or vision changes.
• **Referral to Ophthalmology**: Indicated for any of the following:
	◦ Uncertain diagnosis
	◦ Vision changes (e.g., induced **astigmatism**)
	◦ Growth progression towards the **visual axis**
	◦ Consideration for surgical excision
sections.complications:
• **Disease-related**:
	◦ Progressive irregular **astigmatism**.
	◦ **Corneal scarring** and thinning.
	◦ Obstruction of the **visual axis** leading to significant vision loss.
	◦ Chronic ocular surface irritation and dry eye syndrome.
• **Surgery-related**:
	◦ **Recurrence**: The most common complication, although much lower with modern techniques.
	◦ Infection, diplopia, **scleral melt** (thinning of the sclera), persistent inflammation.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is generally **excellent**.
• It is a **benign condition** that, if monitored, can be managed effectively.
• **Vision loss is preventable** with timely surgical intervention.
• With modern surgical techniques (excision with autograft), the cosmetic and functional outcomes are very good, with low rates of recurrence.
sections.preventionEducation:
• **UV Protection**: Patient education on aggressive UV protection is paramount in all cases to prevent progression.
	◦ Emphasize wearing **sunglasses** (wrap-around, 100% UVA/UVB blocking).
	◦ Recommend the use of **wide-brimmed hats**.

sections.overview:
• A **pinguecula** is a common, benign degenerative condition of the **bulbar conjunctiva**.
    ◦ Presents as a yellowish, slightly raised, triangular or amorphous deposit.
    ◦ Typically located in the **interpalpebral fissure**, the area of the eye exposed between the eyelids.
    ◦ Represents a degeneration of collagen fibers within the conjunctival stroma.
    ◦ Key feature: A **pinguecula** **does not** grow onto the **cornea**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ The primary cause is chronic exposure to **ultraviolet (UV) radiation** from the sun.
    ◦ Other contributing factors include chronic irritation from wind, dust, sand, and low humidity.
    ◦ It is essentially an "actinic" or sun-related injury.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ UV radiation induces damage to the fibroblasts in the conjunctival stroma.
    ◦ This leads to the pathological process of **elastotic degeneration**, where fibroblasts produce excessive and abnormal elastic and collagen fibers.
    ◦ This accumulation of degenerated connective tissue (hyaline and yellow elastic fibers) forms the visible lesion.
sections.epidemiology:
• Extremely common, with prevalence increasing significantly with age.
• More prevalent in populations living in sunny, windy, and dusty climates (i.e., closer to the equator, in "Sun Belt" regions).
• Higher incidence in individuals with significant outdoor occupations (e.g., farmers, sailors, welders, construction workers).
• Often **bilateral**.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Chronic UV light exposure (most significant risk factor)**
• Outdoor occupation or hobbies
• Living in a dry, dusty, or windy environment
• Advancing age
• Male gender (likely due to higher rates of outdoor occupations)
• Dry eye syndrome
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient, typically middle-aged or older, presents with a "spot" or "bump" on the white of the eye that has been present for years.
    ◦ Often an incidental finding during a routine eye exam or noticed by the patient themselves.
    ◦ The lesion is usually asymptomatic but can become intermittently red and irritated, a condition known as **pingueculitis**.
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ **Often asymptomatic.**
    ◦ If symptomatic, symptoms are typically mild:
        ▪ Foreign body sensation
        ▪ Grittiness or irritation
        ▪ Dryness
        ▪ Redness and inflammation (during episodes of **pingueculitis**)
        ▪ Cosmetic concerns
sections.physicalExam:
• **Location**: **Bulbar conjunctiva**, within the **interpalpebral fissure**.
    ◦ More common on the **nasal side** than the temporal side.
• **Appearance**: Yellowish, slightly elevated, triangular (with base towards the limbus) or amorphous lesion.
• **Key Differentiating Feature**: The lesion is **strictly confined to the conjunctiva** and **does NOT cross the limbus** or encroach onto the **cornea**.
• **Pingueculitis**: If inflamed, the lesion and surrounding conjunctiva will exhibit **conjunctival injection** (redness) and mild edema.
sections.diagnostics:
• The diagnosis is **purely clinical**, made by visual inspection, often with a slit-lamp examination.
• **Slit-lamp exam**: Confirms the diagnosis by providing a magnified view of the lesion, showing its elevation, characteristic color, and, most importantly, its confinement to the conjunctiva without corneal involvement.
• **Biopsy**: Rarely indicated.
    ◦ May be considered if the lesion has an atypical appearance (e.g., rapid growth, unusual pigmentation, prominent feeder vessels) to rule out malignancy such as **conjunctival carcinoma in situ** or **squamous cell carcinoma**.
sections.treatment:
• **Asymptomatic Pinguecula**
    ◦ **Reassurance** and patient education.
    ◦ **UV Protection**: Strongly recommend sunglasses with UV-A and UV-B protection and a wide-brimmed hat to prevent further growth and irritation.
• **Mildly Symptomatic (Irritation/Dryness)**
    ◦ **Artificial tears** or lubricating eye ointments for symptomatic relief.
• **Pingueculitis (Acute Inflammation)**
    ◦ **Topical NSAIDs** (e.g., ketorolac tromethamine) can reduce inflammation without the risks of steroids.
    ◦ **Mild topical corticosteroids** (e.g., loteprednol, fluorometholone) for a short course (1-2 weeks) in more significant inflammation.
        ▪ *Use with caution due to risks of increased IOP and cataracts.*
• **Surgical Excision**
    ◦ **Rarely indicated.**
    ◦ Considerations for surgery include:
        ▪ Chronic, severe **pingueculitis** unresponsive to medical therapy.
        ▪ Significant cosmetic concerns.
        ▪ Chronic irritation that interferes with contact lens wear.
sections.management:
• **Patient Education**: Educate the patient on the benign nature of the condition and the critical role of UV protection in management and prevention.
• **Follow-up**: Routine follow-up is not necessary for asymptomatic cases. Patients should be advised to return if the lesion changes in size or color, becomes chronically painful, or if they experience changes in vision.
sections.complications:
• **Pingueculitis**: The most common complication, characterized by acute inflammation, redness, and irritation.
• **Progression to Pterygium**: While a distinct entity, chronic inflammation and continued irritation of a **pinguecula** may predispose an individual to the development of a **pterygium** in the same location.
• **Corneal Effects (Rare)**: An extremely large or elevated **pinguecula** can disrupt the normal tear film, leading to localized dry spots on the adjacent cornea.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent.** A **pinguecula** is a benign condition that does not threaten vision.
• It may enlarge very slowly over decades, but this is typically of little clinical consequence.
• With appropriate UV protection, growth can be minimized.

sections.overview:
• **Keratitis** is an **inflammation of the cornea**, the transparent, dome-shaped anterior part of the eye that covers the iris and pupil.
• Considered an **ophthalmologic emergency** as it can rapidly lead to corneal scarring, perforation, and permanent vision loss.
• The condition can be broadly categorized into infectious and non-infectious causes.
• A **corneal ulcer (ulcerative keratitis)** refers to keratitis that involves an open sore or epithelial defect on the cornea.
sections.etiology:
• The underlying pathophysiology involves a breach in the corneal epithelium, allowing pathogenic organisms or inflammatory mediators to invade the underlying corneal stroma.
    ◦ This triggers a robust inflammatory response, characterized by the influx of white blood cells (creating an infiltrate), edema, and potential tissue necrosis.
• **Infectious Keratitis**
    ◦ **Bacterial**: Most common cause.
        ▪ *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*: Aggressive, rapidly progressing. Strongly associated with **contact lens wear**, especially extended-wear lenses. Produces a mucopurulent, often greenish discharge.
        ▪ *Staphylococcus aureus*: Common, often associated with ocular surface disease like blepharitis.
        ▪ *Streptococcus pneumoniae*: Often follows corneal trauma.
        ▪ *Moraxella catarrhalis*: Associated with alcoholism, diabetes, malnutrition.
    ◦ **Viral**
        ▪ **Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV)**: Most common cause of viral keratitis and infectious corneal blindness in the US.
            ▪ Caused by reactivation of the virus from the trigeminal ganglion (CN V1).
            ▪ Characterized by its classic **dendritic (branching) appearance**.
        ▪ **Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV)**: Reactivation of VZV in the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (**Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus**).
            ▪ Look for a vesicular rash in the V1 dermatome and **Hutchinson's sign**.
        ▪ **Adenovirus**: May cause keratitis as part of epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC).
    ◦ **Fungal**: Less common but difficult to treat.
        ▪ *Candida*: Yeast. Seen in chronic ocular surface disease or immunocompromised patients.
        ▪ *Aspergillus* & *Fusarium*: Molds. Classically associated with **trauma involving organic/vegetable matter** (e.g., tree branch injury).
    ◦ **Protozoan**
        ▪ *Acanthamoeba*: Rare but devastating. Strongly associated with **poor contact lens hygiene**, such as rinsing/storing lenses in tap water or swimming/showering with contacts.
• **Non-Infectious Keratitis**
    ◦ **Exposure Keratitis**: Due to incomplete eyelid closure (e.g., Bell's palsy, severe exophthalmos, coma), leading to corneal drying and breakdown.
    ◦ **Neurotrophic Keratitis**: Caused by damage to the trigeminal nerve (CN V), leading to loss of corneal sensation, reduced tear production, and impaired healing.
    ◦ **Photokeratitis ("Welder's flash")**: Caused by intense UV light exposure.
    ◦ **Allergic/Immune-mediated Keratitis**: Associated with conditions like atopic disease or rheumatoid arthritis.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Bacterial keratitis** is the most common form, with an estimated 30,000 cases annually in the US.
• The incidence is dramatically higher in **contact lens wearers**.
    ◦ Soft contact lens wearers account for the vast majority of cases.
• **Fungal keratitis** is more common in tropical and agricultural regions.
• **HSV keratitis** is the leading cause of unilateral infectious blindness in developed nations.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patient typically presents with an **acute onset** of a **painful, red eye** and changes in vision over several hours to days.
• The history is critical for identifying risk factors.
    ◦ Always ask about **contact lens wear** (type, hygiene, sleeping in them), recent trauma (especially with plant matter), and any history of cold sores (HSV) or shingles (VZV).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Diagnosis is often made based on history and physical exam findings, especially with **slit-lamp examination**.
• **Fluorescein Staining**: Essential for any painful red eye.
    ◦ It highlights **epithelial defects**, confirming an ulcer.
• **Corneal Scraping for Culture and Staining**: Indicated for large, central, vision-threatening ulcers, or those not responding to empiric therapy.
    ◦ Samples are sent for:
        ▪ **Gram stain** (bacteria)
        ▪ **KOH prep** or Giemsa stain (fungi)
        ▪ **Culture** on specialized media (blood agar, chocolate agar, Sabouraud agar for fungus).
• **Confocal Microscopy**: Non-invasive imaging that can visualize fungal hyphae or *Acanthamoeba* cysts in vivo.
• **PCR**: Can be used to rapidly identify HSV or VZV DNA from a corneal swab.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly variable and depends on the causative organism, size and location of the ulcer, and timeliness of treatment.
• Small, peripheral bacterial ulcers treated promptly often heal well with minimal scarring.
• Central ulcers, aggressive organisms (*Pseudomonas*), fungal keratitis, and *Acanthamoeba* keratitis have a much more guarded prognosis and are more likely to result in significant vision loss.

sections.overview:
• A **corneal ulcer**, or **ulcerative keratitis**, is an **open sore** on the cornea, the transparent outer layer of the eye
    ◦ Involves disruption of the **corneal epithelium** with underlying inflammation of the **stroma**
• Considered an **ophthalmic emergency**
    ◦ Can rapidly lead to **corneal scarring**, **perforation**, and **permanent vision loss** if not treated promptly and aggressively
sections.etiology:
• Fundamental pathology involves a **breach in the corneal epithelium**
    ◦ Allows pathogens or inflammatory mediators to access the underlying **corneal stroma**
• The host's inflammatory response contributes to stromal tissue destruction (**liquefactive necrosis**)
    ◦ Involves **neutrophils** and **cytokine release**
    ◦ Can lead to scarring and thinning
sections.epidemiology:
• Incidence in the U.S. is approximately 30,000-75,000 cases per year
• **Bacterial keratitis** is the most common etiology
• Risk is significantly elevated in **contact lens wearers**, accounting for a large percentage of cases in developed nations
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient, frequently a **contact lens user**, presents with the acute onset of symptoms:
    ◦ **Painful, red eye**
    ◦ **Photophobia**
    ◦ **Blurred vision**
    ◦ Rapid progression over 24-48 hours
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Primarily based on history and characteristic **slit-lamp** findings
• **Fluorescein Staining**: Essential to confirm and delineate the size of the **epithelial defect**
• **Corneal Scraping for Cultures and Stains**: **Gold standard** for identifying the causative organism
    ◦ Indicated for any ulcer that is **large**, **central**, **vision-threatening**, or not responding to initial therapy
    ◦ Samples are plated on various media
        ▪ **Blood agar**, **chocolate agar**
        ▪ **Sabouraud dextrose agar** (fungi)
        ▪ Non-nutrient agar with E. coli overlay for ***Acanthamoeba***
    ◦ Stains include:
        ▪ **Gram stain** (bacteria)
        ▪ **Giemsa/KOH prep** (fungi)
• **Confocal Microscopy**: Non-invasive imaging that can visualize **fungal hyphae** or ***Acanthamoeba* cysts** in vivo
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is highly dependent on the **size and location** of the ulcer, the **virulence** of the organism, and the **time to effective treatment**
• Small, peripheral bacterial ulcers treated promptly have an **excellent prognosis**
• Large, central ulcers and those caused by ***Pseudomonas***, **fungi**, or ***Acanthamoeba*** have a more **guarded prognosis**
    ◦ High likelihood of **permanent vision impairment**

sections.overview:
• **Herpes Simplex Keratitis (HSK)** is an infection of the cornea caused by the **Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV)**.
• It is a major cause of infectious blindness in developed nations.
• The infection is characterized by its potential for recurrence, leading to progressive corneal scarring, thinning, and vision loss.
• The hallmark finding of the most common form (epithelial keratitis) is a **dendritic ulcer**, which is pathognomonic.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**:
    ◦ Primarily **Herpes Simplex Virus Type 1 (HSV-1)**, which is typically associated with orofacial infections.
    ◦ Less commonly, HSV-2 (genital herpes) can be the cause, especially in neonates or from autoinoculation.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Primary Infection**: Usually occurs in childhood and is often subclinical or presents as a mild blepharoconjunctivitis (eyelid and conjunctiva inflammation).
    ◦ **Latency**: The virus travels via sensory axons to the **trigeminal ganglion (cranial nerve V)**, where it establishes a lifelong latent infection.
    ◦ **Reactivation**: Various triggers cause the virus to reactivate. It then travels back down the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V1) to infect the ocular tissues, most notably the cornea.
• **Types of Keratitis**:
    ◦ **Epithelial Keratitis**: The most common form.
        ▪ Caused by active viral replication in the corneal epithelium. This leads to the classic **dendritic ulcers**.
    ◦ **Stromal Keratitis**: Primarily an **immune-mediated** response to viral antigens within the deeper corneal stroma. It is not an active infection. Can present as:
        ▪ **Disciform Keratitis**: A disc-shaped area of corneal edema due to an inflammatory reaction against the corneal endothelium (endothelitis).
        ▪ **Necrotizing Stromal Keratitis**: Severe inflammation leading to stromal destruction, ulceration, and scarring.
    ◦ **Neurotrophic Keratopathy**: Chronic, non-healing epithelial defect resulting from impaired corneal innervation and decreased sensation caused by viral damage to corneal nerves.
sections.epidemiology:
• HSK is the most common cause of infectious corneal blindness in the United States.
• The vast majority of adults are seropositive for HSV-1.
• Recurrence is common, with a rate of ~25% at 2 years after the first episode, increasing with each subsequent episode.
• No significant gender or racial predilection.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Systemic or emotional stress**
• **UV light exposure** (e.g., intense sunlight)
• **Fever** or systemic illness
• **Immunosuppression** (e.g., corticosteroids, chemotherapy, HIV)
• Ocular trauma or surgery
• Menstruation
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Typically **unilateral**.
• Patients present with the acute onset of a painful, red eye.
• A key historical clue is a **history of prior, similar episodes**.
• There may or may not be a concurrent or recent history of a "cold sore" (herpes labialis).
• **Symptoms** may include:
    ◦ **Pain** (often described as a foreign body sensation)
    ◦ **Photophobia** (light sensitivity)
    ◦ **Blurred vision**
    ◦ **Redness**
    ◦ **Epiphora** (excessive tearing)
    ◦ Vesicular rash on the eyelids (in some primary infections or severe recurrences).
sections.physicalExam:
• **Visual Acuity**: Almost always decreased in the affected eye.
• **Eyelids/Conjunctiva**: Possible vesicular lesions on the eyelid skin. Conjunctival injection, particularly a **ciliary flush** (a ring of redness around the cornea).
• **Cornea**:
    ◦ **Decreased Corneal Sensation**: A classic and highly suggestive finding. Test by gently touching the central cornea with a wisp of cotton from a cotton-tipped applicator and comparing the blink reflex to the unaffected eye.
    ◦ **Slit Lamp Examination with Fluorescein Stain**: This is the key diagnostic examination.
        ▪ **Dendritic Ulcer (Epithelial Keratitis)**: The **pathognomonic** finding. A thin, linear, branching epithelial ulcer. The ends of the branches have characteristic swellings called **terminal bulbs**. Fluorescein stains the base of the ulcer, while Rose Bengal or Lissamine Green stain the borders.
        ▪ **Geographic Ulcer**: A larger, amoeba-shaped epithelial defect that can form if a dendritic ulcer is misdiagnosed and treated with topical steroids.
        ▪ **Disciform Edema (Stromal Keratitis)**: A central, disc-shaped area of stromal and epithelial edema without a true epithelial ulcer.
        ▪ **Keratic Precipitates (KPs)**: Inflammatory cells clumped on the corneal endothelium, often seen underlying the area of stromal inflammation.
• **Anterior Chamber**: May show cells and flare, indicating an associated iritis (uveitis).
• **Intraocular Pressure (IOP)**: Can be elevated due to associated trabeculitis (inflammation of the trabecular meshwork).
sections.diagnostics:
• The diagnosis is primarily **clinical**, based on the characteristic history and slit lamp findings.
• **Fluorescein staining** is the most critical diagnostic tool to visualize the dendritic ulcer.
• **Viral culture or Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR)** of corneal scrapings can be performed in atypical or non-resolving cases but is not routinely necessary.
sections.treatment:
• **Epithelial Keratitis (Active Infection)**:
    ◦ **Topical Antivirals**:
        ▪ **Ganciclovir 0.15% gel** (preferred due to lower toxicity)
        ▪ Trifluridine 1% drops
    ◦ **Oral Antivirals**:
        ▪ **Acyclovir** 400 mg 5 times/day
        ▪ **Valacyclovir** 1 g TID
        ▪ Used as an alternative to topicals or as adjunctive therapy in severe cases or immunocompromised patients.
    ◦ **Cycloplegic agents** (e.g., Cyclopentolate) may be used to relieve pain from ciliary spasm associated with iritis.
    ◦ **CRITICAL**: **Topical corticosteroids are contraindicated in active epithelial HSK.** They can potentiate viral replication, leading to a large geographic ulcer and corneal melting.
• **Stromal Keratitis (Immune-Mediated)**:
    ◦ Managed exclusively by ophthalmology.
    ◦ Treatment involves a **topical corticosteroid** (e.g., Prednisolone acetate) to control inflammation, given concurrently with a **prophylactic oral antiviral** (e.g., Acyclovir) to prevent epithelial reactivation.
sections.management:
• **Immediate ophthalmology consultation is mandatory.** A PA should not manage this condition independently.
• **Prophylaxis**: For patients with frequent (2 episodes/year) or sight-threatening recurrences, long-term, low-dose oral antiviral prophylaxis (e.g., **Acyclovir** 400 mg BID) is highly effective in reducing the frequency and severity of recurrences (supported by the HEDS trial).
sections.complications:
• Corneal scarring and opacification
• Neovascularization (growth of new blood vessels into the cornea)
• Neurotrophic keratopathy (persistent epithelial defects)
• Corneal thinning and perforation
• Secondary glaucoma
• Cataract formation (from chronic inflammation or steroid use)
• Permanent vision loss
sections.prognosis:
• With prompt and appropriate treatment, a single episode of epithelial keratitis has a good prognosis for visual recovery.
• The prognosis worsens with each recurrence due to the cumulative effect of scarring and nerve damage.
• Stromal and neurotrophic disease carry a more guarded prognosis and are more likely to result in permanent vision loss.
sections.preventionEducation:
• Counsel on the recurrent nature of the disease and the importance of seeking immediate care if symptoms return.
• Advise on trigger avoidance (e.g., UV protection).

sections.overview:
• **Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus (HZO)** is a sight-threatening medical emergency characterized by the reactivation of the latent **Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV)** in the **ophthalmic division (V1)** of the **trigeminal nerve (CN V)**
    ◦ It presents as a painful, unilateral, dermatomal vesicular rash on the forehead, scalp, and nose, often accompanied by direct ocular involvement
    ◦ Prompt diagnosis and treatment are critical to prevent permanent vision loss and other serious complications
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**: Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV), also known as Human Herpesvirus 3 (HHV-3)
• **Primary Infection**: The initial infection with VZV causes varicella (chickenpox)
• **Latency**: After the primary infection resolves, the virus travels up sensory nerves and establishes a lifelong latent infection in the dorsal root ganglia
    ◦ For HZO, the virus lies dormant specifically in the **trigeminal ganglion**
• **Reactivation**: A decline in VZV-specific cell-mediated immunity allows the virus to reactivate
    ◦ It then travels anterograde down the axon of the trigeminal nerve's **ophthalmic division (V1)** to the skin and eye
• **Anatomic Correlation**
    ◦ The V1 division of the trigeminal nerve has three main branches: frontal, lacrimal, and **nasociliary**
    ◦ The **nasociliary branch** innervates the tip of the nose (via the external nasal nerve) as well as the cornea, iris, and ciliary body (via the long ciliary nerves)
        ▪ This is the anatomical basis for **Hutchinson's sign**
sections.epidemiology:
• Herpes Zoster (shingles) affects approximately 1 in 3 people in the U.S. during their lifetime
• HZO accounts for 10-20% of all herpes zoster cases
• Incidence sharply increases with age, particularly after 50 years
• No significant gender or racial predilection
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation typically occurs in two phases:
    ◦ **Prodromal Phase (pre-eruptive)**
        ▪ Lasts 2-3 days before the rash appears
        ▪ Characterized by unilateral facial or periorbital pain, which can be described as burning, tingling, aching, or stabbing
        ▪ May be accompanied by systemic symptoms like malaise, fever, and headache
    ◦ **Eruptive Phase (acute)**
        ▪ A unilateral, dermatomal maculopapular rash develops on the forehead, scalp, and upper eyelid
        ▪ The rash rapidly progresses to vesicles on an erythematous base, then pustules, and finally crusting over 7-10 days
        ▪ The rash **strictly respects the midline**
        ▪ Ocular signs and symptoms may develop concurrently or shortly after the rash appears
sections.diagnostics:
• Primarily a **clinical diagnosis** based on the characteristic unilateral, dermatomal V1 rash
• **Confirmatory Testing (if diagnosis is uncertain)**
    ◦ **Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR)**
        ▪ Test of choice
        ▪ High sensitivity and specificity for VZV DNA from a swab of an unroofed vesicle or corneal scraping
    ◦ **Viral Culture**
        ▪ Less sensitive and slower than PCR
    ◦ **Tzanck Smear**
        ▪ Shows multinucleated giant cells but cannot differentiate between VZV and HSV
        ▪ Rarely used
• **Mandatory Evaluation**
    ◦ Urgent **slit-lamp examination** by an ophthalmologist
    ◦ **Fluorescein staining** to assess for corneal involvement
    ◦ **Tonometry** to measure intraocular pressure
sections.prognosis:
• With prompt antiviral therapy and ophthalmologic care, the prognosis for vision is generally good
• Prognosis is worse in elderly or immunocompromised patients and in cases with significant ocular inflammation (uveitis, keratitis) at presentation
• **Delay in treatment (>72 hours)** significantly increases the risk of severe complications and vision loss
• **PHN** can develop in up to 20% of patients and severely impacts quality of life

sections.overview:
• Inflammation of the anterior uveal tract, which includes the **iris (iritis)** and the **ciliary body (iridocyclitis)**
• Most common form of uveitis
• Core pathophysiology involves the breakdown of the **blood-aqueous barrier**, leading to the leakage of inflammatory cells and protein into the anterior chamber of the eye
• It is an **ophthalmologic urgency** that requires prompt diagnosis and treatment to prevent vision-threatening complications
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The fundamental process is a breakdown of the tight junctions in the blood vessels of the iris and ciliary body (the **blood-aqueous barrier**)
    ◦ This increased permeability allows leukocytes (**cells**) and protein (**flare**) to extravasate into the aqueous humor of the anterior chamber
    ◦ This inflammatory response leads to pain, photophobia, and potential structural damage
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Idiopathic**
        ▪ The most common cause (approx. 50-70% of cases), with no identifiable underlying systemic disease
    ◦ **Systemic Autoimmune / Inflammatory Disease (Seronegative Spondyloarthropathies)**
        ▪ **HLA-B27 Associated**: This is the strongest genetic link
        ▪ **Ankylosing Spondylitis**: Most common association; uveitis may be the presenting sign
        ▪ **Reactive Arthritis (Reiter's Syndrome)**: Classic triad: "Can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree" (uveitis, urethritis, arthritis)
        ▪ **Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD)**: Crohn's disease, Ulcerative Colitis
        ▪ **Psoriatic Arthritis**
        ▪ **Other Systemic Diseases**
            • **Sarcoidosis**: Often presents as **bilateral, granulomatous uveitis**
            • **Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA)**: A common cause in children; can be asymptomatic ("**white eye**") initially
            • **Behçet's Disease**
    ◦ **Infectious**
        ▪ **Viral**: Herpes Simplex (HSV), Varicella Zoster (VZV) - often associated with high **intraocular pressure (IOP)**
        ▪ **Bacterial**: Syphilis ("the great masquerader"), Tuberculosis (TB), Lyme disease
    ◦ **Trauma**
        ▪ Blunt trauma to the eye can cause acute traumatic iritis
    ◦ **Masquerade Syndromes**
        ▪ Conditions that mimic uveitis, such as intraocular lymphoma
sections.epidemiology:
• Most common form of uveitis, accounting for ~75% of all cases
• Annual incidence is approximately 8-15 cases per 100,000 people
• Peak onset is in young to middle-aged adults (20-50 years old)
• No significant gender predilection, though **HLA-B27-associated uveitis** is more common in males
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with the **acute onset of a unilateral red, painful eye** that has developed over hours to days
• They will complain of significant **light sensitivity (photophobia)** and may have blurred vision
• A history of low back pain and stiffness (**Ankylosing Spondylitis**), joint pain, recent GI illness (**IBD**, **Reactive Arthritis**), or rash (**Psoriasis**, **Zoster**) is a critical clue
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is **primarily clinical**, based on the slit-lamp exam findings of **anterior chamber cells and flare**
• **Laboratory Workup**
    ◦ A workup is **NOT** typically needed for a first-time, unilateral, non-granulomatous episode without systemic symptoms
• **Indications for workup**
    ◦ Recurrent, bilateral, granulomatous, or severe uveitis
    ◦ If systemic symptoms are present
• **Targeted Labs based on H&P**
    ◦ **HLA-B27**: For suspected spondyloarthropathy
    ◦ **Chest X-ray, ACE level**: For suspected **Sarcoidosis**
    ◦ **RPR/VDRL & FTA-ABS**: For suspected **Syphilis**
    ◦ **PPD or Quantiferon-TB Gold**: For suspected **Tuberculosis**
    ◦ **ANA**: For suspected **JIA** in a child
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for acute, idiopathic cases that are treated promptly
    ◦ Most resolve without long-term sequelae
• **Guarded** for chronic, recurrent, or granulomatous uveitis, especially when associated with a systemic disease
    ◦ These cases have a higher risk of vision-threatening complications

sections.overview:
• **Episcleritis** is a common, benign, **self-limiting inflammation** of the **episclera**, the thin layer of vascular connective tissue lying between the **conjunctiva** and the **sclera**.
    ◦ Characterized by **acute onset** of **sectoral** or **diffuse redness** with **mild discomfort**.
    ◦ Crucially, it is **not** typically associated with **severe pain** or **vision loss**, distinguishing it from the more serious condition of **scleritis**.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• **Age**: Typically affects young to middle-aged adults (30s-50s).
• **Gender**: Slight female predominance.
• **Recurrence**: Common, occurring in over 50% of patients.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Onset**: Acute, typically over hours.
• **Laterality**: Usually **unilateral**, but can be **bilateral** (especially when associated with systemic disease).
• **Chief Complaint**: Sudden onset of a "**red eye**" with **mild discomfort**.
• **Course**: Episodes usually resolve spontaneously within 1-3 weeks.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**
    ◦ Diagnosis is primarily **clinical**, based on history and physical exam findings (especially the **slit lamp exam** and positive **phenylephrine test**).
• **Laboratory Workup**
    ◦ **Not indicated** for a first-time, uncomplicated, unilateral episode.
    ◦ **Consider** if episodes are recurrent, bilateral, severe, nodular, or if the review of systems is positive for systemic disease.
    ◦ Targeted labs based on suspicion:
        ▪ **CBC, ESR, CRP**: General inflammation markers.
        ▪ **RF, anti-CCP**: Rheumatoid Arthritis.
        ▪ **ANA**: Lupus and other connective tissue diseases.
        ▪ **ANCA**: Vasculitides (e.g., GPA).
        ▪ **ACE, Lysozyme**: Sarcoidosis.
        ▪ **RPR/VDRL, FTA-ABS**: Syphilis.
        ▪ **PPD / Quantiferon Gold**: Tuberculosis.
        ▪ **Chest X-Ray**: To screen for sarcoidosis or TB.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**; the condition is **self-limiting** and does not cause long-term ocular damage or vision loss.
• The main morbidity is patient discomfort and the high rate of recurrence.

sections.overview:
• **Scleritis** is a **severe**, **painful**, and often **destructive inflammatory disease** of the **sclera**, the white outer layer of the eyeball
• It is a deep inflammation, distinct from the more common and benign **episcleritis**
• **Scleritis** is frequently associated with underlying **systemic autoimmune or infectious diseases** and can be **sight-threatening** if not diagnosed and treated promptly
• It is considered an **ophthalmologic emergency** requiring urgent referral
sections.etiology:
• The pathophysiology involves a deep, **immune-mediated vasculitis** of the **scleral and episcleral vessels**, leading to a destructive inflammatory cascade, causing vessel occlusion, **collagen degradation**, and scleral tissue remodeling
• **Idiopathic**: Approximately 50% of cases have no identifiable underlying cause
