• **Systemic Autoimmune/Inflammatory Disease**: The most common cause (about 50% of cases), where scleral inflammation is a manifestation of the systemic disease
    ◦ **Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)**: The most common systemic association
    ◦ **ANCA-Associated Vasculitides**: Especially **Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA)**, formerly Wegener's
    ◦ **Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)**
    ◦ **Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD)**: Ulcerative Colitis, Crohn's Disease
    ◦ **Relapsing Polychondritis**
    ◦ **Sarcoidosis**
• **Infectious**: A less common cause, but must be considered, especially in unilateral or atypical cases
    ◦ **Bacterial**
        ▪ ***Pseudomonas aeruginosa*** (post-surgical)
        ▪ ***Mycobacterium tuberculosis***
        ▪ ***Treponema pallidum*** (syphilis)
    ◦ **Viral**
        ▪ **Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV)**
        ▪ **Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV)**
    ◦ **Fungal**: Rare, often post-traumatic or surgical
• **Trauma/Surgical**: Can occur post-ocular surgery (e.g., pterygium excision, strabismus repair)
• Classification by location and type:
    ◦ **Anterior Scleritis (90%)**
        ▪ **Diffuse**: Widespread inflammation of the anterior sclera. Most common and most benign form.
        ▪ **Nodular**: Presence of firm, tender, immovable nodules on the sclera.
        ▪ **Necrotizing with Inflammation**: The **most severe form**. Associated with **extreme pain** and high risk of **scleral perforation** and **vision loss**. Often linked to systemic vasculitis (e.g., GPA, RA).
        ▪ **Necrotizing without Inflammation (Scleromalacia Perforans)**: Rare, **pathognomonic for long-standing rheumatoid arthritis**. Characterized by scleral thinning and melting without significant pain or redness.
    ◦ **Posterior Scleritis (10%)**
        ▪ Inflammation of the sclera posterior to the ora serrata
        ▪ Symptoms can be vague (pain, decreased vision) and the globe may appear white externally, making diagnosis difficult
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Relatively uncommon, estimated at ~4 per 100,000 person-years
• **Age**: Typically affects individuals in their 4th to 6th decades
• **Gender**: Slight female predominance, likely reflecting the higher prevalence of autoimmune diseases in women
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient with scleritis presents with a **subacute onset** of a **red, painful eye** over several days
• The patient often appears in **significant distress** due to the **severity of the pain**
• The presentation is typically **unilateral** but can be **bilateral**, especially when associated with a systemic condition like RA or GPA
• Vision may be affected
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Diagnosis is primarily based on history and physical exam findings, especially the characteristic pain and appearance confirmed by slit-lamp
• **Ophthalmology Consultation**
    ◦ **Slit-lamp exam** is essential
    ◦ A **B-scan ultrasound** may be used to evaluate for posterior scleritis, which shows scleral wall thickening and a characteristic **"T-sign"** (fluid in Tenon's capsule)
• **Systemic Workup** (to find underlying cause): This is mandatory for all new cases of non-infectious scleritis
    ◦ **Inflammatory Markers**
        ▪ **CBC with diff**, **ESR**, **CRP** (usually markedly elevated)
    ◦ **Autoimmune Panel**
        ▪ **Rheumatoid Factor (RF)** and **Anti-CCP** (for RA)
        ▪ **Antinuclear Antibody (ANA)** (for SLE and other connective tissue diseases)
        ▪ **Anti-neutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibody (ANCA)**: Especially **c-ANCA** for GPA
    ◦ **Infectious Workup** (if suspected)
        ▪ **RPR** or **VDRL** (Syphilis)
        ▪ **PPD** or **IGRA** (Tuberculosis)
        ▪ Consider viral titers (VZV, HSV)
    ◦ **Imaging**
        ▪ **Chest X-ray** (to look for signs of sarcoidosis, TB, or GPA)
        ▪ **Sinus CT** (if GPA is suspected)
sections.prognosis:
• **Non-necrotizing**: Generally good visual prognosis with appropriate treatment, but relapses are common
• **Necrotizing**: **Guarded prognosis**. High risk of **significant vision loss** (up to 75% in 1 year without treatment). Also associated with an **increased mortality rate** due to the severity of the underlying systemic vasculitis.

sections.overview:
• Any **opacification** or clouding of the eye's normally clear **crystalline lens**
• Obstructs the passage of light to the retina, resulting in a **progressive and painless loss of vision**
• Leading cause of **reversible blindness** worldwide
• Most often **bilateral**, though typically asymmetrical in its progression
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Senile (Age-related):** The most common cause (>90%), occurring as a natural part of the aging process
    ◦ **Congenital:** Present at birth
        ▪ Causes include genetic mutations (e.g., Down syndrome, Marfan syndrome), intrauterine infections (**TORCH**: **T**oxoplasmosis, **O**ther, **R**ubella, **C**ytomegalovirus, **H**erpes), and metabolic disorders (e.g., galactosemia)
    ◦ **Traumatic:** Can result from blunt or penetrating eye trauma, electric shock, or infrared/ionizing radiation
    ◦ **Secondary (Metabolic/Systemic):** Associated with systemic diseases, most notably **Diabetes Mellitus**. Also seen with hypocalcemia and atopic dermatitis
    ◦ **Drug-induced:** Most commonly caused by long-term systemic or topical **corticosteroid** use, which classically causes a posterior subcapsular cataract. Other implicated drugs include phenothiazines and amiodarone
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The lens is primarily composed of water and proteins called **crystallins**, arranged to allow for transparency and light refraction
    ◦ **Protein Aggregation:** With age and exposure to oxidative stress, **crystallin** proteins denature, misfold, and aggregate
    ◦ **Loss of Transparency:** These protein aggregates form insoluble clumps that scatter light rays, leading to lens opacification
    ◦ **Water Content Changes:** Lens fiber cells lose their ability to regulate water and electrolyte balance, leading to swelling and disruption of the lens's architecture
• **Types of Age-Related Cataracts**
    ◦ **Nuclear Sclerotic:** Hardening and yellow-brown discoloration of the central part (nucleus) of the lens. Progresses slowly and affects distance vision more than near vision
    ◦ **Cortical:** Opacities form in the lens cortex (periphery) and appear as white, wedge-shaped "spokes" that point inward, causing significant glare
    ◦ **Posterior Subcapsular (PSC):** Opacities form as a plaque-like lesion on the back surface of the lens capsule. Tends to progress rapidly and disproportionately affects near vision and vision in bright light. Strongly associated with **steroid use** and **diabetes**
sections.epidemiology:
• The leading cause of blindness and visual impairment globally
• Prevalence is strongly correlated with age
• By age 80, more than 50% of Americans either have a cataract or have undergone cataract surgery
• No significant gender or racial predilection, although access to care creates disparities in surgical rates
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The typical patient is an older adult presenting with a **gradual, progressive, and painless** decrease in vision, often in both eyes
• Patients may report increasing difficulty with activities such as:
    ◦ Night driving
    ◦ Reading fine print
    ◦ Seeing in bright sunlight (glare)
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on history and a comprehensive ophthalmologic exam
• **Slit-lamp examination with pupillary dilation is the standard for diagnosis**
• No lab tests or imaging are needed for routine age-related cataracts
• For pre-operative planning, **biometry** is performed to calculate the power of the required intraocular lens (IOL)
    ◦ Uses ultrasound A-scan or optical methods
    ◦ Measures the axial length of the eye and corneal curvature (keratometry)
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis following cataract surgery is **excellent**
• Over 95% of patients achieve significantly improved vision (often 20/40 or better), provided there is no other underlying ocular pathology (e.g., advanced glaucoma, macular degeneration)

sections.overview:
• Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma (POAG) is a chronic, progressive, and typically bilateral optic neuropathy characterized by a distinctive pattern of optic nerve head damage ("cupping") and a corresponding, progressive loss of visual field.
	◦ It is the most common form of glaucoma.
	◦ The intraocular pressure (IOP) is typically, but not always, elevated.
	◦ The anterior chamber angle is open, as determined by gonioscopy.
	◦ Because it is painless and affects peripheral vision first, it is often called the **"silent thief of sight."**
sections.etiology:
• The exact etiology is multifactorial, but the core pathophysiology involves an imbalance between aqueous humor production and drainage, leading to a gradual increase in intraocular pressure (IOP).
	◦ **Aqueous Humor Dynamics:** Aqueous humor is produced by the ciliary body, flows into the posterior chamber, through the pupil into the anterior chamber, and drains primarily through the **trabecular meshwork** into Schlemm's canal.
	◦ **Pathologic Mechanism:** In POAG, there is increased resistance to aqueous outflow through the trabecular meshwork. This is thought to be due to cellular dysfunction, extracellular matrix deposition, and reduced porosity of the meshwork tissue.
	◦ **Optic Nerve Damage:** The resulting elevated IOP (and potentially other factors like vascular compromise) exerts mechanical stress and ischemic damage on the retinal ganglion cell (RGC) axons at the optic nerve head. This leads to RGC apoptosis, thinning of the neuroretinal rim, and enlargement of the optic cup.
	◦ **Nerve Fiber Layer Loss:** Axonal death follows a characteristic pattern, most commonly affecting the inferotemporal and superotemporal nerve fibers first.
		▪ This corresponds to the **ISNT rule** (the normal neuroretinal rim is thickest **I**nferiorly > **S**uperiorly > **N**asally > **T**emporally). In glaucoma, this rule is often violated.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** Second leading cause of blindness worldwide and the leading cause of **irreversible** blindness.
• **Age:** Prevalence increases significantly with age, affecting ~1% of people over 40 and up to 10% of those over 80.
• **Race/Ethnicity:** Significantly more common, occurs at an earlier age, and is more aggressive in individuals of **African descent**. Also has a higher prevalence in Hispanic populations.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is insidious and asymptomatic in the early to moderate stages.
• Patients are most often diagnosed during a routine comprehensive eye exam.
• Late-stage presentation occurs only after significant, irreversible vision loss has occurred.
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is made based on a constellation of findings: characteristic optic nerve damage and corresponding visual field loss.
	◦ **Comprehensive Ophthalmic Exam:** As detailed above.
	◦ **Tonometry:** Measures IOP. **Goldmann applanation tonometry** is the standard.
	◦ **Gonioscopy:** Essential to visualize the drainage angle and confirm it is open.
	◦ **Automated Perimetry (Visual Field Testing):** Maps and quantifies visual field loss.
		▪ **Characteristic Defects:** Arcuate scotoma, nasal step, paracentral scotoma.
	◦ **Pachymetry:** Measures Central Corneal Thickness (CCT).
		▪ Used to adjust IOP readings (thin cornea -> artificially low reading; thick cornea -> artificially high reading).
	◦ **Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT):** Provides high-resolution, cross-sectional images of the optic nerve head and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL).
		▪ Quantifies RNFL thickness, which can detect damage before visual field defects are apparent.
sections.prognosis:
• With early detection and consistent treatment, the prognosis for maintaining useful vision throughout a patient's lifetime is **good**.
• Vision that has already been lost **cannot be recovered**.
• Prognosis is worse for patients with advanced disease at diagnosis, poor adherence to therapy, or more aggressive forms of the disease.

sections.overview:
• **Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma (AACG)** is a true **ophthalmic emergency** characterized by a **sudden, severe increase in intraocular pressure (IOP)** due to the **obstruction of aqueous humor outflow** from the eye.
    ◦ The peripheral iris bows forward and physically **blocks the trabecular meshwork** at the iridocorneal angle.
    ◦ This rapid rise in IOP can quickly lead to ischemic damage of the optic nerve and **permanent vision loss** if not treated emergently.
sections.etiology:
• The underlying cause is an **anatomically narrow anterior chamber angle**.
• The acute attack is triggered by **pupillary dilation (mydriasis)**.
    ◦ **Pupillary Block (Most Common Mechanism)**:
        ▪ In a predisposed eye, the lens and iris are in close apposition.
        ▪ When the pupil dilates (e.g., in dim light, due to stress, or from medications), the iris tissue bunches up peripherally.
        ▪ This blocks the normal flow of aqueous humor from the posterior chamber (behind the iris) to the anterior chamber (in front of the iris).
        ▪ Pressure builds in the posterior chamber, causing the peripheral iris to bow forward (**iris bombé**).
        ▪ The forward-bowed iris makes contact with the trabecular meshwork, physically obstructing the drainage angle.
    ◦ **Aqueous Humor Outflow Obstruction**:
        ▪ With the trabecular meshwork blocked, aqueous humor cannot drain from the eye.
        ▪ Aqueous humor production continues, leading to a rapid and dramatic rise in intraocular pressure (IOP), often exceeding 40-50 mmHg (normal is 10-21 mmHg).
    ◦ **Ischemic Damage**:
        ▪ The extremely high IOP compresses the blood vessels supplying the optic nerve and retina, leading to ischemia and subsequent optic neuropathy and irreversible vision loss.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Age:** Primarily affects individuals >50 years old, as the lens thickens with age, narrowing the anterior chamber.
• **Sex:** More common in females (3:1 ratio).
• **Ethnicity:** Highest prevalence in Asian and Inuit populations due to anatomical predisposition (shallower anterior chambers). It is less common in individuals of African descent.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is **abrupt and severe**.
• Patients often present to the emergency department in significant distress, frequently in the evening when ambient light is low.
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is primarily clinical, confirmed with pressure measurement and ophthalmologic examination.
    ◦ **Tonometry**:
        ▪ **Key diagnostic test**.
        ▪ Reveals **severely elevated IOP**, typically >40 mmHg.
        ▪ Can be performed with a Tono-Pen, Perkins tonometer, or Goldmann applanation tonometer.
    ◦ **Slit Lamp Examination**:
        ▪ Confirms physical exam findings like corneal edema, shallow anterior chamber, and a mid-dilated, fixed pupil.
    ◦ **Gonioscopy**:
        ▪ **The gold standard for diagnosing angle closure**.
        ▪ Allows direct visualization of the iridocorneal angle to confirm physical closure.
        ▪ Usually performed by an ophthalmologist, often after the acute attack has been controlled to avoid further corneal injury.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent:** If treated emergently within a few hours of onset. Vision can be completely preserved.
• **Poor:** If treatment is delayed >24 hours. Significant and **permanent vision loss** is likely. The extent of optic nerve damage is directly related to the magnitude and duration of the IOP elevation.

sections.overview:
• **Ocular Hypertension (OHTN)** is a clinical condition characterized by an **intraocular pressure (IOP)** that is consistently elevated above the statistically normal range (> 21 mmHg) in the absence of any detectable **optic nerve damage** or **visual field loss**.
    ◦ It is not a disease itself but is the most significant risk factor for developing **Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma (POAG)**.
    ◦ The central clinical challenge is to identify which patients with OHTN are at high risk of converting to glaucoma and require treatment versus those who can be safely monitored.
sections.etiology:
• The intraocular pressure is maintained by a balance between the production and drainage of **aqueous humor**.
    ◦ **Aqueous Humor Production:** Produced by the **ciliary body** in the posterior chamber.
    ◦ **Aqueous Humor Flow:** Flows from the posterior chamber, through the pupil, into the anterior chamber.
    ◦ **Aqueous Humor Drainage:** Exits the eye primarily through the **trabecular meshwork** into the Canal of Schlemm (conventional outflow).
        ▪ A smaller portion drains through the **uveoscleral pathway** (unconventional outflow).
• **Pathophysiology of OHTN:**
    ◦ The underlying mechanism is an **imbalance between aqueous production and drainage**.
    ◦ In OHTN, the cause is almost always **decreased outflow** of aqueous humor through the **trabecular meshwork**, leading to a gradual increase in IOP.
        ▪ The trabecular meshwork becomes less porous or "clogged" over time, increasing resistance to drainage.
        ▪ Aqueous humor production remains normal.
• **Key Concept:** OHTN is a "plumbing" problem—specifically, a clogged drain, not a faucet that's turned on too high.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** Affects approximately 4-10% of the US population over the age of 40.
• **Age:** Prevalence increases significantly with age.
• **Race:** More common and often occurs at a younger age in individuals of **African** or **Hispanic** descent.
• **Conversion to Glaucoma:** Without treatment, approximately 10% of individuals with OHTN will develop glaucoma over a 5-year period.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Higher IOP:** The higher the baseline IOP, the greater the risk of conversion.
• **Thin Central Corneal Thickness (CCT):** A CCT < 555 microns is a major independent risk factor.
    ◦ Thinner corneas may lead to an underestimation of true IOP by Goldmann tonometry and may also indicate a structurally weaker optic nerve.
• **Advanced Age:** Risk increases with each decade of life.
• **Large Cup-to-Disc (C/D) Ratio:** A larger vertical C/D ratio (>0.5) at baseline suggests the optic nerve may already be more susceptible to damage.
• **Family History:** A first-degree relative with glaucoma significantly increases risk.
• **Race:** **African ancestry** is a significant risk factor.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Ocular hypertension is almost always **asymptomatic**.
    ◦ The complete lack of symptoms is a hallmark of the condition.
• It is typically discovered as an incidental finding during a routine comprehensive eye examination.
• Patients do not experience pain, redness, or changes in vision.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Goldmann Applanation Tonometry:** The gold standard for measuring IOP.
    ◦ IOP should be measured at different times of the day if possible, as it can fluctuate.
• **Pachymetry:** Measures the **Central Corneal Thickness (CCT)**.
    ◦ This is essential for risk stratification.
• **Gonioscopy:** A special lens is used to directly visualize the **anterior chamber angle** to confirm it is open and rule out **angle-closure glaucoma**.
• **Dilated Fundoscopic Exam:** Detailed evaluation of the **optic disc** (nerve head) is mandatory to look for any signs of glaucomatous damage (e.g., **cupping**, asymmetry, notching, nerve fiber layer defects).
• **Automated Perimetry** (e.g., Humphrey Visual Field): Provides a detailed map of the patient's **visual field** to establish a baseline and confirm that no glaucomatous field loss is present.
• **Optic Nerve Imaging** (e.g., **OCT - Optical Coherence Tomography**): Provides a highly detailed, quantitative measurement of the **retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL)** and optic nerve head.
    ◦ This is the modern standard for establishing a baseline and detecting subtle, early structural changes of glaucoma.
sections.treatment:
• **Indications for Treatment:**
    ◦ Patients with **high-risk features** (e.g., IOP > 30 mmHg, very thin CCT, large C/D ratio, strong family history).
    ◦ Patients with moderate risk who desire treatment or have other comorbidities (e.g., only one functional eye).
• **Medical Therapy:**
    ◦ **First Line: Prostaglandin Analogs**
        ▪ *Examples:* Latanoprost, Travoprost, Bimatoprost
        ▪ *Mechanism:* Increase **uveoscleral (unconventional) outflow** of aqueous humor.
        ▪ *Dosing:* Once daily at bedtime.
        ▪ *Side Effects:* **Iris color darkening** (irreversible), eyelash growth, conjunctival hyperemia.
    ◦ **Second Line / Adjunctive:**
        ▪ **Beta-Blockers:** (e.g., Timolol) - Decrease aqueous production. *Caution in asthma, COPD, bradycardia.*
        ▪ **Alpha-2 Agonists:** (e.g., Brimonidine) - Decrease aqueous production AND increase outflow.
        ▪ **Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors:** (e.g., Dorzolamide, Brinzolamide) - Decrease aqueous production.
• **Laser Therapy:**
    ◦ **Selective Laser Trabeculoplasty (SLT):** A laser is used to stimulate the **trabecular meshwork**, improving its drainage function.
        ▪ It is increasingly used as a first-line treatment alternative to drops, especially for patients with adherence issues.
sections.management:
• **Referral:** All patients with suspected or confirmed OHTN should be referred to an **Ophthalmologist** for a complete workup, risk assessment, and management plan.
• **Monitoring:** The follow-up interval is determined by the patient's risk profile.
    ◦ **Low Risk:** Annual monitoring with IOP check, dilated exam, and visual field/OCT every 1-2 years.
    ◦ **High Risk / On Treatment:** More frequent monitoring, often every 3-6 months.
• **Patient Education:** Counsel patients on the asymptomatic nature of the condition, the importance of lifelong monitoring, and proper eye drop administration if prescribed.
sections.complications:
• The primary and most feared complication is **progression to Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma (POAG)**.
• If POAG develops and is left untreated, it can lead to progressive, irreversible **peripheral vision loss**, eventually leading to **"tunnel vision"** and potential blindness.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis for OHTN is **excellent** with appropriate ophthalmologic monitoring.
• The majority of patients will never develop glaucoma.
• For high-risk patients who are treated, the risk of conversion to glaucoma is reduced by approximately 50%.
• With early detection and management, significant vision loss is preventable.

sections.overview:
• Age-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD) is a chronic, progressive neurodegenerative disease affecting the macula, the central part of the retina responsible for sharp, detailed central vision
    ◦ It is the leading cause of irreversible blindness in developed countries in individuals over age 60
    ◦ **Dry AMD**, also known as **non-exudative** or **atrophic** AMD, is the most common form, accounting for 85-90% of all cases
    ◦ Characterized by the slow, progressive breakdown of the macula, leading to the accumulation of waste products (**drusen**) and gradual thinning (**atrophy**) of retinal tissue
    ◦ Vision loss is typically slow and insidious
sections.etiology:
• The pathophysiology is multifactorial, involving a combination of oxidative stress, chronic inflammation in the complement pathway, and impaired metabolic processes within the retina
    ◦ **RPE Dysfunction**: The disease begins with dysfunction of the **Retinal Pigment Epithelium (RPE)**, a single layer of cells that supports the overlying photoreceptors (rods and cones)
    ◦ **Drusen Formation**: Dysfunctional RPE cells are unable to effectively process cellular debris from photoreceptors
        ▪ This waste material, primarily composed of lipids and proteins, accumulates between the RPE and **Bruch's membrane**
        ▪ These extracellular deposits are called **drusen**
    ◦ **Inflammation & Ischemia**: **Drusen** trigger a local inflammatory response, activating the complement cascade, which further damages the RPE and surrounding tissues
        ▪ The thickening of **Bruch's membrane** by these deposits impairs nutrient transport from the choroid to the retina, causing further stress and ischemia
    ◦ **Atrophy**: Over time, this chronic process leads to the death of RPE cells and the overlying photoreceptors
        ▪ This results in patches of retinal thinning known as **Geographic Atrophy (GA)**, the advanced form of dry AMD, which corresponds to dense central scotomas
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Leading cause of permanent vision loss in patients >65 years in developed nations
• **Incidence**: Increases exponentially with age
    ◦ Rare before age 50
    ◦ Affects ~10% of people aged 65-75 and ~30% of people over 75
• **Form**: Dry AMD accounts for ~85-90% of cases
    ◦ While less severe in its progression, it can convert to the more aggressive wet form
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Patient Profile**: Typically an individual over 60 years of age
• **Onset**: Insidious, gradual, and often asymptomatic in the early stages
• **Laterality**: Usually bilateral, though often asymmetric in severity
• **Chief Complaint**: Patients may present for a routine exam or with complaints of difficulty with tasks requiring fine visual acuity, such as reading small print, threading a needle, or recognizing faces
sections.diagnostics:
• **Comprehensive Eye Exam**: Includes visual acuity, Amsler grid, and dilated fundus exam
• **Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT)**
    ◦ **Gold standard for imaging**; provides a high-resolution, cross-sectional image of the retina
    ◦ **Findings in Dry AMD**: Shows **drusen** as elevations of the RPE. In GA, it reveals profound thinning of the outer retinal layers and RPE loss
    ◦ **Crucial Role**: Differentiates dry AMD from wet AMD by confirming the **absence of subretinal or intraretinal fluid**
• **Fundus Photography**: Documents the extent of **drusen** and atrophy for monitoring progression over time
• **Fundus Autofluorescence (FAF)**: A non-invasive imaging technique that highlights RPE health
    ◦ Areas of GA appear dark (hypoautofluorescent)
• **Fluorescein Angiography (FA)**: Used primarily if there is suspicion of conversion to wet AMD
    ◦ In dry AMD with GA, it shows **"window defects"** (hyperfluorescence due to RPE loss) without the characteristic leakage seen in wet AMD
sections.prognosis:
• The course is chronic and progressive
• Vision loss is **slow** and occurs over many years to decades
• **Peripheral vision is always preserved**, so patients do not experience total "black" blindness
• Prognosis worsens with the presence of numerous large, soft **drusen** and pigmentary changes, which increase the risk of progression to GA or conversion to wet AMD

sections.overview:
• Wet Age-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD), also known as **neovascular** or **exudative AMD**, is a chronic, progressive eye disease that causes severe, irreversible **central vision loss**.
• Characterized by the **abnormal growth of new blood vessels** (choroidal neovascularization) from the choroid into the subretinal space.
• These vessels are fragile and **leak fluid and blood**, damaging the macula.
• Accounts for 10-15% of all AMD cases but is responsible for approximately 90% of severe vision loss attributed to the disease.
• Considered an **ophthalmologic emergency** requiring prompt diagnosis and treatment to preserve vision.
sections.etiology:
• Wet AMD is a progression from dry (atrophic) AMD.
• The pathophysiology is centered on a response to chronic hypoxia and inflammation within the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and Bruch's membrane.
    ◦ **Chronic Inflammation & Oxidative Stress:** Accumulation of metabolic byproducts (drusen) between the RPE and Bruch's membrane leads to chronic inflammation and oxidative stress.
    ◦ **Hypoxia:** This inflammatory environment impairs nutrient transport and leads to ischemia and hypoxia of the outer retina.
    ◦ **VEGF Upregulation:** In response to hypoxia, retinal cells, particularly the RPE, upregulate the production of **Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF)**.
    ◦ **Choroidal Neovascularization (CNV):** VEGF is a potent angiogenic factor that stimulates the proliferation of new, abnormal blood vessels from the choroid.
    ◦ **Exudation:** These new vessels lack tight junctions and are highly permeable. They grow through breaks in Bruch's membrane and leak serous fluid (exudate) and blood into the sub-RPE and subretinal spaces.
    ◦ **Photoreceptor Damage:** The leakage causes separation and elevation of the retina (pigment epithelial detachment, serous retinal detachment) and direct damage to photoreceptors (rods and cones), leading to rapid vision loss.
    ◦ **Fibrosis:** If left untreated, the process culminates in the formation of a **disciform scar**, a fibrovascular membrane that permanently destroys the macular architecture.
sections.epidemiology:
• Leading cause of irreversible blindness in individuals **>65 years** in developed countries.
• Affects approximately 1.5% of the US population over 40.
• The prevalence increases dramatically with age.
• Wet AMD develops in about 10-15% of all AMD patients but causes the majority of severe vision loss.
• More common in Caucasians.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Age:** The single greatest risk factor.
• **Smoking:** Strongest modifiable risk factor (doubles the risk).
• **Genetics / Family History:** Strong association with complement factor H (CFH) and ARMS2 gene variants.
• **Race:** Caucasians have the highest prevalence.
• **Cardiovascular Disease:** Hypertension, hyperlipidemia, obesity.
• **Diet:** Low intake of antioxidants, omega-3 fatty acids, and leafy green vegetables.
• **Sunlight Exposure:** Chronic, high levels of UV light exposure may increase risk.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is an elderly patient with a **sudden or subacute onset** of **painless**, **unilateral central vision distortion or loss**.
• Patients often notice the change when covering the unaffected eye.
• The onset can be dramatic over days to weeks.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Symptoms:**
    ◦ **Metamorphopsia:** A key symptom where straight lines appear wavy or distorted.
    ◦ **Central Scotoma:** A blind spot or gray/dark area in the center of the visual field.
    ◦ **Rapid decline in visual acuity:** Difficulty with reading, recognizing faces, or other tasks requiring fine central vision.
    ◦ Decreased color vision or brightness perception.
    ◦ Painless.
• **Exam Findings:**
    ◦ **Subretinal Hemorrhage:** Blood located beneath the retina, appearing as a dark red lesion in the macula.
    ◦ **Subretinal Fluid:** A grayish-green or gray-yellow discoloration or elevation of the macula, indicating fluid accumulation.
    ◦ **Hard Exudates:** Yellow, lipid-rich deposits in the macula, often arranged in a circinate (ring-like) pattern, signifying chronic leakage.
    ◦ **Pigment Epithelial Detachment (PED):** A well-demarcated elevation of the RPE.
    ◦ **Signs of underlying Dry AMD:** May see concurrent soft drusen and RPE changes.
    ◦ **Disciform Scar:** In late-stage, untreated disease, a white or yellow fibrovascular scar is visible in the macula.
    ◦ **Amsler Grid:** Patient will describe the grid lines as wavy, distorted (**metamorphopsia**), or missing (**scotoma**).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Visual Acuity Testing:** Quantifies the degree of central vision loss.
• **Fundus Photography:** Documents the appearance of the macula for baseline and monitoring.
• **Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT):** **Gold standard for diagnosis and monitoring.**
    ◦ Provides high-resolution, cross-sectional images of the retina.
    ◦ **Key OCT Findings:**
        ▪ **Intraretinal or subretinal fluid** (anechoic/dark spaces).
        ▪ Thickening of the macula.
        ▪ **Pigment epithelial detachment (PED)**.
        ▪ Can directly visualize the **Choroidal Neovascular Membrane (CNV)**.
• **Fluorescein Angiography (FA):** Definitive test to identify the location and type of CNV.
    ◦ Injected intravenous fluorescein dye is used to visualize retinal and choroidal circulation.
    ◦ **Key FA Finding:** Identifies the **"leaky" new vessels** as dye leaks from the CNV into the subretinal space in the mid-to-late phases of the angiogram.
sections.treatment:
• **Intravitreal Anti-VEGF Injections:** The **standard of care**. These agents bind to and inhibit VEGF.
    ◦ **Bevacizumab (Avastin):** Off-label, most cost-effective.
    ◦ **Ranibizumab (Lucentis):** FDA-approved fragment of bevacizumab.
    ◦ **Aflibercept (Eylea):** A fusion protein that acts as a VEGF "trap."
    ◦ **Brolucizumab (Beovu):** Newer agent, potential for longer duration but carries a risk of intraocular inflammation.
    ◦ **Faricimab (Vabysmo):** Dual inhibitor of VEGF-A and Angiopoietin-2.
• **Photodynamic Therapy (PDT):** Verteporfin dye is injected IV and activated by a non-thermal laser to close abnormal vessels. Now used less commonly, often in combination with anti-VEGF for specific cases.
• **Laser Photocoagulation:** A thermal laser was used to destroy the CNV, but this also destroys overlying retina, creating a permanent scotoma. Rarely used today for CNV under the fovea.
sections.management:
• **Urgent Referral:** Immediate referral to an ophthalmologist (retina specialist) upon suspicion.
• **Dosing Regimen:** Treatment is initiated with a series of monthly injections. The long-term strategy is often a **"treat-and-extend"** regimen, where the interval between injections is gradually increased as long as the disease remains inactive on OCT.
• **Monitoring:** Regular follow-up every 4-12 weeks with visual acuity testing and OCT to assess for recurrence of fluid.
• **Patient Education:** Instruct patient on at-home **Amsler grid monitoring** to detect new changes.
• **Risk Factor Modification:** **Smoking cessation is critical.** Control of hypertension and hyperlipidemia.
• **AREDS2 Supplementation:** While primarily for slowing the progression of dry AMD, it is recommended for patients with wet AMD in one eye to reduce the risk of developing it in the fellow eye.
• **Low Vision Rehabilitation:** Referrals for magnifiers, assistive technology, and occupational therapy to maximize remaining vision.
sections.complications:
• **Untreated Disease:**
    ◦ Progressive and permanent **central vision loss**.
    ◦ Legal blindness (visual acuity ≤ 20/200).
    ◦ Formation of a **disciform scar**.
• **Treatment-Related:**
    ◦ **Endophthalmitis** (rare but devastating intraocular infection from injection).
    ◦ Retinal detachment.
    ◦ Vitreous hemorrhage.
    ◦ Increased intraocular pressure.
sections.prognosis:
• **Without Treatment:** Very poor. Most patients progress to legal blindness within 2 years.
• **With Anti-VEGF Therapy:** Significantly improved.
    ◦ Approximately 90% of patients can maintain their baseline vision.
    ◦ 30-40% may experience a significant improvement in vision.
    ◦ Early diagnosis and consistent treatment are crucial for a better outcome.
    ◦ The goal is often stabilization of vision rather than complete restoration.

sections.overview:
• Retinal detachment (RD) is an **ophthalmic emergency** characterized by the separation of the neurosensory retina from the underlying retinal pigment epithelium (RPE).
    ◦ The RPE is crucial for providing oxygen and nutrients to the photoreceptors.
    ◦ When separated, the photoreceptors become ischemic and dysfunctional, leading to progressive and potentially permanent vision loss if not treated urgently.
• There are three main types:
    ◦ **Rhegmatogenous:** (Most common) A tear or break in the retina allows vitreous fluid to seep underneath, separating the layers.
    ◦ **Tractional:** Fibrovascular membranes on the retinal surface contract and pull the retina off the RPE.
    ◦ **Exudative (Serous):** Fluid leaks from the choroid and accumulates beneath the retina without a retinal break, pushing it off the RPE.
sections.etiology:
• **Rhegmatogenous RD:**
    ◦ This is the most common type (~90%).
    ◦ The process begins with a full-thickness retinal tear or hole.
    ◦ **Pathophysiology:**
        ▪ A posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) is the most common initiating event.
        ▪ As the vitreous gel liquefies and shrinks with age, it pulls away from the retina.
        ▪ If there are strong points of adhesion, this pulling (traction) can create a retinal tear.
        ▪ Once a tear exists, the liquefied vitreous passes through the break into the subretinal space, separating the neurosensory retina from the RPE.
• **Tractional RD:**
    ◦ Occurs secondary to another condition causing fibrous scar tissue formation.
    ◦ **Pathophysiology:**
        ▪ Conditions like proliferative diabetic retinopathy or sickle cell retinopathy lead to neovascularization.
        ▪ These fragile new vessels can bleed and lead to the formation of fibrovascular membranes on the retinal surface and in the vitreous.
        ▪ These membranes then contract like scar tissue, pulling the retina off the underlying RPE.
        ▪ No retinal break is required.
• **Exudative (Serous) RD:**
    ◦ Caused by the breakdown of the blood-retinal barrier.
    ◦ **Pathophysiology:**
        ▪ Damage to the RPE or choroidal vessels from inflammation, tumors, or severe hypertension allows fluid (exudate) to leak into and accumulate in the subretinal space.
        ▪ This fluid pressure pushes the retina away from the RPE.
        ▪ The key feature is the absence of a retinal tear.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence:** Approximately 1 in 10,000 people per year.
• **Peak Incidence (Rhegmatogenous):** 50-70 years of age, often coinciding with the age of PVD onset.
    ◦ A second peak can occur in younger individuals with high myopia or following trauma.
• The lifetime risk is ~3% for phakic (natural lens) patients and increases to ~5% for pseudophakic (post-cataract surgery) patients.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • A typical patient is a 60-year-old myopic male who presents with a sudden onset of flashing lights in his peripheral vision followed by a shower of new floaters and a progressive, painless "shadow" or "curtain" blocking a portion of his visual field.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis:** The diagnosis is primarily made through history and a thorough **dilated funduscopic exam** by an ophthalmologist using indirect ophthalmoscopy.
• **Ocular Ultrasound (B-scan):** **Test of choice when the fundus view is obscured** (e.g., by dense vitreous hemorrhage or cataract).
    ◦ It can visualize the detached retinal flap, which appears as a bright, mobile, linear echo in the posterior globe.
• **Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT):** Not used for primary diagnosis of RD but is very useful for confirming and assessing **macular involvement** (macula-on vs. macula-off).
sections.prognosis:
• **Macula-on Detachment:**
    ◦ This is a more urgent surgical emergency.
    ◦ If repaired successfully before the macula detaches, the visual prognosis is **excellent**, with many patients returning to their baseline vision.
• **Macula-off Detachment:**
    ◦ The visual prognosis is **guarded**.
    ◦ Even with successful anatomical reattachment, central, fine, and color vision are often permanently impaired.
    ◦ The longer the macula is detached, the worse the visual outcome.
• **Anatomic Success:**
    ◦ With modern surgical techniques, the single-operation anatomic reattachment rate is >90%.

sections.overview:
• **Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO)** is an **ophthalmologic emergency** characterized by the sudden, complete blockage of the central retinal artery, the primary blood supply to the inner retina.
• This event is often described as a **"stroke of the eye."**
• The resulting retinal **ischemia** leads to rapid and often permanent vision loss in the affected eye.
• Immediate recognition and referral are critical, as the window for potential intervention is extremely narrow.
sections.etiology:
• CRAO results from the acute obstruction of blood flow through the central retinal artery, leading to **retinal ischemia** and subsequent infarction of the inner two-thirds of the retina.
• **Primary Causes of Obstruction:**
    ◦ **Embolism (Most Common):**
        ▪ **Carotid Artery Atherosclerosis:** Cholesterol emboli (**Hollenhorst plaques**) are the most frequent cause.
        ▪ **Cardiogenic Emboli:** Thrombi from **atrial fibrillation**, valvular disease, or ventricular aneurysm.
        ▪ **Calcific Emboli:** From calcified heart valves.
        ▪ **Fat Emboli:** Following long bone fractures.
    ◦ **Thrombosis:**
        ▪ In-situ thrombus formation at an atherosclerotic plaque within the central retinal artery itself (less common).
    ◦ **Vasculitis / Inflammatory:**
        ▪ **Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA):** A critical consideration in patients >50 years old. An arteritic cause that requires immediate high-dose corticosteroids.
        ▪ Other vasculitides (e.g., lupus, polyarteritis nodosa).
    ◦ **Hypercoagulable States:**
        ▪ Antiphospholipid syndrome, Factor V Leiden, protein C/S deficiency.
    ◦ **Other:**
        ▪ Orbital compression, trauma, sickle cell disease, vasospasm.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence:** Approximately 1 in 100,000 people.
• **Age:** Typically affects older individuals, with a mean age of 60-65 years. Rare in patients <40.
• **Gender:** Slightly more common in males.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Hypertension (HTN)**
• **Diabetes Mellitus (DM)**
• **Hyperlipidemia (HLD)**
• **Carotid Artery Disease / Atherosclerosis**
• **Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)**
• **Atrial Fibrillation**
• **Smoking**
• **Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA)**
• **History of TIA or CVA**
• **Hypercoagulable states**
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is an abrupt, profound, and **painless loss of vision** in one eye that occurred **"like a curtain falling."**
• **Symptoms:**
    ◦ **Sudden, profound, painless monocular vision loss.**
    ◦ Vision loss is typically central and dense.
    ◦ Patients may describe the vision as completely black or may only be able to perceive **hand motion or light**.
• A history of **amaurosis fugax** (transient, painless monocular vision loss) may precede the event, representing transient ischemic attacks (TIAs) of the retina.
sections.diagnostics:
• Immediate evaluation is focused on confirming the diagnosis and initiating a systemic workup to identify the underlying cause and prevent further ischemic events (e.g., stroke).
• **Ophthalmic Evaluation:**
    ◦ **Slit-lamp and dilated fundoscopic exam:** To confirm physical exam findings.
    ◦ **Intraocular pressure (IOP):** To rule out acute angle-closure glaucoma.
    ◦ **Fluorescein Angiography (FA):** Confirmatory test showing delayed or absent arterial filling and a prolonged arteriovenous transit time.
    ◦ **Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT):** Shows swelling and hyper-reflectivity of the inner retinal layers in the acute phase.
• **Systemic Workup (Treat as a Stroke Workup):**
    ◦ **Immediate Labs for GCA (if patient >50):**
        ▪ **Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR)**
        ▪ **C-Reactive Protein (CRP)**
        ▪ If **GCA** is suspected, start high-dose steroids immediately without waiting for results.
    ◦ **Vascular Imaging:**
        ▪ **Carotid Duplex Ultrasound:** To assess for carotid artery stenosis.
        ▪ **CT or MR Angiography (CTA/MRA):** Of the head and neck.
    ◦ **Cardiac Evaluation:**
        ▪ **Electrocardiogram (ECG):** To check for **atrial fibrillation**.
        ▪ **Echocardiogram (TTE and/or TEE):** To look for cardiac vegetations, thrombus, or patent foramen ovale.
    ◦ **Additional Labs:**
        ▪ CBC, CMP, Lipid panel, HbA1c
        ▪ Hypercoagulability panel in younger patients without clear risk factors.
sections.treatment:
• **Ocular Massage:** Firm, intermittent digital pressure on the globe (10-15 seconds on, 5 seconds off) to lower IOP and potentially dislodge the embolus.
• **IOP Lowering Agents:**
    ◦ **Topical:** Timolol, Brimonidine
    ◦ **Systemic:** IV Acetazolamide, IV Mannitol
• **Anterior Chamber Paracentesis:** An ophthalmologist rapidly removes a small amount of aqueous humor to cause a sudden drop in IOP.
• **Carbogen Therapy / CO2 Rebreathing:** Inhaling 5% CO2 or rebreathing into a paper bag to induce vasodilation. Limited evidence.
• **Hyperbaric Oxygen (HBO):** May improve retinal oxygenation while waiting for reperfusion.
• **Thrombolysis:** Intra-arterial (via interventional radiology) or intravenous tPA. Highly controversial, significant risks, and only considered in specialized stroke centers within a very short time window (<4.5 hours).
sections.management:
• **STAT referral to a Stroke Center/Neurology.**
• **Antiplatelet Therapy:** Aspirin, Clopidogrel.
• **Statin Therapy:** High-intensity statin regardless of LDL level.
• **Blood Pressure Control:** Manage hypertension.
• **Glycemic Control:** Manage diabetes.
• **Lifestyle Modification:** Smoking cessation, diet, exercise.
• **Address Underlying Etiology:** Anticoagulation for **atrial fibrillation**, carotid endarterectomy for significant stenosis.
sections.complications:
• **Permanent, Severe Vision Loss** (most common outcome).
• **Neovascularization:** Growth of new, abnormal blood vessels on the iris (**rubeosis iridis**) or retina, occurring weeks to months later.
• **Neovascular Glaucoma:** A severe, painful type of glaucoma resulting from neovascularization of the iris, which blocks the trabecular meshwork.
sections.prognosis:
• **Visual Prognosis:**
    ◦ Generally very poor. Most patients have permanent, severe vision loss.
    ◦ If perfusion is restored within 90 minutes, some recovery is possible, but this is rare.
    ◦ The presence of a patent **cilioretinal artery** (supplies the fovea in ~20% of people) can lead to preservation of central acuity (e.g., 20/50), but peripheral vision is still lost.
• **Systemic Prognosis:**
    ◦ Patients with **CRAO** have a significantly increased risk of subsequent **ischemic stroke** and **myocardial infarction**.
    ◦ The 5-year mortality rate is higher than in age-matched controls.

sections.overview:
• Central Retinal Vein Occlusion (CRVO) is a common retinal vascular disorder often called a "**stroke of the eye**"
• Occurs when the central retinal vein is blocked, typically at the **lamina cribrosa**
• The blockage increases venous pressure, causing blood and fluid to leak into the retina, leading to **retinal hemorrhages**, **edema**, and **ischemia**
• Vision loss is typically **acute, unilateral, and painless**
• Classified into two main types:
    ◦ **Non-Ischemic (Perfused)**
        ▪ Milder form (~75-80% of cases)
        ▪ Characterized by good capillary perfusion and a better visual prognosis
    ◦ **Ischemic (Non-Perfused)**
        ▪ More severe form (~20-25% of cases)
        ▪ Characterized by significant **capillary non-perfusion**, severe vision loss, and a high risk of complications like **neovascularization**
sections.etiology:
• The underlying mechanism is compression of the central retinal vein by an adjacent **atherosclerotic** central retinal artery where they share a common sheath at the lamina cribrosa
• **Pathophysiological Cascade**:
    ◦ **Compression**: A rigid, atherosclerotic central retinal artery compresses the softer central retinal vein
    ◦ **Thrombosis**: Compression and turbulent blood flow lead to endothelial damage and **thrombus formation (Virchow's Triad)**
    ◦ **Occlusion**: The thrombus obstructs venous outflow from the retina
    ◦ **Increased Venous Pressure**: Blood backs up in the retinal venous system
    ◦ **Vascular Leakage**: High pressure damages the capillary endothelium and breaks down the blood-retina barrier, leading to retinal and **macular edema** and **retinal hemorrhages**
    ◦ **Ischemia**: Blood flow stagnation leads to retinal hypoxia, stimulating the production of **Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF)**, which drives macular edema and neovascularization
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Second most common retinal vascular disease after diabetic retinopathy
• **Incidence**: Increases significantly with age
• **Age**: Primarily affects individuals > 50 years old
    ◦ If seen in a patient < 40, a workup for **hypercoagulable states** is warranted
• **Gender**: Slightly more common in males
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients typically present with a chief complaint of **sudden, unilateral, painless vision loss** that developed over hours to days
• The severity of vision loss can range from mild blurriness to counting fingers only
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is primarily clinical based on the fundoscopic exam
• Further testing is performed to confirm, classify severity, and guide treatment
    ◦ **Ophthalmologic Testing**
        ▪ **Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT)**
            • The **gold standard for diagnosing and quantifying macular edema**
            • Shows intraretinal and/or subretinal fluid in the macula
            • Essential for monitoring treatment response
        ▪ **Fluorescein Angiography (FA)**
            • An intravenous dye test that helps differentiate between ischemic and non-ischemic types
            • Shows delayed venous filling, vessel wall staining/leakage (indicating macular edema), and areas of **capillary non-perfusion**
                • >10 disc areas of non-perfusion defines ischemic CRVO
    ◦ **Systemic Workup (PA's Role)**
        ▪ Check **blood pressure**
        ▪ Lab work: **HbA1c** (for diabetes), **lipid panel** (for hyperlipidemia)
        ▪ In patients < 50 or with bilateral disease, consider a **hypercoagulability workup** (e.g., PT/INR, PTT, Factor V Leiden, protein C/S)
        ▪ Carotid ultrasound if ocular ischemic syndrome is suspected
sections.prognosis:
• The visual prognosis is highly variable and depends on two key factors:
    ◦ **Initial Visual Acuity**: The single best predictor of final visual outcome
    ◦ **Perfusion Status (Ischemic vs. Non-Ischemic)**
        ▪ **Non-Ischemic CRVO**
            • Better prognosis
            • Approximately 50% of patients will return to a visual acuity of 20/40 or better without treatment
            • Approximately 15-20% may convert to the ischemic form within 3 years
        ▪ **Ischemic CRVO**
            • Poor prognosis
            • Final visual acuity is typically 20/200 or worse
            • High risk (~50%) of developing **neovascularization** of the anterior segment (iris/angle) within months

sections.overview:
• Nonproliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (NPDR) is the earlier and more common stage of diabetic retinopathy.
• A chronic, progressive microvascular complication of diabetes mellitus characterized by retinal vascular damage, including increased permeability and occlusion, **without** the formation of new blood vessels (neovascularization).
• Vision loss in NPDR is primarily caused by the development of **diabetic macular edema (DME)**.
• It is the leading cause of new blindness among working-age adults in developed countries.
sections.etiology:
• Chronic hyperglycemia is the primary driver of a cascade of events leading to retinal damage.
    ◦ **Microvascular Damage & Weakening**
        ▪ Hyperglycemia damages retinal capillaries. A key early event is the **loss of pericytes**, cells that provide structural support to capillary walls.
        ▪ Loss of pericytes leads to weakening of the vessel walls, resulting in the formation of **microaneurysms** (focal outpouchings), the earliest clinical sign of NPDR.
    ◦ **Increased Vascular Permeability**
        ▪ The blood-retinal barrier breaks down, causing capillaries to become leaky.
        ▪ This leakage allows plasma fluid, proteins, and lipids to seep into the retina.
        ▪ Fluid accumulation causes **retinal edema**. When this occurs in the macula, it is called **Diabetic Macular Edema (DME)**, the main cause of vision loss in NPDR.
        ▪ Lipid deposits form **hard exudates** (waxy, yellow lesions).
    ◦ **Vascular Occlusion**
        ▪ Capillary basement membranes thicken and endothelial cells are damaged, leading to occlusion and retinal ischemia.
        ▪ Ischemia in the nerve fiber layer results in **cotton-wool spots** (fluffy, white patches representing nerve fiber layer infarcts).
        ▪ Occlusion also leads to deeper retinal hemorrhages (**dot-and-blot hemorrhages**), venous caliber changes (**venous beading**), and the formation of **intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMAs)**, which are shunt vessels that bypass occluded capillaries.
sections.epidemiology:
• Leading cause of new-onset blindness in adults aged 20-74 in the United States.
• Prevalence is directly related to the duration of diabetes.
    ◦ **Type 1 DM**: After 20 years, >95% of patients have some form of retinopathy.
    ◦ **Type 2 DM**: At diagnosis, ~20% of patients already have some retinopathy. After 20 years, >60% have retinopathy.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Most patients are **asymptomatic**, especially in the early stages.
• The condition is typically discovered on a routine screening dilated funduscopic exam.
• If symptomatic, the patient may report a gradual, painless blurring or distortion of central vision, which usually indicates the presence of diabetic macular edema.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Dilated Funduscopic Exam**: The gold standard for screening and diagnosis, performed by an ophthalmologist or optometrist.
• **Fundus Photography**: Documents retinal findings and allows for objective monitoring of disease progression.
• **Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT)**
    ◦ **Gold standard for detecting and quantifying Diabetic Macular Edema (DME)**.
    ◦ Provides high-resolution, cross-sectional images of the retina, showing retinal thickness and presence of intraretinal or subretinal fluid.
• **Fluorescein Angiography (FA)**
    ◦ An invasive test where fluorescein dye is injected intravenously to visualize retinal circulation.
    ◦ Identifies leaking microaneurysms, areas of capillary nonperfusion (ischemia), and helps differentiate IRMAs from early neovascularization.
sections.prognosis:
• With early detection and strict systemic control, the visual prognosis is good.
• The development of DME significantly worsens the prognosis, but treatment with anti-VEGF agents has dramatically improved outcomes and can often restore lost vision.
• Once NPDR becomes severe, the risk of significant vision loss increases substantially due to the high likelihood of progression to PDR.

sections.overview:
• Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR) is the advanced, most severe stage of diabetic retinopathy and a major cause of vision loss in patients with diabetes.
    ◦ The defining characteristic is **neovascularization**—the growth of new, abnormal blood vessels in the retina and on the optic disc.
        ▪ These new vessels are fragile, grow in response to widespread retinal ischemia, and lead to severe, vision-threatening complications such as **vitreous hemorrhage** and **tractional retinal detachment**.
sections.etiology:
• **Chronic Hyperglycemia**: Leads to the formation of advanced glycation end-products (AGEs), oxidative stress, and activation of inflammatory pathways.
• **Microvascular Damage**: Capillary basement membranes thicken, and pericytes (cells that support capillaries) are lost. This leads to capillary incompetence, leakage, and breakdown of the blood-retina barrier.
• **Capillary Occlusion & Retinal Ischemia**: Widespread capillary nonperfusion occurs, resulting in significant areas of retinal hypoxia and ischemia.
• **VEGF Upregulation**: In response to hypoxia, ischemic retinal tissue upregulates the production of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and other angiogenic factors.
• **Neovascularization**: VEGF is a potent stimulus for angiogenesis, causing the proliferation of new, abnormal, and fragile blood vessels.
    ◦ On the surface of the retina (**Neovascularization Elsewhere - NVE**)
    ◦ On the optic disc (**Neovascularization of the Disc - NVD**)
• **Complications**: These new vessels lack structural integrity.
    ◦ They easily break and bleed into the vitreous cavity (**vitreous hemorrhage**).
    ◦ They also grow with associated fibrous tissue, which can contract and pull on the retina, causing a **tractional retinal detachment**.
sections.epidemiology:
• PDR is a leading cause of new-onset **blindness** in working-age adults (20-74 years) in the United States.
• The risk of developing PDR increases significantly with the duration of diabetes.
    ◦ **Type 1 Diabetes**: After 20 years, >60% of patients will have some form of retinopathy, with a significant portion progressing to PDR.
    ◦ **Type 2 Diabetes**: At the time of diagnosis, ~20% of patients already have some degree of retinopathy. The risk increases with disease duration.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient with a long history of diabetes (often poorly controlled) may be **asymptomatic** or may present with a **sudden, dramatic change in vision**.
    ◦ The onset of symptoms often indicates a significant complication has already occurred.
• Due to the initial asymptomatic nature, regular **screening** is critical.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Dilated Funduscopic Exam**: The primary tool for diagnosis and screening.
• **Fundus Photography**: Used to document the extent of the disease and monitor progression.
• **Fluorescein Angiography (FA)**: Gold standard for visualizing **neovascularization**.
    ◦ IV dye is injected, and photographs are taken of the retinal circulation.
    ◦ In PDR, the dye will leak profusely from the abnormal new vessels.
    ◦ It also highlights areas of capillary nonperfusion.
• **Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT)**: High-resolution imaging of the retina.
    ◦ Primarily used to assess for co-existing **diabetic macular edema (DME)** and to evaluate for traction on the macula.
• **B-scan Ultrasonography**: Used when the view of the retina is obscured by a dense **vitreous hemorrhage** to rule out an underlying **tractional retinal detachment**.
sections.prognosis:
• **Without Treatment**: The prognosis is poor.
    ◦ High-risk PDR has a >50% chance of leading to **severe vision loss** within 5 years.
• **With Timely Treatment**: The prognosis for preserving vision is good.
    ◦ Panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) reduces the risk of severe vision loss by over 90%.
    ◦ Anti-VEGF therapy is equally or more effective, especially for preserving central vision.
    ◦ However, vision that has already been lost is often not recoverable.

sections.overview:
• **Hypertensive Retinopathy** refers to the spectrum of **retinal microvascular damage** caused by chronically elevated systemic **blood pressure**.
• The retina is unique as its arterioles can be **directly visualized** non-invasively, providing a "window" into the state of systemic vascular health.
• Findings are a direct result of **vasospasm**, increased **vascular permeability**, and **arteriosclerosis** of the retinal circulation.
• The presence and severity of hypertensive retinopathy are strongly correlated with **end-organ damage** in the brain, heart, and kidneys, serving as a powerful prognostic marker for cardiovascular morbidity and mortality.
sections.etiology:
• **Vasoconstrictive / Vasospastic Phase (Acute)**
    ◦ In response to acutely elevated BP, retinal arterioles undergo autoregulation and constrict to protect the capillary beds from high pressure.
    ◦ This leads to **generalized or focal arteriolar narrowing**.
• **Sclerotic Phase (Chronic)**
    ◦ Persistent hypertension leads to structural changes in the vessel walls.
    ◦ **Intimal thickening**, **medial hyperplasia**, and **hyaline degeneration** occur, causing the vessel walls to become stiff and thickened.
    ◦ This manifests as:
        ▪ **Copper Wiring**: Thickened arteriolar walls reflect more light, giving them a brownish-red, coppery appearance.
        ▪ **Silver Wiring**: With further sclerosis, the vessel wall becomes opaque and white, resembling a silver wire.
        ▪ **Arteriovenous (AV) Nicking / Tapering (Gunn's Sign)**: A hardened arteriole crosses over and compresses a softer venule, causing the venule to appear to "taper" or "disappear" on either side of the crossing.
• **Exudative Phase (Advanced / Severe)**
    ◦ Sustained, severe hypertension leads to the breakdown of the **blood-retinal barrier**.
    ◦ Damage to the endothelial lining results in leakage of blood and plasma into the retina.
    ◦ This manifests as:
        ▪ **Flame-shaped Hemorrhages**: Bleeding into the superficial nerve fiber layer.
        ▪ **Dot-and-Blot Hemorrhages**: Bleeding into the deeper retinal layers.
        ▪ **Cotton-Wool Spots (Soft Exudates)**: Fluffy, white lesions representing microinfarcts in the nerve fiber layer from arteriolar occlusion and subsequent axoplasmic stasis.
        ▪ **Hard Exudates**: Waxy, yellow lipid deposits from chronic plasma leakage. When centered around the fovea, they can form a **macular star**.
• **Malignant Hypertension Phase**
    ◦ Extremely high BP (e.g., >220/120 mmHg) overwhelms all autoregulatory mechanisms.
    ◦ This results in fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles and optic nerve ischemia and edema, leading to **papilledema** (swelling of the optic disc).
    ◦ This is an ophthalmologic and medical emergency.
sections.epidemiology:
• Prevalence is directly related to the prevalence and control of **systemic hypertension**.
• Found in approximately **10-15%** of non-diabetic adult patients with chronic hypertension.
• The severity of retinopathy increases with the duration and severity of hypertension.
• More common and often more severe in patients of **African and Caribbean descent**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Most patients, especially in the early stages (Grades 1-2), are **asymptomatic**.
• The condition is often discovered incidentally on a routine fundoscopic exam.
• When symptoms are present, they typically indicate **advanced disease (Grades 3-4)** or complications.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Fundoscopic Examination**
    ◦ The primary diagnostic modality.
    ◦ A dilated fundus exam by an ophthalmologist provides the best view.
• **Blood Pressure Measurement**
    ◦ Essential for diagnosis and management.
    ◦ Confirm elevated BP in both arms.
• **Systemic Workup for End-Organ Damage**
    ◦ **Labs**: Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP) to assess **creatinine** (kidney function), Urinalysis (UA) for **proteinuria**.
    ◦ **EKG**: To assess for **left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH)** or ischemia.
    ◦ **Chest X-Ray**: To assess for **cardiomegaly**.
• **Ophthalmology Tools (not for initial diagnosis by PA)**
    ◦ **Fluorescein Angiography**: Can identify areas of capillary non-perfusion, leakage, and microaneurysms.
    ◦ **Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT)**: Quantifies macular edema and serous retinal detachments.
sections.prognosis:
• **Visual Prognosis**
    ◦ Generally good if BP is controlled before irreversible damage to the macula or optic nerve occurs.
• **Reversibility of Signs**
    ◦ **Reversible**: **Arteriolar narrowing**, **hemorrhages**, **cotton-wool spots**, and **retinal edema** typically resolve over months with good BP control.
    ◦ **Irreversible**: Sclerotic changes like **copper/silver wiring** and **AV nicking** are permanent.
• **Systemic Prognosis**
    ◦ The presence of retinopathy, particularly Grade 2 or higher, signifies significant systemic vascular disease and portends a worse prognosis for cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events.

sections.overview:
• **Retinitis Pigmentosa (RP)** is a group of inherited retinal dystrophies characterized by the progressive degeneration of **photoreceptor cells (rods and cones)** and **retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)**.
    ◦ It is a **"rod-cone dystrophy,"** meaning **rod photoreceptors** are typically affected first and more severely than **cones**.
    ◦ This leads to the hallmark symptoms of **night blindness** and progressive **peripheral visual field loss**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Genetic**: **RP** is a genetic disorder caused by mutations in over 100 different genes responsible for photoreceptor or RPE structure and function.
    ◦ **Inheritance Patterns**:
        ▪ **Autosomal Recessive (AR)**: Most common form (~50-60%).
        ▪ **Autosomal Dominant (AD)**: (~30-40%).
        ▪ **X-Linked (XL)**: Most severe form (~5-15%).
    ◦ **Syndromic Forms**: **RP** can be a feature of systemic diseases, such as **Usher Syndrome** (RP and hearing loss) and **Bassen-Kornzweig Syndrome**.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Rod Degeneration**: The primary event is the apoptosis (programmed cell death) of **rod photoreceptors**.
        ▪ Since rods are concentrated in the mid-periphery of the retina and are responsible for scotopic (low-light) vision, their loss causes:
            • **Nyctalopia** (night blindness).
            • **Peripheral visual field constriction**.
    ◦ **Cone Degeneration**: Cone photoreceptors, responsible for central, high-acuity, and color vision, degenerate later in the disease process.
        ▪ This secondary loss leads to:
            • Loss of central vision.
            • Impaired color vision (dyschromatopsia).
            • Photophobia.
    ◦ **RPE Changes**: The breakdown of photoreceptors leads to the migration of RPE cells into the retina, where they deposit pigment around blood vessels, creating the characteristic **"bone spicule"** appearance.
        ▪ This is accompanied by retinal arteriolar narrowing and optic disc pallor.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Approximately 1 in 4,000 individuals worldwide.
    ◦ It is the most common inherited retinal dystrophy.
• **Age of Onset**: Typically presents in adolescence or early adulthood, but can manifest at any age depending on the specific genetic mutation.
• **Demographics**: No significant racial or ethnic predilection.
    ◦ X-linked forms primarily affect males, while female carriers may have milder or no symptoms.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A typical patient is a young adult or adolescent who presents with a gradual onset of bilateral visual complaints.
• The classic history involves:
    ◦ Difficulty navigating in dim light or at night (e.g., trouble finding a seat in a dark movie theater).
    ◦ A history of being "clumsy," frequently bumping into furniture or doorframes due to loss of peripheral vision.
• The symptoms are slowly progressive over years.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Electroretinography (ERG)**: **GOLD STANDARD** for diagnosis. This test measures the electrical response of the retina to light stimuli.
    ◦ **Key Finding**: Markedly reduced or extinguished **rod response** with a later reduction in **cone response**.
• **Visual Field Testing (Perimetry)**: Characterizes the pattern of vision loss.
    ◦ **Key Finding**: Initially shows a **mid-peripheral "ring scotoma"** (a ring-shaped blind spot) that gradually expands peripherally and centrally, eventually leading to tunnel vision.
• **Fundus Photography**: To document the characteristic retinal findings.
• **Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT)**: Not for initial diagnosis, but essential for detecting and monitoring **cystoid macular edema (CME)** and assessing photoreceptor layer thickness.
• **Genetic Testing**: Identifies the causative mutation, which aids in prognosis, genetic counseling, and determining eligibility for gene-specific therapies.
sections.prognosis:
• The course is **universally progressive**, but the rate of progression is highly variable.
• Prognosis is strongly correlated with the **mode of inheritance** and specific gene mutation:
    ◦ **X-Linked RP**: Most severe, with rapid progression and often legal blindness by age 30-40.
    ◦ **Autosomal Recessive RP**: Intermediate severity.
    ◦ **Autosomal Dominant RP**: Tends to be the mildest form with the slowest progression.
• Most individuals will eventually become legally blind (visual acuity of 20/200 or worse, or a visual field of 20 degrees or less).

sections.overview:
• **Optic neuritis** is an inflammatory, demyelinating condition of the **optic nerve (Cranial Nerve II)**.
• It is a common and often initial manifestation of **Multiple Sclerosis (MS)**.
• The classic presentation involves **subacute, monocular vision loss** accompanied by **eye pain that worsens with movement**.
• While vision often recovers, the event serves as a significant prognostic indicator for the development of MS.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Demyelinating (Most Common)**
        ▪ Strongly associated with **Multiple Sclerosis (MS)**.
        ▪ It can be the first clinical sign (**clinically isolated syndrome**, or CIS) in 15-20% of MS patients.
    ◦ **Other Autoimmune/Inflammatory**
        ▪ **Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder (NMOSD)**, associated with **Aquaporin-4 antibodies**.
        ▪ **MOG Antibody Disease (MOGAD)**.
        ▪ Sarcoidosis, Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), Sjögren's syndrome.
    ◦ **Infectious**
        ▪ Viral (VZV, measles, mumps, EBV), bacterial (Lyme disease, syphilis, cat-scratch disease), or sinus-related (contiguous spread).
    ◦ **Post-vaccination**: Rare association.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The core process is **inflammation and demyelination** of the optic nerve.
    ◦ An autoimmune response targets myelin, the protective sheath around nerve axons, and sometimes the axons themselves.
    ◦ Inflammation leads to edema and conduction block within the nerve, causing impaired signal transmission from the retina to the brain. This results in vision loss, color desaturation, and visual field defects.
    ◦ The inflammation can occur at any point along the optic nerve:
        ▪ **Retrobulbar neuritis (most common, ~2/3 of cases)**: Inflammation occurs behind the eyeball. The optic disc appears normal on fundoscopy. **"The patient sees nothing, and the doctor sees nothing."**
        ▪ **Papillitis (~1/3 of cases)**: Inflammation involves the optic nerve head, causing visible disc swelling (**edema**) on fundoscopy. More common in children.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Peak Incidence**: 20-40 years of age.
• **Sex**: Female-to-male ratio is approximately 3:1.
• **Geography**: More prevalent in higher latitudes (e.g., Northern US, Northern Europe), mirroring the epidemiology of MS.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Established Multiple Sclerosis**: The single greatest risk factor.
• **Genetic Predisposition**: HLA-DRB1 allele.
• **Female sex**.
• **Age 20-40**.
• **Northern latitude residence**.
• **Recent viral illness**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The "classic" patient is a **young woman** who presents with a complaint of **vision loss in one eye** that has developed over the course of a few days.
• She will frequently report that it **hurts to move her eyes**, especially on adduction or abduction.
• She may also notice that colors appear **"washed out"** or "dull" in the affected eye compared to the normal eye.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ **Monocular Vision Loss**: Subacute onset, typically worsening over several days to a week. Severity ranges from mild blurring to no light perception.
    ◦ **Periocular or Retro-orbital Pain**: Present in >90% of cases. Characteristically **exacerbated by eye movement**. The pain may precede the vision loss by a few days.
    ◦ **Dyschromatopsia**: Impaired color vision, particularly **red desaturation** (reds appear pink or faded). This is a very sensitive sign.
    ◦ **Photopsias**: Flashing or flickering lights, often induced by eye movement.
    ◦ **Uhthoff's Phenomenon**: Transient worsening of vision with an increase in body temperature (e.g., during exercise, fever, or a hot shower). This is a classic sign of demyelinating disease.
• **Exam Findings**
    ◦ **Visual Acuity**: Decreased in the affected eye, ranging from 20/25 to no light perception (NLP).
    ◦ **Pupillary Exam**: A **Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD)** or **Marcus Gunn Pupil** is the hallmark sign.
        ▪ *Swinging Flashlight Test:* When light is swung from the normal eye to the affected eye, the affected pupil paradoxically dilates instead of constricting. This indicates a defect in the afferent (sensory) limb of the pupillary light reflex.
    ◦ **Color Vision**: Tested using Ishihara plates or by asking the patient to compare the color of a red object between the two eyes (will appear desaturated/duller in the affected eye).
    ◦ **Visual Fields**: **Central scotoma** (a blind spot in the center of vision) is the most common defect. Other patterns like altitudinal or arcuate defects can occur.
    ◦ **Fundoscopic Exam**:
        ▪ **Normal Optic Disc (in ~65% of cases)**: This is **retrobulbar neuritis**.
        ▪ **Swollen/Edematous Optic Disc (in ~35% of cases)**: This is **papillitis**.
        ▪ **Optic Atrophy (Pallor)**: A late finding that develops 4-6 weeks after the acute event as nerve fibers are lost.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: The diagnosis is primarily based on the characteristic history and physical exam findings (especially the presence of an **RAPD**).
• **MRI of the Brain and Orbits with and without Gadolinium**: **The most important diagnostic test.**
    ◦ **Confirms the diagnosis**: Shows enhancement and swelling of the affected optic nerve.
    ◦ **Prognosticates MS risk**: Identifies characteristic T2/FLAIR hyperintense white matter lesions in the brain (e.g., periventricular, juxtacortical).
        ▪ The number of brain lesions on initial MRI is the strongest predictor of future MS development.
• **Lumbar Puncture (LP) & CSF Analysis**
    ◦ Not routinely necessary for typical optic neuritis.
    ◦ Considered in atypical cases (bilateral, severe vision loss, unresponsive to steroids).
    ◦ Findings suggestive of MS include **oligoclonal bands** and an **elevated IgG index**.
• **Serology**: To rule out atypical causes, especially if presentation is bilateral, severe, or recurrent.
    ◦ **Aquaporin-4 (AQP4) antibodies**: For NMOSD.
    ◦ **Myelin Oligodendrocyte Glycoprotein (MOG) antibodies**: For MOGAD.
    ◦ Infectious workup (Lyme, Syphilis), inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP), and autoimmune panel (ANA, ACE).
sections.treatment:
• **First-Line**: **High-Dose IV Corticosteroids**.
    ◦ **Regimen**: **IV Methylprednisolone** (e.g., 1 gram daily for 3 days).
        ▪ This is typically followed by a course of **oral prednisone taper** (e.g., 1 mg/kg/day for 11 days).
    ◦ **Mechanism & Effect**:
        ▪ **Speeds the rate of visual recovery**.
        ▪ **Does NOT improve the final visual outcome** at 1 year compared to placebo.
        ▪ **Reduces the 2-year risk of developing clinically definite MS** in patients with MS-like lesions on their brain MRI.
    ◦ **CRITICAL POINT**: **Low-dose oral prednisone monotherapy is CONTRAINDICATED**. The ONTT found it increased the rate of recurrent optic neuritis and provided no benefit.
• **Plasma Exchange (PLEX)**: May be considered for patients with severe vision loss who do not respond to IV steroids.
sections.management:
• **Referral**: All patients with a first episode of optic neuritis require a **Neurology referral** for MS workup and management.
• **Ophthalmology follow-up** is essential to monitor visual recovery.
• **MS Disease-Modifying Therapy (DMT)**: For patients diagnosed with MS or deemed high-risk based on MRI findings, initiation of a DMT is the standard of care to prevent future relapses and disability progression.
• **Patient Education**: Counsel on the risk of MS, symptoms to watch for (numbness, weakness, balance problems), and managing **Uhthoff's phenomenon** by avoiding overheating.
sections.complications:
• **Permanent Visual Deficits**: While most recover well, some may have residual deficits in visual acuity, contrast sensitivity, or color vision.
• **Optic Atrophy**: Permanent damage and thinning of the optic nerve, visible as pallor on fundoscopy.
• **Development of Multiple Sclerosis**: The most significant long-term consequence.
• **Recurrence**: Optic neuritis can recur in the same or contralateral eye.
• **Uhthoff's Phenomenon**: Can be a persistent, lifelong symptom.
sections.prognosis:
• **Visual Prognosis**: Generally excellent. Over 90% of patients recover to a visual acuity of 20/40 or better within one year, even without treatment.
• **MS Prognosis**: This is highly dependent on the baseline brain MRI.
    ◦ **Normal Brain MRI**: ~25% risk of developing MS in 15 years.
    ◦ **1+ White Matter Lesion on MRI**: **~72% risk** of developing MS in 15 years.

sections.overview:
• **Papilledema** is swelling of the optic disc secondary to elevated **intracranial pressure (ICP)**.
• It is a critical ophthalmologic sign of an underlying neurologic emergency.
• By definition, papilledema is almost always **bilateral**, though it can be asymmetric.
    ◦ Unilateral optic disc swelling is typically due to other causes and is not termed papilledema.
• The presence of papilledema necessitates an urgent workup to identify and treat the source of the elevated ICP to prevent permanent vision loss and other neurologic damage.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology (Causes of Elevated ICP)**
    ◦ **Space-Occupying Lesions**: Brain tumors, abscesses, large hematomas (e.g., subdural, epidural).
    ◦ **Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) Abnormalities**:
        ▪ **Obstructive Hydrocephalus**: Blockage of CSF flow within the ventricular system.
        ▪ **Communicating Hydrocephalus**: Impaired CSF absorption at the arachnoid granulations.
        ▪ **Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH)**: Also known as pseudotumor cerebri. Elevated ICP with no identifiable cause on imaging.
    ◦ **Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis**: Clot in the dural venous sinuses prevents proper CSF drainage.
    ◦ **Meningitis / Encephalitis**: Diffuse cerebral inflammation and edema.
    ◦ **Severe Systemic Hypertension**: **Malignant hypertension** can cause cerebral edema.
    ◦ **Medications**: Tetracyclines (minocycline, doxycycline), high-dose Vitamin A (isotretinoin), growth hormone.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The optic nerve is surrounded by a sheath that is continuous with the dura mater and subarachnoid space of the brain.
    ◦ **Pressure Transmission**: Elevated ICP is transmitted along the optic nerve sheath.
    ◦ **Axoplasmic Stasis**: The increased pressure compresses the optic nerve axons, impeding axoplasmic transport (the flow of nutrients and organelles within the axon).
    ◦ **Venous Congestion**: The pressure also compresses the central retinal vein, leading to venous stasis and engorgement.
    ◦ **Disc Edema**: The combination of axoplasmic stasis and vascular congestion causes leakage of fluid into the nerve fiber layer of the optic disc, resulting in visible swelling.
sections.epidemiology:
• The epidemiology mirrors that of the underlying causes.
• For the most common testable cause, **Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH)**:
    ◦ Primarily affects **obese women of childbearing age**.
    ◦ Incidence: ~1 per 100,000 in the general population.
    ◦ Incidence rises dramatically to ~20 per 100,000 in **obese women** aged 20-44.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The "classic" vignette is an **obese female in her 30s** presenting with:
    ◦ A **chronic, daily headache** that is worse in the morning and with Valsalva maneuvers (coughing, sneezing, bending over).
