    ◦ Transient episodes of vision loss.
    ◦ A "whooshing" sound in her ears.
sections.physicalExam: • On exam, **bilateral optic disc swelling** is noted.
sections.diagnostics:
• A step-wise approach is crucial and must be done in a specific order.
• **Fundoscopy**:
    ◦ Identifies the presence of **bilateral optic disc swelling**.
• **URGENT Neuroimaging (CT or MRI)**:
    ◦ **THIS IS THE FIRST STEP AFTER FINDING PAPILLEDEMA.**
    ◦ The primary goal is to rule out a **mass lesion**, **hemorrhage**, or **hydrocephalus** that would contraindicate a lumbar puncture.
    ◦ **MRI with MR Venography (MRV)** is the preferred study.
        ▪ It can identify tumors, hydrocephalus, and **cerebral venous sinus thrombosis**.
• **Lumbar Puncture (LP)**:
    ◦ **PERFORMED ONLY AFTER IMAGING HAS RULED OUT A MASS.**
        ▪ A mass can lead to **brainstem herniation** during an LP.
    ◦ **Measure Opening Pressure (OP)**:
        ▪ The patient must be in the **lateral decubitus position** with legs extended.
    ◦ **Normal OP**: < 20 cm H2O
    ◦ **Abnormal OP**: > 25 cm H2O
    ◦ **CSF Analysis**:
        ▪ Send fluid for cell count, glucose, protein, and culture to rule out meningitis/encephalitis.
        ▪ In **IIH**, CSF composition is **normal**.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis depends entirely on the underlying etiology.
• For malignant tumors, prognosis is often poor.
• For **IIH**, the prognosis for vision is generally good if diagnosed early and managed aggressively.
    ◦ However, symptoms like headache may persist, and relapses can occur.

sections.overview:
• Amaurosis fugax (Latin for "fleeting darkness") is a **symptom**, not a disease, characterized by **painless, transient, monocular vision loss**.
• It is considered a form of **Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA) of the retina**.
• The episode is abrupt in onset, typically lasts for a few seconds to several minutes, and resolves spontaneously with full recovery of vision.
• Its clinical significance is profound, as it is often a critical warning sign of an impending **cerebrovascular accident (stroke)** or **central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO)**.
• Prompt workup is mandatory.
sections.etiology:
• The underlying mechanism is temporary ischemia of the retina, optic nerve, or choroid due to insufficient blood flow through the ophthalmic artery and its branches.
• **Embolic (Most Common, ~80%)**
    ◦ An embolus travels from a proximal source, temporarily occluding the retinal vasculature.
        ▪ **Arterial Source**: **Cholesterol crystals (Hollenhorst plaque)**, calcific debris, or platelet-fibrin aggregates from an ulcerated atherosclerotic plaque, most commonly at the **ipsilateral carotid artery bifurcation**.
        ▪ **Cardiac Source**: Thrombi from **atrial fibrillation**, valvular vegetations (endocarditis), or ventricular aneurysm.
• **Hemodynamic**
    ◦ Systemic hypoperfusion leading to reduced blood flow to the retina, particularly in the presence of severe, flow-limiting stenosis.
        ▪ **Causes**: Severe carotid stenosis/occlusion, hypotension, cardiac arrhythmia, severe heart failure, subclavian steal syndrome.
• **Vasculitic**
    ◦ Inflammation of the vessel walls supplying the eye.
        ▪ **Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA / Temporal Arteritis)**: **A MUST-NOT-MISS DIAGNOSIS**. Inflammation of medium and large vessels, including the ophthalmic and posterior ciliary arteries. Can lead to permanent blindness if not treated emergently.
• **Hematologic**
    ◦ Hyperviscosity or hypercoagulability syndromes leading to sludging and thrombosis.
        ▪ **Causes**: Polycythemia vera, sickle cell disease, antiphospholipid syndrome, leukemia, multiple myeloma.
• **Vasospastic**
    ◦ Transient constriction of the retinal arterioles.
        ▪ Often a diagnosis of exclusion, more common in younger patients and may be associated with migraines.
• **Ocular/Orbital**
    ◦ Local factors causing intermittent vascular compression or obstruction.
        ▪ **Causes**: Optic nerve head drusen, intermittent angle-closure glaucoma, orbital compressive mass.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Estimated at approximately 14 per 100,000 people annually.
• **Age**: Predominantly affects individuals **> 50 years old**, with incidence increasing with age.
• **Gender**: Slightly more common in **males** than females, reflecting the prevalence of atherosclerotic disease.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Major Modifiable**:
    ◦ Hypertension (HTN)
    ◦ Diabetes Mellitus (DM)
    ◦ Hyperlipidemia (HLD)
    ◦ Tobacco Use (Smoking)
    ◦ Atrial Fibrillation
• **Non-Modifiable**:
    ◦ Advancing Age (>50)
    ◦ Male Sex
    ◦ Family History of vascular disease
• **Other**:
    ◦ Known Coronary Artery Disease (CAD) or Peripheral Artery Disease (PAD)
    ◦ History of TIA or CVA
    ◦ Obesity / Sedentary Lifestyle
• **For GCA**:
    ◦ Age > 50
    ◦ Female sex
    ◦ Northern European descent
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The typical patient is an older adult with vascular risk factors who presents after a self-resolved episode of vision loss.
• They are often **asymptomatic upon arrival**, making a detailed history the most crucial part of the evaluation.
• The presentation is considered a **neurological and ophthalmological emergency** until a life-threatening cause is ruled out.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ **Vision Loss**:
        ▪ **Laterality**: Strictly **monocular** (one eye).
        ▪ **Pain**: **Painless**.
        ▪ **Duration**: **Transient**, lasting seconds to minutes (usually < 30 minutes).
        ▪ **Pattern**: Classically described as a **"curtain" or "shade" descending** (or ascending) over the visual field. It can also be a generalized dimming, blurring, or constriction of vision.
    ◦ **Associated Symptoms (HIGHLY IMPORTANT)**:
        ▪ **TIA/CVA Symptoms**: Contralateral hemiparesis, sensory deficits, aphasia, or dysarthria suggest a larger ischemic event involving the brain.
        ▪ **GCA Symptoms**: New-onset headache (especially temporal), jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, fever, malaise, symptoms of polymyalgia rheumatica (proximal muscle stiffness).
• **Physical Exam Findings**
    ◦ **Visual Exam**:
        ▪ **Visual Acuity**: Usually 20/20 in both eyes.
        ▪ **Pupillary Response**: Typically normal. A **relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD)** may be present if some ischemic damage persists.
    ◦ **Fundoscopic Exam**:
        ▪ Often normal.
        ▪ **Pathognomonic Finding**: **Hollenhorst Plaque** - a bright, refractile cholesterol embolus located at an arterial bifurcation.
        ▪ May also see platelet-fibrin emboli (dull, white plugs) or signs of retinal ischemia (e.g., cotton-wool spots) if viewed close to the event.
    ◦ **Cardiovascular Exam**:
        ▪ Auscultate for **carotid bruits** (low sensitivity/specificity, but significant if present).
        ▪ Palpate pulses, check for an irregularly irregular rhythm (suggests **A-fib**).
    ◦ **Neurological Exam**:
        ▪ A full neurological exam is essential to rule out concurrent focal deficits.
    ◦ **GCA-Specific Exam**:
        ▪ Palpate the temporal arteries for tenderness, thickening, nodularity, or a reduced pulse.
sections.diagnostics:
• The workup is urgent and aimed at identifying the source of ischemia.
• **Initial / Emergent Studies**:
    ◦ **Stat Labs**: CBC, CMP, PT/INR, PTT.
    ◦ **Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR)** and **C-Reactive Protein (CRP)**: **CRITICAL** for all patients >50 to screen for **Giant Cell Arteritis**.
    ◦ **ECG**: To identify **atrial fibrillation** or other arrhythmias.
    ◦ **Non-contrast Head CT**: To rule out hemorrhage if stroke is suspected.
• **Vascular Imaging (KEY to workup)**:
    ◦ **Carotid Duplex Ultrasound**: **First-line test**. Non-invasive, identifies hemodynamically significant stenosis in the carotid arteries.
    ◦ **CT Angiography (CTA)** or **MR Angiography (MRA)**: Provides more detailed imaging of the carotids and intracranial circulation. Often used for surgical planning or if ultrasound is inconclusive.
• **Cardiac Evaluation**:
    ◦ **Echocardiogram (TTE or TEE)**: To identify cardiac sources of emboli (e.g., valvular disease, ventricular thrombus). TEE is more sensitive for left atrial appendage thrombi.
    ◦ **Holter Monitor / Cardiac Event Monitor**: If paroxysmal A-fib is suspected.
• **If GCA is Suspected (Elevated ESR/CRP)**:
    ◦ **Temporal Artery Biopsy**: **Gold standard** for diagnosis. However, treatment should **NOT** be delayed pending biopsy.
sections.treatment:
• **Atherosclerotic/Embolic Disease**:
    ◦ **Medical**: **Antiplatelet therapy** (Aspirin 81-325mg daily, or Clopidogrel) AND **High-Intensity Statin** (e.g., Atorvastatin 80mg).
    ◦ **Surgical/Interventional**:
        ▪ **Carotid Endarterectomy (CEA)**: For symptomatic patients with high-grade stenosis (**70-99%**).
        ▪ **Carotid Artery Stenting (CAS)**: An alternative for high-risk surgical candidates.
• **Cardioembolic Source (e.g., Atrial Fibrillation)**:
    ◦ **Systemic Anticoagulation** (Warfarin or a DOAC like Apixaban, Rivaroxaban).
• **Giant Cell Arteritis**:
    ◦ **IMMEDIATE high-dose systemic corticosteroids** (e.g., Prednisone 60-80mg daily).
        ▪ This is an emergency; **do not wait for biopsy results to initiate treatment**.
sections.management:
• **Specialist Referrals**:
    ◦ **Neurology**: For comprehensive TIA/stroke workup and management.
    ◦ **Ophthalmology**: For a complete dilated eye exam.
    ◦ **Vascular Surgery**: For evaluation for CEA/CAS.
    ◦ **Cardiology**: For management of cardiac etiologies.
sections.complications:
• **Cerebrovascular Accident (CVA / Stroke)**: The most feared complication. The risk is highest in the first few days after the event.
• **Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO)**: Results in profound, permanent monocular vision loss.
• **Permanent vision loss** from untreated **Giant Cell Arteritis**.
• **Complications from treatment**: Stroke or nerve injury from CEA, bleeding from anticoagulation.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis for **visual recovery** from the episode itself is excellent.
• The long-term prognosis depends on the etiology and management.
• Untreated, the risk of stroke after amaurosis fugax from significant carotid stenosis can be as high as **15% within 3 months**.
• Timely diagnosis and appropriate treatment (e.g., CEA) significantly reduce the risk of future stroke.
sections.preventionEducation:
• **Aggressive Risk Factor Modification**:
    ◦ **Blood Pressure Control**: Goal < 130/80 mmHg.
    ◦ **Lipid Control**: High-intensity statin therapy.
    ◦ **Glycemic Control**: A1c < 7% for diabetics.
    ◦ **Lifestyle**: Smoking cessation, diet, regular exercise.
• **Patient Education**:
    ◦ Educate on stroke symptoms using the **F.A.S.T.** acronym (**F**ace drooping, **A**rm weakness, **S**peech difficulty, **T**ime to call 911).
    ◦ Emphasize medication adherence and lifestyle changes.

sections.overview:
• Strabismus is a condition in which the eyes are not properly aligned with each other.
	◦ One eye may be turned inwards (**esotropia**), outwards (**exotropia**), upwards (**hypertropia**), or downwards (**hypotropia**).
• This misalignment can be constant or intermittent.
• In children, if left untreated, strabismus can lead to **amblyopia** ("lazy eye"), a condition of reduced vision in the misaligned eye that is not correctable by glasses alone.
• The primary goals of management are to preserve or restore vision, align the eyes, and achieve **binocular vision** (**stereopsis**).
sections.etiology:
• The underlying cause is often multifactorial, involving a disruption in the neuromuscular control of eye movement.
• **Congenital / Infantile**:
	◦ Often idiopathic extraocular muscle imbalance.
	◦ Typically presents within the first 6 months of life (e.g., infantile esotropia).
• **Accommodative Esotropia**:
	◦ A common cause in children aged 2-5.
	◦ Caused by high **hyperopia** (farsightedness).
	◦ The effort to focus on near objects (**accommodation**) is linked to **convergence** (eyes turning in).
	◦ Excessive accommodative effort leads to excessive convergence and esotropia.
• **Cranial Nerve Palsies**:
	◦ **CN VI (Abducens) Palsy**:
		▪ Most common cause of acquired strabismus.
		▪ Leads to **esotropia** due to paralysis of the **lateral rectus muscle**.
		▪ Patient cannot **abduct** the affected eye.
	◦ **CN IV (Trochlear) Palsy**:
		▪ Leads to **hypertropia** due to paralysis of the **superior oblique muscle**.
		▪ Patients often present with a compensatory **head tilt** away from the affected side.
	◦ **CN III (Oculomotor) Palsy**:
		▪ Leads to a complex strabismus, with the eye deviated "**down and out**."
		▪ Often accompanied by **ptosis** and **mydriasis** (a "**blown pupil**").
• **Sensory Strabismus**: Poor vision in one eye (e.g., from a **congenital cataract**, **retinal detachment**, or **retinoblastoma**) leads to a failure of visual fusion, causing the eye to drift.
• **Mechanical Restriction**: Abnormalities of the extraocular muscles or surrounding orbital tissues restrict movement (e.g., **orbital fracture** with muscle entrapment, **thyroid eye disease**).
• **Central Nervous System (CNS) Pathology**: Brain tumors, stroke, hydrocephalus, or trauma can disrupt the brain's control over eye alignment.
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects approximately 2-4% of the U.S. population.
• **Esotropia** is more common than **exotropia** in childhood.
• No significant gender or racial predilection, though infantile esotropia may be more common in Caucasians.
• Can present at any age, but most commonly diagnosed in infancy and early childhood.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Parental concern about **ocular misalignment** ("crossed eyes" or a "wandering eye").
• Observation of a **compensatory head posture** (e.g., head tilt, face turn, chin up/down) to achieve binocular vision and avoid diplopia.
• Squinting or closing one eye, especially in bright sunlight (common in intermittent exotropia).
• In adults with new-onset strabismus, the chief complaint is often **diplopia** (double vision).
sections.diagnostics:
• Strabismus is primarily a **clinical diagnosis** based on the physical exam.
• **Cycloplegic Refraction**:
	◦ Essential in all children with strabismus.
	◦ Cycloplegic drops (e.g., cyclopentolate) are used to paralyze the ciliary muscle to reveal the full extent of any refractive error, particularly **hyperopia**.
• **Neuroimaging (CT/MRI)**:
	◦ Not routinely indicated.
	◦ Reserved for cases of:
		▪ Acquired, non-resolving **cranial nerve palsies**.
		▪ **Sudden onset** of strabismus accompanied by other neurologic signs (e.g., headache, vomiting, ataxia).
		▪ Suspected orbital or CNS pathology.
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent if detected and treated early.
• The prognosis for visual recovery from **amblyopia** is best when treatment is initiated before age 7.
• Surgical alignment has a high success rate, though some patients may require more than one surgery over their lifetime.
• Delayed diagnosis and treatment significantly worsen the prognosis for both visual function and binocularity.

sections.overview:
• **Amblyopia**, commonly known as "lazy eye," is a functional reduction in the best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) of one or both eyes due to abnormal visual development during early childhood.
	◦ It is a **diagnosis of exclusion**, meaning there is no underlying organic or structural pathology of the eye or visual pathway.
	◦ The brain "learns" to suppress the visual input from the affected eye, leading to a breakdown in normal **binocular vision**.
	◦ It is the most common cause of **monocular vision loss** in children.
sections.etiology:
• Amblyopia develops during the **critical period of visual development** (from birth to approximately 7-8 years of age) when the brain's visual pathways are maturing.
	◦ Any condition that prevents a clear, focused image from reaching the retina can lead to suppression of that eye's input to the visual cortex.
• **Core Pathophysiology**: Use-dependent competition between neuronal inputs from each eye.
	◦ If one eye provides a clear image and the other provides a blurry or misaligned image, the brain actively suppresses the input from the weaker eye.
	◦ This leads to atrophy and reduced synaptic connections in the visual cortex corresponding to that eye.
• **Three Main Types**:
	◦ **Strabismic Amblyopia (Most Common)**
		▪ Caused by misalignment of the eyes (**strabismus**).
		▪ The brain ignores the input from the deviating eye to avoid **diplopia** (double vision) and confusion.
		▪ Most commonly associated with **esotropia** (inward turning eye).
	◦ **Refractive Amblyopia**
		▪ Caused by a significant difference in refractive error between the two eyes (**anisometropia**) or high bilateral refractive error (**isoametropia**).
		▪ **Anisometropic**: One eye focuses much better than the other (e.g., one eye is more farsighted). The brain favors the clearer image, leading to suppression of the blurrier one. This type can be easily missed as the eyes appear straight.
		▪ **Isoametropic**: Both eyes have a severe, uncorrected refractive error (e.g., high hyperopia or astigmatism), leading to bilateral blurry images and **bilateral amblyopia**.
	◦ **Deprivation Amblyopia (Most Severe)**
		▪ Caused by a physical obstruction in the line of sight that prevents a clear image from forming on the retina.
		▪ Examples: **congenital cataract**, significant **ptosis**, corneal opacity, vitreous hemorrhage.
		▪ This is an **ophthalmologic emergency** in infants and requires prompt treatment to prevent profound, irreversible vision loss.
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects **2-4%** of the general population.
• The leading cause of preventable, **monocular vision loss** in children and young adults.
• The **critical period** for development and treatment is from birth until age 7-8, with the highest brain plasticity in the first few years of life.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Often **asymptomatic** and discovered during routine vision screening at a well-child visit or school screening.
• Parents may report a "wandering" or "crossed" eye (**strabismus**).
• Child may squint, shut one eye (especially in bright light), or exhibit head tilting to favor the better-seeing eye.
• **Poor depth perception**, leading to clumsiness or difficulty with tasks like catching a ball.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Comprehensive Ophthalmologic Examination**
	◦ This is the **gold standard** and is required for diagnosis.
	◦ The primary care provider's role is screening and referral.
• **Cycloplegic Refraction**
	◦ Use of mydriatic/cycloplegic drops (e.g., cyclopentolate, atropine) to paralyze accommodation and accurately measure the full refractive error of each eye.
	◦ This is essential for diagnosing **refractive amblyopia**.
• **Slit-lamp and Fundus Examination**
	◦ To rule out any structural eye disease (e.g., **cataract**, **optic nerve hypoplasia**, retinal pathology) that could be causing the decreased vision.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** if detected and treated early (before age 5-6). Most children can achieve significant improvement in vision.
• **Fair to good** if treated between ages 7-10.
• **Poor** if treatment is initiated in late childhood or teenage years, as brain plasticity is greatly reduced.
• **Deprivation amblyopia** has the worst prognosis; **refractive amblyopia** generally has the best.

sections.overview:
• A congenital cataract is an opacification or clouding of the crystalline lens of the eye that is present at birth or develops within the first three months of life. It can be unilateral or bilateral.
• This condition is a significant cause of treatable childhood blindness.
• The primary clinical concern is the prevention of irreversible **stimulus deprivation amblyopia**, a type of "lazy eye" where the brain does not develop normal visual pathways due to a blocked visual signal from the affected eye.
• Prompt detection and intervention are critical.
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The lens is composed of highly organized proteins called crystallins. A cataract forms when these proteins misfold, aggregate, and accumulate, disrupting the lens's transparency and scattering light instead of focusing it cleanly onto the retina.
    ◦ This disruption can be caused by genetic defects, metabolic derangements, or external insults during fetal development.
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Idiopathic (~50%)**: Most cases have no identifiable cause.
    ◦ **Genetic/Hereditary (~25%)**
        ▪ Most commonly an **autosomal dominant** inheritance pattern.
        ▪ Associated with mutations in genes coding for crystallins, lens membrane proteins, or transcription factors.
    ◦ **Intrauterine Infections (TORCH)**
        ▪ **R**ubella: The classic cause, associated with the triad of cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and cardiac anomalies (e.g., PDA).
        ▪ **T**oxoplasmosis
        ▪ **C**ytomegalovirus (CMV)
        ▪ **H**erpes Simplex Virus (HSV), Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV), Syphilis, Zika.
    ◦ **Metabolic Disorders**
        ▪ **Galactosemia**: Classic cause, due to deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT). Presents with characteristic "oil droplet" cataracts. Reversible if a galactose-free diet is initiated early.
        ▪ **Lowe Syndrome (Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome)**: X-linked recessive disorder.
        ▪ **Fabry Disease**.
    ◦ **Systemic Syndromes / Chromosomal Abnormalities**
        ▪ **Down Syndrome (Trisomy 21)**
        ▪ **Edwards Syndrome (Trisomy 18)**
        ▪ **Patau Syndrome (Trisomy 13)**
        ▪ **Marfan Syndrome**
        ▪ **Alport Syndrome**
    ◦ **Ocular Abnormalities**: Often associated with other eye malformations like Persistent Fetal Vasculature (PFV) or aniridia.
    ◦ **Trauma**: Perinatal trauma (rare).
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Occurs in approximately 1-6 per 10,000 live births.
• Represents a leading cause of preventable blindness in children worldwide.
• **Unilateral vs. Bilateral**
    ◦ Bilateral cases are more often hereditary or associated with a systemic disease.
    ◦ Unilateral cases are more likely to be idiopathic or associated with a local ocular anomaly (e.g., PFV).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Often detected during the **newborn nursery eye examination**.
• Parental concern about a "white spot" in the pupil, especially noticed in photographs (**leukocoria**).
• Abnormal visual behavior, such as failure to make eye contact or track objects.
• Development of secondary **strabismus** (misalignment of the eyes) or **nystagmus** (involuntary eye movements).
sections.diagnostics:
• The primary diagnostic step is a referral to a **pediatric ophthalmologist** for a comprehensive, dilated eye examination.
• **Full Ophthalmic Evaluation**
    ◦ Confirms the presence, density, and morphology of the cataract.
    ◦ A dilated fundus exam is crucial to rule out posterior segment pathology (e.g., retinoblastoma).
• **B-scan Ultrasonography**
    ◦ Used if the cataract is too dense to visualize the retina, to rule out coexisting posterior pathology like retinal detachment or retinoblastoma.
• **Systemic Workup (especially for bilateral or syndromic cases)**
    ◦ **Urine Test**
        ▪ For reducing substances (screens for galactosemia).
        ▪ **Crucial to perform before any dietary changes.**
    ◦ **Serology**
        ▪ TORCH titers, VDRL/RPR for syphilis.
    ◦ **Genetic Testing**
        ▪ Karyotyping or specific gene panels if a syndrome is suspected.
sections.prognosis:
• **Highly dependent** on the timing of surgery, etiology of the cataract, and compliance with post-operative management (contact lens wear and patching).
• **Bilateral cataracts** often have a better visual prognosis than unilateral cataracts, as there is no "good" eye for the brain to favor, reducing the severity of amblyopia.
• **Unilateral cataracts** have a guarded prognosis due to the high risk of dense, difficult-to-treat amblyopia.
• With early intervention and aggressive therapy, many children can achieve good functional vision.

sections.overview:
• Preseptal cellulitis, also known as periorbital cellulitis, is an infection of the eyelid and surrounding soft tissues that are **anterior** to the orbital septum.
• It is distinct from the more severe orbital cellulitis, which involves infection of the fat and muscles posterior to the orbital septum.
• Preseptal cellulitis is essentially an infection of the face/eyelid, not the orbit itself.
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The infection is confined to the subcutaneous tissues located **anterior** to the orbital septum, a thin fibrous membrane that extends from the orbital rim to the tarsal plates of the eyelids.
    ◦ This septum acts as a barrier, preventing the spread of infection into the orbit proper.
• **Routes of Infection**
    ◦ **Contiguous Spread (Most Common)**: Infection spreads from an adjacent structure.
        ▪ Upper respiratory infections, particularly **ethmoid sinusitis**.
        ▪ Infections of the eyelid glands: hordeolum (stye) or chalazion.
        ▪ Dacryocystitis (infection of the lacrimal sac).
        ▪ Dental infections.
    ◦ **Direct Inoculation**: Bacteria enter through a break in the skin.
        ▪ Trauma (lacerations, abrasions).
        ▪ Insect or animal bites.
        ▪ Foreign bodies.
        ▪ Cutaneous lesions (e.g., impetigo, eczema).
    ◦ **Hematogenous Spread**: Bacteremia from a distant site seeds the periorbital tissues (less common).
• **Common Pathogens**
    ◦ **Associated with skin trauma**: *Staphylococcus aureus* (including MRSA) and *Streptococcus pyogenes* (Group A Strep).
    ◦ **Associated with sinusitis**: *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae* (less common since the Hib vaccine), *Moraxella catarrhalis*, and anaerobes.
sections.epidemiology:
• Primarily a disease of **children**, with a median age of 5-7 years.
• More common than orbital cellulitis.
• The incidence of *H. influenzae* type b (Hib) as a cause has dramatically decreased since the widespread adoption of the Hib vaccine.
sections.riskFactors:
• Recent upper respiratory infection (URI) or sinusitis
• Local skin trauma, insect/animal bite near the eye
• Eyelid lesions (hordeolum, chalazion, impetigo)
• Dacryocystitis
• Recent dental procedures or infections
• Immunocompromised state
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A typical patient, often a child, presents with the acute onset of a unilateral red, swollen, and tender eyelid.
• The patient may have a history of a recent "cold," bug bite, or minor cut near the eye.
• The globe itself is unaffected, and the patient does not complain of vision changes or pain when moving the eye.
• A low-grade fever may be present.
• Symptoms include:
    ◦ Unilateral eyelid swelling (edema)
    ◦ Eyelid redness (erythema)
    ◦ Eyelid tenderness and pain
    ◦ Epiphora (excessive tearing)
    ◦ Low-grade fever
    ◦ **ABSENCE** of vision changes (no blurriness, no diplopia)
    ◦ **ABSENCE** of deep eye pain or pain on eye movement
sections.physicalExam:
• **Periorbital Tissues**: Unilateral erythema, edema, warmth, and tenderness of the eyelid and surrounding skin. The eyelid may be swollen shut.
• **Visual Acuity**: **NORMAL**
• **Extraocular Movements (EOMs)**: **INTACT** and **PAINLESS**
• **Pupillary Response**: **NORMAL** (pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light; no afferent pupillary defect [APD]).
• **Proptosis (Exophthalmos)**: **ABSENT**. The eye is not bulging.
• **Chemosis (Conjunctival Edema)**: Typically absent or minimal.
• A primary source may be visible (e.g., skin abrasion, insect bite, hordeolum).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primarily a clinical diagnosis** based on the history and physical exam findings that localize the infection anterior to the septum.
• **Labs**
    ◦ A CBC may show leukocytosis with a left shift, and inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) may be elevated, but these are nonspecific.
    ◦ Blood cultures are generally low-yield unless the patient is febrile, systemically ill, or very young.
• **Imaging (CT Orbit with IV Contrast)**
    ◦ Not routinely indicated for clear-cut preseptal cellulitis.
    ◦ **Indications for CT Scan**:
        ▪ Any clinical suspicion for orbital cellulitis (pain with EOMs, proptosis, vision loss, ophthalmoplegia).
        ▪ Inability to perform a complete eye exam (e.g., eyelid is swollen shut in an uncooperative child).
        ▪ Failure to improve after 24-48 hours of appropriate antibiotic therapy.
        ▪ Signs of systemic toxicity.
    ◦ **CT Findings**: Soft tissue swelling and inflammation confined **anterior** to the orbital septum.
sections.treatment:
• **Goal**: Eradicate the infection and prevent posterior extension into the orbit.
• **Setting**
    ◦ **Outpatient**: Reliable patients/caregivers with mild-to-moderate disease who can tolerate oral medications and ensure close follow-up.
    ◦ **Inpatient Admission**: Recommended for children <1 year, patients with signs of systemic toxicity (high fever, hypotension), inability to tolerate oral intake, or concern for noncompliance.
• **Antibiotic Selection (covers *S. aureus*, MRSA, *Streptococcus spp.*)**
    ◦ **Oral (Outpatient)**
        ▪ **Clindamycin** (monotherapy)
        ▪ **OR**
        ▪ **Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX)** PLUS one of the following:
            • **Amoxicillin-clavulanate**
            • **Amoxicillin**
            • **Cefpodoxime** or **Cefdinir**
    ◦ **IV (Inpatient)**
        ▪ **Vancomycin** (for MRSA coverage) PLUS one of the following:
            • **Ceftriaxone** or **Cefotaxime**
        ▪ Alternative monotherapy: **Ampicillin-sulbactam**.
sections.management:
• **Follow-Up**: Patients managed as outpatients must be re-evaluated in **24-48 hours** to assess for clinical improvement.
• **Patient Education**: Instruct the patient/caregiver to return immediately for any "red flag" symptoms:
    ◦ Worsening pain
    ◦ Pain with eye movements
    ◦ Vision changes
    ◦ Double vision
    ◦ Bulging of the eye
• **Supportive Care**: Warm compresses can be applied to the affected eye for 15-20 minutes, 2-4 times a day to help with swelling and comfort.
• **Consultation**: Ophthalmology consultation is warranted if the diagnosis is uncertain, if there is a poor response to treatment, or if any signs of orbital involvement develop.
sections.complications:
• Progression to **Orbital Cellulitis**
• Subperiosteal Abscess
• Orbital Abscess
• Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis
• Meningitis
• Vision Loss
sections.prognosis: • **Excellent**. With timely and appropriate antibiotic therapy, most patients make a full and rapid recovery without sequelae.

sections.overview:
• Orbital cellulitis is a serious infection of the orbital soft tissues **posterior** to the orbital septum.
    ◦ Involves the orbital fat and extraocular muscles.
• This condition is a true **ophthalmologic emergency**, as it can rapidly lead to vision loss and life-threatening intracranial complications.
• It must be distinguished from **preseptal (periorbital) cellulitis**, which is a much less severe infection of the eyelid and soft tissues **anterior** to the orbital septum.
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**: The infection occurs when pathogens gain access to the space behind the orbital septum, a thin, fibrous membrane that acts as a barrier against the spread of infection from the eyelid into the orbit.
• **Primary Routes of Infection**
    ◦ **Sinusitis** (Most Common, ~90%): Infection spreads directly from adjacent paranasal sinuses, most commonly the **ethmoid sinus**. The lamina papyracea, the thin bony wall separating the sinus from the orbit, is easily breached.
    ◦ **Direct Inoculation**: From trauma (e.g., orbital fracture, penetrating injury) or orbital/eyelid surgery.
    ◦ **Hematogenous Spread**: Seeding from bacteremia originating from a distant site.
    ◦ **Dental Infections**: Spread from a maxillary tooth abscess can ascend into the orbit.
    ◦ **Dacryocystitis**: Infection of the lacrimal sac.
• **Common Pathogens**
    ◦ *Streptococcus pneumoniae*
    ◦ *Staphylococcus aureus* (including **MRSA**)
    ◦ *Haemophilus influenzae* (less common since the Hib vaccine)
    ◦ Anaerobes (often in dental or chronic sinusitis cases)
    ◦ Fungi (e.g., ***Mucor***, ***Aspergillus***) in immunocompromised or diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) patients.
sections.epidemiology:
• More common in children than adults, with a median age of 7-12 years.
• Slight male predominance.
• Incidence is higher during the winter months, correlating with the peak incidence of sinusitis and upper respiratory infections.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient, often a child, presents with a recent history of an upper respiratory infection or sinusitis who develops a rapid onset of unilateral eye swelling, pain, and fever.
• The patient appears systemically ill.
• The key is the presence of signs indicating involvement *behind* the orbital septum.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Labs**
    ◦ **CBC with differential**: Leukocytosis with a left shift is common.
    ◦ **Blood cultures**: To rule out bacteremia/sepsis.
    ◦ **ESR/CRP**: Will be elevated but are non-specific inflammatory markers.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **High-resolution CT Scan of the Orbits and Sinuses with IV Contrast** is the **imaging modality of choice**.
        ▪ **Confirms the diagnosis**: Shows inflammation posterior to the orbital septum (e.g., **fat stranding**, muscle enhancement).
        ▪ **Identifies the source**: Opacification of the paranasal sinuses is common.
        ▪ **Detects complications**: Can visualize a **subperiosteal abscess**, **orbital abscess**, or signs of **cavernous sinus thrombosis**.
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent if diagnosed early and treated aggressively with IV antibiotics.
• Prognosis worsens significantly with delayed treatment, the presence of an abscess, vision loss at presentation, or the development of intracranial complications.

sections.overview:
• A hyphema is the presence of gross blood (erythrocytes) in the **anterior chamber** of the eye, which is the fluid-filled space between the cornea and the iris.
• A hyphema is an ophthalmologic emergency as it can lead to a rapid increase in **intraocular pressure (IOP)** and **permanent vision loss**.
    ◦ It is most commonly caused by **trauma**.
• A **microhyphema** refers to suspended red blood cells in the anterior chamber without a visible layered collection of blood.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Traumatic (Most Common)**
        ▪ **Blunt Trauma:** Accounts for the vast majority of cases. A sudden blow to the eye causes rapid compression and decompression of the globe, creating shearing forces that tear the blood vessels of the iris and ciliary body.
        ▪ **Penetrating Trauma:** Laceration of anterior segment vessels.
        ▪ **Iatrogenic:** Post-operative complication following intraocular surgery (e.g., cataract, glaucoma surgery).
    ◦ **Spontaneous (Non-traumatic)**
        ▪ **Neovascularization:** Abnormal blood vessel growth (e.g., **proliferative diabetic retinopathy**, retinal vein occlusion).
        ▪ **Ocular Tumors:** Juvenile xanthogranuloma, iris melanoma.
        ▪ **Uveitis:** Certain inflammatory conditions can cause bleeding.
        ▪ **Blood Dyscrasias / Coagulopathies:** Leukemia, hemophilia, von Willebrand disease, **sickle cell disease**.
    ◦ **Medication-Induced:** Anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin) or antiplatelets (e.g., aspirin) can contribute, but rarely cause hyphema without underlying pathology or trauma.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ A force (usually blunt trauma) tears a vessel in the iris or ciliary body.
    ◦ Blood leaks into the **anterior chamber**, mixing with the aqueous humor.
    ◦ Due to gravity, the red blood cells settle inferiorly, forming a visible, layered line.
    ◦ The blood, cells, and fibrin can obstruct the **trabecular meshwork**, the eye's drainage system.
    ◦ Blockage of the trabecular meshwork leads to increased **intraocular pressure (IOP)**, which can damage the optic nerve (**secondary glaucoma**).
sections.epidemiology:
• Incidence is approximately 12 per 100,000 people.
• Strong bimodal distribution:
    ◦ Most common in children and adolescents (10-20 years old), primarily due to sports-related injuries and altercations.
    ◦ A second smaller peak occurs in the elderly, often related to falls or post-surgical complications.
• Male-to-female ratio is approximately 3:1.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with a history of recent, direct **trauma** to the eye.
• They will complain of a **painful red eye** and **vision changes** that began shortly after the injury.
• The presentation can range from minimal symptoms with a tiny hyphema to severe pain and near-total vision loss with a large one.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**
    ◦ Diagnosis is made by history and physical exam findings, primarily with a **slit lamp**.
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **Sickle Cell Screen:** Mandatory for all African American and Mediterranean patients due to significant management implications.
    ◦ **Coagulation Studies (PT/INR, PTT):** If a bleeding disorder is suspected or the patient is on anticoagulants.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **B-scan Ocular Ultrasound:** Useful if the posterior segment cannot be visualized due to a dense hyphema, to rule out **retinal detachment** or **vitreous hemorrhage**.
    ◦ **CT Scan of Orbits:** Indicated if there is suspicion of a **ruptured globe** or **orbital fracture**.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is generally excellent for uncomplicated microhyphemas and Grade I hyphemas, with most patients recovering full vision.
• Prognosis worsens significantly with larger hyphemas, **re-bleeding**, and development of **secondary glaucoma**.
• An **"8-ball hyphema"** (Grade IV) has a poor prognosis, with only a ~50% chance of recovering useful vision.

sections.overview:
• Blunt ocular trauma refers to injury to the eye and surrounding structures from a non-penetrating force.
• The injury spectrum ranges from minor contusions (e.g., "black eye") to severe, vision-threatening emergencies.
• The most critical distinction in ocular trauma is between a **closed globe injury** (contusion; eyewall is intact) and an **open globe injury** (rupture; full-thickness scleral or corneal laceration).
• An **open globe** is an ophthalmologic emergency requiring immediate surgical intervention to preserve vision and the eye itself.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Assault**: Fists, blunt objects
    ◦ **Sports**: Balls (racquetball, baseball, soccer), elbows, fingers
    ◦ **Motor Vehicle Accidents (MVAs)**: Airbag deployment, striking the steering wheel/dashboard
    ◦ **Workplace Accidents**: High-velocity objects, machinery-related trauma
    ◦ **Falls**: Especially in the elderly
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ A blunt force strikes the orbit, causing a sudden, dramatic increase in intraocular pressure (IOP).
    ◦ The globe rapidly compresses in the anteroposterior (AP) dimension and expands along the equator.
    ◦ This force can cause two types of damage:
        ▪ **Coup-Contrecoup Injury**
            • **Coup**: Damage at the direct site of impact (e.g., corneal abrasion, traumatic mydriasis).
            • **Contrecoup**: Damage at the opposite pole of the eye from the impact (e.g., optic nerve avulsion, retinal detachment).
        ▪ **Equatorial Expansion**: The stretching force tears internal structures like the iris root (iridodialysis), ciliary body, lens zonules (lens subluxation/dislocation), and retina.
    ◦ **Globe Rupture**: If the force exceeds the sclera's elastic limit, the globe ruptures. This typically occurs at the eye's weakest points:
        ▪ The limbus (corneoscleral junction)
        ▪ Posterior to the insertion points of the extraocular muscles (where the sclera is thinnest)
        ▪ Sites of prior ocular surgery (e.g., cataract, LASIK flap, glaucoma surgery scars)
sections.epidemiology:
• Ocular trauma is a leading cause of monocular blindness, particularly in young people.
• **Highest incidence in young males** (ages 10-30).
• Bimodal distribution: one peak in young adulthood (sports, assault) and a second in the elderly (falls).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents to the emergency department after a direct blow to the eye.
• History will involve a specific mechanism (e.g., "was struck by a baseball," "punched in the face," "airbag deployed in MVA").
• The patient's primary complaints are usually acute pain and vision loss in the affected eye.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Bedside Exam**
    ◦ Visual acuity, pupillary exam, external inspection.
    ◦ Use Seidel test only if suspicion is low-to-moderate and you need confirmation; avoid if rupture is obvious.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **CT Orbit** (axial and coronal views, thin cuts, no contrast): **Test of choice.**
        ▪ Excellent for identifying **globe rupture** (e.g., "flat tire" sign), intraocular foreign bodies (especially metallic or inorganic), and associated orbital fractures.
    ◦ **B-scan Ocular Ultrasound**
        ▪ Can be performed by ophthalmology to visualize posterior structures (e.g., retinal detachment, vitreous hemorrhage) when the view is obscured.
        ▪ **Contraindicated if open globe is suspected** due to pressure from the probe.
sections.prognosis:
• The **initial visual acuity** at the time of presentation is the single most important prognostic factor for final visual outcome.
• **Poor prognostic indicators**:
    ◦ Poor initial visual acuity (e.g., light perception only)
    ◦ Presence of an **afferent pupillary defect (APD)**
    ◦ Large posterior scleral rupture
    ◦ Vitreous hemorrhage
    ◦ Delayed time to surgical repair

sections.overview:
• **Otitis Externa (OE)** is an inflammation or infection of the **external auditory canal (EAC)**, the auricle, or both.
    ◦ Commonly known as "**Swimmer's Ear**".
    ◦ Can be **acute** (<3 weeks) or **chronic** (>3 months).
    ◦ Characterized by **otalgia**, **pruritus**, **otorrhea**, and **erythema/edema** of the ear canal.
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ Begins with a breakdown of the protective barrier of the skin and **cerumen** in the EAC.
    ◦ Cerumen provides a hydrophobic, acidic (pH 4-5) environment hostile to bacterial and fungal growth.
    ◦ Disruption of this barrier through **moisture**, **trauma**, or **dermatologic conditions** leads to skin maceration, inflammation, and microbial invasion.
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Bacterial** (accounts for >90% of cases)
        ▪ **_Pseudomonas aeruginosa_** is the most common pathogen.
        ▪ **_Staphylococcus aureus_** is the second most common.
        ▪ Other gram-negatives (_Proteus_, _Klebsiella_) and gram-positives (_Staphylococcus epidermidis_) can also be involved.
        ▪ Often polymicrobial.
    ◦ **Fungal (Otomycosis)**
        ▪ Less common, often seen after treatment with antibacterial drops or in immunocompromised hosts.
        ▪ **_Aspergillus niger_** (black or grey, fuzzy growth) is most common.
        ▪ **_Candida albicans_** (white, creamy discharge) is also a frequent cause.
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects approximately 10% of people in their lifetime.
• Most common during **summer months** due to increased swimming and humidity.
• **Bimodal age distribution**, with peaks in children (7-12 years old) and older adults.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Water Exposure**: Swimming, surfing, excessive bathing/showering (macerates the skin).
• **Trauma**: Use of cotton swabs (Q-tips), earplugs, hearing aids, finger scratching.
• **Occlusive Devices**: Hearing aids, earplugs, headphones.
• **Dermatologic Conditions**: Eczema, psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis affecting the EAC.
• **Anatomic Factors**: Narrow or stenotic ear canals.
• **Immunocompromised States**: Diabetes mellitus, HIV/AIDS, chemotherapy.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Typically presents with a **rapid onset** (within 48 hours) of ear discomfort, often following recent water exposure or minor trauma to the ear canal.
• The presentation is almost always **unilateral**.
• **Symptoms**
    ◦ **Otalgia (Ear Pain)**: The **cardinal symptom**. Can range from mild to severe and is exacerbated by chewing or touching the ear.
    ◦ **Pruritus (Itching)**: Often an early symptom before pain develops.
    ◦ **Aural Fullness / Pressure**: A sensation of blockage in the ear.
    ◦ **Otorrhea**: Discharge from the ear, which can be scant, watery, or purulent and malodorous.
    ◦ **Conductive Hearing Loss**: Due to occlusion of the canal by edema and debris.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Hallmark Sign**: **Pain upon manipulation of the tragus or traction of the auricle (pinna)**. This finding is highly specific for OE.
• **Otoscopy**
    ◦ **Erythema and edema** of the external auditory canal skin.
    ◦ **Purulent debris or discharge** within the canal.
    ◦ The canal may be so edematous that it is narrowed (**stenosis**), preventing visualization of the tympanic membrane (TM).
    ◦ If the TM is visible, it is typically **normal in appearance and mobility**, which helps distinguish OE from Acute Otitis Media (AOM) with perforation.
• **Periauricular Findings**
    ◦ Erythema of the pinna or surrounding skin (cellulitis) and tender regional lymphadenopathy (preauricular or postauricular) may be present in more severe cases.
sections.diagnostics:
• Primarily a **clinical diagnosis** based on history and physical exam findings.
• **Otoscopy** is essential to confirm inflammation of the EAC and assess the TM.
• **Culture of discharge**
    ◦ Not necessary for routine, uncomplicated cases.
    ◦ Indicated for:
        ▪ Recalcitrant or chronic cases.
        ▪ Post-operative infections.
        ▪ Immunocompromised patients.
        ▪ Suspected fungal etiology.
• **Imaging (CT Scan of Temporal Bone)**
    ◦ Only indicated if invasive infection, such as **Malignant (Necrotizing) Otitis Externa**, is suspected.
sections.treatment:
• **Aural Toilet (Debridement)**
    ◦ Gentle cleaning of the EAC to remove debris, cerumen, and purulent material, allowing topical medications to penetrate.
    ◦ Can be done via suction or irrigation (only if TM is confirmed intact).
• **Topical Medications (First-Line)**
    ◦ **Fluoroquinolone Otic Drops** (e.g., Ciprofloxacin, Ofloxacin)
        ▪ Excellent broad-spectrum coverage, including *_Pseudomonas_*.
        ▪ Non-ototoxic, making them safe even if TM perforation cannot be ruled out.
        ▪ Examples: **Ciprodex** (Ciprofloxacin/Dexamethasone), **Ofloxacin Otic**.
    ◦ **Neomycin/Polymyxin B/Hydrocortisone** (e.g., Cortisporin Otic)
        ▪ Effective but contains **neomycin**, which is potentially **ototoxic** and can cause **contact dermatitis**.
        ▪ **Avoid if TM is perforated or not visualized**.
• **Fungal OE (Otomycosis)**
    ◦ Thorough debridement is critical.
    ◦ Topical antifungal agents such as **Clotrimazole 1% solution** or **Acetic Acid 2%**.
• **Systemic Antibiotics**
    ◦ **Generally NOT indicated** for uncomplicated, localized OE.
    ◦ Reserve for cases with deep tissue infection, extension of cellulitis beyond the EAC, or in immunocompromised patients. Oral **Ciprofloxacin** or other anti-pseudomonal agent may be used.
• **Pain Management**
    ◦ NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen) or acetaminophen for mild to moderate pain.
    ◦ Opioids may be required for a short duration for severe pain.
sections.management:
• **Ear Wick Placement**
    ◦ If the EAC is too edematous for drops to enter, a compressed sponge (ear wick) is inserted into the canal.
    ◦ The patient then applies drops onto the wick, which expands and delivers medication to the medial canal.
    ◦ The wick is typically removed in 2-3 days.
• **Follow-up**
    ◦ Re-evaluate in 48-72 hours if symptoms do not improve.
    ◦ Re-evaluate in 1-2 weeks to confirm resolution.
sections.complications:
• **Malignant (Necrotizing) Otitis Externa**
    ◦ An invasive, life-threatening **osteomyelitis of the temporal bone**.
    ◦ **Classic Patient**: Elderly, **diabetic**, or immunocompromised.
    ◦ **Pathogen**: Almost exclusively **_Pseudomonas aeruginosa_**.
    ◦ **Presentation**: Severe, deep-seated otalgia (out of proportion to exam findings), persistent purulent otorrhea.
    ◦ **Key Finding**: **Granulation tissue** at the bony-cartilaginous junction of the EAC floor.
    ◦ **Diagnosis**: **CT or MRI** showing osseous erosion.
    ◦ **Treatment**: Requires hospitalization and prolonged IV anti-pseudomonal antibiotics (e.g., IV Ciprofloxacin, Ceftazidime).
• **Periauricular Cellulitis**
• **Canal Stenosis**: Chronic inflammation can lead to permanent narrowing of the ear canal.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for uncomplicated acute OE. With appropriate treatment, symptoms typically improve within 48-72 hours and resolve completely within 7-10 days.
• **Guarded** for **Malignant Otitis Externa**, which has significant morbidity and potential mortality if not treated aggressively.
sections.preventionEducation:
• **Keep the ear canal dry (Water Precautions)**
    ◦ Avoid swimming and water sports for 7-10 days.
    ◦ During showering, protect the ear with a cotton ball coated in petroleum jelly.
• Instruct on proper administration of ear drops (lie with affected ear up, fill canal, pump tragus to facilitate entry).
• Avoid instrumentation of the ear (e.g., Q-tips, hairpins).

sections.overview:
• **Malignant (Necrotizing) Otitis Externa (MOE)** is a **severe**, **invasive**, and potentially **life-threatening** infection of the external auditory canal (EAC) and surrounding soft tissues, cartilage, and bone.
    ◦ It is essentially an **osteomyelitis of the temporal bone and skull base** that originates in the EAC.
    ◦ Despite the name **"malignant,"** it is not a cancer but is named for its aggressive clinical course and high mortality rate if not treated promptly and aggressively.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• Primarily affects **elderly patients with diabetes mellitus** (over 90% of cases).
• Also seen in other **immunocompromised** individuals (HIV/AIDS, chemotherapy, chronic steroid use, organ transplant).
• Rare in children, but can occur in the setting of pediatric immunodeficiency.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is an **elderly diabetic patient** with a history of otitis externa that has **failed to resolve** with standard topical antibiotics.
• The patient complains of **progressively worsening, severe ear pain** that is **out of proportion** to the findings on initial physical exam.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Laboratory Studies**
    ◦ **ESR and CRP**: Almost always **markedly elevated**. These are essential for diagnosis and for monitoring response to therapy.
    ◦ **Culture and Sensitivity**: Swab of ear discharge/tissue is mandatory to identify the pathogen and guide antibiotic choice.
    ◦ **CBC**: May show leukocytosis.
    ◦ **HbA1c / Glucose**: To assess glycemic control.
• **Biopsy**
    ◦ A biopsy of the granulation tissue is often performed to rule out malignancy (e.g., squamous cell carcinoma) and confirm the diagnosis histologically.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **CT of the Temporal Bones with Contrast**: **Best initial imaging study**. Excellent for assessing **bony erosion**, **osseous destruction**, and extent of disease.
    ◦ **MRI with Gadolinium**: Superior for evaluating **soft tissue involvement**, **dural enhancement**, **abscess formation**, and **intracranial extension**.
    ◦ **Radionuclide Scanning** (less common now, but classic for boards):
        ▪ **Technetium-99m bone scan**: Highly sensitive for osteomyelitis (shows increased uptake) but not specific.
        ▪ **Gallium-67 scan**: More specific for inflammation. Excellent for tracking treatment response, as uptake decreases with successful therapy.
sections.prognosis:
• With modern antibiotic therapy, the **mortality rate is approximately 10-20%**.
• The prognosis is significantly worse if **cranial nerve palsies** are present at diagnosis (mortality can exceed 50%).
• Neurological deficits, especially facial nerve palsy, may be permanent despite successful eradication of the infection.
• **Recurrence** is possible if the full course of therapy is not completed or underlying risk factors are not controlled.

sections.overview:
• Cerumen impaction is the accumulation of cerumen (earwax) in the external auditory canal (EAC) to a point where it causes symptoms or prevents necessary assessment of the ear, such as visualization of the **tympanic membrane (TM)**.
• Cerumen itself is a normal, protective substance, but its excessive buildup leading to obstruction is a common clinical problem.
sections.etiology:
• **Normal Cerumen Physiology**
    ◦ Cerumen is composed of desquamated keratinocytes and secretions from sebaceous and apocrine (ceruminous) glands in the cartilaginous outer third of the EAC.
    ◦ It is hydrophobic, acidic (pH ~6.0), and contains lysozymes, which helps to lubricate the canal, trap debris, and inhibit bacterial/fungal growth.
• **Self-Cleaning Mechanism**
    ◦ The ear is typically self-cleaning.
    ◦ Epithelial migration, aided by jaw movements (chewing, talking), moves cerumen and debris from the TM outwards, where it is naturally expelled.
• **Pathophysiology of Impaction**
    ◦ Impaction occurs when this self-cleaning mechanism is disrupted. This can be due to:
        ▪ **Overproduction**: Some individuals naturally produce more cerumen.
        ▪ **Anatomical Obstruction**: Narrow or tortuous EACs, osteomas, or exostoses can hinder normal cerumen migration.
        ▪ **Mechanical Obstruction / Disruption**: The most common cause is iatrogenic. Use of **cotton-tipped applicators**, earplugs, or hearing aids pushes cerumen deeper into the bony, non-secretory part of the canal, preventing its natural expulsion and causing it to become impacted.
        ▪ **Age-Related Changes**: In older adults, ceruminous glands atrophy, leading to drier, harder cerumen that is more difficult to expel.
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects approximately 10% of children, 5% of healthy adults, and up to 60% of the elderly and institutionalized populations.
• It is one of the most common reasons for primary care and otolaryngology (ENT) visits.
• More prevalent in patients with cognitive impairment and those who use hearing aids.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Anatomical**
    ◦ Narrow, tortuous, or collapsed external auditory canals.
    ◦ Presence of osteomas or exostoses (bony growths).
    ◦ Excessive hair growth in the canal.
• **Iatrogenic/Mechanical**
    ◦ **Use of cotton-tipped applicators (Q-tips)**.
    ◦ Use of hearing aids, earplugs, or in-ear headphones.
• **Physiological**
    ◦ Overproduction of cerumen.
    ◦ Age-related changes (drier cerumen in the elderly).
• **Patient-Related**
    ◦ Cognitive impairment (e.g., dementia, developmental delay), leading to inability to recognize or express symptoms.
    ◦ History of previous cerumen impaction.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient, typically elderly or a known hearing aid user, presents with a chief complaint of unilateral or bilateral gradual **hearing loss**.
    ◦ The symptoms may have an **acute onset**, often after showering or swimming, as water can cause the impacted cerumen to swell and create a complete occlusion.
    ◦ The patient may also complain of ear fullness, tinnitus, or dizziness.
• **Associated Symptoms**
    ◦ **Conductive Hearing Loss (most common symptom)**
    ◦ **Otalgia (ear pain)**
    ◦ Sensation of ear fullness or pressure
    ◦ **Tinnitus** (ringing or buzzing in the ear)
    ◦ Dizziness or vertigo
    ◦ Pruritus (itching) in the ear canal
    ◦ **Reflex cough or hiccups** (rare, due to stimulation of Arnold's nerve, a branch of the vagus nerve)
sections.physicalExam:
• **Otoscopy**
    ◦ The key to diagnosis.
    ◦ Cerumen is visualized obstructing the external auditory canal.
    ◦ The **tympanic membrane cannot be fully visualized** due to the obstruction.
    ◦ The cerumen may vary in color (light yellow, brown, black) and consistency (soft, firm, rock-hard).
• **Weber Test**
    ◦ Sound lateralizes to the **affected ear** (indicative of **conductive hearing loss**).
• **Rinne Test**
    ◦ **Bone conduction > Air conduction (BC > AC)** in the affected ear (a **negative Rinne test**, indicative of **conductive hearing loss**).
sections.diagnostics:
• The diagnosis is **clinical**, made by **direct visualization with an otoscope**.
• No imaging or laboratory studies are required for an uncomplicated cerumen impaction.
• Audiometry may be performed if hearing loss persists after the impaction is cleared to rule out an underlying sensorineural component.
sections.management:
• **Asymptomatic Patients**
    ◦ Observation is a reasonable option unless visualization of the TM is required for other diagnostic purposes.
• **Follow-up**
    ◦ Not typically required if symptoms resolve completely after removal.
    ◦ If symptoms persist (hearing loss, tinnitus, dizziness), further workup and/or referral to ENT or Audiology is indicated.
sections.complications:
• **Associated with the Impaction**
    ◦ Conductive hearing loss
    ◦ Otalgia
    ◦ Vertigo
• **Associated with Treatment**
    ◦ **Tympanic membrane perforation** (most serious)
    ◦ Laceration or abrasion of the EAC skin
    ◦ **Otitis externa** (from retained water or canal trauma)
    ◦ Vertigo (from using water that is too cold or warm during irrigation)
    ◦ Pain, bleeding, or tinnitus can also occur during the removal procedure.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**: Symptoms typically resolve completely and immediately upon successful removal of the obstructing cerumen.
• Recurrence is common if underlying risk factors are not addressed.
sections.preventionEducation:
• Counsel patients to **avoid using cotton-tipped applicators** or other objects to clean their ears.
• Prophylactic use of cerumenolytics or mineral oil (1-2 times per week) may be beneficial for patients with recurrent impactions or those who use hearing aids.

sections.overview:
• A **foreign body (FB)** in the **external auditory canal (EAC)** is the presence of any object, animate or inanimate, within the ear canal that is not naturally occurring.
• It is a common otologic problem, particularly in the **pediatric population**.
• While often benign, it has the potential to cause significant morbidity, including **infection**, **canal trauma**, **tympanic membrane (TM) perforation**, and **hearing loss**, especially if removal is delayed or improperly attempted.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology:
• **Predominantly a pediatric issue**, with a peak incidence between ages 2 and 4.
• Slight **male predominance** in children.
• In adults, it is often seen in tropical climates (insects) or in hearing aid users.
• The **right ear** is slightly more commonly affected than the left, likely due to right-handedness in the majority of the population.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation varies widely based on the type of FB, duration, and presence of complications.
• Often **asymptomatic** and discovered incidentally on routine examination or after being witnessed by a caregiver.
• Patients may present with a chief complaint of **ear pain**, **discharge**, or **hearing loss**.
• A high index of suspicion is required for any child presenting with **unilateral, foul-smelling otorrhea**, as this may be the only sign of a retained, chronic FB.
sections.diagnostics:
• The diagnosis is **clinical**, made by direct visualization with an otoscope.
• **Imaging is rarely required**.
• **Indications for Imaging (CT scan of the temporal bone)**:
    ◦ Suspicion of **TM perforation** with middle or inner ear involvement.
    ◦ Penetrating FB with suspected **ossicular** or **facial nerve injury**.
    ◦ Inability to visualize the FB due to severe **edema** or **bleeding**, but history is highly suggestive.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** with timely, appropriate, and atraumatic removal.
• The prognosis worsens with:
    ◦ Delayed presentation
    ◦ Complicated FBs (e.g., batteries, sharp objects)
    ◦ Multiple failed removal attempts leading to iatrogenic injury.

sections.overview:
• Acute Otitis Media (AOM) is an acute infection and inflammation of the middle ear space, the area behind the tympanic membrane (TM).
• It is one of the most common pediatric illnesses and a frequent reason for antibiotic prescriptions in children.
• The diagnosis is **clinical**, based on the presence of **middle ear effusion (MEE)** coupled with acute signs of inflammation and **rapid onset** of symptoms.
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**: AOM almost always follows a preceding event that causes **Eustachian tube dysfunction**, most commonly a viral Upper Respiratory Infection (URI).
    ◦ **Eustachian Tube Dysfunction**: A viral URI causes inflammation and edema of the nasopharyngeal mucosa, leading to obstruction of the Eustachian tube.
    ◦ **Negative Pressure & Effusion**: The obstruction prevents proper ventilation and drainage of the middle ear. Trapped air is resorbed, creating negative pressure that pulls fluid from the surrounding mucosa into the middle ear space, forming a sterile transudate (effusion).
    ◦ **Bacterial Colonization & Infection**: The static, nutrient-rich fluid becomes a culture medium for pathogens that colonize the nasopharynx. These pathogens enter the middle ear via the Eustachian tube, leading to a suppurative infection.
• **Causative Organisms**
    ◦ **Bacterial (Most Common)**
        ▪ ***Streptococcus pneumoniae*** (~40-50%)
        ▪ ***Haemophilus influenzae*** (non-typeable) (~30-40%)
        ▪ ***Moraxella catarrhalis*** (~10-20%)
        ▪ *Streptococcus pyogenes* (Group A Strep) is less common.
    ◦ **Viral**
        ▪ RSV, Influenza, Rhinovirus, Adenovirus.
        ▪ Viruses can cause AOM alone or predispose to bacterial superinfection.
• **Anatomic Predisposition in Children**: Children's Eustachian tubes are shorter, wider, and more horizontal than adults', making them less efficient at draining and more susceptible to pathogen entry.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Peak Incidence**: Age 6 to 18 months.
• By age 3, over 80% of children have experienced at least one episode of AOM.
• Slightly more common in males.
• Incidence peaks in the fall and winter, paralleling the seasonality of viral URIs.
• The introduction of the **pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13)** has decreased the incidence of AOM caused by *S. pneumoniae*.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a young child with a recent history of URI symptoms (cough, rhinorrhea) who develops a **rapid onset** of **fever**, **otalgia**, and **irritability** over hours to a few days.
• Preverbal infants may present with non-specific signs like inconsolable crying, poor feeding, or changes in sleep patterns.
sections.diagnostics:
• AOM is a **clinical diagnosis** based on history and physical exam.
• No lab or imaging studies are routinely required.
• **Diagnostic Criteria (AAP Guidelines)**
    ◦ **Rapid onset** of signs and symptoms.
    ◦ **Presence of Middle Ear Effusion (MEE)**, confirmed by one of the following:
        ▪ **Bulging** of the TM
        ▪ Limited or absent mobility of the TM on pneumatic otoscopy
        ▪ Air-fluid level behind the TM
        ▪ **Otorrhea**
    ◦ **Signs and Symptoms of Middle Ear Inflammation**:
        ▪ Distinct **erythema** of the TM
        ▪ Distinct **otalgia** (interfering with normal activity or sleep)
• **Ancillary Tests (not for routine diagnosis)**
    ◦ **Tympanometry**: Measures TM compliance. A flat (Type B) tympanogram indicates MEE. Useful for confirming effusion but not for differentiating AOM from OME.
    ◦ **Tympanocentesis**: Aspiration of middle ear fluid for culture. Reserved for treatment failure, neonates, or immunocompromised patients.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis for uncomplicated AOM is excellent.
• Most episodes resolve completely, often without antibiotics.
• Spontaneous resolution occurs in ~80% of cases.
• Hearing loss is typically transient and resolves once the middle ear effusion clears, which can take up to 3 months.

sections.overview:
• Definition: A pattern of distinct and well-documented episodes of **Acute Otitis Media (AOM)**
    ◦ **Three or more episodes** within a **6-month period**
    ◦ **Four or more episodes** within a **12-month period**, with at least one episode in the preceding 6 months
• A common pediatric condition resulting from a cycle of **infection, inflammation, and Eustachian tube dysfunction**
• Management focuses on treating acute infections, addressing underlying risk factors, and considering surgical intervention to prevent further episodes and complications.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology (Pathogens)**
    ◦ Causative organisms are the same as for a single episode of AOM
    ◦ **Bacterial (most common)**
        ▪ **Streptococcus pneumoniae** (most common overall, though incidence reduced by PCV13 vaccine)
        ▪ Nontypeable **Haemophilus influenzae** (increasingly common, often associated with **biofilm formation**)
        ▪ **Moraxella catarrhalis**
    ◦ **Viral**
        ▪ Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), Influenza virus, Rhinovirus
        ▪ Viral URIs often precede bacterial superinfection by causing Eustachian tube inflammation and dysfunction
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The core mechanism is persistent **Eustachian tube dysfunction (ETD)**, often exacerbated by other factors
    ◦ **Key Contributing Factors:**
        ▪ **Anatomy:** In young children, the Eustachian tube is shorter, more horizontal, and floppier, leading to inefficient drainage and pressure equalization
        ▪ **Inflammation:** A viral URI or allergic rhinitis causes inflammation and edema of the nasopharyngeal mucosa, including the Eustachian tube orifice
        ▪ **Obstruction & Negative Pressure:** The inflamed tube swells shut, air is absorbed, and negative pressure pulls fluid (**transudate**) into the middle ear space, creating an effusion
        ▪ **Bacterial Colonization:** Nasopharyngeal bacteria are aspirated into the sterile fluid, where they proliferate, leading to a purulent infection (AOM)
        ▪ **Biofilms:** In ROM, bacteria may form a persistent, antibiotic-resistant **biofilm** on the middle ear mucosa, serving as a nidus for repeated infections
        ▪ **Adenoidal Hypertrophy:** Enlarged adenoids can physically obstruct the Eustachian tube opening or act as a reservoir for pathogenic bacteria
sections.epidemiology:
• **Peak Incidence:** 6 to 18 months of age
• One of the most common reasons for pediatric healthcare visits and antibiotic prescriptions in the United States
• Approximately 10-20% of children will meet the criteria for ROM during early childhood
• Incidence dramatically decreases after age 5-7 as the Eustachian tube anatomy matures
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Characterized by a **pattern of repeated AOM episodes**
• Each individual episode presents as classic **AOM**
• The child often has a recent or concurrent URI
• The parent reports a history of multiple ear infections requiring antibiotics over the past several months
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis:** Based on meeting the specific frequency criteria and a physical exam confirming AOM at each visit
    ◦ **Frequency Criteria:** 3 episodes in 6 months, or 4 episodes in 12 months
• **Pneumatic Otoscopy:** Essential tool to confirm **middle ear effusion** by assessing tympanic membrane (TM) mobility
• **Tympanometry:** An objective measure of middle ear function
    ◦ **Type B Curve (flat):** Indicates **middle ear effusion**, confirming lack of TM mobility
    ◦ **Type C Curve (negative pressure peak):** Suggests **Eustachian tube dysfunction**
• **Audiometry (Hearing Test):** Recommended for all children with ROM or persistent middle ear effusion to evaluate for **conductive hearing loss**, which can impact speech and language development
• **Tympanocentesis:** Aspiration of middle ear fluid for culture
    ◦ Not routinely performed
    ◦ Reserved for neonates, immunocompromised patients, or failure of multiple courses of antibiotics
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is generally **excellent**
• Most children outgrow the tendency for ear infections by school age as their anatomy matures
• **Tympanostomy tubes** are highly effective at reducing the frequency and severity of AOM episodes while they are in place
    ◦ They typically fall out on their own in 6-18 months
• Long-term hearing and developmental outcomes are excellent with appropriate management

sections.overview:
• Otitis Media with Effusion (OME), also known as Serous Otitis Media, is characterized by the presence of non-purulent fluid (effusion) in the middle ear space without signs or symptoms of an acute infection.
    ◦ A common cause of **conductive hearing loss** in children.
    ◦ Often a sequela of Acute Otitis Media (AOM) or **Eustachian tube dysfunction**.
    ◦ Frequently called **"glue ear"** when the effusion is particularly thick and mucoid.
sections.etiology:
• The central mechanism is **Eustachian Tube Dysfunction (ETD)**.
    ◦ The Eustachian tube normally ventilates the middle ear, equalizing its pressure with the nasopharynx and allowing for fluid clearance.
• Pathophysiology:
    ◦ **Pressure Dysregulation**: When the Eustachian tube is blocked or fails to open properly, oxygen within the middle ear is absorbed by the surrounding mucosa. This creates **negative middle ear pressure**.
    ◦ **Transudation**: This negative pressure acts as a vacuum, pulling a sterile, serous transudate from the capillaries of the mucosal lining into the middle ear space.
    ◦ **Inflammation & Metaplasia**: Persistent ETD and inflammation can cause the middle ear mucosa to undergo goblet cell metaplasia, producing a thicker, mucoid fluid (**"glue ear"**).
• Common causes of ETD include:
    ◦ **Viral Upper Respiratory Infection (URI)**: Inflammation and edema of the nasopharyngeal mucosa surrounding the Eustachian tube orifice.
    ◦ **Adenoidal Hypertrophy**: Enlarged adenoids can physically obstruct the Eustachian tube opening.
    ◦ **Allergic Rhinitis**: Mucosal inflammation can lead to ETD.
    ◦ **Anatomic Factors**: In young children, the Eustachian tube is shorter, more horizontal, and floppier, making it more prone to dysfunction.
    ◦ **Following AOM**: Inflammation persists after the acute infection resolves, impairing Eustachian tube function and trapping sterile fluid.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Peak Incidence**: 6 months to 4 years of age.
• Extremely common; nearly all children experience at least one episode of OME by age 10.
• More common in males.
• Increased incidence during fall and winter months, paralleling the seasonality of URIs.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is often **subtle and insidious**.
• OME is frequently asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on a well-child exam or an exam for another complaint.
• When symptoms are present, they are related to the effusion and pressure changes, not acute infection.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Pneumatic Otoscopy**: The single most useful diagnostic tool in the primary care setting for assessing TM mobility.
• **Tympanometry**: Objective measure of TM compliance and middle ear pressure.
    ◦ **Classic Finding: Type B ("flat") tympanogram**.
        ▪ Indicates poor TM mobility due to middle ear fluid.
        ▪ The tracing shows a flat line with no peak compliance.
    ◦ **Type C tympanogram**:
        ▪ Indicates significant **negative middle ear pressure** (peak < -200 daPa).
        ▪ Often a precursor to or a sign of resolving OME.
• **Audiometry**: The gold standard for quantifying hearing loss.
    ◦ Indicated for OME lasting **3 months** or if there are concerns for speech/language delay.
    ◦ Reveals a mild to moderate **conductive hearing loss** (typically 20-40 dB).
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**. The vast majority of cases resolve spontaneously without intervention.
• ~50-60% of cases resolve within 3 months.
• ~75-90% of cases resolve within 6 months.
• Recurrence is common, especially in younger children.
• Hearing loss is reversible with resolution of the effusion or with tympanostomy tube placement.

sections.overview:
• Chronic Suppurative Otitis Media (CSOM) is a chronic inflammation of the middle ear and mastoid cavity, characterized by a **non-intact (perforated) tympanic membrane (TM)** and **persistent or recurrent purulent otorrhea** lasting more than 6 weeks.
• It is one of the most common causes of persistent **hearing loss**, especially in developing nations.
• There are two primary subtypes, which dictate management and prognosis:
    ◦ **Tubotympanic (Mucosal) CSOM**:
        ▪ Also known as the **"safe" type**.
        ▪ Involves a perforation in the **pars tensa** (central perforation).
        ▪ Disease is limited to the mucosa of the middle ear cleft.
        ▪ Associated with a lower risk of serious complications.
    ◦ **Atticoantral (Squamous) CSOM**:
        ▪ Also known as the **"unsafe" type**.
        ▪ Involves a perforation in the **pars flaccida (attic)** or a **marginal perforation** of the pars tensa.
        ▪ Frequently associated with **cholesteatoma**, a destructive sac of keratinizing squamous epithelium.
        ▪ High risk of bony erosion and serious intratemporal and intracranial complications.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**:
    ◦ CSOM is a polymicrobial infection, with pathogens that thrive in a chronically draining, aerobic/anaerobic environment.
    ◦ **Most Common Aerobes**: *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, *Staphylococcus aureus* (including MRSA).
    ◦ **Other Aerobes**: *Proteus* species, *Klebsiella pneumoniae*.
    ◦ **Anaerobes**: *Bacteroides*, *Peptostreptococcus*.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Prerequisite**: A persistent **TM perforation**, which usually arises from:
        ▪ An episode of **AOM** that caused TM rupture and failed to heal.
        ▪ Traumatic TM perforation.
        ▪ Long-standing pressure-equalizing (PE) tubes.
    ◦ **Colonization**: The non-intact TM allows bacteria from the external auditory canal (EAC) to enter and colonize the normally sterile middle ear space.
    ◦ **Inflammatory Cycle**: The presence of bacteria incites a chronic inflammatory response in the middle ear mucosa, leading to edema, granulation tissue, and polyp formation, producing the characteristic purulent discharge (**otorrhea**).
    ◦ **Cholesteatoma Formation (in Atticoantral type)**:
        ▪ A retraction pocket forms in the weaker pars flaccida or at the TM margin.
        ▪ Keratin debris builds up within this sac, forming a **cholesteatoma**.
        ▪ This mass expands and produces proteolytic enzymes that erode surrounding bone (ossicles, mastoid, facial nerve canal, inner ear, and tegmen tympani).
sections.epidemiology:
• More prevalent in developing countries due to factors like poor nutrition, overcrowding, and limited access to healthcare.
• A leading cause of preventable **hearing impairment** worldwide.
• Can occur at any age but often begins in childhood, following recurrent **AOM**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a patient with a history of recurrent ear infections who now presents with **painless, persistent, or intermittent foul-smelling ear drainage** and **gradual hearing loss** in the affected ear.
• The patient is typically **afebrile** and does not appear acutely ill unless a complication is present.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Diagnosis is primarily made based on the characteristic history (chronic **otorrhea** >6 weeks) and physical exam finding of a **TM perforation**.
• **Audiometry**:
    ◦ Essential for all patients to quantify the type and severity of hearing loss and to establish a baseline.
    ◦ Typically reveals a **conductive hearing loss**.
    ◦ A mixed or sensorineural component suggests inner ear involvement.
• **Culture of Discharge**: Useful for guiding antibiotic therapy in cases refractory to initial treatment.
• **CT Scan (Temporal Bone, without contrast)**:
    ◦ Not needed for routine diagnosis.
    ◦ **Indicated if**:
        ▪ **Cholesteatoma is suspected**.
        ▪ Intratemporal or intracranial complications are suspected (e.g., new onset of pain, vertigo, facial nerve palsy, headache).
        ▪ Pre-operative planning for surgical intervention.
    ◦ CT findings can show **bony erosion**, ossicular chain destruction, extent of mastoid disease, and soft tissue masses (**cholesteatoma**).
sections.prognosis:
• **Tubotympanic CSOM**: Good prognosis for eradicating infection with medical and surgical (**tympanoplasty**) therapy. Hearing may or may not fully recover.
• **Atticoantral CSOM (with cholesteatoma)**:
    ◦ Requires surgery to prevent life-threatening complications.
    ◦ The primary goal of surgery is to create a "safe" and dry ear.
    ◦ Hearing preservation/restoration is a secondary goal.
    ◦ Recurrence of **cholesteatoma** is possible.

sections.overview:
• A **Tympanic Membrane (TM) Perforation** is a rupture, hole, or tear in the eardrum, the thin membrane that separates the external auditory canal from the middle ear space
	◦ This breach can lead to **hearing loss**, pain, and an increased susceptibility to middle ear infections
sections.etiology:
• The TM can be perforated through several mechanisms, broadly categorized as traumatic, infectious, or iatrogenic
• **Infection (Most Common Overall)**
	◦ **Acute Otitis Media (AOM)**: Increased pressure from purulent effusion in the middle ear space builds until it causes the TM to rupture. This provides a channel for drainage, often resulting in a sudden decrease in pain
• **Trauma**
	◦ **Direct Penetration**: Injury from objects inserted into the ear canal (e.g., cotton swabs, bobby pins, pencils)
	◦ **Barotrauma**: Caused by a sudden, significant pressure differential between the middle ear and the external environment
		▪ **Positive Pressure**: Slap to the ear, explosion/blast injury, forceful Valsalva
		▪ **Negative Pressure**: Rapid altitude changes (flying, scuba diving)
	◦ **Temporal Bone Fracture**: **Basilar skull fractures** can disrupt the TM and ossicular chain
		▪ Look for associated signs like **hemotympanum**, **Battle's sign**, or **CSF otorrhea**
• **Iatrogenic**
	◦ Perforation occurring during medical procedures such as foreign body removal, myringotomy (without tube placement), or ear canal irrigation
sections.epidemiology:
• TM perforation is a common otologic condition seen in all age groups
• In children, **AOM** is the most frequent cause
• In adults, **trauma** is a more common cause than infection
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The patient's history is crucial and often points directly to the diagnosis
• **Infectious Etiology**
	◦ A patient (often a child) presents with a history of preceding upper respiratory infection symptoms, progressing to severe **otalgia**, fever, and irritability
	◦ This is followed by a sudden episode of **otorrhea** (purulent or bloody drainage) and an **immediate relief** of the severe ear pain
• **Traumatic Etiology**
	◦ A patient reports an acute event (e.g., a slap to the ear, a loud blast, or inserting an object) followed immediately by severe **pain**, **hearing loss**, and sometimes **tinnitus** or **vertigo**
sections.diagnostics:
