• **Profuse, brisk, arterial bleeding**.
• Bleeding is often seen from **both nares** as blood pools in the nasopharynx and overflows to the contralateral side.
• The hallmark is the sensation of **blood dripping down the posterior pharynx** or active bleeding seen in the oropharynx on examination.
• Patient may present with nausea, **hematemesis** (vomiting of swallowed blood), **hemoptysis**, or **melena**.
• Signs of **hemodynamic instability** (tachycardia, hypotension, pallor) may be present with significant blood loss.
sections.diagnostics:
• Posterior epistaxis is primarily a **clinical diagnosis** based on the presentation and failure to identify an anterior source.
• **Labs**
    ◦ **CBC**: To establish baseline hemoglobin/hematocrit and assess for anemia or thrombocytopenia.
    ◦ **PT/INR, aPTT**: To evaluate for coagulopathy, especially in patients on anticoagulants or with liver disease.
    ◦ **Type and Screen/Crossmatch**: Crucial for patients with severe hemorrhage who may require transfusion.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ Generally not required for the initial diagnosis.
    ◦ **CT Scan**: Considered if there is a history of trauma (to rule out facial fractures) or if a neoplasm is suspected.
    ◦ **Angiography**: Can be both diagnostic and therapeutic (for embolization) in refractory cases.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is generally **excellent** if the bleeding is identified and managed promptly and aggressively.
• Morbidity and mortality are typically related to the complications of treatment (e.g., TSS, airway compromise) or severe blood loss in elderly patients with significant comorbidities.

sections.overview:
• A nasal foreign body (NFB) is any object lodged in the nasal cavity that is not naturally occurring.
• It is a common pediatric complaint, typically seen in **toddlers and preschool-aged children** who insert objects into their own nose.
• While often benign, certain objects (like **button batteries** and **magnets**) constitute a medical emergency.
• The classic presentation of a delayed diagnosis is **unilateral, foul-smelling, purulent nasal discharge**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Inorganic**: Beads, pebbles, small toy parts (e.g., Lego), crayons, paper wads.
        ▪ Generally better tolerated as they are inert.
    ◦ **Organic**: Food particles (beans, peas, nuts, seeds), sponges.
        ▪ These tend to swell with moisture and decompose, causing a more significant inflammatory reaction and odor.
    ◦ **Dangerous (Urgent Removal)**
        ▪ **Button Batteries**: Cause severe damage via three mechanisms:
            ▪ Direct **pressure necrosis**
            ▪ Leakage of alkaline contents causing **liquefaction necrosis**
            ▪ Generation of a low-voltage electrical current
            ▪ Can cause **septal perforation** in hours.
        ▪ **Paired Magnets**: One magnet in each nostril can cause pressure necrosis of the nasal septum, leading to perforation.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Obstruction**: The object physically blocks the normal drainage of mucus from the sinuses and nasal cavity.
    ◦ **Inflammation**: The presence of the foreign object triggers a local inflammatory response, leading to mucosal edema, rhinorrhea, and granulation tissue formation.
    ◦ **Infection**: Stagnation of secretions proximal to the obstruction creates a breeding ground for bacteria, leading to **purulent, malodorous discharge** and secondary sinusitis.
    ◦ **Pressure Necrosis**: The object can exert direct pressure on the nasal mucosa or septum, leading to tissue death and potential perforation.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Peak Age**: 2-5 years old.
    ◦ This corresponds to a developmental stage of curiosity and body exploration.
• **Prevalence**: Accounts for a significant number of pediatric emergency department visits for ENT complaints.
• **Gender**: Slightly more common in males.
• **Location**: Most commonly found in the anterior nasal cavity, just inferior to the inferior turbinate, or in the narrow space between the septum and middle turbinate.
    ◦ The right naris is slightly more common in right-handed children.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation can be acute (witnessed insertion) or delayed (unwitnessed).
    ◦ **Acute/Witnessed**: The child is brought in immediately after the event.
        ▪ The object may be easily visible, and symptoms are minimal (e.g., mild discomfort, sneezing).
    ◦ **Delayed/Unwitnessed**: This is the classic board presentation.
        ▪ The child presents days or weeks later with persistent **unilateral nasal symptoms**.
        ▪ The history of insertion is often unknown or denied.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primarily a clinical diagnosis** made by history and direct visualization on physical exam.
• **Imaging is generally not required** unless:
    ◦ The object is not visible, but suspicion remains high.
    ◦ A **button battery** or **magnet** is suspected.
    ◦ There is concern for complications like sinus involvement or aspiration.
• **Radiography (Plain X-rays)**
    ◦ Useful for **radiopaque objects** (metal, batteries, magnets, glass).
    ◦ **Button Battery on X-ray**: Shows a characteristic **"double-halo" or "step-off" sign** on AP and lateral views, respectively, which helps distinguish it from a coin.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** with timely and successful removal.
• The vast majority of cases resolve without long-term sequelae.
• Prognosis is worse with significant delays in diagnosis, dangerous objects (especially **button batteries**), or complications such as **aspiration**.

sections.overview:
• Viral pharyngitis is an **inflammation of the pharynx**, including the tonsils and posterior oropharynx, caused by a viral infection.
• It is the **most common cause of sore throat (odynophagia)** in all age groups, accounting for the vast majority of pharyngitis cases.
• The primary clinical challenge is **differentiating it from Group A Streptococcal (GAS) pharyngitis** to avoid unnecessary antibiotic use.
• The illness is typically **self-limiting** and managed with supportive care.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology (Most Common Pathogens):**
    ◦ **Rhinovirus:** The most frequent cause overall.
    ◦ **Adenovirus:** Classic cause of **"pharyngoconjunctival fever."**
    ◦ **Influenza A & B:** Associated with systemic symptoms like myalgias and fever.
    ◦ **Parainfluenza Virus:** Common cause of croup but can also cause pharyngitis.
    ◦ **Coronavirus:** (Non-COVID-19 strains and SARS-CoV-2)
    ◦ **Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV):** Causes **infectious mononucleosis**.
    ◦ **Coxsackie A Virus:** Causes **Herpangina** and **Hand-Foot-and-Mouth Disease**.
    ◦ **Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV-1, HSV-2):** Causes herpetic pharyngitis/gingivostomatitis.
    ◦ **Cytomegalovirus (CMV):** Can cause a mononucleosis-like syndrome.
• **Pathophysiology:**
    ◦ The virus directly invades the epithelial cells of the nasopharynx and oropharynx.
    ◦ Viral replication leads to cell lysis and triggers a local inflammatory response.
    ◦ This response involves the release of inflammatory mediators (cytokines, prostaglandins), leading to vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, and stimulation of pain receptors.
    ◦ This results in the characteristic clinical findings of erythema, edema, and **odynophagia** (painful swallowing).
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence:** Extremely common; the leading cause of pharyngitis, accounting for **85-95% of cases in adults** and **~70% in children**.
• **Age:** Affects all age groups, but peak incidence is in children and adolescents.
• **Seasonality:** Predominantly occurs in the **fall, winter, and early spring**, mirroring the seasonality of common respiratory viruses.
• **Transmission:** Spread via **respiratory droplets** from coughing/sneezing, direct contact with an infected person, or contact with contaminated fomites.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is typically one of a **gradual onset of sore throat** in the context of other upper respiratory infection (URI) symptoms.
• A patient with viral pharyngitis will often complain of a **"cold."**
• The presence of a constellation of URI symptoms (the **"coryzal complex"**) is the strongest indicator of a viral etiology.
sections.diagnostics:
• Viral pharyngitis is primarily a **clinical diagnosis**.
• Testing is performed to exclude other causes, mainly GAS pharyngitis.
• **Centor Criteria (or Modified/McIsaac Criteria):** Used to assess the probability of GAS pharyngitis and guide testing.
    ◦ **C** - Absence of **C**ough (+1)
    ◦ **E** - Tonsillar **E**xudates (+1)
    ◦ **N** - Tender anterior cervical **N**odes (+1)
    ◦ **T** - **T**emperature > 100.4F (38C) (+1)
    ◦ **OR** - Age modifier: 3-14 years (+1), 15-44 years (0), >45 years (-1)
    ◦ **Interpretation & Action:**
        ▪ **Score 0-1:** Low probability of Strep. No testing or antibiotics recommended.
        ▪ **Score 2-3:** Intermediate probability. Perform **Rapid Antigen Detection Test (RADT)**. If negative in children/adolescents, follow with a **throat culture**.
        ▪ **Score ≥4:** High probability. Can treat empirically for GAS or perform RADT/culture to confirm.
• **Monospot Test (Heterophile Antibody Test):**
    ◦ Order if **infectious mononucleosis (EBV)** is suspected based on **posterior LAD**, **splenomegaly**, and **profound fatigue**.
    ◦ Note: Low sensitivity in the first week of illness.
• **CBC with Differential:**
    ◦ May show **lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes** in EBV.
• **Influenza Swab:**
    ◦ If influenza is suspected during peak season and the patient is within 48 hours of symptom onset.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is **excellent**.
• Most cases are **self-limiting** and resolve completely without sequelae within one week.
• Symptoms related to infectious mononucleosis (especially **fatigue**) can linger for several weeks to months.

sections.overview:
• **Group A Streptococcal (GAS) Pharyngitis**, commonly known as "**strep throat**," is an acute infection of the oropharynx and tonsils caused by ***Streptococcus pyogenes***.
    ◦ It is a common cause of pharyngitis, especially in **children**.
    ◦ Accurate diagnosis and treatment are crucial not only to alleviate symptoms and prevent local spread but, most importantly, to prevent the serious non-suppurative sequelae of **acute rheumatic fever (ARF)** and subsequent **rheumatic heart disease**.
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**: ***Streptococcus pyogenes***, a **Group A β-hemolytic Streptococcus**.
    ◦ **Microbiology**: **Gram-positive cocci** that grow in chains.
    ◦ **Culture**: Exhibits **β-hemolysis** (complete hemolysis) on sheep blood agar, creating a clear zone around colonies.
• **Transmission**: Spread via **respiratory droplets** from an infected individual or, less commonly, through direct contact with contaminated surfaces.
• **Incubation Period**: 2 to 5 days.
• **Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Adherence**: The bacteria adhere to pharyngeal epithelial cells using virulence factors like **M protein** and **lipoteichoic acid**.
    ◦ **Invasion & Inflammation**: GAS produces numerous exotoxins and enzymes that damage host tissue and evade the immune system, leading to the classic inflammatory response (sore throat, fever, erythema, edema).
• **Key Virulence Factors**:
    ◦ **M Protein**: The major virulence factor; it is **antiphagocytic** and inhibits complement activation. The host develops type-specific antibodies to the M protein, which provides immunity but can also lead to **molecular mimicry** (the basis for rheumatic fever).
    ◦ **Streptolysins O and S**: Exotoxins that lyse red and white blood cells (responsible for β-hemolysis).
    ◦ **Pyrogenic Exotoxins (SpeA, B, C)**: **Superantigens** responsible for the rash of **scarlet fever** and the systemic effects of **streptococcal toxic shock syndrome**.
    ◦ **Hyaluronidase ("spreading factor")**: Breaks down connective tissue, facilitating the spread of infection.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Peak Incidence**: Children aged **5 to 15 years**.
• **Prevalence**: Accounts for **15-30% of pharyngitis cases in children** and 5-10% in adults. The vast majority of adult pharyngitis is viral.
• **Seasonality**: Most common in **late winter and early spring**.
• **Setting**: Outbreaks are common in settings of close contact, such as schools, military barracks, and households.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • The classic presentation is a school-aged child who presents in the winter with a **sudden onset** of **high fever**, **severe sore throat**, **headache**, and **abdominal pain**, but notably **lacks cough** or other viral symptoms.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Scoring (Centor Criteria)**: Used to estimate the probability of GAS and guide testing. One point for each:
    ◦ **C** - **Cough** (Absence of)
    ◦ **E** - **Exudates** (Tonsillar)
    ◦ **N** - **Nodes** (Tender Anterior Cervical)
    ◦ **T** - **Temperature** > 38°C (100.4°F)
    ◦ **McIsaac Modification**:
        ▪ Age 3-14: +1 point
        ▪ Age 15-44: 0 points
        ▪ Age 45+: -1 point
    ◦ **Interpretation of Score**:
        ▪ **0-1**: Low risk; no testing or antibiotics recommended.
        ▪ **2-3**: Intermediate risk; perform **Rapid Antigen Detection Test (RADT)**.
        ▪ **≥4**: High risk; can perform RADT or consider empiric antibiotic treatment.
• **Laboratory Tests**:
    ◦ **Rapid Antigen Detection Test (RADT)**:
        ▪ **Method**: Throat swab immunoassay that detects GAS carbohydrate antigens.
        ▪ **Pros**: Fast (5-10 minutes).
        ▪ **Cons**: High specificity (~95%) but moderate sensitivity (70-90%).
        ▪ **Clinical Use**: A positive result confirms GAS. In **children and adolescents**, a **negative RADT must be confirmed with a throat culture** due to the risk of missing a case and subsequent **rheumatic fever**. In adults, a negative RADT is generally sufficient.
    ◦ **Throat Culture (Gold Standard)**:
        ▪ **Method**: Throat swab cultured on sheep blood agar.
        ▪ **Pros**: Highest sensitivity and specificity (>95%).
        ▪ **Cons**: Takes 24-48 hours for results.
    ◦ **Serology (ASO Titer)**:
        ▪ **Anti-streptolysin O (ASO)** titers are **NOT used to diagnose acute pharyngitis**.
        ▪ They are used retrospectively to confirm a recent GAS infection when investigating potential complications like **rheumatic fever** or **glomerulonephritis**.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**. With antibiotic therapy, symptoms typically improve within 24-48 hours and resolve in 3-5 days.
• Untreated infections resolve spontaneously but carry a significant risk for the development of complications, particularly **ARF**.

sections.overview:
• **Chronic tonsillitis** is a persistent inflammatory condition of the palatine tonsils
• Unlike acute tonsillitis, it is characterized by **long-standing or recurrent symptoms**, including:
    ◦ Persistent **sore throat**
    ◦ **Halitosis**
    ◦ Presence of **tonsilloliths**
• The underlying pathology involves a **polymicrobial biofilm** within the tonsillar crypts
    ◦ This leads to a low-grade, ongoing infection and inflammation that is often resistant to short courses of antibiotics
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ Primarily **polymicrobial**, caused by a community of bacteria, not a single pathogen
• **Common Aerobes**
    ◦ *Streptococcus pyogenes* (**Group A Strep**)
    ◦ *Haemophilus influenzae*
    ◦ *Staphylococcus aureus*
    ◦ *Moraxella catarrhalis*
• **Common Anaerobes**
    ◦ *Bacteroides*
    ◦ *Fusobacterium*
    ◦ *Prevotella*
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Biofilm Formation**
        ▪ The core pathophysiologic feature
        ▪ Bacteria colonize the deep, avascular tonsillar crypts and form a structured **biofilm**
        ▪ This biofilm shields bacteria from host immune defenses and antibiotics, leading to a persistent, low-grade infection
    ◦ **Tonsillar Crypts**
        ▪ The unique anatomy with deep, branching crypts provides an ideal **anaerobic environment** for bacterial sequestration and biofilm development
    ◦ **Chronic Inflammation**
        ▪ The persistent biofilm triggers a continuous, low-grade host immune response
        ▪ This results in chronic inflammation, tonsillar hypertrophy, fibrosis, and the production of caseous, malodorous debris (**tonsilloliths**)
sections.epidemiology:
• Most common in **children, adolescents, and young adults**
• Represents one of the most frequent reasons for outpatient ENT consultation
• A primary indication for **tonsillectomy** in adults and children
• Prevalence has decreased in some regions due to more stringent criteria for tonsillectomy, but it remains a common clinical problem
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The typical patient is a child or young adult with a history of **persistent or recurrent throat discomfort** for **at least 3 months**
• Patients often report feeling "unwell" or having a **"constant scratchy throat"** even between acute episodes
• May have a history of **multiple antibiotic courses** for "strep throat" with only temporary relief
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primarily a clinical diagnosis** based on a characteristic history and physical exam findings
• **Throat Culture**
    ◦ Often performed to rule out acute **Group A Strep (GAS) pharyngitis** during an exacerbation
    ◦ A positive culture does not differentiate between active infection and chronic carriage and fails to identify the polymicrobial/anaerobic nature of the condition
• **Monospot Test (Heterophile Antibody Test)**
    ◦ Useful to rule out **infectious mononucleosis** (caused by EBV), especially in adolescents and young adults with tonsillitis, fatigue, and lymphadenopathy
• **Labs (CBC)**
    ◦ Generally not indicated or helpful
    ◦ May show a **mild leukocytosis** during acute flares
sections.prognosis:
• **Without surgery**
    ◦ Symptoms are **likely to persist or recur**, although they may wax and wane in severity
• **With tonsillectomy**
    ◦ Prognosis is **excellent**
    ◦ The vast majority of patients experience **complete resolution of their symptoms** (sore throat, halitosis, tonsilloliths)

sections.overview:
• A **peritonsillar abscess (PTA)**, also known as **quinsy**, is a localized collection of pus in the **peritonsillar space**, which is a potential space between the fibrous capsule of the palatine tonsil and the superior constrictor pharyngeal muscle.
• It is the most common **deep neck infection** and typically arises as a complication of **acute tonsillitis**.
• A PTA is considered a medical emergency due to its potential for rapid **airway compromise**.
• The classic presentation involves:
    ◦ Severe **unilateral sore throat**
    ◦ **Fever**
    ◦ Muffled **"hot potato" voice**
    ◦ **Trismus**
    ◦ **Drooling**
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ PTA is typically a **polymicrobial infection**, involving a mix of aerobic and anaerobic bacteria.
    ◦ **Common Aerobes**:
        ▪ ***Streptococcus pyogenes*** (Group A Strep, GAS) is the most classically cited pathogen.
        ▪ Others include ***Staphylococcus aureus*** (including MRSA) and ***Haemophilus influenzae***.
    ◦ **Common Anaerobes**:
        ▪ ***Fusobacterium necrophorum***
        ▪ ***Peptostreptococcus*** species
        ▪ ***Prevotella*** species
        ▪ ***Bacteroides*** species
        ▪ Anaerobes are often the predominant organisms.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Origin**: The infection usually begins as **acute exudative tonsillitis**.
    ◦ **Spread**: The infection spreads from the tonsillar crypts through the tonsillar capsule into the surrounding peritonsillar space.
    ◦ **Progression**:
        ▪ The initial stage is **peritonsillar cellulitis** (phlegmon), an inflammatory reaction without a drainable pocket of pus.
        ▪ As the infection progresses, tissue necrosis and liquefaction occur, leading to the formation of a mature abscess.
    ◦ **Alternative Theory**: Obstruction of the **Weber's glands** (minor salivary glands in the peritonsillar space) may also lead to inflammation and subsequent abscess formation.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Most Common Age Group**: Adolescents and young adults (20-40 years old).
• It is the most frequent **deep neck infection** in adults.
• Incidence has decreased since the widespread use of antibiotics for streptococcal pharyngitis, but it remains a common ENT emergency.
• Slight male predominance.
• Often occurs during the late fall and early spring, mirroring the seasonality of pharyngitis.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic patient is an adolescent or young adult with a history of pharyngitis that initially improved with antibiotics (or was untreated) and now presents with a sudden worsening of a severe, **unilateral throat pain**.
• They appear ill, are often febrile, and may be dehydrated due to **odynophagia**.
• The key features are a triad of **trismus**, muffled **"hot potato" voice**, and **uvular deviation**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: PTA is primarily a clinical diagnosis based on the characteristic history and physical exam findings.
• **Imaging** (used when diagnosis is uncertain or for complications):
    ◦ **CT scan with IV contrast of the neck** is the gold standard imaging modality.
        ▪ **Indications for CT**:
            ◦ **Trismus** is so severe that it prevents adequate oral examination.
            ◦ Suspicion of spread to **deeper neck spaces** (e.g., parapharyngeal or retropharyngeal space).
            ◦ Failure to improve after initial drainage attempt.
            ◦ Atypical presentation (e.g., minimal oropharyngeal findings but significant neck swelling).
        ▪ **CT Findings**: A well-defined, rim-enhancing, hypodense fluid collection in the peritonsillar space.
    ◦ **Intraoral Ultrasound**:
        ▪ Can be used at the bedside to differentiate cellulitis from a drainable abscess and to guide needle aspiration.
        ▪ It is highly sensitive and specific.
• **Labs** (Supportive, not diagnostic):
    ◦ **CBC**: **Leukocytosis** with a left shift.
    ◦ **CMP/BMP**: Assess for dehydration (elevated BUN/Cr).
    ◦ **CRP/ESR**: Elevated inflammatory markers.
    ◦ **Monospot test** if suspicious for infectious mononucleosis.
• **Aspiration**: Aspiration of pus is both **diagnostic and therapeutic**.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is **excellent** with timely diagnosis and appropriate treatment (drainage and antibiotics).
• Most patients recover fully without long-term sequelae.
• Mortality is rare and is almost always associated with complications like **airway obstruction** or spread of infection to the **mediastinum**.

sections.overview:
• A **retropharyngeal abscess (RPA)** is a collection of pus in the potential space between the posterior pharyngeal wall and the prevertebral fascia
• It is a deep neck space infection that is considered a **medical emergency** due to its potential for rapid **airway compromise** and spread to contiguous structures
• It most commonly affects young children but can also occur in adults
sections.etiology:
• The pathophysiology differs significantly between children and adults
• **Pediatric Pathophysiology (Most Common):**
    ◦ Results from suppuration (pus formation) of the **retropharyngeal lymph nodes**, also known as the **Nodes of Rouviere**
    ◦ These nodes drain the nasopharynx, adenoids, paranasal sinuses, and middle ear
    ◦ A primary infection (e.g., URI, pharyngitis, otitis media, sinusitis) leads to suppurative adenitis, which progresses to cellulitis and then liquefaction, forming an abscess
    ◦ These lymph nodes typically **atrophy by age 5-6**, which is why RPA is primarily a disease of young children
• **Adult Pathophysiology:**
    ◦ Usually occurs from **direct extension** of a nearby infection or **penetrating trauma**
    ◦ Causes include:
        ▪ Pharyngeal trauma (e.g., fish bone, instrumentation like endoscopy or intubation)
        ▪ Extension from a contiguous infection (e.g., dental abscess, tonsillitis, parotitis)
        ▪ Vertebral body osteomyelitis
• **Microbiology:**
    ◦ Almost always **polymicrobial**
    ◦ Common pathogens include:
        ▪ **Group A Streptococcus (*S. pyogenes*)**
        ▪ ***Staphylococcus aureus*** (including MRSA)
        ▪ **Anaerobes** (*Bacteroides*, *Peptostreptococcus*, *Fusobacterium*)
        ▪ Respiratory flora (*H. influenzae*, *Moraxella catarrhalis*)
sections.epidemiology:
• **Peak Incidence:** Primarily affects children between **2 and 4 years of age**
• Over 95% of cases occur in children under 6 years old
• Slight male predominance
• Less common in adults but often associated with higher morbidity due to underlying conditions or trauma
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a young, **febrile**, and **irritable** child who appears **toxic** and **refuses to eat** or **move their neck**
• The onset is typically acute and progressive
sections.diagnostics:
• **Labs:**
    ◦ **CBC:** **Leukocytosis** with a **left shift** (neutrophilia)
    ◦ **Inflammatory Markers:** Elevated **ESR** and **CRP**
    ◦ **Blood Cultures:** To rule out bacteremia and identify the pathogen, though often negative
• **Imaging:**
    ◦ **1. Lateral Neck Soft Tissue X-ray:**
        ▪ Often the initial imaging study, especially in a stable patient
        ▪ **Key Finding:** **Widening of the prevertebral space**
        ▪ Normal space at **C2 is <7 mm**; at **C6 is <14 mm** in children (<22 mm in adults)
        ▪ A helpful rule of thumb: the prevertebral space should be **less than half the width of the adjacent vertebral body**
        ▪ Other findings: loss of normal **cervical lordosis** (straightening of the spine), presence of **air-fluid levels**
    ◦ **2. CT Scan with IV Contrast of the Neck:**
        ▪ **GOLD STANDARD** and definitive diagnostic test
        ▪ **Confirms the diagnosis** and differentiates between cellulitis (phlegmon) and a drainable abscess
        ▪ Shows a well-defined, **rim-enhancing fluid collection** with central low density
        ▪ Crucial for surgical planning by defining the abscess size and extent
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent if diagnosed and treated promptly
• Mortality is low (<1-3%) with appropriate airway management, antibiotics, and surgical drainage
• Prognosis worsens significantly with the development of complications, especially mediastinitis

sections.overview:
• Infectious Mononucleosis (IM) is a clinical syndrome most commonly caused by the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), characterized by the classic triad of **fever, pharyngitis, and lymphadenopathy**.
• The oropharyngeal manifestations are often the most prominent and are the patient's chief complaint.
• While typically a self-limiting illness in immunocompetent individuals, its presentation can be dramatic and it carries a risk of significant complications.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiologic Agent:**
    ◦ Primarily **Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV)**, a member of the Herpesviridae family (Human Herpesvirus 4, HHV-4).
    ◦ Less common causes of a "mono-like" syndrome include Cytomegalovirus (CMV), Human Herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6), acute HIV infection, and Toxoplasma gondii.
• **Transmission:**
    ◦ Transmitted via oropharyngeal secretions (saliva), earning it the name **"the kissing disease."**
• **Pathophysiology:**
    ◦ **Initial Infection:** EBV initially infects the epithelial cells of the oropharynx and salivary glands.
    ◦ **B-Cell Invasion:** The virus then spreads to underlying lymphoid tissue, where it infects **B-lymphocytes** using the CD21 receptor.
    ◦ **Immune Response:** The host's immune system mounts a vigorous response. **Cytotoxic T-lymphocytes (CD8+)** proliferate to control the infected B-cells.
    ◦ **Clinical Manifestations:** This T-cell proliferation is responsible for the clinical signs:
        ▪ **Lymphadenopathy & Splenomegaly:** Proliferation in lymph nodes and spleen.
        ▪ **Atypical Lymphocytes:** These reactive T-cells are the characteristic finding on a peripheral blood smear.
        ▪ **Pharyngitis:** Caused by intense inflammation and lymphoid hyperplasia in Waldeyer's ring (tonsils and adenoids).
    ◦ **Latency:** Like other herpesviruses, EBV establishes a lifelong latent infection within memory B-cells.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:**
    ◦ EBV is ubiquitous; >90% of adults worldwide are seropositive.
• **Age:**
    ◦ Infection in early childhood is often asymptomatic or presents as a mild, nonspecific illness.
    ◦ The classic IM syndrome occurs most frequently when primary infection is delayed until **adolescence and young adulthood (peak age 15-24)**.
• **Setting:**
    ◦ Common in settings with close personal contact, such as high schools, colleges, and military barracks.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient, typically an adolescent or young adult, presents with a 1-2 week history of gradual onset symptoms.
    ◦ A prodrome of malaise, fatigue, and headache often precedes the more specific symptoms.
• The chief complaint is almost always a **severe sore throat** and fever.
• The fatigue is often described as profound and disproportionate to other symptoms.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Heterophile Antibody Test (Monospot):**
    ◦ **Description:** Rapid screening test that detects IgM antibodies that agglutinate non-human erythrocytes (e.g., sheep or horse).
    ◦ **Utility:** Good initial test, but has limitations.
    ◦ **False Negatives:**
        ▪ Sensitivity is low in the first week of illness (~75%).
        ▪ Can remain negative in up to 10% of adults and 50% of young children.
        ▪ If suspicion is high with a negative Monospot, retest in 7-10 days or order specific serology.
• **Complete Blood Count (CBC) with Differential:**
    ◦ **Hallmark Finding:** **Lymphocytosis** (>50% of total WBCs) with **>10% atypical lymphocytes**.
    ◦ Atypical lymphocytes are larger than normal lymphocytes with abundant cytoplasm and an indented nucleus; they are the activated CD8+ T-cells.
    ◦ Mild thrombocytopenia or neutropenia may be present.
• **EBV-Specific Serology (Gold Standard):**
    ◦ Used when Monospot is negative but clinical suspicion is high, or in atypical cases.
    ◦ **VCA-IgM (Viral Capsid Antigen IgM):** Indicates **acute infection**. Appears early and disappears after 3-6 months.
    ◦ **VCA-IgG (Viral Capsid Antigen IgG):** Indicates **current or past infection**. Appears during acute illness and persists for life.
    ◦ **EBNA-IgG (EBV Nuclear Antigen IgG):** Indicates **past infection**. Appears 6-12 weeks after symptom onset and persists for life. **Its absence in the presence of VCA-IgM confirms acute primary infection.**
• **Liver Function Tests (LFTs):**
    ◦ Mild to moderate elevation of transaminases (AST, ALT) is seen in >80% of cases.
• **Throat Swab (Rapid Strep & Culture):**
    ◦ Essential to rule out concomitant or primary Group A Streptococcal (GAS) pharyngitis.
    ◦ Co-infection occurs in up to 30% of patients.
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent in immunocompetent individuals.
• The acute illness is self-limiting and resolves in 2-4 weeks.
• Fatigue is the most common lingering symptom and can last for 6 months or longer in some individuals.

sections.overview:
• Self-limited **inflammation of the larynx** (voice box) and **vocal cords**, lasting **less than 3 weeks**.
    ◦ The hallmark symptom is **dysphonia (hoarseness)**.
    ◦ It is most commonly caused by a **viral upper respiratory infection (URI)** but can also result from **vocal strain** or exposure to **irritants**.
• The condition is typically **benign** and resolves with **supportive care**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Viral (Most Common >90%)**
        ▪ **Rhinovirus**
        ▪ **Influenza A and B**
        ▪ **Parainfluenza virus**
        ▪ **Adenovirus**
        ▪ **Coronavirus**
        ▪ **Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV)**
    ◦ **Bacterial (Less Common)**: Often a secondary infection or co-infection.
        ▪ ***Moraxella catarrhalis***
        ▪ ***Haemophilus influenzae***
        ▪ ***Streptococcus pneumoniae***
    ◦ **Non-infectious**
        ▪ **Vocal Strain**: Excessive use of voice (e.g., yelling, singing, public speaking).
        ▪ **Irritants**: Inhaled substances like tobacco smoke, pollutants, or chemicals.
        ▪ **Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)**: Reflux of gastric acid can cause chemical irritation of the larynx.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ An infectious agent, irritant, or trauma causes **inflammation of the laryngeal mucosa**.
    ◦ This leads to **edema** and **erythema** of the **vocal cords** (vocal folds).
    ◦ The swelling disrupts the normal, smooth vibration of the vocal cords during phonation.
    ◦ The altered vibration results in the characteristic hoarse, raspy, or breathy voice (**dysphonia**) or complete voice loss (**aphonia**).
sections.epidemiology:
• Extremely **common**, affects individuals of all ages.
• Incidence **peaks in the fall and winter months**, corresponding with the prevalence of viral URIs.
• No significant gender or racial predilection.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The typical patient is an adult who presents with a **1-3 day history of hoarseness**.
    ◦ Hoarseness was preceded by or is concurrent with symptoms of a **common cold** (e.g., coryza, malaise, mild sore throat).
• The **primary complaint is the change in voice quality**.
• The patient generally **appears well** and is in **no respiratory distress**.
sections.diagnostics:
• Primarily a **clinical diagnosis** based on the characteristic history and physical exam findings in the context of a URI.
• **No laboratory or imaging studies are necessary** for typical, uncomplicated acute laryngitis.
• Referral for **Laryngoscopy (by ENT)** is indicated if:
    ◦ Hoarseness persists for **> 3 weeks**.
    ◦ Suspicion of a more serious pathology (e.g., malignancy in a smoker).
    ◦ Presence of **"red flag" symptoms**:
        ▪ **Stridor**
        ▪ **Respiratory distress**
        ▪ **Hemoptysis**
        ▪ **Severe dysphagia**
    ◦ The patient is a **professional voice user** and requires a definitive diagnosis.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent**.
• Most cases **resolve spontaneously within 7-10 days**.
• The voice may take up to **3 weeks** to return completely to its baseline quality.

sections.overview:
• Laryngeal inflammation lasting **longer than 3 weeks**
    ◦ A common cause of persistent hoarseness resulting from prolonged exposure to irritating stimuli
    ◦ Can lead to inflammatory changes and, in some cases, premalignant or malignant transformation of the laryngeal mucosa
sections.etiology:
• Pathophysiology involves chronic irritation leading to mucosal inflammation, edema, epithelial hyperplasia, and potentially dysplasia
    ◦ **Laryngopharyngeal Reflux (LPR)**: The most common non-smoking cause; retrograde flow of gastric contents irritates the posterior laryngeal mucosa
    ◦ **Inhaled Irritants**
        ▪ **Tobacco Smoke**: The single most common cause, leading to inflammation, ciliary dysfunction, and squamous metaplasia
        ▪ **Environmental/Occupational Exposures**: Dust, chemicals, secondhand smoke
    ◦ **Vocal Misuse/Abuse**: Chronic phonotrauma (e.g., yelling, improper singing) causes microtrauma to the vocal cords
    ◦ **Chronic Rhinosinusitis / Post-Nasal Drip**: Constant drainage of inflammatory secretions acts as a direct irritant
    ◦ **Inhaled Corticosteroids**: Can cause mucosal thinning and predispose to **Candida** infection
    ◦ **Infectious (less common)**: Fungal (e.g., *Candida albicans*) or mycobacterial (Tuberculosis) laryngitis
    ◦ **Systemic Inflammatory Disease**: Autoimmune conditions like Rheumatoid Arthritis, Sarcoidosis, and Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA)
sections.epidemiology:
• Commonly affects adults, particularly those between **40-60 years of age**
• Higher prevalence in individuals with specific occupations (teachers, singers, factory workers) or habits (smokers, heavy alcohol users)
• **LPR** is an extremely common contributing factor
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Hallmark presentation is **persistent, progressive hoarseness** (raspy, rough, or "gravelly" voice)
    ◦ Onset is insidious
    ◦ Associated symptoms may include a constant need to clear the throat, a non-productive cough, or a globus sensation (feeling of a lump in the throat)
    ◦ Systemic symptoms like fever are absent
• **Red Flag**: Any patient with hoarseness lasting **> 3 weeks**, especially a smoker or older adult, must be evaluated to rule out laryngeal carcinoma
sections.diagnostics:
• **Laryngoscopy**: **Gold standard for diagnosis**
    ◦ **Flexible Fiberoptic Laryngoscopy**: Performed in the office to visualize laryngeal anatomy and function
    ◦ **Videostroboscopy**: Uses a strobe light for a "slow-motion" view of vocal cord vibration; best test to assess vocal function and subtle mucosal abnormalities
    ◦ **Biopsy**: **Mandatory** for any suspicious lesion (leukoplakia, erythroplakia, ulceration, or mass) to rule out dysplasia or **squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)**
• **Ancillary Testing** (if indicated by history)
    ◦ **24-hour Ambulatory pH/Impedance Monitoring**: Most sensitive test to confirm **LPR** if empiric therapy fails
    ◦ **Chest X-ray**: To evaluate for primary lung cancer or pulmonary tuberculosis
    ◦ **CT/MRI of the Neck**: To evaluate for suspected malignancy, deep space infection, or extralaryngeal pathology
sections.prognosis:
• Good for most patients if the offending agent is removed and the underlying cause is treated
• Voice quality may not fully return to baseline
• Prognosis is poor if **squamous cell carcinoma** develops and is not detected early

sections.overview: • Epiglottitis is an acute, life-threatening inflammatory condition of the epiglottis and adjacent supraglottic structures (aryepiglottic folds, arytenoids). • Considered a true medical emergency due to the risk of rapid and complete upper airway obstruction and death. • The classic presentation has shifted from predominantly pediatric to adult cases since the widespread introduction of the Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) vaccine.
sections.etiology: [NO CONTENT PROVIDED]
sections.epidemiology: • Pre-Hib Vaccine Era ◦ Primarily a disease of children aged 2-6 years. • Post-Hib Vaccine Era ◦ Incidence in children has decreased by >90%. ◦ Now more common in adults than in children. ◦ Mean age in adults is 45-50 years. ◦ When it occurs in children today, it is often in un- or under-vaccinated individuals.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • Presentation is typically acute and fulminant, evolving over hours. • The patient appears toxic, anxious, and acutely ill. • The classic description is a patient sitting upright, leaning forward with the neck hyperextended and chin thrust forward ("tripod" or "sniffing" position) in an effort to maximize airway diameter.
sections.diagnostics: • This is primarily a clinical diagnosis. ◦ Diagnostic studies should never delay securing the airway. • Definitive Diagnosis: Direct laryngoscopy in a controlled setting (i.e., operating room). ◦ Allows for direct visualization of a swollen, "cherry-red" epiglottis. ◦ The team must be prepared for immediate intubation or surgical airway (cricothyrotomy/tracheostomy). • Imaging: ◦ Lateral Neck X-ray: Only to be performed in a stable patient where the diagnosis is uncertain. ▪ The classic finding is the "Thumbprint Sign"—a radiopaque, swollen epiglottis that looks like the distal phalanx of a thumb. • Labs: ◦ CBC may show leukocytosis with a left shift. ◦ Blood cultures should be drawn to identify the causative organism (often positive). ◦ Epiglottic cultures can be obtained during intubation.
sections.prognosis: • With prompt diagnosis and airway management, the prognosis is excellent. ◦ Mortality is <1% in treated patients. • If treatment is delayed or the airway is lost, mortality is significantly higher.

sections.overview:
• Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) is a common pediatric respiratory illness from inflammation and edema of the larynx, trachea, and large bronchi, leading to subglottic narrowing
    ◦ Presents with a hallmark clinical triad of a **barking cough**, **inspiratory stridor**, and **hoarseness**
    ◦ Primarily a viral infection most prevalent in young children
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ **Parainfluenza virus type 1** is the most common cause (~75% of cases)
    ◦ Other viral causes include Parainfluenza virus types 2 & 3, Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), Adenovirus, Influenza A & B, and Human Metapneumovirus
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ A viral infection causes an inflammatory response (edema, cellular infiltration) primarily affecting the **subglottic region** (below the vocal cords)
    ◦ The subglottic space is the narrowest part of the pediatric airway (cricoid cartilage is a complete ring), making it susceptible to significant narrowing
    ◦ Turbulent airflow through the narrowed passage produces **inspiratory stridor**
    ◦ Inflammation of the larynx and vocal cords causes **hoarseness**
    ◦ Inflammation and irritation of the trachea cause the characteristic **barking cough**
sections.epidemiology:
• **Age**: Peak incidence between **6 months and 3 years** of age
• **Season**: Most common in the **fall and early winter**, coinciding with parainfluenza virus season
• **Gender**: Slight male predominance (M:F ratio ~1.5:1)
sections.riskFactors:
• Age (**6 months - 3 years**)
• **Fall/Winter season**
• Daycare attendance
• Family history of croup
• Airway hyperreactivity
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Begins with a 1-3 day **viral prodrome** including low-grade fever, coryza (runny nose), and mild cough
• Followed by the acute onset of classic croup symptoms, which characteristically **worsen at night**
• **Hallmark Triad**
    ◦ **Barking cough** (seal-like)
    ◦ **Inspiratory stridor**
    ◦ **Hoarseness**
• **Other Symptoms**
    ◦ Low-grade fever
    ◦ Coryza
    ◦ Respiratory distress (tachypnea, retractions)
sections.physicalExam:
• **General**: Observe for signs of respiratory distress; note if stridor is present only with agitation or at rest
• **Vitals**: Tachypnea, tachycardia, possible low-grade fever, and pulse oximetry (hypoxia is a late and ominous sign)
• **HEENT**: Hoarse voice or cry; **no drooling or dysphagia** (key negative findings to distinguish from epiglottitis)
• **Respiratory**
    ◦ **Auscultation**
        ▪ **Inspiratory stridor** is the key finding
        ▪ Biphasic stridor (inspiratory and expiratory) indicates severe obstruction
        ▪ Air entry may be diminished in severe cases
        ▪ Wheezing is less common but can be present
    ◦ **Inspection** (Signs of increased work of breathing)
        ▪ **Suprasternal, subcostal, and intercostal retractions**
        ▪ **Nasal flaring**
        ▪ Cyanosis (late sign)
• **Severity Scoring (Westley Croup Score)**
    ◦ **Mild (<2)**: Barking cough, no stridor at rest
    ◦ **Moderate (3-7)**: Stridor at rest, mild/moderate retractions
    ◦ **Severe (>8)**: Significant stridor at rest, severe retractions, agitation, or lethargy; indicates impending respiratory failure
sections.diagnostics:
• Croup is a **clinical diagnosis** based on history and physical exam
• **Imaging** (not routinely required)
    ◦ **Anteroposterior (AP) soft tissue neck X-ray**
        ▪ **Classic Finding**: **Steeple Sign** (subglottic narrowing of the trachea)
        ▪ Indicated for atypical presentations, severe cases, or to rule out other causes (e.g., foreign body aspiration)
        ▪ Note: The absence of a steeple sign does not rule out croup
• **Labs**
    ◦ Generally not indicated
    ◦ Pulse oximetry is essential
sections.treatment:
• **Supportive Care (All Severities)**
    ◦ Cool, humidified air (evidence is weak but commonly used)
    ◦ Keep the child calm and comfortable (crying worsens stridor)
    ◦ Hydration and antipyretics (acetaminophen, ibuprofen)
• **Mild Croup (No stridor at rest)**
    ◦ **Dexamethasone**: A single oral (PO) or intramuscular (IM) dose (0.6 mg/kg; max 10-16 mg)
        ▪ Reduces airway inflammation and edema; onset of action is 1-6 hours
• **Moderate to Severe Croup (Stridor at rest, retractions)**
    ◦ **Dexamethasone** (as above)
    ◦ **Nebulized Epinephrine**
        ▪ A potent alpha-adrenergic agonist that causes vasoconstriction of precapillary arterioles, rapidly decreasing subglottic edema
        ▪ Onset is rapid (within 10-30 minutes); duration is ~2 hours
        ▪ Indicated for moderate to severe distress
sections.management:
• **Disposition**
    ◦ **Discharge**: Most patients with mild croup and those with moderate croup who respond well to treatment (dexamethasone + one dose of nebulized epinephrine) and remain symptom-free during a 3-4 hour observation period
    ◦ **Admit**: Patients with severe croup, persistent stridor at rest, hypoxia, those requiring multiple epinephrine treatments, or concerns about follow-up
• **Patient Education**
    ◦ Counsel parents that symptoms often worsen at night for 2-3 nights
    ◦ Instruct on supportive care at home
    ◦ Provide strict return precautions: return for worsening stridor, increased work of breathing, cyanosis, altered mental status, or poor oral intake
sections.complications:
• Respiratory distress / failure (most critical)
• Bacterial superinfection (e.g., **bacterial tracheitis**, pneumonia)
• Dehydration
• Pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum (rare)
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent; croup is a self-limiting illness
• Symptoms typically peak in 2-3 days and resolve within a week
• Hospitalization is required in less than 5% of cases

sections.overview:
• Vocal cord nodules and polyps are common, benign, non-cancerous lesions of the true vocal folds (vocal cords).
    ◦ They are a primary cause of **dysphonia** (hoarseness).
    ◦ The key distinction lies in their etiology and appearance:
        ▪ **Vocal Cord Nodules ("Singer's Nodes"):** Typically **bilateral** and symmetric lesions that arise from chronic vocal abuse. They are analogous to calluses.
        ▪ **Vocal Cord Polyps:** Typically **unilateral** lesions that can arise from acute vocal trauma or chronic irritation. They are more fluid-filled and analogous to blisters.
    ◦ Both lesions typically occur at the **junction of the anterior and middle thirds** of the membranous vocal fold, which is the point of maximal vibratory stress during phonation.
sections.etiology: • The underlying cause for both is **phonotrauma** (trauma from voice use).
sections.epidemiology:
• **Nodules:**
    ◦ Most common in **women** (aged 20-50) and **children** (especially young boys, often called "screamer's nodes").
    ◦ High prevalence in professional voice users (singers, teachers, coaches).
• **Polyps:**
    ◦ Most common in **adult males**.
    ◦ Strong association with **smoking**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a patient with a chief complaint of **progressive or persistent hoarseness**.
    ◦ **Nodule Patient:** A 35-year-old female elementary school teacher presents with several months of a progressively worsening raspy voice. Her voice is worse at the end of the workday and improves with rest.
    ◦ **Polyp Patient:** A 45-year-old male smoker presents with a more sudden onset of a rough, breathy voice after shouting at a football game last weekend.
    ◦ In both cases, the patient denies pain, difficulty swallowing, or constitutional symptoms.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical History:** Detailed history focusing on vocal demands, onset of symptoms, and risk factors (smoking, reflux).
• **Laryngoscopy with Videostroboscopy:**
    ◦ This is the essential diagnostic test.
    ◦ It confirms the presence of a lesion, distinguishes nodules from polyps and other pathologies, and assesses the impact on vocal fold function.
• **Biopsy:**
    ◦ Rarely needed unless there is a high suspicion for malignancy (e.g., atypical appearance, ulceration, leukoplakia, rapid growth, or significant smoking history).
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for both conditions when managed appropriately.
• **Nodules:** The vast majority resolve completely with voice therapy alone.
• **Polyps:** Voice outcomes are excellent following surgical excision combined with voice therapy.
• The key to long-term success is the patient's adherence to vocal hygiene and behavioral changes taught in voice therapy.

sections.overview:
• Laryngopharyngeal Reflux (LPR) is a condition where stomach contents (acid, pepsin, and bile salts) reflux past the **upper esophageal sphincter (UES)** into the laryngopharynx (voice box and throat).
    ◦ Unlike classic **Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)**, LPR often presents with extra-esophageal symptoms like **hoarseness**, **chronic cough**, and **throat clearing**, frequently in the absence of typical **heartburn**.
    ◦ It is often referred to as "**silent reflux**" because patients may not experience the classic esophageal symptoms of GERD.
    ◦ The laryngeal and pharyngeal mucosa are significantly more sensitive to acidic and enzymatic injury than the esophageal mucosa, leading to symptoms with even minimal exposure.
sections.etiology:
• **Core Mechanism**: Dysfunction of the **Upper Esophageal Sphincter (UES)**, which allows retrograde flow of gastric contents into the upper aerodigestive tract.
    ◦ This is distinct from GERD, which is primarily a failure of the **Lower Esophageal Sphincter (LES)**. Both sphincters can be dysfunctional in LPR.
• **Refluxate Composition**: The damage is not solely from acid (hydrochloric acid). The enzyme **pepsin** and **bile salts** are also highly caustic to the delicate laryngeal epithelium.
    ◦ **Pepsin** remains stable at a neutral pH and can be reactivated by subsequent acidic events (e.g., from food/drink).
• **Mucosal Susceptibility**: The laryngeal epithelium lacks the protective mechanisms of the esophagus (e.g., bicarbonate secretion, robust peristalsis for clearance).
    ◦ Therefore, even small, intermittent reflux events can cause significant inflammation and injury.
• **Pathophysiological Steps**:
    ◦ Gastric contents (acid, pepsin) reflux from the stomach into the esophagus due to LES relaxation.
    ◦ The refluxate travels the length of the esophagus and breaches a dysfunctional UES.
    ◦ The refluxate makes direct contact with the mucosa of the pharynx, larynx, and potentially the trachea and bronchi.
    ◦ Direct chemical injury leads to inflammation, edema, and mucosal damage, causing the characteristic symptoms.
sections.epidemiology:
• LPR is a very common condition, but its true prevalence is difficult to determine due to varied presentations and diagnostic criteria.
• It is estimated to be a contributing factor in:
    ◦ ~50% of patients with **hoarseness**.
    ◦ ~25-50% of patients with **chronic cough**.
• Affects adults of all ages, with no significant gender predilection.
• Often underdiagnosed or misdiagnosed as allergies, asthma, or chronic sinusitis.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Dietary**: **Fatty foods**, **spicy foods**, **acidic foods** (citrus, tomatoes), **chocolate**, **mints**, **caffeine**, **carbonated beverages**, **alcohol**.
• **Lifestyle**: **Obesity** (increased intra-abdominal pressure), **smoking**, excessive voice use (vocal abuse), tight-fitting clothing.
• **Anatomic/Physiologic**: **Hiatal hernia**, **LES** and/or **UES hypotonia**, **delayed gastric emptying**, **pregnancy**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The "classic" LPR patient presents with chronic, nagging upper aerodigestive symptoms, often without the hallmark **heartburn** of GERD.
    ◦ They may have seen multiple specialists (PCP, allergist, pulmonologist) without a definitive diagnosis.
    ◦ Symptoms are often worse in the morning (due to nocturnal reflux) and after meals.
    ◦ **Less than 50%** of patients with LPR report significant **heartburn** or **regurgitation**.
• **Most Common Symptoms ("The Big Three")**:
    ◦ **Hoarseness (Dysphonia)**: Often described as a rough or strained voice.
    ◦ **Globus Sensation**: A persistent feeling of a lump or fullness in the throat.
    ◦ **Chronic Throat Clearing**: Constant need to clear mucus or irritation from the throat.
• **Other Key Symptoms**:
    ◦ **Chronic Cough**: Typically dry and non-productive, can be triggered by talking or lying down.
    ◦ **Dysphagia**: Difficulty swallowing or a sensation of food getting stuck.
    ◦ **Sore Throat (Chronic Pharyngitis)**: Persistent, low-grade throat irritation.
    ◦ **Excessive Throat Mucus / Post-Nasal Drip Sensation**: Thick, tenacious mucus.
    ◦ **Halitosis**
    ◦ **Laryngospasm** (rare)
sections.physicalExam:
• **Laryngeal Erythema and Edema**: Particularly of the posterior larynx, involving the arytenoid cartilages and the interarytenoid space (**posterior laryngitis**).
• **Pseudosulcus Vocalis**: Edema of the Reinke's space below the vocal folds, creating the appearance of a false sulcus.
• **Ventricular Obliteration**: Swelling of the false vocal cords.
• **Vocal Fold Edema/Erythema**.
• **Contact Ulcers or Granulomas**: Often on the medial surface of the arytenoid cartilages.
• **Thickened Endolaryngeal Mucus**.
• A scoring system, the **Reflux Finding Score (RFS)**, is often used to grade these findings, though its specificity is debated.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Empiric Therapeutic Trial (Most Common Approach)**
    ◦ A trial of high-dose **Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs)**, typically **twice daily (BID)** for 2-3 months.
    ◦ Improvement of symptoms is considered a positive, presumptive diagnosis.
• **Laryngoscopy**
    ◦ Essential for visualizing the laryngeal signs of inflammation and ruling out other pathology (e.g., malignancy).
• **24-Hour Ambulatory Dual-Probe pH Monitoring**
    ◦ **The Gold Standard**.
    ◦ Uses a catheter with two pH sensors: one in the distal esophagus (to detect GERD) and one in the proximal esophagus/pharynx (to detect LPR).
    ◦ Positively diagnoses reflux events reaching the pharynx.
• **Multichannel Intraluminal Impedance with pH (MII-pH) monitoring**
    ◦ Detects both **acidic** and **non-acidic reflux**, increasing sensitivity.
• **Barium Esophagram**
    ◦ Can identify anatomical abnormalities like a **hiatal hernia** or **stricture** but is not sensitive for diagnosing LPR.
sections.treatment:
• **Lifestyle and Dietary Modifications (First-Line & Foundational)**
    ◦ **Diet**: Avoid triggers (**caffeine**, **alcohol**, **acidic/spicy/fatty foods**, **chocolate**, **mints**).
    ◦ **Behavioral**:
        ▪ Elevate head of bed by 6-8 inches (use blocks or a wedge, not just pillows).
        ▪ Avoid eating within 3 hours of bedtime.
        ▪ Eat smaller, more frequent meals.
        ▪ **Weight loss** if overweight.
        ▪ **Smoking cessation**.
• **Pharmacotherapy**
    ◦ **Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs)**: Mainstay of treatment.
        ▪ **Dosing**: Requires higher doses than for GERD. Typically given **30-60 minutes before breakfast and dinner (BID dosing)**.
        ▪ **Duration**: An initial trial of **3-6 months** is often needed to see significant laryngeal healing and symptom improvement.
        ▪ Examples: Omeprazole, Pantoprazole, Esomeprazole.
    ◦ **H2 Receptor Antagonists (H2RAs)**:
        ▪ Can be added at bedtime to suppress nocturnal acid breakthrough.
        ▪ Examples: Famotidine, Cimetidine.
    ◦ **Alginates (e.g., Gaviscon Advance)**:
        ▪ Forms a viscous foam raft that floats on top of stomach contents, creating a physical barrier to reflux.
        ▪ Often taken after meals and before bed.
• **Surgical Management**
    ◦ Reserved for severe, refractory cases confirmed with objective testing (pH monitoring).
    ◦ **Laparoscopic Nissen Fundoplication**: Surgical procedure to reinforce the LES.
sections.management:
• **Initial Step**: Initiate a 2-3 month trial of empiric therapy with aggressive lifestyle/dietary modifications and a **twice-daily PPI**.
• **Follow-up**:
    ◦ If symptoms improve, continue therapy for at least 6 months before considering a slow taper.
    ◦ If symptoms do not improve, refer to ENT and/or Gastroenterology for further workup (**laryngoscopy**, **pH monitoring**) to confirm the diagnosis and rule out other causes.
• **Long-term**: LPR is often a chronic condition.
    ◦ Many patients require long-term or intermittent therapy to control symptoms.
    ◦ Lifestyle modification is key to long-term success.
sections.complications:
• **Subglottic Stenosis**: Narrowing of the airway below the vocal cords.
• **Laryngeal Granulomas** and **Contact Ulcers**.
• **Laryngospasm**.
• Worsening of co-existing asthma, bronchitis, or sinusitis.
• **Barrett's Esophagus** (if co-existing GERD is significant).
• A potential (though controversial) role as a co-factor in the development of **laryngeal cancer**.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is generally good for symptom control with consistent treatment and lifestyle changes.
• Laryngeal healing and voice improvement can take several months.
• It is a chronic condition, and relapse is common if therapy is discontinued or lifestyle modifications are not maintained.

sections.overview:
• Recurrent Aphthous Stomatitis (RAS), or canker sores, are painful, recurring, solitary or multiple ulcers of the oral mucosa.
• One of the most common oral mucosal diseases.
• Characterized by well-defined, round or oval, shallow ulcers with a yellow-gray pseudomembranous center surrounded by an **erythematous halo**.
• Unlike herpes labialis (cold sores), aphthous ulcers are **not contagious** and are **not caused by the Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV)**.
• They occur exclusively on **non-keratinized** oral mucosa.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ The exact cause is **idiopathic**.
    ◦ The leading theory suggests a multifactorial etiology involving a localized, cell-mediated immune dysregulation.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The process is thought to be a **T-cell mediated immune response** targeting the oral epithelium.
    ◦ An unknown trigger (e.g., local trauma, microbial antigen) initiates an inflammatory cascade.
    ◦ This involves infiltration of T-lymphocytes (specifically CD8+ cytotoxic T-cells and later CD4+ helper T-cells) and pro-inflammatory cytokines like Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha (TNF-α).
    ◦ This localized immune attack leads to epithelial necrosis and ulceration.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** Affects approximately 20% of the general population.
• **Age of Onset:** Typically begins in childhood or adolescence (ages 10-19).
• **Gender:** More common in females.
• **Socioeconomic Status:** Higher prevalence in higher socioeconomic groups.
• **Recurrence:** The defining feature; frequency varies from a few times a year to near-constant outbreaks.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Local Trauma:** Minor injury from dental work, accidental cheek bite, toothbrush abrasion.
• **Stress:** Strong association with emotional or psychological stress.
• **Genetics:** Positive family history in ~40% of patients.
• **Hormonal Changes:** May correlate with the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle.
• **Food Sensitivities:** Chocolate, coffee, nuts, strawberries, cheese, acidic foods.
• **Nutritional Deficiencies:** Iron, Folate, Vitamin B12, and Zinc deficiencies.
• **Medications:** NSAIDs, beta-blockers, nicorandil.
• **Chemicals:** **Sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS)**, a common ingredient in toothpaste, can be a trigger for some individuals.
• **Systemic Disease Associations (High-Yield):**
    ◦ **Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD):** **Crohn's disease**, **Ulcerative colitis**.
    ◦ **Celiac Disease**
    ◦ **Behçet's Disease:** A classic triad of recurrent oral ulcers, genital ulcers, and uveitis.
    ◦ **HIV/Immunosuppression:** Ulcers may be larger, more persistent, and more frequent.
    ◦ **Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)**
    ◦ **Cyclic Neutropenia**
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patient presents with a chief complaint of a "painful mouth sore" and often reports a history of similar, recurrent sores.
• **Prodrome:** Localized burning, tingling, or pain 24-48 hours before the ulcer appears.
• **Primary Symptom: Pain**
    ◦ Described as a burning sensation, often disproportionate to the size of the lesion.
    ◦ Exacerbated by contact with food (especially acidic or spicy), drink, or by talking.
• Patients are **afebrile** with no systemic symptoms unless the ulcers are a manifestation of an underlying systemic disease.
• No fever, malaise, or lymphadenopathy in uncomplicated RAS.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Location:** Found exclusively on **non-keratinized (movable) mucosa**.
    ◦ Buccal mucosa (inner cheeks)
    ◦ Labial mucosa (inner lips)
    ◦ Ventral tongue (underside)
    ◦ Floor of the mouth
    ◦ Soft palate
• **Types of Ulcers:**
    ◦ **Minor Aphthae (Most Common)**
        ▪ **Size:** < 1 cm in diameter.
        ▪ **Number:** Usually 1-5 lesions per episode.
        ▪ **Appearance:** Round or oval, shallow, yellow-gray fibrinous center with a distinct **erythematous halo**.
        ▪ **Healing:** Heal within **7-14 days without scarring**.
    ◦ **Major Aphthae**
        ▪ **Size:** > 1 cm in diameter.
        ▪ **Appearance:** Deeper, crater-like, often with rolled borders.
        ▪ **Pain:** More severe and debilitating.
        ▪ **Healing:** Take **weeks to months to heal** and frequently **cause scarring**.
    ◦ **Herpetiform Aphthae**
        ▪ **Appearance:** Multiple (10-100) small, 1-3 mm pinpoint ulcers that can coalesce into larger, irregular lesions.
        ▪ **Note:** Name is a misnomer; **not related to HSV**.
        ▪ **Healing:** Heal within 1-2 weeks without scarring.
sections.diagnostics:
• Primarily a **clinical diagnosis** based on history of recurrence and characteristic physical exam findings.
• **Laboratory studies are not typically required** for simple, recurrent cases.
• **Consider a workup if ("Red Flags"):**
    ◦ Ulcers are unusually large, numerous, or persistent (>3 weeks).
    ◦ Patient has systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss, rash, diarrhea).
    ◦ Onset is in later life.
• **Potential Workup ("Red Flag" cases):**
    ◦ **CBC with differential:** To rule out neutropenia or anemia.
    ◦ **Iron studies (ferritin), Vitamin B12, Folate:** To rule out nutritional deficiency.
    ◦ **Celiac serologies (tTG-IgA):** If GI symptoms are present.
    ◦ **HIV test:** In at-risk patients or with severe, atypical ulcers.
    ◦ **Biopsy:** Rarely needed. Indicated for any ulcer that persists >3 weeks to rule out **Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)** or other pathology.
        ▪ Histology shows a non-specific inflammatory infiltrate.
sections.treatment:
• **First-Line / Mild-to-Moderate:**
    ◦ **Topical Corticosteroids (Mainstay):**
        ▪ **Triamcinolone acetonide in Orabase 0.1%**
        ▪ Fluocinonide 0.05% gel
        ▪ *Instructions: Dry the ulcer with a cotton swab, then apply a thin layer directly to the lesion 2-4 times daily, especially after meals and at bedtime.*
    ◦ **Topical Anesthetics:**
        ▪ Viscous lidocaine 2%
        ▪ Benzocaine preparations (e.g., Orabase-B)
        ▪ Provides temporary pain relief, especially before eating.
    ◦ **Barrier Pastes/Gels:**
        ▪ Sucralfate suspension (swish and spit) can coat and protect ulcers.
        ▪ Hyaluronic acid gels.
    ◦ **"Magic Mouthwash"**
        ▪ A compounded prescription with variable ingredients, but commonly contains a topical anesthetic, antihistamine, and an antacid.
        ▪ May also include a steroid, antibiotic, or antifungal. Used as a "swish and spit" rinse.
• **Second-Line / Severe or Recalcitrant Disease:**
    ◦ **Systemic Corticosteroids:** A short course of oral prednisone (e.g., 40 mg/day with a taper) for severe, debilitating outbreaks.
    ◦ **Colchicine:** Used for frequent recurrences, especially in **Behçet's disease**.
    ◦ **Immunosuppressants:** Azathioprine, thalidomide (requires specialist management).
sections.management:
• **Patient Education:**
    ◦ Reassure the patient that the condition is benign and **not contagious**.
    ◦ Discuss identifying and avoiding personal triggers (e.g., specific foods, stress).
• **Oral Hygiene:**
    ◦ Recommend a soft-bristled toothbrush to minimize trauma.
    ◦ Suggest trying an **SLS-free toothpaste**.
• **Diet:**
    ◦ Avoid acidic, spicy, or abrasive foods during an outbreak.
• **Follow-up:**
    ◦ Advise the patient to return if an ulcer persists for **more than 3 weeks** to rule out malignancy.
sections.complications:
• Severe pain leading to difficulty eating or drinking, potentially causing dehydration or weight loss (especially with major aphthae).
• **Scarring** of the oral mucosa (only with **major aphthae**).
• Secondary bacterial infection (rare).
• Significant impact on quality of life due to chronic pain and recurrence.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent.** Aphthous ulcers are self-limiting.
• While the condition is chronic and recurrent, the frequency of outbreaks often decreases with age.
• Minor and herpetiform types heal without long-term sequelae.
• **Major aphthae** are the only type to cause **scarring**.

sections.overview:
• Herpes Labialis, commonly known as cold sores or fever blisters, is a recurrent viral infection of the skin and mucous membranes, most frequently affecting the lips and perioral area
    ◦ Characterized by the eruption of painful, clustered vesicles on an erythematous base
    ◦ The infection is caused by Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), which establishes lifelong latency in sensory nerve ganglia, leading to periodic reactivation
sections.etiology:
• **Causative Agent**: Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), a double-stranded DNA virus
    ◦ **HSV-1**: The primary cause of orofacial herpes (>80% of cases)
    ◦ **HSV-2**: Less common cause, typically associated with genital herpes but can be transmitted to the oral area via oral-genital contact
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Primary Infection**: The initial exposure to HSV, often occurring in childhood. It may be asymptomatic or present as a more severe clinical syndrome called herpetic gingivostomatitis (fever, oral ulcers, lymphadenopathy)
    ◦ **Transmission**: Occurs through direct contact with active lesions or infected secretions (e.g., saliva, even during asymptomatic shedding)
    ◦ **Latency**: After the primary infection resolves, the virus travels via retrograde axonal transport along a sensory nerve (most commonly the **trigeminal nerve**) to the sensory ganglion (the **trigeminal ganglion** for orofacial HSV). It remains dormant/latent within the ganglion for the life of the host
    ◦ **Reactivation**: Various triggers can cause the virus to reactivate. It then travels down the same sensory nerve (anterograde transport) to the initial site of infection on the skin or mucosa, causing a recurrent outbreak
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Extremely common worldwide. Seroprevalence of HSV-1 in the adult population is estimated to be 50-80% in the United States and higher globally
• **Acquisition**: Most primary HSV-1 infections are acquired asymptomatically during childhood
• **Recurrence**: Approximately 20-40% of individuals with latent HSV-1 will experience recurrent herpes labialis
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The clinical course follows a predictable pattern over 7-10 days:
    ◦ **Prodromal Stage (Day 0-1)**: Patients experience localized symptoms of tingling, burning, itching, or pain at the site where the lesion will appear. This is the optimal time to initiate antiviral therapy
    ◦ **Erythema/Papule Stage (Day 1-2)**: A red, slightly raised papule forms at the prodromal site
    ◦ **Vesicle Stage (Day 2-4)**: The classic lesion appears: **grouped, small, fluid-filled vesicles on an erythematous base**
    ◦ **Ulcer/Weeping Stage (Day 4)**: The vesicles coalesce and rupture, leaving a shallow, painful, erythematous ulcer that may ooze clear or straw-colored fluid. This is the most contagious stage
    ◦ **Crusting Stage (Day 5-8)**: The ulcerated lesion dries and forms a characteristic **"honey-colored" or serosanguinous crust**
    ◦ **Healing Stage (Day 8-10)**: The crust flakes off, and the underlying skin heals, typically **without scarring**
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Diagnosis is almost always made based on the characteristic history (recurrent nature, prodrome) and classic physical exam findings
• **Confirmatory Testing** (if needed for atypical cases, immunocompromised patients, or clinical trials):
    ◦ **Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR)**: **Test of choice**
        ▪ Highly sensitive and specific. Can differentiate between HSV-1 and HSV-2
        ▪ Performed on a swab of vesicle fluid
    ◦ **Tzanck Smear**: A classic, though less common, test
        ▪ A scraping from the base of an unroofed vesicle is stained (Wright-Giemsa)
        ▪ Finding of **multinucleated giant cells** is suggestive of a herpesvirus infection (HSV or VZV) but is not specific for HSV-1 vs. HSV-2
        ▪ Less sensitive than PCR
    ◦ **Viral Culture**:
        ▪ Vesicle fluid is cultured
        ▪ High specificity but lower sensitivity than PCR, and results are slower
    ◦ **Serology (IgG)**:
        ▪ Not useful for diagnosing an acute outbreak
        ▪ It indicates past exposure but does not confirm that the current lesion is herpetic
sections.prognosis:
• **Immunocompetent Host**: Excellent. Herpes labialis is a self-limiting condition. The primary morbidity is pain, discomfort, and cosmetic concern
• **Recurrence**: Variable among individuals. The frequency and severity of recurrences often decrease over time and with advancing age
• **Immunocompromised Host**: Outbreaks can be more frequent, severe, prolonged, and have a higher risk of complications

sections.overview:
• Oral Candidiasis, or **thrush**, is an opportunistic fungal infection of the oral mucosa caused by an overgrowth of **Candida** species, most commonly ***Candida albicans***.
• **Candida** is a normal commensal organism; its proliferation is typically checked by the local immune system and competing bacterial flora.
    ◦ Symptomatic infection occurs when host defenses are compromised.
• The hallmark presentation is **creamy white plaques** on the oral mucosa that can be **scraped off**, revealing an underlying erythematous base.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiologic Agent**
    ◦ Primarily ***Candida albicans*** (~80% of cases).
    ◦ Other species like ***C. glabrata*** or ***C. tropicalis*** can also be responsible, particularly in refractory cases.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ Infection is caused by the overgrowth of a commensal organism due to a disruption in the host's local or systemic immunity, or an alteration of the normal oral flora.
    ◦ **Adhesion**: **Candida** yeast cells adhere to the epithelial cells of the oral mucosa.
    ◦ **Proliferation**: A change in the local environment (e.g., pH change, reduced competing bacteria, immunosuppression) allows the yeast to multiply rapidly.
    ◦ **Invasion**: The yeast transforms into its pathogenic hyphal form, which can invade the superficial layers of the epithelium, causing the characteristic inflammatory response and plaque formation.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Infants**: Very common due to their immature immune systems. Can be acquired during passage through the birth canal.
• **Elderly**: Common, especially in **denture wearers** and those with **xerostomia** or multiple comorbidities.
• **Immunocompromised**: High prevalence in patients with:
    ◦ **HIV/AIDS** (it is an **AIDS-defining illness** when it extends into the esophagus)
    ◦ Patients undergoing **chemotherapy**
    ◦ **Organ transplant recipients**
    ◦ Those on long-term systemic **corticosteroids**
• Prevalence in HIV patients is strongly correlated with CD4 count; it is most common when **CD4 < 200 cells/L**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation varies depending on the type of candidiasis; the most common form is **Pseudomembranous Candidiasis**.
• A patient, often with risk factors, will present with complaints of:
    ◦ Mouth soreness
    ◦ A "**cottony**" feeling
    ◦ **Loss of taste**
• An infant may present with **feeding difficulties** or fussiness.
sections.diagnostics:
• Primarily a **clinical diagnosis** based on characteristic physical exam findings (**white plaques** that can be scraped off) in a patient with risk factors.
• **Confirmatory Testing** (if diagnosis is uncertain):
    ◦ **KOH Prep**: A scraping of the lesion is placed on a slide with potassium hydroxide (KOH).
        ▪ Microscopic examination reveals **budding yeast and pseudohyphae**, which is diagnostic.
• **Further Workup**:
    ◦ In a healthy-appearing adult with no obvious risk factors, new-onset oral thrush should prompt an investigation for an underlying systemic disease (e.g., **HIV test**, **HgbA1c** for diabetes).
    ◦ **Endoscopy** is required to diagnose suspected **esophageal candidiasis**.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** in immunocompetent patients who receive treatment and have their underlying risk factors addressed.
• **Recurrence is common** if the predisposing condition (e.g., steroid inhaler use without rinsing, uncontrolled diabetes) is not corrected.
• In severely immunocompromised patients, thrush can be **recurrent and difficult to manage**, often serving as a clinical marker for the severity of their immunodeficiency.

sections.overview:
• A clinical term for a white patch or plaque on the oral mucosa that **cannot be scraped off** and cannot be characterized as any other disease
• It is a diagnosis of exclusion
• Considered a **premalignant lesion**, meaning it carries an increased risk of developing into oral squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)
sections.etiology:
• **Pathophysiology**: Represents a protective reaction of the mucosal epithelium to chronic irritation, leading to **hyperkeratosis** (thickening of the outer keratin layer)
    ◦ **Cellular Changes**: The key concern is the potential for **dysplasia**, which represents disordered cell growth and is the histologic precursor to malignancy
        ▪ The progression is often from simple hyperkeratosis to mild, moderate, or severe dysplasia, then to carcinoma in situ (CIS), and finally to invasive SCC
• **Etiology**: While often idiopathic, the vast majority of cases are linked to chronic irritants
    ◦ **Tobacco**: The single most common and significant etiologic agent, including smoked and smokeless forms
    ◦ **Alcohol**: Acts synergistically with tobacco to significantly increase risk
    ◦ **Chronic Irritation**: From sources like ill-fitting dentures, rough teeth, or chronic cheek biting
    ◦ **Infectious Agents**:
        ▪ **Human Papillomavirus (HPV)**, particularly HPV-16 and HPV-18, has been implicated in a subset of cases
        ▪ ***Candida albicans*** can colonize leukoplakic lesions (candidal leukoplakia), which may increase malignant potential
• **Note on Oral Hairy Leukoplakia (OHL)**: This is a distinct entity caused by the **Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV)** in immunocompromised individuals (esp. HIV/AIDS) and is **not** considered premalignant
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects approximately 2-3% of the adult population worldwide
• **Age**: Primarily a disease of older adults, with peak incidence in individuals aged 50-70
• **Gender**: More common in men than women (approx. 2:1 ratio), likely reflecting historical differences in tobacco and alcohol use
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients are often **asymptomatic**
• The lesion is typically discovered as an incidental finding during a routine dental or medical examination
• Presentation is highly variable, ranging from a small, discrete white patch to extensive involvement of the oral mucosa
sections.diagnostics:
• **Biopsy is mandatory** for definitive diagnosis and to rule out malignancy
    ◦ **Incisional biopsy** is performed on larger lesions, taking a sample from the most clinically suspicious area (e.g., red, ulcerated, or indurated areas)
    ◦ **Excisional biopsy** (complete removal) may be appropriate for smaller, localized lesions
    ◦ **Histopathology**: The pathologist will determine:
        ▪ The presence and grade of **dysplasia** (mild, moderate, severe)
        ▪ The presence of **carcinoma in situ (CIS)** or **invasive squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)**
• **Adjunctive Tools**: Toluidine blue staining can help identify high-risk areas within a lesion to guide biopsy, but it does not replace the need for histopathology
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis depends directly on the degree of **dysplasia** found on biopsy
    ◦ **No dysplasia**: Excellent prognosis if risk factors are eliminated, but surveillance is still required
    ◦ **Mild dysplasia**: Good prognosis, small risk of transformation
    ◦ **Moderate to Severe dysplasia**: Guarded prognosis, with a significantly higher risk of malignant transformation. Complete excision improves prognosis
• Location also impacts prognosis, with floor of mouth and tongue lesions carrying a worse outlook

sections.overview:
• A clinical term for a chronic, **fiery red patch** or plaque on an oral mucous membrane that cannot be attributed to another disease.
    ◦ It is a **diagnosis of exclusion**.
• Considered a significant **oral potentially malignant disorder (OPMD)** due to an extremely high rate of **malignant transformation**.
    ◦ Carries a much higher risk for dysplasia or carcinoma compared to its white counterpart, **leukoplakia**.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ The exact etiology is multifactorial but is overwhelmingly linked to **chronic exposure to carcinogens**.
    ◦ The primary causative agents are **tobacco** and **alcohol**.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ Erythroplakia represents a lesion with significant **epithelial abnormalities**.
    ◦ **Cellular Changes**
        ▪ The lesion is characterized by **severe epithelial dysplasia**, **carcinoma in situ (CIS)**, or **invasive squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)**.
    ◦ **Appearance**
        ▪ The characteristic red color is due to **epithelial atrophy** (thinning) and a **lack of surface keratin production**.
        ▪ This allows the underlying, **highly vascular submucosal connective tissue** to be visible.
    ◦ **Molecular Basis**
        ▪ **Chronic irritation** from carcinogens leads to the accumulation of **genetic mutations** (e.g., in TP53), promoting uncontrolled cell proliferation and **malignant transformation**.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**
    ◦ Much less common than leukoplakia, with an estimated prevalence of 0.02% to 0.83%.
• **Age**
    ◦ Predominantly affects middle-aged and older adults, typically over the age of 50.
• **Sex**
    ◦ Historically more common in males (M:F ratio ~2:1), though this gap is narrowing with changing smoking habits.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presents as a well-demarcated or ill-defined **erythematous (red) macule or plaque** on the oral mucosa.
    ◦ **Texture**: Often described as soft and **velvety**.
• **High-Risk Locations**
    ◦ Most commonly found in areas at high risk for oral cancer:
        ▪ **Floor of the mouth**
        ▪ **Ventrolateral tongue**
        ▪ **Soft palate**
        ▪ Retromolar trigone
• **Variants**
    ◦ **Homogenous Erythroplakia**: Uniformly red in appearance.
    ◦ **Speckled Erythroplakia (Erythroleukoplakia)**: A mixed lesion with red patches and white keratotic flecks (leukoplakia), carrying a particularly **high risk of malignancy**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Scalpel Biopsy is the mandatory gold standard** for any persistent, unexplained red lesion in the mouth.
