    ◦ **Incisional Biopsy**: Preferred for larger lesions to obtain a sample from the most suspicious area.
    ◦ **Excisional Biopsy**: May be both diagnostic and therapeutic for small, well-defined lesions.
• **Histopathology**
    ◦ This is the definitive step to evaluate for the degree of **epithelial dysplasia**.
    ◦ Findings will be one of the following:
        ▪ Mild, Moderate, or **Severe Dysplasia**
        ▪ **Carcinoma in situ (CIS)**
        ▪ **Invasive Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)**
    ◦ **High-Yield Fact**: Approximately **90%** of true erythroplakias will demonstrate severe dysplasia, CIS, or invasive SCC upon biopsy.
• **Adjunctive Tools**
    ◦ **Toluidine blue staining** can help identify high-risk areas for biopsy but is not a substitute for histopathology.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is entirely dependent on the **histopathologic findings** from the biopsy.
• For lesions showing **severe dysplasia** or **CIS** that are completely excised, the prognosis is **excellent**.
    ◦ The lifetime risk for a new primary cancer remains elevated.
• If **invasive SCC** is diagnosed, the prognosis is determined by the **stage at diagnosis**.
    ◦ **Early-stage** oral cancers have a much better prognosis than late-stage disease.
• The presence of erythroplakia is a powerful predictor of future **oral cancer risk**.

sections.overview:
• **Temporomandibular Disorder (TMD)**, often referred to as TMJ, is a heterogeneous group of musculoskeletal and neuromuscular conditions affecting the temporomandibular joint, the muscles of mastication, and associated structures
• It is a major cause of **non-dental facial pain**
• The conditions are generally categorized into:
    ◦ **Myofascial Pain and Dysfunction (MPD)**: The most common form, involving pain and dysfunction of the masticatory muscles
    ◦ **Internal Derangement**: A disorder involving the articular disc, condyle, and fossa (e.g., disc displacement)
    ◦ **Degenerative/Inflammatory Joint Disease**: Conditions such as osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis affecting the TMJ
sections.etiology:
• The etiology of TMD is considered **multifactorial**, with no single causative agent
• **Myofascial Pain**
    ◦ Caused by hyperactivity or overuse of masticatory muscles (masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoids)
    ◦ Leads to muscle fatigue, spasm, and development of localized **trigger points**
    ◦ Strongly associated with parafunctional habits like **bruxism** (teeth grinding/clenching), gum chewing, and nail-biting, often exacerbated by psychological stress
• **Internal Derangement**
    ◦ Refers to an abnormal relationship of the articular disc to the mandibular condyle
    ◦ **Anterior Disc Displacement with Reduction**
        ▪ The disc is displaced anteriorly when the jaw is closed but returns ("reduces") to its normal position upon opening, typically producing an audible **click or pop**
    ◦ **Anterior Disc Displacement without Reduction**
        ▪ The disc is displaced anteriorly and fails to reduce upon opening, resulting in a mechanical obstruction
        ▪ This presents as a **"closed lock"** where jaw opening is restricted
• **Degenerative Joint Disease (DJD)**
    ◦ Primarily osteoarthritis resulting from chronic overloading of the joint, leading to deterioration of articular cartilage and subchondral bone
    ◦ Presents with **crepitus** (grating/grinding sound) rather than a distinct click
    ◦ Can also be secondary to systemic inflammatory conditions like rheumatoid arthritis
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects up to 15% of adults
• **Gender**: Significantly more common in **females** (F:M ratio ~4:1)
• **Age of Onset**: Peak incidence is between **20 and 40 years old**
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with a primary complaint of unilateral, dull, aching **facial pain** located in the preauricular area, jaw, or temporal region
    ◦ The pain is often chronic and waxes and wanes
    ◦ It is commonly exacerbated by jaw function (chewing, yawning, talking) and may be worse upon awakening due to **nocturnal bruxism**
• Patients may also report mechanical symptoms like **clicking or locking**
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is **primarily clinical**, based on history and physical exam
• **Imaging**
    ◦ Not routinely required for uncomplicated myofascial pain
    ◦ Indicated if there is a history of trauma, suspected degenerative joint disease, severe pain, or locking
• **Panoramic Radiograph (Panorex)**
    ◦ Good initial screening test to rule out dental pathology or gross bony abnormalities (fractures, severe arthritis)
• **MRI**
    ◦ **Gold standard** for evaluating soft tissues, particularly the position and morphology of the articular disc
    ◦ It is the best test for diagnosing internal derangement
• **CT Scan**
    ◦ Superior for evaluating fine bony detail (e.g., fractures, erosions, ankylosis)
• **Labs**
    ◦ Not indicated unless a systemic inflammatory cause is suspected (e.g., order ESR, CRP, RF, anti-CCP if suspecting Giant Cell Arteritis or Rheumatoid Arthritis)
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for most patients
• Approximately **80-90%** of patients experience significant improvement with conservative, non-invasive therapies alone
• A small subset of patients will develop chronic, refractory TMD that significantly impacts their quality of life

sections.overview:
• A dental abscess is a localized collection of pus associated with a tooth.
    ◦ It represents an acute infection originating from either the tooth pulp or the surrounding periodontal tissues.
• There are two main types:
    ◦ **Periapical Abscess**: Occurs at the apex (tip) of the tooth root, typically as a result of **pulp necrosis** secondary to dental caries or trauma.
    ◦ **Periodontal Abscess**: Occurs in the supporting gum and bone tissues of the tooth (periodontium), often as a complication of advanced gum disease (periodontitis).
• A dental abscess is a common reason for patients to present to urgent care or the emergency department and requires prompt management to prevent serious, life-threatening complications.
sections.etiology:
• A dental abscess is a **polymicrobial infection**, dominated by anaerobic bacteria.
• **Periapical Abscess Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Dental Caries (Cavity)**: Bacteria erode through the enamel and dentin to reach the tooth's inner pulp.
    ◦ **Pulpitis**: Inflammation of the pulp. Initially reversible, it progresses to irreversible pulpitis.
    ◦ **Pulp Necrosis**: The pulp tissue dies, creating a nutrient-rich, anaerobic environment for bacterial proliferation.
    ◦ **Infection Spread**: Bacteria and their toxins exit through the apical foramen (the opening at the root tip) and into the periapical tissues of the alveolar bone.
    ◦ **Abscess Formation**: The body's immune response walls off the infection, forming a localized collection of pus (neutrophils, dead tissue, bacteria).
• **Periodontal Abscess Pathophysiology**:
    ◦ **Chronic Periodontitis**: Bacteria in plaque cause inflammation and destruction of the gums and bone, forming deep "periodontal pockets" between the tooth and gum.
    ◦ **Obstruction**: A foreign body (e.g., food particle) or calculus can obstruct the opening of a deep periodontal pocket.
    ◦ **Bacterial Proliferation**: Bacteria are trapped within the pocket, leading to a rapid inflammatory response and pus formation within the gingival tissues.
• **Common Pathogens**:
    ◦ **Aerobes**:
        ▪ *Streptococcus* species (especially the *S. anginosus* group, a.k.a. *S. milleri* group)
    ◦ **Anaerobes (predominant)**:
        ▪ *Peptostreptococcus*
        ▪ *Prevotella*
        ▪ *Fusobacterium*
        ▪ *Bacteroides*
sections.epidemiology:
• Extremely common worldwide.
• Affects all age groups but is more prevalent in individuals with **poor oral hygiene** and limited access to dental care.
• Incidence is directly correlated with the prevalence of untreated dental caries and periodontitis.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with a primary complaint of **severe, localized tooth pain**.
• They may appear distressed, systemically unwell, and have visible facial swelling.
• The presentation can range from a simple, localized abscess to a life-threatening, **deep-space neck infection**.
sections.diagnostics:
• Primarily a **clinical diagnosis** based on history and physical exam.
• **Imaging**:
    ◦ **Dental Radiographs (Periapical or Panorex)**: The primary imaging modality.
        ▪ Can reveal a **periapical radiolucency** (dark area at the root apex), bone loss, or widening of the periodontal ligament space.
    ◦ **CT with IV Contrast (Neck/Face)**:
        ▪ Indicated for suspected **deep space infections**, **airway compromise**, **osteomyelitis**, or **cavernous sinus thrombosis**.
        ▪ It is essential for determining the extent of the infection and planning for surgical drainage.
• **Labs**:
    ◦ Not necessary for uncomplicated abscesses.
    ◦ Consider **CBC** (for leukocytosis) and **CRP/ESR** in patients with systemic signs of infection or who appear toxic.
    ◦ **Blood cultures** if sepsis is suspected.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for uncomplicated abscesses that receive prompt drainage and definitive dental care.
• **Poor** if complications like **Ludwig's angina**, **cavernous sinus thrombosis**, or **sepsis** develop.
    ◦ Mortality for these conditions can be significant.

sections.overview:
• **Acute Bacterial Sialadenitis** is a bacterial infection and subsequent inflammation of a salivary gland, most commonly the **parotid gland** (~85%), followed by the **submandibular gland**.
    ◦ Also known as suppurative sialadenitis.
    ◦ The infection typically results from **salivary stasis**, which allows for the retrograde migration of bacteria from the oral cavity into the salivary duct system.
    ◦ Presents as an acute, painful, unilateral swelling of the affected gland, often in elderly, dehydrated, or post-operative patients.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology (Causative Organisms):**
    ◦ **_Staphylococcus aureus_ is the most common pathogen (including MRSA).**
    ◦ Other common organisms include:
        ▪ _Streptococcus_ species (_S. viridans_, _S. pyogenes_)
        ▪ _Haemophilus influenzae_
        ▪ Oral anaerobes (e.g., _Peptostreptococcus_, _Prevotella_, _Fusobacterium_)
    ◦ Often a polymicrobial infection.
• **Pathophysiology:**
    ◦ **Salivary Stasis:** A decrease in salivary flow is the primary predisposing factor. Saliva has antimicrobial properties and its constant flow mechanically flushes bacteria from the ducts.
    ◦ **Retrograde Contamination:** Reduced flow allows oral bacteria to ascend from the oral cavity into the ductal system.
        ▪ **Stensen's duct:** Drains the parotid gland.
        ▪ **Wharton's duct:** Drains the submandibular gland.
    ◦ **Infection & Inflammation:** Bacteria multiply within the gland parenchyma, leading to an inflammatory response, suppuration (pus formation), and potentially abscess formation.
sections.epidemiology:
• Most commonly affects the **elderly, debilitated, or hospitalized patients**.
• Can occur in any age group, including neonates (neonatal suppurative parotitis).
• Incidence has decreased with improved post-operative care, particularly hydration and oral hygiene.
• **Parotid gland** is affected in ~85% of cases.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Dehydration:** The single most important risk factor.
• **Post-operative state:** Especially after major abdominal surgery (due to NPO status, dehydration, and anticholinergic medications).
• **Advanced Age**
• **Sialolithiasis (salivary stones):** Causes ductal obstruction and stasis.
• **Medications that reduce salivary flow (antisialogogues):**
    ◦ Anticholinergics (e.g., atropine)
    ◦ Antihistamines
    ◦ Diuretics
    ◦ Beta-blockers
    ◦ Antipsychotics
• **Poor Oral Hygiene**
• **Chronic Illness:** Diabetes mellitus, renal failure, Sjögren's syndrome, hypothyroidism.
• **Immunosuppression**
• **Radiation therapy** to the head and neck.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The "classic" patient is an elderly, post-operative individual (often day 5-7 post-op) who develops the **acute onset of unilateral cheek or jaw swelling, pain, and fever**.
• The patient may complain of a **foul taste** in their mouth and difficulty opening their jaw.
• **Acute, unilateral pain and swelling** over the affected gland (parotid or submandibular area).
• **Fever and chills.**
• **Foul taste (cacogeusia)** due to purulent drainage into the mouth.
• **Trismus:** Pain and difficulty opening the jaw due to inflammation of the nearby masseter muscle (especially with parotitis).
• **Dysphagia:** Difficulty swallowing.
• **Malaise** and general systemic illness.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Inspection:** Obvious, often unilateral, erythema and edema over the affected gland.
• **Palpation:** Gland is firm, indurated, and **exquisitely tender** to palpation.
• **Intraoral Exam:**
    ◦ **Pathognomonic Finding:** Expression of **purulent or cloudy saliva** from the ductal orifice (Stensen's or Wharton's) upon gentle massage of the gland.
    ◦ Orifice may be red and inflamed.
    ◦ Check for obstructing stones (sialoliths).
• **Systemic Signs:** Fever, tachycardia.
• **Cervical lymphadenopathy** may be present.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primarily a clinical diagnosis** based on history and physical exam findings.
• **Imaging (indicated if diagnosis is unclear, patient fails to improve, or abscess is suspected):**
    ◦ **Ultrasound (US):** Excellent initial imaging modality. Can differentiate between simple inflammation (cellulitis/phlegmon) and a drainable fluid collection (abscess). Can also identify sialoliths.
    ◦ **CT with contrast:** The modality of choice for assessing the extent of infection and detecting abscesses or deep neck space involvement. Provides superior detail compared to ultrasound.
• **Laboratory Studies:**
    ◦ **CBC:** May show **leukocytosis with a left shift**.
    ◦ **Blood Cultures:** If the patient appears septic.
    ◦ **Culture of Purulent Discharge:** Gram stain and culture of expressed pus from the duct can guide antibiotic therapy, especially for non-responders or hospital-acquired infections.
sections.treatment:
• **Antibiotics:**
    ◦ Must cover **_S. aureus_** and oral **anaerobes**.
    ◦ **Outpatient (Mild cases):** Oral antibiotics.
        ▪ **Dicloxacillin** 500 mg QID
        ▪ **Clindamycin** 300-450 mg QID (good anaerobic coverage, alternative for penicillin allergy)
        ▪ **Amoxicillin-clavulanate (Augmentin)** 875 mg BID
    ◦ **Inpatient (Severe cases, toxic appearance, unable to tolerate PO):** IV antibiotics.
        ▪ **Nafcillin** or **Oxacillin** + **Metronidazole** or **Clindamycin**.
        ▪ **Vancomycin** if **MRSA** is suspected or prevalent.
• **Supportive Care (Crucial):**
    ◦ **Hydration:** Aggressive intravenous or oral rehydration to promote salivary flow.
    ◦ **Sialogogues:** Measures to stimulate saliva production and flush the ducts.
        ▪ Examples: Lemon drops, tart candies, vitamin C lozenges, chewing gum.
    ◦ **Gland Massage & Warm Compresses:** Applied to the affected area.
    ◦ **Analgesia:** NSAIDs or opioids for pain control.
    ◦ **Oral Hygiene:** Encourage regular tooth brushing and mouth rinsing.
sections.management:
• **Admission Criteria:** Dehydration, sepsis, inability to tolerate oral intake, immunosuppression, or failure to improve on outpatient therapy.
• **Surgical Intervention:**
    ◦ **Incision and Drainage (I&D):** Required if a discrete abscess is identified on ultrasound or CT. Usually performed by an otolaryngologist (ENT).
• **Follow-up:** Patients should be re-evaluated in 24-48 hours to ensure clinical improvement. If no improvement, consider imaging and broadening antibiotic coverage.
• **Recurrent Sialadenitis:** Investigate for an underlying cause such as an obstructing stone, ductal stricture, or autoimmune disease.
sections.complications:
• **Abscess formation** (most common)
• **Sepsis** and bacteremia
• **Osteomyelitis** of the mandible
• **Ductal stricture or fistula**
• **Ludwig's Angina:** Spread of infection from the submandibular gland to the sublingual and submylohyoid spaces, causing elevation of the tongue and potential airway compromise (a **medical emergency**).
• **Lemierre's Syndrome:** Septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein.
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent for most patients with prompt and appropriate treatment.
• Morbidity and mortality are significantly higher in elderly, immunocompromised, or medically frail patients, especially if treatment is delayed.

sections.overview:
• **Chronic Sialadenitis** is a condition characterized by **recurrent or persistent inflammation** of a salivary gland, most commonly the **parotid or submandibular glands**.
    ◦ The chronic inflammation leads to **progressive, irreversible damage** to the gland's functional tissue (acini), resulting in **ductal ectasia (dilation)**, **strictures**, and **parenchymal fibrosis**.
    ◦ This process impairs salivary function, leading to symptoms of **pain**, **swelling**, and often **xerostomia**.
sections.etiology:
• The underlying pathophysiology involves a cycle of **ductal obstruction**, **salivary stasis**, and **inflammation**.
    ◦ **Hyposecretion & Stasis**: Reduced salivary flow is the initial trigger, which can be caused by dehydration, medications, or systemic disease.
    ◦ **Obstruction**: Salivary stasis promotes the formation of microliths, mucus plugs, or stones (**sialolithiasis**), which obstruct the salivary duct. Ductal strictures from prior inflammation or trauma can also cause obstruction.
    ◦ **Inflammation & Infection**: Stagnant saliva is an excellent culture medium for bacteria. Retrograde migration of oral flora (e.g., ***Staphylococcus aureus***, ***Streptococcus viridans***) up the duct leads to infection and inflammation.
    ◦ **Repetitive Cycle**: Each inflammatory episode causes further damage to the ducts and acini, leading to scarring, fibrosis, and more strictures. This worsens the obstruction and stasis, creating a vicious cycle of recurrent inflammation.
    ◦ **Glandular Destruction**: Over time, this cycle leads to **acinar atrophy** (loss of saliva-producing cells) and replacement with fibrous tissue, permanently reducing gland function.
• **Specific Causes**:
    ◦ **Obstructive**:
        ▪ **Sialolithiasis (Salivary Stones)**: Most common cause, especially in the submandibular gland (**Wharton's duct**).
        ▪ **Ductal Strictures**: From prior infection, trauma, or surgery.
        ▪ **Mucous Plugs**.
    ◦ **Non-Obstructive**:
        ▪ **Autoimmune Disease**: **Sjögren's syndrome** is a classic cause, leading to lymphocytic infiltration and destruction of the glands.
        ▪ **IgG4-Related Disease**: Causes a fibroinflammatory condition, leading to **chronic sclerosing sialadenitis (Küttner's tumor)**, which can mimic a neoplasm.
        ▪ **Post-Radiation**: Radiation therapy for head and neck cancers damages salivary glands, causing fibrosis and xerostomia.
        ▪ **Radioactive Iodine (RAI) Therapy**: Used for thyroid cancer, can cause "**RAI Sialadenitis**."
        ▪ **Juvenile Recurrent Parotitis**: An idiopathic, recurrent inflammatory condition in children.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Most common in adults aged 40-70.
• **Gland Involvement**: **Parotid** and **submandibular** glands are most frequently affected.
• **Specific Populations**:
    ◦ **Sjögren's Syndrome-associated**: Predominantly affects middle-aged females.
    ◦ **Chronic Sclerosing Sialadenitis (Küttner's tumor)**: Typically affects middle-aged to older males.
    ◦ **Juvenile Recurrent Parotitis**: Affects children, usually resolving after puberty.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents with a history of **recurrent episodes** of **unilateral gland swelling and pain** that may last for hours to weeks.
    ◦ These episodes are often **triggered by meals**, which stimulate salivary flow against an obstruction.
    ◦ Between acute flare-ups, the gland may remain **firm, enlarged, and mildly tender**.
    ◦ Over time, the frequency and severity of episodes may increase, while the functional capacity of the gland decreases.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Often made based on history and physical exam findings.
• **Imaging** (Crucial for confirmation and identifying cause):
    ◦ **Ultrasound (US)**: Excellent initial test. Non-invasive and can identify stones (**sialoliths**), ductal dilation (**ectasia**), parenchymal heterogeneity (**fibrosis**), and **abscesses**.
    ◦ **CT Scan with Contrast**: Best for evaluating for an **abscess** or **deep neck space infection**. Can clearly visualize calcified stones and assess the extent of glandular involvement.
    ◦ **MRI**: Superior for soft tissue evaluation and differentiating inflammation from a **neoplasm**.
    ◦ **Sialography**: A historical gold standard, now less common. Involves cannulating the duct and injecting contrast to visualize the entire ductal system.
        ▪ Classic findings include **"sausage-link" appearance** (alternating areas of ductal dilation and stricture).
    ◦ **Sialendoscopy**: A minimally invasive procedure where a micro-endoscope is inserted into the salivary duct.
        ▪ It is both **diagnostic** (direct visualization of stones, strictures, polyps) and **therapeutic** (stone removal, stricture dilation).
• **Lab Studies**:
    ◦ Generally non-specific. CBC may show **leukocytosis** during an acute bacterial flare.
    ◦ If autoimmune cause is suspected: Order **ANA**, **Anti-Ro/SSA**, **Anti-La/SSB** (for **Sjögren's**).
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is generally good for symptomatic control, although the underlying **glandular damage is irreversible**.
    ◦ Conservative measures are effective for many patients.
    ◦ For those with refractory disease, interventional or surgical procedures are often curative but carry procedural risks, particularly **nerve injury** with gland excision.

sections.overview:
• Sialolithiasis is the formation of calculi (stones) within the ductal system of a salivary gland.
• It is the most common non-neoplastic cause of salivary gland swelling.
• The obstruction of the salivary duct by a stone leads to stasis of saliva, which can cause intermittent painful swelling of the gland and predisposes it to secondary infection (**sialadenitis**).
sections.etiology:
• The exact etiology is not fully understood, but the pathogenesis involves **salivary stasis** and changes in salivary composition, leading to precipitation of mineral salts.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ **Nidus Formation**: A nidus, typically composed of desquamated epithelial cells, bacteria, mucus, or foreign bodies, forms within the duct.
    ◦ **Mineral Deposition**: Salivary stasis and altered saliva biochemistry (e.g., increased calcium concentration, alkaline pH) promote the deposition of organic and inorganic materials around the nidus.
    ◦ **Growth**: The stone grows in layers, gradually increasing in size and leading to partial or complete ductal obstruction.
• **Stone Composition**
    ◦ Primarily calcium phosphate and hydroxyapatite, with smaller amounts of magnesium, carbonate, and ammonia.
• **Anatomic & Physiologic Rationale for Submandibular Gland Predominance**
    ◦ **Wharton's Duct**: Is longer, wider, and has an **antigravity (upward) flow**, promoting stasis.
    ◦ **Submandibular Saliva**: Is more alkaline, has a higher concentration of calcium and phosphate, and is more mucoid (thicker) than saliva from other glands.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects approximately 1.2% of the population.
• **Peak Incidence**: Ages 30-60 years.
• **Gender**: Male-to-female ratio is approximately 2:1.
• **Gland Distribution**
    ◦ **Submandibular Gland (Wharton's Duct)**: Most common, accounting for **80-90%** of cases.
    ◦ **Parotid Gland (Stensen's Duct)**: Second most common, ~10-20%.
    ◦ **Sublingual & Minor Salivary Glands**: Rare, <2%.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is recurrent, **painful swelling** of the affected salivary gland, particularly associated with meals.
• **Classic Triad**
    ◦ **Post-prandial pain**
    ◦ **Post-prandial swelling**
    ◦ Intermittent symptoms
• The patient typically reports sudden onset of swelling and pain in the preauricular area (parotid) or submandibular triangle just before or during a meal, when salivary flow is stimulated.
• The swelling and pain usually subside gradually over 1-2 hours after the meal as the backed-up saliva is slowly released.
• If the obstruction becomes complete or a secondary infection (**sialadenitis**) develops, the pain and swelling become constant and more severe.
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is often made clinically, but imaging can confirm the presence, size, and location of the stone.
• **Ultrasound**
    ◦ **First-line imaging modality.**
    ◦ Non-invasive, no radiation, readily available.
    ◦ Highly sensitive for stones >2 mm.
    ◦ Appears as a **hyperechoic focus with posterior acoustic shadowing**.
    ◦ Can also show ductal dilation.
• **Non-Contrast CT Scan**
    ◦ Excellent for visualizing **calcified stones** and assessing the gland itself.
    ◦ Modality of choice to evaluate for a concurrent **abscess**.
    ◦ ~80% of submandibular stones and ~60% of parotid stones are radiopaque.
• **Plain X-rays (Mandibular occlusal view)**
    ◦ Can visualize **radiopaque stones** in the floor of the mouth.
    ◦ Limited utility as it misses radiolucent stones and stones outside the field of view.
• **Sialography**
    ◦ Involves injecting contrast into the duct. The stone appears as a **filling defect**.
    ◦ Both diagnostic and potentially therapeutic (can flush out small stones).
    ◦ **Contraindicated in acute infection** and largely replaced by ultrasound and CT.
• **Sialendoscopy**
    ◦ Allows for direct visualization of the ductal system.
    ◦ Can be both diagnostic and therapeutic (stone retrieval).
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is **excellent**.
• Over 90% of patients are successfully treated with conservative measures or minimally invasive procedures.
• Recurrence is possible (around 10-20%), but can be minimized by managing underlying risk factors like dehydration.

sections.overview:
• Parotitis is the inflammation of one or both parotid glands, the largest of the major salivary glands.
• "Non-mumps parotitis" refers to a heterogeneous group of conditions with various etiologies, including bacterial, other viral, autoimmune, and obstructive causes.
    ◦ The most common form in adults is **acute bacterial (suppurative) parotitis**, which is a serious infection requiring prompt diagnosis and treatment.
sections.etiology:
• The underlying pathophysiology typically involves reduced salivary flow (stasis) and retrograde seeding of bacteria from the oral cavity into the parotid gland via **Stensen's duct**.
• **Bacterial (Acute Suppurative Parotitis)**
    ◦ **Most Common Organism**: **Staphylococcus aureus** (including MRSA).
    ◦ **Other Organisms**: *Streptococcus spp.*, *Haemophilus influenzae*, oral anaerobes (*Peptostreptococcus*, *Bacteroides*).
    ◦ **Pathophysiology**: Salivary stasis allows for ascending infection from the oral flora up Stensen's duct, leading to inflammation, suppuration, and potential abscess formation.
• **Viral**
    ◦ Causes are less common than mumps but include: Influenza A, Parainfluenza, Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV), Coxsackievirus, Cytomegalovirus (CMV), and Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV).
    ◦ **HIV-associated parotitis** often presents as bilateral, cystic enlargement (lymphoepithelial cysts).
• **Obstructive (Sialadenitis secondary to Sialolithiasis)**
    ◦ A calculus (sialolith) forms within Stensen's duct, obstructing salivary flow.
    ◦ This stasis leads to painful glandular swelling, especially with meals (salivatory stimulus), and creates a nidus for secondary bacterial infection.
• **Autoimmune**
    ◦ **Sjögren's Syndrome**: Chronic autoimmune disorder characterized by lymphocytic infiltration of exocrine glands, leading to dry mouth (xerostomia) and dry eyes (keratoconjunctivitis sicca). Presents as firm, chronic, often bilateral, and less tender parotid enlargement.
• **Granulomatous**
    ◦ Rare causes include Tuberculosis (TB), sarcoidosis (**Heerfordt's syndrome**: uveitis, parotitis, fever, facial palsy), and cat-scratch disease.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Acute Bacterial Parotitis**: Most common in the **elderly**, **debilitated**, **dehydrated**, and **post-operative** patients (typically within 2 weeks of surgery). It is the most common cause of infectious parotitis in adults today.
• **Viral Parotitis**: Can affect any age group, dependent on the specific virus.
• **Sjögren's Syndrome**: Predominantly affects middle-aged females (9:1 female-to-male ratio).
sections.clinicalPresentation: • The "classic" patient with acute bacterial parotitis is an **elderly**, **post-operative**, or **dehydrated** individual who develops **sudden onset of unilateral facial swelling and pain**.
sections.diagnostics:
• Primarily a **clinical diagnosis**.
• **Labs**
    ◦ **CBC**: Leukocytosis with a left shift is common.
    ◦ **Blood Cultures**: Indicated if the patient appears septic.
    ◦ **Serum Amylase**: May be elevated due to salivary gland inflammation (distinguish from pancreatitis).
    ◦ **Culture**: A sample of purulent material from Stensen's duct should be sent for Gram stain, culture, and sensitivity to guide antibiotic therapy.
• **Imaging** (used to confirm diagnosis or evaluate for complications)
    ◦ **Ultrasound (US)**: Excellent initial imaging test.
        ▪ Can differentiate between cellulitis, a phlegmon, and a drainable abscess.
        ▪ Can also identify sialoliths.
    ◦ **CT with IV Contrast**: **Test of choice** to confirm the diagnosis, define the extent of inflammation, and identify an abscess or deep neck space infection.
sections.prognosis:
• With prompt antibiotic therapy and supportive care, the prognosis is generally excellent.
• Recurrence is possible if underlying risk factors (e.g., dehydration, poor oral hygiene, obstructive stone) are not corrected.
• Mortality is low but increases in the presence of sepsis or significant comorbidities.

sections.overview:
• **Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA)** is a sleep-related breathing disorder characterized by repetitive episodes of complete (**apnea**) or partial (**hypopnea**) upper airway obstruction during sleep.
    ◦ These events lead to intermittent **hypoxemia**, **hypercapnia**, **sleep fragmentation**, and surges in sympathetic nervous system activity.
• From an Ear, Nose, and Throat (ENT) perspective, OSA is primarily a disease of upper airway anatomy, where specific sites of narrowing or collapse contribute to the obstruction.
sections.etiology:
• The core pathophysiology involves a combination of two factors:
    ◦ **Anatomical Narrowing**: A congenitally or acquired small upper airway.
    ◦ **Loss of Pharyngeal Muscle Tone**: A normal physiologic event during REM sleep that, in a susceptible individual, allows the narrowed airway to collapse.
• **The Apneic Cycle**:
    ◦ Airway collapse → Respiratory effort against obstruction → ↓O2, ↑CO2 → Sympathetic surge (↑HR, ↑BP) → Cortical arousal (micro-awakening) → Airway muscle tone restored, airway opens (often with a gasp/snort) → Patient falls back asleep → Cycle repeats.
• **ENT-Specific Sites of Obstruction** (Can be single-level or multi-level):
    ◦ **Nasal Cavity**:
        ▪ **Deviated nasal septum**
        ▪ **Inferior turbinate hypertrophy**
        ▪ **Nasal valve collapse**
        ▪ **Nasal polyps**
    ◦ **Nasopharynx**:
        ▪ **Adenoid hypertrophy** (a primary cause in children)
    ◦ **Oropharynx (Velopharynx)**:
        ▪ Redundant or elongated **soft palate** and **uvula**
        ▪ **Tonsillar hypertrophy** (a primary cause in children, significant in adults)
        ▪ Lateral pharyngeal wall collapse
    ◦ **Hypopharynx (Tongue Base)**:
        ▪ **Macroglossia** (enlarged tongue)
        ▪ **Retrognathia** or **micrognathia** (jaw positioned posteriorly, causing tongue base to fall back)
        ▪ Lingual tonsil hypertrophy
        ▪ **Epiglottic collapse** (floppy epiglottis)
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects an estimated 9-38% of the general adult population.
• Prevalence increases with **age** and **obesity**.
• More common in **men** than women (approx. 2:1 to 4:1 ratio) until menopause, after which the gap narrows.
• Significantly **underdiagnosed**.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a middle-aged, **overweight male** whose partner reports loud, disruptive **snoring** with periods of silence followed by **gasps**.
• The patient's chief complaint is often **excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS)** that interferes with daily function, work, or driving.
    ◦ They may be unaware of the nighttime events.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Polysomnography (PSG)**: The **gold standard** for diagnosis.
    ◦ An overnight, in-lab sleep study that measures:
        ▪ **EEG** (sleep staging)
        ▪ **EOG** (eye movements)
        ▪ **EMG** (muscle tone)
        ▪ Airflow, respiratory effort, oxygen saturation (**SaO2**), ECG.
• **Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI)**: The number of apneas and hypopneas per hour of sleep.
    ◦ Used to grade severity:
        ▪ **Normal**: < 5 events/hour
        ▪ **Mild OSA**: 5 - 15 events/hour
        ▪ **Moderate OSA**: 15 - 30 events/hour
        ▪ **Severe OSA**: > 30 events/hour
• **Home Sleep Apnea Test (HSAT)**: A simplified, portable monitor for uncomplicated patients with high suspicion for moderate-to-severe OSA.
    ◦ Measures airflow, effort, and **SaO2**.
• **Screening Questionnaires**:
    ◦ **Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS)**: Quantifies daytime sleepiness.
        ▪ Score >10 suggests significant sleepiness.
    ◦ **STOP-BANG Questionnaire**: Screens for high risk of OSA (**S**noring, **T**iredness, **O**bserved apnea, **P**ressure (high BP), **B**MI, **A**ge, **N**eck size, **G**ender).
sections.prognosis:
• Excellent with consistent and effective treatment (e.g., high **CPAP adherence**).
    ◦ Patients experience improved quality of life, reduced daytime sleepiness, and decreased risk of long-term complications.
• Untreated moderate-to-severe OSA is associated with significantly increased **all-cause mortality**.

sections.overview:
• **Oral Cavity Squamous Cell Carcinoma (OCSCC)** is a malignancy arising from the **squamous epithelium** of the **oral mucosa**.
    ◦ It represents over 90% of all oral cancers.
    ◦ The oral cavity includes the lips, buccal mucosa, floor of the mouth, gingiva, hard palate, and the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
    ◦ OCSCC is a significant subtype of **head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC)**.
    ◦ Early detection is critical as advanced disease is associated with high morbidity and mortality.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**
    ◦ Primarily caused by chronic exposure to carcinogens, leading to genetic and epigenetic alterations in the oral mucosa.
        ▪ The most significant carcinogens are **tobacco** and **alcohol**.
        ▪ **Human Papillomavirus (HPV)**, particularly type 16, is a known cause, though it is more strongly associated with *oropharyngeal* SCC than OCSCC.
• **Pathophysiology**
    ◦ The development follows a multi-step process of carcinogenesis:
        ▪ **Hyperplasia**: Increased cell proliferation in response to chronic irritation/carcinogens.
        ▪ **Dysplasia**: Pre-cancerous, disordered cell growth and maturation. Clinically may appear as **leukoplakia** (white patch) or **erythroplakia** (red patch).
        ▪ **Carcinoma in situ (CIS)**: Full-thickness dysplasia of the epithelium without invasion of the basement membrane.
        ▪ **Invasive Squamous Cell Carcinoma**: Malignant cells breach the basement membrane and invade the underlying lamina propria, submucosa, muscle, and bone.
    ◦ Metastasis occurs primarily via the **lymphatic system** to cervical lymph nodes.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Accounts for approximately 3% of all cancers in the United States.
• **Demographics**: Primarily a disease of older adults, with a median age at diagnosis of ~64 years.
• **Sex**: Historically, much more common in men (Male:Female ratio was ~6:1). The gap is narrowing due to changes in smoking habits, with the ratio now closer to 2:1.
• **Geography**: Higher incidence in South and Southeast Asia due to the prevalent use of **betel quid (paan)** and **areca nut**.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Major Risk Factors**
    ◦ **Tobacco Use**: Cigarettes, cigars, pipes, and especially **smokeless tobacco (chewing tobacco/snuff)**. Risk is dose- and duration-dependent.
    ◦ **Alcohol Consumption**: Heavy alcohol use is a major independent risk factor.
    ◦ **Synergistic Effect**: Tobacco and alcohol together have a multiplicative, not additive, effect on risk (risk increases >15-fold).
• **Other Significant Risk Factors**
    ◦ **Human Papillomavirus (HPV)**: Primarily HPV-16. More strongly linked to oropharyngeal cancer but is a recognized risk for OCSCC.
    ◦ **Betel Quid/Areca Nut Chewing**: A major cause in Asia.
    ◦ **Sun Exposure**: Key risk factor for SCC of the **vermilion border of the lip**.
    ◦ **Poor Oral Hygiene** and chronic dental inflammation.
    ◦ **Chronic Irritation**: From ill-fitting dentures or jagged teeth.
    ◦ **Immunosuppression**: Organ transplant recipients, HIV/AIDS.
    ◦ **Diet**: Low intake of fruits and vegetables.
    ◦ **Precursor Lesions**: History of leukoplakia or erythroplakia.
    ◦ **Genetic Syndromes**: Fanconi anemia, Plummer-Vinson syndrome.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients often present with a persistent, non-healing lesion in the mouth.
    ◦ The presentation can be subtle initially and is often **painless**, leading to delays in diagnosis.
• **High-risk locations** for malignancy within the oral cavity include the **ventrolateral tongue** and the **floor of the mouth**.
• Presentation may also be an asymptomatic **neck mass**, representing a nodal metastasis.
• **Early Symptoms**
    ◦ A non-healing sore or ulcer (>2-3 weeks).
    ◦ A persistent red patch (**erythroplakia**) or white patch (**leukoplakia**).
    ◦ A lump or thickening in the cheek or on the gums.
• **Late Symptoms**
    ◦ **Oral pain** or **odynophagia** (pain on swallowing).
    ◦ **Dysphagia** (difficulty swallowing).
    ◦ Unexplained bleeding in the mouth.
    ◦ Loose teeth or poorly fitting dentures.
    ◦ **Trismus** (lockjaw), indicating invasion into the muscles of mastication.
    ◦ **Dysarthria** (difficulty speaking), often from tongue involvement.
    ◦ **Referred otalgia** (ear pain) via CN IX or X.
    ◦ Unexplained weight loss.
    ◦ A palpable, firm neck mass.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Inspection of the Lesion**
    ◦ **Appearance**: May be **exophytic** (growing outward), **endophytic** (growing inward/ulcerated), or a flat patch.
    ◦ **Color**: Can be red (**erythroplakic**), white (**leukoplakic**), or mixed (**erythroleukoplakia**). Erythroplakia has the highest malignant potential.
    ◦ **Borders**: Typically **irregular** and **indurated** (hardened).
    ◦ **Surface**: Often **friable** (bleeds easily on contact).
• **Palpation**
    ◦ **Lesion**: **Induration** (firmness) of the lesion and surrounding tissue is a hallmark of malignancy.
    ◦ **Local Invasion**: Assess for fixation to underlying structures like the mandible or tongue musculature.
    ◦ **Cervical Lymphadenopathy**: Meticulously palpate all cervical lymph node levels (submental, submandibular, jugular chains). Malignant nodes are typically **hard, non-tender, and fixed** (immobile).
• **Cranial Nerve Exam**
    ◦ Assess for deficits, particularly **CN XII** (tongue deviation away from the lesion) and **CN VII** (facial muscle weakness).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Definitive Diagnosis**
    ◦ **Incisional or Punch Biopsy**: **This is the gold standard.**
        ▪ An adequate sample including underlying stromal tissue is required to assess for invasion.
        ▪ Brush biopsy is for screening only and is insufficient for definitive diagnosis.
• **Staging Workup (to determine the T, N, and M stages)**
    ◦ **CT Scan with Contrast (Neck)**: Best for evaluating **bony invasion** (e.g., mandible) and for detecting and characterizing **cervical lymph node metastases**.
    ◦ **MRI**: Superior for evaluating **soft tissue extent**, **perineural invasion**, and **tongue infiltration**.
    ◦ **Chest Imaging (CT Chest)**: To rule out synchronous lung primary or **pulmonary metastases** (the most common site of distant spread).
    ◦ **PET/CT Scan**: Increasingly used for advanced stages to detect unknown primary tumors, regional and distant metastases, and to assess for treatment response.
    ◦ **Panendoscopy**: Examination under anesthesia including laryngoscopy, esophagoscopy, and sometimes bronchoscopy to rule out **synchronous primary tumors** in the upper aerodigestive tract, which occur in 10-15% of patients.
sections.treatment:
• Treatment is complex and managed by a **multidisciplinary team** (Head & Neck Surgeon, Radiation Oncologist, Medical Oncologist, Dentist, Speech Pathologist).
• Treatment modality depends on the **stage, location, and patient factors**.
• **Early Stage (I & II - small tumor, no nodes)**
    ◦ **Single-modality therapy**: Typically **surgical excision** with adequate margins OR **definitive radiation therapy**.
        ▪ Surgery is often preferred for resectable oral cavity lesions.
• **Advanced Stage (III & IV - large tumor and/or positive nodes)**
    ◦ **Combined-modality therapy**:
        ▪ **Surgery followed by adjuvant radiation therapy (RT) or chemoradiation (CRT)**. This is the most common approach.
            ▪ Adjuvant therapy is given for high-risk features like **positive margins**, **extracapsular extension (ECE)** in nodes, or perineural invasion.
        ▪ **Definitive Chemoradiation**: For patients who are poor surgical candidates or have unresectable disease.
sections.management:
• **Pre-treatment**
    ◦ Dental clearance is mandatory to prevent osteoradionecrosis.
    ◦ Nutritional assessment and possible G-tube placement.
    ◦ Smoking and alcohol cessation counseling.
• **Post-treatment Surveillance**
    ◦ Regular follow-up every 1-3 months for the first year, with decreasing frequency thereafter.
    ◦ Includes complete head and neck exam and flexible laryngoscopy.
    ◦ Imaging (CT/PET) as clinically indicated for suspicion of recurrence.
• **Supportive Care**
    ◦ **Speech and Swallow Therapy**: Crucial for rehabilitation.
    ◦ **Nutritional Support**: Diet modification, supplements.
    ◦ **Pain Management**.
    ◦ **Management of Treatment Toxicities**: **Xerostomia** (dry mouth), **mucositis**, **trismus**.
sections.complications:
• **From Disease**
    ◦ Local invasion into bone, nerves, and muscle.
    ◦ Regional metastasis to cervical lymph nodes.
    ◦ Distant metastasis (most commonly to lungs, liver, bone).
    ◦ Airway compromise, malnutrition, pain.
• **From Treatment**
    ◦ **Surgery**: Scarring, disfigurement, impaired speech/swallowing, nerve damage (e.g., spinal accessory nerve, marginal mandibular nerve).
    ◦ **Radiation**: **Xerostomia** (dry mouth), **mucositis**, **osteoradionecrosis of the mandible**, fibrosis, trismus, dental caries.
    ◦ **Chemotherapy**: Systemic side effects (nausea, fatigue, myelosuppression, nephrotoxicity).
sections.prognosis:
• The **stage at diagnosis** is the single most important prognostic factor.
• **Nodal involvement** significantly worsens prognosis. The presence of **extracapsular extension (ECE)** is a particularly poor prognostic sign.
• **5-Year Overall Survival Rates (approximate)**
    ◦ Stage I: >85%
    ◦ Stage II: 65-80%
    ◦ Stage III: 45-65%
    ◦ Stage IV: <40%
• Unlike oropharyngeal cancer, HPV status does not confer the same strong positive prognostic benefit in OCSCC.

sections.overview:
• Oropharyngeal carcinoma is a malignancy arising from the tissues of the oropharynx, which includes the tonsils, base of the tongue, soft palate, and posterior pharyngeal walls.
    ◦ The vast majority (>95%) of these cancers are **Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)**.
    ◦ There are two distinct etiologic pathways:
        ▪ One driven by infection with high-risk **Human Papillomavirus (HPV)**.
        ▪ The other associated with traditional risk factors like tobacco and alcohol.
    ◦ These two pathways result in clinically, biologically, and prognostically different diseases.
    ◦ **HPV-positive (HPV+)** disease now accounts for the majority (~70%) of cases in developed nations and carries a significantly better prognosis.
sections.etiology:
• There are two primary, distinct molecular pathways:
    ◦ **HPV-Positive Oropharyngeal SCC (OPSCC)**
        ▪ **Causative Agent**: Primarily **high-risk HPV type 16** (>90% of cases), and less commonly HPV-18.
        ▪ **Mechanism**:
            ▪ The virus integrates its DNA into the host epithelial cell genome.
            ▪ It expresses two key viral oncoproteins: **E6** and **E7**.
            ▪ **E6 Oncoprotein**: Binds to and promotes the degradation of the **p53 tumor suppressor protein**, blocking apoptosis and allowing for DNA damage accumulation.
            ▪ **E7 Oncoprotein**: Binds to and promotes the degradation of the **retinoblastoma (pRb) tumor suppressor protein**, leading to uncontrolled cell proliferation.
        ▪ **p16 Overexpression**: The inactivation of pRb by E7 disrupts a negative feedback loop, leading to the marked **overexpression of p16INK4a**. This is so consistent that **p16 immunohistochemistry (IHC)** is used as a highly reliable surrogate marker for a transcriptionally active HPV infection.
    ◦ **HPV-Negative OPSCC**
        ▪ **Causative Agents**: Chronic exposure to carcinogens, primarily tobacco and alcohol.
        ▪ **Mechanism**:
            ▪ A stepwise accumulation of multiple genetic and epigenetic mutations.
            ▪ Common mutations include inactivation of the **TP53 tumor suppressor gene** (distinct from E6-mediated degradation in HPV+ disease).
            ▪ This pathway often involves progression from dysplasia to carcinoma in situ to invasive carcinoma.
            ▪ These tumors are genetically more unstable and complex than their HPV+ counterparts.
sections.epidemiology:
• A tale of two diseases with diverging trends:
    ◦ **HPV-Positive OPSCC**
        ▪ Incidence is **rapidly increasing**, reaching epidemic proportions in North America and Europe.
        ▪ Represents **>70% of all new oropharyngeal cancers** in the US.
        ▪ Typically affects a **younger demographic** (ages 40-60).
        ▪ More common in males (3:1 to 4:1 ratio).
        ▪ Often occurs in patients with no history of significant tobacco or alcohol use.
    ◦ **HPV-Negative OPSCC**
        ▪ Incidence is **decreasing** in developed countries, paralleling the decline in smoking rates.
        ▪ Typically affects an **older demographic** (ages 60-80).
        ▪ Strongly associated with a long history of heavy tobacco and alcohol use.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The initial presentation is often subtle. The classic patient for **HPV+** disease is a healthy, non-smoking male in his 50s who presents with a persistent, **painless neck mass**.
    ◦ **Most Common Presentation (especially HPV+)**: A persistent, non-tender **cervical neck mass** representing nodal metastasis.
        ▪ The primary oropharyngeal tumor may be small, asymptomatic, and difficult to visualize.
        ▪ HPV+ nodal metastases are frequently **cystic**.
    ◦ **Local Symptoms**: A persistent, **unilateral sore throat** or a foreign body sensation in the throat that does not resolve.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Biopsy (Definitive Diagnosis)**
    ◦ **Fine-Needle Aspiration (FNA)**: Often the first step for a suspicious neck mass. Can confirm metastatic SCC and provide tissue for p16 testing.
    ◦ **Incisional or Excisional Biopsy**: Required for the primary tumor, typically performed in the operating room during a panendoscopy.
• **Histopathology & HPV Testing**
    ◦ All oropharyngeal SCC biopsies must be tested for HPV status.
    ◦ **p16 Immunohistochemistry (IHC)**: The standard, widely available surrogate marker. Strong, diffuse nuclear and cytoplasmic staining is considered positive.
• **Staging Workup (To determine the extent of disease)**
    ◦ **CT with contrast (Neck)**: Excellent for evaluating bone invasion, tumor extent, and identifying necrotic or enlarged lymph nodes.
    ◦ **PET/CT (Whole Body)**: The standard for initial staging. Identifies the primary tumor, regional nodal metastasis, and distant metastases. Also used to assess treatment response.
    ◦ **MRI**: May be superior to CT for delineating soft tissue involvement, particularly at the base of the tongue and for perineural invasion.
    ◦ **Panendoscopy**: Examination under anesthesia (direct laryngoscopy, esophagoscopy, bronchoscopy) to fully evaluate the primary tumor, obtain biopsies, and rule out synchronous primary cancers (more common in the HPV-negative population).
sections.prognosis:
• **HPV status is the single most powerful prognostic factor.** The AJCC 8th Edition Cancer Staging Manual created separate staging systems for p16-positive and p16-negative disease to reflect this.
    ◦ **HPV-Positive OPSCC**
        ▪ **Excellent prognosis**; highly sensitive to both radiation and chemotherapy.
        ▪ 3-year overall survival: **~85-90%**.
    ◦ **HPV-Negative OPSCC**
        ▪ Significantly **poorer prognosis**; more resistant to treatment.
        ▪ 3-year overall survival: **~45-50%**.

sections.overview:
• Laryngeal carcinoma is a malignancy arising from the tissues of the larynx (voice box) and is a subset of head and neck cancers
	◦ The vast majority (>90%) of laryngeal cancers are **squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)**, originating from the epithelial lining
	◦ The larynx is anatomically divided into three regions, and tumor location significantly impacts symptoms, prognosis, and treatment:
		▪ **Glottis**: The true vocal cords (most common site, ~60%)
		▪ **Supraglottis**: Area above the vocal cords, including the epiglottis and false cords (~35%)
		▪ **Subglottis**: Area below the vocal cords, extending to the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage (rarest site, ~5%)
sections.etiology:
• The primary driver of laryngeal SCC is chronic irritation and inflammation of the laryngeal mucosa, leading to a sequence of cellular changes
	◦ **Carcinogen Exposure**: Toxins, primarily from tobacco smoke and alcohol, damage cellular DNA
	◦ **Cellular Progression**: This damage initiates a progression from normal epithelium to **hyperplasia** and **dysplasia** (premalignant lesions like leukoplakia or erythroplakia)
	◦ **Malignant Transformation**: Accumulation of genetic mutations (e.g., in tumor suppressor genes like **TP53**) leads to **carcinoma in situ** (full-thickness dysplasia without basement membrane invasion) and finally to **invasive squamous cell carcinoma**
	◦ **Metastasis**: The tumor can spread via direct local invasion, lymphatic drainage to cervical lymph nodes, and hematogenous spread to distant sites (most commonly the lungs)
		▪ Supraglottic tumors have rich lymphatic drainage and a high rate of early nodal metastasis
		▪ Glottic tumors have sparse lymphatics, leading to later metastasis
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Represents ~1% of all new cancer diagnoses in the U.S.
• **Age**: Primarily a disease of older adults, with a peak incidence between ages 50 and 70
• **Sex**: Historically a strong male predominance (10:1), but the ratio is decreasing (~4:1) as smoking rates in women have increased
• **Trends**: Overall incidence is decreasing in the U.S., mirroring the decline in tobacco use
sections.riskFactors:
• **Tobacco Use**: The single most important risk factor. Risk is dose- and duration-dependent.
• **Alcohol Consumption**: Synergistic effect with tobacco; together they increase risk more than 15-fold.
• **Human Papillomavirus (HPV)**: A minor risk factor for laryngeal cancer compared to its strong association with oropharyngeal cancer.
• **Occupational Exposure**: Asbestos, wood dust, paint fumes, mustard gas, nickel, sulfuric acid mist.
• **Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)**: Chronic acid exposure may contribute to inflammation and dysplasia.
• **Poor Nutrition**: Diet low in fruits and vegetables.
• **Genetic Predisposition**: Rare genetic syndromes (e.g., Fanconi anemia).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The "classic" patient is a 65-year-old male with a significant smoking and drinking history who presents with persistent hoarseness
	◦ The specific presentation depends heavily on the tumor's subsite
sections.physicalExam:
• **Comprehensive Head and Neck Exam**:
	◦ **Cervical Lymphadenopathy**: Palpate for firm, fixed, non-tender lymph nodes, which suggest metastatic disease. Note the level and size.
	◦ **Laryngeal Crepitus**: Gently palpate and move the larynx side-to-side over the cervical spine. Loss of the normal "clicking" or "grating" sensation suggests post-cricoid or prevertebral space invasion.
• **Laryngoscopy**:
	◦ **Flexible Nasolaryngoscopy (in-office)**: Initial visualization of the larynx to identify suspicious lesions (e.g., ulcerative mass, exophytic growth, leukoplakia, erythroplakia) and assess vocal cord mobility.
	◦ **Direct Laryngoscopy (in OR)**: Performed under general anesthesia for complete tumor visualization, mapping, and biopsy. Allows for palpation of the tumor base.
sections.diagnostics:
• **History and Physical**: As detailed above.
• **Laryngoscopy with Biopsy**: This is the **gold standard for diagnosis**.
	◦ A tissue sample is taken during direct laryngoscopy and sent for histopathologic confirmation.
• **Staging Workup (Imaging)**: Determines the extent of the disease (TNM staging).
	◦ **CT with Contrast (Neck)**: The primary imaging modality. Assesses tumor size, local invasion (especially cartilage), and cervical lymph node involvement.
	◦ **CT (Chest)**: Standard of care to rule out synchronous lung primary or pulmonary metastases (the most common site of distant spread).
	◦ **PET/CT Scan**: Often used for advanced-stage disease (Stage III/IV) to detect distant metastases or an unknown primary tumor, and to assess treatment response.
sections.treatment:
• **Early Stage (I-II) / Carcinoma in situ**: **Single-modality therapy**.
	◦ **Radiation Therapy (XRT)**: Excellent cure rates with voice preservation.
	◦ **Transoral Endoscopic Surgery**: Transoral Laser Microsurgery (TLM) or transoral robotic surgery (TORS) to resect the tumor while preserving the larynx.
	◦ *Choice between XRT and surgery depends on tumor specifics and patient preference; outcomes are similar.*
• **Locally Advanced Stage (III-IVa)**: **Combined-modality therapy**.
	◦ **Chemoradiation (CRT)**: The **standard of care for larynx preservation**. Concurrent chemotherapy (typically cisplatin) acts as a radiosensitizer to improve the effectiveness of radiation.
	◦ **Total Laryngectomy**: Surgical removal of the entire larynx. Reserved for very large tumors with cartilage destruction, a non-functional larynx prior to treatment, or as salvage therapy after failed chemoradiation. Results in loss of natural voice and a permanent tracheostoma.
	◦ **Induction Chemotherapy**: Chemotherapy given before CRT, used in select cases to shrink the tumor.
• **Metastatic / Recurrent Disease (IVb, IVc)**: **Palliative intent**.
	◦ **Systemic Therapy**: Chemotherapy, Immunotherapy (e.g., Pembrolizumab), or Targeted Therapy.
	◦ **Palliative radiation** for symptom control (e.g., pain, bleeding).
sections.management:
• **Pre-treatment**: Dental evaluation, nutritional assessment (possible G-tube placement), smoking and alcohol cessation counseling.
• **Post-treatment Surveillance**: Regular follow-up with physical exams, laryngoscopy, and imaging for 5 years to monitor for recurrence.
• **Rehabilitation**: Crucial for quality of life.
	◦ **Speech Therapy**: Voice rehabilitation after laryngectomy (**tracheoesophageal puncture (TEP)**, electrolarynx, esophageal speech). Swallowing therapy (dysphagia is common after CRT).
	◦ **Physical/Occupational Therapy**: Management of neck fibrosis and shoulder dysfunction.
	◦ **Nutritional Support**: Managing diet and hydration, especially with dysphagia and xerostomia.
sections.complications:
• **From Disease**:
	◦ **Airway Obstruction**: Can be a medical emergency requiring tracheotomy.
	◦ Aspiration Pneumonia
	◦ Metastatic Spread
• **From Treatment**:
	◦ **Radiation**: **Xerostomia** (dry mouth), **mucositis**, dysphagia, skin changes (radiation dermatitis), neck fibrosis, hypothyroidism, osteoradionecrosis of the mandible/larynx.
	◦ **Surgery**:
		▪ **Laryngectomy**: Permanent tracheostoma, loss of natural voice, pharyngocutaneous fistula, dysphagia.
		▪ **Endoscopic Surgery**: Bleeding, dysphonia, aspiration.
	◦ **Chemotherapy**: Nausea/vomiting, nephrotoxicity (cisplatin), myelosuppression, neuropathy.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is primarily dependent on the **stage at diagnosis** and the **tumor subsite**.
	◦ **Glottic Cancer**: **Best prognosis**. Presents early due to hoarseness when the tumor is small (T1/T2) and has a low rate of nodal metastasis. 5-year survival for Stage I is >90%.
	◦ **Supraglottic/Subglottic Cancer**: **Worse prognosis**. Presents at a later stage, often with nodal metastasis already present.
• **Overall 5-Year Survival**:
	◦ Stage I: ~90%
	◦ Stage II: ~70%
	◦ Stage III: ~55%
	◦ Stage IV: ~30%

sections.overview:
• A malignant tumor arising from the epithelial lining of the nasopharynx, the area behind the nose and above the back of the throat.
• Distinct from other head and neck squamous cell carcinomas due to its unique epidemiology, strong association with **Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV)**, and high radiosensitivity.
• The most common site of origin within the nasopharynx is the fossa of Rosenmüller.
• NPC frequently presents with nodal metastasis, and a painless **neck mass** is often the first sign.
sections.etiology:
• The development of NPC is a multifactorial process involving viral, genetic, and environmental factors.
• **Viral**
    ◦ **Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV)** is the primary etiologic agent, particularly for the non-keratinizing subtypes (WHO Types II and III).
    ◦ The virus integrates into the nasopharyngeal epithelial cells, establishing a latent infection.
    ◦ Expression of viral oncoproteins (e.g., LMP1, LMP2) disrupts normal cell cycle control, promotes proliferation, and inhibits apoptosis, leading to malignant transformation.
• **Genetic Susceptibility**
    ◦ There is a strong genetic predisposition, evidenced by its prevalence in specific ethnic groups.
    ◦ Certain Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) haplotypes (e.g., HLA-A2) are associated with increased risk.
• **Environmental Factors**
    ◦ Dietary habits are a major contributor.
        ▪ Consumption of **salt-cured fish and preserved meats**, which are rich in volatile **nitrosamines**, is a well-established risk factor, especially with early childhood exposure.
    ◦ Tobacco smoking is a weaker risk factor compared to its role in other head and neck cancers.
• **Histological Classification (WHO)**
    ◦ **Type I:** Keratinizing Squamous Cell Carcinoma
        ▪ Less common, weaker association with EBV, similar behavior to other head and neck SCCs, poorer prognosis.
    ◦ **Type II:** Non-keratinizing Differentiated Carcinoma
        ▪ Intermediate features.
        ▪ Strong EBV association.
    ◦ **Type III:** Non-keratinizing Undifferentiated Carcinoma
        ▪ **Most common type**.
        ▪ Strongest association with EBV.
        ▪ Has a prominent lymphocytic infiltrate (sometimes called lymphoepithelioma).
        ▪ Most radiosensitive and has the best prognosis of the three types.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Geographic Distribution:** Endemic in **Southern China**, Southeast Asia, North Africa, and the Arctic (Inuit populations).
    ◦ It is rare in North America and Europe.
• **Age Distribution:** Bimodal peak:
    ◦ A smaller peak in adolescence/young adulthood (15-25 years).
    ◦ A larger peak in later adulthood (50-60 years).
• **Sex:** Male-to-female ratio is approximately 2-3:1.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• NPC often presents late because the primary tumor is in a clinically silent location.
• The presentation is classically described by a triad of symptoms related to local invasion and regional metastasis.
• **Most Common Presenting Sign (75%):** A painless, enlarging **cervical neck mass** representing metastatic lymphadenopathy.
    ◦ Nodes are typically in the upper jugular chain (Level II) and posterior cervical triangle (Level V).
• **Otologic Symptoms (50%):** Due to tumor obstruction of the Eustachian tube orifice.
• **Nasal Symptoms (45%):** Due to the primary tumor mass in the nasopharynx.
• **Neurologic Symptoms (20%):** Due to skull base invasion and involvement of cranial nerves.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Definitive Diagnosis:** **Endoscopic-guided biopsy** of the nasopharyngeal mass.
• **Laboratory Studies:**
    ◦ CBC, CMP.
    ◦ **Quantitative plasma EBV DNA:**
        ▪ This is a crucial biomarker.
        ▪ High levels are strongly associated with NPC.
        ▪ It is used for diagnosis, staging, monitoring treatment response, and detecting recurrence.
• **Imaging:**
    ◦ **MRI of the Head and Neck with contrast:**
        ▪ **Best modality for evaluating the primary tumor**, soft tissue extent, perineural spread, and intracranial invasion.
    ◦ **CT of the Head and Neck with contrast:**
        ▪ Superior for evaluating **bony erosion** of the skull base.
        ▪ Also used for initial evaluation and staging of the neck.
    ◦ **FDG-PET/CT Scan:**
        ▪ **Standard of care for staging**.
        ▪ It is the most sensitive test for detecting regional nodal involvement and distant metastases (bone, lung, liver).
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is **highly dependent on the stage** at diagnosis.
• NPC is curable, especially when caught early.
• **5-Year Overall Survival Rates (approximate):**
    ◦ Stage I: >90%
    ◦ Stage II: 80-90%
    ◦ Stage III: 70-80%
    ◦ Stage IV (non-metastatic): 60-70%
    ◦ Stage IV (metastatic): <40%
• The non-keratinizing, undifferentiated (WHO Type III) subtype generally has a better prognosis than the keratinizing (Type I) subtype due to its higher radiosensitivity.

sections.overview:
• Salivary gland tumors are a heterogeneous group of neoplasms from major (parotid, submandibular, sublingual) or minor salivary glands.
• The **parotid gland** is the most common site.
• Approximately 80% of salivary gland tumors are **benign**, and 80% of these occur in the parotid gland.
• The most common benign tumor is the **Pleomorphic Adenoma**.
• The most common malignant tumor is the **Mucoepidermoid Carcinoma**.
• Clinical presentation is typically a **slow-growing, painless mass**.
• Red flag signs suggesting malignancy include **rapid growth**, **pain**, and **cranial nerve involvement** (especially **CN VII**).
sections.etiology:
• **Origin**: Tumors arise from the ductal and myoepithelial cells of the salivary glands.
• **Pathogenesis**: The exact etiology is unknown for most tumors, linked to genetic and environmental factors.
    ◦ Specific chromosomal translocations are identified in certain subtypes (e.g., MECT1-MAML2 fusion gene in mucoepidermoid carcinoma; PLAG1 gene rearrangement in pleomorphic adenoma).
• **Malignant Transformation**: A long-standing benign tumor, most notably a pleomorphic adenoma, can undergo malignant transformation into a "**carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma**."
• **Anatomic Consideration**: The **facial nerve (CN VII)** exits the stylomastoid foramen and courses directly *through* the parotid gland, dividing it into a superficial and deep lobe.
    ◦ This anatomy is critical, as tumors can compress or invade the nerve, and surgery places the nerve at high risk.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Relatively rare, accounting for <5% of all head and neck neoplasms.
• **Location Distribution**:
    ◦ **Parotid Gland**: ~80% of all salivary tumors.
    ◦ **Submandibular Gland**: ~10-15%.
    ◦ **Sublingual & Minor Glands**: ~5-10%.
• **Benign vs. Malignant Ratio (Critical Concept)**: The likelihood of malignancy increases as the size of the gland decreases.
    ◦ **Parotid**: ~80% Benign / 20% Malignant.
    ◦ **Submandibular**: ~50% Benign / 50% Malignant.
    ◦ **Sublingual & Minor Glands**: ~20% Benign / 80% Malignant.
• **Age**: Peak incidence between ages 40-70. Benign tumors tend to present earlier than malignant ones.
• **Warthin Tumor**: Strong association with elderly male **smokers**; often bilateral.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Radiation Exposure**: The most well-established risk factor, particularly low-dose radiation to the head and neck during childhood.
• **Tobacco Use**: Strongly associated with **Warthin tumors**.
• **Viral Infections**: Possible association with Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) and HIV.
• **Occupational Exposures**: Nickel compounds, rubber manufacturing, silica dust.
• **Genetic Predisposition**: Certain genetic syndromes may increase risk, but this is rare.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is an **asymptomatic, slow-growing, firm, mobile mass** located over the parotid or submandibular area.
    ◦ The patient may have noticed it for months or even years.
    ◦ Malignant tumors may present similarly initially but are more likely to exhibit "red flag" signs over time.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Inspection**: Note any facial asymmetry, erythema, or skin ulceration over the mass.
• **Palpation**:
    ◦ **Location**: At the angle of the mandible (parotid), below the mandible (submandibular).
    ◦ **Size & Consistency**: **Firm, rubbery** (benign) vs. **rock-hard, indurated** (malignant).
    ◦ **Mobility**: **Mobile** (benign) vs. **fixed** to underlying tissue or skin (malignant).
    ◦ **Tenderness**: Usually non-tender, but tenderness may suggest inflammation or malignancy.
• **Neurological Exam**:
    ◦ **CRITICAL**: Meticulously assess **CN VII (Facial Nerve)** function. Ask the patient to:
        ▪ Raise eyebrows
        ▪ Close eyes tightly against resistance
        ▪ Smile or show teeth
        ▪ Pucker lips
        ▪ Puff out cheeks
    ◦ Assess **CN V (Trigeminal Nerve)** sensation in V1, V2, and V3 distributions.
• **Neck Exam**: Palpate for **cervical lymphadenopathy**, a sign of metastatic disease.
• **Intraoral Exam**: Bimanual palpation of the floor of the mouth for sublingual/submandibular masses. Inspect the palate and oropharynx for bulging, which could indicate a deep lobe parotid tumor.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Fine Needle Aspiration (FNA)**:
    ◦ **First-line diagnostic procedure**.
    ◦ Differentiates benign from malignant with ~90% accuracy.
    ◦ Guides surgical planning.
    ◦ Performed with or without ultrasound guidance.
    ◦ **Note**: An open incisional biopsy is generally **contraindicated** due to the risk of tumor seeding.
• **Imaging**:
    ◦ **Ultrasound**: Excellent initial study to characterize the mass (solid vs. cystic) and guide FNA.
    ◦ **CT with Contrast**: Best for evaluating **bone invasion**, defining tumor extent, and assessing cervical lymph nodes.
    ◦ **MRI**: Superior for soft tissue detail, evaluating **perineural invasion** (a hallmark of adenoid cystic carcinoma), and assessing deep lobe parotid tumors.
sections.treatment:
• **Surgical Excision**: The primary treatment for nearly all salivary gland tumors. The specific procedure depends on the gland and tumor characteristics.
    ◦ **Parotid Gland**:
        ▪ **Superficial Parotidectomy**: Removal of the superficial lobe with careful dissection and preservation of the facial nerve. Most common procedure.
        ▪ **Total Parotidectomy**: Removal of both superficial and deep lobes, also with facial nerve preservation if possible. Required for deep lobe tumors or malignancy.
    ◦ **Submandibular/Sublingual Gland**: Complete excision of the gland (sialadenectomy).
    ◦ **Neck Dissection**: Performed for clinically or radiographically evident cervical node metastasis, or electively for high-grade malignant tumors.
• **Adjuvant Radiation Therapy**: Used post-operatively for malignant tumors with high-risk features:
    ◦ High-grade histology
    ◦ Positive surgical margins
    ◦ Perineural or lymphovascular invasion
    ◦ Nodal metastasis
• **Chemotherapy**: Generally has a limited role. Reserved for palliative treatment of recurrent or metastatic disease.
sections.management:
• **Benign Tumors**: Surgical excision is typically curative. Follow-up is to monitor for recurrence and surgical complications.
• **Malignant Tumors**: Requires a multidisciplinary approach (ENT/Head & Neck Surgery, Radiation Oncology, Medical Oncology).
• **Post-operative surveillance** is crucial for detecting recurrence. This includes regular physical exams and may involve periodic imaging.
• Patients with **Adenoid Cystic Carcinoma** require very long-term follow-up due to its propensity for late recurrence and distant metastases (often to the lungs).
• Management of surgical complications (e.g., facial nerve weakness, Frey's syndrome).
sections.prognosis:
• **Benign Tumors**: Excellent. Recurrence rate is low (<5%) with complete excision.
• **Malignant Tumors**: Highly variable and depends on:
    ◦ **Histologic Grade (Low vs. High)**: The single most important factor.
    ◦ **Stage (TNM)**: Tumor size, nodal status, and distant metastasis.
    ◦ **Perineural Invasion**: A poor prognostic sign.
    ◦ **Surgical Margins**: Positive margins increase recurrence risk.
• **5-Year Survival Rates (Approximate)**:
    ◦ Low-grade tumors: >90%
    ◦ High-grade tumors: 30-50%

sections.overview:
• **Retinoblastoma (Rb)** is the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood.
• It is a neuroblastic tumor arising from the developing retina.
• It can be **heritable** or **non-heritable** and typically presents in early childhood.
• Early diagnosis and treatment are critical to save the patient's life, preserve the eye, and optimize vision.
sections.etiology:
• **Genetic Basis**: Caused by mutations in the **Retinoblastoma (*RB1*) gene** located on chromosome 13q14.
    ◦ The *RB1* gene is a **tumor suppressor gene**.
• **Knudson's "Two-Hit" Hypothesis**: This is the classic model for retinoblastoma development. Two separate mutations ("hits") are required to inactivate both alleles of the *RB1* gene in a retinal cell, leading to uncontrolled cell growth.
    ◦ **Heritable / Germline (40% of cases)**:
        ▪ **First Hit**: An inherited germline mutation is present in all cells of the body.
        ▪ **Second Hit**: A second, somatic mutation occurs in a retinal cell.
        ▪ **Clinical Features**: Patients often present at a younger age (avg. 12 months), frequently have **bilateral** and/or **multifocal** tumors, and have a significantly increased risk of developing secondary non-ocular cancers (e.g., **osteosarcoma**, soft tissue sarcomas, melanoma).
    ◦ **Non-heritable / Sporadic (60% of cases)**:
        ▪ **First & Second Hits**: Both mutations are somatic and occur randomly within the same retinal cell.
        ▪ **Clinical Features**: Patients present at an older age (avg. 24 months), and tumors are almost always **unilateral** and **unifocal**. There is no increased risk for other cancers.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Incidence**: Approximately 1 in 15,000 to 20,000 live births.
• **Age of Onset**: 95% of cases are diagnosed before the age of 5.
    ◦ **Heritable**: Mean age of diagnosis is ~12 months.
    ◦ **Non-heritable**: Mean age of diagnosis is ~24 months.
• **Demographics**: No significant racial or gender predilection. Occurs with equal frequency worldwide.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Primary Risk Factor**: A germline mutation in the ***RB1* gene**.
• **Family History**: A parent or sibling with a history of retinoblastoma. About 10% of newly diagnosed patients have a positive family history.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The most common presentation is a parent or family member noticing an abnormality in the child's eye, often from a photograph taken with a flash.
• The child is typically otherwise well-appearing.
• Delay in diagnosis can lead to orbital invasion, metastasis, and death.
• **Leukocoria**: A white pupillary reflex (**"cat's eye reflex"**). This is the most common presenting sign (>50% of cases).
• **Strabismus**: Misalignment of the eyes (esotropia or exotropia). This is the second most common presenting sign (~20% of cases), caused by the tumor interfering with the central visual axis.
• **Decreased vision** (may be inferred by the child's behavior).
• **Nystagmus** (involuntary eye movements).
• **Proptosis**: Bulging of the eye, indicating extraocular extension.
• **Painful, red eye**: Often associated with secondary glaucoma or inflammation.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Leukocoria**: An abnormal white reflex seen instead of the normal red reflex when using an ophthalmoscope. Best assessed in a darkened room from a distance.
• **Strabismus**: Ocular misalignment detected on the cover-uncover test.
• **Fundoscopy (by ophthalmologist)**:
    ◦ A chalky-white to creamy-pink intraocular mass.
    ◦ May see retinal detachment or vitreous "seeding" (small tumor fragments floating in the vitreous).
• **Proptosis, hyphema (blood in the anterior chamber), or buphthalmos (enlarged globe from glaucoma)** may be seen in advanced disease.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Initial Step**: Urgent referral to an **ophthalmologist** for any child with suspected leukocoria or new-onset strabismus.
• **Definitive Diagnosis**: Made via a **dilated fundoscopic exam under anesthesia**. This allows for a complete and detailed examination of the entire retina.
• **Imaging**:
    ◦ **Ocular Ultrasound (B-scan)**: First-line imaging. Quick, non-invasive, and excellent for identifying **intraocular calcification**, which is highly characteristic of retinoblastoma.
    ◦ **MRI of the Brain and Orbits with contrast**: Essential for all diagnosed cases.
        ▪ Assesses for optic nerve invasion and extraocular extension.
        ▪ Rules out intracranial tumors, specifically a **pinealoblastoma** (associated with **trilateral retinoblastoma**).
• **Contraindicated Procedure**:
    ◦ **Biopsy is NEVER performed**. It carries a high risk of tumor seeding and extraocular spread. Diagnosis is clinical and radiographic.
• **Metastatic Workup (if high-risk features are present)**:
    ◦ Lumbar Puncture (LP) for CSF cytology.
    ◦ Bone Marrow Aspiration and Biopsy.
    ◦ Bone scan.
sections.treatment:
• **Systemic Chemotherapy**: Often used as first-line treatment to shrink the tumor (**chemoreduction**) before focal therapies are applied. Common regimen is **VEC (Vincristine, Etoposide, Carboplatin)**.
• **Intra-arterial Chemotherapy (IAC)**: Super-selective delivery of chemotherapy (e.g., melphalan) directly to the eye via the ophthalmic artery. Minimizes systemic side effects.
• **Focal "Consolidative" Therapies**:
    ◦ **Laser Photocoagulation (Transpupillary Thermotherapy)**: For small posterior tumors.
    ◦ **Cryotherapy**: For small anterior tumors.
• **Enucleation (Surgical Removal of the Eyeball)**: Indicated for:
    ◦ Large tumors with no hope of useful vision.
    ◦ Tumors that do not respond to chemotherapy.
    ◦ Evidence of optic nerve invasion.
    ◦ Uncontrolled secondary glaucoma.
• **Radiation Therapy**: External beam radiation (EBRT) is used less commonly now due to the high risk of secondary malignancies and orbital deformities, but may be necessary for orbital disease.
sections.management:
• **Multidisciplinary Team**: Requires collaboration between pediatric ophthalmology, pediatric oncology, radiation oncology, and genetic counseling.
• **Genetic Counseling**: Essential for all patients and their families to determine if the mutation is germline, assess risk for relatives, and guide surveillance for secondary cancers.
• **Surveillance**:
    ◦ Lifelong monitoring is required.
    ◦ Patients with germline mutations need regular screening for secondary malignancies, particularly **osteosarcoma**. This may include whole-body MRIs.
    ◦ Siblings and offspring of patients with germline mutations require regular ophthalmic screening from birth.
sections.complications:
• **Disease-Related**:
    ◦ Blindness
    ◦ Retinal detachment
    ◦ Metastasis (most commonly to the CNS, bone, and bone marrow)
    ◦ Death
• **Treatment-Related**:
    ◦ Hearing loss (from platinum-based chemotherapy like carboplatin).
    ◦ Renal toxicity.
    ◦ Orbital developmental abnormalities (following enucleation or radiation).
    ◦ Cataracts or retinopathy from radiation.
• **Secondary Malignancies**: The most feared long-term complication in patients with germline *RB1* mutations. The risk is significantly increased by radiation therapy. The most common secondary tumor is **osteosarcoma**.
• **Trilateral Retinoblastoma**: The combination of bilateral (or unilateral) retinoblastoma with an intracranial midline neuroblastic tumor, typically a **pinealoblastoma**. Occurs only in patients with germline mutations.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for intraocular disease in developed countries, with a survival rate >95%.
• **Poor** if there is extraocular extension or metastasis to the CNS. The prognosis drops to <50% with optic nerve involvement and is very poor with CNS metastasis.

sections.overview:
• **Major Depressive Disorder (MDD)**, also known as unipolar depression, is a common and serious mood disorder characterized by a persistent feeling of sadness or a loss of interest or pleasure (**anhedonia**).
• To be diagnosed, symptoms must:
    ◦ Be present for at least **two consecutive weeks**.
    ◦ Represent a change from previous functioning.
    ◦ Cause clinically significant **distress or impairment** in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning.
    ◦ Not be attributable to the physiological effects of a substance or another medical condition.
sections.etiology:
• The etiology of MDD is multifactorial, involving a complex interplay of genetic, biological, environmental, and psychosocial factors.
• **Biogenic Amine (Monoamine) Hypothesis**: The most classic theory posits a deficiency in the central nervous system of key neurotransmitters:
    ◦ **Serotonin (5-HT)**: Regulates mood, sleep, appetite, and obsession/compulsion.
    ◦ **Norepinephrine (NE)**: Regulates alertness, energy, and interest.
    ◦ **Dopamine (DA)**: Regulates motivation, pleasure, and reward.
• **Neuroendocrine Dysregulation**:
    ◦ Dysregulation of the **Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Adrenal (HPA) axis** is frequently observed, leading to elevated cortisol levels (**hypercortisolemia**).
    ◦ Chronic stress is a major contributor to HPA axis dysfunction.
• **Neuroplasticity & Neurogenesis Hypothesis**:
    ◦ Chronic stress and depression are associated with reduced **Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor (BDNF)**, leading to decreased neurogenesis and neuronal atrophy, particularly in the **hippocampus**.
    ◦ Antidepressant treatment may work by increasing BDNF and promoting neuronal recovery.
• **Genetic Factors**:
