    ◦ Strong genetic component; first-degree relatives of individuals with MDD are ~3 times more likely to develop MDD.
    ◦ Twin studies show higher concordance rates for monozygotic twins (~40-50%) than dizygotic twins (~20%).
• **Inflammatory Hypothesis**:
    ◦ Elevated levels of **pro-inflammatory cytokines** (e.g., IL-6, TNF-alpha) are associated with depressive symptoms, suggesting a link between the immune system and mood regulation.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Lifetime Prevalence**: 15-20% in the general population.
• **Gender**: Twice as common in **women** than in men (2:1 ratio).
• **Age of Onset**: Mean age of onset is in the late 20s, but it can occur at any age.
• **Public Health Impact**: A leading cause of disability worldwide.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients may not explicitly state "I feel depressed." They often present with somatic or vague complaints.
• **Chief Complaint**:
    ◦ Fatigue
    ◦ Insomnia
    ◦ Chronic pain
    ◦ Headache
    ◦ Digestive issues
• **History**:
    ◦ The patient or family may report social withdrawal, irritability, decreased productivity at work or school, and loss of interest in hobbies.
• **Mental Status Exam**:
    ◦ May reveal **psychomotor retardation** (slowed speech/movement), **psychomotor agitation** (restlessness, hand-wringing), poor hygiene, flat or constricted affect, and a sad or irritable mood.
sections.diagnostics:
• MDD is a clinical diagnosis based on **DSM-5 criteria**.
• No lab test can diagnose depression, but labs are crucial to rule out other conditions.
• **Screening Tools**:
    ◦ **PHQ-9 (Patient Health Questionnaire-9)**:
        ▪ A 9-item questionnaire that mirrors the DSM-5 criteria.
        ▪ Used for screening, diagnosing, and monitoring treatment response.
    ◦ **PHQ-2**:
        ▪ A 2-item screen asking about depressed mood and anhedonia.
        ▪ If positive, proceed to the PHQ-9.
• **Laboratory Studies (to rule out organic causes)**:
    ◦ **TSH**: To rule out hypothyroidism.
    ◦ **CBC**: To rule out anemia.
    ◦ **CMP**: To assess electrolytes and renal/hepatic function (important for medication choice).
    ◦ **Vitamin B12 / Folate**: Deficiencies can cause depressive symptoms.
    ◦ **Urine Drug Screen (UDS)**: To rule out substance-induced mood disorder.
sections.prognosis:
• MDD is often a **chronic, recurrent illness**.
• With treatment, ~70% of patients experience significant improvement.
• Without treatment, a single episode can last 6-12 months or longer.
• Risk of recurrence:
    ◦ After one episode is ~50%.
    ◦ After three episodes, it is >90%.
• **Negative prognostic factors** include longer episode duration, psychotic features, and comorbid psychiatric or medical conditions.

sections.overview:
• Persistent Depressive Disorder (PDD), formerly Dysthymia, is a chronic depression with a depressed mood for most of the day, more days than not, for at least two years.
    ◦ Symptoms are less severe than Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) but are persistent and long-lasting.
    ◦ Patients often describe their mood as their "normal" baseline, stating "I've always been this way."
    ◦ A key feature is the potential for superimposed Major Depressive Episodes, known as "**double depression**."
sections.etiology:
• The etiology is multifactorial, involving a combination of genetic, neurobiological, and environmental factors.
    ◦ **Neurobiological**
        ▪ Similar to MDD, involves dysregulation of key neurotransmitters, primarily **serotonin**, norepinephrine, and dopamine (monoamine hypothesis).
        ▪ Dysfunctional circuits involving the prefrontal cortex, amygdala, and hippocampus are implicated.
    ◦ **Genetic**
        ▪ Strong heritable component.
        ▪ Having a first-degree relative with a depressive disorder significantly increases risk.
    ◦ **Psychosocial**
        ▪ Often associated with early life stress, trauma, loss, or chronic stress.
        ▪ Certain personality traits, such as neuroticism and pessimism, are predisposing.
    ◦ **HPA Axis Dysregulation**
        ▪ Chronic stress may lead to hyperactivity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis.
        ▪ This results in elevated cortisol levels which can be neurotoxic over time.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Lifetime Prevalence:** Approximately 3-6% in the general population.
• **Gender:** More common in **women** than men (approx. 2:1 to 3:1 ratio).
• **Age of Onset:**
    ◦ Typically has an insidious and **early onset**, often in childhood, adolescence, or early adulthood.
    ◦ Early onset (<21 years) is associated with a higher likelihood of comorbid personality disorders and a worse prognosis.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients typically present with a long history of feeling "down," "sad," or "empty."
    ◦ They are often pessimistic, self-critical, and anhedonic.
    ◦ They may function adequately in daily life but experience significant subjective distress and social/occupational impairment.
• The onset is insidious, and patients may not recognize their mood as a treatable illness, often integrating it into their self-concept.
• Patients may seek treatment only when a superimposed Major Depressive Episode occurs ("**double depression**").
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primary Tool:** Clinical diagnosis based on a thorough history and mental status exam (MSE) using **DSM-5 criteria**.
• **Laboratory Studies (to rule out organic causes):**
    ◦ **TSH:** To rule out hypothyroidism (classic mimic).
    ◦ **CBC:** To rule out anemia.
    ◦ **CMP:** To check for electrolyte abnormalities, renal, or hepatic dysfunction.
    ◦ **Vitamin B12 / Folate:** Deficiencies can cause depressive symptoms.
    ◦ **Urine Drug Screen:** To rule out substance-induced mood disorder.
• **Screening Tools:**
    ◦ Patient Health Questionnaire (**PHQ-9**) can be used to screen for and monitor the severity of depressive symptoms.
sections.prognosis:
• PDD is a chronic condition with a high rate of relapse.
• Prognosis is guarded, especially with early onset and comorbid conditions.
• Spontaneous recovery rates are low without treatment.
• With consistent, long-term treatment (psychotherapy and/or pharmacotherapy), many patients can achieve significant symptom reduction and improved functioning.

sections.overview:
• Bipolar I Disorder (BP-I) is a chronic, severe psychiatric illness characterized by the occurrence of **at least one manic episode**
    ◦ Major depressive episodes (MDEs) are common and are typically part of the illness course, but they are **not required** for the diagnosis
    ◦ The defining feature is **mania**
• Episodes of mania and depression are often interspersed with periods of euthymia (normal mood)
• The illness causes significant functional impairment and is associated with a high risk of suicide
sections.etiology:
• The exact etiology is unknown but is understood to be multifactorial, involving a complex interplay of genetic, neurobiological, and environmental factors
    ◦ **Genetics**: This is the strongest risk factor
        ▪ First-degree relatives of individuals with Bipolar I Disorder have a 10-fold increased risk
        ▪ Concordance rate in monozygotic twins is high (40-70%)
    ◦ **Neurobiology**
        ▪ **Monoamine Hypothesis**: Dysregulation of neurotransmitters
            ▪ **Mania**: Believed to be associated with **increased** levels of dopamine and norepinephrine
            ▪ **Depression**: Associated with **decreased** levels of serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine
        ▪ **Neuroanatomy**: Structural and functional changes in brain regions responsible for emotional regulation, including the prefrontal cortex, amygdala, and hippocampus
    ◦ **Environmental Factors**
        ▪ Stressful life events, childhood trauma, or abuse can act as triggers for initial or subsequent episodes in genetically predisposed individuals
        ▪ Sleep deprivation can precipitate manic episodes
sections.epidemiology:
• **Lifetime Prevalence**: Approximately 1%
• **Age of Onset**: Typically late adolescence or early adulthood (mean age ~18-20 years)
• **Gender**: Affects males and females equally (1:1 ratio)
    ◦ Males are more likely to have their first episode be a manic one
    ◦ Females are more likely to have their first episode be a depressive one and have higher rates of rapid cycling and mixed features
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient's presentation depends on their current mood state (manic, depressed, or euthymic)
    ◦ **Manic Episode**
        ▪ Patients rarely present voluntarily, as they often lack insight (**anosognosia**) and feel "better than ever"
        ▪ They are typically brought in by family, law enforcement, or EMS due to erratic, impulsive, or dangerous behavior
        ▪ May appear euphoric, expansive, irritable, or agitated
        ▪ Speech is often loud, rapid, and difficult to interrupt (**pressured**)
        ▪ May be dressed in flamboyant or sexually provocative clothing
    ◦ **Depressive Episode**
        ▪ The presentation is indistinguishable from that of Major Depressive Disorder (MDD)
        ▪ The patient reports low mood, anhedonia, fatigue, and feelings of guilt or worthlessness
        ▪ It is **critical** to screen any patient presenting with depression for a past history of manic or hypomanic episodes to avoid misdiagnosis and inappropriate treatment (e.g., **antidepressant monotherapy**)
sections.diagnostics:
• **Diagnosis is clinical**, based on DSM-5 criteria obtained through a thorough patient history and MSE
    ◦ Collateral information from family is often essential
• **Laboratory Studies** (to rule out other causes and for pre-treatment baseline)
    ◦ Complete Blood Count (CBC)
    ◦ Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP) - check electrolytes, renal and liver function
    ◦ Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH) - to rule out hyper/hypothyroidism
    ◦ Urine toxicology screen
    ◦ hCG (in females of childbearing age)
    ◦ EKG - especially before starting certain antipsychotics or TCAs
• **Screening Tools**
    ◦ The Mood Disorder Questionnaire (MDQ) is a common screening tool for a lifetime history of mania
sections.prognosis:
• Bipolar I Disorder is a chronic, lifelong illness that requires long-term management
• It is a relapsing and remitting course
    ◦ With treatment, many individuals can achieve significant periods of euthymia and lead functional lives
• Poor prognostic indicators include early age of onset, presence of psychotic features, comorbid substance use, and poor treatment adherence

sections.overview:
• Bipolar II Disorder is a chronic mood disorder characterized by at least one **hypomanic episode** and at least one **major depressive episode**
	◦ The defining feature that distinguishes it from Bipolar I Disorder is the **absence of any history of a full manic episode**
• Patients typically seek treatment during their depressive phases and may not recognize their hypomanic episodes as pathological, often viewing them as periods of high productivity and well-being
	◦ This frequently leads to misdiagnosis as **Major Depressive Disorder (MDD)**
sections.etiology:
• The etiology is multifactorial, involving a complex interplay of genetic, neurobiological, and environmental factors
• **Genetics**
	◦ Strongest risk factor
	◦ High heritability (up to 80%)
	◦ First-degree relatives of individuals with bipolar disorder are ~10x more likely to develop the disorder
• **Neurobiology**
	◦ **Monoamine Hypothesis**
		▪ Dysregulation of key neurotransmitters, including **serotonin (5-HT)**, **norepinephrine (NE)**, and **dopamine (DA)**
		▪ The model suggests an imbalance rather than a simple deficit or excess
	◦ **Neuroanatomic Changes**
		▪ Structural and functional abnormalities in brain regions responsible for emotional regulation, including the **prefrontal cortex**, **hippocampus**, and **amygdala**
• **Environmental Factors**
	◦ Stressful life events, childhood trauma, or abuse can act as triggers for mood episodes in genetically predisposed individuals
sections.epidemiology:
• **Lifetime Prevalence**: Approximately 1.1% of the U.S. adult population
• **Age of Onset**: Typically late adolescence or early adulthood (average age ~25)
• **Gender**
	◦ Slightly more common in women than men
	◦ Women may experience more depressive episodes and a more rapid-cycling course
• **Diagnostic Delay**: Often a significant delay (5-10 years) between symptom onset and correct diagnosis due to misdiagnosis as MDD
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a patient seeking help for symptoms of a **major depressive episode**
	◦ They report **low mood**, **anhedonia**, **fatigue**, and **feelings of worthlessness**
• The key to diagnosis is eliciting a history of a distinct period of elevated mood and energy that meets the criteria for **hypomania**
• **Patient History**
	◦ Patients often do not volunteer information about hypomania
	◦ They may describe it as a time they "felt great," were "highly productive," or "didn't need much sleep"
• **Collateral Information**
	◦ Family, partners, or friends are often crucial sources of information
	◦ They may report observing the patient being unusually energetic, talkative, irritable, or engaging in impulsive behaviors
• **Course**
	◦ The clinical course is characterized by recurrent mood episodes, with depressive episodes typically being more frequent and longer-lasting than hypomanic episodes
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is made clinically based on a thorough history and DSM-5 criteria
• There are no pathognomonic lab or imaging findings
• **Clinical Interview**
	◦ The most important diagnostic tool
	◦ Meticulously screen for any past episodes of **hypomania** in all patients presenting with depression
• **Screening Tools**
	◦ **Mood Disorder Questionnaire (MDQ)** is a common and useful tool to screen for a history of manic or hypomanic episodes
• **Laboratory Studies (to rule out other causes)**
	◦ **TSH**: To rule out hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism
	◦ **CBC**: To rule out anemia
	◦ **CMP**: To assess electrolytes and renal/hepatic function (important for baseline before starting medications like lithium)
	◦ **Vitamin B12 / Folate**: Deficiencies can cause depressive symptoms
	◦ **Urine toxicology screen**: To rule out substance-induced mood disorder
• **Imaging**
	◦ Brain MRI or CT is not routinely indicated unless there is a focal neurologic deficit, late-age onset, or an atypical presentation suggesting an organic cause (e.g., brain tumor, stroke)
sections.prognosis:
• Bipolar II Disorder is a **chronic** and **recurrent** illness
• With effective treatment and consistent adherence, many individuals can achieve good functional outcomes
• However, depressive episodes often predominate the course of the illness and are associated with significant morbidity
• Negative prognostic factors include **early age of onset**, **high frequency of episodes**, and **comorbid substance use**

sections.overview:
• **Cyclothymic Disorder** is a **chronic**, **fluctuating mood disturbance** characterized by:
    ◦ Numerous periods of **hypomanic symptoms** and periods of **depressive symptoms** that are distinct from each other.
    ◦ A persistent and **unstable mood state**.
• It is considered a milder form on the **bipolar spectrum**.
• The key feature is that symptoms are **subthreshold**; they are not severe enough in number, duration, or pervasiveness to meet the full criteria for a **hypomanic** or **major depressive episode**.
sections.etiology:
• The exact etiology is unknown but is believed to be **multifactorial**, similar to other **bipolar spectrum disorders**.
• **Genetic Factors**
    ◦ There is a strong genetic component.
    ◦ Individuals with a **first-degree relative** (parent, sibling, child) with **Bipolar I Disorder** are at a significantly higher risk of developing cyclothymia.
• **Neurobiological Factors**
    ◦ Imbalances in key **neurotransmitters**—including **serotonin**, **norepinephrine**, and **dopamine**—are implicated.
    ◦ Dysregulation in the brain's **limbic system**, particularly the amygdala and prefrontal cortex involved in emotional regulation, is also thought to play a role.
• **Psychosocial Factors**
    ◦ **Environmental stressors**, traumatic life events, and childhood adversity may act as triggers in genetically predisposed individuals.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**
    ◦ Lifetime prevalence is estimated to be between 0.4% and 1.0% in the general population.
    ◦ It is likely **underdiagnosed** as individuals may not seek treatment or may be misdiagnosed with other conditions.
• **Age of Onset**
    ◦ Typically begins in **adolescence** or **early adulthood**.
    ◦ An early onset is associated with a higher risk of developing **Bipolar I** or **Bipolar II Disorder** later in life.
• **Gender**
    ◦ Affects males and females equally (1:1 ratio).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients often present due to the consequences of their **mood instability** rather than the mood swings themselves, such as being brought in by family members concerned about their **erratic behavior** or seeking help for depressive symptoms.
• **Subjective Report**
    ◦ Patients may describe themselves as "**moody**," "**temperamental**," or "**unpredictable**."
    ◦ They often report a lifelong pattern of "**ups and downs**."
• **"Up" Periods (Hypomanic Symptoms)**
    ◦ These periods may be viewed as positive, productive, or creative times by the patient and may not be reported as a problem.
    ◦ Symptoms include **increased energy**, **decreased need for sleep**, **heightened self-esteem**, and **increased talkativeness**.
• **"Down" Periods (Depressive Symptoms)**
    ◦ These periods are more likely to cause distress and lead the patient to seek help.
    ◦ Symptoms include **low energy**, **anhedonia**, **hypersomnia**, feelings of inadequacy, and social withdrawal.
• **Functional Impairment**
    ◦ The primary issue is often **social and occupational dysfunction** resulting from the unpredictable mood shifts (e.g., strained relationships, inconsistent work performance).
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is **clinical**, based on **DSM-5 criteria**.
• **DSM-5 Diagnostic Criteria**
    ◦ **Duration**: For at least **2 years** (in adults) or **1 year** (in children and adolescents), there have been numerous periods with **hypomanic symptoms** (that do not meet criteria for a hypomanic episode) and numerous periods with **depressive symptoms** (that do not meet criteria for a major depressive episode).
    ◦ **Persistence**: During the above period, the hypomanic and depressive periods have been present for **at least half the time**, and the individual has not been without the symptoms for more than **2 months at a time**.
    ◦ **Exclusion of Major Episodes**: Criteria for a major depressive, manic, or hypomanic episode have **never been met**.
    ◦ **Exclusion of Other Disorders**: The symptoms are not better explained by **schizoaffective disorder**, **schizophrenia**, schizophreniform disorder, delusional disorder, or other specified or unspecified schizophrenia spectrum and other psychotic disorder.
    ◦ **Exclusion of Substance/Medical Condition**: The symptoms are not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance (e.g., a drug of abuse, a medication) or another medical condition (e.g., **hyperthyroidism**).
    ◦ **Clinical Significance**: The symptoms cause clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning.
• **Labs/Imaging**
    ◦ **Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH)**: To rule out **hypothyroidism** or **hyperthyroidism**.
    ◦ **Complete Blood Count (CBC) & Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP)**: To establish a baseline before starting medications (e.g., lithium) and rule out other metabolic causes.
    ◦ **Urine Drug Screen (UDS)**: To rule out **substance-induced mood disorder**.
sections.prognosis:
• Cyclothymia is a **chronic**, **lifelong illness**.
• The course is variable.
    ◦ With consistent treatment (medication and therapy), many individuals can achieve significant stabilization and lead functional lives.
    ◦ Without treatment, the prognosis is poorer, with a high likelihood of **functional impairment** and progression to a more severe **bipolar disorder**.

sections.overview: • Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD) is a severe form of Premenstrual Syndrome (PMS) with affective, behavioral, and somatic symptoms recurring cyclically during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle. ◦ It is classified as a Depressive Disorder in the DSM-5. ◦ The defining feature is the presence of clinically significant mood symptoms (e.g., marked irritability, depression, anxiety) causing severe distress and functional impairment. ◦ Symptoms begin the week before menses, peak around onset, and resolve within a few days after menstruation starts, followed by a symptom-free follicular phase.
sections.etiology: • The exact etiology is not fully understood; it is considered an abnormal central nervous system response to normal cyclical fluctuations in ovarian steroids, not caused by abnormal hormone levels. ◦ Serotonergic (5-HT) Dysregulation: ▪ The leading theory suggests individuals with PMDD have an abnormal sensitivity to the effects of progesterone and its metabolite, allopregnanolone, on the serotonin system. ▪ Normal luteal phase hormone changes appear to trigger a decrease in central serotonergic activity in susceptible individuals, leading to mood and behavioral symptoms. ▪ This is supported by the rapid efficacy of SSRIs. ◦ GABA System: ▪ Allopregnanolone is a potent positive modulator of GABA-A receptors. ▪ In individuals with PMDD, there may be a paradoxical or altered response to this modulation, leading to increased anxiety and irritability instead of the expected anxiolytic effect. ◦ Genetic Predisposition: ▪ There is evidence for a heritable component. ▪ Studies have identified specific gene complexes (e.g., ESC/SET complex) that may confer susceptibility by altering hormone sensitivity at the cellular level.
sections.epidemiology: • Prevalence: Affects approximately 3-8% of menstruating individuals. • Age of Onset: Can occur any time after menarche but most commonly presents in the late 20s to early 30s. • Course: It is a chronic condition that persists until menopause.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • A patient typically presents with a history of severe, recurrent mood and physical symptoms that reliably begin 1-2 weeks before her period and significantly interfere with her life. ◦ The key to the history is the timing: symptoms are limited to the luteal phase, and she experiences a symptom-free period after menses (follicular phase). ◦ She will report feeling "like a different person" during this time. ◦ The primary complaint is often the profound negative impact on relationships, work productivity, or social activities.
sections.diagnostics: • The diagnosis of PMDD is clinical and relies on confirming the cyclical nature of the symptoms. ◦ Gold Standard: Prospective symptom charting for at least two consecutive menstrual cycles. ▪ Patients use a daily rating scale, such as the Daily Record of Severity of Problems (DRSP), to track symptoms. ▪ This documentation is essential to confirm that symptoms are confined to the luteal phase and to differentiate PMDD from a premenstrual exacerbation of another underlying disorder. ◦ Laboratory Studies: There are no specific lab tests to diagnose PMDD; labs are used to rule out other conditions. ▪ TSH: To rule out hypothyroidism/hyperthyroidism. ▪ CBC: To rule out anemia, which can cause fatigue and mood changes. ▪ Hormone levels (estrogen, progesterone, FSH) are not indicated as they are typically normal in PMDD.
sections.prognosis: • PMDD is a chronic condition that, if untreated, will likely persist throughout the reproductive years. • Symptoms resolve completely with menopause (either natural or surgically/medically induced). • With appropriate treatment, the prognosis is excellent, and most individuals achieve significant or complete symptom relief.

sections.overview:
• Depression with Peripartum Onset is a **Major Depressive Episode (MDE)** with an onset during pregnancy or within the 4 weeks following delivery, according to the **DSM-5**.
    ◦ Clinically, the timeframe is often extended to the first year postpartum as symptoms may not present or be recognized immediately.
• It is a common and serious medical condition that negatively impacts the mother, infant, and family.
• It is distinct from the milder, transient "**postpartum blues**" and the severe, rare "**postpartum psychosis**."
sections.etiology:
• The etiology is **multifactorial** and not fully elucidated, believed to be a combination of biological, genetic, and psychosocial factors.
• **Hormonal Fluctuations**:
    ◦ The rapid and dramatic decrease in **estrogen**, **progesterone**, and **cortisol** levels immediately following childbirth is thought to be a primary trigger.
        ▪ These hormones have significant effects on mood-regulating neurotransmitter systems.
    ◦ Dysregulation of the **hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis** is also implicated.
• **Neurotransmitter Dysregulation**:
    ◦ Alterations in **serotonergic**, **noradrenergic**, and **dopaminergic** systems, similar to non-peripartum major depression.
• **Thyroid Dysfunction**:
    ◦ **Postpartum thyroiditis**, an autoimmune condition, can present with hypothyroid symptoms (**fatigue**, **depression**) or hyperthyroid symptoms (**anxiety**, **irritability**), mimicking or contributing to a mood disorder.
• **Psychosocial Stressors**:
    ◦ **Sleep deprivation**, the physical and emotional stress of childbirth and recovery, feelings of being overwhelmed, lack of social support, and changes in personal/professional identity contribute significantly.
• **Genetic Predisposition**:
    ◦ A personal or family history of mood disorders strongly increases susceptibility.
sections.epidemiology:
• Affects approximately **10-15%** of mothers.
• About 50% of postpartum MDEs actually begin during pregnancy (**antenatal depression**).
• Peak onset is typically within the first **3 months** postpartum.
• It is one of the most common complications of childbirth.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents weeks to months after delivery to her OB/GYN, PCP, or her infant's pediatrician.
• She may not volunteer feelings of sadness but may present with somatic complaints like **fatigue**, **insomnia**, or **anxiety**.
• The core feature is a **depressed mood** or **anhedonia** for at least two weeks.
• She may express feelings of inadequacy, guilt about not feeling "happy," or excessive worry about the baby's health.
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is clinical, based on **DSM-5 criteria**.
• **Screening Tools**:
    ◦ **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)**: A 10-item self-report scale.
        ▪ A score of **10-13** suggests depression and warrants further assessment.
        ▪ A positive answer to question #10 (**suicidal thoughts**) requires immediate evaluation.
    ◦ **Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9)**: A general depression screening tool also used in this population.
• **Laboratory Studies** (to rule out organic causes):
    ◦ **TSH**: To rule out **postpartum thyroiditis**.
    ◦ **CBC**: To rule out **anemia**.
    ◦ Consider **Vitamin B12** and **Folate** levels.
sections.prognosis:
• With adequate treatment, the prognosis is very good, and most women experience a full recovery.
• However, there is a high risk of recurrence (~**50%**) with subsequent pregnancies.
• If left untreated, the episode can last for months to years and may become chronic.

sections.overview:
• Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is a chronic psychiatric condition characterized by **excessive, persistent, and uncontrollable anxiety and worry** about a variety of everyday life events or activities (e.g., finances, health, work, family)
    ◦ The worry is out of proportion to the actual likelihood or impact of the feared event
    ◦ It must occur for at least **6 months** and cause significant distress or functional impairment
    ◦ It is often accompanied by physical symptoms like fatigue, muscle tension, and sleep disturbance
sections.etiology:
• The exact cause is multifactorial, involving a combination of neurobiological, genetic, and environmental factors
    ◦ **Neurobiology**
        ▪ **Neurotransmitter Dysregulation**
            • **GABA:** Decreased inhibitory tone from GABAergic interneurons
            • **Serotonin (5-HT):** Dysregulation in serotonergic pathways. SSRIs are effective, supporting this theory
            • **Norepinephrine (NE):** Overactivity in noradrenergic systems (e.g., locus coeruleus)
        ▪ **Brain Circuitry**
            • **Amygdala:** Hyperactive, leading to an exaggerated fear response
            • **Prefrontal Cortex (PFC):** Hypoactive, leading to diminished top-down control and inability to regulate the anxiety response generated by the amygdala
            • Dysfunction in the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical (CSTC) loop
    ◦ **Genetics**
        ▪ Strong genetic component; GAD runs in families
        ▪ Heritability is estimated to be around 30%
    ◦ **Psychosocial Factors**
        ▪ Learned behaviors (e.g., parental modeling of anxiety)
        ▪ Cognitive distortions (e.g., catastrophizing, overestimating threats)
        ▪ History of childhood trauma or adversity
        ▪ Chronic environmental stress
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** Lifetime prevalence is approximately 5-9%. One-year prevalence is ~3%
• **Gender:** **Females are affected twice as often as males (2:1 ratio)**
• **Age of Onset:** Median age of onset is around 30 years old, but it can begin at any point in life. The onset is often insidious
• **Course:** It is a chronic condition with a waxing and waning course
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients often present to primary care with somatic complaints rather than chief complaints of "worry"
• They may describe being "**stressed out**," "**worried all the time**," or "**unable to relax**"
• The history reveals pervasive worry about multiple, everyday domains that is difficult to control
• They may report significant time spent worrying each day, leading to procrastination and difficulty making decisions
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis:** Diagnosis is made based on history and meeting DSM-5 criteria
• **Screening Tools**
    ◦ **GAD-7 (Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item scale):** A widely used tool to screen for and measure the severity of GAD symptoms
        ▪ A score of 10 suggests a probable diagnosis
• **Laboratory Studies (to rule out organic causes)**
    ◦ **TSH:** To rule out hyperthyroidism
    ◦ **CBC:** To rule out anemia (can cause fatigue)
    ◦ **CMP:** To assess for electrolyte abnormalities
    ◦ **Urine toxicology screen:** To rule out substance-induced anxiety (e.g., stimulants, caffeine)
    ◦ **EKG:** If palpitations or chest pain are prominent symptoms, to rule out arrhythmias or ischemia
sections.prognosis:
• GAD is a **chronic illness** with a **waxing and waning course**
• Full remission is uncommon, but most patients can achieve significant symptom reduction and improved functioning with consistent treatment
• Relapse rates are high, particularly after medication discontinuation
• Poorer prognosis is associated with early age of onset, severe symptoms, and high comorbidity

sections.overview:
• Panic Disorder is an anxiety disorder characterized by **recurrent, unexpected panic attacks**
	◦ The core feature is the subsequent development of:
		▪ **Persistent concern or worry** about having additional attacks or their consequences (e.g., losing control, having a heart attack, "going crazy")
		▪ A **significant maladaptive change in behavior** related to the attacks (e.g., avoidance of exercise or unfamiliar situations)
• A panic attack is an abrupt surge of intense fear or discomfort that reaches a peak within minutes
sections.etiology:
• The exact etiology is multifactorial, involving a combination of genetic, neurobiological, and environmental factors
	◦ **Neurobiology**
		▪ **Neurotransmitter Dysregulation**: Imbalances in key neurotransmitters are implicated
			• **Norepinephrine (NE)**: Overactivity in the **locus coeruleus** is thought to trigger autonomic symptoms
			• **Serotonin (5-HT)**: Dysregulation of serotonin pathways, which normally modulate anxiety and fear
			• **GABA**: Decreased inhibitory effect of GABA leads to CNS hyperexcitability
		▪ **"Suffocation False Alarm" Theory**: Hypersensitivity to carbon dioxide (CO2) may trigger a flawed feedback loop, causing the brain to misinterpret benign CO2 changes as suffocation
		▪ **Fear Network**: An overly sensitive and poorly regulated network involving the:
			• **Amygdala** (fear processing)
			• **Hippocampus** (contextual memory of fear)
			• **Prefrontal cortex** (regulation of fear)
	◦ **Genetics**
		▪ There is a strong genetic component
		▪ First-degree relatives have a significantly higher risk of developing the disorder
sections.epidemiology:
• **Lifetime Prevalence**: 2-3% of the U.S. adult population
• **Gender**: **Females are affected 2-3 times more often than males**
• **Age of Onset**: Typically occurs in late adolescence or early adulthood (median age 20-24 years)
• **Comorbidity**: High rates of comorbidity with other psychiatric disorders, especially **Major Depressive Disorder (MDD)**, other anxiety disorders, and substance use disorders
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a patient presenting to the Emergency Department convinced they are having a **heart attack, stroke, or dying**
	◦ The patient appears intensely anxious, fearful, and may be hyperventilating
	◦ They report an overwhelming **"sense of impending doom"**
• The attacks are typically **unexpected** (uncued), occurring without an obvious trigger
• After the event, the patient's primary concern shifts to the fear of having another attack
sections.diagnostics:
• Panic disorder is a **clinical diagnosis** based on DSM-5 criteria
• The primary purpose of diagnostic testing is to **rule out underlying medical conditions** that can mimic a panic attack
	◦ **Essential Workup (especially in ED)**:
		▪ **ECG/EKG**: Rule out MI, arrhythmia
		▪ **Cardiac Enzymes (Troponin)**: Rule out acute coronary syndrome (ACS)
		▪ **TSH**: Rule out hyperthyroidism
		▪ **Urine Drug Screen (UDS)**: Rule out intoxication (e.g., cocaine, amphetamines) or withdrawal
		▪ **Complete Blood Count (CBC) & Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP)**: Rule out anemia, electrolyte abnormalities
		▪ **Blood Glucose**: Rule out hypoglycemia
sections.prognosis:
• With treatment, the prognosis is generally good, with most patients experiencing significant improvement
• Panic Disorder is often a **chronic condition with a relapsing and remitting course**
• Full remission is possible, but many patients require long-term management
• Early and consistent treatment is associated with a better outcome

sections.overview:
• **Agoraphobia** is an anxiety disorder characterized by marked, irrational fear or anxiety about situations from which escape might be difficult or in which help might not be available in the event of developing panic-like symptoms or other incapacitating or embarrassing symptoms.
• This fear leads to the **active avoidance** of these situations, significantly impairing daily functioning.
• While often associated with **Panic Disorder**, agoraphobia is a distinct diagnosis in the **DSM-5** and can occur independently.
sections.etiology:
• **Neurobiological**
    ◦ **"Fear Circuitry" Dysregulation**: Involves the **amygdala** (fear processing), **hippocampus** (contextual memory), and **prefrontal cortex** (cognitive control). An overactive amygdala and insufficient top-down control from the prefrontal cortex are implicated.
    ◦ **Neurotransmitters**: Imbalances in **serotonin** (mood, anxiety), **norepinephrine** (fight-or-flight), and **GABA** (primary inhibitory neurotransmitter) are key targets for pharmacotherapy.
• **Cognitive-Behavioral Model**
    ◦ **Classical Conditioning**: A neutral public space (conditioned stimulus) becomes associated with the intense fear of a panic attack (unconditioned stimulus), leading to a conditioned fear response.
    ◦ **Operant Conditioning**: Avoidance of feared situations is **negatively reinforced** because it temporarily reduces anxiety, thus strengthening the avoidance behavior.
    ◦ **Catastrophic Misinterpretation**: The individual misinterprets benign bodily sensations (e.g., tachycardia) as signs of an impending catastrophe (e.g., heart attack, "going crazy"), which fuels the panic and fear cycle.
• **Genetic Predisposition**
    ◦ Strong familial link. First-degree relatives of individuals with agoraphobia are at an increased risk.
    ◦ Heritability is estimated to be around 60%.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Approximately 1.7% of adolescents and adults have a 12-month prevalence.
• **Age of Onset**: Typically late adolescence or early adulthood; mean age of onset is ~17 years. Onset after age 40 is rare.
• **Gender**: Diagnosed twice as often in **females** as in males (2:1 ratio).
sections.riskFactors:
• **Temperamental**: **Neuroticism** (negative affectivity), anxiety sensitivity (belief that anxiety symptoms are harmful).
• **Environmental**
    ◦ Stressful or traumatic life events in childhood (e.g., parental death, abuse).
    ◦ Reduced warmth and overprotective parenting styles.
• **Genetic/Physiological**
    ◦ Family history of anxiety disorders.
    ◦ Personal history of **panic attacks** or **Panic Disorder** is the strongest single risk factor.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a patient who reports significant distress about leaving their home. They may describe being "**house-bound**."
• They will describe **actively avoiding** specific situations like grocery stores, crowded malls, bridges, or using buses/subways.
• If they do enter these situations, it is with intense dread or the requirement of a "**safe person**" (e.g., a spouse or friend) to accompany them.
• The patient's primary fear is not of the situation itself, but of experiencing **panic-like symptoms** (e.g., dizziness, palpitations, shortness of breath) and being unable to escape or get help.
• The history will reveal significant **functional impairment** (e.g., inability to work, go to school, or attend social functions).
• **DSM-5 Criteria**:
    ◦ **A.** Marked fear or anxiety about **2 or more** of the following 5 situations:
    ◦ **B.** The individual fears or avoids these situations because of thoughts that **escape might be difficult** or **help might not be available** if they experience panic-like or other incapacitating symptoms.
    ◦ **C.** The agoraphobic situations **almost always** provoke fear or anxiety.
    ◦ **D.** The agoraphobic situations are **actively avoided**, require the presence of a companion, or are endured with intense fear or anxiety.
    ◦ **E.** The fear or anxiety is **out of proportion** to the actual danger posed by the situations.
    ◦ **F.** The fear, anxiety, or avoidance is persistent, typically lasting for **6 months or more**.
    ◦ **G.** The symptoms cause **clinically significant distress or impairment** in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning.
    ◦ **H.** The symptoms are not better explained by another medical condition or mental disorder.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Typically unremarkable**.
• The physical exam is primarily performed to **rule out organic causes** that can mimic anxiety symptoms.
• **Vital signs**: May show resting **tachycardia** or **hypertension** due to anxiety during the visit.
• **General**: Patient may appear **anxious**, **tremulous**, or **diaphoretic** during the interview.
• **Focused exams**:
    ◦ **Thyroid**: Check for goiter, proptosis (ruling out **hyperthyroidism**).
    ◦ **Cardiopulmonary**: Listen for murmurs, arrhythmias (ruling out MVP, etc.).
    ◦ **Neurological**: Assess for vestibular dysfunction (if dizziness is a primary complaint).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Primarily a clinical diagnosis** based on a thorough history and fulfillment of **DSM-5 criteria**.
• **Laboratory studies (to rule out medical causes)**:
    ◦ **TSH**: To rule out **hyperthyroidism**/**hypothyroidism**.
    ◦ **CMP**: Check for electrolyte abnormalities, liver/kidney function.
    ◦ **Urine Drug Screen**: To rule out substance-induced anxiety (e.g., stimulants, caffeine).
• **Other Tests**:
    ◦ **ECG / Holter Monitor**: If palpitations or chest pain are prominent, to rule out arrhythmia.
    ◦ **Neurology/ENT consult**: If vertigo or dizziness is the main symptom, to rule out vestibular causes.
sections.treatment:
• **First-Line**: **CBT + SSRIs**
• **Psychotherapy**:
    ◦ **Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT)**: The gold standard. Involves:
        ▪ **Psychoeducation**: Teaching the patient about the fight-or-flight response.
        ▪ **Cognitive Restructuring**: Identifying and challenging catastrophic thoughts.
        ▪ **Exposure Therapy**: Gradual and systematic exposure to feared situations (*in vivo* or imaginal) to extinguish the fear response and break the cycle of avoidance. This is the most crucial component.
• **Pharmacotherapy**:
    ◦ **First-Line**: **SSRIs** (e.g., Sertraline, Paroxetine, Escitalopram).
        ▪ Start at a low dose and titrate up slowly to minimize activating side effects.
        ▪ Inform patient that full therapeutic effect may take 4-6 weeks.
    ◦ **Second-Line**: **SNRIs** (e.g., Venlafaxine XR).
    ◦ **Adjunctive/Short-Term**: **Benzodiazepines** (e.g., Alprazolam, Clonazepam).
        ▪ **CAUTION**: Use only for short-term management of severe symptoms while SSRIs take effect.
        ▪ High risk of **tolerance, dependence, and abuse**.
        ▪ Can impede the effectiveness of exposure therapy by acting as a "safety behavior."
sections.management:
• **Collaborative Treatment Plan**: Develop a plan with the patient, emphasizing that recovery is gradual. Set realistic goals for exposure therapy.
• **Patient Education**: Reassure the patient that their symptoms are real and treatable. Explain the rationale for treatment, medication adherence, and potential side effects.
• **Lifestyle Modifications**:
    ◦ Encourage regular physical activity.
    ◦ Promote good sleep hygiene.
    ◦ Advise reduction or elimination of caffeine, alcohol, and other stimulants.
• **Follow-Up**: Schedule regular follow-up visits (e.g., every 2-4 weeks initially) to monitor symptom improvement, assess for medication side effects, and provide support.
• **Duration of Treatment**: Continue pharmacotherapy for at least **6-12 months** after symptom remission to prevent relapse.
sections.complications:
• **Severe functional impairment**: Becoming "**house-bound**," unable to work or maintain social relationships.
• **High comorbidity**:
    ◦ **Major Depressive Disorder** (~50% of cases)
    ◦ Other anxiety disorders (**Panic Disorder**, **Social Anxiety**)
    ◦ **Substance Use Disorders** (often alcohol as a form of self-medication)
• Increased risk of **suicidal ideation and attempts**.
• Demoralization and feelings of hopelessness.
sections.prognosis:
• The course is often chronic and persistent if left untreated.
• With evidence-based treatment (**CBT + SSRIs**), the prognosis is **good**, with many patients achieving significant reduction in symptoms and improvement in functioning.
• Relapse rates can be high, especially if treatment is discontinued prematurely.
• **Negative prognostic factors**: high severity of avoidance at presentation, long duration of illness before treatment, and presence of comorbid personality disorders or major depression.

sections.overview:
• **Social Anxiety Disorder (SAD)**, also known as **Social Phobia**, is a psychiatric disorder characterized by a marked and persistent fear of social or performance situations in which the individual is exposed to unfamiliar people or to possible scrutiny by others.
• The core fear is of acting in a way (or showing anxiety symptoms) that will be **negatively evaluated**, leading to humiliation, embarrassment, rejection, or offending others.
• Exposure to the feared social situation almost invariably provokes anxiety, which may take the form of a situationally bound or situationally predisposed **Panic Attack**.
• The fear is recognized as out of proportion, and the situations are either avoided or endured with intense distress, leading to significant impairment in functioning.
• **Key Feature**: Intense fear of **negative evaluation**.
• **DSM-5 Duration Criteria**: Symptoms must persist for **≥ 6 months**.
• **Specifier**: **Performance only** - fear is restricted to public speaking or performing in front of others.
sections.etiology:
• The etiology is multifactorial, involving a combination of genetic, neurobiological, and environmental factors.
• **Genetic Predisposition**
    ◦ Strong familial link; first-degree relatives have a 2-6 times greater risk.
• **Neurobiological Factors**
    ◦ **Amygdala Hyperactivity**: The brain's fear center shows an exaggerated response to social cues (e.g., faces with negative or neutral expressions).
    ◦ **Prefrontal Cortex (PFC) Hypoactivity**: Reduced top-down regulation from the PFC fails to inhibit the overactive amygdala.
    ◦ **Neurotransmitter Dysregulation**
        ▪ **Serotonin (5-HT)**: Decreased serotonin activity is strongly implicated. This is the primary target for SSRIs.
        ▪ **Dopamine (DA)**: Dysfunctional dopamine pathways in the striatum and PFC may contribute to reward processing deficits and fear of social situations.
        ▪ **Norepinephrine (NE)**: Overactivity in the noradrenergic system can contribute to the physical symptoms of anxiety (tachycardia, tremor).
• **Environmental Factors**
    ◦ **Behavioral Inhibition**: A temperamental trait in early childhood characterized by shyness, fearfulness, and withdrawal from unfamiliar situations is a major predictor.
    ◦ **Adverse Social Experiences**: History of bullying, public humiliation, or rejection.
    ◦ **Parenting Styles**: Overly critical, controlling, or overprotective parenting can contribute.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: One of the most common anxiety disorders.
    ◦ Lifetime prevalence is ~12%.
    ◦ 12-month prevalence is ~7%.
• **Age of Onset**: Typically begins in adolescence, with a median age of onset around **13 years old**. Onset is rare in late adulthood.
• **Gender**: More common in females in clinical settings, but prevalence is nearly equal in community samples.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Temperamental**: **Behavioral inhibition**, shyness in childhood.
• **Genetic**: First-degree relative with social anxiety disorder.
• **Environmental**: Childhood maltreatment, teasing, bullying, or other negative social events.
• **Comorbidities**: Presence of other anxiety disorders, depression, or substance use disorders.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient will often present with complaints of debilitating shyness or physical symptoms that occur in specific social contexts.
• They may report avoiding important life activities like job interviews, dating, attending classes, or speaking in meetings.
• The chief complaint might be a somatic symptom (e.g., "my heart races when I have to talk to my boss," "I get stomach cramps before a party").
• **Common Feared Situations**
    ◦ Public speaking
    ◦ Meeting new people
    ◦ Speaking to authority figures
    ◦ Eating or drinking in public
    ◦ Using public restrooms
    ◦ Attending parties or social gatherings
    ◦ Being the center of attention
• **Cognitive Symptoms**
    ◦ Intense fear of being judged, scrutinized, or negatively evaluated.
    ◦ Belief that others can see their anxiety (e.g., blushing, sweating).
    ◦ **Anticipatory anxiety**: Worrying for days or weeks before a feared event.
    ◦ **Post-event rumination**: Mentally replaying social interactions and criticizing their own performance.
    ◦ Negative self-talk ("I'm going to look stupid," "No one will like me").
• **Physical Symptoms (Autonomic Arousal)**
    ◦ **Blushing (Erythrophobia)**
    ◦ Tachycardia, palpitations
    ◦ Trembling, shaking
    ◦ Sweating (diaphoresis)
    ◦ Nausea, GI distress
    ◦ Dizziness, lightheadedness
    ◦ Shortness of breath
    ◦ Muscle tension
• **Behavioral Symptoms**
    ◦ **Avoidance**: Actively avoiding feared social situations.
    ◦ **Safety Behaviors**: Actions taken to prevent or minimize feared outcomes (e.g., rehearsing sentences, avoiding eye contact, wearing makeup to hide blushing, drinking alcohol before an event).
    ◦ Leaving situations prematurely.
    ◦ Speaking very quietly or minimally.
sections.physicalExam:
• The physical exam is typically **unremarkable** and serves to rule out organic causes of symptoms.
• During the clinical interview, the patient may exhibit signs of anxiety if the interaction itself is perceived as a performance situation:
    ◦ Poor eye contact
    ◦ Tremor
    ◦ Diaphoresis
    ◦ Tachycardia
    ◦ Blushing
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is clinical, based on DSM-5 criteria.
• **DSM-5 Criteria Highlights**
    ◦ Marked fear/anxiety about one or more social situations involving possible scrutiny.
    ◦ Fear of showing anxiety symptoms that will be negatively evaluated.
    ◦ Social situations almost always provoke fear or anxiety.
    ◦ Situations are avoided or endured with intense fear/anxiety.
    ◦ Fear is out of proportion to the actual threat.
    ◦ **Duration is at least 6 months**.
    ◦ Causes clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning.
    ◦ Not attributable to a substance or another medical condition.
    ◦ Not better explained by another mental disorder (e.g., Panic Disorder, Body Dysmorphic Disorder).
• **Screening Tools**
    ◦ **Social Phobia Inventory (SPIN)**
    ◦ **Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale (LSAS)**
sections.treatment:
• **First-Line Treatment**
    ◦ **Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs)**: Sertraline, Paroxetine, Escitalopram.
    ◦ **Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT)**: Specifically with an exposure component.
• **Pharmacotherapy**
    ◦ **SSRIs**: First choice. Start low, titrate slowly. Full effect may take 4-12 weeks.
    ◦ **SNRIs (Serotonin-Norepinephrine Reuptake Inhibitors)**: **Venlafaxine XR** is an effective alternative.
    ◦ **Benzodiazepines** (e.g., Clonazepam): Can be used for short-term, rapid relief but are not ideal for long-term management due to risks of tolerance, dependence, and abuse.
    ◦ **Beta-Blockers** (e.g., Propranolol, Atenolol)
        ▪ Used for **performance-only ("stage fright")** specifier.
        ▪ Taken 30-60 minutes before a performance event.
        ▪ Manages peripheral symptoms (tachycardia, tremor) but not the cognitive component of anxiety.
    ◦ **MAOIs** (e.g., Phenelzine): Highly effective but reserved for treatment-resistant cases due to dietary restrictions (tyramine) and side effect profile.
• **Psychotherapy**
    ◦ **Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT)**: Gold standard. Includes:
        ▪ **Psychoeducation**: Understanding the nature of anxiety.
        ▪ **Cognitive Restructuring**: Identifying and challenging maladaptive thoughts and beliefs about social situations.
        ▪ **Exposure Therapy**: Gradual, systematic, and repeated exposure to feared social situations until the anxiety subsides (habituation). This is the most crucial component.
    ◦ **Mindfulness-Based Therapies & Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT)** are also emerging as effective options.
sections.management:
• **Initial Phase**: Start with either an **SSRI** or **CBT**. For severe cases, a combination is superior.
• **Medication Titration**: Start SSRIs at a low dose (e.g., Sertraline 25 mg) and increase every 1-2 weeks as tolerated to a therapeutic dose.
• **Continuation Phase**: Once a response is achieved, continue medication for at least **6-12 months** to prevent relapse.
• **Patient Education**: Crucial for adherence. Explain the rationale for treatment, time course for medication effects, potential side effects, and the importance of therapy exercises (exposure).
• **Monitoring**: Regularly assess symptoms, functional improvement, and side effects. Screen for suicidality, especially at the start of SSRI therapy in young adults.
sections.complications:
• **High rates of comorbidity**
    ◦ **Major Depressive Disorder** (~50%)
    ◦ Other anxiety disorders (GAD, Panic Disorder)
    ◦ **Substance Use Disorders** (especially Alcohol Use Disorder, used as a social lubricant/self-medication)
• **Functional Impairment**
    ◦ Lower educational and occupational achievement.
    ◦ Unemployment or underemployment.
    ◦ Difficulty forming and maintaining romantic relationships and friendships.
    ◦ Overall reduced quality of life.
• **Increased risk of suicidal ideation and attempts**.
sections.prognosis:
• SAD is typically a chronic disorder, but the prognosis with treatment is good.
• CBT has durable effects, even after treatment ends.
• Pharmacotherapy is effective but has a higher relapse rate upon discontinuation if coping skills have not been learned.
• Negative prognostic factors include early age of onset, severity of symptoms, and the presence of comorbid psychiatric conditions.

sections.overview:
• A specific phobia is an anxiety disorder characterized by a **marked, persistent, and excessive or unreasonable fear** of a specific object or situation.
• Exposure to the phobic stimulus almost invariably provokes an immediate anxiety response, which may take the form of a situationally bound or situationally predisposed **panic attack**.
• The phobic object or situation is **actively avoided** or endured with intense fear or anxiety.
• The individual recognizes that the fear is out of proportion to the actual danger posed.
• The fear, anxiety, or avoidance causes clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning.
• There are five DSM-5 specifiers (types) of specific phobia:
    ◦ **Animal Type**: (e.g., spiders, insects, dogs)
    ◦ **Natural Environment Type**: (e.g., heights, storms, water)
    ◦ **Blood-Injection-Injury (B-I-I) Type**: (e.g., needles, invasive medical procedures, sight of blood)
        ▪ Distinctive for its **vasovagal syncopal** or near-syncopal response.
    ◦ **Situational Type**: (e.g., airplanes, elevators, enclosed places)
    ◦ **Other Type**: (e.g., situations that may lead to choking or vomiting; in children, loud sounds or costumed characters)
sections.etiology:
• The etiology is multifactorial, involving a combination of neurobiological, genetic, and environmental factors.
    ◦ **Neurobiological**:
        ▪ **Amygdala Hyperactivity**: The amygdala, the brain's fear center, shows an exaggerated response to phobic stimuli.
        ▪ **Prefrontal Cortex (PFC) Hypoactivity**: The medial PFC, which normally exerts inhibitory control over the amygdala and extinguishes fear responses, is often underactive.
        ▪ **Insula & Anterior Cingulate Cortex**: These areas, involved in processing disgust and monitoring internal bodily states, are also hyperactive, particularly in B-I-I phobia.
    ◦ **Behavioral / Learning Theories**:
        ▪ **Classical Conditioning (Mowrer's two-factor model)**: A neutral object/situation becomes a feared stimulus after being paired with a traumatic or aversive event (e.g., a dog bite leads to cynophobia).
        ▪ **Observational Learning**: Acquiring a phobia by observing the fearful reaction of others (e.g., a child developing a fear of storms after seeing a parent's panicked reaction).
        ▪ **Informational Transmission**: Developing a fear after being told about dangers (e.g., repeated parental warnings about spiders).
    ◦ **Genetic / Familial**:
        ▪ There is a clear familial aggregation, especially for the **Blood-Injection-Injury type**.
        ▪ First-degree relatives of individuals with specific phobias are more likely to have a specific phobia themselves.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: One of the most common mental disorders.
    ◦ Lifetime prevalence in the U.S. is approximately **7-9%**.
• **Gender**: More common in females (approx. **2:1 ratio**).
• **Age of Onset**: Typically begins in early childhood or early adolescence.
    ◦ Median age of onset is around **7-11 years**.
    ◦ Situational phobias tend to have a later onset (e.g., mid-20s).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents due to the phobia's interference with their life, not just its presence.
    ◦ **Vignette**: A 28-year-old male with a new job that requires frequent travel presents for "anxiety."
        ▪ He reports intense fear of flying (**aviophobia**).
        ▪ For years, he has driven everywhere, but now he is at risk of losing his job.
        ▪ He experiences **palpitations, diaphoresis, and a sense of dread** even when thinking about booking a flight.
        ▪ He tried to board a plane once and had a full-blown **panic attack**, forcing him to deplane.
        ▪ He knows his fear is "ridiculous" but feels powerless.
• Patients with B-I-I phobia may present after a **syncopal episode** during a blood draw or medical procedure.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical diagnosis** based on a thorough history and application of the DSM-5 criteria.
• No specific laboratory tests or imaging studies are required for diagnosis.
• Labs (e.g., TSH, CBC, CMP) or imaging may be used to rule out medical conditions that can cause anxiety symptoms if the presentation is atypical.
    ◦ Examples: **hyperthyroidism**, pheochromocytoma, cardiac arrhythmias.
sections.prognosis:
• With treatment, especially exposure therapy, the **prognosis is excellent**.
    ◦ Many individuals achieve significant and lasting symptom reduction.
• Without treatment, specific phobias are often **chronic and persistent**, though the intensity may wax and wane.

sections.overview:
• Separation Anxiety Disorder (SAD) is an anxiety disorder characterized by developmentally inappropriate and excessive fear or anxiety concerning separation from home or from attachment figures.
    ◦ While some separation anxiety is a normal part of development (peaking between 8-14 months), SAD is distinguished by its severity, persistence, and significant functional impairment.
    ◦ It is the most common anxiety disorder in children under 12 but can persist or have an initial onset in adolescence and adulthood.
sections.etiology:
• The etiology is multifactorial, involving an interplay of genetic, neurobiological, and environmental factors.
    ◦ **Genetic Factors**
        ▪ Strong heritable component; SAD often runs in families.
        ▪ Higher concordance rates in monozygotic twins.
        ▪ Family history of anxiety disorders, panic disorder, or depression increases risk.
    ◦ **Neurobiological Factors**
        ▪ **Amygdala Hyperactivity**: The amygdala (the brain's fear center) may be overly sensitive.
        ▪ **Neurotransmitter Dysregulation**: Imbalances in neurotransmitters, particularly **serotonin** and **norepinephrine**, are implicated.
        ▪ The HPA (Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Adrenal) axis may be dysregulated, leading to an exaggerated stress response.
    ◦ **Environmental & Psychosocial Factors**
        ▪ **Life Stressors**: Traumatic events such as the death of a relative or pet, parental divorce, or moving to a new school can trigger the onset.
        ▪ **Parenting Styles**: Overprotective or intrusive parenting can foster dependence and anxiety.
        ▪ **Attachment Style**: An insecure attachment to a primary caregiver is a significant risk factor.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: The most common anxiety disorder in children < 12 years old.
    ◦ Children: ~4%
    ◦ Adolescents: ~1.6%
    ◦ Adults: ~1-2%
• **Age of Onset**: Most commonly begins in childhood, around age 7-8. Adult-onset is also possible.
• **Gender**: More common in females than males.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a child who refuses to go to school or an adult who has extreme difficulty being away from a spouse or child.
    ◦ **Children/Adolescents**
        ▪ **School Refusal**: Often the presenting complaint.
        ▪ **Somatic Complaints**: Frequent headaches, stomachaches, nausea, or vomiting, especially on school days or when separation is anticipated. These symptoms resolve once the child is allowed to stay home.
        ▪ **Clingy Behavior**: Follows parents around the house ("shadowing"), unwilling to be in a room alone.
        ▪ **Sleep Difficulties**: Refusal to sleep alone, insisting on co-sleeping, recurrent nightmares with themes of separation (e.g., kidnapping, family dying).
        ▪ **Excessive Distress**: Crying, tantrums, or pleading when separation is imminent.
    ◦ **Adults**
        ▪ Extreme worry about the well-being of a spouse or children.
        ▪ Discomfort being alone; may need to know the exact whereabouts of attachment figures at all times.
        ▪ Difficulty with work or social obligations that require travel or independent functioning.
        ▪ Can present as an over-involved, "helicopter" parent.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Based on a thorough history and evaluation using DSM-5 criteria.
    ◦ It is crucial to gather collateral information from parents, partners, and teachers.
• **Screening Tools**: Standardized rating scales can aid in diagnosis and monitoring.
    ◦ **SCARED** (Screen for Child Anxiety Related Disorders)
    ◦ Spence Children's Anxiety Scale (SCAS)
• **Labs/Imaging**: No specific diagnostic tests for SAD.
    ◦ Workup may be performed to rule out medical causes for somatic symptoms (e.g., basic labs for recurrent abdominal pain).
    ◦ Should be used judiciously to avoid reinforcing the anxiety.
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis is generally **good** with early identification and evidence-based treatment (CBT and/or SSRIs).
• Without treatment, the disorder can have a chronic, waxing and waning course, often persisting into adulthood.
• Factors associated with a poorer prognosis include early age of onset, greater symptom severity, and comorbid psychiatric conditions.

sections.overview:
• **Selective Mutism (SM)** is a childhood **anxiety disorder** characterized by a consistent failure to speak in specific social situations where there is an expectation for speaking (e.g., at school), despite speaking in other situations (e.g., at home).
• It is considered a **phobia of speaking**.
• The lack of speech is a manifestation of **severe anxiety**, not due to a language deficit, communication disorder, or willful refusal.
sections.etiology:
• The etiology is **multifactorial**, involving a combination of genetic, temperamental, and environmental factors.
• It is **NOT** considered an oppositional or manipulative behavior.
• **Neurobiology**
    ◦ Strong association with anxiety disorders.
    ◦ There is thought to be an over-activity of the **amygdala**, the brain's threat detection center, which is triggered by social situations requiring speech.
    ◦ This initiates a **freeze response**, leading to mutism.
• **Genetics**
    ◦ A significant genetic component is observed.
    ◦ There is a high incidence of **social anxiety disorder (SAD)**, avoidant personality traits, and selective mutism in first-degree relatives.
• **Temperament**
    ◦ A predisposition often exists in the form of **behavioral inhibition**.
    ◦ These children are often timid, cautious in new situations, shy, and prone to withdrawal from a very young age.
• **Environment**
    ◦ Parental modeling of anxiety or social avoidance can contribute.
    ◦ Overprotective parenting styles may inadvertently reinforce the child's avoidance.
    ◦ **Negative reinforcement** (e.g., others speaking for the child, removing the demand to speak) can maintain the mutism.
    ◦ **Bilingualism is NOT a cause**, but the stress of speaking a less familiar language can be a contributing factor in vulnerable children.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Relatively rare, affecting approximately **0.3% to 1%** of the pediatric population.
• **Age of Onset**: Typically occurs **before age 5**. The condition is often first recognized when the child enters a new social setting, such as preschool or kindergarten.
• **Gender**: Slightly more common in **females** than males.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a child who is described by parents as very talkative, outgoing, and even "bossy" at home with immediate family but is **completely non-verbal** at school or in other social settings.
• **In School/Public**
    ◦ Does not speak to teachers or peers.
    ◦ May use non-verbal communication (pointing, nodding, writing).
    ◦ Often has a **"frozen"** or blank facial expression.
    ◦ **Avoids eye contact**.
    ◦ May appear socially withdrawn or disinterested.
• **At Home**
    ◦ Speaks freely and at a normal volume with trusted family members.
    ◦ Behavior is typically age-appropriate when in a comfortable setting.
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is **clinical**, based on a comprehensive history and fulfillment of **DSM-5 criteria**.
• There are no specific lab tests or imaging studies.
• **Detailed History**
    ◦ Obtain **collateral information** from multiple sources, especially parents and teachers, to establish the situational nature of the mutism.
• **Rule out other conditions**
    ◦ **Audiology Referral**: To rule out hearing impairment.
    ◦ **Speech-Language Pathology (SLP) Evaluation**: To rule out a primary communication disorder.
    ◦ **Psychological/Psychiatric Evaluation**: To assess for comorbid anxiety disorders, ASD, or other psychiatric conditions.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is generally **good** with early and intensive behavioral intervention.
• Younger children (<8 years old) tend to respond more quickly to treatment.
• **Negative prognostic factors** include:
    ◦ Older age at diagnosis
    ◦ Severity of mutism
    ◦ The presence of significant comorbid psychiatric conditions (especially ASD)

sections.overview:
• **Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD)** is a trauma- and stressor-related disorder that may develop after exposure to a terrifying event or ordeal in which grave physical harm occurred or was threatened
    ◦ Characterized by a constellation of symptoms including **intrusive recollections** of the trauma, **avoidance** of trauma-related stimuli, **negative alterations in mood and cognition**, and marked **alterations in arousal and reactivity**
    ◦ For a diagnosis, these symptoms must persist for more than one month and cause **significant functional impairment**
sections.etiology:
• The pathophysiology of PTSD is complex and involves dysregulation of neurobiological, neuroendocrine, and neurochemical systems
    ◦ **Neurobiological Model**
        ▪ **Amygdala**: **Hyperactive**. This region is central to fear processing and conditioning. Its hyperactivity leads to an exaggerated fear response and emotional dysregulation
        ▪ **Medial Prefrontal Cortex (mPFC)**: **Hypoactive**. The mPFC is responsible for executive function and emotional regulation; its diminished activity results in an inability to inhibit the hyperactive amygdala
        ▪ **Hippocampus**: **Reduced volume** and **hypoactivity**. The hippocampus is crucial for memory consolidation and contextualization. Dysfunction leads to difficulty distinguishing past trauma from present safety, contributing to flashbacks and re-experiencing
    ◦ **Neuroendocrine System**
        ▪ **Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Adrenal (HPA) Axis Dysregulation**: Chronic stress from PTSD leads to altered HPA axis function. While acute stress causes a cortisol surge, chronic PTSD is often associated with a **blunted cortisol response** or enhanced negative feedback sensitivity, which is a paradoxical finding
    ◦ **Neurochemical Systems**
        ▪ **Norepinephrine**: **Increased levels** contribute to hyperarousal, hypervigilance, and an exaggerated startle response
        ▪ **Serotonin (5-HT)**: **Decreased levels** are linked to mood dysregulation, anxiety, and intrusive symptoms. This is the rationale for using SSRIs
        ▪ **Dopamine**: Dysregulation can contribute to anhedonia and other mood symptoms
        ▪ **Glutamate**: Excitatory neurotransmitter implicated in fear conditioning and memory formation
sections.epidemiology:
• **Lifetime Prevalence**: Approximately 7-8% in the general U.S. population
• **Gender**: **Women are twice as likely** to develop PTSD as men (approx. 10% vs 4%)
• **Trauma Type**: The likelihood of developing PTSD varies by the type of trauma
    ◦ **Sexual assault** is associated with the **highest risk**
    ◦ Combat exposure and interpersonal violence also carry high risks
• **High-Risk Populations**: **Military veterans**, **first responders**, survivors of **sexual violence**, and refugees
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents weeks to months after a **traumatic event**
    ◦ They may not directly mention the trauma, instead complaining of **insomnia**, **irritability**, **anxiety**, **relationship problems**, or **difficulty concentrating**
    ◦ The history often reveals exposure to a **life-threatening event** (e.g., combat, assault, natural disaster, serious accident)
    ◦ The patient may appear **withdrawn**, **anxious**, or **"on edge"** during the interview
    ◦ **Functional impairment** in social, occupational, or other important areas is a key feature
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Based on DSM-5 criteria obtained through a thorough psychiatric history and mental status examination
• **Screening Tools**
    ◦ **PC-PTSD-5 (Primary Care PTSD Screen for DSM-5)**: A 5-item screen, quick and effective for primary care settings
    ◦ **PCL-5 (PTSD Checklist for DSM-5)**: A 20-item self-report measure that assesses the 20 DSM-5 symptoms of PTSD. Can be used for screening and monitoring symptom severity
• **Labs/Imaging**: No specific labs or imaging confirm PTSD
    ◦ Used to rule out other medical conditions that may mimic or contribute to symptoms (e.g., **TSH** for thyroid disorders, **urine toxicology** for substance use, **CBC/CMP** for general medical status, **CT/MRI head** if TBI is suspected)
sections.prognosis:
• The course is variable. Approximately 50% of individuals achieve spontaneous recovery within 3 months of the trauma
• For those who develop chronic PTSD, symptoms can wax and wane over a lifetime
• **Favorable Prognostic Factors**: Strong social support, early intervention, absence of pre-existing psychiatric conditions
• **Poor Prognostic Factors**: History of prior trauma (especially in childhood), comorbid psychiatric disorders, ongoing stressors, lack of social support

sections.overview:
• **Acute Stress Disorder (ASD)** is a trauma- and stressor-related disorder characterized by the development of severe anxiety, dissociative, and other symptoms that occurs within one month after exposure to a traumatic event.
    ◦ It is considered a precursor to **Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD)**.
• The key distinguishing feature from PTSD is the **duration of symptoms**.
    ◦ Symptoms last from **3 days to 1 month** following the trauma.
sections.etiology:
• ASD results from the overwhelming of the body's normal coping mechanisms following a severe traumatic stressor.
• The pathophysiology involves a persistent and dysregulated stress response.
• **Neurobiological**
    ◦ **HPA Axis Dysregulation**: Persistent activation of the Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Adrenal (HPA) axis leads to elevated cortisol levels.
    ◦ **Sympathetic Nervous System**: Overactivation of the sympathetic nervous system leads to a hyperadrenergic state (elevated norepinephrine, epinephrine), causing **hypervigilance**, **exaggerated startle response**, and sleep disturbances.
    ◦ **Amygdala Hyperactivity**: The brain's fear center remains overactive, leading to a persistent state of fear and anxiety.
    ◦ **Prefrontal Cortex (PFC) Hypoactivity**: Decreased activity in the medial PFC, which normally inhibits the amygdala, leads to impaired fear extinction and emotional dysregulation.
    ◦ **Hippocampus**: Impaired function can contribute to fragmented and intrusive traumatic memories.
• **Psychological**
    ◦ **Cognitive Model**: Maladaptive appraisals of the trauma and its aftermath (e.g., "the world is completely dangerous") perpetuate the symptoms.
    ◦ **Conditioning**: The traumatic event becomes an unconditioned stimulus, and subsequent reminders (triggers) act as conditioned stimuli, eliciting an intense fear response (conditioned response).
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Varies significantly depending on the nature and severity of the traumatic event.
    ◦ Approximately 10-20% of individuals exposed to trauma that meets DSM-5 criteria (e.g., assault, MVA) will develop ASD.
    ◦ Rates are higher following interpersonal violence (e.g., sexual assault, mass shootings), with some studies showing rates up to 50%.
• **Gender**: More common in **females** than males (2:1 ratio).
sections.riskFactors:
• **Pre-traumatic:**
    ◦ Pre-existing mental health condition (e.g., anxiety, depression, prior PTSD).
    ◦ History of prior trauma.
    ◦ Female gender.
    ◦ Lower socioeconomic status or education level.
• **Peri-traumatic (During the event):**
    ◦ **Severity of trauma** (perceived life threat, physical injury).
    ◦ **Type of trauma** (interpersonal violence, especially sexual assault, carries the highest risk).
    ◦ **Peritraumatic dissociation** (feeling detached or "unreal" during the event).
• **Post-traumatic:**
    ◦ Lack of social support.
    ◦ Ongoing life stressors.
    ◦ Avoidant coping styles.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient typically presents within days or weeks of a known traumatic event (e.g., serious accident, physical/sexual assault, natural disaster, combat exposure).
• The patient appears highly anxious, distressed, irritable, or emotionally numb.
• Patients may report being unable to sleep, having nightmares, and feeling constantly **"on edge."**
• They often describe avoiding reminders of the event and may report feeling disconnected from themselves or reality.
• The symptoms cause **significant impairment** in social or occupational functioning (e.g., unable to return to work, avoiding social contact).
sections.physicalExam:
• The general physical exam is typically non-specific for ASD but is essential to evaluate for injuries sustained during the trauma.
• **Mental Status Exam (MSE)** is key:
    ◦ **Appearance/Behavior**: May appear restless, jumpy, or withdrawn. Psychomotor agitation or retardation possible.
    ◦ **Mood**: Anxious, irritable, dysphoric.
    ◦ **Affect**: Constricted, labile, or incongruent.
    ◦ **Thought Process**: May be preoccupied with the traumatic event.
    ◦ **Thought Content**: Ruminations about the trauma, potential for suicidal ideation.
    ◦ **Cognition**: May report difficulty with concentration and memory (especially for aspects of the trauma).
    ◦ **Insight/Judgment**: Often fair, but may be impaired by distress.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Diagnosis is clinical**, based on DSM-5 criteria.
• **DSM-5 Criteria Summary:**
    ◦ Exposure to a traumatic event.
    ◦ Presence of **9 or more symptoms** from the 5 clusters (Intrusion, Negative Mood, Dissociation, Avoidance, Arousal):
        ▪ Recurrent, involuntary, and intrusive distressing memories.
        ▪ Recurrent distressing dreams (**nightmares**) related to the event.
        ▪ Dissociative reactions (e.g., **flashbacks**) in which the individual feels or acts as if the event were recurring.
        ▪ Intense psychological or physiological distress at exposure to internal or external cues that symbolize or resemble an aspect of the event.
        ▪ Persistent inability to experience positive emotions (e.g., happiness, satisfaction, loving feelings).
        ▪ An altered sense of the reality of one's surroundings or oneself (e.g., seeing oneself from another's perspective, being in a daze, time slowing) - **Derealization/Depersonalization**.
        ▪ An inability to remember an important aspect of the traumatic event (**dissociative amnesia**).
        ▪ Efforts to avoid distressing memories, thoughts, or feelings associated with the event.
        ▪ Efforts to avoid external reminders (people, places, conversations, activities, objects, situations) that arouse distressing memories.
        ▪ Sleep disturbance (difficulty falling/staying asleep, restless sleep).
        ▪ Irritable behavior and angry outbursts.
        ▪ **Hypervigilance**.
        ▪ Problems with concentration.
        ▪ **Exaggerated startle response**.
    ◦ **Duration**: Symptoms last from **3 days to 1 month** after trauma exposure.
    ◦ Symptoms cause clinically significant distress or functional impairment.
    ◦ Symptoms are not due to a substance or another medical condition (e.g., TBI).
• **Screening Tools**:
    ◦ While not required for diagnosis, scales like the **Acute Stress Disorder Scale (ASDS)** can be used to assess symptom severity.
• **Laboratory/Imaging**: No specific labs diagnose ASD. Workup is done to rule out other causes:
    ◦ **Urine toxicology screen**: Rule out substance intoxication/withdrawal.
    ◦ **TSH**: Rule out thyroid dysfunction.
    ◦ **Head CT/MRI**: If **traumatic brain injury (TBI)** is suspected.
sections.treatment:
• **First-Line**: **Trauma-Focused Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (TF-CBT)**.
    ◦ Considered the gold standard.
    ◦ Involves psychoeducation, anxiety management skills (e.g., breathing retraining), cognitive restructuring of maladaptive beliefs, and imaginal/in-vivo exposure to trauma-related memories and cues in a safe, controlled manner.
    ◦ Goal is to reduce the risk of progression to **PTSD**.
• **Pharmacotherapy**:
    ◦ **No FDA-approved medications specifically for ASD.**
    ◦ Medications are used as **adjuncts** for specific, severe symptoms.
    ◦ **Insomnia/Nightmares**:
        ▪ **Prazosin** (alpha-1 antagonist) can reduce trauma-related nightmares.
        ▪ **Trazodone** is often used for insomnia.
    ◦ **Severe Anxiety/Arousal**:
        ▪ **SSRIs** are NOT typically initiated in the acute phase but may be considered if symptoms are severe and transition to PTSD seems likely.
        ▪ **Propranolol** (beta-blocker) can be used to blunt the physiological hyperarousal response.
    ◦ **AVOID BENZODIAZEPINES**: 
        ▪ Generally contraindicated. They can interfere with emotional processing of the trauma, increase the risk of developing PTSD, and carry a risk of dependence.
sections.management:
• **"Watchful Waiting"**: For patients with mild symptoms, supportive care and monitoring may be sufficient, as many cases resolve spontaneously.
• **Psychoeducation**: Educate the patient and family that their symptoms are a common reaction to an extreme event. This helps normalize the experience and reduce self-blame.
• **Supportive Care**:
    ◦ Ensure physical safety and basic needs are met.
    ◦ Encourage mobilizing social supports (family, friends).
    ◦ Teach grounding techniques and relaxation skills.
    ◦ Promote a return to normal routines as tolerated.
• **Follow-up**: Schedule a follow-up appointment around the **1-month mark** post-trauma to reassess symptoms.
