    ◦ **TSH:** Rule out hypothyroidism, which can cause weight gain and mimic depressive symptoms.
    ◦ **EKG:** Consider in patients with significant obesity, HTN, or before starting certain medications (e.g., stimulants).
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is generally better than for Anorexia or Bulimia Nervosa.
• With treatment, remission rates are high (up to 80%).
• However, relapse is common, and the course can be chronic and fluctuating.
• Negative prognostic factors include earlier age of onset, higher frequency of binging, and more severe comorbid psychopathology.

sections.overview:
• Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID) is an eating disorder characterized by a persistent failure to meet appropriate nutritional and/or energy needs.
◦ This leads to clinically significant consequences such as weight loss, nutritional deficiencies, dependence on nutritional supplements, or marked psychosocial impairment.
◦ The core distinction from other eating disorders like Anorexia Nervosa is the **absence of body image disturbance or a fear of gaining weight**.
◦ The avoidance is based on other factors, typically categorized into three main presentations:
    ▪ **Lack of interest** in eating or food.
    ▪ **Sensory-based avoidance** of food characteristics (e.g., texture, smell, color, taste).
    ▪ **Concern about aversive consequences** of eating (e.g., fear of choking, vomiting, or abdominal pain).
sections.etiology:
• The etiology is multifactorial, involving a complex interplay of genetic, psychological, and environmental factors (biopsychosocial model).
◦ **Biological/Genetic:**
    ▪ Higher concordance in monozygotic twins.
    ▪ Potential link to sensory processing sensitivity, which has a genetic component.
    ▪ Often co-occurs with heritable conditions like Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and anxiety disorders.
◦ **Psychological:**
    ▪ **Anxiety:** High rates of co-occurring anxiety disorders. Food avoidance becomes a negatively reinforced behavior (avoiding food reduces anxiety).
    ▪ **Trauma:** A past negative or traumatic experience with food (e.g., a severe choking or vomiting episode) can trigger a conditioned fear response.
    ▪ **Temperament:** Traits like neophobia (fear of new things) and high anxiety sensitivity are common.
◦ **Environmental/Social:**
    ▪ Parental anxiety regarding feeding can inadvertently reinforce avoidant behaviors.
    ▪ Learned feeding behaviors within the family.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** Estimated at 3-5% in the general pediatric population; much higher rates (up to 20-30%) are seen in pediatric gastroenterology clinics and specialized feeding disorder programs.
• **Age of Onset:** Typically begins in infancy or early childhood, but can persist or even present for the first time in adolescence or adulthood.
• **Gender:** Unlike anorexia and bulimia, ARFID is more evenly distributed between genders, with some studies suggesting a slight male predominance, especially in childhood.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation varies based on the underlying driver of the food avoidance.
◦ **Vignette (Fear of Aversive Consequences):** A 7-year-old boy presents with a 15-lb weight loss over 3 months. History reveals he choked on a hot dog at a birthday party and now refuses all solid foods, accepting only smoothies and yogurt. He expresses intense fear of choking again. He denies any concerns about his weight or body shape.
◦ **Vignette (Sensory Sensitivity):** A 10-year-old with a history of ASD is brought in for "extreme picky eating." His diet consists of only 5-6 "safe foods" (e.g., plain pasta, chicken nuggets from one brand, one type of cracker). He gags or has a meltdown when presented with new foods, particularly those with "slimy" or "mixed" textures like casseroles or stews. He is falling off his growth curve.
◦ **Vignette (Lack of Interest):** An adolescent presents with fatigue and low energy. He reports "never feeling hungry" and "eating is a chore." He often forgets to eat meals, consumes very small portions when he does, and shows no enjoyment in eating. He has a low BMI but expresses no desire to be thin.
sections.diagnostics: • ARFID is a clinical diagnosis based on DSM-5 criteria, after ruling out other causes.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is variable and often depends on the age of onset, severity, and presence of co-occurring conditions.
• Early and intensive intervention is associated with better outcomes.
• ARFID can be a chronic condition, but significant improvement in weight, nutrition, and psychosocial functioning is achievable with treatment.

sections.overview:
• Paranoid Personality Disorder (PPD) is a **Cluster A** (odd, eccentric) personality disorder characterized by a pervasive and unjustified pattern of distrust and suspiciousness of others.
	◦ Individuals with PPD interpret the motives of others as malevolent, beginning in early adulthood and present across various contexts.
	◦ They assume others will exploit, harm, or deceive them, even without sufficient basis.
	◦ This disorder leads to significant impairment in social and occupational functioning.
sections.etiology:
• The exact etiology is unknown, but it is believed to be multifactorial.
	◦ **Genetic Factors**: PPD is more common in individuals who have a family history of Schizophrenia or other psychotic disorders, suggesting a genetic link.
	◦ **Psychosocial Factors**: Early childhood experiences, such as severe physical or emotional trauma, abuse, neglect, or growing up in a household with pervasive hostility and rage, are strongly implicated.
		▪ These experiences may foster a worldview that others are untrustworthy and malicious.
	◦ **Biological Factors**: No specific neurobiological markers have been definitively identified, but dysfunction in brain regions associated with threat perception (e.g., amygdala, limbic system) may play a role.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Estimated at 2.3% to 4.4% of the U.S. general population.
• **Gender**: More commonly diagnosed in **males**.
• **Co-morbidity**: High rates of co-occurrence with other psychiatric disorders, including Major Depressive Disorder, Substance Use Disorder, Agoraphobia, and other personality disorders (especially Schizotypal, Schizoid, Narcissistic, and Avoidant).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The patient will often present as guarded, defensive, tense, and argumentative.
	◦ **Rapport**: Extremely difficult to establish a therapeutic alliance. The patient may be hostile, sarcastic, and question the clinician's motives.
	◦ **Affect**: Often cold, serious, and lacking in tender feelings. They may appear humorless.
	◦ **Insight**: Poor. The condition is **ego-syntonic**; patients do not see their suspiciousness as a problem. They view their beliefs as rational and justified responses to the actions of others.
	◦ **History**: They may provide a detailed history of being wronged, betrayed, or mistreated by others, often with a litigious or grudge-bearing tone. They rarely seek treatment voluntarily and are often brought in by family or due to legal issues.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Diagnosis is clinical**, based on a thorough psychiatric history and collateral information (if obtainable, though patients will often refuse).
	◦ The key is establishing a **longitudinal pattern of behavior** that is inflexible, pervasive, and causes significant functional impairment.
• **Labs/Imaging**: No specific tests for PPD. Labs (e.g., TSH, CMP, urine toxicology) and imaging (e.g., head CT/MRI) are used to rule out organic causes of paranoia, especially in new-onset cases or with atypical presentations.
sections.prognosis:
• Generally **poor**.
• PPD is a chronic, stable condition that is highly resistant to change.
• Patients rarely recognize their own role in their difficulties, making them resistant to therapy.
• With long-term, consistent treatment, some individuals can achieve modest improvements in social and occupational functioning.

sections.overview:
• Schizoid Personality Disorder (SPD) is a **Cluster A** ("weird, odd, eccentric") personality disorder characterized by a pervasive and lifelong pattern of social detachment and a restricted range of emotional expression in interpersonal settings.
    ◦ Individuals with SPD are classic "loners" or "hermits" who have no desire for close relationships, including sexual ones, and seem indifferent to the praise or criticism of others.
    ◦ Their condition is ego-syntonic, meaning they typically do not see their isolation as a problem.
sections.etiology:
• The exact cause is unknown, but it is believed to be a combination of genetic and environmental factors.
    ◦ **Genetic**: Increased prevalence in families with a history of **schizophrenia** or **schizotypal personality disorder**, suggesting a shared genetic vulnerability.
    ◦ **Neurobiological**: Some theories suggest a possible link to dopaminergic pathway abnormalities, similar to but less severe than those in schizophrenia.
    ◦ **Environmental/Psychological**: Theories point to a childhood environment that was cold, neglectful, or emotionally detached.
        ▪ The individual may have developed detachment as a maladaptive defense mechanism to cope with a non-responsive or unempathetic upbringing.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Estimated at 3-5% of the general population.
• **Gender**: Diagnosed more frequently in **males**.
• **Clinical Setting**: Rarely seen in clinical settings because individuals with SPD do not seek treatment on their own.
    ◦ They may be brought in by family members or present for a comorbid condition (e.g., depression due to profound isolation).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The patient often presents at the urging of a family member. During the interview, they will appear **aloof, detached, and emotionally cold**.
    ◦ **History**: They provide sparse personal history and have difficulty describing their feelings. They will report having no close friends and no desire for them.
    ◦ **Interaction**: They maintain poor eye contact and a formal, distant demeanor. They rarely smile or show changes in facial expression.
    ◦ **Speech**: Monotonous, slow, and lacks emotional inflection.
    ◦ **Interests**: May have a rich fantasy life and be highly engaged in solitary intellectual or abstract pursuits (e.g., mathematics, computer programming, philosophy).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Based on a comprehensive psychiatric history, MSE, and fulfillment of DSM-5 criteria.
• **Collateral Information**: Speaking with family members is often essential, as the patient may be a poor historian regarding their social functioning.
• **Psychometric Testing**: Personality inventories like the Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI-2) can provide supportive evidence but are not diagnostic.
• **Rule out other conditions**: It is critical to rule out medical conditions or substance use that could cause social withdrawal.
sections.prognosis:
• The course is **chronic and stable**, with little change over the lifespan.
• Prognosis for significant social or emotional change is **poor**, as the traits are deeply ingrained and ego-syntonic.
• Individuals may achieve a stable, albeit isolated, level of functioning, especially in occupations that suit their solitary nature (e.g., night security guard, archivist, lab researcher).

sections.overview:
• Antisocial Personality Disorder (ASPD) is a **Cluster B** (dramatic, emotional, erratic) personality disorder characterized by a pervasive and persistent pattern of disregard for, and violation of, the rights of others.
    ◦ Individuals with ASPD commonly engage in **criminal behavior**, are deceitful, manipulative, impulsive, and lack remorse for their actions.
• The diagnosis requires evidence of **Conduct Disorder** before the age of 15.
• Cannot be formally diagnosed until the individual is at least **18 years old**.
sections.etiology:
• The etiology is multifactorial, involving a complex interplay of genetic, neurobiological, and environmental factors.
• **Genetic**
    ◦ There is a strong genetic component, with higher concordance rates in monozygotic twins compared to dizygotic twins.
    ◦ Adoption studies show that children of parents with ASPD are at higher risk even when raised in different environments.
• **Neurobiological**
    ◦ **Prefrontal Cortex (PFC) Dysfunction**
        ▪ Reduced volume and activity in the orbitofrontal and ventromedial PFC, areas crucial for decision-making, impulse control, and empathy.
    ◦ **Amygdala Abnormalities**
        ▪ Reduced amygdala volume and reactivity, leading to a blunted fear response and impaired fear conditioning.
        ▪ This contributes to recklessness and a failure to learn from punishment.
    ◦ **Neurotransmitter Dysregulation**
        ▪ **Serotonin (5-HT):** Low levels are linked to impulsivity, aggression, and irritability.
        ▪ **Dopamine (DA):** Dysregulation may contribute to reward-seeking behavior and substance abuse.
• **Environmental**
    ◦ Adverse childhood experiences are major contributors.
    ◦ Childhood physical, sexual, or emotional **abuse** and **neglect**.
    ◦ Unstable or erratic parenting and inconsistent discipline.
    ◦ Parental criminality, substance abuse, or violence in the home.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** 1% to 4% in the general population.
• **Gender:** Significantly more common in **males** (Male-to-female ratio is approx. 3:1).
• **Setting:** Prevalence is much higher in specific populations, particularly forensic settings.
    ◦ **Prison populations:** Estimates range from 40% to 75%.
    ◦ **Substance abuse treatment centers:** High comorbidity and prevalence.
• **Course:** The pattern is chronic but may become less evident or "burn out" as the individual ages, particularly after age 40.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients rarely present for treatment of their personality disorder. They are more often encountered when:
    ◦ Mandated by the **legal system** (court-ordered evaluation).
    ◦ Seeking treatment for a **comorbid condition** (e.g., substance use, depression, anxiety).
    ◦ Brought in by family members due to distress caused by their behavior.
• **Demeanor**
    ◦ Can be superficially **charming**, charismatic, and manipulative.
    ◦ May become irritable, hostile, or aggressive when confronted or challenged.
• **History**
    ◦ A detailed history will reveal a chronic pattern of irresponsible and antisocial behaviors starting in childhood/adolescence:
        ▪ Unstable employment history (frequent job changes, firings).
        ▪ Chaotic interpersonal relationships (multiple divorces, short-term partners).
        ▪ History of arrests, legal troubles.
        ▪ Financial irresponsibility (debt, failure to pay bills or support dependents).
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical diagnosis** based on a thorough psychiatric interview and meeting **DSM-5 criteria**.
• **Collateral information is CRITICAL.**
    ◦ Information from family, friends, employers, and legal/school records is essential, as patients are often unreliable historians and may minimize or lie about their past behaviors.
• **Screening Tools**
    ◦ While not diagnostic, tools like the Psychopathy Checklist-Revised (**PCL-R**) may be used in forensic settings.
• **Labs/Imaging**
    ◦ No specific tests for ASPD.
    ◦ Used to rule out other conditions or assess for comorbid substance use (e.g., **urine toxicology screen**).
    ◦ A head CT/MRI might be considered if a TBI is suspected as a cause for personality change.
sections.prognosis:
• Generally **poor**, as it is a chronic, lifelong condition.
• Prognosis is worse with early onset of severe conduct problems, a high degree of psychopathy (**callous-unemotional traits**), and comorbid **Substance Use Disorder (SUD)**.
• Symptoms, particularly criminal behavior and impulsivity, may decrease with age (often after 40).
• The presence of a stable, supportive relationship or steady employment (though rare) can be a positive prognostic factor.

sections.overview:
• Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) is a **Cluster B** (dramatic, emotional, erratic) personality disorder characterized by a pervasive pattern of instability in interpersonal relationships, self-image, and affects, accompanied by marked impulsivity.
    ◦ The core features are **emotional dysregulation**, **identity disturbance**, and **unstable relationships**.
    ◦ It typically begins in early adulthood and presents in a variety of contexts.
sections.etiology:
• The etiology follows a **biopsychosocial model**, with no single cause.
    ◦ **Genetic/Biological**
        ▪ **Heritability**: BPD is about 5 times more common in first-degree biological relatives of those with the disorder.
        ▪ **Neurobiology**: Key findings involve dysfunction in the neural circuits responsible for emotion regulation.
            ▪ **Hyperactive Amygdala**: Leads to exaggerated fear and anger responses (emotional intensity).
            ▪ **Hypoactive Prefrontal Cortex (PFC)**: Diminished top-down control over emotional impulses, leading to poor executive function and impulsivity.
            ▪ **Neurotransmitters**: Dysregulation of serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine systems may contribute to impulsivity and affective instability.
    ◦ **Environmental/Psychosocial**
        ▪ **Childhood Trauma**: A very strong association exists with adverse childhood experiences, particularly sexual abuse, physical abuse, neglect, and early parental loss or separation.
        ▪ **Invalidating Environment**: Growing up in an environment where one's emotional experiences are consistently dismissed, punished, or trivialized can prevent the development of healthy emotional regulation skills.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects ~1.6-5.9% of the general population.
• **Clinical Settings**: Much higher prevalence in clinical populations; ~10% of psychiatric outpatients and ~20% of psychiatric inpatients.
• **Gender**: Diagnosed more frequently in females (approx. 75% of cases or a 3:1 ratio).
• **Age**: Symptoms typically emerge in adolescence or early adulthood. The greatest functional impairment occurs in young adulthood, with potential for improvement with age.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients often present in **crisis**, frequently to the emergency department, following a **suicide attempt**, **self-harm**, or an intense interpersonal conflict.
• The history reveals a pattern of **"stormy" relationships**, occupational instability, and a life characterized by chaos and crisis.
• They may initially present as engaging and friendly but can quickly become demanding, hostile, or manipulative when they feel slighted or **fear abandonment**.
• Their mood is highly reactive to interpersonal stressors.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Based on a thorough psychiatric history and fulfillment of DSM-5 criteria.
    ◦ A longitudinal history is essential, as personality traits are enduring.
• **Collateral Information**: Speaking with family, previous providers, or partners can be invaluable, as the patient's self-report may be unreliable or lack insight.
• **Screening Tools**: McLean Screening Instrument for BPD (MSI-BPD).
• **Labs/Imaging**: No specific tests for BPD.
    ◦ Lab work (CBC, CMP, TSH, UDS, blood alcohol level, pregnancy test) is performed to rule out medical or substance-induced causes for presenting symptoms and for medical clearance in cases of overdose or self-harm.
sections.prognosis:
• BPD is a serious and chronic illness, but the prognosis is more optimistic than previously believed.
• With appropriate, long-term treatment (especially DBT), a significant proportion of patients experience **symptomatic remission** and improved functioning.
• **Impulsive symptoms** tend to decrease with age (by the 30s-40s).
• **Affective and interpersonal symptoms** (e.g., chronic emptiness, anger) may be more persistent.
• While symptomatic remission is common, full recovery of social and vocational functioning is less so.

sections.overview:
• Histrionic Personality Disorder (HPD) is a **Cluster B** (dramatic, emotional, erratic) personality disorder characterized by:
    ◦ A pervasive and excessive pattern of **emotionality** and **attention-seeking behavior**
    ◦ Individuals are often described as **dramatic**, theatrical, and overly expressive
    ◦ They feel uncomfortable or unappreciated when they are not the **center of attention**
    ◦ Behavior is often inappropriately **seductive** or **provocative**
    ◦ Emotions, though expressed with great flair, are typically **shallow and shift rapidly**
sections.etiology:
• The exact cause is unknown; believed to result from a combination of biopsychosocial factors
• **Genetic**
    ◦ Higher incidence among **first-degree relatives** of individuals with HPD
    ◦ Likely genetic link to other **Cluster B** disorders, particularly **Antisocial Personality Disorder**
• **Neurobiological**
    ◦ Potential dysregulation in **catecholaminergic** (especially norepinephrine) and **serotonergic** systems
    ◦ The amygdala and prefrontal cortex may be implicated in **emotional lability**
• **Psychosocial/Psychoanalytic**
    ◦ **Parenting**
        ▪ Theories suggest parenting styles that were inconsistent, overly indulgent, or delivered affection contingent on attention-grabbing behaviors may contribute
    ◦ **Learned Behavior**
        ▪ Children may learn that dramatic or emotional displays are the only way to get parental attention and care
    ◦ **Defense Mechanisms**
        ▪ Individuals may use **repression** and **dissociation** to avoid painful feelings, resulting in shallow emotional experiences
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Affects approximately **1.8%** of the general population
• **Gender**: Diagnosed more frequently in **females**
    ◦ This may reflect a diagnostic bias, as similar traits in males may be labeled as narcissistic
• **Setting**: Prevalence is higher in **clinical settings** (inpatient and outpatient psychiatric facilities)
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient with HPD will often present for a comorbid condition like depression or anxiety, or due to interpersonal or romantic difficulties
• **Initial Interaction**
    ◦ May be **charming**, engaging, and energetic
    ◦ Often dress and groom themselves in a way that **draws attention** (e.g., flashy clothing, heavy makeup)
• **History Taking**
    ◦ The patient's narrative is often **dramatic**, emotional, and filled with exaggerated stories
    ◦ Their speech is **impressionistic and lacking in detail**
        ▪ Example: Might say "The whole situation was an absolute catastrophe!" but struggle to provide specific facts about what happened
• **Provider Interaction**
    ◦ May be inappropriately **flirtatious** or **seductive** with the provider, regardless of gender
    ◦ May lavish the provider with praise but can become **demanding** or **theatrical** if they feel they are not receiving enough attention
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Based on a thorough psychiatric interview confirming **DSM-5 criteria**
• **Collateral Information**: Interviewing family members or friends is crucial to establish a **pervasive** and long-standing pattern of behavior, as the patient's self-report may be unreliable or exaggerated
• **Labs/Imaging**
    ◦ **No specific tests** for HPD
    ◦ Laboratory studies may be ordered to rule out medical conditions or substance use that could mimic symptoms
        ▪ Examples: TSH, urine toxicology screen
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is **guarded** as personality disorders are chronic and **ego-syntonic** (the patient does not perceive their behavior as a problem)
• Patients often **lack insight** and may terminate therapy prematurely, especially when their behaviors are challenged
• Symptoms, particularly overtly **seductive behaviors**, may **decrease with age**
• Prognosis improves for individuals who can engage in and commit to **long-term psychotherapy**

sections.overview:
• Narcissistic Personality Disorder (NPD) is a **Cluster B** (dramatic, emotional, erratic) personality disorder.
    ◦ Characterized by a pervasive pattern of **grandiosity** (in fantasy or behavior), a constant need for **admiration**, and a **lack of empathy**.
    ◦ Patients often have an inflated sense of self-importance and **entitlement**, while simultaneously possessing a fragile self-esteem that is vulnerable to criticism.
    ◦ The disorder causes significant impairment in social, occupational, and other important areas of functioning.
    ◦ It is considered an **ego-syntonic** disorder, meaning the patient often does not perceive their own behavior as a problem.
sections.etiology:
• The exact cause is unknown but is believed to be multifactorial, involving a complex interplay of biopsychosocial factors.
• **Genetic Factors**
    ◦ Higher incidence in individuals with a family history of NPD suggests a heritable component.
• **Neurobiological Factors**
    ◦ Some studies suggest abnormalities in brain regions associated with **empathy**, compassion, and emotional regulation (e.g., prefrontal cortex, insula), but this is not well-established for diagnostic purposes.
• **Psychodynamic & Developmental Factors**
    ◦ This is the most widely cited theory, suggesting NPD stems from early childhood experiences, such as:
        ▪ **Excessive parental adoration** and praise that was not contingent on realistic achievements.
        ▪ **Chronic parental criticism, neglect, or abuse**, leading to the development of a grandiose exterior to mask feelings of inadequacy and low self-worth.
        ▪ **Inconsistent or unreliable caregiving**, preventing the development of a stable sense of self.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**
    ◦ Estimated at 0-6.2% in community samples.
    ◦ Higher prevalence in clinical settings.
• **Gender**
    ◦ Diagnosed more frequently in **males** (50-75% of cases).
• **Onset**
    ◦ Narcissistic traits are common in adolescence but do not necessarily indicate the development of NPD.
    ◦ The persistent, pervasive pattern required for diagnosis typically becomes evident in early adulthood.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients rarely present for treatment of NPD itself; they typically seek help for comorbid conditions like **depression, anxiety, or substance use**.
    ◦ These presentations are often triggered by interpersonal rejection or a significant blow to their self-esteem (a "**narcissistic injury**").
• **History**
    ◦ The patient will describe a history of "special" achievements, superior talents, and relationships with "important" people.
    ◦ They often blame others for their problems and failures.
    ◦ They may express frustration with others not recognizing their superior abilities.
• **Interaction with Provider**
    ◦ May be initially charming and flattering ("You're the best PA I've ever seen") but can quickly become demanding, **devaluing**, and dismissive if their needs are not met or if they feel criticized.
    ◦ They demonstrate a clear sense of **entitlement** regarding appointment times, treatment plans, and attention.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**
    ◦ Diagnosis is made based on a thorough psychiatric history and meeting the **DSM-5 criteria**.
    ◦ A longitudinal history is crucial to establish the pervasiveness and stability of the traits.
• **Collateral Information**
    ◦ Information from family, friends, or previous providers can be invaluable in confirming the pervasive pattern of behavior, as patients often lack insight.
• **Screening Tools**
    ◦ Structured clinical interviews (e.g., **SCID-5-PD**) or questionnaires can be used but are not sufficient for diagnosis alone.
• **Labs/Imaging**
    ◦ Not used for diagnosis of NPD itself but may be ordered to rule out differential diagnoses (e.g., TSH for thyroid dysfunction, urine drug screen for substance use, head CT/MRI if a neurological condition is suspected).
sections.prognosis:
• **Poor**; NPD is a chronic condition that is highly resistant to change.
• Patients have **poor insight** and are often unwilling to engage in the long-term, intensive psychotherapy required for meaningful improvement.
• Prognosis is slightly better for those who acknowledge their problems, have some capacity for introspection, and are motivated to change.
• Function may decline with age as physical health and appearance wane.

sections.overview: • Dependent Personality Disorder (DPD) is a Cluster C (anxious, fearful) personality disorder characterized by a pervasive and excessive need to be taken care of. ◦ This need leads to submissive and clinging behavior, as well as profound fears of separation and abandonment. ◦ Individuals with DPD struggle with self-confidence and believe they are incapable of functioning adequately without the help of others, leading them to subordinate their own needs to the needs of those they depend on.
sections.etiology: • The exact etiology is multifactorial, involving a combination of genetic, environmental, and psychosocial factors. ◦ Genetic Factors ▪ Higher concordance in monozygotic twins. ▪ A genetic predisposition to anxiety, insecurity, and submissiveness may play a role. ◦ Psychosocial Factors ▪ Parenting Styles: Overprotective or authoritarian parenting that discourages autonomy and reinforces dependent behaviors. ▪ Childhood Trauma: Chronic physical illness, separation anxiety disorder, or the early loss of a parent can contribute to the development of DPD. ▪ Learned Behavior: Children may learn dependent behaviors by observing a dependent parent or being rewarded for passivity and compliance.
sections.epidemiology: • Prevalence: Estimated at ~0.5% - 0.6% of the general population. • Gender: Diagnosed more frequently in females in clinical settings, though some studies suggest similar prevalence rates in the community, indicating potential diagnostic bias. • Onset: The pattern of behavior begins by early adulthood and is present in a variety of contexts.
sections.clinicalPresentation: • Patients often present not for the personality disorder itself, but for a comorbid condition like depression or anxiety, often triggered by the loss or threatened loss of a supportive relationship. ◦ History ▪ The patient's history will reveal a long-standing pattern of relying on others for major and minor life decisions (e.g., where to live, what job to take, what to wear). ▪ They may report a series of overlapping relationships, with an urgent need to find a new relationship as soon as one ends. ▪ They describe themselves as helpless or incompetent when alone. ◦ Demeanor ▪ In the clinical setting, they may appear passive, overly agreeable, and self-deprecating. ▪ They may look to a spouse, parent, or friend who has accompanied them to the appointment to answer questions.
sections.diagnostics: • Primary Tool: A comprehensive psychiatric interview and detailed patient history. • DSM-5 Criteria ◦ Diagnosis is made by meeting the symptomatic criteria. ◦ The pattern of behavior must be inflexible, pervasive across a broad range of personal and social situations, and stable since early adulthood. ◦ It must cause clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning. • Collateral Information: Information from family members or partners can be highly valuable in establishing the pervasiveness and long-term nature of the behaviors. • Labs/Imaging: No specific labs or imaging studies are used for diagnosis. They are used to rule out other medical conditions.
sections.prognosis:
• Prognosis is variable and considered guarded, as personality disorders are chronic and resistant to change.
• With long-term, motivated engagement in psychotherapy, patients can achieve significant improvements in functioning and quality of life.
• The patient's insight and motivation to change are key prognostic factors.

sections.overview:
• **Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder (OCPD)** is a **Cluster C** (anxious, fearful) personality disorder characterized by a pervasive pattern of preoccupation with orderliness, perfectionism, and mental and interpersonal control, at the expense of flexibility, openness, and efficiency.
    ◦ Individuals with OCPD are excessively devoted to work and productivity, are overly conscientious and inflexible about matters of morality, and are often rigid and stubborn.
• A key feature is that the traits are **ego-syntonic**, meaning the individual perceives their behavior as correct, normal, and desirable, in stark contrast to Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD), which is ego-dystonic.
sections.etiology:
• The exact etiology is unknown but is believed to be multifactorial.
    ◦ **Genetic Factors**:
        ▪ Higher concordance in monozygotic twins.
        ▪ Family history of OCPD or other anxiety disorders increases risk.
    ◦ **Neurobiological Factors**:
        ▪ Potential dysregulation in serotonergic systems, similar to what is seen in OCD and depression, though less clearly defined.
        ▪ Imaging studies are inconclusive but may suggest alterations in the prefrontal cortex related to decision-making and impulse control.
    ◦ **Psychosocial Factors**:
        ▪ **Upbringing**: Often associated with rigid, overly controlled, or authoritarian parenting styles where conformity and high achievement are heavily emphasized.
        ▪ **Learned Behavior**: Children may model parental OCPD traits or develop them as a coping mechanism in a chaotic environment.
        ▪ **Psychodynamic Theory**: Fixation at the "anal stage" of development, leading to traits of orderliness, stubbornness, and miserliness (anal-retentive character).
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Most common personality disorder in the general population, estimated at **2-8%**.
• **Gender**: Diagnosed about twice as often in **males** than females.
• **Setting**: Frequently seen in outpatient mental health settings, often presenting for comorbid anxiety or depression rather than the personality traits themselves.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Patients typically do not present with a chief complaint of "I am too perfectionistic." They often seek treatment for secondary issues like:
    ◦ **Anxiety or stress**: "I'm overwhelmed at work," "I feel constantly on edge."
    ◦ **Somatic complaints**: Headaches, GI distress, hypertension.
    ◦ **Interpersonal conflict**: "My spouse says I'm too controlling," "My employees are incompetent."
    ◦ **Depression/Anhedonia**: Due to inability to relax, social isolation, or a sense of failure when perfection is not achieved.
• During the interview, the patient may appear formal, stiff, and serious.
    ◦ They often provide excessively detailed, circumstantial histories and may be critical of the clinician's process.
    ◦ They lack a sense of humor about their situation and struggle with ambiguity.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Interview**: The primary diagnostic tool. A thorough psychiatric history focusing on longitudinal patterns of behavior across different contexts (work, relationships, personal life).
• **Collateral Information**: Interviewing family members or partners can be crucial as patients often lack insight into how their behavior affects others.
• **DSM-5 Criteria**: Confirm that the patient meets at least 4 of the 8 criteria, that the pattern is enduring and pervasive, and that it causes significant functional impairment or distress.
• **Psychological Testing**: Structured interviews (e.g., SCID-5-PD) or personality inventories (e.g., MMPI-2) can be used as adjuncts.
sections.prognosis:
• The course is chronic and stable, as personality traits are enduring.
• Prognosis is considered fair to good with motivated patients who engage in long-term psychotherapy.
• Patients with good insight and a willingness to change have a better prognosis.
• Prognosis is poorer in individuals with severe rigidity, multiple comorbidities, or lack of motivation for treatment.

sections.overview:
• Insomnia Disorder is a common sleep disorder characterized by persistent dissatisfaction with sleep quantity or quality, associated with:
    ◦ **Difficulty initiating sleep**
    ◦ **Maintaining sleep**
    ◦ **Early-morning awakening** with an inability to return to sleep
• The nocturnal sleep disturbance must cause **clinically significant distress or impairment** in social, occupational, educational, academic, behavioral, or other important areas of functioning
• For a diagnosis of chronic insomnia, symptoms must occur at least **3 nights per week** for at least **3 months**, despite adequate opportunity for sleep
sections.etiology:
• The underlying pathophysiology is best explained by the **Hyperarousal Model**, suggesting that insomnia is a disorder of being "too awake" rather than an inability to sleep, involving dysregulation in neurobiological systems that balance sleep and wakefulness
• **Behavioral Model (3-P Model):**
    ◦ **Predisposing Factors:** Genetic predisposition, personality traits (e.g., anxiety, perfectionism), innate tendency toward hyperarousal
    ◦ **Precipitating Factors:** Acute stressors (e.g., job loss, death of a loved one), medical illness, medication changes, environmental changes that trigger an acute episode of insomnia
    ◦ **Perpetuating Factors:** Factors that turn acute insomnia into chronic insomnia
        ▪ Include maladaptive behaviors (e.g., spending excessive time in bed, napping, irregular sleep schedules) and dysfunctional cognitions (e.g., worry about sleep, catastrophizing)
        ▪ This leads to **conditioned arousal**, where the bed and bedroom become associated with wakefulness and anxiety rather than sleep
• **Neurobiological Model:**
    ◦ **Increased activity in wake-promoting systems:** Overactivity of the ascending reticular activating system (ARAS)
        ▪ Key neurotransmitters include **orexin (hypocretin)**, histamine, acetylcholine, and norepinephrine
    ◦ **Decreased activity in sleep-promoting systems:** Insufficient signaling from the ventrolateral preoptic nucleus (VLPO)
        ▪ Key neurotransmitter is **GABA**, the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS
    ◦ **HPA Axis Dysregulation:** Elevated evening and nocturnal **cortisol levels** contribute to a state of physiologic arousal
sections.epidemiology:
• Most common sleep disorder
• **Prevalence:**
    ◦ ~30-35% of adults report some insomnia symptoms
    ◦ ~10% meet the full diagnostic criteria for Insomnia Disorder
• More common in **women** and **older adults**
• High comorbidity with psychiatric disorders (e.g., depression, anxiety) and medical conditions (e.g., chronic pain)
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A patient with insomnia typically presents with a primary complaint of poor sleep but the focus of the interview should be on the **daytime consequences**
• The patient often appears fatigued or irritable and may express significant worry and frustration about their inability to sleep and its impact on their daily life
• The classic presentation is a patient who feels "**wired but tired**" at night
• **Sleep-Onset Insomnia:**
    ◦ Difficulty falling asleep at the beginning of the night
• **Sleep-Maintenance Insomnia:**
    ◦ Difficulty staying asleep, with frequent or prolonged awakenings during the night
• **Late Insomnia (Terminal Insomnia):**
    ◦ Waking up too early in the morning and being unable to return to sleep
sections.diagnostics:
• **Diagnosis is primarily clinical**, based on a thorough history using DSM-5 criteria
• **Sleep Diary/Log:**
    ◦ The most important diagnostic tool
    ◦ The patient records bedtimes, wake times, sleep latency, number and duration of awakenings, and daytime symptoms for at least 1-2 weeks to identify patterns and maladaptive behaviors
• **Screening Questionnaires:**
    ◦ **Insomnia Severity Index (ISI):** A 7-item questionnaire to assess the severity of insomnia
    ◦ **Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS):** Helps differentiate insomnia from primary hypersomnolence disorders like OSA or narcolepsy
        ▪ Patients with pure insomnia often have a normal ESS score despite feeling fatigued
• **Actigraphy:**
    ◦ A wrist-watch-like device that measures activity and rest, providing an objective estimate of sleep patterns over several weeks
• **Polysomnography (PSG) / Sleep Study:**
    ◦ **NOT routinely indicated for the diagnosis of insomnia**
    ◦ Indicated only when there is suspicion of another primary sleep disorder (e.g., OSA, periodic limb movement disorder), when the diagnosis is uncertain, or when initial treatment fails
• **Labs:**
    ◦ Generally not needed unless history/exam suggests a secondary cause (e.g., TSH for thyroid disease, iron studies for RLS)
sections.prognosis:
• Acute insomnia often resolves spontaneously or with brief intervention
• Chronic insomnia tends to follow a relapsing and remitting course if untreated
• Prognosis is **excellent** with CBT-I, which produces durable, long-term improvements in sleep
• Prognosis is fair with pharmacotherapy alone, as relapse is common upon discontinuation

sections.overview:
• Characterized by **excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS)** despite a main sleep period lasting at least 7 hours.
• Key features include:
    ◦ Recurrent periods of sleep or lapses into sleep within the same day.
    ◦ A prolonged main sleep episode of more than 9 hours that is non-restorative.
    ◦ Difficulty being fully awake after abrupt awakening (**sleep inertia**).
• It is a diagnosis of exclusion, made after ruling out other causes of sleepiness such as narcolepsy, insufficient sleep, **obstructive sleep apnea (OSA)**, and medical or psychiatric conditions.
sections.etiology:
• **Largely Idiopathic**: The exact cause is unknown in most cases.
• **GABA-Related Hypothesis**: 
    ◦ A leading theory suggests there is an endogenous substance that enhances the effects of the inhibitory neurotransmitter **GABA** (gamma-aminobutyric acid) at the GABA-A receptor.
    ◦ This increased GABAergic activity leads to a state of central nervous system depression, manifesting as profound sleepiness.
    ◦ This substance has been isolated from the **cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)** of some patients.
• **Genetic**: A familial link is sometimes observed, suggesting a potential genetic predisposition.
• **Post-infectious/Traumatic**: Some cases have been reported following viral illnesses (e.g., Epstein-Barr virus, Guillain-Barr syndrome) or head trauma.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence**: Considered rare, but prevalence is difficult to determine accurately. It is less common than narcolepsy.
• **Age of Onset**: Typically insidious, beginning in adolescence or early adulthood (usually before age 25).
• **Gender**: Affects males and females relatively equally, with some studies showing a slight female predominance.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Family History**: Positive family history of hypersomnolence.
• **Prior Viral Infection**: History of mononucleosis, Guillain-Barr, or other significant viral illness.
• **Head Trauma**.
• **Comorbid psychiatric conditions**: Association with depression, anxiety, and bipolar disorder.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• A typical patient is a young adult who presents with a chief complaint of "always being tired" or "sleeping all the time" despite getting what appears to be adequate or even excessive amounts of sleep (e.g., 10-12 hours/night).
• They report significant difficulty waking in the morning, often sleeping through multiple alarms.
• The sleepiness profoundly impacts their academic, occupational, and social functioning, and they may be perceived by others as lazy or unmotivated.
• **Cardinal Symptom: Excessive Daytime Sleepiness (EDS)**
    ◦ A persistent, daily, irresistible urge to sleep, or unintended lapses into sleep.
• **Prolonged Nocturnal Sleep**
    ◦ Regularly sleeping for more than 9 hours, yet feeling unrefreshed upon waking.
• **Sleep Inertia ("Sleep Drunkenness")**
    ◦ This is a hallmark feature, characterized by a prolonged period of grogginess, confusion, disorientation, and impaired cognitive/motor performance upon awakening.
    ◦ This can last for minutes to hours and is often very distressing.
• **Long and Unrefreshing Naps**
    ◦ Patients may take very long naps (often >1 hour) that do not alleviate the feeling of sleepiness.
    ◦ This is a key contrast to narcolepsy, where naps are typically short and refreshing.
• **Automatic Behaviors**
    ◦ Performing activities without full conscious awareness or memory of the event (e.g., driving past an exit, nonsensical conversations).
• **Cognitive Dysfunction ("Brain Fog")**
    ◦ Difficulties with attention, concentration, and short-term memory.
sections.physicalExam:
• The physical and neurological exams are **generally unremarkable**.
• The exam is primarily focused on ruling out other causes of sleepiness:
    ◦ **Oropharyngeal Exam**: Check for signs of **OSA** (e.g., crowded airway, large tonsils, high Mallampati score).
    ◦ **Neck Circumference**: A large neck circumference (>17" in men, >16" in women) is a risk factor for **OSA**.
    ◦ **Thyroid Exam**: Check for goiter (**hypothyroidism**).
    ◦ **Cardiopulmonary Exam**: Assess for underlying cardiac or pulmonary disease.
sections.diagnostics:
• The diagnostic process is essential for excluding other, more common causes of **EDS**.
• **Subjective Assessment & Initial Workup**
    ◦ **Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS)**: A questionnaire to quantify the severity of daytime sleepiness. A score >10 suggests significant **EDS**.
    ◦ **Labs**: CBC (for anemia), TSH (for hypothyroidism), CMP (for electrolyte/renal/hepatic issues).
    ◦ **Medication/Substance Review**: Rule out sedative effects from medications or substances.
• **Objective Sleep Documentation**
    ◦ **Sleep Diary**: Patient-recorded log of sleep/wake times for at least 1-2 weeks to rule out Insufficient Sleep Syndrome.
    ◦ **Actigraphy**: Wrist-watch-like device that tracks rest/activity cycles to objectively confirm a sufficient sleep duration.
• **Gold Standard: Polysomnography (PSG) followed by Multiple Sleep Latency Test (MSLT)**
    ◦ **Overnight Polysomnography (PSG)**
        ▪ **Purpose**: To rule out other sleep disorders, especially **OSA** and **Periodic Limb Movement Disorder (PLMD)**.
        ▪ **Findings in Hypersomnolence Disorder**: Normal or long total sleep time (>10 hours is suggestive), high sleep efficiency, and an absence of significant sleep-disordered breathing or limb movements.
    ◦ **Multiple Sleep Latency Test (MSLT)**
        ▪ **Purpose**: To objectively measure the physiological tendency to fall asleep and to identify sleep-onset REM periods (SOREMPs).
        ▪ **Procedure**: Performed the day after the PSG. The patient is given 4-5 opportunities (naps) to sleep, scheduled 2 hours apart.
        ▪ **Diagnostic Criteria for Hypersomnolence Disorder**:
            • Mean Sleep Latency (MSL) **≤ 8 minutes**.
            • **< 2** Sleep-Onset REM Periods (SOREMPs). *Note: Differentiates from narcolepsy, which requires ≥ 2 SOREMPs.*
sections.treatment:
• **First-Line Pharmacotherapy**:
    ◦ **Modafinil** or its R-enantiomer, **Armodafinil**. These are wakefulness-promoting agents with a lower abuse potential than traditional stimulants.
• **Second-Line / Alternative Pharmacotherapy**:
    ◦ **Traditional CNS Stimulants**: **Methylphenidate**, **Dextroamphetamine**, Mixed Amphetamine Salts. More potent but have a higher risk of side effects.
    ◦ **Sodium Oxybate**: Effective for consolidating sleep and improving **EDS** and **sleep inertia**. It is a C-III controlled substance with a REMS program.
    ◦ **Newer Agents**: **Pitolisant** (histamine H3 receptor inverse agonist) and **Solriamfetol** (dopamine/norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor) are sometimes used off-label.
sections.management: • **Follow-up**: Regular follow-up appointments are needed to monitor treatment efficacy, titrate medications, and assess for side effects.
sections.complications:
• **Occupational & Academic Impairment**: Poor performance, absenteeism, job loss.
• **Social & Interpersonal Difficulties**: Strain on relationships due to social withdrawal and perceived laziness.
• **Increased Risk of Accidents**: Particularly motor vehicle accidents due to severe sleepiness.
• **Comorbid Psychiatric Conditions**: High rates of depression and anxiety, either as a cause or consequence of the disorder.
• **Decreased Quality of Life**.
sections.prognosis:
• Hypersomnolence Disorder is a chronic, stable, and often lifelong condition.
• Spontaneous remission is rare.
• While there is no cure, treatment with medication and behavioral strategies can significantly improve daytime alertness, function, and quality of life for most patients.
sections.preventionEducation:
• **Patient Education**: Crucial for setting realistic expectations. This is a chronic condition that is managed, not cured.
• **Behavioral & Lifestyle Modifications**:
    ◦ **Sleep Hygiene**: Maintain a regular sleep-wake schedule, even on weekends.
    ◦ **Avoidance of Sedating Agents**: Counsel patients to avoid alcohol, sedating medications, etc.
• **Safety Counseling**:
    ◦ **Driving**: Advise patients about the significant risks of drowsy driving. Depending on state law and symptom severity, they may need to cease driving until sleepiness is well-controlled.
    ◦ **Occupational Hazards**: Discuss risks related to operating heavy machinery or other safety-sensitive tasks.

sections.overview:
• Narcolepsy is a chronic, debilitating neurologic disorder characterized by the brain's inability to regulate sleep-wake cycles normally.
• The cardinal symptom is **excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS)**.
• Its most specific symptom is **cataplexy**.
• The pathophysiology involves dysregulation of **Rapid Eye Movement (REM) sleep**, leading to the intrusion of REM-associated phenomena (like muscle atonia and dreaming) into wakefulness.
• There are two main types:
	◦ **Narcolepsy Type 1 (NT1):** Characterized by EDS and definite **cataplexy**, and/or low cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) **hypocretin-1** levels.
	◦ **Narcolepsy Type 2 (NT2):** Characterized by EDS without **cataplexy**, and with normal CSF **hypocretin-1** levels.
sections.etiology:
• The central mechanism is a deficiency in the neuropeptide **hypocretin** (also known as **orexin**), which is produced by a small group of neurons in the lateral hypothalamus.
• **Hypocretin** is a key promoter of wakefulness and a suppressor of **REM sleep**.
• **Narcolepsy Type 1 (NT1):**
	◦ Caused by a **selective, irreversible loss (>90%) of hypocretin-producing neurons**.
	◦ Strongly believed to be an **autoimmune process**, triggered by environmental factors in genetically susceptible individuals.
	◦ The autoimmune attack is linked to the **HLA-DQB1*06:02 allele**.
	◦ Loss of hypocretin leads to an unstable sleep-wake state, allowing for rapid, inappropriate transitions between wakefulness, NREM, and REM sleep.
	◦ This '**REM intrusion**' into wakefulness manifests as **cataplexy**, **sleep paralysis**, and **hypnagogic hallucinations**.
• **Narcolepsy Type 2 (NT2):**
	◦ Pathophysiology is less understood.
	◦ **Hypocretin-producing neurons** are generally intact, and CSF hypocretin levels are normal.
	◦ The condition is likely heterogeneous, with the final common pathway being dysfunction in the sleep-wake regulatory systems.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** Approximately 1 in 2,000 individuals (~0.05% of the population).
• **Age of Onset:** Typically presents with a bimodal distribution:
	◦ First peak in adolescence (**age 15-25**).
	◦ Second, smaller peak around **age 30-35**.
• **Gender:** Affects males and females equally.
• **Delay in Diagnosis:** There is often a significant delay (average 8-15 years) from symptom onset to formal diagnosis.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic patient is an adolescent or young adult presenting with a chief complaint of being '**constantly tired**' or '**falling asleep at inappropriate times**' (e.g., in class, during conversations, while driving).
• They may report a normal or even extended amount of nocturnal sleep but never feel rested.
• The history may reveal bizarre episodes of **muscle weakness** triggered by laughing or joking with friends, which the patient may be embarrassed to discuss.
sections.diagnostics:
• Diagnosis is based on a combination of clinical history and objective sleep studies.
• **Clinical Evaluation:**
	◦ A detailed history focusing on the classic symptoms.
	◦ Sleep diaries and questionnaires (e.g., Epworth Sleepiness Scale) are useful.
• **Overnight Polysomnography (PSG):**
	◦ **Primary Purpose:** To rule out other sleep disorders that cause EDS, most importantly **Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA)**.
	◦ Findings suggestive of narcolepsy include a **short sleep latency (<10 minutes)** and a **short REM latency** (sleep-onset REM period, or **SOREMP**).
• **Multiple Sleep Latency Test (MSLT):**
	◦ **The gold standard and confirmatory test for narcolepsy.**
	◦ Performed the morning after the overnight PSG.
	◦ Consists of 5 scheduled nap opportunities given every 2 hours.
	◦ **Diagnostic Criteria (must meet both):**
		▪ **Mean sleep latency ≤ 8 minutes.**
		▪ **Two or more Sleep-Onset REM Periods (SOREMPs).** A SOREMP is the occurrence of REM sleep within 15 minutes of sleep onset during a nap.
• **CSF Hypocretin-1 Measurement:**
	◦ Performed via lumbar puncture.
	◦ Not routinely required but can be diagnostic for NT1, especially in ambiguous cases.
	◦ **Diagnostic for NT1:** **CSF hypocretin-1 level ≤ 110 pg/mL.**
	◦ Levels are normal in NT2 and healthy controls.
sections.prognosis:
• Narcolepsy is a lifelong condition with **no cure**.
• It is **not a progressive or neurodegenerative disorder**.
• With appropriate diagnosis and consistent treatment, most patients can manage their symptoms and lead productive, fulfilling lives.
• **EDS** is typically stable over a lifetime, while **cataplexy** may lessen in severity with age for some individuals.

sections.overview:
• Parasomnias are undesirable physical or experiential phenomena that occur during entry into sleep, within sleep, or during arousals from sleep.
• They represent an abnormal activation of physiological systems at inappropriate times during the sleep-wake cycle.
• They are broadly classified based on the sleep stage from which they arise.
    ◦ **NREM (Non-Rapid Eye Movement) Parasomnias**: Disorders of arousal from deep, slow-wave sleep (Stage N3). The brain is "stuck" between being asleep and awake.
        ▪ **Sleepwalking (Somnambulism)**
        ▪ **Night Terrors (Sleep Terrors / Pavor Nocturnus)**
    ◦ **REM (Rapid Eye Movement) Parasomnias**: Occur during REM sleep and are associated with dream content.
        ▪ **Nightmare Disorder**
        ▪ **REM Sleep Behavior Disorder (RBD)**
            • *Note: Distinct from the others; involves acting out dreams due to lack of normal REM atonia.*
• This guide focuses on Nightmares, Night Terrors, and Sleepwalking.
sections.etiology:
• **General Pathophysiology**: Parasomnias often involve a "state dissociation," where elements of wakefulness intrude into sleep, or vice-versa. There is often a strong genetic predisposition.
• **Night Terrors & Sleepwalking (NREM Parasomnias)**:
    ◦ **Mechanism**: Incomplete arousal from **NREM Stage N3 sleep** (slow-wave sleep). The motor cortex is activated, allowing for complex behaviors, but higher cortical areas responsible for consciousness and memory remain asleep.
    ◦ **Cause**: Thought to be related to CNS immaturity in children. In adults, it's often triggered by factors that increase N3 sleep or cause arousals.
    ◦ **Genetics**: Strong familial link; often runs in families.
• **Nightmares (REM Parasomnia)**:
    ◦ **Mechanism**: Occur during **REM sleep**, a stage characterized by vivid dreaming and muscle atonia. Nightmares are intensely dysphoric and well-remembered dreams.
    ◦ **Cause**: The pathophysiology is linked to dysfunction in emotion-regulating brain circuits, including the amygdala and prefrontal cortex. Often associated with stress, anxiety, and trauma (e.g., PTSD).
sections.epidemiology:
• **Nightmares**:
    ◦ Extremely common in children (3-6 years), with up to 50% experiencing them.
    ◦ **Nightmare Disorder** (recurrent, causing significant distress/impairment) affects 1-4% of adults. More common in females.
• **Night Terrors**:
    ◦ **Prevalence**: 1-6% of children.
    ◦ **Peak Age**: 3-7 years.
    ◦ Rare in adults (<1%). Usually resolves by adolescence.
• **Sleepwalking (Somnambulism)**:
    ◦ **Prevalence**: Up to 17% of children have at least one episode.
    ◦ **Peak Age**: 4-8 years.
    ◦ **Prevalence in adults**: 1-4%.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• **Sleep Stage**
    ◦ **Nightmares**: **REM**
    ◦ **Night Terrors**: **NREM (Stage N3)**
    ◦ **Sleepwalking**: **NREM (Stage N3)**
• **Time of Night**
    ◦ **Nightmares**: Latter half of the night
    ◦ **Night Terrors**: **First third** of the night
    ◦ **Sleepwalking**: **First third** of the night
• **Arousal**
    ◦ **Nightmares**: Complete and rapid awakening
    ◦ **Night Terrors**: Partial/incomplete arousal
    ◦ **Sleepwalking**: Partial/incomplete arousal
• **Autonomic Signs**
    ◦ **Nightmares**: Mild (tachycardia)
    ◦ **Night Terrors**: **Intense** (tachycardia, tachypnea, diaphoresis, mydriasis)
    ◦ **Sleepwalking**: Minimal
• **Vocalization**
    ◦ **Nightmares**: Crying or talking after awakening
    ◦ **Night Terrors**: **Piercing scream**, crying, moaning
    ◦ **Sleepwalking**: Mumbling, sleep-talking
• **Motor Activity**
    ◦ **Nightmares**: Minimal during dream (due to REM atonia)
    ◦ **Night Terrors**: Thrashing, sitting up, may get out of bed
    ◦ **Sleepwalking**: **Complex behaviors**: sitting up, walking, dressing, eating
• **Recall of Event**
    ◦ **Nightmares**: **Vivid, detailed recall** of a frightening dream
    ◦ **Night Terrors**: **No recall** of dream content; amnesia for the event
    ◦ **Sleepwalking**: **No recall** of the event; amnesia
• **Consolability**
    ◦ **Nightmares**: **Easily consoled** and oriented once awake
    ◦ **Night Terrors**: **Inconsolable**, confused, disoriented
    ◦ **Sleepwalking**: Difficult to awaken; confused if aroused
• **Return to Sleep**
    ◦ **Nightmares**: Often difficult due to fear
    ◦ **Night Terrors**: Rapidly falls back asleep
    ◦ **Sleepwalking**: May return to bed or wake up confused elsewhere
sections.diagnostics:
• **Clinical Diagnosis**: Diagnosis is primarily based on a thorough history from the patient and a bed partner or family member.
• **Sleep Diary**: Can be used to document the frequency, timing, and characteristics of episodes.
• **Polysomnography (PSG) / Sleep Study**: Not routinely indicated unless:
    ◦ Diagnosis is uncertain.
    ◦ There is a risk of injury.
    ◦ Symptoms are atypical for a parasomnia (suggesting seizures).
    ◦ There is suspicion of a comorbid sleep disorder (e.g., OSA, RLS).
• **Video-EEG-PSG**: The gold standard to differentiate NREM parasomnias from **nocturnal seizures**.
    ◦ **Parasomnia Finding**: Shows arousal from Stage N3 sleep without epileptiform activity on EEG.
    ◦ **Seizure Finding**: Shows stereotypical movements and epileptiform discharges on EEG.
sections.prognosis:
• **Excellent** for childhood-onset NREM parasomnias. The vast majority resolve spontaneously during adolescence without any long-term sequelae.
• Adult-onset or persistent NREM parasomnias may be more chronic and are more likely to be associated with an underlying trigger.
• Nightmare disorder can be chronic if untreated but generally has a good prognosis with appropriate treatment (IRT, prazosin).

sections.overview:
• **Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD)** is a chronic, relapsing brain disorder characterized by a problematic pattern of alcohol use leading to clinically significant impairment or distress.
	◦ It is a spectrum disorder, ranging from mild to severe, based on the number of diagnostic criteria met.
	◦ The diagnosis is made using the criteria outlined in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th Edition (**DSM-5**).
sections.etiology:
• AUD is a complex condition resulting from the interplay of genetic, neurobiological, and environmental factors.
	◦ **Neurobiology**
		▪ **Reward Pathway:** Alcohol increases **dopamine** release in the brain's reward pathway (ventral tegmental area [VTA] and nucleus accumbens), producing feelings of pleasure and reinforcing its use.
		▪ **GABA System:** Alcohol is a **CNS depressant** that enhances the effect of **GABA** (gamma-aminobutyric acid), the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter. This leads to sedation and anxiolysis. Chronic use leads to downregulation of GABA receptors.
		▪ **Glutamate System:** Alcohol inhibits the activity of **NMDA receptors** for **glutamate**, the primary excitatory neurotransmitter. This causes cognitive impairment, memory loss, and slurred speech. Chronic use leads to an upregulation of NMDA receptors to compensate.
		▪ **Withdrawal:** The abrupt cessation of alcohol in a dependent individual leads to a state of **CNS hyperexcitability**. This is due to the combination of reduced GABAergic inhibition (downregulated receptors) and increased glutamatergic excitation (upregulated receptors), causing symptoms like tremors, **seizures**, and **autonomic hyperactivity**.
	◦ **Genetics**
		▪ A strong genetic predisposition exists. Individuals with a **first-degree relative** with AUD are at a 3-4 times higher risk.
	◦ **Environmental Factors**
		▪ Social norms, peer pressure, stress, history of trauma/abuse, and co-occurring psychiatric disorders (e.g., depression, PTSD, anxiety) significantly contribute to the development of AUD.
sections.epidemiology:
• **Prevalence:** One of the most common substance use disorders in the United States.
• **Gender:** More prevalent in **men** than **women** (approx. 2:1 ratio).
• **Age:** Highest prevalence is in **young adults (ages 18-29)**.
• **Morbidity/Mortality:** A leading cause of preventable death and disability worldwide.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• Presentation is highly variable. Patients may present for a seemingly unrelated complaint (e.g., **pancreatitis**, **falls**, **hypertension**, **anxiety**) and deny or minimize their alcohol use.
• They may be brought in by family due to behavioral changes or present directly requesting help for their drinking.
• Be alert for signs of **acute intoxication**, **withdrawal**, or chronic **end-organ damage**.
sections.diagnostics:
• **Screening Tools**
	◦ **CAGE Questionnaire:** (Cut down, Annoyed, Guilty, Eye-opener). 2 positive answers is a positive screen.
	◦ **AUDIT-C (Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test - Consumption):** A 3-question screen on consumption quantity and frequency. Score ≥3 for women and ≥4 for men is positive.
• **Laboratory Findings**
	◦ **Liver Function Tests (LFTs)**
		▪ **AST:ALT ratio > 2:1** is highly suggestive of **alcoholic liver disease**.
		▪ Elevated **GGT (gamma-glutamyl transferase):** Sensitive but not specific.
	◦ **Complete Blood Count (CBC)**
		▪ **Macrocytosis (elevated MCV)** is a common finding, with or without anemia.
		▪ **Thrombocytopenia**, **leukopenia** (due to bone marrow suppression or hypersplenism).
	◦ **Other**
		▪ Elevated triglycerides.
		▪ Electrolyte abnormalities (**hypomagnesemia**, **hypokalemia**, **hypophosphatemia**).
		▪ Elevated blood alcohol level (BAL).
	◦ **Phosphatidylethanol (PEth):** A highly specific blood test to detect recent heavy alcohol consumption.
• **Imaging:** Not for diagnosis of AUD, but for assessing complications.
	◦ **Abdominal Ultrasound:** To evaluate for **hepatic steatosis (fatty liver)**, **cirrhosis**.
	◦ **Head CT/MRI:** May show **cerebral or cerebellar atrophy** in chronic users.
sections.prognosis:
• AUD is a **chronic, relapsing disease**.
• Relapse rates are high, particularly within the first year after treatment.
• Prognosis improves significantly with engagement in long-term treatment, strong social support, and treatment of co-occurring psychiatric disorders.
• The development of severe complications like **cirrhosis** or **alcoholic cardiomyopathy** carries a poor prognosis.

sections.overview:
• Alcohol intoxication is a **transient**, **reversible** condition resulting from the recent ingestion of **ethanol**.
• It causes a spectrum of dose-dependent behavioral, psychological, and physiological changes primarily due to the depression of the central nervous system (**CNS**).
• Clinical effects range from mild euphoria and disinhibition to severe **respiratory depression**, **coma**, and **death**.
• It is one of the most common reasons for an emergency department visit.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology**: Ingestion of ethanol (ethyl alcohol).
• **Absorption**
    ◦ Rapidly absorbed from the stomach and small intestine.
    ◦ Peak blood concentrations occur 30-60 minutes after the last drink on an empty stomach.
• **Mechanism of Action**: Ethanol is a **CNS depressant**.
    ◦ **GABA Agonism**: Potentiates the effect of Gamma-Aminobutyric Acid (**GABA**) at the **GABA-A receptor**, the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS.
        ▪ This leads to sedative, anxiolytic, and ataxic effects.
    ◦ **NMDA Antagonism**: Inhibits the N-methyl-D-aspartate (**NMDA**) receptor, which is activated by the primary excitatory neurotransmitter, glutamate.
        ▪ This contributes to cognitive deficits, memory impairment (**"blackouts"**), and sedation.
    ◦ **Dopamine & Opioid Systems**: Increases dopamine release in the brain's reward pathway (nucleus accumbens), leading to feelings of euphoria and contributing to its addictive potential.
• **Metabolism**
    ◦ **Ethanol → Acetaldehyde**: Primarily metabolized in the liver by **Alcohol Dehydrogenase (ADH)**. This is the rate-limiting step.
    ◦ **Acetaldehyde → Acetate**: Acetaldehyde is further metabolized by **Aldehyde Dehydrogenase (ALDH)**.
        ▪ Acetaldehyde is a toxic substance responsible for flushing, headache, and nausea.
    ◦ **Acetate → CO2 + H2O**: Acetate is broken down in peripheral tissues.
sections.epidemiology:
• Alcohol is the most commonly used substance of abuse in the United States.
• Alcohol intoxication is a frequent presentation in emergency departments worldwide.
• A major contributing factor in approximately 50% of all **traumas**, including **motor vehicle accidents (MVAs)**, **assaults**, **falls**, and **drownings**.
• **Binge drinking** (consuming 4+ drinks for women or 5+ drinks for men in about 2 hours) is a common pattern leading to acute intoxication.
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The presentation is highly variable and depends on the **BAC** and the patient's **tolerance**.
• Patients are often brought to the ED by friends, family, or law enforcement due to **altered mental status**, abnormal behavior, or injury.
• The primary focus should be on identifying and treating life-threatening conditions, as intoxication can mask serious underlying pathology (e.g., **intracranial hemorrhage**).
sections.diagnostics:
• The diagnosis is often made **clinically**.
• Workup is aimed at ruling out other causes of **altered mental status** and identifying complications.
• **Labs**
    ◦ **Fingerstick Blood Glucose**: **ALWAYS THE FIRST TEST!** **Hypoglycemia** can mimic intoxication and must be treated immediately.
    ◦ **Serum Ethanol Level (BAC)**: Confirms diagnosis but **correlates poorly with the degree of impairment** due to individual tolerance. A patient should "act their level"; if not, search for another cause.
    ◦ **Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP)**: Check for **hypoglycemia**, **electrolyte disturbances** (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia), and an elevated **anion gap**.
    ◦ **Serum Osmolality**: To calculate an **osmolal gap**. An elevated osmolal gap disproportionate to the ethanol level suggests ingestion of a **toxic alcohol** (methanol, ethylene glycol).
    ◦ **Urine Drug Screen (UDS)**: To assess for **co-ingestions**.
    ◦ **Creatine Kinase (CK)**: If patient was found down or immobile for a prolonged period, to rule out **rhabdomyolysis**.
    ◦ **Urinalysis/Urine hCG**: In all females of childbearing age.
• **Imaging**
    ◦ **Non-contrast Head CT**: Indicated for any patient with suspected **trauma**, **focal neurologic deficits**, persistently **altered mental status**, or mental status that does not improve as expected.
        ▪ Crucial to rule out **intracranial hemorrhage**.
    ◦ **C-Spine Imaging**: If there is any concern for **neck trauma** (e.g., fall, MVA).
sections.prognosis:
• The prognosis for **uncomplicated** acute alcohol intoxication is **excellent** with appropriate **supportive care**.
• Morbidity and mortality are significantly increased by associated **trauma**, **aspiration**, **co-ingestions**, or severe complications like **respiratory arrest**.
• Long-term prognosis is dependent on the patient's underlying **alcohol use disorder** and their engagement in treatment.

sections.overview:
• **Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome (AWS)** is a potentially life-threatening condition that occurs when a person who has been drinking heavily for a prolonged period suddenly stops or significantly reduces their alcohol consumption.
    ◦ The syndrome represents a state of central nervous system (CNS) hyperexcitability and ranges in severity from mild tremors and anxiety to severe complications such as seizures, hallucinations, and delirium tremens (DTs).
sections.etiology:
• The pathophysiology of AWS is centered on the neuroadaptive changes that occur in the brain with chronic alcohol use.
    ◦ **GABA System (Inhibitory):** Alcohol is a CNS depressant that enhances the effect of the main inhibitory neurotransmitter, gamma-aminobutyric acid (**GABA**), by acting on **GABA-A receptors**. This leads to sedation and anxiolysis. Over time, the body downregulates the number and sensitivity of GABA-A receptors to counteract this chronic inhibition.
    ◦ **Glutamate System (Excitatory):** Alcohol also inhibits the action of the main excitatory neurotransmitter, **glutamate**, at the N-methyl-D-aspartate (**NMDA) receptor**. To compensate, the body upregulates the number and sensitivity of NMDA receptors.
• **Cessation of Alcohol:** When alcohol is abruptly withdrawn, the system is left with downregulated inhibitory (GABA) tone and upregulated excitatory (glutamate) tone. This imbalance results in a state of profound **CNS hyperexcitability**, causing the signs and symptoms of withdrawal.
sections.epidemiology:
• Approximately 50% of individuals with **Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD)** will experience withdrawal symptoms upon cessation.
• About 3-5% of those experiencing withdrawal will progress to severe symptoms, including **delirium tremens (DTs)**.
• Alcohol withdrawal is a common reason for admission to general medical and surgical wards, as well as intensive care units (ICUs).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The onset and progression of symptoms follow a predictable timeline after the last drink.
• **6-24 hours:**
    ◦ **Minor (Uncomplicated) Withdrawal**
        ▪ Anxiety, insomnia, GI upset (nausea/vomiting), headache, palpitations, diaphoresis, mild tremors.
• **12-48 hours:**
    ◦ **Withdrawal Seizures**
        ▪ Single or multiple generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Often occurs in patients with no prior seizure history.
• **12-72 hours:**
    ◦ **Alcoholic Hallucinosis**
        ▪ Visual, auditory, or tactile hallucinations **with a clear sensorium** and stable vital signs.
• **48-96 hours:**
    ◦ **Delirium Tremens (DTs)** *(Medical Emergency)*
        ▪ **Altered sensorium (delirium)**, severe agitation, hallucinations, profound autonomic instability (tachycardia, hypertension, fever).
sections.diagnostics:
• Alcohol withdrawal is primarily a **clinical diagnosis** based on history and physical exam.
• Diagnostic tests are used to rule out other etiologies and assess for complications.
• **Clinical Assessment Tool:**
    ◦ **CIWA-Ar (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol, Revised):** Gold standard for quantifying withdrawal severity and guiding symptom-triggered therapy. A score >8-10 often indicates the need for pharmacotherapy.
• **Laboratory Studies:**
    ◦ **CMP:** Check for electrolyte abnormalities (**hypomagnesemia, hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia**), hypoglycemia, and liver function (AST:ALT ratio >2:1 is suggestive of alcoholic liver disease).
    ◦ **CBC:** To assess for anemia (macrocytic), thrombocytopenia, and leukocytosis (infection).
    ◦ **Blood Alcohol Level (BAL):** Can be elevated, low, or zero at the time of presentation. A high BAL with withdrawal symptoms suggests significant tolerance.
    ◦ **PT/INR/aPTT:** To assess for coagulopathy from liver disease.
    ◦ **Ammonia:** To rule out hepatic encephalopathy.
• **Imaging:**
    ◦ **Head CT:** Indicated for patients with a first-time seizure, head trauma, or focal neurologic deficits to rule out intracranial pathology (e.g., subdural hematoma).
• **Other:**
    ◦ **ECG:** To screen for arrhythmias (e.g., atrial fibrillation, "**holiday heart syndrome**") and prolonged QTc.
sections.prognosis:
• With early recognition and appropriate treatment, the prognosis is generally good.
• Untreated or delayed treatment, especially for **DTs**, significantly increases morbidity and mortality. Mortality of treated DTs is <1%.

sections.overview:
• **Delirium Tremens (DTs)** is the most severe manifestation of Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome (AWS), a life-threatening medical emergency.
	◦ Characterized by a classic triad of **delirium** (altered sensorium), **hallucinations** (most commonly visual), and severe **autonomic instability**.
	◦ Typically occurs **48-96 hours** after the last alcoholic drink in individuals with chronic, heavy alcohol use.
	◦ Prompt recognition and aggressive management, typically in an **ICU setting**, are critical to prevent morbidity and mortality.
sections.etiology:
• **Etiology:** Abrupt cessation or significant reduction in alcohol consumption in a person with chronic alcohol dependence.
• **Pathophysiology:**
	◦ Chronic alcohol use enhances the effect of the brain's primary inhibitory neurotransmitter, **GABA** (gamma-aminobutyric acid), at the GABA-A receptor, causing the CNS to down-regulate these receptors.
	◦ Simultaneously, alcohol inhibits the primary excitatory neurotransmitter, **glutamate**, at the NMDA receptor, causing the CNS to up-regulate these receptors.
	◦ **During withdrawal:** The sudden removal of alcohol leaves the CNS in a state of severe hyperexcitability.
		▪ Decreased GABA-ergic inhibition ("no brakes")
		▪ Increased glutamatergic excitation ("all gas")
	◦ This unopposed excitatory state leads to global neuronal excitation, autonomic overdrive, and delirium.
sections.epidemiology:
• Approximately 50% of individuals with alcohol use disorder will experience symptoms of alcohol withdrawal.
• Of those who experience withdrawal, only about **3-5%** will progress to Delirium Tremens.
• DTs occurs more commonly in males and typically in patients in their 30s and 40s with a long history of heavy drinking.
sections.riskFactors:
• **Prior history of DTs or alcohol withdrawal seizures (strongest predictor)**
• Long duration and high quantity of daily alcohol consumption (>10 years of heavy use)
• Concurrent acute medical illness (e.g., pneumonia, pancreatitis, GI bleed, post-operative state)
• Older age (>30)
• Presence of significant withdrawal symptoms despite a high blood alcohol level.
• Pre-existing electrolyte disturbances (e.g., hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia).
sections.clinicalPresentation:
• The classic presentation is a patient with a known history of heavy alcohol use who is admitted to the hospital for an unrelated reason (e.g., trauma, infection) and develops symptoms **2 to 4 days** into their hospital stay.
• The patient becomes acutely confused, agitated, and appears profoundly unwell.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Symptoms:**
	◦ **Altered Mental Status:** Severe confusion, global disorientation (person, place, time), impaired attention, short-term memory loss.
	◦ **Hallucinations:**
		▪ **Visual (most common):** Seeing bugs, rats, snakes, or other frightening images.
		▪ **Tactile:** **Formication** (sensation of insects crawling on or under the skin).
		▪ **Auditory:** Less common than in alcoholic hallucinosis.
	◦ **Psychomotor Agitation:** Severe restlessness, combativeness, anxiety, and panic.
	◦ **Profound Insomnia** and vivid, disturbing dreams.
• **Exam Findings:**
	◦ **Vital Signs (Autonomic Hyperactivity):**
		▪ **Tachycardia** (HR > 100 bpm)
		▪ **Hypertension**
		▪ **Hyperthermia** (Fever > 38°C / 100.4°F) without an infectious source.
		▪ **Tachypnea**
	◦ **General:** Profuse **diaphoresis** (sweating).
	◦ **Neurologic:**
		▪ Diffuse, coarse **tremor** (most prominent in the hands).
		▪ **Hyperreflexia**.
		▪ **Mydriasis** (dilated pupils).
		▪ Nystagmus.
	◦ **Note:** In contrast to minor withdrawal, the patient's sensorium is **clouded** and they cannot be easily reoriented.
sections.diagnostics:
• Delirium Tremens is a **clinical diagnosis** based on history and physical exam; the workup aims to rule out other causes of delirium and identify comorbidities.
• **Labs:**
	◦ **CMP (Comprehensive Metabolic Panel):** Crucial to check for electrolyte abnormalities (**hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypophosphatemia**), hypoglycemia, and assess renal/hepatic function.
	◦ **CBC:** To check for infection (leukocytosis), anemia, and thrombocytopenia.
	◦ **Magnesium and Phosphate levels:** Must be ordered separately and repleted aggressively.
	◦ **Blood Alcohol Level (BAL):** May be elevated or zero. A high BAL with withdrawal symptoms indicates severe dependence.
	◦ **PT/INR, aPTT:** To assess for coagulopathy from liver disease.
	◦ **Cardiac Enzymes (Troponin) & CK:** To rule out MI and rhabdomyolysis.
	◦ **Urinalysis & Urine Drug Screen:** Rule out other intoxications.
• **Imaging/Other Tests:**
	◦ **Head CT (without contrast):** Indicated for patients with head trauma, new focal neurologic deficits, or new-onset seizures to rule out intracranial hemorrhage.
	◦ **Chest X-Ray:** To rule out aspiration pneumonia.
	◦ **EKG:** To screen for arrhythmias and QT interval prolongation.
	◦ **Lumbar Puncture:** If meningitis or encephalitis is suspected (fever with nuchal rigidity).
sections.treatment:
• **First-Line Therapy: Benzodiazepines**
	◦ **Mechanism:** Potentiate GABA-A receptor activity, substituting for the effect of alcohol.
	◦ **Administration:** **IV administration is preferred** for rapid onset and reliable absorption.
	◦ **Dosing Strategy:** Symptom-triggered therapy using the **CIWA-Ar scale** is superior to a fixed-dose schedule. The goal is to keep the patient calm but arousable.
	◦ **Choice of Agent:**
		▪ **Long-acting (preferred for smooth withdrawal):**
			▪ **Diazepam (Valium):** Rapid onset, long half-life.
			▪ **Chlordiazepoxide (Librium):** Long half-life. *Avoid in severe liver disease due to active metabolites.*
		▪ **Intermediate/Short-acting (safer in liver failure/elderly):**
			▪ **Lorazepam (Ativan):** No active metabolites, metabolized outside the liver (the "L" in "**LOT**").
• **Refractory DTs (requiring massive doses of benzodiazepines):**
	◦ **Phenobarbital:** A barbiturate that also enhances GABA-A activity; can be used as an adjunct or alternative.
	◦ **Propofol:** Requires intubation and mechanical ventilation.
